## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age to the Time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with certain manuscripts, corrected with the greatest care; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority and influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any topic may be surveyed at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers, and in what passages of their works, commented on the text of the individual books of Scripture. An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily to be preferred to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the whole work, the low price, and above all this collection—one, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but gathered together for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and literary form.

### Second Series

In this series appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Under the direction of J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. — Two hundred volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,000 francs; three hundred of the Greek-Latin edition for 1,800 francs. — The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are provided in it only in Latin translation.

## The Book of the Day of the Roman Pontiffs

The work and scholarship of J. Garner, priest of the Society of Jesus, edited for the first time in 1680 from a most ancient manuscript codex, with notes and dissertations.

[Col. 0009]

## Dedication

To the Most Illustrious Lord, Lord Jacques-Nicolas Colbert, Abbot of Bec,

J. Garner, priest of the Society of Jesus.

I offer you, Most Illustrious Abbot, the Book of the Day of the Roman Pontiffs, which, after having long lain hidden in the darkness of a library, now emerges into the light, having until now been eagerly desired or diligently sought out by learned men.

Although it remained hidden from ordinary people for so long, it was not unknown to the ancient collectors of canons. Ivo of Chartres saw it; Anselm of Lucca, Cardinal Deusdedit, and Gratian saw it, as did certain more recent writers, though only a very small portion. Nevertheless, that portion created so great a desire for the whole and gave it such value that many learned men found it difficult, and even resented, that the work had remained concealed for so long.

Behold, it now appears, summoned forth by so many and such great wishes; and, in order to come forth secure in its reputation, it seeks no other patronage than yours. First, because you possess toward letters the same disposition as your Most Illustrious Father, whose name, on account of his lavish generosity toward men of learning, deserves to receive as a tribute whatever scholarly labor is brought into the light.

Moreover, because you are a lover, as well as a constant and inquisitive investigator, of ecclesiastical antiquity, you can properly appreciate those ancient monuments which others either undervalue through arrogance or disdain through love of empty novelties. You also favor with a grateful spirit the College in which you first undertook your training in piety and learning, and you esteem whatever scholarship proceeds from it to promote the glory of God and the good of the Church.

Let it also be added, if this may have any weight, that the work has been enlarged with notes and dissertations by one who has always honored you and your Most Illustrious Family with singular reverence.

I have no intention of praising this Family at length with an ambitious display of encomiums. For what need is there, when merely to name it surpasses every form of praise? It is such a family that its father was rightly loved by Louis, greatest and wisest of kings, was placed in charge of the highest affairs, and was regarded, because of his foresight, as an assistant in all victories and great counsels.

Its firstborn son surpasses his age in virtue and, following in his father’s footsteps, is equal to the kingdom’s highest administrators.

You, its second-born son, shine in the Church with a dignity that is surely destined for the highest degrees, since it rests upon merits to which nothing can fail to be owed. You increase the distinction of your family through piety, virtue, learning, and humanity, so that you arouse great expectations of yourself; and, as much as one may hope, you will surpass them.

You will indeed do this if God grants my prayers. For I pray that he may make you in the Church what your father is in the kingdom: namely, a faithful, active, magnanimous, courageous, prudent minister, loving the one whom you serve; and, in turn, worthy to be loved in return and justly advanced to the highest honors.

[Col. 0011]

## Preface to the Reader

[Col. 0011A]

### I

The Book of the Day of the Roman Pontiffs, which long remained hidden, now comes into the light. Why should it continue to lie concealed, when nothing is more suitable for satisfying the desires of scholars, more useful for ancient ecclesiastical history, more necessary for silencing the mouths of slanderers, or more honorable to the dignity of the Apostolic See against the detractors of Honorius?

### II

The book is called the Roman Book of the Day. It is a codex containing, besides the formulas of correspondence that the supreme pontiffs customarily used in the sixth, seventh, and eighth centuries, and also in the ninth, the ordinances of the supreme pontiff and of the suburbicarian bishop, with all their accompanying matters; professions of faith; privileges, precepts, concessions, and many other things of this kind.

[Col. 0011B]

### III

It was not unknown to ancient or more recent writers, whether collectors of canons or other distinguished authors. In former times, certainly, Ivo of Chartres, Gratian, Anselm of Lucca, and Cardinal Deusdedit remembered it; in our own age and that of our fathers, Anthony Augustine, Baronius, Labbe, and those who received it from him also remembered it.

### IV

Ivo of Chartres, in part 4 of his Decree, chapter 132, entitled “On the Eight Universal Councils,” reports from the Book of the Day part of the Roman pontiff’s profession of faith:

> “I profess that I will preserve the eight holy universal Councils—that is, the First Council of Nicaea, the Second of Constantinople, the Third of Ephesus, the Fourth of Chalcedon, the Fifth, again of Constantinople, the Sixth, again of Nicaea, and the Seventh and Eighth, likewise of Constantinople—unaltered in every respect down to the last point; that I will hold them worthy of equal honor and veneration; that I will follow and proclaim in every way what they preached and decreed; and that I will condemn with mouth and heart whatever they condemned.”

[Col. 0011C]

### V

The same material is found in book 2 of the Panormia, chapter 103, and also in Gratian, distinction 16, where the notes state:

> “Cardinal Deusdedit reports the complete profession of faith, made when someone was promoted to the Roman pontificate, in his Collection of Canons, which is preserved in the Vatican Library.”

### VI

When Anthony Augustine called this passage up for examination in dialogue 20, he added the following:

That book—the Roman Book of the Day—does not, so far as I know, exist under this title; [Col. 0011D] nevertheless, I have seen several copies of the profession. Indeed, in book 5, title 10, chapter 54, of the Epitome of Ancient Pontifical Law, he presents a considerable part of the same profession. Baronius incorporated the whole from Augustine’s papers into the Annals under the year 869, though with many interpolations. Although these are absent from the Book of the Day, they were nevertheless needed to adapt it to the usage of the ninth century.

### VII

The learned Labbe had seen one or two quires of the most ancient codex and had shared a fragment from it with the Most Illustrious Marca and Jean Launoy. Marca intended to insert what he had received into a dissertation that he was planning to write on Honorius. Launoy used the material in his Letters and in various other writings.

[Col. 0012A]

### VIII

Although known only in a very small part, it has long been desired by learned men. That portion created a desire for the whole, and the desire was all the greater because it was believed—not on the basis of a slight or rash opinion—that from a monument so important, so celebrated, and so ancient, much might be drawn that would illuminate ecclesiastical history and assist the cause of the faith.

### IX

Now, for the first time, it is brought into the light through my work, such as it is, complete, in my judgment. The reason it was suppressed for so long was a pressing occupation elsewhere, [Col. 0012B] which impeded me. The reason it now appears is this one, whether sole or at least principal: to show that the controversy concerning Honorius, which had been stirred up and harassed rather than merely debated amid intense agitation of minds, could be settled by the judgment of nearly a hundred supreme pontiffs, in such a way that neither the faith of the Apostolic See—whose cultivation I would not wish to be surpassed by anyone—could ever be said to have been corrupted; nor incredible corruptions of the acts of the Sixth Synod and other ancient monuments be invented, something utterly contrary to historical scholarship; nor the Sixth Synod, which was presided over by legates of the Apostolic See, be accused of error; nor should Honorius, although he was entirely free of Monothelitism, be thought to have been free from blame.

[Col. 0012C]

### X

The manuscript codex from which this edition is prepared is, besides being of the finest quality, itself gives evidence of its age—about nine hundred years—through the characteristic manner of its Latin script. Even if the script were silent, the remaining evidence would suffice. When the supreme pontiffs, councils, and emperors are listed, the list stops at a point from which its age can easily be recognized. Among the pontiffs, the last named are Martin I and Agatho: the former died in 665, the latter in 682. Among the general councils, the last mentioned is the Sixth, held in 680, although there would have been every reason to mention others, especially if they had already existed. Among the emperors, Constantine Pogonatus occupies the final place, and is said recently to have summoned the Sixth Council. Pogonatus, however, died in 685.

[Col. 0012D]

### XI

The Book of the Day was therefore compiled after 685. But at what time? Among the formulas concerning the ordination of the supreme pontiff are two letters addressed to the exarch. Since exarchs were instituted in 567 and expelled in 752, it must be acknowledged that the collection was compiled during the interval extending from 567 to 752.

### XII

If the two things that Baronius reports from Anastasius the Librarian were true—first, that Constantine Pogonatus restored to the Roman Church its right to elect and ordain the pontiff, and remitted the obligation of seeking the assent of the emperor and the exarch; and second, that John V and the successors who followed him were thereafter consecrated with that freedom up to the time of Charlemagne—it would have to be affirmed that this collection was made before 685, since John V ascended the Apostolic See on July 22 or 23, 685.

[Col. 0013A]

But what Baronius relates requires explanation, and the date inferred from it is inconsistent with the truth of history. For two professions of faith remember Constantine, who had already died. He died in September 685, about two months after John’s ordination.

### XIII

I think nothing more probable can be said, nor anything more certainly established, than that the work belongs to the earliest years of Gregory II and was compiled shortly after 714. If this is assumed, everything will fit together and agree both internally and with history, as will be noted in the observations, according as the circumstances and chronological indications present themselves.

[Col. 0013B]

### XIV

This Book is later in date than Marculf’s Formulas, if it is indeed correctly asserted that Marculf wrote in 660. It is nevertheless superior in its subject matter. For it contains formulas more commendable than Marculf’s royal and provincial formulas because they are ecclesiastical, because they are pontifical, because they are more useful to history, because they are not confined within the limits of a single kingdom, because much of their Latin is of better quality, and because they have been excerpted from earlier sources.

Many of them were taken from the letters of Gregory the Great and other pontiffs—sometimes complete or altered only slightly, sometimes only in part. We shall indicate this in the notes.

[Col. 0013C]

### XV

What I have said about the formulas, with respect to the source from which they were drawn, should not be understood in the same way of the professions of faith and of the other materials relating to the ordination both of the supreme pontiff and of the bishop. For these appear to have been taken, either almost entirely or to a large extent, from what took place in the ordination of pontiffs shortly after the Sixth Synod. The professions of faith issued by earlier pontiffs when they assumed the pontificate differ considerably from those that we publish, as comparison will make clear.

[Col. 0013D]

### XVI

I scarcely believe even myself how much labor had to be expended in correcting the codex, which an unskilled hand had damaged in copying. Nevertheless, I scrupulously took care to correct nothing except solecisms and absurd forms of words, transpositions, separations, combinations, repetitions, and even omissions. Whenever possible, I corrected the text from no other sources than the books from which the formulas had been taken, especially the Register of Gregory the Great and the letters of other pontiffs.

### XVII

I added the notes that were necessary—something that no one who reads them will easily deny. I did not, however, relegate them to another part of the volume, as some do. Experience has taught me that notes placed far from the text are read only with difficulty, so that the reader either fails to obtain the desired benefit or, when he encounters something obscure, throws the book aside in disgust.

[Col. 0014A]

### XVIII

Three things seemed especially in need of explanation in the notes: historical, dogmatic, and what are called critical matters. I call historical whatever contributes to illuminating history; dogmatic, whatever sets forth the faith of the Apostolic See in explicit and formulated words; critical, whatever contributes to understanding ancient terms and rites.

### XIX

In monuments of such venerable antiquity, so precious and useful, some interpolator, as I suspect, has dared either to insert or at least to add certain more recent and inferior materials. Such are some privileges of Apostolic authority that do not differ greatly from those which are not highly approved by learned men. For the threats of condemnation, made by the supreme pontiffs against even the successors of the Apostolic See, together with Satan and his pomps and the traitor Judas, for matters that are not very serious, are either spurious or belong to a later age.

But we shall discuss each item individually in the notes.

[Col. 0014B]

### XX

The Book of the Day, which, in my opinion, we are publishing complete, comprises altogether 104 titles. In the manuscript codex they are written in continuous sequence, without any division of the work into parts, any distribution of the parts into chapters, or any distinction of chapters according to their different subjects.

This is not surprising, since such things often occur in ancient works. For, to say nothing of the many exceedingly confused collections of canons, what order is there in Marculf’s Formulas? What principle of arrangement?

[Col. 0014C]

### XXI

Nevertheless, the order that appears to be lacking can easily be supplied if the entire Book of the Day is divided, as it truly is, although this is not indicated, into two parts: the first part containing six chapters, and the second one lengthy chapter. Thus there are seven chapters altogether.

**First:** On superscriptions and subscriptions, under which are twelve titles.

**Second:** On the ordination of the supreme pontiff, under which are eleven titles.

**Third:** On the ordination of a bishop by the supreme pontiff, under which are nineteen titles.

[Col. 0014D]

**Fourth:** On the use of the pallium, under which are four titles.

**Fifth:** On sacred persons and places, under which are likewise nineteen titles.

**Sixth:** On administering and alienating the property of the Church, under which are twenty-one titles.

**Seventh:** On various privileges of Apostolic authority, or on exempting, endowing, granting, confirming, and uniting monasteries and pious places; on the office of provost; and so forth.

### XXII

With regard to what I said about the continuous sequence in which the formulas are written in the manuscript codex without a suitable division, it should also be added that several matters are mixed together in great confusion which reason requires to be separated because they have no affinity [Col. 0015A] and restored to their proper order.

I have tried to accomplish this, and I think no one who has observed the confusion will disapprove of what I have done. To make this clear, I present two different and conflicting tables of contents for the Book of the Day: one from the Roman codex, the other from ours.

### XXIII

The copy sent from Rome many years ago reads as follows.

## Index of the Formulas of the Most Ancient Manuscript Codex

An outline of a letter to be written [lacuna]. Superscription to the prince [lacuna]. “To the most pious lord,” etc. [Col. 0015B] “To Victor, conqueror and triumphant” [lacuna]. No traces of the remaining chapters or formulas survive.

The fifth leaf then begins with these words: “They who aspire to offices should not be admitted for any reason,” etc., which appears to be a form or outline concerning the office of a bishop.

If the discrepancy between the two exemplars is as great as it is presented here, and if the confusion proper to each is likewise so extensive, then, I think, it was necessary to escape from that confusion and to follow nature as our guide—nature which both assigns an order to the individual titles and shows in advance to which headings each item should be referred. This we have done, unless I am mistaken, with reasonable probability, grouping the material under the seven headings set out above.

That confusion, moreover, detracts nothing from the value of the book, since almost all ancient collections of matters of this kind suffer from the same defect. The formulae of Marculf have scarcely any order; so too do the books of the Canons, whether those commonly called the canons of the universal Church or those of the Roman Church. In the one recently published and presented as the most ancient, there is scarcely any chronological order, no careful selection of materials, and sometimes an unlearned arrangement of the titles, so that what the Editor says on page 670 of volume II appears deserved: “the work of a rough and ignorant compiler, stitched together.”

[Col. 0021]

# THE DIURNAL OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS. (C)

## CHAPTER ONE. THE FORMULARY FOR WRITING A LETTER

### 1. Summary

In letters written by the Supreme Pontiff, three things must be observed: the superscription, the subscription, and the address. The superscription is placed before the letter; the subscription is appended; the address is inserted within it. The form of the first two is found in the Diurnal; the third is absent, but it can easily be supplied either from the other two or from the letters of the Pontiffs, especially those of Gregory the Great.

The letters of the Supreme Pontiff are addressed either to secular persons or to ecclesiastical persons. Among secular persons the Emperor, the Empress, the King, and those who hold the highest positions at court are prominent—men such as Patricians, Exarchs, Counts, and Consuls. Among ecclesiastical persons at that time were reckoned the Patriarch, the Archbishop of Ravenna, bishops both foreign and subject to the ordination of the Apostolic See, presbyters, deacons, First Notaries, and Second Notaries. For these persons, under whose number the others are included, there are eleven letter-formulas; a twelfth is added for subscribing to a decree.

As for the words “formulary for writing a letter,” observe that the ancient forms of superscriptions and subscriptions cannot fruitfully be sought in the published Register of Gregory the Great, although there might otherwise have seemed to be some hope of finding them there. For the compiler, omitting honorific titles, inscribed on almost every letter’s opening only the bare indication of who wrote to whom. Nevertheless, letters of Gregory inserted in the works of ancient authors are found bearing the complete and solemn formula. It is therefore clear—something also understood from John the Deacon—that the omission was not made by the Pontiff but by the compiler, to no small loss for historical knowledge of antiquity. The same happened with the letters of Leo the Great. Accordingly, those should not be heeded who have dared to assert that the letters of either Pontiff were superscribed in no other way than that in which they were collected into the codex.

## TITLES

### TITLE I. To the Emperor

[Note: To the Emperor of the Eastern Empire. The Western Empire had long since been destroyed by the barbarians, and Rome, at the time when the Diurnal was compiled, after the barbarians had been expelled, was under the rule of the East, together with the exarchate and the islands.]

### Superscription

[Note: The superscription. This was used before the Sixth Council by Leo the Great when writing to the younger Theodosius, by Gregory the Great, Martin I, Agatho, and others; and after the Sixth Council by Leo II, etc.]

To the most devout and most serene lord, victorious and triumphant son, lover of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, Ill. Augustus, Ill., bishop, servant of the servants of God.

[Note: “Lord.” This form of address, customary in earlier times, fell out of use around the ninth century. John the Deacon, Book IV of the Life of Gregory the Great: “Gregory called all priests brothers and fellow ministers, and clerics of the various orders his most beloved sons; but in his letters he called laymen ‘lords’ and laywomen ‘ladies.’”]

[Note: “Most devout,” etc. The reason for this and the other appellations that occur is to be sought in the fact that, in a Christian Emperor, there is acknowledged both the dignity by which he is called Augustus; the power by which he is called lord; the devotion to religion by which he is called a lover of God and of Christ; the affection toward the Church by which he is called son; the power against enemies by which he is called victor and triumphant; the love toward his subjects by which he is called devout, which means the same as father of his country; and the manner of governing by which he is serene or tranquil—that is, peaceful—and a giver of tranquillity, which follows peace. Sometimes “beloved and crowned by God” is added, as well as “glorious,” so that his right to rule and the manner of his life may be proclaimed. But if the feeling of the peoples is considered, two names surpass all others: “most devout” and “most serene.” Hence the frequent mention on coins of the father of his country, tranquillity, and peace.]

[Note: “Ill.” Thus the ancients used this where we now place N., when they wished to indicate the place of a name.]

### And his subscription

[Note: The subscription. This very formula is read in the letters of Martin I, Agatho, and Leo II to Constantine Pogonatus, etc. It should also be observed that the subscription was written by the Pontiff’s own hand, while the superscription and the letter were written by the Notary. Thus it is chiefly from the subscription, rather than from anything else, that the Pontiff’s disposition toward the person to whom he was writing can be determined. In place of the wish or prayer formerly contained in the subscription, the addition of the name is now appended. One should also observe the ancient custom of the Supreme Pontiffs of placing the name of the person to whom they were writing before their own, without regard to rank.]

May the grace from above preserve the most devout authority of our lord, and subject to him the necks of all the Gentiles.

[Note: “The necks of the Gentiles.” In those times, because kings ruled in Italy, it was not safe to mention Gentiles—let alone heretics or enemies.]

## TITLE II. To the Empress

[Note: To the Empress. The compilers of the letter collections of the holy Leo and Gregory deprived us, for the most part, of the formula by which the Pontiffs’ letters to Empresses were superscribed and subscribed. Nevertheless, I have no doubt that it was the same as, or not very different from, the form I infer from Gregory the Great’s letter to Constantia, Book III, Letter 30, which begins: “The serenity of your devotion.” Later it says: “But since the religious desire of the most serene lady,” etc.; or as it appears in the first part of the Council of Chalcedon: “To the most glorious and most humane daughter Pulcheria, Leo, bishop.” From this one can construct the superscription: “To the most devout and most serene lady, daughter and Empress Constantia.”]

### Superscription

To the most devout lady, daughter, Ill. Augusta, Ill., bishop, servant of the servants of God.

And his subscription:

May grace from above preserve the authority of your devotion, lady daughter.

[Col. 0024A] Another:

May the divine majesty preserve your serenity unharmed, lady daughter.

## TITLE III. To the Patrician

[Note: To the Patrician. He is called by this name not, as formerly, because he was born of a senatorial father, but because, after holding the higher magistracies, he was summoned to the Emperor’s more sacred council.]

### Superscription

To the most excellent and pre-eminent lord and son, Ill. Patrician, Ill., bishop, servant of the servants of God.

His subscription:

May grace from above preserve your excellence unharmed.

## TITLE IV. To the Count of the Imperial Service and the Exarch

[Note: To the Count, etc. The same superscription formula is used in letters to a Patrician, to a Count of the Imperial Service, and to an Exarch, because of the equality of their rank. Under the general title “Count of the Imperial Service” were included all who held the highest offices at court, such as Masters of the Soldiers, Masters of Offices, Counts of the Sacred Largesses, and others.]

[Note: To the Exarch. The Emperor of Constantinople’s prefect in Italy. This office lasted for nearly two hundred years: Longinus was the first Exarch, appointed by Justin the Younger in 567; the last was Eutychius, expelled by Aistulf, king of the Lombards, in 752. The power of the Exarchs was so great that it sometimes became tyrannical, as is clear from the letters of Saint Gregory. An Apocrisiarius was sent to him from the Apostolic See, just as to the Emperor, as is established by chapter 2 of this Diurnal, where there is a form of letter to the Apocrisiarius of Ravenna concerning the election of the Pontiff. Their power, and the arrogance arising from that power, had four chief causes: first, that the Exarchs were far from Constantinople, the imperial city; second, that they controlled a substantial army against the barbarians; third, that, if they feared anything from the Emperor, they could easily make an alliance with the barbarians and protect themselves by it; fourth, that the office was long-lasting, so that Isaac, the eighth of the Exarchs and the plunderer of the ecclesiastical treasury under Pope Honorius, ruled for twenty-five years, while Theodore Calliopas, persecutor of Saint Martin, ruled for thirty-five or even thirty-six. Certainly, during the 185 years in which the exarchate existed, no more than eighteen men held this office, according to the more probable opinion.]

To the Count of the Imperial Service and the Exarch.

### Subscription

May your excellence remain safe through grace from above, lord son.

## TITLE V. To the Consul

[Note: To the Consul. At that time the consulship, which had once been the summit of dignities, had declined so far that it was almost an empty title. Justinian nearly suppressed it; although later emperors restored it in some fashion, it did not regain its former splendor.]

[Col. 0025A]

### Superscription

To the most eminent lord and son, Ill. Consul, Ill., bishop, servant of the servants of God.

His subscription:

May God preserve you unharmed, lord son.

## TITLE VI. To the King

[Note: To the King. No superscription or subscription has been appended. Nor was there need, since it was the same as the formula addressed to a Patrician. Thus, in Bede, Book II of the Ecclesiastical History of the English, chapter 17, Honorius writes to Edwin, King of the English: “To the most excellent and pre-eminent lord and son, Edwin, King of the English, Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God.” Subscription: “May grace from above preserve your excellence unharmed.” Likewise, in Book III, chapter 24, Vitalian writes to Oswy, “the most excellent lord and son, King of the Saxons,” etc., with the same subscription. Leo II uses the same formula in superscribing and subscribing a letter to King Ervig. Hadrian I uses almost the same form to Charlemagne, King.]

To the King.

## TITLE VII. To the Patriarch

[Note: To the Patriarch. The same form of superscription and subscription was used from the earliest times. Certainly in the fifth century [First Part of the Council of Ephesus, chapters 15, 18, 20], Celestine superscribed letters sent to Cyril of Alexandria, John of Antioch, and Nestorius of Constantinople, “To the beloved brother”; but he subscribed the latter two, “May God preserve you unharmed, dearest” or “most honorable brother.” Leo the Great wrote to Flavian of Constantinople: “To the most beloved brother Flavian, Leo, bishop.” In the same form Simplicius wrote to Acacius of Constantinople, Gelasius to Euphemius, bishop of that same city, and Gregory the Great to John of Constantinople and other Patriarchs.]

### Superscription

To our most beloved brother, Ill., Ill.

His subscription:

May God preserve you unharmed, most beloved brother.

## TITLE VIII. To a Foreign Bishop

[Note: To a foreign bishop. Someone might wonder which bishop is meant by “foreign.” I infer partly from the origin of the word and partly from the order of the title, in which the foreign bishop is placed between the Patriarch and the Archbishop of Ravenna—an office of great authority when the Diurnal was composed—that it means either a bishop of a city outside Italy or an Exarch, that is, a prelate subject to no bishop but nevertheless possessing authority over even metropolitan bishops, such as the bishop of Carthage in Africa, Caesarea in Cappadocia, Ephesus in Asia, and Thessalonica in Illyricum. For the word “foreign” may be derived either from *foris*, “outside,” or from *forum*, “jurisdiction.” I incline more to the former conjecture because that derivation is more common and Ravenna is a city of Italy. The latter is suggested by the order of rank, which seems to have been preserved among the persons to whom the Pontiffs wrote. The conjecture receives some support from the fact that Leo superscribes his letters to Anastasius of Thessalonica in the same way as those sent to Patriarchs: “To the most beloved brother.” Yet this argument is not very strong, since he also used the same form when writing to bishops.]

### Superscription

To our most beloved Ill., Ill.

His subscription:

May God preserve you unharmed, most beloved of us.

## TITLE IX. To the Archbishop of Ravenna

[Note: To the Archbishop of Ravenna. As stated, at the time when the Diurnal was composed he possessed great authority, partly because the seat of the Exarch was located at Ravenna; partly because his own intercession was necessary with the Exarch for ecclesiastical affairs to be advanced; and finally because, following the example of the Exarchs, the prelates of Ravenna thought they could with impunity inflict injury upon the Romans, since the Exarchs ruled them despotically. Two points should be observed: first, that the prelate of Ravenna is not called a bishop but an archbishop; second, that he is addressed more honorifically even than the Patriarch himself. The latter is called “most beloved brother,” whereas the former is called “most reverend and most holy brother.” Both circumstances were produced by the miserable condition of the times, when prudence required flattery and administrative necessity required some relaxation of Saint Gregory’s strictness. The prelates of that city consequently assumed so much for themselves that, out of arrogance toward the Roman Pontiffs—the vicars of Christ, successors of Peter, and heads of the Church—they refused to submit, and could scarcely be brought back to their duty by the complete exertion of the Supreme Pontiffs.]

### Superscription

To the most reverend and most holy brother, Ill., fellow bishop, Ill., servant of the servants of God.

[Col. 0026A] And his subscription:

May God preserve you unharmed, most reverend and most holy brother.

## TITLE X. To a Bishop

[Note: To a Bishop. This formula, uncommon in earlier centuries, became solemn after the Diurnal was published. Thus Gregory II, Gregory III, and Zacharias address Saint Boniface, the Apostle of the Germans, as well as other bishops.]

### Superscription

As above.

His subscription:

May God preserve you unharmed, most reverend brother.

## TITLE XI. To a Presbyter, Deacon, First Notary, and Second Notary

[Note: To a Presbyter. Thus Leo the Great addresses Eutyches in Letter 6 and Faustus in Letter 98; Gregory the Great likewise addresses many persons who were not only presbyters but also deacons, subdeacons, notaries, defenders, and administrators of the patrimony.]

### Superscription

To our most beloved son, Ill., Ill., servant of the servants of God.

His subscription:

May God preserve you unharmed, most beloved son.

## TITLE XII. Subscription for a Person Appointed

[Col. 0026B]

I, Ill., bishop of the holy catholic and apostolic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed for Ill., appointed by us.

[Note: “For the person appointed.” Thus Gregory the Great in 594, Gregory II in 721, and Zacharias in 743 each subscribed in his own Roman Synod.]

# CHAPTER II. ON THE ORDINATION OF THE SUPREME PONTIFF

[Col. 0027]

### Summary

In the sixth, seventh, and eighth centuries the following practices were observed in the ordination of the Supreme Pontiff.

I. As soon as the Supreme Pontiff had died, a message was sent to the Exarch by those who exercised the authority of the Apostolic See.

II. After the customary rites had been performed for the deceased and a three-day fast proclaimed, a Pontiff was elected, with the votes of the clergy, the leading men, and the people converging; a decree was drawn up and subscribed by the electors.

III. The election was then reported to the Emperor—that is, the Emperor of Constantinople—and approval of the election was requested.

IV. It was likewise reported to the Exarch of Ravenna, with a request that he either confirm the election in the Emperor’s name or arrange for its confirmation.

V. Letters were also written to the judges, the Archbishop, and the Apocrisiarius of Ravenna, and, as seems certain, to the Patrician, the Bishop, and the Apocrisiarius of Constantinople, by their peers.

VI. Once confirmation had been received, the elected man was ceremonially led to the confession of Saint Peter.

VII. There, although not yet ordained, he professed the faith at the tomb of the Prince of the Apostles.

VIII. Soon after being ordained, he set it forth again.

IX. Finally, he delivered a discourse on the faith in the city and sent it to the whole Church of God.

Each of these matters has its own formula in the Diurnal. Two might be thought missing: one for the Emperor’s reply and another for the Exarch’s. Yet nowhere are they found, at least nowhere that I remember having read. The eleven formulas contained in this chapter are drawn from events that occurred at the ordinations of four Pontiffs: Boniface V in 617, Leo II in 682, Conon in 686, and Gregory II in 714, insofar as it is permissible to determine this by conjecture.

## TITLES

### TITLE I. Message to the Exarch concerning the death of the Pontiff

[Note: To the Exarch. If what we shall say concerning the following titles is correct, the Exarch to whom the letter was written, which became a solemn formula, was Scholasticus, who is mentioned in Anastasius’s Life of Pope Constantine.]

[Note: Concerning the death of the Pontiff. Constantine, who preceded Gregory II. For the entire message concerning the death of the Pontiff corresponds to the report to the Exarch concerning the election. That report concerns the election of Gregory II, as will be explained later. Moreover, that great mourning suits the funeral of Constantine, who, if we trust Anastasius the Librarian, was both exceedingly gentle toward everyone and generous toward the Romans.]

### Superscription

To the most excellent and pre-eminent lord, and by God to be preserved for us for a long life and prosperously in the principal offices, Ill., former consul, Patrician and Exarch of Italy, Ill., archpresbyter; Ill., archdeacon; Ill., First Notary.

[Note: “Those serving in place of the Apostolic See.” Observe in whose hands the power of administration lay at that time while the see was vacant. It lay with the archpresbyter, the archdeacon, and the First Notary; today people live according to other customs. Not only when the see was vacant but also when the Supreme Pontiff was absent, supreme authority lay with those three. We know this from other sources as well as from Letter XV of Martin I to Theodore, in which he writes of his sufferings before Eugenius had been substituted in his place: “In the absence of the Pontiff, the archdeacon, archpresbyter, and First Notary represent the place of the Pontiff.” Observe that Martin names the archdeacon first, whereas here he is listed only second. A nearly similar superscription is found among the letters of John IV to the bishops and presbyters of Scotland: “To our most beloved and most holy, etc. Hilary, archpresbyter, serving in place of the Apostolic See; John, deacon and, in God’s name, elected; likewise John, First Notary and serving in place of the Apostolic See,” etc. In this superscription note that John, although elected Roman Pontiff, is nevertheless listed second after the archpresbyter. Four conclusions follow. First, the elected man had no authority to administer affairs until he had been ordained. Second, when it is said that the Apostolic See was vacant for a time during the age of the Exarchs and even earlier, when the Goths ruled, the period must be calculated not from the Pontiff’s death to the election of his successor but to his ordination; for, when there were no schisms, the election was scarcely ever delayed beyond three days. Third, it was a special privilege of Gregory the Great and certain of his successors that, with the consent of the clergy, they administered affairs before their ordination. Finally, the elected man did not describe himself in letters as Roman Pontiff but as the elected man.]

Those serving in place of the holy Apostolic See.

Although not without profound lamentation and a truly mournful voice, we make known through these humble words of ours to the excellence of our lord, preserved by God, that by the judgment of God—by whose dispensation the whole world is governed—our most holy Pontiff, Lord Ill., has been taken from this life; all truly mourned his departure, and, if it must be said, even the stones themselves mourned it.

[Note: “On the Ill. day of the present month.” On the ninth of April, as is established by Anastasius the Librarian under the year 713, indiction 13, during the reign of Anastasius, or Artemius.]

For he died on the Ill. day of the present month. Because of his funeral, which, as we have said, has thrown us all beneath a great burden of sorrow, we lift the eyes of our hearts toward the sole mercy of Christ our God, so that he himself may deign to help the despairing and provide a worthy ruler for the Church founded by him, who also promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18). After divine assistance, we all place our confidence in your excellence, most excellent lord Ill., whom God has granted to us for many years. Behold, we have announced the mournful event, since we have no other human refuge to which we may flee for consolation.

## TITLE II. Decree concerning the election of the Pontiff

[Note: Decree concerning the election. Observe who are said to have subscribed the decree made by them, and from this judge by whom the election was made at that time. Are these and the other forms of subscription the forms of laymen who merely consent to and praise the election, or of those who actually elect together with the clergy?]

[Note: Of the Pontiff. If it did not happen by chance that, at the end of the formula, a particular and definite month and indiction were mentioned—a possibility I scarcely think likely, since in other formulas not a definite month and definite indiction are given, but merely, according to custom, “month Ill., indiction Ill.”—if, I say, this was not accidental, the conjecture can fit no one more suitably than Boniface V. He began to occupy the see in December 617, according to Baronius on the authority of Anastasius, after the see of his predecessor Deusdedit had been vacant for one month and six or sixteen days. The seven points mentioned seem to correspond to the ordination of Boniface V: first, that he was elected as a presbyter; second, that he was adorned with every virtue and was exceedingly gentle; third, that he was elected by unanimous agreement; fourth, that he followed a predecessor greatly mourned; fifth, that the see was not vacant for long; sixth, that the election was completed in November; seventh, that it occurred in the fourth indiction. For Boniface was made Pontiff from among the presbyters of the Roman Church, a most gentle, merciful, and generous man, without any party dissension, after a predecessor most holy and dear to all; he was ordained soon after his predecessor’s death in December, and therefore was elected in November—on the 14th or 24th—of December, in the fifth indiction according to Anastasius. Yet an error could easily have entered in either place, especially in the Diurnal, which was copied by an unlearned hand. What we have said about Boniface V is established by his Life written by Anastasius and by the epitaph which Honorius placed for his predecessor. For after six verses serving as witnesses to his grief, the following follows:]

Here was a man nourished from his birth in Peter’s fold,

Yet he deserved to stand as shepherd of the holy flock.

The man’s pure faith, cleansed by kindly prayers,

Exults in the hymn-filled songs of Christ.

Wise simplicity, lively skill, simplicity itself:

He flourished with serpent-like simplicity.

And when he had completed forty years as a presbyter,

Though late in old age, his mind remained noble.

He honored the Apostolic summit for nearly three years,

Completing the perfect number three times four.

For his great merits, his successor Honorius

Built this gift of an epitaph for you in marble.

Among the other matters arranged by the counsel of supreme divinity, the sublimity of pontifical promotion is granted by him from whom everything good proceeds, who both predestines and bestows it. [Col. 0029A] Divine providence, of course, knows how to come to the aid of human affairs and turn the tears and groans of the sorrowful into rejoicing, so that those who had recently been cast down in affliction may afterward appear exceedingly consoled.

[Note: “Divine providence knows how to aid human affairs,” etc. These words and what follows, up to and including the confirmations by subscription, are found verbatim in the report concerning the election of the Pontiff to the Exarch, Title IV, with this one difference: here the elected man is said to have been a presbyter, whereas there he is said to have been an archdeacon.]

For the words which the Holy Spirit sounded from the temple of the prophetic heart belong to the singing King: “In the evening mourning shall remain, and in the morning joy” (Psalm 29:6). And again, giving thanks to God, he sings and proclaims the greatness of his benefits: “You turned my mourning into joy for me; you tore off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with sorrow” (ibid., vv. 12–13). For he himself cares for us (1 Peter 5:7), as the integrity of the vessel of election teaches. Indeed, he mercifully leads the things that are sorrowful toward joy; and this heavenly favor has also shown assistance to us, insignificant sinners awaiting help from his mercy.

For indeed, when the lord Ill., pope of venerable memory, was summoned from present cares to eternal rest, as commonly happens in human affairs, [Note: [Col. 0030C] “A great mass of sorrows,” etc. Deusdedit, Boniface’s predecessor, left behind a great longing for himself because of his outstanding holiness, also renowned for miracles, and his lavish generosity toward the clergy. His memory is recorded in the Roman Martyrology on 8 November; he is plausibly believed to have died on that day.] a great weight of sorrows had overwhelmed us, deprived of our own steward. But [Note: [Col. 0030D] “Not for long,” etc. The see was vacant for only one month and six or sixteen days—the readings in Anastasius vary. It is therefore clear that Boniface was elected only a few days after the death of his predecessor. That period of vacancy was short indeed, considering that the decree of election had to be carried from Rome to Constantinople and the emperor’s approval from Constantinople to Rome.] the accustomed goodness of our God did not abandon us, who hoped in him, to remain long in affliction. While we persevered in prayer, divine grace supported us, and, as heavenly favor demonstrated whom it commanded to be chosen as worthy to succeed to the apostolic office, inspiring the minds of all and bringing us together into one, [Note: [Col. 0030D] “As is customary.” The power of electing the pontiff, who was to preside over the whole Church, had not yet been restricted to the cardinals. It was first restricted by Nicholas II in 1059, and thereafter by Alexander III, Gregory X, and Clement V.] as is customary—that is, with all the priests and principal men of the Church, the entire clergy and the nobles, the whole military presence, or respectable citizens, and the entire general body of the people of this God-preserved city of Rome, from the least to the greatest, if one may so speak—the election converged upon and consented to the person of Ill., the most holy presbyter of this holy apostolic see of the Roman Church, with God cooperating and the blessed apostles exerting their support.

The advancement of this God-loving man in a good and chaste way of life had earned so much merit in the consciences of all that no one dissented from his election, no one was absent, and no one withdrew himself. The incomparable and unfailing providence of our God had evidently predestined him for this office of the apostolic succession. How could the unanimous agreement of human minds fail to converge upon what was undoubtedly fixed in the presence of God?

Accordingly, solemnly drawing up his decree and confirming by the signatures of our hands the desires of our hearts concerning his election, we profess that our God-loving elect is chaste, modest, sober, kind, and perfect in every pious work, as well as a defender and most steadfast observer of the orthodox faith and the tradition of the holy Fathers.

We have unanimously chosen this man, [Note: [Col. 0030D] “Most gentle.” Anastasius says: “The most blessed Boniface was gentler than all men and merciful.”] certainly most gentle, as our pastor and pontiff because of his exceptionally gracious and good-willed constancy. Therefore, for the integrity of his pious conduct, we offer immense praises to our Redeemer, singing with the Prophet in harmonious voice: “Great are you, Lord our God, and great is your power” (Psalm 146:5). “Who can speak of your mighty acts, Lord, and make all your praises heard?” (ibid. 105:2). For, hearing the prayers of those who petition you, you have bestowed upon us a devout pastor, who, under your protection, Lord God and our Savior, may be able to rule and govern your holy universal Church and all the Lord’s rational sheep entrusted to him.

Having confirmed this decree made by us below with our own hands, as has been stated, we ordered it to be deposited, for the security of future generations, in the lordly archive of our holy Roman Church, namely, in the sacred [Note: [Col. 0031B] “Lateran archive.” Alongside other ecclesiastical documents, it preserved decrees of election and professions of faith, whether issued by supreme pontiffs or by other bishops at their ordination, as well as the guarantees and undertakings of lower-ranking prelates. Thus Anastasius, in the Life of Pope Constantine, speaks of Felix, bishop of Ravenna: “Contrary to the custom of his predecessors, he did not wish to provide the customary guarantees in the archive, but through the power of the judges he brought forward whatever he wished.”] Lateran archive, in the month of November, in the fifth indiction.

I, Ill., humble presbyter of the holy Roman Church, have consented and subscribed to this decree made by us in favor of Ill., the most holy presbyter; likewise, the entire clergy, the nobles, and the soldiers or citizens subscribe.

## 14. TITLE III. Report concerning the election of the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0031C] “To the emperor.” The emperor of Constantinople, as we explained in the notes to chapter I.] to the emperor

[Col. 0031B] Since it is not without the prompting of divine mercy that, after the death of the supreme pontiff, the votes of all converge upon the election of one man and unite in agreement, so that no one at all is found who could remain in opposition, it is necessary that we humbly pour out united prayers to our most serene and devout lord. It is certain that he both rejoices in the concord of his subjects and graciously grants what is requested for the sake of unity.

When, therefore, our pope Ill., of blessed memory, died, [Note: [Col. 0031C] “In the election of Ill.” It will not be far from the truth, as it seems to me, to suppose that whoever composed this formula intended it as a petition presented by the Romans to the emperor Anastasius or Artemius in 714, seeking consent to the election of Gregory II. All the circumstances of the election fit this supposition very well. They are six: (1) The man said to have been elected was archdeacon. (2) He was the one who had long previously been desired. (3) There was complete unanimity in the election. (4) From an early age he had been devoted to every ministry of the Roman Church. (5) He had zealously supported his predecessor. (6) He possessed outstanding learning and eloquence. The consistent opinion of the sources is that Gregory II was made pontiff from the office of archdeacon, when everyone had long desired this and had assented to his election with the greatest eagerness. According to Anastasius, he was “brought up from childhood in the patriarchium; under Pope Sergius of holy memory he was made subdeacon and sacellarius, then prefect of the library, and afterward advanced to the order of deacon. With his predecessor, the holy man Constantine, he went to the royal city. He was a chaste man, learned in divine Scripture, eloquent in speech and steadfast in spirit, a defender of ecclesiastical affairs and a most vigorous opponent of those who resisted.” Two points may seem to contradict this. First, Anastasius says in the Life of Benedict II: “He received the imperial commands of the most merciful Constantine [Col. 0032B] the Great to the venerable clergy, people, and most fortunate army of the Roman city, by which he granted that whoever had been elected to the apostolic see should immediately and without delay be ordained pontiff.” From this it might be concluded that no petition concerning Gregory II was sent to the emperor and that his consent to the election was not requested; Gregory was ordained nearly thirty years after the death of Benedict II. But Constantine’s grant was valid for only three years, during which John V and Conon were ordained. In the schism following Conon’s death, however, there was a tumult, and the matter was referred to the exarch, who did not allow a pontiff to be ordained until he had extorted money, as may be gathered from Anastasius. From then until the exarchs were expelled—that is, until 752—the oppression introduced by the Goths remained. Binius, wholly occupied with following Baronius’s footsteps, seems not to have attended to the history of events; otherwise he would not have written that from the time of Benedict II the Roman Church had been free from this tyranny. The second apparent contradiction is that the report mentions several emperors, whereas only Anastasius was reigning when Gregory II was created. It should be observed, however, that Anastasius’s sons were also called emperors. Indeed, after the emperor Justinian, even the empresses themselves were included under the titles “lords” and “emperors.”] the assent of all, God willing, converged upon the election of Ill., the venerable archdeacon of the apostolic see, because from the beginning of his life he had served that holy Church and had conducted himself so diligently in all things that, with divine grace supporting him, he deserved to be placed over its ecclesiastical government. This was especially so because he had formerly been formed in such a manner that, through his constant association with the aforementioned most blessed pontiff Ill., he had advanced, with Christ’s help, to the marks of such great merit with which that bishop of holy memory is known to have been adorned. By his words he had always kindled in those who desired it a longing for heavenly joys, so that we confidently trust that whatever good we lost in that man we shall unquestionably find in this one.

Therefore, we, all your servants, tearfully beg [Col. 0032B] that the piety of our lords may graciously hear the entreaties of their servants and, by granting an order expressive of their kindness, command that the desires of those who petition, as a reward for their imperial rule, reach fulfillment in his ordination. Thus, [Note: [Col. 0032D] “Through the sacred,” etc. Some call the command and grant mentioned here merely consent and approval, although John the Deacon, in Book I of the Life of Saint Gregory, chapter 40, calls it a *praeceptio*, an authoritative order. It is probable that there was a solemn formula for this matter, but I do not know whether it survives anywhere.] through the sacred letters of their clemency, once we have been placed under this same pastor, we may continually pray to almighty God and to the prince of the blessed apostles, whose Church they permit to be provided with a worthy governor, for the life and empire of our most serene lords.

### Subscription of the priests

[Note: [Col. 0032D] “I, Ill.” The elected man did not subscribe; indeed, he did not even send private letters, lest he appear ambitious. Gregory the Great earnestly asked the emperor Maurice, on account of their longstanding friendship, not to consent to his election; nevertheless, he did not succeed.] I, Ill., by the mercy of God presbyter of the holy Roman Church, consenting to this decree made by us in favor of Ill., the venerable archdeacon of the holy apostolic see and our elect, have subscribed.

### Subscription of the laity

I, Ill., servant of your piety, consenting to this decree made by us in favor of Ill., the venerable archdeacon of the holy apostolic see and our elect, have subscribed.

## TITLE IV. Concerning the election of the pontiff, to the exarch

### Superscription

To the most excellent and pre-eminent lord, preserved by God for a long life and prosperously in the principal offices, Ill., former consul, patrician, and exarch of Italy, [Note: [Col. 0033C] “The priests,” etc. The elected man did not subscribe to letters of this kind, lest he appear to suffer from the vice of ambition. Gregory the Great sent letters to Constantinople in which he urgently asked his friends—he had won many while serving as apocrisiarius to the emperor—to prevent consent to his election. I have spoken of letters of this kind, for it is clear from the letter of John IV, discussed above, that the opposite was true of other letters concerning ecclesiastical affairs.] the priests, deacons, and the entire familiar clergy, together with the dignitaries, or [Col. 0033B] the army and people of this Roman city, as suppliants.

[Note: [Col. 0033D] “Divine providence knows,” etc. These words, up to “confirming,” are taken from the formula of the decree concerning the election of the supreme pontiff.] Divine providence knows how to come to the aid of human affairs and to turn the tears and groans of the sorrowful into exultation, so that those who recently lay afflicted in dismay may afterward appear exceedingly comforted. For these are the words of the singing King, which the Holy Spirit sounded forth from the temple of the prophetic heart: “In the evening weeping shall tarry, but joy comes in the morning” (Psalm 29:6). Again, giving thanks to God, he sings of the magnificence of his benefits and says: “You have turned my mourning into joy; you have cut off my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pierced with sorrow” (ibid., vv. 12–13). For he himself cares for us (1 Peter 5:7), as the integrity of the vessel of election and of the true faith teaches; indeed, he mercifully leads sorrows toward joy. This heavenly favor has also displayed itself to us, insignificant and sinful though we are, as we await help from his mercy.

For indeed, when Ill., pope of venerable memory, was summoned from present cares to eternal rest, as commonly happens in human affairs, a great weight of sorrows had overwhelmed us, deprived of our own steward. But the accustomed goodness of our God did not abandon us, who hoped in him, to remain long in affliction: [Note: [Col. 0033D] “For three days,” etc. In 606 Boniface III, as Anastasius reports, “issued a decree in the church of Saint Peter, where seventy-two bishops, thirty-four Roman priests, the deacons, and the entire clergy assembled under anathema, so that no one, while a pontiff was alive—or while the bishop of his city was alive—might presume to speak of a successor or form factions for himself. Instead, on the third day after his burial, when the clergy and the sons of the Church had assembled, an election was to be held, and each person was to have the freedom to choose the priest he wished.” During those three days, people devoted themselves to fasting and public prayers.] for three days, while we insignificant persons remained in prayer, heavenly favor demonstrated to the minds of all whom it commanded to be chosen as worthy to succeed to the apostolic office. With its grace supporting and inspiring the minds of all, [Note: [Col. 0034D] “When we came together into one,” etc. This is almost the same as in the report to the emperor, making it evident that both reports concern one and the same elect, and therefore Gregory II.] when we came together into one, as is customary, [Note: [Col. 0034D] “The familiar members of the clergy.” In his decree Boniface calls these the “sons of the Church.”] the familiar members of the clergy and the people, [Note: [Col. 0034D] “The principal men also,” etc. It is therefore clear that at that time the principal men and other laypeople did not assemble at the election of a pontiff merely to give assent to the clerical electors or to testify to the candidate’s character, but to elect him truly. Thus Leo the Great says in Letter 89: “Let the man who is to preside over all be elected by all.” Gregory the Great used this statement more than once.] together with the principal men and the military presence, from the least to the greatest, if one may so speak, the election, with God cooperating and the blessed apostles exerting their support, converged upon and consented to the person of Ill., the most holy archdeacon of this holy apostolic see of the Roman Church.

The perfection of this God-loving man’s good and chaste conduct had earned such merit in the consciences of all that no one dissented from his election, no one was absent, and no one withdrew himself. The incomparable and unfailing providence of our God had destined him for this office of the apostolic succession; how could harmony fail to arise in human minds? It was undoubtedly fixed in the presence of God.

Accordingly, solemnly drawing up his decree and confirming by the signatures of our hands the desires of our hearts concerning his election, we have sent, through the bearers of these letters, Ill., the most holy bishop; Ill., the venerable presbyter; Ill., the regional notary; Ill., likewise the regional subdeacon; Ill. and Ill., respectable citizens; and, from the military rank, Ill., the most eminent consul, together with Ill. and Ill., distinguished military tribunes, our fellow servants. We humbly and jointly implore with the greatest earnestness that, for the preservation of your pre-eminence, you may cause your customary goodness to concur with our pious wishes. For a man has been unanimously elected from our service in whom, so far as human knowledge can judge, no stain of reprehensible conduct will appear.

Therefore, we humbly ask that, with God inspiring his lofty lordship, he command us quickly to become possessors of our desire. There are especially many matters, and others are daily born from them, which await the care and remedy of pontifical favor. Provincial concerns, too, and whatever other useful affairs arise, await the judgment of perfected authority. [Col. 0035A] [Note: [Col. 0035C] “The ferocity of the approaching enemies,” etc. He means the Lombards who were lying in wait for the city. To defend Rome against them, Gregory ordered the walls to be repaired at the beginning of his pontificate, after the lime-kilns had been fired, as Anastasius says. We have restored a passage so confused that it was meaningless. It had read as follows: “The ferocity of the approaching enemies, which, unless the power of God alone and of the prince of the apostles, through his vicar—that is, the pontiff of the city—sometimes bends and renders tractable by exhortation, requires the singular intervention of him alone, etc.”]

The ferocity of the approaching enemies, which only the power of God and of the prince of the apostles, through his vicar—that is, the pontiff of the Roman city—sometimes bends and renders tractable by exhortation, requires a singular intervention. For, out of reverence for the prince of the apostles, they offer voluntary obedience to the pontifical admonitions of this one man; those whom the power of arms does not humble are inclined by pontifical rebuke, together with observance.

Since these things are so, again and again, with the greatest earnestness, we humbly ask you, most exalted lord preserved by God, that, with God working and inspiring your hearts, you may order the apostolic see to be adorned by the complete ordination of this same father and pastor of ours, [Note: [Col. 0035D] “May you command,” etc. The prayers appear to be addressed to the exarch as though the entire matter depended upon his single will and all imperial power had been transferred to him. This prayer contains no more than an obscure reference either to imperial consent or to the exarch’s intercession and insistence with the emperor. I would readily believe that in the time of Gregory II the exarchs, through a kind of tyranny, sold the emperor’s consent for money in his name, and that they were therefore entreated with humble prayers as though they were masters of the matter.] since through Christ’s grace you are successfully and faithfully carrying out the ministry of the imperial dignity. Thus, when we insignificant servants see our desire fulfilled more quickly, we may offer unceasing thanksgivings to God, to imperial clemency, and to your distinguished and God-pleasing lordship; and, together with the pontiff advanced to the apostolic see, our spiritual pastor, we may pour out continual prayers for the life, safety, and perfect victories of our most tranquil and Christian lords, Ill. and Ill., the great, victorious emperors. May merciful God grant their royal virtues multiplied victories, cause the Christian commonwealth to triumph through the subjection of all peoples, and grant joy of heart through the fuller restoration of the ancient devotion of the Roman Empire.

For we know that the prayer of the man whom, by God’s will, we have elected to the height of pontifical dignity will bend and appease divine omnipotence through his prayers and prepare increases of the desired prosperity for the Roman Empire. It will preserve, for the administration of this [Note: [Col. 0036D] “Servile.” That is, both obedient to you and largely enduring servitude under Lombard domination. Pope Agatho uses the same word in his letter to Constantine Pogonatus, where he says of the legates that he “inquired what sort of persons could be found according to the deficiencies of the present time and the condition of a servile province.”] servile Italian province, your power, which is to be guarded by God, and will preserve the protection and aid of all of us servants through long campaigns of arms.

### Subscription of the priests

[Col. 0036A] I, Ill., humble archpresbyter of the holy Roman Church, consenting to this decree in favor of Ill., the most holy archdeacon and our elect, have subscribed.

### Subscription of the laity

I, Ill., consul in the name of God, consenting to this decree made by us in favor of Ill., the most holy archdeacon and our elect, have subscribed.

## TITLE V. Concerning the election of the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0036D] “To the archbishop,” etc. No one who has read all these letters, even superficially, will deny that both letters—one to the exarch and one to the archbishop—and the following two were written at the same time concerning the same election.] to the archbishop of Ravenna

### Superscription

To the most holy lord Ill., our spiritual father, archbishop; Ill., archpresbyter; Ill., archdeacon; and Ill., first of the notaries, serving the place of the holy apostolic see.

Among the other matters ordered by the counsel of the supreme Divinity, the sublimity of pontifical promotion is granted by him from whom every good thing proceeds, through his predestination and gift. Since this is beyond doubt, we have taken care to inform your holy and fatherly blessedness that, when Ill., pope of venerable memory, was summoned from present cares to eternal rest, the customary goodness of God wiped away and soothed the burden of sorrows that had briefly overwhelmed us because we had been deprived of our former steward. For, lest the blow of affliction wound us for long, she deigned to give us a prudent and God-pleasing successor to the apostolic office.

Indeed, after three days, [Note: [Col. 0036D] “After three days, as is customary,” etc. That custom originated, or at least received confirmation, from the decree issued by Boniface III 128 years earlier. Since Pope Constantine died on 9 April, Gregory’s election must have taken place after three days, while his ordination was postponed until 22 May, until the consent of the emperor and the exarch had arrived. Gregory is said to have begun to sit as pontiff on 22 May.] when we had assembled, as is customary—that is, the priests and all the remaining clergy, the most eminent consuls and illustrious judges, the whole body of citizens, and the flourishing Roman army—we cast the votes of election upon the person of your beloved and our lord’s spokesman, Ill., the most holy archdeacon of this apostolic see. In this election, devoted to God, no one was absent, with the grace of the Holy Spirit illuminating us, but the votes of all converged in concord. Having solemnly drawn up decrees in favor of his holiness, we sent, through the bearers of these letters, [Note: [Col. 0036D] “The most holy bishop,” etc. The size of this embassy is noteworthy: it was sent not only because of the dignity of the person to whom it was addressed, but also, and especially, to give authority and credibility to the harmonious election—a bishop representing the province, a presbyter the clergy, and respectable men the city. The consul and tribunes served as representatives of the army.] the most holy bishop Ill., the venerable presbyter Ill., the regional notary Ill., the regional subdeacon Ill. likewise, Ill. and Ill., respectable citizens, and from the military rank the most eminent consul Ill. and the distinguished tribunes Ill. and Ill., to the feet of your exalted and God-preserved son, the exarch. We earnestly beg that, with God inspiring his mind, he may quickly adorn the see of the prince of the apostles with the complete ordination of the elect, especially in view of the various dangers that threaten and require aid for the province, while also bearing upon the imperial service. May there be, in the watchtower of the apostolic see, one who may rule the Church of Christ, wisely administer the flock of rational sheep, and pray without ceasing for the stability of the Roman Empire decreed by God, for the long-lasting health and prosperity of the times of the aforesaid distinguished lord exarch.

Therefore, we ask you, most holy and blessed Father, to labor with the bearers of these letters, your reverers and sons, and to intervene most diligently with the aforesaid lord exarch. Return to your patron, blessed Peter, the favor due to him, and press forward with all your strength so that, God commanding, the business of the desired ordination may be hastened. Thus, through the episcopal support of your fatherly blessedness, this apostolic Church may rejoice and exult, we may offer thanksgivings, and the charity of our designated lord, the elect and future apostolic pontiff, may be more abundantly extended toward your present holiness.

## TITLE VI. [Col. 0037C] Concerning the election of the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0037D] “To the judges.” Either the title should be emended so that it agrees with the superscription, and the singular *judici* should be read, “to the judge”; or it was written to several persons of equal rank; or, as I rather think, the letter was addressed to the entire assembly of judges, with only its presiding officer, namely the consul, being named.] to the judges of Ravenna

### Superscription

To the most eminent lord and our brother in Christ, Ill., consul; Ill., archpresbyter; and Ill., archdeacon; Ill., first of the notaries, serving the place of the holy apostolic see.

If benefits bestowed upon secular affairs are not undeserving of reciprocation, there is certainly no one who doubts that those things performed with pious intent are repaid with the reward of eternal life.

Since this is so, although we recognize from many documents the purpose of your illustrious eminence—to support with all your strength the interests of this holy apostolic Church of God, your spiritual mother—we have thought it appropriate, with fraternal affection, to exhort and ask you that, when the bearers of these letters, Ill. and Ill., whom we have sent [Col. 0038A] with decrees and earnest supplication for the speedy promotion of your spokesman and beloved lord, Ill., the archdeacon and elect, to the exalted and God-preserved lord exarch, meet with you, [Note: [Col. 0037D] “With decrees,” etc. It may be inferred that the decree of election was sent to the exarch and also to the emperor for subscription; this was a sign of approval.] you may join them and assist them in praying to God for the desired outcome with the aforesaid lord exarch. Thus, when those who have been sent return successfully, by God’s favor, and announce to our aforesaid elect lord the favorable goodness of your eminence, they may make his holiness not only more favorably disposed toward your eminence, but also ensure that the reward and recompense of your good service, from the prince of the apostles, to whose service you especially devote yourselves, may be multiplied in the present life and repaid in the heavenly kingdoms.

## TITLE VII. Concerning the election of the pontiff, to the apocrisiarius of Ravenna

### Superscription

To our most beloved brother Ill., presbyter and apocrisiarius; Ill., archpresbyter; Ill., archdeacon; and Ill., first of the notaries, serving the place of the holy apostolic see.

We know well that your most beloved fraternity learned some time ago of the death of Ill., the pope of holy memory. We inform you that, after his passing, on the third day, as is customary, we assembled—that is, the clergy, the *axiomati*, and the entire body of the army and citizens—and, with the grace of God supporting us, cast the votes of election upon the person of the lord Ill., the most holy archdeacon. Having drawn up his solemn decree, confirmed by the subscription of all, we sent it to the distinguished and God-preserved lord exarch through the bearers of these letters, Ill. and Ill. Your most beloved fraternity should meet with them and intervene with the aforesaid lord exarch to request the speedy advancement of the pontifical ordination, so that those who have been sent, with Christ as their companion, may return to us with the matter accomplished and, bringing favorable news, may courageously lift up the apostolic Church of Christ and the spirits of us all.

## TITLE VIII. [Note: [Col. 0037D] “The rite of ordaining.” This entire formula—if it is a formula and not rather a rubric—is contained in the same words in the most ancient Roman Order of the Corbie Library, as the Benedictine Dom Hugues Ménard testifies. It is also found, with a few additions, in the published Roman Order.] The rite of ordaining the pontiff.

[Note: [Col. 0038D] “They sing according to custom.” This custom, when the ordination of a bishop is being performed, is found in the Roman Ordo: “After the procession from the sacristy to the place of ordination, the Schola sings the Introit, as they call it: ‘The Lord has chosen you for himself as a great pontiff, and, opening his excellent treasury, he will make you abound in all good things.’ Psalm: ‘May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation; may the name of the God of Jacob protect you.’]

They sing according to custom. The elected candidate proceeds from the sacristy, [Note: [Col. 0038D] “With seven candle-bearers.” Some think that a mystery lies hidden in the number seven, although we learn from the Roman Ordo that there were seven candle-bearers, corresponding to the number of the city’s regions.] with seven candle-bearers, and comes [Col. 0039A] [Note: [Col. 0039B] “To the confession.” There, at the body of Saint Peter, the first profession of faith is made, and the entire ordination is performed—a prerogative of the supreme pontiff, according to a decree of Gregory the Great.] to the confession, and [Note: [Col. 0039B] “And after the litany.” That is, after the Introit has been sung by the Schola and the customary Kyrie eleison has been said, the pontiff’s ordination is performed. When it has been completed, the pontiff says “Glory to God in the highest” and finishes the rest of the Mass.] after the litany [Note: [Col. 0039B] “They ascend to the seat.” Not the seat proper to the supreme pontiff, but that of the presiding bishop, to whom the bishops of Albano and Porto, together with the presbyter, lead the man to be ordained in the customary manner.] the bishops and presbyters ascend to the seat together. Then the bishop of Albano gives [Note: [Col. 0039B] “The first prayer.” The Roman Ordo adds: “Over the pontiff: Almighty God, attend to our supplications,” and so forth—the prayers found in the ordination of a bishop, as well as the two other prayers that follow.] the first prayer; then the bishop of Porto gives [Note: [Col. 0039C] “The second prayer.” The Roman Ordo adds: “Be favorable, Lord, to our supplications,” and so forth.] the second prayer. [Note: [Col. 0039C] “Afterward the Gospels are brought forward.” In the ordination of a bishop, the Roman Ordo states that the Gospels are held over the head of the elected candidate not by deacons but by two bishops. Alcuin comments on this passage: “That two bishops hold the book of the Gospels over his head, while one pours a blessing over him and the other bishops present touch his head with their hands, is found neither in ancient nor in recent authority, nor yet in Roman tradition.”] Afterward the Gospels are brought forward, opened, and held over the elected candidate’s head by deacons. Then the [Note: [Col. 0039C] “Bishop of Ostia.” This was the privilege of the Church of Ostia before any bishops were counted among the cardinals. Now, however, since there are several bishops among them who surpass the others in age, they enjoy the right of consecrating the pontiff. Moreover, on the day when he ordained the pontiff, the bishop of Ostia wore the pallium, by decree of Pope Mark.] bishop of Ostia [Note: [Col. 0039D] “Consecrates him pontiff.” The Roman Ordo has: “God of all good things,” and so forth.
