In this prayer the following words must be added at the appropriate place: “And therefore, Lord, we ask that you grant this grace to your servant N., whom you have appointed bishop of the Apostolic See, primate of all the priests throughout the world, and teacher of the universal Church, and whom you have chosen for the ministry of the supreme priesthood.” A little later it adds: “Grant him the pontifical chair for governing the universal Church,” and so forth.] consecrates him as pontiff. [Note: [Col. 0039D] “After this,” and so forth. If the elected candidate is a deacon, he is consecrated a presbyter; for the words that are read here belong to that consecration. In the book of sacred rites by Augustine Patritius—incorrectly attributed to Christopher Marcello—that rite is described as follows: “When the prayers have been said, the pope, still without the mitre, approaches the altar; and, with the second of the deacons assisting the first, he takes the pallium from the altar and places it on the pontiff, saying: ‘Receive the pallium,’” and so forth.] After this the archdeacon attaches the pallium to him; then [Note: [Col. 0039D] “And he ascends to the seat.” The seat proper to the supreme pontiff, and the throne of the universal Church; from there he begins both the celebration of the Mass and, as an act of thanksgiving, the angelic hymn.] he ascends 25 to the seat and gives peace to all the priests, [Note: [Col. 0040B] “And he says ‘Glory.’” Innocent III, *Decretals*, title “Quod sicut,” *De Electione*, § “Super eo”: “Since only the Roman Pontiff, who is consecrated before the angelic hymn and afterward, once consecrated, begins and completes the solemn celebration of the Mass, is able to celebrate the orders on the day of his consecration,” and so forth.] and says, “Glory to God in the highest.”

## TITLE IX

[The document called an *indiculum* in this place is called a profession of faith by Ivo, Gratian, Antonius Augustinus, and Baronius, in the places cited in the preface. All of them report that they received this profession from the *Liber Diurnus*; yet none reproduces it in its pure form, as it appears here, but rather in an expanded and interpolated form adapted to the usage of the ninth century. It seemed worthwhile to present both versions in parallel (*παραλλήλως*), so that everyone might more easily observe the differences and understand with less difficulty what conclusions should be drawn from comparing them.]

[Note: [Col. 0040] The following two divisions of the texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### Indiculum [Note: [Col. 0040B] “Of the pontiff.” I think this refers to Conon, who was created after the death of Constantine Pogonatus, or to Sergius, who succeeded Conon; for both were elected while they were presbyters and after Constantine’s death—two features that appear in the *Indiculum*. Moreover, that this profession of faith was issued after the time of Gregory the Great is clear from the fact that Gregory made a very different profession, which John the Deacon calls a Symbol, at his own consecration.] of the pontiff

In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, etc. In the third indiction, in the third month, I, N., by the mercy of God, [Note: [Col. 0040C] “Presbyter.” The name “cardinal” had not yet been adopted to display the eminence of the dignity. It was adopted in the ninth century, as is clear from the comparison of the professions. Earlier, no one in the Church was called a cardinal except one assigned to the care of a particular holy place, as we shall explain in the notes to chapter three, where the incardination of a bishop will be discussed, and to chapter five, where the appointment of a cardinal presbyter will be treated.] presbyter and [Note: [Col. 0040C] “Elected.” He was professing the orthodox faith, like one of the faithful, before taking his seat on Peter’s chair to teach the Church. This profession seems to have been the beginning of the entire ceremony. It is shorter than the profession issued by one who had been ordained, for this was the profession of one making a declaration, whereas the other was that of one teaching.] elected, and by God’s grace destined to become the humble bishop of the Apostolic See, profess to you, blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, ( [Note: [Col. 0040C] “To whom he entrusted the keys,” and so forth. Unless attention is paid to it, this long parenthesis disturbs the sense, as does the following one, though it is shorter. In the other profession these words, which are enclosed within two brackets, must either be deleted or a missing verb restored—for example, *profiteor*—lest the rules of grammar be violated. For what is the infinitive *custodire*, “to guard,” doing after the conjunction *quod*, “that,” together with the subjunctive *non deseram*, “I will not abandon”?] to whom the Lord and Creator and Redeemer of all, Jesus Christ, entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven for binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven”) and to your holy Church, which today I have undertaken to govern with your protection.

This rectitude of the true faith—which, handed down by Christ its author through your successors and disciples, I have found in your holy Church and which has been brought down to my insignificance—I shall guard with all my strength, even to soul and blood, and, with your help, endure patiently the difficulties of the times.

Both concerning the mystery of the holy and undivided Trinity, which is one God, and concerning the dispensation accomplished according to the flesh of the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and concerning the other doctrines of the Church, as they have been commended in the [Note: [Col. 0041C] “Universal Councils.” Observe the order of the rules of faith established by the supreme pontiffs before the Church.] universal councils, in the constitutions of the most approved Apostolic Pontiffs, and in the writings of the Doctors of the Church, [Note: [Col. 0041C] “And likewise whatever,” and so forth. The reading of the other version seems preferable: “which,” and so forth.] I shall likewise preserve whatever pertains to the rectitude of your orthodox faith and ours, handed down by you.

[Note: [Col. 0041C] “The holy councils as well.” Gregory the Great, newly ordained, says nearly the same thing in his synodal letter to the other four patriarchs of the Church concerning the five universal councils held before his ordination.] I shall also preserve, without mutilation to a single jot, the holy universal councils: Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, Chalcedon, and the Second Council of Constantinople, which was celebrated in the time of the pious-emperor Justinian. [Note: [Col. 0041D] “To a single jot.” Thus the pontiffs promised, before their ordination, to preserve all the canons of the Fifth Synod without any mutilation, including canon eleven, which was issued against the writings of Theodoret. How, then, can it be proved that Theodoret had always been wholly free from error?]

And with them, with equal honor and veneration, I shall preserve the holy Sixth Council, which [Note: [Col. 0041D] “Recently.” That is, the last one held, and indeed five years earlier, if this profession belongs to Conon. For Conon was ordained on 20 October 686; Constantine Pogonatus, whose death is mentioned, died in September 685; and the Sixth Council began on 10 November 680 and ended on 16 September 681.] recently [Note: [Col. 0042C] “Under Constantine, of pious memory,” and so forth. The profession was therefore issued by an elected candidate after the death of Constantine Pogonatus—that is, after September 685—and thus either by Conon, who was the first elected after Constantine, or by Sergius, or by another elected not long afterward.] met under Constantine, the prince of pious memory, with my Apostolic predecessor Agatho, preserving it thoroughly and completely; and whatever they proclaimed I shall proclaim, and whatever they condemned I shall condemn with mouth and heart.

But I shall confirm more diligently and more energetically all the [Note: [Col. 0042D] “Decrees of my predecessors.” That is, concerning faith and morals, as the context itself shows. For matters belonging to discipline correspond to different times and consequently are changed from time to time.] decrees of my Apostolic predecessors, the pontiffs, and whatever they established synodally and approved; I shall preserve them without diminution and guard them in the stability of their force, exactly as they were established by them. Whatever, or whomever, they condemned or rejected by a judgment of similar authority, I shall condemn by a judgment of similar authority.

[Col. 0042C] [Note: [Col. 0042D] “The discipline and rite of the Church.” By both terms is meant the universal ordering of sacred matters, of which the subsequent professions speak—not, similarly, a form of living, judging, and so forth.] I shall preserve intact the discipline and rite of the Church, as I found them and as I found them handed down by my holy predecessors.

I shall preserve the possessions of the Church without diminution and take care that they be preserved without diminution.

[Col. 0043A] 30 [Note: [Col. 0043C] “Nothing concerning the tradition.” This does not mean the tradition that came from Christ or the Apostles, but that which originated with human beings and is nothing other than praiseworthy customs and ordinances. Ivo of Chartres quotes this entire *pericope* (*περικοπή*, “section”) in the following words: “In the book of the pontiffs, which is called the *Liber Diurnus*, the following is likewise contained concerning the profession of the Roman Pontiff: ‘I shall diminish or change nothing of the tradition which I have found handed down and preserved by my most approved predecessors, nor admit any novelty; but fervently, as their disciple and follower, I profess that with all the efforts of my mind I shall observe and venerate whatever I find canonically handed down.’ Blessed Gregory likewise,” and so forth. He mentions the same passage in Letter 57 to Bernard, abbot of the Monastery of the Greater. “For the supreme Pontiff himself,” he says, “before receiving the grace of consecration, professes that he will inviolably observe the customs of the Roman Church and the ordinances of his predecessors.” These two passages make it clear that the supreme pontiffs, even in Ivo’s time—about the year 1115—made the profession of faith placed first in the *Liber Diurnus* before their consecration.] I shall diminish or change nothing of the tradition which I have found preserved by my most approved predecessors, nor admit any novelty; but fervently, as truly their [Note: [Col. 0043D] “As their disciple and follower.” A form of expression customary in those times. Leo II writes to the emperor Constantine, “As their foot-servant,” and so forth. Agatho writes to the emperor Constantine: “My littleness desires to become the foot-servant of those predecessors.”] disciple and follower, I shall preserve and venerate with all my strength and efforts whatever has been handed down.

If anything should arise contrary to canonical discipline, I shall correct it; and I shall guard the sacred [Col. 0043B] canons and the constitutions of our pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0044C] “As divine and heavenly commands.” They were established through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, who governs the Church.] as divine and heavenly commands, knowing that I shall have to render to you a strict account in divine judgment of everything I profess, since by divine favor I occupy the place whose office I perform and, aided by your intercessions, fulfill its function.

If I should presume to do anything beyond these things, or permit anything to be presumed, may you be unfavorable toward me on that terrible day of divine judgment.

[Col. 0044A] Since I am placed in this corruptible life, I beg you also to grant assistance to me as I strive for these things and carefully seek to preserve them, so that I may appear blameless before the presence of the Judge of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, when he comes in terror to judge what has been committed, that he may make me share in the right-hand portion and a companion among your faithful disciples and successors.

32 This profession of mine, written as set forth above by Ill., the notary and scriniary, at my command, I have subscribed with my own hand and sincerely offered to you, blessed Peter, Apostle and Prince of all the Apostles, with a pure mind and devoted conscience, under bodily oath.

**Subscription.** I, the aforesaid unworthy presbyter Ill., elected by the grace of God bishop of this Apostolic See, the Roman Church, having made this profession of mine as stated above, have offered it bodily under oath to you, blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, with a pure mind and conscience.

[Note: [Col. 0040D] “The Pontifical Profession.” Although Cardinal Baronius refers it to the year 869, it was not used in the form in which it is reported until well into the tenth century. It mentions a cardinal bishop who, if elected supreme pontiff, would become pope, and this as though by a certain common right. Yet the right of a bishop to be advanced to the supreme pontificate was not acknowledged until long after the time of Formosus. Formosus was infamously accused of having transferred from the bishopric of Porto to the supreme see; he died near the beginning of the ninth century.] **The Pontifical Profession**

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. I, N., deacon or presbyter of the holy Roman Church, or cardinal bishop elected to become, by God’s grace, the humble minister of this holy Apostolic See, profess to you, blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, (to whom our Lord and Creator and Redeemer entrusted the keys of the heavenly kingdom for binding and loosing in heaven and on earth, saying: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven” [Matthew 16:19]) and to your holy Church, which today I undertake to govern with your protection, [Note: [Col. 0041D] “That as long as I remain in this wretched life.” Such an explicit promise not to abandon the Church, whatever the cause and however great the fear imposed, plainly belongs to the period when the supreme pontiffs were both installed and expelled by the more powerful tyrants of Italy.] that, as long as I remain in this wretched life, I shall not abandon it, leave it, deny it, or renounce it in any way; nor, for any reason or on account of any fear or danger, shall I relinquish it; nor shall I separate myself from it.

But I shall preserve with all my strength, even to blood, the rectitude of the true faith—which, handed down by Christ its author through you, your most blessed fellow apostle Paul, and your disciples and successors, I have found brought down to my insignificance in your holy Church.

Both concerning the mystery of the holy and undivided Trinity, which is one God, and concerning the dispensation accomplished according to the flesh of the only-begotten Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, and concerning the other doctrines of the Church, as they have been commended in the universal councils, in the constitutions of the Apostolic Pontiffs, and in the writings of the most approved Doctors of the Church—that is, whatever pertains to the rectitude of our orthodox faith and yours, handed down by you—I shall preserve.

I shall preserve without mutilation to a single jot the eight holy universal councils: Nicaea, [Col. 0042A] Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, Chalcedon, the Fifth and Sixth Councils, likewise of Constantinople, and the Seventh Council, likewise of Nicaea; [Note: [Col. 0042D] “The Eighth Council of Constantinople as well.” It was celebrated in 869, under Adrian II, concerning Ignatius and Photius. See Baronius under the year already mentioned, and Raderus in his notes on that council. From them one will learn how necessary it was in subsequent times, for the honor of orthodoxy, to accept this eighth ecumenical synod. I call it ecumenical because two other councils were held by schismatics who attempted to counterfeit the name of the Eighth Synod.] and the Eighth Council of Constantinople as well.

I shall hold them worthy of equal honor and veneration, follow and proclaim in every respect what they proclaimed and established, and condemn with mouth and heart whatever they condemned.

[Col. 0042B] More diligently and energetically, as long as I live, I shall confirm and preserve without diminution all the canonical decrees of our Apostolic predecessors, the pontiffs, whatever they established synodally and approved. I shall guard them in the stability of their force exactly as they were established by them; and whatever, or whomever, they condemned or rejected, I shall likewise condemn or reject.

[Col. 0042C] I shall preserve intact the discipline and rite as I have found them canonically handed down by my holy predecessors, for as long as life remains with me in this world.

I shall preserve the possessions of the Church without diminution, and shall not alienate them or give them in fief, census, or emphyteusis [Col. 0043A] in any manner or for any reason; and I shall take care that they be preserved without diminution.

I shall diminish or change nothing of the tradition which I have found canonically handed down and preserved by my most approved predecessors, nor admit any novelty; but fervently, as their disciple and follower, I shall preserve and venerate with all the efforts of my mind whatever I find canonically handed down.

If anything should arise contrary to canonical discipline, I shall correct it with the communication [Col. 0043B] [Note: [Col. 0044C] “Of my sons,” and so forth. It seems that *brothers* should be written instead, partly because pontiffs usually speak in this way and partly because at that time some bishops were counted among the cardinals.] of my sons, the cardinals of the holy Roman Church, with whose counsel, direction, and reminders I shall conduct and complete my ministry; or I shall patiently endure it, except in the case of serious offense against the faith and Christian religion, through the intercession of you and your most blessed [Note: [Col. 0044C] “Fellow apostle Paul.” This suggests a later period, since in earlier times mention was made only of Peter.] fellow apostle Paul. With God’s help, I shall guard the sacred canons and the decrees of the sacred pontiffs as divine and heavenly commands, knowing that I shall render to God and to you a strict account in divine judgment of all that I profess, do, or forget [Col. 0043C] as long as I live, since by divine favor, with you as my patron, I preside over this most holy see and fulfill its function through your intercessions.

[Col. 0044A] On that terrible day, be favorable toward me as I strive for these things and diligently seek to preserve them.

I also beg you to grant assistance to me, placed as I am in this corruptible life, so that I may appear blameless before the presence of the Judge of all, our Lord Jesus Christ, when he comes in terror to judge what has been committed, that he may make me share in the right-hand portion and a companion among your faithful disciples and successors.

I have subscribed this profession of mine, written by the notary [Col. 0044B] and scriniary of the holy Roman Church at my command, with my own hand, and I have sincerely offered it to you, Apostle Peter and Prince of all the Apostles, with a pure mind and devoted conscience, over your holy body and your altar. Done, etc.

[Note: [Col. 0044C] “The Second Profession.” It displays three features by which its author may plausibly be identified. First, the one who makes the profession was elected by concurrent votes. Second, the profession is highly learned and explains the Catholic faith handed down in the councils so clearly that scarcely any equal can be found in ancient monuments. Third, it was issued after the death of Constantine Pogonatus and before the *Liber Diurnus* was compiled. Constantine died toward the end of 685; the compilation of the *Liber Diurnus* dates to 715. From Constantine’s death until the compilation of the *Liber Diurnus*, thirty years elapsed, during which period seven pontiffs were established in the Apostolic See: Conon, Sergius I, John VI, John VII, Sisinnius, Constantine, and Gregory II. The first feature shows that the profession must belong to one of these seven pontiffs; the second excludes Conon and Sergius, whose elections were preceded by a violent schism; the third plausibly makes Gregory II its author. He was ordained after the death of Constantine Pogonatus, in 714, and by concurrent votes, and he is celebrated above the other four for his singular learning and eloquence. Moreover, the letters of Gregory, especially those written to the emperor Leo, contain certain characteristic expressions found here, as well as the same style and, as it were, the same spirit. This formula has two parts: one is a sermon, the other a profession of faith. In the first, the pontiff confesses that his virtue is unequal to so great a dignity, gives thanks to God and to the electors, and asks to be aided by prayers in fulfilling his office. On the very day of his accession Saint Leo delivered a sermon similar to this one, except that he did not append the profession of faith in the same way. Perhaps it had not yet become customary to issue a second profession besides the one made at the body of Saint Peter; or, as I rather think, the profession was omitted by the compiler of Leo’s sermons because the formula was common and did not differ from the Roman Apostolic Creed. But concerning Saint Leo’s sermon, see the appendix of notes.]

### Second Profession of Faith

[Col. 0044C]

[Note: [Col. 0044D] “Bishop Ill.” Since this profession of faith has the form both of a sermon, as its opening shows, and of a letter, as its inscription and conclusion indicate, it may have been delivered in the following manner, like the Paschal homilies of the Alexandrian pontiffs: namely, it was first issued as a sermon in the Roman Church and then transmitted in writing to all the Churches, at least those subject to the ordering of the Apostolic See. [Col. 0045C] Seven pontiffs in all were established in the Apostolic See during this period: Conon, Sergius I, John VI, John VII, Sisinnius, Constantine, and Gregory II. The first feature shows that the profession must belong to one of the seven. The second excludes Conon and Sergius, whose elections were preceded by a violent schism. The third makes Gregory II a plausible author. For he was ordained after the death of Constantine Pogonatus, in 714, and by concurrent votes, and he is celebrated above the other four for singular learning and eloquence. Add that Gregory’s letters, especially those written to the emperor Leo, contain certain characteristic expressions found here, together with the same style and almost the same spirit. This formula has two parts: one is a sermon, the other a profession of faith. In the first, the pontiff confesses that his virtue is unequal to so great a dignity, gives thanks to God and to the electors, and asks to be aided by prayers in fulfilling his office. On the very day of his accession Saint Leo delivered a sermon similar to this one, except that he did not append the profession of faith in the same way. Perhaps it had not yet become customary to issue a second profession besides the one made at the body of Saint Peter; or, as I rather think, the profession was omitted by the compiler of Leo’s sermons because the formula was common and did not differ from the Roman Apostolic Creed. Concerning Saint Leo’s sermon, however, see the appendix of notes.]

Ill., bishop of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church of the city of Rome, to the most reverend brothers and beloved sons, or to the entire people.

[Col. 0045A] Beloved, we reflect that we ought to receive the office of the Apostolic See, to which, through the providence and assistance of heavenly grace, we have attained, with as much astonishment and humility of heart as we recognize our littleness to be incomparably unequal to approaching it. For we do not perceive that this has been conferred upon us because of preceding merits, nor do we allow that it was entrusted to us because of skill in governing. Rather, the majesty of our most merciful God, mercifully inclined, consented that this should take place through your supplications, and impressed upon us the judgment of those who elected us and those who concurred in the election as a yoke of pious stewardship.

Therefore, dearest ones, assist the faint-heartedness that you see in us with frequent prayers; intercede for us before the mercy of God [Col. 0045B] with tears, so that the omnipotence of our God may strengthen the weakness that is in us, and that he who has deigned to redeem all his children with his precious blood may, being appeased, deign also to regard the duty of our frailty.

Although the disposition of the virtues is by no means in us, nevertheless the saving integrity of the Gospel and Apostolic faith, undefiled and perfect, by Christ’s favor is now in us and will remain so to the end.

Although, therefore, we can neither imitate nor worthily measure the merits of the pontifical predecessors, we nevertheless preserve their spiritual rules in our inmost being and rely upon the saving teachings of the holy Fathers. Girded with these as with an impregnable wall, [Col. 0045C] [Note: [Col. 0045D] “We trust,” and so forth. Such confidence was not presumption but trust in Christ. It led Leo to write to Leo the Isaurian, inflamed with zeal against the iconoclast, and, after recalling the holy Fathers as witnesses of Catholic truth and reproaching the emperor for despising so many witnesses, to say: “Hear our humility, Emperor, and desist. Follow the holy faith as you found and received it. These are not the doctrines of emperors but of pontiffs, since we possess the mind of Christ. One is the institution of ecclesiastical constitutions, and another the understanding of secular affairs,” and so forth.] we trust that we shall destroy all the weapons of the enemies of the faith [Col. 0046A] and overthrow, by their support and authority, minds that attack the truth.

Instructed according to our capacity by their traditions, with devoted mind we profess before the whole Church [Note: [Col. 0046C] “To the whole Church.” When Pelagius I wished to prove his faith to the whole Church, he wrote a letter to the entire people of God resembling the sermon here published, as can be established by comparing the two.] and, with God as witness of consciences, we declare that we shall do whatever accords with the stability of the Christian religion and the rectitude of the Catholic faith—something which the eager expectation of the faithful awaits from us and [Note: [Col. 0046C] “The gaze signifies that it is listening.” Hence it is clear that, although this profession of faith appears to have the form of a letter, it was nevertheless delivered in the Church; for these words can refer only to listeners who, by their present nod, show their desire.] which the gaze of those listening indicates.

Let your love therefore know and trust that we shall proclaim, hold, defend, and proclaim in the future the faith of Christ, which the Apostles handed down, the disciples of the Apostles taught, and their Apostolic successors and our most approved predecessors [Note: [Col. 0046D] “Immutably,” and so forth. It should be noted that this is said first after the death of Honorius, then in the sermon by which the Sixth Synod is received, and finally in the passage where Honorius is expressly said to have “provided support for the wicked assertions of heretics.” Thus that great pontiff is not branded as a Monothelite, as some ineptly proclaim, but as a supporter of the Monothelites—not a supporter in the sense of one who aided them, but one who did not restrain them as he ought to have done; that is, not one who used approval, but one who used dissimulation and imprudent accommodation.] have preserved immutably [Col. 0046B] and defended.

For we shall inviolably guard the norm of this Apostolic tradition, which the venerable council of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, assembled at Nicaea under the great emperor Constantine, formulated in the Creed by the revelation of God’s grace; which proclaimed the Son consubstantial with the Father; which, confirming that the Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, is true God, expelled Arius, who blasphemed the deity, together with his associates, and condemned them as ministers of the devil by an eternal anathema.

Next, the equally holy Council of Constantinople, composed of one hundred and fifty Fathers, assembling in the imperial city under Theodosius the Elder, of pious memory, [Note: [Col. 0046D] “Which was thought to be lacking in the Creed.” The Nicene Fathers said only this concerning the Holy Spirit: “And in the Holy Spirit.” Something more had to be expounded against Macedonius and Apollinaris, who agreed with Macedonius. The Arians reproached the Catholics for this exposition as though it were an innovation and an addition to the faith rather than a mere explanation, as appears in Theodoret’s first dialogue against the Macedonians.] explained what was thought to be lacking in the Creed [Col. 0046C] and, with the grace of the Holy Spirit illuminating it, added that the Holy Spirit is God, to be worshiped together with the Father and the Son as consubstantial. Thus it struck down Macedonius, the rebel against the Holy Spirit, and Apollinaris with his sacrilegious accomplices, under the sentence of perpetual anathema.

Through these two sacred councils [Note: [Col. 0047C] “The holy and inseparable Trinity,” and so forth. Nowhere is a fuller or clearer exposition of the mystery of the Trinity to be found; hence Anastasius the Librarian rightly called our Gregory learned in divine Scripture and eloquent in speech.] we know and have learned openly to proclaim that the holy and inseparable Trinity is one God and that the substance of the Trinity is one; and that there is a Trinity in unity and unity in Trinity. Thus we confess one God because of the unity of essence, and we teach an inseparable Trinity because of the distinction of substances and persons: the Son is eternally born from the Father; the Holy Spirit is affirmed to proceed from the Father; the Son of God is said to receive him from what is his own; and he makes clear that the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father in his own name. Ascending into heaven, he sends the Paraclete to the disciples as he had promised, and, breathing upon the disciples, he proclaims him to proceed from himself. [Note: [Col. 0047C] “Proceeding from himself.” What is expressed less clearly in this profession is explained more clearly in the one that follows: “The Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son.” These words occur in the Symbol of Gregory the Great, though not in the faith of Pelagius. In both professions of the *Liber Diurnus*, however, the tradition is contained which the supreme pontiffs of the seventh century taught had been “immutably preserved and defended by the Apostolic and most approved predecessors.” In the Roman Ordo, in the interrogation of the bishop to be ordained, we read: “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit, full, perfect, and true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son,” and so forth. The same appears in the sermon on faith that follows the interrogation in the same Ordo.] proceeding from himself.

From this, therefore, we are vividly instructed both to proclaim the one essence of divinity and to proclaim a perfect Trinity because of the unconfused properties of the subsistences. Just as the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit truly have one divinity, so they have one glory, dominion, majesty, virtue, and power; likewise, they have one natural will and one operation.

To these two universal and venerable Councils there was added a Third General Council of two hundred holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0047D] Of two hundred. Marius Mercator counts two hundred and seventy-four, and has Saint Cyril as his supporter, who writes that there were more than two hundred. The complete number has therefore been given, as is customary, with the additions omitted.]—a Council which was held under Theodosius Augustus, of revered memory [Note: [Col. 0047D] Theodosius Augustus. He calls him Augustus in order to distinguish him from the Great, that is, the younger from the elder, the grandson from the grandfather.]—yet, under the authority of Coelestine, president of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0047D] Yet under the authority of Coelestine, etc. Coelestine did not summon the Council, but approved its convocation: it was summoned by the Emperor Theodosius, who had been deceived by Nestorius’s schemes, since Nestorius wished to evade the judgment of the Apostolic See. Although Coelestine did not know that the Council had been summoned, as is clear from Nestorius’s letters to him, he may nevertheless be said to have approved it, partly by the letters sent to Theodosius and the Synod, and partly by sending three legates: the bishops Arcadius and Projectus, and the presbyter Philip.]—and which first assembled at the city of Ephesus with blessed Cyril, bishop of the Alexandrian Church. At that Council the union of the natures joined in Christ—that is, the connection, according to subsistence, of divinity and humanity in Christ—was salutarily proclaimed; and the profane “man-worshipper” [Note: [Col. 0048C] Man-worshipper. Cyril repeatedly makes the same charge against Nestorius.] Nestorius, hostile to the Lord’s dispensation, since he had separated and disjoined God from man by separating the mystery of the Incarnation, which must be adored, and had attacked the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, with blasphemous words, was cast down with his associates by twelve venerable chapters, under a perpetual condemnation of multiple anathemas [Note: [Col. 0048C] By twelve chapters, etc. Observe the following concerning them. I. They were issued by order of Pope Coelestine by Saint Cyril at a Synod in Egypt, and sent by four bishops to Constantinople to Nestorius, together with letters from the Roman and Egyptian Synods, by which he was ordered to subscribe to them within ten days unless he wished to be deposed. II. They were attacked through the machinations—or rather the entreaties—of Nestorius by Andrew of Samosata and Theodoret of Cyrus. III. They were later reread and approved at the Council of Ephesus. IV. After the time of Dionysius Exiguus they were accepted as the definition of the Synod of Ephesus. V. Although Cyril’s faith was under discussion, they were read neither at Chalcedon nor at the Fifth Council nor at any subsequent council; only two other letters were read, namely, the second to Nestorius and the peace-making letter to John of Antioch.], because he obstinately refused to confess truthfully that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:12)—that is, that God the Word, who is also the Son of God, became man for us [Note: [Col. 0048D] Remaining what he was, etc. This Catholic doctrine is maliciously attacked by that Nestorian, Eutherius, bishop of Tyana. After he had been deposed by the Council of Maximian, he could not be restored to his see, although Paul of Emesa strove with all his strength to accomplish this while conducting the negotiations for peace between the Churches. The Sermons on Various Propositions, published among the works of Saint Athanasius in volume II, should be attributed to this Eutherius, as we have shown in the Appendix to the Works of Theodoret; for M. Mercator demonstrates the falsity of the common opinion that attributes them either to Athanasius or to Maximus the Monk.]—remaining what he was, he became what he was not; and because, being flesh and at the same time the Word’s flesh animated by a rational soul, it had this very subsistence in the Word.

Therefore, in order to explain such rules concerning the incarnation of God the Word, the Fourth Holy Council also assembled at Chalcedon: six hundred and thirty holy Fathers, under the Emperor Marcian, of revered memory. Pope Leo of the Apostolic See presided through his legates and representatives. By God’s grace revealing the truth, the Fathers, strengthened by his venerable Tome [Note: [Col. 0048D] Venerable Tome. The dogmatic letter to Flavian against the errors of the deranged Eutyches.], solemnly promulgated as their judgment [the doctrine] that, from two natures and in two natures, or substances—that is, divinity and humanity—there is one and the same Son of God, the Lord Jesus Christ; and that the distinction of the natures was in no way destroyed, but rather that, with the property of each preserved, both natures came together into one person and subsistence [Col. 0048C]. For, from the things in which we truly believe him to subsist [Col. 0049A], in those same things we likewise proclaim that he both exists and is contemplated, without confusion, inseparably, and indivisibly. Dioscorus the blasphemer and Eutyches the deranged, who refused to submit to these teachings, were struck down by the just sentence of anathema, together with their supporters [Note: [Col. 0049B] With his supporters. The manuscript continued: “With these, the letter called that of Ibas to Maris the Persian, and the writings of Theodoret against the most blessed Cyril, were also cast out with condemnation.” But this passage was restored to its proper place, from which it had been displaced through the carelessness of scribes: it belongs where mention is made of the Fifth Council.].

These four holy and universal Councils were followed by the venerable Fifth Holy Council. It was assembled near Constantinople under Justinian, of pious memory. By its salutary deliberation, our Lord Jesus Christ was truly proclaimed to be one of the Holy Trinity [Note: [Col. 0049C] One of the Holy Trinity. These words refer to canon 4 of the Fifth Synod: “If anyone does not confess that the union of God the Word with flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul was made according to composition, or according to subsistence, as the holy Fathers taught, and therefore that his one subsistence is composite—the one who is our Lord Jesus Christ, one of the Holy Trinity—let him be anathema.”]. Those who confused or divided the mystery of his sacred incarnation were struck down by the spiritual sword of this expression.

In this Council Origen, together with his impious disciples and followers Didymus and Evagrius, and those who pursued the Creator of all things, God, and all his rational creation in pagan fables, were consigned to eternal condemnation [Note: [Col. 0049C] Origen, etc. See the Dissertation on the Fifth Council appended to the Breviary of Liberatus, edited by us.].

In it Theodorus of Mopsuestia, the author of Nestorius’s teaching, and likewise Diodorus, together with all the disciples of that detestable division, who were also called Semi-Nestorians, were cast out of the Church of God under the eternal sentence of anathema. Together with these, the letter called that of Ibas to Maris the Persian, and the writings of Theodoret against the most blessed Cyril, were also cast out with condemnation [Col. 0050A].

In this Council Severus the Acephalite, together with Peter and Zoara and the rest of the partners and followers of their impious confusion, were struck down by perpetual condemnation, as were all who refused to acknowledge, from two natures and in two natures or substances, with their properties, one and the same Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Although he is God, consubstantial with the Father and coeternal with him, he descended from heaven for us and for our salvation and was incarnate from the Holy Spirit—that is, by the operation of the Holy Spirit the virgin conceived the Son of God—in flesh possessing a rational and intellectual soul. In this flesh he was crucified, died, and on the third day, as he willed, rose from the dead, destroying the dominion of our death. In this flesh, which he assumed from us without sin alone, he sits at the right hand of the Father, and in it he will come to judge the living and the dead; his kingdom will have no end [Note: [Col. 0049C] Although he is God, etc. This passage corresponds to canon 2 of the Lateran Council under Martin I. It should be observed that this confession and the one that follows, as well as the confession issued by the bishop, were taken from the Fifth and Sixth Synods and from Agatho’s letter.].

Among these venerable universal Councils we also proclaim the holy Sixth Universal Council, consisting of one hundred and seventy-five venerable bishops. By God’s favor, and by his merciful fulfillment of the desire of our lord Constantine, the great prince of revered memory [Note: [Col. 0049D] Of pious memory. This profession was therefore issued after the death of Constantine Pogonatus.], it was celebrated in the royal city while he presided [Note: [Col. 0049D] While he presided. That is, while occupying and directing the principal place, like a supreme kind of judge, as Gregory II writes that it was fitting for the Emperor to do in his letters to Leo the Isaurian. The old Breviary of the Roman Church reads “while he was resident”; the new one, “while he was present.” Albert Pighius, otherwise a man deserving well of the Church, maintained that the Sixth Synod was merely a political assembly presided over by the Emperor Constantine. But he is excellently refuted by the writers on controversies of faith, so that there is no need for us to revive a conflict long since settled.]. Pope Agatho, of Apostolic memory, presided through his legates and representatives [Note: [Col. 0050C] Through his legates and representatives. Saint Agatho writes thus to the Emperor Constantine concerning them: “In accordance with the most pious command of Your Clemency, out of the obedience we owed, not out of confidence in their knowledge, we send these fellow servants of ours, our most reverend brothers the bishops Abundantius, John, and John; our dearest sons the presbyters Theodore and George, together with our dearest son John the deacon and Constantine the subdeacon of this holy spiritual mother, the Apostolic See; and also Theodore, presbyter and legate of the holy Church of Ravenna, and the religious servants of God, the monks, etc.” Five observations should be made concerning this passage. I. The presbyters Theodore and George and the deacon John represented Pope Agatho; Abundantius and the two Johns served as legates of the Western Council. Hence the former are listed before the patriarchs, the latter after them. Thus the acts read: “When the holy and universal Synod had assembled, etc.”, namely, with Theodore and George, venerable presbyters, and John, venerable deacon, acting in the place of Agatho, the most holy and most blessed Archbishop of ancient Rome; with George, venerable and most holy Archbishop of great Constantinople, New Rome; with Peter, priest beloved of God and monk, occupying the place of the see of the great city of Alexandria; with Macarius, venerable Archbishop of Theopolis, Antioch; with George, religious presbyter and monk; with the apocrisarius Theodore, venerable representative of the see of Jerusalem; with John, bishop of Porto; Abundantius, bishop of the city of Paternus; and John, bishop of the city of Rhegium, representing one hundred and twenty-five venerable bishops of the holy Council of ancient Rome.” II. It is thereby clear from which cities Abundantius and the two Johns were bishops; but from which Churches Theodore and George were cardinal presbyters, and to which deaconry John belonged, is unknown. John had succeeded Benedict II five years earlier, after Leo II had succeeded Agatho and Benedict had succeeded Leo. III. The monks mentioned by the pope are listed in the acts. They were: “Theophanius, presbyter and venerable abbot of the monastery in Sicily called at Baiae; George, presbyter and monk of the monastery of Renatus, situated in ancient Rome; Conon and Stephen, presbyters and monks of the monastery called the House of Arsicia, likewise situated in elder Rome.” IV. Constantine the subdeacon is not mentioned in the acts, because in Councils there was no place for anyone except bishops, presbyters, and deacons. V. Of those who were sent, three later held the pontificate: John, Conon, and Constantine, although I am somewhat uncertain about the monk Conon. Theodore twice became the cause of schism: once when Conon was elected, and again when Sergius was elected.], and, solemnly embracing his venerable Tome [Col. 0051A], they demonstrated most clearly that those who were striving to pollute the spotless Church of God with a new and heretical doctrine had erred; and, together with the authors and supporters of their error [Note: [Col. 0051C] With the authors and supporters. Also, if one may speak in this way, with the “negatives,” who remain silent when they ought to cry out and restrain themselves through cowardly prudence when iniquity must be resisted at God’s command. Innocent I: “I do not think there is much difference between the disposition of one who connives and the favor of one who consents.” And afterward: “Care must be taken lest, by permitting wolves, we appear to be hirelings rather than shepherds.” Letter to the Council of Milevis. Coelestine I to the bishops of Gaul: “In such cases silence is not free from suspicion, since truth would confront the matter if falsehood were displeasing; rightly, therefore, the matter concerns us if we favor error by our silence.”], they condemned them by perpetual anathema.

They rightly and truthfully decreed that, just as we acknowledge two natures of our one Lord Jesus Christ, namely divinity and humanity, and know that he has two births—one from the Father, from eternity, and one from the mother, from whom humanity came to him, in time—so also we confess two substances of one and the same person, united according to subsistence, from which and in which the same Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, is proclaimed and believed. For he is wholly God and wholly became man; remaining entire in what is his own [Col. 0051B], he also appeared perfect in what is ours [Col. 0052A], without sin alone, because he had come to save the whole human being in himself. They likewise decreed, according to the teaching of the holy Fathers, that he possesses two natural wills and two natural operations.

But the authors of the new heretical doctrine—Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0051C] Authors of the new doctrine, etc. By “doctrine” he means the doctrine of one will in Christ, which, although in reality it did not differ from the Eutychian doctrine, disguised itself under a different appearance.]—together with Honorius, who supplied encouragement to their corrupt assertions [Note: [Col. 0051D] Together with Honorius. Hadrian II says concerning Honorius in the Roman Synod reported in the Eighth General Council, act 7: “This presumption is intolerable, and the ears of our hearts cannot bear it. Who among you has ever heard such a thing? Or who, even by reading, has encountered the enormity of such temerity? We read that the Roman Pontiff has judged all the prelates of the Churches; but we do not read that anyone has judged him. Although anathema was pronounced against Honorius after his death by the Easterners, it must nevertheless be understood that he had been accused of heresy, on account of which alone it is lawful for inferiors to resist the conduct of their superiors or freely reject corrupt opinions. Yet even there, no patriarch or other prelate was permitted to pronounce judgment against him unless the authority of the Pontiff of that first See had preceded it.” This is how Anastasius’s translation reads; the Greek text differs somewhat. It should be observed that Hadrian II began his pontificate in the year 867 and therefore issued this very profession of faith when he first took his seat. It should likewise be observed that all the usual disputes on this matter can be resolved from Hadrian’s words: who could assert that the pope was either ignorant of so serious a matter or had pronounced judgment rashly?]—and likewise Theodore of Pharan and Cyrus of Alexandria, together with their imitators, as well as those who stubbornly defended heretical doctrines against the truth declared and proclaimed synodally [Col. 0052A]—were condemned.

They also bound the most wicked and God-hated Macarius [Note: [Col. 0052B] Macarius. The bishop of Antioch, against whom the Sixth Synod cried out in act 8: “Anathema to the new Dioscorus! Let such a man be deposed. Cast out the new Dioscorus! Evil days to the new Apollinarius! Let him rightly be removed from the bishop.”], together with his disciple and teacher of impiety, Stephen [Note: [Col. 0052B] Stephen. He was a monk and presbyter of Antioch, Macarius’s disciple and syncellus, obstinate in error. Against him the Synod shouted in act 9: “Cast out the heretic! Evil days to the new Eutyches! Evil days to the new Apollinarius! Cast out the heretic!” And Stephen, Macarius’s disciple, was driven out and expelled. He himself later had a disciple named Tyrannus Bardanes, as appears in the concluding speech of Agatho the Deacon.], and Polychronius, that deranged old man [Note: [Col. 0052C] And Polychronius, the deranged old man. He is called deranged not only because of the name, which signifies a man of advanced age, but also because of his age: he was then more than eighty. He is called an old man, and indeed a deranged one, for in his letter to the Emperor he relates visions resembling delirious fantasies and dreams.], the “new Simon” [Note: [Col. 0052C] The new Simon. Hence correct the old Roman Breviary, in the feast of Saint Leo II, at the fourth lesson, where it reads “Polychronius, Novus, and Simon,” as though these were three men rather than three expressions referring to one. He was called by the people the new Simon, namely, the Magus, after the imposture was exposed by which he attempted, like that ancient Simon Magus, to prove his faith by a miracle; but each man was deceived by his hope. Simon did not fly unharmed, as he had promised in order to attest his divinity; nor did Polychronius raise the dead man, which he had pledged as testimony to his faith. The matter is related in act 16 of the Sixth Synod: “When the most glorious judges and the holy Council had gone out, and a great crowd had gathered in the atrium of the public bath called Zeuxippus, a dead man was brought before the most glorious judges, those who belonged to the holy Council, and the numerous Christ-loving people gathered there, laid out in a silver funeral bier. Polychronius, standing over him, placed upon the dead man a written statement of his faith and, continuing for many hours and whispering over him, was unable to accomplish any of the things he had foolishly and blasphemously promised. Then Polychronius declared that he could in no way raise the dead man. The people who were present therefore cried out, saying: ‘Anathema to the new Simon! Anathema to Polychronius, the deceiver of the people!’” Macarius, Stephen, and Polychronius were sent by the Emperor to Rome to Leo II; because they obstinately retained their error, they were thrust into monasteries and died unrepentant.], together with all their heretical writings and followers [Col. 0053A], under the bond of perpetual anathema. They wickedly asserted one will and one operation in Christ, which they could demonstrate to be neither divine nor human, neither uncreated nor created, but only something confused and blended. Just as the impious Eutyches did concerning the natures, so they tried, according to the deceits of the heretics, to defend confusion concerning Christ’s natural wills and operations.

They also inflicted the same anathema upon those who dared to speak of one and two wills and operations together in Christ, or of neither one nor two; and upon those who attempted or attempt to confuse or extinguish the properties of Christ’s natures.

Therefore, whoever or whatever the six holy universal Councils rejected, we too strike with a similar condemnation of anathema,

together with the aforesaid heretics: Sabellius, Paul of Samosata, Maris the Persian [Note: [Col. 0053C] Maris the Persian. In the Lateran Synod under Martin I, canon 18, the name is Theodulus the Persian. I think he is the same as Theodulus, the commentator’s name, that is, the disciple of Theodorus of Mopsuestia, whom Hebed-Jesu mentions in his catalogue.], Montanus, Donatus, Eunomius, Novatian, Sabbatius, Acacius, Anthimus, Julian of Halicarnassus, Theodosius, Gaianus, Priscillian, Pelagius, Caelestius, and Julian their disciple [Note: [Col. 0053C] Julian, etc. The bishop of Eclanum, who learned the heresy from Caelestius, whom Pelagius had corrupted; subsequently, from being a disciple he became the teacher of the whole faction. Marius Mercator reports about him what no one else relates distinctly. See our notes on the first part of Marius Mercator’s Works and the dissertation on the first authors and defenders of the Pelagian heresy.], and, together with them, all heretics and their followers, we curse and condemn.

But whoever or whatever the same six holy Councils received as companions of the true faith, we receive, and with the same reverence we venerate them in word and heart.

Moreover, with Christ’s assent, we promise your charity that everything which the aforementioned Apostolic Pontiffs, our predecessors in this Apostolic See, established synodally, we shall preserve with the whole devotion and purity of our mind; and that, with their support, we shall keep pace before men in defending the purity of the true faith.

Therefore we subject to the prohibition of a strict anathema anyone—whether ourselves or another—who at any time presumes to introduce anything new against this evangelical tradition and the integrity of the orthodox faith and the Christian religion; or who attempts to alter or remove anything from the integrity of our faith; or who, with sacrilegious audacity, consents to those presuming such things.

So that the sincerity of our perfect faith might shine more clearly before your charity, we have deposited this page of our profession, written by the illustrious notary and bearing our own subscription, after it was reread before everyone, at the confession of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, as though he himself were testifying to the purity of our conscience—he to whom the Savior and Lord of all entrusted the keys of binding and loosing on earth and in heaven.

I, Illustrious, by the grace of God bishop of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church of the city of Rome, have subscribed this profession of right and orthodox faith, as it is written above, and have offered it to you, blessed Apostle Peter, to be confirmed at your body.

[Note: [Col. 0053D] Ill. Bishop, etc. This profession of faith itself seems to state by whom and at what time it was first issued; for it has four marks by which both matters may be determined. I. It mentions the Sixth Synod, whose definition it receives. II. The name of the Emperor Constantine is invoked, who convened the Synod. III. The Emperor’s name is not accompanied by the phrase customarily added after death—and not omitted in the other two—“of pious memory,” but rather by the phrase “crowned by God.” IV. Its opening is drawn from an exhortation to concord and mutual forgiveness of injuries. It is apparent from the first and second marks that this faith was issued after the conclusion of the Sixth Synod; from the third, however, that it was not issued after Constantine’s death, since otherwise he would have been called “of pious memory”; and finally, from the last, that it was issued after dissensions had arisen in the election of some Pontiff. Now the Sixth Synod was concluded on 16 September 681. Constantine died in September 685, four years after the Synod’s conclusion. During this interval exactly three supreme Pontiffs were created: Leo II, Benedict II, and John V. Of these three, Benedict and John are reported to have been elected immediately; Leo, however, was not, but succeeded Agatho after the see had long been vacant. Nor is there any doubt that the chief cause of the vacancy was the struggle of minds divided over electing a Pontiff. It is therefore necessary to acknowledge that this profession was issued by Leo II in 682, since Agatho died—or at least was buried—on 10 January 681, and, as Baronius reports from Anastasius, the see was vacant for one year, seven months, and seven days.]

## Third Profession of Faith, after ordination

I, Illustrious, bishop of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church of the city of Rome, send greetings in the Lord to my most beloved and sweetest sons [Note: [Col. 0054C] Most beloved and sweetest sons. The fact that he does not mention brothers, but only sons, indicates that this profession of faith was directed to the whole people of God, whereas previously it had been issued at Rome before the people. Thus Pelagius I, when he sent his faith to the people of the universal Church, mentioned only sons, not brothers. Nor is there any difficulty in the fact that the words concerning charity and the forgiveness of offenses suit the Roman people: it was customary for a sermon delivered before an assembly to be sent from the Church to all peoples whenever the whole world was to be instructed about some important matter. See the paschal homilies of Saint Cyril of Alexandria on this subject.].

The festive joy of this day invites us, my beloved, to exhort your brotherly concord in Christ in a humble voice. May this eager gathering of your devotion advance not toward human favor but toward the praise of the almighty Creator, who, while abundantly heaping vow upon vow, will deign to enlarge the joys of our humility with heavenly joys.

For who, as the Prophet says, will speak of the Lord’s mighty acts, or who will be able to make heard all his praises (Psalm 105:2)? Or who could worthily recount his great and wondrous works (Ecclesiasticus 17:8)? For it is not my merits, dearest ones, which are nothing, but the prayers of your Christianity before the Most High that have obtained this: you see me, though unworthy, rejoicing from above, so that the Almighty might raise the needy from the earth and lift the poor from the dung heap (Psalm 113:7), grant the privilege of the priesthood, and appoint me steward of his household.

Therefore, dearest ones, the distinguished solemnity of this day has compelled me, through this page of my mediocrity [Note: [Col. 0055C] Page. From this it is clear that this was not merely a sermon spoken aloud, but also a letter that was afterward to be sent in writing.], to discharge a twofold duty toward your charity, pleasing to God [Note: [Col. 0055C] To discharge the office. It is established by several testimonies and examples of the Roman Pontiffs themselves that, immediately after ascending the Apostolic See, they customarily informed the whole Church about their ordination and faith. Gelasius, Letter 2, in the year 492, to Laurentius of Lignidum: “Since it is the custom of the Roman Church for a newly appointed priest to extend the form of his faith to the holy Churches, I have endeavored to recall it here in a very brief summary, so that the reader may perceive without weariness, in this letter, according to the decrees of the Fathers, the faith according to which one ought to live. Therefore we confess, etc.”].

And first of all, it is fitting for me, with paternal affection, to ask my dear children to pray suitably to Christ the Lord for the poverty of my weakness, so that, through the intercession of his Apostles, he may grant me to fulfill without blame this office of piety which, by the Lord’s generosity and through your prayers, I have received. Thus may I not be condemned by the punishment of presumption because of the height of the episcopate, but may I deserve, on the day of the Lord’s coming, together with the souls entrusted to me by him, to receive an unfading crown of glory [Note: [Col. 0055D] And first of all, etc. Following the custom of his predecessors, he asks that he be assisted by prayers. Thus Leo the Great in a sermon delivered on the very day of his elevation; Pelagius I in a letter to the whole people of God; Gregory the Great in a synodal letter to the patriarchs of the Eastern Church; and others, from whom writings concerning their promotion have reached us. Hilary too, writing about the beginning of his ordination, in Letter 5 to Leontius of Arles, after asking that all the bishops throughout the province be informed about the Apostolic See entrusted to him, adds: “so that, just as they join in the joys of exultation, they may also join the prayers of their supplications for the good of the universal Church.”].

Next, my beloved, I have another and very extensive exhortation of charity to offer to you for your sake [Note: [Col. 0056C] A very extensive exhortation to charity. The Pontiff urges clergy and people to lay aside the enmities which they had fiercely conceived and nourished during the disagreement over the election, for nearly twenty months, and had not yet entirely abandoned, although they had agreed to Leo’s election.], so that, if any one of you has had or still has a grievance against another, through the intervention of my entreaty—because of him, namely, who is the author of peace and charity—you may release one another from it in your hearts. “Forgiving one another” (Colossians 3:13), according to the apostolic exhortation, “as God in Christ forgave you,” so that, God forbid, we may not be deceived by any stratagem of Satan, the enemy and author of peace-destroying discord (2 Corinthians 2:11).

Let enmities and dissensions, I ask, come to an end, so that the tinder of hatred may not reign in your chaste body, but peace and charity, which God loves; so that you may be obedient children of your Father who is in heaven (Matthew 5:45). For it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (ibid., verse 9). And again: “Pursue peace and holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews 12:24). “Forgive,” the Lord says in the Gospel, “and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). “By this,” he says, “everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you preserve love for one another” (John 13:35), so that the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, may guard your hearts and minds in Christ Jesus our Lord (Philippians 4:7).

Just as the Most High has today multiplied your joy through the promotion of my insignificance [Note: [Col. 0056D] Today. The sermon was therefore delivered at Rome on the very day of his elevation and afterward sent in writing to the provinces, or at least to those subject to the Pontiff’s ordination.], so may the joy of my mind be more abundantly multiplied through the concord of your unanimity and peace, so that with fitting common assent we may be able, with harmonious melody and inward agreement of mind, to cry out gladly with the holy angels, before the venerable body of the Prince of the Apostles: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14) [Note: [Col. 0056D] Hymn of glory. The hymn called that of Ambrose and Augustine was not yet sung at Rome in solemn thanksgiving. I say at Rome, for it may be inferred with some clarity that it had previously been sung in Gaul.].

With these matters prefaced, my beloved, I hasten to address you with the speech of my humility concerning that singular remedy of our hope. I perceive before my eyes your desire that I be continually attentive and concerned, through the breath of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0056C]; and in the profession of my humility I willingly undertake to bring forth for your edification those things which your devotion, devoted with fervor to the Catholic and orthodox faith and the Christian religion, longs to hear suitably through the ministry of my tongue [Note: [Col. 0056D] Address. I have corrected a passage miserably corrupted. It originally read: “I took the greatest care concerning the place, to which your desire, through the affection of the Holy Spirit, was continually anxious and attentive, furnished by him with spotless things, those which my humility, etc.”].

Therefore, since by God’s grace we are disciples of Christian and evangelical teaching, imitators of the paternal tradition, and followers of the orthodox faith, just as we believe in our heart unto righteousness (Romans 10:10), so it is fitting for us, for the edification of your salvation, to profess openly, with a devoted mind, properly and truthfully, before the whole Church [Note: [Col. 0057C] Before the whole Church. Not merely the Roman Church, but the whole metropolitan Church, or the universal Church spread throughout the world. Hence I conclude that the sermon was not delivered only to the Romans, but sent to all the faithful of the world, or at least to all the Churches of the West, or to those subject to the Apostolic ordination.], with a free voice, the things which we have undertaken to preach through the holy Apostles and the bishops of this Apostolic See.

48 [Note: [Col. 0057D] “We believe,” etc. If this faith is compared with that portion of Agatho’s second letter to the Emperor Constantine that contains an exposition of Catholic doctrine, the agreement of one with the other will immediately be seen to be so great that this appears to have been taken from that one, if not in wording, at least in meaning. Nor should it trouble you that in Agatho’s letter the Holy Spirit is said to proceed from the Father, and *Filioque* is not added, whereas it is read in this faith: for the Latins complained at the Council of Florence that this had been deleted by the Greeks when they translated the Latin letter into Greek.]

We believe in one God, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, an inseparable Trinity: namely, the Father, from whom all things are; the Son, through whom all things are; the Holy Spirit, in whom all things are. The Father is unbegotten, but the Son is the only-begotten from the Father; [Note: [Col. 0057D] “But the Holy Spirit,” etc. In the Roman *Ordo*, as has already been stated, the bishop to be ordained is questioned concerning the faith of the Holy Spirit in this manner: “Do you also believe in the Holy Spirit, full, perfect, and true God, proceeding from the Father and the Son, etc.”] but the Holy Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son. We believe in one essence of the Holy Trinity, one power, one dominion, one natural will, and one operation. We have been baptized in the name of the Trinity, and we faithfully proclaim that it must be believed.

We therefore believe that one of the Holy Trinity—that is, God the Word, who was born from the Father before all ages—is the same one who descended in the last times, was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and from the blessed ever-virgin Mary, the Mother of God, and became man: consubstantial with the Father according to divinity, and the same one consubstantial with us according to humanity; born from the Father timelessly and eternally, but from his mother in time and without seed. Hence we proclaim two births of him, and one and the same Son of God, and the same Son of Man, from two natures and in two natures—that is, divine and [Col. 0057C] human, uncreated and created, impassible and passible—converging into one person and substance, while the same natures remain in their own properties, unmixed and unchangeable. From these there came about an ineffable union, and God was united, through a rational soul, to the flesh that he assumed from the holy and immaculate Virgin.

Therefore we truly and properly proclaim her Θεοτόκον, that is, “Mother of God,” holy and ever-virgin, because she gave birth to one and the same God and our Lord Jesus Christ, not divided into two persons or two sons, but the same one—impassible in divinity, yet suffering in the flesh—crucified and buried [Col. 0058A] in the flesh, rising again and ascending into heaven in the flesh, from which he never departed in divinity; seated at the right hand of the Father in that same flesh, and thus coming to judge the living and the dead, and remaining forever in that same flesh.

[Note: [Col. 0058C] “Therefore we detest,” etc. He is referring simultaneously to the Eutychians and the Nestorians, in opposition to the popular error of the sixth century, according to which, as Facundus reports, it was believed that there was no middle way between the two errors in which the Catholic faith could stand.]

Therefore we detest and condemn all who assert in error that there were two natures before the union and one nature of Christ after the union; and likewise those who blaspheme by dividing our one Lord Jesus Christ into two persons or two sons.

Thus, following in all things the decrees of the five holy Synods, as well as the venerable traditions of the approved Fathers and Doctors of the Catholic Church, we confess and proclaim [Col. 0058B] the properties of the two natures of Christ united, while nevertheless acknowledging two natural wills and two operations of one and the same Lord Jesus Christ.

Moreover, we also profess that we will observe in all things all the decrees of the Pontiffs, my predecessors in the Apostolic See, especially those that were defined and decreed by Pope Martin of holy memory, [Note: [Col. 0058D] “Martin.” He departed this life crowned with martyrdom in the year 655. Six years earlier he had held at Rome the Lateran Synod of 105 bishops against the Monothelites, and had issued a profession of faith that the Sixth Synod received and followed in act 18. Nevertheless, while condemning the other patriarchs on account of heresy, it also numbered Honorius among them, which Martin had not done.] in confirmation of the five Synods mentioned above, and especially those promulgated against the new controversies by which the scandals of the weeds have been scattered here and there.

Strengthened and relying upon the authority of these holy Fathers and Pontiffs of the Apostolic See, we accept and proclaim without any diminution whatever they received synodically or proclaimed. In the same way, whatever they condemned, together with its authors and adherents, we condemn under anathema.

We also profess that, in accordance with the decisions established by my predecessors, we will never accept anything new against the Catholic and orthodox faith; nor will we in any way give consent to those who rashly presume such things, even if it should be necessary to die, with God’s grace strengthening us, [Note: [Col. 0058D] “Give consent in any way.” That is, neither explicitly, by assenting to errors, nor tacitly, by conniving at them; for sincere faith, the duty of a teacher, and prudence instructed by the example of Honorius forbid both. Honorius is referred to here, and mention of the Sixth Synod immediately follows.] no matter what form that consent might take.

Moreover, I accept, embrace, and venerate the definition made, with God’s favor, by the holy, universal, and great Sixth Synod, which recently met in the imperial city of Constantinople, in which it is evident that the legates of the Apostolic See presided, and which was convoked by the decree of the most Christian and devout Prince Constantine, crowned by God. What it received, I receive; and those whom or whatever it rejected, I reject; likewise, those whom it anathematized and condemned, I anathematize and condemn.

Finally, my beloved, holding this norm of the orthodox and Apostolic faith in all things, and adhering to the sacred teachings of the spiritual Fathers, as though to the brightest lights of the age, we ought, with the religious devotion of our humility, to confess freely with our mouth what we have conceived in our heart through their instruction, illumined by heavenly grace, so that on the day of the coming of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, standing at his right hand, [Col. 0059B] we may deserve to hear that desirable Gospel voice saying: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

Having thus laid these foundations, my beloved, we ought, with knees fixed upon this most sacred and venerable body of the blessed Prince of the Apostles, to beseech the Lord Jesus Christ earnestly to preserve and guard the most faithful and most Christian Roman Prince, established by God, rich in the worship of religion, [Note: [Col. 0059B] “Rich in the worship of religion.” This was a particular praise of Constantine Pogonatus, whose father Constans was the author of the *Typos*, and whose great-grandfather Heraclius approved the *Ecthesis*, while Constantine himself was more religious.] with life and victory, throughout a long course of years in his holy fear; and, reigning peacefully far and wide, to deem him worthy—together with the most faithful and valiant armies of the Roman commonwealth of Italy—to subdue and overthrow the rebellious enemies of the Empire, with the blessed Princes of the Apostles going before him, not by the sword’s edge, but by prudent counsels, and without the loss of his flourishing army. [Note: [Col. 0060B] “Against the imperial city,” etc. See Zonaras on Constantine, where he relates that the Bulgarians, threatening the imperial city and Constantine’s army, were restrained by no other means than the payment of tribute. This is what is meant here by “not by the sword’s edge, but by prudent counsel, without loss to the flourishing army.”] May commendable triumphs over the savagery of those hostile both to the imperial city and on every side ensue, so that every sex and rank, rejoicing in such victories, may with one voice be invited to offer worthy praises and thanks to our God and Lord Jesus Christ, with whom, together with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, there is glory throughout all ages of ages. Amen.

52 **CHAPTER III. ON THE ORDINATION OF A SUBURBICARIAN BISHOP BY THE SUPREME PONTIFF**

[Col. 0059]

## ARGUMENT

I. When one of those bishops who were subject to the ordination of the Apostolic See had departed this life, the Pontiff was immediately informed of his death, either by letters from the Clergy and People of the widowed Church or by the defenders of the patrimony stationed there. — II. Once informed, the Pontiff wrote to the Clergy and People of the widowed Church concerning the election of a bishop. — III. He also wrote to a neighboring bishop, to whom he entrusted the care of the Church until it should have a shepherd. — IV. The election took place through the concurrence of the votes of the Clergy, the Order, and the People, and the decree was confirmed by the subscription of all. — V. The decree of election was brought to the Pontiff, together with prayers that he approve the election and ordain the bishop whom they had chosen for themselves. — VI. The Pontiff replied and summoned the bishop whom he had approved to Rome for consecration. — VII. When the elected man traveled to the Apostolic See, the Archdeacon of the widowed Church and other distinguished men accompanied him, and they carried with them further letters from the Clergy and People, by which the ordination was urged more insistently. — VIII. The ordination was performed at Rome with solemn rite, preceded by an examination concerning faith and morals; and during the ordination admonitions were given to the bishop by which he would be helped in governing his Church. — IX. At the ordination the bishop made a profession of faith at the body of Saint Peter. — X. He also gave a written undertaking in which he promised to observe ecclesiastical discipline. — 53 XI. He added a memorandum concerning the obedience owed to the supreme Pontiff and the fidelity to be maintained toward the Prince. — XII. After the ordination he received from the Pontiff letters to the Clergy and People of his city, informing them what the bishop had received as commands and what he had promised, and with what respect he ought to be honored by his subjects. — XIII. When he was dismissed, he also received from the Archdeacon of the Roman Church a *formata*, so that it might be established by whom the ordination had been performed, on what day, in what month, in what indiction, under which emperor, and so forth. — XIV. If a bishop had lost the Church to which he had been ordained because of the violence of the barbarians, and there was no hope of recovering it, the supreme Pontiff appointed him by letter over another widowed Church; this was called incardination. — XV. But if circumstances opposed this, so that no one was appointed over a widowed Church, the neighboring bishop received letters from the supreme Pontiff by which the Churches were united and one bishop was placed over both. — XVI. When a bishop was seated in his own Church, the supreme Pontiff was accustomed to invite him by letter to celebrate the Pontiff’s natal feast more solemnly at Rome. — XVII. If the man who had been invited could not come because of illness or some other important matter, and excused himself by letter, the Pontiff sent an excusatory reply—that is, a letter in which he approved the excuse. — XVIII. At fixed times the bishops who were subject to the ordination of the Apostolic See were required to present themselves before the Pontiff. If they ever neglected this duty, they received from the Pontiff an exhortatory letter, by which those who delayed were admonished and even terrified with threats. — XIX. If they suffered some adversity, the Pontiff gave them letters of consolation: such was the humanity and kindness of those times. — Thus there were nineteen formulae concerning the ordination of a suburbicarian bishop and the instruction of the one ordained: eleven belonged to the Pontiff who wrote; three to the bishop; the remainder to others. Among the Pontifical letters, neither the exhortatory letter to the Clergy concerning the election, nor the commendatory letter to the widowed Church is found in the *Diurnus*; but both are found everywhere among the letters of Gregory the Great.

The form of the decree after the election is also not found; yet it is read in the Roman *Ordo*. The missing items will be appended after the Notes, as an appendix, so that the practice of the times under discussion may be more evident.

## [TITLES]

### TITLE I. Decree concerning the elected bishop, which the Regional Notary will read

[Note: [Col. 0061B] “The Regional Notary.” Each of Rome’s Regions had its own notaries assigned to it, who took turns performing service for the supreme Pontiff. They reported to him on the affairs of the suburbicarian regions assigned to them.]  

[Col. 0061A]

**Superscription.** To the holy Lord, deservedly Apostolic and adorned with divine blessing, Ill. [Note: [Col. 0061C] “Pope of the Fathers.” This title had been used since the age of Constantine the Great, though not so frequently; in later times it became more frequent and more solemn.] Pope of the Fathers, Prelate of the supreme See, your servants, the Clergy and People of the Church of Ill.
