We nevertheless believe that it pertains to the praise of your Apostolate if the Church, which appears deprived of the office of its Pontiff, should, by God’s favor, be adorned during your pontificate. Therefore, holy and deservedly Apostolic Lord, we ask your Apostolate that your Apostolate may graciously consecrate as bishop for us your servant, the venerable man Ill., Deacon of our Church, whose life and honorable conduct among us we have found well and most fully tested; [Col. 0057B] so that, when the Church of God and yours has been adorned during your pontificate, it may return insufficient thanks to God and to your Apostolate.

[Note: [Col. 0061C] “Your Apostolate.” Although this title seems to belong to the prelate of the supreme and Apostolic See, from which the Roman Pontiff is also often called “the Apostolic,” it was sometimes attributed to lower bishops as well; examples of this attribution occur everywhere.]

55 **And their subscription.** I, Ill., have consented to and subscribed this decree made by us concerning the venerable man Ill., our Deacon and elected bishop, etc.

### TITLE II. [Note: [Col. 0061C] “Summons.” Letter 183 of John VIII is a summons; yet it is not addressed to bishops and priests, etc., but to the elected man himself, who had informed the Pontiff by letter of his election. He was Theodosius, Deacon and elected bishop of the Church of Nonna in Illyricum, under the Metropolitan of Jadera. Since this letter contains much useful material for ecclesiastical history, it is also especially worthy of reading.] Summons

To our most beloved [Note: [Col. 0061D] “Brothers and sons.” This summons seems to concern the elected bishop of a metropolitan Church: thus “brothers” will refer to the bishops of the province, and “sons” to the priests, etc.] brothers and sons, the priests, deacons, clerics, distinguished men, possessors, and the entire People of the Church of Ill., and likewise to Ill., summoned as the future bishop, with the Lord’s help, of the holy Church of Ill.

[Note: [Col. 0061D] “We address your affection.” A similar letter is read in the Roman *Ordo*, except that it has this entirely superfluous clause: “For this reason we have sent this admonition, because it was long ago decreed by the holy Synod that a bishop should not be received without a summons, lest the obscurity of a doubtful ordination be incurred.”]

We address your affection for your welfare, because we are compelled to ordain as bishop the venerable man Ill., chosen by you. We rejoice and pray to Christ Jesus that he who gave you the devotion of making this election may also grant us the power to complete it. Now hold that man fast with religious force and hasten to bring him to our holy See; for perhaps he will be more worthy of it if he should wish to hide himself. [Note: [Col. 0061D] “If he should wish to hide himself.” Gregory the Great did this; consult the *Life of Saint Gregory*, where John the Deacon, chapters 39 and following, explains the pious devices by which the holy man attempted to avoid the supreme ecclesiastical dignity of the world.]

56 ### TITLE III. [Note: [Col. 0061D] “Decretal.” This *decretal* may appear to differ from the *decree* only in wording; by this one distinction, the following two formulae differ from the *decretal*. But the contrary is indicated. First, the superscription of each is different, and the following formulae are not similarly inscribed. Further, the decretal, unlike the preceding decree, was to be read not by a Notary but by a Deacon. Again, the decree was sent after the bishop had been elected, whereas the *decretal* was sent after he had been designated. Finally, a minister of the widowed Church, sent to the Pontiff, brought the decree so that the election might be approved; the *decretal* was brought by the Deacon, companion of the future bishop, so that the ordination might be performed. The distinction between an elected and a designated man is that the elected man is one upon whom the Clergy and People have agreed, whereas the designated man is one who has been approved by the supreme Pontiff and ordered to come for ordination. Alcuin, in his book *On Divine Offices*, mentions this *decretal* when he says: “When the bishop of a city has died, another is elected by the clergy or People, and a decree is made by them; then they come to the Apostolic One with their elected man, bringing with them a petition or letters of request, so that he may consecrate the bishop for them.”]  

**Decretal, which the Deacon will read to the designated bishop**

[Note: [Col. 0062C] “The Deacon.” Not, in any case, of the Roman Church, but of the widowed Church over which the bishop was to be placed; for the reference is not to the reading of the decree that would take place during the ordination itself. Otherwise it would not be said merely that a Deacon read it, but that an Archdeacon did, since it was his duty to report on the election.]

[Col. 0062B]

To the most blessed Lord Pope: the assembled priests, deacons, and People of the holy Church of Ill.

**Another hand.** [Note: [Col. 0062D] “With the neighboring parishes.” That is, the Churches of neighboring cities; for the word “parishes” signifies Churches, as is clear from many passages of the *Diurnus*. Moreover, another hand shows that the parishes were distinct from the widowed Church, whose clergy included all who ministered in rural Churches.] Greetings in the Lord, together with the neighboring parishes.

It belongs to your Pontifical office to assist Churches deprived of their pastors, lest the People devoted to God should appear for long to be without their own ruler. Therefore, most blessed Lord Pope, we beseech your Apostolate to deign to consecrate for us as pastor our venerable man Ill., our Deacon, approved in life and conduct, [Note: [Col. 0062D] “Deacon.” As is clear from the ancient documents relating to this matter, it was customary to elect Deacons rather than priests, for many reasons. First, Deacons knew the affairs of the Church thoroughly, not only temporal but also spiritual, for a Deacon is the bishop’s eye and assistant. Moreover, they were better known to all the orders of the city because of their administration of affairs. Further, since they had everything in their power, they could easily win the goodwill of the clergy. Finally, they generally brought more dignity than others, since Archdeacons—who are meant here under the name of Deacons—if they had conducted themselves well, had shown that they excelled in all the qualities of character useful for governing others.] and elected by the whole body, [Col. 0063A] as shepherd.

**Another hand.** We wish you good health for many years, most blessed Lord Pope.

Ill., Archpriest, subscribed. Ill., priest, subscribed. Ill., archdeacon, subscribed. Ill., deacon, subscribed. Ill., subdeacon, subscribed. Ill., primicerius, subscribed. Ill., acolyte, subscribed. Ill., lector, subscribed. The cantor and the others subscribed.

### TITLE IV. Another example

We readily believe that a desire should be granted when what is requested accords with ecclesiastical discipline. Our Church, therefore, is deprived of its own pastor, for whom your Apostolate ought to provide. Therefore, most blessed Lord Pope, we beseech your Apostolate to deign to consecrate for us as bishop the venerable man Ill., our Deacon, distinguished in life and conduct and elected by the judgment of the whole body.

### TITLE V. Another example

[Note: [Col. 0063C] “The Paschal festival.” As Easter approached, the widowed Church needed a bishop, not only because of the solemnity of the greatest feast, but also for these three matters: the preparation of the chrism, solemn baptism, and the reconciliation of penitents. See the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory*.]

The Paschal festival urges us to hasten to the remedies of your Pontificate, in whose power the adornment of all [Col. 0064A] Churches consists. Therefore we beseech your Apostolate, most blessed Lord Pope, to deign to consecrate for us as pastor the venerable man Ill., our Deacon, approved in life and conduct and elected by the whole body, so that, with the Lord granting your approval, we may celebrate venerable Easter together with him.

### TITLE VI. [Note: [Col. 0063C] “Profession of faith.” The Roman *Ordo* does indeed show by what rite a bishop was consecrated by the Pontiff in those times; yet it does not provide the profession of faith and the memorandum found here, but instead an interrogation made by the Pontiff who ordained him. From this it may be inferred that the Roman *Ordo*, as it is read in published books, is later than the *Diurnus*: the interrogation replaced the profession. This form of faith, as it is read here, has three features that reveal its age. It mentions Martin I, who died in 655; the Sixth Synod, completed in 681; and Constantine Pogonatus, still living at the time, who died in 685. It was therefore issued before 685 and belongs to the period between 682 and 685; indeed, it should be attributed to Leo II, who began to sit in 683. I have said “as it is read here,” that is, with the additions that, so to speak, were attached to its body. I think two parts must be distinguished in it: one, as it were, the body; the other, the additions. The former may perhaps be traced back to the period close to the Council of Chalcedon; the latter accrued at different times successively. Thus the mention of the Seventh and Eighth Councils was added to the first Pontifical profession in later times. I have asserted that it was issued while Pogonatus was alive because, although the emperor is named, the words “of pious memory” were not added, while he is nevertheless called most pious, most Christian, and crowned by God. People of that age applied these epithets—at least the last one—only to the living.]

**Profession of faith [Note: [Col. 0064C] “Of the bishops.” Not of bishops of every region, but of those regions whose bishops were subject to the ordination of the Apostolic See. Those subject to it were bishops subordinate to no other metropolitan, such as the Latins, Bruttians, Lucanians, Apulians, Sicilians, etc.] of the bishop**

In the name of the Lord, and so forth. I, Ill., bishop of the holy Church of Ill., promise to my most holy and thrice-blessed lord, Ill., the supreme Pontiff, [Note: [Col. 0064C] “Or universal Pope.” In the force of the words, “supreme Pontiff” and “universal Pope” mean the same thing. Saint Gregory nevertheless recoiled from the title “universal Pope,” as is clear from Letter 30 of Book VII to Eulogius of Alexandria. Later Pontiffs were not equally reluctant after Boniface III obtained from Phocas that the bishop of Constantinople be forbidden to assume a title belonging solely to the Roman Pontiff and conferred upon him by the Council of Chalcedon. What I have said about the later supreme Pontiffs is known from the superscriptions of several letters addressed to them: when they were called universal Popes, they did not trouble those who wrote to them about the matter, as Gregory did Eulogius. Gregory, moreover, interpreted the term “universal Pope,” out of the disposition of his remarkable humility, somewhat differently from those who used it. They did not mean—as Gregory seems to have supposed—that there was one patriarch of the whole Church, or one bishop whom they called universal, but that the Roman Pope possessed authority bounded by no fixed limits, unlike the other patriarchs. Consult the cited letter and the many others written on the same subject to the Emperor Maurice, the Empress Constantina, the bishops of Alexandria and Antioch, and also to John of Constantinople, who arrogantly claimed this title for himself, and to Sabinianus the *Apocrisiarius*, etc.] or universal Pope, and through you to your holy Catholic Church and the Apostolic See, with devoted integrity of mind, a pure conscience, and the firm purpose that is required, to profess what accords with the confirmation and rectitude of the Catholic faith and orthodox religion.

Therefore I promise and pledge to you, my most holy and blessed lord Pope, and through you to blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and to his holy Church, that I will hold, preach, and defend the faith that we have received from the Apostles and that the venerable Council of Nicaea of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, [Note: [Col. 0064D] “The venerable Council of Nicaea.” From these words to the words indicated below, this is called the *Tome*. The greater part of the faith contained in it is found, with very few alterations, in the letter of Pelagius II to Elias and the bishops of Istria.] having received it by revelation of the Holy Spirit, set it down in the Creed; this faith had been preserved through their successors.

Then the three other holy Synods: that of Constantinople, of the one hundred and fifty Fathers, held under the Emperor Theodosius the Elder of blessed memory; the First of Ephesus, over which Pope Celestine, pontiff of the Apostolic See, of blessed memory, and blessed Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, presided; and the Council of Chalcedon, of six hundred and thirty Fathers, which assembled under the Emperor Marcian of blessed memory, and over which Pope Leo of holy remembrance presided through his legates and representatives. In accordance with the diversity of the various heresies requiring condemnation, they more fully set forth the same faith, with one and the same meaning and Spirit.

[Col. 0065B] Whoever among those condemned at different times by these holy Fathers in the four aforementioned Synods, or in the Fifth Synod held under Justinian of blessed memory, I and my Church, following the venerable authority of those Fathers, strike with irrevocable condemnation. Likewise, all whom the Pontiffs of the city of Rome, of blessed remembrance, condemned on account of various errors or heresies, we condemn.

With the support of spiritual grace, we also profess that we will preserve inviolably in every respect and in all things the letter of Leo, holy and blessed in memory, prelate of the Apostolic See, addressed to Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, which is also called the *Tome*, as well as all his letters written concerning the firmness of the faith; and we will always preach them freely, as you preach them.

Among other things, these letters most clearly contain the teaching that one and the same God, Lord, and Savior Jesus Christ, the Son of God, and the same Son of Man, is to be proclaimed as existing from two natures and in two natures—that is, divine and human—converging into one person and subsistence, while remaining in their own properties and distinction; not divided into two persons and two sons, but, as has been said, one and the same Son of God, our God and Lord Jesus Christ. We believe that he took from the womb of the holy Virgin Mary, his Mother, from that same holy ever-virgin Mary, true flesh animated by a rational soul, and united it to himself; and thus, born from the womb of the Virgin Mary, Mother of God, he is the same true God in the flesh; the same one who suffered in the flesh, was crucified and died in the flesh, rose again in the flesh, and ascended in that same flesh into heaven, from which he never departed in divinity; and thus he will come in that same flesh to judge the living and the dead, [Col. 0066B] and will remain forever in that same flesh.

And although what has been said above is sufficient in abundance for the sincerity of the orthodox faith, nevertheless, since you wished this especially to be professed by us, as is fitting, [Note: [Col. 0065C] “Since this especially.” This supports the opinion mentioned earlier, that the profession was made immediately after the Council of Chalcedon against the ravings of Eutyches. At that time it was necessary for each person, in order to prove his orthodoxy, to detest Eutyches’ madness concerning two natures before the union and one after the union. If this opinion concerning the age of the profession is probable, then the other matters that follow, at least insofar as they concern the faith, must have been added by Leo II.] we also detest, abominate, and condemn all who in their delirium have presumed to say or believe that in our Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ there were two natures before the union and one after the union.

We also profess that we will preserve all the decrees of the Pontiffs of the Apostolic See, namely, of Severinus, John, Theodore, and Martin, of holy remembrance, [Note: [Col. 0065D] “Of Severinus,” etc. From Honorius, during whose pontificate the new controversies arose and the impious *Ecthesis* was issued in the name of Heraclius, until Leo II, under whom we suppose this formula either to have been issued or at least enlarged by an addition, nine supreme Pontiffs presided over the Church: Severinus, John IV, Theodore, Martin I, Eugenius, Vitalian, Adeodatus, Donus, and Agatho. It may reasonably be asked why the first four are mentioned while the other five are passed over; and especially why no mention is made of Agatho, who, after convening a Synod of 125 bishops at Rome, wrote two distinguished letters concerning the faith. The reason, however, is immediately evident. Against the *Ecthesis*, which asserted one operation of Christ, Severinus issued a decree condemning and anathematizing it. John, while the Exarch Isaac was relentlessly persecuting the clergy with banishments, convened a Council at Rome that proscribed the Monothelite heresy. Theodore likewise convened a gathering of bishops against the same *Ecthesis* and the *Typos*, and sent two synodal letters from it to Constantinople. Martin assembled that celebrated Lateran Synod, where he condemned the Monothelite heresy by twenty published canons. These four Pontiffs attacked the Monothelites with all the greater vigor because they resented more deeply the action of Honorius, who, through imprudent accommodation and connivance, “did not illumine the Apostolic Church with the teaching of apostolic tradition, but promised that the immaculate faith would be stained by profane tradition,” as Saint Leo II says. Eugenius, when he was brought in during troubled times in place of Saint Martin, who had been deported to Cherson, could not raise a controversy because of the tyranny of the Exarch, nor ought he to have done so after the careful exposition of the faith delivered in the Lateran Council. The latter reason also applies to Vitalian, Adeodatus, and Donus, especially since the condition of the Church seemed calmer, or rather the storm was silent; when it broke out again, Agatho convened a Council of 125 bishops and, after the Monothelite errors had been condemned, sent two letters to Constantinople, which the Sixth Synod followed κατὰ πόδας, “step by step.” Therefore, to receive the Sixth Synod means nothing other than to adhere to Agatho’s decrees.] who are known to have cut away all the scandals of the weeds that arose in the imperial city against the new controversies and in defense of their own teaching, professing two natural operations in accordance with the movement of the two natures. Whatever they condemned, we condemn under anathema; whatever they received, we receive; and we venerate it with the full integrity of faith.

62 Moreover, I accept, embrace, and venerate the definition made, with God’s favor, by the holy, universal, [Col. 0067A] and great Sixth Synod, which assembled in the imperial city of Constantinople, in which it is evident that the legates of Lord Agatho of the Apostolic See presided, and which was convened by the decree of the most Christian and devout Constantine the Great, [Note: [Col. 0067B] “And crowned by God.” No one, I think, will have read this epithet attached anywhere to anyone other than a living person. Examples of its application to the living occur everywhere.] crowned by God. Whatever they received, we receive; whatever or whomever they rejected, we reject; likewise, those whom they anathematized and condemned, we anathematize and condemn.

We also profess that we will never accept anything new that is clearly contrary to the Catholic faith and orthodox religion.

[Note: [Col. 0067C] “Moreover, I promise.” Some light may be shed on this passage by the testimony of Gregory II, writing to Serenus of Fréjus: “When, at the prayers of our distinguished son the king, I was induced to add to the height of your honor, and moved by the uprightness of the faith which we have learned that you and your Church embrace, we sent you the pallium, forbidding and prohibiting, among other things, that you should ever invade another’s rights or usurp anyone’s jurisdiction through presumptuous boldness, but should be content with what you have possessed until now; yet now you are striving to invade the rights of the patriarch of Grado, etc.” From this it is clear that this was imposed upon bishops of the outer provinces when the pallium was sent, just as it was imposed upon the suburbicarian bishops at their ordination, namely, that they should remain within their own boundaries.]

Moreover, I promise never to usurp, under the jurisdiction of my episcopate, a parish or rights belonging to any other Church whatsoever.

[Col. 0067B] And so that the integrity and purity of our faith might be demonstrated to your Apostolate and to its holy Catholic Church, we dictated the text of this present promise, 63 to be written by the illustrious notary, [Note: [Col. 0067C] “The sacred archive,” etc. The Lateran archive, of which we spoke above, chapter 11, title 2, toward the end.] and we deliver it to the sacred archive of the holy Apostolic See of Your Beatitude.

And the bishop’s subscription:

I, Ill., unworthy bishop of the holy Church of Ill., having reread everything contained above, and agreeing with this promise and undertaking concerning the orthodox faith, faithfully made by me, have subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0067C] “The subscription of the priests.” One priest subscribes in the name of all, indeed in the name of the entire particular Church.]

And the subscription of the priests of that same Church:

I, Ill., [Col. 0068A] unworthy presbyter of the holy Church of Ill., having reread everything professed above, and agreeing with this promise and undertaking concerning the orthodox faith, made by Ill., my most holy bishop, have subscribed.

## TITLE VII

[Note: [Col. 0067D] “Security.” By *cautio* is understood a document by which someone binds his faith in writing to fulfill a promise; hence Pope Zacharias calls it a *chirographum* in canon 4 of the Roman synod held in 743. To make this security more readily intelligible, it should be compared with the synodal declaration received by a bishop when he is ordained and with the exhortation of the ordaining bishop, such as is found in the Roman Order. For the most part, this appears to have been composed from Letter 9 of Gelasius. It contains thirteen sections, almost all of which reflect the discipline of Gregory’s age.]

### The Bishop’s Security

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, while Ill. is emperor, etc.

Among the other salutary instructions of doctrine by which the Lord Ill., most blessed and Apostolic See Pope, has deigned to lead and instruct me, Ill., bishop, for receiving and governing the episcopate of the Church of Ill., you have also admonished me that [Note: [Col. 0067D] “Without any reward,” etc. The subject is the bishop’s gratuitous ordination; what did the Church not undertake to secure it? There were, moreover, those who put forward the names of compensation, *pastellus*, and reward as a pretext for simony, lest the word “price” create horror; but Gregory the Great tore off this mask when he forbade even compensation to be received for the pallium, though the custom had become established.] the priesthood should be granted without any reward, 64 [Note: [Col. 0067D] “Except for the services.” This entire passage concerning rewards and services is illuminated by Letter 44 of Book IV of Gregory the Great, if indeed it is a letter and not rather a decree enacted in a Roman Council by Gregory in 595: “Following the ancient rule of the Fathers, I decree that nothing is ever to be received from those who ordain, neither for the giving of the pallium, nor for the delivery of documents, nor under that name of *pastellus* which a new pretense, devised through ambition, has invented. For since the pontiff lays his hand upon the one being ordained, while the minister reads the Gospel and the notary writes his letter of confirmation, just as it is unfitting for the pontiff to sell the hand which he lays upon him, so it is unfitting for the minister or notary, at his ordination, to sell either the spoken word or the document. I altogether forbid the person who is to be ordained or has been ordained to give anything for ordination, the pallium, documents, or *pastellus*. If anyone should presume to demand or accept anything from these matters under the name of a benefit, he shall be liable to guilt at the strict judgment of almighty God. But if the person who has been ordained, without having agreed to it, without being required or solicited, should, after receiving the documents and pallium, wish to give something to anyone from the clergy merely as a token of gratitude, we in no way forbid its acceptance, since his offering bears no stain of guilt, not having proceeded from the recipient’s greed.”] except for the services which, according to ancient custom, are usually given; for it is right that what I have received freely I should, with God’s help, freely bestow.

[Note: [Col. 0068D] “I promise that I will accept nothing for ordination,” etc. This evil was born almost with the Church, always opposed by good men and often concealed by others beneath various plausible arguments. Would that it might at last be overcome.]

I promise that I will accept no reward for the ordination of clerics, from the doorkeeper up to the presbyter; rather, those whom I shall choose for the clerical office out of regard for God, I shall ordain freely.

I likewise confess [Note: [Col. 0068D] “Nor from those being baptized.” In the earliest centuries those who received baptism used to give money to presbyters and other ministers. But what was initially given as an honorarium for the service, when later demanded through the ministers’ greed as though it were a debt owed by right, the Church, in its salutary prudence, entirely forbade to be given. Thus Gregory of Nyssa sharply rebukes some who delayed baptism until they had something to give, in his discourse *Against Those Who Delay Baptism*.] and promise under oath by the divine judgment that I will never demand or accept any reward, in any matter or form, from those being baptized and sealed as Catholics, for any person whatsoever.

I also promise that I will carefully and faithfully preserve ecclesiastical estates, urban or rural, and all immovable and movable property, as well as the Church’s ornaments and sacred furnishings. If any pledges have been given by anyone, or are being wrongfully withheld, I promise that, through my own efforts, labor, and expense, insofar as the needs of the time permit, I shall strive to recover them, and that they shall not be alienated by me under any title. 65

I affirm that I shall conduct or defend, effectively and faithfully, ecclesiastical legal affairs that must be brought or answered, without regard to favor, collusion, bribery, or fraud—bringing actions against those who withhold property or answering those who bring claims—yet with justice considered in all things, since justice must be preferred to every advantage, with God’s help.

I promise that I will not alienate any urban or rural estate belonging to ecclesiastical law, whatever its value, whether useful or excessive, nor slaves of either sex or any age, during the time of my episcopate, so that the Church in which I was ordained may suffer no loss.

I promise each year to provide the fourth portion to the clerics or to the fabric funds without any diminution, and not, out of favor, to attach to ecclesiastical offices any person, whatever his worth.

[Note: [Col. 0069B] “The buildings kept in repair.” That portion of the goods which was assigned to the fabric funds was at that time held by the bishops throughout the entire parish; churches endowed as benefices had not yet been established.]

I profess that I shall maintain the buildings of all my Churches in good repair, with every diligence and care, each year and according to the expenses I possess; nor, during the time of my episcopate, shall the aforementioned furnishings be pledged as security for any reason.

[Note: [Col. 0069B] “Moreover, I promise.” The promise has two parts: one concerning not going to the imperial court without the permission of the Apostolic See; the other concerning not roaming through other cities or provinces while abandoning one’s own Church. Both serve to preserve residence; the former additionally serves to promote peace and charity, restrain ambition, and preserve holiness of conduct. Necessity and charity in Christ drew only a few bishops to the imperial court; accusations against their brothers, devotion to secular life, and desire for honors drew the greater number.]

Moreover, I promise that, [Note: [Col. 0069C] “Without the permission of the Apostolic See,” etc. From this it is evident that this security pertains only to bishops ordained by the Apostolic See; for it is certain that others sought permission from their metropolitans. See the letters in which Gregory the Great sends the pallium to metropolitans and admonishes the subject bishops who receive it, for in each he mentions that ecclesiastical rule, since they were to remain in their own Churches. Remember also that metropolitans gave an account in provincial synods of the canonical letters delivered to their subjects.] without the command of the Apostolic See I will in no way proceed to the imperial court, 66 nor roam through various provinces or cities, so that I may not appear to abandon my Church without serious cause.

[Col. 0070B] I also promise that, [Note: [Col. 0069C] “To the feast of the Apostles.” Bishops and others came to Rome for the solemnity of the Apostles on three occasions: at the feast of Saints Peter and Paul, at the dedication of the Basilica of the Apostles, and around the Ides of May. Concerning the feast, there is a clear testimony in Paulinus, Letter 13 to Severus: “We set out for Rome for the venerable day of the Apostolic solemnity, promising ourselves your attendance there in a meditation that was indeed dutiful, yet festive.” And in Letter 16 to Delphinus, concerning Pope Anastasius: “When we had come to Rome, as was customary, for the feast of the blessed Apostles, he received us as graciously as he did honorably. Later, after some time had passed, he also deigned to invite us to his own feast, which he usually extended only to his fellow priests, and he was not offended by our excuse. And later: ‘If the Lord grants us leave to return to him at the customary solemn season, etc.’” That assembly was optional for bishops who were not subject to ordination by the Apostolic See, but mandatory for those who were. The *Liber Diurnus* suggests this, and Gregory the Great’s Letter 70 of Book I proves it explicitly: “Because we wished our brothers and fellow bishops residing on the island of Sicily to assemble for the feast of the blessed Apostle Peter,” etc. Shortly afterward, having stated that they were prevented for a legitimate reason, he “orders them to come as soon as possible, but not before winter.” I interpret this as referring to another gathering for the dedication of the Basilica of the Holy Apostles on 18 November. The words of Valentinian, Galla Placidia, and Eudoxia to the Emperor Theodosius and the Empress Pulcheria should also be understood of this gathering; some have taken them, contrary to the clear evidence of history, as referring to the feast of the Apostles on 29 June. It is not equally clear when this kind of command was first imposed upon bishops subject to ordination by the Apostolic See. In the Roman Synod held by Zacharias in 743, canon 4, he decreed that “according to the statutes of the holy Fathers and the canons, all bishops subject to the ordination of the Apostolic See, those who are near, should appear annually at the thresholds of the holy principal Apostles Peter and Paul on or around the Ides of May. Those who are far away should fulfill this according to their written undertaking. Whoever proves contemptuous of this constitution—unless he is prevented by serious illness—should know that he is subject to the penalties of the canons.” Yet we are not sufficiently informed by this concerning what statutes these were, or which Fathers and canons issued them, for the present question to be settled. Zacharias is not speaking of the feast of the Apostles, which falls on 29 June, but of the Ides of May. I know of no reason why bishops were summoned at that time, unless perhaps to pay homage to the primate, when neither the great heat nor their absence would harm the Churches—namely, after the solemn rites of Pentecost, which are completed as quickly as possible around the Ides of May. I have said that this command was imposed upon bishops subject to ordination by the Apostolic See, that is, those who had to be ordained by the supreme pontiff. Those who presided over the suburbicarian Churches had to be so ordained. By “suburbicarian” I understand the term in Ruffinus’s sense, for at that time no primates other than the Roman bishop presided over such Churches.] I shall attend annually the feast of the Apostles, unless prevented by some necessity.

If I should be proved to have acted or done anything contrary to the foregoing provisions, or to any one of them, I affirm that I shall restore, both by myself and through my heirs, not only whatever belonging to my Church I may have lost or perhaps unjustly received, but I also promise that I shall undergo the loss of my honor.

[Col. 0071A] 67 [Note: [Col. 0071C] “I further promise.” Whatever came to a bishop not by succession but by legacy was judged to have been given not to a private person but to the head of the Church, and therefore to pass into the rights of the Church. Indeed, “it is known to have been defined by the sacred laws of the canons that, in those things which a bishop acquires during the time of his episcopate, no one else succeeds, but the Church alone.” Gregory the Great, Book IX, Letter 14, to Scholasticus the Defender.]

I further promise that, apart from all persons related or connected to me, if anyone should name me heir for the judgment of his soul, or should perhaps bestow anything upon me by donation, I, Ill., bishop of the holy Church of Ill., promise to transfer it to that Church. If I fail to do so, let the aforesaid holy Church, or its priests, have the right, on the basis of this profession and promise, to reclaim it without question, as though everything had been acquired or bestowed upon them by me.

[Note: [Col. 0071C] “This also,” etc. From this it is clear what the Church understood concerning the bishop’s obligation, and that of the entire clerical order, to celebrate vigils and perform the divine office. It is equally clear what the arrangement of the office was according to the differing seasons, so that one form corresponded to the longer nights and another to the shorter. The longer nights were those from the autumnal equinox until Easter; the shorter, those from Easter until the autumnal equinox.]

I also promise above all that at all times, every day, from cockcrow until morning, I shall celebrate vigils in the Church with the whole order of my clergy, so that during the shorter night—that is, from Easter until the equinox, [Col. 0071B] the twenty-fourth day of the month of September—[Note: [Col. 0071D] “Three readings,” etc. Nothing is decreed concerning the psalms, which were said to number twelve, according to the ancient custom said to have originated from an angelic revelation, as Cassian reports in Book II, chapter 5, of the *Institutes*. The statements concerning antiphons and responsories reflect the age of Gregory the Great; for I know of no older antiphonary than the Gregorian one. What if the holy pontiff wished his *Antiphonary* to be observed by bishops of his ordination and required an undertaking that it be observed?] three readings, three antiphons, and three responsories shall be said; but from this equinox until the next vernal equinox, and until Easter, four 68 readings shall be said with their responsories and antiphons. On Sundays, at all times, we profess that we shall offer God nine readings with their antiphons and responsories.

[Note: [Col. 0071D] “Litanies,” etc. Litanies were instituted to appease God and avert evils. It is uncertain by whom and at what time they were first instituted. Some refer them to the time of Constantine, when the Church of Christ, released from captivity, publicly displayed the signs of its piety. The litany of Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, in the fifth century is famous; others are mentioned as even more celebrated in later centuries, though they were performed as necessity required. Gregory the Great once urged the bishops of Sicily to celebrate litanies against the enemies threatening the island (Book IX, Letter 45): “I urge you, dearest brothers, to appoint a litany without fail every Wednesday and Friday, and to implore the aid of heavenly protection against the assaults of barbarian cruelty.” I believe that this exhortation later developed into a command; but I suspect that the frequency was simultaneously reduced, so that litanies were now held twice not in one week but only in one month. Yet, so far as I know, no such command exists anywhere. What if “year” should be read instead of “month,” and the litanies understood as the two solemn ones, the greater and the lesser? The matter would be more easily resolved, for both were prescribed by Apostolic command to be performed annually; the others only as circumstances required or by decree of a particular synod.]

I promise that I shall celebrate litanies twice each month at all times. I also promise, with God’s help, that I shall institute all these observances in my Church with fear and discipline, so that God may be appeased, and shall preserve them throughout the days of my life.

I dictated this security of mine to be written by the notary of my Church. I also subscribed it below in my own hand, and asked the witnesses to write, having made a solemn promise, at the exhortation of the Lord and of the most blessed Pope Ill., with you, Lord Ill., the primicerius, or Lord Ill., the secundicerius of the holy Apostolic See, acting as stipulators concerning all that is contained above. [Col. 0072A] Done at Rome on the day of Ill., in the reign of Emperor Ill., during the consulship of Ill.

And the bishop’s subscription:

I, Ill., unworthy bishop of the holy Church of Ill., having reread and agreed with everything written above concerning this security and undertaking of mine, have subscribed, and I have asked the witnesses to subscribe.

The subscription of the witnesses:

I, Ill., tribune, having been asked by Ill., bishop of the holy Church of Ill., have subscribed as a witness to this security and undertaking made by him, etc.

69 The subscription of the writer:

I, Ill., notary and also scribe of the holy Church of Ill., have completed the testimony with my subscription.

## TITLE VIII

[Note: [Col. 0072D] “The memorandum.” By this formula Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz, bound himself to the Apostolic See. Among the letters of Gregory II there is a memorandum of the oath which Boniface issued at Rome when he was ordained bishop and presented with his own subscription. It was worthwhile to display it and set it parallel to the formula, so that one might correct one from the other and also understand from both, and from the following document, what distinction existed in such an oath when it was given by an Italian, a Lombard, or someone situated outside Italy.]

### The Bishop’s Memorandum

In the name of the Lord, etc., the emperor being Ill.

I, Ill., bishop of the Church of Ill., promise to you, blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and to your vicar, the most blessed Pope, Lord Ill., and to his successors, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the inseparable Trinity, and by this most sacred body of yours, that I shall exhibit every faithfulness and purity of the holy Catholic faith and, with God’s help, persevere in the unity of that same faith, in which the salvation of all Christians is demonstrably found, and in no way consent, at anyone’s persuasion, to anything against the unity of the common and universal Church. Rather, as I have said, I shall in every respect exhibit my faithfulness, purity, and cooperation to you and to the interests of your Church, to which the Lord God has given the power of binding and loosing, and to your aforesaid vicar and his successors.

Moreover, if I learn that bishops are behaving contrary to the ancient institutions of the holy Fathers, I shall have no communion or association with them; rather, if I am able to prevent them, I shall prevent them. If not, I shall immediately report the matter faithfully to my Apostolic Lord.

But if—which God forbid—I should in any way, by device or pretext, attempt to do anything contrary to the terms of this promise of mine, may I be found guilty at the eternal judgment and incur the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira, who presumed to defraud you even of their own property and to tell a lie.

[Col. 0073C] 71 I, Boniface, an insignificant bishop, have written this memorandum of the oath with my own hand, and, placing it upon the most sacred body of blessed Peter, I have taken the oath as written, with God as witness and judge; and I promise to keep it.

### Memorandum of Boniface of Mainz

[Col. 0072A]

In the name of the Lord God [Col. 0072B] and our Savior Jesus Christ. In the reign of Lord Leo, crowned by God, the great emperor, in the sixth year after his consulship; and also in the third year of Constantine, his son, the great emperor; indiction six.

I, Boniface, by the grace of God bishop, promise to you, blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and to your vicar, the blessed Pope Gregory, and to his successors, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the inseparable Trinity, and by your most sacred body, that I shall exhibit every faithfulness and purity of the holy Catholic faith and, with God’s help, persevere in the unity of that same faith, in which the salvation of all Christians is undoubtedly found. I shall in no way consent, at anyone’s persuasion, to anything against the unity of the common and universal Church; rather, as I have said, I shall in every respect exhibit my faithfulness and purity, which [text uncertain] to your Church, to which the Lord God has given the power of binding and loosing, and to your aforesaid vicar and his successors.

I likewise promise that, if I learn that anything is being done by anyone against the commonwealth or against our most pious ruler, I shall not consent but, insofar as my strength permits, shall oppose it, and shall report it to your vicar, my Apostolic Lord, by whatever means I can, and shall act and conduct myself so that I may demonstrate my faithfulness in all things to be most sincere.

But if—which God forbid—I should in any way, by device or pretext, attempt to do anything contrary to the terms of this promise of mine, may I be found guilty at the eternal judgment or incur the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira, who likewise presumed to defraud you, blessed Peter, of their own property and to tell a lie.

[Col. 0073C] I, Ill., bishop, have written and subscribed this memorandum of the oath with my own hand, and have placed it upon your most sacred body; and, as written above, with God as witness and judge, I have taken the oath, which I promise to keep.

### Memorandum of the Bishop [Note: [Col. 0073C] “From Lombardy.” This formula has two features from which one may to some extent infer the time when it was first issued. First, it resembles the formula by which Saint Boniface bound his faith to the Apostolic See in the year 722; it was therefore already in use at that time. Second, it was issued when the Lombards not only held dominion over that part of Italy whose bishops were subject to ordination by the Apostolic See, but also maintained peace with the Romans. This occurred especially for as long as Queen Theodelinda lived—that is, before the year 626, when she is believed to have died. It therefore appears to have been written, or at least used, in the age of Gregory the Great, although it had already long been in use. I would readily believe that the body of the text itself belongs to an earlier period, while the appendix concerning the Lombards belongs to the Gregorian period.]

### From Lombardy

[Col. 0074A]

In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ, the emperor being Ill., etc.

I, Ill., bishop of the holy Church of Ill., promise to you, blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, and to your vicar, my most blessed lord Pope Ill., and to his successors, by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the inseparable Trinity, and by this most sacred body of yours, that I shall exhibit every faithfulness and purity of the holy Catholic faith and, with God’s help, persevere in the unity of the faith, in which the salvation of all Christians is undoubtedly found. I shall in no way consent, at anyone’s persuasion, to anything against the unity of the common and universal Church; rather, as I have said, I shall in every respect exhibit my faithfulness, purity, and cooperation to you and to the interests of your Church, to which the Lord God has given the power of binding and loosing, and to your aforesaid vicar and his successors.

I likewise promise to hasten with every effort so that the peace which God loves may always be preserved between the commonwealth and us—that is, the nation of the Lombards—and that I shall in no way act or do anything against it, so that I may demonstrate my faithfulness in all things to be most sincere. 72

But if—which God forbid—I should in any way, by device or pretext, attempt to do anything contrary to the terms of this promise of mine, may I be found guilty under Catholic law at the eternal judgment and incur the punishment of Ananias and Sapphira, who likewise presumed to defraud you, blessed Peter, of their own property and to tell lies.

I, Ill., bishop, have written this memorandum of the oath with my own hand, and have placed it upon your most sacred body, blessed Peter; and I have sworn the oath which, as written above, with God as witness and judge, I promise to keep.

## TITLE IX

[Note: [Col. 0073D] “The Synodal Letter.” This formula occurs in more than one place, although with only minor alterations. Before the *Liber Diurnus* was compiled, it is found among the letters of Gelasius I, who died in 498, and in Gregory the Great, Book II, Letter 25. After the compilation of the *Liber Diurnus*, it is found in Gregory II, writing to the Thuringians in 723, and in Hincmar’s letter to the people of Laon. I omit mentioning that it is reproduced for the most part by Anselm, Book VI, chapter 39, and by Gratian, Part II, Question 12, chapter 26—but from Gelasius, not from Gregory. It is called “synodal” partly because it was sent by the supreme pontiff from the Roman synod *ἐνδημούσᾳ* (*endēmousāi*, “resident” or “permanent”); partly because it was read in the synod of the Church over which the bishop presided. We understand from the Roman Order that bishops gathered for an ordination performed at Rome; and from the *Liber Diurnus* and the custom of the times we know that neighboring bishops, together with the clergy and people of the Church that was to receive the bishop, gathered to celebrate the anniversary feast. Observe that when such letters were sent from the synod of the supreme pontiff, the pontiff alone subscribed; when they were sent from the synod of a metropolitan, not only the metropolitan but all the bishops who were present added their subscriptions. The former practice concerning the supreme pontiff is solemn and known to everyone; the latter concerning other metropolitans we learn from the aforementioned letter of Hincmar, after whom Odo of Beauvais, Raginelmus of Noyon, John of Cambrai, Willebert of Châlons, Hildebold of Soissons, Gerold of Amiens, and Hadebert of Senlis subscribed as bishops.]

### The Synodal Letter Received by the Bishop

To the clergy, order, and people residing at Ill., our most beloved sons in the Lord, greetings.

We have not delayed granting your reasonable requests. [Col. 0075A] We have ordained as your priest our brother and fellow bishop, Ill., 73 and have instructed him as follows:

1. He must never presume to perform unlawful ordinations.

2. He must not permit a bigamist, or one who has not taken a virgin as his wife, nor an unlettered person, nor anyone disfigured in any part of the body, nor one who has not completed penance, nor anyone subject to the curia or to any other condition, or marked by infamy, to advance to sacred orders. If he should happen to find anyone of this kind, he must not dare to promote him.

3. [Note: [Col. 0075B] “Africans indiscriminately.” Gregory the Great likewise takes precautions concerning Africans in Book II, Letter 25, to John, bishop of the Church of Lisbon, which had been captured by barbarians, whom he incardinates—as the expression goes—in the widowed Church of Squillace. The words concerning ordinations found here have been copied from that letter word for word. It reads: “We command that you never perform unlawful ordinations; that you do not ordain a bigamist, or one who has not taken a virgin as his wife, or one ignorant of letters, etc.”]

He must in no way receive Africans who present themselves indiscriminately for ecclesiastical orders, because some of them have repeatedly been found to be Manichaeans and some rebaptized.

4. He must strive not to diminish the furnishings or ornament of the Church, nor anything belonging to its patrimony, but to increase them.

[Col. 0075B] 5. From the Church’s income or from the offerings of the faithful, he must make four portions: one he shall retain for himself; a second he shall distribute to the clergy in proportion to their devoted service; a third shall be assigned to the poor and strangers; and the fourth he must know is to be reserved for the fabric of the churches, concerning which he will have to render an account at the divine judgment.

6. [Note: [Col. 0075C] “Ordinations, however.” This passage concerning the times of ordination appears to have been taken from Letter 9 of Gelasius to the bishops of Lucania, Bruttium, and Sicily, chapter 11: “They should know that the ordinations of presbyters and deacons must be performed only at the appointed times and days: that is, during the fast of the fourth, seventh, and tenth months, as well as at the beginning of Lent and on mid-Lent day, on the Saturday fast toward evening.”]

He must know that the ordinations of presbyters or deacons are to be celebrated only during the fasts of the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth months, 74 and also at the beginning of Lent and at mid-Lent, on Saturday evening.

7. [Note: [Col. 0075C] “The sacrament of holy baptism,” etc. This passage too is taken from the same letter, chapter 10: “Let no one believe that he may confidently baptize at random at any time, except at the solemn sacrament of the Paschal feast and Pentecost, with the sole exception of an attack of very serious illness, in which it is to be feared that, as the danger of the disease increases, the sick person may depart, overcome by death, without the saving remedy.” The Eastern Church had another custom, for baptism at Epiphany was solemn.]

He must know that the sacrament of holy baptism is to be administered only at the Paschal feast and Pentecost, except to those who are pressed by imminent death; such persons must be aided by these remedies lest they perish forever.

8. [Note: [Col. 0075D] “The litanies, however,” etc. This command is not contained in Gregory II’s letter. It may have been omitted through the carelessness of copyists, or because the letter was written to peoples living outside Italy, among whom that rite had either not yet been introduced or—more likely, in my opinion—was being consistently observed. What if this command was imposed upon the bishops of Italy at that time because a praiseworthy custom, as it was declining through the negligence of pastors, had to be revived by Apostolic command?]

He must celebrate litanies for three days before the day of the Ascension of the Lord.

Therefore, you ought to obey with devout hearts this man who observes the commands of our See, so that the body of the Church may become irreproachable and pleasing, through Christ our Lord, who lives and reigns with God the almighty Father [Col. 0076B] and the Holy Spirit, throughout all ages of ages.

And his subscription:

May God preserve you unharmed, our beloved ones.

# TITLE X

**[Note: [Col. 0075D] “Formata.”** Three very learned men—Baronius, Sirmond, and Ferrarius—have written about *formatae* letters; Priorius has recently joined them. They discussed at length both the name and the form of such letters, and produced several examples, especially Sirmond in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*. Nevertheless, I do not recall reading in them anything corresponding to this formula of the *Diurnus* concerning *formatae* given by the supreme Pontiff to a bishop after his ordination. That such letters were nevertheless customarily given cannot be doubted. For, following the example of the principal see, this canon was enacted by the African Fathers in the year of Christ 402:

“Let it be decided that, from now on, all who are ordained by bishops throughout the African provinces shall receive from their ordainers letters written by their own hand, containing the consulship and the day, so that no dispute may arise concerning what was earlier or later.”

Bernardinus Ferrarius indeed reports from the *Roman Order* a form of such letters, which we shall presently present. But it says nothing about the archdeacon’s subscription when he dismissed the bishop, nor about adding the day of Easter to those very *formatae*, although the African Fathers enacted in canon 106 “that *formatae* given by primates or by any bishops to their own clergy should bear the day of Easter. But if the day of Easter for that same year is still uncertain, the preceding one should be added, as is customarily written after the public acts of the consulship.”

Concerning *formatae*, however, which were given to a bishop after ordination, they do not issue an equally explicit command. As for the day of Easter, we nevertheless learn from the *Diurnus* that the common practice was observed in these letters also. It is useful, therefore, to transcribe a *formata* from the *Roman Order*, so that, by comparing both examples with one another and with what has already been said, the whole matter concerning such letters may be understood.

**A *formata* to be given to a bishop.** [Col. 0076D]

“To our most beloved brothers and sons, the priests, deacons, clergy, persons of rank, property-holders, and the entire people of the church of Ill.; with the help of the Lord, the archbishop of the holy Catholic See.

Approving your election as most acceptable to God, we have consecrated the venerable man Ill. as a priest in the first order among you. Therefore we earnestly admonish your affection to honor the aforesaid with that veneration with which you wished him to be consecrated bishop for you. For this reason we have sent such a messenger from our see, since it has been most satisfactorily established by the holy Synod that no bishop should be received without a *formata*, lest he incur an obscure or doubtful mark concerning his ordination.

I, Ill., have verified this. Ill. drew this up at the ordination of the bishop of the church of Ill. I, Ill. of the church of Ill., have subscribed.”

**[Note: [Col. 0076D] “Receives.”** Not from the metropolitan himself, as in the *formata* of the *Roman Order*, but from the archdeacon of the Roman Church, who, when dismissing the consecrated bishop, gave him letters to the clergy, so that he might inform them about the ordination of their bishop and the circumstances accompanying it.] The bishop receives the *formata*.

“To the priests, deacons, and assembled people of Ill., greetings from the brothers of Ill. [Col. 0077A]

Through our most beloved Ill., the bishop, we greet you, our most beloved; those of ours also greet you.”

**[Note: [Col. 0077C] “Through our most beloved.”** If this reading were genuine, that remarkable designation *most beloved* would deserve notice. It would show how great was the dignity of the archdeacon at Rome, since the supreme Pontiff called him “his most beloved brother,” while he was content to call the bishop “his most beloved.” But without doubt the text is corrupt. The scribe, instead of what was actually written in the customary manner—“your most reverend bishop”—carelessly directed his eyes to the following line, where *our most beloved* occurs, and wrote *our most beloved*. For what could be more absurd than to address a bishop less honorifically than clergy of inferior rank?]

“And his subscription: Farewell, brothers, in the name of the Lord. Easter will be on the Ill. day of the Ill. month, in the Ill. indiction.

**Subscription of the archdeacon.** I, Ill., archdeacon of the holy Apostolic See, have subscribed and dismissed him. Given on the Ill. day of the Ill. month, [Col. 0077C] under the reign of Ill., after the consulship of Ill., in the Ill. indiction.”

**[Note: [Col. 0077C] “Under the reign of Ill., after the consulship of Ill.”** This *formata* was therefore customary while the consulship—or at least the post-consulship—was still used in dating documents. Its use ceased as the sixth century was declining; consequently, this formula was employed before the age of Gregory the Great. Indeed, it seems to have been extremely ancient and proper to the Roman Church in every period, although it had different dating notices in different ages.]

# TITLE XI

**A synodal letter, so that a bishop of one city may be incardinated in another church.**

**[Note: [Col. 0077D] “Incardinated.”** In this passage the term means assigning, with ordinary authority and as though making him its proper priest, to a vacant church a man who has lost his own church because of invading barbarians. I have specified “in this passage,” because properly *incardination* means assigning to a particular church as its own priest a presbyter, deacon, or even subdeacon. Incardination, commendation, and ordination have considerable affinity, but there is nevertheless this distinction: incardination remained valid only until the church of the incardinated man, occupied by barbarians, was liberated; commendation lasted until the bishop was either ordained or sent back; ordination conferred perpetual right and, correspondingly, perpetual obligation.

This is evident both from the nature of ordination—for it is a kind of sacred marriage, like that which exists between Christ and the Church—and from the letters of Saint Gregory when he incardinated or commended men. Thus he wrote to John, bishop of the Lyssitanian Church, which had been occupied by barbarians:

“Therefore we have judged it necessary to establish you, John, bishop of the city of Lyssa, captured by enemies, as a cardinal priest in the Squillitanian Church, so that, mindful of future reward, you may fulfill the care of souls once entrusted to you. Although you have been driven from your church by the enemy’s threat, you must govern another church that is without a shepherd. Yet this is to be done in such a way that, if it should happen that the city is freed from its enemies and, with the Lord’s protection, restored to its former condition, you may return to the church in which you were previously ordained. But if the aforesaid city continues to suffer the calamity of captivity, you must remain in this church, in which we have ordained—or incardinated—you. We command, and so forth.”

The formula of incardination is found in Gregory, book II, part I, letter 25. Its heading should be corrected: it now reads, “He enjoins the visitation of a certain church.” For it is not temporary visitation that is enjoined upon the incardinated man, but governance. See book I, letter 77.]

“To the clergy, the order, and the assembled people of Ill., our most beloved sons, greetings in the Lord.

Both the necessity of the times presses us and the reduction in the number of persons requires us to come to the aid of your deserted church with a salutary arrangement. Therefore, in accordance with your desire, we have appointed our brother and fellow bishop Ill., whose church is occupied by enemies, as cardinal priest of your church, as you requested, so that, with God’s favor, he may diligently strive to govern you both by ordaining and by keeping watch.

**[Note: [Col. 0078C] “Cardinal of your church.”** See book I, letter 15.]

We have charged him, moreover, never to presume to perform unlawful ordinations, and so forth, according to custom.

**[Note: [Col. 0078C] “To whom we have given instructions.”** A common formula whenever someone was sent to govern a church.]

# TITLE XII

**A directive concerning the union of churches.**

**[Note: [Col. 0078C] “Concerning the union of churches.”** This formula is found almost word for word in Gregory, book II, letter 59, to Gratiosus, bishop of Nomentum, whose church he united with that of Saint Anthemius, situated in the territory of the Sabines at Cures. It is also found in book V, letter 19.]

[Col. 0078A]

“After the impiety of the enemy, through the working of sins, has so devastated the churches of various cities that, because their people have diminished, no hope of restoring them remains, we are compelled by very great concern to consider how, after their priests have died, the remnants of the people may not, lacking any pastoral governance, be caught—God forbid—in the snares of the crafty enemy of the faith through his malice.

**[Note: [Col. 0078D] “Governed.”** In Gregory: *while governing*.]

**[Note: [Col. 0078D] “Through the envy, etc.”** Gregory has: “through the byways of faith, etc.”]

Therefore, having often been urged by concern for this matter, we resolved that these churches should be entrusted to neighboring bishops for governance.

**[Note: [Col. 0078D] “We should entrust them to bishops.”** Gregory: “we should entrust them to pontiffs.”]

Accordingly, we have provided for the care and governance of the church of Ill. to be entrusted to your fraternity,

**[Note: [Col. 0078D] “Of the church of Ill.”** Gregory: “of the church of Saint Anthemius, situated in the territory of Cures among the Sabines.”]

**[Note: [Col. 0078D] “We have decided that it should be joined and united.”** Gregory: “it must be joined and united.”]

and we have decided that it should be joined and united to your church, [Col. 0078B] so that, with Christ’s help, you may rightly be the priest of both churches and may arrange, with vigilant and canonical care, whatever seems necessary to you concerning its patrimony or the ordering and advancement of its clergy, since, as its proper bishop, you have free permission by virtue of our present

**[Note: [Col. 0078D] “Authority.”** Gregory: “permission.”]

authority.

Therefore, dearest brother, remembering the Lord’s salutary commands, watch carefully over the governance of the people entrusted to you and over the winning of souls,

**[Note: [Col. 0078D] “So that to our Redeemer, etc.”** Gregory: “so that, having been placed before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, you may present to our Redeemer the fruit of good works that belongs to your reward and in which you may rejoice.”]

so that you may offer our Redeemer the fruit of good works in which you may rejoice.”

# TITLE XIII

**An invitation to a bishop on the pope’s feast day.**

**[Note: [Col. 0079B] “On the pope’s feast day.”** The bishops of Italy assembled for the feast day of the supreme Pontiff. Concerning Anastasius, Paulinus writes to Delphinus in letter 16:

“After some time had passed, he also deigned to invite us to his feast day, an honor that he usually extends only to his fellow priests, and he was not offended by our excuse, etc.”

Observe from this that only fellow priests—that is, bishops summoned by ordinary right—were invited; the others were invited by privilege. Sixtus writes in his letter congratulating Cyril on the peace established between the divided churches:

“The whole brotherhood assembled at blessed Peter. Behold an audience suited to its hearers and suited to what was to be heard. Our fellow bishops had as witness of their congratulation him whom we have as the beginning of our honor. For in the holy and venerable Synod, which the favor of the Lord had gathered on my feast day, as must be believed, he himself presided, etc.”

And in his letter to John of Antioch:

“The whole brotherhood that had assembled for my feast day heard, etc.”

Observe that the gathering of bishops is called a synod and that matters arising were discussed in it. [Col. 0079D]

Saint Leo, Sixtus’s successor, writes in the sermon commonly called the second on the anniversary of his accession:

“The desired and honored presence of my venerable brothers and fellow priests is all the more sacred and devoted to me if, in the piety of this duty in which they have deigned to be present, they chiefly honor him whom they know to be not only the bishop of this see but also the primate of all bishops.”

Hilary, Leo’s successor, writes in his first letter to Ascanius:

“After reading your letters in the assembly of the brothers whom the celebration of my feast day had gathered, etc.”

And in letter 8:

“While a numerous council of brothers presided, gathered by God’s grace from various provinces on our feast day in honor of blessed Peter the Apostle, etc.”

Three things should be observed here: the custom of assembling, the custom of inviting, and the form of the invitation. We learn the ancient custom of assembling both from these testimonies and from the *Diurnus*; the custom of inviting by letter from Paulinus’s letter 16 to Delphinus, and much more clearly from these words of the *Diurnus*: “according to the custom, you are invited by a letter sent by me”; and the form of the letters from the *Diurnus* alone.

This formula is therefore unique. It is not found among the careful investigators of ecclesiastical letters—Baronius, Sirmond, and Ferrarius—nor are the two letters of excuse found there, although all of them could not improperly be classified as *tractoriae*, since the assembly to which the bishops were invited was a synod at which ecclesiastical matters, if any were pressing, were dealt with. We learn this partly from the examples of Sixtus and Hilary and partly from the *Diurnus*.

Although only those bishops subject by ordination to the Apostolic See were summoned, we learn from both of Hilary’s letters that bishops assembled from all the provinces of Italy and even from more distant regions. Both letters concern the Roman Council held in 465, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. Besides the suburban bishops, Ingenuus of Embrun, Sabinus of Avignon, Maximus of Turin, and the Africans Restitutus and Octavius attended it.

The *Diurnus* and Saint Leo explain why the bishops were summoned: namely, so that in an assembly of priests the Pontiff might give thanks to God for his accession; then, so that whatever ecclesiastical affairs required might be jointly confirmed; and finally, so that by such service the bishops might acknowledge their own Pontiff as their prince.

It may be conjectured that other primates also had the custom of inviting their fellow bishops to their feast-day celebrations. Augustine’s address to the people of Carthage suggests this (*Sermon 32, On the Words of the Lord*). After the sermon had ended, he said:

“As your charity knows, we announce to you that tomorrow dawns the anniversary of the aged Lord Aurelius. Through my humility he asks and admonishes your charity that you deign to come most devoutly to the basilica of Faustus.”

[Col. 0079A]

“With the mercy of our God favoring us, the day of Ill., on which the anniversary of my episcopate falls, is approaching. In accordance with custom, you are invited to it by letters sent by me. For it is fitting, dearest brother, that you share in this celebration and offer the presence of your affection to the gathering of the brothers, so that we may confirm among ourselves those matters that ecclesiastical custom requires.”

# TITLE XIV

**A letter of excuse.**

**[Note: [Col. 0080D] “A letter of excuse.”** This is not a letter by which an invited bishop excuses himself, but one by which the supreme Pontiff accepts an excuse based on weakness and old age.]

“We have reread the letter of your fraternity that you sent and that was presented to us, and we have granted the pardon you requested for the weakness and old age of your fraternity, because you were unable to come. We have recognized that your fraternity did not fail to come to us through any deliberate attempt at making an excuse.”

# TITLE XV

**A letter of excuse when a bishop is ill.**

“Both the celebration of our feast day and the solemnity of custom require that, with all the priests assembling and present, the thanks owed to almighty God for our advancement should be rendered. But since you report that your affection has been prevented from coming to the gathering of devotion by bodily infirmity, we must grant pardon for whatever your physical illness requires. For where necessity is present, the will is not held culpable. Nevertheless, once health has been restored, we desire that, when the time permits, you make amends with the affection that is fitting.”

# TITLE XVI

**A letter exhorting a bishop.**

“We are greatly astonished at the reverence of your fraternity, because you have forgotten the promise **[Note: [Col. 0080D] “Promise.” See the bishop’s undertaking, in the section dealing with attendance at the feast day of the Apostles. Consult also the notes on this passage.]** that, at the time of your consecration, you made to blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles: that after two years you would come to this Apostolic See to present yourself to your Pontiff.

Behold how much time has passed, and you have not come. But now I admonish your reverence that, as soon as you receive the letter of our command, you come to us as quickly as possible, without any excuse. If you delay, carried away by the arrogance of pride, know that by the authority of my lord, the supreme Prince of the Apostles, blessed Peter, you are to be suspended from the solemn celebration of Mass until you present yourself to us.”

# TITLE XVII

**A letter of consolation.**

“Taking the beginning of our speech from the Apostle, we cry out: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak?’ (1 Cor. XI, 27). He also says elsewhere: ‘If one member suffers, all the other members suffer with it’ (1 Cor. XII, 16).

For we ourselves, grieving over your sorrows, suffer as though from continual illness. Since the opportunity permits, we address your holiness as though present, with the fervor of charity; and, with our pen flowing, we recall to your mind that apostolic consolation by which the sorrowful are comforted: ‘Consider it all joy, my brothers, when you fall into various trials’ (James I, 2).

The Truth itself also teaches: ‘You will be blessed when people hate you, persecute you, and speak every evil against you’ (Matt. V, 11), and what follows. For this he promises that abundant reward has been stored up for them in heaven.

Since tribulation is the exercise of life in this world, we admonish your united affection to endure events with equanimity, lest this misfortune inflict any faintheartedness upon you. It is a labor through which we believe that you receive spiritual fruit from Christ.

Recall, then, the saying of the prophet who sings:

‘Going, they went and wept, casting their seed; but coming, they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves’ (Ps. CXXV, 6).

Having first said these things, take comfort, holy brother, and be strong. We trust that, under the protection of him for whose love you endure such dishonor in exile, you will return to your own see. For our unceasing prayer before Christ is that he himself, restraining the madness of those who rage, may restore you to your own see.

We do not cease to labor with all our strength so that, supported by his help in whatever ways we can, we may restore you to your see. Do not hesitate in anything, and do not let excessive sadness oppress you. For we confidently hope and believe that Christ our Lord will soon favor our prayers and that, through his mercy, you will joyfully recover the see granted to you to govern, so that with glad heart we may offer praises to Christ.”

# CHAPTER IV  
## ON THE USE OF THE PALLIUM

[Col. 0081]

### SUMMARY

The supreme pontiffs sometimes gave the pallium to those who were present and sometimes sent it to those who were absent. The ancient rite of giving it to those present is displayed by the *Roman Order*. Four formulas of letters by which it was sent are contained here.

## TITLES

# TITLE I

[Col. 0081B]

**[Note: [Col. 0081C] “If shepherds.”** I have no doubt at all that this formula was taken from Gregory the Great, although perhaps not entirely from one place but from various passages here and there. This is shown by certain fragments inserted into different letters; it is also suggested by the style, which is wholly Gregorian, and by Gregorian expressions.

Although this is clear in itself, it may be shown even more plainly by comparison with the letters that the holy Pontiff wrote to various people when he sent the pallium or instructed newly ordained bishops with admonitions, especially his letter to Maximus, bishop of Salona.

John VIII used this formula for the most part when, in the year 878, he sent the pallium to Walo, bishop of Metz. He copied it word for word up to the words “lest he find.” Leo VII also used it in 935 when he granted the pallium to Gerard of Lauriacum, as did Alexander II in 1062 when he likewise sent the pallium to Peter, bishop of Dalmatia.

It is useful to compare the letters of John, Leo, and Alexander with the formula of the *Diurnus*, for this will make both the use of the formula clearer and contribute something to ecclesiastical learning.

In the *Roman Order*, when a bishop is ordained, the ordaining bishop’s exhortation begins with words very similar to the beginning of our formula:

‘If shepherds of animals, for temporal advantage, subject themselves to such labor that they may guard their masters’ sheep without loss and acquire profit, what shall we say in turn on the day of the strict judgment, when the Shepherd of shepherds appears, etc.’]

“If shepherds of sheep are content to endure sun and frost day and night for the protection of their flock, and constantly watch with vigilant eyes lest any of the sheep perish by wandering or die torn by the bites of wild beasts, let us consider with how much exertion and care we ought to remain vigilant, who are called shepherds of souls.

Let us not cease to perform the office entrusted to us in guarding the Lord’s sheep, lest on the day of divine judgment the guilt of negligence torment us before the supreme Shepherd because of our laziness, since for the time being we are judged more exalted than others by the dignity of our office.

We have sent the pallium to your fraternity according to custom, for celebrating the solemn rites of Mass. We grant you permission to use it only in the manner in which your predecessors and their predecessors are known to have used it, while the privileges of your church remain in their established condition.

Since the honor of this garment must be preserved by the modest vitality of your conduct, we exhort you to make the ornaments of your character correspond to it, so that, with God as author, you may rightly be distinguished in both respects.

Therefore let your life be a rule for your sons. If any sluggishness has entered them, let them rise up through it; let them look in it for what they should imitate; let them always advance by contemplating it, so that, after God, it may appear that their living well is your doing.

**[Note: [Col. 0082D] “Therefore let the heart neither…”** What Gregory the Great writes to Maximus of Salona in book VII, letter 130, is so similar that what the *Diurnus* contains seems to be nothing other than an expanded version of Gregory’s exhortation:

‘We have sent the pallium according to custom for use at the sacred solemnities of Mass, and we wish you to claim its meaning in every respect. For the honor of this garment is humility and justice. Therefore let your fraternity hasten to show itself with all its mind humble in prosperity and, if adversity should ever arise, upright with justice; friendly toward the good and opposed to the perverse; never suppressing the face of anyone who speaks for the truth; devoting itself to works of mercy according to the measure of its substance; yet desiring to persist even beyond its means; showing compassion to the weak; rejoicing with those who are well; counting the losses of others as its own; exulting in others’ joys as though they were its own; raging against vices when correcting them; soothing the minds of assistants when fostering virtues; maintaining judgment in anger without anger; and, in tranquility, not abandoning the strictness of its severity.

This, dearest brother, is the meaning of the pallium you have received. If you preserve it carefully, you possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly.’]

Therefore let neither the heart be lifted up by prosperous things that flatter temporarily, nor cast down by adversity. Whatever it may be, let it be overcome by the virtue of patience.

Let hatred find no place with you, nor indiscriminate favor. Let the good find you kindly; let the wicked recognize you as strict. Let evil suggestion not make you condemn the innocent; let favor not excuse the guilty. Do not show yourself lenient toward offenders, lest by failing to punish what you have not avenged you permit it to be committed.

Let there be in you both the gentleness of a good shepherd and the severity of a strict judge: the one to cherish the innocent who live uprightly, the other to restrain the restless from wickedness by striking them.

But since at times the zeal of superiors, when it wishes to act as the strict avenger of the wicked, goes too far, when correction turns into cruelty, restrain anger by judgment. Use the discipline of censure in such a way that you strike at faults while not withdrawing affection from the persons whom you correct.

Show yourself merciful to the poor insofar as virtue permits. Let your defense assist the oppressed; let a modest firmness oppose their oppressors. Accept no one’s person against justice. Let justice not despise anyone who complains. Let the protection of equity excel in you, so that neither the power of the rich may persuade them to dare anything outside the path of reason, nor the humility of the poor concerning themselves cause them to despair.
