Thus, with God’s mercy, you may be such as sacred Scripture commands when it says: ‘A bishop must be blameless’ (1 Tim. III, 2).

You will be able to use all these qualities beneficially if you have charity as your teacher. Whoever follows it does not depart from the straight path.

Behold, dearest brother, among many other things, these are the duties of the priesthood; these are the duties of the pallium. If you carefully preserve them, you possess inwardly what you have shown that you received outwardly.”

**[Note: [Col. 0083C] “But the faith.”** In the following formula faith is likewise mentioned, though explained less fully than would be proper. From both formulas the following conclusions are established:

1. Bishops customarily sent a profession of faith to the Apostolic See when they requested the pallium in writing.
2. Both formulas concern bishops who were not subject to the ordination of the Apostolic See; for those bishops were ordained at Rome and professed the faith at their ordination.
3. Both formulas were composed shortly after the Fifth Synod. At that time it was necessary to explain one’s faith more precisely because many schismatics did not accept the Fifth Synod, and thus receiving it would be evidence of orthodoxy.
4. Their author—or rather their compiler—was Gregory the Great. No one was more exacting in requiring the profession of the faith and of the Fifth Synod. Consequently, in professions of faith issued by supreme pontiffs or bishops, explicit mention of both occurred so frequently.

For illuminating this passage, what Gratian cites in the chapter beginning “Optatum,” Distinction C, from John VIII’s letter to Wilibert, bishop of Cologne, is especially useful:

‘We have not been able to confer the pallium upon you at present, because we have found that the document of your faith is less complete than it ought to be. In it you have made no mention, as is customary, of any of the holy universal Synods in which the symbol of our faith is contained, nor of the decrees established by the Roman pontiffs. Nor have you secured it with your own subscription, or sent someone to confirm it by oath.’]

“Although you should have explained more fully the faith that you briefly set down in your letters, we nevertheless give thanks to our Redeemer because we have recognized that, even in its brevity, it is orthodox.

**[Note: [Col. 0084C] “The Holy Trinity, etc.”** This clause reflects an earlier age of the Church. In this formula, as also in the following three, there is no mention of the fullness of power, nor of a special fidelity and obedience toward the Apostolic See, nor of apostolic vicariate or authority over bishops, nor finally—except in the third formula—of an urgent petition. There is only language of honor and encouragement toward a holier way of life.]

May the Holy Trinity surround your fraternity with the protection of its grace and direct us in the path of its fear, so that, after the bitterness of this one life, we may together deserve to attain eternal sweetness.

# TITLE II

**Another formula.**

**[Note: [Col. 0084D] “The priest’s office.”** There is no room for doubt that this second formula was taken from Gregory the Great. The style, the ideas, and the fact that nearly half of it is repeated in four places in Gregory in almost the same words make this clear. The preface up to the words “may gladden with reward” is found in Leo IX’s letter 11 to John of Salerno.]

“If, with inward vigilance, we consider the assumption of the priestly office, it is more a burden than an honor. For it is not enough for the priest to care for his own concerns unless he also manages those of others beneficially. The care of pastoral governance rises to this point: that, with devout foresight, it receives responsibility for others and vigilantly arranges itself for their protection, so that the lurking wolf may have no opportunity to break in through him or inflict injury upon the sheep.

Since we have assumed this continual care, we must exercise constant vigilance, so that we may close the way to the crafty and ancient enemy of the human race and resist his voracity with all our strength. Let us ensure that, through our negligence, he does not—God forbid—devour anyone with his ravenous jaws, so that the destruction caused by dreadful negligence may not justly be charged to our punishment.

Let us therefore exhibit what we say. By the dispensation of divine providence it has happened that we preside; let us hasten to be useful as much as we can, so that, when the creditor comes to settle accounts with us, he may find that we have made a profit and may gladden us with his promised reward.

Consider this, therefore, dearest brother, and recognize that you have undertaken the position you have obtained not for rest but for labor. Strengthen the hearts of the faithful by exhortation; convert the unbelieving. To deserve to achieve this more easily,

**[Note: [Col. 0084D] “Let your life commend your preaching.”** A related passage occurs in Gregory’s letter 113, book VII, indiction 2, when he sent the pallium to Syagrius of Autun:

‘Your fraternity must exercise itself with the greatest zeal in all pursuits, and must watch carefully over the conduct of those subject to you, so that your example, instruction, and life may be their teacher, etc.’]

let your life commend your preaching. Let it itself be their instruction; let it itself be their teacher. Under your instruction, let them sigh for the desire of eternal life; living according to your example, let them reach it. Let them despise temporal things, and, scorning what will pass away, always long for those things that are closed by no end.

Apply your effort to these things, therefore, and persist in them with the full attention of your mind, so that when they have attained these things through your preaching and imitation, you may receive greater things from our God, in proportion as you have not ceased to exercise the duties of your office with fitting concern for winning souls for him.

Moreover, according to ancient custom, we have sent the pallium to your fraternity. Remember to use it in the manner in which our predecessors granted it to your predecessors,

**[Note: [Col. 0085C] “With the integrity of the privileges preserved.”** When the pallium was sent, privileges were either granted for the first time or those previously granted were confirmed. Gregory the Great first granted them to Syagrius:

‘Lest we seem merely to have bestowed the splendor of this garment upon you, we have also taken care to grant this along with it.’

And afterward:

‘The order of reason altogether admonishes us that, when we must grant some privileges along with the use of the pallium, etc.’

Examples of confirmation of privileges once granted occur everywhere.]

with the integrity of your privileges preserved.

Although you ought to have explained the faith of your fraternity carefully in the letter that you sent, we nevertheless rejoice in the Lord, who has taught us through your confession of the solemn symbol that it is orthodox.

**[Note: [Col. 0085C] “Moreover, it has come to us, etc.”** This entire passage concerning the conferral of sacred orders through simony extends up to the words “for which reason I admonish” and is taken from Gregory the Great’s book IV, letter 50, to Virgilius of Arles, when he sent him the pallium, and from letter 55 to John, bishop of Corinth. It is drawn especially from letter 56 of the same book to the bishops of Greece, in which, with a few changes, the exhortatory conclusion occurs that is lacking in the other two. It is also found in book V, letter 7, to the bishops of Epirus, up to the words “We pray, etc.”; that conclusion, however, has a nearly corresponding counterpart there.

From this one may gather how widely the plague of simony was raging at that time and how greatly the most holy Pontiff labored to abolish it. Letter 44 of book IV explains clearly enough what was included under the name of simony. Consult that passage, and, if you wish, turn your eyes from it toward our own times. The same passage is inserted in letter 94 of John VIII, in which he sent the pallium to Rostagnus of Arles, volume IX of the new edition of the general councils.]

“Moreover, it has come to us that in those regions sacred orders are conferred in exchange for payment. If this is so, I say it with tears and denounce it with groaning: when the priestly order has fallen inwardly, it will not long be able to stand outwardly either.

For we know from the Gospel what our Redeemer himself did: entering the temple, he overturned the seats of those selling doves (Matt. XXI, 12). To sell doves means to receive temporal profit for the Holy Spirit, whom almighty God, consubstantial with himself, gives to human beings through the laying on of hands. From this evil, as I have said, it is already indicated what follows. For those who presumed to sell doves in the temple of God had their seats fall by God’s judgment, because error spreads among their subjects with increase. The man who is advanced to sacred honor for a price is already corrupted at the very root of his advancement and is prepared to sell to others what he bought.

And where is what is written: ‘You received without payment; give without payment’ (Matt. X, 8)?

Since the Simoniac heresy was the first to arise against the holy Church, why do you not consider, why do you not see, that whoever ordains or promotes for a price thereby acts so as to become a heretic?

For this reason I admonish and earnestly entreat you to be entirely vigilant, so that no payment, no favor, and no entreaty from any persons may claim anything for itself in sacred orders. Rather, let the office be conferred upon the man whom the gravity of his character and his actions commend. For if—which we do not believe—we should perceive anything of this kind taking place, we shall correct it with canonical severity, as it deserves.”

[Note: [Col. 0085D] “We pray,” etc. Nearly the same epilogue occurs in Gregory’s letter to Virgilius of Arles.] We pray almighty God to surround you with his protection and grant you to fulfill by your works the office of the priesthood that you have undertaken.

## TITLE III. Another formula.

[Note: [Col. 0085D] “The use of the pallium.” In this form Symmachus sent the pallium in the year 501 to Theodore, bishop of Lauriacum, as appears in the new collection of councils, among the letters of Symmachus, letter 11, which is said to have been taken from the appendix to the Chronicle of Reichersperg and from Hondius’s *Metropolis Salisburgensis* [Col. 0086C]. It is also found in Goldast’s appendix of documents. There can scarcely be doubt that by this same form Symmachus sent the pallium to Caesarius of Arles. Although the learned Thomasinus laments that Symmachus’s letter to Caesarius has perished, I nevertheless think that the loss may thereby be repaired. We learn that Symmachus sent the pallium to Caesarius from Pope Vigilius’s letter to Auxanius of Arles, written in the year 543: “Because we believe it fitting that this should be fulfilled, so that the pallium’s adornment may not be lacking to one acting in our place, we grant you, by the holy authority of blessed Peter, its use, just as our predecessor Symmachus of holy memory is said to have bestowed it upon your predecessor.” Some believe that before Symmachus no pontiff gave a pallium to any bishop except the bishop of Ostia, to whom Pope Mark gave one in the year 336, so that he might be distinguished as the ordainer of the supreme pontiff; and they interpret Vigilius’s mention of Symmachus alone, and not of other predecessors, in this sense [Col. 0086D]. But the words of this formula, “according to the custom of our forefathers” and “according to the custom of your church,” overturn that assumption: mention is made both of forefathers, who are plural, and of a custom, which cannot be established by a single instance. Paschal I also used this form, with a few alterations, when he sent the pallium to Bernard, bishop of Vienne, in the year 817. “With a few alterations,” I say: for he prefixed a preface of five lines and added the solemn closing formula of that period, mentioning the notary; he also added confirmation of the privileges, about which this formula is silent; and he omitted a few words of the ancient formula that would have been better retained. See the appendix to volume VII of the general councils, latest edition, p. 1869, and observe in passing that this formula was in use for at least three hundred years—namely, from the year 501, when Symmachus was alive, to 817, when Paschal wrote [Col. 0087B]. I say “at least,” for since it is the simplest and the first of all those that have come down to us with an explicit mention of the pallium, it also appears to be the oldest. The additions seen in other forms are indications of later periods that departed from the original simplicity.]

You requested, as was proper, the use of the pallium, both for the adornment of the priestly office and to display the unanimity that the whole flock of the Lord’s sheep entrusted to blessed Peter the Apostle unquestionably possesses with him. Since you are a bishop of a Church founded by those same apostles, we have willingly granted the petition of your predecessors; and, to display toward you and your Church the love of that Apostolic See, we signify that we have sent you, from the use of our own pallium, one that you may use according to the custom of your Church. We fittingly and necessarily admonish your Fraternity that, considering both the work of the Church entrusted to you and the benevolence and affection of the Apostolic See toward you, you should, with God guiding your heart, strive to carry out the governance committed to you in such a way that, having attained the dignity of the office with which you are adorned, you may strive still more to adorn it by uprightness of conduct, vigilant diligence, and preservation of the integrity of the faith.

## 90 TITLE IV. Another formula for the bishops of Sicily.

[Col. 0088A]

[Note: [Col. 0087B] “The benevolence of the Apostolic See,” etc. The whole passage, word for word, is contained in book V, letter 8, of Gregory the Great, written in the year 595 to the bishop of Messana; it is also contained in letter 18 of the same book, addressed to John of Syracuse. The preface up to the words “we have determined should be granted” had appeared in book IV, letter 54, to Marinianus of Ravenna.] Moved by the benevolence of the Apostolic See and [Note: [Col. 0088B] “By ancient custom.” In Gregory: “according to the order of ancient custom.” Three points are thereby confirmed. First, that pallia were sent to bishops by the supreme pontiffs even before Symmachus’s time; for there could not be an ancient custom that had existed for less than a hundred years. Second, that pallia were sent not only to metropolitans but also to bishops generally; for in Gregory’s time there was no prelate in Sicily who possessed metropolitan rights. Third, by what stages the city of Messana rose to become an archiepiscopal see.] prompted by ancient custom, we have foreseen granting the use of the pallium to your Fraternity, which is known to have undertaken the office of governing the Church of Ill.; namely, at those times and in that order in which, as you do not doubt, your predecessor also used it [Note: [Col. 0087B] “You do not doubt.” In Gregory: “we do not doubt.”].

Nevertheless, we admonish you that, just as you rejoice to have received from us the use of this distinction for the honor of the priestly office, so you should strive to adorn the priestly office undertaken by our authority, for the glory of Christ, by the uprightness of your conduct and actions. For you will be conspicuous in reciprocal honor if, together with this bodily garment, the good qualities of your mind also correspond [Col. 0088B].

We also confirm by our authority all the privileges that are known to have been previously granted to your Church, and decree that they remain inviolate.

## 91 CHAPTER V. ON THE SUPREME PONTIFF’S INSTRUCTIONS TO BISHOPS OF HIS ORDINATION, ON SACRED PLACES AND THE RELICS OF THE SAINTS.

[Col. 0087]

### SUMMARY

The formulas contained in this chapter set out the supreme pontiff’s instructions to bishops of his ordination concerning sacred places and the relics of the saints. He orders sacred places—that is, basilicas, oratories, baptisteries, and altars—to be consecrated; shrines to be installed; relics to be granted or deposited; the bodies of saints to be raised and placed in a more honorable location; and priests to be appointed over oratories and basilicas. Here there are not only formulas of instruction but also formulas of petition.

### TITLES

## TITLE I. To a bishop, concerning the ordination of a priest.

[Col. 0087C]

The priest who had presided over the basilica of the estate of Ill. is said to have been deprived of this present life. In his place, those concerned request that the deacon Ill. be substituted. Let your Charity investigate his life and conduct with careful scrutiny; and, if the authority of the venerable canons supports him in every respect by the merits of his life, [Note: [Col. 0087C] “On the evening of the Sabbath.” That is, at the appropriate times of the fasts [Col. 0087D]. If “the evening of the Sabbath” is understood according to the ancient custom, it means nothing other than that part of the day during which the fast had not yet been broken; and therefore it may also include the first part of the Lord’s Day if the fast extended until then. See Saint Leo’s letter to Dioscorus.] you shall solemnly ordain him priest on the evening of the Sabbath, without intercession, so that under observance of ecclesiastical discipline he may be worthy to govern the aforesaid Church blamelessly.

## 92 TITLE II. Another formula.

[Col. 0087C]

Our son Ill. has requested that a priest be ordained for him in the oratory consecrated at his own insistence. Therefore, if your Fraternity sees that it is expedient, and that what has been donated can suffice without complaint for those serving there, we decree by this present instruction, in fulfillment of the aforesaid desire, that your Charity should ordain at that place, at a suitable time, a priest distinguished by worthy conduct and perfect in faith.

## TITLE III. Petition for the dedication of an oratory.

To the holy and most blessed Lord, Father of Fathers, Pope Ill., your servant.

[Col. 0089A]

Whenever venerable places are consecrated to divine worship in honor of the saints, this contributes to the growth of the Catholic religion.

I submit that I have built at my own expense, on the estate of Ill. belonging to me, a basilica which I desire to have consecrated in honor of the saints Ill. and Ill., martyrs. For the lighting and support of those serving in that basilica, I offer Ill. and Ill.

Therefore I beseech your Apostolate to issue your instructions to the venerable Ill., bishop of the city of Ill., so that he may consecrate the aforesaid basilica with the sacred mysteries, and so that by this act holy veneration may grow during the time of your Beatitude.

I likewise promise that I will claim nothing further for myself from that place except the privilege of procession, which is owed in common to all Christians.

## 93

With an equal petition I ask that, when you have issued your instructions to the venerable Ill., bishop of the city of Ill., he may solemnly hand over to me relics of the saints mentioned above.

## TITLE IV. Reply concerning the dedication of an oratory.

[Note: [Col. 0089C] “Petition.” Pelagius I is found to have used this formula twice, once when writing to Eleutherius and again to the bishop Alterius, if we trust Holstenius, who excerpted those two letters, together with others, from the collection of Cardinal Deusdedit [Col. 0089D]. Gregory the Great subsequently used it in three places: book VII, letter 85, indiction 2; book VIII, letter 63, to Decius of Lilybaeum; and book XI, letter 20, to Passivus of Firmum.] He has submitted to us in a petition, the contents of which follow, that he founded, out of his devotion, an oratory on the estate of Ill., belonging to Ill., and desires it to be consecrated in honor of Saint Ill.

Therefore, if the aforesaid building lawfully belongs within your parish and it is established that no body has been buried there, after first receiving a lawful donation—namely, Ill. and Ill., or Ill., free from fiscal claims, amounting to so many solidi, with the municipal records cited—you shall solemnly consecrate the aforesaid oratory without public Masses, so that neither a baptistery may be built there in the future nor you appoint a cardinal priest.

But if he should perhaps prefer Masses to be celebrated there, let him know through your Love that a priest must be requested for this purpose, so that no such thing may in any way be presumed by any other priest. As for the shrines received, you shall place them there with due reverence.

## 94 TITLE V. Reply concerning shrines to be requested.

[Col. 0090A]

[Note: [Col. 0089D] “Shrines,” etc. This entire formula, as well as the two that follow, is taken from book IX, letter 26, of Saint Gregory; it is also found in book VII, letter 107. “Shrines” here are either the relics of the saints themselves or, more properly, the containers of the relics, that is, reliquaries.] In a petition submitted to him, Ill. requests that the shrines of blessed Ill. and Ill. be granted to him, so that a basilica built at his own expense in their name may be solemnly consecrated. Therefore, dearest brother, it is fitting that by our instruction you should comply with the desire of the aforesaid person, so that he may attain the fulfillment of his devotion in the consecration he requests.

## TITLE VI. Concerning the granting of shrines.

In the oratory built by Ill., which is said to have been consecrated by order of our predecessor in honor of blessed Ill. and Ill., let your Love return, with appropriate devotion, the shrine of blessed Martyr Ill. that you have received [Col. 0090B], so that the holy and devout petition of the aforesaid person may, through the ministry of the priestly office, attain its fulfillment.

## TITLE VII. Concerning the granting of a relic of the holy angel.

Ill. [Note: [Col. 0089D] “The relics of the holy archangel.” We learn from Saint Gregory’s book II, letter 72, that “relics” (*beneficia*) means relics: there mention is made of a cross sent by the supreme pontiff to Dynamianus, in which relics of Saint Peter’s chain and Saint Lawrence’s grill were inserted. But someone may ask what relics of Saint Michael can be imagined; for it is certain that “the angel” signifies Michael. It may be answered that perhaps it was a fragment from the stone on which the archangel once appeared, either on Mount Gargano [Col. 0090D] or somewhere else. It seems more credible, however, that it was a pallium placed upon the altar or memorial of the holy archangel and given as a gift to those who requested a blessing. This conjecture is strengthened, and rendered almost certain, by an excerpt communicated to me by the distinguished Stephanus Baluzius from the manuscript history of the monastery of Saint Michael of Cuxa in the diocese of Elne, composed around the year 1030 by Garsias, a monk of that place. It reads: “These are relics of the glorious archangel Michael himself, namely, from the pallium of his holy memorial.”] requests in a petition that the relics of the holy Archangel be granted to him, so that an oratory built at his own expense in his name may be solemnly consecrated. Therefore, dearest brother, it is fitting that by our instruction you should comply with the desire of the aforesaid person, so that he may attain the fulfillment of his devotion in the consecration he requests.

## 95 TITLE VIII. Reply concerning the dedication of an oratory within a monastery of monks.

[Note: [Col. 0090D] “The religious,” etc. The same words are found in Gregory, book VII, letter 49. It is thereby established that bishops and priests possessed rights in consecrated oratories, while monks possessed rights in offerings.] Religious desires ought to be fulfilled without difficulty. Since Ill. said that an oratory had been founded, at his own request, at the place where the monks live, we have thought it necessary to admonish your Love by these present instructions that, whenever requested, you should proceed without delay to the aforesaid place and perform the venerable solemn rites of dedication, so that, whenever necessary, the priests serving in the Church at the place mentioned above may celebrate the venerable sacrifices of the Mass. Let neither your Fraternity nor the priests at that monastery inflict any annoyance there, apart from the careful observance of discipline; and if anything of benefit should accrue through the devotion of various persons, let them consider it theirs to claim, since whatever is evidently offered ought to benefit the monks serving at that place.

## 96 TITLE IX. Concerning the depositing of relics within a monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] “Religious desires,” etc. This formula is taken from book II, letter 98, of Saint Gregory, who wrote to Fortunatus of Naples concerning the consecration of the monastery of the abbess Gratiosa. Letter 52 of book I, addressed to John, bishop of Sorrento, is also related to it.] Religious desires ought to be fulfilled without difficulty. Therefore, since Ill., abbot of the monastery of Ill., or Ill., who belongs to the aforesaid monastery, has said that an oratory was founded according to his wish and requests that it be dedicated, we have thought it necessary to admonish your Love by these present instructions that, whenever requested, you should proceed without delay to the aforesaid place and perform the venerable solemn rites of dedication, so that, whenever necessary, the priests serving in the Church at that place may celebrate the venerable sacrifices of the Mass.

Let neither your Fraternity nor the priests there inflict any annoyance, apart from the careful observance of discipline; or, if anything of benefit should accrue through the devotion of various persons, let them consider it theirs to claim, since whatever is evidently offered ought to benefit the monks serving at that place.

As for the shrines received, you shall place them there with due reverence.

## TITLE X. Concerning the depositing of relics within the episcopal residence.

[Note: [Col. 0091D] “Within the episcopal residence.” Observe the discipline of the period, by which a bishop of a suburban city was indeed permitted to have a domestic oratory, but one that had to be duly consecrated; and not before permission had been granted by the supreme pontiff. Thus Gelasius, letter 9, to the bishops of Lucania, chapter IV: “They must not dare to dedicate newly established basilicas without having requested the customary instructions.” From these words it may be inferred that this practice had been observed from ancient times [Col. 0092D].] Since your Love requests that the shrines of blessed Ill., granted to you by our will, be deposited in the oratory which you assert that you built in the name of the same blessed martyr within the episcopal residence of your city, so that the place itself may be consecrated in his honor [Note: [Col. 0092D] “Consecrated.” The practice of private, as I might call it, and hidden oratories had not yet become established. Each oratory had its own fixed stone altar and its own building, separated from the roof of the secular house.], we grant your request—provided it is clear that no body has been buried there—so that, with God as author, you may attain the fulfillment of your desire.

## TITLE XI. Petition of a bishop.

It certainly belongs to the praise of the supreme Pontiff whenever the number of holy basilicas appears to increase. I acknowledge that I have built at my own expense, on the estate of Ill. situated in our territory, a basilica which, with God as author and with your favor, I desire to consecrate in honor of Saint Ill., the martyr [Col. 0091D]. For that basilica, toward repairs or the support of its custodians, I offer from the same estate of Ill. and Ill. [Note: [Col. 0092D] “For that basilica,” etc. Again observe the custom of the period, according to which anyone who built a basilica was also required to provide what was needed for repairs, the support of the custodians, and the lights.] Therefore I beseech your Apostolate that, once your order has been issued, I may dedicate the basilica in honor of the aforesaid Saint Ill., the martyr.

## TITLE XII. Another reply.

We grant permission to dedicate the basilica which your Love states that you recently built in honor of blessed Apostles Ill. and Ill., especially if you affirm that the areas in which the building was founded belong to your Church. In it we have also ordered blessings from the Apostolic shrines to be placed—namely, [Note: [Col. 0092D] “Little pallia.” Saint Gregory also calls them *brandea* and veils.] little pallia taken from their confessors’ shrines. With the prudent devotion of a pontiff, you shall also prudently ensure that you formally transfer, with solemn devotion, the property you have set aside from your own resources for the benefit of those serving there [Col. 0092B].

## TITLE XIII. Another reply.

Ill. states in a submitted petition that he formerly founded a monastery on land granted to him by Ill., on the estate of Ill., and says that he has recently built in it the oratory that was lacking, requesting that it be dedicated in honor of Saint Ill.

[Note: [Col. 0092D] “And therefore.” This is the solemn form of an instruction used in the titles that follow.] Therefore, dearest brother, if the aforesaid foundation lawfully belongs within your diocese, you shall, upon receiving this instruction, consecrate the oratory mentioned above with the customary blessing. Only ensure that its founder does not in any way retain it for public processions; you shall celebrate the sacred mysteries there only for the congregation known to be present, so that the religious community may pray to the Lord day and night without the disturbance of the crowd.

## TITLE XIV. Another reply.

We have received your Love’s petition, rejoicing in the completion of a good work, with appropriate congratulations. Therefore the basilica which you assert formerly to have been a cave of the Arian heresy, but which you have now, through your diligence, adapted to the Catholic faith, with Christ our God and our Savior reigning, we grant for consecration in honor of blessed Ill. and Ill., the martyrs.

## 99

Therefore, dearest brother, if the aforesaid building lawfully belongs within your parish and it is established that no body has been buried there [Col. 0092D], know that by our instructions the authority to reconcile and consecrate the aforesaid basilica has been granted to you.

## TITLE XV. Concerning the dedication of an altar.

[Col. 0093A]

After reviewing the tenor of your report and also the petition submitted by Ill., it was necessary to give a reasonable reply. Therefore, let your Love’s consecration be applied to the altar said to have been constructed in the basilica of Saint Ill., formerly dedicated, so that the builder’s devotion may attain the full fulfillment of his desire.

## TITLE XVI. Concerning the depositing of the body of a saint.

Our son Ill. has informed us in his submissions that the body of blessed Ill. was recently found in the region of Ill.; and that his glorious father Ill. has determined to place the same body in the basilica that he recently built. He requests that the same church [Note: [Col. 0093D] “Solemnly,” etc. Observe the two modes of consecration: one ordinary, of which the preceding formulas speak, and another solemn, for which neighboring bishops are summoned. Such was the dedication of the basilica that occasioned the Second Synod of Orange.] be solemnly consecrated.

Therefore, dearest brother, if the aforesaid building lawfully belongs within your parish and it is established that no body has been buried there, after first receiving from the aforesaid man a lawful donation sufficient to provide suitably for the lights of the same basilica, you shall diligently dedicate the same church solemnly, summoning the other brothers and our fellow bishops who are your neighbors, so that he may attain the fulfillment of his devotion in the consecration he requests.

## 100 TITLE XVII. A basilica repaired after a fire.

Your Love states that the basilica in the fortress of Ill. was repaired after a fire, and that the inhabitants of that place desire it to be consecrated in honor of blessed Ill. [Col. 0093C]. We grant you, by the sequence of our instruction, the authority to dedicate it, so that the devotion of the faithful may attain its proper fulfillment. [Note: [Col. 0093D] “Know that the shrines have been sent.” Relics were sent from Rome, or at least their reception elsewhere was ordered by a special instruction. In this way the Pontiff appeared in some measure himself to construct the holy place.] Know that the shrines have recently been sent; and you shall place the shrines received with due reverence.

## TITLE XVIII. A basilica built beside another after the latter’s collapse.

You state that the basilica of blessed Ill., once built of brick, completely collapsed, and that the ruin itself became so filled with rubbish and other refuse that it would have been more difficult to clean than to build. You also report that in a place quite near it, you constructed another basilica in honor of the aforesaid Martyr, not of brick but of lime [Col. 0094A] and sand, and that it rose in a far better condition than the former one. Now you desire that authority be granted to you to dedicate this basilica, and that the relics themselves be transferred from the aforesaid ruins to the new basilica.

Therefore, since what your Fraternity requests is pious and just, with God’s favor we grant you permission to dedicate the aforesaid place; and also to transfer the relics with due honor [Note: [Col. 0093D] “To transfer.” Just as it was not permitted to consecrate a basilica without the shrines sent from Rome, so neither was it permitted to transfer them from one place to another for the purpose of consecration.] and place them in the basilica that you have built. These things are recognized as contributing to the joy of the sons of the Church and to the benefit of your reputation and reward.

## 101 TITLE XIX. Petition for the dedication of a baptistery.

[Col. 0094B]

The solemnity desired by the faithful calls for the basilica’s enlargement, so that the devotion of the people may grow more greatly for the good of religion. Therefore, because I have established a baptistery in the basilica of Saint Ill., on the estate of Ill. belonging to me [Note: [Col. 0093D] “Baptistery.” This is not the sacred font itself but an additional building attached to the basilica; hence it is called an enlargement of the basilica. It was generally round, like a vault, with the sacred font in the center. In some churches, especially cathedrals, such a building can still be seen; although it is not under the same roof as the basilica, it has its own rite of consecration. It was customarily decorated with images of the baptisms celebrated in the New Testament—Christ’s baptism by John, the eunuch’s by Philip, and so forth. It was also adorned with statues and relics of the saints, and in former times even had its own altar. These facts are established partly from ancient writers and partly from surviving traces of the ancient religion.], I desire that the relics of the holy martyrs Ill. and Ill. be introduced into the same place. Therefore I prostrate myself before the dignity of your Apostolate and beseech you, by the See over which you preside as vicars of the Divinity by divine appointment, to issue instructions to our venerable bishop Ill., in whose diocese the building appears to have been constructed, ordering that the baptistery be dedicated with the aforesaid martyrs' favor, so that the relics may be placed there in the Catholic faith, while the people increase and give thanks to your Beatitude. I promise to assign to that basilica [Note: [Col. 0094D] “To that basilica.” Wherever a baptistery was established, it had its own congregation and thus became, in our terminology, a parish. Hence Pope Zacharias prohibited baptisteries from being established in private oratories. Hence also the formula says that the people’s devotion may increase.] the estates of Ill. and Ill., with the deed of donation executed.

## 102 TITLE XX. Reply concerning the dedication of a baptistery.

[Col. 0094C]

[Note: [Col. 0094D] “Our son,” etc. This formula was taken for the most part from the same source as the following one, with a few words adopted elsewhere.] Our son states in a submitted petition that a basilica on the estate of Ill., belonging to him, was dedicated some time ago, and reports that he has built in the aforesaid basilica the baptistery that was lacking. He desires it to be consecrated with a solemn blessing, and requests that the shrines of Saints Ill. and Ill. be placed in the same baptistery.

Therefore, dearest brother, if the aforesaid foundation lawfully belongs within your diocese, you shall, upon receiving this instruction, satisfy the founder’s desire. Nevertheless, a solemn donation of the first offerings must precede it [Note: [Col. 0094D] “Solemn donation.” This would suffice for the support of the cardinal priest, that is, the titular priest. It is called lawful by Pelagius I and Saint Gregory, though neither specifies the amount.], and you shall declare according to custom that the founder is to retain no further right there except the privilege of procession [Col. 0095A], which is owed in common to all Christians. Thus both the founder’s desires may be fulfilled in every respect and the stains of sin may be washed away from those regenerated there through the sacred bath.

## TITLE XXI. Another reply.

[Note: [Col. 0095A] “The petition,” etc. The formula has been taken, with a few alterations, from book XI, letter 24, of Saint Gregory, addressed to Honorius, bishop of Tarentum.] Ill. has informed us in a petition, the contents of which follow, that he built a baptistery on the estate of Ill. belonging to him [Col. 0096A].

Therefore, dearest brother, upon receiving this instruction, you shall satisfy the founder’s desire, so that the stains of sin may be washed away there through the venerable bath.

## 103 CHAPTER VI. ON ADMINISTERING AND ALIENATING THE PROPERTY OF THE CHURCH.

[Col. 0095]

### SUMMARY

When a steward is sent to administer a patrimony, he is first given authority to manage it; then letters are written to the tenants, so that they may obey; to the Governor of the Province, so that he may provide protection; likewise to the judge, so that he may assist in the causes of the poor; and to the local bishops, so that they may lend support. Afterwards authority is granted to draw up lawful leases, to exchange estates or slaves, and to grant slaves or boys. Finally, after the accounts of the administration have been rendered, immunity is granted. Formulas for all these matters are found here, together with three additional formulas: one by which a slave is granted freedom, and two *tractoriae* (official letters of conveyance), by which those sent to conduct the business of the Apostolic See, or those returning to their homeland after properly paying their respects at the Apostolic threshold, are furnished with credentials.

### TITLES

## TITLE I. Instruction issued when a layman is tonsured and made a regional notary.

[Col. 0095B]

We do not disdain to admit into the ecclesiastical fold those whom a reputation for good life and the merit of excellent conduct commend.

And since, from the report of many persons, we have been satisfied concerning the modesty of your conduct, and since you are a man of refined life, we have judged it fitting to enroll you among the clergy of this Apostolic Church of God and, by this document of instruction, to record you from this day among the Regional Notaries, by the authority of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, whose representatives we are, though unequal to him in merits, by God’s gracious appointment. Thus, remembering such a benefit or promotion, you shall throughout the days of your life [Col. 0095C] 104 faithfully and sincerely serve in whatever your superiors enjoin, and display obedience and uprightness in all things, so that you may appear acceptable to God and to blessed Peter the Apostle, our author and protector, and may be found among us more highly commended for faithful service and worthy of praise.

## TITLE II. Instruction issued when an absent subregional notary is made a regional notary.

Whoever faithfully displays his integrity in the responsibilities entrusted to him, and can thereby be acceptable to the Prince of the Apostles and his Vicar, is rightly advanced to greater dignity and, through the stronger support of our instruction, enriched with greater honor.

[Col. 0095D] Therefore, although long ago, yet also now, having been satisfied by the report of Ill. concerning your faithful services, we grant you the munificence of promotion. Accordingly, by the authority of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, whose representatives we are, though unequal to him in merits, by God’s gracious appointment, know that from this day you are enrolled among the Regional Notaries, so that, mindful of such a benefit, you may also be able and eager to demonstrate better services.

## TITLE III. Instruction for one going to administer a patrimony.

With salutary foresight, we believe that whatever the Church’s interests require should be entrusted to persons whom purity of faith or devotion to approved conduct commends by a praiseworthy reputation. Therefore, with God’s grace assisting you, Ill., we entrust to you by this present instruction the entire patrimony belonging to the holy Roman Church of God, which we serve with God as its author, established on the island of Ill. [105]. You are to assess and administer it. We charge you to consider the means of the tenants under the judgment of God and carefully determine how much they should contribute as rent from the present indiction [Col. 0096C], so that none of them is compelled to pay more than suffices, or pays less or more than is appropriate. Whatever you determine through prudent deliberation in the fear of God, arrange under the protection of the right hand of our Creator. If you judge that someone’s rent should be reduced, let him find relief; and if you believe that something should be added, compel him to pay what is just. For what is distributed to the poor is far removed from reward if it has not been dispensed justly and mercifully among those from whom it is collected.

## TITLE IV. Another formula, for the administrator of an estate.

Since, in organizing or examining the patrimony of the holy Roman Church—which we serve with God as its author—situated in the province of Ill., we order you to proceed as administrator during the present indiction [Col. 0096D], you are to act well and conduct yourself without burdening the tenants. Mindful of the divine judgment and of our admonition, you must show yourself so effective and faithful that, God forbid, you are not found liable for anyone’s neglect or fraud [Col. 0097A]. Rather, act in such a way that you may be commended to divine grace for your fidelity and diligence. We have also sent instructions, according to custom, to the households of the same patrimony, so that they may in no way impede the performance of the duties enjoined upon you.

## 106 TITLE V. To the tenants and households of the estates or properties established in the Province.

[Note: [Col. 0097C] “To your care,” etc. This has been copied, with very few alterations, from book VII, letter 52, of Gregory, addressed to the tenants of Syracuse; it is also found in exactly the same words in the Codex Thuaneus.] Our arrangement has determined that your care is to be subject to the administration of Ill., the Notary and Administrator of our See. We order you to hasten to obey his commands concerning the interests of the Church and the cultivation of the fields, and to follow his salutary instructions. We have given him authority to punish with strict severity those who prove rebellious [Col. 0097B]. For you must know that you have been entrusted under this condition: if any slaves are hiding outside, or if boundaries have been seized, he is not to delay reclaiming them for the rights of the Church through his diligence. You have likewise been warned, at your own peril, never to presume to use violence against another’s property or perhaps to carry anything away by force.

## TITLE VI. Instruction commending a departing administrator of the patrimony to the Provincial Judge.

[Note: [Col. 0097D] “Whoever, placed in office,” etc. In the Codex Thuaneus it appears under this heading: “Ill., bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ill., the glorious Judge of the island of Ill.” At the end several lines are added, which occur word for word in the following formula; it may reasonably be suspected that the copyist of the Codex Thuaneus combined the two formulas into one through negligence.] Whoever, placed in office, strives to commend himself to almighty God by good works is certainly preparing for himself a path by which he may arrive safely at his desired goal and, with Christ’s help, advance ever toward greater things.

Therefore, after the foregoing salutation, we commend to your greatness Ill. the notary, bearer of this document, whom we have sent to administer the ecclesiastical patrimony situated on the island of Ill., so that you may most willingly commend him to the favor and grace of your goodness in matters concerning the poor, and assist him in everything, as is truly fitting for Christians. Thus, while, with your cooperation, he carries out the task entrusted to him, may you be able to find, before the eyes of almighty God, with blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, interceding, the reward for your actions, and may you always have His Church as your debtor.

## TITLE VII. To the Patrician of the Province

[Note: [Col. 0097D] “To Patricius.” By “prefects of the province” understand either those whom the Constantinopolitan emperors sent into the West to govern provinces not yet occupied by other kings, or those whom the kings of Gaul appointed within their own dominions. Gregory has more than one letter to Patricius of Sicily; there are also several letters to the patricians of Gaul—Arigius, Dynamus, and others. These letters so closely resemble this one that they may reasonably all be said to have had one author.]

[Col. 0098A]

Whoever protects those things from which the poor are known to receive some sustenance, what else is he doing than supplying alms to the needy from his own possessions? Since this is plainly known to be the case by your Excellency, we willingly write to you what we confidently believe you will do voluntarily.

Therefore, saluting you with due honor, and commending to you in this letter the bearer of the present document, Ill., to whom the care of the ecclesiastical patrimony situated in those regions has been entrusted, we ask that the protection of your assistance graciously support him, and that you help him in whatever circumstances may require it. Thus, in return for the good services of your patronage, we may be all the more earnestly moved to pray for the safety of your Excellency, and blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, to whom you lend your service, may repay you with a worthy recompense both in this life and in the future. For it is not new for you to do what we ask: many who have come from there have testified so greatly about you that we ought to place greater confidence in the goodness of your high rank than we formerly did, since one who is asked is undoubtedly believed to provide what he is accustomed to provide even when not asked.

[Col. 0098B]

May almighty God protect you from every evil and always grant us joy in your well-being.

## TITLE VIII. Likewise, to Bishops

[Note: [Col. 0097D] “To the notary.” In the Thuaneus manuscript the inscription reads: “Ill., Bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Ill., his fellow bishops.” It then continues: “You should know that Ill., the notary of our holy Church, has been entrusted, with God’s help, with administering from the present year of the Lord’s Incarnation M. Ill. the patrimony of our holy Church situated on the island of Ill.” [Col. 0098D] “Concerning this matter, etc.”]

You should know that the notary Ill. has been entrusted, with God’s help, from the present Ill. indiction onward, with administering the patrimony of our holy Church situated on the island of Ill. Therefore, wherever necessary, let your affection hasten to provide the aforesaid notary with assistance, so that, aided by your help, he may accomplish without hindrance what we have entrusted to him. Thus, when he reports your obedience to us, you may, with God’s favor, be more favorably commended in our minds.

## TITLE IX

[Note: [Col. 0098D] “Tractoria.” Nine years ago, when I was adding notes to Mercator’s *Commonitorium*, I published both of them on the occasion of that letter which Pope Zosimus sent to all the bishops of the world concerning the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, and which Mercator reports as having been called a *tractoria*. In that place I criticized Jacobus Gothofredus, commentator on the Theodosian Code, because, when he wished to criticize Bernardinus Ferrarius, he had written that bishops, when they were summoned to a synod by the pontiffs with *tractoriae*, were indeed received on the road by the faithful with Christian charity, but that this was neither prescribed nor included in the *tractoriae*, and that it could not yet be proved from any passage. For I said that from these two *tractoriae*, by which provision is made for persons of lower rank, it could not improbably be inferred—on the basis of exhortation and command addressed to the faithful—what ought to be thought concerning bishops summoned to a synod. The author of the dissertation *De Litteris Canonicis* did not approve my criticism of Gothofredus; [Col. 0099D] but, just as he had read what I wrote hastily, so he attributed to me the opposite of what I had said. He wanted me to have spoken of the emperor’s *tractoriae*, although I was discussing pontifical ones, and to have denied a command to provide assistance, although I had expressly affirmed it. May such a thing be far from me: it was merely the result of careless reading. There is some resemblance to these letters in several letters of Pelagius I, excerpted by Holstenius from the collection of Cardinal Deusdedit, in which he commends to John, the Count—or rather, I would prefer, the Curator—of the patrimony, the presbyter Luminosus, sent to conduct some business of the Apostolic See. In Marculfus, book I, formula 11, there is also a celebrated *tractoria* by which a king grants a mounted escort to a legate.]

### Tractoria

The interests of the Church do not permit delay; therefore we have sent Ill., the notary of our holy Church, to our most excellent son, King Ill. We exhort you to have your charity procure for him, without delay, horses with which he may readily reach the neighboring city, so that the task entrusted to him may, with divine favor and your assistance, quickly achieve its fulfillment.

## TITLE X

[Note: [Col. 0100D] “Likewise, a *tractoria*.” Related to this *tractoria* is the one numbered tenth among the old formulas, by which a penitent, while visiting holy places as a pilgrim in order to expiate his crime, is commended to the faithful so that he may receive lodging, a fire, bread, and water from them.]

### Likewise, a Tractoria

The bearers of this document, having presented themselves, out of devotion, at the thresholds of the blessed Princes of the Apostles, requested that, released by us, they might return to their own homes. Therefore we command you to release them, providing them without hindrance with assistance and suitable aid—[Note: [Col. 0100D] “To release”: to set free.]—so that, refreshed by your support, they may return safely and guiltlessly to their own homes. Provide them with sustenance, assistance for their journey, and strength, undoubtedly awaiting from God, the rewarder of all good things, the recompense to be granted to you in return.

## 110 TITLE XI. Authoritative Precept Concerning the Preparation of Documents

Just as it is beneficial for pontifical counsel to provide prudently for whatever concerns the leasing and contracting of ecclesiastical properties, so it is necessary that the scrutiny of that prudent authority be present, so that the property of God’s Church may be entrusted to those who request it not only legally but also according to ecclesiastical rule.

Since, therefore, various persons request that the vineyards and farmsteads belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, situated in the patrimony of Ill. entrusted to your care, be leased to them by written instruments, each for himself, and that the lease itself be extended for many years, let your experience, supported by this authority, not delay giving the aforesaid vineyards and farmsteads, with everything belonging to them, after solemn documents have been drawn up, at a fair rent to be paid each year into the ecclesiastical accounts.

You must take care, however, never to presume to remove the tenants of our holy Church, nor in any way to usurp a place belonging to them and lease or let it to anyone else. For everything you do will be null and void if you prove to be a transgressor.

Thus, through the intervention of a lease and tenancy contract, their labor may be useful to them, and the advantage and security of our holy Church may be secured.

## TITLE XII. Likewise, Another Concerning the Preparation of Documents

[Col. 0100A]

Although what is done legally cannot be overturned by any opposition, nevertheless, so that there may be no uncertainty in the contracting, our authority must necessarily intervene.

Since, therefore, Ill. requests that approximately so many vineyard-plots belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, situated in the patrimony entrusted to your care, be leased to him by written instruments, and desires that the lease itself be extended for many years, let your experience, supported by this authority of ours, not delay giving the aforesaid vineyard, with everything belonging to it, after solemn documents have been drawn up, at a rent of one gold solidus to be paid each year into the ecclesiastical accounts.

[Note: [Col. 0100D] “Gold solidus.” If the Roman gold solidus is valued at six thousand denarii, as Cassiodorus maintains, and each Roman denarius at three and a half asses, as common opinion holds, the gold solidus is worth one thousand French pounds and somewhat more.]

Thus, through the intervention of a lease and tenancy contract, their labor may be useful to them, and the advantage of our holy Church may be secured.

## TITLE XIII. Precept Concerning the Exchange of an Estate

Although an exchange of property can be made firm by the actual physical transfer itself, and although what is done legally cannot be overturned by any opposition, nevertheless, so that there may be no uncertainty in the contracting, the support of our authority must intervene.

Since, therefore, Ill. has requested and desires to exchange the estate Ill., situated in the place Ill., belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, and wishes to grant in its place the estate Ill., situated in the place Ill., belonging to him in his own right, let your experience, supported by this authority of ours, exchange and transfer, from the present Ill. indiction, the aforesaid estate Ill., existing in its entirety as the property of the holy Roman Church, as stated above. In return, receive from him, in exchange, into the right and ownership of our holy Roman Church, the estate named Ill., in its entirety and with everything belonging to it, whatever its designations may be; for the security of future times, it is fitting that this be delivered to the archivists of our holy Church for our ecclesiastical archive.

Thus, through this intervention, he may obtain the result of his petition, and the security of our holy Church may be preserved.

## TITLE XIV. Precept Concerning the Exchange of a Bondservant

It is evident that your strenuous service has raised, as belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, a boy named Ill., and has kept him for so many years in the service of your household; you have asked us to exchange him with you, and have requested that in his place we grant a young man, a boy named Ill., of the nation of Ill.

Moved at last by your prayers, by this document of our precept and exchange we receive the aforesaid boy into the rights of our holy Church, and from the present Ill. indiction grant and give to the aforesaid Ill., in irrevocable right, the aforementioned boy Ill. We decree that from now on our holy Church shall have no part of jurisdiction over him.

As confirmation of this precept and exchange, we have delivered to you this document, strengthened by our hand.

## TITLE XV. Likewise, Another Concerning the Exchange of a Bondservant

[Col. 0101B]

The abbot of the monastery of Ill. reported to us personally that a certain male slave of the aforesaid monastery, in the possession of Ill., had taken as his wife a female servant of our Church.[Note: [Col. 0101D] “Had taken”: either had chosen, or had married.]

## 113

Therefore, by the authority of this present precept of ours, we instruct your experience—[Note: [Col. 0101D] “Your experience.” It is clear that the precept is addressed to the curator of the patrimony, from the title by which Gregory everywhere commonly calls the curators of the patrimony “Ill.”]—that, going to the place Ill. in the patrimony Ill. entrusted to you, you are to receive from the people of the aforesaid monastery a substitute for the aforesaid female servant of the Church and, in exchange, release the Church’s own female servant, since she has taken a monastery tenant as her husband, so that henceforth she may serve in the monastery’s possession without any further claim being made.

For the firm accomplishment of this matter, we have deemed it appropriate that this present precept of ours intervene, so that the aforesaid exchange may possess the full strength of permanence in the future.

## TITLE XVI

[Note: [Col. 0101D] “Precept concerning the granting, etc.” There are two similar examples, or at least examples not very different, in Gregory the Great: one in book 2, letter 57, by which the boy Acosimus is given to Theodore the counselor; the other in book 10, letter 52, by which the boy John is given by letter to Felix, bishop of Porto.]

### Precept Concerning the Giving of a Boy

No one diminishes what belongs to himself by giving something to those who diligently serve him, since our Lord God says: “Blessed is that servant whom, when the Lord comes, he finds watching” (Luke 12:37).

Therefore, by apostolic authority, we give you, for service, a boy named Ill., belonging by right to the hospice of Ill., granting him to you in a spirit of compassion, in return for your good offices and the faithful service you have rendered to us. We establish that he is to be under your control on this condition: after your death, if he has served well, he is to be released from the yoke of servitude, secured in freedom by you.

[Col. 0101D] Whoever should choose to violate this precept of our authority, let him be bound by the chain of eternal condemnation.

## 114 TITLE XVII. Likewise, a Precept Concerning the Granting of a Boy

[Note: [Col. 0101D] “A precept, etc.” This and the following formula differ from the preceding one in that the former adds the condition of granting freedom by testament, whereas the later ones add no such condition.]

[Col. 0102A]

The souls of the faithful, and especially those who serve in ecclesiastical rank, are kindled by the example of pastoral goodness, so that they may not only themselves perform faithful service in what has been entrusted to them, but also encourage others to do so.

Therefore, satisfied with your faithful services, we give, cede, and grant to your affection, Ill., by apostolic authority, the boy Ill., who is known to have arisen from the tenancy of the estate Ill. of the patrimony Ill., belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, bestowing him upon you. We transfer the same boy Ill. to your right and ownership, so that from this day, as his proper master, you may enjoy his service, and whatever you may wish to do with him, you may have free power by our authority. Thus, having obtained this benefaction, you may be encouraged to offer us still better and more faithful service.

## TITLE XVIII. Likewise, a Precept Concerning a Grant

We believe that it contributes to the growth and praise of the holy Church if, from the gifts of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, whose place, although unequal to him in merit, we nevertheless occupy by God’s favor, we grant something to those who provide faithful service for its interests. For what is bestowed upon them does not count as a loss, when the generosity of apostolic munificence encourages them to watch over the ministries entrusted to them with greater zeal and energy, and to devote diligent care and devoted effort to the interests committed to them.

## 115

Therefore, moved by your faithful and sincere services, as a small recompense for your purity, from the generosity of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, in the present Ill. indiction we give and grant to you a boy named Ill., of the nation of Ill., from the household of the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve. We transfer him into your rights, so that you are to have over him the right and ownership that you have over your own servants. No one may ever have permission to remove from your right whatever we are known to have bestowed upon you in good will as a small recompense for your services.

We have delivered this document of donation, strengthened by our hands, to your affection as future security.

## TITLE XIX

[Note: [Col. 0102D] “Security.” This is not merely an *acceptilatio* or receipt, but testimony that the accounts had been properly rendered, by which the procurators of ecclesiastical property lived securely. The word is understood in this sense in Gregory the Great, book 1, letter 42. I suspect that these two formulas of security belong to a later period, for the form of subscription in which the notary’s name is appended to both is scarcely found before the ninth or even the tenth century. Moreover, the *actionaria* of the city gates, which is mentioned, points to a later period, when the supreme pontiffs already ruled Rome. In addition, that terrifying threat appended to the later formula reflects the spirit of the ninth and tenth centuries. Add, if you wish, the more corrupt Latin.]

### Security

[Col. 0102D]

It is recognized as consistent with justice that those who faithfully serve ecclesiastical interests should be protected by complete security, so that henceforth they may suffer no loss from anyone.

Since the patrimony Ill., belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, has been entrusted to your care, and you are known to have carried out its collection by our arrangement, in the present Ill. indiction, concerning the *nuntiatica* or other incidental matters, and you are known to have made its collection by our direction, you delivered to us from the aforesaid patrimony, for the aforesaid Ill. indiction, namely ten gold solidi, ten oxen of equal number, ten horses, ten cows, and pigs. The final printed words, *accepturi tui tenorem*, are corrupt or uncertain.

## 116 TITLE XX. Security

It is evident that we entrusted to your greatness the *actionaria* from various gates of this city of Rome, to collect the lord’s due—[Note: [Col. 0103C] “Lord’s due”: the right of the lord.]—and that, for the past indiction, you are known faithfully to have collected it. Whatever you were able to take and exact from it, you have visibly presented and assigned in full, without any fraud, and we have been fully satisfied by you concerning the same *actionaria*. It is clear that nothing has remained with you, since you have plainly presented everything faithfully and with complete integrity.

By apostolic censure and by the authority of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, we decree that no one ever, whether a person of great or small rank, presume in any way to trouble you or your heirs concerning the same *actionaria*, or to bring any dispute over a claim against you or your heirs. Therefore we have decided that you and your heirs must be protected by the most ample security and complete safeguard. We order this to be written by Ill., the notary and archivist of our see; we have subscribed it with our own hand and delivered it to you, on the day Ill., under the emperor, our lord and son, and so forth.

## TITLE XXI

[Note: [Col. 0103C] “Precept of freedom.” This formula may in part have been taken from Gregory the Great, book 5, letter 12, where Montana and Thomas are granted freedom and made Roman citizens. There are also several formulas of enfranchisement in the collection of the most distinguished Bignon; and several learned notes on them, whether those found in Marculfus or those contained in the three other collections of ancient formulas. Nevertheless, none is comparable with ours, which, while granting the full measure of freedom, declares the recipient a Roman citizen, states that he owes nothing to anyone except a simple greeting, and permits him to live according to the complete rite of freedom. It is clear that all the rights of enfranchisement are included here. This singular formula therefore deserves to be carefully observed.]

### Precept of Freedom

We believe that our Lord God is pleased when compassion, guided by consideration of piety, pursues what is fitting, since He says: “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6; Matthew 9:13). For we read in His own words that He gave a reward to hired laborers.

In imitation of Him, therefore, we who, by His dispensation, hold the place of a shepherd ought to return the rewards of labor to those who render faithful service, so that what we do in mercy may be acceptable to Him.

## 117

Therefore, in return for the services you have rendered with as willing a mind as you wished, by which you have satisfied our mind in the matters entrusted to us, we decree that you, Ill., a servant of the holy Church which by God’s authority we serve, are, by the authority of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, through this document of our precept, as a recompense, from the present Ill. indiction, granted the full measure of freedom—[Note: [Col. 0104C] “The full measure of freedom”: that is, the fullest freedom, which is called lawful freedom, *Institutes*, On Freedmen, title 5.]—and are to be free from every servile fortune and condition. We decree that you are a Roman citizen, released from every burden of subjection, and that you owe nothing to anyone except a simple greeting, so that, wholly freed from the servile yoke, you may live according to the complete rite of freedom throughout the days you have left, giving thanks to God in the manner of free persons, for whose love and command you are known to have earned this.

# CHAPTER VII. VARIOUS PRIVILEGES OF APOSTOLIC AUTHORITY GRANTED TO MONASTERIES, DIACONIES, AND HOSPICES

[Col. 0103]

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0103] This chapter contains various privileges of apostolic authority granted to monasteries, diaconies, hospices, and other pious places. No other order seemed necessary than the one found in the manuscript codex, in which everything is mixed together in disorder. Nevertheless, because of its singularity, the *Prologue in Judicatum* is placed at the beginning. I do not possess the date of all formulas of this kind; for I suspect that the same thing happened to this collection as to the Roman Order, which, having initially been simpler and shorter, was enlarged by additions. I think that certain material from a later age was inserted into this part by an audacious hand. For these texts are not filled with the gentler spirit of the earlier age, but threaten terribly—the characteristic spirit of the ninth and tenth centuries. We have made only a very few observations on the individual formulas, since they contain almost nothing pertaining to ecclesiastical antiquity and no particularly hidden doctrine. Any words belonging to a declining Latin usage that may occur will easily be understood from the Glossary of the distinguished Cangius.

## [PRIVILEGES]

### PROLOGUE IN JUDICATUM

[Col. 0103D]

Since pastoral solicitude is recognized as greatly impelling us to carry out the advances of justice and to silence the evasions of disputants, we therefore apply ourselves more vigilantly, so that, if any deception arises between the parties, the law may immediately be investigated by a clear inquiry and refined, through the moderation of equity, until everything is brought into harmony.

And since it is evident, etc.

## I. Privilege

[Note: [Col. 0105D] “Since, etc.” Pope Zacharias granted Boniface, founder of the monastery of Fulda, a privilege by this formula around the year 750.]

Since whatever accords with reasonable desires should always be granted, it is fitting that devotion to the founder of a pious institution should by no means be denied when privileges are being granted.

Therefore, since you have asked us that the monastery of Saint Ill., situated in the place Ill., be adorned with the privileges of the Apostolic See, so that, established under the jurisdiction of the holy Church which by God’s authority we serve, it may be subject to the jurisdiction of no other Church—

## 119

[Col. 0105B]—we, favoring your pious desires, by this authority of ours commit to effect what is requested. Accordingly, we forbid any priest of any Church to exercise any authority or jurisdiction in the aforesaid monastery, except the Apostolic See, so that no one may presume to celebrate the solemnity of Masses there unless he has been invited by the abbot of the monastery. Through this document of our decree we establish and absolutely prohibit all prelates of every Church, and all persons endowed with power of whatever rank, under the imposition of anathema, from doing so. Whoever presumes in any way to violate this constitution granted by us to the aforesaid monastery, etc.

## II. Privilege

[Col. 0105C]

[Note: [Col. 0105D] “Since, etc.” With several interpolations, Stephen II used this formula in 757 when he sent Abbot Fulrad of Saint-Denis a diploma concerning the freedom of monasteries which he himself or his successors were to found throughout Francia.]

Since always, as above, up to the words “to violate.”

Moreover, by apostolic censure, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment and by strong and most terrible prohibitions of anathema, we decree that no priest ever, nor anyone else, presume to claim what has been given and offered in that holy place, or what may later be granted there. Rather, it is to remain the firm and stable property of the aforesaid monastery forever. As stated, no person, great or small, may have permission to remove anything from it or from anything belonging to the monastery, so that this venerable place may remain, without disturbance, endowed according to the tenor of the apostolic constitution and privilege granted to it.

But if anyone—which we do not wish—should presume by wicked audacity to oppose or in any way transgress what we have established for the praise of God and the stability of the aforesaid monastery, let him know that he is bound by the chain of anathema and is to be assigned to be burned with the Devil and his most atrocious [Note: [Col. 0105D] “Pomps.” Leo IX, in the eleventh century, letter 11 to the bishop of Salerno: “But if anyone should presume to act against the privilege of this our precept, or consent to those presuming to do so, or prove to be their supporter, etc., let him know that by the authority of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles and key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, and by the chain of our anathema, he is bound and alienated from the kingdom of God, and, with the Devil and his most atrocious Pomps, assigned by the canonical tradition of the transgressing holy Fathers, etc.” Two hundred years earlier, John VIII, in a privilege of the monastery of Torny, had written “Angels” for “Pomps,” [Col. 0106D] following Scripture: “to be burned in everlasting fire with the Devil and his angels.” If this passage permitted more recondite speculation, one might perhaps say that the reading should be emended to *Pompaeis*. For the *Pompaei* are conductors of souls to the underworld, and *πομπαῖος* was once an epithet of Mercury in Sophocles’ *Ajax*. Nevertheless, the word *Pompis* may be retained to signify attendants, and, as Scripture puts it, the angels of the Devil. For by *pompa* the ancients understood not only spectacles but also the attendants and bearers of splendid objects; hence Cicero spoke of the *pompa* of the lictors.] Pomps, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ, to the punishment of eternal fire. But whoever proves to be observant in all things out of pious devotion, keeping this precept of our apostolic constitution, which concerns the worship of God, shall receive in many ways the grace of blessing from our most merciful Lord and God and shall deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

## III. Privilege of a Monastery

We are impelled by the care of our entrusted oversight, and also by the ardor of Christian religion and the zeal to advance divine worship, to consider the stability of venerable places and of those who serve God, so that, through this pious labor, the souls dedicated to Christ—who have resolved to serve Him throughout the days of their life—may persevere undisturbed, and so that those things constructed by Christians for the praise of God may remain firm to the end.

Since, therefore, it is altogether evident that the monastery of the holy martyr of Christ, Stephen—[Note: [Col. 0106D] “Stephen.” Leo IV, who became pope in 847, is said to have restored the monastery of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr after it had collapsed. But since that monastery is said to have been near the basilica of Saint Lawrence, whereas the monastery discussed here was within the atrium of Saint Paul, it must necessarily be a different one.]—which was founded within the atrium of blessed Paul the Apostle, had, with the passage of time, been stripped of its congregation of male or female servants of God and handed over to solitude, with no superior or monks living in it, we have therefore been moved by compassion for so great a sacrilege and compelled by grief. By apostolic authority we have provided that the same monastery be joined to the monastery entrusted to you, so that from the present Ill. indiction and forever it may be administered in its entirety by you and your successors, together with everything subject to it, and governed in the fear of God, so that it may remain joined to your monastery. Thus, in that venerable place, you are to offer praises to our Lord God. By this authority of ours we establish that you are to render no account thereafter for it or for anything belonging to it, except to God alone. The building and the provision of lamps, however, are without doubt to be carried out by your diligent care.

Let there therefore be no delay in offering praises to God or in preparing the lamps. Hasten to carry this out with devoted sincerity, and, lest fear of the future judgment shake you because of the fault of heedless negligence, strive rather to labor so that divine clemency may be pleased by your effort, and so that what has been decreed by us after proper deliberation may remain undisturbed and perpetual for all future time.

## IV. Privilege

When episcopal authority sends the abundance of spiritual rewards to religious men living a chaste life, thereby contributing fully to the accumulation of future recompense, it can win eternal remembrance before the Creator of all by a praiseworthy exchange.

## 122

Therefore, having confidence in the steadfast religious solicitude of your care, which always clings to pious pursuits and excels in sober conduct, we entrust to you, by this document of our precept, for governing and administering throughout all the days of your life, the aforesaid venerable places Ill. of the blessed Ill., situated in the place Ill., which we have found overwhelmed by extreme poverty through the negligence of their predecessors. We grant the monastery Ill., situated in the place Ill., to your religiousness and to your successors forever, joining to it the place called Ill., which is situated in the place Ill., together with all urban and rural properties belonging in full to these same venerable places.

This is to be done on the condition that you diligently complete, without setting aside any neglect, all the construction, restoration, and preparation of lamps required by the aforesaid places, so that, when you have completed these works, you need not fear that anyone will in any way expel you or alienate them. Rather, keep striving, with divine recompense in view, to promote the increase and advantage of all these venerable places, as stated above, and to complete their construction and improvement. We charge all our descendants and successors to preserve this pious disposition inviolate to the end.

## V. Privilege

Since the care of watching over all Churches and pious places presses upon us with great solicitude, lest they suffer any loss through want, but rather receive the resources necessary for their own benefit, it is therefore fitting that, with the full integrity of our pastoral mind, we provide for the greatest stability of these venerable places and diligently confer resources for their benefit. Thus, whatever we are known to have bestowed upon venerable places for our almighty God’s holy things, and for the honor, praise, and glory of His divine majesty, may be acceptable to Him, and may recompense for such a pious work be granted to us by His most abundant hand in the heavenly courts.

## 123

Therefore, since you have asked us to grant, by issuing a precept, the estates Ill. and Ill., situated in the place Ill., to your religiousness to hold forever, on the condition that from you, etc.,

we decree, by apostolic censure and by the authority of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, under the solemn appeal to divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, that no one ever—neither any of our successor pontiffs nor any other person, great or small—may lawfully remove or alienate the aforesaid places from the power and jurisdiction of the aforementioned monastery. Rather, they are to remain in its own possession.
