But if any person, great or small, should presume by reckless audacity to act against this apostolic decree of ours, let that person know that he or she is bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the impious to eternal fire and punishment. But whoever proves to be an observer of the precept shall deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from our most merciful God.

## VI. Privilege

[Note: [Col. 0107D] “It is fitting, etc.” Agapetus II used the beginning of this formula when, in 949, he granted a privilege to Aymard, abbot of Cluny. John XIII also used it when writing to Berengarius, bishop of Verdun, to confirm by apostolic privileges the monastery which Berengarius had built in his diocese. Finally, Leo IX used it in 1049 when granting immunity to Hugh of Cluny.]

It is fitting for apostolic governance to come to the aid of those who ask in pious religion with benevolent compassion, and to grant the minds of those who ask assent with willing devotion. For the greatest reward is then stored up with God, the Creator of all, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

## 124

Therefore, since you have asked us that the estate Ill., etc.,

we decree, by the authority of blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, whose place we occupy—although unequal to him in merit, yet with divine grace assisting us—under the prohibition of anathema and the solemn appeal to divine judgment, that no one may in any way overturn what has been decreed by us out of compassion. Rather, it is to remain firm, stable, and undisturbed forever.

## VII. Privilege

[Col. 0108D]

Ecclesiastical affairs make all the greater progress through more extensive growth insofar as, out of a spirit of piety, something from them has been bestowed either upon those in need, upon those serving Christ, or upon venerable places. For we do not doubt that whatever, by God’s mercy, we have received in trust will be restored through the excellent stewardship of his power; and we hold confidence in obtaining the future reward.

[Col. 0109A] Therefore, since you have asked us that we should grant the estate of Ill., etc.,

We therefore decree, by apostolic authority and under threat of the future judgment, that none of our successors, nor anyone else whatsoever, may in any way overturn these pious provisions decreed by us with good purpose; rather, we define that they shall remain firm, stable, and unshaken, and shall be observed perpetually under the bond of anathema.

## VIII. Privilege

The divine and saving commandments, together with the effective instruction of the sacred Canons and venerable Fathers, teach us that, with pious consideration and indeed through the zeal of apostolic governance, we must secure the usefulness of all the churches of God and complete their integrity of stability, so that the assistance procured for their needs may remain unshaken and those persons dedicated to divine worship may be able to persevere for a very long time in offering praises to God.

[Col. 0109B] For, among the other struggles of suitable pastoral activity that we continually strive to undertake, the responsibility entrusted to us undoubtedly urges us, with pious consideration, to decree that no church whatsoever established under episcopal governance should in any way suffer want or deprivation. Therefore justice requires that we promulgate, with impartiality, the privileges of each church, the rights of parishes and dioceses, and those of monasteries, so that they may possess them under apostolic sanction; thus the institutions of the sacred Canons may remain unimpaired, and we may receive from God, the creator of all things, the most profitable reward.

Therefore, etc.

## IX. Privilege

Since a pious desire of the will and a praiseworthy intention concerning good works should always be assisted by apostolic efforts, diligent care must be taken that what is lawfully done and accords with the forms of equity cannot be disturbed by any opposition, but must remain, by God’s authority, under an unanswerable right. For this reason, apostolic sanctions having been promulgated, justice requires that each person’s possessions, insofar as they are available, be confirmed for ownership.

[Note: [Col. 0109D] Paschal I uses this entire preface in writing to Petronacius, bishop of Ravenna, up to the words “and therefore, since it is established.” But the words in volume VII of the General Councils, p. 1502, have been so mutilated, corrupted, and disordered that they are wholly meaningless; nevertheless, they can be emended from this passage.]

And therefore, since it is established that Your Excellency has both built and acquired very many monasteries and has dedicated them all in honor and under the name of your patron, blessed Peter; and since you appear to have bestowed upon them various estates and possessions of land, as well as a multitude of servants; and since you have asked that all these things be confirmed by the privileges of the Apostolic See, so that the same monasteries and estates of land, together with all their original servants and resident dependants

[Col. 0110A] or all things belonging to them, may perpetually remain under the authority of Your Excellency, or of your wife, Ill., queen, and the lineage of your children, for them to retain—just as the same places and estates of land are shown below to contain, namely, etc.

## X. Privilege

It accords with apostolic governance to assist, with benevolent compassion, those who ask in pious devotion, and to grant the minds of those who ask their assent with eager devotion. For by this we undoubtedly earn the most profitable reward from God, the creator of all things, when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since you have asked us that we should grant you, by an issued command, the monastery of Saint Ill., situated in the place Ill., belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, for you to govern and administer with the fear of God, we have been moved by your prayers. By the tenor of this command, we grant you the aforesaid monastery in its entirety, with all that belongs to it, from the present indiction Ill. and for as long as you shall live, by God’s will, to govern and administer with the fear of God.

This is subject to the sole condition that you cherish and govern, like a father of a household, the servants of God, the monks who are in the same monastery or whom you may gather there, in chastity and moderation, under regular and monastic discipline, so that they must sing continual praises to God by day and by night. You are also to see without delay to all the preparation and restoration of the lamps.

[Col. 0110C] If you discover that any urban or rural places of the monastery have perhaps been taken away or diverted by certain persons, you are to labor through your own efforts to restore them to the right of the venerable monastery, so that, according to the office entrusted to you by us, showing the care of pious zeal in all things and toward everyone, you may receive a reward from God, and so that what has been decreed by us may remain with unshaken firmness throughout all the days of your life.

## XI. Privilege

We willingly assent to the requests of those who live religiously and chastely. Therefore, since you have asked us, together with your congregation, concerning the monastery of blessed Ill., belonging to our holy Church and established in this Roman city, in the district Ill., that those who dwell there and continually devote themselves to pious works should daily sing praises to God,

[Col. 0110D] by the tenor of this command of ours we have perpetually granted that monastery to you and your congregation, namely on the condition that neither you nor your congregation may ever leave it, but that you must always dwell there; for, as has been said, out of regard for piety and in compassion for your pilgrimage, the monastery has been granted to you by us.

But just as we have decreed that you must not leave it at all, so we establish and decree that none of our successors shall have permission to expel you from it. Rather, it shall always be a monastery in which your congregation must sing praises, throughout all days, to our Lord Jesus Christ, the redeemer of the human race.

In this command and disposition of our pious mind we have subscribed, and for that reason have delivered it to you and your congregation for your eternal protection.

## XII. Privilege of a monastery in another province

[128] If those things that accord with pious desires should always be granted, how much more should those things not be entirely denied that are requested for the advancement of divine worship, for these are things that ought not merely to be requested from benefactors, but undoubtedly to be exacted by the force of charity.

You therefore ask us to grant the privileges of the Apostolic See to the monastery of Saint Ill., established in the place Ill., over which you are recognized as presiding, so that, since it has been established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it may be subject to the jurisdiction of no other church.

Favoring your pious wishes in this matter, by this authority of ours we commit to effect what your religious devotion requests. Therefore we entirely prohibit any priest of any church from extending any jurisdiction or authority over the aforesaid monastery, or from celebrating the solemnity of Mass there on his own authority, unless he has been invited by the provost of the monastery.

Let it therefore be your concern to adorn the brothers of the monastery over which you preside with excellent conduct and an irreproachable life, so that your charity, which has preferred those subject to apostolic privileges to be endowed with unshaken security, may desire—or rather ardently long—for them to be adorned by the inviolable gift of heavenly abundance through the daily prayers of holy discipline.

Let their life truly be communal and sincere; let the sincerity of their fellowship be sober, so that, since the world has died and been buried for them, the vices may not be aroused by the incentives of contention. For a person is known to labor in vain and fruitlessly if he is perceived to submit his neck to pride, the author of vices. Let humility in God be exalted,

[Col. 0111D] because through it the elect will possess the citadel of heavenly gifts.

Let the rule of the traditions of the Fathers therefore stand before the eyes of mind and body, so that every prelate may know how he ought to command his subjects, lest, when harsh things and things not suited to every brother appear to be imposed, the subjects break out into contempt because of the ruler’s lack of discernment.

Let there therefore be moderated vigor and outstanding zeal for diligence among the brothers, so that all who devote themselves wholly to God, duly rendering temporal service according to the rule of obedience, may attain the everlasting joys of the heavenly homeland. And let it suffice to have said these things concerning what belongs to diligence.

But above all, let us earnestly await, with sobs and sighs, the mercy of our Redeemer, whose redemption we groan while awaiting it, so that the human frailty of our condition may sufficiently and confidently fulfill, with the support of its author, what piety demands.

## XIII. Command concerning the granting of a hospice

[Note: [Col. 0111D] “The desires of petitioners,” etc. This entire preface, down to the words “Therefore, since you have asked,” is found in the diploma by which Stephen II grants Fulrad, abbot, a hospice and house in Rome in the year 772, indiction 10, in the month of January.]

It is fitting for us to grant assent to the desires of those who ask in such a way that, nevertheless, in subsequent times no ecclesiastical utility may be subjected to loss. For a petition appears then to attain its proper effect when venerable places, suitably ordered, have without doubt been brought to a better condition.

Therefore, since you have asked us that we should grant you, by an issued command, the hospice called Ill., established in the Roman district Ill., belonging to the holy Roman Church, which by God’s authority we serve, for you to govern, we have been moved by your prayers. By the tenor of this command we grant you the aforesaid hospice, with everything belonging to it, from the present indiction Ill. and for the days of your life, to administer under the condition written below.

[130] The precise condition is that, in the same venerable place, beds with their coverings be prepared through your efforts, in which you may always receive the sick and the needy, care for them, and provide them with necessities. You shall have suitable preparations made and supplied for the sick and needy, as well as everything useful to the needs of the infirm, bringing in physicians and providing care for the sick, so that by such devotion Christ our God may be appeased, and this present command may remain undisturbed throughout all the days of your life. Otherwise, if you neglect these duties, you may incur divine indignation and be deprived of the just reward of your administration.

## XIV. Another

Those who hasten to show unimpaired faithfulness in the responsibilities entrusted to them—especially when the welfare of the poor may result from them—are believed to do nothing other than distribute alms to the needy from their own possessions.

Since this is undoubtedly so, we have determined, with God’s help, to entrust you, Ill., notary of our holy Church, with the hospice Ill. for all the days of your life. You are to keep the judgment of almighty God before your eyes and conduct yourself purely and faithfully; with the safeguard of this matter before your eyes [the intervening reading is uncertain], you are to perform your office faithfully and piously. You must conduct yourself in the responsibilities of the same hospice

[Col. 0113A] so that you hasten to provide diligent, faithful, and effective care for the sick lying there, in order that you may gain praise in human opinion and may not subject yourself to almighty God under any stain of reproach for neglect.

We establish that these things, decreed by us through the authority of this present command, are also to be preserved in every way unshaken by our successors in the future.

## XV. [131] Command concerning a provostship

To the extent that the moderate sincerity of the faithful and the discerning purity of administrators gladden us, so much does the care of pastoral foresight urge us to accumulate the support of merit in those subject to us. For by this means the integrity of piety is preserved, and the Apostolic Church of God, entrusted to us, is kindled toward a better condition.

Therefore, having learned through clear and reliable indications of the certain effectiveness of your sincerity that you place God before your eyes, by this page of our command we decree that you shall be provost of the aforesaid Basilica of Blessed Ill., situated in the place Ill., for all the days of your life, from the present indiction Ill.

The following condition is to be observed: if the aforesaid basilica should need any expense or payment for any matter, including the preparation of the lamps, it is to be paid from your resources. In this way you are likewise to show the greatest diligence and care toward the same sacred basilica, so that you may be able to please almighty God and his Martyr.

By this page of our command, and under the adjuration of the divine judgment, we prohibit anyone from persuading you during the days of your life to relinquish that provostship, provided that you diligently procure its welfare in all things. Rather, we devoutly decree that what has been determined by us shall be preserved.

## XVI. Command concerning granting a boy to a monastery

We believe that nothing is diminished from the rights of the Church whenever we bestow something from the apostolic possessions upon pious places, especially upon those who, with providence favoring them, continually offer praises in the name of Jesus Christ our God.

[Col. 0113D] Therefore, to you, Ill., abbot and priest, and through you to the aforementioned venerable monastery, we give, cede, and grant by irrevocable right, for the congregation of the monk-brothers and for the provision of their allowance and food, from the present indiction Ill., to be possessed under the right and lordship of the monastery, as stated above, persons of the nation Ill. from the estate of Ill. or from the monastery Ill., or from the family written above. They are to serve in the same monastery throughout all the days of their lives, and all are to render obedience to you, as are those who may be born from them, like servants belonging to their own lordship.

[Col. 0114A] No one shall have permission to remove or alienate any one of them. Rather, by perpetual right they shall remain subject to serving the venerable monastery or the deaconry, rendering all the services that they are ordered and assigned to perform by the congregation established there, as servants belonging to their own lordship.

But if anyone should attempt to act against this page of our command and donation, let him be bound by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, with the bond of anathema and subjected to perpetual condemnation.

We have delivered this page of the command, subscribed by us, to you, Abbot Ill., and to your monastery, for future security.

## Privilege of the Deaconries. XVII

[Col. 0114B] Since, without doubt, offerings must be devoted to the worship of divine majesty in order to attain the eternal joys of the heavenly kingdom, justice altogether requires us, with whatever zeal we possess, to complete carefully whatever is recognized as pertaining to the stability and advancement of venerable places—especially those in which praises are offered to almighty God and sustenance is diligently supplied to our brothers—so that abundant assistance may advance the welfare of all the needy, including impoverished newcomers. By this means, what we are recognized as having provided for the glory of his holy name may be acceptable to our Redeemer, and remuneration may be bestowed upon us by the same Lord God our creator in the heavenly heights.

[Col. 0114C] Therefore, since your fidelity asks us that the estate of Ill., etc.,

From the present indiction Ill. we grant it perpetually to Your Magnitude, and through you to the same venerable deaconry, to be retained. But the administrator who shall at that time be in the same venerable deaconry—that is,

[Note: [Col. 0113D] “When lucina is completed,” that is, at the time when the lamps are lit and, consequently, the evening prayers are completed.]

when the lamps are lit, shall see that all the diaconites and poor of Christ who gather there cry out in the same deaconry, for the remission of our sins, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”). This is to be done in such a way that, in every indiction, the rent is paid three times, without delay, by Your Magnitude and by your successors as administrators, according to the accounts of the Church, perpetually; and that whatever defense or improvement is needed is undoubtedly provided for you without distinction. Moreover, there shall be no delay on the part of Your Magnitude or your successors as administrators in paying the annual rent; rather, it is to be paid voluntarily to the agents of our holy Church at the proper time.

By the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, under the adjuration of the divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that none of our successors, the pontiffs, nor anyone else, of great or small rank, may ever in any way remove or alienate the aforesaid estate. Rather, it shall remain perpetually for the proper benefit, use, and possession of the venerable

[Col. 0115A] deaconry, for the support and sustenance of our brothers, the poor of Christ.

But whoever observes this apostolic command of ours shall receive the greatest grace and deserve to obtain eternal life from our most merciful Lord God.

## XVIII. [134] Privilege

With regard to the consideration of heavenly mercy, we have undertaken the care of governance so that we may assist the prayers of those who ask justly, and all persons in their needs, with the balance of equity—especially those who, for the name of the redeemer, the Lord Jesus Christ, have devoted themselves for the whole course of their lives to diligent service and to singing his mighty deeds, under the religious habit and within monastic enclosures. For we are adorned with pontifical merits when, as divine command and reason require, we restore to each person what rightfully belongs to him, and when, through pastoral compassion, we console those whom necessity constrains.

But since, after many years had passed, you, Abbot Ill., in charge of the monastery of which your religious devotion is the head, informed us before the synodal assembly, by presenting a petition, that you had possessed by unshaken right the estate Ill. and the estate Ill., and that a predecessor of blessed memory had restored the aforesaid estate to your congregation, we decree, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles—whose representatives we are by divine favor, although unequal to him in merits—that from the present indiction Ill. and throughout perpetuity, your monastery and your congregation shall possess the same estate Ill. and the estate Ill. without any annual payment, defend it under their own right, and claim it for their own uses. No one is to attempt or dare to take it from you by any device or pretext, but it shall remain perpetually in the right and ownership of the venerable place.

If anyone, which we do not wish, should dare to act against this page of our decree or attempt to inflict harm upon your party, let him be bound by the bond of anathema and struck with the curse of Judas the betrayer. But may those who observe it, through the merits and prayers of the Apostles and of Christ’s Confessor Martin, enjoy the rewards of the life to come.

## XIX. [135] Privilege

With the greatest concern for venerable places, insofar as possibility is granted through divine assistance, we strive to care for their stability. By this zeal divine clemency is appeased, praise for Christ and his Church is advanced, and we dare with greater confidence to implore eternal mercy for the forgiveness of our sins.

Therefore, through the wrongdoing of certain petitioners, it happened some years ago that the provost of the aforementioned place, overcome by greed, leased the estate Ill. and the estate Ill. of the orphans, by which the necessities of their food were supported. As the term of years was extended, death occurred; the places mentioned above were alienated from the right of the said orphanage, and they were deprived of their proper lord. Meanwhile, as the place was pressed by the need for sustenance, the attendance of the children ceased because provision for their expenses was lacking.

[Note: [Col. 0115D] “The order of singers.” From this we learn that the singers’ school was supplied from the orphanages. Saint Gregory further decreed in the Roman Synod that neither priests nor deacons should sing in the church, but only subdeacons, the minor orders, and boys. That custom did not last long, although it had been established by the holy pontiff for no weak reason; the discipline of the Church has varied at different times.]

Therefore, lest the order of singers should fail and thereby an insult be inflicted upon the Church of God, we carefully investigated the same places, from which they were being withheld beyond all reason, and, by command, restored them to the venerable place. We judged it just that the things cultivated for the uses of outsiders should serve those who nourish orphans for the praise of God.

We therefore command that from the present indiction Ill. and for all future time, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, whose representatives we are, although unequal to him in merits, by God’s mercy, the said estate, restored with all its rights, shall remain the property of the aforementioned orphanage under unshaken security, to be devoted to its benefit and to that of the children. No one, great or small, may lease it or alienate it from its benefit; rather, it shall always be preserved for the uses and needs of the venerable place.

[Col. 0116C] If anyone should therefore arise as a violator or attempt to act against this page of the decree, let him be indissolubly bound by the bond of anathema and condemned by the curse of Judas the betrayer.

## XX. [Note: [Col. 0115D] Privilege of confirmation. A bishop had founded a deaconry, apparently on an estate under his own authority. He asked that what he had contributed for the support of the poor be confirmed by a privilege of the Apostolic See, lest anyone at some time defraud the poor. If that bishop held an apostolic ordination, nothing can be inferred from this except that the power of bishops of this kind was restricted within very narrow limits. If he was an outsider, one may understand what opinion the bishops of those times held concerning the authority of the Roman pontiff.]

### Privilege of confirming a place

Whatever is done out of regard for piety ought to remain with unshaken firmness. It is therefore fitting to strive so that the rights of all may remain established for perpetual time, especially when, with devoted sincerity, provision for the necessities of life is made for the poor of Christ for the praise of our Lord God. For he says: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5:7); and he teaches that what is done to one of the least is done to him.

Relying on this hope, you are recognized, venerable brother, as having founded a deaconry in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, our Lady, in the place Ill., confidently trusting that you will obtain rewards for your merits in the future. For this reason you have contributed things there, and others strive to offer them, out of love for our almighty God, for the administration of aid to his poor and for the redemption of sins.

Lest anyone, acting as a violator out of some rivalry against salvation, overcome by greed, remove or defraud anything once dedicated to God, you have hoped that the venerable place might be secured by a command of our authority.

Therefore, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, through this page of the decree we command all persons, whatever dignity and power they possess, that no one presume to remove anything whatsoever from the possessions of the same venerable deaconry. Rather, whatever it may be, let it always possess by its own right and claim all that has been granted to it, or whatever may have been offered, so that it may remain under the protection, governance, and administration of the place Ill.

Under fear of the eternal judgment, establishing this by pontifical sanction and under the prohibition of anathema, we decree that no violator may exist.

## XXI. Privilege granted in its own proper place

Since great concern presses upon us to consider the stability of all holy places, so that the integrity of their most devout usefulness may advance, it is fitting that we act accordingly. We certainly bear the greatest concern for both the Church Ill. and the Church Ill., lest the preparation of the lamps there appear to be insufficient. For this reason, from its own estates—namely, the places Ill. below the road Ill., in the aforesaid venerable title—we confirm the estates Ill. written above for the use and benefit of that holy place and of the priest who at all times shall have cared for the same venerable title. They are to remain for perpetual and everlasting times, from the present indiction Ill. and forever, for the use and benefit of the aforesaid title, as has been said.

By apostolic sanction, under the adjuration of the divine judgment and the prohibitions of anathema, we decree that none of our successor pontiffs, nor any person great or small, presume to remove or alienate the aforesaid estates from that venerable title and from the priest’s use.

Nor may the priests

[Note: [Col. 0117D] “Or visitors.” Just as churches deprived of their bishops were entrusted to visitors, so pious places were entrusted to visitors through their priests. This may perhaps be the original source of what are called commendams, when a mandate degenerated into a grant.]

or the Visitors who in their time shall have cared for that holy place dare to issue anyone a charter or any other document of security concerning them. Rather, as we have said above, they shall remain with firm stability for the use and benefit of that holy place and of all its priests throughout perpetual time.

## XXII. Privilege for the confirmation of a monastery

[Note: [Col. 0118D] “The desire, etc.” This preface is partly found in letter 70 of Paschal II to Hugh of Cluny.]

The desire that is shown to pertain to a religious purpose and to the stability of holy places must, by God’s authority, be fulfilled without delay, so that whenever the assistance of our assent and of the customary apostolic authority is sought for certain benefits and advantages of those places, it may be fitting for us to come forward willingly, out of regard for benevolence, and to strengthen their rights on rational grounds for complete security. Thus the safety and protection of the venerable place Ill. may advance, and for us too the most profitable reward may be prepared by God, the creator of all things, in the starry heights.

It is fitting that we should have been implored by Ill. to fortify the aforesaid monastery of Saint Ill. through an authoritative instrument and to confirm that everything belonging to it shall remain there inviolably by perpetual right.

Therefore, moved by your prayers, through this page of the command we establish and decree that all urban and rural places—that is, estates, homesteads, various cultivated or uncultivated properties, tenants, and households—which were granted by command through Ill., Ill., and Ill. to the same venerable monastery, or which may also have come to that pious place through other notifications, shall be possessed by you now with complete security and in peace, just as your monastery possessed them in the times of Ill. and Ill., our predecessors of blessed memory.

[Col. 0118B] You and, through you, your venerable monastery or your successors, the abbots, shall also have the power to possess and retain them, so that, enjoying jurisdiction perpetually, they may defend them and continually advance the interests of the same pious place.

For this reason, promulgating the decree under the adjuration of the divine judgment, we determine that no official of public authority, nor any person of whatever dignity, great or small, may in any way have jurisdiction over the said monastery, its estates, lands, homesteads, properties, cultivated or uncultivated, or other possessions, including tenants and households, wherever you appear to retain them. No one may presume to remove or seize any of these things from the same pious place, nor dare to inflict any injury or evil opposition upon that monastery of blessed Ill. or upon all things attached and belonging to it, by any device or pretext whatsoever.

Rather, as was stated above, they shall perpetually advance in the same venerable monastery by perpetual right, and the authority and possession of disposing of and holding them shall remain perpetually with your religious devotion and with all your successors, the abbots.

[Col. 0118D] But if anyone should attempt to act or proceed against the tenor of this apostolic command of ours, piously promulgated by us, with rash boldness, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema of our Lord and of the prince of the Apostles, Peter, and that he will be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most atrocious pomp, and with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ; and, cast down together into chaos with the impious, let him perish.

But may those who, out of regard for piety, prove themselves guardians, obedient, and observant of this salutary command of ours obtain the grace of blessing and the everlasting joys of heavenly recompense from the just Judge, our Lord God.

## XXIII. [140] Privilege restoring to their former uses places that have been taken away from a monastery

The words of the divine command admonish everyone that whenever another’s property is held by anyone contrary to the order of reason, it ought to be restored when equity demands it.

It is established that the estate Ill., situated in the place Ill., which had long been held by your monastery, was unlawfully invaded there by Ill. and Ill. and has been held up to the present.

Now therefore, since, with the grace of heavenly piety assisting us, we once again confirm your aforesaid monastery as it was from ancient times, we establish that it must receive without delay what belongs to it.

For this reason, confirming the matter by the authority of this privilege, we establish the aforementioned place in the aforesaid monastery, so that it may return to the right of the same monastery from which it had been taken and remain without ambiguity in its ownership.

We decree, etc.

[Col. 0119]

# DISSERTATIONS ON THE *LIBER DIURNUS*

## FIRST DISSERTATION. APPENDIX TO THE NOTES ON CHAPTER ONE, concerning the index for writing a letter

[Col. 0119B] **143 I.** There can be no doubt that pontifical letters were at times so addressed that the pontiff placed his own name after the name of the person to whom he wrote; for very many letters of pontiffs plainly teach this.

**II.** At what time this practice first began cannot be determined, since the letters circulated as having been issued before the age of Damasus and Siricius are either doubtful or certainly spurious, apart from a few inserted in the books of approved writers.

**III.** How long it remained is clear from the fact that, from the times of Damasus and Siricius, a tradition can be traced down to the ninth century, during which it is shown to have been observed.

**IV.** The tradition is all the more certain because the two arguments that can be brought against it are weaker. The first is that letters of one and the same pope are reported as addressed in both ways. The other is that the registers of Leo the Great and likewise of Gregory the Great—than which none were more numerous in the early centuries—are full of letters in which the pontiff’s name is placed first.

**V.** It must be admitted that toward the end of the fourth century and the beginning of the fifth, both forms of address were in use; but it must likewise be admitted that, from Leo the Great, who entered upon the pontificate in 440, down to John VIII, who began to occupy the see in 872, one custom prevailed: namely, that of placing the pontiff’s name after the other name.

**VI.** Nor should reliance be placed on the registers of Leo and Gregory on the ground that the compilers neglected the formal addresses and subscriptions of letters, which other approved authors inserted in their writings. For, since the compilers wished to spare their readers the tedium caused by the continual repetition of the same formula, they were content to state who wrote to whom and concerning what matter; but more will be said of this below. For the present, the sequence of the tradition must be set forth, though six cautions must first be given.

**144 VII. First.** The custom of which we speak was not introduced suddenly, but gradually, letters of the same pontiff being addressed differently in different cases, until it at last prevailed completely in the fifth century; the manner of its disappearance seems to have been the same as that of its beginning.

**Second.** As I have already observed, the registers of the pontiffs who sat from the fourth century to the ninth are not to be consulted on this question; for the compilers omitted the formal addresses and subscriptions. Thus the letters of St. Leo which, in the more recent edition of his Works, bear the formal formula, were obtained by the recent editor from elsewhere and added to the older collection.

**Third.** Where the letters of pontiffs have been truncated by their compilers and, as it were, deprived of head and feet, if they are ever found inserted in other writings by approved authors, they are for the most part complete; and they must therefore be sought from that source.

**Fourth.** When pontiffs write either sentences of condemnation against persons—as Vigilius wrote against Rusticus and Sebastian—or to persons deprived of communion—as Felix wrote to Acacius—then they place their own name first, as both judicial procedure and faith require.

**Fifth.** Some think that pontiffs placed their own name after that of certain highly eminent persons when writing to them, but before it when writing to inferiors. To show that this is far from the truth, in setting out the sequence of the tradition we shall use examples of letters addressed to emperors, assemblies of bishops, and private persons.

Sixth. In the sequence of the tradition, the order of the pontiffs succeeding one another will be preserved [Col. 0120D]; and no one will be omitted whose letters are available, whether genuine or containing an honorable inscription and subscription. For this indication teaches that the letters were not mutilated by the collectors and compilers.

A letter to the same men concerning Aurelianus, to whom he entrusts his own responsibilities, bears the same inscription. In short, there is no letter of Vigilius—not even the Constitutum itself—that does not bear this same form of inscription, except the one containing the sentence of excommunication against Rusticus and Sebastianus, and the one addressed to the universal Church. In the former, a judge writes to the accused; in the latter, the head writes to his members.

“To the lord son, the most glorious and most excellent Childebert, king, Pelagius the bishop.” Three other letters to the same man are likewise inscribed in the same way.

Pelagius II, in the year 577.

“To the most beloved brother Annacharius, Pelagius, bishop of the city of Rome.”

“To the most beloved brothers Elias and the other bishops, and to all the sons established in the regions of Istria, Pelagius, bishop of the holy Catholic Church of the city of Rome.” Two other letters of the same kind are addressed to the same men.

Gregory I, in the year 590.

There is no letter in his entire Register that has not been stripped by the compiler [Col. 0123C] of the solemn formulas that he possessed. That all of them nevertheless had such formulas is clear from this one fact: many were sent to secular men and women, yet none of the letters as they now stand bears the name “Lord” or “Lady” in its heading, although John the Deacon reports that this was never omitted. Moreover, since Gregory, according to the same Deacon’s testimony, after the insolent arrogance of John of Constantinople, always styled himself “servant of the servants of God” in his letters, none of the letters as they are now preserved bears this inscription. Further, since he wrote the letters of Pelagius II to the bishops of Istria and preserved the customary form in them, it is not credible that he departed from the custom of his predecessor.

What is more, it seems contrary to reason that one who, out of humility, called himself “servant of the servants of God” [Col. 0123D] would place his name first, either after the manner of an emperor giving orders or like a praetor issuing an edict. Finally, the letter of recommendation to Aetherius of Arles for Augustine, who was setting out for England, lacks every formal element in the Register, but is quoted by Bede, Book I, chapter 25, with a suitable inscription and subscription:

“To the most reverend and most holy brother Aetherius, fellow bishop, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.”

And at the end:

“May God keep you safe, most reverend brother.”

Bede likewise quotes a letter of the same form to Virgilius, Aetherius’s successor, and to Augustine, bishop of York, in chapters 28 and 29. Indeed, in chapter 30, he gives the following letter to Mellitus the abbot:

“To the most beloved son Mellitus, abbot, Gregory, servant of the servants of God.”

[Col. 0124A]

And to King Æthelberht:

“To the lord, the most glorious and most excellent son Æthelberht, king of the English, Gregory the bishop.”

And at the end:

“May heavenly grace keep your Excellency safe, lord son.”

## NINTH CENTURY

After the three Gregories—II, III, and IV—who were not consistent in retaining a single manner of writing, but used sometimes one form and sometimes another [Col. 0126D], Leo IV consistently placed his name first, and the pontiffs who followed Leo followed his example. Once, however, Formosus, and once also Benedict VII, placed his name afterward: Formosus when he wrote to the bishops of England, Benedict when he wrote to the Gauls and Germans. Yet neither letter inspires much confidence. The one commonly attributed to Formosus is not free from defects; the one attributed to Benedict emerged from hiding only recently. And since it restores what Symmachus had formerly established, Benedict’s inscription may also be said to imitate Symmachus’s inscription.

The pontiffs of that period also refrained from the titles “Lord” and “Lady” when they wrote [Col. 0127A] to secular persons, even to emperors and queens. John VIII, nevertheless, once inscribed letter 92 as follows:

“To the most beloved daughter, the lady Angelberga, empress, wife of Louis, the invincible emperor, of pious memory, the most serene Augusta.”

Indeed, Nicholas I regularly omitted the solemn subscription used by his predecessors, and no longer prayed that the person to whom he wrote be kept safe by heavenly grace; instead he added either “we wish,” and so forth, or “farewell,” or something similar. He nevertheless retained the custom received from his predecessors in letters 36 and 67. His successors imitated Nicholas, except that John VIII observed the old custom once or twice.

Gregory VII introduced the custom that subsequently prevailed [Col. 0127B]: that he bestow greeting and the Apostolic blessing upon those to whom he sent letters.

From the material presented thus far, certain conclusions useful to ecclesiastical history may be drawn.

I. Around the beginning of the ninth century, the formulas contained in the *Diurnum* gradually fell out of use.

II. This occurred at the time when great changes in political affairs took place: after the Exarchs had been expelled from Italy and the Lombard kingdom overthrown, the Apostolic See acquired considerable dominion.

III. The old custom was not abolished suddenly, but gradually, as it were in stages, lest the world be surprised and perhaps object.

IV. It is surprising that Bernardinus Ferrarius [Col. 0127C] reports in Book II of *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Letters* that greeting and the Apostolic blessing were bestowed by the supreme pontiffs at the beginning of the letters they sent. “This custom,” he says, “just as Polydore Vergil in *On the Invention of Things*, Book VIII, chapter 2, and Gilbert Genebrard in the *Chronology*, Book III, under the year of Christ 93, in the notice on Cletus, report that it was first introduced by Cletus, the Roman pontiff, so they affirm that the remaining pontiffs thereafter borrowed it from him and consistently retained it.”

But who would not be surprised at this, when before Gregory VII, who sat in the eleventh century, either no one or scarcely anyone is found to have used that greeting? How, moreover, can it be asserted that Cletus was the author of this greeting? I know no basis on which this can be asserted, since no letters of his exist [Col. 0127D], nor did writers earlier than Polydore Vergil and Genebrard transmit anything on this matter in written records. It is highly credible that he wished them greeting and the grace of God, in the manner of the Apostles. But the issue here is not greeting, but the Apostolic blessing, which no Apostle prefaced to his letters by saying that he bestowed it.

Perhaps someone will wish that, after it has been explained in what form a pontiff inscribed and subscribed the letters he sent to others, it should next be shown what form of inscription and subscription was used in letters he received from others. But since this does not pertain to the *Diurnum*, in which the things prescribed for the pontiff to do are set out, not the things done by others, it may rightly be omitted [Col. 0128A]—especially since everyone seems to have written according to his own judgment, and no single form is found to have been consistently observed by all, even by persons of the same rank, such as emperors, Augustae, and so forth.

Nevertheless, it will not be irrelevant to the subject to report briefly what was used at the end of the sixth century, when Gregory the Great was seated, and throughout the two succeeding centuries by princes, Augusti, patricians, and others. Very few examples are found either in collections of papal letters or among the writers of Ecclesiastical Annals; and it is not worthwhile to investigate the matter more carefully elsewhere.

**Emperor to the supreme pontiff, in the year 682.** “Flavius Constantine, emperor faithful in Jesus Christ God, to Leo [Col. 0128B], most holy and most blessed archbishop of the ancient and most illustrious city of Rome, and ecumenical pope.” Subscription of the most pious emperor: “May God preserve you for many years, most holy and most blessed Father.”

**In the year 687.** “The emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, faithful in Jesus Christ, peaceful, pious, perpetual Augustus, to John, most holy and most blessed, of the ancient and life-giving city of Rome, and universal pope.” And in the imperial hand: “May the Divinity preserve you for many years, most holy and most blessed Father.”

**The Ecumenical Synod:** “The holy and universal Council, assembled by the grace of God and by the pious decree of the most pious and most faithful great emperor Constantine, in this [Col. 0128C] new Rome, Constantinople, preserved by God and royal city, in the secret chamber of the sacred palace called the Trullus, sends greeting in the Lord to Agatho, most holy and most blessed pope of elder Rome.”

**The universal African Synod to the supreme pontiff:** “To the most blessed lord, exalted to the Apostolic summit, Father of Fathers, Theodore the pope and supreme pontiff of all prelates: Columbus, bishop of the first see of the Council of Numidia; Stephen, bishop of the first see of the Council of Byzacena; Reparatus, bishop of the first see of the Council of Mauretania; and all the bishops of the three aforesaid Councils of the African province.”

**Patriarch to the supreme pontiff, in the year 712:** “To the most holy and most blessed brother and fellow minister, the lord [Col. 0128D] Constantine, John, an unworthy bishop, greeting in the Lord.” Subscription: “Strong in the Lord, pray for us, most holy and most blessed brother.”

**Primate of Africa to the supreme pontiff:** “To the most blessed and honorable holy brother, Theodore the pope, Victor.”

**Bishop to the supreme pontiff, in the year 741:** “To the dearest lord, endowed with the insignia of the supreme pontificate, an Apostolic man, Zacharias, Boniface, servant of the servants of God.”

“To the most reverend Father, most beloved Lord, revered with fear and trembling as Master, endowed with the privilege of Apostolic honor and exalted by the insignia of the Apostolic See, Zacharias, Boniface, your insignificant servant [Col. 0129A], although unworthy and last, yet your most devoted Germanic legate, sends the desired greeting of unfading charity in Christ.”

**Observation I.** Constantine Pogonatus and Justinian II place their names before the name of Leo II, the pontiff, and do not follow the example of Marcian in his letter to Leo I: “To Leo, most reverend bishop of the glorious city of Rome, Marcian.” They nevertheless follow the form of Justin and Justinian I. The former wrote to Hormisdas: “Victor Justin, pious, fortunate, illustrious, triumphator, perpetual Augustus, to Hormisdas, most holy and most blessed archbishop of the life-giving city of Rome, and patriarch.” The latter wrote to John II: “Victor Justinian, pious, fortunate, illustrious, triumphator, perpetual Augustus, to John, most holy archbishop of the life-giving city of Rome, and patriarch.” And to Agapetus: “The emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, Alemannic, Gothic, Frankish, Germanic, Antic, Alanic, Vandalic, African, pious, fortunate, illustrious, victor and triumphator, perpetual Augustus, to Agapetus [Col. 0129D], most holy archbishop of the life-giving city of Rome, and patriarch.”

**Observation II.** Neither in the collections of papal letters nor in Baronius is there found a letter of any Augusta to the supreme pontiff in solemn form, except that of Pulcheria to Saint Leo, which has the same form as that used by Marcian.

**Observation III.** The Sixth Ecumenical Synod placed the pontiff’s name after its own, imitating the example of the Fourth Synod’s report to Saint Leo I concerning the proceedings at Chalcedon. For the report is inscribed as follows:

“The holy, great, and universal Synod, assembled by the grace of God and by the decree of our most pious emperors, lovers of Christ, in Chalcedon, metropolis of the province of Bithynia, to Leo, most holy and most blessed archbishop of the Romans [Col. 0129C].”

[Col. 0130A]

It is uncertain whether the Council of Ephesus preceded the Council of Chalcedon in this respect, for the inscriptions of the report vary in different manuscripts.

The fathers of neither Council explicitly call the supreme pontiff “brother,” “Father,” and “Lord,” although the Chalcedonians, in the body of their report itself, sometimes call themselves brothers and sometimes sons. Let those, therefore, who think they can derive much from the fact that the Chalcedonians called themselves Leo’s sons consider how they are to defend their position.

**Observation IV.** The four greater patriarchs—the Alexandrian, Antiochene, Constantinopolitan, and Jerusalemite—and also the bishop of Carthage, who is primate of the entire African diocese, when they send letters to the supreme pontiff, call him “brother and fellow minister,” but at the same time call him “Lord.” The pontiff, for his part, does not use the title “Lord” when he inscribes his letters to them [Col. 0130D].

**Observation V.** Provincial synods, over which neither patriarchs preside and whose African primate is not equal in rank to the patriarchs, call the supreme pontiff both “Lord” and “Father” in their letters, and in this differ from the Ecumenical Synods. This was preserved from ancient times. For in the year 416, the fathers of the Council of Milevis, presided over by Silvanus, primate of Numidia because of his age, inscribed their letter to Innocent I as follows:

“To the most blessed Lord, deservedly venerable and honored in Christ, Pope Innocent, Silvanus, Valentinus, Aurelius, Donatus, Restitutus, Lucianus, Alipius, Augustine, and the others.”

The letter of the Council of Carthage [Col. 0130C], however, over which the primate of all Africa presided, reads as follows:

“To the most blessed and most honored brother, holy Pope Innocent, Aurelius, Numidius, and the others.”

156 **DISSERTATION II. APPENDIX TO THE NOTES ON CHAPTER II, ON THE ORDINATION OF THE SUPREME PONTIFF**

[Col. 0129C] Chapter II is divided into three parts. The first comprises the letters by which, before the ordination [Col. 0129D] of the elected pontiff, either the death of his predecessor was announced, or the decree of election was conveyed, or approval of the decree was requested. The second concerns the rite by which the pontiff’s consecration was carried out. The third concerns professions and explanations of the Catholic faith. For each of these, the following observations remain to be made—observations which the brevity and rationale of the notes prevented from being appended to the text of the *Diurnum*.

### § I. On the letters pertaining to the ordination of the supreme pontiff

I. In the notes I said that letters were sent not only to Ravenna but also to the imperial city by the clergy of the Roman Church and the Roman people, to obtain approval of the elected man from the prince; and to the Antistes, the patricians, and the leading men of the palace, as well as to the *apocrisiarius* of the Apostolic See, so that they might be informed of the business to be advanced before [Col. 0130C] the prince. This is readily understood from the letters of Gregory the Great: to John, [Col. 0130D] bishop of Constantinople; to another John, former consul and patrician; and finally to Philip, Count of the Excubitors.

When those men, by whatever influence they possessed with the emperor, had done what they had been asked—of course, by the clergy in letters sent from Rome—to do, the holy pontiff complains to them of the friendship that had been violated. To Bishop John he writes (Letter 4):

“I know with what zeal you wished to avoid the burdens of the episcopate; and yet, so that these same burdens of the episcopate might not be imposed upon me, you did not resist. It is therefore clear that you do not love me as you love yourselves, since you wished me to undertake those burdens that you did not wish to be imposed upon you.”

To John the patrician (Letter 30):

“I am not a little saddened by this contradiction of love, because you learned that I was seeking quiet and [Col. 0131A] led me into unrest, and so forth.”

Finally, to Philip, Count of the Excubitors (Letter 31):

“Unworthy as I am to undertake the burdens of the episcopate, I submitted myself to the command of almighty God and to your will; and you wished me to preside over it by the generosity of grace rather than by an assessment of judgment.”

There is no doubt that he wrote to Honoratus, the *responsalis* of the Apostolic See, in the same sense.

II. I also said that no one ought to suspect that the *Diurnum* lacks the formula for letters of this kind. For letters were indeed issued in corresponding forms to peers, with a few alterations, as usual: namely, the same forms to the Constantinopolitan Antistes as to the Ravennate, and so forth. Two considerations establish this. First, the reason for writing to the Constantinopolitans and the Ravennates was the same, as were the subject [Col. 0131B] and the necessity. Second, it was customary in those times to send similar letters to everyone when several letters were dispatched concerning the same matter; this was called writing “from an equal”—that is, with an equal subject. This is evident from the letters of Gregory the Great.

III. I added that nowhere is there found a form by which either the Exarch or the emperor, after approving the election, granted authority to ordain the pontiff by subscribing, as I believe, the decree brought to him. I think no one who has read books produced in that period will call this into doubt, although in Marculfus, Book I, there is found a pair of royal commands concerning the ordination of a bishop, by which the king responds to the people requesting that a bishop be granted to them. Those three formulas, which are extremely corrupt in Bignon’s edition, are appended in Sirmond’s corrected version [Col. 0131C], volume II of the Councils of Gaul.

IV. Cassiodorus also preserves a letter from Athalaric to the senate of the city, in which he declares that it was most agreeable to him that they had approved the judgment of his grandfather Theodoric, who had chosen Felix IV as pontiff, and that the former dispute between the clergy and laity, divided into factions, had been ended by their acceptance of the pontiff chosen by the prince.

### § II. On the rite by which the supreme pontiff was ordained

I. This rite varied at different times. One form is described in the *Diurnum* and in the ancient Roman *Ordo*; another by Cencius Camerarius in the coronation of Celestine III; another by Augustine Patricius in the *Book of Ecclesiastical Rites*; and yet another, somewhat different, is now observed.

[Col. 0131D] II. It is not clearly evident whether, before the seventh century, any rite other than the one customary in the consecration of other metropolitans, and indeed of bishops, was observed. Certainly, in that period the supreme pontiffs were not made from among bishops. This was first attempted in the case of Formosus. For the most part they were chosen from the deacons and priests of the Roman Church, as the *History of the Pontiffs* teaches. Thus at that time three rites could occur together: the elected man would immediately be made priest, bishop, and supreme pontiff.

158 III. He was made priest and bishop according to the custom used for others; but supreme pontiff by the imposition of the pallium received from the altar of Saint Peter, and by *enthronement* (*enthronismos*). This is shown by the words: “The archdeacon fastens the pallium [Col. 0132A] upon him, and he ascends to the seat.” The pallium signified the fullness of authority, and *enthronement* (*enthronismos*) signified presidency. There is as yet no mention of a coronation, while Rome still served a secular power.

IV. The sign of supreme authority over the universal Church was not precisely the reception of the pallium, for that was common to all patriarchs, but its reception from the altar of Saint Peter, to whom God entrusted the feeding of his flock and in whose place the pontiff succeeds.

V. What rite the Eastern Church formerly observed in ordaining its patriarchs is not explicitly transmitted in the Greek ritual books. Liberatus the Deacon reports the following concerning Alexandria:

“It is the custom at Alexandria for the one who succeeds the deceased to keep vigil [Col. 0132B] over the body of the deceased, to place the deceased’s right hand upon his own head, and, after burying him with his own hands, to receive around his neck the pallium of blessed Mark, and then to be legally seated”—that is, to be enthroned.

These words should not be understood as though someone were made a bishop from a presbyter solely by this rite and no other consecration were employed, as some rashly have imagined. Rather, in addition to the common ceremony for ordaining a bishop, this was the solemn method of constituting a patriarch. Something comparable occurs in the election of the supreme pontiff, even if he has not yet been a bishop.

VI. For I can scarcely accept what some say: that the presbyters of the Alexandrian Church mentioned by Jerome were all chorepiscopi, and indeed possessed an episcopal [Col. 0132C] character. Although I admit that there were several bishops in the suburbs and neighboring places of Alexandria, I nevertheless know that in the days of Alexander, who expelled Arius, and of Cyril, who overthrew Nestorius, there were many presbyters in the Alexandrian Church, such as Eulogius, to whom Cyril wrote the *Commonitorium* inserted in the third part of the Council of Ephesus.

### § III. On the professions of faith issued by the supreme pontiffs at their ordination, in general

I. It is beyond doubt that the supreme pontiffs made a profession of their faith when they were ordained. For we learn from various passages of the writers, and especially from the letter of Eusebius of Caesarea to his people, preserved in Theodoret, Book I of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter XII, that a confession of faith was made not only by catechumens when they received baptism, but also by the faithful when they received the presbyterate and [Col. 0132D] episcopate. Since this was required of each bishop because they must be teachers of their own Church, the Roman bishop certainly did not omit it, since he is the teacher of the whole Church.

II. It is not equally certain, or at least not so generally known, in what form those who were elected to the supreme pontificate before the seventh century professed the faith. It is therefore useful, for the illumination of ecclesiastical history, to investigate this matter. But, lest an error mislead the unwary during the investigation, it is necessary at the outset to distinguish [Col. 0133A] two professions: one issued by the man being ordained, and the other issued by the man already ordained.

### III

John the Deacon distinguished the two in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, giving the former the name “Symbol” and the latter “Synodical Letter.” The former belonged to a private individual; the latter to a teacher of the Church. By the former, the Elect professed his faith; by the latter, the Pontiff explained what all ought to believe and taught God’s people from the seat of Peter. The former is scarcely mentioned before Gregory the Great; numerous examples of the latter survive.

### IV

John the Deacon writes of Gregory’s Symbol:

> “Standing upon the watchtower of the holy universal Church, a man of complete orthodox humanity and authority, from which the herald of the Gospel might be seen and heard more clearly, [Col. 0133B] he fortified the right faith with the divine sword of his mouth and dispersed all heresies with a single Symbol. The Symbol of this sacred confession is as follows:
>
> “I believe in one almighty God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: three Persons, one substance. The Father is unbegotten; the Son begotten; the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, but coeternal, proceeding from the Father and the Son.
>
> “I confess the only-begotten Son, consubstantial with the Father and born from the Father without time; the creator of all visible and invisible things; light from light, true God from true God, the radiance of glory, the likeness of substance. Remaining the Word before the ages, he was made perfect man at the end of the ages, conceived and born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and assumed our nature [Col. 0133C] without sin. He was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate; on the third day he rose from the dead. On the fortieth day he ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead, setting all the hidden things of each person before the eyes of all; giving the just the everlasting rewards of the heavenly kingdom, but punishments of eternal fire to the wicked; renewing the age by fire, and bringing about the resurrection of the flesh.
>
> “I confess one faith, one Baptism, one Apostolic and universal Church, in which alone sins can be forgiven, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

### V

Of the Synodical Letter he writes:

> “Gregory also sent his Synodical Letter, [Col. 0133D] according to the ancient custom of his predecessors, to John of Constantinople, Eulogius of Alexandria, Gregory of Antioch, John of Jerusalem, and Anastasius, Patriarch of Antioch. It reads as follows:
>
> “When I consider that, unequal to the merits required and resisting with all my heart, I have been compelled to bear the burdens of pastoral care, a darkness of sorrow comes upon me, etc. A sorrowful heart sees nothing except those shadows that permit nothing to be seen. For why is a bishop chosen for the Lord except to intercede for the sins of the people? With what confidence, then, do I come before him as an intercessor for the sins of others, when I am not secure concerning my own? [Col. 0134A] If someone were to seek to have me become his intercessor before a powerful man who was angry with him and unknown to me, I would immediately reply: ‘I cannot come to intercede, because I have no acquaintance with him through diligent familiarity.’ If, therefore, I would be ashamed to become an intercessor before a man concerning whom I had presumed nothing, how great is the audacity of my occupying the place of intercessor before God for the people, when I do not recognize myself as familiar to him through the merit of my life?
>
> “In this matter I must fear something still more serious. As we have all plainly recognized, when one who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the angered mind is provoked to worse things. I greatly fear that the people of the faithful entrusted to me may perish through the addition of my guilt, although until now the Lord has patiently endured their sins.
>
> “[Col. 0134B] When I somehow suppress this fear and apply my consoled mind to the duties of the pontifical office, I am frightened when I consider the very magnitude of the task. I reflect that the ruler must be watchful with every care, pure in thought, distinguished in action, discerning in silence, useful in speech, near to each person through compassion, raised above all through contemplation, humble companionship to those who do good, and, through zeal for justice, upright against the vices of those who sin, etc.”

> “Moreover, because one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation, I acknowledge that I receive and venerate the four Councils just as I do the four books of the holy Gospel: namely, the Council of Nicaea, in which Arius’s perverse doctrine was destroyed; the Council of Constantinople, in which the error of Eunomius and Macedonius was refuted; [Col. 0134C] the First Council of Ephesus, in which the impiety of Nestorius was judged; and the Council of Chalcedon, in which the depravity of Eutyches and Dioscorus was rejected. I embrace them with complete devotion and preserve them with the fullest approval, because in them, as in a square stone, the structure of the holy faith rises and the rule of every life and action stands firm. Whoever does not hold their solidity, even if he appears to be a stone, nevertheless lies outside the building.
>
> “I likewise venerate the Fifth Council, in which the letter called ‘of Ibas,’ full of error, was rejected; Theodore was shown to have fallen into impious treachery by separating the person of the mediator between God and human beings into two substances; and the writings of Theodoret, by which the faith of blessed Cyril was attacked, were refuted as produced with mad presumption. [Col. 0134D] I reject all the persons whom the aforesaid venerable Councils reject, and embrace those whom they venerate. Since they were established by universal agreement, whoever presumes either to release those whom they bind or to bind those whom they release destroys himself, not them. Therefore, whoever thinks otherwise, let him be anathema.”

### VI

These are John’s accounts of the Symbol and Synodical Letter of Saint Gregory. To explain them more usefully and clearly in relation to our subject, two points must be observed.

First, one and the same thing had three names: “Faith,” “Symbol,” and “Indiculum.” It was called “Faith” from its content; “Symbol” from the order and brevity of its articles and its resemblance to a token; and “Indiculum” from the form in which it was transmitted in writing, like an instrument secured with all its accompanying details—person, time, and witnesses—and preserved in the archive. [Col. 0135A]

Second, the other document likewise had three names: “Exposition of the Faith,” “Sermon,” and “Synodical Letter.” It was called an “Exposition of the Faith” because it was an explanation more extended than the Symbol and better adapted to condemning heresies; a “Sermon” because it was delivered before an assembly of the faithful; and a “Synodical Letter” because it was sent from the Roman Synod to the Patriarchs and had to be read at the Synod of the Patriarchs, so that the whole Church might recognize the faith of its teacher.

### VII

Concerning the form of faith that we have called the Symbol and that the Elect used before ordination, two questions arise.

First, what was it in ancient times? By “ancient” I mean the period preceding Gregory the Great. [Col. 0135B] Was it only the Symbol called the Apostolic Symbol, and that in the form we use, or was it once used differently at Rome?

Second, what was the ancient Symbol of the Roman Church?

### VIII

To resolve the first question fully, the ancient period must first be divided, and then the Roman Symbols distinguished.

In the earlier period—that is, before the year 400—when Rufinus, Presbyter of Aquileia, writes that nothing had yet been added to the Roman Symbol, I think that the Elect professed no other faith than that contained in the unaugmented Roman Symbol.

In the later period—that is, from about the year 400 until Gregory the Great—I believe that the same Elect recited the [Col. 0135C] Apostolic Symbol, but with additions, sometimes fewer and sometimes more, as the circumstances of the times required and as the seventh century approached. At that time the profession of faith contained in the *Liber Diurnus* was issued, and it remained in use until the fifteenth century and even later.

### IX

To make this clearer, the second question must be resolved: what was the Apostolic Symbol used at Rome, to which Rufinus, shortly before the four-hundredth year of Christ, wrote that nothing had yet been added?

From the ancient records it is understood to have been as follows:

> “I believe in God the almighty Father, and in Jesus Christ, his only-begotten Son, our Lord, who was conceived from the Holy Spirit, born from the Virgin Mary, suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, [Col. 0135D] and was buried; on the third day he rose from the dead, ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of God the Father, and from there will come to judge the living and the dead.
>
> “I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy Catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins, and the resurrection of the flesh.”

Three elements found in the common form are absent from it: “creator of heaven and earth,” “he descended into hell,” and “everlasting life.”

### X

From this arises a third question: when and for what reason were these three elements added? No one, as far as I know, has investigated the matter, although it is useful to know, even by conjecture.

### XI

Rufinus seems to provide some basis for conjecture when he reports that the Roman Symbol lacked additions [Col. 0136A] when he wrote:

> “Because no heresy had originated there; whereas in other places, as far as can be understood, certain additions appear to have been made on account of some heretics, by which the meaning of novel doctrines might be excluded.”

### XII

From this I seem able, not implausibly, to conclude that the need for additions arose when the three principal heresies of Origen, Mani, and Arius attempted to infiltrate the Roman Church.

They made such attempts when Origen’s book *περὶ ἀρχῶν*—*On First Principles*—appeared at Rome; when the Manichaeans, secretly lying in concealment, were detected by definite indications and brought into public view; and when the Eutychian error, a kind of offspring of Arianism, spread widely.

### XIII

The book *On First Principles* came to Rome [Col. 0136B] during the time of Anastasius I. Leo the Great attacked the Manichaeans in the year 443. Under the same Pontiff, the Eutychian heresy caused disturbances everywhere on the occasion of the Ephesian Robber Council.

Against Origen’s teaching of the temporal and mutable blessedness of the saints, eternal life was professed. Against Manichaeism’s doctrine that the sensible world was created by a demon, the confession was made that God is the maker of heaven and earth. Against Arius’s error that Christ had no soul, the descent of the soul into hell was confessed while the body lay in the tomb.

### XIV

This threefold addition alone was made to the Symbol as it was transmitted to catechumens and recited at Baptism. But a much greater addition appears to have been made when it was professed by those being ordained, so that they might prove their faith pure from error. This is clear from the Symbol of Gregory the Great, which everyone can see is very different from the common form. [Col. 0136C]

### XV

In the seventh century, when the supreme Pontiffs were ordained, the earlier Symbol was no longer used. Instead, there was a form of faith such as that presented in the *Liber Diurnus*.

That form remained in force not only until at least the tenth century, when Yvo of Chartres lived, but also until the time of the Council of Basel, as will be said later. For Yvo makes it sufficiently clear that even in his time the supreme Pontiffs issued that profession at their ordination, citing a substantial part of it from the *Liber Diurnus*; and the Fathers at Basel required it of the Pontiff being ordained.

### XVI

A fourth question also arises: at what time was the Symbol changed into the form of faith contained in the *Liber Diurnus*?

I think this happened after the first [Col. 0136D] six ecumenical Councils had established the two principles of the Christian religion: the consubstantiality of the divine Persons and the truth of the Incarnation. For it was then an unquestionable mark of orthodoxy—*ὀρθοδοξίας*—to receive the Councils and execrate the heresies they had proscribed.

### XVII

A fifth question also arises: did the supreme Pontiffs and other bishops, at least those consecrated at Rome—whether they were from outside Rome or subject to the ordination of the Apostolic See—profess their faith without distinction?

There was, indeed, a very great distinction: the Pontiffs bound themselves by oath to Saint Peter *ἀμέσως*, immediately, whereas the bishops bound themselves to Saint Peter’s successor.

### XVIII

There is also this final question: how far is it true—or rather, what examination does it require—that Euthymius Zigabenus reports in chapter XII of his *Panoplia*, [Col. 0137A] drawing from a dissertation by Photius of Constantinople on the procession of the Holy Spirit:

> “Until the time of Sergius of Constantinople, who was ordained in the year 608, the Roman Pontiffs, at the beginning of their episcopate, inserted without alteration the Symbol in the canonical letters transmitting the faith they professed to all the patriarchal sees.”

First, the alteration of which he speaks is solely that by which the Holy Spirit was said to proceed from the Father and the Son. Moreover, his claim that the supreme Pontiffs appended the Symbol to their canonical letters until the time of Sergius of Constantinople, and that they did not place the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in their Symbol, is refuted by the example of Gregory the Great. Gregory began to sit as Pontiff in the year 590; nevertheless, he both professed in his Symbol [Col. 0137B] that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and did not append the Symbol to his letters to the Patriarchs.

### XIX

With regard to the Synodical Letters that the supreme Pontiffs, immediately after ascending the Apostolic See, sent to the Patriarchs and to bishops equal in rank to the Patriarchs, seven questions may usefully be asked, in addition to what has been stated in the notes: how ancient was this custom; when did it begin; to whom were the Synodical Letters sent; what did they contain; what was the purpose of sending them; when did they cease to be sent; and whose Synodical Letters have come down to us?

### XX

That the custom was ancient is taught by Gelasius in his first letter to Euphemius, his second to Laurentius, Bishop of Lignidum, and his third to the Bishops of Dardania.

To Euphemius of Constantinople, who complained that he had not yet received a Synodical Letter from Gelasius, the Pontiff replied in these words: [Col. 0137C]

> “You have said that it was necessary for the one newly established as priest of the Apostolic See to announce this by a preceding letter. This was once the ancient ecclesiastical rule among our Fathers, among whom the one Catholic and Apostolic communion remained free from every pollution of transgressors. But now, since you prefer an alien fellowship to returning to the pure and undefiled communion of blessed Peter, how shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land? How shall we offer to men of an alien communion the ancient covenants of the Apostolic dispensation?”

[Col. 0137D] To Laurentius, Bishop in Macedonia:

> “Because it is the custom of the priest newly established in the Roman Church to send in advance the form of his faith to the holy Churches, I have endeavored to renew that same practice in an excessively brief summary, so that the reader may recognize from this letter, without weariness because of its brevity, according to what faith one must live, in accordance with the statutes of the Fathers.”

To the Bishops of Dardania:

> “Having attained the government of the Apostolic See, and being delayed by public disturbances, we have been unable to announce by our own letters, as was customary, the sacred office of administration entrusted to us, so that your fraternity might rejoice with us in the Lord’s gift of communion.”

He then sets forth the faith against the spreading Eutychian heresy [Col. 0138A] and adds at the end:

> “Let your affection also cause this to reach all the neighboring provinces and the bishops nearby, so that the presidents of the Churches, having received instruction in the whole truth, may be able to avoid the deadly falsehood.”

### XXI

When this ecclesiastical “ancient rule” among the Fathers began is obscure. Nevertheless, something of the truth may be discerned if two elements in such letters are distinguished: first, what they announced concerning their ordination; second, what contained the exposition of the faith.

Someone might reasonably suppose that the first element had always existed, and the testimony of Cyprian’s reply to Cornelius, recently ordained, may usefully be cited for this purpose.

Although no mention of the second element is found before [Col. 0138B] the time of Gelasius, it nevertheless existed long before him and originated as early as the time of the Emperor Aurelian, that is, about the year 270 after Christ.

For in the year 493 Gelasius testifies:

> “It was the custom of the priest newly established in the Roman Church to send in advance the form of his faith to the holy Churches.”

That custom, therefore, had already long been established. He also testifies that it was an ancient rule among the Fathers; therefore it had existed for a long time. But from when? Certainly not from the Church’s origin, nor during the first two centuries, since there is neither any surviving trace nor any basis for conjecture, while the Church then lay hidden beneath the imperial swords threatening it from every side.

It remains, therefore, that this custom arose when the faith of the Roman Church could be publicly disclosed, with the Emperors themselves [Col. 0138C] willing it, so that it might serve as a standard of belief and a rule of orthodoxy.

This first occurred under Aurelian and later under Constantine.
