For although Aurelian was a pagan, he decreed against Paul of Samosata, deposed by the Second Synod of Antioch, that the house belonging to the Church of Antioch should be granted to whichever person the Bishop of the Roman Church judged worthy to receive it—as though he were saying that the Catholic bishop of the Church of Antioch should be regarded as the one whose faith the Bishop of the Roman Church approved.

Constantine, however, who freed the Church from servitude, caused the privilege possessed by the Roman Church from Christ—the privilege of teaching the faith to the world—to burst forth freely into action and to be recognized by all.

[Col. 0138D] This opinion, then, took root in my mind: from the time of Aurelian onward, when the Roman Bishop first succeeded to the seat of Peter, who was commanded to strengthen his brethren, he sent to all God’s people the form of his faith—that is, the Catholic faith.

### XXII

As stated earlier, he sent it to the Patriarchs and to autocephalous bishops equal in rank to the Patriarchs.

This is established partly from Gelasius and partly from Gregory the Great. Gelasius wrote letters to the Macedonians and the Dardanians; Gregory wrote to John of Constantinople, Eulogius of Alexandria, Gregory of Antioch, John of Jerusalem, and likewise Anastasius of Antioch, sending letters to his peers in which he included his profession of faith (*Book 1, Letter 24*).

[Col. 0139A] It should further be observed from Gelasius and Gregory that the Pontiffs did not send their Synodical Letters to bishops divided by schism. They did send them to those who, although forcibly and wrongfully driven from their thrones, nevertheless remained in communion with the Apostolic See, which condemned what had been done.

Thus Gelasius wrote neither to John of Constantinople nor to the Bishop of Thessalonica, because both were obstructed by the Acacian schism. He did write to the Dardanians subject to the Patriarch of Constantinople and to Laurentius, Bishop of the Church of Lignidum, subject to the Bishop of Thessalonica, so that those who did not consent to their schismatic primates would not lack communion in the faith.

[Col. 0139B] Gregory sent a letter to that distinguished Anastasius, called the Sinaitic, who had been unjustly expelled from the see of Antioch, just as he did to the other Patriarchs, although Gregory had been installed in his place. Not content with sending him a similar letter, he sent another in which, among other things, he wrote:

> “Moreover, just as I have sent a Synodical Letter to the other Patriarchs who are your equals, so I have sent one to you, because in my eyes you have always been what you received by the gift of almighty God, not what you are thought by human will not to be.”

### XXIII

The Synodical Letter contained three or four elements: news of the ordination of the supreme Pontiff, the form of faith, a request for prayers, and also an exhortation to fulfill the office. This is established partly from the Synodical Letter of Gregory the Great and partly from the formulas of the *Liber Diurnus*.

[Col. 0139C]

### XXIV

From these matters it is apparent what purpose the letter served: namely, that Christ’s sheepfold might be one; that the sheep might hear and follow the voice of their shepherd; and that the unity of the Church—whose bond is faith and the agreement of the members with the head—might be preserved intact.

For through the letters, when they were sent, the shepherd recognized the sheep; and through the letters, when they were received, the sheep recognized the shepherd.

### XXV

That custom continued as long as the Eastern Church had not departed from the Western. But after the dreadful schism tore one away from the other, it was no longer appropriate either to write the form of faith to people who accused the Apostolic See of error or to embrace with the bond of paternal charity those who, through pride, rejected paternal embraces.

### XXVI

[Col. 0139D] The Synodical Letters of only a few Pontiffs have come down to us. I investigated carefully and found no more outside the *Liber Diurnus* than four: those of Gelasius I, Pelagius I, Gregory the Great, and Leo IX—if, strictly speaking, the last of these ought to be called a Synodical Letter.

It is worthwhile to place these here. When compared with those presented in the *Liber Diurnus*, they contribute considerably to ecclesiastical doctrine.

### XXVII

In the letter mentioned above to Laurentius, Bishop of Lignidum, Gelasius says:

> “We confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten before all ages, without beginning, from the Father according to divinity. In the last days, the same one was incarnate from the most holy Virgin Mary and became perfect man through the assumption of a rational soul and body; *homoousios* (consubstantial) with the Father according to divinity and *homoousios* (consubstantial) with us according to humanity.
>
> “[Col. 0140A] For the unity of two perfect natures was ineffably accomplished. Therefore we confess one Christ, the same Son of God and of man, the only-begotten from the Father and the firstborn from the dead. We know that he is coeternal with his Father according to divinity, according to which he is the maker of all things, and that he deigned to be born after the consent of the most holy Virgin, when she said to the angel: ‘Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.’
>
> “Ineffably he built a temple for himself from her and united it to himself. He did not bring down from heaven a body coeternal with him and of his substance, but received it from the mass of our substance—that is, from the Virgin—and united it to himself. God the Word did not turn into flesh, nor did he appear as a phantom; rather, he preserved his essence unchangeably and unalterably, and, assuming the first fruits of our nature, united them to himself.
>
> “[Col. 0140B] For God the Word, in great goodness, deigned to unite these first fruits of our nature to himself. He appeared as one and the same in the substance of both, without mixture, as it is written: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’ Christ Jesus is destroyed according to the true substance that he assumed, and he raises up the destroyed temple as his own; he himself is so according to the divine substance, according to which he is also the maker of all.
>
> “[Col. 0140C] After the resurrection he never departed from his own temple, nor can he depart from it because of his ineffable goodness. Rather, the same Lord Jesus Christ is passible and impassible: passible according to humanity, impassible according to divinity.
>
> “God the Word therefore raised up his temple and effected in himself the resurrection and renewal of our nature. After rising from the dead, our Lord Christ God showed this to his disciples, saying: ‘Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have.’ He did not say, ‘as you say that I am,’ but ‘as you see me have,’ so that, considering both the one who possesses and the thing possessed, you might recognize not mixture, conversion, or change, but a unity that has been made. For this reason he also displayed the marks of the nails and the wound of the spear, and ate with his disciples, so that he might show in every respect the resurrection of our nature renewed in himself.
>
> “[Col. 0140D] And because, according to the blessed substance of divinity, he is unconvertible, unchangeable, impassible, immortal, needing nothing, and perfecting all things, he permitted sufferings to be inflicted upon his own temple, which he raised by his own power; and through the perfection of his temple he effected the renewal of our nature.
>
> “[Col. 0141A] But those who say that Christ was a subtle man, or that God was passible, or that he was changed into flesh, or that he had a body co-born with him, or that he brought it down from heaven, or that he was a phantom, or that he was mortal; those who say that God the Word needed the Father to raise him, or that he assumed a body without a soul, or a man without sensation; those who say that Christ’s two substances were confused by mixture and became one substance; and those who do not confess that our Lord Jesus Christ has two unconfused natures but one person, since he is one Christ and one identical Son—the Catholic and Apostolic Church anathematizes them.”

This entire exposition of the faith concerns the truth of the Incarnation against the heresies then spreading, especially the Apollinarian, Nestorian, and Eutychian heresies.

### XXVIII

[Col. 0141B] Pelagius I, in his letter to King Childebert, before whom he had been falsely accused as though he did not hold the same view concerning the Incarnation of the divine Word as Saint Leo, first praised the Tome of Leo, which he had received in another letter, and honorably mentioned the first four Synods. He then wrote:

> “I believe in one God, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: namely, the almighty, eternal, unbegotten Father; the Son, begotten from the substance of that same Father before absolutely every beginning, whether of time or of anything else, almighty from the almighty, equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with his begetter; and the almighty Holy Spirit, equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with both, namely the Father and the Son. Proceeding timelessly from the Father, he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son.
>
> “[Col. 0141C] These are three Persons, or three subsistences, of one essence or nature, one power, one operation, one blessedness, and one authority, so that there is a triune unity and a single Trinity, according to the voice of the Lord’s truth, which says: ‘Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’
>
> “He says ‘in the name,’ not ‘in the names,’ thereby showing one God through the undivided name of the divine essence and teaching the distinction of the Persons through their proper attributes. Since there is one name of divinity for the three, the equality of the Persons is shown; and, again, the equality of the Persons permits nothing foreign or accidental to be understood in them. Thus each one of them is true and perfect God, namely from the fullness of divinity: nothing less is to be understood in each, and nothing more in the three.
>
> “[Col. 0141D] From this holy, most blessed, and consubstantial Trinity, I believe and confess that one Person—that is, the Son of God—descended from heaven in the last times for the salvation of the human race, without abandoning either his paternal seat or the governance of the world. When the Holy Spirit came upon the blessed Virgin Mary and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, the same Word and Son of God mercifully entered the womb of that holy Virgin Mary and united flesh from her to himself, animated by a rational and intellectual soul.
>
> “[Col. 0142A] The flesh was not created first, with the Son of God coming afterward. Rather, as it is written, ‘Wisdom building herself a house,’ flesh was immediately formed in the Virgin’s womb, immediately became the flesh of the Word of God, and thereafter, without any alteration or conversion of the nature of the Word and flesh, the Word and Son of God became man. One Christ Jesus, true God and the same true man, proceeded—that is, was born—in both natures, divine and human, while the integrity of his mother’s virginity was preserved, because, remaining a virgin, she gave birth to him just as she had conceived him while a virgin. For this reason we most truly confess that the same blessed Virgin Mary is the Mother of God: she bore the incarnate Word of God.
>
> “[Col. 0142B] There is therefore one and the same Jesus Christ, true Son of God and the same true son of man, perfect in divinity and likewise perfect in humanity, wholly in what belongs to him and the same wholly in what belongs to us. Through his second birth he assumed from a human mother what he was not, without ceasing to be what he was through his first birth, by which he was born from the Father.
>
> “For this reason we believe him to exist from two natures and in two natures, which remain undivided and unconfused. They are undivided because, even after the assumption of our nature, one Christ, the Son of God, remained and remains. They are unconfused because we believe the natures to have been united into one person and subsistence in such a way that, while the property of each was preserved, neither was converted into the other.
>
> “[Col. 0142C] Therefore, as we have often said, we confess that he is one and the same Christ, true Son of God and the same true son of man, consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and the same consubstantial with us according to humanity, like us in every respect except sin, passible in flesh and the same impassible in divinity.
>
> “We confess that he willingly suffered in the flesh under Pontius Pilate for our salvation; was crucified in the flesh, died in the flesh, and rose on the third day in the same flesh, glorified and incorruptible; that after the resurrection he lived with his disciples and clearly demonstrated to them in many ways the reality of his body; and that on the fortieth day, in the sight of those same disciples, he ascended into heaven.
>
> “[Col. 0142D] I believe and confess that he also sits at the right hand of the Father and, according to the testimony of the angels, will come from heaven just as he ascended, to judge the living and the dead. I confess that all human beings born and dead from Adam until the consummation of the age, including Adam himself and his wife, who were not born from other parents but were created—the one from the earth, the other from the man’s rib—will then rise and stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive what belongs to his body according to what he has done, whether good or evil.
>
> “He will grant to the just, through the most abundant grace of God, as vessels of mercy prepared for glory, the rewards of eternal life; they will live forever in the company of the angels, without any further fear of falling. But the wicked, who remain by their own free choice as vessels of wrath fit for destruction, having either not recognized the way of the Lord or, after recognizing it, abandoned it when captured by various transgressions, he will by his most just judgment hand over to the punishment of eternal and unquenchable fire, so that they may burn without end.”

[Col. 0143A] No mention is made of the Fifth Synod, since at that time it still had a bad reputation in Gaul, as though it opposed Chalcedon. Predestination and the vessels of mercy are mentioned because questions concerning this matter were still being debated in Childebert’s kingdom, although the Second Synod of Orange, held in 529, had issued its judgment and Boniface II had confirmed it.

### XXIX

Gregory I, writing to the Patriarchs according to the custom of his predecessors, after setting forth at length the difficulties of the pastoral burden and imploring the prayers of his brethren to help him fulfill his office, writes as follows: [Col. 0143B]

> “Moreover, because one believes with the heart unto righteousness, but confession is made with the mouth unto salvation, I acknowledge that I receive and venerate the four Councils just as I do the four books of the holy Gospel . . . I likewise venerate the Fifth Council,” etc., as quoted above on page 160.

### XXX

In those times, acceptance of the five Synods constituted a complete and certain exposition of the Catholic faith. The Fifth Synod was mentioned more distinctly and explicitly because many had not yet received it, and because in Italy itself and the neighboring regions schismatics were still causing disturbances. It was in the interest of Catholics to distinguish themselves from them.

## § IV. On the First Profession of Faith

### XXXI

[Col. 0143C] Thus far we have discussed professions of faith in general; now we turn to the individual professions.

Concerning the first, we have observed two things. First, around the seventh century it succeeded the Symbol that had been in use until then, although that Symbol had received certain additions according to the circumstances of the times. Second, the new profession itself acquired further additions as the period from the seventh century, when it began to be used, advanced toward the time when it ceased to be used. Both points have been amply established in the notes.

### XXXII

It remains to inquire when it ceased. It was still in use in the time of Yvo of Chartres, as we stated in the preface—that is, in the year 1115—and even in the year 1294, when Boniface VIII succeeded Saint Celestine V. Boniface issued it at his ordination, according to Bzovius, from a Vatican manuscript.

It is worthwhile to quote its beginning here: [Col. 0143D]

> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Amen. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1294, the eighth Indiction. I, Benedict Cajetanus, Cardinal Deacon of the Holy Roman Church, and elected so that by the grace of God I might become . . .”

The remaining words are exactly the same as those in the Baronian version.

### XXXIII

It appears to have ceased in the following century. For the Council of Constance seems to have wished to restore it to use, at least in some measure, as an antiquated practice, when in session 39 it established the formula by which the supreme Pontiff was to profess his faith before his election was publicly announced. Thus they decreed:

> “[Col. 0144A] The greater the authority with which the Roman Pontiff exercises power among mortals, the more fitting it is that he should be supported by the clearest bonds of faith and bound by the rites that must be observed concerning the ecclesiastical sacraments. Therefore, so that in the future the fullness of faith may shine with singular splendor at the beginning of the Roman Pontiff’s creation, we decree and ordain that henceforth anyone to be elected Roman Pontiff, before his election is publicly announced, shall make the confession and profession written below publicly before his electors.
>
> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Amen.”

“From the year of the Lord’s Nativity one thousand, etc. I, N., elected pope, profess with heart and mouth before almighty God, whose Church I undertake to govern with his protection, and before blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, that, for as long as I remain in this fragile life, I firmly believe and hold the holy Catholic faith [Col. 0144B] according to the traditions of the Apostles, of the general Councils, and of the other holy Fathers—especially of the eight holy general Councils, namely, the First of Nicaea, the Second of Constantinople, the Third of Ephesus, the Fourth of Chalcedon, the Fifth and Sixth of Constantinople, likewise the Seventh of Nicaea, and also the Eighth of Constantinople, as well as the general Councils of Lateran, Lyons, and Vienne—and that I will preserve that faith unimpaired to the last jot, and confirm, defend, and preach it to my very soul and blood. Likewise, I will in every respect follow and observe the rite of the ecclesiastical Sacraments handed down by the Catholic Church.

171 “I subscribed this profession of mine with my own hand, having had it written by the notary [Col. 0144C] and archivist of the holy Roman Church at my command; and to you, almighty God, with a pure mind and devoted conscience, upon such an altar, etc., I sincerely offer it, in the presence of such persons, etc. Given, etc.”

XXXIV. The Basel Fathers likewise decreed this, and established the same form of assent, as they call it, except that they added the Council of Basel to the Councils and added a promise and oath to the confession. “I also faithfully promise to labor for the protection of the Catholic faith, the eradication of heresies and errors, the reform of morals, and peace among the Christian people. I also swear to pursue the celebration of general Councils and the confirmation of elections, in accordance with the decrees of the holy Council of Basel. And this profession, etc.”

[Col. 0144D] To this they added a form by which, every year, on the anniversary of the day of his elevation, during the solemn celebration of Mass, the supreme pontiff was to be admonished by the first cardinal in the performance of his office. This form bears some resemblance to the admonitions which a newly ordained bishop used to receive from the supreme pontiff, as appears in chapter III of the *Diurnus*, title IX.

XXXV. Since approximately 123 years elapsed between the ordination of Boniface VIII and the decree of Constance, the old formula must necessarily have fallen into disuse during that interval. It is uncertain, however, at what precise point in the interval this occurred; it is also uncertain for what reason. For neither should we listen to certain importunate detractors of the Apostolic See who rashly utter what they dream up: namely, that the use of the formula ceased when the question began to arise concerning the relative authority of pontiffs and Councils, because the formula mentioned [Col. 0145A] Councils.

XXXVI. At his ordination, Saint Celestine V issued no other form of profession than that which had been issued by his successor Boniface; accordingly, that most holy pontiff also pronounced the words contained in the form of faith: “I profess to you, blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, and to your holy Church, which today I undertake to govern with your protection, that, for as long as I remain in this wretched life, I will not desert it, abandon it, deny it, or in any way renounce it, nor will I leave it for any reason or on account of any fear or danger whatsoever, nor will I separate myself from it.”

XXXVII. This in particular supplied Boniface VIII’s enemies with an argument for declaring Saint Celestine’s [Col. 0145B] abdication illegitimate, since it had been made contrary to the solemn promise given to God and to the Church. But after the constitution of Boniface, inserted into the *Corpus of Canon Law*, and the books of Giles of Rome and others, nothing remains of this question that can prudently be discussed.

172 § V. On the second profession of faith.

XXXVIII. Concerning the second profession, what must now be treated is what we touched upon in the notes; the reader is referred to this place if he wishes to be informed about the sermon of Saint Leo delivered on the day of his ordination.

XXXIX. This sermon, which the published manuscripts count as the first of all those spoken by the holy pontiff, say—even those recently issued—that it was delivered on the anniversary of his elevation to the summit and [Col. 0145C] burden of the Roman See. The sermon itself shows that the word “anniversary” has crept into the text, and clearly demonstrates that it was delivered on the very day of his elevation. Since this is of some importance for historical truth and fits especially well with the subject before us, it must be explained and established more clearly; but first the entire sermon must be presented:

“Let my mouth speak the praise of the Lord, and let my soul and spirit, flesh and tongue bless his holy name (Ps. 144:21). For it is a sign not of a modest but of an ungrateful mind to be silent about divine benefits; and it is altogether fitting that a consecrated pontiff should begin his service with sacrifices of the Lord’s praise, because the Lord remembered us in our lowliness (Ps. 135:23) and blessed us; because he alone has done great wonders [Col. 0145D] (ibid., v. 5), so that the affection of your holiness might see me present, whom the necessity of a long pilgrimage had made absent.

“I therefore give thanks to our God, and will always give thanks for all that he has bestowed upon me (Ps. 115:3). I also celebrate, with the thanksgiving that is due, the judgment of your favor, clearly understanding how much the devotion of your affection can bestow upon me in reverence, love, and faith, I who, with pastoral solicitude, desire the salvation of your souls, since you have pronounced so holy a judgment concerning me, despite my having no preceding merits at all.

“I therefore beseech you, by the mercies of the Lord, to aid with your prayers the man whom you sought with your desires, so that the Spirit of grace may remain in me and your judgments may not waver; may he who infused into you the devotion of unanimity grant us all together the good of peace. Thus, throughout all the days of my life, devoted to the service of almighty God and ready for your service, may I confidently entreat the Lord: ‘Holy Father, preserve in your name those whom you have given me’ (John 17:11). And, as you continually advance toward salvation, may my soul magnify the Lord (Luke 1:46), and may the account of my priesthood stand before the just Judge at the judgment of future recompense in such a way that through your good works you may be my joy, you my crown (1 Thess. 2:19)—you who, by your good will, have offered sincere testimony in the present life.

“Thus, dearest ones, divine favor has made this day honorable to me; while raising my lowliness to the highest rank, it has shown that he despises none of his own. Therefore, although it is necessary to tremble over my merit, it is nevertheless religious to rejoice over the gift, since he who is the author of my burden will himself become the helper of my administration; and lest the weak man succumb beneath the greatness of grace, he who bestowed the dignity will give strength.

“Thus, as the day returns in its proper order on which the Lord willed me to have the beginning of episcopal office, I have a true reason for rejoicing to the glory of God: he forgave me much so that he might be greatly loved by me; and, in order to make his grace shine forth, he bestowed his gifts upon one in whom he found no merits to plead for them. By this work of his, what does the Lord insinuate and commend to our hearts, [Col. 0146C] except that no one should presume upon his justice and no one despair of his mercy? This is most evident when the sinner is sanctified and the rejected person is raised up. For the measure of heavenly gifts does not depend upon the quality of our works; nor, in this world, in which the whole of life is a trial (Job 7:1), is each person repaid what he deserves. If the Lord were to observe iniquities, no one would withstand his judgment (Ps. 129:3).

“Therefore, dearest ones, magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together (Ps. 33:4), so that the entire meaning of today’s celebration may be referred to the praise of its author. For, as regards what properly belongs to the affection of my heart, I confess that I rejoice greatly in the devotion of all of you; and when I see this most splendid gathering of my venerable fellow priests, I feel that an angelic assembly is present among us in so many holy congregations. Nor do I doubt that we are visited today by a more abundant grace of the divine presence, since so many most beautiful tabernacles of God are present together and shine with one light, so many most excellent members of the body of Christ.

“Nor, as I trust, is the pious favor and faithful affection of the most blessed Apostle Peter absent from this gathering. He has not deserted your devotion, whose reverence has brought us together. He too rejoices in your affection and, among the companions of his honor, embraces the observance of the Lord’s institution, approving the perfectly ordered charity of the whole Church, by which, in the See of Peter, it perhaps beholds Peter, and in its love for so great a shepherd does not grow cold even toward an heir so unequal to him.

“Therefore, dearest ones, so that this devotion which you unanimously display toward my lowliness may attain the fruit of its labor, entreat the most merciful clemency of our God, that in our days he may defeat those who attack us, fortify your faith, multiply your devotion and love, increase peace, and deign to make me, his servant—whom he has willed to preside at the helm of the Church in order to display the riches of his grace—sufficient for so great a work and useful for your defense. May he also prolong the time of our service, so that what he has granted to our age may advance your devotion, through Christ our Lord. [Col. 0147B] Amen.”

174 XXXX. If the sermon is considered more attentively and each of its parts weighed more carefully, everyone will acknowledge that what we intend has been established. What else can these words mean: “It is fitting that a consecrated pontiff should begin his service with sacrifices of the Lord’s praise, etc., so that the affection of your holiness might see me present, whom the necessity of a long pilgrimage had made absent, etc.; I also celebrate the judgment of your favor with the thanksgiving that is due, etc. I therefore beseech you, aid with your prayers the man whom you sought with your desires, so that the Spirit of grace may remain in me and your judgments may not waver, etc. Thus divine favor has made this day honorable to me, while raising my lowliness to the highest rank, etc. Thus, as the day returns on which the Lord willed me to have the beginning of episcopal office, etc.”?

XXXXI. What purpose, I ask, would these words serve if an anniversary day, rather than the very day of his elevation, were intended? Why does he say that the service of a consecrated pontiff is being begun? Why mention his return from a long pilgrimage? Why give thanks for his election? Why use the present-tense verb “raises” if he had already spent at least an entire year in the pontifical See?

XXXXII. Those who added the titles to Leo’s sermons therefore imposed these words: “Thus, as the day returns on which the Lord willed me to have the beginning of episcopal office.” For they seemed to indicate the return of an anniversary day, and not merely of the weekday, after seven [Col. 0147D] weeks.

XXXXIII. Add to this that all the historical circumstances connected with the election and elevation show the same thing. When Sixtus, his predecessor, departed this life on 28 March, Leo—who was far away in Gaul, engaged in reconciling the dissidents Aetius and Albinus—was elected by unanimous agreement. An embassy was sent to recall him to Rome, where he arrived after forty days in order to assume the pontificate. During this interval everything was settled in an extraordinary peace; many prelates gathered for the celebration of his ordination; and the consecration was completed amid the greatest acclaim of all. The day of the election thus returned, so that the man elected on the sixth day of the week, 29 March, might be ordained on that same weekday, 10 [Col. 0148A] May—since the See had been vacant for more than forty days, as it is recorded in the chronicle attributed to Prosper, or, as it appears in the corrected Anastasius, for forty-two days.

§ VI. On the case of Pope Honorius and the Sixth General Synod.

We also touched, in the notes to this profession, upon a few matters concerning Pope Honorius, who nevertheless is condemned in it. It is worthwhile to discuss so important a case, since it is treated differently by different people, and from the passage in which we now find ourselves it can be determined—just as we said in the Preface—while preserving due reverence for both the Apostolic See and the ecumenical Synod.

I. That difficult case has appeared uncertain and perplexing down to the present day—not, in my opinion, because of the matter itself, but because the disposition of men has divided its authors into factions. Almost everyone brings a preconceived opinion to the discussion: some refuse to believe that Honorius was condemned by the Sixth Synod, while others vehemently desire some contrary conclusion. Those who deny that he was condemned generally argue that the acts of the Synod as now preserved have been corrupted; yet some among them contend that the Synod itself erred. Those who maintain that he was condemned partly assert that the Synod erred and partly accuse Honorius of Monothelitism. Yet these three propositions—that the acts were corrupted, that the Synod erred, and that Honorius was a Monothelite—may rightly appear difficult to believe, indeed improbable. No one acting in good faith would now positively maintain that the acts were corrupted; while the other two propositions offend the minds of those who venerate and honor either the Synod, over which the Holy Spirit presided, or the Apostolic See, in which the faith of Peter remains immovable.

II. It is worthwhile to demonstrate the improbability of these three claims, so that, when the clouds of vain speculation have been dispersed, the truth may shine forth and honorably safeguard the integrity of the acts, the judgment of the Synod, and the purity of the Apostolic See.

III. To accomplish this, we must first establish that the acts of the Sixth Synod were not adulterated; then that Honorius was in fact condemned by that Synod; and afterward that neither did the Synod err nor was Honorius infected with the Monothelite heresy. But first something must briefly be said about Monothelitism.

IV. The Catholic faith teaches three things: first, that there are two natures in Christ, divine and human; second, that they are substantially united; third, that this substantial union is hypostatic only. Some, unable to grasp the substantial union of the natures, devised Nestorianism concerning two persons in Christ; others, unable to understand a substantial union that was only hypostatic, produced the heresy of one nature in Christ. Both groups erred, but the former through deficiency, acknowledging only a *relational* union (*σχετικήν*, *schetikēn*); the latter through excess, imagining either that the Word informed the flesh like a soul or mind, or that the two natures had been confused, or that an ineffable transformation of one into the other had occurred, so that although two had existed before the union, only one remained afterward [Col. 0149A]—yet one that retained the appearance of the other and clothed itself in it.

V. The first error belonged to the Arians and Apollinarius; the second to Polemon; the last to Eutyches, or rather to the Armenian monks, who deceived the delirious old man.

VI. Eutyches therefore asserted that the Incarnation took place in almost the same way that Catholics commonly say the consecration of the Eucharist takes place: by the conversion of one substance into another, with the appearance of the substance that is converted remaining and adhering to the other. He said, namely, that when the Word became flesh, the human nature was converted into the Word, so that the human appearance nevertheless remained, by which the incarnate Word would strike the eyes—just as Christ’s body, remaining veiled under the appearance of bread after the conversion had been completed, strikes the senses. [Col. 0149B]

VII. From this followed many consequences, but especially these six. First, that in reality there was one nature after the union, although there had previously been two; thus Eutyches interpreted Cyril’s statement concerning the one incarnate nature of the Word after the union. Second, that Christ was God substantially (*οὐσιωδῶς*, *ousiōdōs*) but man in appearance. Third, that the Word was truly born from the Virgin and truly suffered and was crucified. Fourth, that Christ had one operation, one will. Fifth, that Eutyches adhered to the heresy of the Docetists insofar as he denied that the human nature truly remained. Sixth, that he partly agreed with Arius and Apollinarius, who did not acknowledge perfect humanity in Christ.

VIII. Since that error relied upon two extremely powerful supports—the authority of Cyril, indeed falsely attributed but believed, and the genuine and formidable power of Eutyches, because of the eunuch Chrysaphius—it grew incredibly strong in a very short time. It gained control of almost the whole of Egypt because of Cyril’s name; it dominated Constantinople because of Chrysaphius; and it struck deep roots among the monks of the East because of the reputation and apparent holiness of the monk Eutyches.

IX. Eutyches was first condemned at Constantinople by Saint Flavian; then at Rome by Leo the Great; and finally at Chalcedon by six hundred and thirty Fathers. The error might then have seemed—and in reality was—extinguished, had not a certain vain opinion taken deep possession of the minds of the common people: that there was no middle ground between the parties of Eutyches and Nestorius, and that whoever confessed two natures adhered to Nestorius, while whoever confessed one person adhered to Eutyches. For in this matter the common people did not distinguish nature from person.

X. After the Council of Chalcedon, the East was divided into three parties. Some entirely rejected the Council’s definition; others entirely accepted it; and some partly rejected and partly accepted it. Catholics accepted it in every respect, while the Eutychians rejected it in every respect. Those who entered upon a third path were called by the Greeks *διακρινόμενοι* (*diakrinomenoi*, “those who distinguish” or “hesitate”), and by the Latins *Haesitantes*, “the Hesitants.” From these the Monothelites arose.

XI. Some, compelled by the authority of the Council to confess two natures in Christ, united *according to hypostasis* (*καθ’ ὑπόστασιν*, *kath’ hypostasin*), had nevertheless not yet laid aside the prejudice of Apollinarius, which Cyril reports in his *Apologeticus* to Theodosius: that the natures could not be substantially united, but only relationally (*σχετικῶς*, *schetikōs*), with each being perfect in itself, so that each required the other to supply something lacking in it. Since they could find what was supposedly lacking in neither nature—for both were present in Christ intact and perfect, the divine because it is simple, and the human because the flesh lacked neither a human soul nor a mind—they decided that the matter must be located in operation. Thus they said that Christ had one operation and one *θέλησις* (*thelēsis*), or will, and that this will was divine. Hence they also acquired the name Monothelites.

XII. I admit that there were other arguments by which the heresy afterward attempted to establish itself. But its chief support lay in what I have said, if indeed it can be called a support, since almost all the Fathers commonly considered the Monothelites to belong among the Eutychians, or rather the Apollinarians. For even the Nestorians could bring forward those other arguments on their own behalf; indeed, they were truly Monothelites before this name was heard. They defined Christ as a man *energized* by the Word (*ἐνεργούμενον*, *energoumenon*), and said that the man of the divine Word was merely an instrument, comparable to tools used by an artisan, upon which he impresses movement, since they themselves possess no movement at all.

XIII. Hence it happened that in the letter of Pope Agatho to the Emperor Constantine, which was reread in the Sixth Synod, session 4, the following passage appears among the testimonies of heretics cited in support of one operation, concerning Nestorius [Col. 0150C]:

“Likewise, from Book IV of Nestorius the man-worshipper, which he entitled *Of the Splendid Initiation* (*ἐπιφανοῦς μυήσεως*). ‘We preserve the natures without confusion, united not according to substance but according to will; for this reason we establish one will, operation, and dominion belonging to them, their equality of dignity having been demonstrated. For God the Word, in assuming the man whom he predestined, was not hidden from him by reason of power, because of the affection predetermined.’”

XIV. What will the Monothelites understood, and what they removed from human nature—whether the faculty of willing itself or merely operation—is disputed by more recent theologians. But in my view they dispute this without justification. For they imprudently reduce a controversy of faith, and a very great one at that, to the slight philosophical question of whether the faculties of the soul really differ from its substance. If they do not differ, how could the faculty of willing be absent where the soul is present?

XV. What the heretics therefore wanted to maintain was that the human nature in Christ was an instrument of the divine person—an instrument, I say, not one that acted while being acted upon, as the Church holds, but one that was merely acted upon, or rather suffered, like instruments devoid of life, which of themselves and by their own movement do nothing, but purely suffer action from the artisan.

XVI. If the Monothelite heresy is thus defined, everything that either they themselves advance on their behalf or Catholics object against them harmonizes remarkably well. They advance two principal arguments for themselves: first, that by holding this view they depart very far from the heretics condemned at the Council of Chalcedon; and second, that they safeguard Christ’s dignity as fully as possible.

XVII. “Arius, Apollinarius, Nestorius, Eutyches, and Polemon, the author of confusion, were condemned at the Council of Chalcedon,” they said. “We depart far from all of them: from Arius and Apollinarius because we confess two complete and perfect natures in Christ; from the others because we admit the hypostatic union of the natures, against Nestorius; because after the union we acknowledge two natures, against Eutyches; and because we reject the confusion of the natures, against Polemon.”

[Col. 0151B] XVIII. As far as Christ’s dignity is concerned, two things are especially relevant: unity and impeccability. The Monothelites thought they safeguarded unity. First, because they attributed to the one and same Word everything said about Christ, whether human or divine. Second, because they did not divide the evangelical and apostolic statements concerning Christ. Finally, because they asserted that God was truly born of the Virgin and truly suffered and died.

XIX. They boasted that they preserved Christ’s impeccability intact by uprooting the whole root of sin—namely, the conflict of judgments and wills. For they did not posit two operations or wills in Christ, but one, which belonged to God. Their reasoning was as follows: a will, precisely because it is created, is capable of sin; therefore, if such a will is posited in Christ, Christ is said to be capable of sin. But Christ is not capable of sin; therefore, there is no created will in him. Furthermore, wherever there are two wills, each proper to a different nature, conflict can occur; thus in a human being the will of the flesh and the will of the spirit conflict. But for the human will to conflict with the divine is sin. Therefore Christ could sin if he possessed a human will; but he cannot sin, and therefore he does not possess a human will.

XX. These things the heretics said on their own behalf. Catholics, apart from various passages of Scripture by which Christ’s human soul and will are proved, brought four principal objections. First, that those who asserted one will agreed with the Docetists, Apollinarians, Nestorians, and Eutychians. Second, that they contradicted the Apostle, who teaches that Christ was made like his brethren in all things except sin. Third, that they removed the perfection of the Incarnation. Fourth, that they destroyed the truth of humanity’s redemption through Christ.

XXI. Catholics raised these objections, paradoxical in appearance but true in reality. For although the heretics disguised their error in Catholic language, they nevertheless truly agreed, at least in part, with the Docetists—for there appeared to be a human will in Christ, though in fact there was none; with the Apollinarians—for wherever there is a nature endowed with reason, its natural operation must also be present; with the Eutychians—for, as all the Fathers assert against the opponents of the consubstantiality (*ὁμοούσιον*, *homoousion*) of the Trinity, wherever there is one operation there is also one nature; and finally with the Nestorians—for if Christ’s human nature lacks its own free will, it is merely an instrument of the divine Word, deprived of natural operation, and Christ is nothing other than a man *energized* by the Word (*ἐνεργούμενος*, *energoumenos*).

XXII. Furthermore, the Apostle declares that Christ had to be made like his brethren in all things (Heb. 2:17), except for sin, as the Fathers interpret it. Such complete likeness could not exist if Christ lacked what is most excellent in others: *αὐτεξούσιον* (*autexousion*), that is, the proper operation of a rational soul.

XXIII. Moreover, the Incarnation was accomplished for the purpose of freeing man from slavery to sin. Therefore, if the Word did not assume a human will, he certainly did not free it, although that will, either especially or alone in itself, was enslaved, since it alone was properly guilty. For the Word freed only what he assumed; liberation is effected according to what is naturally joined (*κατὰ τὸ σύμφυες*, *kata to symphy es*), as the Fathers teach.

XXIV. Finally, Christ could not redeem human beings except by merit and satisfaction. But there is neither merit nor satisfaction where there is no free created operation; for it belongs to an inferior being to merit and make satisfaction by freely presenting suitable actions and sufferings to the superior whom it has offended.

XXV. From these points it is clear what the Monothelite heresy was. They denied that there was in Christ any free will besides the divine will, which moved the human nature as an artisan moves a mere instrument.

XXVI. Since that heresy struck at the very foundation of human salvation, it greatly disturbed the minds of Catholics. They immediately perceived that the whole substance of salvation was at stake, and that the devil was secretly contriving, through his agents—men who falsely assumed the appearance of Catholics professing the faith of Chalcedon—to persuade the people either that the doctrine of one operation was pious, or that the question of one or two wills was trivial and ought rather to be silenced than debated.

XXVII. Thus the Christian world was divided into three parties: some defended two operations, each proper to one of Christ’s natures; others declared that there was in reality one operation, proper to God; and still others wished to abstain from the terms “one” and “two,” as though it were sufficient for orthodoxy (*ὀρθοδοξία*, *orthodoxia*) simply to profess the operation of Christ, God and man, and as though a more precise explanation of the rest were superfluous and even harmful. Catholics spoke of two wills and operations; the Monothelites of one. Constans, in the *Typos*, decreed that neither one nor two should be mentioned, claiming that this had been the opinion of Pope Honorius. On what grounds he made that claim must now be examined.

180 XXVIII. In the time of our fathers, many people, when they heard heretics charge Honorius with the crime of Monothelitism and importunately pile up testimonies—false in reality but apparently plausible—rashly believed that the matter was indeed so; and the opinion prevailed as though it had been formally established. But now, after the case has been investigated more carefully and more conscientiously, only a few persons, and those either otherwise suspect in faith or not of the highest authority, condemn Honorius for Monothelitism; many others acquit him.

XXIX. The former group is as inconsiderate in its judgment as the latter is circumspect. For Honorius wrote about the question in no other way than Saint Leo did, except that Saint Leo expounded the dogma of faith more briefly and concisely, while Honorius explained it at greater length. Saint Leo wrote:

“Each form acts in communion with the other what is proper to it: the Word doing what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carrying out what belongs to the flesh.”

Honorius wrote:

“We must confess that both natures, joined in one Christ by a natural unity, act and operate in communion with one another: the divine nature performing what belongs to God, and the human nature carrying out what belongs to the flesh, etc.”

XXX. It therefore seems almost superfluous to dwell longer on this argument, especially since the two letters of Honorius presented in the Sixth Synod, sessions 12 and 13, when compared with the definition of faith composed by that same Synod, are found to differ from it in no respect except that the first mentions one will, and that in both letters, by a certain pastoral accommodation intended to restrain disputes among minds, it is forbidden to use the expressions “one operation” or “two operations” in preaching.

XXXI. The first difference is of no importance; the second is of little relevance to the matter at hand. For the one will mentioned by the pontiff has nothing to do with the Monothelite question. It was the will proper to the human being and to the spirit, excluding only what is called the will of the flesh, which in us, infected by original sin, rebels against reason. Honorius denied only what all Catholics deny: that the nature assumed by the Word was one in which wills would conflict with one another and in which there would exist, as they say, the tinder of sin. This is clearly shown by these words:

“We confess one will of our Lord Jesus Christ, because surely our nature was assumed by the Divinity, not our fault: that nature, certainly, which was created before sin, not that which was corrupted after transgression.”

And afterward:

“Therefore, as we have said above, the Savior did not assume a corrupted nature that would resist the law of his mind; rather, he came to seek and save what had been lost, that is, corrupted human nature. For there was no other law in his members, nor any different or contrary will opposed to the Savior, because he was born above the law of the human condition, etc.”

XXXII. That Honorius’s words must be understood in this sense is taught by three authoritative witnesses: John the Abbot, who composed a letter in the name of Honorius; John IV, the successor of Honorius after an interval of one year, in his *Apology*; and Saint Maximus the Martyr, who defended the holy pontiff on the testimony of both, partly in his disputation with Pyrrhus and partly in his letter to Marinus.

XXXIII. Abbot John therefore says to Maximus [Col. 0154A]:

“We said that there was one will in the Lord—not one will of his divinity and humanity, but of his humanity alone. When Sergius had written that certain people said there were two contrary wills in Christ, we replied that Christ did not have two contrary wills, of the flesh, I mean, and of the spirit, as we have after sin, but only one, which naturally signified his humanity.”

XXXIV. John IV, or the same John the Abbot speaking in his name, says:

“Therefore my aforesaid predecessor, teaching about the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation, said that there were not in him, as in us sinners, contrary wills of mind and flesh. Certain people, twisting this to their own interpretation, supposed that he had taught Christ to have one will of his divinity and humanity; but this is altogether contrary to the truth.”

XXXV. It should incidentally be observed concerning these testimonies that they are of the greatest force for overturning the conjecture of the recent author of the *History of the Monothelites*. Seeking a way to repel the objection, he thought it possible to argue that the corruption which Maximus complains the Greeks introduced into the letters of Honorius consisted in their substituting “one will” for “a new will,” when they translated the Latin words into Greek. But if the matter were so, the method of interpretation used by both Johns would not be appropriate; nor could one tolerate the silence of both men, who say nothing about the corruption. Indeed, one could not excuse the negligence of John the Deacon, who compared the Greek letter with the authentic Latin one at the Synod [Col. 0154C] and did not inform the Fathers of a fraud of such importance.

XXXVI. “What, then,” you will ask, “will become of the Sixth Synod? Did it err—and knowingly so—when, after the solemn exposition of both Johns in letters sent to the Emperor, it condemned Honorius as guilty of asserting one will and convicted him from his own letters?”

The holy Synod certainly did not err, since it was ecumenical. I admit that it condemned Honorius from his own letters; but I deny that it made him guilty of asserting one will. Indeed, I maintain that nothing can be brought from the acts of the Synod from which this conclusion can be drawn. This will soon be demonstrated, once we have discussed the integrity of the acts with Baronius.

XXXVII. We said that the Christian world was divided into three parties because the Monothelites had raised the question of whether Christ had one will or two. To restore peace to the Church and harmony to the world, the Sixth Council was assembled at Constantinople. There the Catholics, zealous and ardent in defending the true dogma, struck with one and the same anathema the *Ecthesis* of Heraclius and the *Typos* of Constans—that is, the Monothelites, defenders of one operation, and the supporters of the Monothelites who wished silence to be kept concerning one and two operations.

XXXVIII. In the acts of the Council as they are now preserved, Honorius is found implicated in this anathema. Baronius believes that these acts are not authentic, and he supports his opinion with conjectures so plausible that he has persuaded even learned men. Others maintain that the preserved acts are authentic and argue their case with many serious proofs.

XXXIX. To establish his opinion, Baronius uses four arguments. He says that Honorius had no cause whatsoever to be condemned; that the Synod had no authority to judge the First See; that the Apostolic See’s legates who were present would not have remained silent if anything of that kind had been attempted; and finally, that the forger and the reasons for the forgery could not have remained unknown.

### XL

He establishes the first point by three arguments. First, that the two letters of Honorius contain nothing of Monothelitism, nor do they in any way condemn two wills, except wills that mutually conflict, such as flesh and spirit—which is Catholic doctrine. [Col. 0155B] Second, that in his letters Agatho, the successor of Honorius, affirms that his predecessors were sound in faith and entirely free from error. Third, that the authority of the ecumenical Synod greatly strengthens the force of Agatho’s letters, since the Synod received them as though they had been written by Peter himself.

### XLI

He concludes the second point chiefly from the argument that the first see is judged by no one; and he confirms this rule of canon law by tradition, practice, and the authority of many persons, both supreme Pontiffs and Fathers.

### XLII

He proves the third point by conjectures. If the Legates, he says, had seen anything attempted against the honor of the Apostolic See in the case of Honorius, they would certainly have resisted it with the same, or even greater, zeal than that with which they repelled the calumny brought against Vigilius at the same Synod. For the reason was not merely equal but far greater, since Vigilius was more remote in memory, whereas Honorius was almost a contemporary.

Moreover, the Cardinal Legates of the Apostolic See—two presbyters and the Deacon John—had been given this single instruction: “that they should presume to add, subtract, or change nothing, but sincerely set forth the tradition of this Apostolic See as it had been established by the Apostolic Pontiffs who preceded them.” The bishops sent by the Western Synod could consent to condemn nothing other than what the Synod itself, whose vicars they were, had previously condemned. Otherwise they would have sinned against the religious character of their office and against their observance of the Apostolic See, whose integrity and faith appeared to be attacked even by the very accusation [Col. 0155D] brought against its head. Yet the Western Synod had decreed nothing against Honorius and had found no fault with a Pontiff so holy.

### XLIII

Finally, he establishes the fourth point as follows. Theodore was condemned [183] at the Sixth Synod, yet nowhere is he mentioned in its acts. Therefore, he falsified the acts—indeed, before they were published—and substituted the name of Honorius after erasing his own.

He proves that Theodore was condemned partly because he was a Monothelite and had subscribed to the faith of Macarius of Antioch, and partly because the Synod wished to spare no one who had belonged to that heresy. He infers that the acts were falsified from the silence about him, and from the insertion, after the Second Session, of gatherings of pages containing the condemnation of Honorius; he further holds that the falsification was carried out before copies of the acts had been published and delivered to the Legates of the Apostolic See and to the other Patriarchs. Who, he asks, would have dared such a crime except one whose interest in it was greatest, and who had an ancient hatred of the Roman Pontiffs—one who had obtained from the Emperor, by importunate petitions, that the name of Vitalian should not be entered in the sacred diptychs?

He was able to accomplish what he had dared to attempt because, after George’s death, he had been restored to the see of Constantinople in the year 682 and had the authentic acts in his power before the Roman Legates departed from the imperial city. He therefore handed them over to the Legates and to the others after corrupting them.

### XLIV

Those who judge otherwise than Baronius concerning so important a matter are, just as they belong to two groups, so also divided in the answers they give to the Cardinal’s first argument. Those who believe Honorius guilty of Monothelitism deny that human conjectures should be indulged in on this matter; instead, they insist upon the judgment of the ecumenical Synod, since the Holy Spirit presided over it, the Legates of the Apostolic See were present, the supreme Pontiffs have shown it the same honor and equal veneration as the other five universal councils, and the entire Catholic Church gave it its assent. The Roman Church itself wished to testify to its veneration publicly in its prayers until the beginning of our own century, when it prescribed the following third and fourth readings for the Office of Matins on the feast of Saint Leo II:

> “He received the holy Sixth Synod, which had recently been celebrated by God’s providence in the imperial city, written in the Greek language, with the most devout and most clement great Prince Constantine presiding and sitting within the palace called the Trullus. Together with him sat the Legates of the Apostolic See, and the two Patriarchs, of Constantinople and Antioch, together with one hundred and fifty bishops. At this Synod Cyrus, Sergius, Honorius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter were condemned, as were Macarius with his disciple Stephen; and also Polychronius, the new Simon, who said or preached that there was one will and one operation in the Lord Jesus Christ, etc.”

### XLV

Now these words are read in a shorter form:

> “He approved the acts of the Sixth Synod, which was celebrated at Constantinople under the presidency of the Legates of the Apostolic See, with the Emperor Constantine also present, together with the two Patriarchs, of Constantinople and Antioch, and one hundred and seventy bishops; and he translated it into Latin. At that Council Cyrus, Sergius [184], and Pyrrhus were condemned, because they preached only one will and one operation in Christ.”

### XLVI

Those, however, who consider Honorius free from error defend the view that he was condemned for another reason—namely, because he “gave support to the wicked assertions of the authors of the new heretical doctrine”; because he “proved to be a supporter, accomplice, and confirmer of the heresy”; because “he did not enlighten the Apostolic Church with the doctrine of Apostolic tradition, but by profane betrayal permitted the immaculate Church to be stained”; because “he did not extinguish, as Apostolic authority required, the flame of the heretical doctrine when it first began, but by negligence fostered it”; and because “he consented to the immaculate rule of Apostolic tradition, which he had received from his predecessors, being stained.”

### XLVII

As for Baronius’s second argument, nothing better can be brought forward than the testimony of Pope Adrian II concerning his predecessor, as reported in Session 7 of the Eighth Synod:

> “This presumption is intolerable, and, I confess, the ears of our inmost hearts cannot endure it. Which of you, I ask, has ever heard such a thing, or who has found, even by reading, the enormity of such rashness? We read that the Roman Pontiff has judged the bishops of all the Churches; but we do not read that anyone has judged him. Although Honorius was anathematized by the Easterners after his death, it must nevertheless be understood that he had been accused of heresy. Only on account of heresy is it lawful for inferiors to resist the movements of their superiors or freely reject perverse opinions. Even there, however, it was not lawful for any Patriarch or other bishop to pronounce any sentence concerning him, unless the authority of the first see had preceded it.”

### XLVIII

As for the Legates, the argument that Baronius derives from their silence has an easy solution. First, some accuse them of timidity, saying that they had yielded fearfully to the Easterners, who held their Sergius in extraordinary honor and could not remove him from the anathema, and who wished to lessen the disgrace of sharing a condemnation with the Roman Pontiff.

Second, some praise their prudent policy, since they preferred the common peace of the universal Church to the honor of one man. Third, it is not implausible that some believe they had been instructed to do precisely this; they support that view by the testimony of Adrian cited above. Fourth, perhaps nothing else was done to Honorius at the Council than what had been done at the Roman Synod and in Agatho’s letters—except that at Constantinople the matter was treated more openly and explicitly, whereas at the Roman Synod and in Agatho’s letters it had been expressed implicitly and somewhat obscurely.

### XLIX

What is said about Theodore as the corrupter of the acts scarcely withstands examination in any respect. First, no ancient writer, and no one before Baronius, records that he was deposed on account of Monothelitism, much less shortly before the Synod. Baronius’s suspicion [185] nevertheless appears not implausible: Theodore had subscribed to the faith of Macarius of Antioch, and by that act deserved the deposition with which Macarius was punished.

Moreover, even if he agreed with Macarius—as did his successor George—he did not remain obstinate. Instead, imitating George, he repented; and for that reason he succeeded him immediately after his death, being restored to the see he had previously left. The Synod, however, proscribed no one except either the dead or the obstinate.

### L

But even if he is said to have falsely professed the Catholic faith out of desire to regain the see, and even if he retained inwardly not only the error but also hatred of the Apostolic See, how could he, however greatly he may have tried, have corrupted the acts every time Honorius was mentioned? How could one man have falsified the profession of faith subscribed by the hands of the bishops themselves, and the very letters of the Emperor Constantine? Was the profession of faith not sealed with seals? Did not Constantine, an eminently Catholic emperor, subscribe his letters with his own hand? Did he recognize what he was about to subscribe with rash and imprudent, rather than careful and mature, reading, as the importance of the matter required? Did the Emperor himself—whom the Synod declared equal to Constantine the Great—also join Theodore in the crime?

Who could persuade himself or others that such a thing was attempted by a prince so devout and so ardently Catholic that he proscribed even the Typus of his own father Constantine and the Ecthesis of his grandfather Heraclius?

### LI

Thus Baronius, although he piously devoted to the defense of Honorius the full force of his intellect and learning, in which he was especially powerful, and although he believed his method of defense to be the only effective one, satisfied only a few learned men to some extent. The majority did not cease listening to the ancient writers, to whom it had never occurred to accuse the acts of the Sixth Synod of error, much less to call the other public instruments of the faith forgeries. They therefore took another path and devised another defense of Honorius.

### LII

John V, who held the Pontificate twelve places after Honorius and was one of Agatho’s Legates to the Sixth Synod, brought the acts of the Synod back to Rome when he returned from Constantinople. He had received them for conveyance to Rome together with the Emperor’s letters.

But what sort of acts did he receive—complete or corrupted? If complete, why are the writings of Leo II concerning Honorius, which agree with the complete acts, called into question? If corrupted, how did he fail to recognize the crime, when he had played such a large part in the events? If he recognized it, why did he not warn the supreme Pontiff and complain of the unspeakable crime? Why did the supreme Pontiff himself remain silent about so abominable a matter? Why did he not accuse the corrupter of this detestable crime before the Emperor? Why did the Emperor write what agreed with the acts, and the Pontiff himself reply in agreement with them?

By what crime did that most holy man not only approve acts corrupted, injurious to the Apostolic See, and full of calumnies against Honorius, but also, while retaining their corruption, translate them into Latin and send them to the Spaniards [186] and Gauls for acceptance? How did he introduce this corruption into the profession of faith to be issued by the supreme Pontiffs? If these things are not incredible, what things are?

### LIII

What, then, shall we say of the Legates of the other great sees? Did they likewise take corrupted acts back to their provinces, or complete ones? If complete, why were those portions that had suffered corruption not corrected from them, especially when the Seventh and Eighth Synods were being convened from the whole world? If corrupted, how could it have happened that none of the more than one hundred and seventy-five bishops, and none of the almost innumerable multitude of presbyters, said or wrote a word about the corruption?

Had the whole world at that time become so stunned that it could neither recognize the corruption nor the crime, despite so many bishops and so many clergy who knew the Synod’s acts and were able to bring an accusation? Or, if they did recognize it, did they flatter one man who was neither especially powerful, nor of the best reputation, nor especially favored by princes?

### LIV

Why pursue the matter further? What shall we say of the silence of subsequent ages, of the supreme Pontiffs, of general Councils, and of distinguished writers concerning either the condemnation of Honorius or the corruption of the acts? What shall we say of the Roman Church itself, which for so long confessed the matter in the Office of Saint Leo II? What shall we say of innumerable arguments of this kind?

### LV

Since, therefore, the integrity of the acts is certain, and the orthodoxy of Honorius is likewise certain, it must be investigated what just cause there could have been for so great a condemnation. To reject the Sixth Synod as spurious, as Albert Pighius did; to condemn it as erroneous in a question of fact, as some have thought; or to accuse it of usurping authority in its judgment of Honorius, as others have attempted—these are not, in my judgment, the actions of a man who wishes to speak consistently.

For if such objections are valid against the sentence pronounced by the Sixth Synod against Honorius, someone may rightly ask why the ancient defenders of Honorius who lived after the Synod did not previously use them; why the subsequent ecumenical Synods, the Seventh and Eighth, either did not reject the Sixth as spurious or did not follow it as an erroneous council; why the supreme Pontiffs not only did not protest against a judgment accused of illegitimacy, but instead pursued it with the same veneration as the five preceding councils; why bishops swore by it when they ascended the Apostolic See; and why, when they swore by it, they not only praised its definition of faith but also expressly mentioned the condemned Honorius.

### LVI

I omit speaking not only of Saint Leo II, who presented the Synod—including the portion in which Honorius is accused—as something to be read and accepted in Latin, but also of the Gallican and Spanish prelates, who accepted it when it was presented to them. I omit also the most learned collectors of canons—Yvo, Anselm, Deusdedit, and Gratian—who counted the Sixth Synod [187] among the others without any exception or criticism.

Was not both exception and criticism especially necessary if the Sixth Synod were either spurious or guilty of error and usurped authority?

### LVII

For the just cause of the condemnation that we are seeking to become manifest, three things seem to me to require demonstration. First, what was asserted earlier: that it cannot be concluded from the acts—or even from the testimony of those who took part in composing or carefully examining them—that the Synod condemned Honorius because he asserted one will in Christ. Second, that another cause of condemnation is both indicated by the Synod and consistently and concordantly transmitted by others of the same age. Third, that the cause they transmit was just.

### LVIII

As to the first point, the cause for which Honorius appears to have been condemned is presented in six places in the acts altogether. In Session XIII, p. 944 of the new edition, it is said that his letter to Sergius disagrees with the Fathers. In the same place, that in everything he followed Sergius’s opinion and confirmed his doctrines. In Session XIV, p. 972, that his letter concurred in one and the same impiety with the writings of the heretics. In Session XVIII, p. 1024, that through him, just as through the others, the devil spread the heresy of one will and one operation. In the same session, p. 1044, that he preached one will and one operation. In the same session, p. 1053, that he followed Theodore, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and others.

### LIX

From these passages, provided that they are reported as they stand, I maintain that it cannot be concluded that the Synod struck Honorius with anathema because he taught that there was only one will in Christ, but only because he favored those who taught it and supplied them with an opportunity to teach.

### LX

The first passage reads as follows:

> “Reviewing the dogmatic letters said to have been written by Sergius, formerly Patriarch of this imperial city, both to Cyrus, who was then Bishop of Phasis, and to Honorius, formerly Pope of ancient Rome, and likewise the letter written in reply by that man—that is, by Honorius—to the same Sergius, and finding these letters to be wholly alien to the Apostolic doctrines, to the definitions of the holy Councils, and to all approved Fathers, but instead to follow the false doctrines of the heretics, we reject them altogether and execrate them as deadly to the soul.”

Yet in this passage there is no explicit mention of one will in Christ, but only a general reference to false doctrines that diverge from the tradition of the Apostles. The doctrines of Sergius and Pyrrhus do indeed diverge from the Apostolic tradition concerning the faith. But Honorius’s thoughtless policy, by which he cowardly refused to resist the heretics, diverges from the generous courage of Paul and the other Apostles, who testified that one must obey God rather than human beings.

### LXI

In the second passage, after the Synod had proscribed the names [188] of those whom Pope Agatho had mentioned in his letter—namely, Theodore of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Peter, and Paul of Constantinople—and had defined that they “should be subjected to anathema as holding opinions contrary to the right faith,” it continues in these words:

> “Together with these we have also foreseen that Honorius, who was Pope of ancient Rome, should be cast out from the holy Catholic Church of God and likewise anathematized, because we have found in the writings composed by him to Sergius that in everything he followed his opinion and confirmed impious doctrines.”

This passage is so far from proving that Honorius was condemned for asserting one will that it can be brought forward to prove the opposite. To have followed Sergius’s opinion does not mean to have agreed with his doctrine, but to have adhered to his plan of imposing silence. For in Greek it reads: **τῇ ἐκείνου γνώμῃ ἐξακολουθήσαντα**, that is, “having followed his counsel,” by which he confirmed his impious doctrines—not by agreeing with them, but by conniving at them.

I observe concerning this passage that casting the names of the dead out of the Church and subjecting them to anathema means nothing other than erasing their names publicly from the sacred diptychs, and either not mentioning them at all in the Church or mentioning them only with a disgraceful and dishonoring epithet.

The third passage contains the Synod’s sentence concerning the booklets, documents, and short works brought forth by the Chartophylax and read before the Fathers. Among them were the two letters of Honorius:

> **τῶν εἴδησιν λαβόντες, ἔγνωμεν εἰς μίαν καὶ τὴν αὐτὴν ἀσέβειαν φέρεσθαι, καὶ συνεῖδομεν ταῦτα εἰς βίβηλα καὶ ψυχοφθόρα παραχρῆμα πρὸς τέλειον ἀφανισμὸν πῦρ παραδοθῆναι.**

“Having examined these, we recognized that they tended toward one and the same impiety, and we judged that, as profane and destructive to souls, they should immediately be handed over to fire for complete destruction.”

But two writings may tend toward the same impiety in different ways: one because it contains a doctrine, the other because it contains a concealment of doctrine. It is therefore not permissible to conclude from this that the letters of Honorius definitely contained heretical doctrine, but only that they contained one or the other of these things without specification.

### LXII

The fourth passage has no greater force. The Synod says:

> “The devil, through his instruments—namely, Theodore, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Peter and Paul, Honorius, and Cyrus, together with Macarius and Stephen—continually raises scandals of error in the Church by spreading among the Catholic people the heresy of one will and one operation in the two natures of Christ.”

But heresy is spread both by teaching and by conniving at those who teach. Therefore, from this passage, which contains what is called the Synod’s definitive sentence, nothing else can legitimately be concluded except that Honorius contributed to the spread of the heresy in one of these two ways.

### LXIII

The fifth passage appears at first sight to have somewhat greater force. When the Emperor asked the Synod whether everyone had willingly subscribed to the definition, it exclaimed as follows:

> “Anathema to Nestorius, Eutyches, and Dioscorus. Anathema to Apollinaris and Severus. Anathema to those [189] who agree with them. Anathema to Theodore of Pharan. Anathema to Sergius and Honorius. Anathema to Pyrrhus and Paul. Anathema to Macarius, Stephen, and Polychronius. Anathema to all heretics. Anathema to those who have preached, preach, teach, or will teach one will and one operation in the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

It seems, indeed, that all those named are called heretics who preached one will. But the force and appearance of the argument disappear once the punctuation is distinguished. Anathema is pronounced against the men named individually, for the same reason in the acclamation as in the definition that follows. Then, after a punctuation mark, it adds: “Anathema to all heretics.” After another punctuation mark: “Anathema to those who have preached, preach, teach, or will teach one will and one operation in the dispensation of Christ our God.”

### LXIV

The final passage, in the address to the Emperor, has very little force for making Honorius guilty of asserting one will, and much for absolving him. It reads as follows:

> “We cast far from the ecclesiastical enclosures and rightly subject to anathema the inventors of superfluous novelties of speech and of these doctrines: Theodore of Pharan, Sergius and Paul, Pyrrhus together with Peter, who held the bishopric of Constantinople; moreover Cyrus, who held the priesthood of Alexandria; and with them Honorius, who was Bishop of Rome, since he followed them in these matters.”

In Greek: **ὡς ἐκείνοις ἐν τούτοις ἀκολουθήσαντα**—“since he followed them in these matters.”

It should be observed that Honorius is separated from the others, as though his condition were different, and is said to have been condemned because he served and followed the others; this is what the word **ἀκολουθήσαντα** signifies. He served their perverse counsels not by resisting them, as he should have done, but by fostering them through an imprudent order of silence. By this silence the heretics attempted gradually and imperceptibly to unteach the peoples the Catholic faith concerning the two wills.

He was therefore not guilty of asserted heresy, but of heresy fostered; not of agreement with the heretics, but of thoughtless concealment.

### LXV

As for the second point, the Emperor Constantine, who attended the Synod, and Pope Leo, who translated its acts from Greek into Latin, report that Honorius was condemned not for heresy but for another crime.

Thus Constantine says in his Edict:

> “We anathematize the authors and supporters of new doctrines: namely Theodore, who was Bishop of Pharan; Sergius, who was Bishop of this city, equal to Theodore in character and to him in impiety; and also Honorius, who was Pope of ancient Rome, the supporter, helper, and confirmer of their heresy,” etc.

He divides the condemned men into two classes: authors and supporters of doctrines. He pronounces anathema upon Theodore and Sergius as authors, and upon Honorius as a supporter.

No one understood the mind of the Synod better than the Emperor [190], who was exceptionally learned in theological matters, attended its sessions tirelessly, and indeed played a leading part in them. A little earlier, speaking of priests who had governed the Churches perversely, he says:

> “These are Theodore, who was Bishop of Pharan; Sergius, who was Bishop of our imperial city preserved by God; and furthermore Honorius, who was Pope of ancient Rome, a confirmer of this kind of heresy, who also contradicts himself,” etc.

He calls Honorius a confirmer of the heresy because of his thoughtless policy. He accuses him of contradicting himself because, although he held Catholic views in reality in his letters, he neither spoke nor acted with the spirit required to overthrow the heresy.

### LXVI

Leo II, in his letter to the Emperor Constantine:
