> “We anathematize the inventors of the new error, namely Theodore, Bishop of Pharan; Cyrus of Alexandria; Sergius; Pyrrhus; Paul; and Peter, the occupants rather than the bishops of the Constantinopolitan Church [Col. 0163A]; and also Honorius, who did not enlighten this Apostolic Church with the doctrine of Apostolic tradition, but by profane betrayal permitted the immaculate Church to be stained.”

In his letter to the bishops of Spain:

> “Theodore of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul, and Peter of Constantinople were punished with condemnation, together with Honorius, who did not extinguish, as Apostolic authority required, the flame of the heretical doctrine when it began, but fostered it through negligence.”

In his letter to King Ervig:

> “Theodore, Bishop of Pharan; Cyrus of Alexandria; Sergius; Paul; Pyrrhus; and Peter, formerly bishops of Constantinople, were cast out from the unity of the Catholic Church, together with Honorius of Rome, who consented to the immaculate rule of Apostolic tradition, which he had received from his predecessors, being stained.”

### LXVII

To assess the force of such testimony, the following points must be observed.

1. No learned person now listens to Baronius when he protests against the letters of the Emperor and the supreme Pontiff as though they were forgeries.

2. Leo read the acts he translated with the greatest diligence:

   > “Reviewing the sequence of the synodal proceedings, and demanding each act with painstaking care, we found that the very things narrated by the Legates of the Apostolic See agreed with the written records. For we discovered,” etc.

3. The Legates of the Apostolic See not only attended the Council’s sessions but presided over the proceedings in which Honorius was discussed. Indeed, they were the first of all to subscribe the definition and the address to the Emperor, in which he is condemned. It would therefore have been impossible for them to allow themselves to be deceived by spurious acts and, after being deceived, to lead the Pontiff into error.

4. By the name “Legates” we must understand not only those who occupied Agatho’s place, but also those sent by the Roman Synod with the monks and counted as participants in the Council [191]. None of them was uneducated or ignorant of the doctrine of the faith. They were highly learned, even if unskilled in secular eloquence. They therefore could not have been deceived so carelessly that they failed either to explain to the Pontiff, who questioned them with sufficient diligence, the Council’s sentence—which they themselves had issued under their presidency—or the integrity of the acts, to which they had subscribed.

5. Honorius was charged with nothing other than agreeing with Sergius and thereby fostering the heresy. But he agreed only in the respect in which Sergius judged that the matter should be concealed under the fictitious name of peace. Both therefore fostered heresy out of a desire for concord: Honorius fostered another’s heresy because he did not destroy it; Sergius fostered his own because he concealed it.

Each subscribed to a writing similar to the two imperial writings that had been condemned: Honorius to the Typus of Constans, which commanded nothing beyond silence; Sergius to the Ecthesis of Heraclius, which, in addition to imposing silence, contained a profession of one will.

The Typus was later condemned by Martin I as impious and rejected by the entire Lateran Synod, with reasons that were worthy of a holy Synod and of irresistible force.

### LXVIII

The third point of the division can now easily be established. Honorius plainly sinned through that policy by which he wished silence to be maintained concerning one or two operations, although religious duty required him openly to defend two operations. Otherwise the faith in the two unmixed, unconfused, and undistinguished natures of Christ—which was being indirectly attacked by the remnants of the Eutychians—might waver.

No sin that harms the Catholic faith exists which the Church cannot rightly punish. But if the offender has died, punishment cannot be inflicted unless his name is erased from the sacred records, his memory disgraced, and his books burned. These are the three things the Synod carried out against Honorius.

To erase a name from the sacred diptychs is, in the case of the dead, precisely the same as casting someone out of the Church. To disgrace the memory means nothing other than condemning someone because of the harm inflicted upon the faith. To burn books is to declare them unworthy of being read.

### LXIX

There is nothing surprising in supporters of error—even negative supporters, if that expression may be used—being subjected to the same punishment as the authors themselves. The supreme Pontiffs teach that both are held by the same guilt.

Pope Innocent I to the Fathers of Milevis:

> “Let pastoral care beware lest the deadly contagion of two sheep perhaps spread through an unwary flock, and lest the ravenous wolf rejoice in his heart within the Lord’s sheepfold over such great flocks of sheep, while the wound of two is deceptively concealed by their guardians. Care must therefore be taken lest, by permitting wolves, we appear more like hirelings than shepherds.”

Celestine I to the bishops of Gaul:

> “I fear that to connive here means to remain silent; I fear that those who permit them to speak in this manner are themselves speaking even more. In such matters silence is not free from suspicion, because truth would intervene [192] if falsehood were displeasing. The matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by silence.”

Leo I, Letter 93, to Turibius:

> “If the hearts of priests do not resist profane errors, with what conscience do they claim the honor owed to them, when they do not labor for the souls entrusted to them? Beasts rush in, and they do not close the sheepfolds; thieves lie in wait, and they do not keep watch; illnesses multiply, and they provide no remedies,” etc.

Felix II to Acacius of Constantinople:

> “To neglect, when one is able to drive out the perverse, is nothing other than to foster them; and he is not free from the suspicion of secret partnership who ceases to oppose a manifest crime,” etc.

The Lateran Synod under Martin I, speaking about the Typus of Constans:

> “Likewise, it is evil to embrace the worse and indiscriminately cast out the better together with it.”

---

## 193. DISSERTATION III  
### APPENDIX TO THE NOTES ON CHAPTER IV: On the Use of the Pallium

[Col. 0165]

### I

By the term *pallium*, in the sense in which it is used here, a certain kind of sacred vestment is understood. Patriarchs were clothed with it when they were ordained, but they were stripped of it if they were deposed.

### II

It is not the place here to discuss what kind of vestment it was in the Eastern Church. The work we are elucidating concerns only the Church of the West. Nor is this the place to explain what its form is in our own time, what rite is used in conferring it, or what use and authority it possesses; anyone can easily learn these things from the interpreters of pontifical law, under the title “On the Use and Authority of the Pallium.”

### III

This brief Dissertation of ours, if indeed it is a Dissertation and not rather a concise observation, concerns only the earlier centuries.

### IV

Among authors of Latin, the word *pallium* signifies that long garment which is placed over other clothing and is put on when one must go out in public, but removed when one is at home.

### V

In sacred vestments the word has an ambiguous meaning. Sometimes it denotes a sacred garment worn over other clothing, such as the *pluviale* (cope), the *cappa*, and the *casula* (chasuble). Sometimes it denotes a certain insignia of exceptional dignity, which is itself placed upon the cope and chasuble. For this reason it is called a *pallium*: either because it is placed upon the pallium, as the pallium is placed over other clothing, or because it is a kind of ornament and adornment of the pallium. Those who torment themselves by anxiously searching into this terminology are wasting their efforts.

### VI

It is now understood in this latter sense, and in the Church signifies proportionately what a torque signifies in military and royal [194] orders: namely, an insignia of a certain pre-eminent dignity and a band added around the sacred pallium.

### VII

Since there is no dignity in the Church greater than the patriarchal, this ornament became proper to Patriarchs, and especially to the one who surpasses all the others and who presides by divine right—namely, the supreme Pontiff, or Roman Bishop.

### VIII

Since authority corresponds to dignity in the Church, the pallium of which we are speaking signifies, together with dignity, the fullness of authority, though according to the rank of the person who wears it. In the supreme Pontiff it signifies authority over the universal Church; in the other Patriarchs it signifies authority over their respective dioceses.

### IX

Just as no definite time can be identified in the Eastern Church when Patriarchs began to wear it, so neither can one be identified in the Western Church. Its use may therefore rightly be called perpetual among the supreme Pontiffs when they celebrated sacred rites or performed duties proper to their office.

It was certainly in use before the year 336. In that year Pope Mark permitted the Bishop of Ostia to wear the pallium when, according to ancient custom, he ordained as supreme Pontiff the person elected by the Roman clergy.

### X

The opinion of those who make Linus, the successor of Peter, the originator of this ornament is therefore not far from the truth. Rupert of Deutz and Augustine Patritius hold this view: the former in Book I, chapter 27, of *On the Divine Offices*; the latter in Book I of *Sacred Rites*, in the section on the pallium.

### XI

It is remarkable what Rupert writes: that Maternus, who was sent by Blessed Peter the Apostle to found the Church of Trier, left the inheritance of the pallium to his successors. If this is true, one must admit that Saint Peter used the pallium and bestowed it upon Maternus, and consequently that from the beginning of the nascent Church the supreme Pontiffs both wore and granted the pallium.

But just as this author, writing in only the twelfth century, asserts such an ancient granting of the pallium without the testimony of the ancients, so he can scarcely obtain credence—at least among people who are not excessively credulous.

### XII

Augustine Patritius, the author of the books on the sacred rites of the Roman Church, took what he wrote from Rupert. Those who attribute these books to Christopher Marcellus of Corcyra seem to have overlooked Marcellus’s preface to Leo X while reading it.

Marcellus wrote the preface in 1516, while Leo X was seated on the papal throne, and dedicated the book to him. But the author composed the book in 1473 or 1474, during the pontificate of Sixtus IV and the reign of Frederick, as he clearly demonstrates.

### XIII

Just as the supreme Pontiffs sometimes communicated their authority to prelates of lesser Churches and appointed them their vicars in distant provinces, so they bestowed an insignia of the authority communicated to them; this is precisely the granting of the pallium.

Consequently, in earlier times, whenever the pallium was granted, mention was made [195] of the authority conferred—authority that properly belongs by itself to the supreme Pontiff: namely, the power to convene Synods, to exercise judgment over bishops and matters of faith, to grant bishops permission to travel farther from their own Churches, and so forth.

### XIV

Since, moreover, vicarious authority was conferred by the supreme Pontiff together with the pallium, justice and equity required that those who received the pallium should in turn pledge a particular loyalty to the supreme Pontiff. Yet the obligation of loyalty, initially confined within the narrow limits of the vicariate, was afterward extended more broadly.

### XV

In the earliest period, when the pallium was sent by letters from the Pontiffs, the letters contained not only an exhortation to order one’s life more holily and to discharge the pastoral office worthily with vicarious authority, but sometimes also commands to eradicate heresies and the tares growing up in the field of the Church. But at that time there was no mention of any particular obedience or subjection; this occurred in a later age, if not always, at least for the most part. What I have said about the earliest period is established by the letters of Symmachus, Pelagius II, and St. Gregory, as well as by the forms in the *Diurnus*.

### XVI

I do not, however, deny that the communication of the pallium and of that sacred collar constituted a somewhat closer union between the receiving Bishop and the supreme Pontiff who bestowed it, so that through the Bishop the Pontiff seemed to exercise his authority in more remote provinces and to be present everywhere in authority, as those who had undertaken to govern the Christian world as Vicars of Christ. Pelagius I indicates this when sending the pallium to Sapaudus of Arles. For he signifies that his own functions were entrusted to him according to ancestral custom,

> “so that the everlasting solidity of that steadfast rock, upon which the Lord our Savior founded his own Church from the rising of the sun to its setting, might firmly retain the summit of its primacy through the authority of its successors, both directly and through its Vicars, etc. Thus, with shared responsibility, our predecessors governed the holy universal Church of God by the grace of God,” etc.

### XVII

Since in the sixth and seventh centuries the pallium was sent even to Bishops situated outside the dominion of the Empire, it happened that, at the very time when the supreme Pontiffs were almost subject to the Exarchs and Emperors, and when the Exarchs and Emperors were all the more suspicious because they could scarcely retain their authority at Rome against invading kings of other peoples, the Pontiffs, when sending the pallium, sought the Emperor’s consent, lest suspicion arise that they were seeking support elsewhere.

Thus Vigilius sought Justinian’s consent, and Gregory the Great sought that of Maurice. Vigilius was groaning under the servile, uxorious tyranny of Theodora and Justinian, while Gregory suffered the Exarch’s calumnies and the Emperor’s insults. Neither of them, in his prudence, wished to offend the feelings of people eager for quarrels, or provoke even the slightest suspicion of an alliance entered into with the kings Childebert, Theodoric, and Theudebert. Neither was unaware of the calumny that had been fabricated against Silverius under a similar appearance, or of how dreadful a fate the supreme Pontiff had endured as a result.

### XVIII

Two conclusions follow from this. First, there is no need to laboriously seek some general cause of the Emperors’ consent that would apply to all Pontiffs, since it is known to have been sought by only two Pontiffs. Nor is it reasonable to derive that cause—if some general explanation is required—from the notion that the pallium was an imperial ornament which, because it had been granted to the supreme Pontiffs by the Emperors, could not be communicated to others without imperial permission. For from whom, then, was this grant of imperial vestments made to the Eastern Patriarchs derived, and from whom to the Romans, unless perhaps from that notorious donation of Constantine made to Sylvester?

### XIX

Second, the explanation recently devised by a certain writer for the Emperors’ demanded consent has no appearance of truth: namely, that the use of the pallium was granted to Gallic Prelates but not to the Spanish.

He says that in the time of Vigilius and Gregory the Great, Gaul was either still subject to the Emperor of Constantinople or at least acknowledged his authority, whereas Spain had already completely thrown off the yoke of the Roman Empire. Therefore, he says, when Gregory the Great sent the pallium to Leander of Seville, he made no mention of obtaining the Emperor’s consent, but did mention it when sending it to Siagrius of Autun.

### XX

This entire argument collapses through its own emptiness. For how does he know that Maurice’s permission was not requested when Gregory sent the pallium to Leander? Is it because the letters are silent, and therefore the act did not occur? The letters are also silent in the cases where either Pelagius sent the pallium to Sapaudus of Arles or St. Gregory sent it likewise to Virgilius of Arles. Does it follow from this that neither of them sought the Emperor’s consent?

If it follows, the man’s reasoning collapses with respect to the Gallic Bishops. If it does not follow, it collapses equally with respect to the Spaniards.

The learned man further proposes that Pelagius did not seek the Emperor’s consent when he granted the pallium to Sapaudus because the custom of granting it had already become established. But this is hardly an adequate reply to the advocate of the Spaniards. For if it were valid, there would have been no reason for that same consent to be sought when Vigilius gave the pallium to Auxanius and Aurelianus, since Symmachus had previously given it to Caesarius of Arles.

Rather, this confirms our view. Pelagius did not seek Justinian’s consent because he was on good terms with Justinian; Vigilius sought it because he was not.

### XXI

Concerning the persons to whom the pallium was conferred in those earlier times with which we are concerned, there is no single, consistent opinion. Some think that it was given to Metropolitans by something like a common law, and to other, lower-ranking Bishops only by privilege. Others, by contrast, believe that it was granted indiscriminately to all, according to the judgment of each supreme Pontiff.

Some divide the matter and say that it was indeed granted to all at the Pontiff’s discretion, but with this distinction: to Metropolitans alone it was granted together with the authority to exercise the functions of the Apostolic See; to lower-ranking Bishops, together with certain lesser privileges, namely for ornament, honorary precedence, and matters of that kind.

### XXII

The first group confirms its opinion by custom and reason. For the functions of the Apostolic See are found to have been entrusted only to Metropolitans, and this was done appropriately, so that supreme authority might, as it were, descend less far, and so that those who were required to obey the Vicars of the Apostolic See might do so with less reluctance, since they were not unaccustomed to rendering the obedience required to Metropolitans.

### XXIII

The second group uses the same arguments, namely custom and reason. For authority belonging to the Apostolic See was entrusted even to Deacons and Presbyters, and indeed in matters of the greatest gravity. Certainly Pelagius, a Deacon of Vigilius, deposed Paul, Patriarch of Alexandria, from his throne; and Philip the Presbyter occupied the place of Caelestine at the Synod of Ephesus.

Nor is this surprising, since the condition of benefices is that they are granted by the Prince at his discretion to whomever he chooses.

### XXIV

The last group adduces the following arguments on its behalf.

1. In the case of lower-ranking Bishops to whom the pallium is recorded as having been granted—such as Maximus of Ostia by Mark in the year 336, Siagrius of Autun by St. Gregory in 599, and Aigilbert of Le Mans by John V in 685, as well as others, including those of Pavia, Lucca, Bamberg, and so forth—no vicarious authority of the Apostolic See is found to have been conferred, but only lesser privileges.

2. No Metropolitan is found to have been endowed with the pallium without the vicariate of the Apostolic See.

So they commonly argue.

### XXV

I, however, hold the following view: the pallium was never granted to anyone from the clergy except Bishops, although on occasion the functions of the Apostolic See were entrusted to Presbyters and even Deacons. For no example of the contrary act is found in the ancient records. Yet the functions of the Apostolic See are frequently recorded as having been entrusted to Presbyters, so that they might preside over Synods, even general ones. Thus Philip the Presbyter occupied the place of the Apostolic See at the Council of Ephesus. They were also entrusted to Deacons for acts of the highest authority: thus Pelagius, in the name of Pope Vigilius and with two Patriarchs associated with him, deposed Paul, the Bishop of Alexandria.

There is scarcely any explanation for this practice other than the will of the Pontiffs. For if someone says that it is inappropriate for a Presbyter to preside over Bishops and even Metropolitans with that full authority whose insignia is the pallium, there immediately arise the examples of the presbyteral presidency at Councils by Presbyters sent by the Pope, of Pelagius the Deacon’s judgment concerning the Patriarch Paul, and of the ordinary jurisdiction exercised in England by Abbots over Bishops.

If someone should again argue that by “pallium” is meant the outer border of the vestment which the Pontiff used when performing sacred rites, and that it would therefore be unfitting for a Presbyter but fitting only for one who is, as it were, the king of sacred rites, the answer may be made that the vestment of the Pontiff performing sacred rites is not now, nor was it formerly, different from that of a Presbyter in any other respect that could be at issue here. Since the pallium is worn either exclusively or more frequently during the solemnities of Mass, it is no less suitable for a Presbyter than for a Bishop, if this single consideration of suitability is taken into account.

If it is pressed that there are other functions besides Mass during which a Bishop wears the pallium, such as ordaining, and so forth, I readily admit this. But just as Bishops ordain without the pallium, why should Presbyters not wear the pallium without ordaining, and so forth?

### XXVI

I likewise think—and indeed I am certain—that the pallium was granted not only to Metropolitans but also to lower-ranking Bishops. This is established by several examples already cited. Add to them the case of John VIII sending the pallium to Wallo, Bishop of Metz, after four predecessors had already obtained it, without the Metropolitans making any objection.

This custom did not become so obsolete that it was absent even in our own times. When the Most Christian King Louis XIII pressed the supreme Pontiff to raise the Church of Paris to an Archbishopric because of the dignity of the city, which was the capital of the realm, the Pontiff, perceiving the difficulty caused by the opposition of the Metropolitan of Sens, offered the pallium to the Bishop of Paris, lest he seem to offend the King’s wishes by a refusal.

More recently, the pallium was granted to the Bishop of Autun by Innocent XI, who is now reigning.

### XXVII

From the fact that a pallium was sent by Benedict IX to St. Odilo, Abbot of Cluny—a fact reported by Hallerius from Glaber in *On the Sacred Orders*, p. 237—someone might think that this mark of dignity was not conferred upon Prelates alone. But such an inference would contradict Glaber himself.

A pallium was indeed sent to Odilo together with a ring, but not for the Abbot to wear. Rather, he was to wear it after becoming Bishop of the Church of Lyons, which the Pontiff ordered him to govern.

Glaber must be heard. After recounting the disputes over the election of a Bishop to succeed Burchard in the see of Lyons, and the report made to the Pontiff concerning those disputes, he continues:

> “The Pontiff immediately sent to that Father both a pallium and a ring, and commanded that he should be Archbishop of the aforesaid city. But the religious man, mindful of the purpose of his humility, utterly refused to become one; and, accepting the pallium and ring, reserved them for the future Pontiff of that see, whoever might prove worthy before God.”

### XXVIII

I admit that the pallium was generally granted to Metropolitans together with the authority of the Apostolic See: thus Vigilius, Pelagius, and Gregory granted it to the Bishops of Arles.

Yet from the letters of the Pontiffs who sent pallia we must determine what privilege was conferred. Symmachus did not entrust the functions of the Apostolic See to Theodore of Laureacum, nor Paschal to Bernard of Vienne, although Theodore and Bernard were Metropolitans.

Conversely, we understand from a letter of Pope Hormisdas to St. Remigius, Bishop of Reims, written in the year 514, that the functions of the Apostolic See were sometimes entrusted to Metropolitans without the pallium.

### XXIX

It is reasonable to believe that in earlier times the pallium was given by the Pontiff only to Westerners. For no example is found of its being given to Easterners before Latin Patriarchates were established in the East.

The account given by Theodorus, Balsamon, and Photius concerning St. Cyril—that he received from St. Caelestine a *phrygium*, which they interpret as the pallium, together with vicarious authority to exercise judgment concerning Nestorius at the Council of Ephesus—rests on a weak foundation. For neither the letters of St. Caelestine nor the acts of the Council contain a single word about authority being entrusted to him to preside over the Council, nor do they contain anything about the pallium.

Indeed, some believe that this tale was fabricated by the Constantinopolitans, at the time when they had withdrawn from the Latin Church, with the aim of diminishing the dignity of the Alexandrians, as though it had originated with the Romans or at least been enhanced by them.

### XXX

In the records of antiquity no trace is found of the pallium having been given to any Africans, at least so long as the African Church retained something of its former splendor. Indeed, reason proves that it was not given at all.

For when the title of Archbishop was attached to the pallium, the African Church so strongly rejected it that at the Council of the year 397 it decreed:

> “The Bishop of the principal see shall not be called the prince of priests, or the high priest, or anything of that kind—that is, Archbishop—but only the Bishop of the principal see.”

### XXXI

Since Gregory’s saying, “the order of reason admonishes us that with the use of the pallium we ought to bestow certain privileges,” applies not only to Metropolitans entrusted with the functions of the Apostolic See, but also to lower-ranking Bishops who received the pallium, something must be investigated concerning such privileges. Something must therefore be investigated concerning such privileges.

Some of these privileges were granted to the Church itself, others only to an individual. The former were enduring; the latter temporary.

Gregory the Great granted Siagrius of Autun the authority to summon to a Synod all the Bishops under the jurisdiction of Theodoric and Theudebert. This was a personal privilege. He also granted him, among the Bishops, the first see after the Primate in the province of Lyons. The Church of Autun retained this privilege even without the pallium.

### XXXII

Some think that the title of Archbishop was also granted to these lower-ranking Bishops. To prove this, they cite the example of Aigilbert of Le Mans, who is recorded as having been called Archbishop in a charter of King Theodoric; of Chrodegang of Metz; and also of Angilram of Metz; indeed, even of Theodulf of Orléans, who, because they had received the pallium, claimed for themselves the title of Archbishop, although they were Bishops subject to Metropolitans.

“For what other reason,” they say, “would they have received so important a title, unless because, on account of the pallium received from the supreme Pontiff, they appeared to excel other Bishops?”

### XXXIII

I make the following observations concerning these examples.

First, I read that the title of Archbishop was granted only to Gauls, not to Prelates of any other nation, although many were distinguished by the pallium.

Second, it was not granted to all Gauls—for who has ever read this of Siagrius of Autun? Who has read it of the Bishop of Paris?

Third, those four who are said to have borne the title of Archbishop were men distinguished either by nobility of birth, by the favor of princes, or by the dignity of chief chaplains at court. For this reason flattery may have bestowed upon them the title of preeminence.

Fourth, the letters of the Pontiffs who sent pallia to Bishops nowhere mention the title of Archbishop, although the title is sometimes expressly used when writing to Metropolitans. Therefore, if any men bore this title, they arrogated it to themselves rather than received it, and did so out of pride, not as a prerogative of dignity.

Fifth, these four examples—except perhaps that of Angilram—are drawn from lesser-known documents, which are certainly not authoritative enough to prove something so extraordinary.

Why should an error not have entered the charter of King Theodoric, whether through the ignorance of the copyist or through friendly flattery toward the King’s associate? Why was Aigilbert called Archbishop because he held the first place after the Metropolitan among the Bishops of the third province of Lyons?

For *archē* (ἀρχή), from which *archiepiscopus* is formed, signifies both “beginning” and “authority.” Why should he not have been called Archbishop by hyperbole—a usage not uncommon in ordinary speech—because he was outstanding among Bishops in holiness of character, devotion to religion, learning and wisdom, and nobility of birth? Perhaps for that reason he was called “prince of the Bishops” in another document.

### XXXIV

If these explanations are probable—as certainly they are—and all the more so because they contradict a deed otherwise unheard of and a title incredible in its extravagance, the entire conjecture concerning Aigilbert’s pallium collapses, since it rests on no other foundation than the title itself.

### XXXV

Furthermore, the prerogative supposed to have been granted to Aigilbert with the pallium—namely, that he either actually occupied or was considered to occupy the first place after the Metropolitan among the Bishops of the third province of Lyons—belonged to the city of Le Mans long before Aigilbert’s time.

For in the *Notice of the Provinces and Cities of Gaul*, placed at the beginning of the first volume of the Councils of Gaul, which the highly learned Sirmond considered to belong to the time of the Emperor Honorius and therefore to precede Aigilbert’s ordination by almost three centuries, Le Mans is listed after the city of Tours in the enumeration of the third province of Lyons.

The same must be said of the city of Metz, which in the same notice is regarded as first after the metropolitan city of Trier. Yet this notice, being arranged for civil affairs, does not thereby provide certain evidence for ecclesiastical matters. For it does not follow that if a city holds a particular place in the political order, it retains the same place in the ecclesiastical order.

Otherwise the privilege which St. Gregory says he conferred upon Siagrius of Autun—that he should hold the first see after the Metropolitan in the first province of Lyons—would not be a privilege, since in the aforementioned notice the city of the Aedui is placed immediately after Lyons.

### XXXVI

Some cite another privilege of the pallium: namely, that one who had been given it could be judged only by the Apostolic See.

But what will they say concerning Theodulf of Orléans, who is said to have received the pallium from Stephen, yet, having been suspected of conspiracy against Louis the Pious, was deposed by Bishops and thrown into a monastery?

He indeed complains that he was condemned by judges from outside his own jurisdiction:

> “This is the task of the Roman Prelate alone,  
> from whose hand I received the sacred pallia.”

But the action of the Bishops shows that such a privilege, if it existed, was not accepted in practice in Gaul.

Moreover, if the matter were as they say, how would the rights of the Metropolitans not have been violated when the pallium was granted to lower-ranking Bishops, even though the Pontiff explicitly wished those rights to remain intact?

Finally, if an example of this privilege can be found, it does not belong to the period with which we are concerned, but to a later period, when common law had been restricted by private benefices.

### XXXVII

From these considerations I conclude that it is by no means clearly established what privileges were granted to lower-ranking Bishops together with the pallium.

Therefore, the opinion of those who have thought that certain men in the provinces were endowed by the supreme Pontiff with this insignia of plenary authority does not seem implausible. They were, as it were, the eyes and hands by which he might see and manage affairs far away. Bound by a particular oath according to the measure of the authority granted, they were summoned to share in the supreme government and ordered to report emerging cases to the Apostolic See and, whenever necessary, to carry out its commands.

This opinion is supported not only by the testimony of Pelagius already cited, but also by the whole of St. Gregory’s letter to Siagrius, if it is read with somewhat closer attention.

### XXXVIII

Just as what we have just said is obscure, so perhaps the matter is doubtful in which those functions of the Apostolic See consisted which are said to have been granted to Metropolitans. Gregory the Great reduces them to three heads: judging the cases of Bishops, and even cases of faith; convening Synods; and giving *formatae* to Bishops who were going farther away.

Yet these functions properly belong to Metropolitans. For according to the decree of the Council of Nicaea, they must summon the Bishops twice a year to a Synod at which, by common deliberation, judgments concerning Bishops are exercised and cases of faith are discussed if any heresies arise.

They must also give *formatae* to Bishops. This is established by the example of the Africans and Gauls and confirmed by the testimony of antiquity; no one disputes it.

What, then, was the distinctive privilege granted with the pallium? The difficulty is increased by the added phrase that the right of the Metropolitans was preserved. For if it was preserved, what remains of the three functions mentioned by Gregory the Great?

### XXXIX

I think the answer should be that Metropolitans could indeed exercise these three functions by their own right, but only over their own provincial Bishops. Over others, including Metropolitans, they could exercise them by the authority of the Apostolic See, whose power is exceedingly broad.

For this reason Vigilius conferred upon Auxanius of Arles authority over all the Bishops in the dominions of King Childebert.

The right of the Metropolitans was preserved in this respect: in their own provinces they continued freely to perform their duties, and lower-ranking Bishops were not granted permission to disregard the commands of their superiors.

### XL

Since the supreme Pontiffs were accustomed to warn carefully the Bishops whom they endowed with the pallium to use it only during the solemnities of Mass—and since Gregory the Great severely rebuked the Bishop of Ravenna for wearing it during litanies, although afterward, worn down by persistent entreaties, he granted permission—it may reasonably be asked what was the reason for so explicit and insistent a warning.

Was it the dignity of the pallium, lest it be cheapened by use? Was it the prerogative of the supreme Pontiff, who used it daily so as to be distinguished from the other Bishops? Was it because it was the proper ornament of the sacred chasuble, which is worn only during Mass? Or, more probably, did all these reasons operate together?

It follows that a precious ornament was formerly added to the precious vestment which is the sacred chasuble, but not to a woolen band and some cheap appendage.

### XLI

Nor can it be objected that the same warning continued in later times, even after the pallium had become woolen. Either the ancient custom of giving this warning was retained because the ancient formulas for sending the pallium were likewise retained, or, once the third reason had disappeared, the first two still seemed to retain some force of their own.

### XLII

From what has been said, a historical question may arise concerning the material of the pallium. Was it always made of the material now used, or was it formerly made of something more precious?

That the Eastern pallium was woolen in the fifth century is attested by Isidore of Pelusium, Letter 136, Book I, and there seems little doubt that it was always so.

It is also established that the pallium is now woolen in the West, although it is marked with red silk crosses. Augustine Patritius even reports in his book on ecclesiastical rites what kinds of wool are used and according to what procedure.

### XLIII

But the question is whether it was once made of another material.

John the Deacon provides grounds for the question when he writes, in Book 4 of the *Life of St. Gregory*, that the pallium worn by Gregory the Great was woven of shining byssus, and that it could still be seen in the tomb of the holy Pontiff in the year 875, when John was flourishing.

Whether one interprets *byssus* as fine linen, as the authors of better Latin do, or as silk thread, as ecclesiastical writers of a later age do, it was certainly not wool. It follows that it was not woolen in earlier times either, if it may reasonably be believed that so eminent a man, so hostile to novelty, would not have wished to depart from the practice of his predecessors, especially in a matter so visible and exposed to everyone’s eyes.

### XLIV

A learned and diligent man who recently published a work on the archiepiscopal pallium foresaw this argument and made two exceptions in order to defend his view that the material was wool.

First, he says that John the Deacon was deceived when he inspected St. Gregory’s pallium and thought it linen, whereas in reality it was wool. The cause of the deception, he says, was the obscurity of the distinction between the two materials, especially when their age had made them worn.

Second, if the Deacon was not deceived—which could scarcely have happened, since an immense crowd saw the pallium—then, if it truly was linen, Gregory acted modestly against the custom of his predecessors.

He thinks both points can be established from John the Deacon’s words. The first follows, in his view, from the fact that John calls the pallium “woven of shining byssus,” whereas byssus is not white but rather yellowish, since it is a coarser part of linen. The second follows from the Deacon’s statement that the mediocrity of the garment worn by the holy man was represented by the material of the pallium.

### XLV

Let me state simply and plainly what I think.

First, I do not sufficiently understand how a linen pallium could be so much cheaper than a woolen one that a man of antiquity—as John calls him—would have wished, out of modesty, to depart from the custom of his predecessors by using it. For byssus is much more precious than wool, as is clear from that passage in Proverbs where the virtuous woman is praised because she made coverings for herself and because “fine linen and purple” were her clothing.

That woman, whose noble husband sat at the gates with the elders of the land—that is, administered the commonwealth—would scarcely have differed greatly from a peasant woman if she used the coarser part of linen.

Furthermore, it seems to me that when John speaks of the holy Pontiff’s pallium, he praises nothing except the man’s antiquity. The mediocrity he mentions, however, refers to the band from which the silver reliquary hung.

For after writing that three objects were honored with the greatest veneration and kissed by those who kept vigil on the anniversary of the feast—the pallium, the reliquary, and the belt—he immediately added:

> “When considered individually, these represent by perpetual signs both the man’s antiquity, the mediocrity of his garment, and the appearance of his religious rule. For since his pallium is seen to have been woven of shining byssus and pierced by no needles, it is recognized that it was wrapped around his shoulders rather than fastened, just as it is shown in the most ancient mosaics and paintings. The fact that his reliquary appears to have been made of thin silver and hung from his neck on a cheap pallium demonstrates the modesty of his garment. Moreover, the slenderness of his belt, which never exceeds the measure of one inch, makes it clearer than daylight that he preserved the appearance of the rule once established by St. Benedict.”

Add to this that, unless I am mistaken, John the Deacon’s words lead rather clearly to the opposite conclusion from that asserted by the learned man: namely, that Gregory did not depart from the custom of his predecessors in using a pallium made of byssus.

The Deacon teaches five things about the pallium: that it was woven of shining byssus; that it was pierced by no needles; that it was wrapped around the shoulders; that the same practice was displayed in very ancient mosaics and paintings; and that these features represented the man’s antiquity—that is, in my judgment, his devotion to preserving antiquity, by which the holy man was bound.

Thus both the material of the pallium and the manner of wearing it bore the mark of antiquity. Gregory was therefore so far from abandoning his ancient predecessors as they were depicted in mosaics that he deliberately imitated them.

Finally, if Gregory followed antiquity in wearing a pallium woven of shining byssus, it must be admitted that the pallia of the ancients were likewise woven of shining byssus. Accordingly, if by “byssus” is understood the finest linen, as all interpreters of the word hold, they were made of linen rather than wool.

But if someone wishes that the word signify not ordinary linen but the particular byssus mentioned by Pliny in Book 19 of his *Natural History*, then the pallia of the ancients must have been precious, since Pliny reports that “its scruples were exchanged at four denarii each, like gold.”

And it was indeed fitting that the ornament placed upon the precious garments worn by the supreme Pontiffs during the sacred rites should itself be precious.

### XLVI

From what has been said thus far, it is clear that the question of what material the pallia worn by the supreme Pontiffs were made of in the earliest period is not raised without reason.

Was it wool, symbolizing the humility of the shepherd? Or was it something more precious, befitting the dignity of the priest?

### XLVII

The question seems incapable of being resolved in either direction except by four arguments, apart from the common presumption: the testimony of ancient writers, tradition or usage, the agreement of both Churches, and an argument derived from the mystical meaning of wool.

### XLVIII

But, as far as I know, the Latin authors earlier than John the Deacon transmitted nothing in writing concerning this matter. Therefore, I think no argument can be drawn from authority that would create a presumption for the Latin Church in either direction.

### XLIX

Nor is what the Greeks possess—or rather what one Greek, Isidore of Pelusium, possesses—any more effective concerning the pallium of the Prelates of the Eastern Church. For it does not support the Latins, with whom we are concerned, as will be shown later.

### L

Nor does the present usage seem to provide an adequate argument, as though what is now in use must always be said to have been used, and to have existed for a long time, even though the time when it began cannot be demonstrated.

For John the Deacon’s passage is not rashly believed to point in the opposite direction and sufficiently to prove that before the sixth century the custom now prevailing had not yet been established.

### LI

Nor does the argument drawn from reason possess enough force to resolve a historical question. For the claim made concerning the mystical meaning of the woolen pallium—as though it represented the skin of the lost sheep which the good shepherd, having found it wandering, placed upon his shoulders and carried back to the fold—is neither relevant to our question nor weighty in itself.

The author of that mystical interpretation, Isidore, is speaking first about the pallium of the Easterners, whereas the question concerns the Latin pallium. Moreover, he says things that cannot be transferred without violence to another meaning. Finally, different people have devised such varied mystical explanations that anyone can find one to use on his own behalf.

### LII

But since Isidore’s testimony is highly valued by recent writers, and is almost the sole support of the common presumption, it must be subjected to a somewhat more careful examination. Indeed, the whole of Letter 136 must be set out.

> **“To Count Hirminus.**
>
> “As intensely as you burn with an insatiable desire to learn, so readily and willingly am I prepared to explain what you ask, provided that God, moved by your prayers, grants me insight from heaven.
>
> “That linen cloth with which Deacons perform their office in the sacred mysteries recalls to us the humility of the Lord, who washed and wiped the feet of his disciples.
>
> “But that garment which the Priest wears upon his shoulders, woven from wool and not from linen, signifies the skin of that sheep which the Lord sought when it had gone astray and, having found it, lifted upon his shoulders. For the Bishop, who bears the figure of Christ, performs Christ’s office and, by that very garment, shows to all that he is an imitator of that good and great shepherd who undertook to bear the weaknesses of the flock.
>
> “And pay close attention. For when the true shepherd himself approaches through the opening of the venerable Gospels, then the Bishop rises and lays aside the garment of imitation. This signifies that the Lord himself, the guide and God and master of pastoral art, is present.”

### LIII

First, it must be observed that Isidore’s entire purpose is to explain the mystical meanings of sacred things. There is no argument more open to the vanity of conjecture than this.

Second, Count Hirminus asked Isidore what mystery was signified either by the linen cloth carried by Deacons or by the shoulder-garment carried by Bishops during the sacred mysteries. Concerning the Deacons’ linen cloth, Isidore replied with an interpretation that can scarcely be approved by investigators of sacred matters: he says that it recalls the humility of Christ, who washed and wiped the disciples’ feet.

But interpreters of such matters think otherwise, and those who interpret it more simply do so more plausibly: namely, that it is an ordinary sign of those serving at the table.

Finally, what he says about the Bishops’ shoulder-garment is no more plausible, if by “shoulder-garment” he means what in this discussion is called the pallium.

### LIV

Since this is so, I do not see how the perpetual use of a woolen pallium in the Latin Church can be defended. Yet I would not only refrain from overturning the opinion confirmed by an age extending over ten centuries and by a considerable multitude of authors; I would not even weaken it.

For three considerations still prevent me from yielding entirely to John the Deacon’s side: the continuous use of the garment for ten centuries; the difficulty of showing when and for what reason its use began; and the number and antiquity of the authors who agree that its material was wool.

### LV

Although I see that the force of these three arguments can be weakened, the multitude of authors does not press very strongly. All those usually cited wrote about what was used in their own times, not about what had been used in earlier times.

Those who addressed liturgical matters are partly ancient and partly more recent. The former devoted themselves entirely to devising and explaining mystical interpretations; the latter adhered to the ancients without conducting any more searching examination.

Moreover, from John the Deacon one may infer with some clarity that the use of the woolen pallium began around the beginning of the ninth century. For he seems to have mentioned Gregory’s byssus pallium while at the same time praising the man’s antiquity, thereby silently reproaching his contemporaries for their novelty. For what other reason would he have done both things?

Now, I think that the continued use of wool from the time of the change onward should be attributed to the ceremonies by which, because of the analogy of the name, good people of the ninth century began, at the annual celebration, to offer lambs to the virgin Agnes, from whose wool cloaks would be made. For nothing is more enduring than what is devoted to ceremonies of this kind.

### LVI

Although I see that the force of these three arguments can be weakened in roughly the manner I have described, I nevertheless suspend judgment, content to have proposed the question to learned men together with its 207 considerations. Let them deliver whatever opinion they judge more consistent with reason, but only after they have more carefully weighed two points.

### LVII

The first is that Gregory the Great never mentions wool when writing about the pallium to those to whom he sent it; yet he would undoubtedly have mentioned it if truth had permitted him to do so. For, being extraordinarily fond of allegories, he would have drawn from the material of the pallium an argument for preaching humility, to which he so earnestly exhorted those who received the pallium. Yet he did not do so, although the opportunity was most suitable—especially when he sent the pallium to Maximus of Salona:

> We have sent, according to custom, the pallium to be used at the sacred solemnities of Mass, and we wish you to claim its significance in every respect; for the honor of this garment is humility and justice, etc.

[Col. 0178A]

### LVIII

The second is that the pallium may be called the fullness and completion of power, the sign of full authority, and an emblem of honor; and, if we believe some writers, it was the border and fringe of the imperial pallium which the Emperor Constantine gave to Sylvester. But who could believe that these things apply to a woolen band?

### LIX

Before bringing this Dissertation to an end, a question must be resolved, occasioned by Gregory the Great, who prescribed to Marinianus of Ravenna how he ought to use the pallium. According to the latest edition of the Councils, his instruction reads as follows:

> Remember that you must use it only in the church of your own city, after the sons have been dismissed, proceeding from the salutatorium to celebrate the sacred solemnities of Mass; but when the Masses have been completed, you shall take care to remove it again in the salutatorium.

[Col. 0178B]

### LX

Before the question is proposed, the arrangement of the words must be corrected, since it has been disordered. For what does the phrase “after the sons have been dismissed, in the church,” etc., mean? Some read: “unless in the church of your own city, after the sons of the Church have been dismissed,” etc. This reading too is faulty, for it does not agree with what follows, since the salutatorium mentioned there is not a part of the city but of the church. It is possible to restore the text from Book IV, chapter 5, of the Life of Gregory, where John the Deacon reports Gregory’s entire letter to Marinianus and reads:

> except in the church of your own city, after the sons have been dismissed, proceeding, etc.

### LXI

The question is who those sons were after whose dismissal the bishop, wearing the pallium, proceeded from the salutatorium to the altar. A learned man thinks that they were laymen who came, as a mark of honor, to greet the bishop. Hence, he believes, the place received the name salutatorium. In their presence the bishop was forbidden to put on the pallium, but once they had been dismissed, only the clergy remained.

### LXII

Three considerations support the learned man’s opinion. First, what we read about Proclus in Socrates, Book 7, chapter 47: Proclus seized Thalassius, among the leading men who had customarily come before the solemnities of Mass to greet the bishop, and appointed him Bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, 208, after he had been prefect of Illyricum. Second, laymen were accustomed to be called “sons of the Church.” Finally, Gregory wished in that passage to restrict as much as possible the use of the pallium, which John, the predecessor of Marinianus, had extended in an improper manner.

Another learned man holds that by the name “sons of the Church” clergy could be understood. Once they had already gone out from the salutatorium, the pontiff would put on the pallium and proceed. This conjecture is also supported by the fact that in our *Diurnus* the supreme pontiffs address the clergy as “sons” in the second and third professions of faith.

I admit that both conjectures are probable and learned. Nevertheless, I think something simpler may be proposed: namely, that the name “sons” referred to the School of Singers (*Schola Cantorum*), which, when the pontiff proceeded to the altar to celebrate the sacred rites, was dismissed from the salutatorium at a given signal and went ahead in the manner described in the appendix to the *Sacramentary of St. Gregory*, p. 261 of the edition of Dom Hugh Menard.

[Col. 0179]

# Supplement to the *Diurnus* of the Roman Pontiffs

[In Mabillon, *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, part II, p. 32.]

## Reply to a Bishop’s Petition

*(To p. 97.)*

You should know that authority has been granted to you, by the sequence of our command, to consecrate the basilica which, as your devotion reports, you have completed in honor of the holy [N.]. Therefore, dearest brother, after first making the donation attached to the petition, and fulfilling the desire of your devoted vows, you may rejoice in the completion of the celebration.

### Another Reply

We have received, with appropriate congratulations, the offering of your devotion, rejoicing in the completion of a good work. Therefore you shall consecrate as soon as possible, by the sequence of our command, the basilica which you report to have been built in the name of blessed [N.], so that the glory of the prince of the apostles may be consecrated through the attendance of all in reverence for him; and so that the surrounding people may have one through whose intercession they may soon deserve to obtain the fulfillment of their petition. Take care to complete without delay whatever you say has been contributed, or report that you are going to contribute, for its proper end.

[Col. 0179B]

## Decretal Read by the Deacon When a Bishop Is Being Examined

*(To p. 54.)*

Your Holiness, in whom the primacy of the priesthood also resides, has been accustomed to assist churches deprived of the service of their own pastor. Therefore, prostrate before you, most blessed lord pope, we beseech your apostolate that, while we seek a shepherd, you may deign to consecrate as bishop such a one as [N.], whose merits are attested by the unanimous assent of all of us in requesting him. We wish you good health for many years, most blessed lord pope.

### Another Text Read by the Deacon

An election in which no one dissents rejoices with the affection of one who desires the candidate. Therefore, having long been deprived of episcopal leadership, we have united all our votes in favor of such a one as [N.], so that, with your approval, he may be substituted in the place of the deceased. Accordingly, we beseech your apostolate, most blessed lord pope, that you may deign, in your kindness, to approve [N.], whom religious zeal is known to have led us to request.

### Another of the Same Kind

The desires of those who ask to be assisted by the judgment of Your Beatitude do not conflict with the tradition of the venerable canons. Therefore, since our church has long been deprived of its own pastor, we have taken refuge in the authority of your pontificate, from whose see all honor of priests proceeds. For this reason we beseech your apostolate, holy and venerable lord pope, that you may deign to consecrate as bishop [N.], our priest, whom the agreement of the whole community has chosen. We wish you good health for many years, most blessed lord pope. And they subscribed.

# Various Privileges of Apostolic Authority

## I

[Col. 0180A]

[N.] bishop, servant of the servants of God, to [N.], the religious abbot of the venerable monastery of holy Mary, ever-virgin, Mother of God and our Lady, and through him to the same venerable monastery forever.

Since the summit of supreme apostolic dignity is recognized as shining forth in the splendor of divine providence, and since in carrying out the praises of God it ought to display with particular zeal the contest of its labor, the proper care of the same apostolic pastoral solicitude has compelled us to publish abundantly whatever is recognized as pertaining to the stability of holy places and to confirm it by the authority of apostolic institution.

Therefore, because you have asked us that the monastery of holy Mary, ever-virgin, Mother of God and our Lady, situated in the place called Plumbariolum, in the territory of Aquino, be adorned with the privileges of the apostolic see, so that, established under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, which by God’s authority we serve, it may not be subjected to the jurisdiction of any other church, we, favoring your devout desires, commit by this authority of ours to effect what is requested.

And therefore, by this authority, we forbid any priest of any church to exercise any jurisdiction whatever in the aforesaid monastery, except the apostolic see. Thus, unless invited by the abbot of the monastery, no one may presume to celebrate the solemnity of Mass there. By apostolic censure, under threat of divine judgment and by the force of the most severe anathemas, we absolutely decree that no other person, whatever power or dignity he may possess, nor any person of high or low standing, may ever presume to interfere in the same monastery or in its affairs, to remove or alienate in any way its property and possessions, or anything else that appears to belong to it; nor may anyone inflict upon it any malice or harm, whether in a time of peace or in a time of barbarian disturbance.

We decree that it is to remain perpetually secure under the jurisdiction of our holy Church, both in time of peace and, as stated, in time of barbarian disturbance. We further promulgate and establish, by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, before God and the terror of his future judgment, through this apostolic desire and constitution of ours, that the places exchanged or granted by the abbot of any monastery to the aforesaid monastery of holy Mary at Plumbariolum, as well as the other properties of places given and offered to that holy site by kings, dukes, gastalds, and other Christians, or that may later be granted there, shall belong securely by right to the said monastery and its superior and shall remain so forever.

Nor shall anyone have permission, as stated, to take away from it, or from anything belonging to the monastery, anything whatever, whether from a person of high or low standing, so that this venerable place, in accordance with the apostolic constitution and privilege to which it is subject, may remain securely endowed.

If anyone—which we do not wish—should presumptuously oppose or in any way violate what we have established for the stability of the aforesaid monastery and for the praise of God, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema and assigned to be burned in the punishment of eternal fire with the devil and his most atrocious pomps, and with Judas, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whoever, with devout regard, observes and guards all the matters in this apostolic constitution of ours that concern the worship of God shall receive in many ways the grace of blessing from the most merciful God and Lord, and may deserve to become a participant in eternal life.

## II. Privilege

Since the proper care of pastoral solicitude has compelled us to set down the praises of God, it is fitting that whatever is recognized as pertaining to the stability of holy places be published abundantly and confirmed by the authority of apostolic institution in privileges and decrees.

Indeed, under apostolic governance, the aforesaid venerable places, which had long lain in ruins and suffered great want and poverty, and which [lacuna] have again been built from the ground and enriched on every side, [lacuna] to restore them without doubt to a better state—especially where things are sought that concern not temporal advantage but the enduring care of souls serving God: namely, that the aforesaid venerable places, which have been gathered together and joined into one by us, together with the nearby [lacuna] congregations of saints which regularly [lacuna]. The rest is missing.

## III. To a Bishop Concerning the Removal of Relics

[Col. 0182B]

Let your fraternity know that, concerning the relics of the blessed martyr [N.], it is necessary that they be placed in the site which is to be dedicated to his veneration. Therefore, do not fail to entrust to the present representatives of [N.] of our see the relics that have been raised according to the customary reverence, so that they may be transported to us as quickly as possible, in accordance with what has been entrusted to them.

[Col. 0181]

# Mabillon’s Observations on the *Diurnus* of the Roman Pontiffs

[Col. 0181C]

1. The *Diurnus* of the Roman pontiffs, once held by them in such authority, although now entirely obsolete, should nevertheless not be neglected because of the distinction conferred by its antiquity. Accordingly, when an ancient copy eight hundred years old came into our hands—the copy used by Lucas Holstenius in preparing the edition of this book which he had planned—we thought we should perform a useful task by comparing the aforesaid copy with Garner’s edition.

Garner possessed a copy of the manuscript which Hilary Rancatus, a Cistercian monk, had lent Holstenius for a single night, as we said in our *Itinerary*. Garner calls it a Roman manuscript, and a very ancient one, and reports its chapters, with a few omissions, in his preface. For some reason unknown to me, perhaps because of a defect in the copy, several chapters escaped him; we have reported them below.

2. The most important item is the privilege concerning the monastery of Plumbariolum. Tasia, the wife of Duke Ratchis, and their daughter Rattruda built at their own expense a monastery for women not far from Cassino, in a place called Plumbarola, as Leo of Marsica testifies in Book I, chapter 8, of the *Chronicle of Cassino*. There they ended their days, living under strict observance and great caution according to the rule. It is said that St. Scholastica lived and died there.

Leo calls it a monastery for women, yet the privilege above is addressed to the religious abbot of the venerable monastery of holy Mary, Mother of God. Perhaps there were two monasteries there, as often occurs. Certainly, in a manuscript of Cassino marked no. 219, the monastery of virgins at Plumbariola is said to have been dedicated not to the Virgin Mother of God but to St. Petronilla, in these words:

> “Bernard, abbot of Cassino, sends this missal to the sisters of our monastery of St. Petronilla of Plumbarola, so that they may pray for him.”

In the same manuscript, under the month of June, appears:

> “The death of Beatrice, abbess of the monastery of St. Petronilla of Plumbarola.”

It is now an estate of the monastery of Cassino.

3. Various readings and emendations are not lacking in the Roman copy, by which Garner’s edition can be embellished in many places. It may be useful to set down here some of the more significant passages.

Column 29, line 26: “For while we remain in prayer, so that the heavenly favor …”; more correctly in the Roman copy: “For while we remain long in prayer, so that the heavenly favor may be present to the minds of all …”

In the same place, line 34: “If it is said”; our manuscript has: “if it is lawful to say.” The same correction should be made at column 34, line 6.

Likewise, at column 30, line 3, “priests”; in the Roman manuscript, “deacons,” as also at the end of the same formula: “I have consented and subscribed in that most holy deacon and our elect.”

Similarly, “the whole clergy together with the leading men and soldiers or citizens subscribed” at column 31, line 21, should read, instead of “of the united petition,” “of our petition.”

And at column 32, line 23: “blessed Peter, prince of the apostles.”

At column 35, line 1, it should be restored as follows: “the fierceness even of approaching enemies, which, unless the power of God alone and of the prince of the apostles through his vicar—that is, the pontiff of the Roman city—as is known to all, sometimes restrains by warnings, and sometimes also bends and moderates by exhortation … with entreaty …”

At column 40, line 8, “priest”; in our manuscript, “deacon.”

Likewise, at column 48, line 16: “at once the Word flesh, at once flesh endowed with life and reason.”

At column 53, line 32, after “synodally,” the manuscript adds: “and by decree.”

At column 57, line 22, *inhumanatum* should be read as *humanatum* (“made human” or “incarnate”).

In the same place, line 41, read “subsistence” for “substance”; our manuscript corrects this serious error.

At column 59, line 4, “Constantine”; ours adds “the Great,” which is necessary for the customary formula.

At column 60, line 10, add “and accompanying” after “preceding.”

At column 66, line 24, after “they presumed,” add likewise: “they presume and shall have presumed.”

In the same place, line 29, read “through their own doctrines.”

Likewise, line 30: “according to the mode of the two natures, so also two natural wills and two natural operations.”

At column 73, line 4: “my purity and my cooperation for you and for the interests of the Church,” etc.

At column 76, line 10, the words “but to celebrate the litanies for three days before the day of the Lord’s Ascension” are entirely absent from the Roman manuscript, as also from the letter of Gregory II.

At column 84, line 17, read “for indeed” as “who are souls.”

In the same place, line 22, after “devour,” correct as follows: “and his destruction may justly be applied to our punishment, since we neglect to guard those entrusted to us with vigilant care”; and at line 25, after “we say,” add: “and by which divine …”

At column 90, line 31, read “in the place of [N.]”; and at line 33, after “founded,” add: “requesting that it be dedicated, your devotion, etc.”

At column 91, line 44, read: “in [N.], namely in the estate, [N.], in the territory”; and at line 47: “you should judge it to be dedicated in honor of the martyr [N.], so that, with God’s favor and your prayers preserved, I may rejoice that I have fulfilled my desire.”

We shall pass more lightly over the remainder.

[Col. 0184A]

At column 109 there is a privilege granted to a certain queen in favor of monasteries founded by her. The printed editions do not give the queen’s name; the Roman manuscript calls her Cynedrida.

Line 1 of the privilege: instead of “praiseworthy concerning goods,” read “of praiseworthy devotion.”

Likewise, line 11: “which she had acquired justly”; and line 13: “to establish and dedicate.”

Line 16: “your [N.], Queen Cynedrida”—who was undoubtedly queen of the English, or at least the daughter of the king of England.

At column 112, line 34, instead of “suitable,” the manuscript has “of oils.”

And at column 115, line 11, after “with vows,” it adds “may you favor.”

These are a few examples from many.

# In the Year of Our Lord 821. Theodulf, Bishop of Orléans

[Note: [Col. 0187B] We reprint this according to the edition of Jacques Sirmond.]

[Col. 0187A]

## Historical Notice on Theodulf

(Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*)

[Col. 0187A] Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, lived in the ninth century. His homeland is uncertain. He is commonly regarded as an Italian, because in an old chronicle, preserved by Quercetanus, volume I, page 36, it is said that Charlemagne brought him from Italy into Gaul. This opinion is quite weak. No better is the alternative by which Mabillon, Nicolás Antonio, and Eccard, *Rerum Francicarum* XXXVIII, 169, make him a Spaniard, because Theodulf called the remnants of the Gothic people in Hesperia, or Spain, his kinsmen. For the word “kinsmen” could have been used metaphorically for a companion of the same faith and religion. His homeland, therefore, is not yet known with certainty.

Before coming to Gaul, he had a wife, by whom he had a daughter, Gisla, to whom poem 4 of book III is addressed. He was first abbot of Fleury, as the *Catalogue of the Abbots of Fleury* attests, volume I of Baluze’s *Miscellanies*, page 492, and afterward bishop of Orléans. In 794 he took part in the Council of Frankfurt against Felix; in 811 he was a witness to Charlemagne’s testament. At first he enjoyed favor with Louis the Pious, but afterward, when he seemed to favor Bernard, king of Italy, more strongly, he was expelled from his see in 818 and confined in prison in the city of Angers. Because he steadfastly defended his innocence, he was restored in 821, in which year he also died.

Mabillon published his epitaph in *Analecta*, volume I, page 426; see the notes there, pages 433–434; in the recent edition, pages 377–378; and Eccard, at the cited place.

His works were published together by Jacques Sirmond, Paris, 1646, octavo, and later reprinted in his *Works*, in the following order:

1. **Chapters for the priests of his parish.** These were first published by Baronius under the year 835, no. 5; afterward by Joannes Buseus together with the letters of Hincmar of Reims, Mainz, 1602, octavo; and further by Sirmond in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, page 211. Sirmond considers that they should be assigned much more accurately to the year 797 or thereabouts. They are also found in Spelman, volume I of the *Councils*, page 584, and Hardouin, volume IV, page 911. The canons of the Sixth Ecumenical Council, printed in volume III of Hardouin’s *Councils*, page 1719, are spurious and were copied almost entirely from these chapters.

2. **On the Order of Baptism.** This book was written in 812, when Charlemagne had been considering the subject. Eccard, *Rerum Francicarum* XXVIII, 18. It is addressed to Magnus, archbishop of Sens. In one Corbie manuscript, however, from which Menard published it in his edition of Gregory the Great’s *Sacramentary* (Paris, 1642, quarto), page 113, it is addressed to John of Arles—a mistake that Sirmond had thought erroneous. Mabillon, in volume I of the *Analecta*, page 24 (new edition, page 76), resolved the matter by maintaining that different copies were addressed to each of the two men.

3. **On the Holy Spirit.** This book was published in 809 and dedicated to Charlemagne, for in that year the Council of Aachen had dealt with the procession of the Holy Spirit. See Eccard XXVII, 63.

4. **Poems in six books.** Polyc. Lyser treats them with sufficient accuracy in his *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, page 223 and following, though some matters must nevertheless be supplied. He published in Paris the *Exhortation to the Judges*, which constitutes book I but had lost its beginning. Afterward Gey. Elmenhorstius published it at Leiden, 1618, quarto; and later Andreas Rivinus published it, together with certain poems from Canisius and the Cologne *Library of the Fathers*, Leipzig, 1653, octavo, [Col. 0189A] along with Drepanius, Florus, and others.

Mabillon subsequently published ten previously unpublished poems for the first time in *Annals*, volume I, page 376 and following (new edition, page 410). Baluze published two epigrams in *Miscellanies*, book I, pages 492–493. Christian Daumius observes in his *Catalogue of Christian Poets* that two hymns—on the Nativity of the Lord and to the holy martyrs Sergius and Bacchus—were omitted from Sirmond’s edition, although they had already been printed in the *Libraries of the Fathers* and in Rivinus’s edition.

A poem on the entire instruction of the Old and New Testament is found in Goldast’s *Biblical Manual*, page 34. In the *Works*, book II, poem 1, it is entitled: “Verses at the Beginning of the Bible, which he himself had copied.” Martène and Durand published a short poem on luxury in the *New Thesaurus of Anecdotes*, volume I, page 399.

5. **Fragments of two sermons, together with another fragment of a work on the sacred interpreters,** were published by Lucas Dacherius in *Spicilegium*, volume V, page 117 (in the recent edition, volume I, page 254). That these are Theodulf’s is shown both by their style and by the fact that the beginning of his chapters was appended at the end. [Col. 0190A]

6. Arnold Wion, in *The Wood of Life*, and after him Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, page 757, say that Theodulf wrote the *Annals of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious*. A fragment of such annals under Theodulf’s name is preserved in the Vatican Library. Bernard de Montfaucon, *Bibliotheca Bibliothecarum Manuscriptorum*, page 35. Perhaps he is one of those anonymous annalists, several of whom survive for that period.

7. In the *Catalogue of the Abbots of Fleury* mentioned above, an **Explanation of the Athanasian Creed** and a **Mystical Explanation of the Mass** are also attributed to him. Both are likewise found in a manuscript of Fleury.

8. A **Mirror of Biblical Passages** is also attributed to him; it appears elsewhere among Augustine’s works, volume III, page 680.

More information will be supplied by the *Literary History of France*, volume IV, page 459.

[Col. 0189]

## Several Testimonies of Writers of the Same Period Concerning Bishop Theodulf

### Alcuin in a Letter to King Charles

When he had received from him the task of refuting the book of Felix of Urgell:

“But I beg that a copy of that little book be sent to the apostolic lord; another also to Paulinus the patriarch; likewise to Richbod and Bishop Theodulf, doctors and teachers, so that each may answer independently.”

### Einhard in the *Life of Charlemagne*

Listing the bishops who signed Charlemagne’s testament:

“Bishops Hildebald, Richolf, Arnold, Wolfar, Bernoin, Laidrad, John, Theodulf, Jesse, Hetto, Waltgaud.”

### Hincmar, *On the Divorce of Lothar and Tietberga*, Reply to Question 6

“And from the sacred Scriptures and the statements of Catholics, a certain orthodox and distinguished poet wrote, among other things, saying:

‘But if the cause of swearing presses and constrains you,

[Col. 0189C] do it with pure words, do it with a devout mind.’

And the rest that is read in the *Exhortation to the Judges*, verse 833.”

### Lupus, Abbot of Ferrières, in Letter 20 to Alcuin

“I read *nundinas* in Theodulf’s poem with the penultimate syllable lengthened. Whether reliance should be placed on his authority or on that of the teachers lies with you to determine.”

(He alludes to verse 357, chapter 3, on Palm Sunday, book II.)

### Author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*, under the Year 814

(Apud André Duchesne, volume II of the *History of the Franks*)

“After his father’s death, Rampo was sent to him so that he might learn of his death promptly and in no way delay his arrival. When he had reached the city of Orléans, Theodulf, bishop of that city, a man learned in every respect, perceived the reason for his arrival and very quickly made every effort to inform the emperor through a messenger.

The same author, speaking under the year 816 of the arrival of Pope Stephen:

‘The emperor decided to await his arrival at Reims. He ordered Hildebald, archchaplain of the sacred palace, Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, John of Arles, and a large number of other officials to go out to meet him, clothed in sacerdotal vestments.’

Again, under the year 817, speaking of the conspiracy of Bernard, king of Italy:

‘Very many clerics and laymen were aware of this crime. Among them the storm of that time engulfed several bishops, namely Anselm of Milan, Wlfold of Cremona, and also Theodulf of Orléans.’

And afterward:

‘He consigned to monasteries the bishops bound by this atrocity, having deposed them through the other bishops.’”

## The Old Chronicle

(Apud the same author, volume III, page 366)

“Also flourishing in these times near the city of Orléans was Theodulf, bishop, who, because of the excellence of his learning, was brought from Italy into Gaul by the aforementioned emperor Charlemagne, and received from him both the abbacy of Fleury and the bishopric of Orléans.”

## From the Book of the Miracles of Saint Maximin, Abbot of Micy

By Letald, a monk of Micy, who began to flourish toward the end of the tenth century.

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictines*, century I, page 601)

“During the time of the blessed-memory emperor Charles Augustus, when the Lord of all things was arranging to restore that place to its former nobility, Theodulf, most noble in both character and birth and of exceptionally keen intellect, was appointed bishop of the Church of Orléans.

He therefore strove with great diligence to restore that place to its ancient dignity. When he found in the neighboring regions monks insufficient for accomplishing this, he summoned others from the regions of Septimania. He gave them the place and, adding from his own resources the property assigned to it, handed it over to them.

He did not regret this action. Indeed, during his time the glory of that place shone so brightly that the honor that followed cast the disgrace of its former ignominy into shadow, and later gains compensated for earlier losses.

Among his other works, Bishop Theodulf built a basilica of marvelous workmanship, modeled on the one constructed at Aachen, in a village called Germigny. There he elegantly expressed his memory in the following verses:

[Col. 0190D]

‘These temples, Theodulf, I consecrated in honor of God.

Whoever enters them, I beg, let him remember me.’

This venerable priest was accused before the king of conspiracy, deprived of his bishopric, and confined for many days. Later, through a marvelous reversal of circumstances, he promptly cleared himself of the charge, regained the king’s favor, and recovered the chair of his former dignity, though he was not to live long afterward.

For it is said that he was killed by poison by those who, while he was in exile, had already conceived the desire to seize his property once they had obtained freedom.”

## Theodulf’s Epitaph

[Note: [Col. 0191A] They report that Theodulf was Italian by nation—that is, as Sirmond believes, from Cisalpine Gaul. His epitaph makes Speria, or Hesperia, his homeland; but this name is ambiguous, sometimes signifying Italy and sometimes Spain. An old chronicle edited by Chesne, in volume III of the *History of France*, settles the matter on page 336 in these words:
