“Also flourishing in these times near the city of Orléans was Theodulf, bishop, who, because of the excellence of his learning, was brought from Italy into Gaul by the aforementioned emperor Charlemagne, and received from him both the abbacy of Fleury and the bishopric of Orléans.”

But against this stands the fact that Theodulf himself rather clearly indicates that he came from Spain in the *Exhortation to the Judges*, in these verses:

“Soon we touch, Narbonne, your seats and your splendid city,

where a joyful company meets me.

The remnants of the Gothic people, together with the Hesperian crowd,

rejoice in me as their kinsman and leader.”

There Theodulf calls the peoples of Hesperia dwelling in Septimania his kinsmen, since they had flowed there from Spain. Unless he calls them “kinsmen” on the grounds that both those Gothic peoples of Septimania and the Ostrogoths dwelling in Italy, from whom Theodulf himself was descended, had come from the same nation.

Theodulf died in 821, in the seventh year of his exile, killed by poison—either on his return, as the aforementioned chronicle says, or after his return at Orléans, as reported by Letald, the monk of Micy, in his book on the miracles of Saint Maximin. Theodulf’s death is placed in the necrology of our monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, written more than eight hundred years ago, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October.]

(Mabillon, *Analecta*, volume I, from a very old Vitonian manuscript)

“His ashes are preserved in this stone,

he who once was bishop and abbot for the peoples.

[Col. 0192A]

Not born among us, yet let him be regarded as our foster son:

Speria produced him, but Gaul nurtured him.

The populous city of Orléans upon the Loire,

once rejoiced while this Father dwelt here.

Alas! A malign man drove him from his own see;

he is said to have been an exile within these walls, and he was an exile.”

[Col. 0191C]

[Note: [Col. 0191D] **Theodulf.** They report that Theodulf was brought from Italy—that is, as I believe, from Cisalpine Gaul—to our country by Charlemagne and endowed with the bishopric of Orléans. This is established by Theodulf himself, and also by the fact that, through Charlemagne’s favor, he exercised the very extensive office of *missus dominicus* in both provinces of Narbonne and remained, throughout his life, among the emperor’s closest associates.

After Charlemagne’s death, he enjoyed no less favor during the first years with his son Louis, by whom he was also ordered to go out honorably to meet Pope Stephen when the pope came into Gaul.

Later, accused of taking part in the conspiracy of Bernard, king of Italy, against his uncle, he was stripped of his bishopric and exiled to a monastery near Angers. Although he consistently denied the crime in every respect, there were nevertheless people who claimed that it had been fabricated through envy. At last he was acquitted, but while returning to his own people he is said to have died, apparently in 821.

The rest will be supplied by his books. If in them, especially in the verses, there are passages that seem less pleasing because they depart from common usage, let the reader remember that these are blemishes in the wording, compensated for by the abundant fruit and usefulness of the work.]

# Theodulf, Bishop of Orléans

[Note: [Col. 0192D] **Chapters for the Priests.** Theodulf, and after him similar writers such as Herard of Tours and Riculfus of Soissons, called this book—and others like it—*chapters* and *capitularies* because they were composed and divided into individual chapters. The practice of that period likewise gave the law books of kings the same names, for the same reason. Thus among the Greeks too such works were similarly called *kephalaia* (κεφάλαια, “chapters”): for example, the ascetic treatises of Mark the Ascetic, Diadochus, Nilus, and others, as well as the paraenetic, or exhortatory, work of Agapetus and other writings of that kind composed “by chapters” (διὰ κεφαλαίων).]

## Chapters for the Priests of His Parish

[Col. 0191]

Theodulf to our brothers and fellow priests, the clergy of the parish of Orléans: greeting in the Lord.

### I. That They Must Care for the Progress of the Peoples Entrusted to Them, and on the Dignity of Priests

[Col. 0191B]

“I beg you, dearest brothers, to labor with the most vigilant care for the progress and correction of the peoples entrusted to you, so that, by showing them the way of salvation and instructing them by word and example, you may bring to our Lord Jesus Christ fruitful sheaves from their progress, and we from yours, with his help.

I also beg your fraternity to read these chapters, which I have briefly arranged for the correction of life, continually, to commit them to memory, and by reading them and the holy Scriptures to shape your conduct and amend your life. With the Lord’s help, strive to proceed with the peoples entrusted to you toward the heavenly kingdom.

You must know truly and always remember that we, to whom the care of governing souls has been entrusted, shall have to give an account for those who perish through our negligence; but for those whom we win by word and example, we shall receive the reward of eternal life.

For the Lord has said to us: ‘You are the salt of the earth’ (Matthew V, 13). And if the faithful people are God’s food, we are the seasoning of that food.

Know that your rank is second to and almost joined with ours. For just as bishops hold in the Church the place of the Apostles, so priests hold the place of the other disciples of the Lord. The bishops hold the rank of the high priest Aaron, while you hold that of his sons.

Therefore you must always remember such great dignity; remember your consecration; remember the sacred anointing that you received into your hands. Thus you will neither degenerate from that dignity, nor make your consecration void, nor pollute by sinning the hands anointed with sacred oil. Rather, preserving purity of heart and body, offering the peoples an example of good living, provide those over whom you preside with guidance toward the heavenly kingdoms.”

### II. That They Must Devote Themselves Constantly to Reading and Prayer

“You must be assiduous in reading and earnest in prayer, because the life of a just man is instructed, adorned, and fortified by reading; and through continual reading a person is protected from sin, in accordance with the words of him who said: ‘I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you’ (Psalm CXVIII, 11).

These are the weapons—reading and prayer—by which the devil is conquered. These are the instruments by which eternal blessedness is acquired. By these weapons vices are restrained; by this nourishment virtues are fed.”

### III. That Work Should Follow Reading

“But whenever you cease reading, manual labor should follow, because idleness is hostile to the soul, and the ancient enemy, when he finds a person free from reading or prayer, easily drags him toward vices.

Through the practice of reading you will learn how to live and how to teach others. Through the practice of prayer you will be able to benefit both yourselves and those joined to you in charity. Through manual labor and bodily discipline you will both deny nourishment to vices, assist your own needs, and have something to offer to those suffering want.”

### IV. With What Equipment They Must Come to the Synod

“When you assemble for the synod in the customary manner, bring with you the clothing, books, and sacred vessels with which you perform your ministry and the office entrusted to you. Also bring two or three clerics with whom you celebrate the solemnities of the Mass, so that it may be demonstrated how carefully and diligently you perform God’s service.”

### V. What Care Must Be Taken with Bread, Wine, and Water in Celebrating Mass

[Col. 0193D]

“The loaves that you offer to God as a sacrifice must be made either by yourselves or by your servants in your presence, cleanly and carefully. It must be diligently observed that the bread, wine, and water, without which Mass cannot be celebrated, are handled with the greatest cleanliness and care, and that nothing cheap or unapproved is found among them, in accordance with what Scripture says: ‘Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and perform everything diligently’ (2 Chronicles XIX, 9).”

### VI. That Women Must Not Approach the Altar While Mass Is Being Celebrated

“Women must never approach the altar while the priest is celebrating Mass. Rather, they should stand in their appointed places, and there the priest who is to offer their offerings to God should receive them.

Women must remember their infirmity and the weakness of their sex, and therefore fear touching anything sacred in the ministry of the Church. Laymen too ought to fear this, lest they suffer the punishment of Uzzah, who died when the Lord struck him because he attempted to touch the Ark of the Lord in an unauthorized manner (2 Samuel VI).”

### VII. That the Priest Must Not Celebrate Mass Alone

“A priest must never celebrate Mass alone. For just as it cannot be celebrated without the priest’s greeting, the people’s response, the priest’s instruction, and likewise the people’s response, so it must certainly not be celebrated by one person alone.

There must be people standing around him, whom he may greet and from whom he may receive a response. He must also recall the Lord’s saying: ‘Wherever two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them’ (Matthew XVIII, 20).”

### VIII. That Nothing Besides Sacred Things Is to Be Stored in Churches

“We frequently see harvests and hay gathered in churches. Therefore we wish this also to be strictly observed: that nothing be stored in a church except ecclesiastical vestments, sacred vessels, and books. Otherwise, if activities other than those proper to the place are carried on there, we may hear the Lord say: ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer; but you have made it a den of thieves’ (Matthew XXI, 13).”

### IX. That Henceforth No One Except a Few Who Are Worthy of It Is to Be Buried in a Church

[Col. 0194C]

“In these regions there was formerly a custom of burying the dead in churches, and places dedicated to divine worship and prepared for offering sacrifices to God were commonly made into cemeteries, or burial grounds.

Therefore we wish this practice to cease from now on, and no one is to be buried in a church unless perhaps the person is a priest or some exceptionally righteous individual who, by the merit of his life, acquired such a place for his dead body through the way he lived.

Bodies that were buried in churches in ancient times must not be thrown out. Rather, the tombs that are visible should be sunk deeper into the earth, and, after a pavement has been laid over them so that no trace of the tombs remains visible, the reverence due to the church should be preserved.

Where, however, there is such a multitude of corpses that this is difficult, let that place be regarded as a cemetery, after the altar has been removed from it and erected in a place where sacrifice may be offered to God reverently and in purity.”

### X. That Idle Talk and Profane Actions Are to Be Prohibited in the Church

“You must not assemble in church for any other reason than to praise the Lord and perform his service. Disputes, disturbances, idle talk, and other such activities must be entirely prohibited from that holy place.

For where God’s name is invoked, sacrifice is offered to God, and the presence of a multitude of angels is beyond doubt, it is dangerous to say or do anything unsuitable to the place.

If the Lord angrily expelled from the temple those who bought and sold the victims offered to him, how much more will he angrily drive out those who defile a place dedicated to divine worship with lies, idle talk, laughter, and similar nonsense (Matthew XXI, 12)?”

### XI. That Mass Must Not Be Celebrated Anywhere Except in a Church

“The solemnities of Mass must never be celebrated anywhere except in a church—not in just any houses or in lowly places, but in the place that the Lord has chosen, according to what is written: ‘See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place that the Lord will choose, so that he may place his name there’ (Deuteronomy XII, 13).”

### XII. That Women Must Not Live with a Priest

[Col. 0195B]

“No woman is to live in the same house with a priest. Although the canons permit a mother, sister, or persons of this kind, concerning whom there can be no suspicion, to live with him, we nevertheless prohibit this entirely because other women, who are not related to him, come in their service or on their account and entice him to sin.”

### XIII. That Priests Must Abstain from Drunkenness and Taverns and Must Not Recklessly Dine with Just Anyone

“You must take care both to abstain from drunkenness yourselves and to preach that the peoples entrusted to you abstain from it. Do not go through taverns drinking or eating; do not roam through houses or villages out of curiosity; and do not hold banquets with women or with any impure persons.

Unless perhaps some head of a household has invited you to his home and wishes to rejoice with you, together with his wife and children, in spiritual joy, to receive nourishment from your words, and to offer you bodily nourishment as an act of charity. For whenever any of the faithful refreshes you with bodily food, it is fitting that you refresh him with spiritual food.”

### XIV. That They Must Not Try to Draw the Faithful of Other Churches to Their Own

“No priest is to persuade the faithful of God’s holy Church from another priest’s parish to assemble at his own church, abandoning their own church, and to give him their tithes. Rather, each priest should be content with his own church and people, and must never do to another what he does not wish done to himself, in accordance with the Gospel saying: ‘Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them’ (Matthew VII, 12).

Whoever acts against these regulations or attempts to resist these admonitions of ours shall know that he will either lose his rank or be detained in prison for a long time.”

### XV. That They Must Not Solicit Other Clerics

“We also prohibit this in every way: that none of you solicit or receive another’s cleric, because the sacred canons pronounce a severe judgment on this matter.”

### XVI. On Those Who Seek Other Churches by Means of Gifts

“If a priest is found to have given, or to be giving, gifts to a cleric or layman in order to steal away another priest’s church, let him know that, for this robbery and savage greed, he will either lose his rank or be detained for a long time in the misery of prison, doing penance.”

### XVII. That They Must Not Refuse Baptism to Sick Children from Other Parishes

“If a sick child is brought to any priest from any parish for the sake of baptism, the sacrament of baptism must in no way be refused. If anyone refuses to grant this gift to one who requests it, and [Col. 0196B] the child dies without the grace of baptism, let the one who did not baptize him know that he will have to give an account for the child’s soul.”

### XVIII. That Sacred Vessels Must Not Be Turned to Other Uses

“No priest or layman is to presume to turn a chalice, paten, or any sacred vessel dedicated to divine worship to other uses. For whoever drinks anything else from a consecrated chalice besides the blood of Christ received in the sacrament, or uses a paten for any purpose other than the service of the altar, must be deterred by the example of Belshazzar, who, when he took the Lord’s vessels for common uses, lost his life together with his kingdom (Daniel V).”

### XIX. To Which Schools They May Send Their Relatives, If They Wish

[Col. 0196C]

“If any priest wishes to send his nephew or another relative to school, we grant him permission to do so at the church of the Holy Cross, at the monastery of Saint Aignan, at that of Saint Benedict, at that of Saint Lifard, or at any of the other monasteries entrusted to us for governance.”

### XX. That They Themselves Must Have Schools in Which They Teach the Children of the Faithful Free of Charge

“Priests must have schools in villages and hamlets. If any of the faithful wishes to entrust his children to them to learn letters, they must not refuse to receive and teach them, but must teach them with the greatest charity, mindful of what is written: ‘Those who are learned will shine like the splendor of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness will shine like the stars forever and ever’ (Daniel XII, 3).

When they teach them, they must demand no payment from them for this, nor accept anything from them, except what their parents may voluntarily offer them out of charitable devotion.”

### XXI. A Brief Rule of Christian Life

“Since the pages of all the holy Scriptures are filled with the instruments of good works, and throughout the fields of the holy Scriptures weapons can be found by which vices are restrained and virtues nourished, we have wished to insert into this our collection of chapters the teaching of a certain Father concerning the instruments of good works. In it, what must be done and what must be avoided is contained in great brevity.

First, love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; then, your neighbor as yourself.

Then: do not kill; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not covet; do not bear false witness; honor all people; and do not do to another what one does not wish done to oneself.

Deny yourself in order to follow Christ. Discipline the body; do not embrace luxuries; love fasting; refresh the poor; clothe the naked; visit the sick; bury the dead; assist those in tribulation; console the sorrowful.

Make yourself a stranger to the actions of the world. Prefer nothing to the love of Christ. Do not carry anger through to completion; do not reserve time for wrath; do not keep deceit in your heart; do not offer false peace; do not abandon charity.

Do not swear, lest you perhaps commit perjury. Speak truth from the heart and mouth. Do not repay evil with evil; do not commit injury, but patiently endure injury when it is done to you.

Love your enemies. Do not curse those who curse you, but rather bless them. Endure persecution for the sake of justice.

Do not be proud, drunk, excessively gluttonous, sleepy, lazy, querulous, or a detractor. Commit your hope to God.

When you see some good in yourself, attribute it to God, not to yourself. But always know that evil comes from yourself, and attribute it to yourself.

Fear the day of judgment. Dread hell. Desire eternal life with every spiritual longing. Keep death daily before your eyes.

Guard the actions of your life at every hour. Know with certainty that God watches you in every place.

When evil thoughts come into your heart, immediately dash them against Christ, and disclose them to your spiritual elder.

Guard your mouth from evil or corrupt speech. Do not love speaking much. Do not speak empty words or words suited to laughter. Do not love excessive or uncontrolled laughter.

Gladly listen to holy readings. Apply yourself frequently to prayer. Confess your past sins to God every day in prayer, with tears or groaning. From now on, amend those sins. Do not fulfill the desires of the flesh.

Hate your own will. Obey in everything the commands of the priest and teacher, even if he himself, God forbid, acts otherwise, remembering the Lord’s command: ‘Do what they say, but do not do what they do’ (Matthew XXIII, 3).

Do not wish to be called holy before you are holy; first be what you are more truly called.

Fulfill God’s commandments daily in deeds. Love chastity. Hate no one. Do not have jealousy or envy. Do not love contention. Flee arrogance. Revere elders. Love the younger.

In the love of Christ, pray for your enemies. With those who are at odds with you, return to peace before sunset. Never despair of God’s mercy.

Behold, these are the instruments of the spiritual craft. When we have fulfilled them continually, day and night, and presented them again on the day of judgment, that reward will be repaid to us by the Lord which he himself promised: ‘What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him’ (Isaiah LXIV, 4; 1 Corinthians II, 9).”

### XXII. That All the Faithful Must Learn the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed

“The faithful must be admonished so that all of them, from the least to the greatest, learn the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed. They must be told that the entire foundation of the Christian faith rests upon these two statements, and that unless someone both retains these two statements by heart, believes them with his whole heart, and repeats them very frequently in prayer, he cannot be a Catholic.

It has been established that no one is to be anointed with chrism, baptized, received after the washing at the font, or hold anyone before the bishop for confirmation unless he knows the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer by heart, except those whom age has not yet enabled to speak.”

### XXIII. That Everyone Must Pray to God at Least Twice Daily, Morning and Evening

“They must be told that every day, if they cannot pray more often, they should pray at least twice, namely morning and evening, saying the Creed, or the Lord’s Prayer, or ‘You who formed me, have mercy on me,’ or also, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner.’

They should give thanks to God for the provisions of daily life, because he has deigned to create them in his own image and to set them apart from the beasts. After these things have been done, and after worshiping God alone as their Creator, they should invoke the saints, so that they may deign to intercede for them before the divine majesty.

Those for whom a church is nearby should do this in the church. But whoever is traveling, or on any occasion is in the woods or fields, should do it wherever that very hour of morning or evening finds him, knowing that God is present everywhere, as the Psalmist says: ‘In every place of his dominion’ (Psalm CII, 22), and: ‘If I ascend into heaven, you are there’ (Psalm CXXXVIII, 8), and so forth.”

### XXIV. On Observance of the Lord’s Day

“The Lord’s Day must be observed with great solemnity, because on it God created light; on it he rained manna in the desert; on it the Redeemer of the human race freely rose from the dead for our salvation; and on it he poured out the Holy Spirit upon the disciples.

Nothing should be done on that day except prayers, the solemnities of Mass, and what pertains to eating. If there should be necessity for sailing or traveling, permission is granted, provided only that Mass and prayers are not omitted on that account.

Every Christian should assemble at church on Saturday with lamps; they should assemble for vigils or the morning office. They should also gather with offerings for the solemnities of Mass.

And while they are assembling at church, no case should be pleaded or heard, and no quarrels should take place. They must devote themselves solely to God: to the celebration of the sacred offices, to the giving of alms, and to feasting spiritually with friends, neighbors, and strangers in the praises of God.”

### XXV. That Everyone Must Love Hospitality and Offer It Freely
Admonish them to love hospitality, to refuse hospitality to no one, and, if they happen to offer hospitality to anyone, to accept no payment from him—unless, perhaps, the one received by you freely gives something. They should also be told how many have pleased God through the ministry of hospitality, as the Apostle says: “For through this some pleased God, receiving angels as guests” (Hebrews 13:2). And again: “Be hospitable without grumbling” (1 Peter 4:9). The Lord himself will say at the judgment: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matthew 25:35). Let all who love hospitality know clearly that, in their guests, they receive Christ. For that form of hospitality is not only inhuman but also cruel in which a guest is never received into a house until the payment for the hospitality has first been made, and what the Lord commanded to be done for the attainment of the heavenly kingdom is instead done for the acquisition of earthly possessions. [Col. 0199B]

### XXVI. That the faithful should beware the crime of perjury

It must also be preached that the faithful should beware perjury and abstain from it with the utmost care, knowing that it is a grave crime, prohibited both in the Law and the Prophets and in the Gospel (Matthew 5:33). For we have heard that some regard this crime as insignificant and impose upon perjurers a somehow light form of penance. They must know that penance for perjury is to be imposed in the same manner as for adultery, fornication, homicide, and the other criminal vices. If, after committing perjury or any criminal sin, anyone refuses to come to confession because he fears the long hardship of penance, he is to be expelled from the church—that is, from communion and fellowship with the faithful—so that no one may eat or drink with him, pray with him, or receive him into his house. [Col. 0199C]

### XXVII. That the faithful should abstain from false testimony

They must be told to abstain also from false testimony, knowing that this too is a most serious crime, prohibited by the Lord himself on Mount Sinai, when that same Lord said: “You shall not give false testimony” (Exodus 20:15); and: “A false witness will not go unpunished” (Proverbs 19:5). Whoever has committed this must know that he is either to be cleansed by such penance as was stated above concerning perjury, or condemned with such condemnation and excommunication as was set forth above. They must also be told that it is the height—not merely of folly but of wickedness—for the sake of greed for silver and gold, clothing, or anything whatever, or, as very often happens, because of drunkenness, to fall into so great a crime that one must either remain for seven years in severe hardship or be expelled from the church. The Lord says: “What does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” (Matthew 16:26). For while he may appear pious to others, he is cruel toward himself. [Col. 0199D–0200A]

### XXVIII. That presbyters should be ready to teach the peoples

We exhort you to be ready to teach the peoples. Let the one who knows the Scriptures preach the Scriptures; but the one who does not know them should at least say to the peoples what is very well known: “Let them turn away from evil and do good; let them seek peace and pursue it, because the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are attentive to their prayers,” and so forth. No one, therefore, will be able to excuse himself by saying that he has no tongue with which he can edify anyone. As soon as he sees anyone going astray, let him draw him back from error as he is able and has the strength—by admonishing, entreating, or reproving him—and encourage him to carry out a good work. When, with the Lord’s help, we have assembled together in synod, each one must be able to tell us how much he has labored with the Lord’s assistance or what fruit he has gained. And if anyone happens to need our help, let him admonish us with charity; and we likewise will not delay in offering him, with charity, whatever assistance lies within our power. [Col. 0200A–B]

### XXIX. In what manner the faithful should pray

You must admonish the faithful to be constant and diligent in prayer. Their manner of praying should be as follows: first, after reciting the Creed, as though reviewing the foundation of their faith, each person should say three times, “You who formed me, have mercy on me,” and three times, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner,” and should complete the Lord’s Prayer. If the place or time requires it, let him beseech the holy apostles and martyrs to intercede for him. With his brow armed by the sign of the cross, and with heart, hands, and eyes raised, let him give thanks to God. If there is insufficient time to carry out all these things, it is enough to say only, “You who formed me, have mercy on me,” and, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner,” together with the Lord’s Prayer alone, with groaning and contrition of heart. [Col. 0200B–C]

### XXX. Concerning the daily confession of sins to God

Every day, in our prayer, we ought to confess our sins to God either once, twice, or as often as we can, as the Prophet says: “I made my offense known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my iniquities against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the wickedness of my sin” (Psalm 31:5). After confession has been made to the Lord in prayer, with groaning and tears, Psalm 50, or Psalm 24, or Psalm 31, together with other psalms relevant to the matter, is to be recited, and thus the prayer is to be completed.

For the confession we make to priests also brings us this assistance: after receiving from them salutary counsel, most beneficial practices of penance, and mutual prayers, we wash away the stains of our sins. The confession that we make to God alone helps us in this way: the more mindful we are of our sins, the more the Lord forgets them; and conversely, the more we forget them, the more the Lord remembers them, as the Prophet says: “I will remember your sins no more” (Jeremiah 31:34). You, however, should remember what the prophet David testifies that he did when he says: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm 51:4). [Col. 0200C–0201A]

### XXXI. Those who come to confession must confess everything and be examined concerning everything

Confession must be made concerning all sins committed either in deed or in thought. There are eight principal vices, without which scarcely anyone can be found. They are: first, *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony of the belly; second, fornication; third, *acedia*, or sadness; fourth, avarice; fifth, vainglory; sixth, envy; seventh, anger; eighth, pride.

Therefore, when anyone comes to confession, he must be carefully questioned how and on what occasion he committed the sin that he confesses having committed, and penance must be assigned to him according to the nature of the deed. He must be persuaded to confess his depraved thoughts as well. He must also be instructed to make confession concerning the eight principal vices; and the priest must name each vice to him individually and receive his confession concerning it. [Col. 0201A–B]

### XXXII. That each person should spiritually perform for himself the works of mercy that he performs for others

The hungry are to be fed, the thirsty given drink, the naked clothed, the sick and those who are in prison visited, and guests welcomed, as the Lord says: “For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink,” and so forth (Matthew 25:35).

For each person must also perform all these things spiritually in himself and fulfill them bodily in others, because all these things contribute almost nothing toward attaining eternal life if someone lives luxuriously, proudly, and enviously—or, not to enumerate each vice, viciously and disorderly—and neglects the other good works.

Whoever sees that he does not possess Christ, who said, “I am the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:41), and does not possess charity, which is the nourishment of the soul, is indeed hungry. But if, through good works, he joins himself to Christ and fills himself with the sweetness of charity, then he has wholly fed the hungry person within himself.

Whoever lacks the teaching of the Holy Spirit and the streams of the holy Scriptures is thirsty. But if he waters himself with the streams of God’s word and intoxicates his mind with the sweetness of the spiritual cup, he gives drink to the thirsty person within himself.

Whoever sees himself stripped of righteousness or of the other manifestations of good works, and clothes himself with righteousness or with the other virtues, undoubtedly clothes the naked person within himself.

If he lies in the bed of his vices, suffers from the disease of his iniquity, is bound by the cords of his sins, and is covered by the wall of his vices in the darkness of his iniquity, he is indeed sick. But if, through confession, he comes out of the mud of his vices, is released from the bonds of his sins through the lamentation of penance, and emerges into the light of good works, he undoubtedly visits the sick person and the prisoner within himself. [Col. 0201B–0202A]

If, on the road of this life, he sees himself laboring and disturbed by the storm of vices, as though by some disorder of the air, and lacking a shelter of good works, let him know that, being on a journey, he needs lodging. But if he leads himself to the house of the virtues and takes refuge under their protection, he receives the guest within himself. When he spiritually offers all these things to himself, he feeds, gives drink to, clothes, visits, and receives Christ within himself, of whom he himself is a member. [Col. 0202A]

### XXXIII. Concerning the duty of children toward parents and of parents toward children

The faithful of the holy Church of God must be admonished to teach their sons and daughters to show obedience to their parents, as the Lord says: “Son, honor your father” (Ecclesiasticus 7:29). Parents themselves, moreover, ought to conduct themselves moderately toward their sons and daughters, as the Apostle says: “And you, parents, do not provoke your children to anger” (Ephesians 6:4).

They must also be told that, even if, out of natural affection, they wish to pardon injuries committed by their children, the Lord does not permit these to go unpunished unless worthy penance is perhaps offered; for it is less burdensome for children to receive whatever chastisements their parents impose than to incur the wrath of God. [Col. 0202A–B]

### XXXIV. What true charity is

The people must be admonished that true charity is this: to love God more than oneself, and one’s neighbor as oneself; and to wish to do nothing to another except what one wishes to have done to oneself, along with many other things that it would take too long to recount.

For those who think that charity consists only in drinking and eating and in giving and receiving things are greatly mistaken, as the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink” (Romans 14:17). These things themselves, when done with charity, are good and are to be counted among the virtues. [Col. 0202B–C]

### XXXV. What merchants engaged in trade must beware

Those who devote themselves to business and the trading of goods must be admonished not to desire earthly profits more than eternal life. For whoever thinks more about earthly possessions than about the salvation of his soul has greatly strayed from the way of truth and, according to a certain wise man, “in his life has lost his inmost self.” [Col. 0202C–D]

In this matter, as in others, the apostolic word must be followed: “Let no one transgress or defraud his brother in business” (1 Thessalonians 4:6), for God is the avenger of all these things.

Just as tithes and alms are to be given by those who devote themselves to the labor of the fields and to other work, eagerly acquiring food, clothing, and the necessities of human use, so too must this be done by those who engage in business for their needs. For God has given every person a craft by which he may be sustained, and each person ought, from the craft by which he obtains the necessities of the body, also to provide the soul with what is more necessary: its support. [Col. 0202D]

### XXXVI. What must be taken care of before Lent, and the seven ways in which sins are forgiven

[Col. 0203A]

One week before the beginning of Lent, confessions are to be made to priests, penance received, those who are at odds reconciled, and all quarrels settled. They must forgive debts to one another from their hearts, so that they may say more freely: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” Thus, entering the season of blessed Lent with minds cleansed and purified, they should approach holy Easter and renew themselves through penance, which is a second baptism. For just as baptism cleanses sins, so penance purifies them. And because, after baptism, a sinner cannot be baptized again, the Lord has given this remedy of penance, so that through it sins committed after baptism may be washed away in place of baptism. [Col. 0203A–B]

The holy Scriptures demonstrate that sins are forgiven in seven ways.

First, in baptism, which was given for the remission of sins.

Second, through martyrdom, according to what the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the one whose sin the Lord did not reckon” (Psalm 32:2). For according to the judgment of that same David: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered” (ibid., verse 1). Sins are remitted through baptism, covered through penance, and not reckoned through martyrdom.

Third, through almsgiving, according to Daniel, who said to the impious King Nebuchadnezzar: “Redeem your sins with almsgiving, and your iniquities with mercy toward the poor” (Daniel 4:24); and according to this saying: “As water extinguishes a burning fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin” (Ecclesiasticus 3:33). The Lord also says in the Gospel: “Nevertheless, give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41).

Fourth, when someone forgives the sins of one who has sinned against him, according to this saying: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Mark 11:25); and: “So also your Father will forgive you your sins, if you forgive each one from your hearts” (ibid.).

Fifth, if someone, through his preaching and the exercise of good works, converts others from their error, according to what the Apostle says: “Whoever brings a sinner back from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover a multitude of sins” (James 5:19).

Sixth, through charity, according to this saying: “The charity of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord, covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8).

Seventh, through penance, according to what David says: “I have returned to my distress while the thorn is being driven in” (Psalm 32:4). [Col. 0203B–D]

### XXXVII. That the fast of Lent must be observed with the utmost care

Lent itself must be guarded with the greatest observance, so that the fast during it is in no way broken except on Sundays, which are excluded from abstinence, because these days are the tithes of our year, which we ought to pass with complete devotion and holiness. There must be no occasion for breaking the fast on these days, since at another time the fast may be dissolved for the sake of charity, whereas during this period it must not be dissolved at all.

For at another time it is left to each person’s will and discretion whether to fast; during this period, however, not to fast is to transgress God’s command. At another time, fasting is the acquisition of a reward for abstinence; during this period, however, whoever does not fast—apart from the sick and little children—acquires punishment for himself, because the Lord consecrated these same days by sacred fasting through Moses, Elijah, and himself. [Col. 0203D–0204A]

### XXXVIII. That almsgiving must be joined to fasting

On the days of fasting, almsgiving must be practiced, and the food or drink that a person would have consumed if he were not fasting must be distributed to the poor, because to fast while reserving the foods of the midday meal for the evening is an increase not of merit but of food. [Col. 0204A–B]

### XXXIX. That the fast should not be broken before the evening service

Many who think that they are fasting eat as soon as they hear the signal for the ninth hour. Such people must in no way be considered to be fasting if they have eaten before the evening service has been celebrated. For they must attend the Masses, and, after hearing the solemnities of the Masses or the evening services and distributing alms, they should take food.

If anyone is constrained by necessity and cannot assemble for Mass, he should reckon the evening hour, complete his prayer, and then end the fast. [Col. 0204B–C]

### XL. From what things one should abstain while fasting

Abstinence on these days must extend to every delicacy, and one must live soberly and chastely. Whoever can abstain from eggs, cheese, fish, and wine displays great virtue. But whoever cannot abstain from these because of illness or because of any work may use them—provided that he solemnly observes the fast until evening and drinks wine not to drunkenness but to restore his body.

To abstain from cheese, milk, butter, and eggs and yet not to fast is utterly foolish and contrary to all reason. For drunkenness from wine and sexual excess are forbidden, [Col. 0204D] not milk and eggs. The Apostle does not say, “Do not eat milk and eggs,” but, “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Ephesians 5:18).

[Note: [Col. 0203D] “Wine” appears to be missing.]

### XLI. On which days the faithful should receive Communion during Lent, and concerning the celebration of Holy Week

On each Sunday in Lent, except for those who have been excommunicated, the sacraments of Christ’s body and blood are to be received. All are to receive Communion without exception on the Lord’s Supper, on Good Friday, at the vigil of Easter, and on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection; and all the days of Holy Week itself are to be honored with equal devotion. [Col. 0204D–0205A]

### XLII. That lawsuits and quarrels must cease on the days of fasting

On these days of fasting there must be no lawsuits and no quarrels; rather, one must persist in the praises of God and in necessary work. The Lord reproves through the Prophet those who engage in quarrels and lawsuits during Lent and demand debts from their debtors, saying: “Behold, on the day of your fast your own desires are found, and you demand all your debts. Behold, you fast for lawsuits and quarrels, and you strike with an impious fist” (Isaiah 58:3). [Col. 0205A]

### XLIII. That one should abstain from sexual relations on the days of fasting

On these most sacred days one must abstain from one’s spouse and live chastely and devoutly, so that these holy days may be spent with heart and body sanctified, and thus one may arrive at holy Easter. For a fast that is defiled by marital intercourse and not commended by prayers, vigils, and almsgiving is worth almost nothing. [Col. 0205A–B]

### XLIV. Concerning holy Communion: how and how frequently it should be received

The people must be admonished not to approach the most sacred sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood carelessly, nor to abstain from it excessively. Rather, each person should carefully choose a time when he will abstain for a while from marital intercourse, cleanse himself from vices, adorn himself with virtues, devote himself to almsgiving and prayers, and then approach so great a sacrament.

For just as it is dangerous for anyone impure to approach so great a sacrament, so it is also dangerous to abstain from it for a prolonged period. This is without prejudice to those who have been excommunicated and receive Communion not whenever they wish but at designated times, and to any devout persons living holy lives who do this almost every day. [Col. 0205B–C]

### XLV. That on Sundays the people should not be drawn away from the public Masses by private Masses

The Masses that priests celebrate privately on Sundays must not be celebrated so publicly that through them the people are drawn away from the public solemn Masses, which are canonically celebrated at the third hour. For some have a very bad custom: on Sundays or on any feast days, as soon as they hear that a Mass is being celebrated—even if it is for the dead—they leave, so that throughout the entire day, from early morning onward, they may serve drunkenness and gluttony rather than God. [Col. 0205C–D]

### XLVI. That all should assemble at the mother church to hear the solemn Mass and the preacher, and should not eat before the service has been completed

[Col. 0206A]

The people must be admonished not to take food before the public service has been completed, but all should assemble at the holy mother church to hear the solemn Mass and the preaching. Priests must in no way celebrate Masses in chapels before the second hour unless they do so with such care that the people are not drawn away from the public solemnities.

Rather, priests who are in the environs of the city or in the city itself, as well as the people, should assemble together, as we have said, for the public celebration of Mass, except for women consecrated to God, whose custom is not to go out in public but to remain within the cloisters of the monastery. [Col. 0206A–B]

[Note: [Col. 0205D] Cardinal Baronius was the first to publish these canons of Theodulf. Since he had no certain knowledge of the time in which they were written, he assigned them to the year of Christ 835, considerably later than was appropriate. For Jonas, his successor in the see of Orléans, shows that Theodulf did not live to those times: Jonas was sent by Louis the Pious to Pope Eugenius after the synod of Paris in the year 824. Although we likewise had no certain information about the year, it nevertheless seemed more suitable to refer them to this period, which lay nearer to the beginning of Theodulf’s pontificate. Alcuin’s letter to King Charles shows that during these years, and before the Council of Frankfurt, Theodulf was already a bishop.]

[Note: [Col. 0206D] What follows, since it was later revised and reprinted at the end of Theodulf’s works in Sirmond’s edition, we bring back here. EDITOR.]

Beloved brothers, most holy fellow priests, and helpers in our ministry: with humble spirit I beseech you, in the presence of our Lord Jesus Christ and his saints, to serve God worthily in all religious devotion, charity, and chastity, and to be teachers and guides of God’s people in every good example, so that God’s people may be instructed both through your holy conduct and through your devoted preaching, to the praise and glory of the holy name of our Lord Jesus Christ and for the eternal salvation of your souls.

Conduct yourselves before God and before all the people in bodily chastity and humility of soul, and show holy charity toward everyone, doing nothing by which the priesthood of your holiness may become blameworthy, nor allowing anything to be found in your life that anyone could justly criticize.

Let your conduct be without evil desire, without avarice, without feasting and drunkenness, as befits God’s holy priests, who are to preside over God’s people and govern the churches of Christ.

Learn the Catholic faith, preach it most diligently, and preach it to the people, each one in his own church. Perform your offices at the appointed times for the honor of almighty God, so that almighty God may be honored and his holy name praised by all who see you honorably exercising your priesthood and service to almighty God.

Preach worthily to the people that they should confess their sins and receive penance, since they cannot obtain forgiveness of their offenses from God unless they make a pure confession and perform just penance, and abstain from the sins they previously committed. For this is true penance and the surest pardon: that a person not commit again the offenses for which he sought forgiveness.

Let them abstain from fornication. Those who have women should use them lawfully at the appointed times, honor their women, and preserve the trust of chastity toward their wives, just as they wish their wives to preserve it toward them.

Let them educate the sons and daughters they have in the fear of God and in holiness, so that they are not thieves, robbers, or fornicators, and do not commit any other uncleanness in their bodies to satisfy lust. Let them be obedient to their parents in every good thing, so that they may be worthy to receive a blessing from the Lord.

Preach to everyone that they should love truth, be kind to the poor, strangers, and the wretched, and, from the substance God has given them, not only refrain from taking what belongs to others but also generously give what is their own.

If they wish to have God’s blessing, let them not give false testimony and not commit perjury, because God condemns false and wicked witnesses forever. [Col. 0206B–0207B]

Admonish them to perform faithfully whatever they owe their masters in every labor and task assigned to them; to come more frequently to the churches, especially on feast days, for prayer and to hear the word of God; and not to remain there for prayer with idle words. Let them maintain among themselves pure and holy humility, patience, and charity, which is the head and foundation of every good thing.

Preach to them that there is one almighty God, creator of heaven and earth, who redeemed the world in his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and opened the kingdom of heaven to all the faithful, in which he will judge the world.

Preach to them about the future judgment and the everlasting punishments of the wicked; that they should confess and do penance for their sins, or abandon those sins.

Name the sins that blessed Paul, teacher of the nations, enumerated when he said: “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor perjurers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6:9–10).

Those who commit these or similar things, if they neglect to confess and do penance, will be condemned to eternal torments and flames with the devil. But those who desire to enter the kingdom of God should practice justice, mercy, truth, kindness, and obedience, and also almsgiving according to their means. Let them also practice fasting and prayers, possessing charity toward almighty God and doing good to every person as far as they can.

Let them live in chastity and piety, in humility, obedience, and good faith, and let them trust in God’s mercy, so that he may forgive them all their offenses and deign to grant them eternal joys with his saints. [Col. 0207B–D]

These things, most holy priests of Christ, summoned to eternal life with the holy bishops and apostles, preach to the people; and make yourselves worthy in all religion and chastity before almighty God, so that he may grant you, together with the abundant fruit of your labor, to receive the glory of eternal blessedness.

May almighty God cause you to advance in every good work, beloved brothers. [Col. 0207D–0208A]

## ADDITION TO THE CAPITULARY OF THEODULF

The two final chapters are combined into one in the Soissons manuscript, with additions beyond the published text. They are as follows:

It has been decreed that the Masses which priests celebrate privately on Sundays must not be celebrated so publicly that the people can hear them and thereby withdraw from the public solemn Masses, which are canonically celebrated at the third hour. For some have a very bad custom in this matter: on Sundays or on other solemn days, when they happen to seek out Masses—even Masses for the dead—or any other Masses celebrated privately by priests, they serve drunkenness, feasting, and idle chatter throughout the entire day from early morning rather than serving God.

Therefore provision must be made that all assemble at the public holy mother church to hear the solemn Mass and the preaching. It has also been decreed that, in the city where the bishop is established, all the presbyters and people, both of the city and of the suburbs, should stand in that Mass, clothed in their vestments, with devoted minds until the bishop’s blessing and Communion; afterward, if they wish, they may return to their own titular churches with permission, having received the blessing and Communion.

The priests must take the greatest care never to presume to celebrate Masses in chapels, suburban monasteries, or suburban churches before the second hour, and then only with the doors open and with such caution that the people cannot, on that account, withdraw from the public solemnities, from the Mass, or from the bishop’s preaching. Rather, all the suburban priests and those established in the city, together with the entire people, should assemble, as we have said, for the public celebration of Mass.

No one, except little children and the sick, whether in the cities or in the parishes, may presume to eat or drink before the public service has been completed, even if he has already heard Mass. If anyone attempts to transgress these statutes, he is to be subjected to canonical judgment until satisfaction has been made. [Col. 0208A–D]

[Col. 0207]

## THEODULF’S CAPITULARY TO THE SAME RECIPIENTS

(Baluze, *Miscellanea*, volume II, page 99.)

[Col. 0207D] From the first fall of humanity, in which the good of nature, as though the very root of the human race, was corrupted, the seedbed of vices implanted in nature has continued to sprout. Hence it comes about that we learn with difficulty and forget without difficulty, rise with difficulty to the virtues, and easily slip into vices.

Therefore, beloved priests, we must strive with every watchfulness of mind to apply labor in learning and to devote practice to retaining what we have learned—especially we who hold a place in governance and those similar to us in this order.

Accordingly, priests of the Lord, we admonish you both to retain the Catholic faith by heart and to understand it in your hearts; that is, “I believe,” and, “Whoever wishes to be saved must, before all things, hold the Catholic faith.”

All the priests of the Lord must be examined as to whether they know the canon of the Mass and the Secret—or “Therefore, O Lord”—by heart and distinguish them properly; whether they recite the names of the dead and the living in their proper places, in an orderly manner and with complete devotion; whether they properly perform baptism and can pronounce the correct words; and whether, through negligence in baptizing the sick, they presume to baptize a healthy person under the pretext of illness, except on the appointed days of Easter and Pentecost.

They must be admonished not to demand anything for the ministry of baptism, either from those being baptized or from their parents—not the smallest gift and absolutely no price—but to perform it with thanksgiving and the greatest devotion. If, however, their parents, or those who receive them from the sacred font, wish to give you some gift freely and without compulsion, accept it without hesitation. [Col. 0208D–0209B]

Priests must likewise be instructed and admonished to understand that the tithes and offerings they receive from the faithful are the support of strangers and the poor, and that they are not to use them as their own but as entrusted goods. They must know that they will have to render an account concerning all these things and suffer condemnation.

As for how they should be distributed, the sacred canons establish that they should be divided into four parts: one to assist in maintaining the church building, another to be distributed to the poor, a third to be held by the presbyter with his clerics, and a fourth reserved for the bishop, so that whatever he orders may be carried out through prudent counsel. [Col. 0209B–C]

It must be forbidden and emphatically enjoined in every way that no priest, deacon, or subdeacon keep in his house women of the kind specified in the canon, concerning whom suspicion could arise; indeed, they should not keep even those whom the canons permit, because, at the devil’s instigation, a crime is frequently committed even with such women, or with their female attendants.

Therefore we do not permit a mother, aunt, or sister to continue living in the same house with a priest. But if anyone has among these a woman in such need that she requires the support of a presbyter, deacon, or subdeacon, he should have her live in a house in a village or estate far from the presbyter’s daily association, where he can provide her with what is necessary. [Col. 0209C–D]

This too must be prohibited in every way according to the authority of the canons: when Mass is being celebrated, no woman may presume to approach the altar, assist the presbyter, or stand or sit within the chancel. [Col. 0209D]

They must be admonished that on Sundays each priest should, according to his ability and understanding, deliver a sermon of preaching to his people. First, he should admonish the people to love one another and to possess fraternal charity; to love the Lord more than themselves and their neighbor as themselves; then to abstain from every evil deed; not to do to others what they do not wish done to themselves; and to do for others what they wish people to do for them. [Col. 0209D–0210A]

Then, if the Lord grants understanding, let the priest tell them as much as he can of what he truly understands from the Gospel and from the Epistle of Saint Paul. Let him admonish them to hasten frequently to the church, faithfully offer their oblations, and make confession to God and to priests.

Let there be no one among them who has not confessed adultery, incest, or fornication with women, males, or beasts; let them not consent among themselves [the wording is unclear]. But if anyone among them has fallen into these crimes, let them correct him and have him make amendment publicly with his priest. [Col. 0210A–B]

With these and other matters, as far as he can, let him instruct his people on each Sunday.

Let him also admonish them that on every Saturday night and every Sunday, together with the nights following them, and likewise on solemnities and fasts, they should abstain from carnal pleasure, so that they may approach the church pure in body and heart and not presume to defile the solemnity with the impurity of pleasure. [Col. 0210B]

According to canonical authority, the priests of the Lord must be commanded not to demand any gift for burials or for burying people, unless the person being buried, while alive, ordered that something from his possessions be given to the church in whose atrium he is buried, or unless, after his death, those entrusted with distributing his alms freely wish to give something from his possessions.

Nevertheless, the presbyters must in no way demand anything from them, nor from those who preside over the places and villages, nor from those whose possession the church itself is, whether by hereditary or benefice right. [Col. 0210B–C]

It must also be prohibited, according to the ordinances of the elders, that they be buried anywhere inside the church; rather, they are to be buried in the atrium, portico, or outer hall of the church. Within the church itself, near the altar where the Lord’s body and blood are consecrated, they must under no circumstances be permitted to bury anyone.

If a presbyter keeps an adulterous man or woman in his house and—what is forbidden—consents to adultery being committed in his house, he must know that he is to be deprived of the honor of his rank. [Col. 0210D] But if he discovers this in the people entrusted to him, and does not immediately correct it, if he has the strength to do so, but consents to the adulterers either out of fear of their power or for the sake of benefit, profit, or friendship with them, then, when the matter has been exposed, he is to be excommunicated. If, however, he excommunicates the offender as far as he can and is unable to prevent that evil, he has freed his own soul. Nevertheless, he must report the matter with every diligence to his archdeacon, and the archdeacon to the bishop.

Incestuous relations must be diligently investigated by priests through truthful men who keep the fear of God before their eyes. If such a thing is discovered, they must immediately strive either to correct it themselves or, with the assistance of the archdeacon or bishop, endeavor to correct and eradicate it, lest they be polluted and perish through so great a crime and incur the wrath of almighty God through the proximity of others. [Col. 0211A]

Priests must be admonished and instructed that they themselves should first be free from every incitement of the flesh, and that they should preach this both in words to the peoples subject to them and demonstrate it by their example: they must abstain from all fornication and from every irrational lust and pollution, such as that of animals. They must prepare themselves pure in body and mind before God to receive and judge the confessions of the faithful, using gentle counsel. For although the time of penance must be established in proportion to the measure and extent of the sin—long or short, strict or mild, or moderate—for the priest when he receives the confession of any of the faithful, yet he must consider whether the sin was committed once, or repeated afterward, or committed frequently; whether it was done willingly or under compulsion, through drunkenness, or by any other device. When he discovers from what source the root of that sin arose, he must then apply an appropriate remedy. [Col. 0211B]

But the manner in which the remedy for sin is to be applied must be according to the canons and the authoritative teachings of the holy Fathers, and not according to human preference or will. In this matter the will or favor of any person is not to be pursued; rather, the will of God must be sought in all things in the Holy Scriptures, so that the vengeance of almighty God, provoked by human fault, may be appeased through worthy prayers and fitting repentance.

The people must be admonished concerning penance in this manner, since it is often evident that, through the weakness of our nature, we are inclined toward vices, although provision has been made for us through Christ’s Passion, so that what the deserts of sin demanded might be redeemed by Christ’s Passion. And although we are washed in holy baptism, granted for the remission of all sins through saving ordinances, nevertheless, because we cannot pass through the course of this life without the turmoil of vices, nor lead a life free from the stain of sin while the offenses of our weakness continually creep upon us, [Col. 0211C] the most merciful goodness of God has granted the remedy of true confession and the washing away of sins through penance. The Lord declares through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live.” And the Gospel says: “Produce fruits worthy of repentance.” The Apostle says: “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another, so that you may be saved.”

There is indeed fruitful penance in true confession: not admitting sins that ought to be repented of; mourning with contrition of heart those that have been committed; cutting away, through genuine penitential satisfaction, the causes of sin; allowing no access to their suggestions; and not falling again into the vices once committed. [Col. 0211D]

Capital and mortal crimes must be publicly mourned according to the institution of the canons and the holy Fathers. Yet we do not deny that mortal crimes may also be absolved through secret satisfaction, provided that the intention of the mind is first changed and worldly boasting is laid aside at the same time, while the penitent submits himself through correction of life and continual—indeed perpetual—mourning, with a devout and religious confession. Nevertheless, no one should despair of the mercy and boundless goodness of almighty God, because it is written: “On whatever day the sinner turns from the error of his way and turns away from evil deeds, all his iniquities will be forgotten.” [Col. 0212A]

The measure of penance depends upon the priest’s judgment. The priest, carefully examining and understanding the ordinances of the holy Fathers, must impose penance upon those who confess according to their authority. The authority of the canons and the institution of the holy Fathers is indeed most firm.

If anyone commits homicide voluntarily or by ambush, he must submit himself to continual penance. If it is established that the act was public, then, if he is a layman, he must lay down his weapons and abandon all secular military service, and make public satisfaction, so that for forty days he prays outside the church, at the door. After completing those days on bread and water, he is to be excluded from communion in the prayers for five years. After five years he is to be admitted only to communion in prayer; he must not offer, nor touch the Lord’s body at all. Remaining in this condition for fourteen years, he is then to be received into full communion with the prayers. Near the end of his life he is to receive this consideration: he may receive the Eucharist as viaticum. His abstinence is to be left to the priest’s judgment; according to the person and his ability, abstinence from foods is to be imposed upon him. If the matter is secret, he is likewise to act secretly, as prescribed above. [Col. 0212B]

Whoever commits homicide accidentally and unwillingly was formerly assigned seven years of penance with exclusion from communion, according to the established degrees. But this definition of the Council of Ancyra assigns five years of penance: he is to stand outside at the church door for forty days. After these have been completed, he is to be separated for two years from the prayer of the other faithful; he must neither communicate nor offer. After two years he is to be received into communion in prayer and may offer, but he must not communicate. After five years he is to be received into full communion. Abstinence from food is to remain at the priest’s discretion; according to the person and character of the individual, so also shall be the measure and duration of abstinence. [Col. 0212C]

If someone, while traveling along a road, whether in his own house, in the street of a city, or in a village, is suddenly attacked by another or becomes involved in a quarrel, and, wishing to defend himself, kills a man without previously having hatred against him, he must do penance for seven years according to the institution of the canons. He is to be deprived of communion for three years; for four years he is to be received into communion in prayers and offerings. It will depend upon the priest’s judgment whether he is worthy to receive the body of Christ or must be separated from it until the completion of his penance. Abstinence from food is to be determined by the priest’s prudence, according to the penitent’s ability, devotion, and disposition to shed tears. [Col. 0212D]

Women who fornicate and kill their children, or act so as to expel what has been conceived in the womb, were formerly removed from the church until the end of their lives. More humanely, however, they are now subjected, according to the definition of the Council of Ancyra, to ten years of penance, so that they pray outside at the church door for forty days. After these have been completed, they are removed for four years from communion with the faithful and from offerings. Then, received into communion in prayer, they complete the ten-year period and, out of consideration for human weakness, may receive the Eucharist after completing their penance. [Col. 0213A] It nevertheless remains to the priest’s discretion whether they should approach the body of Christ before completing their penance, according to whether he sees them contrite, consumed with tears, and possessed of great devotion. Abstinence from food is to be entrusted to the priest’s care, according to how he sees them repenting and according to the condition of their persons.

A woman who has married two brothers must be rejected until the day of her death. But out of consideration for human weakness, she ought to be reconciled to the sacraments at the point of death, provided that the marriage is first dissolved and she remains unmarried; and her husband must likewise undergo corresponding penance without a wife.

If two brothers have fornicated with one woman, [Col. 0213B] neither knowing of the other’s fornication, as soon as they learn of the adultery, the one who has her as his wife must dismiss her. After completing his penance, if the wife has died, he may be joined to another; while she is alive, he may not. She, however, may never afterward be taken in marriage, and, having been subjected to continual penance, she is to receive the grace of communion at the end of her life.

A woman who has suffocated her son while sleeping, and he has died, must do penance for six years. Her husband, if he was in her house, must do penance for four years. If he was in the same bed and acted in the same way, he must do penance for two years on bread and water; for the remaining four years the priest is to impose abstinence upon them according to what he sees them capable of. Likewise, a married man who has committed adultery must do penance; after three years he may communicate.

[Col. 0213C] [Note: [Col. 0213D] Council of Nantes, chapter 12.] If someone’s wife commits adultery, and this is discovered and made public by her husband, he may dismiss his wife, if he wishes, on account of fornication. She, however, is to do penance according to what has been inserted above. Her husband, while she is alive, has absolutely no permission to take another wife. Or, if he wishes, he may have permission to reconcile the adulteress to himself, provided that he and she do penance together and, once the penance has been completed, approach the grace of communion as prescribed above. The same rule is to be observed in the case of a woman. If her husband commits adultery against her, she has the power to dismiss her husband on account of fornication, but must remain unmarried as long as her husband lives, because neither does he have power to take another wife while the first is alive, nor may she marry another man while the first is still alive. [Col. 0213D] Nevertheless, they have the power to reconcile themselves to one another.

If an unmarried woman or an unmarried man commits fornication, they must do penance for five years.

If an unmarried man commits adultery with another man’s wife, or an unmarried woman with another woman’s husband, both are adulterers, and they must do penance according to what is contained and prescribed above.

If anyone commits theft, he must do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. The measure of penance is to correspond to the character of the theft. If he committed the theft out of necessity, the penance is to be lightened. For Solomon says: “It is not a great fault when someone has stolen”; for “he steals in order to fill the hungry soul.”

Whoever commits perjury must likewise do penance for seven years.

Whoever gives false testimony, and his testimony harms someone, must do penance for seven years, provided that the person who gave the testimony restores all the damage to the one whom his false testimony harmed. Only then can he attain pardon through penance. If he refuses to do this, he must know that he is performing his penance in vain.

Those who behave irrationally are to be dealt with according to what is contained in the canons, in the title where there are Greek words translated into Latin, from the Council of Ancyra, chapter 16. Its meaning is threefold: concerning those who have intercourse with animals; those who, like animals, commit incest with relatives; and those who have intercourse with males.

Therefore, all who committed such a crime before their twentieth year are, after completing fifteen years of penance, to begin participating only in the prayers. After remaining for another five years in simple communion, they are to be received into communion with offerings after twenty years [of penance]. Their conduct during the period of penance must also be examined, and they are to receive this leniency accordingly. If any, persisting in these crimes, require a longer period of submission, such persons can never be advanced to the priesthood.

All who have fallen into these crimes after completing twenty years of age, including those who have wives, are, after doing penance for twenty-five years, to be received only into communion in prayer. After remaining another five years, they are to be received into full communion with offerings. If married men who are over fifty years of age have sinned in these matters, they are to merit communion only at the end of their lives. [Col. 0214C]

Those, however, who have lived like dumb animals and have contaminated themselves and others with the defilement of this kind of sin—that is, with relatives, animals, or males—must, during the appointed period of penance, stand and pray only among those who are thrown to the ground by lunar madness and tormented by an unclean spirit, that is, among the possessed. Just as it is more abominable to have intercourse with an animal than with a male, so an irrational crime with a male is worse than with a woman. To sin with a female relative and with a nun is an equal crime. The law of Moses judges it worthy of death: those who have intercourse with an animal, a male, or a female relative.

It is an equal crime for a woman to sin with a woman as for a male to sin with a male, and the penance must be equal. Concerning such people the Apostle says: “Their women exchanged natural use for that which is against nature. Likewise the males, abandoning natural use of the female, burned in their desires for one another, males committing shameful acts with males.” [Col. 0215A]

What we said above applies to those who have come publicly to confession and have performed public penance. But if the act was secret, and they came secretly to the priest and made a pure confession, they are to do penance secretly according to the measure of their age as prescribed above. Thus, if someone did this before the age of twenty, or through ignorance, or perhaps did not know that it was such a crime, he is to be dealt with more leniently; this is to depend upon the priest’s judgment. The priest must investigate how he fell into this crime and for how long he remained involved in it. According to what he confesses, the measure of penance is to be applied to him.

If he did this once or twice through ignorance—that is, with a male, an animal, or a female relative—and, as soon as he learned that it was a grave crime, abandoned it, then, to speak more humanely, he must do penance for seven years, abstain from meat for three years, and not communicate for one year, not even on Easter Day, nor offer. He must submit himself wholeheartedly so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. For the remaining period, according to the measure of his weakness, he is to practice abstinence from food at the priest’s discretion. [Col. 0215B]

But if he remained longer in this crime and, after being warned that the offense was a great sin, committed it again and again, he is to do penance as prescribed above. First, he is to be separated from all communion for five years; after those fifteen years, he must neither offer nor communicate in prayer, nor enter the church with the other Christians. When these years have been completed, he is to be received only into communion in prayer. Then, after completing twenty years of penance, if he has performed his penance well, with tears and complete devotion, he is to be received into full communion and reconciliation. The same rule is to be observed concerning the other periods specified above.

If, God forbid, someone has committed such a crime in holy places, his penance is to be doubled. In Scripture, the crime is called “the worst” whether it is with an animal, a male, or a female relative. To have intercourse unnaturally with a woman is called uncleanness, or a detestable sin; thus Onan, the son of Judah, was struck by God because, having entered a woman, he spilled his seed upon the ground. [Col. 0215D]

Uncleanness is also called softness, whether it arises through touch, sight, or remembrance of a woman, so that some pleasure occurs while one is awake, or when someone exercises impurity alone with himself or with another between his thighs. Concerning these the Apostle Paul says: “The unclean shall not possess the kingdom of God.” Again: “Let no uncleanness even be named among you.” And elsewhere: “The soft shall not possess the kingdom of God.” Whoever falls into these practices must do penance as for a crime that excludes one from the kingdom of God.

If a presbyter commits adultery, whether it is exposed and publicly known, he must cease from the priestly order and be cleansed through ten years of public penance. But if he commits it secretly and comes secretly to confession, secret penance is to be imposed upon him. It is to be left to his own judgment whether he ought to cease from that ministry or whether, remaining in it, he can thereafter offer the Lord worthy satisfaction. [Col. 0216A] If he washes himself daily with tears and prayers in the deepest devotion and strives to extinguish his sins through the giving of alms, then, if the matter is secret, he may remain secretly in his rank and perform penance. If he commits fornication, he is to be cleansed in the same manner for seven years. If he has fallen into sodomy—that is, with a male—he is to be expiated in the same manner for fifteen years.

The same rule is to be observed concerning deacons and those established in the sacred orders, as follows: a deacon is to do penance for seven years for adultery, five years for fornication, and ten years for a sodomitical act; for adultery, five years, for fornication, three years, and for a sodomitical act, seven years. Such observance is to be maintained according to the stated degrees, up to the lowest ecclesiastical rank.

No one should excuse himself on the basis of what the Apostle Paul says: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife.” They must know that this was said only concerning those established in the lay order or those who have not yet entered the subdiaconate. For the canons in no way permit anyone to enter the subdiaconate unless he has promised that he will henceforth observe perpetual continence and chastity.

The priests of the Jews, indeed, were commanded by the Lord through Moses to take wives; and priests came from no tribe except Levi, so that one lineage might be preserved through succession. [Col. 0216C] Now, however, people from all nations are permitted to approach the priesthood just as they are permitted to approach baptism. There is no necessity for them to take wives, since they are appointed to the priesthood not through succession of the flesh but through imitation of conduct.

Even the Jewish priests themselves, although they did not have such a holy sacrifice as we have, during the period of their service remained far from their homes and, removed from conjugal relations, kept watch in chastity beside the Temple until they had completed the time of their ministry. Now, since priests must always minister, they must likewise always remain continent. For they handle not the victims of animals but the very immaculate body and blood of the Lord.
