Deacons and subdeacons likewise approach the altar in the Lord as ministers of the handling of so great a sacrament, and must observe the same continence. [Col. 0216D]

To laymen, however, and to those who do not approach the ministry of the altar, the Apostle gives this command: those who cannot remain continent should marry, “for it is better to marry than to burn.” That is, it is better to take a lawful wife than to burn through acts of fornication, adultery, sodomy, or uncleanness.

Presbyters must be admonished to show a holy example to their subjects by maintaining mutual charity among themselves, far from all arrogance of pride and the bitterness of envy, both to the clergy and to the laity. They must not be rapacious, greedy, drunkards, insolent, quarrelsome, or calumniators of anyone; rather, they must guard themselves irreproachably in all things and provide the clergy and the peoples with a pattern of salvation, so that those who advance toward eternal life and upright conduct through their example may be raised up by humility. [Col. 0217A]

They must also be admonished never to practice usury, and they must preach to the peoples subject to them and to the clergy that they abstain from this vice in every way, according to the institution of the canons. Whoever, by any device, receives more than he gives must know that he has practiced usury. For if someone lends wheat or another kind of grain and does not receive the same kind in return, but either receives money in the amount for which it could have been sold at the time he lent it, or receives something else, he has unquestionably committed usury.

If anyone from the clerical order presumes to do this, he must know that he will incur the danger of losing his rank. If he is a layman, he must know that he is to be excommunicated. Therefore it is fitting that, first, all those established in the clerical order abstain from these practices and strictly enjoin upon the peoples that no one dare do such a thing at all. [Col. 0217B]

When a priest receives the confession of the faithful, among other things he must admonish the person confessing to make confession concerning the eight principal vices, promise amendment, and accept penance as medicine for his soul. He must ask about the names of the eight principal vices one by one, as they are listed, and the penitent must confess and make confession concerning all of them, as stated above. Then the remedy of penance is to be applied to him.

The eight principal vices, without which scarcely anyone can be found, are these:

1. First, *gastrimargia*, that is, gluttony of the belly.
2. Second, fornication.
3. Third, acedia or sadness.
4. Fourth, avarice.
5. Fifth, vainglory.
6. Sixth, envy.
7. Seventh, anger.
8. Eighth, pride. [Col. 0217C]

If the priest sees that someone is ashamed and blushes to confess and disclose the sins he has committed, he should admonish him, saying:

“My brother, the Lord frequently exhorts us to the remedies of true confession—not because God needs our confession, since he knows everything we do, say, and think. But we cannot be saved in any other way unless, in repentance, we confess whatever we have done through negligence. The devil grieves when someone confesses his sins and desires us to conceal what we have done; for the one who accuses himself of his sins the devil cannot accuse again on the day of judgment, provided that the person confessing washes away through repentance what he has done and does not renew what he has committed.

“Therefore the Apostle James says: ‘Confess your sins to one another.’ Paul says: ‘With the mouth confession is made unto salvation.’ Solomon says: ‘Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper; but whoever confesses and abandons them will obtain mercy.’ The evangelist John likewise says: ‘If you confess your sins, God is faithful and just to forgive you your sins and cleanse you from all iniquity.’ The Psalmist similarly says: ‘I said, “I will declare my transgressions against myself to the Lord,” and you forgave the iniquity of my sin.’

“But it must be understood that this great medicine of salvation does not consist in repeating impious deeds, nor in reopening earlier scars with new wounds.” [Col. 0218A]

In the first week before the beginning of Lent, confession must be made concerning all sins committed either in deed or in speech. The priest must then name to them individually the eight principal vices mentioned above.

The first is gluttony, by which the devil deceived Adam and by which he tempted Christ when he said: “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.” It is to be healed through abstinence.

The second principal vice is fornication, concerning which Solomon says: “A prostitute is a deep pit and a narrow well.” The same teacher says: “Who is stronger than Samson? Who is wiser than Solomon?” Yet this man was deceived by women’s sons, and the vice is to be healed by chastity.

The third principal vice is acedia, that is, instability of place. It does not allow a person to persevere in what is good. It is to be healed through perseverance in good work, because, as Gregory says, “he labors in vain at a good work if he abandons it before the end of life.” [Col. 0218B]

The fourth principal vice is avarice, through which the avaricious man becomes like hell. Nothing is more wicked than an avaricious man. This vice is to be healed through generous almsgiving, because just as avarice plunges a person into hell, so generosity customarily raises him to heaven.

The fifth principal vice is vainglory. It is deprived of every good work; for just as a stone thrown upward does not reach heaven, so prayer accompanied by vainglory does not reach God. This vice is to be healed by love of God.

The sixth principal vice is envy, concerning which Solomon says: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world.” It is to be healed by charity. Charity does not envy; it bears all things.

The seventh principal vice is anger, concerning which Christ says: “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment.” Paul says: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger. Give no place to the devil.” And again: “Do not defend yourselves, but give place to wrath.” It is to be healed by patience: “Blessed are the peacemakers,” says the Lord, “for they shall be called sons of God.” And again: “Love your enemies; do good to those who persecute you and slander you.” And elsewhere: “In your patience you shall possess your souls.”

Sadness itself is not properly the same as anger. Sadness belongs to acedia; worldly sadness produces death. Evil sadness produces despair and instability of place. Hence the person afflicted with acedia is called sad. The Apostles were not angry, but they were sad. Their sadness was turned into joy. Sadness, or acedia, which is the vice mentioned above, is to be healed by spiritual joy. [Col. 0218D]

The eighth principal vice is pride, concerning which Christ says: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.” Solomon says: “Where there is pride, there will be disgrace.” Jesus, son of Sirach, says: “Pride is hateful before God and human beings.” Augustine says: “Why such great pride in us—the pride that deceived the angels? How much more does it desire to plunge human beings down with itself?” Thus the angels became demons. Just as pride is the origin of all crimes, so it is the ruin of all virtues.

Saint Gregory says: “A rotten fruit is useless to farmers, and the fruit of the proud is useless to the Lord.” Just as the weight of fruit breaks a branch, so pride overturns the beauty of souls. Pride cast down the archangel and made him fall like lightning. [Col. 0219A] It is to be healed by humility, because through humility human beings are made equal to the angels.

Unless someone cleanses these eight principal vices and those that arise from their roots here through confession and penance, they cannot be cleansed on the day of judgment; rather, they lead people into hell. Why is a person ashamed to confess, when he was not ashamed to be defiled by sins? Through confession what is contracted by sinning is washed away. How can a physician heal a wound that the sick person is ashamed to show? The sinner is the sick person; the wise priest is the physician.

Whoever confesses should kneel with the priest before God, and then confess whatever he can remember from his youth, concerning all the ways in which he has acted. If he cannot remember all his crimes, or perhaps is ashamed, the priest must ask him about whatever is prescribed in the penitential book, whether he has fallen into that or another crime. Nevertheless, he must not disclose all crimes to him, because many vices are recited in the penitential book that it is not fitting for a person to know. Therefore the priest must not question him about everything, lest, after leaving him, he fall—at the devil’s suggestion—into one of the crimes of which he was previously unaware. [Col. 0219B]

After he has confessed all his sins, the priest must make him recite the Creed, forgive all who have sinned against him, promise amendment to God, and not return again to those sins. When he has done all this, the priest shall consider the gravity of his offenses and impose upon him a period of penance according to their measure. Then he shall recite over him the seven penitential psalms with the prayers found in the sacramentary, and absolve him in peace. [Col. 0219C]

It must also be understood that if any bishop has been defiled by one of the eight principal vices, he must do penance for fourteen years; a presbyter, twelve; a deacon, eight; a cleric, six; and a layman, four.

A woman who kills her own child must do penance for fourteen years. If she kills her son, she must do penance for fifteen years. If she kills him in the womb before birth, she must do penance for seven years. If an infant dies without baptism, its parents must do penance for one full year and must never be without some form of penance.

There are certain sins which, as Isidore says, can be cleansed by purgatorial fire. These include excess in eating and drinking, sleeping, talking, and being slow to visit the sick, to come to church, or to give alms; sudden anger that is not retained in the heart; and drunkenness, if it is not frequent. Anger that remains in the heart, however, generates hatred and desires revenge, and is counted among the principal vices. [Col. 0219D]

Some have said that the following are lesser sins: a minor act of perjury, if it is not habitual; speaking while joking or becoming angry; theft of a small thing; marrying a wife whom one has polluted in sleep; striking a person so that blood flows; amputating a person’s limb so that he does not die; having intercourse with one’s wife on Sunday or on days when it is not permitted; violating the graves of the dead in order to build a house there; neglecting the sacrifice, so that one does not perform it with the diligence required; drinking a magical potion or an unclean substance; lending at usury; taking small possessions belonging to others; committing sacrilege in small matters, that is, stealing something from a church, or stealing or defrauding ecclesiastical money; burning a house without causing great damage; making others drunk for the sake of amusement; and eating carrion, that is, an animal killed by a beast or bird, or one that died of disease.

For these and similar offenses, a bishop is to do penance for seven weeks, a presbyter for five, a deacon for four, a subdeacon for three, a cleric for two, and a layman for one. If a greater crime is found among these matters or others, the measure of penance is either to be increased or lightened according to the seriousness or assessment of the sin. Whoever hates his brother must live on bread and water for as long a period as he has maintained that hatred. [Col. 0220B]

Priests must also be admonished concerning the anointing of the sick, penance, and viaticum, so that no one dies without viaticum. If someone seeks penance during illness, and, when the priest comes to him, it happens that he has been deprived of the use of speech, it has been established that suitable men who have been with him from the beginning of his illness should give true testimony concerning what they heard from him while he was able to speak—whether about penance, shaving his beard, or entering the monastic life. Then, once informed, the priest must complete the ministry toward him, impose his penance upon him through his guarantors, and have them fulfill it on his behalf.

If a bishop is so ill that he may be anointed, and no other bishop is present to perform the ministry of anointing for him, a presbyter is permitted to consecrate him through the ministry of anointing. For in the earliest period of the Apostles’ preaching there was no distinction between bishops and presbyters; nor would there still be one, had many presbyters not taught different and contradictory things on account of the dissensions of heretics. [Col. 0220C]

First, let penance be given to the sick person. Then, if his illness permits it, after his body has been washed, let him be dressed in white garments, carried into the church, and lie there on sackcloth with ashes spread over it. Let a cross and blessed water be brought there, so that when they have come to him—namely, three presbyters—they may say the chapter:

“Peace to this house and to all who dwell in it. Peace to those entering and departing, in the name of the Lord.”

Then let the priest pour consecrated oil into the blessed water and sprinkle it, saying the antiphon:

“Bless, O Lord, this house and all who dwell in it, for you, O Lord, have said: ‘Peace to this house,’” etc. “Bless, O Lord, those who fear you, the small together with the great. You are blessed by the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

And again let him say the antiphon:

“You shall sprinkle me, O Lord, with hyssop,” etc.

After the prayer has been said, let him place consecrated ashes on the sick person’s head and breast in the form of a cross, saying:

“By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread until you return to the earth from which you were taken. You are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

Then let them begin the seven penitential psalms on his behalf. If he is able, let the sick person stand with bent knees and bowed head, or prostrate himself with his whole body.

After the litany and prayer have been said, let him begin the anointing, while the others sing suitable psalms and an antiphon. Let him make twelve signs of the cross with oil over him, as follows: first, a large cross between the shoulders, extending up to the neck and transversely across to the shoulders, with a prayer; then on the neck up to the nape; the third over the head up to the forehead, transversely from ear to ear; then the fourth and fifth on the faculty of sight, that is, on the eyebrows of the eyes; the sixth on the faculty of smell, that is, on the nose or nostrils; the seventh on the faculty of taste, that is, on the lips; the eighth and ninth crosses on the faculty of hearing, that is, on the outer parts of the ears; the tenth on the throat; the eleventh on the breast; the twelfth and thirteenth on the faculty of touch, that is, on the outside of each hand; and the remaining two on the feet.

We make this number of fifteen crosses with holy oil over the sick person because of the mystery of the Trinity and the significance of the five senses. For three times five makes fifteen. And since it has more often been customary to sanctify through an odd number, some wish to make twenty crosses over the sick person; others, according to the unclear printed phrase *ex quatuor*, make them as follows: three between the shoulders, three over the shoulders, three on the neck, nape, and brain; three on the forehead and eyebrows; three on the nostrils and lips; two on the ears; two on the throat and breast; two on the hands; and two on the feet. Some add two on the temples and make two on the inner parts of the hands. Some say that no cross of oil ought to be made on the forehead of anyone or on the inner parts of the priest’s hands. Nevertheless, it does no harm.

For a bishop places not the oil of the sick but chrism on the foreheads of all the baptized and on the hands of priests. Indeed, before baptism the presbyter touches the breast and the space between the shoulders of the baptized, making a cross with exorcised oil, not with the oil of the sick. Therefore, we see no harm in touching these same places during the anointing of the sick with the oil of the sick.

The apostles, however, when anointing the sick with oil, made no more than three crosses with oil over them. Hence the Greeks, who imitate that very apostolic tradition, likewise make only three crosses with oil, pouring the oil of the sick from a flask in the form of a cross over the head, garments, and entire body of the sick person. They begin the cross at the head and extend it to the feet, transversely from the right hand to the arms, and across the breast to the left hand, saying once over those three crosses:

“I anoint you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, so that the prayer of faith may save you, and the Lord may raise you up; and if you are in sins, may they be forgiven you.”

Those garments drenched with oil are not buried with the sick person [so printed: *infirmandus*]. If he recovers, they are washed in a clean place, and he uses them again.

Such anointing is to be given not only to clerics but also to laypeople, and not only to men but also to women, if necessary, because we read that certain holy men anointed paralyzed girls with holy oil and healed them. We also read that possessed persons were anointed with holy oil and healed.

Therefore, if a sick person has become insane, nevertheless, in accordance with the Council of Orange, let every ministry of compassion be shown to him, including Communion itself, provided that in his soundness he had believed the Catholic faith. For it is written in that council:

“Let whatever belongs to compassion be bestowed upon the insane.” [Col. 0222A]

And rightly so: at the hour when someone suddenly becomes mute, he may be baptized or receive penance if there are reliable testimonies of his previous will. Thus, as long as life remains apparent in the sick person, he may be commended to all the ministries of compassion, even if testimony of his will is lacking.

Nevertheless, on the basis of the faith of his friends, every sacramental aid ought to be supplied to him, following the Gospel example in which Jesus, looking not to the faith of the paralytic but to that of those who carried him, said:

“Man, your sins are forgiven you.”

This must be observed in every case: after death, Communion of the Eucharist is [not] to be placed in a corpse’s mouth under any pretext of mercy, since the canons strongly prohibit this. Only penance may be received from friends on behalf of the dead after his death, if they possess such great charity.

Anointing is also necessary for children themselves, since we read that some holy men anointed children’s limbs with consecrated oil and restored them to their former health. For penance appears so necessary for children that we read that certain children, because of the merits of their sins, were handed over to the ministers of Satan and died without penance.

As we have already said, it is likewise permitted for presbyters to anoint bishops in illness, just as the Council of Carthage grants presbyters permission to confirm the faithful with chrism according to the custom of bishops, if they see someone in danger of death who has been confirmed with holy chrism by a bishop. Similarly, they are granted permission to reconcile penitents in danger of death. For presbyters, although they do not possess the summit of the episcopate, are nevertheless second to bishops. [Col. 0222C]

After the sick person has been anointed with the prayers prescribed above, let the priest instruct him to say the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, commend his spirit into the hands of God, fortify himself with the sign of the cross, and bid farewell to the living. Then let the priest give him the peace and communicate him, saying:

“May the body and blood of the Lord be for you the remission of all your sins, and may he preserve you unto eternal life.”

After the prayer has been said, at the end let the priest say:

“Let us bless the Lord.”

And let everyone answer:

“Thanks be to God.”

Then the rite is complete. On the following day, and for up to seven days, let the priest visit him and pour over him prayers appropriate to the occasion.

The priests must also be told that, whenever they impose the manner and duration of penance upon penitents, they should say these words to them:

“Brother, all penance is effective in this: to repent of past sins, to abstain from future sins, and to apply oneself diligently to labor, vigils, prayers, fasts, almsgiving, and the pardon of enemies. For God does not require long periods of penance, as it is said through the prophet: ‘When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved.’ And again: ‘Turn back to me, and I will return to you.’

“The merciful Lord does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live. And in the Gospel he says: ‘There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents more than over ninety-nine who have no need of repentance.’ And again: ‘On the day when the sinner turns before me, I will blot out all his iniquities.’

“See, therefore, my brother, by how many testimonies you have learned the remedies for sins, and know that you cannot merit pardon in any other way unless you have turned with your whole heart. Make for yourself, therefore, one burden out of all your sins, a burden that can never depart from your eyes, because continual prayer and constant groaning are more acceptable to God than long and lukewarm penance.”

Let the priest know, however, that he ought not to investigate the individual faults of those who confess. When he finds a greater one, he should judge the case according to it.

We have endeavored to say these things to you priests concerning the winning of Christ’s sheep, with the help of the Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever.

[Col. 0223]

THEODULF, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS  
[Note: Concerning the order of baptism. Of the four copies of this book that have come into my hands, three—those of Verdun, Dijon, and the Vatican—teach that the work was sent to Bishop Magnus; the fourth, the Corbie copy, has John in place of Magnus, erroneously, as I believe. There is indeed among us a short booklet by that same Magnus, bishop of Sens, *On the Mystery of Baptism*—for that is what he calls it—not yet published, addressed to the Emperor Charles, in which he testifies that he was impelled to write by royal command. There is also among the works of Alcuin a book *On Holy Baptism*, likewise addressed to the same Charles, assigned to Alcuin by a false conjecture because it lacked a title, although the author is actually Bishop Amalarius, as we learned from the Petavian manuscript. Indeed, the words read near the end of that book—“You have said, most serene Augustus, that you wished to know how we and our suffragans teach the people of God concerning the sacrament of baptism”—are such as cannot apply to Alcuin, who was not a bishop, but fit especially well with Bishop Amalarius of Trier.]  

A BOOK ON THE ORDER OF BAPTISM, ADDRESSED TO MAGNUS, BISHOP OF SENS.

[Col. 0223B]

Theodulf sends greetings to the most reverend and beloved brother Magnus, bishop.

I have carried out your command, venerable Magnus, and, if not with diligent effectiveness, at least with complete obedience. For you commanded me—or rather, through you charity commanded me—to respond briefly and quickly to certain questions concerning the order of baptism that the lord and glorious Emperor Charles had sent to you.

Thus, pressed on one side by brevity, which compelled me to dispatch great matters in a short discourse, and on the other by the narrowness of time, in which I wished to fulfill quickly what you had commanded, I completed your order. Would that this work had been completed as effectively as it was willingly undertaken!

Although, because various occupations hindered me, I had no opportunity to treat the subject at length or to turn through the volumes of the Fathers, and although charity moved me to fulfill the command, I wrote rapidly on each matter that occurred to me and sent it to your brotherhood, so that, even if the answers should bring no benefit, obedience might at least bear fruit.

Meanwhile, as I am certain you know, these questions were not posed by royal necessity because of a need to learn, but from a desire to teach; nor so that, once they had been answered, he himself might be instructed in things he did not know, but so that others might be roused from the sleep of sluggish torpor to the useful completion of their duties.

For it has always been characteristic of him to urge bishops to investigate the holy Scriptures and to pursue sound and sober doctrine; the whole clergy to discipline; philosophers to knowledge of divine and human affairs; monks to religious observance; everyone generally to holiness; leading men to counsel; judges to justice; soldiers to expertise in arms; prelates to humility; subjects to obedience; and everyone generally to prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance, and concord.

Through these and similar endeavors, that excellent man, with God favorable to him, never ceases to increase the eminence of holy Church. He is extraordinarily energetic in the administration of ecclesiastical and civil affairs, overflowing with the fountain of wisdom, and triumphant in the display of virtue.

## I. Why an infant is made a catechumen

The practice by which infants are now made catechumens preserves an ancient custom. For all who came to the apostles as believers to be baptized were instructed and taught by them; and, once instructed and taught concerning the sacrament of baptism and the other rules of faith, they received the holy mystery of baptism.

Hence the Apostle says:

“Do you not know, brothers, that all of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” (Rom. 6:3)

These words show that those who were baptized were not ignorant of the mysteries of the sacrament of baptism.

The Lord likewise did not simply say, “Go, baptize,” but:

“Go and teach all nations, baptizing them” (Matt. 28:19),

so that we may understand that the person who is to be baptized must first be instructed and taught, and afterward baptized.

Infants, therefore, both hear and become catechumens—not because they can at that age both be instructed and taught, but so that the ancient custom may be preserved, according to which the apostles first taught and instructed those whom they were going to baptize, as has already been said.

## II. What a catechumen is

A catechumen is interpreted as “one who hears,” or “one who has been instructed.” For the human race hears and is instructed before it comes to baptism.

What it once heard through Moses—“Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4)—and what it was instructed through the Law and the Prophets concerning the worship of the one true God, it now hears through the ministry of priests and is made capable of instruction, so that, abandoning the rite by which it served the creature, it may serve God the Creator alone.

Thus catechumens believe in Christ while still carrying their sins. Concerning them, I think, it is said in the Gospel:

“While they believed in Jesus, Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them” (John 2:24).

Accordingly, all who were taught or instructed by John and were baptized—since his baptism could not erase sins—must be recognized as having prefigured the type of catechumens.

## III. Why the exsufflation is performed

On their face, therefore, the priest makes the sign of the cross by exsufflation, so that the devil may be driven away and a way may be prepared for Christ. The devil, who by his seductive persuasion had become the inhabitant of the human race, which at its beginning had received the breath of life, is compelled by the power and most sacred sign of Christ, through the ministry of priests, to depart. Christ is the one who is read to have breathed upon his disciples and rebuked unclean spirits.

## IV. Why the exorcism is performed

For this reason that malignant spirit is also exorcised, so that it may depart and withdraw from the creature that it had long possessed through the sin of the first man.

And because, according to the Apostle, “Christ has no agreement with Belial, nor does light share fellowship with darkness” (1 Cor. 6:15), let darkness depart and Christ, the true light, enter.

He is also read in Zechariah to have symbolically worn filthy garments on account of our sins, which he bore in his body (Zech. 3:3). Rebuking Satan, he chose Jerusalem—namely, the holy Church, whose name means “Vision of Peace”—so that he might daily make her fruitful with new offspring. To her it is said through the prophet:

“Your sons shall come from afar, and your daughters shall rise at your side” (Isa. 60:4).

Moreover, an exorcism is a word of rebuke or adjuration. Hence exorcists are also read to have existed in the Acts of the Apostles, and the holy Church includes the ministry of exorcists among the ecclesiastical orders.

For it must be understood that, when an exorcism is performed, the one being exorcised is undoubtedly he who is opposed to baptism, to the salvation of the faithful, and to all its virtues. Once he has been exorcised or expelled, the seasoning of the divine word is given to believers.

## V. Why a catechumen receives salt

For this reason those who are to be baptized receive salt as part of the sacrament, so that through its taste they may perceive the seasoning of wisdom, may not be deceived concerning the savor of Christ, and may not become tasteless and foolish.

The one who said to his disciples, “You are the salt of the earth” (Matt. 5:13), also said:

“No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 9:62).

Thus, so that those who are baptized may be fit for the kingdom of heaven, and so that they may not repeat their former sins and look back, becoming a pillar of salt and, by remaining senseless, seasoning others by the example of their own punishment, they ought to receive the salt of wisdom. Whatever in them is unstable and fluid must be healed by the salt of God’s word, and, according to the Apostle, they must remember Lot’s wife.

And just as Elisha healed the barrenness of the water by casting in salt, so the true Elisha, our Lord Jesus Christ, by the savor of his word brings the fluid barrenness of the human race to the sweet savor of faith and good works.

The firmness of this faith then begins clearly to shine forth when the one who had heard that the worship of God alone must be maintained—whence he was called a “hearer”—and had begun to be instructed in the worship of true religion—whence he was called a catechumen—and had been freed from the malignant spirit through exsufflation and exorcism, begins, through the giving of salt, to possess a taste for the divine word. Then the Creed is delivered to him, that is, the complete and unwavering confession of the true faith, so that the house, after its former inhabitant has been abandoned, may be adorned with faith, and so that, after the thorns of unbelief have been uprooted from it, the teachings of true faith may begin to be planted there.

For the thorns of unbelief or vices must first be uprooted, and afterward the beginnings of faith and good works must be planted.

Hence the Lord first crushed, before the children of Israel, the seven nations symbolizing vices, and in their place established the Israelite people as a type of the virtues. And he says to the prophet Jeremiah:

“Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to tear down, to destroy and to demolish, to build and to plant” (Jer. 1:10).

First he mentioned uprooting, tearing down, destruction, and dispersal; afterward he added building and planting. Through the same prophet he says:

“As I watched over them to uproot, demolish, dissipate, scatter, and afflict, so I will watch over them to build and plant” (Jer. 31:28).

This is because after exorcism and exsufflation comes the handing over of the Creed.

## VI. The interpretation of the Creed according to the Latins

The word *symbolum* is interpreted in Latin as “indication,” “sign,” or “conferring.”

It is an “indication” because through it the integrity of the faith is indicated. It is a “sign” because, when it is rightly retained and understood, the faithful are distinguished from the unfaithful. It is “conferring” because in it the apostles conferred the whole integrity of the faith.

What they all retained in their hearts with equal sincerity of faith, they confessed with their mouths. Each contributing his own statement, they produced the *symbolum*, that is, the “conferring of the whole faith.”

As they were about to depart from one another, they established together the rule of their future preaching, so that, though departing from one another geographically, they would not preach anything divergent or discordant. For it was most fitting and useful that those whose soul and heart were one in the Lord, and whom the breath of the Holy Spirit enlivened, should also be adorned by one confession of faith. Those bound together by the bond of one faith neither could nor ought to be divided in anything.

Meanwhile, many wish the “abbreviated word” mentioned through the prophet Isaiah to be understood as referring to the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. In the one, the completeness of faith is contained; in the other, the completeness of prayers. Thus in the twelve statements are contained the teaching of the twelve apostles, and in the seven petitions is contained everything pertaining to the ordering of the present and future life.

The “abbreviated word” may also be understood as the whole of doctrine, because what the Law and the Prophets previously contained in the breadth of their commandments, the Lord, when he came, summarized and declared:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Matt. 22:37).

In these two sayings he plainly abbreviates the Prophets and the Law.

Let this suffice concerning the Creed and its name.

## VII. On belief: how one is to believe in God the Father almighty, in Jesus Christ his Son, and in the Holy Spirit, in the holy catholic Church, and in the other articles that follow in the same Creed

The faith contained in this Creed must be understood by those who are to be baptized in such a way that they believe in God the Father almighty, creator of all things visible and invisible. He alone is called “unbegotten” because he is not from another.

They must believe in Jesus Christ, his Son, through whom all things were made: true God, the only-begotten, true Son of God—not made or adopted, but begotten and of one substance with the Father, and in every respect equal to God the Father, so that he cannot be inferior in time, rank, or power, and so that the one who was begotten is as great as the one who begot him.

They must also believe that he was born from the Holy Spirit and from Mary, ever-virgin; that is, that, with the Holy Spirit cooperating, the same Son of God assumed a true body from a virgin, so that the one who was the Son of God the Father in divinity became, in humanity, the Son of a human mother.

They must also believe that at the end of time he descended from the Father for the redemption of the world—the one who never ceased to be with the Father—and became truly human, so that a human being might free the human race.

And they must believe that the one who, without beginning, possesses eternity with the Father and the Holy Spirit assumed, at the end of the ages, a complete human being of our nature, and that the Word became flesh by assuming humanity, not by changing his divinity.

They must also believe that he endured suffering and death, not in the power of divinity but in the weakness of humanity; that he died a true death of the flesh, rose in a true resurrection of the flesh, and by his resurrection conferred upon us the hope of resurrection—so that, just as he rose alive from the dead on the third day, so we too may rise at the end of the ages in the same flesh in which we now live.

They must also believe that, in the same body that he assumed from the virgin, in which he endured suffering and rose again, he ascended into heaven; that he now exists in that same body; that he will come to judgment; and that, after all have been raised, he will give to some the sentence of eternal punishment for their sins, and to others the reward of eternal blessedness for the merits of their righteousness.

They must also believe in the Holy Spirit, true God proceeding from the Father and the Son, equal in every respect to the Father and the Son in will, power, eternity, and substance. There are no degrees in this holy Trinity by which anyone could be called lower or higher.

They must also believe in the holy catholic Church, that is, the universal Church—not “in the holy Church,” as they believe in the Trinity. They must believe that the holy Church is the house of that same holy Trinity.

They must believe that those who depart from communion with it are called schismatics and heretics and are punished with eternal damnation, while those who remain in its communion are members of Christ, receive the remission of sins, and belong to eternal life.

Since little children, not yet possessing reason, cannot understand these things at all, they must be taught when they reach an age capable of understanding, both the sacraments of faith and the mysteries of their confession, so that they may truly believe these things and guard them with diligent care.

We have rightly spoken of their confession, because although they cannot yet speak, those who receive them from the baptismal font confess and speak on their behalf. Nor is it without reason that those who are liable for the sins of others should, through the mystery of baptism, receive remission of original sins through the confession of others.

## VIII. On the scrutiny

Those who are already of an age at which they can give an account of their belief must be examined with careful scrutiny, to determine whether they truly believe or whether some stain of falsehood is concealed within them.

Otherwise, if they come to the sacrament of baptism either through fear of or favor toward earthly powers, or for the acquisition of certain possessions, while the ministers of the Church are unaware of it, what is holy may be given to dogs, pearls cast before swine, and wolves clothed in sheep’s skins.

The Church has been accustomed to observe this practice: for a number of days, those who are to be baptized at the solemnity of Easter are scrutinized, so that the sacraments of life may be imparted to those who have been instructed and taught and who come to the true faith with a sincere heart.

To make them more suitable for the sacrament of baptism, and to make their faith more approved, certain bodily actions are performed which, when tasted with spiritual discernment, convey something mystical and spiritual.

## IX. Why the ears and nostrils are touched with spittle

The nostrils and ears are therefore touched with spittle, and the word “Ephphatha” is spoken.

The nostrils are touched so that they may follow Christ in the fragrance of perfumes and say:

“Draw me; we shall run after you” (Song 1:3),

and, with the Apostle, profess:

“We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (2 Cor. 2:15),

and become members of the one to whom it is said:

“The fragrance of your garments is above all spices” (Song 4:10).

He will be able to possess this fragrance rightly if, together with Mary—whose name is interpreted as “lady” or “illuminatrix”—they anoint Jesus’ feet with an alabaster jar of ointment, that is, with the purity of sacred faith and the practice of good works. In this way they fulfill the admonitions of the apostles or of whatever preachers Christ walks through, and the house—that is, the world or the universal Church—may be filled with their good reputation as with a certain sweet and pleasant fragrance.

And because the sweetness of fragrance and various incenses often belong to dissoluteness and lovers of pleasure, these people, on the contrary, having become continent and lovers of Christ, should always embrace only his life-giving fragrance.

The ears are also touched so that, hearing the words of God and doing them, they may resemble, according to the Gospel, the wise man who built his house upon a rock (Matt. 7:24), and so that with spiritual hearing they may always listen to spiritual things. Thus, with David, they may say:

“I will hear what the Lord God speaks within me” (Ps. 84:9),

and, with Isaiah:

“The Lord God opened my ear, and I do not contradict; I did not turn back” (Isa. 50:5).

Hearing spiritually what is spoken spiritually, they may attain the benefits of spiritual works.

When the Lord says in the Gospel, “Let the one who has ears to hear hear” (Matt. 11:15), and John says in his Apocalypse, “Let the one who has ears to hear hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Rev. 2:7), bodily ears are not being sought here, but spiritual ones; and by the name “ears” the hearing of the inner person is signified.

For in sacred Scripture the spiritual powers of the soul are often understood through the limbs of the body. Since the divinity, by assuming humanity, made a kind of eye-salve through the union of two substances in the one person of the Son of God, by which it might illuminate the human race, born blind from its first parents, the ears and nostrils are rightly touched with spittle.

The one who, by spitting, touched the tongue of the mute, made clay with spittle, and opened the eyes of the man born blind now, through the ministry of priests, grants spiritual hearing to those who are to be baptized, gives them the ability to speak rightly—that is, to confess the true faith—and opens their nostrils so that they may receive the good fragrance of Christ.

The breast of the one who is baptized must always be filled with the nectar of the divine fragrance and moistened with spiritual anointing.

## X. Why the breast is anointed with oil, and the shoulders are marked or smeared

For this reason the breast of those who are to be baptized is also touched with oil, as are their shoulders, so that, softened by the anointing of that holy oil—that is, of the Spirit, concerning which the Apostle says, “His anointing teaches us about everything” (1 John 2:27)—they may be fortified before and behind.

That is, being watchful whether things are prosperous or adverse, and, in imitation of the heavenly living creatures, being full of eyes before and behind, they should look toward the past and the future and not lose custody of their salvation.

Their breast is touched so that with David they may say:

“His mercy shall go before me” (Ps. 59:11).

Their shoulders are touched so that with the same David they may say:

“His mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 23:6).

That is, the anterior parts are touched so that they may will what is good; the posterior parts, so that they may not will in vain. To will what is good and to accomplish it are given to us by the one from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes.

And because the mind is often signified by the word “heart,” as in the saying, “With my whole heart I have sought you” (Ps. 119:10), and because anointing by the Holy Spirit, or works of light and mercy, is understood by the word “oil,” the place of the heart is fortified by anointing on both sides, front and back. Thus the Christian’s mind may abound everywhere both in the richness of the Holy Spirit and in works of light and mercy.

## XI. What renunciation is

The person in whom these things abound does well if, by renouncing the devil and his works, he rejects his dominion, and if the yoke that weighed upon him is weakened by the anointing of that oil. Thus the prophetic saying may be fulfilled:

“The yoke shall rot before the face of oil” (Isa. 10:27).

To renounce is ordinarily used in the sense of despising, rejecting, contradicting, or expressing something else that can be conveyed by this word in the present sense.

Although the meaning of the word *nuntio* (“announce”) is evident when it is used without a preposition, and although, when the preposition is added, it sometimes does not depart far from its meaning, as in:

“I will tell and announce” (Ps. 55:18),

at other times it changes into another meaning, as in:

“Thus, therefore, everyone among you who does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33),

nevertheless *abrenuntiare* (“to renounce”) is always customarily used in the sense mentioned above.

The person confesses that he renounces Satan, all his works, and all his pomps. This renunciation is rightly followed by the confession of the holy Trinity, so that where sin abounded, grace may abound all the more; and where the devil’s yoke has rotted before the face of the anointing of the Holy Spirit, the yoke of the one who said, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:29), may come upon him.

Satan, who is also called the devil, is renounced by the faithful so that they may serve God the Savior more freely, because, according to the same Lord’s saying:

“No one can serve two masters” (Luke 16:13).

## XII. On the renunciation of Satan, all his works and pomps, and what the devil’s works and pomps are

His works are also renounced because his works are contrary to the works of the Savior. Because he subjected the human race to himself by his weapons—that is, by vices—the Lord conquered him with his weapons—that is, with virtues.

In the devil’s service—that is, while remaining in the sins of our servitude—one incurred death. In the service of the Lord—that is, in the virtues—we receive eternal life.

We may therefore appropriately call the seven principal vices with which the devil afflicts the human race the works of Satan; opposed to them are the seven principal virtues, which are undoubtedly saving works.

His pomps are likewise renounced. They too are certainly works of Satan, but they seem to be distinguished from his other works because in them pride is in some way displayed—pride of which he is the author and which cast him down.

His pomps, therefore, are ambition, arrogance, vainglory, and other things of this kind, which are recognized to proceed from the fountain of pride.

That “pomp” is to be understood as ambition, boasting, and similar things is demonstrated by the prophetic word when it says:

“Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria, nobles, heads of the peoples, entering pompously into the house of Israel” (Amos 6:1).

Clement Prudentius, moreover, a most eloquent and most Christian poet, used *pomp* in this sense in his book *Psychomachia*, where he says:

> The pomp that displays the empty splendor of vanity  
> is stripped off, laid bare of its covering.

Although every sin may be called pride, because when someone sins he appears to oppose God, who forbade sinning, nevertheless it is one thing to sin sluggishly, another maliciously, another knowingly, another ignorantly, another negligently, and another arrogantly.

Whatever the manner in which someone sins, if he refuses to repent, he plunges himself into a great abyss of pride, from which he can emerge only through confession of his sins, correction of his conduct, and the aid of saving penance.

A person is proud against God in two ways: either when he is disobedient to God’s commands and commits what has been forbidden, or when he neglects to repent of what he has committed.

Therefore, whether those who are to be baptized or we who have already received the sacrament of baptism must place before our eyes the covenant made with God in baptism, in which Satan, his works, and his pomps are renounced.

That covenant is made void if a person either remains in the faith while submitting to vices, or deviates from the faith and submits to the worship of idols or to the errors of heresies.

## XIII. On the sacrament of baptism
Since it is therefore established that believers make two covenants—one in which they renounce the devil, his pomps, and all his works, and another by which they profess their belief in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—these must be held with unwavering concentration of mind. In order that they may be preserved undefiled, we must always seek the help of him who bestowed the sacrament of baptism for the salvation of the human race. Its mystery was prefigured in the Old Testament through Moses, when the people were baptized in the cloud and in the sea, and was most clearly demonstrated for us in the New Testament through the mediator of God [Col. 0231D] and humanity. For he himself said: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3). John said of him: “I baptize in water for repentance; but in your midst stands one whom you do not know; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3:11; John 1:26).

Through this we, who are born into the world, are reborn to God; and we who through sin were children of wrath are through grace made children of God. By this immersion and this washing the Church is invigorated. Woman was fashioned from the bone of the sleeping first-formed man; the Church was formed from the side of Christ sleeping upon the cross. For blood and water flowed from his side: the two principal sacraments of the holy [Col. 0232A] Church, so that through the one consecration and through the other cleansing might be granted to that same Church. We are indeed regenerated from the washing, so that we may be consecrated also by the blood. Hence the people crossed the Red Sea, because the baptism of Christ is consecrated by his blood.

Since, therefore, the element of water in this world is more suitable than all the other elements for cleansing, giving life, and refreshing, the dignity of baptism is rightly conferred upon it. For it conceived both the efficacy of human regeneration, when the Spirit of God hovered over it at the beginning of the world, and the dignity of cleansing, when it flowed from the side of Christ. Through this visible element that invisible reality is signified, so that just as the body is cleansed outwardly by water, so inwardly, through its mystery, the soul may be purified by the Holy Spirit [Col. 0232B].

When God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, by sanctifying the waters, grants them the power of purification. From them the human being, restored to the image of the holy Trinity in whose likeness he had been created, is driven forth; and he who had entered them old through the sin of the first human being emerges from them new through the grace of Christ, changed for the better by the Spirit of grace and made something far different from what he had been. He had been foul with the deformity of sins; there he is restored, beautiful through the whitening of virtues.

The mystery of baptism can in no way be completed except under the invocation of the holy Trinity, for the Lord also said to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). The same Lord confirmed this sacrament when, at his baptism, the Father was declared by the voice, the Son by the body, and the Holy Spirit by the appearance of a dove [Col. 0232C].

O glorious and wondrous sacrament, which makes children of God from children of wrath, new people from the old, and beautiful people from the defiled; in it we are regenerated and cleansed, and imitate the example of Christ’s death. Let the Apostle say how we should imitate this example. “Do you not know,” he says, “that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:3–4).

We die to sin, therefore, when we renounce the devil and everything that belongs to him; we are buried with Christ when, under the invocation of the holy Trinity, through a threefold immersion, we descend into the baptismal font as into a kind of tomb; we rise with Christ when, stripped of all sins, we emerge from the font as from a tomb. Nor is the mystery of the three days and nights during which the Lord is said to have been in the tomb passed over, when, after invoking the holy Trinity—which is truly the light—we descend into the font. For the Father is light, and in his light, because the Son exists, we see the Holy Spirit, the light.

We also enact three nights when we contradict the father of darkness and ignorance, together with the lie born from him—which is itself false, just as its father is—and when he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own resources [Col. 0233A]. Third, we destroy the spirit of error that inspires false prophets to say, “Thus says the Lord,” although the Lord has not sent them. We destroy and trample these things if we have been buried with Christ, in accordance with what he himself says: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10:19). Each of these is opposed to the holy Trinity as night to day, darkness to light, and falsehood to truth.

The baptismal font likewise bears the likeness of Christ’s tomb, which is said to have been new. For whoever is buried with Christ in it and rises with him must, according to the same Apostle, walk in newness of life. The seven steps of this font seem to signify three nights in the descent and three days in the ascent, of which we have spoken above. The seventh, which is also the fourth, is that of which someone said: “And the appearance of the fourth was like a son of God” (Daniel 3:92). He extinguishes the fiery furnace; he is the support of the feet and the foundation of the water, in whom, according to the Apostle, “the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9).

Baptism is not repeated because Christ also dies only once. Sins committed after baptism are wiped away by the tears of repentance, almsgiving, and the practice of other good works, not by repeating baptism. Meanwhile, the Lord’s body is buried with the purest linen cloths and spices, because the person who desires to be buried with Christ—even if he has died through original sin, which he still bears, and if age permits—must nevertheless burn with the practice of good works and be clothed in clean garments, of which the prophet prays that priests be clothed when he says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 131:9).

If, therefore, before he is reborn, cleansed of original sin, and buried with Christ, he ought to burn with spices, give forth fragrance, and be clothed in the purest garments, how much more, once reborn, cleansed, brought to life together with Christ, walking in newness of life, and made a new creation, ought he to abound in fragrant odor and shine with the splendor of white garments?

## XIV. Why he is clothed in white garments

So that we, who die to the world and rise with Christ, may be clothed in the brightness of good works and strengthened by hope of heavenly joys, the angel who announces his resurrection is most fittingly described as sitting in white garments; those who announce his return to the apostles appear in white garments; and after baptism we too are clothed in white garments, so that we may preserve in our conduct the purity we received in regeneration, maintaining both our renewal and the beauty of angelic splendor.

White robes are also given individually to us as the hope of immortality and eternal blessedness, so that with the prophet we may say: “I will rejoice greatly in the Lord, and my spirit will exult in my God. For he has clothed me with the garment of salvation and covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10). May he who gave us these garments enable us to preserve them, so that what is written in the Apocalypse may be said of us: “Blessed is the one who keeps watch and guards his garments” (Revelation 16:15).

Since, therefore, all things in the rite of baptism are fragrant with mysteries and overflow with sacraments, it was fitting that the new human being should receive new garments and, cleansed from the pollution of his former offense, be clothed in the brightness of white vestments. Moses first washed Aaron and his sons with water and afterward clothed them in linen garments, because our true Moses also—the one who frees the people from Egyptian slavery, that is, from the error of paganism, the mediator of God and humanity—purifies us with the water [Col. 0234B] of his ineffable sacrament and adorns us with the garments of good works.

His face—that is, the manifestation of his divinity—shines like the sun on the mountain of the Church, as testified by the Law and the prophets; and his garments, that is, all the saints, become white like wool or like snow. Let us give thanks to him with the Apocalypse, who washed us from our sins in his blood and made us a kingdom and priests for his God and Father, to whom be glory forever and ever (Revelation 1:5–6). For this kingdom and priesthood are anointed by the Lord both with the visible oil of chrism through the ministry of priests and with the invisible grace of the Holy Spirit.

## XV. Why the head is anointed with sacred chrism

The sacrament of this ointment is first recorded as having been composed by Moses at the Lord’s command in Exodus, and in the New Testament it is truly declared by the Lord, who was anointed by the Father with the oil of gladness above his companions. God gives him the Spirit without measure, because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

The Church says to him: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women have loved you” (Song of Songs 1:2), because the name “Christian” arose both from Christ’s chrism and from Christ. Before his coming, only kings and priests were anointed, and they too were called “Christs”; after his coming, however, not only kings and priests but the whole Church is consecrated by this anointing, since it is established that she is both kingdom and priesthood, and that her children are kings and priests.

The heads of the baptized are therefore anointed with chrism so that, consecrated into the kingdom and priesthood of the Church, they may receive the distinction of the Christian name and become members of him who redeemed them and is their head.

## XVI. Why he is covered with a mystical veil

Since our same Redeemer is a king, of whom the prophet says, “Your kingdom, Lord, is a kingdom of all ages, and your dominion is throughout every generation” (Psalm 144:13), and who wondrously triumphed over the devil, death, and the world; and since he is a priest, of whom the same prophet says, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109:4), and who offered himself in sacrifice to God the Father [Col. 0235A]—it is most fitting that his holy Church, which is certainly his body, should be both kingdom and priesthood, and that we, regenerated in her and being her members, should be kings and priests.

We are kings so that we may fight manfully against the devil and govern the administration of our life with admirable stewardship; and we are priests so that, in the holy temple of God that we are, building the altar of faith, we may offer him the peaceful sacrifices of good works and say with the Apostle: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:3). From this altar may the smoke of our prayers rise to him daily, in accordance with what the prophet says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140:2).

The heads, therefore, of those who are regenerated from water and the Holy Spirit are covered with a mystical veil, so that it may be said to them through Peter: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for acquisition” (1 Peter 2:9). By this veil both a royal diadem and the covering of a priestly head are signified. Since “head” is often understood in sacred Scripture as the mind, according to the words, “Look up and raise your heads” (Luke 21:28), may the minds of the reborn possess the ornaments of royal dignity and the covering of a priestly crown, so that they may be fortified against vices by a priestly veil, spiritually adorned with the jewels of virtues, and anointed with the unction of the most holy chrism.

Through the anointing with chrism they are also granted the sevenfold Spirit of grace, so that they may be worthy to become not merely the dwelling place of the Spirit who is of one substance with the Father and the Son, but the dwelling place of the entire holy Trinity.

## XVII. Why the one confirmed by the bishop receives the sevenfold Spirit of grace through the laying on of hands

That priests are permitted to anoint the baptized with chrism but are not permitted to confer the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands is an ancient custom handed down to the Church by the apostles. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

“When Apollos was at Corinth, Paul, after passing through the upper regions, came to Ephesus and found certain disciples. He said to them, ‘Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?’ But they said to him, ‘We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.’ He said, ‘Into what, then, were you baptized?’ They said, ‘Into John’s baptism.’ Paul said, ‘John baptized the people with a baptism of repentance, telling them to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, in Jesus.’ When they heard this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus; and when Paul had laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied” (Acts 19:1–6).

Likewise, in another passage:

“When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet come upon any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name [Col. 0236A] of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”

It must therefore be understood that, just as the other sacraments of baptism are performed visibly by priests but consecrated invisibly by God, so also the grace of the Holy Spirit is bestowed upon the faithful through the laying on of hands and the ministry of bishops. Priests, although they are priests, do not possess the fullness of the episcopal office.

That this belongs to bishops alone—that they may either sign or confer the Paraclete Spirit—is demonstrated not only by ecclesiastical custom but also by the earlier passage from the Acts of the Apostles, which states that Peter and John were sent for the purpose of giving the Holy Spirit to those already baptized. Priests, whether bishops are absent or present, may baptize and anoint the baptized with chrism, but only with chrism consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, sign the forehead with that same oil, since this belongs exclusively to bishops when they confer the Paraclete Spirit.

This Paraclete Spirit is also called the sevenfold Spirit of grace because of the mystery of the number seven, in which complete perfection is understood. For seven is composed of the first even number in its entirety and the first odd number in its entirety: of the first even number, which can be divided, and of the first odd number, which cannot be divided. The number three contains the mystery of the Trinity, and the number four that of the Gospel. Whether three is multiplied by four or four by three, the result is twelve, because the mystery of the holy Trinity and the teaching of the Gospel were spread through the twelve apostles into the four regions of the world: east and west, north and south [Col. 0236C].

This number is customarily used in sacred Scripture to signify perfection. When God had completed his works, he rested on the seventh day; and Enoch, who is seventh from Adam, walked with the Lord, and his translation gave us hope of eternal rest. Hence the Jubilee year, in which complete rest is signified, is completed through seven weeks of weeks. Seven times seven makes forty-nine, which is completed by adding the one—the unity of our gathering together.

The prophet commends the perfection of this number when he says: “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118:164). In another psalm, explaining this almost explicitly, he says: “His praise is always in my mouth” (Psalm 33:2). John also, in his Apocalypse, is generally believed to have written to the whole Catholic Church when he wrote to seven churches. Hence he himself says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 2:7).

Much is found in both the Old and New Testaments concerning the number seven, which in some passages of Scripture signifies universality or perfection and in others the sevenfold Spirit of grace; to pursue all of it would be lengthy. Let us now see how the prophet Isaiah enumerates the gifts of this sevenfold Spirit.

When he prophesied concerning Christ, who is the rod of the Lord’s strength, he said: “A rod shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:1–2).

Upon this flower, which came forth from the rod of Jesse—that is, from the birth of blessed Mary, ever-virgin—the Spirit of the Lord rested, because in him it pleased the whole fullness of divinity to dwell bodily. It was not distributed in parts, as among the other saints, to whom one is given the word of wisdom, another the word of knowledge, another the grace of virtues, and so forth, each receiving according to measure, but was given in complete fullness.

Hence the Apostle says: “God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34); and the prophet says: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my chosen one in whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him; he will bring judgment to the nations” (Isaiah 42:1). So that the Spirit might rest in him in perpetual dwelling, it came upon him, in accordance with the testimony of John the Baptist, who said:

“I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him. I did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me, ‘The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’” (John 1:32–33).

The Spirit of the Lord is called the spirit of wisdom because Christ is the wisdom of God, concerning whom it is written: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). The Psalms also sing: “How magnificent are your works, Lord; you have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24).

In another passage, where the Trinity is openly displayed, it is written: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power” (Psalm 32:6) [Col. 0237C]. Through Christ, who is the Word of the Lord—that is, of the Father—of whom it is written, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1), the heavens, namely the holy preachers who proclaim the glory of God, were made; and through the Holy Spirit, who is consubstantial with them and proceeds from both, all their power exists, because the beauty and strength of all the saints subsist through the inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

The Apostle writes: “Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24). And in Proverbs it is read: “God founded the earth by his wisdom and prepared the heavens by understanding” (Proverbs 3:19).

Just as the same Word of the Lord is called light, life, and resurrection, so he is called the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, and of knowledge, piety, and the fear of the Lord—not because he is different according to the differences of these names, but because he is one and the same source and beginning of all virtues.

Without Christ, therefore, no one can be wise, understanding, a counselor, strong, learned, or filled with the fear of the Lord. It must also be understood that the Spirit of the Lord—of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and strength, of knowledge and piety, and of the fear of the Lord—that is, the sevenfold number, which Zechariah calls seven eyes in one stone (Zechariah 3:9)—rests upon the rod and flower that arose from Jesse and, through him, from the stock of David.

This Spirit, which proceeds from the Father and the Son, the same Lord granted to the apostles and, through the ministry of the apostles and their successors, to his holy Church. Although its gifts proceed from the one fountain of the Spirit, they appear in some way to possess distinct properties.

To have wisdom is one thing and to understand another, because many have a taste for eternal things but are quite unable to understand them. Wisdom therefore fills the mind it inhabits with hope and certainty concerning eternal things; understanding, because it penetrates hidden matters, enlightens the heart it touches by restoring its darkness.

Counsel, by restraining someone from acting rashly, fills the mind with reason. Strength, when it does not fear adversity, gives confidence to a trembling mind. Knowledge, when it drives away ignorance, enlightens with its light the one whom it fills. Piety permits the one whom it fills to abound in works of mercy. Fear, while restraining the mind from becoming proud over present things, strengthens it concerning the future by restoring hope [Col. 0238B].

Thus these virtues assist one another through their mutual support, so that, while one aids another, the order and condition of life may be most fittingly arranged. Wisdom is lesser if it lacks understanding, and understanding is very useless if it does not proceed from wisdom, because when it penetrates higher things without the weight of wisdom, its lightness lifts it only to make its fall more severe.

Counsel is worthless when it lacks the strength of fortitude, because what it discovers through deliberation it cannot bring to completion without power. Fortitude is also greatly weakened unless it is supported by counsel, because the more it sees that it can accomplish, the more disastrously virtue rushes headlong without the moderation of reason.

There is no knowledge if it does not possess the usefulness of piety, because when it neglects to carry out the good things it has learned, it binds itself more tightly for judgment. Piety is also very useless if it lacks the discernment of knowledge, because when no knowledge enlightens it, it does not know how to show mercy.

Fear itself, too, if it does not possess these virtues, undoubtedly rises to no good work, because while it trembles at everything, it remains inert through the very dread that belongs to it and is empty of every good deed.

We must therefore observe with the utmost care and implore the help of the Holy Spirit himself: that wisdom may not exalt us; that understanding, while running subtly, may not go astray; that counsel, while multiplying itself, may not confuse us; that fortitude, while granting confidence, may not precipitate us; that knowledge, while knowing but not loving, may not puff us up; that piety, while inclining beyond righteousness, may not distort us; and that fear, while trembling more than is right, may not plunge us into the pit of despair.

It must certainly be understood that these distributions of spiritual gifts in the body of Christ, which is the Church, are supported by such aids. But in him who is the source of light and origin of goodness, they reign fully, perfectly, incomparably, and ineffably.

Wisdom—which fashioned a body for itself in the Virgin’s womb and built the Church in the world—possesses the spirit of wisdom, by which it does all things wisely; of understanding, by which it searches out all the hidden secrets; of counsel, by which it manages everything with great stewardship, because it is the Angel of great counsel; of fortitude, because it reaches powerfully from end to end and can be overcome by no one; of knowledge, because it is ignorant of nothing except those to whom it will say, “I do not know you” (Matthew 25:12); of piety, because it created the human being in goodness, condemned him in justice, and redeemed him in piety; and of fear, on account of those who need the fear of the Lord because they are little ones. To them it says through the Prophet: “Come, children; hear me: I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm 33:12).

Since, therefore, he descended to our weakness, emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, humbled himself even to death, and bent himself down so that he might raise us, who were lying prostrate, to himself, it is not inappropriate that the Spirit of the Lord who rests upon him should begin with wisdom and descend through most fitting stages all the way to fear.

We, however, coming from fear—which love casts out—arrive at the chaste fear that endures forever and ever. We proceed to piety, so that, adorned with works of piety, we may come to knowledge—not knowledge that puffs up, but that which love builds up [Col. 0239B]. From knowledge we proceed to fortitude, so that, adorned with the beauty of knowledge, we may fight bravely against vices; from fortitude to counsel, so that we may fortify with the gravity of counsel what we have done bravely; and, with our actions obeying counsel, we may enter into the secrets of understanding and come to that wisdom which has the fear of the Lord as its beginning.

Thus, completing all things wisely and possessing good understanding through our conduct, we may be admitted to that wisdom through which all things were made: wisdom which was ineffably begotten by the Father before the ages and, at the end of the ages, deigned to take flesh for our salvation. He granted that flesh to his faithful to eat when he said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:55–56).

## XVIII. Why he is perfected by the Lord’s body and blood

To obtain this life we are baptized, nourished by his flesh, and given drink from his blood, because we cannot pass into his body unless we are imbued with these sacraments. For he himself says: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6:54); and: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:55).

It is a saving sacrifice, which in the Old Testament Melchizedek, king of Salem, offered as a type of the Lord’s body and blood, and which in the New Testament the same mediator of God and humanity fulfilled before he was handed over, when he took bread and the cup, blessed them, and, giving them to his disciples, commanded that these things be done in remembrance of him.

Therefore, after the old sacrifices had been abandoned and brought to an end, the Church celebrates this mystery of sacrifice, offering bread on account of the living bread that descended from heaven, and wine for the one who said, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1), so that through the visible offering of priests and the invisible consecration of the Holy Spirit, bread and wine may pass into the dignity of the Lord’s body and blood.

Water is mixed with this blood, either because it flowed from the Lord’s side together with the blood, or because, as the elders wish it to be understood, just as Christ is signified by the wine, so the people are signified by the water. Wine and water are inseparably mixed in the cup because the Church is also inseparably joined and united to Christ, her head.

The Church therefore maintains the custom of receiving the Eucharist handed down by the Lord: when someone is reborn from water and the Holy Spirit, he is nourished by the Lord’s body and given drink from his blood. Thus, when he has been transformed into the body of Christ, he remains in Christ and Christ in him. Strengthened by the power of this food, he may, following the example of Elijah, reach the mountain of God—namely Christ, the mountain of the house of the Lord prepared upon the summit of the mountains—and, by his gift, draw near to the glory of eternal blessedness, where his desire may be satisfied with good things and he may say with the prophet: “But I shall appear in your presence with righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Psalm 16:15).

[Note: [Col. 0239C] “Behold, venerable man.” The three copies I mentioned add this clause; it is absent only from the Corbie manuscript.]

Behold, venerable man: what you wisely commanded, I have humbly fulfilled. I beseech your holiness that, when you discover more elevated answers to these questions, you may, after incorporating them, not reject these answers, provided that everything is tested by apostolic authority and whatever is good is retained.

[Col. 0239]

# THEODULF, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS

[Note: [Col. 0239D] “On the Holy Spirit.” The preface also teaches that this book was written by Theodulf at the command of Charlemagne; from it we inferred even the title, which was missing in our manuscript [Col. 0240D]. It could also have been formulated differently, as we saw in another book on the same subject and of the same character, but by an uncertain author, written to the same Charles, in these words: “Testimonies collected from the sacred volumes, from which it is clearly shown that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.” The title could likewise have resembled that borne by the three books of Saint Cyprian’s Testimonies against the Jews. There were also those who called books of this kind Testimonies—because these excerpts had been extracted and collected from various sources—Eclogues, as Gennadius relates concerning Pelagius, chapter 42: “Pelagius,” he says, “before he was exposed as a heretic, wrote one book of Eclogues from the divine Scriptures for practical conduct.” Thus the best manuscripts read there, not *Eulogiarum*.]

## ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

The opinions of the ancient Fathers: that he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

## PREFACE TO THE EMPEROR CHARLEMAGNE

Following the commands of your imperial authority, illustrious king,

I, Theodulf, gladly bring these documents.

That the gracious Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son,

you read, while the trumpet of Scripture resounds.

The Gospel proclaims this; the Apostle, its author, announces it;
