the devout and unanimous voice of the holy Fathers sings it.

Go swiftly, little book, to the feet of the lofty Charles,

the king; and say: “Hail, O pious emperor.”

Prostrate upon the ground, give grateful kisses to the soles of his noble feet;

then rise and promptly seek his knee, as is fitting.

And if he fixes upon you the bright circles of his eyes,

and his gracious hand takes you up,

and he asks where you come from, what you want, where you are going, or who you are,

you shall immediately answer him humbly with these words:

“Under Theodulf’s guidance I ran through many meadows;

behold, you see me here, laden with flowers.

I strive to establish, by the teachings of faith,

that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father or from the Son.

And I come prepared to contend with those

who walk otherwise and flee this path.”

Say this. If he then says, “You cannot,” respond:

“Thus I shall be able, I shall be able, O king; God will add his help.”

The illustrious judgment of the holy prophets is with me,

those whom the good breath of this Spirit guides.

And you, whom that Spirit quickens, will lend your hand

to the cause that began to be debated in your time.”

You are the glory of the world, the light of the kingdom, the guardian and defender of justice,

the wall and the weapon of the Catholic faith alike.

You command what is just and forbid what is unjust;

you bestow honors and rightly provide nourishment for the liberal arts.

You love these arts, command that they be loved, restore and foster them,

and drink deeply from the abundant cups of their streams.

What more can I say? You shine in virtue and overflow with piety;

in all good things, I know, no one surpasses you.

If such a person should say to you, “You who are about to impose your hand upon the contest,

bring forth now whatever virtue you possess,”

then immediately behold the weapons of the Fathers,

drawn from the vast stream, which the New or Old Law has taught.

While our battle line is fortified by these and does not know how to give way,

you will truly conquer, since you yourself are their follower.

A splendid victory, flowing with radiance, will appear,

and, pious king, you will attain the fulfillment of your holy desire.

## LIST OF AUTHORS CITED

Athanasius. Cyril. Hilary. Ambrose. Didymus. Augustine. Vigilius Afer. Proclus. Agnellus. Gregory. Isidore. Prosper. Fulgentius. Hormisdas. Leo. Cassiodorus. Prudentius.

[Note: [Col. 0242D] “Athanasius against the Arians.” The testimonies presented here under the name of Athanasius, with one exception, are all taken from the eleven books *On the Trinity*, which circulate in Latin alone among the works of Athanasius. It had already become customary to attribute them to Athanasius; under his name they are also frequently cited by Hincmar against Gottschalk, *On the Non-Trinal Deity*. That all of them are spurious is clear. Perhaps one would not be mistaken in thinking that they were composed by that same Vigilius who also fabricated the disputation of Athanasius with Arius. This conjecture is certainly strengthened by an ancient manuscript of good reputation from Fleury, in which these eleven books are joined with Vigilius’s books against Nestorius and Eutyches, and with the disputation I mentioned, as though they belonged to the same author.]

## ATHANASIUS

Concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, in the book he wrote against the heretical Arians, he says as follows (Book VIII):

“I believe in the Son in the Father and the Father in the Son, and also in the Paraclete Spirit, who proceeds from the Father and belongs both to the Son and to the Father, because he also proceeds from the Son, as it is written in the Gospel that through his breathing he gave the Holy Spirit to his disciples, saying: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven, and whose sins you retain are retained’ (John 20:22–23).

“Therefore I confess the Trinity to be inseparable, and I do not say that the Son or the Holy Spirit is alien from God, as heretics speak. I say that the Son is from God the Father, because the Son, who is the wisdom of God the Father, is himself also the will of the Father, which has always been in him; and he himself is the angel of great counsel.”

Likewise, the same author in the same work (Book VIII).

Concerning the Holy Spirit, there is no doubt that he is ignorant of nothing, nor is he alien from the Father; for it is the height of madness to say that the Father ever existed without the Holy Spirit, since he searches, as the Apostle says, as has often been stated, “the deep things and the heights of God” (1 Cor. 2:10). It has also been proved by many testimonies of Scripture that this same Spirit is the Spirit of the Son; and that he wholly remains in the Son, and, just as he proceeds from God the Father, so he proceeds from the Son, so that the whole Trinity may be believed to be one God.

There is therefore nothing that the Father does or ordains without his Wisdom, and nothing that he knows or ordains without his Holy Spirit, concerning whom the Prophet says: “The Spirit, the Paraclete; the Spirit of wisdom and understanding; the Spirit of counsel and might; the Spirit of knowledge and piety” (Isa. 11:2)—all of which subsist in God, who is the Trinity.

Again, in the same book (Book VIII), that the Son and the Holy Spirit are in the Father, and that the Holy Spirit proceeds from God, where the name of the Son is not excluded:

Therefore Christ the Son must be served, because he is both perfect God and the true Son. Whoever faithfully serves the Son serves the Father, and the Holy Spirit who is in him; and whoever worships the Father worships the Son and the Holy Spirit in him, because the Son and the Holy Spirit are in the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father. The Lord himself says: “I am in the Father and the Father is in me” (John 14:11). Concerning the Holy Spirit also he says: “The Paraclete, who proceeds from my Father” (John 15:26).

And when someone worships the Son, he worships the Father and the Holy Spirit in him, because the Father is in him. He says: “Whoever sees me sees my Father also” (John 14:9); and again: “The Father, remaining in me, himself does the works” (ibid., v. 10). Concerning the Holy Spirit he says: “He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:14); and: “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said to you that he will receive from what is mine” (ibid., v. 15).

The Spirit of the Father is therefore the Spirit of the Son, as the Apostle says: “But because you are sons of God, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Gal. 4:6); and again: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9); and again: “For I know that this will turn out for my salvation through your prayer and the assistance of the Spirit of the Lord Christ” (Phil. 1:19).

In the Gospel also the Lord himself says: “The Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). And in the Acts of the Apostles we read: “Passing through Phrygia and Galatia, they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. When they had come to Mesopotamia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of the Lord did not permit them” (Acts 16:6).

By these most manifest testimonies, therefore, it is proved that the Holy Spirit—the Paraclete Spirit, the Spirit who proceeds from the Father—is the Spirit of the Son, the Spirit of Christ, the Spirit of Jesus. For the whole Trinity must be worshiped, honored, proclaimed, and loved inseparably, in one substance, divinity, and power.

Again, the same author in the same book (Book I): that the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but exists as God by nature, proceeds from the Father, and receives from the Son.

This Holy Spirit, who is neither the Father nor the Son, and who moreover has neither begotten nor been born—since one person is the begetter, another person is the Only-Begotten who is from him, and yet another person, as I have said, according to the Scriptures, is neither the Father nor the Son—this is the Holy Spirit; but he is plainly of one and the same nature.

Therefore, in the deity there is one common name for them, as the Son testifies in the clarity of the Gospel concerning the Paraclete Spirit, saying: “He proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26), and continuing: “He will receive from what is mine” (John 16:14). Consequently, wherever the persons are being distinguished, they are differentiated by their proper names. But wherever the deity is being indicated, one name is given to them, because we are shown to be plural when the names of the persons are spoken, and by this fact they are one in deity and three in the names of the persons.

Again, the same author in the book [Note: In the edition: On the United Deity, Book IV, On the Individual Names.] that he wrote against the objections of a certain Potentinus.

Just as the Son cries out to the Father, “Father, glorify your name,” and a voice came from heaven, “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again” (John 12:28), so in another place he himself repeats: “I came forth from the Father and have come” (John 16:28).

Surely, if the Father himself were the same person as the Son, he ought to have said, “I came forth from myself and have come,” since without doubt one is he who came forth, and another is he from whom he came forth.

To this he added concerning the person of the Holy Spirit: “When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will testify about me” (John 15:26). Is it not therefore the case that one is he who sends, another person is he from whom he proceeds, and another is this very one who comes? Finally, if there were one person, from whom would he be sent, or from whom would he proceed?

The Apostle likewise confirmed these matters in his greeting to the Corinthians, saying: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God”—that is, of the Father—“and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen” (2 Cor. 13:13). Did he not openly distinguish, through each name, just as is also stated above, that separate persons are present?

Therefore one is the Father in person, who begot; another is the Son, who is the Only-Begotten from him; and another is the Paraclete Spirit, who proceeds from one nature. But you say to me, heretic: How does the Spirit subsist from one nature? Behold, the Son testified concerning him that he proceeds from the Father, and continued: “And he will receive from what is mine” (John 16:14).

Again, the same author in the book On the Profession of the Catholic Rule (Book VII):

“By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their host” (Ps. 32:6). Certainly, he declared the Word to be the Son, indicated the Lord as his Father, and showed that the spirit of his mouth is the principal Spirit.

You see how briefly he distinguished the several meanings as belonging to the persons: the Word, the Lord, and the Spirit. But he also showed that there is one operation in them. For if ambiguity still holds you, I repeat the very same point: when he says, “By the word of the Lord,” do not understand this as an insubstantial sound of the voice, such as, when someone emits it loudly, ordinarily resounds as an echo—whose resonance is heard only in the imagination and, once produced, is nothing.

Rather, concerning this Word of our Lord the Father, who is our salvation, as divine Scripture everywhere testifies, the Son of God is substantial, through whom all things were made. Therefore, because he said, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth their host,” recognize that this substantial Word was properly born from none other than the Father, and that he called “the spirit of his mouth” the Spirit who proceeds from that very united substance, as we find it authoritatively established—not from another nature, but from that very one.

Accordingly, the substance of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is united; the Greeks call this *ὁμοούσιον* (*homoousion*, “of one substance”). The operation also of the united and same Trinity in creation is one.

Again, the same author in the book that he wrote against heretics (Book XI), that the Holy Spirit is the inspiration of the Father and the Son, and that the Son is the fountain of the Holy Spirit; from this it is gathered that he also proceeds from the Son.

“The light of the Lord is the inspiration of human beings, which searches the innermost parts of the belly” (Prov. 20:27). It is clear that the Spirit searches all things, as Paul writes (1 Cor. 2:10), and that, when Adam had been formed in the beginning, God breathed the Holy Spirit into his face, as Moses says: “And God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7).

For what was breathed by God is not the soul, as the Jewish fabulists claim; otherwise, how could God condemn to eternal fire what was breathed by him? Rather, it is the life-giving Spirit, concerning whom Paul says: “The Spirit, however, gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). And he breathed, he says, into Adam’s face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul (Gen. 2:7).

Therefore the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of life, from whom certain people, while alive, have fallen away and become dead, as Paul wrote: “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives” (1 Tim. 5:6).

Otherwise, how can Solomon’s statement be heard: “The light of the Lord is the inspiration of human beings, which searches the innermost parts of the belly,” if you do not say that the souls of human beings are the light of God’s words? Unless you confess the Holy Spirit to be the light of the Lord and believe him to be the inspiration of the Son, with Moses saying, “God breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life,” and the Son of God saying, “I am life” (John 14:6).

Solomon’s Wisdom also introduces the Savior as saying: “Behold, I will proclaim to you the confession of my inspiration” (Prov. 1:23). For thus it says in Proverbs:

“Wisdom sings aloud at the outset; in the streets she speaks boldly; at the gates she takes her stand with greater power; and on the walls of the city she speaks confidently. As long as the simple possess righteousness, they will not be ashamed; but the foolish, since they are eager for insult, have become impious and have hated understanding, and have become liable to rebukes. Behold, I will proclaim to you the confession of my inspiration; I will teach you my word” (Prov. 1:20 ff.).

And Isaiah, proclaiming the promise of the Holy Spirit, says:

“Thus says the Lord who made heaven and fixed it in place, who established the earth and the things that are in it, who gives inspiration to the people who are upon it, and spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isa. 42:5).

Tell me: who is the people that receives inspiration? Do you also say here that inspiration is the soul? Or will you grant that a people was established upon the earth without a soul? But it is not so. For the prophet, proclaiming the promise of the Holy Spirit, said these things.

Finally, Luke wrote that the promise was fulfilled upon the believers who were living at that time:

“When the days of Pentecost had been completed, they were all together in one place. Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent wind being carried along, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting. And divided tongues appeared to them as of fire, and one rested upon each of them; and they began to speak in other languages, as the Spirit granted them utterance” (Acts 2:1 ff.).

In a similar way, the great Job also spoke against his friends, when they had been deprived of the Holy Spirit and said nothing true, nor supposed that they were speaking before God. Job therefore said: “Are you not speaking before God?” and again: “To whom have you announced your words? Whose inspiration is this that proceeds from you?” (Job 26:4).

One of them, speaking grandly, said: “It is the Spirit who intercedes for mortals; but the inspiration is the Almighty, who teaches me” (Job 32:8). The Almighty is immediately the Son of God, concerning whom Zechariah says: “Therefore thus says the Almighty: After the glory he sent me against the nations that plundered you” (Zech. 2:8).

Let us also hear Solomon saying: “The light of the Lord is the inspiration of human beings” (Prov. 20:27), and, instructed by Moses, that “the Lord breathed into Adam’s face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7).

But as we hear the Savior saying, “I am life” (John 14:6), and Paul writing, “For the law of the Spirit of life” (Rom. 8:2), and again, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying out” (Gal. 4:6); and as we see the Only-Begotten breathing upon the faces of the apostles and saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22), let us be taught that the inspiration of the Son, remaining in his own life and substance, is the Holy Spirit.

Let us believe that he was neither begotten nor created by the Son, and that he is not the Word of the Son. The Word of God, however, was begotten: the Son of God remains in his own life and substance, since he himself is life. Therefore the Spirit is not begotten by him, because he is not his word. But it is impious to call the Holy Spirit created. Nevertheless, we have been taught by the holy Scriptures that he is the inspiration of the Son of God.

We say that the Son of God is the fountain of the Holy Spirit, since the Son himself says through Jeremiah: “For this people has committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves cracked cisterns that could not hold water” (Jer. 2:13).

The living water is the Holy Spirit, as John taught that the Savior said to the Samaritan woman: “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is who says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water” (John 4:10); and again: “Whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will never thirst” (ibid.).

For in the middle of the temple he also cries out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7:37). And it was interpreted in this way: “He was speaking about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (ibid.).

Isaiah likewise says that the Lord declared: “For I will give water in thirst to those who have traveled in a dry land, and I will place my Spirit upon your seed, and my blessings upon your children; and they will spring up as grass beside water, and like a willow among streams of water” (Isa. 44:3).

Thus, with the holy Scriptures openly confessing that the living water is the Holy Spirit, we recognize this truth. The Lord said that he is the fountain of the Spirit in the words: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water” (Jer. 2:13).

David likewise sings in the thirty-fifth Psalm (v. 10), saying to the Lord: “For with you is the fountain of life.” Therefore, apart from the Lord, show another fountain of life that is with him. For he did not say, “You are the fountain of life,” but, “With you is the fountain of life.” “With you,” that is, with God; and the Son exists as the fountain of the Spirit.

Concerning this Paul writes to the Romans: “But the Spirit is life because of righteousness” (Rom. 8:10). Thus he calls the Spirit not alien but the Father’s own. For after he had confessed, “With you is the fountain of life,” he added, “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:10)—that is, “In your Son we shall see the Spirit.”

The Spirit is also called by the name of God’s power, and is shown to be life and wisdom. For we heard the Savior promising his disciples in the Gospel that he would send the Holy Spirit, saying to them: “Behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you; but remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49).

In the Acts of the Apostles the same Lord says: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you” (Acts 1:8). We later learn that this too was fulfilled when the fiftieth day had been completed.

Therefore either confess that the power of the Lord is the Holy Spirit, or, like Sabellius, since the Paraclete is the power of God, proclaim him to be the same as the Son of God. And as we hear Paul saying, “The Spirit is life because of righteousness” (Rom. 8:10), we are again taught that the Son is the fountain of the Spirit.

Again, the same author (In the Creed), that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

[**Note:** “The Father was made by no one.” These words are from the Creed of Athanasius, if indeed it already bore that name at that time. It was more usually called the Faith of Athanasius, or the Sermon on Faith, or the Exposition of the Faith of Athanasius. The uncertain author whom we mentioned, using this very testimony, says: “Blessed Athanasius, in the catholic exposition of the faith which that outstanding teacher himself composed, and which the universal Church confesses, declares the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, saying thus: ‘The Father was made by no one,’ and so forth.” The Greeks show that this was the ancient and proper designation, interpreting it as *ἔκθεσις* or *ὁμολογία τῆς καθολικῆς πίστεως* (“exposition” or “confession of the catholic faith”). The Latins later called it a creed; and I do not know whether Hincmar was the first of all to do so, in his work against Gottschalk, chapter 35. For this creed was held in such high esteem among the Gauls that Hincmar himself orders in his capitularies that it be entrusted to priests’ memory together with the Apostles’ Creed, as does the Synod of Autun for all clerics.]

The Father was made by no one, neither created nor begotten. The Son is from the Father alone, not made, nor created, but begotten. The Holy Spirit is from the Father and the Son, not made, nor created, nor begotten, but proceeding.

Therefore there is one Father, not three fathers; one Son, not three sons; one Holy Spirit, not three holy spirits. And in this Trinity there is nothing earlier or later, nothing greater or less, but all three persons are coeternal and coequal with one another. Thus, in all respects, as has already been said above, both the Trinity in unity and the unity in Trinity must be venerated. Whoever therefore wishes to be saved must think this way concerning the Trinity.

In his Epistle to Nestorius (Epistle 3, On Excommunication), Cyril says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son:

When he says concerning the Spirit, “He will glorify me” (John 16:14), we, rightly understanding this, confess one Christ and Son—not as though he needed another’s glory—to have received glory from the Holy Spirit, because his Spirit is not superior to him. But because, in performing wondrous works as a demonstration of his divinity, he used the Spirit by his own power, he is said to be glorified by him, just as one might assert of human beings that someone glorifies each person by his own power or discipline.

Although Christ exists in his own substance, and the personal property of the Spirit is understood according to the fact that he is Spirit and not Son, nevertheless the Spirit is not alien to Christ. For he is called the Spirit of truth, and Christ is the truth. Therefore the Spirit proceeds from Christ in the same way as from God the Father.

Finally, this same Spirit, performing glorious miracles even through the hands of the holy apostles, glorified God Jesus Christ after he had ascended into heaven. Christ was believed to be God by nature, effecting mighty works through his own Spirit; therefore he said: “He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:14).

The same Spirit is by no means said to be wise or powerful through participation in another, since he is perfect in every respect and entirely lacks nothing good. For this same Spirit is believed to be the Spirit of the Father’s power and wisdom, and therefore he is proved to be both the substance of power and wisdom itself.

Again, the same author in his dialogue held with Theodoret, bishop of Cyrus (Anathema IX, addressed to Euoptius), that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son:

We remember Christ openly saying concerning the Holy Spirit: “He will glorify me” (John 16:14). We know that the operation of the Holy Spirit overthrows the most wicked and unclean powers. But we do not say that he uses the Holy Spirit’s power as something alien, as each of the saints ultimately does. For he was and is his Spirit, just as he is the Spirit of the Father. Most holy Paul explains this sufficiently to us when he writes: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:8–9).

The Holy Spirit proceeds from God the Father, according to the Savior’s word, but he is not alien to the Son. For he has everything with the Father, and the Son himself taught this when he said concerning the Holy Spirit: “Everything that the Father has is mine. Therefore I said to you that he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you” (John 16:15).

Therefore the Holy Spirit will indeed glorify Jesus while he performs extraordinary works. Nevertheless, he is his Spirit, not an alien power, and he is not superior to him insofar as he is understood to be God.

Hilary teaches that the Holy Spirit’s proceeding from the Father and receiving from the Son is one and the same thing as being sent, in the eighth book On the Trinity:

“When the Advocate comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from my Father, he will testify about me” (John 15:26). The Advocate will come, and the Son will send him from the Father; and he is the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father.

Let every school of heretics sharpen the goads of its ingenuity and now seek what it might be able to lie about to the ignorant, and let it explain what it means that the Son sends him from the Father. Whoever sends displays his authority in the one whom he sends. But what do we understand by the fact that he sends him from the Father? Does it mean received, released, or begotten? For one of these must necessarily be signified by the one whom he is going to send from the Father, and he is going to send from the Father that Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father.

But where procession has been demonstrated, there is no reception. It remains for us to confirm our judgment concerning him: whether we should understand this as the going forth of one who subsists, or as the procession of one who has been begotten.

Nor, in this matter, do I now constrain the freedom of understanding by arguing whether they think the Paraclete Spirit is from the Father or from the Son. For the Lord did not leave the matter uncertain. In the same discourse he spoke as follows:

“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all truth. For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will announce to you things to come. He will glorify me, because he will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said, ‘He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you’” (John 16:12–15).

He therefore receives from the Son, because he is sent by him, and he proceeds from the Father. And I ask whether receiving from the Son is the same thing as proceeding from the Father. If it is believed that there is no difference between receiving from the Son and proceeding from the Father, then receiving from the Son will certainly be considered the same and one thing as receiving from the Father.

For the Lord himself says: “He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said, ‘He will receive from what is mine and will announce it to you’” (John 16:14–15).

Whatever it is that he will receive—whether power, strength, or teaching—the Son said that it was to be received from him, and again he signifies that this same thing is to be received from the Father. For when he says that everything the Father has is his, and that for this reason he said that it would be received from his own, he also teaches that it is to be received from the Father, yet is received from him, because everything that belongs to the Father belongs to him.

This unity has no diversity, nor does it matter from whom that which was given by the Father is said to have been received, whether from the Father or from the Son. Is the unity of will alone being asserted here? Everything that the Father has belongs to the Son, and everything that belongs to the Son belongs to the Father. For he himself says: “Everything that is mine is yours, and what is yours is mine” (John 16:15).

This is not yet the place to demonstrate why he said, “He will receive from what is mine.” The expression indicates a future time, when he is shown as going to receive. At present, however, he says that he will receive from him for this reason: that everything belonging to the Father was his.

Dissect, if you can, the unity of this nature, and introduce some necessity of dissimilarity by which the Son would not be in unity of nature. For the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, but he is sent by the Son and by the Father. Everything that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son; and therefore whatever he receives, the one who is to be sent receives from the Son, because everything belonging to the Father belongs to the Son.

Nature therefore preserves its law in all things. What both are as one is a manifestation in both of the same divinity through generation and birth, since the Son acknowledges that what the Spirit of truth receives from the Father is to be given by him.

Again, the same author on the sending of the Holy Spirit by the Son, in the book On Synods, which he wrote to Germany, Belgic Gaul, Lyonnaise, Narbonese, Novempopulania, Toulouse, and Britain:

We believe in the Holy Spirit, that is, the Paraclete, whom, after promising him to his apostles, the Son sent after his return to heaven, to teach them and remind them of everything. Through him the souls of those who sincerely believe in him are sanctified.

Again, the same author in the same book, in the exposition of the same faith:

If anyone, while calling the Holy Spirit the Paraclete, calls him the unbegotten God, let him be anathema. The addition of the word “Paraclete” now makes the proclamation that he is the unbegotten God liable to anathema. For it is utterly impious to call him the unbegotten God who was sent by the Son for our consolation.

If anyone, as the Lord taught us, does not say that the Paraclete is another than the Son—for he said, “And the Father will send you another Paraclete, whom I will ask him to send” (John 14:16)—let him be anathema.

We remember that the Paraclete was sent by the Son, and the faith itself stated this at the beginning. But because the Son frequently said that his own works were the Father’s works through the power of their undifferentiated nature, saying, “I do the works of my Father” (John 10:37), when he was also going to send the Paraclete, as he frequently promised, he sometimes said that the Paraclete was to be sent by the Father, since he was accustomed piously to refer everything he did to the Father.

From this heretics frequently seize an opportunity to say that the Paraclete is the Son himself, whereas, in saying that he would ask the Father to send another Paraclete, he indicates a distinction between the one who is sent and the one who asks.

If anyone says that the Holy Spirit is a part of the Father or of the Son, let him be anathema. The foolishness of heretical frenzy compelled these matters to be recorded in writing—not a question of inquiry. For since the name “Holy Spirit” has its own meaning, and since the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, has both the function and the order of his own substance, and since the immutable Father and Son are proclaimed everywhere, how can the Holy Spirit be asserted to be a part of either the Father or the Son?

But because, among the other kinds of madness, this too is often put forward by the impious, it had to be rejected by the holy ones.

If anyone says that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three gods, let him be anathema.

Ambrose teaches that the Holy Spirit does not pass from place to place when he proceeds from the Father and the Son, in the first book that he wrote to the emperor Gratian (Chapter 10):

For if the Spirit proceeds from a place and passes to a place, and the Father himself is found in a place, and likewise the Son, if the Spirit exits from the place from which the Father or the Son sends him, then the Spirit, passing and proceeding from a place, appears—according to impious interpretations—to leave behind both the Father, as though he were a body, and the Son.

I speak in accordance with those who think that the Spirit has a downward-moving motion. But the Father, who is above all things—not only corporeal nature but also invisible creation—is not confined within any place. Nor is the Son enclosed by the places or times of his works, since he is above every creature and the maker of the whole creation.

Nor is the Spirit of truth, as the Spirit of God, confined by any bodily boundaries. Since he is incorporeal, he surpasses every intelligible created substance by the ineffable fullness of divinity, breathing where he wills and inspiring as he wills, possessing authority over all things.

Therefore the Spirit is not sent as though from a place, nor does he proceed as though from a place when he proceeds from the Son. Likewise, when the Son himself says, “I came forth from the Father and have come” (John 8:42), he destroys all opinions that suppose movement from place to place, as can be considered with respect to certain bodily things.

Similarly, when we read that God is either within or outside, we do not confine God within some body or separate him from some body. Rather, weighing this with profound and ineffable understanding, we comprehend the mystery of the divine nature.

Finally, Wisdom says that she came forth from the mouth of the Most High in such a way that she is not outside the Father but with the Father, because “the Word was with God” (John 1:1). Not only with the Father, but also from the Father; for he says: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 10:38).

But when he comes forth from the Father, he does not withdraw from him as though from a place, nor is he separated as body from body. Nor, when he is in the Father, is he enclosed in him as body in body.

The Holy Spirit likewise, when he proceeds from the Father and the Son, is not separated from the Father and is not separated from the Son. For how can he be separated from the Father, since he is the Spirit of his mouth? This expresses both a sign of eternity and the unity of divinity.

He therefore exists and always remains the Spirit who is of the mouth. Yet he appears to descend when we receive him so that he may dwell in us, lest we be alien from his grace. It appears that he descends to us—not that he descends, but that our mind ascends to him.

We would speak more fully about this if we did not remember that the earlier books already stated that the Father said, “Come, let us descend and confuse their languages” (Gen. 11:7), and that the Son said: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23).

Thus the Spirit comes in the same way as the Father comes, because where the Father is, there also is the Son, and where the Son is, there also is the Spirit. The Holy Spirit therefore should not be thought to come separately.

He comes not from place to place, but from the disposition of the established order to the salvation of redemption, from the grace of being made alive to the grace of sanctification: so that he may transfer us from earth to heaven, from dishonor to glory, and from servitude to the kingdom.

Thus the Spirit comes in the same way as the Father comes. For the Son said: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him.” Did the Father come bodily? Therefore the Spirit also comes in this way: when he comes, the full presence of both the Father and the Son is in him.

Who, moreover, can separate the Spirit from the Father and the Son, since we cannot even name the Father and the Son without the Spirit? “No one can say, ‘Lord Jesus,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3).

Therefore, if we cannot name the Lord Jesus without the Spirit, we certainly cannot proclaim him without the Spirit. But if the angels too proclaim the Lord Jesus, whom no one can proclaim without the Spirit, then the gift of the Holy Spirit also operates in them.

We have therefore proved that the presence of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is one, and their grace is one—so heavenly and divine that for this reason the Son gives thanks to the Father, saying: “I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10:21).

Again, the same author in the third book (Chapter 1), that the Holy Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son, where “sending” is understood as “procession”:

The Father also sent the Spirit, and the Son sent him. The Father sent him, because it is written: “But the Paraclete, that Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name” (John 14:26). The Son sent him, because he said: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from my Father, the Spirit of truth” (John 15:26).

Therefore, if the Son and the Spirit send one another, just as the Father sends, this is not an insult of subordination but a sharing of authority (Chapter 2).

The Father not only sent the Son but also gave him, just as the Son gave himself. For it is written: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins” (Gal. 1:3).

If they think that he was subordinate because he was sent, they cannot deny that he is an object of grace because he was given. He was given by the Father, as Isaiah said: “A child has been born to us; a son has been given to us” (Isa. 9:6).

I dare to say that he was also given by the Spirit, who was sent by the Spirit. Since he did not specify by whom he was given, he showed that he was given by the grace of the Trinity.

But when the Son himself gave himself, he certainly could not, according to his divinity, be subject to himself. Therefore what was given could not involve divine subjection.

The Holy Spirit also was given, since it is written: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16); and the Apostle says: “Therefore whoever rejects these things rejects not a human being but God, who has given his Spirit in us” (1 Thess. 4:8).

Isaiah likewise shows that both the Spirit and the Son were given. He says:

“Thus says the Lord who made heaven and fixed it in place, who established the earth and the things that are in it, and gives the Spirit to the people who are upon it, and spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isa. 42:5).

And concerning the Son:

“I, the Lord God, have called you in righteousness; I will hold your hand, strengthen you, and have given you as a covenant for my people, as a light for the nations, to open the eyes of the blind and lead the bound out of their chains” (ibid., v. 6).

Therefore, since the Son has been sent and given, and the Spirit likewise has been given and sent, they certainly possess unity of divinity, because they possess unity of operation. Hence the Spirit has also been called the finger of God.

Again, the same author in the same book (Chapter 20), that the river proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb is the Holy Spirit, whereby his procession from the Father and the Son is understood:

The Spirit therefore possesses what Christ possesses. He therefore possesses what God possesses, because everything that the Father has the Son also has. For this reason he said: “Everything that the Father has is mine” (John 16:15).

Nor is this a minor matter: we read that a river goes forth from the throne of God. For, as you have it in the words of John the Evangelist:

“He showed me a river of living water, bright as crystal, proceeding from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and in the midst of its street and on either side was the tree of life, producing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit each month; and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of all the nations” (Rev. 22:1–2).

This is certainly the river proceeding from the throne of God—that is, the Holy Spirit, whom the one who believes in Christ drinks, as he himself says:

“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” This he said concerning the Spirit (John 7:37–39).

Therefore the Spirit is the river.

Him also, as proceeding from the Father, Jerome teaches in the book of Didymus (Book II, near the beginning), which he translated from Greek into Latin. He teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and is sent by the Son, not according to the ministry of angels, prophets, and apostles, but as it is fitting that the Spirit of God should be sent by the Wisdom of God; from this it follows that he proceeds also from the Son.

Since, then, the Holy Spirit is taught to inhabit the mind and the inner person, in the same way as the Father and the Son, it is not merely foolish but impious to call him a creature. Disciplines, virtues—I mean arts—and their contrary disturbances, ignorances, and affections can indeed dwell in souls, [Col. 0253B] but not as subsistent entities [some books: substances], but as acceding qualities. It is impossible, however, for a created nature to dwell in the understanding. If this is true, and the Holy Spirit, subsisting without any ambiguity, is an inhabitant of the soul and of the heart, no one can doubt that he must be believed, together with the Father and the Son, to be uncreated. From everything, therefore, that the preceding discussion has set forth, the Holy Spirit has been shown to be incorruptible and eternal according to the nature of the Father and the Son. He has removed every ambiguity concerning himself, as well as the suspicion that he who is the Spirit of God might be one of the created substances—the Spirit whom the words of the Savior in the Gospel declare to proceed from the Father: “When the Comforter comes,” he says, “whom I will send to you, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he himself will bear witness concerning me” (John XV, 26). [Col. 0253C]

He calls the Holy Spirit who comes the Comforter, giving him this name from his operation, because he not only comforts those whom he finds worthy of himself and makes them strangers to every sadness and disturbance, but also bestows upon them an incredible joy and gladness, to such an extent that a person, giving thanks to God for being deemed worthy of such a guest, may say, “You have put gladness in my heart” (Psalm IV, 7). For eternal joy dwells in the hearts of those whose inhabitant is the Holy Spirit. This Spirit, the Comforter, is sent by the Son, not according to the ministry of angels, prophets, and apostles, but as it is fitting that the Spirit of God should be sent by Wisdom and Truth, possessing an undivided substance with that same Wisdom and Truth [some books: “with the Father and the Son”].

[Col. 0253D] The same author in the same book, shortly afterward.

Although the Savior frequently says that he has come forth from God, he nevertheless assumes from the name of the Father the special relationship and, so to speak, intimacy about which we have often spoken, saying, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV, 11), and elsewhere, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30), together with many similar statements, which a careful reader will find by observing the Gospel. This Holy Spirit, therefore, who proceeds from the Father, will, the Lord says, “bear witness concerning me” (John XV, 26), bearing testimony similar to that of the Father, of whom he says, “The Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John VIII, 18). When the Son sends the Spirit of truth, whom he called the Comforter, the Father also sends him at the same time; [Col. 0254A] for the Father does not fail to send when the Son sends, since the Spirit comes by the same will of the Father and the Son. The Savior also speaks through the prophet, as will be clear to anyone who reads the entire passage: “And now the Lord God has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah XLVIII, 16). For God sent not only the Son but also the Spirit. The Apostle likewise says: “The things that have now been announced to you through those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven” (I Peter I, 12).

And in the Wisdom entitled *Panaretos*, a voice giving thanks to God is uttered by those who have received divine gifts: “But the things that are in heaven, who has searched them out? And who has known your will, unless you gave wisdom and sent your holy Spirit from on high? And thus the paths of those who were on [Col. 0254B] earth were made straight, and human beings were taught the things pleasing to you” (Wisdom IX, 16). In the present reading also, it is not only the Wisdom of God—that is, his only-begotten Son—that is given by the Father, but the Holy Spirit too is sent. In the same Gospel it is proclaimed that the Holy Spirit is given by the Father and sent, the Savior saying: “And I will ask my Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John XIV, 16); and again: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything” (ibid., verse 26). For in these sayings the Father is said to give “another Paraclete,” not another in relation to the one sent by the Son, according to the statement: “But when that Paraclete comes whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth” (John XV, 26). He called him “another Paraclete,” not according to a difference of nature, but according to a diversity of operation.

The same author in the same work (Book II), shortly afterward.

Since, then, the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father in the name of the Son, possessing the Son’s property insofar as he is God, though not sonship, so that he might be his Son, he shows by what unity he is joined to the Son. Hence he is also called the Spirit of the Son, making those who wished to receive him sons through adoption. “Because you are sons,” he says, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians IV, 6). This Holy Spirit, who came sent by the Father in the name of the Son, will teach everything to those who are perfect in the faith of Christ. By “everything” he means all spiritual and intellectual things, and, to sum up everything briefly, all the mysteries of truth and wisdom. He will teach not as a doctor and teacher of a discipline that he acquired elsewhere—for that is characteristic of those who have learned wisdom and particular arts through diligence and study—but as the art and teaching itself, and as the Spirit of wisdom and truth, invisibly instilling knowledge of divine things into the mind.

The same author in the same work (Book II), shortly afterward.

Then, introducing an interpretation of how he had said, “He will take from what is mine,” he immediately added: “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said, ‘He will take from what is mine and will announce it to you’” (John XVI, 15). He speaks, as it were, in this way: Although the Spirit of truth proceeds from the Father, [Col. 0255A] and God gives the Holy Spirit to those who ask him, nevertheless, because everything that the Father has is mine, this very Spirit of the Father is mine as well, and he will take from what is mine. But when these things are said, beware lest you fall through a perverse understanding into error and suppose that there is some object or possession held by the Father and the Son. Rather, whatever the Father has according to substance—that is, eternity, immutability, incorruption, immortality, and goodness subsisting from itself and in itself—the Son has these same things. And, to go further, whatever the Son himself subsists as, and whatever belongs to the Son, the Father likewise has.

The same author in the same work (Book II, near the end).

“But you,” he says—without doubt addressing the disciples of Christ, who have received the wisdom of the Spirit, and life and [Col. 0255B] peace—“are not in the flesh” (Romans VIII, 9), that is, in the works of the flesh; for you do not commit its works, since you have the Spirit of God within you. This same Spirit of God is also the Spirit of Christ, bringing and joining to the Lord Jesus Christ the one who possesses him. Hence it is written in what follows: “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this person does not belong to him” (ibid.). Again, in the present passage we learn the fellowship that the Holy Spirit has with Christ and with God. In Peter’s Epistle also, the Holy Spirit is shown to be the Spirit of Christ: “Searching and investigating,” he says—that is, the prophets of whom he had spoken above—“into what or what sort of time the Spirit of Christ who was in them was indicating, testifying to the sufferings in Christ and the decrees that were to follow afterward; to them it was revealed [Col. 0255C] that they were serving not themselves but us in the things that have now been announced to you through the Holy Spirit” (I Peter I, 11–12).

This Holy Spirit is also called the Spirit of God, not only in the present passage but in very many other places, as in the statement: “No one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (I Corinthians II, 11). Then, after the statement, “But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this person does not belong to him” (Romans VIII, 9), there follows: “But if Christ is in you.” And it is most clearly demonstrated that the Holy Spirit is inseparable from Christ, because wherever the Holy Spirit is, there also is Christ, and from wherever the Spirit of Christ departs, Christ likewise departs. For if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him. If someone were to assume the contrary of this and say, “If anyone belongs to Christ, so that Christ is in him, in that person is the Spirit of God,” the same reasoning must also be applied to God the Father. If anyone does not have the Spirit of God, that person does not belong to him. Again, someone may assume the contrary and say, “If anyone belongs to God, in that person is the Spirit of God.” Hence it is written: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (I Corinthians III, 16). And in the Epistle of John, God is recognized as dwelling in certain people when the Spirit whom he gave them remains in them. From all these passages the indivisible and inseparable substance of the Trinity is demonstrated.

The same author in the same work (Book III, at the end), shortly afterward.

Since, then, Holy Scripture says no more about the Trinity than that God is the Father of the Savior and that the Son was begotten by the Father, we must believe only what is written. Once it has been shown that the Holy Spirit is uncreated, we must consequently understand that the one whose substance is not created is rightly joined to the Father and the Son. These statements, made here according to the poverty of our speech, may suffice for the present.

Augustine, on the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, says the following in the book he wrote against the heretic Maximinus (Book III, chapter 17, near the end):

“You appear to yourself to be saying something important when you say, ‘The Son was in the beginning before anything existed, but the Father was before the beginning.’ Where did you read this, that you should believe it? From where did you presume to say it, when there is neither authority nor reason for it? For what is ‘before the beginning’? Whatever existed before would itself be the beginning. If, then, the Father is before the beginning, he is before himself, because he himself is also the beginning.

“But what does ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (John I, 1) mean except that the Son was in the Father? And when the Jews asked that same Son who he was, he answered, ‘The beginning, who also speaks to you’ (John VIII, 25). The Father, therefore, is beginning, not from beginning; the Son is beginning from beginning. Yet the two together are not two beginnings but one beginning. Just as the Father is God and the Son is God, but the two together are not two gods but one God, so I will not deny that the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, is also beginning. But these three together, just as I say that they are one God, so I say that they are one beginning.”

The same author in the same book (Book III, chapter 9).

[Col. 0256C] “You ask me: If the Son is from the substance of the Father, and the Holy Spirit is also from the substance of the Father, why is one the Son and the other not the Son? Behold, I answer, whether you understand or do not understand. The Son is from the Father; the Holy Spirit is from the Father. But the one is begotten, while the other proceeds. Therefore the one is the Son of the Father from whom he was begotten, while the other is the Spirit of both, because he proceeds from both.

“But when he was speaking of the Spirit, he said, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John XV, 26), because the Father is the source of his procession: he who begot such a Son gave him, by begetting him, that the Holy Spirit should proceed also from him. For unless he proceeded also from the Son, the Son would not say to the disciples, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John XX, 22), and would not give him by breathing upon them, thereby openly showing through his breathing what he was giving secretly through his inspiration, signifying that the Spirit proceeds also from himself.

“If he were born not only from the Father or not only from the Son, but from both, he would certainly be called the Son of both. Accordingly, because in no way is he the Son of both, he ought not to be born from both. The Holy Spirit, therefore, belongs to both, proceeding from both.

“But who can explain, speaking of that most excellent nature, what the difference is between being born and proceeding? Not everything that proceeds is born, although everything that is born proceeds—just as not everything that is two-footed is human, although everyone who is human is two-footed. I know this distinction; but I do not know, cannot, and am not capable of distinguishing between that generation and this procession. Therefore, since both are ineffable, just as the prophet says of the Son, ‘Who will recount his generation?’ (Isaiah LIII, 8), so it is most truly said of the Holy Spirit: ‘Who will recount his procession?’

“Let it suffice for us, then, that the Son is not from himself but from him of whom he was born; and that the Holy Spirit is not from himself but from him from whom he proceeds—and because he proceeds from both, as we have already shown. Hence he is called the Spirit of the Father, where it is written: ‘But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you’ (Romans VIII, 11); and the Spirit of the Son, where it is written: ‘But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this person does not belong to him’ (Romans VIII, 9).

“For there are not two Holy Spirits, as though they were individually one for each—one the Father’s and the other the Son’s—but rather one Spirit of the Father and the Son. Of this one Spirit it is written: ‘For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slaves or free, and we all drank one Spirit’ (I Corinthians XII, 13); and elsewhere: ‘One body and one Spirit’ (Ephesians IV, 4). What, then, is this Trinity except of one and the same substance? For the Son is not from some matter or from nothing, but from him from whom he was begotten; likewise the Holy Spirit is not from some matter or from nothing, but from where he proceeds.”

The same author in the book *On the Incarnation of the Lord* [Note: In the Appendix to volume IV of Saint Augustine there are two books *On the Incarnation of the Word*; but these statements cited by Theodulf are not found in them].

“And the Holy Spirit likewise is neither unbegotten nor begotten, but proceeds from the Father and the Son, since he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son; he himself is consubstantial and coeternal with both. Nor was the Holy Spirit whom he gave by breathing upon them one Spirit and the one whom he sent after his ascension another. For there is one Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit, the same God who works all things in all, so that the Trinity is believed to be perfect on account of the distinct properties of the persons, and one God on account of the inseparable Trinity.”

The same author, in the book [Saint Fulgentius’] *Exposition of the Faith to Peter* (chapter 1).

“Just as, then, the Son is neither later nor lesser than the Father, so the Holy Spirit is neither later nor lesser than the Son. For eternal and without beginning is the fact that the Son came forth born from the Father’s nature; and eternal and without beginning is the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the nature of the Father and the Son. Therefore we rightly believe and say that the three are one God, because there is wholly one eternity, one immensity, and naturally one divinity of the three persons. Let us therefore hold that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are naturally one God. Nevertheless, the Father himself is not the one who is the Son, nor is the Son himself the one who is the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit himself the one who is the Father or the Son. For there is one essence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, which the Greeks call *οὐσία* (*ousia*, ‘essence’).”

The same author in the same work, shortly afterward (chapter 1, near the end).

“In that holy Trinity, therefore—a point repeated by us so often that it may be fixed more firmly in your heart—there is one God the Father, who alone essentially begot one Son from himself; and one Son, who alone was essentially begotten from one Father; and one Holy Spirit, who alone essentially proceeds from the Father and the Son. But all this could not belong to one person: namely, both to beget oneself, to be born from oneself, and to proceed from oneself. Since, then, to have begotten is one thing, to have been born another, and to proceed is something different from both begetting and being born, it is clear that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.”

The same author likewise in the same work (chapter 2, at the beginning).

“For in that Trinity it would not be proper to the Father alone that he himself was not born but begot one Son; nor would it be proper to the Son alone that he himself did not beget but alone was born from the Father’s essence; nor would it be proper to the Holy Spirit that he himself was neither born nor begot, but alone proceeds from the Father and the Son in unchangeable eternity [Note: The printed editions of Fulgentius omit ‘in unchangeable eternity’].”

The same author in the same work (chapter 11).

“Hold most firmly, and do not doubt in any way, that the same Holy Spirit, who is the one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeds from the Father and the Son. For the Son says: ‘When the Spirit of truth comes, who proceeds from the Father’ (John XV, 26), where he taught that the Spirit is his, because he himself is the truth.

“That the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son is commended to us by prophetic and apostolic teaching. Isaiah says of the Son: ‘He will strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the Spirit of his lips he will kill the wicked’ (Isaiah XI, 4). Of this the Apostle also says: ‘Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the Spirit of his mouth’ (II Thessalonians II, 8). Whom the only Son [the editions add: ‘of God’] himself also shows to be the Spirit of his mouth [the editions read: ‘showing’], when, after his resurrection, he breathed upon his disciples and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John XX, 22).

“Of the mouth of the Lord Jesus John says in the Apocalypse that it was a two-edged sword (Revelation I, 16). The Spirit of his mouth is himself the sword that proceeds from his mouth [the edition: ‘the sword, sharp on both sides, proceeded’].”

The same author, in the disputation (118, among Augustine’s letters) that he held against Pascentius, a count of the Arians, in the presence of Laurence, the judge chosen by both sides.

[Col. 0258D] “Behold what *ὁμοούσιον* (*homoousion*, ‘consubstantial’) means, which is unjustly made a reproach. For it is not merely a word, but also the reality expressed in the word; it is not merely speech sounding in the ears, but one substance that must be believed in the minds. If, among human beings who believe in him, God in his entirety is believed to dwell, how can the Father not be believed to receive the Son in his entirety, or the Son the Father in his entirety? Accordingly, he himself remains in the Father, and the Father in him; and the Holy Spirit must be believed not only to have proceeded from the Father or the Son [the printed editions of Augustine: ‘from the Father out of the Son’], but always to proceed wholly for carrying out the works of the Trinity.”

[Col. 0259A] The same author, saying that the Holy Spirit is in the Father and the Son, speaks as follows in the book he wrote against the Pagans, Jews, Manichaeans, Sabellians, and Arians:

“We have spoken about the Father and the Son as much as we could, and as far as we could—if indeed we were able to say anything worthily. We have been silent about the Holy Spirit, but not because we passed him over [the editions: ‘separated him’]. For whatever we have said about the Father and the Son, we have also said about the Holy Spirit. He is in them and with them, one equal and true God, not a lesser or third God.

“What more should I say, exhausted as I am, to those who are exhausted? Whoever separates the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son in eternity and substance or communion, and denies that he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, is full of an unclean spirit and empty of the Holy Spirit. For this is why it is said, ‘God is love’ (I John IV, 8): he does not divide unity into parts, but ineffably binds the Trinity together. For the Trinity itself is one God, a tower of strength against the enemy, who guards those who believe in him forever and ever.”

The same author, teaching that the Holy Spirit belongs both to the Father and to the Son and is coequal, consubstantial, and coeternal with the Father and the Son, says the following in Book I, chapter 4, *On the Trinity Which Is God*:

“All the Catholic interpreters of the divine books, old and new, whom I have been able to read and who wrote about the Trinity, which is God, intended to teach according to the Scriptures that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, by an inseparable equality of one and the same substance, signify the divine unity. Therefore they are not three gods but one God, although the Father begot the Son and therefore is not the Son; and the Son was begotten by the Father and therefore is not the Father; and the Holy Spirit is neither the Father nor the Son, but solely the Spirit of the Father and the Son, himself also coequal with the Father and the Son and belonging to the unity of the Trinity.”

The same author in the same book (chapter 8), saying that the Holy Spirit is inseparably the Spirit of the Father and the Son, and that, since this is so, it is a great madness not to profess that he proceeds from the Father and the Son:

“Finally, because of this very inseparability, sometimes only the Father is named, or only the Son is named, as the one who will fill us with joy by his countenance; yet the Spirit of both—that is, the Spirit of the Father and the Son—is not thereby separated. This Spirit is properly called the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive (John XIV, 17). For this is our complete joy, beyond which there is no more: to enjoy the Trinity, God, in whose image we were made.

“For this reason he sometimes speaks of the Holy Spirit as though he alone were sufficient for our blessedness. And he is sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Son. The Father likewise is sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Son and the Holy Spirit; and the Son is sufficient alone because he cannot be separated from the Father and the Holy Spirit.”

The same author in Book III (in the prologue), saying that the Holy Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son:

“When we had come to the point at which we wished to show that the Son is not therefore lesser than the Father because the Father sent and the Son was sent, nor that the Holy Spirit is therefore lesser than both because he is read in the Gospel to have been sent both by the one and by the other, we undertook to inquire into this. The Son was sent to a place where he already was, since he came into this world and was in this world; likewise the Holy Spirit was sent to a place where he also already was, since ‘the Spirit of the Lord has filled the world,’ and that which contains all things has knowledge of the voice (Wisdom I, 7).”

The same author clearly teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son as well as from the Father, in Book IV of the same work (chapter 20):

“When the Father is known by someone in time, he is not said to be sent; for he does not have one from whom he is or from whom he proceeds. Wisdom says: ‘I came forth from the mouth of the Most High’ (Ecclesiasticus XXIV, 5), and of the Holy Spirit it is said, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John XV, 26), but the Father is from no one. Just as, then, the Father begot and the Son was begotten, so the Father sent and the Son was sent. But just as the one who begot and the one who was begotten are one, because the Father and the Son are one, so the Holy Spirit is also one with them, because these three are one.

“For just as being born is, for the Son, being from the Father, so being sent is, for the Son, being recognized as being from him. And just as being the gift of God is, for the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father, so being sent is being recognized as proceeding from him.

“Nor can we say that the Holy Spirit does not also proceed from the Son; for it is not without reason that the same Spirit is called the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. Nor do I see what else he wished to signify when, breathing upon the faces of the disciples, he said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John XX, 22). For that bodily breath, proceeding from the body and touching the body with a bodily sensation, was not the substance of the Holy Spirit; rather, it was a demonstration through an appropriate sign that the Holy Spirit proceeds not only from the Father but also from the Son.

“For who, utterly deranged, would say that the Holy Spirit whom he gave by breathing was one, and the one whom he sent after his ascension another? For there is one Spirit, the Spirit of God, the Spirit of the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit, who works all things in all.”

The same author in Book VI (chapter 10), saying that the Holy Spirit is the sweetness of the Son and the Father; hence whoever denies that he proceeds from both must consequently deny [Col. 0260D] that sweetness proceeds from the Father and the Son:

“That love, delight, happiness, or blessedness—if indeed it can be worthily expressed in any human word—is called, in brief, “use” by him, and in the Trinity is the Holy Spirit: not begotten, but the sweetness of the begetter and the begotten, pouring over all creatures with immense generosity and abundance according to their capacity, so that they may keep their proper order and rest in their proper places. All these things, therefore, which have been made by divine art both display in themselves a certain unity, form, and order. For whatever one of these things is, it is also one thing.”

The same author in Book XV (chapter 17), saying that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son:

“I do not know why, just as Wisdom is said to be both the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, while all together they are not three wisdoms but one Wisdom, so love should not likewise be said to be the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, while all together they are one love. For the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; yet all together they are one God.

“Nevertheless, it is not without reason that in this Trinity the Word of God is said to be the Son alone, the gift of God the Holy Spirit alone, and the one from whom the Word was begotten and from whom the Holy Spirit principally proceeds is God the Father alone. I added ‘principally’ because the Holy Spirit is also found to proceed from the Son. But the Father also gave this to him—not to one who already existed and did not yet possess it, but whatever he gave to the only-begotten Word, he gave by begetting him. Thus he begot him in such a way that the common gift would also proceed from him and the Holy Spirit would be the Spirit of both.

“This distinction of the inseparable Trinity, therefore, must not be passed over casually but must be examined carefully.”

The same author in the same book (chapter 26):

“Then, in that supreme Trinity which is God, there are no intervals of time by which it could be shown, or even asked, whether the Son was first born from the Father and afterward the Holy Spirit proceeded from both, since Holy Scripture calls him the Spirit of both. For he is the one of whom the Apostle says: ‘Because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts’ (Galatians IV, 6). And he is the one of whom the same Son says: ‘For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you’ (Matthew X, 20). By many other testimonies of the divine utterances it is also proved that he who is properly called the Holy Spirit in the Trinity is the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

“Of him the Son himself likewise says: ‘Whom I will send to you from the Father’ (John XV, 26); and in another place: ‘Whom the Father will send in my name’ (John XIV, 26). That he proceeds from both is taught as follows: the Son himself says, ‘He proceeds from the Father’; and when he had risen from the dead and appeared to his disciples, he breathed upon them and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’ (John XX, 22), so that he might show that the Spirit proceeds also from himself. He is also the power that went out from him and healed everyone, as we read in the Gospel (Luke VI, 19).

“But what the reason was that after his resurrection he first gave the Holy Spirit on earth and afterward sent him from heaven, I believe to be this: through that gift of God, love is poured into our hearts, by which we love God and our neighbor, according to those two commandments on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend. Signifying this, the Lord Jesus gave the Holy Spirit twice: once on earth, on account of love of neighbor, and again from heaven, on account of love of God.”

The same author in the same book (the same chapter), shortly afterward.

Can we therefore ask whether the Holy Spirit had already proceeded from the Father when the Son was born, or had not yet proceeded, and whether, after the Son was born, he proceeded from both, where there are no temporal intervals? We could ask this where we find temporal succession: namely, whether the will first proceeds from the human mind, so that what has been found may be called offspring; for once that will has been produced or begotten, it is brought to completion, coming to rest in this end: that what had been the desire of one seeking should be the love of one enjoying; and that it should then proceed from both—that is, from the generating mind and from the begotten conception—as from parent and offspring.

Such questions cannot at all be raised there where nothing begins in time in order to be completed subsequently in time. Therefore, whoever can understand the Son’s generation from the Father without time should understand the Holy Spirit’s procession from both without time. And whoever can understand that, in the words of the Son, “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26), the Father did not give life to the Son as though the Son had previously existed without life, but begot him without time in such a way that the life which the Father gave the Son by begetting him is coeternal with the life of the Father who gave it—let that person understand likewise that, just as the Father has in himself the power for the Holy Spirit to proceed from him, so he gave the Son that the same Holy Spirit should proceed from him also. Both occur without time. Thus the statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father is to be understood in such a way that what also proceeds from the Son is from the Father and from the Son.

For if whatever the Son has, he has from the Father, then surely he has from the Father the fact that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. But no temporal intervals are to be conceived there—intervals that involve a before and an after—because there are absolutely none there. How, then, would it not be most absurd to say that the Holy Spirit is the Son of both, since, just as the generation of the Son from the Father gives the Son his essence without any beginning in time and without any change of nature, so the procession from both gives the Holy Spirit his essence without any beginning in time and without any change of nature?

For this reason, although we do not call the Holy Spirit begotten, we nevertheless do not dare to call him unbegotten, lest in that term someone suspect either two fathers in that Trinity or two who are not from another. For the Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called “unbegotten”—not, indeed, in Scripture, but in the customary usage of disputants, who express themselves about so great a matter as they are able.

The Son, however, was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds principally from the Father and, with the Father giving without any temporal interval, proceeds jointly from both. He would be called the Son of the Father and the Son if—as all sound minds reject—both had begotten him. He is therefore not begotten from both, but the Spirit of both proceeds from both.

Yet because in that coeternal, equal, incorporeal, ineffably immutable, and inseparable Trinity it is extremely difficult to distinguish generation from procession, let what we said on this subject in a certain discourse delivered to the ears of the Christian people, and then committed to writing, suffice for the time being for those who cannot extend their inquiry further.

Among other things, after I had demonstrated through the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures that the Holy Spirit proceeds from both, I said: “If, then, the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, why did the Son say, ‘He proceeds from the Father’ (John 15:26)? Why do you think, unless it is because he is accustomed to refer to the Father even what belongs to himself, since he himself is also from the Father? Hence the statement: ‘My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me’ (John 7:16). If here the teaching is understood to be his, although he said that it was not his but the Father’s, how much more must the Holy Spirit be understood to proceed also from him in the passage where he said, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ without saying, ‘He does not proceed from me’?

“From the one from whom the Son has that he is God—for he is God from God—from him he certainly has also that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. And consequently, for the Holy Spirit to proceed also from the Son, just as he proceeds from the Father, he has this from the Father.

“Here, too, we understand, insofar as such matters can be understood by people like us, why the Holy Spirit is not said to have been born but rather to proceed. For if he too were called a son, he would necessarily be called the son of both, which is utterly absurd. No one is the son of two unless he is the son of a father and a mother. But far be it from us to suspect anything of this kind between God the Father and God the Son, since not even a human son proceeds simultaneously from father and mother: when he proceeds from the father into the mother, he does not then proceed from the mother; and when he proceeds from the mother into this light, he does not then proceed from the father.

“The Holy Spirit, however, does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son toward the sanctification of creation; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both, although the Father gave this to the Son, so that he should proceed from the Son also, just as he proceeds from the Father. For we cannot say that the Holy Spirit is not life, since the Father is life and the Son is life. Consequently, just as the Father, having life in himself, gave the Son to have life in himself, so he gave him to be life proceeding from him, just as the Holy Spirit proceeds from him.”

I have transferred these words from that discourse into this book, speaking to the faithful, not to unbelievers. But if they are not sufficiently capable of contemplating this image and seeing how true these things are—things that exist in their mind, although the three are not so constituted that they are three persons, but all three belong to one human being, who is one person—why do they not believe, concerning that supreme Trinity which is God, what is found in the sacred writings, rather than demand that a perfectly clear explanation be given them, an explanation which cannot be grasped by the human mind, slow and weak as it is? Certainly, once they have firmly believed the holy Scriptures as most truthful witnesses, they should act by praying, seeking, and living well, so that they may understand—that is, so that, insofar as it can be seen, what is held by faith may be seen by the mind.

### Again, the same author, in his Homily on John (Tractate 99 on John)

Here someone may perhaps ask whether the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son. The Son is the son of the Father alone, and the Father is the father of the Son alone; but the Holy Spirit is not the spirit of one of them, but of both.

You have the Lord himself saying: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:20); and you have the Apostle saying: “God sent the Spirit of his Son, crying in our hearts” (Galatians 4:6).
