Are there two spirits, one of the Father and another of the Son? Far be it from us. For when he was signifying the Church, he said, “One body,” and immediately added, “and one Spirit” (Ephesians 4:4). And see how in that passage he completes the Trinity: “Just as you were called,” he says, “in one hope of your calling, one Lord.” Here he certainly intended Christ to be understood; it remains for him also to name the Father. He therefore continues: “One faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all, and in all.”

Since, therefore, just as there is one Father and one Lord—that is, the Son—so there is also one Spirit, he is unquestionably the Spirit of both, since Christ Jesus himself says, “the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you,” and the Apostle says, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts” (Matthew 10:20; Galatians 4:6).

You also have the same Apostle saying elsewhere: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you” (Romans 8:11). Here he plainly intended the Spirit of the Father to be understood; yet elsewhere he says: “But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9).

There are many other testimonies by which this is clearly demonstrated: that the Spirit who in the Trinity is called the Holy Spirit is himself the Spirit of the Father and of the Son. I do not think he is called “Spirit” in a special sense for any other reason than this: even if we are questioned about each of them individually, we can call both the Father and the Son spirit, since “God is spirit”—that is, God is not a body, but spirit (John 4:24). Therefore, what they are each called in common ought properly to be the name of him in whom the commonality of both appears, since he is not the spirit of one of them but of both.

Why, then, should I not believe that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son, since he is himself likewise the Spirit of the Son? For if he did not proceed from him, the Son, appearing to his disciples after the resurrection, would not have breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). What else did that breathing signify except that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from him?

The same point is also relevant to what he said about the woman who suffered from a flow of blood: “Someone touched me, for I perceived power going out from me” (Luke 8:46). That the Holy Spirit is also called by the name “power” is clear from the passage where the angel replied to Mary, who said, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?”: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:34). And the Lord himself, promising him to his disciples, said: “But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49); and again: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses” (Acts 1:8).

### Again, the same author, in Book 13 of *The City of God* (Chapter 24)

The Holy Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and of the Only-Begotten, and is one Spirit belonging to both. Since this is so, there is no doubt that he proceeds from both.

Therefore, in what the Lord did when he breathed and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22), he plainly wished it to be understood that the Holy Spirit is not only the Spirit of the Father but also the Spirit of the Only-Begotten himself. For that same Spirit is the Spirit both of the Father and of the Son, with whom the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—is not a creature but the Creator.

That bodily breath, proceeding from the mouth of flesh, was not the substance and nature of the Holy Spirit, but rather a sign by which we might understand, as I have said, that the Holy Spirit is common to the Father and the Son, since they do not each have a separate spirit, but one Spirit belongs to both.

### Fulgentius, on the Father alone begetting the Son, the Son alone being begotten by the Father, and the Holy Spirit alone proceeding from the Father and the Son, says in Book 3, which he wrote against Fabianus:

“For we truly confess that the Father alone begot, that the Son alone was born from the Father; and we also truly say that the Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son.”

### Again, the same author, in Book 5 against the same Fabianus

“Behold, insofar as I could, although briefly, I have given the explanation by which we call the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit one God. And in that image of God I have displayed a certain indication of divine knowledge. In that image, memory, understanding, and will do not have separate and proper persons.

“For this is an image, not born but made, not begotten but created. The purpose is that, just as in this one image a certain distinction of names is found, so in that one divinity the distinction of persons may be recognized; and that the natural unity may show that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, while the property of the persons may demonstrate that the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another.

“The Father is other, not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is Father; and the Son is other, not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is Son; and the Holy Spirit is also other, not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is the Spirit of the Father and of the Son.

“The Father is therefore other because he begot; the Son is other because he was born from the Father; and the Holy Spirit is other because he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Yet the Father is not one God and the Son another God and the Holy Spirit another God; rather, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.

“For unity does not confuse the Trinity, nor does the Trinity divide unity: what is distinguished in the property of the persons is shown to be one naturally through the communion of the one essence.”

### Again, the same author, in Book 7 of the same work

“He will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:13–14).

Here he first shows that the Holy Spirit’s things are no different from the Son’s; then, to show that everything belonging to the Father belongs to him, he adds: “Everything that the Father has is mine. Therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:15).

Let us therefore first attend to what he says: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears he will speak.” Who, however, can comprehend what the speech of that simple nature is like, or what its hearing is like, where hearing is nothing other than being?

The Holy Spirit therefore hears whatever the Father and the Son say, and speaks these same things in the same way, just as the Son sees whatever the Father does and does these same things in the same way. For in that nature where there is supreme and true simplicity, the Son sees what the Father does, and the Holy Spirit hears what the Son says with the Father, because through the communion of the natural essence the Son exists as born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

For the Holy Spirit, “to hear,” means to proceed from the nature of the Father and the Son; and “to speak” means to communicate ineffably to our hearts through grace.

### Again, the same author, in the same book

“And no one snatches them from my hand. My Father, who gave them to me, is greater than all, and no one can snatch them from the hand of my Father. I and the Father are one” (John 10:28–30).

This, then, is the voice that his sheep hear. In the fact that no one snatches them from the hand of the Son or from the hand of the Father, they understand the one power of the Son and the Father; and when they hear from him that he and the Father are one, they recognize the true unity of the natural essence in the Father and the Son.

This is the voice of the Son; this is the speech of the Holy Spirit, because the Son was born from the nature of the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from him. The Holy Spirit also hears this from the Father and the Son, because he proceeds from the equality of the common divinity of the Father and the Son.

The Holy Spirit therefore does not speak from himself, because he does not have natural speech from himself but from the Father and the Son; and, proceeding naturally from them, he possesses the truth of his origin. This is certainly the meaning of what he says: “He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and declare it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine” (John 16:14–15).

How well truth itself has preserved the truth of its teaching! If he had said this in such a way as to show that the Spirit belonged to him alone, he would have done so; but by saying, “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine,” he showed that the Holy Spirit is one Spirit belonging both to the Father and to himself. He preserved the same line of thought in the preceding passage, saying: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you everything I have said to you” (John 14:26).

The Father sends him, but sends him in the name of the Son. The Spirit sent by the Father teaches, but the Son speaks. The same is demonstrated in the passage where the Lord says: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26).

Here the Father sends the Paraclete in the name of the Son, and the Son himself sends him from the Father. He sends the Spirit of truth from the Father; he therefore sends his own Spirit from the Father, because he himself is the truth. The Father sends him in the name of the Son, because he is one Spirit of the Father and the Son. The Son sends him from the Father, because he proceeds from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father.

The same Spirit is the Spirit of the Father and the Spirit of truth. Therefore he receives from the Son, and everything that the Father has belongs to the Son, which the Holy Spirit receives, because he proceeds not from the Father alone nor from the Son alone, but simultaneously from both.

The term “procession” is not found granted to any creature from the Father, so that this particular procession may be shown to belong solely to the natural essence. For we read that the Son was begotten from the Father; and although, in the designation “Only-Begotten,” natural generation alone is indicated, nevertheless, because of the grace of adoption, God the Father also voluntarily begot us by the word of truth.

The Only-Begotten, therefore, is the one and only Son born from the Father’s essence. Yet we too are called sons of God by adoption and are said to be born from God, as the blessed Evangelist says: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (John 1:12–13).

Although the divine sayings thus show that we are both sons of God and begotten from God and born from God, nevertheless no one can demonstrate that the term “proceeding from God” has been granted to any creature. Why is this, unless it is because natural birth could show the Only-Begotten Son to be true God, and demonstrate without doubt that he is not adoptive or of a different nature, but consubstantial with the Father?

No creature is therefore said to proceed from God, so that the one who proceeds from the Father and the Son may be believed to be God just as the Father and the Son are. This property of procession from the Father and the Son belongs solely to the Holy Spirit, whose nature is common with the Father and the Son.

For he proceeds from the Father and the Son, but does not depart from them; he is not in any respect less or subordinate, since from the boundless Father and the boundless Son he proceeds inseparably, both as one and as whole. Thus what he speaks cannot be commanded to him, just as what he performs wondrously cannot be commanded to him.

### Again, the same author, in Book 8 of the same work

The Son was therefore sent by the Father, not the Father by the Son, because the Son was born from the Father, not the Father from the Son. Likewise, the Holy Spirit is read to have been sent by the Father and the Son, because he proceeds from the Father and the Son.

But because “sending” is not expressed in only one way in the holy Scriptures, the Son was sent in the mystery of the Incarnation not only by the Father but also by the Holy Spirit, because Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and human beings, was formed through the action of the entire Trinity.

In another way the Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son: he proceeds naturally from the Father and the Son. The Holy Spirit is sent by the Father and the Son when the effect of spiritual grace is given by the Trinity itself, the one God.

### Again, the same author, in Book 9 of the same work

We therefore confess God the Father to be the author not of the entire Trinity, but of the Son and the Holy Spirit: from him the Only-Begotten Son has the origin of eternal birth, and the Holy Spirit the origin of eternal procession. Natural unity, however, indicates that the Creator Son came forth by natural birth from the Creator Father, and that the Creator Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

### Again, the same author, in Book 10 of the same work

Having completed our confession of the true divinity and true humanity of the only Son of God, we confess that we believe in the Holy Spirit, who is one Spirit of the Father and the Son, proceeding from the Father and the Son, naturally remaining in the Father and the Son, and naturally possessing from the Father and the Son the truth of one divinity.

### Again, the same author, to demonstrate that the Holy Spirit is equal to the Father and the Son, testifies in Book 2, written to King Thrasamund (*Book 2 to Monimus*, chapter 6), that the same Holy Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son, and that the Son was sent by the Father and the Holy Spirit

Now we must consider again that question concerning the mission of the Holy Spirit: namely, why, if sacrifice is offered to the entire Trinity, only the mission of the Holy Spirit is required for the sanctification of the offering we make.

As though, so to speak, God the Father himself, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds, could not sanctify the sacrifice offered to him; or as though the Son himself could not sanctify the sacrifice of his body which we offer, although he himself sanctified the body which he offered in order to redeem us; or as though the Holy Spirit must be sent to consecrate the Church’s sacrifice as though the Father or the Son were absent from those who offer it.

First, then, we must remember that in the term “mission” the Holy Spirit should be understood to be neither lower nor lesser. For if he is lesser, he is certainly lower; and if he is lower, he is certainly lesser. We have stated this beforehand because we know that heretics have frequently brought this objection against our faith in particular: that the Holy Spirit must be believed to be lesser than the Father and the Son because he was sent by both the Father and the Son.

But if the sender is to be believed superior to the one sent, they will discover that their own impiety is refuted here, because just as the Holy Spirit is read to have been sent by the Father and the Son, so the Son is found to have been sent by the Father and the Spirit.

The Son himself said this through the prophet long before he was sent, and after he had been sent confirmed it by his own testimony. For when he came to Nazareth and entered the synagogue, and, having been handed the book of the prophet Isaiah to read, unrolled the passage where it is written, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor” (Luke 4:18; Isaiah 61:1), he returned the scroll and testified by the present fulfillment to the truth of that prophecy, saying: “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:21).

Also, in another passage of the same prophet, he showed that he had been sent by the Lord and by the Lord’s Spirit, in these words: “And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isaiah 48:16).

He also declared that the Holy Spirit was sent by him, speaking to his disciples before his Passion in this way: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me” (John 15:26).

Earlier he had taught that the same Spirit was also sent by the Father, saying: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you everything” (John 14:26).

The Son, therefore, was sent by the Father and by the Spirit, and the Spirit was sent by the Father and the Son. Nevertheless, no Christian should understand the mission of either the Son or the Holy Spirit as having taken place locally. Rather, by the term “mission” we should understand the work of a manifestation that was granted.

For the Son was not sent locally, nor is the Holy Spirit sent locally, just as the Father himself does not have a local advent anywhere.

### Hormisdas, Roman bishop, on the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, says the following in a letter sent to the emperor Justin against the blasphemies of Nestorius and Eutyches

Let us worship the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit: the undistinguished [or: undivided] Trinity distinctly, the incomprehensible and indescribable substance. Although reason admits number in the persons, unity nevertheless does not lose the separation of essence. In such a way, however, let us preserve what belongs properly to the divine nature, and preserve what belongs properly to each person, so that neither the singularity of divinity is denied to the persons nor what is proper to the names is transferred to the essence.

Great is the holy and incomprehensible mystery of the Trinity: God the Father, God the Son, God the Holy Spirit, the undivided Trinity. Yet it is known that it belongs properly to the Father to beget the Son; it belongs properly to the Son of God to be born from the Father as an equal from the Father; and it belongs properly to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son within the one substance of the Godhead.

### Leo, Roman bishop, on the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, says the following in a letter sent to Turibius, bishop of Astorga

The first chapter demonstrates how impiously those think about the divine Trinity who assert that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one and the same person, as though the same one were now called Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit; and as though the one who begot, the one who was begotten, and the one who proceeds from both were not distinct, but a singular unity were to be understood under three names, though not in three persons. They took this kind of blasphemy from the opinion of Sabellius.

### Gregory, Roman bishop, on the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, says the following in Homily 26

Thus it is rightly said: “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21)—that is, I love you with the charity with which the Father loves me, who caused me to come to endure sufferings, when I send you amid the scandals of persecutors.

Although “being sent” may also be understood according to the nature of divinity. For the Son is said to be sent by the Father precisely in that he is generated by the Father. The Son likewise declares that he himself sends the Holy Spirit, who, although he is equal [Edition: coequal] to the Father and the Son, was nevertheless not incarnate: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father” (John 15:26).

If “being sent” must be understood only as being incarnate, then surely the Holy Spirit could in no way be said to be sent, since he was not incarnate at all. But his mission is itself his procession, by which he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Therefore, just as the Spirit is said to be sent because he proceeds, so the Son is not improperly said to be sent because he is generated.

“When he had said this, he breathed on them and said: ‘Receive the Holy Spirit’” (John 20:22). We must ask what it means that our Lord gave the Holy Spirit once while remaining on earth and once while presiding in heaven. For the Holy Spirit is not plainly shown to have been given elsewhere except here, when he is received through the breathing, and afterward, when he comes from heaven and is manifested in various tongues.

Why, then, is the Spirit first given to the disciples on earth and afterward sent from heaven? Is it not because there are two commandments of charity: namely, love of God and love of neighbor? The Spirit is given on earth so that the neighbor may be loved; the Spirit is given from heaven so that God may be loved. Thus, just as there is one charity and two commandments, so there is one Spirit and two gifts: first from the Lord while he remained on earth, afterward from heaven. For through love of neighbor one learns how one must arrive at love of God.

### Again, the same author, in Book 2 of the *Moralia* (chapter 28)

If the spirit of prophecy were always present with the prophets, the prophet Nathan would never have granted King David’s request for advice about the construction of the temple, only to deny it shortly afterward. Hence it is rightly written in the Gospel: “Upon whoever you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes” (John 1:33).

For the Spirit comes upon all the faithful, but in the one Mediator alone he remains continually in a singular way, because he never abandoned his humanity, from whose divinity he proceeds. He therefore remains in the one who alone can do everything and always.

### Again, the same author, in the same book (chapter 29), after a short interval

In these gifts, therefore, without which one cannot attain life, the Holy Spirit always remains, whether in his preachers or in all the elect. But in those gifts by which our life is not preserved through the manifestation of the Spirit, but the salvation of others is sought, he does not always remain in preachers. For he always presides over their hearts for right living, yet he does not always display signs of power through them. Sometimes he withdraws from them the manifestation of signs, so that his virtues may be held in greater humility precisely because what has been possessed cannot be retained.

But Christ Jesus, the man who is Mediator between God and human beings, continually and always has the Spirit present in every respect, because the same Spirit is substantially brought forth from him. Therefore, although the Spirit remains in holy preachers, he is rightly said to remain in the Mediator in a singular way: in them he remains by grace for a particular purpose, but in him he remains by substance for all purposes.

### Again, the same author, in Book 5 (chapter 26), that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and receives from what belongs to the Son, whereby he is understood also to proceed from the Son

“And I heard a voice like a gentle breeze” (Job 4:16). For what is signified by “the voice of a gentle breeze” except the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, who, proceeding from the Father and receiving from what belongs to the Son, is poured gently into the frail capacity of our understanding?

Yet when he comes upon the apostles, he is manifested through an external sound as a mighty wind, when it is said: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like that of a rushing mighty wind” (Acts 2:2).

For the Holy Spirit, when he insinuates himself into the frailty of human understanding, is expressed both by the sound of a mighty wind and by the voice of a gentle breeze. He is both mighty and gentle when he comes: gentle because he tempers his knowledge for our senses, insofar as they are at all able to know it; mighty because, however much he tempers it, nevertheless by his coming he illumines and disturbs the blindness of our frailty.

### Isidore, in Book 7 of the *Etymologies* (chapter 3), on the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and the Son, says:

The Holy Spirit is proclaimed to be God because he proceeds from the Father and the Son. He is not called begotten, lest two sons be suspected in the Trinity; he is not proclaimed unbegotten, lest two fathers be believed in the Trinity.

He is called “proceeding” on the testimony of the Lord, who says: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now [According to Isidore: ‘the things that I will speak to you, but you cannot hear them now’]. But the Spirit of truth will come, who proceeds from the Father and will receive from what is mine; he will teach you everything” (John 21:12).

He proceeds not only by nature, but also proceeds continually to carry out the works of divinity without ceasing. The difference between the Son who is born and the Holy Spirit who proceeds is that the Son is born from one, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. And therefore the Apostle says: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9).

### Again, the same author, in the same work (chapter 4), after a short interval

The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are Trinity and unity. They are the same one and the same three: one in nature, three in persons; one because of the communion of majesty, three because of the property of the persons.

For the Father is one, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another—but one “other,” not one “other thing,” because they are equally simple, equally immutable, good, and coeternal.

The Father alone is not from another; therefore he alone is called unbegotten. The Son alone is born from the Father; therefore he alone is called begotten. The Holy Spirit alone proceeds from the Father and the Son; therefore he alone is called the Spirit of both.

### Again, the same author, in the Book of *Differences* (Book 2, chapter 3)

[Note: Some portions of this chapter are read differently in the printed editions of Isidore.]

The person of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is distinguished in this way: the Father is neither made nor born; the Son is born, not made; but the Holy Spirit is neither born nor made, proceeding instead from the Father and the Son.

Accordingly, the Father has eternity without birth; the Son has birth together with eternity; but the Holy Spirit has procession without birth. The Father derives his beginning from no one; the Son takes his origin from the Father; but the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

Yet what we say about the Trinity is expressed only insofar as human understanding can grasp it [Edition: in whatever way]. For who is sufficient to contemplate the inner mysteries of the Trinity itself? How are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit three persons but one nature? How is the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit neither begotten nor unbegotten, while seeming to be not a creature but uncreated? How is the Son born from the Father, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and from the Son? How does the Son proceed by being born, while the Holy Spirit does not come into being by being born but by proceeding? How is the Father never without the Son, and yet, without the Son, the Father begot the Son? How is the Son never without the Spirit, and yet says, “Unless I depart, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16:7)?

How is the Son not from himself but from the Father, and yet not later than the one from whom he is? How does the Holy Spirit proceed from the Father and the Son, and yet is not preceded by those from whom he proceeds? How are the three one, and the one three? How are they three in relation to one another, but essentially one?

Who could contemplate these things? Who could comprehend them? If we do not grasp the mysteries of Christ’s human birth, how shall we grasp the mysteries of the divine nature?

### Again, the same author, in the Book of *Sentences* (Book 1, chapter 17)

The Holy Spirit is Creator, just as the Father and the Word are, as the prophet testifies: “The Spirit of God made me, and the breath [Edition: ‘the spirit’] of the Almighty gave me life” (Job 33:4).

The Holy Spirit belongs to the Father and the Son. The Father and the Son are therefore one because the Father has nothing that the Son does not have. For one thing, consubstantial with two persons, could not proceed simultaneously from them and simultaneously be present in them unless those from whom it proceeds were one.

### Prosper, in Book 1 of *The Contemplative Life* (chapter 18), teaches that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as follows:

But since, according to the Apostle, we must not only provide an example for the faithful [Col. 0272C], but must also instruct those very faithful people who have been divinely entrusted to us for instruction—concerning the Father, how he alone is understood to be unbegotten; concerning the Son, how he alone is said to be begotten [Edit., “how he is begotten from him”]; and concerning the Holy Spirit, how, proceeding from the Father and the Son, he can be called neither unbegotten nor begotten; and concerning how these three are one, and how this one is not divided but distinguished into three; and concerning how neither the Father nor the Holy Spirit, but the Son alone, ineffably born from the Father alone, assumed the whole human being without any change in his substance, proved himself true God and true man through miracles and sufferings, allowed himself to be apprehended, and willed to be killed, rose again on the third day, raised to heaven by his own power the man assumed from us [Col. 0272D], granted to us, reborn in him, the happy hope of rising again through the example of his resurrection, made us his members, threatened punishment to those who did not believe in him or withdrew from him, and promised the heavenly kingdom to those who adhered to him—(chapter 19).

A priest ought to know these and other matters in order to teach them, and the people ought to believe them so that they may understand what they are taught, as the Apostle says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah VII, 9). From this it is understood that faith does not arise from understanding, but understanding from faith; and that it is not the one who understands who believes, but the one who believes who understands, and that the one who has understood should act well.

[Col. 0273A] [Note: [Col. 0273D] Vigilius, African bishop. Here the error of those who have hitherto published these books under the name of Vigilius of Trent becomes clear. Moreover, in the codex of Saint Eugendus, as I hear, this Vigilius is designated bishop of Thapsus, a city of Africa in the province of Byzacena. And in the Catalogue which we published, among the bishops of that province who came to Huneric on account of the faith, Vigilius of Thapsus is listed last. Whether this is the same man as ours or another, we leave for our Vigilius Chiffletius to examine, in view of his zeal and diligence; from him we hope shortly for more accurate and fuller works of Vigilius.]

Vigilius, African bishop, demonstrates in these words that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, in the books which he wrote at Constantinople in defense of Pope Leo against the Eutychianists (Book I, after the middle).

“Likewise, let them raise some question for us concerning the Trinity, so that, because there are certain properties of the Father which do not belong to the Holy Spirit [Edit., ‘nor to the Son, nor to the Spirit, etc.’], and certain properties of the Son which belong neither to the Father nor to the Holy Spirit, and also certain properties of the Holy Spirit which are shown to belong neither to the Father nor to the Son, they may accuse us Catholics of worshiping three gods separated from one another. But lest perhaps you be disturbed by an unexpected question, listen to each matter individually. The dispensation of the assumed man belongs neither to the Father [Col. 0273B] nor to the Spirit, but to the Son alone [Edit., ‘Consider each matter individually. The dispensation of the assumed flesh belongs neither to the Father, etc.’]. For the Son alone, not the Father, was born from a virgin. Again, that voice which has often been heard, ‘This is my beloved Son’ (Matthew III, 17), belongs neither to the Son nor to the Holy Spirit, but to the Father alone. Likewise, the appearance of a dove which appeared in the Jordan, and the distribution divided into tongues of fire, are shown properly to belong to the person of the Holy Spirit. But lest you still doubt these properties, listen more clearly. It is proper to the Father to have begotten; it is proper to the Son to have been born; it is proper to the Holy Spirit to proceed from the Father and the Son. What is specially proper to each person is not at all transferred to another person [Col. 0273C]. If, therefore, these three persons, each possessing their own properties by which they are more significantly distinguished, not separated, are one God, how is the Son, while the property of each nature remains intact, not one Christ?”

Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, in a letter addressed to the Armenians against the heretics, teaches in these words that the Holy Spirit proceeds inseparably from the divine essence.

“Let us therefore flee the counsels of seduction—I mean the destructive and God-hating streams of the heretics—the madness of Arius, who divides the inseparable Trinity among substances; the audacity of Eunomius, who confines the incomprehensible nature within the limits of human knowledge; [Col. 0273D] the fury of Manichaeus [Edd. omit “Manichaeus”], and the madness of Macedonius, who separates from the essence of the Godhead the Holy Spirit, who proceeds inseparably.”

[Note: [Col. 0274D] Agnellus, in a letter to Nennius. It was first published at Basel under the title, “Of Agnellus, bishop, to Arminius, concerning the rule of faith.” The name “of Ravenna” was later added from another copy, I think; he governed that see in the final years of Justinian.]

Agnellus, in his letter to Nennius, teaches in this way that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

“Therefore the Son is from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. Nor, as some say, does God have two sons, Christ and the Holy Spirit; rather, he has an invisible Son, just as he himself is invisible. In order that he might be visible, he assumed the body of our frailty—not so that he would cease to be invisible, but so that in Christ himself he might remain invisible to unbelievers.

“For when he says, ‘Blessed are the eyes which see what you see’ (Luke X, 23), then all the Jews, and those who crucified him, would have been blessed—those of whom it is said through David, ‘They themselves looked upon and saw me’ (Psalm XXI, 19). You see, therefore, that he remains invisible and is perceived by a pure and believing mind. Thus, if the Father is invisible, the Son is invisible, and the Holy Spirit is invisible.

“And to bring you back to the matter from which it arose that we should teach this concerning fragile man, tell me, Arius: are these three invisible things, undivided, gathered together into one, and overflowing with the effectiveness of their power—namely, the voice that gives birth to the word, the effectiveness proceeding from the word together with the voice, which makes one man consul and another be slaughtered—one, or are they not? If they are not one, divide the voice from the word, and the effectiveness from the voice and the word. But if, in fragile man, these three—voice, word, and effectiveness—are so one, then they are indeed three persons, but one power of subsistence.

“If such power exists in the most fragile man, as we have said, how much more does it exist in the omnipotence of God, so that the Father is the almighty begetter of the Son, and the power proceeding from the Father and the Son is the Holy Spirit.”

Cassiodorus, in his exposition of Psalm 50, says in this way that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and establish me with a governing spirit” (Psalm L, 14). We should not think it without purpose that the holy man, illumined by the radiance of his heart, named the Spirit three times, unless it was because, devoted to the undivided Trinity, he asked that forgiveness be granted him by it.

“For, with respect to the essence of the Godhead, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are rightly called one God. But for the distinction of persons, it is proper to the Father that naturally, without beginning, before the ages, he begot the Son; it is proper to the Son that he was naturally begotten by the Father; it is proper to the Holy Spirit that he proceeds from the Father and the Son. Through their ineffable love and cooperation, their consubstantial eternity and power accomplishes everything it wills in heaven and on earth.

“Although we now know that these things are incomprehensible and inexpressible, nevertheless some Fathers propose the following likeness from bodily things existing together. For in the sun we find these three properties: first, the bodily substance itself, which is the sun; next, its radiance, which remains in it; and third, the heat which reaches us from its radiance. If some likeness to so great a reality can be found, I think they should be understood in this way: what in the sun is its bodily substance may in some manner be understood in the Trinity as the person of the Father; what in the sun is its radiance may in the Trinity be the person of the Son, as the Apostle says, ‘the radiance of his glory’ (Hebrews I, 3); and what in the sun is its heat may in the Trinity be the person of the Holy Spirit, as we read, ‘Who can hide himself from his heat?’ (Psalm XVIII).

“Another example may also be drawn from incorporeal things, namely from the soul, which is known to have been made in the image and likeness of God. The soul, therefore, is itself an incorporeal, rational substance, in which understanding and life are present. What in the soul is substance may, if it is lawful to say so, be understood in the Trinity as the person of the Father; what in the soul is power and knowledge may be understood in the Trinity as the Son, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God; and what in the soul is the property of giving life may likewise be understood in the Trinity as the Holy Spirit, through whom the work of giving life is proclaimed in many places to be accomplished, as the Apostle Peter says in his letter: ‘Put to death in the flesh, but made alive in the spirit’ (1 Peter III, 18). The Apostle likewise says: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit gives life’ (2 Corinthians III, 6); and in the Gospel the Lord says: ‘It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no benefit at all’ (John VI, 64).

“Yet these three things which we have mentioned are never found separated individually, although our understanding can perceive them as distinct. Rather, they are naturally united in such a way that whenever one of them presents itself, all three are always encountered together. Through these likenesses, therefore, some conception of the truth of so great a reality is disclosed to us. There are also other similar examples in the discussions of the Fathers. But what the weakness of the flesh now prevents us from understanding clearly, those who are blessed will then be able to comprehend more fully, when they see the Godhead in its majesty.

“Whoever desires to recognize this more fully should not cease reading the books of Saint Hilary, Saint Ambrose, and Saint Augustine [Cassiodorus: ‘the books of the Trinity’]. For this subject is as great for discussion as it is long. Blessed Jerome also discussed the Trinity lucidly and briefly against the heretics in this psalm.”

Likewise, the same author on Psalm 61:

“For from him comes my salvation” (Psalm LXI, 4), that is, the only-begotten Son, who is salvation to those who rightly believe. When it is said, ‘from him,’ the Son is signified. The holy Trinity, the one God, possesses these particular properties: the Father is unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. This is what sound faith professes; this is what the Catholic Church confesses [Col. 0276A].

“You therefore rightly profess that you, O Jeduthun, are subject to God, from whom you testify that you have received an immeasurable benefit. But so that the holy word may be honored with a single and equal veneration, consider what follows: ‘For he himself is my God and my salvation; my helper, I shall not be moved again’ (ibid., verse 3).

“Above, he had called the author of salvation begotten from the Father; now he embraces this Savior with a threefold confession. First, lest you think him lesser, he says, ‘He himself is my God,’ just as above he speaks of God the Father [Edd., ‘God’]. For the equality of the supreme name displays the unity of substance and power.

“Therefore Father Augustine, in the fifteenth book of his work on the Trinity (chapter 3), says: ‘Once the reason has been given, it is clear to those who understand that, in the substance of truth, the Father is not only not greater than the Son, but that the two together are not anything greater than the Holy Spirit alone; nor are any two in that same Trinity anything greater than one; nor are all three together anything greater than each individually.’ Thus he demonstrated, with wondrous truth, the perfect and singular nature of the Holy Trinity.”

Prudentius, in his book Against Marcion [Harmartigenia, verse 931], in heroic meter:

> O God, Father of all, giver of the soul, O Christ, O God,  
> Whose Spirit, one God, subsists from your mouth.

Likewise, in his Book of Hymns [Cathemerinon, hymn 6, verse 5], in iambic meter:

> O single power  
> Of this Trinity,  
> O single light,  
> Everlasting God from God,  
> God sent from both.

Likewise, in his Book of Hymns [hymn 5, verse 5], in choriambic meter, called Asclepiad:

> Good creator, guide of the shining light,  
> Who divide the seasons in fixed succession,  
> When the sun has sunk and dreadful chaos presses in,  
> Restore the light to your faithful, O Christ.

> (Ibid., verse 157) Through Christ, your begotten Son, O highest Father,  
> In whom your visible glory stands for you,  
> Who is our Lord, your only Son,  
> He breathes forth the Paraclete from his Father’s heart.

> Through him your splendor, honor, praise, wisdom,  
> Majesty, goodness, and devotion  
> Continue the kingdom under a threefold name,  
> Weaving age upon age forever.

[Col. 0275]

## SOME FRAGMENTS OF SERMONS OF THEODULF, BISHOP OF ORLÉANS

[Col. 0275D] We rise with difficulty toward virtues, but slide into vices without effort. The latter are downhill, the former steep. We endure great exertions so that we may be able to climb to heaven [Col. 0276D]. Just as those who strive toward the summit of virtues do not begin at the highest points but at modest ones, so that they may gradually reach greater heights, so those who slide into vices do not immediately begin with great crimes, but become accustomed to them through lesser ones and thus plunge into the greatest.

It is no use doing good with evil mixed in; first one must be restrained from evil, and then good must be practiced. The prophet indicates this when he says: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good” (Isaiah I, 16). Vices must first be uprooted from a person, and virtues then planted. Truth cannot cling and be joined to falsehood, modesty to wantonness, faith to treachery, or chastity to lust.

The lust of the flesh is conspicuous to everyone because it is immediately shameful in itself; nevertheless, in God’s reckoning, pride is the lesser evil. But one who is held by pride and does not perceive it falls into the lust of the flesh, so that he may be humbled by it and rise from shame and from [Col. 0277B] pride.

Everyone who sins is proud, because by doing what is forbidden he contemptuously disregards the divine commandments. Pride is therefore rightly the beginning of every sin, because unless disobedience to God’s commands comes first, the guilt of transgression does not follow. As pride is the origin of all crimes, so it is the ruin of every virtue. It is first in sin and last in conflict. It either throws the mind down through sin at the outset or finally casts it down from virtues.

It is therefore also the greatest of all sins, because through both virtues and vices it destroys the human mind. From the guilt of pride one generally proceeds to the detestable uncleanness of the flesh, for one depends upon the other. But just as through pride of mind one proceeds into the prostitution of lust, so through humility of mind the chastity of the flesh is preserved.

God sometimes casts down hidden pride of mind through the manifest ruin of the flesh. That uncleanness of lust is born from hidden pride of spirit is revealed by the example of the first man: as soon as he swelled with pride against God, he immediately felt the lust of the flesh and covered his nakedness.

Sometimes a Christian is attacked by the devil with a twofold vice: secretly through arrogance and openly through lust. But God’s servant, weighing both carefully, avoids lust in such a way that he does not fall into arrogance, and fears arrogance in such a way that he does not relax his spirit into lust.

Demons are especially favorable to the lustful and the proud. While evil spirits serve in other vices, they are joined to these with greater familiarity and serve them more fully according to their desire [Col. 0277D]. Through these two vices above all—the pride of mind and the lust of the flesh—the devil rules the human race.

Thus the Lord speaks to Job concerning the devil: “He sleeps under the shade, in the secret of the reed, in moist places” (Job XL, 16). By the reed, empty pride is signified; by the moist places, the lust of the flesh. Through these two vices the devil possesses the human race, either by raising the mind into pride or by corrupting the flesh through lust.

Fornications must first be removed from the heart, so that they do not burst forth in action. Hence it is said through the prophet: “Gird your loins over your breasts” (Isaiah XXXII, 11); that is, cut away lusts in the heart.

[Col. 0278A] When, therefore, the mind is driven by the impulse of demons toward the pleasure of fornication, let the torments of divine judgment and the eternal fire be placed before its eyes. Every punishment restrains a temptation by fear of a heavier penalty; remembrance of the heat of Gehenna drives out the heat of lust.

Continence is given by God, but “ask, and you shall receive.” It is granted when God is called upon with inward groaning. The beauty of chastity is to be loved; once tasted, its pleasure is found sweeter than that of the flesh. Chastity is the fruit of sweetness, the undefiled beauty of the saints, health of body, and security of mind.

For whoever trusts that he possesses continence but does not withdraw himself from other earthly desires, although the lust of the flesh does not defile him, is nevertheless stained by the various activities of worldly life. Every sin, however, receives healing for its wound through repentance.

No one can pass through spiritual battles unless he has first subdued the heat of desire. The mind cannot be free to contemplate God when it is occupied with the desires of this world.

Avarice and the love of money are worse than every sin. Hence Solomon says: “There is nothing more wicked than loving money” (Ecclesiasticus X, 10). Desire is the material of every crime. Hence the Apostle says: “The desire for money is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy VI, 10). If, therefore, the root of crimes is cut off, the other shoots of sins do not sprout.

Desire sold Christ; it sold life and purchased death. Nor is this surprising, since those who, while alive, did not extinguish the flame of their desire are assigned, when they die, to the fires of hell.

It is useful to beware of gluttony and desire for food. For what is more harmful than that the mind should serve the belly and foods which are destined to be destroyed, as the Apostle testifies: “God will destroy both it and them” (1 Corinthians VI, 13)? Food should be used not for lust or satiety, but only so that the body may be sustained for the work of God.

Just as all carnal desires are cut away by abstinence, so all the virtues of the soul are destroyed by the vice of overeating. No one can attain the perfection of virtues unless he has first subdued the greed of the belly. No one can rule over the other vices unless he has first restrained the vice of gluttony. No one can easily drive unclean spirits from himself except through abstinence from gluttony.

For then the enemies outside us are overcome more powerfully by us, when the vices within us have first been extinguished. A person fights uselessly outside who has danger within.

Food generates overeating, and drink generates drunkenness. Drunkenness produces disturbance of mind, fury of heart, and the flame of lust. It so alienates the mind that a person does not know where he is.

Hence in Proverbs it says: “The powerful are wrathful; let them not drink wine, lest when they have drunk they forget wisdom” (Proverbs XXXI, 5). Many people regard it as praise to drink much and not become drunk. Let them hear the prophet speaking against them: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isaiah V, 22).

Isaiah rebukes those devoted to much wine and living luxuriously, saying: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they may burn with wine” (Isaiah V, 11).

Of such people it is said elsewhere: “Woe to you, city, whose king is a boy and whose princes eat in the morning” (Ecclesiasticus X, 16). Many serve drunkenness and the pleasures of gluttony from morning until sunset. They do not understand why they were born, but, held captive by beastlike habit, serve luxury and banquets throughout the day.

The prophet Joel cries out to those who serve drunkenness, saying: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep; howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness” (Joel I, 5).

The care of the flesh must therefore be carefully moderated with discernment, so that there may be nothing excessive. Whatever is excessive and beyond measure is harmful; whatever is done with measure and restraint is salutary. In every undertaking, therefore, one ought to maintain measure and restraint.

For this reason, some commandments are given to the faithful who live an ordinary life in the world, and others to those who renounce this world. The former are told to manage all their possessions well; the latter to abandon all their possessions.

For perfection, however, it is not enough to renounce all one’s possessions unless one also renounces oneself, according to the Gospel—that is, unless one abandons one’s own desires and renounces evil habits: so that the one who was proud becomes humble; the adulterer chaste; the angry person strives to become gentle; the hot-tempered person strives to become patient; the miser generous; and the one who wastes away in hatred or envy against his neighbor retains in his heart pure love of God and neighbor.

Thus he should set one contrary virtue against each vice and strive to adorn himself with good habits, so that he may obtain forgiveness for his vices and a reward for his good deeds. For the Lord says: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew XVI, 24).

Therefore those who do not pursue the monastic profession with firm purpose, but seek the goal of heavenly love loosely, are more easily led back again to love of the world. An imperfect profession returns to the desires of the present life. Even if such a person does not yet bind himself to them in deed, he does so through the love of his thoughts. It is therefore good to resist evil thoughts with strength.

Whoever undertakes the profession of holiness in order to desire someday to rule over others is not a disciple of Christ but a follower of wickedness, because he strives to bear the labor of Christ’s cross not for God but for love of the world.

Those who abandon the world but follow the virtues of the commandments without humility of heart fall, as it were, heavily from a height, because through the pride of their virtues they are cast down more disastrously than they could have slipped through vices.

No servant of God should be lifted up by his merits when he sees that others who were beneath him can become superior to him. The conscience of God’s servant should always be humble and sorrowful: humble, so that he does not become proud; and usefully sorrowful, so that his heart does not relax into frivolity.

God’s servant ought without interruption to read and work, lest the spirit of fornication steal upon a mind devoted to idleness. Pleasure yields to labor, but it quickly seizes a vacant mind. Consider Solomon, who through leisure became entangled in many fornications and through the vice of fornication fell even into idolatry.

Those who renounce the world out of fear of God but remain entangled in worldly affairs withdraw themselves from divine love to the extent that they involve themselves in worldly concerns. Those who try both to obey earthly cares and to exercise themselves in divine matters cannot embrace both, as Christ says: “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew VI, 24).

Unless the oppressive multitude of worldly cares is first driven from the secret places of the heart, the soul lying within can in no way rise again.

The tepidity of those who wish to be free for God and renounce the world, while despising their own concerns, is reproved when, in caring for the interests of their relatives, they separate themselves from the love of God. A spiritual person ought to benefit his relatives, but must beware lest, while striving to show them the favor of the flesh, he himself decline from his spiritual purpose.

Many monks, through love of their parents, have become entangled not only in earthly cares but also in legal disputes, and have lost their souls for the temporal safety of their own people.

Just as our soul itself is not to be hated by us, but its carnal affections, so our parents are not to be hated by us, but their impediments, which hinder us from the right path. Yet the Lord commanded us to hate our parents in the same way as our own souls.

No one can appreciate how serious it is to turn away from good and do evil unless he first turns toward God with the full effort of his mind.

The progress of every convert is described as threefold: first, correction from evil; second, doing good; third, receiving the reward of good work. Therefore everyone should hasten to God through repentance while he can, lest, if he is unwilling while he can, when he wishes too late he be altogether unable.

Therefore the prophet says: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah LV, 6). And where can he be found except in this life, in which Jesus Christ our Lord is also near to all who call upon him in truth? He will prepare eternal life and glory for all who truly and faithfully believe in him.

## CONCERNING ALL THE ORDERS OF THIS WORLD

Let every sin which has pleased us or stolen upon us remain in our memory. Since our sins have now been wiped away, let us not lose the reward of Christ’s blood, nor stain the garment of the soul through wickedness, robbery, or desire.

We had fallen; now we have been raised. We had been wounded; now we have been healed. There will be no excuse. However much the devil may invite someone to evil, he cannot drag him there. He brings pleasure, not power; he introduces a suggestion, not a struggle.

Now, therefore, because of the childbirth of blessed Mary, let my speech be directed to virgins, whether men or women; to widows; to the powerful and the poor; to slaves. With God there is no distinction except that of merits.

Listen to me, therefore, all of you who by Christ’s gift are virgins in body. I speak generally to everyone. Listen to me, then, whoever recognizes himself as being what I describe: strive to be a virgin also in heart. Rejoice in the gain of the body in such a way that you do not suffer loss of soul.

Yet rejoice in this precious gift of Christ; rejoice with humility; weep with devotion; give thanks because you carry so great a happiness in integrity; rejoice because you will follow the Lamb wherever he goes—provided that, as we read in the Apocalypse, no lie is found in your mouth.

Pray for perseverance, lest any worldly pleasure, however slight, or the devil’s envy take away so great a gift, cloud so great a brightness, and darken so great a radiance. Hold it firmly; do not lose what cannot be restored; do not lose the grace of the body in a single moment of pleasure; do not contract the soul’s shame through the beauty of a corrupted form; do not let desire conquer you.

If you listen to me, you will remain. If you do not listen, you will lose what you will never recover.

Again I speak to you who have wives: I urge you to keep them chastely. For Elizabeth, who had lived chastely with her husband for many years, and both of whom had been faithful before God, merited to have a son from a dead seed, who would both adorn the holiness of his parents and convert many unbelievers through his preaching.

Again I speak to you who are widows: guard your widowhood. Do not be talkative, but await the Lord in silence, for he will receive the orphan and the widow. A widow is good when she is devoted to prayer and humility and ready to give alms. If she truly has no means of doing so, let her have a good and sincere will and thought.

Women, do not curse; do not swear; do not be quick to speak. Perhaps you say that what I am saying is intrusive. I may not [perhaps: “be silent”]. I fear the one who commands more than the one who criticizes.

I speak so that the one who recognizes himself may correct himself; the one who does not recognize himself in it should rejoice and retain what he has heard, so that he may be able to say it to others for their salvation.

Now I speak to you, penitents, who have received and are practicing penance in the Church: persevere in weeping, in compunction; weep intelligently. What does “weep intelligently” mean? Do not seek a temporal thing in prayer, but eternal blessedness and remission of sins. Whoever prays in this way weeps intelligently.

Let your tears not fall uselessly to the ground, for the one who says through the prophet is truthful: “I have placed my tears in your sight” (Psalm LV, 9).

Now you ought to love God greatly and pass from fear to love. For we read in the Gospel of that sinful woman: “She to whom much is forgiven loved much” (Luke VII, 47). Therefore you ought to love God greatly, because he has deigned, by waiting for you and not punishing you, to lead you to repentance.

Now I speak to you, the poor. I mean you poor who beg and live on the alms of Christians: be comforted. Your tribulation will be changed into joy, and your sorrow into gladness.

Do not regard it as an insult that you beg, nor therefore say anything in your heart against the Lord. For he is just and merciful in all his works. He made you poor so that, by enduring want, you might acquire eternal life; and he made another rich so that, by giving you what was superfluous, he might acquire a remedy for his sins. Therefore be patient and await the Lord.

I also speak to you, slaves, whoever has earthly masters and whoever has the condition of servitude: obey your masters; love them from the heart. Do not serve merely for outward appearance, but perform your service out of love.

For God appointed them to rule over you and you to serve. Serve well, because you will receive a reward for good service. If you are good, you will be better than evil masters.

For with the Lord the soul of each person is not distinguished by nobility but by conduct, not by lineage but by action.

Therefore I have now spoken to everyone, because Christ died for us. Preserve what I have said, so that I may obtain fruit from you; and may the merciful Lord admit all of you into the heavenly places where the grain is to be gathered. He lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0281D] What follows seems, through the negligence of a copyist, to have been attached to Theodulf from another source. The sermon itself is read among the sermons attributed to Saint Augustine, no. 117. EDIT.]

Do you now wish, dearest brother Desiderius, that I should tell you a few things concerning writers who have been able to bring forth very clearly for us much about the obscurities which, because of carnal understanding, hinder us from the splendor of spiritual contemplation—writers like the lights of the firmament that shine throughout the whole world?

I fear that I may fulfill against myself the judgment of Susanna, daughter of Helcias, who spoke against the unjust judgment of the elders: “Distress is all around me, and I am likewise in distress.” For if I wish to criticize some of them, I shall stir up adversaries and hostilities everywhere; but if I wish to do what you have asked, you will never find what you seek. Yet it seems that I would condemn the will of one person and pass over or despise the counsel of many, each of whom has deserved to be diligently praised in the Holy Scriptures.

But let the most august bishop, flying over the peaks of the mountains like an eagle, gently and lightly, with complete affection—as though to fulfill both purposes peacefully—proclaim all this in clear speech, without considering what takes place at the roots of the mountains, while surveying the great spaces of the heavens, the arrangement of the earth, and the circuit of the waters.

For whoever wishes to climb a fruitful tree hastens gradually toward what is higher and greater, while leaving the nearby branches to little ones [perhaps: “leaving them”]. We are little ones. I beseech you, most beloved brothers, to labor with the most vigilant care for the progress and correction of the peoples placed under your authority.

[Col. 0283]

# THE POEMS OF THEODULF

## BOOK ONE

[Note: [Col. 0283D] “Exhortation to Judges.” Peter Daniel invented this title for himself; he was the first to publish this poem from a headless copy that had no title. In the Alta-Silva and Petavian manuscripts, in which the poem survives complete, the inscription is simpler: “Against Judges.” We have retained Daniel’s title, but with the help of those same manuscripts restored the twenty-nine verses that were missing at the beginning, as well as others in other places, and corrected many things that were defective throughout.]

## EXHORTATION TO JUDGES

[Col. 0283A]

> Judges, take hold of the path of judgment, righteous censors,  
> And let your feet disdain crooked byways.  
> This road leads to heaven; that one drags toward the shades.  
> A godly life holds this one; yawning death possesses the other.  
> Therefore beware, men, of approaching the chasms of Acheron,  
> Where Styx lies, where Cocytus lies, where all fury dwells.  
> But, O paradise, nothing is more pleasing than your dwellings,  
> Where no evils exist and all good things remain.  
> If I had a thousand tongues in a hundred throats,  
> And an iron voice gave bronze words to all,  
> I could not, I confess, utter all the joys  
> Of that delightful dwelling, which those who govern laws well attain.  
> Nor could I run through in speech the monsters of punishments  
> Which the troop friendly to fraud endures.  
> Let piety be given to judgment, and diligence to piety,  
> So that savage bribes may find no place.

> The page of the ancient law cries out that this must be accomplished;  
> No blessed tongue of any prophet keeps silent about it.  
> The evangelical trumpet roars this through the crossroads of the world;  
> The apostolic sermon also thunders it forth.  
> This thing raised the name of the patriarchs to the heights;  
> From it the holy company of prophets derives its renown.  
> Whoever among leaders and kings obtained this holy path  
> Possesses all good things.  
> But those who, driven by error, were carried along rough byways  
> And abandoned this road—all good things likewise abandoned them.  
> Moses, the most faithful interpreter of the gracious God,  
> Enjoys converse with God while the people marvel.  
> For forty years through the trackless ways of the wilderness  
> He led the wealthy people with the honor of God.

[Col. 0283C] Always loving what is just, always despising savage rewards,

He was, by example and by words, a standard of salvation.

Samuel, born through his mother’s prayers and faith,

And through the gift of him who creates all good things.

He who brings about beforehand what he shows established in time,

For whom at once the past and the future are present.

He spurned every kind of fraud, pursuing all good things.

Nor did he make use of your price, contemptible little ass.

What shall I say of the king who modulates his song in resonant verse,

Who strove with all his mind to please God?

For whom all things together rightly obey in praise of the Thunderer:

Art, flesh, mind, plectrum, voice, lyre, strings, and chorus?

[Col. 0284A] By songs and deeds, and with every effort,

This man warns against vices that must be avoided and teaches laws that must be observed.

“The Lord is just,” he says, “a lover of balanced justice,

Whose triumphant countenance sees all that is just.”

Thus he rebukes corrupt judges with these words, hissing them out,

And moves his lips with such admonitions:

“Why do you so often persist in unjust judgments,

And together assume the savage faces of sinners?

Hasten to the case of the poor, or of the orphan,

So that the wretched man may go away upright and acquitted.

Rescue the needy from the cruel hands of sinners.”

With his pen he sings many such things at length.

His revered power extends without limit;

He who yesterday was blessed was able to be his own father.

Here he was repeatedly tempered in the furnace of adversity.

[Col. 0284B] Hence he became renowned for virtue and surpassed vices.

Because his most illustrious offspring lacked these qualities,

He therefore abandoned the right path with a leftward mind.

The more the curved ploughshare wounds the soil beneath it,

The fewer thorns there are, and the more abundant the harvest produced.

He had been a wise king, just in the administration of laws,

Had he not been captured by women’s snares.

Alas, abandoning so many and such great blessings, he was overturned by disgrace;

Thus you wickedly lose sweet nectar by turning it into sour wine.

The glory of the revered king Hezekiah also grew,

Through the merits of justice and the aid of piety.

To him the Father of All wished to add three more periods of fifteen years,

And through the setting of death his pious life returned.

Here he teaches the people to proclaim their ancestral laws

And to flee the impediments of the evil of error.

[Col. 0284C] On the high mountain he destroyed the fashioned *chelydrus* (serpent),

Which had first been a cause of life and afterward of death.

So too the physician who pierces himself with a sharp scalpel:

From this comes health to others, but black disease to him.

Such was your observance, prince Josiah,

And by this your celebrated name was carried to the heights:

You removed the impious monuments of ancient crime

And renewed the ancestral laws as far as you could.

To the departing kingdom this pious glory was given to him,

Which the order of the evening time bestowed.

Thus purple closes the border; thus wine concludes the feasts;

After the fruits of the fertile year, the olive flourishes.

A great crowd of fathers must undertake this work,

[Col. 0284D] Whom the pious law retains, and whom it would take too long to recount.

[Col. 0285A] Often I see judges, seduced by promises, abandon the laws

And pursue gold with greedy throat and mouth.

Often I strive to call back those who wish to seize it.

There are some whose willingness is greater, and for whom refusal is scarcely less so:

While someone divides a broad river into channels,

The smaller part flows in the channels, the greater in the river.

Often, while I accuse the wicked of such things,

They secretly say among themselves that I too am their equal in this respect.

Often, even when they are not such, I suspect that they are;

Since they are numerous, I shall be free from this disease.

A sick man cannot be confined by every illness;

At least one disease among many can be absent.

[Note: [Col. 0285D] “My prefecture.” He means the legation which, by the command of King Charles, the *missus dominicus* carried out in Narbonese Gaul together with Laidradus, later bishop of Lyons. Under this title he describes, in poetic fashion, the boundaries of that province and his journey from Lyons all the way to Narbonne. How extensive the authority of this office was is shown by the words of the bishops to Charles the Bald at the palace of Verberie: “We ask that the perpetrators of crimes and despisers of apostolic discipline be restrained, without regard to persons or blindness caused by gifts, by legates of proven faith sent from your side.” From this legation, therefore, Theodulf found the occasion to judge that he ought to teach in this poem what judges must chiefly avoid and what they must perform.]

My prefecture had been assigned to me to carry out,

A great undertaking in practice, and an office of power.

Second to none in force, zeal, pious efforts, or arms,

[Col. 0285B] King Charles, foremost in every good thing, gave this to me.

To him obey Wales, the Rhône, the Meuse, the Rhine, and the Inn,

The Seine, the Weser, the Vardo, the Garonne, and the Po;

The fields, the Moselle, the Loire, the Volturnus, the Marne, and the Lez;

The Danube, the Aude, the Gabarus, the Olitis, the Elbe, and the Saône.

So that the holy law might bind clergy and people in synod,

And so that the leader might be a rule for all along his own path.

So that the holy order of Mother Church might grow,

And pious custom and dignity in the strong cities—

Those which the Saône and the Vardo, the swift Rhône, wash,

As well as Elauris, or the Aude, which must be counted among them;

Those which the Alps and the Libyan sea divide from Latium,

And those from which the Pyrenees separate your world from Iberia;

Or those which Lyons tears away toward the Bear or the North Wind,

And the beautiful Aquitanian territories in your region of Toulouse.

[Col. 0285C] Laidradus, my companion, had been attached to us for this task,

So that the great labor might be lightened by his assistance.

Noricum gave him birth; Lyons, you hope that he will become

Your future bishop through the aid of religion.

He is renowned for skill, vigorous in understanding, and overflowing with virtue.

For him this life remains a passage to the world above.

Now, leaving your lofty walls of Lyons behind us,

We undertake the journey which the business requires.

We seek stony Vienne, built in a valley,

Which cliffs confine on one side, while the gaping river presses on the other.

From there we gave ourselves to the Valentian lands and the fallen city,

And from there, to you, Morenate, we entrusted ourselves to your rock.

Then we touch the lands of Orange and the fields of Avignon,

And the boundaries once held by the Goths.

[Col. 0285D] From there we gradually hasten toward the Nemausian citadels,

Where there is a spacious city and a sufficiently demanding undertaking.

Here Madalona held the left, Sextantio the right:

The latter is girded by rugged hills, the former by the sea.

When we had safely passed these places, with Agatha soon on the left,

[Col. 0286A] We left them behind, and Béziers received us beneath its roofs.

Soon we touched your seat, Narbonne, and the beautiful city,

Where a joyful crowd came out to meet me:

The remnants of the Gothic people, together with the western crowd,

Made themselves joyful under my leadership, as their kinsman.

From there, revisiting Carcassonne and Redas,

We quickly carried ourselves into your walls, Narbonne.

Peoples and throngs of clergy gather from every side,

And synod governs the clergy, while the holy law governs the forum.

After these affairs had been well arranged, the wealthy city of Arles

At last received us—the city which its own citizens established.

The city of Arles, which surpasses many other cities,

Is nevertheless first in rank, while Narbonne, you are second.

In synod of the clergy and by the administration of laws over the people,

We subdued their hearts through the power of law and skill.

[Col. 0286B] Marseille, founded by a Greek people, received us;

And the countryside and city of Aquae, or yours, Cavaillon.

But circumstance forbids me to visit the others individually,

Although all the people among whom we are go to them.

Their neighborhood is afflicted by the savage proximity of the raging sea,

And a sickening odor exhales from the corrupted air.

Some are lifted by hills, others strangled in the depths of valleys;

Savage winter, hail, frost, and snow strike them.

There the road continues through thickets and sharp stony ground,

And through abrupt hollows.

Valleys occupy the lowlands; mountains rise toward the clouds;

Steep rivers plunge from the mountain heights.

A great assembly often throngs to us in crowds,

Containing every age and sex that one could name:

Little child, old man, young man, boy, unmarried woman, bachelor,

[Col. 0286C] Elder, youth, old woman, man, married woman, and younger person.

Why should I linger? The common people urgently promise gifts,

And believe that what they desire will be accomplished if they give.

They strive to break the wall of my mind with this assault,

So that my mind, badly battered by such a ram, may collapse.

One promises crystal and eastern gems

If I arrange for him to possess another man’s fields.

Another brings coins of heavy weight, rich gold,

Which Arab speech or script has engraved,

Or which the Latin stylus stamps upon shining silver,

Provided that he acquires estates, fields, and houses.

Someone secretly summons our official in a subdued voice

And utters these words, which I must repeat:

“I have a vessel marked with ancient figures,

In which there is pure metal of high quality and no small weight.

[Col. 0286D] On it are revealed the sculpted traces of Cacus’s crimes,

And the faces of men loosened by corruption and by stakes.

Iron-bound rocks, or varied images of robbery,

And a field stained with human and animal blood.

There the Herculean fury crushes the bones of Vulcan’s son;

[Col. 0287A] The savage man belches his ancestral fires from his mouth.

Or with his knee he breaks the stomach, or with his heels the flanks,

And with his smoke-belching club strikes the throat and face.

There, in a hollow rock, you may see bulls coming forth,

And again being dragged in terror behind him.

On one part of the hollow, whose mouth is a level circle,

Not too broad and bearing small figures,

The Tirynthian child struck twin serpents;

Ten deeds are also marked there in order.

But the outer portion, polished by frequent use,

Has been worn smooth, and the old image has grown thin and vanished:

There Alcides, the river Calydon, and misshapen Nessus

Compete for the beauty of your Deianira.

The deadly robe smeared with Nessus’s blood

Is visible, and the dreadful fate of wretched Lychaeus.

[Col. 0287B] Antaeus also loses his life between his hard arms,

Although he is forbidden to be thrown down upon the earth in the customary way.

I shall bring this to my lord—for he happened to call me ‘lord’—

If he favors my requests.

A numerous portion of the people is involved: mothers and men,

Children and young people, both sexes together.

Their father and mother abandoned them under the protection of liberty,

And from that time they have remained a free multitude.

If I invalidate their documents, you will soon possess them,

Together with that old vessel, through these gifts of mine.”

Another says: “I have cloaks dyed in various colors,

Which, I think, the grim Arab sent.

As the calf follows its mother, and the heifer the bull,

The heifer matches the calf in color, and the cow the ox.

[Col. 0287C] You may admire the brilliance and the art joined to the colors,

And how the smaller figure is skillfully joined to the great wheels.

I have a dispute with someone over some fine cattle,

For which I am preparing to give these suitable gifts.

For calves I offer a calf, for bulls a bull,

For a heifer a heifer, and for an ox I give an ox.”

Someone promises that he will give beautiful cups,

If only I give him what he asks to have given to him:

Gold adorns the interior, while blackness decorates the exterior,

And when touched by sulfur the silver-colored hue disappears.

“Look how the supports shine beautifully, and the lovely embossed work. We shall give cloths,”

Another says, “if you give me what I ask.

A field adorned with vines and olives, herbs and gardens,

And watered by irrigation, was left to me at my father’s death.

[Col. 0287D] Now my brothers and sister demand their shares from me,

And I wish to possess it alone, without any co-heir.

I shall obtain my wish if my desires please you;

If you accept what I give, you will rightly give what I ask.”

One wants to steal his partner’s household, another his fields.

Both deal with what belongs to another: one holds it, the other desires it.

One burns with desire to acquire, the other lest he lose;

The former is ready to give a sword and helmet, the latter shields.

One brother possesses the father’s property; the other wants to possess it,

And one wishes to give mules, the other horses.

One part of the people is rich in resources; the rest presses forward,

And all have something they seek and something they complain about.

Nor did they lack a ready willingness to give;

Each used resources of differing strength.

[Col. 0288A] Just as the greater produce great gifts, so the lesser produce small ones,

Believing that what they desire will be theirs by this method.

One brings Córdoba leather, named after you;

Another draws out white skins, another red ones from there.

One who can afford linen brings linen gifts, and one who cannot brings wool;

One offers a covering for the head, another for the foot, another for the hand.

Another has a woven gift to give, with which we commonly wipe

Our faces and palms with a light moisture.

Some prepare *serinia* to be given, nor was there a lack of one

Who eagerly wished to give little wax rolls.

Who could recount each item? Everyone trusted in a gift,

And no one thought that he possessed anything unless he gave something.

O criminal disease, spread throughout every part!

O crime, O madness, with mouths excessively savage,
