Which wickedly claims the whole world as its captive,

[Col. 0288B] And lacks neither one to give nor one to carry away what has been wickedly seized!

Thus they hasten to bend me, yet they would not have thought me

To be such a man, had someone of this kind not previously been there.

No one seeks boars in the waters, scaly gifts in the forests,

Water upon funeral pyres, or water in a torch.

The Sabaean land has frankincense, the Ganges ivory monsters,

The Gryphons [Gryphes] and Hyrcania have them, Syria has balsam.

Each thing is sought according to its own law and through continual practice,

And mortals think that what once existed will exist again.

But when they see the points of their words broken,

And the weapons of their promises achieving nothing,

And see me standing firm, like a strong city after battle,

Unable to be captured by their skill,

Then each seeks his own property, each recovers his own rights,

[Col. 0288C] And they no longer oppress me or their own people with snares.

Thus anyone who sees the entrance through which he was often accustomed

To steal has been closed passes by without hope.

But so that a noble sense of propriety would not abandon our actions,

And so that these matters would not be thought to have been acted out merely as a show,

And so that I myself would not be conspicuous to many through novelty,

Nor would good be made abhorrent by its proximity to evil,

I did not refuse the gifts which concord, the foremost virtue, bestows—

Concord, which willingly joins and receives minds,

And makes something common whose proper use demands it,

Although, possessing much, it teaches that nothing is one’s own.

As I considered these matters, I gladly accepted small gifts,

Which a savage hand did not give, but a beloved one:

Tree fruits and the produce of a green garden,

Eggs, unmixed wine, bread, and food for hoofed horses.

[Col. 0288D] We also accepted tender chickens and small birds,

Whose bodies were small but suitable for food.

O happy every virtue, if discernment

As the nurse of virtues moderates, adorns, and nourishes them!

My Muse, which had wandered a little from my deeds,

Let it return to the melody it began.

Let the scales of a just balance have equal weights for you as judge,

So that, when you grant, each person may willingly receive his own.

Let neither greed, nor love, nor jealousy, nor fear—

Which disturb things—be present; let the summit of your mind stand firm.

Alas, by these things piety is quickly driven from justice,

And fraud and deceit invade its place.

These four are guilty things, for one is guiltier than the other three:

Greed, the terrible root of every evil.

[Col. 0289A] The acceptance of gifts commonly turns weak minds away

From truth and drives righteous justice away.

This disease does not grow only through silver and gold,

Or through the swift horse’s claw that tears up the fields,

Or through purple, scarlet, gems, or beautiful embroidered cloth,

Or through various objects that sails are accustomed to carry.

It also grows through light words and words that fly on equal winds,

Through flattery, by whose breeze the stirred mind swells.

The honor of clothing is color; purses rejoice in their weight;

The breath of favor vanishes into thin air.

To some, at least, it is the earthly glory of material gain;

To others, by contrast, there is nothing but air.

A rich gift quickly disturbs the judge’s understanding;

The poor man trembles because he cannot bear it.

One promises that he will often give more, another even more,

[Col. 0289B] Yet the man who gives the better gift will acquire what he seeks.

There is one whom neither witnesses, nor law, nor document supports,

And so he comes to the court stripped of all these things.

He carries everything with him and says, “If you wish, accept it”;

He relies on everything, if only he can give more.

Do not, judges, be angry with the labor of this man,

Who seeks to remove the crime, not to commit it.

I do not spread the guilt of some over everyone;

Let each person have praise or shame according to his own merit.

Alas, it is a crime to abandon truth for any things,

Or to sell, whether freely or for payment, what everyone ought to give.

Do not suppose yourself free of deceit or bitter fraud,

Even if you bring gifts for what is just.

One judge strives to sell what is just and what is unjust;

One commits a single crime, the other two.

[Col. 0289C] The one because he sells justice, which he ought to give freely;

The other because he despises it, yet nevertheless accepts payment for it.

He who seeks savage rewards in judgment instead of what is right,

You are carrying out his crime, hostile fraud, and wickedness:

The greedy man sets against an unworthy price

The pious services of justice which he ought to give freely.

If by chance the madness of greedy disease has seized you,

Let reason stand firm and sing to you in a teachable voice:

See that the Most High watches you from above,

And notes individually everything that you do with supreme attention.

He is at once judge, witness, and avenger of evil,

Knowing how to give worthy things to the good and evils to the wicked.

If, nevertheless, the contrary phrase “Accept the gift” resounds,

What you now give to your associates, afterward beware of accepting.

[Col. 0289D] Let victorious reason, standing against it, say:

“Shameful disease, depart, and give yourself wholly over to me.”

This thirst, in which you burn fiercely, must not be satisfied for you;

The more you drink of it, the greater it will become for you.

The more wood the fire receives, the more it boils;

So each person desires to possess more, the more he possesses.

A swallow always grows larger as blood is heaped up,

And the more it drinks, the more it thirsts thereafter.

Therefore, I beg you, strive to drive away this frenzied disease;

With me as physician, you will be healed from the savage wound.

When his kindly hand has healed you, sick man,

Let this disease reign in you no longer; let the bitter plague go far away.

When the clamor of cases calls you to the troubled courts

And the business of your office must be carried out,

First willingly seek the holy places to be approached,

[Col. 0290A] And while you seek them, offer pious prayers to God.

Ask him humbly to direct your actions

And not allow anything to be done unless it pleases him.

For this is the rule to be observed in all actions,

Whenever any matter must be begun by you.

We are judged to seek first the kingdom and justice of God,

So that through this help all things may be added to us.

If you cast the first foundations upon such marble,

Every pious work rises more firmly from it.

O work blessed once, four times, and beyond all numbering,

To which you, glorious Christ the stone, adhere.

Soon, according to the custom of the resonant court, hasten to its doors,

Where perhaps a quarrelsome crowd awaits you.

As you return, if a poor man utters words of supplication,

Who afterward says that he cannot speak to you,

[Col. 0290B] Go surrounded by the people, or through the splendid doors;

With the people waiting outside, you yourself will be received within.

Let a faithful, just, and pious official go near you,

So that under his guidance the poor man may afterward have access to you.

Tell him to bring the man into our presence,

The man who was uttering the beginnings of a great complaint.

After you sit down, first examine his case carefully,

Then let each matter proceed in its own order.

Perhaps you ask when and at what hour one should come to the courts.

Take my advice: come in the morning.

The labor will not burden you throughout the whole day;

The harvest is greater the more each person ploughs.

He who fasted greatly in order to receive the law

Is said to have continued fasting for this entire undertaking.

I have seen judges slow in the duties of justice,

[Col. 0290C] But, I confess, quick to accept gifts.

They arrive at the fifth hour and know how to leave at the ninth;

If the third hour brings them, the sixth takes them away.

For if they must give, they are present at the ninth hour;

If they must receive, at the first—and the man who was late is suddenly prompt.

Thus, as soon as a horse feels its mouth controlled by the bit,

It leaps forth and seeks its pasture of its own accord.

He who is always ready to harm and never to help

Comes quickly, although he ought never to come.

Always avoid drunkenness, especially during the time

When the pious reins of justice must be guided.

For he who buries himself in excessive banquets and sleep

Blunts himself and deprives his body and soul of strength.

When he comes to cases with his sharpened sense stripped away,

[Col. 0290D] He sits slack, sluggish, and mindless.

While the skill of the case must be held in suspense,

And the question must be examined at length, back and forth,

That lazy, soaked, belching, drunken, panting man

Yawns, withers, feels sick, suffers, and grows dull.

Now he says that he has pains in his joints, now that he has phlegm,

And now that all his limbs are burdened at once.

Sleep first infects him after wine and banquets;

Next comes the labor of indulging in luxury.

Therefore beware of excessive food, cups of Bacchus,

And sleep: each of these often weighs down the mind.

Just as these things in small amounts nourish the stomach,

So in greater amounts they burden it.

Much water destroys grain, whereas a moderate amount nourishes it.

A drunkard will be laughed at secretly by the whole people;

One man signals to another, and soon you will be marked out.

[Col. 0291A] As a sober man moving his lips, you will be respected by the whole people,

And they will eagerly do whatever you command them to do.

Those whom honorable integrity and just action commend,

Bring each one in by name, calling him forward.

Let these men handle and examine matters with you in great care,

And investigate the path that leads to better things.

Meanwhile let the doorkeeper restrain the gaping crowd,

So that the lawless, raging people do not rush inside.

Let the buildings not be packed with tumultuous complaints;

The less someone is heard, the louder he roars.

The doorkeeper himself must be warned not to seek gifts—

Those which the people often offer when they come.

It is a crime to expect payment from a complaining petitioner.

Alas, every doorkeeper loves this crime.

Every doorkeeper loves it, yet the judge does not hate it;

[Col. 0291B] Scarcely one out of a thousand will recoil from it.

Their strengths are various, but their love of possessing is one;

It should more properly be called madness than love.

This harmful disease flies around the whole world,

And in its fury devours a great part of humanity.

Every age and every rank is exhausted by this corruption:

Virgin, child, old man, and both sexes together.

Just as the great desire great things, so the small desire small things;

The cat does to the mouse what the grim lion does to the sheep.

When, therefore, everything has been arranged in its individual parts,

And the time and order of your office require it,

When the senate of the people is seated in its seats and ranks,

And the curule chair has received you,

Looking around at them, address them with these beginnings,

And admonish them with the pious love of your mind:

[Col. 0291C] “Learn justice; learn the commands of heaven,

Which the Father enthroned on high established from the axis of heaven.

God examines this, the prophets examine it, the laws examine it, and the ruler also;

Let this force govern our hearts.

If it governs us, we shall rightly govern the peoples;

A mind rules all things well when God himself rules it.”

Remain for a while on these admonitions and words,

And give them an excellent taste of the law from its stream.

But if light, airy pride should seek you with a slight effort

And wish to tear you apart,

With savage eyes, dreadful hand, most foul mouth,

And a swollen, viperous head and body,

Whose mind is swollen, whose action is frivolous, whose voice is bloated,

And for whom food and drink remain black poisons,

[Col. 0291D] Replacing walking with leaps, and feet with the wing of a bird,

By which he was able to glide away from the axis of heaven,

Remembering the ancient crime committed above the heavens,

Using his skill by which he seeks the depths of Styx—

By which he hisses within you, “How high and exalted you are,”

So that you may think it beneath you to mingle with the common people—

Behold, you struggle to become one part of the humble people,

While wishing to be pious and merciful toward everyone.

Your order and rank raise you to sublime heights;

Why do you willingly abase yourself when you hold lofty places?

For if you examine yourself, you are greatly in error here,

When you make yourself degenerate through simplicity.

When no one is able to resist you, no one to oppose you,

Why, poor fool, do you turn yourself from head to tail?

[Col. 0292A] Once a blind wound begins to live beneath your breast,

Or, what is worse, begins already to flow outward,

Let humble power immediately leap forth, whose companion is prudence,

Carrying arms with pious strength.

Those whose faces shine and whose garments radiate with light

Will have a gracious expression, everything sufficiently beautiful.

Let only one noble pair rise up terribly against the enemy,

And say from afar, “Shameful disease, depart from here.”

Let them say, “Depart, join yourself to the spirits of the dead,

Whose fate has been heaped together with yours.

Go, seek Cocytus; plunge into the depths of Phlegethon,

Where your savage inventor will be tortured.

He who wished to ascend with you to the seat of God

Has fallen with you from the pious seat into the depths.

Without you he would have fallen there; with you he could have ascended,

[Col. 0292B] While remaining in the seat of the firmament.

You are a heavy burden to the worthy and a load for the unjust.

You are a driver for evils and an enormous weight for the good.

Those whom, unhappy one, you seek and strive to harm,

Are not your people, but the blessed flock that follows Christ.

He came from heaven and opened a path to heaven,

Where the way had long been closed but now lies open.

He continually draws people from earthly things to heavenly ones,

While you continually drag them from the heights to the depths.

He places his followers in their heavenly seat;

You plunge yours into the fearful realms of Tartarus.

Struck by these darts and driven away by this spear,

Let the disease yield, as snow departs when the sun drives it away.

From here let the savage tracks of the wounding monster flee,

And let the friendly hand heal the wound inflicted by the enemy.

[Col. 0292C] Let the iron drive away this enemy, and medicine this disease;

Let healing be given to you by his voice as well.

See that swollen pride does not corrupt your heart,

While you hold the public face of elevated places.

While the people favor you, and you alone are surrounded by many,

Do not think yourself enclosed everywhere by prosperity.

And lest sluggish forgetfulness remove anything from your mind,

Let the final day always be kept in view.

To be able to remain free from every stain of vice,

Look at what you are, not at what you possess.

Although you sit adorned with gems and purple,

After the passage of the flesh you will be rotting dust.

For the body now girded with yellow gold,

Which a silk cloak of varied color covers,

Will, alas, be pressed into foul, filthy, stinking, icy, decaying earth,

[Col. 0292D] Uncovered by any garment.

What the sea, earth, and air carry for consumption,

And the beautiful cups which you prepare to distribute,

Alas, must be eaten by the mouth of wasting corruption;

Alas, afterward it will be nothing but dirty ashes.

And the flesh which smells of fragrant moss and amomum,

And which carries the scent of foreign musk,

When it has fallen apart will give off a stench and be wet with corruption,

Containing everything offensive and nothing lovable.

You whom coffered palaces beneath lofty roofs shelter,

And who complain that small ceilings are large enough,

Will be shut within a narrow and modest urn,

And scarcely will your dwelling be larger than your body.

You whom the people visit in crowds from every side,

[Col. 0293A] And whom this or that commoner is ready to obey,

Afterward you will be the solitary inhabitant of a solitary cave:

What reason for seeing you will there be except mourning?

Nor will there be companions except those who gnaw your entrails,

Whose food is their mother, without whom their life is short.

Even if a thousand flocks and a thousand herds return to you,

And no neighbor confines your land,

Deprived of everything, beneath the covering of an unloved tomb,

Poor in possessions, you will seek things poorer still.

Several bodies are not needed to carry one person,

And one suitable color is chosen for the whole fitting body.

Nevertheless, you may then be carried on four pairs of shoulders,

When the final and tearful honor is already being paid.

The iron sleep will dissolve your cold limbs,

[Col. 0293B] And you will undertake a brief journey from which there is no return.

Why should I enumerate more? What is pleasing to the sight,

What delights and pleases human eyes,

After life the worm will possess, after the worm the dust,

Until the voice of the Thunderer returns it to the place from which it came.

This is the law of the body formed from earthly substance;

The soul has another power, whose origin is heavenly.

The noble soul, which has been thrust into a perishable prison,

Is confined and weighed down by an earthly dwelling.

The merciful Creator joins these two elements together

So that the human being remains alive and mortal.

Joined together, they provide life; separated, death.

To live is for them to be present to one another; to be absent is to die.

But by different courses they return to their origins:

For the heavenly origin gives itself back to its own,

[Col. 0293C] As air yields to heaven and the lowest earth to air,

So everywhere the body must yield to its own soul.

Alas, what a crime it is to place the body before the soul,

And to prefer what is mortal to what does not die,

To prefer the servant to the mistress, pepper to hemlock,

Lead to gold, and filthy stones to gems and precious things.

Let God preside over the mind; let this also care wisely for the flesh;

Let the flesh live through the soul that gives it strength, and let the soul live through God,

So that, upright in this order, you may be drawn to the heights,

And your mind may flee the depths and seek the high places.

And when that day comes which shakes nothing but bodies,

Let earth cover the body, and let the spirit seek the stars.

Set this before your eyes; turn it over constantly in your mind,

As a certain king once wisely said:

For these are your final concerns, so that you may be free from dark sin;

[Col. 0293D] You must remember them in all your actions.

For if your diligent meditation considers what you will be,

You will be stained by few or no evils.

If you weigh these things, after death there is everlasting life;

You will exist in the better part of yourself and soon live again.

And when the heavy blast of the trumpet shakes the world,

And you emerge from the urn, a human being restored to life,

And your mind once more takes its place in its former dwelling,

You will be numbered among the angelic assemblies.

When these things are finished, you will immediately establish a tribunal within your own mind,

To carry out its commands voluntarily.

Let its members ascend, sit together, teach, and govern

Every movement of the soul from the citadel of your mind.

[Col. 0294A] Fortified by this help and supported by such aid,

Let your foot run swiftly along an unobstructed path.

Go quickly, boy; choose some from among the many

Who live in places not nearer to the neighboring districts.

And for their own cases they have come there; or choose those

Who, although they are near, nevertheless belong to the needy people.

If one of your own citizens is mixed among them, do not cast him out;

His case shall be heard within, wherever it falls in the order.

If you cast him out, do not let him, upon returning, obstruct those who are coming,

And let them not hinder one another while one goes and another returns here.

Examine everyone’s cases with vigilant investigation,

So that you may be able to conclude each in its proper order.

First learn these matters well, as much as you ought to learn them.

Words are prepared for you from Job as an example; he says:

“I was eyes to the blind, and guidance for the lame;

[Col. 0294B] the poor man was safe when he had found me a father.

I diligently searched out the hidden recesses of an unknown case,

By what efforts I might make it known to me.”

Do not hasten too quickly toward the end of the case,

Nor roll it along lazily, with a slow or excessively sluggish step.

Let torpor not cloud your slowness, nor error your speed;

Let your foot proceed safely between the two evils.

Imagine something else while the case remains hidden; soon the case will become clear.

So that you are not badly deceived, first deceive properly.

The threatened death of the infant exposed the false mother’s lies,

And the true mother received her dear burden.

This matter carried Solomon’s reputation to the heights,

And became for the people a source of fear and for him a path of praise.

The great often and habitually twist their own cases,

While the poor man goes away without his own affair.

[Col. 0294C] Add these men to yourself as companions in the cases of the lesser,

And, setting aside their own matters, let each one rightly help you.

Whoever is deprived of a father or mother, or of a husband,

Let it be your care to pursue the cases of such people.

Remain their advocate and their protection;

Let one group know you as a mother, another as a husband.

If the weak, infirm, child, sick person, old woman, or old man comes,

Offer them pious aid with compassion.

Let him sit who cannot stand; grasp the hand of one who cannot rise.

Help the one whose heart or voice, foot or hand trembles.

Raise up the man cast down by words; calm the threatening man.

Give strength to the one who fears, and add fear to the one who rages.

The crowd stirs lawsuits and battles of many voices;

Strike them sharply with your voice and with a grave sound,

Like hoarse geese, crows, and blackbirds,

[Col. 0294D] Whose custom is that they all sing out together.

If they do not keep silent, impose threats, but always beware

Lest your hand become too ready for savage words.

Let no one's breast be struck there by your staff.

The various crowds will come together with unequal force:

This one cannot, that one can; this one refuses, that one wishes.

Govern their various movements with a skillful moderation,

And prudently give each person whatever is useful in his place.

Restrain the swift one; rebuke the slower one,

So that this one may be swifter and that one slower.

Instruct the foolish one; draw the clever one back with reins,

So that the former does not lose what is his and the latter does not seek what belongs to another.

Willingly moderate the slow-speaking man and the excessively talkative one;

[Col. 0295A] Let one hand bring help to two.

Lest the slow man lose his business by remaining silent,

And lest he seek more of another’s than is just.

Or lest the verbose man, in the whirlwind of his windy tongue,

Bury the undertaking he has begun and the proper measure of the matter.

While you allow the empty hours to pass halfway through speeches,

Let both matters and days go by without result.

There is one who cannot complete his business by speaking,

And through an ignorant tongue badly mutilates his own affair.

Just as when someone, with a bow bent taut,

While intending to strike an enemy, strikes himself and his own people,

So, while such a person speaks to his own harm,

Alas, he is soon pierced by his own arrow.

Supply this person’s oarage with healthful words;

[Col. 0295B] Hold him back if he falls, and lift him if he has fallen.

When the perplexed case resounds throughout the entire forum

And its ambiguity wearies you and your people,

Command silence to the advocates on both sides,

So that they do not disturb justice while each one shouts for his own case.

Then, with a few men and the whole crowd silent,

Willingly consider and reconsider the matter for a long time.

Until at last a path without guilt is found,

Let the savage dispute be settled and let justice give each person his own.

Moreover, observe whoever sits near you,

In case he wishes to corrupt justice by a prayer or gifts.

Perhaps his ear has already been touched by a gentle whisper,

And a clever man is hinting something to him from one side, a crafty man from the other.

One may make a sign with his eyes, another with his hands,

Or there may be any kind of conduct in this matter.

He may wish to favor these men but not wish to reveal himself to you;

He wavers uncertainly, desiring and fearing at once.

[Col. 0295C] No differently from an adulteress contemplating adultery:

Here she desires the crime, there she fears the scourging.

Often wicked companions injure their companion with their contagion,

As one animal is injured by the proximity of another.

Do not think the man who hides himself just if he is unjust,

Lest, while you are unaware, he draw you into his crimes.

Thus a thief pretends to be someone’s companion so that he may enter to do harm;

Thus poisons lie hidden mixed with sweet wine.

Be attentive also concerning the wife who belongs to you,

Lest she stain your mind by seducing you.

The kisses which she will softly give to your knees, hands, neck, and cheeks,

With which she mixes gentle words,

Accustomed to arm her prayers with such poison,

As the bow-bearing man arms his swift arrows,

[Col. 0295D] If your mind has been protected by a strong helmet,

So that it sees her arrows rebound from it,

She will return groaning, offering feigned sighs,

And weeping that her prayers have carried no weight.

Soon a boy, nurse, or perhaps a deceitful little maidservant

Will say, “Why do you despise the words of my mistress?”

With turned face, this person will quietly whisper these things:

“What is now merely noticed is always an honor to me;

What other women ask for they receive, and it benefits or harms them,

But I alone obtain none of what I desire.”

At last, they will say, let her ask and run to embrace you,

And say to you, “Why do you allow her to be troubled by you?”

[Col. 0296A] But let your mind fight and resist her return like an enemy,

And fear lest renewed battles overcome you.

And lest she do something harmful and say that you ordered it,

Be watchful and, as far as you can, take care continually.

Long ago, without her husband’s knowledge, a queen carried out a deed

So that a stony hail might crush an innocent man.

Nor should less care be applied to your own officials.

What sort of retinue do you have? Those who are near you are many:

Let not the savage disease injure them, nor let them wound your heart,
And let them stain your inmost parts with their own corruption.

As they seek to seize, may you seize them; as they may be able to take, may you take them. If they can compel you, be vigilant and take care. Anyone from the crowd will force you to withdraw; let the others withdraw, but one will remain nearby.

Whoever seems to you to be closer to them will give you these words and counsel:

“Please do not reject the prayers I address to you, for behold, your kindness makes me bold. If you favor my requests, there is someone who seeks to give rewards; the gifts are good, and the giver himself is good. This or that person is preparing to give you this or that gift, which you can possess without the burden of sin.”

Then the cunning man will add persuasive words to entice you, whose hand is already laden with coins.

Avoid this hydra, this *cenchris*, this horned serpent; here will be a *seps*, here a *dipsas*, here a *prester* for you.

A censor commonly has stern and savage attendants, though he himself is both pious and strong in piety.

[Col. 0296B]

Thus, they say, Scylla appears to you with a human face, but her loins bristle with savage dogs.

The matter remains uncertain: one persists, another denies. “It is” and “it is not” resound, and these two assertions produce many more.

From the seed of these things, which stir human concerns, arise the shoots of cases, or a broad harvest grows.

Let witnesses be sought, so that they may dispel the clouds of the case and drive away doubt as truth approaches.

Diligently investigate their reputation and origin, their names or character, their places or trustworthiness.

If one is upright, receive him; if corrupt, remove him entirely, as you reject bitter fruits from food and accept those that are suitable.

Let neither suspicion, nor something heard, nor money support these men; let them report only what appears true to them.

And to draw out the truth, examine those same men separately, and note individually the words each one utters.

[Col. 0296C]

If there are two, question both; if there are more, separate the several witnesses. If there are three, let this same rule apply to the three separately.

The knower of the secret, guardian of the chaste woman, and kindly youth performed this deed in the Achaemenian land.

From there he crushed the wicked old men beneath a stony rain, those whom the black cloud of wickedness had previously oppressed.

Separate the wicked; join the trustworthy in firm fellowship, so that the one group may do less harm and the other help more.

As worse things do more harm, so good things are more beneficial: just as more sheep provide more milk, so wolves bring greater losses.

Do not let the deceitfulness of these men, prepared beforehand, overcome you; see that false speech does not proceed as though it were the only speech.

[Col. 0296D]

Having properly detected them, and questioning them again and again, draw them out by varying the ambiguity and wording.

Despise witnesses who speak falsely and conceal the truth; although their methods differ, both kinds harm.

The one who conceals the truth and the one who speaks falsely both err wickedly: the former because he contributes nothing, the latter because he wishes to cause harm.

One is wicked, the other less useful; although they differ, error holds them both.

For although one transgresses less and the other more, neither is far removed from error.

The one casts down a man who is standing; the other scorns to raise up one who has fallen. The former harms by doing injury; the latter harms by refusing to act.

Often, because of those in power, justice is wrongly abandoned, and favor and fear suppress the truth by silence.

[Col. 0297A]

Hence the anger of the heavenly Judge remains to be feared, when he sees human affairs placed above his own.

Be vigilant meanwhile, lest, while you wish to bring forth the truth, someone perish through your betrayal.

The guilty man deserves death; do not betray the guilty, and let your voice not open the path to his blood.

Blessed is the man who can rescue the wretched from destruction and bring the aid of salvation by deed and by speech.

If an innocent man perceives something tending to his condemnation, the judge will be credulous and the witness malign.

An unjust witness is hostile to three persons: to the censor, to the innocent man, and to you, supreme God.

By swearing wickedly, he scorns God through his perjuries, and vainly invokes his lordly name.

[Col. 0297B]

He is hostile also to the censor, whom his lies deceive, and whom he binds in the chains of his own error.

Finally, he is hostile to the innocent man, whom he injures with unjust statements and for whom, through wicked ingenuity, he prepares dreadful harms.

As the kite hastens toward the flesh, the fish toward the hook, the bear toward honeycombs, and cattle toward salty places, so the unjust witness rushes to seize a reward and receives agreeable payment for great evil.

If it is a crime to sell the truth, what is it to sell falsehood?

Do you wish, savage witness, to join one crime to another?

I beg you, such men, refrain from selling your lies. If you give me these pleasing things, they will be pleasing to the ungrateful.

They were neither good things to be bought nor goods to be sold for money; dust was being purchased with empty dust.

[Col. 0297C]

O merchandise, merchandise more harmful than every payment, which kills both the giver and the taker at once.

From this comes the wicked plague of perjury, while someone wishes false matters to be believed.

Those who deceive by entreaty, by tears, or by false murmuring often obtain belief even in this way.

Whoever you are, I warn you constantly: beware of swearing, because, believe me, it is a matter sufficiently dreadful to swear.

Not because the matter itself is evil or removed from holy law, but because, when it is done repeatedly, one enters gaping into crime.

No one who does not speak can lie; no one can see dreams unless he sleeps.

No one falls in battle unless he attempts savage combat, nor is anyone wounded by a boar’s tooth unless he attacks the boar.

[Col. 0297D]

No one is shipwrecked unless he cuts the waves with his vessel; no one perishes in fire if he remains far from fire.

And no one who does not swear commits perjury; unless someone fears it, he will be seized by this plague.

When a harsh or uncertain hearer seizes upon your words, let “yes, yes” and “no, no” bind all these matters.

There are also words that excuse the burden of swearing, by which perhaps you can avoid guilt without defilement.

If he persists in doubting, support the truth for him by examples, reasoning, and arguments.

If he still does not believe and carries a heart of stone, leave him, and then go away safely.

[Col. 0298A]

But if the necessity of swearing presses and constrains you, do it in pure words and with a pious mind.

Do not think that by verbal skill you can deceive the Thunderer, to whom nothing is hidden and before whom all things are fully open.

He judges not according to what you swear, but according to what the person to whom you swear believes you have sworn, and thus you are liable to both.

You are liable to God, whose name you wish to take in vain, and to the companion whom you intend to deceive by a dark fraud.

If you swear in order to commit a crime, let your vows be null: this is more serious than that, although both are wounds.

Lesser wrongful wounds afflict less, greater and still greater ones more; blessed is the person who departs wounded by no wound.

If censure comes first and piety afterward, let rewards never be present in judgment; Christ too is there.

The law commands that the guilty heads of criminals be removed; their legs, their generative organs, their eyes, their backs, and their hands be burned on pyres; molten lead be poured over their mouths—or whatever punishments have been established by human law.

Such measures were devised to restrain disgraceful acts. Let piety moderate them through a balanced goodness:

[Col. 0298B]

let there be neither connivance at disgraceful deeds nor a dark hand that takes away life or limbs.

Be toward the guilty such as you wish the Thunderer to be toward you; continue to strive to spare them whenever you can.

Perhaps someone, having read our poem, will say: “This man commands no one to restrain the reins of evil.”

Read this advice of mine, which I give you in this poem, so that your vigilant mind may avoid evil on both sides.

Do not go too far in leniency, nor be savage and dark; a broad remedy will benefit a doubtful evil.

Let justice not be cruel, nor mercy sluggish, for if either exceeds what is equitable—whether more or less—it causes harm.

Often a plague lies hidden under the appearance of virtue, and it does more harm because it is less apparent.

[Col. 0298C]

Thus, for example, someone may have carried out cruel deeds while thinking that he had followed the path of justice.

Bind criminals with chains; correct them with whips, and let the vicious populace know that you are harsh toward it.

Nevertheless, do not dip steel into the blood of the wretched; bring out the sword for enemies and the whips for the guilty.

Lest, if you dissemble, you be called a supporter of vices; if you use the sword, let the name “savage” attach to you.

When others come forward, ready to defend the laws and to tear criminals apart in various ways, and say, “It is not we but the ancient law that slays them,” this death is useful, since it prevents many evils.

The axe of our office ought to fulfill the laws, and that obedience will not itself be a crime.

Let me be the one who redeems the many companies of the wretched;

let me be the one who rescues more people from the cross and from destruction.

[Col. 0298D]

Let the unhappy crowd watch me with tearful eyes; let the trembling, helpless assembly long to see me.

When they see me, let their almost lifeless bodies recover their strength; let hope increase at the sight, and warmth return to both sides.

I was about to lower the sails and seek the shores, so that the weary vessel might enjoy welcome rest for you.

Yet, after crossing the whirlpool, a small part of the great sea still remains for us to traverse.

A brief concern must properly be joined to you, little book, concerning the impoverished crowd oppressed by the rich.

For the final part of the work will sing of the care owed to the poor, whereas the preceding part was concerned with preserving the rights of the powerful.

Whoever presides over the poor, be most gentle, and know that by nature you are equal to them.

[Col. 0299A]

It was not their condition but their fault that subjected them to you, a fault that caused one human being to be subject to another.

Their labor and their consolations enrich you; when joined with many of them, you alone are richer.

Rivers grow greater through the confluence of smaller streams, and the rich man benefits from the increase brought by the poor.

Bodies grow fat when fed on another body, and flesh lives when restored by another’s death.

The stronger oppresses the weak, the great the small; one grows larger from the point at which the other diminishes.

The hawk and the sparrowhawk do this along the winding shores; the wolf does it in the forests, and the fish in the river.

Thus often beast is slain by beast, serpent by serpent, and the helpless animal remains nothing but prey.

[Col. 0299B]

O mortal race, flee this example of wild beasts, and let no human being be to another human being what a savage beast is to a beast.

Let the poor man not be stripped of his possessions; let the wretched man, condemned by a false accusation, not be forced to surrender his own property.

Ah, how often greedy corruption advances under the name of justice, and madness begins to bear the name of law!

Whatever the wretched man loses is said to have been lost justly; whatever the rich man seizes, he thinks he has taken lawfully.

One is a thief, another a fugitive; the latter’s mind is conscious of fraud.

One lies wickedly; another robs and steals.

[Col. 0299C]

The latter has wickedly tried to despise our servitude; the one whom he has long fled is our neighbor.

Fasten stocks to their feet; let them join chains around their arms, so that they may confess their unjust deeds and endure leather whips.

They inflict such things when they prefer to injure the wretched, when they wish to strip them of their property rather than their vices.

Yet the man who endures unjust deeds is more pitiable than the one who commits them.

The latter perishes by acting; the former grows strong by enduring.

Thus the cruel deeds of the wicked benefit the good, just as gold is refined by harsh fire.

For the harsher practice of the wicked commonly benefits the just, since, afflicted by it, they seek the heavenly kingdom.

The more the Egyptian people oppressed the Hebrew nation,

[Col. 0300A]

the more eagerly it prepared to reach the promised land.

Do not go violently against the wretched; be gentle toward them, whose vows are perhaps better than your own.

Let neither concealed fraud nor open license harm them; let them be secure and safe from either evil.

Do not count severe sins, but be sure to forgive them, since no one can live in this life without sin.

You who always ask that your debts be forgiven, do for the poor what you yourself ask of God.

If your indulgence does not lift any wretched person, when you ask for this indulgence, may you yourself be deprived of his help.

Thus, when the servant refused to spare his fellow servant, he soon called upon himself the anger of his just master.

As a mortal, be prepared to spare mortals, since one law of nature remains for you all.

[Col. 0300B]

Although each person’s course may be different through prosperity, their rising and setting are equal to yours.

The sacred fountain blesses them with you; the ancestral ointment anoints them, and the flesh or blood of the Lamb satisfies them.

The author who is life for you also died for them, and he calls each one to his own gifts according to his merits.

Here let the sails of the completed book be lowered; at this shore the anchor holds the vessel.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0299]

## I. [Note: Verses at the front of the Bible]

[Col. 0299D]

To this day there remains in the Memmian library the distinguished monument of an excellent work: the very Bible codex which Theodulf once commissioned to be written, with these same verses placed at the front of the book in letters of gold. We now publish them from that source, much more accurately corrected than before. From these verses and from the preface to the work, which I shall append after the poem itself, it is possible to see what Theodulf’s Bible was like, and what number and order the sacred books in it possessed.

[Col. 0300D]

## VERSES AT THE FRONT OF THE BIBLE WHICH HE HIMSELF CAUSED TO BE COPIED

Whatever the Greek and Latin style has taken from Hebrew, reader, you have here in this entire codex.

Genesis holds the first place, singing of the world’s beginnings, the Flood, and the great deeds of the fathers.

Exodus strips Egypt, cuts through the Red Sea, opens the road through the wilderness; there water and law are given.

Then Leviticus adorns the nation of the priests and explains the typological gifts with sacred rites.

The Book of Numbers describes wars, men, and deeds, by which Moses shattered idols, disgraces, and leaders.

Afterward it repeats the law, blesses the people, gives holy ordinances, and dies victorious at the word of the song.

From this point the hero Navegius divides the land in his own book, with the cities and places destroyed.

The following book sings of what order and deeds formerly proceeded under the Judges, continuing the same style.

Then comes what Ruth, the Moabite woman, accomplished, illustrious in pious merits and illustrious through her pious descendant.

[Col. 0301A]

Here you have the deeds of the Psalm-singer and the deeds of wicked Saul, followed first and next by the books of Samuel.

The third and fourth books, to which the name *Malachim* has been attached, sing in order of the deeds of the Hebrew kings.

Then comes Isaiah, who sings that Christ will be born from a virgin and calls the nations to pious laws.

Near him is Jeremiah, who watches over the rod and the pot and constructs a mournful work in fourfold order.

Ezekiel is obscure in his highest and lowest parts; here is he whom the Lord calls, in human fashion, “son of man.”

Afterward comes the pious order of the twelve lesser prophets, signifying something far different from what their words themselves sound.

Hosea repeatedly thunders of the adulteress and Joseph’s offspring, Samaria, Ephraim, Jezreel [Ms. Reg., *Gesrahel*], and the widow.

[Col. 0301B]

Then Joel sings of the world previously overturned by dark calamities and of the arrival of the holy Spirit.

Amos rebukes kingdoms for three offenses, indeed for four, and loudly proclaims that he has seen many mystical things.

Obadiah strikes Edom with the point of his holy word, and his rival falls from the mouth of his brother.

Christ’s Passion is marked by Jonah’s shipwreck, and the world possesses life in the name of Nineveh.

The daughter of the robber is devastated by the famine of Micah, because she had wounded the face of the leader of Israel.

With his voice Nahum strikes the city of steadfast blood, and loudly proclaims the feet of the peacemakers upon the mountain’s height.

[Col. 0301C]

With his inward eye Habakkuk beholds Christ on the cross; in these horns is power, and its hidden meaning resounds [Mss. Reg., Colb., and Mem., *tonat*, “thunders”].

Zephaniah brings forth what he hears from the gate and the hill; he also brings lamentation to your native people.

Haggai restores the temple and sings that the lofty Thunderer will move the seas, the fields, and the sky.

After seeing many mystical things in order, Zechariah calls the Lord your rider, O little donkey.

Malachi says that the offerings of the former people have been rejected, and that the companies of the nations are beloved by God.

Then the little book of Job is placed, preserving both words and deeds; though small, it carries great burdens.

Next the sweet song of the Psalms brings forth the sweet Christ, psalms which lyric feet have composed.

Immediately three books of Ididia are set in order, whose name is Solomon, or Qoheleth.

[Col. 0301D]

The first addresses everyone under the name of a son and corrects morals by ethical law.

The second sings that all things are vanity beneath the radiant sun; its task is to enumerate physical realities.

The third adorns the bridal chamber of the Church and of Christ, and its work turns upon logical matters.

Then comes the historical Daniel of the whole world, who sings of all kingdoms being shattered by a stone.

Next are placed two books called *Verba dierum* (“Words of Days”); their task is to bring forth the deeds and lineage of leaders.

Then Ezra is placed, restoring the law and the temple and singing of Israel’s return to its kingdoms [Mss. Reg. and Colb., “lands”], while soon afterward Esther is written as a type of the Church.

[Col. 0302A]

She was both the praise and the glory of the exiled people.

After this is placed the book called Wisdom, in which Christ’s coming and death are revealed.

The book Ecclesiasticus is immediately fitted to this one, in which pious laws resound and the blessed praise of the fathers is heard.

Here, in your book, blessed one, pious poverty, piety, and abundant goodness are duly recorded in Tobit.

Next is written the distinguished woman Judith, through whose striking the frenzy of incest fell.

Then two books of the Maccabees are placed, in which the noble deeds of four brothers are contained.

Here the open trumpet of the new law brings forth Christ [Ms. Colb.: “here the trumpet of the law brings forth Christ”], whom the ancient work brought forth under a typological veil.

Matthew, Mark, Luke, and holy John—the voice of all four thunders as one.

[Col. 0302B]

Because the first began to bring forth his account from the human race, he accordingly bears the form of a human figure.

The second begins with a terrible voice and is therefore represented by the form of a lion.

Since the third began with matters of the priesthood, the form of a young bull is properly assigned to him.

The fourth travels upon the wings of words above the heavens and therefore bears the likeness of an eagle soaring toward the heights.

The fourteen writings of Paul follow these four, writings which the sheep who was formerly a wolf sent to the world.

The first recalls the descendants of Romulus from the burden of the law and urges them to embrace evangelical faith.

The second calls the Arcadians, led astray by varied error, back to true faith through its saving writings.

[Col. 0302C]

The third praises their repentance, consoles them, and at the same time exhorts them toward better things.

The fourth leads the Galatians toward the vigor of faith, from which they had turned away under a great burden.

The fifth extols the people of Ephesus with venerable praises because they had by no means abandoned the holy faith.

The sixth consoles, praises, and adorns the Philippians because they steadfastly preserved the glory of faith.

Then the seventh instructs, corrects, and teaches the Colossians, who had been forestalled by false prophets.

The eighth favors the Thessalonian community because, when the times were clouded, it stood firm.

The ninth predicts the final times for them also, and the manner in which the dark plague is to be cast down.

The text of the tenth instructs Timothy and equips him for the affairs and sacred orders of the Church.

[Col. 0302D]

The offenses of the final age are sung in the eleventh, and he is instructed in every good path.

The twelfth, placed after the tenth, instructs Titus, so that he may avoid heresies and be able to be a presbyter.

The thirteenth gives you Philemon’s pious words, which the father sent from the city of Rome while bound.

The final book proclaims through the oracles of the law and the prophets that Christ is the Son of God to the Hebrews.

Following these are the seven Catholic pages in order, which the pen carries forth in apostolic speech.

One belongs to the pious James, two are Peter’s, three are John’s, and one there is your Jude.

Together they complete the whole Church in universal teaching and establish the faith and the law of salvation.

[Col. 0303A]

From there the pen proceeds to the apostolic Acts which Luke brought forth, and which sing of the Church’s new deeds.

The holy Vision that appeared to holy John closes the books and marks them with an arcane boundary.

Under one path this twofold road of the Old and New Testament, plainly revealed, leads upward to the heights of heaven.

Here food satisfies the inmost heart with eternal nourishment and, the more it is possessed, feeds the hunger for righteousness.

Here is drink coming from the stream of paradise; the more a person approaches it, the more he thirsts for every good.

This terrible trumpet bellows through the crossroads of the world and sends the earthly race to the heavenly kingdoms.

This light shakes away the dreadful shadows of error, by which the straight path keeps the feet of your mind.

[Col. 0303B]

Here are the laws of God, stripping the world of darkness, brighter than the stars and whiter than snow.

They command what is just, forbid what is unjust, cut away all evils, produce virtues, and drive away disgraceful faults.

The law of God is precious—for what is more precious than it, since the fountain of life, the light, and the source of goodness give it?

It is powerful doctrine and knowledge surpassing all others; nothing beneath the vault of heaven can be compared with it.

If you should wish to compare any subject with it in understanding or skill, earth will yield to it as earth yields to heaven.

Whatever is learned in the liberal arts of the world runs here along a freer path.

Whatever possesses strength through reason, or whatever is loved in those arts, comes from this fountain and flows from this stream.

[Col. 0303C]

And since it surpasses these subjects in all things, it surpasses them in the order of speech, because in a single utterance it teaches many things worth noting.

Without changing its single path of words, one speech thus powerfully proclaims many matters.

Thus it recounts the text while revealing mysteries; while singing of merely great things, it insinuates greater ones.

Thus it joins great things to small and small things to great, so that what is precious may resound through what is humble.

In narrating a past event, it shows a future one; while reporting one thing, it foretells another in wondrous fashion.

It describes deeds in such a way as to provide a method for acting; in recounting what happened, it urges you toward what must be done.

I say nothing of the weight of its subjects: who could relate individually in speech the things in which this glory shines and flourishes?

[Col. 0303D]

It does not, when closed, inspire fear, nor, when open, produce distaste; nothing here is terrifying, and nothing there is base.

Here hope seeks it; there ready ability holds it. Where it is hidden, it exercises the mind; where it is open, it nourishes it.

It trains the strong for battles in obscure sayings, and in humble speech it cherishes the little crowd.

It is bread for the strong and milk for the small; it nourishes the former with solid food and the latter with the help of milk.

It treats the sick like pure wine and soothes them in the manner of oil; through many modes of adaptation it gives one salvation.

By constant use it also removes distaste, and the more it is received, the more it is sought.

Although many things customarily cause horror when pondered deeply, love for this work grows the more these matters are considered.

It assists the mind of the reader through humble speech and raises it through lofty meanings toward better things.

[Col. 0304A]

For the crowd of uneducated readers thinks it knows this work well, while for the learned it is always fresh.

Why mention that it calls the peoples to heavenly dwellings and joins you to an imperishable life?

Where worldly love flees, heavenly love grows, and it turns the reader’s heart toward a better work.

Add that through examples it instructs worldly actions, and that the way is opened by the counsel it provides.

Certainly, while someone learns the deeds of earlier generations, he gains knowledge of what he can avoid and what he should pursue.

Thus it teaches his own actions through the actions of others, and he does not govern his words or deeds by his own alone.

Who could recount each thing? Its abundance surpasses number, and the rich excellence of the law surpasses the drops of rain.

[Col. 0304B]

Whoever you are, if you devote yourself to reading it with all your strength, seek God with an attentive mind.

Ask that he may graciously refresh your heart with this nectar, and that it may dwell in the chambers of your breast.

When this arrives, may the door of your mind be opened, so that, once it shines, it may be free from every stain.

May it provide hospitality to the one who created it, when he himself, the giver of the law, approaches with the law.

Let pride not penetrate you, nor deceptive glory; let no love of empty or vain praise possess you.

The Holy Spirit flees the savage breasts of the false, nor does he enter bodies oppressed by evils.

Let your mind be humble, your heart prudent, your action pure; let your zeal flourish, and let your work be one of piety.

Let meditation on the holy law be frequent for you; press its admonitions upon yourself by night and by day.

[Col. 0304C]

Carry it in your heart and hand; let it never be absent from your mouth; correct the actions of others, and let it correct your own.

Let it sit at the side of your bed; let your eyes see it; let your neck, knees, and bent arms carry it.

Let it sit at your head when you sleep at the customary hour, and when sleep flees from you, let it hasten toward you.

Love it not only so that you may be learned but also so that you may be just; although both are good, one rises above the other.

For the Almighty will require actions from you, not words.

Nevertheless, you can please him in both.

Learn by reading, grow accustomed through frequent practice, and teach by doing; let this be your path in the pious art of the law.

Let frequent reading educate your mind and give your senses a beautiful path.

[Col. 0304D]

So that it does not quickly slip away, let it gather strength through use; frequent reading preserves what the sharp mind grasps.

Thus a path through a thorny forest, cut by the strength of the axe, becomes a broad road as it is worn by frequent feet.

Let holy examples give strength to holy words; do what you sing, and sing what you do.

Let actions not oppose words, nor words oppose actions; let both run together as a noble pair.

Speak humbly what you grasp well in your mind, lest through pride you lose what you possess through diligence.

It is tedious to report many things; gather much into little, reader whose mind possesses a golden sharpness.

Thus, with a small quantity of seed prepared, the reaper carries away many grains and appears rich in a more fertile yield.

[Col. 0305A]

While you contemplate this work and reread our poems, I beg you, merciful reader, remember Theodulf. Farewell.

# PREFACE ATTACHED IN GOLDEN LETTERS TO THE BIBLE OF THEODULF

The Old Testament is so called because, when the New came, it ceased; the Apostle mentions this when he says: “The old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The New Testament, however, is so called because it renews. No one learns it except people renewed from their old state through grace and already belonging to the New Testament, which is the kingdom of heaven.

The Hebrews, with Ezra as author, accept the Old Testament as twenty-two books, according to the number of their letters, dividing them into three orders: the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa.

[Col. 0305B]

The first order, the Law, consists of five books. The first is *Bresit*, which is Genesis; the second *Ellesmot*, which is Exodus; the third *Vasicra*, which is Leviticus; the fourth *Vagedaber*, which is Numbers; and the fifth *Elleaddabarim*, which is Deuteronomy.

These are the five books of Moses, which the Hebrews call *Torath* and the Latins call the Law; strictly speaking, however, “the Law” is the law given through Moses.

The second order is that of the Prophets, containing eight books. The first is Joshua son of Nun, who in Latin is called Jesus Nave; the second is *Oblim*, which is Judges; the third is Samuel, which is the First Book of Kings; the fourth is *Malachim*, which is the Second Book of Kings; the fifth is Isaiah; the sixth Jeremiah; the seventh Ezekiel; and the eighth *Torsera*, which is called the Twelve Prophets.

[Col. 0305C]

Because these books are joined together on account of their brevity, they are counted as one.

The third order is that of the Hagiographa, that is, of those who write holy things. It contains nine books. The first is Job; the second *Nabla*, which is the Psalter; the third *Masloth*, which is the Proverbs of Solomon; the fourth Qoheleth, which is Ecclesiastes; the fifth *Sirasirin*, which is the Song of Songs; the sixth Daniel; the seventh *Dabreiamin*, which is *Verba dierum*, that is, Chronicles; the eighth Ezra; and the ninth Esther.

All these together—five, eight, and nine—make twenty-two, as was stated above.

Some add Ruth and *Cinoth*, which in Latin is called the Lamentation of Jeremiah, to the Hagiographa, making twenty-four volumes of the Old Testament according to the twenty-four elders who stand before the presence of God.

[Col. 0305D]

Among us there is a fourth order of the Old Testament, consisting of those books that are not in the Hebrew canon. The first is the Book of Wisdom, the second Ecclesiasticus, the third Tobit, the fourth Judith, and the fifth and sixth the books of the Maccabees. The Jews separate these books among the apocrypha, but the Church of God both honors and proclaims them among the divine Scriptures.

In the New Testament there are two orders. The first is evangelical, containing Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The second is apostolic, containing Paul in fourteen Epistles, Peter in two, John in three, James and Jude in one each, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse.

The whole division of both Testaments is distinguished in three ways: history, morals, and allegory. These three are in turn divided in many ways: what was done and said by God, angels, or human beings; what was proclaimed by the prophets concerning Christ and his body; what concerns the devil and his members; what concerns the old and new people; and what concerns the present age, the future kingdom, and judgment.

[Col. 0306A]

The following brief catalogue sets forth in order the books of the Holy Scriptures contained in the present library.

## Order of the Books of the Old and New Testament Received by the Church and Generally Contained in This Volume

### I. The Order of the Law, containing these books

Genesis. Exodus. Leviticus. Numbers. Deuteronomy.

### II. The Order of the Prophets, containing these books

Jesus Nave. Judges. Samuel, two books. Malachim, two books. Isaiah. Jeremiah. Ezekiel. The Twelve Prophets.

### III. The Order of the Hagiographa, containing these books

Job.

[Col. 0306B]

Psalter. Proverbs. Ecclesiastes. Song of Songs. Daniel. Chronicles. Ezra. Esther.

### IV. Books Not Included in the Hebrew Canon

Wisdom. Ecclesiasticus. Tobit. Judith. Two books of the Maccabees.

## The Evangelical Order, containing these books

Matthew. Mark. Luke. John.

## The Apostolic Order, containing these books

Fourteen Epistles of Paul:

To the Romans, one. To the Corinthians, two. To the Galatians, one. To the Ephesians, one. To the Philippians, one. To the Colossians, one. To the Thessalonians, two.

[Col. 0307A]

To Timothy, two. To Titus, one. To Philemon, one. To the Hebrews, one. Two of Peter. One of James. Three of John. One of Jude. Acts of the Apostles. Apocalypse.

## II. VERSES PREFIXED TO THE BRIEF CHRONICLE [Note: Attached to the Chronicle]

[Col. 0307D]

The preceding verses were placed at the front; these were placed at the end of the codex. In them he commends the usefulness of what he had ordered to be added to the Bible: namely, the Chronicle of Isidore and Eucherius’ little work on the interpretation of Hebrew and Greek names, together with a key which some have thought to be by Melito, bishop of Sardis.

## CHRONICLE WHICH WAS ADDED TO THE BIBLE

Theodulf constructed the work of this codex out of love for the one whose blessed law thunders within it.

[Col. 0307B]

Externally it shines with gems, gold, and purple; yet inwardly it glows with an even more splendid honor.

After the venerable volumes of the Catholic law, observe how a small piece of writing occupies a modest place.

Beginning its account from the very beginning, it weaves the work through the names of fathers and kings.

It records the number of years and marks the kingdoms in order, down to your time, Emperor Heraclius.

It gives many deeds to be remembered in a few words: thus a great work is marked by a small indication.

From here are opened the names of the Hebrew language, whose usage is renowned in sacred speech.

After them come the Greek names, whose ancient authority of faith bestowed their riches upon the Church.

A small grove is formed from Latin names, bearing weight worthy of great fruit.

[Col. 0307C]

Within a small body they retain great mysteries: these are the matters enclosed within the limits of this codex.

With these lamps of the law he will be able to explore the river of Scripture, whoever wishes to seek the fish of the law in its stream.

With these nets he will be able to capture precious prey—the skill of seeking nourishment in holy law.

Do not, exultant reader, despise them as though they were worthless.

A worthless container can hold a beautiful object.

An iron key, made from base metal, gives access to a place of silver and gold.

Whatever is a small burden for the person who preserves or carries it shows the way to a burden of great value.

Do not dislike them because they are small in body; great weights lie hidden beneath a small covering.

[Col. 0307D]

A great structure is held together by small keys, and a little hammer polishes great metals.

Thus great crops arise from a small seed, and the weight of a tree from a light shoot.

They open things shut away and reveal many things that lie hidden;

[Col. 0308A]

a small rod lifts a great covering [Ms. Colb., “a small claw lifts a great covering”].

All the great meadows of the books contain flowers; behold, this basket gives them to you here—pluck them with your hand.

Use it, fortunate reader, so that you yourself may become more fortunate, as your life takes possession of everlasting riches.

And, I beg you, deign to remember me in all things while you rule and reread, while you approach this work.

While you approach this work, which my labor has produced, repay me the reward of my effort.

I ask you to seek this reward from the Thunderer on my behalf: that he may grant me forgiveness, or graciously add his help;

that he may drive away harmful things, grant all prosperity, and make me a participant in the blessed life with you.

May he order my morals, strengthen my hope, correct my actions, and, by granting this, bring salvation to my soul.

[Col. 0308B]

And may he cleanse me mercifully from every sin, so that after death he may grant me a place above the stars.

May he join me to the angelic assemblies, by whose gift the earthly race climbs to the stars of heaven.

### Couplets

Live happily for God through many years, reader; I beg you, do not forget your Theodulf.

### Another

The work is finished, and by these words its task has been completed. May peace, life, salvation, and greeting be yours, reader.

## III. VERSES COMPOSED TO BE SUNG BY BOYS [Note: On Palm Sunday]

[Col. 0307D]

This poem is on everyone’s lips, but until now it has appeared mutilated and incomplete; henceforth it emerges into the light full and entire. The evidence indicates that it was written among the people of Angers, and writers agree that it was composed during the reign of Louis the Pious. But because Alcuin mentions this poem in *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 14, and it is certain that Alcuin did not live into the time of Louis, a learned man recently thought that he had sufficient grounds to deny that Theodulf composed it. Nevertheless, although other considerations may be lacking, one cannot doubt that these verses truly belong to Theodulf after the testimony of Lupus of Ferrières, who was nearly contemporary and explicitly attributes them to him in Letter 20. Others have already observed that the book *On the Divine Offices* is not by Alcuin.

[Col. 0308D]

## TO BE SUNG ON PALM SUNDAY

Glory, praise, and honor be to you, Christ the Redeemer and King,

[Col. 0308C]

to whom the children offered their holy “Hosanna.”

You are the King of Israel, the illustrious offspring of David,

who come in the name of the Lord, blessed King.

The whole heavenly assembly praises you in the heights,

and mortal humanity together with every created thing.

The Hebrew people came to meet you with palms;

behold, with prayer, vow, and hymns we come before you.

They offered you gifts of praise as you were about to suffer;

behold, we sing this melody to you as you reign.

They pleased you; may our devotion also please you,

pious King, merciful King, to whom all good things are pleasing.

The glory of noble blood made them Hebrews;

behold, a holy passage makes us Hebrews.

When earthly things have been conquered, what is glorious passes over to the heavens.

Kindly virtue takes us away from filthy vices.

Let us be children in wickedness, grown old in virtue;

grant that we may hold the path our fathers held.

Let us not be degenerate from our fathers in the practice of the pious;

may your holy grace draw us after them.

You are the pious rider, and may we be your little donkey.

[Col. 0309A] May the venerable city of God receive us with you.

May we be clothed in the radiant splendor of the apostolic vestment,  
so that, well covered by it, our company may bear you along.  
Thus may we spread our bodies as coverings for our souls,  
so that through us the way may always be safe for you.

May victory be holy for us in place of palm branches,  
so that we may sing thus to you, perhaps, as you triumph.  
And let pure hearts stand in place of willow branches;  
may the green of our works lead us to pleasant meadows.  
In place of olive branches, let devotion, light, and the teaching  
of the holy Spirit within us be rightly pleasing to you.  
From the tree of the Law let us cut away certain doctrines,  
by which the way of your coming to us may be safe.

And so may our present devotion celebrate the feast,  
so that annual feasts may continually follow it.

[Col. 0309B] With branches and praises we go together to this city;  
make us worthy, by our holy merits, to approach the heights of heaven.  
Look kindly upon this people gathered here in your love,  
and willingly receive its vows and prayers.

Behold the crowds of priests and the wing of the people;  
both sexes sing your praises together.  
These are the people whom venerable Angers possesses  
within the circuit of its city, singing devout hymns with pious mind.  
The city is cherished by the lingering Maine  
and adorned by the golden Loire,  
which the Sarthe beautifies as it aids the smooth passage of boats.  
Abounding in crops, resources, markets, beautiful things,  
it is everywhere richly covered with holy places.

This holy people has come from the see of blessed Albinus,  
bearing songs worthy of the occasion, with vows and branches.

[Col. 0309C] And that company hastens from the citadel of John the Baptist,  
joining melodious words to its branches.  
Nor, blessed Martin, does your company return later than the others;  
it bears branches in its hands and melody in mind and mouth.

The crowd of blessed Saturninus has come, joined to these,  
adorned by the cross, branches, and triumphant praise.  
And the company called by your holy name, Peter,  
eagerly sends those whom it can to this work of praise.  
The venerable martyr Sergius sends his own pupils  
to perform the blessed duties of this holy office.  
To these your company, blessed Maurilius, is joined,  
and thus sings its devout vows with prayer, praise, and song.

The slower crowd of blessed Anianus does not fail to hasten  
so that it may sing these praises to you, Christ the King.  
The people also rush forth from the church of life-giving Mary,  
which your bridge, O Maine, sends here.

[Col. 0309D] The people of blessed Germanus also come here  
from the seat of their distinguished bishop and prelate.  
Behold, we climb the slope to the holy halls of Michael,  
where your sweet love, Christ, joins us together.  
There may its company be joined to its kindly bishop,  
and from head and members may this praise resound to God.

From here let us come to the holy halls of Mauricius,  
where together this voice of praise and prayer may resound.  
There also let one mother gather us under her titles,  
she who is the head and glory of this city.  
May our prayer there and the bishop’s blessing adorn us,  
and send each of us back to his own place with praise.

## IV. How the Season, Place, Circumstances, and Movement Aid the Writer’s Understanding

[Col. 0310A]

Thus the season, place, atmosphere, movement,  
or the manner of an event aids a fitting understanding.

In the evening, in the flower-bearing garden, he seeks the sinner  
and the Lord, creator of the world, asks where he is.  
This is the setting of the time: the light of day had departed  
and he had already turned back into the darkness of night.  
He seeks him, though he knows where he is, because he knew him not to be there  
where he had rightly commanded him to remain after giving the command.  
He asks as though ignorant where he is; but I do not know, after all,  
what God’s not knowing could mean, unless he wished to reprove him.

Meanwhile, time and place often impart  
a perceptive meaning to sacred speech.

[Col. 0310B] Coming from the summit of the Mount of Olives,  
Christ approached the holy threshold of God’s temple in the morning.  
He frees the adulterous woman offered up to those deceitful men,  
and in this deed teaches how merciful and just he is:  
merciful, for he saves her; just, for he condemns her sins.  
“Go,” he says, “and do not follow anything of this kind any longer.”

For the Mount of Olives is the Lord’s lofty mercy,  
from whose citadel in heaven he comes seeking us;  
there he refreshes us, anointed with holy oil,  
and grants us the help both of light and of mercy.

He comes in the morning, bringing back the day after night has fled;  
there the new light has arrived and the shadow of the Law has departed.  
Often, too, the changeable air opens up meaning,  
for heat and cold suggest many mysteries.

[Col. 0310C] Once, in Jerusalem, the Dedication had taken place;  
Scripture, as witness, says that a harsh winter oppressed it.  
The cold of winter is the unbelieving hearts  
of the Jewish people, who remained bare of the warmth of faith.  
This cold also was present when Christ’s Passion was enacted:  
Peter, by denying, you grow rigid; by weeping, warming again, you grow strong.

The Lord’s sitting or standing, or his movement,  
produces living meanings when rightly observed.  
Stephen says that he stood; Mark says that he sat:  
there is no difference here; one person does both.  
Sitting has the force of one who reigns; standing, of one who fights:  
he fights for these and rules those, fulfilling both at once.

The blessed angel announces him standing at his birth,  
and sings of him, now risen, as sitting.  
Here he indicates one who will fight; there, one who will reign:  
he is born for battle and rises for empire.

[Col. 0310D] Standing belongs to the supreme bishop; sitting, to the teacher:  
he is the Father’s sacrifice for us and teaches us.  
He sees, as he goes, the two whom, while standing, he heals of blindness:  
let it be man’s task to pass on, but God’s to stand.

If the manner and sequence of the Lord’s deeds are observed,  
the understanding will begin to grow into a rich harvest.  
Finally, he seeks the mountain heights and descends to the depths,  
teaching there that he is God, here that he is man.  
Those whom he first heals he then feeds with great nectar:  
heals them beforehand through faith, and nourishes them with the Law.

He made us recline upon fragile grass,  
so that the work of mortal flesh might rightly be pressed down.

[Col. 0311A] He gives food to the disciples, and they give it to the crowds:  
thus the disciples are established through teaching, and the devout people through them.

## V. On the Altar of Saint Anianus

[Note: [Col. 0311D] On the altar of Saint Anianus. It is not clear where this was. An inscription shows that a basilica was founded by the same man in the village of Germiniacum:

> “Theodulf dedicated this temple in honor of God. Whoever enters it, I ask you, remember me.”]

I adorn this altar for you, O thunderer on high,  
Theodulf; may God himself favor my vows.

Whoever you are who see this, and you, most holy bishop  
Anianus, I beg you, remember me, the insignificant one.

## VI. To the Monks of Saint Benedict

[Note: [Col. 0311D] To the monks of Saint Benedict. In order to restore the discipline that had collapsed in the monastery of Saint Maximinus at Mitiacum, Theodulf had requested monks from Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Aniane in the province of Narbonne. Since Benedict had first sent two men who had successfully begun the work, Theodulf now asks that more be sent to complete what they had begun. On this matter the author of the Life of Saint Maximinus says briefly: “When discipline had collapsed at Mitiacum, Bishop Theodulf restored it after receiving monks from the province of Septimania.”]

Go, my letter, swiftly to the blessed Benedict’s dwelling,  
and, after greeting him, revisit the dwelling of the fathers.  
Greet him and bid him farewell for me, and tell him everything  
that is prosperous for us through God’s gift.

[Col. 0311B] Then convey many thanks for the gift he sent,  
and kindly ask him to send more willingly.  
May the noble work rise after its foundations have been laid,  
the work that already delights and warms my heart.  
May the summit be better; the order of the foundation is good,  
sanctified by the fortune and distinction of the number two.

Behold: two monks are two commands of salvation,  
so that love of the brother may likewise be joined to divine love.  
Is there an understanding that joins itself to action?  
Thus the two talents enrich the good servant.  
There are also two lives, which the two sisterly actions indicate,  
as do the new Law and the old.

Now work willingly, and do not fear the foundations;  
whatever you add will stand, with God making it firm.  
You can add more; the structure will not know collapse,  
since this holy number supports it.

[Col. 0311C] You sent small seeds through our fields;  
send many more, and a great harvest will arise for you.  
What Benedict was, as rector in the fields of Italy,  
that you, Benedict, are now in our regions.

Do not be inferior in merit to the man from whom you are not distant in name;  
may one fortune bless both in name and merit.  
As the Samian is thought to have sprung in mind from Euphorbus,  
so in you the work of the father of Nursia is renewed.

Through Theodulf, Theodulf’s words of prayer,  
you fulfill his request, and the same name proceeds from here with one prayer.  
Thus, Benedict, may through you Benedict grant him what he desires,  
and may you go as mediator of his vow.  
What this holy father once was to you, O Cassinus,  
in this way let him be to your cell, the city of Orléans.

[Col. 0311D] How aptly ancient times called it Mitiacum,  
which had once been an auspicious place for gentle choirs.  
There Maximinus presided over a flourishing crown of brothers,  
and, joined to them, he ascends to the stars of heaven.

Their bodies lie buried in various tombs,  
but their souls dwell in your bosom, O patriarch.

[Col. 0312A] Savage barbarism, removing the gift of peace,  
cast them down from their seats and left the place deserted.  
It, which held its own ashes, like an eastern bird,  
raises its head from the fall of ashes toward the heights.

When you have finished these matters, hasten to seek the community of brothers,  
and, looking around them, bend your bowed knee.  
First ask that your mouth, which is about to speak a few words, be blessed;  
then, before lingering, receive the sound of their voice.

“Theodulf has sent me to you, blessed company;  
he asks, as one who has prayed, to receive your help.  
He seeks that your planting may grow in his fields,  
from which the fragrance of ambrosial nectar may rise to the stars.  
May a blessed stream of your frequent prayer water it,  
so that the root may be able to stretch out strong branches.”

When you have perhaps finished speaking, then freely revisit the dwelling,  
and tell me everything about the fathers.  
See where the devout company sleeps, where it receives food,  
where it reads and chants psalms, and where it works.  
Look at the mill, and do not disdain the kitchen quarters;  
see where those who are vigorous in mind lie down in body.

Next inspect the guesthouse, and the man who occupies it,  
the one who has now come for the first time as a soldier into the ranks.  
Since the presence of the brother whom you sought will be lacking,  
mourn that he has feared this beautiful journey.

[Col. 0312B] Then revisit the brother whom you must greet in piety,  
to whom I am joined by name, though not by merit.
