From there seek the dwelling of the venerable Father Nebridius,  
and soon let the house of Donatus also be seen by you.  
Nor should you pass by the place of the holy brother Attilus;  
reverently enter the dwelling of my Anianus.

[Col. 0312C] For Attala will kindly look upon you as you offer him gifts of salvation;  
see him, and say, “Farewell, Olemundus.”

But if you happen to be well enough to travel through worldly cities,  
visiting each town, countryside, and cottage,  
proclaim our greetings in verse to the bishops,  
and to all the clergy—though it would take too long to name them all.

Let Attila, Clarinus, Teutfredus, Leubilla,  
and the whole holy company of our fathers hear our farewell.  
What more shall I sing to you? Greet them all in my name,  
and, after greeting them, return quickly to me.

## VII. Verses Written in Golden Letters about Saint Quentin

### On the First Tablet

When King Charles had ruled with his righteous scepter  
for forty-seven years,

[Col. 0312D] and, removed from human affairs, was about to leave  
the heights of his great kingdom to you, King Louis,

the happy Incarnation of Christ added  
eight hundred and fourteen years to the course of time:

Abbot Fulradus, renowned for his nobility,  
began to build this venerable hall.

[Col. 0313A] [Note: [Col. 0313D] Abbot Fulradus. There were two highly distinguished abbots of this name. The first was abbot of Saint-Denis and chaplain to King Pippin, famous for the affairs conducted under him and under Charles in Italy; the annals report that he died in 784. The other is our Fulradus, abbot of Saint Quentin among the Viromandui, a grandson of Charles Martel through Jerome, the brother of King Pippin. Thus it was this Fulradus who, as he says, restored the basilica of Saint Quentin, beginning the work in the year in which Louis the Pious began to reign, namely 814. There is no doubt that this is the Fulradus whom Flodoard, Book II of his History, chapter 18, says attended the Council of Noyon in that very year with other abbots.]

For Jerome was father to this man, and Charles to Jerome,  
and he carried the glory of his own family to the heights.  
Waging wars and guarding peace, he who sent  
the heights of the kingdom to his offspring with God’s aid.

### VIII. On the Second Tablet

Here rest the limbs of the illustrious martyr Quentin,  
whose mind clings to Christ in the citadel of heaven.

In his pious honor this church had been built  
on an ancient foundation and had stood for a long time.  
But when its cracked walls gave grim signs of ruin,  
they gave occasion for it to rise toward better things.

For, with the Lord granting it, I, Fulradus,  
completed this work through pious vows,  
so that this house might rise from its foundations  
greater and more industrious in every respect.

Whoever enters it to offer vows to the Lord,  
I ask you to join me in your vows and prayers.

[Col. 0313B]

### IX. On the Third Tablet

This blessed house of God is the road by which one goes to heaven’s halls;  
here, behold, the tranquil gate of heaven lies open to the good.

This is the way, the life, the salvation. Christ revisits his temples,  
accepting the offerings, vows, and prayers of the righteous.

Here rest well the bones of blessed Quentin,  
who strove rightly to please his Lord.  
By his own blood he purchased the kingdoms of heaven  
and bought himself a place in the citadel above.

The living people, seeking help,  
frequent his martyrdom with devoted mind.

Remembering us, I, Fulradus, ask you to pray  
that God himself may always remember you.

## X. On the Tomb of Saint Nazarius

[Note: [Col. 0313D] On the tomb of Saint Nazarius. This was in the monastery of Lorsch, which thereafter took the name of Saint Nazarius. Paul the Deacon, in his account of the bishops of the Church of Metz, says of Chrodegang: “Finally he requested from Paul, the Roman pontiff, the bodies of three holy martyrs: namely, that of blessed Gorgonius, who rests at Gorze; that of blessed Nabor, who was buried in the monastery at Hilaria; and that of blessed Nazarius, which he placed beyond the Rhine, in the monastery called Lorsch, after building there a basilica of marvelous beauty in honor of that martyr.”]

Beautiful martyr, here Christ buried your limbs,  
while your mind, flying upward, climbs to the heights of the center.  
You have been celebrated by the Tiberine letter through your deeds,  
and now you bless the Rhineland people by the honor of your bones.

Rome, with God’s favor, saw signs in the martyr;  
now the German company sees this work.  
You placed palatial shrines in the woodland countryside, O martyr,  
and a hall gleams amid deserted wastes.

Every nation calls this flower Nazarius,  
for *nazar* means “flower” in the Hebrew language.

Coming hastily from the city of the Vangiones  
while seeking him, I saw snow falling from a cloud.  
I crossed the banks of the fish-bearing Rhine with strength,  
so that I might reach his dwelling more quickly.

## XI. Epitaph of Queen Fastrada

[Note: [Col. 0314D] Epitaph of Queen Fastrada. Everyone writes that after Hildegard’s death Fastrada became the wife of Charlemagne. Einhard says that she was Frankish by birth and the daughter of Count Rudolph; he also records that she died at Frankfurt while a synod was being held there and was buried at Mainz near Saint Alban. This poem by Theodulf had been carved on her tomb. But after the church of Saint Alban was consumed by fire and Fastrada’s ashes were transferred to the metropolitan church, a very different epitaph of inferior quality was attached; it can be seen in Serarius’s History of Mainz.]

Here lie the limbs of the illustrious Queen Fastrada,  
whom cold death carried away from the midst of her flower.

Noble herself, joined to the bed of a powerful man,  
but now nobler in the heavenly marriage chamber.

The better part of her soul, King Charles himself, remains,  
to whom may the gentle God grant abundant years.

## XII. On the Front of the House

[Col. 0314B]

You who stand, or sit, who travel through fields and houses,  
you consume your time in various activities.

Do nothing shameful, since someone from this lofty house may see it;  
there is this, and there is something else you ought to fear even more.

God is above the stars: he sees what the human race does  
and will bring the just weights of the balance.

## XIII. Why He Does Not Write Poems Now

Brothers, you have often brought me poems that delighted me greatly,  
and believe me, those you bring now please me very much.

For I delight in them, praise your zeal and labor,  
and urge you to pursue better things.  
You are growing toward what is better, and from this our joys grow;  
I love you to do so more and more.

[Col. 0314C] I, who once could easily bring forth verses,  
am now in turmoil and cannot compose sweet song as I wish.

You will ask why this new practice has arisen,  
which makes our Erato keep silent.

Now my sins are more properly to be lamented with tears  
than celebrated in lyric metre [F.: “heights” (*culmina*)].

My love, Christ himself, will not seek my poems,  
but rather the great gains of the flock entrusted to me.

For it, and for my own errors, I desire prayer:  
I commit no crime if I do not compose poems.

Play, boys; we have played enough with metrical art.  
The first things you desire are already achieved for me.

Learn in such a way, brothers, that you may be considered learned  
and become companions of the citizens of heaven.

[Col. 0315A] Behold, the venerable solemnities of so great a feast  
now do not allow us to versify very much.

After these preliminary matters, let us celebrate this feast exultantly;  
a more suitable time for producing poems will come.

Thus let us also reverently keep the annual feasts,  
so that God may grant them to us without end.

[Note: [Col. 0315B] “For to you, Wulfine.” There is no doubt that this Wlfinus was that grammarian of Orléans, famous for his poetic skill, to whom Morel long ago published a letter by an unknown author urging him to reply:

> “To Wulfinus, the grammarian of Orléans.
>
> What, brother, are you doing, I ask, keeping such long silence?  
> Why has your love for us been driven away so quickly?  
> Surely the many exceedingly flowery poems of your Muse  
> required no small delay in order to appear.”]

For to you, Wulfine, belong the rewards of praise,  
since from your stream learned verse flows beautifully.

For this we offer you manifold thanks, dearest friend;  
the Lord God himself will grant rewards according to your merits.

## XIV. On the Death of Damasus

He who, walking upon the sea, restrained its bitter waves,  
who grants life to the seeds dying in the earth,  
who was able to release the legal bonds of death,  
who, after darkness and after the sun’s third light,  
gave Martha’s brother back again to his sister,  
will, I believe, make Damasus rise after his ashes.

## XV. On the Bishop’s Chair

[Note: [Col. 0315C] On the bishop’s chair. On the episcopal seat or cathedra. From the same root, *faldistorium*, meaning a seat, is frequently found in the rituals of the Roman Church, for example in the Ceremonial, concerning a bishop who is about to celebrate: “Then he comes to the seat prepared for him, namely the faldistorium placed at the epistle side.” But they distinguished the faldistorium from the episcopal seat. “The proper bishop,” it says, “ought to stand and sit not on the faldistorium but in his own episcopal seat.” I think, therefore, that Theodulf is speaking of his proper seat, on which he had these verses carved, just as Augustine, according to Possidius, had a distich with a similar meaning on his table:

> “Whoever loves to gnaw at the lives of absent people  
> should know that this table is unworthy of him.”]

## On the Bishop’s Chair

May every sitting and action of Theodulf be pleasing, I pray,  
to you, gracious God the King, who delight in all good things.

Without you no good can be done; with you, many things are possible.  
Please grant me the good will and ability to do good.

When your superior approaches, let the people stand;  
let the younger attend you, and ask those standing around with devout speech.

Let your mind be humble, your heart prudent, and your conduct pure;  
as you sit, constantly keep God in mind.

Whoever you are standing here, do not slander anyone.  
To gnaw at the life of the absent is a crime.

Refrain, you who stand, from persisting in empty chatter,  
lest the one who sits judge that you should go outside.

## XVI. On Contempt for the World

[Col. 0316B]

Whoever you are who love the Creator’s rewards, fear the everlasting fires  
which he justly threatens.

then all the glory of this fragile world becomes worthless;  
within you, the blessed love of God prevails.

# BOOK THREE

## I. To King Charles

[Note: [Col. 0315D] To King Charles. From what he says about the recently brought-in treasures of the Huns and about the recent conversion of that people to the faith of Christ, we understand that this poem was written around the year 796, to which the annals assign these events.]

The whole world resounds with your praises and your glory, O king;  
though it says much, it cannot say everything.

If the Meuse, Rhine, Saône, Rhône, Tiber, and Po  
can be measured, then your praise too has a measure.

[Col. 0315D] Your praise is sufficiently immense, and immense it will remain  
as long as the world is passable to beast and man.

Though I cannot fill it adequately through the efforts of speech,  
nevertheless I disdain to keep so great a matter silent.

Let it run through playful jests mixed with sport,  
and let that man often be touched by any hand whatsoever.

Let this page, smeared with praise and jest together, revisit him;  
I shall see him soon, if God grants it.

O face, three times brighter than gold refined by fire,  
happy is he who can always be near you!

And the forehead, worthy enough of the weight of a diadem,  
which has no equal anywhere in the fields of the world.

And the noble head, chin, and beautiful neck,  
and the golden hands that abolish poverty.

Chest, legs, feet—there is nothing that is not worthy of praise;  
all things flourish in beauty, all shine with elegance.

And to hear your thoughts expressed in beautiful speech—  
you are above all, and no one is above you.

[Col. 0316D] No one is above you; your skillful prudence  
shines so greatly that, I think, it has no limit.

You are broader than the Nile, greater than the icy Ister,  
greater than the Euphrates, and not smaller than the Ganges.

What wonder if the eternal Shepherd himself created  
such a shepherd to nourish his own flocks?

In name you restore your grandfather; in the lineage of your understanding, Solomon;  
in strength, David; and in appearance, Joseph.

You are the guardian of wealth, avenger of crimes, giver of honors,  
and therefore all these good things are given to you.

[Note: [Col. 0316D] “Receive manifold treasures.” Einhard, in his Life of Charlemagne, and all the others, recall elegantly and seriously, in his customary manner, the booty acquired in the war against the Huns. The Saxon poet likewise writes:

> “For the royal seat of the Huns, which they call Hring,  
> was stripped bare. Duke Eric had captured it in that year,  
> and from it had brought back to the king many kinds  
> of treasures, gathered through ancient ages  
> by the Huns from the frequent plunder of countless peoples.”]

Receive manifold treasures with joyful heart,  
which God sends you from the Pannonian world.

Then render devout thanks to the Thunderer on high,  
to whom your generous hand is accustomed always to be liberal.

[Note: [Col. 0317C] “Peoples come to Christ.” Alcuin congratulates Charles on the Huns’ approach to the faith of Christ in Letter 7:

> “Christ has subjected to your scepters the nations and peoples of the Huns, once fearsome for their ancient savagery and strength, as they now serve your honor; and, by his prevenient grace, he has bound their long-most-proud necks to the yoke of the holy faith and poured the light of truth into minds blind from ancient times.”

Regarding the conversion of the Avars specifically, the author of the Annals of Engolism says: “In that same year Tudun came to the king with a multitude of Avars and surrendered himself to him together with his people and homeland; both he and his people became Christians and were baptized”—in the year 797.]

Peoples come ready to serve Christ,  
whom you call to Christ as your right hand urges them.

The Hun comes to Christ with his hair braided;  
he who was formerly fierce is humble in faith.

Let the Arab join him; both peoples wear long hair:  
let the one come with braided hair, the other with it loose.

Cordoba, send the treasures gathered over a long period,  
send them swiftly to the king, to whom every worthy thing belongs.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] “As the Arabs come.” The context requires us to read *Abares* or *Avars* instead of *Arabes*. This is clear both from what has just been said about the conversion of the Avars and because otherwise the repeated mention of the Arabs here would be pointless and senseless. He is urging the Arabs, or Saracens, whose royal seat was then at Cordoba, to follow the example of the Avars.]

As the Arabs come [read *Abares*, “Avars”], Arabs and nomads, come;  
bow your necks before the king’s knees.

They were no less savage and fierce than you,  
but he who subdued them will also subdue you.

[Col. 0317B] Namely, he who sits in heaven and reigns through Tartarus,  
who rules the sea, the lands, and the stars of the sky.

Behold, a new spring comes, bringing with it every happiness;  
by God’s gift may they come to you and yours, O king.

Behold, the year is renewed in triumph under the eternal laws,  
and now the earth, its mother, brings forth its offspring.

The forests are green with leaves, the fields are adorned with flowers;  
thus the elements preserve their appointed cycles.

Let envoys come from every side to report good news;  
let peace be the reward, and let all violence be absent.

Then, raising eyes, mind, and hands together toward heaven,  
let him give and return thanks to God.

Let the honor of counsel be celebrated; let prayer be offered in the palace  
where a beautiful structure rises with marvelous domes.

From there let them return to the heights of the palace residence;  
let the people go and return, treading the long halls.

Let the door be opened, and let the few enter among the many who wish to do so—  
the few whom each rank has raised upward.

[Note: [Col. 0318C] “Let offspring surround the king.” He next lists all the male and female offspring of Charlemagne who had been born or were surviving when he wrote, except King Pippin of Italy, who was absent while all the others were with their father. The following words of Einhard clarify Theodulf’s verses: “He took Hildegard, a woman of the Suevian people and of the highest nobility, in marriage. By her he had three sons—Charles, Pippin, and Louis—and as many daughters—Rotrude, Bertrada, and Gisela. He also had three other daughters: Theodrada, Hiltrude, and Rothaid, two by his wife Fastrada, who was of the Eastern Frankish, that is, German, people; and the third by a certain concubine whose name does not now occur to memory. After Fastrada’s death he married Liutgard, an Alamannian woman, by whom he had no children.”]

Let his dearest offspring surround the beautiful king;  
let him stand out above all, as the sun usually does in heaven’s citadel.

Let the boys stand here and the girls gather there;  
thus let the young vine make its father joyful.

Let Charles and Louis stand together, one of them a young man,  
while the other’s youthful beauty is already advancing.

Their vigorous youth is strong in body,  
their hearts capable of study and steadfast in counsel.

They flourish in mind, shine in virtue, and overflow with piety;  
each is the glory of his people and dear to his father.

Now let the king turn his burning eyes toward them,  
now toward the maidenly chorus on either side,

toward the maidenly company, than which none is more beautiful  
in dress, bearing, appearance, body, heart, or faith.

Namely toward Bertrada and Rotrude, with Gisela also present,  
the youngest sister among the three beautiful sisters.

[Col. 0318B] Leutgardis, the beautiful woman, is joined to them,

[Note: [Col. 0318D] “Leutgardis, the beautiful woman.” She was Charles’s last wife, as stated above. No one records where or when she married him; everyone affirms that she died at Tours in 801. Others also praise her appearance and character, including Alcuin, in his account of Pope Leo’s arrival to King Charles:

> “Liutgard, Charles’s most beautiful wife,  
> proceeds with a great crowd accompanying her.”

The Saxon poet likewise speaks of her death:

> “In every virtue of character and life worthy of praise—  
> her name was Liutgard.”]

who shines in intelligence together with the aid of piety.  
Beautiful enough in adornment, but more beautiful still in worthy conduct,  
she favors the people and all the leaders alike,  
generous in hand, merciful in spirit, most gracious in speech,  
ready to benefit everyone and harm no one.

She labors diligently in the pursuits of learning  
and places the liberal arts in the citadel of her mind.

Let the offspring be ready in obedience, most pleasing to the king,  
and strive to please him more through devoted love.

Let Charles quickly receive the double cloaks, or the gentle coverings for the hands,  
and Louis the sword.

When he is seated, let the excellent daughters, amid grateful kisses,  
give him their gift, and let cherished love give its own.

Let Bertrada bring roses, Chrodtrude violets, and Gisela lilies,  
each bringing the rewards of ambrosial nectar.

Let Rothaid bring fruits, Hiltrude grain, and Theodrada wine;  
their appearances vary, but their beauty is one.

This one shines with gems, that one glitters with gold and purple;  
this one is distinguished by a green jewel, that one by a red.

A brooch adorns one, a border embellishes another;  
bracelets adorn this one, and a necklace suits that one.

For one the garment is rusty-colored, for another yellow;  
this one bears a milk-white fillet, that one a red one.

Let one please the king with sweet words, another with laughter;  
let this one charm her father by her walk, that one by her jest.

[Note: [Col. 0319B] “And if perhaps the most holy sister.” Gisela was devoted to God. Einhard, in his Life of Charlemagne, says: “He had one sister, named Gisela, dedicated from girlhood to a religious way of life, whom he honored with great devotion, just as he did his mother. She also died a few years before his death in the monastery in which she had lived.” This was the monastery of Saint Mary at Soissons. Hence the poet calls her the bride of God:

> “What is Gisela, the illustrious and most beautiful bride of the great Thunderer?”

She was ten years younger than Charles. I think the following passage in the old chronicle for 757 refers to her: “The birth of Gislana.” Paul the pope, in Letter 5 to Pippin, and Hadrian, in Letter 4 to Charles, also discuss her, calling her Gisila.]

And if the king’s most holy sister should be present,  
let her give sweet kisses to her brother, and her brother to her.

Let her moderate such joys with a tranquil expression,  
so that in her mind she may bear the joys of the eternal bridegroom;  
and let her ask that the paths of Scripture be opened to her,  
while the king teaches her what God himself teaches.

[Note: [Col. 0319C] “Let the leaders come.” He designates the palace leaders partly by their proper names and partly by conventional names, according to the practice customary among Charles’s companions. Thus Alcuin often calls the king David, and attaches the name Homer to Angilbert; Dametas to Riculfus; Macarius to Ricbodo; and other names to others. Thyrsis here, Lentulus, Menalcas, and many others are likewise not proper names but assumed names. See Alcuin’s poems 221, 222, and 259. Theodulf, however, depicts most of them through the offices they held or other associated characteristics, so that they could easily be recognized.]

Let the leaders come and happily stand around him on every side;  
let each strive to fulfill his own duties.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] “Thyrsis, ready for service.” Alcuin also plays with the names Thyrsis and Menalcas in poem 221:

> “May Thyrsis and Menalcas both remain forever well,  
> and may Flaccus have hot porridge served on his dishes.”

What Theodulf says about Thyrsis seems to indicate the chamberlain; what he says about Menalcas, the official in charge of the royal table or steward.]

Let Thyrsis always be ready for his master’s service,  
active and swift in foot, heart, and hand.

[Col. 0319B] Let him receive many requests from here and there,  
and conceal these while willingly hearing those.  
Let him order one to enter and another to wait a while;  
let him judge one to be inside and another still outside.

Let this active Baldhead stand by the royal throne,  
and conduct everything prudently, everything reverently.

[Note: [Col. 0319D] “Let the bishop stand exultant.” Hildeboldus, the archchaplain. Among other duties, the blessing of the royal table belonged to him. A few years earlier the bishop of Metz, Angilramnus, had been succeeded in this office by Hildeboldus, bishop of Cologne. The Council of Frankfurt, canon 56, says: “The lord king also said at that synod that he had obtained permission from the Apostolic See, from Pope Hadrian, to have Archbishop Angilramnus constantly in his palace because of ecclesiastical needs. He asked the same synod that, just as he had had Angilramnus, so he should also be permitted to have Hildeboldus, since he had apostolic permission concerning him as well. The entire synod agreed, and it pleased them that he ought to be in the palace for ecclesiastical needs.”]

Let the bishop stand present, exultant in spirit and kindly in face,  
bearing a blessed countenance and a devout heart.

Let sincere faith, the dignity of so great a rank,  
and an innocent heart commend him to you, O Christ the King.

Let him stand to bless the king’s drink and food;  
if the king wishes to partake, he too will be willing.

[Col. 0320A] [Note: [Col. 0320C] “Let Flaccus also be present.” Alcuin, whom Theodulf again jokes about below under the name of Father Albinus. Alcuin himself also calls himself a poet, as in poem 201, addressing Angilbert:

> “Sweet Homer, I ask you, remember the poet Flaccus.”

And in poem 209:

> “Albinus the poet had ordered this house to be prepared.”

As for Theodulf’s calling him a sophist as well, this may be understood as meaning learned in sacred wisdom, following Alcuin himself, who speaks of his arrival in Gaul in poem 211:

> “Albinus came from the distant world of poets,  
> whom illustrious Britain sent to these lands.  
> Charles, the renowned king of this whole world, received him,  
> both from piety and from love of sacred wisdom.”]

Let Flaccus also be present, the glory of our poets,  
who can utter much in the lyric measure.

He is both a powerful sophist and a melodious poet,  
powerful in understanding and powerful in achievement.

Let him bring forth devout teachings from the holy Scriptures  
and, with playful wit, untie the knots of number.

Let Flaccus now have an easy question, now a difficult one;  
now let him solve a worldly art, now one that returns to heaven.

Let the king himself, alone among the many who wish it,  
be fully able to solve the Flaccidian problem.

Strong in voice, alert in understanding, polished in speech—

[Note: [Col. 0320D] “Let Riculfus be present.” There were two distinguished men of this name in Charles’s palace, both of whom subscribed his testament according to Einhard: Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, and Riculfus, count, whom I think is intended here. Homer, that is, Angilbert, will have his own place below.]

Let Riculfus be present, noble in skill and faith.

Even if he has stayed in a distant region,  
he does not return from there empty-handed.

I would sing sweet song to you, sweet Homer, if you were not absent;  
but since you are absent, my Muse is silent.

[Note: [Col. 0320D] “Let the presence of Ercambaldus not be absent.” Although he does not state the name, the tablet designates a notary and record-keeper. Ercambaldus, the chief chancellor, is frequently mentioned in the annals. A charter of Charlemagne for the church of Le Mans, issued at Aachen in 794, shows that he held this office during these years; it is subscribed with the words, “Genesius, in place of Ercambaldus.” Another charter, concerning the church of Saint Carilephus, bears the same subscription in 798.]

Let the skillful presence of Ercambaldus not be lacking,  
whose faithful hand is armed with a pair of tablets.

Hanging at his side, they swiftly follow the movements of his hands  
and receive words which they utter without a voice.

Let Lentulus be present, bringing sweet fruits.  
Let him carry fruits in baskets and faith in the citadel of his heart.

His discerning understanding makes everything else slow;  
be swifter, upright Lentulus, in voice and foot.

Nardulus should run back and forth with unceasing step,

so that, like an ant, your foot may repeatedly come and go.

His little house is occupied by a great guest,

and a great affair inhabits the chambers of his little heart.

Now let him carry books laboriously, now other things,

and now prepare little darts suitable for the slaughter of the Scot.

While this life remains his companion, I shall give you these kisses—

the savage wolf gives them to you, long-eared little ass.

The dog will sooner raise hares, or the wicked wolf lambs;

or the cat will turn its back on the timid mouse,

than Geta join a loyal treaty of peace with the Scot.

If he should happen to wish to join one, it will be wind.

Will he pay the penalty, or flee, most like the South Wind?

And, whatever else he may be here, he will be nothing but a Scot.

If you remove from his name the little letter that is third in order,

and the second happens to remain in its own name,

the first letter sounds in *coelum* [“heaven”], and the second in *Scando* [“I climb”],

the third in *Ascensus* [“ascent”], the fourth in *Amicitiae* [“friendships”].

The letter which Salvi uses in your place sufficiently offends you; without doubt, what this sounds like it also will be:

[Note: [Col. 0321D] What sounds like this is also what it will be. Namely, “stupid.” For *Scottus*, if you remove the letter *c*, becomes *sottus*, a word that already at that time meant “dull” and “stupid.” In poem 3 of this book, addressed to Angilbert, [the text reads] “Here is the Scot, the stupid one” (*Hic Scottus sottus*). In a similar kind of taunt, they say that another Scot, John Scottus Erigena, was likewise attacked by Charles the Bald, but that Erigena evaded him with a witty reply. As for this Scot, or Scottulus, whom he again attacks later, I have no grounds for asserting that he was John Scottus, whom they say came to Gaul together with Alcuin.]

[Note: [Col. 0321D] Let the comely deacon Fredegis stand. There survives a little work by Alcuin addressed to this Fredegis, in which he answers questions on the Trinity put to him by Fredegis. For Fredegis was his pupil, as Osulfus also was. There also survives, still unpublished, a letter by Fredegis himself, the deacon, On Nothing and on Darkness, which begins: “To all the faithful and to those standing in the sacred palace of our most serene lord Prince Charles, Fredegis the deacon. The question concerning Nothing, long debated by very many persons, etc.” It has been learned from various diplomas of Louis the Pious that he was later abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin and chancellor.]

Let the graceful deacon Fredegis stand here, accompanied by Osulfus;

both skilled in the art, both thoroughly learned.

[Note: [Col. 0322D] Nardus. He is called Nardulus above because of his short stature. Alcuin, poem 256:

“Although the door is small, and the inhabitant of the house is small,

do not despise Nardus, reader, in a little body.

For nard, with its spiked grass, gives off a powerful fragrance;

an excellent stone bears me to you in a little body.

The pupil of the eye is indeed a small thing—look at it—

yet by its command it governs the movements of the living body.

So Nardulus himself governs this entire house for himself.

‘Nardulus,’ say, as you pass by, reader; little one, farewell.”]

If Nardus and Ercambald are joined to Osulfus,

three tables will be able to stand on one leg.

This one is fatter than that one; this one is also thinner than that one,

but their height has made them equal in measure.

Let skillful Menalcas come from the fruit-bearing seat,

wiping the sweat from his brow with his hand.

How often, entering amid the wedges of bakers or cooks,

he bears the synodal law.

Prudently carrying everything, let him convey the king’s honored feasts and banquets

before the throne.

Let the powerful cupbearer Eppinus arrive, and let him himself

carry beautiful vessels in his hand and agreeable wines.

Now let those appointed take their places around the royal meals;

let the gift of joy be granted from the pole of heaven.

And let Father Albinus sit there, prepared to offer pious words,

and ready to take food gladly with mouth and hand.

Or, if he should command that your cups, Bacchus, or those of your cereal liquor

be served—perhaps he will wish for both—

his pipe may sing the better and teach the better,

if it moistens the chambers of his learned breast.

Let the porridge and the mass of curdled milk be far away,

but let seasoned food be near the table.

Let them share the tables and take their sweet nourishment;

let them drink wine, standing and sitting alike.

When these things have been duly accomplished, and the tables and dishes removed,

let the people go outside accompanied by joy.

[Col. 0322A] While joy remains within, let the Theodulfian Muse resound,

the Muse that warms kings and soothes nobles.

Perhaps the muscular hero Wibodus will hear her;

let him shake his thick head three and four times,

and, glaring fiercely, threaten in face and voice,

and overwhelm me, absent as I am, with his threats:

if the king’s most gracious favor should summon him,

let him go with sidelong step or tottering knee.

Let his swollen belly precede his breast,

and let his foot resemble Vulcan, his voice Jupiter.

While these things are happening, while my poems are being read,

let Scottulus stand there, a lawless, raging creature—

a dreadful creature, a savage enemy, a dull horror, a bitter plague,

a contentious pestilence, a wild creature, a great outrage.

A wild creature, a shameful creature, a sluggish creature, and a detestable creature,

a creature hostile to the pious, an enemy of the good.

With crooked hands and his neck bent slightly backward,

let his arms move toward his stupid chest, not straight.

Uncertain, bewildered, trembling, frantic, panting,

let him stand light in ear, hand, eye, mind, and foot;

now pressing one person, now another, with rapid movement,

now uttering only groans, now savage words.

Now let him turn toward the reader, now toward all

the nobles standing there, doing nothing rational.

Let the savage enemy burn with zeal to criticize,

though his ability is far away, since his will is already near.

He has learned very much, yet has nothing fixed or certain;

whatever he does not know, he supposes that he knows entirely.

He did not learn in order to be regarded as wise,

but to be ready for the weapons of contention.

[Col. 0322C] You know many things and understand none, you ignorant man; you know more still.

What more shall I say of it? You do not understand—and yet you do understand.

Let the king seek his supports, and let each person have his own dwelling;

let the king depart happily, and let the people go happily.

But you, my pipe, ask the pious king to return,

and ask pardon for all whom this place summons [F., “joke”].

May the love of Christ, which endures all things and is pleased with all good things,

offend no one.

Anyone empty of this aid, anyone stripped of so great a gift—

even if he is hostile, I care little.

May he who raised you, O king, to the citadel of the earthly kingdom

grant you better rewards in the everlasting one.

## II. On the Tomb of Pope Hadrian

[Note: [Col. 0322D] On the tomb of Pope Hadrian. It does not seem, however, that this poem was placed on Hadrian’s tomb, but rather another poem, also written in the person of Charles by Alcuin. What can still be seen today engraved in marble at Rome is a singular testimony to the king’s benevolence toward the pontiff, “his chief friend,” as Einhard records, “whose death, when announced to him, he mourned as though he had lost a brother or dearest son.”]

**ON THE TOMB OF POPE HADRIAN**

[Col. 0322D] Golden letters embrace the funeral poem;

the tawny color gives voice to the words and to the tears.

Love and grief compel me to bring them forth,

because of you, beloved bishop Hadrian, loved beyond measure.

Model of pontiffs, light of the people, standard of salvation,

pious man, wise man, man worthy of the highest reverence;

shining in mind, noble in appearance, radiant in understanding,

vigorous in illustrious love, renowned for hope and faith.

You are the Church’s glory, the shining torch of city and world;

you, Father, were extraordinarily dearer to me than daylight.

When the dread day, which would not display you returning,

snatched you from the living, the reality became clear to me.

At once I recognized the traces of my former grief,

and the death of my parents was recalled to my eyes.

I felt the weariness brought by Pippin’s death,

and, alas, alas, this grief recalls Bertrada.

[Col. 0323B] And whenever I remember your appearance, most holy pope,

my heart and my eyes contain nothing but grief.

I had prepared welcome gifts to send you while you lived;

now I prepare sorrowful gifts with mournful heart.

Marble in place of garments, a tearful poem in place of gold—

these are what your small house, the urn, will now bear.

Whoever hastens here from the west, or whoever comes from the east,

you have here a gift to be revered.

Of either sex, old man, young man, child, stranger, citizen—

whoever you are, say: “May rest be pleasant for Hadrian.”

Rome, always remember this pontiff,

who was your guardian of wealth, your wall, and your weapon.

You also, successor sitting in the sacred seat,

remember him, I pray, if God himself remembers you.

May pleasing prayer grant him rest, as may Paul and Peter;

may the entire host of heaven’s inhabitants also help him.

Grant him holy light, grant him rest,

King God, and have mercy on your work.

Behold, what he was has been taken from dust and is now dust,

but you are able to restore the decaying ashes.

I believe that this dust will rise again after death has passed,

and will no longer die in such a way after the tomb.

Whoever reads these lines, recognize that you will become what he is;

all flesh follows this path.

Therefore, wishing your mind to remember future events,

remember him in prayer and supplication. Hail.

## III. To Angilbert

[Note: [Col. 0323D] To Angilbert. He was the abbot, secretary of King Charles, and minister of the chapel, especially dear among his intimates. Everyone calls him “abbot,” and among the abbots present at Charlemagne’s testament Angilbert’s name is also recorded. He was abbot of Saint-Riquier at Centula, a monastery he restored at his own expense, as Alcuin’s poems 116 and 177 show. Charles himself calls him his *auricularius*, or secretary, in letter 83 among the Alcuinian letters, and in letter 84 his *manualis*, that is, his amanuensis. Finally, Pope Hadrian calls him minister of the chapel in his reply to Charles’s capitulary, which he had received through Angilbert. Two further embassies to Rome by him are recorded in the annals. The first was in 792, when he brought Felix of Urgell to the same Hadrian so that he might again renounce his heresy; the second was to Leo in 796, when he offered him gifts from the Hunnish treasury that had been destined for Hadrian had he not died. These are the gifts mentioned in the preceding epitaph: “I had prepared welcome gifts to send you while you lived.”]

**TO ANGILBERT**

[Col. 0324A]

What are swans doing while ravens utter such sounds,

and many songs clatter through my roof?

Now the deceitful magpie counterfeits the guilty speech of a man,

disdaining the birds, it sits among sacred dishes.

The parrot imitates various songs with its voice,

defiling the Muses—your Muses, poet Homer—

[Note: [Col. 0324D] Poet Homer. I have already noted that Angilbert was playfully called Homer. Thus, when King Charles wrote to him about his departure for Leo, he gave the letter the heading “To Homer, the chamberlain,” and concluded it with these words: “Go, Homer’s boy, and return safely.” Alcuin likewise often uses the name, both in letters and poems, but especially playfully and elegantly in letter 92, where he plays on an Ovidian verse: “If you bring nothing, you will go outside, Homer.” This entire poem by Theodulf is full of such changes of names, which perhaps could be understood by those who heard them but now seem impenetrable.]

The little diver, the black fisherman in the waters of the Loire,

now habitually dwells in the woods of Briège.

And he thinks himself handsome as a peacock because of his feathers,

though here is what Lamuel has added to your praises.

I think the voice sounds equal, but the feather deceives the color;

no varied beauty shines here in appearance.

Now the spring cuckoo displays the lights of Phoebus,

while the stammering voice resounds from its hoarse throat.

Now the wicked crow, hanging from the branches, calls for rain,

and deceitfully boasts that it has nine lives.

Let the blackbird’s voice be silent; the marshland goose plucks its strings,

devouring every filthy thing with submerged head.

Let the spring warbler be silent with its sweet songs;

the hostile owl echoes nocturnal sounds.

Behold, the poet of Balen attacks again—the little ass—

and produces unfamiliar sounds with braying voice.

Suddenly the pursuits of things are turned in opposite directions.

Let Tityrus laugh at Orpheus, whose ears resound with music.

Orpheus, feed your rotten little goats in the woods;

Tityrus pursues the delights of the halls.

David remains in the citadel with a few girls,

blowing every song upon his Pierian trumpet.

[Col. 0324C] Above all, Delia of Flaccus makes the Muses shine,

and afterward the other sacred instruments roar together.

Delia now plays the Thracian lyre with her thumb,

and adorns her sacred temples with new flowers.

Vinnula’s sweet-sounding pipe searches out the honeyed Muses;

behold, her throat resounds with fifteen tones.

The old Flaccus departs from the city accompanied by boys;

when the full light returns, then he himself returns home.

He has his age; let him answer for himself,

and give an account for himself and for his boys.

Or he may have ordered them to blow the light reeds,

or to bind garlands upon the head of the old Silenus.

These few songs the psalmist David sees,

now resounding among royal feasts.

Among them he inserts a few threads into the loom,

and Delia, in Virgilian fashion, gives them a woman’s feet.

He suddenly caught sight of Beselel and the idle Lupus.

Therefore he kept silent, fearing to utter sweet words.

When Lupus flees, understanding returns to his heart;

he fills rivers, fields, and houses with songs.

And on whatever day the thyrses grow upon his head,

when his hair is already shining, then he too will sing,

while the gray Lupus searches for his songs in his book-chests;

perhaps he will find them, so that Maro may then resound.

Lucius himself, known for his brevity, paints poems;

perhaps even the raven cannot learn such things.

[Col. 0325B] Scottulus, girded with a sharp sword, watches you,

so that he may pierce your breast, Corvinian.

He does not fear these ravens, nor would he spare any bird,

if only he hopes that Damaetas is far away.

Our Scot is not the pious poet Damaetas;

the insolent game turns into grief upon his lips.

Nevertheless, the Scot, threatening with weapons, now attempts battle,

wishing to strike a Getic head with his sword.

This Scot will bear the threefold name *sottus cottus*,

and he himself cries out “gentle wolf” from his hollow throat.

With smoky verse and a distich issuing from his mouth,

behold, Menalcas has sung this to us in his own way.

He struck the living man, lifeless, with unjust laughter,

but nevertheless these battles are useful to boys.

Three boys rejoice around Daniel’s dishes;

by the nobility of their faith they overcome the flames.

Now Job shines with the honor of his immense number,

and the Psalter shines before pious eyes with love.

In the midst of them David governs all with his scepter,

distributing abundant feasts in peaceful order.

And pious Aaron blesses everything throughout the hall,

sanctifying all the dishes with sacred words.

And Nehemiah, who had now rebuilt Jerusalem,

the bald man, powerful in wine, will carry sweet wines.

What place is there for the black raven amid these banquets?

Let him remain in the woods among the wolves.

Unless Elijah purges the raven’s crimes,

and summons him once more to the sacred dishes.

Hardberd, the miserly keeper of Spanish drink,

is completely armed with Ceres in his own hall.

He stirs the hot cauldron with his scepter in the kitchens,

so that he may drink this cold liquid that makes the heat here.

And the despised little Greek Putifar, perhaps hated by girls,

is uselessly armed, fighting no battles.

Whom do his companions, Bagao and Egeus, accompany together?

Of these three trunks, not one human being will emerge.

I think these men are no longer voluntarily faithful in the chambers:

the doctor’s savage hand compels them to keep faith.

The son of the widow, Hiram, constructs the temple well;

may the work be aided by Christ, the Most High.

Among these, the giant Nimrod shakes his hunting spears,

preparing to strike the raven’s forehead with his weapons.

And the huge Polyphemus, disturbing the sail-bearing sea,

so that the little diver cannot escape upon the water—

these two, unequal in body but threatening in mind:

the one will break the raven’s feet, the other his head.

The Pygmies, desiring only to seek peace,

because of the battles of the cranes, are here for you, black little Raven.

Let these things suffice for you when you come; only three-legged things—

winter, thirst, and hunger—will suffice in words for you.

Let us keep our own people, and what belongs to us, in our hall;

let us keep our three-legged brothers; let your crowd be small.

Hold these verses most sharply in mind, little Raven;

read them often and store them in your heart.

When Flaccus comes accompanied by boys and odes,

then you may hope for better things.

Then, as many greetings to you as there are hairs upon your head,

now turning white. Thus, Corvinian, farewell.

## IV. To Gisla

[Note: [Col. 0325D] To Gisla. His daughter, as he shortly indicates:

“What your father Theodulf gives you here.” He had evidently become her father before assuming the episcopate.]

**TO GISLA**

Gisla, by God’s favor, receive this venerable gift,

which your father Theodulf here gives you.

For I ordered this Psalter to be written for you,

which you see shining with silver and gold.

The earlier page agrees with the Hebrew truth;

as the ancient edition is, so the following one immediately has it.

[Note: [Col. 0325D] Which Jerome handled well. Jerome did two things concerning the Psalter: he corrected the old Latin version according to the Septuagint, and produced another new version according to the Hebrew. He mentions both works near the end of Book I against Rufinus: “The Psalter also, which Rome formerly received through our labor, certainly corrected according to the Septuagint translators, I have again fortified with a preface while translating it according to the Hebrew.” Theodulf indicates that both works are joined together in this own codex.]

Jerome translates this one well and corrects that one;

believe me, both shine with excellent meanings.

Attend to it constantly and diligently,

and vigorously submit your mind to its meanings.

Hold this instrument in your lap, keep its melodies in your mind;

let your hand be full of this plectrum and these rattles.

Let this sweet song refresh you, strike these drums;

let this harp sound for you, and let that lyre resound.

Return to it, sometimes singing, sometimes handling it,

so that divine love may grow greater within you from it.

If you pray constantly, if your reading is frequent,

you yourself speak to God, and God himself speaks to you.

Let your hand be generous, your manners well ordered, your conduct prudent,

so that you may properly please the Creator.

Let there be devotion to wool-working, constant care of the household,

and let your mind soothe your servants and your husband.

Let discretion rule all your actions;

by this willingly adorn yourself, and under this guide let your life remain.

Despise evil, pursue good, conduct everything becomingly,

so that noble salvation may lift you up completely.

Thrive as a chaste wife with a chaste husband,

and may the fruit of children make you both joyful.

And, Gisla, happily make sweet use of your husband Suavaricus—

[Note: [Col. 0326D] Use of *rico*. This should be read from the manuscript, not *erico*. He says that Gisla’s husband was Suavaricus, whose name he divides for metrical reasons. Thus, “And, Gisla, happily make sweet use of your husband,” *suaveque, Gisla, tuo feliciter utere rico*, is expressed by tmesis, as in Virgil’s *septem subiecta trioni* (“the seven [stars] placed beneath the Bear”). Not many years earlier there had been another bishop Suavaricus among the Orléanais; it is a plausible conjecture that this man was related to him both in name and family.]

[Col. 0327A] And grow old happily with him, with God granting it.

May a multitude of grandchildren seek you as grandmother and great-grandmother;

may he who gave this gift to your fathers grant it to you.

May hope, honor, order, faith, piety, concord, virtue,

the grace and peace of God always be yours. Hail.

## V. To the Queen

[Note: [Col. 0327D] To the queen. Luitgard, who has already been mentioned. From her he asks balsam, from which chrism is made, the substance that gives Christians their name. This is what he means when he says, “when the same ointment gives the name of Christ-bearers.” For those who have received chrism are Christians, that is, anointed ones. Cyprian alludes to this in Letter 70: “It is also necessary,” he says, “that the baptized person be anointed, so that, having received chrism—that is, anointing—he may be God’s anointed one and may have Christ’s grace within him.”]

**TO THE QUEEN**

O powerful queen, O glory of the great king,

O living light and glory of people and clergy,

may the Father enthroned on high preserve you for a long age,

and may you benefit the peoples and the Church of God.

You are the light and splendor, the kingdom’s distinguishing glory;

you shine in beauty together with the aid of piety.

You are joined to the pious and meritorious king,

whom God exalts and for whom he prepares every good thing.

[Col. 0327B] Day and night you labor to assist him,

and you continually raise his name on high.

You remain beautiful in body, but in mind you are more beautiful still;

it is doubtful whether you are altogether superior in this respect or that.

You are beautiful in the meaning of your words, but more beautiful in your deeds;

yet in both respects you alone are victor over yourself.

May the Creator, who granted you the will for so many good things,

grant you to complete them and help you without end.

Queen, send me balsamic liquid,

so that the ointment of chrism may go fittingly among the peoples.

From this a rich harvest of reward will grow for you,

when the same ointment gives the name of Christ-bearers.

May the Almighty grant you life and pious gifts of salvation,

and may you remember us without end. Farewell.

## VI. To the King

[Col. 0327C]

Blessed king, farewell; may you prosper through long ages,

and may the highest Good grant you every success.

For your prosperity is the honor and glory of the Christian people,

whose guardian and father you are.

You are guardian of their wealth, avenger of crimes, giver of honors;

whatever you do is accomplished under God’s direction.

You are the weapon of pontiffs, the hope and defense of the clergy;

through you the pontiffs retain their sacred rights.

I am lying—unless Bishop Leo has learned this by experience himself,

which our little pipe sings in its brief measure.

His own people unjustly drove him from city and see,

and preferred death for him rather than life.

Your merciful compassion received him well, O king;

it consoles, soothes, cherishes, adorns, and nourishes him.

[Col. 0327D] A raging hand robbed him of sight and tongue,

[Col. 0328A] of sacred garments and holy orders.

Peter restored what black Judas took away;

this man is Christ’s confessor, while the other is God’s betrayer.

A seditious band followed Judas in this matter,

that one desiring the Lord’s death, this one the pontiff’s.

For they deny that these things were restored and deny that they were taken away,

yet proclaim that they wished to take them away.

It was restored—it is marvelous; it is marvelous that they were unable to take it away.

Yet I do not know whether I should marvel more at this or at that.

For when Peter could have saved him in the Quirinal city,

from black enemies and savage ambushes,

he sent him to you, most merciful king, to be saved,

and wished you to perform his office in his place.

Through himself he restores to him the fearful losses of his limbs,

[Col. 0328B] and through you the dignity of his see and office.

He holds the keys of heaven and ordered you to hold those of his own realm;

you rule the Church, while he rules heaven.

You rule his possessions and govern clergy and people;

he will lead you even to the choirs of the heavenly inhabitants.

Therefore, priest restored to a secure see, sit in your see,

and gladly ask the Lord to aid the king.

Ask that Christ grant him life and bestow salvation upon him,

and always raise his kingdom on high.

May the Father enthroned on high save you, O king, for a long time,

and give you life or the aid of salvation.

May the saints pray and plead with the Lord for you,

those whose souls heaven and whose bodies earth hold.

The people and clergy in these regions thirst to see you;

may I too obtain the fulfillment of my wish.

And would that the Lord lead you to these citadels,

and that the city of Orléans might see its lord.

May you have life, salvation, piety, and Christ’s blessing,

pious king, wise king, king wholly suited to God.

## VII. What Should Be Said to a Friend When He Sees His Friend’s Wealth

When your dear friend looks upon your possessions,

you yourself, happy, shall give him these words, happily:

“These good things that you see are to be shared with me;

whoever is good will also share in these things.

Do not begrudge giving; believe me, it is beautiful to give to me:

if you give nothing, you will receive nothing; if you give, you will carry away [your reward].”

The one who sowed great seeds will reap with a full sickle;

so cultivated land will make its lord glad.

When you see someone known to you by face but not by name,

love him as though he were well known to you in both respects.

Do not begrudge giving pious words or welcome kisses;

while you do so, take care to learn his name.

As commonly happens, you may come to know it when another person calls him,

or he may happen to name himself in some way.

If he remains unknown, there is error; but if you ask his name aloud, shame remains.

If you learn it secretly, both error and shame are absent.

Someone who thinks that he is known to you, or who once was known to you—

if you do not call him by his proper name, he will be sad.

Learn the names or habits of the people you are going to teach;

and while you teach, call each person by his proper name.

Be great with the great, little with the little,

so that you may be all things to everyone, as Paul himself says.

This principle must also be observed in many actions:

some things we conceal, while more things are made public.

## VIII. On a Little Fox Pouncing upon a Hen

[Col. 0329B]

[Note: [Col. 0329D] They call it Carroph. It is a place in the diocese of Poitiers where the monastery of Saint Saviour, the subject here, was founded. Fulbert, in Letter 117, calls it the monastery of Carroficum, and in the Constitution of Aachen concerning monasteries which owe military service or gifts, or do not owe them, it is called the monastery of Carrofinium—unless the reading is corrupt.]

There is a place which the Gauls call Carroph by name,

where the courtly gate of heaven lies open to the chosen.

There the hall shines under the name of the Savior,

and there the beautiful cloisters of a monastery remain.

Here it shines, relying on the radiant pledge of the saints,

and a faithful community lives there in exceptional fashion.

Finally, the great count Rotharius [Rotgarius], an illustrious hero,

founded this work together with his wife Eufrasia.

He adorns it with shining silver, gems, and gold,

and supplies it abundantly with books, vestments, and sacred objects.

He gave estates, meadows, houses, woods, vineyards, tenants,

cattle, flocks, and every kind of good.

[Col. 0329C] By these things, given with generous hands, let dreadful poverty be driven away,

while heaven’s treasury receives the fruit.

May almighty God cleanse him from every sin,

and in his piety join him to the choirs of heaven.

Christ strives to defend this place from dark forces,

having consecrated it himself for his own worship.

A fox had been accustomed, by hostile plundering, to seize whatever food

was needed to nourish men,

and whatever bird, trailing a thousand feathers and spreading a thousand colors,

produces—this too it devoured with crafty jaws.

Then the worthy company of monks did not know

what would bear such losses from the pest.

At once the fox’s cunning seized the winged hen,

and thus the hidden path of the fraud became clear.

The barbarous plunderer, together with the weight of its prey,

stupidly hung of its own accord from part of a stake.

It hung stupidly of its own accord, deprived of every means of escape;

all around, the end had come to its various deceits.

It had consumed the bird’s head with its hollow mouth;

the rest of the limbs remained untouched.

For the alder was lower than the tree but taller than the rods: there, fox, your foot was to be caught by the craftsman,

so that the hand of the man lifting the stones with which the wall might swiftly rise high

could reach higher.

[Col. 0330A] From this the savage plunderer hung, and from there the pest,

twisting its neck and trembling head this way and that.

At this sight the faithful company of monks rejoices,

seeing signs worthy of wonder, by God’s favor.

Let every thief and profane person stay far, far away from here;

depart, error of the demon; come, gracious angel.

Let concord dwell among those oppressed by the arrows of envy,

and let hope and faith reign in this place.

Granting every prosperity, may God drive away adversity;

let minds feed on your nectar, O Christ.

## IX. On a Certain Soldier Who Recovered His Lost Horse by Cunning

[Note: [Col. 0330D] Cunning often provides what strength refused to provide. Peter Pithoeus published this epigram among the ancient poems, but without the author’s name and mutilated by four verses, which we supplied from our manuscript.]

Cunning often provides what you would have thought impossible;

the man who was powerless in strength is master through skill.

Listen to how a certain soldier recovered his horse,

stolen amid the confusion of a military camp.

Having lost his horse, he becomes a herald and calls out at the crossroads:

“Let whoever has our horse make an effort to return it.

Otherwise, compelled by such a reason, I shall do

what our father did in the city of Rome.”

This moves everyone, and the thief lets the horse go,

fearing such losses to himself or to the people.

When its master finds it, he rejoices and takes possession of what he has found,

and those who had previously been afraid congratulate him.

Then they ask what he would have done after the horse had been taken,

or what his father had previously done in the city.

“With a saddle,” he says, “and with a collar of wolf-teeth attached for carrying,

and with other little packs, the poor man would go off loaded.

Having nothing that could prick him, and carrying spurs at his heel,

he who had once been a horseman would return home on foot.”

Following his example, I too would have done such things in sorrow,

had this horse, believe me, not been found for me.

## X. That Power Cannot Endure a Partner

The tale tells that triple Geryon ruled,

because one heart could belong to three brothers.

The blessed page sings again in truthful speech,

surpassing all fictions with its holy law:

earthly kings, because of the heights of royal power,

have by cruel treachery put brothers to death.

This must be avoided with every prayer and every skill,

so that nothing of this kind may occur in our age.

Once, nearly all peoples had this custom:

that one man from the body of brothers should hold the scepter,

while the remaining part strove to be a great senate,

so that the summit of the kingdom might remain solidly united.

This was the custom among Assyrians, Egyptians, and Hebrews,

and among the people that formerly inhabited Achaemenian lands.

The Parthian has this custom, as do the Athenians and Romans;

the swarthy Indian has it, and the Hagarenian has it.

This was the custom among the Getae, Huns, and dark Moors,

and I think that the dreadful Ethiopians have that custom too.

[Col. 0331A] Among Thracians and Phrygians also—whether you are the land of Sparta—

and among every people that now bears the scepter or once bore it.

## XI. On the Front of a House

You who wish to go from Rome to the crowds of Tours, or to return from Tours to Rome, and to climb, look and see.

From here you will behold crops, vines, and the enclosures of wild beasts,

rivers, meadows, roads, and a fruit-bearing grove.

While you gaze upon these things, while you see so many pleasant sights,

remember the God who is their author.

## XII. Itinerary

Yet soon our journey set out from there toward the unwarlike

Limoges, whose entire people were prepared to serve.

Their wealthy city was hospitable to us until

the sun had driven the stars from the sky nine times

and Auredus joined himself to the one waiting for him in the wing.

There the abbots, the clergy, and the rest of the people

often refreshed us with delights in abundant kindness.

When the people, drenched in much wine,

rushed upon our men, and our men strove to defend themselves,

[Col. 0332A] and the impious sword was about to consume the ancient city,

alas for me, and a savage loss was about to come upon us,

had not the presbyter Ephraim—or Mancio—gone there,

and, by restraining the fury, caused death to cease on both sides.

At last, laden with these packs, such as necessity requires,

we departed from there, and the land of Périgueux received us.

[Note: [Col. 0331B] The land of Périgueux. *Petrocorica*. This name does not occur interpolated in this way only here. For in ancient copies of Paulinus also, who wrote six books of poems on the Life of Saint Martin, it is attached to the title of the work and has taught us the author’s homeland.]

From there we sought your backward-flowing banks, Dordogne.

Scarcely had the farther shores become visible,

when, with the mass of the waters turned aside,

you gave orders to the horses to go farther.

Three times we drove them swiftly into the river’s waters,

urging them with cries and even with the throwing of stones;

three times, thrown back by the river’s weight, they were powerless,

through shallows, rocks, leaps, and caverns.

The anxious crowd of those searching found them trembling.

I think that they trembled at the pitiable monster which the farther bank

had created, and feared the earth lying there.

For pale hunger, perhaps overflowing with money,

was ravaging your lands, Gaul of Périgueux.

After this, we crossed the wandering rivers by boat.

We drew the hoofed animals through the wet by tying them with halters;

what lay before us offered itself willingly to our sight.

# BOOK FOUR

## I. On the Books I Used to Read, and on How the Philosophers Treat the Poets’ Fables Mystically

For I was accustomed to reading these books frequently;

that labor occupied me night and day.

Often I reread Gregory, often Augustine,

and the sayings of Hilary, or yours, Pope Leo.

Jerome, Ambrose, Isidore, John with golden mouth,

and you, illustrious martyr and Father Cyprian.

Or others whose names it would be tedious to list,

whom the glory of learning has carried well to the heights.

We also frequently read the pagan writings of the sages,

who distinguished themselves sufficiently in various matters.

Nor was the fitting care of the pious Fathers the least of my concerns;

below, you may see their names written.

[Note: [Col. 0331D] Sedulius, Rutilus. I do not know which poet he means by Rutilus, apart from Rutilius Namatianus. Yet it would be strange to number among Christian poets one who was not a Christian. Therefore Fortunatus, who in Book I of the Life of Saint Martin lists seven others, omits Rutilius.]

Sedulius, Rutilus, Paulinus, Arator, Avitus,

and Fortunatus; and you, thundering Juvencus.

And you, Prudentius, powerful in wisely bringing forth many things

in varied meter, yourself also our father.

Sometimes I read Pompeius, sometimes you, Donatus,

sometimes Virgil, and sometimes you, loquacious Naso.

Although there are many trifles in their sayings,

very many truths lie hidden beneath a false covering.

The poets’ style brings falsehoods; the sages bring truths,

and these falsehoods they often turn into truth.

Thus Proteus depicts truth; thus Virgo depicts justice;

Alcides, virtue; and needy Cacus, theft.

But to expose falsehood so that it may be recognized,

a thousand lies are revealed;

when this has been firmly stripped away, the original form returns.

That force of justice shines unharmed in the manner of Virgo,

which the plague of injustice cannot stain.

The madness that deceives thieves goes with reversed steps;

from their mouths they pour out smoke, denying their foul crimes.

But the power of the mind uncovers, suppresses, and shakes them;

thus their wickedness lies exposed.

Cupid is imagined as winged, naked, and a boy,

carrying a bow and quiver, poisons, arrows, and a torch.

He is winged because he is light; naked because his crime is open;

a boy because he lacks skillful judgment.

[Col. 0332D] A wicked mind is marked in the quiver, ambushes in the bow;

the arrows are first poison, and your torch, O Love, is passion.

For what can be more mobile or lighter than lovers,

whose mind is wandering and whose body is light?

Who can conceal the crime that fierce love commits,

whose evil deeds will always be exposed?

Who will be able to bind him with the coils of reason,

who is an unrestrained boy and devoid of reason?

Who could penetrate the evil hiding places of the quiver—  
how many savage arrows lie concealed within its wicked womb?

Joined with the torch, what poisonous stroke springs forth,  
which flies, wounds as it destroys, burns, and drives onward?

[Col. 0333A] For the demon of adultery is criminal and savage,  
dragging wretched men toward the cruel abysses of lust.

He is ready to deceive and always prepared to do harm,  
since power, activity, and practice belong to the demon.

Sleep, as the poems relate, possesses twin gates:  
one carries true things, the other false.

The horn gate draws forth truth, while the ivory gate produces falsehood;  
the eyes see the truth, but false things pass through the mouth.

For horn is smooth, and the tender eye is translucent,  
while ivory bears the obscured opening of the mouth.

Horn feels neither the eyes’ brightness nor the cold;  
its force and color remain equal to those of tooth and ivory.

The power of those two gates is not the same:  
the mouth conveys falsehood, while the eye sees nothing but truth.

It is enough to have set down these few points,  
compressed into brief chains from many examples.

## II. [Note: [Col. 0333C] On the seven liberal arts

From the Vatican manuscript, by an uncertain author—though, if I am not mistaken, older than Theodulf—we once transcribed these tetrastichs, not unworthy to be presented here.

### Wisdom

My unbegotten Father begot me, coeval with the Word,  
whom no body nourishes and no place contains.

Yet I bring earthborn people to my Father’s banquets,  
for those alone lack them who are reluctant to go together.

### Astronomy

A wondrous appearance and a restless spirit confront me;  
I bear as many eyes as the sky contains stars.

I hold five breasts, one of them scorched by fire,  
two mild and two cold.

### Music

I flow from the fountain of joy, the author of sweetness;  
no part of me exists without joy.

I am harmonious melody, differing in triple modulation;  
when it resounds without me, it lacks usefulness.

### Geometry

Whoever wishes, by diligent study, to penetrate my secrets  
must first approach various locks.

I shine with six lights and three faces,  
and with a radius I construct hexagonal regions.

### Arithmetic

I am slender in appearance and possess many swiftly moving wings;  
whoever wishes to know me should always cultivate me with love.

I am born unequal, with figures arranged wondrously,  
remaining the source and origin of three brothers.

### Rhetoric

A skilled tongue and speech gave me my name,  
yet I often visit unlearned men.

For through me he prevails who had never seen me.  
What more does the one who knows my laws accomplish?

### Dialectic

I concede nothing doubtful in speech, but reveal certainties;  
I am skilled at compressing broad statements into swift formulations.

For in five modes I determine everything that exists,  
neither less nor greater, but singing of the whole as it is.

### Grammar

I become a beautiful remedy when I restore speech to the stammerers,  
for I am a powerful medicine for the defects of the mouth.

With six leaves I also compose a wholesome taste,  
and afterward add the resources of health in a thousand ways. ]**

## On the seven liberal arts depicted in a certain painting

There was a disk formed in the rounded image of the world,  
which the work of a single tree adorned.

Grammar sat at its great root,  
warning it either to generate itself or to retain itself.

Thus every branch is seen to proceed from her,  
because no art can be brought forth without her.

Her left hand holds a whip, or her right a sword,  
so that the former may drive on the sluggish and the latter cut away their vices.

And because Wisdom everywhere holds first place,  
she had adorned her head with a diadem.

And because good sense or judgment gives birth to you,  
both attend you here, lofty Wisdom.

[Col. 0333C] From the tree’s straight trunk, branches  
rise everywhere, facing one another.

The right-hand branch contains Rhetoric and Dialectic,  
while the left bears the four Virtues.

Rhetoric sat with her right hand extended toward the forum,  
and beside her stood the structure of a turreted city.

By great eloquence she accomplishes civil laws,  
and is accustomed to give the reins to lawsuits and the people.

The fortress of her body bore wings,  
and the head of a lion, which the craftsman’s well-trained hand had made.

The lightness of words shown by the wings,  
and the lion’s strength in the head, gave fitting signs of eloquence.

Thus, bearing wings on head and feet like the caduceus-bearer,  
she signified that a lightness of movement resides in words.

Not far from here sat Dialectic, the mother of understanding:  
the former appeared standing, the latter seated.

They were equal in understanding but unlike in most of their activity:  
standing, the one speaks aloud; seated, the other reads.

The one seeks tumultuous seats, the other secluded ones;  
the one continually desires the forum, the other the stylus.

The one arranges the manner of speech, the other the manner of conduct;  
the one remains a fountain of words, the other of meanings.

On the left she displays a head, but conceals her body as a serpent,  
while she holds nothing in her right hand—let anyone who seeks her seek.

[Col. 0334B] She proposes and assumes, then sharply concludes,  
so that she may soon seize the unwary with her skillful serpent.

She struggles with great diligence to distinguish true things from false,  
and knows how to find the path of truth.

This is Logic; but on another branch Ethics had taken her seat:  
the former flourishes through reason, the latter through upright conduct.

Prudence holds the first place in this section,  
for she knows not how to lose the path of holy life.

She stood there with reverent gravity and held a book,  
so that her follower might be imbued with it.

Next to her stood the strongest power, Fortitude,  
marked out by her weapons and offices.

One hand holds a dagger, the other a shield;  
a helmet’s cone covered her entire head.

Thus she may overcome the dreadful apparitions of vices,  
and so that holy liberty may be kept secure.

Near her Justice held a sword and a palm,  
and in one hand a balance or a crown.

She determines who should endure punishments unjustly imposed,  
and who should receive just rewards;  
she approves by proper weight what is rightly said or done.

Near her stood Moderation, offering self-restraint,  
holding either strong reins or whips in her hand,

with which she might spur the sluggish, restrain the swift,  
and ensure that an equal order proceed along balanced courses.

[Col. 0335A] The image of the great tree extended upward,  
and its trunk rose straight and well toward the heights.

The art of numbers embraced it with its arms;  
its feet seemed to stand upon either branch.

One hand held numbers and the other a volume—  
she whom you, Physics, acknowledge as your mother.

Above her, two branches are seen to emerge from the first branches,  
similar and facing one another.

Music occupied one side with her sounding art;  
she seemed to move the strings of a lyre.

And she whose pipe has seven unequal reeds—  
a number famous for containing many mysteries.

Geometry also stood leaning on the left side,  
holding a radius in her right hand and a measuring wheel in her left.

The radius measures a rounded circle nearby,  
and the wheel contains the five heavenly zones.

Of these, the two outermost are pressed by cold,  
while one torrid zone in the middle moderates the two.

Between them the central trunk rose upward,  
and the art cultivated by astrologers held it.

A great circle, reaching toward its lofty head, burdened it;  
outstretched arms held it with both hands.

It was a circle formed in the image of the star-bearing sky,  
which a graceful fiery order of signs fills.

Twelve signs, or seven wandering stars,  
adorn it by their law, succession, courses, orbit, and places.

Here are Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo,  
Virgo with the Chariot, Libra, and the Scorpion;

the Archer, Capricorn, Aquarius, and the two Fishes  
surround the sphere in their signs of the sky.

[Col. 0335C] The Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus,  
and weighty Saturn proceed in the sphere day by day.

Reader, do not be displeased by the pagan names.  
This is the ancient custom handed down by the fathers.

By these seven stars and twelve signs,  
the month, the year, and the day itself are directed.

One is fitted to the days, another to the months;  
the weeks and the year are constituted by them.

The tree possessed these things, as well as leaves and hanging fruits,  
and thus supplied beauty and many mysteries.

In the leaves understand words; in the fruits, meanings.  
The former continually increase; the latter, rightly used, nourish.

Upon this spreading tree our life is exercised,  
so that it may always seek things higher than the small ones.

[Col. 0335D] Let human understanding gradually climb toward the heights,  
and let it long be reluctant to follow what is lower.

Ethics is joined to Grammar, and Logic soon joins them;  
Physics also sits there with its companion arts.

Of these, the highest chose for itself a seat in the citadel,  
which contains the law of the stars and of the sky.

Let eloquence follow morals, and let nourishing Logic follow them,  
so that it may come to know natural things well.

And let it traverse the vault of heaven in song and the lands,  
seeking the lofty ether and the things of the world.

## III. Another painting in which there was [Note: [Col. 0335D] An image of the earth

The Great Goddess, the same as Earth. Therefore the things usually attached to the Great Goddess were referred by some, in different ways, to Earth according to physical reasoning. On this subject Augustine, drawing on Varro, says much in Book VII of *The City of God*, and Isidore in Book VIII of the *Etymologies*, in the chapter “On the gods of the nations.” Concerning the goddess Tellus, I think an ancient Roman inscription not yet brought to light remains:

“Sacred to the goddess Tellus. Marcus Aurelius Threptus made this.”]**

## The image of the earth enclosed in the form of a sphere

[Col. 0336A]

A beautiful woman stood there in the likeness of the earth,  
nursing a child and filling a basket with grain.

She bore a turreted head and a great serpent in her lap,  
and in her hand a key, cymbals, and weapons.

Before her stood roosters, sheep, and fierce lions,  
submissive; and an empty seat was there.

Beneath her was the revolving motion of a great vehicle,  
and the circle of a rounded wheel moved around her.

She nurses the child because she nourishes what is born,  
and because Earth fosters all created things together.

The grain in the baskets, and the great cities in the towers,  
are signified by the farmer’s clever skill in the serpent.

[Col. 0336B] Since the year opens in summer and is closed in winter,  
she carries a key in her hand for this reason.

The cymbals are the sounds produced by rustic instruments,  
or by whatever craftsman practices his art.

And because all must fight for their country,  
the image of Earth therefore bears your weapons.

The sphere is the emblem of the wheel; the roosters signified seeds,  
and the sphere will produce much from conceived seed.

The sheep are placed beneath her because from her  
they obtain pasture and can possess no resource without her.

The hostile rage of the lions lies beneath her,  
because the earthly Earth tames all things.

Although everything is moved, she herself cannot be moved;  
for this reason an everlasting seat was imagined for her.

Through seats, too, the honors of the world are signified,  
since no one approaches them to possess them forever.

One rejoices to sit in another’s chair:  
this one sits, that one sat; this one goes, and the other returns.

For this reason she was carried in a chariot: Earth hangs in the air  
and is supported by the light waters.

Hence the reading concerning the Lord makes a true declaration,  
when it seeks to enumerate his praises:

He stretches out the North over the immeasurable void,  
and hangs the earth upon nothing.

What is carried on wheels signifies the revolving motion of the world,  
which turns with swift and measured movement.

The image of earthly destiny seemed to stand there,  
for the one who cultivates the fields always has work to do.

I, Theodulfus, bishop, arranged this work,  
and duly gave it strength through its twofold purpose:

[Col. 0336D] namely, that bodies might be fed with joyful banquets,  
and that the image of the world, when contemplated, might nourish the mind.

Viewer, love the soul’s banquets more than those of the body:  
the mind is vigorous through the former, while the flesh is dull through the latter.

Let heavenly words resound, and let this table overflow with dishes;  
let envious speech find no place here.

A brief painted image of the entire world is present:  
it will enable one to know a great matter in a small body.

Here Amphitrite, along the long boundary of the lands,  
[Col. 0337A] stretches out her arms, devouring all the rivers.

With puffed cheeks, quarreling brothers from every side  
stand upon the sphere; each has his own place.

## IV. [Note: [Col. 0337D] To Bishop Aiulfus

Aiulfus, or Aigulfus, patriarch of the first see of Bourges—for that is how he calls him. While still alive, he was a man distinguished by a reputation for holiness. He was chosen as a judge together with other bishops by Ebbo of Reims in the year 835.
