From this letter it is clear that he was already a bishop when Theodulfus was exiled at Angers, that is, before the year 820—contrary to the common account of those who have written about the bishops of Bourges.]**

## To Bishop Aiulfus

Theodulfus, an exile from exile, sends this poem  
to you, Aiulfus, most holy bishop.

Once, as a boy, you possessed a noble and beautiful nature;  
now you are a man adorned by the power of nobility.

The teachable skill that belonged to you as a little boy  
now remains in the mature man, bestowed by the Thunderer.

As a boy you always possessed great signs  
of great virtue, indicating that fate would make you a great man.

Thus fruitful seed promises the rewards of a rich harvest;  
thus the form of the bull appears in the tender calf.

At last you applied yourself to learning the liberal arts,  
and your heart was sufficiently cultivated by them.

But now it is your task to hand on the teachings of the divine Word  
and to proclaim the laws of heaven to the peoples.

The cups you once drank from the grammatical fountain  
now refresh minds with an ambrosial dew.

Rumor spreads everywhere that you live holily;  
your great fame flies sufficiently through men’s mouths.

Who could recount all the praises of your merits,  
which this Suitegaudus is accustomed to report?

Suitegaudus, in whom uprightness, truth, faith,  
and all good things remain joined together.

God, the integrity of his life, and the choice of his brothers  
had placed him over the holy flock, with me as intermediary.

[Col. 0337C] But destructive envy, deceit, and treacherous falsehood  
removed him from his own episcopal seat.

There is a God in heaven who will restore him to his own fold;  
let him also care for the flock that was formerly his.

On your behalf he brought me kindly words  
and gave me your presence through his speech.

While he tells me of your goodness, he comforts me in my sickness,  
and my mind remains joyful because of your deeds.

On his behalf he now seeks from us certain matters concerning you,  
and has an answer to carry back to you.

He reported to me the zeal, distinction, and conduct  
with which you bear the burdens of your worthy office.

How, by examples and words, you continue to lead the peoples  
toward the holy kingdoms of heaven.

You are doing great things; we pray that you may do greater still,  
and we ask Christ to grant you the help you desire.

You have the examples of earlier fathers to follow,  
so that you may teach by your example and words.

May your teaching increase with every passing day,  
and may he who is the head proceed through his holy members.

You have been appointed with the patriarchal honor  
[Col. 0338A] of the first see, and the nourishing company of the fathers is subject to you.

Therefore prudent skill must remain with you,  
so that you may be an example, an ornament, an order, and a measure to all.

The higher you are, remember to be all the more humble,  
so that the gracious favor of God, the lofty-throned, may enrich you.

Be a lamb to the good, a fiery lion to the wicked;  
let the former love you as a father, and the latter fear you as their lord.

When you are gentle with the devout and stern with the harsh,  
let this group feel you as a mother and that one as a father.

Let your hand be generous, your heart calm, your words sweet;  
be upright and diligent, ready for every good.

But what am I doing, and where is my little pipe now leading me?  
I have just become like a teacher.

Meanwhile, I ask you to remember our ruin,  
and perhaps lighten our evil circumstances by prayer and supplication.

[Col. 0338B] Perhaps, when you pray and the company of your brothers assists,  
the Almighty will mercifully grant me pardon.

May he mercifully release us from this exile,  
as he released Joseph from prison and Peter as well.

I confess before God that I have committed many sins,  
which exceed in number the sands of the sea,

the drops of rain, the sea’s waves, the stars of heaven,  
the stalks of grass, and all the shoots of the soil.

These are my troubles; why have I been sent into them,  
when such evils are not deserved by me?

Believe that I did not sin against the king or his offspring,  
nor against his wife, so as to bear such great evils as punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0337D] Believe my words

Theodulfus was accused of being a participant in King Bernard’s conspiracy against his uncle, Louis. He emphatically denies that he had any connection with this crime, not only in this letter but also in the following one.

“The bishop did not confess, and yet he perished.” Although hope of pardon was offered to him if he assented, he nevertheless could not be bent. Theganus must therefore be excepted, since he asserted that the bishops deposed in this judgment had admitted their guilt.]**

Believe my words, most holy brother—believe  
that I am in no way guilty of the charge brought against me.

To deprive him of scepter, life, and his own nephew—  
these three things I never plotted.

We add a fourth: I had no such intention,  
whatever evils might result from these circumstances.

This I proclaimed, proclaim, and will proclaim forever,  
as long as the liquid sustains the limbs of my soul.

Whoever does not believe me now will eventually be compelled to believe,  
when we come before the throne of the great Judge.

He will be my witness, a merciful and most just avenger,  
to whom everything always remains naked and open.

He does not accept persons or gifts;  
as a just man, he loves every just good.

In his sight all falsehoods will perish;  
here I need no other witness’s help.

Your sweet compassion, dear brother, sustains me,  
and a great part of my sorrow remains with you.

[Col. 0338D] May the heavenly Father, who governs heaven and earth,  
grant that you may afterward possess our joy.

I know that you are crowned with the flower of every good thing  
and shine brightly enough with the lamp of virtues.

May you have life, health, and the grace of Christ the King;  
may the Almighty everywhere be your helper.

[Col. 0339A] Live happily for long ages, priest devoted to God,  
and duly advance from good to better. Farewell.

## V. [Note: [Col. 0339C] To Bishop Moduinus

The bishop of Autun, who was likewise chosen as a judge by Ebbo when he was deposed. A letter of Florus of Lyon to him survives, formerly printed by the Morellian press. There are also two other letters by the same Florus in the Petavian manuscript 791: one longer, “For the Church of Lyon, to the distinguished man Moduinus,” and another shorter one, in which, because *dun* in the old language of the Gauls means “mountain,” he calls Moduinus the bishop of the Augustan Mountain. He addresses him as follows:

“Greetings, holy father, venerable priest of Christ,  
powerful shepherd of Augustan Mountain’s citadel,

whom the sacred order illumines with shining merits,  
and whose devotion to holy teaching raises to the stars.”]**

## To Bishop Moduinus

Theodulfus sends greetings to his Moduinus.

This Theodulfus, an exile, sends you, Moduinus,  
behold, a humble song to the highest of bishops.

Go, Thalia, swiftly; cross the distance on swift wings;  
let there be no delay or rest for you on the way,

until you reach the dwelling of blessed Moduinus,  
that outstanding bishop and holy pontiff.

When you have reached him, immediately fall prostrate at his knees.  
If he orders you to rise, rise quickly.

At once give kisses to his friendly hands,  
and, gazing at the open ground, remain silent in your weariness.

[Col. 0339B] But if he asks who you are, whose you are, and where you come from,  
come, speak, and reveal each word from your heart.

I am Theodulfus’ Erato, coming from the cavern of his prison,  
where your immense love for him burns.

An exile, helpless, poor, most sorrowful, anxious, and distressed,  
despised and afflicted wherever he is, and grieving.

Perhaps he will also ask what I am doing. You will say that I live  
a life which perhaps would be better replaced by death.

He either reads, teaches, or fulfills the holy duties of praise  
to the Father of all, who rules the fields and the sky.

He asks this on your behalf, on behalf of himself and the order of the clergy,  
and for the safety of the people, the king, and the leaders.

He sent me to you; I convey his greetings to you,  
whose words, submitted to you, are to be sung.

I beg you, loving brother, remember to remember me;  
brother, a great portion of my soul.

May your mind always pity our labors,  
for you know well the cause of our situation.

The more clearly you know it, the more work devote to it;  
thus a physician drives out disease when he sees it, by his art.

You know that the smoky joys of the present world perish,  
but brotherly love never perishes, when it is nourishing.

Now love me more, although you have always loved me;  
a devout mother loves an invalid child more than others.

I gladly desire to come to the definite aid of the weary in their troubles,  
and to stir the devout minds of the brothers.

Although I am only one, this is not the affair of one alone:

[Col. 0340A] what has happened to me can happen to another.

The evil is common; a common remedy must be sought:  
what is ours today will belong to another tomorrow.

Let no brother be so foolish as not to fear these contagions:  
lest this plague creep upon him as it has upon us.

Fever tends to grow from fever, and wound from wound;  
thus many streams flow from a single source.

If my wound should find a peaceful cure,  
and former strength return when the disease departs,

the hostile party will no longer be able to seek anything of this kind,  
and this crime will certainly not be a trivial one.

The servant has his own law, and so does the lying little maid;  
the shepherd, the herdsman, the sailor, the swineherd, and the plowman likewise.

Alas! The bishop alone has lost his law,  
the order that is now being undermined without its law.

[Col. 0340B] He who ought to declare lawful judgments to others  
loses the right of his own office without law.

Acknowledged guilt makes the savage robber perish;  
the bishop did not confess, and behold, he perishes.

And while worldly affairs require their own arrangements,  
by which a just order may be maintained,

our case required the proper weight of reason;  
this matter has no measure except cruelty.

There was no witness there, nor any suitable judge,  
and I myself had confessed no crime.

Suppose I had confessed: whose judgment would have had the authority  
to impose fitting restraints upon me?

That task belongs solely to the Roman bishop,  
from whose holy hand I received the pallium.

[Note: [Col. 0339D] I received the palliums

The *pallium* is normally granted specifically to archbishops. Sometimes, however, it is also granted to non-metropolitan bishops, as it was granted to Syagrius of Autun by Gregory the Great; and Theodulfus testifies that he received it from the hand of the pope himself. I think this was Stephen IV, whom Theodulfus had been sent by Louis the Pious to meet when Stephen came into Gaul. But there was this difference between the pallium granted to the two men: Syagrius’ was given so that it might pass to his successors, whereas Theodulfus’ was not.]**

I was pleased to send you, dear brother, some poems,  
in which our playful Muse amused herself somewhat.

Moreover, at this time certain marvels are said to have appeared;  
of these I shall briefly sing the following.

## VI. [Note: [Col. 0340D] On the river that dried up

This happened in the year of Christ 820, on 8 February. Theodulfus indicates both facts in his verses. He counts this as the seventh year of Louis the Pious, who had begun to reign in 814. He indicates the day by saying that the sun was then in the twenty-second degree of Aquarius. Since in Theodulfus’ age the sun’s entry into Aquarius was usually reckoned from 18 January, the twenty-second day thereafter was necessarily 8 February. As for his reckoning the fourth year of his exile together with Louis’ seventh year, this seems to be understood as including in his exile the time when he was first detained with others toward the end of 817. Otherwise he was deposed and exiled—that is, relegated to a monastery—only in the following year, after Easter. At that time it was not Louis’ seventh year but his eighth.]**

## On the river that dried up

There is a river which earlier Gauls called the Sarta;  
the Perche gives it birth, and the Meduana drinks it.

Flowing through the fields of Le Mans,  
it passes beside the walls of that city.

The citizens usually cross it there in boats;  
there it performed no slight portent for them.

When dawn was driving away the dewy darkness  
and people sought the waters in their customary manner,

[Col. 0341A] that place was found stripped of its own waters,  
which previously had been passable by boat or oars.

With the waters standing still, the people on either side were astonished,  
and the riverbed called the populace into its depths.

No one seeks a boat; no sailor asks for you.  
To the wondering people, the way lies open.

Fear and the novelty of the event at first prevented entry,  
but gradually fear began to depart.

The new thing begins to become familiar: people and livestock  
seek one bank or the other.

Their feet are dry, or the sole is only slightly wet,  
as the crowds continually go and return.

If the young Leander had once possessed such a ford,  
your grief, Hero, would not have been so famous.

No one brings a net or hook for fishing;  
whoever wishes to do so manages it by leaps and with his hands.

A man was to be buried in a field on the farther bank;  
his grieving relatives carried him across the dry places.

That city greatly feared that the swelling waters might approach,  
and at once overwhelm its crossroads, fields, and houses.

Unknown rocks became visible beneath the sky,  
and the sky itself became visible through the rocks,  
as the moisture left its native bed.

Where, Sarta, you had offered no ford to a pedestrian,  
you provided a great one, while your rocks marveled at the boots.

Sarta suffered this same event twice on other occasions,  
neither at this time nor in this place.

Who could deny that the Lord remembered the ancient triumph,  
by which he divided the river and shook Jericho?

The water had flowed down from the first hour to the fourth;  
afterward the swift current returned to its own channels.

[Col. 0341C] We have not written the names of those who reported this,  
since there are many who have sung it to me.

But if you wish to know the time of the event, reader,  
receive it; I shall reveal it to you briefly.

Here the slippery seventh year is running its course,  
since, Louis, your father’s kingdoms have remained yours.

The unhappy fourth year of my exile,  
undeserved in the end, is now passing over me in misery.

Perhaps you wish to know the day; learn that too,  
and I shall sing it, so that the event can contain no uncertainty.

The sun’s solid orb had climbed twice eleven parts of Aquarius,  
and the Moon was in the sixth degree of Pisces.

They assert that you, O Idonea, suffered something of this kind,  
because Sarta, flowing from that city, drinks sufficiently near it.

[Col. 0341D] Seek the place from others; I shall tell you the day:  
the event occurred on the day before the one mentioned above.

They say that Angera also suffered this failure,  
but I know the place and day less well.

For we investigate such things with great zeal,  
because those who report them want to know the future through me.

It does not sing openly, nor will the voice always remain concealed;  
for these things remain to be sung at their proper time.

## VII. On the battle of the birds in the land of Toulouse

Through events and examples we can learn certain things well;  
although I do not prophesy, I know what this event means.

Since many wondrous things were seen at the same time,  
this too was seen, and I am preparing to recount it.

Gairardus reported it to me, and Paschasius to him:  
the latter tells me what he heard, but the former what he saw.

There is, of course, a place in the territory of Toulouse,  
at the outermost edge of Quercy; each district ends there.

There is a plain whose outer edges are encircled by woods,  
with people living not far away.

Many birds filled it with a great rush,  
and a multitude of birds settled on the plain.

Those belonging to river and woodland, to the harsh countryside,  
those accustomed to make nests on crags—

their food, song, color, flight,  
feather, claws, beak, habit, place, and function were diverse.

The west wind had brought some, the north wind others;  
you might think that both groups bore their own standards.

[Col. 0342B] The armies sat opposite one another on the fields,  
and some space extended between them.

You might have thought that envoys were going between the two armies,  
preparing to report the terms of war or peace.

Meanwhile a few birds from each side flew back and forth,  
and one side or the other fulfilled its exchanges.

That accomplished nothing, for after the peace embassy  
had taken place by chance, they stirred up great wars.

As envoys once went between the Carthaginians and the Roman people  
until they rushed into arms,

so, after sufficient flight on both sides,  
they rushed by force into savage war, each according to its strength.

The bands of birds burned for battle on every side;  
wing met wing, and cohort met cohort.

Their military strength was different, but their will was one:  
what the greater soldier wanted, the lesser wanted too.

There were no chariots, and no use of horses;  
there was no use of steel, and no spears flew.

Instead of a helmet there was a crest; instead of a spear, beaks or claws;  
instead of trumpets, each bird sounded its own song.

The light wing served as a shield, the bird’s small feather as a dagger,  
and fine plumage took the place of a breastplate.

Now the sixth day of this assembly had passed;  
from both sides they rushed eagerly into war.

They tear one another in turn, here with bites and there with blows;  
on both sides the battle rises with immense spirit.

Here you might see Rutulians, there Teucrians,  
and savage Mars raging on either side.

[Col. 0342D] An acorn falls from an oak trunk in autumn,  
and a ripe leaf when frost is already approaching.

No differently did the army of birds die there  
and fall, filling the ground with a great slaughter.

As a smooth threshing floor is filled with summer grain,  
so the field was filled with dead birds.

A small part came back from north to north;  
the entire cohort on both sides lies slain.

The event resounds, the people come, and they are astonished at what happened;  
they marvel at the various limbs of the fallen birds.

The bishop of Toulouse himself, Mantio, also came from the city.

[Note: [Col. 0341D] Bishop Mantio

We owe our knowledge of this bishop of Toulouse to Theodulfus alone. Apart from this passage, no mention of him has so far been found.]**

The people ask whether these birds may serve as food.

“Reject what is forbidden and take what is permitted,” he said;  
they load wagons with birds, and each returns home.

## VIII. On a similar battle of birds

News, flying through many mouths,  
has brought us word that something of this kind also happened at this time.

Those who travel to Rome and return from Rome sing of it;  
among them is a good woman, a trustworthy witness.

She went from Tours to Rome to pray; on her return  
she told the matter to the priest Arbalus, and he told it to me.

At last, near the Saône and the swift Rhône,  
a battle of birds took place, as above.

There, amid harsh cliffs and dense marshes,  
a few cultivated fields lie open on level ground.

There, as they report, every kind of flying creature came,  
the various birds nourished by your fertile Europe.

Some sat on the crags, others rested in the level fields,  
and many also sat on branches of trees.

The young warriors were divided into two military sides;  
each side, gaping, prepared for combat.

Four hawks came from one side, four from the other;  
and four *capi* [perhaps “capons”] in equal number on either side.

In their first encounter they killed one another in turn:  
hawk killed hawk, and the capus itself killed the capus.

Beaks pressed against beaks, claws fought claws;  
because they carried equal weapons, they killed one another all the more.

The Roman people did this in the fields of Emathia,  
when savage wars were fought, father-in-law on one side and son-in-law on the other,

when brother killed brother or friend killed friend,  
when they carried equal eagles and equal weapons.

It is said, however, that two great birds escaped,  
which did not fight; the rest of the multitude lies dead.

Each side wins, but victory comforts neither;  
on both sides it leaves the ground filled with slaughter.

As Hannibal’s fury filled Cannae with corpses,  
so these fields remain filled with the corpses of birds.

Who could recount each sign that is repeatedly revealed in time—  
what it is, where, why, when, or from where it is shown?

When will that day come when you enter our garden  
and willingly pluck our roses with your claw?

And when will your great thirst grow ever greater,  
while you are full of the song you always love?

[Col. 0343D] If there should be defects in these songs, as there will be,  
spare me, I beg you; I am not a learned writer.

Please send us your faithful servant,  
to bring me your gracious words. Farewell.

## IX. Moduinus to Theodulfus in exile

Moduinus, an unworthy bishop, to his Theodulfus.

No one can play skillfully in polished verse without rules;  
indeed, one who lacks art cannot speak correctly.

But even a hawk does not attempt to conquer in battle  
before, trained in the custom of its own parent, it undertakes this.

A young man does not serve as a soldier in his earliest years;  
only after experience does the recruit receive worthy rewards.

Nor does Tiphys dare, unprepared, to enter a ship  
and attempt the sea with a sailor’s skill.

Since I am unskilled, I will deny that I can  
reply to your outstanding verses.

My Muse is worthless among learned poets;  
for this reason I strive to compose no work in verse.

But your letter compels me, though I hesitate,  
now to write poems in unequal meters.

I am forced to impress hard iron upon soft wax  
and to weave words in an unfamiliar manner.

Indeed, what your letter sent to me has brought forth  
must properly be called an immoderately small book.

[Col. 0344B] You have heard the ancients thus play with friendly words;  
I have often learned this from your own mouth as well,

that a poet who knows nothing of the Muses  
does not know the Muses’ caves.

But this too can rightly be said of me.

Some assert that poets even go mad,  
when they compose verses while their minds are deprived of reason.

But our own mind remains sound, and it does not dare  
to go too far, abandoning its proper order.

Yet, to avoid stumbling blocks, it does not seek lofty things;  
being moderate, it is content with a modest place.

Theodulfus, kindly attend to my verses;  
let our poems not be despised by you.

I do not want you ever to attack ours with a poisoned tooth;  
let the poems be safe under your judgment.

If there should perhaps be errors in my songs, as there will be,  
please regard them with impartial eyes, bowing down kindly.

Often I lament, mourning the fate of an innocent friend;  
tears flow like a river from my mouth.

Often, repeating your name, I have mourned your ruin in tears:  
alas, you perish, deprived of episcopal honor.

Innocent priest, you endure a most bitter exile;  
renowned bishop, you have experienced a monstrous evil.

Wisdom often benefits some people greatly;  
but, father, behold, you have been harmed by your own intelligence.

Your great wisdom, especially, harmed you alone  
and prepared for you the burden of sorrow that you bear.

Devouring envy roars as it attacks what is lofty,  
attempting to overthrow what the simple-hearted crowd honors with joy.

Do you not know that, because of envy, Naso endured long labors  
and was himself driven from his native land?

[Col. 0344D] [Note: [Col. 0343D] Severinus himself

Boethius. In his own *Consolation* Boethius says little about the causes of his exile. An ancient author gives more, and previously unheard-of, information about them and about his punishment in the *Excerpts* which were long ago published together with Ammianus Marcellinus from our manuscripts by Henri Valois, a man of distinction.]**

Severinus himself was driven down from the great city,  
the famous Roman consul, far from the citadel.

The great poet Virgil was harried by a hostile soldier,  
stripped of his ancestral fields.

The distinguished Seneca is said to have suffered savage wounds  
from his tyrant, and perished in Nero’s slaughter.

Why should I mention the many among our own people  
who have suffered grievously for our holy religion?

The more devoutly one is honored by the great teacher himself,  
the more dreadful an exile John endured.

You too, Hilary, experienced the dreadful prisons,  
sent by royal command to an unknown place.

Peter himself, the key-bearer, and Paul,  
the teacher of the peoples, were in the embrace of prison.

Yet nevertheless the untutored, resistant ferocity of the Gentile did this,

for it was hostile to the devout faith.

I add also that, even then, the ecclesiastical order was still unformed,

and, shapeless and inert, lacked the discipline of its own rule.

With peace now set aside, it ought to have enjoyed serene savagery

and now maintained its proper measure.

The fault of the priests causes this: the highest order of sacred ministry is held in contempt.

Among them no faithful accomplishment is found;

those whom grace commends to the sacred office are without effect.

No one grieves in compassion for another’s hardships,

striking out on behalf of his brother’s welfare.

[Col. 0345B] Each strives to devote himself to earthly profit,

and, fond of pleasure, pursues fragile riches.

Yet do not suppose that I belong to their number,

those who utter varnished words from a frivolous heart;

rather, I shall never cease to contend in prayer,

and I gladly labor for your return.

Therefore I am always concerned for your old friends,

and I shall zealously exert myself on account of your losses.

I think you know this, since news is quickly scattered throughout the whole world,

carrying courtly tidings.

You are to be moved at last from this unhappy region,

and likewise to go to the shining threshold of Caesar.

You will come before his eyes and see with joy

the face that for so long had been sad to you.

He prefers to forgive you every offense committed,

[Col. 0345C] provided that you are willing to acknowledge that you have sinned.

For a sincere confession will be able to benefit you,

if by your own words you prove yourself guilty of the crime.

If you pretend not to know what crime I am speaking of,

know the reason why you were placed here.

[Col. 0346A] But choose what you will do, and whatever seems to you

the better counsel, keep it in mind, I beg.

Yet it has seemed better to me that you should freely confess

what no ingenuity can deny.

I think there is no other way to overcome the prince’s anger

unless you prove yourself guilty of the crime.

He promises that, if you yourself confess that you have sinned,

Caesar wishes to give you counsel.

For he promises you that your former virtue will return,

[Note: [Col. 0345C] To regain the rank that had been lost. As above:

“Alas! Having lost your honor, bishop, you perish.” For the bishops guilty of this conspiracy had been deposed. Einhard, *Annals*, year 818: “By synodal decree he ordered the deposed bishops to be handed over to monasteries.”]

so that you may again regain the rank that you lost.

I do not know, loving brother, what more I could write to you,

since these matters are no less fully known to you.

To me you are dearer than the great light of the sun;

I confess that the world contains nothing I love more than you.

[Note: [Col. 0345C] Matfrid, count and at that time a chief minister of the empire under Louis. Agobard’s letter, entitled “To the most excellent and most illustrious Matfrid,” is addressed to him; from it one can understand how great his authority and influence with the emperor were. How great his later treachery toward the emperor became was shown by the two conspiracies of the emperor’s sons—first Pippin’s and then Lothair’s—against their father, in both of which Matfrid is numbered by Thegan and others among the principal instigators.]

The letter repeatedly addresses Matfrid,

[Col. 0346B] and your words have often been read aloud to him.

He is able to apply the desired remedy to the fallen,

and to offer pious protection to the shipwrecked.

The mournful Muse, her song exhausted, scarcely resounds;

she has nothing more that she can say.

But I wondered why your letter hesitated

to entrust anything to me concerning your service.

For, believe me, I shall never refuse you any service,

but gladly do whatever you yourself command.

For that reason we have sent this messenger of ours to you,

so that he may report back to me whatever you command.

He is, as I believe, without doubt sufficiently faithful,

since you see my words running from his mouth.

He will recount to you without deceit whatever you ask,

[Col. 0346C] and will transact all our business on our behalf without fraud.

As many drops as the rain contains, as many fish as the rivers send forth,

as many leaves as every green wood bears,

as many grains as a threshing-floor usually contains in summer—

so many greetings I send you. Farewell always and everywhere, Father.

# BOOK FIVE

## I. CONSOLATION ON THE DEATH OF A CERTAIN BROTHER

[Col. 0345D]

If the beginnings of such great events were now being made anew,

a new practice would now have to be applied to them.

But since the path of so great a matter has long been well trodden,

the ancient way of our forebears must be followed in regard to it.

The world began from chaos with this varied order,

and by this same allotment it remains destined for completion.

But Adam, greatest inhabitant of the flower-bearing seat,

[Col. 0346D] bore the burden of this condition.

Although Abel was received as a sacrifice by the heavenly fires,

he endured the blows of his brother in dying.

Although harsh death marveled that Enoch had been taken from himself,

it was destined to reach him, though late.

Noah died, hope and second father of the world,

who lived illustriously amid the many waters.

Shem also, by a changed name, is the king whose name means “righteous”

[Note: [Col. 0345D] “A king righteous in name”: Melchizedek, whose name means “king of righteousness.” He speaks according to the opinion of those who held, with the Hebrews, that he was Shem himself, Noah’s son.]

[Col. 0347A]

[Note: [Col. 0347D] “The true offerer of sacrifice.” Because, offering bread and wine, he represented the offering of Christ and his table, at which we are nourished by his flesh and drink his blood under the figure of bread and wine. Inscription on the altar set up at Lyons by Agobard:

“This is Christ’s table; here heavenly food is received;

here the rose-colored liquid is drunk in the blood of the Lamb.

Christ’s people use this food; by wondrous order

the water washes, the blood redeems, the body nourishes.

Agobard, the bishop, brought forth this work with humble prayer

and duly consecrated and dedicated it to Christ,

where silver gleams in rivalry with radiant gold,

and cypress, painted with varied marble, gives off its fragrance. [Col. 0348D] And on the corporal cloth:

“For Christ’s guests the heavenly table is prepared;

here the living bread is received by divine gift;

here water mixed with the Lamb’s blood is also drunk;

thus water washes us, blood redeems us, and flesh feeds us.”]

and duly offered the true sacrifice.

Abraham died, having conquered the fires of Achaemenian conflagration,

the standard and glory of faith.

And holy Isaac, created from a barren mother,

was offered in a figure, O good King Christ, for you.

Nor did Jacob, worthy of the Lord’s wrestling,

escape death—he who became blessed through the help of his father and God.

And his noble offspring, the great assembly,

whose immense glory was righteous Joseph:

after the evils he endured, for which he repaid many good things,

he too closed his final day in death.

Lot, though he fled Sodom, could not flee death;

death devours even one safe from the sulfurous fires.

Moses died, than whom no other was more fit

to bear God’s law and enjoy his converse.

[Col. 0347B] And his priestly brother, clad in purple and gold,

whose holy forehead also bore a sacred burden;

or the sacred offspring of Nun, mighty beside the Jordan’s stream,

who apportions holy lands among the devout people.

This harsh fate was not unknown to the judges,

through whose action the people were freed from the enemy.

Nor was the eminent Samuel exempt from this tribute,

he who shone from childhood in doctrine, law, and faith.

David died, who felled Goliath in slaughter,

adorned with kingship, arms, and sacred songs,

and wise Solomon, builder of the holy sanctuary,

after immense honor, riches, and wealth.

Nor did the pious succession of former kings and prophets,

after scepters and the holy proclamations of God’s word,

escape.

The famous high priests, and Isaiah, greatest of the prophets,

[Col. 0347C] took this path after their holy oracles.

You, Josiah, endured the weapons of the Pharian king,

though, alas, you were suited to the worship of the Lord.

And although Elijah, carried upward, ascended to the heights,

death was delayed for him, not taken away.

Although a dead man rises from Elisha’s bones,

this dead man rises, while that dead man lies.

Jonah has a living tomb, so that he may not die;

but when he rises, he undergoes the death that he conquers.

The savage lions feared to touch each holy man;

the dark day of death does not fear to attack this one.

The boys of holy faith extinguished the furnace with fire,

but they cannot overcome the pyre of death.

Ezekiel dies after seeing the lordly seat,

and afterward sees many of God’s hidden mysteries.

[Col. 0347D] Esdras, retaining the right of priesthood with his blessed offspring,

rebuilds, adorns, and loves the temple.

And those who restore the walls of holy Jerusalem:

righteous Zerubbabel and devout Nehemiah.

[Col. 0348A] And those who weave the oracles of the nation to be restored:

the prophet Zechariah and holy Haggai.

Esther, and Mordecai, who overcame wicked Haman,

rescue the people of the Israelites.

Raphael rescues Tobit and his daughter-in-law from dreadful misfortunes,

yet not at all from the mouth of death.

Judith restrained the incestuous rages with her sword;

the unjust plague of death does not restrain you.

Zechariah and the old woman surpass eloquent laments;

but they do not overcome your blows, bitter death.

Nor is the heavenly man, the earthly angel, who readily prepares

the way for the Lord, free from this fate.

But what will you do, savage death—cruel, wicked, fierce toward others—

when you attack the author of life?

He who crushed you by his death, bent you down, and drove you away,

[Col. 0348B] and who, rising, opened the way of life;

he who plunged your author into the dark Tartarus,

having removed him from devout minds and communities.

Peter, revered prince of apostolic honor,

through whom, as key-bearer, the heavenly kingdoms stand open.

By your teaching, Paul, you live, penetrating the secrets of heaven;

great punishment, labor, and devotion adorn you.

John gives cups drawn from the Lord’s breast,

whom devout virginity and his love adorn.

The sublime and illustrious apostolic order shines,

with its learned companions and disciples.

And the distinguished company of martyrs glows with its lamp,

together with the confessing multitude and the virginal choir.

Although lofty souls, born from mortal stock,

they pay to you, hated death, the debt that is owed.

[Col. 0348C] It is difficult to recount the names of all

who are, who have been, and whom the Lord will grant to be.

Whatever their merit, none of them through the ages

remains free from this condition.

Finally, the great king David and holy prophet,

inspired by sacred song, sings thus:

“Is there any living human being whom you, worst of evils,

will not drag away, O death, and from whose sight you can be absent?

Or who will rescue his own soul from your deepest hands,

and be able to escape their savage grasp?”

This custom, from the beginning of chaos, has oppressed mortal offspring,

and, savage, subjected the world to its own law.

For the brother whose death we commemorate in song

has paid the debt of this condition.

## II. ON THE SEVEN CAPITAL VICES

[Note: [Col. 0348D] On the seven capital vices. We do not know what title the acephalous poem originally had; we have rashly supplied this one, both so that it would not be without a title and because it is not in fact remote from its subject. For it discusses these seven “disasters,” as he calls them.]

[Col. 0348D] ([Note: [Col. 0348D] Much is missing. This gap indicates the loss of one gathering, which did not reach us. [Col. 0349D] (*) Jacob Sirmond, the learned Jesuit priest who published the works of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, issued six books of his poems. In Book V, which concerns the seven capital vices, much is certainly missing at the beginning, a very large gap occurring there; but it can be partly filled by these verses, which seem to belong to that poem. Marten, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. V, p. 400.

“Whoever wishes to be good, whoever seeks an honorable life,

love purity of body and soul.

A clean house will be able to retain the pure Lord;

for it will always be safe with such a guest.

[Col. 0350C] The Almighty is seen by the blessed who are pure of heart,

[Col. 0350D] but the unclean have not deserved to see God.

Flee luxury if you wish to climb the heights,

for the luxurious man seeks the depths of hell.

Luxury has dragged many nobles down to the fire,

alas, and always draws the lowly to the depths.

Luxury utterly cuts away the sharpness of the senses,

infects the mind, wounds, and burdens it.

It lays bare the riches of the soul just as it does gold,

weakens strength, soils, and oppresses.

It always loves to plunge the wretched into pitchy flames,

always loves to subject its companions to demons.

Therefore, prudent one, beware the harmful weapons of lust—

namely, gluttony and the plague of drunkenness [the supplied musticeam is obscure; the rendering follows the surrounding references to wine and intoxication].

When drunkenness has filled the heavy belly of the drinker,

it draws him, in his luxury, to filthy jests.

It always loves laughter, always to wrinkle the face with guffaws;

the fat belly always loves luxury.

Do you seek the lofty kingdoms? Let the reins of the belly be controlled,

lest, running onward, you fall when the reins of the stomach are loosened.

Therefore, brother, if you wish to climb to the kingdoms of heaven,

love purity of body and soul.”]

In it, as I have learned, the first place was occupied by the well-known poem about the Phoenix,

“There is a place in the far East, blessed,” and so forth; thus one may henceforth be permitted to praise Theodulf as the author of a poem whose author was previously unknown.]

Much is missing.)

To prepare sacred offerings of a contrite heart for God.

[Col. 0349A] This sadness is strengthened by reason and held within this law;

it prepares great joys for holy minds.

“Blessed,” says the Lord and King, “are you who now weep,

for afterward an excellent laughter will be yours.”

The wise man said that the heart of the wise is in the place of sorrow,

but that of fools is in the place of joy.

Indeed the venerable Apostle says, “Be wretched,”

and let lamentation and weeping sit within your spirits.

“Let laughter receive mourning, and sorrow your joys”—

he earnestly gave these sacred teachings.

Who could describe on his own pages all the things

that the sacred page sings here and there about this matter?

The second mode is born from fury and confusion of mind,

and from harmful sluggishness possessing no reason.

It does not purify the spirit, but troubles it in an unjust whirlwind;

what it can trouble, it cannot cleanse.

Anxiety nourishes it, despair gives it birth,

and it feeds upon the stream of its own black milk.

The third, wicked mode arises as dreadful anger;

it can even generate passing harms.

When the mind is struck by desire or fear,

or is consumed by the blind fire of sluggishness,

it is usually so blinded by its own fury

that it does not know what to say or what to do.

There is also pain without disaster, sorrow without a name,

but inwardly it contains the clouded error of the heart.

Now sleep possesses it, now sluggish silences seize it;

it walks and snores, murmurs and is silent.

Here the sluggard dreams with open eyes,

[Col. 0349C] and, saying nothing, thinks he is saying many things.

Dull action, inert withdrawal, sluggish forgetfulness—

these are present, and he carries nothing fixed in mind or speech.

Like a ship on the sea without a helmsman, which flies toward no certain place

but wanders aimlessly over the waters,

so the mind, pressed by the sluggish darkness of sadness,

goes and returns across the sea of its own senses.

Frequent conversations with the brothers wear away this fault,

and constant prayer also drives it away.

Speech banishes it, and holy reading banishes it;

the dark cloud flees the clear radiance of this light.

The withered weariness of so great a vice will not endure

if it is driven away by the hand of these virtues.

As wax melts in fire and ice in the sun,

as a fire perishes in a stream,

so the weakened dangers of the disease of sluggishness

will waste away completely under the power that destroys them.

If reason enlivens, composes, and adorns the mind,

the monstrous forms of vices will soon take flight.

Our substance is dull in the limbs of the body;

it flourishes in reason, where the image of God is.

Furious anger follows, hot with foaming jaws,

and twists bloodshot eyes in dark gall.

Impious Bellona gave it a dreadful whip,

with which she stirs human minds into savage quarrels.

From here and there she supplies weapons to provoked companions,

with which they may destroy the bitter good of peace.

So that savage crime takes root and discord grows,

[Col. 0350B] and fraternal love is wickedly assailed.

Then food is given to bloodstained vices,

and every wickedness thrives with its legion.

The same band of virtues, when it comes, breaks apart,

and God’s holy commandments are made void.

They cannot settle in a mind unless it is pacified;

where black fury is present, they cannot exist at all.

The law sees the angry man, but he himself neglects to see it;

the law wishes to avenge, while he, blinded, wanders inert.

When anger comes, modesty, peace, and piety depart;

it hurls every good from the citadel of the mind.

As the black battles of winds stir the waves of the sea

and do not allow its elements to remain tranquil,

or as a peaceful grove is disturbed by Zephyr and Eurus,

the trees resound and the struck oaks fall,

[Col. 0350C] so treacherous anger moves human minds

and does not permit the unhappy heart to be at peace.

Its madness drives minds headlong

and does not allow them to retain their proper state.

It cuts off the senses, imitating the frenzies of the brain,

and maliciously prevents one from knowing what one does or says.

Hence envy covers the face; hence trembling shakes the limbs;

the eyes flash with a fire more savage than the Gorgon’s.

He roars with his mouth and strikes with his hands, rages in a great assault,

and cannot remember anything he has done.

He is joined, unsound of mind, to the Stygian dances of the Eumenides,

and to the savage maidens of Phlegethon,

far removed from the choirs of heaven, where, with Christ as prince,

[Col. 0351A] the glorious army receives rewards according to its merits.

There peace reigns in triumph, renowned love, and blessed order;

there the holy citadel gleams beneath the heavenly vaults.

There is also at times a zeal called provident anger,

when it is employed in support of what is right,

by which one steadfastly resists black vices,

and at whose prompting an evil thing is driven away.

It is evil to favor vices and resist what is worthy;

the angry man drives this away, while the sluggish man nourishes it.

Yet if the angry man wishes the person being corrected to become capable of amendment,

that anger remains light.

But if good things become burdensome and the worst things delight,

this is serious anger, and an exceedingly bitter matter.

It plunges into the muddy chasms of malicious hatred,

which leads wretched men to the depths of Styx.

[Col. 0351B] For anger is hatred when it grows old through long persistence,

and learns to go from evil to worse evil.

“You see,” says the Lord, “the splinter in your brother’s eye,

but you neglect to look at the beam in your own.”

Light anger is the splinter; hatred is the enormous beam.

The former quickly passes by; the latter, by delaying, grows heavy.

The one makes a slight sound; the other grows weighty in the silent heart.

The one desires blows; the other desires destruction.

Levity of spirit creates anger; it creates malicious hatred—

a thistle, first a plant, afterward a heavy thorn.

From a light word arises a grave and black crime,

just as a deadly basilisk comes from a smooth egg.

Thus, long nourished, the evil seeds of things do harm;

once torn out, they immediately cease to harm.

If there is love of the brothers, one does not proceed to savage anger;

[Col. 0351C] If this anger is absent, no hatred remains.

The honesty of reason, in an even-tempered spirit, moderates this vice;

love of what is just crushes its head.

And modest patience destroys this dreadful crime,

which is the protection of good and the ruin of evil.

The mother, nurse, and vigilant defense of the virtues,

it helps and cherishes these amid adversity.

It knows how to break the savage darts of vices

and to wear down their fearful weapons by its own weapons.

Faith is the shield, hope the breastplate, and love the helmet;

the sword of steel perishes when dashed against these.

The steel sword, ordinarily rebounding when dashed against these,

has its edge blunted and lies in savage fragments and tiny pieces.

The greater the blow, the greater the fracture appears,

and the broken pieces fly farther and more widely scattered.

[Col. 0351D] After humanity lost the joys of immortal life

and received the bitter plague of wretched death,

until it returns to the beginnings of its ancient life,

there is always labor on one side and fear on the other.

By this your nourishing patience renews our strength,

and by your weapons we are a protected company.

This glorious virtue granted comfort to all the saints,

and was a venerable city in which they might be safe.

The brevity of this poem forbids me to enumerate

those who patiently earned the riches of heaven.

Among them was Job, a most faithful companion of this virtue,

and that faithful power had clung to him as his companion.

Virtues flourished in him, together with abundance of possessions,

and he was renowned as powerful in every good thing.

[Col. 0352A] Blessed with children, a household, and a troop of livestock and servants,

and, more rightly than all these, with fear of God.

The envious enemy arms his darts against him at close quarters

and strikes the wall of his mind with a great engine.

In a moment, deprived and stripped of everything,

he ceased to be a master and ceased to be a father.

Prosperity fled him, and the gracious gifts of health fled;

there was nothing to bear or possess except disease.

Instead of servants, worms remained; instead of possessions, corruption;

instead of offspring, dung; instead of clothing, putrefaction.

From one side torments press him; from the other his wife’s mouth strikes him;

the wall [of his mind] receives the darts of his friends.

Mindful of the ancient sin, you thought through his wife’s mouth

that this man could be overcome as at first.

But reason helps him, and motherly patience helps him;

by these two his mind was well protected.

Prosperity had borne him as a righteous man, and adversity as a patient one;

from the former he builds up good things, from the latter destroys evil.

Reason provides him a helmet, patience a shield;

by these your furious anger is weakened.

This is followed by guilty pride, the mother of vices,

the queen of evil, the leader and origin of deceit.

Although it supplies nourishment to all vices,

since no human being can sin without it,

it nevertheless rises as a double, gaping thing,

and one thing has two forms with two heads.

The first remains as the openly disgraceful disease of pride;

the second is the empty crime of vainglorious praise.

Whether it is its sister, niece, or daughter,

one savage nature nevertheless belongs to both.

[Col. 0352C] Fourfold vain glory and boastfulness grows in you,

and with four blows you strike dark wounds.

There are some who possess a gift but do not acknowledge the giver;

they refuse to render due thanks to God.

There are others who invent for themselves the insignia of merits

and attribute their gifts to those merits rather than to God.

[The supplied word order, Atque illis tribuunt non sua dona Deo, is difficult; this rendering takes illis (“to those merits”) and non ... Deo (“not to God”) as the contrast.]

Still others neither possess a gift nor will be able to possess one,

but in their swollen hearts imagine that they do.

I think no boastfulness is greater in a human being than that of one who

believes himself alone to be able to do or to be something.

Hence the angel fell, because he thought that he alone possessed

power and radiance;

and, in exchange for the bright heaven, he purchased gloomy Avernus,

and, cast out, became wretched instead of angelic in honor.

Inflated pride is split into three parts,

[Col. 0352D] and thus the three-headed Cerberus devours with triple mouth.

First among these is transgression of the law,

for while someone despises it, he is rightly proud.

The law is abandoned whenever one resists it;

a person sins when he does what it forbids.

Therefore the law proclaims that it is the beginning of sin,

since no one can abandon what God has commanded without it.

Let the pious law therefore command what is to be done

and forbid what is foreign;

then every honorable work is far away.

Moreover, others desire to despise all their companions

and think that whatever they possess belongs to them alone.

This is the second of these: those whose keeping of the law

immediately makes their proud hearts swell.

From the place where they ought to be humble, they strive to be proud,

and purchase great evil with a good gift.

This Pharisaic practice is performed in the sacred vaulted chamber of the temple;

alas for me, many act in precisely this way.

As treasure remains safe when entrusted to a learned guardian,

so a humble mind preserves every good work.

The third part belongs to those whose conduct is inflated,

whom the swelling of an exalted mind lifts to the heights.

They disdain subjection to honorable authority

and strive to reject the words or deeds of their elders.

And because they refuse to be disciples of integrity,

they become a crowd that teaches error.

They cannot know what they do not know, because they think themselves capable of knowing it.

Thus their wandering mind deceives them as they rush downward.

For this is the one pattern common to all the proud:

[Col. 0353B] always to think themselves possessed of great worth.

Never to give assent to the speech of their brothers,

and to think that they speak better than everyone else;

to use their own senses and intelligence rather than anyone else’s,

and to reject the help of better counsel.

To bear false proclamations of praise for their own affairs,

and at the same time to despise another’s words or deeds.

Despising equals, inferiors, and superiors alike,

they think that neither they nor their own have anything communal.

They do nothing with calm reason; thus, taking crooked byways,

they abandon the straight road.

But God’s medicine excludes wicked diseases

and makes dutiful health return.

Therefore, while the mind fears being deprived of the light of virtues

and dreads being covered by the blackening cloud of vices,

[Col. 0353C] your disease, O boastfulness, is immediately driven away,

and vain glory does not smear the mind it has enticed.

Fear casts off diseased contagion and pestilence,

just as a harsh broom drives dirt from a house.

So the proud plague, fury, and vanity are repelled from you

by the example and love of the humble king,

and by fear of the angelic fall from the heavenly citadel,

from which the wretched one fell headlong with swelling heart.

He, speaking proudly, was plunged from heaven into Tartarus;

he is a dreadful demon who had previously been an angel.

But the humble Lord, coming from the citadel of heaven,

joins earthly ranks to the heavenly citizens.

Let that dark fall therefore terrify the human race,

and let the ascent of the redeeming Lord bring comfort.

The lofty human mind falls, and, cast down, rises again;

the more closely joined to earth, the more closely joined to heaven.

In descending it rises; in climbing it suffers downfall;

everything proceeds by numbers and advances according to its stages.

All things must be dispensed according to heavenly judgment,

which weighs down the proud and raises the humble.

Muse, who have wandered briefly through the meadows of vices,

bring your step to a halt at the end of this slight little book.

These seven disasters had devastated the whole world,

and through them the conqueror had ruled the entire world.

Through these vices the savage enemy held the human race captive

and had subjected it to himself by these weapons.

As that disgraceful one first struck the parent,

so he turns his weapons against his entire offspring.

[Col. 0354A] And by the weapons with which he subjected him in his guilty mind,

he savagely strives to subject his descendants to himself.

For there is voracious gluttony, followed by shameful adultery,

fraud and avarice, or the crime of envy;

then sluggish sadness, and the disease of furious anger,

and afterward the proud plague, leader of them all.

But God has set weapons opposed to these phantoms,

so that their work may be wisely annulled.

Thus the wise physician applies weapons contrary to diseases,

weapons from the opposite direction, so that nourishing health may be given:

combining cold with hot, moist with dry,

soft with hard, and rough with smooth.

Holy fasts overcome the foul gluttony of the belly,

which afflicts, constrains, and drives mortal humanity.

[Col. 0354B] Virgin chastity, adorned with beautiful dignity,

extinguishes your flames, dreadful lust.

The fortunate practice of giving conquers avarice,

when a generous right hand performs the work of piety.

Love of the Lord and of the brothers overcomes envy,

and by their action all its work wastes away.

Brotherly conversation and the practice of prayer,

or holy reading, drive away sluggish sadness.

Secure, gentle patience breaks savage anger

and wears down its cruel darts.

Inflated pride is broken by Christ’s examples;

fear of punishment and nourishing love dissolve it.

Thus this physician often heals by opposites

and often brings the aid of salvation from contrary things.

Often, too, his nourishing hand is accustomed

to apply healing to these wounds through similar things.

He gives long things to long things, and applies rounded

plasters to rounded wounds, fitting them to the measure of the injury.

Death entered through wood, and glorious life returned through wood;

one was brought about by the taste, the other by the exalted honor of the cross.

The old virgin brought death; the new virgin brought salvation—

the one by persuading the man, the other by giving birth to God.

The ancient woman brought death to the man, but the new woman

announces to her devout disciples that Christ lives.

Through the speaking serpent the disease enters; when it hangs, it wastes away—

the scaly serpent brings about the one, the bronze serpent the other.

Food gave death, and food also grants life:

then guilty Eve gave it; now, powerful Christ, you give it.

The staff departs into a serpent and returns from there to staff-like limbs;

[Col. 0354D] Christ goes into death and returns alive from it.

The staff signifies power, and the water-serpent death;

hence these things rightly succeed one another.

It divides the ground, or accomplishes dreadful signs—

the staff that you hold, illustrious Moses, in the figure of the law.

And it is fitting that a serpent should be able to bear the image of death,

since through it accursed death entered.

Muse, who have wandered briefly through the meadows of vices,

the time has come—bring your step to a halt at this end.

## III. EXHORTATION TO BISHOPS

[Note: [Col. 0353D] The fourth little book. Theodulf had divided this part of his work into four little books, the contents of each of which he now explains at the beginning of the fourth. Of these, the first two are missing, together with part of the third. I think that the second part of the third is the section on the conflict of the vices that immediately preceded this. Since, moreover, in the old manuscript there was nowhere any division into separate books in the rest of the work, we have arranged all the poems into six books. We also supplied from our own resources the title that this little work lacked.]

Having completed three little books, now proceed to the fourth,

and follow the order of the brothers, which summons you onward.

He who gives speech to the mute and steps to the lame,

he who has brought them help—may he grant you aid.

A general doctrine had to be poured out for all of them,

but this work will now be special to you.

The first contains certain teachings of the holy faith

and matters by which its devout summit is known.

The second briefly sings how it ought to be held,

and what places are prepared for the reprobate and what for the devout.

The third teaches that a dreadful war must be waged against the hostile people,

and arms its companions with whatever aid it can.

The foundation of faith and the healthy increase of the structure—

these together establish devout laws in their proper place.

They resist vices, arm the citizens with virtues,

and order the city with soldiers, law, and faith.

Call the priests themselves to our walls,

[Col. 0355B] and let care for their devout service be yours.

Remember first to prostrate yourself at their knees,

and then, bowing low, ask that you may be blessed.

When you have been received by holy hands and into holy laps,

prepare to offer kisses to their mouths and necks.

When they have given kisses, receive their kisses humbly nevertheless,

and, of course, announce that you are about to speak.

But when permission to speak has been granted to you,

excuse your author as fully as you can.

Say that I have not rashly undertaken this matter,

nor has a presumptuous mind forced me to this task.

I do not set myself, a teacher, above the holy bishops,

whose life is for me a standard of salvation.

But although I am a small part of the great Levitical company,

[Note: [Col. 0356D] “In the Levitical throng.” He indicates that, when he wrote this, he was merely a deacon or a cleric of a lower rank. For that reason he excuses himself for daring to admonish bishops concerning their duty.]

I am pleased to help the fathers as best I can.

And because I wish, am accustomed, or am obliged by a devout vow

to serve them humbly and gladly favor them,

we take care that the seat should rise properly from the ground,

and that its cushion should be sufficiently suitable to the father’s needs.

We see that linen garments suitably cover the legs and feet,

and that the graceful *campagus* be placed over them.

We strive to pour water over their hands and bring towels;

we provide a long hem for the tunics.

So that the white dalmatic may shine with its extended folds,

and so that its light fringe may not hang untidily.

So that the cloaks may be arranged and the *chlamys* itself hang properly,

and an attendant hand carefully accompany the head.

It is also a task for the fingers to remove whatever dirt there may be

and to polish the father’s soles and entire body.

If wax or olive oil flows down from a lit lamp,

[Col. 0355D] it is likewise wiped away with the fingers from the clothing.

If sweat occupies the face, we wipe it;

if dust is on the garments, it must be shaken out.

To drive away the cold, we spread cloaks beneath the feet;

the breeze drives away the heat of the false blast.

“The blind cannot lead the blind,” says the Lord;

both will fall together into a pit.

Both the wicked and the unlearned must be reproved:

the first because he does what is unjust, the second because he keeps silent about what is holy.

[Col. 0356A] One ruler is accustomed to be bound by both feet,

if he is rightly to be called a ruler:

he who harms by his example and does not help by the art of teaching,

by which neither his own mind nor another’s can be governed.

The holy Isaiah condemns unlearned rulers in these words,

singing the sacred words of the Lord:

“The shepherds themselves do not know you, O wisdom,

but the assembly of watchmen is deprived of light.

Blind ignorance heavily oppresses them all,

and the pack of barking dogs lacks strength.

Alas for the crime, alas for the great wickedness,

when the one who ought to be a standard of salvation becomes the path and leader of evil.

By his example, how many have perished!

For all of them, I think, he himself will pay the punishments.

He is guiltier than a thief, guiltier than a savage robber,

[Col. 0356B] because he himself harms minds more than possessions.

The one steals external riches; the other lays waste the inner ones,

for who could deny that the soul is superior to the flesh?”

There is also one who teaches what is right but, by doing what is wrong,

destroys by his action what he builds by the work of his mouth.

In his madness he wounds himself by his perverse conduct,

while with his mouth he strikes the evil deeds that he himself commits.

He benefits others but refuses to benefit himself,

and, living for others, is himself dead to himself.

He advises others to be something, but becomes senseless himself;

he is wax for others, but becomes ash for himself.

There is also that serious form in which no one can rightly drive away disgrace,

so long as he himself commits disgraceful acts.

By what method, I ask, can a filthy person wipe away filth,

when deep sleep holds the one who is supposed to awaken others?

Or what face, lying down, will strive to lift up those who lie down,

or seek to heal wounds while bearing a wound himself?

A bishop ceases to restrain the people from gluttony

if he himself lies weighed down by food.

He does not forbid wine if he guzzles it himself;

drunk, he will not proclaim the people sober.

He does not advise the vices to be despised when he himself is burdened by them,

and, lacking virtues, he does not set out the road to them.

His voice cannot wear away avarice

when he is bound by the hooked hand of that plague.

He cannot loosen the biting knots of hatred

when his mind bears the monstrous horrors of hatred.

He cannot establish the people in tranquil peace

when he himself is bound to the people by no peace.

By what weapons will he be able to break the goads of anger,

[Col. 0356D] when anger has made him its lurid prey?

Or can the one over whom empty pride blows like a hollow wind

sit still, if he goes about swollen by its blasts?

How will he be able to urge contempt for the world?

Unless he despises this, he who admonishes is himself despised.

The favor of human beings has taught him to flatter the powerful;

when will such a man proclaim that judges must observe justice?

Or will he say that the wretched are to be protected by the law of mercy,

if he oppresses them in every way he can?

[Col. 0357A] The boastfulness that hangs from an airy rope lifts him,

and ambitious corruption carries him into worse things.

He does not restrain the boaster who boasts of living boastfully,

nor will he say to anyone, “Be free from ambition.”

By what right will this man proclaim the great judgment to be feared—

alas for me—if perhaps he himself does not fear it?

His tongue is restrained by the curb of his own deeds;

he keeps silent about the faults of others lest he bring them to his own ears.

He does not urge the good things that perhaps he has not performed,

and does not forbid the evils that he himself, wretched man, commits.

I do not, while writing of the lives of wicked bishops,
Either you yourself are an adornment to the devout, or my Muse is one for you.

Nor do I burn beautiful lilies with rough nettles,  
nor do your harsh buckthorns destroy the crops amid the bushes.

In soft meadows soft things are mingled with hard,  
[Col. 0357B] when the field bears harmful seeds among the shining ones.

A garden fragrant with the most aromatic herbs  
often bears the stench of your hemlock.

For who could deny—or, doubting, refuse to confess—that  
bad things mixed with good, and good with wicked, pass through the ages?

For the master orders the pure crop, once the corrupt seed has been uprooted,  
to grow until the appointed season.

Kids remain in Christ’s fold together with gentle lambs,  
and the right hand awaits the devout, the left the guilty.

The mystical third catch contained fish mingled together:  
the good portion, selected, thrives; the bad, cast away, perishes.

Since the field, the fold, and the nets belong to the Church,  
why should this poetic work not possess them as well?

Or why should it not strive to depict the character of many,  
as it prepares to cleanse the character of all?

[Col. 0357C] Her distinguished garment shone with light,  
and it offered its allure to the eyes of men.

But may the ornaments of the virtues give you beauty,  
and may you continually favor them with the eyes of your heart, as far as you can.

She possessed powerful reverence in sacred worship,  
and distinction in the vesture of pontifical office.

Holy reverence is yours toward your holy mother,  
and toward the pursuits and deeds of a devout life.

A golden plate encircled the pontiff’s forehead,  
on which a twice-twelve-pointed diadem bore the Lord’s name.

But let the forehead of your mind be encircled with kindly thoughts,  
and let your voice thunder forth Christ from an evangelical mouth.

May the deeds of faith, uprightness, and justice be manifest,  
so that this may be the order of four virtues for you.

For these closely observe the deeds of all,  
[Col. 0357D] as a prudent shepherd is accustomed to do with his own fold.

Thus they love the good and rightly acknowledge them as worthy of love,  
and call those whom they have thus strengthened toward better things.

But those whom the immense weight of vice restrains,  
they raise up by whatever means they can.

And if they cannot lift some from the burden of their vices,  
they take upon themselves the task of carrying them by enduring them.

Who would not say that the life or patience of these people bears fruit,  
when they undertake to correct some and tolerate others?

This is a blessed company—oh, how far it differs from that one  
which greedily pursues its own profits rather than the Lord’s!

It refuses to be useful and strives only to preside;  
it sleeps at the former task and remains wakeful at the latter.

The sins of the people never grievously trouble it,  
[Col. 0358A] nor do good deeds performed by its people make it rejoice.

It laments its own concerns,  
though it never deems itself blessed by troubling over the crimes of the wicked.

It gapes so as to become richer, for it refuses to become holier;  
it receives the gifts of military service but flees the weapons.

For it likes not work but wealth, not burden but honor;  
cutting away what is well joined, it keeps this and casts away that.

Those who seek only their own advantage rather than that of the people  
wish to be called shepherds, but do not wish to be shepherds.

Nor do they concern themselves with feeding or protecting the flock;  
they attend only to whatever can be seized from it.

If the excellent prophet does not sing these things falsely,  
since he now sounds them forth in divine words:

Alas for the wicked shepherds of the Israelites,  
[Col. 0358B] who provide many pastures for themselves, but none for the flock.

For milk supplied food for you,  
and wool, stripped from the fleece, was clothing.

If anything was fat, the ravenous crowd devoured it,  
and it was no labor for you to strengthen the weak.

You supplied no remedies to the sick flock,  
and your hand disdained to bind up what was broken.

No one took care to bring back the banished to the fold,  
nor did you trouble yourselves to seek the lost.

Instead you imposed harsh commands by malignant authority,  
and you were a fierce or powerful multitude toward them.

Therefore the flocks of my bleating sheep are scattered,  
not because there was any shepherd to feed them.

The hostile fury of beasts devours them,  
and they become prey for the monsters carried across the fields of the world.

[Col. 0358C] They have not yet laid down the dreadful burden of their vices,  
though they have sought a place of high distinction.

They cannot go before their subjects on the path of holy life,  
for those subjects do not know this way well.

By what manner, I ask, can one be a guide to his companions  
who does not even know the road he is to follow?

If it is hot, we seek shade; if cold, fire;  
and in whatever definite way I can help, I will help.

Who would forbid the teacher to be adorned inwardly with words,  
when our hand is accustomed to adorn him outwardly?

Why should I not prepare to apply purity of life,  
when I cannot tolerate dirt even on a garment?

Why should I not desire the benefits of eternal life,  
when I now prepare, as far as I can, so many benefits?

The people ought wholly to submit themselves to this Church,  
[Col. 0358D] which remains worthy of praise throughout all ages.

She is its honor and splendor, its founder and its nurturer,  
the names of the great men after the twelve.

She is the firmest order of columns in Christ,  
fixed, upon which the diligent company rightly rests.

Her starry dwelling’s radiant gate—  
through it whoever longs for Christ enters rejoicing.

Those entrusted with governing souls  
bear the great burdens allotted to the people.

They offer fervent prayers for the people’s sin,  
and lament the evils mingled with their own.

They turn away the wrath of the immeasurable Judge from the people,  
as Moses, together with his brother, once performed this work.

That choir is the herald of the Lord’s will,  
[Col. 0359A] under whose leadership the believing people climb to the heights of heaven.

Defender of truth, enemy of perverse doctrine:  
this he summons and retains; that he drives away and banishes.

The people fear that the consciousness of their wickedness may be seen,  
but perceive that good things, sweeter than honey, are present in him.

He is the protector of the oppressed people and their kindly avenger;  
the entire Catholic assembly calls him father.

They promise the lofty rewards of the light-filled kingdom,  
where the angelic choir and the devout company of the fathers dwell.

That kingdom receives the holy soldier who toils in arms  
and flies victorious from the dreadful enemy to the stars.

While they offer devout evidence of good works,  
they are a holy model and adornment for God’s people.

This is the ministering company which, with kindly keys,  
both shuts and opens, binds and looses.

[Col. 0359B] Through whose dispensing of the sacred things of the supreme King,  
the dutiful company shines upon its appointed steps.

Ambition did not raise them, but the glory of their life,  
to the higher places of the lofty steps.

No wing of human favor lifted them up,  
but your gift, kindly God, bore them to the heights.

They never applaud themselves from the summit of their primacy;  
their mind is humble and devout.

Accepted honor does not inflate them with empty breath,  
but the lordly burden imposed upon them weighs them down.

Their minds hold not primacy but a burden,  
and consider not how lofty the honor is, but how heavy the load.

Thus a horse adorned with trappings and proud bosses  
groans while its rider applies the spur.

If the true matter is made manifest and simulation is absent,  
[Col. 0359C] he who rightly gives himself to follow also often brings help.

[Col. 0360A] For the Redeemer commanded that your works be observed,  
so that those who see them may glorify your Father who is above the stars.

Therefore a shining mitre covered his head;  
may justice and piety also cover your mind.

The head is the citadel of the body, the mind of the soul;  
if the latter clings to the love of its Creator, what greater thing does a human being possess?

In it the image of divine goodness is expressed,  
if it remains well joined to holy conduct.

Certainly one may take an example from small things:  
if a ring presses an image into wax for you.

Let doctrine be your hidden treasure of beautiful weight,  
which the belt of limited authority properly fits.

If too many things are disclosed to untrained minds, they do harm;  
more things, unless spoken in their proper order, cause injury.

[Col. 0360B] Thus foods benefit some and harm others;  
each has its time and order, and each its proper place.

Let circumspection gird the tunic of doctrine for you;  
let this multicolored garment of the virtues lie above the ephod.

Let the kindly cloak be pure, shunning every stain,  
and let it be varied with the other good qualities of the virtues.

For the most holy hero David prays that priests  
may possess devout garments of righteousness.

### IV. THAT GOD IS NOT TO BE SOUGHT IN A PLACE, BUT TO BE WORSHIPED IN PIETY

It is not so much going to Rome that is beneficial as living well,  
whether in Rome or wherever a human life is lived.

I believe that it is not the road of the feet but of character that leads to the stars;  
God, from his citadel, observes what each person does everywhere.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0359]

### I. ON THE GRACE OF GOD

[Note: [Col. 0359D] “Such is the goodness of God.” An uncertain but ancient author expressed the same thought, not inelegantly, addressing God in these rhythms:

“From what is yours we serve you, your own little servants;  
from what is yours we are strong, and from what is yours we are fervent;  
we bear the burden of the day and no small heat.

You give us everything here, Father and householder.  
You call us to labor, you urge us to desire to go,  
and at the same time you inspire the ability and renew our strength there.

And when you do these things for us, afterward you reward us in such a way  
that it seems as though both the will and the ability  
to bear every hardship had come from us.

Shall we remain silent about such great grace of God, unworthy as we are,  
seeking our own unhappy glory rather than yours?  
Shall we not proclaim this mercy to all?”]

Such is the goodness of God: it instructs and adorns us, though fragile,  
so that from what is his own he may accomplish our merits.

And the good things without which nothing good is done,  
and which his grace brings about, are to be reckoned among our good deeds.

The devout One gives the will to do good and also grants its accomplishment;  
his work precedes us here and follows us there.

[Col. 0359D] Hence it happens that both the beginning and the completion are given,  
and thus the sacrifice is pleasing to God in head and tail alike.

And, in his mercy, he grants rewards for our own good deeds,  
if our effort is rightly in harmony with his.

### II. ON THOSE WHO RETAIN ONE THING IN THEIR HEART AND UTTER ANOTHER WITH THEIR MOUTH

Nor does the wicked heed what the renowned prophet prays,  
when he wishes to be rescued from such people:

“Do not join me,” he says, “with the sinner in their tumult,  
nor destroy me with those who always do evil.”

Their neighbor hears their peaceful words,  
but within their hearts many savage things lie hidden.

“Give them, O God, the just return for their works,  
and according to the dreadful evil of their own invention.

Give them what is fitting for the deeds of their hands;  
grant them, I pray, recompense according to their deserts.

Since they have not understood the work of the Lord, nor his devout deeds,  
destroy them, and do not build them up.”

The illustrious ordinance of blessed law commands this,  
when its terrible voice thunders such words:

“Let there not be for you a double measure or an unjust weight;  
let there be simplicity in your mind, and let your mouth speak what is right.”

Let your bushel be just and your sextarius fair,  
so that no deception may take possession of us.”

[Col. 0361A] The heavenly-throned One always detests double deceit;  
he loves a straight heart and a simple, impartial judge.

### III. WHAT FASTING AND WHAT FRUGALITY ARE ACCEPTABLE TO GOD AND ABLE TO OBTAIN WHAT IS REQUESTED

For by means of the holy fast proclaimed through the distinguished prophet,  
God the King himself declares what is acceptable to him:

“Loose the bonds,” he says, “of wicked impiety;  
undo the bundles that so often oppress unjustly.

See that the one who was previously bound goes free;  
let every burden be completely broken for you.

Do not refuse to break your bread for the hungry;  
bring the homeless and needy into your house.

Clothe the naked, and do not despise your own flesh,  
since you are of the same condition.”

[Col. 0361B] “Then your light will break forth like the dawn,  
and your salvation will quickly arise.

The devout judgments of the Thunderer will go before your face,  
and the holy glory of God will gather you to itself.

Then, when you call, the mercy of your kindly Lord will hear you;  
he himself will say to you, ‘Here I am.’” [Note: [Col. 0361D] Isa. 58:6ff.]

### IV. AGAINST SIMULATORS AND DECEIVERS

You firmly practice none of these things, yet you pretend to practice them all,  
you simulator who possess only imitations of goodness.

The wicked person who certainly does evil, or maliciously pretends to do good,  
hates what he loves and loves what God hates.

The wise king says that the things God hates are finally six,  
and that there is a seventh which his soul detests:

Lofty eyes, a lying tongue,  
and hands from which the blood of the innocent flows;

a heart that frequently entertains wicked thoughts,  
and swift feet that walk toward every evil;

a false witness uttering savage lies,  
and one who sows dreadful quarrels among brothers. [Note: [Col. 0362D] Prov. 6:16ff.]
