The wicked, mad person has done, does, and will do all these evils;  
his mind is continually filled with shameful wrongdoing.

### V. THAT THE GREEDY PERSON CANNOT BE SATISFIED BY AMASSING VARIOUS WEALTHS

Whatever the world, filled with diverse nations, possesses,  
would not suffice for him if all of it were his own.

His greed will always have an open abyss for receiving,  
nor can the foul chasms of Styx be filled.

Whatever Chryse and Argyre possess, and whatever the world of Taprobane,  
whose wealth is said to be exalted;

whatever India has—gems, spices, and ivory monsters—  
and the land of Ophir, rich in refined gold;

let Assyria come full of fragrant amomum,  
and Persia itself bring its riches;

let the Sabaean, almost neighboring in his incense, come,  
and let Arabia of Eudaemon bring its gifts.

Let Bagata come laden with Agarene treasures,  
the city that once stood high in Achaemenian lands.

Whatever the Tigris and Euphrates possess, and the Jordan himself,  
and whatever the blessed Palestinian soil produces;

[Col. 0362A] whatever beautiful Bactra possesses, and worthy Hyrcania,  
and whatever the Bosphorean mountain ranges, well ruled by the plow, contain;

whatever the Seric Ocean carries, and the Caspian kingdoms,  
and whatever the Seres, rich in their own fleece, possess;

whatever the cruel Scythian, the savage Ceta, and the harsh Sarmatian possess;  
whatever is yours, Hydaspes, whatever is yours, Araxes;

whatever the fierce Gelonian and Thracian Hebrus possess,  
and the fields forever wrapped in Riphaean frost;

whatever the Hyperborean people, fixed beneath the axis of the Wain, possess,  
or the Tanais, or Pontus and the Ister;

whatever the long-haired Dane and the fair-haired Suebe prize,  
and every people that lies beneath the farthest North;

whatever the Moesian, Dacian, Thracian, Attic, and Arcadian possess,  
and whatever thrives in your city, Constantine;

whatever wise Greece possesses, whatever strong Germany produces,  
whatever misshapen Abar and Pannonian Gipes possess;

whatever the illustrious city of Jerusalem, long promised to blessed fathers,  
the holy city of God, possesses;

whatever the people scorched by Pelusian vapors possess,  
whatever the black Troglodyte and the people of Meroe possess;

if the discolored whole multitude of Ethiopians should give all its goods,  
and every people that lies beneath the sign of Cancer;

whatever the nomadic peoples possess, and whatever your kingdoms, Jugurtha, possess,  
and whatever cuts through the Syrtes and traverses the African fields;

whatever the Libyan world or the land of Mauretania possesses,  
whatever belongs to the place of Antaeus and to the gardens of the Hesperides;

whatever the Galaurians, fortunate in their fields, offer,  
whose island produces manifold riches;

whatever the fiery region of the Atlantic Moors provides,  
and whatever people there may be who knows your source, Nile;

whatever Latium possesses, whatever fertile Calabria possesses,  
and the fields and pleasant lands of the Veneti, Ligurians, and Po;

and your city, once the city of demons, now devoted to Christ—  
whatever the rejoicing capital of the world and the devout mother possesses;

she who despises the shades stained with fraternal blood,  
seeks the heavenly kingdoms, and flees profane shrines;

she does not worship the winged she-wolf, but the one born of a virgin,  
and stands renowned, fixed in apostolic strength;

whatever wealthy Gaul possesses, whatever beautiful Spain produces,  
and whatever fertile Córdoba possesses;

whatever the Briton possesses, and whatever Scotland’s Ireland produces,  
and whatever useful thing the farthest Thule may bring;

and whatever the most powerful Astur brings with his native goods,  
he who is the glory of the Hesperides and vigorous in arms;

if the rich cultivator of Gallic soil should come,  
who surpasses his neighbors in beautiful possessions—

if all these things were heaped together and given to him at once,  
his greedy hand would not thereby be richer.

### VI. THAT PROSPERITY OFTEN BELONGS TO THE WICKED

David, praying, says: “Rescue me from many waters  
and from the foreign hand, whose offspring is bitter;

whose mouths stand in empty, frenzied speech,  
and whose right hand is a right hand of wickedness;

whose sons flourish like a new planting,  
nurtured from the first day of their tender age;

whose daughters, everywhere arranged and adorned,  
are like the courtly form of God’s splendid temple.”

Their storerooms overflow into one another, full,  
and their pantry exults in abundant wine.

Their sheep return bearing many young,  
and their bodies are exceedingly fat like cattle.

No breach in the wall displays any sign of ruin,  
nor does any outcry at their going forth trouble their affairs.

These are the people whom many have called blessed:  
‘Happy is the people whose Lord is their God.’” [Note: [Col. 0363D] Ps. 143:7ff.]

### VII. THE SAME SUBJECT IN JEREMIAH

Jeremiah rejoices that he addressed the Thunderer in these prayers  
and uttered such words concerning this matter:

“Why is the way of sinners prosperous, most righteous ruler?  
Why do all who do every evil prosper?

Planted by you, they grow green from a beautiful root;  
they advance and bring forth their fruits.

You are near their mouth in their feigned speech,  
but far away from the inner citadel of their mind.

And you, supreme God, to whom all things are open,  
know them well and see them well.

Gather them together for yourself as a flock for sacrifice,  
sanctifying them justly at the time of death.” [Note: [Col. 0363D] Jer. 12:1ff.]

### VIII. THE SAME SUBJECT IN JOB

Job, your soldier of patience, sings in the same way,  
and presents this matter in his own poem:

“Why, then, does the faction of the wicked live in exaltation?  
Why are they strengthened by your riches?

Their offspring remains before them in all its wickedness,  
and a crowd of relatives surrounds them on every side.

They preside over secure and peaceful houses,  
and your rod, O God, is not over them.

Their ox breeds, and suffers no harmful miscarriage;  
their cow is not deprived of her young.

Their little flock advances in the measure of the herds,  
exulting in various games and amusements.

They hold tambourines in their hands and sounding lyres,  
and the music of instruments provides them joy.

They pass the days of their life amid many good things,  
but in a moment they go to the foul chasms of Styx.” [Note: [Col. 0364D] Job 21:7ff.]

### IX. THAT THE LORD IS TO BE IMITATED BY US AND LOVED AND FEARED WITH ALL OUR HEART

For the one who imitates him in piety or благeful deeds  
imitates the one who is both our Lord and our благeful Father.

His mercy is boundless and his clemency sweet;  
he is always accustomed to be present to worthy prayers.

He not only grants forgiveness of sins, but also rewards  
those who turn back, kindly and always loving to spare.

If the renowned God is our Father and Lord,  
his piety, conduct, and character in faith must be followed.

A child will learn to love his father and fear the infernal realms;  
let love join him to the one, and fear to the other, toward better things.

[Col. 0364A] If a child is degenerate or a proud servant,  
he horribly disgraces both with immense shame.

### X. ON THE STUPIDITY OF SIMULATORS AND FOOLS, WHO DO NOT KNOW HOW TO BE TURNED FROM THEIR WICKEDNESS BY GOOD EXHORTATION

Salt does not preserve one, nor wisdom the other;  
instruction cannot overcome this person, nor salt him.

It is useless to apply instruction to his innermost nature;  
the more you teach him, the more foolish he becomes.

It is like someone trying to wash an unbaked brick:  
the more he washes it, the more mud he makes.

What do good words accomplish where there is no благeful will?  
Or what good do seeds cast among nettles accomplish?

What good is yellow honey when poured into dreadful pits?  
What does a shore or oil mixed with dung accomplish?

[Col. 0364B] What good does a lyre accomplish if it plays for an ass with long ears,  
or a trumpet if it rings skillfully for a horned ox?

As much as your sight thrives when the sun rises, though you are blind,  
so much does his understanding usually benefit after good words.

Songs can accomplish many things, though not everything;  
even pagan literature sings this too.

The renowned Circe is said to have changed  
the companions of Ulysses into various beasts by the art of song.

Though many things can be done, they will not be able to heal the itch,  
nor will a moth become healthy through their murmuring.

Yet just as those things benefit nothing when a hernia remains,  
and when it appears the entire operation is wasted,

so the work will be wasted for you, wicked simulator,  
if you try to insinuate some good.

Finally, since the wise king has said many things about this,  
I would like to offer this one example:

If a fool is beaten in a mortar until he is bruised like meal,  
his stupidity will not leave him. [Note: [Col. 0364D] Prov. 27:22.]

I have set down the words of the leader; I will now set down what the rustic people  
often say, speaking aptly of such a person:

“You cannot make this happen by habit or by beating,  
so that an owl will ever become a hawk that seizes cranes with its talons.

Nor can you make a vulture perform your office,  
for it is sluggish, greedy, and heavy in flight.”

He desires to learn no good things, but wishes to learn every evil.  
Do you want to know why he does this? He is a fool.

This man, worse than Judas, wishes to appear better than you, Peter;  
his pretence conceals many evils beneath its cloak.

He considers small good things great and many evils nothing;  
the wretch deceives himself when he wishes to deceive others.

### XI. WHY THE SCARS THAT THE LORD RECEIVED IN HIS PASSION WERE NOT COVERED OVER IN THE RESURRECTION

For the Lord’s scars, inflicted for humanity,  
will be a cause of honor for the holy martyrs.

Thus the Savior returns from the Phlegethontic shades  
bearing the marks on his foot, side, and hands.

This is not because he was unable to cover all the wounds,  
as foolish pagan error often dreams,

for he who was able to conquer every danger of death  
retained them because his deeds were filled with holy purposes.

[Col. 0365A] These four celebrated reasons convey mysteries:  
the author of life possesses the marks of death.

First, so that the disciples might know that they had seen a body,  
not a breath of spirit, and might lodge this knowledge in the citadel of their hearts;

so that certain faith in the risen Lord might adorn them,  
and through the long ages they might proclaim the hope of resurrection.

Next, so that, by praying in the human condition he assumed for us,  
he might show the Father in himself our wounds—

the sufferings he endured as a human being for the human race—  
and might mercifully display them continually in his service.

He calls to remembrance him whom forgetfulness never holds,  
so that, acting kindly, he may always have mercy.

He urgently reminds him to remember humankind for ever  
and always to desire mercy with kindly love,

since the only-begotten Son shares their nature  
and for them was willing to suffer such great wounds.

Third, so that the elect may never cease to render  
the work of praise while they behold the marks of your Passion.

Seeing in his dark scourges their salvation,  
their courses, once toward Styx, turn toward the stars;

through his death their life is made glorious in every respect,  
and golden crowns are granted to them for the sake of the thorns.

Fourth, so that at the final time, seeing him,  
the faction of the reprobate may grieve, crushed by heavy sorrow.

As Scripture sings, “They will see the one whom they pierced.” [Note: [Col. 0365D] John 19:37.]

And another passage of Scripture says again:

“Every eye will see him, and the people who pierced him;  
every tribe on earth will mourn over him.” [Note: [Col. 0365D] Matt. 24:30.]

And they will recognize that they are to be condemned by a just judgment  
and to suffer fiery scourges for their deeds.

Those hands will not be saved that the wicked crowd laid upon the Lord,  
nor those that wish to disregard what was commanded,

whether pressing down upon what they had undertaken,  
or refusing to undertake it,  
or looking furiously upon those whom they ought to retain.

O cruel wickedness of humanity, O mad insanity,  
O monstrous fury, O utterly childish evil!

Whether God is not worshiped, or whether he is worshiped,  
this is not unpunished, because it is a great crime.

### XII. ON FAITH, HOPE, AND CHARITY

At last blessed faith, hope, and concord  
jointly hold the kingdom in the minds of the people.

These are the ancient foundations that God laid for the Church,  
so that the structure of heaven might rightly rise.

Faith gives us to him, hope carries us, and renowned love unites us;  
this threefold good arouses, prepares, and directs us.

By these our minds possess strength, are invigorated, and nourished;  
we ask for and receive them when God the Father gives them.

“Surely,” says the Lord, “when one asks his father for welcome gifts,  
will anyone receive insults instead?

Will anyone, by giving the hardness of a stone instead of bread,  
satisfy the petitioner’s request?” [Note: [Col. 0366D] Luke 11:11.]

For bread signifies the love of God and of the brothers;  
whoever lacks it carries a heart of stone.

Will he give a winding snake instead of a fish,  
when the fish nourishes but that wicked creature kills?

[Col. 0366A] The fish signifies faith, which grows in rushing waters  
and shines joyfully amid the whirlwind of storms.

Unbelief is opposed to it, like a savage serpent;  
the tongue of faithlessness strikes and kills.

Or if he asks for an egg, will he be given a scorpion,  
which strikes with the hooked sword of its tail or threatens savagely?

For devout gifts are symbolized by the smooth egg,  
shaded by its shell and bearing life within.

As eggs cover the chick, so the present conceals hope;  
the one, stripped of its shell, is manifest; the other prepares what is future.

Opposed to it is harmful despair,  
which strikes the person it attacks from behind and does not allow him to go forward.

If worthy forgetfulness puts to sleep what strikes from behind,  
extend yourself toward those things to which what lies ahead calls you.

With Paul you will grasp the palm above the ether,  
carrying a joyful crown of beauty in the citadel.

And since the fish signifies faith, the egg hope, and bread love,  
whoever lacks these three remains utterly wretched.

While now just things ebb and return, and unjust things painfully return,  
these three have grown lukewarm together with many good qualities.

And because wickedness is strong, presses upon us, prevails, and abounds,  
alas, the love of many often grows cold.

### XIII. ON DIVINE DISPENSATION, WHICH IS OFTEN HIDDEN BUT NEVER UNJUST

O power, O splendor, O glory of the exalted mind,  
which all can admire, but no one can understand!

We see many things variously ruling the human race,  
but in ignorance we do not know why or from where each thing comes.

[Col. 0366C] For evils often follow the good, and good things the reprobate;  
good things often follow the good, and evils the wicked.

Often the good person is oppressed and the wicked raised on high;  
the wicked falls, while the good rises to the heights.

All these things are governed by heavenly judgments.  
They are often hidden, but never dishonorable.

The Lord orders everything with a gentle and powerful nod,  
from beginning to end, and governs all things.

God therefore judges some things, but not always none or all  
of the wicked deeds that now take place without his law.

If no judgment were exercised in this present time,  
would not what dark fury does be unpunished?

Soon the wicked, thinking that God takes no care of mortal affairs,  
would rush unrestrained into every evil.

But if worthy vengeance immediately struck sinners,  
and all things were securely struck by judgment,

the laws of the supreme day would remain useless,  
and the time of judgment would have no work to perform.

Therefore he judges certain things, so that we may know that he cares for us  
and that God observes what we do from his citadel;

for this reason he does not judge everything, but reserves much,  
so that the great final day may have something to do.

This is what the law, the prophets, and the Lord himself proclaim,  
and it is known to all who possess reason:

[Col. 0367A] that God will come, supported by a red cloud,  
to set a just balance with a just weight.

He is merciful and just: from one side he comforts, from the other he deters.  
I fear him as just, and I am compelled to love him as merciful.

What mercy pardons, justice cuts away as sin;  
from one side he soothes with oil, from the other reproves with wine.

### XIV. THAT THE END IS SHOWN TO BE NEAR BY MANY SIGNS

It can be seen how the world is progressing toward its end  
and, though its voice is silent, singing of its own ruin.

It speaks through events, even if we remain silent about  
all the teachings of divine law that loudly proclaim this future.

The winter climate is no longer what it once was,  
able to nourish grasses, trees, and crops.

[Col. 0367B] There is less abundance of sunlight to sustain the burning labor of summer,  
and spring is no longer joyful in its own function.

Autumns do not overflow so greatly with sweet new wine,  
nor do trees flourish, burdened with fruit.

The earth now produces nothing good as it once did,  
and shows itself to be exhausted and barren.

There is less abundance in all things,  
and it fails more in some places and grows less everywhere.

The minister who performs every duty is rarer than before,  
and nothing stands firm as it once stood.

The cultivator in the fields, the soldier in camp, the sailor at sea,  
fairness in judgments, and piety in the marketplace—

concord in friendships, skill in any art:  
where does благeful discipline in character flourish?

It does not flourish as it once did, when invigorated by youthful strength;  
dreadful old age devours everything with blackened mouth.

For it is necessary that what sees its end approaching  
become diminished, and that it see the sunset not far away.

The sun, moving toward its setting, gives rays with diminished brilliance,  
and the waning moon bears darkened horns.

The tree that, young, blossomed with flowers and leaves  
sends forth rare shoots in a disfigured form.

The spring that used to spread overflowing streams  
often has, in its old age, only a thin trickle.

A cracked wall displays signs of impending ruin,  
though in its youth it stood solid, painted, and skillfully built.

And as songs, amusements, games, standing, riding, walking,  
and speaking playful words now weary the old man,

while frequent breath badly shakes his trembling limbs,  
he sighs and utters repeated groans,

[Col. 0367D] so all pleasant things have left the aged world,  
and none of the vigor it once possessed remains.

Dreadful desire, filth, perjury, luxury,  
devouring envy, falsehood, quarrels, strife, deceit—all flourish.

### XV. A POEM FROM THE LETTER TO THE CORINTHIANS, COMPOSED FOR THE PRAYER OF A CERTAIN MONK

Thus things usually sit together in orderly fashion,  
when one work is joined together from many parts.

In many matters this most beautiful order prevails;  
it is also sufficiently powerful in the art of eloquence,

where the broad meadows of sacred Scripture overflow  
and the holy grove breathes an ambrosial fragrance.

[Col. 0368A] As I wander through these things and run among the flowerbeds,  
I cut with my fingernail the roses carried by this basket.

This poem has taken its sacred material from the sacred doctrine of Paul,  
which his Arcadian pen conveyed.

It adorns a composed and holy discourse with language,  
after he had enumerated the virtues in this way:

“By various words, words are fittingly joined,  
and the order of an excellent meaning is opened along its path.

We exhort you,” he says, “holy people of the brothers,  
not to receive the holy grace of God in vain.

For he says: ‘In an acceptable time I heard you,  
and on the day of salvation I came to your aid.

Behold, now is the acceptable time;  
behold, now is the day of salvation.’

Let no offense be given to anyone by anyone,  
[Col. 0368B] so that our ministry may not rightly become worthless.

Rather, let us adapt ourselves in every matter  
so that all of us may be the ministers of the supreme God.

Let great patience flourish in us,  
so that the storm of evil may not overcome us.

Let harsh circumstance pressing upon us, distress causing pain,  
and the impiety of the wicked become occasions of approval through the test of justice.

In the filth of prisons or amid dark seditions,  
it is fitting for the purified to climb to the heavenly kingdoms.

Let our mind be exercised by laborious cares;  
let us be sleepless, and let every heart be watchful.

Let purity be chaste for us, and knowledge skillful;  
let us be long-suffering and free from every stain.

Let the mind bear the yoke of the Lord as tranquil and gentle,  
so that it may be able to receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0368C] Let love not be false but true affection,  
so that the true voice may soon utter true things.

Let us act in the power of God, by which all created things are governed,  
which holds the vaults of heaven, the fields, and the sea.

Now he begins to set opposites against one another,  
and to adorn his eloquence with a changing style:

‘Let the weapons of righteousness be borne on the right and on the left,  
so that the soldier of the Most High may shine victorious on both sides.

By honor on one side and by restrained disgrace on the other,  
we are seen as infamous; let good reputation belong to the good.

Let a sentence, as it were, be pronounced against us as seducers;  
nevertheless, we ought to be truthful.

As unknown, yet at last recognized, we are a people;  
as dying, behold, we live nonetheless.

As chastened, yet not put to death, we remain;  
as sorrowful, we are always a joyful multitude.

As needy, we weep, yet enrich many in our company;  
as having nothing, we nevertheless possess immense riches.’” [Note: [Col. 0367D] 2 Cor. 6:1ff.]

### XVI. ON THE HUNDRED-FOLD, SIXTY-FOLD, AND THIRTY-FOLD FRUIT

The field of the Church is divided into these parts,  
animated by the Lord’s good seed.

The first part is a hundredfold, the second a sixtyfold,  
and the third contains a thirtyfold degree.

When the first has perished, the second cannot immediately proceed;  
the third takes its place according to the order of things.

The third follows the first, and the second follows it in turn;  
yet no one is able to return to the first.

[Col. 0369A] The third leaves the wretched condition and seeks the second,  
but the first cannot be sought again.

### XVII. THE SAME SUBJECT

For good seed rightly fell as good into the fields,  
sown by the sower out of love for the peaceful crop.

Thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruits abound,  
which the field of the mind brings forth from the seed of faith.

The thirtyfold shines in marriage, the sixtyfold in widows;  
the third order of good surpasses these two.

The glory of the hundredfold fruit is given to virgins,  
and this number corresponds to the holy martyrdom.

The bending of the fingers sufficiently marks the matter in numbers,  
a thing rightly discovered by men of old.

[Col. 0369B] For when the highest finger is lightly joined to the thumb,  
it is known to hold the place of thirty in the numbers.

The soft embrace of the fingers signifies  
the sweet kisses of marriage, which remain pleasing to the couple.

But when the thumb, bent inward, is pressed by the index finger,  
it shows sixty and, in the symbolic figure, widows.

As one finger constricts another, so anguish often constricts them;  
the renowned lament of the turtledove adorns them.

If a transition is made in order from the left hand to the right,  
and the index finger is joined to its thumb,

and a peaceful circle is formed in a smooth round shape,  
this figure contains the number one hundred.

This figure bears a crown of beauty,  
which is rightly given to holy virgins and devout martyrs.

This transition admonishes us to despise present things on the left  
and to seek future things on the right through good deeds.

To pursue nothing perishable, but to fix the mind on enduring things;  
to despise the passing world and love God;

to follow heavenly things, to put all earthly matters second,  
and to grasp holy work with mouth, hand, heart, and faith.

### XVIII. ON HYPOCRITES; AND THAT IN THE TIMES OF THE APOSTLES, OR OF THEIR SUCCESSORS, THE VIRTUES OF THE CHURCH FLOURISHED MORE THAN IN THESE LAST TIMES

False virtue flourishes, while true virtue fades uselessly;  
the former has raised its head, while the latter seeks the depths with groaning.

Now, just as true goodness gives help, false goodness will harm;  
the one prepares to advise, while the other yearns to deceive.

Then the doctrine of devout priests flourished,  
[Col. 0369D] and their speech and conduct were a model of salvation.

Now the double heart of simulators and deceitful words prevail,  
and only pretense retains its place.

Then the care of pontiffs bore honor and distinction,  
for whom the apostolic order bestowed the throne.

They were given authority to loose and bind,  
and by their key the kingdoms of heaven were able to be opened.

To them the Shepherd of shepherds commended sheep and lambs,  
and entrusted the pledge of his own loving work.

Thus then all things moved on one course, but now on another:  
the foot is above the head, and the head inclines to the depths.

Then the apostolic cloaks bestowed from the see flourished,  
and the right of authority consisted in vesture and order.

[Col. 0370A] Now a simulated garment has appeared, and a simulated wearer,  
whose mind and outward habit suit one another well.

Loose hair covers the head; a dark will conceals the mind;

rough wool covers the limbs, and a sheep’s garment [conceals] the wolf.

A double cloak is outwardly displayed, but within there is a double heart;

the honor of simplicity is far removed from both.

They wear ample footwear bulging with swollen cloth,

and a cheap shoe is fitted to the swift foot.

The left side also carries a knife and a double writing-tablet;

a covering and a stylus are commonly found there.

Pallor holds his face, and weary sighs his breast;

his groaning voice sounds in a thin murmur.

A groaning voice sounds, uttering feigned and pleasing words,

so that they may draw the pure hearts of men after their own desires.

[Col. 0370B] Though they cannot weep, they desire to seem to have wept,

watering their unkempt cheeks with a deceitful shower.

They strive to seem just, holy, and devout,

so that human praise may be purchased.

In this guise the image veils his face with piety;

these men wish to be seen as holier than they actually are.

This class of men also knows no other way than to go through the towns,

nor does it cease to inspect crossroads, fields, and cottages.

They do this so that they may thrust their way into purses

and obtain shameful profit, filling their greedy bosoms.

These men perform many good deeds ostentatiously, and many evils secretly;

the former are open to human eyes, the latter to God’s.

Whoever has performed a worthy deed for the sake of human praise

receives his reward—alas! Wretched is that man.

[Col. 0370C] Thus the trumpet of the Gospel’s word sounds out mightily,

and triumphantly resounds through the roads of the world:

“Let not your left hand know what your right hand does”;

then everything you do will be acceptable to God [Note: [Col. 0369D] Matthew 6:3].

That is, the mind should be ignorant of human praise

when the renowned deed is performed by the right hand.

The present life is signified by the left, the future life by the right;

God’s holy page teaches this.

For a certain powerful philosopher, a famous king, once

gave forth such words from such considerations:

“Long life is in her right hand,

and in her left are glory, honor, and riches” [Note: [Col. 0370D] Proverbs 3:16].

Her left hand likewise rests beneath our head,

and her holy right hand will give pious embraces.

For in her left she gives the comforts of the present life,

and in her right she prepares those of perpetual life, without end [Col. 0370D].

For the two disciples who wished, while the Lord was seated, to hold the left and the right

signify this.

In the right hand is Christ’s powerful wisdom,

which grants eternal rest to spirits.

The governance of this life remains in his left,

until we arrive at eternal riches.

True riches are the glory and norm of faith,

which rightly protect us in this exile.

For your left hand, powerful Christ, generally signifies

the Church of this present life.

While I sing of those who exist only outwardly in the guise of saints,

I would not wish to condemn the innocent, provided that I speak truthfully.

[Col. 0371A] Yet by singing these things I do not disparage righteous monks,

whose heart is heaven and whose holy mind thirsts for God;

whose faith is devoted, whose hope is pious, whose love is sweet;

for whom Christ is life, and holy gain is death.

They left everything when they heard the voice of the Thunderer,

and strive to follow the Lord with the love of their minds;

and to stand upon the foundation of the apostolic life,

so that the former way of the Church may endure.

All things are shared by those who possess an excellent common purpose,

to whom God himself has given one mind and one spirit.

Yet many things run together in mixed course through each individual,

and good things are found among the wicked, and evil things mixed with the good.

So wine contains dregs, olive oil contains foul lees,

and the ambrosial liquid of honey has its sediment.

[Col. 0371B] Surely the Lord said that there were two in the field, two likewise in the bed,

and two at the mill.

Of these, one is taken up and the other left behind;

this portion, taken, shines forth, while that, left behind, perishes.

The Church’s bosom therefore bears these three classes,

which one faith binds together in different orders.

The clerical order is in the field, the monk beneath the lot of quiet,

and in the circle of the mill is the common people.

The former governs peoples; the latter enjoys holy rest,

while the one who follows worldly actions runs through the world.

And these three are rightly divided at a gaping fork,

for each part contains a portion destined for destruction.

One part seeks heaven, another goes toward the Stygian shades,

and life thus prepares different places for them.

[Col. 0371C] This threefold order, and the threefold harmony of life,

has been signified in three holy men.

The blessed Noah contains the pattern of rulers,

who governs the hope of cattle and human beings amid the waters.

The unmarried man and the monk flourish in the choir of Daniel,

who triumphantly overcame luxury and gluttony.

Job represents those whom the activities of the world either drive onward or make repentant—

he who was without stain in the actions of the age.

[lacuna]

XIX. EPITAPH OF HELMENGALD.

[Note: [Col. 0371C] Epitaph of Hermengald. At this time the name of the count Helingand was similar to his. Helingand was sent by Charlemagne to Constantinople, together with Jesse, bishop of Amiens, as an envoy to Irene in 802; and two years earlier he had taken part at Rome, with other nobles of Charlemagne, in the trial of those who had most outrageously assaulted Pope Leo III. I could not easily affirm, however, that this is the same man.]

[Col. 0372A]

Here in this earth lies Helmengald, a noble hero,

who was the glory and entire distinction of his homeland.

Rich in wealth and understanding, shining in nobility,

adorned with character and every virtue;

powerful in counsel, perhaps strengthened by arms and bodily force,

versed in laws, mighty in speech and action.

For he was prefect of the palace

while pious Charles ruled with tranquil scepter.

He enriched churches with many resources,

and made them heirs to his possessions.

He was a foot to the lame, the glory of eyes to the blind;

every weak person found comfort in him.

He was accustomed alike to drive hunger and thirst,

and terrible cold, away from the bodies of the poor.

Jerusalem possesses his earthly body,

but his spirit seeks the blessed realms above.

You who read this inscription, or behold this tomb,

say: “May Helmengald’s rest be without end.”

The holy company of monks will do this also,

as it frequently returns and goes forth, while it undertakes this journey.

May it itself remain mindful of him throughout all ages,

and pray that the heavenly realms be granted to him.

XX. TO FARDULF, ABBOT.

[Note: [Col. 0371D] To Abbot Fardulf. Alcuin mentions him in poem 117. Verses under Fardulf’s own name were also published long ago, inscribed on the magnificent buildings that he had constructed in Charlemagne’s honor; in them he declares in these words that he was Italian by birth and a Lombard by nation: “Verses of Abbot Fardulf inscribed on the buildings of Saint-Denis.”

“Reader who sees the roofs, bring forth the letters:

Fardulf built these for his own Charles.

Once, while he followed and guarded the scepters

of his own people, fate carried him along hostile roads.

Yet here he preserved the honor of loyalty to his lords,

although this was the final limit of their kingdom.

At last he yielded to the fortunate arms of Charles his ruler,

and fate gave his journey a better course.

While he also preserved the gifts of loyalty to the king,

the exalted king gave him many gifts.

Among them, peaceful Charles granted that he should become

ruler of the church of Saint-Denis and of its palace.

The prudent man built this house for his benefactor,

in which he himself might rejoice with his servants.

May the mighty prince give joy to his servants,

whom the bonds of loyalty join to him.

Yet he ordered the roofs to rise in the manner of ancient ancestors;

the buildings shine forth with the king’s honor,

so that whenever he surveys the splendid palaces of the kingdom,

he may remember Fardulf, his own servant.”]

What he says here about his loyalty to Charles must be referred to the conspiracy of the illegitimate Pippin, which Fardulf exposed. Both the Dionysian Annals indicate this, and Einhard explicitly records it in the Chronicle under the year 792:

“While the king was spending the summer there,” he says, “a conspiracy was formed against him by his elder son, named Pippin, and by certain Franks who maintained that they could not endure the cruelty of Queen Fastrada, and who therefore had conspired to kill the king. When this had been discovered by Fardulf the Lombard, he, in return for the merit of having preserved his loyalty, was given the monastery of Saint-Denis.”

It is plainly evident that Fardulf, not Ardulf, ought to be read in that passage.]

TO FARDULF, ABBOT OF SAINT-DENIS.

Receive gladly the little gifts I have sent,

my sweet friend, sweet and most fittingly so.

Although they are small, great affection sends them;

it is not the gift but the work of love that compensates.

May life, health, and every happiness be yours,

and may God the King add heavenly help to you.

And may the merciful one lead you through the prosperity of the world,

so that your foot may seek the heights along an unobstructed path.

And may he who granted you worthy honor in this life

give you a place above the stars after death.

XXI. REPENTANCE MUST BE SERIOUS.

What good does it do to abandon for a time the phantoms of trifles,

if an unsound man eventually takes them up again?

What good is it to rise, if at once that person falls again—

the person who, weakened, lay upon the inert earth?

A boy is said to have begged his aged mother,

and laid before her prayers such as these:

“O mother, whose care for us always gnaws at you,

you are dearer to me than life, and I myself am dear to you.

As soon as the bird that announces the light gives its song,

take care to awaken me immediately.”

She replied, “I shall do what you love; but tell me, my son, what will you do?”

“Perhaps,” he said, “I shall be able to fall asleep again.”

Meanwhile no lesser madness had seized the man

who reported no gain from his hunt.

In the end, hunting is practiced wisely when

it is either amusement, profit, or both at once.

[Col. 0373B] When caught, roe deer, stag, elk,

beaver, fallow deer, bison, buffalo, bear, and boar usually provide profit.

For hares, there are javelins to strike them and mastiffs to seize them.

In modest profit there is an attractive spectacle.

The dog and the hare, both flying, have different lots:

one seeks prey, the other assistance.

The dog seeks food with its claw; the hare itself seeks safety with its claw;

thus, with different desires, their labor is one.

Love and mad passion for these things had invaded him,

who, after capturing nothing, began as follows:

“Roaming through the valleys below and the broad countryside,

I found no hare anywhere in it.

Now I was returning to my house without profit from the hunt,

and, because I had been unable to catch anything, I was sad.

There is a small thicket surrounded on every side by fields,

which, sparsely wooded, lies not far from our house.

Who would ever believe that a wild creature, or a hare, was there,

since the place was so near the farm?

Whenever on this day no hope of hares remained to me,

I thought that profit from them was absent.

I inspected the place, sent in the dogs, and set the nets.

Though eager in my efforts, I found nothing there.”

XXII. DISAPPOINTED EXPECTATION.

When something extremely worthless in speech has a grand beginning,

you give birth to a small mouse, great elephant.

Thus a certain son reported his dreams to his father,

bringing forth from his mind trifling words.

“O father, I shall tell you what marvelous things I saw in dreams;

such visions stirred my mind.

Last night an ox uttered our human speech;

it was speaking, and we were amazed,” he said.

Then the astonished father questioned him about the matter:

“Tell me what it said.”

He replied, “Nothing.”

XXIII. THAT THE WICKED GENERALLY SUFFER EVILS, AND ON THE TIME OF ANTICHRIST.

He who rules the world with virtue and governs it with piety

then dealt well and triumphantly with human affairs,

when he brought against the unspeakable, savage monster

hostile forces to complete its wicked deed,

and from evil provided a gentle remedy for the wicked,

while tempering the fearful harms intended for his own good people.

If a fierce scorpion is killed in shining olive oil,

that liquid overcomes its venom.

If a fresh wound is smeared with this liquid,

it acts against the poison, so that the poison cannot harm.

Thus vice departs through vice, disease through disease;

one thing often yields in this way to another.

A wedge drives out a wedge, a nail a nail,

and when one comes upon another, the former perishes.

So stone blunts stone, and wood blunts wood,

while steel forges and polishes steel through skill.

By restraining this evil Christ grants relief,

or by shortening, Antichrist, your days.

[Col. 0374B] So that the deadly evil might not grow strong through dark measures,

it is confined within a narrow span of time.

The prophetic trumpet reveals the shameful dangers of that time,

you, pious King Christ, being its herald.

“Then,” says the author, “there will be great tribulation,

such as there was not, nor shall be, from the beginning of chaos.

Those days will be shortened by exact reckoning;

otherwise no flesh would be saved.”

In accordance with this consideration of the Lord,

by whom all things are accomplished, the course of events will proceed

according to an appointed and fitting time:

the impious and savage plague will exceed three years

but not complete four.

“Time, times, and half a time,” Daniel says,

the fierce times of that evil which must run their course.

Thus, by forty-two months,

he explains and sings of this very matter.

By “one time” he signifies one year, by “times” two,

and by “half” he properly teaches that there will be six months.

Thus the total number of months comes to this:

three and a half years, neither more nor less.

XXIV. ON THE SOLEMN ANNUAL DAY.

For our peoples, the clergy, and the sacred ministers,

the solemn annual joys of the feast have returned.

For who would not desire duly to venerate with abundant

praises and prayers so great a treasure of wisdom?

From it the ages are adorned with everlasting riches;

from it a golden understanding shines with heavenly doctrine.

Its eloquence surpasses silver and the radiance of light;

by its brightness all the gems of the virtues are dimmed.

By it the regions of Libya are strong, the Frankish kingdoms,

the peoples of Hesperia, and the British nations flourish;

sacred Rome, the world and the head of the world, gleams,

and the believing people shines illustriously throughout the whole earth.

XXV. TO KING CHARLES.

[Note: [Col. 0373D] To King Charles. Not to a king, but to the king’s son, famous under his father in many military expeditions and victories. He nevertheless died before his father in the year 814. Hence the Saxon poet, praising him after his death, wrote:

[Col. 0374D] “He was his father’s equal—not in name alone,

but in the bright integrity of his mind and the uprightness of his character;

and he would have reflected his father in every virtue,

if Francia had deserved to enjoy such a ruler.”]

TO KING CHARLES.

O my great salvation, O hope, O glory of the kingdom,

Charles, farewell, with heaven’s King favoring you.

You multiply the joys of your father and your country,

and you prepare every distinction for the entire senate.

Brighter than amber, purer than gold refined three times,

all metals yield to your splendor.

Lighter than birds, yourself stronger than a lion,

surpassing in arts and ready-handed in war.

Our two eyes thirst too greatly for the sight of you,

and the deep love of our heart longs to see you.

For when you began to touch the western regions,

I, a servant and a friend, felt my master nearby.

Lighter than the south wind, swifter than winged Eurus,

I immediately wished to approach your feet prostrate.

The king’s command restrained me from this desire

and gave me another road to travel.

Now, willing again and again, I remain restrained without offense;

twice I prepared to come, and twice the road was denied me.

When your Gomis spoke sweet words to me,

and the little servant heard his master greet him,

a tearful winter soon flowed back in a cloud over my eyes,

and the foreign brow drenched my cheeks with rain.

Joy, therefore, is accustomed to produce such springs,

and, when its direction is reversed, joys give tears.

I ask that you load this slave with twin bonds:

if you bind my arms, I shall not be a fugitive.

By these bonds your great-grandfather, grandfather,

and father himself bound the armies that earned them the throne of the kingdom.

From there they have laid low many ranks of the proud

and, by striving, have subdued very many kingdoms for themselves.

But you, great boy, be safe and fare well forever;

may the Lord of heaven protect, adorn, and nourish you,

so that, radiant, you may be able to ascend to your ancestral seats

and, with God’s help, hold the scepters in your hand.

[Col. 0375C] And thus may you leave behind the earthly heights

of the worldly kingdom, so that afterward you may possess those of heaven.

XXVI. TO CHARLES THE EMPEROR.

May he who rules the fields and heaven be your helper everywhere, O king;

may he who rules the fields and heaven always assist you.

May he who gave you the scepters give you long years of life;

may he who gave you the scepters grant you joys.

God has placed the European kingdoms beneath your laws;

may God incline the whole world beneath your laws.

As you yourself crush wild beasts, so restrain barbarian necks;

as you yourself crush wild beasts, so restrain Hesperia.

As the boar yields to you, so may the Moor and the Arab yield to you;

may the Sarmatian submit, as the boar yields to you.

Trample proud necks, as a flock of capons tramples ducks;

as a hawk does a goose, trample proud necks.

[Col. 0376A] May eternal joys follow these pleasures and games;

carry joys or games through the boundless ages.

May God’s great grace unfold the gifts of life to you;

may God’s great grace govern and protect you.

May you possess long joys, and rejoice forever, O king;

may you possess long joys with your offspring and household.

You, the glory of every kind, hold long-lasting health,

with clergy and people, you, the glory of every kind.

For your welcomed safety is a light to these eyes;

your welcomed safety is desired by the good.

Good fortune to you, glory of the people, most powerful Caesar, son;

holding famous scepters, good fortune to you, glory of the people.

Hail, Emperor, while the Thunderer grants you long life;

gladly receive my greeting, Emperor, hail.

XXVII. ON THE OUTER SIDE OF THE FIRST TABLET OF THE LIBRARY.

[Col. 0376B]

If you wish to know who I am, know that I am called the Library,

and I bear the authority of the old law, or of the new.

Please do not despise me because you see that I am small in body:

I am small in body, yet great in strength.

Whoever sees me, I ask you to remember Theodulf,

whose study founded me, fitted me, and loves me.

He adorned me externally with silver, gems, and gold,

and polished my interior with the file. Hail.

XXVIII. ON THE OTHER TABLET.

If you wish to be good, if you seek an honorable life,

seek me, I advise you: I am God’s holy law.

I am the way, I am the light, I am the teacher, I am the witness of truth;

who obeys me possesses an unextinguishable light.

I prepare the heavenly kingdoms, I lay open worldly sophistries;

I prevail in all things, or I am renowned.

Use me, reader, and place me in the seat of your mind;

and when you seek this book, let your hand be washed.

XXIX. ABOVE THE DOOR.

May your door always stand open to the poor, bishop;

with the wretched, Christ himself enters too.

May the needy poor man be fed from your banquets,

so that you may be able to be received as God’s guest.

XXX. ABOVE THE DRINKING VESSEL.

May he who once changed water for the use of wine

and made it take on the appearance of pure wine,

himself bless our cups with pious hands,

and make us possess a joyful day.

APPENDIX. SOME POEMS OF THEODULF,

published by J. Mabillon in the Ancient Analecta.

[Col. 0377]

The poems of Theodulf published by Sirmond and divided into six books survive in the same form, in continuous sequence, in a very ancient codex of the monastery of Saint-Vaast, together with many others absent from Sirmond’s edition. Some verses by other authors, inserted without the names of their authors, are also included. The most distinguished scholar Jean Mabillon testifies to this in the first volume of the Ancient Analecta. He then says:

“Of the pieces that seemed to be Theodulf’s, I selected only those that may be useful to literary studies; but the others, which deal with moral matters, I thought it sufficient merely to note.”

I. ON THE ARRIVAL OF LOUIS AUGUSTUS AT ORLÉANS.

[Note: [Col. 0377C] The first poem, on the arrival of Louis Augustus in the city of Orléans, has already been printed in volume 6 of Canisius under the name of Jonas, Theodulf’s predecessor. Yet it ought rather to be attributed to Theodulf as author, both because it is listed among his metrical works in the Saint-Vaast manuscript, and because this arrival of Louis Augustus in the aforesaid city took place during Theodulf’s episcopate, as we learn from Louis’s own Life under the year 814, where the following is read about Louis:

“When he had arrived at the city of Orléans, Theodulf, bishop of that same city, a man learned in every respect, perceived the reason for his arrival; and, having very swiftly sent a messenger, he took care to inform the emperor, ordering him to ask only whether he should await him as he came into the city, or meet him on some road as he approached the city,” and so forth.

On this occasion Theodulf seems to have sung the first and second poems. The first is reprinted here because of its variant readings, although perhaps it would rather have been omitted. Moreover, the first verse of the third stanza is mutilated in the Saint-Vaast manuscript. MABILL.]

ON THE ARRIVAL OF LOUIS AUGUSTUS AT ORLÉANS.

Behold, the pious and gracious Caesar is here,

he who shines resplendent throughout the whole world,

and surpasses all others in goodness,

by Christ’s gift.

Bowed in reverence, prudent, wise, and modest,

gentle and merciful, moderate in conduct,

self-controlled, brave, upright, and honorable,

a censor and judge.

He, the glory (Sudam [uncertain]) and father of the Church, diligently

adorns, renews, cherishes, educates,

fortifies, honors, and instructs her

with abundant doctrine.

Powerful in arms, with the Lord’s favor,

he restrains proud peoples by his strength,

and, victorious, tramples their necks

as he triumphs.

O populous city, namely Orléans, your face,

at his arrival, greatly brightens

and grows serene,

through Christ’s mercy.

Therefore give praises to God through the years [C.: everlasting],

at whose command he hastened to you,

and who, behold, has granted you

to see his face.

Let the clergy sing these praises, and all the people together;

let old men, boys, and little children compose them;

let poor and rich resound them joyfully

with pure hearts.

Let this chorus of clergy and multitude of people,

singing again a Sapphic [C.: supplicatory] song, pray:

“May God grant Louis

long years for action.”

May the merciful one always bring him prosperity,

drive away and repel adversity far from him,

and mercifully protect his life

through the ages.

May the noble spouse of this Caesar,

or his illustrious offspring, endure forever;

may the happy people and household rejoice

in perpetual peace.

May faithful nobles fortify this city,

who have dedicated their pure bodies

to the wars they must endure

for pious Christ against the hostile enemy.

[Col. 0378A] May these holy leaders be present and return [C.: let these holy leaders come],

so that they may favor you, Caesar; 

and by their intercession may you overcome your enemies—

we all ask this.

May you please the Thunderer in all your actions,

and meditate upon God’s holy laws,

so that you may be able to keep the way of life

along the straight path.

When the span of this time has been completed,

may you ascend on high and enter the heavens;

may the pious choir of angels receive you

and join you to itself.

O glory of the kingdom, offspring of empire,

may you always flourish, Lothair, good fortune to you.

May you powerfully hold your father’s seat [C.: his father’s seat]

through the broad ages.

To the Father and Son, and to you, Spirit,

be eternal splendor, honor, and everlasting praise,

now and in the present, and likewise in the future,

always through the ages.

II. ON THE SAME SUBJECT.

O father of the clergy, glory of the people,

Caesar, powerful in distinguished piety,

we all ask that you willingly

approach our doors.

O worshiper of God, nourisher of the wretched,

guardian of orphans and widows,

highest and merciful king, we ask you

to heed our prayers.

Therefore, at last, entreated by our prayers,

return to our prepared homes,

and enjoy happy days in them,

blessed king.

The choir of priests and all the clergy,

and the entire multitude of the people,

both great and small alike,

greatly desire to see you.

Prudent, venerable king, farewell and hail;

king, receive our greeting, we pray;

we ask Christ to grant you health,

with knees bent.

May Christ everywhere save you,

your offspring, and your consort in life,

committed to you by a fortunate lot,

through the prayers of blessed Albinus.

[Col. 0379A] After the days of the age, may you happily enter

the realms of the Thunderer;

may you possess rest among the elect,

with Christ granting you everlasting completion.

III. ON THE BILINGUAL MAN.

Behold, a certain chatterer, whispering a fixed thread of words with his lips,

now sings jokes, now laments, and now something shameful.

He trembles out flatteries, now flits about like a cicada;

he repeats them in the ears that the wanderer of the east seeks.

Like a crow, he strikes hard breasts with his beak,

when, shamelessly, he devours rain-bringing luxury.

Or, like a swift swallow, he tries to inspect

the pools pressed by rapid wings, singing with a sweet voice.

No differently, he runs through unstable minds,

an enemy of youths whom a light breeze drives.

IV. TO SOMEONE ABOUT GIFTS.

Come now, do not, as is your custom, turn my poem away;

take care that it not return empty.

Otherwise the impatient hoof of your foaming horse

may now trample your tracks backward. Return the gifts.

Like a garment of reddish-purple cloth, named from Rome,

which the Fathers call by that name, let it press your neck.

So that, happily endowed with a beautiful gift,

you may receive my thousand sweet thanks.

But if perhaps you come empty to our house,

you will go out, fool, beaten with a thousand whips.

V. ON THE PASSION OF THE LORD.

The sacred people should fittingly proclaim with holy mouth

the sacred work of the Almighty in such praises.

That the Creator of the great world deigned

of his own will to suffer the lowest things—this deserves to be loudly praised.

At last, born in human form,

Christ endured everything that belonged to human salvation.

VI. ON THE DAY OF THE RESURRECTION.

[Col. 0379C]

Come, Muse, willingly, sing songs now, I ask;

now sing a melody, I ask—come, Muse, willingly.

Strive now to bring forth beautiful feasts with me,

so that afterward you may receive beautiful feasts.

A day worthy of song is present; let us all compose songs:

this radiant day is present, worthy of song.

Because death lies conquered, slain when Christ arose,

let us all rejoice, because death lies conquered.

Tartarus lies conquered, the blessed being visited by Christ;

the Prince having been conquered, Tartarus lies conquered.

From there he drove out the upright and left the reprobate behind;

having trampled the enemy, he drove out the upright.

After the dreadful depths of Tartarus, the blessed seek the heavenly realms;

rescued from darkness, they seek the heavenly realms.

Turn your step, Muse, lest you add weariness to the brothers;

I ask you, quickly turn your step this way, Muse.

Say, “Hail, bishop,” with neck and knee bent,

and here and forever say, “Hail, bishop.”

VII. ON A TABLET.

I am a small, brief tablet, superior and useful for two functions,

suitable in appearance within and without.

I add an external appearance of adornment for its bearer;

within, I preserve words bound together by letters.

VIII. ON THE TALAMASCA.

[Note: [Col. 0379D] What a talamasca, or talamascae, is, learned men explained long ago: Vossius in book 2 of On the Vices of Speech, and especially the distinguished scholar Étienne Baluze in his notes on Regino. They cite a passage from an ancient Council of Reims:

“We prohibit under anathema the masks of demons, which the common people call talamascas.”

Hence the word masque, meaning a mask, is common among our French people. Even hidden signs in writing are called talamascas, as Baluze observes, because they present one thing while signifying another. Here, therefore, Theodulf is speaking of a masked little boy.]

When a little boy covers his face with an empty mask,

what trembles here frightens, and what flees there drives away.

I think he even lay prostrate and stretched out his palms,

moving his little limbs before the Redeemer.

IX. VERSES ON AN ALTAR.

This altar, Creator of heaven and earth,

Theodulf, bowed down, adorns for you with a pious vow.

Whoever approaches it, I ask, bringing sacred gifts or prayers [F.: offering them],

remember me, if God himself remembers you.

Shepherd, feed the Lord’s sheep here with heavenly nourishment,

for through it life is given and the court of God stands open.

There is a pious shepherd above the stars, by whom we are all fed;

when you love him as shepherd, you yourself are also part of the flock.

Do you see this company panting at the manger?

Here it receives nourishment from the Lamb’s blood and flesh.

The dragon whom you dread, savage one, the lion who conquered you, faithless one,

bore the sins of the world, grown old through time.

And he has granted us here to share

in his heavenly drink and consecrated food,

in him who is the way, the life, and the salvation,

through whom, toward whom, and in whom one travels more safely;

with whom the pious must now reign without end.

X. IN A HOSPITAL FOR STRANGERS.

[Col. 0380C]

Behold, this house stands open, built with modest means,

yet in every way suitable for human use.

May God, from the citadel of heaven, mercifully visit its servants,

drive away every adversity, and bring every prosperity.

May modesty and truth, piety and uprightness abound here;

may holy faith be present, and every wickedness far away.

May the hungry find food here, the thirsty drink, and the guest honor;

may the naked find clothing.

May the weary bring away help, the sick medicine, and the sorrowful joys;

may this house provide for everyone.

May the Father enthroned on high grant this gift to those who dwell here,

so that it may be open to citizens and to you, traveler.

May the love of brothers and of God reign forever,

and may all virtues come together under its guidance.

May every benefit soon follow these things through God’s mercy.

May there be no path here for envy or savage deceit.

May justice govern minds here, and may material prosperity remain;

may thirst and hunger be far, far away.

You who seek these dwellings of Theodulf, I ask you to remember

the man who built these roofs with God’s favor.

[Col. 0381]

A MIRROR OF SACRED SCRIPTURE.

(This little work, attributed by some—though doubtfully—to our Theodulf, may be found among the works of Saint Augustine, volume 34 of Patrologia, column 887.)

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 822. SAINT EIGIL, ABBOT OF FULDA.

THE LIFE OF SAINT EIGIL, BY CANDIDUS, A MONK OF FULDA.

[Col. 0381A]

PRELIMINARY NOTICE.

(Mabillon, Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict, volume 5, p. 226.)

[Col. 0381A] 1. Candidus, a monk of the same monastery under Eigil, composed two books on the Life of Eigil, or Aegil, the fourth abbot of Fulda: one in prose, the other in strict verse. Eigil, with the pious affection of a father, allowed him to enter into his intimacy and companionship, as Candidus himself writes in section 23 of the prose Life.

Candidus’s subscription at the end of the metrical preface to his companion Modestus should be noted. He dedicated both little books to him:

“Here ends Candidus’s preface to Modestus, who is called Bruun and Reccheo by his proper name.”

It seems that the plural should be read, “who are called,” so that Candidus and Modestus each had a double name, one Latin and one German, according to the custom of that age: namely, Candidus [was also called] Bruun, as appears from chapter 17 of the metrical Life; and Modestus [was also called] Reccheo, who is called the younger, from chapter 7 of the same Life.

Perhaps someone will suspect that this Candidus is the same as Candidus, the disciple of Alcuin, whom Alcuin himself mentions in more than one place. But what chiefly moves me to think that he was another man is Alcuin’s preface to Ecclesiastes, addressed to the priest Onia and the presbyter Candidus. In it he writes that they had flown from the nest of paternal devotion—not into the cloister of monks, but into the public air of secular business—and he warns them away from the desire for riches.

Letters 93 and 97 also move me, in which he indicates that Candidus came from the island of Britain, not from Germany. In a manuscript list of the abbots of Fulda, a fragment of which I shall shortly quote, our Modestus and Candidus are said to have been sent by Abbot Ratgarius to Clement the Scot for the purpose of studying grammar. According to the monk of Saint Gall, Charles ordered this Clement to reside in Gaul.

2. I read of no public testimony or cult honoring the memory of Eigil, although Christopher Brower, who was the first to publish his Life, repeatedly calls Eigil a saint. Rabanus nowhere in his Martyrology, nor any other ancient writer, bestows the title on Eigil.

Nevertheless, people of that age were persuaded that Eigil had been received by God into heaven. Candidus, in his metrical book, proclaims that he was second to none of the ancients in piety, and Rabanus sings in his epitaph, which he himself composed, that Eigil remains above the stars.

I shall nevertheless refrain from calling him holy or blessed and shall call him venerable, until his sanctity has been attested to me by more certain arguments. The day of his death is likewise still unknown; it will be discussed in the notes at the end of the prose book.

There was also another Eigil living at approximately that time: abbot of Prüm, then of Flavigny, and finally bishop of Sens. I shall give his encomium below.

3. Before relating Eigil’s Life, certain things must be prefaced concerning his predecessors, so that what is here recorded about him may be clearer.

The first abbot of the monastery of Fulda was Saint Sturmius, whose Life I related in part 2 of the preceding century. He had as his successor Baugolf, or Paugolf, in the year 779.

According to the Annals of Fulda, Baugolf “in the year 802, having relinquished the authority he had held, received Ratgarius as his successor.” He survived for thirteen years and died in 815, as Brower testifies.

Trithemius is mistaken in writing that he died in 804, in his Life of Rabanus, where Baugolf is said to have attained among all the Germans a glorious reputation for sanctity.

It is certainly established that he survived long beyond the year assigned by Trithemius from the following inscription, which appears in Brower’s Book 2 of the Antiquities of Fulda, chapter 12:

“In the year 812, the church at Slitisse was dedicated at the request of Baugolf by Richolf, venerable archbishop of the church of Mainz, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, in honor of Saint Margaret the virgin.”

Ruodolf also discusses him below in the Acts of Rabanus.

Candidus recorded the Life of this same Baugolf in writing at Eigil’s command, but his work on this subject has until now lain in darkness.

Of Abbot Ratgarius it is written as follows in the list of abbots preserved by Brower in his notes on Rabanus’s poem 13:

“Ratgarius, born in the regions of Germany to noble parents, was received by Saint Sturmius into the monastery of Fulda. He succeeded Baugolf in the government of the abbey in the year 802 and was deposed in the year of the Lord 817.

“He governed the monastery nobly for sixteen years. Like a wise architect, joining the western church to the other with marvelous skill and immense size, he made one church.

“He sent Rabanus and Hatto to Tours to Master Albinus for the study of the liberal arts; Bruno to Einhard, a most learned teacher of various arts; and Modestus and Candidus, with others, to Clement the Scot for the study of grammar.

“He also advanced the place gloriously with gold and silver, crowns, lamps, and every good thing.

“This venerable Father also built a monastery on the mountain, of praiseworthy and measured proportions, to which the precious martyr Boniface, bishop, gave his name. He caused it to be dedicated by Haistolf, archbishop of the church of Mainz, in honor of holy Mary, the Mother of God; and at the entrance to the cloister of that church, on the right, he was given an honorable burial as an old man full of days.

“He was succeeded by Eigil, namely in the year 818.”

4. This encomium of Ratgarius may seem excessive if you consider how disturbed the condition of the monastery became under that abbot, and what the cause of these disturbances was: namely, Ratgarius’s harsh severity toward his monks, which grew so fierce that they themselves were compelled to present Charlemagne with a petition, to be produced below after this Life, in which they laid their complaints before the emperor and requested that the customs and laws of the monastery be restored to their former condition. And lest you think that these disturbances were stirred up merely by a faction of certain worthless men, all the good men—in fact, the entire congregation of Fuldensian monks—were shaken by this storm, Rabanus above all, as he himself testifies in poem 30, *On the Departure of the Monks*—those who withdrew from Abbot Ratgarius.

That this occurred in the year 811 is shown to us by the manuscript *Saxon Chronicle*, in these words:

> “In the same year mentioned above, 811, a very serious disturbance arose at Fulda in the monastery of Saint Boniface. Twelve brothers from that household proceeded together with Abbot Ratgarius to the judgment of the emperor Charles; yet that agitation did not cease. Later Ricolfus, archbishop of Mainz; Bernharius, bishop of the city of the Vangiones; Hatto, bishop of Augsburg; and Wolgarius, bishop of Würzburg, assembled by the emperor’s command for this same cause and healed it.”

The same words occur in the *Chronicle of Hildesheim* and in the oldest annals, which end in the fourth year of Louis Augustus and which Petrus Lambecius published in volume II of the *Imperial Library*, book II, chapter 5. There it is said that these events occurred in the forty-fourth year of Charlemagne.

After Charles’s death, when Ratgarius did not cease harassing his monks, Louis Augustus, moved by the repeated complaints of the monks of Fulda, sent Western—that is, Frankish—monks there. Then, in the year 817, he ordered Ratgarius to be deposed and exiled, and appointed another abbot in his place. Eigil was subsequently elected. He restored the condition of affairs for the better and, through the common consent of his monks—an act of kindness and compassion on the part of that pious man, and indeed of the monks of Fulda—recalled Ratgarius from exile.

5. Eigil was succeeded by Rabanus in the year 822, and he governed the monastery for twenty years. Later compelled to resign, he subsequently became archbishop of Mainz; we shall relate his Life under the year 856.  
[Col. 0384B]

6. One thing remains for me to observe concerning Eigil: he wrote a little book on the Life of Saint Sturm, the first abbot of Fulda. Rabanus seems to praise this book in poem 14, entitled *To Eigil, on the Book He Wrote*. In the following poem he commends Eigil’s gentleness in these and other verses:

> Priest in age and merits, kindly priest,  
> Eigil, may Christ God save you throughout the world.  
> Be for me what I ask; and in what I desire, be kind:  
> Teacher, shepherd, always my friend and honor.  
> Nor do your admonishing words distress me,  
> Since I know that you always harbor a friendly heart.  
> I speak the truth, and my judgment does not deceive me:  
> I wish to hold you alone, among many, in my heart.  
> Always be the same for me, since I am always the same for you.  
> The friend always loves; he will always be worthy of love.

Candidus likewise praises Eigil’s gentleness, courtesy, and affability in the following Life. From this it is clear that Eigil possessed those qualities which were necessary for correcting Ratgarius’s ferocity.  
[Col. 0384C]

[Col. 0383D]

# LIFE OF SAINT EGIL, BY CANDIDUS, A FULDENSIAN MONK

## AUTHOR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0383]

1. Candidus sends perpetual peace and blessedness in Christ to his most beloved brother and fellow presbyter, Modestus.  
[Col. 0383C]

I also make known to your Charity that last year, when I complained to the lord Abbot Rabanus that I had no companion with me with whom I might advance by disputing and reading in divine literature, he gave me this answer:

> “Exercise yourself,” he said, “by reading, and add some useful work by composing. For when I once lived in the same place where you now reside, I began, under divine inspiration, a book in prose and verse in praise of the holy cross, and completed it through diligent labor for the faithful to read.”  
> [Col. 0383D]

Therefore, brother, relying upon this permission, I completed, by God’s gift, two books on the Life of our abbot Eigil, composing and writing them: I set out one in prose and the other in verse. I nevertheless asked that they be joined into a single work, so that in the narration of events each might assist the other.

In them I have reverently expressed the clemency shown toward us by Louis, the most serene Augustus. Although I could not explain in full his admonition and instruction exactly as they were delivered by him, I nevertheless took care to unfold his benevolent intention according to the law of God and the teachings of the holy Fathers, so that through this work of mercy his memory and that of his descendants might always remain in holy prayer among us and our successors.  
[Col. 0384D]

This work, therefore, most beloved brother, I have gathered, by God’s gift, for the advancement and benefit of its readers, and have dedicated it to you, servant of God, so that it may remain continually with you in memory of your former teacher. Farewell.

# THE LIFE BEGINS

[Col. 0385]

2. From the time when the venerable Father Eigil persuaded me, by his intimate exhortation, to set down in writing the Life of Baugulf, our dear abbot, who had already been released from the prison of the body—  
[Note: [Col. 0385D] I suspect that this Life has been lost, since Browerus, who examined the records of the monastery of Fulda, did not see it. See the preliminary observations, no. 3.]  
—from that time onward I was pleased to commend to memory the benevolence, zeal, and gravity of so great a Father.

3. This man, born of freeborn parents in the province of Noricum, was transferred not long after the martyrdom of blessed Boniface, for the sake of serving God, to the monastery situated in the Bochonic forest beside the bank of the river Fulda. Because of its proximity, this monastery is commonly called Fulda. There the martyr of Christ, Boniface, rests in his sacred body; and at that time the venerable Styrm, his kinsman, of whom we are speaking, appeared to govern the company of monks by a worthy manner of life. To him the still very young Eigil was brought from his homeland and honorably presented by his parents. Having softened him with paternal affection and caresses, his father ordered him to be associated, for the sake of learning, with the school community, where divine law is learned and taught through constant practice with the utmost diligence. There, with divine grace supplying his aid, he soon advanced daily so far in the contemplation of the knowledge contained in Scripture that he seemed even to imitate hungry bees in gathering flowers.  
[Note: [Col. 0385D] That is, “schools,” as the following passage requires, not the novices’ cells, which are sometimes understood by the word “school,” as our Menardus noted in chapter 15 of the *Concordia Regularum*.]

4. But after not many years had passed, strengthened in God’s service, he became a monk. He was dear to his abbot and gracious to the entire congregation, keeping in mind the justice of God, which God had taught him from his youth, so that he might proclaim His wonders. From this point onward, as time passed and by divine dispensation he was promoted, he was ordained priest by Lullus, bishop of the church of Mainz, who, after Saint Boniface, the great and chosen pontiff of God, was the first to hold the episcopate of that city.  
[Col. 0385C]

5. Meanwhile Styrm, the first abbot and founder of the monastery of Fulda—whom Saint Boniface, his teacher, was accustomed to call “his hermit”—worn out by illness and old age, began to grow weak. Not long afterward, an old man and full of days, he departed in peace from this temporal light to the light which, we believe, endures without end.

Baugulf the German, a monk of that same monastery, succeeded him. When he had ceased to hold office, Ratgarius was elected father of the monastery by the brothers’ remarkable unanimity. When Ratgarius had already been deposed because of a certain discord which the members of the head of all quarrels had sown between him and his brothers, the care and assistance of Louis, the most serene Augustus, immediately arose on our behalf.

[Note: [Col. 0385D] That is, deposed. The *Fulda Annals*, under the year 817: “Ratgarius, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, accused by the brothers and convicted, is deposed.”] Our misery had moved his heart so deeply that he said he had never experienced such sorrow, except that which had befallen him through the death of his father, Charles, of blessed memory.

Accordingly, he sent his messengers Aaron and Adalfrid with their companions, namely, Western monks, to console and support us in the trial of our temporal misery and, if anything concerning the observances of the Rule had either been begun or fallen into neglect among us, to correct it by fraternal love and admonition.  
[Note: [Col. 0386D] That is, Frankish monks: Gaul is western Germany, New Francia, and at that time was called “the West.” I do not wish to guess from which monastery Aaron and Adalfrid came. Among the enrolled brothers of the monastery of Saint Gall, an Aaron is listed as a monk from the monastery of Saint Peter at the fountain of Bosua in Burgundy.]

6. For a long time we lived in the monastery, leading a quiet life under their direction, with a provost and deans appointed by them. Later the community of brothers, having taken counsel with Aaron and his companions, sent Adalfrid, one of them—a man who, as it seemed to us, was well-mannered—and with him some of our own brothers, to the emperor’s clemency, to see whether he might perhaps deign to advise those who were unworthy concerning the election of an abbot.

After receiving them kindly, he granted permission for the election and explained clearly that the election should be conducted according to the authority of the Rule, repeatedly recalling the severity of an undiscerning shepherd. When this delegation had returned and entered the monastery of Fulda, it assembled the brothers and explained the emperor’s mandate as follows:

> “Brothers, Louis, the serene Augustus, sends you greetings. The election you requested he has granted with a cheerful countenance. Moreover, he repeatedly insisted that you should elect for this office a man—if such a one exists—who wishes and is able to be your father according to God and the authority of the holy Rule.”

When the brothers heard these words, they bowed down in worship and gave thanks to the emperor. Afterwards the elders persuaded the entire congregation to strive to commend this matter to God’s will through earnest prayers, and always to refer it to His will by conferring and discussing together.  
[Col. 0386C]

7. In the meantime, however, when a question arose, considerable disagreement developed, as often happens among a crowd of differing wills. Such a crowd, tossed and wavering in tumult, cannot reach the harbor of truth unless it submits to unity. Speeches among the brothers increased in turn; words came out into the open, while more often murmuring took place in secret. Some insisted that one man, others that another, should preside over them.

One group desired a man whom another rejected. In all these conversations the severity of the abbot they had lost was constantly held up as an example: it was not so much his own wickedness as that of his flatterers and accusers that had overthrown him.

Some of the brothers tried to create an abbot for themselves from a noble family, saying:

> “If we accept this man, he will defend us against counts and those more powerful than ourselves; indeed, by his rank he will make the emperor favorable toward us. Do you know why? Because he has noble connections at the palace.”

Another opposed this argument, saying:

> “Cease, brothers, from this lofty and noble election, for God has chosen the weak and contemptible things of the world. Weakness in God is innocence, while low birth is humility. Innocence without God is considered weakness, and humility not undertaken for God is judged lowliness. If we bow our necks to such a man—not to nobility, I say, but to lowliness—where will we turn if he who oppresses us turns against us? If we humbly urge him to keep quiet, perhaps, moved by even greater anger, he will not keep quiet, because he trusts in his relatives.”

While they were arguing in this way, another, seated somewhat nearer, affirmed that a father endowed with learning ought preferably to be chosen; another favored a young man, and another a man of moderate qualities.

Others, on the contrary, reconsidering the matter, said:

> “If we promote a learned and excessively eloquent man, and later he abandons sound teaching and becomes angry and obstinate against the commandment of truth, what shall we do? He knows many syllogisms, and he crushes us when, with severity, we humbly bring some matter before him, even if we have a just complaint. Or perhaps—and this is both to be feared and lamented—if we give a necessary reply to his obstinacy, he will say: ‘Why are you contending with me, when the Rule forbids a monk to contend with his abbot?’ Thus, whenever he wishes and as often as he wishes, he will call a necessary admonition contention. Therefore, brothers, fearing everything that might be dangerous, we are afraid and do not know where to turn.

“We have indeed been terrified in many matters, because, as the common saying goes, ‘A burned man fears fire.’ Do not the things we have mentioned seem to us either already to have happened or capable of happening in the future? Some of our own men, whom your fraternity knows well by name, under the pretext of some usefulness, have been sent into exile to other monasteries because of some very small reply or necessary word, and deprived of their proper place. And what at that time was truly pitiable both to say and to see: old men and the decrepit were dragged unwillingly to various places without any compassion. Do you know, brothers, whether these things are so? We certainly know that you do, and nothing concerning these matters can be hidden from you, since you have long possessed knowledge of them.”

Thus, brother Modestus, the question that had arisen was discussed, and those who held differing opinions about such persons spoke in this way and that. Nor were companions of the same age absent from this exchange of words. Although they stood in a corner, they whispered as follows:

> “If we set you or you over us, tell us, we beg you, truthfully whether you would then do us good. We certainly think you would and would do so, for you know under what tribulation, and with what danger to body and soul, we lived together in this monastery under a contentious abbot. Therefore we believe that you would have pity on us. You know where he went astray, and you will not turn in that direction.
