“It would be shameful in your case if you later did what you previously hated; and if you once blamed another who had been placed in authority for many things, but were later found blameworthy in the same authority for the same things. This would be especially shameful because now you detest these actions with us, reject them, and judge the actions of your ruler.

“What do you say to this? Perhaps you promise us every good thing according to your ability. But when you have been elected to this office, which we desire, we shall fear that a time may come when you forget your brotherly and humane concern for us and become like a lion, after the manner of your predecessor, overturning your household in your own house and oppressing those subject to you.  
[Note: [Col. 0387D] Namely, Abbot Ratgarius.]

“You also know the weakness of our character and bodies, and none of the secrets of our condition is hidden from you. Therefore, above all, we suspect that, if you become estranged from us, you will set the claws of detraction upon our backs and, by deriding us, disgrace us on the basis of some suspicion concerning the wrongful actions of our youth.”

Such was the conversation of minds divided in different directions, and in this way the wandering of their hearts came out into the open.  
[Col. 0388B]

8. At that time the crowd of our brothers was therefore greatly confused, and no sign of simplicity had yet appeared among them. But when this disagreement had arisen and was coming to an end, the leading group of the elders raised its voice and, with sounder counsel, said:

> “Let us first pray, brothers, to the goodness of almighty God, that according to His will He may hear us as we pray, and grant us to ask for what He Himself knows to be expedient for us, so that, praying according to His will, we may deserve to be saved through Him who wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

After this holy and salutary instruction from the elders, and after the prayer had been completed, the brothers gathered and sat together. The leading group of the elders then strengthened them again with these words:

> “Take courage, brothers, take courage, and let there be among you one heart and one soul in God. For the love of God and neighbor, let none of you seek what is useful only to himself, but what is useful to many, so that in this love we may be called and may truly be Christ’s disciples.

“Moreover, under the inspiration and guidance of the Holy Spirit, it has seemed good to us—if this accords with your will—that Father Eigil, because of his mature age and, indeed, the gravity of his character, would be a more suitable successor to the office from which the man who previously presided over us was removed.”

At these words the entire multitude of monks immediately consented to their counsel and action, although a few, seized by fear because of his firmness of mind, faltered in this agreement.

For he was steadfast and sound-minded, firm of heart and severe toward the undisciplined, but gentle toward the meek and well-mannered, so that they might advance toward better things. He was cheerful in face, joyful in mind, discerning in action, and cooperative in what was useful. He did not consent to hear the trifles and empty babblings of accusers, knowing that such things disturbed rather than delighted him. As one who loved the peace of his mind, he allowed no suspicion whatsoever to rule it; nor did this simple man take pleasure in the crooked ambushes of secret plots. He prohibited every harmful practice, but pursued especially the crimes of thieves, and by firm action condemned the manifest evils of the guilty.  
[Col. 0389A]

9. After the younger brothers, as has been said, had agreed with the elders concerning the election of an abbot, the brothers openly asked Eigil to undertake the government and care of that monastery: for his own reward and for the brothers’ example, and for the common salvation of both, with divine grace going before and following after.

Although he resisted at length with many arguments, the concord of the brothers consoled him with gentle words:

> “Do not be afraid, father, because we are ready willingly to bear the burden of this labor together with you. We shall not leave you to sweat alone under so great a weight, especially if you now come to our aid of your own free will in this necessity.”

10. At last, scarcely overcome by the brothers’ prayers, he accepted responsibility for the governance imposed upon him, though with great fear.  
[Note: [Col. 0389D] Namely, in the year 818, for which year the *Fulda Annals* state: “Eigil was elected and ordained abbot of the monastery of Fulda.”]

He openly declared that he had not avoided so great a labor for the sake of human praise, but because, on account of his old age and weakness, he had wished to withdraw from so difficult and arduous a task.  
[Col. 0389C]

11. Not many days afterward, this newly appointed father, together with Aaron the presbyter, the first among the Western monks, and accompanied by a crowd of brothers, approached the emperor. After greeting them mercifully, he addressed them in these words:

> “You, fathers, brothers, and my beloved sons, know—and I know, and nearly my entire kingdom also knows—how many dangers have surrounded you from the time of my father Charles, of blessed memory, until now. But since by divine mercy you have now been saved, lift up your hearts in the Lord and drive away the sorrowful fear of this storm and the dreadful anxieties of your minds.

“Order your way of life according to the fear of God and the authority of the holy Rule, so that, remaining in it, you may be heirs of the kingdom of God. For if you accepted the very small Rule at the beginning  
[Note: [Col. 0390D] Thus Saint Benedict modestly calls his Rule in the final chapter of the Rule.]  
and placed your confidence in it, trusting the promise of the blessed man of God Benedict that you would attain eternal life, why did you neglect so great a good by abandoning your place and your law because of the obstinacy of one fellow servant? Who bewitched you so completely that you did not obey the truth?

“My father, recently mentioned above, once thought—and I myself, born to the empire, supposed—that if I had wished to violate your law and observance, God forbid, you would in no way have consented to me. For you have not yet resisted unto blood. It is shameful to abandon so easily the law of truth and the holy place because of the threats of one man, when many saints have struggled to the death for the law of their God and have not feared the words of the wicked.

“Why did they do this? Because they were founded upon Christ, the firmest rock.

“You, brothers, possess knowledge of the divine Scriptures; you possess the examples of the holy Fathers who came before you; and you also possess the Rule specially established for you. In these things, without doubt, you can contemplate yourselves as in a mirror: what sort of people you are and toward what you are striving.

“For whatever things were written,” the apostle Paul says, “were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we might have hope” (*Romans* 15).

“The first ordinance of the law, given to Moses on Mount Sinai, was this: ‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your mind, with all your strength, and with all your soul; and, secondly, your neighbor as yourself’ (*Deuteronomy* 6). The love of God is empty unless the love of neighbor is added to it. Therefore the commandment of truth is complete when the indivisible rule of charity remains in the mind.

“The complete care of monastic discipline is love; it urges this bond of charity and peace without greed. In sincere love, therefore, a sufficient measure is found for those who are present, and those who love one another are called children of the kingdom because they love one another perfectly. These are the ones who eat bread in the kingdom of God; they live without blemish and are strangers to the wrinkle of discord.

“Strive, therefore, brothers, to please God, living a spiritual way of life and preserving His divine commandments. Let the precepts of the law, with wisdom, be in the darkness of your hearts. Do not be wise beyond what the simplicity of God’s Scriptures affirms. For many who thought differently about God have fallen away from love of God and of their neighbors.

“If you have any disagreements among you, cast them away from one another, knowing that God is not a God of sedition but of peace. Forgive one another, and let each one, according to the commandment of the Gospel, release his brothers from their debts and from their griefs and resentments. If there is any quarrel, let it be driven away from the choir of the saints.

“Free your hearts through the fear of God, so that, falsehood having been expelled, truth may rule, and, wars having ceased, the tranquility of peace may return. Then you may walk in it before God and human beings.

“I urge you all equally to love one another in Christ, so that you may serve God and concord, not the various desires of your eyes, the deceitful frauds of swelling knowledge, or the vices of the flesh. From these arise schisms, contempt for the law of God, contention, and evil thoughts, which, boiling with the fire of anger, burst out like water and foam over the pleasures of the body.

“The Book of Wisdom plainly proclaims that because of sins human beings have suffered hunger, pestilence, mortality, and beasts. The human race is known to have labored under these misfortunes from the beginning of the world until now, and especially now, because, as the Apostle says, ‘perilous times are at hand, and people are lovers of themselves, accumulating teachers for themselves according to the desires of their hearts’ (*2 Timothy* 4).

“This wickedness appears to reign in certain monasteries, neither to a moderate degree nor secretly, but openly and unhappily, when certain more powerful persons in a congregation attempt, through presumptuous contention, to appoint as abbots men who agree with them, so that, once those men are in power, they themselves may likewise dominate everyone and all the offices of the monastery may be arranged solely according to their counsel, whatever its quality.

“From these things arise presumptuous behavior toward companions, indignation, unjust judgments, evil counsels, blind accusations, whisperings, and other evils that are shown to be unfit for monastic life. From this also burst forth animosities, contradictions, enmities, constant murmurings, and other harmful things, by which those ensnared will be subjected to danger.

“But once these matters have been exposed wherever they exist, all faithful people in Christ must hasten to act, so that the authors of dissension may be rebuked by zeal for justice and those who produce it may be removed from the midst of the brothers, according to the Apostle’s command: ‘Remove the evil one from among yourselves’ (*1 Corinthians* 5), until they are healed of such a disease by worthy satisfaction.

“All these things, therefore, my most beloved brothers, I have carefully explained to you, insofar as I could, for the warning and salvation of your souls.

“For this reason also, brothers, be prudent, and keep watch in this election with the gaze of your minds, so that it may be according to God and the institution of the holy Rule. For if someone, as Cassian says (*Institutes*, book II, chapter 3), has not been trained under an elder according to the institutions of the Rule, he will never be able in any way to preside over a congregation of brothers. He has not learned through obedience what he ought to command those younger than himself who will obey him, nor has he first acquired from the institutions of his elders what he ought to hand on to his juniors.

“No one will ever be able to give saving precepts to disciples who listen to him unless he has first been trained in every discipline of the virtues. For our Fathers truly said that governing others well is the highest gift and grace of the Holy Spirit.

“Moreover, each of these evils is mentioned by blessed Pope Gregory in the *Pastoral Book*: the evils that are often committed by subjects against prelates and often by prelates against subjects. Those who preside consider all their subjects less wise than themselves, while those who are subject judge the actions of their rulers and think that, if they themselves happened to hold authority, they could act better.

“Consequently, it often happens that rulers see less wisely what ought to be done, because the very cloud of exaltation darkens their eyes. And sometimes the one who was subject, once he has become a prelate, does what he had previously criticized when he was subject; and although he perpetrates the things he had judged, he is ashamed merely because he had judged them.

“Nor do I pass over what the same pope says in the same book concerning the empty fear of certain prelates. ‘We often know,’ he says, ‘that those who preside commonly demand from their subjects an improper fear of themselves, and wish to be revered not so much for the Lord as in place of the Lord. Within themselves they exalt themselves through the swelling of their hearts and despise all their subjects in comparison with themselves. They do not advise by condescending to them, but presume by dominating them. In lofty thought they raise themselves up and do not recognize as their equals those over whom they have happened to preside.’

“Against this swelling the book of Ecclesiasticus says: ‘They have appointed you a leader; do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of them’ (*Ecclesiasticus* 32). The Lord rebukes this swelling in shepherds through the prophet, saying: ‘But you ruled over them with harshness and power’ (*Ezekiel* 34).

“Therefore, whenever a ruler exalts himself in the fact that he governs others, he is separated through the fall of pride from the service of the supreme Ruler; and when he despises subjects who are his equals, he does not acknowledge the dominion over him of the One under whom all are equal.

“Such men, my brothers, when they are compelled by those who agree with them not so much to benefit the congregation as to preside over it, resist by pretending incapacity. Yet they fear not to attain the office to which they are supposedly dragged unwillingly; and when they have perhaps attained it, they later reveal in various ways how eagerly they had previously desired it in their minds.”

12. And when the emperor’s goodwill had offered these and many other things to the brothers collectively, he said:

> “Bring forward the Father whom you have chosen, so that I may see him and know who he is.”

At these words Father Eigil was immediately and hurriedly presented before him—a man, clearly, of mature age and grave appearance. Looking at him, the emperor said:

> “Is this that brother whom the entire harmonious congregation, with one voice and according to the fear of God and the authority of the holy Rule, approves and requests for itself?”

They replied: “He is.”

> “This man, then, brothers, I now entrust to you according to the fear of God and the authority of the holy Rule, so that he may be your father, shepherd, and brother, in accordance with the monastery of blessed Benedict, who, filled with the Holy Spirit, composed this same Rule for monks with great discernment and commanded his disciples to observe it with him. You, however, as sons, honor this old man, your Father, by your holy conduct and love him with sincere affection. Take care also to show obedience not only to him but eagerly to one another in every good work.
>
> “But you, my Father, strive with every diligence and prudence to preserve your younger brothers according to the will of God, so that, persevering in this holy concord, you may deserve to reach him who descended from heaven for this one purpose: to reconcile the world to God the Father through himself.
>
> “To you who know the law of God I speak. Concerning it I urge nothing else than that you read it and, according to the ability the Lord grants, turn its words into deeds. As for immense buildings and unnecessary works, by which the dependents outside and the congregation of the brothers inside are wearied, dismiss them henceforth altogether in favor of moderation.

> [Note: Candidus brought this maxim—certainly most true and worthy of observance—here from the petition-book of the men of Fulda and adapted it to Louis as speaker. For one must not suppose that the emperor’s exhortation was so verbose. On the moderation to be observed in religious buildings, the letter of Abbot William to the brothers of Mont-Dieu is especially noteworthy.]

Remember how often complaint about this excess disturbed the ears of my father and of us.
>
> “For this purpose divine power, although I am less suitable, has nevertheless appointed me to this empire: that I might be eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, father to the poor, and investigate most diligently any case of which I was ignorant. Therefore I cannot refrain from speaking of what is beneficial to this religious community.
>
> “That John Chrysostom, while eloquently recalling these matters—those who build martyrs’ shrines and adorn churches—says [Homily 35 on Matthew]:
>
> “ ‘For behold,’ he says, ‘those who build martyrs’ shrines and adorn churches seem to be doing a good work. But if they also observe the other justice of God, if the poor rejoice in their goods, and if they do not make the goods of others their own by violence, know that they build for the glory of God. But if they do not observe the other justices of God, if the poor do not rejoice in their goods, if they make the goods of others their own either by violence or by fraud, who is so senseless as not to understand that they build those structures not for the glory of God but for human esteem? And rightly they build martyrs’ shrines where the poor, having suffered violence at their hands, appeal against them. For the martyrs do not rejoice when they are honored with those monies over which the poor weep. What sort of justice is it to reward the dead and strip the living—to take from the blood of the wretched and offer it to God? That is not offering to the Lord; it is wishing to make God an accomplice in one’s violence, as though he would willingly accept money bound to him by sin and consent to sin.
>
> “ ‘Do you wish to build the house of God? Give faithful poor people the means by which they may live, and you have built a rational house of God. Human beings dwell in buildings, but God dwells in holy people. What, then, are those who strip human beings and build martyrs’ shrines? They construct dwellings for human beings and destroy dwellings for God?
>
> “ ‘As for the property of the monastery entrusted to you, my Father, beware lest you recklessly squander it through an audacious judgment, or unjustly order or establish anything, as though you possessed unrestricted authority. Jerome also teaches you this when he writes to Paulinus not to squander the possessions of Christ’s poor. “What benefit,” he says, “is there in walls glittering with gems while Christ dies of hunger in the poor? What you possess is no longer yours; a stewardship has been entrusted to you. Remember Ananias and Sapphira.” They cautiously kept what belonged to them; you must consider lest you recklessly squander Christ’s property—that is, lest through immoderate judgment you give the poor’s property to those who are not poor—and, as the most prudent man said, lest generosity perish through generosity.
>
> “ ‘For many monks, according to the saying of a certain Father, becoming entangled in secular activities and legal business, while wishing to benefit their relatives, have lost their souls. You must therefore take the utmost care lest, through immoderate—or rather audacious—judgment, you give the poor’s property to those who are not poor: namely, the alms of faithful laypeople, which they have offered to the Lord for the salvation of their souls, so that Christ’s poor might be fed.
>
> “ ‘Do not even consent to those subject to you, so that they may dare impudently to distribute to relatives and friends—or, worse still, to rebels—the possessions given to Christ’s poor. For, as it is written, not only those who do evil but also those who consent to evildoers are worthy of punishment.
>
> “ ‘The man of God Benedict composed the Rule in lucid language. It contains no hidden teaching and no obscurity; therefore it needs not exposition but admonition. For this is the narrow gate and the difficult way that leads those who follow it to God. It teaches you to possess such discretion, moderation, and charity that, even when exhorting with charity, you may prevail in cutting away vices, doing everything moderately for the weak, reflecting on the discretion of holy Jacob, and always recalling your own frailty to yourself in all these matters.
>
> “ ‘But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning while she dwelt amid the delights of God’s paradise, so your mind may be corrupted—God forbid—by flatterers and accusers, the vessels, so to speak, of the intelligible serpent, and that you may be cast down with the animals subject to you into a place of misery and calamity.
>
> “ ‘Just as we live in this most perilous world as though upon the sea, where the storm is never absent—and even when there is sometimes no storm, there is always fear of a storm—so those living in this world are never without temptation. Even if temptation does not sometimes occur, there is always fear of temptation. Therefore let us ask divine clemency to grant us the assistance of his grace, so that we may not be overcome by evil but may ourselves overcome every evil.’ ”

13. While recalling these things, the emperor’s benevolent will commended itself to the brothers’ prayers, and he dismissed them to go in peace.

Father Eigil then left the palace with his companions and traveled through Mainz. When he reached the city, he was honorably received by Heistolf, archbishop of that city, and after prayer they sat down. Later the bishop of the city began as follows:

> “Father, let us first praise the Lord our God and offer him abundant thanks, who in his kindness has brought us together and granted us the joy of mutual conversation. In addition, Father, I shall try to remind your beloved familiarity that in this government which you have undertaken you should order your life and teaching in such a way that it may contribute to eternal salvation both for you and for all who are subject to your authority.
>
> “Strive to show yourself to your sons as the kind of father whom you shortly before requested to be made for yourself and your brothers. The model of that request and desire was dictated and written out by you in the following manner and presented to Augustus Charles:

> “[Most merciful emperor, this above all we judged necessary for us and desired above all else: to have unity and concord with our abbot, as we had with our former abbots; to experience in him mercy and familiarity, kindness and moderation; and that he should be kind toward the sick, merciful toward offenders, approachable to the brothers, a comforter of the sorrowful, a helper of those who labor, an assistant to the well-disposed, an encourager of those who strive well, a restorer of the weary, a supporter of those who yield, and a restorer of those who fall; that he should love all the brothers, hate none, and persecute no one through the deceit of jealousy or envy; that he should be neither turbulent in appearance, nor anxious in mind, nor excessive in judgment, nor obstinate in counsel, but cheerful in face, joyful in mind, discerning in action, and cooperative in what is beneficial.
>
> “ ‘And when one of the brothers had been caught in some offense, he should not immediately torture him with tyrannical vengeance, but hasten to correct him with merciful discipline; and when he had reformed, he should receive him kindly, neither wearying him again with a wicked suspicion nor driving him out through perpetual hatred.’]”

> [Note: This petition, enclosed in brackets, is found as no. 20 of the petition submitted by the monks of Fulda to Charlemagne, which we shall later see in full.]

“What more elevated or clearer statement could be made, Father, about such a person? It is therefore clear what sort of father you first wished to be made; now be such a one to your brothers, and you will have praise from God and from people of good will.”

14. While he was offering these and other admonitions, he ordered the servants to prepare a more worthy meal for the guests than usual. Meanwhile he himself returned to the church to offer praise to God. Afterwards he honorably received the abbot and his company into his house, and when the table had been set they ate together with thanksgiving.

A reading was plainly given at table according to the priest’s arrangement. When it had ended, spiritual conversation arose among them, so that spiritual nourishment might assist bodily food; and the varied benefits of the churches of God were discussed in many forms. Both men were joyful in God. The watchman—the archbishop—rejoiced that he had been worthy to receive Christ in his guest; the Father rejoiced that true reception of Christ had shone forth in Christ’s minister.

15. After they had mutually strengthened one another through various benefits, Father Eigil requested leave from the bishop and, having been blessed, set out for Fulda.

> [Note: The blessing, or ordination—or consecration—of an abbot by a bishop was ancient. It is mentioned in several letters of Gregory the Great, namely Book VII, Letters 18 of the first indiction and 94 of the second indiction; also in chapter 93 of the Rule of the Master; in Books I and II of Bede’s History of His Monastery; in the Councils of Becanceld toward the end of the seventh century and of Celichyth, chapter 8, at the beginning of the ninth century, in Spelman; and finally in the Roman Ordinal.]

When he arrived, his monks came out to meet him. Receiving him with due honor, they led him to prayer. After prayer had been completed, they prostrated themselves on the ground in the oratory and greeted the abbot. He kindly and humbly returned their greeting and kissed them peacefully, singing together with them, according to the custom of the Fathers, this song of David:

> “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together.”

And great joy arose in the church, where they had assembled in the Lord’s name.

16. Not long afterwards this venerable man, moved by great love for the worship of God, began to cleanse the places of the church. He ordered the pavements to be renewed and likewise commanded altars to be made in suitable places, covered above with polished stones. In the same church he constructed two crypts in magnificent workmanship: one facing the rising sun and the other extending toward the setting sun.

17. After he had placed these and many other ornaments of various kinds in the temple of God, he sent a letter, with the brothers’ advice, to Archbishop Heistolf, asking him to come to dedicate the church constructed in praise of almighty God, so that through these pious services of work a reward from God might remain for both men in the future and the kindly memory of holy prayer might be frequently renewed among people in the world.

The archbishop therefore came at the time appointed for him, in accordance with the abbot’s request. Many other bishops, abbots, priests, and counts also came, honorably invited by the abbot of the monastery. Moreover, summoned by fame, the common people of the lower orders came from different directions and gathered together for the dedication of this temple.

> [Note: This took place in the year 819, according to Rabanus in the poem addressed to Heilstulf and prefixed to the books on the Instruction of Clergy, which he dedicated to him. The dedication is also said to have taken place on the Kalends of November in Rabanus’s Martyrology. Rabanus likewise recorded the day and year in his notation—as he calls it—of this event in Browerus, Book II of The Antiquities of Fulda, chapter 3.]

Meanwhile the blessed day of the dedication arrived, illumined by the flashing light of the perpetual sun. The bishop proceeded in full ecclesiastical vestments and dedicated the temple constructed in the monastery of Fulda in honor of the holy Savior, namely our God and Lord Jesus Christ. The body of Christ’s martyr Boniface was transferred to the place that Father Eigil had prepared for him together with his brothers, as the following book makes perfectly clear (Book II, chapter 17).

At the dedication of the temple the people of God sang praise to God, and a sweet sound resounded from their mouths. Great joy filled the church of God, gathered together in his name.

18. When the work of God had been completed, the bishop was invited to the table so that, refreshed with spiritual food, he might also be restored with bodily food because of his bodily weakness. A reading from the law of God had been given at table, with a question from the reading interspersed from time to time. When it had been read through, spiritual conversation arose among them, grave and distinguished as they were in mind, and the various benefits of the churches of God were discussed among them in many ways.

After the meal they rose from the table and recited a verse. Then, after celebrating the evening praises and completing Compline, they were overcome by sleep and rested.

[Col. 0397A]

19. On the following day Humbert, chorepiscopus,

> [Note: I would prefer *coepiscopus*; for Humbert, bishop of Würzburg, suffragan of the archbishop of Mainz, seems to be intended here. At Rabanus’s request he transferred the relics of the martyrs in the monastery of Holzkirchen, as Rabanus records in epigram 63. Rabanus also wrote Bishop Humbert a letter on the question of in which degree marriage between blood relatives is permitted.]

at the command of his archbishop Heistolf, consecrated the two crypts of the church and reverently completed the whole work entrusted to him by divine authority with the utmost reverent fear of God.

Rabanus the teacher carefully committed to memory in writing the day, time, number, and year of this dedication, as well as the names of the saints whose relics had been planted there.

> [Note: These verses are extant among the poems of Rabanus, as are others concerning the blessing of a cemetery, which will be mentioned below.]

When this holy and salutary solemnity had been completed, the bishop and all the people returned joyfully to their dwellings.

20. Thereafter the diligent Father of the monastery, learning the joys of common life, built, with the advice and consent of the brothers, a small round church,

> [Note: Benedict, abbot of Aniane, likewise ordered the Oratory of Saint John to be built in the brothers’ cemetery. It was also the custom of our order to have a separate cemetery with a chapel outside the cloister.]

where the bodies of deceased brothers, committed to burial, rest. They call it a cemetery, which in Greek is κοιμητήριον (*koimētērion*) and is translated into Latin as *dormitorium*, “sleeping place.”

The structure of this building rises powerfully beneath the ground, where a passageway encircles a cavern, from one stone column placed in the center, with arches joined to it on either side. Above, it is raised on eight columns, and at the summit of the work it is closed with a single stone.

This venerable and aforementioned Father, together with his companions, fashioned this building—though I do not know what great thing they had in mind—having been taught by divine instruction. Nevertheless, without prejudice to the faith, I think that it can signify the figure of Christ and the Church.

The apostle Paul, himself also called by the Lord a vessel of election, clearly declared to his hearers that the Church of Christ, joined together from living stones—that is, holy human beings—is the dwelling place of God:

> “For the temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3).

Christ Jesus is the chief architect and founder of this structure, its foundation and column, remaining always immovable through the power of perpetual majesty. In him every building constructed grows into a holy temple in the Lord.

What is signified by the fact that the completion of this building is brought to perfection at the top by one stone is suggested by the same teacher, who teaches us to pray with attentive mind that he who began a good work in us may perfect it until the day of Christ Jesus (Philippians 1), so that all our work may always begin from God and, having begun through him, be brought to completion.

The eight columns standing in this temple of the Lord appropriately correspond to the eight beatitudes that the Lord himself set forth in the Gospel, so that all who fulfill these sayings of Jesus, four times two, may deserve to be regarded as supports in this church of Christ.

The circle of the church, which is bounded by no end and contains within it the paths of life—that is, the divine sacraments, the kingdom of everlasting majesty, the hope of eternal life, and the enduring rewards with which the righteous are crowned forever—seems not inappropriately to signify these things.

21. This temple, which the venerable man constructed with great love of piety, was dedicated by Heistolf, bishop of the Church of Mainz, as he passed through the fields of Thuringia, in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, Saint Michael the archangel of Christ, and the other saints.

The same teacher mentioned above also elegantly expressed in verse and prose the day, number, time, and year of its dedication, together with the names of the saints whose relics were buried there, as the following volume clearly demonstrates to attentive readers.

> [Note: Browerus records both accounts in Book II, chapter 5. In prose: “In the year 822 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fifteenth indiction, this cemetery was dedicated by Heilstulf, archbishop of the Church of Mainz, in the month of January, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, in honor of Saint Michael the archangel, Saint John the Evangelist, Saint Abundus the martyr, Saint Amandus the confessor, and many other holy martyrs and confessors of Christ.” After the oratory had been renovated, another dedication was performed by Foleram, bishop of Minden, in 1092, on the fourth day before the Nones of December, at the request of Abbot Ruthard.]

22. After the matters pertaining to the worship of God had been carried out in this way, this same venerable man, although already worn down by old age and illness, nevertheless conceived the plan of building the monastery cloister anew.

The brothers were summoned for counsel. The question was where the cloister could most suitably be placed. Some advised that it be constructed on the southern side of the basilica, according to the former custom. Others maintained that it would be better, in the Roman fashion, to place it on the western side,

> [Note: Note the ancient custom of the Italians of turning cloisters toward the west.]

because of the proximity of the martyr, who rested in that part of the basilica. The elders accepted their counsel, and the rest of the brothers likewise agreed.

When they had thus been gathered into unity, the dimensions of the work were immediately laid out. The earth was dug up, and the master builders accordingly laid the foundations.

In this work—and not only in this one but also in all the monastery’s undertakings—the brothers and the abbot displayed equal care, will, and zeal. He willingly listened to the brothers’ counsel and very often enjoyed their conversations. For he knew what is written:

> “Do everything with counsel” (Proverbs 13).

Therefore he did not consider himself superior or wiser than the others, nor did he, in empty pride, suppose that he had no need of another’s consultation [possibly *consolation*, “comfort”]. Nevertheless, whenever he made an error through insufficient prudence in some matter, he conceived it more through the introduction of others who were less prudent than through his own invention.

23. He therefore loved his brothers, as the holy Rule teaches (Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 2), especially those whom he knew to be zealous in the service of God and in divine reading. Among them he permitted me also—although unworthy and the least of God’s servants—to enter into his familiarity and joy through the affection of a devoted Father.

He also often received a discussion with the teacher Rabanus, who was bound to him by special familiarity.

> [Note: Some call such discussion of spiritual matters *collatio*, “conference,” as has been observed elsewhere. Candidus uses the word in the same sense in the preface to this Life, where he laments that he had no companion with whom he could make progress in divine reading by discussion and reading.]

Frequently, while engaged in discussion, he stirred us together with Rabanus in his presence for this one purpose: that, according to Solomon’s saying, “the wise man who hears becomes wiser” (Proverbs 1).

With every diligence and prudence he labored to guard the flock entrusted to him in God’s service, with the help of divine grace. He persecuted no one through the deceit of jealousy or envy; he wearied no one with wicked suspicion, nor did he drive anyone out through perpetual hatred.

In his days there was peace among the brothers, one heart and one soul in God; no one disturbed the monastery, strengthened as it was in such delightful concord. They rejoiced to show the good of obedience, not only to the abbot but also to one another, with the greatest reverence, knowing that by this way of obedience they would go to God.

This venerable man remained so safe and cheerful in the government he had undertaken until the end of his life that neither the congregation seemed to cause him any disturbance nor he to cause any disturbance to the congregation of monks. This is not surprising, because, as was said above, they were one heart and one soul in God.

24. As he had always been accustomed to do, he likewise established and decreed, with the advice and consent of his brothers, that the brothers who were known to oversee ministries outside the monastery should, during each week of the year, serve the brothers remaining inside the monastery in food, drink, and every other convenience appropriate to monastic life, beyond the allowance assigned to them, for their proper refreshment—not under compulsion, but voluntarily, insofar as their expenses permitted, according to the arrangement of the provost or deans.

> [Note: Saint Benedict exempts the cellarer, the sick, and those who happen to be occupied with more important business from service at table in chapter 35 of the Rule.]

He himself, however, first undertook the beginning of this service on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, with joy, as an example to the others.

> [Note: The Lives of Saint Salaberga and others teach us that abbots and abbesses served their subjects in the kitchen, either in rotation or on certain days of the year. The Rule of Saint Ferreolus likewise prescribes this three times a year in chapter 38, as does the manuscript Ritual of Bec. Finally, at Cluny the abbot and cellarer took charge of the kitchen at Christmas, as Udalric records in Book I, chapter 46, of The Customs of Cluny.]

He imposed these arrangements upon the brothers living outside precisely so that through these works of charity they might obtain a reward from God and might not, despite their distance, depart from the command of the Rule, which orders the brothers to serve one another.

25. With similar counsel and devotion this man of good will also decreed that the anniversary of Sturmi [correctly, Stirmi], the first abbot and founder of the monastery of Fulda, and the commemoration of all our brothers who had died from this life should be celebrated on the feast of Saint Ignatius, martyr of Christ, which is counted shortly below from this anniversary. He established that the commemoration should be observed, through the intercession of so great a patron, in the celebration of Masses, in psalmody, and in holy prayer.

> [Note: The anniversary of Abbot Sturmi and the founders of the monastery had already been observed before Eigil’s administration, as is clear from the beginning of the petition. But Abbot Eigil restored it by his decree and ordered it to be celebrated more solemnly, namely on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January.]

When this decree had been read to the entire congregation and they had then been asked whether it pleased them, all replied: “It pleases us.”

But lest anyone perhaps consider this celebration superstitious and empty, let him read the Conferences of the holy Fathers; there he will find an example of this festival.

> [Note: Namely, in Conference 19, chapter 1.]

On that same day, out of reverence for so great a solemnity, he ordered the brothers’ meal to be prepared with greater care and greater pleasure than usual, in accordance with the requirements of monastic life.

He also commanded that the book which, by the grace of Christ, he had recently composed about the life of the aforesaid abbot and the origin of the monastery should be read to the brothers at table, so that, hearing in it the wonders of divine action, they might strive to give thanks to divine majesty and that all the joy of the festival might resound to his praise.

26. Among his other works of piety, he is rightly praised for having performed this act of mercy: he freed from exile his predecessor, whom he had once avoided with his companions by fleeing as though from a persecutor, after that man had been sent into exile by the emperor as the cause of their disturbance. He did this at the request of his brothers.

Augustus admired their faith and mercy so greatly that he said they had truly prayed for their persecutor, in accordance with the command of the Truth.

Therefore, brother Modestus, according to the Apostle’s admonition, humble yourselves beneath the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you in the time of tribulation, casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you.

Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. May God grant you aid to resist his most wicked will, for without God human frailty can accomplish nothing good.

Let it not seem to the reader that the frequent mention above of this disturbance is a calumny, since no harm is recognized as having come from the threefold denial of Peter, chief of the apostles, even though it is often recited in the Church. Struck by divine visitation, he wiped it away with the bitterest tears.

There is no doubt that this happened to him so that he might know that he should place his confidence not in a human being but in him of whom the Psalmist said:

> “It is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes.”

It also happened so that he might learn through his own fault how, when later placed in authority, he ought to show mercy to others.

The apostle Paul likewise became a persecutor of Christ in the members of Christ; but he who had once been a teacher of error, rebuked by a divine voice, became a disciple of truth.

Lot’s wife, too, while fleeing the fires of Sodom, was changed into a pillar of salt, as seasoning for the faithful; for the punishment of the guilty is the instruction of the righteous.

Even dung spread around a barren tree is often known to benefit it. In the same way, for a person who acts negligently regarding God’s commandments, remembrance of his sins often contributes to eternal salvation: struck by divine mercy through it, he comes back to life and produces from himself the fruits of good works, a most fragrant offering to the Lord God.

I have recorded these testimonies from divine reading in this book, brother Modestus, so that no one may place hope in himself but may place his hope in God; and so that whoever thinks he is standing may take care lest he fall. Whoever falls through pride, when corrected by divine reading, should strive to rise again through humility with God’s help. Thus every sinner established in the Church may, with right faith, hope for forgiveness from God through humble confession and true repentance.

27. As I mentioned above, when the construction of the cloister had already advanced upward in part, the same venerable Father was struck by illness and began to grow seriously weak.

When he then saw the time of his death approaching, he asked to be carried for the sake of prayer to the cemetery mentioned above. Afterward, taking a mattock, he marked out the place of his grave on the eastern side of the cemetery. As far as his illness permitted, he himself struck the earth first and dug.

He prepared a sarcophagus in the place of the tomb and humbly requested that after his death they bury him in it.

When he had been brought back from there into the house, he fell hopelessly onto his bed and realized that he was going to die. When the brothers heard this, they came to visit him and pour out prayers to God for the departure of his soul. Seeing them, he rejoiced at their arrival, and his soul delighted in their prayer.

28. Meanwhile the brothers asked him to cleanse himself, by confession—though hidden—and worthy repentance, so that he might depart from this world purer: if he had injured anyone, he should ask forgiveness; or if he had been injured by anyone, he should simply grant forgiveness.

He willingly listened to the brothers’ admonition and said:

> “If I have injured anyone, I ask forgiveness with humble supplication; and if I had been injured by anyone, let God forgive him [the text reads *dicitur*; corrected to *Deus*], and I truly forgive him from the depths of my heart.”

When he had spoken these words as one already dying, he commended himself to God and to the prayers of his brothers. Drawing his body together upon the bed, he breathed out his spirit.

> [Note: The year 822 is recorded by the Annals of Fulda in these words: “Eigil, abbot of the monastery of Fulda, died, and Rabanus succeeded him.” The day has until now been unknown. In Book II of The Fulda Traditions, pages 527–528, there is a grant made to Abbot Eigil “on the sixth day before the Nones of August, in the ninth year of the reign of Emperor Louis”; and on pages 532–533 I find a donation made to Abbot Rabanus “in the year 822 of the Lord’s incarnation, in the fifteenth indiction, in the ninth year of Louis’s reign, in the month of October, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.” From these facts I conclude that Eigil’s day of death fell within the period extending from the sixth day before the Nones of August, when the earlier grant was made to him, to the fifth day before the Kalends of November, when the other was made to his successor Rabanus.]

When the brothers saw this, terrified and already placed in anguish, they mourned the Father’s death, knowing what sort of Father they had possessed and not knowing what sort they would receive.

For no one, brother Modestus, can know—except one who has learned it through experience—how great a misery it often is for sons when their lawful father is taken from them and a stepfather follows: their own mother falls, and a stepmother succeeds her.

This was clearly shown by those two women who quarreled over a living child before the judgment seat of Solomon, king of Jerusalem.

After this the brothers, according to the custom of the Fathers, carried the body of their beloved elder. Singing and praying, they bore it into the church. When the prayer had been completed there, they lifted his body and buried it in the tomb that he had prepared for himself while alive, trusting in resurrection on the day of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power forever. Amen.

[Col. 0401]

## A Metrical Life by the Same Author, Candidus the Monk

### Preface: Candidus to His Brother Modestus

This poem, behold, Candidus sang

Spontaneously for his own brother Modestus,

Recalling the glorious deeds of the chosen Father,

And his departure [transit] and subsequent noble end.

Therefore he asks this plowman [arator],

And all who read, whether eager or idle,

Not rashly to tear apart this slender heap of grain

With the teeth of an ant.

Rather he asks, with bowed head

And humbled breast,

That a brother properly reread this work

And consign it not to dark bears and birds.

The preface of Candidus to Modestus ends. They are called Bruun and Reccheo by their proper names [the text has the singular *nuncupatur*, “is called,” but the plural is required by the context].

## The Life Begins: Candidus to Modestus

Ever since that aged Father,

Eigil, son of Baugolf, whose years were passing away,

Once bearing the memorable name of Common Father,

Ordered me to commit his life to little letters,

After the blessed man’s command

And his solemn wishes,

I have not been reluctant—and am not now reluctant—to remember

His grave character and manly spirit.

Therefore, brother—than whom no other is superior—it delights me

To consecrate to you, Modestus,

The heights of this famous old man’s life:

All that I saw, already as a young man and later as an old man,

In his exceptional deeds,

And all that I sometimes heard with my own ears

From the sayings of religious men concerning his pious actions,

Gathered together into one collection.

### Chapter I. The Boy Eigil Is Brought to the Monastery of Fulda

This boy, once noble, arose in the serene region of Noricum.

After spending not much time there,

He was brought away from his ancestral lands

And led into the forest called Buchonia,

Named from the beech tree.

There the river Fulda, loud with its waters, glides along;

From it this place, where now you see mighty walls,

Once took its name at the beginning of its origin.

Meanwhile they traveled a long way

By various roads

To the holy and chosen place,

And to the dedicated temple.

Here the blessed martyr Boniface, who once did not fear to succumb to cruel death for God’s law, is revered with worthy honor for the praise of God.

## Chapter II. Sturmi receives him and sends him to school

Here this boy, Eigil, appears, standing before the doors, by chance before the man who at that time governed the Fulda monastery beneath these humble walls. Sturmi immediately received him when he saw him, with gentle murmuring words, and the shepherd embraced him with his weary arms and gave kisses to the young kinsman.

Under such auspices, he began to be Christ’s soldier from his earliest years. What his later outcome would be, what thoughts would already have been in his youthful breast, and what firmness of mind would grow in the maturing man—if life remains my companion, if the spirit within continues to nourish my body, if my tongue retains its customary gift, and if advancing age grants me honorable and worthy success, I shall begin to set forth these matters in a few songs.

After this, the beardless boy was led from the abbot’s dwelling and brought to the citadel of the school, where the eternal law of God is learned by boys through Christ’s gift and taught by the mouths of elders. Without delay he began to master the elements.

As a hungry bee, at the beginning of spring, flies eagerly over the meadows on balanced wings and strives to pluck for itself the flowers of the fields, then flying higher, with buzzing wings, gathers from the pale willows, the pear, and the plane tree shining with flowers, and from the linden, newly fervent, endeavors to store honey beneath its hidden roof—so this young man first fed upon the song of books, as one feeds upon sharp leaves scraped from bark. At last, progressing not by his own strength but by Christ’s gift, and advancing together in age and keen understanding, he became worthy to feed upon draughts of shaded nectar.

## Chapter III. He becomes a monk and is ordained priest

From that time he already adhered to the customs and habit of the Fulda monks, inflamed by love of the heavenly life. With the counsel of the brothers and of the Father, he was joined to them and girded with the shining arms of Christ, an intrepid standard-bearer relying on Christ’s protection.

Meanwhile he became the Father’s companion and faithful minister, managing everything successfully. As a suppliant, he often walked with the elders together to the high oracles. Often, while a large crowd awaited him, he was ordered to give judgments before them all, and again to forbid things unspeakable. At that time, distinguished in merits and teaching and born of a fortunate father in fortunate years, he had received in baptism the name Eigil.

He deserved to serve as a priest under the holy bishop Lull, rescued from the hostile floods of the world.

## Chapter IV. Catalogue of the abbots of the monastery mentioned above

Meanwhile it came to pass that Sturmi, worn out by old age and illness, who had been the first founder and abbot of the Fulda monastery, departed from this light—which, we believe, remains forever in the everlasting light.

After his death, with the harmonious voice of the assembled brothers, Baugolf, generous German stock, was duly chosen as Father, put forward by the mouth of his predecessor.

## Chapter V. The poet introduces a metaphor

When this man ceased, the Unicorn succeeded him—namely Ratgar, whom Modestus depicted here in Candidus’s principal copy as seated upon a unicorn, marking by this symbol the man’s eruption or scabby disorder (*impetigo*). He—

perhaps with what sort of expression I do not know—drove the flock entrusted to him with foolish goads; until, compelled by excessive force, it abandoned its pasture and flowing springs, its pleasant places and lofty stalls, and by flight withdrew from its ancestral kingdom.

What more should I pursue? While the burden of these volumes remains in these matters, if someone wished, traveling from mouth to mouth, to report all these things, the entire flock, gathered together into one by a certain impulse from a single wool-bearing shepherd, is collected with care; and, having at least recovered its stolen hope and strength, it hastened back again to its unfamiliar pasture.

## Chapter VI. Royal care for the Fulda brothers

After the savage Unicorn had been removed, the unexpected royal care of Ludwig quickly arose—he who was always a lover of the better life and loved the monks with chaste affection. May almighty God place him safe from his paternal seat in the kingdom of light and the blessed dwelling.

From the west he sent monks who would urge our brothers, and also those living nearby, lying here and there, to begin again the customs, studies, rules, and teachings of the fathers, and to renew what had fallen away.

## Chapter VII. The brothers’ embassy sent to the emperor

Meanwhile, with the harsh guardian removed, we remained subject—until Brother Adalfrid, one of those from the west, accompanied by our brothers, approached the oracles of the exceptional king and asked that Fulda, deprived of its place and stripped of its cruel master, might again be clothed with a pious Father.

To him the gracious offspring replied:

“Go now, call a council, and greet the brothers. Seek for yourselves whichever father they wish, rightly and duly found, and grant him from us for this labor.”

He spoke, and joyfully dismissed him from the bright hall.

When he had received the mighty king’s answer and revolved these very words within his breast, he repeatedly encouraged his companions, ordered them to be ready, compelled them to undertake the journey, and urged them to carry a swift step through the darkness of places, across lands, grasses, and waters, over mountains and valleys together, through the dense lairs of wild beasts, where the wolf, wandering apart and howling terribly with bloody mouth, often turns ambushes over in his heart.

There was no delay. When day had overcome the shadows of night and the red light of the Titan shone high upon the world, he was immediately sent back by the king with his companions. Together they hastened competitively toward the lofty walls of Fulda, carrying back with them the good gifts they had obtained.

Meanwhile, winged Fame flew over the broad fields and, exulting, reached the ears of the brothers of the Fulda monastery with suitable rumors. She displayed, by chance, a man safely accomplished without mishap and warned them to fear nothing with a troubled mind.

While he was still recalling these things, the envoy sent by the gracious king arrived, and together with our prince, the brothers Odilhoh and Reccheo the elder—now deceased, each a priest and monk—were ordered, joyful in spirit, to seek their lodging. For not many days afterward, when the brothers had been summoned, the king’s messenger began thus.

*Note:* There were two Fulda monks of this name. One was the elder Reccheo, mentioned here, a deacon who wrote in 800 the charter of donation of Einhilt, abbess of Milz, for the Fulda monastery, in Book II of the *Traditions of Fulda*, p. 511; as a priest, he wrote another in 819, p. 531. The other was the younger Reccheo, also called Modestus, to whom this *Life* is dedicated. Nothing occurs to be noted concerning Odilhoh, except that a brother of nearly the same name, Odiileoz, is mentioned in Alcuin’s Letter 64, addressed to the brothers in the church of Saint Liudger, bishop.

## Chapter VIII. The emperor’s reply is disclosed to the brothers

“Ludwig, the peaceful king and serene Caesar, has already sent you greetings in his own voice. Whichever father your concordant community desires, rightly, justly, and worthily found, he has granted to your desire with *laesis luminibus* (‘with injured/altered eyes’; the transmitted reading is uncertain).”

He spoke, and closed the breaths of his mouth within.

Without delay, the whole company of brothers, suppliant and needy in their affairs, bearing the answer before them, fell prostrate upon the ground on their knees; then, giving worthy thanks to the giver of these gifts, they rose.

## Chapter IX. The poet’s rebuke and exhortation

What thoughts did the brotherly company then have in your breast? What desire, rather, was in your mind as you revolved such matters? What trembling voices did you summon with your body gathered together?

Did not the simple path of the brothers bend in both directions, discolored, while discord entered secretly behind it, and troubled concord, divided in two, fell backward?

If you proceed farther into such things, sociable community, permit me to admonish you in a slender voice. Do not fear; learn to trust in God alone. Ask for what pleases God, if you know how. If you do not know how to ask, or if you lack the wisdom of true speech, bow your face before him who reigns in living and lofty faith. He will give all good things and repay no one with reproaches.

## Chapter X. Permission is given to aspire to the abbatial election; the elders deliberate and an abbot is elected

A broad opportunity for speaking was granted to the brothers concerning this matter, and afterward each had the power to breathe freely in turn. Suddenly the brothers everywhere gathered together into one assembly. In the long porticoes of the cloister, a long consultation was to be seen.

From there, lifted up in varied speech, a discordant matter burst quickly into the midst. It revolved, poured forth on every side, sharpening anger with various rumors—the offspring of Discord, born of an ill-fated mother.

“Shall I speak, or shall I remain silent?” The opinion of the crowd declares that whoever has been strongly touched by a flame-bearing fire fears the fire with a mind that trembles before the flame.

One man seeks this Father; another demands that one. One party desires him; the other rejects him. The young man dares to address the old man, and one man challenges another with hostile voices and harsh words.

No one now secretly professed his personal preference. They hastened at least to their customary consolation in their prayers. A profound prayer was offered to God by all together. They earnestly begged that the brotherly will might be shown—what the right hand of the Almighty had decreed concerning this matter.

See now, I pray, most confident brother, how easily God himself, the king and possessor of the transparent heavens, in pity provides for the faithful in their need. Discord and foolishness flee, while, suddenly, Concord enters through gates opened on both sides, joyfully accompanied by faith.

Meanwhile the bell was shaken with repeated force, so that, perhaps warned, though not equal in strength of mind, the brothers might gather into one with their order mixed together. Then, according to the customary practice, a reading was made from the verses. After this, when prayer had at last been duly completed, the more prominent part of the brothers broke into a solemn voice and then, with wholesome counsel, spoke as follows:

“We, faithful company, have often, amid various disturbances, partly labored beneath adversity. Yet it has happened that we have all endured together the dangers of a common illness and the mixture of evil; and this would still happen, unless the lightning-bearing right hand of the High Father, suddenly coming from above, should willingly take pity on us.

“But because the ruler of mighty Olympus has wished us to possess these places again rather than abandon them, and to restore us once more to the ancient form of our life, let each person now remember his own soul and his whole strength. Put forward as Father a brother who is capable, even if he refuses with humble speech—not one who desires the office yet cannot bear it, but one distinguished in conduct, in sacred teaching, and in a pious mind, worthy to lead so great a crowd.”

Having recalled these things carefully, the prominent party of the Fathers raised them up; then, repeating them, brought forward the remaining matters and reformed them in dense discussion.

Without delay, with united mind, the aged Eigil was sought as Father. He had once come from the serene Noric region, a noble man of the smallest beginnings, and was then a grave investigator of the elders of old.

To him, though he resisted, they said a few words with composed hearts:

“You ought to remember that you previously entered into a brotherly covenant with us. Take pity on your companions. If you have any strength, the concord of the brothers says, do not withdraw it from our prayers, whether in body or in soul.”

## Chapter XI. His excuse, the brothers’ objection, and the old man’s consent

Then the long-lived man, his heart stirred, replied:

“Do you not see that this body is weighed down by exhausted old age? It shakes the head and twists the footsteps. The sight grows weak; coughing tears at the inward parts; and diseased breath shakes all the limbs of the body. Therefore, I confess, I alone cannot bear such burdens.”

Thus the elder resisted in speech and drenched his muddy little eyes with tears.

“Say no more, Father,” one replied, “and yield to this monastery’s request. I beg you, do not let concern for your old age break you. The concord of the brothers, together with you, willingly undertakes to bear the labor with exhausted strength. It will not allow you alone to suffer beneath the burden.”

At this the old man’s hard breast began to soften, and he addressed the brothers with friendly words:

“I declare that I do not wish to purchase flight for myself as the price of praise in this undertaking; nor has this dreadful labor terrified my heart. But weakened old age, swelling illness, and the pestilential enemy frightened me.

“Now I yield to your commands and shall carry them out. You, meanwhile, concord of the brothers, share the labor with me, with equal and exhausted strength.”

## Chapter XII. They go to the king concerning confirmation of the abbot

When these things had been said, the authority of the brothers selected brothers and companions from their own body, who, together with the Father newly received as elder, might return to the distinguished king concerning his decision on this matter.

When these arrangements had been made, they set out. Aaron accompanied them, the first among them. The royal care had sent him and others for our common good at the time when the wicked and threatening Unicorn had at last ceased, with furious attempts, to terrify the fugitives.

After some days had properly passed, this same embassy came to the western lands, humbly seeking the old Caesar’s oracles.

At that time the western monk and priest Aaron, first invited to the presence of the lofty king, came forward and openly explained before the king that the Fulda brothers had come for the sake of their life and their brothers, and that they were standing outside the closed doors.

When Caesar perceived them at the doors, he is said to have ordered them to enter. Then the elder, surrounded by a crowd of brothers, entered, fell upon his knees, and, rolling upon his knees together with his companions, honored the face of the ruler.

Without delay the king himself beckoned with his shining right hand and ordered them to stand. The elder then began:

“O sons, my brothers and chosen fathers, hope of the fatherland, our kingdom’s honor and glory, previously you were pressed by exceedingly dreadful dangers from the deadly plague. At least now, rescued, raise up your hearts and shut out sorrowful fear. Hold with attentive heart to what your rule teaches.

“That rule is the gate and the narrow way that leads to the lofty kingdoms of heaven. Strive now to enter through it, so that, running along it, you may come to him who, in mercy, brought you from darkness and the blind prison into marvelous light—not on account of your merits.

“Run now, brothers, while you possess the light of life, lest darkness seize you. Above all, preserve peace—true peace, I say—without which not even a gift brought to the altar is useful. Nor does property poured out upon the poor benefit anyone, nor has a martyr ever carried gifts away from the lofty Judge. I admonish you: preserve peace.”

Saying this and many other things in a long sequence, he said:

“Bring forward the Father whom you have desired.”

The brothers proceeded into the middle. Eigil, suddenly sprinkled with white hair, advanced in steadfast old age. At the king’s command he had come farther forward.

When the lofty king saw him, he said:

“Is this the shepherd whom the unanimous concord of all the brothers advances and approves with one harmonious voice?”

The brothers’ embassy, humbly, answered the king in a few words:

“This is he, good king. Now, bowed down, the whole assembly rests its request upon you: decree that he be retained, O our hope and the honor and glory of our life.”

## Chapter XIII. The king’s confirmation and instruction

“Behold, this old man whom you seek stands here before you. Have him as Father; preserve him as your parent.

“And you, Father, learn to preserve your lesser brothers, with every care. Always love diligently to join pious bonds in turn. Reprove those who fall backward from peace, lest they perish, and teach them to return to peace by a gentle and wholesome restoration.

“Be discerning and a counselor in every matter. Hold with attentive heart to whatever the established rule of the community teaches.

“There you will find fixed what the shepherd who goes before the flock undertakes, and what the tender flock following behind accomplishes; together, this work benefits the well-fed wool-bearing sheep and suits the lambs. Nor should the careful investigator neglect to examine what care must be given to the sick and weak, and what provision remains for those who must be nourished.

“Benedict, rejoicing and filled with sacred inspiration, established this law as the proper master of monks and commanded his disciples to observe it with him. I now entrust it to you; receive the rule.

“And under its firm covenant, shepherd, I entrust to you the entire Fulda monastery, together with all the neighboring places which I now decree must be protected.”

Having spoken these things, the illustrious king, in response to the brothers’ pious prayers, dismissed them all to depart in peace.

## Chapter XIV. Father Eigil returns through Mainz

After this, traveling from there with a company of companions, this joyful Father directed his steps toward the city, once wealthy in resources and built by ancient workmanship. It appears above the bank of the frozen water of the Rhine, into which, flowing with swelling waves, the river Mogoin pours itself. There, where the Rhine’s icy water flows with swelling waves and the river Mogoin runs into it, Mainz—so report has it—takes its name from Mogoin. [The text reads *Non*; perhaps *Nam*: “for on the other side the great fortress is seen.”] Not far above stands the bridge which King Charles once caused to be made over the Rhine while his realm prospered; it burned in the last year of his life. [This is the wooden bridge over the Rhine mentioned by Einhard and other annalists of that period.]

Meanwhile Eigil came as a most welcome guest to Haistolf, the holy bishop of the Mainz church, and was received with fitting honor. First he was led to the church. After the prayers had been completed, he suddenly appeared before the bishop’s sight and, going humbly to the kisses of peace, reverently bowed.

When the two men, advanced alike in age and equally distinguished in doctrine—the bishop of the law of justice and the aged shepherd—had sat down together, the city’s bishop, arriving first, began to speak:

“Father, first let us praise the All-Powerful and joyfully give him worthy thanks, who by his own gift has safely brought us, devoted to him, together with our companions, into one place.

“Moreover, you ought to know what burdens, and how oppressive, once pressed upon you and your companions under the undiscerning rule of a tyrant—especially now, since the ruler of Olympus has wished to place you over familiar sheepfolds as their vigilant guardian.

“Do not, Father, at some time, while troubling your subjects in the manner of your predecessor, wander away from them in anger.

“Let the false and fleeting power of this pompous age not deceive you, nor let proud arrogance possess you. Restrain anger; flee the name of the greedy. Do everything with counsel. Thus once Idida—apparently recounting the King of Jerusalem—spoke; thus your own lawgiver himself said. Then, after the deed, may the punishment of the guilty not torment you, nor may harsh words remain for you afterward.

“Take counsel with all your people in fatherly compassion; take counsel with all your brothers. For often the Omnipotent, who sees the things stored up in the present, reveals the best goods to the lesser person and discloses worthy things.

“Often a stratagem confuses an empty mind when the arrow of the perverse enemy strikes from behind. Error will either steal upon a person in this way and disturb his understanding, since no human being remains in the flesh without weakness, or, though someone may possess great intellectual power and surpass another in wisdom, he may still conceive something false with a blunted mind. Conversely, someone less wise and of lesser merit may sometimes perceive in the dwelling of his heart what is more correct and truer.

“Therefore no one placed in this life should presume upon himself, nor proudly say that he has no need of another’s counsel. Even if devilish guile (*zabolica gannatura*; “fox-like cunning”) does not deceive his judgment, he will not easily overcome the heavier snares of pride set here and there.”

Having recalled these things to the Father, together with many others in a long discourse, the bishop immediately ordered men to be present who would duly provide water, grain, wine, and tables.

Meanwhile he himself walked to the sacred altar with the clergy to perform the lofty melodies of the Mass. When the praises of Christ had been completed, the venerable bishop, distinguished by honor, received the abbot and his companions into the open hall. Water was poured for them into their hands, and a table was suddenly set before them, laden with graceful fare for the priest and his guests.

When these things had been completed, a sacred reading followed, which the bishop briefly treated in his customary speech, at times satisfying those present with heavenly sweetness.

When it had been explained, the men’s mouths murmured sweet conversations, and peace resounded everywhere around. The city’s chief man, the aged shepherd, and all the lesser people became deeply joyful in the hall; both groups were carried along in high rejoicing.

Then this pious Father, with the circle of brothers revolving around him, after the meals, conversations, and joyful cups, departed happily, with bowed head but at least conscious of the familiar parting, blessed by the bishop.

Not many days passed, nor much time elapsed, before the joyful company of brothers returned again with the Father to the place from which he had come.

The old man Eigil, of famous name, arrived with his companions and was first received with fitting honor. Then his own brothers carried him to the lofty church, where Christ’s martyr rests adorned in his coffin, once put to sleep by a sharp weapon together with his companions.

After the prayer had been completed, the crowd of monks flowed together. When the elder had been seen in the western part of the church, they immediately fell prostrate and greeted the Father according to custom.

After he had returned their greeting, he ordered them to come nearer; entering into peace and giving suitable kisses, he himself, together with the brothers, suddenly sang the melodies of David’s Muse:

“How good, brothers, and how lofty is the joy—when the rancor of bile has been removed—to live a common life in holy conduct!”

When this song had been completed, the tired abbot proceeded toward the desired dwelling. The mixed crowd—young and old—accompanied him as he went. They looked upon him, rejoiced together, and burned with the desire to behold him.

That very day the joyful Father arranged to be held as a day of complete joy for all, displaying to the brothers the gladness deep within his breast, shining through the appearance of his body, his tongue, and his face.

## Chapter XV. The unfinished work of the basilica is completed

From that time this man began, with great love of piety, to cleanse the church’s spaces. He ordered the pavements to be relaid and placed square altars around them.

At the summit he had fixed polished stones, joined by arches, under the direction of the master Racholf—both a monk and a blameless minister of the brothers. [Was this the same Racolf, chancellor, who wrote the charter of donation made by a certain Walto to the Fulda community in the thirty-third year of Charlemagne’s reign, in Book II of the *Traditions*, p. 516?]

I ask you, and all who read, to remember him, so that the Lord’s piety may grant his soul the honor of rest for this work and confer everlasting light.

As I have said, under the direction of that same master, both monk and blameless minister of the brothers, he magnificently raised two crypts in beautiful order, with arches and columns inserted here and there.

The first of these faces east. It has three windows toward the East, where light from the standard-bearing axis of the heavens, amid rainy weather and resounding storm, first scatters its golden rays over the earthly world. Within it contains one adorned altar, duly furnished with the relics of the saints, which I intend to list below.

This cave also bears an altar at the crown of its head, which Saint Boniface himself consecrated to the Almighty in ancient times; the matters added above he left to others to consecrate.

But another noble chamber, where the martyr now lies, is seen to have been constructed in the western part. It is very rich in workmanship and internally in the spoils of the pious, looking toward the west through three fixed windows behind it.

It is darkened on both sides and closed by two openings toward sunset, where Phoebus, following his customary course, sinks down as the golden light turns toward its accustomed path, so that by traversing it he may once again rise toward the east.

At the summit of this chamber, firmly resting upon stout supports, it bears an altar. Upon it now lie the remains of the exceptional martyr of Christ, together with his companions, sacred and blessed forever.

## Chapter XVI. The bishop is invited to dedicate the church

When these things had been constructed, the entire council of the brothers, together with the Father of the brothers, duly invited Haistolf, the metropolitan, to consecrate the church.

Meanwhile, flying Fame, with lofty rumors, stirred the pious hearts of many worshipers of Christ to the praise of Christ and to the necessity of coming. Behold, suddenly the priest departed from his own seat: first the metropolitan proceeded, and after him a crowd of priests, abbots, and powerful counts, together with a rejoicing company of lesser people of every rank.

Thus, with a great multitude, they gathered together for so magnificent and holy a festival.

**Candidus to Modestus**

“Consider now, brother, for whom no other is more excellent, with the eyes of your mind, and establish these sacred things with me.”

## Chapter XVII. The church is dedicated and the body of Christ’s martyr Boniface is transferred

The blessed day had come, illuminated by a flashing ray. The bishop of the perpetual Sun proceeded to the hall that was to be consecrated. Then the relics were lifted up to be placed within.

The pontifical chief had gone before in bright order; the red banners of the magnificent King of victory were likewise raised into the air. After them came the crowd of priests, monks, and powerful counts, properly surrounded by rose-colored lights, together with the lesser people of every rank, shouting behind them and calling upon Christ with a voice that thundered three times.

For Christ was invited by powerful virtue, and the holy Mother of God herself, the virgin Mary. The heavenly armies were summoned by prayers for aid, and thereafter the entire army of the saints.

When the bishop had completed three circuits with these prayers, and the following crowd likewise advanced in a joyful procession, the doors of the temple were opened before the eyes of the people and the faces of the men at the command of the herald of the King of virtues and the victorious God.

The bishop entered, led by divine power. The priests and ministers of the altar entered with him, according to their custom, to perform within the commands of the powerful one.

The relics of the saints were brought in, surrounded by joyful choirs. The rest of the crowd remained outside, watching through their prayers, excluded from the inner space, until the good bishop consecrated all the altars to the high-throned King, except five, which I shall mention again below.

Immediately afterward, at the command of the attendant, the lofty and blessed house of almighty God was opened again. The rejoicing crowd rushed in; suddenly they pressed against one another and against the doors as they hurried inside.
