One man took another’s right hand and led him in, each giving kisses on the cheeks according to the custom of laymen.

When the shouting had subsided and the tumult had been removed, the ecclesiastical order gathered together from every side and immediately turned toward the martyr’s tomb, which was then known to stand in the middle of the church.

The people were also present as witnesses, and the Almighty Creator himself became a witness, he who remains everywhere forever in everlasting majesty, together with all his army. For at that very hour, when the presence of the high divinity arrived and Christ’s martyr was carried away from his former resting place, the event became clearly known to many in the sacred hall.

Meanwhile the venerable old age of Haistolf, the bishop, persisted in prayers, seeking Christ’s consolations, so that by divine gift he might bring the sacred work begun to a holy conclusion together with his companions.

After this, relying on Christ’s protection, the same bishop proceeded and ordered the venerable body to be lifted. He himself lifted it first and powerfully rendered a hymn filled with the magnificent fragrance of praise to the Begetter, the Begotten, and the life-giving Spirit:

“We therefore praise you as God; we confess you as Lord. The earth venerates you as everlasting Begetter.

“The entire angelic and wondrous order stands before you, and all the venerable powers of heaven, the Cherubim and Seraphim together, reverently and justly cry out to you alone with unceasing voice:

“Holy, holy, holy, for the Lord God is one, Sabaoth. Heaven and earth are filled with the great gifts [or, according to the correction, *doxa*: ‘glory’] of everlasting majesty.

“The apostolic assembly, strong in power, and the illustrious order praise you; the praiseworthy company of prophets praises you equally; the shining and burning army of witnesses praises you.

“The holy Church, spread throughout the world, sings to you, venerating the Father of immeasurable majesty, and your true Son, born from your own breast, and the holy Paraclete, breathed forth with equal divinity.

“You are king of glory and light, Christ, lofty light. You are the eternal Son of the Father, born before time began.

“You assumed humanity to liberate the world, and your exalted power did not shrink from the virgin’s womb.

“Having conquered the sting of death, you are victorious everywhere, for in mercy you have opened the kingdoms of heaven to the faithful.

“You reign at the Father’s right hand with everlasting power, coming from above as the certain judge of the world.

“Prostrate, we ask you: defend your own servants, whom you, Savior of the world, redeemed with your own blood. Save the people led back from the enemy’s jaws.

“Deign, God, to bless your inheritance; rule it and exalt it for ever by your help. For every day we bless you highly, and throughout all ages we praise your name.

“On this day, powerful Christ, deign to guard us, and do not let the contagions of an impure life defile us.

“Have mercy upon us, our God; have mercy upon us. May your mercy toward us be abundant, as we trust in you with steadfast heart.

“In you, highest God, I hope; may I not be disturbed forever.”

The ecclesiastical order, startled, suddenly received this hymn from the bishop’s mouth and sang praise to the high-throned one in lofty melody.

The coffin of the tomb, in which the sacred limbs of the blessed martyr lay enclosed, was carried first by two grave and aged men, Haistolf and Eigil. Behind them went the monk and priest Ercanberctus, brother of Baugolf, and the abbot Theolgarius; also Bruunwar, perhaps Brunward, the chorepiscopus to whom a poem of Rabanus survives; and Rabanus himself, priest and monk, rightly master of many.

*Note:* Perhaps Brunward, the chorepiscopus to whom Rabanus’s poem 12 is addressed. Browerus thinks that he was the very abbot of Hersfeld mentioned by Lambert under the year 846. I do not know whether Theotgarius was abbot of that place, of Fritzlar, or of the monastery of Saint Alban.

They proceeded in equal number, singing of Christ. With pious companies of priests mingled among them on either side, and a crowd pressing around with lights, the people rejoiced to touch the coffin with eager hands.

The royal road that led to the great altar of the everlasting King had been suitably spread with gleaming cloths. The same priest, Ercanberctus, devoted to Christ’s love, joyfully offered them on behalf of the martyr, adding above them a stiff purple covering and enlarging the display by his own efforts and those of his companions.

When these things had been received, the pontifical chief, accompanied by great honor, extended his steps toward the altar, which had been completed in the western part according to Roman custom.

Meanwhile the newly arrived people suddenly raised their voices with “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”); the cry rose to the stars. The worshipers of Christ burned inwardly with the fresh fervor of the divinity poured into them.

Yet, marvelous to say, you know that the voice of praise was not produced equally by all in the customary manner. They shed tears, the joy of their minds: tears of gladness and songs were mingled together.

Then he sang another hymn in a similar measure, filled with the great sweetness of praise to the Lord, the Begetter, the Begotten, and the life-giving Spirit:

“Glory in the highest to the great Lord,

and peace of good will to earthly beings.

We also praise and sanctify you

because of your magnificent and lofty honor.”

For a long time the jubilation of the lofty voice resounded, until they enclosed the remains in the stony tomb and, having closed it, left them there to rest.

The martyr, buried with this honor in the western part, lies high in the adorned altar of the high-throned King, above which a great apse has been built and rises overhead.

I myself, once nourished in this hall of Christ, a priest and monk, Bruun, an insignificant master, painted it. With modest talent and small Minerva, I fashioned and represented the various faces in pigment.

## Chapter XVIII. The painter’s and poet’s supplication

I ask every reader to remember him who produced this work, praying to the Lord in a spirit of love and piety, so that he may confidently obtain forgiveness for his sins from him who does not wish anyone to perish by the death of sin, but rather, returning, to live by blessed virtues.

When these things had been accomplished, the celebration of the solemn Mass resounded with worthy praises. After it had been duly completed, Haistolf and Eigil, tired and accompanied by their companions and by a great murmuring crowd, were led back beneath the lofty walls to the dwelling, where the joyful bishop and shepherd himself likewise returned.

The lesser people of both groups soon approached, swift ministers of the Father at that moment, carrying the gifts of Ceres in baskets after much labor. Others busied themselves bringing food sprinkled with various fragrances; still others, in carefully arranged order, mixed the illustrious cups of Bacchus in glass.

Nor was sacred reading absent from the paternal banquet, for it is the strong and solid food of men, satisfying those who listen with the richness of the heavenly word.

## Chapter XIX. The dedication on the following day and what followed

When the following day had removed the dark wings of night and the shadow-bearing mist had withdrawn from the fields, he left the lodging once the sun’s light had appeared. Humberet, the chorepiscopus, was ordered to fly forth with his companions to the two chambers of the church that were to be consecrated and that the bishop had left unfinished the previous day.

First he approached the cave facing east, visible in the rigid vestment of the bishop’s office, acting in the bishop’s place. Once it had been consecrated together with its titular dedication, he soon consecrated in like manner the chamber facing west, which looks toward the sunset.

Two altars left unconsecrated were then consecrated. One stood where the martyr had previously been beneath the central vault of the church; the other where Sturmi’s body rests and worthy Liobgid, Boniface’s niece—perhaps *Bonifacia*—lies alone, buried in the portion assigned to women.

On his return in the following year, the bishop dedicates it together with the titular dedication of James and Philip.

To contain the whole matter in a few words: Haistolf, bishop of the Mainz church, a soldier of Christ from his earliest years, with great zeal and great love of piety, and, above all, with great honor for the saints, consecrated this hall, fulfilling in the prescribed order the promises made to the petitioner.

## Chapter XX. Commemoration of Master Rabanus and His Work

[Col. 0415C] Rabanus, rightly called “the master,” has entitled in verse part of the day, its number, season, and year mentioned above, together with the offices and some of the saints’ names; part he has set out again in prose.

I have unfolded in orderly fashion what I thought worthy of being inserted here in flower-bearing verse, so that in this book, which is to preserve their memory, those matters might remain unharmed and untouched forever.

All this, my brother, which I saw, perceived, and was able to learn concerning these things, I have set forth for you here in solemn verses. Now, having drawn a boundary here, I leave what has been added above to be written by another.

[Note: You may find Rabanus’s verses and prose on this subject in Book II, chapter 5, of the *Antiquities of Fulda*.]

## Chapter XXI. The Building of the Round Basilica and the Design of Its Structure

[Col. 0415D] When these things had been done, Eigil, diligently learning everywhere the common joys of life and bound to those under him by sacred love, wisely pressed on. At the counsel of the brothers he founded a small, devoutly rounded church, beside which the bodies of the deceased brothers lie; beneath it a passable crypt lies hidden under the earth. The structure begins properly with a single column and rises above on eight columns, being closed most beautifully at the top by a single stone.

This work, then, the learned pastor and at the same time the honorable teacher of the young, together with his companions, undertook in the deep recess of his mind, conceiving by fruitful art I know not what great thing. Yet I myself believe—with sound mind and faith—that it presents the figure of this Church and of Christ.

For the holy temple of God is plainly what Paul himself declares Christ’s people to be: Christ’s vessel. God himself stands as the master and founder of its roof, and as its foundation and its unshaken column, remaining forever in enduring strength.

By the merit of faith, the newly arrived people are now raised up here to Christ, and the temple grows together for God into a nourishing structure.

[Note: That is, “grows together.”]

But the fact that the building is closed at the top by one stone teaches us that the distinguished teacher himself urges us to ask with attentive mind that Jesus, who began the pleasing work in us by his mighty power, may deign to bring it to completion on high, until the manifest and renowned day of Christ shines forth and advances throughout the world.

The eight columns standing within, on this side and that, correspond to the eight beatitudes, so that those who fulfill these sayings of the Thunderer—four times two—may rightly deserve to be regarded as the supports of God’s house.

The circle of the church, rounded and enclosed without end, seems to signify within it the blessings of life, as well as hope of eternal life, the everlasting kingdom, and rewards that will endure after this life: the life in which the righteous are crowned forever by their merit.

## Chapter XXII. The Dedication of the Same Church, Which They Call a Cemetery, etc.

This temple, then, which that tireless old man had built for the gracious Lord, Haistolf the metropolitan dedicates at the appointed time with three altars, having departed from the city and made for the fields of Thuringia.

The excellent teacher of the young, whom I have often mentioned, also embraces in varied fashion, worthily, learnedly, and devoutly, the number, time, year, and day of the office, together with the holy rites.

## Chapter XXIII. The Structure of the Cloister and the Abbot’s Illness

But behold, as the new work had begun and he was weighed down by bitter old age, mention was at last suddenly made of the cloister. Some proposed that it be established according to the earlier custom. Others, however, put forward the Roman practice: that it should be placed toward the setting sun, where the excellent martyr lies behind it. The elders yielded to this proposal, and the rest of the community humbly agreed with it.

What more need I say? At once the measure of the work was laid out, and, after the ground had been dug up, they set down the foundations. The work was hotly pursued, and at the same time it supplied courage and strength. All shared the same care and the same determination to carry out the work.

Meanwhile, however, another completed what had been left unfinished. Immediately afterward he was seized by the peril of a serious illness, and the violence of the disease quickly overcame his exhausted limbs. The concord of the brothers was shaken; murmuring arose, and the brothers were terrified, groaning over the Father’s hateful illness.

Yet he himself, gathering his strength, with his bodily dwelling opening under his feeble power, was the first to open it and, with his own hands, to uncover—

## Chapter XXIV. His Death, Burial, and Epitaph

[Col. 0417A] From that point the fierce power of the disease grew ever hotter and threatened death. At last, as pain pressed upon him, he was brought to the final moment and death stood at the threshold.

All gathered around him, close on this side and that; old men and young men alike stood there. A holy prayer was offered jointly to God for the Father, dear to them all.

Then, commended at least by the prayers of the brothers—

[Note: *commenditus* is a barbarous form for *commendatus*, in the same way that Alcuin uses *commendite* for *commendate* in epigrams 124, 164, and 267.]

—and thus, as he was dying, he had stretched his weary limbs upon the bed, breathing forth his surging soul toward the heavenly breezes.

Shaken in spirit by this death, a deep groaning passed through them all. Here they lamented the loss of the joys of their father.

[Col. 0417B] But what can you do, man, against this? For by rightful law a day appointed for each person and an irreversible time remain fixed. Thus he died according to the customary law of those who came before, and left these places to be guarded by others.

Then, following the custom of the Fathers, the brothers soon carried the lifeless corpse beneath the roof of the church as they prayed. There, amid their hands, asking for rest for him whom he himself had made, they laid him beneath the roof of the tomb.

At that time our Rabanus—himself a father and shepherd, eminent in merit and learning—exultantly set down his epitaph in verses with celebrated teaching.

### Commemoration of the Dear Father and Shepherd

You see how nothing is; you see, my beloved brother, how vain and perishable is the power of the wandering world.

Behold, he lies covered by a tomb, whom once a great crowd of old and young, gathered together, used to cover.

Although for the present he lacks these affections, he always rejoices in the honorable prayers of the brothers.

For this wretched condition, and the grim fates ordained beneath the sky, await all afflicted mortals [the text prints *fama*; perhaps *fata*, “fates”].

Our first parents rightly earned this law; because of one person’s fault, kings and mighty nobles alike, rich and poor, master and servant, the afflicted and the needy, the innocent and the guilty, receive it. No distinctions bring it to an end.

This deadly condition will continue until that final day, swift, strong, and blazing, which, amid the cloud, the trumpet blast, and wrath, will carry the whole world together beneath the realms of Tartarus.

But this Father left his native soil, his homeland, and his parents while still an infant, and sought the fields of Buchonia.

Proceeding gradually along the steps of justice, he earned by divine favor the exalted place he holds in this church; in piety he was second to none of the ancients.

The mother of the virtues, Discernment, nourished him with twin breasts; grace be to Christ on high. Thus he never willingly commanded his own people when he saw them overcome by terror, nor, when terrified by them, did he ever withdraw.

The Father’s prudence rejected admission to his ears of frivolous, empty talk; nor did that gloomy sleepless suspicion prevail over him, which above all torments the unwary.

Nor was he easily stirred to anger, nor did he bring forth dreadful, flame-vomiting fires from his mind.

Turning aside and removing both lines of attack, he took care that they should not behold the empty things of the pestilential enemy.

He was deeply grieved whenever he saw anyone take flight, yielding too greatly to escape and grim fear; often, with gentle speech, he restrained that fear in them.

Thus, here and there, the malicious offspring of discord, born from an ill-fated mother, was lulled to sleep.

From that point onward the concord of the brothers could not be broken.

His vigor did not allow the affairs of the monastery of Fulda to be torn into factions; he did not fear the grim looks of the powerful or the haughty honors of the nobles.

He forbade every harmful thing, but most of all he forbade thieves. He pursued and exposed evils by acting steadfastly.

He properly drove the evildoers far from himself.

[Note: That is, “wrongdoers.”]

He was our glory, our helper in the honor of life; he was, in this church of God, the support of our work and our labor, together with the saving teaching of Noah.

I ask you and all who read to remember him through this work, so that the great and abundant mercy of the Lord may preserve him forever in everlasting rest.

[Col. 0417]

# Appendix

In which Eigil’s two epitaphs and the supplicatory booklet presented by the monks of Fulda to Charlemagne are reported.

[Col. 0417D] 1. It is fitting to insert here the two epitaphs of Abbot Eigil: one composed by Rabanus, the other by Eigil himself. Candidus copied both, and the one by Rabanus with this title:

### Epitaph dictated by Rabanus for Abbot Eigil

Entering, reader, the chamber of the very small house,  
Read the inscription and learn the fate of the man.

This abbot was Eigil, a man of renowned name;  
He lies in a tomb, but remains above the stars.

He himself also ruled this monastery happily,  
And properly accomplished many good deeds with joy.

Therefore, together with the bishop, he transferred the sacred bones of the martyr,  
And likewise dedicated these two churches.

After this he sought the heights and sent his soul to the stars;  
Here too he laid the limbs of his feeble body.

For him, I, Rabanus, his unworthy successor, composed  
This inscription with affection. May Christ help us both.

Eigil composed the other in the manner of the epitaph of Pope Damasus, which Candidus likewise reported as follows.

### Verses that Abbot Eigil himself dictated for himself

Here I, Abbot Eigil, lie buried and rest by the lot of fate,  
I who was once known to many throughout the world.

Here my limbs are enclosed in a small tomb,  
Which, while alive, I myself took care to build.

Here I await the Lord, who will release the bonds of death;  
When he comes, I believe that he will make me rise.

2. I shall also add the supplicatory booklet which the monks of Fulda presented to Charlemagne during the raging schism of Ratgar. This distinguished monument of antiquity is of considerable value for illuminating both the affairs of Abbot Eigil and those of the monastic order. It survives in Book II, chapter 15, of the *Antiquities of Fulda*, in the following form.

## Supplicatory Booklet of the Monks of Fulda Presented to the Emperor Charles

The entire monastery of Fulda also asked  
Augustus Charles to renew its rights.

The excellent Caesar judged all these requests honorable,  
And ordered that the petition contain pious prayers.

[Col. 0419B] First of all, most merciful emperor, we ask your piety that we may be permitted to maintain the measure of prayers, psalmody, and vigils which our fathers observed for our living and deceased friends: namely, a daily prayer for you, Lord Augustus, for your children, and for the whole Christian people.

In the morning, when we assemble together and a chapter from the Rule is read before the brothers, after the reading we rise and, singing three times the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” together with “Glory be to the Father,” we sing Psalm 50 on bended knees, along with the verses and the collect.

On the second day of every week, we offer a prayer for all who give us alms: that is, the same Psalm 50, which the whole congregation, prostrate together before the body of the blessed martyr, sang with the Lord’s Prayer, the verses, and the prayer.

For our deceased brothers, that commemoration which we have every day twice—after the celebration of Matins and at Vespers—namely the antiphon “Eternal rest,” together with the first part of the psalm “You are worthy of praise, O God,” the verse, and the collect.

On the first days of every month, one vigil and fifty psalms.

For Abbot Sturmi and the founders of this monastery, on the anniversary of their death, one vigil and one psalter each year.

### II

That priests be permitted to celebrate Mass more frequently, and that time be granted to them for this, as it was granted by our predecessors.

Furthermore, that those be chosen for the sacred order who are learned in the word and approved in holy conduct—not thieves, criminals, or men wholly ignorant of the rights and duties of the priesthood.

### III

That the honor and feast of the saints not be despised, but that worthy commemoration be made of them at vigils and Masses.

On those feasts which deserve greater veneration, may the brothers be permitted to leave their work for readings and psalmody, as was permitted under our predecessors: namely, on the feast of holy Mary, of the twelve apostles, of Saint Stephen, Saint Lawrence, and the others whose memory is celebrated in the churches of Germany, as well as those whose bodies are kept in these regions.

### IV

That receiving the communion of the broken bread before food each day not be rejected, according to the examples of the Fathers who came before us.

### V

That greater care and compassion be shown to the sick, especially the elderly and the weak; that they not be afflicted by a shortage of food or worn down by inadequate clothing; and that they not be harassed by any foolish practices.

They should not be forbidden to carry a staff for support or to cling to a support, which we call a *formola*, while walking. A blind or lame person cannot walk properly without the support of a staff, nor can a feeble old man bend his knees without a support.

We ask that such men not be expelled from the monastery out of disgust, lest, placed in cells among the laypeople, they die without confession and without the necessary provision for life.

### VI

That suitable compassion be shown to all who come to the monastery out of love for this way of life; that the sick, the elderly, and the delicate not be driven away by harshness, but that all be received with mercy; and that the comfort they request be honorably provided according to their infirmity.

### VII

That no one be received before a period of probation, nor joined to the body of the monastery, lest someone wish to associate himself with the monastery more for earthly advantages than for love of eternal life and, once received, disturb the brothers by his dishonorable conduct.

### VIII

That no one, deceived by false promises and blandishments concerning money or earthly property, should perish in worldly grief and regret after being received into the monastery when he does not possess what had been promised him. Rather, the truth should be spoken to everyone and fulfilled in deed.

### IX

That no one be forced to become a monk or tonsured for the clergy against his will, whether free or enslaved; for such men, once received into the monastery, become authors of crimes and perpetrators of vices.

### X

That we be permitted to have food and clothing as our predecessors established for us. For our first abbot, Sturmi, after spending a year living in the monastery of Saint Benedict, returned here and, according to the judgment of Saint Boniface, who assessed their clothing and food, established this arrangement for us. Several witnesses to this matter still survive.

### XI

That common governance of all the brothers be exercised by the deans and the provost; for the divisions now made are causes of scandals, dissensions, and opposition.

We believe that, for the preservation of peace and charity, it is expedient, according to the earlier constitution, that all the deans be appointed jointly for the brothers, so that common care may provide vigilance and show affection.

### XII

That immense and superfluous buildings, and other useless works by which the brothers are exhausted beyond measure and the households outside are ruined, be omitted; but that everything be done according to measure and discretion.

Let the brothers also, according to the Rule, be permitted at fixed hours to devote themselves to reading and likewise to work at fixed hours.

### XIII

That the reception of pilgrims and the washing of their feet not be neglected, but that, according to the Rule and the custom of our predecessors, whenever they come they be mercifully received, and that all the brothers wash their feet.

### XIV

That the ancient hospitality not be forgotten, but that fitting honor and every kindness be shown to all guests.

When several arrive together, as at the Mass of Saint Boniface, let refreshment be provided for all by those who care for the cells, with consolation offered on every side.

### XV

That private business, secular benefits, and the division of possessions and fields not be conducted within the monastery itself; for from these arise quarrels, disputes, rivalries, anger, strife, enmity, dissension, envy, secret feasting and drunkenness, and almost every evil contrary to our salvation.

Rather, let all fields and cells belong in common to all the brothers, and let all the people who live in the same monastic establishment receive clothing from one wardrobe, according to what the provost or cellarer distributes.

Let no commercial dealings be carried on there by anyone; rather, let everything be held in common by all.

### XVI

That the monastery’s own services be organized by the brothers—namely, the bakery, garden, brewery, kitchen, agriculture, and the other services—as they were under our predecessors; for every duty will be performed more devoutly and worthily by brothers than by a hostile layman or slave.

### XVII

That men of malicious and frenzied mind, extremely ready to commit every disgrace, not be gathered into the monastery, as happened with that murderous cleric who killed a monk and was placed in the monastery against the will and agreement of all the brothers.

For we fear that the relatives of that monk, inflamed by the devil’s persuasion in desire for revenge, may increase the killing.

Nor should those who, because of their crimes and wickedness, could not remain among secular people be scattered in groups throughout the places near the monastery; for they plunder the monasteries by theft and infest every nearby place with banditry.

### XVIII

That the abbot himself be corrected, so that he does not disparage the institutions of Saint Boniface by saying that his decrees were condemned by a synod, and so that he does not criticize our elders and the other monasteries as though they did not live according to the Rule.

### XIX

That the glorying of the Cross take place on every Sunday before Mass, with all the brothers following the Cross around the neighboring places of the monastery while singing hymns and antiphons, as was customary among our predecessors when, on Sundays, the glory of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection was celebrated.

And on days of fasting decreed by the bishop, may we be permitted to carry the Cross and perform the Litanies.

### XX

This above all, which we judged especially necessary for us, we desired before everything else: namely, to have unity and concord with our abbot, as we had with our earlier abbots; to find in him mercy and intimacy, piety and moderation; and that he should be kind to the sick, lenient toward offenders, approachable by the brothers, a comforter of the sorrowful, a helper of those who labor, a supporter of the willing, an encourager of those who strive well, a refresher of the weary, a sustainer of those who yield, and a restorer of those who fall.

Let him love all the brothers, hate none, and persecute no one through the deceit of jealousy or resentment.

Let him be neither turbulent in countenance, nor anxious in spirit, nor excessive in judgment, nor obstinate in counsel, but cheerful in face, glad in mind, discerning in action, and agreeable in what is useful.

When one of the brothers has been caught in some offense, let him not immediately torture him with tyrannical vengeance, but hasten to correct him with merciful discipline; once he has reformed, let him receive him kindly, neither wear him down again with a wicked suspicion nor drive him out through perpetual hatred.

[Col. 0422B] In these and similar matters, Lord Emperor, we lived under our earlier abbots. We have very often asked this abbot for the same things, but up to the present day we have not been able to obtain them.

[Col. 0421]

# Life of Saint Sturmi, First Abbot of Fulda, by Saint Eigil, Fourth Abbot of Fulda

[Col. 0421C]

## Mabillon’s Notice

1. No one who has considered the author’s authority, piety, and age can doubt how authoritative the book on the life of Saint Sturmi ought to be. The ancients call him *Sturmin*; some later writers call him *Sturmio*.

For Eigil, the fourth abbot of Fulda, from 818 to 822, a pious and holy man, committed to writing the principal deeds of his teacher, “in whose discipleship,” as he himself affirms in his Prologue, “he had lived for more than twenty years,” and he was also present at his death.

Indeed, he submitted his work more than once to the judgment of the monks of Fulda. “For he orders the reading at table of that book which, by the grace of Christ granted him, he composed concerning the life of the aforementioned Abbot and the origin of the monastery of Fulda,” according to the monk Candidus in Eigil’s own Acts, “so that, hearing these wonders of divine activity, they might give thanks to the divine majesty, and that all the joy of the feast might resound in his praise.”

2. By “feast,” understand the annual commemoration established by Abbot Eigil for Sturmi. Candidus relates the matter as follows:

“Sturmi, the first abbot and founder of the monastery of Fulda, whom Saint Boniface, his teacher, used to call his hermit, began to grow ill, worn out by sickness and old age. Not long afterward, an old man full of days, he departed in peace from temporal light to light which, as we believe, endures without end.

“With similar counsel and devotion, Eigil, a man of good will, decreed that the annual memory of Sturmi, the first abbot and founder of the monastery of Fulda, and of all our brothers who had died from this light, should be celebrated on the birthday of Saint Ignatius, martyr of Christ” [the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, on which Sturmi had died] “through the intercession of so great a patron, in the celebration of Masses, psalmody, and holy prayer.

“When the constitution of this observance had been read before the whole congregation, and they had afterward been asked whether it pleased them, all replied: ‘It pleases us.’

“But lest this celebration perhaps seem superstitious and empty to anyone, let him read the *Conferences of the Holy Fathers*, and there he will find an example of this feast.”

This is found, of course, in *Conference* XIX, chapter 1; we discussed the matter in the Preface.

From these facts it is understood that those annual prayers were instituted for the welfare of Sturmi and the other brothers. For although he was later numbered among the saints, he had neither a festive celebration nor a place in the ancient martyrologies—not even in that of Rabanus Maurus—until, in 1139, Pope Innocent II, at the Lateran Council, decreed by letters written to Chuonrad, abbot of Fulda, that solemn honors should be paid to him after his sanctity had been approved.

[Col. 0422D] 3. Browerus and others think that Saint Sturmi is mentioned in Boniface’s Letter 17, where, after Wigbert, abbot of Fritzlar, had died, Boniface arranges the offices of that monastery so that “Stirme” should be in the kitchen.

Indeed, Saint Sturmi received the beginnings of monastic life at Fritzlar. But in 747, the year in which we have established that Saint Wigbert the abbot died, Sturmi was already presiding as abbot over the monastery of Fulda, as is clear both from his Acts and from a charter of Boniface concerning the boundaries and limits of the monastery of Fulda, preserved by Browerus in Book I, chapter 4, of the *Antiquities of Fulda*. Sturmi the abbot subscribed it in March of the year of the Lord’s incarnation 747. Therefore the Fritzlar monk “Stirme,” whom Boniface assigned to the kitchen, must have been someone other than Sturmi.

4. It is impossible to express adequately in words how much praise Saint Sturmi deserves, since he established and governed the monastery of Fulda with such religious devotion.

The discipline of the monastery was such that, according to Boniface, Sturmi’s assistant, in a letter to Pope Zacharias, there lived there “monks living under the Rule of the holy Father Benedict, men of strict observance, without meat, wine, or servants, content with the labor of their own hands.”

It is said below, no. 13, that King Pippin later moderated this institution.

Rudolf the monk adds, in the previously related *Life of Saint Lioba*, the praiseworthy custom of this monastery: “because, from the time that the place began to be inhabited by monks, entrance was denied to women. Such permission, however, had been granted to Lioba because Saint Boniface the martyr had entrusted her to the elders and had decreed that her body should be buried there.”

“Our predecessors observed this principle so sacredly,” says Browerus in Book I, chapter 8, of the *Antiquities of Fulda*, “that it was expressly inserted into the privileges granted by Pope Martin to Abbot Hadamar in the ninth century, by Sylvester to Erkembald in the tenth century, and later by John, Richard, and other pontiffs, and was religiously observed by posterity.”

This is proved both by the case of the wife of King Lothair, who on the holy day of Pentecost was not permitted to attend the sacred rites in the principal church of the monastery, and by the case of the wife of Emperor Frederick, “who, because she was queen in his retinue, was not permitted to enter the city of Fulda.”

Browerus further observes that, after that discipline had once been relaxed by Pope Boniface IX at the request of John Merlavius, abbot of Fulda, “in the year 898 the church of Fulda was struck by lightning from heaven and burned on the seventh day of June.” Later generations believed that this had happened as punishment for the violation of the discipline.

5. A wholly praiseworthy institution also flourished in the same monastery: namely, the establishment by Sturmi of schools for the benefit of the young. From these emerged so many brilliant lights that the chief ornament of the ancient glory of the men of Fulda must be traced to this source.

Browerus produces a clear example of the reputation of the schools from the age of Sturmi in the *Life of Abbot Eigil*. Candidus says that “there was a school for the congregation, where divine law was learned and taught through continual exercise,” plainly according to the institution of Saint Benedict, in imitation of which Boniface established teachers of the young at Fritzlar and in other monasteries built by him, as he himself says in Letter 17.

From the academy of Fulda, where Alcuin taught for a time, came Haimo, Usuard—not, however, the author of the Martyrology—Freculfus, Rabanus, Liutbertus, Walafrid Strabo, Servatus Lupus, Rudolf, Aserchus and Ruodbertus, Modestus and Candidus, Gerungus, Meginfridus, and countless others.

Indeed, the great academy of Hirsau among the Nemetes also derived from this source: Liutbert gave its beginnings to the disciples of Alcuin and Rabanus, and Gerungus its development.

Christophorus Browerus should be read in his illuminating work on the *Antiquities of Fulda*, chapters 9 and following, where he treats this subject clearly and learnedly; we have also discussed it here in our Preface.

6. Yet nothing recommends and illuminates the monastery of Fulda as much as the piety and holiness of the men who flourished there. For the moment, let us say nothing of the distinguished men who were taken from there to the episcopal mitre, among whom nine pontiffs were claimed by Mainz.

There lived piously and holily there Sturmi, the leader and standard-bearer of the others, in the eighth century; Eigil and Rabanus Maurus in the ninth; and Bardo, surnamed Chrysostom, in the eleventh. Rabanus and Bardo were both archbishops of Mainz.

7. The monastery of Fulda still endures and flourishes today, enlarged by a town and its own territory. It lies in the district of Buchonia, formerly called Grapfeldt, by the river Fulda or Wulda, bordering eastern Francia and Wetterau.

Its abbot, archchancellor of the Empire and primate of the abbots of Germany, exercises spiritual jurisdiction over his subjects.

Recently, at the time when he laid aside his honors together with Luther’s errors and assumed monastic dress, the most illustrious margrave of Baden became coadjutor of the abbots of Fulda and Kempten, and was soon to receive other honors.

Albericus, in his *Chronicle*, observing the matter from William of Malmesbury and the monks Helinandus, says that the abbot of Fulda has “the ancient privilege of sitting at the emperor’s right hand on great festivals.” Read the account of the dispute over this matter in Lambert of Hersfeld under the year 1063.

8. The abbey of Fulda has had, and still possesses, numerous monasteries subject to it; Browerus gives a list of them in Book II, chapter 10, of the *Antiquities of Fulda*.

In that list, however, he omitted several, including the convent of Miliz, whose transfer to Fulda is recorded as having been made by Abbess Einhild “in the year 800, the thirty-first year of King Charles of the Franks.” This is clear from a charter in Book II of the *Traditions of Fulda*, a distinguished document of great antiquity; the tradition is found as no. 38 in Book II.

This Einhild, or Emhild, was the abbess and founder of the monastery of Miliz, as is clear from the preceding tradition, in which these words occur:

“I, Emhilt, abbess, grant, for the remedy of my soul, to our almighty Savior God, and to holy Mary, God’s mother, and to the handmaids of God who in my monastery at Miliz serve the Lord God day and night under the Rule of Saint Benedict and have promised to remain there, the land of my own inheritance in various places … together with the monastery mentioned above, which I myself built and constructed through my own labor.

“Everything in its entirety, with sound mind and sound counsel, as I have said above, I give, deliver, and transfer to our almighty Savior God, to holy Mary, God’s mother, and to the handmaids of God who in this monastery rightly and regularly serve God faithfully according to the Rule of the monks, without any falsehood …

“This donation I now deliver, in the presence of witnesses standing by, to the Lord God and to holy Mary, for those relics of holy Mary which are specifically mine, which I myself acquired and which are in my own chest, together with the chrismal. To these relics the handmaids of God who serve the Lord God in this same monastery first promised the vow of holiness, the monastic way of life, and the order of religion, etc.”

This was enacted in the year of the Incarnation 783, the sixteenth year of King Charles of the Franks. Saint Willibald, bishop of Eichstätt, subscribed the charter.

[Col. 0423D]

# Life of Saint Sturmi

## Author’s Prologue to Angildrutha

[Col. 0423] 1. I have always recognized you, virgin Angildrutha, as constantly aflame with divine love and continually filled with holy zeal. Therefore I complied with your requests.

For you asked me to set out for you the beginnings and life of the holy and venerable abbot Sturmi, and to write down the origins of the monastery of the Holy Savior, which he founded and established, and which is also called by another name, Fulda. You also asked me to set forth and truthfully recount the causes of that monastery’s establishment.

I have done, according to the smallness of my abilities, what you requested. Just as I learned from sufficiently trustworthy men—or rather from Christ’s vessels—the beginnings and way of life of that man and the foundations of the aforementioned monastery, so I have inserted them into this little book as best I could.

[Note: That is, virgins or consecrated women, over whom Abbess Angildrutha perhaps presided in the nearby convent at Bischofsheim or Kitzingen. The Apostle Paul calls a woman a “vessel” in 1 Thessalonians 4:4. Donatus, bishop of Besançon, entitled the Rule he composed for the nuns of the monastery of Jussan “to the most precious vessels of Christ”; and the Second Council of Chalon, chapter 52, commands abbesses to watch over themselves and the virgins entrusted to them as over holy vessels prepared for the Lord’s service.]

I have likewise inserted the various events which the course of this world continually undergoes, as I experienced them either from their own account or by my own observation.

For I too, Eigil, lived in his discipleship for more than twenty years, and from childhood until this present age I was nourished and instructed under the discipline of that monastery.

Therefore I have testified that I saw some of the things I have written.

Here you have what you requested, nominally dedicated to your name and left in your keeping. You answer the curses of the envious; defend me as more benevolent than presumptuous; and sustain me before Christ, your true bridegroom, by your holy prayers.

# The Life Begins

[Col. 0425]

## 2

At a certain time the holy and venerable Archbishop Boniface entered the region of Noricum [Note: That is, Bavaria, subject to Duke Tassilo, which the ancients called Noricum. Concerning it Paulus Warnefridus writes in Book III, chapter 31, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*: “The province of Noricum, inhabited by the people of the Bavarians, has Pannonia to the east, Suavia to the west, Italy to the south, and the waters of the Danube to the north.” Hence Charlemagne’s reason for sending Sturm to Tassilo in order to restore peace: a man of the country seemed likely to accomplish this more easily. Boniface also often visited the Bavarians, having found Duke Hucbert a supporter on his return from the pilgrimage to Rome undertaken in 732; perhaps he brought Sturm with him to Germany.] While he was instructing the priests and all the orders of the Church in the Catholic faith, and driving all the errors of the heretics from the churches there, he also restrained the Christian people of that nation—although they were Christians—from the ancient contagions of paganism and perverse doctrines by the true teachings of Christ.

Then noblemen began, in eager rivalry, to offer their children to him to be raised in the service of the Lord. At that time the boy Sturm was also entrusted to him at the entreaty of his parents. He was born in the province of Noricum, descended from and raised by noble Christian parents. Having abandoned his fleshly kinship and followed the counsel of our redemption [add: “the counsel”], he gladly undertook the road of pilgrimage with the bishop to whom he had been entrusted, while all his relatives wept.

After they had crossed several provinces and had finally reached the holy man’s monastery at Fritslari in the territory of the Hessians, the holy bishop commended the noble boy to one of his priests named Wigbert [Note: Namely, Saint Wigbert, the first abbot of Fritslari]. The holy priest then applied every diligence to train the boy Sturm for the service of almighty God. Having committed the Psalms to his retentive memory and firmly fixed very many readings in perpetual remembrance, the boy of Christ began to understand sacred Scripture in its spiritual sense. He took the greatest pains to learn the mysteries of Christ contained in the four Gospels; and, as far as he was able, he carefully stored the New and Old Testaments in the treasury of his heart through constant reading.

For, as it is written, his meditation was in the law of the Lord day and night; profound in understanding, discerning in thought, prudent in speech; handsome in appearance, orderly in gait, honorable in conduct, and blameless in life. Through charity, humility, gentleness, and cheerfulness he drew everyone’s love to himself.

## 3

After not a long time, the priest was ordained by the will and unanimous consent of all the servants of God. He began earnestly to preach the mystical words of Christ to the surrounding peoples at suitable times. Many sacred miracles were also performed through him by the divine gifts of the Holy Spirit.

How often, through the holy devotion of prayer, did he drive out, in the name of God, the dwelling of unclean spirits from sinful Christians! How often, through the laying on of hands and humble prayer, did he heal the sick from hostile diseases! How often, coming to the aid of hearts infected with the serpents’ poisons through saving instruction, did he cure by his healing the deadly venom that lay hidden and spread like a plague!

He commanded those who were at odds, with peace broken, to return to the harmony of charity before sunset. He taught everyone to possess patience, gentleness of disposition, humility of spirit, long-suffering of heart, faith, hope, and charity.

## 4

When he had exercised the office of his priesthood for nearly three years in preaching and baptizing among the people, a thought entered his heart through heavenly inspiration: that he should bind himself to a stricter life and to the harshness of the wilderness. He carried the constant memory of this thought in his breast at every moment and hour, until, instructed by divine admonition, he revealed to the man of God, Archbishop Boniface, what he had secretly conceived in his mind, as to his spiritual teacher.

When the holy man learned this, he understood that the inspiration had descended from God. He rejoiced that the Lord had deigned to admonish him by His grace and became, with the greatest devotion, a willing supporter of the plan. He therefore assigned him two companions, instructed them all carefully, prayed, and gave them his blessing. Then the bishop said:

“Go into this wilderness called Bochonia and seek a place suitable for the servants of God to inhabit. For God is able to prepare a place for His servants in the desert.”

Thus the three of them proceeded to the wilderness. Entering its wild and solitary places, where they saw almost nothing besides the sky, the earth, and immense trees, they devoutly entreated Christ to direct their feet into the way of peace.

On the third day they reached the place that to this day is called Hersfelt [Note: Here Christophorus Browerus unjustly attacks Trithemius, who attributes the beginnings of the Hersfeld monastery to Lullus and its governance to Sturm, its first abbot. Browerus is moved by the fact that the foundations of the Hersfeld basilica were first laid in the year 830, according to Lambert, a native of the place. He therefore supposes that the beginnings of the Hersfeld abbey were formed later, when Charlemagne was already flourishing, and that the relics of Saint Wigbert were transferred there from Fritslari. But Lambert himself expressly places the beginning of the Hersfeld monastery in the year 736, although the foundations of the smaller basilica in honor of Saint Wigbert were laid in 830, ninety-four years after the monastery’s origin.]

After seeing and examining the places situated all around, they asked Christ to bless the place for them to inhabit. In that spot where the monastery now stands, they built small dwellings covered with tree bark, and remained there for a considerable time, serving God with sacred fasts, vigils, and prayers.

## 5

After some time, Sturm, filled with holy zeal, left the wilderness and went to the holy Archbishop Boniface. He described to him in order the position of the place, the quality of the land, the course of the water, the springs and valleys, and everything that pertained to the site.

When the holy Archbishop Boniface had listened carefully and considered the matter prudently within himself, he received his hermit [Note: Saint Boniface habitually called Sturm his hermit, as Candidus testifies in the *Life of Saint Eigil, Abbot*] with every affection of charity and ordered him to live with him for a while.

After the sweet conversation he had with his teacher, and the abundant consolations of the sacred Scriptures, the bishop spoke as follows:

“I fear that you will inhabit the place you have found because of the proximity of the barbarian people. For, as you know, fierce Saxons are nearby. Therefore seek for yourselves a more distant and lower dwelling in the wilderness, which you may cultivate without danger to yourselves.”

Then blessed Sturm, having learned everything that had been commanded him by the Blessed One, instructed by his sacred teachings and strengthened in spirit, eagerly returned to the wilderness, concerned with the search for a place.

When he reached his companions, he found them anxiously awaiting his arrival in the dwellings mentioned above. When he saw them, he greeted them with peaceful words from the bishop and greatly consoled them both concerning his own arrival and concerning the bishop’s account.

After he had explained the holy bishop’s words to them in order, they took two brothers with them, boarded a boat, and sought the upper reaches. They began to travel by boat along the channel of the river Fulda, examining everywhere the mouths of all the streams and springs.

After leaving the boat, they walked around and examined the land, exploring the mountains, hills, higher and lower ground, to see where the Lord might show a suitable place for His servants to inhabit in the wilderness. Finally, on the third day they reached the place where the river called the Ludera enters the Fulda.

They then returned by boat and began to make their way back to their own cell, having found nothing that pleased their eyes, except that they lingered for a short while at a place called Rohenbah, where it seemed to them that the servants of God might somehow remain. Yet they did not think that it would altogether please the venerable bishop.

As they sailed back along the channel of the same river, after not a long time they reached their poor little dwellings. There they continually entreated Christ to show them the desired habitation in the wilderness, where, according to the command of Bishop Saint Boniface, they could serve the Lord perpetually and in safety.

Thus persevering day and night in the service of the Lord with fasts, vigils, and prayers, they did not lose the remembrance of the Lord their God, saying in their hearts: “I kept the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I shall not be moved” (Psalm 15). Continual praise of Christ also resounded alike in their mouths and hearts, as they fulfilled the Psalmist’s words: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33).

## 6

Then the holy Bishop Boniface, remembering his hermit Sturm and wondering what progress he had made in searching for a place, sent a messenger to ask him to come to him quickly.

When the messenger hastened there, he found him staying in the dwellings mentioned above. After greeting him honorably, he said:

“Our venerable father the bishop greatly desires to see you and has asked you to come to him, if it is not burdensome. For he has many matters to discuss with you.”

After hearing these words, the zealous man Sturm gave a humble reply:

“I give thanks to Christ God that so great a bishop, remembering my smallness, has deigned to send his messenger to me in this wilderness.”

He then called the brothers to him and ordered them to show the arriving messenger the service of charity. Carefully fulfilling his command, they set a table for him and offered him the food they had.

When he had recovered his strength, the brothers asked his permission to depart. Then the man of God called the messenger to him, thanked him for his weariness, and said:

“Greet the holy bishop Boniface from us, his peaceful servants, with words of peace, and tell him that I shall hasten to him after you as soon as I can.”

He blessed him and allowed him to depart.

On the following day, after asking the brothers for their blessing, the man of God Sturm immediately set out. Taking the road, he hastened to Seleheim, where he learned that the holy bishop was staying.

On the second day after his departure, he reached the bishop on foot and found him at the place mentioned above, Frideflar. When the holy bishop was informed that his hermit Sturm had arrived, he immediately ordered him to be brought before him.

When he had been brought in, Sturm humbly prostrated himself on the ground. After greeting the bishop, he asked for his blessing. When he had been blessed and greeted in return, the bishop ordered him to come nearer, kissed him, and commanded him to sit beside him. He rejoiced at his arrival with every affection of charity and asked him, for love of him and because of his presence, to relax his appointed fast for a little while.

The man of God, exercising great discretion, consented out of reverence for the supreme priest and teacher.

“I believe all that has been commanded me by you,” he said.

A table was set in the bishop’s presence, and food was brought before him, which the bishop ordered him honorably to eat.

When Sturm had been refreshed and the dish removed, the bishop rose and took his hermit with him to a more secluded place. There they spoke at length about spiritual matters and discussed the monastic way of life extensively.

For the holy pontiff was greatly intent—as later became clear—on establishing a monastic way of life in the wilderness. Accordingly, among their other conversations, he asked what progress had been made in exploring the place.

The hermit Sturm replied:

“We sailed upward along the channel of the river Fulda, but for several days we found nothing of which we dare to speak in your praise.”

The holy bishop understood that the place predestined by God had not yet been revealed. He therefore spoke to him in a prophetic voice:

“A place in that wilderness has indeed been prepared by God; Christ will show it to His servants when He wills. Therefore do not cease searching, knowing and believing that without doubt you will find it there.”

Having thus made him confident that the place would be found, stirred up in love of the monastic life, and thoroughly instructed in spiritual warfare against the devil, he allowed him to return to his beloved wilderness.

When Sturm reached his cell, which had been built at the place already mentioned above, Hersfelt, he greeted the brothers he found there and explained to them the holy bishop’s command and promise.

## 7

After he had rested briefly among them, he saddled his donkey, took provisions, and set out alone, commending his journey to Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life. Sitting entirely alone upon the donkey, he began to travel through the vastest regions of the desert.

Eagerly exploring the places, he surveyed everywhere with keen attention the mountainous and level ground; he looked at the mountains, hills, and valleys, and examined springs, streams, and rivers as he went.

Keeping the Psalms in his mouth, he prayed to God with sighs, lifting his mind toward heaven. He rested only wherever night forced him to stay.

Whenever he spent the night somewhere, he cut wood with the iron tool he carried in his hand and made a circular fence as protection for his animal, lest the wild beasts—which were extremely numerous there—devour it. But he himself, having impressed the sign of the cross of Christ upon his forehead in the name of God, rested without fear.

Thus the holy man, richly adorned with spiritual weapons, clothed his whole body in the breastplate of righteousness, fortified his breast with the shield of faith, protected his head with the helmet of salvation, and girded himself with the sword of the word of God; then he advanced to battle against the devil.

One day, as he was traveling, he reached the road leading to the region of the Thuringians, along which merchants traveling to Mainz went. There, where the road crosses the river Fulda, he found a great multitude of Slavs immersed in the channel of the same river, washing their bodies [lacuna in the source].

His animal, frightened by their naked bodies, began to tremble, and the man of God himself recoiled from their stench. They mocked the servant of the Lord in the manner of pagans, and when they wished to harm him, they were restrained and prevented by divine power.

One of them, who served as their interpreter, asked him where he was going. He replied that he was going toward the upper part of the wilderness.

## 8

Thus the man of God continued alone through the dreadful wilderness. Seeing nothing there besides beasts, of which there was an abundance, the flight of birds, immense trees, and the wild places of the solitude, he finally, on the fourth day, passed beyond the place where the monastery now stands and proceeded toward the upper reaches, where the river called the Gysilaha joins the channel of the Fulda.

Then, going a little farther upstream, where there was a path that in the ancient language was called Ortessueca, he arrived after sunset and began to take precautions for himself and his donkey against nighttime attacks.

While he was preparing his nighttime camp there, he heard in the distance the sound of water, though he did not know whether it had been caused by a wild animal or a human being. Standing silently, he listened with attentive ears. Again he heard the sound of water.

Because the man of God did not wish to shout, he struck a hollow tree with the iron tool he carried in his hand, understanding by God’s providence that a human being was there.

When the other man heard the sound of the striking, he hurried toward it and called out. As he approached, they saw one another and mutually exchanged greetings.

When the man of God asked where he came from, he replied that he came from Wedereiba and was leading his lord Orcus’s horse by the hand.

They settled there and spent that night together. For the man was extremely knowledgeable about the places in the wilderness.

When the man of the Lord revealed to him what he had in mind and what he was doing, the other began to tell him the names of the places and to point out the courses of the streams and springs.

Since they were then at the place that in the ancient language is called Ahloh, they rose in the morning and blessed one another. Immediately the secular man began to proceed along his own road toward Grapfelt.

## 9

The servant of the Lord immediately returned from there, commending his journey and all his hope to the Lord Christ, and continued alone through the wilderness in his customary manner.

As he traveled through Ailoha, he disliked the land there and came to the stream that to this day is called Grezibach. After seeing the character of the place and the quality of the land, he remained there for a short while.

Returning a little way from there, he reached the place blessed and long ago prepared by the Lord, where the holy monastery now stands.

When he arrived there, the holy man Sturm was immediately filled with immense joy and went forward cheerfully and exultantly. For he understood that such a place had been revealed to him by the Lord through the merits and prayers of the holy Bishop Boniface.

Then, going around and examining each thing he saw, he gave thanks to the Lord. The farther and wider he walked, the more he rejoiced.

After spending a considerable part of the day there, delighted by the beauty of the place and circling around to explore it, he blessed the place, carefully marked it, and departed joyfully.

## 10

Accordingly, when the man of God reached Hersfelt for the second time, he found his companions engaged in holy prayers. He told them of the discovery of the place and ordered them to hasten with him to the site where they were to go.

After asking the brothers for their prayers, he suddenly set out to seek the bishop at Selehim [Note: Adalger the cleric had granted this place, near Amanaburg and the monastery of Fritslari in Hesse, to Boniface; see Othlonus, Book II, chapter 18].

When he reached the bishop on foot after a few days and had been kindly received by him, he began to describe the place he had found, praising it.

“I think,” he said, “that the place beloved by you has now been found.”

When he had disclosed to him the site’s condition, the quality of its land, and the course of its water—which to this day are sufficient for the monastery—he made the bishop very cheerful. Rejoicing together and giving thanks to the Lord, they held a pleasant conversation for a long time about the life and conduct of monks.

## 11

After these sweet conversations, the holy bishop kept his hermit with him for a while and carefully instructed him with holy speeches and the sayings of sacred Scripture, urging him toward love of the monastic life.

Thus, having watered him from the richer fountain of teaching and strengthened him with very many admonitions from sacred Scripture, the holy bishop allowed his hermit Sturm to return to the wilderness.

He himself, in order to confirm the place found in the wilderness, went to the king’s palace.

But after Sturm had reached his companions in the solitude and wished to discuss with the brothers the place he had found, he returned from Hersfelt in the ninth year after he had begun to live in the wilderness [Note: The reading “ninth” seems preferable. Sturm’s companions indeed inhabited the Hersfeld wilderness for a long time while he carried out the matters mentioned above. Thus they had enough time to sketch out a monastery by rough workmanship, as the frugality of such men permitted. Certainly, between the year 736, when Lambert places the beginnings of the Hersfeld monastery, and 744, when the Fulda monastery was built, there intervened a period of nearly nine years.]

The devil, jealous of every good thing and fearing the life of God’s servants in the wilderness, stirred up the minds of wicked men so that they opposed the holy place to the servants of Christ.

Since the holy servants of God were not yet able to endure the obstinacy of the wicked—or rather, the attacks of the devil—they withdrew from there and retired to a place called Chrilhari.

## 12

As I have said, the holy Bishop Boniface went to Carlmann, king of the Franks, and spoke to him humbly and wisely:

“For your perpetual reward, if almighty God wills and your aid is present, I intend to establish the life of monks and found a monastery in your eastern kingdom—something that no one before us has begun in former times.

“Therefore we now ask for your pious assistance in this matter, so that an unfading gift may remain for you before Christ, the supreme King, in the future and endless kingdom.

“For we have found in the wilderness called Bochonia, beside the river called the Fulda, a place suitable for the servants of God to inhabit, and it belongs to your jurisdiction.

“We now ask your piety that this place be granted to us, so that there we may be able to serve Christ under your protection.”

When the king heard this, he rejoiced by God’s providence. He gathered all the princes of his palace, commended the bishop’s request, and, in their presence, handed over to the holy bishop the place he had requested, saying:

“The place you seek, which, as you assert, is called Eihloha (Aiclocha), on the bank of the river Fulda, and which I appear on this day to possess there as my own, I transfer wholly and intact from my right into the right of the Lord. Thus, from that place in every direction around it—from the east and west, from the north and south—a boundary (that is, a limit) shall extend for four thousand paces.”

The king then ordered a charter of his grant to be written, which he confirmed with his own hand.

He sent his messengers to gather all the noblemen who lived in the region of Grapfelt [Note: Thus Gregory II calls the inhabitants who cleared the vast solitude of Bochonia “Graveldi” in a letter addressed to them, preserved in Othlonus, Book I, chapter 29], so that they might ask them in the king’s words that anyone who appeared to possess anything of his own in that place should make a grant in the same way as the king had done.

When all had assembled on the appointed day, the king’s messengers arrived and said:

“The king commands all of you to be greeted in his words. He asks and orders that everyone who appears to possess any property in the place called Eihloha surrender the whole of it for the servants of God to inhabit.”

When they heard this, immediately, by God’s providence and with every diligence, they handed over to the man of God Sturm everything they were able to possess there.

## 13

When this grant had thus been confirmed on every side and the place had been transferred from human ownership into the right of the Lord, blessed Sturm went to the brothers at Dryhlar (Chrichlar).

Not many days afterward he rose from there, took with him seven brothers, and moved to the place where the holy monastery now stands.

In the year of Christ’s Incarnation 744, while two brothers, Carlmann and Pippin, ruled this people of the Franks, in the twelfth indiction, in the first month, on the twelfth day of that month, he entered the holy place long before predestined by God.

They implored the Lord Christ always to guard it and to defend it with His unconquerable power [variant: “to defend”]. Serving the Lord day and night with sacred psalmody, fasts, vigils, and prayers, they applied themselves, as far as they were able, to cutting down the forests and clearing the place by their own labor.

After two months had been completed, the venerable Archbishop Boniface went to them with a multitude of men. Having seen all the advantages of the place and examined its immense usefulness, he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit, giving thanks and praise to Christ because He had deigned to grant His servants such a dwelling in the wilderness.

He ordered the men who had come with him to cut down the thickets and all the brushwood at the place where it seemed suitable to him and to the servants of God who were with him to build a church.

He himself withdrew to the mountain that to this day is called the Bishop’s Mountain. There he continually prayed to the Lord and labored in examining the sacred books; for this reason he gave the mountain its name.

After one week had been completed, countless forests and trees had been felled, and *rase* had been arranged for making lime [Note: Browerus says that *rase* means “sod” in German. Our French people call that type of sod *des troubles*. They prepare it as follows: they pull sods from rich soil, dry them in the sun, and then, once dried, apply fire to them as fuel and material, either for making lime or for domestic use].

The bishop blessed the brothers, commended the place to the Lord, and departed with the workers who had come with him.

The following year the holy bishop again hastened there and reached his new monastery, which by then had begun to be called Fulda because of the course of the river.

After seeing and greeting the brothers, he spent several days among them. During that time he instructed his new monks and did not cease establishing among them the disciplines of the monastic rule according to the tradition of sacred Scripture.

When he had expounded the sacred Scriptures to the brothers and said that he nowhere read that monks possessed wine, it was decreed by common consent that no strong drink capable of causing intoxication should be drunk among them, but only weak beer [Note: Hence Boniface writes to Pope Zacharias, in Othlonus, Book II of *The Life of Saint Boniface*, chapter 12: “Building a monastery, we established monks living under the Rule of our holy father Benedict, men of strict observance, without meat, wine, or servants, content with the labor of their own hands.” See also the privilege of Zacharias in the same work, chapters 1 and 14, and that of Pippin, chapter 17. From this it is clear that the Fulda monastery was devoted to the Benedictine Rule from its very beginnings, and that Sturm had no other reason for his journey to Italy than to learn the regular way of life perfectly; below, he had already absorbed it as a young man at Fritslari].

After several years, when the community had grown, this was changed by a synodal decree during the reign of King Pippin, on account of the sick and weak. Nevertheless, some of the brothers abstained from wine and other strong drinks until the end of their lives.

After a private conversation with Sturm, in which he taught him how he ought to preside over the others, and after giving abundant instructions and admonitions by which he trained the brothers in how they ought to obey and submit, he greeted them, commended them to Christ, and departed.

He himself often used to visit them and, as often as his episcopal duties—which were very extensive among the people—allowed, he would come and stay there each year. He also strove to work with his own hands, and often sat upon the mountain mentioned above, which was beloved by him, examining the mystical Scriptures and praying familiarly to Christ.

## 14

Since the brothers eagerly desired to observe the Rule of the holy Father Benedict, and had bent their bodies and minds wholeheartedly toward the discipline of monastic life, they formed a useful plan: some of them should be sent to great monasteries elsewhere, so that they might perfectly learn the concord of the brothers there and the regular way of life.

When this was reported to the holy bishop, he approved their prudent plan and entrusted this mission to the zealous Sturm.

After preparing what was necessary for the journey and taking two brothers with him, in the fourth year after entering the place mentioned above he set out for Rome. After visiting all the monasteries in that land [Note: Among them was Monte Cassino, which at that time, under Abbot Petronax, had begun to rise again and flourish from its ruins], and fully learning the customs of all the brothers living there and the traditions of the monasteries, he remained among those monasteries for a whole year.

In the second year he returned, filled with the virtues he had witnessed.

As he was reaching this land with the Lord’s help, he was seized by illness at the monastery of Chitzzinga [Note: “Among the monasteries of virgins that Saint Boniface built,” says Trithemius at the end of his *Chronicle of the Franks*, “the monastery in the town of Kitsingen beside the Mogonum [the river Main, called *Moyn* in the vernacular] still stands out. Saint Hadelonga, a holy virgin whom he named Thecla, born in England, presided over it.” Othlonus preceded Trithemius in Book II, chapter 25. But this town in eastern France, having been handed over to the ruler of the new religious foundation—that is, the margrave of Ansbach—lost even this distinction of virginity, says Browerus], and remained ill for four weeks.

Then he recovered from his illness and went to Bishop Boniface, who happened at that time to be in Thuringia.

When the bishop saw him, he rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to the Lord for his arrival. He questioned him at length about the regions from which he had come.

When he learned from Sturm’s prudent account about the customs of that people and the disciplines of the monks, he said:

“Go and establish the new monastery of Fulda, as far as you are able, according to the customs of the monks whose life you observed there.”

Immediately the blessed man Sturm asked the bishop for his blessing and went to the wilderness. Welcome to his brothers, he arrived among them on the fourth day, to live with them.

He explained to them in prudent words, and demonstrated by his own example, what he had learned from the holy Fathers in the monasteries of the Italian regions and the province of Tuscany.

For in every discipline that he imposed upon the brothers, he first made sure to practice it himself, lest anyone should be able to say of him: “Why do you not do the things you teach?”

The brothers then possessed an immense desire to adapt themselves with all their strength to everything that had been told or shown to them through the examples of the saints. They observed in everything the Rule of Saint Benedict, which they had promised to fulfill (printed *implesse*, perhaps *impleturos*, “that they would fulfill”).

Living for many years in these holy ways, the monastery grew through the arrival of many people, since many surrendered themselves and their possessions there to serve the Lord.

As Christ’s household grew and the place began to multiply, its good reputation spread through every province, and its exceptional renown reached the ears of all the holy brothers in distant monasteries.

Since a very large congregation of monks there led a strict life under the discipline of the holy Rule, the holy bishop devoted many periods to visiting them. Taking pity on their poverty, he gave them several small estates from which to obtain the necessities of food.

## 15

In the tenth year after the holy Archbishop Boniface moved to the holy place, he took counsel with the king and the other Christians and entered the more distant regions of the Frisians, devoted to pagan worship. There, by teaching and baptizing, he won an immense multitude of people for the Lord.

After a long time he departed from there and returned safely to his churches in Germany.

The following year [Note: That is, the eleventh year after the founding of the Fulda monastery, corresponding to the Christian year 754, since Sturm began to inhabit the place at the beginning of 744, above, no. 13. Yet Willibald assigns the martyrdom of Saint Boniface to the year 755] he again reached the watery fields of the Frisians, desiring to complete the work of preaching he had begun.

When he had arrived and one day summoned the people to hear his teaching, they came each from his own place—not humbly, as though to hear the word of the Lord, but swollen with an evil spirit. With hostile weapons they rushed upon the sacred assembly of the Lord’s preaching and slaughtered the holy bishop of Christ with the sword; they also killed all his companions with swords.

After the bishop and many others with him had been crowned with martyrdom, faithful brothers came from Upper Frisia, from the monastery called Trech [Note: Thus we correct the printed books, in which the reading is “to Trech, a monastery,” and so forth]. They carried away the bodies of the holy martyrs and buried some there, while they took others with them—namely, the body of the holy Bishop Boniface and those of the holy priests and deacons who had suffered with him.

They also took the body of a bishop named Eoban, but when they took it up they could not find his head, which had been cut off by the enemies.

When they arrived, they placed the holy Bishop Boniface in the smaller church nearer to them, together with the bier on which he had been carried from the ship [Note: That is, a coffin, as the author explains his meaning shortly afterward; medieval authors commonly use the word in this sense]. They committed the other bodies of the martyrs to burial.

Then all the inhabitants of that place held a great council, wishing that the body of the holy martyr Boniface should thereafter rest among them forever, since they would have a great aid if they were protected by so great a martyr.

They proclaimed fasts and prayers and entreated the Lord that the holy martyr might deign to remain with them. They honorably prepared a place for him to rest in the larger basilica.

But the holy martyr wished his body to be carried to the place in the wilderness that he himself had chosen for it by God’s providence. This immediately became clear.

When they wished to carry him to the other church and place him there in a sarcophagus, those who approached put their hands to the bier but could not lift it [Note: Nothing similar is found written by Willibald or Othlonus in the Acts of Saint Boniface].

Many more joined them, but even then they could not move the bier on which the holy corpse lay.

### 16

They therefore understood that it was not his will that he remain in the same place; rather, they declared that he ought to be taken to the city of Mainz. Immediately lifting the bier without any difficulty, carrying it to the river, and placing it on the stern of a boat, they began to tow the vessel along the channel of the Rhine and make for the upper reaches. When Sturmi heard this, he hastened to come meet them from the monastery of Fulda, situated in the wilderness, and proceeded with them until they reached the city of Mainz by a favorable and easy passage [Col. 0436B].

The priests and all the clergy of that city immediately approached, took up the body of the holy martyr, and placed it honorably in their basilica. Then all the priests, clerics, and the entire people declared with one accord that it was not lawful for the holy martyr of God to be carried elsewhere, but that where, while alive, he had held the episcopal see, there also he ought to rest in body.

Moreover, a messenger came from the royal palace, saying that the king had ordered that the body of the holy martyr be placed in that same city, if it was his wish. But Sturmi and those who had come with him from the wilderness firmly maintained that the holy bishop, since he had often remained among them, had shown them the place where they should lay his body, and that without a doubt he had wished to rest bodily there in the wilderness.
