Meanwhile, while they were disputing in this way, and Lullus, the bishop of that city, was determined by every means to prevent the blessed martyr’s body from reaching the wilderness, the holy bishop appeared by night in a vision to a certain deacon [Note: [Col. 0436D] Othlonus calls him Otpertus in Book II of the Life of Saint Boniface, chapter 24.]. “Why,” he said, “do you delay carrying me to my place at Fulda? Rise,” he said, “quickly, and take me without delay into the wilderness, to the place that God destined for me.”

The man arose and first related to Sturmi, then to all the leading men, the sequence of the vision that had been shown to him. Then all were seized by excessive fear and dared no longer oppose the holy martyr’s passage from that place. Nevertheless, Lullus, who was bishop there, refused entirely to believe the holy martyr’s revelation until the man who had seen the vision had placed his hand upon the sacred altar and confirmed under oath what he had seen.

Then, according to the power of the Lord, whose will cannot be resisted, the body of the blessed martyr was lifted with the highest honor, carried to the river amid spiritual song, placed on a boat, and conveyed by water as far as the village of Hohheim, which stands on the bank of the Main. A few days later—namely, on the thirtieth day after his passion—they carried the holy priest’s corpse to the monastery of Fulda [Col. 0437A] and placed it in a new tomb.

The next day Bishop Lullus departed from there with the clerics and the rest of the company with whom he had come. At that time the venerable abbot Sturmi and his brothers gave thanks to Christ that they had deserved to have so great a patron, namely Boniface, the holy martyr of God, dwelling beside them.

After the arrival of the holy martyr, that holy place, chosen by God, began to grow, to be held in high esteem by everyone, and the monastery to increase—especially because many noblemen, hastening eagerly and competitively, surrendered themselves and all that they possessed to the Lord there. Thus, as the number of the monks increased daily, they were strengthened in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0437D] Before Saint Sturmi’s death, “he was father and teacher of about four hundred monks, apart from the bell-ringers and other lesser persons, whose number in the monastery was very large,” says Liudger in the Life of Saint Gregory, abbot of Utrecht, no. 10.], and the brothers serving the Lord there maintained the discipline of holy conduct with tireless and unceasing perseverance [Col. 0437B]. How many miracles were then performed there, and how many are still performed daily, I leave to others more expert to record.

### 17

Now Sturmi, beloved by everyone in the monastery and admired by the people outside it, carried out his ministry with the greatest devotion, always presenting himself first as an example to the others: what he taught in words, he demonstrated beforehand by his deeds.

Only Lullus disliked his good reputation and, out of envy, was always acting against him [Note: [Col. 0438D] This is expressed somewhat harshly against Saint Lullus.]. When Sturmi had preached the word of the Lord everywhere with persistence and everyone had listened to him attentively, the envious enemy of the human race, unable to tolerate such great benefit among the people, began to sow discord among the brothers and stirred up the minds of three false brothers [Col. 0437C] to fabricate deceitful charges, so that they might accuse Sturmi, the servant of God and faithful to all, before King Pippin.

Having been led astray by such diabolical suggestions, they formed a wicked plan among themselves, placed their confidence in the support of Bishop Lullus, and went to the king. There they accused the blessed man, bringing against him some charge—whose nature I do not know—of hostility toward the king.

When the man of God Sturmi was brought before him, he patiently endured their falsehood and did not wish to defend himself at length. Instead he said: “Behold my witness and my conscience on high; the Lord God is my helper, and therefore I am not confounded.”

Then the will of the wicked prevailed, and King Pippin ordered that the blessed man be removed and sent into exile with a few of his clerics [Note: [Col. 0438D] That is, monks.], namely to the great monastery called Unnedica [Note: [Col. 0438D] Browerus considers the word suspicious, and so do we, since he regarded conjecture as improper. Nevertheless, he suggests the related forms Venedica and Inda; but the monastery of Inda had not yet been founded.]. There he was received kindly and honorably by the abbot who then governed that monastery and by all the brothers, and for two years he lived there in exile, beloved by everyone.

When the brothers at the monastery of Fulda heard this and were informed about their abbot—how he had been taken away from them—they were deeply disturbed and suffered beyond what can be expressed. For there was then great turmoil in the house of God. Some wanted to leave the monastery; others wanted to go to the palace [Col. 0438A]; others entreated almighty God through fasts and prayers to come to their aid in his mercy.

Then an extraordinary rumor had filled the ears and mouths of everyone alike: that the blessed abbot Sturmi had been taken away from the monastery of Fulda through the counsel of Bishop Lullus. They all bore this grievously. There was no church in that eastern region that did not mourn his exile.

### 18

Meanwhile Lullus obtained from King Pippin, by offering unjust gifts, that the monastery of Fulda be granted into his dominion. Having received this authority [Perhaps: jurisdiction], he appointed there as abbot a certain man, his own [Supply: familiar associate] [lacuna], called Marcus, who would obey him in every respect.

But because the brothers turned their affections away from him out of love for their former abbot [Col. 0438B], he was like a stranger to them, and their ways did not accord with his. Because of this incompatibility of character, although they lived together bodily, they were separated from one another in mind.

While they were living amid such discord, and the brothers were continually considering how they might once again obtain Sturmi as their abbot through God’s grace, they could no longer endure the quarrel with Marcus, whom they had unwillingly received as abbot over them through Lullus. They formed a good plan, expelled him, and unanimously opposed his becoming their abbot any longer.

After he had been removed, all the brothers wished to leave the monastery and go to King Pippin’s palace, to ask the king to restore their abbot Sturmi to them. When Lullus heard this, he tried to calm them with soothing arguments, promising them that they themselves might choose from among their own brothers an abbot whom they liked [Col. 0438C].

When this pleased everyone, the brothers chose one of their number who was altogether a good brother, truly a servant of God, and adorned with every good character: a man named Preszoldus. Blessed Sturmi had taught him from childhood and had loved him greatly. They ordained him abbot over them solely so that he and they might confer together every day about how, with the help of the holy martyr Boniface and by the grace of almighty God, they might attain their purpose and request from King Pippin that their former master Sturmi be granted back to them.

Preszoldus himself governed the brothers for a considerable time and kept them united in charity. Day and night he considered together with them how, with Christ’s favor, they might recall to themselves their master and abbot Sturmi through the will of King Pippin [Col. 0438D].

### 19

Now while Preszoldus was thinking deeply about his father and master Sturmi, and the holy brothers were suffering great grief with him because of Sturmi’s absence, they continually sought the protection of almighty God in prayer, asking that he, for whom nothing is impossible, might by his unconquerable power grant that their master be permitted to return to them [Col. 0439A].

After they had done this for a long time on their own, and unceasing prayers for him were being offered to God throughout all the churches of the East and in every monastery of God’s servants and handmaids in the surrounding region, God, the comforter of the humble, heard the prayers of those who entreated him.

And because he had decreed that this should be requested, he inclined his ear to the prayers of the faithful and stirred the heart of King Pippin, so that the king began to think about the blessed Sturmi and ordered him to be brought honorably from the exile in which he was to his palace.

When Sturmi had been brought hurriedly to the palace and had spent several days there praying to God in the king’s chapel, awaiting what the king would command him, it happened one day that the king set out to hunt. As was his custom, he came at first light to pray, while the other servants of God rested after the morning vigils [Note: [Col. 0439D] That is, the monks who lived at the palace and over whom the abbot, called the palatine abbot, presided.].

Sturmi alone was awake. Watching for the king’s arrival, he opened the church doors for him and went before him to prayer with a bright light. When the king had humbly entreated God the King before the sacred altars, he rose and looked cheerfully at Sturmi:

“The Lord,” he said, “has now brought us together. We do not know what it was that your monks accused you of before us, nor do we know why we became angry with you.”

Sturmi replied firmly: “Although I am not free from sins, I have committed no offense against you, O king.”

But the king said: “Whether you have ever thought wickedly against me or done anything unjustly, may God forgive you everything; and I, from my heart, forgive you. From now on,” he said, “be in my favor and friendship forever.”

Then, taking a thread from his own cloak, he threw it onto the ground and said: “Behold, as a testimony of complete forgiveness, I throw this thread from my cloak onto the ground, so that it may be clear to all that our former hostility is henceforth annulled” [Note: [Col. 0439D] An outstanding passage concerning the symbolic act of forgiving an injury, and almost unique.].

Thus reconciled and firmly established in friendship, the king resumed the journey he had begun.

### 20

Shortly afterward, Preszoldus and the other brothers of the monastery of Fulda learned that their beloved master Sturmi had been received into the favor and friendship of the lord king. They decided to go to the palace and plead with the king on behalf of their master. They sent messengers to the palace, asking the king to give them back their abbot.

Everything that God wills to happen occurs easily and without effort. The king kindly received the brothers’ petition and promised to send the venerable abbot Sturmi back to them. We believe this was brought about through the many prayers of God’s servants and handmaids [Col. 0439D].

After not much time had passed, the king ordered Sturmi to be summoned before him. He entrusted to him the governance of the monastery of Fulda [Col. 0440A], which he had previously held, released him from every authority of Bishop Lullus, and ordered him to go with all honor to the monastery of Fulda. He also ordered him to govern the monastery according to the privilege that blessed Pope Zacharias, supreme pontiff of the apostolic see, had formerly given to Saint Boniface—and which the brothers have preserved in the monastery down to the present day. He further commanded that Sturmi seek the defense of his own cause and that of the monastery from no one other than the king.

Having received authority from the lord king, together with the aforesaid privilege, which he had received from the king’s hand [Note: [Col. 0439D] A diploma of King Pippin concerning this matter exists, though it is addressed to Boniface while he was still alive, in Othlonus, Book II, chapter 17; and to Zacharias in chapter 14. In Book III of the Antiquities of Fulda, chapter 8, a privilege granted to Sturmi by Pope Stephen is recorded as confirming the immunity of Fulda; in it Stephen orders that Sturmius “direct his brothers according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.”], he proceeded to his monastery.

It was immediately proclaimed throughout all these provinces that Sturmi was going to return to this land. Everywhere, among God’s servants and handmaids in all the monasteries, his return from exile soon became known [Col. 0440B], and they all gave immense thanks to Christ.

When the brothers learned that he had drawn near to the monastery, they took a golden cross and the relics of the saints and went out a long distance from the monastery to meet him. After greeting him and those who had come with him, they led him into the monastery amid spiritual song and rejoicing, and praised their Lord, who had given them the abbot they had long desired. Great joy arose among them.

### 21

Sturmi himself, devoted to his task with great zeal, began by reforming the brothers’ life and correcting their conduct, and by organizing their monastic duties. He adorned the temple—that is, the church—that they then possessed, and strengthened all the monastery’s buildings with new columns, massive beams, and new roof structures [Col. 0440C].

Not long afterward, considering how what the holy Rule says could be fulfilled—namely, that various crafts should be maintained within the monastery (chapter 66), so that the brothers would not perhaps need to wander outside because of some necessity—he gathered as many diggers as he could. Being sharp-minded, he carefully investigated the course of the river Fulda, then, at some distance from the monastery, diverted the stream of that river from its natural course and caused it to flow into the monastery through sizeable ditches, so that the force of the river might bring joy to God’s monastery.

How much that work benefited the brothers, and how much use it still provides every day, is evident both to those who see it and to those who use it.

Over the tomb of the blessed martyr Boniface he erected a shrine fashioned from gold and silver [Col. 0440D], which we usually call a “resting-place” [Note: [Col. 0439D] From this seems to have been derived the French word *Poisle*, as though one said “a place of repose” or “resting-place,” denoting the honorific canopies placed over the tombs of important persons. It is indeed very likely that the *ciboria*, *repas*, and *fredae* of the ancients—or little structures supported by four columns, sometimes made of gold cloth and other textiles of that kind—were so fashioned. This is relevant to Bede, Book III, chapter 2, where, speaking of the relics of Saint Oswald, king of the Mercians, he says: “They placed his standard, made of gold and purple, over the tomb.” More precisely, Gislebertus, bishop of Limerick, in Letter 30 among Usher’s Irish Letters, interprets *ciborium* as an umbrella or canopy over an altar; in printed editions *cimbarium* is mistakenly read.] and which he had made with beautiful workmanship, as was then customary. It remains to this day above the tomb [Col. 0441A] of that martyr of Christ, together with the golden altar.

### 22

Since, however, this just and perfect man of God was held in high esteem by everyone, and especially by King Pippin, he obtained from the king by his own speeches—for he enjoyed no small degree of familiarity with him—that the royal estate, namely Omunstat [Note: [Col. 0441D] In the Book of Traditions, no. 21, there is a copy of this donation, made at Orléans on the third day before the Ides of February. Among other things, Pippin is introduced as saying: “We piously give and devotedly transfer, for the remedy of our soul and in memory of our brother Carloman, to the monastery of Fulda . . . a certain estate called Omenestat in the district of Moynecgowe, with all its boundaries and appurtenances, etc.” This is Browerus’s note on the passage.], together with everything that the ancient kings possessed in that estate, should be granted to the aforesaid, often-mentioned monastery as his alms, and confirmed by a written charter, as was customary.

When Pippin died in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 768, in the twenty-third year of his reign, his son Carl succeeded him in the kingdom. Since this young king was then winning over with great gifts all those who had previously enjoyed honors under his father, he also summoned the venerable abbot Sturmi and joined him to himself in close friendship, often honoring him with many marks of distinction and royal gifts.

At one time the Lord put it into his heart to begin deliberating with a view to eternal reward. He summoned Abbot Sturmi to him, took counsel with him, and transferred Hamelenburc [Note: [Col. 0441D] According to Browerus, the donation charter identifies the place as a royal estate of ours beside the river Saale, and also mentions the neighboring village Dietpach and Hunfeld, now a small town.] with everything belonging to that estate, by the authority of his power, from his own right into the right of the Lord and of Saint Boniface, for the monastery of Fulda.

The brothers gratefully received this transfer and continue to offer prayers to the Lord for the king’s safety to this day. From then on Saint Sturmi lived throughout the rest of his life in the favor of the venerable King Charles.

### 23

In those same times, having undertaken an embassy between Charles, king of the Franks, and Tassilo, duke of the Norican province, he established friendship between them for many years [Col. 0441C].

While the lord King Charles was reigning successfully, the Saxon people remained for four years cruel and extremely hostile to all, and excessively devoted to pagan rites. King Charles, however, always devoted to the Lord and being most Christian himself, began to consider how he might win this people for Christ.

After taking counsel with God’s servants, he asked them to obtain by their prayers that the Lord might grant his wishes. Having assembled a very large army and invoked the name of Christ, he set out for Saxony, taking with him all the priests, abbots, presbyters, and all orthodox people and worshipers of the faith, so that they might cause the people, who from the beginning of the world had been bound by the chains of demons, to submit through faith to the gentle and sweet yoke of Christ by means of sacred teachings.

When the king arrived there, he converted most of that people to the faith of Christ, partly by wars, partly by persuasion, and partly also by gifts. After not much time had passed, he divided the whole province into episcopal parishes [Note: [Col. 0442D] A metropolitan province was called *ἐπαρχία* (*eparchia*), an episcopal province *παροικία* (*paroikia*), and the territory of a primary see, such as those of the patriarchs, was formerly called *διοίκησις* (*dioikēsis*), as appears from canon 9 of the Council of Antioch. The ancients preferred *parochia* for an episcopal diocese rather than *paroecia*. Certainly, says Nonius Marcellus, “the word *parochus* is derived from the Greek, because he provides vehicles.” For all provisions are called *παροχαί* (*parochai*). Today the word “parish” is commonly used more narrowly for any portion of an episcopal diocese placed under a single parish priest.] and gave God’s servants authority to teach and baptize.

Then the greater part of that people and land was entrusted to blessed Sturmi for administration. Having undertaken the office of preaching, he devoted himself in every way to acquiring a considerable people for the Lord. He took advantage of suitable opportunities, teaching them through sacred discourses to abandon idols and images, accept the faith of Christ, destroy the temples of their gods, cut down the sacred groves, and build holy basilicas.

### 24

After he had spent a long time preaching and baptizing there with his presbyters and had built churches throughout each of the various regions, the wicked and perverse Saxon people later deviated from the faith of Christ and entangled themselves in empty errors. Having assembled an army, they went beyond their own borders and reached as far as the Rhine, laying waste and devastating everything.

When they turned back from there, they slaughtered with hostile carnage everyone they could find. When their army had encamped in Loganacinse, which lies near the aforesaid monastery, they conspired to send a chosen multitude of men from the army against that very monastery, burn everything they found with fire, and kill the servants of God with the sword.

When Saint Sturmi learned of this, he immediately summoned the brothers, informed them of the danger threatening them, and advised them to take up the body of the holy martyr and hasten to Hamelanburg [Col. 0442C]. The man of God Sturmi himself went out toward Wedereiba, intending, if he could in any way, to restrain the conspiracy of the wicked.

We, his brothers and disciples, took the body of the holy martyr from the tomb in which it had lain for twenty-four years [Note: [Col. 0442D] The Fulda Annals agree with this reckoning, reporting that the event took place in the year 778.]. Together with all God’s servants, we began to depart from the monastery.

We stayed the first night at a nearby cell, where the waters of the Fledena join the channel of the Fulda. Rising from there in the morning, we reached the more distant Sinn and pitched our tent there. In it we placed the most sacred body of the martyr of Christ, while the soldiers of Christ made camp around it.

After we had spent three nights in the tents, our messengers arrived on the fourth day and reported that some of our people had gathered to wage war against the Saxons and that, after being defeated, the Saxons had fled to their own lands [Col. 0442D].

When we heard this, we lifted the sacred bones of the blessed martyr and returned joyfully to the monastery from which we had departed. We buried the holy bones of the martyr of God in the tomb where they had previously been [Col. 0443A], giving thanks to Christ the Lord that peace had been granted and we were allowed to dwell in our monastery [Note: [Col. 0443C] Yet above, at no. 20, it says that Sturmi had erected a shrine, or canopy, over Saint Boniface’s tomb. The bodies of the saints therefore were not buried in the upper part of the canopy, since it was almost solid, but in the tomb itself; this was then the usual practice.].

### 25

Then King Charles again went with an army into that land, to strengthen the Christian faith that had been begun. He ordered the venerable Sturmi, who was ill and already worn out by old age, to remain at Heresburg with his companions to protect the city.

After arranging everything according to his will, the king returned and ordered the holy man to remain for a few days in the aforesaid city after his own departure. When this period had ended, the man of God returned to the monastery, taking with him the physician of Lord King Charles, named Wintarus, to assist him in his illness.

One day, when the physician had administered to him some potion of his art—I do not know what kind—with which he ought to have reduced his illness, he instead increased it, so that the grievous disease grew more severe and acute. In distress, Sturmi began to say that the physician, who ought to have lessened the illness, had inflicted a great evil upon him.

He ordered that they run quickly to the church and that all the *gloggas* (bells) be rung together [Note: [Col. 0443C] This is what they called bells. Willibaldus and Othlonus, near the end of the Life of Saint Boniface, call them *gloccae* and *cloggae*; Boniface himself, in Letter 9, uses *clocca*, although Bede had already used the word *campana* in Book IV, chapter 23. From this and other evidence we gather that the statement made here concerning the ringing of the church bells during the final struggles of Sturmi’s dying is almost unique.]. After the brothers had assembled, he ordered them to be told that his death would soon come and asked them to pray earnestly for him.

First he had the entire household gathered and brought into the house where he lay. Then he addressed the whole community in these words:

“You, brothers, have known my efforts, how until this day I have labored for your welfare and peace. Above all, I have taken care that after my death this monastery might persevere in Christ’s will and that you, my sons, might be able to serve the Lord here sincerely and in charity [Col. 0443C].

“Now persevere throughout all the days of your life in the purpose you have undertaken [Col. 0444A]. Pray to the Most High God for me. If I have acted wrongly among you or unjustly offended anyone, forgive me. And from the depths of my heart I forgive everyone all reproaches and insults offered to me, including Lullus, who was always opposed to me.”

After these and several other good words, he bade the brothers farewell and dismissed them.

When the brothers had gone out, the holy man began to grow gravely weaker and to be driven toward his end. Everyone was sorrowful, and great sadness occupied the hearts of the brothers. With tearful voices they implored the mercy of God alone and commended the death of their holy and venerable abbot Sturmi to the Lord with the greatest prayers.

### 26

On the following day, that is, the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, as his weakness grew worse, he was brought to the point of death [Col. 0444B]. As we stood around him and saw that his end would come quickly, one of us began to speak:

“Father, we do not doubt that you are going to depart to the Lord and reach everlasting life. Therefore we beseech your fatherhood to remember us and there to pour out prayers to the Lord for your disciples. We confidently believe that it will benefit us to send on ahead such a patron.”

He suddenly looked at us and said: “Make yourselves worthy, and so conduct yourselves in your behavior that I may rightly be able to pray for you; and I shall do what you ask.”

After these words, that holy soul was released from the flesh, rescued from the prison of the body, and, filled with good merits, departed to Christ, whose kingdom endures forever. Amen.

## In the Year of the Lord 824. Bernowinus, Bishop of Clermont

### Historical Notice on Bernowinus

(*Hist. Franc. litt.*, vol. IV, p. 481.)

For a long time there was deep silence among all writers concerning Bernowinus, bishop of Clermont. Mabillonius was the first to rescue his name from oblivion; he published several poems bearing his name from a manuscript in the Ottobonian Library.

It is entirely uncertain when he was elevated to the see of Clermont and in what year he died. Assisted by the munificence of Charlemagne, Bernowinus built a large church in honor of Saint Alliri in his episcopal city. Only four poems by Bernowinus survive, among them his epitaph.

### Poems of Bernowinus

#### First Poem

(Mabillonius, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, p. 717.)

Almighty Lord, who govern the heights and the depths,

God, powerful in majesty, always and everywhere,

Look down from the highest throne of the saints’ glory,

And give aid to your servants, good King.

Grant peace to rulers and salvation to their subjects;

Drive away the threats of the enemy and restrain savage wars.

May these shining heights of the temple also,

Which I, Bernowinus, have established, be pleasing to you, O God.

And grant to Augustus Charles, by whose power I completed them,

The great joys of his empire.

And whoever from this place shall knock at the highest ears with prayers,

May God always grant his prayer to be fulfilled.

Bernowinus, rejoicing and led by the love of God,

Built this honorable work, reader, which you behold [Col. 0445B],

Also out of love for that great father of his,

Whose body rests in the sanctuary of the holy house.

In that place the merciful God has already and repeatedly

Displayed many miracles on account of his merit.

Whoever comes, rich in the gift of faith,

Finds what he asks for; behold, he possesses what he desires.

You brothers, petitioners for pardon, I beg you:

Ask the Maker of this house for heavenly gifts.

These things I established for you, great priest Illidius,

Which shines here—the Lord’s bright house . . . [syntax uncertain].

I am Bernowinus, a small lover of the saints,

Who offer vows and prayers especially to you.

I humbly ask you: plead with the Thunderer for me in prayer,

That by pardon he may cleanse all my sins [Col. 0445C].

And may he grant to Augustus Charles, by whose piety we are sustained,

Abundant rewards in the heavenly realm.

#### Poem II

(Mabillonius, same work.)

If some traveler, eager to learn about things,

Should wish to know the author of this poem or work,

When he returns, I ask him to pause briefly on his journey

And read this inscription, which tells him everything.

For I am called Bernowinus, the most humble bishop,

Who made these heights and sang these poems.

Whoever comes to ask pardon for sins with tears,

Let him pass through these gates to the holy places,

Where Illidius, lofty in merits and powerful in piety,

Rests bodily in the exalted sanctuary.

There he will find certain comforts of salvation,

And the pardon he seeks with tears, he receives [Col. 0445D].

#### Poem III: The Epitaph of Bernowinus

(Mabillonius, same work.)

You who seek the sacred heights of this venerable temple,

Which possesses the splendid ornaments of piety,

Read again this mournful poem about my unhappy fate,

Which the final hour of life brought upon me.

Once I was rich, famous throughout the wide world,

And greatly beloved by pious princes [Col. 0446A].

The glory of abundant possessions distinguished me,

But the friendship of kings was customarily valued more highly.

Therefore the people honored me with generous esteem,

With excessive gifts and the favor of their prayers.

But suddenly, torn by fate from so great a height,

This narrow resting place now holds me.

These examples of my condition, reader, show you

The whole road of life along which you travel:

Do not pursue riches or shameful profits,

Nor, yourself doomed to perish, seek them while blindly pursuing riches.

While such things are kept, immersed in profound darkness,

They send their own [possessors] into the abyss, into consecrated caves [sense uncertain].

What does it profit you to become accustomed to delicate banquets?

What does elaborately worked purple profit you?

For an unhappy body is given, for which such things are prepared,

Only to become soon both dust and food for worms [Col. 0446B].

But now I ask you to return a favor to me for this poem,

And say: “May God have mercy on him.”

Whoever you are who succeed me, grant me this honor,

I who laid down my limbs in this place:

May no hand violate it, I pray, until the Almighty says from on high:

“Rise; now our trumpet commands it.”

Life, salvation, rest, hope, glory, grace, virtue—

Grant pardon to me, your servant, O Christ, and so forth.

Give Bernowinus, merciful nourisher, your shining kingdoms,

You who send light to human beings through their eyes,

You who freely grant it to one subdued beneath a great burden, and so forth.

Thus, for yourself and all your people, return vows to the Lord,

And, I beg you, remember his servants [Col. 0446C],

This sanctuary which he founded while Charles was triumphant.

Whoever wishes to enter the house and enjoy good things,

Let him say as he goes, I beg you, humbly:

“Peace be to this house,

Which Christ and his disciples commanded to be kept.”

When these things have been done, as you go out I humbly ask you to say:

“Have mercy on Bernowinus, O King, most high God,

Who built this house and adorned it with poetry.

In this house shines the holy, wondrous cross of Christ,

On which the ineffable Victor—salvation, light, and life—

Hung and freed the people from the enemy’s ambushes.”

(The following verses by the same Bishop Bernowinus are also found for a cross. Likewise, verses on a chalice and paten, which read as follows:)

Bernowinus the humble returns his vows to the Thunderer.

This body of the humble . . . grants blessed life.

#### Poem IV: Verses to the Cross

(Marten, *Ample Collection*, vol. VI, p. 820.)

Eternal Creator, whom I praise in these verses,

King, give Bernwin rest, O gracious and merciful Father and Redeemer.

Virtue of virtues, Victor, victory, Jesus—

Christ, you righteous judge, now, as king, have mercy on me.

Almighty Lord, maker and author of the world,

Be gracious and merciful; be my only hope of life.

Receive this gift; I humbly beg you, accept it.

## In the Year of the Lord 826. Dungalus the Recluse

### Historical Notice

(From Fabricius, *Library of Medieval and Late Latin Literature*.)

Dungalus the Recluse, or a monk leading a solitary life, wrote a letter to Charlemagne concerning a double solar eclipse that was said to have occurred in the preceding year, 810. Lucas Dacherius published it in volume X of the *Spicilegium*, p. 143 (in the new edition, vol. III, p. 324; there also appears the critique of Ismael Bullialdus, repeated from the preface to volume X of the earlier edition).

The same man—or another Parisian deacon—composed around the year 828 a book of *Responses Against the Opinions of Claudius of Turin*, which discouraged the veneration of images, addressed to the emperor Louis and his son Lothair Augustus. Papyrius Massonus first published it at Paris in 1603; from there it was inserted into the *Libraries of the Fathers*, Paris 1624, vol. IV; Cologne, vol. IX; and Lyon, vol. XIV, p. 196.

# DUNGALUS THE RECLUSE

[Note: [Col. 0447A] Dungalus’s Letter. The author of this letter is Dungalus the Recluse—that is, a solitary, leading a monastic life far from the company both of monks and of secular persons. Since in this letter we had found several obscurities, we consulted the distinguished man Ismael Bullialdus, who was exceptionally versed in mathematical matters, as well as in every kind of sound learning, asking him to explain to us what he thought of it. Accordingly, he wrote the following brief observation, which we thought worth transcribing here. [Col. 0447B]

“This letter of Dungalus, although it does not answer the question proposed by the emperor either skillfully or clearly, nor demonstrate what it ought to have demonstrated, is nevertheless useful in showing that at that time several people, and the Emperor himself, were in doubt about what was being asserted by certain persons carried away by rashness and empty boasting: namely, that two eclipses of the sun had occurred and been observed in our Europe in the year of Christ 810. Those who were guided by reason rightly doubted this.

For it could not have happened in that year, 810, on the seventh day before the Ides of June, that the sun was eclipsed, or that its eclipse was recorded in Europe. Calvisius made an excellent annotation concerning this year and judged most correctly that this solar eclipse on the seventh day before the Ides of June had been predicted by someone who wrote a calendar, on the basis of a calculation derived from more imperfect astronomical tables, [Col. 0448A] but that it had not actually taken place (I add: nor had it been seen by our Europeans). Nevertheless, the chronologers wrote in their chronicles that it had been seen, following the opinion—or rather the error—of the common people.

It seems to me that one should add that the calculator of that year 810 was mistaken in failing to point out that this eclipse would appear in places situated under, or south of, the equatorial line, and would be visible in the southern hemisphere. For it is impossible that in places somewhat distant from the equatorial line two solar eclipses should be seen within a period of six months; this can occur under the equatorial line, or in places lying along parallels not far removed from it. Within a period of five months, however, two solar eclipses can be seen in the same northern or southern hemisphere. All these matters can be demonstrated, since they are true.

But the author of this letter, Dungalus, seems to have been unaware of these distinctions. And when, on the day before the Kalends of December of that same year 810, the solar eclipse observed by Europeans occurred, he ought to have asserted that the earlier eclipse of the seventh day before the Ides of June had taken place in the regions opposite ours and among our antipodes, or at least had been seen in the southern hemisphere, if he wished to satisfy the question fully.”

Thus far Ismael Bullialdus. Our own Jean Mabillon collected Dungalus’s letter from a manuscript of San Remigio.] 

## LETTER ON THE TWO SOLAR ECLIPSES OF THE YEAR 810, TO CHARLEMAGNE

(From Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, vol. III, p. 324.)

[Col. 0447]

[Col. 0447A] In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.

To the most glorious lord Charles, most serene Augustus, exceptionally devoted to all the noble and honorable gifts and exercises of royal virtues possessed by all preceding Roman princes: long life, faithful safety, continual benevolence, peace, an unfading crown, glory without end.

I have therefore heard, most beloved lord—I, Dungalus, your faithful servant and petitioner—that you sent a letter to Abbot Waldon, so that through it he might question me in your words concerning the cause of the sun’s obscuration, which, as you said you had learned from the report of several people, had occurred twice in the preceding year, 810 from the incarnation of the Lord. As you recalled having read, not only the ancient philosophers of the pagans but also a certain Constantinopolitan [Col. 0449A] bishop had previously declared that this was a natural effect of the collision of the elements, known through customary and certain investigation, before it occurred.

It therefore seemed good to your most blessed and renowned serenity to command that I should be questioned, as though I were a student of wisdom, about what I thought and what I knew, and that my confession should be set down in writing as I gave my opinion and answer, and that what was written should be brought to you.

I shall not delay, then, nor shall I conceal my willingness, according to my abilities, to obey your most holy and useful command. Would that I might prove as effective as I am willing, so that I could not merely desire what I wish but also attain it in accordance with my hope. Yet before the supreme Ruler a devoted and eager intention is reckoned as though the deed had been accomplished and fulfilled.

[Col. 0449B] Since, then, my lord, investigation and knowledge of this subject properly and especially belong to philosophers—that is, to natural philosophers—as your letters indicate, I believe that, had I possessed their more elaborate and diligent books, in which they treated these matters and subjects in a more practiced style and with clearer expression, I could have answered you more fully and learnedly concerning what you asked.

Nevertheless, according to the simple, slight, and condensed little books that are at hand, insofar as the sluggishness of my dulled heart and my slow understanding—creeping and moving only with laborious effort and lazy exertion—can manage to offer a preliminary account, I shall answer as best I can, lest, according to the common proverb, “the wolf in the story,” I should seem to be restrained by fearful and foolish silence. I know beyond all doubt that your most serene and devout long-suffering clemency will readily grant me pardon if I say anything deficient or otherwise than I should, and that, with paternal correction, it will moderately chastise me as one who has erred through frailty and weakness rather than through lack of diligence or zeal.

The origin of this question must first be retraced, so that, as is customary in other discussions, the reasoning may proceed in order from the beginning and an appropriate answer may be given to what has been asked.

Macrobius Ambrosius, in his exposition of Cicero, among other matters mentions nine circles that surround the *aplanes*—that is, the greatest sphere in which the twelve signs are seen fixed—and beneath which are placed seven other spheres through which the two luminaries, the sun and the moon, and the five wandering stars travel. Of these orbits—that is, of the circles mentioned above—the first is the *galactias*, which is interpreted in Latin as “milky.” It alone lies subject to the eyes; the other circles are apprehended more by thought than by sight.

The second is the zodiacal circle, that is, the sign-bearing circle, so called because it bears and contains signs—that is, stars and constellations. The other five circles are called parallels, given this name because they are neither equal in every respect nor unequal. Virgil mentions them in the *Georgics*.

Besides these there are two others, the colures, whose name derives from an incomplete revolution. Two additional circles, which are added to the number given above—the meridian and the horizon—are not drawn on the sphere, because they cannot have a fixed location; rather, they vary according to the differences among those who look around or inhabit a place. There is no need here to explain all these matters, which have merely been named and counted in passing.

The two luminaries mentioned above—that is, the sun and the moon—and the five stars called wandering stars have divided among themselves the seven spheres placed beneath the greatest sphere containing the twelve signs, which is called the *aplanes*. Each, having occupied its region, has obtained it as though it were its own particular inheritance.

In the first of the seven spheres is the star called Saturn’s; in the second, Jupiter’s; in the third, Mars’s; in the fourth, which is the middle one, the sun; in the fifth, Venus’s; in the sixth, Mercury’s. The moon occupies the seventh, which is the outermost and lowest of them all.

Cicero describes the arrangement in this way, and Archimedes and the Chaldean system agree with him. Plato, however, confirms that the sun holds the second place upward from the moon—that is, the sixth place from the top among the seven—following the Egyptians, the parents of all the philosophical disciplines, who wish the sun to be placed between the moon and Mercury.

Although Cicero’s opinion, and that of his authorities, strengthened by certain pronouncements and plausible arguments, has prevailed and has been adopted for practical use by nearly everyone, Plato’s more penetrating observation nevertheless seems to have discovered the truer order. Apart from the evidence of sight, the following reasoning also recommends it: since the moon lacks light of its own and borrows it from the sun, it must be situated beneath the source of its light.

This reasoning makes the moon lack its own light, while all the other stars shine with their own, because they are located above the sun in the purest ether. In that ether, as I may put it in the words of the Philosopher, everything that exists possesses natural and proper light. The whole of it, together with its fire, rests upon the sun’s sphere in such a way that the regions of the heavens far from the sun are oppressed by perpetual cold.

The moon, however, because it alone is beneath the sun and is near the region of perishable things, which lacks light, could not shine from itself. Finally, because the lowest part of the entire world is the earth, while the lowest part of the ether is the moon, they called the moon an earth, but an ethereal one.

It could not be motionless like the earth, because in a revolving sphere nothing remains motionless except the center. The earth is the center of the world’s sphere and therefore alone remains motionless.

Again, the earth becomes bright by receiving the sun’s light but does not itself shine. The moon, like a mirror, emits the light with which it is illuminated. Although it is a denser body than the other heavenly bodies, it is nevertheless much purer than anything earthly and becomes penetrable to the light it receives, so that it emits it again from itself. Yet it conveys to us no sensation of heat, because when a ray of light comes to us from its source—that is, from the sun—it carries with it the nature of the fire from which it arises. But when it is poured into the body of the moon and shines back from it, it reflects brightness alone, not heat.

A mirror likewise, when it sends back from itself the radiance of a fire placed opposite it at a distance, displays only the likeness of the fire, without any sensation of heat.

To this it must be added that, apart from the sun, the moon, and the five stars called wandering stars, all the remaining stars are fixed in the heavens and move only with the heavens. Others, whose assertion is closer to the truth, have said that these stars too advance by their own motion, in addition to being carried along by the revolution of the heavens. But because of the immensity of the outermost sphere, they consume many ages in completing their course, exceeding any number that can be reckoned; and therefore no human being can perceive the motion of any of them. The span of human life is insufficient to detect even the briefest point of such a slow advance.

The sun, the moon, and the five stars to which the name “wandering” has been given, besides being carried from east to west by the daily revolution of the heavens, proceed by their own motion from west toward the east. This is demonstrated by arguments that lead to the truth.

That they move and are not fixed in the heavens is affirmed both by sight and by reason: they are seen now in one region of the heavens and now in another, and often, when two or more have come together in one place, they later separate both from the place where they were seen together and from one another. Fixed stars do not do this; they are always seen in the same places and never disperse from their conjunction with one another.

That they revolve from east to west by a motion contrary to their nearer motion is demonstrated not only by the clearest reasoning but also by the evidence of the eyes.

For, considering the order of the signs into which we see the zodiac divided or distinguished, let us take our beginning from any one sign in its sequence. When Aries rises, Taurus emerges after it; Gemini follows Taurus, then Cancer, and the remaining signs in order.

If these stars proceeded from east toward the west, they would not revolve from Aries to Taurus, which is placed behind it, nor from Taurus to Gemini, the following sign. Rather, they would proceed from Gemini to Taurus and from Taurus to Aries, advancing in a straight motion corresponding to the world’s revolution.

But since they revolve from the first sign to the second, from the second to the third, and thence to the remaining signs that lie behind, while the signs fixed in the heavens are carried along with the heavens, it is beyond doubt that these stars move not with the heavens but against them.

To make this fully clear, I shall present the course of the moon, which is more remarkable both for its brightness and for its speed.

Around sunset on approximately the second day, it is seen, as though near the sun that it has recently left. After the sun has descended, the moon itself occupies the edge of the heavens, preceding it in the west. On the third day it sets later than on the second. Thus each day it withdraws farther from the west, until on the seventh day, around sunset, it is seen in the middle of the sky.

After another seven days, when the sun is setting, the moon rises; thus, during the middle of the month, by withdrawing from west to east, it traverses half the heavens—that is, one hemisphere. Again, after another seven days, around sunset it occupies the summit of the hidden hemisphere, as is indicated by the fact that it rises at midnight.

Finally, after the same number of days has elapsed, with approximately two additional days, it overtakes the sun again, and the rising of both appears close together. It continues to follow the sun until, moving away from it once more and continually retreating toward the east, it leaves the west behind.

The sun itself also naturally moves from west toward east, and by gradually retreating toward the east leaves the west behind. Although it completes its retreat more slowly than the moon—for it traverses one sign in the same length of time in which the moon travels through the entire zodiac—it nevertheless offers clear signs of its motion, visible to the eyes.

Let us suppose that the sun is in Aries, which, because it is an equinoctial sign, makes the hours of night and day equal. When the sun sets in this sign, we see Libra—that is, the claws of Scorpio—rise immediately, and Taurus appears near setting. For we see the Pleiades and the Hyades, the brighter parts of Taurus, setting not long after the sun.

In the following month the sun withdraws into the next sign, that is, into Taurus. Consequently neither the Pleiades nor any other part of Taurus is seen during that month. For the sign that sets together with the sun is always hidden, so that the stars near it are concealed by the sun’s proximity.

The Dog likewise is not then seen, because it is near Taurus and is covered by the proximity of the light. This is what Virgil says:

> With gilded horns bright Taurus opens the year,  
> And the Dog, yielding to the opposing star, sets.

He does not mean that, when Taurus rises with the sun, the Dog—which is near Taurus—immediately sets. Rather, he says that it sets when Taurus carries the sun, because then it begins not to be seen, with the sun nearby.

At that time, however, when the sun sets, Libra is found so far above that the whole of Scorpio appears to have risen; Gemini, meanwhile, is seen near setting. Again, after the month of Taurus, Gemini is not seen, which signifies that the sun has moved into it.

After Gemini the sun returns to Cancer, and then, when it sets, Libra is immediately seen in the middle of the sky. It is therefore clear that the sun, after passing through three signs—Aries, Taurus, and Gemini—has withdrawn to the middle of the hemisphere.

Finally, after the following three months, during which it has passed through the three succeeding signs—Cancer, Leo, and Virgo—it is found in Libra. Libra again equalizes night and day, and when the sun sets in that sign, Aries immediately rises, in which the sun used to set six months earlier.

We have chosen to emphasize its setting rather than its rising because the later signs are seen after sunset. When the sun has set and those signs ordinarily become visible, by showing that the sun returns to them we demonstrate beyond doubt that it withdraws by a motion contrary to that of the heavens.

What we have said about the sun and the moon is also sufficient to establish the retreat of the five stars. For, moving into the later signs by the same principle, they always turn with a retreat contrary to the world’s revolution. Their courses and returns are said to be governed by the sun itself.

There is a fixed limit of distance: when each wandering star, retreating, reaches the sun, it seems to be driven backward, as though forbidden to proceed farther. Again, when, by retreating, it reaches a certain point, it is recalled to its customary direct course. Thus the sun’s force and power regulate the movements of the other luminaries according to a fixed measure.

A circle, therefore, is understood as the complete and accomplished revolution of each star: that is, its return to the same place after it has traversed the circuit of the sphere through which it moves.

This is a line surrounding the sphere and forming, as it were, a path through which the sun and moon travel; within it the proper wandering of the stars is confined. The ancients called them “wandering” because they are carried along in their own course and, contrary to the impulse of the greatest sphere—that is, of the heavens themselves—revolve from west toward east in a motion opposed to the heavens.

All have equal speed, a similar motion, and the same manner of travel, but they do not all complete their circles and orbits within the same period of time.

The unequal extent of the spheres through which the individual stars travel causes the difference in duration despite the same speed. From Saturn’s sphere, which is the first of the seven, to Jupiter’s sphere, which is second from the top, the intervening distance is so great that the former completes the circuit of the zodiac in thirty years, while the latter completes it in twelve.

Jupiter’s sphere is again so far from Mars’s that Mars completes the same course in two years. Venus, however, is so much lower than the region of Mars that one year is sufficient for it to traverse the zodiac.

Mercury’s star is now very close to Venus, and the sun is close to Mercury, so that these three complete their own heavens in approximately the same period, namely, one year. Cicero therefore called these two—the courses of Venus and Mercury—companions of the sun, because within an equal interval they never withdraw far from it.

The moon, however, has withdrawn so far downward from them that what they complete in a year it completes in twenty-eight days.

When Cicero wishes the sun to be fourth among the seven, and the fourth among seven is not merely approximately middle but is wholly and literally middle, he did not simply call the sun middle, but “almost middle,” using these words: “Next, the sun occupies almost the middle region among the seven.”

The addition by which this statement is qualified is not without purpose. The sun, holding the fourth place, occupies the middle region numerically but not spatially. Saturn’s star, which is highest, traverses the zodiac in thirty years; the sun occupies the middle and does so in one year; the moon, at the bottom, does so in less than one month.

There is therefore as much difference between the sun and Saturn as between one and thirty, and as much between the moon and the sun as between twelve and one. Hence it is apparent that the division of the entire space from top to bottom is not made at the sun’s region as an exact midpoint.

But insofar as number is concerned, the sun is called middle as the fourth among seven, although, because of the unequal distances, the expression is qualified by the addition of the word “almost.”

The zodiacal circle is therefore one of the eleven mentioned above, and it alone could acquire the breadth in the manner I have described. The nature of the heavenly circles is incorporeal, and a line is conceived by the mind in such a way that it is judged only by length and cannot possess breadth.

In the zodiac, however, the extent of the signs required breadth. The breadth of space occupied by the extended stars is therefore bounded by two lines, while a third line drawn through the middle is called the ecliptic. This is because, when the sun and moon complete their courses together along that same line, an eclipse of one of them must occur: an eclipse of the sun if the moon then follows it; an eclipse of the moon if it is then opposite the sun.

The sun therefore never suffers an eclipse except when it is the thirtieth day of the moon’s course, and the moon knows an eclipse only on the fifteenth day of its course. For it happens either that, when the moon is placed opposite the sun in order to borrow from it a complete light, the cone of the earth is found beneath the same line and obstructs it, or that, when the moon follows the sun, it drives its light away from human sight by its interposition.

In an eclipse the sun itself suffers nothing; rather, our sight is deprived. The moon, however, is affected in its own eclipse because it does not receive the sun’s light, by whose benefit it colors the night.

Virgil, who was most learned in all the disciplines, knew this when he said:

> The various eclipses of the sun, and the moon’s labors.

Although the drawing of three lines both encloses and divides the zodiac, antiquity wished it to be called one circle, according to certain philosophers. The breadth of the zodiac is measured by twelve lines. By the nature of an even number, two of these must be middle lines. Those who assert that only the sun traverses these two lines say that the moon travels through all the others.

For this reason, wandering back and forth, it does not allow an eclipse to occur every month. Nevertheless, they establish that eclipses of both luminaries occur every year on appointed days and at appointed hours, although they are not always visible. The reason is that they sometimes occur beneath the earth, in the portion of the hidden hemisphere, and sometimes above it.

But because of clouds and because of the earth’s spherical and convex shape, they cannot be seen everywhere or at the same hours by everyone. It is therefore certain that these events occur more often than they are seen, and, when they are seen, do not appear equally to all.

Thus people in the East do not perceive evening eclipses of the sun and moon, nor people in the West morning eclipses, because the cone of the earth obstructs and blocks the sight.

We have learned through credible reasoning and tradition that an eclipse of the moon can sometimes occur in the fifth month after a previous one; that an eclipse of the sun can occur twice within thirty days in the seventh month after a previous solar eclipse; that it can be seen by others; and that at one time both luminaries can be eclipsed within twelve days.

I have therefore answered, most blessed Augustus, as it seems to me, in accordance with the demands of your letters. I have explained, on the authority of those same ancient philosophers, how they both knew and predicted how a solar eclipse would occur and when it would occur.

For those men, most learned in every discipline and ignorant of none of the schools approved by antiquity, with the keenest and most refined attention of a purified mind, and with the sharpest and purest acuity of their inward understanding, investigated most subtly and persistently, through natural inquiry, the natures, principles, causes, and origins of all things.

They found with the greatest care and effectiveness what they sought from him who offers every good gift and every perfect gift; and what they had found and discovered they observed with the greatest diligence and concentration.

From this, the natural philosophers who devoted themselves especially to astronomy, observing and testing the risings and settings of the stars with long and deliberate care, investigated most fully the courses and returns, approaches and retreats, of the sun, the moon, and the five remaining wandering stars.

They investigated them so thoroughly that, by their inquiry, they knew beyond doubt how many lines of the zodiacal circle each wandering star traversed, through which particular line it was presently directing its course, and in what sign and in what part of that sign it was located.

Since they knew so certainly and diligently about the subtler, though true and natural, motions of the other stars, why would they have been ignorant of the courses of the sun and moon, which are genuinely more conspicuous and easier to know? How could it have been hidden from them how or when these bodies would travel along the same ecliptic line of the zodiac, traverse that one same line, come together in one sign and in one part of it, and, coming together there, produce a solar eclipse when the moon followed the sun?

The philosophers mentioned above therefore not only knew in advance of an eclipse—that is, the obscuration of the sun—and, knowing it beforehand, predicted when it would occur after one month; they also predicted, through the sagacious investigation and careful observation described above, when it would occur after a year, or after twenty, or after one hundred thousand years, having experienced such events long beforehand.

But, to make you wonder still more, they extended such calculations as far as fifteen thousand years.

Cicero, reporting the vision of Africanus, says:

> People commonly measure the year only by the return of the one star, the sun. But when, in truth, all the stars have returned to the same place from which they once set out, and have again brought back the same configuration of the whole heaven after long intervals, then that may properly be called the “turning year.” In it, I scarcely dare say how many generations of human beings are contained. For just as once the sun seemed to mankind to fail and be extinguished, when the spirit of Romulus entered these very temples, so, when at some future time the sun shall again fail in the same region and at the same time, then, with all the signs brought back to the same beginning and the stars restored, consider the year completed. Know, however, that not yet a twentieth part of that year has revolved.

The Ambrosian exposition of Tullius clarifies and expands these words in the following manner:

The year is not only what common usage now calls the year. Rather, for each individual luminary—that is, the sun and the moon—or for each star, the completion of the entire circuit of the heavens and the return from a fixed place to the same place constitutes its own year.

Thus the moon’s month is its year, within which it traverses the circuit of the heavens. The month is named from the moon because the moon is called *mēnē* (Greek: μήνη).

Finally, wishing to distinguish the lunar year, which is short, from the year produced by the course of the sun, Virgil says:

> Meanwhile the sun revolves through the great year.

He calls it the great year in comparison with the lunar year. The course of Venus and Mercury is nearly equal to that of the sun; the year of Mars, however, lasts almost two years, for it takes that long to circle the heavens. Jupiter’s star spends twelve years, and Saturn’s thirty, in the same revolution.

These matters concerning the sun, the moon, and the wandering stars have now been explained, as I related above.

The year called the world-year, which is truly a turning year because it is produced by the complete revolution of the whole universe, unfolds over immense ages. Its principle is as follows.

All the stars and constellations that appear fixed in the heavens, whose proper motion human sight can never perceive or detect, nevertheless move. Besides the revolution of the heavens, by which they are always carried along, they also advance by their own motion so slowly that no human life is long enough, through continuous observation, to detect the change of position produced by that motion from the place in which one [Col. 0456A] first saw them.

The end of the world-year therefore occurs when all the stars and all the constellations contained by the *aplanes* have returned from a fixed place to the same place, so that not one star of the heavens is in a different place from the one in which it was when all the others, having moved away from that place and returned to it, completed their own years.

Thus the sun and the moon, together with the five wandering stars, must be in the same places and parts in which they were at the beginning of the world-year. According to the natural philosophers, this occurs after fifteen thousand years have been completed.

Therefore, just as the moon’s year is one month, the sun’s year twelve months, and the years of the other stars are those which we mentioned above, so the world-year consists of fifteen thousand years of the kind we now reckon.

That, then, is truly to be called the turning year—not the year measured by the return of the sun, that is, of one star, but the year enclosed by the return of all the stars that are in any heaven to the same place, under the same configuration of the entire heaven.

It is called the world-year because the heavens are properly called the world.

Therefore, just as we call the sun’s year not only the period from the Kalends of January to the same Kalends, but also the period from the day following the Kalends to that same day, and the return from any day of any month to the same day is called a year, so each person may make the beginning of this world-year whatever point he chooses.

Thus Cicero himself takes as the beginning of the world-year the solar eclipse that occurred near the end of Romulus’s life. Although solar eclipses occurred very frequently afterward, the world-year is not said to have been completed by the repetition of a solar eclipse. It will be completed only when the eclipsed sun is again in the same places and parts and finds all the stars and constellations of the heavens once more in the positions they occupied under Romulus.

After fifteen thousand years, as the philosophers assert, the sun will again be eclipsed in such a way that it will be in the same sign and the same part, at the same beginning at which it was under Romulus, with all the stars and signs likewise restored.

In the preceding year, 810 from the incarnation of the Lord, it is therefore not surprising that a solar eclipse occurred, as your letters indicate: on the seventh day before the Ides of June, when the new moon was just beginning; and again in the same year, on the day before the Kalends of December, when the thirtieth moon was beginning.

The latter occurred in the seventh month after the former eclipse—that is, with December beginning. A solar eclipse is defined as occurring at the last or first moon and in the seventh month after a previous eclipse, although it may sometimes not appear at all even though it certainly occurred; or, if it appears, it may not always be seen everywhere; or, if it is seen everywhere, not all people may see it occurring at the same hours, because of the causes mentioned above.

If, then, even in the present age someone endowed with such keenness of understanding, sustained by such prolonged application, and devoted with such diligence to investigation and observation should apply himself to the pursuit of astronomy or of any discipline, with the same leisure and curiosity as those born in the earlier age, would he not easily be believed capable of attaining the same knowledge and foreknowledge as the ancients?

It is difference of will, not of nature—for nature is one and equal—that makes human beings differ so greatly from one another, although we have discovered that among the first human beings there was greater willingness because of the youth of the world, the strength of their bodies, and the vigor of their senses.

Here, then, let this be the end of what I have to say about the solar eclipse—not because I think I have perhaps said enough, but because the smallness of my own ability has been unable at present to recall anything more.

Pliny the Second and the other books through which I might judge that I could supplement these matters are not available to us in this region, and I dare not or presume to invent anything about such subjects on my own.

But you, most devout Augustus, to whom God has distributed an abundance of wisdom above all others, as well as the other holy virtues, I humbly ask to deign to instruct and guide me wherever I may seem to you ignorant of this matter or to judge otherwise than is right.

“For God chose the foolish things of the world”; and, “There is no partiality with him.” Thus the light of your most pure and renowned wisdom may shine not only upon those who are near but also upon those who are far away; and not only may it illuminate those who travel across the open fields, but the ray of your most serene splendor, extending even through cracks and joints, may also suffuse recluses.

It is therefore greatly necessary for everyone, with attentive and constant prayers, to ask and entreat that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ grant and bestow upon his people the joy, for many years, of possessing such a great prince and teacher—one who is regarded equally by all as the foremost teacher of every good work, virtue, and honorable discipline, and as the perfect model for rulers in governing their subjects well, for soldiers in practicing their lawful military service, for clergy in rightly observing the rites of the universal Christian religion, and for philosophers and scholars in philosophizing and reasoning honorably about human matters and in thinking and believing reverently and orthodoxly about divine matters.

Why should I strive to say more about the supreme virtues and outstanding qualities of our lord Augustus Charles, when, however much I might wish to labor, I could not recount them all?

We can say this truthfully: everyone proclaims with one voice that, in this land in which, by God’s gift, the Franks now rule, from the beginning of the world no king or prince such as our lord Augustus Charles has ever been seen—a man so strong, wise, and religious.

As for what remains, perhaps through his holy and exalted merits such a one may arise from his offspring.

Only this remains for all of us Christians: with the loftiest voices and most devout hearts, let us unanimously cry out to the Lord and ask that he multiply the triumphs of our excellent lord Augustus Charles, enlarge his empire, preserve his sacred lineage, strengthen his health, and extend his life through many courses of years.

Hear, hear, hear, O Christ.

Thus, most revered and most beloved lord, just as you commanded the faithful servant of God and your servant, Abbot Waldon, to question me about such matters by reminding me of your words and to press me by demanding an answer—he who was faithful to you was also, in this matter, a serious and importunate examiner toward me, although he acted with moderation—I return the answer to you through him.

You should therefore give him thanks if I have said anything well in these matters, which I resolved, willingly or unwillingly, because of his urgent demands. But if I have said anything badly through my own negligence, impose upon me mercifully whatever penance you wish.

I desire that you may always be well in God, excellent lord—and not merely excellent lord, but also most devout and most loving Father.

# BOOK OF DUNGALUS THE RECLUSE AGAINST CLAUDIUS OF TURIN, TO LOUIS AND LOTHAR, THE AUGUSTI

(From the *Library of the Fathers.)

[Col. 0457D]

## PREFACE

To the bishops and clergy of Gaul, Papirius Massonus.

[Col. 0457D] Among other things, I think this was very wisely said by L. Florus, the historian of Rome: that the bites of dying beasts are generally the most deadly. Nor do I doubt that heresy ought rightly to be called by this name. I hope that the Catholic Church will one day, after the beast has grown old and died, find consolation and rest from its death. For your ancestors always believed that this plague or poison, after it had done harm for a long time, would come to an end when the priests of the Lord had diligently examined themselves and the flocks entrusted to them, and had resolved to order their lives in such a way that they could no longer be reproached.

In earlier ages, very many heresies reigned, whose names you could not even enumerate; so it will also happen to those that now afflict the world: after they have raged for a long time, they will disappear.

Claudius, bishop of Turin, who formerly held very wicked opinions about images, caused Jonas, bishop of Orléans, to write against that heresy. This was done in the time of Charles the Bald. In that work many things are said about Charlemagne, and many about his father Louis, the pious prince, son of the holy Church of God, against a presbyter of Spanish nationality named Claudius.

But Dungal, whom we now humbly offer to you, himself an outstanding theologian, lived under that same Emperor Louis and his most noble son, Augustus Lothar. He calls his little book *Responses containing extracts and selections from the authority and teaching of the holy Fathers*, under the name and in honor of the most glorious and most Christian princes, rulers of the holy Church, the lord Louis, most great and serene emperor, and his son, Augustus Lothar, against the insane and blasphemous ravings of Claudius of Turin.

Among the first things to be noted in this book is the following statement by Dungal:

> “What insane arrogance and empty presumption it is that one man should dare to blaspheme, criticize, trample underfoot, cast away, and blow away what, from the earliest age of Christianity for almost 820 years or even longer, has been permitted, established, and commanded by holy and most blessed Fathers and afterward by most religious princes to be done in churches and in every Christian home for the glory and praise of the Lord—as though during all that long period there had been no author in the Church of God so holy or wise, possessing in his heart such ardent zeal or such subtle understanding, as this man who dares to attack what the others, as though fearful, did not dare to undertake, or to condemn what others, as though foolish, did not understand ought to be condemned.”

But before Claudius of Turin rose up against the Church of God, Felix of Urgell was troubling the Church in the time of Charlemagne, as this passage of Dungal shows:

> “The lord Charles, of most blessed memory, most flourishing and most vigilant guardian and defender of the Catholic faith, crushed with a powerful iron rod the head of the most wicked viper—Felix, the teacher of this error—hissing against the unity of the Church under the authority of the Apostolic See.”

But that foolish bishop of Turin would have tried, if he could, to silence the most illustrious lights of the Church—Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory of Nyssa, John Chrysostom, and Gregory, Roman pontiff. Yet those men, far superior to him in life, conduct, and knowledge, are sufficiently protected against the accusations of the rabid dog by the single name of holiness.

Dungal also uses the testimony of Paulinus of Aquitaine and bishop of Nola, concerning whom St. Augustine says in Book I of *The City of God*: “Our Paulinus, bishop of Nola, from being an exceedingly wealthy man became by choice exceedingly poor and abundantly holy.” Dungal says of the same man: “Endowed with holiness and wisdom, and like a certain lighthouse and an impregnable tower.”

He also uses the authority and testimony of Aurelius Clemens Prudentius, a man of consular rank and the most learned of the Iberians, whose poems in the times of Theodosius the Younger and Honorius were judged worthy of the highest praise.

He also invokes the authority of Priscian, concerning whom Dungal likewise says: “Priscian, because of the brilliance of his most noble intellect, deserved to be called the light of Roman eloquence.” Cassiodorus, in his little book *On Orthography*, says: “These things have been excerpted from the modern author Priscian,” and in its twelfth chapter: “These matters have been collected from Priscian the grammarian, who in our time was a teacher at Constantinople.”

He also cites the poets Sedulius and Fortunatus; the latter, afterward bishop of Poitiers, Dungal cites in defense of his cause.

Therefore embrace this author as a singular gift. In him he gathers very many arguments from Holy Scripture by which he proves that the veneration of saints is rightly approved by the Church, while God himself is adored by the Christian people and humbly worshiped as the eternal Creator of all things.

Dungal himself plainly and candidly testifies at the beginning of his book that he came into this land from elsewhere; but where he came from is uncertain. His book appears to have been written in the monastery of Saint-Denis on the Seine, [Col. 0460C] where it was seen by many in the hands of Velii, a Benedictine of noble birth and a learned librarian. It eventually came into the hands of Paul Petau, an eminent Parisian senator, skillfully written on ancient parchment. Just as he kindly showed it to me, so he will extend the same favor to those who wish to see the parchment itself.

Fifteen years ago Nicholas Faber, a Parisian citizen, made a copy of the manuscript for me. I have thought it necessary to name these men so that no one may suspect me of falsehood, when I am so devoted to truth that I would rather die for it.

Farewell. Paris, 25 July 1608.

[Col. 0459]

# APOLOGETIC STATEMENT AND REPLY OF CLAUDIUS, BISHOP, AGAINST THE ABBOT THEUTMIR

[Col. 0459D] I received your letter, together with the chapters appended below, full of loquacity and stupidity, through a certain rustic courier. In these chapters you declare that you have been disturbed because a rumor has spread from Italy about me throughout all Gaul as far as the borders of Spain—as though I had preached some new sect against the rule of the Catholic faith. This is entirely false.

Nor is it surprising that the members of the devil have said such things about me, since they proclaimed our very head to be both a seducer and a demoniac.

For I do not teach a sect; I maintain unity and proclaim the truth. But sects, schisms, superstitions, and heresies, insofar as I have been able, I have restrained, crushed, fought, and defeated; and, with God’s help, I do not cease to defeat them insofar as I can.

This has happened because, after I was compelled to undertake the burden of pastoral office, sent by the pious prince Louis, son of the holy Catholic Church of the Lord, I came to Italy, to the city of Turin. I found all the basilicas, contrary to the order of truth, filled with filthy, accursed images. Since I alone began to destroy what everyone was worshiping, they all opened their mouths to blaspheme me; and unless the Lord had helped me, they might perhaps have swallowed me alive.

## Elsewhere in the same work

[Col. 0461A]

Since it is expressly said that no likeness is to be made of anything that is in heaven, or on earth, or beneath the earth, this is understood not only of likenesses of foreign gods, but also of heavenly creatures, or of anything that the human mind has been able to devise in honor of the Creator.

To adore means to praise, revere, ask, entreat, implore, invoke, and pour out a prayer. To render cult or honor (*colere*) means to govern, observe, perform one’s duty, frequent, revere, love, and cherish.

## Elsewhere in the same work

They say, against whom we have undertaken to defend the Church of God: “We do not think that anything divine is present in the image that we adore. We adore it with such veneration merely for the honor of the one whose likeness it is.”

To them we reply that if those who have abandoned the worship of demons venerate images of the saints, they have not abandoned idols but merely changed their names. If you write on a wall or paint images of Peter and Paul, Jupiter and Saturn, or Mercury, neither the former are gods nor the latter apostles; neither the former nor the latter are the persons themselves, and thus the name is changed. The error, however, both then and now, always remains exactly the same.

Certainly, if human beings were to be adored, the living ought rather to be adored than the dead—that is, where they possess the likeness of God, not where they possess the likeness of animals, or, more truly, of stones or pieces of wood lacking life, sensation, and reason.

From this we must consider most carefully that if the works of God’s hands are not to be adored and venerated, how much more must the works of human hands not be adored and venerated, [Col. 0461C] not even in honor of those whose likenesses they are said to be.
