For if the image that is adored is not God, it must in no way be venerated in honor of the saints, who in no way claim divine honors for themselves.

## Elsewhere

Therefore we must understand most carefully that not only the person who venerates visible images and figures, but also anyone who venerates any creature—whether heavenly, earthly, spiritual, or bodily—in place of the name of God, and expects from them the salvation of his soul, which comes from God alone, belongs to those of whom the Apostle says: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator.”

## Elsewhere in the same work

Why do you humble and bow yourself before false images? Why do you bend your captive body before senseless statues and earthly figures? God made you upright, and while the other animals are prone and directed toward the earth, you have an elevated posture, and your face is raised toward heaven and toward God. Look there; raise your eyes there; seek God in the heights, so that you may escape the depths below.

Lift up your breast, suspended toward the high heavens. Why do you cast yourself down into the fall of death together with the senseless image that you venerate? Why do you fall through it, and with it, into the ruin of the devil? Preserve the exalted state in which you were born; remain such as the Lord made you.

## On the cross, elsewhere

But these worshipers of false religion and superstition say: “We venerate, revere, and adore the cross painted and represented in his honor, in remembrance of our Savior.” They find nothing else pleasing in our Savior except what also pleased the impious: the disgrace of suffering and the mockery of death.

They believe about him what impious people believe, whether Jews or pagans, who doubt that he rose again. They know nothing else to think about him except that he was tortured and died, and they believe and retain in their hearts that he remains forever in his passion. They do not attend to or understand what the Apostle said: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way.”

## Elsewhere in the same work

To them we must reply that if they wish to adore every piece of wood made in the form of a cross because Christ hung upon a cross, then many other things that Christ did in the flesh will also be incumbent upon them.

He hung upon the cross for scarcely six hours, yet he was in the Virgin’s womb for nine lunar months and more than eleven days, which together amount to 276 solar days—that is, nine months and six days beyond them.

Therefore let young virgins be adored, because a virgin gave birth to Christ. Let mangers also be adored, because as soon as he was born he was laid in a manger. Let old pieces of cloth be adored, because immediately after he was born he was wrapped in old cloths.

Let ships be adored, because he frequently sailed in ships, taught the crowds from a small boat, slept in a boat, commanded the winds from a boat, and ordered the net to be cast on the right side of the vessel when that great prophetic catch of fish took place.

Let donkeys be adored, because he reached Jerusalem riding a young donkey. Let lambs be adored, because it is written concerning him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

But these worshipers of perverse doctrines wish to devour living lambs and adore lambs painted on a wall.

Let lions also be adored, because it is written concerning him: “The lion of the tribe of Judah, the root of David, has conquered.”

Let rocks be adored, because when he was taken down from the cross he was placed in a stone tomb, and the Apostle says of him: “The rock was Christ.” But Christ is called a rock, a lamb, and a lion figuratively, not literally—by signification, not by substance.

Let the thorns of bushes be adored, because a crown of thorns was placed upon his head at the time of his passion. Let reeds be adored, because soldiers struck his head with them. Finally, let spears also be adored, because one of the soldiers opened his side on the cross with a spear, from which blood and water flowed—the sacraments from which the Church is formed.

All these things are ridiculous and should be mourned rather than written. We are compelled to set foolish things against fools, and against hearts of stone to hurl not arrows or judgments of words, but blows of stone.

Return to your senses, transgressors, you who have departed from the truth, who love vanity and have become vain; you who crucify the Son of God again and expose him to public disgrace, and thereby have masses of wretched souls made companions of demons. By alienating those souls from their Creator through the abominable sacrileges of images, you have them cast down and thrown into everlasting damnation.

## Elsewhere in the same work

[Col. 0463A]

God commanded one thing; these people do another. God commanded that the cross be carried, not adored. They wish to adore it, although they are unwilling to carry it with them either spiritually or bodily.

To worship God in this way is to depart from him. For he said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” For unless someone fails himself, he does not draw near to the one who is above him; nor can he grasp what is beyond himself if he does not know how to put to death what is—

## Elsewhere

As for your claim that I prevent people from going to Rome for the sake of penance, you are speaking falsely. I neither approve nor disapprove of that journey, because I know that it harms neither everyone nor benefits everyone, neither helps everyone nor hinders everyone.

I wish first to ask you yourself whether you know that going to Rome is an act of penance. Why have you destroyed so many souls for so long, keeping them in the monastery, receiving them into the monastery for the sake of penance, and not sending them to Rome, but rather making them serve you?

For you say that you have a crowd of 140 monks, all of whom came to you for the sake of penance and entrusted themselves to the monastery, yet you permitted none of them to go to Rome.

If, as you say, going to Rome is an act of penance, what will you do with that sentence which the Lord says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be cast into the depths than that he should cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble”?

There is no greater scandal than preventing a person from taking the road by which he might proceed to everlasting joys.

## Elsewhere in the same work

We know that, because the words of the Lord Savior spoken by the evangelist to the blessed apostle Peter were not understood—“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven”—an ignorant class of people, in order to obtain eternal life, setting aside all spiritual understanding, wishes to go to Rome.

And shortly afterward:

Whoever understands the keys of the kingdom of heaven in the manner stated above as an intercession of blessed Peter does not seek it locally. For if we carefully consider the literal meaning of the Lord’s words, he did not say to him: “Whatever you loose in heaven will be loosed on earth, and whatever you bind in heaven will be bound upon earth.”

Therefore we must understand that this ministry was granted to the bishops of the Church only so long as they themselves are pilgrims in this mortal body. But when they have paid the debt of death, others succeed to their place and receive the same judicial authority, as it is written: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth.”

## Elsewhere in the same work

Return, blind people, to the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world; the light that shines in darkness, and the darkness does not comprehend it. You are in darkness because you do not behold this light; you walk in darkness and do not know where you are going, because darkness has blinded your eyes.

## Elsewhere

Hear this also, you senseless among the people, and learn wisdom at last, you who seek the intercession of the apostle by going to Rome. Consider what the same often-mentioned blessed Augustine says against you. In Book VIII of *On the Trinity*, among other things, he says:

> “Return, then, with me, and let us consider why we love the apostle. Is it perhaps because of the human appearance that we know so well, since we believe that he was a human being? Certainly not; otherwise he is not now someone whom we can love, since that human being no longer exists. For his soul has been separated from his body. But what we love in him we believe even now to be alive.”

## Elsewhere in the same work

Everyone ought to believe God when he makes a promise—how much more when he swears an oath.

What does it mean when he says: “If Noah, Daniel, and Job were in the midst of it”? It means that even if someone possessed as much holiness, justice, and merit as they did, he would not deliver either son or daughter.

He says this so that no one may rely upon the merit or intercession of the saints. For unless he possesses the same faith, justice, and truth that they possessed, by which they pleased God, he cannot be saved.

## Elsewhere in the same work

Your fifth objection against me is that you say you are displeased because the apostolic lord was angry with me. You said this about Paschal, bishop of the Roman Church, who has now departed this life.

“Apostolic” means either “guardian of the apostle” or “one who performs the apostle’s office.” Certainly, the one who sits in the apostle’s chair but does not fulfill the apostolic office should not be called apostolic.

Concerning those who occupy that place but do not fulfill its office, the Lord said: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat. Therefore observe and do everything they tell you, but do not act according to their works; for they say and do not do.”

*(The book from which we have excerpted these passages is as large as the Book of Psalms plus fifty Psalms.)*

[Col. 0465]

# DUNGAL’S REPLIES AGAINST THE PERVERSE OPINIONS OF CLAUDIUS, BISHOP OF TURIN

[Col. 0465A] I, Dungal, have devoted and resolved that this little book, containing responses drawn and excerpted from the authority and teaching of the holy Fathers, should be composed and dedicated under the name and in honor of the most glorious princes, the most Christian rulers of the holy Church, the lord Louis, most great and serene emperor, and his son, the most noble Augustus Lothar, in the service of God and of them, against the insane and blasphemous ravings of Claudius, bishop of Turin.

I do this not because, from the time long ago when I came into this land, no abundant opportunity had arisen for me to protest and complain continually about this matter. I have seen the Lord’s harvest everywhere bristling with evil tares and unfruitful darnel, and I have sighed over it. Rather, I feared that our efforts might, as the saying goes, beat the air, or that by asserting uncertain things as certain we might be mocked.

Therefore, under a long and anxious observance of silence, I kept my mouth closed, grieving and sorrowfully murmuring much over the ancient dispute concerning the body of Christ—that is, the Church—which was now taking place everywhere among the crowds, though formerly the dispute had concerned the Head.

For at that earlier time, as John says, some were saying, “He is good,” while others said, “No, but he deceives the crowds.”

In a similar way even now, with the people of this region separated from one another and divided into two parties, Catholics murmur and contend about ecclesiastical observances—that is, about the image of the Lord’s passion and holy painting. They say that painting is good and useful, and contributes almost as much to instruction as the sacred Scriptures.

The heretic, on the other hand, together with the faction he has led astray, says: “No, but it is the seduction of error” [Col. 0465C] “and idolatry.”

A similar dispute is held concerning the cross. The Catholics say that it is good and holy, the triumphant banner and sign of everlasting salvation. The opposing party, with its teacher, replies: “No, but it contains and displays and commemorates nothing except the disgrace of the passion and the mockery of death.”

In the same way they oppose the memorials of the saints, which people visit for the sake of prayer, and the veneration of their relics. Some affirm that it is good and religious custom to frequent the basilicas of the martyrs, where their sacred ashes and holy bodies are buried with honor appropriate to their merits, like certain venerable vessels acceptable to God, in which they endured every kind of torment for the faith of Christ even unto death.

There, through their intercession, bodily and spiritual illnesses are daily healed in great abundance and with immediate effect, by the hand of God at work and by his grace shining forth.

Others, however, resist, saying that the saints do not help anyone after death and cannot aid anyone by interceding, knowing nothing at all of what is done on earth; nor does any reverence accompany their relics, any more than it accompanies the worthless bones of animals or ordinary earth.

Thus Augustine says in his exposition of the holy Gospel according to John:

> “This is now said concerning all his servants: whoever has excelled in some grace, some say, ‘He is good’; others, ‘No, but he deceives the crowds.’ Why is this? Because our life is hidden with Christ in God.
>
> “Therefore it is permissible to say to people: ‘During winter this tree has died’—for example, a fig tree, a pear tree, or some such fruit tree; it resembles a dry tree, and as long as winter lasts it is not visible. Summer proves it; judgment proves it. Our summer is the revelation of Christ.
>
> “Our God will come openly and will not remain silent; fire will go before him. This fire will inflame his enemies; it will seize the dry trees. On the other side, on the right, the fertility of the fruits and the dignity of the leaves will appear. Greenness will be eternity.
>
> “To those who are like dry trees it will therefore be said: ‘Go into the eternal fire.’ For behold, the axe has been placed at the root of the trees. Every tree, therefore, that does not produce fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire.
>
> “This is said concerning the whole body of Christ. The body of Christ is still on the threshing floor: see how it is blasphemed by the chaff. They are threshed together, but the chaff is crushed and the grain is cleansed.”

We earnestly beseech our most Christian and most religious lords, moved by zeal for God, graciously to come at the proper time to the aid of their holy mother Church, who is groaning and in danger, and not to allow her to be torn apart any longer by the savage bites of serpents.

Since the lord Charles, of most blessed memory, the most fervent and vigilant guardian and defender of the Catholic faith, crushed with a powerful iron rod the head of the most wicked viper—Felix, the teacher of this error—against the hissing unity of the Church under the authority of the Apostolic See, it is right that the aforesaid beast’s tail, which infects everything with its dreadful venom, should be crushed by the same blessed generation with the same staff.

Let it be restrained by repeated blows, beaten and struck down so long as it moves with evil force to do harm, until, its strength exhausted, it ceases to writhe.

For since the perverse disciple has tried not merely to equal his perverse and pestilential teacher, but even to surpass him by corrupting and blaspheming, as it is written, “From the root of the serpent a basilisk will emerge,” let him be corrected with punishment even stronger than that which his predecessor received, so that the others may be afraid.

Let them not, inflamed by the most wicked spirit of pride, dare to devise such depravity again, presuming to defame and violate the Church, the bride of Christ, whose overseers and defenders God has appointed you.

As Augustine says in his exposition of the Gospel according to John:

> “If, whenever God wishes to rouse the powers against heretics, against schismatics, against those who tear the Church apart, against those who insult Christ, and against those who blaspheme his saints, he does so, let them not be surprised that God rouses them, so that Hagar may be beaten by Sarah. Let Hagar recognize this, lower her neck. But they are surprised that Christian powers are stirred against the detestable destroyers of the Church.
>
> “If they were not stirred, how would they render an account of their rule to God? Let your charity attend to what I say, for this concerns the Christian kings of this world: in their time they should wish their mother, the Church from whom they have been spiritually born, to be at peace.”

We read the visions of Daniel and the deeds recorded in prophecy. Three boys praised God in the fire. King Nebuchadnezzar marveled at the boys praising God and at the harmless fire around them. When he had marveled, what did King Nebuchadnezzar say? Was he not a Jew or a circumcised man? He had erected his statue and compelled everyone to adore it.

Yet, moved by the praises of the three boys and having perceived the majesty of God present in the fire, what did he say?

“I will issue a decree to all tribes and languages throughout the whole earth.”

What decree?

“Whoever speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be put to death, and his house shall be destroyed.”

See how a foreign king rages lest the God of Israel be blasphemed, because he was able to free three boys from the fire. Yet they do not wish Christian kings to rage when Christ is insulted—Christ by whom not three boys, but the whole world together with its kings, is freed from the fire of Gehenna.

## The Prologue ends

Therefore the ambiguity that compelled us to remain silent for so long, and because of which we have until now been unable to give or send a definite reply, has been removed from our midst like an obstacle. We have received a document composed by Claudius, bishop of Turin, which, as is stated at its end, has been excerpted from a book that he calls his *Apologetic Statement*, written against Theutmir, the abbot.

According to the proper meaning of the Greek word, *apologia* is without the sense of opposition; it is ordinarily said not against some person but only in defense of someone or something.

Although this letter was published in an uncultivated and rustic style, as might be expected from a man inexperienced in scholarly learning, I did not take much trouble to examine or investigate that matter. Rather, the divergent meaning, contrary to the Catholic faith, moved and disturbed me profoundly.

For he says that those who adore and venerate the idols and images of the pagans—at the devil’s prompting, and through them deceiving people, believing that they are gods and goddesses by whom all things are governed or bestowed—and Christians who paint and venerate an image of Christ and his saints, out of love and honor for the Savior and Redeemer of the world and for his chosen ones, whom they also love and honor, though far less than God, because they were first chosen and loved by God and served him faithfully during their lives, enduring everything for him with the greatest devotion even unto death, believing in no one else except the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as contained in the holy Creed and the Catholic faith—all these, he says, are equally in error and ought to be called by the same name: idolaters.

He also says that the Lord’s cross must be cast away and trampled underfoot, as though it were the disgrace of the passion and the mockery of death. He calls those who honor it, paint it, or adorn it by fashioning it worshipers of false religion and superstition; moreover, he calls them foolish, stony-hearted, and transgressors, and condemns them.

He also detests those who go to Rome—that is, to the places of the most glorious blessed apostles and of the countless other saints lying there—for the sake of prayer, with unwavering faith that, by God’s merciful providence, because of the labor of the journey undertaken for God and especially through the intervention of the most pious patrons whom they devoutly visit, as though they had greater merit and influence with God, they will obtain more easily and quickly whatever they rightly and justly ask.

He calls these people an ignorant class, blind, senseless, and foolish.

Concerning the matter of painted images, which he proposes at the beginning of his letter, an investigation was conducted, as I believe, about two years ago, in the palace before the most glorious and religious princes. There, by examples and authority from divine Scripture, from holy books, and from the most approved men who wrote them, it was discovered, confirmed, and sufficiently clearly determined with what moderation and discernment images are to be treated.

Thus no one, however foolish or dull of heart, may henceforth excuse himself for giving divine honor either to angels, even holy ones, or to human beings, even holy ones, or to their images, or to any creature whatsoever in the world. Divine honor belongs only to the one Creator of all things, God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Nor, on the other hand, may anyone presume to destroy, erase, despise, or abominate the beings mentioned above—whether holy angels, holy human beings, or their images—or anything faithfully made in honor, praise, and glory of the one true and supreme God.

Thus Saint Gregory corrected and reproved Serenus, bishop of Marseille, saying:

> “It had indeed been reported to us that, inflamed by inconsiderate zeal, you had broken the images of the saints under the pretext, as it were, that they ought not to be adored. We praised you greatly for forbidding them to be adored, but we reproved you for breaking them.
>
> “Tell me, brother: from what priest have you ever heard that what you did was right? Even if nothing else, should not this have restrained you—that, despising the other brothers, you alone should believe yourself holy and wise?
>
> “It is one thing to adore a picture; it is another, through the history represented in a picture, to learn what ought to be adored. For what Scripture provides to readers, a picture provides to uneducated people who look at it: in it the ignorant see what they ought to follow; in it those who do not know letters read.
>
> “Therefore, especially for the pagans, a picture serves in place of reading. This ought to have been carefully considered by you, who live among pagans, lest, while you were incautiously inflamed by proper zeal, you should create a scandal among fierce minds.
>
> “Therefore what had been placed in the churches not for adoration but solely for the instruction of the minds of the ignorant ought not to have been broken.
>
> “And since antiquity, not without reason, permitted histories of the saints to be painted in holy places, if you had tempered your zeal with discretion, you could undoubtedly have obtained what you sought in a beneficial manner and gathered rather than scattered the flock entrusted to you, so that the name of shepherd would have been honored in you rather than the guilt of one who disperses.
>
> “But while you carried out these actions in the excessively reckless agitation of your spirit, you are said to have scandalized your sons so greatly that most of them withdrew from your communion.
>
> “When, then, will you bring wandering sheep to the Lord’s fold, when you cannot retain those whom you have?”

What insane arrogance and empty presumption it is that one man should dare to blaspheme, criticize, trample underfoot, cast away, and blow away what, from the earliest age of Christianity for almost 820 years or even longer, has been permitted, established, and commanded by holy and most blessed Fathers and afterward by most religious princes for the glory and praise of God to be done in churches and in every Christian home.

It is as though during all that long period there had been no author in the Church of God so holy or wise, possessing in his heart such ardent zeal or such subtle understanding, as this man who dares to attack what the others, as though fearful, did not dare to undertake, or to condemn what others, as though foolish, did not understand ought to be condemned.

Some, on the other hand, among the ancient Fathers took pains to paint not only images of the saints who had fallen asleep in Christ but also of living friends. Thus Saint Severus, bishop, painted in his church not only the image of blessed Martin, who had departed from this world to God, but also the image of Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola, who was still alive.

Both were holy bishops, both spiritual philosophers; yet neither attempted anything of this kind. When Paulinus heard of it, he humbly excused himself, unwilling to be likened to Martin as though he were his equal. But, recognizing the holy devotion of his friend toward him, he consented and composed the following verses in a humble comparison:

> Wealthy in possessions, yet poor for Christ in himself, Severus  
> Established splendid edifices with sacred fountains.  
>   
> And because he was building a heavenly hall for sacred acts,  
> Where people might be renewed by font and by God,  
> He painted a double image fitting for the sacraments,  
> So that the reborn person might learn the gifts of life.  
>   
> A venerable image of the man represents Martin;  
> The other figure portrays humble Paulinus.  
>   
> The former arms faith with examples and strong words,  
> So that it may bear undefiled palms of merit.  
>   
> The latter teaches, redeeming his sins with coins poured out,  
> That possessions are of less worth than each person’s salvation.

Concerning him Saint Augustine says in Book I of *The City of God*: “Our Paulinus, bishop of Nola, from being an exceedingly wealthy man became by choice exceedingly poor and abundantly holy.”

He had nearly all the histories of the Old and New Testaments in his churches, represented in paintings, and he displayed them in sequence to Saint Nicetas, bishop of the Dacians.

For this reason he says in Book IX, which he composed in verse concerning the virtues of the holy martyr Felix:

> Now I wish you to see the paintings in a long procession  
> Along the porticoes painted with colors,  
> And to tire your slightly upturned neck—
While you read through everything with your head inclined,

He who sees these things, recognizing truths in empty figures,

Feeds his faithful mind on an image that is not empty;

For the picture holds in faithful sequence

All that Moses the elder wrote in five books,

And all that Jesus, marked with the Lord’s name, accomplished.

And a little later:

[Col. 0470B] Perhaps someone may ask for what reason

The plan of painting holy dwellings,

In an unusual fashion, with living creatures depicted,

Seemed fitting to us.

Listen, and I shall attempt briefly to explain the reasons.

No one is unaware of the gatherings that the glory

Of holy Felix draws here; but the crowd is larger still:

Country people, not lacking in faith, though untrained in reading—

People long accustomed to serving profane things,

Now, as strangers, converted to Christ and finally to God,

While they marvel at the works of the saints displayed in Christ.

See how many assemble from every countryside,

And how piously they wander, deceived by their uneducated minds;

They have left their distant homes, despised the frosts,

Not chilled by the fervor of their faith; and now, behold, in great numbers

[Col. 0470C] They extend their vigils and celebrations through the whole night.

Joy keeps sleep and darkness at bay with torches.

Also, in the same work:

Therefore it seemed to us a useful undertaking

To adorn all the houses of Felix with holy paintings,

So that perhaps, through these spectacles,

The colored shadow might capture the astonished minds

Of the country people.

The same author:

While the painting deceives hunger, and the honesty

Of holy deeds steals upon the reader of the histories,

Led on by pious examples, sobriety is drunk

By the open mouth, and forgetfulness of excessive wine enters in.

And while they spend the day gazing for a longer time,

The cups grow fewer, because, as time is drawn out by the miracles,

Only a few hours remain for the banqueters.

[Col. 0470D] Saint Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, among other matters composed a discourse on Abraham. “I saw,” he says, “an image of the Passion, and I did not pass beyond the sight without tears, bringing the history into visible form.”

Warned, therefore, by these examples, we believe that forming holy paintings for the honor of God—as I may put it in Paulinus’s words—is not blameworthy for any Christian, but rather a sign of religion.

The letter says:

“For when it is distinctly stated that no likeness is to be made of all that is in heaven, or on earth, or beneath the earth, this is understood not only of the likenesses of foreign gods, but also of heavenly creatures, or of whatever human understanding could devise in honor of the Creator.”

He ought to have expressed and explained this more clearly and truthfully. For likenesses made not for divine honor but for foreign honor—that is, not for the Creator’s honor, as the letter has distorted it, but for the honor of a creature—are forbidden.

Therefore, knowing that the people were stiff-necked and inclined to worship idols, and that they would quickly transgress and fashion an image for themselves to worship, the Lord prohibited them from possessing any likeness of the things in heaven, on earth, or in the waters, lest, abandoning him and neglecting his honor, they should worship and venerate those things in his place.

But when he saw that something pertained to his own honor, he not only did not forbid it; he even commanded that holy likenesses be made. Thus we read in the Book of Exodus:

“Moreover, you shall make two cherubim of gold, beaten out, on both sides of the oracle. [Col. 0471A] Let one cherub be on one side and the other on the other. Let them cover both sides of the mercy seat, spreading their wings and covering the oracle; and let them face one another, their faces turned toward the mercy seat, by which the ark is to be covered, in which you shall place the testimony that I will give you. From there I will command and speak to you above the mercy seat, namely from between the two cherubim that will be over the ark of the testimony” (Exod. 25:18).

Again, later in the same book, the making of them is described:

“He also made two cherubim of beaten gold, which he placed on both sides of the mercy seat: one cherub at the top of one side, and the other cherub at the top of the other side—two cherubim at each end of the mercy seat. They spread their wings and covered the mercy seat, facing one another and looking toward it” (Exod. 37:8).

Again, in the Book of Numbers:

[Col. 0471C] “And he prayed for the people, and the Lord spoke to him: ‘Make a serpent and set it up as a sign; whoever has been bitten and looks at it shall live.’ Moses therefore made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; and those who had been bitten and looked at it were healed” (Num. 21:7).

Therefore those who possess holy divine paintings, recalling through them the histories to the praise and honor of God, are not to be reproached. Rather, that wordy man should be condemned who imputes false crimes to the innocent; who, like a lethargic patient, has set down almost all the words of his letter in contradiction to one another and in mutual conflict.

For he said that no one ought to adore or worship anything except God alone. And because he understood none of the precise or proper meaning of these words, he handled them in a confused fashion, saying:

“To adore is to praise, venerate, ask, entreat, supplicate, invoke, and pour out a prayer. But to worship is to govern, observe, perform a duty, frequent, venerate, love, and cherish.”

If we were to examine and criticize everything in this explanation that deserves examination and criticism, our response would become excessively long. For this reason, and also because these matters are apparent to those skilled in grammatical learning, we have left their investigation to them. This much, however, must be noted: the interpretations he supplied apply to many different matters, and some of them in no way suit God, contrary to the author’s purpose and intention.

Again, in the next volume of the heretic he says:

[Col. 0472A] “For if those who have abandoned the worship of demons venerate images of the saints, they have not abandoned idols but merely changed their names. For if you write or paint on a wall images of Peter and Paul, Jupiter and Saturn, or Mercury, neither the former are gods nor the latter apostles; neither the former nor the latter are human beings. Thus the name is changed, but the error remains always the same, both then and now.”

More fully, these matters are found at the beginning of this written booklet.

In this way Eunomius and Vigilantius, heretics, and their followers customarily blaspheme Catholics, calling them idolaters and worshipers of dead men, just as the pagans were, because they venerate the relics of martyrs who suffered for Christ.

To them we reply that we do not adore images of the saints painted on walls, nor their bodies buried in tombs, as though they were God; nor do we offer sacrifices to them. This is so abominable that it is written: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be destroyed, unless it be to the Lord alone” (Exod. 22:20). Rather, we venerate only those whose likenesses or bodies are present in God, and through their intercessions we ask that divine assistance be present to us.

Thus Augustine says in Book VIII of *The City of God*:

“So that those who read these things with a hostile and perverted mind may think that the gods were worshiped by the pagans in temples, while by us the dead are worshiped in tombs.”

The same author shortly afterward says:

“Indeed, the deceitful spirit, at whose prompting Hermes said these things, was compelled through that very man to confess that the land was already full of tombs and of the dead whom they worshiped as gods. But the demons’ grief was speaking through him, because they mourned that their future punishments were impending at the memorials of the holy martyrs. For in many such places they are tormented and confess, and they are expelled from the bodies of the possessed.

“Yet we do not establish temples, priesthoods, sacred rites, or sacrifices for those same martyrs, because it is not they but their God who is our God. We honor their memorials as those of holy men of God who contended for the truth even unto death, so that the true religion might become known when falsehood and fabrication had been convicted.

“But who has ever heard a priest among the faithful, standing at an altar—even one built in honor and worship of God over the holy body of a martyr—say in his prayers: ‘I offer sacrifice to you, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian’? Yet at their memorials sacrifice is offered to God, who made them both human beings and martyrs and joined them in heavenly honor to the holy angels. In this celebration we give thanks to the true God for their victories and, invoking him for help, encourage ourselves to imitate such crowns and palms by renewing the memory of them.

“Whatever religious observances, therefore, are performed at the places of the martyrs are ornaments of their memorials, not sacred rites or sacrifices offered to the dead as though they were gods.”

Accordingly Jerome, writing to the presbyter Riparius against Vigilantius, says:

[Col. 0473A] “After first receiving your letter, not to reply would be arrogance; to reply, presumption. For you ask about matters that it is sacrilege both to state and to hear.

“You say that Vigilantius—who is called by this name κατὰ ἀντίφρασιν, ‘by contrariety’ (for ‘Dormitantius,’ ‘Sleepy-man,’ would be a more appropriate name)—has once again opened his foul mouth and spoken the vilest stench against the relics of the holy martyrs; and that he calls us, who have received them, ash-men and idolaters because we venerate the bones of dead men.

“O unhappy man, worthy to be mourned with every fountain of tears! In saying these things he does not understand that he is a Samaritan and a Jew, who regard the bodies of the dead as unclean and even suspect that vessels which have been in the same house are polluted—following the letter that kills and not the life-giving spirit.

“We, however, do not worship or adore—I do not say the relics of martyrs, but not even the sun or the moon, angels, archangels, seraphim, cherubim, or any name that is named in the present age or in the age to come, lest we serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.

“But we honor the relics of the martyrs so that we may adore him whose martyrs they are. We honor servants so that the honor paid to the servants may redound to the Lord, who says: ‘Whoever receives you receives me.’”

Again Jerome, against the same Vigilantius:

[Col. 0473B] “For who, you madman, has ever adored martyrs? Who has thought a human being to be God? Did not Paul and Barnabas, when the Lycaonians thought them Jupiter and Mercury and wished to sacrifice victims to them, tear their garments and declare that they were human beings?

“Not because they were not once better than dead men such as Jupiter and Mercury, but because, under the error of paganism, the honor due to God was being offered to them. We read the same concerning Peter, who raised Cornelius with his hand when Cornelius wished to adore him and said: ‘Rise, for I too am a human being.’”

Again, the words of the letter:

“Certainly, if human beings were to be adored, the living ought to be adored rather than the dead. That is, where they possess the likeness of God, not where they possess the life, sense, and reason of animals—or, more accurately, of stones or pieces of wood.”

What profound, raging, insane folly, what utterly deranged drunkenness and most empty presumption it is to equate and compare the bodies of Christ’s blessed ones—the apostles and holy martyrs—with the corpses of animals, with wood and stones—through which the words of divine preaching rang out into the world as through sacred instruments, and in which, even unto the glorious death of martyrdom and triumphal palms, they fought with all their strength for Christ against the devil and his father, thereby deserving to become living victims and sacrifices most peaceful and acceptable to God.

Hence Saint Augustine says in Book X of *The City of God*:

[Col. 0473D] “Therefore the human being consecrated by the name of God, insofar as he dies to the world in order to live to God, is a sacrifice. For this too belongs to the mercy that each person exercises toward himself; therefore it is written: ‘Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God.’

“When we chastise our body with temperance, if we do this for God as we ought, so that we do not present our members as weapons of iniquity to sin but as weapons of righteousness to God, it is a sacrifice. The Apostle urges us to this when he says: ‘I beseech you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, that you present your bodies as a living, holy, acceptable sacrifice to God, your rational service.’

“If, then, the body—which the soul uses as a subordinate servant or as an instrument—becomes a sacrifice when its good and proper use is referred to the Lord, how much more is the soul itself a sacrifice when it refers itself to God; when, kindled by his love, it casts off the form of worldly desire and is refashioned in submission to him as an unchanging form; when it is pleasing to him because it has received its beauty from his beauty?

“The same Apostle adds immediately: ‘And do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what is the will of God, what is good, pleasing, and perfect.’”

For if the relics of martyrs are to be held so cheap and despised that they differ in no way from the corpses and bones of brute animals, Christian emperors, all bishops, and all the peoples of the churches must be convicted of having acted foolishly and sacrilegiously, since they appear at times to have transferred and honored them with such great ceremony and reverence.

Hence Saint Jerome, against Vigilantius:

[Col. 0474C] “Was the emperor Constantine, then, a sacrilegious man, because he transferred the holy relics of Andrew, Luke, and Timothy to Constantinople, where demons roar and the inhabitants of Vigilantius confess that they feel their presence? Must Augustus Arcadius also now be called sacrilegious, because long afterward he transferred the bones of blessed Samuel from Judea to Thrace?

“Must all the bishops be judged not only sacrilegious but foolish, because they carried a worthless object and scattered ashes in silk and a golden vessel? Must all the peoples of the churches be called fools because they went out to meet the holy relics and received them with such joy as though they saw them present and alive, so that crowds of people joined together from Palestine to Chalcedon and resounded with one voice in praise of Christ?

“Indeed, with heavenly grace accompanying them and the divine hand working daily along the journey, wherever those holy burdens were set down, rested, or remained, signs and miracles of heavenly powers flashed forth. In all those places basilicas and oratories were afterward built, which the same grace of healings continually ennobles and most beautifully adorns to this day.

“Moreover, many of the holy and faithful men who accompanied them—bishops, abbots, and other religious elders—asked that portions be given to them from the holy bodies, so that each might receive these dearest and most precious pledges and bring them back to his private home as the reward of his service and the payment for his labor. This was granted, and thereafter it happened that from the tiniest drops there remained immense fountains of spiritual grace and the greatest rivers of life.”

Accordingly Paulinus says in his ninth poem:

For while Constantine was founding a city

Bearing his own name, and was the first of Roman kings

To bear the Christian name, he received in his mind

A divine plan: since, with the walls of Rome

Vying with his magnificent undertaking, he was then building walls,

He should also follow Rome in these endowments,

So that, rejoicing, he might fortify his walls

With apostolic bodies. Then he brought Andrew from Achaea

And Timothy from Asia. Thus, rising with twin towers,

Constantinople stands, a great capital vying with Rome.

More truly does it resemble Rome in the height of its walls,

Because God compensated it with Peter and Paul in equal measure:

It deserved to receive Paul’s disciple,

Since, together with Peter’s brother, how great a benefit

Has grown for the duties of our life along this long road

Across the intervening lands of the saints—

The very places today bear witness where that spacious wagon,

[Col. 0475B] Carrying its burden, halted at a station.

Everywhere that there was a stopping-place or rest

For the holy bodies and those who carried them,

The places cried out with wondrous signs

For the consecrated ashes.

For the divine hand, with healing power,

Worked there along every road where the holy bodies

Imprinted living traces in their sacred passage.

Then, with faith urging them and opportunity granted to the faithful,

He earned from the zeal of the companions the favor

Of plucking some portion from the holy bones,

So that each might carry back to his private home

A protection as the reward of his service and the payment for his labor.

From that time, the sacred ashes, like seeds of life,

Were scattered in different places. Wherever a tiny drop

Fell from a small fragment of bone, a minute piece

From the little stock of the sacred body,

There the pious grace generated immense fountains

And rivers of life from a drop of ash.

Nor would Saint Ambrose, bishop of Milan, and all the Catholics who were present have shown such public rejoicing or so celebrated the discovery of the bones of oxen, sheep, asses, pigs, and other animals as they did when, through the Lord’s revelation, the relics of the saints Gervasius and Protasius were found—although Claudius asserts that both groups are equal.

Accordingly Ambrose, in the book he wrote to his sister about this matter, says:

[Col. 0475D] “We found two men of extraordinary stature, as the ancient age produced them; all the bones were intact, and there was a great deal of blood. A huge crowd of people gathered throughout those two days. Why say more? We placed them intact in due order and transferred them, as evening was already approaching, to the basilica of Fausta. There were vigils there throughout the night and the laying on of hands. On the following day we transferred them to the basilica that is called Ambrosian.

“During the transfer, a blind man was healed. This was my sermon to the people: When I considered the great and unprecedented solemnity of your assembly and the gifts of divine grace that had shone forth in the holy martyrs, I confessed that I judged myself unequal to this task. I did not think it possible to complete in speech what I could scarcely grasp in my mind.”

The same author shortly afterward says:

[Col. 0476A] “‘Day unto day utters the word.’ Behold the true days, which no darkness of night interrupts. Behold the true days, full of light and eternal radiance, which uttered the word of God not in a perfunctory speech but from the depths of their hearts—steadfast in confession, persevering in martyrdom.

“Another psalm was read, saying: ‘Who is like the Lord our God, who dwells on high and looks upon the humble in heaven and on earth?’ Truly our God looked upon the humble when he revealed the relics of the holy martyrs of his Church, lying hidden beneath an ignoble covering—those whose soul is in heaven and body on earth. ‘He raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dung heap,’ those whom you see, ‘to place them with the princes of his people.’

“Who else should we judge to be the princes of the people but the holy martyrs? Among their number, long unknown, Protasius and Gervasius are now reckoned. They have made the Milanese Church, previously barren of martyrs but now the mother of many children, rejoice in the titles and examples of their own passion.

“This too is not contrary to the truth: ‘Day unto day utters the word’; soul to soul, life to life, resurrection to resurrection, and night indicates knowledge to night. That is, flesh to flesh: their passion revealed the true knowledge of faith to all.

“Good are those nights, luminous nights, which have stars. For as star differs from star in brightness, so also is the resurrection of the dead. It is not without reason that many call this the resurrection of the martyrs. I shall see whether it is so for them; for us, certainly, the martyrs have risen.

“You have recognized—indeed, you yourselves have seen—many cleansed from demons, and very many freed from the illnesses from which they suffered when they touched the garment of the saints with their hands. You see the miracles of ancient times restored, when, at the coming of the Lord Jesus, a more abundant grace had poured itself over the earth; through a kind of shadow of the holy bodies you see very many healed.

“How many cloths are thrown upon them! How many garments are placed upon the most sacred relics and requested as curative through the very touch! Everyone rejoices in touching the outermost edge, and whoever touches it will be saved.

“Thanks be to you, Lord Jesus, that in this time you have raised up for us such spirits of the holy martyrs, at a time when your Church desires greater protections. Let all learn what sort of defenders I seek—those who can defend and cannot be attacked. These are the ones I have acquired for you, holy people: beneficial to all, harmful to no one.

“These are the defenders I desire; these are the soldiers I possess—not soldiers of the world, but soldiers of Christ. I fear no jealousy concerning such men, whose patronage is safer the greater it is. I even wish these protections upon those who begrudge me their possession.

“Let them come, then, and see my guards; I do not deny that I am surrounded by such weapons: ‘Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we will glory in the name of the Lord our God.’

“Our eyes were closed as long as the bodies of the saints lay buried and hidden. The Lord opened our eyes; we saw the aids by which we had often been defended. We did not see them, yet we possessed them. Thus, as though the Lord had said to us in our trembling: ‘Look at how many martyrs I have given you,’ our eyes being opened, we behold the glory of the Lord, which is present in the martyrs’ former suffering and present activity.

“We have escaped, brothers, a considerable burden of shame. We had patrons and did not know it. We have found one respect in which we may seem superior to our ancestors: the knowledge of the holy martyrs, which they lost, has been granted to us.

“Noble relics are brought out from an ignoble tomb; trophies are displayed to heaven. The tomb is wet with blood; the triumphal marks of gore appear; the inviolate relics are found in their proper place and order; the head of a living man has been severed.

“The city had lost its own martyrs, which had seized those belonging to others. And although this is God’s gift, I cannot deny the grace that the Lord Jesus has granted in the time of my priesthood, because, although I do not deserve to be a martyr myself, I have acquired these martyrs for you.

“Let the triumphal victims enter the place [Col. 0477B] where Christ is the victim. He is upon the altar, he who suffered for all; they are beneath the altar, they who were redeemed by his suffering.

“I had destined this place for myself. For it is fitting that the priest should rest where he was accustomed to offer sacrifice. But I yield the right-hand portion to the sacred victims. This place was owed to the martyrs.

“Let us therefore bury the most holy relics and bring them into worthy seats, and let us celebrate the entire day with faithful devotion.”

Saint Augustine also commemorates what happened in the city of Milan in this matter, in Book XXII of *The City of God*:

[Col. 0477C] “The miracle that occurred at Milan, when we were there, when the blind man was given sight, could become known to many, because the city is large and the emperor was then there, and the event took place before an immense crowd, which had gathered at the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius. Their bodies had been hidden and entirely unknown, but they were revealed to Bishop Ambrose in a dream and were found. There the blind man, the old darkness having been driven away, saw the daylight.”

Likewise, the second proposition of that same man concerns the Lord’s cross. He reproaches its venerators as practitioners of false religion and superstition, babbling and belching forth from a foul, muddy mouth that the holy cross possesses no honor or dignity whatsoever, except merely the disgrace of the Passion and the mockery of death.

As though to confirm this, he takes an example from the Apostle: “And if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer in that way.” He does so incongruously and improperly, like one who does not understand Scripture, or who, if he understands it, wishes deliberately to corrupt it.

For the Apostle, as Augustine says in his book against Faustus, according to his custom contemplates our future life—which has already been completed in the man Christ Jesus, our mediator and head, when he rose again—with certain hope as though it were already present and grasped. That life will not be according to the flesh, just as Christ’s life is no longer according to the flesh.

For by “flesh” here he does not mean the substance of our body itself, which the Lord also calls flesh after his resurrection when he says: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have bones and flesh as you see me have.” Rather, he means the corruption and mortality of the flesh, which will not then exist in us, just as it no longer exists in Christ.

He called this specifically “flesh” even when he spoke quite plainly about the resurrection itself and said: “Flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God, nor will corruption possess incorruption.”

We therefore knew Christ according to the flesh—that is, according to the mortality of the flesh—before he rose again; but now we know him no longer in that way, because, as the same Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer have dominion over him.”

For if the Apostle, as this false accuser maliciously charges him, as heretics habitually do when interpreting his words, believed that there was no dignity or power of any kind in Christ’s cross except the disgrace of the Passion and the mockery of death, and if for this reason he did not want it honored, known, or remembered by anyone, why does he say elsewhere, in contrast:

[Col. 0478B] “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me and I to the world”?

Jerome says:

“Only he can glory in the cross of Christ who takes it up and follows the Savior; who has crucified his flesh with its vices and desires; who has died to the world and does not contemplate the things that are seen but those that are unseen; who sees the world crucified and its form passing away; for whom the end of the world has come; who has become worthy of a new heaven, a new earth, and a New Testament; who sings a new song and receives a new name written on a stone, which no one knows except the one who receives it.

“It must be understood that all the Apostle’s glorying is in the cross, and that whatever worthy deed is accomplished in the virtues is accomplished because of the Lord’s Passion.”

The Lord did not wish his cross or Passion to be unknown or hidden from his faithful, as though he wanted it mentioned on account of the insult and disgrace of his death. For if that were so, his disciples would consequently also be ashamed to suffer or die for him.

On the contrary, he commanded that his Passion be recalled and celebrated daily in the Church. Hence the Apostle says:

[Col. 0478C] “For I received from the Lord what I also delivered to you: that the Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread, and giving thanks broke it and said: ‘This is my body, which will be delivered for you; do this in remembrance of me.’ Likewise also the cup, after he had supped, saying: ‘This cup is the new covenant in my blood; do this whenever you drink it in remembrance of me.’ For whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes.”

Therefore the saints too, when they endure adversity and afflictions in this world for the Lord, rejoice and glory in them. Hence the Apostle says in the Second Letter to the Corinthians:

[Col. 0478D] “I will gladly glory in my infirmities, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. Therefore I am pleased with infirmities, insults, necessities, persecutions, and distresses for Christ; for when I am weak, then I am strong.”

The same author says in the Letter to the Philippians:

“But I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has turned out rather for the progress of the Gospel, so that my chains have become manifest in Christ throughout the whole praetorium and among all the others.”

The same author says to Timothy:

“Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner, but labor with the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with his holy calling.”

Again, in the Acts of the Apostles:

“They went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus.”

For, as the Apostle says, “the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God.”

And shortly afterward:

[Col. 0479A] “Because the Jews ask for signs and the Greeks seek wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified: to the Jews, indeed, a stumbling block; to the Gentiles, foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

The same author shortly afterward says:

“And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come with excellence of speech or wisdom, proclaiming to you the testimony of Christ. For I judged myself not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.”

The Apostles, therefore, and all humble and faithful people who follow their teaching love, honor, praise, celebrate, and glory in the cross of Christ, as his triumphant sign by which he conquered the devil and redeemed the world.

But impious, proud, and unbelieving heretics disdain to hear of his humility or to believe that any power exists in it. The Apostle laments them, saying:

[Col. 0479B] “For many walk—of whom I often told you, and now tell you even weeping—as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction; their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame.”

Hence Augustine says in his exposition of the Gospel according to John:

“Jesus therefore went to the place where he was to be crucified, carrying his cross: a great spectacle. But if impiety observes it, a great mockery; if piety, a great mystery. If impiety observes it, a great lesson in disgrace; if piety, a great bulwark of faith.

“If impiety observes it, it laughs at the king carrying, in place of the rod of his kingdom, the wood of his punishment. If piety, it sees the king carrying the wood on which he was to be fastened—the wood that he would also fix upon the foreheads of kings; in that same thing he is despised by the eyes of the impious in which the hearts of the saints would glory.

“For when Paul was about to say: ‘But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ,’ he commended that very cross by carrying it upon his shoulder, and he carried the lampstand for the lamp that was about to burn and that he knew must be placed beneath a bushel.”

Since Claudius has learned none of the liberal disciplines, knows nothing of the meanings and properties of letters, and does not know how to join gender with gender, number with number, or case with case in a rational construction, he nevertheless dares to compose, as is reported, enormous treatises.

He falsely claims these as the work of his own labor and industry, although he extracts them by transferring—or rather scattering and corrupting them—from the books of others in the manner of a glossary. He then presents them with wretched and empty arrogance as his own, torn from the expositions of the authors from whom he presumes to snatch and steal them.

He also permits no books except his own to be read in his city, inscribing the authority of his name on the title pages of each in this fashion: “Here begins the commentary, treatise, or exposition of Claudius, bishop of Turin.”

Of the ancient holy teachers and doctors of the Church, he praises and accepts some after assuming the judicial robe, while he blasphemes and reviles others, though he agrees in faith and teaching with none of them.

He appropriates Augustine, although he is exceedingly far removed from Augustine’s subtle intellect and the rectitude of his Christian understanding. Apart from him, he rejects almost everyone, calling one a great “mentioner,” another a compiler, and another a rustic, a brute, insensible, and ignorant of every good thing.

Yet he would customarily wish that all of them might exist at one and the same time and in one place with him, so that, having easily and swiftly overcome them all, the wedge of his superior wisdom might appear and shine forth.

He attacks Jerome above all others and heaps excessive abuse upon him. He declares that, had they lived in the same age, he would have been Jerome’s fiercest and most hostile enemy.

The only reason, I think, is that he learned that Jerome had written against Vigilantius, the heretic who was his neighbor and the author of his madness, and had vigorously crushed that man’s head, as he was accustomed to strike down the heads of others of the same sort, with the club of Catholic teaching.

This accuser of the brethren, ignorant of the proper uses of the words “I adore” and “I worship,” and supposing that these expressions belong exclusively to God, blasphemes Christians excessively, not understanding either what is read or what he himself asserts according to the Apostle.

For the following is written in his letter, to which we must respond:

[Col. 0480C] “If they wish to adore every piece of wood fashioned in the shape of a cross because Christ hung upon the cross, then many other things that Christ did in the flesh also apply to them.”

The man whose objection and argument is of this kind shows that he is entirely ignorant of the power of this saving wood, through which life was restored to the human race that had perished by tasting the fruit of the forbidden, deadly tree. Hence Fortunatus says:

Sing, tongue, the battle of the glorious contest,

And tell upon the cross’s trophy the noble triumph:

How the world’s Redeemer, sacrificed, conquered.

Grieving over the fraud of the first parent,

When he fell to death by biting the noxious fruit,

The Maker himself then marked the wood,

So that by it he might undo the damage of the wood.

The order of our salvation required this work:

That the art of the many-shaped betrayer might be outwitted,

And that it might bring healing from the place

From which the enemy had inflicted the wound, and so on.

The same author in another poem:

The exalted power of the cross rightly fills the whole world,

For through it he restores all the things the world had lost.

And whatever the savage serpent infected with the gall of poison,

Christ’s blood on this cross washes clean with its sweet stain.

Whatever had been the prey of the fierce wolf and ravager,

The Virgin’s Lamb restores upon the cross.

Stretching his arms with his feet fastened to these branches,

He himself, hanging upon the cross, establishes the Church.

In his goodness, upon this wood he repairs what had long been lost,

The good that the fruits of the forbidden tree had taken away.

[Col. 0481A] On account of this ignorance just mentioned, he regards it as idolatry for anyone to adore or venerate the Lord’s cross, just as neither should any girls whatsoever, unmarried women, mangers, old cloths, ships, asses, lambs, lions, rocks, thorn-bushes, reeds, or spears be adored, because Christ used all these things for a time. As though no special privilege ought to be accorded to the Lord’s cross above these things, as we demonstrated earlier. Rebuking and chastising its venerators severely and shamefully, he reprimands them in these words:

“Return to your senses, transgressors, you who have withdrawn from the truth and love vanity, and have become vain; you who crucify the Son of God again, hold him up to contempt, and thereby, in a crowd, have made the souls of wretched people companions of demons; by your abominable sacrileges [Col. 0481B] of images you have alienated them from their Creator and cast them down and thrown them into everlasting condemnation.”

There is therefore no doubt that a deceitful and malignant spirit belches forth and breathes through the mouth of this deranged slanderer, bringing forward and reproaching the faithful with the crimes of unbelievers, calling them transgressors and apostates from the truth and lovers of vanity, while naming the divine cross a wicked and sacrilegious image surpassing every blasphemy of the past. From this he is most clearly proved to be the utterly perverse destroyer and overthrower of the Catholic faith.

But we, against whom he directs so many and such disgraceful slanders, believing with our whole heart and, by divine assistance, confessing with our mouth, with humbled spirit and lowly bodily bearing, bear witness against his false testimony that God alone is to be adored and venerated, as it is fitting for the creature to adore and venerate the Lord and Creator of all things, since we believe in him alone, hope in him, and sacrifice to him daily.

We also adore and venerate God’s holy and good creature—that is, a holy angel, a holy human being, or the holy cross—according to the diversity of their dignity. This means that we humbly honor, love, and embrace them for God’s sake and in God, in a manner altogether different from that in which we venerate and adore him. But he slanders this in ignorance, raging while refusing to know; in indignation, fury, and madness he raves, having often heard sung in the Church:

“We adore your cross, O Lord, and we praise and glorify your holy resurrection,” and so forth.

[Col. 0481D] For if these words could not appropriately be applied to creatures, then the following words would no longer be read in the book of Genesis concerning Lot:

“Two angels came to Sodom in the evening, while Lot was sitting at the gate of the city. When he saw them, he rose and went to meet them, and bowed down with his face to the ground.”

Likewise in the same book:

“Abraham rose and bowed down before the people of the land,” namely, the sons of Heth.

Again in the same book concerning Jacob:

“And he himself, going out, bowed down with his face to the ground seven times, until he drew near to his brother.”

A little later:

“Leah also came with her children, and when they had likewise bowed down, Joseph and Rachel, the last, bowed down.”

Again in the same book:

“And he said to them”—that is, Joseph said to his brothers—“Hear my dream, which I saw. I thought that we were binding sheaves in the field, and that my sheaf, as though rising up and standing, was being adored by your sheaves standing around it.”

Again in the same book:

“When his brothers had bowed down before him and he had recognized them, he spoke to them harshly, as though to strangers.”

Again in the same book:

“Joseph entered his house, and they offered him gifts, holding them in their hands, and they bowed down with their faces to the ground.”

A little later:

“They answered: ‘Your servant, our father, is safe; he is still alive.’ And they bowed down and adored him.”

Again in the book of Joshua:

“When Joshua was in the field of the city of Jericho, he lifted his eyes and saw a man standing opposite him, holding an unsheathed sword. He went toward him and said: ‘Are you one of ours or one of our adversaries?’ He answered: ‘By no means; I am the prince of the army of the Lord, and now I have come.’ Joshua fell on his face to the ground, and, adoring, said: ‘What does my Lord speak to his servant?’” and so forth.

Again in the book of Psalms:

“And adore the footstool of his feet, for it is holy.”

For this reason Jerome explains:

“What is this footstool of Jesus’ feet, since it is holy? We read elsewhere: ‘Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet’; and now it is said: ‘Adore the footstool of his feet.’ If the earth is the footstool of Jesus’ feet, and it is said that his footstool is to be adored, then the earth is to be adored. How, then, do we read in the Apostle that, apart from the Creator, we ought not to adore a creature?

“‘To adore’ is used in Scripture in two ways. Adoration is spoken of as directed toward God, and ‘to adore’ is also used in the sense of honoring. When we are said to adore the Lord, ‘adoration’ properly refers to God. But when the word is used of a human being—for example, ‘Sarah adored Abraham’ and ‘Elijah adored Ahab’—it does not mean ‘as God’; rather, adoration is used there in the sense of greeting.

“Let us therefore now examine what is meant by ‘adore the footstool of his feet’: does it mean that we adore the footstool of God’s feet as God, or that we adore and greet it as a human being? We read in the Lamentations of Jeremiah, and in another prophet as well: ‘How,’ he says, ‘the Lord sanctified the footstool of his feet’; and there Jerusalem, or the temple, is called his footstool.

“According to the historical sense, then, we read also in another place: ‘And adore the footstool of his feet.’ If feet do not stand except upon a footstool, then this means: ‘And we adored where his feet stood’; the reference is to the footstool. According to the letter, therefore, we can say, for example, that it is the place where he was born, where he was crucified, and where he rose again.

“Otherwise, Jesus’ footstool is the soul of the believer. Blessed is the one in whose breast Jesus’ feet are placed daily. Would that his feet also be placed in my breast! Would that his footprints always remain impressed upon my heart! Would that I too might say with the bride: ‘I will hold him fast and will not let him go.’ The bridegroom is quickly offended; he always loves purity, and wherever he sees filth, he quickly departs.

“‘And adore the footstool of his feet, for it is holy’—not every footstool of his feet, but whatever is holy, whatever perseveres in holiness. For example: adore Peter and Paul, the footstool of his feet, and adore the other apostles—that is, honor them. It is holy; adore those who persevere in holiness. But those who were a footstool and are not holy, do not adore them. For example, Judas the traitor was God’s footstool; but since he is not holy, do not adore him.”

According to the one sense of the word mentioned above that applies to human beings, it is written in the Book of Kings:

“When the sons of the prophets who were in Jericho saw him opposite them, they said: ‘The spirit of Elijah has rested upon Elisha.’ And they came to meet him, bowed down with their faces to the ground, and adored him.”

Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles:

“When Peter entered, Cornelius came to meet him, fell at his feet, and adored him. But Peter raised him up, saying: ‘Rise; I too am a human being.’”

Bede explains this as follows:

“By the gesture of his body Cornelius demonstrated what devotion he possessed within his heart. The hearer came to meet his teacher, receiving the word of faith with a pure breast, an attentive and diligent ear, and eager desire. For one who is slow to come to faith is, as it were, raised up by his teacher while lying on the ground. But one who, ashamed of the stains of his life, falls upon his face and thereby displays signs both of humility and of shame, rightly deserves to be raised up by his teacher. Peter, however, said…” and so forth.

The holiness of his conduct deserved fellowship in equality.

Again in the Apocalypse:

“And he said to me: ‘See that you do not do this, for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers who bear witness to Jesus.’”

On this subject Saint Gregory explains:

“Because the King of heaven assumed the earth of our flesh, that angelic sublimity no longer despises our weakness. The angels return to peace with us; they set aside their former hostility, and those whom they had previously despised as weak and rejected, they now honor as companions.

“For this is why Lot and Joshua adore angels and are not forbidden to adore them. John, however, in the Apocalypse, wished to adore an angel, but that same angel restrained him from adoring him, saying: ‘See that you do not do this; I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers.’

“What does it mean that, before the Redeemer’s coming, angels were adored by human beings and remained silent, whereas afterward they refuse to be adored? It means that, after they saw our nature—which they had previously despised—assumed above them, they feared to see it subjected and bowed down beneath them. They no longer dared to scorn as weak the nature that they venerate above them in the King of heaven. Nor do they disdain to have as their companion the human being whom they adore as God above them.”

[Col. 0483D] For blessed John the Apostle and Evangelist, Christ’s most beloved disciple, did not wish to be estranged from God by the spiritual visions revealed to him by God, nor to commit sacrilege by improperly offering to another the honor due to God alone, nor to oppose God, who had exalted him with such honor. Nor did the angel refuse because apostolic worship had been offered to him as though he were divine; rather, as stated above, out of humility he merely refused to see subjected and bowed before him the substance of human nature which he knew God had assumed into the unity of his person.

Although Scripture, as usual, has multiple senses, we have learned that other teachers understand these passages differently. Numerous examples of the same argument are likewise found in the other holy books of the authors.

Paulinus, in Book IX, which he composed in verse concerning the virtues of Saint Felix:

“Behold, filled with joy, I adore the priest’s return,

Receiving Christ, who dwells in his humble breast.”

The same author:

“And although hidden by the ancient age in tombs,

And concealed beneath the earth because he was mortal,

Yet, while God gives life, grace surviving in the limbs

Glorifies for the peoples the divinely breathing bones

Of the martyr, deservedly living though buried;

A throng, gathered continually from diverse lands,

Adores the brief shrine of the great confessor.”

Likewise Prudentius, in the book entitled *Apotheosis*:

“Nor does Hammon return answers in the Libyan Syrtes.

Rome’s Capitol itself mourns that Christ,

God, shines upon its princes; its temples destroyed,

The purple of the commanders having fallen,

Now humbly prostrates itself before the halls

Of the Aenead ruler, Christ,

And the supreme ruler adores the standard of the cross.”

The same author, to Bishop Valerian, concerning the passion of Saint Hippolytus:

“Every young person hastens to greet him in the morning;

All adore him; they go and return until the sun’s setting.”

The other word, *colo*, is shown by Priscian—who, on account of the distinction of his most noble intellect, deserved to be called the light of Roman eloquence—to have three meanings. He says:

“*Colo* is also understood as ‘I love,’ ‘I inhabit,’ and ‘I till.’”

For this reason Augustine says in Book X of *The City of God*:

“Our writers have translated *latria*, wherever it is found in the holy Scriptures, as ‘service.’ But the service owed to human beings—the service according to which the Apostle commands servants to be subject to their masters—is usually called by another name in Greek. According to the usage of those who composed the divine utterances for us, *latria* means either always, or so frequently that it is almost always so, the service that pertains to worshiping God.

“Therefore, if only worship itself is intended, it does not seem to be owed to God alone. For we are said to worship distinguished human beings whom we regularly approach either in honor or in remembrance. Nor are only those things said to be worshiped to which we subject ourselves with religious humility; certain things that are subject to us are also said to be worshiped.

“For from this verb come the words ‘farmer,’ ‘tenant,’ and ‘inhabitant.’ The gods themselves are called *heaven-dwellers* for no other reason than that they inhabit heaven—not by venerating it, but by dwelling in it, as tenants of heaven. They are not like those tenants who, because of agriculture, owe a condition to their native soil under the authority of its possessors. Rather, as a great author of Latin eloquence says:

‘There was an ancient city, which Tyrian settlers held’ (*Virgil, Aeneid* I.12).

“He called them settlers from inhabiting, not from agriculture. Hence cities founded by larger cities, as though by swarms of peoples, are called colonies.

“Accordingly, it is entirely true, according to a certain proper meaning of this word, that worship is owed to God alone. But because worship is also spoken of in relation to other things, what is owed to God cannot be signified in Latin by this one word alone.”

[Col. 0485A] It is clearer than daylight that this word refers not only to the Creator but also to creatures, though in a different manner, as we said above. God is worshiped in one way, an angel or human being in another, and the earth in another, according to the variety of crops and trees that are tended upon it by manifold and laborious care—building, ploughing, sowing, planting, irrigating, watering, and the like.

In another way Christians worship and celebrate the holy cross of the Lord, the offices, and the feasts of Christ and his saints in the holy Church. These matters are so familiar and almost universally known that they require little demonstration or confirmation by examples. Nevertheless, a few examples should be added for the sake of confirmation and experience.

[Col. 0485B] On venerating the Lord’s cross, Sedulius says in Book IV of *The Paschal Poem*:

“He himself was the peace of the cross; illuminating

The violent wood with his own limbs,

He clothed punishment with honor

And made the penalty more truly a sign of salvation;

Sanctifying the torments in himself,

He blessed them.

“Lest anyone fail to know that the form of the cross is to be venerated,

The cross that bore the Lord in triumph, by a powerful design,

From it gathers the four regions of the square world.

The shining East gleams from the crown of its Author;

The sacred feet are touched by the setting star.

Its right hand holds the North; its left raises the central axis;

All nature lives from the limbs of its Creator,

And Christ governs the whole world, embraced by the cross.”

Likewise, on venerating the holy Church, Paulinus says in Book X:

“You see these newly born works shining forth,

Surrounded on every side by lofty structures,

With equal splendor and adornment.”

A little later:

“Rivaling one another, they join their roof-beams,

And stand forth, various yet beautiful in equal adornment.”

The same author on the same subject, in his letter to Severus concerning the cross:

“And so, with the ready assent of the emperor’s son, the Augusta mother, opening her treasuries for holy works, expended the entire fisc. With whatever expense and adornment the queen could furnish and religion urged, she built basilicas throughout and adorned and embellished all the places.”

On venerating the saints, Prudentius says in the *Passion of the Apostles*:

“Behold two gifts of faith, bestowed by the supreme Father

Upon the city wearing the toga, gifts he gave to be venerated.”

The same author, *de civi. col.*:

[Col. 0485D]

“Noble in birth, Eulalia,

And nobler still in the character of her death,

The holy virgin adorns her own Emerita—

From whose breast she was born—

With her bones, and cherishes it with love.”

Likewise Fortunatus, to the clergy of Paris:

“The honor and dignity of an illustrious order,

The fathers whom I venerate in heart, faith, and devotion,

Having long forgotten to strike the lyre with accustomed song,

You compel me to renew my ancient lyre.”
