The same author concerning the Church’s worship and the veneration of the saints’ feasts:

“Those summits which Placidina adorned with sacred veils—

Here they rival one another; there she venerates them.”

On venerating the feasts of the saints, Prudentius, commemorating the birthday of the holy martyr Hippolytus, says:

[Col. 0486A]

“If I remember rightly, beautiful Rome venerates him

On the Ides of the month of August, as she herself calls it.”

And there are many other examples that it would take too long to produce.

Just as he therefore went astray in these words, from which, as I think, the origin of his perversity began, so now, in the term *Apostolicus*, although at less risk, he has likewise been deceived by similar ignorance. For, attempting to discuss it according to the principles of grammatical learning, after the manner of ancient teachers—who, though they had been educated in every branch of wisdom, whenever an opportunity arose in their books or explanations to examine some matter concerning them, would fully disclose and unravel it—this man, imitating or even surpassing them, strives to express the meaning and derivation of the word *apostolicus* as though it were composed of the complete *apostoli* and a corrupt *-cus*, as though it meant “guardian of the apostle,” recklessly and presumptuously asserting what he does not know and defining uncertain matters as certain.

For *apostolicus* is a simple derivative noun, derived from *apostolus* by adding *-cus* to its genitive, and it does not have the meaning he ignorantly devised. For one does not say *Italicus*, “guardian of Italy,” *Gallicus*, “guardian of Gaul,” or *Germanicus*, “guardian of Germany”; rather, these names correspond to the meaning of their respective originals. We need not concern ourselves greatly with these matters. For if someone were to investigate them more carefully, he would find that almost everything had been stated crudely and incorrectly.

Let us therefore return to matters of greater necessity, about which we spoke earlier.

[Col. 0486C] Just as a person who is compelled by unavoidable necessity to cross a very turbulent and dangerous sea cannot have any hope of escaping or prospering if he has no ship to carry him, so no perverse or unbelieving person who refuses to hold the faith of the life-giving cross, and who therefore lacks its protection, will be able to reach the harbor of his heavenly homeland from the sea of this world.

For this reason Augustine says in his exposition of the Gospel according to John:

“It is as though someone were to see his homeland from a distance, with the sea lying between him and it. He sees where he must go, but he has no means by which to go there. Therefore, so that there might be a way by which we could go, the one to whom we wished to go came from there. And what did he do? He established the wood by which we might cross the sea. For no one can cross the sea of this world except carried by the cross of Christ.

“Sometimes even one weak in sight embraces this cross; and one who does not see clearly from afar where he is going should not depart from it. The cross itself leads him to his homeland, where it will no longer be needed, because no sea will be crossed.

“It is therefore better not to see mentally what truly exists, yet not to depart from the cross of Christ, than to see it mentally and despise the cross of Christ.”

This saving sign was therefore prefigured long beforehand in the Law and the Prophets. Thus in Genesis we read of Abraham and his son Isaac:

“He also took the wood for the burnt offering and placed it upon his son Isaac.”

The bundle of wood which Isaac carried, after his father had placed it upon him, to the place appointed by God, so that he might be sacrificed upon it, signifies the cross which the mystical Isaac—that is, Christ—carried, by the will of God the Father, to the place of Calvary.

For this reason Paulinus says in Book IX:

“May Isaac offer the living victim to God like a boy,

And may I, carrying my wood, follow the gracious Father beneath the cross.”

Again in Exodus:

“Moses called all the elders of Israel and said to them: ‘Go, take an animal according to your families, sacrifice the Passover, dip a bundle of hyssop in the blood that is at the threshold, and sprinkle from it upon the lintel and both doorposts’” (Exod. XII.21).

For this reason Augustine says in his exposition of the Gospel according to John:

“Passover is called ‘passing over’ in its own language, that is, in Hebrew, because the people of the Lord first celebrated the Passover when, fleeing from Egypt, they crossed the Red Sea.

“Now that prophetic figure has been fulfilled in reality, when Christ is led like a sheep to be sacrificed. With his blood staining our doorposts—that is, with the sign of the cross upon our foreheads—we are freed from the destruction of this world as from Egyptian captivity or slaughter, and we accomplish a most salutary passage when we pass from the devil to Christ and from this unstable world to his firmly established kingdom.”

The same author says on this matter in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*:

“Let him therefore remember those who at that time celebrated Passover through the imaginary figures of shadows, when they were commanded to mark the doorposts with the blood of a lamb: they were commanded to mark them with hyssop.

“This plant is lowly and gentle, and nothing is stronger or more penetrating than its roots. Being rooted and grounded in love, we might comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth—that is, the cross of the Lord.

“And there is also in hyssop a purifying power, so that, when knowledge puffs up concerning the riches taken from Egypt, the swollen breast may not breathe out something arrogantly. ‘You shall sprinkle me with hyssop,’ he says, ‘and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow. You shall make me hear joy and gladness.’ Then he immediately adds, to show that purification from pride is signified by hyssop: ‘And the bones that have been humbled shall rejoice.’”

Augustine says in Book X of *The City of God*:

“Who would say that the enemies who confronted them, obstructed their passage, and fought against them, were struck down and overthrown while Moses prayed and extended his hands in the form of a cross, with none of the Hebrews falling?”

Again in the Book of Numbers:

“Moses therefore made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign; those who had been bitten and looked upon it were healed.”

Augustine says:

“The Lord commanded Moses to make a bronze serpent, raise it upon a piece of wood in the wilderness, and remind the people of Christ, so that if anyone had been bitten by a serpent, he would look upon that serpent raised upon the wood.

“It was done. The people were bitten; they looked, and they were healed. Meanwhile, brothers, so that we may be healed from sin, let us look upon Christ crucified. For, as Moses,” he says, “raised up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be raised up, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.”

Just as those who looked upon that serpent did not perish from the serpents’ bites, so those who look upon Christ’s death in faith are healed from the bites of sins. But they were healed from death to temporal life, whereas here he says that they should have eternal life.

This is the difference between the figurative image and the reality itself: the figure provided temporal life, while the reality of which it was the figure provides eternal life.

Again in the Book of Joshua we read of Rahab the prostitute, who, having received the Israelite spies, was saved from death together with her entire household by a certain sign of blood-red color—that is, by a scarlet cord. This signified the Church, violated among the nations by the manifold worship of idols, later saved by Christ through the sign of the blessed cross marked with blood.

For this reason Paulinus says in Book VIII:

“Rahab alone, the prostitute who carried chaste faith

Among a wicked people, did not trust in escaping by her walls,

But, having gained God’s favor, obtained the reward of piety.”

A little later:

“She marked her own dwelling with a purple-red fleece

And received her salvation while her homeland perished,

Signifying those who are to be sheltered as the world collapses,

Whom the blood of the unconquered cross marks.

“From this learn how much that blood is worth,

The blood whose image was saving her.”

Again Isaiah:

“A child is born to us; a son is given to us, and the government has been placed upon his shoulder.”

Jerome says:

“Although, from what he had said above—‘Emmanuel,’ that is, ‘God with us’—he had shown that he was the Lord, nevertheless he now says that his government was placed upon his shoulder, either as though he himself had carried his cross, or indicating through the shoulder the strength of his arm, as the same Isaiah says: ‘The Lord God has revealed his holy arm to all the nations.’”

Again Ambrose, in the book he published on the holy Trinity:

“The cross of the Lord is the beginning of strength, by which the way was opened for the holy martyrs to the passion of the sacred contest. Isaiah saw this beginning, and therefore said: ‘A child is born to us; a son is given to us.’

“The Magi also saw it, and therefore, when they beheld the child in the manger, they adored him, saying: ‘A child is born to us.’ When they saw the star, they proclaimed: ‘A son is given to us.’ One gift came from the earth and another gift from heaven, and they adored both as one; they offered gifts to show that the one who was seen in the manger is himself Lord of heaven.”

Again in the Book of Ezekiel:

“And the Lord said to him: ‘Pass through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and mark a *taw* upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over all the abominations that are committed in its midst’” (Ezek. IX.4).

Jerome explains this as follows:

“The final letter, *taw*, has the likeness of the cross, which is painted upon the foreheads of Christians and marked by the frequent inscription of the hand. Those who groan and grieve are therefore saved: they not only do not consent to evil deeds, but also lament the sins of others. And the six men are commanded to kill everyone except those who can say: ‘The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us’; they are to spare none of those who, without the sign of Christ, believe themselves to be something.”

[Col. 0489A] What, then, remains for a person crossing the stormy sea of this world without the saving ship of the cross? Nothing, as one must suppose, except that he remain dead amid the waves and be plunged into the depths of hell with the Egyptians.

And what awaits the person whose forehead is neither armed nor inscribed with this same sign? Nothing except that, according to the prophet, he be slain with the transgressors of Israel by the sword of divine vengeance.

But the true and saved Israelites, chosen in the number of twelve thousand from the twelve tribes of Israel—that is, all the faithful and orthodox throughout the world, children of the holy and Catholic mother Church, who gaze upon the Lord with right faith and a pure heart and observe the sound doctrine of the twelve apostles—are inscribed by the angels of the Lord upon their foreheads with this most glorious and salutary sign of the Lord’s cross, and through it they are saved.

Blessed John, as we read in the Apocalypse, had seen them standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb; therefore he says:

“And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun, having the sign of the living God. And he cried out with a loud voice to the four angels to whom it had been given to harm the earth and the sea, saying: ‘Do not harm the earth, nor the sea, nor the trees, until we have marked the servants of our God upon their foreheads.’ And I heard the number of those who were marked: one hundred and forty-four thousand, marked from every tribe of the children of Israel” (Apoc. VII.2).

The Lord, born in the flesh, who is the angel of the great counsel—that is, the messenger of the Father’s will—visited us, rising from on high and bringing the standard of the cross with which he would mark the foreheads of his own.

“And he cried out with a loud voice,” and so forth—that is, with exalted preaching:

“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near.”

“Do not harm,” and so forth, “until we have marked the servants of our God upon their foreheads.”

For this purpose the empire of the nations was broken, so that the faces of the holy might freely be marked with the sign of faith which they had resisted. The very figure of the cross signifies that the Lord’s kingdom has been extended everywhere.

As an ancient couplet proves:

“Behold the square world divided into distinct regions,

Showing that all things bear the sign of faith.”

Nor was the name of the Lord—the tetragrammaton—written without reason upon the forehead of the high priest, since this is the unique and simultaneously four-sided sign upon the foreheads of the faithful. Concerning it Psalm 8 is sung:

“O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth,”

and so forth, until it says:

“that you may destroy the enemy and the defender.”

It continues:

“Clothed in white robes, and palms in their hands.”

The robes signify baptism; the palms signify the triumph of the cross.

[Col. 0489D] For this wondrous and ineffable sacrament of the divine cross the Apostle prays, bending his knees before God, that it may be granted to the faithful to understand it. He says in the Epistle to the Ephesians:

“For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, rooted and grounded in love, [Col. 0490A] so that you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth; and to know the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge, and be filled unto all the fullness of the Lord” (Eph. III.14).

For this reason Augustine says in his exposition of the Gospel according to John:

“What are we to say about the cross itself, which certainly was likewise made and fastened upon Christ by enemies and impious men?”

And yet it is rightly understood that the Apostle’s words signify the cross: “what is its breadth, length, height, and depth.”

It is broad in the transverse wood, upon which the hanging hands are extended, and signifies good works in the breadth of love. It is long from the crossbeam down to the earth, where the back and feet are fastened, and signifies perseverance through the length of time unto the end. It is high at the summit, which rises above the crossbeam, and signifies the heavenly end toward which all works are directed. Since all things are done well and perseveringly in breadth and length, they must be done because of the height of divine rewards.

It is deep in the part that is fixed in the earth. There it is hidden and cannot be seen, but all its visible appearance and prominence arise from it, just as all our good works proceed from the depth of God’s grace, which cannot be comprehended or fully expressed.

Again, concerning the passage cited above from the Apocalypse:

“After this I saw a great multitude, which no one could number, from every nation, tribe, people, and language, standing before the throne and in the sight of the Lamb, [Col. 0490C] clothed in white robes, with palms in their hands; and they cried out with a loud voice, saying: ‘Salvation belongs to our God who sits upon the throne, and to the Lamb’” (Apoc. VII.13).

All are marked upon their foreheads and hands—that is, in confession and action.

For the Lord is believed to come to judgment in the form in which he deigned to suffer for us, carrying his cross. With all the faithful obscured, it alone will shine with wondrous and ineffable brilliance, as we read in the Gospel:

“The sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light, and the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of heaven will be shaken; and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven” (Matt. XXIV.29).

[Col. 0490D] Hence John says in the Gospel:

“They will see him whom they pierced” (John XIX.37).

Thus, I say, he will come surrounded and accompanied by very numerous and glorious ranks of heavenly citizens and all the faithful, each of whom will carry this triumphant standard upon his shoulders.

For this reason John Chrysostom says in his homily on the cross and the thief:

“I want you to learn other reasons as well. He did not leave the cross alone on earth, but lifted it with him to heaven. But you say: ‘From where is this demonstrated?’ Therefore listen: ‘When he comes with it, he will make his second appearance with it.’ For this reason I called the cross glorious.”

A little later:

“And then the sign of the Son of Man will be seen in heaven. Do you see the glory of the sign—that is, of the cross? The light of the sun will be made dark; the moon will not be granted its brightness, but that sign will radiate and shine. Just as royal pomp goes before an emperor, and a military order customarily carries standards upon its shoulders as it advances, thereby announcing his arrival, so, when the Lord comes from heaven, a host of angels and a multitude of archangels will carry that sign upon their exalted shoulders and announce to us the royal arrival.”

For this reason Paulinus says in Book IX:

“By the purple cross, with the crimson of precious blood,

He, lofty in ascent, penetrated into the heights [the printed reading *voluerit* is uncertain].”

The same author in Poem 11, on the same subject:

“Christ is likewise my Alpha and my Omega, who embraces

The highest limits of the highest realms and equally the lowest;

Victor, he seized both the infernal and the heavenly realms,

And, having shattered the abysses, penetrated the opened heavens,

Bringing back victorious salvation after conquering death.

[Col. 0491B] And when victory joined him to the right hand of his homeland,

He fixed the standard of the cross above all the stars.

He established a bodily trophy in the heavenly seat.”

What, then, will the enemy and persecutor of Christ’s cross do on that day, when the entire army of the Lord appears marked and adorned with it? Although he has always hated and persecuted it, he will not deserve to be marked with the others; yet for that reason he will not remain unmarked. For there will be two signs by which all are to be marked on that day, according to the diversity of their merits: one belonging to Christ, the other to the devil; one for salvation, the other for destruction; one for protection, the other for deception; one for guidance, the other for seduction and corruption; one for glorification and exaltation, the other for condemnation and being hurled into the abyss of eternal death. Whoever has not been marked with the one sign, together with Christ and his elect, will be marked with the other, together with Satan and his attendants, who have been designated by his sign and mark.

Hence we read in the Apocalypse:

> If anyone worships the beast and his image and receives his mark upon his forehead or upon his hand, he too will drink of the wine of God’s wrath, mixed with unmixed wine in the cup of his anger; and he will be tormented with fire and sulphur in the presence of the holy angels and before the presence of the Lamb. And the smoke of their torments will rise for ever and ever (Rev. XIV, 9).

It is a sign of the most monstrous and wretched madness, and of certain perdition, for a man called by the Christian name and occupying an episcopal office to despise such a sign and to liken it to an ass and to any cheap, worthless piece of wood—so that, as though by flattering and indiscriminate praise he might earn Christ’s grace, he blasphemes and despises Christ’s cross, as if its praise and commemoration brought disgrace and insulting shame upon himself. But whoever thinks this finds it more displeasing than pleasing, and inflicts injury rather than honor.

Therefore Gregory says:

> But the minds of unbelievers suffered grave scandal at him when, after so many miracles, they saw him dying.

Paul likewise says:

> We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews a scandal, but to the Gentiles foolishness.

It seemed foolish to human beings that the author of life should die for human beings; and from the very thing that ought rather to have caused him greater honor, man took scandal. For the Lord ought to have been honored by human beings with greater dignity in proportion as he had accepted unworthy things for human beings.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “Blessed is the one who is not scandalized in me,” unless by an open declaration he signifies the abasement of his death and his humility? Hence Augustine, in his exposition of the Gospel according to John:

> It was necessary that he should be despised; for if he had not been despised, he would not have been crucified; and if he had not been crucified, he would not have poured out the blood by which he redeemed us. In order to give the price for us, he was crucified; in order to be crucified, he was despised; in order to be despised, he appeared in humility.

Hence the Apostle, in the Epistle to the Philippians:

> He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.

Hence Augustine, in book 78 of the *Questions*:

> He therefore permitted himself to be crucified, so that his passion might benefit us, so that, going forth from here with his sign, we might by no means be held by the second death. For death fears even the servants of him by whom it was conquered.

With this triumphant standard, renowned Sobriety, the warrior, recalled the noble band of Virtue, which was withdrawing and preparing to retreat from the battle line, to the conflict; and she easily and successfully gained victory over the enemy, Luxury, the deceiver of many. Hence Prudentius, speaking figuratively in the book entitled *Psychomachia*, says:

> The gravest outrage was lamented by mighty Virtue,  
> Sobriety, when her allies withdrew from the right wing,  
> And her unconquered hand, once free from slaughter,  
> Was on the point of perishing. The lofty standard of the cross,  
> Which the good commander had borne before the first ranks,  
> She fixes firmly with its spear planted in the ground,  
> And restores the light wing with biting words,  
> Spurring their courage now with reproaches, now with mingled prayers.

The same author shortly afterward:

> “Here I am, Sobriety. If you are ready to unite,  
> I open the way for all the virtues, so that destructive  
> Luxury, surrounded by a great host of attendants,  
> May pay the penalty with her legion beneath Christ’s judgment.”

Having spoken thus, she presents the Lord’s cross to the fiery horses, advancing the venerable wood against their very bridles. When the fierce creatures saw it, shining with raised horns and gleaming upon the highest part of the forehead, they turned and scattered in blind terror, plunging headlong into the precipitous places. The charioteer is carried backward, thrown onto her back, with the reins drawn in vain, and her dripping hair soiled with dust. Then the whirling of the wheels entangles her and excuses her mistress; for she slips forward beneath the axle and, with the torn brake, delays the chariot.

Concerning this most glorious and exalted sign of the venerable and worshipful cross, together with the most revered relics of the saints, Paulinus writes to Severus:

> Brother Victor, amid the accounts of your other works and vows, reported to us that you desired a blessing from the sacred relics of the saints for the basilica which you have now built at Primoliacum, larger than the former one, so that your domestic church may be adorned with it, as is worthy of your faith and grace. The Lord is witness that, if we had possessed even a little sacred ash beyond what will be necessary for the basilica which is soon to be completed and dedicated in the Lord’s name, we would have sent it to your fellowship. But since we did not have an abundance of this gift, and he said that he had great hope of obtaining such grace from holy Silvia, who had promised him relics of many martyrs from the East, we found that we could fittingly send you, both for the sanctification of the basilica and for increasing the blessing of the saints’ ashes, a portion—a tiny fragment of the wood of the divine cross, which blessed Melania brought to us at Jerusalem as a gift from the holy bishop John there.
>
> Receive, therefore, a great gift in something small, and in a splinter scarcely larger than an atom take a brief piece of wood as a defense for the present and a pledge of eternal salvation. Let your faith not be cramped by the smallness perceived by bodily eyes, but let the inward gaze see in this little thing the whole power of the cross. When you think that you see that wood on which our salvation—and the Lord of majesty—hung while the world trembled, rejoice with trembling. Let us remember also the rocks split open at the sight of this cross, and at least in emulation of the stones let us split our hearts with godly fear. Let us also consider the veil of the Temple, torn by the same mystery of the cross, and understand that the veil was torn for this purpose: so that, when we hear the voice of the Lord and the mystery of immense devotion, we may not harden our hearts, but may be separated from carnal things and tear apart the veil of unbelief, so that with the face of our heart unveiled we may see the mysteries of the Lord’s saving gifts.
>
> We do not write this to you so that you may imitate the arrangement by which we enclosed so great a blessing in a little golden tube. Rather, by such an adornment we have imitated your faith, so that we might send you an image of it in the form of gold, because we know that, like gold tested by fire, you have within you the kingdom of God—that is, faith in the cross, by which the kingdom of heaven is seized.

The same author shortly afterward:

> But in the history of the cross receive a great and truly divine miracle. When that venerable queen came to Jerusalem, she carefully and devoutly examined that place and all its divine and remarkable objects, eagerly desiring to absorb with her eyes the faith that she had received through pious ears and writings; and she began with the utmost diligence to seek the Lord’s cross.

Again, later:

> When three crosses had been found together, standing as they had once stood, fixed to the Lord and to the thieves, the joy at their discovery began to be confused by anxious doubt, through the justified fear of the devout: lest they should perhaps choose the thieves’ gallows in place of the Lord’s cross, or reject and dishonor the saving wood as though it were the thieves’ stake. The Lord looked upon the faithful concerns of those who were devoutly troubled and, especially to her who was the leader of such pious solicitude, infused the light of counsel, so that she ordered that someone recently dead be sought and brought in.
>
> There was no delay; the command was carried out. The corpse was brought in, laid down, and one of the crosses was brought near to the body lying there. But death disdained those pieces of wood. At last the Lord’s cross brought forth resurrection: at the touch of the saving wood, death fleeing, the corpse was shaken, and the body stood upright. While the living trembled, the dead man stood; and, freed at once from his funeral bonds, like Lazarus formerly, he walked back alive among the spectators.
>
> Thus the Lord’s cross, hidden for so many ages and concealed by the Jews at the time of the Passion, was not revealed to the Gentiles either, when they were indisputably digging the ground for the construction of the pagan temple. Was it not hidden by the divine hand so that it might now be found when sought religiously, as was fitting for Christ’s cross? Christ’s cross was found and proved by the evidence of resurrection; and soon afterward, with fitting splendor, a basilica was consecrated and built at the place of the Passion. Gleaming with gilded ceilings and rich in golden altars, it preserves the cross, placed in a hidden shrine.
>
> Each year, when the Lord’s Passover is celebrated, the bishop of that city himself brings it forth for the people to venerate, leading the worshipers. Apart from this day, on which the mystery of the cross itself is celebrated, it—the cause of the sacraments—is not brought forth as a kind of insignia of the sacred solemnity, unless exceptionally the most devout visitors request it, those who have come there solely for the sake of pilgrimage, so that its unveiling may be granted to them as the reward of their distant journey. They say that this can be obtained only through the bishop’s favor; and by his gift these small fragments of the same cross are given, to provide great grace of faith and blessing.

This cross, although possessing living power in insensible matter, has from that time lent its wood almost daily to the countless petitions of human beings, without suffering loss and remaining seemingly untouched, being divided daily among those who receive portions while remaining whole for all who venerate it. It has certainly drawn this imperishable power and indestructible solidity from the flesh whose blood it drank—the flesh that, although it suffered death, did not see corruption.

The same Paulinus:

> Hence the inscription indicates that it has been placed beneath the altar of the Holy of Holies:
>
> Here are devotion, here nourishing faith, here the glory of Christ;  
> Here is the cross joined to its martyrs.  
> For a great pledge of the cross is a short splinter of its wood,  
> And the whole power of the cross is in a tiny fragment.  
> This supreme gift, brought from Jerusalem’s city,  
> Was conveyed to Nola by Melania’s holy gift.
>
> The holy altars conceal a twofold honor before God,  
> Joining apostolic ashes with the cross.  
> How well the bones of the devout are joined to the wood of the cross,  
> So that those killed for the cross may have rest in the cross.

The same author, concerning the Lord’s sign painted above the entrance in the form indicated by these verses:

> See the cross crowned above the courts of Christ the Lord,  
> Standing and promising lofty rewards for arduous labor.  
> Take up the cross, whoever wishes to win the crown.

Likewise, on the right and left, these epigrams are written above crosses painted in red pigment:

> The cross is encircled by the lofty crown of the flower-bearing orb,  
> And, stained with the Lord’s shed blood, it glows red.  
> The doves that sit above the heavenly sign  
> Proclaim to the simple that the kingdoms are open to them.

Again:

> By this cross put us to death to the world, and the world to us,  
> Giving life to the soul through the death of sin.  
> You will also perfect us, Christ, as doves pleasing to you,  
> If your portion flourishes in pure hearts.

Above the central arch are these verses:

> As Jesus, our peace, dissolved the middle wall of the enclosure  
> And, destroying division by the cross, made the two one,  
> So, when the division of the old roof has been destroyed,  
> We see the summits of the gates joined by a covenant.  
> The shining basin, flowing with sacred water for the servants,  
> Washes the hands of those entering with its stream.
>
> The twofold people worship Christ in Felix’s basilica,  
> Which Paul the priest governs with apostolic speech.

The same author, in book VIII, concerning the power of the holy cross:

> The sign and confession of the unconquered cross fortify us,  
> And, armed with God, we seek no weapons for the body;  
> Although we may seem unarmed in our limbs,  
> We nevertheless carry weapons with which, even in serene peace,  
> We contend in spirit against bodiless enemies.

Again, in book X:

> We therefore run, relying only on faith and supported by humble prayer,  
> To the neighboring threshold of my Felix; and from there  
> With equal vows we hasten to the adjoining basilica,  
> And ask healing from the power of the apostolic ashes,  
> Bending our faces beneath the altars placed there.
>
> Returning home, I bring a small but great means of salvation,  
> A piece of wood taken from the fragment of the eternal cross.  
> I bring it forth and hold it in my hand, presenting it from afar  
> Against the threatening flames, as though holding a shield  
> Before my breast, with which I might cover myself  
> And repel the enemy, striking him with the joined boss.
>
> Believe me—and do not thank me, but give back  
> Thanks to Christ and offer fitting praises to the Almighty.  
> For our salvation rests upon Christ’s cross and name.  
> From that source our faith, resting upon this cross in danger,  
> Has profited, and the flame recognized our salvation.  
> It was not my voice or right hand that terrified the fire,  
> But the power of the cross; and in the very place  
> From which it had risen, it forced the flame, bounded by the prescribed limit,  
> To settle down and be extinguished with dying roar,  
> And forced the storm, rising from ash, to return to ash.
>
> How great is the power of the cross, that nature itself yields!  
> Fire, devouring all wood, is burned by the wood of the cross.  
> Many hands then sprinkled that fire with water from numerous vessels,  
> Seeking to overcome it with abundant streams.  
> But although they sought to match the flames with torrents drawn from exhausted springs,  
> The fire, with greater force, overcame all the water  
> As the weary pourers scattered it; we extinguished the fire with wood.  
> What water could not overcome, a short splinter defeated in the flame.

The same author, in his letters to Severus, concerning little cloaks:

> May your prayers intervene, so that the needle of the Lord’s cross, threaded with the saving word, may mend my soul, torn apart by much corruption and rashly entangled with the thorns of my senses. For I consider faith and the word of Christ’s cross to be the needle by which the fabric of our life is renewed and our death is pierced. Through the intervention of that mediator, we ourselves are attached to God.

The same author, concluding his eleventh poem with praise of the holy cross:

> Now to you, venerable cross of God, I turn my words,  
> And, having spoken my thanks, I shall conclude with your praise.  
> O great cross, compassion of God; cross, glory of heaven;  
> Cross, eternal salvation of humankind; cross, terror to the wicked  
> And strength to the just, light to the faithful—O cross,  
> You granted God to serve salvation on earth in the flesh,  
> And granted humankind to reign in heaven in God.  
> Through you the light of truth was revealed; impious night fled.  
> You destroyed the temples, torn down for believers;  
> To the nations you are the bond of human peace,  
> Reconciling humankind through the covenants of Christ.  
> You became the ladder of humanity, by which it can be carried into heaven.  
> Be ever a pillar to the devout, and an anchor to us,  
> So that our household may stand well and our fleet proceed safely,  
> Fixed in the cross through faith, or having gained a crown from the cross.

And there are very many other passages contained most abundantly in the Scriptures concerning the praises and proclamations of the powers of this divine sign. Since it would be tedious to run through them and impossible to include them all, let us for now bring this section to a close, so that immediately, with the aid and intercession of the glorious prince of the apostles, on whose behalf we now resolve to contend, we may come to the third question.

For that shameless slanderer argued in his letter chiefly on three matters: first, the breaking and casting away of images; second, that the cross should no longer be honored more than any ass or thorny bush; and finally—that is, third—that the memorials of the saints, and especially the church of Saint Peter, should not be visited for the purpose of prayer. He says that this labor is vain and useless, without any benefit, and calls those who undertake it blind, senseless, and foolish.

For he asserts that relics—that is, the bones of human beings, however holy—are no more worthy of reverence than the bones of animals, or, more truly, than wood, stones, or any other kind of earth. Eunomius was the first author of this heresy. Then came Vigilantius, his neighbor and kindred in this matter, born among the people called the Convenae, whom the consul Pompey, after conquering Spain, removed from their mountain strongholds in the Pyrenees, where they practiced brigandage, and gathered into one place. From this they gave their name to the city of the Convenae.

Against this heresy Saint Jerome wrote, and he fully overcame and confuted it by the authority of orthodox holy Scripture. But that man’s abhorrence of visiting the basilicas of all the saints, and especially Saint Peter’s, for the purpose of prayer—although a larger crowd seeks that church than the others, because of the eminence of the apostles and the countless martyrs resting there—arises, as I think, from the goads of envy and greed. For many votive gifts flow there.

If they were brought to the church of Turin in such abundance, I am certain that he would have labored no less to favor and praise this practice than he now labors to blaspheme and discourage it. He would compose books with no less zeal to persuade everyone to honor the relics of the saints of Turin and commend themselves to their intercessions than he now heaps up arguments against the apostles and brings them forth in perverse opposition.

Therefore, infected with this most loathsome envy, he bursts out saying:

> This error arose from the fact that an ignorant class of people, not understanding the Lord’s words to Peter—“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven,” and the rest (Matt. XVI, 18)—adopted the custom of visiting Rome, as though one could obtain greater benefit there than elsewhere, although Peter knows nothing of it and can neither come to their aid nor help them.
>
> And because the Lord did not say to Peter, “Whatever you loose in heaven will be loosed on earth, and whatever you bind in heaven will be bound upon earth,” Peter, having departed from earth to heaven, left behind that ministry which had been granted to him as long as he lived on earth; and it was handed down to those who succeeded him.

But this invented objection is wholly perverse and wholly empty. For everything in it is presented contrary to the truth: as though the footstool of the feet of the Judge of judges ought to have been his judicial seat, and the proper dwelling of earthborn human beings ought to be considered heaven; as though those who exercise judicial authority there should bind the guilty and release the corrected, while the Lord, sitting lower down as if on earth, should confirm this by giving assent and pardon.

But that this is neither so nor acceptable to all who think and understand rightly is evident. Rather, by these words he declares and confirms that this power of loosing, binding, and interceding for others belongs to Peter himself and to those of his rank only so long as they are pilgrims in this mortal body. Consequently, it must be understood that this ministry was granted to the bishops of the Church only so long as they themselves are pilgrims in this mortal body. When they have paid the debt of death, others succeed them in their place, and they obtain the same judicial authority, as it is written:

> In place of your fathers sons are born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth (Ps. XLIV, 17).

It would be as though any pilgrims—wretched and utterly despised little paupers—ought to obtain and gain more from the emperor than his most glorious princes and most honored elders. For according to this slanderer, the apostles, as though far away and detained because they are dead, are unable to know, hear, or intervene for those seeking their memorials. Yet, on the contrary, we read in the Gospel:

> The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob is not the God of the dead, but of the living (Mark XII, 27).

Of them it is said:

> They follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. XIV, 4).

Hence Jerome says:

> If the Lamb is everywhere, then those who are with the Lamb must also be believed to be everywhere. And if the devil and demons roam throughout the whole world and are present everywhere with extraordinary speed, are the martyrs, after the shedding of their blood, covered by some confinement, shut in, and unable to leave it?

He adds this also in his own letter, saying:

> Hear this also, you senseless among the people, and become wise at last, you fools, who go to Rome seeking the intercession of an apostle. According to the opinion of their master and kinsman Vigilantius, as Jerome says, while we live we might pray for one another. But after we have died, no one’s prayer should be heard on behalf of another—especially since the martyrs, when they beseeched vengeance for their blood, were unable to obtain it.
>
> If the apostles and martyrs, while still in the body, can pray for others, when they ought still to be concerned for themselves, how much more after crowns, victories, and triumphs? One man, Moses, obtained forgiveness from God for six hundred thousand armed men; and Stephen, the imitator of his Lord and the first martyr in Christ, prayed for forgiveness for his persecutors. After they have begun to be with Christ, will they have less power? The Apostle Paul says that two hundred and seventy-six souls were granted to him in the ship; and after he has been released and begun to be with Christ, will he then close his mouth in prayer and be unable to utter a word for those throughout the whole world who believed in his Gospel?

But he fawningly flatters and curries favor with Saint Augustine, preferring him above all others with extraordinary praise, as though he were a supporter of his own folly. Although he is ignorant of all the liberal arts, he most shamelessly attempts to use Augustine’s dialectic by himself, without any teacher, and most recklessly twists it toward what he has chosen to assert.

Thus, by the following example, which he seized from book VIII of *On the Trinity* with a perverse understanding, he tried to establish that the memorials of the saints should not be sought for the sake of prayer and that their relics ought to be despised and hated. He says:

> Hear this also, you senseless among the people, and become wise at last, you fools, who go to Rome seeking the intercession of an apostle. Hear what the same most blessed Augustine, so often mentioned, says against you. For in book VIII of *On the Trinity*, among other things, he says:
>
> “Return with me, then, and let us consider why we love the apostle. Is it perhaps because of the human form which we know very well, since we believe that he was a human being? Certainly not; otherwise there is now no one for us to love, since that man no longer exists—for his soul has been separated from his body. But we believe that what we love in him is still alive.”

He did not understand in what sense Augustine said that the apostle was not to be loved because of his human appearance, nor because he had once been a human being. No one should love a human being because of beauty, or because of the affection of bodily kinship, or because of the desire of the will, or for any other reason, except solely for the sake of God. In and for God, the whole human being—who consists of two substances, soul and body—is to be loved in the manner and measure in which it is fitting to love both.

Hence the same Augustine, in book I of *On Christian Doctrine*:

> But it is asked whether a human being should be loved by another human being for his own sake or for the sake of something else. If for his own sake, we enjoy him; if for the sake of something else, we use him. It seems to me that he should be loved for the sake of something else. For what is to be loved for its own sake is where blessed life is established; and although we do not yet possess it, its hope consoles us in this present time. But cursed is the one who places his hope in a human being.
>
> Nor should anyone enjoy even himself, if he observes the matter clearly; for he should not love himself for his own sake, but for the sake of him whom he ought to enjoy. A human being is then at his best when his whole life proceeds toward unchangeable life and he clings to it with his entire affection.
>
> Therefore, if you ought not to love yourself for your own sake, but for the sake of him in whom the most righteous end of your love lies, a human being should not be angry if you love him also for God’s sake. For this is the divinely established rule of love: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” but God “with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind,” so that you may direct all your thoughts, your whole life, and your entire understanding toward him, from whom you possess the very things you offer.
>
> Whoever therefore rightly loves his neighbor ought to act toward him in such a way that he too may love God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind. For, loving him as himself, he refers the whole love of himself and of the other person to that love of God which does not allow any stream to be diverted away from it and diminish it by being channeled elsewhere.
>
> Not everything that is to be used is to be loved; only those things are to be loved which either, through some fellowship with us, are referred together with us to God, as a human being or an angel; or which, when referred to us, need God’s benefit through us, as the body does. For the martyrs certainly did not love the crime of those who persecuted them, although they used it to win God’s favor.

The same author, in the same book I:

> Since there are four things to be loved—one that is above us, another that is ourselves, a third that is beside us, and a fourth that is beneath us—no commandments needed to be given concerning the second and the fourth. For however far a human being falls away from the truth, love of self and love of one’s body remain with him.

And shortly afterward:

> No one therefore hates himself. On this point there has been no controversy with any sect. Nor does anyone hate his own body; for what the Apostle says is true: “No one has ever hated his own flesh.” And when some say that they would prefer to be without a body, they are altogether mistaken. For they do not hate their body, but its corruptions and its burden.
>
> They do not therefore wish to have no body, but an incorruptible and extremely agile body. Yet they think that, if a body were such, it would not be a body, because they think that the soul is something of that kind.
>
> As for those who appear to pursue their bodies through self-restraint and labors, those who do so rightly do not act in order to have no body, but to have one subjected and ready for necessary works. For they seek to extinguish, through a certain laborious affliction of the body, the lusts that misuse the body—that is, the habits by which the soul is inclined toward enjoying interior things.
>
> They do not kill themselves, and they take care of their health. But those who act perversely in this matter wage war, as though naturally, against their own body, their enemy. They are deceived by what they read: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another” (Gal. V, 17).
>
> This was said on account of the unruly carnal habit, against which the spirit desires—not in order to destroy the body, but so that, once its desire, that is, its evil habit, has been subdued, it may make the body subject to the spirit, as the natural order requires. For since this will occur after the resurrection, when the body, in complete rest, will live immortally in full submission to the spirit, this too must be practiced in the present life: the carnal habit must be changed for the better, so that it does not resist the spirit with disordered movements.
>
> Until this occurs, the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh—not because the spirit resists through hatred, but through authority, since it wants what it loves more to be subject to what is better; nor because the flesh resists through hatred, but through the bond of habit, which has grown old by the law of nature and has become established even through descent from our parents. The spirit therefore acts in subduing the flesh so that it may dissolve the quasi-contracts of evil habit, as it were, and so that the peace of a good habit may be established.

And below:

> “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” On these two commandments hang the whole Law and all the Prophets. The end of the commandment, therefore, is love, and it is twofold: of God and of one’s neighbor.
>
> If you understand “yourself” as the whole of you—that is, soul and body—and “your neighbor” as his soul and body, since a human being consists of soul and body, no kind of thing that ought to be loved has been omitted from these two commandments.
>
> Since the love of God comes first, and the measure of that love is prescribed, so that all other things flow into it, nothing seems to have been said about the love of yourself. But when it is said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” the love of yourself by yourself is also not omitted.
>
> He lives justly and holily who is an exact evaluator of things. He is the one who possesses an ordered love, so that he neither loves what ought not to be loved, nor fails to love what ought to be loved, nor loves more what ought to be loved less, nor loves equally what ought to be loved either less or more, nor loves less or more what ought to be loved equally.
>
> No sinner, insofar as he is a sinner, is to be loved; and every human being, insofar as he is a human being, is to be loved for God’s sake; but God is to be loved for his own sake. And if God is to be loved more than any human being, each person ought to love God more than himself.
>
> Another human being is also to be loved more than our body, because all these things are to be loved for God’s sake, and another human being can enjoy God together with us, whereas the body cannot, since the body lives through the soul, by which we enjoy God.
>
> All are to be loved equally. But since you cannot benefit everyone, you should take particular care of those who, because of the circumstances of place and time or any other opportunities, are more closely joined to you, as though by lot.

And after other matters:

“Moreover, of all those who can enjoy God with us, we love some whom we help; some by whom we are helped; some whose assistance we both need and whose needs we relieve; and some to whom we contribute no advantage ourselves, nor expect any advantage to be conferred upon us by them. Yet we ought to wish that all may love God with us. And everything by which we either help them or are helped by them must be referred to that one end.”

But if Augustine had judged that the memorials of the saints ought not to be sought for the sake of prayer, evidently on the grounds that supplicants received no more abundant or immediate assistance from God there through their merits, it seems strange that so great and distinguished an author, so learned and truthful in his other works, should not have hesitated to teach and affirm things wholly contrary to one another. For he says in his book *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, addressed to Bishop Paulinus:

“There are limits belonging to human affairs, and there are signs belonging to divine powers. Some things happen naturally, others miraculously; although God is present in nature, and nature is not absent from miracles. We should not therefore suppose that the dead can be present at will in the affairs of the living merely because martyrs are present to certain sick persons when they are healed or helped. Rather, we should understand that martyrs are present to the affairs of the living through divine power, since by their own nature the dead cannot be present to the affairs of the living.

“Although this question exceeds the powers of my understanding—namely, how martyrs assist those whom it is certain are helped through them: whether they themselves are present in person at the same time in so many different places, separated from one another by such great distances, whether at the places where their memorials are located or wherever they are perceived to be present apart from their memorials; or whether, while they themselves are in a place suited to their merits, removed from all human intercourse, nevertheless almighty God, who is present everywhere, neither confined among us nor remote from us, hears the martyrs’ prayers, which are spread everywhere through angelic ministries, and provides human beings with these consolations, judging that they ought to be provided amid the misery of this life; and whether, by a wondrous and ineffable power and goodness, he commends the merits of his martyrs wherever, whenever, and however he wishes—especially through their memorials, because he knows that this is useful to us for building up the faith of Christ, for whose confession they suffered—I cannot attain to this matter, since it is too lofty for me, nor investigate it, since it is too hidden.

“And therefore I do not dare to determine which of these two alternatives is correct—or whether perhaps both are correct: whether these things sometimes occur through the martyrs’ own presence, and sometimes through angels who assume the person of the martyrs. I would rather inquire of those who know such things. For it is not the case that no one knows these matters, nor that anyone who seems to himself to know them does not know them. The gifts of God are given in different ways to different people, according to the Apostle, who says that the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for the common good.”

When this grace revealed it, Jerome defined the matter more confidently, explaining that saying of the Apocalypse, namely: “They follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Apoc. XIV, 4). “If the Lamb is everywhere, then those who are with the Lamb must also be believed to be everywhere.”

How great, then, and almost innumerable are the signs of miracles, and how inexhaustible the remedies for bodies and souls, that occur daily at the memorials of the martyrs, while God’s hand works through their prayers, is sufficiently evident from the few examples that Saint Augustine reports in Book XXII of *The City of God*. Since Claudius judges that his own sect can be supported by Augustine’s authority, his words are as follows:

“There is among us a man of tribunician rank, Hesperius. He has an estate in the territory of Fussala called Zubeli. When he discovered that, because of an affliction affecting his animals and servants, his house was suffering the harmful violence of evil spirits, he received from a friend some holy earth brought from Jerusalem, where Christ was buried and rose again on the third day. He hung it in his bedroom, so that he himself might not suffer any harm. From that time his house was cleansed of that infestation.

“He was considering what should be done with the earth, since he did not wish to keep it longer in his bedroom out of reverence. It happened by chance that I and my colleague, Maximinus, then bishop of the Church of Sinicensis, were nearby. He asked us to come, and we came. After he had told us everything, he also asked that it be buried somewhere and that a place of prayer be established there, where Christians might gather to celebrate the things of God. We did not object, and it was done.

“There was there a young peasant who was paralyzed. When he heard this, he asked his parents to carry him without delay to that holy place. When he had been brought there, he prayed, and immediately departed on his own feet.

“There is a village called Victoriana, less than thirty miles from Hippo Regius, where there is a memorial of the Milanese martyrs Protasius and Gervasius. A certain young man was carried there after, while washing a horse at midday during the summer in a deep part of the river, he was attacked by a demon. He lay there, either close to death or very like a dead man.

“Toward evening the lady of the estate entered the place with her servants and certain consecrated women, according to custom, for the hymns and prayers. They began to sing hymns. At the sound of their voices he was as if struck and shaken. With a terrible growl he seized the altar and, unable or unwilling to move it, held it as though he had been tied or fastened to it. With great wailing he begged for mercy and confessed where, when, and how he had attacked the young man.

“At last, declaring that he was going to leave, he named each of the young man’s limbs and threatened, as he departed, to cut them off. While saying these things, he left the man. But the man’s eye had fallen onto his cheek and hung from within by a slender vein, as if from its root. The whole middle part of the eye, which had been black, had become white.

“When those present saw this—for others too had hurried there, summoned by his cries, and all had prostrated themselves in prayer for him—although they rejoiced that he was standing in his right mind, they were again saddened by the condition of his eye and said that a physician should be sought.

“Then the husband of his sister, who had brought him there, said: ‘God is powerful. He who drove out the demon can, through the prayers of the saints, restore his sight.’ Then, as best he could, he replaced the fallen and hanging eye in its proper place and bound it there, thinking that it should not be unbound until seven days had passed. When he did so, he found it perfectly sound.

“There was an old man named Florentius, one of our people at Hippo, a religious and poor man. He supported himself by tailoring. He had lost his cloak and had no means to buy another. In a loud voice he prayed to the Twenty Martyrs, whose memorial is especially celebrated among us, asking that he might be clothed.

“Some young men who happened to be present heard him. They mocked him and followed him as he departed, taunting him. But he walked on silently and saw a large fish, still beating, cast up on the shore. With their assistance and encouragement he seized it and gave it to a certain cook named Cattusus, a good Christian, for the preparation of a meal, explaining what had happened.

“Florentius sold it for three hundred folles, intending to buy wool from the proceeds so that his wife might make him something to wear. But when the cook cut open the fish, he found a gold ring in its stomach. Immediately moved by compassion and struck with reverence, he returned it to the man, saying: ‘See how the Twenty Martyrs have clothed you.’

“Eucharius, a presbyter from Spain who lived at Calama, suffered from the longstanding disease of a calculus. Through the memorial of the martyr mentioned above, which Bishop Possidius had brought there, he was healed.

“Later, when another illness had grown severe, that same man lay dead in such a condition that his thumbs were already being tied. Through the assistance of the aforementioned martyr, when the presbyter’s tunic had been brought back from his memorial and laid upon his prostrate body, he was restored to life.

“There was there a man of first rank in his order, named Martialis, already advanced in age and greatly opposed to the Christian religion. He had a faithful daughter and a son-in-law who had been baptized that same year. When they urged him, with many and great tears, to become a Christian while he was sick, he absolutely refused and drove them away from him in angry indignation.

“His son-in-law decided to go to the memorial of Saint Stephen and pray there for him as earnestly as possible, asking God to grant him belief in Christ. He did so with great groaning and weeping, and with a sincere and ardent devotion of heart. Then, as he departed, he took from the altar some flowers that happened to be there and, since it was already night, placed them near the sick man’s head.

“Then they went to sleep. And behold, before dawn the sick man began to cry out that they should run for the bishop, who happened at that time to be with me at Hippo. When they told him that the bishop was absent, he asked that presbyters be brought. They came, and he declared that he believed. Everyone was amazed and rejoiced, and he was baptized.

“From that time, as long as he lived, he constantly had in his mouth the words: ‘Christ, receive my spirit’ (Acts VII, 19). He did not know that these had been the last words of blessed Stephen when he was stoned by the Jews; yet they were also the last words of this man, for he too died not long afterward.

“Audurus is the name of the estate where the memorial church of the martyr Stephen is located. A small boy was playing in the courtyard when oxen that were drawing a wagon veered off course and crushed him beneath a wheel. He immediately gasped his last breath. His mother seized him and placed him at the same memorial. He not only came back to life but also appeared unharmed.

“A consecrated woman on a neighboring estate called Capaliana was suffering from an illness and had been given up for dead. A tunic from the same memorial was brought to her; before it could be taken back, she died. Her parents nevertheless covered her corpse with the tunic, and when she recovered her spirit she was restored alive and well.

“At Hippo, a certain Syrian named Bassus was praying at the memorial of the same martyr for his sick and endangered daughter, and he had brought her garment with him. Then children came running from the house to announce that she had died. But while he was praying, his friends received them and prevented them from speaking, lest he should mourn publicly.

“When he returned home, already filled with the wailing of his household, and threw over his daughter the garment he had brought back, she was restored to life.

“Likewise, among us, the son of a certain tax collector named Irenaeus died of illness. While the lifeless body lay there and the mourners and lamenters were preparing the funeral, one of his friends, amid the words of the others who were offering consolation, suggested that the body be anointed with oil from the same martyr. This was done, and he revived.

“Again, among us, a man of tribunician rank named Eleusinus placed his little son, who had been rendered lifeless by illness, upon the memorial of the martyrs located on his suburban estate. After he had poured out many tears in prayer there, he lifted him up alive.

“What am I to do? The promise imposed by this work must be fulfilled, so that I cannot mention here everything I know. Without doubt, many of our people, when they read these things, will regret that I have omitted so many events which they themselves know as well as I do. I now ask them to forgive me and to consider how laborious it would be to do what the necessity of the work undertaken here compels me not to do.

“For if I wished to write only the miracles of healings, leaving other matters aside, that were performed through this martyr—namely, the most glorious Stephen—in the colony of Calama and in our own city, many books would have to be completed. Yet even then they could not all be collected, but only those about which written accounts had been submitted to be read before the people.

“We wanted this to be done because we saw that signs of divine power, like those of ancient times, were occurring frequently even in our own day, and that they ought not to perish from the knowledge of many. It is not yet two years since this memorial began to exist at Hippo Regius. Although many accounts of miraculous events had not been submitted—as we know with certainty—and although those that had been submitted had reached almost seventy when I wrote this, at Calama, where the memorial itself had begun earlier and accounts were submitted more frequently, their number surpasses this by an incomparable multitude.

“At Uzalis also, a colony near Utica, we have learned that many distinguished miracles were performed through the same martyr. His memorial was established there by Bishop Evodius long before it was established among us. There was no custom there—or rather, there had not been one—of submitting written accounts, although perhaps it has now begun.

“For when we were recently there, a married woman named Petronia was miraculously healed there of a severe and prolonged illness, in which every medical remedy had failed. At the urging of the bishop of that place, we encouraged her to submit an account to be read before the people, and she obeyed most willingly. In it she also included something that I cannot omit here, although I am compelled to hasten toward the matters that press upon this work.

“She said that a certain Jew had persuaded her to insert a ring into a belt made of hair, so that it could be worn beneath every garment and gird the naked body. Beneath the gemstone the ring contained a stone found in the kidneys of an ox. Bound with this as though it were a remedy, she came to the thresholds of the holy martyrs.

“But after setting out from Carthage, when she had remained at her estate near the boundary of the river Bagradas, she arose to continue her journey and saw the ring lying at her feet. Astonished, she tested the hair belt to which it had been fastened. When she found that it was still held by its very strong knots exactly as before, she suspected that the ring had broken loose and leaped away. When she also found that the ring itself was completely intact, she took it as a kind of pledge of the salvation to come, granted to her through so great a miracle. She then loosened the fastening and threw it, together with the ring, into the river.

“Let those who do not believe that the Lord Jesus was born through the intact virginity of his mother and entered to his disciples when the doors were shut refuse to believe this too. But let them investigate this fact, and, if they find it true, let them believe those other things as well.

“She is a woman of great distinction, nobly born and nobly married, living at Carthage—a large city and a prominent person, so that those who seek the truth cannot conceal the matter. The martyr himself, through whose intercession she was healed, believed in the Son of the Virgin who remained a virgin; he believed in him who entered to his disciples when the doors were shut; finally, and this is why all these things are being recounted by us, he believed in him who ascended into heaven in the flesh in which he had risen. Therefore such things occur through him, because he laid down his life for this faith.

“Many miracles, then, are also occurring now, with the same God performing them through whomever he wishes and in whatever manner he wishes.

“One such miracle occurred among us. It was no greater than those I have mentioned, but it was so clear and remarkable that I think there is no inhabitant of Hippo who either did not see it or learn of it, and no one who could in any way forget it.

“Ten siblings—seven males and three females—of respectable standing among their fellow citizens at Caesarea in Cappadocia, left without their father through his death and recently cursed by their mother, who had suffered their injury most bitterly, were divinely punished with such a penalty that all were horribly shaken by trembling limbs. Unable to endure the gaze of their fellow citizens in this most disgraceful condition, they wandered almost throughout the whole Roman world, each going wherever he thought fit.

“Two of them, a brother and sister named Paul and Palladia, came to us. Their misery had already made them known in many other places. They arrived about fifteen days before Easter and attended the church daily, and in it the memorial of the most glorious Stephen, praying that God might now be appeased toward them and restore their former health.

“Both there and wherever they went, they drew the attention of the city upon themselves. Some who had seen them elsewhere and knew the cause of their trembling explained it to others as best they could.

“Then Easter arrived. On the morning of that Sunday, when a large crowd was already present, the young man was praying while holding the railings of the holy place where the martyr’s shrine was located. Suddenly he fell forward and lay there like someone asleep, though he was no longer trembling, as he had been accustomed to do even in sleep. Those present were astonished; some were afraid, and others grieved.

“When certain people wanted to lift him up, others prevented them and said that they ought rather to wait and see what would happen. And behold, he rose and was not trembling, because he had been healed. He stood unharmed, looking at those who were looking at him.

“Who among those who saw him could restrain himself from praising God? The church was filled everywhere with the voices of those shouting and rejoicing. People ran to me where I was sitting, already preparing to go out. One after another burst in, each later arrival announcing as something new what the previous person had already reported.

“While I rejoiced and gave thanks to God within myself, he too entered with many others, bent down to my knees, and rose for my kiss. We went out to the people. The church was full and resounded with cries of joy: ‘Thanks be to God! Praise be to God!’ Voices rang out from every side, and no one was silent.

“I greeted the people, and again they shouted the same words with even greater fervor. At last silence was made, and the appointed readings from the divine Scriptures were delivered. When the time came for my sermon, I said a few words suitable to the occasion and to the joy of that delightful moment.

“The man dined with us and carefully recounted to us the entire history of his brother and sister’s calamity. Accordingly, on the day after the sermon, I promised that his written account would be read to the people on the following day.

“When this was done on the third day after Easter Sunday, on the steps of the raised platform from which I was speaking, I had both siblings stand while their account was being read. The entire people, men and women alike, looked upon one standing without any disfiguring movement and the other trembling in all her limbs. Those who had not seen the young man saw in his sister what divine mercy had accomplished in him. They saw what they ought to rejoice over in him and what they ought to pray for on her behalf.

“When their account had been read, I ordered them to leave the people’s sight. I had begun to discuss the entire matter rather carefully when, as I was speaking, other voices of renewed rejoicing were heard from the memorial of the martyr. Those who had been listening to me turned toward it and began to run.

“For after she had descended from the steps on which she had been standing, the girl had gone to pray to the holy martyr. No sooner had she touched the railings than she collapsed in the same way, as if into sleep, and rose healed.

“When we therefore asked what had happened and from where the joyful commotion had arisen, they entered the basilica in which we were, bringing her with them, sound from the martyr’s shrine. Then so great a shout of astonishment arose from both sexes that the continuous sound, mingled with tears, seemed unable to end.

“She was led to the place where shortly before she had stood trembling. They rejoiced that she had become like her brother, from whom they had grieved to see her remain different. They rejoiced that, although their prayers for her had not yet been poured out, their prior intention had so quickly been heard. Voices rose in praise of God, without words, with such a volume that our ears could scarcely bear it.

“What was in the hearts of those who rejoiced except faith in Christ, for whom Stephen’s blood was shed?”

But when he says that Saint Peter and the other apostles were removed from the ministry of loosing and binding—that is, from judging in the Church—and that he and others equal to him succeeded to their place, as though they were more worthy and more effective substitutes for those who had grown weary or had been convicted of some falsehood, this is contrary to the truth. For the apostles never ceased to be judges of the holy Church, since the Lord had once entrusted this office to them in principle together with the whole Church, whether they judge through their bodily presence or through the teaching that they left to their successors in their place.

For what ruler of the Church could rightly judge or determine anything on his own, or by himself, without the authority of the Gospel, the apostles, or the canon from which that authority derives?

He attempts to append an example taken from the Psalms:

“Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. XLIV, 17).

This passage is rightly understood both of the apostles and of the various holy bishops who are their successors, just as the Apostle says: “Our fathers were under the cloud” (I Cor. VI, 10). And in the Psalm: “Your friends, O God, have been greatly honored; their principality has been greatly strengthened” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 17).

I would be mistaken if Augustine does not affirm that these things are so in his exposition of the Gospel according to John, where he says:

“This is what the Church does in the hope of blessedness amid this troubled life. The apostle Peter, because of the primacy of his apostleship, represented the Church in a figurative universality. In what properly belonged to him, he was by nature one man; by grace, one Christian; and by a still more abundant grace, one and the same man, the chief apostle.

“But when it was said to him, ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven’ (Matt. XVI, 19), this signified the whole Church, which in this world is shaken by various temptations, as by rains, rivers, and storms, yet does not fall because it has been founded upon the rock, from which Peter received his name. For the name Peter does not come from *petra*, ‘rock’; rather, Peter comes from *petra*, just as Christ is not named from Christian, but Christian from Christ.

“Therefore the Lord says, ‘Upon this rock I will build my Church’ (ibid. 18), because Peter had said, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God’ (ibid. 16). ‘Upon this rock,’ he says, ‘which you have confessed, I will build my Church.’ For Christ was the rock, and upon that foundation Peter himself also was built. No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.

“Therefore the Church, founded upon Christ, received from him the keys of the kingdom of heaven in Peter—that is, the power of binding and loosing sins. What the Church is by its proper reality in Christ, Peter is by signification in the rock. Through this signification, Christ is understood as the rock and Peter as the Church.

“This Church knows that two lives have been divinely proclaimed and commended to it. One is in faith, the other in sight; one in the time of pilgrimage, the other in the eternity of dwelling; one in labor, the other in rest; one on the way, the other in the homeland; one in the work of action, the other in the reward of contemplation.

“The former was signified by the apostle Peter, the latter by John. The whole of the former is lived here until the end of this age, and there it finds its end. The latter is postponed until after the end of this age, but in the age to come it has no end.

“Therefore it is said to one, ‘Follow me,’ while of the other: ‘Thus I wish him to remain until I come. What is that to you? You follow me’ (John XXI, 19, 22). For what is this, as far as I understand it, except: ‘You follow me by imitating me in enduring temporal evils; let him remain until I come to repay eternal goods’? It can be stated more plainly in this way: ‘Let perfected action follow me, formed according to the example of my passion; but let contemplative thought, begun but not yet perfected, remain until I come, to be perfected when I come.’

“Yet no one should separate these two distinguished apostles. In what Peter signified, they were both present; and in what John signifies, both were to be present. By signifying, the one followed and the other remained; but by believing, both endured the present evils of this misery. Both awaited the future goods of that blessedness.

“Nor did they alone do this. The entire holy Church, the bride of Christ, does the same: it is to be rescued from these temptations and preserved in that happiness.

“Therefore, just as the title, honor, dignity, and office of evangelist are not taken away from John, although Peter and the entire holy Church share them with him, so Peter does not lose the primacy of the Church or the power of loosing and binding in it, which the Lord entrusted to him in principle as the reward for his undoubted faith, even though John shares this ministry with him in the integrity of the Church, as has been said.”

Hence Augustine says:

“To all the saints who belong inseparably to the body of Christ, the first of the apostles, Peter, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven for the governance of this exceedingly stormy life, so that sins might be bound and loosed. And for all those same saints, John the evangelist reclined upon the breast of Christ, because of the most secret and tranquil repose of that life. For it is not he alone, but the whole Church, that binds and looses sins.

“Nor did he alone drink from the fountain of the Lord’s breast those sublime teachings concerning Christ’s divinity and concerning the Trinity and unity of the whole Godhead—the Word who in the beginning was God with God, and the other things that are to be contemplated face to face in that kingdom, but are now, until the Lord comes, seen in a mirror and in an enigma—and then pour them forth by preaching. Rather, the Lord himself spread the Gospel throughout the entire world for all his people to drink, according to each person’s capacity.”

This verse, “Instead of your fathers,” and what follows, must be read and understood carefully by bishops with humbled and submissive hearts. Indeed, they ought to consider themselves unworthy and less capable of such a great ministry, since spiritual and most excellent men refused to accept it, as though unequal to it, by avoiding and fleeing from it.
