Nor should they swell with pride or insult the holy apostles. Their opponent, adversary, and despiser, puffed up with the emptiest arrogance and presuming with excessive temerity, boasts vainly of such things. Isaiah threatens him and those like him, saying:

“Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. V, 21).

The Apostle likewise says:

“Do not be wise in your own eyes” (Rom. XII, 16).

Therefore Gregory, explaining that saying which the Lord addressed to his disciples after the resurrection—“Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John XX, 23)—invites us to consider to what a height of glory those disciples were led after being summoned to bear such great burdens of humility:

“Behold, they are made secure not only concerning themselves, but also receive the power of releasing and binding others. They receive the principality of heavenly judgment, so that in God’s place they may retain the sins of some and forgive those of others. It was fitting that God should raise them up in this way, since they had humbled themselves so greatly for God.

“Behold, those who fear God’s strict judgment become judges of souls; and those who feared being condemned themselves condemn or free others. The bishops in the Church now hold their place. Those who receive the rank of governance receive the authority to loose and bind.

“Great is the honor, but heavy the burden of this honor. For it is difficult when one who does not know how to govern his own life becomes the judge of another’s life. It often happens that a person holds the place of judgment while his life is entirely unsuited to the place of life. It also frequently happens that he condemns the innocent or releases others whom he himself has bound.

“Often, in loosing and binding those subject to him, he follows the movement of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Thus it comes about that he deprives himself of the very power of binding and loosing because he exercises it according to his own desires and not according to the conduct of those subject to him.”

He also proposes the example of the prophet Ezekiel to confirm that no one who is pleading, repenting, or laboring should place confidence in the merits or intercessions of the saints (Ezek. XIV, 14):

“Even Noah, Daniel, and Job will not deliver a son or daughter.”

Therefore this perversity cannot truly be defended or confirmed by the authority of sacred Scripture, although heretics adulterate the word of God in order to support their own depravity and attempt to force it into such a meaning.

The Prophet says that the impious and transgressors who persist in their crimes cannot in any way be freed from punishments through the intercessions of any others among the saints, without their own earnestness and labor.

Jerome says:

“Therefore neither will a martyr be able to free a transgressing son, nor will a mother of holy conduct give the rewards of chastity to an unchaste daughter. Conversely, the vices of parents will not harm their children, but the soul that sins shall itself die.

“Not only will the saints not free the impious who do not repent of their sins and iniquities, but God himself will not do so. Hence the Apostle says: ‘Do you not know that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works’ (Rom. II, 4–6).

“But we believe that those who repent and turn back, afflicting themselves with weeping and lamentation, redeeming their sins through almsgiving, bringing in presbyters, visiting the memorials of the saints, and devoting themselves with every diligence to satisfaction, can be freed by the Lord through his ineffable mercy and through these exercises.”

Claudius, therefore, that new and remarkable philosopher, unskilled in the liberal arts, directs all his ingenuity and the subtlety of his intellect toward tearing apart and lacerating the body of Christ, the Church. For this he continually struggles, presses forward, studies, and keeps watch.

The ancient teachers and spiritual philosophers, however, had this as their one and singular concern: to praise the apostles, to compose hymns and songs in honor of the martyrs with joyful understanding and sweet-sounding melody, to visit their places, and to commend themselves to their intercessions with the greatest reverence and devotion.

One of them was Bishop Paulinus, a man of the greatest learning and holiness, as many have testified concerning him. He published a noble book divided into fifteen poems in honor and praise of the holy martyr Felix. In it he discussed the many miracles and acts of power that, by divine clemency, were performed daily through Felix’s merits and intercessions at his tomb, especially on the anniversary of his feast. It could not easily be excerpted or culled by anyone, because everything in it is made of flowers, spices, roses, fragrant lilies, and honeyed sweetness.

His first poem begins in this manner:

Illustrious confessor Felix, in merits and in name,

Mind mighty in devotion, mind dwelling near the highest heaven,

No less experienced in power throughout all the earth,

You who, confessing the Lord Christ with an unfettered voice,

By despising cruel punishments deserved to escape them,

And, having been commanded, willingly gave your devoted soul

To Christ through every torment, surrendering your limbs,

You left your body empty for the savage executioners,

Carried without blood into the honor of a martyr in heaven.

O father, O lord, although we are unworthy servants, grant our request:

While at last we drag out this life in a fragile body,

May we be permitted to celebrate this day

At the desired dwelling and in the palace where you rest,

To offer devout vows before you,

And, rejoicing, to rejoice amid the crowds.

Let it now, I beg, be enough that we have endured this punishment

With deserved impiety, for so many years as we have lived without you,

Far from your seat—alas! although not far from you in mind.

Now attend to us, worn out by immense longing;

Now, even if late, remember and have mercy on your people.

Across the world, which the great expanse of sea

Separates from us, and hostile obstacles delay us,

Open easy roads. And if an envious enemy hinders

Those hastening toward you, drive away the barriers in our path,

Stronger against adversity, and speed your friends upon their journey.

Whether the road across the land pleases you, be a companion

To your people along a safe highway;

Or whether great confidence in you urges us

To travel across the long sea, run with us over gentle waves,

And send favorable winds from the stern to your servants,

So that, carried under Christ’s guidance,

We may soon, borne to the Campanian shores under Christ’s guidance, be swept in eager course to your heights,

And find a tranquil harbor at your threshold.

Let Vigilantius, that enemy of the cross of Christ and violator of sacred images, now hear that illustrious men, outstanding throughout the world in wisdom and holiness, praise everything that he condemns; that they confirm what he, in his unbelief, denies; and that they command the practice of everything that he forbids. In every respect he is unlike and opposed to the holy religion and wisdom of the orthodox.

For, as the Apostle says, “What participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has the faithful person with the unbeliever?” (I Cor. VI, 14–15).

Let him hear, I say, holy and wise men, while still living in the flesh, pray and earnestly and devoutly entreat the holy dead, departed from the body but living with Christ and reigning, that they may deign to intercede for them before the Lord.

Let him hear them praise, love, and venerate the holy cross of the Lord and the relics of the saints with fitting, faithful, and religious devotion.

For this reason we first set before him blessed Paulinus, endowed with holiness and wisdom, as a kind of most brilliant beacon and an impregnable tower. He discussed this subject at length in a most eloquent and fertile discourse, speaking as follows in the second poem of the holy martyr Felix:

The time has come to pour forth thanks to you with vows fulfilled.

O father, O lord, although we are unworthy servants, best of all,

At last we have obtained, in answer to prayer, leave to celebrate

Your feast within your thresholds.

Three five-year periods have passed since, in these solemn rites

I dedicated my vows and my heart to you before your presence.

From that time you have known what labors, by land and sea,

Have kept me far from your distant dwelling.

For I have always called upon you as near to me everywhere,

Amid the hardships of the road and the uncertainties of life.

And I entered the seas under your guidance, because concern for danger

Yielded to love of you; nor was I without you, for I felt your protection.

In the Lord Christ, I overcame the roughness of the sea.

Always safe because of you, both on land and on the waves.

The same, in the same work.

Behold, a variegated people marks out the roads with a many-colored throng:

Within one city we marvel at innumerable cities.

O Nola, happy in your Felix as bishop,

Illustrious in your holy citizen, secure in your heavenly patron;

After these things, Rome herself, having acquired a second title,

Which formerly was first only in empire and victorious arms,

Is now also first among the tombs of the apostles throughout the world.

[Col. 0511D] Be good, O Felix, to your people, and entreat the almighty Lord

That, when Christ’s favor has been won,

After the waves of the sea, and after the waves of the world have been crossed,

I may stand safely in your harbor, a tranquil station.

The same, in poem 3.

Ask, I pray, that this day may be serene for us in everlasting peace;

May I be permitted to rejoice in returning once more,

And here to render annual offerings, vows, and songs

At your festival, under the tranquil favor of appeased Christ.

This is our love, this our labor; receive these vows of your people

And commend them to God, so that, when our diligent service

Has been offered to you through a long age,

Then at last, with a hand that sends them forth, he may release

The peaceful children of pious labor;

And do not refuse to carry the souls of your people,

Placed before your eyes, in the Father’s bosom,

To the presence of the radiant Lord.

[Col. 0512A] The same, in poem 4.

Give me a word from your fountain; without you I cannot speak of you.

For the praise of your martyr is also your praise,

O Almighty, who make human beings prevail through divine power,

And, overcoming the strong through the weak, triumph over the flesh.

The same, in poem 6.

A long subject, then, remains for me; and for as long as life endures,

So long will there be words with which to recount the deeds of Felix,

If only my mouth possesses as much abundance

As the abundance of his works and merit that remains.

For from the time when this day first placed Felix

In a blessed end, giving his flesh to the earth and his soul to the stars,

Almost every day seems to be at work through

[Col. 0512B] God’s confessor, and Christ proves him alive without a body,

To show that greater power remains in the death of the righteous

Than the force of wickedness in life.

The same, in the same work.

After the bier containing the body to be buried had been placed in the tomb,

The people, gathered from every side in a dense assembly,

Surround the limbs with such a throng, vying with one another;

A devout struggle of loving people is carried on:

Each strives to press upon another and stand nearer to the relics,

And rejoices to touch the body with his hand.

Nor is it enough to have seen it once; they delight to linger continually,

To fix their eyes upon the exposed limbs,

And, wherever possible, to press kisses upon them;

The united people render due praise to Christ.

The same, in the same work.

When the arrangements had thus been settled, it was right to cover the pious corpse with a tomb;

The grace divinely implanted in the holy limbs

Could neither die nor be buried with the flesh.

Rather, once the bones had been laid down, a light shone forth,

Which has never ceased from that time to give signs

Of the powerful merit by its healing powers.

And throughout the whole age in which the world shall endure,

That same light will shine, a guardian through the ages

Of the holy ashes.

The same, in the same work.

Yet, however spacious, these heights are overcome by the crowds;

For, as faith increases, the grace of Christ overflows,

Which grants Felix to the peoples as a healer

To live. Even after the age of his body has passed,

He himself, holy, presides over his own bones;

And the bones of the holy body, not covered in the tomb

[Col. 0512D] by the dust of death,

But endowed with the secret seed of eternal life,

Breathe forth the life-giving fragrance of the victorious soul;

By it powerful healing is granted to those who entreat.

One may conjecture what power and glory will surround him when he rises,

When such glory already surrounds the buried,

And with what renewed splendor the bodies will shine

When so great a light exists in obscure ashes.

What will the crowns of such men be sufficient to bestow upon us wretched people,

Whose ashes themselves give benefits to the living?

The same, in the same work.

For you see what still remains for you to do; but [in me,

Who stand close by your threshold with eyes almost blinded,

For I have drowned my eyes in much weeping,

Weeping not only in grief but even amid rejoicing.

[Col. 0513A] You have removed the cause of my tears; now take away the wounds

That have arisen from those tears. Have pity, holy one, on the loss of my oxen;

Have pity likewise now on the loss of my eyes.

You gave me back my cattle; give me back my eyes also.

For what good is it that the cattle have been restored

If, while my sight is failing, I am absent from those present?

The people standing there laughed at the man making such a complaint,

But the ears of the hidden martyr, approached from afar,

Received the pious words of the foolish suppliant;

And soon his eyes, restored, felt the holy hand.

Then, rejoicing in the recovery of his eyes and oxen,

He returned home, while the people praised God,

And a joyful victory of his double prayer followed him.

The same, in poem 7.

[Col. 0513B] Holy one, I pray, come to the aid of your servant; I know that you are near,

And that, from the neighboring shrine, with ears attentive to those who call,

You, Felix, heard the weeping of your unhappy fosterling.

Whether now you cling, joined to the exalted side

Before the throne of the great King, acknowledged as his friend,

Receive, through the clouds, this voice of your poor and reverent servant

With the ear of God; do not despise it, but seek there

The salvation which, by Christ’s mercy, you may bring to me.

The same, in the same work.

The Creator himself, our light, God, wished to adorn

The birthday of his friend Felix with such a great healing,

In order to display by a mighty gift the sublime merit

Of the confessor—not to increase the honor

Of the martyr, to whom long ago he granted

[Col. 0513C] Palms with noble titles and a blessed name,

And upon whom the mercy of the Lord Christ continually bestows

Every kind of virtue without weariness.

But God wished at this time to grant us special joy,

And, by working such a sign through our own patron

For his own servants, to give something of that kind

To those who belonged to him.

The same, in poem 8.

Perhaps this act of piety will bring us greater salvation

If, for that reason, it pleases us to lay aside our cares,

So that we may bring rejoicing hearts to the confessor,

In whose honor God rejoices, because the martyr

Scorned his own honor for the name of the Lord Christ,

Making himself of less account to himself, so that he might be more precious to Christ.

The same, in the same work.

As former ages once possessed these things, so now, if our age

Has gained Felix as its salvation, let it ask whatever it dares,

And, trusting in such a patron, hope for whatever it desires.

Holy Felix, beloved of God, you are God’s right hand;

Be, I pray, our most strongly fortified tower.

The same, in the same work.

But just as the dew-laden breath, while children sang eternal hymns,

Scattered the burning fires,

So may the grace of Felix, with peaceful breath,

As God breathes upon us, temper the fires of war,

Suppressing the fires that have arisen in the Roman lands,

Cooling the anxious heats now in tranquil peace,

And releasing weary hearts from their extinguished cares.

The same, in the same work.

A certain man was for no long time so tormented by a prodigious

[Col. 0514A] demon that he would no longer consume merely the familiar

Food of human beings, even if a rich table were offered

With a plentiful feast, in an easy swallow;

Rather, he would snatch hens from the thresholds of their owners,

And as soon as he had seized them, tear them apart with his ravenous mouth,

Swallowing them, feathers and all, without being choked.

Indeed, he thirsted for funeral gore and licked bones,

Chewing the discarded carcasses of animals,

An unclean banqueter of dogs. Now, freed from so great a demon,

Behold, sober, he cultivates a little leased farm.

Restored to himself by God’s care in the holy shrine of Felix,

He clearly demonstrates, by a sufficient testimony,

That Felix is powerful through his merits and through the name of Christ.

The same, in poem 9.

[Col. 0514B] Hail, dear day; hail, my light; hail,

Always a festival for me. But in this year you have shone more brightly for me,

Because, together with the honor of Felix,

You bring back Nicetas, so that, through love for the two saints,

I may have a double birthday today:

Celebrating the departure of the martyr taken from the body,

And [the celebration] of one ready in body.

The same, in the same work.

Now Felix himself is needed for this task, and for this gift:

Let him obtain from Christ the things which Christ himself may bestow upon me,

So that I may give him worthy thanks for his gifts.

And now I could wish that perennial rivers of living water

Would flow from my breast,

So that I might recount my joy not with my own mouth,

But through Christ’s gift—my joy which, by Christ’s gift,

Overflows into my peaceful heart more abundantly than usual.

The same, in the same work.

[Col. 0514C] For, like chambers whose ceilings are joined to sacred roofs,

The altars look out through secure windows from above;

Beneath them the bodies of the saints have their dwelling within.

For apostolic ashes too, placed beneath the heavenly altar,

Give forth a peaceful fragrance breathing toward Christ,

Returning the scent of their dust among the sacred offerings.

Here is Father Andrew; here is he who, sent as a fisherman to Argos (the Argives),

Taught boastful tongues to grow gentle.

The same, in the same work.

Here too is the martyr Nazarius, whom, through the faithful gift

Of noble Ambrose, I received within my prostrate mind.

He himself deigns to honor the heights of Felix as a fellow guest

And adds brotherly dwellings to private residences.

Although all the saints, together throughout the whole world,

[Col. 0514D] Are one in God wherever they are,

And are presented everywhere as their bodily members dedicated to God,

Places nevertheless belong to the bodies of the saints;

Nor does the grace of those placed there live only where the whole body rests.

Wherever any part of the pious body is present,

And a hand remains, it bears witness before God

To the proofs of the blessed man’s merit;

And the great power in the small dust of the saints

Proclaims, in an unmistakable word, the power of an apostolic body.

Therefore whoever, in purity, dwells beneath heavenly roofs

Will be near them; and whoever comes from afar,

Moved by a proper devotion, hastens to the holy shrines,

When he wishes, in private, to approach Christ in prayer,

Whether by day or by night he wishes to utter his vows:

Let the guest come forth diligently from the neighboring threshold.

The same, in the same work.

[Col. 0515A] Whatever remains of the things that we see done and painted,

I offer you as material for prayer, asking you

To undertake Felix’s cause and pray diligently for me.

And it is fitting that the one whom you accompany with a pious mind

You should also reproduce before your mind’s eye

And follow in spirit, equal in love for me.

For, wretched though I am, I do not doubt that I am loved

By the martyr, who has deigned to love even a little puppy,

Since through Felix, by God’s gift, my life, my home, my possessions,

My favor, my glory, and my bread exist.

With him as bishop, ask that my foundations be laid

Upon the holy mountains,

And that the tower I have begun may be completed

With its structure unbroken.

The same, in poem 18.

If stars may be absent from the sky,

Grass from the earth, honey from honeycombs,

Water from springs, and milk from udders,

[Col. 0515B] Then the praises of the righteous might also cease from tongues,

In whom God himself is both the virtue of life and the glory of death—

God for whom they chose to bargain away their lives,

And by dying to establish the pious faith of peoples.

The same, in the same work.

One of that number of eminent confessors, Felix was given in this city;

His name shone far and wide throughout the world.

But Nola, made the home of the buried man,

Applauds as though he were its own star.

For every martyr, wherever he has been entrusted to a region,

Is at once the star of that place and the medicine of its worshipers.

For the Creator, taking pity on a world darkened by ancient gloom

And on souls languishing throughout the earth,

So arranged the earthly defenses of the righteous

That he scattered them like the lights of the stars across the night sky.

The same, in the same work.

[Col. 0515C] Wishing therefore to avert these diseases from us,

The Lord, healer of all things, brought forth saints among mortal sufferers

As physicians, through various nations, with healing piety.

And, so that divine power might display its care more clearly,

He placed them in the more important cities.

Although some towns retain their martyrs in small communities,

God brought others into cities with great walls,

And divided those who had completed their course among a few regions;

Yet before their death he made them teachers for the whole world.

Thus he fixed Peter and Paul in the city of Rome,

Because the head of the world needed the chief physicians.

The same, in the same work.

So too, bestowing pious gifts upon the remaining lands,

God scattered his great members everywhere throughout the cities.

Thus he gave Andrew to the Parthians and John to Ephesus,

So that through them he might heal Europe and Asia together,

And scatter the heavy darkness through such great lights.

Parthia embraces Matthew; India, Thomas;

Libya received Lebbaeus; the Phrygians received Philip;

Crete took Titus for itself; Antioch—and perhaps Ostia, in the damaged text—Luke;

Alexandria received you, Mark, with the ox driven on.

The same, in the same work.

Powerful Carthage rejoices in the martyr Cyprian,

From whose mouth, poured forth together with his blood,

Springs made fruitful the sands of thirsty Libya.

The same, in the same work.

Nor has grace shone less brightly in the western lands:

[Col. 0516A] Ambrose in Latium, Vincent in Iberia;

Gaul took Martin, Aquitania took Delphinus;

And many other seeds of saints, spread abundantly

Through those same regions after their tombs were established,

Illuminate the whole world with heavenly powers.

The same, in the same work.

Thus, through the love of merciful Christ,

Our Nola too deserved to be fortified by the tomb of Felix,

And at the same time to be cleansed;

For the world, mingled with blind ruins,

And Nola herself, were lying dying in night.

The same, in the same work.

The personages who had been gods through a false divinity howl in punishment—

Those who, under a deceitful name, had given themselves to human beings as gods,

Though before the worship of God they saw nothing heavenly in themselves—

Now, when the true faith has been revealed in the light of Christ,

Cannot bear the buried saints.

The same, in poem 13, on the destruction of the Gothic army with its king.

For this cause was cared for by many patrons,

So that Roman safety and the life of the commonwealth might remain:

Here were Peter, here Paul, here all the eminent martyrs,

Whom the circuit of the great City holds in its embrace,

And whom the Church venerates within the Roman boundaries,

Though they are scattered along an uncountable path through innumerable peoples.

Together they kept anxious watch with earnest prayer.

My Felix was, as it were, one of them

And a great participant in their prayers;

But the supreme result of what was sought is referred to all,

And is not assigned privately to anyone.

The same, in poem 14.

Now to you, venerable father, eternal patron,

[Col. 0516C] My protector, and Felix, most beloved of Christ,

I shall repay you with grateful words in return.

You have bestowed many gifts upon me through various blessings.

I remember that I owe you all that belongs to the present life,

And all that begets hope for the future;

Christ gave me to you as a servant from my earliest years.

If eloquence flowed for me in river-like streams,

And I possessed a thousand mouths, each endowed with a hundred tongues,

Perhaps, even refreshed by these resources and by such a fountain,

I could traverse all the gifts of Felix,

How many Christ the Lord bestowed upon his friend,

And the confessor transmitted to me, his servant and fosterling.

The same, in the same work.

If, returning to the beginning, I should recount everything

That he has bestowed upon me through equal piety at various times,

I could sooner adorn my own head with gifts

Than recount your gifts toward me, good Felix.

The same, in the same work.

With its resting-place unharmed and its tomb never gaping open,

the martyr’s body, enclosed on every side by a solid defence,

and his merit were exposed to no profanations.

The bones worthily retain the pious honor of their holy flesh,

because the Spirit never ceases to be present with the saints.

Thus living grace abides at pious tombs,

proving that all who are buried in Christ are without death,

and that their bodies sleep for a time in peaceful slumber.

The same, in poem 15.

Come forth, spring, with songs; let an articulate voice

Flow in modest rhythms.

Be present, Felix, rich source of speech for me,

And glide into my heart with silent breath.

Your spirit will run through my mouth;

Be the fountain of my words.

I shall be the pipe of your streams,

Which you will offer me from the river of the divine word.

The same, in the same work.

Rise, then, and enter my breast with your gentle breath,

O father Felix, lord, and patron.

You are my home, my medicine, and my wisdom, Felix.

Now sharpen my dulled mind after its long inactivity,

Reviving my heart with your fiery light.

The same, in the same work.

But my discourse is not to be poured out upon this expanse

So that I may run through the merits or miracles of the saints,

And attempt to weave into verse all that God has accomplished

And continues to accomplish through all the saints

From the beginning of things.

[Col. 0517B] The human mind cannot contain these things,

Nor can the tongue express them.

And what wonder is it if a whole scroll cannot contain

What the whole world itself cannot contain?

The maker of the world, God the King himself, is greater than the world.

He fills earth and heaven; this world cannot contain him.

The saints contain him—not in bodily vastness,

But because they are humble in piety

And capable of him through purity of heart.

The same, in the same work.

Now, therefore, as I recount the divine deeds of my patron Felix,

Or the benefits of life that he has bestowed upon me,

Or those that, through heavenly aid, he does not cease to bestow

Upon many people through pious gifts almost every day,

Granting various gifts through signs,

The order of his merits demands that Christ be praised.

I shall seem to praise not the man,

But rather him through whom Felix, powerful by his author,

Receives his venerable name

And grants healing powers by which he restores sick bodies

And, with God prevailing, frees captive souls from the power of the dark demon.

Nor does Felix work Christ’s gifts only in this kind of aid;

He is also most powerful in triumphing over the serpent-like enemy.

Likewise, so that the spiteful accuser may marvel—or rather, that he may rage and waste away—let him hear Paulinus, whom Augustine calls the bishop of Nola: from a most wealthy man, made by choice the poorest of the poor, and exceedingly holy; not puffed up by knowledge of wisdom but humbled by it, because he burned with the fire of charity and was built up by its adornment. Let him hear, I say, such a Paulinus speaking in his letter to Sulpicius Severus:

[Col. 0517D] “Will that time, I ask, ever come, and will that day ever dawn,

When I may receive your brotherhood, coming with the chosen company of God,

In the bosom of the common patron of my estate, Felix?”

The same, to the same person, in the letter *On the Little Cloaks*:

“Our hut, which, raised above the ground, extends farther as an upper room, with one portico set between the guest chambers, as though enlarged by the grace of the Lord, offered its narrow spaces not only to the holy people who accompanied it in great numbers, but also to the crowds of those wealthy men; in it, the neighboring heights of our estate of Felix resounded with the groups of boys and virgins.”

The same, to the same person, concerning the holy presbyter Clarus, companion of Saint Martin:

“Therefore I dared to compose verses in memory of that holy man—not because I could say anything worthy of his divine merits, but in order to express the great devotion of charity in his soul—and to send them to your unanimity. As you recite them before the Lord, in the presence of his holy soul, which always dwells with you as a fellow guest in the Lord, you will excuse my boldness and commend my service.”

Here lies the presbyter Clarus, distinguished by merits and by name,

A companion of Martin in devotion, and now a sharer in his merit.

This house is worthy of a pious altar, beneath which

His lifeless limbs are buried, while his spirit rejoices in heaven,

And joins the disciple to his equal master above the stars.

Clarus in faith, most renowned in conduct, brightest in fruitfulness,

You who make the title of your name equal to your merits,

Chaste altars worthily veil your body,

So that the altar of God may cover Christ’s temple.

But you are not held in this place where your body lies,

Since in heavenly merit your spirit flies.

Whether you recline in the bosoms of the fathers,

Or are buried beneath the Lord’s altar,

Or are nourished in a sacred grove,

In whatever region of heaven or paradise you are placed,

Clarus, you live blessed beneath eternal peace.

Receive these good prayers of sinners who entreat,

That you may remember Paulinus and Therasia.

Through Severus’s intercession, love those entrusted to you,

Whom you did not know in the body, though they are so worthy.

Let a united and common love be a bond for both of us

In the supreme covenant in the Lord.

You cannot tear apart those joined together; if you draw one,

The other, clinging to him, will be drawn wherever he is taken.

[Col. 0518C] Therefore embrace us, inseparable brothers, together;

And love us as we are, making us sharers in your affection.

Thus God summoned us; thus Martin loved us;

So also, Clarus, protect your equals together.

Equal not in merits but in love: you, holy one, will be able

To entreat that we may become equal in merit,

If, with Martin, you labor in joined devotion,

So that your prayers may overcome our sins.

And may we together be led into the destiny of your Severus,

And may your wing protect both of us within its bosom.

The same, concerning these three sacred things collected together as one—that is, the sacred painting, the divine cross, and the holy relics of the saints—about which the blasphemer, like another, more savage, Tartarean Cerberus, opening three raging throats and making a threefold din with his barking, and like a bristly, foul-smelling goat trying with its poisonous tooth to tear apart the lovely vine of Christ and his Church and inflict an ugly scar upon it, spoke as follows:

[Col. 0518D] “But if the Lord should fulfill the desire of your soul according to your faith, adding to the adornment and sanctification of your works that you should obtain sacred ashes from the blessed relics of glorious apostles or martyrs—for we have learned that, in the presumption of this vow, you have prepared another basilica at Primuliacum, larger than the former one—then, since the dedication of a work faithfully undertaken is without doubt most celebrated and worthy of your work of faith, we judge that it is fitting for the relics of the saints that you should also venerate this object which we have sent from the cross, deposited and consecrated together with them.

[Col. 0519A] If this should please you, these verses, if you wish, will announce your decision.”

The altars worthy of veneration cover the divine covenant,

With the martyrs arranged together with the cross in sacred union.

All the saving sufferings of Christ come together:

The cross, the body, the blood—God himself is the martyr.

For God always preserves his gifts for you,

And wherever Christ is, there are the Spirit and the Father.

So too, wherever the cross is, there is the martyr;

Where the martyr and the cross are, there is the holy cause of martyrdom.

It produced both food for mortals and crowns,

Which make the Lord’s servants sharers in him.

On the cross the flesh is fixed, by which I am fed;

From the cross flows the blood by which I drink life and wash my heart.

[Col. 0519B] O Christ, may these gifts of yours come together for Severus;

May this bearer also be a witness of your cross.

May he live by your flesh, and may your blood

Offer him cups; may he live in your word and act according to it.

And by whatever means your own gift carried Martin

To ascend with his companion Clarus,

May this man also go, borne by your gift.

“If, however, it should please you more to have this blessing from the cross available for daily protection and healing, lest, once it has been deposited in the altar, it not always be at hand when use requires it, that blessing alone is sufficient for the consecration of the basilica—namely, the Lord together with the apostles and martyrs. Their venerable ash, if it is placed beneath the altars without the companionship of the cross, is indicated by this title:

The glory of the divine table veils the pledges of the saints,

Brought forth through apostolic bodies.

The Spirit of the Lord attends with healing powers,

And proves the sacred ashes alive through its signs.

Thus doubled grace breathes upon pious vows,

Acted from above upon the sacred martyrs below.

The priest’s vows and the benefits of the living,

The precious death of the saints helps with a little dust.”

The same, concerning the same three sacred things.

Indeed, this little basilica also will be consecrated by the sacred ashes of the blessed relics of apostles and martyrs, in the name of Christ—the Holy One of saints, the Martyr of martyrs, and the Lord of lords. For he himself has testified that he will in turn be the confessor of his confessors. Therefore, beyond the painting, this title concerning the painting has been doubled by grace:

[Col. 0519D] The labor and reward of the saints rightly cling together;

The arduous cross, and the lofty crown, are the price of the cross.

God himself is our prince and our crown,

In the heavenly grove of flowering paradise.

Beneath the bloody cross Christ stands in a snow-white lamb,

The Lamb given as an innocent victim for an unjust death.

The Holy Spirit, as a gentle bird, bathes him as he opens his mouth,

And the Father crowns him from a gleaming cloud.

Likewise Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man of consular rank and the most learned of the Iberians, burning with the same zeal of faith and devotion, composed many things in metrical form concerning the praises of the saints and the seeking of their intercession. Thus, with remarkable humility, turning inward and exhorting his own soul, he says in the preface to the book Καθημερινῶν (*Daily Songs*):

But at the final end,

Let the sinful soul cast off its folly.

At least let it celebrate God with its voice, if it cannot do so by its merits.

Let it continue the day with hymns,

And let no voice utter anything without singing of the Lord.

Let it fight against heresies and examine the Catholic faith.

Let it trample the sacred things of the nations,

And, Rome, let it bring disgrace upon your idols.

Let it dedicate a song to the martyrs and praise the apostles.

While I write or speak these things,

Would that I might burst free from the chains of the body,

Free at the last sound carried by my moving tongue!

The same, in the poem on the Roman martyr.

[Col. 0520B] I would wish that, destined to be among the herds of goats on the left,

I might be recognized from afar; and that, at this prayer,

The excellent King might say:

“Romanus is praying; transfer this goat to me.

Let it be a sheep on the right and be clothed in wool.”

The same, in the hymn of the holy martyrs Emeterius and Chelidonius of Calahorra.

The names of two martyrs have been written in heaven,

Which Christ recorded there in letters of gold,

And likewise transferred in marks of blood to the earth.

This blessed Iberian land is powerful throughout the world through this distinction.

This place seemed worthy to God to hold their bones,

A chaste host for the bodies of the blessed.

Here, stained with a twofold slaughter, it drank the hot waters.

The inhabitants now throng the sands marked with holy blood,

[Col. 0520C] Entreating with voice, vows, and gifts.

A settler from abroad, and from the rest of the world as well, comes here;

For the revealing fame has spread through every land:

Here are the patrons of the world whom suppliants surround.

No one has gathered pure prayers here in vain when entreating.

Here the suppliant returns joyful, with cleansed tears,

Sensing that everything justly requested has been obtained.

So great is the care of those who intercede for our dangers

That they do not allow anyone to pour out a useless murmur in prayer.

They hear, and immediately carry it to the ear of the eternal King.

From that very fountain abundant gifts flow down upon the earth,

Watering the cases brought before them with the remedies sought.

Good Christ has never denied anything to his own witnesses.

The same, in the same work.

They leave behind the standards of Caesar and choose the sign of the cross;

And instead of the windswept dragon emblems that they carried on their cloaks,

They bear before them the marked wood that subdued the dragon.

The same, in the same work.

By these means the power of the martyrs shakes the filthy robber;

It restrains him, tortures him, burns him, and puts chains upon him.

The tormented plunderer strips himself of his very marrow.

He abandons his unharmed prey and flees with parched jaws;

From the bottom of his claw to the hair of his head,

He returns everything untouched,

Confessing that he himself is burning—for he is an inhabitant of hell.

Why should I speak of bodies cleansed of long diseases,

When icy horror shakes their discolored limbs?

Here the swelling leaves the face; here true color is restored.

The Savior himself granted us this benefit to enjoy

[Col. 0521A] When he consecrated the limbs of the martyrs in our city,

Which now bring healing to the inhabitants whom the Iberus waters.

The same, speaking in prayer concerning the passion of Saint Lawrence:

Wipe away this disgrace, O Christ;

Send forth your Gabriel,

So that wandering Jewish blindness

May recognize the true God.

And now we hold the most faithful pledges of this hope:

Here, surely, the two princes of the apostles already reign.

One was the caller of the nations;

The other, possessing the first chair,

Opens the doors of eternity

Entrusted to him.

[Col. 0521B] Depart, adulterous Jupiter,

Who forgot the violation of your sister;

Leave Rome free,

And flee the people who now belong to Christ.

Paul drives you out from here;

Peter’s blood expels you.

What you yourself had armed against him—

Nero’s deed—works against you.

The same, in the same work.

O thrice, four times, and seven times blessed

Is the inhabitant of the City

Who celebrates you and the seat of your bones

Close at hand,

Who may fall prostrate beside you,

Who sprinkles the place with tears,

Who presses his breast upon the ground,

Who pours out vows in a murmur.

The Iberian Vasco separates us,

Keeping us distant by two Alps,

Beyond the ridges of the Cottian Alps,

Beyond the snowy Pyrenees.

Scarcely does fame make known how full of saints Rome is,

Hidden though it is,

How rich the urban soil flowers

With sacred tombs.

But we who lack these blessings

And cannot behold before our eyes

The traces of the blood,

Look toward heaven from afar.

The same, at the end of the same passion.

What power has been entrusted,

And how great a gift has been given,

The rejoicing of the Quirites proves,

For you grant what is asked.

Whatever each suppliant requests,

He carries away successfully obtained.

They ask, they offer sacrifice, they make it known,

And no one returns sad.

As though you were always present,

You embrace your urban fosterlings

Within your nursing bosom

And nourish them with paternal love.

Among these, O glory of Christ,

Hear also the rustic poet,

Confessing the sins of his heart

And revealing his own deeds.

I acknowledge and know myself unworthy,

One whom Christ himself would hear;

But through the patron martyrs

He can obtain healing.

Hear kindly the suppliant,

Prudentius, guilty before Christ,

And serving the body;

Release him from the chains of the world.

Likewise, at the end of the hymn of Saint Eulalia.

Gather purple violets,

And harvest blood-red crocuses.

[Col. 0522B] The genial winter is not without these,

And, as the warming ice loosens the fields,

It heaps baskets with flowers.

Virgin and child, offer these gifts

From the leafy foliage;

But I shall carry into the middle of the choir

Garlands woven in dactylic verse—

Worthless and withered, yet festive.

Thus I delight to venerate the bones,

And the altar placed upon the bones.

She, lying beneath the feet of God,

Looks upon this place and cherishes her people,

Made favorable by song.

The same, in the passion of Saint Vincent the martyr.

Happy is that retreat of the pleasant shore

Which, cherishing the sacred entrails in its sands,

Provided a path to the tomb.

While pious care, mourning, adorns the mound

And entrusts the body to the tomb,

It preserves it for the life to come.

But soon, after the enemies had been subdued,

When peace had been restored to the righteous,

The altar grants the blessed bones

The rest they were owed.

The same, in the same passion.

Be present now and receive

The suppliant voices of those who pray,

An effective advocate for our guilt

Before the Father’s throne.

Through you, through that prison,

An increase of your honor;

Through chains, flames, hooks,

Through the prison stake,

Through that potsherd,

By which your glory grew,

Through which trembling descendants

Kiss the little bed.

Have mercy on our prayers,

So that Christ, appeased by his own,

May incline his favorable ear

And not charge all our offenses against us.

If we duly venerate the solemn day

With mouth and heart,

If we prostrate ourselves with joy

Beneath the traces of your footsteps,

Glide down here for a little while,

Bringing Christ’s favor,

So that burdened minds may feel

The relief of indulgence.

The same, from the hymn of the eighteen holy martyrs of Caesaraugusta.

Twice nine of our people preserve

The ashes of martyrs in one tomb.

We call the city Caesaraugusta,

A city endowed with such a thing.

House full of great angels,

Do not fear the ruin of the fragile world,

Bearing in your bosom so many gifts

To be offered together to Christ.

When God comes, shaking his flashing right hand,

Supported upon a red cloud,

To place a just balance before the nations

With an even weight,

Each city, raised from the great world,

Will hasten to meet Christ,

Carrying precious gifts

In baskets.

African Carthage will bring forth your bones,

Cyprian, eloquent teacher;

Corduba will give Ascisclus and Zoellus,

And three crowns.

You, mother of the righteous, will offer Christ

A beautiful diadem of three gems,

Tarraco, for which Fructuosus

Wove a seamless bond.

This name is bound into a jeweled band;

Twin stones gleam beside it,

And the equal splendor of the two

Burns with flashing fire.

Small Gerunda, rich in holy limbs,

Will display the glory of Felix;

Our Calahorra will carry both

Whom we venerate.

Barchino, relying on illustrious Cucufas,

Will rise; and Narbo, made splendid by Paul;

And powerful Arelas will possess you,

Holy Genesius.

[Col. 0523D] The chief city of the Lusitanian towns,

Seizing the ashes of the maiden who was worshiped,

Will carry her to meet Christ

And present her at the altar.

Complutum will gladly bear in its bosom

The blood of Justus, to whom a shepherd clings,

A double burden and a twofold gift—

The limbs of two men.

Tingis will offer Cassianus,

A festive monument of the kings of Massylia,

Whose ashes compelled conquered peoples

To the yoke of Christ.

The same, shortly afterward.

The citizens honor these, as though their own turf

Enclosed the very limbs

And, embracing them in their ancestral tomb,

Preserved the bones of the blessed martyr.

The same, at the end of the same passion.

Grant that we may wash with pious tears

The grooves of the marble beneath which hope lies covered,

That it may release me

From the bonds of my restraints.

Prostrate yourself, noble city, entirely with me

Before the holy tombs; then,

You will follow the souls and limbs

That will soon rise again.

The same, at the end of the passion of Saint Agnes.

O happy virgin, O new glory,

Noble inhabitant of the heavenly citadel,

Look upon our defilements,

With your face adorned by a double diadem.

The All-Father alone has given you the power

Even to restore the vault itself.

I shall be cleansed if you fill

Our inward parts with the radiance of your merciful face.

Nothing is unchaste that you, pious one,

Deign to behold or touch with your nourishing foot.

The same, in the hymn of the blessed martyrs Fructuosus, bishop of Tarraco, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons.

Then the ash from the sacred bodies

And the bones drenched with wine were gathered,

Each person hastily claiming them for himself.

So great was the brothers’ love to carry home

The dedicated gifts of the holy ashes,

Or to bear a faithful pledge in their bosom.

But lest they divide the relics destined to rise again,

And soon to be together with the Lord,

Among separate tombs,

They are seen clothed in white robes;

They order the sacred dust to be restored

And shut up together in hollow marble.

O triple honor, O threefold summit,

By which the head of our city is raised,

Surpassing all the cities of Iberia.

It is a joy to exult in the three patrons,

By whose protection all the peoples

Of the Pyrenean lands are cherished.

The same, in the passion of Saint Cassianus of Forocornelium.

[Col. 0524D] Here, when I was seeking you, mighty Rome,

A hope arose that Christ would be favorable.

Stretched upon the ground, I was prostrate beside a tomb,

Which the holy martyr Cassianus adorns with his dedicated body.

While weeping, I considered with myself my wounds,

All the labors of life, and the sharp points of grief.

I raised my face toward heaven; directly before me stood

A painted image of the martyr, depicted with colors,

Bearing a thousand wounds, lacerated throughout his limbs.

The same, shortly afterward.

When consulted, the custodian said:

“What you see, guest, is not an empty tale

Or an old woman’s story.

The painting recounts a history which, handed down in books,

Shows the trustworthy account of ancient times.”

The same, at the end of the same passion.

These are the things painted in clear colors

That you marvel at, guest: this is the glory of Cassianus.

Present, if you have one, a just or loving vow;

If you have any hope, if anything burns within you.

Believe me, the most favorable martyr hears all prayers,

And makes those he sees to be worthy come true.

I obey; I embrace the tomb; I pour out tears as well.

The altar grows warm from my lips, the stone from my breast.

Then I review all the hidden matters of my labor.

[Col. 0525B]

Then I murmur what I was asking for, what I feared,

and the house left behind under an uncertain fate,

and perhaps my wavering hope of future prosperity.

I am heard; I reach the City and enjoy favorable success;

I return home and proclaim Cassianus.

Likewise Fortunatus, in praising and honoring the saints and their memorials, both believed and taught that those who devoutly and faithfully commend themselves to their prayers can be helped by them. Thus, speaking of the basilica of Saint Gregory, he says:

> He who, powerful in virtue, lies buried in the eastern region,
>
> behold, beneath the western sky he offers aid.
>
> Therefore remember him in your prayers and pay your vows, traveler;
>
> here pious faith obtains by his merits what it seeks.

Likewise, concerning Saint Mauritius and his fellow soldiers:

[Col. 0525C]

> Fortunatus, through the shining gifts of the Thunderer,
>
> lest I be tormented in darkness, I beg you to offer help.

Likewise, concerning Saint Medardus:

> I, Fortunatus, piously bringing these few words out of love,
>
> ask for help; grant my prayers, I beg.

Likewise, in the epitaph of Gregory, bishop of the city of Langres:

> If you ask about his merit, the miracles of events bear witness:
>
> through him friendly salvation is said to come to the weak.

Likewise, in the epitaph of Caletricus, bishop of the city of Chartres:

> These few words, holy Father, I whisper as though they were great;
>
> for your Fortunatus, I beg you, pray.

Likewise, concerning Gregory, bishop of Tours:

[Col. 0525D]

> By the merits of Martin, through long ages, Gregory,
>
> as shepherd, cherish the flock of Tours;
>
> may you be a standard in sacred councils and the life of your predecessors,
>
> and through your example may the honor you have gained increase.
>
> May your tongue minister apostolic light to the peoples,
>
> and may heaven’s gift shine forth as you radiate.

We also read that the Lord’s chosen have entreated the Lord through the merits of earlier saints, as is recalled in Daniel concerning Azariah praying in this way:

> “Do not, we beseech you, hand us over forever because of your name,
>
> and do not destroy your covenant,
>
> nor take away your mercy from us because of Abraham, your beloved,
>
> and Isaac, your servant,
>
> and Israel, your holy one,
>
> to whom you spoke, promising that you would multiply their offspring
>
> like the stars of heaven and like the sand that is on the seashore” (Dan. III).

They certainly would never have done this unless, through the revelation of the divine Spirit, they had known with complete certainty that the saints, after laying aside the corruptible and mortal burden of the flesh and clinging inseparably to God, have greater standing with the Lord than those still living in this troubled life, where the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh. For although such people may be perfect, their earthly dwelling nevertheless weighs them down and presses upon them, and they must always be concerned for themselves.

Hence the Apostle complains, although the hope of the freedom to come consoles him, saying:

> “For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. But I see another law in my members opposing the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin which is in my members. Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. VII).

But not only are the living, in their various needs, wonderfully and presently assisted by the Lord through the intercession of the saints; we also believe and read that divine aid is granted to faithful departed persons buried near their memorials—namely, to those who prepared and merited this beforehand through their bodily life—so that sacrifices, prayers, and alms performed for them by the Church or by any surviving friends may benefit them after death.

Therefore Augustine, in his book *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, addressed to Bishop Paulinus, says:

> “You wrote to me asking whether it benefits anyone after death that his body is buried near the memorial of some saint.”

And shortly afterward:

> “For you say that it seems to you that the religious and faithful movements of souls caring for their own in this matter are not empty. You add that it cannot be without purpose that the whole Church is accustomed to supplicate for the dead; so that from this it may also be inferred that it benefits a person after death if, through the faith of his relatives, a place is provided for the burial of his body in which the assistance of the saints, sought even in this manner, may be seen. But although these things are so, you indicate that you do not sufficiently see how this is not contrary to what the Apostle says: ‘We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil’ (II Cor. V, 10). For this apostolic judgment warns that before death something may be done which can benefit a person after death—not at the time when what each person did before death must already be received.

> “This question is therefore resolved in this way: by a certain manner of life, while one lives in this body, one acquires the possibility that these things may help the dead; and thus, according to what they did through the body, they are helped by what is religiously done for them through the body. For there are some whom these things do not help at all: either because they are done for those whose merits are so evil that they are not worthy of being helped even by such means, or because they are done for those whose merits are so good that they do not need such assistance. Thus it is by the kind of life each person lived through the body that it is determined whether whatever is piously done for him after he has left the body will help or not. For if no merit by which these things might help was acquired in this life, it is sought in vain after this life.

[Col. 0527A]

> “Thus it happens that neither the Church nor the care of relatives acts religiously in vain when it offers what it can for the dead; and yet each person receives according to what he did through the body, whether good or evil, since the Lord repays each according to his works. For the ability of what is offered to benefit someone after death was acquired in the life he lived in the body.”

And after much more:

> “The provision of a place for bodies to be buried near the memorial of the saints is an expression of human affection toward the remains of one’s relatives. For if there is some religious significance in their being buried, there can be no complete absence of it when attention is paid to where they are buried. But when such consolations of the living are sought, by which their loving disposition toward their own may become evident, I do not see what benefit this brings to the dead, except that, when they recall where the bodies of those they love have been placed, they commend them in prayer to those same saints, as patrons who have received them before the Lord, so that the saints may help them. Some could do this even if they were unable to bury them in such places.”

And immediately afterward:

> “When, therefore, the mind recalls where the body of a beloved person has been buried, and the venerable name of a martyr comes to mind, the affection of the person remembering and praying commends the beloved soul to that martyr. When this is done for the dead by their dearest faithful friends, there is no doubt that it benefits those who, while living in the body, merited that such things should benefit them after this life.”

For this reason, I think, Ambrose buried his brother Satyrus, whom he had loved exceedingly, beside the holy martyr Victor. On this subject he published three excellent books: one on his mourning, and two consolatory books on the resurrection and paradise. His epitaph is composed in this quatrain:

> Ambrose brought Uranio Satyro, his brother,
>
> the final honor at the martyr’s left hand.
>
> Such is the reward of his merit, that the moisture of the sacred blood,
>
> penetrating nearby, bathes his remains.

This reasoning agrees with what is read in the Book of Kings: the corpse of a certain man, when it touched the bones of the prophet Elisha, was immediately restored to life. For the passage reads:

> “So Elisha died, and they buried him. In that same year bands of Moabites came into the land. Some men were burying a man, but when they saw the raiders, they threw the corpse into the tomb of Elisha. When it touched the bones of Elisha, the man came back to life and stood on his feet” (IV Kings XIII).

With all these matters treated above, it is entirely and most clearly evident that sacred images, the holy cross of the Lord, and the sacred relics of God’s chosen must be venerated by Catholics and orthodox Christians with fitting and appropriate honors, in God and for God—not so that anyone should offer them, by sacrificing to them, the divine honor and worship owed to God alone, the Creator of all things, but so that, in love, honor, praise, and glory of God, all the faithful and religious may honor and embrace each of their holy, distinguished, and venerable vessels, as is proper, with sound and sincere faith.

But that Eunomian and Vigilantian, enemy and blasphemer of all the saints, enemy of the cross of Christ, destroyer and melter-down of its holy image, and thus advancing step by step to become a mocker and despiser of Christ’s incarnation and passion—wherever he sees the sacred image of the Crucified, narrowing his eyes and twisting his mouth with swollen cheeks, he persists in jeering and cackling, shouting:

> “Behold Christ, dead and tortured!”

For this reason the Jews in this region praise him above all others and put him forward everywhere; and because he differs in nothing from their tradition and religion, they call him the wisest of Christians. They mockingly and insultingly urge Christians, as though ignorant and uninstructed, to learn from him and become his disciples; while he, for his part, extols them in turn—and especially his kinsmen, the Saracens—with excessive, hyperbolic and “perbolic” praises.

Thus, since he obstinately and so completely resists the holy Catholic faith and sound doctrine, and argues and prattles against it with such shamelessness, he must be rebuked as a most perverse schismatic and a thoroughly wicked heretic; and, as an useless vessel filled with the most bitter gall and deadly poison, he must be crushed—indeed, broken—by the mighty rod of apostolic and canonical authority.

To pass over the rest: how could a bishop who abhors, tramples upon, violates, and destroys the Lord’s cross perform the offices of the Church—namely, baptizing, making chrism, laying on hands, giving any blessing, performing any consecrations, or celebrating Mass—without the inscription of that saving sign, without which none of these sacred acts can rightly and undefiledly be performed?

Hence Saint Augustine says in his exposition of the Gospel according to John:

> “Finally, what is the sign of Christ that everyone knows, if not the cross of Christ? Unless this sign is applied either to the foreheads of believers, or to the water from which they are reborn, or to the oil with which they are anointed in chrism, or to the sacrifice by which they are nourished, none of these things is rightly accomplished. How, then, is nothing good signified through what evil men do, when through the cross of Christ—which evil men made—every good thing is signified for us in the celebration of his sacraments?”

How, I ask, can he truly be counted among Christ’s worshipers when he rejects and detests what the Catholic Church practices? For in the litanies and other offices of the Church he does not wish any of the saints to be remembered or named, nor their annual festivals to be celebrated; despising these as a vain observance and useless custom, he omits everything.

Lest he appear to ask anything from God through their intercessions, he puts himself before them, comparing their relics with the bones of animals, dry wood, and stones. He forbids lamps and candles to burn in the Church during the day, and forbids the eyes to be lowered to the ground in prayer, as though God were not everywhere and as though this were not an indication of humility and devout prayer.

Yet in the Gospel we read of the publican:

> “He did not even dare to raise his eyes to heaven” (Luke XVIII, 10).

And Stephen, praying for those who were stoning him, placed his knees on the ground (Acts VII, 60). Paul, too, is described as having prayed prostrate on the ground when Simon Magus was lifted by demons into the air.

For the present, it is enough to have said these things. The many other matters that we have learned by hearing them reported to us by other faithful and truthful men, after they had heard them from him, are so impious and sacrilegious that a Christian mind both refuses and fears either to commit them to writing or to repeat them to others. Therefore, omitting the task of writing them down, we have confined ourselves to replying to the words of his letter.

Because of this utterly insane perversity, he refused to attend the assembly of the bishops, calling their synod a gathering of asses. But those bishops, although exceedingly patient, ought not to have tolerated these things any longer; nor should such a man have been spared, lest the ruin of souls be increased and the deadly cancer nourished—for, as the Apostle says, he does not please God and is hostile to all people.

For my part, I burn with zeal because of his contempt for the divine cross, and, moved by that zeal, am unable to pass over the blasphemy against the saints with deaf ears, since contempt shown to the members redounds to the injury of their head, as he himself says:

> “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke X, 16).

Taking these few passages from the holy books, I have brought them together; if necessary, with Christ’s help I shall add other material as he himself grants it, for resisting the devil.

[Col. 0529]

# THE POEMS OF DUNGAL

(Marten., *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, p. 811.)

## POEMS I, II, III, IV. ON CHARLES THE GREAT

[Col. 0529B]

(See *Patrologia*, vol. XCVIII, col. 1443.)

### V. Verses for a church

> This is a wondrous house, painted with varied metal,
>
> noble in its clergy, renowned for pious doctrine.
>
> Its roof gleams with gold; its silver wall shines white;
>
> the floor, pressed from radiant marble, groans.
>
> This beautiful house, conqueror, you must recognize:
>
> it contains within it the bodies of three saints.

### VI. Verses for the fonts

> Here an irrigating fountain supplies life-giving gifts,
>
> and, renewing the peoples, sends them to the stars, to God.
>
> Behold, Christ is present there, the source of the first fountain,
>
> who washes away every crime and purifies every wickedness.
>
> Run now, boys, to the waters and sacred streams;
>
> bring gifts to God with your stains immersed [in the waters].

### VII. Verses for a window

> Lest the crafty tempter enter David’s bed,
>
> may this window be marked with the Lord’s hand.
>
> May the fourfold number of the Gospel defend every
>
> body within, and the almighty one defend the soul.

### VIII. Verses for a door

> May that God who once marked the doorposts of the Egyptians
>
> with the blood of the lamb mark our doorposts also.

### IX. Verses for the ministry

[Col. 0529D]

> May he who ordered streams to issue from the hard rock
>
> here often command pure wine to flow.
>
> May supreme salvation be yours, always blessed without end.
>
> This Martin, a lover of your salvation, wishes for you
>
> and will ask the gracious Lord for it with constant prayers.
>
> May he also grant that you receive the eternal palm.
>
> For remember to carry the Lord in a pure heart,
>
> so that you may always have him as your ruler, etc.

### X. Epitaph of Folradus (abbot of Saint-Denis)

[Col. 0530D]

> Blessed for men and precious for the good is that death
>
> which glory, life, salvation, and rest follow.
>
> Those who return to their homeland, leaving the world’s foreign lands,
>
> after miserable sorrows possess long joys.
>
> One of their number, already rightly a distinguished priest,
>
> lies here in this tomb, having laid aside his body.
>
> Distinguished in the merits, hope, and name of his life,
>
> shining everywhere with the radiance of his virtues.
>
> He was a father and teacher to all through his goodness,
>
> admonishing some by his skill and guiding others by his piety.
>
> A worshiper of the Church, a supporter of pilgrims, an avenger of the needy,
>
> he benefited all by speech and by equal piety:
>
> sweet in speech, upright in deeds, serene in countenance,
>
> with a nectar-like heart, ready for every good.
>
> But since it is certain, patron, that you have merited the palm,
>
> for your pilgrim I ask you to pray.

### XI. Epitaph of Fardulfus (abbot of Saint-Denis)

> Fardulfus had been a father through his piety, a shepherd,
>
> and a master through his care,
>
> tranquil, gentle, ready for every good,
>
> a worshiper of the Church, generous and compassionate toward the poor.
>
> Here he lies in this tomb;
>
> in this house of God he merited to be raised up
>
> under a distinguished name to eternal praises and prayers.

### XII. Other verses

[Col. 0530D]

> The excellent princes Clothar and Dagobert,
>
> son and father, are commemorated here with everlasting praise.
>
> But Dagobert enriched this church more greatly,
>
> together with his Nanthild, whose golden busts adorn it.

### XIII. Other verses likewise

> Here shine the images and illustrious names of kings:
>
> of eminent Charles and of strong Pippin, his offspring;
>
> the excellent Augustus Caesar, who shines through so great a father,
>
> whom the most beautiful mother Berta bore.

### XIV. Epitaph of Pippin, king of Italy

[Col. 0531A]

> Here in this tomb lies the venerable King Pippin;
>
> he ruled Hesperia; here in this tomb he lies.
>
> France bore him, filled with beautiful piety;
>
> now Hesperia holds him, whom France bore.
>
> Noble in lineage, shining from a beautiful stock,
>
> whom noble Charles begot, noble in lineage.
>
> Dispelling every cloud, he hastened toward the stars;
>
> now he remains without end, dispelling every cloud.
>
> In his face he surpassed the beautiful lilies;
>
> the clear day shone from his face.
>
> More noble in merits than anyone can express in speech,
>
> beautiful in appearance, more noble in merits.

[Col. 0531B]

> One love of the people, one virtue, one peace for all;
>
> the one love of the people loved everyone.
>
> A good and gentle king, surpassed by none in mercy,
>
> he rightly ruled others, a good and gentle king.
>
> From his pious mouth the people reaped their desires;
>
> from his pious mouth they drank every sweetness.
>
> He was swiftly snatched from the world, a generous shepherd of the needy;
>
> [lacuna] He was snatched from the mouth.

### XV. Epitaph of Motharius

> You who hold this book in your hands, reader,
>
> here you can learn the sacred commandments of God.
>
> If you wish to know the author of the work,
>
> I do not want his name to remain hidden from you.
>
> Motharius himself, a priest, produced this book;
>
> he wrote this work with his own fingers,
>
> and that holy man gave it in honor of holy Mary,
>
> so that he might obtain everlasting rest.
>
> Whoever you are, O reader, who read this book,
>
> say: “May the Lord grant him everlasting rest.”

### XVI. Another, likewise

> In this tomb lies that priest Motharius,
>
> who earlier lived in the world with devout love.
>
> He was happy: he abandoned the earthly things of the world,
>
> and chose to learn sound letters,
>
> so that he might more fully proclaim the Lord’s commands.
>
> Before this, he was humble and full of the love of God.

### XVII. Epitaph of Dungal

> Whoever you are who sees this inscription, say with a pure heart:
>
> “May there be rest for him, excellent reader, I beg.”
>
> I beg you, almighty Creator of the square-shaped world,
>
> that Dungal, your soldier, may flourish everywhere,
>
> and that you may continually protect his body forever,
>
> so that the wolf may not tear him apart while he is unguarded.
>
> May he rightly be able to grasp starry Olympus,
>
> and may he be able to share life with the saints.
>
> He does not cease seeking divine help night and day,
>
> so that, as he asks, he may conquer all evils.
>
> He despises the varied riches of the perishing world;
>
> he bears a heart free from the cares of the world,
>
> and rules his own flesh with just restraint,
>
> lest his soul perish through the fault of the flesh.
>
> He asks to despise the deadly splendors of the world;
>
> he asks to seek the rewards of the heavenly kingdom.
>
> Meditating on the Lord’s law with all his strength,
>
> his devout mind rightly serves the Lord.
>
> He illuminates his disciples with sacred light,
>
> like a bright lamp set in a lofty place.
>
> From a chaste heart he brings forth the sacred Scriptures,
>
> teaching the weak and the strong alike.
>
> Watering the children with milk and giving food to those who can receive it,
>
> here he gives milk for them to take, there food as well.
>
> Like a pious mother, he nourishes her children with a kindly mind,
>
> giving food to the grown and milk to the inexperienced.
>
> Why should I enumerate more of these holy virtues?
>
> I cannot say them, nor am I able to write them.
>
> If words flowed from my heart like rivers,
>
> even then I would not suffice to recount what is worthy for you.
>
> May you be well and flourish for long ages;
>
> may God grant you everlasting rest—ask him for it.
>
> This world is dissolved amid uncertain events,
>
> and the human race is destroyed by the worst of deaths.
>
> When the end comes, long years are of no benefit;
>
> no one is found released from the law of death.

### XVIII. Epitaph of Authelmus the monk

> The limbs of Authelmus the monk lie beneath this tomb;
>
> hostile death took him in the early years of his life.
>
> Happy at the beginning of life, he abandoned earthly things;
>
> he despised the world and now shines above the stars.
>
> Noble in lineage, gentle, good, and fair to all,
>
> nobler in merits than speech can express.
>
> He was wise, humble, and filled with piety;
>
> strong in understanding, he shone powerfully in the world.
>
> Whoever you are, O reader, who read this inscription through,
>
> ask, “O God, grant him everlasting rest.”

## In the year of the Lord 826. Saint Adalhard, abbot of Corbie in Gaul

[Col. 0533]

# Historical Notice on Saint Adalhard

(Mabill., *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, vol. IV, p. 306.)

[Col. 0533A]

1. Adalhard’s father was Bernartus or Bernard, son of Charles Martel, brother of King Pippin, and uncle of Charlemagne. Some say that this Bernard was born of a legitimate wife, others of a concubine. Their basis is that Charles Martel, in the division of the kingdom, took account only of Carloman, Pippin, and Grifo; he would also have taken account of Remigius, Jerome, and Bernard if they had been legitimate in the same way as the others.

This is Bernhart, uncle of Charlemagne, who, together with Charles himself, went to Italy “over Mount Jovis with part of the army” against Desiderius, king of the Lombards, in the year 773, as Einhard bears witness; and he is counted among the brothers recorded in the monastery of Saint Gall.

It has not yet been possible to learn the name and lineage of the wife by whom he had three sons—Adalhard, Wala, and Bernarius—and two daughters, Gundrada and Theodrada. I infer that she was Saxon from what Radbertus reports in Book I, chapter 12, of *The Life of Abbot Wala*: that Wala—and the same must be said of Adalhard—was “of Saxon descent.” Since this cannot be said of the paternal line, it must be understood of the maternal line.

Their paternal cousins through Jerome were Saint Folcuin, bishop of the Morini, and Fulradus, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Quentin. Saint Folcuin will be discussed below in his proper place.

2. Mejerus, Molanus, John Cosinus, and others report that Adalhard was born in a village of Belgium called Hustia (Huise). The place lies in the diocese of Tournai near the town of Aldernand (Audenarde), and is celebrated for the fountain and cult of Saint Adalhard.

Yet the following consideration causes difficulty: Hustia is said to have come into the possession of the monastery of Corbie not through Adalhard, but through Count Conrad. For in a more recent manuscript chronicle of that monastery I read that Odo, formerly abbot of Corbie and later bishop of Beauvais, having made an agreement with Aginelm, bishop of Tournai, “built the church of Hustia in the year 874, in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul, on the condition that it should remain under the jurisdiction of Corbie, and that the bishop of Tournai should provide the holy oil and chrism each year.”

Then these words are added:

> “And a certain Count Conrad had given this village of Hustia to the church of Corbie in the preceding year.”

Nevertheless, the same chronicle shows that Saint Adalhard possessed extensive property in Belgium. It says, concerning Abbot Hildebert, that in his time the Northmen, in the year 882, destroyed in many places the monastery of Corbie, then renowned among everyone, and burned all the patrimony of blessed Adalhard—namely Biringuae, Montem-Aquarum, Gomplae, and Molae, together with the neighboring castles.

All these estates lie in Belgium: Biringuae, commonly Beringhen, in the county of Liège, as also Montes-Aquarum, Montenac; Gomplae and Molae in the Brabant district called Campine. Many other properties in those regions are also said to have belonged to Saint Adalhard. All were alienated in the previous century; I do not know whether they will soon return to the possession of the abbey of Corbie.

Certainly, Einhard lists Adelhartus among the counts and leading men of Carloman, who was reigning in Austrasia, under the year 771. This shows that our Adalhard, who was then a count, belonged to the Austrasian kingdom, to which the province of Belgium belonged.

3. After making his profession of monastic life, the holy man held various offices piously and successfully. First of all, he was abbot of both Corbies: the old one in Gaul and the new one in Saxony, of which he was the principal founder together with his brother Wala. An ancient parchment codex contains a catalogue of the abbots of that place, ending with Abbot Ratoldus; other abbots are written in by a second hand.

4. In addition, Adalhard was the first of our number whom Charlemagne summoned to administer the kingdom:

> “so that he might form the kingdom of Italy, which had been entrusted to him, and its king, the younger Pippin, more honorably, usefully, justly, and prudently according to the condition of the state and the practice of religion.”

So says Radbertus, who also reports an outstanding encomium of him by Pope Leo. Adalhard’s brother Wala later undertook the same office, sent there by Emperor Louis together with Gerungus, master of the ushers:

> “so that Lothair might use their counsel both in household affairs and in matters pertaining to the advantage of the kingdom.”

After returning from Italy, Adalhard was regarded as “first among the counselors” of Charlemagne, as is clear from Hincmar; and he retained that dignity under Louis, as Paschasius testifies in chapter 52 of his *Life*.

5. Moreover, in the year 809 Charles Augustus sent him to Rome to Pope Leo, together with Bernarius, bishop of Worms, and Jesse, bishop of Amiens. Smaragdus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael in the county of Verdun, was also assigned to them as a companion, so that the dispute concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, which had arisen through John, a monk of Jerusalem, might be brought to an end.

This is established both from the records of the Councils of Gaul, from a conference held at Rome on this matter—which conference Smaragdus committed to writing—and from a letter of Leo to Bishop Riculfus.

Our abbot also attended the synod of Noyon at Oise in the year 814, according to Frodoardus, Book II, chapter 18.

6. Finally, he devoted himself not only to secular studies, in which he especially excelled for his time, but also to sacred learning. In this respect he was

> “a most distinguished imitator, as it were a follower, of the works of Father Augustine,”

and for this reason was called Aurelius Augustine, as Paschasius records in chapters 14 and 21 of the *Life*. In chapter 18 Paschasius also gives an excellent specimen of his eloquence and fearless zeal: a fragment of one of the many letters of Adalhard, all of which we lament have perished.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, praises his likewise-lost book *On the Order of the Palace* in his letter *On the Proper Instruction of a New and Young King*, chapter 12, in these words:

> “In my youth I first saw the old and wise Adalhard, related by blood to our lord Emperor Charles and abbot of the monastery of Corbie, first among the chief counselors. I read and copied his little book *On the Order of the Palace*.”

In volume IV of the *Spicilegium* there is a book *On the Statutes of the Monastery of Corbie*, composed at Adalhard’s command. In the published editions it is incomplete and interpolated, under this title:

> “A brief work which Adalhard, having returned to Corbie in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 822, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction, and in the eighth year of the reign of the glorious Louis Augustus, ordered to be made.”

In the same parchment codex from which these statutes were copied are found *The Chapters of Lord Abbot Adalhard on Admonitions in the Congregation*—that is, as I interpret them, summaries of the matters that he used to impress upon his monks while preaching.
