Finally, Frodoardus, in Book III, chapter 23, of his *History of Rheims*, testifies that Hincmar wrote to Odo, bishop of Beauvais,

> “concerning the date of the paschal moon and the reading which Abbot Adalhard composed on that subject.”

# Ancient Statutes of the Abbey of Saint Peter of Corbie, Prescribed for His Monks by Saint Adalhard, Abbot

(Apud Canisium, *Spicilegium*.)

[Col. 0535]

## Canisius’s Preliminary Notice

[Col. 0535B]

We have extracted the fragments of the statutes of old Corbie, which the most noble Adalhard, a most holy abbot, once prescribed for his monks after returning from exile in the year of Christ 822, from parchment papers belonging to the archive of that same abbey. They had indeed been written at that time, but had been somewhat damaged by decay and mildew; the characters repeatedly disappeared from sight, so that I was almost forced to guess.

I thought it worthwhile to clarify the obsolete and colloquial words used by that age, so that nothing would delay the reader. Moreover, the biographer of Saint Adalhard, Blessed Gerardus, mentions these statutes with praise in chapter 8, as follows:

> “Anyone who wishes to know how effective Adalhard was in the arrangements of his rule may read, not without great astonishment, in the book written about these matters. There he will also see how wisely the house of the church of Corbie was arranged by a wise man.”

Besides the fragments that I rescued from darkness and decay, only an index of sixty-one chapters remains.

That excellent abbot also published another book for forming the king’s mind in Christian morals and for properly and prudently instructing and restraining the ministers of the court, as Hincmar, an eyewitness, testifies in chapter 12 of his fourteenth letter:

> “In my youth I first saw the old and wise Adalhard, kinsman of our lord Emperor Charlemagne and abbot of the monastery of Corbie, first among the chief counselors. I read and copied his little book *On the Order of the Palace*, in which, among other things, it is stated that the condition of the entire kingdom consists principally in two divisions, with the judgment of almighty God always and everywhere placed first.”

[Note: The book to which Hincmar refers has been lost.]

[Col. 0535D]

## Ancient Statutes of the Abbey of Saint Peter

### Brief work that Adalhard ordered to be made after returning to Corbie in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 822, in the month of January, in the fifteenth indiction, and in the eighth year of the reign of the glorious Louis Augustus

## Book I

### Chapter One

[Col. 0535C]

These are the prebendaries [Note: *Provendarii*. If Acherius is to be believed, they were so called from *providere*, “to provide,” and are those whom we call in the vernacular *pourvoyeurs*; but Baluzius is much more correct when he maintains that this concerns a fixed number of canons, whom they call *praebendarii*.] who must always be equal in number and fully present in our days.

If one of them dies, another must immediately be appointed in his place, so that the number may always be complete, and no additional person may be added to that number.

Although there are now other superfluous clerics, such as Savaricus and several others assigned to that cell, or certain laymen there at the same cell, such as those Winedus, Geriola, and Bruningus the Saxon, or Germanus Bituradus, or any other clerics or laymen who may yet be sent there, they are not to be added to that number of 150. They must always be kept separately, and are then to be supplied according to what the person placed over them orders to be given to each at the proper times.

These 150, however, are always to be supplied according to one uniform arrangement in our days, just as they are supplied today through the individual offices—some in one way, others in another. It was unnecessary to write the details here, because daily practice makes them well known both to those who give and to those who receive; and the officials themselves each have their own brief instructions concerning this: the chamberlain, cellarer, and seneschal.

#### Concerning the clerics

There are twelve bell-ringers and seven other clerics. Of these, two are assigned to the cellarer, one to the brothers’ laundry, one to the abbot’s garden, and three to the infirmary. The other tasks that the clerics must perform are to be carried out by the bell-ringers.

It is therefore necessary to appoint there men who can perform all the interior tasks, who belong to our household, and who dare not refuse anything. As far as possible they should be officials, and, within their office or religious order, after the provost and dean they should answer to the keeper of Saint John. They must not be left entirely without supervision, lest, because of some disgraceful conduct, their religious order bring blasphemy upon the monastery.

#### Concerning the laymen likewise

There are twelve matricularii [Note: *Matricularii*. Acherius continues explaining the obscure names. *Matricularii*: *marguilliers*—church wardens, guardians, or administrators of churches, or even those who care for the poor. *Cavalarii*: horsemen or drivers. *Pergaminarius*: one who prepares parchment. *Saminator* or *samiator*: one who sharpens a whetstone. *Fusarii*: the same as *fusores* (founders or casters). *Gararii*: those whom we call *gruyers*, who oversee the cutting of woodland. *Mattiones*: those who prepare food.] and thirty laymen.

To the first chamber: six; three shoemakers; two horsemen; one fuller.

To the second chamber: fourteen. Of these, one to the chamber; six heavy smiths; two goldsmiths; two shoemakers; two shield-makers; one parchment-worker; one sharpener; three founders or casters.

To the third chamber: three.

To the cellar and pantry: two doorkeepers.

To the infirmary: one.

Woodland wardens: two.

To the woodshed at the bakery: one.

To the middle gate: one.

Carpenters: four.

Cooks or food-preparers: four.

Doctors: two.

To the vassals’ house: two.

These are inside the monastery.

These, however, are outside the monastery:

To the mill: twelve.

To the fishery: six.

To the stable: two.

To the gardens: eight.

To the laundry [Note: *Buria*. Acherius continues: *buria* is a place where linen is whitened, or where dirt is washed away with lye, French *buerie*. *Arboreta*: a place planted with trees. *Berbicarii*: shepherds of sheep, French *bergers*. *Vivarium*: a place where fish are raised, a fishpond.]: seven.

To the new orchard: two.

Shepherds: two.

To the fishpond: five.

### Chapter II
These, then, are the thirteen days on which, for the love of God and in honor of the holy days, they are to be given—apart from their regular allowance, and, if possible, in addition to it, or at least such a consolation is to be provided: namely, one vassal’s loaf between two men, of the kind made thirty to the modius; and to each person half a pound of every kind of pottage; and to each a full cup, if there is enough, of wine, or otherwise of the brothers’ beer. The Nativity of the Lord; the Theophany; the Mass of Lady Balthildis; and on that same day, from the chamberlain’s department; the Purification of Saint Mary; Sunday, the beginning of Lent; Maundy Thursday; Easter; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; the Mass of Saint John the Baptist; of Saint Peter; of Saint Martin; and of Saint Andrew.

Likewise, these are the days on which they are to be excused from secular labor [*opere dominico*: from service owed to their lords, as Acherius understood it]—except for whatever pertains to preparing food: the Nativity of the Lord; Saint Stephen’s Day; Saint John’s Day; the Feast of the Innocents; the Octave of the Lord; the Theophany; the Mass of Lady Balthildis; the Purification of Saint Mary; the first day of the Lenten fasts, so that they may have time to renew their confessions; Maundy Thursday; Good Friday; Holy Saturday; Wednesday in Easter week; the Rogations, for three days; the Ascension of the Lord; Saint John the Baptist’s Day; Saint Peter’s Day; Saint Marcellinus’s Day; Saint Firminus’s Day; Saint Martin’s Day; Saint Andrew’s Day; the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord; and those days of the four Ember seasons.

## CHAPTER III

These are the things that are to be given to our clerics, the canons written above, who are specifically called the bell-ringers.

As clothing: two white tunics and a third of another color; four hose; two pairs of breeches; two felt socks [*soccos filtrinos*: the more obscure names occurring in this chapter are interpreted by Acherius as follows. *Socci* are a type of footwear, French *soques*; they are to be made of felt, that is, of the thicker cloth called *feutre*. *Solae* are slippers, *pantoufles*. *Vuanti*, or *guanti*, are gloves, *gants*. To these are added *mulfolae*, elsewhere *mulfulae*, which may be called *mouffles* or *mitaines*, and which are larger gloves. Next comes *pellicia*, apparently either a garment of skins, commonly called a *pellisson*, or what is called an *aumusse*. *Cottum*, also called *lectarium* or *sagum*, is a square cloak or a covering used for beds. *Capella* is a diminutive of *cappa*. *Hroccus*, or *cuculla*, is the outermost garment, covering the whole body from the head; from this comes *rochetum*.]; four shoes with new soles [*solis*], except for eight denarii for footwear; two pairs of gloves; and two pairs of mittens. All this is to be supplied annually.

A cloak of serge, a fur garment, a *cottum* or bed-covering, or a *sagum*, they are to receive in the third year. All these things are to be taken from the clothing that the brothers return when they receive new garments, and the most useful items that can be found among them are to be selected for these men. As for the small cloak and the *hroccus*, or *cuculla*, of serge—or the serge from which a *hroccus* can be made—that is to be left to the prior’s discretion.

## CHAPTER IV

We decree that forty-five loaves made of mixed grain [*de mixtura*: what we call *de méteil*, mixed loaves; *spelta* is a kind of grain, which some call *vicia*], each weighing three and a half pounds, and five loaves of wheat or spelt, of the kind received by the vassals, are to be given daily to the hospital of the poor, making fifty loaves in all.

These loaves are to be distributed as follows: the twelve poor who remain there overnight are each to receive one loaf, and on the following day each is to receive half a loaf for the journey. The two hospital attendants who serve there are each to receive one loaf from the number specified above. The five wheat loaves are to be divided among the clerical travelers who are brought to the refectory for provisions and the sick who are maintained there. We nevertheless entrust the distribution of these loaves to the hospital attendant’s judgment, so that, if a larger number of poor arrive, or if some need more or less—such as those weakened by hunger or very small children—he may distinguish among them according to what is appropriate.

If at any time fewer poor should happen to arrive, the hospital attendant and his senior, the gatekeeper, are to keep fully in mind how much less than the number specified above has been distributed because of the small number of arrivals, so that, when more come, what remained may be distributed.

To the other poor who arrive and depart on the same day, a *quartarius* is customarily given—or, as we have said, a portion of *companaticus* according to what the hospital attendant judges suitable for a greater or smaller number or for their need.

As for drink, half a modius is to be given daily, that is, eight *sextarii*. Four *sextarii* are to be divided among the twelve persons mentioned above, so that each receives two cups. Of the other four, six cups are to be given to the clerics whose feet are washed by the brothers, one cup to each, and one cup to Willerannus the servant. Whatever remains we leave to the hospital attendant’s discretion, so that he may distribute it among the sick or the other poor.

As for wine, the matter is to be left to the prior’s discretion [*Prioris*. Another manuscript adds: “As for the laymen who, because of the benefice they hold, serve the abbot, the prior, or the provosts, inside or outside, whether riding or performing service, we decree that at the Nativity of the Lord and at Easter they are to have either two *sextarii* of beer or one *sextarius* of wine—not by hereditary right, but as an act of charity or in honor of the place. This, however, is to be at the will of the abbot, the prior, and the provosts.”].

The senior gatekeeper is to provide, according to his ability, for the needs of the sick, whether in food or drink, using whatever supplies the hospital attendant lacks for the care of the sick.

If travelers from distant provinces should arrive in numbers exceeding those specified above, the gatekeeper is to provide them with what is necessary, so that nothing is diminished from what has been allocated for the ordinary days.

## CHAPTER V

We also add, for the *companaticus* of the poor’s food, thirty *pensas*, distributed between cheese and bacon, and thirty modii of legumes; one fifth of the tithe that the gatekeeper receives from the cellarer in eels or fresh cheese, which he is appointed to provide from ten sheepfolds; and likewise of that which is given as a tithe from the lord’s demesne estates.

Similarly, one fifth of the entire tithe from livestock—that is, from calves, sheep, and everything given from the flocks to the gatekeeper, including horses—is to be added.

Moreover, we have arranged that the hospital attendant himself is to receive one fifth of all silver that comes to the gate, through the hands of the senior gatekeeper. We wish the following arrangement to be made concerning this silver: not less than four denarii are to be given each day; and if the amount of that fifth is insufficient for making this daily distribution, the abbot, if he wishes, is to supplement it from elsewhere; if it increases beyond that amount, nothing is to be withheld.

The gatekeeper is to provide wood for the poor according to custom, as well as the other things not written here, such as cloth for beds, vessels, and everything else of that kind. All the things written above that come to the gate are to be given for the purpose of supplementing the silver, as mentioned above.

In addition, the hospital attendant is to receive from the chamberlain old clothing or footwear belonging to the brothers, to be given to the poor according to custom.

We therefore beseech all to whom an office in this monastery has been assigned to attend, in generosity and distribution, rather to God’s will than to the example of our parsimony, since each person will render an account for himself.

## CHAPTER VI

The account, or quantity, of grain or bread—how, from where, and how much is to come annually to the monastery, and how the keeper of the bread is to distribute it.

We wish seven hundred and fifty well-winnowed and cleaned *corbi* of spelt to arrive each year, each *corbus* containing twelve modii, well leveled and scraped according to this new modius which the lord emperor established.

This grain is to come from those estates which the provost specifically holds in his office; if necessary, from all of them, but otherwise from those which he has considered with the abbot.

We have arranged this quantity in this way so that for each day of the year, of which there are 365, there will always be two *corbi*. Together these amount to 730 *corbi*. We ordered twenty to be added so that there would be a surplus rather than a shortage.

Although this grain sometimes yields better flour and sometimes worse, and at times more and at times less, we nevertheless estimate moderately and hope that ten modii can always be obtained from those two *corbi*. Thus, thirty modii produce three hundred loaves each day.

Since we are certain that at all times there will always be at least three hundred people permanently residing inside, together with those who arrive at the monastery—although at present we number no more than 350—and since at times we may perhaps number fewer than four hundred and at other times more, we wish to arrange matters as though we were always four hundred, so that when we are fewer than four hundred a surplus will accumulate from which an abundant provision can be made when we are more numerous. It nevertheless rarely happens that we are more numerous, whereas it happens very often that we are far fewer than four hundred.

Let us therefore add four modii, which come daily from the mills and produce 120 loaves; add these together, and there are 420 loaves. Thus we have provision not only for the four hundred, who are rare, but also daily for twenty more, who are rarer still.

But because we always prefer that all our resources, which are to be distributed by our officials, should increase rather than fall short, we add one further modius from what comes from the mills. This produces 450 loaves daily, from fifteen modii.

Taken together, the daily total is fifteen modii; over the year it is 5,475 modii. Let us also add twenty from those mills, and the total becomes 5,500. Of these, 3,650 modii are to come from spelt; the remaining 1,850 are to come from the mills.

Therefore, since, as we said above, we prefer that there be a surplus rather than a shortage, we ordered twenty *corbi* to be added at the outset, as well as a daily provision of loaves beyond the 400 allowance, and a further twenty-five modii, although, as stated above, we are usually fewer than 400, or certainly more than 400.

And since oxen, pigs, various birds, dogs, and sometimes horses must be fed at the mill itself, we add another 150 modii from those mills. The total that is to come from the mills thus becomes 2,000 modii.

For the present, let these provisions be stated and maintained in this form, until we can consider together whether it is necessary to add or subtract anything. Nevertheless, we admonish and beseech the keeper of the bread not to neglect learning with the utmost diligence whatever can be known from measures or from the number of days in the weeks or months of the whole year, so that when the time for alteration comes he will know how to report to us how the present year has passed under his administration.

To make this easier for him to determine, let him first set aside the provisions for the servants, which are always measured and distributed in equal quantities, and whose number is always fixed—unless it should occasionally be smaller, for it is never larger.

Next, let him assess the brothers’ bread: when they eat once a day and when they eat twice a day. Let him always keep separate the amount assigned for their use, and consider how much is consumed during the period when they always eat once a day, how much when they always eat twice a day, how much in one week during the time of minimum consumption, and how much in one week during the time of maximum consumption. We believe that he will thereby be able to determine approximately how much bread, or how many modii, must be allocated for their use.

All who receive the brothers’ bread are to be included in this number, except guests, who do not receive it daily. He must take care not to prepare so much of the brothers’ bread at one time that too much remains and becomes hard. If he does so, when he is testing that quantity, the bread itself is to be removed and another portion put in its place.

Since, as we have said, we eat once a day at one time and twice a day at another, and since now we are more numerous and now fewer, and can never determine exactly what our number ought to be, if he can find another and better method for testing this, let him adopt it with God’s help.

The same applies to our vassals, and likewise to those at the gate. Their number cannot be fixed; but if he begins to estimate, in the sense described above, how much is given by days, weeks, and months—at the minimum, the average, and the maximum—we believe that he will be able to determine what will suffice for the whole year.

For the bell-ringers, the schoolboys, and the remaining clerics or laymen, whether ours or outsiders, it can easily be determined how he is able to provide for them.

We also admonish him not to neglect considering that the bread distributed is not given to everyone according to one measure: to some a larger amount is given, and to others a smaller amount. It is therefore necessary for him to consider, for each of the various measures of bread, how many larger, medium-sized, or smaller loaves can be made from one modius. We hope that, once this has been done, everything will become clear to him.

Behold, this is what we have been able to devise—not in order to establish it permanently in this exact form, but so that, by beginning to test it, we may learn how in the future we ought to maintain what grain must come to the monastery under the divisions set out above. We hope that this can be determined properly: first, the provision for our servants or registered poor, who are always to be counted equally; second, for the brothers; third, for the vassals; fourth, for the guests; fifth, for the bell-ringers or schoolboys; sixth, for the individual recipients of allowances here and there. Of the last group, however, as we have said, we cannot establish any number that will always remain constant.

## CHAPTER VII

Concerning mills and exchanges, we wish the following arrangement to be observed.

First, each miller is to be given a homestead and six *bonuaria* of land [*Bonuaria*: an obscure word, which can be understood only conjecturally. Acherius suspects that it should be read as “six *bovaria*,” that is, areas which six oxen can plow in a day], because we wish him to have the means to accomplish what is ordered of him and to preserve his milling income. That is, he is to have oxen and the rest of the livestock with which he can work; enough to support himself and his entire household; to raise pigs, geese, and chickens; to repair the mill; to bring all the timber and other materials needed to repair it; to repair the sluice; to bring millstones; and to possess and perform everything else required there.

For this reason, we do not wish him to perform any other service—whether with a cart, with a horse, by working with his hands, plowing, sowing, gathering crops or hay, making malt, carrying manure, hauling wood, or doing anything else for the lord’s work. He is to serve only himself and his mill.

The pigs, geese, and chickens which he is required to fatten from the resources of his mill are to be fed from those resources; he is to pay the eggs; and he is to take care only of those things which, as we have said, must be done for the mill or which must come from the mill.

When we said above that two modii were to come from the mills to the monastery for our use, we did not mean that this other milling income should be separated from the granary. We meant that he should test this year whether it is necessary to add or subtract anything, and whether it will suffice for the specified recipients and for the works carried out each year in the monastery, such as the grape harvest, the gardens, the meadows, and similar activities, so that it can sustain this number throughout the year.

We also wish him to have the earlier modii assessed before those millers according to this new modius, with complete equality, determining how many modii of the former measure make up the present measure; and according to these modii, let them henceforth pay their rent, whether in grain or in malt.

We wish each of the millers to have full responsibility for maintaining six mill wheels. If they do not wish to maintain six, but only half of that responsibility—that is, three wheels—he is to have only half of the land belonging to the homestead, namely three *bonuaria*, and his associate the other three. Between the two of them they are to render the full milling income and perform the full service required for that one mill, whether concerning the work, the sluice, the bridge, or everything else assigned to the individual mills.

# BOOK II

This is the regulation of the gardens.

## CHAPTER I

So that the brothers who are required to work in the gardens may fulfill the office entrusted to them for the common benefit without annoyance or any improper inconvenience, we decree that the reeves of the following estates are to make the necessary dwellings and fences, and repair them whenever necessary:

For the first gate, which is beside the fishpond, the estates of Waniacum and Cipiliacum; for the second, the estate of Villa; for the third, the estates of Albiniacum and Cerisiacum; for the fourth, those of Vernis and Taziacum.

Those same reeves are likewise to provide, each for the garden he serves, in the third year, one plow with a yoke, an *amblacium*, and *conjuncti*, whenever necessary; and in the fourth year, a harrow [*erptia*, or *erpica*, an instrument for breaking up clods, French *herse*], for cultivating the garden, always by the feast of Saint Marcellinus.

When the season arrives in which it is necessary to clear the gardens of harmful weeds—that is, from the middle of April to the middle of October—every twenty days, without negligence or any withholding, each of these reeves is to come to the brother who tends the garden, whom he is required to assist, in order to see and ask when it is necessary to send weeders there.

Once the young leeks and leeks have been transplanted, and likewise the shallots, garlic, and onions, the reeves are to weed only these whenever necessary, as has been said. Whenever the household comes together for this weeding, the reeve himself, or the dean—one of the two—is absolutely to be present there to ensure that the workers perform their task diligently and usefully.

The gardeners are to receive carts from the *bura* every year according to custom. They are to receive all iron tools from the chamberlain, who provides the smiths according to the common custom. If any tools are broken, the gardener is to show them to the chamberlain, who is to have them repaired or give him another tool and take back the broken one. Likewise, whenever they need to be repaired in any manner, they are to be requested from the chamberlain.

Each gardener is to have, for cultivating the garden or meeting other needs, six digging tools, two flat spades, two axes, one adze, two large and small drills, one chisel, one *gulbium*, and two sickles, one scythe, two wooden chests, one knife, and one saw [*fossorii*, that is, mattocks; *bessi*, flat mattocks, called *bêches*; *taratra*, augers, *tarières*; *scalpra*, *ratissoires*; *gulbium*, or *gurbium*, a tool for extracting obstructing objects; *falcilia*, sickles; *trunci*, wooden chests. Next come *banstae*, that is, flailing sticks suitable for threshing, *fléaux*].

The other vessels belonging to this office, such as winnowing baskets, flails, or any other similar items, are to be requested by the gardener from the abbot whenever the old ones wear out; the abbot is to provide assistance by which he can acquire others.

We also decree that, for hiring workers to raise the beds in autumn, to assist with planting at the proper time, and to weed in summer whenever necessary, each gardener-brother is to receive, in installments, one hundred provision-loaves. The brother responsible for supplying the brothers’ bread is to provide these loaves; they are not to be given all at once, but the dispenser is to distribute them to the gardener as the gardener needs them, until the prescribed number has been completed, if the gardener requires the whole amount.

Each gardener is also to receive from the cellarer one modius of beer, in the same manner as the bread is supplied—not all at once, but in portions, when and as much as the gardener needs and requests, until the stated measure has been completed. Each is also to receive one modius of legumes.

The abbot is to give each gardener five solidi per year for hiring workers, as we have said. They are not to seek hired labor elsewhere unless it is within the monastery.

For the rest, each brother is to bring to the abbot, at the proper time and without any reduction, whatever he is able to obtain from his garden beyond the garlands [*servidas*, or *servias*, garlands or bundles made from herbs or flowers] that they are required to make for the brothers.

We have arranged that each of them is to have an ox of his own, so that without hindrance he may cultivate only those things required for the gardens.

We especially admonish the gardeners to avoid entirely making any dishonest profit or asking anything from the neighbors.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning the *meirae* on the feasts of the saints.

At the Nativity of the Lord, three; on Saint Stephen’s Day, two; on Saint John’s Day, two; on the Feast of the Innocents, one; on Saint Silvester’s Day, one; on the Octave of the Lord, one; on the Theophany, two; on the Octave of Epiphany, one; on Saint Agnes’s Day, one; on the dedication of Saint John and of Balthildis, one; on the Purification of Saint Mary, two; on Saint Agatha’s Day, one; on Saint Vedast’s Day, one; on Saint Gregory’s Day, one; on Saint Benedict’s Day, one; on the Annunciation of Saint Mary, one; on the feast of Philip and James, two; on Saint John the Baptist’s Day, one; on Saint Peter’s Day, two; on Saint Paul’s Day, one; on Saint Martin’s Day, one; on Saint James’s Day, one; on the dedication of Saint Peter, one; on the dedication of Saint Stephen, one; on Saint Lawrence’s Day, one; on the Assumption of Saint Mary, one; on Saint Bartholomew’s Day, one; on Saint John’s Day, one; on the Nativity of Saint Mary, one; on Saint Matthew’s Day, one; on Saint Maurice’s Day, one; on Saint Firminus’s Day, one; on Saint Michael’s Day, one; on Saint Dionysius’s Day, one; on the feast of Simon and Jude, one; on All Saints’ Day, two; on Saint Quentin’s Day, one; on Saint Martin’s Day, one; on Saint Cecilia’s Day, one; on Saint Andrew’s Day, one; on Fuscianus and Victoricus, one; on Saint Thomas’s Day, one; on Maundy Thursday, two; on Holy Saturday, one; on Holy Easter, three, and throughout the whole week, two; on the Ascension of the Lord, two; at Pentecost, three; after the grape harvest, one; on Sundays, forty-eight; likewise forty-eight on Saturdays; and on the feasts of the saints, fifty.

[*De meiris*: Acherius interprets *meirae* as that which is temporarily handed over as payment for service rendered. In French, *mereaux*: a token, or counter; later, when the opportunity arose, the counter was returned and money was counted out.]

## CHAPTER III

A record of the meals which the cellarer is to provide.

From the estate-farms, one for Bishop Hilmerad and his brother Hengarius, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June. Another, on the day before the Nones of June, for Herirardus and Gundrado. On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May: the anniversary of Judith [*Anniversary of Judit*: the reading was *vidit*. These events certainly cannot belong to Adalhard, since not only Judit but also Louis the Pious survived him by many years.].

The anniversary of Judit. On the Ides of June, the Nativity of King Charles. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of July, the anniversary of the emperor Louis.

In administering the refectory, until something better is found—as we have likewise said concerning our other dwellings—the following arrangement may perhaps appropriately be maintained.

First, the junior cellarer is to place each brother’s double portion before him in equal measure. Then, if because of some need arising at any time—because of guests or irregular weather—it should be necessary, a mature brother is to be assigned to him, whose conscience will make everyone confident that he will add or subtract nothing from anyone except according to legitimate measure.

If the lord abbot, the provost, or the dean orders the drink of a sick person to be changed for one, two, three, or somewhat more days, the junior cellarer himself, the person assisting him, or anyone else is in no way to presume either to give the same change to another person or to extend it to the same person beyond the days specified.

All other matters belonging to proper decorum, whether they are to be administered or provided for the sake of guests, the table of the seniors, or the brothers generally, are to fall under the care of the junior cellarer, so that no one entering, leaving, or staying there—or arriving, as has been said—may encounter anything in its use or in any less worthy arrangement that has not been properly cleaned.

Those matters that specifically belong to the cooks are indeed to be provided for by the cooks themselves with the greatest diligence. Nevertheless, the aforementioned cellarer must not set aside this concern, but must always provide cautiously and admonish them, lest the aforesaid cooks presume in any way to neglect what has been entrusted to them, until, at the end of the week, they return the vessels of their ministry clean and intact, as the Rule commands.

The senior cellarer, both inside and outside—that is, in the refectory, in the kitchen, and in all the rooms belonging to the kitchen—is to exercise care in every matter and for every person, so that no one there, by acting or speaking immoderately, may presume to handle either himself or the things he is doing except in a manner wholly appropriate to our religious life.

The same cellarer is not to be asked or required to involve himself, as though from personal devotion, in preparing the pottages, thereby postponing the aforesaid care in any way. Rather, according to the authority of the Rule, he is to seek another assistant if necessary, so that he himself may remain free to attend on every side to the matters of God.

We do not say this to obstruct his devotion when it can be practiced without hindering the concern mentioned above, but so that, while he immerses himself more devoutly in matters that do not belong to him at that time, he may not presume to postpone the definite duty imposed upon him of providing proper oversight.

Nor should the cellarer claim that he does not know in what matters or concerning what things the aforesaid cooks are to be admonished to act or not to act.

## CHAPTER IV

The following matters are especially to be observed among the rest.

First, concerning every matter that does not contribute to this office at the time, silence is to be maintained.

Next, so that this silence may be maintained there by all with the fruit of another reward, psalms are to be sung without interruption. As long as two of them are present, those same psalms are never to be omitted.

If it should happen that one of them goes farther away to attend to some necessary duty, and for this reason is perhaps unable to continue singing the psalm alone, as soon as he returns to the place where he finds the others singing psalms, he is to enter and strive to sing with them for as long as he remains with them.

The same applies to another, or a third, if he has gone away from there: upon returning, he is to join those singing psalms.

If a circumstance should arise—as sometimes happens—in which all of them are so occupied that no one can run through the psalm from memory while singing, as soon as anyone recalls the interrupted psalm, he is to resume it at the place where he left it, and all the others who are free are to move their mouths together with him in praise of the Lord.

If it should happen that no one remembers where he left off the psalm he had begun, he is to begin at the nearest point that he remembers having sung previously. They are not to neglect the work they have begun until, after everything has been completed with which and in which this same practice could be maintained, each returns, as reason dictates, to the remaining tasks, always preserving silence as far as possible.

Lest these matters also fall from anyone’s mind because of the earlier discussion, we repeat briefly that there are three things on which the whole arrangement depends: either to refrain from unnecessary speech, to say what is necessary, or to sing psalms.

Nor is the following ever to be neglected as though it were merely a matter of maintaining order. It may happen that the same order requires all the younger brothers, or even those who are less prudent or less steadfast, to be sent into the kitchen. In that case, leaving aside the same arrangement, a mature and steadfast senior is to be added to the younger men, one who, moved by zeal for God, will strive to guard both himself and the others.

When his period of service has ended, the person who was transferred for this reason is again to enter together with the seniors. Thus it is to be observed in every way at all times that only those who are foolish because of advanced age, or less perfect because of youth, are never sent alone—those in whom there is no confidence that they can preserve this sort of justice. Rather, as stated above, one or two mature men are always to be sent each week, so that both the will of God within, like sons, and proper sobriety outwardly may always be maintained.

If anyone wishes to teach that this should not be done, but that the order should always be maintained according to the arrangement by which they sit at the tables, he is not to be listened to. Instead, he is to be firmly rebuked for thinking otherwise; and if he does not desist from this presumption and become patiently obedient, he is to be restrained more severely until he obeys the sounder counsel.

We say these things so openly and repeatedly for the sake of the simpler—and, to put it more strongly, the more foolish—lest anyone excuse himself on the grounds of ignorance.

To ensure that these provisions can be maintained, the dean and the cellarer are always, several days in advance, to arrange matters so that this assignment is not disturbed in any way: neither because of someone’s illness, nor because of a journey, if one should occur, nor because of any new necessity that arises, nor even because of any command of the lord abbot or the provost.

After these provisions have been made for continual observance, the following must not be omitted: whenever he has time, the cellarer is always personally to place those portions before the individuals, lest another, out of favor toward someone, give him more or less than he ought to receive. He himself is to distribute according to the definite and proper need, since he ought to know the infirmities and needs of each person.

If he does not have time, the person whom he appoints is to do this in his place, always taking care that no fault begins to arise there.

## CHAPTER V

As for the laymen, there is one definite rule: as long as food is being prepared or prepared food is being served—whether when the brothers are first fed together or when they eat afterward—no layman is to enter.

If there are things of this kind that must either be prepared beforehand or cleaned or cared for afterward, a window, doorway, or some other designated place outside the kitchen is to be established where the brothers may either receive what is to be prepared or return what has been cleaned, and where the laymen may place those things or receive what has been set down, so that they have no occasion to enter the kitchen.

Among such things, the following come to mind: herbs of every kind, which are to be brought in, cleaned, and arranged for making pottage. Likewise, whenever necessary, fish are to be gutted and scaled; legumes of various kinds are to be washed or prepared; and other things of this sort are to be handled completely and decently outside the kitchen, in the places assigned to them, whenever necessary.

They are to take the greatest care to place or arrange these things in a suitable location where the brothers can properly receive them. Nevertheless, as has been said, at the times specified above they are to abstain utterly from entering the kitchen.

Wood likewise, which must be carried in, split, or suitably prepared, is to be brought abundantly through the window, as we have said, or through a suitable entrance, so that neither the laymen need enter among the brothers nor the brothers need go out to them for this reason.

Perhaps such a multiplicity of instructions will not seem burdensome to anyone, since we have chosen to set out each matter individually according to its apparent necessity rather than leave anyone, as though ignorant of what he ought to do, an opportunity for overstepping the rule.

The cellarer is to strive, as he has time each day, to oversee all these matters, so that no fault may arise there, until, by God’s authority, everything that ought properly and decently to be done there becomes customary, and no novice may transgress through ignorance.

We assign all these matters to the cellarer’s oversight because we neither wish nor permit anyone in that office or workplace to be rebellious or contradictory toward him. But if—God forbid—it should happen that the senior or junior cellarer does not carefully observe these and similar rules belonging to the office, and, after being admonished a second time, does not correct himself, then, if he is not worthy to remain, he is to leave with a fitting reprimand; but the order is to remain undisturbed and unconfused.

## CHAPTER VI
These matters too, briefly recalled concerning what is to be observed inside the church at the hours when the Work of God is celebrated, seem not improperly to be added here—subject always, as before, to whatever more careful or superior arrangement the Lord may grant. [Col. 0548C] If it is summer, after these hours have been completed, following which everyone must immediately proceed together to the refectory, all ought to remain silently in the church until, on hearing the signal, they reverently give due honor to God and depart. Entering, sitting down, and leaving the refectory in the prescribed silence, each person should attend to whatever, according to the time, reason indicates or command has required. If it is winter and the need for warming oneself arises, then, as the person in charge sees fit, an interval may be made either before or after some office has been completed, so that they may warm themselves; otherwise, they should wait in the church, as stated above. This too concerning these matters.

Concerning the dormitory: for those who wish to understand the matter properly, everything can be summed up in this—that [Col. 0548D] at no time should anything improper be done there, nor should anything be done improperly. To recall some of these rules, so that the others resembling them may not be neglected through forgetfulness: when speaking is permitted—for conversation must always be regulated there—whether two, three, or even more persons join together, as usually happens when they rise from chapter, they should do so accordingly. But when it is time to sleep, whether by day or by night, just as complete silence must be maintained in the mouth, so also the utmost care must be exercised in one’s movements, so that no one suffers injury. No one should shake out his clothing, climb into or descend from bed carelessly, or do anything else of the kind that produces noise through clatter or causes inconvenience to anyone. [Col. 0549A] At all times, therefore, as has been said, every precaution must be observed there, both for the sake of propriety and for the rest of the sick, lest, if someone is compelled by necessity to seek rest there, he be disturbed by another’s misconduct. If anyone sits on his little bed to read, he should by no means invite another there for conversation. But if they have a need to speak at length, they should go outside and talk there. For, even if one is placed far from the other, the sound carries; and, for the propriety or custom of the house itself, two persons should never sit or stand together there for conversation. These matters, briefly stated among the many others that must be observed in the dormitory, lest they be despised as though worthless by foolish persons or by those who press matters more harshly than they ought, must be supervised [Col. 0549B] at all times not only by the superior, the dean, or the other deans, but also by the attendants themselves during the hours when the brothers are free for reading; and any violations discovered must be punished more strictly. In the *piselum*, however, when it is necessary to use that place, nearly the same care and propriety must be observed in all respects—except for what concerns sleeping—as we have said concerning the dormitory. If anything pertains particularly to that same building, such as soaked cloths being hung up, or those who are sluggish and sleepy, or those who read less attentively because of the pleasant warmth, and any similar matters, no one who bears even a small share of the responsibility imposed for supervising such things is unaware, from daily practice, what must be done about them. [Col. 0549C] When the unsuitable hours have passed and the permitted time for conversation and joining together has arrived, propriety—often mentioned above—must nevertheless always be observed there, as in every other place, whether there are few or many present, in speaking and in acting; it must never be postponed or despised.

## Concerning the provisioned servants

Concerning the monastery gate and matters pertaining to it, we have deliberately inserted nothing among the subjects treated above, because we judged that whatever concerns the gate or its ministers, from the tithes, should be arranged separately by itself, with the Lord indicating the way. First, therefore, it must be stated that a definite measure must be maintained regarding the provisioned servants who are to serve there, so that they are sufficient in number but in no way more numerous than necessary. [Col. 0550A] Since they are to be fed and clothed from that same tithe, they should receive the measure appropriate to them, so that they suffer neither shortage nor excessive abundance.

It has therefore seemed to us that ten provisioned servants should be sufficient for those who must receive and serve guests. Likewise, these provisioned servants should be supported with food and drink of the same quality and quantity as our other provisioned servants: that is, they should receive a monthly allowance according to the custom established for the others, and likewise bread and drink according to that same custom. Clothing and footwear, as stated above, they should receive in due measure, so that they are neither filthy from nakedness [Col. 0550B] nor marked by any other disgrace; but, on the other hand, they must not presume to demand more than their proper measure. This concerning the provisioned servants.

It therefore seems to us that, if the entire tithe from everything and in every respect is given as has been established, it ought to be wholly sufficient for all such needs, whether of the rich or of the poor. This includes whatever, for the sake of almsgiving, is freely granted to churches or to the brothers for the monastery in various bodily provisions or movable goods. Likewise, whatever is acquired in any manner through various kinds of labor, or is raised among different kinds of livestock, or is spontaneously produced in those livestock by God’s dispensation without human provision, such as milk and wool. Likewise hay, and whatever grows freely on trees, such as fodder or fruits of various kinds, should be supplied, as far as circumstances permit, according to the quality and quantity of each thing and as the season allows, so that they may suffice. And so that what we are saying may become clearer, first everything from our estates situated in the Ambianese, Atrabatine, or Beauvais territory should be supplied fully, as mentioned above. Then, if perhaps the distance makes it impossible to bring the household dependents, a good solution remains [Col. 0550C], with the Lord indicating it: because of this, neither should the tithe remain unused, nor should any fault arise among the poor.

[Col. 0549]

## Epitaph of Saint Adalhard

(*Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 426.)

Here lies the venerable abbot, eminent in merits,  
Our Adalhard, an old man worthy of honor.  
Of royal lineage, by right a citizen of paradise,  
A good man in charity, character, and faith.  
You who recall him beneath the tomb, whoever you are, traveler,  
See what you are and what you will be, since death snatches everything away.  
For after the Lord’s octave he was released from the flesh here,  
And on the following day he joyfully sought the stars.

[Col. 0551]

## Charters of Corbie

(See vol. CIV of *Patrologia*, among the diplomas of Louis the Pious.)

[Col. 0551]

## In the Year of the Lord 826

Ermoldus Nigellus: *The Elegiac Poem of Ermoldus Nigellus Concerning the Deeds of Louis the Pious, from the Year 781 to the Year 826*, first published by Ludovico Antonio Muratori from a very ancient codex of the imperial library at Vienna.

[Col. 0551]

## Bouquet’s Notice Concerning Ermold’s Poem

[Col. 0551A] I had read in Peter Lambecius, *Commentaries on the Imperial Library at Vienna*, book II, chapter 5, that the same library possessed a manuscript codex containing the poem of Ermoldus Nigellus concerning the deeds of Louis the Pious. Lambecius himself had indeed promised to publish the poem, but death destroyed his plan. I had also heard that Johann Benedikt Gentilott, prefect of that library, had undertaken the task; but, when the work had been prepared for the press, he was summoned to Rome to serve as auditor of the Rota and, finally, scarcely after he had been appointed bishop of Trent, he died.

When it seemed that no hope remained that the Nigellian poem—so often promised, so eagerly desired, and destined to be a great ornament to our Collection—would soon come to light, I resolved to leave nothing unattempted in order to obtain a copy. I had already asked Dom Bernard de Montfaucon to arrange, through his many friends in Germany or, if necessary, through the Most August Emperor—whose kindness and benevolent disposition toward him he had often experienced—for a transcript of the poem to be made for me. Then, behold, the most learned man Philipp Argelati, a leading member among the Palatine associates who assist Ludovico Antonio Muratori in collecting and illustrating the writers of Italian affairs, sent me the second part of the second volume of the Muratorian Collection.

I was exceedingly delighted when, on opening this volume, the elegiac poem of Ermoldus Nigellus first presented itself to me. But I was filled with far greater joy when, after reading it attentively, I discovered outstanding material that would shed much light on the history of that period.

[Col. 0552A] Muratori adorned the poem with a very learned preface and highly learned notes. In his preface he endeavors at length to show that Ermold was abbot of the monastery of Aniane. He correctly observes that the monastery from which Ermold had been torn away, and to which he asks to return, belonged to Pippin’s kingdom, or to Aquitaine. But he wrongly places the monastery of Aniane in Aquitaine, for it is clear from Louis the Pious’s constitution concerning the monasteries that must provide gifts and military service to the king [Note: [Col. 0551D] See *Patrologia*, vol. XCVII, col. 423] that it was situated in Septimania. Moreover, the charter concerning the division of the empire among the sons of Louis the Pious, made in the year 817 [Note: [Col. 0552D] See the same volume, col. 373], makes it clear that Pippin possessed nothing in Septimania except the district of Carcassonne.

It therefore remains uncertain what abbey Nigellus governed, if indeed he attained the dignity of abbot. For from the entire poem nothing more can be extracted than that he was a monk, since, as Muratori himself reasons, military service was the duty of abbots, not of monks. If Ermold truly was an abbot—a possibility I do not wish to deny—nothing prevents his being identified with Ermold the abbot whom Astronomus, in his *Life of Louis*, states was sent to Pippin by Louis the Pious in the year 834. For Mabillon’s assertion is futile: he says that it is wholly unlikely that a supporter of Lothair’s party, and therefore one thrust into exile, would later have been honored by Louis with an embassy. Yet, as Muratori rightly proves, Ermold was already in exile in 826, when he was composing his poem; whereas the conspiracy of the sons against Louis the Pious did not begin to break out until 830.

We follow Muratori’s edition and publish at the same time his preface and notes.

[Col. 0553]

## Muratori’s Preface

[Col. 0553A] Peter Lambecius, formerly prefect of the imperial library at Vienna, a man of great renown and one who deserved well of the republic of letters through his books—and especially because, in his *Commentaries*, at the command of the Most August Leopold, formerly emperor of the Romans, he laid open the treasures of that library for the benefit of all—Lambecius, I say, was the first to give the learned world a proper knowledge of Ermoldus Nigellus and of the poem now to be published.

For although Marquard Freher had earlier published several of his verses and had partially uncovered an entirely unknown writer, he spoke of him so meagerly that he left among learned men no desire for the man or his poem. Moreover, before Lambecius, Gerardus Joannes Vossius had mentioned this author [Col. 0553B] in book III, chapter 4, *On Latin Historians*, but only in passing. Speaking of Ermenoldus, or Ermenricus, a deacon and monk who committed the *Life of Saint Solus the Abbot* to writing around the year 840, published by Canisius and subsequently by Mabillon, he writes:

> “If this Hermenricus and Ermenoldus are the same person, then Ermoldus too would be the one who celebrated Louis the Pious in an elegiac poem.”

For this reason Vossius did not even include our Ermold among the historians, since he knew him scarcely by name; certainly, this omission must not be repeated in the future. But Lambecius, in *Commentaries*, book II, chapter 5, no. 25, p. 395, discussed him fully, describing manuscript codex 249 of the Latin Historical collection of the Vienna library. After listing Ermold’s name, period, exile, and poem, he also presented the beginning and end of the poem as a specimen, adding the hope—indeed, the promise—that he would later publish the complete work.

The poem was therefore eagerly awaited by lovers of literature, so that Lambecius might at last fulfill his pledge by publishing the book. I do not doubt that he would have done so, had envious death not taken that excellent and distinguished man from us in 1680 and thereby brought all his literary plans to an end. From this point Ermold’s name began to become increasingly well known. William Cave consequently added him to his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers in the *Literary History*, under the year 834, calling him Ernold instead of Ermold. John Hallervord likewise did so in his *Collection of Latin Historians*, while also recalling what Lambecius had promised concerning such a book.

Nor should the most learned Daniel Nessel be omitted. In his *Outline of the Great Historical Corpus*, published at Vienna in 1692, he promised that he would make this work, together with many others not yet published, available for public use. Concerning the single manuscript codex in which this poem lay hidden, he adds:

> “The writing of the codex is extremely ancient and very similar to the other manuscript codices of the periods of the emperors Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. I would therefore dare to affirm that this is either the very authentic codex that was presented to the emperor Louis the Pious, or at least a copy made from it in the same age. Before it was transferred to the Most August Imperial Library, it once belonged to the distinguished Wolfgang Lazius, as appears not only from his own hand, visible in several places in the margin, but also from the testimony of Johann Jakob Frisius, which appears in the expanded edition of Gesner’s library, in these words: ‘Four books of Ermoldus Nigellus, an exile, addressed to Louis the First, emperor, concerning his deeds, written in elegiac verse, are preserved at Vienna in Austria in the possession of Wolfgang Lazius.’”

The distinguished man and notable glory of the Benedictine order, John Mabillon, also mentioned our Ermold in the *Benedictine Annals*, as will appear below. Nor did he merely mention him: the celebrated Godefridus Guilielmus Leibniz also used his authority. Leibniz had read the Vienna manuscript in order to confirm his opinion concerning the origin of the Franks. When the learned Johann Georg Eccard reprinted and annotated Leibniz’s dissertation, he too remarked in his notes that Ermold still lacked an edition, and that an edition was to be hoped for from the distinguished Johann Benedikt Gentilott, who was then in charge of the imperial library.

The fame of Ermold, however, increased in this way only to intensify the thirst of learned men [Col. 0554C]—and especially my own thirst, once I had resolved to collect into one body the history of Italy, while also bringing forth whatever had thus far escaped the ravages of time and could be gathered for the common good. Immediately it occurred to me how well the desired edition of Ermold would suit this undertaking, and how closely the deeds of Louis the Pious corresponded with our history, since nearly all Italy was then under his authority. Indeed, the Augusti belong by a special title to the Italian sphere because they are kings of Italy and emperors of the Romans, and for this reason a magnificent title is conferred upon them above all others.

Meanwhile the illustrious Gentilott, mentioned above, had gone to the Roman Curia to serve, as they say, as auditor of the Rota for the German nation. The learned and outstanding man Pius Nicolaus Garellius had been appointed prefect of the imperial library; he was a knight of the Order of Christ, a counselor and personal physician to the Most August Roman Emperor and King of Spain, Charles VI.

I therefore approached the illustrious Garellius, whose exceptional goodwill toward me I had always experienced whenever circumstances required it, with repeated letters, asking in my most humble prayers that, by bringing my requests to the ears of the most merciful Emperor, he might arrange for Ermold to be restored to life through me and might not allow the learned world to be wearied any longer by waiting for him.

The Most August Prince’s willing disposition, inclined and ready for every benefit and advancement of learning, readily accommodated my wishes. But since Gentilott had not only undertaken to publish Ermold but had also incorporated the complete work into extensive commentaries that he had prepared and was preparing for the further illustration of the imperial library, the Emperor resolved that the poem should be granted to me only with Gentilott’s consent.

Gentilott, however, was far from willing that the edition of this author should be taken from him. Although the most eminent nobles—the Marquis of Rialpe, one of the Emperor’s most trusted secretaries and counselors, and Hieronymus Colloredo, then an excellent governor of the Insubrians, later elevated to honors at the imperial court and soon afterward taken to heaven—supported my cause out of their generous devotion to this Collection; although the Palatine associates themselves, moved by equal zeal, had submitted to the Most August Emperor, through Count Colloredo, a petition on this very matter; and although the illustrious Count Carlo Pertusati, senator of Milan and regent in the Supreme Council of Spain, an outstanding cultivator of both law and learning, had also used his influence on my behalf, the fate of Ermoldus Nigellus nevertheless remained uncertain.

Then, unexpectedly, the knot was untied. The excellent Gentilott, scarcely appointed bishop and prince of Trent, was carried off at Rome by his final destiny, amid the sorrow of all good men, in the year just past, 1725, leaving lovers of learning with a profound sense of his loss. I therefore once again began to hope that I might obtain what I desired. I asked the most courteous Garellius that, since the publication of Ermold’s long-promised work had become much more difficult and remote than before because of Gentilott’s death, he would finally obtain from the Most August Emperor—also the most merciful patron of my Collection—permission for me to publish it.

What more is there to say? My prayers prevailed, and Garellius obtained the gift. For the magnanimous Emperor, born for the happiness of our age, who never ceases to win glory and immortal renown for himself through the arts of peace no less than through those of war, ordered that Ermold be handed over to me. In particular, whether the learned republic receives Ermold through Gentilott’s commentaries or through me, this benefit must always be attributed to the generosity of the most glorious Emperor Charles VI and to his rich and celebrated library, which alone preserves the manuscript of Ermold’s poem. The benefit is all the more valuable because it was conferred so promptly.

What the most learned Garellius, prefect of the imperial library, wrote to me on that occasion I consider worth making public here, both for its own sake and as an expression of my grateful mind.

[Col. 0556A]

> “Pius Nicolaus Garellius sends greetings to the illustrious and most learned Lord Ludovico Antonio Muratori, librarian of the Most Serene Duke of Modena.
>
> “You rightly request, most distinguished sir, that now, after you had formerly and repeatedly been refused the Nigellian work because it had been entered by Gentilott into his catalogue and was expected shortly to be published, I—who had been the one to resist—should now revive your prayers before the Most August Emperor. You ask this with excellent justification, since, as the pitiable vicissitude of human affairs has brought about, the learned world has suffered the loss of so great a man and has now been deprived of the hope of enjoying, at least so soon, Gentilott’s eagerly desired labors. For the work is indeed vast, and many of its contents, having been prepared by the author for the use of himself and the imperial library, would require the censor’s approval if they were to be published, lest they offend the more delicate ears of some readers. For not everything that recalls the memory of ancient times pleases everyone in our own age.

> “Indeed, he had more than once intimated to me from Rome by letter and, in accordance with his kindness toward me, had granted ample authority to remove whatever might seem necessary, if the Emperor wished to hasten the edition. But many serious and equally weighty reasons discouraged me from assuming, so to speak, at my own risk, such a burden—especially while the author was alive. You can readily imagine these reasons, and it is quite unnecessary for me to press them upon you at greater length here.

> “There are also the most serious cares with which I am constantly occupied; moreover, my disposition is averse to unpleasant disputes and exceedingly fond of tranquility. Every day I see before my eyes the fate of distinguished men who, in publishing the works of others, have experienced the unjust judgment of unreasonable critics. Nor do those of us attached to the library now have enough leisure; and even if we did, the task could not be accomplished so quickly and rashly, if I wished to entrust this responsibility to them.

> “You have, most honorable sir, as it were in passing (*ὡς ἐν παρόδῳ*), the reasons that may delay the publication of Gentilott’s work, especially after the author’s death. Nevertheless, I am of the opinion that whatever serves either to illuminate antiquity or to satisfy the curiosity of scholars should not by any means be kept permanently in libraries, so that it may provide an aged feast for cockroaches and moths. Rather, I will strive to bring such material into the light for the benefit of all, with as much accuracy and diligence as I can, and I will endeavor to compensate by a ready and frank willingness for whatever may be lacking in intellectual ability for advancing and enlarging the benefit of the learned world.

> “I have always been so disposed, and hereafter, whenever occasion arises, I shall not hesitate to advise this course, especially since I daily experience that the Most August and most merciful Lord himself, the patron—indeed, I may say the author—of this institution, is so favorable to it that I have never seen my wishes and prayers concerning the advancement of learning fall fruitless from his generosity.

> “You may ask what all this is for, as though anyone could be so blind as to doubt the generosity of so great a prince toward learning, when so many monuments of his exceptional glory survive. I have no other purpose than to clear myself—for I confess it—if you should accuse me of obstinacy because I formerly and repeatedly refused to comply with your requests. I make a practice of using the Emperor’s generosity modestly and not without caution. But now, when time and circumstances advised it, I received your letters, immediately approached the Emperor, and explained the matter to him; and to explain it was to plead it. Who could ever refuse you, an excellent man who has deserved so well of the republic of letters, something that no reason prevented?

> “You shall therefore have a copy of the Nigellian poems, transcribed in perfect good faith and carefully collated. Meanwhile, let those who desire ancient histories accept it as a pledge on your behalf, and let them form hope concerning the other monuments of the imperial library and soothe their long-standing desire for this author.

> “This, however, is granted to you on the condition that nothing be lost from the labors of our Gentilott. Rather, the judgment that he himself placed before this little work must be printed, pure and unaltered, as a preface, with the scrupulous care due to material issued from the imperial library and from Gentilott’s commentaries. In this way, I judge that through the generosity of the Most August Emperor nothing has been diminished from Gentilott’s dignity or glory, and that the republic of letters has been adequately served by me.

> “This codex was formerly numbered among the historians as 249; now, according to Gentilott’s recension, it occupies the place of 992 among the secular historians.

> “There is also one small favor I should like to ask of you. Since I have heard from our Forlosia that you have decided to reprint the *Annals of the Franks* published by Lambecius, I thought it would be in your interest to add to them Gentilott’s judgment together with the variant readings. I have appended all this after copying the Nigellian material. In this way you will conveniently spare yourself and also serve the memory of that most friendly and distinguished prelate, which I must honor forever, lest all this labor disappear.

> “For the rest, I earnestly ask you to love me; and if there is anything more I can do for you, command me. Farewell.

> “Written at Vienna, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, 1725.”

At last, therefore, the elegiac poem of Ermoldus Nigellus concerning the deeds of Louis the Pious, never before published, now appears. If I say that through this work the value of my Collection, and especially of this volume, will be greatly increased, I shall perhaps find no one who disagrees.

But before I declare what judgment should be formed concerning the poem itself, the circumstances require me first to establish who its author was. In the preface he expressly calls himself Ermoldus Nigellus, and through a double acrostic, at the beginning and end of the verses, he offers us this line [Col. 0557C]:

> Ermoldus cecinit Hludovici Caesaris arma.  
> “Ermold sang the arms of Caesar Louis.”

There, in another verse, he also reveals his other name, saying:

> Suscipe gratanter profert quae dona Nigellus.  
> “Receive gratefully the gifts that Nigellus offers.”

He therefore had a double name. If anyone prefers to call one of them a surname, I shall readily agree. In those times there flourished Flaccus Albinus, whom we call Alcuin; Amalarius Fortunatus; Lupus Servatus; Walafridus Strabo; Paschasius Radbertus; Rabanus Maurus; and others whom I omit, to whose names some additional designation was attached.

Nor am I unaware that the distinguished Sirmond, in his notes on Ennodius and in his preface to Sidonius, argues that among men of the Middle Ages it was customary for nobles alone to use several names, of which only the last was their proper name, while those preceding it were adopted names, as it were, or forenames. But although what he observes concerning the periods of Ennodius and Sidonius is correct according to his customary method, I fear that this cannot be applied to the age of Charlemagne. It seems more likely that Albinus, Strabo, Servatus, Maurus, Nigellus, and names of that kind were additional surnames placed after the proper name.

But let us proceed. It is clear not only that Ermold was a contemporary of Louis the Pious, whose deeds he sings, but also that by order of that same Emperor he was punished with exile for some offense. The place of exile was Strasbourg, called *Strazbure* by the poet, a name it still retains among the Germans. To appease the angered Caesar, Ermold undertook in this poem to sing his praises and narrate his outstanding deeds, repeatedly imploring the mercy of the pious prince and pleading for an end to his exile. At the conclusion of the poem he says especially:

> Hoc tibi, Caesar, opus stolida crocitante cicuta,  
> Porrigit Ermoldus, exsul, egenus, inops.
>
> “This work Ermold, an exile, needy and destitute,  
> Offers you, Caesar, while the foolish hemlock croaks.”

He then asks Christ to lead Louis to know and weigh his case more closely, adding:

> Veridicis poteris forsan cognoscere verbis,  
> Criminis objecti me minus esse reum.  
> Non tamen excuso me illius, crede, reatus,  
> Infelix quo sum trusus in exsilium.
>
> “Perhaps through truthful words you will be able to learn  
> That I am less guilty of the charge brought against me.  
> Yet do not think that I excuse myself from that offense,  
> Because of which, unhappy man, I was thrust into exile.”

[Col. 0558B] But who this Ermoldus Nigellus was is nowhere recorded, and therefore, in order to identify him, we must proceed only by conjecture. In the *Life of Louis the Pious* written by Astronomus, under the year 834, we read:

> “The emperor instructed his son Pippin, through Ermold the abbot, to restore without delay to the churches the ecclesiastical properties in his kingdom, whether those which he himself had assigned to his own people or those which they had seized for themselves.”

Referring to this passage, the distinguished Mabillon, in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year of Christ 818, where he discusses the abbots of Nantua, presents Ermold, abbot of Nantua, who flourished in the year 833. He then adds:

> “Perhaps this is the Ermold who was abbot and through whom Louis Augustus, in the following year—that is, in the thirty-fourth year—ordered his son Pippin to restore the ecclesiastical properties, and so forth.”

But Mabillon himself then seems to turn to another, and indeed more plausible, opinion. Under the year 834 he writes:

> “Who that abbot Ermold was who was sent to Pippin is not sufficiently known, unless he was Ermenald, abbot of Aniane, who in the following year obtained a privilege from the Emperor Louis. I do not, however, think that he was Ermoldus Nigellus, sent into exile by Louis himself, who composed in four books a poem in his praise, published by Lambecius in the second volume of the *Imperial Library*.”

Here Mabillon was lacking his usual diligence. For Lambecius never published those books anywhere; he published only the beginning and the end. Mabillon continues:

> “He was undoubtedly a supporter of Lothair’s party and was therefore driven into exile and imprisonment. But although he was restored to freedom, it does not seem likely that Louis later honored that same man with an embassy.”

This is Mabillon’s view. Yet although he wished to prophesy and openly contradicted his own prophecy, I nevertheless conjecture—or rather, I am convinced—that he stumbled upon the truth. Let us examine the matter closely, now that the complete poem of Ermold is before our eyes, whereas Mabillon lacked it for forming a correct judgment.

Anyone who reads Ermoldus Nigellus’s poem will immediately understand that he was a monk devoted to the Benedictine rule. For there is scarcely any passage in which the poet’s pen does not range over the praises of the Benedictine order, its abbots, monasteries, and Rule. I say nothing of his ecclesiastical learning, which reveals him to have been by no means a layman and which in those times was more often observed among monks than among secular clerics.

That he was also an abbot is indicated, unless I am mistaken, by what he says in book IV, where he narrates the expedition against the rebellious Bretons in the year 824. He says:

> Huc egomet scutum humeris, ensemque revinctum  
> Gessi, sed nemo me feriente dolet.  
> Pippin hoc aspiciens risit, miratur, et infit:  
> Cede armis, frater: litteram amato magis.
>
> “Here I myself carried a shield upon my shoulders  
> And a sword fastened at my side, but no one suffers from my striking.  
> Pippin, seeing this, laughed, marveled, and said:  
> ‘Give up arms, brother; love letters more.’”

The first point is thereby confirmed: our Ermold had professed the monastic life. Pippin would not have burst out laughing when he saw him for any other reason than that he saw a man girded with weapons who was so far removed from the military profession, and weapons so ill suited to a monastic habit. He therefore laughingly encouraged him to withdraw from military service and to devote himself to literary studies, as befitted a monk and as was his custom.

Moreover, he called him “brother.” That name—now so strongly rejected by monks, who wish it reserved solely for religious mendicants—formerly designated monks above all, as the monuments of those times demonstrate; indeed, this very poem confirms it in more than one passage.

From this second point it may also become clear that Ermold presided over some monastery with the title of abbot. The very learned Thomassinus demonstrates at length, in part III, book I, chapter 40, *On Benefices*, that under Charlemagne and his successors both bishops and abbots were accustomed to undertake military service themselves and to lead their own troops into the king’s service. This was the duty of abbots, not of monks.

And although Charlemagne and other Frankish kings sometimes exempted ecclesiastical nobles from this burden, as is recorded in their capitularies, and although there were monasteries regarded as exempt from supplying military forces to the king, nevertheless, whenever the gravest necessity of the commonwealth demanded it, all bishops and abbots were compelled either to join military expeditions or at least to contribute their contingents.

That our Ermold did this is learned from the passage just cited. He also declares that he abstained from shedding anyone’s blood and that he did not bear arms to anyone’s destruction. By these words he clears his military service of guilt and shows that he avoided the bond of irregularity, as we now call it.

Therefore there are indications that present Ermoldus to us as abbot of some monastery. It remains now to inquire which monastery he governed. When I read in Duchesne and Baluze, in the capitulary of Louis the Pious concerning the year 817, that the monastery of Nigellus was listed among those required to provide gifts and military service, I wondered whether our Ermoldus might have been designated under the name Nigellus. For it was not at all difficult to show that there had been monasteries which received their names from their founders. But when Mabillon, in his *Annals*, maintained that this monastery was so called [Col. 0560A] because it was situated beside the river Nigella, I turned from that conjecture to others.

My view—or, if not my view, at least my conjecture—is therefore founded, as I believe, on sound grounds: namely, that our Ermoldus was none other than Ermenaldus, abbot of the monastery of Aniane, contrary to what the aforementioned Mabillon recently thought unlikely. To demonstrate this, readers should know that the monastery of Aniane, named from the river Aniane, lies on the shore of the Mediterranean in Occitania, now Languedoc, in the diocese of Montpellier. In the year 822 it was subject to an abbot named Trutesind, as that same Mabillon clearly established in the preface to the *Life of Saint Benedict, Abbot of Aniane*, in the fourth century of the Benedictine collection, part I, p. 192. He cites Louis the Pious’s charter concerning this matter. Then, according to the same authority, in the years 835 and 837 three privileges were granted by Louis himself to Ermenaldus, abbot of the monastery of Aniane. Thus there is nothing to prevent us from supposing that, after the year 822, this Ermenaldus began to govern that same monastery.

Moreover, that Ermenaldus and Ermoldus were the same name even Mabillon himself does not deny, when he suspects—as I noted above—that this same Ermenaldus was the Ermoldus who was sent by Louis Augustus to King Pippin in the year 834. For Ermenaldus and Ermenoldus were formerly one name. For that reason, in Labbe, vol. I of the *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum* under the *History of the Bishops of Auxerre*, there also appears a count of the district of Auxerre named Ermenoldus; and in Bollandus [Col. 0560C], under 6 January in the *Acts of the Saints*, there is a *Life of Saint Ermenoldus or Erminoldus*. In the same way, in ancient books one finds equally Arnaldus and Arnoldus, Rainaldus and Rainoldus, Bertaldus and Bertholdus, Hunaldus and Hunoldus, Athelbaldus and Adelboldus, and other names of this kind.

Now let the considerations that impel me to suspect that Hermenoldus, abbot of Aniane, and our Ermoldus were one and the same man be brought forward. We have already seen that their names, dignity, and period agree. I now add that it is clear from the poem itself that the monastery from which our poet had been torn away and sent into exile belonged to Aquitaine—that is, to the kingdom then governed by Pippin, son of Louis the Pious. Near the end of Book I Ermoldus expresses this wish:

[Col. 0560D]

> May he, joyful though exiled, go to the realms of mighty Pippin;  
> May the Most High and the Caesar himself, mighty as he is, grant it.

Likewise, before closing Book III he sings:

> May this same devotion—for I faithfully ask and ask again—  
> Restore me, flourishing, to the pious Pippin.

Do you see how our Ermoldus had not only a place in the kingdom of Aquitaine, but also very great favor with Pippin, who was king there? The monastery of Aniane in Aquitaine therefore immediately presents itself to us; and we have just seen that Ermenoldus, or Ermoldus, was then its abbot.
