It is further significant that our Ermoldus, toward the end of Book II, praises at length Benedict, the monastery’s founder, a man renowned for holiness and its first abbot, who was later transferred to the monastery of Inda and was dearer to Louis the Pious than all other [Col. 0561A] monks; he likewise launches into praise of the monastery of Aniane itself. Moreover, at the end of Book III he reports the death of that same Saint Benedict, which occurred in the year 821, five years before our Ermoldus completed his poem. There, addressing the saint himself, he says:

> Behold, this third little book brings its end  
> In your name, holy father, so that you may remember your Ermoldus.

Why, I ask, does he entreat Benedict, formerly abbot of Aniane, to remember “his Ermoldus,” unless Ermoldus himself had succeeded Benedict in governing the same monastery, and had perhaps also been his disciple? All these considerations converge finally upon this conclusion: led by an exceedingly probable line of reasoning, we should recognize that our author is to be identified with Ermenaldus, abbot of Aniane, and that he was the same Ermoldus who was sent by Louis the Pious as envoy to his son Pippin in the year 834.

For what Mabillon objected against this opinion—that it was in no way likely that Louis Augustus would entrust such a task to a man who had previously belonged to the party of Lothair—rests on no foundation. That distinguished writer would have recognized this more clearly if he, like us, had been able to read the whole poem of Ermoldus. The utterly detestable conspiracy of the sons against Louis the Pious finally burst forth as though from an egg in the year 830. But anyone who reads our Ermoldus attentively will easily see that the poem was completed in the year 826 and, consequently, [Col. 0561C] that the author’s offense and exile preceded by a considerable interval that most disastrous tragedy of the Franks. His narrative concerns events confined to the same year; and, after recounting them, he immediately adds at the end of the work:

> While I was singing these things, I was kept under guard at Strasbourg,  
> Conscious and guilty of my own offense.

Thus he was composing his poem in that same year, 826. It is also relevant that Ermoldus repeatedly mentions and praises Lothair, Pippin, the sons of Augustus, the counts Matfrid and Hugh, and others, seeking to win their goodwill—even though they took the leading roles in the many disturbances raised against the most pious emperor. If that most dreadful [Col. 0561D] upheaval of their minds had already occurred while Ermoldus was writing, and he himself had been involved in it, he would certainly have refrained from praising these princes so often, since he was writing to Louis, whom they had treated so badly, and seeking from Louis forgiveness for his offense and restoration to his former freedom.

Our poet therefore must not be mixed up with the grave disturbances of the year 830 and those that followed. He must have been driven into exile before 826 for an entirely different offense. We may now reasonably conjecture that, shortly after presenting this poem to Louis Augustus, he was restored to the prince’s favor, and that by the year 834 his integrity and loyalty had become so well established that Louis chose him as envoy to his son Pippin. Indeed, since from this very poem we have sufficiently understood that our Ermoldus was especially devoted to Pippin himself and dear to him, we are also led to see more clearly why the Emperor Louis, preferring him to others, chose to use him to communicate his mind to his son and judged him better suited to negotiate with Pippin himself the restoration of ecclesiastical affairs in the kingdom of Aquitaine.

These, then, are the matters that occurred to me to say about the author of the poem. Let us now add a few remarks about the poem itself. Certainly, for the history of those times, the Franks possess approved and trustworthy writers. Yet it must be observed that it is neither the duty nor the practice of historians to pursue every minor detail. This should especially be evident to readers of the great [Col. 0562B]—and certainly valuable, though meager—*Annals of the Franks*. Poets, however, are not only permitted but are generally compelled by the principles of their art to describe events, whether real or invented, in such a way that they descend even to the smallest particulars.

You can see that our Ermoldus often fulfills this rule, and that by this means the customs and practices of those times are vividly delineated. Thus the storehouse of learning has material by which it may be enlarged, since poets supply what is generally lacking in historians. I shall refrain from examples, for anyone can readily collect them independently.

As for the poem itself, it was certainly composed with a rough Muse; in places it is obscure and interrupted by speeches that offer no pleasure and sometimes even some tedium. No one should approach it as though it were some outstanding model of poetic art. Nevertheless, so far as my purpose is concerned, I present an excellent, trustworthy, contemporary historical source. I do not want readers to come here for poetic flowers, but rather to attain the single truth of history.

You will receive that truth clearly from our Ermoldus, a suitable witness of his own age, and especially unlike the better poets in that he nowhere mixes fables into his narrative. In addition, he commemorates for us the principal courtiers and nobles of the imperial palace, together with other distinguished men flourishing at that time, excepting Abbot Wala, whom he perhaps knew to be hostile to him. He seems to remember each of them for the purpose of winning everyone’s favor, so that he might have each one favorably disposed toward him before Augustus [Col. 0562D] Louis and thus assist him in recovering his liberty.

Above all, notice how he flatters the empress Judith: he heaps praises upon her and presents her child Charles, later called the Bald, as exceedingly dear to the Graces. He also portrays Louis himself as so illustrious in a chorus of virtues, especially religion and piety, that it is perfectly clear how justly—or perhaps even at that time—the title “Pious” was transferred to him.

In a word, Italy, Germany, and Gaul, over which that pious prince then ruled, have reason—indeed abundant reason—to give thanks to the Most August Emperor Charles VI, second to none of his predecessors in piety, courage, and prudence, because he granted permission; to the most illustrious Garellius, because he obtained it; and, I may finally add, to me, because I have at last published an author of great usefulness to literary scholarship, who until now had been condemned to a second exile longer than was fitting.

From the Catalogue of Manuscript Codices of Profane History by John Benedict Gentilotti, no. 992, formerly 249.

A parchment manuscript consisting of 66 leaves, which appears to have been written in the same century in which the author lived, or at least not long afterward; and which, as is evident from the Gesner–Simler Library, enlarged by Frisius, formerly belonged to the library of Wolfgang Lazius. It contains the poem of Ermoldus Nigellus on the deeds of Louis the Pious, divided into four books.

I have discovered nothing about the author except that he himself mentions having served in the military expedition to Brittany in the year 824. It is clear from what he relates near the end that he was in exile at Strasbourg. [Col. 0563B] He nowhere states the reason for which he was punished with exile, nor is it known whether he was recalled from it. Nevertheless, if he was expelled into exile because he had conspired with other factional men against the Emperor Louis, there can scarcely be any doubt that he was recalled from exile along with the others who had belonged to that party and whom Louis forgave.

The Astronomer, in his *Life of Louis*, does indeed mention an abbot Ermoldus and relates that he was sent by the emperor to his son Pippin with instructions “to restore without delay to the churches the ecclesiastical possessions in his kingdom, whether he himself had assigned them to his own men or they had seized them for themselves.” But the most learned Mabillon believes this man to have been different from Ermoldus, the author of this poem, in the *Benedictine Annals*, Book XXXI, no. 22.

I readily agree with him, although in the whole work I find no argument by which the person who holds them to be the same can be refuted. For what Ermoldus says in praise of the Rule and [Col. 0563C] monastic discipline suggests that our poet belonged to the Benedictine family, either as abbot or monk; so too do Pippin’s words to him when he saw him armed during the expedition to Brittany:

> Lay aside your arms, brother; love letters more.

That monks as well as abbots served in the military at that time is known to everyone. Nor does it seem contrary to the indulgence and clemency of a most gracious prince—who sometimes bestowed benefits in place of punishments—to send to his son Pippin a man from whom he had obtained pardon for an offense, especially since the poem itself makes it clear enough that Ermoldus had been of great use to Pippin.

Be that as it may, and whoever the author of this poem ultimately was, it is certainly most deserving of publication and has long been eagerly sought by all learned men. For, contrary to what Mabillon seems to imply in the passage mentioned shortly before, not all four complete books were published by Lambecius in Book II of his *Commentaries*, beginning at p. 359; only the prologue, the beginning, and the end of the work were printed.

I once suspected that the whole poem was commonly available when I read the most learned notes of Marquard Freher on the treaty between Louis of Germany and Charles of Gaul, the sons of Louis the Pious, concluded at Strasbourg in the year 842, and noticed that in them certain verses from Ermoldus were cited as though from any other readily available author. Then I came upon the autograph letters of Janus Gruter and the same Marquard Freher to Sebastian Tengnagel. From these I learned how Freher had come to know of this poem—of which, as far as I know, the imperial manuscript is the sole copy—and had taken from it the verses he cites. I thought it worthwhile to place these letters before Ermoldus, so that the whole matter might be seen in a better light.

## Letter of Janus Gruter to Sebastian Tengnagel

“Greetings, most illustrious sir, and forgive me if I reply briefly to your most welcome letter. I am called away elsewhere, and wish, if possible, that this may reach you in time. I owe you much for your pious consolation in this grief of mine, which I bear patiently, certain that all things are sent by God to the good of those who are good.

If you send back our Arabic manuscript, another one that you request will soon be available to you. As for the catalogue of the library of His Imperial Majesty, which you were kind enough to share with me, I love you greatly and am greatly indebted to you. My Livy has indeed been published, but not yet the notes in which I explain the textual emendations. Thus, if there is with you a very old copy, or one transcribed from an ancient original, I would not decline it—nor would I decline a Julius Caesar, for whom I am now preparing a collection of variant readings.

But above all, if there is a Martial of good quality there, I should like it. Do not hesitate to send it to me, provided this can conveniently be done. You will learn from this note of Freher what he wishes done with Ermoldus. The Wegenmeyers obstinately remain silent; I interpret their silence as a refusal. I cannot determine their reason, unless it is a difference of religion, which they perhaps obstinately uphold [Col. 0564B] and exercise with a hatred they ought least of all to show.

Those last missives of yours also caught my eye, but in such a way that they might have imposed cleverly upon someone else, though not upon me. Therefore, *Memneso apistein* [Greek: “Remember to distrust”]. I do not know whether Heinsius is continuing his emendation of Nonnus; otherwise, we too possess the very oldest manuscripts of that author, which he has nevertheless never requested. Still, today I shall convey to him your kindly intention.

This is all I have briefly to say in reply to your letters. Farewell and greetings, my dear sir, together with my most beloved friend and master, Mr. Blotius.

“Heidelberg, 30 January 1608.  
“Your servant, Janus Gruterus.”

**Address:** To the most distinguished and illustrious gentleman, Mr. Sebastian Tengnagel, librarian of His Imperial and Royal Majesty.

### Freher’s note, mentioned by Gruter in the preceding letter

“Greetings. Who would not embrace with open arms the humanity [Col. 0564C] and kindness of so distinguished a man, who voluntarily undertakes to assist our undertaking, offering booklets concerning the life of the Emperor Louis the Pious by a contemporary writer, a writer hitherto unknown even by hearsay to me, and therefore all the more eagerly desired?

Therefore, when you write to him, please convey my warmest greetings, offer him my studies and services most fully, and ask that whatever there is of the archetype of the book be sent to us at the next fair so that we may examine and transcribe it. It will faithfully return to its owner with the interest of gratitude that is properly owed. Farewell and greetings, dearest of friends.”

T. Freherus.

“The writer Rabanus Maurus, of the same period, abbot of Fulda and archbishop of Mainz, also composed several books in verse concerning the deeds of the Emperor Louis and his sons. What if that distinguished man has heard something about them as well?”

**Address:** To Monsieur Gruterus.

## Letter of Marquard Freher to Sebastian Tengnagel

[Col. 0564D]

“Greetings. For many years no matter, although less expected, has come to me more agreeable to my mind or better suited to my studies than this matter from you, noble and most distinguished sir. You convey greetings through our Gruterus to a man unknown to you; you offer to advance our studies a copy of an old, unpublished manuscript from the imperial library; and then you promptly send the very archetype itself, a rare author of any value, hitherto unknown even by hearsay to us, yet, for his age, not without charm, and altogether deserving to appear publicly, with some notes, among our *anekdotoi* [Greek: “unpublished”] Frankish writers.

Such humanity exceeds all admiration; the magnitude of the benefit surpasses our powers; we are overcome by the readiness and timeliness of your service. At last, in whatever way I can, I offer and willingly give you my most heartfelt thanks, as you rightly deserve, prepared to repay you in any way permitted.

I shall also acknowledge you publicly when I publish this most delightful little book, at least for those who take pleasure in the monuments of every age and every nation. Among these, the Frankish name seems certainly to hold a foremost place, both by the greatness of its empire and by the glory of its deeds.

How many beautiful and exceptionally interesting observations I have already extracted and noted from it! For on the day before I left home, I took it with me as a companion on my journey to the Danube and, amid the business and tedium, transcribed it with my own hand during my free hours. How often, meanwhile, I silently weighed your kindness with grateful mind and prayed that all good things might come to you! I resolved to repay you with thanks.

And now, behold, the manuscript itself, religiously guarded by me, returns safely to you with a great store of thanks. Yet there is a danger that your readiness may henceforth encourage us to request more, thereby causing you a little additional trouble.

There is also something I can scarcely refrain from begging, all the more boldly because it is not for my own sake but for the public. Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz, wrote in heroic verse a book about the internal dissension among the sons of Louis the First, as Gesner and others indicate. I have long desired it with many prayers but have so far been unable to obtain it by any search, so that we should now despair of it entirely unless that imperial library supplies it.

I am pleased to hope that it exists there. For what could be missing from so vast a number, where this Ermoldus is catalogued under no. 4709? [Note: [Col. 0565B] According to the old arrangement, in which manuscripts were mixed together with printed books. In Tengnagel’s manuscript catalogue the codex is historical no. 249.]

See, I ask you, most distinguished sir, whether you can assist our desire, and continue at the same time to serve the public good:

> May the gods above grant you what you deserve for such piety;  
> May your sweet right of friendship be dear to me.

“Farewell, distinguished sir.

“From Augsburg, our native city, revisited at last after many years, 13 December 1608.  
“Marquardus Freherus.”

### Another letter of the same man to the same recipient

[Col. 0566A]

“Greetings. Your letter was delivered to me at Frankfurt. It was welcome for many reasons, but especially because I learned that the manuscript of Ermoldus had been properly returned to you; I had been somewhat anxious about it. I hope that it will soon emerge, together with a few more works of that kind, furnished with some notes, and thus return to you with interest. To you, I say, since the precaution you mention will be observed.

Nor do I doubt that more unpublished works of this kind are held there; if you share them with the republic of letters, you will benefit my studies no less than the public. Cuspinianus, in his work on Frederick III, mentions, unless I am mistaken, that at his command the books of feudal law were arranged in better order by a certain jurist. [Note: [Col. 0565C] This is Antonius Minuccius of Prato Vecchio, whose six books *On Feudal Law* were published by Johann Schilter from a manuscript codex of the Royal Library of Paris, together with the Alemannic feudal codex at Strasbourg in 1695, in quarto.] Please look up the passage and consider how that book might be brought to light. I offer my efforts for its publication and illustration with notes.

I also hear that the collections of Sambucus and Lazius—antiquities, coins, statues, and similar objects—remain with their heirs and are for sale, while scarcely finding a suitable buyer. If this is so, I might perhaps spend something on them, provided it were clear what and of what quality they are. Please reply at your convenience. And think kindly of those volumes on German affairs of mine.

“I wrote hastily at Frankfurt, 21 April 1610.”

**Address:** To the noble and most distinguished gentleman, Mr. Sebastian Tengnagel, Doctor of Laws, director of the imperial and royal library, respected lord and friend, Vienna in Austria.

Thus far the letters. Now let us examine the poem of Ermoldus.

[Col. 0567] [Col. 0567]

[Col. 0569A]

## Prologue of Ermoldus Nigellus. “The Royal Work of Ermoldus” [Note: [Col. 0569A] The title was added by a second hand.]

[Col. 0569]

> **Editor** [Note: [Col. 0569A] Ermoldus begins with an obscure word. The word appears to have been used for *Creator*, although I rather suspect that the poet wrote *editus* or *edite*, meaning “born” or “O born one.” For he is addressing Christ.], you who shine in the heavenly citadel of the Father,  
> Ruler, patron, Redeemer, and author of the world,  
> You who open to worthy soldiers the realms of heaven,  
> Once shut in Avernus through the guilt of the mother [Eve],  
> You who, O Christ, restore the tribunal of eternal light—  
> David the psalmist, prophetically singing of this before,  
> With a voice wondrous to recount, a seer who uttered  
> The sacred doctrines of things to come—  
> Grant that I, a rustic, may fittingly recount in a slight, measured poem  
> The deeds of the outstanding Caesar. [Note: [Col. 0569A] The reading is apparently *poscito* for *postulato* (“requested”). Below occurs *pectine parvo* (“with a little plectrum”), and so I doubt this word.]
>
> I do not invoke the nymphs here, as the mad pagans of old did;  
> Nor do I ask the Pierian Muses, nor enter Apollo’s threshold  
> By Apollo’s path to seek help. [Note: [Col. 0569A] Lambecius printed *lumen*, “light.” But the manuscript plainly has *limen*, “threshold”; the following verse, “I shall enter,” also persuades us that it should not be read otherwise.]
>
> When I did such things [Note: [Col. 0570A] Rather, “when they did such things,” so that the sense is: when the pagans did this, Satan darkened their hearts.],  
> The grim and loathsome Behemoth [Note: [Col. 0570A] For *Behemoth*, that is, the devil; the ancients allegorically interpreted this beast, mentioned in Holy Scripture, in this way.] pressed down their hearts.
>
> I seek instead the thresholds of heavenly light, so that the true Sun  
> Of justice may deign to grant the gifts I ask. For I do not demand  
> To run through in verse, on a little plectrum, all the deeds  
> In which even great masters may fail  
> To bend their imperial gaze; [Note: [Col. 0570A] For *deficere* (“to fail”). Nigellus perhaps wrote *certare* (“to contend”).]  
> But here I shall begin to celebrate them in song.
>
> Favor, Christ, the poems of one who prays,  
> So that, because of them, you may now mercifully relieve me in exile;  
> You who, high in your palace, lift up the fallen, spare sinners, and scatter  
> Far and wide, in place of the bright sun’s rays,  
> The lofty lights of Christ the King.
>
> Greatest prince, who holds the lofty scepters of Christ the King,  
> Pious King Louis, Caesar renowned  
> For the gift of piety, distinguished in the teaching of Christ,  
> Graciously receive the gifts that Nigellus offers,  
> Though he has dared [Note: [Col. 0570A] Or rather *ausus*, “having dared,” which the following *tangere* seems to require.] to touch your deeds in song,  
> Since the love of the eternal King has always remained  
> In your heart. Caesar, raise up your fallen servant,  
> So that Christ the Most High may exalt you in heaven.

[Col. 0569D]

## The First Book of the Poem of Ermoldus Nigellus in Honor of Louis the Most Christian Caesar Augustus Begins

[Col. 0569]

[Col. 0569B]

> You surpass the Augusti renowned for wealth and arms,  
> But, Louis, Caesar, even more through the love of God.
>
> I desire to speak readily of the praises of the gracious prince;  
> May the Almighty, who has power, furnish me with arms.
>
> I attempt to describe the deeds of the arms-bearing Caesar,  
> Which the world rightly recounts with devoted affection.
>
> Perhaps it would be better to remain with the task begun,  
> To lament the dreadful deeds of my offense.
>
> Since I am a rustic, I know neither the retreats of the Camenae  
> Nor can I produce polished measures in the art.
>
> But as I hesitate, the King’s mercy restores me;  
> For he prefers a prayer to gifts.
>
> Exile also compels me, I confess, to such things;  
> Lacking gifts, I offer what I possess.
>
> I shall not run through every deed in detail:  
> It is neither permitted, nor possible, nor within my talent.
>
> If Maro, Naso, Cato, Flaccus, Lucan, Homer,  
> Tully, Macer [Note: [Col. 0571B] He means Aemilius Macer, an ancient poet whose poems, now lost, may perhaps still have been extant in Ermoldus’s time. But note the poet’s license—or rather his childishness—in writing “Tully and Macer, Cicero,” as though Tully were someone other than Cicero. One could hardly call this a poetic flourish.], Cicero, or Plato;
>
> Sedulius, Prudentius, and Juvencus,  
> Or Fortunatus and Prosper themselves, were here,
>
> They would scarcely be able to set everything down  
> On their famous pages and twice multiply their celebrated melody.
>
> But I, a sailor in a rough little craft, with a leaking oar,  
> Wish to approach this expanse of the boundless ocean. [Note: [Col. 0571C] Added to the manuscript by a recent hand.]
>
> The right hand that raised faithful Peter above the overwhelming waves,  
> So that he would not perish, and also added strength to the boat—  
> May that hand, in mercy, preserve me as I plunge through the waves  
> And bring me, generous Caesar, to your harbor.
>
> Now let my song go forth to recount the deeds of Louis,  
> And let my page read a few things from among many.
>
> In the time when the scepters of Charles of the Franks were flourishing,  
> Whom the whole world celebrates with the honor due to a father,
>
> While Francia had spread its broad thunder everywhere  
> And its famous name was celebrated throughout the world,
>
> Then wise Charles, with the council of the nobles,  
> Divided the insignia of sovereignty among his offspring.
>
> Certainly, Francia by lot had passed to the namesake [Note: [Col. 0571C] That is, to Charles, the firstborn son of Charlemagne, whom Queen Hildegard had borne to him in 772. His father had assigned the Frankish kingdom to him, and confirmed that division in the year 806 in his final testament, which is preserved in Baluze and in part II of volume I of this collection, p. 125. But Charles died before his father, frustrating his father’s plan and hope.]  
> Of his father, if he was able to become his successor.
>
> The kingdom of Italy fell to beloved Pippin [Note: [Col. 0571D] Namely, to another son of that same Charles, who ruled the Italian kingdom for a long time while his father was alive, as the Lombard laws published in this same collection and countless other documents attest. But premature death also carried him away before his father.].
>
> But to you, Louis, he gave the kingdoms of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0571D] It is not easy to determine what part of his kingdoms Charlemagne, while still alive, gave to his son Louis to govern under the royal title. The western boundaries of Aquitaine were certain, namely Spain; but its eastern boundaries were not sufficiently known, since some writers of antiquity set the Garonne as its eastern limit, others the Loire. De Marca, in Book III, chapter 14 of his work on the Spanish March, “assigns to this kingdom first and second Aquitaine, Vasconia, the county of Toulouse, Septimania, and all the territories that then belonged to the Spanish March.” [Col. 0572B] I regard this as beyond dispute. In the testament mentioned above, Charles enlarged the portion of territory assigned to Louis himself.].
>
> When the territories had been apportioned, the report spread increasingly throughout the world,  
> And Louis, exulting, went to claim the kingdom entrusted to him.
>
> It was an omen that his parents had called him so,  
> For he would be distinguished in war, powerful, and pious.
>
> For Louis, derived from the name *ludus* (“play”),  
> Suggests that he would “play with” his subjects by pacifying them.
>
> Or, if anyone prefers to unlock the Frankish language  
> So that he may learn the meaning of the name,
>
> That is, *Hluto* means “famous,” and *Wigch* likewise means Mars [war];  
> Thus it is clear that his name was composed from these elements. [Note: [Col. 0572C] Johann Georg Eccard cites these two verses from the Viennese Caesarean manuscript in his *History of Etymological Study* (Hanover, 1711), judging that *Hlutowigch* means “famous warrior.” Gottfried Philippi informed me by letter that in Otfrid, the most ancient writer, *Liuthi* means “light, I shine”; and, as Johann Goropius Becanus notes in his *Origines*, *Wigch* denotes “warlike.” See also the aforementioned Leibniz, *Archaeologia Teutonica*, letter W, p. 189. Ermoldus undertakes to explain this name as Latin *Ludovicus*, but with poetic licence offers us *ludus* (“play”) instead of the truth.]

[Col. 0572B]

> Already a boy [Note: [Col. 0572C] A boy indeed. For, as the Astronomer—or the anonymous author of Louis the Pious’s *Life* in Duchesne, vol. II of the *Frankish Historians*—writes, Louis was crowned in Rome while still being carried in a cradle, namely in the year 781, as we have already seen above. Then Charlemagne his father sent him to Aquitaine to reign; he was carried in a cradle as far as the city of Orléans. But why was Louis, who was no longer nursing, carried in a cradle, when he had already been born in 778? Because among the warlike Franks horses were indeed in daily use, but an infant could not use them. On the other hand, wagons, chariots, carts, and vehicles of that kind—supports for laziness, which in our time are held in such honor and use—were then scarcely employed.] lofty and filled with holy inspiration,
>
> He enlarged his realm in honor through war and faith.
>
> Hurrying to advance the Christian people, he enriched the heights  
> With gifts; he restored ancient gifts to the sacred churches.
>
> With ordered government he renewed his subject kingdoms,  
> Ruling the people by law with the aid of piety.
>
> He, the pious one, subdued the raging Vascones [Note: [Col. 0572D] Now Gascony. Henry Valois, in his *Description of Gaul*, already noted that among the ancient Franks the Aquitanians were improperly also called Vascones, because, in my opinion, the kingdom of Aquitaine then included Vasconia. Louis himself, according to the author of his *Life*, around the year 786 met Charlemagne his father at Paderborn dressed in the costume of the Vascones, together with boys of his own age.], by the mastery of his skill,  
> And from savage wolves he produced sheep.
>
> Finally, turning his swift arms against the Spaniards,  
> He drove them far away from his own borders.
>
> As for the heights of the earth, and however many fortresses he traversed,  
> He subjected them to his rule, with God carrying the arms;
>
> They are less known to me; or, had they been known,  
> My foolish style could not have recorded everything.
>
> But what fresh report has carried to my astonished ears  
> I shall begin to sing; the rest I leave to the learned.
>
> Meanwhile there was a city inhospitable to the Frankish troops,  
> More closely allied with the wishes of the Moors,
>
> Which the ancient Latins called Barcelona [Note: [Col. 0573C] Around the year 711, after occupying Africa, the Saracens, or Arabs, invaded Spain and gradually subjected most of its peoples to their rule by force of arms. It also seems likely that Barcelona was captured by that profane people at that time. The Moors were entrenched there and ruled it when Louis the Pious undertook the expedition against them narrated here.],
>
> And which had been very finely polished in the Roman fashion.
>
> It was always a refuge for Moorish brigands,  
> And was sufficiently filled with armed enemies.
>
> Whoever came from Spain or returned there  
> Entered it quietly, and everything was safe for him.
>
> It was always accustomed to ravage our troops,  
> And joyfully seize the spoils of those returning.
>
> Many leaders, with varied efforts of war,  
> Had long besieged it; but their desire [Note: [Col. 0573C] The sense is obscure. Perhaps the meaning is: “but their efforts dissolved into mere wishes”; the city was never captured.] came to nothing.
>
> With arms, ingenuity, or whatever skill anyone possessed,  
> Yet it drove their eagerness for battle far away.
>
> For it was strongly protected by massive walls,  
> Built of exceedingly hard marble, ancient and venerable.
>
> When June leads the whitening crops into the heavens  
> And ripe Ceres approaches, ready for the sickle,
>
> The Frank, rushing through the countryside and dwellings,  
> Seizes the planted crops and ravages the gifts of the fields,
>
> Or, when accustomed to gather the very sweet wines of Bacchus  
> Together with the vineyards [Note: [Col. 0573D] That is, the Franks did not ravage the fields of Barcelona only at harvest time, but also during the grape harvest, thereby relieving the Saracens of the labor and burden of gathering the grapes: the Franks themselves seized them.]; that labor was not theirs.
>
> Just as in autumn, with their ranks thickened, thrushes,  
> Or various birds whose food is the grape,
>
> Fly through the vineyards, seizing and carrying off the clusters;  
> By claws and beaks the beautiful grape is destroyed.
>
> The unhappy vinedresser in vain shakes his mournful cymbal  
> At the top of the fortress, or summons sounds by his skill;
>
> Nor is it easy work to prevent the hostile birds  
> From gathering in dense formation and plundering the feast.
>
> In no other way do the Franks, when the first season  
> Of crops arrives, seize the gifts of the countryside [Note: [Col. 0573D] For *ager*, “field,” “county,” or “district,” as we now say; the same word is sometimes found used in this sense by ancient writers.].
>
> Yet this circumstance could not break the stubborn Moors,  
> Nor could the varying fortunes and frequent arms of their leaders.
>
> Nor, indeed, did the Franks carry off the spoils as easily as did so many birds.

How many riches the swift sailor has sent him across the sea.

For many periods this matter remained uncertain and doubtful: on either side they say that harsh wars would arise.

When, in springtime, the countryside, warmed, grows green with renewed strength, and winter flees as the starry dew drives it away; when the returning year brings back the scents it had taken away, and fresh grass ripples with new moisture:

[Col. 0574B] Kings set in motion the laws of the realm and renew customary practices [Note: Thus the Caesarean manuscript, instead of *solita* or, as I think, *solemnia*. For in springtime arms and soldiers are prepared, both to defend one’s own borders and to invade those of others, whenever fear or necessity of war presses.],

and each goes forth to guard his own boundaries.

No less, in accordance with the ancient custom of the Franks [Note: Namely, in ancient times it was customary for Frankish kings to hold the solemn assembly of the realm on the Kalends of March, with nobles, counts, and other officers of the state gathering there. The poet calls the chosen men of the people, or “the heights of the realm,” the leading men summoned to that place. Fredegar, in his *Chronicle*, writes: “When the year had passed, the aforesaid king [Pippin] ordered all the Franks to come to him from the Kalends of March at Berny, as is the custom of the Franks.” I omit the other very ancient witnesses to this practice, adding only that the kings of the Lombards likewise customarily held the public assembly of the realm on the Kalends of March, and there enacted laws and declared war, as is especially clear from the prefaces to King Liutprand’s laws, part II, volume I of this collection.], he summons the familiar armies already established by Charles.

That is, the chosen men of the people, or the heights of the realm, on whose counsels the matter to be undertaken depends.

The foremost hasten to appear and obey his command willingly; the unarmed populace, sufficiently numerous, follows close behind.

They sit down when instructed. The king ascends his ancestral throne; the rest of the crowd prepares suitable gifts [Note: From ancient times this custom had also prevailed: when the assembly of the realm was held on the Kalends of March, the people brought gifts to the king. In the Fulda and Lambecian Annals under the year 750 one reads: “On a fixed day, once each year, according to ancient custom, gifts were offered by the peoples to those kings in the Field of Mars.”] outside.

They begin to speak. Then the descendant of Charles began and gave these words from his own heart:

“Great-hearted nobles, worthy by your merits of such a reward,

whom Charles appointed over the borders of our fatherland [Note: The sense would require *liminibus*, or rather *limitibus*. The nobles meant are those whom my father, Augustus Charles, appointed to protect the borders of the kingdom.],

for this reason the All-powerful has granted us the summit of honor,

so that we may duly bring aid to the people.

The annual cycle returns, when nations press upon nations,

and, as Mars takes his turn, they rush into arms.

This matter is well known to you, but unknown to us:

Tell us the counsel by which we may carry out our expedition.”

Thus spoke the king; and Lupus Santio [Note: As is stated plainly below, this Lupus was a prince of the Wascones. In the *Life of Charlemagne* written by the monk of Angoulême, the same Charles made an expedition in 769 against Unaldus, or Hunaldus, who had invaded the duchy of Aquitaine; his army was led by “Lupus, prince of the Wascones, who knew the places.” He was captured …] replied as follows [Note: This has been added to the manuscript by a more recent hand. “Hunold was captured,” and, according to Einhard’s testimony in his *Life of the same Charles*, the king “sent word through envoys to Lupus, duke of the Wascones, that he should surrender the fugitive.” Similar statements occur in Einhard’s own Annals and in the Annals of Saint-Bertin. I would not dare affirm with certainty that this was the same Lupus whom our poet introduces here as speaking, for a great deal of time passed between the year 769 and the year 799, when the siege of Barcelona described here was undertaken. But if he was not the same man, he was doubtless his son; for that reason he seems to be called here by a double name, Lupus Santio, to distinguish him from his father. He is said to have surpassed his ancestors in ability and fidelity; these words indicate that his forebears, too, had ruled Wasconia. *Santio* is nothing other than *Sancius*, and in Italian *Sancio*, a name commonly used among the ancient Spaniards. “Count Sancius, son of Sancius” occurs in a letter of Eulogius of Córdoba.] in opposition:

“Santio, who was carrying out the work of his own people,

prince of the Wascones, relying on Charles’s upbringing [Note: That is, he had been raised in the court of Charlemagne from childhood. The word occurs in this sense among the ancients; hence he was a familiar and household member of King Charles, a circumstance that gave him the greatest confidence in speaking. From this we can understand that the Lupus mentioned here is not the one recorded in Einhard’s Annals, but rather his son.],

and surpassing his ancestors in ability and fidelity.

O king, it is necessary for us to obey your judgment,

since a draught of counsel flows from your mouth.

But if this matter must now be conducted on our side,

I declare that, on my side, there will be peace and quiet.”

Then Duke William of Toulouse spoke [Note: In the *Life of Louis the Pious* written by the Astronomer, under the year 789, we read: “When Chorso had been removed from the duchy of Toulouse, William was substituted in his place. He quickly subdued the nation of the Wascones, light by nature as they are, both in action and in strength.” This is the same man who, after various demonstrations of military valor and various victories over the Saracens, having gained a great breath of secular glory, finally renounced the world, entered the monastery of Gellone founded by him in 806, and spent the rest of his life there with such an abundance of virtues that he was numbered among the saints. His Life, written anonymously not long after his death and published by Charles Stengel, was again published and annotated by the distinguished Mabillon among the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century four, p. 70; consult it if you want more information. Some records call him a count. Mabillon, however, thinks that the title of duke should by no means be denied him, since his predecessor enjoyed the same title. And rightly so. Here our poet expressly calls him Duke of Toulouse.] from the city;

bending his knee, he kissed the king’s feet with his mouth [Note: Observe this custom of kissing the feet of kings, so often performed when the leading men of the realm were about to address them; other examples will occur below. You owe this information to the poet, who describes the minor customs of his own age—things which a historian would scarcely ever have recorded.].

“O light of the Franks, O king and father, arms and glory,

who surpass your fathers in merit and your ancestors in skill,

lofty virtue is yours, and, great ruler, wisdom;

the consent of our fathers flows with harmonious agreement.

O king, if I am worthy, heed my counsels;

and, king, in your mercy favor my wishes.

There is a very savage people, called by the name of Sarah,

which habitually lays waste our borders,

strong, trusting in its horses, and no less in the strength of arms;

a people well known to me, and to whom I myself am well known.

I have often surveyed its walls, camps, places, and other features;

I can lead you by a peaceful route.

There is also, in those regions, a savage city [Note: That is, Barcelona, a refuge for Moorish pirates and raiders.],

which remains joined to the cause of so great an evil.

If, by God’s mercy and through your labor,

it is captured, there will be peace and rest for your people.

Turn your steps there, O king; bring gifts to the estates [Note: What “to bring gifts to the estates” means, Oedipus may explain. *Massa* signified nothing other than villages, estates, or farms in those times. Perhaps he understood “gifts of war,” an expression used more than once below.],

and William, gracious king, will be your guide.”

Then the king, smiling at these friendly words,

embraced his servant and gave and received kisses:

“Our gratitude to you; may you have the gratitude of my father Charles.

Good duke, for your merits you will always have honors [Note: For *honorem*, with the good leave of Priscian. It occurs below as well, and not only once.].

What you now recite has long been a concern

to place within the citadel of my heart; now that it has been recited, it pleases me.

I heed your counsels, as you ask; I heed your wishes:

Believe, O Frank, that my arrival will be swift.

For I confess that I must tell you one thing, William:

receive my words now with eager mind.

If, by the Lord’s gift, life remains with me,

as I think it will, and he prospers my journey,

I may either see your savage walls, Barcelona,

which has been gladdened by so many wars of mine,

I swear by both heads [perhaps leaning upon the shoulders

of Count William, he also spoke these words]:

or, if the profane Moorish host stands against me

and, covering itself and its own, wages the battles of Mars,

you, Barcelona, whether willingly or unwillingly,

will order the forbidden gates to be opened [Note: For *jubes*, “you will order”], and will seek my commands.”

At these words the nobles murmured in various speech

and pressed kisses upon the king’s beneficent feet.

Then the king addressed Bigo, his beloved, in words [Note: I think this was none other than the man who was later made count of Paris under Louis the Pious and founded the monastery of Fosses. In a diploma of Charles the Bald, king of France, from the year 844, preserved by Baluze in volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1454, the monastery of Fosses is said to have been received, at the petition of Bigo, formerly its illustrious count, under the protection and defense of Louis the Pious, emperor. The distinguished Mabillon mentions the same Bigo in his Benedictine Annals under the year 816, when that count died, citing two diplomas of the same Louis for the monastery of Fosses, in which the same Bigo is called an illustrious count; Mabillon calls him Begon or Biegon. From this you can also see how greatly Louis loved him, since the poet calls him “beloved Bigo.” It is therefore not surprising that Louis made him count of Paris after the death of his father Charles. His death is narrated below.],

in whose ears his sweet words sounded.

“Go quickly, Bigo; proclaim these things to the crowds of our people,

and sound our words through your heart” [Note: A scribal error. Thus it is found in the manuscript. Write *sona*, “sound.”].

As soon as the Titan has climbed the Virgin’s constellation,

and the sister follows her course in her own station,

let our army, in dense formation, joyfully seize

the walls of that city, bearing arms.

Bigo departs, skillfully carrying out the orders of his gracious master,

and goes and returns, swiftly bearing the famous commands.

Meanwhile the pious king, inflamed with love of Christ,

gives the Christians walls [Note: At first sight one might think *munera*, “gifts,” should be read. Nevertheless, we understand that here *moenia*, “walls,” signifies monasteries and churches, which Louis the Pious endowed.] worthy of their faith.

For they say that he duly established many companies of monks

under God’s authority.

If anyone wishes to know this, let him travel through the kingdoms of Aquitaine,

among which our little document sings of one.

There is a distinguished place, notable for its worship or religion,

to which the king himself first gave the name Conques [Note: Mabillon writes in his Benedictine Annals under the year 768 that there were those who claimed that the monastery of Conques in Aquitaine, situated in the diocese of Rodez, had been founded by Pippin, king of the Franks. Then, under the year 812, he discusses the origin of that monastery, uncertain and conjecturing that its foundation might be attributed to the Pippin mentioned above, to Louis the Pious, or to Pippin, king of Aquitaine and son of Louis himself. We now have Nigellus as a suitable witness, assigning the origin of that monastery, or cell, to Louis the Pious, then king of Aquitaine. The most ancient author of Louis’s Life had previously taught us the same thing under the year 811.],

for formerly it was suited to wild beasts and singing birds [Note: For *canoris*, “singing.”],

and, because of its wildness, was unknown to human beings.

Now it shines with a company of Christian brothers,

whose fame reaches farther through the heavens.

This cell, too, was built by the pious king’s gift;

he founded it, enriched it with possessions, and adorned it with services.

It lies in a broad valley, girdled by a pleasant river [Note: As is clear from a diploma of Louis the Pious issued in 819, that Augustus receives the monastery of Conques in the county of Rodez, on the stream called the Dourdou, under the name Conques, under his protection.],

with vineyards, orchards, and varied foods.

Through rocks cut away by vigorous, sweating labor,

a path is made by which the place may be reached:

A brother once lived there, called Datus by name [Note: Everything agrees with the diploma of Louis the Pious Augustus from the year 819, published by the distinguished Baluze in volume II, p. 1416, of the *Capitularies*. There the first rector of the monastery of Conques is called “a religious man named Dado,” who in our own times began to inhabit that place, where some Christians had taken refuge through fear of the Saracens.],

whom they report to have first inhabited that place.

While he was preserving his ancestral home from enemies [Note: That is, from the Saracens, who afflicted Aquitaine with frequent raids.],

his mother, still safe, shared the household with him.

Then, alas, while an immense tumult surrounded the county,

the Moors devastated Rodez [Note: Or Ruthenicum, now Rouergue.] severely [Note: For *vastavere*, “they devastated,” carrying away immense booty.].

They say that his mother was among this very great booty,

and that all the household’s possessions were taken.

When the enemies had departed, the exile hastened to see his own house

and each person to return to his familiar hearth.

When Datus recognized that his mother and his own house

had been plundered, he turned a burden of conflicting thoughts in his heart.

Straightaway, adorning a horse with trappings, and no less with arms,

he prepared, with his assembled companions, to follow them.

By chance there was a fortress, strong with rampart or stone,

to which the Moors were returning with their spoils.

Swiftly Datus and his companions, and the entire little populace,

gathered there in rivalry and prepared to break the gates.

Just as a hawk, gliding through the clouds on its wings,

seizes a bird with its talon and flees to its familiar caves,

while its companions croak and uselessly repeat their harsh cries

through the sky and follow the bird,

so, sitting safely, it grips and strikes its prey,

and turns it in whatever direction it pleases.

In the same way the Moors, possessing the rampart and the booty,

fear Datus’s battles, arrows, and threats.

Then one of them, from the fortress tower, addresses the young man,

uttering shameful words in a mocking voice:

“Tell me, clever Datus, what business has just brought you

to our fortress, and your companions with you, I beg you.

If you wish, for such a reward, to give us the horse

on which you ride, richly caparisoned,

then let your mother go safely to you, along with the rest of the booty;

but otherwise, before your eyes, you have your mother’s death.”

Datus replied with words unworthy of repetition:

“Bring about my mother’s death; I have no great concern for it.

For the horse you demand, I would never deem it worthy to give it:

wretch, it is not fitting for your reins.”

Without delay the cruel man halted Datus’s mother in the fortress

and tore her apart before her son’s eyes.

For they say that he first cut off her breasts with a sword,

and, after severing her head, said, “Here is your mother” [Note: Or rather: “Here is your mother,” he says.].

The wretched Datus rages over his mother’s death;

now here, now there, he wavers and groans.

He has no access, nor the strength to avenge his mother’s limbs;

sad and bereft of reason, he flees.

After losing everything and taking up his best weapons,

he soon began to live piously as a dweller in the wilderness.

Once he had been made harsher by the savage death of his mother,

from then on he returned more firmly to your yokes, O Christ.

For a long time he alone reflected on these things,

because he had despised every worldly sin.

When the fame of the pious king reached his ears,

he immediately summoned the servant of the Lord to his own dwelling.

For the entire day the king and the servant of God conversed in similar speech,

equal in religion.

Then the king and Datus first set the foundations at Conques

and prepared for the monks the camp that was to be.

Where lately wild beasts had lain in a mighty company,

there now a harvest pleasing to God is restored.

Meanwhile the king’s nobles and the people’s ranks,

long since summoned, willingly carry out the commands.

Companies gather from every side according to Frankish custom,

and a dense ring surrounds the city’s walls [Note: That is, the walls of Barcelona.].

Before all others came the descendant of Charles with a splendid host;

he gathered the leaders for the city’s destruction [Note: Einhard writes in his Annals under the year of Christ 801: “That very summer the city of Barcelona in Spain was captured, after having been besieged for two years.” Therefore the siege began in 799. Similar statements may be read in the Fulda, Saint-Bertin, and Loiselian Annals.].

On his own side Prince William pitched his tents,

with Heripreth [Note: In the *Life of Louis the Pious* written by the contemporary author known as the Astronomer, under the year 808, these words occur: “King Louis decided to return to Tortosa in person, taking with him Heribert, Liutard, Isembard, and a strong reinforcement of Franks.” No one will deny that this is the same man who here is called Heripreth instead of Heriperth. Around that time there also lived Herebert, count of Vivarais, perhaps a different person.], Liuthard [Note: As we have recently seen from the *Life of Louis the Pious*, he accompanied the king himself toward Tortosa. Before Barcelona surrendered, however, according to the author of that same Life, “King Louis, having assembled the people of his kingdom at Toulouse, deliberated and considered what seemed necessary to be done. For after Burgundio’s death, his county of Fidentiacus was assigned to Liutard.”], and Bigo, or Bero [Note: As Einhard testifies in his *Life of Charlemagne*, among the others who signed the final documents of that famous emperor was Count Bero. After Barcelona was captured, the *Life of Louis the Pious* says that Count Bera was left there for its protection. He was the first count of Barcelona, as Peter de Marca has already noted in book III, chapter 17 of the *Marca Hispanica*, and as will be confirmed below in book III of this poem, where he will again be mentioned. Baluze, in volume II of the *Capitularies*, p. 1490, reports a judgment held in 869 in which this same Count Bera, already long dead, and his daughter Rotrudis are named.],

Santio [Note: He has been mentioned above. He was prince of Wasconia.], Libulfus [Note: I find no trace of this man among the ancients, except that in his Benedictine Annals under the year 828 Mabillon mentions a certain illustrious man named Leybulfus who made a benefaction to the monks of Lérins; perhaps he had nothing to do with this Libulfus.], Hilthibret [Note: For Hiltiberth, or, below, Hildibert, whom I think was a count.], and Hisimbard [Note: As we saw above from the *Life of Louis the Pious*, that Augustus took Heribert, Liutard, and Isembard with him to Tortosa in 808. Earlier, in 806, he sent Isembard, Hademar, Bera, Burrellus, and the rest against the Saracens. I think this man was a count, and perhaps the father of Count Isembard, who is mentioned in a capitulary of King Charles the Bald from the year 853.],

and many others, whom it would delay us to name.

The remaining youth is scattered in camps across the fields:

Frank, Wascon, Goth, and the Aquitanian host.

The din rises to heaven; the sky resounds with trumpets;

within the city there is shouting, terror, weeping, and every kind of distress.

While these things are being done, evening star brings back its shadows,

and the enemy possesses your wealth, Barcelona.

When bright dawn first returns to human beings,

the summoned counts seek the royal tents;

each sits down in his proper order upon the grass,

and with attentive ears asks for the king’s words.

Then the offspring of Charles delivered this speech with wise mouth:

“Receive this counsel in your hearts, nobles.

If this people worshiped God and pleased Christ,

and were anointed with the oil of holy baptism,

peace would have to be established and maintained between us,

so that it might be joined to God through religion.

But now it remains accursed and rejects our salvation,

following the commands of the demon.

Therefore the mercy of the Thunderer is able

to render it a servant to us [Note: That is: God will deliver each of them to us into servitude.].

Now, now, let us hasten at once to the walls and fortresses,

O Franks, and let the former strength return to your hearts.

As winds swiftly fly at the command of Aeolus,

roaring through countryside, forests, and every strait,

and houses are plundered, crops and forests tremble,

while the bird can scarcely hold its sunny perch on hooked feet;

so the wretched sailor, suddenly abandoning sail and oar,

drags his loose canvas across the wandering sea.

In the same way, at the command of the Franks, the entire army

goes and returns in continual movement toward the city’s destruction.

They run into the forests; everywhere the sound of axes rings;

pines are cut down, and the tall poplar falls.

One makes ladders, another arranges stakes;

one carries arms swiftly, another gathers stones.

Dense arrows fall, and missile iron as well;

the gates thunder beneath the battering ram, and frequent sling-stones strike.

Meanwhile the thick Moorish host,

remaining in the towers, prepares to hold the camp.

The prince of the city was a Moor named Zadun [Note: The Astronomer, in the *Life of Louis the Pious*, calls him Zaddo, duke of Barcelona. In the Saint-Bertin and Metz Annals under the year 801 it is said that “the city of Barcelona in Spain was captured, and Zatun, its governor.”],

who had ruled this city with powerful skill.

He runs to the walls, accompanied by a sorrowful crowd:

‘What is this strange new sound, my companions?’ he asks.

But one of his companions answered him who asked,

singing harsh omens in words of doom:

‘The prince, that hero [Note: I think this is for *heros*.] of the Goths,

does not mingle battle with us;

our spear has driven him away so many times.

But Louis, the illustrious offspring of Charles, is here;

he himself orders the leaders and wields arms in his hand.

Unless swift Córdoba now comes to the aid of the wretched [Note: Córdoba was then also subject to the Saracens, and King Abbaca ruled there; but because he was at war with his uncles, he was forced to refrain from defending the people of Barcelona. Roderic of Toledo, in his *History of the Arabs*, chapter 25: “While Albacan was waging war against his uncles, the Christians acquired Barcelona, and the Arabs suffered devastation and burning.”]—us,

we, the people, and the revered city will fall.

He utters these sad words with lowered heart,

and from the tower, not far away, sees the weapons.

‘Come, friends, let us defend the walls from the enemy;

perhaps Córdoba will bring us aid.

But there is something greatly displeasing to my mind, people,

which troubles me as I prepare to tell it to you.

You see this lofty people that besieges our fortresses;

it is strong, armed, harsh, and swift.

For I will now confess something hard to say,

whether I remain silent or speak, though it will not please you.

Whomever that famous people has met in its war,

whether willingly or unwillingly, it has subjected to servitude.

It brought under its empire and dominion

the Roman city [Note: It had recently happened that Charlemagne was proclaimed emperor of the Romans—that is, on Christmas Day in the year 800, while the siege of Barcelona continued and was prolonged into the following year.] which once founded this city [Note: It would be difficult to show that Barcelona was founded by the Romans. Indeed Ausonius calls it Punic Barcelona, words that seem rather to attribute its origin to the Carthaginians. That a Roman colony was established there is beyond dispute. Pliny, book III, chapter 3: “On the seacoast is the colony of Barcelona, surnamed Faventia.” This is also taught us by the surviving inscriptions.],

along with its power.

They always bear arms; their youth is accustomed to war;

the young man carries them, and the old man practices the craft.

For I shudder whenever I repeat the very name of the Franks:

the Frank bears a name derived from his savagery [Note: Many maintain that the people called Franks signify nothing other than “free,” especially Cluverius in book III, chapter 20 of *Germania Antiqua*, and Adrian Valesius in his *Notitia Galliarum* under the word *Francia*. But Sigebert of Gembloux, at the beginning of his *Chronography*, writes: “Valentinian called the Franks by the Attic word which in Latin is interpreted as ‘savage.’” The same is the view of Paulus Aemilius and of the anonymous author of Erfurt in Pistor’s collection. Against them, Cluverius, fearless as usual in correcting others, cries: “Paulus Aemilius, Sigebert, and all who have published such things with them or on their authority were delirious.” Good words, Cluverius. However that may be, and even if Valentinian must be excluded here, behold a very ancient witness—or at least what was commonly believed under Augustus Louis the Pious—that the Franks received their name from their savagery. Those men certainly understood the force of the German language of their own age better than later writers.].

What more can I say now, citizens, with sorrowful heart?

Alas, I know it well, and do not wish to recount it.

Let us strengthen the walls with a powerful guard to hold them:

a watchman at the gates, trusting and watchful.”

Meanwhile the young men, with a dense crowd accompanying them,

wear away the gates with the battering ram; Mars resounds everywhere.

The walls, enclosed with squared stone, are struck;

dense arrows fall and strike the wretched defenders.

Then the Moor Durzaz shouts from the lofty tower,

singing shameful words in a loud, mocking voice:

“O exceedingly harsh people, spread throughout the wide world,

why do you shake our holy camps and disturb the peaceful?

Do you not think that you can suddenly overturn from their foundations

these buildings, the work of a thousand years of Rome?

Flee, savage Frank; withdraw yourself from our sight.

Neither your appearance pleases us nor your commands.”

In reply, Hilthiberth uttered words that were not shameful;

behold, he seizes his bow in his hand.

Finally he stood swiftly opposite the shouting enemy,

holding the horn bow, and drew and bent it.

The arrow, flying from the bow, entered the black brain

and drove its deadly shaft into the shouting mouth.

Falling, he unwillingly abandoned the lofty walls,

and dying stained the Franks with dark blood.

The Franks raised shouts with joyful hearts;

the wretched Moors, by contrast, were filled with weeping.

Then various men send various men down to Orcus in death:

William kills Habirudar, and Liuthard kills Uriz.

Zabirizun’s spear pierces Uzacus with its thrusting iron;

the sling strikes Colizan, and the sharp arrow Gozan [Note: Added by a second hand in place of the earlier erased word.].

The Franks could not otherwise approach them in battle,

but now with missiles, now also with sling-stones.

The fierce Zadun had ordered them neither to trust the battle

nor, by any chance, to retreat from the camp.

For twice ten days this opposing struggle [Note: That is, twenty days; ancient poets commonly spoke in this way. Nevertheless, I cannot refrain from suspecting that Nigellus intended *menses*, “months,” instead of *solibus*. For the Frankish Annals state that the siege of Barcelona was prolonged for two years, and what follows seems to indicate that the Franks had already remained in the same siege for a long time, since King Louis addresses the nobles.] occurred,

and fortune brought various outcomes.

No machine was able to break through the gates of the walls;

the enemy found no entrance into the fortifications.

Yet the war did not cease from its undertaking,

but the battle continually battered the gates with its barrier.

Meanwhile the illustrious offspring of powerful Charles,

carrying the scepter in his hand, advanced with an accompanying choir,

and encouraged the leaders, encouraged the ranks in due order,

calling them to the weapons of Mars in the manner of his father.

“Believe me now, young men; believe me now, all nobles,

and let these words remain in your hearts:

I will not first return to see my father’s dwellings,

by the Lord’s gift, or my own kingdoms,

before this city and its people,

overcome by war and famine, come swiftly as suppliants under my rule.”

Then again one of them scattered words into the air,

holding the walls securely and uttering mocking speech:

“Frank, why are you mad? Why do you assail our walls?

This city cannot be captured by clever means.

We have enough food: meat and honeyed gifts

remain in the city; you are afflicted by dreadful hunger.”

William replied with contrary words,

and, scornful, spoke such things in a voice:

“Listen, Moor, I beg you, proud man, to words that are not gentle,

not pleasing to you, but, I believe, entirely true.

You see the horse fitted with spots and varied colors,

on which I ride, directing my gaze from afar toward your walls.

Before my host abandons your exceedingly forbidden walls,

he will perish as food for our unworthy mouths

and will have to be chewed by our teeth;

never will the battles we have begun fall away.”

Then he struck his dark breast with dark fists,

and, in misery, disfigured his black face with hooked nails.

Struck through with fear in his heart, he fell on his face,

the wretched man beating the sky of heaven with his cries.

His companions abandoned the fortresses and, in great astonishment,

marveled at the Franks and their exceedingly harsh words.

Zado ran furiously through the immense heaps:

“Where are you fleeing, citizens, and where are you directing your course?”

Zado, the Franks now send you this reply:

“What now stands pleasing to us [Note: Is it sufficiently pleasing? Or should one perhaps read *stant placitura*, “the pleasing things stand”?]—but first hear what follows.

They will first gnaw their horses with shameful teeth

before they will ever wish to abandon your camp.”

“O wretched citizens, long ago I foretold these things to you,

when someone asked what battles were to be fought.

Now also tell me whatever counsel is useful to you,

so that I may be able to complete the rest.

For everywhere you see the walls bursting apart in dense ruin,

and your people dying as iron tears them to pieces.

Córdoba sends you none of the promised aid;

everywhere we are harassed by war, hunger, and thirst.

What remains now, except to seek peace from the Franks,

and send envoys who will go swiftly?”

Gnashing his teeth, he tore his garment,

ripped apart his dark hair, and lacerated his face.

Then he continued in words, again and again calling

upon Córdoba with profane voice, and weeping for a long time:

“O swift Moors, where has your confidence now gone?

Now, companions, bring forth your accustomed strength.

If any concern for our people still remains,

I beg one thing of you; with this single favor I shall be glad.

I myself have observed the place where, as the army withdraws,

the dense camps leave a space and the tents are sparse [Note: The sense is: “I have noticed a place where the enemy’s tents are sparse and an opening lies through which I can escape past the enemy.”].

I shall be able to pass unharmed through those ambushes;

perhaps I can run to familiar allies for assistance [Note: And perhaps I may be able to reach the sultan of Córdoba and obtain his aid.].

Only guard the gates with the greatest effort,

unafraid, brothers, while I return here.

Let no circumstance compel you to abandon the fortresses,

nor do I urge you to go out into the fields to battle.”

After giving his people many instructions, he withdrew from the city

and secretly passed joyfully through the ranks.

Already he was making his way through the pleasant silence of night,

when suddenly the wretched horse neighed loudly.

At that cry the guards stirred their troops in the camp

and immediately pursued it.

Leaving the road in fear, he turned the horse

and threw himself headlong into the dense ranks.

He sees the hated companies, with no happy expression,

and the wretched man has no means of escape by his ingenuity.

Soon he is captured [Note: The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* reports the same thing in these words: “Zaddo, duke of Barcelona, was persuaded by someone whom he thought his friend to proceed as far as Narbonne. When he was captured, he was brought to King Louis.”]; deservedly overcome, he is without delay bound with straps.

Trembling, he is led to the king’s canvas-covered tents.

Flying rumor fills the entire city with terror

and announces with its own voice that the king has been captured.

Mothers and fathers, and the young people, redouble their mourning;

the little boy carries this message, and the girl carries that.

Nor is there a lesser sound in the camp, beating the sky everywhere;

the people resound with unanimous joy.

Meanwhile black night falls, and dawn brings back

the gracious day: the Franks seek the royal camp.

Then Charles’s offspring speaks with peaceful heart

and gives kind words to his servants:

“Zadun, wishing to hasten to the Spanish ranks,

seeking aid, arms, and men of equal strength,

is here captured against his will, bound and unarmed,

before our doors, though he had not been before our eyes.

Arrange, William, that he be able to see his walls,

and order them swiftly to open the gates for us.”

Without delay Zado follows, bound by ropes,

and from afar raised his outstretched hand by a gesture.

For earlier, as he was departing, he himself had told his companions:

“Whether evil fortune or prosperity befalls us,

I do not know; if by chance I should encounter the Frankish troops [Note: I would write *incurrero*, “I shall encounter,” as the sense requires.],”

Yet I beg you nevertheless, as I said, hold the camp.

Then, stretching his hands toward the walls, he called out to his friends:

“Open now, comrades, the gates that have long been forbidden.”

At the same time he craftily bent his fingers and fixed his nails into his palms, performing this gesture deceptively.

By this signal he indicated that the camp should be held; yet unwillingly he called out, “Open!”

Recognizing this, Vilhelmus, in a sudden rush, struck him with his fist—not acting deceptively.

Gnashing his teeth, he turns over anxieties beneath his breast; he marvels at the Moor’s ingenuity, but even more at his cleverness.

“Believe me, if the love and fear of the king did not forbid it, this day, Zado, might well be your last.”

Meanwhile Zadun is guarded by a Frankish custodian, while his companions [Note: That is, the Saracens of Barcelona continue to prepare to hold the city.], weeping, prepare to hold the camp.

[Col. 0585A] The following moon was completing its allotted circuit,

When the king and the Franks together approached the forbidden camp.

The dense siege-engine resounds, and the walls are battered everywhere;

Mars rages, and before this there had been no battle like it.

Arrows fall thickly; the twisted sling exhausts itself:

The king directs the work, urging on the commanders.

Now the wretched Moors dare neither climb the lofty walls

Nor look out from the tower upon the camp they desire to see.

And just as, on a little stream, a chance flock of waterfowl swims,

When it settles down trembling, trusting vainly in the river,

Behold, Jupiter’s armor-bearer descends from high heaven,

And flies around them for a long time after finding them.

Some thrust their heads into the depths and raise them again beneath the air;

One reclines among the seaweed, another is pressed down into the mud,

But that one hovers above them on wings and harasses the trembling birds;

The one that lifts its head into the winds, he snatches away.

So, throughout the city, the sword and death and terror

Pursue the frightened Moors as they flee.

Then the pious king himself, brandishing a spear in his arm,

Forced it swiftly to fly against the hostile city.

The flying spear passed through the winds into the middle of the city

And was driven deeply into the marble pavement beneath.

At this sign, the Moors, shaken in heart by fear,

Marveled at the weapon, and even more at the deed of the one who had thrown it.

What could they do? The king was already gone, and the fighting was cooling;

The sword had carried off the foremost of the Moors.

At last, defeated and exhausted by war and hunger,

They unanimously wished to surrender the camp.

The gates are opened [Note: Barcelona came into the submission of Louis the Pious in the year 801, as the concordant Frankish annals testify. Pagi, however, long ago observed that the Astronomer, the author of the Life of Louis the Pious, had been deceived when he wrote that the city had been taken from the Saracens at a later date.], and all the inner chambers are laid open;

The shaken city comes into the king’s service.

[Col. 0585C] At once the desired arrangements are established in the city;

The victorious Franks rule over the enemy without delay.

It was the sacred Sabbath when this deed was accomplished,

The day on which the city was first opened to the Franks.

For on the following festival day the king,

Louis, ascended the city in triumph to fulfill his vows to God.

He cleansed the places where they had worshipped the demon’s sacred rites,

And himself rendered devout thanks to Christ.

By God’s permission, the victorious king returns with the guards

To his own dwelling, and so does his people.

Meanwhile, the spoils are led in a long procession to Charles,

The Moorish plunder and the gifts of the commanders:

Weapons, corselets, richly adorned garments and helmets,

A Parthian horse with trappings, and golden bridles as well.

[Note: Compare the corresponding passage in Einhard’s Annals, where the same events are repeated in other respects: “Zatus, his prefect—that is, of Barcelona—and several other Saracens were captured. Zatus and Roshelmus were brought on the same day into the emperor’s presence and condemned to exile.”]

Zado, trembling greatly and unwilling to see the Franks again,

Moves forward as well, accompanied by a slow companion’s step.

[Col. 0586A] The shrewd Bigo, hurrying, flies ahead of the column and is

The first to reach Charles’s hall, bearing joyful news.

Fresh rumor quickly threw the whole palace into confusion

And soon reached the emperor’s ears in triumph.

Bigo is summoned and appears; he kisses the lofty feet,

And in order follows the commands given to him in words:

“Behold, the pious king Louis sends gifts to his father,

The emperor Charles—

Gifts which, victorious, he took from the Moors

By sword, shield, and his own arm, to be held as his.

He has also sent you the king of the city he captured by arms:

Zadun is here before the emperor’s eyes.

The city that once devastated many of the Franks

Now lies defeated in war, seeking the just rule of the king.”

Then Caesar Charles spoke these words with calm expression,

[Col. 0586B] Raising his eyes and hands toward heaven:

“May the grace of the One enthroned on high accompany my beloved son;

May our grace remain with him.

What thanks can I render for such a gift,

Son worthy of God through your own merits?

O most illustrious son, whom I have always loved,

Holding you in my heart, as the patriarch Paulinus [Note: Patriarch of Aquileia, a most holy man, as the Continuator of Paul the Deacon calls him in Freher. In the *Lives of the Patriarchs of Aquileia*, which I edited in vol. IV of the *Anecdota Latina*, p. 240, it is written of him: “He went to the glorious Emperor Charlemagne to enlarge the rights of the Church. This man, of remarkable holiness, obtained many privileges from Emperor Charles.” See also what Ughelli has on him in vol. V of the *Italia Sacra*.] once told me.

It is said that the kindly patriarch

Had come to the holy sees at the king’s command.

One day, while he was seated in the venerable church

And, astonished, was singing a melody to Christ,

It happened that the illustrious son of Charles [Note: Namely, the eldest son of Charlemagne, who died before his father in the year 811.]

Came to his father, strengthened by the support of the nobles.

As he hurried toward the altar and approached it,

Where the holy bishop was performing his sacred duties,

Paulinus immediately asked who he was.

The attentive servant gave him in reply the answer he had begun to speak. [Note: The same expression occurs elsewhere. In Virgil, Aeneid 11, one finds *orsa referre*, ‘to report begun words,’ as Servius explains it. Our poet took the expression from there.]

When he learned that this was to be the king’s first-born son,

He fell silent; and the prince continued on his begun course.

At last, after some time, the hero Pippin [Note: The second son of Charlemagne, king of Italy, whom untimely death carried off in the year 810.]

Came with a company accompanying the great-hearted youth.

Paulinus, hastening, addressed the same servant,

And asked him again; the servant prepared to give the true answer.

When the bishop recognized the name and recalled the king [Note: Rather, *regemque*: that is, remembering that he was king of Italy, he immediately uncovered his head.],

He immediately bowed his head; the other continued swiftly on.

At last Louis came, and, approaching the altar more quickly,

Embraced it, prostrating himself suppliantly upon the ground.

Shedding tears for a long time, he prayed to Christ reigning in heaven

That he might bring him help.

When the holy man [Note: For *sacerdos*, ‘priest.’ Our poet uses the same form in many other places.]

Saw this, he rose burning with zeal from his seat

[Col. 0586D] To address the sacred man with reverence.

Earlier, when Pippin and Charles had passed by,

He had remained seated and had uttered no words.

At last the king [Note: That is, Louis. The “prophet” is the patriarch.] worshiped the prophet with his body prostrate,

And behold, Paulinus received the pious king.

He gave him hymn-like words filled with varied expression:

‘Go,’ he said, ‘to Charles in devotion. Farewell.’

When the prophet first reached the emperor’s ear,

He recited everything to him in due order:

‘If God appoints as king from your Frankish seed,

This man will be suited to your realms.’ [Note: This prophecy of Louis the Pious’s succession to the empire after the death of his father Charlemagne is attributed to the celebrated Abbot Alcuin by the nearly contemporary author of his Life, part I, ch. 10, p. 156 of the fourth century of the Benedictines. When the holy abbot was asked by Charles who would succeed him in the empire, he replied: “You shall have Louis the humble, an outstanding successor.” Then, turning to those present, he said: “Do you see Louis, humbler than his brothers? You will indeed see him as his father’s most exalted successor.” Let others judge to which of these writers greater credence should be given. Perhaps to both.]

The wise Charles disclosed these words to a few attendants,

Whom he trusted, or who were pleasing to him. [Note: I do not know whether *causa* is used here for *res*, ‘matter.’ The obscure sense seems to be explained as follows: Charles disclosed these things to his intimates, in whom he had greater confidence and whom he favored above the others.]

He recalls the messenger once more and asks him in due order

How the famous city had been brought under his rule;

By what ingenuity the king had brought Zadun there as a captive,

And which commanders he himself had overthrown in savage war.

Good Bigo recounts it, and tells the whole truth,

And the pious Caesar honors his words.

Caesar, rejoicing, offers him the cup from which he happened to be drinking;

He eagerly drinks the wine he has drawn.

Then, honoring the servant with gifts and many distinctions,

He sends great gifts to his own son.

Loaded with praise and gifts, Bigo proceeds swiftly

And, joyful, reaches his own king.

May the Thunderer grant that the exiled poet [Note: That is, the poet Ermoldus Nigellus himself, an exile, begs that he may return to the kingdom of Pippin if liberty is granted him. This Pippin was the son of Louis the Pious; his kingdom was Aquitaine. See my Preface to this poem.]

May joyfully go into the realms of the powerful Pippin,

And may Caesar himself, powerful as he is, grant it.

Therefore, little book, bring your ending beneath this name,

As you proceed in fellowship with three brothers.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0587]

[Col. 0587C] And now, with God’s favor, peace held the Franks everywhere,

For Mars and God had struck down their adversaries.

For the venerable old man, Caesar Charles, renowned throughout the world,

Summoned a new assembly to his palace.
