[Note: Einhard, in his Annals under the year 813, writes: “After a general assembly had been held, he summoned his son Louis, king of Aquitaine, to Aachen, received him, placed the crown upon him, and made him his associate in the imperial title.” The author of Louis’s Life gives a fuller account of this under the same year, 813.]

Seated upon a golden throne, he thus began from on high,

While the chosen nobles sat around him:

“Hear, nobles, who rely upon our nurture:

I shall tell things that I know and believe sufficiently true.

While strength remained in my youthful body,

It was my concern to sport with strength and arms.

I confess that neither through my sluggishness

Nor through shameful fear did an enemy people seize the borders of the Franks.

Now my blood is growing weak, and dreadful old age grows numb;

My flowering white hair presses upon my milk-white neck.

My right hand, once famous throughout the world for war,

Now, with its blood grown cold, falls trembling.

The son born to me has departed from the shores above [Note: His premature death carried off Pippin in 810 and Charles in 811, both sons of this Charlemagne.],

Having fulfilled his appointed course; alas, he lies buried.

But she who once seemed more excellent and more pleasing to the Lord

[Col. 0588C] Has now also been left to me [Note: That is, left behind.],

And yet Christ has not abandoned you, Franks:

He now preserves for you a beloved offspring from our stock.

She, always illustrious and delighting in my commands,

Obeyed and carried out my authority.

Always through the love of God she renewed the rights of the churches

And improved the kingdoms entrusted to her.

You saw what she once sent at the death of the Moors [Note: The verse exceeds the meter, since it consists of seven feet. The word *dona*, “gifts,” should be deleted as superfluous and as having been added by some ignorant person; the reading should be: “You saw what she once …”],

A king, arms, and captives together as great trophies.

Give me counsel, Franks, from a faithful heart;

Tell me, and let us promptly carry out the same deed.”

Then Heinardus [Note: The Heinardus named here by our poet is the same as Einhard, a very celebrated man, called Heinardus by other ancient writers as well. He was the author of the Life of Charlemagne and, as many believe, also of the Frankish Annals; he was the emperor’s notary and intimate, and dear to him among the few, as Ermoldus himself testifies. He is also said to have married one of Charles’s daughters, though this is not equally certain.] was present, beloved by Charles,

Shrewd in intelligence and strong in goodness.

He falls before his feet and kisses his venerable footprints;

Learned in counsel, he begins first with these words:

[Col. 0588D] “O Caesar, famous in heaven, on earth, and on the sea,

Who grants your own people the imperial name,

It is not within our power, nor has Christ granted it to any mortal,

To add anything to your counsels.

What God, in his mercy, has bestowed upon you in your heart,

I urge you to complete at once, as a parent.

You have a son, gracious one, exceedingly sweet in character,

Who, by his merits, is able to hold your kingdoms.

All of us, great and small alike, ask for him;

The Church asks for him, and Christ himself favors him.

After your sorrowful death,

He is able to maintain the empire’s rights by arms, intelligence, and faith.”

The delighted Caesar assents and prays to Christ.

Then he sends quickly to his son.

For at that time the good Louis,

As I have sung above, held the kingdom of the Aquitanians in triumph.

Why delay? He immediately reached his father’s palace;

The clergy, people, and nobles of Aachen rejoice, as does his father. [Note: That is, Aachen, which Charlemagne had chosen as his principal residence.]

Charles again begins, and recounts and explains everything

Word by word to his beloved son:

“Son dear to God, to your father, and to the obedient people,

Whom God has allowed me to have as my consolation,

You yourself see my old age hastening toward its end

And the time of death approaching for me. [Note: In fact, death took him in the following year, 814.]

The first administration of my kingdom remains in place,

Which God himself undeservedly bestowed upon me.

What I say to you is prompted not by human favor

Or by the fickleness of the human mind, but by the love of devotion.

Francia gave me birth; Christ granted me honor;

Christ gave me possession of my father’s kingdoms.

I held these same kingdoms, and received even greater ones;

I was both shepherd and weapon to the flock devoted to Christ.

I was the first of the Franks to obtain the imperial name,

And I gave the Franks the Roman name.

[Col. 0589C] He said this and placed upon his son’s head a crown of gems and gold. [Note: All the annals agree that Louis, the son of Charles Augustus, was not only made Charles’s associate in the imperial title with the agreement of the whole kingdom, but was also crowned with the imperial diadem. This coronation, however, was later repeated and confirmed by Stephen, the Roman pontiff, as will be related below.]

‘Receive, son, the crown that Christ grants me,

And receive, son, together with it the glory of empire.

May he who, in his mercy, granted you the summit of honor

Grant you the power to please him.

Then father and son, rejoicing in this great gift,

Celebrate a great banquet with devotion to God.

O festive day, memorable for many years!

Frankish land, you hold two closely joined twins.”

France, rejoice gladly; let golden Rome rejoice with you [Note: That is, Rome, outstanding above all other cities. This title later became so established that it was used on the seals of the emperors. A diploma of Otto I, written in 972, bears a hanging lead seal whose front shows a head with the inscription *AUREA ROMA* (“Golden Rome”), while the reverse reads *OTTO IPERATOR ROMANOR* (“Otto, Emperor of the Romans”). Similar expressions may be read on several other imperial seals.]

The remaining kingdoms look toward your empire.

Then wise Charles urged his attendant repeatedly

To love Christ and honor the Church.

Embracing him with great affection, he gave and received beautiful kisses;

He grants him leave [Note: That is, he gives permission or pardon and allows him to return to his own kingdom, namely Aquitaine.] and speaks his final words.

Not long afterward, mature in age and worn by years,

The emperor visits his ancient ancestors in death. [Note: The most glorious emperor ended his life in the year 814, as noted above.]

They prepare an honorable funeral, and his body is entrusted to a tomb

In his own basilica, which he had built at Aachen.

[Col. 0590B] Meanwhile, someone is sent to report the father’s funeral

To his son; Rampho [Note: The Life of Louis the Pious relates the same matter in these words: “After the death of his father of pious memory, Rampho was sent by those who arranged his burial, so that Louis might learn of his death promptly.” He is called both Rampo and Rampho, with the same freedom by which *Campio* and *Camphio* were once written. In a precept of Louis the Pious dating from 823, preserved by Baluze, one reads: “How the illustrious man Rapo, count, approached our serenity, seeking a privilege for the monastery of Bagnols in the diocese of Girona, which the same count had enriched with many estates.” But *Rampo* should be read; this is established by another diploma of Charles the Bald, in which, in 844, he confirms several things for the same monastery, which Abbot Domnulus had built with his own hands, with the permission of the margrave Rampo. If the count Rampo and the margrave Rampo were indeed one and the same—for they could have been father and son—we now learn that he was count of Girona and subsequently elevated by the title of margrave because he defended the borders of the Spanish March against the Saracens.] prepares to make the journey swiftly.

Night and day he flies, traversing broad lands,

And at last reaches the place where Louis was.

Beyond the Loire there is a fertile and suitable place;

On one side it is enclosed by woods, on the other by open plain.

In the middle it flourishes amid the calm river’s current;

It is rich in fish and abundant in wild animals.

There Louis, in triumph, built lofty palaces.

“Do you ask where? It bears the name Thedwat [Note: In the Life of Louis the Pious mentioned above, it is reported that when Charlemagne died, Louis proclaimed “a general council at a place whose name is Tehotvadus.” A palace of this kind stood in the diocese of Angers, and its remains are said still to survive. It is now called Doadum or Dove and is mentioned under various names by Einhard, Thegan, Hincmar, the annalist of Tilianus, and others. More may be found about it in Adrian Valesius’s *Notitia Galliarum* and in Mabillon’s *Diplomatics*, book 4, chapter 142.] is here, my friend,

Where he judged that the pious duties of the subject people

Should be performed, governing clergy and people with devotion.”

Suddenly Rampho entered and threw the entire palace into confusion,

Bringing the sad news of pious Charles’s death.

When this report reached the ears of the good king,

He immediately grieved, wept, and lamented his father.

Among the hesitant ministers Bigo came running;

He was accustomed to see his lord in the morning.

He urged him to dry his cheeks and put aside his tears:

[Col. 0591A] “Another matter,” he said, “must now be undertaken by you.

When these things are known and remain within your breast, prince,

This is the lot that holds men of the human race.

We shall all, I confess, hasten there;

Yet none of those men is able to return.

Rise, and let us all hasten to the venerable church:

It is time to sing hymns and offer prayers to God.”

Listening to his servant, he at last rose,

And urged everyone with him to fulfill their vows to God.

That night was filled with psalms and hymns,

And the day was completed with the melodies of Masses.

Already the third day was rising in the bright heavens,

And Phoebus shone with his rays across the world.

When from every side the excited multitude rushed from the Frankish realms,

All the people came joyfully to meet the king.

[Col. 0591B] The nobles of Charles, the leading men of the kingdom,

And the friendly company of priests also came running.

The roads grew crowded and the entrances to the houses were filled;

The house could not contain them, and they climbed onto the heights.

Neither rivers held back the anxious people, nor the dreadful forest,

Nor icy winter, nor the rainy day.

Whoever could not cross by boat, striving here perhaps by swimming,

Contended to reach the farther bank of the Loire first.

O how many peoples you would see from the lofty cliff

Throwing themselves headlong into the river without a boat!

The people of Orléans [Note: The distinguished city of Orléans lies on the Loire, above Angers, from which city, and especially from Aachen and Paris, the populations chiefly gathered to visit the new emperor. As is recorded in the Life of Louis, Rampho himself, before reaching Thedwat, “came to the city of Orléans.”] laughed at those swimmers:

From the highest tower they called: “Love the shore, men!”

All shared one love and one desire:

To see the king’s face, if only they could.

At last they assembled, and the pious king received them all,

Each according to his rank, with devoted assistance.

The emperor soon visited Orléans in triumph,

Where the banners of the cross [Note: There the largest of all such churches still stands, the cathedral dedicated to God Most Good and Most Great under the title of the Holy Cross. Anianus, Euvertius, Maximinus, and Avitus were holy men under whose names other distinguished basilicas in the city of Orléans were frequented with greater devotion.] or the remains of Anianus are found.

Happy Heburtius, if you first completed this sanctuary,

Or you, Maximinus, or holy Avitus, if you shine here.

From there they hasten to visit the Parisian churches,

Where the martyr Stephen holds the highest heights;

Where, Germanus, your most holy body is honored;

Where Genevieve, the virgin dedicated to God, shines.

Irmino [Note: Or Hirminus. He was abbot of the celebrated monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, whose renown the illustrious monks of the Congregation of Saint-Maur greatly increased and continue to increase. According to Einhard, this abbot also subscribed the final documents of Charlemagne. Mabillon records some of his deeds in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 823.], rejoice gladly, since you often asked for this:

By the Thunderer’s gift, you see the emperor’s arrival.

Nor did he pass by your heights, Dionysius, martyr,

Without approaching you and asking your help.

From there they set out and travel through the Frankish realms;

By a peaceful road the king enters Aachen.

Come, Muse, it remains for us to implore God with suppliant prayers,

That he may grant us eloquence.

What should I begin with first, when all the deeds he performs

Stand complete and shine with the man’s gracious actions?

At last, after establishing the boundaries of the kingdom in due order

And arranging the limits of the empire as well,

He immediately lavishly expended his ancestral treasures

As payment for his father and for the repose of his soul.

Whatever wealth the strength of his forefathers and Charles had amassed,

He distributed to the poor and to the holy churches.

[Col. 0592B] He gave golden vessels, garments, and many cloaks;

He heaped up broad talents of pure silver.

He scattered various wealth and innumerable weapons;

He distributed gifts for you, poor man, to possess.

O fortunate Charles, who left such an offspring in the world,

Who strives to enter the heavenward path by which his father entered.

He orders the prison chambers to be opened and releases those confined;

Out of devotion he lifts men from exile.

He performs wondrous deeds, wholly worthy of being recounted in lasting memory,

And from these his fame now remains above the stars.

Immediately he chooses envoys [Note: Learned men know well this distinguished custom of the ancient Frankish kings, but do not praise it sufficiently. Eminent men were selected who, acting in the king’s place and with great authority, traveled through the provinces to hear and decide the cases of individual people, as they themselves declared. Through their virtue and care abuses were removed, disputes settled, and fear and punishment inflicted upon the powerful. They are frequently mentioned in the Lombard laws, in the capitularies of the Frankish kings, and by other ancient authors. Many of their judgments exist, both published and unpublished; and in selecting these men the prudence and charity of Louis the Pious shone forth above all.] whom he will send throughout the world,

Men whose life is upright and whose loyalty is noble.

Men whom neither gifts can bend, nor the savage flattery

Of the powerful, nor favor, nor clever corruption.

Let them travel swiftly through the vast Frankish realms,

[Col. 0592C] And administer justice and judgment together.

Those whom their father, or oppressive servitude in their father’s time,

Had crushed, let them set free,

Whether by gift [Note: This word, like *dolo*, is to be referred to *servitium*, ‘servitude.’ Many powerful men had unjustly made free persons their slaves, either by money given or by deceit, that is, by cunning means, as the laws put it. There is more than one law concerning such persons among the Lombard laws and the capitularies of the Frankish kings.] or by deceit.

O how many and what kind of men, whom harsh laws

And the golden law oppress through the power of money,

The powerful Caesar himself liberates,

Granting them the honor of possessing their freedom through love of his father!

And by this benefaction he confirms the charters with his own hands [Note: Many ancient charters of manumission survive. Individuals, when they were granted freedom, obtained such charters from their manumitting lords so that, if necessary, they could thereafter defend that freedom in court. It was then customary to call them charters of free status. The supremely pious emperor Louis did this above all: he was accustomed to sign the charters of those manumitted with his own hand.],

So that they may be able to live under the law for all time.

[Col. 0593A] His father, a warrior, while acquiring kingdoms by arms,

Was occupied with wars and constantly engaged in battle.

Then this vice grew everywhere, with thick ears of grain [Note: Under Charlemagne this practice had become universal, and for many years this evil had grown like a field thick with ears of grain: free men, their wives, and their children were dragged into slavery, not only from among defeated enemies but also from among those subject to the Frankish kingdom. Louis the Pious applied the most immediate remedy to this disease. See the law of that emperor among the Lombard laws, “First of all.”],

But as soon as you arrived, Louis, you cut it down.

What deeds he performed throughout the world against the evil chelydrus [Note: Or *chelydrus*, namely Satan.]!

How great were the gifts that fell to the people devoted to Christ!

The rejoicing world sings these things far and wide, and the common people echo them;

They resound more loudly among the people than any melody could sing them.

Whose doctrine shines and grows throughout the world [Note: Or perhaps *cujus*, “whose”?],

He orders, arms, and nourishes the empire entrusted to him.

Then he orders a patron from the Roman see to be summoned,

To whom Stephen [Note: The fourth of that name, whom others customarily call the fifth, is meant. Our poet says that Louis the Pious summoned him to Francia. Thegan, however, seems to hold a different view, writing of this pope: “As soon as he assumed the pontificate, he ordered all the Roman people to promise fidelity to Louis by oath; and, sending his legates to the aforesaid prince, he announced that he would gladly see him wherever it pleased him.” Einhard’s account in the Frankish Annals does not seem different. Anastasius, in his Life, says only that he undertook the journey to Francia “to confirm the peace and unity of the holy Church of God.” He passes over the other events there, which must be sought in the Frankish chroniclers.] gives a name to the happy ages.

The holy priest [Note: For *sacerdos*. The same form occurs several times below.] obeys out of love and complies with his gracious commands;

He gladly hastens to visit the Frankish kingdoms.

Caesar joyfully awaits him at Rheims [Note: I read *Caesar eum*. And in fact Louis Augustus, as Einhard writes, “decided to meet Pope Stephen at Rheims”; or, as the author of Louis’s Life has it, “decided to await his arrival at Rheims.”],

[Col. 0593B] Where he had earlier ordered the council to be held [Note: I restore *quo sibi*, “where.” That is, in the place where, at Louis’s command, the clergy and nobles of the kingdom had earlier been compelled to assemble to receive the pontiff.].

Various envoys gather and return in due order,

Carrying Caesar’s good wishes and those of the holy priest.

A messenger flies ahead to report, with burning zeal,

The Roman bishop’s arrival, hastening swiftly.

Then Louis leads the clergy, people, and senate,

Orders, arranges, prepares, and assigns each his place:

Those who are to hold the right side and those who are to hold the left,

Who is to approach first and who is to follow.

The company of priests holds the right in a long procession;

Singing psalms, they reverently await the father.

On the other side the chosen nobles and foremost leaders

Stand in place; the people occupy the rear.

In the middle stands Caesar, gleaming with gems and gold;

Though his clothing may shine, he shines more brightly in devotion.

[Col. 0594A] At last the two come together from opposite sides;

One is powerful in rank [Note: Namely, the pontiff Stephen, superior to the king in dignity.], the other strong in goodness.

When each fixed his eyes upon the other,

They quickly ran to a devout embrace.

Yet first the prudent king worshiped with bent knee [Note: Louis Augustus not only showed obedience to Stephen by bending his knee, but seems to have done even more, judging from the words of Thegan, a contemporary author: “Each descended from his horse, and the prince, prostrating his whole body upon the ground, bowed three times before the feet of so great a pontiff; and at the third time he rose and greeted the pontiff,” and so forth.],

Three and four times, for God and in honor of Peter.

Suppliant Stephen received him and with consecrated hands

Raised him from the ground and willingly kissed him.

Now the eyes, now the mouths, now the head, now the breasts and necks,

The king and the holy priest kiss one another.

Then, holding each other’s palms with their hands and fingers,

Caesar, together with Stephen, enters the gleaming palace.

First they pass through the church and address the Thunderer with prayers;

They sing thanks and vows that must be offered.

Soon they return to the palace, hastening to the great banquet;

They sit down, and servants pour water over their hands.

They celebrate a worthy feast, taste the gifts of Bacchus,

And already move pious conversation across their lips.

[Col. 0594B] “O holy bishop [Note: For *antistes*, “bishop.” So in the manuscript.], shepherd of the Roman flock,

Who, in apostolic succession, feed the sheep of Peter,

[Note: Earlier the poet told us, and will repeat below, that the pontiff was summoned by Louis the Pious into Francia. Now he represents Louis as asking why the pontiff came into Gaul. These points do not cohere well. The latter account agrees with the other chroniclers of the period, who report that Stephen IV went there of his own accord.]

What cause,” Caesar began, “has brought you to this

Land of the Franks? Give me your answer.”

He, calm as he was and peaceful in heart, spoke,

Constantly surveying the king with his eyes:

“The same cause that once carried the queen of the South, through love of the wise man,

Across many peoples, across straits, and through snows—

That cause has brought me, Caesar, to your citadels,

You who rightly bear Solomon’s banquets for me.

The report reached my ears long ago, prince,

Of how much aid you bring to God’s people as a father,

And how your doctrines shine throughout the world,

Surpassing your fathers in skill and faith. [Note: Nigellus may perhaps have written *praecellis ... tuos*, ‘you surpass your fathers.’]

Yet nothing could stand in the way of my desire

[Col. 0594C] To see your deeds for myself.

No speech was able to report to me as much

As the gracious deeds which you now set before my eyes.

Therefore I repeat to you the words of that queen

Which she herself brought to Solomon’s ears.

[Col. 0595A] ‘When she beheld the king, the servants, and the garments arranged in order,

And his cupbearers and his various dwellings:

Happy the servants, happy indeed the slaves

Who stand and behold your illustrious deeds.

Happy is the one who drinks in your teachings with a receptive ear,

And happy the people, happy the kingdoms as well.

May the Most High God be remembered with complete love,

Who granted you, as a father, such doctrines;

Who delights in you and grants you to retain your father’s throne,

And who loved his own people by setting you over them.

With these words the queen of Sheba addressed powerful Solomon;

With these words I, suppliant, dared to approach you.

Yet you are superior; you truly stand more powerful:

He retained a shadow, whereas you cultivate the truth.

[Col. 0595B] He was exceedingly wise, but he yielded to love;

You live wisely in chaste love of God.

He was the ruler of Israel alone, within a single citadel;

You, pious one, powerfully possess the kingdoms of Europe.

Therefore let us all strike God with rich prayers,

That he may preserve you for his own people through long ages.’”

With these and many other words the holy priest addressed the gracious king,

And Caesar himself addressed the holy priest.

Full cups fly around, and Bacchus touches willing hearts;

The people resound with unanimous joy.

When the banquet was over, they rose and left the tables,

And Caesar went with Stephen to private chambers.

They passed that night amid cares and various matters in due order;

Sleep itself fled from their eyes.

At the new morning Caesar summoned Stephen and the assembly of nobles,

[Col. 0595C] And they obeyed the royal commands.

Caesar, robed, took his seat upon the lofty throne,

Holding in his mind many things he was preparing to begin.

He placed the holy priest beside him on a golden seat as a friend,

While the nobles sat each in his proper order.

Then the pious Caesar first uttered these golden words,

Speaking to the holy priest and his obedient attendants:

“Hear this, nobles, and you, most holy bishop;

Receive this common good with unanimous agreement.

Behold, God the Almighty Father, in his mercy,

Has granted me possession of my ancestral kingdoms and all their glory.

Not, as I believe, because of my own merits,

But Christ, in his mercy, granted me this honor because of my father.

Therefore I ask my faithful men, and you, illustrious priest,

To provide me with fitting assistance in counsel.

[Col. 0595D] And you also, servants, who preserve our kingdoms with me,

And you, blessed holy priest, provide your help,

So that my clergy and people, poor and powerful alike,

May be able, through me, to follow the rights of their fathers.”

## Rule

[Note: The poet is hinting at a book on the life of clerics, or on the institution of canons, which this pious Caesar was then contemplating and which, under his direction, the bishops subsequently established in the same year, 816, at the Council of Aachen. This pious institution, introduced earlier into only a few churches, soon began to spread throughout all the Frankish kingdoms and even throughout Italy itself. Ademar says this about Louis in his *Chronicle*: “He ordered a Rule to be made for the canons, excerpted from various writings of the Fathers, and decreed that the canons should observe it, so that, just as monks look to the book of the Rule of Saint Benedict, so the canons should read among themselves the book of the Life of Clerics.” Here the poet says nothing about nuns, for whom Louis nevertheless also took care to prescribe a rule.]

May the holy Rule of the Fathers bind the clergy in order,

And may the venerable law of the Fathers join the people to it.

May the order of Benedict’s monks grow through his teaching,

And may it seek the sacred pastures through morals and life.

Let the rich practice the law, and let the poor be held by the same;

Let there be no place or distinction for persons.

Let savage gifts, adorned with no precious metals,

Have no standing; let wicked presents withdraw far away.

If by right we also feed the Lord’s nourishing flock,

Which the beloved Shepherd has entrusted to me or to you:

We correct the wicked, reward the righteous,

And make the people follow the laws of the Fathers.

Then the Most High God, in mercy, will grant to us

And to the obedient people the blessed kingdoms of heaven,

And in the present life will preserve our honor,

Driving hostile enemies far away here. [Note: Perhaps, “driving them far away from here.”]

Let us be an example to the clergy, or a standard for the people:

Let each bishop teach justice to his own.

That Israel, God’s people, beloved in his affection,

Which crossed the sea on dry feet,

For whom God, after so many passing years in the wilderness,

Provided manna as food and flying delicacies from the rock;

For whom God was weapon, sword, and shield on the journey,

And led it honorably to the promised land;

Which preserved the commandments of the teaching God to the end,

Cultivated justice, and administered judgment;

And while it loved the same Lord with devout love,

Followed no foreign things, but the pious words of God:

He cast down hostile nations before it by his power,

Gave it every prosperity, and removed its enemies.

O, if that happy people had always followed the Lord’s commands,

It would possess the eternal kingdoms in triumph.

But when at first it carelessly indulged in rich possessions,

It abandoned justice and every good together,

And deserted God, soon worshiping empty idols:

For that reason it rightly suffered so many evils.

But the Father, who holds the heavenly helm, corrected it

With blows and various scourges, and restored its former laws,

So that, when afflicted in misery, it wished to remember the Lord,

The merciful Nourisher soon received it.

This nation alone knew God, and part of it

Obeyed the Thunderer’s commands and worshiped him.

The rest of the crowd indeed observed the commands of the water-snake (*celidrus*),

While ignorant of the Creator and following the demon’s enterprises.

He, alas, ruled the world in three parts [Note: For *triquetrum*, that is, through the three parts of the world, or throughout the whole earth, which they then divided into three parts; America was, of course, entirely unknown at that time.],

And gave the human race over to his kingdoms.

Already priests, kings, and solemn laws

Had wholly ceased, as had sacrificial offerings.

Then the merciful Father grieved, and sent the Word of salvation

Into the world, so that in mercy he might rescue us.

He washed the world in pity with his own blood,

Gave clear teachings, and taught justice.

By his divine power he shattered the gates of the infernal realm,

Rescued the elect, and took away the demon’s weapons.

Then, seeking the heights, he ascended victoriously into the ether,

And granted us the name of Christians.

Now everyone who wishes to bear Christ’s name must strive

To take the path to where the Head has departed.

Although, by God’s gift, the whole world now abounds

In crowds of Christians and in the faith of the Church,

And there is no need for the servants of the Lord to be slain for the name,

Since the name of Christ resounds everywhere in the world;

And although the wicked and faithless band that rejects the Lord’s teaching

Has already been driven far away by the Christian spear;

Although death has indeed carried off the Fathers of the Church and our forebears,

They now dwell in God’s palace:

Though we cannot follow them through death, let us strive joyfully

To follow them with a pure heart, in justice and faith.

Let every person love his brother, as John admonishes,

Whom he sees, so that in his mind he may be able to behold Christ.

He says to Peter: “Simon, do you love me, or not?”

Three times Peter replies: “You know that I love you.”

“If you love me,” says Christ, “I exhort you: feed my lambs, Peter,

With the help of devotion.”

Therefore, Sacer, it is your task to care for the people entrusted to us,

Whom the Lord has appointed us to feed.

You are the sacred bishop; I am king of the Christians:

Let us preserve the people through teaching, law, and faith.

But Caesar added these few words,

Which the holy bishop received with attentive ear.

If the rights of Peter remain intact,

You who care for Peter’s kingdom

And feed his flock in your allotted portion;

But if anything is otherwise, I urge you earnestly, priest,

Tell me everything: I shall gladly act at once on your words. [Note: That is: “Tell me, most holy pontiff, whether the temporal rights of Saint Peter remain untouched, or whether anyone has diminished or usurped them.”]

Just as my forebear preserved Peter’s honor,

So I shall preserve it, bishop, through the love of God.

Then he recalls the beloved servant Helisachar, [Note: He was Louis the Pious’s chancellor, and many charters of that emperor survive, subscribed by the deacon Durandus on behalf of Helisachar. Einhard and Agobard call him a priest and abbot. Indeed, he presided over many monasteries in that age under the title of abbot, so that we should no longer be surprised by the customs of our own times, which are scarcely different.]

Who, speaking aloud, uttered these pious words:

“Receive this, go quickly, and commit these words to firm documents [Note: Sadly, these documents perished many centuries ago.],

Which I wish to remain fixed forever.

I decree this throughout the kingdom enclosed under our rule,

And throughout my empire, granted to me by the Thunderer:

That the possessions of Peter’s Church and his everlasting see

May always flourish unharmed, in the honor of God.

As this Church formerly, supported by the ministry of its shepherds,

Held the highest summit, [Note: The primacy of the supreme pontiff in the Church of God, and his archieratic rights, derived from Saint Peter to his successors; Louis the Pious also confirms these.]

So we wish it to hold it still.

May Peter’s honor grow in our time: it grew

In the days of my father Charles and also in mine.

But, bishop, we add only this, as I have said above:

Let him who sits upon Peter’s throne recall justice.

This is the reason, Sacer, for which I asked you to come to me.

Be a strong helper to me, blessed one.”

Then Sacer, raising his eyes and hands toward heaven,

Prayed, repeating these words to God:

“O God, thundering on high—Christ the Son and the holy Spirit together—

Who created all kingdoms;

You, Peter, illustrious keeper of heaven’s keys,

Who draw your net and lead the people to the heavenly kingdoms;

And you, heavenly citizens, whose bodies Rome

Now guards and for whom it provides worthy, diligent services:

I beg you, preserve this king for the governance of the people,

For the adornment of the kingdom and the Church, through long ages.

In teaching, warfare, and faith he surpasses his ancestral customs,

Cares for the Church, and governs the empire.

He endows Peter’s see with the highest honor,

And is Father and Sacer, nourisher and defense to his own.”

Having said this, he quickly clung to him in a friendly embrace,

Rejoicing in his own honor and in Peter’s gift.

He begins, and, admonishing everyone, gives orders for silence;

Then the pious man kindly reports these words to the pious man:

“Rome, Caesar, sends you Peter’s gifts,

Fully worthy of one worthy, and honor suited to him.”

Then he orders a crown adorned with gems and gold to be brought,

Which had formerly belonged to Caesar Constantine. [Note: The coronation of Louis the Pious is described here; the other Frankish annals also record it under the year 816. No one but our poet, however, attributes a crown then used by Pope Stephen to Constantine the Great.]

He himself takes it in his hands, blesses it with words, and prays,

Holding the shining insignia [Note: That is, holding the crown in his hand.] while turning his eyes toward heaven:

“You who rule the empire of the world and govern the age,

Who have appointed Rome to possess the world’s capital, [Note: Who ordained that Rome should be the capital of the world.]

Hear me, and, I ask, incline your kindly ear to my prayers,

Christ; pious King, I beg you favor his vows.

May Andrew, Peter, Paul, and John help,

And Mary, the noble Mother of the good God.

Preserve this emperor Louis for long ages;

Let every sorrow depart far away.

Grant him every prosperity, and, I ask, drive harmful things far away;

Let him be happy and powerful for a long time.”

He said this, then quickly turned toward him,

And touched with his hand the sacred height of his head.

May the Almighty, who increased Abraham’s seed, grant you

To see descendants from whom you may be called grandfather.

May he grant offspring, and double and triple your grandchildren,

So that from your seed a rich harvest may grow,

Men who will rule the Franks and powerful Rome as well,

As long as the name of Christians resounds in the world.”

After pouring on the oil and reciting the hymns in due order,

He immediately placed the honor upon the imperial head.

“Peter, rejoicing, has granted you this very gentle gift,

Because you permit him to possess justice.” [Note: That is: “Peter sends you this gift because you also grant his successors the right and justice [Col. 0599C] to exercise authority over the Roman people.” By this, I believe, temporal authority is meant, which the Frankish emperors granted to the pontiffs in the City.]

Then he sees the empress and married consort,

Irmingard, [Note: I would write *Irmingart*, since I see her elsewhere called Irmingarda. She was, of course, the first wife of Louis the Pious.] whom he receives and embraces completely.

After looking at her for a long time, he soon places an honor upon her blessed head,

And blesses her: “Hail, woman beloved by God.

May you have life and health marked by long years;

May you always preserve your husband’s marriage-bed, beloved.”

The bishop also heaped many gifts upon her,

Gold and garments, which Rome had given him.

He gives gifts to the Augustus, the Augusta, and their lovely offspring,

And distributes gifts in due order to their servants.

The wise Caesar repays him with abundant thanks;

Then orders that Stephen be loaded with gifts.

He gave him two cups, polished with gems and gold,

With which that holy man might drink the draughts of Bacchus.

He also gathers outstanding bodies of high-stepping horses,

Such as the land of the Franks customarily produces.

They bring golden gifts, followed by silver vessels,

Red cloaks, and at the same time white linen cloths.

Why should I recount more here? For the Roman received gifts

Multiplied a hundredfold, which he had carried away from the citadels. [Note: If I see correctly, one should write *Romanis*, so that it may be joined with *arcibus*. Other writers of Frankish history also mention the gifts exchanged between Pope Stephen and Louis the Pious, but none so lavishly as our poet. Agnellus writes this about that pontiff in his *Life of Martin, Archbishop of Ravenna*: “And this pope went to Francia to the emperor Louis [supply: ‘having departed’], and obtained from him whatever he requested.”]

These he gave to Sacer; and Caesar, filled with goodness toward the servants,

Gave suitable gifts according to his devotion.

Dyed cloaks, and also coverings suitable for the body,

Made well according to Frankish custom.

He gives horses of various kinds, bearing splendid necks,

Whose backs their riders could scarcely mount.

Sacer and the servants, rejoicing in the gift,

Now prepare to return to Rome as they please.

Chosen envoys too are sent with honor,

To conduct the holy Stephen back to his own kingdoms.

But the pious Caesar himself returns to the house at Compiègne [Note: After these events, if we follow Thegan, the emperor, departing from Rheims, “came to the palace at Aachen.” But the author of the *Life of Louis* writes more accurately: “The emperor withdrew to Compiègne … Having stayed there twenty days or somewhat more, he set out to winter at Aachen.”]

Happy with his own wife and offspring.

Faithful Bigo dies; his funeral is announced to the king,

And, unwillingly, alas, he leaves his own lord.

The Caesar divided his feasts [Note: For “possessions”; this usage occurs more than once in this poet. “He divides the honor,” as one sometimes reads, sufficiently shows that Bigo’s dignities were divided among his sons. Therefore one of them must have been appointed Count of Paris.] and also divided his honor

Among his own offspring, with a father’s love.

At last the widely circulated report sounds throughout the world

That the pious emperor has begun to renew his kingdoms [Note: Or perhaps “wishes to renew.”].

He appoints chosen members of the clergy and trusted men,

Whose life is known to him and pleasing,

To travel through the cities, monasteries, and fortresses of the kingdom,

Fulfilling all the benevolent commands of their lord.

“Come,” he says, “servants sustained by our nourishment,

Whether you are those whom the teaching of our father Charles instructed well,

Attend wholly to our commands,

And receive my words with a devout heart.

A truly difficult task remains to be performed by you,

But I believe it good and suitable for Christians.

Behold: through God’s working and the faithful labor of the Fathers,

The frontiers of the kingdoms remain inviolate;

The fame of the Franks has driven black enemies far away;

We live joyful, peaceful, and piously.

But since we must not contend through wars, we deem it fitting

That we give fitting laws to our subjects.

For first I shall seek the Church’s summit and honor,

Whence my fathers raise their name to the stars.

For I have sent out into the world

Legates who may govern peoples with devotion.

Now, now, envoys, attend to definite matters,

And run properly throughout my empire.

Examine the canonical flock, the male sex,

And also the female sex [Note: That is, nuns, whose conduct and enclosures the imperial envoys once also customarily inspected and corrected, just as they did those of monks and canons. See the Capitularies of the Frankish kings, as well as the Lombard Laws, where similar admonitions to envoys occur.], who cultivate the pious camps of religion:

What kind of life, beauty, teaching, and discipline there are,

How great their religious observance, and what work of devotion;

What relationship joins the shepherd to the flock,

So that the flock loves the shepherd and he the sheep;

Whether the prelates provide them with enclosures, houses, drink,

Covering, and food at the proper time and place.

They cannot otherwise complete divine worship in due order

Unless the pious care of the Fathers supplies these things.

Yet let the resources of the church be assessed, and its lands,

Whether suitable or less fertile places.

Commit everything you discover to written records,

And it pleases me that you report everything carefully to me:

Who lives well, who less well, who moderately, and who not at all—which God forbid—

Or whether they maintain the ancient teachings of the Fathers.

I insert these few words into your ears;

But you ought yourselves to inquire into more matters.”

He also orders legates chosen from among the monks [Note: It was customary to send two envoys together through the provinces, one a layman and the other attached to the clergy. Bishops or abbots were therefore chosen for this office, and their names are also found in the records of those times. The Capitulary of Louis himself, concerning the year 823, presents only bishops and counts, in Baluze, vol. I, p. 640. But these matters concern the years 816 and 817 and the period of the Councils of Aachen.] to be present,

Who might observe his commands,

And whom he might send again through the sacred monastic camps;

He asks them to investigate so that pious life may proceed.

Benedict was a man worthy of that name, [Note: The very pious and celebrated abbot of Aniane, and later of Inda, whose Life is found in the *Acta Sanctorum Benedictinorum*, fourth century, part I, p. 194. His monastery was situated in Narbonese Gaul, or Occitania, and formerly in the diocese of Maguelonne.]

Who led very many men to the stars. [Note: Thus the manuscript reads. One should read: “a man who led very many men.”]

He had formerly been recognized by the king in the lands of the Goths, [Note: The same Benedict, as his Life written by a contemporary relates, “was of the race of the Goths and came from the regions of Gothia.” Occitania was formerly so called, now Languedoc, because the Gothic people had established their seat there and had spread into Spain as well.]

And I wish to report a little about his life.

He was deservedly placed over the flock at Aniane, [Note: A formerly distinguished monastery, situated on the Anianus River, now in the diocese of Montpellier. It was founded by that holy man Benedict.]

A shepherd and abbot, a gentle rule for his flock.

When the nourishing love of the sacred King filled his heart,

So that the order and life of monks might prosper,

He was helper, standard, and exemplary teacher,

Through whom the pious camps now please God.

In sacred conduct a beautiful will ruled him:

As far as it is permitted a human being to discern, he was holy.

He was gentle, beloved, kind, calm, and modest,

His rule fixed in his sacred heart.

He benefited not only monks but everyone;

He himself had become a father to all.

For this reason the pious Caesar had loved him,

And had brought him with him at the same time to the Frankish kingdoms.

The king sends his disciples through the monasteries,

To be an example and standard to the brothers wherever they might be.

He orders them to correct whatever they can;

Whatever they cannot, they are to report to him, everything recorded in writing. [Note: The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*, under the year 817, says: “Likewise that God-loving emperor appointed Abbot Benedict, and with him monks of vigorous life in every respect, who, going and returning through all the monasteries of monks, should hand down to all the monasteries, both male and female religious, an unchanging way of life according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” These matters are treated more fully in Mabillon’s *Life of that holy Benedict of Aniane*.]

Meanwhile the pious king and Benedict, himself a priest,

Were turning over in their hearts duties beloved by God.

Soon the emperor addresses him first with gentle words,

As he was accustomed, always with affection and piety:

“You know, Benedict, I think, what concern I have had for this order

From the beginning, from the time when it became known to me.

Therefore I should like to dedicate a chapel of its own

Not far from our seat, for the love of God.

Believe me, this desire has arisen in my heart for three reasons,

Of which I now wish to tell you.

You see how the weight of my empire presses upon my heart

With its burden, and the great rights of affairs weigh heavily.

There I might perhaps rest for a little while, [Note: Perhaps the poet wrote *potero*, “I shall be able.”]

And offer private vows, pleasing to God.

A second reason urges me: you yourself admit

That this work is contrary to your wish;

Nor is it fitting for monks to be involved in civil affairs,

Or willingly to bear palace responsibilities. [Note: This deserves notice. In that century abbots frequented the royal court and were willingly employed in palace duties. Benedict of Aniane himself behaved no differently; he spent a long time at court and wore out the palace doors. From this, however, we learn that he did not do so willingly, since he disapproved of monks’ involvement in civil affairs.]

But there you could care for the brothers’ labors,

And piously arrange services for guests.

And, renewed, you could visit our seats again

And bring your customary protection to the brothers.

A third reason is clear: what profits this place near Aachen

Would bring to us and to our subjects: [Note: That is, the third reason is evident why it would be most useful to me and to my people to have a monastery near Aachen.]

If the end of the human body should suddenly come,

The bodily members could be committed for burial in this place.

There converts [Note: Namely, those who decide to renounce the world and choose the monastic life; a monastery will be available to them, to which they can transfer themselves without delay.] could at once take up Christ’s duties,

And a willing person could receive welcome counsel.”

When Sacer heard these things, he fell at his friend’s feet,

And praised God for the honor, and Caesar for his faith.

“This desire of yours, Great One, has always been known to me,” he said,

“May God confirm it, who has given every good thing.

There is a place called Inda, [Note: The author of the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane* says this about the building of this monastery, §48: “There was a nearby valley, which, I believe, was no more than six miles from the palace.” (Our poet says that it was only three miles distant.) “It pleased the eyes of the man of God; and there the emperor ordered a monastery to be built with marvelous workmanship, called Inda, taking its name from the stream of the same valley.”]

Long ago built by those very men,

Retaining the name of the water that flows before its doors.

It lies three miles from the royal palace,

Which is now widely known by the name Aachen.

Once it was a most pleasant dwelling for antlered stags,

Suitable for bears, buffaloes, and wild goats.

But Louis, acting, cleared out the haunts of wild beasts,

And by his skill established a place pleasing to God.

He founded it carefully and endowed it with rich possessions,

So that your holy Rule, Benedict, might flourish there.

For that same Benedict was father of the establishment,

And Caesar Louis is present as abbot as well.

He often visits these places and hastens to revisit the enclosures,

Arranges their expenses, and prepares generous gifts.”

Stop, Muse, your melody: behold, a little book hastening to its brother

Is arriving to be joined with it, joyful in its conclusion.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0603]

The arms of Caesar, through the gift of the exalted God, were growing,

And peace among all peoples was increased through faith.

The fame of the Franks, through the bounty of great Louis,

Crossing all seas, flew up and sought the sky of heaven.

Yet, following the ancient custom of kingdoms, Caesar orders

The frontier regions [Note: He seems to be referring to those who in that same century began to be called *marchiones* or *marchisi*, from their guardianship of the kingdom’s borders.] and chosen leaders to appear first.

They all assemble at the public court and obey his command;

Each speaks words appropriate to his own region.

Among them came the noble Lantpreth, [Note: For *Lantpertus* or Lambertus. According to Mabillon in the *Benedictine Annals*, he was Count of Angers, and therefore bordered in his jurisdiction on Lesser Britain, which is discussed below. The author of the *Life of Louis* calls him simply Lantbert under the year 825, and under the year 829 names Count Lambert. I think he was Count of Nantes, not of Angers, for reasons noted below.]

Of Frankish stock, hurrying quickly to his place.

He had charge of the borders [Note: Hence you learn that the protection of the borders of neighboring Britain was entrusted to Lantbert. Einhard, under the year 826, mentions guardians of the Breton frontier. Adrevald of Fleury, in Book 2 of the *Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 33, writing of events after the death of Louis the Pious, says: “When the marquises of the Breton frontier were quarreling among themselves, war arose. Although, after Rainald fell, Lambert emerged victorious, he nevertheless did not bring back entirely victorious standards from the enemy,” and so forth.] which an enemy people had formerly

Captured by ambush, sailing across the sea in boats.

This people, coming from the farthest part of the world, the Britons [Note: That is, from Greater Britain, now England, which that people abandoned and crossed into Celtic or Armorican Gaul, establishing there a settlement and later a dominion. In his *Annals*, under the year 786, Einhard recalls the older history: “When the island of Britain had been invaded by the Angles and Saxons, a large part of its inhabitants crossed the sea and occupied the farthest regions of Gaul, the territories of the Veneti and Coriosolitae.”],

Whom the Frankish language now calls Bretons,

Needing land, tossed by wind and rain,

Seized fields and prepared to pay tribute.

At that time the Gaul also possessed this countryside,

When that same people, driven by the waves, arrived. [Note: That is, when the Franks had not yet subjected Gaul to themselves. Sidonius Apollinaris, Jordanes in his *History of the Goths*, Gregory of Tours, and others sufficiently indicate that an incursion of this kind occurred in the fifth century of Christ.]

But because this people had been anointed with the oil of baptism,

It was soon permitted to spread out and cultivate the fields as well. [Note: In the manuscript the earlier hand read *ex priore manu*, while the second hand wrote *licet*. I have preferred to retain the latter word for the sake of the sense.]

When their period of rest was granted, they soon began terrible wars,

And prepared to fill the countryside with a new guardian.

A spear instead of tribute, a gift instead of the right of war [Note: I think the sense should be constructed as follows: in place of a right—that is, in place of justice being done to their Gallic hosts—the Breton newcomers offer a gift of single combat. Below also you have: “he carries the gifts of war according to custom.”],

Is returned to their hosts, through the arrogance of their devotion.

Francia was striking against the kingdoms of another [Note: Something such as *partis* or *gentis* seems to be missing. The sense is that the Frankish people, having set aside concern for Cisrhenane Britain, devoted all their attention to conquering other kingdoms which they thought could oppose or harm them more seriously.]

With triumphs, indeed those that seemed more difficult to it.

For that reason this matter was neglected for so many years;

The people grew more and more and filled the countryside.

Now it challenges the Frankish kingdoms, too proud, [Note: Under the very line of the Merovingian kings the Cisrhenane Britons rebelled several times, as Gregory of Tours and Fredegar testify in their *Chronicles*. In 786 Charles the Great “suppressed the insolence of the faithless people with remarkable speed,” as Einhard records. His words under 799 are also relevant: “Count Guido, prefect of the Breton frontier, had traveled through the whole province of the Bretons with his fellow counts and brought back the arms of the leaders who surrendered, with each man’s name written on them.” Other Frankish annals report the same. The anonymous but contemporary author of the *Life of Charlemagne*, preserved by Duchesne, relates it thus: “Count Guido, who governed the Breton march, entered Britain with his companions, traveled through the whole region, and received it into submission; and he presented to the king the arms of the leaders who had surrendered, with each man’s name written on them … and the whole province of the Britons was subjected by the Franks, something that had never happened before.” These words sufficiently show that those marquises, or prefects of the Breton frontier—one of whom was Lantbert, Count of Nantes—had no jurisdiction over Lesser Britain, but were merely charged with protecting the borders of the Franks from the Bretons, whom their own counts or leaders, also called kings, had formerly governed, though they were not wholly free from the supreme authority of the Frankish kings.]

And, not content with the soil in which it was foreign,

Unhappy and at the same time inexperienced, accustomed to contend,

It hoped to overcome the agile Franks.

But, as I have said, Caesar addresses Lantpreth in the ancestral

Manner, asking him to report everything to him:

“How that people honors God through worship and faith,

And how abundant the honor paid to God’s churches is;

What love the people bear, what justice and what peace;

What the king’s honor is like, and what work of devotion;

Moreover, what security exists for our frontiers.

Tell me everything in its proper order, Frank; I wish you to do so.”

Lantpreth answered him from his faithful heart,

Bowing and kissing the imperial knee with his mouth. [Note: We have seen above more than once that it was customary for nobles, before addressing the king, first to kiss his feet. Here you see Lantbert kissing only the knee. Perhaps this was granted to some as a mark of prerogative and higher rank; the cardinals of the Holy Roman Church still do the same, kissing the knee of the supreme pontiff.]

“That people,” he said, “is deceitful, proud, and rebellious,

And until now has remained without goodness.

The faithless people retains only the name of Christians,

For its deeds, worship, and faith are far away.

No care for orphans, widows, or churches remains:

Brother and sister come together.

One brother seizes another’s wife, and all

Live in incest and commit abominable acts.

They live in thickets and make their beds in wild places,

And delight in living by plunder like beasts.

The virtue of justice claims no court for itself;

The straight line of judgment flees far away.

Their king Murman is present, called by that name, [Note: Here one who ruled the Armorican Bretons at that time is called king. The designation is not recent. Jordanes, in *History of the Goths*, chapter 45, mentions Riothimus, king of the Britons; Gregory of Tours, in Fredegar’s *Epitome* according to Freher’s edition, mentions Cunobert, king of the Britons, though other manuscripts call him merely a count. Fredegar himself, under the year 635, mentions Judicael, king of the Britons. Even after the time of Louis the Pious, the *Annals of Bertin* under the year 866 mention Erispoe, king of the Britons. For the rest, they were usually called counts or leaders. Certainly they should be called not kings but petty kings.]

If it is permissible to call him king, since he rules nothing.

They have often come along the path to our frontiers,

Yet they have not returned unharmed to their own.”

Lantbert spoke; Caesar, distinguished in merit,

Peaceful and pious, replied these words to him:

“This is an exceedingly harsh matter, and foolish to report,

Which you, Lantpreth, utter to my ears.

That a foreign people should freely inhabit my soil,

And in its arrogance stir up wicked wars against my people!

It is right and lawful to drive this deed away by force,

Unless the sea that brought them offers them refuge.

It is better that an envoy be sent to that very king,

Who may first properly convey our words to him.

That king too has been washed in sacred baptism;

Therefore it is fitting that we admonish him first.”

And he calls Witcharius, [Note: Below he is called an abbot. At that time there was an Abbot Wicardus at Inda. I fear, however, that *Witebarius* and *Wicardus* are different names.]

Who had perhaps arrived there,

A good and shrewd man, capable of sound judgment.

“Go quickly, Wichart, and report these commands of ours

To the tyrant—commands that must not be doubted.

Behold, he widely occupies my lands,

In which he wanders as an exile, borne across the sea,

Together with his entire people.

Indeed, he forbids tribute, attempts battles,

Sends threats to the Franks, and prepares weapons.

For after, by God’s gift, I received my ancestral kingdoms

And the honor of empire, with the people asking it as well,

I tolerated him to some extent, waiting to see whether he would perhaps prove faithful

And wish to obey our laws.

But now his wicked mind wavers more and more,

And, with weapons moreover deployed, disavows shameful wars.” [Note: I sense an error here. I would write *movet*, “he stirs up.”]

“Now, now the time has come; let him not deceive himself or his people:

Let him seek the Franks by asking for peace.

If he does otherwise, go quickly, return,

And report everything to me.” The pious Caesar said these words.

Witchar prepares to go swiftly on horseback and carries out the pious commands;

The king, his household, and the place were known to him.

Near that king’s borders Abbot Wiccharius

Had possessions granted by Caesar’s gift.

The place is enclosed on one side by woods, on the other by a pleasant river,

And is situated among hedges, furrows, and marshland.

Inside was a rich house; on every side it bristled with arms,

And was by chance filled with a varied soldiery.

Murman always especially loved these places;

They provided him secure rest and a suitable site.

By chance swift Wicchar quickly arrived there,

And sought an opportunity to speak with the king.

When Murman recognized that the noble Caesar Louis’s

Envoy had arrived, his mind immediately recoiled.

Yet, so that he might learn the outcome of so great an affair,

He feigned hope in his face and concealed his fear.

He became cheerful, and immediately compelled his companions to be cheerful;

At last he invited Witcharius into his house.

“Welcome, Witchar,” he said. “Murman gives you the greeting

Of the warlike, peaceable, and pious Caesar.”

Murman, looking up fully, replied these words to him,

And gave him kisses in the customary manner: “You too, Wicchar, welcome.

May health and everlasting life attend the peaceful Augustus,

And may he rule his empire through broad ages.”

Then they sat down and ordered all attendants to remain far away;

They exchanged words in alternating voices.

Wicchar began first and reported the commands given to him;

Murman, with doubtful heart, listened and received them in his ear.

“Louis Caesar, the glory of the Franks and the honor of Christians,

Has sent me to you,

First in peace and faith, second to no one in warfare,

Supreme in teaching and in the work of piety.

Behold, you occupy his lands widely,

In which you, an exile and wanderer, have arrived borne across the sea,

Together with your entire people.

Indeed, you forbid tribute, attempt battles,

And send threats to the Franks,</source>
You are preparing arms against the Franks as well, and threats.

Now, now the time has come; do not, unhappy man, deceive yourself and your people by coming there to seek peace.

These are the emperor’s words; but I shall add a few of my own, Murman, out of affection for you.

[Col. 0606D] If now, of your own accord, you abandon the royal commands,

[Col. 0607A] as he himself first urges, out of his piety;

and if you desire to preserve perpetual peace with the Franks,

as is fitting and also necessary for you and yours:

hasten onward, and accept the pious laws of the pious king;

give back to the land not what is yours, but what is owed.

Take thought—alas!—for your country; I beg you, take thought for all your people;

take thought for your offspring and your wife’s marriage bed.

Especially since you cultivate vain doctrines and do not observe the teachings,

and you and your people pursue crooked, wandering paths.

Perhaps that pious ruler will send you back to your own land,

and perhaps he will grant you still greater gifts.

Suppose you were great, ruler of a great territory,

with many men at your command and a warrior’s renown,

and nations and peoples came to you for aid,

as the Rutulians came to Turnus, or swift Camilla,

[Col. 0607B] and all the Italian Latin host;

even so, they were not able to defeat Aeneas.

Even if you had Pyrrhus, the descendant of Odysseus, or the grim Achilles,

or Pompey with his father-in-law, and with them prepared for war,

still it is not lawful for you to wage war against the Franks,

in whose territory you dwell and remain in piety.

For whoever once begins to test them in battle,

even though he himself and all his people may undertake it,

will find that the Frankish nation is second to none in valor;

it conquers through the love of God and surpasses all in faith.

It always loves peace, and, unwillingly, takes up arms;

yet once they have been seized, no one will wish to confront them.

Whoever has sought their faith and their arms

lives gladly, peacefully, and piously.

Come now, break off the delays, and do not let your hostile mind,

[Col. 0607C] wandering in different directions, lead you astray through ambushes.

He, keeping his face and eyes fixed intently on the ground,

strikes the earth with his foot.

By now Wicchar had begun, in polished speech,

to bend the hesitating man with the threats properly delivered.

With her mind poisoned, his treacherous wife,

proud in her manner, approached Murman’s embrace.

First she lightly kissed his knee, then his neck;

she kissed his beard, his face, and his hands.

She went around him and back again, and touched a certain part with practiced skill [Note: [Col. 0607D] The poet cannot have written it quite this way. Yet I do not wish to guess what he did write. [Col. 0608D]],

and craftily desired to perform her service.

At last the wretched man received her, clasped her with his arm,

and yielded to her desire; his wife’s actions pleased him.

Then the unhappy woman sought his ears and whispered for a long time,

[Col. 0607D] and immediately turned her husband’s understanding and mind away.

Just as, in the forests, during a cold year,

a band of shepherds hurries to bring cut wood to the fire:

one swiftly carries suitable straw and dry kindling,

another brings fuel, while another eagerly feeds the flames.

Now the leaping pyre gave off flames and touched the lofty

stars; the shepherds’ chilled limbs grew warm.

Suddenly thunder, hail, rain, and frost

came crashing down, and the whole woodland resounded;

under the frequent rains the fire unwillingly collapsed,

and from where the heat had come, smoke returned.

[Col. 0608A] In no other way did the deadly woman extinguish

the words of Wicchar, fixed in the good man’s marital heart.

Then she also looked disdainfully at the envoy who had been sent,

gazing upward at him, and artfully asked:

“O king and glory of the noble Brittonic people,

whose grandfather’s right hand bears his name into heaven,

where has such a husband reached your strongholds?

Is he a guest,” she asked, “announcing peace or singing of wars?”

Smiling at her, Murman immediately pretended to say:

“This man has been sent to me by the Franks.

Whether he brings peace or war, that is a matter for men.

Perform your own duty properly, woman.”

When Wicchar heard words contrary to his own,

he immediately spoke these words in turn:

“Murman,” he said, “return to the king whatever message you wish:

[Col. 0608B] the time has now come for you to report his commands to me.”

But he, turning gloomy concerns over in his heart,

said: “Let these be for me the hours of deliberation [Note: [Col. 0608D] That is, of counsel and examination.] during the night.”

Sleep had overwhelmed the country-dwellers, and already

the horses of the sun were bringing back dawn over the summit.

At first light Wiccharius the abbot came to Murman’s doors,

hastening, and asked that an answer be given.

At last the wretched man appeared, buried in drink and sleep,

barely able to open his eyes.

Drunkenly belching these words with lips scarcely parted,

he uttered a speech that would never afterward please him:

“Hasten and quickly repeat these words to your king:

I neither cultivate his lands nor desire his laws.

Let him have the Franks; Murman properly holds

the Brittonic kingdom and forbids the census and tribute.

If the Franks stir up war, I shall immediately stir up war in turn,

nor does our right hand remain so powerless.”

Wicchar replied: “Our predecessors always used to say—

and now my mind will declare it with certainty—

that your people possess wholly unstable minds,

with counsels in their hearts changed by every disturbance.

A woman alone could soften a man’s mind

and turn his plans by whispering.

So, he said, the teachings of King Solomon testify,

which the Church frequently reads and venerates.

Take the wood away from the fire: immediately the flame dies.

So, with the whisperer removed, all quarrels fall silent.

But since you are now unwilling to obey our counsels,

I shall speak the truth as a prophet, and I shall be your prophet.

When Francia first hears the words of your wicked speech,

it will soon come snarling against your kingdom.

Then a thousand shields of men will converge upon you,

and you will be filled, perhaps, with Frankish spears.

They will densely fill your lands with soldiers,

and carry you and your captives into their own kingdom.

Or you will die miserably and lie upon the thirsty sand,

while the victor alone exultantly possesses your arms.

Nor should you be deceived by the thickets and trembling marshes,

though your house is enclosed by woodland and a rampart.”

Murman answered him with a furious heart;

the Briton raised himself from his seat and proudly sang:

[Col. 0609A] “A thousand wagons stand ready for me, filled with missiles,

with which I shall rush fiercely to meet them.

My shields are painted, but they are bright to you;

many are ready, and there is no fear of war.”

With such words the two men answered one another,

though their minds were not united.

Wicchar quickly departed, carrying these replies,

and reported to the pious king the impious words.

Meanwhile the emperor reviewed the Frankish realms

and urgently ordered arms to be prepared for him.

There is a city fixed beside the sea, where the water of the Loire

plows the broad surface and enters it in a rushing stream.

Veneda [Note: [Col. 0609B] Hear the author of the Life of Louis the Pious: “After holding a general assembly among the Venedes, he enters the province.” Our poet quite plainly reveals that this city stood at the mouth of the Loire and on the seacoast. [Col. 0609C] Search for such a city now on geographical maps: you will find none. From this you understand that it was destroyed. Baudrand, Brietius, and others are therefore mistaken in thinking it identical with Venetiae, or the ancient city of the Veneti situated in Celtic Gaul, now called Vannes; nor do they distinguish Vannes from ancient Dariorigum. I observe that on the Peutinger Map the Veneti are placed far from the Loire. It is more probable that a province, not a city, is indicated there. Dariorigum is located there by the Loire. Adrian Valesius is rather to be followed, since in the *Notitia Galliarum* he writes that this was the ancient name of the territory of the Veneti.]—the Gauls of old gave it this name—

is filled with fish and also rich in the resources of salt.

The harmful band that so often attacks the Britons

visits it and brings the customary gifts of war.

Therefore the emperor orders the Franks and the subdued peoples

to be there at the appointed time, and he himself proceeds there as well.

The Franks assemble under their ancient and original name,

accustomed to war, and carry their prepared weapons.

The fair-haired Suebi come across the waters of the Rhine,

assembled in hundreds of thousands of men.

The Saxon cohort arrives, girded with broad quivers,

and the Thuringian force comes in alliance with it.

Burgundy sends a multitude of varied peoples

and increases the number of the Franks by joining its men to them.

I shall recount the peoples of Europe and release the nations

[Col. 0610A] into the narrative, which cannot be confined by enumeration.

The emperor traveled safely through his own realms,

until in his majesty he reached the regions around Paris.

Now, Dionysius, your martyr, he joyfully revisits your shrine,

where Abbot Hilthuin [Note: [Col. 0609C] The very celebrated man better known as Hilduin, who served as archchaplain under Louis the Pious and was abbot of Saint-Denis at Paris, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and other monasteries in Gaul. I proceed here without dwelling on a well-known matter.] prepares gifts for him.

From there he passed the summit of your church, Germanus,

and of the martyr Stephen’s, and yours, Genevieve.

Then he gradually visits the fields of Orléans,

and the pious ruler now enters the estate of Victriacum [Note: [Col. 0609C] Now Vitry. Those who consider Victoriacum and Victriacum identical report that there was more than one place in Gaul with this name; I would not readily affirm this. Adrian Valesius and Mabillon, in *Diplomata*, p. 340, locate a double Victriacum in the Forest of Orléans, though one is an appendage of the other. There was formerly a palace of the Frankish kings there, which our poet designates by the name *villa*, that is, a royal estate.].

There, Matfrid [Note: [Col. 0609D] He was count of Orléans, frequently mentioned in the Frankish Annals of Thegan and in the Life of Louis the Pious written by the Astronomer. His treachery against the most pious emperor later broke out.]—for whom you prepared the fairest dwelling—

you gave great gifts, gifts pleasing to him.

From there, as he traveled, he repeatedly visited the city just mentioned,

seeking to arm himself with the gift and aid of the cross [Note: [Col. 0609D] In those times the practice had not yet been introduced of marking oneself with the cross when undertaking a military expedition for the Christian religion. Nevertheless, these words seem in some way to show that something similar was already practiced. I think the passage should be construed thus: he seeks to arm himself with the gift and assistance of the cross.].

Behold, the most holy bishop Jona [Note: [Col. 0609D] Bishop of Orléans, very famous from the history of the Franks and from his writings.] comes to meet him;

you prepare to return worthy gifts, as a willing debtor.

And now, hurrying onward, he revisits your stronghold, Aniane [Note: [Col. 0610B] Clearly the monastery of Saint-Aignan, situated in the city of Orléans, which he had also mentioned above; now Saint-Aignan of Orléans.],

and demands that assistance be provided for him.

Then, Durand [Note: [Col. 0610B] The celebrated Mabillon, in the *Benedictine Annals* [Col. 0610C] under the year 826, records a diploma of Louis the Pious and his son Lothair, granted to Abbot Durand for a monastery recently built in the district of Narbonne in honor of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Anianus. Mabillon adds: “Who that Abbot Durand was is not known. He does not seem to have been attached to any monastery, but rather to have been one of those distinguished abbots who accompanied the emperor.” As far as I can see, I infer from our poet’s words that this abbot was the abbot of the Orléans monastery of Saint-Aignan, who, under the name of that same holy confessor, later built or arranged for the building of other monasteries, as was customary in those times.], you come frequently and return again, and offer

what remains to you, ceded as an imperial gift.

From there he approaches Tours and the shrine of lofty Martin,

and that of the martyr and pious Maurice.

Come now, Fridugis, the time has come—master [Note: [Col. 0610C] He was abbot of the celebrated monastery of Saint-Martin at Tours, and, according to Einhard, subscribed the final charters of Charlemagne. He is often mentioned in the Benedictine Annals; in 822 and for some time afterward he served Louis the Pious in the important office of chancellor. In those days monks—or rather abbots—were brought into or entered the courts of kings and emperors with remarkable ease. He is called “master,” just as Aldric, bishop of Sens, is said in his Life to have been trained by Louis the Pious as *praeceptor palatinus*, that is, one who wrote royal commands or diplomas, as Mabillon interprets it.]—

and you rejoice to see the emperor’s arrival.

You offer great gifts: the blessed Martin demands

that God grant him a safe journey [Note: [Col. 0610D] For *iter*, “journey.” Examples are not lacking in ancient Latin.].

The emperor joyfully reaches the city of Angers [Note: [Col. 0611D] For *Andegavensem*, which may also be what the poet wrote. The writers of that period use the city-name *Andegavis*. Perhaps the original of Nigellus read not *Andegavensis* but *Andegavis ovans*.],

and seeks, with due honor, your body, sacred Albinus.

His dear friend Helisachar [Note: [Col. 0611D] We have already discussed him above. He was the chancellor of Louis the Pious and, according to the custom of his age, presided as abbot over many monastic houses. From this it is easy to conclude that the monastery of Saint-Albinus at Angers, now Saint-Aubin of Angers, had been entrusted to Helisachar.], comes to meet him with a joyful heart

and diligently increases his substantial wealth.

For the emperor sends himself into the city of Nantes,

and by prayers and petitions seeks all its shrines [Note: [Col. 0611D] That is, the principal churches of the city of Nantes.].

Now, Lantbertus [Note: [Col. 0611D] He was discussed above. Mabillon thought him count of Angers. The present passage proves that he was count of Nantes, since he received the emperor there. At that time, as we saw above, Count Matfrid governed the people of Angers. The passage in Mabillon’s *Miracles of Saint-Denis*, Benedictine century, vol. III, part II, p. 826, when examined carefully, refers not to the count of the district of Angers but to the count of the neighboring royal domain.]—at last you receive the king,

desired by your prayers, and powerfully offer him gifts.

You ask that the emperor hasten against the hated Britons

and deign to send himself to you as aid.

The remaining crowd of counts and other powerful men remains hidden,

whose number cannot be counted, nor their wealth enumerated.

At last the illustrious emperor reaches Veneda;

he prepares for battle in the ancestral manner and appoints his commanders.

[Col. 0611B] Meanwhile the proud Briton Murman was busy

preparing war with arms and with his own skill.

The emperor, acting once again out of his customary piety,

immediately sent a messenger to bring him every word.

“Tell me,” he said, “what madness torments the wretched man,

and what is he planning, that he is preparing to make war against me?

Does he not remember the sworn faith, or the right hand

so often given to the Franks, and the services rendered to Charles?

Where is he rushing? In his madness he wishes to become a traitor

to himself, to his offspring, and likewise to the exiles!

Above all, let him have one common faith [Note: [Col. 0612D] Is this a common expression? That is, one thing held in common.] with our people and his own.

God granting, he will perish, alas, without faith.

This will be his end, if he persists [Note: [Col. 0612D] Nigellus surely wrote *perstat*: that is, if he persists with a resolute mind in his plan, this will be his end.]. Let him do what our command

urges him to do; let him quickly submit to my reins.

Let him join the Christian flock in peace and faith,

[Col. 0611C] and, for the love of God, let the wretched man abandon the devil’s arms.

If he chooses otherwise—for I shall act unwillingly, but I shall stir up war—

I shall kindle a war sufficiently fierce and terrible for him.”

The messenger went and returned swiftly, ordered to proclaim

the king’s excellent words, rebuke him, and plead with him.

But that wretched man, deservedly devoted to an evil plague,

did not know how to keep faith, but fled from the pious commands.

More deeply pierced in mind, he bore a heart inflamed

by the entreaties of his proud wife.

He desired war and called all the Britons to war;

he arranged ambushes and prepared his deceits.

Meanwhile the emperor heard the proud Briton’s words

and ordered them to be recited to the Franks.

Enraged by these words, the host, long prepared for war,

struck camp; the trumpet gave a terrible blast.

[Col. 0611D] But the pious emperor placed excellent guards

[Col. 0612A] over everything and commanded them in the love of God:

“Protect the churches, men, and do not touch the sacred buildings;

let peace, for the love of God, be maintained in the churches.”

The field trumpets [Note: [Col. 0612D] Medieval writers derived *salpix* from the Greek σάλπιγξ, meaning a trumpet or bugle. Vossius, book III, chapter 45, *On the Vices of Language*, and Du Cange in his Latin Glossary have collected examples from Alcuin, Althelmus, and Fulcher of Chartres.] now resound across the countryside;

the whole woodland echoes, and the hollow bugle groans as it is blown across the fields.

Everywhere they march; the forest opens distant roads to the peoples,
