and the countryside remains filled with Frankish soldiers.

They search for provisions hidden in thickets and marshes,

and for provisions deposited in the ground, in furrows and by human ingenuity.

They plunder the wretched people, livestock, and oxen;

nothing is hidden, nor did any stratagem remain concealed.

No safety exists in any marsh, nor do hidden enclosures in the thickets

protect the men: the Frank ravages wealth everywhere.

They loved the churches, as the emperor had commanded them;

the other buildings they consigned to flame-belching fires.

[Col. 0612B] Yet no faith met the Franks openly in the fields:

proud Briton, you flee from war.

Hidden far away among thorny places and dense thickets,

the Britons appear only rarely and wage war by shouting.

As the leaf falls from the oak tree when frost comes,

as rain in autumn and dew on a hot day,

so the wretched Britons filled the forest clearings

and the marshlands with the slaughter of wild beasts.

They carried on wicked warfare through narrow paths,

shut inside their houses and offering no battle.

Now, Murman, your sands are traversed everywhere;

the pathless forests lie open, and your proud house is exposed.

Meanwhile Murman, pressing through the wooded valleys,

vigorously drives his horses and takes up his familiar weapons.

He joyfully addresses his people and, proud in his own

[Col. 0612C] heart, speaks these words, rebuking them at length:

“Wife, children, and servants, guard your leafy homes

without fear.

But I, with a few companions, so that I may roam the ranks more safely,

am preparing to go there accompanied by these men.

I believe that, clothed in spoils and laden with plunder,

I shall swiftly return on horseback to my house.”

He arms his horse and himself, and arms his faithful companions.

He himself arms both hands with missiles.

Swiftly he mounts his horse and fixes sharp spurs to its sides,

holding the reins; the four-footed beast makes various circuits.

As he leapt about, he ordered huge vessels of drink

to be brought in the usual manner; he accepted them and drank.

Joyfully he sought the embraces of his wife, children, and servants alike,

and gave lingering kisses to them all.

[Col. 0612D] Then, repeatedly brandishing his spear in his hands, he spoke:

[Col. 0613A] “Wife, listen to the words I shall give you.

The little lances you see,” said Murman, your beloved,

sitting joyfully on his horse and turning them in his hands,

“if I have firm confidence, you will see them stained

with Frankish blood when I return home today.

I believe, my beloved, that Murman’s right hand

will not cast any of them in vain. Farewell, beloved woman; goodbye.”

With these words he hurried into the sunny woods,

drunk, wretched man, seeking you, Louis.

With a resolute heart he urges his companions to arms.

All hasten eagerly to go, driven by love of Mars.

“Do you see, young men? The entire Frankish army

is ravaging the fields, carrying off the people and all the livestock.

O strength of the fatherland! O noble fame of our ancestors,

alas, it is shameful that you are now remembered in vain.

[Col. 0613B] Behold, you see the wretched citizens trusting to the forests,

and not daring to bring arms against the enemy in the fields.

Nowhere is faith safe: where is the right hand promised for a year?

Now no one wishes to approach the Franks.

Behold, they rule widely, rejoicing, raging, and carrying off

the great gifts of the Britons, long prepared for them.

If only fortune allowed me to see the king,

for I would boldly present him with a missile;

in place of tribute I would give him these iron gifts,

and, forgetful of myself, would hasten into battle.

Indeed, I would be glad to give myself voluntarily to death

for the glory of my country and the safety of the land.”

One of his companions, following him into battle, answered,

speaking the truth too plainly, though it was not suitable for him:

“O king, empty words fall from a sorrowful heart;

[Col. 0613C] what is left unsaid has more force than what is now repeated.

You see many thousands of Franks occupying the plains,

and countless men rushing through the deep forests.

The king himself, surrounded by a varied host of soldiers,

securely travels the well-trodden road through your lands.

Alas! A people excessively broad, spread throughout the world,

to whose dominion every human being is subjected.

If it pleases you, Murman, pursue the few whom you see passing;

there is no faith in advancing against the king.”

He turned his head and at last spoke, saying:

“You speak the truth indeed, though it will not please me.”

His cheeks were not without tears, nor his heart without grief;

his unsound mind rushed in different directions.

Soon he swiftly threw himself against the opposing enemy:

[Col. 0613D] he struck their backs and pierced their broad chests with iron.

Now here, now there, he raged among the weapons already prepared,

at one moment acting in his father’s manner by fleeing, then returning.

Already a great many of Murman’s swineherds, struck by his fury,

lay scattered about, and the wretched shepherd likewise—

as a ravenous she-bear, having lost her newborn cubs,

goes roaring back and forth through the countryside and forests.

There was a certain Coslus, born of Frankish stock,

though not of the first rank, nor from a noble family.

He was merely a Frank, previously little known by reputation;

afterward his right hand gave him a name.

[Col. 0614A] Murman, as he advanced, saw him at a distance,

and, trusting his horse, prepared to rush fiercely against him.

Nor did the other, trusting in his faithful arms, fail to pursue him swiftly;

both were exceedingly bold.

Immediately Murman addressed him with harsh words:

“Frank, I shall first give you these gifts of mine.

These gifts have long been kept in store for you;

but when you receive them, remember me afterward.”

Saying this, he brandished his weapon and hurled his spear from afar;

the other, shrewdly, drove it away with the aid of his shield.

Coslus, then superior in arms and spirit,

and exulting, spoke these words with his own mouth:

“Proud Briton, I have received the gifts of your right hand;

now it is fitting that you receive such gifts as a Frank possesses.”

Immediately, pressing his iron-shod heels against his horse,

[Col. 0614B] he made it rush toward Murman.

This was no time to fight with small missiles:

with his Frankish spear he pierced Murman’s broad temples.

He had covered his head and the rest of his limbs

with prepared iron; nevertheless, the Frank struck him by skill.

Murman fell to the ground, transfixed by the spear [Note: [Col. 0613D] The British war began and was completed in the year of Christ 818. For that year Einhard states in the *Annals*: “Morman, who in Britain, contrary to the customary practice of the Britons, had claimed royal power for himself, was killed by the army.” We have seen above that others as well had previously assumed the royal title.],

and, sad and unwilling, pressed his body into the earth.

Coslus fell from his horse, drew his sword, and cut off his head;

with a groan, his life soon fled far away.

Murman’s companion struck Coslus,

and you perish, alas, Coslus, victorious yet unwary.

For Coslus’s boy, bound by his master’s affection,

immediately pierced the enemy’s sides with a sharp weapon.

The wounded man, suffering, transfixed the boy;

each, overcome by the other’s wound, died.

[Col. 0614C] These four fought upon the field in proud battle.

For victor and vanquished alike, the outcome was one.

Meanwhile the camp grew somewhat more crowded,

and the news filled the thin air, proclaiming the recent deeds.

For word spread through the camp that the hostile and proud Murman

had fallen by his fate, and that his head was there.

From every side a crowd of Franks rushed together,

greatly delighted by the desire to see it.

Soon the head was brought, severed from the neck by the sword,

defiled with blood and stripped of its former dignity.

They ordered Witchar to be summoned and begged him to report

whether he should declare the news true or false.

He immediately washed the head with liquid and arranged it

with a comb; at once he recognized it.

“This is Murman’s head,” he said; “all of you may trust me.

That neck is very well known to me.”

But the pious emperor ordered the corpse, out of compassion,

to be committed to the earth according to custom.

The bodies of the Franks were indeed entrusted to burial

with pious observance and the proper offering of hymns.

A second report raced through the Britons’ forests;

it thundered aloud that a grim fate had carried off their king.

“Alas, wretched citizens, come together! It is fitting to seek

the laws of the gracious emperor while life is still granted.”

[Col. 0615A] Our Murman has died, struck by a Frankish spear,

too trusting of his wife’s entreaties.

The Britons, compelled, seek the royal authority,

and now all Murman’s offspring and entire lineage come.

Soon Louis joyfully receives the Brittonic submission,

grants law and faith; peace and rest are bestowed.

Then, victorious, he renders abundant thanks to God

and joins the kingdoms long lost to his empire.

But afterward the emperor gladly returns, leaving only a few behind,

and, with God’s help, seeks his lofty realms.

Meanwhile the envoys [Note: [Col. 0615C] That is, the royal messengers whom Louis had sent through his realms to administer justice and regulate the conduct of both clergy.] whom the emperor had previously sent throughout the world,

so that the honor of the Church might increase,

having carried out the pious commands and set all matters in order,

assemble from every side and bring their prepared report.

They had properly visited countless cities and all the monastic camps,

[Col. 0615B] the canonical communities, and, Benedict, your own,

wherever the greatest emperor had ordered them to go;

and they speak the following words:

“By God’s favor and through your faithful labor,

we saw many things adorned and piously completed.

Affairs, examples, and the entire order of worship

proceeded along a straight course, God granting it.

For many matters previously neglected in practice and administration

were not properly carried out in God’s service.

Nevertheless, under the compelling force of your word, we firmly ordered

that each should fulfill these matters in his proper order.

And, assigning themselves measures under your guidance,

they might always be able to proceed

along the lawful path.

We also gave them the book [Note: [Col. 0615D] Namely, the book on the life of clerics and nuns, which the fathers of the Council of Aachen, at the command of the most pious emperor, compiled from the judgments of the holy Fathers; it was published in Labbe’s collection of councils.], which your authority

drew from the teaching of the Fathers and completed through its power.

[Col. 0615C] For the cities and monasteries we leave what each sex requires;

men present, read these things.

The pastor loves it peacefully, and the diligent flock reads it through;

the attentive crowd always honors it.

There young and old, as well as teachers, find

what they should hold, what they should teach,

and whatever they should cherish with love.

But we add this, Caesar: from the time of Christ,

after the holy Church first grew throughout the world,

we speak the truth—during no king’s reign

had the Church [Note: [Col. 0615D] Better: “the Church’s.”] grown, or its honor and faith,

as it now grows in your time, through the mercy of the Thunderer,

in the love of God and in its own splendor.

[Col. 0616A] Your right hand causes all harmful men to remain far away

and protects your pious servants with your right hand.

Your offices teach whatever the ancients taught,

and you yourself constantly make your people remember these things [Note: [Col. 0615D] Written above the text by another hand.].

Terrible toward the fierce, pious and gentle toward your subjects,

you make the world abound in the benefit of your merits.”

Then the emperor returned thanks to them from his heart

and rewarded them equally with munificent gifts.

It was always the ancient custom of the Franks, and it remains so;

as long as it endures, it will be the honor and glory of the nation:

if anyone refuses to preserve perpetual faith toward the king

by cunning, gift, or deceit,

or if the wretched man desires by some device to bring against the king,

his offspring, or his scepters anything that lacks faith,

then, if a brother is present who also speaks [Note: [Col. 0615D] The sense is obscure, but it may be explained thus: it is the Frankish custom that, if anyone raises suspicion of treachery against the king and someone brings the charge against him, the two must enter single combat before the king and the nobles of the Franks.],

[Col. 0616B] it is fitting that the two should fight a savage battle

before kings and Franks and the entire senate.

For Francia detests this crime.

For there was once a certain man named Bero [Note: [Col. 0615D] The same man mentioned above in Book I, also called Count Bera.],

exceedingly rich in possessions and powerful in wealth and rank,

who held Barcelona when Charles granted it to him,

governing the authority entrusted to him for many years.

Another man, Sanilo [Note: [Col. 0616C] The Astronomer, author of the Life of Louis the Pious, briefly describes the matter under the year 820: “At the palace also, Count Bera of Barcelona, when he was attacked by a certain man named Sanila and accused of treachery, fought with him in mounted combat according to their own law, since both were Goths, and was defeated.” Our poet, however, says that the challenge was offered and accepted according to Frankish custom as well; among the Franks, too, single combat was clearly practiced. The Goths differed from the Franks only in this respect: the former fought on horseback, the latter on foot. See below.],

whose native land gave him his name,

attacked him; each was a Goth [Note: [Col. 0616D] For *uterque*, “both.” Indeed, according to the Astronomer, both Bera and Sanilo were Goths.].

He came before the king and the assembled people and senate

and uttered wicked words, all of which Bero denied.

They sprang forward together and moved honorably on foot,

and asked that weapons of war be given to them.

[Col. 0616C] Then Bero first said: “Emperor, for the love of piety,

I beg that I be permitted to deny these charges.

Yet, according to our custom, allow me to remain on horseback

and carry my weapons.” He asked this repeatedly.

The emperor said: “The Franks may settle this matter:

thus it is lawful, thus it is fitting, and we order the same.”

After judgment had been given according to the ancient custom of the Franks [Note: [Col. 0616D] Not according to the custom of the Goths, but of the Franks: Louis ordered this dispute to be settled by a foot-combat. Perhaps they were also permitted to use no other weapons than clubs and shields, as several Frankish royal capitularies prescribe; the Lombard laws show that this custom was introduced into Italy as well.],

they prepared their weapons, eager to rush into the fight.

The emperor, out of love for God, addressed them briefly,

speaking words appropriate to his piety:

“Whoever among you admits to me that he is guilty

of this offense,

[Col. 0617A] I shall pardon him out of compassion for his error

and remit all his debts of sin, bound by the love of God.

For believe me, it is better to obey my counsels

than to engage in the savage battles of destructive Mars.”

But they quickly and repeatedly begged him:

“Battles please us; let battles be prepared.”

The wise emperor said to them [Note: [Col. 0617B] That is: “I grant you permission, setting aside the Frankish custom, to enter combat according to the custom of the Goths.”]: “Let the laws of the Franks be set aside,”

he commanded; and they immediately obeyed his order.

There is a remarkable place near the royal palace,

widely known for its fame, called Aachen,

enclosed by marble stones or surrounded by an embankment,

planted with trees, where fresh grass grows green.

A river gently washes through its middle;

various birds and wild beasts inhabit it.

Whenever the king wishes, accompanied by a few men,

he often enters there for the pleasure of hunting,

to pierce the great bodies of antlered stags with iron,

or to strike does and goats.

Or, when winter’s frost binds the ground,

he chases winged creatures with *capes* (birds which the common people call falcons) [Note: [Col. 0617C] The Synod of Pavia in 850, canon 4, says: “He shall not himself engage in hunting with dogs, hawks, or falcons, which the common people call *falcones*.” These birds are thought to have been so named from *capere*, “to catch.” Du Cange gathers other examples in his Latin Glossary. Accordingly, Gerricus *capis praelatus*, mentioned in the Life of Louis the Pious under the year 813, should rightly be understood as the chief falconer of the royal court. Certainly, in a letter of Charlemagne to his son Pippin, falconers are listed among the royal officers. Hincmar of Reims also mentions them among the palace dignities in his book *On the Order of the Palace*.].

[Note: [Col. 0617C] The description of this combat contains several noteworthy features that one seeks in vain among other writers of that period.] Therefore the trembling Bero and Sanilo come there;

the men sit upon the large bodies of their horses,

carry shields on their backs and spears in their hands,

and await the king’s signal to be given from the palace.

The royal company follows them closely,

carrying shields as well by royal command,

so that, if one should strike his companion with a sword, [Note: [Col. 0617C] Since the detestable practice of duels could not once be abolished altogether, they nevertheless had to be conducted in the sight of everyone; and at least this showed some humanity, since the defeated were usually rescued from death. But in more recent centuries combat is carried on in secret, and no one is present to secure life for the defeated; so far had this madness advanced.],

they might [Col. 0618A] piously rescue him and drag him from the jaws of death.

Soon Gundoldus arrives [Note: [Col. 0617D] This custom deserves careful notice: if anyone fell in the combat, he was immediately carried away. Gundoldus had been accustomed to do this. Thanks are due to Nigellus for explaining this ancient practice to us.], and orders the customary bier

to be brought afterward, as he had been accustomed to do.

The throne gives its assent; then they provoke battle

by a new technique previously little known to the Franks.

They hurl spears and then, with swords drawn,

attempt an ineffective battle according to their custom.

Now Bero spurs his horse and begins to make the horse

run in circles; then he flees swiftly across the broad meadows [Note: [Col. 0617D] For *cornipes*, “horse.”].

The other pretends to follow him, then finally lets go the reins

and strikes with his sword; Bero [Note: [Col. 0618C] That is, Count Bero. Hear Einhard in the *Annals* under the year 820: “Count Bero of Barcelona, who had long been accused by his neighbors of fraud and treachery, attempted to fight his accuser in mounted combat, but was defeated.”] declares that he is guilty.

The strong young men rush together and, at the emperor’s command,

rescue the exhausted Bero from death.

For Gundoldus is astonished and sends the bier back,

empty, to the house from which it had come.

[Col. 0618B] The Caesar granted him life, and granted him safety,

and, taking pity on him, [Note: Eginhard again: “And although he had been condemned to capital punishment as guilty of treason, he was spared through the emperor’s mercy and was sentenced to exile at Rouen.” Therefore, when our poet says that he was permitted by Louis to have his own meals, this must be understood to mean that only his personal property was left to him, not the prefecture of Barcelona. In the Life of Louis, under the year 834, Count Sanila appears. It seems likely that he was the same man who defeated Bera and was later elevated to the dignity of count as a reward.] allowed him to keep his own provisions.

O immeasurable pity! It loosens the bonds of sins;

it yields wealth, it allows the condemned to possess life.

May this same pity—this I ask and faithfully ask again—

restore me, Pippin, rich in virtue, to the pious man.

Now, Benedict, [Note: Namely Benedict of Aniane, later abbot of Inda, a man renowned for the holiness of his conduct, already mentioned above by Nigellus. Death carried him into heaven in the year 821, as appears from his Life in Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Benedictini*, century IV, part I. Accordingly, you can see that Nigellus preserves chronological order in these narratives.] you have completed your course in due order,

and kept the faith, as Paul proclaims with his voice.

Now, seated joyfully in the heavenly court,

you follow the one of the same name, [Note: That is, Benedict, patriarch of the Western monks, whom Benedict of Inda imitated in his virtues. Theodulf of Orléans, writing to the same man in Book II, chapter 6, compares him with Benedict of Monte Cassino in these verses:

“You do not differ in merit, though you do not differ in name;

one lot makes both alike in name and merit.

What Benedict was in the Ausonian fields, a ruler,

that, Benedict, you now are in our regions.”] whom here you had imitated.

Behold, the third little book in your collection ends

with a title, so that you may be remembered, gracious Ermold. [Note: See my Preface.]

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0617]

[Col. 0617D] At last the pious king’s care was spreading everywhere,

and the loyalty of the Franks had risen to the heavens.

[Col. 0619A] From every side, peoples and nations came together

to behold the Christ-worshiping Caesar and his faith. [Note: Or rather, “the Christ-worshiping man and the faith of the Caesar”?]

Meanwhile there was a people whom the deceitful serpent had left in their ancient error

and had deprived of God.

For a long time it had maintained pagan and wicked rites,

worshiping empty idols instead of its Maker.

Neptune stood in place of God; they retained Jupiter,

to whom they entrusted all their sacred rites.

These peoples, moreover, were formerly called by the ancient name of Danes, [Note: That is, *Dani*. Their region is called *Denmark* in German, and therefore the poet calls them *Deni*, as the Germans still do, rather than *Dani*.]

and they are still called so.

They are also called by the Frankish name Northmen, [Note: Namely, Northmen, or Northerners, a name once applied to all the peoples settled north of Europe who, practicing piracy, harassed the Frankish kingdoms. This kind of scourge arose under Charlemagne. Other writers of those times call them sometimes Danes and sometimes Northmen.]

swift, agile, and exceedingly well armed.

That people is widely known indeed:

in a boat it seeks its food and inhabits the sea.

It is handsome in face and graceful in appearance and bearing,

[Col. 0619B] and rumor reports it to be related to the Franks. [Note: The distinguished Leibniz published a dissertation on the origin of the Franks, later reprinted in an expanded and annotated form in 1720 by Johann Georg Eccard—who has thus far served the republic of letters most admirably—at the end of the *Salic Law*. Leibniz argues there that the Franks originated “from the homeland of the Normans, which was called Denmark by the ancients,” and that they formerly settled beyond the River Elbe. He borrowed these words from the Anonymous of Ravenna, published by Porcheron and Gronovius. Yet perhaps that Anonymous is not as ancient as Leibniz believed; and it remains to be investigated whether he is actually Guido of Ravenna, from whose *Cosmography* I once read excerpts in a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library, where his name is plainly given, though previously known otherwise to Raphael Volaterranus. I would venture to affirm nothing here: for many things found in the Anonymous of Ravenna occur in those excerpts, which are otherwise insufficiently corrected, while other things found there are nowhere present in the Anonymous. For example, the following:

“Then there is the city of Lyctia, the city of King Idomeneus, about which Virgil says:

‘Idomeneus of Lyctia besieged

the fields of the Salentines with his troops.’

Of this city only the theater remains; the rest of the walls having been leveled with the ground, it was once approached with solemn devotion. Its inhabitants have now made for themselves, at its summit, a small and nearly ruined municipal settlement preserving the ancient name, a structure that expresses more the appearance of a city than the city itself. In its suburbs innumerable monuments of the ancients, exposed beneath the open sky and carved from solid stone, can be seen. The city of Rugae is recognized next to it. From there to Hydruntum, which lies on the shore and in the harbor of the same Lyctia, is calculated to be about thirty miles,” and so forth. He also writes that Romuald, prince of Benevento, possessed Brundisium and Tarentum, and reports that he leveled those cities to the ground.] [Note: Leibniz, mentioned above, did not rely on the authority of the Anonymous of Ravenna alone in placing the ancient settlements of the Franks near the Baltic strait; he also relied on our poet, whom he had seen in the Imperial Library at Vienna before he was published. Leibniz cites these very verses in support of his opinion. Certainly the testimony is not to be dismissed: Nigellus, an author of such antiquity, gives this account of the origin of the Franks. Below the same poet writes that Louis the Pious, moved by his ancestral lineage—that is, by the Danes, who were still devoted to the worship of false gods—…]

Moved by love of God and pity for his ancestral race,

the Caesar also attempts to win these people for God.

He grieved long that, with no one to warn them, so many peoples,

so many flocks of the Lord, had perished.

After taking counsel, he seeks someone whom he might send there

to seek the great gains for God that had long been lost.

For this work Bishop Ebo of Rheims is sent, [Note: Bishop of Rheims, a man famous in ecclesiastical history both for preaching the Christian faith among the Danish peoples, who at that time were still serving idols, and for the disturbances that he later stirred up against Louis the Pious. Pagi, following Baronius, places Ebo’s mission in the year 823 and cites Eginhard’s words in support. But Eginhard writes under the year 822: “Ebo, archbishop of Rheims, who, at the emperor’s counsel and by the authority of the Roman pontiff, had gone to the borders of the Danes to preach, and during the previous summer had baptized many of them who were coming to the faith, returned.” Therefore Ebo’s sacred expedition, and the events reported here by our poet, belong to the year 822. Pagi should not be corrected; rather, the *Annals of Fulda* should be followed, which under the year 822 state: “Ebo, bishop of Rheims, preached the word of God to the Northman people.”]

through whom they may indeed come to believe in God.

For Louis had himself brought up this boy,

and had made him skilled in liberal arts.

The Caesar therefore addresses him, and flashes with words;

singing many things, he gives his servant pious commands:

“Go, holy one, first address the fierce people

with gentle speech, whether at an earlier or at the present time.

There is a God in heaven, creator of the world and of all things,

whatever the earth contains, whatever the sea and sky contain.

He first made man, our ancestor,

and placed him in Tempe and in your paradise, [Note: *Tempe*, a most pleasant little region of Thessaly, exceedingly celebrated among ancient poets. Lesser poets therefore sometimes used that word to signify a pleasant place.]

so that he might serve Him joyfully through all ages,

and, with the Creator’s gift, remain ignorant of evil.

But because he sinned, he soon fell; from that point onward,

through the devil’s envy, the whole race of his descendants fell.

Yet the offspring increased and filled the forests and fields;

[Col. 0620B] they did not worship God, but images made by human hands.

At last the flood buried them beneath its rushing waters, [Note: Nigellus took this from Festus, who writes that the waves of the sea, when they are still, or when there is a calm, are called *flustra*.]

except for the few whom the pious ark redeemed from the waters.

From this a noble company grew from a small seed,

from which some worshiped their God with devotion.

But the rest, infected with various poisons,

took crooked byways, worshiping savage idols.

Again, in pity, He sent the Son into the fields,

the partner of His kingdom, who holds the heights of heaven.

He joined mortal humanity to His own honor;

[Col. 0621A] He frees mankind from the first sin.

Although He was able, with the Father, powerfully to save the world,

He wished in His goodness to die on earth.

Fastened to the cross, He willingly gave Himself to death,

so that He might graciously give His kingdoms to His soldiers.

Now He sits at the Father’s right hand, sharing His power;

He invites His servants: ‘Run, I shall give you kingdoms.’

He commands the chosen to call back all the sheep,

and duly to bestow the sacred gifts of baptism.

No one will otherwise ascend into heaven’s court,

unless he does what that Son of God commanded.

Therefore, once the worship of the black demon has been abandoned,

let him soon receive the sacred gifts of baptism.

To this faith, Ebo, strive to recall the people:

this is our faith; this is what the Church worships.

[Col. 0621B] It is right to abandon vanities. To serve metals fashioned by hand—

alas, it is a crime for a human being endowed with reason.

What benefit is there in following Jupiter or Neptune, or any of them,

or in the metals fashioned by their own hands?

The wretched worship vanities, praying to deaf and mute things,

and sacrifice to demons what should be given to God.

It is not lawful for us to appease God with the blood of beasts;

the merciful One loves the kindly prayers of human beings more.

Enough time has now been given to profane error;

the time has come to abandon unlawful rites.

The last hour of the waning day now calls these people;

a portion of the Lord’s vineyard still remains.

Now it is fitting to break the slow idleness, while the kindly light

still permits a person to seek God.

Lest the falling black night seize the wretched while they lie inactive,

[Col. 0621C] and immediately hand them over, as is right, to fiery hearths. [Note: So it stands in the manuscript. Elsewhere he uses the word *ignivomis*.]

But you, holy Ebo, after reading through the books,

receive the Testaments of the new and ancient teaching.

First draw sweet cups from this sacred fountain,

so that, having drunk, they may recall the true doctrines of God.

Then give harsh passages at suitable places,

so that they may come to know the false things they have hitherto practiced. [Note: So it stands in the manuscript; a word has fallen out. The sense is: “so that they may come to know the false things they have hitherto practiced.”]

Approach, in brief, Herdolt, the king from our regions, [Note: The man whom he later calls Herordus and Heroldus, king of the Danes at that time.]

and report to him these words of ours.

Pierced by the piety of God and by the teaching of our faith,

we give him these words.

If now he prefers to obey kindly counsels,

let him receive our words in a pious heart.

Alas, let him hasten to abandon his ancestral error,

[Col. 0621D] we ask, and give pious vows to pious Christ.

Let him offer himself entirely and most willingly to God,

whose creation he is and who created him.

Let the monstrous things be far away; let dreadful Jupiter be absent;

let him abandon Neptune and worship the Church.

Let him receive the gift of salvation from the consecrated fountain,

and, I pray, let him bear Christ’s cross upon his forehead.

Do not suppose that I advise this so that his kingdoms may pass to me,

but so that I may win God’s creature for God.

If he wishes, let him hurry to our strongholds,

and receive the washing of God from the true fountain.

Once washed, nourished with food and supplied with weapons,

let him then return to his kingdom and live in the love of God.

This true faith and the commands of the divine Thunderer

urge us to say these things, which I desire to accomplish.”

At once he orders Ebo to be given a great gift.

[Col. 0622B] “Go,” says the emperor, “and may God be with you.”

Meanwhile a messenger from the Britons, [Note: This new revolt of the Britons on this side of the sea belongs to the year 824. Eginhard—or whoever he was whose *Annals of the Franks* I continue to cite under Eginhard’s name—reports among other things: “The emperor, intending to conduct the Breton expedition in person, came to Rennes. From there, dividing the army into three parts and entrusting two parts to his sons Pippin and Louis, he entered Brittany and devastated the whole region with fire and sword.”]

from the rebel side, arrives as usual,

bringing savage news.

They have broken the pledge that the Caesar had recently secured from them,

and, in addition, their sworn faith.

After summoning the peoples and duly preparing the weapons,

the Caesar, rejoicing, prepares to hurry there.

All Francia rushes forward; conquered peoples come as well;

and you, Pippin, prepare to come with your contingent. [Note: Pippin is meant, the son of Louis the Pious and at that time king of Aquitaine.]

He divided all the people into three contingents

and appointed commanders and arranged the nobles.

He entrusts one division to his namesake in war, [Note: That is, to his son Louis, king of Bavaria.]

and joins Matfrid to it, many thousands together. [Note: We noted above that he had been appointed count and prefect of Orléans.]

To King Pippin, Helisachar and powerful men

are joined; the rest of the multitude has no number.

[Col. 0622C] The rejoicing Caesar himself takes the middle column,

a warrior and a wise man, and conducts the war in ordered fashion.

Lantpert leads these men, Matfrid leads those in the ranks, [Note: Namely the count of Nantes, as we saw above. The counts of Orléans and Nantes were chosen as commanders of the war above the others because each held territory bordering on the Bretons, and the Frankish frontier in that region had been entrusted to their protection.]

and you, Louis, as a boy, wage your father’s wars. [Note: He was the son of Louis the Pious, whom his father had already established as king of Bavaria in 817. Eginhard has just told us that he also took part in the Breton expedition of 824.]

Pippin and his own men, mingled with the Frankish host,

bear arms and ravage the people’s honors everywhere.

The Caesar, leading the Franks, directs them along broad roads;

thus the Breton kingdoms lie open as they are traversed.

I myself carried here a shield on my shoulders

and a sword strapped to my side, but no one suffers from my blows.

Seeing this, Pippin laughed, marvels, and says:

“Give up arms, brother; love letters more.”

Then they traverse fields, forests, and trembling marshes;

the people are devastated, and all the livestock perishes.

[Col. 0622D] The wretched are led away captive, and die by the sword;

[Col. 0623A] at last the survivors seek the Caesar’s weapons. [Note: That is, those who had survived free from sword and chains surrendered to the soldiers of Louis Augustus.]

For the Caesar places excellent commanders as guards,

so that, if they wish, they cannot renew the war.

But then the victorious and pious Caesar returned,

and the victorious Franks soon sought their own homes.

For a long time the holy Ebo had traversed the Northman kingdoms,

performing illustrious duties worthy of God’s name.

Now the bishop had reached your strongholds, Herordus, [Note: The same man whom we saw above, the king of the Danes.]

and filled your hearts with the teaching of Christ.

He had begun, in obedience to God’s commands and to the king’s words,

to believe, and now preached to his own people.

“I believe, holy one, but only if deeds follow words.

Go,” he says, “to the king and report these words to him.

For it pleases me to behold the Frankish kingdoms,

the Caesar’s faith, weapons, food, and the glory of Christ-worshipers,

[Col. 0623B] and the worship of God, to whom all power is subject

like a dog, and whom a blessed faith holds firmly.

Then, if your Christ, whom you proclaim in your teaching, grants me

the help I request, I shall immediately perform the deed.

Let the gods also be preserved, whose altars we have consecrated,

until I may be able to behold the temples of your God.

If that God of yours is preferred to ours in honor

and is able to give more gifts to one who prays,

his command urges me to leave the others; it will be a joy to obey Christ,

and to carry the fashioned metals from the flame-belching hearths.”

He orders gifts to be brought, and also gives the holy man a gift,

such as the land of the Danes is able to possess.

Ebo returns rejoicing, and, like a prophet of future gains,

burns with excitement and reports vows pleasing to the king:

how Herold, the excellent ruler of the Danes,

[Col. 0623C] requests that he be received in the sacred washing of God.

Then the pious Caesar offers rich thanks

to the Lord, Father of All, who gave every good thing.

And he orders that immediately, throughout the subjected empire,

all should eagerly pay their vows to God,

so that Christ, who saved the whole world by His blood,

might also redeem these people from the evil enemy.

The pious emperor himself flies by a peaceful road to Ingelheim, [Note: Namely Ingelheim, now a town in the Rhenish Palatinate. There a splendid palace was founded by Charlemagne, of which the Saxon Poet writes in the *Annals of Charlemagne*, in the final chapter:

“Ingelenheim is the name of the place where he founded a palace,

to which our age has seen nothing comparable.”

Eginhard places this royal estate not far from Mainz.]

with his wife and offspring.

That place lies near the streams of the swift Rhine,

adorned with various decorations and banquets.

There the gracious house stands open, marked by a hundred columns,

with various approaches and buildings of many kinds.

A thousand entrances, exits, and a thousand chambers of the buildings,

the work of masters and craftsmen.

[Col. 0623D] The temples of God are wrought in the finest metal, [Note: I would gladly write *summi*—“of the highest”—and I judge that the poet wrote it thus.]

with bronze doors and little golden gates.

The illustrious deeds of God and the series of memorable men

are displayed in remarkable paintings, there to be read.

As the left side first recounts, God having placed them,

human beings inhabit you, new paradise.

How the treacherous serpent tests Eve’s heart,

ignorant of evil; how she touches the man, and he the food.

How, when the Lord comes, they cover themselves with a fig-leaf covering,

and, because of their sins, thereafter cultivate the ground.

How, because of envy and the first gift, one brother

struck down his brother—not with a sword, but with wretched hands.

From there the painting proceeds through countless successors,

and in order and sequence recounts the ancient doctrines.

How the water, deservedly poured throughout the whole world,

increased and brought every race to an end.

How, when God showed mercy, the ark lifted up a few,

and the service of the raven—or yours, O dove.

Then Abraham and his descendants are depicted, along with their deeds,

and Joseph, his brothers, and the work of Pharaoh.

How Moses liberated the people from Egypt by God’s gift,

how Egypt perished and Israel journeyed forth.

[Col. 0624B] And how the law, given by God, was written on twin tablets,

and rivers flowed from the rock, and food came from the birds.

And how the land long promised was given back as a dwelling,

and Jesus had become a good leader for the people.

Then the great multitude of prophets and kings

is painted, and their deeds, celebrated together, shine forth.

The work of David, and the deeds of mighty Solomon,

and the temples built by divine workmanship.

Then the leaders of the people, whatever their stature and greatness,

and the high offices of priests and nobles.

The other side preserves the life-giving deeds of Christ,

which, sent into the world by the Father, He performed on earth.

How the angel first descended into Mary’s hearing,

and how Mary says: “Behold, the servant-girl of God.”

How Christ was born, long before known

to the sacred prophets, and how, as God, He was wrapped in swaddling clothes.

How the pious shepherds soon receive the commands of the Thunderer,

and how the Magi deserved to see God.

How Herod rages, believing that Christ will succeed,

and how he struck down the children who deserved to die.

How Joseph fled to Egypt and brought back the child,

how the child himself grew, and how he was obedient.

How He who had come to save all

who had long perished by His blood wished to be baptized.

How Christ, in human fashion, endured such great fasts,

and how by His skill He struck down His tempter.

How, piously, He soon taught the Father’s commands throughout the world,

and how, in His goodness, He restored the ancient gifts to the sick.

How He even restored dead bodies to life,

and removed the demon’s weapons and drove them far away.

[Col. 0624D] How, betrayed by a fierce disciple and a savage crowd,

He, though God, wished in human fashion to die.

How, rising, He appeared to His own ministers,

and how openly He ascended to heaven and rules the earth.

This palace of God is filled with these paintings,

properly polished and completely finished by the craftsman’s hand.

For the royal house gleams, richly carved throughout,

[Col. 0625A] and sings through its artistry of the greatest deeds of men.

It sings of the deeds of Cyrus, and also of the many wars

and exceedingly harsh deeds in the time of Ninus.

Here you may see the fury of a king raging against the river,

and how at last he avenges the death of his beloved horse.

Next, the unhappy victor seized the realm of a woman;

then her head was placed in a vessel of blood.

Nor are the impious deeds of wicked Phalaris omitted,

or how here he kills savage peoples by cruel art.

How Pyrrilus, a certain craftsman in bronze and gold, [Note: Whom others called Perillus,]

is joined to Phalaris, the wretched man in his impiety,

and how he skillfully forged a bull of bronze, with excessive splendor,

so that the savage man might thrust human limbs inside.

Then the tyrant shut him inside the bull’s belly,

and the art brought death to its own craftsman.

[Col. 0625B] How Romulus and Remus laid the foundations of Rome,

and how that impious man struck down his brother.

How Hannibal, always accustomed to unjust wars,

was himself deprived of his sight.

How Alexander also took the world for himself by war,

and how the Roman power grew ever upward to the heavens.

On another part of the roof they admire the deeds of the fathers,

and those more closely connected with pious faith.

The excellent deeds of the Roman imperial seat

are joined with the deeds of the Franks, and wondrous actions appear together.

How Constantine, out of love, abandoned Rome

and built Constantinople for himself.

The fortunate Theodosius is depicted there,

with his illustrious deeds added to his achievements.

From this point Charlemagne’s first ancestor, [Note: Namely Martel, the grandfather of Charlemagne and mayor of the palace of Francia: the man who defeated the extremely fierce people, the Frisians, in a celebrated expedition and added them to his dominion in 733 and 734.]

Charles Martel, is painted as master of the Frisians through Mars,

and with him his hand’s great deeds.

From this point you, Pippin, shine, restoring the Aquitanian rights, [Note: Pippin was engaged in the Aquitanian war for several years, and, scarcely having completed it, paid his debt to nature.]

and, with Mars favoring you, joining Aquitaine to your kingdom.

And wise Charles displays his open features,

and bears his head duly crowned with a diadem.

From this point the Saxon host stands opposed and attempts battles;

he strikes, subdues, and draws them under his laws.

By these and other deeds that place shines brightly,

and the eye is nourished by the sight; everyone delights to look upon them.

There, therefore, the pious Caesar gives laws to the subdued,

and in his customary manner duly administers the work of the kingdom.

Behold, a hundred ships fly along the streams of the Rhine,

their sails joined in shining white array,

laden with gifts for the people of the Danes; one vessel also carries

King Herold [Note: Three arrivals of Herold, king of the Danes, at the court of Louis Augustus must be distinguished. The first belongs to the year 814, as I shall note below. The second is reported by Eginhard and other chroniclers under the year 823, when he approached Louis “seeking assistance against the sons of Godefrid, who were threatening to drive him from his homeland.” The third belongs to the year 826, when, as Eginhard writes, “Heriboldus, coming with his wife and a great multitude of Danes, was baptized at Mainz at Saint Alban’s.” Our poet seems to have recognized this last arrival of Herold.] in the first ship,

[Col. 0625D] seeking you, Louis. This gift is owed to you,

who properly cause the Church’s glory to increase.

Now they were approaching the banks and taking possession of the harbor;

the pious Caesar sees this from his lofty fortress,

[Col. 0626A] and orders Matfrid, accompanied by a company of young men,

to hurry out in devotion to meet the men.

He sends many horses, fitted with trappings and purple,

to carry the newcomers back to their homes.

Mounted on a Frankish horse, Herold approached;

his wife and the whole household prepared to come as well.

The Caesar joyfully received him from his lofty court,

arranged the expenses, and distributed food.

Herold, bowing, addresses the excellent king,

and first begins to speak his vows:

“Excellent Caesar, the business that has brought me to your stronghold

has brought me, my household, and my entire race as well.

If your authority commands it, I shall begin to tell the story;

ready for the ears of the Caesar, I shall sing it.

For a long time I followed the laws of my forefathers,

and until now I have continued to live according to the custom of my race.

I have always humbly paid my sacred rites to my gods and goddesses,

and offered pious vows,

so that their support might preserve my father’s kingdoms,

the people, the estates, and the household shrines,

and might powerfully remove hunger and every harmful thing,

while granting all prosperity to their own people.

Your holy Ebo, entering the Northman lands some time ago,

preaches and proves something different.

For he proclaims that the creator of heaven, earth, and sea

is the true God, to whom all glory is due.

He had made two human beings from the first substance of clay,

from whom the race of men grew throughout the world.

That most high God sent the Son into the fields,

from whose side blood and water flowed.

[Col. 0626C] This washed the world, in pity, from every sin, [Note: The poet probably wrote *hac lavit*, “with this He washed.”]

and gave heavenly kingdoms to the reborn.

That Son of God is called Christ Jesus,

whose anointing now blesses the whole pious race.

Unless each person confesses that He is the Thunderer

and receives the pious gifts of baptism,

he will unwillingly hasten to the depths of the Tartarean abyss,

where he will be joined, to his misery, with the demons.

But whoever wishes to ascend to heaven’s seat,

where all good remains and all evil is far away,

let him now confess that He is truly both God and man,

and let him cleanse his body in the sacred fountain.

In the name of the Father, the Son, and the gracious Spirit,

let him wash his limbs three times in saving waters.

[Col. 0626D] This is one God, although the names are three;

equal honor and glory belong to Him—He was, is, and will be.

The other things, metals fashioned by human hands,

the bishop calls empty idols and declares to be nothing.

[Col. 0627A] Your most holy bishop Ebo, loving Caesar,

declared to me in his own words that this is your faith.

By his example, revived by his honorable words,

I believe in the true God and reject things fashioned by hands.

For that reason I hastened by oars to your kingdom,

so that your faith might be joined with mine.”

The Caesar replied: “Herold, what you ask of me as a friend

I shall duly give you, and for it I return thanks to God.

Through whose mercy, having long followed the commands of the *celidrus* [a kind of serpent],

you now seek to approach the faith of Christ-worshipers.

‘Make ready; come together, all of you,’ commands the Caesar;

‘it is fitting to prepare the gifts of baptism.’ [Note: Perhaps, “it is fitting to prepare.”]

Prepare white garments such as Christ-worshipers should wear,

fountains, chrism, and waters.”

When these things had been completed in due order

and the sacred preparations had also been properly made,

[Col. 0627B] the Caesar and Herold proceed to the consecrated buildings.

The Caesar received Herold from the waters in God’s honor, [Note: Hear Thegan on the *Deeds of Louis the Pious*: “In the following year” (that is, 826), “he was at the palace of Ingelheim, and there Eriolth of Denmark came to him, whom the emperor raised from the baptismal font.”]

and with his own hand adorned him in whitish garments.

The beautiful empress Judith raised Herold’s queen

from the sacred font and clothed her in garments.

Caesar Lotharius, the son of the gracious Louis,

lifted Herold’s son from the water.

The king’s honored nobles raised and adorned the others,

while the crowd raised many more from the waters.

O Louis, great one, how many hosts you give to God!

How great a fragrance moves forth through you, as you make them Christ’s!

These gains, prince, preserved for you for a long time, will remain yours;

you draw from the wolf’s mouth those whom you make God’s own.

Herold, clothed in white and reborn in heart,

now enters the bright house of his excellent father.

[Col. 0627C] The lofty Caesar gives him enormous gifts,

such as the fields of the Franks can produce.

A gem-studded cloak of red purple, [Note: I leave the examination and elucidation of this matter to the distinguished Dom Bernard de Montfaucon, of the Congregation of Saint Maur, an outstanding ornament of letters and of our age, who has recently undertaken to describe the antiquities of the Franks.]

whose golden border also circles it,

the Caesar gives him the distinguished sword that he himself had carried,

[Col. 0628A] adorned with golden belts properly bestowed.

Golden fastenings soon bind both arms,

and a gem-studded belt encircles his thighs.

His head is duly given a splendid crown,

and golden ornaments [Note: An arc, or the plectrum with which the strings of cithara players are struck. This is the genuine meaning of the word. But what it signifies here is not easy to determine. According to Sipontinus, a *plectrum* was sometimes also called a bronze spur, which was formerly attached to fighting cocks when they were made to fight one another—a practice that continues among the Britons. Does the poet therefore refer to spurs here? Or should *plectra* be read as *plata*, or something else? I understand footwear to be meant here, which the monk of Saint Gall, Book I, chapter 36, says was externally gilded for the kings of the Franks.] adorn his feet.

Golden coverings gleam broadly across his back,

and his hands are adorned with a white covering.

Meanwhile the royal matron Judith also gives gifts

appropriate to her station and pleasing in their beauty.

Namely, she makes a tunic stiff with gold and gems,

such as Minerva herself might fashion by her art.

A golden band encircled with gems crowns her head,

and a large new necklace covers her breast.

A flexible circle of twisted gold passes around her neck,

and women’s bracelets hold her arms.

[Col. 0628B] Soft golden and gem-studded belts cover her thighs,

and a golden cloak covers her back.

Meanwhile Lotharius, moved by affection no less,

adorns Herold’s son in gold-bearing garments.

The rest of the company is outfitted according to Frankish custom;

the Caesar gave them their clothing out of affection.

Meanwhile the sacred rites of the Mass were already prepared,

and the customary signal calls the people to the sacred heights. [Note: That is, the bell. See Ducange’s *Latin Glossary*, where other ancient examples are collected.] [Note: That is, the church. But which church of this kind? If the Astronomer in the *Life of Louis the Pious*, Eginhard, and the Annals of Fulda and Saint-Bertin are believed (the latter give matching accounts, since they derive from one source), Heriold was baptized at Mainz, at Saint Alban’s. Accordingly Mabillon, in the *Benedictine Annals* under 826, treats this as certain. The monastery of Saint Alban at Mainz was indeed famous. But our author says nothing of Mainz or Saint Alban’s basilica; rather, he states quite clearly that the event took place in the district of Ingelheim, and therefore in the magnificent basilica there which Nigellus has just described. Thegan too, as we have just seen, wrote no differently. I would more readily follow these two contemporary writers, and especially Nigellus, who describes the matter so vividly. For the Annals attributed to Eginhard do not have as certain an author as the poem before us. This is so unless the church of Saint Alban and the basilica at Ingelheim were the same church.]

[Col. 0627D] The buildings shine, filled with the glittering clergy;

in magnificent order the lovely house blooms.

A crowd of priests is constituted according to Clement’s teaching, [Note: I think this refers to the Roman pontiff, in whose spurious books much is found concerning priests. Perhaps the following verse also alludes to another Roman pontiff, to whom some ordinance concerning deacons is attributed, though I do not know on what good authority.]

and the Levites shine, pious in their order.

Theuto arranges properly the choir of the singing clergy, [Note: Some one of the nobles of the palace, as was also Adbalvitus, mentioned below. Around that time there was a Theoto who, a few years later, is still mentioned in the diplomas of Louis the Pious as distinguished by the dignity of chancellor. There was also a Theoto who was abbot of the Greater Monastery. But perhaps neither belongs to this passage.]

and Adhallvitus appears, carrying a staff in his hand.

He strikes and arranges the men who press forward,

[Col. 0628C] arranging the way in honor of the Caesar, the nobles, his wife, and his offspring.

The rejoicing Caesar crossed the broad courts toward the palace,

often diligently present at the sacred offices.

Resplendent beyond measure with gold and flashing gems,

he joyfully proceeded, leaning upon servants.

[Col. 0629A] Hilduin holds his right hand, while Helisachar

supports his left; Gerung himself goes first, [Note: He was the chief doorkeeper of the sacred palace. Frothar, bishop of Toul, grants him this title in Letter 2, in Duchesne, volume II, page 712, *Scriptores Francici*. In the *Life of Louis the Pious*, the Astronomer also states under the year 822 that Lotharius was sent by his father to Italy, together with Wala, a monk related to him, and also Geruntius, the doorkeeper. It should be written *Gerungum*, whom Eginhard likewise calls *Gerungum ostiariorum magistrum* under the same year 822.]

carrying a staff in the customary manner and preserving the king’s footsteps,

whose head, of course, bears a golden crown.

Pious Lotharius and Herold himself, clothed in robes,

follow behind them, shining with their gifts.

Before his father, the handsome and illustrious boy Charles, [Note: The man whom we customarily call Charles the Bald. He was the youngest son of Louis the Pious, born of the empress Judith; indeed, in the year 826, when these events occurred, he was still a small child, having been born on 13 June 823.]

adorned with gold, proceeds happily, triumphantly striking the marble with his feet.

Meanwhile Judith, supported by royal gifts,

advances, resplendent in her magnificent attire,

while two nobles accompany her with the highest honor.

Matfrid, or Huc [Note: [Col. 0629C] I correct this to *sive Hug*, or even *sive Huc*: for *Hugo* and *Huco* occur among the ancients with differing pronunciation, yet denote the same name. If two nobles accompanied the Empress, then, besides Matfrid, count of Orléans, another ought to be mentioned. [Col. 0629D] This was Hugo, I conjecture—the count whose daughter Irmingard Lothar, the eldest son of Louis the Pious, had married in 821. In the *Life of Louis the Pious*, under the year 827, Louis himself is said to have sent his son Pippin against the Saracens, “and with him sent from his side the counts Hugo and Matfrid.” Here we find both counts joined together, just as they are joined in our poet in this solemn ceremony. And since it is established that, in the impious conspiracy against Louis Augustus himself, the counts Hugo and Matfrid took the leading roles, while Theganus wrote that Hugo, Lothar’s father-in-law, had sown the seeds of such great disloyalty as early as 821, we must understand that the Hugo referred to here was Irmingard Augusta’s father, “who was of the lineage of a certain duke named Edith,” as Theganus reports.] joining them in procession.

And the crowned men [Note: [Col. 0629D] It should not be passed over that these counts too are said to have worn crowns upon their heads—different, certainly, from the imperial crown, but nevertheless a sign of distinguished rank. In the Continuator of Aimoinus, Boso appears adorned with a ducal crown. I do not know whether any ancient writer has mentioned the crown of counts. Yet these men already enjoyed the office of margraves, though not yet the name. In Great Britain the custom of such crowns still survives when the king is inaugurated.] venerate the honorable lady;

Each of the two shines nobly in golden garments.

Herold follows more closely; then at last comes his wife,

[Col. 0629B] Gladly bearing the gifts of the pious Empress [Note: [Col. 0630C] I read *munere*, “with the gift.”].

And Fridugisus [Note: [Col. 0630C] Whom we saw above as Louis the Pious’s chancellor and simultaneously abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours.] proceeds, followed by the shrewd

Crowd of disciples, radiant in clothing and in faith.

Next, in ordered array, follows the rest of the youth,

Adorned with garments bestowed by the Caesar.

When the Caesar reaches the church with dignified step,

He seeks the Lord with prayers, according to his custom.

Soon the trumpet of the Germans loudly gives forth its proper blast,

Immediately followed by the clergy and the choirs.

Herold marvels, and his wife and all his children

And companions marvel at such lofty heights of God;

[Col. 0630A] They marvel at the clergy, and finally they marvel at the temple,

And at the priests and their pious service.

Above all, they marvel at the rewards of the great king,

Under whose commands they see so many things proceed.

Tell me, Herold, I ask: which will you value more—

The exalted king’s faith, or your worthless carved images?

Carry to the furnaces the metals of gold and silver,

And from them have honor prepared for yourself or your people.

If it should be iron, perhaps it will suffice for cultivating the fields;

Order knives to be forged from it.

The plowshare fixed in the earth will bring you greater wealth

Than that god of yours can bestow upon you by his art.

This is the true God, whom the Franks and the Caesar himself

Rightly worship in prayer: worship him, and abandon Jupiter.

[Col. 0630B] From Jupiter make black pots

And dusky cauldrons, so that they may always love the fire,

As their maker himself does.

For Neptune let a water-carrier be forged for you,

A pitcher, and honor will always belong to its liquid.

Meanwhile the lordly provisions were reverently prepared,

And various foods and many kinds of wine.

Peter, chief of the bakers [Note: [Col. 0630C] He is here called chief of the bakers; this dignity also formerly flourished at the court of the kings of France. In later centuries he was called the great baker, or master panetier of France, the official placed in charge of this duty.], on one side, and Gunto [Note: [Col. 0630C] He is called chief of the cooks. This too was an illustrious dignity in the palace of the Frankish kings. Theodulf of Orléans, in Book III of his *Poems*, presents one of these officials of the kitchen, surrounded by ranks of cooks:

“Wisely managing everything, he brings the king’s

Honored dishes and feasts before the throne.”

Herimann too, in his *Book on the Restoration of Saint Martin of Tournai*, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, calls Bishop Fulcher the son of the king of France’s chief cook.] of the cooks,

Hasten forward and arrange the tables in their proper order.

They set out white tablecloths with snowy nap [Note: [Col. 0630D] Although we commonly write *mantilia*, nevertheless, as Dausquius has already noted in his *Orthographia*, the most ancient Vatican manuscript of Virgil and other old manuscripts have *mantelia*. Perhaps these *mantelia* with snowy *villi*, that is, shaggy nap, spread upon the tables may seem strange to you here. But our poet is playing the scholar, having borrowed this mode of expression from Virgil or Ovid, in whom occur: “. . . and they carry tablecloths with shorn nap”; and: “And . . . a tablecloth with loosened nap.” Servius is the authority for the assertion that larger cloths had nap. So it was among the Romans; whether also among the Franks, or whether this is said merely for the verse’s sake, let others judge.],

[Col. 0631A] And arrange the dishes upon a marble platter [Note: [Col. 0631C] Note the customs of the ancient Franks.].

Here one is accustomed to serve Ceres, here meat offerings.

You see golden vessels resting across the platter.

No less, the eager boy Otho commands the cupbearers [Note: [Col. 0631C] This too was formerly one of the court dignities. Those who received it were called *buticularii* by Hincmar and other writers of that period, whence our word *bottigliere*. Abbot Hermeland, in his *Life* [Col. 0631D] preserved by Mabillon, is said to have been first appointed by the king chief of the cupbearers. See Du Cange, *Glossary of Medieval Latin*.],

And prepares the slow gifts of Bacchus, the rich wine.

When the beneficent rites have duly been completed,

The golden Caesar prepares to depart from the place

From which he had earlier come; and his wife, his children,

All the gilded company, and finally the shining clergy depart.

Then the pious ruler, controlling his step, reaches the palace,

Where provisions are prepared for him in imperial fashion.

Beautiful Judith too sat down happily at his side,

Having been ordered to do so; and she kisses the king’s knee [Note: [Col. 0631D] Above we saw that certain nobles approached not to kiss the emperor’s feet but his knee. Now it deserves notice and astonishment that, at that time, it was customary for the wives of the Frankish emperors or kings to kiss their own husbands’ knees. Times have changed, and customs have changed with them.].

Caesar Lothar, and also Herold, the guest,

By order of the king, take their places beside him on the couch.

[Col. 0631B] They marvel at the food, and they marvel at the weapons

Of the Caesar, at the servants, and at the honor of the boys [Note: [Col. 0631D] Instead of *pueris*, meaning those whom we now call pages. For I have no doubt that kings and emperors formerly had honorary boys attached to their service. Those raised in the royal court would have belonged especially to this number. Above, in Book II, there also occurs:

“Relying on the nurture of Charles, the chief of the Gascons.”

Below the same honor of the boy occurs twice again.].

That joyful day was for the Franks and for the newly converted Danes,

And rightly it will thereafter be remembered.

For another day was already approaching with the first eastern dawn;

The stars withdraw from the sky, and the earth grows warm beneath the sun.

The Caesar prepares to go hunting, as the Franks are accustomed to do,

And orders Herold to go with him.

There is an island nearby, enclosed by the Rhine’s waters,

Where the fresh grass grows green and a shady grove stands.

For many different wild animals were there,

And a host lay scattered inertly through the woods.

Bands of hunters filled the place from every side,

Together with a great pack of Molossian hounds.

[Col. 0631C] The Caesar, riding a swift horse, traverses the fields,

With Wito [Note: [Col. 0631D] The same as Wido and Guido. I suppose that he was in charge of the hunt, a dignity formerly counted among the chief offices in the palace of the Frankish kings, as Hincmar testifies in his *Book on the Order of the Palace*. Charlemagne also lists hunters among his officials in a letter published among the Lombard laws [Col. 0632D] in Part II of Volume I of this collection. Around this time the Widones, or Guidones, flourished, but it is uncertain whether they had any connection with this man.] riding beside him, armed with a quiver.

A great crowd of young men and boys streams forth,

Among whom swift Lothar rides on horseback.

Deni too is there, together with Herold, the guest,

Happily present also to watch the spectacle.

Now pious Judith, the Caesar’s most beautiful wife,

Mounts her horse, magnificently adorned and arrayed.

The highest nobles, or the crowd of powerful men,

[Col. 0632A] Pass before her [Note: [Col. 0632D] That is, they precede her.] and follow her with the honor due to the pious king.

Now the entire grove resounds with repeated barking,

Here with the voices of men, there with the furious blast of the trumpet;

The wild animals leap apart and flee through the rough thickets.

Neither flight offers safety, nor the grove nor the stream;

A doe too falls among the branching stags.

The tusked boar itself falls, pierced by a spear.

For the joyful Caesar himself strikes many wild animals

And brings their bodies to death with his own hand.

Swift Lothar too, flourishing and confident in his youth,

Strikes many bears with his own hand.

The rest of the men slaughter here and there across the meadows

Wild animals of many kinds and various species.

By chance a little doe, pursued by a pack of dogs,

Flees through the shady grove and leaps through the willows.

[Col. 0632B] Behold the place where the powerful crowd and Caesar’s wife Judith [Note: [Col. 0632D] Excessive freedom, good Nigellus. Of course *Caesara* means “the Caesar’s wife,” or *Caesarea*. In the *Miscellaneous History*, *Caesara* is mentioned as the wife of the Persian king.],

Together with the boy Charles himself, had taken their stand.

It rushes past; its only hope lies in its feet;

Unless flight brings help, behold, it will perish.

When the boy Charles sees it, he desires to follow his parent

In the customary manner, and eagerly begs for a horse.

[Note: [Col. 0632D] These events took place in 826. Charles, however, had been born in 823 and was therefore scarcely four years old. I would not deny that the little boy asked for weapons and wished to pursue the wild animal; but at the same time one must acknowledge that our poet is here flattering and speaking sweetly to Augusta Judith, so that through her he too might be freed from exile and restored to Louis’s favor. Read what follows.]

He eagerly asks for weapons, a quiver, and swift arrows,

And longs to follow, as his father himself is accustomed to do.

He multiplies his entreaties upon his entreaties; but his beautiful mother

Forbids him to go and does not grant a path to his desire.

Unless his tutor and his mother restrain him as he wishes,

The boy, in the manner of a boy, will already want to go on foot.

Meanwhile the other young men proceed and catch the fleeing

[Col. 0632C] Little creature, soon bringing it back unharmed to the boy.

Then he takes up weapons suitable for his tender age,

And the boy strikes the wild animal’s terrible back.

The honor of boyhood surrounds and adorns him on every side;

His father’s valor and his grandfather’s name adorn him.

Like Apollo shining as he walks upon the heights of Delos,

Bringing great joy to his mother Latona.

Now the distinguished father Caesar, and the rest of the youth,

Heavy with the hunt, prepare to return to the dwelling.

Yet in the middle of the green forest

[Col. 0633A] Judith wisely constructs and covers a sheltered enclosure

With stripped wicker and trimmed boxwood,

She surrounds it with little cushions and covers it with linen cloths,

And herself prepares a seat for the pious king

On the green grass of the countryside, and arranges the food.

Soon, after washing their hands, the Caesar and his beautiful wife

Sit down together upon a golden couch.

Beautiful Lothar, and Herold, the beloved guest,

Take their places at the table by order of the pious king.

The rest of the young men sit upon the grassy ground

And rest their weary bodies in the shady grove.

Soon the young men bring rich, roasted entrails of wild animals;

Venison joins the Caesar’s dishes.

Hunger, driven away by the food, flees;

They offer cups to their mouths, and thirst itself is dispelled by the wholesome liquid.

[Col. 0633B] Good Bacchus soon makes their brave hearts joyful.

The men happily return to the palace.

When they reach the palace, they soon refresh their hearts with Lyaeus [Note: [Col. 0633C] Our Nigellus frequently mentions Bacchus and Lyaeus. Take note of this, lest you criticize our times as though temperance once sat at table but now is often excluded from it.],

And proceed to the evening services [Note: [Col. 0633C] Namely, to the evening office sung by the clergy in the church.].

When these too have been completed in the customary, proper, and reverent manner,

They then enter the palace chambers.

Behold the hands of the young men, carrying the gifts of the hunt;

A great stream approaches, eager to appear before the king’s eyes.

They bring enormous antlers of stags,

And the hides and heads of bears.

They bring back many bodies of bristling boars,

And the boys carry young roe deer and does.

That pious man distributes the prey among all the servants

According to his custom; a large portion also falls to the clergy.

Meanwhile, when Herold the guest saw such things,

[Col. 0633C] He turned many thoughts over in his heart.

Seeing the royal laws, he marvels that imperial power, faith,

And the service of God proceed according to their proper order.

But at last he wipes uncertain emotions from his heart,

And takes the counsel that God himself has given.

Behold, full of faith, he speaks these words to the king;

Coming of his own accord, he falls before his feet.

“Excellent Caesar, worshiper of God and ruler of your people,

Whom almighty God, your gracious Lord, has entrusted to you,

[Col. 0634A] I see that, by God’s gift, you are distinguished, patient, strong, and pious,

A warrior and merciful.

Exceedingly rich in wealth, and also a giver to the needy,

Gentle toward your subjects and tranquil in your conduct.

I see that all the streams of virtue have been entrusted to you, Caesar;

Your heart is drenched with heavenly dew.

Your persuasion has subdued my neck beneath Christ’s yoke,

And has drawn me away from eternal fires.

It has taken away my evil error and my subjugated household,

And filled my heart with the true fountain.

Moreover, aided by various gifts and weapons,

My heart full of God, my body abounds in resources.

Who would do such things, unless inflamed by love of Christ,

Bearing such great gifts to an ungrateful people?

I believe that you are now the head of good things on earth,

And rightly hold the honor of the Christ-worshiping empire.

Just as all idols yield before me in the name of Christ,

So too do the powers yield before your name.

Let the glory of the ancient age now give way,

While your empire flourishes by the gift of the Thunderer.

Perhaps someone might have been your equal in gifts and arms;

But in love of God you surpass them all.

But what am I doing now? Why do my words delay me?

I wish to reveal such great matters in a brief speech.”

Then, with hands joined, he voluntarily surrendered himself to the king [Note: [Col. 0633C] To surrender oneself to someone with joined hands is to promise him, by an oath, fidelity and submission. I do not find in the annals of that period that Herold submitted himself and the kingdom of Denmark to Louis Augustus. For what Astronomus writes in the *Life of that emperor*, under the year 814—“Herold, to whom supreme authority over the Danish kingdom seemed to belong, and who had previously been expelled from the kingdom by the sons of Godfrey, fled to Emperor Louis and, according to the custom of the Franks, surrendered himself into his hands”—does not establish the matter clearly enough; the sense of the words is ambiguous. Einhard has instead: “and commended himself into his hands.” Nevertheless, I think our Nigellus will have such authority in this matter that no one will wish any longer to deny what he narrates so plainly. Accordingly, Hermann Conring must be corrected. In Book I, chapter 4, *On the Boundaries of the German Empire*, he argues that Denmark was by no means transferred under Louis the Pious into the jurisdiction of the empire, although Louis established the bishopric of Hamburg over Denmark as well; he maintains that this was first done under Henry I, the Fowler, king of Germany. Herold’s fidelity soon passed away lightly into the winds; nevertheless, we are compelled to believe that he gave it at that time.],

And with himself the kingdom that had been his by right.

“Accept me, Caesar,” he says, “and also the kingdoms I have subdued;

Of my own will I place myself at your service.”

[Col. 0634C] The Caesar himself received his hands in his honorable hands [Note: [Col. 0634C] The rite by which the one receiving an oath ratified the oath of the person swearing. The matter is well known to learned readers and therefore does not require explanation from me.];

The Danish kingdoms are joined to the pious Franks.

Then, rejoicing in the ancient Frankish manner [Note: [Col. 0634D] Ah, good Ermoldus! *Veternus* is one thing, *vetustus* another; the latter is the word you intended.],

The Caesar gives him a horse and, as usual, weapons [Note: [Col. 0634D] Here too one must note the custom of the ancient Franks. When someone subjected himself to the king, binding himself to him by an oath of fidelity, the king in turn bestowed gifts upon him, especially a horse and weapons. I shall be content with one example. The Continuator of Fredegar, under the year 764, says: “Remistanus came to the king and promised many oaths and his fidelity to the aforesaid King Pippin, so that he would always be faithful both to that king and to his sons. The king received him into his authority and enriched him by giving him many gifts of gold and silver, precious garments, horses, and weapons.”] at the same time.

Again a festive day rises, renewed and shining,

Celebrated with solemn rejoicing by Franks and Danes.

Meanwhile the Caesar, now that Herold is faithful,

Honors him with a gift of wealth, out of his piety.

But on account of his conflicts he grants him borderlands [Note: [Col. 0634D] The sense is not entirely clear. It is uncertain whether this means “he grants him territories,” that is, a region adjoining the Danish kingdom, “because of his battles”—that is, because rebellions against Herold had hitherto existed and still existed in his kingdom—or whether we should read *praemia*, “rewards,” rather than *praelia*, “battles,” meaning gifts that Louis bestowed upon him near, or in the vicinity of, the borders of Denmark. Einhard teaches us the correct sense in his *Annals*, under the year 826, where he writes that Herold returned “through Frisia, by the route on which he had come.” “In that province he was given the district called Rhiustri, so that, if necessity required, he could withdraw there with his possessions.” Other Frankish annals have the same account, as does Astronomus in the *Life of Louis*.] borders,

And vineyards and many kinds of food.

So that he may properly adorn the worship of God through his office,

The powerful Caesar also gives him all the necessary vessels.

To the sacred orders he gives garments,

And he gives priests and Catholic books.

He sends monks there as well [Note: [Col. 0635C] Especially Ansgar, the apostle of the northern peoples, later the first bishop of Hamburg and afterward of Bremen, a man renowned for the holiness of his life. His *Life* may be found in Bollandus, *Acta Sanctorum*, under 3 February.], willing to undertake the task,

So that they may lead the peoples back to the pious kingdoms of heaven.

The number and quality of the gifts he grants to be possessed

Surpass and overwhelm both ingenuity and song.

Meanwhile the sailors, who knew the treasures of the sea,

Load the ships with provisions and royal food.

Already the breezes call for the sails, and the wind rebukes

Those who linger, warning of the dreadful signs of winter.

At last, with the ships made ready and the sails renewed,

With permission [Note: [Col. 0635C] That is, with the leave or permission granted by Augustus to depart; our poet has used the word above as well.] Herold honorably boards the vessel.

[Col. 0635B] The king’s son and grandson keep watch in the palace

As guards [Note: [Col. 0635C] Namely, these were hostages whom King Herold had left with Louis as pledges of his sworn fidelity.], honoring Frankish law.

Herold, laden with food and various weapons,

Makes for his own kingdom across the wave-tossed sea [Note: [Col. 0635C] He did indeed seek his own kingdom; but not long afterward he renounced the Christian religion and returned to his former superstition. Saxo Grammaticus, in Book IX of his *Danish History*, despite the many Romanesque fables with which he filled his narrative, nevertheless acknowledged Herold’s conversion to the Christian faith at Louis the Pious’s urging. He then adds that Herold first destroyed the temples and proscribed the sacrificers; but afterward, driven out by Regner, “he transferred his fortune to sacrilege. For just as he had been the chief example of the religion he had begun, so he became the first spectacle of its neglect, and from a glorious promoter of holiness he became its infamous deserter.”].

These are the gains, Louis, that you give to almighty God,

And you join illustrious kingdoms to your own.

Kingdoms which their fathers’ weapons could never win in any battle

Now freely seek to submit to you.

[Col. 0636A] What powerful Rome never held, nor Frankish law,

You retain in its entirety, father, in Christ’s name.
