Even organs [Note: [Col. 0635D] The first musical organs brought into France once appeared so remarkable to the Franks that they judged the matter worthy of being reported to posterity as something extraordinary. In their oldest annals, Volume II of Du Chesne, pages 4 and 8, it is noted under the year 757: “Organs came into France.” Einhard writes that this instrument was sent to King Pippin by the Greek emperor—for at that time Greece alone supplied craftsmen capable of constructing such ingenious machines. It is also testified by the Monk of Saint Gall, in Book II, chapter 10, of his *Life of Charlemagne*, that “every kind of organ” was sent to Charlemagne by the Greek Augustus. But in 826, as the Annals of Fulda report, “a certain George, a priest from Venice, came with Count Baldwin of Friuli and made a hydraulic organ at Aachen.” Although you hear it called a hydraulic organ here, do not suppose that anything other than pneumatic organs is meant—the kind now commonly used in churches [Col. 0636C]. Einhard writes under that year that George came from Venice, “claiming that he knew how to make an organ. The emperor sent him at Aachen with Thencolf the chamberlain, and ordered that everything necessary for making the instrument be supplied to him.” The monk of Saint Gall mentioned above explains this by saying: “That most excellent musical organ was constructed from bronze vessels, with bull-hide bellows blowing wonderfully through bronze pipes, and so forth.” In any case, organs were known and used even in the age of Augustine, Isidore, and Cassiodorus. I have perhaps been permitted to provide curious readers with additional information on such a subject.], which France had never before seen,

From which the proud kingdoms of the Greeks swell excessively,

And which Constantinople thought it alone had surpassed,

Your palace at Aachen now possesses, Caesar.

Perhaps this will be a sign that the Franks lower their necks,

When their distinctive glory is taken from them.

France, rejoice—it is fitting: offer pious thanks to Louis,

By whose virtue you receive such gifts.

May almighty God, creator of heaven and earth,

Grant that his name resound throughout the world for many ages.

While I was singing these things, I was guarded at Strasbourg [Note: [Col. 0636D] As everyone knows, this was formerly Argentoratum and is now called Argentina by the Italians. This city had been assigned to our Ermoldus as a place of custody or imprisonment, and he was living there in exile when he composed these verses.],

Conscious of my own offense and guilty.

[Col. 0636B] O Virgin Mary, your temples shine for you,

Where your honor is rightly revered on earth.

They say that the heavenly citizens often visit these shrines,

And that angelic choirs worship in them.

They report many marvelous things, but I shall recount only a few.

Take up the song, Thalia, if the gracious Virgin favors you.

The church’s guardian was once Theutramus [Note: [Col. 0636D] Why the poet calls this priest worthy of his name was explained to me by the very learned Godefridus Philippi. According to Aventinus, *Teuto* is the same as “king,” and according to Leibniz, *Theodo* signifies “man,” “hero,” or “prince.” Again, *ram* in compounds means fame and glory, as can be seen from *Adelram* and *Adalram*. We may therefore interpret Theutramus as “an eminent and celebrated man.”] by name,

[Col. 0637A] And he was worthy of that name.

He, ever watchful by night and day, was accustomed

To supplicate God before the sacred altar of the Virgin.

Therefore, relying on heavenly grace,

He often deserved to see the angelic citizens, the holy ones.

One night, after the psalms and hymns had been completed,

When he wished to lay his weary limbs upon his bed,

He suddenly saw the temple grow bright with light

Like the sun, and the serene day itself burst into flame.

He rose from his bed and wished to learn the cause,

To discover why the holy house shone with such great light.

By chance a bird resembling an eagle had spread its wings before the altar;

Yet this was no bird born upon the earth.

Its beak was of gold, its talons more precious than gems,

And an ethereal color was poured across its wings.

[Col. 0637B] The light itself shone from its eyes. The priest was astonished,

And could not direct his gaze against it.

He marvels at the bird, and likewise marvels at its wings,

Especially at its eyes and at its entire body.

For a long while he remains there, until the rooster’s chattering triple

Cry resounds and awakens the brothers for their duty.

Then the wondrous creature, raising itself, spontaneously opens the window

Before it and loosens itself [Note: [Col. 0637C] In Italian, *si lascia andar fuori*, “it lets itself go out.”] to depart.

As it departed toward the heavens, the light too withdrew;

It thereby appeared to have been a citizen of God.

At another time the same teacher [Note: [Col. 0637D] A little earlier he had said that organs had never before existed in France. What, then, does Ermoldus mean by this word? He used *crevit* for *vidit*, deriving it from *cerno*, “I see,” on the authority of Priscian, who quotes Titinnius in the *Gemini*: “As soon as I saw these girls sighing at night,” that is, “I saw.” But the statement that organs were entirely unknown to the Franks before Louis the Pious is clearly inconsistent with the truth, as we have already seen above.] saw, and recounted to me

The many marvels of a band of brothers.

As he was accustomed to psalmodize before the altar of the aforesaid church,

He pondered the darkness, seeking God in his heart.

His disciples were with him, keeping watch through the night;

[Col. 0637C] [Note: [Col. 0637D] Rather, *servabat*, “he was keeping.” The sign mentioned next, as I noted above, means a bell.] They vigilantly observed the times of the signal.

Suddenly a sound, thunder, and an urgent wind

Violently shook the lofty roof of the house.

The disciples fell to the ground, and trembling throughout the hall

They threw themselves down, while their minds fled in fear.

But the undaunted Sacer, with his palms spread toward the stars,

Wished to learn what that sound signified.

He saw the holy house’s roof suddenly open,

And saw three men enter with reverence.

They were bathed in light and clothed in white garments;

Their bodies were whiter than snow, their heads like milk.

The third, an elder, went in the middle, supported

[Col. 0638A] by the other two servants, and entered reverently.

As soon as their feet touched the ground, they sought the Virgin’s altar

With reverence and sang their vows in prayer.

Following the path and custom of men, they approach the other altars [Note: [Col. 0637D] This must be understood as referring to the altars.],

They sound forth words with their mouths and offer prayers in order.

The right side of the church rejoices in Paul’s gift,

While the left is supported by the name of Peter.

Here is the distinguished teacher, there the key-bearer of heaven;

Between them shines the glorious Mother of God.

Michael claims the middle, or the cross claims the central nave,

And the last of John’s ointment [Note: [Col. 0637D] Thus in the imperial manuscript. Perhaps *unguine*, “ointment,” or blessed oil from the relics of Saint John, was intended. For the passage concerns the relics of the saints kept there, as the following lines show; this was also indicated above by the words “the church rejoices in Paul’s gift.”] shines joyfully.

These heavenly citizens too came to earth in prayer,

Those whose souls they often see before God.

What idiot [Note: [Col. 0637D] Above the word *idiota* in the manuscript there is written a gloss in the Theotisc language, *Heimi Kizogener* [Col. 0638C]. The sense is: “Who is so insane and unlearned as to deny that the bodies of the saints ought to be venerated?”] or fool would maintain that the bodies

[Col. 0638B] Of the holy Fathers ought not rightly to be venerated on earth,

When God is rightly honored in his beloved servants,

By whose prayers we ascend to the heights of heaven?

Peter is not God, but I believe that through Peter’s prayer

I may be freed from the guilt of my sin.

For as far as the men advance through Mary’s temple,

The roofs always stand open above them.

When their vows have been completed, they return upward to the stars;

The opened roofs resume their proper place.

Seeing this, Sacer goes on and visits his companions,

Who for a long time hold their astonished hearts upon the ground [Note: [Col. 0638D] I suspect this should be *humi*, “on the ground”; otherwise a corruption lies hidden.].

“Rise,” he says, “my companions, for what circumstance has compelled you

To sleep now, when you ought to be awake?”

Shaken by sobbing, they can scarcely utter words,

[Col. 0638C] And declare that they are entirely ignorant of the matter.

“Come,” he says insistently, “mark the hour and the time;

Perhaps this event too will bring us something further.

I believe [Note: [Col. 0638D] That is: “As I suppose, the venerable man whom I saw carried to heaven was some priest already shining with episcopal dignity, whom the angels were bearing into paradise.”] that he was a prophet, consecrated with episcopal honor,

Whom an angelic choir also carried into the heavens.

What wondrous testimony of events! The blessed Boniface [Note: [Col. 0638D] Namely, that most celebrated archbishop of Mainz, apostle and martyr of Germany, whose precious death occurred in Frisia in the year of Christ 755, although some assign it to the preceding year, 754. His *Acts* are found among the distinguished Bollandists under 5 June. You therefore have the period in which this Theutramus flourished at Strasbourg; I leave the visions described by our poet to the judgment of sensible people.] at that time

Had died—the one whom that Sacer saw—

When he wished to break the iron hearts of the Frisians

With Christ’s teaching and give them the road to the heavenly kingdoms.

Alas, the diseased people soon killed their excellent physician

With its own wound, and thereby prepared kingdoms for him.

As he hastened to heaven, accompanied by a twin companion [Note: [Col. 0638D] I do not know whether this hints at a companion of Saint Boniface by this name, whom the *Acts* nevertheless do not mention, or rather at his brother, born with him in the same birth. In the supplement to the *Life of this holy man*, page 476 of Volume I of the *June Saints*, it is said: “After him his brother Habmunt the deacon also died.”],

[Col. 0639A] He will wish to visit your temples, Virgin Mary [Note: [Col. 0639B] For *voluit*, or perhaps *voluerit*.].

Great is your power in heaven and your authority on earth,

You who are able to give birth to the Father of the world.

Grant me, though undeserving, help; grant me healing

In my exile, whose threshold I often inhabit.

And if the fierce glory of the present age eludes me,

Under your guidance, gracious Virgin, I shall seek the heavenly kingdoms.

This work, Caesar, Ermoldus, an exile, poor and needy,

Offers you while the senseless hemlock croaks.

Lacking gifts, I bring a few songs to the powerful;

Free of wealth, I offer song.

Christ, who grips and adorns royal hearts with his hand,

Turns them in whatever directions he wishes.

[Col. 0639B] He who filled your heart above all with the flower of virtue,

[Col. 0640A] And caused it to overflow with piety,

May he grant that, illustrious king, you look more closely upon my cause,

Giving it a kindly hearing.

Perhaps you will learn from truthful words

That I am less guilty of the crime brought against me.

Yet do not think that I excuse myself for that guilt—

Unhappy man that I am, banished into exile [Note: [Col. 0639B] The manuscript is defective here; Lambecius supplied *illud*. In the same place it reads *exsilio* instead of *exsilium*.].

But I beg that the boundless mercy that loosens what is owed by the guilty

May remember my exile.

You too, Judith, most beautiful wife, worthy of him,

Who rightly share with him the heights of empire,

Grant help to the fallen; comfort the wretched man who has been struck down;

Raise up the one who is sinking; free the condemned man from prison.

May the Most High exalt, save, enrich, honor, and love you

[Col. 0640B] Through the many ages of the world. [Note: [Col. 0639B] After learned readers have read this poem, let them judge, I ask, whether P. Jacques Le Long was right or wrong to include our Ermoldus—whom he had never seen—in the class of fabulous writers of Frankish history, which he appended to his recently published and highly accurate catalogue on page 1099. If the argument is valid that Ermoldus wrote Louis’s life in metrical language—which is not valid, in view of Aristotle’s authority, since in his *Poetics* he teaches that historian and poet do not differ because one writes in bound meter and the other in prose, for history may be written either with meter or without it, but because one reports what has happened whereas the other reports what might or ought to happen—if, I say, that argument is valid, why should it not also classify the Saxon poet, a contemporary of Emperor Arnulf, who bound the life of Emperor Charlemagne into verse, and others among writers of narrow credibility, indeed among authors to be avoided?]

[Col. 0639]

IN THE YEARS OF THE LORD 824–827. EUGENIUS II, ROMAN PONTIFF.

[Col. 0639]

HISTORICAL ACCOUNT OF EUGENIUS II.

(From Mansi, *Amplissima Collectio Conciliorum*, p. 411.)

[Col. 0639C] [Note: [Col. 0639C] (a) Eugenius. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the year 824, Eugenius II was elected as Paschal’s successor amid such a schism that, to settle it, the emperor Louis sent his son Lothar to Rome. When Lothar had arrived in Rome and had been honorably received by Eugenius, “he corrected,” says the author of the *Life of Louis*, “the condition of the Roman people, long since corrupted by the perversity of certain prelates, through the pope’s aforementioned benevolent consent, in such a way that all who had been grievously despoiled by the seizure of their possessions were magnificently consoled by the restoration of their goods, which, through his arrival and by God’s gift, had been recovered.”

While he was in Rome, with the consent of the pope, who held the primary civil authority of the city, he issued a constitution concerning the papal election and the restoration of property. It is preserved in Sigonius, *On the Kingdom of Italy*, under the year 825, in the section on Louis, in these words:

“We decree that no one, whether free or enslaved, who might offer any impediment, dare come to the election of the pope, except only those Romans to whom the ancient custom of electing the pope was granted by the constitution of the holy Fathers. If anyone should dare to act against our command, let him be punished with exile.

“We decree that the entire Roman people be asked under what law they wish to live, so that they may live according to the law which they have professed that they wish to follow; and it shall be announced to them so that everyone may know this—dukes, judges, and the rest of the people alike. If they should act against that same law to their own detriment, they shall be subject, by the constitution of the pope and ourselves, to the law which they profess.

“Concerning the property of churches unjustly occupied on the pretext of having received permission from the pope, and concerning whatever has not yet been restored but was nevertheless seized without the authority of the popes, we decree that it be restored through our legates.

“We wish all judges—whether those who are to preside over all matters, or those through whom judicial authority is exercised in this city of Rome or ought to be exercised in the other provinces—to come into our presence. We wish to know their number and names and to admonish each one concerning the office entrusted to him.

“Finally, we admonish all men that, just as they desire to possess the grace of God and our favor, so they should show obedience and reverence in all things to this pope.”

At the beginning of Eugenius’s pontificate, an embassy was sent from Michael, emperor of the East, to Louis. “Among other matters,” say the Frankish annals in the *Life of Louis*, “pertaining to their embassy, they presented certain arguments concerning the veneration of images and said that they ought to go to Rome and consult the bishop of the apostolic see. After hearing their embassy and giving a reply, he ordered them to be led to Rome, as they said they wished.”

The envoys—if the booklet of the pseudo-synod of Paris is to be believed—reached Gaul in October, while the emperor Louis was on campaign against the Bretons. After hearing them in November and dismissing them, the emperor Louis joined to them his own envoys to the Roman pontiff. These were to ask not for permission to convene a synod, but only for permission to arrange some kind of meeting at which learned men might inquire into and debate among themselves the cult of images.

On Louis’s side, Jonas of Orléans carried out the embassy. In these times he wrote three books against Claudius the Iconoclast, a disciple of Felix. In the first he attacks the destruction of sacred images; in the second he defends the adoration of the holy cross against the same opponent; in the third he advocates and defends the veneration of the saints and the pilgrimage to Rome undertaken to the thresholds of the blessed apostles.

After the death of Theodore the Studite, who had followed the example of John the Baptist in fearlessly reproving sinners, the emperor Michael became more confident, married the nun Euphrosyne, and by this act brought himself, together with the entire Eastern Empire, into the utmost ruin.

The Danes were converted to the faith through the preaching of Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims. Crantzius, *Metropolis*, book I, chapter 9, [signature] SEV. BIN.]

Eugenius was a Roman by nationality, the son of Boemundus, [Col. 0640C] [Note: [Col. 0640D] (b) He occupied the see for four years. Baronius asserts that Eugenius occupied it for only three years, and that the four years assigned to Eugenius here are erroneous; he confirms this by the authority of Aimoinus and other writers of this period. ID.] and occupied the see for four [three] years, two months, [Col. 0641A] and twenty-three days.

For this venerable and distinguished man was possessed of great simplicity and humility. Learned in knowledge, outstanding in speech, handsome in appearance, generous to those who asked, and rejecting the world, he thought day and night only of what was pleasing to Christ.

During the time of this aforementioned pontiff, no small abundance spread throughout not only Rome but nearly the whole world. For whatever he received from his subjects by a just assessment, he distributed continually to everyone—not only to the poor and widows but also to the wealthy. In his days there was the greatest peace and rest throughout the Roman world. Since he himself was a friend of complete peace, what else did those under him do except what he himself practiced through his honorable conduct, and what they likewise practiced?

For he was archpresbyter of this most sacred and universal Church. In it he governed his office with great distinction for no brief period. Afterwards, on account of the pious report of his merits, he was elected by all the Romans and made pontiff after the death of the most holy lord Pope Paschal.

During the time of his presbyterate he held the church of the blessed martyr Sabina, situated on the Aventine Hill. By God’s dispensation, after the pontifical grace had been conferred upon him, he brought it to a better state of worship and adorned it everywhere with paintings.

In his days the Roman judges who were being held captive in Francia returned. He permitted them to enter the property of their parents and gave them no small amount of goods from the Lateran patriarchate, since they had been deprived of nearly all their resources.

In the aforementioned church of the blessed martyr Sabina he made a ciborium of the purest silver, weighing pounds . . . . . The same venerable prelate offered it in the place mentioned above.]

[Col. 0641]

DIPLOMA OF POPE EUGENIUS II. From the *Appendix of Various Diplomas of the Pontiffs of the Holy Roman Church*, published after the *Chronicle of Reichersberg* by Gewold at Munich in Bavaria in 1611.

[Col. 0641C] Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Rathfredus of the holy Church of Faviana; to Methodius of the Church of Speculum Julium, also called Soriguturensis; to Alewinus of the holy Church of Nitravia; and likewise to Anno, bishop of the Church of Vetuarum; and also to Tuttundus and Moymarus, dukes and nobles, and to the armies of the people of Hunnia, also called Avaria, and of Moravia.

Most beloved sons in Christ, desiring the salvation of your souls, when we heard of your most Christian way of life and of your progress in holy faith and good works, we were filled with the greatest joy and gladness. For, as the Apostle says, through the divine clemency working in you, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more”; and thus the holy Church of God in our times receives daily growth through your election.

The most reverend Yrolfus, archbishop of the holy Church of Lauriacum, and our most holy brother, but your spiritual father, was the herald of this desirable report. Through his holy preaching he has begotten you as adopted sons for God.

Accordingly, when he came to the thresholds of the apostles for the sake of prayer, he earnestly commended to us a new church to be formed by our apostolic blessings, since, with the Lord’s help, he had undertaken to govern it according to the Catholic faith.

For, as is certain from reading, in the time of the Romans and formerly of the Gepids, his predecessors had possessed by metropolitan right a diocese divided into seven episcopal parishes. By this justice and law, the aforementioned archbishop, most worthy of God, is bound by duty to scatter the heavenly seeds of life throughout that land, formerly Christian and entrusted to the care of his ancient predecessors, which you now possess as though it were an inheritance through the hidden judgment of almighty God; and, as an evangelical farmer, he is to raise again from you a fruitful harvest for the Lord Christ in the winning of souls.

Recognizing that this most learned minister of the divine oracle is in every respect necessary for your salvation, proven in faith and example, we rightly preserve toward him the apostolic judgment which says: “How will they believe without a preacher? And how will they preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10).

Therefore, from the holy Roman Church, our mother, we have sent you a governor together with him. In the aforementioned regions of Hunnia, also called Avaria, and likewise in the provinces of Moravia, Pannonia, and Moesia, we entrust to him and to his successors, by canonical authority, our apostolic representation and our diocese, together with the right to exercise ecclesiastical jurisdiction and the usage and power of his predecessors, namely the archbishops of the holy Church of Lauriacum. We confirm the decree of this constitution of ours by the privilege of our signature.

Moreover, according to ancient custom, we have given His Holiness the pallium. We have granted it in the same manner as our predecessors granted it to their predecessors, while preserving the full integrity of their privileges. Although we would have permitted this to his affection as a due right, because of your petitions—since you urgently requested this matter for his honor—we have further increased our apostolic representation and authority. This was never granted to his predecessors.

Thus you, his brothers and fellow bishops, may know that henceforth you are to show him greater reverence and obey, as wise sons, his sound teaching of heavenly instruction for your edification. And you, lay nobles and common people, should humbly obey his salutary commands, not as those of a man but as those of God, and remain steadfast in the Catholic faith which you have obtained through the Lord Jesus.

For the devil, the artificer of every deceit, whose dominion and pomps you renounce in baptism, suffers with displeasure the loss and injury caused by your salutary conversion. By sowing the weeds of unbelief on various occasions, he rages as though suffering a great wrong, and continually strives to make one of you turn his back on the holy profession.

Therefore, give kindly attention to the teachings of the aforementioned archbishop, your shepherd appointed by God. He instructs you to beware of Satan’s craftiness and to escape his eternal torments; and on the day of judgment he himself will present you before the Lord of the ages, to be rewarded with perpetual glory for your good works.

For the complete and necessary salvation of your instruction, however, as we have learned, the few bishops who have now been appointed do not suffice for you, since many are still detained there in the error of paganism, and, because of the shortage of heralds of the divine word, knowledge of Christ has not yet reached them.

Therefore, so that the number of the faithful may increase, let your diligence, for the reward and remission of your sins, provide assistance and support to the most reverend Archbishop Yrolfus, so that the number of the bishops formerly established there may be completed. If properly appointed, they can be useful both to you and to your descendants.

For the restoration of the churches, therefore, in the name of the Lord, from your possessions—which, as you know from widespread report, once served as the revenues and endowments of those churches—provide and bestow upon those same churches sufficient lasting resources. Let suitable men be chosen for this ministry, and let bishops be ordained especially in those places where opportunity and usefulness recommend it, and where the remains of churches and buildings demonstrate that episcopal sees once existed.

If not, we grant to his judgment and deliberation the determination of whom and where bishops are to be appointed, since we have entrusted our representation among you in all matters of ecclesiastical government to him.]

[Col. 0643D]

[Note: [Col. 0644C] A letter under the name of Pope Eugenius II, written by the pseudo-assembly of Paris to the emperor Michael concerning the veneration of images, appears in that pseudo-booklet of the Paris synod, which was published in 1595 by the Wechel printing house at Frankfurt without any mention of its author or of the place from which it had been taken. SEV. BIN.]

LETTER OF POPE EUGENIUS II TO BERNARD, ARCHBISHOP OF VIENNE.

[Col. 0643]

[Col. 0643C] Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the most reverend brother Bernard, archbishop of Vienne.

I rejoice greatly, because, although detained by certain matters, I have nevertheless received, out of the great love of the apostle Peter and of us, the letter of Your Holiness. Through it we have learned with admiration what kind of love you desire to exercise toward us. Therefore you must not be forgetful of us, since the affection of your love has taken up residence in our inmost heart.

And so, wherever you may have gone to carry out the business of your church, we desire that the right hand of Peter, the bearer of the keys, may surround and guide you.

Concerning the matter, dearest brother, which you took care to make known to us in your letter, we wish you to know that, as far as we were able, we searched for it through repeated reading in our archives. Whatever we found after the authority of Rome, and also in the Justinian law, we communicate to Your Holiness in our letters.

In chapter 511 of that same law we found the following:

“Let the *descriptio* [read *praescriptio*, ‘prescription,’ Hardouin] of forty years be suitably applied to venerable places; and let neither a prescription of twenty nor even of thirty years be applied to religious houses, but let only the period of forty years have force, not only in legacies and external property but also in sacred inheritances.”

Accordingly, through the tenor of our authority, which we send to your love, if the matter is as your letter has reported to us, do not doubt that it has been granted to your church. Likewise, know that your privilege has plainly been restored to you—the privilege which our predecessors granted to your see. For we ought to desire nothing other than what they established by unbreakable rules.

May almighty God always preserve the honor of you and your church from enemies.

Written by the hand of Agatho, notary and archivist, in the month of July, indiction 15. [Col. 0644D] [Note: [Col. 0644D] False indiction.]

Farewell.

Given on the eighth day before the Ides of July, by the hand of George, librarian of the holy apostolic see, while the most pious lord Augustus Louis was reigning, in the fourth year of his empire. [Note: [Col. 0644D] The year is false, since Eugenius began to occupy the see in the eleventh year of Louis.]

[Col. 0645]

[Note: [Col. 0645B] These decrees pertain for the most part to Eugenius III.] DECREES OF POPE EUGENIUS II FROM THE COUNCIL OF RHEIMS.

I.

We decree that anyone who knowingly presumes to associate with an excommunicated person, until he has been absolved by the one who excommunicated him or by another acting with the authority of the apostolic see, is himself to be held under sentence of excommunication.

II.

We order that it be observed that those who, being in the order of subdeacon or above, marry wives or keep concubines are to lose their ecclesiastical office and benefice.

III.

We establish that nuns and women who are called canonesses and live irregularly correct and amend their way of life for the better according to the Rule of the blessed Benedict and Augustine, and abandon extravagance and indecency in dress. If they do not fulfill this, then, if any one of them dies, she is to be denied Christian burial. We also prohibit anyone from being received into their communities unless she is going to live according to a rule.

IV.

We have decreed that laymen are not to presume to settle ecclesiastical affairs.

V.

By apostolic authority we prohibit any advocate from presuming to seize or usurp anything beyond his ancient right and benefice. If anyone attempts this, he is to be denied Christian burial.

VI.

[Col. 0646A]

No one is to be appointed dean or archdeacon unless he is a deacon or priest. If anyone should refuse to be ordained, he is to be deprived of the honor he has received.

VII.

We entirely prohibit, under anathema, the rash audacity of many who customarily come to the detestable fairs arranged for the display of their strength. If anyone should die there, penance and viaticum are not to be denied him; nevertheless, he is to be denied ecclesiastical burial.

VIII.

We have decreed that if anyone lays violent hands upon a cleric or monk, he shall be subject to anathema, and none of the bishops shall presume to absolve him, except in urgent danger of death, until he has been brought before the apostolic presence.

IX.

We renew the decree that if anyone, out of vengeance or hatred, sets fire to something or causes it to be set on fire, he is not to be absolved unless, according to his means, he has made good the damage he caused and swears that he will never again set fire to anything. Let penance also be imposed upon him, so that he may do penance for a year in Jerusalem or in Spain in the service of God.

X.

We order that no payment be demanded for receiving chrism, sacred oil, or burial.

XI.

We order that churches not be entrusted to hired priests.

[Col. 0645]

YEAR OF THE LORD 827. VALENTINUS, ROMAN PONTIFF.

[Col. 0645]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON POPE VALENTINUS.

(From Mansi, *Amplissima Collectio of Councils*, vol. XIV, p. 501.)

[Col. 0645D] [Note: [Col. 0645D] Valentinus. Almost all the Frankish annals, as I said above, attest that Eugenius died in the year 827. They disagree among themselves about the month in which he died. We therefore, following Anastasius, think that the beginning of Valentinus’s pontificate should be referred to the year of Christ 827 and to the eleventh of August. Anastasius reports that, on account of his distinguished virtues, he was made archdeacon by Pope Paschal after having been a subdeacon. Some say that he held the pontificate for forty days, others scarcely thirty. SEV. BIN.]

Valentinus was a Roman by nationality, the son of Peter, from the district of Via Lata. He occupied the see for forty days. This man remained filled with great holiness and great blessedness, and suffused with the grace of the Holy Spirit.

While he was in this Roman city, which by God’s authority retains the dignity of the supreme priesthood and royal excellence, he was born of freeborn and pious parents and was entrusted to an attentive teacher for the study of letters. He diligently explored the sacred writings of the divine law with a receptive and abundant understanding and retained them in the memory of his intellect.

As was fitting for a nobleman, he avoided the empty and disgraceful games of boys. He uttered no unsuitable or dishonorable tales from his own mouth, and engaged in no unlawful actions. From the very first flower of childhood he was devoted to pious modesty and sobriety, and, filled with the splendid spirit of divine inspiration, he kept his lips adorned amid every ornament of speech and wisdom. By the exceptional wealth of his language and the light-bearing merits of his deeds, he revealed the elegance of his bodily mind.

Especially, in accordance with the outstanding saying of the teacher of the nations, he showed himself to all without offense and offered himself with a kindly spirit. Causing no one the scandal of opposition, he earnestly sought to render to his neighbors the due service of perfect love. And, in accordance with the command of the Lord’s voice, he kept his loins girded with chastity and carried burning lamps in his hands—shining brightly in speech and likewise radiant in the judgment of his conduct and teaching, with a magnificent example.

[Col. 0647B] With the virtue of God from above assisting him, when he had fully entered upon maturity and the favor of his goodness and prudence was spreading far and wide like the fragrance of incense, this report reached the ears of the most blessed prelate, the lord Paschal of revered memory, through the truthful account of the faithful. When he had learned, as the people praised him, that Valentinus was truly distinguished and renowned in all things, he immediately advanced him through the ecclesiastical orders to the honor of the subdiaconate from the Lateran palace and ordered him to serve him.

Recognizing his manner of life, patience, and character, Paschal loved him greatly above the others. The aforementioned man, with divine grace from above favoring him, to which he had devoted himself with complete mental devotion and integrity of virtue, shone with the light of truth and wisdom.

[Col. 0647C] He was affable in speech, distinguished in learning, conspicuous in appearance, modest among his brothers in pious devotion, and faithful to his neighbors. Supported by a prudent heart, he did not entangle himself in any affairs that might cause anyone even slight sorrow.

Furthermore, when the aforementioned pontiff observed him, together with so many virtues and such great merits of his deeds, adorned with an elegant and outstanding bodily form, he consecrated him as a levite of his apostolic see. Because of the merit of his life, which shone splendidly, and because he was loved with great affection by the entire people of the Church and by the illustrious Roman people gathered together, he bestowed upon him many goods and benefices in abundance, and afterwards made him archdeacon.

When that pontiff, at Christ’s command, ascended to the heavenly heights, Eugenius was raised by all to pontifical honor and placed upon the apostolic see. Recognizing that Valentinus was splendidly adorned with all the virtues we have mentioned, Eugenius kept him throughout his life in the place of a beloved companion and rejoiced in him with his heart as a father rejoices in his own son; he desired him to remain continually in his presence.

When the appointed span of this prelate’s passing light had been completed and divinely brought to an end, the entire Roman assembly prayed to the Lord with frequent fasts and prayers at the summit of the sacred see, asking that he might deign to reveal to their minds who was worthy of the honor of so great a see.

But could the divine majesty, now appeased, show by the hidden sign of its power anyone else to be chosen from the list of priests except him whom it had adorned from his mother’s breasts with all the virtues mentioned above and with the fairest flowering of learning, and whom it had nurtured as a steadfast and faithful disciple in all things? Surely it was to him that it would entrust the governance of the most sacred see.

Accordingly, when the venerable bishops, the glorious nobles of the Romans, and the entire population of the great city had assembled together in the Lateran palace, so that what all already held equally revealed in their hearts from heaven might resound in the single voice of the many, they loudly acclaimed with one accord: “Valentinus, the most holy archdeacon of the apostolic see, is worthy; Valentinus is to be adorned with the insignia of the supreme pontificate.”

[Col. 0648B] After these honey-sweet words, all remaining together in a single bond of peace immediately hurried to the church of the holy Mother of God, our Lady, ever-virgin Mary. There, the sacred clergy and the Roman nobles, together with the people, found him giving the Lord manifold thanks and praises according to custom.

Although he resisted greatly and for a long time, vigorously declaring that he was unfit for so great a government, he was nevertheless elected to the papal see by the joyful voices of the gracious populace and of both orders of the Roman soldiery. Then he was led by them to the Lateran patriarchate with fitting praises of glory and great honor and was placed upon the pontifical throne.

After the entire Roman senate had joyfully kissed his feet and everything that had to be completed had been performed properly and reverently, great sobriety and great joy prevailed among people of every sex and age. When the day of his consecration had already dawned clear, all the Romans together led the aforementioned bishop from the palace, with lights, to the church of the blessed Peter, prince of the apostles. There, with the help of the divine majesty, they consecrated him as supreme pontiff upon the high throne.

Having immediately ascended the heights of the beneficent see of the blessed apostle Peter, bearer of the keys of the heavenly kingdom, he returned to the palace amid the great joy of a splendid and magnificent gathering of Romans, after piously offering divine praises and sacrifices to God. After taking sumptuous meals, he enriched the sacred clergy, senate, and Roman people with many and various gifts of his loving generosity. For he was renowned for liberality, outstanding in action, eloquent in speech, close to all in compassion, and eager to provide timely consolation to those enduring poverty.

Adorned with these manifold virtues, when Christ called him to the heavenly realms, he passed through a precious death, overcome by bodily illness, and ascended joyfully into the presence of the supreme Majesty with the desirable fruit of a most blessed work, reigning and rejoicing with the Lord forever.

[Col. 0649]

YEAR OF THE LORD 831. HALITGAR, BISHOP OF CAMBRAI.

[Col. 0649C]

HISTORICAL NOTICE ON HALITGAR.

(From Leglay, [Note: [Col. 0649D] The most learned Leglay compiled *Christian Cambrai* in 1849. The most illustrious librarian will not be displeased that we have drawn the historical notice on Halitgar from *Christian Cambrai*. EDIT.] *Christian Cambrai*.)

[Col. 0649A] Halitgar, or Halitcharius, began his episcopal office in the year 817. In the following year, at the request of Elefantus, whom King Charles the Great, his relative, had placed in charge of the monastery of Cellensis, or Saint-Ghislain, he consecrated an oratory, in which he lay, recently built in a more honorable manner. This provided the occasion for raising the sacred body from the earth.

“For when the bishop came,” it says, “he declared that it ought not to be blessed—the oratory—while the body of some saint or certain relics of the saints remained inside . . . . . Thus the basilica was blessed in honor of the apostles Peter and Paul and the other saints, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the time of King Louis, son of the illustrious Charles. Afterwards, when the abbot asked the bishop what ought to be done with the sacred body, the bishop is said to have replied: ‘Let the saint rest there until God’s mercy deigns to make his merits more clearly known to all people.’”

In the year 822, Ebbo, archbishop of Rheims, went to Rome and obtained from Pope Paschal permission to preach the Gospel to the northern peoples, together with Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai. Accordingly, at the beginning of this year, having taken a companion, “with the counsel of the emperor Louis and the authority of Paschal, Roman pontiff, he went as far as the borders of the Danes for the purpose of preaching and baptized many of them who came to the faith,” says Flodoard.

The annalist of Lorsch relates that Ebbo returned to Gaul in the same year and was present at the assembly of Compiègne in November; he is silent, however, about Halitgar’s return. It is nevertheless probable that Halitgar did not leave the company of his metropolitan. Writers of those times report that Ebbo shortly afterwards undertook another journey for the purpose of preaching the faith.

After Halitgar’s return, he permitted the raising of Saint Ursmar, abbot of Lobbes, from his old tomb. In the year 825, Halitgar was present at the assembly held at Paris concerning the veneration of sacred images. He was one of those who collected the opinions of the Fathers on the veneration of images, which he and Amalarius, archbishop of Trier, collected with excessive haste and brought to Louis Augustus, as the emperor himself teaches at the beginning of his memorandum:

“Halitgar and Amalarius, bishops, came into our presence on the eighth day before the Ides of December, bringing collections from the books of the holy Fathers which you collected at the assembly held at Paris.”

In the year 828 the same emperor sent him as ambassador to Constantinople with Ansfrid, abbot of Nonantula, to Michael Augustus. These envoys were honorably received, as those who committed the deeds of Louis the Pious to writing teach us. We think that they were sent to confirm the treaty between the two emperors, which Michael’s envoys had recently requested from Louis at Compiègne.

In the year 829 he attended the council held at Paris on the eighth day before the Ides of June by the bishops of the provinces of Belgica Secunda and Lugdunensis Secunda, Tertia, and Quarta, for the correction and reform of Christian morals, especially those of ecclesiastical men, kings, and princes.

In the year 831 he attended the translation of Saint Moabulus, formerly a disciple of Saint Fursa. Halitgar himself and Achard, bishop of Noyon, transferred his body to the basilica of Saint Peter. On this matter see Mabillon, *Benedictine Centuries*, book II, and the *Annals* under the year 650, no. 4.

He died in the same year, 831, on June 25, and was buried in the monastery of Mount Saint Eligius. He was distinguished not only by his excellent achievements but also by his writings. In particular, he wrote a work on vices and virtues, remedies for sins, and the order or judgments of penance, completed in six books.

Canisius published the first five books in volume V, part II; they are also read in volume XIV of the *Library of the Fathers*, p. 906. The sixth, which is the penitential book of the Roman Church, was inserted into Canisius’s supplement, prepared by Stevartius, and is found among the notes of Dom Hugh Menard on the *Book of the Sacraments of Saint Gregory the Great*, volume III of the new edition of his works.

[Col. 0649]

J. BASNAGE’S OBSERVATION ON HALITGAR’S SUBSEQUENT PENITENTIAL BOOK.

[Col. 0649D] I. The use of penitential booklets was frequent in the centuries of the Middle Ages. Books are called penitentials when they explain the penalties to be inflicted for each crime according to the canons.

When the Decian persecution raged, some Christians who had lapsed hastened back to communion, while others scarcely grieved over the idolatry they had committed. When peace had been restored, the bishops assembled and weighed a remedy with salutary moderation, so that peace would neither be entirely denied to the lapsed nor evangelical discipline dissolved. For this reason, the letters of Cyprian form, as it were, a penitential book.

Morinus considers the earlier penitentials much older, because he believes that the Apostolic Canons were either composed in earlier times or produced by the apostles themselves. This is entirely untrue.

When barbarians were devastating Pontus, Christians had committed heinous crimes together with them. Gregory Thaumaturgus was consulted about this matter and sent them a letter instructing them in the methods of penance.

After the persecution of Diocletian had ceased, the same necessity demanded that bishops or councils enact new laws. Peter of Alexandria did this; afterwards the Council of Ancyra was followed by other decrees of Basil and of councils, observed in various ways according to the custom of the churches. Nevertheless, no penitential book had been sanctioned by public authority.

II. In the seventh century, as the old discipline was weakening, other laws had to be promulgated. Bede, or Egbert, bishop of York, attempted this; Theodore of Canterbury, who understood Greek because he was Greek, accomplished the same task.

But perhaps those earlier books, which were used by the English, were also desired by others, especially by the Gauls. In the ninth century the Gallic priests possessed booklets according to whose standard penitents were punished.

Nevertheless, the judgments concerning penitents in the booklets of the priests were so confused, and so diverse, contradictory, and unsupported by any authority, that they could scarcely be distinguished [Note: [Col. 0651C] Ebbo, letter to Halitgar, below.]

This necessity moved Ebbo, a man exceedingly distinguished at that time, to urge his friend Halitgar, bishop of Cambrai, to copy the canons of the ancients and compose, as it were, a new penitential, lest the Church be disturbed while priests—often inexperienced—made different judgments concerning one and the same sin.

Halitgar therefore composed this work for the benefit of his friend and of the Church.

III. It is scarcely possible to determine the year in which he wrote it. Morinus maintains that he published the work before or around 830, because Ebbo was then deposed on account of his abominable conspiracy against the emperor Louis.

There was another most compelling argument: Halitgar had died in 831, whereas he had been promoted to the episcopate in 816. Supported by this reasoning, we think that the work was published much earlier than the most learned man believed.

In 823 Halitgar went to the Danes with Ebbo for the purpose of propagating the religion; in the same year he returned and attended the assembly at Compiègne. [Col. 0652A] In 825, as a delegate of the Paris synod, he collected the opinions of the Fathers concerning images. In that same year, or perhaps the preceding one, he excerpted the canons concerning penance at the urging of Ebbo of Rheims, with whom he was joined in friendship.

At least, he could scarcely have worked on it later. For from that time onward Louis sent him to the East, to Michael, emperor of the Greeks. He returned from there in 829 and died in 831. Therefore he could not have devoted himself to this little work around the year 835.

IV. Both Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, book II, chapter 19, and Baldric, in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, testify that Halitgar elaborated six books *On Vices and Virtues*. But the sixth book was missing from all the manuscripts, and therefore Canisius published only five.

After the publication of his *Ancient Readings*, however, Stewart came upon that sixth book, containing the Roman Penitential, and published it with a preface by Halitgar. Menard and Morinus later published it as well, and we have placed it at the end of Halitgar’s work, drawing on Stewart and Morinus.

But whether that book was genuinely copied by Halitgar, we reasonably doubt; for he himself professes that he published five books.

V. In his earlier books Halitgar has precepts of the greatest usefulness for virtue. But, in keeping with the custom of those centuries, he produces nothing from himself. All those statements which he gathered into one collection were compiled from the writings of the ancients.

VI. It contains the Roman Penitential, certain laws intended for the punishment of sinners. Yet I scarcely believe that it is a genuine Penitential of the Roman Church. At least no one will deny that very much was added to it in Halitgar’s time, since more recent writers mention certain matters that are not found in it. Nor should one say that Halitgar abbreviated a larger work; the text does not suggest this, but rather that he copied a penitential book such as he had taken from the archives of the Roman Church. Moreover, the codex from which this sixth book of Halitgar was extracted, according to Morinus, who had carefully examined it, is not more than five hundred years old; hence further doubts arise concerning the authority of that book. Finally, it praises forged decretals, which had then begun to come to light.

[Col. 0651]

# HALITGAR, BISHOP OF CAMBRAI: FIVE BOOKS ON VICES AND VIRTUES AND ON THE ORDER OF PENITENTS

*(In Galland, Bibliotheca veterum Patrum, vol. XIII, p. 521.)*

## In the name of the Lord

To the most reverend brother and son in Christ, HALITGAR, bishop, EBO, an unworthy bishop, sends greetings.

I do not doubt that your Charity knows how greatly we are constrained by concern for ecclesiastical discipline, by the many needs of our subjects, and, beyond this, by the oppressions of worldly affairs with which we are daily troubled. [Col. 0652D] For this reason, although I discussed it with you, I was quite unable to extract from the sayings of the Fathers and also from the judgments of the canons a Penitential for the work of our fellow priests, because the mind, when divided among many things, becomes less capable of attending to each one. This in particular causes me great anxiety: the judgments concerning penitents in the little works of our priests are so confused, so diverse, [Col. 0653A] mutually inconsistent, and supported by no authority, that they can scarcely be distinguished because of their discord. Consequently, those who resort to the remedy of penance are in no way able to help them, both because of the confusion of the books and because of the slowness of their understanding.

Therefore, dearest brother, do not deny us yourself—you who have always flourished with a fervent spirit in divine disciplines and with diligent care in meditating upon the Scriptures, enjoying the most perfect leisure. I ask you: take up, without a word of excuse, the burden of this task, imposed upon you by me, but to be made light by the Lord, whose burden is easy. Do not fear or dread the magnitude of this work, but approach it confidently, because he will be with you who said: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it.” For you know very well that small things suffice for the small, and that a crowd of poor people cannot approach the table of the great. [Col. 0653B] Do not withhold from us the knowledge of your devotion. Do not put the lamp kindled within you under a bushel; rather, set it upon a lofty lampstand, so that it may shine for all your brothers who are in the house of God. Bring forth for us, like a learned scribe, what you have received from the Lord.

His grace will be with you along the road of this labor—he who, when two disciples were traveling, added himself as a third companion on the road and opened their understanding so that they might comprehend the holy Scriptures. May the Spirit, the Paraclete, cause your heart to shine with every teaching of truth and with perfect knowledge of charity, dearest brother. Farewell.

To the lord and venerable father in Christ, EBBO, archbishop, HALITGAR, the least servant of Christ, sends greetings.

After I received, venerable Father, the letters of Your Beatitude, in which you deigned to urge me not to submit the keenness of my mind to idle and sluggish leisure, but to devote myself watchfully each day to the knowledge and meditation of sacred Scripture, and, in addition, to gather into a single volume a Penitential from the judgments of the holy Fathers and of the canons, this command also seemed harsh, very difficult, and terrifying to me: that I should undertake this burden, which I know has been abandoned by prudent men. I resisted your will at length, not with insolent stubbornness, but warned by awareness of my own weakness. For I considered it necessary, out of this concern, to suspend myself for a while from the rashness of writing. But just as I understood the difficulty of the task imposed, so also did I recognize the authority of the one imposing it; and I neither wished nor ought entirely to resist. I was certain that the dignity of your command would assist my weakness far more than the difficulty of my ignorance would weigh me down. Farewell.

# PREFACE ON THE USEFULNESS OF PENANCE

[Col. 0653]

[Col. 0653C] Although it is truly believed that, in the gift of baptism, all original sins are abolished by the grace of the Mediator—for that spiritual regeneration alone is sufficient—nevertheless, when one reaches the age that already receives a command and can be subjected to the authority of the law, war must be undertaken against vices and fought fiercely, lest one be brought back again to damnable sins.

Very few are so fortunate that, from the beginning of adolescence, they commit no damnable sins—whether in shameful acts, crimes, murders, or the error of some unspeakable impiety. Yet, through the great generosity of the Spirit, it is necessary to suppress whatever carnal pleasure can or could dominate within them. Vices are then to be considered conquered when they are overcome by the love of God—whom no one gives except God himself, and in no other way than through the Mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, who became a sharer in our mortality in order to make us sharers in his divinity.

Nevertheless, in the grievous yoke laid upon the sons of Adam, from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all, this evil too is miserably found. Therefore let us be sober and understand that this life has been made punitive for us because of that most unspeakable sin committed in paradise, and that everything done with us concerns nothing except the inheritance of the new age, so that, having received the pledge here, we may in its proper time obtain that of which this is the pledge.

But how the children of God, so long as they live mortally, struggle with death, and are thus stirred by the Spirit of God and, as children of God, advance toward the Lord—yet also, burdened by corruptible flesh and as children of human beings, fail in certain human impulses and thereby sin—this is a matter of distinction. For there is a great difference: not every sin is a crime, but every crime is a sin. Thus the life of holy people, which is lived in this death, can be found without crime, but never without sin, as it is said: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” Scripture, however, customarily uses one term for the other.

In the practice of penance, when a crime has been committed such that the person who committed it is separated from the body of Christ, the measure of time should not be considered so much as the measure of sorrow, for “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.” Since, however, one person’s sorrow of heart is often hidden from another, periods of penance are rightly established by those who preside over the churches, so that satisfaction may also be made to the Church, in which sins are forgiven.

Therefore, when the wound of sin is so great that the remedies of the body and blood of the Lord must be postponed, each person must, by the authority of the bishop, withdraw from the altar in order to perform penance and be reconciled by that same authority. For it is to receive the body and blood of the Lord unworthily if one receives them at a time when one ought to be doing penance.

Indeed, when the cause is such that penance ought to be performed according to the custom of the Church, penance is often not performed because of weakness: shame too is fear of displeasing, when a person’s reputation pleases him more than the justice by which he humbles himself in penitence. Let whoever he is remember that “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” What is more perverse or more wretched than not being ashamed of the wound itself, which cannot be concealed, but being more ashamed of the bandage?

Let no one suppose that he ought therefore to despise the salutary counsel of this penance because he notices and knows that he approaches the sacraments of the altar while he is not unaware that he retains such crimes within himself. Many are corrected, like Peter; many are tolerated, like Judas. Many are unknown until the Lord comes and “brings to light the things hidden in darkness and reveals the thoughts of hearts.”

We cannot, however, prohibit anyone from communion, although this prohibition is not yet deadly but medicinal, unless the person has either confessed voluntarily or has been accused and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical judgment. Many, however, observe that numerous people in ecclesiastical offices themselves—their superiors and ministers—do not live in accordance with the words and sacraments that they administer to the people.

O wretched human beings, who, by looking at these men, forget Christ! [Note: [Col. 0655D] Perhaps: “those who look at these men, or at others.”] He himself long before foretold that the law of God should rather be obeyed than that people should imitate those who say things but do not do them; and, although he tolerated his betrayer to the end, he sent him even to evangelize with the others.

Perhaps some despairing person will say: “I, already baptized in Christ, from whom all my former sins were forgiven, have become vile, repeatedly returning to my ways, and have become, in the eyes of God, a horrible dog returning to its vomit. Where shall I go from his spirit, and where shall I flee from his face?” Where, brother, except to his mercy through repentance—to whose power you showed contempt by sinning? Whatever you have done, whatever you have sinned, you are still alive; otherwise he would entirely remove you if he did not wish to heal you.

It is therefore necessary to approach penance with complete confidence and to believe with faith, without hesitation, that sins can be abolished by penance, even if one repents of sins committed in one’s final breath and exposes them through public lamentation. For God’s purpose, by which he decreed to save what had perished, stands immovable. Therefore, because his will does not change, whether through a reformed life, if time is granted, or through humble confession, if life is immediately cut short, forgiveness of sins should confidently be hoped for from him who does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that the sinner turn away from perdition through repentance and, saved by God’s mercy, live. The keys of the Church are utterly certain and completely trustworthy: whatever is loosed on earth is promised to be loosed also in heaven.

These things have been said about public satisfaction, by which a person humbles himself not only before the Church, which possesses the key of the kingdom of heaven and in which the remission of sins takes place.

[Col. 0656A] I do not deny that mortal crimes may also be absolved through secret satisfaction, provided that the secular clothing is first changed, and that, through correction of life, unceasing—indeed perpetual—mourning, and the mercy of God, one acts contrary to the things of which one repents. Daily and lighter sins, without which this life is not lived, are cleansed by the Lord’s Prayer, which begins: “Our Father, who art in heaven,” and so forth. There we say: “Forgive us our debts,” because it is itself an almsgiving to forgive a person who asks forgiveness. Hence the Lord says: “Give alms, and everything is clean for you.”

There are therefore many kinds of almsgiving by which, when we practice them, we are helped so that our sins may be forgiven. Yet none is greater than this: when we forgive from the heart whatever each person has sinned against us.

There are certain sins that are thought extremely light, unless the Scriptures showed them to be more serious than people suppose. Who would think that someone who says to his brother “Fool” is liable to Gehenna, unless the Truth said so? Or who would judge it a very great sin to observe days, months, years, and seasons—as do those who, on particular days, months, or years, wish or do not wish to begin something—unless the Apostle said: “I fear that I may have labored over you in vain”?

How many other sins there are—whether in speaking about the affairs and business of others, which do not concern you; or in empty laughter; or in the very foods prepared for the necessities of this life, in which appetite is too greedy; or in selling and buying goods, where the desires of charity and usefulness are perverted.

There are also other sins of this kind, committed through offenses in speech and in thought, as the apostle James says: “For we all offend in many things.” We ought daily and repeatedly to entreat the Lord and say: “Forgive us our debts,” and not lie in what follows: “As we also forgive our debtors.” For these sins too, let us not cease, according to our strength, to offer sacrifices of almsgiving and fasting.

For those sins, therefore, which the Decalogue contains, and about which the Apostle says that neither the greedy, nor the rapacious, nor adulterers, nor men who lie with males, and so forth—for those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God—the discipline of penance must be undertaken in which each person ought to exercise greater severity toward himself, so that, judged by himself, he may not be judged by the Lord.

This discipline of penance will be perfect and acceptable if a person raises a tribunal against himself in his mind and sets himself before his own face, so that what God threatens the sinner may not later happen to him. Once judgment has thus been established in the heart, accusing thought, conscience as witness, and fear as executioner should be present; then the blood of the confessing soul should flow forth in tears. Finally, in his conscience he should judge himself unworthy [Col. 0657A] of participation in the body and blood of the Lord.

Let the image of the future judgment be placed before his eyes, so that, when others approach the altar of God while he himself does not, he may consider how dreadful is the punishment by which, while some receive eternal life, others are driven into eternal death.

The canons do not set out the measure of time for performing penance with sufficient precision for each individual crime, but rather decree that it should be left to the judgment of the bishop, because before God the measure of sorrow has greater force than the measure of time. Nor is it merely abstinence from food, but rather the mortification of vices.

For this reason they prescribe that the periods of penance be shortened according to the faith and conduct of penitents, and extended because of negligence. Nevertheless, the canons contain prescribed forms of penance for certain faults, according to which other faults are to be assessed, since through these same forms it is easy to estimate the penalty and censure of the canons.

Let no one suppose that this letter is mine, lest it become worthless to him because of the insignificance of my name. [Col. 0658A] Rather, let him know that it has been collected by our predecessors from the judgments of the saints and excerpted by me, so that its excessive length might not generate boredom in negligent readers.

We place first, after this preface—which we have excerpted—a little book on the eight principal vices and their remedies, which we have excerpted from the books of Gregory, Augustine, and Prosper.

The second little book contains a few chapters on the active and contemplative life, as well as the names of the principal virtues. These too have been collected from the sayings of the holy Fathers. We have placed in the margins the names of the authors whose judgments they are, [Note: [Col. 0657B] In the manuscript the names of the authors are given, but not citations of books or chapters, which we have added in some places. CANISIUS.] in order to avoid the excessive length of repeating their names and so that no envious person might call us a compiler. [Col. 0658B]

The third concerns the order of penitents, with the names of the councils from which it was taken.

The fourth concerns the judgments of laypeople.

The fifth concerns the orders of the clergy and their rules, should they deviate.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0657]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Eight Principal Vices and Their Origins

[Col. 0657C]

After the human race was expelled from the joys of paradise, eight criminal vices have, by origin, held dominion over the sons of Adam. [Note: [Col. 0657D] Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, in his letter to the clergy; Evagrius to Anatolius, Book *On the Eight Vicious Thoughts*; St. Nilus, Book *On the Eight Vicious Affections*, [Col. 0658D] and others enumerate eight principal vices.] We must by no means believe that they can be abolished except through the grace of the Savior and the renewal of baptism. Hence blessed [Note: [Col. 0658D] Gregory the Great, on chapter 39 of Job, Book 31 of the *Moralia*, chapter 17.] Gregory speaks in his exposition of Job:

“Those tempting vices which wage an invisible war against us fight under the banner of the opposing pride above them. Some advance like commanders; others follow like an army.” [Note: [Col. 0658D] Saint Gregory; the Roman edition reads “reigning.”]

For pride itself, the queen of vices, as soon as it has completely seized a conquered heart, immediately hands it over to the seven principal vices, as though to certain commanders of its own, to be ravaged by them. The army then follows these commanders, [Col. 0657D] because from them, without doubt, arise the troublesome multitudes of vices. We shall show this more clearly if, as far as we can, we enumerate and set forth the commanders and the armies themselves.

Pride is indeed the root of every evil, concerning which Scripture attests: “Pride is the beginning of every sin.” From this poisonous root the seven principal vices also spring, namely: vainglory, envy, sadness, avarice, gluttony of the belly, and lust. Because our Redeemer grieved that we had been taken captive by these seven vices of pride, he came to the battle of spiritual liberation filled with the Spirit of sevenfold grace. Yet each of these has its own army against us.

From vainglory arise disobedience, boasting, hypocrisy, quarrels, obstinacy, discord, and presumptuous innovations.

From envy arise hatred, whispering, detraction, rejoicing in one’s neighbor’s misfortunes, and distress at his prosperity.

From anger arise quarrels, swelling of mind, insults, shouting, indignation, and blasphemies.

From sadness arise malice, resentment, faintheartedness, despair, sluggishness concerning the commandments, and wandering of the mind toward unlawful things.

From avarice arise betrayal, fraud, deceit, perjury, [Col. 0658D] and restlessness; and, contrary to mercy, hardness of heart.

From gluttony of the belly arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, uncleanness, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding.

From lust arise blindness of mind, lack of consideration, inconstancy, rashness, self-love, hatred of God, attachment to the present age, and horror of—or despair concerning—the future.

Since, therefore, the seven principal vices produce such a multitude of vices from themselves, when they come to the heart they drag along, as it were, the bands of a following army. Of these seven, five are spiritual and two carnal. Yet each is joined to the others by such kinship that one always proceeds from another.

The first offspring of pride is vainglory. When it has corrupted the oppressed mind, it immediately gives birth to envy. For, while it desires the power of a celebrated name, it wastes away lest someone else should be able to attain it.

Envy also generates anger. The more deeply the mind is wounded by the inner injury of jealousy, the more completely it loses the tranquility of gentleness. And because it is like a painful limb being touched, the hand of an opposing action is felt as though pressing it more heavily.

From anger sadness also arises. For the disturbed mind is confused by the very movement with which it agitates itself. Once it has lost the sweetness of tranquility, nothing nourishes it except the sorrow that follows from disturbance.

Sadness in turn is directed toward avarice. When the confused heart has lost the good of joy within, it seeks outside itself something by which it may be consoled. The more it lacks an inward joy to which it may return, the more eagerly it desires to acquire external goods.

After these, the two carnal vices remain: gluttony of the belly and lust. It is clear to everyone that lust is born from gluttony of the belly, since the genital organs appear to be attached to the belly in the distribution of the limbs. [Note: [Col. 0659D] Saint Gregory; “joined beneath.”] Thus, when one is improperly nourished, the other is undoubtedly aroused to shameful acts.

The commanders are rightly said to encourage, while the armies are said to howl: the first vices enter the deceived mind as though according to some rational design, but the countless vices that follow, as they drag along both this vice and every madness, overwhelm it with something like a bestial cry.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the Vice of Pride

Let us therefore consider what causes precede and what vices follow. Prosper says: [Note: [Col. 0659D] Prosper, Book 3, *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 2.] “To make this seem more credible, let the divine Scripture, when consulted, give its answer.” He then brings forth the answer he sought, saying: “Pride is the beginning of every sin.” Not of some sin, but of every sin. How could it be not only itself a sin, [Col. 0659D] but also the case that no sin can be, could have been, or will be committed without it? For every sin is nothing other than contempt of God, by which his commandments are trampled underfoot.

Finally, the devil himself, the inventor of pride, fell from the heavenly places through it, although God had made him without any sin. And this is the cause of all evils. Hence the first human being, corrupted by the elevation of the proud spirit, subjected all his posterity, which was radically present in him, to the necessity of corruption and mortality. Concerning this the Apostle said: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed into all human beings.” [Col. 0660A] A proud will causes God’s commandments to be despised, and it turned angels into demons.

Therefore let the proud hear this: all the things they seek are transitory, while the things they lose are eternal. Also: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.” And again: “Why is earth and ashes proud?” And: “Before destruction the spirit is exalted.” And: “God knows the high from afar.” Concerning their leader, the devil, it is also written: “He is king over all the sons of pride.”

[Note: [Col. 0660D] The following is from Prosper, Book 3 of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 8.]

“Now let us see by what signs pride can be detected.” A little later he continues:

“Dress and the manner of walking also reveal the proud: their raised neck, grim face, fierce eyes, and frightening speech loudly proclaim naked pride. They confuse human and divine laws; they swell with honors, seize what belongs to others, and, corrupted by the disease of pride, do not understand themselves. There is also a hidden pride that secretly captures those who have made some progress. By a deceitful exercise of domination it casts them into the depths of evil and continually tramples them down, so that they may never be able to rise.

“Thus those whom the festering corruption of a proud mind has infected do not observe the commands of their elders but judge them. When rebuked for their negligence, they either rebel or murmur. They detract from the higher position, desire to be preferred to their betters, boldly vaunt their own opinions, and do not preserve reverence in obedience. These are the signs of the swelling of pride, by which God is offended and by which the devil, nourished by these evils, rejoices.” [Col. 0660C]

## CHAPTER THREE. On the Remedy for Pride

Humility, the mother of all virtues, utterly crushes pride, as Scripture testifies: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted.” And: “Humility precedes glory.” And again: “Upon whom shall I look, except upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” And: “God looks upon the humble.” [Note: [Col. 0660D] Something similar is found in Saint Gregory, Book 32 of the *Moralia on Job*, chapter 27.]

Hence Gregory says: “Let this be said to the humble: by casting themselves down, they rise to the likeness of God.” And: “What is higher than humility? By lowering itself into the depths, it is joined to its Creator, who remains above all things.”

There is, however, another matter that must be carefully considered in them, because they are often deceived by the appearance of humility. Some are misled by ignorance of their own exaltation. Therefore everyone must be vigilant, so that the stain of pride may be wiped away by showers of tears, and so that contrition of heart and a humble spirit may exclude every source of vices.

Whoever has inflicted injury upon his neighbors should reconcile himself to them by satisfaction and forgiveness. Whoever has taken away the goods of the poor should wash away the theft through the mercy of generosity, and should mercifully return, if he can, whatever he unjustly took from those whom he injured. Moreover, he should by no means neglect the fruits of almsgiving. By correcting his life through other good works, he should diligently seek the mercy of the Lord, [Col. 0661A] as it is written: “Have mercy on your soul, pleasing God.”

For this reason the canons do not prescribe a fixed measure of time for performing penance for each crime, but rather establish that it should be left to the judgment of the bishop. For before the Lord the measure of sorrow has greater force than the measure of time, and the mortification of vices matters more than abstinence from food alone.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On the Vice of Vainglory

[Note: [Col. 0661D] Gregory.]

Vainglory is accustomed to exhort a conquered heart as though with reason, saying: “You ought to seek greater things, so that, by whatever power you wish, you may surpass many and thereby be able to benefit even more people.” But Scripture, on the contrary, reveals the sign of vanity when it says:

[Note: [Col. 0661D] This is from Prosper, Book 3 of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 10.]

“For there is a certain inflated vanity concerning the pleasures of a languishing mind: eager for honor yet ignorant of how to possess it; puffed up by the disease of empty excellence; hollow, diseased, turbulent; mistress of shallow minds; flattering toward all who are badly founded; smoky toward those who resist; seductive toward those who can be captured; invincible over those who have been captured. It is a kind of imitation of virtues, [Note: [Col. 0661D] Prosper: ‘the soul of vices, the source of carnal pleasures, the stain of morals, the desire for dignities.’] a desire for dignities, sweet to the wretched and bitter to the perfected.

“The inflated serve it; the exalted lie beneath it. They shamefully boast of works of which they themselves are not conscious. They wickedly desire to be praised by everyone. By their own disparagement they diminish holy men. [Note: [Col. 0661D] Prosper: ‘by comparison.’] Vanity overwhelms these and similar people when it has soothed them, and does not allow them either to feel their disease or to come to the physician.

“And what is it to come to the physician except for a sick person to recognize his illnesses? Yet the fire of human praise inflames them so greatly that they willingly undertake and diligently perform laborious works which the people may admire and through which their fame may spread. Thus they fast, abstain, keep vigils, attend church, or sing psalms—although they do none of these things without labor, they do them even with pleasure—so that they may be seen by human beings, whom they desire to please, rather than by God.” [Note: [Col. 0662D] Up to this point from Prosper.]

Hence the Truth says: “Truly I tell you, they have received their reward.”

## CHAPTER FIVE. On the Remedy for Vainglory

The apostolic statement must be brought forward here: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” The medicine of salvation for this disease is remembrance of divine goodness, through which all the good things that we seem to possess have been bestowed upon us.

There is also the perpetual love of God himself. We ought to do everything for his praise, whatever good we accomplish in this age, and to desire more to be praised by God on the day of eternal recompense than by any mortal human being in this transitory life.

As we have already said, this vice of vainglory must also be abolished by floods of tears, together with the practice of other good works. In everything we do, consideration of our own weakness must depress us, lest the swelling of empty praise extinguish these works before the eyes of the hidden Judge. [Col. 0662A]

## CHAPTER SIX. On the Vice of Envy

Envy is also accustomed to exhort a conquered heart as though with reason, saying: “In what respect are you less than this person or that? Why, then, are you not equal or superior to them? How much are you capable of doing that they are not? Therefore they ought not to be either superior or even equal to you.” [Note: [Col. 0662D] Saint Gregory is cited here; he discusses envy most beautifully in Book 5 of the *Moralia on Job*, chapter 31.]

The apostolic statement cries out against this: “Through the envy of the devil, death entered the world.”
