[Note: [Col. 0662D] This is from Prosper, Book 3 of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 5.]

“An envious person makes another’s good his own punishment through envy. He seems to be stirred by no desire toward the envious person’s object, but only to be tormented by the disease of pride, by which he continually laments that the person whom he envies is preferred to him. Through this he pursues the divine gift in another, although a person ought rather to be loved for the holiness of his merit.

“An envious person has as many torturers by just punishment as the envied person has praisers. Nothing can be more wretched than envy, which is tormented by the goods of others. Therefore, from whatever source a good person advances, from that same source the envious person wastes away. Envy bites the understanding, burns the breast, and afflicts the mind. Whoever envies is like the devil, who through envy cast the human being down from the happiness of paradise.”

(Prosper.) We must miserably observe how much envy corrupts their good: whenever envious people hear anything good done or said by holy persons, they either do not believe it at all or turn good deeds into evil by interpreting them maliciously. Every evil that lying rumor has spread about them they immediately believe as though they themselves had seen it.

(Gregory.) When they do not cast jealousy out of their hearts, they fall into the open wickedness of their deeds, because every evil plan begins with oneself, and before harming another it prepares destruction for oneself. Murders arise from this vice. For if Cain had not envied his brother’s accepted offering, he would never have proceeded to destroy his life.

## CHAPTER SEVEN. On the Remedy for Envy

The Apostle threatens terribly, saying: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”; and, “Whoever envies his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness.” Therefore, if we wish to resist this vice vigorously, let us show charity toward God and our neighbor, from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. We easily resist sin if we abound in every good thing, despise the blandishments of the world, and, while guarding these commandments of love, accomplish with affection everything that is difficult or harsh for human weakness.

(The same.) Nevertheless, those people pervert the order of love and do not observe the proper measure of loving who either love the world, which ought to be despised; or love their own bodies, which ought to be loved less; or fail to love their neighbors as themselves; or perhaps do not love God more than themselves.

We love our neighbors as ourselves when we love them not for any advantage of our own, nor for benefits hoped for or commandments, but solely because they share our nature. Therefore the entirety of love for one’s neighbor is this: that you wish for your neighbor the good that you wish to be conferred upon yourself. A person can therefore make another’s good his own by loving in another what he himself does not do.

(The same.) Let the envious therefore consider how great is the power of charity, which makes the works of another’s labor ours without labor on our part. It must therefore be said to the envious that, because they do not guard themselves against jealousy, they fall into the ancient wickedness of the crafty enemy.

The greatest vigilance must consequently be exercised so that this vice may quickly be torn out by the roots from their hearts and cleansed by good works, as prescribed, though with the counsel of a priest. Each day they should pray for the person whom they hated, offer him the services of charity, and, if they are able, frequently assist him in his needs—the person to whom, when they did not love him, they showed less affection than they ought.

## CHAPTER EIGHT. On the Vice of Anger

(The same.) Anger too is accustomed to exhort a conquered heart as though with reason, saying: “What is done against you cannot be borne with equanimity. Indeed, to tolerate these things patiently is a sin, because if one does not resist them with great irritation, they will thereafter accumulate against you without measure.” [Col. 0663C]

The apostolic statement responds to this: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.” Hence the Truth also says that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment. And: “If each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive your sins.”

If it is not lawful to be angry, or to say “Raca” or “Fool,” it is much less lawful to retain anything in the mind so that indignation may be converted into hatred. Anger is a fury of the mind. If it is fixed in the heart, it removes all foresight from the act: the person can neither seek the judgment of right discernment, nor possess the virtue of honorable reflection, nor have the maturity of counsel. Rather, he appears to do everything through a kind of precipitous impulse. From this arises murder.

(Gregory.) It must be said to the impatient that, because they neglect to bridle their spirit, they are swept away into many precipices of iniquity that they do not even desire. Fury drives the mind where desire does not lead it; and, once agitated, it acts as though unaware of what it will later regret, though it knows that it will regret it.

Through this vice of impatience the fault of arrogance also often pierces the mind. Because a person cannot bear being despised in this world, he tries to display whatever good things he has that are hidden, and through impatience he is led even to arrogance.

## CHAPTER NINE. On the Remedy for Anger

Patience is known to overcome fury and every vice of anger through remembrance of God’s commandments, when charity, the mother of all virtues, is recalled to memory. For the vice of impatience does not arise unless charity, the mother of the virtues, is cut away. It is written: “Charity is patient.” Therefore, when a person is not patient, charity is not in him.

(Gregory.) Through this vice of anger also the very teaching that nourishes the virtues is scattered. Hence it is written: “A man’s teaching is known by his patience.” Therefore, the less patient someone is shown to be, the less learned he is proved to be. For it is written: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than he who conquers cities.” [Col. 0664B] Hence Truth says to his chosen ones: “By your patience you will possess your souls.” The Lord has thus shown patience to be the guardian of our condition, since by it he taught us to possess ourselves. Elsewhere, too, he says: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you.” To tolerate adversaries is therefore a virtue before human beings; but before God, it is a virtue to love them.

The apostle Paul also urged the possession of patience when, by exhorting his disciples, he instructed them with this command: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice.” For indignation, shouting, and blasphemy are removed from the exterior in vain if, within, [Col. 0664C] malice—the mother of vices—holds sway. Those who are patient must therefore be admonished to fortify their hearts after victory, lest the cunning enemy later rejoice with greater exultation in their deception, because it now tramples upon the stiff necks of those who conquered it, once rigid against it. Whoever has long been consumed and destroyed by this vice of anger ought, by humbling himself again, to make satisfaction to the person against whom he became angry, lest he be judged guilty before God, who does not otherwise erase our crimes unless the offenses of our brothers are completely cut away from our hearts.

## CHAPTER X. On the vice of sadness

(Gregory.) Sadness, too, having conquered the heart, commonly urges it on as though by reason, saying: “What do you have [Col. 0664D] from which you can rejoice, when you bear so many evils from those around you? Consider with what grief all those must be regarded who turn against you with so much gall of bitterness.” Against this the apostolic judgment says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress?” And so forth.

There are two kinds of sadness: one salutary, the other deadly. Sadness is salutary when the mind is grieved by the remembrance of sins, so that it seeks to make confession and do penance, and desires with its whole heart to turn back to God. The other is the sadness of this world, which produces death for the soul and is able to accomplish nothing in the desire for good works. It disturbs the mind, often casts it into despair, and withdraws the hope of future goods; for one afflicted by this vice, the present life also has no delight. [Col. 0665A]

## CHAPTER XI. On the remedy for sadness

This wickedness is overcome by spiritual joy, by hope in future things, by the consolation of the Scriptures, and by fraternal conversation in spiritual gladness; or when one brings to mind how small are the things that appear, as it is written: “For the things that are seen are temporal.” Hence Ecclesiastes says: “All things are subject to vanity, and all go to one place, because they were made from the earth, and together they will return to the earth”; but “the things that are not seen are eternal.”

(Prosper.) To speak and think of these things and those like them is nothing other than to reject all vices and cut away every kind of sadness. [Col. 0665B] From these sorrowful evils, therefore, we must ascend to those sublime things by which the minds of those who make progress rise in hope of earning blessedness; and, once earthly things have been renounced, they desire heavenly things, where God will be seen forever and ever. But whoever wishes to be free from this vice should devote himself frequently to prayer and place the death of the soul daily before his eyes. And because “all flesh is grass,” he should not neglect, with great reflection—whether meditating by himself or hearing from others—to consider wholeheartedly the mercy and goodness of God toward all who hope in him. Let him mercifully give whatever he is able to the poor and pilgrims, widows and orphans, as well as the sick and strangers, and let him not fail in the works of the other virtues. [Col. 0665C]

## CHAPTER XII. On the vice of avarice

(Gregory.) Avarice, too, having conquered the mind, commonly urges it on as though by reason, saying: “It is entirely without blame that you desire to possess certain things, because you do not seek to multiply them but fear to be in need; and what another wrongly retains, you yourself spend more rightly.”

Against this the apostolic judgment cries: “Neither the avaricious nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God.” Hence Solomon also says: “The miser will not be satisfied with money”; and, “He who loves riches will reap no fruit from them.” And again: “Riches preserved to the harm of their owner”; for “they perish in the worst affliction.” Shortly afterward he says: “There is nothing more criminal, nothing more unjust, than for the miser to love money.” And again: “When a man dies, he will inherit serpents, beasts, and worms.” [Col. 0665D] Hence the Lord also says: “For it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven.” And again: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolation.” Elsewhere: “You cannot serve God and mammon.” Hence the Apostle says to his disciple concerning the rich: “Command the rich of this world not to be proud, nor to place their hope in uncertain riches.”

Avarice is an excessive desire to acquire, possess, or retain riches. Hence Gregory says: “Avarice is not only a matter of money but also of status.” [Col. 0666A] This plague is insatiable, like the disease of dropsy: drinking does not extinguish the thirst of the dropsical person, but it increases through drinking. So too with avarice: the more one possesses, the more one desires. And when there is no limit to possessing, there will be no limit to desiring. From it arise envy, thefts, robberies, murder, and the rest.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the remedy for avarice

When someone asked the Lord what he should do to possess eternal life, he replied: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have, give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven.” Elsewhere:

(Gregory.) “If you truly desire to be rich, love true riches.” [Col. 0666B] Let the rich therefore learn that they cannot in any way retain the riches they see. Therefore, let them mercifully give away what they see themselves to possess superfluously, because “God loves a cheerful giver.” Those who already give away their possessions mercifully must also be admonished to take diligent care lest, while they redeem committed sins through almsgiving, they continue to commit sins that will have to be redeemed. Let them not suppose that God’s justice is for sale: when they take care to give money for their sins, they must not imagine that they can sin with impunity. For “the soul is more than food, and the body more than clothing.” Therefore, whoever gives food and clothing generously to the poor, but defiles either soul or body with iniquity, has offered to justice what is lesser and to guilt what is greater: he has given his possessions to God, but himself to the devil. [Col. 0666C]

Again, those who intend to seize what belongs to others must be admonished. Let them hear what is written: “Woe to him who increases what is not his.” Certainly, whoever eagerly seeks to increase his wealth neglects to avoid danger, since “the desire for money is the root of all evils.”

(Prosper, Book V of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 4.) Hence it must be asked: if pride is said to be the beginning of every sin, why is desire affirmed to be the root of all evils? The answer is that desire and pride are so much one evil that neither can a proud person be found without desire, nor a desirous person without pride. Moreover, if I cannot commit any sin unless I consent to my own pleasure—which is characteristic of desire—and despise God’s commands—which is the evil of pride—how does every sin not proceed from desire, which is the root of all evils, and from pride, which is called the beginning of every sin? [Col. 0666D]

This vice is also conquered by generosity to the poor, by visiting the sick, and by clothing the naked; moreover, if anyone has unjustly taken something away, it must be restored fourfold, according to the Lord’s judgment. The fear of the Lord must never depart from the heart; in addition, the soul must be cleansed continually through weeping and tears, with contrition of heart, lest, on account of uncertain riches, it lose eternal life.

Let what has been said thus far concerning the five spiritual vices, from the testimonies of the holy Fathers, suffice. It remains for us to treat of the two carnal vices, namely gluttony and lust. [Col. 0667A]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the vice of gluttony

(Gregory.) Gluttony of the belly, too, having conquered the heart, commonly urges it on as though by reason, saying: “God created everything in the world for eating; and one who refuses to be satisfied with food—what else does he do but oppose a gift that has been granted?”

(Prosper.) But, on the contrary, let us see how those first human beings committed such a great sin, one that drove them from paradise into the exile of this penal life and, in them, condemned the entire human race by original sin. The Lord had indeed forbidden them to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; but, deceived by the vice of gluttony, they ate. [Col. 0667B] For if they had not eaten, they would have remained immortal forever, had they lived under their God and kept the commandment they had received. Nor would they have been abandoned by God unless they had first abandoned God themselves. And so they were cast down and handed over to the misery of this afflicted life, to the offense of gluttony and to death. Here every human being is born through sin, lives through labor, and dies through pain.

(Gregory.) Therefore those devoted to gluttony must be admonished not to transfix themselves with the sword of lust while they give themselves over to the pleasure of food. Let them observe how much talkativeness and how much light-mindedness of mind lie in wait for them through eating, lest, while they serve the belly softly, they be cruelly bound by the snares of vices. Let them hear the Apostle saying: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them”; and again: “Not in feasting and drunkenness”; and again: “Food does not commend us to God”; and again: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame,” because lust follows gluttony. [Col. 0667C]

## CHAPTER XV. On the remedy for the vice of gluttony

Since the first human being fell through this vice of gluttony, together with his descendants, it is necessary that we rise again through abstinence. Yet even in abstinence there is something that we must weigh with vigilant care.

(Gregory.) Often, when the flesh is worn down through abstinence more than is necessary, humility is displayed outwardly, but inwardly one takes grave pride in that very humility. [Col. 0667D] Therefore those who practice abstinence must always watch carefully, lest, while they flee the vice of gluttony, they generate more severe vices from it, as though from virtue. The body is therefore worn down through abstinence in vain if, after its disordered impulses have been let loose, the mind is scattered by vices.

(Prosper.) Those who desire to abstain not only from the quality but also from the quantity of foods strive for nothing else than to allow themselves as much as seems sufficient to restore the stomach and relieve hunger. They do not satisfy their appetites through greedy consumption but restrain them; and it is not the fullness of eating that sets their limit, but their will. They abstain both from the desire for expensive foods and from excessive consumption of cheap ones. They do not wish to dissolve the flesh luxuriously with finer foods, nor to burden the belly with cheap foods by stuffing it. For abstinent men are accustomed to be neither delicate nor greedy. [Col. 0668A]

What shall I say about abstaining from wine? The Apostle established a definite rule concerning it when he said: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is lust,” as though he were saying: excessive consumption of wine causes and nourishes lust, not the nature of wine itself. Therefore, “I do not forbid you to use wine, but I forbid you to become drunk.” Hence he commanded Timothy, saying: “Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for the sake of your frequent illnesses.” Accordingly, those who take wine not for drunkenness but only for the health of the body do nothing contrary to abstinence.

One thing, however, must be considered: it benefits nothing to abstain from foods if one serves vices. For a possession is more easily cast away than the will. [Col. 0668B]

(Gregory.) Those who practice abstinence must know that they offer God an abstinence pleasing to him when they give to the needy what they take away from themselves in food. A person fasts not for God but for himself if he does not give to the poor what he temporarily withdraws from his belly, but preserves it in order to offer it afterward to his belly. Again, those who practice abstinence must be admonished both always to preserve it without diminution and never to regard it before the hidden Judge as an outstanding virtue, lest, if it is believed to be of great merit, the heart be lifted up in pride.

Hence Joel says: “Sanctify a fast.” To sanctify a fast is, by joining other good works to it, to show a bodily abstinence worthy of God. [Col. 0668C] For it will profit us to chastise our bodies, or the other incitements of the body, with the rigor of stricter abstinence only if, freed from carnal desires, we flourish in holy virtues. Therefore, if through the pleasure and desire of delight we fell from the joys of paradise, we ought to return through fasting and the laments of repentance.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the vice of lust

(Gregory.) Lust, too, having conquered the heart, commonly urges it on as though by reason, saying: “Why do you not now expand yourself in your pleasure, when you do not know what will follow you? You ought not to waste the time that has been granted in desires, because you do not know how quickly it may pass. For if God had not wished human beings to mingle in the pleasure of intercourse, at the very beginning of the human race he would not have made male and female.” [Col. 0668D]

God did not create male and female—as divine authority testifies—for the purpose of enjoying carnal desire or living in the pleasure of the flesh, but so that they might be joined to one another for the begetting of children with blessing. And if there had then been no transgression of the commandments, no pleasure would certainly have been felt in the intercourse of married couples. Lust is bodily impurity, which ordinarily arises from the lack of restraint of desire and from the softness of the soul, which consents to sin with its own flesh. For every sin is committed in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent.

(Prosper.) Does one who is enslaved to the desire of the flesh [Col. 0669A] not seem to have nothing of pride, especially since the passion itself appears to humble him through lust? Yet unless he had first existed as a rebel against God—whose salutary command concerning the preservation of chastity he contemptuously disregards through the presumption of a proud spirit—no wanton desire would provoke him. In his mind, contempt for God and fear contend for a long time [read: *disceptant* for *deceptant*]. Either contempt for God prevails, and the proud mind loses chastity after receiving desire; or fear prevails, and the mind subject to God resists both desire and pride.

Many are shamefully loosened into lust by gluttony and an abundance of wine; in others, sordid thoughts inflame them against chastity. Some are overthrown by opportunities that arise after they have laid aside chastity; others are brought under the yoke of immodesty by the examples of those who live disgracefully. [Col. 0669B] There are others whose life is inflamed by a disgraceful life and reveals a shameful conscience: first they willingly utter or listen to immodest speech, and then, as the disease gradually grows, they fall away from honesty. For it is thought that pollutes the mind when it is shameful, just as it purifies it when it is honorable.

Hence that bodily emission which occurs in sleepers, without guilt, sometimes occurs in those who are awake through guilt. What happens in a sleeping person is one thing; what an awake person does is another. In the former, the fullness of bodily fluid is expelled naturally; in the latter, desire is shamefully manifested. But this desire elicits such an emission in those who are awake when obscene conversation has stirred their polluted appetite.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the remedy for lust

[Col. 0669C]

The apostle Paul gives a solemn admonition, saying: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none,” and so forth.

(Gregory.) He has a wife as though he did not have one who uses her for carnal consolation in such a way that he is nevertheless never turned by love for her from the uprightness of a better intention toward evil works. He has a wife as though he did not have one who, seeing that all things are transitory, endures care for the flesh out of necessity but awaits the eternal joys of the spirit out of desire.

Hence he says again: “Concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman. But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. But I say this by way of concession, not by way of command.” [Col. 0669D] What is granted by concession is thereby indicated to be a fault; yet it is relaxed all the more quickly when, after this, nothing illicit is done, but what is lawful is not held without moderation. This is well expressed by Lot in himself: he fled burning Sodom, but, when he came to Segor, he did not immediately climb into the mountains. To flee burning Sodom is to avoid the illicit fires of the flesh. The height of the mountains is the purity of those who practice continence. To stand on the mountain is not to cling to the flesh. [Col. 0670A]

On the other hand, those who are not bound by marriage must be admonished to serve the heavenly commands all the more rightly, since the yoke of carnal union does not incline them toward worldly cares.

The unmarried must be admonished not to think that they may associate with available women without condemnation. When Paul included fornication among so many execrable crimes, he indicated its guilt, saying: “Neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the avaricious, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor rapacious persons will possess the kingdom of God.” [Col. 0670B] And again: “God will judge fornicators and adulterers.”

On the other hand, those who are ignorant of carnal sins must be admonished to fear precipitous ruin all the more anxiously the higher they stand. Through John it is said to them: “These are they who have not been defiled with women. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes.”

Therefore, when the mind begins to incline toward the pleasure of the flesh, it is necessary to bring the fear of judgment back to mind and carefully consider the punishments of hell, where no one is thrust except those who are guilty, and what punishment awaits the unjust in eternal torments. Hence it is written: “Send them into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth”; where “their worm does not die, and their fire is not extinguished.” [Col. 0670C]

(Prosper.) What excuse could we put forward? What shall we do beneath the majesty of so great a Judge on that day? By what art of defense shall we cleanse ourselves? What repentance, which we despised in this flesh, will come to our aid? To think of these and similar things is nothing other than to reject all vices and restrain every blandishment of the flesh.

But since, concerning the eight principal vices and their remedies, our pen has briefly gathered and touched upon the judgments of the holy Fathers, insofar as the Giver of all good things granted, let this little book now come to an end, so that in the following work, with the Lord’s gift, we may discuss more fully the virtues of which we have touched here only briefly. [Col. 0670D]

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0669]

In the preceding book I gathered, as far as the Lord may grant strength, an account of the eight principal vices. As I promised, I have likewise taken care to collect from the sayings of the Fathers material concerning the active and contemplative life, as well as the virtues.

## CHAPTER I. On the active life

(Prosper.) The active life is a religious manner of life that teaches how superiors should govern and love those subject to them, and, being no less concerned for their salvation than for their own, should provide with paternal care whatever they know to be expedient for them; and how those subject to their superior, like members to a head, should serve him and preserve his commands with the greatest love, as though they were God’s command.

For the active life gives bread to the hungry, teaches the ignorant by the word of wisdom, corrects the erring, recalls the proud neighbor to the way of humility, cares for the sick, distributes what is expedient to each person, and diligently provides how those entrusted to it may be able to endure. Although these things are performed in the present and cease with the body, the reward of this life remains forever. [Col. 0671A]

## CHAPTER II. On the contemplative life

[Col. 0671B]

The contemplative life takes its name from contemplating, that is, from seeing. (Prosper, Book I of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 1.) In it, the intellectual creature, purified from every sin and healed in every respect, will see its Creator.

But even if we wish to consider carefully, in this fragile tabernacle where we groan daily, we can in some manner become participants in the contemplative life; no one should doubt this, because (Prosper, cited above, chapter 13) the leaders of the Churches can and ought to become followers of the contemplative life. For whether, according to the opinion of some, the contemplative life is nothing other than knowledge of hidden and future things; or withdrawal from all worldly occupations; or study of the divine Scriptures, no impediment seems capable of preventing holy priests from attaining the virtues, since their concern is to flee worldly occupations and cling to the study of the divine Scriptures. [Col. 0671C]

They do not lie idle in leisure, but devote themselves to the work of their perfection; they give themselves tirelessly to the word of God, truly become wise, savor heavenly things, despise earthly things, instruct the obedient, and apply themselves to the holy virtues by which they become daily nearer to God. This life begins in the present age through faith and hope, but remains with the Lord in the future.

## CHAPTER III. On faith

Faith is the foundation of righteousness, and no good works precede it; from it all things proceed. [Note: [Col. 0671D] Prosper has *ex quo*, “from which.” Prosper explains this in Book I of *The Calling of the Nations*, chapter 25, and in *Reply to the Excerpts of the Genoese*, reply to the first three questions.] It cleanses us from all sins, illumines our minds, reconciles us to God, joins us to all who share our nature, inspires in us hope of future reward, increases holy virtues in us, and confirms us in their profession. [Col. 0671D] [Note: [Col. 0672D] Up to this point from Prosper, Book III of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 21.]

Faith is also the stairway of ascent by which every step of the passing life is directed, so that one may flee the errors of human life and reach the heavenly realms securely. The priest ought to know faith in order to teach it, and the people ought to believe in order to understand what is taught, as the Apostle says: “Unless you believe, you will not understand.” Hence it is understood [Col. 0672A] that faith does not arise from understanding, but understanding from faith. Therefore the teacher of the Church ought to preach that one should strive to understand in order to act well, and believe in order to understand, so that the hearer may believe: for without preaching there will be no hearing. It is written: “How will they hear without one who preaches?” The word of faith must be preached so that the hearer may believe, the believer understand, and the one who understands persevere in good works; for neither works without faith nor faith alone without works justifies. And therefore, “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Whoever does not believe, having no faith, can possess neither righteousness of heart nor salvation.

Faith, as the Apostle says, is “the substance of things hoped for, the proof of things not seen.” [Col. 0672B] For by it the elders received testimony. By faith we understand that the ages were prepared by the word of God, so that visible things might be made from invisible things. By faith Abel offered a greater sacrifice than Cain. By faith Enoch was translated so that he would not see death. By faith Abraham offered Isaac when he was tested, since, as the same Apostle says, “without faith it is impossible to please God.” And again: “Therefore, justified by faith, let us have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. Through him we also have access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we glory in the hope of the glory of the children of God.”

## CHAPTER IV. On hope

(Prosper.) Hope is spoken of when something is promised although it is not seen, as the Apostle says: “For we have been saved in hope. But hope that is seen is not hope. For what does anyone hope for that he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience.” [Col. 0672C]

Therefore let us walk in hope, progressing day by day, and mortify the deeds of the flesh by the spirit. For the Lord knows who are his. And “as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God”—by grace, not by nature. For the only-begotten Son of God by nature, through mercy, became the son of man for our sake, so that we, who are by nature sons of man, might through him become sons of God by grace.

In the active life, in which and through which the Church makes its pilgrimage, faith and hope are to be acquired with the praise of charity. Hence the Apostle says: “Now faith, hope, and charity remain; but the greatest of these is charity.” And it is the greatest because it does not pass away with the world destined to perish, but begins here and remains in the future. [Col. 0672D]

## CHAPTER V. On charity

(Augustine.) Now charity, which the Apostle said was greater than these two—that is, faith and hope—the greater it is in anyone, the better is the person in whom it is. When it is asked whether a person is good, one does not ask what he believes or hopes, but what he loves. For whoever loves rightly undoubtedly believes and hopes rightly. But whoever does not love believes in vain, even if what he believes is true; and hopes in vain, even if what he is taught to hope for is said to belong to true happiness—unless he believes and hopes that what he asks may be granted to him, so that he may love. [Col. 0673A]

Through charity, therefore, all the good things that are believed and hoped for are justified.

(Prosper, Book III, chapters 13 and 14 of *The Contemplative Life.)* The Apostle calls charity “the more excellent way”: it is not climbed by the way of the feet, but by the way of conduct. For charity is a right will utterly turned away from all earthly and present things, inseparably joined and united to God by a kind of fire of the Holy Spirit, subject to no defect of mutability; exalted above all things loved carnally, eager for divine contemplation, always unconquered in all things, the death of crimes and the life of virtues. [Col. 0673B]

(Prosper, Book III, chapter 13 of *The Contemplative Life.)* Faith conceives it, hope runs toward it, and the progress of all things serves it. Without it no one has pleased God; with it no one could sin, nor will anyone be able to sin. This is true, genuine, perfect charity, and altogether the way that leads those who walk by it to their homeland. For just as no one can arrive where he is going without a road, so without charity—which has been called the way—people cannot walk but only go astray. [Note: [Col. 0673D] Up to this point from Prosper.]

Hence the Apostle says: “Charity is patient, is kind, does not envy, does not act improperly, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, and does not seek what is its own.” And again: “It bears all things, hopes all things, endures all things.” It bestows all these goods that it possesses upon those in whom it is found. And what could be more perfect in this life for those who abound in such things, with charity reigning in them through these virtues? [Note: [Col. 0673D] Up to this point from Prosper, chapter 14 of the same work.]

Therefore charity is necessary here in the present: it separates us from the devil, cleanses us from sin, and reconciles us to God. But in the future it will be perfect, when it has joined the perfected to God, from whom it was given. [Col. 0673C]

## CHAPTER VI. On virtue

Before anything is said about the four principal [Note: [Col. 0673D] Perhaps *principalibus*, that is, “cardinal.”] virtues, one must first learn, through inquiry into the truth, what virtue is, or why it is called virtue. It excels in such honor of name that nothing, however upright it may appear, is acceptable to God without virtue.

(Prosper, Book III of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 16.) Every virtue is a holy, divine, wholly incorporeal, and utterly pure reality. Minds do not stain it with iniquity; rather, it cleanses those stained by iniquity. Through participation in it, the weak are strengthened, the dead are raised, the infirm are healed, the crooked are corrected, and adversities are reconciled. [Col. 0673D] [Note: [Col. 0673D] Prosper has *formantur informia*, “the formless are formed.”] No one possesses it except God and the one to whom God gives it. It dwells in the soul, but sanctifies both soul and body. No one approaches it unwillingly, and no one loses it except one deceived by his own will.

Elsewhere it is said again: [Note: [Col. 0674D] Up to this point from Prosper.] Virtue is also a disposition of the soul, the adornment of life, the rule of conduct, the worship of piety, the honor of Divinity, and the merit of eternal blessedness. Its parts, as we have said, are four principal ones: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. [Col. 0674A]

## CHAPTER VII. On prudence

Prudence is knowledge of divine and human matters, insofar as this has been granted to human beings. In it one must understand what should be avoided and what should be done. Hence the Psalmist says: “Turn away from evil and do good.” For there is no better wisdom than that by which God is understood and feared according to the measure of the human mind, and his future judgment is believed—at which the good receive good things and the wicked evil things according to the quality of their merits.

(Prosper, cited above, chapter 29.) Many place prudence and wisdom in the investigation and discovery of truth. [Col. 0674B] For no one can rightly be called wise if he lacks prudence, nor prudent if he lacks wisdom. Therefore, if the office of prudence and wisdom is understood to be nothing other than the inquiry into and comprehension of truth, whoever is able prudently to seek and wisely to discover the truth will rightly be called prudent and wise. And whatever is discussed concerning prudence may all be understood concerning wisdom.

Those who, made prudent through participation in prudence, draw near to their God not by their feet but by holy conduct cannot perish in the part in which they are prudent by God’s gift, either through their own sin or through another’s. But because their prudence is not yet as perfect as it will be in that life where no error will be able to creep upon those living perfectly, [Col. 0674C] even prudent people sometimes yield to sins that deceive them—not corrupted in will, but falling as human beings through human error. Nor are they yet perfected in the entire perfection of prudence and wisdom, as they will be there, where they can neither be ignorant of anything nor sin any longer.

The Lord commanded such people to become prudent in the Gospel, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.” For the simple cannot deceive anyone, nor do the prudent allow themselves to be deceived. This virtue differs greatly from the secular and worldly prudence that corrupts sound things, whereas this virtue heals vices, with corruption itself added. [Note: [Col. 0674D] Prosper reads *sanat vitii accessione corrupta* (“heals [things] corrupted by the addition of vice”).] Thus the truly prudent hastens to benefit all whom it can, so that through its merits the fruit of all who are acquired for the Lord through it may increase. [Col. 0674D] [Note: [Col. 0674D] Up to this point from Prosper, chapter 29.]

But since the order of the discussion requires that we also speak of prudence, which is a principal virtue, and place it first, it remains to disclose what justice is.

## CHAPTER VIII. On justice

Justice is nobility of soul, granting to each thing its proper dignity. In it the worship of Divinity, the rights of humanity, just judgments, and the equity of the whole of life are preserved. For what is more just than [Col. 0675A] to love God and keep his commands? Through him we were created when we did not exist; when we were lost, we were recreated and freed from diabolical slavery. He granted us all the good things that we possess.

Justice is rightly and reasonably so called because through it those who practice it are made just.

(Prosper, Book III of *The Contemplative Life*, chapter 22.) From it flows equity, which makes us say that the needs of all human beings are our own, and believe that we were born not for ourselves alone but also for the human race. [Note: [Col. 0675D] Up to this point from Prosper, chapter 22.]

Therefore, if in this life we strive to fulfill justice, whose proper work is to give each person his own, let us return ourselves to God, by whom we were made, and not permit those things over which we have been placed by nature [Col. 0675B] to rule us. Let reason rule the vices, let the body be subjected to the soul, and the soul to God: then the justice and complete perfection of the human being have been fulfilled. [Note: [Col. 0675D] Up to this point from Prosper, the same work, chapter 26.]

From the source of justice there further proceed generosity, beneficence, charity, and other things of this kind, by which human beings can be helped in many ways. Generosity is that which overflows even toward those who appear to lack nothing. In this generosity lies the abundance of one’s household goods. The works of beneficence are many, by which the needs of those who labor are mercifully relieved; and from earthly wealth the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom is acquired. [Note: [Col. 0675D] Up to this point from Prosper, the same work, chapter 24.]

## CHAPTER IX. On fortitude

(Prosper.) Fortitude is great patience of soul, [Col. 0675C] long-suffering, perseverance in good works, and victory over every kind of vice.

The fortitude of the soul, therefore, must be understood as that which not only remains unshaken when assailed by various troubles, but also does not yield to any allurements of pleasure. Otherwise, if it breaks the assault of the evils that follow, if it withstands whatever calamities strike it, if it persists without weariness amid savage injury, amid the storms of oppressive afflictions, amid enmities, present losses, and persecutions of every kind. Those, however, whom the love of God makes strong for the endurance of sufferings are corrupted by no delight of the flesh, by no deceptively pleasing pleasure. For the fortitude of the soul comes to us from him to whom, with the Prophet, we sing: “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” [Col. 0675D]. He is our strength, because he strengthens us against every vice with unconquerable protection, so that neither seductive things dissolve our spirit nor adversities cast it down. And then the Lord becomes our praise, if we desire not that we ourselves be praised for God’s gifts, but that the divine gifts in us be proclaimed. Certainly, the fortitude of the soul must shake off the cowardice of despair and oppose itself to boastfulness. [Note: [Col. 0675D] Up to this point from Prosper, the same work, chapter 20.]

And what is better than this fortitude: to conquer the devil, to overcome all his suggestions, and courageously to endure the adversities of the world for the sake of God’s name? [Col. 0676A]

## CHAPTER X. On temperance

Temperance is the measure of the whole of life, so that a person neither loves nor hates anything to excess, but carefully regulates all the changes of this present life with due consideration. Hence one of the philosophers said that in life it is especially useful to do nothing to excess.

(Prosper.) Temperance, therefore, makes a person temperate, abstinent, frugal, sober, moderate, chaste, silent, serious, and modest. If this virtue dwells in the soul, it restrains lusts, moderates affections, multiplies holy desires, and chastises vicious ones; it orders everything confused within us and strengthens what has been ordered; it removes wicked thoughts and implants holy ones; it extinguishes the fire of lustful pleasure; and it reduces all our intemperance to an honorable measure in food and drink themselves, so that we are content with what is set before us.

It belongs to temperance that we show reverence to our elders, honor our equals as brothers, and extend to our juniors the favor of paternal affection. [Note: [Col. 0675D] Up to this point from Prosper, Book III of *The Contemplative Life*, [Col. 0676D] chapter 19.]

Therefore, [Note: [Col. 0676D] The following is from Prosper, the same work, chapter 18.] it is indeed difficult to identify the names of the virtues that arise from these four principal virtues. Nevertheless, we must know and hold fast to this: that these four virtues, and all those that proceed from them, are gifts of God. No one has had, has, or will have them except the one to whom God—who is the very nature and origin of all virtues—has granted them.

[Note: [Col. 0676D] The following is from Prosper, the same work, chapter 18.] Not only do philosophers hold that there are four principal virtues, but our own writers agree, since scarcely anyone is unaware that the number four is sacred as a number of progression. For the whole world is found to be bounded by four regions: east, west, north, and south. Adam himself, who is the father of the human race—or the general name *man*—is expressed by four letters. The body too, constructed from four elements, contains within itself the mystery of the number four. There are likewise four affections of the soul itself, which we employ either for good or for evil. There are also the four rivers that proceed from the fountain of Paradise, or the four Gospels. Therefore we must carefully consider these virtues, which contain so much perfection in their number, [Col. 0676D] and how much holiness they confer upon the Christian soul; and how no progress whatsoever ever occurs [Note: [Col. 0676D] Prosper has *usquam sit*, “exists anywhere,” rather than *fit*, “is made.”] that does not occur through these virtues. For if prudence makes a person prudent, justice makes a person just, and temperance makes a person temperate, because such a person acts prudently, justly, courageously, and temperately, nothing can be more perfect. [Note: [Col. 0676D] Up to this point from Prosper, chapter 18.]

Therefore, just as by the number of the elements the structure of the world is completed, and human bodies as well, in which are veins, nerves, and other things useful to the body [*Forte corpori*, perhaps “useful for the body”], so no one should doubt that, by the number of the principal virtues, everything that has been established for right living is joined together. [Col. 0677A]

These, then, are the virtues expounded by the most sacred men. The priests of the Lord, who hold the laws of the Church and possess the power of binding and loosing, ought carefully to understand them and proclaim them frequently, so that the people may be free from vices and, with the help of heavenly assistance, each person may strive according to his strength to cling to the virtues. I think that enough has been discussed concerning the three heavenly degrees—faith, hope, and charity—and also concerning the four virtues by which one ascends to the heights of virtue. Now, in a brief book of the work that follows, it remains to insert how each vice must be cleansed by priestly judgment.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0677]

## CHAPTER I. That the periods of penance should be determined according to the character of the sin

[Col. 0677B]

[Note: [Col. 0677D] From the African Council.] For those doing penance, the bishops shall determine the periods of penance according to the distinction among their sins.

Likewise, in the same council:

A priest shall impose the laws of penance upon one who seeks penance, without respect of persons.

## CHAPTER II. That final penance is to be denied to no one

[Note: [Col. 0677D] From a letter of Pope Celestine.] True conversion to God among those placed at the point of death is to be judged more by the mind than by the time, as the Prophet declares in these words: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved.” [Note: [Col. 0677D] See the notes of Antonius Augustinus on Rabanus’s *Penance*.] Since, therefore, the Lord is the examiner of the heart, penance is not to be denied at any time to one who asks for it, since the person binds himself to that Judge to whom he knows that all hidden things will be revealed.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning those who, when death is pressing, ask simultaneously for penance and the viaticum; and concerning those who become speechless before the priest who is to give them penance can approach them

[Col. 0677C]

[Note: [Col. 0677D] From a letter of Pope Leo to Bishop Theodore.] The need of such persons must therefore be assisted in such a way that neither the practice of penance nor the grace of communion is denied them. Even after the loss of the faculty of speech, they should be shown to seek it by signs indicating an unimpaired understanding. But if they have been so weighed down by illness that they cannot indicate in the presence of others what they had shortly before requested, the testimony of the faithful standing around them ought to benefit them. Nevertheless, let them obtain together both the benefit of penance and that of reconciliation.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning those who delay doing penance

[Col. 0677D]

[Note: [Col. 0677D] In the decree of Pope Leo, chapter 21.] Delay may arise not from contempt for the remedy, but from fear of committing a more serious offense. Therefore, when the penance that was delayed has been sought with greater earnestness, it should not be denied, so that the wounded soul may in some way reach the medicine of forgiveness.

## CHAPTER V. That one who seeks forgiveness for illicit acts ought also to abstain from many lawful things

[Note: [Col. 0678D] In the decretal of the same pope.] It is one thing to demand back what is justly owed; it is another to despise one’s own possessions out of love of perfection. But one who seeks forgiveness for illicit acts ought also to abstain from lawful things, as the Apostle says: “Everything is lawful, but not everything is beneficial.” Therefore, if penitents have a case that perhaps they ought not to neglect, it is better for someone to seek an ecclesiastical judgment than a civil one.

## CHAPTER VI. That it is not fitting for a penitent to conduct any profitable business

[Note: [Col. 0678D] In the same work, chapter 23.] The character of trade either excuses or condemns, since there is both honest and dishonorable profit. Nevertheless, it is more beneficial for a penitent to suffer losses than to be bound by the dangers of commerce. [Note: [Col. 0678D] These words are inserted in the *Capitula*, Book VII, chapter 62, p. 1040.] For it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the exchange between buyer and seller.

## CHAPTER VII. That after penance they ought not to return to secular military service

[Col. 0678C]

[Note: [Col. 0678D] In the same council, chapter 24.] It is altogether contrary to ecclesiastical rules, after performing penance, to return to secular military service, since the Apostle says: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs.” Therefore, the person who wishes to entangle himself in worldly military service is not free from the snares of the devil.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning those who have not observed their penance

[Note: [Col. 0678D] In a decretal of Pope Siricius, chapter 5.] Those who, after performing penance, return like dogs and pigs to their former vomit and wallowing, and again seek the military belt, theatrical pleasures, new marriages, and forbidden sexual relations—the children born after their absolution having exposed their professed lack of continence—concerning these, since they now have no further refuge in doing penance, we have determined the following: they are to join the faithful within the church only in prayer; they are to attend the solemn celebration of the sacred mysteries, although they do not deserve to do so. But they are to be separated from the banquet of the Lord’s table, so that, corrected at least by this severity, they may chastise their own errors in themselves and provide an example to others, so that they may be drawn back from obscene desires. Nevertheless, since they have fallen through carnal weakness, we wish them to be aided by the gift of the viaticum through the grace of communion when they begin to depart to the Lord. We judge that this same rule is to be observed concerning women who, after penance, have bound themselves by such defilements.

## CHAPTER IX. On the remedy of penance, and that the absolution of penitents is to be effected by the bishops’ supplications through the laying on of hands

[Note: [Col. 0679D] In a decretal of Pope Leo to Theodore, Bishop of Forum Julii.] For those who, in a time of necessity and amid dangers of urgent crisis, seek the assistance of penance and immediately afterward reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied. For we can neither set a measure nor define times for God’s mercy, before whom conversion suffers no delay, as the Spirit of God says through the Prophet: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved.” [Col. 0679B] And elsewhere: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified.” Likewise: “With the Lord there is mercy, and with God there is abundant redemption.” Therefore, in dispensing God’s gifts, we ought not to be difficult, nor neglect the groans and tears of those who accuse themselves, since we believe that the very disposition to repent comes from God’s inspiration, as the Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will.”

## CHAPTER X. Concerning those who ask for communion at the time of death; or, if one who was despaired of and received communion recovers again

[Note: [Col. 0679D] From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 13.] Concerning those who are approaching death, the ancient and regular law shall still be observed, so that if anyone is departing from the body, he shall by no means be deprived of the final and necessary viaticum. But if one who was despaired of, after receiving communion and becoming a participant in the offering, recovers again, he is to be placed among those who receive only communion in prayer. In general, however, to anyone at the point of death who asks that the grace of communion be granted to him, the bishop ought reasonably to give it from the offering.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning penitents, that they are not to be reconciled by priests except at the command of the bishop

[Note: [Col. 0679D] From the Council of Carthage, chapter 10.] Let the bishops determine the periods of penance for penitents according to the distinction among their sins; and let a priest not reconcile a penitent without consulting the bishop, except when the bishop’s absence compels this by necessity. But if any penitent’s crime is public and notorious, so that it has stirred the whole Church, hands are to be laid upon him before the apse.

## CHAPTER XII. On the same matter

[Note: [Col. 0679D] From the Council of Carthage, chapter 7.] Bishop Aurelius said: If anyone is placed in danger and asks to be reconciled to the divine altars, and the bishop is absent, the priest must certainly consult the bishop and, at his command, reconcile the person in danger. We ought to strengthen this matter by a salutary decree.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the time for remission of penance

[Note: [Col. 0680D] From a decretal of Pope Innocent, chapter 7.] Concerning penitents who are doing penance either for graver offenses or for lesser ones, the custom of the Roman Church shows that, unless illness intervenes, their penance is to be remitted on the Thursday before Easter. In other respects, it belongs to the priest to judge the gravity of the offenses, so that he may attend to the penitent’s confession and to the weeping and tears of the one correcting himself, and order remission when he sees that satisfactory amendment has been made. Certainly, if anyone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, his penance is to be relaxed before Easter, lest he depart from this world without communion.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning those deprived of communion, and those who die in that state

[Note: [Col. 0680D] From a letter of Pope Leo, chapter 20.] Their case must be reserved for the judgment of the one in whose power it was to delay the death of such persons until the remedy of communion. But we, who did not give communion to them while they were alive, cannot give communion to them when they are dead.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning those who have earnestly fulfilled penance for various offenses

[Note: [Col. 0680D] From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 21.] Concerning those who have sinned through various crimes, and who, persevering in prayer, confession, and penance, have achieved a complete conversion from all evils [Col. 0680C] according to the character of their offense: because of God’s clemency and goodness, communion is to be granted to such persons after the period of penance assigned to them.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Letter of Saint James the Apostle, in which he commands prayer for the sick and anointing with oil

[Note: [Col. 0680D] From Pope Innocent, chapter 8.] The Apostle James wrote: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the priests, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.” There can be no doubt that this must be received and understood concerning sick believers. They can be anointed with holy oil, which, prepared by the bishop, is to be used not only by priests but certainly by all Christians in their own need or that of their families. For this reason it was said to the priests: because bishops, occupied with other duties, cannot go to all the sick. But if the bishop is able, or considers someone worthy of being visited by him, he can without hesitation bless and touch him with chrism, since he is the one who prepares the chrism itself. This, however, cannot be poured upon penitents, because it is a kind of sacrament. For those to whom the remaining sacraments are denied—how can it be thought that one kind may be granted?

# BOOK FOUR. On the judgment of lay penitents

[Col. 0681]

[Col. 0681A] Since homicides arise, as was arranged above, from the rancor of envy, anger, lust, and also avarice, we have rightly judged, as I think, that it should first be shown how the vice itself is to be thoroughly corrected canonically by priestly judgment. Then, according to the order of the vices, the remedy will follow, so that wherever a penitent wishes to be cleansed, he may more easily find it without delay in each matter.

## CHAPTER I. Concerning homicides committed voluntarily

[Note: [Col. 0681D] From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 21.] Those who have committed voluntary homicide shall indeed continually submit themselves to penance, but they shall attain perfection toward the end of their life.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning those who committed homicide involuntarily

[Col. 0681B] [Note: [Col. 0681D] In the same council, chapter 21.] Concerning homicides committed involuntarily, the earlier decree ordered that perfection be attained after seven years of penance. The second, however, prescribed the completion of a period of five years.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning those who in various ways kill their own offspring conceived through fornication

Concerning women who kill their own offspring, or who take measures against themselves to expel what has been conceived in the womb: the ancient decree indeed removes them from the Church until the end of their life. But now we define more humanely that we grant them a period of ten years according to the prescribed stages of penance.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning those who kill their slaves without judicial authority

[Col. 0681C] [Note: [Col. 0681D] From the Council of Agde, chapter 35.] If anyone kills his own slave without the knowledge of the judge, he shall cleanse the guilt of bloodshed through excommunication or two years of penance.

## CHAPTER V. If a mistress kills her maidservant out of jealousy

[Note: [Col. 0681D] From the Council of Elvira, chapter 5.] If a woman, inflamed by jealous fury, beats her maidservant with whips so that she gives up her life in torment within three days, and it is uncertain whether she killed her voluntarily or accidentally: if voluntarily, she is to abstain from communion for seven years; if accidentally, for five years, with lawful penance. But if she falls ill during the prescribed periods, she is to receive communion.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning those who inflict death upon themselves through any negligence; and concerning those who are punished for their crimes

[Note: [Col. 0681D] From the Council of Braga, chapter 6.] It has been decreed that those who inflict death upon themselves, whether by sword, poison, falling from a height, or by any violent means whatsoever, are not to be commemorated in the offering, nor are their bodies to be escorted to burial with psalms [Col. 0682A]. Many have also, through ignorance, arrogated this [practice] to themselves. The same has likewise been decreed concerning those who are punished for their crimes.

# ON LUST

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning those who fornicate irrationally—that is, those who have intercourse with animals or defile themselves with males

[Note: [Col. 0682D] From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 15.] Concerning those who have behaved, or are behaving, irrationally: all who committed such a crime before the age of twenty shall, after completing fifteen years in penance, be deemed worthy of communion in prayers. Then, remaining in this communion for five years, let them finally touch the sacraments of the offering. Their life, however, must be examined, what it was during the time of their repentance, and they are then to receive mercy. But if they have clung to these crimes insatiably, let them spend a longer period in doing penance. Those who, after reaching the age of twenty, have wives and have fallen into this sin are to be received into communion in prayers after doing penance for twenty-five years. Remaining in that state for five years, let them then receive the sacraments of the offering. But if, while having wives and being over fifty years of age, they have committed such an offense, let them receive the grace of communion at the end of their life.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning those who have formerly been defiled with animals or males, or who are still wasting away in this vice

[Col. 0682C]

[Note: [Col. 0682D] The same, chapter 16.] Those who have lived irrationally and have defiled others with the leprosy of the crime of incest, the holy synod commanded to pray among those afflicted by an unclean spirit.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning those who have adulterous wives, or who themselves are proved adulterers

[Note: [Col. 0682D] The same, chapter 18.] If anyone’s wife has committed adultery, or if he himself has committed adultery, he ought to attain perfection through seven years of penance, according to the former stages.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning those who leave their wives, or women who leave their husbands, in order to remain in that state

[Col. 0682D] [Note: [Col. 0682D] From the Council of Africa, chapter 69.] It has been decreed that, according to evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may be joined to another. Rather, let them remain as they are or be reconciled to one another. But if they despise this rule, let them be brought to penance.

## CHAPTER XI. That those who, after a divorce, have entered another marriage are shown to be adulterers

[Col. 0683A]

[Note: [Col. 0683D] In a decretal of Pope Innocent, chapter 26.] Those who, while their wife is alive, although the marriage may appear to have been dissolved, hasten to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers. To such an extent that even the persons to whom such men or women have joined themselves appear themselves to have committed adultery, according to what we read in the Gospel: “Whoever dismisses his wife and marries another commits adultery.” Likewise, one who marries a woman who has been dismissed commits adultery. Therefore, all such persons are to be kept from the communion of the faithful. Concerning their parents or relatives, however, nothing of this sort can be decreed unless they are discovered to have encouraged the illicit union.

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning a man who has a wife and also a concubine

[Col. 0683B]

[Note: [Col. 0683D] From the Council of Toledo, chapter 81. See Berardus on canon 4, distinction 34.] Concerning a man who has a wife: if he has a concubine, he is not to receive communion. But one who has no wife and has a concubine in place of a wife is not to be excluded from communion, provided only that he is content with the union of one woman, whether wife or concubine, according to his choice. Otherwise, while he is living, let him be cast out until he ceases or returns to penance.

## CHAPTER XIII. If anyone’s wife commits adultery, or a husband violates another man’s wife

[Note: [Col. 0683D] From the Council of Braga.] If anyone’s wife commits adultery, or a husband violates another man’s wife, let him do penance for seven years.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning women who marry two brothers, or men who take two sisters as wives

[Col. 0683C]

If a woman marries two brothers, let her be cast out until death. Nevertheless, at the point of death, out of mercy, if she promises that, once restored to health, she will dissolve the bonds of this union, let her obtain the fruit of penance. But if a woman or man dies in such a marriage, penance will be difficult for the one who remains alive.

## CHAPTER XV. That it is not lawful to take another person’s betrothed as a wife

[Note: [Col. 0683D] From the letter of Pope Siricius to Himerius, Bishop of Tarragona, chapter 4.] You have inquired concerning the nuptial veil, whether another man may receive in marriage a girl betrothed to someone else. We absolutely forbid this, because the blessing that the priest bestows upon those about to marry is, among the faithful, like a sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning abductors

[Note: [Col. 0684D] From a letter of Pope Symmachus.] We therefore detest the abductors of widows or virgins because of the enormity of so great a crime, pursuing with still greater severity those who have attempted to join consecrated virgins to themselves in marriage, whether willingly or unwillingly; because of the atrocity of so unspeakable a crime, we order such men to be hanged.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning those who abduct girls

[Note: [Col. 0684D] From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 27.] Concerning those who abduct women, and those who cooperate with abductors under the pretext of living together or who live with the abductors, the holy synod decreed that, if they are clerics, they shall fall from their proper rank; if laymen, they shall be anathematized.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning betrothed girls who are violated by others

It has been decreed that betrothed girls who are subsequently violated by others are to be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that force was inflicted upon them by their abductors. [Col. 0684B]

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning veiled virgins who go astray

[Note: [Col. 0684D] Pope Innocent, chapter 24.] Likewise, those who spiritually marry Christ and are veiled by a priest, if afterward they either marry publicly or secretly defile themselves, are not to be admitted to perform penance unless the man to whom they joined themselves has departed from the world. For if this rule is observed among human beings—so that any woman who, while her husband is alive, marries another is regarded as an adulteress and is not granted permission to do penance unless one of them has died—how much more must it be maintained concerning the woman who had first joined herself to an immortal Bridegroom and afterward passed over to human marriage?

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning unveiled virgins who go astray

[Col. 0684C]

[Note: [Col. 0684D] In the same council, chapter 20.] But those who have not yet been covered by the sacred veil, although they have always professed that they would remain in the virginal commitment, even though they were not veiled, if they should perhaps marry, are to do penance for a certain period, because their pledge was held by the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning those who join themselves to close relatives, so that they are separated from the communion of Christ

[Note: [Col. 0684D] In the Council of Toledo.] We rightly decree that this too must be carefully guarded against, lest any of the faithful desire to join in marriage with a blood relative, as far as the lines of kinship are known through the succession of the generations. For it is written: “No man shall approach his nearest blood relative, to uncover his nakedness.” And again: “The soul that does any of these things shall perish from the midst of his people.” Certainly, those who are forbidden an illicit union will have the freedom to enter into a better marriage.

## CHAPTER XXII. Saint Gregory on incestuous unions

If anyone takes a nun—whom they call a servant of God—as his wife, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0685A] If anyone takes his spiritual co-mother as his wife, let him be anathema.

If anyone takes his brother’s wife as his wife, let him be anathema.

If anyone takes his niece as his wife, let him be anathema.

If anyone takes his stepmother or his daughter-in-law as his wife, let him be anathema.

If anyone takes as his wife a woman from his own kin, or one whom a relative has had, let him be anathema.

If anyone abducts a widow as his wife, or consents to one who does so, let him be anathema.

If anyone abducts a virgin as his wife without betrothing her, or consents to one who does so, let him be anathema.

[Col. 0685B] If anyone consults fortune-tellers, diviners, or enchanters, or uses amulets, let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning those who marry repeatedly

[Note: [Col. 0685D] From the Council of Neocaesarea, chapter 4.] Concerning those who have entered into many marriages: the prescribed period is indeed clear, but their conduct and faith shorten it.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On questions concerning marriage

Those who are married shall abstain from intercourse for three nights and days before receiving communion.

A husband shall abstain from his wife for forty days before Easter and through the octave of Easter. The Apostle says concerning this: “So that you may be free for prayer.” [Col. 0685C] A woman ought to abstain from her husband for three months when she has conceived, before childbirth; and afterward, during the time of purification—that is, for forty days and nights—whether she has given birth to a male or a female child.

# ON SACRILEGE

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning those who seek divinations

[Note: [Col. 0685D] From the Council of Ancyra, chapter 23.] Those who seek divinations, or follow pagan custom, or bring such people into their homes to inquire into something by magical arts or for the purpose of purification, shall be subject to the rule of five years, according to the defined stages of penance.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That Christians may not attend to various observances

[Col. 0685D]

[Note: [Col. 0685D] From the Council of Braga.] Christians may not observe pagan traditions or worship the elements, or the course of the moon or stars, or the empty deception of signs, whether for building a house, for crops, for planting trees, or for joining marriages. For it is written: “Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God.” [Col. 0686A]

In the same council:

It is not permitted, when gathering medicinal herbs, to observe any omens or use incantations, except only with the divine Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, so that God and the Lord may be honored.

Likewise:

Christian women may not observe vanity in their weaving; rather, let them invoke the Lord as helper, who has given them the wisdom to weave.

IN THE SAME COUNCIL.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning augury

Anyone serving auguries or incantations is to be separated from the assembly of the Church.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning perjury

Whoever knowingly commits perjury shall submit himself to seven years of penance and then return to communion.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning theft

Whoever, seized by greed, commits theft shall return what he took and do penance for five years.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning false witnesses

False witnesses are to be removed from ecclesiastical communion unless they have washed away the crimes they committed by the satisfaction of penance.

## CHAPTER XXXI. [Col. 0686C] Concerning those who are at odds

[Note: [Col. 0685D] From the Council of Carthage.] The offerings of disputing brothers are not to be received either in the sacristy or in the treasury.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning those who, out of hatred, do not return to peace

[Note: [Col. 0686D] From the Council of Agde.] It has also been decreed, as frequently happens, that those who have parted from one another in hatred or after a prolonged dispute, and who cannot be recalled to peace despite prolonged effort, are most justly to be expelled from the assembly of the Church by excommunication.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning those who bind themselves by oath not to return to peace

[Note: [Col. 0686D] From the Council of Lérida. Manuscript: “Ohelerdense.”] Whoever has bound himself by oath that, while engaged in a dispute, he will in no way return to peace shall, for perjury, be separated from communion of the Lord’s body and blood for one year. Let him absolve his guilt by almsgiving, tears, and as many fasts as he can; but let him hasten quickly to charity, which covers a multitude of sins.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That Christian laymen ought not to exact interest

[Note: [Col. 0686D] From a letter of Pope Leo.] We have thought that this too should not be passed over: we grieve that certain persons, seized by a shameful desire for profit, practice usury and wish to grow rich through interest. We say this not only concerning those who are established in clerical office, but also concerning laymen who desire to be called Christians. We decree that harsher punishment is to be imposed upon those who are found guilty of this, so that every opportunity for sin may be removed. [Col. 0687A]

[Col. 0688A] Up to this point what is contained in the canons concerning the offenses of laymen has been collected. Now we must proceed to the judgments concerning clerics.

# BOOK FIVE. Here begin the rules canonically issued concerning ministers of the Church if they go astray

[Col. 0687]

## CHAPTER I. Concerning priests who have taken wives or committed fornication

[Note: [Col. 0687D] From the Council of Caesarea.] If a priest takes a wife, let him be deposed from his order. [Col. 0687B] But if he has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled even more decisively and brought to penance.

## CHAPTER II. Concerning deacons likewise

[Note: [Col. 0687D] In the same council.] In the same way, if a deacon falls into the same sin, let him be removed from the order of ministry.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning those promoted to the priesthood who are conscious of sins committed before ordination

[Note: [Col. 0687D] In the same council.] If a priest, charged with a carnal sin, confesses of himself that he sinned before ordination, he shall not consecrate the offerings, but shall remain in the other offices because of his good zeal. But if he has not confessed it himself and it cannot be clearly proven against him, let the matter be left to the authority of his judge.

## CHAPTER IV. On the apostolic canon

A priest or deacon who is caught in fornication, perjury, theft, or homicide is to be deposed. Nevertheless, he is not to be deprived of communion. For Scripture says: “The Lord will not judge twice for the same thing.”

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the various orders’ abstinence from wives

[Note: [Col. 0687D] From the Council of Carthage, chapter 4.] The priests and deacons of God, and those who handle the sacraments, as guardians of chastity, shall abstain from their wives.

## CHAPTER VI. That priests and Levites ought not to have intercourse with women

[Col. 0687D] [Note: [Col. 0687D] In a decretal of Pope Innocent, chapter 16.] Moreover, the Church must uphold in every way what is fitting, chaste, and honorable: that priests and Levites, who are occupied with the necessities of their daily ministry, should not have intercourse with women. For it is written: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.”

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the incontinence of priests and Levites

[Note: [Col. 0687D] Pope Innocent, chapter 21.] Concerning priests and deacons, the discipline of the divine laws is that those who are incontinent while placed in such offices are to be deprived of every ecclesiastical honor and are not to be admitted to a ministry that ought to be fulfilled by continence alone.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning women introduced into clerics’ households

[Note: [Col. 0688D] From the Council of Nicaea, chapter 3.] The great synod absolutely forbids a bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone at all who is in the clergy to have a woman introduced into his household.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning clerics who receive interest

[Note: [Col. 0688D] In the same council, chapter 16.] Since many who are established under the rule pursue avarice and shameful profits, forgetting the divine Scripture that says, “Whoever has not given his money at interest,” and, when lending money, exact one-percent interest, the holy and great synod rightly decreed that if anyone is found, after this definition, receiving interest, or conducting business through some invention or by any means whatever, or demanding a *hemiolia*—that is, one and a half times the principal—or contriving anything of this kind for the sake of shameful profit, he shall be deposed from the clergy and shall be an outsider to the rule.

## CHAPTER X. That no priest or deacon should be a tenant or manager, and that clerics should abstain from interest-seeking

[Col. 0688D]

[Note: [Col. 0688D] From the Council of Carthage, chapter 26.] Presbyters and deacons are not to be contractors or agents, nor are they to seek their livelihood through any disgraceful or dishonorable business, since they ought to heed what is written: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs.” If anyone has lent money, let him receive money; if goods, let him receive the same kind of goods that he had given.

## CHAPTER XI. That clerics or continent persons are not to approach virgins or widows.

[Col. 0688D]

[Note: [Col. 0688D] From the African Council, chapter 5.] Clerics or continent persons are not to approach virgins or widows; unless by the command or permission of the bishops, they are not to approach them.
