## CHAPTER XII. Concerning clerics or monks who do not remain in their chosen state.

[Note: [Col. 0688D] From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 7.] Those who have once been enrolled in the clergy, or have chosen the monastic life, are not to enter either military service [Col. 0689A] or any secular dignity. Those who attempt this and do not repent, so as to return to what they originally chose for God’s sake, are anathematized.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning monks or virgins who do not keep their commitment.

[Note: [Col. 0689D] At the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 15.] A virgin who has consecrated herself to the Lord, and likewise a monk, may not enter into marital rights. If they are found to have committed this, let them be excommunicated. For those who confess, however, we have decreed that the bishop of the same place has authority to grant mercy and clemency.

## CHAPTER XIV. That women are not to enter the sacristy.

[Note: [Col. 0689D] From the Council of Laodicea, chapter 44.] Women ought not to enter the altar area.

## CHAPTER XV. That it is unlawful for women to minister at the sacred altars or to perform any of the duties assigned to men.

[Col. 00689B]

[Note: [Col. 0689D] From a letter of Pope Gelasius, chapter 26.] We have nevertheless heard with indignation that such contempt is shown for divine matters that women are asserted to minister at the sacred altars, and to perform everything assigned exclusively to the service of men, for a sex to which this is not appropriate. Unless, indeed, the entire guilt and crime of all the offenses we have individually touched upon rests upon those priests who either commit these things or, by failing to expose those who commit them, show that they favor their wicked excesses.

## CHAPTER XVI. That no priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons.

[Col. 0689C] [Note: [Col. 0690D] Of Pope Celestine, chapter 20.] No priest is permitted to be ignorant of his canons, or to do anything that could contradict the regulations of the Fathers.

## CHAPTER XVII. Augustine’s question concerning pollutions, and Gregory’s answer.

[Note: [Col. 0690D] Augustine’s question.] After the illusion that usually occurs in a dream, may anyone receive the Lord’s body, or, if he is a priest, celebrate the sacred mysteries?

### Gregory’s answer.

Indeed, the Testament of the Old Law, as we have already said in the preceding chapter, calls such a person unclean unless he has been washed with water. He is not permitted to enter the church until evening. Yet the spiritual people, understanding this in another way, will receive it according to the interpretation we have given: for the person who is tempted by impurity and defiled in thought by real images is, as it were, deceived in a dream. But he must be washed with water, so that he may wash away the sins of his thought with tears. And unless the fire of temptation has first withdrawn, let him recognize himself as guilty, as it were, until evening.

Yet in this same illusion a very necessary distinction must be made, and careful consideration must be given to what causes it in the mind of the sleeper. For sometimes it arises from overeating, sometimes from an excess or weakness of nature, and sometimes from thought. If it has arisen from an excess of nature, this illusion is not at all to be feared, because the mind, not knowing that it has endured this, should be pitied more for having suffered it than blamed for having caused it.

But when the appetite of the palate is carried beyond measure in taking food, and consequently the receptacles of the bodily fluids are weighed down, the mind incurs some guilt as a result—not, however, to the point of forbidding the reception of the sacred mystery or the celebration of the solemn rites of Mass, when perhaps a feast day requires it, or necessity compels the mystery to be offered because another priest is absent from the place. If others are present who can fulfill the ministry, the illusion caused by overeating ought not to prevent reception of the sacred mystery; but, as I think, the priest ought humbly to abstain from offering the sacred mystery, provided that no shameful image has disturbed the mind of the sleeper.

For there are some in whom such an illusion commonly arises without their mind, even while their body is asleep, being polluted by shameful imaginings. In this matter one thing is shown: the mind itself is not then guilty but free in its own judgment, since it remembers nothing shameful seen in the sleeping body, yet while awake it remembers having fallen into gluttony.

But if the illusion in the sleeping mind arises from a shameful thought entertained while awake, the mind’s guilt is evident. It sees from what root that pollution proceeded: for what it knowingly thought, it unknowingly endured. Yet we must consider whether the thought fell into suggestion, into pleasure, or—what is more serious—into consent to sin.

For every sin is completed in three ways: suggestion, pleasure, and consent. Suggestion comes through the devil, pleasure through the flesh, and consent through the spirit. The serpent suggested the first fault; Eve, as flesh, took pleasure in it; Adam, as spirit, consented.

A great distinction is necessary between suggestion and pleasure, and between pleasure and consent. The mind must preside as judge over itself. When an evil spirit suggests sin to the mind, if no pleasure in sin follows, the sin has not been committed at all. But when the flesh begins to take pleasure, sin begins to be born. If, after deliberation, the person descends even to consent, then sin is understood to be completed.

Thus, in suggestion there is the seed of sin; in pleasure, its nourishment; in consent, its completion. It often happens that what the evil spirit sows in thought the flesh draws into pleasure, while the soul nevertheless does not consent to that pleasure. Although the flesh cannot take pleasure without the mind, the mind itself, resisting the pleasures of the flesh, is nevertheless unwillingly bound in carnal pleasure, so that it opposes it by reason and does not consent, yet remains bound by pleasure and bitterly laments that it is bound.

Hence that foremost soldier of the heavenly army also groaned, saying: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members.” [Col. 0691A] If he was captive, he was not fighting; yet he was fighting. Therefore he was both captive and fighting [Note: [Col. 0691D] Vulgate: “he was not fighting; therefore he was captive and was not captive, but was fighting.” CANIS.].

The law that is in the members therefore opposed the law of the mind. Yet if he was fighting, he was not captive. Here, then, is a person who is a free captive: free because of the righteousness he loves, captive because of the pleasure he bears unwillingly. Amen.

## CHAPTER XVIII. That it is of no benefit to a priest, even if he lives well, if he does not correct those who live badly by reproving them.

[Note: [Col. 0692D] This is chapter 20 of book I of Prosper’s *Life of the Contemplative*.] As the Apostle says, we ought to offer ourselves as an example to the faithful. But what benefit will there be if the person entrusted with the care of exhorting the good and chastising the wicked presents himself as an example for the good by living well, yet does not correct the wicked through silence?

For this reason, unless I am mistaken, the priest must live holily. Otherwise his words are emptied of force by deeds that contradict them: if he does not do what he preaches ought to be done, or if he presumes to preach what he himself does not do, he accomplishes nothing among those who know his life.

He has been placed over the Church of God for this purpose: not only to instruct others by the example of his conduct while living well, but also, by preaching boldly, to set each person’s sins before his eyes; to show what punishment awaits the obstinate and what glory awaits the obedient. He must not contemptuously despair of anyone’s salvation. He must mourn for those who refuse to amend, imitating the Apostle who says: “That I may mourn for many of those who sinned before and have not repented.” And again: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?”

Therefore, knowing that if he spares or favors any rich or powerful persons who live badly, he will destroy them together with himself and perish, he must live holily for the sake of example and teach because of the duty of his administration. He must be certain that his own righteousness will be of no assistance to him when the soul of one who perishes is required from his hand. When someone else perishes, someone upon whom no obligation of teaching rests, that person alone will suffer the punishment of his crime. But the one entrusted with the ministry of the word, even if he lives holily, will perish with all those who perished while he remained silent, if he is ashamed or afraid to rebuke those living wickedly.

And what will it profit him not to be punished for his own sin, when he must be punished for another’s? I am mistaken if the Lord does not proclaim this through the prophet Ezekiel under a terrifying warning, saying to him: “And you, son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel.”

Nor should we pass over without attention the fact that he calls the priest a watchman. Just as it is the watchman’s duty to look out from a higher place and observe more than everyone else, so the priest must be appointed in a position higher than all others and possess a greater measure of knowledge, by which he can instruct those living beneath him.

Let us now see what the divine word continues: “You will hear a word from my mouth,” it says, “and you will announce it to them from me.” Thus the priest must say what he has learned from divine reading, what God has inspired in him—not what he has discovered through the presumption of human understanding. “You will announce it to them from me,” it says: from me, not from yourself. You will speak my words; there is no reason for you to puff yourself up before them as though you were God. “Announce it to them from me,” he says.

But let us hear what he is to announce: “If, when I say to the wicked man, ‘Wicked man, you will surely die,’ you do not speak so that the wicked man may guard himself from his way, that wicked man will die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand.”

What could be expressed more forcefully or said more clearly? “If,” he says, “you do not speak to the wicked man so that he may guard himself from his wickedness, and he perishes, I will require his blood from your hand.” This means: if you do not announce his sins to him, if you do not rebuke him so that he may turn from his wickedness and live, I will cast both you, who did not rebuke him, and him, who sinned while you were silent, into everlasting flames.

Who, I ask, could be so stony-hearted? Who so hard as iron that this sentence would not terrify him? Who could be so alien to faith as not to believe it? [Note: [Col. 0692D] Up to this point from Prosper, chapter 21, book I, in the same work.]

## CHAPTER XIX. A sorrowful description of priests living according to the flesh.

But we, delighting in present things, while seeking our comforts and honors in this life, hasten to become not better but richer, not holier but more honored than others. We think carnally not about the Lord’s flock, which has been entrusted to us to feed and protect, but about our own desires, domination, wealth, and other enticements.

We wish to be called shepherds, yet we do not strive to be shepherds. We avoid the labor of our office and desire its dignity. We do not drive away the wild beasts of unclean spirits as they tear the flock apart; and what they had left behind, we ourselves consume, since we not only fail to rebuke sinful rich or powerful people but even honor them, lest they be offended and stop sending us their customary gifts or withdraw the services we desire.

Thus, captured by their gifts and services—or rather, through these things made their dependents—we fear to speak to them about their sin or the future judgment. Therefore the divine word sternly crushes our arrogance, but our hearing admits nothing by which we might improve, because, captivated by the sweetness of the present life, we do not wish to consider what eternal punishment awaits our negligence.

These words, then, are spoken against shepherds, whose empty title we use to flatter ourselves.

“Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. Are not the flocks fed by the shepherds? You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool; you slaughtered what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen what was weak; you did not heal what was sick; you did not bind up what was broken; you did not bring back what was cast away; you did not seek what had perished. Instead, you ruled over them with authority and power. And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd. And they became food for all the beasts of the field.”

And a little later:

“Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. As I live, says the Lord God: because my flocks have become prey and my sheep food for all the beasts of the field, because there was no shepherd—for the shepherds did not seek my flock, but the shepherds fed themselves and did not feed my flock—therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord.

Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself am against the shepherds, and I will require my flock from their hand. I will make them cease, so that they will no longer feed the flock; nor will the shepherds feed themselves any longer.”

Who would not tremble at this? Who could receive it without intolerable fear of the future judgment, unless he either does not understand or does not believe what is to come? Yet God has set down everything he wished to be observed so openly and established it with such authority in his name that we more easily—though it is unspeakable to say so—despise it than fail to understand or believe it.

Let us now take as manifest and divine what we hear, when we hear, “Thus says the Lord.” Who would not believe that what God says will come to pass, unless he does not believe God? And when he says, “Woe to the shepherds,” who would not understand that this “woe” is spoken as a curse and that by the name of shepherds he means us, unless he gives no thought to what is to come?

We undertake the care of the Lord’s flocks as shepherds appointed to feed them, yet we ourselves are fed when we do not look to the welfare of the flocks but attend to whatever nourishes and increases our own pleasures. We gladly receive the milk and wool of Christ’s sheep through their daily offerings and the tithes of the faithful, while we lay aside the care of feeding and restoring the flocks from whom we perversely wish to be fed.

We do not heal with spiritual counsel the person weakened by sins. We do not strengthen or restore with priestly help the person broken by various tribulations. We do not recall the erring to the way of salvation. We do not seek with pastoral solicitude the person already lost through despair of forgiveness. We have become powerful only for this purpose: to claim tyrannical domination over our subjects, not to defend the afflicted against the violence of the powerful who rage against them like wild beasts.

That is why some are grievously worn down and perish both by the powerful of this world and, what is worse, by us. The Lord threatens terrifyingly that he will require them from our hand, saying: “I will require my sheep from the hand of the shepherds, and I will make them cease, so that they will no longer feed.”

What else does this mean but that I will strip the shepherds who feed themselves rather than my flocks of the eminence of their dignity and cast them among the reprobate because they refused to preserve their honor?

Terrified by the consideration of these things and of those like them, fear and trembling came upon me, and darkness covered me. And I said: “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and rest?”

This is the whole reason why, remembering my incompetence and the end that is to come, I groaned and wished, laying down the burden of my episcopate, to flee far away, remain in solitude, and there await God, who would save me from my faintheartedness and from the very storm of anxieties intolerable to me [Note: [Col. 0693B] Up to this point from Prosper.]

# [BOOK OF PENITENCE]

[Col. 0693]

## HERE BEGINS THE BOOK OF PENITENCE, TAKEN FROM THE ARCHIVE OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

## HALITGAR’S PREFACE

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693C] We have also added to this work of our excerpting [Note: [Col. 0693C] In Stewart’s manuscript he was composing Halitgar’s sixth book.] another Roman Penitential, which we took from the archive of the Roman Church. Yet we do not know by whom it was published. Therefore we decided to append it to the foregoing statements of the canons, so that, if some of these statements should perhaps seem superfluous to anyone, or if someone should be unable to find there what he desires concerning individual crimes, he may at least find in this final brief work all offenses explained.

## HOW PENITENTS ARE TO BE RECEIVED, JUDGED, OR RECONCILED

Whenever Christians approach penitence [Note: [Col. 0693D] These words are found verbatim in Rubertus’s *Penitential*, published by Morinus at the end of the *Treatise on Penance*, p. 13.], we impose fasts, and we too ought to share their fast for one or two weeks, or as much as we can, lest what our Lord and Savior said to the Jewish priests be said to us: “Woe to you, lawyers, who burden people and place heavy and unbearable burdens on their shoulders, while you yourselves do not touch those burdens with one of your fingers.”

For no one can lift up a person falling under a burden unless he bends down to extend his hand to him. Nor can any physician heal the wounds of the sick unless he shares in their foulness. Likewise, no priest or bishop can heal the wounds of sinners or remove sins from souls unless he does so with watchful care and prayers of tears.

Therefore, dearest brother, we must be solicitous for sinners, because we are members of one another. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. Therefore, if we see someone lying in sins, let us hasten to call him to penitence through our instruction.

Whenever you give counsel to a sinner, immediately assign him a penance: how long he must fast and redeem his sins, lest you forget how long he ought to fast for his sins and thus have to inquire about his sins again. He may perhaps be ashamed to confess his sins again and to be judged again and more severely.

For not all clerics who find this writing should make use of it or read it [Col. 0695B], but only those for whom it is necessary, that is, presbyters [Note: [Col. 0695D] Similar material may be found in the book *On Duties*, attributed to Alcuin.]. Just as no one except bishops and presbyters, to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted, ought to offer the sacrifice, so no others ought to usurp those judgments.

If necessity should arise and a presbyter not be present, let a deacon receive the penitent for satisfaction or holy communion [Note: [Col. 0695D] This is absent from Egbert; nor does he speak of satisfaction or communion. Many deny that a deacon could perform such functions.].

As we said above, bishops and presbyters must humble themselves and pray with sighs of sorrow and tears, not only for their own sins but also for those of all Christians, so that they may say: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?”

When someone comes to the priest to confess his sins, let the priest tell him to wait a little until he enters his room for prayer. If he does not have a room, the priest should nevertheless say this prayer in his heart.

### Let us pray.

Almighty Lord God [Note: [Col. 0696D] This prayer is found in full in the Roman Order. Bill. *Pat.* vol. X, p. 27.], be gracious to me, a sinner, so that I may worthily give you thanks, since through your mercy you have made me, unworthy as I am, a minister of priestly office and have appointed me, a humble and insignificant sinner, to pray and intercede before our Lord Jesus Christ for those who sin and return to penitence.

Therefore, Lord and ruler, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, who does not desire the death of a sinner but that he should turn and live, receive my prayer, which I pour out before your clemency for your male and female servants who have come to penitence, through our Lord.

When the person who has come to penitence sees the priest sorrowful and weeping over his crimes, he himself is more deeply struck with fear of God, and grieves and abhors his sins more intensely.

If you see each person approaching penitence standing firmly and persevering in penitence [Col. 0696A], receive him. If he is able to fast according to what has been imposed upon him, do not forbid him but permit him to do so. Those who hasten to discharge the burden owed them quickly are more worthy of praise, because the fast is owed.

Therefore give this instruction to those who do penance: if they fast and complete what the priest has commanded, they will be cleansed from their sins. But if they return again to their former habit or sin, it is as with the dog that returns to its vomit.

Every penitent, therefore, ought not to fast only what the priest has commanded him. After completing what has been ordered, he ought also to fast as much as seems appropriate to him, whether you assign it on Wednesday or on Friday. If he does what the priest has instructed him, his sins will be forgiven; but if afterward he fasts of his own accord, he acquires a reward and the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore, whoever fasts throughout the entire week for his sins should eat and drink on Saturday and Sunday whatever is set before him. Yet let him guard himself against overeating and drunkenness, because wantonness is born from drunkenness. Hence blessed Paul forbade it, saying: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is wantonness”—not because wantonness is in wine, but in drunkenness.

If someone is perhaps unable to fast and has the means to give something in redemption [Note: [Col. 0696D] Regino has the same words in his ancient manuscript collection, book II, chapter 44. BASN.], then, if he is rich, let him give twenty solidi for seven weeks. If he does not have enough to give that much, let him give ten solidi. If he is very poor, let him give three solidi.

Let no one be troubled because we have ordered twenty solidi, or less, to be given. For if someone is rich, it is easier for him to give twenty solidi than for a poor person to give three. But each person must consider to whom he ought to give: whether for the redemption of captives, or upon the holy altar, or to be distributed to poor Christians.

And know this, brothers: when male or female slaves come to you seeking penitence, do not burden them or compel them to fast as much as the rich, because slaves are not in their own power. Therefore impose upon them half the penance.

### The prologue ends.

# HERE BEGIN THE PRAYERS FOR ASSIGNING PENANCE

First, let the priest recite Psalm 37: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” Afterward let him say, “Let us pray,” and Psalm 111: “I will bless,” up to “he will be renewed.” [Col. 0696D] Again let him say, “Let us pray,” and Psalm 50: “Have mercy,” up to “blot out all my iniquities.” After this, Psalm: “O God, in your name.” And let him say, “Let us pray.” Then Psalm: “Why do you boast in wickedness?” up to “the righteous will see.” And let him say this prayer:

### Let us pray.

O God, whose pardon no one fails to need, remember, Lord, your servant N., who is stripped naked in the frailty of a slippery and earthly body. We ask that you grant forgiveness to the one who confesses and spare the suppliant, so that we who are accused on account of our merits may be saved through your compassion. Through the Lord, etc.

### Another prayer.

O God, beneath whose eyes every heart trembles and all consciences quake, be gracious to the groans of all and heal the wounds of all, so that, just as none of us is free from guilt, so no one may be excluded from forgiveness. Through the Lord, etc.

### Another prayer.

O God of infinite mercy and boundless truth, be gracious to our iniquities and heal all the sicknesses of our souls, so that, having received the forgiveness of your mercies, we may always rejoice in your blessing. Through the Lord.

### Another prayer.

I beseech the majesty of your clemency and mercy, Lord, that you may deign to release forgiveness to your servant who confesses his sins and crimes, and pardon the guilt of his past offenses. You brought back the lost sheep upon your shoulders; you heard and were appeased by the publican’s prayers and confession. Be appeased also, Lord, toward this your servant; look favorably upon his prayers, so that he may remain acceptable in confession, and so that his petition may quickly obtain your perpetual clemency. Restored to the holy altars and sacraments, may he again be devoted to the hope of eternal life and heavenly glory. Through the Lord.

### Imposition of hands.

Holy Father, almighty, eternal God [Col. 0697C], who through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, have deigned to heal our wounds, we, your humble priests, suppliantly ask and beseech you to incline the ear of your goodness to our prayers. Forgive all crimes and pardon every sin, and grant this your servant, Lord, forgiveness in place of punishment, joy in place of sorrow, and life in place of death, so that, trusting in your mercy, he may deserve to attain eternal life. Through the Lord.

# FROM THE ROMAN PENITENTIAL: HOW INDIVIDUAL PENITENTS ARE TO BE JUDGED

## First, concerning homicide.

If a cleric commits homicide, let him do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water. If a layman, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. A subdeacon, six years; a deacon, seven; a presbyter, ten; a bishop, twelve.

If someone consents to the commission of homicide, let him do penance for seven years, three on bread and water. If a layman voluntarily commits homicide, let him do penance for seven years, three on bread and water.

If someone crushes an infant, let him do penance for three years, the first of them on bread and water. A cleric likewise is to observe this.

## Concerning fornication, from the same Penitential.

If a cleric commits fornication as the Sodomites did, let him do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water.

If a cleric commits adultery—that is, with another man’s wife or betrothed—and begets a son, let him do penance for seven years [ann.]. If he does not beget a son and the matter has not come to public knowledge, then, if he is a cleric, let him do penance for three years, the first of them on bread and water [Col. 0698A]. If he is a deacon or monk, seven years, three on bread and water. A bishop, twelve years, five on bread and water.

If a cleric or anyone of a higher order who has a wife has intercourse with her again after his conversion or ordination, let him know that he has committed adultery; therefore let him do penance as established above.

If someone fornicates with a nun or a woman dedicated to God, let him recognize that he has committed adultery. According to the earlier regulations, let each one do penance according to his order.

If someone fornicates by himself, or with an animal, or with any quadruped, let him do penance for three years. If this occurs after ordination or a vow, let him do penance for seven years.

If a cleric desires a woman but cannot sin because the woman does not accept him, let him do penance for half a year on bread and water and abstain entirely from wine and meat.

If a cleric, after vowing himself to God, returns to secular dress, like a dog to its vomit, or takes a wife, let him do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water, and afterward let him not be joined to her in marriage. If the holy synod or the apostolic see so wishes, it shall separate them from communion with Catholics.

Likewise, if a woman, after vowing herself to God, commits such a crime, she shall be subject to the same sentence.

If a layman fornicates as the Sodomites did, let him do penance for seven years. If he begets a son by another man’s wife—that is, if he commits adultery and violates his neighbor’s marriage bed—let him do penance for three years. Let him abstain from more luxurious foods and from his own wife, and in addition give the husband of the violated wife a payment for her chastity [Col. 0698C].

If someone wishes to commit adultery but cannot—that is, he is not received—let him do penance for forty days.

If a virgin man has intercourse with a virgin, let her become his wife if her parents wish it. Nevertheless, let them do penance for one year and remain married.

If someone fornicates with an animal, let him do penance for one year. If he has no wife, let him do penance for half a year.

If someone abducts a virgin or widow, let him do penance for three years.

If a man who has a betrothed woman perhaps brings disgrace upon her sister and has intercourse with her as though she were his own, and then takes her as his wife—that is, the woman to whom he was betrothed—while the other woman who suffered the disgrace perhaps kills herself, let all who consented to this deed be reduced to ten years on bread and water, according to the regulations of the canons.

If someone kills the children born to women who have committed fornication, or hastens to cause abortions, the original ruling forbids communion until death. This is indeed the true definition. But so that they may receive something more humane, let us establish for them a period of ten years, and let them do penance according to the degrees that have been established.

## Concerning perjury.

If a cleric commits perjury, let him do penance for seven years, three on bread and water. A layman, seven; a subdeacon, six; a deacon, seven; a presbyter, ten; a bishop, twelve.

If someone commits perjury under compulsion from some necessity, or unknowingly, let him do penance for three years, one on bread and water. And let him redeem a soul on his behalf—that is, free a male or female slave from servitude—and perform many acts of charity.

If someone commits perjury out of greed, let him sell all his possessions and give them to the poor, have his hair tonsured, enter a monastery, and serve there until death.

## Concerning theft.

If someone commits capital theft—that is, steals a quadruped, breaks into something, or steals anything of greater value—let him do penance for seven years. A layman, five; a subdeacon, seven; a deacon, eight; a presbyter, ten; a bishop, twelve years.

If someone commits a minor theft once or twice, let him make restitution according to his means and do penance for one year on bread and water. If he cannot make restitution, let him do penance for three years.

If someone violates a tomb, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water.

If a layman commits theft, let him return to his neighbor what he stole and do penance for three Lents on bread and water. Let him give alms to the poor from his labor, and let him be joined to the altar according to the priest’s judgment [Col. 0699B].

## Concerning magic.

If someone destroys another person through his magic, let him do penance for seven years, three on bread and water.

If someone becomes a magician out of love and harms no one, then, if he is a layman, let him do penance for half a year; if a cleric, one year on bread and water; if a deacon, three years on bread and water; if a priest, five years, two on bread and water.

But if by this means someone deceives a woman’s childbirth, let each person add six Lents, lest he be guilty of homicide.

If someone causes storms, let him do penance for seven years, four on bread and water.

## Concerning sacrilege.

If someone commits sacrilege [Possibly *sortilegium*, divination by lot]—that is, those whom they call *haruspices*, who practice augury, whenever they have practiced augury—or by any evil device, let them do penance for three years on bread and water.

If someone is a diviner, those whom they call *divini*, and practices any divination, because this is demonic, let him do penance for five years, three on bread and water.

If someone does what many do on the Kalends of January, and what they call “in the little deer,” or rides in a vehicle, let him do penance for three years.

If someone possesses lots, which they irrationally call “of the saints,” or possesses any lots, or draws lots by any evil device, or practices divination, let him do penance for three years, initially on bread and water [Note: [Col. 0699D] The “lots of the saints” were divinations from the words of Scripture, concerning which Saint Augustine writes near the end of letter 55, otherwise 119. For these and similar matters, consult Berardus on canon 16, cause 26, question 7.].

If someone makes a vow or fulfills one at trees, springs, a barrier, or anywhere else except in a church, let him do penance for three years on bread and water [Col. 0699D], because this is sacrilege or demonic. But whoever eats or drinks there, let him do penance for one year on bread and water.

If someone is a mathematician—that is, if through invocation of demons he has taken away a person’s mind—let him do penance for five years, initially on bread and water.

If someone makes amulets or magical bindings, which is detestable, let him do penance for three years on bread and water.

If some go together to a festival in the abominable places of the pagans and, bringing their own food, eat there, it has been decided that they are to be received through two years of penance. But whether they are received with an offering, let each bishop, having approved their life, examine their individual acts.

If someone eats or drinks beside a pagan shrine through ignorance, let him promise that he will never repeat it and do penance for forty days on bread and water.

But if he does this contemptuously—that is, after the priest has preached to him that it was sacrilege—and shares in the table of demons, then, if he did it solely through the fault of gluttony, let him do penance for three Lents on bread and water. But if he did it for the worship of demons and the honor of an idol, let him do penance for three years.

If someone has appeared as sacrificed a second and third time, let him do penance for three years and receive communion for two years without an offering.

If someone eats blood, carrion, or what has been sacrificed to idols, and was not compelled by necessity, let him fast for twelve weeks.

## Concerning various chapters.

[Col. 0700B] If anyone voluntarily cuts off any member of his body, let him do penance for four years, initially on bread and water. If anyone voluntarily causes an abortion, let him do penance for three years, at first on bread and water. If anyone, by force or by any device, wrongfully invades or takes another’s property, let him do penance in the same manner as in the preceding sentence, and give many alms. If anyone by any device reduces a slave or any other person to captivity, or hands him over to captivity, let him do penance as above. If anyone burns down a church, let him do penance for fifteen years, diligently restore it, and distribute its value to the poor. If anyone voluntarily burns the field or house of another, let him do penance as above. If anyone, in anger, strikes another and sheds his blood or disables him, let him first pay him compensation [Col. 0700C] and seek a physician. If he is a layman, let him fast for forty days on bread and water; if a cleric, forty-five days; a deacon, seven months; a priest, one year. If anyone engages in hunting, let a cleric do penance for one year, a deacon for two, and a priest for three. If anyone cheats or neglects any duty belonging to the ministry of the holy Church, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. If any have sinned with animals and are not yet twenty years old, after completing fifteen years in penance let them be admitted to communion in prayer. Then, after remaining for five years in this communion, let them receive the sacrament of the offering. Their life during the time of penance must also be examined, and thus let them obtain mercy. But if they have clung persistently to these crimes, let them spend a longer period in performing penance. Those, however, who, after reaching the age of twenty and having wives, have fallen into this sin, are to be received into communion in prayer after carrying out twenty-five years of penance. After remaining in it for five years, let them then receive the sacrament of the offering. But if any who have wives and are over fifty years old have committed such an offense, let them obtain the grace of communion at the end of life.

## On drunkenness and fornication

Someone becomes drunk on wine or beer, contrary to the prohibition of the Savior and his apostles. If [Col. 0701A] he has made a vow of holiness, let him expiate the offense for forty days on bread and water; a layman, however, shall do penance for seven days. A bishop who commits fornication shall be degraded and shall do penance for twelve years. A priest or deacon who commits natural fornication [Note: [Col. 0701D] “Before the monastic vow.” These words were missing in Stewart’s manuscript.] before taking the monastic vow shall do penance for three years and ask forgiveness at every hour. He shall perform prostrations each week, except on the days of Pentecost.

## On minor matters

If anyone, through accidental negligence, loses the sacrifice by leaving it outside, and it is devoured by someone, let him do penance for forty days; but if not [Note: [Col. 0701D] That is, if it did not happen accidentally.], let him do penance for one year. If anyone unknowingly receives communion with an excommunicated person, let him do penance for forty days. If anyone knowingly communicates with an excommunicated person by word, association, food, or drink, let him do penance for forty days [Col. 0701B] on bread and water and salt. If the sacrifice falls to the ground through negligence, let a superposition be performed. If the sacrifice falls from the hand of the one offering it to the ground, and nothing is found, whatever is found shall be burned in the place where it fell; the ashes shall be buried beneath the altar, and the priest shall do penance for half a year.

We ought to offer for good things, never for evil ones. Priests are not forbidden to offer for their bishops. Whoever supplies a consecrated thing to barbarians shall do penance for three years. Those who strip monasteries, falsely saying that they are redeeming captives, shall do penance for three years and shall give the poor everything they have taken away. Whoever eats the flesh of animals whose death he does not know shall do penance for a third of a year. Let us bring forth the statutes of the ancient Fathers. Children who merely converse and transgress the rules of their elders shall make amends with three prostrations. Those who give a simple kiss shall make seven prostrations. But those who do so with defilement, without an embrace, shall be corrected with fifteen prostrations.

## On the handling of the sacrifice

Whoever does not guard the sacrifice properly, and a mouse eats it, shall do penance for forty days. Whoever loses his corporal cloth (*chrismal*) [Note: [Col. 0701D] It should not be read as though fifty years of penance were being assigned, nor does the letter L denote the number; it should be read as *Chrismal*. What is meant here, however, is the corporal cloth.] or the sacrifice alone, in any region, so that it cannot be found, shall do penance for three Lents or one year. If anyone spills the chalice upon the altar when the linens are being removed, let him do penance for seven days. If it falls [Note: [Col. 0702D] Or, if the sacrifice falls within the table. This is how it stands in Menard’s manuscript; nevertheless, *in stramen*—“into the straw”—is preferable. In the penitential manuscript of the Colbert Library, no. 1348, it reads: “If the sacrifice falls from the hand into the straw, let the one responsible do penance for seven days.”] into the straw, let him do penance for seven days. One who vomits [Alternative reading: “takes”] the sacrifice because he is burdened by fullness of stomach shall do penance for forty days; if he throws it into the fire, for twenty days. A deacon who forgets to offer the offering without a linen cloth shall do penance in the same way until the offerings have been made. Those who receive the sacrifice after food or any very small refreshment, except as a viaticum, shall do penance: children for three days, adults for seven, and clerics for twenty.

If unclean little creatures are found in flour or in any dry food, or in honey or milk, whatever is around their bodies shall be thrown away.

[Note: [Col. 0702D] Gregory III has almost the same provisions in the *Judgments*, chapter 28; see *Concilia*, vol. VI, p. 1483. Yet many things concerning the Eucharist are required here that Gregory omits.] Whoever has been negligent regarding the sacrifice, so that it is consumed by worms and reduced to nothing, shall do penance for three Lents. If he finds it intact but with a worm in it, it shall be burned, and its ashes shall thus be hidden beneath the altar; the negligent person shall do penance for forty days. If it is found as described above, let it be cleansed; if it has fallen only as far as the altar, let a superposition be performed. If anything drips from the chalice onto the ground through negligence, let the tongue lick it up; let the board be scraped and burned in the fire [Col. 0702B]; and let the person do penance for fifty days. If the chalice drips upon the altar, let the minister suck it up, and let the linen touched by the drop be washed three times; let him do penance for three days. If the priest stumbles once over the Lord’s Prayer as it is being said—dangerously—or over the psalms, let him do penance with fifty psalms; for a second time, with one hundred blows.

## Likewise, on homicide

If anyone kills a person without cause during a public military expedition, let him fast for twenty-one weeks. But if he kills someone while defending himself, his parents, or his household, he shall not be guilty. If he wishes to fast, it is in his power, because he did this under compulsion. If he commits homicide during peacetime, and it was not because a crowd compelled him or because of enmity, in order to seize the victim’s property, let him fast for twenty-eight weeks and [Col. 0702C] return the property of the person he killed to his wife or children.

## On sick penitents

If anyone comes to perform penance, and illness comes upon him, so that he cannot complete what the priest has commanded him, let him be admitted to holy communion. And if the Lord wishes to save him, let him fast afterward. If anyone does not repent and perhaps falls ill, and asks to receive communion, let him not be forbidden. Rather, give him holy communion and command him that, if it pleases God’s mercy and he escapes from that illness, he should afterward confess everything and thus do penance.

## On excommunicated persons who die

If an excommunicated person dies after having already confessed, and no opportunity arises but death overtakes him [Col. 0702D], whether on the road or in the house, let one of his relatives offer something for him at the holy altar, or for the redemption of captives, or in commemoration of his soul.

## On incest

[Col. 0703A]

If anyone takes his wife’s daughter, you cannot judge him until they have first been separated. After they have been separated, impose fourteen weeks on each of them, and let them never unite again. But if either the man or the woman wishes to marry, he or she shall have the power to do so—but not the woman whom he abandoned. If anyone takes a kinswoman, a stepmother, or his uncle’s widow—and likewise those who take their father’s wife or their wife’s sister—the offense is a grave one; let them be condemned according to the canons. But because many do not know the number of women with whom they have fornicated, let them fast for fifty weeks.

## On food sacrificed to idols

If anyone, while still an infant, unknowingly tastes [Col. 0703B] food that has been sacrificed to idols, or carrion, or anything abominable, let him fast for three weeks. If anyone unknowingly eats food sacrificed to idols or carrion, forgiveness shall be granted him, because he did it unknowingly; nevertheless, let him fast for three weeks.

## On theft caused by necessity

If anyone, because of necessity, steals food, clothing, or a four-footed animal because of hunger or nakedness, forgiveness is granted him. Let him fast for four weeks. If he returns it, do not compel him to fast. If anyone steals a horse, ox, beast of burden, or cow, or food or anything that sustains an entire household, let him fast as above.

## On adultery

[Col. 0703C] If a woman deceives her mother’s husband, she cannot be judged until she leaves him. When they have been separated, let her fast for fourteen weeks. If anyone who has a lawful wife abandons her and takes another, the woman he has taken is not his. He shall neither eat nor drink nor speak at all with her, because he took her unlawfully, nor with her relatives. If they nevertheless consent to one another, let them be excommunicated. If a woman persuades another woman’s husband, let her be excommunicated from the Christians. If a Christian sees a Christian wandering about or lost, who is his relative, and sells him, he is not worthy to have rest among Christians until he redeems him. But if he cannot find the place where he is, let him give the price he received for him, and redeem another [Col. 0703D] from slavery, and let him fast for twenty-eight weeks.

## On the penance of those married three times

If anyone’s wife dies, he has the power to take another; likewise a woman. If he takes a third, let him fast for three weeks. If he takes a fourth or fifth, let him fast for twenty-one weeks.

## On one who has mutilated himself

If anyone cuts his hair or tears his face with a sword or with his fingernails, let him fast for three weeks after the death of his parents. After he has fasted, let him receive communion.

## On sorcerers

A male or female herbalist, or a killer of infants, when he or she comes to the end of life, if he or she seeks penance with mourning and tearful weeping, accept him or her if the practice has ceased; let him or her fast for fifty weeks. [Col. 0704A]

## On strangled animals

If a dog, fox, or hawk kills something; or if an animal dies from a club, a stone, or an arrow without an iron point, all these are considered strangled animals; they must not be eaten. Whoever eats them shall fast for seven weeks.

## On animals torn apart

If anyone strikes a deer or another animal with an arrow, and it is found after the third day, and perhaps a wolf, bear, dog, or fox has tasted it, no one shall eat it. Whoever eats it shall fast for four weeks. If a hen dies in a well, the well shall be emptied. If anyone knowingly drinks from it, let him fast for one week. If a mouse, hen, or anything else falls into wine, no one shall drink from it. If it falls into oil or honey, let the oil be used in a lamp, as medicine, or for some other necessity. If a fish dies in a fishpond, it must not be eaten. Whoever eats it shall fast for four weeks. If a pig or hen eats part of a human body, it must not be eaten or kept for breeding; rather, it shall be killed and given to the dogs. If a wolf tears an animal and it dies, no one shall eat it. But if it survives and a human being later kills it, it may be eaten.

## On polluted animals

Whether with a goat, sheep, or another animal, if a man has sinned, no one shall eat its flesh [Col. 0704C], nor may it be cooked; rather, it shall be killed and given to the dogs. If anyone wishes to give alms from money that came from plunder, he has the power to do so if he has already performed penance.

## On the reconciliation of penitents on Wednesday and Friday before Easter

First he says the psalm with the antiphon: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”

### Prayer

Most kind creator of the human race and most merciful restorer, who, in the reconciliation of those who have fallen, have willed that I too, who first need your mercy, should serve the effects of your grace through the priestly ministry, so that, when the merit of the suppliant ceases, the clemency of the Redeemer might become more wondrous. [Col. 0704D]

### Another

Almighty and everlasting God, in your goodness release the sins of your servant who confesses to you, so that the guilt of conscience may not harm him more unto punishment than the indulgence of your mercy benefits him unto pardon.

### Another, for others

Almighty and everlasting God, who have placed the forgiveness of sins in speedy confession, come to the aid of those who have fallen and have mercy on those who confess, so that those whom the chain of transgressions has bound may be released by the greatness of your mercy.

### Prayer over the sick

O God, who granted your servant Hezekiah fifteen additional years of life, rescue this your servant also from the bed of illness unto salvation. Through the Lord. [Col. 0705A]

## How the year imposed upon someone in penance, to be fasted on bread and water, is to be observed

### From the Roman Penitential

The penance of one year, which is to be fasted on bread and water, must be as follows: each week he shall fast three days—that is, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—on bread and water. On three days—that is, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday—he shall abstain from wine, mead, honey-drink, beer, meat, lard, cheese, eggs, entrails, and fatty fish. He may eat small fish, if he can obtain them; otherwise, he shall eat one kind of fish, legumes, [Col. 0705B] vegetables, and fruit, and drink beer. On Sundays, on the four days of the Nativity of the Lord, on one day of the Epiphany of the Lord, from Easter through the eighth day, on four days at the Ascension of the Lord and Pentecost, and on the feasts of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Mary, the twelve apostles, Michael, Saint Remigius, All Saints, Saint Martin, and the feast of whichever saint is celebrated with distinction in the diocese, he shall show charity with the other Christians—that is, he shall use the same food and drink as they do. Nevertheless, he must always avoid drunkenness and distension of the stomach in every circumstance.

### From the same Penitential

[Col. 0705C]

This is the second year after the one that is to be observed on bread and water, and is to be fasted after it. It is also to be imposed upon those who voluntarily kill ecclesiastics; those who habitually commit the Sodomitic crime and the sin against nature; those who voluntarily commit homicide in churches; and those who perpetrate other acts of this kind. The penance of that year must be as follows: on two days—that is, Monday and Wednesday—of every week, he shall fast until evening; then he shall refresh himself with dry food—that is, bread and dry but cooked legumes, or fruit, or raw vegetables. He shall choose one of these three and use it, and he shall drink beer, but moderately. He shall observe Friday on bread and water, and fast three Lents: one before the Nativity of the Lord, the second before Easter, and the third after Pentecost. During these three Lents [Col. 0705D] he shall fast two days each week until the ninth hour and eat dry food, as noted above. He shall fast Friday on bread and water. On the feast days listed in the preceding section, he shall use the food and drink used by the other Christians. Nevertheless, he must always avoid drunkenness and distension of the stomach in every circumstance.

## What those who cannot fulfill the prescribed fast should do

Whoever can fast and fulfill what is written in the Penitential does well and should give thanks to God. But for those who cannot, we give this counsel through the mercy of God, so that no one need perish or despair, either himself or anyone else. For one day that he ought to fast on bread and water, let him recite fifty psalms on bended knees, if possible in a church or another suitable place, and feed one poor person. Or, if he cannot stand so long on bended knees, let him recite seventy psalms standing and feed a poor person. Or, kneeling one hundred times, let him ask forgiveness one hundred times. Or let him give three denarii as alms, or feed three poor persons. Whoever redeems one day that was to be fasted on bread and water by one of the five methods mentioned above may eat on that day whatever he wishes, except wine, meat, and lard. [Col. 0706A]

## The remedy for one week, from the same Penitential

For one week that he ought to fast on bread and water, let him recite three hundred psalms on bended knees. Or, without kneeling, let him attentively sing three psalters. After singing the psalms, he may eat whatever he wishes, except wine, meat, and lard. [Col. 0706B]

## The remedy for one month

For one month that he ought to fast on bread and water, let him recite, kneeling, twelve hundred psalms, or, without kneeling, one thousand six hundred and eighty psalms. Each day, if he wishes and cannot abstain, he may eat at the sixth hour, except on Wednesday and Friday; on those days he shall fast until the ninth hour. He shall abstain from meat, lard, and wine for the entire month. After reciting the psalms, he may eat other food. By this arrangement the whole year is to be redeemed.

## Another form of redemption, from the same Penitential

But whoever does not know the psalms and cannot fast shall give twenty-two solidi in alms to the poor for one year that he ought to fast on bread and water. He shall fast every Friday on bread and water. During the three Lents of that year, let him estimate the amount prepared for himself in food or drink, determining what its value might be; let him distribute half that value as alms to the poor, and pray to God continually. [Col. 0706C]

## On priests whose examples are evil

### From the great council under King Louis

If any priest, negligent in his way of life, allows people to suspect evil of him because of his bad example, and the people, compelled by the bishop through an oath or the ban of Christianity, expose his infamy, while definite accusers of his crime are lacking, the bishop shall first admonish him privately [Col. 0706D]; then, before two or three witnesses, if he has not amended, the bishop shall admonish him publicly with a rebuke in the assembly of priests. If he still does not correct himself, he shall be suspended from office until he gives suitable satisfaction, so that the faithful people may not suffer scandal through him. But if there are legitimate accusers who attempt to prove his crimes by manifest indications, and he denies them, then he himself, together with six companions of the same order, if he is able, shall clear himself of the crime. If a deacon is accused of the same crime, let him examine himself together with three others.

Different faults produce different penances. For bodily physicians also compound different medicines, so as to treat wounds in one way, disease in another, [Col. 0707A] swellings in another, putrefactions in another, dimness in another, fractures in another, and burns in another. Thus spiritual physicians must also cure the wounds of souls by different kinds of treatment. But because only a few possess the ability to know, treat, and heal all these matters perfectly and restore a person completely to a sound state of salvation, we therefore earnestly admonish every learned priest of Christ to arrange everything not according to his own judgment but according to the statutes of the canons and the traditions of the Fathers. He must consider the contrition of either sex, age, persons, poverty, cause, condition of each person performing penance, and the very heart of the penitent; and, according to these matters, he must judge each case individually, as seems appropriate to him, like a wise physician.

## From the sayings of blessed Jerome the priest

### Why the canons do not prescribe a measure for each crime

[Col. 0707B]

The canons do not establish the measure of time for performing penance sufficiently explicitly for each crime, so as to state how each offense must be corrected. Rather, they determine that the matter should be left to the judgment of an understanding priest, because with God the measure of time is not as valuable as the measure of sorrow, nor abstinence from food as much as the mortification of vices. For this reason they command that the periods of penance be shortened according to the faith and conduct of penitents, and they consider that they should be extended because of negligence. Nevertheless, certain forms of penance have been imposed for particular faults, and other faults must be assessed in accordance with them, since through these same forms it is easy to estimate the punishment and judgment of the canons. [Col. 0707C]

[Col. 0707C]

## Saint Leo the pope to all bishops (chapter 11)

### On not publishing the confession of penitents

[Col. 0707B]

That presumption which I recently learned is being committed by certain persons through unlawful usurpation against apostolic rule, I decree must be removed by every means. Concerning the penance requested by the faithful, namely, that a written declaration of the individual kinds of sins be made public, it is sufficient for consciences to be disclosed by secret confession to the priests alone. Although the fullness of faith may appear praiseworthy when it does not fear being ashamed before human beings for the sake of the fear of God, nevertheless, because not everyone’s sins are of such a kind that those seeking penance will not fear making them public, let the reprehensible practice be removed. Otherwise many may be kept from the remedies of penance because they are ashamed or fear that their deeds will be disclosed to their enemies, who may attack them through the force of law. That confession is sufficient which is first offered to the Lord and then to the priest who approaches as an intercessor for the penitents’ offenses. More people will then be encouraged to undertake penance if the conscience of the one confessing is not made public to the ears of the people. [Col. 0707D]

## From the decrees of Pope Evaristus (chapter 5)

Let priests, at the bishop’s command, reconcile penitents concerning hidden sins and, as we have written above, absolve and give communion to the sick.

## From the sayings of Saint Augustine

### That the canonical remedy should first be indicated to those who confess secretly

[Col. 0708A]

If anyone secretly commits incest and secretly confesses it to a priest, let the canonical remedy be indicated to him which he would have had to undergo if his crime had been made public. But because the act remains hidden, the priest should give him counsel so that, through hidden penance, he may advance the salvation of his soul: namely, that he confess from the heart that he has grievously sinned; that he strive to cleanse himself through fasting, almsgiving, vigils, and sacred prayers with tears; and that he thus confidently hope to attain the expectation of forgiveness through mercy.

## From the decrees of Pope Pius (chapter 10)

### That penitents should not receive communion before completing their penance

[Col. 0708B]

Penitents ought not to receive communion before completing their penance. Penitents must abstain from banquets, adornments, and white clothing; and those who are at odds with one another must be expelled from the church until they return to peace.

## From the decrees of Pope Julius

### That anyone who denies reconciliation for a gift or grants it to the unworthy is a simoniac

Let no priest accept a present or any temporal profit—or rather, any spiritual harm—from anyone who is publicly sinning or committing incest, so that he may conceal that person’s sin from the bishop or his ministers. Nor, out of regard for any person, kinship, or friendship, should he hesitate to make the matter known to the bishops by sharing in the sins of others. Let him not presume to accept grace, favor, or a gift from any penitent; or bring a less worthy penitent to reconciliation and provide him with a certificate of reconciliation; or, through any ill will, exclude another penitent who is more worthy of reconciliation, because this is simoniacal and contrary both to God and to human beings. [Col. 0708C]

## From the decrees of Pope Lucius (chapter 5)

### That no one should deny penance to a dying person

If any priest denies penance to the dying, he is guilty concerning souls, because the Lord says: “On whatever day the sinner turns back, he shall live and shall not die.” True conversion can indeed take place at the last moment, because the Lord is an observer not only of time but also of the heart. [Col. 0708D]

## From the Council of Toledo

Let bishops have no doubt that they have been entrusted with the care of protecting and defending the people. Therefore, when they see powerful men and judges acting as oppressors of the poor, let them first rebuke them through priestly admonition; and if they disdain correction, let them report their insolence to the ears of the king, so that those whom priestly admonition does not bend toward justice may be restrained from wrongdoing by royal power.

## On illegitimate children

Children begotten before marriage from such a blameworthy union [Col. 0709A], being less commendable, must in no way be promoted to ecclesiastical dignity. Nor should those born from such a marriage be admitted to ecclesiastical orders, unless perhaps the greatest utility and necessity of the Church demands it, or an evident preeminence of merits commends them.

## From the decrees of Pope Hyginus (chapter 4)

If the altar has been moved, the church shall be consecrated again. If the walls are altered but not the altar, let it be exorcised only with salt.

## What custom may be permitted in the Church

From the *Register* of Saint Gregory, chapter 65:

“In accordance with the tenor of your report, we grant that the custom—which is nevertheless recognized as usurping nothing contrary to the Catholic faith—remain unchanged. For the edification of all the churches and the benefit of the entire people, we have decided that we should grant priests the power to preach not only in the cities but also in all parishes. Thus, if a priest cannot preach by himself because of some infirmity, let the homilies of the holy Fathers be read by deacons. For if deacons, whom Christ deigned to govern in the Gospel, are worthy, why should they be judged unworthy publicly to read the interpretations of the saints?” [Col. 0710A]

[Col. 0709]

# Notes of Father Hugh Menard on the preceding book

(*Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*)

[Col. 0709B] In the preface, the word “second” should be noted. He calls this the “second Roman Penitential” because earlier, in Book IV, he placed a Penitential excerpted from the canons of ancient councils.

Burchard cites the first chapter in Book XIX, chapter 33, up to the words “for not all clerics,” from the Penitential of Theodore, bishop of the English, in a somewhat abridged form. The words “you will give counsel to the penitent” should be understood as meaning: you will instruct the penitent how henceforth to be more cautious in avoiding sins. He later says that penance should be imposed by the priest while he recalls the sins confessed, lest, if the penitent refuses to disclose his sins again, he should be judged more severely by the priest.

The words “let the deacon receive the penitent into communion” should be explained as follows: when necessity presses, especially the danger of death, the deacon ought to give holy communion to a penitent whom he knows to be genuinely repentant from the outpouring of his tears or similar signs, even though, because no priest was present, he has not been absolved. Burchard cites this passage in Book XIX, chapter 154, from the Roman Penitential.

Precisely the same rule is established in the Roman Order, in the same words, in the order for Wednesday in the week of fasting at its beginning. We read of something similar in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.36, although not through the ministry of a deacon, in the case of a certain Serapion. Overcome by the force of torments, he sacrificed to idols, was expelled from the Church, and, repentant of his deed, repeatedly begged in vain to be admitted to the communion of the faithful. At last, stricken by a serious illness, he remained for three days without the use of any sense or voice. When he recovered and regained his voice, he sent his grandson to the priest at night, asking him to come to him as quickly as possible. But the priest, prevented by illness from approaching the old man who was sick, gave a particle of the Eucharist to his grandson and ordered him, after moistening it, to pour it into the old man’s mouth. When the grandson returned from the priest and did this, the old man immediately rested in peace.

The words “bishops or priests ought to humble themselves” are also found in Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 2. Saint Ambrose did the same, as the priest Paulinus testifies in his *Life*:

“Indeed, whenever anyone who had fallen came to him to confess his sins in order to receive penance, he wept so much that he compelled that person also to weep. He seemed to himself to lie prostrate while the other remained silent.”

In former times, when the penitents, drenched in tears, fell at the feet of the bishop after the solemn rites of the Mass had been completed, the bishop likewise, wet with tears, prostrated himself at the feet of the penitents, as Sozomen testifies in Book VII, chapter 16, of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

That rite—“let the priest command him,” and so forth—also appears in the chapter cited above and in the manuscript *Order* of the Library of Saint Remigius at Rheims, concerning the imposition of penance, with the prayer that follows. In it, as in the aforesaid Order of Saint Remigius, the reading “to adore” is incorrect; it should be read “to pray,” as in Burchard. [Col. 0709C]

[Col. 0710B]

The following chapter is found in Burchard, chapter 32, cited from the Roman Penitential; in some places it is mutilated, and it is not found in the cited manuscript *Order* of Saint Remigius. The word “tetrads” derives from the nominative *tetras*, that is, Wednesday of each week, just as *parasceve* means Friday, on which Christians, especially Eastern Christians, fast according to ancient custom, as we have explained at length in the notes and observations on the *Concord of Rules*.

Below, in the same chapter, it says: “On Saturday and Sunday he shall eat.” This is how it stands in Burchard; but the word “Saturday” seems to have been added by those who followed the custom of the Greeks, who did not fast on Saturdays, especially since this little penitential book belongs to the Roman Church, as is clear from Burchard, who often cites it under this name.

Finally, at the end of this chapter these words appear: “The prologue ends.” But I think they should be moved to the end of the following chapter [Col. 0710C], since they seem to be part of the preceding section. The words “if anyone cannot fast,” up to “and know this,” are cited by Burchard, chapter 22, from the Penitential of Theodore.

Among the ancient Romans, a *solidus* was a gold coin. Cassiodorus gives its value in Book I of the *Variae*, letter 10: “They determined that a solidus was six thousand denarii.” The Frankish solidus was formerly reckoned as forty denarii, as Hincmar teaches in his book on the *Life of Saint Remigius*, and as is evident from the Second Synod of Rheims, canon 41. It was eventually reduced to the value of twelve denarii.

Several psalms follow for the giving of penance; they are also found in Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 7, but there they are to be recited in full. The prayers are the same in number, but the second and third are different. In Canisius, the word *Oremus* (“Let us pray”) is not present; instead it says, “Say the prayer.”

The prayer of the laying on of hands follows; in Burchard it is the second among the prayers mentioned above. This prayer is called the prayer of the laying on of hands because formerly, when giving penance, the priest placed his hand upon the head of the penitent while reciting this or another similar prayer. The Council of Agde, canon 15, says: “At the time when penitents seek penance, they are to receive from the priest the laying on of hands and sackcloth upon the head, as has been established everywhere.”

The following prayer is not complete in Henry Canisius; you have it in full in the Roman Order, in the order for Thursday at the Lord’s Supper. I have restored the word “also me,” because in our manuscript, as in Canisius, it incorrectly reads “also I.” In the third prayer it reads “so that what,” as also in Canisius. But in Burchard and in the Roman Order it reads “so that those whom.” [Col. 0710D]

[Col. 0711A]

In the first chapter of the second part, the words “If a cleric commits homicide” appear to be superfluous. After the words “if he is a layman,” supply “not voluntarily,” because shortly afterward it deals with the voluntary homicide of a layman.

In the second chapter, “a cleric whose rank is higher” means a bishop, priest, or deacon. After the words “if he has the rank,” supply “has it” (*habuerit*). The end of the chapter is corrupt and, in my judgment, should be corrected as follows:

“If any woman who has committed fornication kills what is born, the original decree forbids her, as a supplicant, to communicate until the end of life. But, so that she may receive something more humane in accordance with what has been determined, we establish that she perform penance for ten years, according to the stages that have been established.”

These words are nothing other than canon 21 of the Council of Ancyra.

### Chapter 3: On Perjury

1. These words, “but if anyone, compelled by necessity, etc.,” are cited by Burchard, Book II, chapter 6, from the Roman Penitential in this form:

> “Nevertheless, the Roman Penitential prescribes: if anyone, compelled by the need to save his life, or by any other cause or necessity, commits perjury, because he loved his body more than his soul, let him do penance for three periods of forty days—or, as others judge, for three years—one of them on bread and water.”

2. These words also, “if anyone commits perjury through greed, etc.,” are cited by Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 7, from the Roman Penitential as follows:

> “Nevertheless, the Roman Penitential prescribes that, if anyone commits perjury through greed, he sell all his possessions, distribute them to the poor, and, having entered a monastery, submit himself to perpetual penance.”

### Chapter 4

After “a four-footed animal,” one should read “he has stolen,” or something similar. These words, “or any better protection,” are corrupt. I think one should read: “or any better livestock; if [the reading is] *praesidium*.” This chapter 4 is cited by Burchard, Book II, chapter 58, from the Penitential of Theodore, but in a shorter form. If anyone does not approve of the earlier emendation, we shall correct it as follows:

> “If any cleric commits a capital theft—that is, if he carries off four-footed animals, or breaks into or breaks open a house, or steals property.”

Here *praesidium* means the substance that someone possesses among his movable goods. The First Council of Orléans, canon 14, says: “While property of every kind remains under the authority of the bishops.” The Fourth Council of Paris, canon 8, says: “We have learned that, when an abbot, presbyter, or those who serve in the various churches have died, whatever property they left behind in danger of death is seized by the bishop or archdeacon.” Gregory of Tours, *History*, Book VI, chapter 4, says: “They rushed upon the houses of Lupus, and, having seized all his property, pretending that they were storing it in the king’s treasury, carried it into their own houses.” Marculphus, formula 67, on the division of an inheritance among relatives, says:

> “Thus the aforesaid person received the aforesaid named estates, situated in the aforesaid place, with so many slaves. As for the property, consisting of cloths, manufactured goods, or every household utensil that can be described or named, they appeared to have divided it among themselves in equal shares.”

Formula 69 speaks of “property of either sex,” by which words it seems to mean male and female slaves.

There follows the punishment of those who violate tombs. In order to excavate the treasures buried with the dead according to the custom of those times, people violated tombs, as may be seen in Cassiodorus, Book IV, letter 18, concerning a certain presbyter Laurence who had violated a tomb in order to seize the gold from it. In earlier times, this crime was punished by the laws with many and varied penalties. In the Edict of King Theodoric, chapter 110:

> “Whoever destroys a tomb shall be put to death.”

In the Salic Law, title 17, law 2:

> “If anyone digs up and strips a dead man, he shall be judged guilty and fined eight denarii, which make two hundred solidi.”

In the Lombard Law, Book I, title 12, law 2:

> “If anyone breaks open the burial place of a dead man and strips the body, he shall pay eighty solidi to the dead man’s relatives.”

These and many other similar laws were enacted because of the treasures hidden in tombs and the costly clothing of the dead, about which more will be said below.

### Chapter 5

By these words, “if anyone is a sorcerer for love,” is meant someone who draws the love of women or boys toward himself by love potions or erotic incantations, as we see in the *Pharmaceutriae* of Theocritus and Virgil, and in Lucian’s *False Prophet*, where he calls them *τὰς χάριτας ἐπὶ τοῖς ἐρωτικοῖς*—that is, “the Venuses or Graces for winning love.”

Most of this chapter is quoted by Ivo of Chartres, Part XV, chapter 116, from the Penitential of Theodore, though it varies in certain places. At the end of the chapter, a penalty is established against one who sends storms, as in Burchard, Book X, chapter 28, from the Roman Penitential. But in chapter 8 of the same book, from that same Roman Penitential, a penalty is established against one who believes that there are people who send storms; these two provisions appear to conflict.

Agobard, bishop of Lyon, published a treatise in which he condemns those who believe that there are people who send storms. The author of the questions included among the works of Saint Justin Martyr, Question 31, writes that such things cannot be brought about by the activity of magicians, and says that such people are called *νεφοδιώκται*, “cloud-drivers.” The Latins call them *tempestarii*, “storm-makers,” as Agobard writes in the same place, and Benedict the Levite, Book I, title 64. Agobard says that this storm is called *aura levatitia*, “a rising wind.”

### Chapter 6

These words are noteworthy: “if anyone on the Kalends of January, as many do, leads about a little deer or goes about as an old woman.” They are taken from the Council of Auxerre, canon 1:

> “It is not permitted on the Kalends of January to perform the old-woman or little-deer rite.”

Burchard mentions it in Book XIX, chapter 5:

> “Have you done something of the sort that the pagans did, and still do, on the Kalends of January, with the little deer and the old woman? If you have done so, do penance for thirty days on bread and water.”

Saint Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona, says in his exhortation to penance:

> “I also think that this little deer recently served a useful purpose, so that the more carefully it was marked, the more carefully it might be corrected; and that all that reproach, expressed and repeatedly renewed, seems not to have suppressed but to have instructed wantonness. Wretched me! What crime have I committed? I think they would not have known how to perform the little-deer rite if, by reproaching them, I had not shown them.”

This was the superstition: on the Kalends of January, people assumed the forms of wild animals and cattle and ran about here and there with excessive license, as we explained in the notes and observations on the *Concordia of the Rules*, chapter 50, § 4.

In the same chapter of our Penitential the following also occurs: “if anyone has lots which, contrary to reason, they call those of the saints.” Burchard reports something similar in Book X, chapter 9, from the Roman Penitential, as follows:

> “Auguries or lots, which are called false lots of the saints or divinations: whoever observes them, or any sort of writings, or makes or fulfills a vow at a tree, a stone, or any object whatsoever, except at a church, let all such persons be excommunicated.”

There follows: “if anyone goes to trees or springs, etc.” These provisions are taken from the Council of Agde, canon 42; the Second Council of Tours, canon 22; and the Council of Auxerre, canons 3 and 4.

There follows: “if anyone is a mathematician, etc.” Here *mathematicus* means a magician. More precisely, however, it is someone who, having examined the hour of birth, investigates what is going to happen to each person. Saint Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chapter 21:

> “Those who are called genethliaci because of their examination of birthdays are now commonly called mathematici.”

Spartianus, in his life of Severus, says:

> “Then, in a certain African city, he anxiously consulted a mathematician; when the hour had been given, the astrologer saw great things.”

Lampridius, in his life of Antoninus Diadumenus, says:

> “On the days on which he was born, the mathematicians, having received his horoscope, exclaimed that he himself was both the emperor’s son and the emperor.”

Their art is called *mathesis*. Spartianus, in his lives of Aelius Verus and Severus, says:

> “He investigated the horoscopes of brides, for he himself was also highly skilled in astrology.”

“To take away a person’s mind” means to disturb his imaginative power so greatly that he thinks himself to be a beast of burden or some other brute animal. Such was the woman mentioned by Palladius who believed herself to be a beast of burden and whom the blessed Macarius of Egypt healed, as well as the daughters of Proetus and those whom Circe drove mad, according to the stories told by the ancient poets.

In Book VI, title 2, law 3, of the Visigothic Law it is said:

> “And those who, through the invocation of demons, disturb the minds of men.”

There follows the prohibition of charms, concerning which Saint Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chapter 20:
