> “To this category also belong all charms and remedies which the medical profession likewise condemns, whether they consist of certain signs that they call characters, or of things hung up and tied on.”

And in chapter 29:

> “For it is one thing to say, ‘If you drink this crushed herb, your stomach will not hurt,’ and another to say, ‘If you hang this herb around your neck, your stomach will not hurt.’”

Ammianus Marcellinus mentions the matter in Book XV:

> “If anyone carried around his neck remedies for quartan fever or for another pain,” etc.

Saint Boniface, in his letter to Pope Zacharias, says:

> “They also say that they saw women there who, according to pagan custom, wore amulets and charms on their arms and legs.”

See what we have written about amulets and talismans in the *Concordia of the Rules*, chapter 3, § 6.

What follows—“if some eat together at a festival, etc.”—is nothing other than canon 7 of the Synod of Ancyra. There, “to be subject for two years” means to be in the third grade of penitents, which is called *ἀπόπτωσις*, that is, “prostration.” In this grade, penitents prostrate themselves before the bishops while the bishops lay hands upon them, as noted above.

The words “and thus be received” should be explained in this way: after the grade of prostration, he is to be received into the grade of those who stand, so that he may pray at Mass with the faithful, as stated above.

The words “which it is necessary to obey, and after the offering, etc.” are corrupt and should be corrected from the same synod as follows:

> “And afterward, whether they should be admitted with the offering, it is necessary to test each person’s spirit and to learn the life of each one.”

The words “if each one has committed this vice alone” are corrupt. One should read: “if he has committed this only through the vice of gluttony.”

The words “let him communicate without the offering” are to be understood of participation in the communion of prayer: he is to be present at the entire Mass with the faithful, but without the offering—that is, without receiving the Eucharist.

Finally, there follows: “if anyone has eaten blood, etc.” The Acts of the Apostles, chapter 15, are said to have forbidden the eating of blood, as did the Sixth Synod, canon 67. There the eating of the blood of any animal is prohibited, not only when prepared by some particular technique but however it may be eaten. This reflects the practice of the Eastern Church.

The same practice was also observed at some time in the Western Church, as is clear from the letter of the churches of Lyon and Vienne to the churches of Asia and Phrygia, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 1. There the martyr Biblias, responding to the slander of the pagans, says:

> *Πῶς ἂν παιδία φάγοιεν οἱ τοιοῦτοι οἷς μηδὲ ἀλόγων ζῴων αἷμα φαγεῖν ἐξόν;*  
> “How could such people eat children, when they are not even permitted to eat the blood of irrational animals?”

But this was not universally customary in the Western Church. Some interpret the passage in Acts as referring to homicide and the shedding of human blood, as does Saint Pacianus, bishop of Barcelona, in his exhortation to penance.

### Chapter 7

The statute against mutilating one’s own limbs is taken from canon 23 of the Apostles, which decrees that a layman who mutilates himself is to be subject to excommunication for three years.

As for voluntarily induced abortion, this crime is punished by capital punishment in Book 39 of the *Digest*, under “Penalties,” and in canon 92 of the Council in Trullo.

The prohibition of usury is taken from canon 17 of the First Council of Nicaea, where usury is forbidden.

The sale of another person’s slave, as well as of a freeborn person, is prohibited in Book V, title 4, laws 11 and 17, of the Visigothic Law. In the Penitential of Theodore, cited by Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 85, this crime is punished by three years of penance.

These words, “if anyone burns a courtyard, etc.,” are cited by Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 86, from the Roman Penitential:

> “If anyone intentionally burns anyone’s house or courtyard, he shall restore everything that was taken away or burned and shall do penance for three years.”

In the same author, Book V of the same work, in the examination of a penitent, we find:

> “Have you burned down a house or another person’s courtyard out of hatred? If you have done so, repay the damage and do penance for one year on the appointed weekdays.”

This decree, “if anyone through anger, etc.,” is reported by Burchard in Book XIX, chapter 101, from the Roman Penitential as follows:

> “Whoever, during a quarrel, makes a man lame or deformed by a blow shall pay the physician’s expenses and do penance for half a year. If a layman intentionally sheds blood, he shall repay him as much as he has harmed him; and if he has nothing with which to repay him, he shall work for his neighbor as long as the injured man is ill, and afterward do penance for forty days on bread and water.”

There follows: “if anyone takes something from the ministry of the church, etc.” Here “the ministry of the holy church” means sacred vessels, whether gold or silver. After *ecclesiae*, a preposition *ad* seems to be missing. It should therefore read: “if anyone takes something from the ministry of the church for any kind of work, etc.”

Finally, there follows: “if anyone sins with animals, etc.” This is nothing other than canon 16 of the Synod of Ancyra, where *ἀκοσαετεῖς* is read—that is, twenty years—whereas here it is thirty years.

The remainder is mutilated. In the words “may merit communion,” *orationum*, “of prayers,” is missing. Add afterward: “when he has persevered in communion for five years, let him participate in the offering.” For *eorum*, read *ejus*. The words “unceasingly for sinning” are superfluous. After the words “let them be subject,” add “and let them receive the communion of prayers.” After the word “five,” understand “years.”

### Chapter 8

This constitution, “A bishop committing fornication, etc.,” is found in canon 25 of the Apostles and in Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 39, from the Penitential of Theodore.

But this passage, with “the monk’s vow” placed before it, is corrupt. It should be read from the same Penitential of Theodore as follows:

> “But a presbyter, before taking a monk’s vow,”

that is, one who is not bound by any monastic vow.

Here *superpositio* means abstinence from food for a complete and entire day. *Superponere* means to abstain from food for an entire day. It is also an addition or extension of the fast. *Superponere* means to prolong the fast, in Greek *ὑπέρθεσις*, that is, “superimposition.” Saint Cyril of Jerusalem uses this term in Catechesis 18:

> *Διὰ τοὺς κόπους τοὺς προερχομένους ἐκ τῆς ὑπερθέσεως τῆς νηστείας τῆς παρασκευῆς καὶ τῆς ἀγρυπνίας*,

“because of the labors arising from the prolongation—that is, the extension or addition—of the fast of Friday and of the vigil.”

Likewise, *ὑπερτίθεσθαι* means “to impose additionally,” “to prolong the fast,” or “to add to it.” Dionysius of Alexandria uses the term in his letter to Basilides, as does Saint Epiphanius in his *Exposition of the Faith*.

Finally, the word *quinquagesimis* is corrupt and should be read *quinquagesimae*. It means the Easter Pentecost—that is, the fifty days intervening between the two solemnities of Easter and Pentecost—which, according to ancient custom, are free from fasting.

### Chapter 9

For “if the cause is negligent,” read “if the cause is negligence.”

In the words “to offer for good things,” the word *rebus* appears superfluous. But more will be said about this passage below.

There follows: “If anyone provides a guide to barbarians.” Burchard gives this differently and more fully in Book XIX, chapter 103, from the Roman Penitential:

> “If anyone provides guidance to barbarians against Christians so that they may plunder them, and no slaughter of Christians occurs, let him do penance for three years; but if it does occur, let him, having cast away his arms, live as one dead to the world until death.”

Afterward, eating the flesh of animals whose death is unknown is forbidden, lest one happen to eat carrion or something strangled.

These words, “boys conversing, etc.,” through the end of the chapter, are cited from the Roman Penitential by Burchard, Book XVII, chapter 56. There one reads “boys conversing alone,” namely, among themselves, about pederastic fornication, as he said shortly before.

After *osculum*, “kiss,” the cited passage has the particle *non*, “not.” The sin is there punished by five extensions of the fast.

### Chapter 10

The following chapter has a corrupt title. It should read: “On defects concerning the sacrifice.”

Some of these sins concerning the sacrifice of the Mass appear in the manuscript Penitential of Saint Columbanus, abbot of Luxeuil in Burgundy. This chapter, however, is lengthy. I think that several matters were included under a single title and that the copyist of this Penitential used a corrupt manuscript, or at least lacked sufficient care in copying.

Those matters in this chapter that concern the sacrifice of the Mass are found in Burchard, Book V, chapters 51 and 52, from the Roman Penitential, though they vary in certain places.

What *chrismal* means was explained above in the discussion of the dedication of a basilica.

These words, “so that, being burdened, he may take,” are corrupt. One should read: “so that, when receiving the sacrifice, he is burdened by an affliction of the stomach, etc.”

The following words, “a deacon forgetting to offer the offering, etc.,” are corrupt. In Burchard, chapter 51 of the cited book, we read:

> “A deacon who forgets to offer the offering until the cloth is offered, when the names of the departed are recited, shall do penance in the same manner.”

There follows: “But if it is in the flour, etc.” Some words appear to be missing before this, since the passage does not connect with what precedes.

For *quadragenas*, Burchard reads *quadragesimus*, “the fortieth.” After *negligens*, “negligent,” add *fuerit*, “has been.” Burchard reads: “and whoever has been negligent shall make satisfaction for his negligence over four days.”

In place of the words “and if something is found,” Burchard reads “so that nothing is found.” The earlier reading is preferable, because it makes clear what must be done when something from the sacrifice is found.

The words “so that if it is found” are expressed differently in Burchard:

> “But if the sacrifice has been found, let the place be cleansed with brooms; let the straw be burned, as above; let the ashes be stored away, as above; and let the priest do penance for twenty days.”

Here one should read “let it be given to the fire.”

What follows, “if something from the chalice through negligence, etc.,” is found in Burchard, Book V, chapter 47, from the decrees of Pope Pius, chapter 3. There the corrupt reading is *linguabitur*; it should be written *lingua lambatur*, “let it be licked by the tongue.”

In the following article, where *vicibus*, “times,” is written, a word expressing the number is missing. In the cited chapter of Burchard, *vicibus* is also absent.

The Lord’s Prayer is here called dangerous because formerly priests recited it at Mass with such reverence and caution that they thought they had committed a grave offense if they stumbled even slightly while reciting it.

The words “if anyone does not do penance” refer to those who, while healthy, do not come to penance but seek it during illness.

These three articles on penance are taken from the Council of Carthage IV, canons 76, 77, 78, and 79.

The words “but not the one who dismissed” are corrupt. One should read: “but not the woman whom he dismissed,” that is, from whom he separated.

The words “if anyone unwillingly kills a man of his relatives” should be explained as follows: “if anyone, against his will, kills the slave of his relatives or kinsmen.” Here *parents* means relatives and kinsmen, and *man* means someone of servile status. For this word, consult Cujacius, *Feud.* Book I, and Frederick Lindenbrog in his *Glossary* and in his notes on Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, Book IV, chapter 3.

The words “if a woman persuades another woman concerning [her] husband” are mutilated. One must add *dimittere*, “to dismiss,” or *relinquere*, “to leave,” or something similar.

The words “if anyone among the Christians sees a Christian walking, etc.” are extremely corrupt. I conjecture that they should be corrected as follows:

> “If any Christian sees a Christian walking or wandering and does not show him the way, let him be excommunicated,”

or something similar should be restored.

Likewise, before the words “has sold his parent,” *si quis*, “if anyone,” must be placed, so that it reads: “if anyone has sold his parent.”

This constitution, “if he has taken a third wife, etc.,” deserves notice. Although the Church permits men with two or three marriages, and so forth, nevertheless, because this polygamy or repetition of marriages indicates some lack of continence in a man, it formerly wished such persons to be subject to certain additional penalties besides the stigma of irregularity.

Saint Basil, in his First Canonical Letter to Amphilochius, excluded men with two marriages from the fellowship of the faithful for two years and those with three marriages for five years.

The constitution of the Emperor Constantine Porphyrogenitus, issued in the year of the world [the transmitted numeral is corrupt], orders that men with four marriages, as long as they remain in that condition, be separated from every ecclesiastical assembly and barred from entering the church, as Theodore Balsamon reports in his commentary on the cited letter.

What, indeed, would that emperor have decreed concerning the man who, in the time of Saint Jerome at Rome, had survived twenty wives, and concerning the woman who had already buried twenty-two husbands? At last the two were joined in marriage, while the Romans eagerly awaited which of the two would carry the other out. When the event befell the man, he was crowned and, carrying the palm, preceded his wife’s bier, as Saint Jerome writes in his letter to Ageruchia.

The Emperor Leo the Philosopher was expelled from the Church because he had four wives, as Cedrenus writes.

What follows, “if anyone cuts his hair, etc.,” is prescribed because of pagan superstition. For when pagans carried out and buried the dead, they hired women for payment to mourn the deceased, praise him, excite others to do the same, cut their own hair, and tear their cheeks. These women were called *praeficae*.

Nonius Marcellus, chapter 1, says:

> “Among the ancients, *praeficae* were women who were customarily brought to funerals to weep and praise brave deeds.”

The old glosses say of *praeficae*:

> *Ἡ πρὸ τῆς κλίνης ἐν τῇ ἐκφορᾷ κοπτομένη θρηνῳδὸς ἐπ’ ἐκφοράν*,

“a woman who, preceding the bier during the carrying-out of the dead, sings a lament.”

Old manuscript glosses from the library of Corbie mention them:

> “The leaders of the mourning.”

Servius explains this custom in his commentary on Book XII of the *Aeneid*:

> “It was the custom among the ancients that before the pyres human blood should be shed, whether that of captives or gladiators; and if such persons were not available, they tore their cheeks and shed their own blood.”

This appears to be reflected in the Twelve Tables, quoted by Cicero in Book II of *On the Laws*, where such madness is prohibited:

> “Women shall not tear their cheeks, nor shall they perform a funeral lament on account of the dead.”

Here *lessus* is a funeral song, elsewhere called a *naenia*.

Such women also tore their hair, as is prohibited here. This is clear from Lucilius, Book XXII, quoted by Nonius in the cited passage:

> “Hired for pay, they weep loudly at another’s funeral and tear their hair.”

Cutting and shaving the hair at funerals was also customary among the Greeks as a sign of mourning. Euripides, *Alcestis*, Act I:

> *Ἢ τεμῶ τρίχα*  
> *Καὶ μέλανα στολμὸν πέπλων*  
> *Ἀμφιβαλώμεθ’ ἤδη;*

“That I should cut my hair, or should we now put on the dark clothing of mourning?”

And Act II:

> *Πένθος γυναικὸς τῆσδε κοινωνεῖν λέγω*  
> *Κουρᾷ ξυρηκέῃ καὶ μελαμπέπλῳ στολῇ*

“I command that they share in this woman’s mourning by shaving the hair and wearing dark garments.”

Likewise, formerly among the Egyptians, whenever a dog had died in any household, all the household members shaved their entire bodies and were overcome with great mourning, as Eusebius writes in Book II of *Preparation for the Gospel*, chapter 1.

The *ungulae* mentioned at this point in the chapter are iron instruments, curved forward and sharp, suitable for tearing flesh in the form of a claw. Formerly executioners used them in the tortures of martyrs. They are also called *fidiculae*, as is clear from Saint Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book V, chapter 27:

> “They are called *ungulae* because they dig out; they are also called *fidiculae*, because by them criminals are stretched on the rack so that the truth may be discovered.”

The same is clear from Cyril’s glosses:

> *Ὄνυχες οἱ εἰς τὰ βασανιστήρια*,

“claws or claw-like instruments used in tortures or interrogations.”

The same may readily be gathered from Prudentius’ *Peristephanon*, concerning the holy martyr Romanus:

> “While the raging Asclepiades interposes, let the executioner turn the blow against the speaking mouth and bring his hand onto the cheeks; transfer the sharp furrows and the claw-like instruments.”

And shortly afterward:

> “The wicked lictor fulfills the commands of the one ordering it; with writing claws he scores both cheeks.”

Here one sees that when the governor ordered the martyr’s cheeks to be torn with *fidiculae*, the poet afterward says that the martyr’s cheeks were scored by servants with writing claws. From this it is perfectly clear that these words have the same meaning.

Isidore derives the name from *fides*, “faith,” but it is a verbal noun from the past form *fidi* of the verb *findo*, “to split.” Such claws were forked or cleft, that is, they had two curved points, as is clear from the same hymn:

> “Freely offering his naked ribs to be cut apart by forked claws.”

Hence below the instrument is called a “gaping point”:

> “The most savage soldiers split both sides of the hanging man’s body with a gaping point.”

So much for the claw-like instruments.

The *herbarius* that follows means a poisoner, because of the poisonous herbs and herbal poisons used by a poisoner. Hence the French word *enherber*, “to kill someone with poison.” An old poet says:

> “Beneath it lies the cool serpent in the grass;  
> Flee, children, for it poisons.”

Before the words “if he ceases to receive him,” some material is missing, for these words do not connect with what precedes.

The word *acceptor* is corrupt; read *accipiter*, “hawk.”

Here penance is imposed for eating carrion and strangled meat, which is also prohibited by canon 63 of the Apostles and canon 67 of the Sixth Synod.

The following passage of Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 5, is relevant:

> “Have you eaten carrion—that is, animals torn apart by wolves or dogs and found dead? If you have done so, you must do penance for ten days on bread and water. Have you eaten birds that a hawk had struck down, without first killing them with some weapon? If you have done so, let him do penance for five days on bread and water.”

There follows: “If a hen has died in a well, etc.” Almost the same provisions are reported by Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 106, from the Roman Penitential:

> “If anyone gives someone a liquid in which a dead mouse or weasel is found, if he is a layman, let him do penance for seven days; if it happened in a monastery, let him sing three hundred psalms. Whoever afterward learns that he drank such a potion shall sing one hundred and fifty psalms.”

There follows: “If a mouse or hen, etc.” Something similar is reported by Burchard from the same Roman Penitential:

> “Whoever eats or drinks something contaminated by a household animal—that is, by a dog or cat—and knows it, shall sing one hundred psalms; if he does not know it, he shall fast for two days. Or, if he wishes to redeem the penalty, he shall sing fifty psalms.”

There follows: “If a fish has died in a fishpond, etc.” Similar is the passage reported by Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 5:

> “Have you eaten a fish that was found dead in a river? If you have done so, do penance for three days on bread and water.”

In the words “let no one eat its flesh,” *its* refers to the animal with which the man has had intercourse.

The following words, “if he wishes to give for his soul, etc.,” are corrupt and do not sufficiently connect with what precedes. I think they should be read as follows:

> “If he wishes to give alms for his soul from the money that came from the spoils, and he has performed his penance, he has the authority to do so.”

Up to this point extends the Corbie manuscript, in which, as I think, the end of this Penitential is missing.

We have touched on these matters briefly so that we might shed some light on this Penitential. We shall not write more about the penance of the ancient Christians, since many learned men before us have already traveled this field, especially Gabriel Albaspineus, bishop of Orléans, in Book II of his *Observations*; Jean d’Artis, professor of law at the University of Paris and royal professor, in his book on the canonical discipline of the Church concerning the sacraments, etc.; and Denis Pétau of the Society of Jesus, in his *Annotations on Saint Epiphanius*, on Heresy 59, which is that of the Novatians.

# APPENDIX TO HALITGAR

[Col. 0717]

## ANONYMOUS

[Note: We judged that this book, excerpted by an anonymous author, should be reprinted here in order to preserve chronological order, because, according to Canisius in the *Ancient Readings*, it should be assigned to the year 825. Although the book of Halitgar’s Penitential is represented in the work we are presenting with only a few variations, it will nevertheless be worthwhile to compare the two. EDITOR.]

## PENITENTIAL BOOK

Taken from the archives of the Roman Church.

*(In Canisius, the* Ancient Readings*.)*

## HOW PENITENTS ARE TO BE RECEIVED, JUDGED, OR RECONCILED

[Note: These words are found verbatim in Rubertus’ Penitential, which Morinus published at the end of his *Treatise on Penance*, p. 13. BASN.]

Whenever Christians come to penance, we impose fasts, and we ought to share their fast with them for one or two weeks, or as much as we can, so that it may not be said to us what the Lord our Savior said to the lawyers of the Jewish people:

> “Woe to you lawyers, who burden men and lay heavy and unbearable burdens upon their shoulders, while you yourselves do not touch those burdens with even one of your fingers.”

For no one can lift up a person burning under a burden unless he bends down to extend his hand to him. Nor can any physician heal the wounds of the sick unless he shares in their foulness. Likewise, no priest or bishop can heal the wounds of sinners or remove sins from souls unless he does so with devoted concern and tearful prayer.

Therefore, dearest brother, we must be concerned for sinners, because we are members of one another. If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. Therefore, if we see someone lying in sins, let us hasten to call him to penance through our instruction.

And whenever you give counsel to a sinner, immediately assign him penance, telling him how much he must fast and redeem his sins, lest you forget how much he ought to fast for his sins and need to inquire about his sins again. He may perhaps be ashamed to confess his sins again and to be judged further.

[Note: Similar material may be seen in the book *On Duties*, attributed to Alcuin. EDITOR.]

For not all clerics who find this writing should use or read it, but only those for whom it is necessary—that is, presbyters. For just as no one except bishops and presbyters, to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted, ought to offer the sacrifice, so no others ought to assume these judgments.

But if necessity arises and no presbyter is present, let the deacon receive the penitent for satisfaction or holy communion.

[Note: These words are absent from Egbert; nor does he speak of satisfaction or communion. Many deny that a deacon could perform such acts. BASN.]

As we said above, bishops and presbyters ought to humble themselves and pray with the groaning of sorrow and with tears, not only for their own sins but also for those of all Christians, so that they may say:

> “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?”

When someone comes to a priest to confess his sins, the priest should tell him to wait a little while he enters his room for prayer. If he has no room, the priest should nevertheless say the following prayer in his heart.

### Let us pray.

[Note: This prayer is found complete in the Roman Order, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. X, p. 27. EDITOR.]

Lord God almighty, be merciful to me, a sinner, so that I may be able worthily to give you thanks, since through your mercy you have made me, though unworthy, a minister of the priestly office, and have appointed me, a humble and insignificant sinner, to pray and intercede with our Lord Jesus Christ on behalf of sinners and for those returning to penance.

Therefore, sovereign Lord, who desire all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, who do not desire the death of a sinner but that he should turn and live, receive my prayer, which I pour out before your mercy for your male and female servants who have come to penance; through our Lord.

When the man who has come to penance sees the priest sorrowful and weeping over his offenses, he himself is struck more deeply with the fear of God, becomes more sorrowful, and shudders more intensely at his sins.

And whenever you see any person approaching penance who remains firmly and persistently in penance, receive him. But whoever is able to fast what has been imposed upon him, do not prevent him; allow him to do so. Those who hasten to discharge the debt imposed upon them are more deserving of praise, because fasting is a debt.

Give this instruction to those who are doing penance: if someone fasts and completes what the priest has commanded him, he will be cleansed from his sins. But if he returns again to his former habit or sin, he is like a dog returning to its vomit.

Therefore every penitent ought not to fast only what the priest has commanded him, but, after completing what has been ordered, he ought also to fast as much as seems right to him. Whether you assign him Wednesday or Friday, if he does what the priest has commanded him, his sins will be forgiven. But if afterward he fasts of his own will, he earns a reward and the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore, whoever fasts the entire week for his sins should eat and drink on Saturday and Sunday whatever is set before him. Nevertheless, he must guard himself against gluttony and drunkenness, because wantonness arises from drunkenness.

For this reason blessed Paul forbade it, saying:

> “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is wantonness”—

not because wantonness is in the wine, but because it is in drunkenness.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] Regino has the same text, in exactly the same words, in his old manuscript Collection, Book II, chapter 44. ID.] If anyone perhaps cannot fast, but has the means to give something in redemption, then, if he is rich, let him give twenty solidi for seven weeks; but if he does not have so much that he can give it, let him give ten solidi; and if he is very poor, let him give three solidi. Let no one, however, be troubled because we have ordered twenty solidi or less to be given: for, if he is rich, it is easier for him to give twenty solidi than for a poor man to give three. But let each person consider to whom he ought to give: whether for the redemption of captives, or upon the holy altar, or for distribution to poor Christians. And know this, brothers: when servants, male or female, come to you seeking penance, do not burden them, nor compel them to fast as much as the rich, because servants are not their own masters; therefore impose half the penance upon them.

The prologue ends.

# HERE BEGIN THE PRAYERS FOR IMPOSING PENANCE

[Col. 0720A]

First, let the priest say Psalm 37: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.” Afterwards let him say, “Let us pray,” and Psalm 3, “I will bless,” as far as “It shall be renewed.” And again let him say, “Let us pray,” and Psalm 50, “Have mercy,” as far as “Blot out all my iniquities.” After this, Psalm “O God, save me by your name,” and let him say, “Let us pray.” Then Psalm “Why do you boast in wickedness?” as far as “the righteous shall see.” And let him say this prayer:

## Let us pray.

O God, whose indulgence no one fails to need, remember, Lord, your servant N.; and since he is stripped bare in the frailty of a slippery and earthly body, we ask that you grant forgiveness to him who confesses and spare him who pleads, so that we, who are accused by our merits, may be saved by your mercy. Through the Lord, etc.

### Another

O God, beneath whose eyes every heart trembles and all consciences quake, be favorable to the groanings of all and heal the wounds of all, so that, just as none of us is free from guilt, so no one may be excluded from forgiveness. Through the Lord.

### Again, another

O God of infinite mercy and immeasurable truth, be favorable to our iniquities and heal all the sicknesses of our souls, so that, having received remission through your mercies, we may always rejoice in your blessing. Through the Lord.

### Another

I beseech, Lord, the majesty of your clemency and mercy: deign to release forgiveness to your servant who confesses sins and crimes, and pardon the guilt of his former offenses—you who brought back the lost sheep upon your shoulders, who, appeased by the publican’s prayer and confession, heard him. Be appeased also toward this servant of yours, Lord; in your kindness look favorably upon his prayers, so that he may remain acceptable in confession, and so that his petition may swiftly entreat your perpetual clemency; and, restored to the holy altars and sacraments, may he again be entrusted to the hope of eternal life and heavenly glory. Through the Lord.

[Col. 0720C]

## Laying on of hands

Holy Lord, almighty Father, eternal God, who through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, have deigned to heal our wounds: we humbly, as your priests, implore and ask you to deign to incline the ear of your compassion to our prayers; forgive all crimes and pardon every sin; and grant this servant of yours, Lord, forgiveness in place of punishment, joy in place of sorrow, and life in place of death, so that, trusting in your mercy, he may be worthy to attain eternal life. Through the Lord.

# FROM THE ROMAN PENITENTIAL: HOW EACH PENITENT IS TO BE JUDGED

[Col. 0720D]

## First, concerning homicide

If a cleric commits homicide, let him do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water. If a layman, let him do penance for three years, one of them on bread and water. A subdeacon: six; a deacon: seven; a priest: ten; a bishop: twelve. If anyone consents to the commission of homicide, let him do penance for seven years, three on bread and water. If a layman voluntarily commits homicide, let him do penance for seven years, three on bread and water. If anyone suffocates an infant, let him do penance for three years, the first of them on bread and water. A cleric likewise shall observe this.

## Concerning fornication, from the same Penitential

If a cleric fornicates as the Sodomites did, [Col. 0721A] let him do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water. If a cleric commits adultery—that is, with another man’s wife or betrothed—and begets a son, let him do penance for seven [years]; but if he has not begotten a son and the matter has not come to public knowledge, then, if he is a cleric, let him do penance for three years, the first on bread and water. If he is a deacon or monk, seven years, three on bread and water; a bishop, twelve years, five on bread and water. If a cleric, or anyone of a higher order, who has a wife, has intercourse with her again after his conversion or ordination, let him know that he has committed adultery; therefore let him do penance as established above. If anyone fornicates with a nun or a woman dedicated to God, let him acknowledge that he has committed adultery; according to the earlier statutes, let each person do penance according to his order. If anyone fornicates by himself, or with an animal, or with any quadruped, let him do penance for three years. If it occurs after ordination or a vow, let him do penance for seven years. If a cleric desires a woman but cannot sin because the woman does not accept him, let him do penance for half a year [Col. 0721B] on bread and water, and abstain entirely from wine and meat.

If a cleric, after dedicating himself to God, returns to secular dress like a dog to its vomit, or takes a wife, let him do penance for ten years, three of them on bread and water, and thereafter not enter into marriage. If the holy synod or the apostolic see so wills, it shall separate them from the communion of Catholics. Likewise, a woman, after dedicating herself to God, if she commits such a crime, shall be subject to the same sentence. If a layman fornicates as the Sodomites did, let him do penance for seven years. If anyone begets a son by another man’s wife—that is, commits adultery and violates his neighbor’s marriage bed—let him do penance for three years. Let him abstain from richer foods and from his own wife, and in addition give the violated woman’s husband the price of her chastity.

If anyone wishes to commit adultery but cannot—that is, is not accepted—let him do penance for forty days. If someone, a virgin (virgo), is joined to a virgin (virgini), then, if their parents wish it, let her be a wife. Nevertheless, let them do penance for one year and be married. If anyone fornicates with an animal, let him do penance for one year. If he has no wife, let him do penance for half a year. If anyone abducts a virgin or widow, let him do penance for three years. If a man has a betrothed woman and perhaps brings disgrace upon her sister and unites with her as though she were his own—then takes her as wife, that is, the betrothed woman—while the one who suffered the disgrace perhaps kills herself, let all who consented to this act be reduced to ten years on bread and water, according to the statutes of the canons. If anyone kills the offspring born to women who have fornicated, or hastens to cause abortions, the initial rule forbids communion until death. This is indeed the true definition. [But] so that they may obtain something more humane, let us establish for them a period of ten years; according to the orders established, let them do penance.

## Concerning perjury

[Col. 0721D]

If a cleric swears falsely, let him do penance for seven years, three on bread and water. A layman: seven; a subdeacon: six; a deacon: seven; a priest: ten; a bishop: twelve. If anyone swears falsely under compulsion, from some necessity, or unknowingly, let him do penance for three years, one on bread and water, and make satisfaction for his soul—that is, free a male or female servant from slavery—and give many alms. If anyone swears falsely out of greed, let him sell all his possessions and give them to the poor, have his hair cut, enter a monastery, and serve there until death.

## Concerning theft

If anyone commits capital theft—that is, steals a quadruped, or breaks in, or steals anything of greater value—let him do penance for seven years. A layman: five; a subdeacon: seven; a deacon: eight; a priest: ten; a bishop: twelve years. If anyone commits lesser theft once or twice, let him make restitution for his soul and do penance for one year [Col. 0722A] on bread and water. And if he cannot make restitution, let him do penance for three years. If anyone violates a tomb, let him do penance for seven years, three of them on bread and water. If a layman commits theft, let him restore to his neighbor what he stole, and do penance for three Lents on bread and water. Let him give alms to the poor from his labor, and be joined to the altar at the priest’s judgment.

## Concerning sorcery

If anyone destroys someone by his sorcery, let him do penance for seven years, three on bread and water. If anyone becomes a sorcerer for love, but destroys no one: if he is a layman, let him do penance for half a year; if he is a cleric, one year on bread and water; if a deacon, three years on bread and water; if a priest, five years, two on bread and water. If by this means anyone destroys a woman’s child, let each person additionally add six Lents, lest he be guilty of homicide. If anyone causes storms, let him do penance for seven years, four of them on bread and water.

## Concerning sacrilege

[Col. 0722B]

If anyone commits sacrilege [or divination], that is, practices what they call haruspicy, or always practices augury, or by any evil art, let him do penance for three years on bread and water. If anyone is a fortune-teller, whom they call a diviner, and performs any divinations, because this is demonic, let him do penance for five years, three on bread and water. If anyone does what many do on the Kalends of January, and what they call “the little deer,” or rides in a cart, let him do penance for three years. If anyone possesses lots which, contrary to reason, they call those of the saints, or possesses any lots, or by any evil art casts lots or divines, let him do penance for three years, the first on bread and water. If anyone makes a vow at trees, springs, a chancel-rail, or anywhere except in a church, or fulfills such a vow, let him do penance for three years on bread and water, because this is sacrilege or demonic. But whoever eats or drinks there shall do penance for one year on bread and water. If anyone is a mathematicus—that is, has taken away the human mind through invocation of demons—let him do penance for five years, the first on bread and water. If anyone makes amulets or magical bindings, which is detestable, let him do penance for three years on bread and water. If people go together to a festival in the abominable places of the pagans and eat there, bringing their own food, it has been decided that they should be received into penance for two years. But whether they are to be admitted with an offering, let the individual bishops, after approving their life, examine each of their actions. If anyone eats or drinks near a shrine through ignorance, let him promise thereafter never to repeat it, and do penance for forty days on bread and water. But if he does this contemptuously—that is, after the priest has preached to him that it was sacrilege—and shares in the demons’ table: if he did it merely through the vice of gluttony, let him do penance for three Lents on bread and water; but if he did it for the worship of demons and the honor of an idol, let him do penance for three years. If anyone, having made sacrifice, obeys a second and a third time [the wording is uncertain], let him do penance for three years and communicate for two years without an offering. If [Col. 0722D] anyone eats blood, carrion, or anything sacrificed to idols, and was under no necessity, let him fast for twelve weeks.

## Concerning various chapters

If anyone voluntarily cuts off any member of his body, let him do penance for four years, the first on bread and water. If anyone voluntarily causes an abortion, let him do penance for three years, the first on bread and water. If anyone exacts interest from any source, let him do penance for three years, the first on bread and water. If anyone, by authority or by any device, wrongfully invades or takes another’s property, let him do penance in the same manner as under the preceding sentence, and give many alms. If anyone by any device takes a slave or any person captive, or sends him away, let him do penance as above. If anyone burns a church, let him do penance for fifteen years, carefully restore it, and distribute his wealth to the poor. If anyone voluntarily burns anyone’s field or house, let him do penance as above.

(From the decree of Pope Julius.) If anyone strikes another in anger and sheds blood or maims him, let him first pay him compensation and seek a physician. If he is a layman, let him fast for forty days on bread and water; if a cleric, five forty-day periods; a deacon, seven months; a priest, one year. If anyone practices hunting: a cleric shall do penance for one year; a deacon, two; a priest, three. If anyone cheats or neglects any work belonging to the ministry of Holy Church, let him do penance for seven years, three on bread and water.

(In the Council of Ancyra, canon 5.) If those who have sinned with animals are not yet twenty years old, after completing fifteen years in penance, let them be admitted to communion in the prayers. Then, after remaining five years in this communion, let them receive the sacrament of the offering. Their life during the period of repentance must also be examined, and thus let them obtain mercy. But if they have clung to these crimes immoderately, let them spend a longer period in doing penance. [Col. 0723B] But all those who, having passed the age of twenty and having wives, have fallen into this sin shall, after carrying out twenty-five years of penance, be received into communion in the prayers. After remaining in it for five years, let them finally receive the sacrament of the offering. But if those who have wives and are over fifty years old have offended in this way, let them obtain the grace of communion at the end of life.

## Concerning drunkenness and fornication

A person becomes drunk on wine or beer, contrary to the prohibition of the Savior and his apostles. If he has made a vow of holiness, let him expiate the offense for forty days on bread and water; but a layman shall do penance for seven days. A bishop who commits fornication shall be degraded and do penance for twelve years. A priest or deacon who commits natural fornication: a prelate before a monk’s vow shall do penance for three years, continually ask for forgiveness, and perform a superposition each week, except on the days of Quinquagesima.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] “A prelate before a monk’s vow” was absent from Stewart’s manuscript. BASN.]

## Concerning minor matters

[Col. 0723C]

If anyone carelessly loses the sacrifice by accident, leaving it outside, and it is eaten by something, let him do penance for forty days; but if it was not accidental, let him do penance for one year. If an excommunicated person receives communion unknowingly, let him do penance for forty days. If anyone willingly communicates with an excommunicated person by word, report, food, or drink, let him do penance for forty days on bread and water and salt. If the sacrifice falls onto the ground through negligence, let a superposition be performed.

[Note: [Col. 0723D] Gregory says the same in his Judgments: “If anyone loses the Eucharist, that is, the sacrifice, through negligence, let him do penance for one year or three Lents; but if it falls to the ground through negligence, let him sing fifty psalms.” ID.]

If the sacrifice falls from the hand of the one offering it onto the ground and nothing is found, whatever is found shall be burned in the place where it fell, and the ashes shall be stored beneath the altar; and the priest shall do penance for half a year.

We ought to offer for good things, never for evil ones. Priests are not forbidden to offer for their bishops. Whoever gives the barbarians guidance shall do penance for three years. Those who strip monasteries, falsely saying that they are redeeming captives, shall do penance for three years [Col. 0723D] and give to the poor everything they took away. Whoever eats the flesh of animals whose death he does not know shall do penance for a third of a year. Let us bring forth the statutes of the former Fathers. Children who merely converse and transgress the rules of their elders shall make amends with three superpositions. Those who give a simple kiss, with seven superpositions. But those who do so with defilement, without an embrace, shall be corrected with fifteen superpositions.

## Concerning the handling of the sacrifice

Whoever does not properly guard the sacrifice and a mouse eats it shall do penance for forty days. But whoever loses his chrismal [Note: [Col. 0723D] Entirely wrong; it should not be read as though fifty-six years of penance were being assigned, nor does the letter L denote the number; read “Chrismal.” Here “chrismal” must be understood as the corporal cloth. ID.], or the sacrifice alone, in any circumstance so that it cannot be found, shall do penance for [the corrupt reading “IIIXL ms8”] or one year. If someone spills the chalice over the altar when the cloths are removed, let him do penance for seven days. If it falls [Note: [Col. 0724D] Or, if the sacrifice falls inside the table. So the Menard codex; “into straw” is nevertheless better. In the Penitential manuscript of the Colbert Library, no. 1348, it reads: “if the sacrifice falls from the hand into straw, let the one from whose hand it fell do penance for seven days.” ID.] into straw, let him do penance for seven days. [Note: [Col. 0724D] Alternatively, “taking.” ID.] If he vomits the sacrifice because burdened by fullness of stomach, let him do penance for forty days; if he throws it into the fire [Note: [Col. 0724D] These words are omitted in other manuscripts. ID.], let him do penance for twenty days. A deacon who forgets to offer the offering without a cloth shall do penance similarly until it is offered. Whoever receives the sacrifice after food or even the smallest refreshment, unless as viaticum, shall do penance: children, three days; adults, seven; clerics, twenty.

(Pope Eutychianus, chapter 11.) If unclean little creatures are found in flour, dry food of any kind, honey, or milk, let whatever is around their bodies be thrown away. [Note: [Col. 0724D] Gregory III has almost the same in his Judgments, chapter 28, which see in the Councils, volume VI, page 1483. Gregory omits many of the regulations here concerning the Eucharist. ID.] Whoever has been negligent regarding the sacrifice, so that it is consumed by worms and comes to nothing, shall do penance for three Lents. If it is found intact but there is a worm in it, let it be burned, and let its ashes be hidden beneath the altar; and let the negligent person do penance for forty days. If it is found as above, let it be cleansed; if it has fallen only as far as the altar, let it be placed upon it. If something drips from the chalice onto the ground through negligence, let the tongue lick it up, let the board be scraped and burned with fire, and let him do penance for fifty days. If the chalice drips upon the altar, let the minister suck it up, and let the cloth touched by the drop be washed three times; and let him do penance for three days. If the priest stumbles over the Lord’s Prayer, which is dangerously [uncertain reading] said once, or over the psalms, let him sing fifty psalms; the second time, let him do penance with a hundred blows.

## Again, concerning homicide

[Col. 0724C]

If anyone kills a man without cause on a public expedition, let him fast for twenty-one weeks. But if perhaps he kills someone while defending himself, or his parents, or his household, he shall not be guilty. If he wishes to fast, it is within his power, because he did this under compulsion. If he commits homicide in peacetime, when there is no crowd, whether by force or out of enmity, in order to seize the victim’s property, let him fast for twenty-eight weeks and return the property of the one he killed to his wife or children.

## Concerning sick penitents

If anyone comes to penance, and illness occurs, and he cannot complete what the priest has imposed upon him, let him be admitted to holy communion. And if the Lord wishes to save him, let him fast afterward. If anyone does not repent and perhaps falls ill and asks to receive communion, let him not be prevented; but give him holy communion and command him that, if it pleases the mercy of God and he escapes that illness, he should afterward confess everything and thus do penance.

## Concerning excommunicated dead persons

If an excommunicated person dies who had already confessed, but death overtakes him before he can appear, whether on the road or at home, let one of his relatives offer something on his behalf at the holy [Col. 0725A] altar, or for the redemption of captives, or in commemoration of his soul.

## Concerning incestuous unions

If anyone takes his wife’s daughter, you cannot judge him until they have first been separated. After they have been separated, impose fourteen weeks upon each of them, and let them never unite again. But if either the man or the woman wishes to marry, he or she shall have the power to do so—but not the woman whom he dismissed. If anyone takes a kinswoman, a stepmother, or his uncle’s widow—and likewise those who take their father’s wife or their wife’s sister—this is a grave judgment: let them be condemned canonically. But because of fornication many do not know the number of women with whom they have fornicated, let them fast for fifty weeks.

## Concerning food sacrificed to idols

If anyone, while still an infant, through ignorance tastes something sacrificed to idols, or carrion, [Col. 0725B] or anything abominable, let him fast for three weeks. If anyone unknowingly eats something sacrificed to idols or carrion, forgiveness shall be granted him, since he did it unknowingly; nevertheless, let him fast for three weeks.

## Concerning theft from necessity

If anyone, because of necessity, steals food, clothing, or a quadruped because of hunger or nakedness, forgiveness is granted him. Let him fast for four weeks. If he makes restitution, do not compel him to fast. If anyone steals a horse, ox, beast of burden, or cow, or food or anything that nourishes an entire household, let him fast as above.

## Concerning adultery

If a woman deceives her mother’s husband, she cannot be judged until she leaves him. When they have been separated, let her fast for fourteen weeks. If anyone who has a lawful wife dismisses her and takes another, the woman he took is not his. Let him neither eat nor drink nor speak at all with her, because he took her unlawfully; nor with her relatives. They themselves, however, if they consented, shall be excommunicated. If a woman entices another woman’s husband, let her be excommunicated from the Christians. If a Christian sees a Christian wandering about, or his own wandering relative, and sells him, he is not worthy to have rest among Christians until he redeems him. But if he cannot find the place where he is, let him give the price he received for him, redeem another from slavery, and fast for twenty-eight weeks.

## Concerning the penance of those married three times

If anyone’s wife dies, he has the power to take another; likewise a woman. If he takes a third wife, let him fast for three weeks. If he takes a fourth or fifth, twenty-one weeks.

## Concerning one who tears himself

If anyone cuts his hair or tears his face with a sword [Col. 0725D] or fingernails after the death of his parents, let him fast for three weeks; and after fasting, let him receive communion.

## [Concerning poisoners]

A man or woman who prepares herbs, murderers of infants, when he or she comes to the end of life, if he or she seeks penance with mourning and weeping tears, and has ceased, receive him or her; let the person fast for fifty weeks.

## Concerning suffocated animals

If a dog, fox, or hawk kills something—whether it has been killed by a stick, a stone, or an arrow without an iron point—all these animals are suffocated; they shall not be eaten. Whoever eats one shall fast for seven weeks.

## Concerning animals wounded by arrows

If anyone strikes a deer or another animal with an arrow, and it is found after the third day, and perhaps a wolf, bear, dog, or fox has tasted it, [Col. 0726A] no one shall eat it. Whoever eats it shall fast for four weeks. If a hen dies in a well, let the well be emptied. If anyone knowingly drinks from it, let him fast for one week. If a mouse, hen, or anything else falls into wine, let no one drink from it. If something falls into oil or honey, let the oil be used in a lamp, in medicine, or for another necessity. If a fish dies in a fishpond, it shall not be eaten. Whoever eats it shall fast for four weeks. If a pig or hen eats from a human corpse, it shall not be eaten or kept for breeding; rather, it shall be killed and given to the dogs. If a wolf tears an animal and it dies, no one shall eat it; but if it survives and a human later kills it, it may be eaten.

## Concerning polluted animals

If a man sins with a goat, sheep, or any other animal, no one shall eat its flesh, nor its cook; rather, it shall be killed and given to the dogs. If anyone wishes to give alms from money that came from plunder, he has the power to do so if he has already done penance.

## Concerning the reconciliation of penitents on the Wednesday and Friday before Easter

First he says the psalm with the antiphon: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”

### Prayer

Most kind creator of the human race and most merciful restorer, who in the reconciliation of the fallen first need your mercy—even I—have willed that I serve the effects of your grace through the priestly ministry, so that, when the merit of the suppliant ceases, the clemency of the Redeemer might become more wondrous.

### Another

Almighty and eternal God, release, in your goodness, the sins of your servant who confesses to you, so that the guilt of his conscience may not harm him more unto punishment than the indulgence of your mercy benefits him unto forgiveness.

### Again, another

Almighty and eternal God, who have placed the forgiveness of sins in swift confession, help the fallen and have mercy on those who confess, so that the greatness of your mercy may release those whom the chain of offenses binds.

### Prayer over a sick person

O God, who granted your servant Hezekiah fifteen additional years of life, so also rescue this servant of yours from the bed of illness unto salvation. Through the Lord.

# HOW THAT YEAR IS TO BE OBSERVED WHICH IS IMPOSED UPON SOMEONE AS A PENANCE TO BE FASTED ON BREAD AND WATER

From the Roman Penitential.

The penance of one year, which is to be fasted on bread and water, must be as follows: each week, let him fast for three days—that is, Monday, Wednesday, and Friday—on bread and water. And for three days, namely Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, let him abstain from wine, mead, honey-drink, beer, meat, animal fat, cheese, eggs, offal, and fatty fish. He may eat small fish, if he can obtain them; otherwise, one kind of fish, legumes, vegetables, and fruit, and he may drink beer. On Sundays, and for the four days of the Nativity of the Lord, and on one day at the Epiphany of the Lord, and from Easter through the eighth day, and for four days at the Ascension of the Lord and Pentecost, and at the Masses of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Mary, the twelve apostles, Michael, Saint Remigius, all the saints, Saint Martin, and the saint whose feast is celebrated in the diocese: on these aforesaid days let him show charity with the other Christians, that is, use the same food and drink as they do. Nevertheless, let him always beware of drunkenness and distension of the belly in all things.

## From the same Penitential

[Col. 0727A]

This is the second year after that which is to be observed on bread and water; after that, it is to be fasted. It is also to be imposed upon those who voluntarily kill ecclesiastics, who habitually commit the Sodomitic crime and the sin against nature, who voluntarily commit homicides in churches, and who perpetrate other offenses of this kind. The penance of that year must be as follows: on two days, Monday and Wednesday, let him fast each week until evening; then let him refresh himself with dry food, that is, bread and dry legumes, but not cooked, or fruit, or raw vegetables. Let him choose one of these three and use it, and drink beer, but moderately. Let him observe Friday on bread and water, and fast for three Lents: one before the Nativity of the Lord, the second before Easter, and the third after Pentecost. In these three Lents let him fast two days each week until the ninth hour and eat dry food, as noted above [Col. 0727B]. Let him fast Friday on bread and water. On the feast days listed in the preceding chapter, let him use the same food and drink as the other Christians. Nevertheless, let him always beware of drunkenness and distension of the belly in all things.

[Note: [Col. 0727D] The word “not” is absent from the manuscript.]

## What those who cannot fulfill the prescribed fast should do

Whoever can fast and fulfill what is written in the Penitential does well and should give thanks to God. But for one who cannot, we give this counsel through God’s mercy, so that no one need perish or despair, either himself or anyone else. For one day that he ought to fast on bread and water, let him sing fifty psalms on bended knees, if possible in a church or another suitable place, and feed one poor person. Or, if he cannot stand so long on bended knees, let him sing seventy psalms standing and feed a poor person. Or, bending his knees a hundred times, let him ask forgiveness a hundred times. Or let him give three denarii as alms, or feed three poor persons. [Col. 0727C] Whoever redeems one day to be fasted on bread and water by one of the five methods mentioned above may, on that day, except for wine, meat, and animal fat, take whatever he wishes.

## The remedy for one week, from the same Penitential

For one week, which he ought to fast on bread and water, let him chant three hundred psalms on bended knees. Or, without bending his knees, let him sing three Psalters attentively. After singing the psalms, he may take whatever he wishes except wine, meat, and animal fat.

## The remedy for one month

For the one month that he ought to fast on bread and water, let him sing twelve hundred psalms on bended knees, or, without bending his knees, one thousand six hundred and eighty psalms. Each day, if he wishes and cannot abstain, let him eat at the sixth hour, except on Wednesday and Friday; on those days let him fast until the ninth hour. Let him abstain from meat, animal fat, and wine for the entire month. After singing the psalms, let him take other food. The entire year is to be redeemed by this arrangement.

## Another redemption, from the same Penitential

Whoever does not know the psalms and cannot fast shall, for one year which he ought to fast on bread and water, give twenty-two solidi as alms to the poor. Let him fast every Friday on bread and water. During the three Lents of that year, let him estimate the amount prepared for himself in food or drink according to what it might be worth, and distribute half that value as alms to the poor, and pray continually to God.

# CONCERNING PRIESTS WHOSE EXAMPLES ARE WICKED  
From the great council under King Louis

If a priest who is negligent in his life permits suspicion of himself through wicked examples, and the people, compelled by the bishop under oath or by the bond of Christianity, expose his infamy, but there are no certain accusers of his crime, let the bishop first admonish him privately, then before two or three witnesses. If he does not amend, let the bishop admonish him publicly with a rebuke at the assembly of priests. But if he still does not correct himself, let him be suspended from office until he gives worthy satisfaction, lest the faithful people suffer scandal through him. But if there are legitimate accusers who strive to prove his crimes by clear indications, and he denies them, then let him, if able, purge himself of the crime with six companions of the same order. But a deacon, if accused of the same crime, shall examine himself with three others.

Different faults produce different penances. For physicians of the body also prepare different medicines: they treat wounds in one way, illness in another, tumors in another, rottenness in another, dimness in another, fractures in another, and burns in another. So spiritual physicians must cure the wounds of souls by different kinds of treatment. But because it belongs to few to know and cure, heal, and restore everything completely to a sound condition of salvation, we therefore earnestly admonish every learned priest of Christ to arrange everything not according to his own judgment but according to the statutes of the canons and the traditions of the Fathers; and to consider the objections of either sex, the age, persons, poverty, cause, condition of each penitent, and the penitent’s own heart; and according to these things, as seems right to him, to judge each matter as a wise physician.

# FROM THE SAYINGS OF BLESSED JEROME THE PRIEST  
Why the canons do not prescribe a measure for each crime

The canons do not define the length of time for performing penance sufficiently explicitly for each crime, by saying how each individual offense is to be corrected; rather, they establish that this should be left to the discretion of an understanding priest. For before God, the measure of time is not as important as sorrow, nor abstinence from food as much as the mortification of vices. Therefore they command that the periods of penance be shortened according to the faith and conduct of penitents, and they judge that they should be prolonged because of negligence. Nevertheless, for certain faults measures of penance have been imposed, according to which other faults are to be assessed, since by these same measures it is easy to estimate the punishment and censure of the canons.

# SAINT LEO THE POPE TO ALL BISHOPS, CHAPTER XI  
Concerning the confession of penitents not being made public

I decree that the presumption which I recently learned is being committed by some through unlawful usurpation must be removed by every means. As for the penance requested by the faithful, let no written declaration of consciences, setting out the individual kinds of sins, be made public; it is sufficient that it be disclosed to priests alone in secret confession. Although the fullness of faith may seem praiseworthy when, for fear of God, it is not ashamed before human beings, nevertheless, because not everyone’s sins are of such a kind that those seeking penance are unafraid to make them public, let the reprehensible custom be removed, lest many be kept from the remedies of penance while they either feel shame or fear that their deeds will be disclosed to their enemies, who may punish them under the provisions of the law. For that confession is sufficient which is first offered to the Lord and then to the priest, who approaches as intercessor for the sins of penitents. More people will then be moved to penance if the conscience of the one confessing is not made public to the ears of the people.

# FROM THE DECREES OF POPE EVARISTUS, CHAPTER V

[Col. 0729A]

That priests, at the bishop’s command, reconcile penitents for hidden sins; and, as we have written above, absolve and admit to communion those who are ill.

## From the Sayings of Saint Augustine

### That the canonical remedy should first be indicated to those who confess secretly

If anyone has secretly committed incest and has made a secret confession to a priest, the canonical remedy that he would have had to undergo if his crime had been made public should be indicated to him. But because the deed remains hidden, the priest should give him counsel so that, through hidden penance, he may advance the salvation of his soul: namely, he should confess from his heart that he has sinned grievously; he should strive to cleanse himself through fasts, almsgiving, vigils, and sacred prayers with tears; and thus he should trust that, by God’s mercy, he may attain the hope of pardon.

## From the Decrees of Pope Pius, Chapter X

### That penitents should not receive communion before completing their penance

Penitents ought not to receive communion before completing their penance. Penitents must abstain from banquets, ornaments, and white clothing; and those who are at odds with the Church should be expelled until they return to peace.

## From the Decrees of Pope Lucius, Chapter V

### Whoever denies reconciliation to the deserving or grants it to the unworthy for a reward is a simoniac

No priest shall accept a gift or any temporal profit—in fact, any spiritual detriment—from anyone who publicly sins or commits incest, in order to conceal that person’s sin from the bishop or his ministers. Nor, out of regard for any person, kinship, or familiarity, shall he refuse to make the matter known to the bishop, thereby sharing in another’s sins. Nor shall he presume to accept from any penitent gratitude, favor, or a gift; nor bring a penitent who is less worthy to reconciliation or furnish him with a certificate of reconciliation; nor, out of any spite, exclude another penitent who is more worthy of reconciliation. For this is simoniacal and contrary both to God and to human beings.

## From the Decrees of Pope Julius

### That no one should deny penance to a dying person

If any priest has denied penance to the dying, he is guilty concerning their souls, because the Lord says: “On whatever day the sinner turns back, he shall live and shall not die.” True conversion can indeed take place at the final hour, because the Lord is the examiner not only of time but also of the heart.

## From the Council of Toledo

Let bishops have no doubt that they have been charged with protecting and defending the people. Therefore, when they see that the powerful and judges are oppressors of the poor, they should first rebuke them with priestly admonition; and, if they refuse to amend their ways, they should report their insolence to the king, so that those whom priestly admonition does not bend toward justice may be restrained from wickedness by royal power.

### Concerning illegitimate sons

Sons born before marriage from such a blameworthy union, and therefore less praiseworthy, are in no way to be promoted to ecclesiastical dignity. Nor are those born from such a marriage to be admitted to ecclesiastical orders, unless perhaps the Church’s greatest usefulness and necessity should demand it, or an evident preeminence of merits should commend them.

## From the Decrees of Pope Hyginus, Chapter IV

If the altar has been moved, the church must be consecrated again. If the walls are altered but not the altar, they are to be exorcised only with salt.

### What custom may be permitted in the Church

From the Register of Saint Gregory, chapter 65. We, in accordance with the tenor of your report, grant that the custom—which, as is clear, usurps nothing contrary to the Catholic faith—shall remain unaltered. We have also decided, for the edification of all the Churches and for the benefit of the whole people, that we should grant priests the authority to preach not only in cities but also in all parishes. Thus, if a priest is unable to preach in person because of some infirmity, the homilies of the holy Fathers may be read aloud by deacons. For if deacons are worthy—those whom Christ deemed worthy to choose in the Gospel—why should they be judged unworthy publicly to recite the explanations of the saints?

[Col. 0729]

# In the Year of the Lord 827: Jeremiah, Archbishop of Sens

[Col. 0729]

## Historical Notice Concerning Jeremiah

*(From Gallia Christiana.)*

[Col. 0729D] Jeremiah was referendary, or chancellor, in the thirteenth year of Charlemagne’s reign, according to a Corbie charter. He then became a monk and treasurer of the monastery of Saint Richarius at Centula. Fearing the Normans, who at that time were ravaging the district of Ponthieu, he carried away with him the relics that Charlemagne had given to Centula and brought them to Sens, to the monastery of Saint Columba, with which Centula had maintained an association since the time of Abbot Guelfo.

While he was staying there, after Magnus died in 818, Jeremiah—a nobleman endowed not only with monastic but also with secular wisdom, highly eloquent and devoted to every branch of philosophy—was elected archbishop by the clergy and the entire people. After his consecration in the church of Saint Stephen, he transferred the relics that he had brought from Saint Richarius. Since he was highly familiar with the king, he obtained from him that the abbey of Saint Columba, which his predecessors had recently lost, should be placed under the protection of the archbishop of Sens. Hence we suspect that Hariulf called him abbot of that place, although Clarius says nothing at all about him, unless perhaps he was its rector under James, the canonical abbot.

At the request of Frodobert, abbot of Saint Peter, he built a cell near the Arverni, in honor of Saint Peter, around January 822, on land belonging to that monastery, which Theodechildis, its foundress, and Basolus, count of the Arverni, had given to it for the support of the monks. The place, called Mauriacus by Jeremiah Novicus, still retains its ancient name. There regular monks from the abbey of Saint Peter were established under the supervision of Abbot Frodobert and his successors, to administer the estates and churches subject to that abbey in the Arvernian and Limousin districts of Aquitaine.

[Col. 0731A] Jeremiah and Abbot Frodobert also obtained from Louis Augustus a privilege concerning that cell and all its dependencies belonging to Saint Peter. The same emperor, at the request of the archbishop of Sens, confirmed Jeremiah’s authority over the monasteries of the diocese on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, 822. In that same year he was sent by Louis Augustus to Sens as royal envoy together with Count Donatus; and three years later, together with Jonah of Orléans, he was sent as a delegate to Rome to Pope Eugenius II, so that they might present to him the collections from the books of the holy Fathers concerning the veneration of images, which they themselves had compiled at the council held at Paris, which they had attended in 825.

The *Commonitorium* of Louis the Pious to them on this matter, and the letter that he himself wrote to Eugenius II, are mentioned in the charter of the emperors Louis and Lothar for the monastery of Micy, in the year 825. Jeremiah also obtained further privileges from Louis the Pious, on the seventh day before the Ides of May and the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the thirteenth or fourteenth year of his reign, for the church of Sens and its monasteries against judicial authorities. Among these, the most outstanding is a monument of the most venerable antiquity: an autograph preserved in the archives of the church of Sens. We could not publish it among the documents of that church because a copy had not yet been made available to us; but after it was made, we insert it here for the benefit of scholars and lovers of documents of this kind, and because it is lacking in other writers who have published the diplomas of Louis the Pious.

> “In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Louis, by the divine … [lacuna] … to honor reverently the places dedicated to God … and to render them immune and tranquil from the disturbances of secular affairs … [lacuna] … those who are known to live gathered in those places for his service … [lacuna] … and we confidently trust that, from the just Judge and Lord of all rewards, who will repay each according to his works, temporal goods may be preserved and increased, and that the crown stored up for us … [lacuna] … rewards may be faithfully repaid with an undoubting mind.
>
> “Therefore let the goodwill of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable man Jeremiah, archbishop of the holy church of the city of Sens, which was built in honor of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of blessed Stephen the protomartyr and blessed John the Baptist, presented to our sight the charter of our immunity, which a few years ago, in the time of his predecessor, Archbishop Magno, we ordered to be made for the protection of that church. He also presented the immunity of our lord and father, Charles, the most pious Augustus, and of our predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks. In these it was inserted that they had caused that holy church, from remote and ancient times, to remain under the protection of their defense, together with all the possessions belonging to it, with monasteries and cells of both men and women, with fields and estates and its other possessions, and with all the families and free persons living upon the land of that bishopric.
>
> “But for the security of the matter, the aforesaid Archbishop Jeremiah requested our serenity that we should confirm the aforementioned charters, at this time, by our own order, for the love of God and the reverence of the saints in whose honor that holy church is known to have been founded, and for the increase of our reward. We readily granted his requests and decided that this charter of our protection and immunity should be made for that church, for love of divine worship and for the remedy of our soul. Through it we prescribe and command that the aforesaid holy church of Sens, remaining fully under the protection of our defense and immunity, together with monasteries and cells of both men and women—including the monastery of the blessed and holy virgin Columba, which we recently added to that bishopric by confirmation of our authority—and with the other cells in which companies of monks serve the heavenly mercy, namely the cell of Saint Peter, the cell of Saint John, the cell of Saint Heraclius, the cell of Saint Remigius, and, beyond the Loire in the district of the Arverni, the cell in honor of Saint Peter which that bishop began to build in a place called Noviacus;
>
> “and also with the cells of women established in the same city, namely the cell of Saint Maximinus and the cell of Saint Hilary; and with the places belonging to Saint Mary the Virgin established in the territory of the Wastinenses; and in the same district, at the fortress of Nantoni, the cell of Saint Severinus; likewise, in the district of Miliduinus, at the place called Milidunum, the church of the blessed ever-virgin Mary and of blessed Stephen the protomartyr, with its cells, villages, fields, and all other places belonging to that church; and likewise in the other districts and territories, both within and beyond the Loire;
>
> “and with all the possessions in Aquitaine belonging to the aforementioned bishopric, wherever they may lie—in whatever kingdoms, provinces, or districts subject to our imperial rule, which has been granted to us by God—we command and establish, as stated above, that under the complete protection of immunity, through the confirmation of this imperial authority of ours, they shall be so free and secure from every disturbance and interference by judicial power that no public judge, nor anyone supported by the authority of judicial power, shall dare to enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions that the aforesaid church now justly and legally holds or possesses in any districts or territories within the domain of our empire, or those which divine mercy may hereafter add to the dominion of that church, in order to hear cases, exact fines or tribute, demand lodging or provisioning services, or forcibly constrain sureties or the men of that church, whether free or servile, who live upon its land.
>
> “Nor shall anyone seek any restitutions or unlawful pretexts, nor collect tolls, banns, wheel-tolls, portage-tolls, or riverbank-tolls, either now or in the future; nor shall anyone presume to exact anything whatsoever of those matters mentioned above. Instead, whatever you might have been able to demand from the aforesaid possessions of the church, we grant in full to that same mother church, so that it may serve perpetually as an increase and support for carrying out the service of God.
>
> “And let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess peacefully, under the fullest protection of our defense and immunity, and free from every disturbance by judicial authority, the possessions of the aforesaid church, together with the monasteries and cells mentioned above that are subject to it, and all possessions and persons belonging or pertaining to them; and faithfully to obey our empire; and, together with the clergy and people subject to him, to pray to the divine mercy for our safety, for that of our wife and offspring, and also for the preservation of our entire empire through an immense succession of years by his most merciful compassion.
>
> “If anyone is found wickedly to have violated this constitution issued by us and fully confirmed for the love of God and desire for the heavenly homeland, and to have violated what we have most piously decreed or strengthened, let him be struck with a penalty of six hundred solidi of refined gold, so that by his example the insolence of all the wicked may be restrained and may learn to preserve inviolably whatever is known to have been established by us through devotion to piety.
>
> “It was also contained in those same orders how, through the negligence and envy of the rectors and ministers of that church of Sens, the written documents of its charters had been lost, and how our lord and father, Charles Augustus, at the request of Bishop Gumbert, had repaired that loss. For we too, embracing this work of piety in every way, as was fitting, long ago confirmed it with a kindly mind at the request of Archbishop Magno, namely that the rectors of that church, and the possessions and serfs that had been lost in those written charter-documents, as well as those that had subsequently been given to that church, should remain securely at all times in its right and power.
>
> “Nevertheless, for the security of the matter, Jeremiah requested our gentleness that we should strengthen those same charters with a new confirmation, for the love of God and the increase of our reward. We graciously assented to his requests and by this authority of ours command and establish that, if a dispute should arise concerning those possessions, already mentioned, which the aforesaid church now lawfully possesses or possessed before the written charter-documents were lost, and if it should be necessary for the matter to be argued legally in court, then through this authority of ours those possessions and serfs of the churches shall be defended just as they could have been defended by those same documents had they not been lost.
>
> “Since we wish this authority to possess fuller force in the name of God and to be preserved inviolate for all future time by all the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own people, we confirm it below with our own hand and order it to be sealed with the impression of our ring.
>
