> “Given on the seventh day before the Ides of May, in the thirteenth year, by Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, the most pious Augustus, in the fourth indiction. Done at the royal palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.”

Jeremiah died on the seventh day before the Ides of December 827 and was buried in the monastery of Saint Columba.

[Col. 0733]

# Letters of Jeremiah

## Letter I: To Amalarius

*(See below among the letters of Amalarius.)*

## Letter II: To Frotharius, Bishop of Toul

*(In Chesnius, volume II, page 722.)*

Jeremiah, the least of Christ’s servants, wishes perpetual health to his most beloved and ever-to-be-loved and embraced brother, Frotharius, venerable bishop.

I do not know what thanks I should offer for the things that you deigned, through the present messenger, to send back in reply to my humble request. I write only this: your charity, as it is accustomed to do, has promised to act generously. Indeed, if your sincerity had indicated otherwise, I could in no way have believed it, although you are wholly known and most manifestly evident to me.

Now I have sent this boy of ours ahead with our carts and the other provisions, so that you may deign to give orders concerning them, just as it pleased your affection to instruct me—namely, in such a way that everything may be brought safely to the place to which we are ordered to go.

Moreover, it has happened that salt is very dear in our province this year, because, on account of the rains, it could not be produced in the coastal saltworks where it was usually made until this time. It seems to us that perhaps some of it can now be produced there, though not in full quantity. Therefore I have sent a pound, so that you may consider how our carts might return to me from there loaded with salt, since, as you know, without the taste of salt the Christian life becomes insipid.

Do this as I ask, or keep the money for your own uses. May the power of the Almighty protect you from every evil and make you pursue with your whole mind the things that are pleasing to him.

[Col. 0733]

# In the Year of the Lord 833: Saint Ansegisus, Abbot of Fontenelle

## Life of Saint Ansegisus, Abbot

By an anonymous contemporary chronicler of Fontenelle.

*(Mabillon, *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, fourth century, part I, page 630.)*

[Col. 0733D]

## Preliminary Observations

### 1

Apart from what is reported below from the chronicle of Fontenelle, little remains for us to say about Ansegisus, except that he himself was the author of the collection of Capitularies circulated under the name of Abbot Ansegisus. Some have thought that it should be attributed to Ansegisus the abbot who later became archbishop of Sens. Jacobus Sirmondus refutes them in a letter to Constantine Cajetanus, believing it to be the work of Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes, on the authority of Sigebert in his *Chronicle* under the year 827, an authority supported by Trithemius.

Sirmondus rightly refutes the authors of the earlier view; but when we seek Ansegisus the abbot among the abbots of Lobbes, we do not find him. In the Chronicle of Lobbes, whose author was Abbot Folcuin, no abbot of that name appears.

We should hear Adso, or Hermiricus, abbot of Luxeuil, who wrote a book in the tenth century about the miracles of Saint Waldebert and his predecessors. Writing about Ansegisus, he says:

> “At that time the dignity of the people of Luxeuil, which among other things was wasting away from its former rigor, was already tottering almost to ruin. Caesar Louis, having observed this, placed in charge as pastor Ansegisus, a most worthy man, distinguished in character and pre-eminent in the splendor of wisdom. He repaired what had collapsed, gathered together what had been scattered, extended the boundaries of the Church farther, enlarged the surrounding workshops with broader spaces and higher walls, and decorated the walls of the church, together with its other ornaments, with beautiful variety.
>
> “He collected the capitularies of the Frankish kings, which had been enacted in various councils, and caused them to be contained in a single volume. Since he was dear to the kings of the Franks among the nobles of the kingdom, he devoted himself to just and pious works, brought his life to an end, and received a worthy burial in the place where he had extended the church more spaciously.”

From this it is clear that this Ansegisus was the compiler of the aforementioned Collection. It is nevertheless surprising that this was omitted by the Fontenelle chronicler, who is certainly a careful and authoritative writer.

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, mentions in his *Opusculum* 46 “two capitularies taken from Abbot Ansegisus, compiler of the imperial capitularies from all the synods and decrees,” namely the seventy-seventh and seventy-eighth chapters of the first book of the Capitularies, concerning the non-division of church property and the election of bishops.

### 2

The following is read about Ansegisus in the Calendar of Luxeuil: “On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, the death of blessed Ansegisus, abbot.”

It should be read “the thirteenth day before the Kalends,” as is clear from the following Life and from the ancient Breviary of Fontenelle printed by order of Claudius of Poitiers, abbot. In that Breviary there is an entry on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August commemorating Anchisilus, a monk of that place.

In the aforementioned Calendar of Luxeuil, under the twentieth day of May, there is also recorded the discovery of the body of Saint Ansegisus, abbot and confessor of Christ, although our people of Luxeuil do nothing concerning him in the ecclesiastical offices. The people of Fontenelle honor Ansegisus on 20 August and likewise on 19 November.

[Col. 0735]

# Life of Saint Ansegisus, Abbot

## The Life Begins

### 1

A distinguished, glorious, and tranquil man, sufficiently instructed in every kind of knowledge—both divine and human philosophy—Ansegisus was born to a father named Anastasius and a mother named Himilrada. By the ordering of divine mercy, he received the governance of this place in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 823, which was the tenth year of Louis, the most glorious Augustus, and approximately the seventh year of the apostolic Paschal, on the fourth day of the Nones of April, in the first indiction.

Concerning his illustrious origin, life, conduct, character, and deeds, it is fitting to insert into the present work only those things that will not offend the reader’s mind. For, according to the dignity of this age, he sprang from a noble lineage of the Franks, which he made nobler by the examples of his splendid works.

Two especially distinguished virtues shone forth in him: the first was to live well, the second to teach rightly. Finally, while his kinsman Girowald was governing this monastery as abbot, Ansegisus came to the monastery and received from him the tonsure of his head. Not long afterward, Girowald brought him to the palace and took care to commend him into the hands of the glorious King Charles.

### 2

After Geroald’s death, Trasarius obtained this monastery. Not long afterward, the aforesaid lord Ansegisus received from Lord King Charles, as a benefice, the monastery of Flaviacum, founded by Saint Geremar, whose body rests there. It is situated in the district of Beauvais. This occurred in the year of the incarnation of the Lord Jesus Christ 807, which was the thirty-ninth year from the time when Charles the Great had been established as king of the Franks, and the seventh year from the time when he had been called emperor and Augustus.

He found the monastery almost destitute of buildings, reduced to poverty and abandoned, but within a short time he strove to restore it through his noble industry. He caused all the buildings there, both public and private, after removing and discarding whatever had been consumed by age, to be constructed from their foundations and restored with greater elegance, as is evident to all who come there.

He was exceptionally skilled in the management of agricultural affairs. Consequently, an abundant supply of various crops was never lacking for him, and he always knew how to distribute it with a generous hand to all who were in need. He was indeed a great almsgiver, a nourisher of the poor, a lavish benefactor and defender of churches, a provider for clerics, a most true father to monks, a most joyful receiver of pilgrims, and a great helper of widows and orphans.

Before the monastery of Flaviacum, two other monasteries had been entrusted to him for governance by the unconquered King Charles: one situated near the walls of the city of Reims, built in honor of Saint Sixtus, the first bishop of that city, and under the jurisdiction of that same city; the other in the territory of the fortress of Châlons, where Saint Memmius, the bishop, rests buried in body.

[Note: [Col. 0735D] It is now the parish church of Saint Sixtus within the city walls.]

After these had been abandoned, he was appointed rector of Flaviacum in the year written above. Moreover, while he held the aforesaid monastery of Flaviacum by right of lease and benefice, he was also appointed by the lord king as superintendent of the royal building works at the royal palace of Aachen, under Abbot Einhard, a man most learned in every field.

He administered this office with great distinction and conducted himself wisely in all his works. By order of the same king he also carried out very energetically a great many embassies.

[Note: [Col. 0736D] That is, appointed over the royal buildings.]

### 3

Meanwhile, after Charles the Great, emperor and Augustus of blessed memory, had died, his son Louis was raised to the empire. The same lord Ansegisus deserved to be honored magnificently by him.

In the fourth year of his reign, Louis entrusted to Ansegisus, by right of benefice, the famous monastery of Luxeuil, renowned among the Gauls. In that year Pope Stephen died on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the third month after returning to Rome from the Franks; Paschal succeeded him in that see.

The moon underwent an eclipse on 9 February, at the second hour of the night. Abdiraman, king of the Saracens, sent envoys to the emperor at Compiègne to seek peace. They were heard at Compiègne, then proceeded again to Aachen, were detained for three months, and were sent back to their king.

In that same year Bernard, king of Italy, surrendered himself to the emperor at Chalon. But, leaving these matters aside, let us return to what we began.

### 4

In the third year of the reign of Lord Louis Augustus, Trasarius, rector of this monastery, returned to the place of his birth with the permission of that same emperor. On his way back to Benevento in Campania, he was honorably received by Duke Sigo, whom he had received from the baptismal font of holy regeneration.

After him, Einhard held this monastery for approximately seven years. When it was finally abandoned voluntarily, Lord Ansegisus undertook its governance in the year already mentioned, by divine command—as it is right to believe—and through the generosity of the most glorious Emperor Louis.

He ennobled it with such attentive care and supreme industry that he could be believed to be a new Wandregisilus, or that the great Bishop Ansbertus had returned to renewed life. Just as those men had ennobled the monastery at its beginning with buildings, increased the clergy [Note: [Col. 0737D] That is, the number of clerics, a term commonly applied to monks at that time.], and instructed them in ecclesiastical disciplines, so Ansegisus strove to repair what had been ruined and restored what age had consumed with greater elegance.

He increased the clergy most splendidly and strove in many ways to ensure that they lived according to the regular order and the rule of the distinguished Father Benedict. Through the negligence of earlier fathers, who had discharged less devotedly the care of the flock entrusted to them, the state of the holy Rule of the aforesaid Father Benedict already seemed almost ready to collapse, although those who served the Lord in canonical order conducted themselves irreproachably.

For, as I have said, through the carelessness of the superiors, who had delayed imparting what the authority of the Rule commanded to be given, the situation had come about. But the aforesaid most reverend Father Ansegisus strove in every way to restore it to its former state and rule, in accordance with what he knew to be the will of the lord emperor concerning this matter; and he did not neglect in any way to give what the authority of the Rule commanded to be given.

Finally, from the monastery of Luxeuil—which, in religious observance and regular discipline, appears even to the present day to be second to none in the lands of Gaul—he brought here with him monks who feared God and religious men. They would teach the monastic rule here and display salutary examples.

Yet formerly, men seemed to have been learned in this philosophy through the just man Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Fosses. They spent many days living in this monastery and left behind there some examples of their teaching and goodness. For, to speak truthfully, this monastery was in no respect inferior in religious observance to the monasteries of France or Gaul.

### 5

Nor is it surprising that, in the time of such an excellent leader, the soldiers of Christ proceeded along the royal road, even though now the love of Christ has not grown cold; for he himself was the standard-bearer of the most holy discipline and appeared worthy to be imitated by all.

Whoever heard him giving commands did not reproach him while acting otherwise. He rendered testimony to truth, not to friendship. They knew that his speeches were useful rather than witty. He abstained entirely from shameful words, knowing that license in such matters nourishes shamelessness.

Four virtues also shone forth in him, virtues on which every person ought especially to rely: prudence, fortitude, temperance, and justice. His speech was never empty; rather, toward his subjects and others, he either persuaded them to do good, or urged them to teach what was right; he either consoled the sorrowful, or commanded them to preserve faith inviolate toward the eternal and immortal God and toward the earthly king. He himself took care to fulfill these things first in his own actions.

Whatever he possessed among transitory things he considered of no great importance; rather, he believed it fleeting. Therefore he strove to distribute his treasures among monasteries and the needy, storing up treasures for himself in heaven, where the thief does not approach and the moth does not consume.

He was in every respect a fugitive from vices; toward the faults of others he was neither a harsh critic nor a meddlesome investigator. Finally, he was kind toward all, steadfast in adversity, cautious and humble in prosperity.

How magnificently he held to the virtue of justice is shown by the embassies that he frequently undertook at the command of the Augusti, especially the one carried out, at the order of the great Emperor Louis, in the Spanish March against Gautselmus, guardian of that frontier.

He was absolutely truthful in speech, steadfast in faith, ready in good works, just in judgment, prudent in counsel, distinguished in goodness, excellent in charity, Catholic in faith, rich in almsgiving, alert in intelligence, fluent in speech, and ardent in zeal. Truly, he was a useful vessel in the house of the Lord: serving God diligently, correcting those who went astray, encouraging those who had been corrected, disregarding the obstinate, always loving the humble, subject to the earthly king, and devoted to Christ, ruler of all.

### 6

How devoted he was to ecclesiastical concerns is demonstrated by the countless gifts that he himself bestowed upon the monasteries under his care.

In the monastery of Luxeuil he offered the following gifts: a beautifully made golden cross decorated with the most precious gems, having a staff covered with silver, which he was accustomed to carry with him on journeys; a golden offertory dish with its golden paten, of marvelous workmanship; three gilded silver chalices, made in repoussé work; a silver cup of excellent workmanship, with four golden snails attached externally at its base; a silver basin and ewer of marvelous workmanship.

He adorned the altar in honor of Mary, perpetual virgin, with a wooden panel, which he covered with various silver images.

Among vestments he gave one excellent *rodinum*, five *planetae* or chasubles, twelve *cindadi* of various colors, three dalmatics, six embroidered pallia, and eight excellent carpets.

He raised the church of Saint Peter higher in its construction, elevating its walls, and covered it with iron nails. He also built anew the portico that leads from the church of Saint Peter to Saint Martin; and, covering it, he fastened its shingles with iron nails.

### 7

At this Fontanellense monastery, therefore, he bestowed the following gifts. A large portion of the wood of the Lord’s life-giving Cross, enclosed in gold fashioned in a round design, with a crystal set in its center, so that the form of the wood of the holy Cross appeared within to those looking at it. Later, because of intervening sins—or through some other circumstance—thieves carried it away from the front of the bed of our protector, the blessed Wandregisilus, after breaking through the wall of the Basilica of Saint Peter. This happened on the day before the Nones of December, a Sunday, three months and sixteen days after the death of that glorious Father.

A golden chalice, wonderfully made, with two handles on either side, decorated with the most precious gems, weighing one pound; another, silver, made in repoussé work, of admirable workmanship, with its silver paten; a silver offertory vessel for the same chalice, bearing an image of marvelous workmanship; other silver offertory vessels with their corresponding silver patens; one large silver crown with its excellent silver lamp. Also, one silver lamp; one excellent silver censer; three silver candlesticks containing ninety solidi, that is, thirty each; two marvelous golden seals with precious stones; one excellent silver ewer with its basin; two glass cups adorned with gold, and one ivory cup, wonderfully made. Two ivory boxes; one excellent glass hanap.

He ordered four Gospels to be written in gold letters, in Roman script, on purple parchment. Of these, he completed Matthew, John, and Luke; but when his death intervened, the remainder was left unfinished. He likewise ordered a lectionary to be written on purple parchment and decorated with ivory boards; likewise an antiphonary on purple parchment, written in silver letters and adorned with ivory boards.

Of ecclesiastical vestments he gave three pallia called fundata; two stauracia; one Spanish coverlet; four carpets; six dalmatics suitable for the ministry of the ministers; one subdiaconal roccus; one scarlet garment; one priestly tunic of Indian color, with a complete vestment; four planetas or chasubles; three chasubles likewise of Indian-colored cindatus; three likewise of green cindatus; one of red or blood-colored cindatus; one chasuble likewise of purple-red color; two Roman capes, one made of red cindatus and ornamented around its circumference with green fringes, the other made of Pontic marten-fur, which the common people call beaver, likewise decorated around its edge with fringes of its own color; one excellent linen cloth; one excellent facistergium [perhaps facitergium]; two excellent fanones, one decorated with gold, the other with stauracium; likewise two of cindatus; two large silk cushions suitable for Gospel services, and one smaller; two belts made in Roman workmanship and decorated with gold; two small napkins; two stoles.

### 8

As for books, he gave the following abundance: an excellent library containing the Old and New Testaments, with prefaces and beginnings of the books decorated in gold letters; one volume of the blessed Augustine’s Expositions of Genesis Literally; likewise one volume of his Enchiridion; three volumes of his explanations of all the Psalms; one volume of his work Against Julian the Heretic; likewise one volume of his letters to various persons; likewise one volume of his book called *Whence Evil?*; likewise one volume of his book entitled *On Christian Doctrine*; his book of the Ten Chords; his work on the Epistle of John; likewise one volume Against the Epistle of the Foundation; one volume of his homiliary.

One volume of the blessed Ambrose’s Exposition of the Gospel of Luke; one volume of his Letters to Various Persons; likewise one volume of his book called *On the Good of Death*; likewise one volume of his work on Joseph and the Twelve Patriarchs.

One volume of the letters of the blessed Jerome; one volume of the letters of Saint Sixtus, Bishop; one volume of Josephus’s Histories; one volume of the *Sentences* of Taius.

[Note: This is Taius, also called Tagius or Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, who compiled four books of sentences from the works of Saint Gregory the First, pope.]

One volume of Paterius’s Excerpts from the Old and New Testament, drawn from the little works of Pope Gregory; one volume likewise of Evipius’s excerpts from the little works of Saint Augustine; one volume of Gregory on the middle portion of Job; one volume of the book of Fulgentius, bishop of Carthage; one volume of the book of Ferrandus, deacon of the Church of Carthage; one volume of Bede’s Exposition of Genesis; one volume of the same author’s work on the computation and reckoning of time; two volumes of Paul the Deacon’s Collections on the yearly cycle.

[Note: Namely, homilies on the Gospels for the entire year; on this matter, see Charlemagne’s letter to Paul.]

Two books of glosses; one volume of the canons of various councils.

### 9

The public and private buildings begun and completed by him are as follows. First, he had an exceedingly noble dormitory for the brothers built, two hundred and eight feet in length and twenty-seven feet in width. Its entire structure rises to a height of sixty-four feet. Its walls were built of very strong and adhesive lime, reddish and excavated sand, and porous but sound stone. In its middle it also has a solar furnished with an excellent floor, above which is a ceiling decorated with noble paintings. The house contains glass windows above, and its entire structure, except for the masonry wall, is constructed of durable oak timber. All its tiles are fastened above with iron nails; it has beams above and below.

After this he built another house called the refectory. He had it divided through the middle by a wall constructed for that purpose, so that one part would be the refectory and the other the storeroom. It was made of the same material and in the same dimensions as the dormitory. He had it decorated with various paintings on the walls and ceiling by Madalulfus, an outstanding painter of the Church of Cambrai.

He also had a third excellent house built, which they call the greater house. Facing east, it touches the dormitory at one end and adjoins the refectory at the other. There he ordered a chamber, a heated room, and many other structures to be built; but when his death came, this work remained partly unfinished.

These three excellent roofs were arranged as follows: the dormitory faced the northern quarter at one end and the southern quarter at the other, and on one side adjoined the Basilica of Saint Peter. The refectory likewise faced these same quarters and was almost contiguous, on its southern side, with the apse of the Basilica of Saint Peter. The greater house, as we have said above, was situated toward the east.

The Church of Saint Peter itself was situated on the southern side, though it faced east. On its western side it was enlarged by thirty feet in length and the same in width, with an upper dining hall constructed. He preferred that it should be dedicated in honor of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ. But this work too remained unfinished because of his very sudden death.

In the same Basilica of Saint Peter he ordered a square pyramid, thirty-five feet high and made of turned wood, to be placed at the summit of the tower of that church. He ordered it to be covered with lead, tin, and gilded copper, and placed three signs there, since previously this structure had been excessively low. He likewise ordered the tower itself, together with the apse, to be newly covered with lead tiles.

He further ordered another house to be built beside the apse of the Basilica of Saint Peter, on the northern side, which he decided should be called the Convent or Curia, which in Greek is called *Beleuterion*.

[Note: *Βουλευτήριον*—a place where deliberation takes place. At that time they also called the chapter-house, as we do now, the *Capitolium*. The chapter-house was called the *Capitulum* from the chapter of the Rule, which in ancient times was accustomed to be read there after Prime. Hence, among some people, the hour of Prime itself is also called the Chapter, according to the Roman Order.]

The brothers were accustomed to gather there to deliberate about any matter and seek counsel. There, on the raised platform, the divine reading is recited daily; there, whatever the authority of the Rule advises should be done is discussed. In it, moreover, he ordered a monument bearing his name to be placed, so that when he had reached the end of his present life, his own people might lay him there.

[Note: Thus it appears that even at that time it was customary for abbots to be buried in the chapter-house. Bertharius, abbot of Monte Cassino, provides another example in Book II, page 44, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*.]

Likewise, in front of the dormitory, the refectory, and the house that we have called the greater house, he ordered dignified porticoes with various balconies to be built. He placed beams upon them and extended them lengthwise according to the dimensions of those buildings. In the middle of the portico that appears to stand before the dormitory, he established the house of documents. The house in which the abundance of books would be preserved, called in Greek *pyrgiscos*, he placed before the refectory and had its tiles fastened with iron nails.

[Note: Greek *Πύργος*, Latin *turris*, “tower.”]

### 10

We have judged that the gifts he offered at the monastery of Flaviacum should also be recorded here. There, in generous kindness, he gave ten various silver chalices; a silver basin with its silver ewer; seven silver candlesticks; approximately forty various pallia; thirty various chasubles, planetas, and cindati, whose colors seem burdensome to describe. The number of fanones and linens is not preserved in memory.

In honor of the Holy Trinity he built a basilica. Before its altar he placed a panel decorated with silver images, and upon the altar itself he set a silver cross. He ordered the entire basilica to be decorated with various paintings.

The names of the books that he gave to that place are as follows: the *Pandect*, translated by the blessed Jerome from the Hebrew or Greek language; his exposition of the twelve prophets, comprising twenty books in one volume; his eighteen books on the prophet Isaiah, in one volume; his book of letters, in two volumes; one volume of his work on Solomon’s Proverbs; his work on the prophet Daniel; his work on the Gospel of Matthew, containing in the same book the decrees of Pope Gelasius concerning books to be received and not to be received, together with some excerpts from the books of Saint Ambrose the bishop’s *Hexameron*, in one codex.

Thirty-two [L.: twenty-two] books of Saint Augustine’s *City of God*, in one codex; one volume of his exposition of the Gospel of Saint John; one volume of his homiliary containing 147 sermons; one volume containing his fifteen books on the Holy Trinity; one codex of his harmony of the Gospels; one codex of his *On Christian Doctrine*; one codex of his exposition of the Creed; one codex of his eighty questions; his three books to Marcellus on the baptism of infants; two books on the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount; one sermon on the providence of God; one sermon on his own Nativity; one volume of a letter to Flactianus.

[Note: This work does not survive.]

Three books of his *Academics*; two books of his *Soliloquies*; one book on immortality; one book on the magnitude of the soul; one book on the Teacher; two books on order; one book on seeing God, in one volume; one codex of his *Confessions*; one codex of his book called the *Enchiridion*; one codex of his exposition of the Psalms; one volume of Saint Ambrose’s exposition of the Epistles of Paul.

[Note: Thus, in the ninth century, those commentaries on Paul that scholars now establish as Julian’s were being attributed to Ambrose, as is also clear from Hincmar and others.]

Seven books of Hesychius the presbyter on Leviticus, in one codex; the exposition of Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, on Matthew; the Apocalypse of Saint John, also containing Saint Isidore’s book of *Differences*, in one codex; one codex of Saint Hilary the bishop’s work Against the Heretics; one codex of the homilies of Pope Gregory on the final part of the prophet Ezekiel; one codex of his letters; one codex of Bede the presbyter’s exposition of the Acts of the Apostles; one codex on the seven canonical Epistles and the Apocalypse of John; one codex of the same author’s work on Mark’s Gospel; one codex of the same author’s work on Luke the Evangelist; one codex of Isidore’s *Testimonies* concerning Christ and the Church; one codex of his *Etymologies*; one codex of his *Rotae* addressed to King Sisebut.

[Note: If I remember correctly, this book does not exist among Isidore’s published works.]

One codex of Prosper’s *On the Active and Contemplative Life*.

[Note: This book is not by Prosper, but by Julianus Pomerius.]

One codex of the *Prognosticon of the Future Age*; one codex of a disputation of the faith between Arius the heretic and Athanasius the Catholic; one codex of the letters of Saint Cyprian the martyr; one codex containing Alcuin’s book on the Trinity; one codex containing the Rule of the blessed Basil, bishop, and the Rule of the blessed Benedict; one codex of the Ecclesiastical History of Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea; one codex of his Chronicle; one codex containing the ecclesiastical histories of three men, namely Sozomen, Theodoret, and Socrates; one codex of the canons of various Fathers; two volumes of sacramentaries; one volume of Cassiodorus on arithmetic; one volume of his exposition of the Psalms; two volumes of Origen’s homilies on the Old Testament; two volumes of his exposition of the Psalms; the Lives of the blessed confessors Jerome, Augustine, and Gregory.

[Note: Namely, the Life written by Paul the Deacon, since John the Deacon had not yet written on this subject.]

Also, one codex containing the passion of the blessed virgin Columba; one volume of an institution and collection by a certain person concerning the canonical life; one codex of the Deeds of the Franks; and many others, whose names do not now come to mind.

### 11

How solicitous he was in distributing alms is attested by his very actions. For at one time, namely in the eighteenth year of his rule, he suffered the illness that physicians call paralysis. He immediately summoned his household members, his faithful attendants, and his intimates, and took care, with a generous spirit, to make the following distribution of his possessions.

This gift or distribution was issued at his command and request by the venerable Hildemann, bishop of the city of Beauvais, together with the laymen Berteningus and Gerlo, and also the monk Lando. Its text is as follows.

At this monastery of Fontanella he gave ninety pounds to the brothers, since he had been accustomed to give thirty annually as a census; ten pounds to the lay servants; ten solidi to the elderly in that hospice and in the other dwellings of the poor; and forty pounds to the entire household of this monastery. I shall list individually the names of the other monasteries to which this same distribution of alms was sent.

To the monastery of Gemmeticum, he sent five pounds.

[Note: Gemmeticum was a monastery of men on the Seine below Rouen, near Fontanella, formerly very famous and commonly called Jumièges.]

To Logium, one pound.

[Note: Logium was a nunnery, now destroyed, situated on the Seine near the town of Caudebec, at the place now called the Port of Loges.]

To Fiscamnum, one pound.

[Note: An important monastery, at that time for women and now for men.]

To Villare, one pound.

[Note: Villare, commonly Montivilliers, was an important Benedictine monastery for women in the region of Caux.]

To Longogilum, one pound.

[Note: I have nothing to add concerning Longogilum.]

To Saint Walericus, one pound.

[Note: Saint Walericus at the mouth of the Somme.]

To the blessed Richarius, two and a half pounds.

[Note: Saint Richarius of Centula.]

To Saint Audomarus, two and a half pounds.

[Note: Saint Audomarus. The monastery of Sithiu was sometimes called this; it had two churches, Saint Bertinus and Saint Audomarus, both originally belonging to monks. Saint Audomarus is now the cathedral, while the other remains a monastery.]

To Saint Audoenus at Rouen, five pounds. To Saint Mary in the same church, two pounds; to Saint Martin in the same city and to the other cells, twenty-five solidi. To Ragnoardus, archbishop of that city, ten pounds, namely, so that he might distribute five to priests and five to the poor.

[Note: The monastery of Saint Audoenus still exists at Rouen. There, the cathedral church is dedicated to the blessed Mary, and there are two parish churches of Saint Martin.]

To the monastery of Penthale, fifteen solidi; to Penante, fifteen solidi.

[Note: The monastery of Penthale was situated on the Lirizinus River, the Lizaine, which flows into the Seine. It was founded by King Childebert in honor of Saint Samson, bishop of Dol, as is clear from his Life. Penante appears to have been the monastery of the same Samson at Dol, where he was buried; it is called Penetale in another Life of that saint by John a Bosco and is now the cathedral church of Saint-Malo.]

To Pratellos, likewise.

[Note: The monastery of Pratellum, commonly Préaux, likewise in Neustria, still survives. It was restored six hundred years ago by the nobleman Humphrey.]

To the city of Évreux, one pound; to the Cross of Saint Audoenus, two pounds.

[Note: The Cross of Saint Audoenus was also called the monastery of Saint Leutfredus, in the diocese of Évreux in Neustria.]

To the city of Lisieux, one pound; to the monastery of Fontanas, twelve solidi.

[Note: Fontanas seems to me to be what is called Fontenay, in the diocese of Bayeux, built by Saint Evremund, the abbot.]

To the city of Bayeux, two pounds; to the monastery of the Two Twins, two pounds.

[Note: The Two Twins, near Bayeux, is said to have been built by Saint Martin, abbot of Vertou; it now lies in ruins.]

To Saint Martin of Tours, five pounds; to those canons in the house, one pound.

[Note: From this it is clear that the monasteries of Saint Martin of Tours and Saint Anianus of Orléans had already been converted into houses of canons.]

To Saint Anianus of Orléans, one pound; to those canons in the same city, one pound.

To Saint Benedict at Fleury, one pound.

[Note: The monastery of Fleury, as well as Ferrières and Saint-Calais, has already been mentioned several times; these monasteries still survive.]

To Ferrières, two pounds.

To Saint Calais, one and a half pounds.

To the monastery of Curbion, one pound.

[Note: Curbion was the monastery built by Saint Launomarus.]

To Saint Columba at Sens, two pounds for the monks; to those canons in the same city, two pounds. Also, to Saint Peter, one pound for the monks in the same city.

[Note: The monasteries of Saint Columba and Saint Peter at Sens still survive and belong to our order. The monastery of Saint Remigius, likewise situated in the suburb of this city, has now been destroyed except for the oratory, which is now a parish church.]

In the city of Auxerre, one pound for those canons. Likewise, to Saint Remigius, one pound for those monks; to Saint Heraclius in the same city, likewise one pound. Also at Auxerre, to Saint Germanus, one pound for those monks.

[Note: The monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre still survives.]

At Troyes, to the monks at Saint Peter, one pound.

[Note: The monastery of Saint Peter at Celle near Troyes is discussed below, in connection with the translation of Saint Frodoaldus, the abbot; it still flourishes.]

To the monks at the Holy Cross of Meaux, likewise one pound.

[Note: The monastery of the Holy Cross at Meaux is now called Saint-Faron.]

To the monks at the monastery of Fossés, two pounds.

[Note: The monastery of Saint Maurus at Fossés, discussed below in connection with the translation of Saint Maurus, was given secular status a century ago.]

To Saint Genevieve at Paris, two pounds. To Saint Germanus at Paris, three pounds; to those canons in the same city, one pound. To Saint Dionysius, five pounds. To the monastery of Cala, two pounds.

[Note: At Paris, the monastery of Saint Genevieve belongs to regular canons of the Order of Saint Augustine. The monasteries of Saint Germanus and Saint Dionysius still flourish under our order.]

To Saint Lucianus, two pounds for the monks. To the canons at Beauvais, one pound. To the canons at Flaviacum, fifteen pounds. For the use of their servants, ten pounds. To Bishop Hildemann, ten pounds for priests and the poor. To the monastery of Oratorium, fifteen solidi. To the monastery of Fontanidum, ten solidi. To the monastery of Insula, ten solidi.

[Note: These are the monastery of Saint Lucianus at Beauvais; the Flaviacense monastery of Saint Geremar, so called after its founder; Oratorium, Oroer, formerly belonging to Saint Ebrulfus and later to Saint Angadrisma, now destroyed, as is Fontanidum; and the monastery of Insula, the very monastery that Saint Geremar is remembered to have built. Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, also mentions this monastery in his letter to Hincmar of Laon, preserved in Part II, chapter 3, of the Council of Douzy: “The monastery called Isla, in the parish of Beauvais,” and so forth.]

To the monastery of Andelagum, twelve solidi.

[Note: Andelagum was a monastery for women, commonly Andely, on the Seine four leagues above Rouen. It was praised by Bede the Venerable and collapsed long ago.]

To the valley of Malardum, ten solidi.

[Note: I have no observation to offer concerning the valley of Malardum.]

To the monastery of Resbace, one and a half pounds.

[Note: Resbace in the district of Brie, Rebais, whose first abbot was Saint Agilus.]

To Saint Salvius at Brago, ten solidi.

[Note: I cannot determine whether this is Saint Salvius at the town of Monstrol, or Saint Salvius at Brago. Unless one should read Saint Salvator at Brago or Brajaco, on the Seine in the district of Sens, which is mentioned in the Life of Saint Paternus.]

To the monastery of Mala, one pound.

[Note: I do not know which monastery Mala is. Nor do I think this passage should be explained by the monastery of Malas, in the diocese of Carcassonne, now called Montolieu; perhaps it refers to Malmedy.]

To Saint Vedastus at Arras, two pounds.

[Note: The abbey of Saint Vedastus at Arras is still famous.]

To Cambrai, two pounds; to Saint Gaugericus, one pound.

[Note: Saint Gaugericus is the collegiate church of secular canons at Cambrai, commonly Saint-Géry.]

To Corbie, five pounds.

[Note: The monastery of Corbie is frequently praised in the Lives of the abbots Saint Adalhard, Wala, and Paschasius Radbertus, and of Saint Ansgar.]

To Saint Eligius in the city of Noyon, one pound. Also, to the canons in the same city, one pound.

[Note: The monastery of Saint Eligius in the city of Noyon is now being restored from its foundations by our people.]

Also, to the canons in the city of Soissons, one pound; to Saint Crispinus, fifteen solidi; to Saint Medardus, one pound for the monks; to those nuns, three pounds.

[Note: The abbeys of Saint Crispinus and Saint Medardus for men, and of Saint Mary for women, still survive.]

At Rheims, one pound for those canons; to Saint Remigius in the same city, one pound for the monks.

[Note: Also at Rheims is Saint Remigius.]

To Saint Memmius at Châlons, one pound. To the same city, fifteen solidi.

[Note: The abbey of Saint Memmius at Châlons belongs to regular canons.]

To the monastery of Hautmont, where Saint Ansbertus was once forced into exile and, having thereby been removed from human society, fifteen solidi.

[Note: Hautmont, commonly Haumont, lies at the headwaters of the Sambre and still belongs to our order.]

To the monastery of Maubeuge, one pound.

[Note: Maubeuge, one league from here, is a house of secular canonesses or noble maidens. This house was once founded by the blessed Aldegund for holy virgins.]

To the monastery of Castrilocus, likewise one pound.

[Note: The same should be said of the nunnery of Castrilocus, built in the hills of Hainaut by Saint Waldetrude, the sister of Aldegund.]

To the monastery of Laubias, one pound.

[Note: Laubias on the Sambre is still an important monastery; it is discussed in the Lives of Saints Landelinus and Ursmarus, the abbot.]

To the monastery of Inda, two pounds. To the canons at Langres, one pound.

[Note: Inda lies near Aachen and was discussed in the Life of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane.]

To Luxovium, twenty-five pounds, namely, ten pounds to the monastery itself. To the cell of that monastery at Fontanas, one and a half pounds. To Cusantia, likewise one and a half pounds. To Anagrates, two pounds.

[Note: Luxovium, still a celebrated monastery in the Vosges, had Fontanas and Anagrates—Fontaines and Anegray—under it; they are still priories dependent on Luxovium. Cusantia, Cusance, was once a monastery founded by Saint Ermenfredus and made subject to Luxovium; it is now a priory subject to the Abbey of Saint Claudius.]

To Mount Romaricus, one pound.

[Note: The monastery of Habendum, Saint Romaricus, commonly Remiremont, is a Benedictine house of canonesses, formerly of nuns; it is discussed in the Life of Saint Romaricus.]

To Balma, likewise one and a half pounds.

[Note: Balma, La Baume, in the diocese of Besançon.]

To the monastery of Morbach, one pound; to Saint Gregory, one pound.

[Note: Morbach, or the monastery of Murbach, still exists in the diocese of Basel in the Vosges mountains. The monastery of Saint Gregory in Alsace, in the diocese of Strasbourg, commonly Münsterthal, still observes the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

To Maurus-Monastery, one pound.

[Note: Maurus-Monastery, formerly founded by Saint Leobardus in Alsace, was so called after the abbot Maurus, who lived under Theuderic IV; it is commonly Maurmunster and still survives under the congregation of Saint Vanne.]

To Melundas, one pound.

[Note: The monastery of Melundum, commonly Molesmes, in the diocese of Langres and the district of Tonnerre, is said to have been founded by Clovis the Great in the village of Melundis, situated in a narrow valley, and later transferred to the Armançon River. It is said to have been dedicated from the beginning to Saint Michael; it is now called Saint Martin.

For this reason, I think the following words in the catalogue of the enrolled brothers of the monastery of Saint Gall should be explained not by this Melundense monastery but by the monastery of Saint Peter at Milidunum: “The names of the brothers from the monastery of Saint Peter at Melondis: Epelinus, abbot; Abel, monk; Ratbaldus, monk.” If this is so, both monasteries were at some time called by the same name.

Certainly, the monastery of Saint Peter at Milidunum is said by Orderic Vitalis, in Book VII of his *History*, to have been restored—not originally built—by Sewinus, archbishop of Sens. Bernard was abbot of the Melundense monastery; he subscribed to the letters of Jonas, bishop of Autun, in the eighteenth year of Charles the Bald, in volume VIII of the *Spicilegium*, page 145.

In the Flavigny Necrology, on the seventh day before the Ides of March, Wido, abbot of Melundum, is commemorated; and on the third day before the Nones of July, Hugh, abbot of Meludum, a monk of Flavigny, though I do not know whether the same man is again entered under the same designation on the third day before the Ides of October.

Peter the Venerable, in Book I, Letter 27, mentions an abbot of Melundum, whose monastery William, abbot of Dijon, is said to have restored to better discipline. I found these notes among my papers to shed some light, however imperfectly, on that passage. See the Chronicle of Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, in Volume I of the Labbe collection, page 248.]

At Saint Reginbertus, where he had first learned the rudiments of letters, he spent twenty pounds on the needy through the hands of his mother.

[Note: I believe that the monastery of Saint Reginbertus is none other than that of Saint Ragnebertus in the district of Lyon, formerly called Bebronnum after the Bebronna stream, and still surviving. The difficulty is that Ansegisus, being a Frank, ought rather to have been educated in a Frankish monastery than outside Francia; by that name the ancients usually understood the kingdom of Neustria, though sometimes also Austrasia.

Alcuin speaks of a teacher named Regenberchtus in poem 264, but what has that to do with this passage? To note this in passing, during the reign of Charlemagne the cell of Bebronnum was held by Nantharius, abbot of Sithiu, the second to bear that name, as is evident from a letter of a certain Ertharius preserved in the chartulary of Folcuinus the Levite. It begins: “To the venerable father in Christ, Nantharius, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, or of the cell called Bebrona, where Ebrogerus appears to be provost.” It ends: “Done at Bebrona in the month of October, in the thirty-ninth year of the reign of King Charles, the sixth year of his empire.”]

In the same way, through the hands of Berteningus, he caused twenty pounds to be distributed; and he caused forty pounds to be given to those serving him in his own household. Three times he had all his possessions distributed to the needy and the poor, reserving nothing for himself.

[Note: From this it is clear that regular abbots at that time also possessed wealth as if it were their own, as is shown by the example of many abbots who made wills.]

I shall pass over how these things were carried out, lest I seem to have caused weariness or disgust. For by almsgiving he prepared his way, since he knew every human being to be a stranger [L.: that the last day of every human being is], whether for punishment or for glory. Therefore he strengthened himself by alms and by the prayers of God’s servants, so that he might pass peacefully through the course of this life and live forever in happiness.

That glorious man ruled this monastery for ten years, five months, and eighteen days. At that time Lord Ansegisus departed this life, as Sunday was dawning, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August. On the same day, amid the greatest mourning, he was buried outside the Basilica of Saint Peter, on the northern side, in the portico where the brothers were accustomed to hold their assembly and to lend their ears to counsels worthy of God. The office of governance then remained vacant for thirty-eight days.

[Note: Yet Adso, cited above in the preliminary observation, suggests that Ansegisus was buried at Luxovium. Nevertheless, the authority of this contemporary chronicler is to be preferred.]

## THE CONSTITUTION OF ABBOT ANSEGISUS

I have thought it appropriate to insert into this work the constitution that he established for the servants of God living in this monastery concerning food and clothing. Its text is as follows:

A memorandum of how the lord and venerable abbot Ansegisus, together with the agreement of the brothers, orderly arranged clothing, footwear, and food for the brothers staying in the monastery of Fontanella, so that, with every form of want excluded and without anyone having cause for complaint, they might fulfill their vows to God and at all times bring the undertaking of their pledged service to completion.

From the Bononian and Tarvanesian districts he decreed that sixty complete garments should be supplied, twenty white cloths [Note: Thus at that time undershirts were made of white cloth, and for this reason are called *stamineae* below. This corresponds to what I remember reading in the cartulary of Folcuin, deacon and monk of Sithiu, concerning a donation made by the cleric Deodatus to Odlando, abbot of Sithiu, in a charter dated to the thirty-second year of Charlemagne’s reign. In that charter Deodatus grants several estates for the use of the monks living in the monastery of Sithiu, namely, for purchasing cloth for overseas shirts, commonly called *berniscrist*. See Menardus, commentary on chapter 62 of the *Concordia*.], from which twenty shirts could be made; five assembled oxhides for soles; twenty modii of beans; twenty-one weights of cheese, at seventy-five pounds each; one thousand eggs; two hundred pounds of wax for that church; one hundred pounds for the use of the brothers; two hundred pounds of tallow; twenty-four shoes from Corialinse; sixty *bragal*. For making sacks, two white cloths, from which ten *stamineae* could be made; two *toaculas*; five assembled oxhides; ten modii of beans; twenty modii of peas; fifteen weights of cheese, at seventy-two pounds each; twenty-five modii of salt.

In the month of September, one thousand eggs; sixty from that rural estate; from Irtio and Idtio, three tablecloths, ten cubits long and two wide; from Apuliacum, one tablecloth of the same measurements. Three hairy linen cloths for drying the hands, each five cubits long and three wide; from Gera, three *camsiles* for making small tablecloths, thirteen cubits long and three wide; from Clariacum, one tablecloth ten cubits long and three wide. Likewise, from Hirtio, one *camsile* twelve cubits long and three wide, for drying the feet. From Campomis, one *toacula*; likewise from Rosontium; likewise from Floriacum. From the aforesaid rural estate, thirty weights of cheese, at seventy-two pounds each. Twelve felt coverings for making sacks [Note: In ancient usage, *filtrum* means anything made from wool that has been matted and compressed, such as the material from which hats are made, commonly called *du feutre*.]; for the beds, as much as necessity requires.

Sixty fattened pigs for fat and lard, together with their grease, and more as needed. From the estate of Rosontium, three modii of beans and five modii of peas. For the Nativity of the Lord, three *aucipastae* [Note: Thus they called meat-pies made from ducks or geese, and *pullipastae* those made from chickens; the eating of these was permitted to monks on the feasts of the Nativity and Easter by the Council of Aachen.], twenty *pullipastae*, sixty chickens, and 250 eggs; and likewise at Easter. Three pounds of wax, three sextarii of honey; and in the month of November, 500 eggs, firewood, sixty wagonloads.

Between that cross-estate of Paldriacum and Bladriciaga, three modii of beans and five modii of peas. For the Nativity of the Lord, four *aucipastae*, twelve *pullipastae*, sixty chickens, and 250 eggs; likewise at Easter. Three pounds of wax and three sextarii of honey.

In the month of December, 500 eggs, firewood, sixty wagonloads; from Campani, three modii of beans and eight modii of peas. For the Nativity of the Lord, four *aucipastae*, seven *pullipastae*, seventy chickens, and 250 eggs; likewise at Easter. One sextarius of honey and one pound of wax.

In the month of January, 500 eggs, firewood, sixty wagonloads; from Sadanma and Bubulo-captiva, two modii of beans and four modii of peas. For the Nativity of the Lord, two *aucipastae*, ten *pullipastae*, thirty chickens, and 100 eggs; likewise at Easter. Two sextarii of honey and two pounds of wax.

In the month of February, 500 eggs, firewood, twelve wagonloads; from Gariciaga, Duno, and Gera, three modii of beans and four modii of peas. For the Nativity of the Lord, three *aucipastae*, twelve *pullipastae*, eleven chickens, and 250 eggs; likewise at Easter. One sextarius of honey and one pound of wax.

In the month of March, fifty eggs, firewood, twelve wagonloads; from Petreopons and Wirto-laicum, two *toaculas*; five modii of beans and fifteen modii of salt. For the Nativity of the Lord, two *aucipastae*, twenty-six *pullipastae*, 105 chickens, and 500 eggs; likewise at Easter. Two sextarii of honey.

In the month of April, 500 eggs; from Idcium, one modius of beans and one modius of peas. For the Nativity of the Lord, one *aucipasta*, four *pullipastae*, twenty-five chickens, and fifty eggs; likewise at Easter. One sextarius of honey and one pound of wax.

In the month of May, fifty eggs, firewood, fifteen wagonloads; from Irtio, one modius of beans and two modii of peas. For the Nativity of the Lord, one *aucipasta*, four *pullipastae*, twenty-five chickens, and fifty eggs; likewise at Easter. One sextarius of honey and one pound of wax.

In the month of June, 500 eggs. Likewise, from Rosontium in the month of August, 166 eggs; from that cross-estate and from Campani, 168 eggs. From Revereis-curtis, forty-eight modii of wine; 255 eggs; wine from Alpiacum, 350 modii; from the estate of Riparensis, 150 modii; from Abriacum, fifty modii; from Burgundy, fifty modii: in all, 600 modii. Thirty-two modii of *adumaticum*. Cider and hops, as much as necessity requires.

Two hundred pounds of wax for that church; 130 pounds of oil; eight modii of fat. For the use of the brothers, 100 pounds of wax and 100 pounds of oil. Sixty prepared goat hides, three pounds. Forty *cordebisae* to be purchased, three pounds. Twenty oxhides, three pounds. Eight black hats, at thirty-two solidi; four others, each at three solidi, making twelve solidi. The three remaining ones, at seven solidi, together make two and a half pounds. One pound for purchasing thirty excellent *stamineae*; one pound for thirty pairs of trousers; one pound of honey and spices for the care of the sick.

Ten pounds for purchasing fifteen gray, dry *sicciscos* for sacks, from which cloaks are to be made—that is, according to this arrangement: each at ten solidi. Two excellent hats at thirty solidi; five remaining ones at thirty-six solidi; nine at fifty-four solidi, that is, each at six solidi, for making *rocci*, of which there are eighteen. Altogether they amount to ten pounds.

Two and a half pounds for placing fifteen *sagi* on the beds. Ten solidi for sheep-hides from which fur garments are to be made. One pound for gloves; one pound for bandages: altogether thirty-one pounds.

For the care of the sick, we have granted a lodging-estate called Bothmeregus and, whatever is suitable, *saura*, that is, pigs, wethers, sheep, chickens, eggs, and our entire tithe for that house of the sick. From our provisions and from those of our vassals we have given, at the monastery gate, the estate of Noviomum and the lodging-estates called Gisimacas, Strotella, Saint Stephen, Luviccina, Bantana, Cisternas, and Lenticulosa, for their illnesses and needs out of charity, as well as cheese and butter, and also for feeding their servants, and we have granted whatever else is necessary.

# In the Year of the Lord 834. Fredegis, Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Martin of Tours

## Historical Notice

*(In Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin Literature.)*

Fredegis, or Fredegisus, a prominent contemporary of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, is celebrated by Theodulf of Orléans in Book III of his *Poems*, verses 175–176:

> Let the teaching deacon Fredegis stand, accompanied by Ofulsus,  
> Each skilled in the art, each well spoken of.

On these verses Sirmondus notes [Note: Volume II of Sirmondus’s works, p. 1066; also in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XIV, p. 6.]:

> “There exists a little work by Alcuin addressed to this Fredegisus, [Note: Alcuin’s works, volume CI of Migne’s *Patrologia Latina*, col. 57. The same man is called Fridugisus; to him Alcuin’s letter on the three kinds of visions was addressed, and Dacherus published it.] in which he answers questions posed by him concerning the Holy Trinity; for he had been Alcuin’s pupil, as was Ofulsus. There also exists a letter by Fredegisus himself, the deacon, concerning Nothing and Darkness, not yet published, whose opening is as follows: ‘To all the faithful and to those of our most serene prince Charles who are present in his sacred palace, Fredegisus the deacon. The question concerning Nothing, long debated by many people, etc.’ It is established from various diplomas of Louis that he later became abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin and chancellor.”

This letter of Fredegis concerning Nothing and Darkness, addressed to the nobles of the palace [Note: Hilduin, bishop of the sacred palace; Wala, abbot; and others. Agobard’s letter to the same nobles is in volume XIV of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 280.]—in which he attempts to prove that Nothing and Darkness are something—was published by Baluze, volume I of the *Miscellany*, pp. 403–408.

His letter to Agobard has perished; but Agobard’s book against the objections of Abbot Fredegis survives and has often been printed among Agobard’s works and in volume XIV of the Lyons edition of the *Library of the Fathers*, pp. 275–280. It deals with various problematic expressions that are raised for discussion or voluntarily defended on both sides.

# Fredegisus’s Letter on Nothing and Darkness to the Nobles of the Palace

*(Baluze, Sacred Miscellany.)*

To all the faithful and to those of our most serene prince Charles who are present in his sacred palace, Fredegisus the deacon.

Having diligently revolved and examined with myself the question concerning Nothing, long debated by many people, which they left undiscussed and unexamined as though it were impossible to explain, I finally decided to undertake it. Breaking apart and untying the powerful knots in which it seemed to be entangled, I restored it to the light after wiping away its cloud of obscurity; and I judged that it should be entrusted to the memory of posterity for all future ages.

The question is this: Is Nothing something, or is it not? If someone answers, “It seems to me that Nothing exists,” the very denial by which he thinks to deny it compels him to admit that Nothing is something, when he says, “It seems to me that Nothing exists.” This is equivalent to saying, “It seems to me that Nothing is some thing.” But if it appears to be something, it cannot in any way appear not to be. Therefore it remains that it appears to be something.

If, however, the response is made, “It seems to me that Nothing is neither anything nor something,” this response must first be met by reason, insofar as human reason permits, and then by authority—not just any authority, but reason alone, which is itself authority and alone possesses immovable firmness.

Let us therefore proceed by reason. Every finite noun signifies something, such as “human being,” “stone,” or “wood.” Once these words have been spoken, we understand at once the things that they signify. For the noun “human being,” apart from any particular distinction, designates the universality of human beings. “Stone” and “wood” likewise embrace their respective general classes. Therefore Nothing refers to what it signifies. From this too it is proved that something cannot be nothing.

Here is another argument: every signification is what it is. But Nothing signifies something. Therefore the signification of Nothing is something that is—that is, an existing thing.

Since it has been shown briefly by reason that Nothing is not only something but also a great something, although countless examples of this kind could be brought forward, I wish to turn to divine authority, which is the protection and firm foundation of reason. For the universal Church, divinely instructed, which arose from Christ’s side and was nourished by the food of his most sacred flesh and the drink of his precious blood, and which from the very cradle of its mysteries was taught, professes with unshaken faith that divine power produced from Nothing the earth, water, air, and fire, as well as light, the angels, and the human soul.

The mind’s gaze must therefore be raised to the authority of so great a height—an authority that cannot be annulled by any reasoning, refuted by any arguments, or attacked by any force. For it proclaims that the things which are first—indeed, first and chief—among creatures are not to be estimated [the transmitted wording is defective; the manuscript reads “first” twice]. Indeed, since none of the things generated from it can be valued as it truly is, who has fully measured the nature of the elements? Who has grasped the substance and nature of light, or of angelic nature, under its veil?

If, then, we have been unable to comprehend these things by human reason, how shall we establish how great or what kind that thing is from which they derive their origin and kind? I could add many other points, but I believe that these are sufficient to make the matter clear to all teachable minds.

## Whether Darkness Exists

Since I have suitably concluded these matters with this brief statement, I immediately turned my attention to resolving questions that rightly seemed worthy of inquiry to inquisitive readers.

There is indeed an opinion held by some that darkness does not exist and that it is impossible for it to exist. A prudent reader will recognize how easily this can be refuted by the authority of Sacred Scripture. Let us therefore see what the history of the Book of Genesis teaches on the matter. For it says: “And darkness was over the face of the abyss” (Genesis 1). If darkness did not exist, with what consistency is it said that it did exist?

Whoever says that darkness exists establishes the thing. Whoever says that it does not exist removes the thing by denying it. Thus, when we say, “A human being exists,” we establish the thing—that is, the human being. When we say, “A human being does not exist,” we remove the thing by denying it—that is, we remove the human being.

For the verb of substance has this in its nature: whenever it is joined to any subject without a negation, it declares the substance of that subject. Therefore, in the statement “Darkness was over the face of the abyss,” a thing is established, and no negation separates or divides it from existence. Moreover, “darkness” is the subject, while “was” is declarative. By predicating, it declares darkness to exist in some manner.

Behold: invincible authority accompanied by reason, and reason confessing authority; both proclaim one and the same thing, namely, that darkness exists.

But although these examples, set forth to demonstrate what we have proposed, are sufficient, nevertheless, so that no opportunity for contradiction may remain to our opponents, let us make the matter clear by adding a few divine testimonies from among many, so that, struck with fear, they may no longer dare to hurl their most foolish words against them.

When the Lord was punishing Egypt with harsher plagues because of the affliction of the people of Israel, he enveloped it in darkness so dense that it could be felt. It not only deprived human eyes of sight, but, because of its thickness, was also subject to the touch of their hands. Whatever can be touched and felt must exist. Whatever must exist cannot fail to exist. Therefore it is impossible for darkness not to exist, because its existence has been proved by the fact that it can be touched.

Nor should we pass over the fact that when the Lord of all made a division between light and darkness, he called the light “day” and the darkness “night.” If the name “day” signifies something, the name “night” cannot signify nothing. Day signifies light, and light is certainly something great. What, then, are we to say? Is darkness without significance, when the same Creator who gave light the name “day” impressed upon darkness the name “night”? Is divine authority therefore to be annulled? In no way.

For it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for divine authority to be altered from its established state. The Creator impressed names upon the things he created, so that each thing might be recognized when called by its own name. He did not form any thing without a name, nor did he establish a name unless there existed something for which it was established. If he had done so, it would appear entirely superfluous—something that it is impious to say God did.

If it is impious to say that God established anything superfluous, the name God imposed upon darkness cannot in any way be considered superfluous. If it is not superfluous, it is appropriate. If it is appropriate, it is also necessary, because it was needed to distinguish the thing signified by it.

It is therefore established that God formed things and names appropriately, and that the names are mutually necessary.

The holy prophet David, filled with the Spirit and knowing that darkness does not denote something empty and insubstantial, plainly expressed that it is something. He says: “He sent darkness” (Psalm 104). If darkness does not exist, how can it be sent? Whatever can be sent can be sent to a place where it is not. But what does not exist cannot be sent anywhere, because it is nowhere. Therefore darkness is said to have been sent because it existed.

Likewise: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17). He made what existed, and in a certain manner he made the darkness that existed his hiding place.

Likewise: “As is his darkness” (Psalm 138). Here it is shown that darkness is possessed, and consequently its existence is made clear. For everything that is possessed exists. Darkness, however, is possessed. Therefore it exists.

But although these proofs are sufficient in number and strength, and hold a very secure stronghold against every attack from which they can easily repel the weapons against their attackers, something must nevertheless be requested from the firmness of the Gospel.

Let us therefore set forth the words of the Savior himself: “The children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness” (Matthew 8). Attention must be paid to the fact that he calls it “outer darkness.” For “outside,” from which “outer” is derived, signifies a place. Therefore, when he says “outer darkness,” he demonstrates that it is local. For it would not be outer unless there were also inner darkness.

Whatever exists must necessarily be in a place. What does not exist is nowhere. Therefore outer darkness not only exists but also exists in a place.

In the Lord’s Passion the Evangelist likewise records that darkness came over the land from the sixth hour of the day until the ninth hour. Since it came into being, how can it be said not to exist? What has been made cannot be made not to have been made. But what has never existed and never was, never exists. Darkness, however, came into being. Therefore it cannot be made not to exist.

Again, in the Gospel: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great will the darkness be?” (Matthew 6; Luke 11). I believe no one doubts that quantity is attributed to bodies, since all things are distributed according to quantity. Quantity, moreover, is an accident of bodies. Accidents either exist in a subject or are predicated of a subject.

Therefore, by saying “how great will the darkness itself be,” quantity is shown to exist in a subject. From this it is reasonably inferred that darkness not only exists but is also corporeal.

I have therefore taken care to write these few points, gathered together by both reason and authority, to your greatness and prudence, so that, holding fast to them firmly and immovably, you may not be led astray from the path of truth by any false opinion. If someone should perhaps advance an argument contrary to ours, return to this teaching as to a rule, and from its judgments you will be able to overthrow foolish contrivances.

*Here ends the treatise on Darkness.*

# In the Year of the Lord 834. Haiminius, Monk of Saint Vedast of Arras

## Historical Notice

Haiminius, a monk of Saint Vedast of Arras, of the Order of Saint Benedict and a disciple of Alcuin, wrote the *Miracles of Saint Vedast, Bishop of Arras and Cambrai*, who died around the year 540, as well as a sermon for Saint Vedast’s feast on 6 February concerning eleven children healed through his merits. These works are found in the *Acts of the Saints*, volume I for February, p. 801 and following.

# Haiminius’s Sermon on the Feast of Saint Vedast: On Eleven Children Healed through His Merits

*(Bollandus, Acts of the Saints, February.)*

## 1

I beseech you, children of light: let your hearts rise to divine praises for the benefits bestowed. Let what already burns in the mind break forth into speech, so that those whom faith illumines may be strengthened by a pure confession.

The material for praise is present; the cause for rejoicing is at hand. It is seen by the eyes, held by the hand, and experienced through its usefulness. Those who have never learned to deceive bear witness. Those who have not yet fully learned to speak are already eloquent.

“For out of the mouth of infants and nursing children,” says the Psalmist, “you have perfected praise” (Psalm 8:3). The one Lord of all, rich toward all who call upon him, makes the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom 10:21). They teach by faith, although they cannot yet teach by speech; indeed, Christ teaches through those to whom he grants such grace. He himself illumines inwardly, while outwardly he shines through miracles.

Wonderful and astonishing things happen in every way, and the rarer they are, the more they must be proclaimed. Ancient things return; former events recur; things often heard are revealed. For what we read in the sacred books, we see repeated before our eyes.

A man blind from birth sees. For Christ works in the Church what he once did in the Synagogue (John 9): he illumined that man in both heart and body. This child, because he had been reborn, he illumined in body, so that he might awaken in the minds of the sluggish a faith that had grown numb.

You who were present certainly know what the Lord Jesus did today through the merits of his servant, our blessed Father Vedast; indeed, he completed what was lacking. He healed two sick persons: to one he gave the light of his eyes, rather than restored it; to the other, because he was lame, he restored the power of walking.

## 2

I am about to speak of marvelous things, which all of you know equally well with me. Our own Father Vedast, though still sacred in his tomb, continues to provide what he accomplished while living in the flesh in the world. This illustrious senator of the heavenly court decrees the salvation of his children. Through outward miracles he shows that in the sanctuary of the saints he intercedes for our souls.

He repeats, as I have said, the very thing he once accomplished. You remember, dearest brothers—and you can remember—that when blessed Vedast was sent by Saint Remigius to preach the word of God to the nations, at the entrance to the city of Arras he cured two poor sick men, a blind man and a lame man, so that by the miracle he was about to perform he might demonstrate what he would accomplish through the word. For just as he opened the eyes of the body to see the world, so through faith he illumined human hearts with the seed of God’s word to know God. And just as he restored the movement of the foot, so he directed the steps of the faithful toward the path of good works.

But because—alas!—our hearts are now growing sluggish toward good works, they must be awakened by the display of miracles. Attend, I ask you, beloved brothers, to what has happened and in whom it has happened. For God’s mercy not only foresaw what it would accomplish through the merits of his servant, but also the persons to whom it would apply such great remedies of salvation.

Those who consider God’s benefits less carefully are accustomed, whenever healings take place in the bodies of people through the merits of the saints, to say—alas!—that they have not been healed, because they think that they had suffered infirmities. What will they say about these children, whose age does not permit them to feign illness? With what charges will they be able to accuse them?

Here are nurses and mothers who brought them weak and are taking them back healthy. One is from the estate of Corbie, called Walgiacus [Note: A town of Picardy on the Somme River.], and the other is a tenant of the church of blessed Vedast. The child from Corbie has been given sight; the servant of blessed Vedast has been given the ability to walk. Both are children; both are innocent; both are humble and upright.

Because our Lord is the salvation of little ones—that is, of the humble—he has now healed little ones, so that we may say that we ought to be humble, that is, to be little ones. For he still cries out: “Let the little children come to me, for the kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Mark 10:14). Behold, he embraced them and healed them; he received them from their parents, blessed them, and gave them back.

## 3

Let each of us give thanks; let us all give thanks to the Almighty, who deigns to visit us again and to reveal to us the fatherly heart of the most sacred bishop. Let us be roused from the sleep of laziness, and through the things we see outwardly as marvelous let us be impressed inwardly with the form of piety.

Let us open the eyes of our minds, so that we may deserve to see eternal light. Let us wash ourselves with tears, so that we may deserve to be purified. Let us run while we have the light, lest darkness overtake us.

Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of mind and body. Let the word of God be a lamp for our feet; let unfailing light be continually our desire. Let us seek and perform works of light, not of darkness and wickedness.

Let us run along the way of God’s commandments. Let us say to our God with mouth and heart: “Direct me, Lord, in your truth and teach me, and direct my steps according to your word, so that no injustice may rule over us.”

Let us implore the Lord’s mercy through the intercession of so great a patron. Let us guard our heart with every care, because from it life proceeds. With humble heart and supplicant voice, let us go before the face of the Lord in confession, so that we may experience in our minds what the children have now merited in the restoration of their limbs.

Let us return to our consciences; let us confront ourselves; let us punish the evils we have committed. Let us consider what we shall say on the day of the judgment of the great God. For those who refused to listen to him, he will no longer heed.

What more could he have done? While living, he ministered the word of God night and day to those who listened; he rained down words and flashed forth miracles. And now he reigns with Christ in heaven, yet he does not cease to care for our salvation.

Let us implore the Lord’s mercy through the intercession of the holy Father, so that here we may remain in his teaching and there rejoice in eternal and shared glory. Let us therefore obey his admonitions here in this life, so that we may rejoice there in a common reward.

Let us prepare here on the road what we may possess in our homeland. May the Lord Jesus, who wills all people to be saved, grant that by doing good we may come to such a patron and rejoice with him forever in eternal joy. Amen.

# Haiminius’s Letters

*(Bollandus, in the same place.)*

## First Letter: Milo the Deacon, Later Priest, to the Venerable Father Haiminius

To the most reverend Father Haiminius, Milo, your most devoted son, offers an unfading joy of eternal happiness.

Once I enjoyed the most kindly conversation of your gentleness, at the time when, received by you, I, though unworthy, deserved to be gladdened by your address and warmed by its honeyed sweetness. I now offer my thanks.

For such great kindness toward my smallness flourished in your excellence that thereafter the fire of love for you, already kindled in my heart, did not cease to burn—and not without reason. Since, filled with the honey of the purest love, you poured forth the deeds of heart and body that had their dwelling in the inner chambers of your breast, you easily obtained that your beloved memory should never at any time slip from my innermost being, but should be preserved and endure eternally, renewed and blooming with unfading blossom.

Therefore, trusting in your most praiseworthy fatherhood, I, as a son, have placed in your hands the foolish verses of my inexperience—an exercise, as it were, for my little talent in the *Life of the Blessed Amandus*. I humbly beg you: if you find in them anything less consonant with the Catholic faith or inconsistent with metrical law, mercifully and as a father bring it back to the standard of a reliable rule, and do not abandon me to my error. I testify and beseech you by the blood of Christ, which was poured out for the salvation of the Christian people.

If, with the mercy of the heavenly Majesty going before us, my poetic text should receive an equitable judgment, then together with me offer due praises with rejoicing to the giver of this gift, namely the Holy Spirit, by whose grace I have been able, however inadequately, to construct so great a work.

My rusticity must be forgiven, since, as someone says, rusticity was created by the Most High. And although in some places I could have employed more difficult verbal circumlocutions, I was restrained from doing so because I also believed that this work would be more pleasing if it were accessible to the hearing of all the brothers.

May your excellence therefore favor not my faults but my labors, so that you may receive in heaven what the mortal eye does not see. We wish you eternal health for the benefit of all the faithful.

## Second Letter: Haiminius to Milo

Haiminius, the lowliest servant of Christ, sends greetings to his Milo.

The poem that you presented, dearest brother, I read with eager attention. But since reading it once was not enough, I was glad to continue examining it. Returning to the beginning, therefore, and not without critical judgment, I reread and rehearsed the entire work from start to finish—what I had previously touched only lightly—applying all the powers of my attention to it.

At first, I confess, I thought I had set foot upon level ground. But when I discovered that my smallness would not merely be watered by a cup from the spring but would be overwhelmed by the floods of eloquence, I thereafter showed the whole stream to the brothers who were with me, taking care that they might know how it should be navigated.

And because I encountered in it neither a reef that impeded the faith nor anything contrary to metrical law, I urge our brothers, who do not shrink from such studies, gladly to accept this gift. I beg them to prefer being summoned to a similar study rather than being consumed by the fires of envy.
