For we know that citizens always envy their fellow citizens and, according to the Savior’s saying, no prophet—or, as you are accustomed to say, no poet—is accepted in his own homeland. But since envy kills the small, the one who envies is recognized to be lesser than the one who is envied.

Good heavens! I marvel that he has been able to prepare an elaborate banquet for the rich whom I thought he could scarcely provide even a taste for the poor. I plainly attribute this to the merits of the most beloved Amandus, whose praises I never cease to celebrate and in whose honor I never cease to praise Christ.

The language is therefore sweet, and the poem pleasing with wit; the discourse flows with gentle movement and plain speech. What more? Let my associates speak and judge as they wish. I, however, reveal the secret of my heart: my dear friend, you have sufficiently and abundantly illuminated the praises of so great a Father in your poem.

Do not, I beg you, desist from what you have begun. Do not succumb to laziness or idle leisure. Do not neglect the grace that accompanies you. Instead, while you have the opportunity, always exercise yourself in good studies, and do not deny to others what you have received freely. Do not wish to possess the common good alone. This is the only wealth that knows how to increase through expenditure; this alone grows when scattered and gains profit when distributed; this is also the wealth that condemns its hoarder to punishment and adorns the good steward with the glory of an eternal reward.

> Excel in new virtue; farewell, Milo, excellent poet;  
> And say, “God, have mercy,” as your Haiminius asks.

# In the Year of the Lord 834. Hilderic, Abbot of Cassino

## Historical Notice Concerning Hilderic

*(In Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin.)*

Hilderic, abbot of Cassino for a few days in the year 834, wrote verses on the origin, life, education, teaching, religion, and manner of life of his teacher Paul the Deacon. Peter the Deacon calls them “very lucid” in chapter 9 of *On the Illustrious Men of Cassino*. John Baptist Marus published them in his notes on Peter’s chapter 8. There are no more than forty-two verses.

[Note: We have found no verses by Paul the Deacon. Who Marus is, who annotated Peter the Deacon’s *Chronicle*, completely escapes us. EDIT.]

I scarcely doubt that this Hilderic is different from the author whose metrical letter is quoted by the Anonymous of Salerno in the second part of his *Chronicle*, published by Muratori, *Italian Historical Sources*, volume II, p. 265. That letter is addressed to the emperor Louis II, to whom he offers every good wish. It begins:

> This is the world’s creator, who by his word created all things,  
> From nothing, surely, fashioned everything at once.

Perhaps, however, the author of this Hilderic’s letter lived somewhat later than can be reconciled with Hilderic of Cassino. For the former presented this letter around the year 876, whereas the Cassinian Hilderic governed that monastery as abbot in the year 834. Yet the reliability of the Anonymous of Salerno in chronological matters during those years is by no means certain.

# Hilderic’s Metrical Letter

*(In Muratori, *Italian Historical Sources*, volume II, part II, p. 266.)*

> This is the world’s creator, who by his word created all things,  
> From nothing, surely, fashioned everything at once.  
>   
> Labor without labor, for whom to be able and to know is to exist;  
> Whose willing is his work, whose labor is profound repose.  
>   
> Let heaven henceforth praise him, and all heavenly things always,  
> The exceedingly blessed camps of angelic light.  
>   
> Let earth praise him, and every creation of the world,  
> Every race of humankind, creeping thing, and winged beast.  
>   
> They say—and let us say: To you, O King, be everlasting glory,  
> You who retain all things and rule them by your right.  
>   
> Every honor is fitting for you; to you virtue and grace have yielded;  
> You whom the underworld, the fields, and the heavens rightly fear.  
>   
> One and three, God, true Light and Wisdom,  
> You hold an immortal kingdom without end.  
>   
> You alone establish the ages, reigning without time;  
> Truly, as you are the beginning, so you have no end.  
>   
> You are beginning and end, first and last,  
> Through whom times, ages, and days run below.  
>   
> You restrain all things and change them, yet you yourself are never changed.  
> You always were as you are now, and you will always remain.  
>   
> You whom cherubim and seraphim, together with all the heavenly world,  
> Proclaim holy, celebrate together, and tremble before.  
>   
> You are compassion, goodness, repose, patience, and peace,  
> Life, salvation, honor, chaste love, and fear.  
>   
> You are prudent simplicity and simple prudence;  
> The world rightly fears, adores, and loves you.  
>   
> We ask that you quickly grant me heaven’s covering, O Christ,  
> So that, your members together with their head, we may praise you.  
>   
> Long-suffering, truthful, strong, wondrous, gracious,  
> Terrible and gentle, receive the prayers we offer.  
>   
> Maker of all, judge, guardian, and nourisher,  
> King of kings, feared one, spare your people.  
>   
> Bring aid to your servants, grant pardon, destroy their sins;  
> Drive out demons; put every harmful thing to flight.  
>   
> Lead to heaven the people whom your Lamb’s blood purchased,  
> Whom the Spirit and the water have brought forth anew.  
>   
> Look kindly upon the groaning, sighs, and voices  
> Of those who cry out to you, and have merciful compassion.  
>   
> Holy Jesus, Redeemer, protect us by your death,  
> Lest the destructive lion or dragon destroy us.  
>   
> May blessing and power be yours, Almighty One,  
> Through endless ages; may all strength be yours. Amen.

# In the Year of the Lord 836. Ahyto, or Hetto, Bishop of Basel

## Historical Notice Concerning Hatto

*(In Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Later Latin.)*

[The supplied source ends here.]

[Col. 0761C] Hatto or Haddo, Hetto, Ahyto, Haydo, Haitho, Otto, formerly abbot of the monastery of Augia, became bishop of Basel in the year 806. In 811 Charlemagne sent him, together with Hugh [Note: [Col. 0761C] In the Pithaean Annals, among the Twelve Writers, p. 22, and in the Anonymous of Melk, ch. 43, [Col. 0762C] he is called Bugo.] of Tours and Aio of Auville, to Nicephorus, emperor of the Greeks, concerning the establishment of peace and the boundaries of the empire. But the Itinerary in which he described that journey of his nowhere survives today. Having returned as an old man to the monastery of Augia, he died in the year 836 [Note: [Col. 0762C] Miraeus, Cave, and others, following Hermannus Contractus.]. The Visions of Saint Wettin, a monk of Augia, appeared together with the visions of Hildegard, mentioned below, and in Mabillon, *Benedictine Centuries*, century IV, p. 263. He published a capitulary for the priests of the diocese of Basel, promulgated around the year 827, in twenty-five chapters. Dacher, vol. VI of the *Spicilegium*, p. 961 (new edition, vol. I, pp. 584, 586), from which it was repeated in the volumes of the Councils by Labbe, Hardouin, and Coletus.

[CAPITULARY.]

[Col. 0763]

## HETTO’S CAPITULARY

(Hartzheim, *German Councils*)

The following chapters were ordained for the priests of his diocese by Hetto, bishop of the Church of Basel and abbot of the monastery called Augia [Note: [Col. 0763D] Augia Dives is a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict on the Rhine, in the diocese of Constance.], so that they might be shown how they ought to govern themselves and the people entrusted to them chastely and justly, and how they ought to strengthen them in religion.

### I

[Col. 0763A]

First of all, the faith of priests must be examined: how they believe and teach others to believe; and here examples must also be proposed, so far as the Creator can in some measure be understood from the creature.

### II

Second, it must be commanded that everyone learn both the Lord’s Prayer, in which all things necessary for human life are contained, and the Apostles’ Creed, in which the Catholic faith is comprehensively contained—both in Latin and in the vernacular [Note: [Col. 0763D] That is, in German, the language spoken by the Franks, and therefore called “barbarian” by Latin-speakers]—so that what they profess with their mouths may be believed and understood in their hearts.

### III

Third, it must be made known that suitable responses to the priests’ greetings are to be learned. Not only clerics and those consecrated to God are to offer the priestly response, but the entire devout people must respond with one harmonious voice.

### IV

Fourth, priests are to learn the faith of Athanasius and recite the Athanasian Creed by heart [Note: [Col. 0763D] Literally, “from the heart”; that is, from memory.] on Sunday at the appointed hour.

### V

Fifth, they are to know what the sacrament of baptism and of confirmation is, and what mystery the body and blood of the Lord constitute: how visible creation is seen in these same mysteries, while invisible salvation is supplied for the soul’s eternity, which is contained in faith alone.

### VI

[Col. 0763C] Sixth, they are to learn those things necessary for priests, namely: the sacramentary, lectionary, antiphonary, baptistery, computus, penitential canon, the Psalter, and homilies suitable for the Sundays throughout the year and for each individual feast. If one of all these is lacking, the name of priest will scarcely remain in such a man, because the evangelical threats are exceedingly dangerous, in which it is said: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into a pit” (Matthew 15).

### VII

Seventh, they are to know the proper times for baptizing during the year, namely Holy Saturday of Easter, so that the threefold immersion in baptism may imitate the Lord’s three-day death, made glorious by the resurrection. Therefore, until the eighth day, this sacred rebirth is to be celebrated by all the Christian people. The other time for baptism is to be celebrated on Holy Saturday of Pentecost. If necessity arises, however, help must be given at any time, because necessity scarcely has a law. The vessel used for the baptismal font must never be used for other purposes.

### VIII

Eighth, it must be announced that they are to know the times of abstaining from work throughout the year: namely, every Sunday from morning until evening, lest they be caught in Judaism. The days of abstaining from work throughout the year are the following, as we began above: the Nativity of the Lord; Saint Stephen; Saint John the Evangelist; the Holy Innocents; the octave of the Lord; the Epiphany; the Purification of Saint Mary; Holy Easter, as contained in the preceding chapter; [Col. 0764B] the Rogation Days for three days; the Ascension of the Lord; Holy Saturday of Pentecost; Saint John the Baptist; the twelve apostles, especially Saints Peter and Paul, who illuminated Europe by their preaching; the Assumption of Saint Mary; the dedication of the basilica of Saint Michael the Archangel; and the dedication of any oratory, or of any saint in whose honor that church was founded. The last is to be announced only to the neighbors living around it, not generally to everyone.

When a fast has been proclaimed from the palace or from the household [Note: [Col. 0764D] The kings of the Franks are said to have imposed fasts upon their subjects; see the laws in Gregory of Tours, Book XIX, chapter 2.], it must be observed generally by all. The remaining feasts during the year—Saint Remedius [Note: [Col. 0764D] Perhaps Saint Remigius.], Saint Maurice, and Saint Martin—are not to be imposed as days of abstaining from work; yet neither are they to be forbidden if the people wish to observe them chastely and with zeal for God.

### IX

Ninth, the same priests must be commanded not to permit unrelated women to live with them, in accordance with the Council of Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0764D] Council of Nicaea, canon 3, vol. I, p. 137], except only those concerning whom no suspicion of ill repute can arise.

### X

Tenth, they are not to enter taverns, whether sitting at home or occupied on a journey. If they nevertheless need to purchase something there, they are to send their messengers, have what is offered brought to another house, and receive it faithfully with thanksgiving.

### XI

[Col. 0764D] Eleventh, they are not to attend secular courts, [Col. 0765A] nor become sureties. They are not to keep dogs for hunting, hawks or falcons, sparrowhawks, or any license for games or spectacles. For it is enough for them that it is written in the Psalm: “Their will is in the law of the Lord, and on his law they meditate day and night” (Psalm 1); and that the Apostle commands: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Timothy 2:4).

### XII

Twelfth, they are to know that no one is to be ordained for money, nor should anyone seize control of a church through gifts. If this is done, both the candidate and his ordainer are to be deposed, because it is manifest that those who do such things are afflicted with the Simoniac heresy. According to the words of the Gospel, such a man does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way and is a thief and a robber. Not only those who do this, but also those who consent to those doing it, are to be excommunicated.

### XIII

Thirteenth, no one is to dare receive a wandering cleric from another parish, allow him to live with him, or let him celebrate Mass without our permission. Nor is anyone to assume the governance of any church or people without our prior approval [Note: [Col. 0765D] Some words are missing: namely, “let him grant permission” or “give authorization.”]. Whoever acts otherwise will be excommunicated.

### XIV

Fourteenth, they are not to celebrate the mysteries of the Mass in huts, unconsecrated churches, or houses, except perhaps for the sake of visiting those confined by illness. If they do so, they are to know that they must be degraded for disobedience.

### XV

Fifteenth, the tithe given by the faithful is to be called God’s due [Note: [Col. 0765D] Perhaps *census* should be read.], and is to be rendered wholly to God. According to the canon of Toledo [Note: [Col. 0765D] The Ninth Council of Toledo.], one third of it should belong to the bishops. We, however, do not wish to exercise this authority, but wish to have only a fourth part of it, in accordance with the decrees of the Roman pontiffs and the practice of the Holy Roman Church. If anyone is found contentious in this matter, whether he is a cleric or a deacon, he will be deprived of communion and judged by synodal censure.

### XVI

Sixteenth, each person is to see to it that women do not approach the altar, and that women consecrated to God are not involved in any ministry of the altar. If the altar cloths must be washed, they are to be removed by clerics [Note: [Col. 0765D] Namely, from the altar.], handed to the women at the chancel screen, and received back there. Likewise, when offerings are presented by these women, they are to be received there by the priests [Note: [Col. 0765D] For “by the presbyters.”] and carried to the altar.

### XVII

Seventeenth, the priests themselves are to preach by word and [Col. 0766A] example that no one should accept interest, whether a one-and-a-half-fold return (*sesculpa*) or one thing in exchange for another. For the one who does this is exceedingly faithless and rebellious against God’s commands. This is known to be forbidden equally to all Christians, but especially to priests, who ought to be the form and example of faith for everyone.

### XVIII

Eighteenth, no ordained person, nor anyone about to be ordained, is to move from his own parish to another, nor go to the thresholds of the apostles for the sake of prayer while abandoning the care of his church [Note: [Col. 0766D] For “deserted.”], nor go to the palace to lodge an appeal; nor may anyone suspended from communion receive communion from another without the permission and prior knowledge of his own bishop. If he does so, such communion, ordination, or departure is invalid. This is also to be announced to all the faithful: those who wish to go to the thresholds of the blessed apostles for the sake of prayer are to confess their sins at home and then set out, because they must be bound or absolved by their own bishop or priest, not by a stranger.

### XIX

Nineteenth, nothing is to be read or sung in the church except those things whose authority is divine and which the authority of the orthodox Fathers has sanctioned. Nor are false names of angels to be venerated [Note: [Col. 0766D] See the decrees of the Roman Council in volume I concerning the names of angels, p. 65.], but only those taught by prophetic and evangelical Scripture, namely Michael and Raphael.

They are not to hold divergent judgments in the cases of penitents, when one wishes to please one person by being more lenient and another by being harsher, flattering one and disparaging another. Rather, after considering the status of the person, the judgment of punishment is to be applied according to the measure of the fault.

### XX

Twentieth, they are to be admonished to weigh that whatever is given by the faithful is the redemption of sins. Therefore they are not to boast of using such revenues, but should rather excel in what was said to the priests in the Old Testament: “They must bear the iniquity of the people” (Numbers 18:1, 23). For this reason they must be solicitous with great fear concerning those whose gifts they share, because it is a grave danger to become responsible for another person’s life when one does not know how to govern one’s own.

### XXI

Twenty-first, they are to know and understand what the crime of incest is. Each person is to see to it in his own parish that it does not occur; and if it does occur, it is to be corrected as quickly as possible. Namely, no one is to take a spouse from among his relatives as far as the fifth degree [Note: [Col. 0766D] For “degree” or “fifth generation.”].

If it is claimed to have occurred unknowingly, that claim is not to be readily believed, but is to be tested by God’s judgment. They are not to be separated in the fourth degree, but are to persevere in penance throughout all the days of their union. Likewise, a man may not have two wives joined to each other by the same relationship, nor a wife two husbands joined to each other in the same way; nor may there be a co-father or co-mother, a spiritual son or spiritual daughter from the font or from confirmation, a woman consecrated to God, another man’s wife while her husband is alive, or another woman’s husband while his wife is alive. No one may lawfully be joined in marriage with such persons.

If those in the first or second degree are found to have committed the crime of fornication, they are to know that they have utterly forfeited the rights of marriage forever. If those in the third degree are found to have been polluted by such a crime, suitable penance is to follow; nevertheless, the rights of marriage are not to be denied to them with other persons [Note: [Col. 0767C] For “they are not to be joined to each other at the same degree.”].

Where slaves belonging not to one master but to different masters have been joined, such a union will not be valid unless both masters consent. Whatever is found to have been neglected and is not corrected with whatever strength is possible—whoever consents to such negligence will be responsible for that union. Many other matters could have been written concerning the crime of incest, such as unions involving a mother and daughter, a stepmother, and almost innumerable cases that do not come to mind for writing. Nevertheless, marital union is forever denied to persons of this kind and to those similar to them.

### XXII

Twenty-second, they are to be admonished to know how to announce to the people what the works of mercy are, together with their fruits, as set forth in the Gospel and the Apostolic writings, by which one reaches life; and what the works of iniquity are, together with their manifold fruits, by which one proceeds by the left-hand path toward eternal destruction. They are also to avoid the crime of perjury in every way, because perjury is recognized as a crime not only when committed in the Gospel or upon the relics of the saints, but also in the Truth, who is God, if one lies.

### XXIII

Twenty-third, they are to be admonished to know that in the churches over which they preside they have become bridegrooms. Therefore, with all vigilance, they are to devote the care of their whole life to adorning those churches and serving them without ceasing.

### XXIV

Twenty-fourth, they are in no way to omit the canonical hours, both by night and by day. For just as the Roman Church sings the psalms, so must all who pursue [Note: [Col. 0768C] Perhaps “who hold to.”] the way of the same discipline do. The reason is clear: not only the precepts of the New Testament, but also those of the Old Testament, require observance of the same form. The Prophet, inspired by the Holy Spirit, declares: “Seven times a day I have praised you,” and, “At midnight I rose to confess to you” (Psalm 118:62, 164).

### XXV

Twenty-fifth, they are to announce to the people that the spiritual sons and daughters whom they receive in baptism, for whom they become sureties and sponsors, renouncing on their behalf the devil to whom they had previously been enslaved, are to remain under their care until they have reached adulthood and have explained and rendered to them the pledge of their faith and renunciation. What they promised on their behalf, they must require from them in the same responses, in full.

## APPENDIX

[Col. 0767]

## DIPLOMA OF THE EMPEROR LOUIS THE PIOUS

Granted to Hetto, bishop of Basel, for the monastery of Sintleozesavia, or Reichenau, on 14 December 816.

(From Grandidier, *History of Strasbourg*, vol. II, p. 16.)

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus [Col. 0767D] Christ, Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor Augustus.

If, for the love of God, we bestow suitable benefits upon places devoted to divine worship and upon those who serve him in those places, we confidently trust that a reward of eternal recompense will be repaid to us by the Lord. Therefore let the diligence—or advantage—of all our faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable Hetto, bishop of the Church of Basel and abbot of the monastery of Sintleozesavia [Note: [Col. 0767D] That is, the abbey of Reichenau, called Sintleozesavia after a noble Suevian, Sintlaus, prefect of Alemannia, who granted the estate of the aforesaid abbey to Saint Pirminius, its founder. *Augia*, *Ow*, and *Au* signify “meadow” in German. The monastery was first called Sintlausowa, then Augia, and finally, with the passage of time, because of its wealth, Augia Dives, or Reichenau. The aforesaid abbey is now united to the episcopal mensa of Constance. On the growth of Augia Dives, consult Eckhart, vol. I of the *Commentaries on the Affairs of East Francia*, p. 348, and Calmet’s *Helvetic Journal*, p. 93.], situated in the duchy of Alemannia, namely in the county of Undresinse [Note: [Col. 0768D] Besselius, in the *Prodrome of the Chronicle of Göttweig*, and his predecessor Paulinus, in *The Counties of Ancient Germany*, say nothing about the county of Undersinse. Those learned men omitted many counties that unpublished charters are gradually bringing to light. The county of Undresinse comprised the region surrounding Lake Constance, called Untersée. Lake Constance, also called Lake Bodamicus or Podamicus (*der Bodensée* or *Bodmer See*), was divided into two parts: the upper lake, Obersée, and the lower lake, Untersée.], built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin, and of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, has placed before our eyes the immunities of our lord and father, the pious Augustus Charles, of blessed memory [Note: [Col. 0768D] The privilege of Charlemagne for Sintleozesavia, issued in 813, is found in Crusius, *Swabian Annals*, vol. I, part II, book X, p. 10, and in Lunig, *Ecclesiastical Spicilegium*, part III, vol. IV, p. 188; this is plainly the document that Louis the Pious mentions here.]. In them we found inserted how he himself and his predecessors, the earlier kings of the Franks, had always held the aforesaid monastery, together with the monks dwelling there, under their fullest protection and the safeguard of immunity, for the love of God and their tranquility.

Nevertheless, for the security of the matter, the aforesaid Bishop Hetto requested that we confirm by our authority, for the love of God and reverence for that holy place, the authorizations of those same kings. We willingly granted his petition, conceded everything accordingly, and confirmed it through this decree of ours.

Therefore we command and order that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, dare enter, in our time or in that of our successors, the churches, estates, places, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid monastery which it now justly and reasonably possesses within the dominion of our empire, or which divine mercy may hereafter cause to be added to the rights of that holy place, for the purpose of hearing legal cases, exacting fines, requiring lodgings or provisions, taking sureties, unjustly coercing the monastery’s people—whether free or unfree—who dwell upon its land, or seeking any payments, bans, or unlawful exactions; nor presume to demand anything at all of what has been mentioned above.

Rather, let the aforesaid bishop and his successors be permitted to possess the property of the monastery in peace, under the protection of our immunity. Whatever the fiscus might hope to receive from it, we grant entirely to the aforesaid monastery for eternal recompense, so that it may perpetually increase for the support of the poor and the maintenance of the monks serving God there.

And whenever, by divine calling, the aforesaid abbot or his successors depart from this life, so long as the monks themselves are able to find among their own number men capable of governing that congregation according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, they shall have, by this authority and consent of ours, permission to elect abbots. Thus may it please the monks who serve God there continually to beseech the immeasurable mercy of the Lord on behalf of us, our wife and offspring, and the stability of our entire empire.

Therefore, so that this authority may possess fuller force in the name of God, and so that it may be more truly believed and more carefully preserved by the faithful of the holy Church of God and by our own faithful, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

[Col. 0770B] Sign of Louis, the most serene emperor. I, Durandus the deacon, have reviewed it in place of Helisachar. Given on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the second year, with Christ’s favor, of the reign of our lord Louis, most pious Augustus, in the ninth indiction. Issued at the royal palace of Aachen [Note: [Col. 0770B] The Annals of Einhard, in Bouquet, vol. VI, p. 176, attest that Louis the Pious spent the winter of 816 at Aachen.], prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

# BOOKLET ON THE VISION AND DEATH OF WETTIN, MONK OF AUGIA

Written by HETTO, former abbot of Augia and former bishop of Basel, on the basis of Wettin’s own account.

(Mabillon, *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, century IV, part I.)

[Col. 0769]

## PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

### 1

Concerning the vision or dream of Wettin, or Guettin, a monk of Augia in Alemannia, Hermann, a monk of that monastery, records the following under the year 824, when it occurred:

“At Augia, Wettin, a monk, was led out of his body and brought back again; after three days he died. His visions were written in prose by Bishop Hetto and in heroic meter by Walafrid.”

Walafrid’s poem was printed by Henry Canisius in volume VI of the *Ancient Lections*. The prose work of Heito or Hetto, never previously published, was taken from two manuscript codices and generously entrusted to me by the man of outstanding learning and humanity, Stephen Baluzius, prefect of the Colbert Library. He also honored his kindness to me with an elegant letter, which will take the place of my observations here.

“To the distinguished and learned man John Mabillon, Benedictine monk, Stephen Baluzius of Tulle sends greetings.

“Religious susceptibility, distinguished sir, is the greatest and most powerful incentive to our credulity. The age of Louis the Pious was inclined toward piety, eager for signs and miracles, and exceedingly desirous of acquiring sacred relics; it was also especially devoted to visions and revelations, and especially fertile in them. The Book of the Revelations of Audradus bears witness; the Vision of Bernold the priest bears witness, as does also that of an English priest, which is reported by the author of the Annals of Bertin; finally, lest I try uselessly to mention each one individually, this vision of Wettin, a monk of Augia, bears witness. I send you a copy of it [Col. 0770C] taken from two ancient manuscript codices of the royal library: one of them belonged to the Parisian senator Claude Puteanus, the other to John Besly of Poitiers, men whom, as you know, were exceedingly learned.

“Walafrid Strabo identifies the author of this little work as Hetto, abbot of Augia. Strabo had been Wettin’s disciple and auditor, and later rendered the work in hexameter verses, placing almost word for word the prose account into poetry. Yet you, excellent sir, thought that one might reasonably doubt whether this was genuinely Hetto’s writing, because at the beginning of Strabo’s poem—which is said to have been taken from Hetto’s narrative—many details concerning the history of the monastery of Augia are read that do not appear in the royal codices.

“But I discovered that Strabo did not perform the office of interpreter so strictly that he did not sometimes remember that he was also a paraphraser and poet. It follows that I believe the earlier part of the poem, which was not necessary in a simple narrative, was added by Strabo in the manner of poets, who generally describe the location and antiquity of the places in which the events they intend to write about took place.

“That vision was both the most celebrated and the most favorably received of all those that occurred in that age. It was believed immediately and immediately spread and became known throughout all the peoples of the Frankish empire. Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, reports that he read it in a letter concerning the vision of Bernold the priest: ‘But also, in the time of our lord Emperor Louis, in our own age, I reread the revelation made to a certain religious man named Witino.’ Ratpert, in chapter nine of *The Origin and Misfortunes of the Monastery of Saint Gall*, while listing the books of that monastery, says that the Visions of Wettin and Barontus were written in one of them. That it reached Aquitaine is clearly inferred from the fact that it is inserted in the Chronicle of Malleac, in the Besly codex. Its authority was so great that the monks of Saint Vincent of Metz later wished to share in its glory. For this is the beginning of that Vision in the Puteanus codex, which undoubtedly belonged to Saint Vincent of Metz:

“‘The Vision of Guettin, formerly a canon and afterward a monk, which God showed him through an angel; and we, his brothers, wrote it down as he narrated it, servants of Saint Vincent of Metz.’

“Strabo and the manuscript Chronicle of William, archbishop of Mainz, state that these events occurred in the year 824. Epidannus, however, assigned Wettin’s death to the preceding year. But the matter is not important enough to require anyone’s critical judgment, much less yours, excellent sir. It would also be easy to illuminate this narrative, which contains a great deal of hidden history of those times. It will be for your prudence to judge what ought to be done. Meanwhile, farewell—not only in mind, as you always do, but also in body, which you possess in a weak and extremely delicate state—and always love me, who am ever devoted to your name and reputation. Paris, 21 June 1673.”

### 2

Thus far the letter of that most learned man, which plainly elucidates Hetto’s work, written by Hetto on Sunday, 30 October 824, from Wettin’s own account. Later, the monks of Saint Vincent of Metz transcribed this Vision of Wettin as he himself narrated it—that is, from Wettin’s account given to Hetto.

### 3

In the following year, namely 825, at the request of Grimoald, archchaplain and later abbot of Saint Gall, Walafrid turned Hetto’s prose narrative into verse at the Easter festival, when he was eighteen years old. This shows that he was a young man of precociously mature talent for his age, as is also demonstrated by [Col. 0771C] the verses he published in his fifteenth year to Ebo, archbishop of Reims, in the person of his teacher Tatto, and by others addressed to Agobard in the eighteenth year of his life. Certainly, the additions Walafrid made to Hetto’s narrative display judgment mature for the author’s age; and the names of the persons whom Hetto passed over in silence he expressed obscurely, just as he had received them from Wettin’s own mouth.

### 4

Perhaps some will ask why Wettin’s Vision is published by me here, since Wettin was not enrolled in the canon of the saints. I answer that Wettin, if not a saint, was at least a pious and religious man, as Hincmar calls him, and that he died a pious kind of death. His Vision could nowhere be reported more suitably than in these Acts, since it contains much worthy of knowing concerning the history of that age and concerning the proper ordering of morals. The condition and various names of the monastery of Augia were discussed in the Life of Saint Pirminius, in part II of the third century. [Col. 0771D] The history of the Vision must now be presented; its title appears as follows in the royal manuscript codex.

[Col. 0771]

## [BOOKLET ON THE VISION AND DEATH OF WETTIN]

## THE VISION OF GUETTIN

The following vision appeared to Brother Guettin in a monastery situated in the region of the people of Alemannia, called Auva in their language, during the reign of the Frankish prince named Louis, who was also ruler of the Roman Empire, under the abbot of the aforesaid monastery, named Heido [Note: [Col. 0771D] It is clear from Walafrid’s poem and Hermann’s Chronicle that Hetto had relinquished the administration one or two years earlier.], on the day before the death of the aforesaid brother.

### 1

When the aforesaid brother, on Saturday, had taken a drink with some of our brothers for the preservation of his bodily health, while the others digested it beneficially, he began to vomit it back with great difficulty, undigested, and immediately after taking the food which he ought to have consumed to restore his body, he began to loathe it. At dawn on the following day, Sunday, he felt somewhat better, and together with the others whom he had associated with himself to attend to the aforementioned bodily needs, he took nourishment, but he continued in the aforesaid state of loathing.

Nevertheless, he did not at all think that he would suffer danger to his bodily life on this account, because the nourishment he took on Monday and Tuesday, as his loathing diminished, had encouraged him without any remaining distrust. On Tuesday, however, as evening twilight began, when the brothers were seated with him for a meal, he said that he could not remain there with them until the meal was finished. While they were dining, therefore, he had the bedding of his bed carried from the place of the aforesaid confession [perhaps: meeting] into another cell adjoining that cell, separated from it only by the intervention of one wall, so that he might rest there while awaiting the end of their meal and his own return once more to the place of his bed.

### 2

With his limbs arranged on the bed, his eyes merely closed but, as he himself acknowledged, not yet surrendered to sleep, an evil spirit came, presenting the appearance of a cleric. Its face was so deformed, blind, and dark that no signs of eyes appeared in it. It carried various kinds of instruments of torture in its hands and stood at his head, terribly and exultantly, as though it were going to torture him the following day.

While that torturer threatened him, suddenly a throng of evil spirits appeared, filling the entire space of his cell. Armed with small shields and spears and encircling him on every side, they seemed to be constructing a certain building, prefigured in the form of Italian cupboards [Besly’s codex reads: “little cupboards,” or “prefigured in various forms”], for his confinement.

The aforesaid brother was surrounded by such horror and intolerable terror, and became so anxious, that he no longer had any hope whatsoever of escaping the signs of this death. But behold, divine mercy suddenly appeared. For at once magnificent men, honorable in appearance and dressed in monastic habit, appeared in the same cell, seated on benches. One of them, sitting apart from the others, said to them in Latin, in the very words written here, as he himself reported:

“It is not right that these useless fellows should do such things, for the man is resting. Order these men to withdraw.”

After his voice, the assembly of evil spirits vanished and withdrew. When the immense terror had been removed, an angel came, shining with incredible beauty, clothed in a purple garment and standing at his feet, addressing him in a friendly voice:

“I come to you, most beloved soul.”

The same brother answered him in Latin:

“If my Lord were to forgive my sins, he would show mercy; but if not, I am in his hand. Let him do what seems good to him. For patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, and every heavenly or earthly dignity, labor for the human race. And you ought now to labor more, because in these times we are more fragile.”

When this conversation between the angel and the aforesaid brother had ended, the first vision came to an end. We who committed these things to writing had it written down from his account, with the very words exchanged between them, omitting nothing and adding nothing of our own.

### 3

The same brother awoke and sat up. Looking around to see whether anyone was with him, he found two men: the superior of the monastery and another brother, who had been left behind to comfort him, while the others had already been dismissed after supper to rest.

When they had been summoned, he explained to them in order everything that had been shown to him in that most confined [Col. 0773B] moment of time, exactly as it is written here. He was already trembling so greatly at the horror of the vision described above that, forgetting the burden of his entire bodily distress, he was tormented by an intolerable fever of fear.

In the immensity of that fear, he anxiously fell to the ground before the aforesaid brothers, stretching out his whole body in the form of a cross, and asked them to intercede for his sins with all the strength they could muster. While he lay prostrate in this way, the aforesaid brothers began to sing on his behalf both the seven penitential psalms and the other psalms suited to such great anxiety that came to their remembrance.

### 4.

When these things had been completed, he rose and sat up on his little bed, asking that the *Dialogues* of blessed Gregory be read to him. Accordingly, the opening of the last book of that same *Dialogue* was read in his hearing [Col. 0773C] up to the completion of nine or ten folios. When the reading had ended, he urged the aforesaid brothers to relieve by bodily rest the weariness they had incurred by keeping vigil for him, and to grant him the little portion of the night that remained for a respite in which to rest.

When they had withdrawn and had placed their bodies in a part of his cell for repose, he too, after such great weariness of both soul and body, had fallen into sleep. Then the same angel who had appeared to him in the earlier vision, standing at his feet, dressed in purple, came to him again, now standing at his head, clothed in white garments and shining with indescribable brilliance. Addressing him in gentle words, he praised the refuge he had made in God when placed in distress, both through his devotion to psalmody and through reading, and urged him thereafter to continue doing likewise without fail [Col. 0773D].

Among other things, he admonished him often to repeat Psalm 118, because moral virtue is described in it. He said that he was greatly pleased whenever he saw anyone devoted to assiduous reading and the repetition of psalmody, and that God could thereby be made propitious, provided that this practice were maintained sincerely and not hypocritically.

After saying these things, the same angel took him and led him along a road of immeasurable beauty. As they proceeded, he showed him mountains of immense height and incredible beauty, which appeared to be almost marble. A vast river of fire flowed around them, and within it an innumerable multitude of the damned were held in punishment [Col. 0774A]. He confessed that he recognized many of them. In other places he had seen people tortured by innumerable torments of various kinds. Among them he had seen many priests, both of lower and higher rank, standing with their backs fastened to stakes and bound tightly with straps in the fire. He had also seen the very women whom they had violated, bound in the same manner before them and submerged in the same fire as far as their genitals.

The angel told him that they were beaten on their genitals with rods without interruption, except for one day’s interval, on every third day. He said that many of them were known to him personally.

“The greater part of the priests,” said the angel, “hungering after worldly profits and serving the concerns of the palace, raising themselves up through luxurious clothing and the display of their dishes, think that gain is piety. They do not watch over the winning of souls. Abounding in pleasures, they rush upon prostitutes; and thus it comes about that they can be intercessors neither for themselves nor for others. For they could have come to the aid of the world, which is suffering from pestilence and famine, by their prayers, if they had been willing to devote their profit to God with all their strength. And therefore they are condemned at the end to such a recompense, because they suffer such things in accordance with their preceding merits.”

### 5.

There also, he confessed, he had seen a certain structure, like a castle, very disorderly in its construction of wood and stone and disfigured by soot, with smoke rising high from it. When he asked what it was, the angel replied that it had been the dwelling of certain monks gathered from various places and regions for their purification.

From that same number he singled out one in particular, whom he said had been shut up there in a leaden chest and must await the day of the great judgment because of a peculiar deed which he had previously committed in the case of Ananias and Sapphira, corrupting the integrity of the common life.

Concerning this brother, damnably confined, the same matter had previously been shown, nearly ten years earlier, to a certain pilgrim who had been carried away suddenly at the end of his life, as rumor had then spread; but it had long since been effaced from memory. This brother had never heard of it before, and by a similar vision he recalled the same matter to remembrance.

From this it is evident that when something that produces an evil growth has been cut down twice in one and the same matter, it must be cut down more frequently still, lest among those who are reckoned under the name of monks a peculiar deed there be turned into the burden of lead.

### 6.

There too the height of a certain mountain was shown to him [Col. 0774D]. The angel told him concerning a certain abbot who had died nearly ten years earlier that he had been appointed to its summit for his purification, not for eternal condemnation. There he was suffering all the harshness of the weather, the violence of the winds, and the discomfort of the rains.

The same angel added concerning him that a certain bishop who had recently died ought to have assisted that abbot by the comfort of his prayers in obtaining pardon, just as he had commanded him through one of the abbot’s clerics, appearing to him in a vision.

But the bishop mentioned above, treating this negligently, had not been moved by the warmth of charity to assist him by undertaking the struggle. “And for that reason,” he said, “he will now be unable to help even himself.”

“And where is he?” asked the other.

“Behold,” he replied, “on the other side of that mountain he is paying the penalties of his damnation” [Col. 0775A].

### 7.

Concerning the vision that we have briefly anticipated, we heard from the very man who had dreamed these things three years earlier:

“I came,” he said, “to a certain dwelling lacking the enclosure of surrounding walls. There the same abbot, sitting with bloody shins, called me.

“‘Go,’ he said, ‘to the bishop and tell him that the present dwelling shared by me and my other companion has become foul for this reason: because, while two companions bathe here in the bathhouse, an intolerable stench rises from it and has made the place almost uninhabitable for us. Therefore, somehow, having gathered expenses from every side, let him close the openings. But if he does not have the funds himself to close them, let him send a message to the monasteries named. When assistance has been gratefully supplied from there, they will provide everything necessary for this enclosure’” [Col. 0775B].

When the bishop heard this, he said: “The ravings of dreams are not to be heeded.”

But the angel in the present vision also reproached him for the same thing, saying that, even when summoned by the dead, the bishop had not provided the comfort of his prayers.

The brother who brought these things back, as it were, from the dead to the living had not previously known any of this.

### 8.

There too, he said, he had seen standing a certain ruler [Note: [Col. 0775D] Namely, Charlemagne, as will become clear from Walafrid’s poem, where the names of the aforementioned abbot and bishop are also revealed.], who had once ruled as king the scepters of Italy and the Roman people. His private parts were being torn by the bite of a certain animal, while the rest of his body remained unharmed by this injury.

Struck dumb with immense astonishment, he wondered how so great a man—who in the defense of the Catholic faith and the government of the holy Church had appeared in the present age almost outstanding among all others—could be punished by so hideous a form of penalty [Col. 0775C].

His guiding angel immediately answered him that, although he had done many admirable and praiseworthy things acceptable to God, for which he was not to be deprived of his reward, nevertheless, overcome by the allurements of sexual sin, he had chosen to bring his long life to this end along with the other good works offered to God, as though depraved obscenity and the liberty granted to human weakness could be buried and consumed beneath the weight of so many good deeds.

“Nevertheless,” he said, “he has been predestined to life in the lot of the elect.”

### 9.

There too he had seen magnificent and countless gifts, ostentatiously arranged by evil spirits for display: golden and silver garments, horses, and linens gleaming with fine workmanship.

When he asked whose these things were and what they signified in their representation [Col. 0775D], the angel replied: “These belong to counts who rule the laws of various provinces, so that when they come here they may find them and know that they have been amassed through gifts, plunder, and greed.”

Naming some of them individually, he said that these things would never run out or be destroyed before the men themselves came and received them into their bosoms.

Who could adequately recount the terrible sentence he pronounced concerning the conduct of the counts? He said that some of them were not avengers of crimes but persecutors of human beings in the place of the devil, condemning the just and justifying the guilty, and associating with thieves and criminals.

“Blinded,” he said, “by the anticipation of gifts, they do nothing for the sake of the reward to come. But when they administer worldly laws to restrain the boldness of evil, they store up the legal penalties they inflict upon debtors—without mercy and as though owed to themselves—for their own greed, to be found again here. They never administer justice in hope of future things. Although they ought to offer it freely to everyone as the reward of eternity, they always carry it for sale, just as they do their own souls.”

He said that some of them had already been judged by name, just as the Gospel speaks of unbelievers: “But whoever does not believe,” it says, “has already been judged” (John 3:18).

He also reported that he had seen innumerable others, both from the common people and from the monastic order of various monasteries and regions: some of them in glory, and some of them sunk in punishment [Col. 0776B].

### 10.

After seeing these and countless other things, which for the sake of brevity we have omitted from this running account, he led him to places established by a natural arrangement, with arches seemingly of gold and silver, distinguished by raised work [In the Puteanus, added in the margin: that is, embossed]. They shone with such magnitude and height and such incredible beauty that the immensity of so great a work could neither be conceived by the mind nor expressed by human speech.

Then the King of kings and Lord of lords proceeded with a multitude of saints, shining with such glory and majesty that a human being could not endure with bodily eyes the radiance of so great a light or the dignity of the glory of the saints that appeared there.

Then the same angel [Col. 0776C], who had been his guide and the one who showed him these things, said to him: “You were to depart tomorrow; but meanwhile we are striving for mercy.”

Then, with the angel going before him, he proceeded to where an assembly of holy priests shone in glory and dignity beyond estimation.

Then the angel said to him: “These are crowned before God with the merits of good works, for whom you provide ecclesiastical offices. Let us ask them to obtain mercy for you from God.”

After these words, they became suppliants and prayed that the priests would become intercessors. The holy priests immediately rose and went to the throne. Prostrating themselves before the throne, they asked mercy for the aforesaid brother.

The angel, together with the brother, stood at a distance to one side while they interceded. As they humbly sought mercy before the throne, a voice was heard from the throne in answer to them [Col. 0776D]:

“He ought to have set examples of edification for others, but he did not.”

Nothing further was heard in the response.

In that distinguished company of priests, he asserted that he recognized the holy Dionysius, Martin, Annianus, and Hilary.

### 11.

Then, again at the angel’s urging, they proceeded together to where an innumerable multitude of blessed martyrs shone with glory beyond estimation.

“These,” he said, “are those whom the glorious triumph of their struggle raised to such glory. You honor them in the Church for the honor and praise of God. We must seek them as intercessors for the remission of your sins” [Col. 0777A].

When they saw them prostrated on the ground in a similar supplication, they immediately, without any delay, hastened to the throne of divine majesty and, prostrating themselves, sought pardon.

From the throne a voice was sent forth to them as before, saying:

“If he corrects those whom, by teaching evil and leading them astray through the example of his wickedness, he had enticed and led from the way of truth into the way of error, and if he brings them back to the way of truth, they are forgiven.”

When they again asked how this correction could be carried out by him so that he might attain the pardon he sought, a voice again came to them from the throne:

“Let him summon all those whom he had ensnared by his example or teaching into doing unlawful things. Let him prostrate himself before them, confess that he acted or taught wrongly, and ask their forgiveness. Let him also beseech them, by almighty God and all the saints, neither to do nor to teach these evils any further.”

Meanwhile, they were to stand at a distance to one side, just as in the earlier intercession of the priests [Col. 0777B].

Among these saints he confessed that he recognized Sebastian and Valentinian.

### 12.

From there, with the angel leading them, they proceeded toward a place where an innumerable multitude of holy virgins dwelt, shining with incomparable dignity and the splendor of radiant light.

“These,” he said, “are the holy women to whom you provide ecclesiastical service for the honor of Christ’s name. We must send them ahead as intercessors with God for your long life.”

After these words, as before, they prostrated themselves before them. The virgins immediately hastened to the throne and asked for his long life, while the others, as previously, stood to one side in the meantime [Col. 0777C].

Before they could prostrate themselves on the ground in prayer, the majesty of the Lord appeared before them. Raising them up, he said to them:

“If he teaches what is good, performs good examples, and corrects those to whom he had offered evil, your request will be granted.”

### 13.

After they had departed from there, the angel began to explain to him in how many filthy vices humanity is wallowing.

“Although,” he said, “the human race departs from its Creator into countless varieties of crime, surrendering itself to the devil, God is offended by nothing more than when sin is committed against nature.

“Therefore, all must strive with great vigilance everywhere, lest by the Sodomitic crime God’s dwelling be turned into shrines of demons. For this disease,” he said, “not only creeps in with virulent contagion and infects souls polluted by intercourse between males, but is also found concentrated in married people as a manifold plague, when, turned into a frenzy by the agitation of lust and driven on by the prompting of demons, they lose the good of nature granted by God. Thus, when the undefiled marriage bed has been turned into a stain of sexual sin, both become prostituted to demons.

“Therefore I command you by divine authority to proclaim these things publicly. Do not conceal how great a danger lies in the luxury of intercourse with concubines. For as long as they are polluted by that obscenity, they do not deserve entry into the kingdom of heaven.”

He said to him: “Lord, I do not dare to bring these matters before the public, because on account of the lowliness of my person I do not consider myself suited to this.”

The angel answered him with great indignation: “What God wills and commands you through me, you do not dare to proclaim?”

After this he began to admonish him in another way concerning his amendment.

“I,” said the angel, “have been appointed to guard you. I was once assigned by God from his birth to that Samson whom the Book of Judges describes, and, with God’s favor, I cooperated with him in every effort toward wondrous deeds, until, softened by the allurements of the flesh, he incurred God’s displeasure through Delilah and sold his consecration to a prostitute; then he was abandoned by God. At that time I departed from him.

“You pleased me in your childhood. Now, however, having turned back to God in sorrow and repentance of heart, you please me again.”

[Col. 0778B]

### 14.

In the monasteries of monks, they must indeed be admonished that, when the roots of vices have been dried up, the shoots of virtues may be able to sprout. For a greater number of those are found who come to these spiritual camps because of worldly necessities than those who come through the Spirit of God.

“The natural man,” he said, “does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God. Therefore, everyone must strive with all his strength lest the life of the spiritual grow lukewarm through the multitude of the carnal, and lest, as iniquity abounds, the charity of many grow cold.

“Let greed be avoided. When it dominates, one does not descend into poverty of spirit, and the entrance to heaven is barred. Let the gluttony of food and drink be changed into the scarcely sufficient necessity of sustenance. Water,” he said, “is very useful for drinking, because it is a natural drink.

“Let the splendor of clothing be changed into what is necessary to ward off nakedness and cold. The swelling of pride [Col. 0778C] must be changed into genuine humility. In some people the bending of the neck is seen, but the uprightness of the heart is not laid down.

“For in this above all the life of the apostolic order is brought to shame: virtues are smothered by vices [Codex Beslii: are darkened]. And while a fault that entered under the appearance of piety is retained in practice, it is now defended as though it were a law of right living.

“Therefore, in the western regions—namely, Germany and Gaul—the members of this order must be admonished so that they may be formed in the true humility of Christ and voluntary poverty, lest, while God pronounces these things terribly through me, they be rejected from the gate of life.”

### 15.

He also did not remain silent about how great a fault had grown in communities of women [Col. 0778D], and how the harm done to God had advanced, through confused ordering, into profit for the devil.

“For when dead women are preferred to the living—for a living widow is dead in pleasures—by sharing in their dead works, the living women subject to them become dead.

“And when they are given to secular persons [Note: [Col. 0777D] In the Puteanus it reads *damnantur* (‘are condemned’). There will be someone who thinks that *dominantur* (‘rule’) should be read. But I think *dantur* (‘are given’) should be retained [Col. 0778D], so that the meaning is: ‘When monasteries of holy women are given to secular widows to govern,’ etc.], insatiably thirsting for earthly wealth, the riches amassed by the faithful for the preservation of the chastity of heavenly life are, through confused ordering, turned toward earthly and perishable pleasures.

### 16.

“And where,” he said, “is the uncorrupted pattern of that apostolic life preserved?”

“In the regions beyond the sea,” he replied, “the steadfastness of apostolic strength still flourishes, because, having been endowed beforehand with poverty of spirit, they attain the kingdoms of heaven without the obstruction of any earthly impediment.”

### 17.

After saying these things, he again and again spoke concerning the Sodomitic crime. He mentioned the other vices only once as things to be avoided. But he repeated five times and more that this pestilential disease of the soul, suggested by the devil’s contrivance against nature, must be avoided.

When the other asked why, while the pestilence was raging, such a great multitude of people was perishing, he replied:

“Because the world sins through the immensity of its crimes, this is the punishment of sins; and a sign has been announced by the Lord, showing by its portent that the end of the world will soon come.”

Among other things, he also admonished him that the celebration of the work of God should be carried out in the churches with complete strength and diligence, in orderly fashion, without any intrusion of weariness or negligence [Col. 0779B].

### 18.

Concerning a certain count named Gerolt [Note: [Col. 0779C] He was prefect of Bavaria during the reign of Charlemagne; more about him appears below in the metrical work.], the same angel said that he was in the repose of glory, made equal to the martyrs.

“For, driven by zeal for God, he engaged the throngs of unbelievers in defense of the holy Church and suffered the losses of temporal life. Therefore he became a participant in eternal life.”

### 19.

After these and nearly countless other things had been shown and heard from the same angel—things that, for the sake of brevity, we have omitted from this written account—the same brother awoke again, while the birds were already sounding out the approach of day.

He summoned the same brothers who had spent the night keeping watch over him. Moved by the magnitude of the vision and shaken by intolerable anxiety of fear, he explained in order the secrets of his vision [Col. 0779C], wishing that, as soon as the monastery’s father arrived, his words might be recorded in his presence.

When they told him that the brothers were occupied with nighttime meditation and did not dare to break the silence of the cloister [Codex Beslii: the enclosure of silence], he said:

“Meanwhile, impress these words upon soft wax, so that when dawn has brightened they may be made ready. For I fear that, with my tongue growing numb, the things seen and heard may be unable to be proclaimed. Since I have been charged to bring them into public with so great a burden of obligation, I fear that I may be struck by the guilt of this silence without pardon if, through my silence, they perish in such a way that they are not made known through me.

“For that final intercession of the holy virgins [Col. 0780A], which had been made to God for my long life, has left me uncertain whether it was offered for the lengthening of eternal life or of this temporal life. Therefore, if by that same intercession of which I have spoken the respite of this temporal life is not prolonged for me, then, setting aside every scruple, in accordance with the promise of my guiding angel I shall depart tomorrow.”

Thus encouraged by these words, they recorded in wax everything he had related, in order.

### 20.

Meanwhile, after the morning hymns had been completed, the monastery’s father arrived with some brothers to visit him. As he stood beside the man lying down, the latter asked to speak privately.

When the others had gone out, the abbot remained with four brothers retained there, so that a fifth was present. The tablets that had been hastily impressed during the nighttime silence [Col. 0780B] were then brought forth, and he recapitulated everything in speech and writing.

Rising from his little bed and prostrating himself on the ground, he asked pardon for the things he had committed and begged them to become intercessors for him with God.

When they saw that he was disfigured neither by pallor, nor wasting away through emaciation, nor complaining of pain in his limbs, nor afflicted by any failure of the pulse or by the appearance of any fatal sign, they encouraged him with words of consolation and complete confidence in the hope of his present life.

To them he repeated the same answers as above, asserting that he had no doubt that he would depart tomorrow.

He had thus spent the entire following day and night, and the whole of the next day until evening, explaining his fear of his summons, laboring with groans and sighs, commending himself to each person individually, and seeking intercessors for the absolution of his sins by sending brief messages to various people [Col. 0780C].

At last, when the evening twilight of the following day had already turned into night, he summoned the brothers and declared that the limits of his present life had run their course. Therefore he earnestly asked them to persist in psalmody. Beginning all the antiphons and the openings of the psalms like a precentor, he had them sung for him.

When these things were completed, he breathed for a little while. The brothers returned to their own beds, while he, feverishly agitated, walked back and forth. As the speed of his departure drew near, he fell upon his little bed. Having received the viaticum, he closed the final hour of this unstable life.

**In the year of the Lord 834. Jesse, Bishop of Amiens.**

[Col. 0779]

## Notice from *Gallia Christiana*

[Col. 0779D] Jesse, or Jessaeus, consecrated the altar of Saint Raphael at the eastern gate of the church of Centula on the day before the Nones of September, 799. In that same year, as a royal envoy, he went with many bishops to meet Pope Leo III, who was proceeding toward Charlemagne, and accompanied him, together with two archbishops and three bishops, on his return to Rome, where, along with other bishops, he investigated the pope’s enemies who had been brought to Gaul.

[Col. 0781A] He was present there on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, in the ninth indiction, in the year 800, at Charlemagne’s anointing. On that day he obtained from the supreme pontiff a privilege for the monastery of Centula, namely, that the abbot alone should have ecclesiastical jurisdiction over the entire monastery and the surrounding estate, and that the bishop of Amiens should have no power to establish anything concerning the churches or clergy of that place.

In 802 he was sent by the emperor Charlemagne to Irene Augusta at Constantinople, together with Count Helmengand, to arrange peace and a marriage with her. In the following year he was sent back with envoys from Nicephorus, who, after sending Irene into exile, had seized the empire.

In 805, as a royal envoy, Charlemagne the emperor gave him capitularies to carry with him and make known to all men. About 808 Charlemagne sent him to Ravenna, to Leo III, who complained about him in Letter 7.

He took part in the Council of Aachen in November 809. Some maintain that from there he was sent to Rome with Bernarius, bishop of Worms, and Abbot Adalard, to confer with the pope concerning the Holy Spirit, although the excellent Cointius disagrees.

He was present and subscribed to the arrangement of Charlemagne’s testament in 811.

He appears to have been absent in 812, when he wrote a letter containing a catechism for the priests of his diocese, teaching them how they ought to conduct themselves toward neophytes and catechumens. For he wrote this at approximately the same time that Amalarius and Theodulf composed their works.

It was published by John Cordesius after the works of Hincmar and in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

He attended the synod held by Walfarius, archbishop of Reims, at Noviodunum in 814, as well as the synod at Theodonis Villa in 821 and the Council of Paris in the following year, 829.

Together with the nobles of the palace, Jesse went to meet Louis the Pious as he was approaching Compiègne, with the intention of disturbing the emperor’s rule. Therefore, in that same year, as a participant in the conspiracy of Louis’s sons, who had declared war against their father, he was expelled from his dignity by the judgment of the bishops at the assembly of Nijmegen as guilty of treason and disloyalty.

Later, however, he was restored to his former rank by Ebbo, archbishop of Reims. At the Council of Compiègne he seems to have consented to Louis’s deposition in 833; if not, he was recalled after the council.

But in 834, when Louis was restored, Jesse followed Lothair, who was compelled to flee into Italy by his brothers, avengers of his father [Col. 0782B]. There, at the beginning of September 836, when a pestilence arose that carried off the principal supporters and friends of Lothair, Jesse too, formerly bishop of Amiens, died.

[Col. 0781]

## Jesse’s Letter on Baptism

*(Galland, Bibliotheca vetum Patrum, vol. XIII, p. 397.)*

[Col. 0781B] To the holy priests and to all who worthily serve in Christ in our diocese, Jesse, humble bishop, sends greetings in the Lord.

Since I hesitate to speak to you, although I frequently recognize that I ought to speak about the divine books and the mysteries of priestly office, even though the circumstances of my inability and absence hinder me, I have therefore briefly set down in writing, insofar as the time permitted, how one ought to proceed by stages to the water of holy baptism.

I know, indeed, that many of you know its mysteries well. But because of practice and ignorance, it seems more suitable to me to write the matter for everyone than for some who are uninformed. Therefore I ask that you who are more capable in understanding instruct and encourage those of lesser ability, in the spirit of gentleness and mildness, so that they may attentively seek out the things hidden within it and, with the Lord’s favor, bring what they have discovered to the fruitfulness of God’s holy Church [Col. 0781D].

I always wish that the summit of your blessedness may prosper and flourish in Christ.

First, we must speak about the catechumen, because he is the first to be made in the order.

**Question.** Why is he called a catechumen, in what language is the term used, and at what time or in what order is he made one if no necessity intervenes? How many persons, and what sort of persons, are to be employed for that ministry?

**Answer.** It is read that *catechumen* is derived from hearing or from instructing. For he hears the teaching by which faith is to be received, and he is instructed in how he ought to come to the washing of holy baptism. Hence the term is interpreted as “hearer” or “instructed person.” For *catechumen* is said in Greek; in Latin it means “hearer” or “instructed person.”

This is done at the following time and in the following order.

[Col. 0782C] In the third week of Lent, on Monday, at the third hour, let them come to the church. Before they enter the church, let the names of the infants and of those who are to receive them be written down by the acolyte. Then let the infants themselves be called by the acolyte inside the church and named in order, as they have been written down. Let the males be placed separately on the right side and the females separately on the left.

Then let the priest come and make the sign of the cross on the forehead of each one with his thumb, saying:

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Then let him place his hand upon their heads, saying this prayer:

“Almighty and everlasting God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and the rest.

Then, turning toward the females, let him do the same.

Afterward let him bless the salt in this manner:

“I exorcize you, creature of salt,” and the rest.

When the salt has been blessed, let him place some of it in the mouth of each infant, saying:

“You, N., receive the salt of wisdom, propitiated unto eternal life.”

When this has been completed, let them leave the church and wait outside for the hour when they are recalled.

Meanwhile, let the clergy begin the antiphon for the entrance appropriate to that day. When it has ended, let the priest say:

“Let us pray. Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, to our elect,” and the rest.

When this prayer has ended, let him sit in his chair.

Then let the deacon say:

“Let the catechumens come forward.”

Let the infants be called by the acolyte by name and in the order in which they have been written down, and let them be placed as before.

Afterward let them be admonished by the deacon, who says:

“Pray, O elect; bend your knees.”

After they have prayed, let him say:

“Rise. Complete your prayer together and say, Amen.”

And let them all respond:

“Amen.”

Then let the deacon say:

“Sign them; come forward for the blessing.”

Let the men or women who have received the infants—that is, the godfathers or godmothers—sign the infants on their foreheads with the thumb, saying:

“In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Let him first place his hand upon the men and afterward upon the women, giving the prayer in a loud voice with these words:

“God of Abraham,” and the rest.

After this, turning toward the women, let him do as above and say:

“God of heaven, God of earth.”

Then let the deacon again announce, saying:

“Pray, O elect,” and the rest.

Let those who have received them sign them as before. Then let another acolyte follow, doing in every respect as the first had done, and let him say:

“Listen, accursed Satan,” first over the men and then separately over the women.

Again let him say:

“God of Abraham and God of Isaac,” and the rest [Col. 0783B].

Let the deacon likewise say that the elect should pray, and let those who have received them sign them as before.

After this, let a third acolyte do as the earlier ones had done, saying this prayer:

“I exorcize you, unclean spirit,” first over the men and then over the women.

When it has been completed, let the deacon again announce that the elect should pray, and let them do as before.

When all these things have been completed, let the priest come, make the sign of the cross on the forehead of each one, and place his hand upon their heads, giving this prayer:

“Your eternal and most just mercy,” and the rest.

When these things have been completed, let them again be admonished by the deacon as follows:

“Pray, O elect; bend your knees.”

After a short while let him say:

“Rise; complete your prayer together and say, Amen. Sign them. Stand with discipline and silence.”

After this, let the priest return to his chair. Let the reading be read and the gradual appropriate to that day be sung.

Afterward let the deacon admonish them in this manner:

“Let the catechumens depart. If anyone is a catechumen, let him depart. Let all catechumens depart outside.”

Let the elect leave and wait outside the doors until the Mass has been completed.

Then let the Gospel be read, and let offerings be presented by the parents or by those who have received the infants. Let the priest place them upon the altar and say this prayer secretly:

“Your mercy, O God, for receiving these mysteries,” and the rest.

But when he has said, “Remember, O Lord, your servants and handmaids,” let the names of the men and women who are to receive those infants be recited.

Likewise, at the fraction [*Infra actionem*: “during the action”], after “This offering,” let the names of the chosen men be recited. When they have been recited, let him say that these infants are to be renewed in the baptismal font, and the rest [Col. 0783D].

When the Mass has ended, let everyone receive Communion except the infants.

Again let the priest announce that during that same week, on whichever day he designates, they should all come to the church at the time he announces to them.

When they come to the appointed church, let them undergo a second scrutiny in order, just as they did the first time.

The same is to be done in the third, fourth, and fifth scrutinies during those three weeks, up to the Wednesday before Palm Sunday.

But on the following Wednesday, the fourth feria, let them come to whichever church he directs. Then let them perform the sixth scrutiny in every respect as the previous five were performed, up to the point where he says:

“Sign them; stand with discipline and silence.”

Then, at the opening of the ears, let the reading from the prophet Isaiah be read:

“Thus says the Lord: Listen, you who listen to me, and eat what is good,” up to, “for he is abundant in forgiving.”

The responsory “Come, children” follows.

Likewise, let another reading from the Letter to the Colossians be read:

“Brothers, having stripped yourselves of the old man with his deeds,” up to, “giving thanks to God the Father through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

The responsory “Blessed is the nation” follows.

After this, let four deacons come from the sacristy with the four books of the Gospels, with two candlesticks preceding them, together with censers and incense. Let them place the Gospels at the four corners of the altar.

Before any of them reads, let the priest address them in these words:

“As we are about to open the Gospels to you, dearly beloved children—that is, the divine deeds—we must first explain the order: what the Gospel is, from where it derives, whose words are set down in it, and why there are four who wrote these deeds, or who they are,” and the rest pertaining to these matters.

Then let him say again:

“We have therefore set these things forth beforehand, lest, without an understanding of this order, we leave astonishment in your minds; and because you have come for this purpose, that your ears may be opened, lest your understanding be dulled and blunted.”

Having done this, let the deacon again announce, saying: “Stand in silence, and attend as you listen.” Then one of the deacons, taking the Gospel book from the [corner—perhaps, “angle”] of the altar that is first on the left, preceded by two candelabra with censers, shall ascend to read, and shall read: “The beginning of the holy Gospel according to Matthew,” up to: “For he himself will save his people from their sins” [Col. 0784C]. When this has been read, the subdeacon shall receive the Gospel from him on a cloth and carry it into the sacristy.

Then the presbyter shall address them in these words: “Dearest children, so that we may not impose a delay upon you, we wish to explain to you what meaning and figure each evangelist contains in himself.” And he shall explain the meaning of each of the evangelists, and why they are represented in this way.

When the priest’s account has been completed, the deacon shall again announce: “Stand in silence, and attend as you listen”; and the Gospel according to Mark shall be read up to the place where he says: “I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit.” In the same way the priest shall explain Mark as he did Matthew.

After this the deacon shall again announce as above, and shall read: “The beginning of the holy Gospel according to Luke,” up to: “to prepare a perfect people for the Lord” [Col. 0784D]; and the priest shall speak about Luke as he did about the others.

Again the deacon shall announce as above, and shall read: “The beginning of the holy Gospel according to John,” up to: “full of grace and truth”; and the priest shall explain John as he explained the others.

After this further exposition, the priest shall announce to them the preface of the Creed in these words: “Dearest ones, as you are about to receive the sacrament of baptism,” and the rest.

When this has been completed, the acolyte shall take one of the male infants, holding him on his left arm, and placing his hand upon his head. The presbyter shall say: “Announce their faith, and how they confess the Lord Jesus Christ”; and he shall recite the Creed in chant. When this has been finished, another acolyte shall do the same for one of the females.

Then the presbyter shall continue in these words: “This is the summary of our faith, dearest ones,” and the rest. Afterwards the deacon shall announce as above; and then the presbyter shall say the Lord’s Prayer in this manner: “Our Lord and Savior,” and the rest.

We stated above which persons, and how many, are assigned to this work, namely, specifically four persons, corresponding to the number of the four books of the Gospels, of which mention was made a little earlier, apart from the subdeacons, the other ministers, and the rest. For there are those who receive the infants, acolytes, subdeacons, and presbyters.
