The catechumen, having already received the mystery of faith and bearing the sign of the cross on his forehead, professes that he believes in Christ; but, not yet regenerated by the water of the font, he is worthy to receive the body and blood of the Lord. Hence blessed Augustine, in a Gospel sermon, says from the Lord’s words to Nicodemus:

“‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.’ Jesus therefore entrusts himself to those who have been born again. Behold, those who had believed in him, and Jesus did not entrust himself to them: such are all catechumens. They already believe in the name of Christ, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them. Let your charity attend and understand. If we say to a catechumen: ‘Do you believe in Christ?’ he answers: ‘I believe,’ and signs himself, already bearing the cross of Christ on his forehead, and he is not ashamed of the cross of his Lord: behold, he believes in his name. Let us ask him: ‘Do you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink the blood of the Son of Man?’ He does not know what we are saying, because Jesus does not entrust himself to them.”

## Concerning the competent

**Question.** What difference is there between a catechumen and a competent?

**Answer.** What a catechumen is has been sufficiently explained above; but what a competent is must be stated briefly. A competent is one who, carefully instructed in the faith and attentively imbued with belief, after the doctrine of Christianity, the mystery of the Creed, and the handing down of the Lord’s Prayer have been delivered to him, asks and begs to be able to attain the mystery of holy baptism and the grace of Christ, to become a participant in the holy Church of God, and to be with Christ among the faithful in his service. Hence he is called “competent,” from asking.

## Concerning salt

[Col. 0785D]

**Question.** Why does the catechumen receive salt?

**Answer.** Salt is therefore applied and placed in the mouths of catechumens. Salt, namely, provides seasoning for all foods, drives away insipidity, arouses appetite, and gives relish to every food. Through it, all nourishment becomes more pleasing and agreeable to human taste.

Appropriately, then, salt is taken up for the office of Christianity. For it is made from the substance of water, and, whatever its origin, it can be dissolved in water. Just as in the Law honey is forbidden to be offered in sacrifices, while salt is commanded in every case, so salt is given to those who are about to offer to the Lord and become a sacrifice, so that everything we offer for the honor and worship of Christ may always possess the salt of reason and discernment, without the offering of honey [Col. 0786A].

Therefore the priest truly places bodily salt in the catechumen’s mouth, to signify that, by the salt of divine Wisdom, his transient and sensual sins are driven away from him, and that all his words are seasoned and adorned. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “Let your speech be seasoned with the salt of God’s grace, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person.”

Salt therefore leaps away from fire. For although it is placed in fire, it nevertheless flees the fire, following its nature, since fire and water are enemies to one another. Salt is rightly given to those who are to be baptized and who have escaped eternal fire, so that, abandoning the vanity by which unbelievers, purifying their children through fire, offered them to demons, they may be led to the water of regeneration and offered and consecrated to God. Rejecting unbelief, they may become [Col. 0786B] children of God and receive Christ, who is true peace, as he himself says: “Have salt in yourselves,” that is, peace. And: “You are the salt of the earth.”

It is also fitting that the priests of God, who are the seasoning of the people, apply salt for the office of Christianity, so that, with vices excluded, they may offer to God children seasoned with the salt of good Wisdom and at peace with him.

## The infant is exorcised, or catechized

**Question.** What language is “exorcism,” what does it mean, and what does “to catechize” mean?

**Answer.** *Exorcism* is Greek; in Latin it is called “conjuration” or “rebuke.” A rebuke is: “Nor is it hidden from you, Satan, that punishments threaten you,” and the rest.

It is both a conjuration and a rebuke of one condemned and to be condemned: “Give honor to the living God; give honor to Jesus Christ; give honor to the Holy Spirit; and depart from this male and this female servant of God, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ,” and the rest.

This is said against the devil, so that he may depart and leave the one whom he held, as is made clear in the prophet Zechariah, where it says: “He showed Jesus the priest standing before the angel of the Lord, and Satan was standing at his right hand; and the Lord said to Satan: ‘May the Lord rebuke you, Satan, who has chosen Jerusalem.’” This is exorcism: to rebuke and conjure.

It is not God’s creature in those who are not [the reading is uncertain] that is exorcised, but the evil spirit, so that he may leave God’s creature.

## Concerning exsufflation

For this reason it is not the human being who is exsufflated, but the one under whom are all who are born under sin, because he is the author of evil and the prince of sinners. He is rightly exsufflated and cast out like dust from the face of the wind: the devil, confounded in his wickedness, is driven away, so that the human being who is to be renewed and brought to life, warmed by the divine breath, may be led to the grace of Christ, and that in Christ our God a worthy entrance may be opened for him.

To catechize means to teach or to correct. Hence the Apostle also says: “Let the one who is catechized share the word with the one who catechizes him in all good things.” The one who learns is catechized; the one who teaches catechizes. For he commands that the disciple cling to the teacher and share with him.

**Question.** Why are the nostrils and ears touched with saliva?

**Answer.** Before baptism a person is touched with saliva so that afterward he may be led to baptism. When the Lord gave sight to the man blind from birth, he spat on the ground, made clay from his saliva, anointed the blind man’s eyes, sent him to the pool, and he washed and saw.

“‘When he anointed him,’ says Augustine, ‘he made him a catechumen. When he washed him, he was baptized in Christ. He had been anointed and did not see; he washed and saw. For when, in a certain sense, he baptized him in himself, then he illuminated him. The Lord mixed the spittle that descended from his head with the earth, to signify his divine nature, which is from God, and his human nature, which he assumed from human beings, so that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.’”

The nostrils and ears are touched with a finger so that those who had strayed from the way of truth may hear the gifts of the Holy Spirit and receive them in their hearts; and, having received what they heard, may persevere in faith, so that they may say: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me.” Hence the Lord also says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear,” that is, whoever has understanding to understand, let him understand.

The Lord also took the deaf and mute man from the crowd and put his fingers into his ears. The first door of salvation is for the Lord, when he takes hold of the infirm person, to lead him away from the crowd, that is, from pagan conduct, and call him to faith. He puts his fingers into the ears when, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit, he opens the ears of the heart to receive and understand the words of salvation.

The nostrils are also touched so that, through the invocation of the Holy Spirit, they may perceive the fragrance of good works, with shameful and foul works rejected, and, as the Lord breathes upon them, may deserve to enjoy the delight of the flowers of the virtues. Hence prayers are poured out in this manner for the making of a catechumen:

“Open for him, Lord, the door of your mercy; and, imbued with the sign of your wisdom, may he be free from the stench of all desires, and may he gladly serve you in your Church in the sweet fragrance of your commandments.”

And when we have been made, according to the Apostle, a good fragrance for Christ, let us say: “We run after the fragrance of your ointments.”

## Concerning the anointing of the breast and shoulders with oil

The breast is also touched with holy oil, so that entrance may be forbidden to the unclean spirit. The shoulders are marked with the same oil, so that he may be strengthened on every side by the protection of the cross and, having been led to the grace of Christ, may deserve to participate in and cling to Christ the Lord, who was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

He is touched between the shoulders so that the consecrated shoulder, together with the shoulder blades, may subject his whole self to the power and dominion of God, whose authority and kingdom are shown to rest upon his shoulder. Hence he himself also carried his cross, possessing the name above every name.

Let us likewise incline our shoulders and necks, believing in and adoring him to whom every knee bends. Let us carry the cross and follow him, because his yoke and burden are gentle and light, so that we who believe may deserve to hear: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened.”

Let us bring our works to prayer, running with desire toward faith, because work is understood in the shoulder and shoulder blades, and reason in the breast. For faith, which is received by hearing, is believed in the heart and professed by the mouth for salvation. It must be placed in the secret recess of the mind and entrusted to the very vital organs of our breast. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.”

Hence the Lord also touched the tongue of the mute, and the mute speaks and confesses. The Lord touches the tongue of the mute when he instructs the mouth of those being catechized to confess the faith, as he himself says: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.” That is: open it in confession, and I will fill it with the sacrament of that confession; I will enrich it with mystical speech, so that you too may be able to answer: “I have hidden your words in my heart, that I might not sin against you.”

## Concerning renunciation of the devil and his pomps

After this order of the rite has been set forth, the infant is led to the sacrament of baptism and questioned concerning belief in Christ and renunciation of the devil. He renounces the pomps which, at the devil’s announcement and persuasion, the human being had accepted, so that, having rejected the devil’s works and ancient vices, he may be renewed and stripped of them. Having been cleansed of filthy and torn garments, he may put on white and new clothing and run eagerly to the fonts.

The pomps of the devil are deadly vices, which he first introduced into the human being with that person’s consent: pride, vainglory, and the rest, which reached all human beings, according to the Apostle: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so it passed into all human beings.”

The human being was made in the image of God and clothed in the garment of mortality, which he admitted by consenting to the devil. Now let him cast away the devil’s image, so that, cleansed, he may possess the heavenly image. Hence the Apostle says: “Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly.”

Just as a coin bears the image of the earthly emperor, so the one who does the works of the ruler of darkness bears his image. All who are baptized in Christ reject that image, so that, marked with the banner of Christ, they may bear the image of Christ.

This is the font of holy baptism, where foul and muddy goats descend and spotless lambs ascend. Concerning this baptism the Apostle speaks: “For all who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death; we have been buried with him through baptism.” We must die to sin so that we may be buried with Christ. Burial is owed to one who has died. For the one who lives in sin cannot be buried with Christ.

Therefore, stripping off, according to the Apostle, the old human being with his deeds by renouncing the devil’s pomps and evil works, let us put on the new, who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness, because our old human being was crucified once for all, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin.

The Lord, however, was buried in a new tomb and wrapped in a clean shroud. Whoever wishes to be buried with Christ through baptism, having cast off old age and impurity, should be cleansed and clothed in a new shroud, as the Apostle commands: “Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new human being.”

There the infant is also named, as John says in the Apocalypse: “And I will give him a white stone,” that is, a body made white by baptism and shining with the glory of incorruption in the resurrection, with a new name written on the stone, so that we may be called and may be children of God.

Hence that same John says: “I will write upon him a new name,” that is, the Christian name, so that, being called Christian from Christ thereafter, the one who has been reborn and made new, having abandoned the vices and pomps of the devil, may bear the new name, that is, “Christian,” and follow its works.

## Concerning the Creed

*Symbolum* is therefore Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “sign” or “knowledge.” The apostles, when they were about to depart to evangelize the nations, established this as the sign or token of their preaching.

It contains belief in the Trinity, the unity of the Church, and the sacrament of the whole Christian teaching. This symbol of our faith and hope is not written on paper and in ink, but on the tablets of the heart of flesh.

Just as, in a good sense, the Church hands down the Creed for our salvation, so unbelievers use it in an evil sense, as the apostle John testifies in the Apocalypse: “Whoever has the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name,” that is, the mystery of iniquity, “has permission to buy or sell in the unity of wickedness.”

This is the sign of Antichrist, in whom Satan in his entirety will dwell bodily. For others are said not to be permitted to sell or buy unless they are marked with that sign.

The symbol of the divine sacrament entrusted to us should therefore not be committed to paper or written in letters, because paper and letters express care more than grace. Where the grace of God, the divine gift, consists in a covenant, faith and the elevation of the heart suffice for secrecy, so that a false witness may always remain ignorant of this symbol of salvation, this covenant within you.

A symbol between two people is always strengthened by a duplicated written document, and human caution makes it secure in agreements, lest force creep in or treachery, always hostile to contracts, deceive. But among human beings, fraud harms those between whom it has been committed or by whom it has been committed. Between God and human beings, however, the symbol of faith is strengthened by faith alone. One trusts not the letter but the spirit, because a divine trust does not require human security. God does not know how to commit fraud and cannot suffer it.

But perhaps someone may say: “If he cannot be deceived, why does he demand an agreement? What is the symbol?” He seeks it for your sake, not for his own—not because he doubts, but so that you may believe.

He seeks the symbol because he does not now summon you to a matter but to faith; and through the present agreement he draws the future toward profit, from faith to faith.

## Concerning the threefold immersion

After the works of the devil have been renounced and the mystery of belief received, the infant is immersed in water and baptized.

*Baptism* is Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “dipping” or “immersion.” It is performed under the designation of the Trinity, that is, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, as the Lord says to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”

Accordingly, in a fitting manner, through threefold immersion the human being is restored to the image of the holy Trinity, in whose image he was created in the beginning with God’s cooperation. And rightly, the one who fell into death through the third stage of sin, namely consent, is restored to life through the third reception from the font.

The reason baptism is given through water is this: the Lord wished that the invisible reality should be bestowed through a suitable, indeed tangible and visible, element, over which the Holy Spirit was also borne in the beginning. For just as water cleanses the body outwardly, so through its mystery the soul is secretly purified by the Holy Spirit.

When God has been invoked, the Holy Spirit descends from heaven and, having healed the waters, sanctifies them. From him they receive the power of purification, so that in them flesh and soul polluted by sins may be cleansed.

“For baptism is such,” as Augustine says, “as is the one in whose power it is given, not such as is the one through whose ministry it is given. For it does not harm anyone to be baptized by an evil person, provided that he is baptized correctly.”

## Concerning the anointing of the head

After he has been baptized, the presbyter makes the sign of the cross with chrism on the crown of his head using his thumb. Just as the remission of sins is given in baptism, so sanctification by the Spirit is applied through anointing.

In the Old Testament also priests and kings were anointed, as Aaron was anointed by Moses and David by Samuel. He is anointed on the head because all the senses proceed from it and it receives sensation.

A woman poured ointment of genuine nard over Jesus’ head, signifying the faith of the Church and of the nations through those anointed with the chrism [Col. 0790C] of salvation.

## Concerning the covering of the head

An ornamented cloth is placed over the head of the baptized person. Often the mind is understood under the name “head.” Hence in the Apocalypse they are said to be clothed in white garments and to have golden crowns on their heads; that is, clothed in good works, let them seek the heavenly joys of the mind in everlasting remembrance.

Now the white horse has been made, and the rider upon it has a bow—that is, the Church, which has been whitened like snow by the grace of baptism—and the Lord presides over it, bearing the banner of the cross.

## Concerning the bishop’s confirmation

After this the bishop confirms him on the forehead with chrism. The laying on of hands is therefore performed so that, through the blessing, the invoked Holy Spirit may descend upon them, according to the example of the apostles:

“When the disciples who were at Jerusalem heard,” he says, “that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they came, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit, for he had not yet come upon any of them; they had only been baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”

It must be understood that Philip, who evangelized in Samaria, was one of the seven. For if he had been an apostle, he himself could have laid hands upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. This is due only to the bishops [Col. 0791A].

For when presbyters baptize, they may anoint the baptized with chrism; but if the chrism has been consecrated by a bishop, they may not mark the forehead with that oil, which belongs to bishops alone, so that they may impart the Spirit, the Paraclete, to the baptized.

“For after the Lord had risen from the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Holy Spirit descending upon him like a dove.”

When this mystery has been completed, if the Christian preserves the faith, he will certainly be blessed. “Blessed,” says the Apocalypse, “is the one who has a share in the first resurrection” (Apoc. XX, 6).

The first resurrection is in baptism, as the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above.” This was not said only to bishops and presbyters, but all who preserve what they were reborn into are called Christians, because of the mystical chrism, and are called priests because they are members of Christ, who is the supreme and holy priest.

Peter says of them: “A holy nation, a royal priesthood.”

A faithful Christian is called such from Christ if the name is followed by deeds. One is faithful who truly believes what he does not see. Hence *faith* is so called when what has been said or promised between two people is carried out.

An agreement made between two, and the things that exist between God and a human being, belong to true faith. Therefore what a human being has promised he must keep; for God too, if he has promised a human being that he will keep his promise, will not commit fraud.

## Concerning the confirmation with the body and blood of Christ

Finally, the infant is confirmed with the body and blood of Christ, so that he may be a member of the one who suffered and rose again for him, as the Lord himself bears witness, saying:

“Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him; for my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.”

Hence Augustine also says: “‘If a human being is in the body of Christ,’ he says, ‘let him receive the Spirit of Christ. Just as our body cannot live without the spirit, so no one has the Spirit of life unless he has been incorporated into the body of Christ. Therefore whoever wishes to come, let him approach, believe, and live for God; let him be incorporated into God, so that he may be given life.’”

## Also, the rite of the baptistery

First he is a pagan; afterward he becomes a catechumen. Approaching baptism, he renounces the evil spirit and all his destructive pomps. He is also exsufflated so that, once the devil has been driven away, he may be prepared for the Lord.

He is exorcised, that is, the evil spirit is conjured, so that he may depart and withdraw, giving place to the true God.

The catechumen receives salt so that his rotten and transient sins may be cleansed by the salt of Wisdom, through the divine gift.

Then the faith of the apostolic Creed is handed over to him, so that the empty house, abandoned by its former inhabitant, may be adorned with faith and prepared as a dwelling for God.

Then scrutinies are performed, so that it may be tested repeatedly how firmly, after renouncing Satan, he has fixed the sacred words given by faith in the roots of his heart.

The nostrils are also touched so that, as long as he draws breath through them, he may persevere in the faith he has received. The breast too is anointed with the same oil in the sign of the holy cross, so that entrance may be closed to the devil.

The shoulders are also marked [Col. 0792A] and fortified on every side. Likewise, in the anointing of the breast and shoulders, the firmness of faith and perseverance in good works are marked.

He is baptized in the name of the holy Trinity through threefold immersion, so that the human being, rightly created in the image of the holy Trinity, may be renewed into that same image through the invocation of the same holy Trinity. And the one who fell into death through the third stage of sin, that is, through action—for the human being fell through thought, delight, and action—may, raised up from the font a third time, rise again through grace to life.

Then he is clothed in white garments because of the joy of regeneration, the purity of life, and the beauty of angelic splendor.

Then his head is anointed with sacred chrism and covered with a mystical veil, so that he may understand that he bears the diadem of the kingdom and the dignity of the priesthood, according to the Apostle: “You are a royal race, offering yourselves to the living God as a holy sacrifice pleasing to God.”

Thus he is confirmed with the Lord’s body and blood, so that he may be a member of the one who suffered and rose for him.

Finally, through the laying on of hands by the chief priest, he receives the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, so that he may be strengthened by the Holy Spirit to preach to others. In baptism he had been given the grace of eternal life.

You see how faithfully, reasonably, and prudently all these things have been handed down for us to observe.

“[Note: [Col. 0791D] St. Augustine, *On the Trinity* IV, 6.] No Catholic dares contend against the authority of the Church; no sober person against rational custom; no faithful person against the understanding of piety,” lest he be found a schismatic and not a Catholic.

Let us follow, in the matter of baptism, the authority of the holy Roman Church, so that from the source from which we received the beginnings of the Catholic faith, we may always be able to receive the models of our salvation; lest the members be separated from their head, and lest the bearer of the keys of the heavenly kingdom cast away those whom he recognizes as differing from his teachings.

## Also, concerning baptism and its rite, with the authorities of those who come to the faith named individually

Prayer—so called as the reason of the mouth, because it proceeds from the mouth and from reason—is said over the elect, that is, those who have been summoned, who come from paganism to the faith of Christ.

*Catechumen* is Greek; it is interpreted as “one who hears” or “one who teaches” [perhaps, “one who learns”].

“Almighty,” because he can do all things and created all things without evil and falsehood. “Eternal God,” that is, because he is everlasting and has neither beginning [Col. 0792D] nor end.

“Deign to look upon,” that is, to show mercy.

“Upon this servant,” whom you have deigned to call, that is, summon, “to the beginnings,” that is, to the newness, “of faith.”

“Drive out,” “cast away,” “break apart,” “shatter,” “the blindness,” that is, the darkness or gloom, “of his heart.”

“The snares,” that is, the traps or mousetrap, “of Satan.” This is Greek and is interpreted as “adversary,” because he is always bound against us, that is, constrained.

“Open for him, Lord, the door of your piety,” that is, the door of faith, as the Truth says in the Gospel: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture.”

Thus, through the sign of your wisdom, that is, so that he may be able to understand the sign of Christ—how he was incarnate, how he was born, how he suffered, how he was crucified, how he died, how he descended to the underworld, how he rose, and how he ascended into heaven—may he be imbued, that is, instructed or taught.

“May he be free from stenches,” that is, from filth or defilements belonging to worldly desire; may he not wish to possess them.

“Of your commandments,” that is, precepts; “glad,” that is, cheerful, bright, or joyful; “may he serve you in your Church.”

There is also another church, that of heretics, because he must not believe in the church of heretics but in the Church of Catholics. Therefore I said: “May he serve and advance in your Church,” that is, may he grow or increase, in faith or make progress, from day to day, throughout the whole time of the present life.

“So that he may be fit,” that is, worthy or sufficient, or pure; “may he be made,” that is, may he be able to approach, that is, draw near, “the medicine he has received,” that is, the healing he has received.

“I exorcise you,” that is, I rebuke or conjure you, “for protection,” that is, for defense or healing.

Salt is an element, and after it has been sanctified it becomes a sacrament, in the name of God the almighty Father, that is, through the Father; and in the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, that is, through the Son; and in the power of the Holy Spirit, that is, in comparison with dead gods; and through the true God, that is, in comparison with false gods.

[Note: [Col. 0793D] Perhaps these belong to another author, who lived before the Fifth Synod.]

In the first annotation we took care to inquire what a canon is and what is contained in a canon. *Canon* is Greek; in Latin it is called a rule. It is called a rule because it leads rightly and never stands without rectitude.

Canons began to originate in the time of the emperor Constantine because of Arius, who blasphemed the Son of God, for he denied that he was coeternal with the Father. For this reason 318 bishops assembled in the city of Nicaea in the province of Bithynia, and there set forth the Catholic faith embraced by the whole Church.

The second synod was assembled at Constantinople, consisting of 150 bishops under the elder Theodosius, against Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit was God.

The third synod, the first at Ephesus, consisted of 200 bishops under the younger Theodosius, against Nestorius, who asserted two persons in Christ.

The fourth synod, at Chalcedon, consisted of 630 bishops under the emperor Marcian, against Eutyches, who pronounced one nature of the Word of God and the flesh.

These four principal synods therefore, like the four rivers of paradise, flow forth and irrigate the hearts of the faithful. If any other councils of the holy Fathers, assembled as necessity required and filled with the Spirit of God, have enacted decrees, they must also be guarded and received.

*Synod* is Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “company” or “assembly.”

We have now stated what a canon is; it remains to say what is contained in a canon. A canon, as has been said, is called a rule. It declares that one must live rightly, act rightly, hold divinity and the humanity of our Lord Jesus Christ rightly in faith by confessing them truthfully, trample down the depravity of heretics, and hold to the norm of the holy orthodox Fathers.

For the canon teaches how one ought to live justly and how one who departs from the right path should be corrected. It is, in a certain sense, the law of laws, because it takes precedence over all laws composed by human judgment.

After learning the canonical faith, it must be noted how the Catholic faith is to be believed and observed by all: namely, to confess the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as three persons; but the Trinity is in the names of the persons, while unity must never be separated from majesty, essence, and eternity. Thus the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are consubstantial, coeternal, and co-working, according to the faith set forth at the Synod of Nicaea by 318 bishops, establishing this formula:

“We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of all things visible and invisible, maker of heaven and earth,” and the rest.

We have also judged that the faith of the holy bishop Athanasius should be observed in this work, together with the Creed of the apostles and the traditions and expositions of the holy Fathers noted in these sermons.

## Chapter I

First of all, they must be admonished concerning the rectitude of their faith, so that they themselves may hold and understand it, and may announce it in living speech to the peoples subject to them. Each one must know those whom he has in his ministry, whether men, women, or children, so that he may know the confession and conduct of each, since he will have to render an account to God for all.

## Chapter II

Second, the priests themselves must display to the peoples subject to them a manner of life that can be imitated, namely, as the Apostle said: “In chastity, in sobriety.” They must not serve gluttony and the desires of this age. What they admonish others to observe, they must show in themselves.

They must beware of all avarice and greed, because many labor day and night to acquire temporal goods, namely slaves, wine, and grain with usury, which both God and all divine Scripture and the holy canons forbid.

They must also avoid the company of women and not permit them to live with them, as canonical authority requires.

## Chapter III

Third, they must explain to those subject to them the Lord’s Prayer, that is, “Our Father,” and “I believe in God almighty,” and have both men and women and children recite them.

## Chapter IV

Fourth, the presbyters themselves must withdraw from feasting and drinking, as the Apostle admonishes. For some of them remain with certain neighbors of theirs [lacuna] until midnight and beyond, drinking with them; and those who appear religious and holy do not indeed remain there at that time, but nevertheless return to their churches either full or drunk, and perform the office of God neither by day nor by night in the church entrusted to them. Some even sleep in the same place to which they go for the banquet.

## Chapter V

Fifth, the presbyters themselves must have such schoolboys—that is, boys so trained and instructed—that if it should happen that the presbyters are unable to arrive at the proper time to perform the office in their church, namely, Terce, Sext, None, and Vespers, the schoolboys themselves may ring the signal at the appointed time and perform the office honorably before God.

## Chapter VI

Sixth, you must diligently ascertain, after each presbyter’s ordination, how much each has advanced in his ministry. For those who were poor before ordination, after ordination buy themselves estates, slaves, and other possessions from the resources with which they ought to have served the churches; yet they have made no progress in their reading, nor have they collected books or increased the things belonging to religious worship. Instead, they always live by insults, disputes, and plunder.

## Chapter VII

Seventh, they must take the greatest care to protect their household members—that is, those who are with them in their residence, whether schoolboys [Col. 0795B] or other servants [Col. 0796A]—from every vice, and especially from drunkenness, sexual excess, and various impurities. For, as the Apostle says: “The one who neglects the care of his household will not be able to benefit the conduct of others.”

## Chapter VIII

Eighth, that they be hospitable, because many who know that a guest is about to arrive at their church flee; but although the Apostle commands, and all the rest of divine Scripture teaches, that this should be practiced, they instead flee in the opposite direction and are afraid to assist the poor.

## Chapter IX

Ninth, the Apostle commands all the faithful that their speech should be gracious, always seasoned with salt—that is, that a Christian should speak what accords with religion, so that he may season the minds of others and correct them from the corruption of sins . . . [lacuna]. The remainder is lacking.

[Col. 0795]

### In the Year of Our Lord 836: Saint Aldric, Archbishop of Sens

[Col. 0795]

### Notice from *Gallia Christiana*

After the death of Jeremiah, the clergy of Sens, having obtained from the emperor—through the petitions of Abbot Hilduin—permission to elect, chose one of their own, who was not fully accepted by the emperor. Accordingly, when, at Hilduin’s supplication, they had obtained permission to elect another, they chose one of their own whom they had known well from childhood: a man not disreputable in birth or character, teachable by reason of his age, suitable for this office, not wholly ignorant of letters, not entirely without knowledge of divine matters, and lightly trained also in other arts. When they had presented him with the imperial envoys, he was not received with complete goodwill. Therefore, after complaining of this, the Church of Sens gave Hilduin and Abbot Einhard three letters to the empress Judith, so that they might be permitted to bring their chosen candidate to the emperor.

The candidate elected by the people of Sens does not seem to have been approved by the emperor. For, as Clarius says, “by divine will—or by command of Caesar Louis—Aldric, formerly abbot of Ferrières, was made archbishop of Sens, according to Lupus, and was ordained at the Council of Paris on the eighth day before the Ides of June in the year 829.” Immediately after his election he wrote to Frothar, bishop of Toul, asking for the support of his prayers and those of his friends.

Around that time he arranged the election of Heribald, bishop of Auxerre. At the Council of Paris, Aldric and others were instructed to investigate carefully the manner of life at the chief monastery of Saint-Denis in France. Aldric carried this out, and Louis issued an imperial decree concerning it on the seventh day before the Kalends of September in 832. He subscribed the division of the goods made by Abbot Hilduin for the monks of Saint-Denis on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February in 832.

Around that time, when he had come to Paris on important business, he dedicated the new church of the monastery of Fossatès in honor of the Blessed Mary on the seventh day before the Ides of December, at the request of Abbot Benedict, who had built it. After returning home, Aldric, while standing before the cathedral church, restrained Marrymund, the custodian of the city, who displayed an arrogant spirit, and persuaded him to become a monk.

He transferred the monastery of Saint Remigius, built in the suburb of the city, to Villiers, because the monks had been less able to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict there on account of the site’s inconvenience. He did this on the advice of many bishops and abbots whom he had gathered at Sens during the deposition of Louis the Pious. When Louis was restored, he confirmed this transfer in the year 835. In that same year Aldric attended the Council of Thionville concerning the case of Ebbo, archbishop of Reims.

He dedicated the church of Saint Florentin in the castle of that name, beside the Armentière River, on Sunday, the Nones of May, in 836.

Aldric was always most devoted and acceptable to Louis Augustus. Louis had appointed him royal tutor, so that matters concerning the life of the imperial court and his more important affairs might be determined by Aldric’s judgment. He also sent him with others to settle the disputes between the abbot and the monks of Flavigny concerning the monastery’s property.

But fearing that the merit of his religious life might be diminished by the turmoil of secular affairs, Aldric decided to lay aside the burden of pastoral concern and return to the repose and haven of his former contemplation. He was, however, seized by a fatal illness, which he understood would be his last. Therefore, since this was the one thing remaining to him, he ordered that his body be carried to the monastery of Ferrières and buried there beneath the eaves of the church. This was done after his death, which occurred on the sixth day before the Ides of October in 836. This is established both from his Acts, which say that he was born in 775 and died in the sixty-first year of his age, and from letters 6 and 41 of Lupus of Ferrières.

Lupus, having returned from the school of Fulda, found Aldric dead. In that same year he was brought into the emperor’s presence; in the following year—that is, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October, in the first indiction, corresponding to the year 837—he went to the palace at the queen’s summons.

After his death, Aldric was immediately buried honorably at Ferrières beneath the eaves, near the oratory of Saint Andrew, in a stone tomb that he had prepared for himself while alive. Meanwhile, his sacred body, because of the miracles performed at his tomb, was brought into the inner basilica of Saint Peter and placed in a higher apse, as an anonymous writer of considerable authority reports.

Odorannus and Clarius, writing six hundred years ago, proclaim him a saint. He is venerated in the church of Sens on the sixth of June [Col. 0797A], which appears to have been the day of his ordination; but on the tenth of October at the monastery of Ferrières. There, in 1569, his sacred relics were scattered by the raging Calvinists, except for a few, and the precious reliquary was plundered—the reliquary that Louis de Blanchefort, abbot of Ferrières, had caused to be made in 1487 at a cost of 40,000 silver coins.

# Life of Saint Aldric

By an Anonymous Author, whose date is uncertain.

(From Mabillon, *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, based on a very old manuscript Lectionary of Sens and other sources.)

[Col. 0797]

## Preliminary Observations

1. No evidence establishes when the anonymous author of the following Life lived. I would nevertheless believe that he lived at the beginning of the eleventh century, since he reports no miracles performed by Saint Aldric after that time.

2. Odorannus and Clarius call Aldric a saint in their Chronicles; both were monks of the monastery of Saint Peter at Sens, the former toward the end of the eleventh century and the latter toward the beginning of the twelfth. Certainly, the body of Saint Aldric had been raised from the earth six hundred years earlier, and his feast day was observed with religious devotion, as is clear from the Life that follows.

This saint is venerated in the church of Sens on the sixth of June, which may perhaps be the day of his ordination, since his death occurred on the tenth of October, a day celebrated with festivity at Ferrières. His translation, however, is observed on the thirtieth of July.

3. The monastery of Ferrières, of which Saint Aldric was monk and abbot, is situated on the Clareia River, which flows into the Loing, in the region of Gâtinais, in the diocese of Sens [Col. 0797C]. Its founder anciently named it Bethlehem, as Lupus, abbot of that place, testifies in Letter 13.

They say that at this place the apostles of Sens, the saints Savinian and Potentian, first established a small shrine of the Blessed Mary. They attribute the foundation of the monastery to Clovis the Great, king of the Franks, and its restoration to Duke Wandelbert.

“Buchinus, converted from paganism, who himself afterward became venerable”—that is, a monk—“was placed in charge of the monastery of Ferrières” around the middle of the seventh century, according to Audoenus in Book I of the *Life of Saint Eligius, Bishop*, chapter 10.

Louis Augustus is said, in the book of his Life, to have restored “the monastery of Saint Mary and Saint Peter at Ferrières, which was anciently called Bethlehem, in whose court his father [rather, grandfather] Pippin killed a lion, and in that very church he himself was solemnly consecrated king by Pope Stephen of Rome.”

This may refer, if I am not mistaken, to what the monk of Saint Gall recorded in Book II of the *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 23: namely, that Pippin, having discovered that his leading men secretly despised him, perhaps because of his short stature, ordered a bull to be released against a lion. The lion seized the bull by the neck and threw it to the ground. Then the king said to those standing around that whoever had greater confidence in his strength should pull the lion away from the bull, or at least kill it.

When no one dared undertake this, Pippin himself did it, driving a sword through the lion’s throat. This event can still be seen represented in ancient figures on the greater gate of the church of Ferrières.

But what the anonymous author of Louis’s Life adds—namely, that Pippin was consecrated in the church of Ferrières by Pope Stephen—is said by Louis Augustus in the letter prefixed to the *Areopagitics*, by Anastasius the Librarian in the Life of Pope Stephen, and by Erchempert and several others to have occurred in the church of Saint-Denis.

Perhaps Pippin was crowned in both places, just as his son Charlemagne was crowned in two places, namely at Noyon and Corbeny. Before Stephen’s arrival in Gaul, Pippin himself had received a crown at Soissons from Boniface, archbishop of Mainz; this practice was also adopted by other kings.

It is certain, however, from the Annals of Saint-Bertin, that Louis and Carloman, sons of Louis the Stammerer, were crowned in that monastery by Archbishop Ansegisus. Carloman acknowledges this in the capitulary he issued at Quierzy, appended to Lupus’s works, where Carloman confirms that document “which he granted at the monastery of Ferrières before the altar of Saint Peter.”

4. It is not easy to establish who the abbots of that monastery were after Buchinus, or in what order they succeeded one another. Their order is confused in the fuller *Gallia Christiana*, where Singulf and Adalbert are listed as sixth and seventh. It is clear from the letters of Abbot Lupus and from the following Life that they must be placed between Alcuin and Aldric.

Concerning Singulf, or Sigulf, Lupus writes in Letter 20 [Col. 0798C]:

“Certainly Sigulf, formerly the noble abbot and presbyter of the monastery of Ferrières, which I, unworthy as I am, serve, had lived honorably into old age in the canonical habit. He voluntarily divested himself of authority and assumed our religion—that is, the monastic life—and until the day he died allowed himself to be subject to his own disciple, whom the emperor Louis, with Sigulf’s consent and the agreement of the brothers, had appointed abbot of that place”—namely, Adalbert.

According to the Life that follows, this Sigulf was English by nation and a disciple of Alcuin. His teacher appointed him over the monastery of Ferrières around the year 804, when Alcuin resigned his abbeys to his disciples.

Adalbert succeeded Sigulf at the beginning of Louis Augustus’s reign. Aldric succeeded Adalbert around the year 824. Then, in 829, when Aldric was transferred to the see of Sens, Odo succeeded him. Odo is omitted by Sainte-Marthe. Later, because he favored Lothair, he was expelled by Charles the Bald, as Lupus states in Letter 26; according to Letter 21, he was succeeded by Lupus, the most distinguished man of his age.

Four letters of Odo are preserved among Lupus’s works, written by Lupus in Odo’s name. Odo the abbot is also mentioned in the *Life of Saint Faro*, chapter 118.

The published lists of the abbots of Ferrières must therefore be corrected. In those lists, Odo is omitted and Wenilo is included. Wenilo, however, was not created archbishop of Sens from the abbacy of Ferrières, as some suppose after being misled by the authority of the following Life; after Aldric’s death, he was appointed from the position of chaplain of the royal chapel of Charles the Bald.

Although Abbot Sigulf had been a canon before resigning his office, the monastery of Ferrières was not subject to canons but to monks. Aldric, after all, “received the insignia of monastic discipline from his earliest age under Alcuin,” the teacher and predecessor of Sigulf.

5. Lupus sufficiently indicates what the religious life of the monks of Ferrières was like at that time in Letter 25, written in the name of Odo the abbot to Louis the abbot [Col. 0799A]:

“For since you were brought up not far from us, you were also with us; the character of our monastery is by no means unknown to you. Apart from the zeal for religion by which it has won a name among the other monasteries, there is nothing here that one who thinks highly of himself should desire.”

Hildegarius—or whoever was the author of the book of the *Life of Saint Faro*—gives the same testimony in chapter 118. Speaking of Lupus, he says that he “now exists as shepherd, on account of the religion of holiness, in the most renowned monastery of Ferrières, where the assembly of monks in Christ, together with him, is to be venerated throughout the whole world.”

We read in Lupus’s Letter 45 to King Charles that seventy-two monks lived there under Abbot Lupus in great poverty.

Marcuvardus, later abbot of Prüm and especially close to Lupus, was a monk there. If I am not mistaken, Eigil was also a monk there before becoming abbot of Prüm, then abbot of Flavigny, and finally archbishop of Sens. Ado, bishop of Vienne, should also be counted among them.

Among the abbots besides Alcuin, Sigulf, Adalbert, and Lupus, Louis de Blanchefort was especially distinguished for religious devotion and generosity. He was abbot from 1465 to 1505, and through his efforts almost the entire monastery was rebuilt from its foundations.

Finally, at that place on 18 August 1569, six monks were subjected to cruel deaths by the Calvinists: John Boursiet, subprior; Louis Bouvet, cellarer; James Colombet, provost; Louis Galopin; Louis Gilles; and Claudius Bourdin.

The first and second were strangled with ropes tied around their necks and dragged down the church steps. The third and fifth were pierced by blows from swords and firearms [Col. 0800A]. The fourth and sixth were stabbed through the breast with a sword.

The monastery still exists under the Benedictine Congregation of Saint Maur and is frequented by great crowds of people, who come to the church of the Virgin Mother of God to fulfill their vows.

6. Several of our monks were placed over the church of Sens during the ninth and tenth centuries. Besides Saint Ebbo, who held that see in the seventh century, Jeremiah, formerly a monk of Centula—as is commonly believed—was appointed archbishop by Louis Augustus. He was succeeded by Aldric, monk and abbot of Ferrières; after Wenilo came Eigil, abbot of Flavigny; then Ansegisus, from the monastery of Saint Michael near Beauvais; then Evrard, monk and provost of the abbey of Saint Columba near Sens.

After two Walters and Aldaldus, William, a monk, received the see. He was followed by Gerlannus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre, who had as his successor Hildemannus, a monk of Saint-Denis. Hildemannus was succeeded by Archembaldus, and after him by Sewinus, who were not monks but eminent observers and promoters of the monastic order.

The Life of Saint Aldric must now be presented. Its title in a manuscript of Ferrières reads:

“Here begins the Life of Blessed Aldric, archbishop of Sens and abbot of this monastery of Ferrières, where his body is buried. Therefore his passing is solemnly commemorated on the tenth of October.”

[Col. 0799]

## Here Begins the Life of Saint Aldric

1. In the year 775 from the Incarnation of the Lord, while Charlemagne was reigning, Blessed Aldric was born in the region of Gâtinais from the family of the palatine princes.

While he was still enclosed within the narrow confines of his mother’s womb, the Lord wished to show in the unborn child what he would become as an adult. For he moved with such frequent leaps that his parents were seized by profound astonishment. This movement is believed to have been a sign that he would fight against spiritual enemies.

2. After he came into the light of day, marked by the character of holy baptism, he was given the name Aldric. Brought up, as was customary for nobles, amid the delights of comfort, he began, in the first tenderness of childhood, to anticipate his age through mature deeds. He made his illustrious nobility still more illustrious through the most distinguished vigilance in good works, indicating by his childish beginnings what a great athlete he would become.

For, as a rival of Saint Nicholas, he weakened his tender body with prolonged fasting and made his limbs thin through untimely abstinence. His parents were not the only ones whom such signs of excellent character affected with profound astonishment; they also wonderfully left the minds of all who observed them astonished.

3. From the earliest beginnings of childhood, therefore, he avoided childish amusements and wonderfully exalted himself through the nobility of his nature and the integrity of his conduct. Loving God with all his strength and pressing forward toward what lay ahead, he rivaled those more perfect than himself in the maturity of his works [Col. 0800C].

At length his parents entrusted him to be instructed in the liberal arts. He began to make extraordinary progress and, as his doctrinal knowledge increased, to receive corresponding growth in religion, so that he might be effectively trained not only in the liberal arts but also in spiritual disciplines.

Remembering the saying of the Wise Man that character is formed through association, he delighted in maintaining conversation with monks and was greatly charmed by the discussions of religious men. He rejoiced to share their fasts, to attend the nocturnal vigils, and, out of zeal for holiness, to avoid illicit desires completely.

He also considered privately, at every moment, how he might avoid the deceptive attractions of the world, whose prolonged companionship he feared would obstruct his purpose of holiness. Inflamed by the fires of this zeal, Blessed Aldric ardently resolved to undertake a stricter way of life. In order to conform his external habit to his interior state, he determined to assume the monastic habit.

4. But so as not to trouble his parents excessively, or to do this without their knowledge, when he found a suitable opportunity he revealed to them the pious secret of his heart. Although at first they did not consent out of a certain natural affection, when they saw shining in him an inestimable ardor of charity, they did not wish to oppose his honorable purpose. Instead, they presented him to the monastery to serve God perpetually, a monastery founded in honor of the Blessed Mary [Note: namely, Ferrières, which is dedicated to the Blessed Mary and Saint Peter. Its principal church, as Lupus testifies in Letter 13, is consecrated in honor of Saint Peter and all the other apostles. The less principal church is dedicated to Saint Mary and remains famous even today for the crowds of pilgrims who visit it.].

There, under Abbot Alcuin, his literary teacher, to whom the administration of that monastery had at that time been entrusted, he received the insignia of monastic discipline.

5. When Alcuin died, Singulf was appointed to take charge of the same place. He was English by nation, born of noble lineage, endowed with honorable character, and distinguished by the excellence of his religious life.

Perceiving Blessed Aldric’s future eminence, which the evident signs of his religious devotion proclaimed, he continually instructed him in pious learning. So that the flower of his youth might develop into abundant fruit, he carefully shaped his tender age through pastoral care.

6. Thus, day by day, the diligence of good works increased in the young man, so that he seemed uniformly to rival his teacher in devotion, silence, humility, and concord—or rather, to be preferred to all as an example for imitation.

At length the fame of this blessed youth reached Saint Jeremiah [Note: Jeremiah succeeded Magnus as archbishop of Sens. Clarius, in the Chronicle of the monastery of Saint Peter at Sens, Hugh the monk of the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre in his *Chronology*, and other more recent writers say that Jeremiah had been a monk and steward of the monastery of Saint Richarius. Hariulf preceded them all in Book III, chapter 20 of the *Chronicle of Centula*, where he writes that Jeremiah, monk and treasurer of Saint Richarius, sought safety by flight during the reign of Louis and Carloman, sons of Louis the Stammerer, when the Northmen were threatening the monastery of Centula. He carried away with him the sacred relics, which he first deposited in the monastery of Saint Columba near Sens [Col. 0801D]. There the brothers elected him abbot, and finally he was made archbishop of Sens. Clarius and Hugh also report this, but they wrongly assign it to the time of Louis the Pious.

Since Jeremiah’s withdrawal to the monastery at Sens occurred when the Northmen were ravaging the Franks—a period after the death of Louis the Pious—Hariulf more correctly assigns it to the reign of Louis and Carloman. Therefore Jeremiah the treasurer of Centula cannot be the same as Jeremiah, archbishop and successor of Magnus, who obtained that see at the beginning of Louis the Pious’s imperial reign.

It must therefore be said either that the authors mentioned above, deceived by the similarity of the name, combined two men into one; or, if Jeremiah the monk of Centula was raised to the see of Sens, that two Jeremiahs must be distinguished: one who held it during the time of Louis the Pious, and another who was appointed senior prelate of the church of Sens during the reign of Louis and Carloman, or certainly shortly afterward, from the monastery of Saint Columba, to which he gave many benefactions during his life and where he wished to be buried after his death.]

At that time Jeremiah was successfully presiding over the archbishopric of Sens.

7. Burning with a pious desire to see him, Jeremiah ordered Aldric to be brought into his presence, so that, if the reports of his goodness were true, he might test the hidden qualities of his character through personal observation and experience.

When this had been done, he found in him such admirable perfection that, in the eyes of many, both those who kept silent and those who spoke, the fame that had praised him seemed to have been maliciously inadequate.

Judging him worthy of greater advancement, he distinguished the young man by ordaining him to the diaconate. Later, after two years had passed, he raised him to the priestly dignity.

For the wise administration of the bishop sought to compensate in him, through maturity of character, for whatever his youthful age seemed to lack. After receiving the sacred orders, Aldric applied himself even more earnestly to divine works, so that the marks of virtue might shine more brightly in him and the increase of his charitable purpose might abound.

8. For the greater he became, the more he humbled himself in all things, according to the Apostle’s word: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation” (1 Peter 5:6).

At length the widespread fame of this illustrious man reached the hearing of King Louis, son of Charlemagne, who at that time held the monarchy of the Frankish kingdom.

9. At Charles’s command, Aldric, as the Holy Spirit granted him speech, defeated the subtle arguments of certain unbelievers who were then attacking the Christian faith [Col. 0802B]. He utterly drove away the ruin threatening the endangered faith and restored it from its uncertainty [Note: It is uncertain which heretics Aldric opposed or by what methods. Tavellus, in his *History of the Bishops of Sens*, believes that Louis summoned the synod of Aachen on the advice of this bishop, where clerics were forbidden luxurious clothing. But the council at which this was decreed was held long before Aldric’s episcopate, namely in 817, as the Anonymous author of the *Life of Louis Augustus* testifies. Aldric always remained deeply loyal to Louis, as is clear from the Annals of Saint-Bertin under the year 833, where most of the bishops act in support of the emperor’s succession plans.].

The emperor Augustus, delighted by these achievements, appointed him royal tutor [Note: I interpret this as chancellor, or the composer of royal diplomas, most of which are called *praecepta*. I find that Aldric was chancellor of Pippin, king of Aquitaine and son of Louis Augustus, in two letters reported by Philip Labbe in his *Curious Miscellanies*.

That our Aldric, already a bishop, was a royal envoy is understood both from a diploma of the emperor Lothair, confirming an arrangement that his father Louis had made through his envoys—Haldric, formerly the venerable archbishop of the church of Sens, Alberic of Langres, and others—to avoid disputes between the abbots and monks of Flavigny concerning the monastery’s property, preserved by our George Viollet in his *Apology concerning the Body of Saint Regina*; and from letters edited above under the year 809 for the monastery of Elnone, to which Aldric was sent by Louis Augustus to confirm monastic order there.

He also labored to restore that order at Saint-Denis, at the instigation of Louis the Pious. But I find him described as superintendent of the palace schools only here.] Thus the affairs of the imperial court and the emperor’s greater business were to be determined by Aldric’s judgment.

France rejoiced in so great a patron. Although he surpassed others in power, he nevertheless made himself equal to all. He was affable to everyone, cheerful in the gentleness of his speech, a helper of orphans, a defender of widows, and a counselor to the afflicted. Thus, becoming all things to all, he deserved to obtain everyone’s goodwill and favor.

10. Although the holy man was diligently praised by everyone, he labored, with pious simplicity, to conceal human praise, lest the favorable breeze of glory disturb the conscience made serene by grace [Col. 0802C].

For the height of merit is accustomed to feel weakness whenever the empty pleasure of human praise steals in [Col. 0803A].

Meanwhile, the instigation of the evil enemy aroused the resentment of certain rivals. Through the poisonous envy of detraction they began to malign the holy man of the Lord and to defile his praiseworthy reputation with profane disparagement [Possibly, “to accuse”].

But the man of God, casting his thought upon the Lord, patiently endured the bitterness of his detractors for the love of Christ. Rejoicing in the sweetness of a conscience made serene, he quieted their deceitful machinations by patience alone, relying on the Davidic saying—rather, on the saying of Hannah: “God is the Lord of knowledge, and thoughts are prepared for him” (1 Samuel 2:3).

Envy is indeed softened by modesty, when virtue shines through silence in the face of shameful accusations. Nor is the one protected by heavenly grace crushed by the weapons of raging enemies [Col. 0803B].

11. While these things were taking place, Adalbert, the distinguished abbot of the monastery of Ferrières, departed from this world. Singulf, weakened by old age, had appointed him as his substitute with the common consent of the brothers, preferring to sit with Mary at the feet of the Lord rather than, like Martha, continue laboring amid the many demands of service.

After four years of administration, Adalbert was happily released from the prison of the flesh. When he had been buried, everyone unanimously and canonically chose Aldric, a man of proven religious devotion.

Although he resisted out of pious simplicity, judging himself unworthy of so high a dignity, he was nevertheless overcome by the brothers’ stubborn insistence and finally yielded graciously to their request.

When the venerable Augustus heard this, he gladly gave his assent and favor to the election. Not only did he renew, at his own request, the privileges of the abbey that his predecessors had granted, but he also bestowed new privileges on the monastery that would benefit it in the future.

12. After assuming the governance of the brothers of Saint Peter, Aldric’s good reputation grew from day to day. Although he secretly lived a solitary life and in many ways declared war on the misery of the flesh, he could not hide the lamp beneath a bushel. Against his will, works of holiness came into public view, glorifying the Father who is in heaven.

He built a new monastery in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, together with certain workshops and buildings extremely useful to the needs of the brothers. In caring for his subjects he showed such diligence that, because he had been faithful over a few things, he deserved to be set over many. The evident outcome soon demonstrated this.

For after a short interval of time, Jeremiah, the celebrated bishop of Sens, was stripped of mortal flesh [Note: In the year 828, according to the monk Odorannus in his Chronicle; and indeed on the seventh day before the Ides of December, as Clarius records. Clarius places Jeremiah’s death in the following year, however, and does so incorrectly, as is shown by the annotation at no. 13.]. After the proper rites of humanity had been performed, he was honorably buried in the monastery of Saint Columba [Note: This monastery is situated in the suburb of the city of Sens. Louis Augustus entrusted it to Bishop Jeremiah, as the monk Clarius states, “so that it might remain under the protection of the archbishop of the city of Sens.”

Benedict, abbot of Aniane, restored monastic discipline there while Jacob, the canon-abate of that place, was still living, as is read in a diploma of Louis Augustus appended to the works of Abbot Lupus in the edition of Baluze.

At the request of Abbot Supplicius, Louis confirmed for that monastery the right to elect its abbot. These letters praise “Aufridus and Donatus, nephews of Jeremiah, formerly bishop of the city of Sens,” who had given some lodging or guesthouse to the monastery of Saint Columba.

The previously mentioned Appendix also contains a privilege of Charles the Bald concerning the liberty of this monastery; it is worthy of reading.]

13. When the appointed time for the election had arrived, as is customary in the Church, lest the rapacious wolf scatter the wandering sheep without a shepherd, the entire people gathered with courtesy and devotion to elect a bishop.

After the grace of the Holy Spirit had first been invoked, Blessed Aldric was elected archbishop by canonical procedure, with unanimous agreement, the people acclaiming and giving their support [Col. 0804B].

When the holy man heard that the quiet of his life was to be interrupted by episcopal administration, he offered various excuses, asserting that he was insufficiently suited to so great a burden [Note: Aldric’s letters bearing on this matter to Frothar, bishop of Toul, are preserved below, after this Life.

That he was not chosen in the first election, but that another man was chosen and was not approved by Louis Augustus, is established by letters 15, 16, and 17 of Frothar. Moreover, that Aldric had not yet been ordained at the beginning of 829 is clear both from the capitularies issued by Louis Augustus in the sixteenth year of his empire for the various councils to be held in his kingdom—in the preface to which he orders the archbishop of Paris and whoever the bishop of Sens might be to meet with the others—and from a letter of the same emperor written to the bishops of Gaul and Germany to summon councils in the provinces, including the one held at Paris in 829 on the eighth day before the Ides of June.

In this letter he commands that the future bishop of Sens and the others should come together at Paris. This shows that at the beginning of that year, when the letter was issued, Aldric’s election had not yet taken place or been ratified, and that his predecessor Jeremiah had died in the preceding December.

Clarius and the author of the *Chronicle of Limoges* in volume I of Labbe’s *Library*, who place Jeremiah’s death in 829, must therefore be corrected.].

Nevertheless, putting private tranquility after the public good, he was overcome by the importunate insistence of the clergy and people and at last scarcely consented. As though unwilling and resisting, he was dragged from the monastery to the episcopal vestments and, amid universal applause, was happily enthroned.

Thus, like another Jacob, he endured sleeping with Rachel, so that one day he might be free for her embraces.

14. After undertaking his pastoral office, he began to keep diligent watch over his flock, lest the deceit of the ancient enemy harm it, since that enemy “circles about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” Through frequent exhortations he encouraged his subjects to arm themselves against him with the armor of God.

Meanwhile, he enlightened those whom he had instructed in saving doctrine, and carefully exercised all the duties of a pious shepherd with prudent discernment.

He was a comforter of the sorrowful, a helper of orphans, a defender of widows, compassionate toward everyone’s hardships, distressed by the troubles of all who were in need, a corrector of injuries, and a reprover of those who inflicted them. Always maintaining an even balance of rectitude, he was equally attentive to the afflicted in comforting them and to their oppressors in restraining them.

Thus he joined the office of a judge to paternal compassion, so that strictness would not become excessively rigid, nor compassion lax.

He also instructed the canons of his church with paternal affection, so that they might become simpler in address, more polished in conduct, gentler in speech, and purer in mind. He wished them to avoid corrupting the simple by their example and to be ashamed to exceed the canonical rule.

For the vigor of virtue shamefully withers when the loss of modesty is not perceived in the sinner. Moreover, he carefully kept gifts away from his private presence, lest the slippery path of greed make the judgment of his examination unequal, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Blessed is he who shakes his hands free from every gift” (Isaiah 23:15).

Indeed, he always set his predecessor before him as an example for imitation, so that he might succeed him not only in dignity but also in humility.

The peoples rejoiced in so great a prelate, devoutly giving thanks to God, who had made his mercy marvelous among them by placing under their governance a man of such religious devotion and integrity.

15. Perhaps, while he was on his way to Paris, drawn there by important affairs, at the request of the abbot of Fosses he dedicated the church that he himself had built in honor of blessed Mary.[^c0073-1] Then, returning to his own place, while one day he was sitting before the church of blessed Stephen,[^c0073-2] he saw a certain passerby named Marrymardus.[^c0073-3] As he looked at the man’s face, he discerned in him unmistakable signs of arrogance. His walk was erratic, his gestures ostentatious, his neck held erect, his face grim, his eyes fierce, and his speech terrifying. He summoned him and carefully asked who he was. Since the man was accustomed to speak about everything with a certain haughtiness, he replied that he was the city’s warden. The bishop said to him:

“If you are the guardian of others, why do you disdain guarding yourself? Since you are dust and ashes, why do you conceive such immoderate pride? Why do you glory in empty boasting?”

He then began to preach the word of God, mingling words of gentleness with his reproof, pouring wine and oil into the wounds of the half-dead man. He did not cease until he had effectively restrained the man’s swollen arrogance and humbled his haughty insolence. For the sharp arrows of the Mighty One had been so deeply fixed in the innermost recesses of his heart, and his heart had been so wounded by love, that he immediately begged him to allow him to become a monk, out of gratitude for all that had gone before. And so it was done.

[^c0073-1]: [Col. 0805D] This dedication is mentioned in the book on the miracles of Saint Babolene, abbot, from the second century. The oratory of blessed Mary still exists in the monastery of Fosses, two leagues above Paris toward the Marne; about a hundred years ago it passed to secular canons, as will be said later in the history of the translation of the body of Saint Maurus, abbot, to this monastery.

[^c0073-2]: [Col. 0805D] This is the cathedral church of Sens, dedicated to Saint Stephen.

[^c0073-3]: [Col. 0805D] I read *Marcuvardus*, who later became a monk of Ferrières and subsequently abbot of Prüm; he is discussed below.

16. At that time there was a monastery consecrated in honor of blessed Remigius, a short distance from the gate of the city of Sens. Its proximity was hostile to the monks’ quiet. For they were often compelled by the noise of the populace to devote themselves to divine services with diminished devotion, and at times to grow lukewarm in the fervor of contemplation when empty thoughts crept in. The narrowness of the site also frequently provided an occasion for quarrels and disturbances between the townspeople and the monks’ companions. For concord of minds is usually difficult where character and way of life differ.

Therefore the holy bishop, seeking a remedy for this inconvenience, transferred the aforesaid monastery to Valerias,[^c0073-4] but, being occupied with secular pressures, did not complete the project he had begun.

[^c0073-4]: [Col. 0805D] Others call it *Vallilias*, in the vernacular Vareilles. Concerning this monastery, as well as that of Saint Remigius, see the note attached to the Life of Saint Romanus, abbot, in the first volume. I shall present below the letters of Aldric concerning this matter. Aldric also arranged for the election of Heribald, bishop of Auxerre, as is read in the *Book of the Deeds of the Bishops of Auxerre*, chapter 36.

17. After his glorious deeds and after enduring labors for the establishment of his church, he grew weary of administering his office and directed the sharpness of his mind toward the final days of his life. He began more privately to ponder again Saint Martin’s statement that his virtue had been greater before the episcopate than during the episcopate. Fearing, therefore, that the merit of his religious life might be diminished by the complications of secular affairs, he resolved to lay aside the care of pastoral responsibility[^c0073-5] and began more devotedly to yearn for the tranquility of his accustomed contemplation.

Yet he feared that the ancient robber might scatter the flock left without its shepherd. He therefore began with sobbing prayers to implore God’s mercy, asking that God grant him to enjoy the delight of secure repose and provide his subjects with the protection of a suitable pastor. That this prayer was heard by the Lord became clearly known afterward by what happened.

[^c0073-5]: [Col. 0806D] Lupus, abbot of Ferrières and his disciple, likewise attests this in Letter 29 to Guenilo, Aldric’s successor, in these words: “Moreover, your predecessor, Aldric of blessed memory, who, at the command of the aforesaid emperor and through the remarkable exertion of good men, was taken from us while he was abbot and made bishop of the church of Sens, had firmly resolved to return to us, abandoning his episcopal charge, when, as we believe, he exchanged this life for a happier one.”

18. For the glorious servant of God, having learned through a revelation of the Holy Spirit the day of his death, on which he would pass over to the joys of true rest, summoned his disciples and piously disclosed to them that his final day was near. With his customary solicitude and devotion he urged them to keep the vessel of their own bodies clean and undefiled; to run in such a way that they might obtain the prize; to labor in such a way that they would not be deprived of the rest of eternal blessedness; and to fight in such a way that they might be rewarded with the prize of everlasting joy.

When his preaching was finished, he chose a suitable place for his burial, namely, the monastery of Ferrières. He ordered that his body be carried there and buried in the eaves of the church after the separation of his body and soul had been accomplished. While he was teaching these things, profound astonishment seized everyone, because they could perceive in him no sign of illness.

19. [Col. 0807A] After a short interval, struck by the heaviness of illness, he began to fall sick and to be intolerably tormented by frequent pains, the forerunners of approaching death. Nevertheless, the customary serenity of his face remained completely unchanged, and his devoted mind was established more and more firmly in faith and love of Christ.

As the illness worsened, he was refreshed with the prescribed viaticum. With his eyes fixed upon heaven and his hands raised toward God, he entered the way of all flesh in the sixty-first year of his life,[^c0073-6] and on the sixth day before the Ides of October[^c0073-7] he happily departed to the Lord, receiving the crown of joy from the hand of God.

His body was carried to the aforesaid monastery in accordance with the terms of his command, amid the great wailing of peoples mourning and lamenting that they had been deprived and left desolate of the protection of so great and so kindly a shepherd. It was honorably buried beneath the eaves, near the oratory of blessed Andrew, in a stone tomb that he had built for himself while alive. There, no less after his death than during his life, the Lord revealed through many signs of virtues and miracles how great was the merit of his servant.

[^c0073-6]: [Col. 0807D] Rather, in his sixty-fifth year, since Aldric is here said to have been born in 775; for it is clear from the following notice that he died in 840.

[^c0073-7]: [Col. 0807D] Indeed, in the year of Christ 840, as is established both from Lupus’s letter to Immo, bishop of Noyon, and from the pamphlet of Charles the Bald’s proclamation against Wenilo. In that letter Lupus indicates that, after returning safely from the school at Fulda, he found everything prosperous “except, as far as I am concerned,” he says, “the death, full of misfortune, of my lord and foster-father Aldric.” He returned toward the end of 841, as will be said below in Rabanus’s eulogy. Charles, however, says that at the time when he divided part of the kingdom with his brothers, “the metropolitan see of Sens was vacant of a shepherd.” This division took place immediately after the battle of Fontenay, fought on the seventh day before the Kalends of July 841; consequently Aldric had departed to heaven in the preceding October.

20. After blessed Aldric, Heneaulus obtained the episcopal chair of the aforesaid city.[^c0073-8] Aldric himself had previously appointed him abbot of the frequently mentioned monastery. This man, therefore, keeping constant watch in the practice of good works and clinging in mind to heavenly things, learned by divine revelation where the bodies of the holy martyrs Savinian and Potentian, Eodaldus and Serotinus were resting. So that their veneration would not grow obsolete through time and neglect, he honorably placed the bodies of the blessed martyrs, with all solemn ceremony, in the church of Saint Peter.

He also transferred the body of blessed Lupus, bishop of Sens, and that of blessed Columba, a virgin who suffered martyrdom under the emperor Aurelian, together with another,[^c0073-9] and deposited them in a place where the reverence due to them is still offered to this day. He also completed with the finishing hand the building that his predecessor, blessed Aldric, had begun at Valerias.

[^c0073-8]: [Col. 0808D] Rather, Wenilo—not the abbot of Ferrières, but the chaplain of Charles the Bald’s royal chapel—as Charles himself testifies at the synod held at Saponaria in 859. At that synod he complained against Wenilo, saying: “To Wenilo, then my cleric, serving me in my chapel, I entrusted the metropolitan see of Sens for its governance.” Certainly Wenilo is remembered by Clarius the monk as having done the same things attributed here to Heneaulus. At Ferrières, Odo, Lupus’s predecessor, was then in charge; in Letter 29 he calls Wenilo Aldric’s predecessor.

21. In the aforesaid monastery there were three young men who rendered continual service to Gaubert,[^c0073-10] who had undertaken its care. By allowing their diligence in service to decline through a dissolute way of life, they served their stomachs more devotedly than the Lord. While the monks were sleeping, they stuffed themselves with an excess of food and drink and prolonged the hours of the untimely night with jokes and obscene songs.
