It happened that, weighed down by sleep, they finally sought rest so that they might digest for a while the wine with which they were drenched. With reckless familiarity, in drunken error or the stubbornness of their corruption, they went to the place where the body of blessed Aldric lay at rest, and there, overcome by sleep, they suddenly fell asleep.

But the Lord, unwilling to allow the place consecrated to the sacred limbs of his servant to be profaned, miraculously carried the sleepers away. He placed one across the nearby river on the public road, and the other two beneath a beech tree far away. At length, when dawn was shining, the people found them as they were customarily hurrying to seek the intercession of the saints resting in the aforesaid monastery.

When everyone had been awakened from sleep and confessed the miraculous event, astonishment seized them all, and the name of the holy confessor was glorified more magnificently to the honor of God.

[^c0073-10]: [Col. 0808D] Is this the Gaubert mentioned by Rodulfus Tortarius in chapter 14 of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*?

22. [Col. 0808B] His body was transferred from beneath the eaves of the church, as signs of his miraculous powers shone forth, and was reverently placed in a higher chapel.

23. At that time there was a certain man of consular rank named Mauritius, noble indeed by birth, but making his lineage ignoble by his conduct. At his instigation, his henchmen began grievously to harass the aforesaid monks with unlawful exactions and violently to plunder their property and that of their people. They had become accustomed to doing this so often without resistance that custom seemed to make lawful what was unlawful, and practice in wrongdoing to diminish the offense.

The monks, therefore, constrained by the pressure of so great a calamity and hoping for protection from no one, took counsel together. They resolved to seek a more peaceful place and, by their absence, to deprive their enemies of a malicious opportunity. After loading their possessions onto a cart and taking with them the body of blessed Aldric together with the other sacred relics, they set out in the silence of night.

As they were leading the cart through the winding and trackless roads, a certain ox-driver, advancing carelessly, fell headlong to the ground. The wheel of the heavily laden cart passed over his legs, and he was thought to have been left half dead. All were thrown into confusion by this misfortune; they raised a lamentable cry and with one voice called upon the help of Saint Aldric.

In response to their devotion, the ox-driver rose unharmed, as though he had felt no burden at all. He resumed the journey and continued performing his customary work. Thus, when everyone’s grief had been turned into joy, they gave thanks to God and happily reached the monastery of Villar.[^c0073-11]

When this was heard, a great crowd of men and women devoutly flocked to the protection of the holy confessor. Among them came the consul Mauritius, having heard of the miracle and being greatly terrified by a threatening rebuke delivered to him by blessed Aldric in a nocturnal vision.[^c0073-12] Before the relics, with tears and groaning, he sought pardon for his former offense and promised thereafter to show due reverence to the monastery that he had violated.

After his vow had been praised by all and strengthened by their support, they joyfully returned with the relics of the blessed confessor to their customary place.

[^c0073-11]: [Col. 0808D] Now commonly called Villemonstier, not far from the town of Montargis; in that village there is a priory subject to the monastery of Fleury.

[^c0073-12]: [Col. 0809C] Here one should note what Lupus writes in Letter 53 to King Charles: “Our elders solemnly affirm, from their own experience, that they have discovered this for themselves, and that it was handed down to them as children by their elders: whoever has inflicted some notable injury upon our monastery, unless he quickly repents, has suffered a great misfortune or endured the loss of health and life.”

24. It was customary for the community of the monastery of Ferrières, after the feast of Pentecost had ended, to go each year with solemn ceremony to the Castle of Nantonis[^c0073-13] in order to render the services of devotion and seek the intercession of the saints.

When, therefore, at the appointed time, the pious ashes of Aldric, beloved of God, were being carried to the aforesaid place with due veneration, behold, a rather large girl, whom her mother’s womb had brought forth into the light without light, struggled through the crowd, seized with her hand a cloth laid over the relics in the carriage, and clinging firmly to it could not be pulled away for the entire length of the journey. She continually and fervently sought the help of the pious confessor with the innermost affection of devotion.

When they finally reached the aforesaid castle, and a brief halt had been made at a certain place before the gate, the eternal counsel of God ordained that his saint should be glorified through works of power. There, in the open spectacle of the people, drops of blood burst from the eyes of the aforementioned girl, and through the merits of the holy confessor a new light illuminated her natural blindness.

Immediately everyone ran together, and the servant of God was raised up with marvelous proclamations of praise—he who is always wondrous in his saints.

[^c0073-13]: [Col. 0810C] Commonly called Château-Landon, a town two leagues from Ferrières, situated on a raised hill near the Loing River. This place was mentioned in the Life of Saint Severinus, abbot, in the first volume.

25. As the annual cycle turned, the solemn day of blessed Aldric arrived. While the whole people were venerating it with the celebration that was due, a wicked woman, as though in contempt of the solemnity, opposed the ecclesiastical ordinances through the sin of disobedience.

While this was happening, the evil adversary came upon her in the form of a black dog and attempted to devour her hand. She tried with all her strength to drive it away but could not. Wounded by its deadly bite, she collapsed, shaken; and her own blood, poured forth, pierced her failing hand, so that, as though maimed because of the crime, that hand was deprived of its customary function.

26. As time passed, it happened that a certain man named Tambold had for some time enjoyed considerable wealth. But, advancing into old age, he fell into such poverty that nothing remained to support life except what his wife, named Supplicia, earned by the labor of her hands. He often recalled his former prosperity and therefore bore the heap of his troubles more heavily, since it is the most miserable kind of misfortune to have once been happy.[^c0073-14]

To increase his grief, it happened that his wife, deprived of her usual bodily health, fell into a prolonged illness and could no longer restore her husband’s weakness by her customary assistance, having become his companion in misery. Afflicted by their adverse circumstances, they humbly implored divine help, asking that he who gives food to all flesh not allow them to perish in pitiable want.

When, after excessive weariness from mourning, the man happened to fall asleep, it was revealed to him in a dream that, if his wife humbly sought the help of blessed Aldric, she would effectively receive a remedy for her pain. Awakened from sleep, he told his wife everything he had seen, advising and exhorting her to cast her thought upon the Lord and his confessor and to act with confidence.

She rose, and after a short interval reached the threshold of blessed Aldric with humble devotion. With a contrite spirit, she stood before the tomb in which the pious ashes rested and implored divine mercy. Through the help of him who lives and reigns forever and ever, she was completely freed from her illness and recovered her former health. Amen.

[^c0073-14]: From Boethius, *The Consolation of Philosophy*.

# The Letters of Saint Aldric

## First Letter: To Bishop Frotharius

[Col. 0809D]

Aldric sends everlasting greetings to the distinguished and especially beloved Bishop Frotharius.

I have found it necessary to be supported by the assistance of your prayers, as I myself have often testified to you when requesting them. But now I need them in every way, since—as I think you have heard—the episcopal charge has been imposed upon me, unworthy as I am; and it has found me as unprepared as I am unworthy.

For although, long ago, when I was devoting myself to monastic discipline, I accepted responsibility for the brothers at their insistence, what I am now compelled to bear could in no way have been anticipated. Therefore, apart from the mercy of God, I entrust myself entirely to the familiar protection of your prayers and those of my other friends, begging you to deign continually to assist the weakness of my strength.

And because I have no confidence in my own prudence to carry out so great a task suitably, I ask that your holy intention strive to obtain from God that I may sincerely guard myself and, through his mercy, at least exercise reverently the care entrusted to me.

I hope that the Lord will bless your kindness, which acts well in this matter, with perpetual well-being, most reverend bishop.

## Second Letter: To the Church of Sens

To the most holy and most reverend lords, brothers and fellow bishops, and likewise to the most religious and venerable abbots established within the dominion of our lord the emperor, the most serene Augustus Lothair, Aldric, the least of the servants of Christ, archbishop of the holy church of Sens.

Your excellent, venerable, and God-devoted Holiness knows how great is the care and solicitude required to preserve and administer the pastoral governance entrusted to us. Since we have therefore been placed upon the watchtower of the Church and ought to show the others the way by which they must enter into life, we must strive, insofar as divine mercy has granted us the ability and understanding, to administer with foresight and prudence what has been entrusted to us according to the will of God.

Our administration should benefit not only our subjects while we remain alive in the present age, but also those who, in places devoted to divine worship and entrusted for a time to our diligence for their governance, will serve the heavenly mercy in perpetuity. When they are not burdened with concern for bodily necessities—I mean food and clothing—they may freely fix their minds upon the vision of divine contemplation. Clinging to this supreme and saving good, they continually yearn for it, suspended in complete freedom of hope; and, guided by divine grace, they will rejoice when they have already obtained the reward of eternal life and reached the place toward which they long.

Yet we know that the Church’s possessions are the offerings of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor. Since we have undertaken to administer, manage, and order these possessions, we must remember that we are their stewards and apply their revenues and expenses to the uses for which they are known to have been assigned to the divine altars.

Therefore I have resolved to bring to your most pious attention the manner in which the monks’ cells belonging to the episcopal church entrusted to my smallness are to be arranged—namely, the cell of Saint Remigius, confessor of Christ, built in the suburb of the city. In the time of my predecessors it was once broken up through divisions; because of this negligence, the monks who appeared to be dwelling there for God were unable, on account of poverty and the unsuitable nature of the site, to observe the rule of blessed Benedict as they ought.

For this reason, with the counsel of our brothers—that is, the canons and monks—as well as of the faithful laity, it seemed appropriate to us, because of the site’s unsuitability and the monks dwelling there for God, to transfer the aforesaid cell to Valliculas and build it from the foundations. Rothlaus assigned or handed it over to the aforesaid cell of Saint Remigius by a deed of donation, out of love for God and for the remedy of the soul of her husband Meginarius, as well as for herself and for her children and parents.[^c0073-15] This was done so that divine worship might be conducted there and the reward of those for whose salvation it had been handed over might increase.

We also wish the administrators and monks to possess, without diminution or impediment from anyone, the places upon which the aforesaid monastery was built—that is, the fields, vineyards, meadows, building plots, and everything it possessed within the city walls or outside them—for the use of those who dwell there for God under the rule of blessed Benedict.

For this reason I have presented this written statement, arranged concerning the matter, to your most holy assembly to be reread and confirmed by your subscriptions. Through your unanimity I have resolved to establish that henceforth no bishop—whoever may succeed in time by the grace granted by God—shall presume to diminish, remove, apply to other uses, or give as a benefice, whether to his own people or to outsiders, anything from the possessions that the aforesaid cell presently holds and possesses for the use of the monks.

Rather, as has been stated, whatever it now retains in different places and territories, assigned to the use of the monks, and whatever may later be given to that place by those who fear God, shall remain without any diminution or subtraction with the cell and the monks dwelling there. This includes territories, vineyards, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, and all other appurtenances.

The following are the places assigned for the maintenance of the monks dwelling in the aforesaid cell:

First, Valliculas, where we wish the aforesaid monastery to be built; Staticus with its dependencies, namely Old Ferrières; Petra Ursana with its territories and woods; Chryniacus with neighboring Hermentaria, together with their territories and woods; Fontanicula with its territories; Lausa with its dependencies, namely the village of Saint Sidronius, with its territories and woods, and also Lation; Bracciacus with its territories; Columbarius with its dependencies, namely Esthiniacus and Silviacus, together with their territories and woods; Villamesca with its adjoining bridge and territory; Misceriacus with neighboring Ternanta; Villanova with its dependencies, namely Cavanarias and Capotenus; Noerollis with neighboring Caprencius, together with its territories and woods, and also Puteoli.

In all, there are 190 *mansi* and nineteen guesthouses. Whatever the monks serving divine grace in the aforesaid places or around the same cell are known presently to possess—or whatever else there may be that has escaped my memory but that they nevertheless retain assigned for their maintenance—with territories, vineyards, meadows, woods, waters and watercourses, and other appurtenances, shall belong wholly and exclusively to them and to their uses, as stated above, in perpetual right, without any diminution under the pretext of our aforesaid episcopate, in accordance with the right properly due.

Moreover, the bishop who by God’s authority presides at any given time shall arrange for the abbot of the same monastery to be appointed and ordained by them—namely, the man whom the entire community requests to be appointed and whom the sincerity of his character and the probity of his good works commend, if such a man can be found among them.

If no such man can at all be found among them, the bishop shall provide that someone from the same parish or diocese of Sens be placed over them and ordained, with the consent of the holy fellow bishops of that diocese and the venerable abbots situated around it.

In adding monks, the abbot who presides shall observe this rule: the total number shall not exceed thirty until a greater abundance of resources has accrued. Nor shall the bishop burden the abbot of that place with demands for gifts. It shall suffice for the annual gifts that he receive one horse and a shield with a lance.

If he is ordered to go on a public expedition, two carts shall be added from the same place, one of wine and the other of flour, together with ten rams. Beyond these, he shall in no way presume to burden them with demands for gifts out of desire or greed, lest the monks of the same cell be diverted from their purpose by such business and the bishop, made responsible for their destruction, be compelled to suffer everlasting punishments.

The bodies of the saints that await their blessed translation in the aforesaid parish of ours are also greatly neglected by wicked and negligent custodians, so that they lack both the service of lamps and the custodianship due to them. Therefore, out of love for God, whom they served while living in the flesh, and for the benefit of our soul, and with the will and permission of our lords and most pious kings Louis and Charles, we wish them to be carried to that place, since we have found a suitable location for this purpose.

But because sacred authority forbids scandal to be brought into such and similar churches of Christ through anyone’s negligence, the consent of many bishops is required. We wish all these matters to be brought to the knowledge of your fatherhood, so that thereafter, through your judgment, both the place itself—which, with God’s favor, we have determined to establish—and the aforesaid sacred relics of the saints may be served worthily and commendably by the servants of God serving God there, and so that due prayers may be offered tirelessly for the welfare of our lord and of the whole holy Church of God.

We confirm this work, dedicated to God, with the hand of our smallness, so that, as time passes, it may obtain a firmer condition of rectitude, with all the most holy fathers and brothers consenting in the name of God, and may remain untouched. And so that what has been written may thereafter remain valid, we ask that it be confirmed by the hands of your Holiness.

In the name of Christ, I, Aldric, unworthy archbishop of the church of Sens, resolved that this privilege be made, and I subscribed.

In the name of Christ, I, Landramnus, archbishop of the church of Tours, acknowledged it and subscribed.

In the name of Christ, I, Bartholomew, archbishop of the church of Narbonne, made it and subscribed.

I, Jonas, unworthy bishop of the church of Orléans, subscribed in support of this act.

I, Rainardus, bishop of Rouen, subscribed.

I, Rotualdus, bishop of Soissons, subscribed in support of this act.

Aldric, bishop of the city of Le Mans.

I, Careviltus, bishop of Bayeux, subscribed.

In the name of God, I, Radulfus, bishop of Lisieux, subscribed in support of this act.

I, Acamradus, unworthy bishop of Paris, subscribed.

I, Stephanus, unworthy bishop of Bourges, subscribed.

I, Altadus, bishop of Geneva, subscribed.

I, Adalhelmus, bishop of Châlons, subscribed.

I, Ragnerius, bishop of Amiens, subscribed.

I, Helias, bishop of Troyes, subscribed.

I, Hucbertus, bishop of Meaux, subscribed.

I, Alduinus, bishop of Verdun, subscribed.

I, Delricus, bishop of Basel, subscribed.

I, Fulconinus, unworthy bishop of Worms.

In the name of God, I, Teugrinus, bishop of Alba.

I, Atto, bishop of the city of Nantes.

I, Gerfredus, bishop of Nevers.

I, Facona, bishop.

I, Boso, abbot of the monastery of Saint Benedict, subscribed.

I, Adrevaldus, abbot of the monastery of Noviacum.

[^c0073-16]: [Col. 0813D] In these letters, which breathe Aldric’s solid piety and religion, the name of the monastery over which Adrevaldus presided must be corrected; instead of Noviacum, one should read Flavigny. For Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, states in his *Chronicle* that Adrevaldus presided over that monastery at the time. Deidonus seems to William Marlot to have been abbot of the monastery of Saint Remigius near Reims; but it is established that he was abbot of Reome or Réomé—that is, of the monastery of Saint John in the district of Tonnerre—not of a monastery at Reims. Christianus was abbot of the monastery of Saint Germanus at Auxerre and later became bishop of the same city.

# In the Year of the Lord 836  
## Symphosius Amalarius, Priest of Metz and Chorepiscopus

## Historical Notice on Symphosius Amalarius

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis)*

Amalarius—also called Amularius, Amelarius, Amilarius, Hamularius, Amalharius, Amalhart,[^c0073-17] and Hamalart—chorepiscopus of Metz, approved in the year 816 at the Council of Aachen the book *The Life of Clerics* [alternatively, *of Canons*], consisting of 113 chapters, to which another 32 chapters were added, as well as 28 chapters *On the Life of Nuns*. See the volumes of the Councils: the Royal edition, volume XXI; Labbe, volume VII; Hardouin, volume VI; and Coleti, volume IX. See also Sirmond’s *Councils of Gaul*, volume II, page 329; Cointius’s *Annals*, volume VII, pages 317, 319, 397 and following.

The same Amalarius, in 825, was sent by the Parisian synod to Aachen to Louis the Pious and brought him a collection of testimonies from ten holy Fathers against the worship of images.

He is the same man of whom Sigebert of Gembloux writes in chapter 87:

“Amalarius”—for *Attularius* should be read here—“a monk, wrote a short book on ecclesiastical offices. Later, writing on the same subject to the emperor Louis, he set forth more fully, in four books, the order and reasons for the ecclesiastical offices, as well as one book on the mysteries of the Mass.”

In a manuscript codex of the church of Saint Martial at Limoges, according to Mabillon, volume I, page 419, and volume II, page 140 (new edition, pages 100 and 432), the following words are read at the end:

“Here ends the book of Symphosius Amalarius, venerable priest, on the Divine Offices, which he sent to the kings Louis and Lothair, sons of the emperor Charlemagne; this book was copied at the direction of Ademar, etc.”

From that codex Mabillon published, as a supplement, Book IV, chapter 48,[^c0073-18] concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict, the principal abbot. Also relevant to its elucidation is Mabillon’s dissertation on the monastic life of Gregory the Great, volume II, page 145, and the new edition, page 499.

Amalarius’s *Eclogues on the Office of the Mass* are found in Baluze’s *Capitularies of the Kings of the Franks*, volume II, page 1352. Baluze also noted that the Anonymous *Response on the Body and Blood of the Lord*, published by Dacherius in volume XII, page 39, and in the new edition, volume I, page 149, belongs to this Amalarius.

The four books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, which Honorius IV.3, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, explicitly attributes to the bishop of Metz, appeared together with his book *On the Order of the Antiphonary*—in which he also promised a *Lectionary*, a *Cantatory*, and a *Commentary on the Daily Office*—in Melchior Hittorp’s collection of writers on the Divine Offices, Cologne, 1568, folio; and in Georgius Ferrarius, Rome, 1591, folio; as well as in all the libraries of the Fathers and in the latest Lyon edition, volume XIV.

[^c0073-17]: [Col. 0815B] Another Amalhart, abbot of Hornbach, appears in Mabillon, volume IV of the *Analecta*, page 643, and in the new edition, page 426.

[^c0073-18]: [Col. 0816B] Bostonus Buriensis did not read this supplement, nor chapters 46 and 47 of Book IV, in his codex.

## Form of Institution for Canons and for Nuns Living Canonically

Published in the year of Christ 806 at the urging of Louis the Pious,[^c0073-19] at the Council of Aachen, compiled by Symphosius Amalarius, priest of Metz.

*[Mansi, Amplissima Collectio Conciliorum]*

[^c0073-19]: [Col. 0815C] At the Council of Aachen. At this council, by order of Louis the Pious, a Rule was composed in two booklets, as the preface explains: one for canons, which has often been published up to the present, and the other for nuns, which we are bringing to light for the first time. Amalarius, deacon of the church of Metz, is said to have played a principal role in this work; the books on the divine offices that he wrote to the same Louis are extant. They say that, after books were made available from the palace, he composed this entire work from the various opinions of learned authorities, and that it was approved by the judgment and authority of the council. Among others, Ademar transmits this account in his *Chronicle of Angoulême*. —Jacques Sirmond.

## Preface of the Fathers of the Council

[Col. 0815B]

[Col. 0815C] When, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, the most Christian and glorious Louis, Augustus, victorious by heavenly favor, had summoned and begun a general and holy assembly at the palace of Aachen in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 816, in the tenth indiction, and indeed in the third year of his reign, he diligently and carefully began to discuss many matters appropriate and necessary for the reform of the holy Church, out of love for him who had redeemed it with his holy and precious blood and had promised to remain with it until the consummation of the age, according to the most ardent desire for divine worship inspired in him from heaven.

Among other matters, the discussion reached the point that, with God’s consent, he consulted—or rather, by consulting admonished—that same holy and venerable assembled council about certain superiors of churches who, partly through ignorance and partly through laziness, took little account of the care of their subjects and observed hospitality less carefully than was right, asking what ought to be done. He further urged them that, since the canonical way of life had been set forth piecemeal in the sacred canons and in the sayings of the holy Fathers, they should, for the sake of the simple and those of lesser understanding, extract from those same sacred canons and sayings of the holy Fathers, by equal vote and common consent, some form of institutional rule through which the life of superiors and subjects might plainly be displayed. Thus all who are regarded as belonging to the canonical profession might proceed without stumbling [variant: *in ingressu*, “at the entrance”] along the path of their chosen way of life and might exist more devoutly, unanimously, and harmoniously in the service of Christ.

But, so that this might be accomplished by divine will, he first admonished them humbly to entreat the Lord together, asking that, moved by the importunate prayers of his servants, he might grant that his admonition be carried out according to his will, and that his grace might go before and follow it. At this admonition the sacred assembly, filled with inward joy, raised its hands toward heaven, gave thanks to the Creator of all, and blessed him—indeed, him who had appointed as procurator of his holy Church so great, so pious, and so benevolent a prince, and one so wise and devoted to all its needs.

Therefore, gladly and cheerfully receiving his most salutary admonition, which, by God’s mercy, would be of great benefit, although many, with Christ’s help, devoutly and religiously observed the canonical institution together with those subject to them, and although the same order was observed most fully in many places, nevertheless all were of one mind that, in accordance with the admonition of that prince, relying on divine assistance and aided by the considerable support of that most pious prince—namely, possessing at hand an abundance of books through his most generous liberality—they should extract this institutional rule from canonical authority and the sayings of the holy Fathers, as though gathering little flowers from various meadows, and present it for observance by canons.

Thus, what might perhaps be difficult to grasp because of the labor of those concerned, the slowness of their understanding, or the scarcity of books, when scattered here and there, might be easily found by them, briefly collected through careful diligence [Col. 0818A] in this work. Through it, as stated above, superiors might proceed along the right path, and might salutarily know how to provide their subjects with a rule of life without the obstacle of ignorance.

Accordingly, they diligently labored to collect this institutional rule. It contains in full how superiors ought to live, govern their subjects, administer ecclesiastical resources to them, bind them to the service of God, encourage those who act well toward better things, and correct the obstinate and negligent.

When, therefore, the sacred assembly had extolled with praises this institutional rule, produced before the aforesaid glorious prince, and had proclaimed with one voice that it was supported by ecclesiastical authority, worthy of praise, and most useful and beneficial to the holy Church, declaring that nothing blameworthy could be found in it by those who think soundly, thanks were proclaimed to God by that most victorious prince and by all who were present. And rightly so: for by his hidden dispensation and most gracious inspiration he had compelled the aforesaid prince to admonish that this be done, and by his mercy had helped bring it to completion.

Consequently, by the judgment of all it was decreed that all who serve the Lord in the canonical profession should, according to their ability, observe in every way this institutional rule, compiled through the watchful labor of so many ecclesiastical men and praised with worthy commendations. Thus, reading it and the teachings of the other holy Scriptures with diligent meditation, both superiors and subjects, supported by divine aid in the calling to which they were called, might walk without weariness; and, for the sake of that most pious prince, who, for the gain of souls, had stirred up this sacred and venerable council by salutary admonitions to compile and establish this rule, they might continually entreat God’s immeasurable mercy in the present and future ages.

For in another book the same sacred assembly, at the urging of the same most religious Augustus, carefully extracted a certain form of institution from the sayings of the holy Fathers, collected it briefly and suitably into one work, and judged it to be observed by women living canonically as religious. It contains what kind of abbesses ought to be placed over them, how those religious women ought to live within the enclosure of the monastery, what provisions are to be given them by their superiors, and with what teachings and instruments of virtue they ought to be adorned. Thus, having considered this form of life, humbly received it, and effectively fulfilled it with God providing assistance, they may deserve to appear before the coming Bridegroom with the lamps of good works and to enter his bridal chamber.

[Col. 0815C]

# CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0821A]

*(Isidore, Ecclesiastical Offices, Book VI, Chapter 4.)* The use of the ecclesiastical tonsure, unless I am mistaken, arose among the Nazirites. After first keeping their hair, they then shaved their heads, once their devotion had been completed after continence [variant: *diuturno*, “of long duration”], and they were ordered to place their hair in the fire of the sacrifice, clearly so that they might consecrate the perfection of their devotion to the Lord.

The practice of this example was therefore introduced by the apostles, so that those who are devoted to divine worship and consecrated to the Lord might, like Nazirites—that is, saints of God [*Dei* is missing]—be renewed by cutting their hair. This is also commanded to the prophet Ezekiel, when the Lord says: “You, son of man, take a sharp sword and draw it over your head and your beard” (Ezekiel V). This was evidently because he too served God in the ministry of sanctification, being of priestly stock.

We also read in the Acts of the Apostles that those Nazirites, Priscilla and Aquila, did this first; likewise the Apostle Paul and certain disciples of Christ, who were remarkable in this kind of observance [*cultu* is missing] (Acts XVIII).

Among clerics the tonsure is a certain sign, represented on the body but enacted in the soul: namely, that by this sign vices may be cut away in religion and that we may strip ourselves of the crimes of our flesh as of hair. Then, renewed in our minds, we may shine with fresh locks, stripping off, according to the Apostle, “the old man with his deeds” (Ephesians IV), and putting on “the new man, who is renewed in the knowledge of God” (Colossians III).

This renewal ought to take place in the mind but be displayed on the head [Col. 0821C], where the mind itself is understood to dwell [Col. 0822A].

As for the fact that, after the upper part of the head has been shaved, a circular crown is left below, I believe that the priesthood and the kingdom of the Church are represented in this. Among the ancients, a tiara was placed on the heads of priests. Made of linen [*confecta*; variant *confecto*: “made”], it was round, like half a sphere; this is signified by the shaved portion of the head [variant: *capitis*, “of the head”]. The crown, however, is the breadth of a golden circle that encircles the heads of kings.

Thus both signs are expressed on the heads of clerics, so that what is written, as the Apostle Peter teaches fully, may also be fulfilled through a certain likeness of the body: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter II).

It is asked why, as [*apud* is missing] among the ancient Nazirites, the hair is not first allowed to grow and then cut. But let those who inquire consider what difference there is between that prophetic veil and this revelation of the Gospel, about which the Apostle says: “When you turn to Christ, the veil will be taken away” (2 Corinthians III).

What the veil placed between Moses’ face and the sight of the people of Israel signified, the hair of holy men also signified in those times. For the Apostle too says that hair serves as a veil (1 Corinthians XI). Therefore, the heads of those consecrated to the Lord ought no longer to be veiled with hair, but only revealed, because what was hidden in the mystery of prophecy has now been declared in the Gospel.

# CHAPTER II

*(Isidore, ibid., Chapter 14.)* Doorkeepers [“Also from Isidore, on doorkeepers: Doorkeepers”] are those who in the Old Testament were called gatekeepers of the temple. They presided over the gates of Jerusalem and [variant: *quippe*, “indeed”], appointed in their respective turns, guarded all the inner and outer areas of the temple [words “and outer areas” are missing].

These men indeed—variant: *Iidemque inter*, “and the same men between”—discern between the holy and the wicked and admit into the Church only those who are faithful. We cannot enter the temple except through them. For they have the power both to receive the good and to reject the unworthy.

# CHAPTER III

*(Isidore, ibid., Chapter 11.)* The order of readers [“Also from Isidore, on readers: The order of readers”] derives its form and beginning from the prophets. Readers, therefore, are those who proclaim the word of God, to whom it is said: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah LVIII).

When these men are ordained, the bishop first addresses the people concerning their manner of life [Col. 0823B]. Then, before the congregation, he hands them the book of the divine writings, so that they may announce the word of God.

Whoever is advanced to this rank must be instructed in learning and books and highly adorned with knowledge of meanings and words, so that through the divisions of sentences he understands where a construction ends, where an utterance is still suspended, and where the final sentence is closed.

Thus, being prepared, he will preserve the force of delivery, advancing the minds and understanding of all toward comprehension by learning [variant: discerning] the kinds of delivery and expressing the particular emotions of the sentences: sometimes with the voice of one making a statement, sometimes of one grieving, sometimes of one rebuking, sometimes of one exhorting, or in similar ways, according to the kind of delivery proper to each sentence. It is especially in this matter that knowledge of ambiguous sentences must be applied.

For there are many passages in Scripture which, unless they are delivered in the proper manner, fall into the opposite meaning. Such is: “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect? God, who justifies?” (Romans VIII). If this is said affirmatively, without preserving its proper manner of delivery, great perversity results. It must therefore be pronounced as though it said: “Is it God who justifies?”—with the implied answer, “No.”

In such matters, therefore, intellectual knowledge is necessary, so that each statement may be delivered properly and appropriately. For this reason the reader must also know the force of accents, so that he may know on which syllable the speaker’s voice should be extended.

Very often inexperienced readers make mistakes in the accents of words, and those who appear to possess this knowledge are accustomed to mock us for our ignorance, disparaging us and swearing that we do not know at all what we are saying [Col. 0823D].

The reader’s voice, moreover, should be simple and clear, adapted to every kind of delivery, full of vigorous resonance, avoiding a rustic and uncultivated sound—not low, nor excessively high, not broken, not soft, and sounding nothing feminine; nor should it be accompanied by bodily movement, but only by an appearance of gravity.

*(Isidore, ibid., Chapter 13.)* The reader ought to attend to the ears and the heart, not the eyes, lest he make spectators rather than hearers who await something from him. It is an ancient opinion that readers paid special attention to their voice for the sake of delivery, so that they might be heard amid a tumult. Hence readers were formerly called heralds or criers.

# CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0824A]

*(Also from Isidore, on exorcists: “In the order.”)* In the order and ministry of the Church there ought to be exorcists, corresponding to the offices that had been arranged in Solomon’s temple and later distributed by Ezra.

We find that those whom Ezra mentions as temple administrators [*scilicet* is missing] are now [variant: *eos nunc*, “that they now are”] exorcists in the Church of God. Under Ezra there were temple administrators, the sons of Solomon’s servants, who had the administration of the entire temple under their care and [variant: *aut*, “or”] served the sacred offerings.

Although they belonged to the order and ministry of the temple, they were far from the office [variant: *ab officio*, “from the office”] of the altar of God, since neither psalmists, nor doorkeepers, nor sacred servants were permitted to touch the altar offerings, except the Levites alone.

What, then, was their role? The temple administrators had no other responsibility than to carry out repairs, so that whatever in the temple building [variant: *aedificatione*, “structure”] had been damaged or fallen down might be restored and improved by those same administrators from the Lord’s treasuries [variant: *aut*, “or”].

Thus the temple administrators are exorcists among the people of God. For just as a prudent and good administrator knows the amount of his master’s census and the measure of all his property, and keeps by him the original documents of the entire estate, so an exorcist gathers into his diligence the secrets of the whole kingdom of the Lord, so that he may commit to memory the mysteries of the Scriptures, from which he may exercise [manuscript addition: *scilicet*, “namely”] the gift granted to him by the Holy Spirit, according to the Apostle’s proclamation.

The Apostle mentions exorcists when he says: “Do all possess gifts of healing?” (1 Corinthians XII).

When these men are ordained, as the canon says (Council of Carthage IV, Distinction 23, “On Exorcists”), they receive from the bishop’s hand a booklet in which the exorcisms are written, receiving the power to lay hands upon the possessed, whether catechumens or baptized persons [“or baptized persons” is missing].

# CHAPTER V

*(Isidore, Etymologies, Book VII, Chapter 12.)* Acolytes [“Also from Isidore, on acolytes: Acolytes”]—Greek *acolythi*—are called in Latin *ceroferarii*, “candle-bearers,” because they carry candles when the Gospel is to be read or the sacrifice offered.

At that time they light the lamps and carry them—not to drive away darkness, since the sun is shining at that hour, but to display a sign of joy—so that under the figure of bodily light that light may be shown of which it is written in the Gospel: “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I).

# CHAPTER VI

*(On Offices, Book II, Chapter 10.)* Subdeacons [“Also from Isidore, on subdeacons: Subdeacons”], who are called *hypodiaconi* in Greek, are found in Ezra and are there called *Nethinim*, that is, “serving the Lord in humility” (1 Esdras II and VIII).

Nathaniel, who in the Gospel of John, warned by divine revelation [variant: *praestante*, “granting”], deserved to confess the Savior, belonged to their order. He also shone forth as faithful at the first indication of Christ’s divinity, when the Lord declared: “Behold, truly an Israelite in whom there is no deceit” (John I).

Finally, these men receive the offerings of the peoples in the Lord’s temple. They obey the offices of the Levites. They also carry the vessels of Christ’s body and blood to the deacons at the Lord’s altars (Council of Carthage IV, Distinction 2, “Subdeacons”).

The Fathers decreed concerning them that, since they handle the sacred mysteries [perhaps more correctly, “ministries”; H.], they should be chaste and continent with regard to wives and free from every carnal impurity, according to the command given to them by the prophet: “Be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah LII).

When these men are ordained, like priests and Levites they do not receive the imposition of hands; instead, they receive only the paten and chalice from the bishop’s hand, and from the archdeacon a vessel of water together with a hand basin and towel.

# CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0825B]

*(Isidore, ibid., Chapter 8.)* The order of deacons [“Also from Isidore, on deacons: Deacons”] took its beginning from the tribe of Levi.

For the Lord commanded Moses that, after the ordination of Aaron the priest and his sons, the tribe of Levi should in turn be ordained and consecrated to the service of divine worship in place of all the firstborn, and should serve Israel before Aaron and his sons in the tabernacle of God, keeping watch in the temple day and night.

They themselves were to carry the ark, the tabernacle, and all its vessels; they were also to establish their camps around the tabernacle, and when the tabernacle moved they were to take it down and then set it up again. They were commanded to serve in the tabernacle from the age of twenty-five years and upward. The holy Fathers established this rule also in the New Testament.

In the Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles [“of the disciples”] their beginning is read as follows:

“Then the twelve apostles summoned the multitude of the disciples and said: ‘It is not right [‘It is not pleasing’] for us to leave the word of God and serve tables. Therefore, brothers, choose from among yourselves seven men of good reputation, full of the Spirit and of wisdom, whom we may appoint for this task. But we will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.’

“And the saying pleased the whole multitude. And they immediately chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, and Timon [Timothy], and Parmenas, and Nicholas, a proselyte of Antioch. These they set before the apostles. And when they had prayed, they laid their hands upon them. And the word of God increased, and the number of believers multiplied” (Acts VI).

From that time the apostles and the successors of the apostles decreed that seven deacons should be ordained in all the churches [“should be ordained” is missing], who, set immediately near the others in a higher rank [“immediately placed above the others”], should stand around Christ’s altar like the columns of an altar—not without some mystery connected with the number seven.

These are the seven angels whom we read of in the Apocalypse singing with trumpets (Revelation VIII and X). These are the seven golden lampstands; these are the voices of the thunderclaps. In a clear voice, like that of a herald, they admonish everyone, whether in prayer, in bending the knees, in singing psalms, or in listening to readings. They also cry out that we should have ears for the Lord.

They proclaim the Gospel as well. Without them a priest has the name but not the office. For just as consecration belongs to the priesthood, so the administration of the sacrament belongs to the ministry. The priest directs prayer; the deacon directs psalmody. The priest sanctifies the offerings; the deacon distributes what has been sanctified.

Even priests themselves, because of the danger of presumption, are not permitted to take the chalice from the Lord’s table unless it has been handed to them by a deacon.

The Levites bring offerings to the altars; the Levites arrange the Lord’s table; the Levites cover the ark of the covenant. Not everyone sees the lofty mysteries that are covered by the Levites, lest those who ought not see them should see them, or those unable to preserve them should take them.

For this reason they stand at the altar dressed in white, so that they may possess a heavenly life and may approach the sacrifices white and undefiled, clean in body and incorrupt in modesty. Such ministers ought the Lord to have: men who are not corrupted by any contagion of the flesh, but rather shine with eminent chastity [variant: *eminentia castitatis*, “the eminence of chastity”].

The Apostle Paul writes most fully to Timothy what kind of deacons should be ordained. After first speaking about the election of priests, he immediately added: “Deacons likewise must be blameless” (1 Timothy III)—that is, without stain, like bishops.

They must be chaste, that is, continent from lust; not double-tongued, lest they disturb those who possess peace; not devoted to much wine, because where drunkenness is, there lust and fury rule; not pursuing shameful profit, lest they seek earthly gains from the heavenly mystery [“ministry”].

There is indeed [variant: *quoque*, “also”] a desire for shameful profit when one thinks more about present things than future ones. After this he added: “Let these first be tested, and then let them serve, being without accusation.” Like bishops, they must first be tested before ordination, to determine whether they are worthy, and only afterward minister.

# CHAPTER VIII

*(Isidore, ibid., Chapter 7.)* The order of presbyters [“Also from Isidore, on presbyters: Presbyters”] took its beginning, as has been said, from the sons of Aaron.

Those who were called priests in the Old Testament are the ones now called presbyters. Those who were then called chief priests are now called bishops. *Presbyters* means “elders,” because in Greek those advanced in age are called *presbyteroi*.

To these, as to bishops, the administration of the mysteries of God has been entrusted. They preside over the Church of Christ and share with bishops in the preparation of the divine body and blood.

Likewise they share in the instruction of the peoples [“of the apostles”] and in the office of preaching. Only because of the authority of the high priest [“and only apart from the authority of the high priest”] has the ordination and consecration of clerics been reserved, lest, if Church discipline were claimed by many, it should dissolve concord and generate scandals.

For the Apostle Paul, speaking to Titus, emphatically identifies these same presbyters as true priests under the name of bishops: “For this reason,” he says, “I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what remains to be done and appoint presbyters in the cities, as I directed you. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of dissipation or disobedient—for a bishop must be blameless” (Titus I).

By this statement he shows that presbyters too are designated under the name of bishops. Hence, when writing to Timothy about the ordination of a bishop and a deacon, he said nothing at all about presbyters, because he included them under the name of bishops (1 Timothy III).

For the second rank is joined to the first [variant: *ut veteres sub*, uncertain and apparently corrupt], just as he writes to the Philippians about bishops and deacons, although one city cannot have several bishops (Philippians I). In the Acts of the Apostles, when he was about to go to Jerusalem, he gathered the presbyters of the Church and said among other things: “Watch over the flock in which the Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops” (Acts XX).

Therefore both the Apostle’s letter to Titus and the canons themselves testify that presbyters ought to be appointed in the Church in the same manner as bishops.

Presbyters are rightly called so because of wisdom, not age [Chapter I]. For Moses too is commanded to choose presbyters. Hence it is said in Proverbs: “The glory of the old is gray hair” (Proverbs XX). What is this gray hair? There is no doubt that it is wisdom, of which it is written: “Gray hair is the prudence of human beings” (Wisdom IV).

Although we read that people lived nine hundred and more years from Adam to Abraham, no one else was first [the word *primus*, “first,” is missing in one witness] called *presbyter*, that is, “elder,” except Abraham, who is shown to have lived far fewer years.

They are therefore called presbyters not because of decrepit old age, but because of wisdom. If this is so, it is surprising that foolish men are appointed [“are being appointed”].

# CHAPTER IX
[Col. 0827C] (Isidore, same work, chapter 5.) Let us therefore now come to the most sacred orders, and let us demonstrate in particular what is the foundation of the priesthood, or by whose authority the pontifical order grew in the world. The beginning of the priesthood was indeed Aaron, although Melchizedek had previously offered sacrifice, and after him Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. But these men did so of their own spontaneous will, not by priestly authority. Aaron, however, was the first in the Law to receive the name of priest, and the first to offer victims after being clothed in the priestly robe, when the Lord commanded and spoke to Moses (Exod. XXIX): “Take Aaron,” he said, “and his sons, and bring them to the entrance of the tent of testimony. When you have washed the father and his sons with water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments, that is, the linen garment and tunic, [Col. 0827D] the ephod and the breastpiece, which you shall fasten with a belt; you shall place the tiara upon him and pour the oil of anointing over his head, and by this rite he shall be consecrated. You shall also bring forward his sons, clothe them in linen tunics, and gird Aaron and his sons with a belt; you shall place turbans upon them, and they shall be my priests by an everlasting religious ordinance.”

At this point it must be understood that Aaron was the high priest, that is, the bishop, and that his sons prefigured presbyters. For Aaron’s sons were themselves priests, and the Levites ought properly to have stood by them, just as they stood by the high priest. But the distinction between Aaron the high priest and the sons of that same Aaron, who were themselves priests, was this: Aaron wore over his tunic the long robe (*poderes*), the sacred stole, the golden crown, the tiara, the golden girdle, the ephod, and the other things mentioned above. The sons of Aaron, however, stood at God’s sacrifice wearing only linen tunics, girded and crowned with turbans.

But perhaps this too is asked: Whom did Moses prefigure? If Aaron’s sons prefigured presbyters, and Aaron the high priest, that is, the bishop, whom did Moses prefigure? Without doubt, Christ—and truly Christ in every respect—for he was a likeness of the Mediator between God and humanity, Jesus Christ, who is the true leader of peoples, the true chief of priests, and the Lord of pontiffs. To him be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0828B] Thus far concerning the beginnings of the priesthood in the Old Testament. In the New Testament, however, after Christ, the priestly order began with Peter. For to him the pontificate in Christ’s Church was first given. Thus the Lord speaks to him: “You are Peter,” he says, “and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XVI). He therefore was the first to receive the power of binding and loosing, and he was the first to bring a people to the faith by the power of his preaching.

Indeed, the other apostles also received an equal share of honor and power with Peter. They were scattered throughout the whole world and preached the Gospel; and when they departed, bishops succeeded them. These bishops have been established throughout the [Col. 0828C] world in the seats of the apostles. They are no longer chosen according to flesh and blood, as at first according to the order of Aaron, but according to each person’s merit, whatever divine grace has bestowed upon him. Thus also the Lord foretold to Eli, saying: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I said that your house and your father’s house would remain before me for ever. But now the Lord says: Far be it; rather, those who glorify me I will glorify, and whoever despises me shall be despised” (1 Sam. II).

For there are four kinds of apostles. One is from God alone, as Moses. The second is through a human being and God, as Joshua. The third is through a human being alone, as in these times many are installed in the priesthood through the favor of the people and of the authorities. The fourth kind is from oneself, as with false prophets and [Col. 0828D] false apostles.

What, then, is the meaning of the name “apostles”? In Latin, *apostoli* means “sent,” because the Lord sent them to evangelize for the enlightenment of all peoples.

“Bishop,” however, as one of the wise has said, is the name of a task, not of an honor. For it is Greek, and the term is derived from the fact that the person who is placed in charge supervises, caring for those subject to him (Augustine, *City of God*, book XIX, chapter 19). [Note: [Col. 0827D] The entire following sentence is lacking up to “the purpose is.”]

For ἐπὶ means “over,” while σκοπός means “purpose” or “oversight”; therefore we can render *episcopus* in Latin as “superintendent,” so that one may understand that a person is not a bishop if he prefers to preside rather than to benefit. That bishops are ordained by the laying on of hands of their predecessors, the priests of God, is an ancient institution. The holy patriarch Isaac, placing his hand upon Jacob’s head, blessed him (Gen. XXVII). Likewise Jacob gave his sons a blessing (Num. XXVII). Moses also, placing his hand upon Joshua’s head, gave him the spirit of courage and leadership over the people of Israel.

In the same way our Lord Jesus Christ, the fulfiller of the Law and the Prophets, blessed the apostles by the laying on of hands, as it is written in the Gospel of Luke: “And he led them out as far as Bethany; and he lifted up his hands and blessed them. And it came to pass, when he had blessed them, that he departed from them; and they returned to Jerusalem with great joy” (Luke XXIV).

And in the Acts of the Apostles, [Col. 0829B] at the command of the Holy Spirit, hands were laid upon Paul and Barnabas by the apostles [the source lacks *ab*] for the episcopate, and thus they were sent to evangelize (Acts XIII).

That a person becomes a priest at thirty years of age is taken from the age of Christ, from which age he likewise began to preach. For this age no longer needs the development of children but is full of perfection, vigorous, and prepared for every exercise of discipline and teaching.

That those chosen for the pontifical order must have been married only once was commanded also in the Old Law, and the Apostle writes more fully: “The husband of one wife” (1 Tim. III; Titus I). The Church seeks a priest either ordained from a monogamous marriage or sanctified in virginity.

[Note: [Col. 0829D] Immediately after “sanctified,” the passage beginning “Furthermore, what follows” comes next, with the intervening words omitted and preceded by the heading: “Why a bishop should be ordained by bishops of the same province.”]

For a man who has married twice is not thought fit to exercise the priesthood. Furthermore, the reason why a bishop is ordained not by one but by all the bishops of the province is that no tyrannical authority might undertake anything against the faith of the Church. Therefore he is appointed by all who assemble, and by no fewer than three who are present, while the others give their consent by written testimony.

When he is consecrated, a staff is given to him, so that by its indication he may rule and correct the people subject to him, or bear the infirmities of the weak. A ring is also given, as a sign of pontifical honor or as a seal of secrets. For priests conceal many things from the senses of carnal and less intelligent people and store them, as it were, under a seal, lest the sacraments of God be disclosed to the unworthy.

Moreover, that secular men should by no means be admitted to the ministry of the Church, the apostolic authority teaches and says: “Lay hands hastily on no one” (1 Tim. V). And again: “Not a recent convert” (ibid. III), lest, lifted up with pride, he think that he has attained not a ministry of humility but the administration of secular power, and, like the devil, be cast down into condemnation for his arrogance.

For how will a secular man be able to fulfill the teaching office of the priesthood, when he has held neither its office nor learned its discipline? Or what will he be able to teach when he himself has not learned? Yet now we often see many ordaining such men. They do not choose those who might benefit the Church, but those whom they themselves love, or by whose services they have been won over, or on whose behalf some person of rank has pleaded; and, to speak of worse things, those who have secured ordination by gifts.

I say nothing of the rest. Some make their sons or relatives successors and attempt to leave the dignity of the episcopate to their descendants, although even Moses, the friend of God, could not do this; rather, he chose Joshua from another tribe, so that we might know that leadership among the people is to be defended not by blood but by the merits of one’s life (Num. XXVII).

Sometimes, however, persons are chosen as rulers according to the merit of the peoples themselves. Let the peoples therefore know that they have deserved to receive the rule of a corrupt pontiff.

That a person who, after baptism, has been corrupted by some mortal sin should not be advanced to the priesthood is also attested by the Law itself. For Moses commanded the priests in the Law [Col. 0830B] not to offer any blemished animal upon God’s altar (Lev. I and II). God later reproached the priests of Israel who offered such things through Malachi, saying: “You priests who have profaned my name, and have said, ‘In what way have we profaned it?’ By offering polluted bread upon my altar, and you offered the blind and the lame” (Mal. I).

Therefore also in Numbers the red heifer, whose ashes are the purification of the people, is commanded to be offered to the Lord’s altar only if it has not performed earthly labor, has not drawn the yoke of wrongdoing, and has not been bound by the chains of sins (Num. XIX).

But why should we add more? If a person who has been placed in the episcopate or presbyterate and has committed some mortal sin is removed, how much more must a sinner who is found to be such before ordination be rejected, so that he is not ordained? [If he is found to be a sinner, he must not be ordained.]

Therefore, since the Law excludes sinners from the priesthood, let each person examine himself. Knowing that the powerful will suffer powerful torments [variant: “the powerful will suffer torments”], let him withdraw from this burden—which is less an honor than a load—and not seek to occupy the place of others who are worthy.

For the person who presides over the instruction and education of peoples in virtue must be holy in all things and considered blameworthy in nothing. Whoever reproves another for sins must himself be free from sin. For with what face will he be able to reprove his subjects, when the person corrected could immediately bring against him the same charge? First teach yourself what is right, O bishop. Therefore let the person who neglects to do what is right cease teaching what is right.

For the person who strives to exhort others to live well must first correct himself, so that in all things he may offer himself as a model of living and summon everyone to good works both by teaching and by action.

He also needs knowledge of the Scriptures. For if a bishop has only a holy life, such a life can benefit himself alone. But if he is also instructed in doctrine, he can teach others, instruct his own people, and repel adversaries. Unless they are refuted and convicted, adversaries can easily corrupt the hearts of the simple.

His speech must be pure, simple, and clear, full of seriousness and propriety, full of gentleness and grace. It must treat of the mystery of the Law, the teaching of faith, the virtue of continence, and the discipline of justice, admonishing each person with varied exhortation according to his profession [variant: “profession”] and the quality of his character—namely, so that he may discern what to say, to whom, when, and how.

His special duty above all others is to read the Scriptures, go through the canons, and imitate the examples of the saints; to devote himself to vigils, fasts, and prayers; to keep peace with his brothers and not tear apart any member of his own body. He must condemn no one unless the charge has been established, and excommunicate no one unless the case has been examined.

He must excel equally in humility and authority, so that neither through excessive humility does he allow the vices of his subjects to grow strong, nor through immoderate authority exercise the power of severity. Rather, he must act toward those entrusted to him with greater caution, the more fearfully he dreads being judged more harshly by Christ.

He must also possess that preeminent charity above all gifts, without which every virtue is nothing. Charity is the guardian of holiness; humility is the dwelling place of this guardian.

Amid all these things he must also possess outstanding chastity, so that the mind destined to consecrate Christ’s body may be clean and free from every defilement of the flesh.

Amid all this he must carefully administer care for the poor: feed the hungry, clothe the naked, receive travelers, redeem captives, protect widows and orphans, and display vigilant care in all things through prudent foresight and measured distribution.

In this respect hospitality must also be especially prominent, so that he receives everyone with kindness and charity. For if all the faithful desire to hear that Gospel saying, “I was a guest, and you received me” (Matt. XXV), how much more must the bishop’s lodging be a refuge for everyone? A layman who receives one or two fulfills the duty of hospitality; a bishop who does not receive everyone is inhuman.

In settling secular disputes, he must distinguish the case according to merit, not favor. A bishop must not receive a powerful person in such a way as to distress a poor person contrary to justice, nor, for the sake of a poor person, take justice away from a powerful one. He must not defend the wicked, nor suppose that holy things should be entrusted to the unworthy; nor should he accuse or attack someone whose crime he has not established.

According to the Apostle, he must also possess gentleness, patience, sobriety, moderation, abstinence, or chastity, so that he refrains not only from an unclean action but also from error of the eyes, the mouth, and thought. Thus, while he permits no vice to rule in himself, he may obtain from God forgiveness for the crimes of his subjects.

Whoever pursues these things will be both a useful minister of God and will complete a perfect priesthood.

## CHAPTER X

(Hieronymus, excerpt from the Letter to Titus.) For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might correct what was lacking (Titus I). He left his disciple Titus in Crete to strengthen the beginnings of the nascent Church and to correct anything that seemed lacking; he himself was proceeding to other nations in order once again to lay Christ’s foundation among them.

[Col. 0832A] When he says, “so that you might correct what is lacking” [variant: “what was lacking, so that you might correct it, and so everywhere”], he shows that they had not yet arrived at a full knowledge of the truth. Although they had been corrected by the apostle, they still nevertheless needed correction.

“And appoint presbyters throughout the cities, as I also directed you.” Let us carefully attend to the Apostle’s words: “So that you might appoint presbyters throughout the cities, as I also directed you.” Explaining what sort of presbyter ought to be ordained, he says in what follows: “If anyone is without blame, the husband of one wife,” and so forth. Then he adds: “For a bishop must be without blame, as God’s steward.”

Therefore the presbyter is the same as the bishop. Before rivalries and schisms arose in the religion through the devil’s instigation, and it was said among the peoples, “I am of Paul, I of Apollo, and I of Cephas,” the Churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters. But after each person began to consider those whom he had baptized his own rather than Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be chosen and placed over the others, with responsibility for the whole care of the Church, so that the seeds of schisms might be removed.

Does someone think that the view that bishop and presbyter are one and the same, with one name referring to age and the other to office, is not the judgment of Scripture but our own? Let him reread the Apostle’s words to the Philippians: “Paul and Timothy, servants of Jesus Christ, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons: grace to you and peace,” and so forth (Philipp. I).

Philippi is one city of Macedonia. Certainly, as is now supposed, there could not have been several bishops in one city. But because at that time they called the same persons bishops whom they called presbyters, he spoke indifferently of bishops, as though of presbyters.

If this still seems ambiguous to anyone, let it be confirmed by another testimony. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles that when the Apostle Paul came to Miletus, he sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters of that same church. He later spoke to them, among other things: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to shepherd the Church of the Lord, which he acquired through his blood” (Acts X).

And here observe more carefully how, after summoning the presbyters of one city, Ephesus, he afterward called these same men bishops.

Let us therefore see what kind of presbyter, or bishop, ought to be ordained: “If anyone is without blame, the husband of one wife, having faithful children, not accused of debauchery or disobedience. For a bishop must be without blame, as God’s steward. Not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not desirous of shameful gain” (1 Tim. III).

First, then, he must be without blame—one whom, I think, he calls irreproachable in other words in the letter to Timothy. He must not be without any blame only at the time when he is to be ordained, having erased former stains through a new way of life; rather, from the time when he was reborn in Christ, he must not be troubled by any consciousness of sin.

For how can the ruler of the Church remove evil from its midst if he himself has fallen into a similar offense? Or with what freedom can he rebuke a sinner when, silently, he himself answers that he has committed the same things he reproves?

First, then, it must be said that the name of the priesthood is so holy that even things placed outside us are counted against us—not that we fail to become bishops because of our own vices, but that we ought to be barred from this rank because of the incontinence of our children.

For with what freedom can we rebuke the children of others and teach what is right when the person corrected could immediately say to us, “First teach your own children”? Or with what face do I rebuke an outsider for fornication when my own conscience answers me: “Then disinherit the fornicating son; cast away your children who serve vices”?

But when a wicked son lives with you in the same house, you dare to remove the speck from another’s eye while not seeing the beam in your own? Therefore the just man is not polluted by the vices of his children, but freedom from this charge is reserved by the Apostle for the ruler of the Church, so that he may be such a man as does not fear reproving outsiders for the vices of their children.

“For a bishop must be without blame, as God’s steward.” Therefore a steward is required to be found faithful—not one who, eating and drinking with drunkards, beats the male and female servants, but one who awaits the Lord’s uncertain coming and gives his fellow servants their food at the proper time.

The only difference between a steward and his household is that a fellow servant has been placed over his fellow servants. Let the bishop and presbyter therefore know that the people are their fellow servants, not their slaves.

The other requirements that follow lie within our control. “Not arrogant,” that is, not puffed up and pleased with himself because he is a bishop, but, like a good steward, seeking what benefits the greatest number.

“Not quick-tempered.” A quick-tempered person is one who is always angry and is shaken by the slightest breath of an answer or offense as a leaf is moved by the wind. A person who becomes angry occasionally is not thereby quick-tempered; rather, the quick-tempered person is one who is frequently overcome by this passion.

He also forbids the bishop to be given to wine, lest, with his judgment clouded, he either raise laughter contrary to the dignity of truth [variant: “gravity”] and laugh aloud with loosened lips, or, if he happens to remember some sad matter while drinking, burst into sobs and tears. It would take too long to go through each of the insanities that drunkenness produces and describe them.

After drunkenness he also commands that the bishop not be violent. Understood simply, this edifies the hearer, so that he does not readily extend his hand to strike, or madly burst out to beat another’s face. But it is better to say that the violent man is one who is not gentle and patient, who does not know what ought to be said at the proper time and what ought to be kept silent, and who strikes the consciences of the weak with useless speech.

The desire for shameful gain must likewise be absent from the man who is to become a bishop. For there are many who teach [variant: “say”] what ought not to be taught for the sake of shameful profit; they overturn entire households and think that piety is a source of gain.

According to Solomon, a small possession with justice is better than many fruits with iniquity; and a good name in poverty is more to be chosen than a very bad name in riches (Prov. XVI).

A bishop who wishes to imitate the Apostle, having food and clothing, ought to be content with these alone. “Those who serve the altar should live from the altar” (1 Tim. VI). Let them live, he says, but not become rich. Therefore money is shaken out of our belt, and we wear only one tunic, so that we do not think about tomorrow.

The desire for shameful gain also consists in thinking more about present things than future ones.

Up to this point the Apostle’s words have instructed us concerning what a bishop or presbyter must not possess. Now, conversely, what he ought to possess is explained: “Hospitable, a lover of good things, chaste, just, holy, self-controlled, abstinent, holding fast to the faithful word that accords with the doctrine, so that he may be able to encourage others in sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.”

Above all, hospitality is enjoined upon the future bishop. For if everyone desires to hear that Gospel saying, “I was a guest, and you received me” (Matt. XXV), how much more must the bishop’s house be a common lodging for all? A layman who receives one or a few has fulfilled the duty of hospitality; a bishop who does not receive everyone is inhuman.

Just as gentleness, patience, sobriety, moderation, abstinence from profit, hospitality, and kindness ought especially to exist in a bishop and be eminent among all laymen, so also chastity must be his particular quality—or, so to speak, priestly purity—so that the mind destined to consecrate Christ’s body may be free not only from an unclean act but also from the casting of the eye and the error of thought.

The bishop must also be just and holy, so that he may exercise justice among the peoples over whom he presides, rendering to each what he deserves and showing no partiality in judgment. The difference between the justice of a layman and that of a bishop is this: a layman can appear just in a few matters, but a bishop must exercise justice over as many people as he has subject to him.

## CHAPTER XI

(From the same author, Letter to Oceanus.) If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work. A work, not a dignity; labor, not delights. A work by which he may decrease through humility, rather than swell with pride in high office.

Therefore a bishop must be irreproachable (1 Tim. III). The same is said to Titus: “If anyone is without blame” (Titus I). In one statement he comprehends all virtues and almost demands something contrary to nature. For if every sin, even in an idle word, deserves reproach, who is there who lives in the world without sin—that is, without reproach?

But the future shepherd of the Church is chosen as one beside whom the rest of the flock may rightly be named. Rhetoricians define an orator as “a good man skilled in speaking.” First, an irreproachable life rather than an irreproachable tongue is sought, so that a learned man may be received with good reason. For the speech of a person whose conduct destroys it loses its authority.

“The husband of one wife.” Certainly the Apostle is speaking of baptized men; let no one doubt it.

“Sober, prudent, dignified, hospitable, a teacher, chaste,” and so forth. Priests who minister in God’s temple are forbidden to drink wine and strong drink, lest their hearts be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness (Lev. X), and so that the mind, performing its service to God, may always be vigorous and clear.

When he adds “prudent,” he excludes those who excuse the foolishness of priests under the name of simplicity. For unless the brain is sound, all the members will be diseased.

“Dignified.” A person who has no vices is called irreproachable; a person who abounds in virtues is dignified. We can also understand something else from this word, in accordance with Cicero’s saying: “The chief point of art is to do what is fitting.”

For there are some who do not know their own measure and are so dull and senseless that, in movement, walking, dress, and ordinary speech, they provoke laughter in those who watch them. And, as though they understood what dignity is, they adorn themselves with clothing and bodily finery and prepare luxurious feasts for the table, although every such adornment and cultivation is fouler than filth.

That teaching is required of priests is commanded both by the precepts of the old Law and written more fully in the letter to Titus (Titus I). For an innocent life without speech benefits as much by example as it harms by silence. The madness of wolves must be driven away by the barking of dogs and the shepherd’s staff.

“Not given to wine, not violent.” He sets vices against virtues. We have learned what we ought to be; let us learn what priests ought not to be.

Drunkenness belongs to clowns and gluttons, and a belly burning with wine quickly foams over into lust. In wine there is debauchery; in debauchery, pleasure; in pleasure, impurity. Whoever lives in debauchery is dead while alive; therefore whoever becomes drunk is both dead and buried.

Noah, in a single hour of drunkenness, exposed his thighs, which he had covered through six hundred years of sobriety (Gen. IX). Lot, through intoxication, unknowingly joined incest to lust; and the wines overcame the man whom Sodom had not overcome (Gen. XIX).

The person who condemns a bishop for violence is the one who offered his back to scourging and, when cursed, did not return the curse. But he should be “modest.” He opposed one good to two evils, so that modesty might restrain drunkenness and anger.

“Not quarrelsome, not greedy.” Nothing is more shameless than the arrogance of rustics [the source is defective here], who consider their loquacity authority and, always ready for quarrels, thunder with inflated speeches over the flock subject to them.

Samuel also teaches that greed must be avoided in a priest, proving before the people that he had extorted nothing from anyone (1 Sam. XII). So too the poverty of the apostles, who received the necessities of their expenses from the brothers and boasted that, apart from food and clothing, they neither possessed nor desired anything else. What he calls greed in the letter to Timothy, he most explicitly calls the desire for shameful gain in the letter to Titus (Titus I).

“Managing his own household well.” Not so that he may increase his wealth, prepare royal banquets, arrange engraved dishes [variant: “bowls”], or cook pheasant birds over a slow fire reaching to the bones while not dissolving the surface of the flesh through artful moderation; rather, so that he may first require from his household what he is going to command the people.

“Having children who are obedient with all chastity.” This is so that they may not imitate the incontinent sons of Eli, who slept with women in the vestibule of the temple (1 Sam. II).

“Not a recent convert, lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil.” Yesterday a catechumen, today a pontiff; yesterday in the amphitheater, today in the church; in the evening in the circus, in the morning at the altar; recently a patron of actors, now a consecrator of virgins.

When he says, “lest, being lifted up with pride, he fall into the judgment of the devil,” who could fail to confirm the truth of this by example? A newly appointed priest does not know the humility and gentleness of ordinary people; he does not know Christian kindness; he does not know how to despise himself.
