He is transferred from one position of honor to another. He has not fasted, wept, frequently reproved his own conduct, or corrected it through constant meditation. He has not distributed his wealth to the poor. He is led, so to speak, from one chair to another—that is, from pride to pride.

There is no doubt that the judgment and downfall of the devil consist in arrogance. Those fall into it who, in the space of an hour, are not yet disciples but are already teachers.

“He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside.” As the beginning, so also the conclusion. A man who is irreproachable is praised with one harmonious voice not only by his household but also by outsiders. Those outside are Jews, heretics, and gentiles.

Let the pontiff of Christ therefore be such that those who disparage the religion do not dare to disparage his life.

These canons must be observed in choosing priests.

## CHAPTER XII
*(St Augustine, Book to Pastors.)*

Those who wish to hear the name of pastors but do not wish to fulfill the office of pastors—let us review what is said to them through the prophet, as we have heard it read. Listen attentively, and let us listen with trembling.

“And the word of the Lord,” Ezekiel says, “came to me, saying: Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, and say to the shepherds of Israel” (Ezekiel 34).

We have just heard this reading when it was read; and from it we have resolved to say something to your holiness. He himself will help us speak the truth, provided we do not speak our own words. For if we speak our own words, we shall be shepherds feeding ourselves, not the sheep. But if what we say belongs to him, then through whoever speaks, he himself feeds you.

“These things says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who feed themselves alone. Do shepherds feed the sheep?” That is, shepherds do not feed themselves, but the sheep. This is the first reason why these shepherds are reproved: because they feed themselves, not the sheep.

Who are those who feed themselves? Those of whom the Apostle says: “For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 2).

We, whom the Lord, according to his gracious favor and not according to our merit, has placed in this position, for which an account must be rendered, possess two things. One is that we are Christians; the other is that we are placed over you. That we are Christians is for our own sake; that we are placed over you is for your sake. In that we are Christians, our own benefit is considered; in that we are placed over you, only your benefit is considered.

There are many who, being Christians but not placed over others, reach God by a perhaps easier path, and perhaps walk all the more freely because they carry a lighter burden. But we, in addition to being Christians—which is why we shall render an account to God for our life [alternative: “for our stewardship”]—are also placed over others, which is why we shall render an account to God for our stewardship.

[Note: [Col. 0837D] The whole following period is missing.]

[Col. 0837A] I set this difficulty before you so that, sympathizing with us, you may pray for us. For a day will come when all things will be brought to judgment. Even if that day is far away from the world, the last day of his own life is near to each person. Yet God has willed that both things remain hidden: when the end of the world will come, and when the end of this life will come for each individual.

Do you wish not to fear the hidden day? When it comes, let it find you prepared.

Since those placed over others are appointed for this purpose, that they may care for those subject to them, and since they must not, merely because they preside, attend entirely to their own advantage, but to that of those whom they serve—whoever is placed over others in such a way that he rejoices in his position, seeks his own honor, and looks only to his own advantages, feeds himself, not the sheep.

This is the subject of our discourse. Listen as God’s sheep, and see how God has made you secure. Whatever those who preside over you may be—that is, whatever we may be—he who feeds the sheep of Israel has given you security. For if God does not abandon his sheep, evil shepherds will pay the penalties they deserve, and the sheep will receive what was promised.

Let us see, then, what the divine word addresses to shepherds who feed themselves, not the sheep. It flatters no one:

“Behold, you consume the milk, clothe yourselves with the wool, and slaughter what is fat, but you do not feed my sheep. You have not strengthened what was weak, nor healed what was sick; you have not bound up what was broken, nor brought back what had wandered, nor sought what had been lost; but you have broken what was strong, and my sheep have been scattered because there is no shepherd” (Ezekiel 34).

The word is addressed to shepherds who feed themselves rather than the sheep, and it tells what they love and what they neglect.

What do they love? “You consume the milk.” For this reason the Apostle also says: “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit? Who feeds a flock and does not partake of the milk of the flock?” (1 Corinthians 9).

We therefore find that the flock’s milk is whatever is distributed by the people to those placed over them for the support of their temporal sustenance.

The Apostle was speaking of this when he said what I have recalled. Indeed, although he chose to work with his own hands, and not even to seek the milk of the sheep, he nevertheless declared that he had the right to receive milk, and that the Lord had arranged that those who proclaim the gospel should live by the gospel. He says that his fellow apostles made use of this right—not a right usurped, but one granted.

He did more, so that he would not receive even what was owed him. Thus he gave up what was owed, but did not demand from others what was not owed [Alternative: “but another did not demand what was not owed”]. He did more; perhaps he signified himself when, as he brought the sick man to the innkeeper, he said: “Whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I return” (Luke 10).

What more should we say, then, about those who do not need the milk of the flock? They are more compassionate—or rather, they perform the service of compassion more generously. They can do so, and they do what they can. Let these be praised, and let the others not be condemned.

The Apostle himself did not seek what was given. Yet he wished his sheep to be fruitful, not sterile and without the abundance of milk. Thus, when at one time he was in great need, imprisoned in the confession of the truth, the brothers sent him what could serve his necessity and poverty.

He replied with thanks and said: “You did well to share in my necessities. For I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to abound, and I know how to suffer want. I can do all things through him who strengthens me. Nevertheless, you did well to send something for my needs” (Philippians 4).

But in order to show, through what they had done for him, what he himself was seeking—and to show that he was not among those who feed themselves rather than the sheep—he did not rejoice so much that his own need had been relieved as he rejoiced in their fruitfulness.

What, then, was he seeking there? “Not because I seek the gift,” he says, “but I seek the fruit.” Not so that I may be filled, he says, but so that you may not remain empty.

Those, therefore, who cannot do what Paul did—support themselves by the work of their own hands—may receive the milk of the sheep and support their own necessity, but they must not neglect the weakness of the sheep. They must not seek this as their own advantage, as though the necessity of their poverty were what made them proclaim the gospel. Rather, they must prepare the light of the word of truth for the illumination of human beings.

[Col. 0838C] For they are like lamps, as it is said: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12). And: “No one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house. Let your light so shine before people that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

If a lamp were lit for you in your house, would you not add oil so that it would not go out? But if, after receiving oil, the lamp did not give light, it was plainly not worthy to be placed on a lampstand, but deserved to be broken immediately.

Thus, from where one lives, it is necessary to receive; but to give is a matter of charity. The gospel must not be treated as merchandise, as though what those who proclaim it receive for their livelihood were its price. For if they sell it in this way, they sell a great thing for a small price.

Let them receive from the people the support of necessity, but from the Lord the reward of their stewardship. The people are not capable of repaying those who serve them in the charity of the gospel. Let them not expect a reward except from the place from which the people receive salvation.

What, then, is reproved in these men, and for what are they accused? Because, while they consumed the milk and clothed themselves with the wool, they neglected the sheep. They sought only their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.

Since we have said what it means to consume milk, let us ask what it means to clothe oneself with wool. One who supplies milk supplies drink; one who supplies wool supplies honor. These are the two things sought by shepherds who feed themselves rather than the sheep: the advantage of satisfying their necessities, and the favor of honor and praise.

A garment is rightly understood as honor because it covers nakedness. Every human being is weak. And what is anyone who presides over you except what you are? He bears flesh, is mortal, eats, sleeps, rises, has been born, and will die. If you consider what he is in himself, he is a human being. Yet by honoring him as though he were an angel, you cover what is weak [alternative reading: “and yet, by honoring him more highly, you as it were cover it”].

See what sort of garment the same Paul received from the good people of God when he said: “You received me as an angel of God.” For I bear you witness that, if possible, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me (Galatians 4).

But when such great honor had been shown him, did he, because of the honor shown him—or lest it be withdrawn, and because he was reproving them he should be praised less—spare those who were in error? If he had done so, he would have been among those who feed themselves rather than the sheep.

He would have said to himself: “What does it concern me? Let each person do what he wishes. My sustenance is safe, my honor is safe; milk and wool are enough for me. Let each person go as he can.”

[Note: The entire following period is missing until “I do not want you.”]

Are all things therefore intact for you if each person goes as he can? I do not wish to make you a leader; I place you as one among that very people. If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it.

Accordingly, the Apostle himself, when he recalled to them what they had been toward him, lest he seem to have forgotten their honor, testified that they had received him as an angel of God, and that, if possible, they would have plucked out their own eyes and given them to him.

Yet he approaches the sick sheep, the putrid sheep, to cut the wound and not spare the rot. “Therefore,” he says, “have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?”

Behold: he received the milk of the sheep, as we recalled shortly before; he was clothed with the wool of the sheep. Yet he did not neglect the sheep. For he did not seek his own interests, but those of Jesus Christ.

Far be it from us, then, to say to you: “Live as you wish; be secure; God will destroy no one. Only hold fast to the Christian faith: he will not destroy what he redeemed; he will not destroy those for whom he shed his blood. And if you wish to amuse yourselves with spectacles, go—what harm is there? And these festivals, which are celebrated throughout the city with the joy of those feasting and delighting themselves at public tables—as they think, though in reality they are destroying themselves—go and celebrate them without fear. Great is God’s mercy, which forgives everything. Crown yourselves with roses before they wither. In the house of your God, feast whenever you wish; fill yourselves with food and wine with your companions. For this creation was given so that you might enjoy it. God did not give it to pagans and impious people while withholding it from you.”

If we said these things, perhaps we would gather larger crowds. And even if some people, hearing us say such things, thought that we were not sound in judgment, we would offend a few but win over the multitude.

But if we did this—speaking not the words of God, not the words of Christ, but our own—we would be shepherds feeding ourselves, not the sheep.

After saying what these shepherds love, he also says what they neglect. The faults of the sheep are plainly evident. Very few sheep are healthy and fat—that is, firm in the food of truth and making use of pastures supplied by God’s gift.

But those evil shepherds do not spare such sheep. It is not enough that they do not care for the weak, sick, wandering, and lost; they also kill, insofar as it lies with them, the strong and fat. And if such sheep live, they live by God’s mercy. Yet as far as the evil shepherds are concerned, they kill them.

“How do they kill them?” By living badly and providing a bad example. Was it said without reason to the servant of God who was eminent among the members of the chief Shepherd: “In all things show yourself an example of good works,” and “be an example to the faithful” (Titus 2)?

For even a strong sheep often observes its leader living badly, if it turns its eyes away from the Lord’s commandments. It looks to the human being and begins to say in its heart: “If my leader lives this way, who am I that I should not do what he does?” He kills the strong sheep.

If, then, he kills the strong sheep, what will he do with the others—the man who, by living badly, has killed what he himself had not made fruitful, but had found perhaps strong and robust?

I say to your charity, and I say again: Even if the sheep live, even if the sheep are strong in the word of the Lord and hold fast to what they have heard from their Lord—“Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23)—nevertheless, whoever lives badly in the sight of the people over whom he is placed, insofar as it lies with him, kills the one who looks to him.

Let him not flatter himself because that person has not died. The other lives, and this one is a murderer.

When a lustful man looks at a woman in order to desire her, the woman is chaste, yet he has committed adultery. For the Lord’s true and explicit judgment is: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5). He has not entered her chamber, but already rolls about in the inner chamber of his own heart.

So everyone who lives badly in the sight of those over whom he is placed, insofar as it lies with him, kills even the strong sheep. The one who imitates the evil leader dies; the one who does not imitate him lives. Yet as far as the leader is concerned, he kills them both.

“And what is fat,” he says, “you have slaughtered, and you have not fed my sheep.”

You have now heard what they love; see what they neglect. “What was weak you did not strengthen; what was sick you did not heal; what was broken and shattered you did not bind up; what wandered you did not bring back; what perished you did not seek; what was strong you broke, killed, and slaughtered.”

[Note: In Sirmond’s edition: “A sheep is weakened—that is, it has a weak heart—so that it can yield to temptations coming upon the unwary and unprepared. When the negligent shepherd believes that such a person is weak, he does not say to him, etc.” Hardouin. The reading of the Vatican manuscript agrees with Sirmond’s reading.]

A sheep has a weak spirit when it does not believe that the temptations coming upon it will be beneficial. When a negligent shepherd finds such a weak person, he does not say to him: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

The one who says these things strengthens the weak and makes the weak strong, so that, once he has become a believer, he will not expect the prosperity of this world. For if he is taught to hope for the prosperity of this world, that very prosperity corrupts him; when adversities come upon him, he is wounded, or perhaps extinguished.

He therefore does not build that person upon a rock when he builds in this way, but places it upon sand [alternative reading: “places the foundation upon sand”]. “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10). The sufferings of Christ must be imitated, not pleasures sought by Christians.

The weak person is strengthened when he is told: “Hope.” The temptations of this world are indeed approaching, but the Lord will deliver you from them all, provided your heart does not turn back from him. For he came to strengthen your heart; he came to suffer, he came to die, he came to be smeared with spittle, he came to be crowned with thorns, he came to hear insults, and finally he came to be fastened to the wood. He did all these things for you; you have done nothing for him, but for yourself.

What sort of people are those who, fearing to offend the persons to whom they speak, not only do not prepare them for the temptations that are approaching, but even promise them the happiness of this world—a happiness which God did not promise to the world itself? He foretells labor upon labor coming upon the world until the end, and you wish the Christian to be exempt from those very labors?

Because he is a Christian, he will suffer something more in this world. For the Apostle says: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3).

Now, if you like a shepherd who seeks his own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, let him say: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution”; and you say: “If you live piously in Christ, all good things will abound for you; and if you have no children, you will receive and raise them all, and no one will die among you.”

Is this your edification? Pay attention to what you are doing and where you are placing it. What you are constructing stands upon sand. Rain will come, the river will rise, the wind will blow, and they will strike that house; it will fall, and its fall will be great.

Take it from the sand and place it upon the rock. Let the person whom you wish to be a Christian be in Christ. Let him attend to Christ’s undeserved sufferings; let him attend to the one who, without any sin of his own, paid what he had not taken. Let him attend to the Scripture that says to him: “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Hebrews 12), and prepare himself to be scourged—or certainly let him not seek to be received.

“He scourges every son,” it says, “whom he receives,” and you say: “Perhaps you will be exempt?”

If you are exempt from the scourging of suffering, you are exempt from the number of sons.

“Does he really scourge every son?” you ask.

Certainly he scourges every son, even the only-begotten. The Only-Begotten, born from the substance of the Father, equal to the Father in the form of God, the Word through whom all things were made, had nothing in himself that could be scourged. For this reason he clothed himself in flesh, so that he would not be without scourging.

If, then, he who scourges the sinless Only-Begotten leaves the adopted son with sin [alternative: “leaves the adopted sinner”], what does that mean?

The Apostle says that we have been called to adoption: “We have received the adoption of sons, so that we might be co-heirs with the Only-Begotten and might also be his inheritance” (Galatians 4). “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2). He set before us an example in his sufferings.

But plainly, so that the weak person may not fail in future temptations, he must be neither deceived by false hope nor broken by fear.

You say to him: “Prepare your soul for temptation,” and perhaps he begins to slip, tremble, and refuse to approach. You have another saying as well: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (1 Corinthians 10).

To promise that sufferings will come, and to foretell them, is to strengthen the weak. But when someone is excessively afraid and is terrified by this, to promise him God’s mercy—not because temptations will be absent, but because God does not permit him to be tempted beyond what he can bear—is to enable him to gather fruit.

It follows: “What was weakened,” he says, “you did not strengthen.”

He says this to evil shepherds, false shepherds, shepherds seeking their own interests and not those of Jesus Christ, rejoicing in the advantage of milk and wool, and caring nothing at all for the sheep.

“And what was sick you did not strengthen.”

It seems to me that there is this difference between the weak—that is, the one who is not firm—and the sick—that is, the one who is unwell. Indeed, among these distinctions that we are attempting, however inadequately, to make, perhaps we too could distinguish them better with greater diligence, or someone else who is more experienced or more filled with the light of the heart could do so.

For the present, so that you are not deceived, I speak what I understand.

The weak person fears that temptation may come and break him. But the sick person is already ill with some desire; some desire already prevents him from entering the way of God and taking up Christ’s yoke.

Those who appear fervent in good works but are unwilling—or unable—to endure the sufferings that threaten are weak. But those who, as lovers of the world, are recalled from good works by some evil desire lie languid and sick. In their very sickness, as though weighed down [alternative word order: *gravati tanquam*] and without any strength, they are unable to perform anything good.

It follows: “What wandered you did not bring back, and what perished you did not seek [alternative reading: *requisistis*, ‘sought again’]” (Ezekiel 34).

Here, amid the hands of robbers and the teeth of raging wolves, we are struggling as best we can. The sheep are obstinate because the wandering are sought. In their error and destruction they declare themselves strangers to us:

“What do you want with us?” they say. “Why do you seek us? If I am in error, what do you want with me? If I am perishing, why do you seek me?”

Because you are in error, I want to bring you back; because you have perished, I want to find you.

“I want to wander in this way; I want to perish in this way.”

Do you want to wander in this way? Do you want to perish in this way? How much better that I do not want it!

I dare to say plainly: I am troublesome. I hear the Apostle saying: “Proclaim the word; insist in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4).

In season for whom? Out of season for whom? In season, certainly, for those who want it; out of season for those who do not want it.

I dare to say plainly: I am troublesome.

You want to wander; you want to perish. I do not want it. I will bring back the wanderer; I will seek the lost. Whether you want it or not, I will do this. Even if the thorns of the woods tear me as I seek you [alternative: “the thorns of syllables”], I will force my way through every narrow place. I will search every hedge, as far as the Lord, who terrifies me, grants me strength. I will traverse everything; I will bring back the wanderer; I will seek the one who is perishing.

If you do not want to endure me, do not wander; do not perish.

It is not enough that I grieve over your wandering and destruction. I fear that, by neglecting you, I may also kill the one who is strong.

For see what follows: “And what was strong you have broken.”

If I neglect the one who wanders and perishes, the strong person will take pleasure in wandering and perishing. I desire outward gains, but I fear inward losses even more.

If I treat your error with indifference, the strong person observes that I do not seek you when you are lost, and thinks that it makes no difference to fall into error [heresy].

It is not without reason, therefore, that after he had said above, “You have slaughtered what is fat,” he again placed at the end: “And what was strong you have broken.”

Hear, then, what follows concerning the negligence of these evil—or rather, false—shepherds:

“My sheep have been scattered because there is no shepherd, and they have become food for every beast of the field.”

Wolves lying in wait steal them; roaring lions seize them when the sheep cling to the shepherd. For the shepherd is present, but he is not a shepherd to those who act badly. They cling to shepherds who are not shepherds—those who feed themselves, that is, and not the sheep—and a deadly error [alternative: “such terror”] follows.

They go to beasts that prey upon them and desire to satisfy themselves with the sheep’s death. For all who rejoice in the errors of others are like this.

“My sheep have been scattered and have wandered over every mountain and every high hill”—that is, into every swelling of earthly pride. For mountain and hill are understood as earthly swelling and worldly pride.

There are also good mountains, of which the Prophet says: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to me” (Psalm 121).

“Over every mountain and every hill, and over every face of the earth they shine; and over every face of the earth they have been scattered,” pursuing everything earthly. They love [alternative: “buy”] the things that shine upon the face of the earth; they cherish them.

They do not wish to die, so that their life may be hidden with Christ.

Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord:

“As I live, says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will seek my sheep, and I will visit them as a shepherd visits his flock.”

The evil shepherds did not care for them, for they did not redeem them with their own blood.

“As a shepherd visits his flock,” he says, “on the day”—on what day? When there is rain and cloud, that is, in rain and mist.

Rain and mist are the error of this present world, a great darkness rising from human desires, and a dense cloud crushing [perhaps: covering] the earth.

It is difficult for the sheep not to wander in this mist. But the shepherd does not abandon them. He seeks them; he penetrates the mist with strong and exceedingly sharp eyes [“with strong and …” is missing in the source], and the darkness of the clouds does not hinder him.

He sees everywhere; he brings back the wanderer, provided that what is said in the Gospel comes to pass: “My sheep hear my voice, and they follow me” (John 10).

“In the midst of the scattered sheep, so I will seek my sheep and bring them back from every place where they have been scattered” [the word “there” is missing].

“On the day of cloud and rain”—when it is difficult to find them—“then I will find them.” The mist is thick; the rain-cloud is heavy; nothing escapes his eyes.

“I will bring them out from the nations, gather them from the regions, bring them into their own land, and feed them upon the mountains of Israel.”

He has established the authors of the divine Scriptures upon the mountains of Israel. Feed there, so that you may feed securely.

[Note: The entire following period is missing until “whatever is outside.”]

Whatever you hear from there, let it taste good to you; whatever is outside, reject. Do not wander in the mist. Hear the shepherd’s voice; gather yourselves to the mountains of Holy Scripture.

There are the delights of your heart. There is nothing poisonous, nothing foreign. The pastures are exceedingly rich. You need only come healthy; feed yourselves healthy upon the mountains of Israel, in the streams, and in every habitation of the land.

From the mountains we have pointed out, streams of evangelical preaching flowed, when their sound went out into all the earth. Every habitation of the earth became joyful and fruitful for feeding the sheep.

“I will feed them in good pastures and upon the high mountains of Israel. Their folds will be there”—that is, places where they may rest, where they may say: “It is good; it is true; it is clear; we are not deceived.”

They will rest in the glory of God, as though in those folds, and sleep—that is, rest—in their good delights [alternative: “they will rest and rest in their delights, etc.”]. They will feed in rich pastures upon the mountains of Israel.

It follows—for he repeats what he first cared for:

“These things says the Lord God: I will seek what was lost; I will bring back what wandered; I will bind up what was weakened; I will strengthen what was exhausted; and I will guard what is fat and strong.”

These were things the evil shepherds did not do, feeding themselves rather than the sheep.

The Lord does not say: “I will appoint other good shepherds to do these things.” Instead he says: “I will do them. I will entrust my sheep to no one.”

Be secure, brothers; be secure, sheep. It seems to us that we must fear as though the good shepherd were absent. But he adds:

“And I will feed them with judgment.”

See that he alone feeds them, and feeds them with judgment. For what human being judges another human being with certainty? Everything is full of rash judgments. The one of whom we despaired suddenly changes and becomes excellent; the one in whom we placed confidence suddenly fails and becomes utterly bad.

Therefore neither our fear is certain, nor our love certain. [A middle portion is missing in the source.] What each person is today, scarcely does that person himself know; what he will be tomorrow, not even he knows.

He therefore feeds with judgment, distributing what is proper to those for whom it is proper. He knows what he is doing. He feeds with judgment those whom he redeemed and will judge.

It follows.

Far be it from us that good shepherds should now be lacking. Far be it from us that they should be lacking. Far be it from his mercy that he should not bring them forth and appoint them.

Certainly, if there are good sheep, there are also good shepherds. For good shepherds are made from good sheep. But all good shepherds are one in the One; they are one.

Let them feed; Christ feeds. Let them all be in the one Shepherd and speak the one voice of the Shepherd, so that the sheep may hear and follow their Shepherd—not this one or that one, but the one Shepherd.

And let all of them speak one voice in him; let them not have different voices.

## Chapter XIII
*(Gregory, Pastoral Care, Part I, in the preface.)* [Note: [Col. 0843D] Here the chapters begin to be numbered in the Vatican manuscript, [Col. 0844D] and correspond to those in the printed editions. Here, however, the following title is prefixed: “Gregory, on pastors of souls, and what sort of men ought to be chosen in the Church.” “When necessity requires,” etc.]

When necessity requires it, one must carefully consider how each person comes to the summit of governance; then, once he has properly attained it, how he lives; and, living well, how he teaches; and, teaching correctly, with how much reflection he recognizes his own weakness each day. This is necessary lest humility shrink from approaching, lest one’s life contradict one’s attainment, lest life leave doctrine unsupported, or presumption exalt doctrine.

Therefore, fear must first restrain ambition; afterward, the ministry—which is not assumed by one who seeks it—must be commended by his life. Then it is necessary that the good of the shepherd, displayed in living, be extended through speech. Finally, every perfected work must be humbled by consideration of one’s own weakness, lest the swelling of pride extinguish it before the eyes of the hidden Judge.

Isaiah also says: “Cry out; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58). Whoever approaches the priesthood assumes the office of a herald, so that before the coming of the Judge, who follows in terror, he himself may go forward crying out.

*(Gregory, Pastoral Care, Part II, chapter 11.)*

If a priest is ignorant of preaching, what voice of proclamation will a mute herald be able to utter? Strong and persevering teachers should be sought like incorruptible wood: they must always cling to instruction from the sacred books, proclaim the unity of the holy Church, and, like poles inserted into rings, carry the ark of the Lord.

To carry the ark of the covenant on poles means that good teachers lead the holy Church by preaching to the unformed minds of unbelievers. They are commanded also to be covered with gold, so that, while their speech rings out to others, they themselves may shine with the splendor of their life.

It is therefore necessary that those who keep watch over the office of preaching [Col. 0845C] not withdraw from the study of sacred reading. For this reason the poles are always commanded to remain in the rings of the ark: so that, whenever necessity demands that the ark be carried, no delay may arise from inserting the poles for carrying it. For when something spiritual is sought from those under his care, it is exceedingly disgraceful if the shepherd then seeks to learn what he ought to explain.

Let the poles of the ark of the covenant remain in its rings, so that teachers, always meditating on the sacred words in their hearts, may lift the ark of the covenant without delay, whenever they must immediately teach what is necessary. Hence the first shepherd of the Church rightly admonishes other shepherds, saying: “Always be ready to give an answer concerning the hope that is in us” (1 Peter 3). It is as though he openly said: “Let no delay hinder the carrying of the ark; let the poles never leave the rings.”

*(Gregory, Moralia I.21, chapter 10.)*

When holy men preside, they should attend not to the power of their rank within themselves, but to the equality of their condition; they should not rejoice in ruling human beings, but in benefiting them. For they should know that our ancient fathers are remembered not so much as kings of human beings as shepherds of cattle.

When the Lord said to Noah and his sons after the flood, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” it follows: “And let your terror and dread be upon all the animals of the earth” (Genesis 9). Human beings have been placed above irrational animals by nature, but not above other human beings. Therefore it is said that they should be feared by animals, not by human beings, because it is contrary to nature to become proud and wish to be feared by one’s equal.

*(Gregory, Pastoral Care, Part II, chapter 16.)*

All who preside ought to weigh not the power of their rank within themselves, but the equality of their condition. For, as we have already said, our ancient fathers are remembered as shepherds of cattle, not as kings of human beings.

It is necessary, therefore, that rulers be feared by their subjects when they discover that those subjects do not fear God at all, so that at least through human fear they may fear to sin who do not fear divine judgments. Superiors should by no means become proud of the fear of their subjects, since in this they seek not their own glory but the justice of those under them.

When they demand fear from those who live perversely, they rule them as though they were not human beings but animals. For in whatever respect the subjects are beastlike, in that respect they ought also to lie subjected to fear.

[Col. 0846B] These are the faces of the holy Church: those placed in positions of governance appear foremost, so that from their appearance there may be honor for the faithful people, even if something deformed is hidden in the body. These leaders, set over the peoples, mourn the faults of the weak and are so afflicted by the lapses of others as though by their own.

Often good rulers, when they see some people return to pardon after their sins, while others persist in wickedness, marvel at the hidden judgments of almighty God, but cannot penetrate them.

*(Pastoral Care, Book I, chapter 10.)*

For they are astonished at what they do not understand. The one who is to be drawn in every way toward an example of living must be someone who, dying to all the passions of the flesh, already lives spiritually; who has set aside the world’s prosperity; who fears no adversity; who desires only eternal things [who desires inward things]; whose intention is rightly suited to this, since his body does not wholly resist through weakness [“the body” is missing], nor does the spirit resist excessively through stubbornness [“the body”].

He likewise ought to be advanced to the dignity of pastoral office who is not led to seize what belongs to others, but gives away what is his; who is quickly moved by the compassion of mercy to forgive, yet, in forgiving no more than is fitting, is not bent away from the stronghold of righteousness; who commits no unlawful acts, but mourns those committed by others as though they were his own; who from the affection of his heart sympathizes with another’s weakness and rejoices in the good of his neighbor as in his own advancement.

He rightly attains the dignity of pontifical excellence who so presents himself as worthy of imitation by others in everything he does that among them his mind has nothing for which to blush, at least concerning the past [“the mind” is missing]; who strives to live so that he can irrigate the parched hearts of his neighbors with the streams of doctrine; who through the practice of prayer has already learned by experience that he can obtain from the Lord whatever he asks; to whom the prophetic voice has already said, in a special way [“to whom, at the fulfillment of his word, it is now said in a special way,” etc.]: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Here I am’” (Isaiah 58).

If someone should come to us and ask us to intercede for him with some powerful man who is angry with him but unknown to us, we immediately reply: “We cannot come to intercede, because we have no acquaintance with him through familiarity.” If, then, a human being is ashamed to become an intercessor with another human being whom he scarcely knows, with what state of mind does one who does not know himself to be familiar with the Lord’s grace through the merit of his life undertake a place of intercession before the Lord for the people?

Or how does he ask him for pardon on behalf of others when he does not know whether that Lord is favorably disposed toward him? In this matter, something else must be feared even more anxiously: lest the one believed capable of placating anger should himself, because of his own guilt, deserve to provoke it.

We all know plainly that when someone who is displeasing is sent to intercede, the mind of the angry person is provoked to worse things. Let anyone who is still bound by earthly desires beware lest, while more gravely kindling the anger of the strict Judge, he become an author of ruin to those under him because he delights in the position of glory.

Therefore let each person carefully measure himself, lest he dare assume a position of governance while some vice still reigns damnably within him; lest one whom his own crime corrupts desire to become an intercessor for the sins of others.

# CHAPTER XIV

*(Gregory, introduction to the Pastoral Care.)* [Gregory: “So that the unworthy and inexperienced may not presume to approach pastoral leadership. There are many,” etc.]

There are many shepherds who, because they do not know how to measure themselves, desire to teach what they have not learned. They judge the burden of teaching to be so much lighter because they are ignorant of its magnitude. Since, being unlearned and rash, they seek to hold the citadel of doctrine, they should be driven back from the ventures of their rashness at the very gate of speech.

No art is presumed fit to be taught unless it is first learned through attentive meditation. With what presumption, then, is pastoral leadership undertaken by the inexperienced, when the governance of souls is the art of arts?

Who does not know that the wounds of thoughts are more hidden than wounds of the flesh? Yet often those who have never learned spiritual precepts do not fear to claim that they are physicians of the heart, while those who do not know the power of medicines would be ashamed to appear physicians of the flesh.

There are some who, within the holy Church, seek the glory of honor under the appearance of governance. They desire to appear teachers; they long to surpass others. Truth bears witness to this: “They seek the first couches at banquets and the first chairs in assemblies” (Matthew 23). Such people are less able to administer worthily the office of pastoral care they have undertaken precisely because they reached the teaching office through pride alone.

For the tongue itself is confounded in teaching when one thing is learned and another taught. Against unworthy shepherds the Lord speaks in protest through the prophet: “They have reigned, but not through me; they have become princes, and I did not acknowledge them” (Hosea 8). They reign from themselves, and not by the will of the supreme ruler, who, supported by no virtues and not divinely called, but inflamed by his own desire, seizes the summit of governance rather than attaining it.

The inner Judge both raises up useless priests and does not acknowledge them: those whom he tolerates by permitting them, he certainly does not know through the judgment of rejection. Hence he says to some who come to him even after performing miracles: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know who you are” (Luke 13).

The ignorance of shepherds is rebuked by the voice of Truth when it is said through the prophet: “The shepherds themselves have no understanding” (Isaiah 56). Again the Lord detests them, saying: “Those who hold the law did not know me” (Jeremiah 2).

Truth therefore complains that it is not known by them, and declares that it does not recognize the authority of those who do not know it. For those who do not know what belongs to the Lord are not known by the Lord, as Paul bears witness when he says: “If anyone is ignorant, he will be ignored” (1 Corinthians 14).

Often the ignorance of shepherds corresponds to the merits of those under them. Although they may lack the light of knowledge because their own fault demands it, strict judgment nevertheless brings it about that, through their ignorance, even those who follow them stumble.

For this reason Truth itself says in the Gospel: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into the pit” (Matthew 15). Hence the Psalmist, not with the spirit of one wishing it but with the mystery of prophecy, declares: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and bend their backs continually” (Psalm 78). The eyes are those who, placed at the very summit of honor, have undertaken the office of looking after the way. Those who cling to them afterward are called their backs.

When the eyes are darkened, the back is bent: when those who lead lose the light of knowledge, those who follow are bent down to bear the burdens of sins. They would flee the weight of so great a guilt if they listened attentively in their hearts to the sentence of Truth, which says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (Matthew 18).

Let no one who is unequal to these sacred offices dare to profane them and, through desire for the summit, assume leadership of perdition. Hence James piously forbids this, saying: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers” (James 3).

Hence the Mediator of God and human beings himself avoided receiving an earthly kingdom, though he reigns in heaven before the ages, surpassing even the knowledge and understanding of the heavenly spirits.

Often the heart is pressed under the discipline of adversity; but if it breaks through to the summit of governance, it is immediately transformed into pride through the exercise of glory. Thus Saul, who had earlier considered himself unworthy and had fled, swelled up as soon as he took up the reins of the kingdom. Desiring to be honored before the people, and refusing to be publicly rebuked, he nevertheless cut himself off from the very one who had anointed him king.

The prophet David, pleasing his Maker’s judgment in nearly all his actions, as soon as he was free from the weight of affliction, burst into the swelling of a wound. In the death of Uriah he became cruelly harsh, though in his desire for the woman he had been weakly yielding. He who had previously known how piously to spare the wicked afterward learned, even in the death of the good, to rush forward without restraint.

At first he refused to strike a discovered persecutor; afterward, at the cost of a suffering army, he killed even a devoted soldier. Guilt would have dragged him farther from the number of the elect if scourges had not called him back to pardon.

*(Gregory, Pastoral Care, chapter 9.)*

Often those who desire to undertake pastoral teaching also propose certain good works to themselves. Although they seek it with an intention of pride, they nevertheless contemplate that they will perform great deeds. Thus it happens that one thing is suppressed—or [“creeps in”]—in the depths of the intention, while the surface of thought displays another to the mind of the person considering it.

For the mind often lies to itself about itself: it pretends to love a good work that it does not love and not to love the glory of the world that it does love. Often the mind that desires to rule is timid when it seeks power, but bold when it has attained it. While striving toward it, it trembles lest it fail to arrive; but once it suddenly arrives, it thinks that what it has attained is rightfully owed to it.

When it has begun to enjoy the office of leadership in a worldly manner, it gladly forgets everything it had religiously considered. For whenever thought is drawn beyond ordinary practice, each person must immediately recall the mind to its past works and weigh what he did while subject. Then he suddenly recognizes whether, as a superior, he can do the good he had proposed, since one cannot learn humility at the summit if, while in a lowly position, one has not ceased to be proud.

One who learned to pant after praise when it was lacking does not know how to flee it when it is available. He cannot overcome greed when he reaches out to support many, if what he possessed was not sufficient even for himself alone. Therefore each person should examine himself by his past life, lest an image of thought deceive him in his desire for the summit.

Often, in the occupation of governance, even the practice of good works that had been maintained in tranquility is lost. For on a calm sea even an inexperienced sailor guides a ship correctly, but when it is disturbed by the waves of storms, even an experienced sailor becomes confused.

What is the power of the summit except a storm of the mind? In it, while the ship of the heart is continually shaken by the tempests of thought, it is driven ceaselessly here and there, so that through sudden excesses of speech and action it is shattered as though against opposing rocks.

Among all that we have brought forward, what must be followed and held fast except this: let the person strong in virtues come to governance when compelled; let the person empty of virtues not approach even when compelled.

If he altogether resists, let him beware lest, tying up the money he received in a cloth, he be judged for concealing it. [Note: [Col. 0849D] A section is missing here up to the words “the money.”] To tie money in a cloth means to hide the gifts one has received in the idleness of sluggish torpor.

On the other hand, when this person desires governance, let him beware lest, by the example of wicked conduct, he become an obstacle—after the manner of the Pharisees—to those striving to enter the kingdom. According to the Teacher’s words, they themselves do not enter, nor do they permit others to enter (Matthew 23).

It must also be considered that when an elected bishop undertakes the cause of the people, he approaches like a physician approaching a sick person. If passions still live in his conduct, with what presumption does he hurry to heal the wounded when he bears the wound on his own face?

# CHAPTER XV

*(Isidore, Sentences, Book III, chapter 34.)* [Isidore, “On worthy superiors: They must not be,” etc.]

Those who are still subject to vices must not be promoted to governance of the Church. For this reason David was commanded not to build the visible temple, because he was a man of war and had shed much blood. By this figure those who are still devoted to the corruption of vices are spiritually admonished not to build the temple—that is, not to presume to teach the Church.

He ought not to assume the honor of leadership who does not know how to go before his subjects along the path of a better life. No one is placed in authority so that he may correct the faults of those under him while himself serving vices.

Whoever considers himself unworthy of the episcopate should not presume to occupy the place of one who is worthy [“to occupy” is missing]. For the name of priesthood is so holy that it does not permit itself to be stained by any mark of vice. He who unworthily assumes what he does not deserve will be condemned more severely.

Whoever strives to desire the priestly office should first examine himself to see whether his life corresponds to the honor. If it does not differ from it, let him approach humbly the position to which he is called. One doubles the guilt of his sin if, while guilty, he aspires to the priestly summit.

The fall of each person is a greater crime in proportion as he possessed greater virtue before falling. The greatness of preceding virtues increases the accumulation of subsequent offenses.

Many priests desire to preside more for their own advantage than for that of the flock. They do not wish to become superiors in order to benefit others, but rather in order to become rich and be honored. They assume the summit of high office not for pastoral governance but solely from ambition for governance or honor [“governance or” is missing]; having rejected the work of dignity, they desire only the dignity of the name.

Although evil priests do not become priests without God’s knowledge, they are nevertheless unknown to God, as he himself testifies through the prophet: “They became princes, but I did not know them” (Hosea 8). But this “not knowing” by God means rejecting, for God knows all things.

# CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0850C] *(Isidore, same work, chapter 35.)* [Isidore, “On unlearned superiors: Just as the wicked,” etc.]

Just as the wicked and sinners are prohibited from attaining the priestly ministry, so the unlearned and inexperienced are restrained from such an office. The former corrupt the lives of the good by their examples; the latter, through their negligence, do not know how to correct the wicked.

For what will those be able to teach which they themselves have not learned? Let the person who does not know how to teach cease to assume the place of a leader. The ignorance of superiors does not suit the life of those under them. For if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit (Matthew 15).

Through the prophet Isaiah the Lord condemns unlearned priests in this way: “The shepherds themselves,” he says, “have no understanding” (Isaiah 56). And again: “All his watchmen are blind”—that is, unlearned bishops. “They all,” he says, “are mute dogs, unable to bark”; that is, unable to defend the peoples entrusted to them against evil by resisting through the word of doctrine.

# CHAPTER XVII

*(Gregory, Pastoral Care, Book I, chapter 5.)* [Gregory, “On those who can benefit others in governance but refuse the same office for the sake of their own quiet: There are some,” etc.]

There are some who receive an abundance of virtues and are exalted with great gifts for the exercise of others. They are pure through devotion to chastity, strong through the power of abstinence, filled with the nourishment of doctrine, humble through long endurance in patience, upright through the strength of authority, and strict [“strict” is missing].

If, when called, they refuse to accept the summit of governance, they often deprive themselves of the very gifts they received not only for themselves but also for others. When they think only of their own gains and not those of others, they deprive themselves of the goods they desire to possess privately.

Hence Truth says to the disciples: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; nor do they light a lamp and put it under a measure, but upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house” (Matthew 5).

Hence the Lord says to Peter: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” (John 21). When he immediately replied that he did love him, he heard: “If you love me, feed my sheep.” If pastoral care is the testimony of love, then whoever is strong in virtues yet refuses to feed God’s flock is proved not to love the chief Shepherd.

If we care for our neighbors as we do for ourselves, we are like people who protect both feet with shoes. But whoever thinks only of himself and neglects the benefit of his neighbors is like someone who disgracefully loses the shoe from one foot.

There are some who, enriched with great gifts, burn with zeal for contemplation alone and therefore refuse in preaching to serve the benefit of their neighbors. They love the privacy of quiet and desire the retreat of contemplation. If they are strictly judged concerning this, they are undoubtedly guilty in proportion to how much they could have benefited others by coming out into public life.

For with what frame of mind does one who would shine for the benefit of his neighbors prefer his own seclusion to the benefit of others, when the Only-Begotten of the supreme Father himself left the Father’s bosom and came forth into our public life in order to benefit many?

There are some who withdraw solely from humility, lest they be placed above those to whom they consider themselves unequal. Their humility is truly genuine before the eyes of God, if it is also surrounded by the other virtues, when it is not stubborn in rejecting what it is usefully commanded to undertake.

For one is not truly humble who understands, by the command of the heavenly will, that he ought to preside, yet nevertheless refuses. Subject to divine arrangements and free from the vice of obstinacy, when the summit of governance is imposed upon him, if he has already been preceded by gifts through which he may benefit others, he ought both to flee it from his heart and to obey unwillingly.

# CHAPTER XVIII

*(Isidore, Sentences, Book III, chapter 33.)* [Isidore, “On superiors: An ecclesiastical man,” etc.]

An ecclesiastical man ought both to be crucified to the world through the mortification of his own flesh and, if the administration of ecclesiastical office arises from God’s will, to undertake its governance—unwillingly indeed, but humbly.

Satan ensnares men who are outstanding in the usefulness of their life and understanding through many deceits, when they are unwilling to preside and benefit others. When governance of souls is imposed upon them, they refuse it, judging it more prudent to lead an idle life than to devote themselves to the gains of souls.

Yet they act thus, deceived by the devil’s argument, which beguiles them under the appearance of good: by withdrawing them from pastoral office, it prevents those from benefiting who could have been instructed by their words and examples.

Holy men do not seek the cares of worldly occupations, but they grieve over those secretly imposed upon them. Although they flee them through a better intention, nevertheless, with a submissive mind, they bear them.

They hurry with all their strength to avoid them, if permitted; but fearing God’s hidden dispensation, they accept what they flee and carry out what they are known to avoid. For they enter into their heart and there consider what God’s hidden will desires. Recognizing that they must be subject to the highest ordinances, they bow the neck of their heart beneath the yoke of divine dispensation.

# CHAPTER XIX

*(Saint Prosper, On the Contemplative Life, Book I, chapter 13.)* [Note: [Col. 0851D] Prosper’s. At that time, evidently, the three books On the Contemplative Life were attributed to Prosper; they are ordinarily published among his works and are frequently cited under his name by Gratian and others. In fact, however, they do not appear to be Prosper’s. First, because Gennadius, when listing Prosper’s works, does not mention these books. Secondly, because their author, in Book II, chapter 9, speaks of Hilary of Arles, who was Prosper’s contemporary, in a way that indicates that Hilary was older than the author. Finally, to pass over other arguments, in the ancient collection of canons in the Angers manuscript they are attributed to Saint Pomerius—so the manuscript calls him—as the author, at the place cited, which appears in Prosper’s Book II, chapter 7; and in the manuscript of Saint-Sauveur of the Viscount, now in the library of the most reverend archbishop of Toulouse, abbot of that same place, Julian Pomerius is named as the author of these books. Isidore likewise expressly ascribes these same works to Julian Pomerius in On Ecclesiastical Writers, chapter 2: “He also published three other books,” he says, “on contemplation of the future life, or on practical conduct, and likewise on vices and virtues.” From these words it is perfectly clear that the subjects of the individual books of this work are being described. In addition, he had published eight other books, whose titles Isidore also explains individually in the same place and whose testimonies Julian the Younger, bishop of Toledo, frequently used in his Prognostics of the Future Age. This Pomerius was an African by origin and a Moor; but, as can be understood from the Life of Caesarius and from the letters of Ruricius to Pomerius himself, he first flourished as a rhetorician, then as a priest and abbot, at Arles. Ennodius also appears to have written to this same Pomerius in Book II, Letter 6.]

*(Prosper, “That holy priests can become participants in the contemplative life: Whoever carefully,” etc.)*

Whoever carefully considers the contemplative life and, being sufficiently instructed, understands when and where its perfection can be attained will not doubt that the leaders of the churches can and ought to become followers of the contemplative life.

For whether, according to the opinion of some, the contemplative life is nothing other than knowledge of hidden and future things; or freedom from all worldly occupations; or devotion to divine literature; or—which is judged more perfect than these—the very vision of God, I do not see what obstacle could be placed before holy priests that would prevent them from attaining these four things I have mentioned.

The first and last of them—namely, knowledge of hidden and future things and the very vision of God—will be incomparably more excellent in that blessed life than in this life entangled in various errors. For then both the knowledge of all things and the very substance of God will be seen fully and perfectly.

The two intermediate things—freedom from all worldly occupations and devotion to divine literature—bishops can possess even here. They are the ones who remove themselves from all entanglements of secular business, yet do not languish in idleness; rather, they devote themselves to the work of their perfection. Turning away from the folly of worldly wisdom, they give themselves tirelessly to the word of God; they truly become wise, savor heavenly things, despise earthly things, rebuke those who contradict sound doctrine, instruct those who obey, and devote themselves to holy virtues by which they may daily draw nearer to God.

Renowned for the advancement both of themselves and of all who are instructed through them, they receive here, as it were, a taste of the contemplative life, by which they may be summoned more fervently to it. But there, having become eternally blessed, they will rejoice in its perfection.

Therefore they are not puffed up because here they are honored as the heads of all faithful Catholics; rather, they rejoice because there they will be brighter members of Christ, who is the head of priests and of all the faithful.

But if—which God forbid—they become entangled in secular affairs, extend the boundaries of their estates without any limit to their greed, and devote themselves [variant: “enrich themselves”] everywhere to elaborate luxuries that weaken both soul and body; if, deceived by the honors of a flattering crowd, they seek the glory not of Christ but of themselves; if they trust the speech of others about them more than their own conscience; if they place all their joy not in the reward of future things or in holiness of life, but solely in their own dignity; and if, while such men are loved as though they were what they believe themselves to be [variant: “are believed to love such things”], they never displease themselves and, pleased with themselves, are not concerned about their correction—who does not understand that such men, if they persist in such conduct and do not reform before the end of this present life, cannot participate in the contemplative life?

No one reaches it unless he has striven to be what he has become, and does not seek to seem, but to be, what he is; unless he is distinguished not by the praises of others but by his own conduct; unless he is conspicuous not only for his own dignity but rather for the nobility of priestly life. Such men are pontiffs not merely in name but in virtue, capable of the contemplative life and coheirs of heavenly joys.

# CHAPTER XX

*(Isidore, Sentences, Book III, chapter 35.)* [Isidore, “On the doctrine and examples of superiors: Both doctrine,” etc.]

An ecclesiastical teacher must shine both in doctrine and in life. For doctrine without life makes one arrogant, while life without doctrine makes one useless.

A priest’s preaching must be confirmed by works, so that what he teaches in word he may instruct by example. That doctrine is true which is followed by a pattern of living. Nothing is more disgraceful than for someone to neglect fulfilling in action the good that he preaches in speech [“in speech” is missing].

Preaching is then brought forth usefully [variant: “effectively”] when it is fulfilled with efficacy. Every teacher ought to devote himself both to good action and to good preaching; one without the other does not make him perfect. Rather, let the righteous person first practice good action, so that afterward he may be able to teach well.

Just as metal, shape, and weight are examined in a coin, so in every ecclesiastical teacher one must examine what he follows, what he teaches, and how he lives. By the quality of the metal, doctrine is signified; by the shape, imitation of the fathers; by the weight, humility. Whoever differs from these three will be not metal but earth.

# CHAPTER XXI

*(Gregory, Pastoral Care, Book II, chapters 4 and 16.)* [Gregory, “On the humility of superiors: Let the ruler be,” etc.]

Let the ruler be discerning in silence and useful in speech, lest he either utter what ought to be silent or keep silent about what ought to be spoken. For just as careless speech leads into error, so indiscreet silence abandons in error those who could have been instructed.

Let the ruler, through humility, be a companion to those who act well, but stand upright against the vices of offenders through zeal for justice. Thus he will neither put himself above the good in anything nor, when the guilt of the wicked requires it, fail to recognize the authority of his precedence. In this way, suppressing his honor, he will consider himself equal to subjects who live well, yet will not fear to exercise the rights [variant: “the way”] of righteousness against the perverse.

Nature gave birth to all human beings as equals; but through the varying order of merits, guilt places some beneath others. This very difference, which arose from vice, is administered by divine judgment, so that, because every person cannot stand equally, one is governed by another.

Therefore all who preside ought to weigh not the power of their rank within themselves but the equality of their condition. They should not rejoice in ruling human beings but in benefiting them.

He governs this power well who knows both how to hold it and how to oppose it. He governs it well who knows through it to rise above faults and knows also, with it, to align himself with others in equality.

He rightly administers this power who carefully knows both how to take from it what helps and how to overthrow what tempts; who sees himself as equal to others while possessing it, yet places himself above sinners through zeal for correction.

Let every preacher strive to soften the threats of the powerful through reasoning and, as far as he can, lighten the distress of the oppressed by his help. Let him oppose patience to those resisting from without and, within, display discipline together with patience toward the proud.

Toward the errors of his subjects, let gentleness temper zeal in such a way that it does not weaken his devotion to justice. Let zeal burn for correction, yet not, by burning, cross the boundary of compassion.

It ought to be the ruler’s office to summon the ungrateful to love through benefits and to preserve the grateful in love through service; to remain silent about the evils of his neighbors when he cannot correct them; and to fear that silence may signify consent concerning whatever can be corrected by speaking.

# CHAPTER XXII

*(Isidore, Sentences, Book III, chapter 42.)* [Isidore, “On the humility of superiors: Whoever is placed in authority,” etc.]

Whoever is placed in authority ought to conduct himself toward the discipline of his subjects in such a way that he shines not only through authority but also through humility.

Yet the virtue of humility must exist in him in such a way that the lives of his subjects are not dissolved into vices; and authority of power must be present in such a way that severity does not arise from an excessive swelling of the heart.

This is true discernment in God’s priests: through freedom they do not become proud, nor through humility do they become lax. Hence the saints, with great firmness, rebuked even the vices of rulers. Although they possessed the greatest humility, they nevertheless freely rebuked transgressors of justice whenever the situation required it.

At times we ought even to be humbler in spirit than our subjects, because the actions of our subjects are judged by us, whereas God judges ours.

Let the bishop recognize that he is the servant of the people, not their lord. Yet this is demanded by love, not by status.

# CHAPTER XXIII
(Of the same author, book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 43.) [Further, Isidore, “On the Discernment of Teaching.”] Not one and the same teaching is to be applied to everyone, but the exhortation of teachers must vary according to the character of their hearers. For some are corrected by a harsh rebuke, while others are corrected by gentle encouragement. Just as skilled physicians treat various bodily diseases with different medicines, so that the treatment varies according to the diversity of the wounds, so also the teacher of the Church will apply to each person the remedy of teaching suited to him and will announce what is appropriate to each according to age, sex, and profession.

Not everything that is hidden is to be disclosed to everyone. For there are many who cannot grasp such things; and if they are revealed to them indiscriminately, they immediately either disparage them or neglect them. The first virtue of prudence, indeed, is to consider what sort of person one ought to teach. To uneducated or carnal peoples, plain and common matters—not the highest and most difficult—are to be preached, lest they be overwhelmed rather than instructed by the vastness of the teaching.

Thus the apostle Paul says: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ; I gave you milk to drink, not food” (I Cor. III). To carnal minds, one should preach neither matters concerning heavenly things that are too lofty nor earthly matters indiscriminately, but teach them moderately, as their beginnings and character require.

When a raven sees that its young are white in color, it does not feed them any food; rather, it waits until they darken to their father’s color, and then it restores them with frequent nourishment. In the same way, the diligent teacher of the Church does not disclose the deeper mysteries of spiritual understanding to those whom he teaches until he sees them darkened in likeness to himself through confession of repentance and, having laid aside worldly brightness, clothed in the garment of lamentation through remembrance of sin. They are still concerned with outward things—that is, carnal things. He does this lest, while they cannot grasp what they hear, they begin to despise rather than revere the heavenly commandments. [Col. 0855D]

One must act differently toward those entrusted to our governance if they offend, and differently toward those who are not entrusted to us. If the latter are righteous, they are to be revered; but if they offend, they are to be corrected, as opportunity permits, for the sake of charity alone—not, however, with the severity appropriate to those entrusted to our governance.

The elders of the people should first be taught, so that through them those below them may more easily be instructed. Hence the Apostle says: “Commit these things to faithful people who will be able to teach others also” (II Tim. II).

It is the mark of a good teacher to begin with praise of those whom he wishes to rebuke with salutary correction, as the Apostle does with the Corinthians: he begins with praise and then proves them by his rebukes. Yet there were among the Corinthians people deserving both praise and rebuke (I Cor. I). But the person who speaks indiscriminately is one who speaks both things to everyone in such a way that both seem appropriate to everyone [sic discrete sic utraque omnibus loquitur, etc.].

## CHAPTER XXIV

(Gregory, in the prologue to book III of the *Pastoral Rule*.) [Gregory: How prelates should teach their subjects and, with discerning circumspection, look to themselves.] Since we have shown above what a pastor ought to be, let us now demonstrate how he ought to teach. For, as Gregory Nazianzen, of revered memory, taught long ago, one and the same exhortation is not suitable for everyone, because not everyone is bound by the same quality of character. Often what benefits one harms another. Frequently, too, herbs that nourish some animals kill others. A gentle whistle calms horses but incites puppies; a medicine that reduces one disease strengthens another; and bread that fortifies the life of the strong kills the little ones. [The whole of this passage is absent, from “as Gregory ... taught” onward: Col. 0856B.]

The speech of teachers must therefore be shaped according to the character of their hearers, so that it suits each person’s needs while never departing from the art of promoting the common good. For what are the attentive minds of hearers except—as I may put it—certain tensions of stretched strings on a lyre? The skilled musician strikes them differently so as not to produce a discordant song; and therefore the strings give back harmonious music because they are struck by one plectrum, though not with one and the same stroke. Every teacher, then, in order to build everyone up in the one virtue of charity, ought to touch the hearts of his hearers with one teaching, but not with one and the same exhortation. [Col. 0856C]

(*Pastoral Rule*, book II, chapter 3.) A teacher who is compelled by the necessity of his office to speak of the highest things is compelled by that same necessity to display the highest things in his life. For that voice penetrates the hearts of hearers more willingly which the speaker’s life commends; what he commands by speaking, he helps bring about by showing it.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion” (Isa. XL). This means that the person who makes use of heavenly preaching must appear to stand at the summit of reality, abandoning the lowly things of earthly works; and he will draw his subjects toward better things all the more easily the more he cries out from above by the merit of his way of life. [Col. 0856D]

The priest is also rightly commanded to wear a breastpiece made of gold, hyacinth, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, so that it may be shown with how great a diversity of virtues he ought to shine. In the priest’s attire, gold shines above all, signifying that the understanding of wisdom must especially gleam in him. Hyacinth, which glows with an ethereal color, is joined to it, so that through everything he penetrates by understanding he may rise not toward lowly applause but toward love of heavenly things—lest, while he heedlessly becomes captivated by his own praises [or: “is praised”], he be emptied even of the understanding of truth.

To the gold and hyacinth, and to the purple, twice-dyed scarlet is added, so that all the good works of the virtues may be adorned with charity before the eyes of the inward Judge, and so that everything that shines before human beings may be kindled in the sight of the hidden Arbiter by the flame of inward love. This charity, because it loves both God and one’s neighbor, shines as though from a double dye.

Whoever therefore longs for the likeness of the Creator while neglecting the care of his neighbors, or carries out the care of his neighbors while growing sluggish in divine love, neglects one of these two things and does not know how to possess twice-dyed scarlet in the ornament of the breastpiece. [Col. 0857A]

When a ruler prepares to speak, let him consider with what great care he ought to speak, lest, if he is swept into speech without order, the hearts of his hearers be struck by the wound of error; and lest, while he wishes to appear wise, he foolishly cut apart the bond of unity.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Matt. IX). By salt, the wisdom of the word is signified. Whoever therefore strives to speak wisely must greatly fear lest the unity of his hearers be disturbed by his eloquence. Hence Paul says: “Do not be wiser than it is proper to be, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. XII).

Therefore, lest a ruler rush heedlessly into speech, Truth itself cries out through the disciple in the words already mentioned: “Have salt in yourselves, and have peace among yourselves” (Mark IX); as though he were figuratively saying through the attire of the priest: “Join the pomegranates to the bells, so that in everything you say you may hold fast to the unity of faith with careful observance.”

A priest must always have the voice of preaching, lest by his silence he display the judgment of the heavenly Watcher. [Note: The entire following period, up to “the priest, etc.,” is absent: Col. 0857D.] For it is written: “Let the sound be heard when he enters or leaves the sanctuary in the presence of the Lord, and he shall not die” (Exod. XXVIII). The priest dies when entering or leaving the tabernacle if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes the anger of the hidden Judge if he walks without the sound of preaching.

The bells are appropriately described as inserted into the garments of the high priest. For what else should we understand the priest’s garments to be than right works, as the Prophet testifies when he says: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. CXXXI)? The bells therefore cling to his garments, so that the good works of the priest themselves may proclaim the way of life together with the sound of his tongue. [Col. 0857D]

Because we are frail human beings, when we speak to human beings about God, we must first remember what we are, so that from our own weakness we may consider with what manner of teaching we ought to console weak brothers and sisters. Let us therefore consider whether we are such as those whom we correct, or whether we were once such, even if by the working of divine grace we are no longer so. Thus we shall correct them with a heart all the more restrained and humble, the more truly we recognize ourselves in those whom we amend.

If we priests are neither now nor formerly what those whom we seek to correct still are, let us recall before our eyes other good qualities of those whose faults we correct, lest our heart perhaps grow proud and, because of that very innocence, fall into something worse. If they have no good qualities at all, let us have recourse to the hidden judgments of God. For just as we receive the good we possess without any merits of our own, so grace from above may also be poured into them, so that, awakened later, they may even surpass the good things we received earlier.

Who would have believed that Saul would one day surpass the stoned Stephen in apostolic merit, when at Stephen’s death he guarded the garments of those who were stoning him? The heart must first be humbled by such thoughts, and only then rebuke the iniquities of those who offend.

## CHAPTER XXV

(Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 44.) [Isidore, “On the Silence of Teachers.”] Because of the bad merit of the people, the teaching of preaching is taken away; because of the good merit of the hearer, the teacher’s word is granted. It lies within the divine power whether God wishes to give the word of teaching to someone or to take it away. This occurs either because of the merit of the speaker or because of that of the hearer: sometimes the teacher’s word is taken away because of the people’s fault, and sometimes it is granted for the ruler’s benefit.

For a good person teaches what is good, and a bad person what is bad; a good person may also teach what is bad, and a bad person what is good. Yet this happens according to the merit of the peoples. Not all times are suitable for teaching, according to Solomon’s saying: “A time to keep silence and a time to speak” (Eccl. III).

Not because of fear, but because of discretion, on account of the incorrigible wickedness of the evil, the elect must sometimes cease from teaching. At times the teachers of the Church, burning with the heat of charity, fall silent from teaching because there is no one to listen, as the Prophet testifies: “The cities of the South are closed, and there is no one to open them” (Jer. XIII).

The person who undertakes the office of teaching should sometimes remain silent for a time about deeds that he does not think can immediately be corrected.
