For if he can correct and pretends not to notice, it is true that he shares in another’s error. Many holy teachers, because of the obstinacy of the wicked and their inability to amend the unrighteous, decide to remain silent toward them; but, unable to endure the heat of the spirit by which they are moved, they again leap forth into rebuking the ungodly.

## CHAPTER XXVI

(Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, book I, chapter 20.) [Prosper: That it profits a priest nothing, even if he lives well, if by silence he does not rebuke those who live badly.] What benefit, then, is there in the Apostle’s saying (II Thess. III) that we ought to present ourselves as an example to the faithful, if the person entrusted with the care either of exhorting the good or of chastising the wicked presents himself by living well as an example for the good to imitate, yet does not rebuke the wicked by remaining silent?

For the priest must live holily for this reason—unless I am mistaken in my judgment—that his words may not be nullified by deeds that contradict them. If he does not do what he preaches ought to be done, or if he presumes to preach what he does not do, he will accomplish nothing among those who know his life.

For he has been placed over the Church of God not merely to instruct others by the example of his conduct through living well, but also, by preaching boldly, to set each person’s sins before his eyes; to show what punishment awaits the stubborn and what glory awaits the obedient; to despise no one’s salvation through despair; and to mourn the souls of those unwilling to be corrected, imitating the Apostle who says: “That I may mourn many of those who previously sinned and did not repent” (II Cor. XI). And again: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?” (II Cor. XI).

Therefore, knowing that if he spares or favors any rich or powerful people who live wickedly, he will destroy and perish along with them, he must live holily for the sake of example and teach devoutly for the sake of his administrative office, certain that his own righteousness will avail him nothing, since the soul of the one who perishes will be required from his hand.

When anyone else perishes, one upon whom no necessity of teaching rests, he alone will suffer the punishment of his own crime. But the person entrusted with the stewardship of the word, even if he lives holily, perishes together with all those who perish while he remains silent, if he is ashamed or afraid to rebuke those who live destructively. And what will it profit him not to be punished for his own sin, when he is to be punished for another’s?

I am deceived if the Lord does not speak of this through the prophet Ezekiel under the threat of a terrifying warning, saying to him: “And you, son of man, I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. III). We must not hear this casually, that he calls the priest a watchman. For just as it is the watchman’s task to look out from a higher place and observe more than everyone else, so the priest ought to be higher than all by the sublimity of his calling and possess the gift of greater knowledge, by which he can instruct those living beneath him. [Col. 0859C]

Let us now see what the divine word contains. “You will hear the word from my mouth,” it says, “and you will announce it to them from me” (Ezek. III). The priest must say what he has learned from divine reading and what God has inspired in him, not what he has discovered by the presumption of human judgment. “You will announce it to them from me,” it says. From me, and not from yourself, you will speak my words to them. You have no reason to puff yourself up before them as though they were your own words. “Announce it to them from me,” it says.

But let us hear what he is to announce. “If, when I say to the wicked person, ‘Wicked one, you shall surely die,’ you do not speak so that the wicked person may guard himself from his way, that wicked person will die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood from your hand.” What could be said more explicitly or more clearly? “If,” he says, “you do not speak to the wicked person so that he may guard himself from his wickedness, and he perishes, I will require his blood from your hand.” This means: If you do not announce his sins to him, if you do not rebuke him so that he may turn from his wickedness and live, I will destroy with everlasting flames both you, who did not rebuke him, and him, who sinned while you remained silent.

Who, I ask, could have a heart so stony, who could be so hard as not to fear this sentence? Who could be so alien to faith as not to believe it?

## CHAPTER XXVII

(Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, book I, chapter 2.) [Gregory, on pastors who do not walk rightly.] There are some who examine spiritual commandments with diligent care, but trample underfoot by living what they penetrate by understanding. Suddenly they teach what they have learned not by practice but by reflection, and by their conduct oppose what they preach in words. Hence it happens that when the shepherd walks over precipices, the flock follows toward the brink.

Through the Prophet, the Lord complains against the contemptible knowledge of shepherds, saying: “When you drank the clearest water, you trampled the remainder with your feet [or: disturbed it]; and my sheep fed on what had been trampled by your feet, and drank what your feet had disturbed” (Ezek. III).

Shepherds drink the clearest water when they draw in and rightly understand the streams of truth. But to disturb that same water is to corrupt the pursuits of holy meditation by living badly. The sheep drink the water disturbed by the shepherds’ feet when all those subject to them do not follow the words they hear but imitate only the examples of depravity that they see. Though they thirst for words, they are perverted by deeds; as though from polluted springs, they take mud in their drink.

No one does more harm in the Church than one who acts perversely while possessing the name or rank of holiness. No one dares rebuke such a delinquent, and the fault is greatly extended as an example when, out of reverence for his rank, the sinner is honored. A person elevated to the appearance of holiness who destroys others either by word or by example would surely have been better confined by earthly deeds to death under an outward appearance than shown by sacred offices as someone whom others might imitate in guilt. If he fell alone, the punishment of hell would at least torment him more tolerably. [Col. 0860C]

(Gregory, same work, chapter 4.) Often an undertaking of governance strikes the heart in different directions as it looks upon various matters, and each person is found unequal to individual tasks while being divided among many things with a confused mind. Hence a certain wise man prudently warns, saying: “My son, do not let your activities be among many things” (Eccli. XI).

For the mind is never gathered fully into the consideration of any one task when, scattered among different things, it is divided [“scattered” is absent]. And when it is drawn outward by excessive concern, it is emptied of the firmness of inward fear. While the mind is also anxious about arranging external matters, it is ignorant of itself alone: it knows how to think about many things but does not know itself.

When it entangles itself in external matters more than necessary, it is like someone occupied on a journey who forgets where he was going. Thus, estranged from the work of examining himself, he does not even consider the losses he suffers and does not know in how many ways he falls into wrongdoing.

King Hezekiah did not at all believe that he was sinning when he showed his storehouses of spices to foreigners who came to him; yet he incurred the anger of the Judge for the condemnation of his descendants because of what he considered himself free to do (Isa. XXXIX).

Often, while many resources are available and many things can be done, subordinates admire what has been accomplished, and the mind raises itself in thought, fully provoking the anger of the Judge, although it does not break out into outward works of iniquity. The one who judges is within, and what is judged is within. When, therefore, we sin in our heart, what we do within us is hidden from human beings; nevertheless, with the Judge himself as witness, we sin.

In bringing these things forward, we do not criticize the authority of governance; rather, we protect weakness of heart from its desire, lest the imperfect dare to seize the summit of governance and those who stumble while standing on level ground place their foot on a precipice. [Col. 0861A]

(Gregory, same work, chapter 11.) The blind pastor is one who does not know the light of heavenly contemplation. Pressed by the darkness of the present life, he does not see the light to come by which he should direct himself, and he does not know where to place the step of his work [“of his work” is absent].

The lame ruler is one who sees where he ought to go but, because of weakness of mind, cannot perfectly follow the way of life that he sees. Since he is not raised to the state of virtue from his unstable habit, his steps in action do not effectively follow where he leans by desire.

He has a small nose who is not capable of maintaining the measure of discretion. We distinguish odors and foul smells by the nose. Accordingly, discretion is rightly expressed by the nose, since by it we choose virtues and reject sins.

But there are some who, unwilling to be regarded as dull, often exercise themselves in certain investigations more than necessary and are deceived by excessive subtlety. Hence it is added here: “Or one with a large and crooked nose” (Lev. XXI). A large and crooked nose is excessive subtlety of discretion. When this grows beyond what is proper, it itself confounds the rightness of one’s action.

He has a broken foot or hand who is wholly unable to walk in the way of God and remains completely deprived of good works, so that he does not retain them even as a lame person might, with weakness, but is altogether alien to them. [Col. 0861C]

A hunchback is one whom the weight of earthly concern presses down, so that he never looks toward heavenly things but attends only to what is trodden underfoot below. Even if he sometimes hears something about the good of the heavenly homeland, weighed down by the burden of perverse habit, he does not raise the face of his heart toward it. He cannot lift up the posture of his thoughts, since the practice of earthly concern keeps him bent over.

A bleary-eyed person is one whose natural intelligence shines toward the recognition of truth, but whose carnal works nevertheless obscure it. In bleary eyes the pupils are healthy, but the eyelids become thickened and weakened by the discharge of moisture. Because they are repeatedly worn down by the flow, the sharpness of the pupil is damaged. There are likewise some whose understanding is wounded by the activity of carnal life. By their intelligence they could see what is right with subtlety, but through the practice of wicked deeds they grow dim.

A bleary-eyed person, then, is one whose understanding nature sharpens but whose perverse conduct confounds. To him the angel rightly says: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, so that you may see” (Rev. III). We anoint our eyes with eye-salve so that we may see when, in order to recognize the brightness of the true light, we assist the sharpness of our understanding with the medicine of good works.

A person who suffers from a white film sees nothing. A priest has a white film in his eye when he is prevented from seeing the light of truth because he is blinded by arrogance concerning wisdom or righteousness. The pupil of the eye is black and sees; one who suffers from a white film sees nothing. Thus, if the understanding of human thought recognizes itself as foolish and sinful, it grasps knowledge of inward brightness; but if it attributes to itself the whiteness of righteousness or wisdom, it excludes itself from the light of heavenly knowledge. It penetrates the brightness of the true light no further precisely because it exalts itself arrogantly in its own estimation. As it is said of some: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. I). [Col. 0862A]

He has a perpetual scab on his body in whose mind the wantonness of the flesh rules without ceasing. In a scab, the heat of the inward organs is drawn to the skin; and lust is rightly signified by this, because if temptation of the heart leaps forth into action, the inward heat bursts out as far as the itching of the skin. The body is then wounded outwardly [“scab”], because, when the will is not restrained in thought, it also dominates in action.

Paul sought to wipe away, as it were, the itching of the skin when he said: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (I Cor. X). As though he were plainly saying: It is human to suffer temptation in the heart; but it is demonic to be overcome by the contest of temptation in action.

Whoever is ravaged in mind by greed also has an impetigo on his body. If it is not restrained in small matters, it spreads excessively and without measure. Impetigo occupies the body without pain, and as it grows without troubling the person affected, it disfigures the beauty of the limbs. So greed wounds the captive soul while seeming to delight it; by placing before the mind whatever is to be acquired, it kindles hostility, yet causes no pain in the wound, because it promises abundance to the inflamed mind as the result of guilt.

The beauty of the limbs is lost through impetigo because the beauty of the other virtues is also distorted by greed. It irritates the whole body, as it were, because it undermines the mind through every vice, as Paul testifies: “The love of money is the root of all evils” (I Tim. VI). [Col. 0862C]

A heavy person is one who does not commit shameful acts in deed but is nevertheless burdened in mind by continual and unrestrained thoughts of them. He is not dragged all the way to the shameful act itself, but his mind takes pleasure in the delight of lust without any resistance [or: “impulse”]. The defect of heaviness occurs when the moisture of the inward organs flows toward the genitals, which swell with the distress of disgrace. A heavy person, then, is one who, flowing toward wantonness with all his thoughts, carries the weight of shame in his heart.

Although he does not practice what is wrong in deed, he is not torn away from it in mind; nor can he rise openly to the practice of a good work, because a shameful weight hidden within burdens him. Whoever, therefore, is subjected to any of these vices is forbidden to offer loaves to the Lord, lest he be unable to cleanse the sins of others while his own still devastate him.

(*Moralia*, book XI, chapters 9–10.) When a priest does not perform the good things he speaks about, the word is also withdrawn from him, lest he dare to say what he does not do, as the Prophet says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousnesses and take up my covenant in your mouth?” (Ps. XLIX).

Hence the Psalmist also prays, saying: “Do not take the word of truth from my mouth altogether” (Ps. CXVIII). For he considers that almighty God grants the word of truth to those who do it and takes it away from those who do not. Therefore, when he asks that it not be taken from his mouth, what else does he seek than the grace of good action? As though he were plainly saying:

(*Moralia*, book XI, chapter 10.) Do not allow me to stray from good work, lest, when I lose the order of living well, I lose the rightness of speaking.

Often a teacher who dares to teach what he neglects to do, once he ceases to speak the good things he refused to practice, begins to teach his subjects the evil things he does. Thus, by the just judgment of almighty God, he no longer possesses even a good tongue, since he refused to possess a good life; and as his mind is kindled by earthly love, he speaks constantly about earthly matters.

Hence Truth says in the Gospel: “For the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart. The good person brings forth good things from the good treasure, and the evil person brings forth evil things from the evil treasure” (Matt. XII). John likewise says: “They are from the world; therefore they speak from the world” (I John IV).

## CHAPTER XXVIII

(Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, book I, chapter 13.) [Prosper, on the negligence of a priest who, neglecting his teaching, cannot fulfill the role of teacher.] Recall, then, how many and how serious were the things you used to say, while I listened and approved, about the administration of a bishop who, neglecting the care of the people entrusted to him, desires present goods more ardently than future ones and, forgetting that he will have to render an account not only of himself but also of the flock entrusted to him to the Shepherd of all shepherds, does not consider the losses of himself and his people.

He is not saddened by the sins of those who offend, nor gladdened by the good of those who advance. He is concerned only with himself—or often not even with himself at all—and is ignorant of what good or evil is being done by his people.

He does not preach perseverance to the righteous, repentance to the wicked, contempt for the world to the converted, or future punishments to those who turn away. He cannot say to those who despise his admonition, “Consider the future judgment,” if he himself perhaps does not consider it.

To lovers of the world he cannot say, “Do not love the world,” if the love of the world delights him. To the ambitious he cannot say, “Put an end now to ambition,” if ruinous ambition drives him headlong. To drunkards he cannot say, “Beware of drunkenness,” if he himself stuffs himself with wine to the point of mental alienation.

Loaded with costly banquets, he cannot praise abstinence to his people, which he himself tramples underfoot. Given over to the vice of greed, he cannot dissuade the greedy from loving money. Holding fast to enmities, he will not be able to reconcile the minds of those who disagree with priestly tranquility.

He is ashamed to preach justice to judges, which he himself corrupts through favor toward a powerful person; nor does he defend the oppressed if he either honors or despises persons according to their status. Whatever good he does not do or evil he commits, he will neither command to be done nor forbid, because by the contradiction of his own actions he either loses or diminishes the authority necessary for teaching.

## CHAPTER XXIX

(Isidore, book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 37.) [Isidore, “On Those Who Teach Well and Live Badly.”] Sometimes the teacher’s own life makes even true teaching worthless; and one who does not live as he teaches makes the truth he preaches contemptible.

The tongue of teachers who teach well and live badly is a crooked bow; and so they shoot an arrow, as it were, from a crooked bow, when they pierce their own wicked life with the blow of their own tongue. One who teaches well and lives badly makes a sound for others like bronze or a cymbal, yet remains without feeling toward himself.

One who teaches well and lives badly benefits those who live well through what he teaches; but by living badly he kills himself. Thus a priest who conducts himself as a priest ought to conduct himself, with due dignity, makes his ministry useful both to himself and to others. But living unworthily, he is useful to others by speaking while killing himself by living perversely.

Accordingly, what is dead in him belongs to him; but what lives in him—that is, the sacred ministry—is not his own. One who teaches well and lives badly appears like a candle: he knows how to provide good light to others, yet consumes and extinguishes himself in his evils.

One who teaches well and lives badly appears to join good to evil, mix light with darkness, and exchange truth for falsehood.

## CHAPTER XXX

(The same, chapter 38.) [Isidore, “On the Examples of Wicked Priests.”] Often the disease of sin enters through those by whom righteousness is taught, and death passes to the peoples—either because they teach evil or because they do what is wrong.

Many priests and clerics who live perversely become an example of evil to others, although they ought to have been an example in good. Without doubt they will have to render an account for all whom they destroy by the example of their evil conduct. [Col. 0864C]

From the example of carnal rulers the life of their subjects often becomes worse; and because of the merit of the people such priests are made rulers that they may destroy the people by a worse example rather than build them up. For because of the people’s merit, bishops are sometimes corrupted, so that those who follow may fall more easily.

When the head languishes, the other members of the body are infected. Hence it is written: “Every head is sick, and every heart is sorrowful; from the sole of the foot even to the top of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isa. I).

The sick head is the teacher who commits sin. His evil reaches the body when, through his sinning or teaching perversely, a pestilential sickness passes to the subject peoples.

Those who corrupt the life and character of the good, whether by teachings or by examples, are worse than those who seize the possessions and estates of others. The latter take away things that are outside us, though they are ours; but those who corrupt morals do not properly seize the people themselves, because the wealth of righteous people is their character. Thus the losses of morals differ greatly from the losses of temporal goods: the latter are outside us, whereas morals are within us.

## CHAPTER XXXI

(Isidore, same work, chapter 39.) Often, by the providence of divine counsel, rulers are appointed who pursue worldly and external things, so that, while they devote themselves entirely to temporal matters, spiritual people may practice the safer life of contemplation.

Because the burdens of episcopal cares are hard for those who wish to live in quiet, God often provides people devoted to worldly concerns for the assumption of governance, so that, while these administer external matters without weariness, spiritual people may devote themselves to inward things without the hindrance of earthly affairs.

Therefore those who condemn bishops because they pursue spiritual matters less and earthly matters more accuse the order of God, by whom they have been appointed. For it is established by the divine arrangement of the tabernacle that, in order to endure the injuries of the world and certain storms, bishops are appointed who devote themselves to worldly cares, so that those who inwardly desire heavenly things may attend more freely to what they love, with no earthly business standing in the way.

A disordered ruler is therefore not to be judged by the people, since the people ought rather to know that it was their own merit that caused them to receive a perverse bishop as ruler. For the life of rulers is arranged by God according to the merits of the peoples.

They sin after the example of David [“of David sinning”], in comparison with rulers who transgress because of the merit of the people. The sons of Noah, Ham, are condemned by the sentence because they publicly expose the faults of their rulers, as Ham did when he did not cover his father’s nakedness but displayed it for mockery.

They will have the merit of Shem and Japheth if they reverently cover what they recognize their fathers to have done wrong—provided that they do not love their fathers’ deeds but merely cover them and do not imitate them.

There are some who judge their rulers perversely when they see them more intent on earthly pursuits, even though they themselves know at least a little about spiritual matters.

Rulers are therefore to be judged by God, but they are by no means to be judged by their own subjects, following the example of the Lord, who himself overturned with a whip those selling doves and the tables of the money-changers (John II), and drove them from the temple; or as the Psalmist says: “God stands in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges the gods” (Ps. LXXXI).

But if a ruler deviates from the faith, then he is to be rebuked by his subjects. For reprehensible morals, however, he should be tolerated by the people rather than harshly dealt with.

## CHAPTER XXXII
(Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, Book I, chapter 21.) [Prosper’s sorrowful description of priests living carnally: “But we, delighted by present things,” etc.; columns 0865D–0867B.] But we, delighted by present things, while in this life we seek our comforts and honors—not to be better, but richer, nor to be holier, but more honored—we hasten to preside over others. We do not think carnally of the Lord’s flock, which has been entrusted to us to feed and guard, but of our own pleasures, domination, wealth, and other allurements. We wish to be called shepherds, yet do not strive to be so. We avoid the labor of our office and desire its dignity. We do not drive away from the flock the wild beasts of unclean spirits as they tear it apart; and whatever remains for them, we ourselves consume, when we not only fail to rebuke the rich or powerful who sin, but even honor them, lest, offended, they cease to send us their customary gifts or withdraw the services we desire. As though captured by their gifts and services—or rather, bound to them by these things [the words “or rather … bound to them” are lacking]—we fear to speak to them about their sin or about the future judgment. And therefore divine speech strikes down our pride with threats, but our hearing admits nothing by which we may improve, because, captivated by the sweetness of the present life, we do not wish to consider what punishment will await our negligence eternally.

These words are spoken, then, against shepherds, whose empty title flatters us:

> Thus says the Lord God: Woe to the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves. Are not flocks fed by shepherds? You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool. You slaughtered what was fat, but you did not feed my flock. You did not strengthen what was weak; you did not heal what was sick; you did not bind up what was broken; you did not bring back what was cast away; you did not seek what had perished. Instead, you ruled over them with harshness and with power. And my sheep were scattered because there was no shepherd, and they became food for all the beasts of the field (Ezekiel 34).

And shortly afterward:

> Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. As I live, says the Lord God, because my flocks have become prey and my sheep food for all the beasts of the field, because there was no shepherd—for the shepherds did not seek my flock, but the shepherds fed themselves and did not feed my flock—therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says the Lord God: Behold, I myself will come against the shepherds and require my flock from their hand, and I will make them cease, so that they will no longer feed the flock, nor will the shepherds feed themselves any longer (ibid.).

Who would not tremble at these words? Who could receive them without unbearable fear of the future examination, except one who either does not understand or does not believe in what is to come? But because God placed everything he wished to be observed so openly, and confirmed it by the authority of his name, that we might more easily—an impious thing even to say—despise such open and divine declarations than pretend that we do not understand or believe them, when we hear, “Thus says the Lord,” who would not believe that what the Lord says will come to pass, except one who does not believe God?

As for the statement, “Woe to the shepherds,” who would not understand that this “woe” is placed as a curse, and that we are signified by the name “shepherds,” except one who does not think about what is to come? We assume responsibility for feeding the Lord’s flocks, and we feed ourselves when we do not look to the welfare of the flocks, but consider what may nourish and increase our own pleasures. We gladly receive the milk and wool of Christ’s sheep—that is, the daily offerings and the tithes of the faithful—and we lay aside [neglect] the care of feeding and restoring the flocks from which, in a perverse order, we wish to be fed. We do not heal with spiritual counsel the one weakened by sins; we do not strengthen or restore with priestly aid the one broken by various tribulations; we do not call the wanderer back to the way of salvation; we do not seek, with pastoral concern, the one already lost through despair of forgiveness. We have become powerful only for this purpose: to claim tyrannical domination over our subjects, not to defend the afflicted against the violence of the powerful, who rage against them like wild beasts.

That is why some perish, grievously oppressed not so much by the powerful of this world as by us—which is worse. The Lord threatens terribly that he will require them from our hand, saying:

> I will require my sheep from the hand of the shepherds, and I will make them cease, so that they will no longer feed my flocks.

What else does this mean than that I will strip shepherds who feed themselves, not my flocks, of the exaltedness of their dignity, and cast them among the reprobate because they refused to guard their honor? Terrified by the consideration of these things and of those like them, the Prophet [the Prophet is lacking] says:

> Fear and trembling came upon me, and the darkness of my sins covered me. And I said, “Who will give me wings like a dove’s? Then I would fly away and rest” (Psalm 54).

This is the whole reason why, remembering my incompetence and my future end, I groaned and wished, laying down the burden of my episcopate, to flee far away and remain in solitude, and there to await the Lord, who would save me from my faintheartedness and from the storm of anxieties unbearable to me.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

(Isidore, *Sentences*, Book III, chapter 40.) [Isidore, on angry teachers: “Angry teachers,” etc.] Angry teachers, through the frenzy of rage, turn the discipline of correction into the monstrousness of cruelty; and by the means through which they could have corrected their subjects, they instead wound them. Therefore an angry superior avenges faults without measure, because his heart, scattered among worldly concerns, is not gathered into love of the one God. A mind loosened among many things is not bound by the chain of charity; but, badly relaxed, it is badly moved at every opportunity.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

[Column 0867C]

(Gregory, *On Ezekiel*, Book I, homily 22.) [Gregory, on zeal for the pastoral office: “Every spiritual zeal,” etc.; columns 0867C–0869C.] Every spiritual zeal of a teacher sears the mind, because he is deeply distressed when he sees the weak abandoning eternal things and taking pleasure in temporal ones. For no sacrifice is so acceptable to almighty God as zeal for souls, as the Psalmist says:

> The zeal of your house has consumed me (Psalm 68).

The apostle Paul, afflicted by zeal for souls, said:

> Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire? (2 Corinthians 11.)

What else had he made of his own heart, which he had kindled with zeal for souls, than something like a frying pan in which he burned with love of the virtues against vices (chapter 4)? For it was burned, and therefore it was also cooked in the frying pan, because it was set alight by bitterness, yet from his afflicted reflection it prepared nourishment for the virtues.

But what does the prophet Ezekiel mean by placing an iron wall between this same frying pan and the city, except that the same strong zeal which is now active in the teacher’s mind will, on the day of the final judgment, stand as a witness between him and the soul for which he burns with zeal against vices? Thus, even if the one being taught refuses to listen, the teacher will not be liable for negligence before the Author on account of the zeal he displayed.

The prophet therefore places an iron wall between himself and the city, because at the time of vengeance the teacher is shielded from the danger of condemnation by that very thing through which he now suffers the burning of his heart in his zeal for guardianship.

How pleasing to almighty God is this burning of the heart, produced by spiritual zeal, is clearly shown when the Law commands fine flour to be offered as a sacrifice. For it is written:

> It shall be fried in a pan sprinkled with oil, and the priest who lawfully succeeds his father shall offer it hot, as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, and it shall be wholly burned on the altar (Leviticus 6).

The fine flour is fried in the pan when the pure mind of the righteous person is consumed by the ardor of holy zeal. It is commanded to be sprinkled with oil—that is, to be mingled with the mercy of charity—which burns and shines in the sight of almighty God. Let the mind, therefore, which is fried in the pan be sprinkled with oil, because the strictness of holy zeal must both burn and shine through the virtue of mercy. For it loves the very one whom it seems to pursue.

Hence it is commanded to be offered hot to the Lord as a most pleasing fragrance, because if zeal does not possess love, the fine flour offered from the pan has lost its warmth.

It must be carefully noted who is commanded to offer the fine flour: namely, the priest who has lawfully succeeded his father. For that priest lawfully succeeds his father who demonstrates by his conduct that he is a son of almighty God and does not differ from his inner nobility through the ignobility of his works. It is commanded to be wholly burned on the altar, so that it may become a whole burnt offering.

The fine flour in the pan, then, is the pure mind of the righteous person in the affliction of spiritual zeal, which is fried through concern for souls; and it is reckoned to be not only a sacrifice but also a whole burnt offering to the Lord.

Let us therefore take an iron frying pan and place it as an iron wall between ourselves and the city—that is, let us assume strong zeal, so that afterward we may find this strong fortification between ourselves and the mind of our hearer. We will find this iron wall if we now hold it firmly: by teaching, guarding, persuading, reproving, soothing, and frightening; sometimes acting gently, but sometimes also more severely.

Concerning this severity Ezekiel rightly adds:

> And you shall set your face against it, and it shall be for a siege (Ezekiel 4).

What does it mean to harden one’s face against Jerusalem, which has been depicted on the side, except that when the teacher announces to the soul the vision of heavenly peace, if he sees that it is still weakened in its actions, he should by no means show himself more remiss or more lenient toward it?

Hence it is written:

> Do you have daughters? Preserve their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face (Ecclesiasticus 8).

Weak souls, devoted to worldly desire, are sometimes better preserved by severity, so that the hardened face—that is, the soul drawn away from every vain hope of leniency through the guardianship of severity—may terrify the unstable soul and restrain it from delight in vices by the force of discipline.

When this is done by a teacher, it is always necessary that sweetness and humility be retained in the heart, so that he may love greatly and never become proud toward the person he corrects through arrogance, even though for that person’s benefit he refuses to reveal his love and humility.

It follows:

> And you shall surround it.

The teacher surrounds the soul of his hearer when he warns that the snares of temptations can be laid in everything done in this life, so that, while the mind becomes fearful everywhere and watchful everywhere, it may live all the more vigilantly the more timidly.

(*Moralia*, Book LIX, chapter 33.) For zeal itself for righteousness, while it agitates the mind with restlessness, immediately obscures its sight, so that in its agitation it does not see higher things which it had previously perceived well while tranquil. Yet from the very point where it is temporarily struck so that it cannot see, it is more subtly led back to higher things. For the very emulation of righteousness, directed to inner things (*interna*; printed reading: “eternal things,” *aeterna*), after a little while opens more generously in tranquility what it temporarily closes through agitation; and from the point where the mind is disturbed so that it cannot see, it progresses so that it may become clearer for seeing more truly.

It is like an ailing eye when a medicinal preparation is applied to it: light is entirely denied, but afterward it truly receives light from the very point where it healthfully loses it for a time.

Contemplation, however, is never joined to agitation; nor can a disturbed mind perceive what a tranquil one can scarcely long for. The ray of the sun is not seen when disturbed clouds cover the face of heaven, nor does a troubled spring reflect the image of the one looking into it, which it properly [its own] displays when tranquil, because, trembling in its waters, it obscures within itself the appearance of the likeness.

But when the spirit is moved by zeal, one must take the greatest care that the anger assumed as an instrument of virtue does not dominate the mind. It must not go before as a mistress, but, like a maidservant prepared for service, must never withdraw from behind reason. For it rises more vigorously against vices when it serves in submission to reason.

However much anger may arise from zeal for righteousness, if it overcomes the mind without measure, it immediately refuses to serve reason. It expands all the more shamelessly because it considers the vice of impatience a virtue.

Therefore the person moved by zeal for righteousness must attend above all to this: that anger does not pass beyond the dominion of the mind, but, considering the time and measure appropriate for punishing sin, restrains the disturbance of the spirit as it rises by examining it carefully, suppresses hostility, and orders its heated movements according to equity. Thus he becomes a more just avenger of another precisely insofar as he first becomes the victor over himself.

The person moved by zeal for righteousness should correct the faults of those who offend in such a way that he himself, the one doing the correcting, first grows through patience. He should judge his own fervor by rising above it, lest, excited without restraint, he depart far from righteousness through the very zeal for righteousness.

## CHAPTER XXXV

[Column 0869D]

(Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, Book II, chapter 9.) [Prosper: priests should possess nothing privately and should preserve the Church’s resources as common goods, since they must render account to God: “It is fitting that the resources,” etc.; columns 0869D–0870B.] It is fitting that the resources of the Church be possessed and that private possessions be despised for the love of perfection. For the Church’s resources are not private but common. Therefore whoever, after abandoning or selling everything he possessed, becomes a despiser of his own property, once he has been made a superior of the Church becomes the steward of everything the Church possesses.

Thus Saint Paulinus—as you yourselves know better—sold the large estates that had been his and distributed the proceeds to the poor. But afterward, when he had become a bishop, he did not despise the resources of the Church; rather, he administered them most faithfully. By this action he clearly showed both that private possessions ought to be despised for the sake of perfection and that, without hindering perfection, the common possessions of the Church may be held.

What of Saint Hilary? Did he not also either leave all that was his to his parents or sell it and distribute the proceeds to the poor? Nevertheless, when by the merit of his perfection he became bishop of the Church of Arles, he not only possessed what that Church then had, but also increased it by receiving numerous inheritances from the faithful.

These pontiffs, therefore, so holy and so perfect, proclaim by evident deeds that what they did can and ought to be done. Certainly, if they—men thoroughly learned without ambiguity in both secular and divine literature—had known that the Church’s possessions ought to be despised, they would never have retained them after abandoning everything of their own.

From this it is understood that such great men, who wished to become Christ’s disciples and renounced everything they had, possessed the Church’s resources not as owners but as stewards. Knowing that the Church’s possessions are nothing other than the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor, they did not claim them for their own use as private property; rather, as entrusted goods, they distributed them to the poor.

This is to despise possessions while possessing them: to possess not for oneself but for others, and not to seek the Church’s resources out of a desire to have them, but to receive them from a spirit of compassion in order to provide assistance.

What the Church possesses, it possesses in common with all who have nothing. It gives none of it to those who are self-sufficient from their own resources; for to give anything to those who already have is nothing other than to waste it.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

[Column 0870C]

(Isidore, *Sentences*, Book III, chapter 46.) [On the discipline of priests, concerning those who offend: “Priests,” etc.; columns 0870C–0872B.] Priests are condemned for the iniquity of the people if they either do not instruct those who are ignorant or do not rebuke those who sin, as the Lord testifies to the prophet:

> I have appointed you as a watchman for the house of Israel. If you do not speak so that the wicked may guard himself from his way, he will die in his iniquity; but I will require his blood from your hand (Ezekiel 3).

Thus the priest Eli was condemned for the iniquity of his sons, although he warned them when they were sinning; nevertheless, he did not rebuke them as he ought to have done (1 Samuel 2 and 4).

Priests ought to investigate the sins of the people and examine each person with vigilant care, according to the testimony of the Lord speaking to Jeremiah:

> I have appointed you as a proven examiner among my people, strong; and you shall know and examine their ways (Jeremiah 6).

Priests ought to scrutinize the deeds of their subjects with the zeal of correction, so that they may win them when they have been amended. But just as it is fitting to rebuke the sinner, so the righteous person should not be embittered.

Priests ought to care for those who are perishing, so that by priestly rebuke they may either be corrected from their sins or, if they prove incorrigible, be separated from the Church.

Those are severely rebuked who, by deceiving sinners, not only fail to rebuke them for their sin but also deceive them through flattery, as the prophet says:

> Those who call this people blessed will be deceivers, and those who are called blessed will be overthrown (Isaiah 9).

Again those are severely rebuked who do not receive the sinner but despise and reject him, and do not mourn another’s fault as their own. Concerning such people the Lord threatens through Isaiah:

> Those who say, “Depart from me; do not come near me, for you are unclean”—these will be smoke in my anger, a fire burning all day long (Isaiah 65).

That is why the Apostle became all things to all people (1 Corinthians 9), not by imitating error but through compassionate mercy: namely, so that he might mourn the vices of others as though he himself were entangled in such error.

Good shepherds of the people ought to mourn their offenses and surrender themselves entirely to lamentation, imitating the prophet Jeremiah, who says:

> Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep day and night for the slain of my people? (Jeremiah 9.)

The priest ought therefore to mourn the sins of the people as his own sins, but through the feeling of compassion, not through participation in the deed.

Some bishops of the flock cast certain people out of communion because of sin, so that they may repent; but they do not visit them by exhorting them toward the better way of life. Against such people the divine word appropriately threatens:

> Shepherds who feed my people, you have scattered my flock; you have driven them out and have not visited them. Behold, I will visit upon you the wickedness of your endeavors (ibid.).

The diligent efforts of good priests investigate even the small deeds of their people with great care, so that, by showing themselves extremely severe in the smallest sins of their subjects, they may make their subjects cautious and attentive concerning greater evils.

Just as physicians undertake to cure impending illnesses, but, by applying medicine, anticipate future illnesses through a kind of foreknowledge so that they do not creep in, so good teachers cut away what has been done wrongly in such a way that, with their teaching coming to the aid of their hearers, they prevent what can be committed from being committed.

A person who is not corrected by gentle speech must necessarily be rebuked more sharply. What cannot be healed gently must be cut away with pain.

If someone warned privately neglects correction for his sin, then, like a wound that cannot be healed secretly, it must be corrected openly. Manifest sins are not to be cleansed by hidden correction. Those who do harm openly must be rebuked publicly, so that, while they are healed by open reproof, those who had sinned by imitating them may be corrected. When one person is reproved, many are amended.

It is necessary that one be condemned for the salvation of many rather than that many be endangered for the license of one.

Speech must be directed against the offender in the manner demanded by the salvation of the person being corrected. If it is necessary to add some medicinal healing to the word of rebuke, gentleness must nevertheless be retained in the heart.

Teachers sometimes strike their subjects with harsh rebukes, yet do not withdraw from charity toward those whom they correct. Often ecclesiastical discipline appears arrogant [proud] to the arrogant; and what is done piously by the good is thought to be done cruelly by the wicked, because they do not discern with a sound eye what the good do with a sound intention.

Every pontiff must carefully observe that he should act toward those entrusted to him with all the greater caution the more harshly he fears being judged by Christ. For, as it is written:

> With the measure you use, it will be measured back to you (Matthew 7).

Every day we all sin (James 3), and we stumble in many errors. Since we are merciful concerning our own offenses, we must by no means maintain strictness concerning another’s sin.

Many see the vices of others but do not look at their own; and although they themselves are held liable for the greatest crimes, they do not forgive their brothers’ lesser sins. Hypocrites do not feel the beam standing in their own eye, but fix their attention on the splinter lodged in their brother’s eye.

We more easily criticize the vices of others than our own. Often we perceive less clearly that what we judge perverse in others is harmful in ourselves; and what we criticize in others, we are not ashamed to do ourselves.

We more readily attend to each person’s vices than to his virtues. We do not wish to acknowledge what good each person has done, but scrutinize what evil he has done.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

(Gregory, *Homily* 26 on John 20.) [Gregory, on the authority granted bishops to bind and loose: “Holy preachers,” etc.; columns 0872C–0873B.] Holy preachers, who fear God’s strict judgment, become judges of souls; they condemn and release others, although they feared being condemned themselves. Bishops now occupy their place in the Church. Those who receive the rank of governance assume the authority to release and bind.

Great is the honor of the episcopate, but heavy is the burden of this honor. It is hard that one who does not know how to govern his own life should become judge of another’s life.

It often happens that a person whose life is wholly unsuited to the judicial office occupies that office. Consequently, it often occurs that he either condemns the innocent or, himself bound, releases others.

Frequently, when releasing or binding his subjects, he follows the impulses of his own will rather than the merits of the cases. Thus the person who exercises the power of binding and releasing according to his own desires [pleasures], and not according to the merits of his subjects, deprives himself of that very power.

Often a shepherd is moved toward a particular neighbor by hatred or favor. But those who follow either their hatred or their favor in the cases of their subjects cannot judge their subjects justly.

Hence it is rightly said through the prophet:

> They were killing souls that should not die, and they were making alive souls that should not live (Ezekiel 23).

He kills one who should not die when he condemns the righteous, and he attempts to make alive one who will not live when he strives to release the guilty from punishment.

(*Moralia*, Book XIX, chapter 14.) Almighty God, wishing to restrain us from delivering a hasty sentence, although everything is naked and open to his eyes, nevertheless did not wish to judge the evils of Sodom on hearsay. He said:

> The outcry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave. I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the outcry that has come to me, or whether it is not so, that I may know (Genesis 18).

Why does the omnipotent Lord, who knows everything, appear to doubt before investigation, unless to set before us an example of seriousness, so that we do not presume to believe people’s evils before testing them?

What else are we admonished by this example than never to be hasty in delivering a sentence, not to judge matters not investigated, not to be moved by every evil report, and not to believe words indiscriminately without proof?

(*Homily* 26 on John 20.) Cases must therefore be weighed, and then the power of binding and releasing must be exercised. One must see what fault preceded and what repentance followed the fault, so that the pastor’s sentence may release those whom almighty God visits through the grace of compunction.

The superior’s absolution is then true when it follows the judgment of the inner Judge. The resurrection of the four-day-old dead man signifies this well: it demonstrates that the Lord first called the dead man and gave him life, saying:

> Lazarus, come out (John 11).

Afterward, the one who had come out alive was released by the disciples, as it is written:

> And when the one who had been bound with bandages had come out, he then said to his disciples, “Release him and let him go” (ibid.).

This means that the pastors of the Church ought to remove the punishment deserved by the person who was not ashamed to confess what he had done.

The pastors of the Church should strive either to release or to bind with great moderation. But whether the pastor binds justly or unjustly, the pastor’s sentence must nevertheless be feared by the flock, lest the person who is subject to him, even if perhaps unjustly bound, deserve the very sentence of his binding because of another fault.

Each pastor should therefore fear to absolve indiscriminately or to bind. The person who is under the pastor’s authority should fear being bound, even unjustly, and should not rashly criticize his pastor’s judgment, lest, even if he has been unjustly bound, the fault that did not previously exist be created by the pride of his inflated criticism.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

[Column 0873C]

(The same author, *Homily* 4 on the Gospel, Matthew 10, “The Lord sent,” Acts 8.) [Gregory, on bishops who willingly accept gifts for the ordination of a priest: “Some bishops,” etc.; columns 0873C–0874B.] Some bishops habitually turn the gift of the received Spirit into an occasion for trade and subordinate the signs of miracles to the service of greed. Hence Simon, seeing miracles performed through the laying on of hands, wished to obtain the gift of the Holy Spirit for money, so that he might sell at a worse price what he had wrongly purchased.

Hence our Redeemer made a whip out of cords, drove the crowds from the temple, and overturned the seats of those selling doves (John 2). For to sell doves is to confer the laying on of hands, through which the Holy Spirit is received, not for the merit of life but for a reward.

But there are some who do not accept monetary rewards for ordination and yet bestow holy orders for human favor, seeking from that same generosity only the repayment of praise. These people do not give freely what was received freely, because from the office of holiness bestowed upon them they seek the coin of approval.

Thus the prophet Isaiah, when describing a just man, rightly says:

> He who shakes his hands free from every gift (Isaiah 33).

For he does not say, “He who shakes his hands free from a gift,” but adds, “from every gift,” because one kind of gift comes from service, another from the hand, and another from the tongue.

A gift from service is an improperly rendered submission. A gift from the hand is money. A gift from the tongue is favor.

Therefore the person who bestows holy orders shakes his hands free from every gift when, in divine matters, he seeks not only no money but also no human favor.

It often happens that one of these people refuses to accept bodily goods from others, yet, because he does not accept these, seeks greater praise from them. Perhaps he does not think that he has received a gift because he refuses to accept bodily goods.

As was stated above, a gift is sometimes offered from the hand and sometimes from the mouth. The person who gives a coin gives a gift from the hand; the person who offers a word of praise brings forth a gift from the mouth.

Often a priest, although he refuses to accept external gifts—which perhaps suit earthly necessity—for the laying on of hands, nevertheless desires a greater recompense for himself when, wishing to be praised beyond his merit, he seeks a gift from the mouth.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

(From the Council of Nicaea, canon 3, distinction 32.) [The canon begins from the Council of Nicaea concerning women brought into clerics’ households: “The great synod absolutely forbade,” etc.] The great synod absolutely forbade a bishop, presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all who is in the clergy to keep a woman brought in under his roof, unless perhaps she is his mother, sister, or paternal aunt, or one of those persons alone who give no occasion for suspicion.

## CHAPTER XL

(From the same council, canon 17, question 4, and distinction 47.) [Likewise in the same council, chapter 17, concerning clerics who take interest: “Since many,” etc.; column 0874C.] Since many who are established under a rule pursue greed and shameful profits, and, forgetting divine Scripture, which says, “He who has not lent his money at interest,” lend money and demand interest at one percent per month, the holy and great synod rightly decreed that if anyone is found, after this definition, accepting interest, or conducting business by some device or by any method, or demanding *hemiolia*, that is, one-and-a-half times the amount, or devising anything of this sort for the sake of shameful profit, he is to be deposed from the clergy and regarded as outside the rule.

## CHAPTER XLI

(From the same council, canon 18, distinction 93.) [Likewise, concerning the privileges of presbyters, title XVIII: “It has come,” etc.; column 0874D.] It has come to the attention of the holy and great council that in certain places and cities deacons give priests the grace of holy communion, although neither rule nor custom has handed this down: that those who offer the body of Christ should receive it from those who do not possess the power to offer it. It has also become known that certain deacons touch the sacred offerings before bishops.

Let all these practices therefore be cut away, and let deacons remain within their proper measure, knowing that they are ministers of bishops and are ranked below presbyters.

Accordingly, after the presbyters, they shall receive the grace of holy communion, with either the bishop or the presbyter presenting it to them. Nor is it permitted for deacons to sit among the presbyters, because if this is done, it is shown to be contrary to rule and order. If anyone, even after these definitions, refuses to obey, he must cease from the ministry.

## CHAPTER XLII

[Column 0875A]

(From the same council, canon 5, 21, question 1.) [Concerning excommunicated persons in the same council, title V: “Concerning those,” etc.; columns 0875A–B.] Concerning those who are deprived of communion by bishops, whether from the clergy or from the lay order, a regular sentence shall prevail throughout each province: those who are expelled are not to be received by others. But inquiry must be made, lest it appear that someone has been excluded from the congregation through the bishop’s pusillanimity, contentiousness, or any other fault.

In order that this may be investigated more appropriately, it was well decided that councils should be held twice each year in every province, so that, with all the bishops of the province gathered together, such questions might be examined in common by all. Thus those who have plainly offended against their own bishop may reasonably be regarded by everyone as excommunicated, until either the community or the bishop sees fit to issue a more humane sentence in their case.

One council shall be held before the forty days preceding Easter, so that, with every disagreement removed, the purest offering may be presented to God; the second shall be held around the time of autumn.

## CHAPTER XLIII

(From the same council, canon 15, 7, question 1.) [In the same council, that migration ought not to occur: “Because of the great disturbances,” etc.; column 0875C.] Because of the great disturbances and seditions that occur, it was decided that the custom—which appears to have been admitted contrary to rule in certain regions—should be completely abolished, so that no bishop, presbyter, or deacon may be transferred from one city to another.

If anyone, after the definition of the holy and great council, attempts to do such a thing and commits himself to such a proceeding, the action shall be declared wholly void, and he shall be restored to the Church in which he was ordained bishop, presbyter, or deacon.

## CHAPTER XLIV

(From the Council of Chalcedon.) [In the Council of Chalcedon, title XV, that one must not migrate from city to city; title V, concerning those who migrate: “Concerning those who migrate,” etc.] Concerning those who migrate from city to city, whether bishops or clerics, it was decided that the canons established on this matter by the holy Fathers should retain their own force.

## CHAPTER XLV

(From the Council of Nicaea, canon 16, 7, question 1.) [In the Council of Nicaea, concerning those who did not remain in the churches to which they had gone, title XVI: “Whoever rashly,” etc.; column 0875D.] Whoever rashly and dangerously, without keeping the fear of God before his eyes and without recognizing ecclesiastical rule, departs from the church entrusted to him [“entrusted to him” is lacking]—whether he is a presbyter, deacon, or anyone at all who is fully subject to the rule—must by no means be received into another church. Rather, every necessity should be imposed upon him so that he may return to his own parishes.

If he does not do so, he must be deprived of communion. But if anyone attempts boldly to invade another’s jurisdiction and ordain in his own church [“boldly … to ordain” is lacking], without the consent of the bishop from whom the person subject to the rule departed, such an ordination shall be declared invalid.

## CHAPTER XLVI

[Column 0876A]

(From the same council, canon 20.) [Likewise in the same council, concerning bending the knee, title XX: “Since some people,” etc.; column 0876A.] Since some people kneel on the Lord’s Day and during the days of Pentecost, so that everything may be observed consistently in all places, the holy council decided that vows should be offered to the Lord while standing.

## CHAPTER XLVII

(From the Council of Antioch, chapter 4, 11, question 4, 3.) [In the Council of Antioch, concerning condemned persons who attempt to minister, title IV: “If any bishop,” etc.; column 0876B.] If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, dares to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry, then, whether he is a presbyter or deacon, he may in no way have either the hope of restoration in another synod or a place in which to offer satisfaction.

Moreover, all who communicate with him are to be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against those mentioned, they attempt to communicate with them.

## CHAPTER XLVIII
(From the African Council, canon 29.) And this also should be requested [In the African Council, concerning clerics condemned, title XXVIII, “And this also should be requested,” etc.]: that he deign to establish [variant: “may you deign”] that if a cleric of any rank has been condemned by the judgment of the bishops for any crime, he may not be defended either by the churches over which he presided or by any individual, under penalty of loss of money and rank; and that they prescribe that neither age nor sex is to serve as an excuse.

## CHAPTER XLIX

[Col. 0876C] (From the Council of Antioch, canon 7.) No stranger [In the Council of Antioch, concerning the reception of strangers, title 7, “No stranger,” etc.] is to be received without letters of peace, that is, commendatory letters.

## CHAPTER L

(From the Council of Chalcedon, canon 10, 21 q. 1.) A cleric may not be enrolled simultaneously in the churches of two cities [In the Council of Chalcedon, that a cleric may not minister in the churches of two cities, title X, “A cleric may not,” etc.], but only in the church in which he was ordained from the beginning, not in the one to which he has fled as though it were superior, out of a desire for empty glory. Those who do this must be recalled to their own church, in which they were first ordained, and must minister there alone. But if someone has already been transferred from one church to another, he is in no way to share in the property of the former church, or of the martyr-shrines belonging to it, or of its poorhouses [variant: poor-feeding houses], or of its guesthouses. As for those who, after the decree of this great and universal synod, dare to perpetrate anything of what has been prohibited, the holy synod decreed that they are to be deprived of their proper rank.

## CHAPTER LI

(From the same council, canon 13.) Foreign clerics [Also in the same council, that foreign clerics should not minister without commendatory letters, title XIII, “Foreign clerics,” etc.] and readers must nowhere minister in another city without the commendatory letters of their own bishop.

## CHAPTER LII

[Col. 0877A]

(From the Council of Laodicea, canon 41.) A priest or cleric must not set out without canonical letters [In the Council of Laodicea, that those serving in the sacred ministry must not travel without letters, title XVI, “That it is not proper,” etc.].

## CHAPTER LIII

(From the Council of Sardica, canon 16.) Bishop Hosius [In the Council of Sardica, concerning clerics removed from communion and not to be received by another bishop, title XV, “Bishop Hosius,” etc.] said: “This also pleases everyone: whether a deacon, a presbyter, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his own bishop and has gone to another bishop, if the bishop to whom he has fled knows that he was cast out by his own bishop, he ought not to grant him communion. If he does so, let him know that, when the bishops have been summoned, he will have to give an account of the matter.” Everyone said: “This statute will preserve peace and safeguard harmony.”

## CHAPTER LIV

(From the Council of Carthage, canon 29.) It also pleased the whole council [In the Council of Carthage, title XXIX, “It also pleased,” etc.] that whoever has been excommunicated for his own neglect—whether a bishop or any cleric—and during the time of his excommunication has presumptuously received communion before a hearing, is to be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.

## CHAPTER LV

(From the Council of Sardica, canon 18.) Bishop Januarius [In the Council of Sardica, concerning clerics belonging to another bishop and not to be solicited, title VIII, “Bishop Januarius,” etc.] said: “Let your holiness also establish that no bishop may solicit an ecclesiastical minister belonging to another bishop’s city and ordain him in his own parishes.” Everyone said: “It pleases us, because discord ordinarily arises from such disputes; and therefore, by the judgment of all [the words ‘and therefore … judgment’ are absent], no one should dare to do this.”

## CHAPTER LVI

(From the African Council, canon 57.) It also pleased [In the African Council, concerning those who have once read in church and cannot be promoted by others, title 57, “It also pleased,” etc.] that whoever has read even once in a church may not be taken up by another church for the clerical office. And they subscribed. Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage, [Col. 0877D] consented to this decree and subscribed after it had been read aloud. The other bishops likewise subscribed.

## CHAPTER LVII

(From the Council of Carthage, canon 31.) It also pleased [In the Council of Carthage, concerning clerics promoted by their bishops who refuse obedience and do not remain there from which they were unwilling to depart, title 31, “It also pleased,” etc.] that whatever clerics or deacons, for the needs of the churches, have not obeyed their bishops when the bishops wished to promote them in their own church to a higher rank, must not minister in their former rank in the place from which they refused to depart.

## CHAPTER LVIII

[Col. 0878A]

(From Pope Leo’s Letter 82 to Anastasius of Thessalonica, chapter 9, 19 q. 2.) No one is to receive or solicit another bishop’s cleric against the will of his own bishop, unless perhaps the matter is agreed between the giver and the recipient as an act of charity. For he is guilty of a grave injury who dares either to entice away or to retain from his brother’s church what is more useful or more valuable. Therefore, if the matter occurs within the province, the metropolitan shall compel the fugitive cleric to return to his own church. But if he has withdrawn farther away, he shall be recalled by the authority of the metropolitan’s command, so that no opportunity may be left either for greed or ambition.

## CHAPTER LIX

(From the African Council, canon 9.) No bishops or clerics are to dine together in church [In the African Council, title 9, “That no one,” etc.], unless perhaps, while passing through, they take refreshment there because of the necessities of lodging. The people, too, are to be prohibited from such banquets as far as possible.

## CHAPTER LX

(From the Council of Laodicea, distinction 44.) Those devoted to the sacred ministry, from presbyters down to deacons, and the remaining ecclesiastical order—that is, down to subdeacons, readers, singers, exorcists, and doorkeepers—and those among the continent and monks must not enter taverns [In the Council of Laodicea, title 24, “That it is not proper,” etc.].

[Note: From this point onward, in the Vatican codex the chapter titles are absent, and only the numbers of the canons are noted; these will be given in the present annotations only when they differ from those in the printed editions.]

## CHAPTER LXI

(From the Council of Carthage, canon 5.) Bishop Aurelius said: “The desire for avarice—which no one doubts to be the mother of all evils—must therefore be restrained, and no one must usurp another’s boundaries or, for a reward, overstep the limits established by the Fathers. Nor may any cleric at all receive interest on any matter. If this seems right both to your holiness and to this council, let it be established by the present decision.” (First Council of Carthage, chapter 13.)

Bishop Gratus said: “New proposals, whether obscure or concealed under a general category, will receive their form after we have examined them. But concerning matters that divine Scripture has most clearly decreed, judgment must not be delayed; rather, it must be carried out. Therefore, what is condemned in laypeople must be condemned in clerics with much greater force.”

The whole council said: “No one acts against the prophets or against the Gospels without danger.”

## CHAPTER LXII

[Col. 0878D]

(From the first decretal of Pope Leo, 14 q. 4.) We have also judged that this must not be passed over: some, seized by a desire for disgraceful profit, practice usury and wish to grow rich by lending at interest. We grieve that this falls not only upon those established in clerical office, but even upon laypeople who desire to be called Christians. We decree that this be punished more severely in those who are convicted, so that every opportunity for sinning may be removed.

## CHAPTER LXIII

(From the Council of Ancyra, canon 13.) Concerning those who are presbyters and deacons in the clergy and abstain from meat: it was decided that they may indeed touch meat and, if they wish, abstain from it. But if they abominate it to such an extent that they consider even vegetables cooked with meat unfit to eat, they must cease from their rank, as people who do not consent to the rule.

## CHAPTER LXIV

(From the Council of Neocaesarea, title XIII, canon 14, distinction 93.) There must be seven deacons, even if the city is very large. The Book of the Acts of the Apostles also indicates this.

## CHAPTER LXV

(From the Council of Gangra, canon 2, distinction 30.) If anyone condemns a person who eats meat—apart from blood, meat sacrificed to idols, and strangled meat (Acts 6)—with religion and faith, as though such a person had no hope because of this consumption, let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER LXVI

(From the same council, canon 8.) If anyone gives or receives offerings apart from the bishop, or apart from one appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, let both the giver and the receiver be anathema.

## CHAPTER LXVII

(From the same council, canon 10, distinction 30.) If anyone among those who preserve virginity for the Lord exalts himself against married people, let him be anathema.

## LXVIII

(From the same council, title 19, canon 18, distinction 30.) If anyone fasts on the Lord’s Day because of supposed continence or out of obstinacy, let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER LXIX

[Col. 0879C]

(From the same council, distinction 30.) If anyone among those who practice continence, without bodily necessity, proudly dissolves the fasts handed down in common and observed by the Church, driven by the impulse of his own thought, let him be anathema.

## CHAPTER LXX

(From the Council of Antioch, canon 2.) All who enter the church of God and hear the sacred Scriptures, yet do not join the people in prayer but, because of some intemperance, turn away from receiving holy communion, are to be removed from the church until they show the fruits of repentance through confession and obtain forgiveness through prayers.

## CHAPTER LXXI

(From the same council, canon 3, 7 q. 1.) If any presbyter or deacon, or indeed anyone belonging to the clergy, abandons his own parish and hastens to another, then moves away entirely and strives to remain for a long time in another parish, he must no longer minister there—especially if he has scorned to obey his bishop when summoned and admonished to return to his own parish. If he persists in this indiscipline, he must be removed from the ministry in every way, so that he may never find a place of restoration. But if another bishop receives someone condemned for this reason, that bishop too is to be punished by the common synod, as one who dissolves ecclesiastical constitutions.

## CHAPTER LXXII

(From the same council, canon 6, 11 q. 3.) If anyone has been deprived of communion by his own bishop, he must not be received by others until he has been reconciled with his own bishop; or else he must appear before the synod that is being convened and make satisfaction on his own behalf.

## CHAPTER LXXIII

(From the same council, canon 11, 13 q. 8.) If any bishop, presbyter, or any member of the Church subject to a rule approaches the emperor without the advice and letters of the bishops of the province, and especially of the metropolitan, he must be rejected and cast out—not only from communion but also from the rank of which he appears to be a participant—because he has attempted to trouble the ears of the venerable ruler against the laws of the Church. If necessity therefore demands that he approach the ruler, the matter must be undertaken with the deliberation and advice of the metropolitan [Col. 0880B] and of the other bishops residing in the same province. They must also accompany the departing petitioner with their letters.

## CHAPTER LXXIV

(From the same council, canon 12, 21 q. 5.) If a presbyter or deacon has been condemned by his own bishop, or a bishop perhaps by a synod, and has troubled the emperor’s ears, he must appeal to a greater council of bishops and submit to the many bishops whatever they may judge to be just; then he must await their investigations and judgments. But if, disregarding these matters, they trouble the emperor, we judge them worthy of no pardon, entitled to no place of satisfaction, and not to be granted any hope of future restoration.

## CHAPTER LXXV

[Col. 0880C]

(From the Council of Laodicea, title V, canon 6, distinction 46.) Priests and clerics must not lend at interest or receive what is called *sescupla*, that is, the principal sum together with half of the principal.

## CHAPTER LXXVI

(From the same council, canon 15.) Apart from those who are regularly singers, who sing from the book, no others should ascend the pulpit and sing psalms in the church.

## CHAPTER LXXVII

(From the same council, canon 20, distinction 93.) A deacon must not sit in the presence of a presbyter, but must sit at the presbyter’s command. Likewise, the deacon is to be honored by those who serve under him, that is, by subdeacons and all clerics.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

(From the same council, canon 25, distinction 93.) Subdeacons must not give the bread or bless the chalice.

## CHAPTER LXXIX

(From the same council, canon 26, distinction 60.) Those who have not been ordained by bishops may not perform exorcisms, either in churches or in houses.

## CHAPTER LXXX

(From the same council, canon 28, distinction 42.) Banquets called agapae must not be held in the dwelling places of God, that is, in the churches of the Lord; nor may anyone eat or spread couches within the house of God.

## CHAPTER LXXXI

[Col. 0881A]

(From the same council, canon 42.) A priest or cleric must not set out without the command of his own bishop.

## CHAPTER LXXXII

(From the same council, canon 44.) Women must not enter the altar area.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII

(From the same council, canon 54, distinction 5.) Priests and clerics must not attend any spectacles in theaters or at weddings; rather, before the stage performers enter, they should rise and depart. Nor should priests or clerics hold banquets from collections or feasts. This is not fitting even for laypeople.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

[Col. 0881B]

(From the same council, canon 54, distinction 44.) Offerings must not be celebrated in private houses by bishops or presbyters.

## CHAPTER LXXXV

(From the Council of Chalcedon, title LVII, canon 7, question 3.) Those who have once been assigned to the clergy, or who have chosen the life of monks, are not to enter military service or any worldly dignity. Those who attempt this and do not repent, so as to return to what they first chose for the Lord, are to be anathematized.

## CHAPTER LXXXVI

(From the same council, title IX, canon 9, 11 q. 1.) If a cleric has a case against another cleric, he must not abandon his own bishop and rush to secular courts; rather, the matter must first be aired before his own bishop, or, with that bishop’s advice, they may obtain judgment before whomever both parties choose. If anyone acts otherwise, he is to be subject to canonical corrections. But if a cleric has a case against his own bishop or against another bishop, he is to be judged by the synod of the province. If a bishop or cleric has a complaint against the metropolitan of the same province, he should appeal either to the primate of the diocese or to the see of the royal city of Constantinople, and be judged before him.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII

(From the same council, canon 20, distinction 71.) Clerics ministering in a church, as we have already established, must not be appointed to the church of another city; they must be content with the churches in which they were first worthy to minister, except those who, having lost their own provinces, have necessarily transferred to another church.

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII

(From the same council, canon 22, 12 q. 2.) Clerics may not, after the death of their bishop, plunder property belonging to him, as ancient canons have also established. If they attempt to do this, they will be subject to the danger of losing their ranks.

## CHAPTER LXXXIX

(From the Council of Carthage, canon 32.) It also pleased the council that bishops, presbyters, deacons, or any clerics who were ordained possessing nothing, and who during the time of their episcopate or clerical office purchase fields or any estates in their own name, are to be held guilty of invading the Lord’s property, unless, after being admonished, they transfer those very things to the same church. But if something comes to them personally through someone’s generosity or through inheritance from their family, they may dispose of it in a way fitting their purpose. If they deviate backward from that purpose, they are to be judged unworthy of ecclesiastical honor, as reprobates.

## CHAPTER XC

(From the African Council, canon 7, distinction 44.) Clerics must not enter taverns for the sake of eating or drinking, unless compelled by the necessity of travel.

## CHAPTER XCI

Bishop Epigonius [From the same council, canon 21.] said: “This has been established in many councils and must now also be confirmed by your wisdom, most blessed brothers: no bishop may seize for himself another’s cleric, against the will of the one to whom that cleric belongs.”

## CHAPTER XCII

(From the decretal of Pope Leo, Letter 1, chapter 4.) We have also judged it necessary to warn that, just as no cleric should practice lending at interest in his own name, so no one should attempt to do so in another’s name. For it is an unseemly crime to devote one’s own guilt to another’s advantage.
