The only interest we ought to regard and practice is this: that what we mercifully give here, we may be able to receive from the Lord, who will repay it manifold and with an enduring return.

## CHAPTER XCIII

[Col. 0882C]

(From the decretal of Pope Gelasius, Letter I, chapter 15, distinction 88.) It was fitting that we should not now pass over what a report recently sent to us from the regions of Picenum has announced: namely, that many clerics are intent upon dishonorable business and disgraceful profits, observing without shame the Gospel reading in which our Lord himself is said to have driven the merchants from the temple with whips (Matt. 21), and not recalling the Apostle’s words: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business” (2 Tim. 2). They also pretend not to hear the Psalmist David singing: “Because I have not known business dealings, I shall enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. 70).

Therefore, let such men know that henceforth they must abstain from profits of this kind and cease from every device and desire of business dealings; or, whatever their rank, let them immediately be compelled to withdraw from clerical offices, since the house of God both is and ought to be called a house of prayer, lest it rather become a workshop of commerce and a den of robbers (Matt. 21).

## CHAPTER XCIV

(Excerpt from St. Jerome’s letter to Nepotianus on the life of clerics.) You ask me in letters from across the sea, dearest Nepotianus—and you ask repeatedly—that I set out for you in a short book the rules for living well, and how one who, having abandoned the service of the world, has begun either to be a monk or a cleric may keep to Christ’s straight path and not be swept into the various byways of vice.

*(In the same letter, after much else.)* I know that from your uncle, the blessed Heliodorus, who is now a bishop of Christ, you have both learned holy things and continue to learn them daily, and that you have his way of life as a model of virtue. But receive also what is ours, whatever its quality may be; join this little book to his little book, so that when he has trained you as a monk, this one may teach you to be a perfect cleric.

Therefore, let the cleric who serves Christ’s Church first interpret his title, and, once the definition of the name has been given, strive to be what he is called. For if *cleros* in Greek is called *sors*—“lot”—in Latin, clerics are so called either because they belong to the Lord’s lot or because the Lord himself is the lot, that is, the portion, of clerics. Whoever is himself the Lord’s portion or has the Lord as his portion must show himself such that he possesses the Lord and is possessed by the Lord.

Whoever possesses the Lord and says with the Prophet, “The Lord is my portion” (Ps. 72), can possess nothing outside the Lord. But if he has anything else besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion. For example, if he has gold, silver, estates, or varied furnishings, the Lord does not deign to be his portion together with these portions.

But if I am the Lord’s portion and the cord of his inheritance, and I receive no portion among the other tribes, but, as a Levite and priest, live on tithes and, serving at the altar, am sustained by the altar’s offering, then, having food and clothing, I will be content with these and, naked, follow the naked cross.

I therefore beg you, and again and again I shall admonish you: do not think of the clerical office as a kind of ancient military service; that is, do not seek worldly profits in Christ’s service. Do not possess more than you had when you began to be a cleric, lest it be said to you: “Their portion will not profit them” (Jer. 12).

Let the poor and strangers, and Christ as their fellow guest, know your little table. Flee the cleric who is a merchant, who becomes rich from poverty and glorious from lowliness, as though he were a plague.

“Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15). You despise gold; another loves it. You trample wealth; he pursues it. You cherish gentleness, silence, and privacy; he delights in talkativeness, a hardened brow, forums, streets, and doctors’ shops. In such great discord of character, what harmony can there be?

Let women’s feet seldom, or never, wear out your little dwelling. Either disregard all girls and virgins of Christ equally, or love them equally. Do not remain under the same roof with them, and do not trust in past chastity. You cannot be holier than David or wiser than Solomon. Always remember that a woman drove the inhabitant of paradise from his possession (Gen. 3).

When you are sick, let some holy brother, or your sister, or your mother, or any woman whose faith is approved by all, attend you. If such relatives, chaste persons, are not available, the Church supports many old women who can provide the service and receive a benefit by ministering, so that your illness too may bear the fruit of almsgiving.

I know that some have recovered in body and begun to grow sick in spirit. The person whose face you frequently look upon ministers to you dangerously. If, because of your clerical office, you visit either a widow or a virgin, never enter the house alone. Have companions whose association will not bring you into disrepute.

If a reader, acolyte, or psalmist follows you, let them be adorned not with clothing but with character; let them not curl their hair with a curling iron, but promise chastity by their bearing. Do not sit alone with a woman alone, privately and without an arbiter or witness.

If something must be discussed more familiarly, she has an older nurse of the household—whether a virgin, widow, or married woman. She is not so inhuman as to have no one besides you in whom she dares to confide.

Avoid every suspicion; and whatever can plausibly be fabricated, prevent it from being fabricated beforehand. Frequent little gifts, handkerchiefs, ribbons, garments applied to the face, offered and tasted foods, and flattering, sweet little letters have no place in holy love.

“My honey, my light, and my desire” is Christ. Born in a poor house and a rustic hut, where I could scarcely satisfy my growling stomach with millet and coarse bread, I now despise fine flour and honey. I know the species and names of fish; I know on what shore shells have been gathered; I distinguish the regions by the flavors of birds; and the rarity of foods, and finally even their absence, delight me.

Read the divine Scriptures frequently—indeed, let sacred reading never leave your hands. Pray often, and with the body bent, raise your mind to the Lord. Keep frequent vigils, and often sleep with an empty stomach.

Flee rumors, little boasts, and flattering sycophants as enemies. Distribute relief to the poor and to the brothers from your own hand and expense. Do not seek humble clothing with a proud heart. Avoid the company of worldly people, especially the powerful.

Have the simplicity of a dove, so that you plot no deceit against anyone, and the cunning of a serpent, so that you are not outmaneuvered by the snares of others. For a Christian, it is not much less blameworthy to be able to deceive than to be able to be deceived.

The true temple of Christ is the soul of the believer. Adorn it, clothe it, offer gifts to it, and receive Christ in it. For I do not know how the person who displeases Christ can please the world more.

Now let us bear Christ’s cross, and count riches as mud. Why are we surprised that Christ calls mammon unjust (Luke 16)? Why do we admire and love what Peter declares that he does not possess (Acts 3)? You must detest the banquets of worldly people, especially those who swell with public honors. It is shameful for the lictors of consuls and soldiers to keep watch before the doors of a priest of Christ, who was crucified and poor and even ate food belonging to others; and for the governor of a province to dine more comfortably at your house than in his palace. If you allege that you do these things in order to plead for the wretched and the subject, a worldly judge pays more regard to a continent cleric than to a rich one, and will venerate your holiness more than your wealth. Or if he is such that he does not listen to clerics except among cups, I shall gladly lack a benefit of that kind and pray to Christ for the judge, since he is better able and quicker to help. For it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man; it is better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes.

Never smell of wine, lest you hear that saying of the philosopher: “This is not offering a kiss, but proffering wine.” The Apostle condemns drunken priests (1 Tim. 5), and the old law forbids them. “Those who serve the altar shall not drink wine or strong drink” (Lev. 10). In the Hebrew language, *sicera* is the name for every drink capable of causing intoxication, whether it is made from grain, from the juice of fruits, when honeycombs are boiled into a sweet barbarian drink, or when the fruits of palms are pressed into a liquid and made richer in color by cooked grains. Flee everything that intoxicates and overturns the mind’s settled state just as you flee wine. I do not say this because God’s creation is condemned by us. For the Lord too was called a drinker of wine (Matt. 11), and Timothy, suffering from his stomach, was relieved by a small draught of wine (1 Tim. 5). But in drinking we require moderation according to age, health, and bodily constitution. If, however, I burn with youth without wine, am inflamed by the heat of my blood, and have a vigorous, robust body, I shall gladly abstain from a cup in which there is suspicion of poison.

It is well said among the Greeks, though I do not know whether it has the same force in our language: “A fat belly does not produce a subtle mind.” Impose on yourself only as many fasts as you can bear. Let your fasts be pure, chaste, simple, moderate, and not superstitious. What good is it not to eat oil, while seeking certain troublesome and difficult foods—figs, pepper, nuts, dates, fine flour, honey, pistachios? The cultivation of so many gardens is troubled so that we may not eat coarse bread. Moreover, I hear of some who, contrary to the nature of things and people, do not drink water or eat bread, but take delicate little draughts and crushed vegetables, and drink beet juice not from a cup but from a shell. The strongest fast is water and bread; but because it brings no glory, and we all live on bread and water, it is not thought to be a public and common fast.

Beware of angling for people’s gossip, lest you exchange the praise of the populace for an offense against God. “If I were still pleasing men,” says the Apostle, “I should not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1). He ceased to please men and became Christ’s servant. Through good report and bad, on the right hand and on the left, Christ’s soldier proceeds: he is not puffed up by praise nor broken by reproach; he does not swell with riches nor shrink under poverty; and he despises both glad and sad things. By day the sun does not burn him, nor the moon by night.

I do not want you to pray at the corners of streets, lest the popular breeze divert the straight course of your prayers. I do not want you to enlarge your fringes, display phylacteries, and, while your conscience protests, be surrounded by Pharisaic ambition. On these hang the Gospel, the law, and the prophets. Faithful reader, you understand with me what I leave unsaid and what I say all the more by silence. As many rules as there are kinds of glory may beset you. How much better it would be to wear these things not on the body but in the heart—to have God as one’s patron, not the gaze of men! Do you wish to know what adornments the Lord seeks? Possess justice, prudence, temperance, and courage. With these four parts of heaven enclose yourself, that the four-horse chariot may carry you, like Christ’s charioteer, swiftly to the goal. Nothing is more precious than this necklace, nothing more distinguished than this variety of gems. You are adorned, girded, and protected on every side: they are both your ornament and your defense; the gems are turned into shields.

Take care also that neither your tongue nor your ears itch—that is, neither speak ill of others yourself nor listen to others speaking ill. “Sitting, you spoke against your brother; against the son of your mother you laid a stumbling-block” (Ps. 49), etc. Spare your tongue from detraction, guard your words, and know that by everything you say about others you are judged by your own sentence, and that you yourself will be convicted in the very things you reproved in others. Nor is this a just excuse: “I cannot do harm when others report it.” No one willingly relates matters to an unwilling listener. Therefore, dearest brother, let it be your duty not only to keep your eyes chaste but also your tongue. Never discuss women’s beauty, and let not one household learn through you what is done in another’s house. Love the houses of all Christians as though they were your own. A cleric who is often invited to dinner and does not refuse is more easily despised. Let us never ask; let us rarely accept when invited. For it is more blessed to give than to receive. For somehow even the very person who begs to give, once you have received, judges you more cheaply; and, remarkably, if you have rejected him while he was asking, he venerates you more afterward.

How can clerics be agents and stewards of other people’s houses and estates when they are commanded to despise their own resources? To steal something from a friend is theft; to defraud the Church is sacrilege. To receive what is to be distributed to the poor, while many are hungry, and either to wish to keep it safely or timidly, or—what is the most manifest crime—to take something from it, surpasses the cruelty of all robbers. Another is tormented by hunger, and you decide how much is enough for his stomach. Either distribute at once what you have received; or, if you are a timid steward, release the donor so that he may distribute his own gift. I do not want your purse to be full on my account. No one can keep my property better than I can. He is the best steward who reserves nothing for himself.

You have compelled me, dearest Nepotianus, by writing such things, to expose myself to be pierced by everyone’s tongues. For either nothing should have been written, lest we undergo human judgment—which you forbade me to do—or, if we write, we should know that the weapons of all slanderers are to be hurled against us. I beg them to be quiet and cease slandering. For we wrote not as enemies but as friends. Nor did we attack those who sin, but warned them not to sin. We were severe judges not only of them but also of ourselves, and, wishing to remove the speck from another’s eye, first cast out our own beam. I have injured no one; my writing has named no one. My discourse has assailed no one in particular. It is a general discussion of vices. Whoever wishes to be angry with me will first confess of himself that he is such a person.

## CHAPTER XCV

(Excerpt from blessed Jerome on the training of clerics, from his letter to the presbyter Paulinus.) I beg you, dearest brother, to flee crowds of people, official duties, greetings, and banquets as though they were chains of pleasure. Let your meal be cheap and taken in the evening. Regard vegetables and legumes, and sometimes little fish, as the height of luxury. Whoever desires Christ and feeds on that bread does not greatly concern himself with how precious the foods are from which he produces excrement. Whatever is not perceived after the appetite has been satisfied should be the same to you as bread and vegetables.

Let sacred reading always be in your hand. Pray frequently, and with the body bent, raise your mind to the Lord. Keep frequent vigils, and sleep often with an empty stomach. Flee rumors, little displays of glory, and flattering sycophants as enemies.

With your own hand distribute relief from your resources to the poor and to the brothers. Do not seek the humility of clothing with a puffed-up spirit. Avoid the company of worldly people, especially the powerful.

Have the simplicity of a dove, so that you devise no deceit against anyone, and the cunning of a serpent, so that you are not outmaneuvered by the snares of others. For a Christian, it is not much different in vice whether one can deceive or can be deceived.

The true temple of Christ is the soul of the believer: adorn it, clothe it, offer gifts to it, and receive Christ in it. For I do not know how the person who displeases Christ can please the world more.

## CHAPTER XCVI
*(The same author, from the letter to Rusticus, title XVI.)* I say, then, that if the desire for the clerical state attracts you, learn what you may teach, and offer Christ a rational sacrifice. Do not be a soldier before you are a recruit; do not be a teacher before you are a disciple. It is neither within my humility nor within my competence [Col. 0887D] to pass judgment on clerics or to say anything unfavorable about the ministers of the churches. Let them have their own order and rank. If you maintain that rank, the book addressed to Nepotianus, once published, will be able to teach you how you ought to live in it. I therefore want prayer to be without interruption, and your mind to be ever watchful, not open to wandering thoughts; let body and soul alike be directed toward the Lord. Conquer anger by patience. Love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Nor should your mind be vacant, exposed to various disturbances: if these settle in your breast, they will dominate you and lead you into the greatest sin. Do some work, so that the devil may always find you occupied. Remember that Christ’s apostles too, although they had authority to live from the Gospel [Col. 0888A], worked with their hands so as to burden no one; and they gave others relief, from whom they ought to have reaped material things in return for spiritual things (1 Cor. IX). So act and live in the monastery that you may deserve to be a cleric; that you may stain your youth with no defilement; that you may come to Christ’s altar like a virgin proceeding from the bridal chamber; and that you may have a good reputation among outsiders. Let women who know your name not know your face. When you reach mature age—provided that your life has accompanied you well—and either the people or the bishop of the city chooses you for the clergy, do what belongs to clerics and follow the better among them, because in every condition and rank the worst are mingled with the best. Learn for a long time what you are to teach. Do not believe your flatterers; indeed, do not willingly lend your ear even to your mockers.

## CHAPTER XCVII

[Col. 0888B]

*(The same author, from the letter to Heliodorus: What distinguishes a cleric from a monk.)* To be unwilling to be a perfect monk is to sin. But once expelled from that rank, you will appeal to the clerical state. Dare I say anything about those who certainly remain in their own cities? Far be it from me to speak unfavorably of those who, succeeding to the apostolic rank, fashion Christ’s body with their sacred mouths; through whom we too are Christians; who, possessing the keys of the kingdom of heaven, judge before the day of judgment; and who preserve the Lord’s bride in sober chastity.

But, as I have briefly touched upon above, the cause of monks is one thing, that of clerics another. Clerics feed the sheep; I am fed. They live from the altar; for me, as for a fruitless tree, the axe is laid at the root if I do not bring a gift to the altar (Matt. XVI and XVIII). Nor can I plead poverty, since in the Gospel the Lord praised the old widow who contributed two small coins, all that she had left for herself (Deut. XVII). I may not sit before the presbyter; but he may, if I sin, hand me over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus.

Under the old law, moreover, whoever had not obeyed the priests was either stoned by the people outside the camp or, with his neck subjected to the sword, expiated his contempt in blood. Now the disobedient is cut down by a spiritual blade; or, expelled from the church, he is torn apart by the ravenous mouths of demons.

## CHAPTER XCVIII

*(The same author, from the letter to Oceanus, on the life of clerics.)* You asked me to explain briefly how clerics ought to live. For this reason many of my malicious rivals lie in wait for me, because I do not keep silent about the truth. The first temptations of clerics are frequent approaches to women. This sex displays clerics in a blameworthy light. What have you truly to do with women, you who converse with the Lord at the altar? Everyone in public—farmers and vine-dressers in the countryside—will severely tear you apart if you insist on living with women contrary to the rule of the faith.

And because, as I think, you desire to be found irreproachable, fortify yourself with a good reputation. Were women present in the choir of the apostles? Forbid virgins to live with you, even those who are of your own family. Do you love them? Have them live outside; visit them frequently, accompanied by clerics, so that, while you enter secretly and alone, you do not stain your reputation. Married men and continent men are instructed differently to undertake ecclesiastical ministry and its burden. Cohabitation of women with clerics is in no way prescribed. Woman is the devil’s door, the path of iniquity, the scorpion’s sting, and a harmful kind. When straw approaches, she kindles fire. With flaming fire a woman strikes the conscience of the man who lives with her and burns up the foundations of the mountains.

I judge that if women live with men, the devil’s snare will not be lacking—the devil who from the beginning has trapped sin through them. Lust tames iron minds. “If someone binds fire to his breast, will his garments not be burned? Or if someone walks over burning coals, will he not burn his feet?” Believe me: a man who is joined to the visits of women cannot dwell with the Lord with his whole heart.

But he says: “Whoever walks uprightly,” he says, “walks confidently” (Prov. X). Well and cleverly said; yet one must have a good reputation among those who are outside. Although you walk before the Lord, you must nevertheless provide what is good before men, because the children of darkness are more cunning than the children of light. When you do not cut off this practice, you give your accusers an opportunity. You have handed yourself over to the bites of detractors if you do not abandon the company of *agapetae*—women devoted to religious companionship.

Are you kind? I rejoice. Are you chaste? That is false. If you seek chastity, love in your mind the woman whom you see living well; do not associate with her through frequent bodily display. It is not soft clothing that makes a cleric or a priest, but the chaste intention of the mind. This preserves in you the devotion owed to honor. Honor is more gloriously preserved by the reputation of good works.

Priests—and indeed the other ranks of clerics, as stated above—ought to be separated from women. If, then, you judge that on account of family affection you cannot dismiss them in any way, remember that Tamar was violated by her brother Amnon (I Reg. XIII). This is precisely what I am pursuing, dearest: wherever there is the life of one household, the pleasure of the flesh is not easily removed. When two are together, if one cannot speak of what he desires, he is at least tempted. The removal of the man therefore places the weapons of chastity, builds a camp in better ground, and strengthens the honor of modesty.

Even Mary, the mother of the Lord, could have remained with the choir of the apostles if it had been permitted. After the trial of her suffering at Antioch, Paul forbade Thecla to continue on with him. No soldier goes to war with his wife. I do not begrudge affection: let your enduring love be with chaste virgins; then you will place merit in what is good and improve your reputation.

Concerning the gathering of young women, however, I advise fittingly that in the second week you should come for a visit to bless the community—but not alone, lest gossipers wear you down by tearing you apart with their tongues. Neighbors desire to examine another person’s life, not their own.

Therefore accept worthily the instructions of our words and the admonitions of humility which, at the prompting of fraternal affection, we have expressed with the pen; read them sweetly. Now, so that the priest of the divine altar may not be blameworthy, I shall explain, as far as the Lord grants, a few matters from the Apostle’s remaining testimonies. Let the preceding matters that have been stated suffice.

But lest anyone with little understanding think that the Apostle spoke above about bishops, I am pleased to recall what was prescribed to Timothy concerning deacons and what was prescribed to Titus concerning presbyters. Yet it must not be passed over that I explain the preceding statement. Both the new and the old commandment judged that a priest should be chosen as the husband of one wife. Because many bishops admitted twice-married men to the ministry, they argued as follows: “That woman was a concubine; this one is a wife.” As though these were not the same dealings of shame in the one as in the other, in the woman who is called a wife; or as though, because he had not drawn up marriage documents, there had been no other desire.

By no means is it fitting for twice-married men, or for those entangled in the chains of concubines, to undertake the priestly ministry. It is written and prescribed in Leviticus what sort of priests ought to be chosen. If, then, the cleric is monogamous but his wife has been married twice, do not admit him to the ministry (chap. XXI). The same Apostle gave these instructions to Titus concerning the ordination of clerics (Tit. I).

And because the book is awaiting its conclusion, let us return to the point from which we digressed. Even if two or three handmaids of God are living together, it is not fitting for the priest to enter to them alone. Whoever does not observe these commands is the enemy of his own soul. But if, after our admonitions, some cleric seeks to love *agapetae* more than Christ, let him be summoned according to synodal rule, and let the commands of the Fathers defined at Nicaea be read to him (Council of Nicaea, canon 3). If he then avoids and abandons the aforesaid summons, we have obtained the greatest gain. Otherwise such a man is to be anathematized by the Church.

Women living with men produce thorns and pierce the secrets of minds with a sharp blade. Alas for the crime! It is painful to say, but it must not be passed over. These women know how to marry Christ, not clerics. Solitude makes a cleric, not public association. Read that such a man ought to be solitary, as Jeremiah described: “He will sit alone and be silent” (Lam. III). And Jesus, leaving the apostles, went alone to pray (Matt. XIV). The angel found Mary alone in the inner chamber, not speaking with an *agapeta*, and she trembled at the entrance of a man.

The Apostle prescribed that a cleric to be ordained should be hospitable (Tit. I). In obedience to this command, the patriarch Abraham and Lot received angels, because they loved guests (Gen. XVIII); so too Onesiphorus received Paul, the fountain of teaching. Let these be your examples, and do not allow a resident stranger to pass by without eating bread with you.

It follows: “Not a striker.” The Apostle is not describing a boxer, but one who does not strike the consciences of individuals. Let him be moderate, not puffed up, not drunk, and rule his own household well. It would be exceedingly terrible if a cleric’s household were disparaged. The priest’s reputation among the people is harmed when the people speak ill of his relatives. Above all this, the Apostle commands the cleric to lay the foundations of a good reputation, so that the testimony of good works may be confirmed by a chaste affection.

## CHAPTER XCIX

[Col. 0891A]

*(Isidore, from the book of Offices: On clerics.)* Accordingly, all who have been ordained in the ranks of ecclesiastical ministry are generally called clerics. Our teachers say that they are called *cleros* or clerics because Matthias was chosen by lot, and we read that he was the first ordained by the apostles (Acts I). Likewise, at that time all those whom the leaders of the churches ordained were chosen by lot. For *cleros* means “lot.” Hence inheritance is called in Greek *cleronomia*, and an heir *cleronomos*. Therefore, they say, they are called clerics because they are assigned by lot to the inheritance of the Lord, or because the Lord himself is their lot, as it is written concerning them, with the Lord speaking: “I am their inheritance” (Num. XVIII).

Therefore those who possess God as their inheritance ought to strive to serve God without any impediment from the world and to seek to be poor in spirit (Deut. XVIII), so that they may fittingly say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. XV).

## CHAPTER C

*(The same author, On Offices, book II, chapter 2.)* The law of the Fathers therefore provides that those ordained in this way, separated from ordinary life, should abstain from the pleasures of the world. Let them attend neither spectacles nor public displays; let them avoid public banquets, and cultivate private ones that are not only modest but also sober. Let them not engage in usury, nor pursue disgraceful money-making occupations or any fraudulent enterprise. Let them flee the love of money as the source of every crime; let them reject secular offices and businesses; let them not undertake ranks of honor through ambition; and let them not accept gifts in exchange for the benefits of God’s healing.

Let them beware of deceits and conspiracies; let them flee hatred and rivalry, slander and envy. Let them walk neither with wandering eyes, nor with an unbridled tongue, nor with a bold, swollen manner; instead, let them display the modesty and shamefastness of the mind through simple dress and bearing. Let them utterly abhor obscenity of speech as well as of action. Let them avoid very frequent visits to widows and virgins. Let them in no way seek companionship with unrelated women. Let them also strive perpetually to preserve the chastity of an inviolate body, or at least bind themselves by the bond of a single marriage.

Let them offer due obedience to their elders and not exalt themselves through any desire for boasting. Finally, let them devote themselves constantly to teaching, readings, psalms, hymns, songs, and discipline. For all who seek to dedicate themselves to divine worship ought to be such as these: while they apply themselves to knowledge, they should administer the grace of teaching to the people.

## CHAPTER CI

*(The same author, On Offices, book II, chapter 3.)* There are two kinds of clerics: one, those living under ecclesiastical discipline and episcopal rule; the other, the acephali—that is, “headless” men—who do not know whom they should follow. Neither the pursuit of secular occupations among laymen nor divine religion among clerics holds these men back; instead, once loosed and wandering, they are embraced only by a shameful and aimless life. Since they fear no one, they pursue the license to fulfill their pleasure and, like brute animals, are driven by their freedom and desire. They possess the appearance of religion, but not the duty of religion; like the hippocentaurs, neither horses nor men, they are, as the poet says, “a mixed race and a two-formed offspring” (*Aeneid* VI). Our western region is sufficiently and more than sufficiently distinguished by—or, alternatively, “defiled by”—their squalid and infamous multitude.

## CHAPTER CII

*(Gregory, What clerics ought to be like.)* A cleric must be admonished to live in such a way that he offers secular people a good example of his life. And if anything is rightly censured in a cleric, the reputation of our religion itself is burdened by his fault. Let clerics learn to fulfill what their elders command them, to submit humbly to their orders, so that neither subjection crushes them nor a superior position exalts them.

Let clerics learn how, before the eyes of the hidden Judge, to order their inner selves through humility and obedience, so that they may not be punished with the rejected but may receive eternal rewards with the elect. Clerics must be admonished to live with greater vigilance over themselves in proportion as they are not entangled in the care of others.

Clerics must be told not rashly to judge the life of their superiors if they happen to see them doing something blameworthy, lest, by the impulse of pride, they sink more deeply precisely where they rightly rebuke evil. Clerics must be admonished not to become bolder against their superiors when they consider their faults, but to judge their wrongs inwardly in such a way that, nevertheless, constrained by fear of God, they do not refuse to bear beneath them the yoke of reverence. For the deeds of superiors are not to be struck by the sword of the mouth, even when they are judged rightly deserving of criticism.

Many clerics are restrained from shamelessness only by harsh rebuke, because, while they do not recognize that they are sinning, it is necessary for many to rebuke them.

## CHAPTER CIII

*(The same author, *Pastoral Rule*, book III, admonition 5.)* Subjects must be admonished not rashly to judge the lives of their superiors if they happen to see them doing something blameworthy, lest, by the impulse of pride, they sink more deeply precisely where they rightly rebuke evil. Subjects must be admonished not to become bolder against their superiors when they consider their faults, but, if some of their actions are very wrong, to judge them inwardly in such a way that, nevertheless, constrained by divine love, they do not refuse to bear beneath them the yoke of reverence.

We demonstrate this more clearly if we bring forward David’s action. Saul the persecutor had entered a cave to relieve himself; David was there with his men, having already endured the evils of Saul’s persecution for so long. When his men urged him to strike Saul, he restrained them with rebukes, because they ought not to lay a hand upon the Lord’s anointed. Yet he secretly rose and cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak (II Reg. XXIV).

What is signified by Saul except wicked rulers? What by David except good subjects? Saul’s relieving himself therefore signifies wicked superiors displaying the evil conceived in their hearts in deeds of foul odor, and revealing their harmful thoughts by carrying them out in external actions.

David feared to strike Saul because pious minds of subjects, abstaining from every plague of slander, do not strike the lives of their superiors with the sword of the tongue, even when they criticize their imperfection. When good subjects can scarcely restrain themselves because of weakness, and speak—still humbly—of certain extreme and external faults of their superiors, they silently cut off, as it were, a corner of the cloak. For when they detract, at least harmlessly and secretly, from the dignity placed over them, they are like men cutting the garment of the king set above them.

Yet they return to themselves and condemn themselves most severely even for the slightest tearing of a word. Hence it is rightly written there: “After this David struck his own heart, because he had cut off the edge of Saul’s cloak” (I Reg. XXIV). The deeds of superiors are not to be struck by the sword of the mouth, even when they are judged deserving of criticism.

If the tongue ever slips against them, even in the smallest matter, the heart must necessarily be weighed down through the affliction of repentance, so that it may return to itself. And when someone has sinned against a superior authority, let him dread that authority’s judgment against him—the authority through which that superior was placed over him. For when you sin against superiors, you oppose the ordinance of the one who placed them over us. Hence Moses, when he learned that the people were complaining against him and Aaron, said: “For what are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord” (Exod. XVI).

Well-disposed subjects must be admonished to rejoice in the goods of others in such a way that they desire to possess goods of their own; to praise the deeds of their neighbors by loving them in such a way that they also multiply them through imitation. Otherwise, if in the arena of this present life they stand as devoted supporters but sluggish spectators of another who is striving, they will remain without a prize after the contest, since they do not labor in the contest now; and then, afflicted, they will look upon the crowns of those whose labors they now idly observe.

We sin greatly if we do not love the good deeds of others; but we gain no reward if, insofar as we can, we do not imitate what we love. Well-disposed subjects must be told that, if they do not hasten to imitate the good things they approve by praising them, the holiness of the virtues pleases them as vanity pleases foolish spectators of theatrical arts.

Those spectators loudly praise the performances of charioteers and actors, yet do not desire to be such as those whom they see and praise. They admire that those performers have done what pleases, yet avoid pleasing in the same way.

Well-disposed subjects must be told that, when they observe the deeds of their neighbors, they should return to their own hearts and not presume upon the actions of others, lest they praise good things while refusing to do them. Those who have approved what they did not wish to imitate must be struck with a more serious final punishment.

## CHAPTER CIV

*(Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 17.)* Because of the sin of the first man, the punishment of servitude was divinely imposed upon the human race, so that God might mercifully inflict servitude upon those whom he sees not to be suited for freedom. Although the sin of human origin has been forgiven all the faithful through the grace of baptism, the just God nevertheless divided human life in this way, establishing some as slaves and others as masters, so that the license to do evil might be restrained by the power of those who rule.

For if all had been without fear, who would have been able to prohibit anyone from doing evil? For this reason kings and rulers were also chosen among the nations, so that by their terror they might restrain peoples from evil and subject them to laws for right living.

As far as reason is concerned, there is no partiality with God. He chose the lowly and despised things of the world, and things that are not, to destroy the things that are, so that no flesh—that is, no carnal power—might glory before him. For the one Lord equally provides counsel for masters and slaves. Subjection in servitude is better than arrogant freedom. For many are found freely serving God while placed under wicked masters; although they are subject to them in body, they are nevertheless superior in mind.

## CHAPTER CV

*(Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part III, admonition 9.)* Often subjects placed under pastoral rule, while presuming greatly upon themselves in their pride, disdainfully reproach others, considering everything they do to be exceptional. The works of the insolent must therefore be examined subtly by the one who rebukes them, so that they may be shown that the very things in which they take pleasure displease God.

We correct the insolent more effectively when we show that the things they believe they have done well were done badly, so that useful shame may follow from the very source from which glory is thought to have been obtained. Sometimes subjects, when they recognize that they themselves do not commit the fault of insolence, come more quickly to correction if they are confounded by the reproach of another more obvious fault, sought out from the side, so that from what they cannot defend they may recognize the improper position that they are defending.

When Paul saw the Corinthians insolently puffed up against one another, with one saying that he belonged to Apollo, another to Paul, another to Cephas, and another to Christ, he brought into their midst the sin of incest, which had both been committed among them and remained uncorrected, saying: “It is heard that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as does not occur even among the Gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife. And you are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, so that the one who has done this deed might be removed from your midst” (1 Cor. V).

It is as though he plainly said: “Why do you insolently claim to belong to this or that person, when through the dissolution of your negligence you show that you belong to no one?”

Envious subjects must be admonished to consider how blind they are when they fail because of another’s progress and waste away because of another’s exaltation; how wretched they are when they become worse through the improvement of their neighbor; and how, while they observe the increase of another’s prosperity, they are anxiously afflicted within themselves and die from the disease of their own hearts.

What is more wretched than the envious, whom the happiness they behold afflicts and makes worse through punishment? If they loved the good things of others, which they cannot possess, they would have made them their own (ibid. and *Moralia*, book VI, chapter 4). The goods of others are truly ours when, although we cannot imitate them, we love them in others; and whatever we love becomes ours through our loving it.

Let the envious therefore consider how great a virtue charity is, since it makes the works of another’s labor our own without labor. When the envious do not guard themselves from jealousy, they fall into the ancient wickedness of the crafty enemy. For it is written of him: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II). Because he himself lost heaven, he envied the human being who had been created; and, lost as he was, he increased his own condemnation by destroying others as well.

Let the envious recognize how many stages of growing ruin lie beneath them. For while they do not cast jealousy from their hearts, they slide into the manifest wickedness of their deeds. If Cain had not envied his brother’s accepted sacrifice, he would never have proceeded to extinguish his life. Hence it is written: “The Lord looked upon Abel and his offerings, but upon Cain and his offerings he did not look. And Cain became very angry, and his face fell” (Gen. IV). Thus jealousy of a sacrifice became the seedbed of fratricide. He grieved that the other was better than himself and cut him off lest he should be better in any respect.

The envious must be told that, while they consume themselves inwardly with this disease, they also destroy whatever other good they seem to possess. Hence it is written: “The health of the flesh is a sound heart, but envy is the rottenness of the bones” (Prov. XIV). Through the vice of jealousy, even things that appear strong to human eyes perish before the eyes of God. For the rotting of bones through envy means the destruction even of certain strong qualities.

The truly humble subject is one who is submissive in good things and not a defender of evil. For when a subject is rebuked for his evils and becomes inflamed against the words of the one rebuking him, then, when he hesitates as though humbly concerning his good qualities, he seeks to be adorned by the voice of humility, not instructed by it.

## CHAPTER CVI

*(Prosper, *On the Contemplative Life*, book I, chapter 22.)* To these statements already made I then replied: “Thus you parade these matters in envious complaints and exaggerate them as an accusation against bishops, or at least against the episcopal office, as though, in the place where you read those things by which you are reasonably disturbed, there were not also other matters that you have omitted and that we shall briefly touch upon in defense of the priestly office.

“After the words that reveal the end of negligent priests, the Prophet speaks concerning the bishop who attends to his duty: ‘But if, when you announce to the wicked man that he should turn from his ways, he is not converted from his way, that wicked man will die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your own soul’ (Ezek. XXXIX). Here it is certainly shown clearly enough that, whether hearers make progress or not, priests must not be silent before them. Nor are they guilty if the people perhaps do not heed their words or, having heard them, despise them; they are guilty if they refrain from correcting them.

“For if rebellious people do not improve, corrected neither by the example of life of their superiors nor by the word of teaching, they themselves are the cause of their own destruction, and they will in no way be able to involve in their crimes the teachers whose examples and words they despise alike.

“The same Prophet pursues this more clearly in another passage, saying: ‘When the watchman sees the sword coming upon the land and blows the trumpet and announces it to the people, then whoever hears the sound of the trumpet but does not take heed, and the sword comes and takes him, his blood will be upon his own head. He heard the sound of the trumpet but did not take heed; his blood will be upon him. But if he guards himself, he will save his soul’ (Ezek. XXXIII).

“Here too the divine word sufficiently shows what the man who performs the office of watchman ought to do: namely, when he sees the sword coming upon the land—that is, God’s anger coming upon sinners devoted to earthly works—he must not remain entirely silent. As long as they cling to their iniquities, he must not cease to announce to them that destruction from divine indignation threatens them; rather, he must rebuke them clearly and publicly. For this is what the name ‘trumpet’ indicates: that, by correcting themselves of their crimes, they may escape the punishment of future condemnation.

“But if earthly men despise the one who rebukes them and announces the future anger already threatening the contemptuous, their blood will be upon themselves, and the priest who did not keep silent about their sins cannot be a participant in the punishment awaiting them.”

## CHAPTER CVII

*(The same author, *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 10.)* Nor do those who possess their own property and wish something to be given to them receive, without great sin on their part, what the poor used to live on. Concerning clerics, the Holy Spirit says: “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. IV).

But just as those who possess nothing of their own receive not sins but food, which they appear to need, so proprietors receive not food, of which they have an abundance, but the sins of others. If the poor themselves can provide for themselves through their crafts or labors, they should not presume upon what the weak and infirm ought to receive. Otherwise the Church, which can provide necessities to all who are deprived of every assistance, may be burdened if even those who lack nothing receive, and may be unable to help those whom she ought to assist.

Those who serve the Church, believing that the fruits of their labor ought to be returned to them as dues, and who either willingly accept or demand what they do not need, are thinking far too carnally if they suppose that those who faithfully serve the Church receive earthly stipends and not rather eternal rewards. Secular military service, which has no heavenly rewards, provides earthly ones to those who serve energetically. It is therefore most unworthy if the faithful and diligent devotion of clerics despises eternal rewards for the sake of temporal payment.

If any minister of the Church has no means by which to live, let the Church not return his labor to him as a debt, but provide what is necessary, so that in the future he may receive the reward of his labor, which even in this life he awaits through hope in the Lord’s promise.

Nor can I say what sin those who are apparently capable commit when, although they do not ask to be given anything as a debt, they nevertheless live at the Church’s expense and presumptuously receive the food of the poor. They burden with their expenses the Church, which they ought to have assisted from their own resources—perhaps for this reason living in communities, so as not to feed any poor people, receive visitors, or diminish their own income through daily expenses.

If they have contributed something from their revenues to the Church, as though toward their own expenses, they should not place themselves through empty boasting above those whom the Church feeds and clothes although they possess nothing. For the one who strips himself of the things of the world is more perfect—or the one who, possessing nothing, does not desire to possess—than the one who gives something to the Church from the many things he owns and perhaps boasts about what he has given.

What I say is harsh, and I do not deny it; it is harsh for those unwilling to observe it. But if these things are done, they become immediately easy for those who do them, though difficult for those who do not. It is therefore not impossibility that makes the things we do not wish to observe difficult for us, but unfamiliarity. Let them become habitual, and repeated practice will trouble no one.

For I ask: what is difficult about the things I have said? Is it that a person should not receive from the Church what he does not need, or that he should gratuitously despise what he does not need? If someone does not wish to leave his own possessions for this reason, so that he may have the means to live, why does he receive something for which he must give an account? Why does he multiply his own sins with the sins of others?

## CHAPTER CVIII

*(The same author, *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 11.)* Therefore the priest entrusted with the care of administration receives from the people, without greed and even with praise for his piety, what is to be distributed, and faithfully distributes what he has received. He has either abandoned all his own possessions or added them to the Church’s property, and has placed himself among the poor through love of poverty, so that from what he supplies to the poor he himself also lives as a voluntary poor man.

Clerics too, whom either their own will or their birth has made poor, receive the necessities of life with perfected virtue, whether they live in their own houses or in a community, because it is not desire for possessions that leads them to accept these things, but the necessity of living compels them.

## CHAPTER CIX

*(The same author, *On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 12.)* But those who are so weak that they cannot renounce their possessions, if they leave with the administrator what they would otherwise have received, to be given to those who possess nothing, possess their own property without sin (1 Cor. IX). For they too in a certain way leave their own possessions when, content with what is theirs, they accept none of the things they think are owed to their labor or rank.

But if they think that they ought therefore to receive a share of what is contributed to the Church, lest they appear to cast it away, and that they cannot leave their own possessions because it would be disgraceful for them to be supported among their own poor, let them know that it is more disgraceful for proprietors to be fed from the alms of the poor.

## CHAPTER CX
(Same author, *On the Contemplative Life*, Book II, chapter 13.) Alas, how subtly that craftsman of deception deceives us! With what blindness he covers the eyes of our mind, lest we discern, when eager for joy, from what source we ought more justly to rejoice—or, when desirous of increasing our riches, recognize which riches we should prefer incomparably above others! [Col. 0898A] For to rejoice is indeed good; but if one who rejoices does not rejoice over what he ought, the thing over which he rejoices cannot be good. The robber rejoices, when he has seized what he desired; the drunkard rejoices, when he has found the opportunity for the drinking he longed for; the adulterer rejoices, when he has attained the pleasure of enjoying the body he coveted. Yet although rejoicing is good, to rejoice over such things and things like them is a great evil.

These, and things like them, are what the world—destined to perish with its lovers—wants us to rejoice over. These are what we must reject, so that we may rejoice ineffably over a good conscience, holiness of conduct, the acquisition of virtues, the gift of God, and the promise of the future kingdom.

To be enriched with riches is also a great good. But to be enriched from a source from which one ought not to be enriched is not a resource to be possessed, but a calamity to be detested. [Col. 0898B] Nothing is more calamitous, nothing more wretched, than the person who grows through unjust acquisitions, whom frauds and acts of robbery make wealthy. We should seek those riches that can adorn and protect us at the same time—riches that we cannot acquire unwillingly, nor lose; that arm us against hostile attacks, separate us from the world, commend us to God, enrich and ennoble our souls. They are with us; they are within us.

[Col. 0898C] Our riches should be understood to be chastity, which makes us chaste; justice, which makes us just; piety, which makes us pious; humility, which makes us humble; gentleness, which makes us gentle; innocence, which makes us innocent; purity, which makes us pure; prudence, which makes us prudent; self-control, which makes us self-controlled; and love, which makes us dear to God and to human beings, strong in virtue, despisers of the world, and followers of every good thing.

These are not the holy virtues of everyone, but of the saints; not the resources of proud rich people, but the possessions of humble poor people; the patrimony of hearts, the incorruptible riches of character. No one abounds in them unless from the heart he renounces those bodily riches. Although the latter too are good, since they were created by the good God, nevertheless, because they are shared by the good and the wicked, spiritual men strive to despise them, so that they may attain those incomparably better things that belong exclusively to the good. For the good possessed by the wicked is not of the same kind as that which only the good possess.

[Col. 0898D] When wicked people possess a bodily good, it is their reward; when the just possess it, it is not their reward but a temporary consolation. Likewise, the loss of temporal good becomes an exercise for the just and a punishment for the unjust: for the just person, captivated by desire for heavenly things, feels nothing at all regarding temporal things, whether he possesses or loses them; whereas the wicked person cannot lose without pain what he possessed with delight.

Therefore riches must be fled from with all one’s heart by those who serve God. Those who wish to possess them do not seek them without labor, find them without difficulty, preserve them without care, possess them without anxious delight, or lose them without pain. But the Apostle says to Christ’s soldiers: “I want you to be without anxiety” (1 Corinthians 7); and: “The root of all evils is avarice; by desiring it, some have wandered from the faith and have pierced themselves with many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6).

[Col. 0899A] Thus this earthly wealth, for those who love it viciously, is not material for pleasures but for sorrows. Therefore it is advantageous that the Church’s resources be possessed, so that those who serve not the world—whose fleeting joys they reject—but God, whose ineffable goods they desire, may live from them.

### CXI.

(Prosper.) The Apostle seems to speak about such matters: “Those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and those who serve at the altar share with the altar.” Unless he had wished this to be understood of those who despise their own resources, he would never have confidently added: “So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.”

Those live from the Gospel who do not wish to possess anything as their own—who neither possess nor desire to possess anything, but are possessors not of private goods but of goods held in common. What else is it to live from the Gospel than to receive from the place where one labors the necessities of life for the laborer?

Yet the Apostle, who preached the Gospel in such a way that he did not live from the Gospel but supplied his necessities with his own hands, speaks confidently about himself: “But I have used none of these things.” And he clearly explained why he said this, declaring: “It is better for me to die than that anyone should deprive me of my glory.” He says that his glory would be emptied if he had wished to receive the expenses of temporal life from those to whom he preached. He did not want to receive the fruit of his labor in the present, but in the future.

If, then, the man who possessed nothing did not wish to live from the Gospel, in which he labored, but from his own hands, lest he lose [Col. 0899C] the glory of his reward, what of us, who are unwilling to leave what is our own—not from necessity of living but from love of possessing—and who also wish to receive, not what we may live from, but what may enlarge our wealth by damnable increases?

### CHAPTER CXII.

(Augustine, *On the Life and Conduct of the Clergy*.) For this reason I wished and asked yesterday that you gather here today in greater numbers. What I am about to say is this: We live here with you, and our intention and desire is that, with you, we may live forever with Christ.

I believe that our way of life is before your eyes, so that we too may perhaps dare to say—although we are far from equal to him—what the Apostle said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4 [Col. 0899D] and 11). Therefore I do not want anyone to find in us an occasion for living badly. “We provide what is good,” the same Apostle says, “not only before God but also before human beings” (Romans 3).

Because of ourselves, our conscience is sufficient for us; because of you, our reputation must not be sullied but must shine among you. Hold on to what I have said, and distinguish the two. There are two things: conscience and reputation. Conscience is necessary for you; reputation is necessary for your neighbor. Whoever, trusting in his conscience, neglects his reputation is cruel—especially when placed in this position, of which the Apostle says, writing to his disciple: “In all things, present yourself as an example of good works” (Titus 2).

So that I do not detain you for long—especially since I am speaking while seated and you are laboring while standing—you [Col. 0900A] all, or nearly all, know that we live in the house called the bishop’s residence in such a way that, as far as we can, we imitate those holy people of whom the Book of the Acts of the Apostles speaks: “No one said that anything was his own, but everything was common to them” (Acts 2 and 4).

Perhaps some of you are not such diligent investigators of our life that you know this as I want you to know it. I shall explain what I briefly mentioned.

I, whom by God’s favor you see as your bishop, came to this city as a young man, as many of you know. I was looking for a place where I could establish a monastery and live with my brothers. I had abandoned every hope in the world, and I did not want to become what I could have become; yet I did not seek what I now am. I chose to be despised in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners. I separated myself [Col. 0900B] from those who love the world; but I did not make myself equal to those who preside over peoples. Nor did I choose a higher place at the banquet of my Lord, but a lower and despised one. And it pleased him to say to me: “Come up higher.”

I feared the episcopate so greatly that, since my reputation among God’s servants had already begun to carry some weight, I did not go to a place where I knew there was no bishop. I guarded against this and did as much as I could to be saved in a humble position, lest I perish in a high one. But, as I said, a servant must not contradict his Lord.

I came to this city to see a friend whom I thought I could win for God, so that he might be with us in the monastery. I came almost without concern, because the place had a bishop. [Col. 0900C] I was seized, made a presbyter, and through this rank reached the episcopate. I brought nothing with me; I came to this church with no possessions except the clothing I was wearing at that time.

Since I had planned to live in a monastery with my brothers, the elder Valerius, of blessed memory, having learned of my rule and intention, gave me that garden in which the monastery now stands. I began to gather brothers of good purpose, my companions, possessing nothing as I possessed nothing, and imitating me. Just as I had sold my modest little poverty and distributed it to the poor, so they too were to do this if they wished to be with me, so that we might live from what was common to us. Our common and abundant estate, however, would be God himself.

[Col. 0900D] I reached the episcopate and saw that a bishop necessarily had to show continual courtesy to anyone who came or passed through; if a bishop did not do this, he would be called inhuman. But if this custom were permitted in the monastery, it would be unbecoming. Therefore I wanted to have with me in this episcopal residence a monastery of clerics.

This is how we live. No one in our society is permitted to possess anything as his own. But perhaps some do possess something. No one is permitted to do so; if any do, they are doing what is not permitted.

I have a good opinion of my brothers, and, always trusting them, I have avoided investigating this matter, since even to ask about it seemed like a sign of thinking badly of them. I knew, and still know, that all who lived with me knew our intention and the rule of our life.

[Col. 0901A] The presbyter Januarius also came to us. He seemed to have almost exhausted his possessions by distributing them honorably, but he had not exhausted them. Some money remained to him—silver, he said, belonging to his daughter. His daughter, by God’s favor, is in the monastery of women and is a person of good hope. May the Lord govern her, so that she may fulfill what we hope for concerning her, relying on his mercy, not on her merits.

Because she was underage and could do nothing with her own money—for although we saw the radiance of her profession, we nevertheless feared the instability of youth—it happened that the silver was preserved as though for the girl, so that when she reached the lawful age she might do with it what was fitting for a virgin of Christ, when she could already act with the greatest propriety.

While these things were being awaited, he began to approach death. Having lived for a long time as though the money were his own—for it belonged to him, not to his daughter—he made a will. [Col. 0901B] I repeat: our fellow presbyter, living with us, living from the Church, professing the common life, made a will. He made a will and appointed heirs.

O sorrow of that society! O fruit born not from the tree that the Lord planted! Yet he made the Church his heir. I do not want such gifts; I do not love the fruit of bitterness. I was seeking him for God. He had professed our society; he should have remained faithful to it and practiced it. If he had nothing, he should not have made a will. If he had something, he should not have pretended to be our companion, as though he were God’s poor man.

This causes me great sorrow, brothers. I tell your charity: because of this sorrow I have decided not to accept that inheritance for the Church. Let what he left belong to his children. Let them do with it whatever they wish. [Col. 0901C] For it seems to me that, if I accept it, I shall become a participant in the deed that displeases and grieves me.

I wanted your charity not to be unaware of this. His daughter is in the monastery of women, and his son is in the monastery of men. He disinherited both: her with praise, him with a formal charge (*elogium*)—that is, with reproach.

I have instructed the Church not to accept the small portions belonging to those who were disinherited until they reach the lawful age. The Church preserves these for them.

Then he left a lawsuit between his children, in which I am laboring. The girl says, “It is mine; you know that my father always said this.” The boy says, “Let my father be believed, because when he was dying he could not have lied.” And what an evil is this dispute! But if the children themselves are servants of God, we shall [Col. 0901D] soon settle this lawsuit between them.

I shall hear them as a father, and perhaps better than their father. I shall see what the law requires. As the Lord wills, with a few faithful and honored brothers, by God’s favor from among you—that is, from this people—I shall hear their case, and as the Lord grants, I shall settle it.

Nevertheless, I ask you: let no one criticize me because I do not want the Church to accept his inheritance. First, because I detest his deed; second, because it is my established practice. Many praise what I am about to say, but some also criticize it. It is very difficult to satisfy both groups.

You have just heard, when the Gospel was read: “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we mourned, and you did not lament. John the Baptist came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon.’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a glutton and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors’” (Matthew 11).

[Col. 0902A] What, then, shall I do among those who prepare to criticize me and gnash their teeth at me if I accept the inheritances of those who angrily disinherit their children? What shall I do for those to whom I sing and who do not wish to dance? They say, “See why no one gives anything to the Church of Hippo; see why those who die do not make it their heir: because Bishop Augustine, out of his goodness”—for while praising they bite, they flatter with their lips and sink in their teeth—“gives everything away and accepts nothing.”

Certainly I do accept; I acknowledge that I accept good offerings, holy offerings. [Col. 0902B] But if someone is angry with his son and disinherits him at death, would I not appease him if he were alive? Should I not reconcile his son to him? How, then, can I want him to be at peace with his son while coveting his inheritance?

But let him do what I have often urged him to do. Does he have one son? Let him regard Christ as a second. Does he have two? Let him regard Christ as a third. Does he have ten? Let him make Christ the eleventh, and I shall accept it.

Because I have done this in certain cases, they now want to turn my goodness—or what they call my good reputation—in another direction, so that they may criticize me in another way, claiming that I do not wish to accept the offerings of devout people. Let them consider how many I have accepted. Why should I enumerate them? Here is one example: I accepted the inheritance of the son of Julian. Why? Because he died without children.

[Col. 0902C] I refused to accept the inheritance of Boniface—not from mercy but from fear. I did not want the Church of Christ to become a shipping enterprise. There are many, indeed, who acquire wealth even from ships. Yet suppose there were one temptation: suppose a ship set out and were wrecked, and we were going to hand people over to torture so that, according to custom, the shipwreck might be investigated and those who had been saved from the waves might be tortured by the judge. We would not hand them over; by no means would it be fitting for the Church to do this.

The fiscal burden would therefore have to be paid—but from what would it be paid? We are not permitted to keep a reserve fund (*entheca*). It is not the bishop’s role to store up gold and turn away the hand of a beggar. Every day so many ask, so many groan, so many needy people appeal to us, that we leave more people sad because we do not have enough to give to everyone.

We do not, then, have a reserve fund. I refused the inheritance in order to avoid the danger of shipwreck. Let no one praise me for this, but let no one criticize me either.

[Col. 0902D] Certainly, when I restored to a son what an angry father had taken from him while dying, I did well. Let those who wish praise me; let those who do not wish to praise me refrain.

Why say more, my brothers? Whoever wishes, after disinheriting his son, to make the Church his heir should look for someone else to accept it, not Augustine. Indeed, by God’s favor, may he find no one.

How praiseworthy was the deed of the holy and venerable bishop Aurelius of Carthage! How he filled with praises of God the mouths of all who know of it! A certain man, having no children and no expectation of children, gave all his property to the Church, retaining the usufruct for himself. Children were born to him, and the bishop returned to him, when he did not expect it, what he had given him. The bishop had the power not to return it—but by the law of the earthly court, not by the law of heaven.

[Col. 0903A] Your charity should also know that I told my brothers who live with me that anyone who possesses anything should either sell it, distribute it, give it away, or make it common. He has the Church, through which God feeds us. I granted a delay until Epiphany for those who had either not divided their possessions with their brothers and had left what they possessed with their families, or had not yet done anything with their property because the lawful age was still awaited.

Let them do with it what they wish, provided that they are poor with me and that together we await God’s mercy. But if they do not wish this—and perhaps some do not—I am certainly the one who had determined, as you know, to ordain no one as a cleric unless he wished to remain with me, so that, if he wished to abandon his purpose, I could rightly remove his clerical status from him because he had deserted the promise of the holy society and the fellowship he had begun.

Behold, in the sight of God and of you, I change my decision. [Col. 0903B] Those who wish to possess something as their own, for whom God and his Church are not sufficient, may remain where they wish and where they can. I do not take their clerical status from them. I do not want hypocrites.

It is evil—who does not know it?—to fall away from one’s purpose. But it is worse to pretend to that purpose. Hear me: I say this openly. Whoever abandons the common life already undertaken, which is praised in the Acts of the Apostles (chapters 2 and 4), falls from his vow and collapses from his holy profession.

Let him look to the judge—but to God, not to me. Therefore I do not remove his clerical status; I have placed before his eyes how great the danger is. Let him do what he wishes.

[Col. 0903C] For I know that if I wished to degrade someone who did this, he would not lack patrons or supporters, either here or among the bishops, who would say: “What evil has he done? He cannot endure this life with you; he wants to remain outside the bishop’s residence and live from his own possessions. Must he therefore lose his clerical status?”

I know how great an evil it is to profess something holy and not fulfill it. “Vow and pay your vows to the Lord your God” (Psalm 73); and: “It is better not to vow than to vow and not pay” (Ecclesiastes 5).

A virgin, even if she has never been in a monastery, is nevertheless a consecrated virgin. She may not marry, but she is not compelled to be in a monastery. If, however, she began to be in a monastery and abandoned it, although she remains a virgin, she has fallen halfway.

So too a cleric has professed two things: holiness and the clerical state; inwardly, holiness. [Col. 0903D] For God imposed the clerical state upon his shoulders for the sake of his people. It is more a burden than an honor. But who is wise and understands these things?

He has therefore professed holiness; he has professed the fellowship of living in common; he has professed how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity. If he falls from this purpose and remains a cleric while living outside, he too has fallen halfway.

What is that to me? I do not judge him. If he preserves holiness outside, he has fallen halfway. If he harbors hypocrisy within, he has fallen completely. I do not want him to be forced to pretend.

I know how people love the clerical state. I take it from no one who does not wish to live in common with me. He has God, who wishes to remain with me. If he is prepared to be fed by God through his Church, to possess nothing as his own, but either to distribute it to the poor or [Col. 0904A] put it into the common fund, let him remain with me.

Whoever does not wish this has his freedom; but let him see whether he can possess eternal happiness.

Let these words suffice for the present, my dear people. What I do with my brothers I shall announce to you. I hope for good things: that all will willingly obey me, and that I shall find none possessing anything except because of some necessity of religion, not as an occasion for greed.

Whatever I do, I shall report to your charity after Epiphany, if it is the Lord’s will. And how I settle the lawsuit between the two brothers, the children of the presbyter Januarius, I shall not conceal from you.

I have spoken at length. Forgive my talkative old age—and my timid weakness. As you see, I have now grown old with respect to age; but because of bodily weakness I was old long ago. [Col. 0904B] Nevertheless, if what I have said pleases God, may he now give me strength, and I shall not abandon you.

Pray for me, so that, for as long as there is a soul in this body, and whatever strength remains is available, I may serve you in the word of God. Amen.

### CHAPTER CXIII.

*(The same author’s Sermon 2, on the Life and Conduct of Clerics.)*

Today I must deliver a discourse to your Charity concerning ourselves. For, as the Apostle says, “We have been made a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to human beings” (1 Cor. 4). Those who love us seek what they may praise in us; those who hate us disparage us. We, however, placed between these two groups, must, with the help of the Lord our God, guard both our life and our reputation in such a way that those who praise us may not be put to shame by our detractors.

But how we wish to live, and how, by God’s favor, we already live—although many of you know this from Holy Scripture—the reading itself from the Acts of the Apostles will now be recited for you, to remind you and to show you where the model we desire to fulfill is written. While it is being recited, I want you to listen with the greatest attention, so that after its recitation I may, with the Lord’s help, speak what I have resolved to say for the benefit of your attention.

When the deacon Lazarus was reading:

> “When they had prayed, the place in which they were assembled was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke the word of God with complete confidence to everyone willing to hear.” Now the multitude of believers had one soul and one heart; and none of them said that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them. And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. For there was no needy person among them. For as many as were owners of fields or houses sold them, brought the proceeds of what they had sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet; and distribution was made to each according to his need” (Acts 4).

When the deacon Lazarus had recited this and handed the book to the bishop, Bishop Augustine said:

“I too wish to read, for I take greater pleasure in being a reader of this word than a disputant of my own words.”

> “When they had prayed, the place in which they were assembled was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit; they spoke the word of God with complete confidence to everyone willing to hear.” Now the multitude of believers had one soul and one heart; and none of them said that anything he possessed was his own, but everything was common to them. And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. For there was no needy person among them. For as many as were owners of fields or houses sold them, brought the proceeds of what they had sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet; and distribution was made to each according to his need.”

When the bishop had finished reading, he said:

“You have heard what we desire; pray that we may be able to accomplish it.”

A certain necessity arose, requiring me to attend to these matters more carefully. As you already know, a presbyter established in our community—and the reading we have just recited bears witness to the kind of community it is—died and made a will, because he possessed property from which he could do so. He had something he could call his own, although he lived in a community in which no one was permitted to call anything his own, but everything was common to them.

Suppose one of our admirers and praisers were to commend this community to one of our detractors, saying, “All those who live with Bishop Augustine live as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles.” Immediately that detractor, shaking his head and thrusting out his tooth, would say: “Indeed? Is that how people live there, as you say? Why are you lying? Why do you honor unworthy men with false praise? Did not a presbyter who was recently a member of their community make a will, and dispose of and leave what he possessed as he wished? Surely everything there is common; surely no one calls anything his own.”

Under such words, what could my praiser do? Would not that detractor effectively seal his mouth with lead? Would he not regret having praised us? Would he not, covered with shame and confounded by that man’s words, curse either us or that testator? This was the necessity that led us to undertake this careful examination.

I therefore bring you news in which you may rejoice. I found all my brothers and clerics who live with me—presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and my nephew Patricius—to be such as I wished. There are, however, some who have not yet done what they had resolved concerning whatever poverty they possess. These are Valens the subdeacon, and the subdeacon who was mentioned shortly before, my nephew. His mother’s life was an impediment, because he lived from her property. His reaching lawful age was also awaited, so that whatever he did might be done with complete firmness.

He has not yet acted, however, because he and his brother jointly possess certain small fields, still undivided. He wishes to transfer them to the Church in such a way that those who have undertaken a life of holiness may be maintained from them for as long as they live in this world.
