For it is written, and the Apostle says it: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5).

He likewise still jointly possesses with his brother certain slaves, not yet divided. He intends to set them free, but he cannot do so before they are divided, since he does not yet know what portion belongs to him. The division belongs to him, since he is the elder, while the choice belongs to his brother. His brother too serves God and is a subdeacon with my holy brother and fellow bishop Severus in the church at Milevis. This matter must now be dealt with, and without delay, so that those little slaves may be divided and freed, and so that he may give them to the Church in such a way that it will receive their maintenance from them.

As for my nephew, from the time he was converted and began to live with me, he too was prevented from disposing of anything concerning his small fields against the will of his mother, who held the usufruct. She died this year. There are certain matters between him and his sisters which must be brought to completion quickly, with Christ’s help, so that he too may do what befits a servant of God and what his profession and this reading require.

The deacon Faustinus—as nearly all of you know—was converted here from military service in the world to the monastery, baptized here, and then ordained a deacon. But because the property he appeared to possess was small, as legal experts say, he had left it in law, though not in physical possession, and it was held by his brothers. From the time of his conversion he never thought about it, nor did he himself seek anything from his brothers, nor was anything sought from him.

Now that the matter has reached this point, with my advice he divided the property itself: half he gave to his brothers, and half to the poor Church established in that same place.

You know under what discipline and scourging of God the deacon Severus exists; nevertheless, he has not lost the light of his mind. He had bought a house here for his mother and sister, whom he wished to bring here from their homeland. He bought it not with his own money, which he did not possess, but through the assistance of religious men, whom he named and identified to me when I asked him about them.

I cannot say what he has done or what he will decide concerning that house, except that he placed the whole matter in my will, so that whatever I wished would be done with it. He also has certain legal disputes with his mother, and he asks me to judge them. When those disputes have been settled, let the house be dealt with as I wish. And what can I wish, with God directing me, except what justice commands and piety demands?

He also has some small fields in his homeland. He intends to distribute them in such a way that there too, in that very place, he may give to the poor Church established there.

The deacon of Hippo is a poor man. He has nothing with which to make a contribution. Nevertheless, before he became a cleric, he bought some little slaves from his own labor; today he will free them in your presence through episcopal legal instruments.

The deacon Eradius is before your eyes; his works shine before us. From his work and the money he expended, we have a memorial of the holy martyr. On my advice he also bought a property with his own money. For he wanted the money itself to be distributed through my hands as I thought proper. If I were greedy for money, or if I cared more in this matter for my own necessities, which I have for the poor, I would have accepted the money.

Why? someone may ask. Because that property, bought by him and donated to the Church, still yields nothing to the Church. He had too little for its purchase price. And because he had borrowed the money, the debt is still being repaid from its produce.

I am an old man: how long can I expect produce from that property to come to me? Do I promise myself that I shall live so many years, until it pays its purchase price? What it repays only slowly over a long period would have been entirely available to me immediately if I had wished to accept it. I did not do so; I had another concern.

I confess to you that I was also still suspicious of his youth. I feared that, as happens among human beings, his mother might be displeased by this and say that I had induced the young man to consume his paternal property and leave him in need. Therefore I wanted his money to remain invested in that property, so that if something—which God forbid—should happen contrary to our wishes, the estate could be returned and the bishop’s reputation would not be blamed.

For I know how necessary my reputation is to you. My own conscience is enough for me.

He later bought a plot from this church, as you know, and built a house with his own money; you know this as well. A few days ago, before I spoke with you about this matter, he donated it to the Church. He had been waiting to complete it and then donate it once completed.

He had no need to build the house except that he thought his mother would come here. If she had come earlier, she would have lived in her son’s property; if she comes now, she will live in her son’s work.

I testify on his behalf: he remained poor, but he remained in possession of charity. Some little slaves had also been left to him. They are already living in the monastery, and today he will free them through ecclesiastical legal instruments.

Therefore let no one say, “He is rich”; let no one suppose it; let no one speak maliciously; let no one tear himself and his own soul to pieces with his teeth. He has no money saved up—would that he might repay what he owes.

The rest, that is, the subdeacons, are poor. By God’s favor, they await God’s mercy. They have nothing from which to make a contribution. Possessing no resources, they have brought the world’s desires to an end. They live with us in a common community. No one distinguishes them from those who have brought something.

The unity of charity must be placed before the earthly advantage of inheritance.

The presbyters remain; thus I wished to ascend to them step by step. I shall say briefly: they are God’s poor. They brought nothing to the household of our community except charity itself, than which nothing is more precious.

Nevertheless, because I know that rumors have arisen about their wealth, they must not be compelled by me to anything, but they must be cleared before you by my speech. I am speaking to you who perhaps do not know, although many of you do.

I received the presbyter Leporius, although distinguished by his birth in the world and born in a very honorable position among his people, already serving God and having abandoned everything he possessed, in poverty. Not because he had possessed nothing, but because he had already done what this reading urges.

This man did not do it here, but we know where he did it. Christ’s unity is one; the Church is one. Wherever he did a good work, it belongs also to us, if we rejoice with him.

There is a garden; as you know, he established a monastery there for his own people, for they too serve God. That garden does not belong to the Church, nor does it belong to him. To whom, then? someone may ask: to the monastery established there.

But what is true is that, until now, he managed their affairs in such a way that he kept with himself the expenses by which they were maintained and himself, as it appeared, supplied them. But lest this provide an opportunity for people who gnaw at their own suspicions and do not fill their bellies, it seemed good both to me and to him that they should arrange their affairs as though he had already departed from this world.

For when he dies, will he be the one to administer anything to them? It is better that he should see them conducting themselves well and, with God directing them, living according to Christ’s discipline; that he should rejoice solely in them and not be burdened with their necessities.

He has no money that he can call his own. He had a hospice to build, which you now see built. I assigned it to him; I ordered it. He obeyed me most willingly and, as you see, carried out the work.

At my command he also built the basilica of the Eight Martyrs from what God has given through you. He began with money that had been given to the Church for the hospice. Once he had begun to build, religious people, desiring their works to be recorded in heaven, assisted and built as each wished. We have the work before our eyes.

Everyone sees what has been done. As for the money, since he has none, let them believe me; let them restrain their teeth, lest they break them.

He had bought with the hospice money a certain house on the carriage road, thinking that its stones might be useful to him. But the stones of that house were not needed for the building, since they were supplied from elsewhere. The house itself therefore remained as it was. It yields rent, but to the Church, not to the presbyter.

Let no one say any longer, “To the presbyter’s house,” “at the presbyter’s house,” or “before the presbyter’s house.” Behold where the presbyter’s house is. Elsewhere he has no house, but wherever he has God, there is his home.

What more do you seek? I remember that I also promised to report to you what I had done concerning the two children of the presbyter Januarius, a brother and a sister, because a financial dispute had arisen between them—yet, by God’s favor, without any loss of charity between siblings.

I had promised to hear the matter and settle whatever had to be judged between them. I had prepared myself as judge, but before I judged, they themselves settled what I was going to judge. I found nothing over which to judge, but something over which to rejoice.

They entirely agreed to my will and advice that they should have equal shares in the money their father had left, the Church renouncing its claim after my speech.

People will talk. Whatever people may say, whatever breeze may blow, something will reach my ears from there. If it is such that we must again clear ourselves, I will answer the slanderers, I will answer the detractors, I will answer the unbelievers—not those who believe us, their superiors. I will answer as I can, with what the Lord grants.

For now there is no need, since perhaps they will say nothing. Those who love us will rejoice openly; those who hate us will grieve silently. Nevertheless, if they exercise their tongues—[Hardouin: perhaps read *exseruerint*, “have put forth”]—they will, by God’s favor, hear my response to you, not my quarrel.

I shall not name people and say, “That man said this; this man disparaged us in such a way,” since perhaps what reaches me may even be false—for that too can happen. Nevertheless, whatever is reported, if it seems necessary, I will speak about it to your Charity.

I want our life to be before your eyes. I know that those who seek permission to do evil look for examples of people living badly and defame many others, so that they may appear to have found companions. Therefore we have done what was ours to do; we have no more to add.

We are before your eyes. We desire nothing from you except your good works.

And I exhort you, my brothers: if you wish to give something to the clerics, know that you must not foster their vices against me. Offer whatever you wish, of your own free will. Whatever is common will be distributed to each according to his need.

Pay attention to the treasury, and we shall all have what is needed. It pleases me greatly if it itself becomes our manger, so that we may be God’s beasts of burden and you God’s field.

Let no one give a cloak, a linen tunic, or anything else except for the common use. From the common fund I will take for myself, since I wish to regard everything I possess as common.

I do not want your Holiness to offer such things as I alone might use more fittingly. Suppose, for example, that an expensive cloak is offered to me. Perhaps it suits a bishop, although it does not suit Augustine—that is, a poor man born of poor people.

People will now say that I have acquired costly garments that I could not have possessed either in my father’s house or in my former worldly profession. That is not fitting. I ought to have one of the kind I can have; if I cannot use it, I should give it to my brother. I want to receive the kind that a presbyter can have, or that a deacon or subdeacon can decently have, because I receive it for common use.

If someone gives a better one, I sell it—which I also customarily do—so that when a garment cannot be common, its price may be common. I sell it and distribute the proceeds to the poor.

If he is pleased that I should have something, let him give me something of which I will not be ashamed. I confess to you that I am ashamed of an expensive garment, because it does not suit this profession, this admonition, these limbs, or these gray hairs.

I also say this: if someone in our house or community is sick, or is recovering from illness and needs to be refreshed before the hour of the meal, I do not forbid religious men or women to send them whatever they think appropriate to send. Nevertheless, no one may have lunch or dinner outside.

There—I say it; you hear it, and they hear it. Whoever wishes to have private property, live from private property, and act against these commands of ours, it is too little to say that he will not remain with me: he will not even remain a cleric.

I had said—and I know that I said it—that if they did not wish to accept a communal life with me, I would not deprive them of their clerical office; they could remain apart and live apart, living for God as they understood. Yet I placed before their eyes how great an evil it is to fall away from one’s profession.

For I preferred to have blind or lame men rather than mourn the dead. Whoever is a hypocrite is dead.

Therefore, just as I would not deprive anyone who wished to remain outside and live from his own property of his clerical office, so now, since by God’s favor they have chosen this communal life, whoever lives hypocritically, whoever is found possessing private property, will not be permitted to make a will concerning it; I will erase him from the register of clerics.

Let a thousand councils appeal against me; let him sail wherever he wishes against me; let him be wherever he can. The Lord will help me, so that where I am bishop, he cannot be a cleric.

Have you heard? They have heard. But I hope in our God and in his mercy that, just as they have cheerfully accepted this arrangement of mine, so they will keep it purely and faithfully.

I said that my fellow presbyters who live with me, among whom is the presbyter Barnabas, possess nothing of their own. But I also heard that certain things had been circulated about him.

First of all, it was said that he bought an estate from my beloved and honorable son Eleusinus. This is false. Eleusinus donated it to the monastery; he did not sell it. I am a witness.

What more do you seek? I do not know. I am a witness. He donated it; he did not sell it. But because people did not believe that he could have donated it, they believed that he had sold it.

Blessed is the man who performed so good a work that people did not believe it. Nevertheless, believe it now, and stop listening willingly to detractors.

I have already said it: I am a witness.

It was also said of him that during the year of his superintendence he deliberately contracted debts, so that when I wished the debts to be repaid, he might ask permission to seek the Victorian estate—as though he had said to me, “To repay my debts, give me the Victorian estate for ten years.” This too is false, although there was a circumstance from which the rumor arose.

He incurred debts that had to be repaid, and we repaid part of them as far as we could. Something remained, which was not owed even to that monastery that God established through him.

When something remained, we began to look for a means of repaying the debt. No one undertook the lease of that estate except a person offering a rent of forty solidi. But we saw that the estate could yield more, so that the debt might be repaid more quickly, and I entrusted his good faith with the lease itself, requiring the brothers to seek no profit from it; whatever the estate produced, they were to apply from its produce toward the debt.

This is a matter of trust. The presbyter is prepared for me to appoint another person to repay the debt to the brothers from the produce. Let someone from your number—someone among those who brought such matters to us—come forward, to whom I may entrust this.

There are religious men among you. If any of them were distressed that the rumor had been falsely charged against him and yet believed that it had occurred, let one of those men come to us, take possession of the estate, faithfully sell all its produce at its proper prices, so that what is owed may be repaid more easily; and today the presbyter will be relieved of responsibility for it.

The place itself, where the monastery was established by the aforementioned honorable son of mine, Eleusinus, was donated to the presbyter Barnabas. Before he was ordained presbyter, he established the monastery in that place. But because the place had been donated in his name, he changed the documents so that it might be held in the name of the monastery.

Concerning the Victorian estate, I ask, I exhort, I entreat: if any religious person wishes to act in good faith, let him perform this service for the Church, so that I may quickly repay the debt. But if no layman is found, I will appoint someone else; this man will not take possession of it.

What more do you want? Let no one tear the servants of God to pieces, for it is not advantageous to those who do so. The reward of God’s servants indeed increases through false accusations, but the punishment of those who accuse also increases.

It was not said without reason: “Rejoice and exult when they speak falsely against you, for your reward is great in heaven” (Matt. 5). We do not want to have a great reward there at your expense. Let us have less there, and yet reign there with you.

Amen.

**End.**

Since it is therefore established that the holy Church ought to follow the examples of the Fathers mentioned above—by whose teachings it is known to shine abundantly after the apostolic institutions—not only should superiors imitate them, but subjects too should obey and strive everywhere to learn how, by following their examples and teachings, they may reach the joys of blessedness to which those Fathers have gone before them.

For just as those who obey their teachings and examples with the greatest devotion are led into eternal joys, so surely those who refuse to follow them are handed over to eternal punishments.

Therefore, whoever has professed the canonical life should diligently read through and carefully consider the statements of the holy Fathers mentioned above, by which the clerical order is instructed to live well. When he has thoroughly examined them, he will plainly discover that one must live not feebly, but religiously.

## CHAPTER CXIV

### Which precepts apply particularly to monks, and which generally to other Christians

Because of the words of certain simple-minded people, who often object to religious and learned men when they admonish and rebuke them that only monks are obliged to observe the precepts of Holy Scripture, we have thought it worthwhile to set forth, as briefly as possible, certain evangelical and apostolic precepts, so that these ignorant people, hearing them and lending the ear of their heart to them, may understand which precepts they themselves must observe and which are appropriate specifically to monks.

Whoever wishes in mind and body to despise the world and follow Christ in poverty should hear him saying in the Gospel:

> “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess, give to the poor, and come, follow me.”

And again:

> “Everyone who has left house, or brothers, or father, or mother, or fields for my sake will receive a hundredfold and will possess eternal life.”

And to the disciples:

> “You who have left everything and followed me will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19).

These and similar precepts apply particularly to monks alone; and the more singular they are, the more important they are.

The same Savior also says generally to everyone:

> “Everyone who comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters—and even his own life—cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14).

And again:

> “Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.”

And:

> “Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10).

And again:

> “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Matt. 7).

And again:

> “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them.”

And again:

> “Take care not to practice your righteousness before people so that you may be seen by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father” (Matt. 6).

Likewise:

> “Lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys” (Matt. 6).

Likewise:

> “Take care that your hearts are not weighed down by gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life” (Luke 21).

Likewise:

> “I say to you: Do not resist evil; love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you.”

Likewise:

> “Everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment. Whoever says, ‘Raca,’ will be liable to the council. Whoever says, ‘Fool,’ will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.”

Likewise:

> “Do not swear, either by heaven or by earth. Let your speech be, ‘Yes, yes; No, no’” (Matt. 5).

Likewise:

> “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12).

Likewise:

> “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Luke 6).

Likewise:

> “Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful” (Matt. 18).

Likewise:

> “If your brother sins against you, forgive him seven times; and not only seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

Likewise:

> “If you do not forgive people from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.”

Likewise:

> “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6).

And to a certain rich man he said:

> “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments: you shall not commit murder, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; honor your father and your mother, and love your neighbor as yourself” (Matt. 19).

And to a certain teacher of the Law who asked him what the great commandment in the Law was, he said:

> “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22).

The Apostle Paul also says:

> “Whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the Law. For, ‘You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet your neighbor’s property,’ and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Rom. 13).

Likewise he says:

> “Be patient with everyone. See that no one repays anyone evil for evil, but always pursue what is good for one another and for all. For this is the will of God. Test everything; hold fast to what is good; abstain from every form of evil” (1 Thess. 5).

Likewise he says:

> “Put to death your members that are upon the earth: fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed” (Col. 3).

Likewise he says:

> “But now put away from yourselves anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and let no obscene speech come from your mouth.”

Likewise he says:

> “Clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, bearing with one another.”

Likewise he says:

> “Do not lie to one another.”

Likewise he says:

> “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above.”

Likewise he says:

> “Be kind and compassionate toward one another, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you” (Eph. 4).

Likewise he says:

> “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (ibid., v. 31).

Likewise he says:

> “Fornication, and every kind of uncleanness or greed, must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints; nor obscenity, foolish talk, or coarse joking” (Eph. 5).

Likewise he says:

> “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor idol-servants, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6).

Likewise he says:

> “No fornicator, unclean person, or greedy person has an inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God” (Eph. 5).

Likewise he says:

> “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 4).

Likewise he says:

> “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord” (Heb. 12).

Likewise he says to Timothy:

> “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity” (2 Tim. 2).

The Apostle John also says:

> “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2).

Likewise he says:

> “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (ibid., v. 6).

Likewise he says:

> “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3).

The Apostle James, however, says:

> “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God” (Jas. 4).

Many other legal, prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic testimonies—indeed innumerable ones—could be brought forward, to which Christian devotion ought to submit tirelessly and without excuse. But for the sake of those whom we mentioned above, we have briefly listed these few, since they foolishly assert that only monks are obliged to follow the difficult way, although the Lord says that the way leading to life is difficult and narrow, and that no one can enter eternal life except through it.

Therefore, not only monks and clerics, but also all who are known by the name Christian must enter by this difficult and narrow way.

What, then, is more difficult than what is commanded: “Love your enemies”; “Do not resist evil”; “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment”; and “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5), and other commands of this kind?

These things are indeed difficult, but they are most beneficial; and the more difficult they are, the more excellent and exalted they are.

Therefore all who, according to the Apostle (Rom. 6), have been baptized into Christ and have put on Christ must walk in newness of life and always place before their eyes the covenant that they made with God in baptism, when they renounced Satan, all his pomp, and all his works.

That covenant is then nullified when someone, while remaining in the faith, becomes entangled in vices, or, departing from the faith, becomes entangled in the worship of idols or in the errors of heresies.

Since, as it is written (Wis. 9), “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind occupied with many things,” and since human frailty becomes stained by the allurements of sins after the grace of baptism—and those sins cannot be erased by repeating baptism—it is necessary that they be erased as quickly as possible through the tears of repentance, generous almsgiving, and the performance of other good works.

And because we have one Father, Teacher, and Lord; one faith; one baptism; and one holy mother, the Church, all must strive earnestly and vigilantly—although people run by various paths of giftedness—to reach together the one holy and heavenly Jerusalem, our mother, where we may deserve to live with the Lord without end.

This too must be known: the more someone makes himself despised in the present world for the love of Christ, the happier a reward he will receive in the future.

## CHAPTER CXV

### How the canonical institution, supported by evangelical and apostolic authority, surpasses other institutions

Since it is clear by evident authority that the canonical institution surpasses other institutions, those who are counted under the name of this profession must take care to adorn that same institution in themselves by their life and conduct rather than disgrace it.

For those who possess an institution of such authority and ought to make themselves examples for others must fear lest, if—which God forbid—they deviate from their profession, they become unworthy of the kingdom of God.

Although canons may, because it is not read as prohibited to them in the sacred canons, wear linen, eat meat, give and receive, and possess their own property and the Church’s property with humility and justice—things entirely forbidden to monks, who lead a stricter life according to their rule—nevertheless, in avoiding vices and embracing virtues, their life must not differ from that of monks.

For monks, who follow the evangelical precept and, having sold and renounced their inheritances, have given their possessions to Christ, rightly receive temporal support from the resources of the Church. Since they desire heavenly things with the whole longing of their mind, they are sustained on the expenses of the Lord along the road of this pilgrimage, so that they may not be compelled by any necessity to return to the things they have despised.

And because they have left nothing as their own, it is clear that they need more abundant support from the Church than canons do, since canons lawfully use both their own property and the Church’s property. For, as the Apostle says, “Each person has his own gift from God” (1 Cor. 7).

## CHAPTER CXVI

### What the property of the Church is
The goods of the Church, as they are handed down by the holy Fathers and contained in the preceding chapters, are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sinners, and the patrimonies of the poor. For the faithful, inflamed by the ardor of faith and the love of Christ, and moved by concern for the remedy of their souls and by desire for the heavenly homeland, enriched the holy Church from their own possessions, so that by these means the soldiers of Christ might be fed, the churches adorned, the poor refreshed, and captives, when circumstances required, redeemed. [Col. 0915A] Therefore those who administer her resources must provide for them with vigilant and diligent care, lest they convert them solely to their own uses; rather, according to the capacity of the goods, they must not at all neglect to care for those who serve Christ—indeed, for those in whom Christ is fed and clothed.

The judgment of blessed Jerome, moreover, must be carefully considered not only by prelates but also by the others who use the goods of the Church. In his Commentary on the Evangelist Matthew he says:

> All, therefore, who misuse for other things, by which they satisfy their own will, the revenues of the temple and what is contributed for the uses of the church, are like the scribes and priests who purchase the lie and the blood of the Savior.

Therefore the goods of the Church are to be understood as stipends for the poor and the soldiers of Christ. Hence prelates must strive with all their strength, obeying the words and examples of the holy Fathers, so that from the goods entrusted to them—as stated above—they may govern their subjects, support the poor, and, by faithfully administering everything useful and necessary to the Church, provide for it. In this way they may deserve to be ineffably rewarded for their faithful administration by him whose ministers they are known to be.

## CHAPTER CXVII. That the Canons’ Enclosure Must Be Carefully Fortified

It is the duty of superiors constantly to fortify the minds of their subjects with readings from the holy Scriptures, lest the invisible wolf find an entrance by which he may enter the Lord’s sheepfold [Col. 0915C] and snatch away some of the sheep. Although this spiritual work must be carried out by them with the utmost zeal, it is nevertheless necessary that the enclosure in which the clergy entrusted to them are to live according to canonical rule be surrounded on every side with strong fortifications, so that no one at all may have access to enter or leave except through the gate. Inside there should also be dormitories, refectories, storerooms, and the other dwellings necessary for the use of brothers living together in one community.

Whoever refuses to do these things mentioned above, insofar as his ability permits, is to be regarded as unequal and less capable of carrying out the other ecclesiastical duties. Although he is worthy of divine vengeance, he must nevertheless be struck by synodal judgment.

## CHAPTER CXVIII. That Discretionary Proportion Must Be Observed in Gathering Canons

[Col. 0915D]

The superiors of churches must take the greatest care not to admit into the churches entrusted to them more clerics than reason allows and the resources of the church can support. For if they gather an indiscriminately and extraordinarily large number, they will be able neither to govern them nor, as they ought, to assist with the other needs of the church.

There are indeed some who seek empty glory from human beings and wish to have a numerous body of clergy, while taking no care to provide them with the comforts of either soul or body. Such men, once gathered in this fashion, receive no necessary stipends from their prelates; they observe neither the canonical order nor persist in the divine offices. Abandoning the enclosure and the fellowship of the others, they become wandering and wanton, devoted to gluttony, drunkenness, and their other pleasures; whatever they desire, they make lawful for themselves. [Col. 0916A]

Therefore superiors must provide diligently in this matter and observe a measure of discretion: they must neither admit into the community more than is proper and than the resources of the church can support, nor, through avarice, cast out those whom they can reasonably govern.

## CHAPTER CXIX. Concerning Those Who Gather into the Community Entrusted to Them Only Clerics from the Church’s Household

There are some who gather into the churches entrusted to them only clerics from the ecclesiastical household. They appear to do this so that, if they should ever inflict some hardship on these men or withhold the appropriate stipends from them, these men will not dare to bring any complaint against them—fearing, that is, that they might either be subjected to exceedingly severe beatings or cruelly reduced once more to human servitude.

This is not said to imply that persons of commendable conduct from the church’s household are not to be admitted into the community, especially since with God there is no partiality; rather, it is said because of the occasion we have mentioned, so that no prelate, excluding the noble, may admit only low-born persons into his community.

## CHAPTER CXX. Which Clerics Constituted in the Canonical Community Ought to Receive Ecclesiastical Stipends

Because the judgments of the holy Fathers cited above [Col. 0916C] teach that clerics are not to be seekers after riches and ought not to receive the goods of churches without proper service, we have thought it worthwhile to cite, by way of example, several chapters from Prosper’s book (*On the Contemplative Life*, book II, chapter 20), where we read:

> Those who serve the church and either willingly accept or demand things they do not need are excessively carnal in their thinking.

And again:

> It is indeed most unworthy if the faithful and diligent devotion of clerics, for the sake of a worldly stipend, despises eternal rewards.

And again:

> If someone does not wish to leave his own possessions for the sake of having the means to live, why does he accept something for which he will have to render an account? Why does he multiply his own sins by means of the sins of others?

After carefully considering these statements and those of the other holy Fathers, clerics must take care to avoid endangering themselves when receiving ecclesiastical provisions. Therefore those who possess both their own resources and those of the church, and who contribute to the church’s usefulness either within or outside it, should receive in the community food and drink and shares of alms, and should be content with these, lest, by receiving more, they appear to burden the poor. They should bear in mind Prosper’s judgment (*ibid.*, chapter 11), which says:

> Those who possess their own goods and wish something to be given to them do not, without great sin on their part, receive what the poor person was going to live on.

But those who neither abound in their own possessions nor possess estates of the church, and who contribute greatly to the church’s usefulness, should receive in the canonical community food, clothing, and shares of alms. For concerning such men it is written in Prosper’s book (*ibid.*, chapter 12):

> Clerics whom either their will or their birth has made poor, living in the community, should receive what is necessary for life, because they are led to receive these things not by the desire to possess, but compelled by the necessity of living.

Moreover, if there are men who do not wish to possess either their own property or that of the church, the prelates must provide for their needs through the resources of the church with the most provident administration, bearing in mind what Prosper says (*ibid.*, chapter 9):

> Whatever the church possesses, it possesses in common with all who have nothing. It must also care for those whom either illness or old age weighs down, and who are known formerly to have labored strenuously for the church’s interests.

## CHAPTER CXXI. That Food and Drink Are to Be Received Equally in the Canonical Community

[Col. 0917B]

In most communities of canons it is irrationally and indiscriminately customary for certain clerics who abound in wealth and contribute little or nothing of benefit to the church to receive a larger allowance of provisions than the others who diligently perform the divine office. Yet nowhere can this be found to have been sanctioned in any way, either by the authority of Scripture or by the traditions of the holy Fathers.

Since such a practice is supported by no authority, but is evidently customary rather for the sake of gluttony—or rather, avarice—it remains for it to be cut away by the sickle of justice and wholly abolished from the places where it occurs by the censure of equity.

It is reasonable and just before God and human beings that in every canonical community, from the least to the greatest, all should receive food and drink equally—namely, those who have been admitted among the number of canons for some useful purpose. Although many subjects are rightly accustomed to be honored by their prelates above others in various other matters, nevertheless in this fellowship, with partiality excluded, there ought to be one equality of food and drink.

## CHAPTER CXXII. Concerning the Measure of Food and Drink

We have also judged it most fitting and reasonable that in each place where the Lord is served canonically in community, the canons should receive equal portions of bread, pottage, and alms. Although it would be most proper for them likewise to receive an equal amount of drink, this cannot be done equally in every place: neither the very different resources of the churches, nor the qualities of the lands, nor the variations of circumstances permit it. Therefore we have considered it necessary to set out that a measure of discretion must be observed in this matter.

Accordingly, by common vote and common agreement, it pleased the sacred assembly to establish that in all places, both greater and smaller, each canon should receive four pounds of wine per day. In places where the churches have greater resources—for example, three, four, or indeed eight thousand manses or more—if the region is rich in wine, they should receive five pounds of wine each day, provided that seasonal scarcity does not prevent it. If the region is not fully productive of wine, they should receive three pounds of wine and three pounds of beer. If it produces no wine at all, they should receive one pound of wine and five pounds of beer.

In middling places possessing one thousand, one thousand five hundred, or indeed two thousand manses, if the region is, as stated above, rich in wine, they should receive four pounds of wine; and if it is not fully productive of wine, two pounds of wine and three pounds of drink made from different materials. If it is not at all productive of wine, they should receive four pounds of the aforementioned drink and one pound of wine.

In smaller places possessing two or three hundred manses, they should receive two pounds of wine. If the same region, as has already been said, lacks vineyards, three pounds of beer should be allotted to them and, if resources permit, one pound of wine.

Although in some provinces there is a lack of wine, prelates must nevertheless strive to obtain wine from the surrounding wine-producing provinces. For although vineyards are absent in many regions, by the Lord’s provision the holy Church abounds in supplies of other things, from which the diligence of prelates can obtain wine from other provinces and provide cups for their subjects according to their means.

In places where the church’s resources are very small, or perhaps have been greatly diminished by the removal of certain properties, only a few canons should be appointed, though they should be men of substantial office, so that at least the smaller measure set out above may be given to them without difficulty.

On feast days, as is the custom of the Church, prelates should provide the brothers with food and drink as generously as they can. In those places where certain prelates, following the example of devout prelates, are accustomed to give more to their subjects, they should by no means cease from the good that they do. If anyone, for the sake of eternal recompense, wishes to give his subjects more than required, let him cheerfully give what he can. Otherwise, let him in no way withhold the prescribed measure from them without unavoidable cause.

When a season of scarcity of wine occurs—as often happens when sins impede it—and the prelates cannot give the canons as much wine as they ought, they should distribute what they do give so discreetly and moderately that all may share it in common. They should not receive it with murmuring, but rather with thanksgiving, accepting what can be given and persevering together in their holy way of life.

For this reason the canons should take care to store communally in the storeroom any wine or other drink given to them as alms, so that when such a season of scarcity approaches they may use it together to supply their needs. Nevertheless, the drink due to them should not on this account be wholly withheld by the prelates if there is something from which it can be given.

Those who abound in both their own resources and those of the church should, when the season of scarcity arrives, strive with charity and humility to assist from their own means those whom the Church feeds as poor, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, “Brother should help brother, and both should be comforted” (Rom. XV). Yet they should not exalt themselves in pride on this account, because, as is read in Prosper’s book, such men ought not to set themselves above those whom the Church, though they possess nothing, feeds and clothes through empty boasting.

Meanwhile, prelates must always beware lest they withhold from their subjects by any evasion or parsimony what they ought or are able to give. Otherwise, compelled by poverty, the subjects may be driven to wander about in various places and entangle themselves in shameful occupations; abandoning ecclesiastical service, they may begin to live without discipline and serve their own pleasures. The prelates, who could have been rewarded by the Lord for generously supplying what their subjects needed, will then be judged strictly and severely.

Let them provide pottage for them according to their means, and assign them suitable places in which provisions may be produced, so that they may have the necessary ingredients for pottage, apart from what they receive from the church’s estates or from the offerings of the faithful. [Col. 0919B] Let these same canons therefore have gardens of vegetables, from which, together with other additions, they may prepare some pottage daily and serve it to one another in the refectory.

Because of the differences and inequalities of measures that prevail among many peoples—not equally according to the law of the Lord, but according to the custom of each province—we have judged that the measure of food and drink to be given to the canons should be determined by weight. This is because, although such measures are commonly very different and unequal, the public weight established for provinces, cities, and metals ought to suffer no difference or inequality; so that, just as the same weight remains equal, the same measure may likewise be distributed equally to them.

Let everyone know generally, however, that a pound must consist of no more than twelve ounces.

## CHAPTER CXXIII. That a Twofold Nourishment Is to Be Provided to Subjects by Prelates

Prelates must diligently strive to instruct those whom they govern by words and examples in how to live well. They must keep firmly in their hearts that they are to remember to treat them not as their own but as the flock of their Lord, in accordance with what is said to Peter: “If you love me, feed my sheep” (John XXI). He says, “my,” not “your.”

We say this because there are some who feed Christ’s sheep not out of love for Christ, but for the sake of their own glory, domination, or profit. They must also carefully consider that this same feeding of the Lord’s flock is to be carried out not with a single kind of care but with many kinds: namely, they must diligently provide them with earthly support and carefully offer them examples of virtue together with the word of preaching.

Therefore each prelate should strive faithfully to supply Christ’s household with both spiritual and bodily food, so that he may deserve to become the evangelical servant of whom it is said: “Who is the faithful and wise servant whom the master has set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?” (Matt. XXIV; Luke XII).

Thus, just as they provide their subjects with the necessities of the body, they must likewise strive to ensure that those same subjects observe the canonical order with the greatest religious devotion and humbly render due honor to their prelates and teachers. They must complete the divine office at the canonical hours with the utmost devotion; inside and outside, they must be irreproachable not only in dress and conduct but also in their very manner of walking.

They must not devote themselves to idleness, engage in empty talk, or occupy themselves with slander and the other enticements of vice. Rather, they should devote themselves either to prayer, reading, various duties of the church, or their own useful occupations; or they should be instructed in sound teachings and the disciplines of different arts. In this way no one in the community, being useless or idle, will receive the church’s stipends without proper service.

They should come daily to the reading and conference, where they should read through this institution and readings from other holy Scriptures, ask forgiveness for offenses committed, and receive a sentence according to the character of the offense. There they should also discuss the common progress and welfare of the Church.

They should all sleep in the dormitory, except anyone whom illness or old age prevents from doing so. They should all dine together daily in the refectory, unless necessity has compelled someone to be absent, and even this should not occur without the permission of the master. While they are eating and religiously maintaining silence, a reading should be continued without interruption and listened to with the utmost attention. In the refectory and in the other common necessities, they should serve one another in the duty of brotherhood.

No one should go outside without permission. Once outside, he should give no occasion for anyone to slander him, but should rather show himself worthy of imitation by all.

Let prelates therefore earnestly provide this twofold nourishment to the sheep entrusted to them, since they will render an account to the Lord for their souls. Thus, presenting them unharmed to Christ, the shepherd of all and the supreme pontiff, on the day of the fearsome judgment, they may not be condemned with the reprobate who will be struck by divine vengeance, but may instead be rewarded by the Lord with perpetual happiness together with the elect shepherds.

## CHAPTER CXXIV. That Canons, in This as in Other Matters, Should Observe Discretion in the Cultivation of Clothing

That God seeks the adornment of the heart rather than that of the body is clear from the evident testimonies of holy Scripture. Therefore the canons must labor with all their strength both to possess inwardly the garments of the virtues and to beware lest by immoderate dress they dishonor the dignity of religion outwardly.

How much they ought to restrain themselves from excessive and immoderate clothing can also be learned from many teachings of the holy Fathers. Blessed Jerome says in his letter to Eustochium:

> There are certain men of my order whose entire concern is with clothing: whether it smells good, whether their foot is not swollen by loose leather. Their hair is curled by the mark of the curling iron; their fingers shine with rings; and, lest the damp road splash their soles, they scarcely set down the tips of their feet. When you see such men, he says, regard them as bridegrooms rather than clerics.

And blessed Gregory says (*Homily 6 on the Gospels*):

> Let no one think that there is no sin in luxury and in the pursuit of costly clothing. For if this were not a fault, the Lord would in no way have praised John for the roughness of his clothing. If the adornment of clothing were not a fault, the Apostle Paul would certainly not have restrained women by his letter from desiring costly clothing, saying: “Not in costly clothing” (1 Tim. II).

We must carefully consider what fault it is for men also to desire what the shepherd of the Church took care to forbid to women. Therefore the canons ought to obey the authority of the holy Scriptures and carefully weigh the teachings of the holy Fathers, so that they may show the humility they carry in their hearts in their conduct, dress, manner of walking, and even their manner of riding. They should wish to shine more through holy conduct and outstanding character than through the ornament of clothing.

For if, following the custom of married people, they misuse fine clothing, horse trappings, and the other things of human vanity in arranging themselves, claiming that they ought to use similar things, in what way will their way of life be seen to differ from that of laypeople? Their dress, moreover, should be such that it is free from any occasion of vanity, gives off no scent of novelty or excess, and offers no cause for blame or slander.

No one should presume specially upon something that is not generally observed by all: neither should his clothing be more elegant than is proper, nor unusual and deformed. In either case the fault of either pride or pretence will become evident. Between the two, therefore, the virtue of discretion must be maintained with the greatest moderation.

This is stated most fully in the *Life of Blessed Augustine* (chapter 21), in his praise:

> His clothing, footwear, and bedding were of a moderate and suitable character, neither excessively fine nor greatly inferior. For in these matters most people are accustomed either arrogantly to display themselves or to abase themselves, seeking in both cases not the things of Jesus Christ but their own. But he, as I have said, kept to the middle, inclining neither to the right nor to the left.

## CHAPTER CXXV. That Canons Are Not to Wear Monks’ Cowls

We have learned that among many canons there has arisen a practice deserving reproach and ecclesiastical correction: contrary to ecclesiastical custom, they wear cowls, which are intended for monks alone. They ought certainly not to usurp the habit of those from whose way of life they differ in some respect. For just as it is indecent for them to carry military weapons in the manner of laypeople, so it is plainly dishonorable and highly unbecoming for them to put upon themselves the clothing of another way of life.

The habits of the individual orders have been distinguished from one another in the Church for this reason: so that, when they are seen, it may be clearly known what way of life the wearer follows and in what profession he serves the Lord. For under the Lord’s law also (Deut. XXII), a man is forbidden to wear a woman’s garment and a woman a man’s garment, so that each sex may go about clothed in clothing appropriate to it.

Just as it is shameful for a man to wear a woman’s garment and for a woman to wear a man’s, so it is highly unbecoming for a canon to wear a monastic garment—unless, together with the garment, he also wishes to assume the way of life.

Since this practice is approved by no authority, but is rightly reproved and rejected by those who think soundly, it ought from now on to be entirely prohibited, so that it does not occur.

## CHAPTER CXXVI. By What Authority the Canonical Hours Are Celebrated, Which Canons Ought to Know and Religiously Observe

*(Excerpt from Isidore, Book I of the Ecclesiastical Offices, chapter 9.)*

Daniel and the three young men devoted the third, sixth, and ninth hours to supplications (Dan. VI), so that the three hours extending from the rising of day to the time of supplication might declare to us reverence for the Trinity. Likewise, from the third and sixth hours up to the ninth, marked off by broad intervals of daylight, the Trinity might be honored by being invoked three times a day.

The following also presents itself as proof of the venerable Trinity: the Holy Spirit descended to earth at the third hour—that is, in its proper place, number, and time—to fulfill the grace that Christ had promised. At the sixth hour Christ suffered, and at the ninth he prolonged the torments of the cross. Through this mystery, at the lawful times of prayer, the perfection of the Trinity is either praised in solemn celebrations or sought through prayers at intervals of three hours.

Even if the daytime celebration is counted through the fourfold division up to the evening office—that is, four times three—it signifies that the world, divided into four parts, is saved in the Trinity. Likewise, during the night, the watches of the military vigil are divided into four parts and separated by intervals of three hours, so that in these nocturnal and worldly offices too the mystery of the Trinity may be revered.

## CHAPTER CXXVII. Concerning Vespers

Vespers is the office at the end of the day and at the setting of the alternating light; its solemn celebration comes from the Old Testament. (Isidore, *ibid.*, chapter 20.) In former times it was customary at this hour to offer sacrifices and burn spices and incense upon the altar. The witness is that hymn-singing man who exercised both royal and priestly office, saying:

> Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice (Exod. XX; Ps. CXL).

In the New Testament also, at this time, while the apostles were dining, our Lord and Savior first handed on the mystery of his body and blood, so that the time itself—the evening—might signify the end of the age. Therefore, in honor and remembrance of such great mysteries, it is fitting for us at these times to appear before the presence of God, to resound in his worship, offering him the sacrifice of our prayers and likewise exulting in his praises.

The evening is called *vesper* from the star called Vesper, which rises as the sun declines. Concerning it the prophet says: “And you cause evening to come forth upon the children of human beings” (Job XXXVIII).

## CHAPTER CXXVIII

*(Isidore, ibid., chapter 21.)*

Concerning the celebration of Compline, this too is found in the examples of the Fathers, the prophet David saying:

> If I ascend upon the bed of my couch, if I give sleep to my eyes and slumber to my eyelids, and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob (Ps. CXXXI).

Who would not marvel at such devotion of spirit in the love of God, that he entirely forbade himself sleep—without which human bodies certainly grow weak—until the king and prophet found in his own heart a place and temple to be built for the Lord?

This ought strongly to admonish us that, if we ourselves wish to be the Lord’s dwelling place and desire to be regarded as his tabernacle or temple, we should imitate the examples of the saints as far as we can, lest what is written be said of us:

> All the men of riches slept their sleep and found nothing in their hands (Ps. LXXV).

## CHAPTER CXXIX

[Col. 0923B]

The devotion of vigils is ancient, a familiar blessing to all the saints. (Isidore, *ibid.*, chapter 22.) The prophet Isaiah finally cries out to the Lord, saying:

> My spirit watches for you by night, O God, because your commandments are light upon the earth (Isa. XXVI).

David likewise, sanctified by both royal and prophetic anointing, sings:

> At midnight I rose to confess to you because of the judgments of your justice (Ps. CXVIII).

At this time the destroying angel passed through and struck the firstborn of the Egyptians (Exod. XII). Therefore we too ought to keep watch, lest we be mixed in with the danger of the Egyptians.

The Savior also asserted in the Gospel that he would come at these same hours. Therefore, rousing his hearers to keep watch, he says:

> Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching. And if he comes in the evening, and if at midnight, and if at cockcrow, and finds them watching, blessed are those servants. Therefore you also must be ready, because you do not know at what hour the Son of Man will come (Matt. XXIV; Luke XII).

He taught vigils not only by his words but also confirmed them by his example. For the Gospel testifies that Jesus spent the night in the prayer of God [that is, in prayer to God] (Luke VI).

Paul and Silas are likewise remembered as having prayed at about midnight in the public prison and sung a hymn while all listened. Then suddenly an earthquake occurred, the foundations of the prison were shaken, the doors opened of their own accord, and everyone’s chains were loosened (Acts XIV).

Therefore at these hours we ought to maintain frequent psalmody and prayer in the holy offices and await our end—or, if it should come—securely in such an activity.

There is, however, a certain kind of heretics who consider sacred vigils excessive and unproductive for spiritual work. They say that divine ordinances are being violated, since God made the night for rest just as he made the day for labor. These heretics are called in Greek *Nyctages*, that is, “sleepy ones.”

## CHAPTER CXXX

*(Isidore, ibid., chapter 23.)*

The same prophet David bears witness to the antiquity and authority of Matins, saying:

> In the morning I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper (Ps. LXII);

and elsewhere:

> My eyes went before you at dawn, so that I might meditate on your words (Ps. CXVIII).

Cassian, however, says (*Institutes of the Coenobia*, book III, chapter 4) that the office of the morning solemnity, instituted while the time was still new, was first established in the monastery at Bethlehem, where our Lord Jesus Christ deigned to be born of the Virgin for the redemption of human salvation; and from that time the custom of celebrating it spread throughout the whole world.

Prayer is therefore offered at dawn because the resurrection of Christ is celebrated. As the morning light shone forth, our Lord and Savior rose from the underworld, when the light that had set for sinners at Christ’s death began to rise for the faithful. At that same time, too, the hope of the future resurrection is believed by all, when all the just, rising from this temporal death as from the sleep of slumber, will awaken.

## CHAPTER CXXXI

Canons must strive with the utmost care to guard the hours mentioned above and to perform the divine office at them humbly and devoutly. As soon as the signal is heard, all must hasten to assemble in the church. They should enter it not pompously, dishonorably, or disorderly, but with reverence and fear of God.

They should not carry staffs in the choir, except those who are infirm; rather, they must stand and sing psalms there with the greatest religious devotion.

There are indeed certain clerics who spend almost the entire day tirelessly in worldly business and disputes. As soon as they enter the church to perform the divine office, they appear so exhausted that they can neither devote themselves to prayer nor stand for psalmody. Instead, sitting down, they habitually persist not in divine but in empty conversations, uttering worldly words to one another and—even though it is shameful to say—foul and obscene ones.

This detestable practice must therefore be uprooted completely both from those who engage in it and from those who may wish to imitate them. For, according to the Lord’s judgment, “His house is to be called a house of prayer” (Matt. III).

All should therefore discipline both their hearing and their tongue against idle chatter, and, standing in the church with fear and veneration, should either pray, sing, read, or listen. They should neither utter shameful, malicious, or worldly words themselves nor allow others to utter them. Rather, while offering praises to God together, they should entreat the Lord for their own sins and for the sins of the people whose offerings support them.

Moreover, according to the Apostle (1 Tim. II), first of all supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings should be made by them for all human beings, for kings, and for all who are in positions of authority, so that “we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity.” For, the Apostle says, “this is good and acceptable before God our Savior.”

They must also beware lest, because rest has been granted to them in places dedicated to divine worship, they grow sluggish through idleness. Rather, they should be more ready and devoted in offering divine praises, so that by working well during this rest they may be able to reach that which has no end.

Whoever neglects to attend these hours and to perform the heavenly office at them as is fitting must be rebuked with a worthy reprimand, so that he may be corrected and the others, taking warning, may avoid such negligence.

Since, however, it is one thing to omit an office entirely and another to arrive sluggishly, whoever comes carelessly or late to Matins or to any other divine service should not stand in the choir with the others but as the very last—or, so that he may learn to feel shame, in a place appointed by the prelates for those guilty of such negligence. He must in no way presume to remain outside, lest he devote himself to idleness and gossip and become wholly separated from the praises of God.

Furthermore, the custodians of the church should know the divisions of these hours well, so that they may ring the signals at the appointed times. They should see to it that the lights are prepared with every diligence, and it should be their concern that nothing belonging to the church’s resources entrusted to them be lost.

## CHAPTER CXXXII. That Angels Are Present When the Lord Is Sung to and Praised in Psalms

[Col. 0925B]

The minds of those singing psalms in the church to the Lord ought to accord with their voices, so that they may fulfill the Apostle’s words: “I shall sing with the spirit; I shall sing also with the mind” (1 Cor. XIV). For although we know that the Lord is present everywhere through the power of his divinity, nevertheless we believe that he is especially present to us by grace when we are attending the divine office.

On this subject the venerable presbyter Bede says in his exposition of the Gospel of Luke:

“It is not hidden that angels are often invisibly present with the elect, either to defend them from the snares of the cunning enemy or to raise them up by the greater grace of heavenly desire, as the Apostle bears witness when he says: ‘Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?’ Yet we must believe that angelic spirits are especially present with us when we are devoted in a particular way to divine services—that is, when, having entered the church, we lend our ears to sacred readings, or apply ourselves to psalmody, or devote ourselves to prayer, or even celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass.”

Hence the Prophet says: “In the sight of the angels I shall sing psalms to you” (Ps. CXXXVII). Nor may there be any doubt that, where the mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood are celebrated, the assembly of the citizens above is present.

Therefore we must diligently strive that, whenever we enter the church either to render the due praises of God or to celebrate the solemn rites of the Mass, we may always remember the angelic presence and complete the heavenly office with suitable fear and reverence. Otherwise, if—which God forbid—we perform it negligently, dishonorably, or lukewarmly, and come tardily to complete it, we may miserably fall under the sentence that says: “Cursed is the one who performs the work of God negligently.” Accordingly, we must carefully observe that in the church of God we perpetrate nothing improper, nothing perverse, nothing unbecoming, whether in thought, words, or actions, so that we may be made worthy in the sight of the angels and that, when the Lord comes to us, he may find in us not what he condemns but rather what he rewards.

## CHAPTER CXXXIII. What sort of persons should be appointed to read and sing in the church

Those should be appointed to read, sing, and chant psalms in the church who render the praises due to the Lord not arrogantly but humbly; who, by the pleasantness of their reading and the melody of their singing, both delight the learned and instruct the less learned; and who prefer the people’s edification through reading or song to the exceedingly vain applause of the crowd.

Those who cannot perform these duties skillfully should first be instructed by teachers. Once trained, they should strive to fulfill them, so that they may edify those who listen.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV. What the manner of correction should be

Although despisers of canonical institutions should be punished chiefly by episcopal judgment—a punishment which, as blessed Augustine says, can have no greater severity within the Church—it must nevertheless be explained what manner of correction the other prelates, who are known to be inferior to them in rank, ought to employ in the places entrusted to them against subjects who offend and who are unwilling to observe those matters that properly belong to their calling.

Since every age and the capacity of each person’s understanding ought to have its own measures, and since the measure of correction must be extended according to the measure of faults, and since all these matters rightly depend upon the judgment of the prelates, by whom they must be most judiciously tempered, those same prelates must imitate the conduct of highly skilled physicians toward offenders. That is, with great care and discretion they must apply whatever is suitable and appropriate to each person, carefully considering above all that they should provide remedies according to the size of the wounds, so that they neither give one person what harms nor withhold from another what helps.

Leaving aside those whose offending age ought not to be spared, but whose sides should rather, according to Solomon, be continually beaten with rods lest they become hardened, let it be shown briefly and concisely how, in accordance with divine authority and the examples and traditions of the holy Fathers, this should be done with regard to other offenders.

If any brother established in a canonical community neglects to attend the canonical hours, enters the church not devoutly but ostentatiously or disorderly, performs the work of God negligently, delays coming to the conference, refuses to carry out an obedience enjoined upon him by his teachers, fails to show diligence according to his ability in reading, singing, or the other ecclesiastical disciplines, comes late to the table not out of necessity but through fault, leaves the cloisters without permission, delays beyond the time assigned to him after being permitted to go out, attempts to go into the streets or sit at crossroads, commits anything improper or dishonorable in words or actions in the dormitory, presumes to sleep anywhere other than in the dormitory with the others without unavoidable cause, neglects to serve the brothers obediently in the duty of charity, sows discord among the brothers—which, as Scripture says (Prov. VI), the soul of God detests—or proves obstinate, proud, murmuring, or in any way opposed to this institution, and attempts to do other things of this kind, he should first be admonished according to God’s command—not only once, and a second and third time, but even more frequently. If he does not yield to these admonitions, he should be corrected by public rebuke.

If he resists even this, he should be forbidden all food except bread and water until he has made worthy satisfaction. If he still does not correct himself, he should be separated from the table and removed from the company of the brothers chanting in the choir. He should be compelled to stand apart in a place designated by the prelates for those negligent in this way, so that at least the shame of separation may amend him.

Then, if after being corrected by these measures he remains incorrigible, and if his age permits it, since, according to Solomon’s words (Prov. XVIII), “A fool is not corrected by words,” a suitable punishment of blows should be applied to him. He should be beaten as a son, so that, according to the judgment of blessed Gregory, “those who do not hear the words of command may be admonished by blows,” and punishment may draw toward good desires those whom rewards do not attract.

But if he is such that either his age or the quality of his person does not permit him to be beaten, he should be corrected by public rebuke, the continual affliction of fasts, and the shame of separation, until he obtains pardon through a worthy satisfaction of penance.

If both—the one who is beaten and the one whom age or the quality of his person prevents from being beaten—remain incorrigible, they should, if there is a place within the cloisters of the canons for temporary confinement, as is known to exist in many places, be shut up there for a time and punished according to the measure of their fault, so that, in accordance with the Apostle, “having been handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord” (2 Cor. V).

If they still do not obey after so many salutary admonitions and punishments, the entire community should offer common prayer for them, that they may be healed by the Lord.

Finally, if they appear altogether unamendable and incorrigible, lest their dreadful contagion spread among many, they must be separated from the society of the others like diseased sheep and brought before the bishop, so that they may be publicly condemned by him with canonical authority.

If anyone in the college of canons commits a criminal offense, no delay should be granted him. Either he must voluntarily perform penance for the crime committed, or, if he refuses to do so, he must be brought before the bishop, so that he may be publicly punished by him with penance.

The rectors must remember that the Church is called a dove in the divine Scriptures, which does not tear with claws but strikes gently with its wings (Song of Songs VI). Therefore they must be especially careful that, as stated above, correction be wholly tempered according to the measure of the faults and according to the persons and their ages, so that neither the vice of sloth may grow nor correction exceed the measure of gentleness. Otherwise, as blessed Maximus says, either excessive leniency may provide connivance for the sinner, or immoderate severity may fail to recall the offender from his fall.

They must likewise beware lest, out of resentment over anything, they strike at the offenders’ faults; rather, as blessed Augustine says, they should be persecutors of crimes and liberators of persons. Let them hate vices and love people. Let them hate what has been instilled by the devil and love what has been created by God’s goodness.

Let them hold in their hand both a staff and a rod: the staff, by which they may spiritually support the weaknesses of others’ strength; and the rod, by which they may strike the vices of offenders with zeal for righteousness.

Meanwhile, the other brothers must not in any way favor offending or excommunicated brothers, deceive them by their flatteries, or defend their errors. Rather, they should lend assistance so that they may be corrected strictly by the judgment of equity.

## CHAPTER CXXXV

The rectors of churches must vigilantly ensure that the boys and adolescents who are nourished or instructed in the community entrusted to them are so restrained by continual ecclesiastical disciplines that their wanton age, which is exceedingly prone to sin, can find no opportunity to plunge into sinful wrongdoing.

Therefore, for guarding and spiritually instructing such persons, the prelates must appoint a brother of approved life who will care for them with the utmost diligence and restrain them so strictly that, imbued with ecclesiastical teachings and clothed in spiritual armor, they may be able both to serve the needs of the Church becomingly and, in time, to be worthy of promotion to the ecclesiastical orders.

Moreover, for suitable edification and instruction concerning the matter at hand, we have wished to insert into this work a saying of the holy Fathers, which runs as follows:

“Every age is inclined toward evil from adolescence. Nothing is more uncertain than the life of adolescents” (Gen. VIII). “For this reason it was necessary to establish that, if there is a boy in the clergy or if there are adolescents, they should all live together in one chamber of the courtyard, so that they may spend the years of their slippery age not in luxury but in ecclesiastical disciplines, assigned to a most excellent elder whom they may have both as a teacher of doctrine and as a witness of life, and so forth.”

With these matters thus set forth, the boys ought to be entrusted for supervision to a most excellent elder, even if they are instructed by another. But if the brother to whom this care is committed takes little account of them, teaches them anything other than what he ought, or in any way implants in them a stain of harm, he should be corrected with the utmost severity and removed from office. The responsibility should be entrusted to another brother who will form them by examples of an innocent life and encourage them to perform good works.

## CHAPTER CXXXVI

When the appropriate hours and the daytime offices have been completed by all the canons with the most devout service, they must, at the given signal, come most devoutly to celebrate Compline.

When it has been completed, they must not devote themselves to feasts, drinking, or idle conversations. Rather, putting these things aside entirely, they should go humbly and decently to the dormitory. They must never rest two in one bed, but each in a separate bed.

A lamp should also burn continually in the dormitory during the night. Finally, no one should do anything improper or unbecoming in the dormitory, nor should anyone presume to disturb another or compel him to break into useless and idle talk.

Anyone who despises this chapter should be corrected with the utmost severity by the prelates and teachers.

## CHAPTER CXXXVII

The singers must take the greatest care not to defile with vices the gift bestowed upon them by God. Rather, they should adorn it with humility, chastity, sobriety, and the other ornaments of holy virtues. Their melody should raise the minds of the people standing around to the remembrance and love of heavenly things, not only through the sublimity of the words but also through the sweetness of the tones that are sung.

A cantor, as has been handed down by the holy Fathers, ought to be distinguished both in voice and in skill, and illustrious, so that through the pleasures of sweetness he may stir the minds of those who hear, and so forth.

Therefore singers should not proudly set themselves above the others because of the gift bestowed upon them, but should present themselves humbly as companions. Care must also be taken that the divine office be performed sometimes moderately and sometimes softly: namely, that they extend the singing and regulate their voices according to the number of clergy, the character of the office, and the length of time.

They should also pronounce the sounds of the vowel letters well and with elegance. But those who are less capable of this art should remain silent until they have been instructed. It is better for them to be silent than, by attempting to sing what they do not know, to compel the voices of others to become discordant.

For the psalms in the church should not be recited hurriedly, with loud, disorderly, or uncontrolled voices, but clearly and distinctly, with compunction of heart, so that the minds of those reciting may be nourished by their sweetness and the ears of those listening may be delighted by their pronunciation. Although the sound of song is customarily produced in a loud voice in other offices, such a voice must be avoided when the psalms are recited.

Meanwhile, senior brothers of more exemplary life should be appointed to join the singers’ school in turn at the appointed time, so that those who ought to learn may neither devote themselves to idleness nor persist in empty and superfluous conversations.
