If the singers are proud and refuse to communicate to others the art they have learned with God’s help, they should be judged gravely and severely, so that, once amended and corrected, they may strive to distribute to others the talent bestowed upon them by God.

The prelates must maintain this manner of correction earnestly toward those who are instructed in any kind of skill and who, because of the talent divinely bestowed upon them, are eager to set themselves above others in pride rather than to communicate it with charity.

## CHAPTER CXXXVIII

The prelates of the church ought to choose from the community entrusted to them brothers of good reputation among whom they can safely divide the burdens of governance.

They should also confer upon them such authority that, acting in their place, they may correct the disobedient by canonical discipline and encourage the obedient toward better things by exhortation.

They must not be appointed merely on the basis of person or according to the order in which they were admitted to the college of brothers. Rather, they should be chosen according to the merit of their life and the precedence of their spiritual gifts. They should be constant in the community and care for the brothers with vigilant diligence.

Just as they surpass others in teaching, so they should instruct them by the example of an innocent life, so that, according to the Apostle, they may be examples to the others in word, conduct, charity, faith, and chastity.

If they begin to grow swollen with pride because of their priorate and take no account of the care of the brothers, and if, after frequent admonition, they remain incorrigible, they should be expelled from their ministry and others who can perform it energetically should be appointed in their place.

## CHAPTER CXXXIX

Although all who preside over others are properly called superiors, usage has nevertheless established that those are called superiors who exercise a certain care of a priorate under other prelates.

Those who are called superiors according to this custom must be appointed as men of exemplary life and great vigor. They must faithfully and humbly fulfill the duties assigned to them and, because they preside over others, must not in any way regard canonical institutions as unimportant. Rather, the more they are involved in caring for the brothers, the more they should strive to obey heavenly commands.

They must therefore be useful to the entire community and faithfully benefit it through the ministry entrusted to them. Whatever they ought to give to the brothers, they should provide readily and with charity at the appropriate time, so that they may receive from the Lord a good rank for faithful administration.

Toward such offenders, however, and those who do not properly administer the obedience entrusted to them, the manner described above must be maintained.

## CHAPTER CXL

The prelate must ensure that he appoints as cellarer for the brothers someone who is neither a drunkard, nor proud, nor slow, nor wasteful, but honorable in character and fearing God. He must faithfully preserve the brothers’ supplies and, by administering them with diligent care, never cause the brothers distress.

The brothers’ bakery should also be entrusted to him, so that he may guard it with the utmost vigilance and ensure that the servants assigned there do not squander the brothers’ provisions either by secretly stealing them or by living negligently in some other way.

These servants should be chosen from the Church’s most faithful household and carefully trained for these duties, so that, both in the art of baking and in purity of faith, they may be able to assist the brothers’ needs most suitably.

The same arrangement must be observed concerning the cooks. Finally, useless and disobedient cellarers should be judged according to the sentence set forth above.

## CHAPTER CXLI

We are instructed by evangelical and apostolic teachings that, in gathering guests, we ought above all to apply ourselves so that the Lord may rightly say of us: “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me” (Matt. XXV), and so forth.

Therefore the prelates of the church, following the examples of the Fathers who preceded them, ought to prepare some place of shelter where the poor may be gathered. They should assign there from the resources of the Church only as much as will enable them, according to the means available, to have the necessary expenses, except for the tithes that are contributed there from the Church’s estates.

The canons should also willingly contribute to that hospital for the use of the poor a tenth part both of the crops and of all offerings of alms.

A brother of good reputation from the community itself should be appointed to receive arriving guests and pilgrims as Christ in his members and to provide them willingly with what they need, according to his ability. He must never divert to his own use what ought to be devoted to the poor, lest he receive the sentence of condemnation together with Judas, who stole from the Lord’s money box.

The prelates’ diligence must also remain vigilant lest they allow the person entrusted with the hospital of the poor to diminish in any way the property assigned to the poor or to use it as though it had been granted to him as a benefice. We have learned that this is done by certain prelates who take little account of the care of the poor.

If the clergy cannot do so at other times, at least during Lent they should wash the feet of the poor in the proper hospital, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “If I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet?” (John XIII), and so forth.

Therefore it is advantageous that the hospital of the poor be located in a suitable place where the brothers can easily assemble to visit it.

If the person entrusted with the hospital neglects the care of the poor and turns their property to his own uses, although he is worthy of divine vengeance, he must nevertheless be judged more severely than other offenders by the superiors and removed from his ministry. And rightly so, since he has applied to his own uses what he had no right to use: the price of sinners’ redemption, the sustenance of the poor, and a treasure to be stored in heaven.

## CHAPTER CXLII

Although the canons may lawfully have private dwellings, the prelate must nevertheless establish within the canons’ cloister a residence for the sick and the elderly. Thus those who perhaps do not have their own dwelling may most suitably endure their weakness there, and may be mercifully supported both by the ecclesiastical resources they need and by the assistance of the brothers.

The other brothers ought to show them great charity: they should help them by compassion, by frequent visits, by the consolations of the Holy Scriptures, and also by providing the necessary assistance from their own resources, so that the Gospel saying may be fulfilled in them: “I was sick, and you visited me” (Matt. XXV).

## CHAPTER CXLIII

The prelate must choose from the community entrusted to him a brother of exemplary life whose duty it will be, with complete obedience and suitable humility, to close and unlock the canons’ gate at the proper time, so that no one may enter or leave through it without permission.

He must also take care not to provide an opportunity for those who prefer to devote themselves to leisure rather than to attend to divine services to wander outside, nor become, which is forbidden, a participant in their frivolity.

He must also receive all who arrive with charity and announce their arrival and purpose to the prior.

After the evening office and Compline have been completed and the gates have been locked, the porter must bring their keys to the one who holds the prelate’s place, so that no one may retain the opportunity to enter or leave at unsuitable hours. He should receive the keys back from that same person at the appointed time on the following day.

If the porter is found to be disobedient and insolent, he should be judged as was stated above concerning other negligent ministers.

## CHAPTER CXLIV

The cloisters of the canons must be guarded so diligently that the Lord’s flock may enjoy fraternal peace in harmony.

If a prelate, someone acting in his place, or perhaps any other spiritual brother finds anyone within the cloister behaving dishonorably, or outside at crossroads and in the streets devoting himself to leisure and idle conversations, he should first correct him by private admonition. Then, if necessary, the same negligent person should be judged more severely before the brothers, so that, once amended, he may thereafter advance toward better things.

Women must not dine or rest in the dwellings or cloisters of the canons. Indeed, they must not be granted any opportunity to enter them at all, except the church, because this is recorded as having been strongly forbidden by the holy Fathers.

If anything is to be assigned to them as an act of charity, a place outside the cloister should be designated where they may receive it. No brother may speak with them unless witnesses are present.

Anyone who attempts to act otherwise than has been stated above must be corrected so severely by the prelates and teachers that the example of the correction inflicted upon him may instill fear in the others, lest they dare to do anything similar.

## CHAPTER CXLV

Although the holy Fathers have sufficiently clarified in the earlier parts of this little book how clerics ought to live—so that anyone who reads carefully what has been set forth above can clearly find in it what his devotion of faith, the adornment of his actions and morals, and the performance of divine worship ought to be—we have nevertheless thought it absolutely necessary, for the sake of the many who are simple and less capable, to repeat these matters briefly and concisely.

Those who cannot read these things, or perhaps cannot fully understand what others have read to them, may use this little selection, like a basket filled with the nectar of various blooming flowers, and learn what they ought to do and what they ought to avoid.

Meanwhile, we are admonished by legal institutions and the most salutary evangelical commands to love the Lord our God with all our heart and our neighbor as ourselves, and so forth.

If all the faithful ought to embrace these saving commands with all their strength, how much more should those who are devoted to divine worship and who ought to be an example of virtue to others do so.

Therefore, first of all they ought to love the Lord God with all their heart, with all their soul, and with all their strength, and their neighbors as themselves; and they should know that upon these two commandments the whole law and the prophets depend.

They must not kill or hate their brother, because, as the Apostle says, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III).

They must not commit adultery, steal, covet another’s property, or bear false witness. What they do not wish to be done to themselves, they must not do to another.

They must not be swollen with pride, accustomed to slander, enslaved to drunkenness, weakened by lust, disturbed by anger, or subjected to any other vices. They must not be talkers of vanity, envious, sleepy, lazy, murmurers, whisperers, drunkards, or excessively gluttonous.

They must beware of fraud and deceit, never serve usury, and not swear, lest they commit perjury. They must not repay evil for evil.

When they see something good in themselves, they should attribute it to God; when they see evil, they should attribute it to themselves.

They should flee discord and restore those whom they find at odds to the harmony of charity. In accordance with the Psalmist’s words (Ps. XXXIII), they should turn away from evil and do good.

They should also heed the Apostle’s prohibition: “Not in feasting and drunkenness, not in sleeping places and impurities, not in strife and rivalry; rather, put on the Lord Jesus Christ.”

They should also observe that from the vices prohibited by the Apostle a harvest of every vice arises, and that pride is the mother of these diseases.

They ought to guard their soul and body from every defilement of flesh and spirit, so that, according to the Apostle, their spirit, soul, and body may be preserved whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.

They should live soberly, justly, and piously, and utterly reject worldly affairs, because, according to the same Apostle, “No one serving God entangles himself in worldly business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.”

They should love fasting, gather guests, refresh the poor, clothe the naked, visit the sick, bury the dead, assist those in tribulation, and console the sorrowful.

They must prefer nothing to the love of Christ and must not abandon charity. If possible, they should have peace with all people. They should fear the day of judgment and spiritually desire eternal life.

They should entrust their hope to God, obey their own bishop in all things according to canonical institution, and not rashly criticize their teachers.

Finally, they should devote themselves to spiritual instruction. They should continually apply themselves to readings, psalms, hymns, songs, and exercises in other good works.

Unless illness has detained someone, all should sleep in the dormitory. They should likewise be refreshed together in the refectory and come daily to the conference.

As soon as the signal has been given, all should hasten to the church and celebrate the canonical hours together, not negligently but with complete devotion.

They should enter the church not ostentatiously but reverently. In the choir they should not stand with staffs, nor persist in idle talk; rather, with complete devotion and reverence, they should perform the work of divine service, knowing that the presence of the angels is always there.

They must not leave the cloisters except with permission. Once outside, they should live irreproachably, so that they may have a good reputation among those who are outside. They must not stain their religion and calling with unlawful deeds; rather, they should season all with whom they associate with the salt of wisdom and the examples of good works.

They must not desire the company of women in any way. They must not walk with wandering eyes, or with a wanton and arrogant bearing, or with loosened hips. They must not attend spectacles or worldly pageants, nor serve gaming or any kind of hunting.

For, instructed by the Apostle’s teaching, which says, “Not in costly clothing” (1 Tim. VIII), they must take no pleasure in expensive garments.

They must take the greatest care not to linger outside the cloisters except as the prior has directed and the opportunity of the time has determined.

While inside the cloisters, they must not devote themselves to leisure, but must either attend to divine offices, their own proper tasks, or at least obey the commands of their teachers, lest, growing sluggish through idleness, they hear from the Apostle: “If anyone is unwilling to work, let him not eat” (2 Thess. III).

The elders should love the younger spiritually; the younger should show due obedience to the elders.

The more learned must not set themselves above the less learned, but should rather edify them with charity. Nor should those distinguished by noble birth or endowed with virtues arrogantly exalt themselves above the others.

All members of the community should serve one another in turn through the duty of charity. While they are eating in the refectory and religiously maintaining silence, a reading should be continued without interruption.

They should rebuke and correct offenders together with zeal for righteousness. They should correct negligent boys and adolescents by disciplines of words.

Each person should be instructed according to his capacity in the disciplines of various arts, so that no one may appear useless in the canonical college, nor consume the offerings of the faithful in idleness.

All who have devoted themselves to divine offices ought to be such persons, and ought also to conduct themselves in this way.

Therefore they should strive to read over these matters, gathered together briefly, with careful reflection, commend them to memory, and, with divine grace assisting, fulfill them according to their ability, so that they may more easily and freely carry out the greater things handed down by the holy Fathers.

Let them therefore walk according to the calling by which they were called, turning neither to the right nor to the left, so that, obeying the divine commands, they may, with Christ’s help, be worthy to reach Christ, in whose portion they are known to be, who is the way, the truth, and the life.

# BOOK TWO. ON THE INSTITUTION OF NUNS

[Note: The manuscript codex of this book is now in the Colbert Library, formerly in the Thuana Library. HARD. — We were permitted to see the single codex of this later Rule belonging to Nicolas Fabri, now kept in the Thuana Library; but I hear that another exists in the church of Auxerre. JAC. SIRM.]

[Col. 0935]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0935A]

This constitution was gathered and compiled by the holy assembly in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 816, in the tenth indiction, specifically in the third year of the most glorious Emperor Louis, at the palace of Aachen, at the urging of that ruler, for the salvation of nuns living canonically. With divine grace inspiring it and the authorities of the holy Fathers, as though from blooming meadows, it collected certain little flowers and brought them together into one work, and by common vote and common agreement determined that the nuns should hold and observe it.

[Col. 0935]

III. Likewise, an excerpt from the same author’s letter to Furia.

IV. Excerpt from Cyprian’s letter on the dress of virgins.

XI. That women’s monasteries should be fortified on every side and that necessary dwellings should be prepared within.

XII. That nuns living in one community should receive food and drink equally.

XIII. How nuns ought to receive the allowances necessary for them.

XIV. That a double meal should be provided by abbesses to nuns.

[Col. 0936A]

XX. That nuns should beware of frequent association with men.

[Col. 0936B]

XXIII. That in women’s monasteries there should be a house for old and sick women.

XXIV. What sort of superiors should be appointed.

XXV. What sort of cellarer should be appointed.

XXVII. That priests and their assistants should enter women’s monasteries only at the appointed time.

XXVIII. That the hospital for the poor should be outside the women’s monastery.

## MANSI’S PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE FOLLOWING RULE OF NUNS

[Col. 0935]

The Rule of the Council of Aachen for nuns exists in a very ancient parchment codex of the ninth century, written in the same period in which the council was held. That codex is preserved at Rome in the library of the Fathers of the Cistercian monastery of the Holy Cross in Jerusalem.

The learned monk Father Darius Marinoni, of the same order and librarian of that monastery, informed me by letter that everything in it agrees with the printed editions, except that before the beginning of the first chapter he noticed a sermon attributed to Saint Augustine. He most courteously sent me a copy of it.

Accordingly, on the authority of this codex, I am the first to place this sermon before the Rule given to nuns.

## HERE BEGINS THE SERMON OF SAINT AUGUSTINE TO VIRGINS

[Col. 0935C]

Love the Lord, and he will love you; serve him, and he will illumine your heart. Honor your mother as the Mother of Christ, and do not despise her gray hairs, she who bore you. Love your sisters as the daughters of your mother, and do not abandon the ways of peace. Let the rising sun see the book in your hand, and after the second hour perform your work. Pray without ceasing, and remember Christ, who begot you. Avoid the company of men, lest it become an idol in your soul and a stumbling block at the time of prayer. You have Christ as your beloved; cast away all men, and you will not live a reproachable life. Keep anger far from you also, and do not let the memory of evil linger with you.

Do not say today, “I am eating,” and tomorrow, “I shall not eat,” for you do this without wisdom; [Col. 0936C] it will be harmful to your body and torment your stomach. To eat meat is not good, and to drink wine is not best; but it ought to be offered to those who are infirm. A turbulent virgin will not be saved, and she who lives in luxury will not see her bridegroom. Do not say, “The servant-girl has saddened me, and I shall repay her,” because there is no such servitude among the daughters of God. Do not lend your ear to empty words, and flee tales of evil. Flee drunken revelries of those who celebrate, and do not go to another’s wedding; for a virgin who does these things is unclean.

Open your mouth to the word of God, and restrain your tongue from much speaking. Humble yourself before the Lord, and he will exalt you from his earth. Do not turn away from the poor in a time of tribulation, and the oil of your lamp will not fail. Do everything for the Lord, and do not seek [Col. 0937A] glory from human beings, for human glory is like the flower of hay, whereas the glory of the Lord remains forever. The Lord loves a gentle virgin, but an angry virgin will be hateful. An obedient virgin will obtain mercy, but one who contradicts is exceedingly foolish. The Lord destroys a murmuring virgin, but delivers the gracious one from death. Shameful is laughter, and reproachable is shamelessness; for every foolish person will become entangled in such things. She who adorns her garments will be chaste outwardly.

Do not linger with worldly people, for they will turn your heart away and make righteous counsels void. Ask the Lord with tears at night, and let no one know that you are praying; then you will find grace. Do not imitate the desire for the promenades of others; a gift and a desire turn the disposition of the mind aside and corrupt its ready [Col. 0937B] will. A faithful virgin will not fear, but the faithless one will flee even her own shadow. Envy consumes the soul, and jealousy devours it.

She who despises her sick sister will be far from Christ. Do not say, “This is mine, and that is yours”; for in Christ Jesus all things are common. Do not investigate another’s life, and do not rejoice at your sister’s ruin. Rather, assist virgin women who love [God], and do not be elated by your nobility. Do not utter a word from your mouth in the church of the Lord, and do not lift up your eyes; for the Lord knows your heart and examines all your thoughts. Drive every evil desire far from you, and your enemies will not trouble you.

Sing psalms from a pure heart, and do not merely move [Col. 0937C] your tongue in your mouth. The foolish virgin loved silver, but the prudent one adds also her bread. As the force of fire is difficult to restrain, so the food of a virgin is scarcely curable [i.e. scarcely brought under control]. Do not give your soul over to evil thoughts, lest they pollute your heart, and keep unclean prayer far from you.

Heavy sorrow and intolerable apathy are grievous, but tears from the Lord are stronger than either. Hunger and thirst make evil desires wither, while good vigil purifies the understanding. Gifts confound anger and maliciousness. She who secretly slanders her sister will stand outside the Bridegroom’s chamber, cry out at his doors, and not be heard. The lamp of a merciless virgin will be extinguished, and she will not see her bridegroom coming. A glass falling upon a stone [Col. 0937D] is shattered, and a virgin joined to a man will not remain innocent.

A gentle woman is better than an impetuous and angry virgin. She who draws a man’s words from him through laughter is like one who casts a noose around her own neck. As a pearl in a golden sling, so is virginity covered with reverence. Songs of demons and pipes loosen the soul and destroy its strength; guard it in all things, lest you become reproachable. Do not delight in laughter, and do not rejoice in those who speak abusively, for the Lord abandons such women.

You shall not reproach your sister when she is eating, nor be exalted by your abstinence; for you do not know what the Lord will think, or who will stand in his presence. She has pity on those whom she sees with her eyes and on those wasting away in their misfortunes [reading uncertain]. [Col. 0938A] Severe abstinence is beyond the power of the mind, and chastity is scarcely kept straight.

Nothing is sweeter than the heavenly Bridegroom. The souls of virgins will be illumined, but the souls of the unclean will see darkness. I have seen men corrupting virgins by their teachings and making their virginity vain. But you, hear, daughter, the teachings of the Church of God, and let no stranger persuade you.

God founded heaven and earth, and rejoices in them. There is no angel incapable of evil [Note: That is, at the time when he was created.]; nor is there a demon evil by nature. Both, like man, possess free will and are constituted with a corruptible body and a rational soul. So also our Lord was born without sin; he ate and was crucified, and his appearance was not fictitious in the eyes of human beings. So will be [Col. 0938B] the resurrection of the dead. This world passes away, and we shall receive the spoils. The bodies of the righteous will inherit light, but the wicked will dwell in darkness. The eyes of the virgin will see the Lord, and the virgin’s ears will hear rightly. Amen.

## CHAPTER ONE

*(Excerpt from Jerome’s Letter 21 to Eustochium.)* Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house, and the king will desire your beauty. In the forty-fourth Psalm, God speaks to the human soul, so that, following Abraham’s example, it may go out from its land and its kindred, leave the Chaldeans—who are interpreted, as it were, as demons—and dwell in the land of the living, which elsewhere the Prophet longs for, saying:

> [Col. 0938C] I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living (Psalm XXVI).

Yet it is not enough for you to go out from your homeland unless you also forget your people and your father’s house.

**THE SAME PLACE.** It is not fitting, after taking hold of the plow, to look back, nor to return home from the field; nor, after putting on Christ’s tunic, to descend from the roof in order to take another garment. A great wonder: a father urges his daughter not to remember her father. “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father” (John VIII), it is said to the Jews; and elsewhere: “Whoever commits sin is from the devil” (1 John III).

Begotten first from such a parent, we are black, and after repentance, while we have not yet ascended to the summit of virtue, we say: “I am black, but beautiful also, O daughters of Jerusalem” (Song I). I have gone out from the house of my childhood; I have forgotten my father; I am reborn [Col. 0938D] in Christ. What reward do I receive for this? It follows: “And the king will desire your beauty” (Psalm XLIV).

This, then, is that great mystery. For this reason “a man will leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two will be,” no longer, as there, “one flesh,” but “one spirit.” Your bridegroom is not arrogant or proud; he has taken an Ethiopian woman as his wife. As soon as you wish to hear the wisdom of the true Solomon and come to him, he will confess to you all that he knows, and the king will lead you into his chamber. Then, wondrously, when your color has been changed, that saying will suit you: “Who is this who ascends, made white?”

**THE SAME PLACE.** I do not want pride [Col. 0939A] to arise in you from your purpose, but fear. You walk laden with gold; a thief must be avoided. This life is a racecourse for mortals: here we contend so that elsewhere we may be crowned. No one walks safely among serpents and scorpions. “My sword,” says the Lord, “has become drunk in heaven” (Isaiah XXXIV); and do you imagine there is peace on earth, which produces thistles and thorns and which the serpent eats?

“Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” We are surrounded by great armies of enemies; everything is full of foes. Fragile flesh, soon to become ashes, fights alone against many. But when it has been dissolved, and the prince of this world has come [Col. 0939B] and found nothing in it, then it will hear securely through the Prophet:

> You will not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies by day, nor the business that walks in darkness, nor the attack and the noonday demon. A thousand will fall at your side and ten thousand at your right hand, but they will not come near you (Psalm XC).

But if their multitude troubles you, and you begin to burn at each incitement to vice, and your thought says to you, “What shall we do?”, Elisha will answer you: “Do not fear, for there are more with us than with them” (2 Kings VI).

**CONTINUED IN THE SAME WORK.** As long as we are confined in this fragile little body, as long as we have this treasure in earthen vessels, and the spirit desires against the flesh while the flesh desires against the spirit, there is no certain victory. Our adversary [Col. 0939C] the devil, like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour, prowls about. The devil does not seek unbelieving people, nor those who are outside, whose flesh the Assyrian king burns in a pot; rather, he hastens to snatch people from the Church of Christ. The Savior came not to send peace upon earth, but a sword.

**A LITTLE LATER.** If, after nakedness, fasts, hunger, imprisonment, scourging, and punishments, the Apostle, returning to himself, cries out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” (Romans VII), do you think that you ought to be secure? Beware, I beg you, lest God ever say of you: “The virgin of Israel has fallen, and there is no one to raise her” (Amos V).

I shall speak boldly. Although God can do all things, he cannot raise a virgin after her fall. He can indeed deliver her from punishment, but he does not wish [Col. 0939D] to crown one who has been corrupted. Let us fear that prophecy, lest it also be fulfilled in us: “The good virgins will fail.” Observe what he says: “The good virgins will fail” (ibid. VIII), because there are also bad virgins.

“Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her,” he says, “has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew V). Virginity therefore perishes even in the mind. These are the bad virgins: virgins in the flesh but not in the spirit, foolish virgins who, having no oil, are shut out by the bridegroom.

But if even those who are virgins are not saved by their bodily virginity because of other faults, what will happen to those who have prostituted the members of Christ and changed the temple of the Holy Spirit into a brothel? Immediately they will hear: “Descend, sit on the ground, virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground, [Col. 0940A] daughter of the Chaldeans; you shall no longer be called tender and delicate” (Isaiah XLVII).

It would have been more right to undertake marriage and walk on level ground than, while striving toward higher things, to fall into the depths of hell.

**A LITTLE LATER.** Let the breast-band not be loosened; rather, as soon as lust has tickled the understanding and the sweet fire of pleasure has bathed us in its gentle warmth, let us burst into the words: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what flesh can do to me.” And when the inner person has begun to waver for a little while between vices and virtues, say: “Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall confess him as the salvation of my countenance and my God.”

I do not want you to allow the thought to grow; let nothing Babylonian, nothing of confusion, mature in you. While the enemy is small, [Col. 0940B] kill it; let wickedness be crushed in the seed, lest the weeds grow.

Hear the Psalmist speaking:

> Wretched daughter of Babylon, blessed is the one who repays you with the repayment with which you repaid us! Blessed is the one who will seize and dash your little ones against the rock (Psalm CXXXVI)!

Because it is impossible for the innate heat of the marrow not to rush into the human mind, that person is praised and proclaimed blessed who, as soon as he begins to think of filthy things, immediately kills the thoughts and dashes them against the rock; and the rock was Christ.

**THE SAME PLACE.** But if these things are endured by those who, their bodies exhausted, are attacked only by thoughts, what does the girl suffer who enjoys luxury? Surely what the Apostle says: “While living, she is dead” (1 Timothy V).

If, therefore, there can be any counsel in me, [Col. 0940C] if one may trust experience, this is what I first advise and solemnly urge: let the bride of Christ flee wine as poison. These are the first weapons of demons against youth. Nor does avarice shake us so much, nor pride inflate us, nor ambition delight us. We easily do without other vices; this enemy is shut up within: wherever we go, we carry the enemy with us. Wine and youth are a double fire of pleasure. Why should we supply fuel for flames to a burning little body?

Paul says to Timothy: “Do not continue to drink water, but use a little wine, because of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (ibid.). Observe for what reasons the drinking of wine is permitted: so that by it pain of the stomach and frequent illness may be treated. And lest perhaps we flatter ourselves because of illnesses, he commanded that only a little be taken, more on a physician’s [Col. 0940D] advice than on the Apostle’s.

Otherwise, the same Apostle elsewhere remembered that he had said: “And wine, in which is debauchery” (Ephesians V); and: “It is good for a person not to drink wine and not to eat meat” (Romans XIV).

Noah drank wine and became drunk (Genesis IX). In that still-primitive age, when the vineyard had first been planted, perhaps wine did not yet know how to intoxicate. And so that you may understand the mystery of Scripture in all things—for the word of God is a pearl, and it can be pierced from every side—after drunkenness the uncovering of the thighs followed, and lust was joined to excess. First the belly is stretched, and then the other members are stirred.

“For the people ate and drank, and rose up to play” (Exodus XXXII). Lot, the friend of God, saved on the mountain and found to be the only righteous man among so many thousands of people, is made drunk by his daughters [Col. 0941A] (Genesis XIX). Although they thought that the human race had perished and did this more from a desire for children than from lust, they nevertheless knew that the righteous man would not do such a thing unless he were drunk. Indeed, he did not know what he had done. And although the will is not culpable, error is blameworthy.

**IN THE SAME WORK.** There are countless divine answers from the Scriptures that condemn gluttony and prescribe simple foods. But since it is not now my purpose to discuss fasts, and to pursue the whole subject belongs to its own title and volume, these few remarks from among many will suffice.

Otherwise, following these examples, you can gather for yourself how the first man also, obeying his belly more than God, was cast into this [Col. 0941B] valley of tears; how Satan tempted the Lord himself with hunger in the desert; how the Apostle cries out: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Corinthians VI); and concerning the luxurious: “Their god is their belly” (Philippians III). For each person worships what he loves.

From this it must be carefully provided that hunger should restore those whom satiety expelled from paradise. But if you wish to reply that you were born of noble stock, always surrounded by luxury, always on feather beds, and that you cannot abstain from wine and more sumptuous foods or live under such strict laws, I shall answer: Live, then, by your own law, since you cannot live by God’s.

Not because God, the creator and Lord of the universe, takes pleasure in the growling of our intestines, the emptiness of the belly, or the burning of the lungs, but because chastity cannot otherwise [Col. 0941C] be kept safe. Job, dear to God and, according to God’s own testimony, blameless and simple—hear what he suspects concerning the devil: “His strength is in his loins, and his power in the navel” (Job XL).

All the devil’s strength against men is therefore in the loins; all his power against women is in the navel. Do you wish to know that it is as we say? Take examples. Samson, stronger than a lion and harder than a rock, who alone and unarmed pursued a thousand armed men, grows weak in Delilah’s embraces (Judges XVI).

**CONTINUED A LITTLE LATER.** It pains me to say how many virgins fall each day, how many the mother Church loses from her own bosom, over how many stars the proud enemy sets his throne, how many rocks he hollows out, and how the serpent dwells in their openings.

You may see many widows—before they were married—covering an unhappy conscience [Col. 0941D] merely by a pretended garment. Unless the swelling of the womb and the cries of infants expose them, they boast that they are holy and chaste; and they walk with uplifted neck and dancing feet. Others drink drugs to produce sterility and commit murder before the human being has been born. Some, when they realize that they have conceived through crime, devise poisons for abortion, and often they themselves also die and are led to hell guilty of three crimes: murderers of themselves, adulteresses against Christ, and parricides of their unborn child.

These are the women accustomed to say: “All things are clean to the clean; my conscience is sufficient for me. God desires a clean heart; why should I abstain from foods that God created for use?” And whenever they wish to live elegantly and cheerfully, after gulping down unmixed wine and joining [Col. 0942A] sacrilege to drunkenness, they say: “Far be it from me to abstain from the blood of Christ.”

These are the women who conspicuously walk through public places and draw behind them crowds of young men by furtive glances from their eyes. They constantly hear through the Prophet: “You have acquired for yourself the face of a harlot” (Jeremiah III).

I do not want you to associate with married women; I do not want you to enter the houses of the nobility; I do not want you frequently to see what you despised when you chose to be a virgin. Nor do I wish you merely to avoid the company of those who are puffed up by their husbands’ honors, whom troops of eunuchs surround, and in whose garments metals of gold are woven, attenuated into thread. Flee also those whom necessity has made widows.

Let your companions be those whom fasts make thin, whose faces are pale, and whose lives have been tested; those who [Col. 0942B] daily sing in their hearts:

> Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at noon?

Those who say from the heart:

> I desire to depart and be with Christ.

Let your food therefore be moderate, and never let your belly be full. There are many who, although sober with respect to wine, are drunk with the abundance of food. When you rise at night for prayer, let indigestion produce no belch for you, but rather emptiness.

Read frequently; learn as much as possible. Let sleep steal upon you while you hold the book, and let the holy page receive your falling face. Let daily fasts be yours, and let your nourishment flee satiety. It does no good to carry an empty belly for two or three days if it is then overwhelmed in the same measure, if the fast is balanced by fullness. Immediately the mind, once filled, grows sluggish, and watered soil produces the thorns of lust.

Whenever you sense the outward [Col. 0942C] person sighing for the flower of youth, and, after taking food, when the sweet procession of desires has shaken you as you lie arranged in your little bed, seize the shield of faith, by which the fiery arrows of the devil are extinguished.

> All adulterers are like an oven; their hearts are like it.

**CONTINUED IN THE SAME WORK.** It is difficult for the human soul not to love something, and it is necessary that, whatever affection our mind is drawn toward, the love of the flesh be overcome by love of the spirit. Desire is extinguished by desire: whatever is diminished there grows here. Rather, repeat constantly:

> Upon my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves (Song III).

“Put to death,” the Apostle says, “your members that are upon the earth” (Colossians III). Hence he himself confidently said: “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians II).

[Col. 0942D] Be a cricket of the nights. Wash your bed each night; water your couch with tears. Keep vigil, and become like a sparrow in solitude. Sing psalms in the spirit; sing psalms also with understanding. Bless the Lord, O soul, and do not forget all his recompenses, who is gracious to all your iniquities, who heals all your illnesses, and redeems your life from corruption.

You must also avoid this with greater caution: do not be seized by the ardor of empty glory. “How,” Jesus says, “can you believe, who receive glory from human beings?” (John V). See what kind of evil it is: whoever possesses it cannot believe.

Let us instead say: “For you are my glory” (Psalm III); “Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Corinthians X); “If I were still pleasing human beings, [Col. 0943A] I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians I); “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians VI); and: “In you we shall praise the whole day”; “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Psalm XLIII).

When you give alms, let God alone see it; when you fast, let your face be cheerful. Let your clothing be neither excessively clean nor dirty.

**AND IMMEDIATELY AFTER.** Do not wish to appear excessively religious, nor more humble than necessary, lest in fleeing glory you seek it. For many who avoid witnesses of poverty, mercy, and fasting desire by this very act to please—that is, by despising the desire to please—and, wondrously, praise is sought while it is being avoided.

There are some who disfigure their faces so that they may appear to people to be fasting. [Col. 0943B] As soon as they see someone, they groan, lower their eyebrows, and, with their faces covered, scarcely free one eye for looking. Their garment is dark, their belt is of sackcloth, and their hands and feet are dirty; only the belly—because it cannot be seen—burns with food. To these women that Psalm is sung daily:

> The Lord will scatter the bones of those who please themselves (Psalm LII).

**THE SAME PLACE.** After these things, although the Apostle always commands us to pray, and even sleep itself is prayer for holy people, nevertheless we ought to have different hours of prayer, so that, if we should happen to be occupied by some task, the appointed time itself may remind us of our duty.

There is no one who does not know the third, sixth, and ninth hours, as well as dawn and evening. Food should not be taken unless prayer has preceded it, nor should one depart from the table unless thanks has been returned to the Creator.

[Col. 0943C] At night we must rise two or three times and turn over in our minds what we retain from the Scriptures by memory. In every action and every step, let the hand draw the sign of the cross.

Do not slander anyone, nor place a stumbling block against the son of your mother. And if you have fasted for two days, do not think yourself better than those who do not fast. You fast and become angry; he eats and has a gentle expression. You digest mental distress and hunger of the belly through quarreling; he is nourished more moderately and gives thanks to God.

Therefore Isaiah cries out daily: “The Lord has not chosen such a fast. On the days of your fasts your own desires are found” (Isaiah LVIII).

Do not set before yourself as examples those who care for the flesh and calculate the revenues of their possessions and the daily expenses of their household. And do not say: “That woman and that woman enjoy their possessions and are honored [Col. 0943D] by people; brothers and sisters come to her. Has she therefore ceased to be a virgin?”

First, it is doubtful whether such a woman is a virgin; for God does not see as a human being sees. A human being sees the face, but God sees the heart. Furthermore, even if she is a virgin in body, I do not know whether she is a virgin in spirit. The Apostle, however, defined a virgin in this way: she must be holy in body and spirit (1 Corinthians VII).

All these things that we have set forth will seem harsh to the woman who does not love Christ. But the one who has regarded all the pomp of the world as refuse and considered everything under the sun vain, in order to gain Christ; who has died with her Lord, risen with him, and crucified the flesh with its vices and desires—she will freely proclaim:

> Who will separate us from the love [Col. 0944A] of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?

And again:

> I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angel nor principality, nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor strength, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

Keep in mind how those who remain in virginity are praised in the Apocalypse. “The virgins,” John says, “remained. These are they who follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Apocalypse IV).

Whenever the empty ambition of the world delights you, whenever you see something glorious in the world, pass over in your mind to paradise. Begin to be what you will be, and you will hear from your bridegroom:

> Place me like a shelter [Col. 0944B] in your heart, like a seal upon your arm.

Fortified in work and in mind alike, you will cry out and say:

> Many waters could not extinguish love, nor could rivers cover it (Song VIII).

## CHAPTER II

*(From the same Jerome’s letter to Demetrias.)* I shall proclaim one thing to you, born of God, one thing above all; and repeating it again and again, I shall admonish you: occupy your soul with love of sacred reading, and do not receive into the good soil of your heart the seed of darnel or oats, lest, while the master of the house sleeps, the enemy sow weeds over it. Rather, always say:

> By night I sought him whom my soul loves;

and:

> My soul clung to you; your right hand received me.

When you were in the world, you loved the things that belonged to the world. But now [Col. 0944C], because you have left the world and, in the second stage after baptism, entered into a covenant with your adversary, saying to him, “I renounce you, devil, and your world, and your pomp, and your works,” keep the pact that you made. Be consenting to and observant of your agreement with your adversary while you are on the road of this world, lest perhaps he hand you over to the judge, and you be handed over to the attendant, and not depart from there until you have paid the last farthing—that is, every smallest sin—for we shall also have to give an account for an idle word on the day of judgment.

Let these words be spoken not as an ill-omened prophecy against you, but in the duty of a fearful and cautious admonisher who fears even those things in you that are secure. “If the spirit of one who has authority rises up against you, do not abandon your place.” The enemy wants to move us from our place and make us step down from our position; but our footsteps [Col. 0944D] must be made firm, and we must say: “He set my feet upon a rock,” and so forth.

If a serpent rises into your thoughts, guard your heart, and sing with David: “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others.” Close the chamber of your breast, and frequently fortify your forehead with the sign of the cross, lest the destroyer of Egypt find a place in you.

After the most careful guarding of your thoughts, you must take up the weapons of fasts and sing with David: “I humbled my soul with fasting, and I ate ashes as bread”; and: “When they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth” (Psalm XXXIV).

The Savior of the human race, who left us the example of his virtues and conduct, is immediately after baptism taken up [Col. 0945A] by the Spirit to fight against the devil; and after overpowering and crushing him, he handed him over to the disciples to trample upon. Hence the Apostle also says: “God will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans XVI).

And yet the ancient enemy, after forty days of fasting, plots through food and says: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew IV).

In Job it is written concerning the dragon: “His strength is in his loins, and his power is over the navel of his belly” (Job XL). Our enemy exploits the ardor of youth against young men and girls, inflames the wheel of our birth, and fulfills what Hosea says: “All adulterers are like an oven; their hearts are like it” (Hosea VII). These things are extinguished by God’s mercy and by the coldness of fasts.

These are the devil’s fiery [Col. 0945B] arrows, which both wound and inflame at once. You must fast in such a way that, once the body’s appetite has been broken, you do less than usual neither in reading, nor in psalmody, nor in vigils.

Fasting is not perfect virtue, but the foundation of the other virtues; and sanctification and chastity, without which no one will see God, provide steps for those ascending to the heights.

Let us read the Gospel of the wise and foolish virgins (Matthew XXV). Some enter the bridegroom’s chamber; others, lacking the oil of good works, are shut out when their lamps have been extinguished. Learn what good continence possesses, and what evil fullness possesses in contrast.

Let coarse joking and wantonness have no place in your presence. Never hear an indecent word; or, if you hear one, do not be ensnared by it. People of ruined minds often [Col. 0945C] test the barriers of chastity with a single, slight remark.

Leave laughter and being laughed at to worldly people; seriousness suits your person. I think it superfluous to admonish you against avarice, since the Apostle teaches that avarice is the worship of idols (Ephesians V). Let the bowels of the hungry praise you, not the luxurious feasts of those who belch.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] Some material is missing here, to be supplied from Jerome’s Letter 7 to Demetrias. Hard.]

Clothe Christ in the poor, feed him in the hungry. Besides the order of psalms and prayer—which must always be practiced by you at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, at evening, at midnight, and in the morning—determine how many hours you ought to spend memorizing sacred Scripture and how much time reading it, not as a burden but for the delight and instruction of the soul.

When you have completed these periods, and concern for the soul has frequently roused you to bend your knees, always have wool [Col. 0945D] in your hands. Either draw out threads with your thumb from the warp, or let spindles turn in the baskets for twisting the weft. Gather the spun threads of others into a ball, or arrange them for weaving.

If you are occupied with such varied tasks, your days will never be long. By observing these things, you will save yourself and others, and you will be a teacher of holy conduct. You will make the chastity of many your gain, as Scripture says: “Every soul of the idle is in desires.”

For this reason you must work with everyone: so that, through the opportunity afforded by work, you think of nothing except what belongs to service of the Lord.

I shall speak simply. Even if you distribute all your wealth among the poor, nothing will be more precious [Col. 0946A] before Christ than what you yourself have made with your hands, whether for your own use or as an example to other virgins.

It is good, therefore, to obey those who are greater and to submit to the perfect; and, after the rules of the Scriptures, to learn the course of one’s life from others, rather than to use as one’s teacher the worst instructor of all—one’s own presumption.

Avoid the companionship of married women who serve their husbands and the world, lest your mind be troubled and you hear what either husband has said to wife or wife to husband. Such conversations are poisonous. Taking up a worldly verse concerning their condemnation, the Apostle makes it ecclesiastical:

> Evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Corinthians XV).

Let serious women be chosen as your companions, women whose conduct is approved, whose speech is measured, and whose modesty is holy. Flee the wantonness [Col. 0946B] of girls who adorn their heads and let their hair fall from their foreheads.

Let that woman be beautiful to you, pleasing to you, and fit to be among your companions who does not know that she is beautiful. Blessed is that conscience, and blessed is that virginity, in whose heart no love dwells besides the love of Christ—who is wisdom, chastity, patience, justice, and the other virtues; no other love ever turns there, nor does she sigh at the remembrance of a man, nor desire to see one whom, once she has seen him, she would not wish to release.

The purpose of holy virgins and the comparable glory of heavenly things are disgraced by the name of certain women who do not conduct themselves well.

I join the end to the beginning, and am not satisfied with having warned you only once. Love the sacred Scriptures, and wisdom will love you; cherish it, and it will guard you; honor it, and it will embrace you. Let these necklaces hang upon your breast and in your [Col. 0946C] ears. Let your tongue know nothing except Christ; let it be able to utter nothing except what is holy.

## CHAPTER III
*(The same author, from the letter to Furia.)*

Seize the opportunity, I beg you, and turn necessity into virtue. In Christians, beginnings are not sought, but the end. Paul began badly, but finished well. Judas’s beginnings are praised, but his end is condemned by his betrayal. That harlot in the Gospel, baptized, was saved when she wiped the Lord’s feet with her tears and with the hair by which she had previously deceived many. She had no curled headdresses, no tinkling shoes, no eye-rings blackened with cosmetic; the more repulsive she was, the more beautiful she became.

The widow who has ceased trying to please her husband and is, according to the Apostle, truly a widow needs nothing except perseverance. The devil’s burning arrows [Col. 0946D] must be quenched by the severity of fasts and vigils. Either our speech must correspond to the way we are dressed, or our clothing to the way we speak. Why do we promise one thing and display another? The tongue proclaims chastity, while the whole body exhibits immodesty.

This concerns clothing and adornment. As for the widow who lives in luxury—this is not my statement, but the Apostle’s—“while living, she is dead” (I Tim. V). What does he mean by saying, “while living, she is dead”? To the ignorant she appears to live and not to be dead through sin; but to Christ, who is not deceived by hidden things, she is dead.

The Apostle disciplines his body and subjects it to the authority of the soul, lest he himself fail to observe what he commands others; and is a young woman [Col. 0947A] whose body is inflamed by food secure in her chastity? In saying this I do not condemn the foods that the Lord created to be used with thanksgiving, but I assert that for young men and girls they are incentives to pleasure. Neither the fires of Etna, nor Vulcan’s land, nor Vesuvius and Olympus burn with such heat as the youthful marrow filled with wine and inflamed by rich dishes.

It is therefore a great virtue, requiring vigilant diligence, to overcome what you were born as; to live in the flesh without living carnally; to fight with yourself each day; and to watch the enemy shut within you with a hundred eyes, as Argus is said to have done in the tale.

First, then, if the strength of your stomach permits, until you pass beyond girlhood, drink water, which by nature is extremely cold. Or, if weakness prevents this, hear Timothy: “Use a little wine [Col. 0947B] for the sake of your stomach and your frequent ailments” (I Tim. V).

Next, avoid hot foods of every kind. I speak not only of meats, concerning which the chosen vessel gives this judgment: “It is good neither to eat meat nor to drink wine” (Rom. XIV); but even among vegetables, avoid whatever causes bloating or heaviness. Know that nothing is so beneficial for young Christians as eating vegetables. Hence, in another place, he says: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (Rom. XIV). The heat of the body must be moderated with cooler foods. Nothing inflames the body or tickles the sexual members so much as undigested food and convulsive belching.

I would rather that modesty suffer a little in your case, daughter, than that you be exposed to danger. Consider whatever is a seedbed of pleasure to be poison. Prefer frugal [Col. 0947C] food and a stomach that is always hungry to three-day fasts. It is much better to eat a little every day than to take enough only rarely. The best rain is that which gently descends upon the earth; a sudden and excessive downpour overturns the fields in its violence.

When you eat, consider that you must immediately pray and at once read. Establish for yourself a fixed number of verses from the Holy Scriptures; render this assigned task to your Lord. Do not surrender your limbs to rest before you have filled the basket of your breast with this woven covering.

After the Holy Scriptures, read the works of learned men—but only those whose faith is known. Transfer your love of necklaces, jewels, and silk garments to knowledge of the Scriptures. Make friends for yourself from the unrighteous mammon, so that they may receive you into the eternal dwellings.

Avoid the company of young men. [Col. 0947D] Let the roofs of your house not see long-haired, well-groomed, or lascivious men. Drive away the singer as a harmful person. Expel from your house the flute-girls, harpists, and every such choir of the devil, like the deadly songs of Sirens.

Do not keep appearing in public. It is a very bad custom when a fragile sex and a weak age abuse their freedom and think that whatever they wish is permitted. Everything is lawful, but not everything is beneficial.

## CHAPTER IV

*(An excerpt from the letter of Caecilius Cyprian, On the Dress of Virgins.)*

“Now,” he says, “our speech is addressed to virgins, whose glory is higher and whose responsibility is therefore greater. They are the flower of the ecclesiastical shoot, the honor and ornament of spiritual grace, a joyful growth, a complete and incorrupt work [Col. 0948A] of praise and honor, an image of God answering to the holiness of the Lord, the more illustrious portion of Christ’s flock.

“Through them and in them the glorious fruitfulness of the mother Church rejoices and flourishes abundantly. The more generously virginity increases in number, the more the mother’s joy grows. To these we speak; these we exhort, more by affection than by authority. Those who have devoted themselves to Christ and, withdrawing from carnal desire, have consecrated themselves to God in body and mind alike should complete their work, destined for a great reward. They should no longer strive to adorn themselves or please anyone except their Lord, from whom they expect the reward of virginity.”

**Continues.** If continence follows Christ and virginity is destined for the kingdom of God, what have they to do with worldly dress and ornaments, by which, while they eagerly seek to please human beings [Col. 0948B], they offend God, not considering what has been said: “Those who please human beings are put to shame, because God has treated them as nothing” (Psal. LII)? Paul also proclaimed gloriously and sublimely: “If I were still trying to please human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. I).

Continence and modesty do not consist solely in bodily integrity, but equally in the dignity and restraint of dress and adornment, so that, according to the Apostle, the unmarried woman may be holy both in body and in spirit.

**Continues.** A virgin must not merely be one, but must also be understood and believed to be one, so that when anyone sees her, no one will doubt whether she is a virgin. Let integrity display itself equally in every respect, and let bodily virtue not be disgraced by dress. Why does she go out adorned and carefully dressed, as though she either had or were seeking a husband? If she is a virgin, let her rather [Col. 0948C] fear being pleasing, and let her who is preserving herself for better and divine things not seek danger for herself.

Those who have no husband whom they pretend to please should remain whole and pure, not only in body but also in spirit. For it is not right for a virgin to adorn herself for the sake of appearance or to glory in her flesh and its beauty, when she has no struggle more serious than that against the flesh, and no contest more persistent than overcoming and subduing the body.

**Continues.** It is fitting for no Christian, and especially not for a virgin, to esteem any splendor or honor of the flesh, but only to desire the word of God and embrace the good things that will remain forever.

**Continues.** It is written, read aloud, and celebrated by the mouth of the Church as an example for us: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked [Col. 0948D]” (I John II). We must walk in equal footsteps and strive to advance with emulation. Then the following of truth corresponds to faith in the name, and the believer receives a reward if he also does what he believes.

You call yourself wealthy and rich, but Paul confronts your riches and prescribes, in his own words, a proper limit for your dress and adornment: “Let women adorn themselves with modesty and chastity, not with curled hair, nor gold, nor pearls, nor costly clothing, but as is fitting for women professing chastity through good conduct” (I Tim. II).

Peter likewise agrees with these same instructions and says: “Let a woman’s adornment not be external—the adornment of gold or clothing—but the adornment of the heart” (I Pet. III).

If he [Col. 0949A] admonishes even women, who are accustomed to excuse their adornment on account of their husbands, and urges them to be restrained by religious observance according to ecclesiastical discipline, how much more is it right for a virgin to observe this, since no excuse for her adornment belongs to her, nor can the guilt of her falsehood be transferred to another, but she alone remains at fault?

You call yourself wealthy and rich; but not everything one can do ought also to be done, since it is written: “Everything is lawful, but not everything is beneficial; everything is lawful, but not everything builds up” (I Cor. VI).

But if you dress yourself expensively and walk conspicuously in public, attracting the eyes of the young, drawing the sighs of adolescents after you, nourishing the desire to lust, and kindling fuel for hope—so that, even if you yourself do not perish, you nevertheless destroy others, and offer yourself to those who see you as a sword [Col. 0949B] and as poison—you cannot excuse yourself by claiming that your mind is chaste and modest. Your disgraceful dress and immodest adornment condemn you. You can no longer be counted among the girls and virgins of Christ, since you live in such a way that you may be loved.

The splendor of ornaments and clothing, and the allurements of beauty, belong only to prostitutes and immodest women. Let chaste and modest virgins flee the dress of adulteresses, the clothing of immodest women, the insignia of brothels, and the ornaments of harlots. God condemns this; God marks it out.

Clothed in silk and purple, they cannot put on Christ. Adorned with gold, pearls, and necklaces, they have lost the ornaments of the heart and breast. Virgins, then, to whom this discourse now gives counsel, should not think that they ought to be counted among virgins [Col. 0949C] if they adorn themselves with such arts.

Therefore, virgins, listen to me as to a parent; listen, I beg you, to one who teaches and warns at the same time; listen to one who faithfully counsels you for your advantage and welfare. Be such as God the Creator made you; be such as the Father’s hand fashioned you. Let an uncorrupted face, a pure neck, and a genuine beauty remain in you.

Conquer clothing, since you are a virgin and serve God; conquer gold, since you conquer the flesh and the world. Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life; hard and narrow is the boundary that stretches toward glory. Broad and spacious are the paths of deadly life: there are allurements and fatal pleasures; there the devil flatters in order to deceive, smiles in order to harm, and entices in order to kill.

Preserve, virgins, preserve what you have begun to be; preserve what you will be. A great reward awaits you, a great prize of virtue, the greatest gift [Col. 0949D] of chastity. What we shall be, you have already begun to be. You already possess in this age the glory of the resurrection. You pass through the world without the world’s contamination. When you persevere as chaste virgins, you are equal to the angels of God.

Let only this solid and unharmed virginity remain and endure, and let it persevere continually with the strength with which it began. Let it seek ornaments not of necklaces or clothing, but of character. Let it look to God and heaven, and let it not lower eyes raised on high toward desire for the flesh and the world, or cast them down toward earthly things.

“The first man,” he says, “was from the dust of the earth; the second man was from heaven. As was the one from dust, so also are those who are from dust; and as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the one who is from dust [Col. 0950A], let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven” (I Cor. XI).

Virginity bears this image; integrity bears it; holiness and truth bear it. The disciples of God bear it, remembering and preserving justice together with devotion, steadfast in faith, humble in fear, strong for every endurance, gentle in bearing injury, ready to show mercy, united and harmonious in fraternal peace.

You, good virgins, must each observe, direct, and fulfill these things. Since you are free for God and Christ, you go before the Lord to whom you have dedicated yourselves with the greater and better part of your being.

Make yourselves teachers to those younger than you. Let the younger offer service to their elders and encouragement to their equals. Stir one another up by mutual exhortations; provoke one another to glory through rival examples [Col. 0950B] of virtue. Persevere bravely, advance spiritually, and arrive successfully.

## CHAPTER V

*(From a sermon of Saint Caesarius, bishop, addressed to nuns.)*

Rejoice and exult in the Lord, venerable daughters, and continually offer him abundant thanks, for he has deigned to draw and summon you from the dark way of life in this world to the harbor of quiet and religious devotion.

Continually consider from where you came and where you have been deemed worthy to arrive. You faithfully abandoned the world’s darkness and have happily begun to see the light of Christ. You rejected the fire of lust and reached the coolness of chastity. You rejected gluttony and chose abstinence. You rejected avarice and luxury and held fast to chastity and mercy.

Although [Col. 0950C] the struggle will not leave you until the end of life, nevertheless, by God’s gift, we are confident of your victory. But I beg you, venerable daughters: the more confident you are about the past, the more watchful you should be concerning the future. For all crimes and sins quickly return to us if they are not defeated daily by good works.

Hear the Apostle Peter saying: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about seeking something to devour” (I Pet. V). As long as we live in this body, let us fight against the devil day and night, with Christ as our helper and guide.

For there are some—what is worse, negligent and lukewarm—who boast only of the name of Christianity and think it is enough for them to have changed their clothing and merely assumed the habit of religion [Col. 0950D], not knowing the prophetic saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II).

Nor do they consider the Psalmist’s judgment: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept to difficult ways” (Psal. XVI). Nor what the Apostle said: “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts XIV).

We can put off secular clothing and assume religious clothing in a single hour; but we must retain good character continually and labor, with Christ’s help, against the evil and alluring pleasures of this world for as long as we live, because “not the one who has begun, but the one who has persevered to the end will be saved.”

First, therefore, every soul that desires to preserve religious devotion [Col. 0951A] must strive with the full strength of faith to overcome the desire for gluttony and avoid drunkenness. It should take care to have a temperate meal and a moderate table, so that its flesh is neither weakened by excessive abstinence nor provoked to luxury by an abundance of delicacies.

Next, having cast away pride, which God resists, let it lay the foundation of profound humility. Let it detest and flee envy as viperous poison; restrain its tongue; reject slander as poison; neither utter idle words itself nor willingly admit words uttered by others into its ears.

Let it become accustomed to clothing that is neither excessively shabby nor conspicuously splendid or dangerously elegant. Let it either read frequently itself or receive the words of the reader with the full eagerness of its heart.

Let it continually draw [Col. 0951B] the water of salvation from the divine fountains of the Scriptures—that water of which the Lord says: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII).

Let the holy soul continually strive to adorn itself with the flowers of paradise, that is, with the meanings of the Holy Scriptures. From them let it hang precious pearls continually from its ears; from them let it fashion rings and bracelets for itself while performing good works. There let it seek medicines for wounds, the perfumes of chastity, and the holocausts of contrition.

The woman who desires to preserve religion with an unstained heart and pure body should either never go out in public or do so only because of some great and ineffable necessity.

Do not, I beg you—do not give anyone an occasion or grant anyone familiarity. She who [Col. 0951C] desires, with Christ’s help, to overcome lust must shun familiarity; and she who does not reject unworthy familiarity will quickly destroy either herself or another.

But perhaps one of them says: “I do not avoid familiarity because I want to have something to overcome, and I wish to hold my adversary captive.” Beware lest the adversary begin to rebel against you; beware lest this captivity lead you away as its captive.

Hear the Apostle saying: “Flee fornication” (I Cor. V). Against the remaining vices we must resist with every virtue; against lust, however, it is not expedient to fight, but to flee. Therefore, be a fugitive from lust if you wish to be an excellent fighter for chastity.

But attend carefully to what I have said. When a woman is alone and is stirred by the impulses of lust, with Christ’s help let her resist herself as much as she can [Col. 0951D], because she has nowhere to flee. But when, through the companionship of another, the devil supplies an opportunity for pleasure, let the holy soul shun that very familiarity as much as it can, as we have said.

But so that we may be able to observe all these things, let us maintain reasonable abstinence, for true is the judgment of that most holy man: “As you restrain your belly, so also you restrain its poisonous impulses.”

Let us also preserve true humility as much as we can. For bodily integrity is not long preserved where the mind is corrupted by the swelling of pride, especially when the flame of anger rises frequently; it quickly consumes the flowers of chastity and virginity.

A chaste soul devoted to God ought not to have intimate familiarity not only with strangers but even with its own parents. [Col. 0952A] If vessels offered to the Church so that they may be placed upon the holy altars are called holy by everyone, and if it is unlawful for them afterward to be taken back from the church into a secular home or adapted for human use, consider what dignity a soul created in God’s image has before God.

Therefore, just as holy vessels intended for divine use cannot and ought not to be taken back from the church for human purposes, so a religious woman ought not, is not fitting, and is not beneficial to become entangled in many obligations to her parents or to be bound by the harmful familiarity of any outsiders.

Above all I warn you to flee the evil of rivalry as viperous poison, and to preserve among yourselves the sweetness of charity in such a way that you may prepare spiritual medicines [Col. 0952B] for one another through holy conversations.

For there are some—what is worse—who, when they join together, inflict wounds upon one another by slandering each other or murmuring against their superiors, rather than preparing spiritual medicines.

But you, holy and venerable daughters: if you see someone fainthearted, offer consolation; if you see someone becoming proud, apply the medicine of humility; if you see someone angry, provide the cooling remedy of patience.

If you were born noble, rejoice more in the humility of religion than in worldly dignity. Therefore hold your hands firmly to the plow and do not look back. Remember Lot’s wife, who, looking back, was turned into a pillar of salt.

Never let an oath, never a curse, proceed from a virgin’s mouth. Guard not only [Col. 0952C] your bodies but also your hearts with every care, because it is written: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. IV). And the Lord said in the Gospel: “From the heart come evil thoughts” (Matt. XV).

For if nothing evil is thought in the heart, whatever is holy is brought forth from the mouth, because, as it is written: “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matt. XV). The tongue is accustomed to utter whatever the conscience has supplied from the workshop of the heart. Therefore, if you wish to bring forth good things from your mouth, always think in your heart of what is holy.

You ought to devote yourselves to reading and prayer in such a way that, above all, you may also be able to engage in some work with your hands, according to what the Apostle says: “If anyone does not work, neither [Col. 0952D] let him eat” (II Thess. III).

Dedicate the better part of the day to holy work. Become accustomed to giving time to reading. Let your prayer proceed from the heart in such silence that it is scarcely heard by the mouth. For whoever wishes to pray in a loud voice does great harm both to himself and to another, since by his chatter he distracts another’s mind from holy and secret prayer.

Despise and reject all pompous clothing, which serves not utility but vanity. For many display in their actions what they love in their character: they prepare secular ornaments for themselves because they love the world and serve pleasure or luxury.

Let nothing be shared between you and such people. Let all ornaments by which the flesh is arranged for luxury be rejected from your way of life as hostile and contrary.

For there are some [Col. 0953A]—what is worse—who, for the sake of this world’s vanity, take greater pains to pursue earthly desires than divine reading and righteousness. They wish to prepare beautiful bedspreads, painted tapestries, embroidered hangings, and other similar things at enormous cost and with extravagant expense, for the pleasure of the eyes, not knowing what the Lord proclaims and says through John the Evangelist: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world; for everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age” (I John II).

What does it profit a virgin to guard the integrity of her body if she refuses to avoid the desires of her eyes?

But you, holy souls worthy of God, conduct everything spiritually. Follow Christ, steadfastly holding what you ardently desired.

Again and again [Col. 0953B], holy souls dedicated to God, I beg you, and with all humility I offer counsel for preserving the reward of virginity: strive with all your strength to drive inappropriate familiarity away from yourselves and from your souls.

For, in preserving the dignity of holy religion, solitude is a most holy witness. When anyone’s familiarity begins to become frequent, it sows nothing but corruption, produces vices, conceives lust, gives birth to disgrace, arouses fury, feeds wantonness, nourishes insolence, magnifies falls, builds ruin, purchases confusion, stores up reproach, increases accusations, inflames excuses, and heaps all these things together in a single bundle and in a crowd.

For if a holy soul wishes to guard its secret and flees with all the strength of its mind the evil of constant familiarity [Col. 0953C], that very holy solitude is an unconquerable defense of holiness, a strong defeat of disgrace, an exercise of continence, an emptying out of luxury, a secure peace of the virtues, and a restless assault upon battles; it is the summit of purity and the prison of lust, the harbor of honor and the shipwreck of disgrace, the mother of virginity and the enemy of uncleanness, the dignity of integrity and the renunciation of fornication, the will to perform good works and the affliction of vices, the cooling of modesty and the punishment of insolence, the acquisition of triumphs and the loss of crimes, the rest of salvation and the exile of destruction, the life of the spirit and the death of the flesh.

All these evils will be forcefully repelled, with God’s help, and the good things we have mentioned will happily be acquired if disordered familiarity [Col. 0953D] is rejected by holy souls.

Pay attention, holy souls, because among all the struggles that Christian warfare always entails, the battles of chastity alone are harder: there the struggle is daily and victory rare. The battles of chastity are harsh, but its rewards are greater. No one securely receives the palm of chastity when the outcomes are as difficult as their fruits are glorious.

Therefore, so that you may happily receive the rewards of chastity and the crown of virginity, with God as your rewarder, always exclude dangerous familiarity from yourselves.
