Run faithfully, so that you may arrive successfully, with the help of our Lord [Col. 0954A] Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## CHAPTER VI
*(Of St. Athanasius to the Brides of Christ.)*

[Note: [Col. 0953D] This exhortation is published in a much more complete form in the appendix to the *Codex Regularum*, p. 9, Roman edition, 1661, edited by Luke Holstenius.]

How great a blessedness holy virginity possesses in heaven, we learn not only from the testimony of Scripture but also from the custom of the Church, by which we understand that a special merit belongs to it, since its consecration is distinctive. For although the entire multitude of believers receives equal gifts of grace, and all glory in the same sacramental blessings, these women are chosen by the Holy Spirit from that holy and spotless flock of the Church, as holier and purer offerings, to possess something peculiar beyond the others, according to the merits of their will; and they are offered upon God’s altar by the high priest [Col. 0954B].

Virginity therefore possesses both what others possess and what others do not possess: it enjoys both a common and a special grace and rejoices in the privilege, so to speak, of its own consecration. For ecclesiastical authority permits us to call virgins brides of Christ, since, in the manner of brides whom she consecrates to the Lord, the Church veils them, showing that those who have shunned carnal union are especially destined to have a spiritual marriage. And rightly are they spiritually joined to God through the comparison of marriage, since for love of him they have rejected human marriage. In them above all is fulfilled the Apostle’s saying: “He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (II Cor. VI).

And since many things lack their own goodness unless they are aided by the support of other things, we must look more carefully lest virginity too should require something without which it can in no way bear fruit; otherwise all that labor will be useless, while one vainly believes that what is possessed without the necessary things is beneficial. Scripture testifies that eternal life cannot be earned except through the observance of all the divine commandments. “If you wish,” it says, “to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX). Therefore no one possesses life unless he has kept the commandments of the law; and whoever does not possess life cannot be an heir of the heavenly kingdom.

Accordingly, those who preserve chastity and integrity and hope from God’s justice for its reward must above all keep the precepts of the commandments, lest the labor of glorious chastity and continence be brought to nothing. [Col. 0954D] If you desire to fulfill the divine purpose, keep the commandment above all; if you wish to attain the reward of virginity, embrace the merits of life, so that there may be something for chastity to receive as its reward. For just as observance of the commandments bestows life, so, conversely, transgression of them produces death. And whoever through transgression has fallen into death cannot hope for the crown of virginity, nor can one established in punishment await the reward of chastity.

For I do not want you to think that righteousness consists in this alone: that you do no evil. To fail to do good is also evil, and transgression of the law is committed in both respects, since he who said, “Turn away from evil,” also said, “and do good” (Ps. XXXIII). If you have turned away from evil but have not done good, you are a transgressor of the law, which is fulfilled not only in the rejection of evil deeds but also in the perfection of good works. [Col. 0955A] Do not flatter yourself on this account if you have failed in only some matters, since it is written: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James II).

Adam sinned once and died, and do you think that you can live while repeatedly committing the very thing that killed another when he committed it once? Remember that Adam and Eve sinned while virgins, and that bodily integrity did not profit those who sinned.

It is indeed lawful to enter into marriage, for those who abandon marriage reject not what is unlawful but what is lawful. But if such women swear, curse, slander, tolerate hearing slanderers, repay evil for evil, incur the guilt of covetousness regarding the possessions of others or of avarice regarding their own; if they harbor the poisons of jealousy or envy; if, contrary to legal and apostolic institutions, they say or think anything indecent; if they go out made up and adorned in the desire to please in the flesh; if they commit other unlawful acts, as usually happens, what will it profit them to have rejected what was lawful and to practice what is unlawful? If you wish what you have lawfully despised to benefit you, see to it that you do none of the things that are unlawful. For it is foolish to fear what is lesser and not fear what is greater.

The Apostle says: “The unmarried woman considers the things of the Lord, how she may please God, so that she may be holy in body and spirit; but she who is married considers the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (I Cor. VII). Let the woman who has no husband, yet considers the things of the world, tell me whom she desires to please. Is she not beginning to be placed beneath the married woman? For by considering the things of the world, the married woman at least pleases her husband; but this one can please neither a husband, whom she does not have, nor God.

Nor should we pass over in silence what he said: “The unmarried woman considers the things of the Lord, how she may please God, so that she may be holy in body and spirit.” What, then, are the things of the Lord? Let the Apostle say: “Whatever things are holy, whatever things are just, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report; if there is any virtue, if there is any praise of discipline.” Holy, true, and apostolic virgins meditate upon these things day and night, without any interval of time. It follows: “the things of the Lord, how she may please God”—God, I say, not human beings—“so that she may be holy in body and spirit.” He did not say, “so that she may be holy in one member,” or “in the body only,” but “in body and spirit.”

A member is one part of the body, whereas the body is the union of all the members. Therefore, when he says “so that she may be holy in body,” he testifies that she must be sanctified in all her members. For the sanctification of the other members will not profit if corruption is found in even one; and she will no longer be holy in body, which consists of all the members, if it has been polluted by the defilement of even one.

Therefore, virgin, I beg you, do not flatter yourself on your chastity alone, lest you be disgraced by the integrity of a single member; but, according to the Apostle, preserve the sanctity of your body for God alone. Cleanse your head from every defilement [Col. 0956A], for it is a crime, after the sanctification of chrism, to soil it with the color of any cosmetic or with powder, or to adorn it with gold, gems, or any other earthly appearance.

Cleanse your forehead, so that it may blush at human rather than divine works, and may receive that shame which produces not sin but the glory of God. Cleanse your neck, so that it may not wear golden necklaces hanging from the hair, but rather those ornaments of which Scripture says: “Let mercy and truth not forsake you; hang them upon your neck” (Prov. III).

Cleanse your eyes by withdrawing them from every form of desire and never turning them away from the poor. Cleanse your tongue from lying, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul”; from slander, from oaths, and from perjury: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit.” And remember the Apostle’s saying: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. XII). For it is an abomination that those lips with which you confess, entreat, bless, and praise the Lord should be polluted by the filth of any sin. I do not know with what conscience anyone prays to the Lord with the tongue with which she either lies or slanders. God hears holy lips, and he quickly grants the prayers that an immaculate tongue utters.

Cleanse your ears, so that they may give attention only to holy words; so that they may never receive obscene, shameful, or worldly speech, nor hear anyone disparaging another, in accordance with what is written: “Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to an evil tongue” (Eccli. XVIII).

Let your hands be neither extended to receive nor prepared to strike, but ready for every work of mercy and compassion. Cleanse your feet, so that they do not travel along the broad and spacious way that leads to the splendid and costly banquets of the world, but rather walk the difficult and narrow path that leads toward heaven.

Recognize that your members were fashioned by God the creator not for vices but for virtue. When you have cleansed all your limbs from every stain of sin and have been sanctified in your whole body, then understand that chastity will benefit you, and await the palm of virginity with complete confidence.

O virgin, preserve the commitment destined for you for a great reward. Recognize your state, recognize your place, recognize your commitment. You are called the bride of Christ; see that you admit nothing unworthy of him to whom you appear betrothed. You have Christ as your bridegroom. Ask his household and intimates, and diligently and attentively inquire what especially delights him: what arrangement of clothing he likes in you and what kind of adornment he desires.

Let his closest associate Peter tell you. He does not permit even married women bodily adornment, as he wrote in his Epistle: “Likewise, let women be subject to their husbands, so that even if any do not believe the word, they may be won without a word through the conduct of their wives, when they observe your chaste conduct in the fear of God. Their adornment should not be external, in the braiding of hair, or the wearing of gold, or the dressing of clothes, but the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is precious in the sight of God” (I [Col. 0957A] Pet. III).

Let another blessed apostle, Paul, also tell you: “Likewise, let women adorn themselves in respectable clothing, with modesty and sobriety, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but with what befits women who profess chastity through good conduct” (I Tim. II).

But perhaps you say: Why did these same apostles not command these things? Because they did not consider it necessary, lest such an admonition to virgins appear more an insult than a correction. Nor could they have believed that they would ever be so reckless as to presume even the carnal and earthly ornaments permitted to married women.

Indeed, a virgin ought to adorn and arrange herself. For how could she please her bridegroom unless she came forth arranged and adorned? Let her certainly be adorned, but with inward ornaments, and let her be arranged spiritually, not carnally, because God considers in her not the beauty of the body but that of the soul.

Therefore, you too, whoever you are who desire your soul to be loved and inhabited by God, adorn it with every care and decorate it with spiritual garments. Let nothing disgraceful, nothing foul, appear in it. Let it shine with the gold of righteousness, gleam with the gems of holiness, and sparkle with the most precious pearl of chastity. Instead of fine linen and silk, let it be clothed with the tunic of mercy and compassion, according to what is written: “Clothe yourselves, therefore, as God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved, with compassion, kindness, humility, etc.” (Coloss. III).

God seeks such an ornament and desires a soul arranged in this way. Remember that you are called a daughter of God, according to the saying: “Hear, daughter, and see” [Col. 0957C] (Ps. XLIV). Moreover, whenever you yourself call the Lord “Father,” you testify that you are God’s daughter.

Therefore, if you are God’s daughter, see that you do none of the things that are unfitting for God the Father; but do everything as a daughter of God. Look to your origin, consider your lineage, heed the glory of your nobility. Recognize that you are adorned not with human nobility but with the nobility of God’s divinity. Conduct yourself so that heavenly birth may appear in you, so that divine nobility may shine forth.

Let there be in you a new dignity, admirable propriety, astonishing modesty, remarkable patience, a virginal walk, the bearing of true chastity, and speech that is always restrained and uttered at the proper time, so that whoever sees you may marvel and say: “What is this patience of a new dignity among human beings? What modesty of shame? What restraint of propriety? What maturity of wisdom?” This is not a human formation, nor a mortal discipline; something heavenly breathes upon me from an earthly body. For I think that God dwells in certain human beings.

And when someone learns that you are Christ’s handmaid, she will be held by even greater wonder and will consider what kind of Lord he is whose servant is such a woman.

If you wish to be with Christ and to share in Christ, you must live according to Christ’s example, for he was a stranger to every wickedness. Let no one deceive you; let no one seduce you with deceitful speech. The heavenly court receives only the holy, the simple, the innocent, and the pure, and wickedness has no place with God. Whoever desires to reign [Col. 0958A] with Christ must be free from every evil and deceit.

I do not want you to look to those who are virgins of the world, not of Christ: women forgetful of their commitment and profession, who rejoice in pleasures and delight in wealth. But you, whoever you are who are Christ’s virgin, not the world’s, flee all the glory of the present life, so that you may attain that which is promised in the future.

Avoid contentious speech, causes of hostility, and occasions of lawsuits. For if, according to the Apostle’s teaching (II Tim. II), a servant of the Lord must not quarrel, how much more must God’s handmaid, whose sex is more modest, have a more restrained spirit?

Restrain your tongue from evil speech, and place the bridle of the law upon your mouth, so that you may speak only when silence would be sinful, according to what the Apostle says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth” [Col. 0958B] (Eph. IV). Always accustom your tongue to speak of good things, and direct your hearing more toward the praise of the good than toward the condemnation of the wicked.

See to it that everything you do well, you do for the Lord, knowing that you will receive from the Lord a reward for that act only to the extent that you have performed it for his fear and love. Strive to be holy rather than to appear holy. Take greater delight in fasts than in banquets, remembering that widow who did not depart from the temple, serving the Lord with fastings and prayers night and day.

Love the banquet of divine reading more, and desire to be filled with spiritual food; seek rather those foods by which the soul, not the body, is refreshed. Flee the kinds of meat and wine as fuel for heat and stimulants of lust. Conquer anger, restrain hostility, and avoid whatever brings repentance after it has been done, as the abomination of a neighboring crime.

The mind that desires to be God’s dwelling must be sufficiently tranquil and peaceful, free from every disturbance of rage. When you desire to celebrate prayer, present yourself as though you were about to speak with the Lord. When you recite a psalm, recognize whose words you are speaking, and take greater delight in contrition of spirit than in the sweetness of a ringing voice. For God approves the tears of the one singing the psalms more than the pleasing quality of the voice.

Believe that God observes all your deeds and thoughts, and beware of doing or thinking anything unworthy of the divine eyes. Let grace increase in you with the years, and righteousness increase with age. Consider every time in which you have not felt yourself becoming better to have been lost.

Preserve the commitment to virginity that you have begun until the end, for virtue consists not merely in beginning but in completing. Be therefore a pattern of life to everyone; be an example. Show yourself a virgin in all things. Let your conduct also be inviolate, so that whoever happens merely to hear of your life may understand that such grace is poured forth from your conduct that, while desiring to imitate you, she too may become worthy of God’s sacrifice.

Behold by what most salutary teachings the holiest and most learned men instruct those dedicated to God to preserve their purpose of chastity. Behold with what garments of eminent virtues they adorn them, so that they may become worthy of the embraces of that bridegroom to whom they have dedicated themselves. Therefore the holy women must watch diligently, so that they may obediently obey the admonitions of such fathers: lest by resisting them they be rejected with the foolish virgins, but rather, by obeying, be admitted with the prudent into Christ’s bridal chamber.

Having therefore carefully set forth these sayings of the same holy Fathers, we have judged it fitting and necessary to distinguish, in separate chapters, what must be observed by superiors and what by subjects. And since the life of the subjects must be formed by the examples of their superiors, we have thought it proper to set down first what kind of women should be appointed abbesses, how they should live, how they should govern their subjects, how they should reside in the monasteries, and how they should serve the Lord earnestly with complete devotion of mind and body; then what must specially be observed by the subjects.

## CHAPTER VII

Such abbesses should undertake the care of governing souls as provide their subjects with leadership in holy religion through words and examples; who do not serve their own wills, but rather exercise the most diligent care for their subjects; who know how to guard both themselves and those women, as holy vessels in which the incense of prayer may continually be worthily offered to God, from every stain of vices; and who make them vigilant with themselves in their holy commitment, so that, journeying together toward eternal life, they may deserve to enjoy the fellowship of the citizens above.

By what authority, then, or by what teachings of the holy Fathers, do they claim permission to wander outside, to reside in villages, to wear silk garments, or to serve vain displays? But since they can do none of these things lawfully by any authority—especially since the holy Fathers, in the preceding chapters, expressly forbid such conduct to holy women—it remains that henceforth such practices must be avoided by them in every respect, insofar as the Lord grants ability.

For although women placed in secular dignity commonly indulge voluptuously in pleasures of many kinds, in monasteries, where the brides of Christ are to be maintained in common from the Lord’s resources, this must be entirely prohibited by the standard of justice. They ought to know that they have not been made superiors so that they may feed only themselves, but rather so that they may feed themselves and their subjects, both bodily and spiritually; nor have they been placed over others by the Lord merely to rule, but to benefit them.

Therefore they must diligently bind themselves and their subjects to the purpose of holy religion. And just as they precede others in the honor of the office, so too must they precede them by the example of a pious life; and what they forbid others to do, they must never themselves commit. For rightly, as blessed Gregory says, the person who corrects the errors of others is one who does not do the things she rebukes.

But since the absence of a shepherd commonly makes the sheep prey, it is necessary that abbesses remain continually in the monasteries and exercise the most vigilant care over the sheep entrusted to them, lest, while they are absent, their subjects become prey to the invisible wolf.

What guides of souls should be like is also taught most fully by St. Caesarius in the letter he wrote to the abbess Oratoria. From it we have thought it right to excerpt certain chapters for the instruction of abbesses and append them to this chapter. He says as follows:

“Hear me, therefore, dearest sister and daughter. However much you may always desire to be occupied with spiritual pursuits, you will nevertheless sometimes have to settle external matters for the sake of the sisters. You must therefore take the greatest care that, if you undertake temporal matters as circumstances require, you nevertheless cling always more firmly to spiritual devotion and love, so that, when you have quickly administered temporal affairs, you may immediately return to prayer or reading, as to your mother’s bosom.

“You ought to desire that, having cast aside worldly anxiety, you may always think about the service of Christ, in accordance with what is said: ‘No one serving as a soldier for God entangles herself in secular business’ (II Tim. II), and so forth.

“In everything, according to the Apostle (Tit. II), present yourself as an example of good works, and let your life, like a winged creature, always fly upward through desire, resound through speech, and shine through example.

“When you have resolved to announce the word of God to the sisters, first weigh it with careful consideration, so that what you promise with your mouth you may fulfill in deeds, and what you preach to others you may provide by your works.

“Be found first in the church and leave last. Share the common food with those who sit at table with you as equals. Let the abstinence preached by your tongue be felt by your neighboring jaws and your nearby stomach, lest perhaps the subjects who hear you say in silent thought: ‘How beautifully she preaches abstinence to us with a full belly!’

“And in this and all other matters, know that what befits you is this: the narrow paths along which you admonish your companions to walk, you should yourself walk first.

“Do not be more adorned than the others in clothing, but in conduct. Do not appoint the woman who has pleased you by her face and appearance, whom you have recognized as pleasing to your eye, or by whose more flattering service you have been charmed; appoint the one whom the love of Christ and a more religious life have shown to be worthy.

“For it is necessary that, on account of certain women, you sometimes have a knife at your throat, carry a cautery on your tongue, and bear a rod and staff in your hand: by the knife, cut away vices; by the cautery, restore the wounds to health; by the discipline of the rod, correct; and by the staff, support the one who has been disciplined.

“When you are summoned to converse with secular persons, first arm your forehead with the trophy of the cross and mark your breast with Christ’s banner, so that Christ may deign to accompany you with his little virgin.

“Let your conversation always be mingled with gravity and sweetness, and speak only as the matter and the time require. If they ask for something that you decide to grant, grant it with a cheerful face. If it is not fitting to grant something, at least soften their request by the courtesy of your speech.

“Let many know your name; let many, insofar as you are able, experience your benefits; let few see your face. If, for the needs of the monastery, you must at some time confer privately, do so with two, or certainly three, chosen sisters.

“For the good reputation of your name, as well as the preservation of a blameless life, is necessary for you; and human disparagement is to be despised only when Christ is at stake.

“Let every action of yours always be for God, and let every thought of God always be directed toward God. Except in the case of vices, which deserve not compassion but correction, I desire you to be compassionate toward all, agreeable to all, and a pious superior to all. Thus, according to Paul (I Cor. VII), may you be holy in body and spirit, with the bridegroom and your Lord ruling your mind and directing your holy ways, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”

## CHAPTER VIII

Abbesses must strive with the greatest care to admit into the monasteries such and so many holy women as are commended both for the integrity of their conduct and as can reasonably be supported by the Church’s stipends. Those who are still entangled in carnal pleasures must on no account be admitted into monasteries, because, according to the Apostle Paul (I Cor. VII), it is better for them to marry outside, only in the Lord, than to be admitted into monasteries and live dissolutely under the appearance of feigned holiness.

When women of this kind seek monasteries for the sake of religious life, they must not be granted an easy entrance until these chapters have first been read to them, so that, after hearing them, they may know what must be observed and what avoided in the purpose of chastity. [Col. 0961C] For after they have bound themselves to the Lord in this warfare, it will no longer be lawful for them to follow their own counsels, nor will they be able to become involved at all in secular affairs; nor ought they to maintain the company or familiar conversation of men without unavoidable cause.

Therefore, let them first examine the secrets of their hearts, and at the same time read and reread with continual meditation the sayings of the holy Fathers set forth above, lest, seizing the bond of continence and virginity without deliberation and insufficient caution, they return after Satan and become like a dog returning to its vomit.

## CHAPTER IX

Provision must be made for those who have dedicated themselves to chastity for the love of Christ and have requested admission into the community of holy women, so that, before they enter the monastery, they may deliberate and arrange their property so wisely and prudently that, as they journey toward eternal life, they suffer no disturbance on account of it.

Therefore, if any holy woman has transferred her own property to the Church in such a way that she claims nothing from it as her own but wishes only to be supported by the Church’s resources, let the necessary stipends be generously provided for her in the community.

But if she has handed the property over to the Church and wished to retain its usufruct, let the Church’s steward defend it as belonging to the Church. If she does not wish to transfer it to the Church, let the abbess, with the agreement of the other holy women, entrust it by a publicly authenticated document either to a relative or to any other friend of good faith who will defend it according to the law of the forum. [Col. 0962A]

According to this form of regulation, therefore, let the holy women deliberate about and arrange their own property, and let them entrust it either to servants or, certainly, to others whom they choose, to administer it and faithfully manage its proceeds for them. For, before entering the monastery, everything must be reasonably arranged by them as has been stated, so that, once the occupation of worldly affairs has been removed, they may preserve their purpose more freely and peacefully.

The abbesses must also beware regarding adolescents and those whose conduct commonly causes monasteries to suffer hostility and dissension, lest they admit them into the community carelessly and indiscriminately, lest their admission later generate some scandal.

## CHAPTER X

Those who have bound themselves to the Lord by professing the name of chastity must remember that they ought to reside continually in monasteries and serve the Lord earnestly with the full intention of mind and body, and that the veil of the body alone, without the adornment of the mind, cannot benefit them. For it is useless to veil the body and stain the mind with the monsters of vice. What does it profit to veil the body and have a poisoned spirit? What does it profit to put on black garments and not restrain the tongue from slander, when the Apostle says: “If anyone thinks that she is religious but does not bridle her tongue and deceives her heart, this person’s religion is worthless” (James I)?

Can the veil of the body conceal the desire of the mind? Since all the works of Adam’s children are naked and open to the eyes of God, and humility of clothing is worthless without humility of mind, and since God can be seen only by a pure heart, it is necessary that they complete in their conduct what they display in their dress, and that the humility they wear on the body shine especially in the mind.

For if, as we read in Solomon, women placed in their father’s house must be earnestly instructed by paternal admonitions, and those bound by the marriage bond must, according to the Apostle, be subject to their husbands, how much more must those who have vowed to live religiously in the house of God be instructed in divine disciplines and be subject with all humility and chastity to their bridegroom, Christ the Lord?

What was wholly unlawful for those established in their father’s house and in the marriage bond: by what authority—or rather, by what madness—could women placed in monasteries make it lawful for themselves, except to their own destruction? Especially since blessed Jerome says that it is a most deplorable custom when the fragile sex and weak age abuse their own judgment and think that what is not lawful is permitted.

Therefore, they must by no means make unlawful things lawful for themselves; rather, their will must submit to the Lord’s will—indeed, to his service. While living in monasteries, they must not grow sluggish through idleness, nor devote themselves to slander and obscene conversations; but they must either persist in the singing of psalms, in manual labor, or at least lend their ears to divine readings.

They must avoid by every means the company, familiar associations, and conversations of men, as the holy Fathers have forbidden. Let all sleep in the dormitory, each one in a separate bed. In the refectory let them dine together every day, unless illness or weakness of age prevents someone from doing so. Let them serve one another in turn in the duty of charity.

While they are eating in the refectory and religiously maintaining silence, let a reading be continued without interruption, and let them listen to it with the greatest attention. Let them come daily to the collation, read through this rule or readings from other divine Scriptures, and discuss the salvation of their souls. There also, let offenders be rebuked according to the measure of their offense.

Let them observe the canonical hours with complete devotion and perform the divine office at them reverently. Let them humbly show honor to one another. Let the younger venerate those advanced in age through the service of holiness. Let those advanced in years instruct the younger by words and examples for good living.

Let those noble by birth in no way prefer themselves to those of humbler origin, knowing that God is not a respecter of persons. Nor should those distinguished by chastity, the privileges of other good works, or teachings of knowledge prefer themselves to the rest; rather, giving thanks to God for the gifts divinely bestowed upon them, let them humbly accommodate themselves, in charity, to the weaknesses of the others, always weighing the Apostle’s saying: “Let anyone who thinks that she stands take heed lest she fall” (I Cor. X).

And this saying of Jerome: “It is to be feared and guarded against that a storm lasting one hour may overthrow ancient glory and solid strength.”

## CHAPTER XI

Abbesses must strive with the utmost determination to surround the monasteries of women on every side with such strong fortifications that no entrance or exit is open except through the gate, so that neither men may have the opportunity to do anything improper within their enclosure nor holy women the opportunity to wander outside.

Therefore, let them have prepared within the monastery refectories, storerooms, dormitories, and the other dwellings necessary for their use, so that those who have vowed themselves to the Lord may be able, after setting aside every excuse, to preserve their commitment inviolate.

## CHAPTER XII

We have discovered that a reprehensible practice, deserving correction, exists in certain monasteries of women: the holy women do not receive the Church’s stipends equally, although nowhere can any decree be found establishing that this ought to be done. Since this practice is supported by no authority, but is evidently an unusual custom arising rather from avarice or respect of persons, it is necessary that it be entirely rejected from those places by the judgment of equity.

For it is worthy and just before God and human beings that all those who, for the love of Christ, have resolved to live in the purpose of chastity—that is, in one community—should, with avarice and respect of persons excluded, receive food and drink equally.

## CHAPTER XIII
Because it has become clearly established that certain abbesses negligently and lukewarmly provide their subjects with necessary provisions, it has most opportunely—indeed, reasonably—been decreed that in all monasteries for women in which life is lived according to canonical rule, each religious woman shall receive daily three pounds of bread and, in regions that produce wine, three pounds of wine, unless the season’s barrenness prevents this. If the same region is not fully productive of wine, she shall receive two pounds of wine and two of beer; and if it produces no wine at all, three pounds of beer and, if means permit, one pound of wine. In smaller establishments, they shall receive two pounds of wine; and if that region, as stated above, is not productive of wine, two pounds of beer and, if resources allow, one pound of wine.

Although in certain provinces there is a shortage of wine, the holy Church of God nevertheless abounds, by the Lord’s granting, in supplies of other things, from which the diligence of the superiors can obtain wine from other provinces and provide drinks to their subjects according to their means. Therefore, in places where the Church’s resources are very meager, or perhaps have been greatly reduced by the depredations of certain persons, let only so many religious women be admitted, and of such a number, that at least the lesser measure of drink specified above can be given without difficulty.

In those places, therefore, where certain superiors, following the example of pious superiors, have been accustomed to give more to their subjects, let them by no means discontinue the good that they are doing. If, moreover, anyone wishes, for the sake of eternal reward, to give her subjects more than required, let her cheerfully give whatever she can; but otherwise, let her in no way withhold from them the measure prescribed above.

On feast days, and as is customary in the Church, let them administer provisions to the religious women as well as they can. In providing them with cooked dishes, the abbesses’ diligence must likewise keep especially watchful guard, so that, according to their ability, they provide them with meat, fish, legumes, vegetables, wood, and other necessities, so that, assisted by these things, they may remain more ready for God’s service. They should also establish for them places in which livestock may most suitably be raised and gardens for vegetables may be made, so that they may have cooked dishes from them, apart from what they receive from the Church’s estates and from offerings of alms.

Let them take care lest, through their negligence and misconduct, the monasteries suffer any want, so that this may result neither in sin for themselves nor in the religious women’s falling into murmuring. Let them also be table-companions with the religious women, so that food may be supplied to them more abundantly and whatever is perhaps lacking may be endured together with a more equitable spirit. For if, disregarding their company and care, they privately prepare richer foods for themselves at home—except in the case of illness or guests—they will undoubtedly compel their subjects to fall into the fault of detraction or murmuring.

Let them also give them each year wool and linen, from which they may make the clothing they need, except for the sick and infirm, who, because of bodily weakness, cannot make these things for themselves, and for those who wish to possess nothing of their own; for these they should mercifully endeavor to provide whatever is necessary. Let them receive offerings of alms equally.

## CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 0965A]

Just as the things mentioned above are to be supplied by abbesses to religious women for the needs of their bodies, so it is necessary that they strive to plant instruction in the virtues in the field of the minds entrusted to them, and that in all things—in life, conduct, behavior, dress, and even manner of walking—they show themselves worthy of imitation by living irreproachably, lest through their examples of perversity their subjects fall into pits of destruction.

Let them therefore teach them how to avoid pride, which is the root of all evils; greed, envy, hatred, detraction, whispering, murmuring, buffoonery, double-dealing, dissension, hypocrisy, empty chatter, and all other things of this kind, which drag their followers toward destruction.

[Col. 0965B]

Let them likewise avoid curiosities, by which the female sex is especially entangled. Let them mourn their own faults and not inquisitively question others about theirs, bearing in mind that saying of Jerome: “It is enough,” he says, “for each person to mourn her own faults, not to criticize those of another.”

Let them also instruct them to pursue the virtues of good works—namely, charity, humility, patience, chastity, continence, sobriety, kindness, obedience, gentleness, and the other virtues by which the Christian soul, pressing toward its eternal homeland, must continually serve.

Let them also see to it that they cannot devote themselves to idleness, but rather apply themselves either to prayer, reading, or manual labor, or at least lend an ear to readings from the divine books, so that, by granting their subjects this twofold nourishment—teaching them to avoid what must be avoided and to pursue what must be done—they may deserve not to be condemned by the Lord for unfaithful and negligent administration, but rather to be happily rewarded by him for faithful service.

[Col. 0965C]

They ought therefore to remember and keep before their eyes that they will unquestionably have to render an account to the Lord concerning those entrusted to them.

## CHAPTER XV

With every obstacle of excuse removed, God’s religious women ought to carry out their ministry promptly and honorably. Their most vigilant care should be that, as soon as the signal has been given, they hasten to the canonical hours, and, entering the church with fear of God and reverence, serve the ministry of divine power with the greatest devotion.

They must always take care that nothing dishonorable is committed in the house of God by heart, tongue, or deed, but that they either pray, read, or listen.

If any woman—except those detained either by some bodily infirmity or by an obedience imposed upon them—neglects to attend the aforesaid canonical hours, to observe them diligently, and to perform the heavenly office in them as is fitting, she shall be rebuked with an appropriate denunciation.

The guardians of the church must know the times of these hours well, so that they may ring the signals at the appointed times; and they must also take care that nothing belonging to the church entrusted to them is lost.

## CHAPTER XVI

For imploring the consolations of divine mercy, these words of the Lord instruct the minds of those who ask: “Ask,” he says, “and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7).

But if we desire the door to be opened when we knock, we must open a worthy entrance to the Lord when he comes to us and knocks at the door of our minds, so that the saying may be fulfilled: “If anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him, and I will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3).

Since, therefore, it is evident that forgiveness of sins can be obtained through perseverance in prayer—provided that the lips do not differ from the heart—the religious women should strive to cleanse their minds of harmful thoughts and continually appease God by praying, knowing that the mind contemplates God well in prayer when it is entangled by no cares of earthly things or allurements of vices.

For, as Isidore says, when one stands before the Lord to obtain favors through supplication, it is necessary that the pure and simple gaze of the heart be directed toward him, so that the prayer of the one beseeching may be directed to the place toward which the Prophet wished his own prayer to be directed, saying: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, O Lord” (Psalm 140).

For prayer, as blessed Gregory says, ought to be of the heart, not of the lips, because God does not attend at all to the words of the one beseeching but looks upon the heart of the one praying.

## CHAPTER XVII

After the evening offices have been celebrated with the most devout service and a conference on the divine Scriptures has been solemnly held, when the signal has been given for the celebration of Compline, the religious women shall likewise come together with the greatest devotion.

When it has been completed, they shall not turn to eating and drinking or devote themselves to useless conversation, but, setting these things aside, they shall go honorably to the dormitory.

They must also take care that nothing dishonorable or indecent is done in the dormitory, that no one presumes to disturb another or compel her to break out into useless and idle words. If anyone does so, she shall be rebuked with the severest denunciation.

A lamp shall also burn continually in the same dormitory during the night.

## CHAPTER XVIII

The abbesses must vigilantly strive never to conceal the vices of their subjects, but, as soon as these begin to arise, tear them out by the roots, lest through their sloth and negligence the souls of those women become entangled in the snares of the devil. For the more fragile this sex is recognized to be, the greater the care that must be applied to it.

The following method of correction toward delinquent religious women—except those whose sides, according to Solomon (Ecclesiasticus 30), must be beaten with rods lest they become hardened—must be firmly maintained by the abbesses.

If any woman in the community of religious women neglects to attend the canonical hours, performs the work of God negligently, delays coming to the reading, refuses to carry out an obedience imposed upon her, fails according to her strength to apply herself to learning the instruments of good works, commits anything indecent or dishonorable by words or deeds in the dormitory, presumes without unavoidable cause to sleep somewhere other than in the dormitory, or neglects to serve her sisters with charity;

if she devotes herself to anger, detraction, whispering, buffoonery, double-dealing, loquacity, dissension, hypocrisy, curiosity, or empty chatter; if she sows discord among the sisters; if she proves obstinate, proud, or murmuring toward this rule, or in any way opposed to it; or if she attempts to do anything else of this kind, she shall first be admonished according to the Lord’s command—not only once, and then a second and a third time, but even more frequently. If she does not obey these admonitions, she shall be corrected by a public rebuke.

If she resists this as well, she shall be forbidden all other food and shall eat only bread and drink water until she has made a worthy satisfaction through penance.

If she still does not correct herself, she shall be separated from the table and from the company of the other religious women singing in choir, and shall be compelled to stand apart in a place established by the abbesses for such negligent persons, so that she may immediately be corrected by the shame of separation.

If, after being admonished and punished in these ways, she still remains incorrigible, corporal punishment shall appropriately be applied, if her age permits.

But if she is such that either her age or the status of her person does not permit her to be beaten, she shall be corrected by public rebuke, continued fasts, and the shame of separation until she appears able to obtain forgiveness through a worthy satisfaction of penance.

If both the woman who is beaten and the woman whom either age or status prevents from being beaten prove incorrigible, there shall be a place within the enclosure where they may be confined for a time and punished according to the measure of their fault.

If any woman should descend into such madness that, after so many salutary admonitions and punishments, she still has not corrected herself, the entire community shall pray for her by common agreement, so that she may be healed by the one for whom nothing is impossible.

Finally, if, after all these measures have been applied, she appears uncorrected and incorrigible—since she may in no way be permitted to return to the world—let the bishop be summoned, if necessary. By his most wise and discerning judgment, let her life be regulated within the monastery’s enclosure; by staining herself with so many vices and persisting in obstinacy, she has in a certain sense separated herself from the community of religious women. This regulation should be such that she may profitably perform the penance imposed upon her by him and be unable to inflict upon the others the disease of any contagion.

But if any woman has committed a criminal sin, the benefit of correction must in no way be delayed: either she must voluntarily wash away the crime of her sin through repentance, or, if she refuses to do so, she must receive from the bishop, as stated above and according to the prescribed measure, a sentence of excommunication and the appropriate form of penance.

In punishing and correcting delinquents, the other religious women must not cease to assist the abbesses.

## CHAPTER XIX

The teachings of the holy Scriptures demonstrate that the life of subjects must be shaped by the examples of their superiors. And since, according to the instruction of the Fathers, religious women must avoid familiarity and conversation with men, it is fitting that abbesses, in this as in other matters, should also provide their subjects with a good example in conversations with men.

Whenever necessity presses upon them to converse, let them do so, in accordance with the previously noted judgment of blessed Caesarius, with religious women accompanying them who are commended by age, uprightness of conduct, and innocence of life. Let them deliberate prudently what must be considered and arrange usefully what must be arranged. For if they make use of their counsel and presence, they will both avoid the bite of detraction and provide their subjects with a more salutary example.

Although such religious women may lack experience in these kinds of affairs, nevertheless the abbesses are made capable of good and chaste counsel by their presence.

## CHAPTER XX

Since it is entirely clear, according to the judgments of the Fathers mentioned above, that religious women must completely avoid frequent contact with men, it remains to demonstrate how they ought to act when unavoidable necessity arises.

It is fitting that the abbesses appoint three or four religious women of commendable life. In their presence the other religious women may, at the proper time and in a place established for this business, speak with men who either come with their own horses or with their own servants carrying the things they need, and may receive what has been brought.

The purpose is that such a conversation may be unable to give anyone occasion for suspicion of an unfavorable reputation.

Likewise, at the time of the new harvest, let them receive and store whatever must be received or stored in the presence of the religious women mentioned above.

Similarly, whenever some work must be done in their own small dwellings that cannot be completed without men’s labor, these religious women shall be present, so that in such affairs there may be no opportunity for anyone to engage in detraction or sin.

The abbesses must investigate and scrutinize this carefully—not only through the care of their assistants and the most earnest oversight of the religious women mentioned above, but also through their own diligence, indeed through very frequent inspection—lest anyone in any way commit anything dishonorable in the small dwellings of the religious women or within their enclosures, or anything be accepted from anyone on the pretext of some familiarity, or be secretly hidden.

The religious women ought therefore to possess such confidence in their chastity when conversing with men that they are not at all ashamed in the sight of others.

For, as blessed Jerome says [Col. 0968D] (in his letter to Furia): “The face is the mirror of the mind, and the silent eyes confess the secrets of the heart.” Hence someone also says: “A man’s brow displays the covering of his own mind; whatever his face is, such is the heart he bears.”

If any woman is found to be devoted to such conversations, let her be corrected according to the procedure stated above, so that she herself may be reformed and the others, taking fright, may not dare to do anything of the kind.

## CHAPTER XXI

Since it is permitted to women dedicated to God and living according to canonical rule to have home-born female slaves with them in the monasteries for the purpose of serving them, they must take care to seek in these women the salvation of their souls rather than earthly advantage.

Such women, having become uncontrolled and shameless, commonly walk about adorned in the dress of prostitutes and shamelessly pour into the ears of their mistresses whatever shameful and obscene things they have seen or heard while wandering outside, softening their minds so that they lose the firmness of divine service.

Therefore, when gathering such women, they must exercise discretion: they should gather no more for service than necessity requires, and they should care for those gathered, lest, when these women fall through some sin, their superiors become participants in their downfall.

If these servants—whether of the abbesses or of the religious women—commit anything indecent within the monastery’s enclosure and, after being frequently admonished and corrected, do not reform themselves, they must be driven and expelled far outside the monastery’s enclosure.

## CHAPTER XXII

Ecclesiastical religion teaches that girls who are educated in monasteries should be nurtured with every feeling of piety and the most vigilant care, lest, if they pass the years of slippery youth while living without discipline, they can later be corrected only with difficulty or not at all.

Therefore, let such teachers be appointed over them from among the religious women as are both of commendable life and show them such care that they can in no way wander here and there and become stained by the vice of laziness or wantonness. Rather, let them be imbued with sacred disciplines, so that, devoted to these, they may be free from the leisure of wandering.

But the method to be followed in educating such girls is taught most fully by blessed Jerome in the letter he wrote to Laeta concerning the education of her daughter, saying:

“Therefore, she who was born of a promise should have an upbringing worthy of her birth. Samuel was raised in the temple; John is prepared in the wilderness, fed on locusts and wild honey, and clothed, as a symbol of the repentance he was to preach, in the skins of the most tortuous animal. Thus must the soul be educated that is to become the temple of the Lord.

“Let her learn to hear nothing and to speak nothing except what pertains to the fear of God. Let her not understand shameful words; let her be ignorant of the songs of the world. While her tongue is still tender, let it be imbued with sweet psalms. Let the wanton age of boys be far from her. Let her have a modest maidservant and a serious nurse. Let her learn in childhood for which emperor she is being raised as a recruit. Her very appearance and clothing should teach her to whom she has been promised.

“Let her ears not be pierced, nor the face consecrated to Christ be painted with white lead and purple dye. Let neither gold nor pearls weigh down her neck; let not the sacred head be burdened with jewels. Instead, let her have other pearls, by selling which she may later purchase the pearl of greatest price.

[Note: [Col. 0969D] From Jerome’s Letter 7, to Laeta, it should be read: ‘If her nurse diligently takes care that the child being raised is not struck by a viper, let her take equal care that she does not drink from a golden cup,’ and so forth. HARD.]

“Let her nurse be careful and prudent, so that the child being raised is not struck by a viper. Let her not drink from Babylon’s golden cup; let her not go out with Dinah to see the daughters of the land; let her not play with her feet and drag her garments. For poisons are given only when smeared with honey, and vices deceive only under the appearance of virtues.

“When she has grown somewhat older and, in imitation of her bridegroom, has begun to increase in wisdom, age, and grace before God and human beings, let her go with her parents to the temple of the true Father. But let her not leave the temple with them, and let her be found nowhere except in hearing the holy Scriptures.

“Let her never go outside, lest those who roam about the city find her and wound her chastity, taking away her veil (theristrum) and leaving her naked in her blood. Let her not eat in public, lest she see foods that she desires. Let her learn even now not to drink wine, in which there is wantonness; nevertheless, until she reaches full maturity, let her use a little wine by way of indulgence and be sustained by the eating of meat.

“Let no young man, no curled-haired youth, smile at her. Let her celebrate vigils and solemn night watches in such a way that she does not move even a fingernail’s breadth away from her nurse. Let her not whisper in the ears of maidservants, but let everyone understand what she says to one person.

“Let her companion not be a finely dressed and beautiful woman who modulates a sweet song in her throat, but a serious, pale, somewhat sad woman, experienced in chastity, who may teach her and accustom her by example to rise at night for prayers and psalms, to sing hymns in the morning, and to stand in battle-line like a female warrior of Christ.

“When the course of the hours of the day has been completed and a small lamp has been lit, let her offer the evening sacrifice. Thus let the day pass; thus let the night find her at work.

“Let her food be a little vegetable dish and fine flour, with small fish only rarely. Let her eat so that she is always hungry, so that immediately after food she may be able to read, pray, and sing psalms.

“Let her have no conversations with worldly girls, and let her not mix with the company of wicked virgins. Let her not rekindle the fires lulled by the heat of baths.

“Instead of jewels and silk, let her love the divine books. Let her first learn the Psalter; let her be instructed in the Proverbs of Solomon for life; let her become accustomed in Ecclesiastes to trample underfoot the things of the world. Let her pursue in Job examples of virtue and patience.

“Let her pass on to the Gospels, never laying them aside. Let her absorb the Acts and Letters of the Apostles with the full devotion of her heart, and then, in order, the entire sequence of the New and Old Testament.

“When she has enriched the storeroom of her heart with these treasures, then, adorned with the flowers of the virtues and having trampled underfoot all that belongs to the world, let her strive to please the heavenly bridegroom alone, to whom she has been entrusted.”

## CHAPTER XXIII

Although religious women living according to canonical rule within the enclosure of the monastery are accustomed to have their own small dwellings, nevertheless, for the sake of old women and the sick, the abbesses ought to establish within the enclosure a residence where they may most mercifully assist the weaknesses and illnesses of those who perhaps do not have dwellings of their own.

The abbesses, as spiritual mothers, must care for these women above all, mercifully supplying them with whatever they need.

The other religious women, too, should frequently visit them, comfort them with conversations from the divine Scriptures, provide them assistance from their own resources, and bear their weaknesses and illnesses patiently and lovingly, so that the Lord may rightly say to them: “I was sick, and you visited me,” and so forth (Matthew 25).

## CHAPTER XXIV

Since it is evident that abbesses are weighed down by the burden of external and internal matters, so much so that, hindered by human frailty and ignorance, they are unaware of many things that are negligently done in monasteries, they must appoint such persons under them as can safely share the burdens of governance.

They shall also grant these persons such authority that, acting in their place, they may exhort those who act well to make further progress through words and examples, and may correct the errors of delinquents with the strictest denunciation. Whatever the abbesses themselves cannot complete in the monasteries because of the demands of various responsibilities, these persons should complete worthily and usefully.

They should also make themselves worthy of imitation by the others, so that, by living irreproachably and providing examples of holy virtues, they may deserve to be admitted to the communities of holy women.

But if they live negligently and, although they ought to benefit others by living well, inflict upon anyone the stain of injury through the example of their perversity, let them be judged according to the procedure stated above; and if they prove incorrigible, let them be removed from their ministry and others of commendable life be appointed in their places.

## CHAPTER XXV

It is fitting that abbesses choose from the community entrusted to them such women to whom they may entrust the food supplies of the religious women—women who are not accusers, drunkards, spendthrifts, or enslaved to other enticements of vice, but rather women of commendable life who preserve faithfully and inviolate what has been gathered and administer it faithfully and humbly to the religious women, so that for their faithful administration they may be faithfully rewarded by God, the rewarder of all good things.

Toward such delinquents and disobedient women, the procedure stated above must be firmly maintained.

## CHAPTER XXVI

A religious woman should be appointed at the monastery gate who surpasses the others in age and uprightness of conduct, so that, neither because of favoritism nor because of anyone’s flattery or fear, the monastery gate may be opened except at the appointed hours.

For unless such a woman is appointed at the gate, great danger may undoubtedly arise for those living in the monasteries.

If anyone should attempt, out of favor toward someone, to act against this rule and, after being admonished, does not reform, she shall be corrected with an appropriate denunciation and removed from her ministry.

## CHAPTER XXVII

For the priests who are to celebrate the solemn Masses in monasteries for women, there should be a place and church outside the monastery where they may live with their ministers and fulfill the service of divine worship.

They should enter the monastery of the women only at the appointed time, and with them only a deacon and subdeacon—men who shine in honorable conduct and desire to love not themselves but Christ, seeking not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ. They should remain there no longer than is necessary to celebrate the Masses publicly for the religious women. When these have been duly and devoutly celebrated, they should immediately go outside.

The religious women should celebrate the canonical hours and the solemn Masses with a veil placed before them, as is customary.

They must also take care that none of them has any familiar conversation with these priests or their ministers.

If any woman wishes to confess her sins to a priest, let her do so in the church, where she can be seen by others, as is contained in the sayings of the holy Fathers, except in the case of the sick, for whom it is necessary to do this in their rooms.

The priest should have with him a deacon and subdeacon who are of good reputation, in order to avoid detraction; he should be seen by them, and they should provide good testimony to his innocence.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

Since the authority of the holy Scriptures clearly demonstrates that hospitality must be cherished in every way, and that the Church’s goods are the offerings of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimony of the poor, although a suitable place must properly be maintained at the monastery gate where all who arrive may be received, there should nevertheless be a hospice for the poor outside the monastery, beside the church in which the priests with their ministers perform the divine office.

A person should preside over it who both hates greed and loves hospitality.

Apart from the tithes that are brought there from the Church’s estates, a portion of the Church’s goods should be assigned to the hospice according to the available resources, so that the poor may there be refreshed and cared for.

A tenth of the offerings brought by the faithful to the religious women should likewise be given for the support of those poor.

The person entrusted with the hospice must never divert the property of the poor to personal use, lest, together with Judas stealing from the Lord’s purse, he or she incur a sentence of condemnation.

There should also be within the monastery a shelter where only widows and poor women may be received and fed. If the religious women cannot wash their feet at another time, then at least during Lent, fulfilling the Lord’s command, let them wash the feet of these women, according to the saying: “If I, the Lord and teacher, have washed your feet, how much more ought you to wash one another’s feet?” (John 13).

# LETTER OF LOUIS THE PIOUS

[Note: [Col. 0971D] To Sicharius, archbishop. Copies of the decrees of the Council of Aachen were sent to each province together with the emperor’s letter to the metropolitan of each province. Hence the various titles of the letters that occur in different places. In our copy, because it was sent to Aquitania Secunda, the name is that of Sicharius, archbishop of Bordeaux; in the copy of Auxerre, it is that of Magnus of the city of Sens, which is the chief city of that province’s archbishop. All of them, moreover, have the same subject. JAC. SIRM.]

## TO SICHARIUS, ARCHBISHOP OF BORDEAUX

He sends a copy of the statutes of the Council of Aachen, so that Sicharius may have them carefully transcribed and observed in his province.

Louis, by the divine ordering of providence, emperor Augustus, sends greeting in the Lord to the venerable Sicharius, archbishop in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] This letter must have been an encyclical, for in Goldast, volume IV of *Imperial Constitutions*, p. 12 of the new edition, it is given as addressed to Arno, archbishop of Salzburg. MANSI.]

The sacred and venerable council, recently convened by divine will and through our initiative in the palace at Aachen, in which many matters were carefully discussed and established for the advancement of ecclesiastical dignity, with the grace of Christ preceding and following, we believe cannot in any way have escaped Your Holiness’s notice. But since it happened that Your Paternity was not present at that same holy and venerable council, we have decided to send to Your Beatitude, through our present envoy Adalhelm, the form of canonical institution collected and brought together by that same sacred assembly from sayings scattered throughout the writings of the holy Fathers.

For this reason also we had it carefully copied in our palace, so that it might reach you intact, containing no corruption or mutilation caused by scribal error. Therefore we wish and decree that, in accordance with the canonical dignity conferred upon you in the metropolitan see and with the sanction of our authority, you summon to yourself, at a suitable time and place, the bishops of your diocese and the other prelates of the Church; that you order the aforesaid form of institution to be read aloud to them chapter by chapter in the presence of these men; and that you clearly demonstrate that the sacred assembly issued it for the exaltation of the dignity of the ecclesiastical hierarchy and for the salvation of souls.

You shall also present it for observance to those who live canonically in one community, in the presence of our aforesaid envoy. If anyone’s dullness of mind should prevent him from understanding it, let it be soberly explained to him either by you or by other bishops—namely, your fellow bishops of the province—who shine with the splendor of learning. We likewise admonish your prudence to take care that those who are to copy it transcribe it in such a way that it is neither corrupted through a scribe’s fault nor mutilated by anyone. Rather, just as our aforesaid envoy has shown it to them, let it be copied without any corruption or mutilation.

Know also that a copy of it has been kept in the archive of our palace so that it may plainly be used to establish who copied it carelessly or who mutilated any part of it. For, as we have learned, while it was being read aloud at that same sacred council, before it was presented to us by the council, and before the measure of food and drink had yet been fixed, certain persons, mutilating it to a considerable extent, unwisely copied some chapters from it.

It is therefore necessary that, if you discover anyone in your diocese to have done such a thing, you annul such an act before the assembly of the bishops of your province and before our aforesaid envoy, and that you ensure that this authentic text, as we have said, is carefully transcribed exactly as our envoy instructs them.

Thus all the bishops of your diocese and the other prelates should strive, with vigilant care, to copy it, with diligent zeal to understand it, and, aided by God, to fulfill it in their deeds through the exercise of the most persistent devotion. In this way, when, for the purpose of investigating this matter, we send our envoys throughout the empire—at the coming Kalends of September, as we remember having said to that holy and memorable council that we would do—without any obstacle of difficulty standing in their way, the prelates and subjects of this salutary institution may be found to be vigorous workers, insofar as the Lord grants them ability.

For we shall order a diligent inquiry to be made, while life accompanies us, into which of the prelates has vigorously performed the duty entrusted to him; who has complied with our decree concerning the construction of cloisters for canons and other dwellings, the granting of necessary provisions to them, and the repair of houses intended as shelters for the poor; who has taken care to instruct his clergy in this same institution and in the other spiritual teachings; and who, out of avarice, has driven away those whom the service of Christ could reasonably have supported.

[Note: [Col. 0973D] *Habitationibus constructis* (“dwellings constructed”). The emperor commands two things: that the rule be observed and that monastic dwellings be restored. Hetti, archbishop of Trier, embraced both together in the letter which he then wrote on the same subject to Frothar, bishop of Toul: “You know,” he says, “with what caution we in our diocese, and each bishop in his own parishes, have received the command of the lord emperor: namely, concerning the rule for increasing religious observance and the service-buildings of canons [Col. 0974D], so that, if in any places these were well furnished, they might thereafter be adorned with the utmost diligence. Now an assembly is close at hand, at which the lord who gave the command will doubtless inquire into compliance with it. Therefore examine carefully in your parish, in your own monasteries and those of others, whether the aforesaid rule is worthily observed in every respect, and whether the buildings are maintained, constructed, and renewed in accordance with its decrees; so that, when we are presented before the imperial diligence, with the machinations of others cast far away, the truth concerning all these matters may be reported to him by us together with you,” and so forth, as follows in the sheets of Saint Peter of Chartres, from which we once copied it. JAC. SIRM.]

For we have allowed a period of one year so that, where the promised measures had not yet been carried out, they might readily be completed without anyone’s excuse based on difficulty. Therefore whoever, during this year, neglects to obey our command in this matter to the best of his ability will unquestionably serve as a warning to the others, lest they presume to commit such an offense.

We have indeed sent you the form of institution which the common agreement and equal zeal of that same sacred council carefully extracted from the sayings of the holy Fathers and established for observance by those devoted to chastity who live canonically in one community. We wish you, or your fellow bishops of the province, to order it diligently copied and to have it presented for observance to the monasteries of women situated in your diocese—namely, those in which life is conducted canonically—and to have them taught most plainly how it ought to be observed with the utmost religiousness and devotion by the abbesses and the other holy women.

For, except when we order one of our abbesses to come into our presence, we wish them to remain in the monasteries at other times, to lead their lives according to the form of this institution, and to bind those subject to them to the holy purpose of religious life. None of them is to grant herself permission to wander outside, to take up residence in villages on any pretext, or to devote herself to her own pleasures.

Although some clerics possess monasteries of women, and some laymen possess monasteries of men and even of women, your most diligent industry must nevertheless foresee that, in all places established under your diocese, wherever communities of clerics and holy women exist, they live according to the form of this institution, insofar as their resources and means permit. For there is absolutely no church possessing resources in which persons sufficient in number and of such a character to perform the divine office could not be maintained, and in which hospitality could not be practiced according to its means.

We have therefore sent our aforesaid envoy to Your Holiness so that he might carefully and attentively observe the zeal of you and of the other ecclesiastics residing in your diocese in this matter, and offer you assistance in giving the remaining admonitions. He is also to report to us how readily the male and female prelates have received these forms, how diligently they have endeavored to copy them, and how devotedly they have taken care to fulfill them according to their abilities.

We have ordered him to remain and travel throughout your diocese and those of your fellow bishops together with your envoy until the aforesaid forms have been copied by everyone. Thus, when he has seen to everything and completed it carefully, and the time has come for him to return to us after the work has been completed, let everything that has been done be recorded in writing by both of you and reported to our knowledge through him and through your own representative, so that we may know to whom we ought to render thanks and whom we ought to correct with appropriate reproofs.

But if anyone from your diocese should brazenly resist this institution and your admonition, neglect to observe to the best of his ability what was established and decreed by that sacred assembly, and fail to correct himself after repeated admonition, whoever he may be, let him hasten to come into our presence at your admonition or that of our envoy, so that we may correct him suitably according to the gravity of his fault.

Moreover, we have sent you the weight and measure according to which bread and drink are to be distributed equally to clerics and holy women. We decree that these measures be held most firmly and inviolably by everyone, and we prohibit by every means that anyone increase or diminish them.

At the end of this letter, therefore, we admonish Your Holiness that, in accordance with the ministry conferred upon you by divine gift, you obey our most salutary admonition in this matter obediently and without excuse, and that you offer the others a good example by your obedience. For it is fitting and just that, the more exalted you are above others in the dignity of the priesthood and the more reverently you are loved by us, the more devoted and ready you should show yourself to be in carrying out the will of God and of us.

Farewell in the Lord, and pray for us.

[Col. 0975]

## On the Form of the Institution of Canons and Holy Women, by Aubertus Miraeus

[Col. 0975C]

### Form of the Institution of Canons

This is now commonly called the Rule of Canons. A rule signifies an established manner or form of living piously and rightly. In Greek, a rule is called *kanōn*; from *kanōn* come the *canonici*, that is, clerics living according to regular precepts. Let us hear Isidore speaking in Book VI, chapter 16, of the *Etymologies*: “*Canon* in Greek is called *regula* in Latin. A rule is so called because it leads straight and never draws one elsewhere.” Others have said that a rule is so called either because it governs, or because it supplies a norm for living rightly, or because it corrects what is distorted and wicked.

### Of Canons

Some dispute whether the Fathers of the Council of Aachen, in the year 816, wrote the form of institution or rule of life for Augustinian regular canons, or rather for those whom people now commonly call secular canons. On this question Clemens Reynerus, Doctor and Professor of Sacred Theology at Douai, gives an extensive answer in his book *On the Apostolate of the Benedictines in England*, published at Douai in 1628, p. 131. From it I quote the following:

“Those canons who were instituted at the Council of Aachen were not professed members of the Augustinian Rule; indeed, they were not even religious or regular in the sense in which we now call regular or religious only those persons who have devoted themselves to God through the three vows and complete renunciation of the world.

“First, this is clear from the very preface of the council, where, among other things, it is said that the life of canons is contained here and there in the sacred canons and in the sayings of the holy Fathers. After the preface comes the institution of canons, composed from many canons of ancient councils; from many chapters of Saint Isidore, Prosper, and Gregory; from several letters of Saint Jerome; from two sermons of Saint Augustine on the common life of clerics; and from one of his sermons *On Pastors*. Thus, from Isidore, Prosper, Gregory, and Jerome—that is, from each of these Fathers—far more was taken than from Saint Augustine.

“Furthermore, no mention whatsoever is made there of the Rule of Saint Augustine, nor was anything taken from it—for it was given not to men but to women. For if the matter concerned the formation of Augustinian canons, why was the instruction not taken from Augustine’s Rule, rather and above all? Indeed, if these canons were Augustinians, why—as the Fathers at the Second Council of Aachen, held in 836, send all monks to be formed according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, in these words: ‘Let monks unanimously follow the regular life in all things according to the Rule handed down by Saint Benedict’—do they not likewise refer canons to the Rule of Saint Augustine?

“Although this argument is sufficiently clear, it will become still clearer from another consideration. Everyone knows that the regular canons of Saint Augustine, properly and truly speaking, are religious and profess complete renunciation of the world. Yet the council itself expressly declares, in chapter 115, that the canons whom the Fathers of Aachen prescribed the Rule for, from the canons of the Church and the sayings of the holy Fathers, were not, properly speaking, bound to religious renunciation:

“‘Although canons, since it is not read that they are forbidden this in the sacred canons, may wear linen, eat meat, give and receive, and possess their own property and that of the Church with humility and justice—which is entirely forbidden to monks, who, according to their regular institution, lead a stricter life—nevertheless, in avoiding vices and embracing virtues, their life ought not to differ from that of monks.’

“From this it is clear that, in the time of Louis the Pious, canons living in common, even under abbots and provosts, were not regular in the sense in which the word is now used, but secular. In addition to the prebends or stipends which, as the Fathers of Aachen say, they ordinarily received from the bishop and the church which they served, they were also permitted to retain their own possessions and give them to whomever they wished. They differed from the secular canons of our time only in living in a common house and using a common table and common dormitory, as academic clerics now live in seminaries, and as the Fathers of the Oratory live in Italy, France, Belgium, and elsewhere.

“In France, moreover, many colleges of secular canons belonging to that ancient institution can still be seen. Although we may call them pious and religious on account of their practice of the virtues, we should not call them religious or regular in the sense in which that term is now applied only to those who, having completely renounced the world, retain absolutely nothing under their control which they can dispose of as their own property.”

Thus far, approximately, Clemens Reynerus in the cited passage.

### At the Council of Aachen

Aachen is an imperial city situated in the diocese of Liège. It was so called from some unknown Granus; it is famous for being the residence, tomb, and repository of the relics of Saint Charles the Great, emperor, and also for its baths. To our countrymen it is Aken; to the Franks, Aix-la-Chapelle. Formerly it was called New Castle. Long before the age of Charlemagne, it was a place of delight to princes, as it was to Pippin of Herstal, mayor of the royal palace in Austrasia and great-grandfather of Charlemagne, who generously endowed the basilica of the Blessed Mary at Aachen, as is clear from his charter:

“Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.
