Let the whole multitude of our faithful know that our great-grandfather Pippin, of illustrious memory, formerly mayor of the palace, gave various possessions to the church of Saint Mary constructed at New Castle, for the increase of his reward. Hence the servants of that place have visibly had the consolation of material support up to the present, and appear to possess those same possessions in peaceful order for all time. Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May, in the eleventh and fifth year of our reign. Done happily in the palace at Herstal, in the name of God. Amen.”

In the year of Christ 816, a council was held at Aachen. At it, by order of the emperor Louis the Pious, son and successor of Charlemagne, two Forms of Institution, or Rules, were composed: one for canons, the other for holy women living canonically, whom people commonly call *canonicas* or *canonistas*. The former was published long ago by Surius and Binius in their volumes of the Councils.

When I was in Paris in 1610 on public business, I arranged to have the latter copied from a manuscript belonging to the highly cultivated and very dear friend of mine, Nicolas Fabri of Paris, who had been a fellow student of Pierre Pithou and whom Louis XIII, king of France, later appointed tutor in letters. From that same manuscript, now preserved in Paris in the Thuana Library, Jacobus Sirmondus published this work in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul* in 1629.

It is believed that Amalarius, deacon of the church of Metz, devoted his principal efforts to composing both Rules. He was the man who compiled the four books on the divine offices attributed to that same Louis the Pious. Until now, however, printers have falsely attributed these books to Amalarius Fortunatus, bishop of Trier.

Amalarius of Metz, as I have said, was a deacon—Honorius incorrectly calls him bishop of Metz in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*—and was a man of exceptionally wide learning, of approximately the same age as Amalarius, bishop of Trier. They say that, after a supply of books had been made available from the palace at Aachen, this entire work of canonical institution was arranged by that Amalarius of Metz from the various opinions of learned men and approved by the judgment and authority of the Council of Aachen. Sirmondus observed this from the *Chronicle of Ademar of Angoulême*.

## BOOK ONE

### Chapter I

#### On the Tonsure of Clerics

In the ancient Western Church, those who had girded themselves for the sacred service immediately laid aside their flowing hair. Prudentius writes of Saint Cyprian:

“His flowing hair is restrained into short locks.”

Traces of this custom remain in the sacred rite by which clerics are made: the bishop, when he receives men into the clerical order, removes tufts of their hair here and there. This is called the first tonsure, and clerics of that rank were formerly called the tonsured.

In earlier times they were in fact shaved, and afterward it was not permitted them to grow their hair. Hence canon 44 of the Fourth Council of Carthage: “Let a cleric neither grow his hair nor shave his beard”—or, as other old books read, “nor cut it.” They therefore grew beards, as the Greeks still do today, and many Latins as well. I therefore cannot at all understand what Pope Gregory VII writes to the judge of Cagliari, in Book IX, Letter 10: that the clergy of the entire Western Church, from the very beginnings of the Church of Christ, had maintained the custom of shaving the beard. Nevertheless, most Latins later shaved their beards, and this became the distinction between the Greek and Latin clergy.

That this difference does nothing contrary to our religion is carefully argued by the Synod of Limoges. In the acts of its second day, the canons of the Synod of Bourges are recited; its seventh canon orders all clerics to have the ecclesiastical tonsure—that is, a shaved beard and a crown on the head. So various have been the changes of the ages even in this matter. Thus, approximately, Sirmondus in his notes on Apollinaris Sidonius and Ennodius.

### Isidore

Saint Isidore of Seville, in Baetica, a province of Spain, flourished as a bishop in the year 629 and, according to Bellarmine’s reckoning, died in 636. Baronius may be consulted concerning him and the other Isidores in his notes on the Roman Martyrology, 4 April.

### Below, a circular crown

The clerical tonsure was formerly made in such a way that only a circle of hair remained, like a crown. Gregory of Tours describes it in this way when speaking of Nicetius, bishop of Trier:

“Saint Nicetius,” he says, “was marked out as a cleric from his birth. For when he had been brought forth in childbirth, his entire head, as is customary with children, was seen to be bare of hair; but around the middle of his hair a row appeared, so that you might think that the cleric’s crown had been marked out by it.”

Today, among us, only monks and singing boys retain almost exclusively the ancient form of the crown. For the short circle at the crown of the head, which a large part of the clergy uses, was formerly unusual and unknown in the Church, as canon 40 of the Fourth Council of Toledo teaches. Thus Sirmondus on Sidonius.

### Chapter V

#### Acolytes

Augustine Valerius, cardinal and bishop of Verona, wrote two books on the discipline of acolytes.

### Chapter VI

#### Subdeacons

They were formerly called *obsequentes*, as will be established below, in chapter 77, from the Council of Laodicea.

### Chapter VIII

#### On Priests

Those who were formerly called priests were, as it were, assistants to the bishops; with their counsel they governed the Church entrusted to them. For this reason Saint Cyprian frequently calls them his colleagues and brothers. Saint Augustine valued the importance of this order so highly that Bishop Valerius ordained him priest almost against his will and while he resisted with tears, as Possidius relates in the *Life of Augustine*, and Augustine himself declares in his letter to Valerius.

### Chapter X

#### For This Reason

This chapter, as well as the following one, deals expressly with bishops. The text of both chapters is taken from Saint Jerome. Jerome likewise writes in Letter 50, to Pammachius:

“Bishops, priests, deacons, or virgins are chosen, or widowers, or at least those who, after priestly ordination, remain chaste forever. In the first centuries of the Church, those who were taken from marriage into the priesthood were separated from the marriage bed and thereafter associated with their wives no otherwise than with sisters. Thus Terasia, after becoming the wife of Paulinus of Nola, became his sister, as Hydatius says in his *Chronicle*. Fortunatus writes the same concerning Placidia, the wife of Leontius, bishop of Bordeaux.

“Moreover, bishops are first in the order of clerics, priests second, deacons third, and so on. Optatus of Milevis, Book I: ‘Why should I mention deacons established in the third order, or priests constituted in the second priesthood? The bishops themselves are the summit and leaders of all.’”

The story invented by some about bishops of the first and second orders is pure fiction—as though, if God please, there had once been two bishops in each see.

### Blessed Jerome

He was born in the town of Stridon, which, destroyed by the Goths, was formerly on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia. He died in the year of Christ 420, at the age of ninety-one, on the day before the Kalends of October, as Prosper says in his *Chronicle*. Baronius, however, assigns him only seventy-eight or seventy-nine years.

### Chapter XII

#### Augustine

He was born in Africa during the consulship of Arbetio and Mavortius Lollianus—as he himself relates in Book I of *The Happy Life* and Book I of *The Order*—that is, in the common reckoning, in the year of Christ 355. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, at the age of seventy-six, after thirty-six years as a bishop and forty-three years after his conversion. At that time the Vandals had already been besieging Hippo for three months, as Possidius relates in his *Life*.

### Chapter XIII

#### Gregory

Saint Gregory of Nazianzus had explained the duties of pastoral care in Greek in the book he entitled *Apologeticus*. Emulating him, Pope Saint Gregory the Great, Gregory I, at the beginning of his pontificate, wrote a book *On Pastoral Care* to John, bishop of Ravenna, and sent it to Spain to Leander, bishop of Seville.

Greece valued this book so highly that Amphilochius, patriarch of Alexandria, translated it into Greek soon after it had been published. The Fathers of the Third Councils of Tours and of Chalon II, held in 813, and of the Second Council of Aachen, held in 836, ordered bishops to read it diligently.

Saint Gregory, elected pope in the year of Christ 590, finally departed to Christ in 604, in the seventh indiction.

### Chapter XIX

#### Prosper

At that time—that is, in the age of the emperor Louis the Pious—the three books *On the Contemplative Life*, which are commonly published among Prosper’s works and are frequently cited under his name by Gratian and others, were attributed to Prosper. In reality, however, they do not appear to be his.

First, Gennadius, when listing Prosper’s works, does not mention these books. Second, in Book II, chapter 9, their author speaks of Hilary of Arles—who was Prosper’s contemporary—in such a way as to indicate that Hilary was older than himself. Finally, to pass over other arguments, in the ancient collection of canons in the Codex of Angers they are attributed to “Saint Pomerie”—for that is how the manuscript names him—as author, in the passage which appears in Prosper, Book II, chapter 6. In the Codex of Saint-Sauveur of Vicomte, now in the library of the archbishop of Toulouse, the abbot of that place, Julian Pomerius is assigned as author of these books.

Isidore likewise attributes them without qualification to Julian Pomerius in chapter 12 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

“He also published three other books on the contemplation of the future life, or on active conduct, and likewise on vices and virtues.”

These words clearly show that the subjects of the individual books of this work are being described. The same Julian Pomerius had also published eight other books, whose titles Isidore explains individually in the same passage, and whose testimony Julian of Toledo, the bishop, frequently used in his *Prognostics of the Future Age*.

This Pomerius was an African and a Moor by birth; in Gaul he was first a rhetorician, then a priest and abbot. He flourished at Arles, as may be understood from the *Life of Saint Caesarius, Bishop of Arles*, and from the letters of Ruricius to Pomerius. Thus approximately Sirmondus in his notes on volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*.

Prosper of Aquitaine, moreover, was a priest, not a bishop—if we believe Victor of Aquitaine, Gennadius, Gelasius, Marcellinus, and Bede. “Following the chronology of Eusebius,” to use Victor’s words, “he composed a remarkable *Chronicle* with great brevity and carried it from the beginning of the world to the eighth consulship of the emperor Valentinian and the consulship of Anthemius, that is, to the year of Christ 455,” in its third edition.

For he appears to have brought the first edition to a close during the consulship of Theodosius XIV and Maximus, that is, in the year of Christ 433. In that year he gathers together the epochs and totals of the preceding years, something ordinarily done only at the end of a work, unless some special reason intervenes; none is apparent here.

Prosper appears to have enlarged the second edition by twelve years and extended it to the consulship of Valentinian VI and Nonius, that is, to the common year 445 of Christ. The common *Chronicle* of Prosper, customarily appended to that of Eusebius and Jerome, ends there.

Finally, the third and last edition was the one extending to the eighth consulship of the emperor Valentinian and the consulship of Anthemius, that is, to the year of Christ 455. Andreas Quercetanus recently published it in Paris in the *Library of Ancient Ecclesiastical Historians and Chroniclers*, after it had been collated by Chiffletius, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, with manuscript codices.

Bucherius discusses at length, in his commentary on the Canon of Victorius, chapter 6, the three or four Prospers of this age: the men of Orléans and Riez, the chronicler, and Tiro.

### Chapter XXXIX

#### From the Council of Nicaea

Dionysius, surnamed Exiguus, a Roman abbot—who, abandoning the pagan reckoning of years, was the first to begin counting from the incarnation of Christ—compiled a book of the canons of the Roman Church and dedicated it to Stephen, bishop of Salona. It was first printed at Mainz in 1525 and then at Paris in 1609.

When Pope Hadrian was at Rome in 787, he presented a faithfully copied exemplar of this book to Charles the Great, king of the Franks. This is certainly established by the many copies of this Collection visible in the libraries of Gaul. At the beginning of these copies, as a dedication of the gift presented, there is prefixed a letter of Hadrian to Charles whose initial letters, taken from the beginnings of the individual lines, yield this title:

“To the most excellent lord, his son, King Charles: Pope Hadrian.”

The letter has been printed by Sirmondus in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*. The authority of this Dionysian Collection subsequently became very great among the Franks, as is clear from chapter 39 of this *Institution of Canons* and from many later passages.

### Chapter LXIV

#### Seven Deacons

It is likewise established from ancient canons that once there were seven cardinal deacons of the city of Rome.

### Chapter LXXX

#### Agapes

These were common meals of Christians, so called because they were instituted for the sake of mutual charity. Tertullian writes in Book *Against the Nations*:

“Our dinner reveals its meaning by its name; it is called *Agape*, which among the Greeks means ‘Love.’”

In the course of time, however, abuse, luxury, and drunkenness corrupted this pious custom. They were therefore rightly abolished and condemned by Saints Ambrose, Augustine, and other Fathers. Consult Baronius under the years 377 and 391.

### Chapter LXXXIII

#### Thymetics

Strictly speaking, this was the name given to dancers who, in the orchestra, sometimes danced toward the actors and sometimes toward the people, while the actors were hidden on the stage.

### Chapter CVIII

#### Clerics Living Either in Their Own Houses or in Community

Here the reader should note that Prosper of Aquitaine—or rather Julian Pomerius—explicitly mentions two classes of clerics: clerics living privately in their own houses, and others living in common, or in a community.

The Council of Girona in Spain, held around the year 517, likewise issued a canon for clerics who had households of their own. From the words of that same Prosper, or Pomerius, quoted in the preceding chapter, it may be inferred that many among the clergy retained ownership and control of their property. These are the words:

“But if they contribute something from the produce of their possessions to the Church, as if for its own expenses,” and so forth.

The Fathers of the Oratory in Italy, France, Belgium, and elsewhere do the same today. That the clerics of Spain had a similar manner of life is attested by chapter 4 of the Ninth Council of Toledo, held in 655. The immediately following chapter may also be consulted.

#### Monastery of Clerics

For Saint Augustine, a monastery of clerics is a community of clerics living together like monks. Writers of antiquity and the Middle Ages commonly use the word in this way. Balderic, bishop of Noyon and Tournai—who died in 1112—in the *Chronicle of Cambrai*, Book II, and frequently elsewhere, calls the cathedral colleges of canons at Cambrai and Arras the monasteries of the canons of Saint Mary. Yet it is established that these churches had been clerical or canonical from their very beginnings, not monastic.

The same Balderic, near the end of Book II, mentions the monastery of the canons of Saint Rumold at Mechelen and the monastery of canons founded by the man of God Guntmar. These are the distinguished canonical colleges now known as Mechelen and Lier in Brabant.

#### Carraria

That is, a quarry. Among the Franks, the Gallo-Belgians, the Spaniards, and other peoples, *carrariae*, commonly called *carrières*, are pits or underground chambers from which stones or marble are extracted. Just as anciently Lunense marble was prized, so today Carrara marble is highly valued, named after the nearby town in whose vicinity it is drawn from the bowels of the earth.

#### Let No One Give Linen or a Birrus

From these words it may be inferred that Saint Augustine and his clerics used linen clothing and a *byrrhus* or *birrus*, though not an expensive one. Lipsius, in his *Amphitheatre*, places *byrrhi* among head coverings, citing Vopiscus concerning the emperor Carinus: “Byrri requested from the Atrebates; byrri of Canusium given.”

From *birrus*, Molanus derives *birretum*, the square clerical cap, in his book *On Canons*. Alciatus, in Book I of his *Miscellanies*, interprets *byrrhus* as a cloak, a garment worn over other clothing. Baronius agrees, explaining the *lacernus byrrhus* mentioned at the Council of Gangra as a *byrrhus* made in the manner of a *lacerna*, or cloak.

In Africa, as in Gaul and elsewhere, he also censures stiff or sumptuous *byrri*.

### Explicit

Here ends the first part of the *Institution* or *Rule of Canons*, compiled by the Fathers of the Council of Aachen in the year of Christ 816 from the writings of the holy Fathers and the decrees of ancient councils. The subsequent, or latter, part was dictated almost entirely by the Fathers of that same council.

### Chapter CXV

#### Canons May Wear Linen, Eat Meat, and So Forth

These words prove with complete clarity that this form of institution was not written or given by the Fathers of the Council of Aachen to Augustinian regular canons, as Pennottus and others maintain, but to the canons of our order, whom the common people call secular because they are mingled with worldly society.

#### Monks Are Forbidden to Eat Meat

In the Eastern Church, the eating of meat was forbidden to Basilian monks; in the Western Church, it was forbidden to Benedictine monks, according to their original institution. The regular canons of Prémontré, Val-des-Écoliers, and others, bound by solemn vows like monks, later imitated them in this respect.

#### Dormitories. Refectory

These and other public places of the same kind, which the canons of our order formerly used, still exist and are shown with admiration at Cologne, Tournai, Liège, Bruges, Lille, and elsewhere.

### Chapter CXXIV
Every day they are to come to the conference. That is, to the chapter of discipline, as the Council of Cologne, held in 1536, interprets it in Part III, chapter 14:

> “The chapters of discipline,” it says, “are to be observed with much greater diligence than hitherto. This will happen if sacred matters, rather than profane ones, are treated in them; if inquiries are made into morals; if the life of each individual is examined; and if, as the holy Fathers are known formerly to have done, the brothers are sometimes admonished by an extemporaneous address; and especially if they are urged to take up the sacred Scriptures and encouraged to devote their best hours to them.”

The following constitution of the likewise Cologne Council, held in 1260, also pertains here:

> “The dean and the canonical brothers shall enter the chapter house, and before every discussion of discipline, or even of the chapter’s prebendal table—that is, the table indicating what each person is to sing or read in the choir—they shall listen attentively to a reading; and likewise another reading from the Rule and the life of clerics shall be read.”

Much older than these decrees are the passages that Isidore records in his Rule for Monks and in Book II, chapter 15, of On Ecclesiastical Offices:

> “To hear the Father at the conference,” he says, “the brothers shall assemble three times a week after the celebration of the Third, when the signal has been given for the gathering. They shall listen to an elder teaching and instructing all by salutary precepts; they shall listen to the Father with the greatest attention and silence, showing the purpose of their minds by sighs and groans. The conference itself shall concern either the correction and instruction of morals or other matters pertaining to the welfare of the monastery. If such matters are lacking, the conference nevertheless is by no means to be omitted for the sake of the customary discipline; rather, on the appointed days, when all have assembled together, the regular precepts of the Fathers are to be reviewed, so that those who have not yet learned them may receive what they are to follow, while those who have learned them, reminded by frequent recollection, may carefully preserve what they know. All, however, shall remain silent while seated at the conference.”

Thus far Isidore.

## CHAPTER CXXV

### That canons are not to wear monks’ cowls

A *cucullus* or *cuculla* is properly a covering for the head, pyramid-shaped, resembling those little paper vessels in which apothecaries sell their enclosed wares. Concerning these Martial wittily writes to his little book:

> “Hasten to provide yourself with a defender,  
> lest, quickly snatched into the black kitchen,  
> you cover sardines with wet paper,  
> or become a cowl of frankincense and poppy.”

The Capuchins properly wear the *cucullus* today; Italians now call this covering of the head a *capucium* or *capuccium*. Hence the name “Capuchins” arose among the common people. Cassian, *Institutes*, Book II, chapter 4, should be consulted.

## CHAPTER CXXVI

### The Third and the Sixth Hours

Many have written about the antiquity of the canonical hours; I refer the reader to them. One may also consult Bartholomaeus Gavanti’s *Treasury of Sacred Rites* and Anacletus Siccus’s *Ecclesiastical Hymnody*.

### The solemnities of the Mass

The Mass, the sacrifice of Christians, is so called not from a Hebrew word, nor from *missa*, meaning a dismissed multitude, but from *missa hostia*, “a victim sent”—that is, brought into view or to the heavenly altar. For in this mystery the Church sends Christ as an envoy and intercessor to the Father, offers and displays to Him this singular benefit of the Son, and strives by it to appease Him; she prays to Him for the living and the dead. She does not sacrifice Him again or crucify Him, as blasphemers falsely accuse her; and this has efficacy *ex opere operato*, as they speak in the theological schools—that is, by divine institution, not through the work of the minister.

## CHAPTER CXXXIV

### If any brother

Here we have the manner of capitular correction formerly customary among canons.

## CHAPTER CXXXV

### Boys and adolescents

Let the reader note that formerly very renowned schools or literary academies existed in the cloisters of canons and in episcopal palaces. When Charlemagne founded the bishopric of Osnabrück in Westphalia in the year 804, he ordered Greek and Latin schools to remain there permanently, so that clerics learned in both languages might never be lacking.

Concerning the bishops and other distinguished men who emerged from the school of Norger, bishop of Liège, and likewise concerning Heraclius, bishop of that same city and an outstanding promoter of schools, Anselm may be consulted in his *History of Liège*. Balderic discusses Lietbert, head of the schools of Cambrai and afterward bishop of that city, in Book III, chapter 61, of his *Chronicle of Cambrai*.

## CHAPTER CXXXVII

### The school of singers

That singing is rightly joined to the divine office is clear from the decrees of the Fourth Council of Toledo and others. Concerning the school of singers, Onuphrius Panvinius, continuator of Platina, reports the following:

> “The school of singers lived at common expense and had a prefect of great esteem and dignity in the city, who was called the *primicerius*, or sometimes the prior of the school of singers. Through his care the finest young men were selected and instructed in singing, the reading of sacred books, and excellent morals. From this arose the office of the *primicerii* in the other cathedral churches of the world; their office and dignity are mentioned in Distinction 25. I believe this to be the school whose origin Anastasius the Librarian describes in the Life of Pope Hilary:
>
> ‘He established in the city ministers—that is, clerics—who went around the appointed stations, serving at the sacred rites and singing psalms.’
>
> John the Deacon, however, in Book II of his Life of Saint Gregory I, pope, writes that Saint Gregory established this school himself. I think this should rather be understood of some reform or restoration of it than of its first institution.”

Thus far Onuphrius. In keeping with the customs of our own times, the dignity of cantor is counted among the principal dignities in cathedral and collegiate churches. Consult Molanus’s book *On Canons*.

## CHAPTER CXL

### The cellarer

Also *cellarius*. According to the grammarians, this word has a broad meaning. A *cella* is any place in which something is stored, such as a wine cellar, beer cellar, flour store, fruit store, and places for similar things. Here, however, the cellarer is called the procurator and custodian of provisions, the person in charge of edible and drinkable supplies. Monks today call such a person the household steward, procurator, or dispenser. Plautus calls him the *promus* and *condus*. At Tournai there are still two master cellarers.

### The man who [cares for] the hospital of the poor

He is called the hospitaler and was responsible for the hospital house built for the use of the poor. Houses of this kind can still be seen in many places beside the churches of canons, as at Saint Servatius in the city of Maastricht, at Tournai, and elsewhere in Belgium. Formerly there was likewise a hospital house at Antwerp beside the Church of Our Lady; it was later transferred to the outskirts of the city.

## CHAPTER CXLIV

### The cloisters of canons ought to be closed

The dwellings of canons were formerly enclosed on every side by walls and gates; hence they are still called *cloisters*, although today they are open to everyone day and night. In most places traces of the ancient enclosure nevertheless remain, and in some places the gates are still closed at night. For this reason I judge the canons of Lille in Flanders, and the noble canonesses of Maubeuge in Hainaut on the River Sambre, worthy of praise.

### When the signal has been given

When persecutions were raging, the faithful were formerly summoned to church by a messenger, usually a subdeacon, lector, or acolyte. Once peace had been restored to the Church, the use of bells is thought to have begun; the pagans also used to summon people by them to the baths and to work. Martial’s Epigram 128 suggests this:

> “Return the ball; the bronze of the baths is sounding.”

Polydore Vergil, in Book VI, chapter 12, of *On the Inventors of Things*, attributes this to the time of Pope Sabinian:

> “That the people are invited to the sacred rites by the sound of bells on appointed days was decreed by Sabinian, who succeeded Gregory.”

Certainly Baronius proves in his account of the year 616 that shortly after the time of Sabinian the use of the bronze campana, or bells, had become common in the West. Bede writes in Book IV, chapter 23, of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English*:

> “They were accustomed to be roused or summoned to prayers by the sound of the bell when one of them had been called away from this world.”

Writing of the same objects, Walafrid Strabo says:

> “They assert that the use of the vessels of which we are speaking was first discovered among the Italians. Hence the larger vessels are called *campanae*, after Campania, a province of Italy; while the smaller ones, which are also called *tintinnabula* from their sound, are called *nolae*, after Nola, a city of that same Campania, where such vessels were devised.”

The use of bells is certainly far more ancient, since it was known already in the time of Moses, as may be gathered from Exodus 23 and Book III of Josephus’s *Jewish Antiquities*. Moreover, it is thought that bronze signals passed from the West to the East around the year 815, when Ursus Patricius, doge of Venice, sent several bells as a gift to the emperor Michael, as the historians of Venice relate.

Among the ancients there is frequent mention of the signal summoning people to church. Gregory of Tours, in the *Lives of the Fathers* that he wrote, says of Gregory, bishop of Langres:

> “When the signal had been sounded, the saint of God, like the others, rose as a newcomer for the service of the Lord.”

The same author says of Nicetius, bishop of Lyon:

> “When the presbyter heard this, he ordered the signal to be sounded for the vigils.”

And in Book II, chapter 23, of his *History of the Franks*:

> “The signal for Matins.”

Einhard, *On the Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter*, Book III, chapter 15:

> “The little tower containing the bells of the basilica could have been seen by them.”

The *Capitularies*, Book VI, title 168:

> “That priests touch the bells at the canonical hours.”

In the *Order of Dunstan of Canterbury*, archbishop in England:

> “The blessing of the church signal, that is, the bell.”

The French word *sein* derives from *signum*, “signal,” and from it comes *toc-sein*. In the first centuries, however, the signals were not bronze but wooden. This is clear from the *Book of the Miracles of the Martyr Anastasius*, which is read in the Seventh Synod, act 4:

> “Striking the sacred pieces of wood, they came to meet one another.”

The wooden signals belonged chiefly to monks; we still use such instruments during the last three days of Holy Week in Lent. In some monasteries, however, the doors of individuals were struck with a mallet. Whoever wishes to know more about these matters should consult Baronius under the year 58.

### Let them be instructed in the disciplines of every kind of art

Formerly, every kind of discipline was taught to the young in the cloisters of canons. The Greek letters, as well as the Latin, were explained there.

# BOOK TWO

## On the institution of canonesses living canonically

Today we call them canonical women, or canonesses, as Clemens Reynerus judges in the book cited above. Let the reader further note that in this form of the canonical Institution no mention is made of the Rule given by Saint Augustine to women. Therefore this institution was not written by the Fathers of Aachen for Augustinian canonesses.

## CHAPTER V

### Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles

Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, wrote, in addition to a Rule for monks, another for holy women; this chapter is taken from it. Saint Radegund, abbess of Poitiers, mentions this Rule in her letter to the bishops assembled at the Second Council of Tours in the year 567:

> “For the congregation gathered by me, through Christ’s favor, I adopted the Rule under which Saint Caesaria lived, which the care of the blessed Caesarius, bishop of Arles, suitably collected from the institution of the holy Fathers.”

## CHAPTER VI

### Saint Athanasius

Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria in Egypt. Some write that he died during the consulship of Gratian II and Probus, that is, in the year 371. But it is clear from the letter of Proterius, patriarch of Alexandria, to Pope Leo I—published by Joannes Bucherius in his commentary on Victor’s Easter canon, chapter 2—that Athanasius was still alive in 373.

## CHAPTER X

### Noble by birth

From this it is clear that, from the time of Louis the Pious onward, virgins noble by birth joined themselves, more than others, to canonically living holy women.

## CHAPTER XX

### In their cloisters

Like canons, canonically living holy women formerly had their own cloisters enclosed on every side by walls, as well as common dormitories and refectories. Traces of these still survive in many places. To restore this discipline to use, the outstanding heroine, Lady Margaret de Lalain, countess of Berlaimont, founded and endowed at her own expense, in the city of Brussels, in recent years, a distinguished convent of noble canonical virgins living under the Rule of Saint Augustine, with the approval of Urban VIII, supreme pontiff.

## CHAPTER XXII

### Girls who are educated in the monastery

Let the reader observe that schools for girls also flourished in the cloisters of canonically living holy women. The noble canonesses of Brussels, whom I have already said were founded by the countess of Berlaimont, emulate this pious institution with honor.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### What sort of women are to be appointed as superiors

At Nivelles, Maubeuge, Thorae, and elsewhere, the dignity of provost is still the first dignity among the canonesses after that of the abbess.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### Priests outside the monastery of the girls

At Nivelles, Mons in Hainaut, and in many other places there are colleges of canons who celebrate the solemnities of the Mass in due order in the churches of canonically living holy women. They also have their own particular churches, in which they chant the canonical hours and perform the other sacred duties.

### The Letter of Louis the Pious

Copies of the Institutions or Rules prescribed by the Fathers of the Council of Aachen in 816 for canons and canonically living holy women were sent to each province, together with a letter from the emperor Louis the Pious to the metropolitan of each province, so that they might become known to all. Hence the letters found in manuscript codices bear different titles.

In the copy used by Jacobus Sirmondus in his edition of the Councils of Gaul, the name of Sicharius, archbishop of Bordeaux, appears, because it was sent by Louis the Pious to Aquitania Secunda. In the Auxerre codex the name of Magnus, archbishop of Sens, appears; that city is the chief city of that province. In the Paris codex of Nicolas Fabri—from which I arranged for the Rule of canonically living holy women to be copied at Paris in 1610—the name of Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, appears. All these letters are identical in subject, although some details differ in each according to circumstances.

[Col. 0985]

# FOUR BOOKS OF SYMPHOSIUS AMALARIUS, PRIEST AND CHOREPISCOPUS OF METZ, ON ECCLESIASTICAL OFFICES

[Note: Until this point these books on Ecclesiastical Offices, as well as the book *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, had presented as their author Amalarius Fortunatus, bishop of Trier. But after the authority of Amalarius himself in the prologue of the book *On the Order of the Antiphonary*, and that of Ademarus, monk of Saint Eparchius of Angoulême, in his *Chronicle*, there is now scarcely any disagreement among learned men that they must be attributed to Amalarius the deacon of Metz. Ademarus’s words are these:

> “When the Council had been held at Aachen, the emperor Louis, in the third year of his reign, in the year 816 from the Lord’s Incarnation, ordered a Rule for canons to be made, excerpted from various writings of the Fathers, and decreed that it be observed by the canons, so that, just as monks look to the book of the Rule of Saint Benedict, so canons might read among themselves the book of the Life of Clerics. This book the deacon Amalarius, commanded by the emperor, compiled from various sayings of learned men. The emperor gave him access to the books in his palace, so that from them he might excerpt whatever seemed appropriate; and thus, together with the decrees of the bishops who were present, the life of clerics was strengthened. The aforesaid Amalarius wrote for that same emperor a book on the divine Offices and their variations, and on the order of the psalms according to the ancient usage of clerics.”

It is beyond doubt that Ademarus’s “book on the divine Offices” means the four books that Amalarius composed on the ecclesiastical Office, as they are usually entitled; and by “on the order of the psalms” he means the book *On the Order of the Antiphonary.]

## To Louis the Pious, Emperor

*(Library of the Ancient Fathers.)*

# PREFACE OF AMALARIUS

[Col. 0985]

[Col. 0985C] Most glorious emperor, most magnificent and a hundred times unconquered, crowned by God, and likewise preserved and destined to be preserved? I, your servant, although the least of all, was once moved by a desire to know something about the order of our Mass, which we celebrate according to customary practice, and especially about the diversity that usually occurs in it—namely, that sometimes one epistle is read, sometimes two, and other such matters—as well as about the other Offices.

Last summer it seemed to me, as though I were placed in a crypt, that sparks of light were shining through a window even to my lowliness concerning the matter that I desired. Hungry with a long starvation, I did not allow any bridle of fear of a teacher to restrain me; rather, immediately giving thanks to God, I wrote what I perceived.

Then I began to consider to which wise man I should present what I had written, so that by his authority what had been written in orderly fashion might be established, or what had been written disorderly might be corrected. Among all spiritual minds living in this age, your mind especially came to my attention as excelling: in you there is charity without envy, wisdom without the prejudice of that knowledge which puffs up, and humility with piety, which resists no rectitude and which daily exalts you before the Lord, raising those who look upon your footsteps and follow them from lowly and passing things to sublime and everlasting ones.

Therefore I judged that my lowliness might find access to your most excellent presence. I also recognized myself as a debtor to your service, although I lived in absence, and that I ought not to return empty to your most glorious and most pious presence, since the Lord says in the Law:

> “You shall not appear before me empty” (Exodus 23).

And again in the Gospel:

> “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s” (Matthew 22).

Because of your excessive humility, of which we have spoken, I ventured to offer these things to your most excellent authority, especially since we know that, insofar as human beings are concerned, you are the ruler of the whole Christian religion.

I was eager to know what the earlier authors who established our Offices had in mind. But since it is very difficult for me to affirm that I have repeatedly written what they were meditating, I have nevertheless one refuge: if what I have written should appear to your piety not to depart from the way of charity.

From Augustine’s book *On Christian Doctrine* I shall defend myself against those who may wish to criticize me, as though I had written dangerously because I did not have before me the minds of the authors of our Office. The aforesaid teacher says in the first book of that work:

> “Whoever, however, draws from Scripture a meaning that is useful for building charity, yet does not say what the person whom he reads can be shown to have intended in that place, is not dangerously deceived, nor is he lying altogether. For in the liar there is a will to say what is false.”

And shortly afterward:

> “But whoever in the Scriptures understands something other than the writer intended, while the writers themselves are not lying, is mistaken.”

Nevertheless, as I had begun to say, if the interpretation that builds charity—which is the end of the commandment—is mistaken, it is mistaken as someone would be who, having left the road through error, nevertheless proceeds across the field toward the same destination to which that road also leads. He must nevertheless be corrected, and it must be shown how much more useful it is not to leave the road, lest, through the habit of going astray, he be forced to proceed crosswise or perversely.

It should also be noted that, lest my lowliness seem to interpolate the sayings of the holy Fathers by passing them off as my own words, I inserted at the end and beginning of them the sign of the cross, +.

> For the divine Louis, life.  
> For the new David, perpetuity.  
> Give life, Lord, to the prince.  
> To the new Solomon himself, happiness.  
> You are the peace of the world.  
> Prosperity to the pious ruler.  
> Lord, grant him life.  
> May your faith preserve you.  
> May Christ, whom you honor, Himself preserve you.  
> May God preserve your authority.  
> May God bring peace to your kingdom.  
> Health for many years to Judith, the orthodox, most noble, and most prudent empress.  
> Lord, preserve the lights of peace.  
> Lord, preserve the lights of the world.  
> Your life is the protection of all.  
> Your faith is the glory of the churches.  
> May Christ preserve our most pious imperial lords, the glorious crowned-born Lothar and his brothers.  
> Lord, preserve them orthodox through their forefathers.  
> Lord, preserve the guardians of the faith.

# SECOND PREFACE

### To be placed at the beginning of this work according to the author’s judgment

[Col. 00987]

[Col. 0987C] After I had written the little book that my lowliness calls *On the Ecclesiastical Office*, I came to Rome and asked the ministers of the Church of Saint Peter how many prayers they were accustomed to celebrate before the epistle of the Mass on feast days when we celebrate two solemnities—for example, at the Nativity of the Lord, at the second Mass during the night, in which the Sacramentary contains a double Office: one for the same Nativity of the Lord and the other for Saint Anastasia—and on Sundays, when we frequently commemorate the solemnities of many saints.

They answered me: “Only one.”

Having made this inquiry, because I saw that many people performed the same order in different ways—some using three prayers, others two, according to the inclination of each person’s mind—I was not reluctant to write down what I had learned from the Romans about this matter and to place it at the beginning of the aforesaid little book for the information of my devoted readers. I also wished to repeat what I learned from the writings of Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine concerning the order of prayers in the Mass and in the other Offices, for they followed the order of the blessed Apostle Paul in his letter to Timothy. I have further added what seemed to me to accord with the reason of that order, according to the capacity of my small intellect.

Saint Ambrose counts the aforementioned prayers in the following order: prayers, supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings. He assigns prayer to the times when we ask for good things for ourselves; supplication to the times when we ask for release from evils; and petition to the struggle against all adversities. He often prescribes that we should do this when we assemble together.

Saint Augustine gives the order as follows: entreaties, prayers, intercessions—or, as your codices have it, petitions—and thanksgivings. He says:

> “The whole, or nearly the whole, Church practices these in the celebration of the sacraments.”

An entreaty is every prayer before what is enacted at the Lord’s table. A prayer is whatever is enacted afterward up to Communion. Intercession, or petition, occurs when the people are blessed. Thanksgiving concludes everything.

Where Saint Augustine says “entreaties,” our codices have “supplications.” As has been said, Saint Ambrose subordinates petition to supplication for the absolution of sins. We name the remaining parts in the same way, as was previously explained concerning Saint Augustine, and they have the same force because Saint Ambrose assigned the same function to them, both in the celebration of the sacraments and in the other Offices.

In everything that I write, I submit myself to the judgment of holy and pious men and Fathers; meanwhile, I state what I think.

What is done in the celebration of the Mass is done in the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion, as He Himself commanded, saying:

> “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me.”

Therefore, the bread, wine, and water that the priest offers in the sacrament are Christ’s bread, wine, and water, the sacrament of Christ’s flesh and blood. Sacraments ought to bear some likeness to the things of which they are sacraments. Therefore the priest should in some way be like Christ, just as the bread and liquid are like Christ’s body.

Thus the priest’s sacrifice upon the altar is in some manner like Christ’s sacrifice upon the cross. In some manner a human being is like Christ’s resurrection: he eats His flesh and drinks His blood. Christ rose from the dead and now dies no more.

Through the body of Christ that a person worthily eats, the soul, having received resurrection through baptism or penance, lives until the complete resurrection is fulfilled on the eighth day. Therefore, when a person is at the end of life, so that body and soul are separated, the soul receives the body of Christ as viaticum, so that through that body the person may live in hope until he receives at the resurrection the body that he himself was vivifying—that is, through his own administration.

As long as the soul lived here, it lived because of the body of Christ, and its own body because of the soul. Before He suffered, Christ often prayed alone and spent the night in prayer. He prayed for us, not for Himself.

The whole human race was subject to the devil. For this deliverance Christ descended from heaven and carried out the dispensation He had undertaken. Therefore the priest, standing in His likeness, prays for the absolution of sins before proceeding to the sacrifice.

Many wounds are often healed by a single remedy; likewise, it is believed that by one prayer of the priest many sins of those who obey may be absolved. Let this suffice concerning the priest’s sacrifice. Let us speak about the order of prayers, which we passed over.

This order concerning the Mass began with the Mass during the night of the Nativity of the Lord, where there are two prayers: one for the Nativity of the Lord and the other for Saint Anastasia. Where the relics of Saint Anastasia are found, or where her body is, prayers for Saint Anastasia are to be said according to Roman custom; where this is not found, prayers concerning the Lord’s Incarnation are to be said.

When there is a feast of a saint on Sunday, that prayer may suffice in which the intercession of the saint whose feast is being celebrated is asked to be present together with the priest’s prayer for the intended purpose, namely, for the commemoration of Christ’s sacrifice—especially since the prayer appointed for Sunday is accustomed to continue through the days of the following week.

It benefits many, when time is available for reading, psalmody, and the other prayers, to celebrate the sacraments separately for Sundays and separately for the feasts of the saints. The same applies on other days when a feast of several saints calls for two or three Masses.

The Sacramentary and the *Cantorius* accord with this order, for in them two Offices of saints are often found on one day. The Lord’s command also says:

> “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me.”

In the other prayers of the Mass, prayers for various needs are inscribed according to their subjects: for example, in time of war, for travelers, and for various blessings. Where common prayer without bread and liquid is not sufficient for a person, what else does the priest do than strive, in a certain manner, to remember Christ, who never forgets the blood of His great price, and, according to the greatness of that price, to ask for His greatest assistance?

If anyone wishes to attend carefully to what is prayed there, he will find it in the prayers of the Mass that follow. If a devout person wishes to intercede according to his own conscience, he has a place where he may pray for these things.

After the priest’s greeting and the reading of the Gospel, when the priest says, “Let us pray,” and then proceeds to receive the offerings, the multitude of the people may fittingly intercede for their own consciences before proceeding to give thanks in the Preface. The priest does so for his own concerns when, after receiving the offerings, he first proceeds to the altar.

The singers do so at the point where the priest places the victim on the altar and causes it, through his secret prayer, to pass into the designation of victim, gift, present, sacrifice, or offering.

If he is praying for union with the holy angels, he has in the Preface:

> “With whom we ask You to command that our voices also be admitted.”

If he is striving to intercede for peace, he has in the Canon:

> “Which we offer to You for Your holy catholic Church, that You may grant it peace.”

If he is praying for the unity of the Church, he has there:

> “To unite it.”

If he is praying for his own preservation, he has there:

> “To guard it.”

If he is praying for the direction of the steps of mind or body, he has there:

> “Deign to direct throughout the whole world.”

Here prayer has been offered for the universal Church.

If he wishes to intercede for individual friends, he has there:

> “Remember, O Lord, Your servants and handmaids.”

There he may name whomever he wishes and whatever individual needs he wishes; then he may remember those who are present and offer the present sacrifice.

If anyone wishes to cry out for his own defense, he has there:

> “Communicating with and venerating the memory of the many saints, by whose merits and prayers grant that in all things we may be defended by the help of Your protection.”

Here prayer has been offered for the priests themselves.

If he wishes to cry out for peace throughout the whole time of his life, he has there, in the words added by Saint Gregory:

> “Order our days in Your peace,”

and afterward:

> “Deliver us from eternal damnation and command us to be numbered among Your elect.”

Here prayer has been offered for eternal life.

According to the words of Saint Ambrose, in this prayer we ask for the good things necessary for us. In the prayer that the priest says after Communion, Saint Augustine says that the priest blesses the people and that the people pass to the hands of the priest.

This custom is not observed everywhere among us, unless perhaps the people’s passing to the hands of the priest means receiving from him the sacraments of the Lord’s body, which nearly the entire Roman and Eastern Church performs on all solemn days; and unless “being blessed” means the food that is eaten being blessed as the Lord’s food.

For this is sung in the Canon:

> “That as many of us as have received the most holy body and blood of Your Son through participation in this altar may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace.”

Let the diligent hearer attend to the purposes for which the prayers said by the priest after Communion resound. He will find that they resound for those who have been refreshed with heavenly bread.

According to the order of the prayers and the exposition of the Fathers mentioned above, in the first prayer of the Mass prayer was offered for the absolution of sins. At the table, however, good things are requested for us, in the manner of the prayer and evangelical hymn that Christ sang according to John when He commended His disciples to the Father before His Passion.

In the final prayer the people are blessed. What does this blessing mean? It certainly means that they are to fight against the devil and his snares. Saint Ambrose remembers the same thing in the third order, where there is petition.

According to Augustine, the fourth order of prayers concludes everything with thanksgiving—that is, when the people respond, “Thanks be to God.”

If anyone considers these matters worthy of reading, he will find them more extensively written in the following volume.

Here it should be noted that on the days of Lent, when the people assemble at the ninth hour in the church, a blessing over the people is celebrated among us, and the people humble themselves, prostrate in prayer, according to the words of Saint Augustine.

Some may think that there is a double prayer in the third order of prayers. But if this duplication is carefully considered, it will not be found to be a duplication, but rather a simplification directed toward one matter, namely, the blessing, which nevertheless is necessarily doubled because of the difference among the people.

Not the entire multitude that assembles in the church attends the sacrifice on successive days, as those do who assemble on solemn days. Those who do not communicate, so that they may not be excluded from the blessing, receive the priest’s blessing, which does not touch the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood. Those who do communicate are blessed by the Communion itself, and prayer is offered for them in the earlier prayer after Communion, that they may be suitably united to so great a sacrament.

These are the things that I received from the Roman See concerning what I wish to insert here, although they have already been explained more fully in the following volume.

The first greeting to the people is pronounced:

> “Peace to you,”

not:

> “Peace be with you.”

When the verse of the Alleluia is sung, the deacon removes his chasuble and draws the stole behind his back, beneath the right arm, together with the chasuble. He prepares himself to minister and remains in that vesture until the Pope has departed from the altar.

After the Gospel they do not offer incense over the altar. The chalice, wrapped in a cloth, is brought to the altar, and the cloth is placed at the corner of the altar. The chalice is placed on the altar beside the offering, not behind it.

The litanies are celebrated at the vigils of Easter as our custom formerly prescribed: that is, according to the numbers seven, five, and three.

# CONTENTS OF THE SUBJECT OF THE WRITING THAT FOLLOWS

[Col. 0991]

[Col. 0991C] Here Saint Augustine, explaining that Gospel saying, “Therefore, whatever you wish that people should do for you, do likewise for them,” separates will from desire: he places will in the good, and desire in evil. For it is not fitting that whatever an evil person wishes to be done to himself he should, on the authority of the Gospel passage before us, freely perpetrate against another. For example, if I, as a glutton, wish to become drunk or to be excessively filled by someone else, I ought not therefore to do that freely to others; rather, whatever good I wish for myself, I ought diligently to pursue for others.

The will is, as it were, a kind of stock given to the mind by the Lord; attached to it, as though they were branches, are the appetites. To these is joined the object created by the author of all things, in which the will is to accomplish something; and if reason is present, error will be absent. Reason [Col. 0991D] directs the rays of the appetites toward the true sun of the Lord, so that by his light it may clearly and truthfully know what, or of what kind, the thing it desires is. Hence the one quoted above says: “For no one desires what he entirely does not know to be something or of some kind.”

To those who possess clear light and sound eyes, an exceedingly subtle and excellent object is presented; to those whose sight is darkened by some blemish of sins, a coarser and more obvious object is presented by God, the most equitable governor. Hence the Apostle says: “To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common benefit.”

The stomach receives various foods, from which belching usually rises upward; similarly, there is a kind of belly of the mind that receives thoughts. If these lack an object, they have nothing from which to produce a belch. To me, a sinner, a coarse subject has been given, more for investigation than for exposition: namely, the office contained in the Sacramentary and the Antiphonary, which is known to almost all country people. I shall act confidently before God, who wills that each person should devoutly minister in the gifts entrusted to him for an eternal reward. The humble person, thinking humbly of himself, awaits the reward of humility. Whoever receives gold, silver, and other great gifts in the house of God does not despise goats’ hair.

[Col. 0992D] I possess an ardor for a well-worn and obsolete path, worn away through antiquity, so that I may know what the aforementioned subject contains in its marrow: that is, what was in the heart of the first composers of our office, and what fruit it produces. Thus my first inquiry concerns Septuagesima, whose end falls in the first month.

# BOOK ONE.

[Col. 0993]

## CHAPTER ONE. On Septuagesima.

[Col. 0993A]

Septuagesima is reckoned, according to the headings of the Sacramentary and Antiphonary, nine weeks before the Lord’s Pasch, and ends after the Lord’s Pasch on the seventh day of the week. It begins on Sunday and ends on Saturday.

It signifies the period of captivity of the people of God, who departed from God by sinning and, through his mercy, return to rest. The people of God were held captive in Babylonia under the number seventy; when that number was completed, they returned to Jerusalem. Concerning this people Jeremiah says: “Consider and seek in her streets whether you can find a man practicing justice and seeking faith, and I shall be merciful to him. But even if they say, ‘As the Lord lives,’ they will swear falsely. Lord, are not your eyes directed toward faith?”

And again: “They hardened their faces more than a rock and were unwilling to return. But I said: Perhaps they are poor and foolish, not knowing the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God. I shall therefore go to the great and speak to them. For they have known the way of the Lord, the judgment of their God; and behold, these have broken the yoke altogether and burst the bonds.”

And again: “Every brother will utterly supplant, and every friend will walk deceitfully; a man will mock his brother and will not speak the truth,” and so forth. Shortly afterward: “Shall I not visit these things, says the Lord?”

And again: “Cast them out from my presence, and let them depart. And if they say to you, ‘Where shall we go?’ you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Those destined for death—to death; those for the sword—to the sword; those for famine—to famine; and those for captivity—to captivity.”

And Isaiah says: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they burn with wine. Harp, lyre, tambourine, flute, and wine are in your banquets, but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands. Therefore my people have been led away captive.”

How long they were to remain in captivity Jeremiah makes clear, saying: “I shall remove from them the voice of joy and gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, the sound of the millstone and the light of the lamp; and all its land shall become a desolation and a horror, and all these nations shall serve the king of Babylon for seventy years. And when the seventy years have been completed, I shall visit the king of Babylon,” and so forth.

+ Perhaps the composer of Septuagesima, knowing by the grace of Christ that our sins have been forgiven, changed the seventy years into seventy days—because in certain crimes we share in the guilt of the earlier people—so that what they unwillingly endured because they were slaves, we might willingly endure for our sins because we are free, and might cease along with them from “the voice of joy and gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride,” and so forth.

And Zechariah says: “On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month of Sabbath, in the second year of Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah, son of Barachiah, son of Addo, the prophet.” Jerome, in his commentary on Zechariah, says: “The eleventh month, which is called Sabbath and in our language is rendered ‘rod,’ signifies austerity and correction; it is in the harshest season of winter, which the Romans call February—the season usually touched by Septuagesima.”

After some intervening material he continues: “The angel of the Lord said: ‘Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry?’ This is the seventieth year.” And the Lord answered the angel who was speaking to him with good words and words of consolation.

The same author, in the same work: “But since he asks for complete mercy, so that, when the seventieth year is at hand, God may have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, the teachers of the churches refer this to the understanding that, until true peace comes, and the sabbath-rest and the number of seven decades—that is, the seventieth year—are fulfilled, Jerusalem will not receive complete freedom, that is, the Church, nor the cities of Judah, that is, the soul confessing the Lord.

“Finally, the Lord answered with good words and words of consolation, which we now see in part and prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect has come, the things that are partial will be destroyed, so that, liberated from the Babylon of this age, we may cry out: ‘When the Lord turned back the captivity of Zion, we became like those who are comforted.’”

The day of Pasch gives good words and words of consolation; it raises us toward good works, for on it we are justified.

But perfect rest and liberation are given in the sabbath-rest [Col. 0994C], when the souls of the saints receive eternal rest. John calls Babylon the city of the devil in the Apocalypse: “Babylon the great has fallen, has fallen,” he says.

Bede, in the second book of his commentary on the Apocalypse: “The proud are then cast down by the Lord when they are inflated by the devil, as the psalm says: ‘You cast them down when they were raised up.’”

The number seventy recalls to our memory the entire duration of the present age, during which we are strangers to the heavenly Jerusalem. Therefore the author of our office placed Septuagesima in our offices, so that during that period, by abstaining from the delights of this world, we might show in our conduct how those who, after baptism, estrange themselves from the heavenly Jerusalem through sins ought to live throughout the duration of this age.

Let us spend seventy days as captives in exile, so that the mourning of penitence may be turned into joy at the Lord’s resurrection, through which we return to Jerusalem. Yet let us do so in such a way that during the six succeeding days we are not bound by any desire for the Babylonian city, but travel the road, so that when the seventh day comes we may enter the heavenly Jerusalem.

Let the catechumens, who are bound by original sin, be washed with the water of baptism at the resurrection, and let us be washed by penitence. Let both they and we persevere in the resurrection until the complete Septuagesima, that is, so that we may not die in sins.

Although Cyrus, king of the Persians, surnamed “Christ,” in the first year of his reign released the greater part—almost fifty thousand persons—of the Jewish people’s captivity from Babylonia, nevertheless the seventieth year extends to the second year of Darius, as Eusebius maintains, adducing Zechariah the prophet as a witness. In the second year of Darius the angel says: “Lord of hosts, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry? This is the seventieth year.”

Concerning these seventy years Augustine says in the third book of *On Christian Doctrine*: “The seventy years of the prophet Jeremiah can also be understood spiritually as the whole period during which the Church is among strangers.”

And again, in the twelfth book *Against Faustus* [Col. 0995B]: “For the fact that, after seventy years, according to the prophecy of that same Jeremiah, there is a return from captivity and the Temple is rebuilt—what faithful Christian does not understand that, after the periods have elapsed which pass by through the repetition of the number seven of the days, we too, that is, the Church of God, must return from the pilgrimage of this age to that heavenly Jerusalem? And through whom, except Jesus Christ, the true great priest, whose figure was borne by that Jesus, the great priest of that time, when the Temple was built after the captivity?

“For the present number, from Septuagesima to Pasch, also intimates the Lord’s affliction and a certain abstinence. There are sixty days from Septuagesima to the Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper; by this number the widows who are in great tribulation are signified. This tribulation and affliction is shown by the reckoning on the fingers, which expresses the aforementioned number when the index finger is placed over the thumb.

“The three days that remain until the Lord’s resurrection signify the three-day fast which, according to the Seventy interpreters, the people of Nineveh undertook. In order that our sins, for which we are afflicted, may be abolished in the glorification of the Lord’s resurrection, it is necessary for us to suffer with Christ’s death for three days. After we have already been regenerated in soul through penitence or baptism in Christ’s resurrection, we ought to rejoice together until the rest that is granted after this life on the sabbath.

“The sixty days recall to us our widowhood, during which we are pilgrims away from the Lord. The remaining three days signify the mortification of our pleasure, so that we may not be entangled in the nets of this world, which usually ensnare us through the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life.

“But during the six days that remain until the sabbath, good works are recalled, which we ought to perform so that our house may not be empty on the sabbath—that is, in rest, when we are restored to perfect freedom.”

Jeremiah showed above that the Lord wishes us to cease from the voice of joy as long as we remain in Babylon, saying: “And I shall cause the voice of joy and gladness to cease among you.” Therefore Alleluia is not sung among us during that period, nor the sweetest hymn of the angels, *Glory to God in the highest*; instead of Alleluia there is the Tract, so called from *trahere*, “to draw,” which the Apostle Paul indicated when he said, “with patience and gentleness.” The Tract is drawn out, and it is sweet to the ears.

Alleluia is more excellent because of the honor and breadth of the first language. Jerome, in the eleventh book of his commentary on Isaiah, says: “Compared with the Hebrew language, both Greek and Latin speech are poor.” During the aforementioned days we frequently use the poor language: “Praise to you, Lord, King of eternal glory.”

The psalm says: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” Alleluia and *Glory in the highest* are heavenly songs. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “After this I heard something like the loud voice of a great multitude in heaven saying, ‘Alleluia.’”

There is no doubt that *Glory to God in the highest* is the song of the angels. For we ought, sitting—that is, humbled—beside the rivers of Babylon, to weep while we remember Zion.

There are some who spend the first week of Septuagesima without any element of the new observance, except for the change in Alleluia, the omission of the dalmatics in certain places, and the discontinuation of *Glory to God in the highest*. Whether this is observed everywhere, or whether it is still so, as I once saw it, I do not know.

During the seventy years of captivity, which we change into seventy days, there was fasting among the Jews. Hence the Lord says through Zechariah: “When you fasted and mourned for seventy years, did you indeed fast for me?” The Greeks sanctify the following week with their fast.

But our clergy also observe their own fast, under the authority of Pope Telesphorus, who established a fast of seven weeks before Pasch. Yet the teacher of our office demands a more extensive change, and he knows Augustine’s statement in the book of *Evangelical Questions*: “Fasting is either in tribulation or in joy: in tribulation, to render the Lord propitious for sins; in joy, when bodily things delight us less in proportion as the arrow of spiritual things is greater.”

In establishing his office, he indicated the fast itself, which was mentioned earlier, in the first prayer of the Mass, saying: “that we who are justly afflicted for our sins…”

Here the word signifies affliction. In the Introit he says: “The groans of death surrounded me; the pains of hell surrounded me.”

Augustine, in his commentary on the Psalms: “Among those who surrounded me in order to destroy me were the pains of envy, which bring about death and lead to the hell of sin. Because of these pains we cannot rejoice and be secure; rather, we ought to prepare ourselves for battle, as the Apostle says: ‘Everyone who contends in the contest abstains from everything.’”

Ambrose says: “From all those things which the same discipline teaches must be avoided, since they know that one is to be crowned. How much more ought we to observe this, since salvation has been promised to all? This discipline is known to soldiers. Some of the many things belonging to the abstinence of our warfare must be set before us.”

[Col. 0997A] The Apostle says to the Ephesians: “Fornication, and every impurity or greed, must not even be named among you, as is fitting for saints.”

Our struggle is against these vices, as the same Apostle says: “Our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers,” and so forth. Vices are overcome in these matters. He prepares himself well against them who so abhors them and drives them from his fellowship that they are not even named among his own people.

The battle is future; let us abstain from those things that hinder our fighting. Then follow obscenity, foolish talk, and buffoonery, which have no bearing on the matter; rather, there should be thanksgiving. These things do not belong to the undertaking of the Jerusalem-bound journey; they resist it. Therefore let us abstain from them.

Concerning obscenity Jerome says that, among other things, it signifies a hidden thought, when our mind is inflamed toward lust and the soul, stirred by the ticklings of the flesh, is set ablaze, yet is restrained by the fear of God and the judgment of the mind.

And again, concerning foolish talk and buffoonery: “Foolish talk contains nothing wise in itself or worthy of the human heart. Buffoonery, however, descends from a prudent mind and, without consideration, seeks certain words—polished, rustic, obscene, or witty—which we may call by another word ‘jocularity,’ so that it may provoke laughter in those who hear it. Yet these things too must be utterly driven away by holy men, for whom it is more fitting to weep and mourn, as we also read in the Hebrew Gospel that the Lord said to his disciples:

“‘Never,’ he said, ‘be joyful except when you see your brother in love.’”

Hence John Chrysostom, in his fourteenth homily on the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Have you not heard Paul say: ‘Obscenity, empty talk, and buffoonery must be removed from you’? When he has mentioned obscenity and buffoonery, do you laugh? When he has mentioned empty talk, which has no usefulness, do you laugh altogether and relax your face? You who profess to be a monk, you who have been crucified, you who ought to mourn—do you laugh? Tell me, where did Christ do this? Did you hear of it anywhere? Certainly nowhere; rather, you have often read that he was saddened.”

And after some intervening material: “Let us mourn, therefore, beloved; let us mourn, so that we may truly laugh more sincerely in the time of joy.”

Thus it seems to us that the teacher of our office wishes the time of Septuagesima to be a time of mourning, and for that reason he said: “The groans of death surrounded me,” and again: “A helper in times of opportunity, in tribulation.”

Augustine, on Psalm 9: “The soul is not turned toward the Lord unless it is turned away from this age. Nor is it turned away from this age at a more opportune time than when labors and pains are mingled with its trifling, harmful, and destructive pleasures. Where there are labor and pain, there at least is fasting from friendship with this world; where there is fasting, there is humility of mind; where there is a seventyfold fast, there is compassion for captives. ‘If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.’”

## CHAPTER II. On Sexagesima.

[Col. 0998A]

In Sexagesima we are surrounded by the greatest tribulations, as though there were no way to escape. We have sold ourselves under sin; within us there is no power of release. Hence it is said in the first prayer of Sexagesima: “O God, who see that we subsist by none of our own strength…”

We desire rather than presume that our true Lord may intervene to release us. For a similar reason Joel says: “Who knows whether he may turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?”

Jerome explains this in his commentary on Joel: “I exhort, for my part, to penitence, and I know that the Lord is ineffably merciful.” And shortly afterward: “But because we cannot know the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, I moderate my judgment; and I desire rather than presume when I say: ‘Who knows whether he may turn and forgive?’ What he says—‘who knows’—must be understood as either impossible or difficult.”

Sins separate God and humanity. Why, then, do we doubt in Sexagesima whether the Lord is with us? For this reason we say in the Introit: “Arise; why do you sleep, Lord? Arise, and do not reject us forever. Why do you turn your face away? Do you forget our poverty and tribulation? For our soul has been humbled in the dust.”

Hence Augustine, on Psalm 43: “Among the hands of this dust, among the hands of the wicked and persecutors, our soul has been humbled so that we might call upon you and you might give help in tribulation. ‘Our belly has clung to the earth,’ that is, it has consented to the impiety of this dust.”

And again: “Arise, Lord, help us and redeem us for your name’s sake”—that is, freely, for your name’s sake, not because of my merit: because you are worthy to do it, not because I am worthy that you should do it for me.

In the Epistle there is a good athlete who encourages us to seek a way of escaping captivity and to despise the masters who hold us for destruction. Indignantly he speaks against those who yield to evils: “You gladly tolerate fools. For you tolerate it if someone brings you into slavery, if someone devours you, if someone takes from you,” and so forth.

As obedient captives, we take the next step: that is, we climb out of tribulation to seek our own true Lord. “Let the nations know,” we say, “that your name is Lord.”

Hence Augustine: “Let them know,” he says, “that your name is Lord—as though those others who are called lords were not truly named by that name, nor by their own proper name, because they rule in a servile manner; and compared with the true Lord, they are not lords.”

The Tract, “You have shaken, Lord,” shows the earth shaken by the conscience of sins. After the earth has been shaken, seed is introduced. In Septuagesima we were rebuked because we stood idle; we were led to cultivate forgiveness. In this Sexagesima we sow the seed.

Sexagesima runs within Septuagesima until the Wednesday of Paschal Week. This Wednesday corresponds to the fourth age of the world, in which David and Solomon reigned.

In the fourth age that heavenly people, renowned for faith and glorious through the kingdom of David and Solomon and through the height of the most holy Temple, ennobled the whole world. On our Wednesday, however, David triumphs, he who conquered the lion; the eternal, peace-bringing Solomon reigns, of whom the Apostle says: “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies; death shall no longer rule over him.”

He builds a most noble Temple for God the Father, who at the end will say: “Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the beginning of the world.”

We ought to run toward that kingdom through Sexagesima. For the number six, when reckoned through its parts, is the first perfect number: the sixth is one, the third two, the midpoint three; for one, two, and three make six. This number demonstrates perfection.

Bede, in his book *On Times*: “Here it must be noted that the number six is not perfect because the Lord completed the works of the world in it; rather, as Augustine says, the Lord, who was able to create all things simultaneously, chose to work in that number because the number itself is perfect.”

Six multiplied by ten makes sixty. Ten refers to the reward of works. If anyone seeks the reward of works through six—that is, through perfection—he will receive the kingdom that is promised to us on the Wednesday of Paschal Week.

## CHAPTER III. On Quinquagesima.

Quinquagesima stands at the third stage. Earlier we doubted whether our true Lord was with us or not. Now we hold fast to him and say: “Be for me a protecting God and a place of refuge, so that you may save me.”

We pray to Jesus as the leader of our warfare, saying: “And for your name’s sake you will be my leader, and you will nourish me.”

We are already on campaign. The most learned athlete has arrived; according to his customary manner, he exhorts us and teaches us with what defenses we ought to fortify ourselves, saying: “Now faith, hope, and charity remain—these three.”

Concerning these he says in another Epistle: “In all things take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one; and take up the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.”

God is the victor of our warfare, to whom it is said: “You are God who works wonders.” And again: “By your arm you have redeemed your people.”

The Tract commands us to serve the Lord who made us, not the one to whom we sold ourselves.

In Sexagesima we sowed; in Quinquagesima we gather the fruit. What did the blind man, who prefigures us, ask from the Lord? Nothing other than to enjoy light. He sought fruit and found fruit.

This Quinquagesima, according to its day, touches the first day of venerable Pasch. For just as the number six demonstrates the perfection of works, so the number fifty signifies all good works, which are completed through the five senses of the body. Five times ten makes fifty.

Whoever, through outward observance, fulfills the ten words of the Law in the Holy Spirit does not doubt that he will attain fellowship in the blessed resurrection celebrated at the Lord’s Pasch. Through the sabbath we come to the Lord’s Day; likewise, by fulfilling the Law through the sevenfold Spirit, we come to the resurrection.

These are the three stages of the three offices that we have set out up to this point. The first contains the mourning of captives who do not wish to remain under the masters of vices. The second shows the desire for flight, provided that the Lord in his mercy wishes to receive them and not reject them from himself. The third gives counsel about how to flee; already presuming acceptance, it gains good counsel according to the words of the Introit: “Be for me a protecting God.”
