If anyone wishes to say, whether in silent or spoken discourse, that the other elements contained in the aforementioned office are not to be fitted into these stages in the same way as the excerpts, I shall fly to a certain tree—Augustine—and sit in its branches. Perhaps its density will protect me from rapacious hawks.

He writes in the sixteenth book of *The City of God*: “Certainly not everything that is narrated as having happened should be thought to signify something; but, on account of those things that signify something, even things that signify nothing are joined to them.

“For the earth is not cut only by the plowshare; rather, for this to be possible, the other parts of the plow are also necessary. Nor are only the strings of harps and similar musical instruments fitted for song; rather, so that they can be fitted, there are also the other parts in the joints of the instruments, which are not struck by those who play, but to which the things that resound when struck are attached.

“Likewise, in prophetic history some things are mentioned that signify nothing, but to which the things that do signify are attached, and by which they are bound together.”

We have spoken of three stages of those striving toward battle. In a similar way we speak of three stages of triumph: the first day of the week, the fourth, and the seventh.

Since we have said that our Septuagesima depends upon the seventy years of the earlier people’s captivity in Babylonia, it is good for us to consider those same stages by which that people reached complete freedom.

The first return took place under Zerubbabel as leader and Joshua as great priest, with fifty thousand people, as we have already recorded. Here it must be noted that in the book of Ezra it is written: “The whole multitude was as one man.”

Hence Bede, in his exposition of that book: “Note the grace of the primitive Church, in which the heart and soul of the multitude of believers were one, also to be found in this assembly of those migrating. Thus, although the army was so large that it nearly reached a total of fifty thousand, and although it consisted of different ranks and conditions, nevertheless the whole multitude, because of the same faith and love, appeared to be like one man, through the gift of him who makes those of one mind dwell in a house.”

The second return took place under Ezra, as the same author records: “Therefore we set out from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month, to go to Jerusalem; and the hand of our God was over us, and he delivered us from the hand of the enemy and the ambusher on the way. And we came to Jerusalem and stayed there for three days. On the fourth day the silver and gold were weighed,” and so forth.

But the walls of Jerusalem had not yet been rebuilt. Hence it is also read in what follows: “And it came to pass in the month of Casleu, in the twentieth year, that I, Nehemiah, was in the fortress of Susa. And Hanani, one of my brothers, came, he and men from Judah; and I asked them about the Jews who had remained and survived the captivity, and about Jerusalem. They said to me: Those who remained and were left behind from the captivity there in the province are in great affliction and reproach; the wall of Jerusalem is destroyed and its gates have been burned with fire.”

The third return took place under the same man. For it is written: “The king had sent commanders of the army and cavalry, and Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah, the Ammonite servant, heard of it and were greatly grieved that a man had come seeking the prosperity of the children of Israel. And I came to Jerusalem, and I was there for three days.”

This Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem. We have mentioned these things beforehand in order to fit our own circumstances to those of the earlier people of God. Here let us pass over the Wednesday, when we entered into battle, since it must be treated in another period. We follow the Sundays.

## CHAPTER IV. On Quadragesima.

In Quadragesima part of the battle has been completed. The one whom we invoked as protector in Quinquagesima says to us: “He called upon me, and I shall answer him,” and so forth.

The Epistle says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” And in the Responsory: “The angels of the Lord guard us.” In the Tract: “We are surrounded by the shield of truth.”

In the Gospel we advance toward triumph, so that we may say to the enemy: “Go, Satan, into destruction.”

In the genealogy of the human Christ, in whom triumph rejoices, Matthew sanctifies the present number of Quadragesima, writing that Christ descended to earth through a series of forty generations. Hence Augustine, in the second book of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*: “It has been perceptively observed that Matthew, who undertook to present Christ’s royal character, named forty men in the series of generations, excluding Christ himself.”

The number itself signifies the period during which, in this age and in this life, we ought to be ruled by Christ according to the laborious discipline by which God scourges every son whom he receives, as it is written. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Through tribulation we must enter the kingdom of God.”

Therefore this number reveals the mystery of this laborious period, during which, under the discipline of Christ the King, we fight against the devil. It also shows that the fast of forty days—that is, the humbling of the soul—was consecrated by both the Law and the Prophets, through Moses and Elijah, who fasted for forty days, and by the Gospel, through the Lord’s own fast.

During those forty days he was also tempted by the devil. What else did he prefigure by this except our temptation throughout the whole duration of this age, in his flesh, which he chose to assume from our mortality?

This number forty, which begins on the Sunday following Quinquagesima, ends on the Thursday before the Lord’s Pasch, which is called the Lord’s Supper. We shall write about the variation of the day of the Lord’s Supper, if the Lord grants it, in the aforementioned period.

Here it is enough to mention that, from the Sunday mentioned above, two days remain after the forty, up to the baptism, and they make forty-two. For there were that many stations of the children of Israel, who were baptized in the Red Sea when they came out of the land of Egypt, from harsh slavery, and reached the promised land.

There are also that many generations in Christ’s genealogy, with Jeconiah counted twice and Christ himself included. It is fitting that those who hasten toward the heavenly homeland should make their stations by the same number by which the children of Israel came to the promised land.

And it is fitting that those who pass over to Christ through baptism should reach him by the same number through which Christ chose to come to us. As Jerome says in his book *On the Stations of the Children of Israel*: “Nor is it surprising if, through the mystery of that number, we reach the kingdoms of heaven, under which the Lord and Savior came from the first patriarch to the Virgin, as to the Jordan, which flowed with a full current and overflowed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit.”

## CHAPTER V. Why the Number Forty Is Applied to Temporal Life.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] Augustine, *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*.]

Why this number signifies this temporal and earthly life is, for the moment, immediately apparent from the following reason, although there may perhaps be another, more hidden reason: the seasons of the years run in fourfold cycles, and this world is bounded by four regions. Forty contains four times ten. Moreover, ten itself is completed by the number progressing from one to four.

And again, in his letter to Januarius: “I think that this life is represented by the number forty because the number ten, in which the perfection of our blessedness consists, just as in the number eight, which returns to one, so in this [number] the creature, which is represented by seven, cleaves to the Creator.”

## CHAPTER VI. Why the Observance of Quadragesima Was Established at Such a Time.

[Note: [Col. 1002D] Augustine, same work.]

In what part of the year, then, could the observance of Quadragesima have been established more suitably than in a season bordering upon and contiguous with the Lord’s Passion? For in it this laborious life is signified, and to it this practice is appropriate: that one should fast from friendship with the world, which, with its deceptions, never ceases to flatter and to scatter and cast about the juices of its enticements.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Variations of the Offices Throughout the Day, Up to the Lord’s Resurrection.

On the Wednesday between Quinquagesima and Quadragesima we begin the fast that extends to the Lord’s Pascha. Until this day we have been on campaign; today we engage in battle. The first collect of the Mass makes this clear, saying: “Grant us, Lord, to begin the defenses of Christian warfare with holy fasts.” On this same day there is no other variation, except that until this day we have celebrated Mass at the third hour, as also on Sunday; on this day, at the ninth hour—and thereafter the time was changed.

Joel shows with what weapons we ought to fight, saying: “In fasting and weeping and mourning”; and: “Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room.” The Gospel likewise says: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face,” and so forth.

Some hold that the Lenten fast begins on this day for the reason that, apart from the six Sundays within Lent, there are only forty days from the Wednesday just mentioned up to Holy Saturday. It occurs to us, however, that Saint Gregory indicates only thirty-six days of abstinence for the Lenten season—perhaps because the four days from the Wednesday mentioned above to the Sunday of Lent had not yet been added.

[Note: The material enclosed in brackets was found in only one copy.]

Thus, in order that the total of forty days might be completed, four days of the preceding week are added to those forty-six days. The authority of the holy Fathers and reason itself commend that these days be kept with equal devotion and the same abstinence—that is, by observance of the fast. Hence the Wednesday on which we begin this fast has customarily been called the head of the fast.

There is also another explanation, which does not depart from the truth for anyone who clearly sees that the head and the members joined together constitute one body. From the Wednesday mentioned above to Holy Saturday there are forty-six days. The Temple in Jerusalem was built over the same number of years. Hence Bede, in his exposition of Ezra, says:

“The building of the Temple began in the first year of King Cyrus and was completed in the sixth year of Darius. According to the authority of the chronicles, these amount to forty-five years. Cyrus reigned for thirty years; after him his son Cambyses reigned for eight years. In this volume, as Josephus maintains, he is called Artaxerxes. After him came the Magi who killed him, for one year; after them Darius, for six years, until the Temple was completed and built. These, as we have said, amount to forty-five years.”

The question arises how, when the Lord said to the Jews under the figure of the Temple, referring to his passion and resurrection, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up,” they answered, “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?”—when no more than forty-five years are found between the first year of King Cyrus and the sixth year of King Darius.

But if we read Josephus’s history, in which he adds three further years after the completion and construction of the Temple, we shall see that during these years the *peribolos*—that is, the construction of the fortifications surrounding the Temple—and certain other unfinished works were completed. Thus the total of forty-six years can rightly be reckoned for the building of the Temple, during which its more prominent structures were completed.

This Temple signifies the Lord’s body. Augustine, in his treatise on John, Book Ten, says:

“We are about to celebrate with annual solemnity the destruction and rebuilding of that Temple itself. We exhort you to prepare yourselves for it, if any of you are catechumens, so that you may receive grace.”

Now is the time; let what is then to be born be brought to birth. We know that much. But perhaps what is required of us is to determine whether the Temple’s having been built in forty-six years contains some sacramental meaning. There are certainly many things that could be said about this; but for now we shall say what can be said briefly and understood easily.

Brothers, unless I am mistaken, we said yesterday that Adam was one man and that he himself is the whole human race. For, if you remember, we said that he was as though broken apart and scattered, then gathered together and fused into one spiritual society and harmony; and that one poor man, Adam himself, groans. But he is renewed in Christ, because Christ came without sin—Adam in order to undo Adam’s sin in his own flesh, and to restore to himself the image of God.

Adam, therefore, is Christ’s flesh. Thus the Temple, which the Jews destroyed and the Lord raised up in three days, is from Adam: for he raised up his own flesh. And shortly afterward Augustine says:

“What, then, does the number forty-six signify? For the moment, consider Adam himself, since he is spread throughout the whole world. Yesterday you heard about four Greek letters, the initials of Greek words. If you write these four words one beneath another—that is, the names of the four regions of the world, East, West, North, and South, which together constitute the whole world, from which the Lord says that he will gather his elect when he comes for judgment—if, then, you write these four names:

Ἀνατολή, which is East; Δύσις, which is West; Ἄρκτος, which is North; Μεσημβρία, which is South.

The initial letters of the words Ἀνατολή, Δύσις, Ἄρκτος, Μεσημβρία spell Adam. How, then, do we find there both the number forty and the number six? Because Christ’s flesh was from Adam.

“And again, observe what numerical value these letters have, and there you will find the Temple built in forty-six years. Adam has alpha, which is one: he also has delta, which is four—you have five. He has alpha again, which is one—you have six. He also has mu, which is forty—you have forty-six.”

How we ought to be joined to the body of Christ, which he assumed, he shows in what follows: “Let us,” he says, “always be humble in heart, and let our joy be in him.”

+ Whoever acts in this way, as the singers admonish us on the Wednesday just mentioned, is humble in heart. They say: “Let us change our clothing for ashes and sackcloth; let us fast and weep before the Lord.”

The composer of our office wishes this to be enacted among us in accordance with his admonition. If someone entered the school of Christian discipline on Wednesday, it is not good for him to leave it except after victory. Since we entered when we celebrated the customary offices, it is good that we should triumph with our Head on the day of the resurrection.

Before Saint Augustine discussed the number just mentioned, he urged the catechumens to prepare themselves for the Paschal solemnity. The apostle Peter shows how they ought to prepare, saying: “Repent, and let each of you be baptized in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, for the forgiveness of all your sins.”

The second Adam therefore came so that, through repentance and baptism, the first Adam, who is in the four regions of the world, might be restored to his image. Since Adam was scattered throughout the four regions of the world, let us return by that number to the Adam who gathers him together, whom the whole world contains in his initial letters.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the second variation of the fourth week of Lent

The second variation occurs in the fourth week of Lent, on Wednesday. First, we shall explain what the variation is; then why it occurs; and finally, if the Lord grants it, why it occurs on the Wednesday of the fourth week.

The variation consists in the addition of one reading and one responsory. The first reading is from the prophet Ezekiel: “I will sanctify my great name.” Greek: “Come, children.” The second reading is from the prophet Isaiah: “Thus says the Lord God: Wash yourselves; be clean.” Greek: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord.”

With the Lord’s mercy, we shall set forth the reason. The Wednesday mentioned is called by the ministers of the Church the day of the opening of the ears. On that same day the third scrutiny is conducted, the greatest of the seven scrutinies. On that day the ears and nostrils of the catechumens are touched with the fingers of the priests. On that day they are instructed concerning the authors and beginnings of the four Gospels. On that day they receive the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, to be rendered back on Holy Saturday of Easter.

Hence Augustine, in his book *On Faith and Works*, says:

“Why, then, do we hand over the Creed to those who are to be baptized and demand that they render it back? Nothing of this kind was done with those whom God delivered from the Egyptians through the Red Sea. But if they rightly understand that the preceding mysteries signify this through the blood of the lamb smeared on the doorposts and through the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, why do they not likewise understand that the separation from the Egyptians signifies the departure from sins, which those who are to be baptized profess?”

We may rightly understand the scrutiny as the journey toward baptism. The scrutiny has its own arrangement and its own Mass. Something must now be said about the Mass that we call public. In it a commemoration is celebrated of what takes place in the scrutiny.

Two offices are performed there: the catechumen is instructed in faith and morals. Hence the same author, in the book mentioned above, says:

“Let those who are to be baptized hear not only what they ought to believe, but also how they ought to free themselves from this wicked age. For they must hear how believers ought to live.”

And again:

“There is no doubt that Philip preached the Lord to the eunuch, and that in his catechesis those things were also said which pertain to the life and morals of one who believes in the Lord Jesus. For to evangelize Christ means not only to say what must be believed about Christ, but also what must be observed by one who approaches the joining of the body of Christ.”

In the first reading, which is taken from Ezekiel, it is shown how God gathers the catechumens into the joining of Christ’s body. He rescues them from their former life and makes them believe in Christ. For it is written there:

“I will take you from among the nations, and gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land. I will pour clean water over you, and you shall be cleansed from all your iniquities; and from all your idols I will cleanse you. I will give you a new heart,” and so forth.

Jerome renders the same passage in his commentary on Ezekiel as follows:

“For I am the Creator of all; I took possession of them and sanctified them, and restored them to their former glory, so that over those who believed and turned away from error I might pour the clean water of saving baptism, cleanse them from their abominations and from all the errors by which they had been occupied, and give them my heart, so that they might believe in the Son of God.”

The same matter will be found by anyone who seeks it in the responsory: “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord.” The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord. Whoever first plants the root of faith must know how to fear the Lord. Hence it is written again: “My son, when you approach the service of the Lord, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation.”

In the second reading he discusses morals at length. He says: “Cease to act perversely; learn to do good; seek judgment; assist the oppressed.” And in conclusion: “Come and accuse me, says the Lord”—that is, if you do these things and I do not repay you with a reward, you will rightly accuse me.

The following responsory shows the catechumens passing over to the Name, saying: “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he chose as his inheritance.” The verse shows the good morals of the elect: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.”

It is fitting that those who have offered themselves voluntarily to God after instruction in faith and morals should pass over to his Name and be fortified by his strength, whose inheritance possesses them. As I understand it, it has been demonstrated that two readings are read on the same day because of the faith and morals in which the catechumens are to be instructed.

The Gospel, too, is not at variance with this office. Augustine, in his commentary on John, says:

“He therefore washed his eyes in the pool that is interpreted as ‘Sent’; he was baptized in Christ. If, when he baptized him in himself in a certain sense, he then enlightened him, when he anointed him he perhaps made him a catechumen.”

Now, as we promised, we must explain why this office is performed on the Wednesday of the fourth week of Lent. The number forty signifies the whole span of the world’s time, as was demonstrated above from Saint Augustine’s book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*: the six days of the beginning signify the six ages of the world, and the six ages of one human being.

For now, we must speak only of the fourth. The Wednesday and the fourth week of Lent correspond to the fourth age of the world and to the fourth period of a human being’s life. The fourth age extends from David, as Bede says in his chronicle, to the Babylonian captivity. And elsewhere he says that from this age, as if from youth, the period of kings began among the people of God. For among human beings this age is ordinarily suited to governing a kingdom.

Again, in the same work:

“The fourth age of the world begins not only with the establishment of the rule of the Jewish people, but also with the renewed promise once given to the Fathers; it takes its beginning from the Christian kingdom, when the Lord swore truth to David, that from the fruit of his womb one would sit upon his throne.”

It is not without reason that on the same day and in the same week the catechumens approach the Christian Name. This was prefigured by the fourth age of a human being, namely youth, which is suited to the reins of government, and by the same age of the world, which was renewed through the promise of Christ’s kingdom.

Concerning this kingdom the archangel Gabriel says to Mary:

“He will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High; and the Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever.”

Bede, in his commentary on Luke, says:

“The Lord received the throne, or kingdom, of David so that he himself, the Mediator of God and human beings, might call to the heavenly and immortal kingdom, by deeds, words, gifts, and promises worthy of him, the nation to which David once provided both the governance of a temporal kingdom and examples of righteousness, and which he used to kindle by the melodies of spiritual hymns to faith in and love for its Creator; and so that he might lead it into the very vision of God the Father.”

## CHAPTER IX. On the third variation of the Saturday before Palm Sunday

The third variation occurs on the Saturday before Palm Sunday. This is its variation: in our Sacramentary and Antiphonary it is entitled, “On Saturday there is no office: the Lord Pope gives alms.”

We ought to consider why on that day in particular the almsgiving of the Apostolic is announced, since alms should be given throughout the entire year. Here we must note that the things we commemorate through ecclesiastical rites concerning the Lord’s passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven are performed in remembrance of those events that took place in their own time. Hence every day we say in the sacrifice of the Mass: “Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me.”

We have an earlier act of almsgiving on the present Saturday, which we ought to imitate and recall to our memory. The fellow evangelist John begins:

“Six days before the Passover, Jesus came to Bethany, where Lazarus had been, whom he had raised from the dead; and they made him a supper there.”

And shortly afterward:

“Mary therefore took a pound of costly perfume of genuine nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, and wiped his feet with her hair; and the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.”

In response to the indignation of Judas the betrayer, according to Matthew, the Lord testifies to the woman’s deed:

“Why do you trouble this woman? She has performed a good work for me. For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.”

And shortly afterward:

“Amen, I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done will also be spoken of in remembrance of her.”

The Apostolic man, in memory of this most devoted woman, does for Christ’s members what she did for the Head. Paul says: “Be imitators of me, dearly beloved children, as I also am of Christ.” Again and again the Apostolic says, though not in words but in deeds: “Be imitators of me, my children, as I also am of Mary.”

Hence Augustine, in his commentary on John, says:

“We hear of the deed; let us seek its mystery. If you wish to be a faithful soul who is Mary, anoint the Lord’s feet with the most precious perfume. That perfume was righteousness; therefore it was a pound.”

And again:

“Anoint the Lord’s feet by living well; follow the Lord’s footsteps; wipe them with your hair. If you have anything in excess, give it to the poor, and you have wiped the Lord’s feet. For hair seems to be something superfluous on the body; you have something to do with your superfluities. They are superfluous to you, but necessary for the Lord’s feet. Perhaps the Lord’s feet on earth are in need of them. For of whom but his members will he say at the end, ‘Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me’? You spend your superfluities, but you have served my feet.”

The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume; the world was filled with the woman’s good reputation. The Apostolic follows this most precious example; may we also follow it. For wherever the office of the Roman Church is performed, this report resounds: “The Lord Pope gives alms.” May God grant that it may also resound continually among us, and that what we do may be acceptable before the angels of the Lord in remembrance of us.

## CHAPTER X. On the fourth variation of Palm Sunday

The fourth variation is the one that is called the variation of Palm Sunday. On that day the Lord descended from Bethany to Jerusalem, when the crowd came out to meet him. John relates:

“On the following day, the great crowd that had come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, and cried out: ‘Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.’”

In memory of that event, we customarily carry branches through our churches and cry, “Hosanna.”

Why he came to Jerusalem, Bede explains in his commentary on Mark from the testimony of the Scriptures:

“As the time of his passion drew near, the Lord wished to draw near to the place of his passion and remain nearby, so that at the time established and predetermined before the ages he might be found there by those through whom that same passion was to be completed.”

And shortly afterward:

“Here we must not pass over in silence not only the harmony in events but also the harmony in times between the Old and New Testaments, between shadow and truth, between Law and Gospel. For it is written in the Law, when the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: ‘This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first month of the year. Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel and say to them: On the tenth day of this month, let each man take a lamb for his families and households.’”

And a little later:

“You shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month, and the whole assembly of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening.”

Thus, on the tenth day of the first month, the lamb that was to be sacrificed at Passover was commanded to be brought into the house, because on the tenth day of that same month—that is, five days before Passover—the Lord also entered the city in which he was to suffer.

## CHAPTER XI. On the fifth variation of the Wednesday of Holy Week

The fifth variation is on the Wednesday after Palm Sunday. It includes the variation and addition of one reading and one responsory with five verses, the Lord’s Passion, which is read on that day, and also, as we have written in the booklet called the *Roman Order*, genuflection.

The aforesaid booklet indicates that, according to Roman custom, on that day before the public office the prayers which we are accustomed to say on Friday ought to be recited. With the Lord’s help, we shall show on that day from the sayings of Saint Augustine what rationale these prayers have, whether on Wednesday or Friday; for the present, only a little needs to be indicated.

Let us first say why this variation is observed on Wednesday, and at the same time explain the mystery of the variation. Augustine says in his book to the priest Casulanus on fasting on Saturday: “On the fourth day of the week, which people commonly call Wednesday, the Jews are found to have formed their plan to kill the Lord.” From this it has been shown why the variation is celebrated on the Wednesday mentioned. For the Jews formed their plan to kill the Lord. As their deed, performed on the sixth day of the week, is recalled to memory, so also is their plan.

In both they wronged Christ. The present office contains this mystery: that we may understand that the second Adam died for the first Adam, as the psalm says: “Then I paid for what I had not taken.” Hence Augustine: “He certainly did not take it; but who took it? Adam +.” On this day the cruel plan of the Jews and the gentleness of Christ are recalled to our memory. Of this gentleness the same writer says, on Psalm 44: “So gentle that, while hanging on the cross, he said: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing’ +.” By the example of this gentleness—that is, of our Head—we are taught to arm ourselves against every injury with the weapons of prayer and patience, as it is written in the Gospel: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you.”

After we have touched upon the appointed parts of the office, they themselves will make clear what they contain. The introit is: “At the name of the Lord let every knee bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; because the Lord became obedient unto death, even death on a cross; therefore the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.” In this place we must understand “the name of the Lord” as the reality, not the word. Hence Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Philippians: “It is evident how he means not a designation but a certain reality acquired by him, as in what is written: ‘And they shall know that your name is Lord’—that is, that you are Lord.”

Paul indeed explains what that name is: “At the name of Jesus every knee shall bend,” and so forth. + Although Ambrose discusses these things after the Lord’s Passion, it is nevertheless not contrary to truth if we say that “at the name of the Lord” can be understood as “at the Lord’s command.” Let every knee bend against the adversities of the world, as was said above: “Pray for those who persecute and slander you.” To signify this matter, we shall first set out the prayers from the Roman Order. The instructor of the office omitted: “And let every tongue confess.” The Apostle spoke this good thing well.

The Jews spoke our good in Christ’s death, which intervened for our salvation, but they uttered it wickedly with their tongues. By the silence concerning the tongue, the instructor of the office teaches us to avoid the Jews’ evil. Christ’s gentleness prayed; let us imitate it. Enough concerning the introit, which pertains to the prayer we ought to practise amid the injuries of persecutors. Let us now pass to the prayer of the Mass, in which, as in the following parts, we celebrate Christ’s death, which he was about to suffer for us. The kingdom of death was goading us; Christ came to strike it down. Thus it says: “May we, who are continually afflicted by our transgressions, be delivered through the Passion of your Only-begotten.”

Let us consider the reading, which openly displays the Lord’s Passion, saying: “He was offered because he himself willed it, and he did not open his mouth.” In what follows it reveals why he was offered: “If he shall set his life for sin, he shall see a long-lived seed,” and so forth. Hence Jerome: “If he whom the Lord wished to crush, or to command, shall set his life for sin, he shall see the long-lived seed which he sowed upon good ground, of which it is also written in the Gospel: ‘The one who sows went out to sow good seed.’” + Let us hear the responsory: “Do not turn your face away from your servant,” and so forth. Hence Augustine on the Psalms: “This commendation is from your servant—that is, from the little one who has now been deprived of pride through the discipline of tribulation.” +

The verse runs: “Save me, O God, for waters have entered even to my soul; I am sunk in the mire of the deep.” Hence the same writer, in the same psalm: “Prefiguring and transforming us in himself, he says: ‘Save me, O God, for waters have entered even to my soul.’ Those who persecuted him could even kill him, but they will have nothing further that they can do.” And shortly afterward: “I am sunk in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground.” What does he mean by mire? Perhaps those who persecuted him? For man was made from mire, but was made righteous unto righteousness. And shortly afterward: “But since they were the mire of the deep, I stuck fast in them—that is, they held me, prevailed against me, killed me +.”

The first man suffered two deaths: the death of the soul and the death of the body. In the first reading and the first responsory the death of the soul is recalled; in the second reading and second responsory, the death of the body. Christ died for both. Hence Ambrose, on the Epistle to the Corinthians: “The Lord’s blood redeemed our blood—that is, it made the whole human being safe. For the flesh of the Saviour was offered for the salvation of the body, but his blood was shed for our soul +.” The first man had one soul; therefore the first responsory is followed by one verse. Let us first see how the second prayer accords with our purpose; then how the reading does; and finally how the responsory, which has five verses, does.

The prayer says: “O God, who willed that your Son should undergo the gibbet of the cross for us, so that you might drive the power of the enemy away from us.” The reading is full of the Lord’s Passion, saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bosrah?” And again: “I have trodden the winepress alone.” These words convey nothing other than the angels’ inquiry why Christ had garments dyed with blood, and his answer: “I have trodden the winepress alone.” Why he did this we shall hear at the end of the reading from the thanksgiving that says: “I shall remember the mercies of the Lord, the praise of the Lord for all that he has bestowed upon us.” Jerome on Isaiah: “Pressed down,” he says, “by the weight of evils, I have hope in nothing other than God’s mercy, he who shows mercy to thousands who love him.”

The second responsory, which has five verses, signifies the five bodily senses that had died in Adam and which Christ revived in dying and rising, restoring them to their former state.

* The responsory has five verses. One human being had died through the five bodily senses. Cyprian shows that the devil is the agent of death through the outward senses. “He offers alluring forms to the eyes,” he says, “easy pleasures, so that through sight he may destroy chastity; he tempts the ears through tuneful music, so that in hearing the sweeter sound he may loosen and soften Christian vigour; he provokes the tongue by abuse; and by injuries that provoke, he incites the hand to the wantonness of killing.” + He is silent about smell. May God grant that the instigator of death have no place of entry into our mind through the scent of lust—a matter more to be feared than discussed.

In certain words of the responsory’s verses Adam himself is introduced, from whom we draw our flesh. The verse says: “For my days have failed like smoke.” Augustine says in the same psalm: “Whence like smoke, unless because of the elevation of pride? Proud Adam, from whom Christ took flesh, deserved to receive such days. Therefore Christ is in Adam, and Adam in Christ.” And again: “I have been struck like grass, and my heart has withered.” Look to Adam, from whom comes the human race. From whom else comes this inherited poverty, if not from him? Therefore let him, once despairing in his own body but now placed with hope in Christ’s body, say: “I have been struck like grass, and my heart has withered +.”

The Passion that is read strengthens our hearts. It shows that the Jews’ plan prevailed for a time, and that Christ persevered in gentleness. We proposed only to speak about the variations; therefore we are silent about the sequences of the Mass, because it is fitting that we should recall Christ’s death, through the Jews’ plan—a death which, although he did not undergo it on that day by the gibbet of the cross, we ought to recall in connection with our death, which already existed, and for which he deigned to come to the Passion.

## CHAPTER XII. On the sixth variation of the Lord’s Supper
The sixth variation occurs on Thursday, which we call the Lord’s Supper. On it, “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit” is not sung. On it, oil for three offices is consecrated in three ways. On it, the Lord’s body is reserved until the following day and received in commemoration of Christ’s meal. The brothers’ feet and the church floors are washed, and the altars are stripped until Holy Saturday. On that day penitents come for absolution, and among some people the Creed is handed back by the catechumens, as is contained in the canon of the Council of Laodicea. Nevertheless, following the Roman Order, we retain this handing back until Holy Saturday.

First, if the Lord grants it, we wish to say something about the nature of oil. As Isidore says: “The olea is the tree itself; its fruit is the olive, and its juice is oil.” It is an emblem of peace. It also possesses fatness, by which the limbs of the weary and infirm are restored, and it supplies the grace of light.

Here we must make this point clear: according to the Apostle, invisible things are understood through visible things. For God can heal the infirm without oil, sanctify his own, and drive out demons. Hence Ambrose, in his Letter to the Corinthians, says:

> For we know that the Holy Spirit was given by God even without the laying on of hands, and that one who had not been baptized obtained the remission of sins. Was he not baptized invisibly here, when he received the gift of baptism?

We have heard the nature of oil: it is suited to restoring the limbs of the weary and provides the grace of light. The animal-minded can recognize such things; let them also believe what they cannot see, so that what we quoted earlier from the Apostle may be fulfilled:

> For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made, as are his eternal power and divinity.

Augustine explains this clearly in Psalm 44:

> Visible oil is a sign; invisible oil is in the sacrament; spiritual oil is within.

God can bestow spiritual oil directly, without bodily oil; but visible things are performed for the animal-minded, so that invisible things may be grasped more easily.

If someone says, “If God can do this, why is the rite of the consecration of oil observed with such care?” the answer will be: Could not the ancient righteous please God without circumcision? Certainly they could. But once they had been commanded to be circumcised, if they were not circumcised they were held bound by sin. Hence Augustine, to Seleucia:

> If the ancient righteous were not circumcised, it was not a sin for them; but after God commanded Abraham and his descendants to be circumcised, failure to do so became a grave sin.

The Apostles used this practice—that is, oil—for the restoration of the infirm; apostolic men used it in the sealing of neophytes. Therefore, we cannot omit without sin what their authority consecrated. For it is written in the Gospel:

> Going out, they preached that people should repent; they drove out many demons, anointed many sick people with oil, and healed them.

Hence Bede says:

> The Apostle James says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.” It is therefore clear that this custom of the holy Church was handed down by the Apostles themselves: that the possessed, or any other sick persons, should be anointed with oil consecrated by pontifical blessing.

Of the oil poured over neophytes we do not read anything of this kind, but we retain the apostolic custom and have received its authority from the Roman Church, which must be held as law. Augustine says this to the presbyter Casulanus concerning the Saturday fast:

> In matters about which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of God’s people or the institutions of our ancestors must be held as law.

Now that we have demonstrated the general nature of oil, we must first speak of the oil consecrated for the sick. It is consecrated within the very rite of the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood. It has no separate office: that is, it has neither the words of greeting at the beginning, nor “Let us pray,” nor is it concluded at the end, as the other prayers are, with “Through our Lord Jesus Christ.” Instead, it has only the words “in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

At the place where we ordinarily bless the grapes, the oil for the sick is consecrated, and it is concluded with the formula:

> Through whom, Lord, you always create all good things.

From this we understand that it is an insertion into the office mentioned above. That office concerns only the immolation of Christ and of the Church. For one who lives in sin is not sacrificed to the Lord; one who dies to sin is sacrificed to the Lord.

If infirmity did not arise from sins, James would not say, “And if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.” In the Epistle read on the same day, Paul shows through which sins infirmity occurs, saying:

> Let a person examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup. For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the Lord’s body. For this reason many among you are infirm and weak, and many are asleep.

Here he shows the wounds; James, his fellow Apostle, shows the medicine:

> Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the presbyters of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.

Here he makes clear what saves the sick person—namely, the prayer of faith, whose sign is the anointing with oil.

If they become sick because they eat the Lord’s body unworthily, yet are helped by the anointing with oil—that is, by God’s grace through the presbyter’s prayer—it is fitting that the consecration now under discussion should be joined to the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood. That consecration is made in commemoration of Christ’s Passion, through which the author of sin was eternally overthrown.

Christ’s Passion destroyed the author of death; his grace, signified by the anointing with oil, destroyed the author’s weapons, which are daily sins.

The final prayer of the consecration of the Lord’s body is made on behalf of penitents, of whom it is said:

> A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit.

It is therefore appropriate that oil for penitents should be consecrated there, where their sacrifice is offered to God.

Since we have briefly touched upon the nature of oil, what it signifies, and why it is consecrated in such a place, it follows that we should say something about the words of the consecration. For it says:

> Send your Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, from heaven into this richness of oil, which you have deigned to produce from green wood for the refreshment of the body.

“Paraclete” is added here, and, as I believe, is not found in what follows without some mysterious reason. First we must see what the Holy Spirit accomplishes in each case; then it will become clear why the word is added here.

The exorcism of the oil commands the devil to depart from the catechumen, who is still reckoned among the dead because he has not yet been baptized. The anointing with chrism sanctifies the one who is already living from the dead. Oil for the sick provides healing for the wounded. Hence the prayer says that it is given “to remove all pains, all infirmities, and every sickness of the body.”

Sickness is followed by pain, and pain by consolation. “Paraclete” is interpreted as “comforter.” The one who is dead does not suffer, because he does not feel; nor does consolation follow him. The one who is sanctified in Christ through resurrection does not need consolation from pain.

We must now pass to the principal consecration of chrism. It is called principal because the principal Spirit is bestowed for its anointing. It has an office of its own. It begins with “Lift up your hearts” and ends with “Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives with you.”

It is consecrated at the place where we ordinarily give the peace among ourselves. This is the work of the Lord’s grace: that peace and concord may reign among us. As Isidore says:

> “The olive is an emblem of peace.”

This peace was prefigured long ago in Noah’s ark, as the words of the same consecration testify:

> When the crimes of the world were once cleansed by the outpoured flood, the dove, displaying the likeness of the future gift, announced through an olive branch that peace had been restored to the earth.

Here not only oil but also balsam is consecrated. According to the same Isidore, the balsam-tree is one of the aromatic trees, which are fragrant. Aromatics are substances of a fragrant smell, which India, Arabia, or the regions of Italy send forth. The word “aromatics” appears to have been derived either because they are placed upon altars and seem suited to divine invocations, or because they are thought to enter into and mingle with the air +.

The fragrance of balsam in the oil demonstrates the widely diffused reputation of good virtues, through the working of the Holy Spirit’s grace. Balsam is added to the oil because heavenly splendor shines in Christ’s face.

Hence Jerome, in Psalm 44, to the virgin Principia:

> The Virgin born from a virgin, who was born not by the will of a man but from God. For unless there had been something star-like in his face and eyes, the Apostles would never have followed him immediately, nor would those who came to seize him have fallen down.

That radiance, through God’s working, brightens the faces of the elect, so that with great joy we may imitate their deeds.

Hence the present prayer. David, foreknowing through the prophetic Spirit the mysteries of his grace, sang that our faces would be brightened with oil. A little later it says:

> This anointing with oil makes our faces joyful and serene.

By “our faces” we understand the manifestation of our works. On this subject Augustine, in Psalm 104, says:

> A certain grace, which exists among human beings and is evident for the purpose of establishing holy love, is called oil in the divine brightness; and because it appeared most excellently in Christ, the whole world loves him.

A little later:

> For his grace is so great that many who do not believe in him praise him, and therefore say that they do not wish to believe in him because no one can accomplish what he commands.

Those who once raged against him in reproach are restrained by praising him. Yet he is loved by all and proclaimed by all, because he is excellently anointed—that is, Christ.

The exorcism of the oil follows. As Isidore says:

> “Exorcism” in Greek means “adjuration” in Latin; or it is a speech of rebuke directed against the devil, so that he may depart.

It is concluded in this way:

> Through our Lord Jesus Christ, who will come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire.

Catechumens are anointed with this oil so that, if any stains have clung to body or mind, they may depart after the catechumens have come to examination, and so that through this anointing they may thereafter have protection, preventing the devil from returning.

The words of the prayer demonstrate this, saying:

> So that, at the touch of the holy oil, any remnants of the hostile spirits that have clung to them may all depart; that there be no place for spiritual wickedness and no opportunity for the powers that have been put to flight; and so forth.

This rebuke, or adjuration, directed against the devil is rightly associated with the last judgment, at which the dead and the living and the world will be judged by fire. There the devil knows that he will above all be condemned; he is shaken on every side by fear of it. But those who have already risen and live with Christ hear good things promised to them, through the same one who lives and reigns as God with the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit.

The three consecrations mentioned are made from one and the same substance, namely the liquid of oil. In the same way, the substance of the Holy Spirit is one, though it is divided in many ways through the grace of his gifts:

> To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, to another the grace of healings, and so forth.

These things seem to us suitable for explaining our consecrations.

The word of wisdom signifies a good manner of life, specifically that of those to whom the present Apostle speaks:

> If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is sitting at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above.

He has tasted this wisdom who says:

> By the grace of God I am what I am.

There you have the oil. Let the word of knowledge be added. Knowledge pertains to teaching. Since Paul labored in it, he therefore added:

> And his grace in me was not empty.

There you also have the balsam. When these two are joined together, they make the servant complete.

It follows:

> To another faith.

We introduce faith as ready for two works: namely, for expulsion, as the Apostle says:

> If I have faith so that I can move mountains;

and for protection, of which it is said:

> Taking up the shield of faith.

There you have the exorcism of the oil, as the Truth itself testifies, saying:

> If any remnants of the hostile spirits have clung to them, let them depart at the touch of this sanctified oil.

And again:

> Let there be no opportunity for the powers that have been put to flight.

It follows:

> To another the grace of healings.

There you have oil for the sick. The words of this prayer demonstrate that not only bodily medicine is necessary, but spiritual medicine above all, when it speaks of “the oath of mind and body” (juramentum; the reading is uncertain). The mind is weakened by sins and healed by the Lord’s grace. Without these things, as I believe, no one enters the court of the heavenly kingdom: that is, unless one possesses a good manner of life and teaching, whether in words or conduct. These cannot be hidden, as the Apostle says:

> Likewise, good works also are manifest; those that are otherwise cannot be hidden.

Nor can anyone enter unless he has faith, without which no one can please God, or unless he has the daily grace of healing, because we sin every day.

Therefore priests chiefly invoke these things through the ministry of oil, so that all may receive them generally, since unless God’s grace grants them, people are not fit for the kingdom.

The gifts that follow from God are not all possessed by everyone; they are distributed among many. Yet those who do not possess them are not thereby believed to be excluded from God’s kingdom, even though they may not possess the working of virtues—that is, so as to perform signs and drive out demons—or prophecy, so as to reveal the secrets of Scripture or foretell the future—or the discernment of spirits, or kinds of tongues, or the interpretation of speech. They will not be exiles from the kingdom of heaven, provided that they have faith, which works through love.

By God’s favor we have said where oil is consecrated and what its meaning contains. It remains for us to say something about the order of consecration according to the notation of the Sacramentary and the booklet called the Roman Order.

Concerning oil for the sick, the Sacramentary contains the following:

> Before “Through whom, Lord, you always create all good things” is said, they are lifted from the vessels offered by the people, and both the lord pope and all the bishops bless them.

In Exodus it is written that the people should offer oil, the Lord saying:

> Command the children of Israel to offer you the purest oil from olive trees.

When it is offered by the people, it is a simple liquid. Through the blessing of the priests it is transferred into a sacrament. This administration signifies that earthly administration ought to be present alongside spiritual administration. Hence the Apostle says:

> If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?

Both the lord pope and all the presbyters bless it. It is the custom of the Roman Church that presbyters be present at the preparation of Christ’s sacrifice and perform it jointly with the pontiff by words and hands. But since the consecration of this oil is concluded in the same section, the presbyters ought likewise to prepare the oil together with the pontiff, as with the other elements.

The booklet of the Roman Order says the following about the consecration of chrism:

> Immediately two acolytes hold the wrapped vessels, covered with a white silk cloth, on the left arm, so that they may be visible from the middle.

And a little later:

> Before he blesses it, he breathes three times into the vessel.

And again:

> As soon as the vessel containing the chrism has been blessed, it is covered, so that no one may see it uncovered. While an acolyte holds it, everyone greets it in order; the bishop and deacons greet it first. +

If the present Order is not carried out as it is written, its author’s labor in composing the work has been frustrated. But if it is carried out, it is useless unless it contains something within the sacrament.

Let us first speak about the statement, “He breathes three times into the vessel.” Breath proceeds from the inner and hidden places into public view, and is called spirit; it belongs to the nostrils. Through his breath, the pontiff announces that the substance of the Holy Spirit dwells in the body assumed by divinity, at whose coming all things were renewed.

The vessel containing chrism signifies, in a certain way, the Lord’s body assumed from the Virgin Mary. Before it passed to the altar of the cross, it was covered for a certain period and uncovered for another.

At the beginning it was covered when he fled into Egypt from King Herod as though he were not the King of kings and Lord of lords; when he was carried to the temple as though he were not omnipotent; when, as his parents returned from Jerusalem, he was sought among relatives and acquaintances as though he were not everywhere; when he was found in the temple sitting in the midst of the teachers, listening and asking questions, as though he were not the fountain of wisdom; and when he was subject to his parents as though he were not the author of parents.

In all these things he lay hidden under a covering. The covering was the white cloth, through which we may appropriately understand the utterly pure manner of life with which he was clothed from the beginning.

He was uncovered after he began to perform miracles that exceeded human works. Hence Nicodemus said:

> No one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.

At the same time he preached and demonstrated that he was God, saying:

> I and the Father are one.

Unless Peter understood this to have been said of the divine nature, he would not have said:

> You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.

But after he passed to the altar of the cross—that is, to the immolation, as though to the consecration of a bishop—for he is himself the supreme Pontiff who offered himself to God the Father, he showed his bodily form uncovered for a certain period.

This period is recalled through the uncovering of the vessel, which the bishop and deacons greet. Thomas, who put his fingers into the marks of the nails and his hand into his side, said:

> My Lord and my God!

He greeted Christ’s uncovered body.

By his uncovering we mean the manifestation of his bodily presence. The same is true of those who ate and drank with him after he had risen from the dead.

But after the vessel has been greeted by the pontiff and the ministers of the altar, it is covered so that no one may see it uncovered. Yet the covered vessel is greeted. For after Christ had shown his presence, according to his own disposition, to those whom he wished to be witnesses of his resurrection, he ascended into heaven and became invisible to human beings, as he himself testifies:

> I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.

This plainly means: “I appeared visibly to human beings; when I return to the Father, I shall be invisible.” Although we do not see his bodily presence, we nevertheless greet it every day by venerating it.

Since we have touched upon the nature of oil in order to explain it, it now pleases us, if the Lord grants it, to say why we omit “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

According to the Gospel, the Lord lay in the tomb for three days, which says:

> Just as Jonah was in the whale’s belly for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights.

Augustine explains this in the first book of his *Questions on the Gospels*:

> Taking the part of Friday on which he was buried, together with the preceding night, as a night and day; then Saturday as a whole, night and day; and the Lord’s night with its dawning day—thus taking a part for the whole—you have three days and three nights.

We recall the Lord’s three-day burial, but we do not commemorate it in our celebration unless Thursday and Friday are added to Saturday. For Sunday night is celebrated in great glory, as is clear to all who observe the custom of our church.

Hence Augustine, in a sermon to the people at the Easter vigil, says:

> Then the day of Saturday, beginning from its own night, ended in the evening of the night beginning, which belongs to the beginning of Sunday, because the Lord consecrated it by the glory of his resurrection. Therefore, we now solemnly celebrate the memory of that night which belongs to the beginning of the Lord’s day.

If, according to Augustine, the resurrection was glory, then his death and burial were his humiliation. If, according to the Apostle, “he emptied himself” after taking the form of a servant, how much more so when “he became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross.”

For three continuous days—Thursday, Friday, and Saturday—we celebrate his three-day burial. Thus, so that we may share in the humility of his burial, we omit our exalted things: “Glory be to the Father, and to the Son,” the ringing of the bells, and other matters that will be treated more suitably when we reach their explanation.

The heavenly bread, that is, the Lord’s body, is reserved from Thursday until Good Friday. Augustine says to Januarius:

> There are some who wish to receive the Eucharist every day. What also serves this likeness, he says, is that in the first people the manna tasted in each believer’s mouth according to his own desire: so, in the mouth of each Christian, there is that sacrament through which the world was saved and subdued. One person, honoring it, does not dare receive it every day; another, honoring it, does not dare omit it on any day. This food desires only not to be despised, just as the manna desired not to be treated with loathing.

On Good Friday the Lord’s body is not prepared. Those who wish to communicate must have a sacrifice from the preceding day.

Then one passes to the meal, from which the day is called the Lord’s Supper.

Hence Isidore says:

> It is called the Lord’s Supper because on that day the Savior celebrated the Passover with his disciples.

John the Evangelist relates how that holy meal was celebrated:

> Behold, when supper had taken place—he says—and the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him, Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper, laid aside his garments, and, taking a cloth, girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the cloth with which he was girded.

And a little later:

> Therefore, after he had washed their feet, he took his garments; and when he had reclined again, he said to them: “Do you know what I have done for you?”

Augustine explains this in the same work:

> We must not understand it as though the supper had already been consumed and completed. For supper was still in progress when the Lord rose and washed the disciples’ feet; afterward he reclined again and later gave the morsel to his betrayer. Certainly the supper had not yet ended, since bread was still on the table. Therefore, “when supper had taken place” means that it had been prepared and brought as far as the table of those dining.

I saw a certain religious man take some food first on that day, then wash the feet of pilgrims, and afterward proceed to the table, following the example of our Lord.

On that day we wash not only the brothers’ feet but also the floors of the church. Although their washing may suitably correspond to the adornment of the Paschal festival, there is also a mystery in it.

The walls of a house bear the name “church” because they contain the Church; they themselves are not the Church. We can understand this from the interpretation of the word “Church.” Let us read Bede on the matter. His explanation distinguishes the synagogue from the Church and gives their interpretations. He says:

> There is a true difference between the synagogue, which means “assembly,” and the Church, which means “convocation”: the people of the Old Testament are designated by both terms, but those of the New Testament only by “Church.” For animals and all lifeless things can be assembled together, but only beings endowed with reason can be called together.

Thus the Church is not the walls of the house. Nevertheless, the walls are sanctified by the bishop so that he may wish the angels to come there, and so that people entering it may know that they must refrain from every disgraceful word and vulgarity, and even from useless thought.

Let those who enter the church hear what Moses heard when he wished to see the burning bush:

> Do not come nearer, he said; remove your sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.

And again the angel said to Joshua:

> Remove your sandal from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy.

Sandals are made from dead animals. Adam is a dead animal, from whom we have inherited death. Let us see whether our mind is shod in some manner according to his example.

If he had not become mortal, we would have had no need for sleep, no need to build houses, no need for agriculture; we would not hunger or thirst, nor would we wage wars, because it would have been enough for each person to preserve the image of God within himself and rejoice in the unity of brotherhood. To say nothing of manifest sins: when the mind is occupied with these things, it is shod with the skin of a dead animal.

As we enter the holy places where the Lord and his angel are, let us remove our sandals here and think about the life of angels: where there is rest without sleep, a dwelling through God’s protection, work without labor, fullness without hunger, and perpetual peace without war.

The floor of the church signifies those who hear the teachers. The washing of the house, which is called “Church” by designation, is a sign of the washing of the brothers’ feet; the washing of the brothers’ feet is a sign of the remission of sins, whether when they are forgiven by the Lord or when we forgive one another.

Augustine says concerning this in his work on John:

> The Lord speaks truth when he says that even one who has been washed needs to have his feet washed. What do you think, my brothers? Is it not because in holy baptism a person is washed entirely—not merely the feet, but wholly? Nevertheless, when one afterward lives among human affairs, one certainly treads the earth. Human affections themselves, without which one cannot live in this mortality, are like feet, because we are affected by human things; and we are so affected that, if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth has not remained in us.

Therefore he who intercedes for us washes our feet every day, and every day we need to wash our feet—that is, to direct the paths of our spiritual steps.

In the Lord’s Prayer itself we confess this when we say:

> Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

On that same day penitents return for the remission of sins, according to the Decretals of Pope Innocent, who says:

> Concerning penitents, whether they are doing penance for graver offenses or for lesser ones, if no illness intervenes, the custom of the Roman Church shows that they should be reconciled on the Thursday before the Lord’s Easter.

Innocent fixes the time; Jerome fixes the manner in his letter to Oceanus on the death of Fabiola, praising Fabiola’s penance for the adultery she had committed. He says:

> Why should I linger over things abolished and ancient, seeking to excuse a fault whose penance she herself confessed? Who would have believed that, after the death of her second husband, she would return to herself at a time when careless widows usually shake off the yoke of servitude and live more freely; that she would go to the baths, flit through the streets, display the faces of prostitutes, and put on sackcloth; that she would publicly confess her error; and that, with the whole city of Rome watching, before Easter, she would stand in a public [place] of the Lateran—“which was cut off by the Caesarean sword” is textually uncertain—among the ranks of penitents? Before bishops, presbyters, and the whole weeping people, with disheveled hair, a pallid face, grimy hands, and filthy neck, she submitted herself. What sins would such weeping not cleanse? What aged stains would such lamentation not wash away?

In all these matters we recognize that the present day has been especially consecrated to the remission of sins.

We do not think that this happens by chance on the present Thursday. For the moment, we learned men may say what seems to us to provide the reason: the Lord wished to wash feet on that very day, and following his example we wash feet and other things; this washing signifies the remission of sins. Therefore penitents also return on that same day to the hands of the priests—and this is also why oil is consecrated on that day.

Our Lord came into the world in the fifth age and consecrated the sixth by his coming. Concerning him Gregory says in his book *On the Building of the Temple*:

> He came at the end of the synagogue and before the beginning of the Church, which he gathered from the nations.

But first let us see what the fifth age was like; afterward we shall be able to understand whether the Lord found it in that condition.

The lord Bede says of it:

> On the fifth day the fish and birds were brought forth from the waters.

And a little later:

> Evening followed, when, as the Savior’s coming was already imminent, the Jewish people, because of the magnitude of their crimes, had become tributary to the Romans and, in addition, had been oppressed by foreign kings.

And again in the same work, *On Times*:

> The fifth age, as though a senile age, extends from the Babylonian captivity to the coming of the Lord and Savior.

And a little later:

> In it the Hebrew people, wearied as though by a burdensome old age, were shaken by increasingly frequent evils. +

Isaiah touches upon how it was shaken:

> He will not break the bruised reed, nor extinguish the smoking flax.

Gregory explains this in the *Moralia*:

> What does he signify by the name “reed” if not the temporal kingdom of the Jewish people—outwardly indeed standing upright, but inwardly empty? And because the royal line had already failed among that people and its kingdom was possessed by a foreigner, he plainly calls that same kingdom a bruised reed.

What, then, is expressed by the flax if not its priesthood? It used linen garments, and because at the Lord’s coming it had lost the warmth of charity, it was like a fire whose flame of faith had already been lost: not burning, but smoking.

When the Lord became incarnate, he did not break the bruised reed or extinguish the smoking flax. For he did not strike with the power of judgment either the kingdom of Judea, which had already been nearly destroyed, or its priesthood, which no longer retained the fire of faith; instead, he endured them with the great patience of forbearance.

We have heard of the shaking of the fifth age, which the Lord found. Let us hear of the restoration by which the Lord repaired the sixth age through his coming.

That he came to us at the end of the fifth age is demonstrated by the end of the present Thursday’s festival, on which he also brought the Law to an end, as we shall write later, if God wills. Now we must speak of the things he brought with him.

Daniel writes:

> Seventy weeks have been shortened for your people and for your holy city, so that transgression may be completed, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be wiped away, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed.

[Col. 1021D] Hence Bede writes in *The Reckoning of Time*: “No one doubts that these words designate the incarnation of Christ, who took away the sins of the world, fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, and was anointed with oil above his companions +.” Concerning this anointing Isaiah speaks in the person of the Savior himself: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to evangelize the poor, to proclaim release to captives, and sight to the blind.” Hence Jerome writes on the same passage in Isaiah: “When companions are mentioned, understand the nature of the flesh, for God has no companions of his substance. And because the anointing was spiritual, and in no way an anointing of the human body, as it was among the priests of the Jews, he is therefore said to have been anointed above his companions—that is, above the other saints.” His anointing [Col. 1022A] was completed at the time when he was baptized in the Jordan, and the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained in him.

According to the preceding words, he came for this reason: to make his companions heirs of his kingdom. This anointing takes place on Thursday, because he came to us in the fifth age of the world. Yet a certain mode of anointing was deferred from his birth, according to Isaiah and the Gospel, in the form of the dove, until his baptism. Although we believe that from the beginning, from the moment when he began to become man, the spiritual anointing remained in Jesus, this nevertheless does not conflict with the practice by which the oil is consecrated on Thursday and the anointing is preserved until our baptism.

Ambrose explains this practice in his book on Luke: “‘I will ask the Father,’ he says, ‘and he will give you another Paraclete, [Col. 1022B] to be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive because it does not see him or know him.’ Therefore he rightly manifested himself in bodily form, since he is not seen in the substance of his divinity: we saw the Spirit, but in bodily form. The man Christ Jesus, after he began to be man, was always God; nor do we believe that the gifts of grace increased in him by the growth of his bodily members. For in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.”

Hence Jerome writes on Isaiah: “Let us understand that the infancy of the human body did not prejudice divine wisdom.” And again: “Upon this flower, therefore, which will suddenly rise through the Virgin Mary from the severed root of Jesse, the Spirit of the Lord will rest, because it pleased him that all the fullness of divinity should dwell bodily in him,” [Col. 1022C] not in portions, as in the other saints.

Bede writes on Luke: “The distinction of the words must be noted, because the Lord Jesus Christ, inasmuch as he was a child—that is, had assumed the appearance of human frailty—was to grow and be strengthened. But inasmuch as he was also the Word of God, eternal God, he neither needed nor could be strengthened or increased. Hence he is most rightly said to be full of wisdom and grace. He was full of wisdom because in him all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily; and full of grace because great grace was granted to that same mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ: from the moment he began to become man, he was perfect both as man and as God.”

John writes something similar, saying that he was “full of grace and truth,” commending under the name of truth that same excellence of divinity which [Col. 1022D] Luke commends under the name of wisdom.

And again, the same author writes in the *Acts of the Apostles*: “Jesus, therefore, was anointed not with visible oil, but with the gift of God’s grace, which is signified by the visible ointment with which the Church anoints the baptized. Yet he was not then anointed with the Holy Spirit when, after his baptism, the Spirit descended upon him like a dove. At that time he deigned to prefigure his body, that is, his Church, in which the baptized especially receive the Holy Spirit. Rather, by that mystical and invisible anointing he is to be understood as anointed when the Word of God became flesh—that is, when human nature, without any preceding merits of good works, was joined to the Word of God in the Virgin’s womb, so that with him it became one person. For this reason [Col. 1023A] we confess that he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.”

He himself came to take away the sins of the world, so that, as the prophet mentioned above says, he might release the broken into forgiveness +.

On that day the Law of the Old Testament comes to an end, as the same point is demonstrated from the authority of Scripture in Luke. For when Moses had died, Joshua was appointed leader, because, after the Law had been corrupted by the traditions of the Pharisees, Christ became incarnate. Joshua feeds and is fed by manna beyond the Jordan, because the Lord himself, until the time of his baptism, both observes the ceremonies of the Law and desires them to be observed by all. After bringing the people across the Jordan, Joshua circumcises them with a stone, because, once the grace of baptism had been celebrated, the Savior also, by the rigor of faith, cut away the enticements of thought that the Law had been unable to remove.

And although he nourished them with the customary manna for three and a half years, while gradually calling them toward the heavenly promises, he did not cease to observe the sacraments [Col. 1023B] of the Law, until, at the appointed time, eating the desired Passover with his disciples, and then, when morning dawned, he consecrated the most pure mysteries of his body and blood on the altar of the cross and brought them, like unleavened bread from the promised land, for the faithful to receive.

And again: “He took the cup, gave thanks, and said: ‘Take this and divide it among yourselves.’” This cup also belongs to that former Passover which he desired to bring to an end. Having taken it, he gave thanks, plainly because old things were passing away and all things were to become new.

The Law did not remove sins but punished them. On Thursday Christ brings the old Law to an end and absolves sins. The same thing is expressed in the first prayer of the Mass, when the priest says: “Thus, with the error of antiquity removed from us, may he grant us the grace of his resurrection.” [Col. 1023C]

He also brings the oil with which his companions are to be anointed, of whom Peter says: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood.”

One matter still remains in the Roman Order, where it prescribes that from Thursday until Holy Saturday the altars should be bare. If I am not mistaken, this signifies nothing other than the flight of the apostles, which the Lord himself attests in the Gospel of John: “Now you believe? Behold, the hour is coming when you will be scattered, each to his own, and you will leave me alone.” Augustine explains this in the same work: “Then you will be so troubled that you will even abandon what you now believe” +.

The altar signifies Christ, as Bede relates in his book *On the Tabernacle and Its Vessels*. The golden altar signifies the Lord himself, because, in a wondrous and ineffable order, he truly assumed flesh from Adam while remaining truly free from the sin of Adam’s flesh. Both altars were made from wood of one and the same kind, but both were not covered with gold. Moreover, nothing fleshly was offered on this altar; only spices were burned there, because the Lord, pouring out prayers or tears, did so not for his own sins—for he had none—but for our salvation.

Just as the ark placed within the veil signifies the man who is God, seated at the right hand of the Majesty on high, so the altar placed outside the veil, near its entrance, can figuratively express the same mediator between God and human beings. The vestments of the altar are the holy ones of Christ, concerning whom it is written: “And they left him and all fled.” [Col. 1024A]

## CHAPTER XIII. On the seventh variation: Good Friday
