The seventh variation occurs on the sixth day, which we call *Parasceve*. As Bede says, *Parasceve* means “preparation.” The Jews who lived among the Greeks called the sixth day of the Sabbath—which we now call Friday—the *Parasceve*, because on that day they prepared what was necessary for the Sabbath, according to the command once given concerning the manna: “On the sixth day you shall gather twice as much,” and so forth.

The Jews who live among the Romans, however, more commonly call it in Latin *coena*. This Friday corresponds to the sixth day of the first creation and to the sixth age of this world. Concerning the Friday of the first creation, the author mentioned above says in *The Reckoning of Time*: “On the sixth day the earth is filled with its living creatures, and the first man is created in the image of God; then, from the side of the sleeping man, a rib is taken and fashioned into a woman.” And again, concerning the sixth age: “In the sixth age, while the prophets were proclaiming beforehand, the Son of God appeared in the flesh, to create the human being in the image of God. Sleeping on the cross, he poured blood and water from his side, from which he was to consecrate the Church to himself.”

On the same day the reading from the book of Exodus is appointed, in which the lamb that entered Jerusalem on the Lord’s Day to be sacrificed is slaughtered. The reading says: “On the tenth day of this month each person shall take a lamb for his family and household”—concerning which we shall speak later—“and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; then the entire assembly of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it at evening.” [Col. 1024C]

Our Lord is the lamb who, at the beginning of the fifteenth lunar day, was handed over and ascended the cross on the Parasceve.

The Responsory follows, with four verses; and there is no doubt that Christ as man consisted of the four elements. It is natural for a human being to consist of earth, water, air, and fire. When he assumed human nature, he assumed these four elements. These hung on the cross between the two thieves.

Hence one verse says: “You shall be known in the midst of two animals.” Jerome explains this in Habakkuk: “The simple interpretation, and the common opinion, understands this of the Savior: that he was recognized when crucified between two thieves” +.

Although the same matter admits another interpretation, the person who established this office understood it in the sense that blessed Jerome reported from the common opinion concerning the two thieves.

The following prayer recalls: “O God, from whom Judas received the punishment of his guilt and the thief the reward of his confession.”

There are two kinds of afflicted people. One does not benefit those who suffer, because they are not corrected through punishments; Judas and the unconverted thief belong to this class. The other benefits those who repent fruitfully; the other thief, venerable for his confession, represents their type. Those who are not corrected by affliction belong to the body of Judas the betrayer and the wicked thief; those who are corrected belong to the thief who deserved to hear: “Today you will be with me in paradise.”

The reading from Hosea follows. [Col. 1025A]

Before speaking about this reading, it must be explained why it is added. On Wednesday, when we recalled the Jews’ plot against the Lord’s life, we made our twofold death known, for which Christ had come to suffer. Nevertheless, he reserved his own Passion until Friday, the day on which our first parent was created.

Today, that is, on the Parasceve, we recall his Passion for our imitation. Peter says concerning it: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, so that you should follow in his footsteps.”

We can recall the same thing more clearly from the reading appointed for this day. It says: “It shall be a male without blemish, one year old. According to this rite you shall take a young goat and keep it until the fourteenth day of this month.”

This lamb without blemish signifies the spotless body of Christ; the young goat signifies his body, which is us, since we are sinners. Both animals are mentioned in the rite of the Passover.

Just as we learn from Scripture that “our Passover is Christ’s sacrifice,” so our sacrifice consists in putting our vices to death; and, if necessary, in pouring out all present possessions, even life itself, and thus passing over to the Father.

The following reading from Hosea says: “Come, and let us return to the Lord, for he has taken us and will heal us; he will strike us and will cure us. He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence.”

Jerome explains this passage in Hosea as follows: “The Lord therefore strikes and heals us, because he reproves the one whom he loves and chastises every son whom he receives. And he not only heals us, but revives us after two days; and, rising from the dead on the third day, he raises the whole human race with himself. When he has healed those who were struck, revived those who were healed, and raised those who were revived, then we shall live in his presence, we who lay dead while he was absent” +. [Col. 1025C]

In this resurrection the benefit of our imitation is demonstrated, because “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him.”

The Tract follows: “He who dwells in the help of the Most High.”

In the preface to his exposition of the present psalm, Augustine shows how appropriately we ought to imitate Christ’s Passion through this psalm. “In what,” he says, “are we to imitate the ways of Christ? In that magnificence in which he was God in the flesh? Does he exhort us to this, or require from us that we perform the miracles he performed?”

And shortly afterward: “He does not say to you, ‘You will not be my disciple unless you walk upon the sea, or unless you raise a man who has been dead four days, or unless you open the eyes of one born blind.’” And shortly afterward: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart.” What happened for your sake, you must consider in him so that you may imitate it.

And shortly afterward: “He therefore does not exhort us even to the miracles that he himself performed before he became man. To what does he exhort you? To imitate what could not have been done unless he had become man. Could he have endured sufferings unless he were man? He could not have died, been crucified, or humbled himself unless he were man. Therefore, if you also suffer the troubles of this age, which the devil brings about either openly through human beings or secretly, as in the case of Job, be strong, [Col. 1026A] be patient; you will dwell in the help of the Most High, as this psalm says” +.

This Tract is long because, in what was promised to us in the reading from Hosea—where it says, “He will raise us up on the third day”—we must hold that we shall rise on the third day in hope, not yet in reality.

Hence Gregory writes in *On the Building of the Temple*: “For this reason another prophet saw the human race being raised at the end through the Lord’s resurrection and said: ‘He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence.’”

That resurrection is recalled at the end of the Tract: “I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation.”

Hence Augustine writes on the same psalm: “What is the length of days? Eternal life, brothers. Do not suppose that the length of days means days such as the longer days of summer. He has such days to give us. That length has no end: it is the eternal life promised to us.”

And shortly afterward: “‘I will show him my salvation.’ This, brothers, must not be passed over briefly. ‘I will show him my salvation’ means: ‘I will show him Christ himself.’”

And shortly afterward: “Do we still live by faith and not by sight? When will sight come? When shall we see face to face? This is what the Apostle says and what God promises us as the great reward for all our labors. Whatever you labor at, you labor for this: that you may see.”

And a little later: “He who was seen in humility will himself be seen in greatness, and he will assure us.”

Then the Passion follows. In it we see Christ himself, as it were, on the cross.

The Roman booklet reports what is to be done next, saying: “Immediately two deacons strip the altar of the cloth that had previously been placed beneath the Gospel, in the manner of a thief.” The altar, as we have often said, signifies our Lord, on which we offer our oblations to the Father; the vestments signify the apostles and all the saints.

It is fitting that something should lie beneath the Gospel for the sake of propriety. Once it has been removed, what was placed beneath it is carried away, because, after Christ had been handed over into the hands of the wicked, the apostles fled and hid themselves like thieves.

For what the altar signifies, the Gospel also signifies. In this cloth one may understand John in particular: he remained with the Lord until the cross, and heard, “Behold, your mother”; afterward, because of fear of the Jews, he concealed himself like a thief.

After this, the prayers are celebrated. Here it must be stated, on the authority of the Decretals of Pope Innocent, why Mass is not sung on Friday or Saturday. “For it is certainly established,” he says, “that during these two days the apostles were in sadness and mourning and hid themselves for fear of the Jews. There is no doubt that they fasted so rigorously during those two days that the tradition of the Church holds that the sacraments are not celebrated at all during them.” +

Only the prayers are read.

> [Note: [Col. 1025D] The words enclosed in brackets occurred in one copy; in the other three they were absent.]
>
> For this reason also Mass is not sung today, because on this day the Lord offered himself, and that offering itself is sufficient for the salvation of believers.

Here we shall fulfill what we promised on Wednesday concerning Saint Augustine. First I recall again that, when we are pursued by enemies, we should always return to prayer. Thus the psalm mentioned above says: “In return for their love they slandered me.” What does he say? “But I prayed.” He did not say what he prayed for, but what can we understand better than that he prayed for those very people?

They slandered the Crucified One most of all when, as though he were a man whom they had defeated, they mocked him. Concerning that cross he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

And shortly afterward: “It was nobler and more useful that he should offer an example of patience than that, by destroying his enemies without any delay, he should teach us to hurry impatiently to avenge ourselves on those whom we suffer as wicked, since it is written: ‘The patient person is better than the strong.’”

The divine utterances therefore teach us by the Lord’s example. When we hear: “In return for their love they slandered me, [Col. 1027B] but I prayed,” then, whenever we find people ungrateful—not merely failing to return good, but even returning evil for good—we should pray. They should pray for others, whether those others are raging, suffering, or in danger concerning the faith.

But first we should pray for ourselves, so that, by God’s mercy and assistance, we may conquer our own spirit, which is carried away by the desire for vengeance whenever we are slandered, whether in our presence or in our absence. Then, while we remember Christ’s patience—as though he himself had been awakened, just as happened when he slept in the boat, calming the disturbance and storm of our hearts—we should pray with a settled and peaceful mind even for our slanderers, so that we may confidently say: “Forgive us, as we also forgive.” This is what he did who certainly had no sin for which forgiveness was needed +.

With the firmest admonition, as we have been instructed, let us pray both for ourselves and for the dangers of this life, and for heretics, faithless Jews, and pagans.

Throughout all the prayers we kneel, so that by this posture of the body we may display humility of mind, except when we pray for the faithless Jews. They knelt, but practiced good works wickedly, because they did so in mockery. To show that we ought to flee works performed hypocritically, we avoid kneeling during the prayer for the Jews.

Similarly, during these days we abstain from the kiss of peace—not because the kiss of peace is evil when it is offered sincerely out of charity, but so that it may be shown what injury Christ suffered from his betrayer, and so that we too may avoid inflicting the same injury on our brothers.

What I mean is this: by word and deed we ought to show those under our authority that the evil of Judas must be avoided. Christ was handed over by a treacherous sign. It is therefore no wonder if we interrupt such practices, so that what belongs to us may be distinguished from Judaism, since Saint Augustine says: “For this reason our feast day and our Paschal celebration pass over to the Lord’s Day, so that our festival may be distinguished from the festival of the Jews.”

He says to Januarius: “For the Jews observe only the month of new moons and the moon from the fourteenth through the twenty-first day. But because their Passover, during which the Lord suffered, occurred in such a way that the day of the Sabbath came between his death and resurrection, our fathers judged that it should be added, so that our festival might also be distinguished from the festival of the Jews.” [Col. 1028A]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Adoration of the Holy Cross

After this, the aforementioned booklet instructs that a cross be prepared before the altar, which everyone salutes and kisses.

From the beginning, from the time when the Lord blessed it with his blood, the cross has been glorified by all the faithful in word and deed. Of the many glorifications with which it has been honored, I shall paint a few in the present work.

John Chrysostom says in his homily on the cross and the thief:

“The cross is the hope of Christians; the cross is the resurrection of the dead; the cross is the guide of the blind; the cross is the way of the despairing; the cross is the staff of the lame; the cross is the consolation of the poor; the cross is the restraint of the rich; the cross is the destruction of the proud; the cross is the punishment of those who live wickedly; the cross is triumph over demons; the cross is the defeat of the devil; the cross is the tutor of the young; the cross is the support of the needy; the cross is the hope of the despairing; the cross is the steersman of sailors; the cross is the harbor of those in danger; the cross is the wall of the possessed; the cross is the father of orphans; the cross is the defender of widows; the cross is the counselor of the just; the cross is the rest of the afflicted; the cross is the guardian of children; the cross is the head of men; the cross is the end of the old; the cross is the light of those sitting in darkness; the cross is the magnificence of kings; the cross is the perpetual shield; the cross is the wisdom of fools; the cross is the freedom of slaves; the cross is the philosophy of emperors; the cross is the law of the devout; the cross is the foreknowledge of prophets; the cross is the proclamation of apostles; the cross is the glorying of martyrs; the cross is the abstinence of monks; [Col. 1028C] the cross is the chastity of virgins; the cross is the joy of priests; the cross is the foundation of the Church; the cross is the protection of the whole world; the cross is the destruction of temples; the cross is the rejection of idols; the cross is the stumbling-block of the Jews; the cross is the ruin of the impious; the cross is the strength of the weak; the cross is the physician of the sick; the cross is the cleansing of lepers; the cross is the rest of the paralytics; the cross is the bread of the hungry; the cross is the fountain of the thirsty; the cross is the protection of the naked.”

Almost the whole glorification with which the holy cross is adorned is expressed in the prayers recited by the priest after the Gospel. If anyone wishes to examine what is prayed there and relate it to the present glorification, he will find it in the power of the holy cross.

Jerome likewise writes concerning it in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians: “The cross of Christ benefited not only us but also the angels and all the powers in heaven, and it disclosed a mystery that they had previously not known.”

Sedulius writes in the *Paschal Poem*:

> Let no one fail to know that the form of the cross is worthy of worship.

For the Son of God emptied himself so that he might appear visibly to human beings. On the day when the cross is kissed, he humbled himself for us before the Father unto death, and death on a cross. If we are to be imitators of this death, we must also be imitators of his humility.

Hence we prostrate ourselves before the cross, so that the fixed humility of the mind may be demonstrated through the posture of the body. We cannot display humility of mind more fully than by prostrating the whole body on the ground.

Hence Augustine writes on Psalm 43: “Whoever is humbled in such a way that he merely bends his knees still has something by which he may be humbled; but whoever is humbled so that his belly clings to the earth has nothing further by which he may be humbled.”

Thus I prostrate myself before the cross as Paula prostrated herself. Her panegyrist Jerome says of her in the little book on her life: “She prostrated herself before the cross as though she saw the Lord hanging there.”

And I, lying before the cross, hold in my heart that Christ suffered and was condemned for me; I adore the power of the holy cross, which it received from the Son of God. I do not worship any creature as God, but I venerate it; hence the Apostle says: “Outdoing one another in showing honor.”

Everything that is not God is a creature, and whatever is a creature is not God. With Christ’s cross placed before me, I hold Christ in my mind as though he were hanging upon it.

The very words of our prayer show whom we adore. We say: “We adore your cross, Lord, and we praise and glorify your holy resurrection.” These are not words of prayer, but of the public display of the cross’s worship and of the Lord’s resurrection’s glorification.

In another place we also customarily say: “O God, who in your mercy deigned to redeem the human race through the precious blood of your only-begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, graciously grant that those who come to adore the life-giving cross may be freed from the bonds of their sins.”

I pray to the one whom I adore; I prostrate my body before the cross and my mind before the Lord; I venerate the cross through which I was redeemed, but I pray to the one who redeemed me.

Concerning this adoration it is written in the *Tripartite History*, book one: “For this military standard was more precious than the others because it was customary for it to go before the emperor and to be worshiped by the soldiers.”

Again, in the same work, book two: “I have also heard of Probianus, a man serving in the palace among the physicians, who was afflicted with a cruel attack of gout and was there freed from his pains; and a holy vision wondrously appeared to him.

Although he had long been a pagan, after becoming a Christian he followed the doctrine to some extent; but he refused to adore the most sacred cross, the cause of complete salvation. To this man holding such an opinion, divine power appeared and showed him the sign of the cross that had been placed on the altar of his church. It plainly revealed that, since Christ was crucified, nothing done for the benefit of the human race had been accomplished in any way apart from the power of the holy cross, whether by holy angels or by devout human beings” +.

Some people wanted to say that they wished to adore that very cross on which the Lord was crucified. If only it were possessed by every church, it would rightly be venerated above all others. Although every church cannot possess it, the power of the holy cross is nevertheless not absent from those crosses made in the likeness of the Lord’s cross.

Thus we read in the *History of the English* about Oswald, a faithful and most Christian king. When he was in danger, he suddenly made a cross and fixed it in the ground. After adoring it and praying to God before it, he gave his people victory.

It is written in the aforementioned book, book three, chapter two:

“To this day the place is shown and held in great veneration where Oswald, as he was about to enter that battle, raised the sign of the holy cross and, bending his knees, prayed to God that, in such a great crisis, he might come to the aid of his worshipers with heavenly assistance.

It is said that, after quickly making the cross and preparing a pit in which it was to be set, he himself, burning with faith, seized it, placed it in the pit, and held it upright with both hands until the soldiers piled up earth and fixed it in place. When this had been done, he raised his voice and proclaimed to the whole army: ‘Let us all bend our knees and together pray to the living and true almighty God, that in his mercy he may defend us from the proud and savage enemy.’

For he himself said that we had justly undertaken the war for the salvation of our people. All did as he had commanded. Then, at the beginning of dawn, they advanced against the enemy and, according to the merit of their faith, gained the victory.

At the place of this prayer innumerable miracles of healing are known to have been performed, as a sign and memorial of his faith. Even to this day many people customarily cut small pieces from that sacred wood of the holy cross. When they place them in water and give it to sick people or animals to drink, or sprinkle them with it, they are immediately restored to health.”

Since we accept the other statements of the lord Bede, why should we not also accept this account, in which the Lord’s power is shown through veneration of the holy cross?

If anyone wishes to say that the matter concerning the wood of the holy cross did not happen as Bede relates, and if he is believed, he will be able to tear out many testimonies of the holy Scriptures—which God forbid.

And if anyone wishes to take offense at the event presently described, he appears to rebel against God, who granted this power to the wood of the holy cross: not merely to give his servant victory at that time, but also, in the time that followed, to perform miracles through the merits of the holy cross, as has been related in the present work.

If someone says, “Why do you not adore the donkey, since the Lord sat upon it, or other such things that the Lord touched with his body?” I answer, according to my limited understanding, that I do not read in the authority of the holy Fathers that miracles and healings were manifested through these things as they were through the power of the holy cross.

Nor do I know that I was redeemed through them as I was through the holy cross; nor that the devil’s works were so dispersed through them as through the cross; nor that the gates of hell were broken through them as through the cross; nor that the souls of the righteous were led into paradise through them as through the cross.

The devil, the woman, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil were the sword of our destruction. The grace of God, the Virgin who gave birth, the man, and the tree are the causes of our restoration—not the donkey, not the woman with the hemorrhage, not the stone, not the well from which the Samaritan woman drew water, nor other such things.

Yet birth would not have profited us unless death had profited us. For the Apostle did not say in vain: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come.”

I understand Adam as a type of the one to come in this way: just as the first Adam was the cause of our death, including for us who did not eat from the forbidden tree, so Christ is the cause of eternal life.

The devil approached Adam through the woman and killed him; he knocked at Adam’s door when he made his suggestion to Eve. Eve opened the door, and through her he entered to Adam, as suggestion passes through affection to consent.

The Lord’s grace approached the Virgin Mary and prepared for itself a dwelling in the man Christ; and the human race, which had been killed in Adam, came back to life.

Moreover, the devil, who had begun to reign through death in Adam, approached Christ and tempted him, trying to enter by the same entrances through which he had tempted the first Adam. He found no door by which to enter and was shut outside.

The first Adam received the command not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. If he obeyed the Lord in that command, he would possess the reward of obedience in eternal life—which he himself lost, and we through him.

By its nature the tree of the knowledge of good and evil did not contain death in itself; rather, it served as the occasion on which our parent’s obedience was tested or his disobedience punished. Just as that tree served as the occasion of testing, so the tree of life served as the occasion of eternal life.

Our Lord Jesus Christ brought this tree to us through the wood of the cross in our Church, so that we who were debtors to death through the tree of the knowledge of good and evil might be made capable of life through the wood of the holy cross.

For just as the tree of the knowledge of good and evil did not by its nature contain death, so the tree through which eternal life is granted to us does not possess this power from itself, but from the power of the one who, although he was weak in our nature, lives through the power of God—a power that can never and nowhere be resisted.

Death and the devil began to reign through disobedience concerning the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; that same death and devil were overcome through obedience concerning the wood of the holy cross.

For just as it pleased God to restore the human race through the same nature by which it had been lost—that is, through human nature—so he restored the power of obedience, which had been corrupted in Adam through the eating of the tree, through the abstinence of the one who was obedient to the Father on the wood of the cross.

Just as the obedience of the first Adam would have benefited everyone, had it continued until the reward at which the human race could no longer sin, so this obedience benefits everyone who looks toward it.

The first Adam was killed by the tree of the knowledge of good and evil with the sword of disobedience; the second Adam passed from the cross into eternal life by the palm of obedience, and led us with him.

What was originally destined for the first Adam through the tree of life—that he should live happily if he persevered in obedience to the Lord—has now been granted to us through the tree that Christ, obedient, planted in our Church.

Hence the cross is rightly called life-giving.

Adam’s destruction was dispersed through the four quarters of the world; Adam’s salvation embraced the four quarters of the world through the posture of his body upon the wood.

Hence Sedulius writes in the *Paschal Poem*:

> From there he gathers the four regions of the square world:
>
> The radiant East shines from the head of the Creator;
>
> The sacred feet are bathed by the western star.
>
> [Col. 1032A] His right hand holds the North (*Arcton*); his left raises the middle axis.
>
> All created nature lives from his limbs.

Let the whole world adore this holy cross, by which it has been redeemed, praying to the one who has the power to grant his power according to his will, in accordance with what he determined before the ages for each creature.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Presentation of the Lord’s Body on the Altar, and of the Chalice with Unconsecrated Wine
In the book mentioned above I found it written that, after the greeting of the cross, two presbyters should bring the Lord’s body, which had been reserved from the previous day, and a chalice with unconsecrated wine, which is then to be consecrated, and from it the people are to receive Communion. Concerning this observance I questioned the Roman archdeacon, and he replied: “At that station where the apostolicus greets the cross, no one receives Communion. Whoever, following the order of the little book, consecrates wine by the commingling of consecrated bread and wine does not observe the tradition of the Church, concerning which Innocent says that during these two days the sacraments are not celebrated at all.” The shepherd has been struck down; the sheep of the flock have been scattered. The shepherds who appear to be in the Church, by their abandonment of their office, display the condition of that time which was then being enacted among Christ’s disciples. For the Lord said on the preceding day: “I shall not drink of this fruit of the vine until I drink it anew with you”—which shows that the passage read on the Monday after the Lord’s Pasch was enacted, when Peter says: “We who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead.”

The proper order is for us to wait until our Lord consecrates the sacraments of his body and blood on the cross and makes them new through his resurrection; and then at last we should eat and drink that most wholesome sacrament—not now having eaten beforehand, as the apostles did at the Lord’s Supper, but fasting. And in this order, after the greeting of the cross, each person ought to return to his own place.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the eighth variation, which occurs on the Sabbath

The eighth variation occurs on Holy Saturday. Yesterday we reported from the decretals of Pope Innocent that Mass is not celebrated today; we have found this to be so from today’s office, which illumines the whole coming night. We ought to learn this from the first consecration of the candle, which says: “This is the night in which, when the bonds of death had been destroyed.” And again: “This is the night of which it is written: ‘The night will be illuminated like the day.’”

Vigils are to be held at night, as we recall on the authority of the Fathers. Augustine says in his sermon to the people at the Easter vigils:

“It must be said why, with such great solemnity, we celebrate vigils especially on this night. No Christian doubts that the Lord Christ rose from the dead on the third day. But that this happened on this night, the holy Gospel bears witness.”

And shortly afterward:

“We spend that night in vigilance on which the Lord rose, and we meditate on that life of which we were speaking a little earlier, where there is neither death nor sleep, and which he began for us in his flesh, raising it from the dead in such a way that he no longer dies and death no longer rules over him.”

And again:

“To him, when he has risen, we sing for a little longer in vigilant celebration; he will grant that we may reign with him by living forever.”

“But even if, during the hours in which we keep this vigil, his body was still in the tomb and had not yet risen, we are nevertheless not keeping vigil inappropriately, because he slept so that we might keep vigil; he died so that we might live.”

Jerome identifies the precise hour of the vigils in his Commentaries on Matthew, saying:

“It is a tradition of the Jews that Christ will come in the middle of the night, in the manner of the Egyptian time: when the Passover was celebrated, the destroyer came, and the Lord passed over the tents, and the doorposts of our foreheads were consecrated with the blood of the Lamb. Hence I think that the apostolic tradition has also continued, so that on the day of the Easter vigils the people may not be dismissed before midnight, as they await the coming of Christ; and after that time has passed, with confidence assumed, let everyone celebrate the feast-day.”

## CHAPTER XVII. On blessing lambs made of wax

The Roman little book relates that on this same day wax mixed with oil is blessed, and lambs are made from it and kept until the octave of Easter. At the octave, after Communion, incense made from these is given to the people for burning and for fumigating their houses. It likewise relates that we ought to do the same with the consecrated candle.

For wax signifies Christ’s humanity, as Gregory says in his homilies. The honeycomb, indeed, is honey in wax; and honey in wax is divinity in humanity. + The lambs made by the Romans signify the immaculate Lamb made for us.

Christ must be brought back to our memory more frequently through all things, as Augustine says to Januarius:

“Nevertheless, fools who do not wish these things to be changed for the better should not therefore think that these lights ought to be worshiped, because at times a likeness is drawn from them to represent divine mysteries. For a likeness is drawn from every creature.”

+ When we see a lamb made of wax, the Lamb prefigured and sacrificed at Easter is brought back to our memory. Saint Gregory poured oil over it when he disclosed the mysteries of the Paschal Lamb.

## CHAPTER XVIII. [Col. 1033D] On blessing the candle

Since the Romans act in this way, we too have been commanded by Pope Zosimus to bless the candle. As we have said, wax signifies Christ’s humanity. This candle is intended to possess a unity of meaning with the pillar of fire that illuminated the people of Israel at night. Hence it is said in the consecration of the candle:

“This, then, is the night which dispelled the darkness of sins through the illumination of the pillar.”

And shortly afterward:

“But now we know the praises of this pillar, which the shining fire kindled in honor of God.”

That pillar prefigured Christ, concerning which Jerome says in the Book of the Stations:

“They moved their camps from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month. On the following day after the Passover the children of Israel went out with an exalted hand.”

And shortly afterward:

“In the first month, when winter had passed and gone away, when spring begins, when all things are renewed, we go out on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day after Passover, in the full light of the month, after eating the immaculate lamb.”

And again:

“And setting out from the land of Rameses, the children of Israel encamped at Succoth.”

And a little later:

“Setting out from Succoth, they encamped at Etham, which is at the edge of the wilderness. The third station is offered after the tents; in it the Lord is first seen at night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud, so that he may go before the people and become the guide of their journey. Etham signifies for us strength and perfection.”

And again:

“Let us prepare strength for ourselves; let us assume perfect vigor, so that amid the darkness of error and the confusion of night the light of Christ may appear. Let our day also have a protecting cloud, so that under these guides we may be able to reach the holy land.”

For the pillar of cloud is also understood as representing the Holy Spirit, as Gregory Nazianzen says in his sermon on the Second Epiphany:

“Moses baptized in the sea and in the cloud, but in type and figure; for so Paul declares. The sea, therefore, had the form of water, while the cloud had the form of the Holy Spirit.”

One part of the pillar, in which the cloud is said to have dwelt, protected the people of God; the other part illuminated them. For it is written concerning the Holy Spirit: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you”; and what overshadows also protects.

If the shining candle signifies that humanity which illuminated every person coming into this world, then certainly [Col. 1034C] we must also understand in the same candle the person of the Holy Spirit, who overshadows the chaste body so that it is not defiled by the heat of desire.

This candle, which prefigures Christ’s humanity, is blessed while illuminated, because Christ’s humanity, after it was assumed by divinity, was always illuminated. It is always blessed for this reason. + That pillar went before the children of Israel before they crossed the Red Sea; our pillar, namely the candle, should go before our catechumens. Its light signifies the light of Christ, by which both the present night is illuminated—namely, by the grace of the resurrection—and the catechumens who are to come to baptism.

The readings that are read before baptism signify this illumination, as will be shown below. The candle is therefore blessed because, unless by the blessing of the minister, it cannot pass from its simple nature into the mysteries. The pillar of fire was itself a mystery.

That it is blessed by a deacon follows Roman custom; for the archdeacon makes the lambs there. This candle goes before the bishop, who is the head of the people, for eight days on behalf of the neophytes, because the pillar of fire went before the people as far as the promised land.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the readings

We have said that the light of Christ is signified by the light of the candle, by which the catechumens are illuminated. Now, with the Lord’s mercy, the manner of this illumination must be explained, so that the journey toward baptism may proceed in an orderly and illuminated way.

The teacher of catechumens ought to be a companion at table with catechumens. Christ did this when he feasted with tax collectors and sinners, in order to bring them over into himself.

This was said to Peter in the Acts of the Apostles when a linen vessel was sent down to him from heaven: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” Bede explains it in the same Acts:

“Rise,” he says, “and prepare yourself to evangelize; kill among the Gentiles what they once were, and make them what you are. For whoever eats food placed outside transfers it into his own body.”

The divine voice therefore commanded that the nations, placed outside the door through unbelief, should be joined to the fellowship of the Church, which Peter signifies, after their former life had been slain.

This teaching is signified by the table in the Mosaic tabernacle, which has four feet, because, as Bede says in his book On the Tabernacle, the whole sequence of divine utterances is distinguished according to a fourfold method. Here, I ask you to consider carefully what correspondence the four readings, the songs, and the prayers performed for the instruction of the catechumens have with the four feet of the table.

The same author, in the work mentioned above, says:

“The table of the tabernacle has four feet because the words of the heavenly oracle are customarily understood either historically, or allegorically, or tropologically—that is, morally—or, certainly, anagogically. History is present when some event is reported in plain speech according to how it was literally done or said.”

Let us see whether the first reading corresponds to this foot. Is not what is written there concerning the creation of humanity held according to the historical sense? We certainly believe it to be so, as it is written there:

“Let us make man in our image and likeness, and let him rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the heavens.”

And again:

“He created them male and female.”

And, as it is narrated there, we believe that humanity was made on the sixth day.

The priest prays to God, who wondrously created and redeemed humanity, that the catechumen, who was made in the image of God—that is, with the reasoning power of the mind—may resist the allurements of the world.

It is the teacher’s duty first to instruct the catechumen concerning his formation, then concerning how he fell, provided that he does not consent to carnal things, like Adam to Eve, and that he can be restored to his first formation. From the teacher he receives instruction; from the priest, confirmation is obtained.

The second reading reports in plain speech how the people of Israel were saved from Egypt. Since in the preceding reading the catechumen heard about his own formation, in this one he should hear about his redemption from the masters to whom he sold himself through his sins. He should hear that, just as the Lord freed the people of Israel from the hand of Pharaoh, whom he destroyed in the Red Sea, so he too can free him from the hand of the devil through the water of baptism.

The song of victory follows it: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified.” A song demonstrates great devotion of spirit, which those who are particularly devout are accustomed to perceive, while no general response is made to them. The devout spirit rejoices because it sees devout catechumens through God’s calling, and it sees this from the disposition produced by the teaching.

One song follows these two readings because both stand at the first foot of the table, that is, in allegory. Or the first reading is not followed by a song because in it the parent is intimated in whom all sinned.

The priest confirms the teacher’s instruction by praying in this way: what you conferred on one people by freeing it from Egyptian persecution through the right hand of your power, accomplish now for the salvation of the nations through the water of regeneration. Grant that the fullness of the whole world may pass into the sons of Abraham and into Israelite dignity.

Let us move on to the second foot of the table. The same author mentioned above says in the same work:

“Allegory is present when, through mystical words or events, the present mysteries of Christ and the Church are signified.” +

Let us consider the third reading. Although it is third in the order of the readings, because of the mysteries it contains it is joined to the second foot of the table. In it we have the mysteries of Christ and the Church:

“Seven women shall take hold of one man on that day, saying: ‘We shall eat our own bread.’”

According to the historical sense, we do not read that this event happened; but we know it to be fulfilled in Christ, whom the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit took hold of.

Hence Jerome says in his Commentary on Isaiah:

“At the coming of our Lord and Savior, the seven women—that is, the seven graces of the Holy Spirit, concerning which the same prophet will say in what follows, ‘A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root,’ and so forth—”

And shortly afterward:

“They shall take hold of Jesus, whom they had desired for a very long time, because they could find no other in whom they could rest in an eternal dwelling.” +

Here you have the mystery of Christ. Hear also the mystery of the Church:

“When the Lord has washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the blood of Jerusalem from her midst by the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning.”

The same author, in the same work, says:

“Notice that he washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion by the spirit of judgment, but the blood of Jerusalem by the spirit of burning. What is light is washed; what is heavier is burned.”

Concerning this spirit of judgment and spirit of burning, John the Baptist spoke in the Gospel:

“I baptize you with water; but he who comes after me will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire.”

From this we learn that a human being contributes only water, while God contributes the Holy Spirit, by whom filth is washed away and the sins of blood are purged. +

Here you have the mysteries of the Church. Here the catechumens are shown what they ought to love, so that they may be like the seven women who took hold of one man; and what baptism benefits them: namely, that lesser and greater sins may be cleansed through the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning.

The song “A vineyard was made” follows this reading, and it contains the mystery of the Synagogue. If the Synagogue is not now joined to the man Christ, it will be when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered.

Because of these two mysteries—that is, of the Church and of the Synagogue—the priest prays, saying:

“O God, who instruct us through the pages of both Testaments to celebrate the Paschal mystery, grant us to understand your mercy.”

What the teacher taught—that the Gentiles receive remission of sins through Christianity, and the Jewish people, which is called the vineyard of Soreth, when it becomes the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth, the house of Israel—that is, the man who sees the Lord—the priest prays that the Church may understand this same mercy by which remission takes place and may say: “Show us, O Lord, your mercy.”

Let us seek the third foot of the table. Bede says in the same work, as above:

“Tropological—that is, moral—speech concerns the formation and correction of conduct, whether expressed in open or figurative language.”

It is fitting that after the catechumens have been taught about the cleansing of baptism, they should be instructed concerning conduct.

The fourth reading says:

“Listen, you who listen to me, and eat what is good, and your soul shall delight in abundance. Incline your ear and come to me; listen, and your soul shall live, and I shall make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David.”

Jerome explains this in the same work on Isaiah:

“Divine speech promises them not the goods of the flesh but those of the soul. For if you listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land—or ‘the Good One,’ who says, ‘I am the good shepherd’—and your soul shall delight in good things and in abundance.”

Therefore the good things promised to souls are not riches, bodily health, or the dignities of this world—things which even philosophers call indifferent, that is, neither good nor evil, and which vary according to the character of those who use them—but those things are to be believed in which God exhorts us: “Turn away from evil and do good,” and so forth.

This is what he wishes to teach who says, “Listen, you who listen to me”: let the catechumen turn away from evil conduct and do good. And again:

“Let the wicked man abandon his ways, and the unjust man his thoughts, and let him return to the Lord.”

Just as the first two readings, because of their historical narrative, are concluded by one song, so this one is expanded into two because of two things joined to one another: namely, good conduct and the heavenly homeland.

Hence the Prophet says:

“His soul shall dwell in good things, and his offspring shall inherit the earth.”

And in some places the same words as those in the reading are almost found in the songs. The reading says:

“All you who thirst, come to the waters.”

The song says:

“My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain.”

The reading says:

“I shall make with you an everlasting covenant, the faithful mercies of David.”

The song says:

“Faithful is God, in whom there is no iniquity.”

The reading says:

“And just as rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but soak the earth and water it,” and so forth.

The song says:

“Let the earth hear the words of my mouth; let my speech be awaited like rain,” and “let my words descend like dew.”

Through these words evangelical teaching is shown. The teacher prays that it may be poured over the catechumens; afterward he admonishes them not to remain silent, but to declare what they have in their hearts, and he says:

“Give greatness to our God,” and so forth.

They are already at the very entrance of the baptismal doorway. The priest, sensing from the devotion of their spirit that they have been called by the Lord, prays for their continual protection, saying:

“Mercifully grant that those whom you wash with the water of baptism you may guard with continual protection.”

In the fourth song let us hold to the fourth foot of the table. Bede says in the same work:

“Anagogy—that is, speech whose meaning leads upward—is language that discusses future rewards and the life that is to come in heaven, whether in mystical or open expressions.”

Let us hear what the catechumens say after the teacher’s admonition:

“As the deer longs for springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God.”

Augustine explains it as follows:

“And indeed it is not wrongly understood as the voice of those who, although they are catechumens, hasten toward the grace of the holy washing. Hence this psalm is also sung solemnly, so that they may desire the fountain of the forgiveness of sins as the deer desires springs of water.”

“My soul thirsted for the living God.”

The same author mentioned above continues:

“What did it thirst for? ‘When shall I come and appear before the face of God?’ This is what I thirst for: to come and appear. I thirst in pilgrimage; I thirst in the course of my journey; I shall be satisfied at his coming. But when shall I come? For what is swift to God is slow to desire. ‘When shall I come and appear before the face of God?’ From that desire also comes what is cried elsewhere: ‘One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.’ Everything sounds anagogical.”

The priest prays for this same thing: that, as we celebrate the Paschal feast, inflamed by heavenly desires, we may thirst for the fountain of life.

Between these two songs no reading is necessary because, as we said earlier, one who remains in good conduct has only to learn heavenly things. Nevertheless, because the reading and the two songs correspond, they may suitably be joined without another reading.

## CHAPTER XX. On the two candles

We have said that the consecrated candle signifies Christ’s humanity, and that we use it in place of the pillar of fire to which we have joined the readings. Indeed, its light signifies Christ’s teaching, who is the fountain of all wisdom; by it the darkness of the catechumens has been driven away.

This candle is therefore lit with new fire to signify Christ’s new teaching, which is found in the New Testament, or the new grace by which the night was uniquely illuminated on the Lord’s Day, namely through Christ’s resurrection.

Another candle is also added in the little book mentioned above, where it says:

“And then two candles are illuminated, held by two notaries,” and so forth.

We, however, wish to observe this order with the greatest care, because Christ, the true light that illuminates every person coming into this world, said to the choir of the apostles: “You are the light of the world.”

Let the consecrated candle stand for the person of Christ; let the other candle, illuminated by the first candle, stand for the choir of the apostles. Let both be in the church; let both go before our catechumens to baptism; let them go before us to the promised land.

We must observe with the greatest care the institution of Christ and of the apostles. Christ illuminates the Church by himself, and he also illuminates it through the apostles.

Hence Augustine, in his letter to Januarius, when he explains to him why we receive Communion fasting although the apostles received it without fasting, says:

“For the Savior, in order to commend more forcefully the greatness of that mystery, wished to impress this final act upon the hearts and memory of the disciples from whom he was departing for his passion. For this reason he did not prescribe the order in which it should henceforth be received, so that the apostles, through whom he was going to establish the Churches, might preserve this place.”

We have introduced teachers of the catechumens in two variations: on the Wednesday after the middle of Lent, when they were taught about faith and conduct, and on the present day, when they are instructed more perfectly. In these two variations I do not think that the teachers’ instruction differs, since our life depends on these two things.

Hence Bede says in his book On the Tabernacle:

“Our life in the present consists in faith and right action.”

For this reason the teacher’s work is repeated today: so that, if what the catechumens once learned has perhaps slipped away through forgetfulness, or if some have not yet attended, they may be instructed more fully today.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the pronouncing of the readings at the vigils of Easter and at the vigils of Pentecost

We are bound to speak in the Church to three classes of subjects: namely, to the wise, to the foolish, and to our own household members.

Paul speaks of the wise and the foolish in his Letter to the Romans:

“I am a debtor,” he says, “to the wise and to the foolish.”

Concerning household members he says to the Corinthians:

“Besides those things that are external, there is my daily pressure, the concern for all the Churches.”

By the daily pressure, which he calls concern for all the Churches, he indicates the instruction he gave every day to those who lived with him.

The condition of night, in which we read as though to the foolish, shows the hearts of the foolish, who need to have light from outside. We have both in our church, the wise and the foolish. It is more fitting, however, for the catechumens to be compared with the foolish than with the wise.

Because of this pronouncing that we perform at the vigils of Easter and Pentecost, we touch on these matters so that we may know why the reading is pronounced one way in the office of the Mass and another way in this office. If the Lord grants it, we shall speak more fully about this in the daytime and nighttime offices.

Because of the blindness of heart of the catechumens, who are foolish, we compared their readings with the condition of night. As the reading is pronounced at night, so it should be pronounced in the presence of the catechumens.

The little book of which we have often spoken, which contains the Roman Order, says:

“The reading from the book of Genesis is not pronounced, nor the reading from the book of Exodus, and similarly with the others.”

If this is observed, it seems to us that it can have the following rationale: the same readings should be pronounced to those who, as wise people, know the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, so that, out of love for the sweetness of the name of their fellow citizen, they may drink in the reading more eagerly.

But to these others—namely, the catechumens, who do not yet know the citizens of Jerusalem—it is useless to present an unknown author, since a very firm authority can become worthless to those who are ignorant of it.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the songs

Suppose that the catechumens are soon to belong to the company of the hundred and forty-four thousand who sing the new song, which no one can utter except that one. The priest prays for this on their behalf in the Sacramentary:

“And that, reborn from the spotless womb of the divine font into a new creation, a heavenly offspring may emerge; and that all whom sex in the body or age in time distinguishes, one grace may give birth to a single infancy.”

And in what follows:

“That every person who enters this sacrament of regeneration may be reborn into the new infancy of true innocence.”

Because of the future renewal into true innocence, the cantor now sings, as though what is soon to come had already happened, songs on their behalf which the others, who have been stained after emerging from the womb of baptism, cannot sing.

Thus, as it seems to us, the reading is like the form given by teachers; the song is like the goodwill of the hearer; and the prayer of the priest and the people, who respond “Amen,” is the confirmation of the preceding goodwill.

It belongs to the singer alone, in the sight of the Lord, to rejoice above the others in the innocence with which infants are undoubtedly clothed in baptism.

Although, because they are sung, these may be called songs, nevertheless in the books from which these excerpts have been taken they are called poems or songs.

Of the first it is written:

“Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the Lord and said, ‘Let us sing to the Lord.’”

Of the second Isaiah says:

“I shall sing to my beloved the song of my kinsman concerning his vineyard.”

“A vineyard was made,” and so forth.

Of the third it is written in Deuteronomy:

“Moses wrote this song and taught it to the children of Israel.”

Although the fourth is not entitled “a song” in the Psalter, we have it called a song by Augustine, a most learned man. For he wrote in the preface to the song “As the Deer”:

“The body of Christ is the Church, and such desire is not found in all who enter the Church. Nevertheless, whoever has tasted the sweetness of the Lord and recognizes what is pleasing to him finds it in the song.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the anointing with oil on Holy Saturday

The scrutiny has its own little work, and therefore we ought to pass over it, especially since it has already been performed. But because we found our dearest ones along the way, we cannot pass them by without, at least for the sake of seeing them, giving them a kiss. Accordingly, we now wish to speak about the anointing with oil.

It is said in the Sacramentary:

“On Easter Saturday, for those reciting”—the lord pope says after πιστέφειν [Greek: “to believe”]—“First it must be said, ‘Let them recite’; and afterward, what the pope says.”

Indeed, the reading which they received on the Wednesday after the middle of Lent they recite today.

The pope begins:

“Nor are you unaware, Satan, that punishments threaten you.”

And shortly afterward:

“Give honor to the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, and withdraw from these servants and handmaids of God.”

This is the pope’s exorcism; it preceded the consecration of the oil.

Concerning this office Gregory says in his homilies:

“For holy Church daily performs spiritually what it then performed bodily through the apostles. When her priests, through the grace of exorcism, lay a hand upon believers and forbid evil spirits to dwell in their minds, what else do they do but cast out demons?”

The Sacramentary continues:

“After this he touches each one’s nostrils and ears and says to them, ‘Ephphatha’ [‘Be opened’].”

This office was mentioned beforehand on the Wednesday referred to, but perhaps it is found here because some had not yet come, or because some who had come had lost through negligence what they had received.

The same Sacramentary continues:

“Afterward he touches the shoulders and breast with holy oil.”

As we said earlier, this oil pertains to the gift of God’s grace, concerning which Paul said:

“To one, faith in the same Spirit.”

Oil is applied to the shoulders and breast for the protection of mind and body. Among weapons of defense, the shield usually holds its place. The same Apostle places faith among the other virtues as a shield, saying:

“Taking up the shield of faith.”

The devil corrupts us through evil thoughts and deeds. Therefore we are armed with the oil of exorcism, that is, with the shield of faith, on the shoulders, which are suited to carrying burdens. Through the shoulders we can understand works, so that, once the devil’s works have been expelled, they may have no place to return.

Likewise, the oil is applied to the breast as a protection for thoughts. The external anointing shows what the Holy Spirit accomplishes within at the priest’s invocation.

And he says:

“Do you renounce Satan”—that is, the devil whom you held in your mouth through the sacrifice of idols?

Again:

“And all his works?”

Some of these are carnal, such as the pleasure of the flesh, to which excessive food and drink and every kind of lust belong; others are spiritual, such as pride, envy, and the rest.

Because of these carnal things, so that they may be absent, the shoulders are anointed; because of the spiritual things, so that they may be present to the mind, the breast is anointed.

It continues:

“And all his pomps.”

To put it briefly, by this I understand all vain and excessive honors. I will offer one example from many. When an emperor or a powerful man goes to Mass on feast days, among the other displays of pomp a horse adorned with gold and silver is led with him; no one sits upon it as he goes and returns.

There is pomp; there is honor rendered in vain.

A promise has been made, and so that it may remain firm it must be entrusted to the grace of God, as though to a kind of oil. Concerning this promise the same author says in the passages mentioned above:

“On the day of baptism we promised to renounce all the works of the ancient enemy and all his pomps.”

Therefore let each of you turn the eyes of his mind back upon himself, and if after baptism he keeps what he promised before baptism, let him rejoice, certain that he is now faithful.

Has the former guest been expelled through the present renunciation? Let the second enter through the confession of faith.

Although the confession of faith is questioned after the water has been consecrated, it will nevertheless be recited here by us because of the continuity between the expulsion of the former guest and the introduction of the second.

The priest says:

“Do you believe in God the Father almighty?”

The person questioned confesses that he believes.

Behold, the entrance for the second guest is already prepared through faith.

Afterward, when asked whether he believes in the Son, he answers that he does.

Behold, the entrance of divine works.

For this reason God became human: so that he could address us and show us the works of his will.

After this it is said:

“Do you believe in the Holy Spirit?”

He answers that he believes.

The pomps having been expelled, the true gifts of the Holy Spirit, which Isaiah enumerates, are adopted.

## CHAPTER XXIV. It is demonstrated from the Gospel that catechumens can be saved through the confession of the other faithful

[Col. 1042A]

It is written in the Gospel of Mark that a Syrophoenician woman came to Christ, asking on behalf of her daughter, who had an unclean spirit. The Lord said to her: “Let the children be satisfied first; for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” But she answered and said to him: “Yes, Lord. For even the little dogs under the table eat from the children’s crumbs.” And he said to her: “Because of this saying, go; the demon has gone out of your daughter.”

This Syrophoenician woman prefigured the Church, which daily beseeches the Lord on behalf of her daughter, who is not yet Christian, and offers her faith on her behalf, since, because of her infancy, she is still [Col. 1042B] unable to speak. Yet we believe that she is saved, in accordance with the Gospel saying through the mother’s speech: “When she heard this, because of this saying”—that is, the saying uttered by the mother in humility and faith—“the demon went out from the daughter.” Thus we believe that, through the confession of those who bring an infant to the fonts, demons are expelled from catechumens. That the daughter was saved by the mother’s faith Matthew plainly relates, when the Lord says: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.” And her daughter was healed from that hour.

Accordingly, we find it written in the book which Bede composed on Mark: “Because of the mother’s humble and faithful saying, the demon abandoned the daughter.” Here an example is given for the catechizing and baptizing of infants, since, through the faith and confession of their parents, little children are delivered from the devil in baptism, although they are not yet able by themselves to understand or think anything good or evil.

From this it may be understood that an adult, who can speak, should utter his confession with his own mouth. Others therefore offer the confession on behalf of infants because the infants themselves cannot speak. Concerning this, Augustine says in his letter to Bishop Boniface, in response to an inquiry about infants:

“You ask me whether parents harm their baptized infants when they try to heal them by sacrifices to demons; and, if they do not harm them, how the parents’ faith can benefit them when they are baptized, since the parents’ faithlessness cannot harm them. To this I reply that the power of that sacrament—that is, of saving baptism—is so great within the holy fellowship of Christ’s body that one who was once generated through another’s bodily will, when he has once been regenerated through another’s spiritual will, cannot thereafter be bound by the bond of another’s iniquity, since he consented to it by no will of his own.

“For if, according to Saint Augustine, an infant is regenerated in baptism through another’s will, no one ought to find it incredible that he is saved through another’s faith. For, as is clear to everyone, an infant cannot possess the wisdom of faith, since he does not yet understand or comprehend; and, as I plainly see, he is not very far removed in behavior from the animals. The infant has a soul, which gives life to the body, and animals have this as well. He has memory, but the kind of memory animals possess—that is, memory which enters the soul through bodily sensation. Nevertheless, in his other activities, how far he is separated from them, or not separated from them, can easily be discerned. Nor is it surprising if an infant who is bound by another’s sin is absolved through another’s faith.”

The aforementioned Augustine shows in what follows, in the same work addressed to the person mentioned above, why an infant is regenerated through another’s will:

“But in order that he may be regenerated through the service of another’s will, when he is brought to receive consecration, one Spirit accomplishes this—the Spirit by whom the one brought is regenerated. For it is not written: ‘Unless one has been born again through the will of his parents,’ or ‘through the faith of those who bring or minister’; rather, it is written: ‘Unless one has been born again of water and the Spirit.’ Water, therefore, outwardly exhibiting the sacrament of grace, and the Spirit inwardly effecting the benefit of grace.”

Here it is clearly shown that the Church of Saint Augustine followed the custom of our confession: namely, that the minister offers his faith on behalf of the infant when he says: “For it is not written: ‘Unless one has been born again through the will of his parents, or through the faith of those who bring or minister.’” He says this so that we may understand that the infant is not delivered by the will or faith of those who bring him, but by the Holy Spirit, who is common to the adults who bring him and to the infants who are regenerated. Nevertheless, for this to happen—that is, for the infant to be saved through the work of the Holy Spirit—the will and faith of those who bring him are of great importance.

A little later the aforementioned Augustine says in the same letter:

“Therefore the regenerating Spirit is common to the adults who bring the infant and to the infant who is brought and regenerated; and so, through participation in one and the same Spirit, the will of those who bring him benefits the infant who is brought. In a certain sense the infant is said to have faith because of the sacrament of faith, and to turn toward God because of the sacrament of conversion, since a likeness of faith and a likeness of conversion have been enacted in him.”

For the same reason the same author says in the letter mentioned above:

“For if certain sacraments did not possess a likeness of the things whose sacraments they are, they would not be sacraments at all. From this likeness they often already receive the names of the things themselves. Therefore, just as, in a certain manner, the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood, so also the sacrament of faith is faith. To believe is nothing other than to have faith. Accordingly, when it is answered that infants believe, although they do not possess the disposition of faith, the answer means that they have faith because of the sacrament of faith, and turn toward God because of the sacrament of conversion. For the answer itself belongs to the celebration of the sacrament, just as the Apostle says concerning baptism itself: ‘We were buried with Christ through baptism into death’ … He did not say, ‘We signified burial,’ but plainly said, ‘We were buried.’ Thus he named the sacrament of so great a reality by the name of that very reality.”

+ Through the sacrament, indeed, the infant possesses a likeness, as though the infant himself were answering; from the mouth of those who bring him, he possesses, in a certain manner, faith. Just as, because of the likeness of the Lord’s burial which we receive in baptism, we enact the reality itself—that is, burial—so, through the response of the parents or those who bring the infant, who enact a likeness of the infants’ believing, faith is enacted in the infants.

For we customarily name the infant and say to him: “Do you believe in God the Father?” And the one who brings him answers: “I believe.” It has already been sufficiently demonstrated above, from evangelical testimony, that the faith of the one who brings the infant can save him. From Augustine also we can understand that the same infant answers through the voice of the one who brings him, where Augustine says: “One Spirit accomplishes this, by whom the one brought is generated”; and where the same Augustine argues from the similarity of the sacraments to the realities whose sacraments they are, saying that, when it is answered that infants believe, they do not possess the disposition of faith.

From this we can understand that, through the likeness of the response—as though the infant himself were answering—the sacrament of faith is celebrated in the infant. Elsewhere Augustine says: “Just as they answer that they believe, so also they are called faithful.”

+ Thus I believe that, because of the work of the one Holy Spirit, what the one who brings the infant answers belongs to the one whom he brings. Saint Augustine would not so often have spoken of the sacrament of faith unless there were some effect between the reality itself and its likeness—that is, between the sacrament of faith, which may be called faith, and the faith itself which a person expresses from an understanding soul. For just as there is a difference between our burial, which we receive in baptism, and Christ’s burial, from which he rose from the dead never again to die, so there is a difference between the sacrament of faith and faith itself. Nevertheless, the sacraments themselves serve to lead us to the realities of which they are the sacraments.

Through the sacrament of faith the infant is saved until the time when he can learn his faith. Accordingly, the same author, in what follows in the same letter addressed to the person mentioned above, says:

“Therefore, although the infant does not yet possess that faith which consists in the will of believers, the sacrament of that very faith already makes him faithful. For just as it is answered that he believes, so also he is called faithful—not by assenting to the reality itself, but by receiving the sacrament of that reality. But when a person begins to understand, he does not repeat that sacrament; rather, he understands it, and his will is also conformed to its truth. As long as he cannot do this, the sacrament serves for his protection against hostile powers. It serves so fully that, if he should depart this life before attaining the use of [mature] reason, then, through that sacrament and through the charity of the Church’s commendation, he is freed by Christian assistance from the condemnation which entered the world through one man.”

Whoever does not believe this, and thinks that it cannot happen, is unbelieving, even if he possesses the sacrament of faith. That infant is far better than such a person who, although he does not yet possess faith in his thoughts, nevertheless does not place in the way of faith the obstacle of an opposing thought.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the consecration of the baptistery

In the first prayer, the dwelling of the guest who is to receive God is cleansed and made serene, and his arrival is entreated, as we can understand from the prayer itself. “Almighty, eternal God,” it says, “be present to the mysteries of your great mercy; be present to the sacraments,” and so forth.

In the following prayer he shows that he already has a guest to whom he may speak; therefore he says: “Lift up your hearts” [Col. 1045A]. Then he gives thanks because such a great guest has deigned to descend to so humble a dwelling, as the same prayer demonstrates: “And although,” he says, “we are unworthy to perform such great mysteries,” and so forth.

Then he recalls the miracles which have already been accomplished through water. At the beginning of creation, the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters, so that the nature of the waters might conceive the power of sanctification. He also relates another event, namely what happened at the saving of the ark.

Thus it is written in the prayer mentioned above:

“O God, who, by washing away through the waters the crimes of the guilty world, marked out the likeness of regeneration in the very outpouring of the flood,” and so forth.

Afterward the priest proceeds to the expulsion of the devil, saying:

“Therefore, at your command, Lord, let every unclean spirit depart far from here,” and so forth.

[Col. 1045B] The priest shows by his blowing how much disgrace the guest of the water deserves, so that what the Lord said may be fulfilled: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out” [John 12:31]. Once that guest has been expelled, the water is fortified with the sign of the cross, so that the devil may have no place to return.

Through the invocation of the Holy Trinity, following the example of Christ’s baptism, the Trinity is present in our baptistery through the priest’s invocation.

The first blessing invokes the Father and says:

“I bless you, creature of water, through the living God, through the holy God, who in the beginning separated you from the dry land by his word,” and the rest.

The Son is present in the second blessing:

“I bless you also through Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, who by the wonderful sign of his power changed you into wine at Cana of Galilee” [Col. 1045C], and the rest.

The Holy Spirit is introduced at the end. The entire prayer is a petition that, just as the Lord caused water to obey his commands in the miracles mentioned above, so now, at his command, it may become suitable not only for washing bodies but also for cleansing the mind. As the following words say, beyond the natural cleansing which water can provide for washing bodies, it should also be effective for purifying minds.

At this point—that is, after the priest has said, “In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—the voice changes, as though to a reading that is to be read.

In the present prayer there is a humble petition, or some preparation of the mind for obtaining the coming of the Holy Spirit into the water. Just as in the first prayer God was entreated to come into the priest’s mind, so in what follows the power of the Holy Spirit is entreated to come into the nature of the water.

Thus the priest says: “As we observe these commandments,” as though he were saying: “We do not dare, through our own presumption, to invoke such great power upon the nature of the water, but by the command of our Lord, who ordered us to administer baptism.”

Then he continues: “You, almighty and merciful God, be present; you, gracious one, breathe upon it,” and the rest that follows.

After this humble petition, the priest calls upon the Holy Spirit. In a loud voice—that is, with an intense movement of the mind—he entreats the Spirit to deign to come to the water itself, saying:

“Let the power of your Spirit descend into the fullness of this font.”

The words that follow in the present prayer show what is to be entreated, so that the Spirit may work there [Col. 1046A].

## CHAPTER XXVI. On placing the candles in the water

While the priest cries out that the power of the Holy Spirit should descend into the water, the candles of the neophytes are lowered into the water. Why is this done, unless to show that the candle now signifies the Holy Spirit?

We read that there was one column during the journey of the children of Israel, and that it served both purposes: on one side it was a light for them at night, and on the other it was the protection of the cloud by day. Concerning this Saint Augustine says in Book XII Against Faustus:

“Why, then, is Christ not also a column for us, since he is both straight and curved (*simus*), supporting our weakness, shining by night and not shining by day, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind?”

It is also read as though there were two columns, as our translation has it:

“The Lord went before them to show the way, by day in a column of cloud and by night in a column of fire.”

When, therefore, through the illuminated candle we recall the column of fire which prefigured Christ, by whom the apostles were illuminated and to whom it is said, “You are the light of the world,” just as one blessed candle is illuminated by another candle, so, through the extinguished candles—or, as we may more appropriately say, through one candle on account of the unity of the Church—by which we recall the column of fire, the person of the Holy Spirit is signified.

Accordingly Gregory Nazianzen says in his sermon On the Second Epiphanies:

“Moses baptized in the sea and in the cloud, but in type and figure, as Paul declares.”

The sea therefore had the form of water, while the cloud had the form of the Holy Spirit.

The candle of the neophytes remains without light until the time when the other candles of the church are illuminated. At the time when the other candles are illuminated, the candles of the neophytes are illuminated as well. For after the Holy Spirit has cleansed the hearts of the neophytes and introduced them into the fellowship and unity of the Church, he will then illuminate their hearts.

For just as the Spirit possesses in his own person the role of being the communion of the Father and the Son, so in his operation he joins together the holy Church and holds it in unity.

We customarily postpone the lighting of the candles until the service of the Mass, either because the neophytes must first receive the imposition of the bishop’s hand, and we then believe that they are illuminated by the Holy Spirit, or because of the night in which we celebrate Mass, so that, just as the glory of the resurrection has been illumined, the light of our candles may likewise shine.

It has been stated, as I think, why the candles are lowered into the water at the invocation of the Holy Spirit: namely, because they somehow represent the person of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the anointing with chrism by the presbyter and the imposition of the bishop’s hand upon the neophyte

Before anything is said about the imposition of the bishop’s hand, it must be explained why the neophyte is anointed by the presbyter on the crown of the head.

As it is read in the papal acts, Pope Sylvester instituted that the neophyte should be anointed on the head by a presbyter. Thus it is written:

“He established that the baptized person should be anointed by a presbyter with chrism taken up from the water, because of the danger of the passage of death” +.
