It is clear when Sylvester governed the Church: namely, at the time when the Council of Nicaea was confirmed under the emperor Constantine.

Afterward, as I think, the holy Fathers established that neophytes should be anointed by presbyters with chrism consecrated by a bishop. Accordingly one of their outstanding teachers, Bede, says in his treatise on the Acts of the Apostles:

“For presbyters, whether outside the presence of a bishop or in the presence of a bishop, may anoint those whom they have baptized with chrism, but only with chrism that has been consecrated by a bishop. They may not, however, mark the forehead with the same oil; that is reserved to bishops, when they confer the Paraclete Spirit upon the baptized.”

If what was already being done was superfluously established by Saint Sylvester, then it was already being practiced. According to this institution, I think, the pontiff was formerly awaited for the anointing with chrism so that every anointing with chrism might be performed by the bishop’s hands. Until that time not everyone was baptized generally, especially when emperors and their ministers were pagans. For that reason a bishop could not easily attend the neophytes, nor could the neophytes themselves come to the bishop.

The priest who anoints the neophyte indicates through the words of his prayer the loosening of bonds and the binding up of wounds, saying:

“Almighty God, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who regenerated you from water and the Holy Spirit, and who gave you remission of all sins.”

In these words we understand both the healing of wounds and the loosening of bonds.

Afterward the aforementioned priest adds:

“He himself anoints you with the chrism of salvation unto eternal life.”

In these words we understand a certain salvation which extends to eternal life.

The bishop, however, passes over the words, “May he himself anoint you with the chrism of salvation,” as though he were richer—not only able to save, but also to enrich—and says:

“Send upon him your sevenfold Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, from heaven: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety. Fill him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord, and mark him with the sign of the cross, in your favor, unto eternal life.”

These are the garments with which the king’s son ought to be adorned, so that he may be able to stand in the heavenly court.

Those who are baptized are sons of God, as John the Evangelist relates:

“But to all who received him, he gave power to become sons of God,” and the rest.

The bishop entreats God that, just as he has deigned to wash the human being through baptism, so he may deign to clothe him in royal garments, with which the sons of the king ought to be clothed. Concerning these sons the Apostle Paul says:

“All who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ.”

The neophytes put on Christ there where they are renewed in the image of the one who created them. For the mind clothes itself with Christ when it is clothed with the Spirit who rested in the human Christ after he began to be human.

I heard someone ask whether a neophyte could possess the kingdom of heaven without the imposition of the bishop’s hand.

The thief who confessed the Lord on the cross and heard him say, “Today you will be with me in paradise,” did not receive the imposition of the hand, although we believe that he was baptized by his own blood on the cross.

Concerning this baptism Gregory Nazianzen says in his sermon On the Second Epiphanies:

“For I know also a fourth baptism, by which one is baptized in his own blood through martyrdom. Christ too was baptized with this baptism, so that in this as in the others he might give a pattern to believers and to those who follow him.” +

Concerning this baptism Augustine says in his letter to Seleucianus:

“We should no longer ask when each person was baptized; rather, all whom we read to belong to the body of Christ, which is the Church, we should understand to have been baptized—unless perhaps they were overtaken by the strait of suffering and, unwilling to deny Christ, were killed before they were baptized; for such people the suffering itself is counted as baptism.”

The words of Saint Sylvester also—when, because of the difficulty of obtaining a bishop before the soul’s departure, he ordered that the neophyte be anointed by a presbyter with the chrism of salvation unto eternal life—sound as though one might be received into the kingdom of heaven without the imposition of the bishop’s hand.

For there are different dwelling places in the Father’s house.

Concerning those who through negligence lose the bishop’s presence and do not receive the imposition of the hand, we must consider whether perhaps they are condemned in that righteousness in which they negligently practice righteousness, since they ought to have hastened to receive the imposition of the hand.

For just as Christ says, “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,” so also he says, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”

Truly, in baptism our sins are forgiven, and we are buried with Christ; in the resurrection we are justified, as the Apostle Paul says:

“He died because of our sins and rose because of our justification.”

The same Apostle reveals who raised him from the dead in the Letter to the Romans, saying:

“But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies.”

That the Spirit gives life to our bodies for this work was demonstrated above in the letter mentioned earlier, where the same author says:

“But the Spirit lives because of justification.”

Concerning this justification Saint Augustine says in Book XXI, chapter 27, of The City of God:

“For what benefit is it to anyone that he is baptized if he is not justified? Did not the one who said, ‘Unless one is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God,’ also say, ‘Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven’? Christ rose because of our justification; the Spirit raised him from the dead. The same Spirit gives life—or will give life—to our mortal bodies.”

It is plainly evident that Christ’s bodily resurrection promises us the giving of life, and that this resurrection occurs for the sake of our justification.

Our justification consists in the practice of good works, as Ambrose says in his treatise on the Letter to the Romans. Although a righteous person should also be called good, he distinguished the categories themselves, signifying by “righteous” one engaged in practice, and by “good” one who is naturally innocent through simplicity.

Our faith holds that without the Holy Spirit we can neither think nor do anything upright.

The Apostle Paul indicated through the imposition of hands that believers receive the Holy Spirit. When he came to Ephesus, he imposed hands upon the disciples after asking them:

“Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?”

He afterward baptized them, because they had been baptized with John’s baptism, and he imposed hands upon them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit.

Some people formerly received the Holy Spirit without the imposition of hands, even before they were baptized, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

“The Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word of God.”

Accordingly Bede says in the same work:

“So that Peter might not hesitate to confer baptism on the Gentiles, he is confirmed by the testimony of the Holy Spirit, which in a new order passes through the very waters of washing that it is accustomed to sanctify. This is found to have happened once, as a testimony to the faith of the Gentiles, but never among the Jews.”

Concerning this Gregory Nazianzen says in his sermon On the Second Epiphanies:

“He did not immediately give this as a law to the Churches, merely because such a thing happened once somewhere or rarely. For if a swallow is seen somewhere, spring does not immediately follow. What happens for the sake of a miracle or necessity must not be drawn into customary practice.”

According to Matthew, we are baptized in the Spirit in two ways. He himself says:

“He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.”

We are baptized with the Holy Spirit and fire. We are baptized with the Holy Spirit when we are washed from sins; this washing is signified by the white garments worn over the whole body in baptism. We are baptized with fire when we receive the ardor of the Spirit, as the apostles received it on the day of Pentecost.

We receive the baptism of fire through the imposition of the bishops’ hands. This fire consumes wood, hay, and stubble, because God is a consuming fire; it grants the warmth of eternal life and the light by which we see what is closed to mortal eyes.

This mode of the Spirit’s manifestation was not necessary in Christ’s baptism, because he did not come to show that it was necessary for the works we have mentioned to be performed in the human Christ. In him “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.” But it was necessary in the apostles and in other human beings.

If someone departs this world without this baptism, he undertakes a dangerous journey.

Foreseeing this, Pope Sylvester helped as much as he could; and because bishops were absent, he added, out of necessity, that neophytes should be anointed by presbyters.

We must fear that the difference between the one who dies without the imposition of the hand and the one who receives it may be like the difference between the brightness of the stars. That is, although such people are not excluded from the kingdom of God because of their other good works, they may not possess the place they would have possessed had they received it.

I do not deny that a person may receive the Holy Spirit without the imposition of the hand, if the Lord wishes to give him the Spirit. But the apostolic practice, which they exercised through the imposition of hands, and the present ecclesiastical care, strongly bind him who through negligence loses the imposition of the hand.

Let us compare these same gifts, according to Augustine, with the beatitudes proclaimed on the mountain, and let us see from Augustine’s words how great a danger is incurred by one who negligently leaves the world without the imposition of the hand.

The distinguished teacher compares wisdom with the peacemakers, in whom all things are ordered and no movement rebellious against reason exists. +

According to this comparison, one who does not possess wisdom is not a peacemaker, nor is he a son of God. If he is not a peacemaker, he is not a son of God; therefore he will not enter the heavenly court.

He compares understanding with the pure in heart, who, with their eyes cleansed, are able to see what the bodily eye has not seen, what the ear has not heard, and what has not entered the human heart.

Accordingly, where will one who does not possess understanding go? He is blind and does not know where he is going.

He compares counsel with the merciful, who forgive so that they may be forgiven, and help others as they wish to be helped themselves.

Without this gift no one reaches the kingdom of God, as the Gospel says:

“If you do not forgive each one his brother from your hearts, neither will your heavenly Father forgive you your sins.”

He compares fortitude with those who hunger, who labor by desiring joy from true goods. Who can attain the kingdom of heaven except one who desires the joys of true goods?

He compares knowledge with those who mourn, because they have already learned from the Scriptures by what evils they are held bound—evils which, because they were ignorant of them and regarded them as good and useful, they had opened themselves to.

For unless a person recognizes his error and turns back from it by correcting himself, he is not suited for the kingdom of God.

He compares piety with the meek. Whoever devoutly seeks Holy Scripture, does not criticize what he does not yet understand, and therefore does not resist it—that person is meek and will possess the earth.

He compares fear with the humble, concerning whom the Gospel declares that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them.

The same author, whose words we desire to understand, explains in the conclusion of this comparison that these gifts lead to that reward, saying:

“There is one reward, namely the kingdom of heaven, which has been given various names according to these degrees.”

For just as those who devoutly sought and salutarily awaited the baptismal sacraments were assisted by the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which the same Holy Spirit grants them, although they did not attain them, so it must be feared that those who negligently seek these gifts of God will not be assisted.

Concerning those who negligently bestow them, it is written in the Gospel:

“Wicked and lazy servant, you knew that I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter; therefore you ought to have put my money with the bankers.”

And shortly afterward:

“Cast the useless servant into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Saint Gregory explains the aforementioned gifts as degrees of those who ascend, in his book On the Building of the Temple [Col. 1051A]. We have excerpted some passages from it which are relevant here.

“The prophet,” he says, “because he was speaking from heavenly things down to earthly ones, began with wisdom and descended to fear.

“He has wisdom who believes in the Holy Trinity.

“He has understanding who perceives the divine commands with his mind and fulfills them in action.

“He has counsel who prudently foresees whatever he does.

“He is strong who resists the devil and his will.

“He has knowledge who knows how to distinguish between good and evil.

“He is pious who forgives sins and gives alms.

“He fears God who not only does what is good but also dares not to do what is evil.”

But we, who are striving from earthly things toward heavenly ones, should count the same degrees by ascending, so that we may be able to reach wisdom from fear.

In our mind the first degree of ascent is the fear of the Lord [Col. 1051B]; the second is piety; the third is knowledge; the fourth is fortitude; the fifth is counsel; the sixth is understanding; the seventh is wisdom.

There is indeed fear of the Lord in the mind, but what kind of fear is it if piety is not present with it? Whoever does not know how to show mercy to his neighbor, whoever pretends not to share in his neighbor’s tribulation—such a person’s fear is nothing before the eyes of almighty God, since it has not been raised to piety.

But piety often errs through disordered mercy, if it should perhaps spare what ought not to be spared. Sins which can be struck by the fires of Gehenna must be corrected by the blows of discipline. But disordered piety, when it spares temporarily, drags a person to eternal punishment.

Therefore, in order that piety may be true and rightly ordered, it must be raised to another degree, namely to knowledge [Col. 1051C], so that it may know either what to punish out of mercy or what to forgive out of mercy.

But what if a person knows what ought to be done and does not possess the strength to do it? Our knowledge must therefore grow into fortitude, so that, when it sees what ought to be done, it may be able to do it through strength of mind and not tremble from fear; lest, collapsing through terror, it be unable to defend the good which it recognizes.

But fortitude often falls through its own presumption if it is imprudent and insufficiently watchful against vices. It must therefore ascend to counsel, so that by foresight it may fortify everything which it can bravely accomplish.

Yet counsel cannot exist if understanding is absent. For one who does not understand the evil which burdens the person acting—how can he establish the good which helps him? Therefore let us ascend from counsel to understanding [Col. 1051D].

But what if understanding remains awake with great keenness and does not know how to govern itself through maturity? Let us therefore ascend from understanding to wisdom, so that wisdom may maturely order what understanding has discovered sharply.

Thus, by oil, let us understand upright conduct, which is moderated in the mind through the maturity of wisdom; and by balsam, doctrine, which provides a good fragrance outwardly.

In the same book, elsewhere, he says concerning wisdom:

“Wisdom pertains to life, whereas knowledge pertains to doctrine.”

The anointing with chrism, as we have explained above, pertains to the two gifts of the Holy Spirit, namely wisdom and knowledge: oil pertains to wisdom; balsam, spreading its fragrance far and wide, to knowledge. These two—namely, life and doctrine—are found joined together in the seven gifts. Wisdom and understanding: wisdom pertains to life, understanding to doctrine. Counsel pertains to doctrine, fortitude to life. Knowledge pertains to doctrine, piety to life. These are the ornaments of the garment that God grants to the mind through the laying on of hands. Without them, it is dangerous for anyone to be found at the king’s banquet, lest he hear the terrifying voice saying, “Friend, how did you come in here without a wedding garment?”

Masters commonly recite the prayer in different ways, together with the cross that they make with the thumb on the foreheads of the infants. All the words mentioned above are words of prayer, since the Spirit is not given by those who lay on hands; rather, they beseech him to come. Hence Augustine, in the fifteenth book of *On the Trinity*, chapter twenty-four, says: “For none of his disciples gave the Holy Spirit. They prayed that he might come upon those on whom they laid hands; they did not themselves give him. The Church still observes this practice in its superiors.”

The bishop has prayed above that the Holy Spirit be sent; in what follows he asks that the recipient be graciously sealed for eternal life—that is, that the recipient not lose the same Spirit until he brings his guest into eternal life. Concerning this seal Jerome says in his treatise on the Epistle to the Ephesians: “We have been sealed with the Holy Spirit of God, so that both our spirit and our soul may be impressed with God’s seal, and so that we may receive that image and likeness according to which we were formed in the beginning.”

By this seal of the Holy Spirit, according to the Savior’s word, we are sealed, with God imprinting it. For he says, “The Father, God, has set his seal on him.” Therefore everyone who, because he has believed God, has certified that God is true is also sealed by the Holy Spirit. He is sealed so that he may preserve the seal and display it pure, genuine, and in no respect mutilated on the day of redemption, and thus may be counted among those who have been redeemed.

Without this seal we ought not to be presented before God. Concerning it, as though concerning a garment, Paul said to the Corinthians: “Indeed, while we are in this body, we groan under our burden, because we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.” He shows in what follows what garment he means: “He who prepares us for this very thing is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit.”

Since we have received God’s pledge, so that we may belong to him, we are sealed with the sign of the cross by which we were redeemed. Thus, when the destroyer sees that sign on our foreheads, he may pass over our houses and see that we do not belong to him, but to the one whose sign we bear.

This cross is effected through chrism, which is prepared from oil and balsam. Such a liquid displays the works of our guest. It plants in the mind the charity signified by the oil, with its flourishing leaves, and exhales from us the fragrance of good knowledge, just as a pleasant odor comes from balsam. That only bishops should anoint through the laying on of hands was taken over from the apostles, as Bede explains in his treatise on the Acts of the Apostles.

[Col. 1053A]

It should be noted that Philip, who evangelized Samaria, was one of the seven. For if he had been an Apostle, he could certainly have laid hands on them so that they might receive the Holy Spirit. This is reserved to bishops alone.

The cross itself is fixed in no place more appropriately than where the high priest once wore the golden plate on which the ineffable name of God was engraved. That the Holy Spirit is given through the laying on of hands and prayer was likewise taken from apostolic authority, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the apostles who were in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them. When they arrived, they prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit.” A little later: “Then they laid hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit.”

Following the example of Peter and John, let bishops hasten to the places where those are found upon whom it is necessary to lay hands. Let those who are about to receive the wedding garment hasten there without hesitation, so that, when the king enters, they may persevere at the banquet. If someone is taken from the present age before he can attend so great a ministry, God knows why he compels him to leave the present age earlier.

“The Lord knows those who are his.” And according to the evangelist John: “My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand.”

We must take every precaution lest, through the torpor of false security, negligence find the door open. The Roman booklet, which we have often mentioned, says: “When the prayer has been completed, he makes the sign of the cross with his thumb from the chrism on each person’s forehead, saying: ‘In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Peace be with you, and with your spirit.’” These are words of greeting addressed to the new person, who has been created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Litanies

The litanies performed around the consecration of the baptistery signify the intercessions of the saints on behalf of those being reborn. We can learn this from the reading of the Book of Revelation: “I saw a door opened in heaven.”

In that vision Christ is shown seated upon a throne. There is the Church, above which the Lord sits; there is an indication of water in the color of jasper, and of fire in that of sardius. There the Spirit of God is in seven burning lamps before the throne, which are the seven gifts of the Spirit of God. There is baptism in the glassy sea, as it is written: “And around the throne was something like a glassy sea, resembling crystal.”

Hence Bede, in his commentary on the same book, says: “Because of true faith, baptism is compared to glass, in which nothing other is seen outwardly than what it contains inwardly. Baptism’s grace is also represented by crystal, which is formed from water into ice and a precious stone.”

We have said nothing about the rainbow, because we wish to signify the litanies through it. The same Revelation also says: “And a rainbow was around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald.” Hence the same author, above, in the same work: “The rainbow, which is produced when the sun illuminates the clouds and which, after the flood, first became a sign of reconciliation, signifies that through the intercession of the saints, whom the Lord enlightens, the Church is protected.”

They are rightly compared to an exceedingly green emerald. For the more perfectly they await the imperishable inheritance by faith, the more powerfully they also protect others through prayer. Because the rainbow was around the throne, the litanies are performed both before baptism and after baptism. *Litanies* in Greek means *supplications* in Latin.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the Garment of Those Clothed in White, and a Recapitulation Concerning Septuagesima

Those clothed in white are commonly called *albati* because of their white garments. I know that the meaning of these garments was carefully explained by the archbishops who lived in the time of blessed memory of Charles, at his prompting. It is therefore unnecessary to labor over it in this little work. I shall say only this, according to the Lord’s mercy: the eight days signify the period during which white garments are worn and the neophytes’ candles are illuminated.

For just as seven days pertain to the Old Testament because of the sabbath, so eight days pertain to the New Testament because of the eighth day of the resurrection. Concerning this Solomon says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight.” He was already teaching his people not always to cling to the Old Testament, but at some point to pass over to the New.

From sabbath to sabbath the white garments are worn. They give us an image of what we ought to be in the New Testament and of the kind of bodies we shall receive on the eighth day.

[Col. 1054C]

We wear them from sabbath to sabbath—that is, from the day on which we receive the pledge of the Spirit, who, because of the number seven, is assigned to the sabbath, until the following sabbath, which recalls that sabbath on which we ought to be presented before the Lord with that pledge.

These garments are the white robes of which it is written in the Apocalypse: “And white robes were given to each of them.” For now the souls of the saints, rejoicing in their blessed immortality, each possess a robe. Again, in the same book: “Clothed in white robes, and with palms in their hands.” By the robes he signifies baptism; by the palms, the triumph of the cross. Again, in the same book: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have authority over the tree of life,” and so forth.

He promises a worthy reward for the shining robes—that is, for an immaculate life—namely, that one may enjoy the sight of the Lord, who is eternal life.

From the passages cited we can discern two things: first, that the white garments are a sign of what our bodies ought to be in the New Testament—for bodies are, in a certain sense, garments of the soul—and second, what kind of bodies are promised to us in the future. Concerning these Solomon says: “Let your garments always be white, and let oil never fail from your head.”

Here too we can understand that our works ought always to be such as are represented by the garments of those clothed in white: clean and shining. And just as oil does not fail from their heads throughout the eight days, so charity should never fail from our minds.

The fact that these garments are removed on the sabbath signifies that, on the day when the soul departs from the body, the soul finds the sabbath—that is, rest—and leaves its garment here, namely the body, in order to receive it again on the last day.

It therefore seems to me more fitting, if the garments are to be worn after the eight days and are truly to be worn by the albati, that they should be worn by those who wore them during the consecrated days rather than by those who have defiled themselves with many stains after baptism. For in the future our bodies will receive no other souls than those same souls that governed them in the present.

These garments are customarily double, and a double reward is promised to the saints in eternal life. Hence Isaiah says: “They shall possess double in their land”—that is, joy of soul and the glory of an incorruptible body.

Because we pollute our bodies with impending sins after baptism, let us hasten to return to the earlier cleansing through a second baptism, namely through penance. Who is it that cleanses us from our sins? And who is it that brings us back to the earlier purification except the Holy Spirit?

The Holy Spirit is sevenfold. It is clear that, if we keep his ten commandments, we are joined through obedience to the same Creator from whom we departed through disobedience. Therefore, in the number seventy, which is seven multiplied by ten, let us mourn and lament our misery, so that the Holy Spirit may cleanse us from our sins and lead us through his commandments to the reward of the number ten, so that we may deserve to see the King, our Lord, in his beauty.

[Col. 1055C]

Above we have said, as far as we could, that the number seventy pertains to the mourning of the captives of God’s people who were under Nebuchadnezzar in Babylon. We can also, in a certain way, compare the same seventy with the children of Israel who were in Egypt under Pharaoh.

The first offices—“The groans of death surrounded me”; “Arise, why do you sleep, O Lord?”; and “Be for me a protecting God”—may correspond to that period when the children of Israel saw themselves afflicted by the Egyptians and cried out to the Lord, as it is written in Exodus: “After a long time the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel groaned because of their labors and cried out. Their cry because of their labors rose up to the Lord, and he heard their groaning and remembered the covenant that he had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

The office of Wednesday, which is the beginning of the fast, corresponds to that period when the Lord said to Moses: “Remove the sandal from your feet.” The Epistle read on that same day shows us what it means to remove the sandal from one’s feet. To give one example: “The bridegroom shall go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room.”

The sandal is removed from our feet when the activity that we have derived from the necessities of carnal desire is interrupted.

The office of Lent corresponds to the period when Pharaoh was afflicted so that God’s people might be liberated. Afterward one must come to the Red Sea, that is, to baptism; and then pass through the desert under leaders, just as our neophytes are led for eight days under the guidance of presbyters, namely priests, sponsors, and matrons. Thus at last they come on the sabbath to the promised land.

Those who baptize are the fathers of the baptized, as we can infer from many testimonies of Scripture. Thus Mark is called Peter’s son in baptism. The writings of the apostles abound in such sons.

Because there are more baptized persons than can be led by those who baptize, they are entrusted to other spiritual fathers, so that these may provide them with what ought to have been provided by the presbyters.

Nor is it contrary to the truth that the forty-two encampments of the children of Israel represent, as it were, forty-two days leading us to the promised land. For forty-two days have been appointed for us who have already crossed the Red Sea, so that we who have reduced ourselves to captivity through our sins may return to the promised land through the examples of the patriarchs—not through water baptism.

Our catechumens, who have not yet crossed the Red Sea, can represent the people of Israel who worshiped idols in Egypt and were freed from Egypt through the excellent leaders Moses and Aaron, and crossed the Red Sea.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Illumination of the Candles

The fact that, according to the booklet of the Roman order, the illumination of the candles is awaited until the *Agnus Dei* signifies that each person ought to receive light through that Lamb who takes away the sins of the world.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Mass at Night

[Col. 1056C]

Let us now say, “Glory to God in the highest,” because this present night has been illumined by so great a light, namely the Lord’s resurrection. Let us sing praises to God, because the places in which the devil dwelt are now inhabited by the Holy Spirit.

The bishop says this with mouth and mind, so that we may hold it in our minds, saying: “O God, who illumine this most sacred night with the glory of the Lord’s resurrection, preserve in the new offspring of your family the Spirit of adoption whom you have given.”

Here it should be noted that the ministers’ speech is addressed to the neophytes up to the Gospel. The lector says to them: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.”

[Col. 1056D]

You have here a reading with an anagogical step, in which the catechumens, kindled by the words of the chant, longed like deer to appear before the face of God; what they then possessed in desire they now possess in reality. No one can fully understand the things that are above unless he has first been kindled inwardly by a heavenly savor of the mind.

The lector says to them: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” Through baptism you have died with Christ; your future life is already in Christ. A life has been laid up for you in his life. What you know was accomplished in him through the resurrection, hope will be accomplished in you: “When Christ your life appears”—that is, when he who now preserves your life in himself reveals himself and makes you what he already is through immortality—“then you also will appear with him in glory,” which is now promised to you.

Therefore the minister says: “Do not be idle; offer a sacrifice to God.” Augustine shows us in the one hundred and sixteenth psalm what sacrifice they ought to offer: “We have heard, brothers, the Holy Spirit admonishing and exhorting us to offer God the sacrifice of confession.”

A little later he says: “You yourselves can perceive that in the divine writings confession is customarily named not only in connection with sins but also in connection with the praises of God. What more appropriately can we understand ourselves to be admonished by in this psalm, when we sing Alleluia, which means ‘Praise the Lord,’ than when we hear, ‘Confess to the Lord’? That is, we are to praise the Lord. God’s praise could not have been expressed more briefly than by saying, ‘For he is good.’ I do not see what could be greater than this brevity.”

[Col. 1057B]

A little later he says: “But since the people are addressed in anticipation of future things, having been freed from all the labor and captivity of pilgrimage and from every mixture with the wicked—and this has been granted to them by God’s grace, who not only does not repay evil for evil but even repays good for evil—it has most appropriately been added: ‘For his mercy endures forever.’”

The Alleluia and the Tract that follows depend upon one command: that the neophytes offer God a sacrifice of praise.

The Tract says, on behalf of the neophytes: “Praise the Lord, all nations; praise him, all peoples. For his mercy has been confirmed over us, and the truth of the Lord remains forever.”

Concerning these two virtues the same author as above says in Psalm 112: “Observe in the holy Scriptures how often these two—mercy and truth—are joined together. In his mercy he called the ungodly, and in truth he judges those who, after being called, refused to come.”

The neophytes present have a prepared path for entering the kingdoms of heaven. The gate is open to them; we, who have been polluted by worldly desire after baptism, must knock upon it through good works. For this reason the only matter at issue concerning them is that they offer God a sacrifice of praise.

Alleluia is sung first. It is Hebrew. For Hebrew, as we believe, is the mother of the other languages and is held to be the noblest because of the authority of divine Scripture. Latin is inferior, like a daughter or daughter-in-law whom the son of the Synagogue has taken as his wife. Therefore Alleluia is placed first here, which does not happen in the other offices. Nevertheless, when the discussion reaches the first and eighth days of the neophytes, it is necessary to return to the same gate, whether in this way or another.

Behold, the sacrifice of the neophytes is finished. Next the Lord’s resurrection is recalled, together with the angels’ address to the women and the women’s feelings.

The Gospel according to Mark narrates the women’s arrival and says: “When the sabbath had passed, Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome bought spices so that they might come and anoint Jesus.”

As I suppose, either because of the women’s imitation, or because the Roman booklet doubts whether the Lord had already brought his flesh back from the underworld in the fullness of the gift of light, it says that on this night nothing other than incense is carried before the Gospel. The women offered only this.

[Col. 1058A]

The angel spoke to them, saying: “Do not be afraid. You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified. He has risen; he is not here.”

In what follows the women’s response is made clear: “But they went out and fled from the tomb.” Fear and terror had seized them, “and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.”

Thus Bede comments on Mark: “It is rightly puzzling how Mark can write, ‘They said nothing to anyone,’ when Luke says, ‘Returning from the tomb, they reported all these things to the eleven and to all the others,’ and Matthew likewise says, ‘They went out from the tomb with fear and great joy, running to report to his disciples.’ This may be understood either to mean that they did not dare say anything to the angels themselves—that is, to answer what they had heard from them—or else to the guards whom they saw lying there.”

In recalling the women’s silence and sacrifice, the singers keep silence during the time of the sacrifice. Their sacrifice at that time was the ointment they carried to anoint the Lord’s body.

They sing, “Holy, holy, holy,” which is the angels’ song, because the angels did not remain silent concerning his resurrection—whether the angel who has just spoken in Mark, or those whom John describes as sitting, one at the head and one at the feet.

In place of the women, the singers again keep silence during the *Agnus Dei*: “Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, have mercy on us.” Mary said to the gardener: “Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have placed him.” She believed that he had been secretly removed; she did not believe that he had taken away the sins of the world. Therefore, when she wished to touch the Lord, she heard: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father.”

The priest, Christ’s vicar, performs his office. While the apostles doubt his resurrection, while the women are afraid and say nothing, the angels’ chorus proclaims that Christ has risen from the dead. Christ himself, through his glorious appearance, makes himself manifest to whomever he wishes.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Eight Days of the Neophytes

Augustine says to Januarius: “These things are held most firmly from the Scriptures: Easter and Pentecost; the Church’s agreement has strengthened the observance of the forty days before Easter. Likewise, it has established that the eight days of the neophytes be distinguished from the others—that is, that the eighth correspond to the first.”

The eight offices performed in commemoration of the neophytes are distinguished from the other offices that follow up to Pentecost. The first has two praises, namely Alleluia and “Confess to the Lord,” and the Tract, “Praise the Lord, all nations.” The eighth has two: two Alleluias, “This is the day,” and “Praise the Lord, children.” This is not done on any other sabbath until Pentecost. The six intervening days have the Responsory and Alleluia.

Therefore the first life, as the same author says above to the same recipient, was not eternal for the one who sinned. The final rest, however, is eternal. Accordingly, the eighth will also possess eternal blessedness, because that rest, which is eternal, is received by the eighth, not extinguished by it; otherwise it would not be eternal. Thus the eighth will be like the first, so that the first life may be restored—but eternal.

In remembrance of the first life that Adam first possessed, Alleluia is sung. Since that life was not eternal, the Tract follows, so that the humility of the later life may be recalled in a humbler tongue. The neophytes are still on pilgrimage, yet they ought to praise the Lord because they have been redeemed.

The final rest, which is restored on the seventh day and completed on the eighth, possesses eternal blessedness. Therefore, in memory of the supreme restoration, two Alleluias are sung on the seventh day and in the eighth office: the first because life is restored; the second because it is eternal—Alleluia.

The Hebrew language is the most glorious of all languages. At this point, for the same reason, we can discharge our obligation concerning the octave-days, namely the Sundays of Pentecost, when two Alleluias are frequently sung.

There are two reasons why the soul praises the Lord on the seventh day, that is, in rest: one concerns the joy already received, the other the joy to be received in the resurrection. In another sense, a human being at the resurrection will consist of soul and body, although the body will be spiritual.

In remembrance of that resurrection, two Alleluias are celebrated on the Sundays of Pentecost. Since the Lord’s resurrection occurred beforehand on the eighth day, and what will occur in our resurrection was prefigured by it, we enact this through the Sundays of Pentecost: both mind and body are to praise the Lord.

In the meantime, because the soul praises God without the body, Alleluia is celebrated each day.

At the feasts of the saints there are two Alleluias, because they already rejoice more in the sight of the Lord than do those who possess only the soul’s rest: one because they rest, the other because they see the Lord.

Although the seventh day of the week is the sabbath, the eighth office is nevertheless celebrated on it for the neophytes. The six intervening days, however, retain the Responsory and Alleluia.

Just as the number seven signifies rest, so the number six signifies works. The Responsory, which invites us through the six days to Christ’s resurrection, wishes to signify some activity for us in the resurrection of bodies.

Concerning this activity the same author as above says to the same recipient: “In that rest there is not sluggish idleness, but a certain ineffable tranquility of activity at rest. For at the end one will rest from the works of this life in such a way as to rejoice in the activity of the other life.”

But because such activity is performed in the praise of God, without labor of the limbs and without the anguish of cares, one does not pass into it through rest in such a way that rest itself is replaced by labor. Activity does not begin in such a way that rest ends. One does not return to labors and cares, but remains in activity. For rest consists in neither laboring in one’s work nor wavering in one’s thoughts.

Because through rest one returns to the first life, from which the soul fell into sin, rest is signified by the sabbath. That first life, restored to those returning from pilgrimage and receiving the first robe, is represented by the first day of the week, which we call the Lord’s Day.

In another passage the same author says to the same recipient: “The Lord’s Day was revealed not to the Jews but to Christians through the Lord’s resurrection, and from that time it began to possess its festivity.”

All the souls of the saints are indeed in a state of rest before the resurrection of the body, but they do not yet possess the activity by which they will be strengthened after receiving the body. The eighth day, which is also the first, signifies such activity. It does not take away that rest but glorifies it.

Through the inspiration of Saint Augustine, by the Responsory we understand the activity of the saints in the body, which will occur with complete joy, as the Responsory says: “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.”

Because this joy reaches its fulfillment in glorification, the Alleluia follows. To show that this activity is nothing other than the praise of God, Alleluia is sung continuously after the six days.

It should be noted that all the verses of the Responsory are from the psalm “Confess to the Lord,” which expresses the confession of praise; nevertheless, that praise is concluded with Alleluia because it belongs to the nobler language.

The verses are:

“Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

Again: “Let Israel now say that he is good.”

Again: “Let those who fear the Lord now say, for his mercy endures forever.”

Or: “Let those whom the Lord has redeemed say so.” I have seen both versions written in that place, and I have heard both sung.

Again: “The right hand of the Lord.”

Again: “The stone that the builders rejected.”

Again: “Blessed is he who comes.”

At the end of the verses the order is reversed. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” is placed before the verse “The stone that the builders rejected,” which occurs earlier in the order of the psalm; and this is not without reason. It is sung on Thursday, while “The stone that the builders rejected” is sung on Friday.

The latter especially resounds among the other verses concerning the Lord’s Passion, which took place on Friday. On that day the Jews rejected the Lord while building; on that day he became the cornerstone, joining together two walls that came toward each other from opposite sides.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Same Eight Days

The eight days of the neophytes display the course of the present life. Just as the journey of the children of Israel, after they crossed the Red Sea and proceeded to the promised land, signifies the whole course of the present life, so the way of life of the neophytes signifies the whole course of the present life, in which we ought to live according to Christ’s resurrection.

Concerning this course Augustine says in the twelfth book *Against Faustus*: “The baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood is represented in the Red Sea. The enemies following behind die: these are past sins. The people are led through the desert. All the baptized do not yet enjoy the promised homeland; but because they do not see what they hope for, and await it through patience, they are as though in a desert. There are also difficult and dangerous temptations there, lest they return in their hearts to Egypt. Yet Christ does not abandon them there, for that column too does not depart.”

According to these words, our baptized persons are led daily to the Church, with the illuminated column of the candle going before them. It is already illuminated because the baptized have been transferred into Christ’s body: the Spirit of Christ illuminates the members of Christ.

From what follows it can be discerned how those eight days correspond to the course of our condition.

The first day, when the baptized person descends from the water, is the sabbath—that is, rest—and presents to us the condition of Adam before he sinned. Adam was not made in such a way that, if he had not sinned, he would have had to acquire the fruit of life through labor of any kind; nevertheless, we read that God placed him in paradise to work it.

God grants the baptized on the sabbath the same rest that he granted Adam before he sinned, yet in such a way that afterward they perform good works until the following sabbath, just as Adam was devoted to work without any labor.

That rest is the innocent life Adam possessed on the seventh day, when God rested from all his works. The baptized now receive the same life on the sabbath.

Then, because a way remains for the baptized through the desert, after the Alleluia comes the Tract of the soul, that is, patience, through which they must await the promised land. Six days follow, pertaining to good, holy, and devout work, lest the empty house be invaded.

After those six days comes the sabbath-rest, which introduces them into the promised homeland, where there is eternal rest. It does not return to any labor, but passes from the joy of the glory of souls to the joy of an incorruptible body. Therefore it is not followed by the Alleluia “This is the day” and the Tract, but by the Alleluia “Praise the Lord, children.”

The six days between the two sabbaths recall both periods to our memory: Adam, who was devoted to highly desired work in paradise, and the period in which the children of Israel passed through the desert under leaders. During that time their garments were not worn out, and at last they reached freedom in the promised land, which signifies the homeland where holy souls are received after the age has passed.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Holy Day of Easter
On the holy day of Easter, at the entrance, Christ presents himself through the mouths of the prophets to his Father in his Church, saying: “I have risen, and I am still with you.” The first prayer shows that, through the resurrection of its Head, the entrance into the holy Church of the heavenly kingdom has been opened. The Epistle admonishes us to be separated from the vices against which we struggled during the forty days, and which the neophytes cast off in baptism. Paul sent it to the Corinthians so that the righteous might separate themselves from those who had committed such a sin as was not even heard of among the Gentiles, and who, through penitence, did not return [Col. 1061D] to the assembly of the saints. They were the old leaven, while the others were unleavened because of the newness of life. Thus we too are admonished that, without turning back, we should be strangers to vices on the holy day of Easter. May God grant that, just as his Son, our Lord, rose today from the dead in such a way that death can no longer claim him, so too his past or impending vices may no longer possess his members.

The Responsory shows how greatly those who are cleansed from vices ought to rejoice. In the Alleluia it is shown what is the cause of such great joy: namely, that Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed; “therefore let us feast,” and so forth. The Gospel explains more perfectly the cause of all the joy. Since, in its proper place, if the Lord grants it, we shall speak more fully about the entire office [Col. 1062A] of the Mass, let this suffice for my smallness, which I have touched upon for the reason that I should not seem, in mind, to be alienated from so great a joy as the present day contains.

Moreover, I gladly insert what Saint Augustine says about the prayers of the Mass in the book of Questions, in his questions to Paulinus, bishop of Nola:

“Many things can be said about this which ought not to be rejected, but I choose to understand in these words what the whole, or almost the whole, Church practices: that we should take as ‘prayers’ those which we make in the celebration of the sacraments, before that which is on the Lord’s table begins to be blessed; as ‘prayers’ those made when it is blessed and sanctified and broken for distribution; and the whole of this petition almost the entire Church concludes with the Lord’s Prayer. ‘Intercessions,’ or—as our books have it—‘supplications,’ are made when the people are blessed. For then the bishops, or advocates, offer those entrusted to them by the laying on of hands to the most merciful power. When these things have been completed and so great a sacrifice has been shared, thanksgiving concludes everything; the Apostle also especially commended this as the final element in these words.”

This, however, was chiefly the reason for saying these things: so that, after what has briefly been prescribed and indicated, no one might think that what follows was to be neglected: “for all human beings, for kings, and for all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and charity.” No one should suppose, as human weakness of thought might lead one to do, that these prayers ought not to be made for those by whom the Church was persecuted, since the members of Christ were to be gathered from every kind of human being. Hence he adds and says: “For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.”

And lest anyone should say that there could be a way of salvation through good conduct and the worship of the one almighty God without participation in the body and blood of Christ, he says: “For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” Thus what he had said—“he wills all human beings to be saved”—is understood to be accomplished in no other way than through the mediator: not God, who was always the Word, but the man Christ Jesus, when the Word became flesh and dwelt among us +.

The four prayers mentioned by Saint Augustine are named in this way by our translation: supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings. Here it should also be noted that the prayer which begins, “Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord, from all evils,” is only the conclusion of the Lord’s Prayer, since Blessed Augustine says, “the whole of this petition almost the entire Church concludes with the Lord’s Prayer.” At the same time, it should be noted that the prayer which bishops, or advocates, customarily make over the people with the sign of the holy cross, he used to make after he had broken the Lord’s body for distribution; this prayer he calls “petitions.” Then follow the thanksgivings, when, after hearing the deacon’s voice saying, “Go, the dismissal is made,” or “Let us bless the Lord,” the people respond, “Thanks be to God.”

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### Demonstration that the six Easter days signify the other Sundays and righteous people; that the fifty days from Easter Saturday to the Saturday of Pentecost’s octave signify the future life; and that the daily days—that is, the Sundays of Septuagesima and the Lenten days—signify penitents

Those six Easter days, on which we sing the Responsory and the Alleluia, signify the other Sundays or feast days that we celebrate from the octave of Pentecost until Septuagesima. The Responsory and the Alleluia recall the activity and joy, praise, or thanksgivings of those who persevere in the holiness they received in baptism. For they hold the future kingdom in hope, so that even here, by doing good, they may attain blessedness. Or, to put it another way, through the Responsory we understand the active life, and through the Alleluia the contemplative life.

Action must necessarily be celebrated here, so that through good works we may be able to attain what we hope for and await through patience. The Responsories that we sing during the six days, or during the other Sundays and feast days of the saints, which are followed by the Alleluia, signify such activities as preaching, reading, almsgiving, and visiting widows, orphans, and the sick. In the present age we can perform these every Sunday without turning back. The Alleluia follows these activities—that is, the aforementioned Responsories—because after such action the soul, sanctified from every sin, is transferred into the praise of God.

Those fifty days that follow from Easter Saturday to the octave of Pentecost signify the other life, which we have not yet received. There will be no Responsory there, because no one will be preached to there; rather, all will be taught by God. Nor will anyone be visited, because there will be no widow, orphan, or sick person there. Almsgiving will not be necessary, because no one there will be in need. Only the Alleluia will be celebrated there: that is, the joy of souls at having received immortality and at receiving their bodies, as thanksgiving to God forever.

The number fifty signifies this same joy; among the Hebrews it is called a jubilee (*iubilaeus*), that is, “full of jubilation.” What the other days signify, we can, I think, consider from Saint Augustine’s book *On Faith and Works*. For he says:

“Not because anyone ought to be so exalted that, to say nothing of boasting before others, he would dare even to think to himself that he is without sin in this life. But unless there were certain sins so serious that they ought also to be punished by excommunication, the Apostle would not say: ‘When you are assembled, and my spirit is present, deliver such a one to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus.’ Hence he also says: ‘Lest I should mourn over many of those who sinned before and did not repent of the impurity and fornication they committed.’

“Again, unless there were certain sins that were not to be healed by the degree of penitence given in the Church to those who are properly called penitents, but by certain remedies of correction, the Lord himself would not say: ‘Correct him between yourself and him alone; and if he hears you, you have gained your brother.’

“Finally, unless there were certain sins without which this life is not lived, he would not have placed a daily remedy in the prayer he taught, so that we say: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors’ +.”

The daily days signify those who are accustomed to confess their sins to a priest, so that they may be corrected by him and receive counsel about doing penance. These days pass without the Alleluia, because “praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner.” Although God has been moved to spare us, the shame of sins cannot quickly pass from the heart of the righteous. The verse that says this gives shape to the manner: “There is no health in my flesh because of your anger; there is no peace in my bones because of my sins.”

The words of the Lord to Moses concerning Miriam also give it form: “If her father had spit in her face, should she not have been covered with shame for at least seven days? Let her be separated outside the camp for seven days, and afterward she shall be recalled.” For when someone is spat upon in the face, contempt is shown toward him. When God despises us because of our sins, we ought to be covered with shame until the completion of seven days—that is, until satisfaction has been made.

Through the abstention from the Alleluia on the daily days in the office of the Mass, the Church’s shame is shown: the shame she bears because of her wounded members, who have not yet been healed.

But the Sundays from Septuagesima to the Lord’s Pasch signify those who are stretched out under the temptations without which the present life cannot be completed. The Responsories of those days are not supplied with the Alleluia, but with the Tract, which, although it belongs to contemplation because of its sweetness and union, is nevertheless not accompanied by such great joy as that of which James said: “The one who does not stumble in speech is a perfect man.”

During the forty-day period before Easter, Holy Church signifies those who are properly called penitents, except that they are not excommunicated and do not return at the end of Lent to the hands of the bishops for reconciliation. It signifies them in fasting, abstinence from pleasures, clothing, lowliness, mourning, vigils, quiet, silence, obedience in works, and the other good practices by which, together with penitence, we are reconciled to God.

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### On the days of Pentecost

The time of Pentecost begins on the first day of the resurrection and runs until the fiftieth day [Col. 1064D] after Easter. Concerning this period Augustine says in his book to Januarius:

“When the number forty is computed according to its parts, it adds the ten itself, and they become fifty, as the reward of work and self-restraint. For it was not without reason that the Lord himself spent forty days after the resurrection on this earth and in this life with his disciples; and after he had ascended into heaven, when ten days had intervened, he sent the promised Holy Spirit when the day of Pentecost was complete. This number fifty has another sacramental meaning: seven times seven makes forty-nine, and when one returns to the beginning, which is the eighth and also the first day, fifty is completed. These fifty days are celebrated after the Lord’s resurrection now as a figure not of labor but of rest and joy.”

For this reason fasts are relaxed, and we pray standing, which is a sign of the resurrection. Hence this is also observed at the altar on every Lord’s Day, and the Alleluia is sung, signifying that our action is nothing other than the praise of God, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you.”

Concerning the relaxation of the fast, Ambrose says in his treatise on the Epistle to the Romans +:

“For there are some who have decreed that meat should not be eaten on Wednesday; there are those who do so on Saturdays; and again there are those who eat from Easter to Pentecost.”

And Jerome says to Marcella, concerning our faith and the heretical doctrine opposed to the followers of Montanus:

“We fast one Lent, according to the tradition of the Apostles, at the season appropriate to us. They make three Lents in the year, as though three Saviors had suffered—not that it is not permissible to fast throughout the whole year except during Pentecost, but that it is one thing to offer a gift out of necessity and another out of free will.”

And again, to Lucinus of Baetica:

“And would that we could fast at all times, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Apostle Paul, and the believers with him, did during the days of Pentecost and on the Lord’s Day.”

And again, in the same work:

“I do not say this because I think one ought to fast on feast days and remove the holidays woven into the fifty days; rather, let each province abound in its own judgment and regard the precepts of its elders as apostolic laws.”

And again, in his *Commentary on Matthew*:

“When the wedding has passed and the time of the Passion and resurrection has arrived, then the bridegroom’s sons will fast. Some think that for this reason the fasts ought to be omitted after the forty days of the Passion, although the day of Pentecost and the coming of the Holy Spirit immediately indicate to us a festival. Taking this testimony as their occasion, Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla also keep a Lent after Pentecost, on the grounds that, when the bridegroom has been taken away, the bridegroom’s sons ought to fast. The custom of the Church, however, approaches the Lord’s Passion and resurrection through humility of the flesh, so that through fasting of the body we may be prepared for spiritual nourishment.

“According to the laws of typology, it should be understood that as long as the bridegroom is with us, and we are in joy, we can neither fast nor mourn; but when he has withdrawn from us because of our sins and flown away, then a fast must be proclaimed and mourning received.”

We have two differing practices in our Church concerning the fast observed after the Lord’s resurrection. Some, according to our common usage, set the end of the Lenten fast at the feast of Saint John. Those who do this cannot always exclude the days of Pentecost from the fast. Others wish, according to the traditions of the holy Fathers whom we have cited above and shall cite below, to have all the days of Pentecost in joy. Those who do this cannot always set the end of this Lent at the feast of Saint John. Scripture and the traditions of the Fathers do not establish a fixed point at which the end should be placed.

It sometimes happens that after Pentecost there are enough days to complete the number forty before the feast of Saint John: namely, when Easter Sunday falls on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, or on the tenth, ninth, or eighth of those days. When Easter Sunday falls on the aforementioned eighth day before the Kalends of April, Pentecost is to be held on the second day before the Ides of May. From that day until the feast of Saint John the Baptist there are six weeks.

If anyone wishes to count only forty days, let him do so when Easter Sunday falls on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, or on the sixth of the days mentioned above; in this way he can complete his number between Pentecost and the feast of Saint John.

I think that, on account of the days mentioned above, which in years occurring at intervals coincide with the end that falls at the feast of Saint John, the careful observance of Pentecost has been neglected, and those very days have been included in mourning when, by the authority of the Lord’s manifestation, they ought to be days of joy, so that the customary end might be maintained.

If it should seem good to the teachers to determine when the time of fasting should end for those who voluntarily fast after the Lord’s resurrection because of their sins, it appears to us that a variable practice should be removed from our Church. Why we should rejoice during the days of Pentecost is shown by abundant examples of the holy Fathers; why it is necessary to fast, each person knows from his own heart.

For the feast of the coming of the Holy Spirit is greater than the feast of Blessed John the Baptist. If a feast is to be included within a fast, the feast of Saint John ought more properly to be included than the coming of the Holy Spirit. And if the one who fasts, or the one who proclaims the fast, decrees that the fast should be released at the feast of Saint John, or of Saints Peter and Paul, and then resumed afterward, he does no harm to his soul.

In the fast we presently observe, we do not follow Montanus and his followers; rather, we consider our sins and strive to render worthy fruits of penitence for them. From the Jerome mentioned above we can learn by whom those fasts were at some time adopted: not because Pentecost fasts must necessarily be proclaimed for the whole Church, but because each person may fast voluntarily out of devotion of mind. Those whom the Church properly calls penitents are excluded from this permission and this freedom.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### On the greater litany

One differing practice follows between the octave of Easter and the vigils of Pentecost: namely, a three-day fast on the vigil of the Lord’s Ascension.

I wonder how the custom of this fast arose in our Church, since it is not observed throughout all the Eastern Churches, while the holy Fathers whom we mentioned—Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome—say that fasts should be relaxed during the time of Pentecost. The venerable priest Bede also says of this period in his homilies:

“Rightly, therefore, on these holy days we too devote ourselves to richer meals and heavenly hymns, out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection, in remembrance of the Lord’s fellowship with his disciples, and also in hope of our future rest and immortal life.”

And shortly afterward:

“Rightly also, in the image of our future blessedness, we honor the state of fifty days by relaxing fasts, singing the Alleluia, and praying while standing—things that are most fitting signs in advance of perpetual rest, resurrection, and praise.”

From whom this present fast first took its beginning, Gregory of Tours makes clear in his *History of the Franks*, saying:

“In those times there was a great earthquake in the city of Vienne, where many churches and the houses of many people were shaken and overturned. Many beasts—wandering wolves and fierce bears—entered through the city gate, devouring very many people; they did this throughout the whole year.

“For when the solemnity of holy Easter arrived, Saint Mamertus, who was bishop in that city, was celebrating the solemn rites of the Mass on the vigil itself, and the royal palace that stood in that city was set on fire by divine flame. While these things were happening, as the Lord’s Ascension was approaching, the holy man of God imposed a three-day fast upon the people, with groaning and contrition.”

And shortly afterward:

“Then that tribulation and destruction ceased. From that time onward, all the Churches of God and the priests, imitating this example, have celebrated those three-day litanies everywhere with solemn observance, even to the present.”

When he says “all the Churches of God,” we cannot understand him to mean those outside Gaul. In the places where those people were whom Ambrose mentioned—those who had decreed that meat should be eaten daily until Pentecost—there was no fast according to our custom, nor was there one where Jerome or Augustine was. If there had been, they would not have preached so explicitly the relaxation of the fast during the fifty days.

Roman custom inserts one day—namely, the seventh day before the Kalends of May—which it calls the greater litany, not a fast. A litany, as we said above, is a supplication among us. A serene mind, free from evil intention, can indeed supplicate God even while eating meat temperately at midday and rejoicing in the Lord’s resurrection. Nevertheless, the practice of the earlier Fathers—that is, the Apostles—must be followed.

Perhaps from the office itself we can understand what ought to be supplicated at such a time. The first prayer at the Mass says:

“Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that we who trust in your mercy amid our affliction may always be fortified by your protection against every adversity.”

The offertory agrees with this, saying:

“Help me, Lord my God; save me because of your mercy.”

And again:

“Let those who rise up against me be put to shame.”

At that time—that is, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May—enemies may, I think, stir up war against neighboring kingdoms. The holy Church wisely took care to ask the Lord that, just as he once destroyed Ahithophel’s counsel, so now he might destroy the counsels of those who wish to attack his peace.

The Epistle directs its attention to this when it says: “For the continual supplication of a righteous person is very powerful.”

The Gospel expresses another petition, saying: “Which of you, if his son asks his father for bread,” and again, “or a fish?” and again, “or if he asks for an egg?” In these three things we can understand three temporal and three spiritual things to be requested.

By the bread, all good things that grow from the earth; by the fish, those that come from the waters; and by the egg, the animals that hatch together. For at the time mentioned these things are making progress: the shoots of the harvest sprout; the fruits of the trees emerge from the blossom; the liquid of the vines and the oil burst forth from their trees; and the young animals graze the fields. Since these things are necessary for our uses, they should be requested from the Lord so that they may be preserved.

The spiritual things are understood as follows: by the bread, charity; by the fish, faith; by the egg, hope. Through these three the Divinity is worshiped by us. These things should especially be requested from the Lord at that time when Christ’s resurrection and the Church are celebrated, so that, strengthened by them, we may persevere in justification.

We sing the Roman office and omit the time of its preaching. According to Jerome, there is a distinction between offering a gift to God voluntarily and offering it out of necessity. At all times we can voluntarily offer God a gift through abstinence from things to be consumed, but this ought not to be done out of necessity.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### On the vigil of Pentecost

We must now come to the vigils of Pentecost. At them four readings are read and four songs are sung before the consecration of baptism, as at the vigils of Easter.

At the Easter vigils we read: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” At the vigils of Pentecost: “God tested Abraham.” In the former, a song does not follow; in the latter, one does.

The readings bring two fathers to our remembrance: one according to the flesh, the other according to the spirit. Adam, who is mentioned in the first reading, is the carnal father from whom we all derive our origin. He sinned by not obeying God’s command, and a song of victory does not follow him.

Abraham is the spiritual father, because by imitating his faith we become his children and are called the people of God. By obeying in the sacrifice of his son, he restored what the first man had offended by disobedience. A song of victory rightly follows him, for he killed the vice of disobedience.

The priest’s prayer expresses this very thing:

“O God, who in the deed of your servant Abraham gave the human race examples of obedience,” and so forth.

This reading belongs to history: as it is read, so it happened.

Another reading follows: “Moses wrote a song.” The cantor there shows which song it is, namely, “Hearken, O heaven” (*Attende, caelum*). Concerning this Bede says in his commentary on Luke:

“In memory of the ancient religion, some places were accustomed to recite on Saturday the song of Deuteronomy, in which the entire condition of the ancient people is contained: what they deserved when God was offended and what they deserved when he was propitious. Otherwise it would be out of order for the final song of Moses to be recited after the songs of the prophets had been sung on the earlier days of the week” +.

And therefore, because good conduct had preceded among the children of Abraham before they seized the one man, “seven women shall take hold of one man,” the reading “Moses wrote a song” is proposed. “Hearken, O heaven,” in which Adam is recalled to memory, for he is an image of the whole human race, most of which was unbelieving before Christ’s coming.

“The vineyard was planted”—that is, the sacrament of Christ and the Church, which belongs to allegory—precedes, because unless he had come, good conduct would not have spread throughout the whole world.

The third reading has already been discussed. In it the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit make one man out of those who obey; concerning him Paul said: “Until we all meet in a perfect man,” and so forth.

The fourth reading is from the prophet Jeremiah, who says among other things:

“Learn where wisdom is, where strength is, where understanding is, so that you may know at the same time where long life and sustenance are, where the light of the eyes and peace are.”

By these words he calls the hearers toward a certain thirst—namely, for wisdom, strength, and understanding. Why? So that the hearer may know where long life, the light of the eyes, and peace are.

What he commands them to learn pertains to the desire for the fountain, in accordance with the hearer’s response: “As a deer longs for fountains of waters,” and so forth. When he gives the reason why he desires the fountain, he intimates the higher life by saying where long life, the light of the eyes, and peace are—things that pertain to the anagogical sense.

The priest says likewise:

“Almighty and everlasting God, who have consecrated this solemnity of the coming of the Holy Spirit, grant us, we beseech you, that, inflamed by heavenly desires, we may thirst for the fountain of life.”

When he says “inflamed by heavenly desires,” he speaks in an anagogical sense.

The litany concerning baptism, as well as the Alleluia and the Tract, has already been discussed. It is nevertheless pleasing to recall briefly once more the Alleluia and the Tract.

The Alleluia is sung in remembrance of Adam’s first life of innocence. But because that innocence was not everlasting, it is changed into the Tract.

For example:

“I was a catechumen, captured at Constantinople. My merciful and most compassionate master sought me and found me captive. He killed the one who had seized me because of my negligence, and restored me to freedom, so that I might return to my homeland.

“How great was the glory for me, since I had been rescued from slavery and restored to freedom! Yet because a long, laborious, and dangerous journey remained for me as I returned to my homeland, after great joy I was affected by some weariness, not knowing whether I would reach my homeland. It was as though I descended from a certain level of greater joy—that is, from the Alleluia—to a lesser one, as in the Tract.

“Nevertheless, I patiently endure the journey appointed to me, praising my deliverer, if in some way I may eventually return to my homeland. Moreover, my deliverer sends defenders with me to protect me from barbarian fury, which surrounds my road on every side.

“These defenders are the baptismal sacraments, the candle, and the patron, who remain with me until the seventh day of the washing of the white garments. The seventh day, as has often been said, signifies the rest that we receive when we depart from the world, which will remain without any danger.”

For the distinction between the Alleluia and the Tract that we wish to demonstrate here, this little explanation is sufficient. It is also pleasing to indicate here what difference there is between the readings read at the vigils of Easter and those read at the vigils of Pentecost.

The difference between Adam and Abraham ought to be the same as the difference between the instruction of teachers to catechumens who are baptized at the Lord’s Easter and those baptized at Pentecost. They should tell them of the peril of the human race, almost unto destruction, through Adam’s disobedience, as it was at that time when no human being worshiped God except Abraham alone.

That destruction persisted throughout the whole human race, except for certain people who came forth from Abraham’s stock. In the former—that is, Adam—the devil was first killed through Christ’s coming. Afterwards, through the love of the seven women, the human race was joined to Christ. Then it was directed toward good works. This order is preserved in the vigils of Easter.

There is another order in the vigils of Pentecost. In these, it is recalled how Abraham pleased God through obedience and how his offspring delighted in good conduct. Nevertheless, in the New Testament it was necessary that they be joined to Christ through baptism and thus remain in him until they are led into the heavenly kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### On the seven following days of Pentecost

What we ought to do during the days that follow in the present week, the lord Bede explains in his homily, saying:

“Moreover, no one should think that it is without suitable discernment and a fitting understanding of the mystery that, once the fiftieth day has been completed, we do not immediately bend the knee for prayer, but continue during that week to entreat the Lord while standing; and, although we resume the interrupted fasts, nevertheless sound forth the Alleluia every day.

“Since the grace of the Holy Spirit is sevenfold, the solemnity of his coming is rightly honored for seven days with the fitting praise of hymns and with the celebration of Masses.

“Since at the time of Pentecost the Church throughout the whole world is accustomed continually to gather new peoples to God through the water of regeneration, it is right that, rejoicing with them in their salvation for as long as they are clothed in white robes, and displaying the brightness of their purified minds through the splendor of their clothing, we should offer God a hymn of devoted praise, in accordance with the command of that most compassionate shepherd and redeemer of ours, who says: ‘Rejoice with me, because I have found my sheep that was lost.’

“Rightly also we then pray while standing, as a sign of the liberation of those same people, who through the gift of the Holy Spirit have deserved to be raised and resurrected from the death of the soul to life.
