By his grace, we also hope to be clothed with the immortality of the flesh on the last day and to be led into the joys of the blessed resurrection.”

## CHAPTER XL  
### How long those who do not receive the laying on of the bishops’ hands at the time of baptism, but afterward, ought to remain under the discipline of the chrism

[Col. 1070D]

It is customary to ask among ordinary people how long those who receive the laying on of hands apart from the time of baptism ought to observe the anointing with chrism on their head, so that they may not wash. They may be answered: for as long as the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles is generally celebrated by the Church, let it be celebrated in the case of each person who has received him—that is, for seven days. And not without reason: since the Holy Spirit came to his host in seven women, it is fitting that a banquet be prepared for each woman on each successive day. Of these women Isaiah says: “Seven women shall take hold of one man.” Their banquet is prepared when they themselves satisfy their host from their own resources. Christ held such banquets for his guests, and the Holy Spirit likewise holds such banquets.

The host of the Holy Spirit is the human mind. The mind is nourished all the more abundantly by the richness of the Holy Spirit the less it has been devoted to carnal desires. Thus, the recipient should observe the time of the Holy Spirit’s coming as a dear friend is accustomed to observe the presence of a dear friend. When a dear person comes to a dear friend, the one who has received him wishes to offend him in nothing; rather, whatever he knows to please him, he offers him with a kindly heart. So whatever the recipient of the Holy Spirit recognizes as pleasing to him, let him offer it to him for as long as he is with him. If he does this, perhaps he will be able to reconcile himself to him more quickly when some offense has caused him to withdraw.

When a person who has been chrismated remembers that the anointing with chrism is present in him, then above all he should remember that he is subject to the discipline of the Holy Spirit. That anointing is performed so that we may know what the Holy Spirit invisibly accomplishes in us. Oil ordinarily soothes the limbs of the weary; balsam ordinarily gives off a fragrance. The limbs of our soul are weary when it regrets having done what is contrary to God’s will. The Holy Spirit usually comes to such a soul and shows it the sins that have been forgiven or are to be forgiven. Hence the Holy Spirit himself is called the Comforter. Concerning this David said: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul.”

The apostles received this Holy Spirit on earth when Christ breathed upon their faces and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them.” The Holy Spirit does not accomplish only this—that is, the forgiveness of sins—but also grants good works, which through a good reputation breathe a good fragrance into others: there is the balsam. For on the day of Pentecost the apostles received this gift, namely, that through signs of virtue they might convey to the people the fragrance of their knowledge.

Oil also has another property: it provides light. This too the Holy Spirit accomplishes in a human being, so that he may possess the light of understanding. He also acts as balsam when, through the mouths of those who speak, he brings to the knowledge of others with the sweetness of eloquence the light that he has given inwardly.

For it was not without reason that the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost in wind and fiery tongues. He wished to show the future Church what he would accomplish in the apostles through his coming. He came in a mighty wind to show that he would shake all earthly desire out of the hearts of the apostles. For just as a powerful wind throws dust from the face of the earth, so the coming of the Holy Spirit expels every earthly desire from the human heart.

He appeared in fiery tongues to demonstrate what he would make the tongues of the apostles: speaking and pouring fiery words into the hearts of believers. These fiery words consume sins and kindle hearts to love of the eternal homeland. This is the charity that is poured into the hearts of believers and makes them one heart, in imitation of its own substance—that is, so that they may will one thing, just as the holy Trinity wills one thing. The first thing that the recipient of the Holy Spirit must preserve is this: that he should have no discord with the unity of the Church.

The Holy Spirit’s other appearance, in the form of a dove, also demonstrates in another way the same power of charity—namely, through simplicity. The dove is a simple animal, free from the malice of gall; therefore he wished to reveal himself through it, so that his hosts might understand that they ought to be simple. The Apostle teaches how simplicity should be observed when he says: “Wise in what is good, simple in what is evil.” This means that a person should know how to benefit himself and his other brothers, and should not know how to harm himself or others.

He harms himself who, during the time of the Holy Spirit’s coming, is defiled by carnal desire. Therefore let him restrain himself from embraces with women, which cannot be completed without carnal desire. Let him abstain from gluttony and drunkenness, so that the mind may be nourished with spiritual food. Let him abstain from lying and from every form of pretence, because the Spirit whom he has received flees what is false.

Lying is not a small sin. If we compare lust and chastity, lying and truth, the one who lies will seem to sin no less than the one who is polluted by lust. Chastity is not greater than truth. We call truth the very substance of God. The one who lies corrupts truth, insofar as he is able.

In a person in whom there are two hearts, that Spirit does not dwell who makes people of one mind in a house. Many speak words to one person while signaling to another with their eyes. From one heart he offers sweetness of words to the person with whom he is speaking; from the other heart he offers another person deceit, through which he pours poison into the heart of the one addressed. The Holy Spirit is not in the person who does this.

There is one who laughs with his mouth while plotting evil in his heart against the person to whom he offers the laugh; he too has two hearts, and therefore the Holy Spirit does not dwell in him.

The wretched Adam lost this garment—that is, simplicity—when he realized that he was naked. Concerning this Augustine writes in his book *Against the Manichaeans on Genesis*:

> “The fact that Adam and his wife were naked and were not ashamed signifies the simplicity and chastity of the soul.”

The Apostle likewise says:

> “I desired to present you as a chaste virgin to one man, Christ. But I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and chastity that is in Christ.”

And a little later:

> “How did they see, if their eyes were closed? This was said so that we might understand that their eyes were opened after they had taken from that fruit, and that they saw themselves naked and were displeased with themselves—that is, they had the eyes of cunning, which are displeased with simplicity. For when someone has fallen from that inward and most secret light of truth, there is nothing by which pride wishes to please itself except through fraudulent pretences. From this hypocrisy also arises, in which those who have been able to deceive and trick whomever they wished seem very much to themselves to be wise-hearted.”

Since we have spoken above about the banquet that the host ought to prepare for the Holy Spirit for seven days—yet in such a way that he asks the Holy Spirit himself for this banquet and believes that he receives it—it is good to show him what he can offer his received guest on each day.

By “days” we mean certain advances of the mind. Peter says in his Epistle:

> “Applying all diligence, minister virtue in your faith, and in virtue knowledge, and in knowledge self-restraint, and in self-restraint patience, and in patience godliness, and in godliness brotherly affection, and in brotherly affection charity.”

Bede explains how these foods are to be prepared in his treatise on the Seven Catholic Epistles, saying:

> “He used the word ‘virtue’ here not for strength or miracles, but for good conduct, which must be joined to right faith, lest faith be idle and dead without works. He rightly commands that every effort be applied, because the person who is soft and negligent in his work is a brother to one who destroys his own work.
>
> “In virtue, knowledge, according to the saying of Isaiah: ‘Learn to do good; seek judgment.’ In knowledge, self-restraint: once they have learned to do good, they must immediately abstain from evil, lest knowledge of heavenly things be useless if someone neglects to restrain himself from earthly enticements.
>
> “In self-restraint, patience: self-restraint must always be accompanied by patience, so that whoever has learned to refrain from the pleasures of the world may also endure its adversities with a steadfast heart, armed on the right and on the left with the weapons of righteousness.
>
> “In patience, godliness: toward those whom he patiently endures, he should also be godly, according to the Apostle Paul’s saying: ‘Charity is patient; it is kind.’
>
> “In godliness, brotherly affection: no one should perform works of godliness toward his adversaries with any other aim than brotherly love, seeking this single thing throughout his intention: that those whom he cannot convert to the practice of godliness merely by teaching or rebuking, he may convert by praying or doing good.
>
> “In brotherly affection, charity. Here he calls ‘charity’ specifically that by which we love the Creator. It is rightly joined to brotherly affection as the degrees of virtue advance, because neither can God be perfectly loved without one’s neighbor, nor one’s neighbor without God. Certainly the love of God is greater than love of one’s neighbors, because we are commanded to love them as ourselves, but God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength. Nevertheless, by the habit of brotherly love we ought to ascend to love of the Creator. For whoever does not love his brother, whom he sees daily, how can he love God, whom he does not see?
>
> “For if all these things are present and abound among you, they will not make you idle or fruitless.”

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Mass of the Innocents

It happened that I first wrote and submitted those matters which I had decided to postpone in the order of our little work. In the later part, according to the order of the arrangement of the offices, I ought to have inserted the Mass of the Innocents. But because I then forgot to introduce it, I now think that I have found a suitable place: after the Holy Spirit, who makes innocents, I shall introduce the truth concerning the Mass of the Innocents. Therefore let the discussion of the Mass of the Innocents have its place here.

It is headed as follows in the Antiphoner:

> “Glory to God in the highest is not sung, nor Alleluia, but that day is led along as if in sadness.”

The composer of the present office wishes us to be joined in spirit to the devout women who grieved and mourned at the death of the Innocents. Just as he separates us from the conduct of the wicked Jews on the Lord’s Supper, on Good Friday, and on Holy Saturday by omitting the kiss and the other customary elements, so in the present feast he joins us to the grief of the devout women. Because of their sadness, we omit “Glory to God in the highest” and “Alleluia.”

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1073]

## CHAPTER I. On the Twelve Lessons

Six lessons were read by the ancient Romans in Greek and Latin—a practice that is still observed at Constantinople, if I am not mistaken—for two reasons. First, there were Greeks present to whom the Latin language was unknown, and Latins present to whom Greek was unknown. Second, it was done for the unanimity of both peoples.

They are called twelve lessons because of the twelve readers, not because there are twelve varieties of meaning: there are only six lessons in terms of their content. For if we say “Amen,” meaning “truly,” we must not therefore understand two different meanings, but one.

At the times when we perform the twelve lessons, we customarily fast, even if they fall during the octave of Pentecost, when the sevenfold feast of the Spirit and of the newly baptized is celebrated. Hence the lord Bede says in his homily:

> “The fact that the discipline of fasting is repeated amid these observances, we must believe to have been taken from the example of the apostles themselves. Having received the Spirit, and enjoying more perfectly the sweetness of new heavenly blessings, they lifted their minds all the more deeply away from the memory of earthly delights.
>
> “For that time had already arrived of which the Lord foretold that the disciples could not fast while he was dwelling with them, but that after he had been taken away they would fast. For when the disciples of John questioned him, saying, ‘Why do we and the Pharisees fast frequently, but your disciples do not fast?’ he said to them: ‘Can the children of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.’
>
> “Since, therefore, both before the Passion and after the Lord’s resurrection they could not mourn and fast because of the Lord’s presence, it is certainly clear that after his removal they voluntarily submitted themselves to fasting. For when, refreshed by receiving the Holy Spirit, they had turned their minds completely away from the desire for food, just as from all other worldly enticements, they rejoiced in nourishment for the soul rather than for the body and devoted themselves to salutary prayers and tears in remembrance of the heavenly homeland.”

*Concerning this same fast, Saint Leo writes in a homily:*

> “The custom of celebrating a fast at the ordination of the sacred order has prevailed from the primitive Church. For it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: ‘There were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, among whom were Barnabas and Symeon who was called Niger.’ And a little later: ‘As they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said: Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have taken them. Then, after fasting and praying and laying hands upon them, they sent them away.’ Sent by the Holy Spirit, they went to Seleucia.
>
> “And in another place: ‘When they had appointed presbyters for them in each church and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord in whom they had believed.’ Although a continuous fast over a period of time may also be understood in the words of the Lord Bede quoted above, fasting for those being ordained is nevertheless not excluded.”

Since mention has been introduced of the twelve lessons, it is necessary to begin it from the time of the first month. In the twelve lessons the consecration of the sacred orders is celebrated. For the purpose of that consecration is that a human being may be joined to God. Saint Gregory demonstrates this in response to Augustine, bishop of the English, who asked whether he alone could ordain a bishop. Gregory replied that, if there were difficulty in obtaining the other bishops, he could do so alone; otherwise there should be three or four.

For this reason he says:

> “For in spiritual matters also, so that they may be arranged wisely and maturely, we can draw an example from bodily matters. Certainly, when marriages are celebrated in the world, married people are summoned, so that those who have already preceded in the path of marriage may share also in the joy of the subsequent union. Why, then, should not those also assemble for this spiritual ordination, by which a person is joined to God through the sacred ministry—those who may either rejoice in the advancement of the bishop being ordained or pour out prayers together to almighty God for his protection?”

The first apostles always administered consecrations in the month of December, in which the nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ is celebrated, up to Simplicius, who was the forty-ninth after blessed Peter. He was the first, unless I am mistaken, to consecrate in February, for no other reason than to signify that those who are advanced through the sacred ministry are joined more closely to the body of Christ.

This could in no way be done more suitably than if, through those patriarchs from whom Christ was born, they were spiritually generated. This is impossible according to the flesh, but according to the spirit it is proper and fitting that they should be born in mind through the interpretations of the patriarchs’ names, since they appear to be more familiarly associated with Christ’s genealogy.

And because it would be incongruous for a consecration to be celebrated in each week just as a single week is assigned to each generation, consecration is celebrated at the appropriate seasons corresponding to the virtues and interpretations of the patriarchs who are placed at the stages of the genealogy.

Through three annual *fourteen-week periods* (*τεσσαραδέκαδιας*, “fourteenfold periods”), there are forty-two weeks. According to Matthew, Christ has that many generations, including Christ himself. The same number of weeks is found from the first Saturday of the first month to the fourth Saturday of the tenth month.

The first consecration is celebrated on the first Saturday of the first month, which in a certain sense represents the place of Abraham, through whom Christ is generated. Abraham is interpreted as “father of many nations,” and it was said to him: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” If a consecrated person stands in the seed of many who are converted to the Lord through his example, he is the first patriarch, born from Abraham; the seed itself is Christ, in whose seed it was promised to Abraham that all nations would be blessed.

This consecration is celebrated in spring, a season suitable for procreation. Abraham too was in the third age of this world, an age compared with adolescence, which is suited to the generation of children.

The second consecration is on the second Saturday of the fourth month, which is the beginning of the second catalogue of fourteen weeks. It is assigned to the place of David among the sons. David is interpreted as “strong of hand.” He struck down Goliath—that is, humility struck down pride. Those who are consecrated are consecrated for this reason: that they may be strong through humility and overthrow pride.

It is celebrated in the month of June, when the sun’s heat is greatest over the earth. Everyone knows that David was warlike and burned intensely with zeal for Mars. The time of June is suitable for wars.

The third consecration is celebrated in September, on the third Saturday, which is the beginning of the third catalogue. It is assigned to the generation of Jeconiah. Jeconiah is interpreted as “the preparation of the Lord.” No one doubts that all ought to be prepared for the coming of Christ, and especially those who are consecrated.

This consecration ends at Christ’s nativity. Sometimes it ends in the third week because of the anticipation of the days of the Lord’s nativity, and then there are thirteen weeks; sometimes it ends in the fourth because of the delay, and then there are fourteen. This too is not without reason. For if the catalogue of the final *fourteen* is counted, and Jeconiah is counted once, there are found with Christ no more than thirteen generations; if he is counted twice, fourteen are found.

## CHAPTER II. On the Annual Fast of the Four Seasons

We have spoken of the fast held during the twelve lessons for those who approach ordination. If the Lord grants it—for no one ought to be ungrateful for his gift, neither rich nor poor—we wish to show, on the basis of Saint Augustine’s exposition, the remedies of the fast of the Four Seasons.

Although ordination is not celebrated at the seasons mentioned, just as it was not celebrated by the earliest bishops, it is nevertheless necessary for our religion that we celebrate four fasts annually. Concerning this I think that those seasons came first, and that the twelve lessons were established in them—not the fast because of the lessons, but the lessons because of the preceding fast.

We think that these four fasts are the beginning of the forty-day season. The number ten contains our entire discipline. Our discipline is this: that the creature serve the Creator. God the Creator is worshiped in three persons. He is worshiped by the soul, which loves him with all its heart, all its soul, and all its strength. The body, composed of four elements—hot, dry, cold, and moist—is subjected to the soul for governance.

If the soul governs it well—that is, the three and the four, which make seven—a human being is most devoutly subjected to the Creator, and the result is ten.

The year revolves through four seasons: spring, summer, autumn, and winter. These four seasons often draw us away from love of the Creator through their delights. Therefore we must fast in each season, so that our four elements may be disciplined and not be stolen away by the delights [*love*] of the world.

The four elements themselves are joined in their nature to the four seasons of the year. Spring is hot and moist. In it we perform one fast, so that the element of moisture in us may be disciplined and not consent to the false beauty of spring. From moisture and heat the beauty of the earth is born.

Summer is dry and hot. In it we perform a second fast, so that the element of heat in us may be disciplined and not consent to carnal burning.

The third fast is performed in autumn, which is moist and dry, lest we wither and waste away through some weakness of spirit and be found without the fatness of the olive in the eternal tabernacle. For in that season we gather what we shall enjoy in the future.

The fourth fast is performed in winter, which is cold and moist, lest our limbs be relaxed through dissipation and luxury in feasting and drinking, and thereby the love of God be neglected.

Since the four seasons of the year hinder us from the love of God, we perform four fasts, one in each season, each fast corresponding to its season.

Likewise, the daily cycles of time, four in number, hinder us from the love of heavenly things: morning, midday, evening, and night. Through these also we are daily drawn back from the love of eternal things.

There are three days in each fast because each season has three months, and one day of fasting is consecrated to each month. But since daily sins weigh us down, one fast in each season is not sufficient. Therefore we introduce the forty-day season, in which daily sins are afflicted.

The number ten, which pertains to our discipline, multiplied by four makes forty. Within that ten the holy Trinity of God presides and governs its creature, so that it may be free from the deception of the first parent. What we do well, he himself does in us.

Let us now set down the words of Saint Augustine. He says in Book 83 of the *Questions*:

> “All wisdom and discipline that pertains to instructing human beings consists in distinguishing the Creator from the creature, worshiping him as ruler, and confessing the creature as subject. God is the Creator, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist; and therefore there is the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
>
> “The creature, however, is partly invisible, such as the soul, and partly visible, such as the body. The number three is assigned to the invisible part; for this reason we are commanded to love God in three ways: with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind. The number four is assigned to the body because of its most evident nature, namely, hot and cold, moist and dry.
>
> “The number seven therefore belongs to the whole creature. Hence all discipline, distinguishing and discerning the Creator and the creature, is signified by the number ten.”

And again, in Book Two of *On Christian Doctrine*:

> “The daily and annual cycles are completed by the number four: the daily cycle through the periods of the hours—morning, midday, evening, and night—and the annual cycle through the months of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. We must abstain and fast from love of the seasons while we live in the seasons, for the sake of eternity, in which we wish to live, although through the cycles of the seasons the teaching of despising temporal things and desiring eternal things is itself suggested to us.
>
> “Moreover, the number ten signifies knowledge of the Creator and the creature. The Trinity belongs to the Creator, while the number seven indicates the creature because of life and body: those three belong to it, and therefore God is to be loved with all the heart, all the soul, and all the mind. In the body, however, the four elements, of which it consists, are most clearly apparent.
>
> “Thus, in this number ten, when it is suggested to us temporally—that is, when it is multiplied by four—to live chastely and continently, abstaining from love of temporal things, is to fast for forty days.”

It ought to be remembered on which days these fasts are celebrated: namely, the fourth, sixth, and seventh days. The fourth, because on it the Jews took counsel to kill Christ; the sixth, because they killed him; the seventh, according to Roman custom, is concluded with fasting because of the apostles’ grief at the Lord’s death, as Innocent relates in the *Decretals*.

He says:

> “The clearest reasoning demonstrates that one must fast on Saturday. For if we celebrate the Lord’s Day and the venerable resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ not only at Easter but also every week by regularly observing an image of that day, and if we fast on Friday because of the Lord’s Passion, we must not pass over Saturday, which appears to be enclosed between the sadness and the joy of that time.”

+ Why consecration is celebrated especially on that day, Augustine writes to Januarius:

> “The Sabbath was commended to the former people to be celebrated through bodily rest, so that it might be a figure of sanctification in the rest of the Holy Spirit. For we never read in Genesis of sanctification on all the preceding days; only of the Sabbath is it said: ‘God sanctified the seventh day.’ Since, therefore, the charity of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us, sanctification is commemorated on the seventh day, where rest is commended.”

+ The consecration of the bishop passes over to the Lord’s Day. He is the vicar of the apostles, indeed of Christ himself. On that day he receives the gift of the Holy Spirit, on which day Christ deigned to illumine the hearts of the apostles.

## CHAPTER III. On the Number of Lessons on the Three Days Mentioned

[Col. 1079A]

On the fourth day, two lessons are read, because those who pass into the sacred order ought to be admonished to possess knowledge of the Law and the Prophets. In the fourth age of the world the Law and the Prophets flourished.

The Apostle admonishes concerning doctrine when he says to Titus:

> “Holding fast the faithful word according to the doctrine, so that he may be able to exhort in sound doctrine and refute those who resist.”

Jerome explains this in his Epistle to Titus:

> “Let him hold fast the faithful word according to the doctrine, so that just as the word of God is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, he too may show himself such that everything he says is considered worthy of faith and his words are a rule of truth.
>
> “Let him also be able to console those who are harassed by the storms of this age and, through his teaching, destroy weak and infirm commands. It is called sound doctrine in contrast to sick and weak doctrine. It should also be such as to convict those who contradict it, whether heretics, Jews, or the wise men of that age.
>
> “The things he placed above among the virtues of the bishop pertain to life. But what he says here—‘so that he may be able to console in sound doctrine and refute those who contradict’—must be referred to knowledge. For if the bishop’s life alone is holy, he can benefit himself by living in this way; but if he is also learned in doctrine and speech, he can instruct others as well, not only teaching his own people but also striking back at adversaries who, unless they have been refuted and convicted, can easily corrupt the hearts of the simple.
>
> “This passage is directed against those who, giving themselves over to idleness, leisure, and sleep, think it a sin to read the Scriptures, and who despise those who meditate day and night on the Law of the Lord as talkative and useless people. They fail to notice that after listing the conduct required of a bishop, the Apostle likewise commanded doctrine.”

I have inserted these matters to make the person being ordained attentive to knowledge of the Law and the Prophets.

On the sixth day one lesson is read. It is evident that the Law and prophecy are recapitulated in one Gospel, which is read in the sixth age of the world.

It is unnecessary to say anything else here about the responsories except that a single responsory corresponds to each lesson, as is customary. We reserve them for the future.

On Saturday, when the blessing is given, four lessons are read. There are four orders of those who bless the Lord, whom the Psalmist mentions:

> “House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord; house of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.”

Augustine explains these blessings in this way in his book on the Psalms:

> “‘Bless the Lord, peoples’—that is, the house of Israel in general. ‘Bless the Lord, rulers’—that is, the house of Aaron. ‘Bless the Lord, ministers of God’—that is, the house of Levi. ‘You who fear the Lord from the other nations, bless the Lord.’ Let us all therefore say with one voice what follows: ‘Blessed is the Lord from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem.’”

In these lessons those being ordained are instructed by the examples of the holy fathers of the four orders. If they follow them, they will be able to have a share with them in blessing the Lord, or the blessing of those fathers may come upon them.

From the present lessons of the first fast after Pentecost, let us learn whether the four orders mentioned correspond to the four lessons.

The first lesson says: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh,” and what follows. In these words and those that follow, the house of Israel in general is demonstrated.

The next lesson says:

> “You shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all your habitations, two loaves of firstfruits from two tenths, which the priest shall lift up before the Lord.”

The priest represents the rulers, who are the house of Aaron.

The third lesson says:

> “You shall approach the priest who shall be in those days, and you shall say to him: I profess this day before the Lord your God, who has heard us.”

And a little later:

> “Therefore now I offer the firstfruits of the fruits of the land that the Lord has given me. You shall leave them in the sight of the Lord your God, and after worshiping the Lord your God, you shall feast on all good things.”

Here the offering of the priest is not being described, but that of the minister who carried it; he is included in the third order of those who bless.

The fourth lesson says:

> “If you walk in my precepts, and keep my commandments,”

and what follows. There is no doubt that those who fear the Lord keep his commandments.

The next lesson for the ordination is read from the furnace of fire. No one can properly approach consecration unless he first passes through the furnace and blesses the Lord in the furnace.

Wisdom says:

> “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation tests righteous people through tribulation,”

according to Paul, who says:

> “Let them first be tested, and then let them minister.”

Those who are going to approach the sacred ministry must be proved through the furnace—that is, through many tribulations.

The Apostle shows this present testing in the Epistle for the Mass:

> “Knowing that tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope does not disappoint,”

and what follows.

The Tract demonstrates the gravity that the consecrated person ought to maintain:

> “Praise the Lord, all nations,”

lest, lifted up in pride, he fall into the judgment and snare of the devil.

The Tract is customarily celebrated at a time of humility and is always assigned to a matter of humility. In each prayer during the twelve lessons we customarily show humility of mind by genuflection, except in the octave of Pentecost.

Only in the prayer of the furnace of fire do we not bend the knees, when Nebuchadnezzar compelled the people to worship the statue that he had made, so that the prayer directed to the one true God might be distinguished from the error of the Gentiles.

Only in this prayer, in which we beseech deliverance from the burning of vices, just as the three boys were delivered from the furnace of fire, do we omit genuflection.

## CHAPTER IV. On Clerics, the Name by Which We Are Generally Called

Jerome says to the presbyter Nepotian concerning the life of clerics or monks:

> “A cleric is one who serves the Church of Christ. Let him interpret his first designation and strive, in accordance with the definition of his name, to be what he is called. For *clerus* is called *sors* in Latin, ‘lot.’ Therefore they are called clerics either because they belong to the Lord’s lot or because the Lord himself is the lot—that is, the portion—of clerics.
>
> “But whoever is himself the Lord’s portion or has the Lord as his portion ought to present himself in such a way that he possesses the Lord and is himself possessed by the Lord. Whoever possesses the Lord and says with the Prophet, ‘The Lord is my portion,’ can possess nothing outside the Lord. But if he has anything besides the Lord—gold, silver, possessions, and so forth—whether he is a long-haired man or a pope, if he has anything besides the Lord, he is not a cleric.”

## CHAPTER V. On the Tonsure
Our head signifies the principal faculty of our mind, [Col. 1081B] where the knowledge of God resides. The knowledge of God is in the mind, which is our head. The hairs on the head signify thoughts in the mind. There are two parts of the soul, the higher and the lower. The higher is the mind, in which the knowledge of God resides; we must shave it of superfluous thoughts, so that the eye of our understanding may be able to contemplate eternal things.

Concerning this Gregory says in the *Moralia*: “What, then, is signified by the head, unless it is the mind itself, which is the principal element of each person’s action?” And shortly afterward: “To cut the hair of the head, therefore, is to cut away superfluous thoughts from the mind.”

The lower part, however, has hair—that is, many-flowing thoughts—in which we are accustomed often to think about temporal matters. This part is not in the image of God, as Augustine says in Book Twelve, chapter seven, of *On the Trinity*: “But because sex differs from the appearance of the body, could not the woman rightly have been represented in her bodily covering by that part of reason which is directed toward governing temporal matters, so that the image of God remains only in that part by which the human mind adheres to eternal principles, whether in contemplating or in consulting them?”*

It is not commanded that a Christian never think about temporal matters, without which the present life cannot be lived; rather, the part of the soul that governs temporal matters must be subject to the mind, just as the woman is subject to the man. Therefore the hairs remain on the lower part of the head.

The circle of hair signifies the power of equality that everywhere accords with reason.* Temporal affairs are governed well when they conform to reason. Concerning this, the same author mentioned above, in *On the Quantity of the Soul*, brought forward a verse of Horace speaking about wisdom:

[Col. 1081D] “Strong, and wholly smooth and rounded in himself.”

After the verse, the aforementioned Augustine follows, saying: “And rightly so; for in the soul you find nothing good that agrees with itself in every respect more than virtue does, nor among plane figures anything more than the circle.”

We frequently renew the upper part of the head with the razor when, with vigorous care, we cut away superfluous and temporal thoughts from the higher part of the soul. In the lower part we wear a crown when we bring into harmony with reason those things that, according to the world, we must necessarily govern.

We must take care that the hairs themselves—that is, the cares of this world—do not grow excessively, lest they cover the ears of the heart and obstruct the eyes, for such cares often suffocate the sown word. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “As for what fell among the thorns, these are the ones who have heard, but as they go on their way they are suffocated by the cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and they do not produce fruit.”

Let us also learn from the words of Saint Gregory what is signified by our allowing the hair of the back of the head or the beard to grow beyond its customary length during the time of fasting. The same author says in the same work cited above:

“For what does it mean that the Nazirite lets his hair grow, unless it means that, through a life of great self-restraint, presumptuous thoughts increase? But what does it mean that, when his devotion has been completed, the Nazirite is commanded to shave his head and place his hair in the fire of the sacrifice, unless it means that we reach the height of perfection when we overcome external vices in such a way that we also cut away superfluous thoughts from the mind? To burn these thoughts in the fire of the sacrifice, of course, is to set them aflame with the fire of divine love.”*

No one should prohibit the pious thoughts that usually increase during a period of abstinence; but before they lead our frailty into some dangerous presumption, we must shave them away.

Some ask who was first tonsured according to our custom. I read in a certain man’s letter that it was Peter; but because that letter does not possess sufficient authority for us to establish our opinion on it, we prefer to pass over it in silence. It is nevertheless not unreasonable to say that he, or one of his successors, was first tonsured according to our custom, since such a practice was taken from that Church in which they sat.

But what does this have to do with us, when we do many things according to the custom of the present Church whose authors are not specifically produced, such as the observances of the forty-day period before Easter? We nevertheless know, from the testimony of Saint Augustine, that this practice has been strengthened by the agreement of the Church. Thus we too say that our tonsure has been strengthened by the authority and custom of the Roman Church.

Let us say what Gregory says in the *Moralia* about the writer of the Book of Job: “But who wrote these things is asked with great superfluity, since the Holy Spirit is nevertheless faithfully believed to be the author of the book.” So we too should not be greatly concerned with who first placed the design of the diadem upon the head, since we know that it was formed according to the guidance of reason.

## CHAPTER VI. On the sacred orders that our bishops regularly perform according to customary practice.

First, it should be noted that the Apostle Paul designated the orders that are especially necessary in the Church and portrayed their conduct, without which the offering of the altar cannot rightly be celebrated—namely, without a priest and a deacon. So that the priest may keep watch over the offerings without interruption, a deacon is necessary to minister those things that the priest requires; the other orders were added to these.

As the Church increased, ecclesiastical service increased as well. To provide assistance to the multitude of the Church, lower orders were added to help those placed over them. Thus Ambrose says in his treatise on the Epistle to Timothy:

“It is worth adding this to our remarks: it is not appropriate to be surprised if the Apostle appears to have made no mention either of subdeacons or of lectors. For these ranks of service, which are necessarily present in the Church, were added later, especially for the usefulness of ministry, since necessity demanded that, because of the multitude of believers, what had to be done should subsequently be carried out by others.”

Thus they do not attain to ordination before the altar, since they are not appointed to minister at the mysteries. Some of them perform the office of reading; others prepare within the diaconium those things belonging to the deacon’s ministry, and they also attend to the lamps. Only presbyters and deacons perform the ministry of the mystery: some carrying out the priestly work, others ministering at the sacred rites.

According to Ambrose’s words, we understand that the orders subordinate to the deacon and presbyter should not receive ordination in connection with the altars. Nor, when the bishop prostrates himself before the altar, should he cause others to prostrate themselves with him except those who are being advanced to the priestly ministry or to the office of deacon. Thus the lower orders assist the higher, without excluding the higher from the duties entrusted to them.

According to Augustine, we may understand Christ himself, the supreme Pontiff, as the doorkeeper. Thus he writes in his forty-third homily on the Gospel of John:

“Let us not, therefore, brothers, be reluctant, according to certain comparisons, to understand Christ himself as the door and Christ himself as the doorkeeper. For what is a door? That by which we enter. What is a doorkeeper? One who opens. Who, then, opens himself, unless it is the one who offers himself? Christ deigned to be a lector when, according to Luke, he opened the book and read.”

Saint Gregory joins the office of the exorcist to the ministry of the priest when he says: “For when priests, through the grace of exorcism, lay their hand upon believers, and so forth.”

We find the ministry of acolytes performed by Aaron, the high priest, under the Law, where it is said in Exodus concerning the lamp: “And Aaron and his sons shall set it in place.”

This is sufficient to demonstrate that every priest possesses within himself the ministries subordinate to him, but that, because of the multitude of people, he cannot fulfill them all. Therefore associates have been added to him to perform the lesser duties.

Now the order of the subject requires that, insofar as the Lord grants, we speak about each order individually.

## CHAPTER VII. On doorkeepers.

Doorkeepers have their origin in the Old Testament; there they were called gatekeepers. It is written in the First Book of Chronicles:

“There were doorkeepers toward the four winds,” that is, toward the east, west, north, and south. “Their brothers remained in their enclosures, and they came on their Sabbaths from time to time. To these four Levites—namely, Shallum, Akkub, Elmon, and Ahimah—the entire number of the gatekeepers was entrusted, and they were over the chambers and treasuries of the house of the Lord. They also remained around the temple of the Lord at their assigned guards. When the time came for them to open the doors in the morning, they were from their group and were also over the vessels of the ministry. For the vessels were brought in according to number and taken out again.”

Again, concerning their ministry, the Second Book says:

“He also appointed doorkeepers in the divisions of the house of the Lord, so that no unclean person might enter it at any time.”

And again:

“The doorkeepers kept watch at each individual gate, so that they did not withdraw even for a moment from their ministry; for this reason their fellow Levites prepared food for them.”

When they are ordained, they receive the keys of the church and hear from the bishop:

“Act in such a way that you may be able to render an account to God for the things enclosed by these keys.”

And they receive the door.

Because we are, in general, “a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation,” we must examine how we perform the office of doorkeeper. The doorkeeper opens the door of the church. The Church is the people of Christ. If someone introduces another into the Church through faith, he himself is a doorkeeper.

Hence Augustine says in his forty-second treatise on John:

“I have come so that they may have life”—that is, faith, which works through love. Through this faith they enter the sheepfold so that they may live, because “the righteous person lives by faith.”

The Apostle Paul enumerates this gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit when he says: “To another, faith in the same Spirit.”

Faith has three functions. One is to be a door, which the doorkeeper uses in the present; another is to be an expulsion, which the exorcist uses; and the third is to be a protection, which the presbyter uses in the anointing with oil—a matter that, with the Lord’s mercy, has been discussed in its proper place.

## CHAPTER VIII. On lectors.

Let us take Ezra as a lector in the Old Testament; he will teach us how we ought to read, as it is written in the same book:

“All the people gathered together as one man in the square that is before the Water Gate, and they told Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses.”

And shortly afterward:

“Ezra the scribe stood upon a wooden platform that he had made for speaking, and Ezra opened the book before all the people—for he was above all the people. The Levites kept silence among the people so that they might hear the law; but the people stood in their place, and they read distinctly and clearly from the book of the law of God, so that it could be understood.”

The bishop repeats the work of this priest and scribe, Ezra, in his prayer for the lector, saying that through constant reading he should be fit to pronounce the words of life and, through distinction of mind and voice, to show the people what is intelligible.

This ministry is contained in the gift of God’s grace, of which the Apostle says: “To another, the utterance of knowledge according to the same Spirit.”

We are spiritual lectors when we instruct someone entering the Christian people concerning moral conduct.

## CHAPTER IX. On exorcists.

Bede says in his treatise on the Acts of the Apostles:

“Josephus reports that King Solomon devised and taught his people methods of exorcism—that is, of adjuration—by which unclean spirits, once expelled from a person, did not dare to return thereafter.”

When he is ordained, the exorcist receives a booklet in which the exorcism is written, [Col. 1085A] and he hears from the bishop that he is to have the power to lay his hand upon a possessed person.

This gift of God’s grace pertains to faith. It is the second mode of faith, through the expulsion of the devil. Hence Matthew says:

“Amen, I say to you: if you have faith and do not hesitate, you will not only do this to the fig tree; but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Take yourself up and throw yourself into the sea,’ it will happen.”

In the moral sense: if someone is able through his prayers to expel the vice of the devil from a person, he is an exorcist.

## CHAPTER X. On acolytes.

Let the acolyte take Aaron and his sons as an example of his ministry. It is written in Exodus:

“Command the children of Israel to bring you pure oil from olive trees, crushed with the pestle, so that the lamp may burn continually in the tabernacle of testimony outside the veil that is hung before the testimony; and Aaron and his sons shall set it in place.”

Bede explains this in Book Three of *On the Tabernacle*:

“After the entire adornment of the tabernacle has been arranged, the light of the lamp is next provided for, so that its admirable beauty may be illuminated by the light of the sun during the day and by the flames of the lamps at night, and so that no place in the house of God may ever, at any hour, be overcome by darkness or by any shadow.”

When he is ordained, the acolyte receives a candle-bearing vessel from the archdeacon. Isidore explains why he does this:

“Acolytes are called in Greek *acolythi* and in Latin *ceroferarii*, from carrying candles when the Gospel is to be read or the sacrifice is to be offered. At that time the lights are kindled and carried by them, not to dispel darkness—for the sun is shining at that hour—but to display a sign of joy.”

This gift pertains to prophecy. After a person has been instructed in moral conduct, which is the first gift of knowledge, it is necessary that he be frequently admonished by the sayings of the sacred Scriptures. For just as a kindled fire goes out if fuel is not added, so the first teaching dies out unless it is frequently renewed by various sayings.

The prophet has two duties: one is to clarify obscure meanings in Scripture; the other is to announce future things. That person is spiritually an acolyte who, by preaching, ministers the fire of the heavenly word, by which the brothers may both be illuminated to recognize God and inflamed to love him.

## CHAPTER XI. On subdeacons.

In many places in the Old Testament, subdeacons are called the Nethinim, as in Ezra:

“The sons of the Nethinim: the sons of Isai, the sons of Susan, and so forth.”

And again:

“Each person dwelt in his possession and in his own cities, and the priests, Levites, Nethinim, and sons of Solomon, and so forth.”

As Isidore says, *Nethinim* is interpreted as “those who serve the Lord in humility.” Concerning their ministries he says the same:

“Finally, these receive offerings in the temple of the Lord from the peoples; these obey the duties of the Levites; these also offer to the deacons at the altars of the Lord the vessels of the body and blood of Christ.”

Among the Greeks they are called ὑποδιάκονοι (*hypodiakonoi*), and among us subdeacons.

When they are ordained, they receive from the bishop the paten and chalice. The subdeacons who follow receive from the archdeacon a small vessel for administering wine for the Eucharist of the body of Christ. They also receive a hand-bowl with a towel. They rightly receive these from the archdeacon, because they have been consecrated to assist him.

The regional subdeacon stands before the bishop during the sacrifice. Therefore it is necessary that the subdeacons who follow provide from outside what is necessary.

He is called a subdeacon because he is under the deacon. They are consecrated for a single mystery: the subdeacon carries the altar vessels to the deacon, while the deacon carries them to the altar, in order to arrange there whatever must be arranged and then receive them from there, like a good steward from the table of his lord.

I am surprised that a practice has been adopted in our church whereby the subdeacon very frequently reads the lesson at Mass, since this is not found to have been entrusted to him in the ministry given at his consecration, either in the canonical writings or in his name. As has been shown, he is called a subdeacon because he has been placed under the deacon. His consecration and canonical institution show in what matters he is subordinate to him: namely, that he should minister to the deacon in those things performed in connection with the services of the altar.

In the earliest period the deacon did not read the Gospel, because it had not yet been written. But after our fathers established that the deacon should read the Gospel, they established that the subdeacon should read the Epistle or lesson as well.

## CHAPTER XII. On deacons.

Saint Jerome demonstrates to us the order and authority of the deacon, presbyter, and bishop, as well as the distinction to be drawn from the Old Testament, in his Epistle to the presbyter Evagrius, saying:

“And so that we may know that the apostolic traditions were taken from the Old Testament, where Aaron, his sons, and the Levites were in the temple, let bishops, presbyters, and deacons claim this for themselves in the Church.”

Let us therefore turn through them to the Old Testament and inquire what the ministry of the Levites was in the temple. It is written in the fifth chapter of the Book of Numbers:

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Bring the tribe of Levi near and make them stand before Aaron the priest, so that they may minister to him, keep watch, and guard whatever pertains to the service of the multitude before the tabernacle of testimony; and let them guard the vessels of the tabernacle, serving in its ministry.’”

Behold, we have heard the ministry of the Levites: watches in the temple and the guarding of things pertaining to the service of the tabernacle and its vessels.

And shortly afterward:

“When Aaron and his sons have wrapped the sanctuary and all its vessels during the breaking up of the camp, then the sons of Kohath shall enter to carry what has been wrapped.”

This was their ministry: to carry on the journey all the furnishings of the tabernacle, and even the tabernacle itself, as will be demonstrated in what follows. It is the duty of the family of the Gershonites to carry the curtains of the tabernacle, the covering of the covenant, another covering, and the rest.

The sons of Kohath are said to be under the authority of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest. The others are to be under the authority of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest. It is said that they are to minister in the tabernacle of the covenant from the thirtieth year [Col. 1087A] to the fiftieth.

From this Book of Numbers and from the words of Saint Jerome, who commands us to derive the distinctions of the sacred orders from the Old Testament, we learn that the ministry of the Levites is to guard the church and its vessels and furnishings, and also to carry on the journey those things necessary for the church.

Therefore it was established in the Council of Sardica that whatever petitions bishops might have to present to the palace, the deacons should carry them. Thus it is written in the ninth chapter of the aforementioned council:

“Therefore, whoever has or receives petitions of the kind mentioned above should send them through his deacon, because the person of the minister is not subject to envy,” and so forth.

Since we have heard the ministry of the deacon from the Old Testament, let us see the reason for his consecration from the New.

It is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

“The Twelve summoned the multitude of the disciples and said: ‘It is not right for us to abandon the word of God and minister at tables. Therefore, brothers, choose from among yourselves seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Spirit and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this work; but we will devote ourselves to prayer and the ministry of the word.’”

Hence Jerome says to the same person mentioned above:

“It is not worthy that, while abandoning the word of God, we should minister at tables. Let them know why deacons were appointed; let them read the Acts of the Apostles and remember their condition.”

And earlier in the same work: “What does the minister of tables and widows suffer?” It is clear that their ministry in the New Testament is to bring those things that must be placed on the Lord’s table for the heavenly banquet and to arrange them upon it.

Now let us hear about their consecration. It is written in the aforementioned book, the Acts of the Apostles:

“The saying pleased the whole multitude, and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and the Holy Spirit, and Philip.”

And shortly afterward:

“They placed them before the apostles; and after praying, they laid their hands upon them.”

There is also among us a certain booklet on the sacred orders, by an author I do not know, which says that only the bishop should lay hands upon the deacon, because he is consecrated not to the priesthood but to ministry.

Was the writer of this booklet more learned or holier than the apostles, who laid several hands upon the deacons when they were consecrated? For this reason, should only the bishop lay his hand upon the deacon, as though only he could pray for the power of graces for which several apostles prayed?

Or perhaps a priest does not lay his hand upon the one being consecrated to the office of deacon so that he may not become what the priest himself is—that is, a priest? If so, the bishop too ought not to lay his hand upon him, lest he become a bishop.

But if the bishop ought to lay his hand upon him because the bishop prays for him, he is not the only one who prays; all who devoutly attend to the bishop’s words and retain them in their minds pray as well. The imitation of the bishops is the chorus of the apostles. It is best to follow good leaders who struggled all the way to complete victory.

Since we read about the laying on of hands, which was taken from the Old Testament, it is good to inquire what it signifies. It is a mystery, whatever its nature may be; the things performed in the Old Testament were shadows of things to come.

Let us briefly state what we think. God will provide teachers who will explain our effort better. By the hands we understand works; by the fingers, the gifts of the Holy Spirit. Among human limbs no distinction of members is greater than that among the fingers; consequently, the distinct gifts of the Holy Spirit are displayed through them.

The head signifies the principal faculty of the mind. In the present work we have written, from the sayings of Saint Augustine, that the apostles do not give the Holy Spirit but pray that he may come upon those upon whom they lay hands.

Hence it is written in the Book of Numbers:

“The Lord said to Moses: ‘Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people and their teachers; and you shall bring them to the door of the tabernacle of the covenant and make them stand there with you. I will descend and speak with you, and I will take from your spirit and give it to them.’”

He did not say, “Take from your spirit and give it to them,” but, “I will take and give.” And shortly afterward:

“The Lord descended in the cloud and spoke to him, taking from the spirit that was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men.”

Here too it did not say that Moses gave, but that the Lord gave.

Through the laying on of hands we understand the works of the Holy Spirit. For God is not yet all things in all people. In one there is wisdom, in another faith, in another piety, in another chastity, in another humility. This is the force of the many hands placed upon the head of the one being consecrated: each person prays that the Lord may give him a portion of his Spirit.

If someone wishes to ask, “Why is it necessary to lay hands so many times upon the heads of those being consecrated?” hands are laid upon the deacon, and afterward they are laid upon the presbyter. Why is this, unless it is because through consecration he passes from one work to another, just as he passes from the ministry of the deacon to the priestly offering?

For we can perform neither one work nor the other unless we are aided by the gift of God’s grace, as the Apostle says: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure.”

The laying on of hands and the prayer are repeated: the prayer for the first work passes into a prayer for the second. One ministry is added to the deacon: that he should read the Gospel, which was not read in the earliest period, when Stephen was made deacon. As I suppose, the Gospels had not yet been written.

The reading of the Gospel is appropriate to the deacon; he is a minister. He imitates the one who said: “I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister.” As long as Christ preached the Gospel, Christ became a minister for us—a fact he showed at the end, before his offering, when he washed the feet of the disciples.

The deacon also has the gift of prophecy. And rightly so, because he performs the office of the one concerning whom it was said: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me; you shall listen to him.” And again in the Gospel: “A great prophet has arisen among us.”

## CHAPTER XIII. On presbyters.

Presbyters are appointed in the place of the sons of Aaron. It is written in the Book of Numbers:

“These are the names of the sons of Aaron, the priests who were anointed, whose hands were filled through consecration so that they might exercise the priesthood.”

Our bishops follow this custom: they anoint the hands of the presbyters with oil. It is evident why they do this: so that their hands may be clean for offering the sacrifice to God and generous for the other duties of piety. Both things are signified by oil: the grace of healing and the charity of love.

They preside over the Levites, as the same Book of Numbers demonstrates:

“Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, shall be chief over the chiefs and guardian of the watch of the sanctuary.”

And shortly afterward:

“This is the service of the family of the Gershonites in the tabernacle of the covenant, and they shall be under the authority of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest.”

When they are consecrated, they receive the laying on of hands. What this signifies we have ministered according to what the Lord has granted us.

Let us learn from the authority of the holy Fathers what order presbyters held in the time of the apostles. Ambrose says in his treatise on Timothy:

“Anyone who is unfamiliar with the use of the divine Scriptures might suppose that blessed Paul passed over presbyters. But this is not how the matter stands. For the things he said earlier about the bishop he also says about those who are now called presbyters, because in ancient times both were called by the name ‘presbyter.’”

And shortly afterward:

“But anyone who can know this more accurately may learn it from what the Apostle wrote to Titus. He said: ‘Appoint presbyters in every city, as I instructed you.’ And when he explained what kind of person should be ordained, he added: ‘For the bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward.’ It would certainly have been appropriate for him to say ‘presbyter’; yet he plainly called the same person both presbyter and bishop.”

And Jerome says in his Epistle to Titus:

“Let us attend to the words of the one who says: ‘Appoint presbyters in the cities, as I arranged for you.’ When he subsequently explains what kind of presbyter should be ordained—that is, if anyone is without accusation, the husband of one wife, and so forth—he then adds: ‘For the bishop must be without accusation, as God’s steward.’ Therefore the presbyter is the same as the bishop.”

And shortly afterward:

“Lest anyone think that this is the opinion not of the Scriptures but of ourselves—that bishop and presbyter are one, the one being a name of age and the other a name of office—let him read the Apostle’s words to the Philippians: ‘Paul and Timothy, servants of Christ Jesus, to all the saints in Christ Jesus who are at Philippi, with the bishops and deacons: grace to you and peace,’ and so forth.”

Philippi is a single city of Macedonia, and certainly there could not have been several bishops, as they are now called, in one city. But because at that time they called the same people bishops whom they called presbyters, he spoke indifferently of bishops as presbyters.

If this still seems ambiguous to anyone unless it is confirmed by another testimony, let him consider the Acts. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles that when the Apostle Paul came to Miletus, he sent to Ephesus and summoned the presbyters of that Church. He then spoke to them, among other things, as follows:

“Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops, to shepherd the Church of the Lord, which he acquired through his own blood.”

Here too observe carefully how, after summoning the presbyters of the single city of Ephesus, he later called those same men bishops.

In the same author’s work addressed to Evagrius:

“But Peter also says in his first epistle: ‘I beseech the presbyters among you, as a fellow presbyter, a witness of the sufferings of Christ and a participant in the future glory that is to be revealed: govern the Church of Christ and exercise oversight, not under compulsion but willingly, according to God.’”

The Greek expression is more significant: ἐπισκοποῦντες (*episkopountes*, “exercising oversight”), from which the name “bishop” is derived.

Do the testimonies of such great men seem insufficient to you? Let the Gospel trumpet sound through the Son of Thunder, whom Jesus loved greatly and who drank the streams of teaching from the Savior’s breast:

“The presbyter to the elect Lady and her children, whom I love in truth.”

And in another epistle:

“The presbyter to Gaius, the most beloved, whom I love in truth.”

Let companions not disdain to be what leaders once were.

The priest received his name from leadership, as Bede explains in his exposition of Solomon’s Temple. For the priest received the Latin name *sacerdos* because he ought to provide sacred leadership to those beneath him.

What their consecration was like Jerome explains in the aforementioned Epistle to Evagrius:

“For in Alexandria, from Mark the Evangelist until the bishops Heraclas and Dionysius, one presbyter was always elected and placed in a higher rank, and they called him bishop—just as if an army were to make someone its commander, or the deacons were to choose from among themselves someone whom they knew to be capable and call him archdeacon.”*

The consecration of the archdeacon is well known to us. The archdeacon has the same consecration as the other deacons, but he is placed over them by the election of the brothers.

The same Jerome explains why one person was elected, in his exposition of the Epistle to Titus:

“Before, at the instigation of the devil, factions arose within religion and people began to say, ‘I am of Paul,’ ‘I am of Apollos,’ and ‘I am of Cephas,’ the Churches were governed by the common counsel of the presbyters. But after each person began to regard those whom he had baptized as his own rather than as Christ’s, it was decreed throughout the whole world that one of the presbyters should be elected and placed over the others, so that the entire care of the Church would belong to him and the seeds of schisms would be removed.”

The same author says in the letter mentioned above, addressed to Evagrius:

“But the fact that afterward one was elected to be placed over the other presbyters was done as a remedy against schism, lest each person, by drawing Christ’s Church toward himself, should divide it.”

Let us see why the name “presbyter” passes over to the bishop. Ambrose says in his Epistle to Timothy:

“It is not right to pass over in silence the reason for this, because of that alteration of names which appears at present, and the reason why the names have now been distinguished, so that a bishop cannot be called a presbyter, nor can a presbyter ever claim for himself the designation of bishop, even when he ceases to be a presbyter.

“For in ancient times, when presbyters devoted themselves to piety, they were ordained everywhere, receiving this name in consideration of honor; just as among the Jews those who presided over the people were called presbyters. They were also called bishops because of the work that they appeared to perform: they had been appointed to supervise everything pertaining to the service of piety, so that the administration of all things was entrusted to them. At that time they themselves had been entrusted with the complete administration and authority of ecclesiastical ministry, and everything was governed according to their judgment.”

And in what follows:

“But when the blessed apostles departed, those who were ordained after them to preside over the Churches could not be made equal to those first leaders, nor could they possess an equal testimony of miracles; indeed, they appeared inferior to them in many other respects. They considered it burdensome to claim for themselves the designation of apostles. Therefore they divided the names themselves: they left to those same men—that is, to the presbyters—the name of presbytery. Others, however, were called bishops: those who were endowed with the power of ordination, so that they might fully recognize themselves as the leaders of the Churches.”*

Jerome explains what more the bishop has than the presbyters, saying in the often-repeated passage of his Epistle to Evagrius:

“For what does the bishop do, apart from ordination, that the presbyter does not do?”*

He explains by whose institution the bishop has been established in his treatise on Titus, saying:

“Therefore, just as presbyters know that by the custom of the Church they are subject to the one who has been placed over them, so bishops should know that they are greater than presbyters more by custom than by the truth of the Lord’s arrangement, and that together they ought to govern the Church, imitating Moses. Although he alone had the power to preside over the people of Israel, he chose seventy men with whom he might judge the people.”

Mention was made of these same seventy in the consecration of a presbyter, when it was said:

“When you had set the high priests over the governance of the peoples, you chose men of the next order and second rank to assist them in their fellowship and work; thus in the wilderness you extended the spirit of Moses through the minds of seventy prudent men,” and so forth.

The work of the presbyter pertains to the gift of the Spirit of wisdom, on account of good conduct.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the pontiff.

Aaron prefigures the pontiff in his anointing, of whom it is written in Leviticus: “Moses sanctified the oil, and, pouring it over Aaron’s head, anointed him” [Col. 1091D] “and consecrated him.” And again in the same book: “The pontiff, that is, the chief priest among his brothers, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, and whose hands have been consecrated for the priesthood.” And shortly afterward: “Nor shall he go out from the sanctuary.”

According to the authority of the Fathers—namely, the apostle Paul, Archbishop Ambrose, and the presbyter Jerome—the consecration for offering sacrifice was assigned to the bishop in the ordination of the presbyter. But since canonical authority adds that several bishops should be present, it must be explained why this is added. Gregory the Apostolic responded to Augustine’s question, which we have already presented above in this present work:

“And indeed,” he said, “in the Church of the English, in which as yet you alone are found to be bishop, you cannot ordain a bishop except without other bishops” [Col. 1092A]. And shortly afterward: “When, therefore, by God’s authority, bishops have been ordained in neighboring places, the ordination of bishops ought in every respect not to take place without three or four bishops assembled.”

In what follows he explains why their arrival is necessary. Why, then, should not men of this kind also assemble for this spiritual ordination, through which a human being is joined to God by the sacred ministry—men who may either rejoice in the advancement of the bishop being ordained or pour out prayers to almighty God for his protection?

Gregory explains why many ought to assemble; his brother Innocent shows why it is forbidden for one man to do this alone, in the ninth chapter of the decretals: “Let no single bishop presume to ordain, lest the benefit conferred appear to have been stolen” [Col. 1092B].

Oil is also poured over his head at his consecration. Hence Bede says in the third book *On the Tabernacle and Its Vessels*:

“Once clothed in the sacred vestments, the pontiff is immediately drenched with the oil of anointing, so that the consecration may be completed through the grace of the Holy Spirit—not because we can possess the garments of virtues mentioned above without God’s grace, but because a greater assistance of grace must be granted by the Lord where someone has either ascended to a higher rank or has been set over the governance of many.”

Mystically the Psalmist says: “Like oil upon the head, which ran down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron” [Col. 1092C]. Augustine says in his treatise on the Psalms:

“Who was the priest except the one priest who entered into the Holy of Holies? Who is the priest except he who was both victim and priest, except he who, when he found nothing in the world that he could offer, offered himself?”

The pontiff is made Christ’s vicar; therefore he is anointed on the head. Christ is our head. Our head has been anointed with invisible oil. Because the bishop is Christ’s vicar, he is anointed on the head: by this it is signified that he receives this grace of anointing from him who is the head of the whole body. By imitating him who is the head of the whole Church, through the grace of anointing he too becomes the head of the Church entrusted to him.

Christ intercedes for the whole Church. The bishop, in Christ’s place, is to govern the Church entrusted to him, just as Christ governs the whole Church. This is what the words of his consecration signify: “Grant him an episcopal chair for governing your Church and the whole people.” And elsewhere:

Gregory says in the *Moralia* [Col. 1092D]: “Oil on the head, charity in the mind.” Since he is Christ’s vicar, we ought to find in him the love that Christ showed and taught us, and from him draw it for the increase of our progress.

All these things performed outwardly are signs of inward realities. If anyone possesses the realities themselves in his mind, he is a true priest. Therefore Peter rightly says of all Catholics: “A holy nation, a royal priesthood.”

A certain little book says that, according to the order by which ordination is celebrated among some people, two bishops hold the Gospel over the head of the one being ordained. Yet neither ancient authority, nor apostolic tradition, nor canonical authority mentions this. Nevertheless, the placing of the Gospel over his head may admonish those holding it to pray that the Lord may likewise establish the Gospel in his heart [Col. 1093A], or to admonish the one being consecrated to remember that he is more fully under the yoke of the Gospel than he was before.

For Bede, in his exposition of Solomon’s Temple, speaks generally of the blessing of all the elect:

“He who said, ‘He blessed all who fear the Lord, both small and great,’ himself also said, ‘For you will repay each according to his works.’ Therefore there will be a common blessing there for all the elect; nevertheless, according to the differing quality of their works, there are many dwelling places of the blessed in the one same eternal house of the Father in heaven.”

## CHAPTER XV. On the dress of the sacred leaders

It must first be noted that the dress of clerics has been established in ecclesiastical offices [Col. 1093B] so that in all things it may offer the Christian people an example of good conduct. Jerome signifies this in a certain way in his book *On the Priestly Garment*, addressed to Fabiola:

“We read,” he says, “in Leviticus that, according to God’s command, Moses washed Aaron and his sons. Even then the sacraments of baptism signified the cleansing of the world and the holiness of all things. They do not receive the garments until they have first been washed of their filth, nor are they crowned for sacred service unless they are reborn as new human beings in Christ.”

*From these words we understand that the priestly garments pertain to the conduct of the Christian people.*

## CHAPTER XVI. On not using consecrated garments for ordinary purposes

Stephen, a Roman by nationality and the son of Jobius, as is read in the *Acts of the Bishops* [Col. 1093C], decreed that priests and Levites should not use consecrated garments in the church for ordinary daily purposes.

The Lord speaks of something of this kind through Ezekiel:

“These are the sacred storerooms in which the priests who approach the Lord in the Holy of Holies shall dress.” And shortly afterward: “When the priests enter, they shall not go out from the sanctuary into the outer court; there they shall lay aside the garments in which they minister, because they are holy, and they shall put on other garments; thus they shall go out to the people.” And again: “When they enter the gates of the inner court, they shall be clothed in linen garments; nothing woolen shall come upon them when they minister at the gates of the inner court and within.” And a little later: “When they go out to the outer court, to the people, they shall remove the garments in which they ministered and place them in the storerooms of the sanctuary, and they shall clothe themselves in other garments.”

Although we ought to understand these things spiritually, nevertheless we have been admonished by the Apostolic mentioned above to complete the change of clothing according to the literal sense. For it is good for us, who have been reborn in the Spirit, to keep before our eyes what may pass into our minds.

By the linen garment, which we use only in sacred things, we understand subtle prayer, stripped before the Lord of every carnal thought. But speech addressed to the people must be different and so plain that it can be understood by the people.

Hence Jerome says in the thirteenth book of his exposition of Ezekiel [Col. 1094A]:

“Because he had once commanded what garments the priests should use when they were within, in the ministries, he again orders that, when they go out, they remove their former garments in the storerooms or chambers of the holy places and put on others, lest, if they retain the sacred garments, they sanctify the people placed outside, who have not yet been sanctified and have not prepared themselves in the sanctification of the temple to become the Lord’s Nazirite.”

From this we learn that we ought not to enter the Holy of Holies in daily garments or in garments polluted by ordinary use of life, but with a clean conscience and clean garments to hold the Lord’s sacraments.

And again in the same work:

“Moreover, divine religion has one kind of dress in the ministry and another in ordinary use and daily life. For here too, from Jerome’s words, we have been admonished concerning a change of clothing.”

The same author continues in the same work [Col. 1094B]:

“We make these garments for ourselves by our own labor; they are woven from above, like the tunic that the Lord also had, which cannot be torn. We put them on when we learn the Lord’s secrets and mysteries, and possess the spirit that searches even the depths and profound things of God—things that are not to be shown to the common crowd or brought before the people who have not been sanctified or prepared for God’s holiness, lest, if they hear greater things, they be unable to bear the majesty of knowledge and, as though choked by solid food, perish while they still must be nourished on the milk of infancy.”
