*Among the rules of sacred Scripture, this is one: that we pass from the letter to the spirit, and from the spirit to the letter. Therefore it is not contrary to truth to understand the woolen garment according to the spirit, provided that according to the letter we complete the change of clothing, which we can rightly understand according to both letter and spirit.*

## CHAPTER XVII. On the amict

The amict is our first garment, with which we encircle the neck on every side. The voice is in the neck; therefore the use of speech is expressed through the neck. By the amict we understand the guarding of the voice, concerning which the Psalmist said: “I said, ‘I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue’; I placed a guard over my mouth.” And in another psalm: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth.”

It is called *amictus* because it is thrown around or wrapped about. In this first garment the correction of the voice is signified.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the alb

[Col. 1094D]

Afterward we put on the shirt, which we call the alb. Jerome speaks of it in the aforementioned letter on the priestly garment to Fabiola:

“The second tunic, made of linen, is the *poderis*, that is, the ankle-length garment,” and in what follows:

“This clings to the body and is so close-fitting, with tight sleeves, that there is no wrinkle at all in the garment, and it descends as far as the legs. For the convenience of the reader, I shall make use of a common expression: soldiers commonly have linen garments, which they call shirts, so fitted to their limbs and so tightly fastened to their bodies that they are unencumbered either for running or for battle—for directing a spear, holding a shield, wielding a sword, and for whatever necessity may summon them. Therefore priests, prepared for God’s ministry, should also use this tunic, so that, possessing the beauty of their garments, they may run with the swiftness of men unclothed.”

In this respect that garment differs from ours: theirs is tight-fitting, whereas ours is loose. For those who were in the Old Testament were constrained by the spirit of slavery, concerning which Paul said: “You have not received the spirit of slavery in fear.” But we, because the Son has set us free, are free; we have not received the spirit of slavery in fear, but the spirit of adoption as sons. Therefore their garment is tight, whereas ours is loose, because of the freedom with which Christ has set us free.

Since we have said that the first garment signifies correction of the voice, let us see whether the second signifies some correction of the body. Bede says in his book *On the Tabernacle*:

“This linen garment ought to bind the priest’s hands and arms, lest they do anything except what is useful; his chest, lest he think anything empty; his belly, lest by desiring pleasures beyond measure he presume to make God a glutton; the limbs beneath the belly, lest by behaving wantonly they corrupt the whole beauty of the priestly habit; his knees, lest they grow sluggish in the persistence of prayer; his shins and feet, lest they run toward evil.”

Therefore the priest should first put on a tight linen garment, so that it may restrain both his body from wicked deeds and his mind from evil thoughts. What is signified there by the tightness of the garment is signified among us by the correction provided by linen.

Since Bede reaches the feet in his discussion of linen garments, it is fitting that we explain ourselves concerning the sandals—or, by another name, the *campobi*—which remain on the feet. Sandals cover the foot beneath but leave it bare above. Concerning them the same author says in his treatise on Mark [Col. 1095C]:

“By saying that they are to be shod with sandals or soles, Mark indicates that this footwear possesses a mystical significance: the foot should be neither covered nor bare upon the earth—that is, the Gospel should neither be concealed nor rely upon earthly advantages.”

Just as the linen with which the feet are clothed signifies correction of the feet, so the sandals signify progress toward preaching.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the chasuble

We place the chasuble, which is the general garment of the sacred leaders, before the other garments that follow. In the garments discussed above, correction of the body from vices is signified, except in the sandals. In the garments that follow, works of righteousness will be shown.

Bede says in the aforementioned book *On the Tabernacle* [Col. 1095D]:

“The sacred garments of Aaron, which Moses made for him, are works of righteousness and holiness.”

But the chasuble, which pertains generally to all clerics, ought to signify works that pertain to all. These are hunger, thirst, vigils, nakedness, reading, psalmody, prayer, the labor of work, teaching, silence, and things of this kind. No sacred leader ought to be negligent in these matters. When he is clothed in these works, he is clothed in the chasuble.

These matters are evident and pertain both to the lower ranks and to the highest. The chasuble is double: behind, between the shoulders, and in front, over the chest.

Works are expressed by the shoulders. The garment should be double upon them because we ought to show good works outwardly to our neighbors while preserving those same works inwardly whole before the Lord.

It is double upon the chest because both things ought to be present there: teaching and truth—truth inwardly, teaching toward human beings. These two forms of doubleness should be joined, because ministry is performed well when work and reason come together as one. Work belongs to the shoulders; reason to the chest.

## CHAPTER XX. On the stole

The deacon receives the stole when he is ordained by the bishop. He always uses it in the work of his ministry. The stole signifies the light and gentle burden of which the Lord says: “Take my yoke upon you; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light.”

By the yoke we understand the Gospel. Jerome says in his *Commentaries on Matthew* [Col. 1096B]:

“How is it lighter? Read the Gospel: in the Law homicide is condemned, but in the Gospel anger is condemned.”

And shortly afterward:

“In the Law there are many commandments, which the Apostle teaches cannot be fulfilled completely. In the Law, works are required, and the one who performs them will live by them; in the Gospel, the will is required, and even if it has not achieved its effect, it will nevertheless not lose its reward.”

Because the stole extends to the knees, which are accustomed to bend as a sign of humility, we understand by this what the Lord says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.”

The deacon should know that, with the stole placed upon his neck, he is a minister of the Gospel, not its superior. The Gospel is Christ.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the dalmatic

[Col. 1096C]

The dalmatic was instituted by Pope Sylvester. By the dalmatic we understand holy, undefiled religion, which is with God and the Father: that orphans and widows may be visited in their tribulations, and that those who visit them may keep themselves undefiled from this world.

The dalmatic itself has two scarlet lines at the back and likewise at the front, because the Old and New Testaments shine with love of God and neighbor. Being undefiled pertains to God; visiting the brethren pertains to one’s neighbor.

By the scarlet color we understand works of mercy, which are performed from charity toward orphans and widows; by the whiteness, the purity of those who visit is signified.

This is the garment of which it is said in the forty-fourth psalm: “The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a garment of gold, surrounded with variety” [Col. 1096D]. Hence Augustine says on the same psalm:

“Let there be variety in this garment, but no division.”

Behold, we have understood the variety as the diversity of languages, and the garment as unity. And in what follows: “Surrounded with variety”—beauty inwardly. In the golden borders, variety of the languages of teaching is the adornment.

The borders that project from the dalmatic are the words of that preacher whose religion is holy and undefiled. Just as words are carried away by the breeze of the air, so are the borders carried by the breath of the wind.

Paul displays white borders around his hands for the benefit of the nations when he says: “Rather, let him labor, working with his own hands what is good, so that he may have something to give to the one who suffers need.” What Paul preached, he completed in deed, saying of himself to the Corinthians: “In tribulations, in labors.”

Ambrose explains this in the same Epistle:

“He did not cease to labor with his own hands, lest he be burdensome to anyone.”

Paul bears white borders at his side when he says: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection,” and elsewhere: “In purity”—that is, purity of body—“and in vigils.” Whoever guards this keeps himself undefiled from this world.

He bears scarlet borders around his shoulders and chest when he says: “In unfeigned charity.” Charity is feigned when it abandons widows and orphans in tribulation but helps them in prosperity.

These borders are in front and behind because the commandment of love remains both in the Old Testament and in the New. Hence John says:

“Beloved, I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning. The old commandment is the word that you heard. Again, I am writing a new commandment to you.”

Bede explains it thus:

“The same charity is both the old commandment, commended from the beginning, and the new commandment, because, after darkness has been cast out, it pours into us the desire for new light.”

Some dalmatics have twenty-eight borders, front and back. Here the sevenfold Spirit is repeated eight times, because of the kinds of people whom he fills so that they may praise God: “kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and judges, young men and virgins, old men and youths.”

Others have thirty and thirty. There are fifteen lines on each side, because charity in both the Old Testament and the New produces fifteen branches from itself.

Whoever strives to benefit his brethren in adversity and prosperity has scarlet borders on both shoulders. These two conditions are signified by the left and right shoulders.

The fifteen branches of charity are enumerated as follows: “It is patient, it is kind; it does not envy; it does not act wrongly; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own; it is not provoked; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.”

The line in the middle is like the trunk of charity. For what the lines or borders signify on the right or left shoulder, they signify also on the front of the human being, which pertains to the New Testament.

The left side has borders because the active life is anxious and troubled about many things; the right side does not, because the contemplative life is tranquil. Through it the queen who stands at the right hand is represented.

She is the one dove, perfect and near; she stands at the right hand and has nothing left-sided in herself. The breadth of her arms shows the generosity and cheerfulness of the giver.

A deacon who is not wearing a dalmatic reads while girded in a chasuble, so that he may minister more readily, or because it is his duty to go to the *comitatus* on account of pressing necessities.

The dalmatic has openings beneath the arms because it wishes to imitate Christ, who was pierced in the side by a spear, and wishes us to follow his footsteps—which is signified by its being pierced at the side.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the tunic that the priest puts on over the shirt

Just as the correction of the body is signified in the shirt [Col. 1098A], so the virtues of the soul are signified in the tunic. These pertain only to the exalted. Jerome says of it in his letter to Fabiola:

“This same hyacinth-colored tunic is called the undergarment, and properly belongs to the pontiff. It signifies that the meaning of sublime things is not open to everyone, but to the greater and the perfect. It is the inner garment, and signifies the virtues of the soul, which are known to few and which the perfect person ought always to possess.”

Hence Bede says in his treatise on Luke:

“For who does not know that the bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, patience, modesty, chastity, faith, hope, and similar qualities must be preserved by the faithful without any interruption of time?”

This tunic is not girded by itself, but by the shirt. The shirt is so fashioned that it does not hinder our course toward ministry, because the virtues mentioned provide us with a free path toward contemplation of God.

The shirt is tightened by the belt of continence, as the Lord commands: “Let your loins be girded.” Thus every pleasure is restrained by two virtues: obedience to the Lord and natural reasoning.

These are the garments of which it is written in the Proverbs of Solomon: “Strength and beauty are her clothing.” And above: “And he gave the belt to the Canaanite.”

If anyone wishes to use two tunics, he will show himself to be both deacon and priest—or else there may be eight garments, according to the number of the garments of Aaron the high priest, whose garments are said to have extended around his head and body down to his feet. The garment of the feet and hands is not mentioned.

According to his pattern, as I have said, our high priest has eight garments from head to feet. The first is the amict, the second the shirt, the third the belt, the fourth the stole, the fifth and sixth two tunics, the seventh the chasuble, and the eighth the pallium.

The garment of the feet, however, pertains more to our pontiffs than to Aaron. To our pontiffs it is said: “Go and teach all nations”; Aaron was concerned only with Judea.

The cloth in the hand pertains more to our pontiffs than to Aaron, because there is greater purity in the New Testament than there was in the Old. We possess the good things that they possessed, and more, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

In his office the priest does not remove the chasuble, because, according to the Lord’s command through Moses, he must not go out from the sanctuary, as it is written: “Nor shall he go out from the sanctuary.” From this it is understood that he ought to remain continually in continence and abstinence [Col. 1098D].

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the pallium used by archbishops

The pallium of archbishops is worn over all the other garments, like the plate on the forehead of the pontiff alone. By it the archbishop is distinguished from the other bishops.

The pallium signifies the *torques*—the neck-ring—that those who competed lawfully were accustomed to receive. By this gift the others are summoned to lawful contest.

It has two lines running from top to bottom, both in front and behind. It signifies the beauty of the highest teaching, made acceptable through the discipline of the Lord’s commandments.

The circle around the neck is the discipline of the Lord around the preacher’s speech, so that his preaching may not be one thing and his conduct another [Col. 1099A]. Paul says: “Giving no offense in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed.”

Ambrose explains this in his treatise on the Epistle to the Corinthians:

“For their ministry is blamed if they do not provide examples in their works for the things they taught in words to be done.”

The bishop should bear the commandments of the Old Testament—from the beginning of Genesis to the end—in the line of the shoulder, by working and teaching them upon the breast; and those of the New Testament, from the primitive Church to the end.

Concerning the neck-ring, Solomon said in the Proverbs: “That grace may be added to your head, and a necklace to your neck.”

Bede explains this in the same work:

“Among the ancients it was customary for those who competed lawfully to receive a crown upon their head and a neck-ring around their neck. Therefore, if we preserve the disciplines of our Creator and the decrees of the mother of grace, the splendor of spiritual virtues is increased in us.”

Grace is added to the head when charity, which adorned the chief part of the mind, is kindled more ardently. A neck-ring is added to the neck when the preaching that proceeds through the neck is confirmed by the splendor of perfect action; and, so that it may not be despised by its hearers, it is carried forward by an unbroken chain of virtues.

But for those who, when the Lord came, preserved the decrees of the Mosaic law, the grace of the New Testament was also added, together with the hope of the heavenly kingdom, whose extraordinary splendor, like that of a crown or neck-ring, will never be closed by any end.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the maniple

With a cloth we are accustomed to wipe phlegm from the eyes and nostrils, as well as excessive saliva running over the lips. Therefore, in this place, the maniple signifies the effort to cleanse thought, by which we strive to wipe away our natural and, as it were, innate pleasures.

It is also said to be worn for wiping away the outpouring of tears. Thus we read in Bede’s *Martyrology* that our father Arsenius always had a maniple in his bosom or hand because he needed to wipe away the excess of his tears.

It is carried in the left hand to show that in temporal life we suffer the weariness of excessive moisture—that is, of carnal pleasure.

Again, we carry the maniple so that with it we may wipe away the sweat produced by the labor of our own body. We read that this was customary in connection with the body of Christ. Hence it is written: “And the cloth that had been upon his head.”

Sweat is a weariness to our body. If it were not wearisome, it would not be wiped away so often [Col. 1099D]. The mind too sometimes experiences weariness, as the Psalmist says: “My soul has slumbered from weariness.”

Weariness in the soul is like sweat in the body. Weariness of spirit sometimes arises from consciousness of sins; sometimes from circumstances, such as every scourging suffered from another’s body; and sometimes from weakness of one’s own body, a weakness that can itself sometimes arise from sins.

When the weariness arising from the weakness of sins covers the forehead of our conscience, let us have a maniple made from chastened and pure wood, such as the words of the prophet David: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”

And if there is weakness arising from testing, as in Job, let us say what he said: “As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord” [Col. 1100A].

There was pure thought in David when he said, “Create in me a clean heart, O God,” and pure thought in Job when he said, “As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done.”

Thus, whenever we are affected by some weariness, lest we be swallowed up by greater sadness, let us take, for our consolation, as it were, a maniple—the examples of the holy Fathers mentioned above—to strengthen patience and wipe away weariness.

By the maniple we understand pure and devout affections amid labor.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the variety of sandals

The variety of sandals portrays the variety of ministers. The office of the bishop and the priest is almost one and the same; but because they are distinguished by name and honor, they are also distinguished by the variety of their sandals, so that error may be removed from our sight—an error that might arise because of the similarity of their office.

The bishop has a fastening on his sandals that the presbyter does not have. It is the bishop’s duty to run here and there throughout the parish in order to govern the people; therefore his sandals are fastened so that they do not fall from his feet.

From this it can be understood how necessary it is for him who moves amid crowds of peoples to make firm the steps of his mind. The presbyter, who offers sacrifices at home, walks more securely.

Because the deacon differs from the bishop in office, he does not need different sandals; he too has a fastening, because it is his duty to go to the *comitatus*.

Because the subdeacon assists the deacon and is engaged in almost the same office, he needs different sandals, lest he be thought to be a deacon [Col. 1100C].

Mystically, since sandals signify the preacher’s course, the sole beneath admonishes the preacher not to entangle himself in earthly affairs.

The tongue of white leather beneath the heel shows that the same separation ought to be innocent and without deceit, so that it may be said of him: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” He must not be like the false apostles, who preached out of envy and rivalry.

The tongue that rises from there and is separated from the leather of the sandals represents the tongue of those who ought to give the preacher a good testimony. Paul said of them: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside.”

These are in the lower part and are in some sense separated from the conduct of spiritual people. The upper tongue is the tongue of spiritual people who introduce the preacher into the work of preaching. These things are required in the later life of the preacher.

Within, the sandals are surrounded by white leather. Thus the preacher’s intention ought to be white before God, proceeding from a pure conscience. Outwardly, however, black appears, because the life of preachers seems contemptible to secular people on account of the multitude of pressures belonging to the present world.

The upper part of the sandals, through which the foot enters, is sewn with many threads so that the two leathers do not come apart. At the beginning, the preacher ought to devote himself to many virtues and sayings of Scripture, so that many outward things may not be separated from those that shine inwardly before God.

The tongue of the sandals [Col. 1101A] that lies over the foot can represent the preacher’s tongue. The line made by the shoemaker, running from the tongue of the sandal to its end, represents evangelical perfection; the lines proceeding from either side represent the Law and the Prophets, which are recapitulated in the Gospel. For these themselves are recapitulated toward the middle line, which runs all the way to the end.

The fastening signifies the mystery of Christ’s incarnation. This incarnation, because in certain respects it is open to human senses in a human manner—such as being placed in a manger, wrapped in cloths, and so forth—is represented in this way.

Some sandals are held without fastenings: this signifies preaching.

And in another sense: The Lord says in the Gospel, “Whatever you spend beyond this, when I return I will repay you.” The Lord arranged that those who preached the Gospel should live from the Gospel. Paul spent beyond what was required, because he expounded the Gospel without expense and worked with his hands to obtain the necessities of life.

We can understand Paul’s work, which he added beyond what the Gospel required, as the straps added to the sandals; these are moved here and there by the hands in order to be fastened.

The preacher who is burdensome to no one walks with a firm step.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Recapitulation of the garments

[Col. 1102A]

We wish briefly to recapitulate the entire adornment of clerics.

The head of the cleric is the mind. In its upper part it is uncovered, where the image of God is; in its lower part it is surrounded by hair, as though by certain thoughts of present necessity.

The amict is correction of the voice.

The alb represents the correction of the other lower senses, while reason presides as their mistress and inwardly restrains the pleasure of the flesh through the discipline of continence, as though by a belt.

The linen of the footwear signifies the prohibition against the feet hastening toward evil.

The sandals signify adornment and the preacher’s journey, because he must neither conceal heavenly things nor long for earthly things.

The second tunic signifies works of the mind; the chasuble, works of the body that are devout [Col. 1102B].

The stole signifies Christ’s yoke, which is the Gospel.

The dalmatic of the deacon and his minister, being suited to travel, signifies care for one’s neighbors.

The maniple signifies devout and pure thoughts, with which we wipe away the troubles of the soul arising from weakness of the body.

The pallium of archbishops signifies the neck-ring of most devoted preaching, both in the Old Testament and in the New.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1101]

[Col. 1101B] With the Lord’s help, and with the intercession of the blessed confessor Medard, whose feast is celebrated among us today [Col. 1101C] in the joy of the saints, we are ready in spirit to undertake God’s gift—provided that he himself deigns to purify and brighten the eye in which we may learn, concerning the office of the Mass, what meaning that variety of actions contains which takes place there.

For it would have been sufficient, without singers and readers and the other things performed there, for the blessing alone of bishops or presbyters to bless the bread and wine by which the people might be refreshed for the salvation of their souls—as was done in the earliest times among the apostles.

Therefore we must first speak about the signs.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the signs by which we are gathered together into one
The use of signs is taken from the Old Testament. [Col. 1101D] It is written in the Book of Numbers:

> “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Make for yourself two trumpets of beaten silver, with which you may summon the multitude” (Num. X).

And shortly afterward:

> “When the people are to be gathered, there shall be a single trumpet blast, and they shall not sound alarm blasts. The sons of Aaron the priest shall blow the trumpets.”

And again:

> “Whenever you hold a feast, or festivals, or new moons, you shall sound the trumpets over your burnt offerings and peace offerings, so that they may be for you as a memorial before your God.”

We have heard the sound of trumpets resounding in remembrance of our God. May God grant us that whatever good we are able to do—whether individually in our own cause or collectively in the cause of our brothers, as when the signs are moved—we may do in his memory.

Let us also hear the trumpet calling us to repentance [Col. 1102B] when we are afflicted by adversity, as Joel says:

> “Sound the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call an assembly, [Col. 1102C] gather the people, sanctify the Church, assemble the elders, gather the little ones and those suckling at the breast” (Joel II).

Jerome renders this passage as follows:

> “Blow the trumpet in Zion, and proclaim repentance to the peoples. Sanctify a fast, proclaim a healing—or an assembly—of which we have already spoken. Gather the people, so that those who sinned while scattered may, once gathered, cease from sinning. Sanctify the Church, so that no one in the Church may be unsanctified; lest perhaps your prayers be hindered, and a little leaven corrupt the whole lump” (I Cor. XV). “And assemble, or choose, the elders, so that what is chosen in them may be not age but holiness. Gather also the little ones and those suckling at the breast, so that there may be no age that is not converted to the Lord.”

The little ones and the sucklings are those of whom we read in the Psalms and in the Gospel:

> “From the mouth of infants and sucklings you have perfected praise” (Psal. VIII; Matth. XXI).

The preaching signified by the blast of the trumpets, according to Jerome’s exposition, signifies the sign that resounds in our Church. Our sign is made of bronze. Bronze is a durable and sonorous metal. This sign also has within it an iron striker, with which it is struck so that it may be heard.

The mouth of the bell signifies the mouths of the preachers of the New Testament, which endure longer than the trumpets of the Old Testament and resound more loftily. The mouths of our preachers will endure to the end, and their sound is heard far away, even to the ends of the earth (Psal. LXXV). In the time of the Jews, God was known only in Judaea; but then he was known throughout the whole earth.

The vessel of bronze signifies, as we have said, the mouths of the preachers; the iron within signifies their tongue [Col. 1103A]; and by the rope we understand the measure of our life. Hence Paul said:

> “But they, measuring and comparing themselves by themselves” (II Cor. X).

The measure of my way of life is nowhere shown to me more clearly than in Scripture; and therefore I understand the rope as Scripture. The rope, which has its beginning at the wood, signifies the sacred Scripture of the New Testament, descending from the wood of the Lord’s cross. Yet that wood is held by what is above, because the Lord’s cross is upheld by the prophets and the ancient Fathers. The rope extends to the priest’s hands, for Scripture ought to pass into the works of priests.

Gregory says of it in his book *On the Building of the Temple*:

> “Whoever reads this measures himself by it: how much he advances in spiritual virtue, or how far he remains separated [Col. 1103B] from the good things that have been commanded; how much he is already rising toward the doing of good, and how much he still lies prostrate in evil.”

These last words are very applicable to the work of the presbyter who moves the sign. When he follows the rope upward, he acts so as to reflect within himself on how much he has been raised up toward good works; when he draws it downward, he considers how much he still lies in evil.

The person who measures himself according to the words of Saint Gregory is fit to call his brothers to one heart and one soul. Let the presbyter not despise carrying out this work, so that in this respect he may imitate the sons of Aaron, as he does in many other matters. Whoever recognizes that he is a debtor to preaching ought not to hold back from moving the signs, since through those same signs he can preach to the people.

The cord by which the striker is fastened [Col. 1103C] to the vessel signifies a certain restraint, which knows how to move the striker of the tongue at the proper time, so that the lips may be struck. The cord, when the rope is touched, moves the striker; in the same way, modesty prompts the preacher’s tongue to speak with the authority of sacred Scripture.

## CHAPTER II. On the Arrangement of the Church

The Church is the people summoned together by the ministers of the Church, by him who makes people dwell together in unity in one house (Psal. LXXVII). The house itself is called *ecclesia*, because it contains the Church.

It is called *κυριακή* (*kyriakē*), because it is the Lord’s—*κύριος* (*kyrios*) in Greek, *Dominus* in Latin, “Lord”; hence *κυριακή*, “belonging to the Lord.”

It is called *βασιλική* (*basilikē*), that is, “royal,” from *βασιλεύω* (*basileuō*), “to reign.” *Βασιλεύς* (*basileus*) means “king,” as though from *basis* and *λαός* (*laos*), “people”: *βασιλεύς*, “the foundation of the people.”

Hence Isidore says:

> “Basilicas were formerly called the dwellings of kings, and from this they also derive their name. For *βασιλεύς* means ‘king,’ and basilicas are royal dwellings.”

But now divine temples are called basilicas for this reason: because worship and sacrifices are offered there to God the King.

Josephus, in a similar manner (*On Jewish Antiquities*, Book VIII, chapter 3, and *The Jewish War*, Book VI, chapter 8), calls the house that Solomon built for his own purpose a dwelling, saying:

> “After the construction of the temple, which we have stated was completed in seven years, he began to establish the royal house, whose construction he scarcely completed in thirteen years. For he did not pursue this work with the same ardent zeal as the temple.”

And shortly afterward:

> “These buildings were erected in accordance with the prosperity of the Hebrew land and the dignity of the king. It is necessary to give the whole explanation and arrangement of them, so that from this everyone may infer their greatness when they have read the description of the work. It was a very large and beautiful basilica. It was supported by an immense multitude of columns, which he distributed for the administration of judgments and the deliberation of affairs.”

You have heard from ancient authority that the people came together in the basilica in order to hear judgments. Hear the Apostle concerning the reason for assembling in the Church:

> “Therefore, my brothers,” he says, “when you come together to eat, wait for one another. But if anyone is hungry, let him eat at home, so that you do not come together for judgment” (I Cor. XI).

Paul shows that we come together in the Church in order to eat the Lord’s Supper. You have heard two reasons why the people assemble: one from ancient tradition, namely, to receive judgments and knowledge of affairs [Col. 1104B]; the other from the New Testament, namely, to eat.

We seek both things in the Church: namely, that there we may hear our judgments, whether evil or good, and the knowledge of God, and that we may eat the Lord’s body. Therefore let us set aside whatever lies beyond these things at that time, so that we may be able to receive and retain the Lord’s judgments and eat the Lord’s bread, striving to test ourselves to see whether it can rightly be eaten by us.

In the ecclesiastical assembly the males stand separately and the females separately. We have received this from ancient custom, as Bede says in his exposition of Luke:

> “Someone asks how the Son of God, when he was being raised by such parents, could have been left behind through forgetfulness when they departed” (Tob. II).

The answer should be that it was the custom of the children of Israel, when they came together at festival times—whether journeying to Jerusalem or returning to their own homes—to proceed in separate groups, the men separately and the women separately, while infants and children could go indiscriminately with either parent. Hence blessed Mary or Joseph could each in turn have supposed that the child Jesus, whom they did not see accompanying them, had returned with the other parent (Luc. II).

We may also hold another view in this matter: if the flesh of a man and a woman come too near one another, each is inflamed by the other toward lust. For this reason Solomon says:

> “Keep your way far from her” (Prov. V).

Since we come for the purpose of lamenting carnal pleasures, it is necessary to avoid the incentives to them.

Concerning the dress of women, Paul teaches the Corinthians:

> “Is it fitting for a woman to pray to God unveiled? Does not nature itself teach you that if a man grows his hair, it is a disgrace to him, but if a woman grows her hair, it is her glory, because her hair has been given to her for a covering?” (I Cor. II).

Ambrose says in his Letter to the Corinthians:

> “A woman ought to cover her head for this reason: she is not the image of God, but is shown to be subject; and because transgression began through her, she ought to bear this sign, so that in the Church, out of reverence for the priesthood, she may not have her head free but covered with a veil. Nor should she have authority to speak, because the priest bears the person of Christ. Therefore, just as before a judge, so before the priest, since he is the Lord’s representative, she ought to be seen as subject because of the origin of guilt.”

And in another way:

> “Certain men also grew their hair, while women entered the Church with uncovered heads, glorying in their locks. This was not only indecent but also provided fuel for desire.”

The males stand on the southern side and the females on the northern, so that it may be shown that, through the stronger sex, the stronger saints are always placed amid the greater temptations of the heat of this world, while, through the weaker sex, the weaker saints are placed in a more suitable position, as the Apostle Paul says:

> “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able to bear” (I Cor. X; Apoc. X).

This also relates to what John saw in his Apocalypse: a strong angel who placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth. For the stronger limbs are stationed amid greater dangers, and the others in circumstances suited to them.

Paul makes clear the kind of speech that people ought to have in the Church [Col. 1105B], saying to the Ephesians:

> “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Ephes. V).

Jerome explains this in his exposition of the Epistle mentioned:

> “Whoever abstains from the drunkenness of wine, in which there is lust, and is filled instead with the Spirit, can receive all these things spiritually: psalms, hymns, and songs.”

We learn fully in the Psalter what distinction there is between a psalm, a hymn, and a song. Here, however, we shall say briefly that hymns are those which proclaim the strength and majesty of God and continually marvel at either his benefits or his deeds. All the psalms contain this, when “Alleluia” is placed either before or after them.

Psalms properly belong to the ethical sphere, so that through the organ of the body we may know what must be done and what must be avoided. But whoever discusses higher matters, and as a subtle disputant sets forth the order and harmony of the world and of all creatures, sings a spiritual song.

Or, to express our meaning more plainly for the sake of the simpler: the psalm refers to the body, while the song refers to the mind. Therefore we ought to sing, chant, and praise God more with the mind than with the voice.

We omitted the question of which of the apostles first established that veiled women should enter the church; here, we think, is the place to introduce it. Linus, an Italian by birth, as is read in the records of the bishops, established by the command of blessed Peter that a woman should enter the church with her head veiled.

## CHAPTER III. On the Choir of Singers

Augustine says in the hundred forty-ninth psalm:

> “Many know what the choir signifies. Since we are speaking in the city, almost everyone knows what a choir is. A choir is an agreement among singers. If we sing in a choir, we sing with the heart. In a choir of singers, whoever differs in voice offends the ear and disturbs the choir.”

Isidore says:

> “A choir is a multitude gathered for sacred purposes. It is called a choir because at the beginning they stood around the altars in the form of a crown and thus sang psalms.”

We take the order of singers from David’s institution. When the ark of the Lord was to be brought from the house of Obed-edom into the city of David, David commanded—as the Books of Chronicles relate—that Levites from among their brothers be appointed as singers with musical instruments. The Levites appointed [Col. 1106A] Heman, Asaph, and Ethan to sound the bronze cymbals together (I Paral. XVI).

And after the rest:

> “Asaph was appointed to sound the cymbals, while Benaiah and Jahaziel, the priests, were to blow the trumpets continually before the ark of the covenant of the Lord. On that day David appointed Asaph and his brothers to give thanks to the Lord.”

And again:

> “Heman and Jeduthun were also appointed to sing with the trumpet, striking the cymbals and all the musical instruments for singing to God.”

And again:

> “The singers, the sons of Asaph, stood in their order according to David’s command, and Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun were the king’s prophets.”

The first of the singers, as the Books of Chronicles relate, was Heman. These are the ones who served with their sons, from the sons of Kohath:

> “Eman the singer, son of Joel, son of Samuel, son of Elkanah, son of Geroam, son of Heliel, son of Thohu, son of Suph, son of Elkanah, son of Maath, [Col. 1106B] son of Masat, son of Elkanah, son of Johel, son of Azariah, son of Sophoniah, son of Thahat, son of Asir, son of Abihasaph, son of Chore, son of Saar, son of Caath, son of Levi, son of Israel; and his brothers, who stood at his right hand” (I Par. VI).

Nevertheless, David was the author of their office. Augustine speaks of this matter in Book XVII, chapter 18, of *The City of God*:

> “David was learned in songs. He loved musical harmony not with ordinary pleasure but with faithful devotion, and he devoted it to his God, who is the true God, as a mystical representation of a great reality. For the rational and measured concord of diverse sounds signifies the unity of a well-ordered city, compacted by harmonious variety.”

Therefore let the singers consider what their symphony signifies. Through it they admonish the people to persevere in the unity of the worship of the one God [Col. 1106C]. Even if a deaf person is present, they communicate the same thing through their arrangement in the most orderly choir, so that those who cannot grasp unity with their ears may grasp it with their eyes.

Moreover, singers are praisers of God and rouse others to praise. Jerome says of this in Book I of his exposition of Isaiah:

> “Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman, and the sons of Korah, who are described more fully in the Book of Chronicles, were appointed over the choirs (I Par. VI and XVI), so that worship might gradually pass from the sacrifices of victims to the praise of the Lord.”

This is found very frequently in the Old Testament, where their office is described and their work is said to be thanksgiving to the Lord. This verse is very often assigned to singers:

> “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”

Our singers do not hold cymbals, lyres, harps, or the other kinds of musical instruments in their hands [Col. 1106D], but in their hearts. The greater the heart is than the body, the more devoutly that which is done through the heart is offered to God than that which is done through the body.

The singers themselves are the trumpet, the psalterium, the lyre, the tambourine, the choir, the strings, the organ, and the cymbals (Tob. VIII).

Hence Augustine says in his exposition of the last psalm:

> “The saints themselves are all the musical instruments.”

And shortly afterward:

> “Praise the Lord in his saints. This is expressed in various ways, signifying that those same saints are his own: ‘Praise him with the sound of the trumpet,’ because of the most excellent clarity of praise. ‘Praise him with psalterium and harp’: the psalterium praises God from above; the harp praises God from below, as though from heavenly and earthly things, as the one who made heaven and earth.”

We have already explained in another psalm that the psalterium has above it that sounding piece of wood upon which the series of strings rests in order to produce a better sound, whereas the harp has that wood below.

> “Praise him with tambourine and choir”: the tambourine praises the Lord when, with the flesh transformed, there is no longer any weakness of earthly corruption; for the tambourine is made from hide that has been dried and hardened. The choir praises the Lord when a peaceful community praises him.

> “Praise him with strings and organ”: both the psalterium and the harp have strings, as was mentioned above. Organ is a general name for all musical vessels. Although custom has now established that organs properly mean those instruments inflated by bellows [Col. 1107B], I do not think that kind is signified here. For although *organum* is a Greek word and, as I have said, a general term for all musical instruments, the instrument to which bellows are attached is called by the Greeks by another name. That it should be called *organum* is rather a Latin and popular usage.

Therefore, when he says “with strings and organ,” it seems to me that he wished to signify some organ that has strings. For not only the psalteria and harps have strings; but because, in the psalterium and harp, something was found that can be understood according to the distinction between what comes from below and what comes from above, he admonished us to seek something else in the strings themselves: namely, that they are the flesh, but flesh already freed from corruption.

Perhaps he added the organ for this reason—not so that the individual parts should sound separately, but so that they should harmonize with the greatest concord through their diversity, as the parts are arranged in an organ. The saints, too, will have differences among themselves, but differences that are consonant, not dissonant—that is, agreeing, not disagreeing—just as the sweetest song arises from things that are diverse but not mutually opposed.

> “As one star differs from another in brightness, so also is the resurrection of the dead” [I Cor. XV].

> “Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation.”

Cymbals are struck against one another so that they may sound; for this reason some have compared them with our lips. But I think it better understood that we praise the Lord, in a certain way, with cymbals when each person is honored by his neighbor rather than by himself, and when, honoring one another, they give praise to God (Rom. XII).

## CHAPTER IV. On the Clothing of Singers

The first singers were clothed in byssus, as the Books of Chronicles relate:

> “Both the Levites and the singers—that is, those who were under Asaph, those who were under Heman, and those who were under Jeduthun—their sons and brothers, clothed in linen, sounded cymbals, psalteria, and harps together” (II Par. V).

From the nature of byssus we can understand how closely related these two things are: byssus and the linen that our singers use.

Bede says in Book II, chapter 13, of *On the Tabernacle and Its Vessels*:

> “For byssus, as has often been mentioned, grows green from the earth. But once torn from the earth, it is dried, beaten, boiled, twisted, and through great and prolonged labor brought from green to white. So also our flesh, in order to attain the excellence and beauty of chastity, must necessarily be subdued by the severe labors of fasting, prayer, vigils, and every kind of self-restraint. Through these we may dry up its natural and seemingly innate pleasures and draw near to that dignity of virtue which we desire.”

And in another passage of the same work:

> “What is signified by byssus except bodily chastity, shining white with the beauty of purity?”

In its signification, our linen, with which our singers are clothed, does not differ from byssus. The labors mentioned above are not themselves whiteness, but through them one reaches whiteness. Therefore, as we have said, through the *casula* we can understand those labors themselves; in the shirt, the purity of the flesh itself, which shines before the Lord.

From our own experience we can learn that fasting, prayers, and vigils are one thing, and purity of the flesh another. Many fast, pray, and keep vigils, yet—and this is more serious—fall through the appetite of the flesh.

Hence Jerome says in his exposition of the Epistle to the Ephesians:

> “How many love the Lord, prepared for exile, prepared for martyrdom, prepared to endure poverty and every kind of insult for his sake, and nevertheless are overcome by the passion of the flesh!”

## CHAPTER V. On the Bishop’s Entrance for Mass

The office called the Introit of the Mass begins with the first antiphon, which is called the Introit, and ends with the prayer that the priest says before the reading [Col. 1108C].

The bishop’s entrance for Mass—he who is Christ’s representative—recalls to our memory Christ’s own coming, and the people’s gathering to him, whether through his own preaching or through that of his preachers. The bishop’s entrance is celebrated until he takes his seat. For it touches in part upon the office that Christ carried out bodily on earth, or that his disciples carried out, until he ascended to his Father’s throne.

Celestine added this office to the Mass. As it is contained in the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*, he established that the one hundred and fifty psalms of David should be sung antiphonally before the sacrifice, selected from the whole Psalter. Previously this was not done; only the letter of blessed Paul the Apostle and the holy Gospel were read, and thus Mass was celebrated.

We understand this as meaning that he selected from all the psalms the antiphons to be sung in the office of the Mass. Formerly Mass began with the reading. This custom is still retained at the vigils of Easter and Pentecost.

Christ, the Son of God, who chose his own before the foundation of the world so that they might be holy and blameless (Ephes. I), sent heralds in the Old Testament—leaving aside the others—who would gather his people to the worship of the one God through the sweetness and modulation of their voices.

David was their author. We quoted Augustine above as saying of him (above, chap. 3; Augustine, *On the City of God*, Book XVII, chapter 14):

> “David was a man learned in songs, who loved musical harmony not with ordinary pleasure but with faithful devotion,”

and so forth.

After him came Heman, Asaph, Ethan, and Jeduthun, concerning whom we have already spoken, as well as the meaning of their psalterium, harp, tambourine, strings, organ, and the rest.

All these things are present in work and song. Hence the custom arose that no one should sit in church while the present office was being performed, since they are regarded as the workers and laborers of Christ, or of his heralds, who were predestined and called to the worship of the one God.

Concerning this posture, the little book entitled *On the Roman Order* says:

> “The Pontiff begins ‘Glory to God in the highest,’ if the time permits, and does not sit before he says ‘Amen’ after the first prayer.”

Whoever is drawn to God is drawn by delight, not by necessity. Hence Augustine says in his exposition of John, sermon twenty-three:

> “Moreover, if poets were permitted to say,”

[lacuna]

“Each person is drawn by his own pleasure” [Col. 1109B]—Virgil, *Eclogues*—not by necessity but by pleasure, not by obligation but by delight. How much more strongly ought we to say that a person is drawn to Christ when he delights in truth, delights in blessedness, delights in justice, and delights in eternal life. And therefore the sweet voice of the cantors is devoted to this work, so that by its sweetness it may be suited to exhort the people to give thanks to the Lord.

For thus it is written in the Book of Chronicles (II Chron. V): “Accordingly, when all alike—the trumpets and the voice, the cymbals and the instruments—were sounding together, and singers of various kinds of music raised their voices on high, a distant sound was heard; and when they began to praise the Lord and said, ‘Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever,’ the house of God was filled with a cloud, nor could the priests stand and minister because of the darkness; for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord.”

While the heralds were singing psalms, when it pleased Christ the Lord to come among those singing psalms, he mounted his chariot and came into the world to arrange that same chariot in its appropriate places. Concerning this chariot the Psalmist says: “The chariot of God is multiplied ten thousandfold” (Ps. LXVII). Hence Augustine again, on Psalm LXVII:

> By this name he signified the multitude of saints and believers who, by carrying God, become in a certain manner the chariot of God. He leads this multitude, remaining in it [or: guiding it; the manuscript reading is uncertain], and governs it to the end as his chariot, as though toward some appointed place. The multitude of ten thousand saints is found in the ecclesiastical orders and in their hearers.

There are seven grades of those who have been ordained; the eighth is that of the cantors, and the ninth and tenth are those of the hearers, of both sexes. “Thousands” is added to indicate their perfection.

When the Lord comes, he brings prophets, wise men, and scribes with him; in the Gospel he promises to send these to invite the people: “Behold, I will send you prophets and wise men and scribes,” and so forth (Matt. XXIII).

The deacons occupy the place of the prophets, announcing the life to come from the Gospel. The subdeacons occupy the place of the wise men, who know how to arrange the vessels of the Lord in proper order, and what should be carried first and what afterward. The acolytes occupy the place of the scribes, who kindle the hearts of the faithful from Sacred Scripture.

The incense precedes in the thurible; this signifies the body of Christ, full of a good fragrance [Col. 1110A]. For this body must first be preached among all nations. Hence Paul said to the inexperienced Corinthians: “I judged it necessary to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II).

Then let the candlesticks be carried, so that the light of the preachers may shine before human beings upon the foundation already laid. Once those who have been illuminated have been followed, let the subdeacons follow them, so that the order of the preachers can say: “We speak wisdom among the mature” (I Cor. II).

Let the Gospel be joined to them, in which perfection has been declared: “If you wish,” he says, “to be perfect, go, sell everything” (Matt. XIX). Let the bishop and those joined to him follow the Gospel, according to the Gospel saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI).

The bishop ought very frequently to keep before his eyes what he must always retain in his mind [Col. 1110B]. The seven prophets, or deacons, are in the ministry because Scripture is divided sevenfold between the New and Old Testaments, which serve the Gospel.

The bishop, in the middle as the vicar of Christ, like the Gospel, has in the New Testament ministers of history, such as Luke in the Acts of the Apostles; he has ministers in the seven canonical Epistles; he has ministers in Paul’s fourteen Epistles; he has ministers in the Apocalypse; and in the Old Testament he has ministers in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms. Hence it is written in Luke’s Gospel: “The things written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke XXIV).

But if there are five, this indicates five ministers of books serving in the Gospel. The bishop, in the middle, as the Gospel, has in the New Testament a first order of preachers of history, a second of the Epistles, and a third of the prophets, as in the Apocalypse; in the Old Testament, one of the Law and another of prophecy.

Philip brings these two together in the middle of John’s Gospel, saying: “Him of whom Moses wrote in the Law, and the Prophets, we have found: Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth” (John I).

But if there are three ministries of three books, the Gospel—the fountain of all wisdom—has in the middle two books in the New Testament, namely, the Epistles and the Prophets. The Book of the Acts of the Apostles, which is sent to Theophilus, is joined to the Epistles. It is an Epistle on one account, because it is sent to a certain man; on another account, because it contains only history, it stands by itself.

In the Old Testament there is one. Among the ancients all Scripture is called “the Law,” just as it is said concerning the Psalms: “And in your law it is written, ‘I said, You are gods’” (Ps. LXXXI) [Col. 1110D].

Hence Augustine, mentioned above, in his treatise on John, sermon forty-four:

> The Lord generally called all those Scriptures “the Law,” although elsewhere he specifically calls the Law by that name, distinguishing it from the Prophets, as in: “The Law and the Prophets prophesied until John” (Matt. XI). And again: “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII).

At times, however, he divided those same Scriptures into three, when he said: “It was necessary that everything written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled.”

If there is one, it indicates the one commandment of love, as the Apostle says to the Galatians: “The whole Law is fulfilled in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Gal. V) [Col. 1111A].

The ministry of the prophet is to establish the evangelical truth from the books mentioned above. So that prophecy may be ordered with moderation, it should have before it the wisdom of the subdeacons—that is, they should prophesy at the appropriate time and in such an orderly manner that what is said can be understood by the hearers.

The light of the acolytes should fulfill the work of the teachers, so that they may bring the books mentioned above into manifest light. For whoever goes before Christ to a particular place in order to preach the Gospel must go before him so wisely that he benefits the hearers and explains the obscure meanings of Scripture.

After the vicar passes among the young women with tambourines, concerning whom Augustine, mentioned above, says:

> “In an honorable ministry,” he says, “for thus they are among the ministers, the leaders of the new Churches.” This is what “young women” means: those who, having subdued the flesh, praise God [Col. 1111B].

The wisdom—that is, the subdeacons—goes among the young women with tambourines, so that they may teach the women with tambourines whom they ought to praise. The women with tambourines are the cantors.

The ministry of the cantors resounds with praise, as the same author says on Psalm LXXII:

> Whoever sings praise not only praises, but praises joyfully; whoever sings praise not only praises, but also loves the one whom he sings about.

It is known what the ancient singers loved under the Law; speaking in their person, David said: “I became like a beast before you” (Ps. LXXII)—that is, so that they might have children, abound in wealth, enjoy honor, and rejoice in health.

When Christ, the new human being, came, their hearts had to be changed for the better. The wisdom [Col. 1111C] of the subdeacons renews them, so that whereas previously they spoke only of one God, they now say of God in three persons: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

But we must wait until what the bride prays for in the Song of Songs comes to pass: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song I).

You know that, as the Apostle says, Christ emptied himself and took the form of a servant. Therefore, after he has been presented to the Church, he stands bowed until the fulfillment of his humility, in which he became obedient to the Father even unto death (Phil. II).

In this bowing he gives peace to the ministers who are on his right and left. For he himself is the peace through whom the Church is reconciled to God, whether from the New Testament or from the Old. “He destroyed the dividing wall of hostility and made the two one”; he “gave peace to those who were far away and peace to those who were near” (Eph. II) [Col. 1111D].

He offers the same peace to the cantors who stand behind, fulfilling what he said to the disciples: “My peace I give you; my peace I leave you” (John XIV). He gives it to those who are present and leaves it to those who are absent, whether of the Old Testament or of the New.

This is what we customarily mean when we say: “The bishop gives a sign to the cantor.” When this has been done, the cantors, as though through the arrival of the wisdom of God—that is, of the subdeacons—understand that, having been changed from the Old, they should now praise God in the Trinity, and they say: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

The deacons, as a choir of prophets, stand with him in humility and say: “Lord, teach us to pray” (Matt. VI). By the spirit of prophecy—that is, the spirit of revelation—they understand that they cannot have the proper disposition in prayer toward the Father unless they are taught by his only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father (Luke XI) [Col. 1112A].

What we have said separately about the deacons, subdeacons, and acolytes we understand of each disciple of Christ; but because of certain advances in spiritual dispositions, the work of one preacher is distinguished through multiple orders.

Moreover, the prophet is a deacon and a wise man and a scribe; the wise man is a subdeacon, a prophet, and a scribe; the scribe is an acolyte, a prophet, and a wise man.

Christ teaches the disciples to pray. Therefore the cantors—that is, those who praise the Lord’s coming—announce that the time has come for the hearts of the fathers to be turned toward the children.

Just as Abraham saw three angels (Gen. XVIII) and yet worshiped one God and believed in the Trinity in unity, so now also the children of Abraham ought to believe. And they say: “As it was in the beginning, and is now, and ever shall be,” and so forth [Col. 1112B].

Behold the abundant harvest, of which it is said in the Gospel: “The harvest is indeed abundant, but the laborers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest” (Luke X).

Christ, the Lord of the harvest, sends laborers into his harvest, as it is written in Luke: “After this the Lord appointed seventy-two others and sent them two by two ahead of him into every city and place where he himself was about to come” (Luke X).

In the same way, two deacons at a time go in turn from opposite sides to kiss the sides of the altar. Their kiss signifies the peace that the Lord entrusted to them, saying: “Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house’” (Matt. X).

The altar—or, in another manner, the table that is kissed—signifies the hearts of the elect, whether in Jerusalem or outside Jerusalem [Col. 1112C]. Hence Gregory, in his book *On the Building of the Temple*:

> The hearts of the saints, therefore, are the tables of God.

[+]

Afterward they return to the bishop. Thus, as we read in the Gospel, those who were sent at that time also acted: “And when they returned,” it says, “the apostles reported what they had done” (Luke X). And later: “And it happened that, while he was praying alone, his disciples were with him” (Luke XI).

The disciples are with Christ; Christ alone prays.

Then, when the time arrives for proclaiming the Lord’s Passion, the cantors, in order to recall Christ’s final humiliation, sing a verse from the Psalter. The Psalter is struck on its lower part, while in its upper part it has the place in which the sound resounds. So too the work of Christ’s Passion has striking from below, while above it has the sweetness of the resurrection, which resounds far and wide through the mouths of the preachers [Col. 1112D].

When the time of the proclamation has been completed, Christ goes to Jerusalem, in which there is the altar that is kissed in the middle, because he is the one of whom it is said in the Song of Songs: “He spread a bed of love among the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song III).

The vicar of Christ does all these things in memory of Christ’s first coming. He kisses the altar to show that Christ’s coming took place in Jerusalem; he kisses the Gospel, in which the two peoples return to the foot, so that we too may love those who had been separated from us.

The kisses of Christ’s vicar correspond to Christ’s kiss. Just as Christ first offered a kiss to those who first believed, so the bishop offers one to the first ministers [Col. 1113A]. And just as Christ offers himself freely to those of whom he says, “I have been sent to the sheep that were lost, the house of Israel,” so the bishop offers himself to the altar through which we recall Jerusalem, in which, according to John, the Lord loved his own to the end.

And just as Christ afterward adopted the Gentile people, who were reconciled to God in the New Testament, so too the bishop kisses the Gospel, which is the New Testament.

The Gospel remains on the altar from the beginning of the service until it is taken up by the minister for reading, because from the beginning of Christ’s coming the evangelical teaching resounded in Jerusalem (Matt. XV), and from there it went out into public, as it is written: “From Zion the law went forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II).

Then the bishop moves to the right side of the altar. It is clear to everyone that Christ always lived the life of the right hand after he rose from the dead [Col. 1113B].

The deacons afterward stand in order; to them he said: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI). Those who stand behind him have been strengthened so that they may follow him unto death and pass with him into eternal life.

The greater part stands on the right side and the smaller part on the left. What their number signifies has been stated above.

To signify that we are free to read and retain the Old Testament, as the Apostle says, “Test everything” (I Thess.), some part of the ministers stands on the left side, through which temporal blessing is signified.

Certainly our Church asks the Lord for both: temporal blessing and eternal blessing. We ask for temporal blessing when we pray that God preserve our lords [Col. 1113C], their children, the fruits of our land, and peace in our country; but for eternal blessing when we ask for justice, wisdom, and charity, and so forth.

Amid all these things the acolytes stand and hold candles in their hands. What else does this signify except that every teacher ought to have his teaching in his hands, so that he may strive to teach more by his deeds than by his words?

## CHAPTER VI. On “Kyrie eleison”

When this work has been completed—that is, when a large part of the people of God has been gathered together through Christ’s preaching, in which the cantors have labored with great effort—lest any useless presumption creep into their hearts, the Lord exhorts them to say: “Say, ‘We are unworthy servants.’”

Hence Bede, in his treatise on Luke:

> “We are unworthy servants,” because “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the glory to come that will be revealed in us” (Luke X; Rom. VIII; Ps. CII).

And elsewhere:

> “He crowns you with compassion and mercy” (Matt. XX). He did not say, “with your merits and works,” because by whose mercy we are anticipated so that we may serve God, by that same gift we are crowned so that we may reign sublimely with him.

What we ought to have done, we have done. Indeed, we ought to have done it, because he who came not to be served but to serve made us his debtors—not trusting, to be sure, in our own works, but always fearing his judgment.

And therefore let the cantors say: “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord Father, have mercy.” “Christe eleison”—“Christ, have mercy, you who redeemed us with your blood.” And again: “Kyrie eleison”—“Lord Holy Spirit, have mercy” [Col. 1114A].

It can also be understood simply that “Kyrie eleison” was necessarily instituted by the teachers of the Church so that, after the antiphon has ended, the cantors might implore the Lord’s mercy, which suppresses the empty boasting that often follows cantors.

For they have a certain exultation because of the excellent composition of their melodies, but not the humility of the reading by which they are enlightened for the pursuit of humility (Col. II). In this matter they can be deceitfully deceived through philosophy and empty deceit according to human tradition.

Where there is true philosophy, empty deceit does not follow; where there is ostentatious teaching, boasting of spirit follows.

In another way: before every special prayer of the priests, the Lord’s mercy must precede for three reasons that occur readily to me [Col. 1114B].

The first is that the priest’s mind may be made serene for attending to what he says with his mouth; the second, that he may be worthy to speak to God, insofar as human nature permits; the third, that if, afflicted by some bodily weariness, the spirit should pray without the mind, the Lord may not look upon him in his anger but in the judgment of mercy.

Therefore something of this kind must precede, something that drives away from the mind the overflowing thoughts that arise through sight, hearing, and the other senses, so that in prayer the mind alone may think upon invisible things, since it speaks to the Invisible.

And therefore, in all completed services, “Kyrie eleison” follows before the Lord’s Prayer, as in the morning and evening assemblies. For what we Gauls customarily sing after the nocturnal psalms—the Lord’s Prayer—the Roman Church omits [Col. 1114C].

## CHAPTER VII. On the candles

While the cantors are saying “Kyrie eleison,” the acolytes put the candles down from their hands onto the ground, one on either side and one in the middle. For after good works have been completed, the Holy Spirit leads us to such humility, signified by the light of the candles, that he who resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (James IV) may cause us truly to recognize that we are dust and ashes.

Patriarch Abraham was illumined by this light when, after the Lord had spoken to him, he said: “Since I have once begun, I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes” (Gen. XVIII).

The candle standing in the middle signifies him who said: “Where two or three are gathered in my name, there I am in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII) [Col. 1114D].

The number of the candle-bearers does not exceed the number seven, because the whole Church is illumined by the sevenfold Spirit, who dwells uniquely in Christ as the sevenfold Spirit.

When the bishop ascends to the seat, the candle-bearers change their places into the order of a single line, except for the first, extending toward the altar.

Through the candle-bearers the various gifts of the graces of the Holy Spirit are represented, through which the Church is illumined. In the gifts mentioned above, we must remember two things: the manifold gifts and the unity of the Spirit.

By the candle-bearers placed on either side, the gifts distributed up to this point through the hearts of the elect are signified. By the arrangement in a single line, the unity of the Holy Spirit in the individual gifts is signified. This arrangement extends precisely from the first candle, which we said signifies Christ, from whom the Holy Spirit proceeds and in whom he eternally remains.

For he was sent by Christ on the day of Pentecost, as far as the altar—that is, as far as the hearts of the elect apostles—in tongues of fire [Col. 1115A].

And therefore what is afterward done in the service of the Mass figuratively expresses the time in which the apostles and the successors of the apostles conduct the Lord’s affairs (Acts II). This concludes with the Gospel having been read in full.

The arrangement of the candles may also be understood simply as the unimpeded course of ministering around the altar.

## CHAPTER VIII. On “Gloria in excelsis”

Telesphorus, a Greek by nationality and formerly an anchorite, established [Col. 1115B] that the angelic hymn—namely, “Glory to God in the highest”—should be said before the sacrifice.

Symmachus, the forty-fifth after Telesphorus, established that the same hymn should be sung every Sunday and on the birthdays of the martyrs.

The hymn “Glory to God in the highest” is the praise of God, as we read in the Gospel: “And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God and saying, ‘Glory to God in the highest’” (Luke II).

When the priest says “Glory to God in the highest,” he customarily looks toward the eastern regions, in which we are accustomed to seek the Lord as though his proper dwelling were there, although we know that he is rather everywhere.

It is not fitting for one who wishes to praise the Lord to turn his back toward him and his breast toward servants. We can infer the position itself from the character of the place where the angels sang the hymn mentioned above [Col. 1115C].

The Lord, who is everywhere, was in Bethlehem according to the form of a servant. Bethlehem signifies our Church, which is the house of bread. The angels sang toward the East.

Concerning this position Micah says: “And you, tower of the flock, cloudy daughter of Zion, to you they shall come” (Mic. IV). The Tower of the Flock, which in Hebrew is called *Tower of Eder*, lies approximately one thousand paces east of the city of Bethlehem.

We said above that the bishop’s passage from the altar to the right side signifies Christ’s passage from the Passion to eternal life. Therefore, at this point, we say that “Glory to God in the highest” should be sung, because ineffable glory came to be in the highest when, through his passage, Christ joined the souls of the saints to the fellowship of the angels.

The angel announced this joy at his birth, saying: “Behold, I announce to you great joy, because today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke II) [Col. 1115D].

It is clear for whom he became Savior. When the glory of his resurrection was celebrated, there was peace on earth for those to whom he said: “Peace be with you.”

Great is the peace when heavenly and earthly things are joined under one Lord. The Savior declares that this happened after his resurrection, saying: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII).

## CHAPTER IX. On the first prayer of the Mass

When we say “Peace be with you,” or “The Lord be with you,” which is a greeting, we turn toward the people [Col. 1116A]. When we greet them, we present our face to them, except in one instance: during the preparation of the hymn before “Te igitur.” There, since we are already occupied around the altar, it is more fitting for us to face in one direction than to look backward, so as to signify the most devout intention that we have in offering the sacrifice.

Nor should the plowman, while performing a worthy work, turn his face behind him (Luke IX).

Enough concerning these matters; let us return to the greeting. In the Old Testament the angel greeted Gideon, saying: “The Lord is with you, mightiest of men” (Judg. VI). And again: “The Lord said, ‘Peace be with you.’”

And again, in Ruth: “Boaz said to his reapers, ‘The Lord be with you’; and they answered him, ‘May the Lord bless you’” (Ruth II). No one doubts that Christ himself greeted them in Boaz, since he was in Boaz’s loins [Col. 1116B].

It is written in the Second Book of Chronicles: “Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin: The Lord is with you, because you have been with him” (II Chron. XV).

Our response, “And with your spirit,” is taken from Paul’s Second Epistle to Timothy. For it is written there: “The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.”

When the priest says “Peace be with you,” according to the evangelical Scripture, or “The Lord be with you,” he does what Paul does when he says: “The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit” (II Tim. IV).

By this greeting of the bishop and the response of the people, we understand that the bishop and the people ought to have one disposition, as the guests of one [+] Lord.

After Christ rose, it is clear that he said to the disciples: “Peace be with you.”

Then the bishop returns toward the East and says: “Let us pray.” After this the blessing follows. So also Christ, before he ascended into heaven, blessed them, as it is written in Luke’s Gospel: “He led them out as far as Bethany; and lifting up his hands, he blessed them” (Luke XXIV) [Col. 1116C].

The priest’s prayer is called by both names—that is, by the name of blessing and of prayer.

Concerning blessing the Apostle says: “If you bless in the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the uninstructed say ‘Amen’ over your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?” (I Cor. XIV).

Ambrose calls this blessing a prayer, saying:

> For the uninstructed hearer, hearing what he does not understand, does not know the end of the prayer and does not answer “Amen”—that is, “true”—so that the blessing may be confirmed.

Through these people the confirmation of the prayer to which they respond “Amen” is accomplished.

[+]

The end of the present service is known by comparison with the other services [Col. 1116D]. At the end of the others we customarily say “Kyrie eleison,” and afterward the prayer, and thus finally each person returns to his own place.

To indicate the same conclusion, the candles are moved from one place to another.

Here I wish to cite the authority of Saint Augustine concerning why the custom of the Church has prevailed of directing its prayers toward the East.

He says in his sermon *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount* (Tome IV, ch. 9):

> When we stand for prayer, we turn toward the East, from which the heavens arise—not as though God were there and had abandoned the other parts of the world, for he is present everywhere, not through the distances of places but through the power of his majesty—but so that the mind may be admonished to turn toward the more excellent nature, that is, toward the Lord, when the body itself, which is earthly, is turned toward the more excellent body, that is, toward the heavenly body.

Therefore God is said to dwell in the heavens because the knowledge of that supreme majesty and essence is greater in the heavens—in the angels and in the souls of the saints—than among the saints who dwell on earth, because of the heaviness of their carnal dwelling, which scarcely permits the soul to fly up to the pure light of truth [Col. 1117A].

## CHAPTER X. On the bishop’s sitting

Then Christ ascended into heaven to sit at the right hand of the Father. Since the bishop is Christ’s vicar in all the matters mentioned above, here too he ought to represent for us the memory of Christ’s ascension and session.

Therefore he ascends to the seat after the work and labor of the ministry entrusted to him [Col. 1117B]. Christ, having arranged his chariot in its appropriate places—that is, the presbyters in their order, the subdeacons in theirs, and the other grades in their own places, as well as the hearers—ascends to the seat in his proper place, and sits.

Those who sit with him are the ones to whom he promised: “When the Son of Man sits on the seat of his majesty, you also will sit on twelve seats, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. X).

Concerning them the Apostle Paul says to the Ephesians: “He raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Eph. II).

Of those who ascended with him, some sit and some stand. By those who sit, the members of Christ resting in peace are represented; by those who stand, those engaged in combat.

The head and the members are one body. Thus Christ sits in some and stands in others, as Stephen saw him standing when Stephen was engaged in combat (Acts VII); so among those who ascended, some sit and some stand [Col. 1117C].

The Lord, sitting on high in the heavens, guards his chariot—that is, the city—of which the Psalmist says: “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. CXXVI).

Paul, because he served in Christ’s place, as Augustine says on Psalm CXXVI, declared: “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the purity that is in Christ” (II Cor. XI).

He guarded them; he was their guardian; he watched over those entrusted to him as far as he could. Bishops do this as well. For this reason a higher place has been established for bishops, so that they themselves may attend to and, as it were, guard the people.
