In Greek, what is called *episkopos* is interpreted in Latin as *superintentor*, “overseer,” because he watches over them and sees from above [Col. 1117D].

Just as a higher place is made for the vine-dresser to guard the vineyard, so a higher place has been made for bishops.

And from this elevated place a perilous account must be rendered unless we stand here with such a heart that, in humility, we are beneath your feet and pray for you.

## CHAPTER XI. On the office of the lector and the cantor
The lector is so called because he performs the reading, as Isidore says. A reading is so called because it is not sung like a psalm or hymn, but merely read. In the former there is melody; here only pronunciation is required.

The cantor has many functions. Each function receives its name from what it performs. The reading that is read after the sitting is followed by a song called the responsory. The Italians have handed down the responsory in the same sense as above. They call these songs responsories because, when one person has finished, another responds.

The use of reading and song is taken from the Old Testament, as we read in the Book of Ezra—a matter that ought to be assigned to the nocturnal office, if the Lord grants it (II Esdras VIII). We may also understand the prophet’s office through the cantor’s office. The reading of the Law and of the Prophets was regularly practiced by the ancient people. Hence it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

> And entering the synagogue on the sabbath day, they sat down. After the reading of the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent to them—that is, to Paul and Barnabas—saying: “Men, brothers, if there is in you any word of exhortation for the people, speak.” Then Paul rose, and, indicating silence with his hand, said, and so forth (Acts XIII).

As long as these two things are celebrated—that is, reading and prophecy—we customarily sit, following the practice of the ancients. Hence Ambrose, in his treatise to the Corinthians:

> This is the tradition of the synagogue, which the Apostle wishes us to follow, because he writes to Christians indeed, but to those made from the Gentiles, not from the Jews: that the elders should discuss while sitting, those of dignity in the chairs; those who follow, on benches; and the last, on the floor upon mats.

And again: through the office of the lector and the cantor we can understand the head of a household, who brings forth from his treasury things new and old. Hence Gregory says in his homilies:

> When Truth says, “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder” (Matthew XIII), it may be understood that he was speaking not of those who had been, but of those who could be in the Church. They bring forth things new and old when they speak the teachings of both Testaments with their voices and their lives.

Through the reading we can understand the preaching of the Old Testament, which is more humble; through the responsory, that of the New Testament, which is more excellent. These two teachings are represented by the life of John and of Christ. For when the evangelist Luke says, “We have mourned, and you have not wept” (Luke VII), this pertains to John, whose abstinence from food and drink signified the mourning of repentance. But when he says, “We have piped to you, and you have not danced,” this pertains to the Lord himself, who, by eating and drinking with the others, prefigured the joy of the kingdom. But the Jews wished neither to humble themselves with John nor to rejoice with Christ.

Just as the New Testament is sweeter than the Old, so among the people song is sweeter than reading. The present lectors and cantors, who must stand, as we read above concerning Paul, have the Lord’s business to perform; to them it is said, “Do business until I come” (Luke XIX).

The lector ought to hand on the Lord’s Law to his hearers, as to beginners exercising themselves in the Lord’s school. Those recently called have been invited to the wedding through the offices of the cantors. They are novices; they must listen to a teacher. The teacher and the lector are one. For it is written concerning Ezra that he himself made the Law of the Lord and taught it in Israel. The same book later presents Ezra reading upon a wooden platform.

Concerning teachers Ambrose says in his Letter to the Corinthians:

> By “teachers,” Paul says, he means those who, following the custom of the synagogue, instructed children in the Church by retaining letters and readings, because their tradition has passed over to us.

Again, it seems to me that the relation between reading and the responsory is like that between the elements and the arts themselves. Music also has its elements; geometry begins with the elements of lines; dialectic and medicine likewise have their introductions. Thus the infancy of holy men is educated through the elements of the Old Testament so that it may come to the fullness of the Gospel. The Law of Moses and the whole Old Testament are to be understood as elements, as the beginnings of religion through which we learn about God.

Let lectors—or teachers—give the Lord’s price, that is, the words of the Law, and receive scholarly minds, namely, minds free from the purchase of a field, the purchase of five yoke of oxen, and the taking of a wife (Luke XIV). “School” means release from occupation.

But if someone is still deaf, and, with the ears of his heart closed, remains torpid, let the cantor come with a lofty trumpet in the manner of the prophets and sound into his ears the sweetness of melody. Perhaps he will be awakened. Let what is reported to have happened to the people in the Book of Ezra take place in him. For it is written there:

> The priests stood in their vestments with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise God by the hands of David king of Israel; and they sang together in hymns and praise to the Lord, because he is good, because his mercy is forever upon Israel. And all the people shouted with a great shout in praising the Lord, because the foundation of the Lord’s temple had been laid (I Esdras III).

And shortly afterward:

> Many, shouting for joy, raised their voices; no one could distinguish the voice of the joyful shouting from the voice of the people’s weeping (ibid.).

Hence Bede, in his treatise on Ezra:

> The priests, adorned in holy vestments and sounding their trumpets, as they had been accustomed to do while the temple still stood, kindled the hearts of the people to the sweetness of heavenly praise. The Levites, meanwhile, sang hymns to the Lord on well-sounding cymbals; but the people, with a common shout, displayed the affection of their hearts in praising the Lord.

The cantors who respond to the first singer give voice to the hearers, whom they testify to be praising the Lord. Not undeservedly do the cantors themselves perform the role of prophets, because it is written concerning the sons of their chief, that is, of Asaph, in Chronicles:

> His sons were under his authority, prophesying beside the king (I Chronicles XV).

They raise their voice like a trumpet. To them it is said in the eightieth psalm, “Sound the trumpet”—that is, as Augustine says, “Preach more clearly and more confidently; do not be afraid,” just as the prophet says in one place, “Cry out and raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah LVIII).

The written Law was given on tablets. Scripture belongs to the office of the lector; prophecy was inscribed upon the mind, and the prophets brought it forth with a confident voice, which belongs to the office of the cantor.

The cantor performs the office of a preacher of the faith. After the obedience of the hearers, he ought to sing the verse. What the verse signifies in the preacher’s office we can learn from the Gospel parable that speaks of a servant plowing, saying:

> Which of you, having a servant plowing or feeding cattle, would say to him when he returned from the field, “Come immediately and recline,” and would not say to him, “Prepare what I may eat” (Luke XVII)?

He plows who cuts hearts with the plow of compunction. No one doubts that even carnal hearts are cut by the sweetness of melody and open themselves, like furrows, in the confession of voice and tears. Music has a certain natural power to bend the mind, as Boethius writes in the book he composed on music:

> It is indeed commonly known how often a song has restrained anger, and how many remarkable things it has accomplished either in bodily or in mental conditions.

Far be it that what even the pagans avoided should turn the strength of the Christian mind into perishable softness. Hence it is written in the book mentioned above that the Spartans were angry with Timotheus of Miletus because, by introducing varied music, he harmed the minds of the boys whom he had received for training and hindered them from the moderation of virtue; and because he had changed the harmony that he had received as moderate into the chromatic kind, which is softer. So great was their care concerning music that they believed it could also take possession of the minds.

Let these few remarks about the natural power of music suffice. We must return to the Gospel parable. The servant who plows must not immediately recline when he returns from the field, but prepare his master’s supper (Luke XVII). Concerning this servant Bede says in his treatise on Luke:

> The servant returns from the field when, having interrupted the work of preaching for a time, the teacher returns to his conscience and, coming back from the public forum of speech to the court of the heart, privately reviews with himself his deeds and words.

According to the discipline of the plowing servant, the cantor is admonished not immediately to seek rest after performing his office or to grow torpid through the torpor of security. He has completed his work when, in a certain manner, through his jubilation he has led good people into the exercise of the plow—that is, he has provoked the cantors to cut their hearts with the plow of compunction.

Afterward the verse follows. In the verse he must draw his thoughts back to himself and consider with himself how, or what, he has learned from his teacher. Through fear the verse has not dared to raise the responsory aloud; it does not know how to finish the verse. Here too he imitates another example of the Lord’s teaching, by which the person who wishes to build a tower is commanded first to calculate the cost, to see whether he has what is necessary for completing it.

The aforementioned Bede continues:

> After feeding and farming, he commands him to prepare at home what he will eat—that is, after the labor of open speech, also to display the humility of personal reflection.

This is done by the one who sings the verse. In the repetition of the responsory he raises his voice confidently, no longer fearing the verse. It signifies the preacher who has completed his course, as Paul was when he said:

> I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; for the rest, there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness (II Timothy IV).

We have said that those who are in a certain manner deaf to the Epistle are awakened through the responsory. Let us say how those who are obedient immediately advance through the responsory.

In the reading the hearer is fed, as it were, like an ox. For an ox is fed so that the work of agriculture may be performed through it. The ox is the preacher. Hence it is written in the Book of the Law:

> You shall not muzzle the ox while it is threshing (Deuteronomy XXV).

The ox has been fed; let the work be performed. The cantor is like a herdsman who sings joyfully to the oxen so that they may draw the plow more cheerfully. The cantor belongs among those of whom Paul says:

> We are God’s fellow workers (I Corinthians III).

The oxen are those who respond to the first cantor, concerning whom he says again:

> You are God’s field (ibid.).

As the oxen draw the plow, the earth is cut open, when the cantors stir their innermost sighs, draw forth a sweet voice, and bring it into public expression. Through it they pierce the hearts of their own people and of others to tears, as though by disclosing hidden things and exposing sins to the earth.

In another way: letters are written so that through them what has been erased by forgetfulness may be restored to memory. In a similar way, through a picture we remember what can be entrusted inwardly to memory. Thus through the responsory the preacher is reminded how to put into practice the teaching that preceded it in the reading: first, that by the sweetness of his imitation he may gather many to himself; then, that those joined to him may awaken the hearts of many to compunction and tears; and, finally, that he must not exalt himself over the work of preaching, but be struck by the verse, so that he may recall that he must be judged before the Lord concerning his own affairs.

## CHAPTER XII. What distinguishes the responsory from the tract

This is the difference between the responsory, to which the choir responds, and the tract, to which no one responds: it is the difference between the two sacrifices, namely, those of doves and turtledoves.

The words of the tracts correspond to their office. Those sung in Septuagesima express tribulation, as in “From the depths I have cried to you, Lord” (Psalm CXXIX). Those sung in Sexagesima seek an opportunity for flight, as in “That they may flee from the face of the bow” (Psalm LIX). And so we can infer the rest in order.

“Praise the Lord, all you nations” (Psalm CXVI) signifies the joy of the newly converted and of those recently ordained. Enough has been said about these matters. We must return to the birds, namely, the doves and turtledoves, which signify the responsory and the tract. Concerning them Bede says in his treatise on Luke:

> These birds have the song of a groan. Not undeservedly do they signify the tears of the humble, which we greatly need even in good works themselves, because, although we know that the things we do are good, we do not know with what strictness they will be examined by the Lord or with what perseverance they must be brought to completion by us.

And again:

> There is indeed this difference between the significance of the turtledove and the dove: the dove, which is accustomed to live, fly, and mourn in flocks, represents the frequent activity of the active life. Of this it is said: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and none of them said that anything of what they possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts IV). The turtledove, however, which rejoices in solitude—so much so that, if it happens to lose its mate, it thereafter remains alone—proclaims the heights of the contemplative life, because this virtue belongs to few.

And shortly afterward:

> When, entering my room and shutting the door, I pray to the Father in secret (Matthew VI), I offer a turtledove. But when I seek companions for the same work, singing with the Prophet, “Come, let us adore and fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us” (Psalm XCIV), I bring doves to the altar.

Moses, as though singing a tract of tribulation, ascends alone to the Lord and, lest the same people be struck, obtains mercy through tearful prayers (Exodus XIX and XXXII). Daniel sings a tract of joy when, while his companions flee, he alone remains among the angels (Daniel X). Ezekiel alone marvels at the chariots of the cherubim and the lofty buildings of the heavenly city (Ezekiel XL).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Alleluia

The Alleluia, which is sung on feast days in remembrance of eternal joy, recalls to memory both the joy of the elect and the praise of the Lord. Nothing sinister ought to sound in it, but everything should be right, as it will be in the future life.

Those are the “straight verses” through which we return to the Alleluia, which retain the joy of the Church and the praise of the Lord without sadness, such as:

> The Lord reigns; he has clothed himself with beauty (Psalms XXIX, XCVI).

And:

> The Lord reigns; let the earth rejoice (Psalm CXLV).

And:

> Praise the Lord, my soul (Psalm XCIX).

And:

> Sing joyfully to God, all the earth (Psalm CXXV),

and other verses of this kind. In the responsory we sow; in the Alleluia we reap. Concerning this the Psalmist says:

> Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy.

## CHAPTER XIV. What distinguishes the Alleluia from the tract

The difference between the Alleluia and the tract is that the Alleluia expresses joy or praise of the Lord, whereas the tract sometimes expresses tribulation and sometimes joy.

Tribulation is expressed in:

> From the depths;

> You have moved me;

> He who dwells;

> To you I have lifted my eyes;

> Often they have fought against me;

> God, my God.

Joy is expressed in:

> Sing joyfully to the Lord;

> Those who trust in the Lord;

> Praise the Lord.

After two of tribulation, a third of joy occurs, because after two days of burial there comes the third day of resurrection.

There are indeed two kinds of compunction: one of fear and the other of love. Fear is divided into two parts, concerning which Isaiah says:

> Behold, I am coming to gather their thoughts and works (Isaiah LXVI).

Words are included in thoughts. Thoughts are the words of the mind and the roots of sounding words.

Love is singular. It knows how to love and ask for one thing only, that one thing of which the prophet says:

> One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord (Psalm XXIV).

## CHAPTER XV. On the removal of the chasubles

Ministers remove the chasuble when they assume the office of lector or cantor. In the office of lector and cantor a certain kind of military service is represented, for they fight alone, whether in reading or in the modulation of the voice. By performing these offices they leave the choir.

What else does this signify except the journey that we have undertaken for the common necessity of the brothers? And the works signified by the chasuble are now such that they cannot be observed on the journey. Hence Bede, in his treatise on Luke:

> But if someone thinks that hunger, thirst, vigils, nakedness, reading, psalmody, prayer, the labor of working, teaching, silence, and other things of this kind must always be practiced, he will not only deprive himself of their fruit, but will also incur the stigma of indiscriminate obstinacy, indeed of stubborn foolishness +.

The lector or cantor wears the alb without the chasuble in the solitary performance of his office when he acts prudently and energetically against the pleasures of the world and presents himself to the brothers in temporal necessities in such a way that he can be imitated by many.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the tablets

Bede writes in his treatise on Ezra:

> The Levites will praise the Lord through the hands of David, either with the instruments that he made or by singing the psalms that he established.

In their place, the cantor—or, when the necessity of reading requires it—holds tablets in his hands, to represent the words of the Psalmist:

> Let them praise his name in the choir; let them sing to him with timbrel and psalter.

Hence Augustine, on the same psalm:

> Why does he take up the timbrel and psalter? So that he may praise not with his voice alone, but also by his work.

The tablets that the cantor holds in his hand are usually made of bone, because they signify the strong perseverance of good thoughts and good works, according to the Gospel:

> Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved (Psalm CXLIX).

Or they signify love of God and neighbor:

> What is love if it does not have works? It is vain (Matthew X).

Therefore they are held in the hand, so that love expressed by the voice may be put into practice through work. Hence the same author mentioned above, on Psalm CXLIX:

> When he takes up the timbrel and psalter, the hands sing together with the voice. So, if you sing the Alleluia, give bread to the hungry, clothe the naked, receive the stranger: then it is not the voice alone that sounds, but the hands also harmonize, because deeds agree with words. +

The Alleluia verse touches the cantor inwardly, so that he may consider in what he ought to praise the Lord or in what he ought to rejoice. This jubilation, which the cantors call the Sequence, brings before our minds that state when verbal speech will no longer be necessary, but the mind will show to mind by thought alone what it holds within itself.

Here the second period of preaching ends. The discourse of preaching runs up to the state just mentioned; what follows is veiled beneath the wings of the seraphim.

## CHAPTER XVII. On ascending the pulpit

The lector and cantor ascend a step according to the custom of the ancients, as it is written in Ezra:

> Ezra the scribe stood upon a wooden platform that he had made for speaking (II Esdras VIII).

And shortly afterward:

> For he stood above all the people.

Bede says that Scripture seems to recall this passage in the same book of Chronicles, where it is said that Solomon stood before the altar of the Lord opposite the whole multitude of Israel and stretched out his hands (II Chronicles VI). Solomon had made a bronze platform and placed it in the middle of the basilica; it was five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high, and he stood upon it.

“In the middle of the basilica” means, he says, in the middle of the priests’ court; this basilica, larger than the outer courts, was surrounded on every side by the courts of the temple. Concerning these it was written earlier in the same book:

> He also made the priests’ court and the great basilica.

But because Solomon, as a king, made a bronze platform, whereas Ezra, as one of lesser power, established a wooden platform for speaking, so also Solomon or Moses made the altar of burnt offering from bronze, while the children of the transmigration replaced it with one of stone.

Yet the wooden platform must not be thought to contain a lesser sacramental perfection than the bronze platform. For, as has often been said, just as bronze, because of its enduring permanence or the sweetness of its sound, corresponds to divine mysteries—which do not fail through any length of ages, and whose sound has gone out into all the earth (Psalm XVIII)—so wood is also most suitably fitting for them because of the trophy of the Lord’s Passion.

The bishop therefore stands above all the people when the one who receives the teacher’s step surpasses the common people by the merit of a more perfect life and action. He stands upon the wooden platform that he made for speaking when, by the singular imitation of the Lord’s Passion, he makes himself higher than the others. Hence he rightly obtains the confidence to preach the word of God freely.

For the one who disdains to imitate the Lord’s Passion according to his ability has not yet ascended the wooden platform from which he might stand above the lowly. Therefore such a trembling scribe must preach the Lord’s commands fearfully or shamefacedly, afraid to set before others for practice what he himself has not done.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the deacon’s ascent to the tribunal

Cyprian calls the step upon which the deacon ascends to read the tribunal. He writes to the clergy and people concerning Celerinus, a confessor ordained as a lector. I have thought it fitting, so that the deacon’s more sacred dignity and the greatness of his ministry may be recognized, to set down Cyprian’s own words, and afterward our own exposition:

> What else should have been done with this man, beloved brothers, who came to us with so great a manifestation of the Lord’s favor, made illustrious by the testimony and miracle of the very man who had persecuted him, than to place him upon the pulpit—that is, upon the tribunal of the Church—so that, supported by the height of the elevated place and conspicuous to the whole people in keeping with the distinction of his honor, he might read the Lord’s commands and Gospel, which he follows bravely and faithfully? Let the voice that confessed the Lord be heard in those things that the Lord spoke. Let him see whether there is any further step to which he might proceed [i.e. advance] in the Church. There is nothing in which a confessor can benefit his brothers more than this: when the Gospel reading is heard from his mouth, let whoever hears the lector’s faith imitate it. He ought to have been joined in reading to Aurelius, with whom he has also been joined in the fellowship of divine honor.

And shortly afterward:

> Know, nevertheless, that these lectors have meanwhile been appointed, because the lamp ought to be placed upon the lampstand, so that it may give light to all (Luke XI), and glorious faces ought to be established in a higher place, where, seen by the whole surrounding brotherhood, they may offer to those who look upon them an incentive to glory.

Now let us return to the order. Until now we have been sitting according to the ancient custom, as we stated above, either as a reminder or because we are admonished how we ought to sing to God, according to the Apostle’s words:

> Singing and making melody in your hearts (Ephesians V).

Now we must stand for the words of the Gospel.

Anastasius, a Roman by nationality and the son of Maximus, as it is read in the episcopal records, established that whenever the holy Gospels were recited, the priests should not sit but stand bowed.

Then the bishop places incense in the censer upon the coals, so that it may produce a sweet fragrance. The censer signifies the body of Christ, in which there is fire, namely, the Holy Spirit. From it proceeds a good odor, which each of the elect wishes to draw to himself. The same odor demonstrates the good work proceeding from Christ, which the person who wishes to live draws into his own heart.

After this the deacon asks the priest for a blessing, and the priest says to him:

> May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips.

The deacon must take careful heed that his heart goes forth with the Lord’s words and that the priest’s prayer not be fruitless. Let him hold in his mind the Lord whom he receives through the priest’s blessing; and, so that the words imposed upon him may not escape or harmful things enter, he is protected by the sign of the cross made by the priest’s hand over his head.

Then he goes to the altar to take from it the Gospel for reading. The altar can signify Jerusalem, as we stated above, from which Gospel preaching went forth, as it is written:

> From Zion the Law went forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isaiah II).

Or it can signify the Lord’s own body, in which are the words of the Gospel, namely, the good announcement. He himself commanded the apostles to preach the Gospel to every creature (Mark XVI). He himself said:

> The words that I speak to you are spirit and life (John VI).

Christ is life. The words that he spoke are contained in the Gospel.

The deacon who carries the Gospel of Christ is the foot. He carries the Gospel on his left arm, by which temporal life is signified, in which the Gospel must be preached.

When the deacon gives the greeting, it is fitting that the whole people turn toward him. After this the priest and the whole people turn toward the east until the deacon begins to speak to the Lord, and they make the sign of the cross upon their foreheads.

This too must not be understood as meaningless: what the priest has implanted in the deacon’s heart through his prayer, each of the faithful should strive to implant in his own mind.

Because the deacon is not permitted, on account of the prescribed words, to pray the following Gospel according to whichever Evangelist, the superior gives him a blessing beforehand; or because the one who hands on the seeds of the Gospel needs a greater blessing than the one who receives them.

Meanwhile, let the people entreat God that the devil may not take the words of the Gospel from his heart, that their hearts may not be stony, nor choked with bushes or thorns, but good soil, so that they may be able to receive good fruit and bear fruit.

Let the person who is less ready to grasp the words of the Gospel at least say:

> Glory to you, Lord (Luke VIII).

After praying this, let him fortify himself with the sign of the holy cross, to confirm what he has planted in his mind by thinking and speaking well.

Since mention has been made of the sign of the cross on the forehead, it is good to explain why we make it especially on that part of the body. The seat of shame is customarily located on the forehead. The Jews are ashamed to believe in the one whom they know to have been crucified, as the Apostle Paul says:

> We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling block (I Corinthians I).

But we believe that we are saved through the Crucified One, whose name the Jews are ashamed of, and in whose name we believe that we are fortified. Therefore we make the sign on the forehead, where the seat of shame is, as we have already said.

Until this office we were supported by staffs. Now, as servants ought to stand before the Lord, we stand humbly, laying down the staffs from our hands. This can distinguish us from the work of the Jews, who placed a reed in Christ’s hand. Yet it is not contrary to the truth if our humility is displayed before the Lord by laying down the staffs.

The two candles carried before the Gospel signify that the Law and the Prophets preceded the teaching of the Gospel. The censer, however, signifies the reputation of good virtues proceeding from Christ. The censer itself ascends to the tribunal before the Gospel, so that it may offer a sweet fragrance there. For Christ’s good works preceded the teaching of the Gospel, as Luke testifies in the Acts of the Apostles:

> What Jesus began to do and to teach (Acts I).

He first did, and afterward taught.

The more exalted place in which the Gospel is read signifies the most eminent teaching of Gospel preaching and the most manifest authority to judge. The position of the candles shows that the Law and the Prophets are inferior to the Gospel.

When the Gospel has been returned after the reading to its proper place, the candles are extinguished, because, once the preaching of the Gospel has ended, the Law and prophecy will cease.

The Gospel, which from the first time of the bishop’s coming to rest upon the altar until the deacon’s final trumpet remains there, signifies the period during which it is necessary for the Gospel to be preached. The preceding office represents the preaching of Christ up to the hour of the Passion, and that of his preachers to the end of the world and beyond. The following work represents Christ’s Passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, and likewise the sacrifice or mortification and resurrection of his followers through confession and longing for heaven, where they will hear:

> Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you (Matthew XXV).

## CHAPTER XIX. On the office called the Offertory

When the preceding offices mentioned above have been completed, the office is introduced in which the offering of those who pay their vows to the Lord is celebrated.

First the legal offering must be recalled, then Christ’s offering, and finally our own. The legal offering had two altars: one at the entrance of the tabernacle, the other within the tabernacle. The altar at the entrance prefigured the present office, concerning which it is written in the Book of Exodus:

> He also placed the curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle and the altar of burnt offering in the vestibule of the testimony, offering upon it burnt offerings and sacrifices as the Lord commanded (Exodus XI).

For what reasons offerings were made, the Book of Numbers makes clear, saying in chapter XV:

> Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you have entered the land of your dwelling, which I will give you, and you make an offering to the Lord as a burnt offering or a peace offering, fulfilling vows or offering gifts voluntarily.

There is also another kind of sacrifice, because our offerings are of two kinds: one through the mortification of the flesh, the other through the offering of good works. Both are offered at the entrance of the tabernacle. In the present life we must mortify the flesh and render good works.

Concerning the second sacrifice, the aforementioned book records:

> Its sacrifice shall be like two tenths mixed with a third of a hin of oil, and he shall offer wine for a drink offering, a third of the same measure, as a sweet odor to the Lord (Numbers XV).

That it must be offered by the hand of the priest is made clear in Leviticus XVII:

> Therefore the children of Israel must offer their victims to the priest, which they kill in the field, so that they may be sanctified to the Lord at the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, and they must sacrifice these victims as peace offerings to the Lord (II Chronicles II).

Again, Chronicles shows for what things one ought to offer. The priests entered before King Hezekiah and said:

> We have sanctified the whole house of the Lord, and the altar of burnt offering.

And shortly afterward:

> Rising early, King Hezekiah gathered all the rulers of the city and went up to the house of the Lord. They offered together seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven goats, for sin, for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah. He also told the priests, the sons of Aaron, to offer them upon the altar to the Lord.

We are taught by the Old Testament for what things we ought to offer sacrifices: for vows, for voluntary offerings, for sin, for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah.

When we fulfill what we promised in tribulation, we act for vows. When we give thanks for what we have received, we act for voluntary offerings. When we are pierced with compunction over what we have committed, we act for sin. When we ask kings for upright hearts, we act for the kingdom. When we ask for the stability of the sacred orders, we act for the sanctuary. When we ask for the peace and unanimity of the people, we act for Judah.

Meanwhile, song was celebrated in the temple of the Lord, as the same Book of Chronicles says:

> He also appointed the Levites in the house of the Lord with cymbals, psalteries, and lyres, according to the arrangement of David (II Chronicles XXIX).

And shortly afterward:

> When the burnt offerings were being made, they began to sing praises to the Lord, to sound the trumpets, and to strike the various instruments that King David had devised. While the whole assembly was worshiping, the singers who held the trumpets were performing their office until the burnt offering was completed. When the offering had ended, the king and all who were with him bowed down and worshiped.

But before the priests entered to offer the burnt offerings, they washed their hands, as it is written in the Book of Exodus. The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

> You shall also make a bronze basin with its base for washing, and place it in the tabernacle of the testimony beside the altar. When water has been poured into it, Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet there whenever they enter the tabernacle of the testimony and whenever they approach the altar.

For now, let these remarks about the ancient offering suffice. Let us now consider Christ’s offering.

The office that we call the Offertory begins at the point where the priest says, “The Lord be with you,” and ends where he says in a loud voice, “For ever and ever.” The final words are spoken aloud so that they may be heard by the people and the prayer may be confirmed by the people’s response.

[Col. 1128B] Christ, then, deigned to come to Jerusalem on Palm Sunday and there await the day of his immolation. Every previous immolation prefigured him; in him every immolation was brought to fulfillment. On that day the Lord descended from the Mount of Olives, while a great crowd came out to meet him (Matt. XXI). There is no doubt that he greeted it according to the good custom of ancient tradition, which not only our learned Church but also the common people observe. It is customary, as a form of greeting, to wish something good upon one who meets us. We say especially, therefore, that the Lord greeted the crowd coming out to meet him because this was the custom of the Jews. Or, as Augustine says in his exposition of the psalm “They have often fought against me” (Ps. CXXVIII):

> Among our people, brothers, when one passes by workers, it is customary to say to them, “The blessing of the Lord be upon you.” This custom was even more prevalent among the Jewish people. No one passed by and saw some work in a field, vineyard, harvest, or anything of that kind without a blessing; it was not permitted to pass by without one.

[Col. 1128C] This custom remains to the present day in our Church: when we pass from one office to another, as though we were newly approaching workers, we greet them with words full of blessing.

Afterward the priest says, “Let us pray.” If the power of Christ had not filled the hearts of the crowds for prayer, they would not have sung such magnificent praises to him. For by prayer the heart is made serene for knowing the Lord. The purity of the linen placed upon the altar signifies the purity of mind of those who sang to the Lord. He required this same purity, with which he had filled the hearts of the singers, in the temple when he drove out the sellers and buyers, saying, “It is written: My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. XXI).

[Col. 1128D] While the priest receives the offerings, the singers sing. For as long as the crowd sang, “Hosanna in the highest” (John XII), Christ received their vows. Once the offering has been received, the priest returns to the altar so that either he himself or the deacon may arrange before the Lord the offerings that he will sacrifice to him in the following parts of the Mass (Isa. LVI). For after receiving the vows of the singers, Christ entered Jerusalem and the Lord’s temple, in which there was an altar, and there presented himself to himself and to God the Father for the future immolation.

Afterward the priest says the Secret, so that the secrets of Christ that were taking place at that time may be brought back to our memory. Let us read Augustine on John (Tractate 28), where he explains that Christ came to the feast of Tabernacles, [Col. 1129A] not openly but as though in secret. He says:

> Let what was secret therefore be revealed; let the veil be removed; let what was hidden appear.

Everything that was said to the ancient people of Israel in the various books of the holy Law—what they were to do in sacrifices, priestly offices, feast days, and altogether in every matter by which they worshiped God—whatever was said and commanded to them, was a shadow of things to come, which are fulfilled in Christ. Hence the Apostle says, “For however many the promises of God are, in him also” (2 Cor. I), that is, in Christ, “they have been fulfilled.”

From these statements we can understand in whose stead the priest says the Secret. The paschal Lamb was hidden in Christ, who was to be sacrificed. This was secret from the apostles; it was secret from the other faithful who were with him; it remained secret from the Jewish people [Col. 1129B] until the day of the Supper, when he deigned to reveal his passion more openly. The priest’s Secret extends until that day.

In the moral sense, in the present office our altar is prefigured by the altar of burnt offering, on which victims were sacrificed for sin, for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, for Judah, for vows, and for freewill offerings. We have these offerings daily in our Church; we offer the same through the hands of the priest. Our altar presently signifies the general life of the righteous, who habitually crucify their flesh daily with its vices and desires and offer it to God as a living sacrifice. If the altar prefigured by the altar of burnt offering signifies the general life of the righteous, the offerings made upon it signify their thoughts and good works.

[Col. 1129C] Let us return to the beginning of the present office. The bishop greets the people, entreating that the Lord may be with him. The people, in turn, pray for the priest, that the Lord may be with them together with his spirit. This greeting indicates the entrance into another office.

Afterward he says, “Let us pray,” and admonishes each of the offerers to lead himself into his own conscience. If anyone has something to sacrifice, let him sacrifice it—that is, if anyone is conscious of his own fault, let him ask to be struck by an invisible sword. If anyone has a voluntary sacrifice, whether a freewill offering or one offered for any other matter, let him pray before it leaves his hand that it may be acceptable to the Lord and not rejected, as Cain’s was rejected because he did not offer rightly (Gen. IV).

[Col. 1129D] Meanwhile the shroud is placed upon the altar. By the shroud, which we usually call the corporal, everyone—the people, the ministers of the altar, and also the priest—is admonished that, just as that linen cloth has been cleansed of all natural greenness and moisture, so the mind of the offerers should be cleansed of every carnal desire; and just as it shines with its own brightness, so the intention of the offerers should shine before God with simplicity.

Then the priest proceeds to receive the offerings. Meanwhile the singers sing according to the custom of the ancients, as we have already stated, or of the crowds that sang to Christ as he came to Jerusalem. The people give their offerings, namely bread and wine, according to the order of Melchizedek. The bread and wine that they offer express all the pious desires hidden within, whether they are for an immolation or for a living sacrifice. What is done outwardly is a sign of what lies hidden [Col. 1130A] within.

Hence Augustine, in the tenth book of *The City of God*, chapter 19:

> Those who think that these visible sacrifices are appropriate to other gods, but that invisible sacrifices are appropriate to the invisible God—greater sacrifices to the greater, better sacrifices to the better, such as the duties of a pure mind and good will—plainly do not understand that these are signs of those things, just as spoken words are signs of things. Therefore, just as by praying and praising we direct our sacrificial voices to him to whom we offer in our hearts the things themselves that we signify, so when sacrificing we must know that the visible sacrifice ought to be offered to no one other than him whose invisible sacrifice we ourselves ought to be in our hearts.

+ After receiving the offerings, he returns to the altar, while the deacon arranges the offerings upon the altar, according to the custom of the first seven deacons.

[Col. 1130B] The priest washes his hands according to the custom of the earlier priests, so that they may be cleansed from contact with ordinary hands and with earthly bread. This washing of the hands signifies purity of heart through tears and compunction, as Bede reports in Book III, chapter 14, *On the Tabernacle and Its Vessels*:

> Rightly, at the altar [near the altar] of burnt offering, the basin is placed in which the priests, having been washed, enter the tabernacle and burn incense to the Lord.

For the condition of tears and compunction is distinguished in two ways.

And shortly afterward:

> No one from the people was commanded to wash there, but the high priest himself and his sons, namely priests of a lower rank, because just as the life of great men is more perfect, so their compunction is ordinarily more exalted.

And again:

> If, in the person of Aaron, we wish to understand the Lord and Savior himself as the great high priest, it is clear that he too was washed with the water of this basin before entering to offer at the altar. For before he burned the incense of his most holy body upon the altar of the cross for our salvation, he also shed tears out of love for us, as became especially known at the resurrection of Lazarus.

[Col. 1130C] While the singers are still singing, the priest goes to the altar and prays. He does what he previously instructed the others to do. He prays for the remission of his own sins, so that he may be worthy to approach the altar and touch the offerings, lest what happened to the Bethshemites happen to him: they rashly looked upon the ark of the Lord. Concerning them it is written in the Book of Samuel:

> He struck the men of Beth-shemesh because they had looked upon the ark of the Lord; he struck seventy men of the people, and fifty thousand of the common people (1 Sam. VI).

[Col. 1130D] Then he receives the offerings of the priests and deacons, who are permitted to approach the altar. He also receives two from the archdeacon: one for himself and the other for the deacon. The censer, which he places upon the altar after the prayer, shows through whom God may be propitiated—namely, through our Lord Jesus Christ, whose body the censer signifies. Concerning it, it is written in Exodus, “Let them offer incense to the Lord in it, lest they die” (Exod. XXX).

Hence the aforementioned Bede:

> For death—spiritual and eternal—is to be feared if anyone chosen for service at the altar neglects to offer to God the incense of prayers.

The deacon mixes water with the wine. Why he does this, Cyprian shows in his second book, letter 3, *To Quirinus*, concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s cup:

> When water is mixed with wine in the cup, the people are united to Christ, and the congregation of believers is joined and bound to him in whom it has believed. This union and conjunction of water and wine is so blended in the Lord’s cup that the mixture cannot be separated from one another. Thus no thing will be able to separate the Church—that is, the people constituted in the Church, faithfully and firmly persevering in what it has believed—from Christ, so that its undivided love may not always cling to him and remain in him.

[Col. 1131A] Just as water alone cannot be offered in sanctifying the Lord’s cup, neither can wine alone. For if someone offers only wine, the blood of Christ begins to exist without us; but if only water is present, the people begin to exist without Christ. When both are mixed and joined to one another in a blended union, then the spiritual and heavenly sacrament is completed.

[Col. 1131B] If the Lord’s cup is neither water alone nor wine alone, unless both are mixed together, then likewise the Lord’s body cannot be flour alone or water alone unless both have been united and joined and solidified into one bread. By this sacrament also our people are shown to be united: just as many grains, gathered, ground, and mixed together, make one bread, so in Christ, who is the heavenly bread, we know that there is one body to which our number is joined and united.

Everyone who enters the church ought to offer sacrifice to God. But the singers, who are Levites by descent, because of the pressing necessity of singing do not have permission to run here and there so that each may offer with the others. It has been established for them that they should not be entirely excluded from the sacrifice: they are to guard the water and offer this one offering on behalf of the others. The people offer wine; the singers, water. Just as wine and water become one in the cup, so the people and the singers become one in the body of Christ.

The singers, following the custom of the ancient Levites, who provided everything necessary for the tabernacle, should obtain water from the spring and keep it covered until the time of the sacrifice; then they should offer it clean.

[Col. 1131C] Afterward the deacon places the cup on the altar and his towel at the right corner of the altar. It is suitable for this purpose, so that whatever dirt may come upon it may be wiped away with it and the priest’s towel may remain perfectly clean. If, through the priest’s negligence, any stains from various temptations have clung to him before the hour of sacrifice, let him wipe them away with his towel. At the hour of [Col. 1131D] sacrifice let him keep watch so that, insofar as human frailty permits, none may cling to him, but may immediately be driven back at the gate of suggestion; and with a tranquil mind let him intercede for the sins of others.

Hence Cyprian, in Sermon 6, *On the Lord’s Prayer*:

> When we stand at prayer, beloved, we ought to watch and devote ourselves to prayers with our whole heart. Let every carnal and worldly thought depart, and at that time let the mind think of nothing except what it is praying. Therefore, before the prayer, the priest, having prefaced it with the preface, prepares the minds of the brethren by saying, “Lift up your hearts,” so that when the people respond, “We have them with the Lord,” they may be reminded that they ought to think of nothing other than God.

[Col. 1132A] Let the breast be closed against the adversary and open only to God; let it not permit the enemy of God to approach during prayer. For he frequently creeps in and penetrates, subtly deceiving us, and turns our prayers away from God, so that we have one thing in our heart and another on our lips, when God ought to be prayed to with sincere intention—not by the sound of the voice, but by the mind and understanding.

What negligence is it to be distracted and captured by foolish and profane thoughts while you are entreating God—as though there were something else you ought to think about more than what you are saying while speaking with God? How do you ask to be heard by God when you do not hear yourself? Do you wish God to remember you when you pray, while you yourself do not remember yourself? This is to take no precaution at all against that enemy; this is, when you pray to God, to offend God’s majesty through [Col. 1132B] negligence in prayer. It is to be awake in the eyes and asleep in the heart, when a Christian ought, while his eyes sleep, to keep watch in his heart, as it is written of the Church speaking in the *Song of Songs*: “I sleep, but my heart is awake” (Song V).

Therefore the Apostle earnestly and carefully admonishes us, saying, “Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping watch in it” (Col. IV), teaching and showing that those whom God sees keeping watch in prayer can obtain from him what they request.

Those who pray should not come to God with prayers that are unfruitful and barren. A request is ineffective when prayer is sterile. For since every tree that does not bear fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire (Matt. III and VII), certainly speech that bears no fruit cannot gain God’s favor, because it is fertile in no [Col. 1132C] good work. Therefore divine Scripture instructs us, saying, “Prayer is good with fasting and almsgiving” (Tob. XII).

After this, the priest returns to the people and asks them to pray for him, so that he may be worthy to offer the offering of the entire people to the Lord. The preceding acts of worship are foreshadowed in *Paralipomenon*, where the crowd prays while the Levites sing. After the burnt offering, the king and all the people bent down (2 Chron. VII).

I have heard it said that at this same hour the people sing three verses for the priest: “May the Lord send you help from the sanctuary” (Ps. XIX), and the two following verses.

## CHAPTER XX: On the Secret

The Secret follows. It is called the Secret because it is said [Col. 1132D] secretly. In it the victim, or sacrifice, is first named; in it the priest prays to be thoroughly cleansed through that same victim. It belongs to the priest alone to offer sacrifice to God alone. Therefore, because we speak to God in our thoughts, a resounding voice is not necessary, but words are needed only so that through them the priest may be reminded what he ought to think about.

In the prayer that follows, he cries out to the people so that they may have what he already has—that is, an uplifted heart—and then so that they may give thanks to God for serenity of mind. This, therefore, is necessarily proclaimed aloud. What all may do together, namely give thanks to God, is proclaimed aloud; what belongs to the priest alone, namely the immolation of bread and wine, is done secretly.

[Col. 1133A] As much as the victim in the Old Testament contributed to the Lord’s sacrifice after it had been led to the door of the tabernacle (Lev. IV), so much does the sacrifice contribute at the first placing upon the altar. It can no longer be changed, either for the better or for the worse.

## CHAPTER XXI: On the Hymn before the Lord’s Passion, or the Preparation

It is called a hymn because it is filled with thanksgiving and the praises of the angels; it is called a preparation because it prepares the minds of the brethren for the fitting propriety of the assembly of the holy angels, who are accustomed to be present at the consecration of Christ’s body, and for the reverence due to so great a consecration. Therefore it is sung in a loud voice.

This office begins with the greeting that is said before [Col. 1133B] “Lift up your hearts” and ends with the hymn “Holy, holy, holy.” The present office brings back to our memory that time when Christ, at the Supper, went up into a large upper room furnished with couches and there spoke many things with his disciples (Matt. XXVI), and sang a hymn to God the Father, which John recalls, until he went out to the Mount of Olives. There he gave thanks to God; there he sang a hymn in which he prayed the Father to preserve his disciples from evil, saying, “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil” (John XVII). And that they might remain holy, he added, “Sanctify them in the truth.” And again, “For them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in the truth.” And that they might pass into heaven, he says afterward, “Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may be where I am, and that they may be with me, so that they may see my glory, which you have given me.”

[Col. 1133C] According to this meaning, the altar is the Lord’s table, at which he feasted with his disciples; the corporal is the linen cloth with which he himself was girded; the towel signifies the labor concerning Judas the betrayer.

The priest follows this order. He ascends into the upper room with his hearers when he says, “Lift up your hearts.” The hearers respond, “We have them with the Lord.” What he prayed for himself in the Preface—that his heart might be free from worldly bonds—he now urges his hearers to do, so that for so great a gift they may give thanks to God. The hearers confirm that it is worthy and right, and so forth, until “through Christ our Lord.” Through him we have been reconciled to God; through him we offer our thanksgivings. And because not only the things on earth but also those in heaven have been renewed through Christ, he recalls the praises of the heavenly beings.

[Col. 1133D] Since a sacrifice is being offered, it remains that we understand the thanksgivings which the priest offers for Christ’s sacrifice, and the ministries of the angels recalled in the present hymn, as being for their sacrifice. This should be kept in mind in all the offices of immolation: the visible altar must be regarded as having the character of the heart of those who offer.

At the time when the hymn before the Passion is celebrated, our altar is made like the altar of incense. This signifies the particular life of certain perfect people—namely, those who, with greater perfection of mind, after all the allurements of the flesh have been utterly extinguished and quieted, offer to the Lord the vows of prayers alone. They have nothing of the flesh that attacks them, [Col. 1134A] nothing of the consciousness of sin by which they may be disturbed or terrified; rather, by the outpouring of sweet tears, they desire to come and appear before the face of the Lord.

The offering placed upon the altar in the preceding office has been assigned to God, and thereby sanctified—that is, separated from earthly things and assigned to heavenly ones. There it is kept until it becomes the Lord’s body; afterward it is taken up into heaven.

It has been explained that this preparation, celebrated at the altar of incense, brings to our memory the sacrifice of the angels. Therefore what the priest says, “Whom the angels praise,” is the sacrifice of the angels. By “angels” we understand the archangels. “The sacrifice of dominions” means exhortation, in which we understand the principalities. Just as dominions have under them hosts of angels over which they preside with wondrous power, so the principalities preside over the spirits of good angels for the fulfillment of divine ministries. Those who rule also preside.

[Col. 1134B] “The trembling of powers, and the holy company of the heavenly virtues and blessed seraphim.” By “heavens” we understand thrones, because heaven is called the seat of God; and with these we join the cherubim, above whom God is said to sit, as the psalm says: “You who sit above the cherubim, appear” (Ps. LXXIX).

After these nine orders have been mentioned, the tenth order, that of the human condition, is added. From its voice the priest says, “With whom we ask that you command our voices also to be admitted.”

The following hymn, which was added to the original hymn, was added by Pope Sixtus, as is read [Col. 1134C] in the *Acts of the Pontiffs*. For it is written:

> He established that within the priest’s action the people should begin to sing the hymn: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.”

This same hymn contains the voices of these two orders. The order of angels says, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; heaven and earth are full of your glory.” The order of human beings says, “Hosanna in the highest; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” This is the part of the hymn that the crowd sang on Palm Sunday as it preceded the Lord into Jerusalem.

We have already spoken of what the altar signifies; we must now speak of the towel. The towel lying upon the altar signifies the labor that the angels undertake in human ministry, or that perfect men undertake when they never cease to pray for our weakness. [Col. 1134D] The corporal, however, signifies unfeigned intention.

Meanwhile the bishops, priests, or deacons stand behind the pontiff, while the subdeacons stand facing him. There what the Lord says to his disciples in the aforementioned upper room according to Luke is fulfilled:

> The kings of the nations lord it over them, and those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors. But you must not be so; rather, let the greater among you become like the younger, and the leader like one who serves. For who is greater: the one who reclines at table or the one who serves? Is it not the one who reclines at table? But I am among you as one who serves (Luke XXII).

[Col. 1135A] Christ’s teaching had many disciples, among whom were the one hundred and twenty who were found together in one house on the day of Pentecost. Joseph of Arimathea was one of them, a secret disciple of Jesus because of fear of the Jews (John XIX); so too was the bearer of water, who received him in his upper room and to whom the Lord said, “The Teacher says to you” (Luke XXII).

Whether these men were physically present in the upper room when the Lord supped, or were not, they nevertheless did not fail in his service, just as the man who furnished the large upper room did not fail. We believe that these are represented by the subdeacons, who stand facing the pontiff, just as that man stood either through his own presence or through the ministry of the one to whom the upper room belonged.

Or they may signify the women who persevered during the Lord’s Passion, concerning whom Gregory writes in the *Moralia* (Book XIV, chapter 23):

> But when the hour of the cross arrived, a great fear arising from the persecution of the Jews seized the Lord’s disciples; they fled individually, while the women stood by. Thus, as though his flesh had been consumed and [Col. 1135B] his bone had cleaved to his skin (Job XIX), his strength found women near him while the disciples were fleeing.

Peter did indeed stand for a while, but afterward, terrified, he denied him. John also stood, to whom at the very time of the cross it was said, “Behold, your mother” (John XIX); but he could not persevere, since it is also written of him that a certain young man followed him, wearing a linen cloth over his naked body; they seized him, but he, abandoning the linen cloth, fled from them naked (Mark XIV). Although he later returned to the hour of the cross to hear the words of his Redeemer, he had first fled in terror.

The women, however, are remembered not only as having neither feared nor fled, but also as having stood firm even to the tomb. Therefore he says, “My bone [Col. 1135C] cleaved to my skin after my flesh was consumed” (Job XIX). That is: those who ought to have clung more closely to my strength were consumed by fear at the time of my Passion; but I found those whom I had appointed for external ministries clinging faithfully to me in my Passion without fear.

## CHAPTER XXII: On the Hymn “Holy, Holy, Holy”

When the hymn “Holy, holy, holy” has begun, both those who stand behind and those who stand facing the pontiff bow, venerating the divine majesty and the Lord’s incarnation, which are introduced through the song of the angels and the crowds.

The chorus of the angels, by saying, “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts,” introduces the divine majesty. [Col. 1135D] The song of the crowds, by saying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord; hosanna in the highest,” introduces the Lord’s incarnation.

## CHAPTER XXIII: On “Te igitur” (“You, therefore”)

They remain standing behind, bowed, until the whole prayer presently being said is finished—that is, until, after the Lord’s Prayer, the words are said: “But deliver us from evil.” For what follows, up to “For ever and ever,” is an exposition of the final petition of the Lord’s Prayer. These are the ones to whom the Lord said: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations, and I appoint to you a kingdom, just as my Father appointed one to me” (Luke 22). Hence Bede, in his commentary on Luke, says:

> The glory of the heavenly kingdom is given not to the beginning of endurance, but to perseverance; for perseverance, which is otherwise called steadfastness, is a certain strength and fortitude of mind and, so to speak, the pillar of all virtues. When it stands upright and firm, nothing is more certain, nothing safer for good morals. +

They remain bowed until they are delivered from evil. These are the apostles, who were oppressed by great tribulation; before they heard of the Lord’s resurrection, they did not dare to rise and confess that they were Christ’s disciples. Although they were not present at the Passion, they nevertheless persevered in temptations after Christ’s resurrection. For they do not rise before the light of which the Psalmist says: “It is useless for you to rise before the light” (Psalm 126)—that is, it is useless to glory before you rise from the dead.

Those who stand in front signify the secret disciples, because of fear of the Jews, or the women, who were able to remain openly before Christ. By their inclination the subdeacons signify the sorrow of those about whom the same author says above, in the same work:

> It was not therefore only the mourning of the women that followed him, since an innumerable gathering of the men who were present was also deeply grieved at his Passion; but because the female sex, as though more contemptible, could more freely, in the presence of priests, princes, and magistrates, display what it felt against them. Who could fail to grieve when they saw the one whom they had loved with the greatest affection and knew to be innocent seized by the impious, bound, led before them, spat upon in the face, scourged, and crucified?

What their rising before the prayer has ended signifies will, if the Lord grants it, be shown in its appropriate places. Now we must speak of *Te igitur*.

From the beginning of the prayer up to the place where it says, “and command that we be numbered among the flock of your elect, through Christ our Lord,” the sacrifice of the elect is celebrated—those who have nothing in the flesh that resists them, nor anything in their conscience that disturbs them. For just as there were two altars in Moses’ tabernacle, or in Solomon’s temple—one of incense and the other of holocausts—so there are two sacrifices of the holy Church. One is that in which all carnal impulses have been put to sleep, of which we have spoken and must speak of again now; the other is that in which it is necessary daily to slaughter carnal impulses, of which we shall speak later.

The altar of incense is represented by both offices, that of the head and that of the body, up to the place designated above. Now it must be explained why the present prayer and the Preface are said secretly, from Cyprian’s sermon on the Lord’s Prayer (Sermon 6):

> Let speech and prayer among those who pray be disciplined, containing quietness and modesty. Let us consider that we stand beneath God’s gaze, and that we must be pleasing to the divine eyes both in bodily bearing and in the manner of our voice. For just as it belongs to the shameless to make a din with shouting, so, conversely, it is fitting for the modest to pray with restrained prayers. Finally, by his own instruction the Lord commanded us to pray secretly, in hidden and secluded places, even in our rooms (Matthew 6).

This is especially fitting for faith, so that we may know that the Lord is present everywhere, hears and sees all things, and penetrates even hidden and concealed places with the fullness of his majesty, as it is written: “I am God who is near, and not a God far away. If a man is hidden in secret places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jeremiah 23). And again: “In every place the eyes of the Lord observe the good and the wicked” (Proverbs 15).

And when we gather together with the brethren and celebrate the divine sacrifices with God’s priest, we must remember modesty and discipline. We must not scatter our prayers indiscriminately in unformed voices, nor throw our petition, which should be commended to the modest God, into tumultuous loquacity, because God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart. Nor does the one who sees the thoughts of human beings need to be admonished by shouting, as the Lord proves when he says: “Why are you thinking evil things in your hearts?” (Luke 5); and elsewhere: “And all the churches shall know that I am the searcher of kidneys and heart” (Jeremiah 15).

Anna, bearing and preserving the type of the Church in the First Book of Kings, observes and keeps this practice. She did not pray to God with a clamorous petition, but silently and modestly within the very hiding places of her breast; she spoke in a hidden prayer but with manifest faith. She spoke not with her voice but with her heart, because she knew that the Lord hears in this manner, and she effectively obtained what she asked because she petitioned faithfully. Divine Scripture declares this when it says: “She spoke in her heart, and her lips moved, but her voice was not heard; and the Lord heard her” (1 Kings 1).

Likewise, we read in the Psalms: “Speak within your hearts, and be pierced in your chambers” (Psalm 4). Through Jeremiah also the Holy Spirit suggests and teaches this same thing, saying: “The Lord must be worshiped in your understanding” (Jeremiah 29).

And when he worships, the beloved brethren should not be ignorant of how the tax collector prayed in the temple with the Pharisee (Luke 18): he did not shamelessly raise his eyes toward heaven, nor insolently lift his hands, but, beating his breast and bearing witness to the sins enclosed within, he implored the aid of divine mercy. While the Pharisee pleased himself, the tax collector who prayed in this way deserved more to be sanctified. He did not place the hope of salvation in confidence in his own innocence—for no one is innocent—but, confessing his sins, he humbly prayed, and the one who forgives the humble heard him as he prayed.

Since we have heard from Cyprian the manner of prayer, let us hear from *Te igitur* the prayers themselves. First, in the place of Christ, the priest performs three prayers, just as the Lord did after he went out to the Mount of Olives before his betrayal: one for the universal Church, one for the particular brethren, and one for the choir of priests.

Christ’s first prayer is: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Luke 22). He asks that the cup be taken away from him, not indeed out of fear of suffering, but out of mercy toward the former people, so that they might not drink the cup prepared for them. Hence he significantly did not say, “Take the cup from me,” but “this cup”—that is, the cup of the Jewish people.

Christ’s second prayer is: “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, let your will be done” (John 4). Jerome explains this in the following way:

> The second time he prays that, if Nineveh cannot otherwise be saved unless the gourd withers, the Father’s will may be done.

Third, Christ prayed the same words, as we learn from the Jerome mentioned above, who says that the apostles’ fear, followed by repentance, obtained a teacher who needed correction. We understand that he prayed then for his body—that is, for the apostles.

With the same number, namely three, the priest completes his prayer in the voice of the elect:

> It is a sacrifice of the elect to God the Father, through Christ our Lord. These gifts, these offerings, these holy and unblemished sacrifices.

“Gifts” and “offerings” are one and the same, in accordance with Daniel’s answer to Belshazzar when he promised him purple and a golden chain. “Let your gifts,” he said, “be for yourself, and give the gifts of your house to another” (Daniel 5).

This one thing is found twice because two things are offered to God, namely bread and wine. Neither of the two can properly be called by a plural noun. For in bread there are water and flour, and in wine there are water and wine. The same thing is repeated a third time: “These holy and unblemished sacrifices.” By the singular repetition the two preceding expressions are recapitulated, because these sacraments are contained in one body of Christ.

But since God requires the sacrifice of the heart rather than what is administered outwardly, we wish to interpret “gifts,” “offerings,” and “unblemished sacrifices” in the heart of the priest. Hence Augustine says in Book 10 of *The City of God*, chapter 3:

> His gifts are in us; we also vow and return ourselves to him. On the solemn occasions of his benefits, on feast days and appointed days, let us celebrate and consecrate the memory of them, lest ungrateful forgetfulness creep in through the passage of time. Let us sacrifice to him the offering of humility and praise, fervent with the fire of charity upon the altar of the heart.

According to the same Augustine, if anyone wishes to offer gifts to God, let him offer himself; if anyone wishes to offer offerings, let him recall his benefits more frequently; if anyone wishes to offer unblemished sacrifices, let him offer humility, praise, and charity.

He says the same in the work mentioned above, chapter 5:

> The visible sacrifice, therefore, is the sacrament of the invisible sacrifice—that is, its sacred sign.

And later in the same work, chapter 19:

> Therefore, just as in praying and praising we direct sacrificial voices toward him, offering in our hearts the realities themselves that we signify, so, when sacrificing, let us know that the visible sacrifice must be offered to no one other than the one whose invisible sacrifice we ourselves ought to be in our hearts.

Since, by the Lord’s mercy, we have found the true sacrifice, let us continue with what follows in *Te igitur*. It continues:

> First of all, that you accept for your holy catholic Church what we offer to you, and so forth.

The sacrifice mentioned is offered for three groups: for the universal holy Church; for particular brethren whose alms or offering we have received, or whose sponsors we have become, or whose presence we behold in the service of our Mass—though their sacrifice is praise; and for us priests ourselves, who share with holy Mary and the apostles in the one Lord, so that we may be protected in all things by the Lord’s protection.

And again:

> According to the Prophet, there are three sacrifices that God requires from us: to do judgment and justice, to love mercy, and to be ready to walk with the Lord God (Micah 6).

He does judgment who vows and returns himself to God, whose entire possession he is, together with everything that can be in him from the things that exist. He does the same when he first indicates that prayer must be made for the peace of the universal Church.

Next, he loves mercy who, by giving thanks for past benefits, obtains future benefits for himself. He obtains great mercy for himself who urges God toward better things. He likewise practices mercy toward the brethren when he specially entreats the Lord for them.

He wishes to be ready to walk with the Lord God who says that he shares, in fellowship with the one Lord, with Mary and the choir of the apostles. “These are the ones who follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Revelation 14).

So that the mortal person may not stray from the straight path because of the danger of the present life, he asks to be protected in all things by the Lord’s protection.

In this prayer the sindon, insofar as it concerns the head, signifies Christ’s humility, which he assumed from an earthly condition and in which he prayed to God the Father. The sudarium lying at the corner of the altar signifies the labor he endured in prayer, as Luke says: “And being in agony, he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like drops of blood flowing down upon the earth” (Luke 22).

Having first laid these matters out, the devout heart says:

> “Therefore, Lord, we ask that you graciously accept this offering of our service.”

In this prayer he entreats God to deign to receive the vows of his elect. Therefore they are presented to him through the demonstrative pronoun when he says, “this offering,” to which Saint Gregory later added: “And order our days in your peace,” and so forth.

This shows that no one can be secure in the present age concerning his own stability, however perfect he may seem to be. Therefore it may be necessary that they always pray for their days to be ordered in peace in the present age, that in the future they may be rescued from eternal damnation and numbered among the flock of the elect.

We have spoken of the corporal and the sudarium insofar as they concern the body. After Christ had prayed for his members, he said to his disciples: “Rise, let us go; behold, he who will betray me is approaching” (Matthew 26). Jerome explains:

> Let them not find us as though we were afraid and drawing back; let us go willingly toward death, so that they may see us suffer with confidence and joy.

The devout heart presents the elect; it presents its offering to the Lord; and the devout Lord presents himself to those through whom he was to be sacrificed to God the Father.

In this prayer the sindon signifies the profound humility in which he not only deigned to pray for his own, but also to be handed over into the hands of the impious. The sudarium signifies the labor he endured because of the betrayer.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Lord’s institution in the making of the body and blood

After the first sacrifice of the perfected, which consists of prayers and is joined to the sacrifice of the angels, we descend to the universal sacrifice—namely, Christ’s immolation, which is celebrated before “Nobis quoque peccatoribus.”

For Christ descended to be sacrificed for sinners, as Paul says to Timothy: “This saying is trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into this world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1).

He is the one through whom every sacrifice is offered to God, because in him all things that are in heaven and on earth were created. Although he is Lord of all, he wished to become a victim for sinners, who could not offer sacrifice to God, so that by his immolation they might be reconciled to God and, consequently, might not themselves be fruitless but might be able to offer sacrifice.

Since Christ was offered as one victim for the just and the unjust (Colossians 1), the same sacrifice remains upon the altar that was placed there earlier. Hence the priest now says:

> “Which offering, O God, we ask that you deign to make in all respects blessed, enrolled, ratified, reasonable, and acceptable.”

I believe this should be explained as follows, subject to the understanding of the teachers: “Which offering”—an offering made in the same manner as this one, that is, with the same devotion; “in all respects,” that is, with the whole mind, the whole life, and the whole understanding; “blessed,” just as this one has been blessed, when the priest says, “that you may accept and bless it”; “enrolled for you,” as this one of which it was said, “We ask, Lord, that you graciously accept it”; “ratified”—that is, faithful—like this one extended to you through Christ our Lord. O God, we ask that you deign to make it reasonable and acceptable, so that it may become for us the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The manuscript reads *latam* at this point; in context it apparently represents *ratam*, “ratified.”

The order in which this is to be accomplished is learned from the Lord’s institution. The priest takes the bread in his hands, following Christ’s example, of whom it was said: “He took bread into his holy and venerable hands,” and so forth. Likewise he takes the cup, as Cyprian says to Caecilius concerning the sacrament of the Lord’s cup (Book 2, Letter 3):

> We find that what was commanded is not observed by us unless we also do the same things that the Lord did, and, mixing the cup in the same manner, do not depart from the divine teaching.

Although Cyprian concluded this by speaking about the mixing of wine and water, we can understand it as applying to the whole of the Lord’s institution, in which his command and the observance of the apostles are contained.

As for the crosses that we customarily make in different ways over the bread and wine, I have nothing to say about why they are placed in this or that manner or place, or why there are more in one place and fewer in another. If the Lord made the sign of the cross when he blessed the bread, those who were present know it—especially since the standard of the holy cross had not yet been erected. But now we know that it is necessary, as Augustine says in his exposition of John’s Gospel, homily 64:

> What is the sign of Christ, as everyone knows, except the sign of the crucified Christ? Unless this sign is applied either to the foreheads of believers, or to the water by which they are reborn, or to the oil with which they are anointed in chrism, or to the sacrifice by which they are nourished, none of these things is properly accomplished. +
