It seems to me that, if the cross has once been made over the bread and wine, that could suffice, because the Lord was crucified once. It is not unreasonable if it is made twice, because Christ was crucified for two peoples. But if it must be made at the place where it says, “Taking bread,” then it must be made separately over the bread and separately over the wine, according to the manner Christ used in taking the bread and the cup.

In the bread Christ commended his body, and in the cup his blood, and he added: “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me.” Here the words of the Lord’s table correspond with the whole office of the Mass. Here “Taking bread,” and so forth, is sung, and the priest performs it when he receives the offering in the secret part of the Mass or when he raises it here. He gives thanks in the hymn, “It is truly worthy and just”; he blesses at the present place; he breaks it around the time of Communion.

Here we believe that the simple nature of the mixed bread and wine is changed into a rational nature—namely, the body and blood of Christ.

The sindon lying on the altar signifies the linen with which the Lord was girded, and the sudarium signifies the labor he assumed in washing the feet (John 13), or the labor he endured for Judas. The altar signifies the Lord’s table.

## CHAPTER XXV. On Christ’s ascent onto the cross

In the sacrament of bread and wine, and also in my remembrance, Christ’s Passion is present. He himself said: “Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me” (1 Corinthians 11)—that is, whenever you bless this bread and cup, remember my birth according to my humanity, my Passion, and my resurrection.

Therefore the priest, together with the voice of the people, adds:

> “Therefore, Lord, we, your servants, and also your people, remembering the same Christ, your Son, our Lord, his blessed Passion, his resurrection from the dead, and also his glorious ascension into heaven, offer to your excellent majesty, from your gifts and grants, a pure victim, a holy victim, an immaculate victim.”

Just as above Christ’s body is the wine in the sacrament of bread and wine, and in my remembrance, so here he ascends onto the cross. God attends to the sacrifice of the heart. Hence Cyprian says in his sermon on the Lord’s Prayer (Sermon 6):

> For in the sacrifices that Abel and Cain first offered (Genesis 4), God did not regard their gifts but looked upon their hearts, so that the one whose heart pleased him might please him in his gift. +

We offer a pure victim, a holy victim, and an immaculate victim from God’s gifts and grants when, inflamed with charity, we offer a victim from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Timothy 1).

The institution of the sacrament makes clear what this victim is when it adds:

> “The holy bread of eternal life and the cup of everlasting salvation.”

The bread of eternal life and the cup of everlasting salvation are Christ; or, as I said above, the pure victim is the bread, the holy victim is the cup, and the immaculate victim is both together, because they form one body.

Concerning “gifts and grants,” we may say this: gifts exist in the eternal reality, while grants exist in temporal action. And since God wishes us sinners to offer him his own gifts, we must earnestly pray that he may deign to look upon them.

Hence it follows:

> “Upon which deign to look with a gracious and serene countenance, and to accept them, as you deigned to accept the gifts of your righteous servant Abel, and the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and that which your high priest Melchizedek offered to you, a holy sacrifice and an immaculate victim.”

The priest asks God the Father that, just as at that time he deigned to look upon Abel’s gifts, the patriarch’s sacrifice, and likewise Melchizedek’s, so he may look upon the present vows, which began with Christ’s immolation.

Then he prays that they may be received, saying:

> “We humbly ask you, almighty God: command that these offerings be borne by the hands of your holy angel to your sublime altar, before the presence of your divine majesty, so that all of us who, from participation in this altar, shall have received the most holy body and blood of your Son may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace, through Christ our Lord.”

The priest prays that the present offering may be acceptable in the presence of the divine majesty, so that those who receive it may at the same time become heavenly and be filled with the grace of God.

Wondrous and great is the faith of the holy Church, which sees with its eyes what is lacking to mortals: it sees what it ought to believe, although it does not yet see what exists in appearance. It believes that the present sacrifice is carried by the hands of angels before the presence of the Lord, and it perceives that it must be eaten by a human mouth. For it believes that it is the body and blood of the Lord, and that by this heavenly bite the souls of those who receive it are filled with blessing.

Indeed, Christ prayed upon the cross, beginning with the psalm, “My God, my God,” and continuing to the verse, “Into your hands I commend my spirit.” Then, inclining his head, he gave up his spirit. The priest bows and commends to God the Father that which has been sacrificed in the place of Christ.

Christ’s Passion is made present for us from the place where it says, “Therefore, remembering,” up to this point. The present altar represents the altar of the cross. At this altar we sinners who came from the nations have been reconciled to God in order to offer sacrifices to him.

Here the sindon signifies that humility with which he humbled himself before the Father unto death. It is not contrary to the truth if humility is signified by the sindon. Augustine writes in Psalm 92:

> He who was humble then, when he was girded with a linen cloth and washed the feet of his disciples.

The sudarium signifies the labor of the Passion.

The subdeacons’ inclination up to this point demonstrates the sorrow of those disciples who were permitted to remain in Christ’s presence. When he was scourged and everything that is read concerning his Passion was being done, those who were his followers grieved most intensely. But after he gave up his spirit, knowing that the persecutors no longer had any means by which to vent their rage further upon Christ’s body—as he himself says in Luke’s Gospel, “Do not be afraid of those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do” (Luke 12)—they are consoled in some measure and raise themselves up, gazing upon the body they loved as long as it hangs upon the cross. This is especially so when they see many miracles occurring, by which the persecutors could be disturbed and those who served him consoled.

In the same office the deacons wash their hands, because all the filthy works of their former way of life are cleansed by Christ’s Passion. If the order of our ministry had intended the washing of hands to signify nothing other than that the deacons should first examine, sift, and cleanse their actions and thoughts with more careful attention, and then proceed to participate in the sacraments of faith—a practice that every believer ought to observe, lest he eat and drink the Lord’s body unworthily—then they would in no way wash their hands in such a place, because they could wash them more suitably while standing upright than while bowed.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the Lord’s body after he gave up his spirit on the cross, and on our being put to death in the same way

For Christ tasted death beforehand so that we might die together with our sins. Christ died to sin once, so that we might die to vices. Paul says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Galatians 5).

This crucifixion is accomplished especially through repentance. Many pass through a narrow opening into the stability of continence; therefore, insofar as the moral sense is concerned, the present sacrifice is rightly called the sacrifice of penitence.

And Christ’s Passion is appropriately celebrated before the sacrifice of penitents, so that it may urge the weaker more strongly toward the healing drink. Hence John Chrysostom says in his fourth sermon on Hebrews:

> Just as a physician does not need to taste the foods prepared for the sick person, but, consoling him, first tastes some of the sick person’s food in order to persuade him to accept those foods more readily, so also the Lord, since human beings feared death, persuading them to approach death confidently, himself tasted death, although he had no need to do so.

From the words of blessed John it has been shown that Christ’s Passion and our confession of sins are uttered together so that we would not fear enduring harsh things for our sins.

Christ has now given up his spirit; blood and water flowed from his side. Without these sacraments no one enters eternal life. Concerning these sacraments Augustine says in his sermon 65 on John:

> That blood was poured out for the remission of sins; that water tempers the saving cup; this provides both washing and drink.

And shortly afterward:

> This second Adam, with his head bowed, slept upon the cross, so that a bride might be formed for him from what flowed from the side of the one who slept.

This bride signifies the centurion of whom the Gospel tells us: “When the centurion saw what had happened, he glorified God, saying, ‘Truly this man was righteous’” (Matthew 27).

If it had not been destined that the Gentile world should be imbued with the sacrament of blood and water, the centurion would not immediately have been changed into such deep contrition that he openly cried out from the affection of his heart: “Truly this man was righteous.”

The priest signifies this transformation by a change of voice when he raises his voice and says, “And also for us sinners.” Bede says of him in his commentary on Luke:

> The distinction between nation and nation must be noted. For the Gentiles, fearing God when Christ died, glorify him with an open voice of confession; the Jews, merely beating their breasts, return home.

The beating of the breast is a sign of repentance and an indication of mourning.

“Meanwhile all his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him from Galilee stood watching these things.” This is what the Lord himself asks of the Father in the psalm, having unfolded the sequence of his Passion, saying: “You have put far from me friend and neighbor, and my acquaintances because of misery” (Psalm 87).

The standing subdeacons recall these friends and neighbors as they gaze upon the presbyter’s action.

As they gaze, a man named Joseph arrives. He was a member of the council, a good and righteous man; he had not consented to their counsel and actions. He was from the city of Arimathea in Judea and was himself awaiting the kingdom of God. He approached Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus. After taking it down, he wrapped it in a sindon and placed him in a hewn tomb in which no one had yet been laid (Luke 23; Matthew 27).

Although Joseph was among the number of the secret disciples, he nevertheless surpassed them all in what was openly done—both the disciples and the apostles. While the disciples merely stood at a distance and watched, and the apostles hid themselves in secret places, Joseph purchased a sindon in order to wrap the body of Jesus after it had been taken down.

How distinguished this Joseph was is read in Bede’s commentary on Luke, where he says:

> This Joseph is praised as having been of great dignity in the world, but of still greater merit before God: through the justice of his merits he was worthy to bury the Lord’s body, and through the nobility of his secular power he was able to receive that same body. For not just any unknown person could approach the governor and obtain the body of a crucified man.

The archdeacon recalls this Joseph when he lifts the cup from the altar and wraps it in the sudarium, from one rim of the cup to the other.

Just as that deacon holds primacy among the other deacons who lifts the cup with the priest, so this Joseph held primacy among the other disciples, since he deserved to take the Lord’s body down from the cross and bury it in his own tomb. He is likewise appointed to stand behind with the disciples, because he was hidden through fear of the Jews.

The priest who raises the offering presents Nicodemus, of whom John tells us:

> “Nicodemus also came—the one who had first come to Jesus by night—bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with spices, as is the Jewish custom of burial” (John 19).

The priest makes two crosses with the offering beside the cup, to teach that the one who was crucified for two peoples was taken down from the cross.

The raising of the offering by the priest and the deacon displays Christ’s removal from the cross. It is known that a sudarium was placed over Jesus’ head, as the same John relates when he says that Peter saw the linen cloths lying there and the sudarium that had been over Jesus’ head.

The offering and the cup signify the Lord’s body. When Christ said, “This is the cup of my blood” (John 20), he signified his blood; just as wine is inside the cup, so his blood was inside the body.

What those represented by the subdeacons did afterward is related by Bede in the book mentioned above:

> We read earlier that all his acquaintances stood at a distance, and the women who had followed him. Therefore, after these acquaintances of Jesus returned to their homes following the burial of his corpse, the women alone, who loved him more closely, followed the funeral, wishing to see how he was placed. +

This prayer, “And also for us sinners,” extends up to “For ever and ever.” Up to this point it concerns the funeral rites of Christ’s burial.

The altar represents the cross insofar as it concerns our mortification; it is the altar of holocausts. The sindon and the sudarium are the things I mentioned above.

In the moral sense, the priest raises his voice in the voice of penitents who confess their sins, as though pierced by a certain spur of excessive fear. Such piercing is called, and truly is, “the sacrifice of a contrite spirit.”

The priest’s raised voice in the sacrifice of penitents signifies that the cry in the penitent’s heart ought to be great. Hence Augustine says in his commentary on John, sermon 66:

> Why did Jesus groan and trouble himself (John 11), unless because the faith of a person rightly displeased with himself ought somehow to groan in the accusation of evil works, so that the habit of sinning may yield to the force of repentance?

And again in the same work:

> “When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice; he groaned and wept.” He cried out with a loud voice. How difficult it is for one to rise whom the weight of an evil habit presses down! Yet he rises; inwardly made alive by hidden grace, he rises after the loud voice.

Enough has been said about the raising of the voice; we must speak of the sacrifice.

The sacrifice of penitents is a contrite spirit and a broken heart. Through repentance our sins are buried. The altar of penitents is the altar of holocausts. The altar of holocausts signifies the heart of those who must consume carnal impulses through the fervor of the Holy Spirit.

The sindon is the chastisement of the flesh itself through fasts and vigils and the other virtues. Through these, from innate carnal pleasure—as from natural moisture—the human affection is brought, like a certain flax, to whiteness, so that it may become a corporal in which the Lord can be received.

The one who receives Jesus with a pure mind wraps him in a clean sindon. The sudarium is the very intention by which one hastens to wipe away all the incoming impulses of former temptations before they wound the eyes.

After the voice of the penitents has been uttered, supplication follows, that the Lord may grant them a share in fellowship with his saints. After these have been named, it continues:

> “Among whose fellowship we ask that you admit us, you who are the giver of forgiveness, not the assessor of merit.”

In the completion of the earlier office, which consisted only of prayers, the communion of the saints is mentioned, whose way of life is nearly equal. Here, because we are far removed from their way of life, we pray to be introduced by forgiveness.

“Through Christ our Lord. Through whom, Lord, you always create all these good things”—namely, those mentioned above—“so that they may exist; you sanctify them,” by assigning them to yourself; “you vivify them,” so that they may be alive; “you bless them,” so that they may be useful to us; “and you grant them for our enjoyment”—through that same one, through whom you grant the things mentioned above.

“And with him, who always lives with you; and in him, in whom all things have been restored. To you, God the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, be all honor and glory for ever and ever.”

Wishing with all my effort to show this very thing to you, and to hold it with complete faith, I, an unworthy priest, raise the offerings now present to you, and the deacon does so in the place of the superiors and hearers, because all good things are assigned to you by your whole Church.

The subdeacons who until now stand before the sacrifice, and who now withdraw, recall for us the ministry of the women who withdrew from the tomb after the Lord had been buried. They did not withdraw from the tomb in such a way as to be absent from the Lord’s ministry; rather, they remained silent on the Sabbath. After it had passed, they prepared spices in order to anoint his body.

In the same way, the subdeacons who are present withdraw from the presence of the sacrifice so that on the Sabbath—that is, while the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer are being said—they may remain silent and bowed, just as the apostles and the holy women were at that time. Afterwards they hasten with the patens to seek the Lord’s body around the altar, just as the women sought the Lord’s body around the tomb.

Morally, we can understand the subdeacons as ourselves, sinners who show our face—that is, the conscience of our sins—to the priest, so that he may offer our confession to God. When this has been done, we do not immediately leap into the place of the teachers; rather, after prolonged humiliation, as the fervor of the Holy Spirit increases, our hearts are widened like a paten for receiving the sacraments of the Church.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the presentation of the paten
The Roman booklet, which we have already mentioned, says:

> “When the Canon begins, an acolyte comes beneath the shoulder, carrying a linen cloth tied around his neck, and holding the paten before his breast on the right side until the middle of the Canon. Then the following subdeacon receives it upon the chasuble and comes before the altar, waiting until the regional subdeacon receives it. When the Canon has been completed, the regional subdeacon stands with the paten behind the archdeacon. When he has said, ‘And safe from every disturbance,’ the archdeacon turns, kisses the paten, and gives it to the second deacon to hold.”

The procedure is as follows. The following subdeacon does not dare leave the altar doors, in accordance with the canons of the Council of Laodicea, which state, in chapter forty-three [Col. 1146D], that a subdeacon ought not even for a short while to leave the doors and devote himself to prayers. Therefore the acolyte brings the paten out from the side-chambers when “Lift up your hearts” is said. My humility offers what seems to me consistent with reason, leaving it to the judgment of teachers to determine what ought chiefly to be observed. It seems to me that the paten should be presented at the hour when the disciples or the women were busily occupied around the Lord’s burial.

For after he had gone to the table, they devoted themselves to the mysteries of his Passion. The following subdeacon, in the middle of the Canon—that is, when “You, therefore” is said—receives it from the acolyte and stands at the altar with the paten until it is received by the regional subdeacon; for it is received when “For ever and ever” is said. The regional subdeacon receives it at the end of the Canon—that is, where “For ever and ever” is said—and holds it until it is received by the deacon.

The subdeacon’s withdrawal from the presence of the pontiff may also be understood simply as an approach to the paten. Here it should be noted that the acolyte holds the paten wrapped in a linen cloth, whereas the subdeacon holds it uncovered. It is therefore plainly evident that consecrated vessels ought rightly to be touched only by consecrated clerics.

The priest Ezra expressed this at length when, returning from Babylon, he entrusted the holy vessels to holy persons, saying: “I separated twelve from the leaders of the priests” (1 Esdras 8). A little later: “And I weighed out for them the silver and the gold and the consecrated vessels of the house of our God” (ibid.). And again:

> “And he said, ‘You are holy to the Lord, and the vessels are holy, and the silver and the gold, which were freely offered to the Lord, the God of our fathers. Keep watch and guard them’” (ibid.).

Accordingly, the Council of Carthage records in chapter 25:

> “Bishop Aurelius said: ‘We add, dearest brothers, moreover, since a report had been made concerning the incontinence of certain clerics—even readers—in relation to their own wives, that it was decided, as had been established in various councils, that subdeacons who handle the sacred mysteries, and deacons and priests, as well as bishops, according to their own statutes, should abstain even from their wives.’”

Pope Sixtus, a Roman by birth and the son of Pastor, likewise decreed that sacred ministries should be touched only by ministers.

Daniel also condemned King Belshazzar for drinking from consecrated vessels, as it is written:

> “But you also, Belshazzar his son, did not humble your heart, although you knew all these things; instead, you exalted yourself against the Lord of heaven, and the vessels of his house were brought before you. You and your nobles, your wives, and your concubines drank wine from them” (Daniel 5).

The paten is so called because it is open—*patet*—and it signifies hearts enlarged by charity. Just as the alabaster vessel in which Mary carried the ointment to anoint the Lord signified her heart, in which there was faith without hypocrisy, so the paten can signify the hearts of holy women, which were open in the breadth of charity in Christ’s service.

Indeed, as I have stated above, they themselves were engaged in no minor service in the ministry of Christ’s discipleship. Of them the evangelist Matthew says:

> “There were many women there, looking on from a distance, who had followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering to him. Among them were Mary Magdalene, and Mary the mother of James and Joseph, and the mother of the sons of Zebedee” (Matthew 27).

Yet they themselves did not receive the Lord’s body from the cross; Joseph did—just as the subdeacons do not receive the chalice from the altar, but the deacons do.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the office that commemorates the Lord’s rest in the tomb

The regional subdeacon receives the paten after the Canon has been completed because the women were the first to hear the joy of the Lord’s resurrection. They ran back and forth with ardent devotion around the Lord’s burial.

The deacons and the subdeacons stand bowed until they hear, “But deliver us from evil.” For this is the seventh petition of the Lord’s Prayer. The number seven signifies universality. With the seventh petition, the end is signified of all the sadness and distress that the apostles had experienced because of the Lord’s death.

The prayer that follows, which begins, “Deliver us, we ask, O Lord, from all evils,” is an embolism [*embolion*] of the Lord’s Prayer, so that through it one may come to the customary conclusion, “Through our Lord.” This will be demonstrated more clearly below, if the Lord grants it.

What the apostles did at that time—that is, when Christ rested in the tomb—is not explicitly recorded. But we learn of their fear from John’s Gospel, which says:

> “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered for fear of the Jews” (John 20).

From this we learn that the apostles were sorrowful because of fear. This sorrow is shown by the deacons’ bowing. We learn of the disciples’ sadness from the Lord’s words, according to Luke, to the two who were going on the day of the resurrection to the village of Emmaus:

> “What are these words that you are discussing with one another as you walk, and are sad?” (Luke 24).

For this reason the subdeacons also remain bowed.

Within the limits of my nocturnal study, I have shown what the deacons’ bowing signifies, except that inward prayer is ordinarily represented by the posture of the body. Hence Augustine, in his book to Paulinus, *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, says:

> “For those who pray also do with the members of their body what is fitting for petitioners: they bend their knees, they stretch out their hands, or even prostrate themselves on the ground, and if they do anything else visibly. Although their invisible will and the intention of their heart are known to God, and he does not need these signs in order that the human spirit may be opened to him, a person nevertheless stimulates himself by these actions to pray and groan more humbly and fervently. And somehow, since these bodily movements cannot occur without a movement of the soul preceding them, when the same movements are again performed outwardly and visibly, that inner and invisible movement which causes them is increased. Thus the feeling of the heart, which preceded in order that these actions might occur, grows because they have occurred. Yet if someone is so constrained or even bound that he cannot perform these actions with his bodily members, the inner person does not for that reason cease to pray; before God’s eyes, in the most secret chamber, he is pierced with compunction and lies prostrate.”

The celebration of this office proceeds in such a way as to show what took place at that time concerning the Lord’s Passion and burial, and how we ought to recall, through our own service, what was done for us.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the Lord’s Prayer

It must be explained why the Lord’s Prayer is said aloud, whereas the other prayers are said secretly. Cyprian says in his sermon *On the Lord’s Prayer* (Sermon 6):

> “Above all, the teacher of peace and master of unity did not wish prayer to be made individually and privately, so that when someone prays, he should pray only for himself. We do not say, ‘My Father, who are in heaven,’ nor, ‘Give me my daily bread’; nor does each person ask that his debt alone be forgiven, or pray for himself alone not to be led into temptation and to be delivered from evil. Our prayer is public and common; and when we pray, we do not pray for one person but for the whole people, because the whole people are one. The God of peace and teacher of concord, who taught unity, wished one to pray for all, just as he himself, being one, bore all.”

This law of prayer was observed by the three boys shut up in the fiery furnace, who prayed in harmony and were united in spirit and agreement. The faith of divine Scripture makes this clear; and when it teaches how they prayed, it gives an example that we ought to imitate in our prayers, so that we may become like them. It says:

> “Then those three, as though from one mouth, were singing a hymn and blessing God” (Daniel 3).

They spoke as though from one mouth, although Christ had not yet taught them to pray. Their prayer was therefore effective and obtained what they asked, because it was a peaceful, simple, and spiritual prayer that found favor with God.

The prayer begins as follows:

> “Instructed by saving precepts and formed by divine teaching, we dare to say.”

By “saving precepts” we mean evangelical teaching; by “divine teaching” we mean the tradition that he himself deigned to hand down in the making of the sacrament of his body and blood.

Hence the same author mentioned above, in his sermon to Caecilius on the sacrament of the Lord’s chalice (Cyprian, book 2, letter 3), says:

> “Although I know, dearest brother, that very many bishops, appointed by divine favor over the Lord’s churches throughout the world, preserve the rule of evangelical truth and the Lord’s tradition, and do not teach a human and novel institution apart from what Christ, the teacher, both commanded and did,”

and so forth.

Again, in the same work:

> “We must not depart at all from the evangelical precepts, and the disciples too must observe and do the same things that the teacher taught and did.”

When Cyprian says “the rule of evangelical truth,” and later, “we must not depart at all from the evangelical precepts,” he indicates evangelical teaching. When he says “preserve the rule of the Lord’s instruction,” and later, “the same things that the teacher taught and did,” he indicates the Lord’s institution.

It has been shown with what boldness one should enter upon the Lord’s Prayer: namely, after saving precepts—that is, the Gospel—have cleansed our heart, and divine ordinances have formed us, which we mention where it is written, “Taking bread into his holy and venerable hands,” and so forth. Then we dare to enter upon the Lord’s Prayer.

Here it should be noted that one must not approach him presumptuously, but with reverence and a serene heart.

In commemoration of the seventh day, when Christ rested in the tomb, the Lord’s Prayer is said. It contains seven petitions, corresponding to that seventh day on which the apostles labored under sadness and fear of the Jews. And, if I am not mistaken, they prayed to be delivered from evil, and they obtained what they prayed for through the Lord’s resurrection.

The holy Church also prays now as though on the seventh day. While the souls of the saints already rest, she persists in fasting, keeping vigil, praying, and striving in charity, lest she be torn away by the dangers of this world from the hope of heavenly joys. Who, while he remains in this present age, does not pray to be delivered from evil?

Nor should it be treated carelessly that, before receiving the Lord’s body and blood, a prayer intervenes to cleanse us from sins, lest we eat and drink the Lord’s body and blood unworthily.

How the Lord’s Prayer is completed in the seventh petition, the same author mentioned above explains in his book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, saying (Cyprian, Sermon 6):

> “After all these things, at the conclusion of the prayer, comes a final clause that gathers together and concludes all our petitions and prayers in brief: for at the very end we say, ‘But deliver us from evil,’ embracing all the adversities that the enemy contrives against us in this world. From them there can be secure protection if God delivers us, if he grants his help to those who pray and implore it. When we say, ‘Deliver us from evil,’ nothing remains that should still be requested afterward. Once we have asked for God’s protection against evil, having obtained it, we stand secure and safe against everything that the devil works in the world. For what fear of the world is there for one whose protector is God?”

“What wonder, dearest brothers, if the prayer is such that God taught it—he who by his teaching abbreviated all our prayer in a saving utterance? This had already been foretold through the prophet Isaiah, when, full of the Holy Spirit, he spoke of God’s majesty and mercy: ‘Completing and abbreviating in righteousness,’ he says, ‘for God will make an abbreviated word throughout the whole world’” (Isaiah 10).

When Cyprian says that our whole prayer is concluded in that one petition, “But deliver us from evil,” we may understand that the end of the prayer signifies the end of our persecution.

The prayer that follows is an exposition of the final petition. The former says, “But deliver us from evil”; the latter says from what evils—namely, past, present, and future—and, so that the house may not remain empty, it asks for peace from God through the intercession of the saints. Thus it continues:

> “And grant peace in our days.”

There is no safer peace than to obey the Lord’s commands, turn away from evil, and do good. Hence the Prophet says:

> “Turn away from evil and do good” (Psalm 36).

And the Apostle:

> “Hating evil, clinging to good” (Romans 12).

The prayer repeats the same petition below. He does not trust that he can obtain this from God by his own merits. Therefore he says, “so that, aided by the help of your mercy”; and then he states more clearly from what evils he prays to be delivered—namely, that we may be free from sin—and he again adds what peace he seeks: “and secure from every disturbance.” This cannot happen unless one applies oneself to the virtues.

As we have said, the following prayer contains nothing else than an exposition of the petition already mentioned. The three clauses of the present prayer can be adapted to the period of the Lord’s three-day burial. For this reason, this alone among the Masses may be understood as being celebrated on Good Friday for the three days comprising the burial.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the presentation of the subdeacons to receive the Lord’s body from the altar

[Col. 1151A]

This office recalls the most devout women who presented themselves at the funeral rites of the Lord’s burial.

When the holy women presented themselves at the Lord’s tomb, they found that the spirit had returned to the body, and they saw angels around the tomb; then they announced to the apostles what they had seen. Concerning this, Bede offers a useful admonition in his treatise on Luke:

> “Just as angels are read to have stood beside the Savior’s body when it had been placed in the tomb, so they should also be believed to stand by during the celebration of the mysteries of that most holy body at the time of consecration, as the Apostle warns that women should have a veil because of the angels” (1 Corinthians 11).

When the women were afraid and turned their faces toward the ground, the angels said to them:

> “Why do you seek the living among the dead? He is not here; he has risen” (Mark 16).

That is: “Do not seek among the dead”—that is, in the tomb, which is properly a place of the dead—the one who has already risen from the dead to life.

And we, following the example of women devoted to God, whenever we enter a church and approach the heavenly mysteries, ought to enter with complete humility and fear, whether because of the presence of the angelic power or because of reverence for the sacred offering.

We bow our faces to the ground before the sight of the angels when, contemplating the joys of the heavenly citizens, which are eternal, we humbly remember that we are dust and earth.

After this, the subdeacon presents himself with his paten at the Lord’s tomb. He received it from the following subdeacon, who, as we said above, recalls the most devoted concern of the holy women for the Lord’s burial.

It is not surprising if holy women are joined to the deacons in this office, since Paul joins them to the deacons in ordination. After discussing the ordination of a deacon, he writes to Timothy:

> “Women likewise must be dignified,”

and so forth (1 Timothy 3).

In the entire admonition concerning ordination, he wishes them to be like the deacons. Why, then, they are separated from the fellowship of the deacons, when Paul joins them to the deacons’ ordination, while subdeacons succeed them, about whom Paul said nothing, is known by those who wish to live chastely.

For we also read that women were present in the company of the apostles. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians:

> “Do we not have the right to take along women, as do the other apostles, and the brothers of the Lord, and Cephas?” (1 Corinthians 9).

After the priest says, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” the offerings are placed on the paten. For after Christ gladdened the hearts of the disciples with his greeting, the hopes of the women were fulfilled when they received the joy of the resurrection.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Concerning the placing of the bread into the wine

I observe that among some people the placing of the bread into the wine is performed in different ways. Some first place a portion of the holy offering into the chalice and afterward say, “The peace of the Lord”; others, by contrast, reserve the placing of it until after the peace has been celebrated and the bread has been broken.

Therefore my smallness has taken pains to set down the words of the Roman booklet concerning this matter, and, so far as I believe I can obtain from the Lord, to bring forth what I discover in investigating it.

The booklet mentioned above says:

> “When he has said, ‘The peace of the Lord be always with you,’ he places some of the holy offering into the chalice.”

As I think, this is not without reason. Bodily life consists of blood and flesh. As long as these two are active in a person, the spirit is present. In this office it is shown that the blood poured out for our soul and the dead flesh offered for our body return to their proper substance and, being quickened by the life-giving Spirit, animate the new human being, so that he may no longer die—the one who died and rose again for us.

The cross formed over the chalice by a particle of the offering places before our eyes that very body which was crucified for us. It touches the four sides of the chalice because through it the human race from the four regions of the world has approached the unity of one body and the peace of the Catholic Church.

While doing this, the priest says these words:

> “May the mingling of the body and blood of the Lord bring eternal life to us who receive it.”

These words pray that the Lord’s body may become present in the offering through the resurrection, through which a venerable and eternal peace was given, not only on earth but also in heaven.

Then the laborers of the vineyard of the first, third, and sixth hours ceased to murmur. Then the peace was given that the angels promised on the most holy night when they said:

> “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.”

The priest now recalls that same peace, saying:

> “The peace of the Lord be always with you.”

The people respond to it with gentle kisses. According to this interpretation, I think that one does not err if one first places the holy offering into the chalice and then says, “The peace of the Lord be always with you,” subject to the instruction of teachers.

The aforementioned booklet continues:

> “But first the archdeacon gives the peace to the bishop, then the others in order, and the people. Then the pontiff breaks the offering on the right side, and leaves the particle that he breaks upon the altar; the remaining offerings he places on the paten, which the deacon holds.”

A little later:

> “Then the acolytes go to the right and left among the bishops around the altar; the others descend to the priests so that they may break the hosts. The paten goes first toward the seat, carried by two regional subdeacons to the deacons, so that they may break them.”

And again, after some intervening material:

> “When the breaking has been completed, the lesser deacon, having lifted the paten from the subdeacon, carries it to the seat so that the pontiff may communicate. After he has communicated from the portion he had bitten, he places it between the hands of the archdeacon in the chalice.”

If this is indeed done in the Roman Church, one may learn from them what the bread placed twice into the chalice signifies. Nothing performed in this office according to the institution of the Fathers is without a mystery.

What the placing of the bread into the wine and the peace extended to the people through the priest’s voice seem to signify, we have offered to teachers for clarification.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the kiss of peace

I must be content concerning the peace with what Innocent writes about it to Bishop Decentius in the *Decretals*, chapter one (Gratian, Distinction 11, chapter “Si”; and *On Consecration*, distinction, chapter “Pacem”), because of the authority of so great a man:

> “You assert, then, that some command the peace to the people before the mysteries have been completed, or that priests give it to one another, whereas after everything that I ought not disclose, the peace must be announced as necessary. Through it, it is established that the people have given their assent to everything that is performed in the mysteries and celebrated in the church, and when these things have been completed, this is demonstrated by the sign of the peace that concludes them.”

Some have asked me why men and women do not give kisses to one another during the office of the Mass. Although I did not answer them at the time, I think I ought to answer now.

Carnal embraces, by which men and women are very often joined, must be avoided in the assembly of the church. Therefore men and women are separated in the church, not only from carnal kissing but also in their physical placement.

Mutual kisses in the church are given by those persons who cannot be compelled to arouse any titillation of lustful suggestion.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Concerning the *Agnus Dei*

Pope Sergius established that the *Agnus Dei* should be sung, as it is written in the *Deeds of the Pontiffs*. He decreed that, at the time of the breaking of the Lord’s body, the *Agnus Dei* should be sung by clergy and people.

It is a supplication for the people who are about to receive the Lord’s body, that through the mercy of the innocent Lamb sudden and attacking sins may be taken away—namely, sins of thoughts and words—and that, just as by his Passion he took away the offense of the whole world, so now he may take away the offense of the Church that is about to receive him through the Eucharist.

The following antiphon—that is, the responsive voice—displays the law of brotherhood, so that each person may seek the benefit of the other and take care to summon him to the joys of the resurrection.

This pattern was enacted by the two who recognized the Lord in the breaking of bread. They immediately returned to Jerusalem, found the Eleven gathered together and those who were with them, and heard them say:

> “The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.”

They themselves then recounted what had happened on the road and how they had recognized him in the breaking of bread (Luke 24).

They sang the antiphon by recounting the Lord’s resurrection in turn.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. Concerning the Eucharist

The Eucharist is to be received after the kiss of peace. Just as we are one bread in Christ, so we ought also to have one heart. To preserve this unity, we are admonished through the kisses of peace.

Hence Bede, in his treatise on Luke, says:

> “Let no one think that he has recognized Christ if he is not a participant in his body—that is, in the Church. The Apostle commends the Church’s unity in the sacrament of the bread, saying: ‘We, though many, are one bread and one body’” (1 Corinthians 10).

Through the Eucharist Christ remains in us, and we in him, through the humanity that he assumed. He is the God of peace, through whom heavenly and earthly things have been reconciled.

Within the holy Church there are some who communicate rarely and others who communicate daily. Saint Augustine gives both groups suitable counsel in his inquiry to Januarius on this subject (Letter 118):

> “Perhaps the dispute between them is more rightly settled by someone who urges them above all to remain in the peace of Christ” (*On Consecration*, distinction 2, chapter “Quotidie”).

Let each person do what he devoutly believes ought to be done according to his faith. Neither of them should shrink from the Lord’s body and blood; rather, each should strive eagerly to honor the most health-giving sacrament.

Zacchaeus and the centurion did not quarrel with one another, nor did either place himself above the other (Luke 19; Matthew 8), when one of them joyfully received the Lord into his house, while the other said:

> “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof.”

Both honored the Savior in different and seemingly contrary ways; both were wretched because of their sins, and both obtained mercy.

He also explains the Apostle’s saying:

> “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11).

He continues:

> “For the Apostle calls it ‘unworthily’ received by those who did not distinguish it from other foods by the singular veneration that is due to it. For immediately after saying, ‘He eats and drinks judgment upon himself,’ he added, ‘not discerning the Lord’s body.’”

That it should be received by those who are fasting, he says in the same book:

> “For the Savior, in order to commend the greatness of that mystery more forcefully, wished to impress this final thing upon the hearts and memory of the disciples from whom he was about to depart for his Passion. Therefore he did not prescribe the order in which it should afterward be received, so that he might preserve this place for the apostles, through whom he was going to organize the churches. For if he had instructed them that it should always be received after other foods, I believe no one would have changed that custom [+].”

When a person ought to sanctify himself for the reception of so great a gift, the ancient history teaches. In Exodus the Lord says to Moses:

> “Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will descend before all the people upon Mount Sinai” (Exodus 19).

With the same number of days David said that he and all his servants had sanctified themselves in order to eat the bread of the Presence. Thus it is written in the Book of Samuel:

> “The priest Ahimelech said, ‘I have no ordinary bread at hand, but only holy bread—if the young men are pure, especially from women.’ David answered the priest and said to him, ‘Indeed, if women are concerned, we have abstained from them since yesterday and the day before, when we set out, and the vessels of the young men were holy. This journey, moreover, is profane; yet today it too will be sanctified in the vessels.’ Therefore the priest gave him the holy bread” (1 Samuel 21).

## CHAPTER XXXV. Concerning the portion of the offering that remains on the altar

Christ’s body is threefold, namely, in relation to those who have tasted death and are destined to die.

The first is the holy and spotless body assumed from the Virgin Mary; the second is the body that still walks upon the earth; the third is the body that lies in the tombs.

The particle of the offering placed into the chalice displays Christ’s body, which has already risen from the dead; the portion eaten by the priest or the people displays the body still walking upon the earth; and the portion left on the altar displays the body lying in the tombs.

That same body takes the offering with it to the tomb, and the holy Church calls it the viaticum of the dying, so that it may be shown that those who die in Christ ought not to be regarded as dead but as sleeping.

Hence the place of tombs is called in Greek κοιμητήριον (*koimētērion*), that is, “a dormitory” or “sleeping place.”

Thus Paul says to the Corinthians:

> “A woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives; but if her husband sleeps, she is released” (1 Corinthians 7).

The particle itself remains on the altar until the end of the Mass because, until the end of the age, the bodies of the saints will rest in the tombs.

The corporal that remains on the altar after the Lord’s resurrection teaches purity of mind, which everyone ought always to pursue when receiving the Lord’s body, but especially at the end.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. Concerning the final blessing

Before his ascension into heaven, the Lord led the disciples to Bethany, blessed them there, and ascended into heaven (Luke, last chapter). The priest follows this practice: after all the sacraments have been completed, he blesses and greets the people.

Then he turns back toward the east, to commend himself to the Lord’s ascension. The deacon says:

> “Go, the dismissal has taken place.”

For Christ was sent on a singular mission for us to the Father, carrying with him the marks of his Passion.

First, through these marks he establishes the disciples’ faith in his resurrection. Second, by pleading for us with the Father, he continually shows what kind of death he endured for the life of mortals. Third, he continually renews before those redeemed by his death the signs of that same death, so that they may see how mercifully they were helped. Therefore they do not cease to sing the Lord’s mercies forever; rather, those who have been redeemed by the Lord say:

> “For he is good, for his mercy endures forever” (Psalm 117).

Finally, the scars of the wounds that he received from them, displayed among the other offenses, announce to the faithless at the judgment how justly they will be condemned.

Concerning this mission the Apostle John says:

> “But if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2).

John himself was certainly a just and great man, who drank the secrets of the mysteries from the Lord’s breast. Yet he did not say, “You have me as an advocate with the Father”; rather, he says, “we have an advocate.” He said “we have,” not “you have.” He preferred to place himself among sinners, so that he might have Christ as his advocate, rather than to set himself forward as Christ’s advocate and be found among the proud who are to be condemned.

Nevertheless, it must not be said that bishops or superiors do not pray for the people. The Apostle prays for the people, and the people pray for the Apostle, who says:

> “Praying at the same time for us also, that God may open to us a door for the word” (Colossians 1 and 4).

The Church also prayed for Peter when Peter was in chains, and her prayer was heard (Acts 12). Likewise Peter prays for the Church, because all the members pray for one another.

The Head intercedes for all, of whom it is written:

> “Who is at the right hand of God and also intercedes for us” (Romans 8).

For the only-begotten Son to intercede with the coeternal Father for humanity means that he shows himself to the Father as human and pleads for human nature; that is, he has taken that same nature into the height of his divinity.

The Lord therefore intercedes for us, not by voice but by compassion.

Would that, when we hear the deacon say, “Go, the dismissal has taken place,” our mind might hasten toward that homeland where our Head has gone before us, so that by desire we may already be there, where the One desired by all nations awaits us with his trophy. In this way, by desiring him, we may one day reach him, who thus pleads with the Father for us:

> “Father, I desire that where I am, my minister also may be” (John 17).

The unlearned common people are accustomed to ask at what point in the entire office the Mass begins, so that if someone should perhaps be unable to attend the whole of it, he may know at which offices he ought to be present without uncertainty.

It seems to us that the Mass is called by that name from the point at which the priest begins to offer the sacrifice to God until the final blessing—that is, from the Offertory through “Go, the dismissal has taken place.”

Isidore assigns the office of the Mass to the time of the sacrifice, saying in his book *Etymologies*:

> “The Mass is at the time of the sacrifice, when catechumens are sent outside, the Levite crying out: ‘If any catechumen remains, let him go outside.’ It is therefore called *missa* because those who are known not yet to have been reborn cannot be present at the altar’s sacraments.”

Our custom is to expel catechumens before the Gospel. This does not seem to me to follow reason, since without doubt the preachers of the nations were commanded to preach the Gospel to them. But they cannot participate in the sacrifice at all unless they have been reborn, because the priest does not pray for them in the consecration of the Lord’s body, nor is the completed sacrament given to them.

Thus the priest prays for those standing around:

> “Remember, O Lord, your servants and handmaids, and all who stand here, whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is recognized.”

Those not yet reborn are called unbelievers, not believers. Therefore we cannot perceive that a prayer has been established for them in the office of the making of Christ’s body. For this reason they rightly withdraw at the time when the sacrifice is celebrated.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning the further final blessing

There is a final blessing, which we are now discussing and which we practice especially during Lent. That is, after the final blessing already mentioned, in which spiritual nourishment is commended, this further blessing remains—the one now under discussion—in which Christ’s soldiers are commended for battle against the ancient enemy.

If at all times it is necessary to be prepared for warfare against the ambushes or attacks of enemies, how much more so when one is drawn up for battle? During Lent our adversary knows that a singular contest has been entrusted by the holy Church against him; therefore he presses more fiercely to seize and overthrow someone, if he should find anyone negligent.

Our priest, like a prudent trainer of athletes and a fighter, sees that the soldiers will be in greater danger and therefore fortifies them more fully with his blessing.

Our weapons against the devil are humility and the other virtues. Our priest wishes us to be clothed in these weapons; therefore, through the minister, he commands us to humble our heads before God, and so at last pours the protection of his blessing over the soldiers.

The priest’s blessing follows an ancient custom, being given at the very end. The patriarch Jacob blessed his sons at the end of his life. It is written in Genesis:

> “He blessed each one with his own blessing and commanded them, saying: ‘I am being gathered to my people; bury me with my fathers’” (Genesis 49).

And again:

> “When he had finished the commands with which he instructed his sons, he drew up his feet upon the bed and died” (ibid.).

Similarly, it is written of Moses in the Book of Deuteronomy:

> “This is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the children of Israel before his death” (Deuteronomy 33).

Finally, the Lord and Savior himself, as we stated above, blessed his disciples before his ascension into heaven (Luke 24).

To pass over the other examples of the holy Fathers, I shall say briefly, for the sake of concision: when, according to the custom of our religion, we have a familiar conversation with the servants of God, before we separate from them, we ask for a final blessing.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. Concerning the first morning Mass on the feast of Saint John the Baptist
The blessed John the Baptist is read in the Gospel of Luke as having been filled with the Holy Spirit from his mother’s womb (Luke 1). [Col. 1157C] Therefore, at the beginning of the day’s light, as though at the beginning of his birth, a sacrifice is offered to God in his honor, to the praise of the Creator, who deemed him worthy to honor him from his mother’s womb. Three Masses are celebrated on the feast of blessed John because he shone forth with excellence through three distinguished triumphs. For he came in order to prepare the way of the Lord by the example of his manner of life. This triumph is celebrated at his vigil. He became illustrious through the ministry of baptism; the triumph of this ministry is commemorated in the first Mass. He remained a Nazirite from his mother’s womb; this gift is commemorated in the second Mass during the day.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Offertory *Vir erat in terra*

[Col. 1157D] Meanwhile, a repetition of words occurs to me—the words found in the verses of the offertory, *Vir erat* (“There was a man”). I did not wish to pass over what I understood concerning it, although the order of the subject requires that, after writing about the birth of Saint John, I should write about the birth of Christ.

There is no repetition of the words in the offertory itself; there is repetition in the verses. The words of the historian are contained in the offertory; the words of the sick and suffering Job are contained in the verses. A sick person whose breathing is neither healthy nor strong commonly repeats incomplete words again and again. The author of the office, wishing to bring the sick Job vividly back to our memory, repeated the words several times in the manner of sick people. In the offertory, as I have said, the words are not repeated, because the historian, writing the history, was not sick.

## CHAPTER XL. On the Advent of the Lord

[Col. 1158A]

In ancient books of the Missal and Lectionary, one finds written: “The fifth week before the Nativity of the Lord.” For there are that many readings in the Lectionary, and that many Gospels from the time just mentioned, on the Sundays up to the Nativity of the Lord. The Antiphonary has three daytime offices, and a fourth on the Sunday that follows the twelve readings. It has four nocturnal offices, as I said above, for the Sundays.

The author of the Lectionary stirs up our faith so that we may recall the proclamation of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ into the world through the five ages of the world. The author of the Missal, which is called the Gregorian, and of the Antiphonary touches us so that we may recall the birth of the Lord, [Col. 1158B] celebrated through the three orders of books—namely, the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms—and also through a fourth, that is, the beginning of the Gospel, in which Gabriel the archangel is narrated as having been sent to Zechariah, announcing the birth of the Lord’s precursor, as well as Zechariah’s prophecy concerning the coming of the Lord, and Gabriel’s being sent to the Virgin Mary, announcing to her the conception of our Savior, and other such matters up to the Nativity.

Indeed, the fourth week itself—that is, the week immediately preceding the Nativity of the Lord, or the week in which it is celebrated—is singular, and in the morning office has its own antiphons in the Psalms for each weekday.

In another manner: the author of the Lectionary teaches us how mighty the Lord is who is to come to us and enter our house, in order to dwell in it—a house that we customarily defile through our five senses. Illicit forms enter through the eyes; suspicion of a brother, through the ears; lustful odor, through the nostrils; gluttony pollutes through the mouth; cruelty, through touch. The coming King does not wish to dwell amid filth. Unless the lodging is cleansed so thoroughly that not even the dust of such phantoms remains, the coming guest will not deign to enter it.

Therefore the author writes five readings for the five weeks, to exhort us to circumcise our five senses from every vice and to prepare a dwelling worthy of the King, the Lord, and the true Prophet. The first reading says of that King:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will raise up for David a righteous Branch, and he shall reign as king and shall act wisely.”

And again, concerning the Lord: [Col. 1158D]

“And this is the name by which they will call him: The Lord is our righteous one.”

And again, in the Gospel, concerning the Prophet:

“For this is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.”

The author of the Missal, or of the Antiphonary, urges us to make the same preparation through four weeks. For just as a person acts well or badly toward the soul through the five senses as intermediaries, so through the four elements he either falls into bodily evils or rises toward good things.

Therefore, as I said, the author mentioned above urges us: if until now we have languished through negligence, let us henceforth rise to cleanse our house, so that the one who was not awakened in the fifth week may at least rise in the fourth. This is precisely what the reading read in the fourth week says: [Col. 1159A]

“We know that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep,” and so forth.

For this reason I do not doubt that, in the week mentioned, the cantor raises his voice with his trumpet—“To you I have lifted up my soul”—in order to awaken those who in the fifth week were overwhelmed by the sleep of negligence.

The following reading shows how we ought to prepare our house:

“Not in feasting and drunkenness, not in beds and debauchery, not in strife and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ.”

The Sacramentary impresses the same preparation upon our ears:

“Let us receive, O Lord, your mercy in the midst of your temple, so that with fitting honors we may go before the coming solemnities of our restoration.”

If anyone wishes to challenge what we have said, on the grounds that there are not four full weeks from the Sunday mentioned to the Nativity of the Lord, it seems to me that he is ignorant of the rule of Sacred Scripture, which commonly makes the whole present in a part.

In former times I saw *Gloria in excelsis Deo* omitted during the days of the Advent of the Lord, and in some places the dalmatics as well. This too has a certain rationale, to signify the time of the Old Testament. No one doubts that there is greater glory in the Church of God in the time of the New Testament than there was in that of the Old.

In another way: whatever is done rarely becomes more precious when it is done. Hence it is written in the Book of Samuel:

“Now the boy Samuel ministered before the Lord in the presence of Eli, and the word of the Lord was precious.”

It is called precious because at that time it was rare. Thus Jerome says to Evagrius in his letter: [Col. 1159C]

“Everything that is rare is desired more eagerly. Pennyroyal among the Indians is more precious than pepper.”

And so, when *Gloria in excelsis Deo*, or some other splendor of the sacred order, is interrupted for a time, it is received with much greater eagerness when it is restored; and it shines more brightly in the souls of the devout when it is renewed after being tarnished.

As a new song, *Gloria in excelsis Deo* is restored on the night of the Nativity of the Lord, so that we may be reminded all the more that this same song was first celebrated in the hymns of the angels.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Nativity of the Lord

The Mass that we celebrate on the night of the Nativity of the Lord was established by Telesphorus, the apostolic bishop. Thus it is written in the *Deeds of the Bishops*: “He established that Masses should be celebrated at night on the Nativity of the Lord.” In my opinion, this was because of the remembrance of the angels who sang *Gloria in excelsis Deo* on that night.

For the same Nativity, the author of the office established that a second Mass should be celebrated in the morning. What we stated above concerning the nativity of John, which has a Mass at the beginning of the light, we retain also here, although there is a great difference between servant and Lord.

No one doubts that the man Christ Jesus, after he began to be man, always remained God. Hence Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, says in his letter to Nestorius, bishop of the city of Constantinople:

“For he was not first born as an ordinary man from the holy Virgin, and only afterward did the Word come upon him; rather, united from the very womb, he is believed and said to have undergone a carnal birth.”

## CHAPTER XLII. On the Usual Time of Mass

The aforementioned Pope Telesphorus wrote at what time on the first day it was permitted to celebrate Mass. In the *Deeds of the Bishops* he is read as having said that no one should presume to celebrate Mass before the course of the third hour, the hour at which our Lord ascended the cross.

If, according to the aforementioned pope, the time of the third hour is suitable for the celebration of Mass because it is read in Mark that Christ ascended the cross at that hour, then we too can appropriately say that the time of the sixth hour is suitable, [Col. 1160B] since according to Matthew he ascended the cross at that hour. Likewise, the time of the ninth hour is suitable, when he gave up his spirit.

These three times were consecrated by Christ’s being fastened—by the tongues of the Jews and by the wood.

Those who, before the third hour or after the ninth hour, necessarily offer sacrifice to God, inflamed by divine love, so that the day may not pass without their sacrifice, do not, as I think, act as though they were insolently opposing apostolic ordinances. Rather, they have a serious reason by which they can reasonably excuse themselves, just as the Lord defended the disciples when they were criticized by the Jews for plucking ears of grain, as though they were doing what was not lawful on the sabbaths. He appealed to the example of David, who, driven by hunger, entered the Law in order to eat the consecrated loaves.

Hunger was indeed the reason why David transgressed the law with a credible excuse. Pope Innocent writes something similar concerning this matter, in chapter 55.

Therefore, what necessity discovers as a remedy ought, when the necessity has ceased, likewise to cease, since one thing is the lawful order and another is the usurpation that present circumstances compel one to undertake.

For I saw the apostolic bishop Leo enter to Mass at dawn. I do not know whether he did this because necessity intervened or by authority alone. What we read in the pontifical deeds, we have written. Authority shines when adorned with reason. For the aforementioned Telesphorus brought forward a reason concerning the hour of Mass, and for this reason we willingly submit to his authority.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Meeting (ὑπαντή)

[Col. 1160D] It is written in the pontifical deeds that Pope Sergius ordered litanies to be performed on the day of the Lord’s Presentation in the Temple. For it is written as follows:

“That on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, of the Dormition and Nativity of the holy Mother of God Mary, and of Saint Simeon—which is called the Meeting (ὑπαντή) in Greek—they should go out with a litany from Saint Hadrian, and the people should meet at Saint Mary’s.”

Concerning this feast, Bede, that distinguished priest and teacher, says in his book *On Times*:

“Numa dedicated the second month to Februus, that is, to Pluto, who was believed to have power over purifications; and it was necessary to purify the city in that month, in which he decreed that rites should be performed for the spirits of the dead.

“But Christian religion rightly changed this custom of purification, [Col. 1161A] when, in the same month, the entire devout people of holy Mary, together with the priests and ministers, proceeds through the churches and suitable places of the city with hymns sung in harmonious voices, carrying in their hands the candles given by the bishop and burning brightly. As the good custom increased, they learned to do the same also on the feasts of this same mother and perpetual virgin—not, indeed, as a purification for an earthly empire lasting five years, but as an everlasting remembrance of the heavenly kingdom. For then, according to the parable of the wise virgins, all the elect, coming to meet their bridegroom and king with the lamps of good works shining, will immediately enter with him into the wedding feast of the heavenly city.”

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the Mass for the Dead

[Col. 1161B] The Mass for the dead differs from the customary Mass in that it is celebrated without *Gloria*, *Alleluia*, or the kiss of peace. *Gloria* and *Alleluia* impress sweetness and joy upon our minds.

What should I say about this? I shall explain it in the words of Origen. In the fifth homily on Leviticus he writes:

“But the sacrifice for sin is not made with oil. For he says, ‘He shall not put oil upon it when it is for sin.’ Therefore, what is for sin receives neither the oil of joy nor the incense of sweetness +.”

No one doubts that death is the punishment of the first sin; and therefore Mass is celebrated without *Gloria* and *Alleluia*, as though without oil and incense.

It should also be noted that the office for the dead is performed in imitation of the offices celebrated at the death of the Lord. We have already stated what we know about why, in the offices of the Lord’s Passion, there should not be a kiss of peace. Here we can bring forward nothing else except what we anticipated there: since the kiss of peace is not performed there, neither is it performed here.

The commemoration of the dead is made by name before *Nobis quoque peccatoribus* (“To us also, sinners”). There the memory of the Lord’s death ends, and our death begins through the confession of sins. Therefore it is rightly there that the memory is made of those who die in the Lord. Christ went before them; we follow.

We customarily celebrate their commemorations generally on the third, seventh, and thirtieth days. We have authority for this in the Old Testament. It is written in the Book of Numbers, chapter forty-seven:

“Whoever touches the corpse of a man and is thereby unclean shall be sprinkled with this water for seven days, on the third and seventh day, and thus he shall be cleansed” (Num. 19).

For the celebration of thirty days, we are supported by the observance of Moses and Aaron. Thus it is written in the same book, chapter one:

“For the whole congregation, seeing that Aaron had died, wept over him for thirty days throughout all their families” (Num. 20).

And again concerning Moses, in Deuteronomy, chapter thirty-four:

“And the children of Israel wept over him in the plains of Moab for thirty days” (Deut. 34).

The unclean person on account of a human corpse signifies the soul polluted by dead works. The purification of the dead person through the priest’s sacrifice on the third and seventh days corresponds to human nature. A human being consists of soul and body.

The soul is, in a certain sense, raised upon three pillars, so that it may love God with all its heart, with all its soul, and with all its mind. The body, however, subsists through the four elements known to all.

We humbly confess and offer to God on the third day the sin of the soul that neglected the worship of God in thought, life, and understanding, so that it may be cleansed from these sins. Likewise, we desire to purge the sin committed through the body on the fourth day after the third day—that is, on the seventh day after death.

Sin is committed in two ways: either by doing what we ought not to have done, or by omitting what we ought to have done. Up to the seventh day, by which number totality is signified, we mourn all the sins that he committed and ought not to have committed, and for these we pray separately for the soul and separately for the body. Then, up to the thirtieth day, we pray both for the matters we have just mentioned above and for those things that he ought to have done but did not do.

A month is completed in thirty days. The course of the present life is signified by a month, as can easily be recognized from the state of the moon. Hence Gregory says in the eighth book of his *Moralia on Job*:

“By the name of months, a collection and sum of days is signified. Thus, by a day, each individual action can be expressed; by a month, the completion of actions is indicated.”

When we strive that the works of our friends may be complete before God, we sacrifice for them for thirty days.

I do not suppose that anyone would wish to say that we are not permitted to pray daily and offer sacrifice to God for the dead. But what is done on the third, seventh, and thirtieth days is done publicly and generally by all their friends, who assemble together for this purpose in the prayers of the Masses, in almsgiving, and in other good practices.

We read in the *History of the English* of a certain priest who thought that his brother had died in battle, although he was not dead but wounded and bound. The priest mentioned above did not wait for the third, seventh, or thirtieth day, but very frequently celebrated Masses for him. During the time of Mass, the wounded man’s bonds were released each day.

It is written in the aforementioned volume, book four, chapter twenty-four:

“When the man who had purchased him saw that he could not restrain him with bonds, he granted him permission to return if he could. From the third hour, however, when Masses were customarily celebrated, his bonds were very often released.”

The man promised under oath that he would return, or send him money in his place. And a little later:

“After this, when he had returned to his homeland and reached his brother, he recounted in order everything adverse that had happened to him and every consolation that had come to him amid adversity. When he returned, his brother learned that his bonds had been released especially at those times when the solemn rites of Mass had been celebrated for him.”

The common people usually ask whether it is permitted to celebrate Mass for all Christians. Augustine answers them in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 110:

“Nor should it be denied that the souls of the dead can be relieved by the piety of their living relatives, when sacrifice is offered for them to the Mediator, or almsgiving is performed in the church. But these things benefit those who, while they were alive, earned that they might later benefit from them.

“For there is a certain manner of life that is neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so bad that these things do not benefit it after death. There is also a condition so good that it does not require these things; and again there is a condition so evil that, when this life has passed, it cannot be helped by them. Accordingly, all merit is acquired here by which someone may, after this life, be relieved or burdened.”

And a little later:

“When sacrifice is offered for all baptized believers who have died, whether at the altar or through any kind of almsgiving: for the very good, these are acts of thanksgiving; for those who are not very evil, they are acts of propitiation; for the very evil, even if no assistance is provided to the dead, they are, in some manner, consolations for the living.

“For those whom these things benefit, they either benefit them so that forgiveness may be complete, or at least so that their damnation itself may become more bearable.”

Again, in his second book *To Paulinus, On Care for the Dead*:

“Although these things do not benefit all for whom they are performed, but only those for whom, while they live, it is acquired that they may benefit from them: nevertheless, because we do not distinguish who they are, we ought to do these things for all the regenerate, so that none of those to whom these benefits can and ought to come may be omitted.

“For it is better that these things remain in excess for those whom they neither harm nor benefit than that they be lacking to those whom they benefit.”

The anniversary day is repeated for the dead because we do not know what their condition is in the other life. Just as the anniversary day of the saints is recalled in their honor for our benefit, so the anniversary day of the dead is recalled for their benefit and to fulfill our devotion, as we believe that they will one day come to share in the company of the saints.

Otherwise, it is always good to pray for the dead, even if the day of the deceased is unknown, whether through forgetfulness or ignorance, or is omitted because of some earthly occupation. Nevertheless, their solemnity should be observed according to the decision of the most devout minds. I believe that with him in whom there is no shadow of change it is accepted as though it were an anniversary.

# BOOK FOUR

## PREFACE

[Col. 1163B] In this fourth little book are contained many matters written for investigation, insofar as I was able to ask them from the mercy of the Lord, concerning the daytime and nighttime cycles, whether on feast days or on ordinary days.

The purpose is that, once the order of the composition and the number of Psalms, readings, and responsories appointed for each appropriate time have been considered, God may be attended in the church with greater sweetness and compunction, and may be entreated and remembered both for oneself, who prays, and for those who need intercession; and that those whose remembrance is useful to us may also be remembered.

Some matters from the preceding books are also recapitulated, which my smallness discovered more clearly after the aforementioned books had been written.

## CHAPTER I. That We May Render to God What Is God’s: As Many Hours as the Sun Traverses the World, by So Many Repetitions We Offer Ourselves to God by Day and Night, Except in the Evening, Compline, and Morning Offices, Which Must Be Discussed Separately

We who are reckoned by the Christian name have been redeemed from diabolical slavery by Christ’s precious blood. Therefore we are not our own, but belong to our Redeemer. Concerning this price the Apostle says:

“For you were bought with a great price.”

And he immediately adds what we ought to do:

“Glorify and carry God in your body.”

We glorify him when we give him thanks for his redemption. We carry him in our body when, in our soul—which is carried by the body—he dwells through his love in thought, life, and understanding.

Therefore, by frequently carrying him in our mind through our remembrance and his sanctification, according to his good pleasure the mind commands the body to obedience. Through this obedience, our Redeemer is even more pleased that the soul, which is carried by the body, should cling to him.

To the same Redeemer we are always bound to serve, as a faithful servant serves his master, through the love of justice, sanctification, and other good practices. Concerning this service the prophet Zechariah says:

“That we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies without fear, might serve him in justice and holiness before him all our days.”

The same Lord has granted us two lights of time, namely, day and night, so that the sun might shine for us during the day and the moon during the night. From these two lights our crops derive their growth, so that they may come to serve our needs. From the moon they receive moisture to grow; from the sun, a moderating heat by which they reach maturity.

We can make this clear from the words of the lord Bede—whether he himself took them from whomever he wished is immaterial to me; his authority is sufficient. He says:

“Finally, when the night is clearer and the moon shines throughout it, a more abundant dew is brought to drench the fields; and many who rest beneath the open sky have perceived that, the more they have been under the moonlight, the more moisture they have gathered on their heads.”

And elsewhere concerning the sun:

“There are four seasons of the year, in which the sun, passing through different regions of the sky, tempers the world beneath it.
