Divine wisdom provides that, remaining always in the same places, it should not ravage the ornament of the world through an excess of heat; rather, gradually moving through different regions, it preserves a temperate condition for earthly fruits to be born and brought to maturity.”

Our body is sustained by the fruits of the earth. The body is in the service of the soul, so that in this present age it may be able to serve God. Once the soul has departed from the body through excessive affliction of the body, labor is no longer counted toward fruit; but as long as it is in the body, it must work at what is pleasing to God.

For we do not attend upon God in our offices only for the things that are provided for us in the present age. We also do so because we recognize that we are debtors to his perpetual service, like a faithful servant who always wishes to be present in the service of his master.

Therefore we make twelve repetitions during the day, through the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours, so that at every hour we may be present before God through each repetition. Likewise, at night we do so through twelve Psalms.

Because our father heard, “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,” we sometimes turn to temporal work. Yet, so that because of these necessities we may not omit the service that we owe to God in our soul, our fathers established that as many prayers of psalmody should be performed as there are hours granted to us for laboring to sustain the body.

And because we cannot work continually without some rest following, night comes, in which we cannot work. We give time to rest, so that for this rest itself we may also render service to God; we sing twelve Psalms for the twelve hours of the night.

We strive toward the kind of service that our first father Adam offered to God before he sinned, and that we hope will exist after this life: namely, that we may remain continually in God’s presence.

No one need murmur in this matter because of the unequal length of days and nights. Even those who calculate the hours divide the times of day and night in such a way that the moon shines for twelve hours during the night, whether in summer or winter.

Hence Bede, mentioned above, says in his book *On Times*:

“But in the longest nights of winter, or likewise in the shortest nights of summer—since it is clear that some greatly exceed the span of twelve hours, while others cannot reach it at all—how can we believe that the moon shines for twelve hours, unless perhaps we understand not the equinoctial hours, but divide each night, according to its measure of length or shortness, into twelve equal portions, which we call hours?”

## CHAPTER II. On Prime
Most magnificent, most glorious, and most Christian emperor [Col. 1165D], since he has professed himself your servant, although the least of all, he ventures to paint something concerning the laborers who at every hour wish to attend upon the service of God. It seems to my smallness, through God’s gift, which draws your mind to itself in prosperity and adversity, that I should begin with the hour at which the householder hires laborers for his vineyard.

Without doubt, the holy Church is the householder’s vineyard. It works through laborers in its vineyard so that it may bear fruit for him. We are the vineyard cultivated by the cultivators—that is, by the overseers of the holy Church—or by ourselves. The overseers display the cultivation, and we practice it together with them.

The cultivators dig the vineyard and spread manure when they cut into our hard hearts with words of rebuke and pour in our foul sins; [Col. 1166A] we too dig the earth around the vine and make a trench when we bring our nature to mind and humble ourselves beneath the powerful hand of God, recognizing that we are dust and ashes. Moreover, because by sinning we corrupt that nature itself, we add manure, so that our sins may be around us in the present age but absent in the future; and through these two things—that is, through consideration of our nature and repentance for our sins—our fruit may grow more abundantly, may become wine through the anguish of the winepress and the stripping away of carnal pleasures, and may enter, as though through a certain winepress, into the storeroom of the eternal house.

The wine expressed from the grape by the pressure of the winepress is our ardent desire, which is stripped of carnal desire [Col. 1166B] so that it may be worthy of being stored in the Lord’s treasury.

Many hostile wild beasts lie in wait for the fruit of the vineyard, so that they may seize it and carry it away into their own bodies. The Ziphites can in some sense be compared with these beasts: they were Saul’s agents who wished to seize David and hand him over to Saul to be killed. Nor are those same Ziphites absent from us. Their name is interpreted as “flourishing.” We understand them to be members of the devil, or the devil himself, who may for this reason be called “flourishing,” because he displays fleeting prosperity to his own. Whether through himself or through his members, he lies in wait for us or openly persecutes us, so as to hand us over to eternal death.

And this would happen if the Lord’s vineyard—which is us—did not have a hedge around it and cultivators within it. The hedge is the Lord’s protection around his elect; [Col. 1166C] the cultivators, as we have said, are the teachers and overseers of the Church.

David was surrounded by that hedge when the Ziphites surrounded him; therefore he was saved and sang the psalm, “O God, save me by your name,” and so forth.

Since, by the Lord’s mercy, we are about to begin the daily offices at the hour when the householder called the laborers to his vineyard, it seems proper to us to begin them at the same time when that Gospel is read which contains the hiring of the laborers at the appointed hours—that is, at Septuagesima.

Just as sheep kept by night in folds, when they leave their enclosure after the morning watch and go out into the broad fields for pasture, immediately need a shepherd to protect them from attacking [Col. 1166D] wolves, so we, rising at first light to obey the Lord’s commands, need to have a shepherd and teacher who will lead us into those same commands and defend us from wolves. Concerning these wolves it is written in the Gospel according to John: “The wolf snatches and scatters the sheep.” Nevertheless, we must also be defended from the lion, which prowls around roaring and seeking someone to devour.

How the wolf snatches and the lion devours is evident to those who are attacked by vices. Anyone who observes how he is tempted by his own desire—drawn away and enticed—recognizes whom these aforementioned beasts snatch through gluttony, whom through lust, whom through curiosity about forbidden arts, whom through the contemplation of shameful and pointless spectacles, whom through the acquisition of temporal possessions, whom through inquisitiveness in investigating or criticizing the vices of his neighbors, whom through pride, and whom through boasting.

These are the vices that fall under the three desires with which the whole world is entangled, as the Apostle says: “Everything that is in the world is either the desire of the flesh, or the desire of the eyes, or the pride of life.”

Because of the beasts mentioned above, our shepherd says, “O God, attend to my help; Lord, hasten to help me.” At the beginning of the office he prays that they may not prevail so greatly that, through their craft, they separate anyone from that same assembly.

Moses acted similarly when the ark was raised for carrying. For they said: “Arise, Lord, and let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee from your presence.” Spiritually, we are that ark. Just as the ark was daily surrounded by enemies, so the holy Church will be surrounded by persecutors until the end, whether open or hidden.

After the prayer of our shepherd there follows the Glory of the holy Trinity, whose presence we implore for our help. Our shepherd remembers the Lord’s saying: “Without me you can do nothing.”

Jerome wrote in his letter to Pope Damasus concerning the addition of “Glory be to the Father” in various places. Why, at the time just mentioned—that is, Septuagesima—is Alleluia (“Praise the Lord”) not appended to the doxology of the holy Trinity, “through all ages of ages,” but instead, “Praise to you, Lord, King of eternal glory”? We explained in the little book we composed on Septuagesima that this is for no other reason than that, by the humbler Latin tongue as compared with Hebrew, we might be reminded that during Septuagesima we ought to be formed toward a humbler way of life than at another time.

After this there follows the psalm that David sang when the Ziphites wished to seize him and hand him over to Saul. We must sing it at dawn, in accordance with what is written: “The righteous will set his heart to keep watch at dawn,” so that God may wish to save us, because strangers rise up against us who do not set God before their eyes, and so that he may rescue us from all tribulations and our eye may look down upon all our enemies, as David did in his own time.

Afterward there follow two repetitions of the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled,” which is full of moral instruction. Those whom God has freed from the bonds and prison of their enemies ought to attend upon him with good and devout conduct in complete dedication, as we can infer from the two verses of the two repetitions.

One says: “Would that my ways were directed toward keeping your ordinances.” The other says: “Reveal my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law.”

These three repetitions support and defend the Lord’s ark until the completion of the third hour—that is, through the first, second, and third hours.

Then follows the verse: “Arise, Lord, help us, and deliver us for the sake of your name.” Moses said something similar when the ark was lowered. For it is written in the Book of Numbers, chapter twenty-six, that when it was lowered he said: “Return, Lord, to the multitude of the children of Israel.”

God’s return to Israel’s army means nothing other than that he causes Israel to return to him with its whole heart. God has nowhere to return, since everything is present to him. Thus “Arise, Lord” is to be understood as meaning: “Make us rise from the sleep of sluggishness, and make us industrious and energetic in the work of your commandments.”

From that return the same chant received the name “verse.” For we enact with the position of our bodies the same return of which we are admonished through the verse. When we hear the verse, we immediately turn toward the east. Why do we do this, unless so that every thought that has gone outside us by looking upon and seeing temporal things may return within us, and we may say: “Lord, give me a heart with which to pray to you”?

After this we begin to implore the Lord’s mercy through “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), “Christe eleison” (“Christ, have mercy”), and again “Kyrie eleison.” In the Church we celebrate, in a certain manner, three aspects of the divine majesty and of the Trinity.

The first is before humanity was assumed, when the Trinity was invoked without the union of human nature; therefore we rightly say “Kyrie eleison” three times, or once because of the one substance.

The second is after the human being was assumed, when Christ was seen on earth and nevertheless was believed by his own people to be God and the Son of God. Thus Peter said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” and Paul said of that same Son: “He did not spare his own Son.” Since he is called “Christ” because of the assumed nature, which was anointed with spiritual oil, we say “Christe eleison” in the middle of the three parts.

When we say “Christe eleison” once, we show that he alone was among human beings and had no equal in every respect; and in the third invocation we show that, because of the unity of his person, he was never separated from the substance of the holy Trinity.

The third aspect is from the time when he wished to glorify the assumed human being more than he had been glorified while mortal. Therefore he himself said to the Father: “Glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory that I had before the world existed.”

For this reason, in a similar manner to the first part, we pray the Lord to forgive us in such temptations as are unavoidable in this life. Concerning these it is said in the Proverbs of Solomon: “The righteous man falls seven times a day and rises again”—that is, through ignorance, forgetfulness, thought, speech, surprise, necessity, [Col. 1168D] and the weakness of the flesh.

Every day, whether unwillingly or willingly, we frequently incur guilt; nevertheless, the righteous person rises again, because the fall caused by human weakness does not prejudice his righteousness.

Then follows the Lord’s Prayer, which ought to be sung with great care, so that we keep in mind the very things we pronounce with our words. “Kyrie eleison” very often precedes it; through this God is first reconciled to us, so that with his mercy and favor we may fittingly invoke him as “our Father” and attend to the words of the prayer.

After the Lord’s Prayer there follows our confession of faith, which the holy apostles established concerning the faith of the holy Trinity, the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, and the condition of our Church.

The form of prayer that we have set out concerns those who are compuncted by lesser and daily sins. There are both kinds of people in our Church: those who have remained in goodness and those who have fallen through sin but hasten each day to rise again through repentance.

In the person of the latter it is said: “My soul shall live, and it shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me.” It is as though he said: “If my soul has died because of my errors, afterward it will live through conversion. And your judgments will help me.” For you have said: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should be converted and live”; and again: “There is more joy over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine righteous people who do not need repentance.”

The following verse shows the former error of the one who now, converted, says, “My soul shall live, and it shall praise you”: “I have strayed like a sheep that has perished; seek your servant, for I have not forgotten your commandments.”

From the same person there follows the psalm that David sang after he had been converted through repentance from the evil of adultery and murder.

After that psalm the entire flock commends itself to God—the shepherd together with the sheep—and says: “Look upon your servants and your works, and direct their children.”

With these words we ought to hold this in mind: we should think of our children as the thoughts that arise from the mind, so that God may direct them according to his good pleasure. And in what follows, where it says, “And direct the works of our hands upon us,” it means the works that proceed from our thoughts.

Then the individual shepherd prays for the whole flock, saying: “Direct, Lord, our hearts”—that is, our thoughts; our senses, namely our eyes, ears, and nostrils; our words, which are offered through the mouth; and the works of our hands—so that we may be pleasing in your sight.

Thus at last, secure, we hasten to the necessary works.

No reading precedes the verse set out above, “Arise, Lord,” and therefore no responsory follows it, as in the other offices. This course follows the custom of the holy Church: first to undertake work, and afterward to teach. Christ left us this example, of whom Luke says: “What Jesus began to do and to teach.”

The psalms concern works; the reading concerns teaching. Therefore, if the Lord grants it, we are prepared to explain more clearly in what follows. In the present course we pray for God’s help in carrying out works. Let us work first, and teach afterward in the course of the third hour.

For this reason, as I think, the custom arose that in monasteries devoted to God a reading should be given in the chapter, so that those who are occupied by the Lord’s service day and night may not be without reading. They are eager for heavenly nourishment; they cannot restrain themselves from eating at every hour, however brief, from the food of the Scriptures.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning Terce

The prophet Daniel instituted three hours of the day for us to worship God. Concerning them it is written in his book:

“When Daniel learned of this—that is, of the established law—he entered his house, and with the windows of his upper room open toward Jerusalem, he knelt three times a day.” [Col. 1170A]

Therefore Jerome, in his explanation of the same book, says:

“The three times at which the knees are to be bent before God ecclesiastical tradition understands as the third, sixth, and ninth hours. Finally, at the third hour the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles. At the sixth hour Peter, wishing to eat, went up to the upper room to pray. At the ninth hour Peter and John were going to the temple.”

After reading these things, we find in the Book of Ezra, who lived after Daniel, that the people of God worshiped the Lord and confessed their sins four times a day. For it is written in that book:

“The children of Israel assembled in fasting and sackcloth, with earth upon them; and the offspring of Israel separated themselves from every foreign-born son. They stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers; and they rose to stand, and they read in the book of the law of the Lord their God: four times a day and four times a night they confessed and worshiped the Lord their God.” [Col. 1170B]

Therefore Bede says this in his exposition of the book mentioned:

“Who would not marvel that so great a people showed such exceptional care for devotion, so that four times a day—that is, at first light, at the third hour, the sixth, and the ninth, when they ought to devote themselves to prayer or psalmody—they surrendered themselves to hearing the divine law, so that, with their minds renewed toward God, they might return purer and more devout to imploring his mercy? And at night, after shaking off the torpor of sleep four times, they would rise to confess their sins and ask forgiveness?

“After their example, I think a most beautiful custom arose in the Church: at each hour of the divine psalmody, one reading from either the Old or the New Testament should be delivered by heart to all who are listening, and thus, strengthened by apostolic or prophetic words, they should kneel for earnest prayer. At the nocturnal hours also, when work has ceased, their ears should freely attend to readings from the divine books.”

By the inspiration with which the Lord Bede was inspired, we know that our course of day and night has its beginning in the Book of Ezra. If, following their custom, we assemble to beseech God, we ought to know that we have the work of building the walls of our Church, just as they had the work of building the walls of Jerusalem, and that we are surrounded by enemies, just as they were.

The wall of our Church has Christ as its foundation; upon that foundation have been established the apostles and those who through them believed, believe, or will believe. Today we are engaged in the construction of this wall, which will always be built until the end of the world.

Each of the saints who has been predestined by God for eternal life is a stone of that wall. One stone is placed upon another when the teachers of the Church take younger people into their own discipline for teaching, correcting, and establishing them in the holy Church.

Each person has a stone above him, bearing a brother’s labor. Concerning this building the Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.”

The larger, polished, or squared stones that are placed on the outer sides, with the smaller stones lying in their midst, are the more perfect men who sustain weaker disciples or brothers in the holy Church by their admonitions and prayers. [Col. 1171A]

The wall cannot be stable without mortar. Mortar is made from lime, sand, and water. Burning lime is fervent charity, which joins sand—that is, earthly work—to itself. Concerning this the Apostle Paul says: “Let him labor, working with his hands at what is good, so that he may have something to give to one in need.”

True charity shows the greatest concern for widows, for those worn out by age or illness, for orphans, and for the weak. Therefore it strives to work with its hands so that it may have something with which to do them good. It recalls Solomon’s words: “Honor the Lord with your substance.” And again: “The redemption of a man’s soul is his own wealth.”

Just as lime and earth become useful for building a wall when they are bound together by the mixing of water, [Col. 1171B] so water is the Holy Spirit, as the evangelist John says: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” He said this about the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

For just as the stones of a wall cannot be joined together for the wall’s stability without mortar, so human beings cannot be joined together for the building of the heavenly Jerusalem without charity, which the Holy Spirit produces.

While we are building this wall, Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites are present, wishing to hinder our work. Through these named foreigners we see the devil attacking us with his weapons, which are vices or wicked people.

But, following the custom of the Jewish people, let us hold our weapons in our hands and defend ourselves from our enemies, crying out to God. For it is written in the book mentioned above, Ezra:

“We prayed to the Lord our God and set guards upon the wall day and night against them.” And shortly afterward: “From that day on, half of their young men performed the work, while the other half was prepared for battle, with spears, shields, bows, and breastplates, and with their leaders behind them throughout the whole house of Judah,” and so forth.

Our weapons are God’s protection. We are protected by the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the word.

Let us keep these things in mind when we are gathered together, and let our leader be with us in Christ’s place. He should say, “O God, attend to my help,” teach us through reading, and fortify us through his prayer.

Who knows whether in this way we shall be able to escape from the hands of our enemies?

There were also such diligent men among that people of God that with one hand they held weapons for defense, while with the other they built the wall. So too let our hands—that is, our intentions—be extended, so that with one we resist our enemies and with the other perform good work.

Several verses from Terce express the same idea. In the first section the verse says: “I will answer those who reproach me with a word, because I have hoped in your words.” In the second it says: “The proud acted wickedly beyond measure, but I did not turn aside from your law.” In the third it says: “The iniquity of the proud has been multiplied against me, but I will search out your commandments with my whole heart.”

What the three repetitions in the course of Terce mean was shown in the first section: namely, that we are protected for three hours until we assemble again—through the fourth and fifth hours and until the sixth—yet in such a way [Col. 1172A] that we reach the sixth hour during the course of the third; and when the sixth hour begins, we begin the next course.

If the Lord wills, he who causes his sun to rise upon the good and the wicked may grant us the ability to say something worthy here concerning the variations made in the courses—that is, in psalmody, readings, responsories, and verses. Perhaps we shall proceed more freely in what follows.

Paul says to the Ephesians: “Do not become foolish, but understand what the will of God is. Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Holy Spirit, speaking to yourselves in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord.”

As has been shown to me from the exposition of Saint Jerome, I understand the three changes in our course to be fulfilled in these three apostolic commands: psalms are present in our speech when we sing psalms; hymns when, from reading the sayings of the holy Fathers, we are pierced with compunction for God’s praises; and songs when, through the singing of the responsory, our mind is lifted by a certain joy toward contemplation of our heavenly homeland.

For song is very often celebrated in joy. The minds of the saints have no greater joy than to be lifted anagogically toward the heavenly kingdom.

The words of that aforementioned supreme Teacher ought to be set down, so that his authority may fix in the minds of those who hear what we wish to explain. He says:

“We have spoken most fully in the Psalter about the difference among psalm, hymn, and song. Here, however, we must say briefly that hymns are those compositions that proclaim God’s strength and majesty and always marvel either at his benefits or at his deeds. This is contained in all psalms to which ‘Alleluia’ is either prefixed or appended.

“Psalms, properly speaking, belong to the ethical sphere, so that through the instrument of the voice we may know what ought to be done and what avoided. But the person who discusses higher matters and, as a subtle disputant, describes the world’s assembly and the order and harmony of all creatures sings a spiritual song.

“The work of the psalter, which is struck by hand so that it may resound, pertains to our works. The works of the saints are good conduct, which we practice either in advancing along the spiritual journey or in killing carnal pleasures. Such conduct cannot be practiced without labor.

“Therefore, when we sing psalms, we customarily stand, so that by the posture of our body we may demonstrate the disposition of our mind: namely, that we are ready either to subdue our flesh or to undertake work for ourselves and our brothers.”

After this tropological discourse—that is, one that discusses conduct—there follows the reading, in which those things are found that Saint Jerome assigned to hymns, namely, those that concern the praise of God.

There we find the Lord’s majesty: how, though circumscribed, he contains everything within himself. There we find his strength: how he redeems his created people with a strong hand and outstretched arm. There we find his benefits: how he enriches with every good the very one whom he has redeemed. There we find his deeds: how he made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything that is in them.

In that reading there is no lack of history, allegory, tropology, or anagogy, [Col. 1173A] although tropology is celebrated separately, as we have stated, in the psalms. In the tropology of the psalms we recall our works; in the tropology of the readings, the works of others.

For we do not labor in the Lord’s majesty, strength, benefits, or deeds. Therefore, during the recitation of the reading we customarily sit or stand silently.

In the responsories we customarily raise our voice higher than in the preceding elements, namely the psalms and hymns. By the height of our voice we show the height of our mind, which lifts itself in joy toward the heavenly city.

After good works and the nourishment of the mind from holy Scripture, heavenly joy follows. Why it is called a responsory has been explained in the written account of the Mass.

In this place we compare the responsory with spiritual songs. They are songs because they are sung; they are spiritual because they arise from the rejoicing of the spiritual mind. There are other songs that rejoice in a singular gift, such as those about which we wrote in the baptistery, where the joy of the newly baptized dances because of their singular innocence and no one responds to them. These, however, are songs by which each person incites another toward the heavenly dwelling places, which are many in the Father’s house.

What the verse of the responsory signifies we described in the aforementioned office of the Mass: namely, that there should be two things in the ecclesiastical man—exhortation directed toward the brothers and personal supplication directed toward the Lord.

Glory follows in the anagogical office. No one doubts that nowhere is such glory rendered to God as in the assembly of the holy angels and of those saints who are in the Lord’s presence.

In these readings, namely the daily ones, a blessing is not requested from the superior, because the superior sings them and is accustomed to hold Christ’s place in the Church. The difference between these readings and the one celebrated at Mass is the difference between a domestic admonition and one delivered to a public assembly.

The reading that we conduct at Mass we ordinarily proclaim from the step, so that the whole people may hear it. The reading that we set out in the office concerning the baptistery was presented because of the circumstances of the time—that is, because it is said to be intended for wise people. In it the author is also recalled, so that if one of those who assemble from every place because readings are rare happens not to know the story, he may hear its author, who perhaps is not unknown; and through the author’s authority the words of the reading may be fixed more firmly in the heart.

Such people, nevertheless, may be wise because of their upright conduct. But those who are always occupied with ecclesiastical matters and with divine reading, as the Church’s household members are, do not need to hear the author, because they recognize the author from the reading.

As we read in Ezra, four readings were given each day among the ancient people of God. And rightly four, because the human being consists of four elements, so that each element may offer itself to its Creator at the appropriate hours.

Following our custom, we have presented Prime without a reading. If it had contained a reading, our readings would not be as numerous as those of that ancient people of God. Therefore the holy Fathers arranged for the reading omitted in Prime to be read in the chapter.

It was not omitted there without reason. Since the shepherd of the place wishes to indicate the teacher, he omits his teaching there in order to teach each teacher that one ought first to act and afterward to teach. Concerning this Moses says in the Book of Deuteronomy: “You shall not plow with the firstborn of an ox.”

These three forms may also be understood as encompassing every kind of music that the ancient people practiced in praise of God. The nature of musical art is threefold.

It is produced either by the striking of the fingers, as in the psalter, the lyre, and other instruments touched by the striking of the fingers; or by the voice, as in song; or by blowing, as in trumpets.

These three are mentioned in the Psalter. Psalm thirty-two says: “Give thanks to the Lord on the lyre; sing to him on the ten-stringed psaltery. Sing to him a new song; sing skillfully to him with a shout.” [Col. 1174B]

Again, in Psalm three: “With my voice I cried out to the Lord.” Likewise, in Psalm one hundred fifty: “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with psaltery and lyre. Praise him with tambourine and dance; praise him with strings and organ. Praise him with well-sounding cymbals,” and so forth.

When we sing psalms, we practice that kind of music which is produced by the striking of the fingers. Indeed, the volume of the Psalter received its name from the psalter of musical art.

When we read, we practice the kind that is produced by the voice. The Apostle Paul called the reading “voices” in the Acts of the Apostles: “Not knowing Jesus,” he says, “and the voices of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath.”

When we sing responsories, we raise our voice as though through a trumpet, stirring our brothers toward higher things, until we arrive at the praise of the holy Trinity and say: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

To the extent that our body is better than the musical instruments made by human beings, so much more acceptable to God is the service offered at this time than it was in ancient times.

And to the extent that the law of freedom, which comes through the grace of the New Testament, is better than the law of servitude, so much more fitting is it that we should have praises in our own body, which we may render to God always and everywhere, than in wooden and bronze instruments.

Here again we wish to speak about the verse. The verse has this power: it makes the whole choir turn toward one thing and directs its entire attention to the matter for which the office is being performed.

Thus, at first light, the verse is: “Arise, Lord, help us and deliver us [Col. 1174D] for the sake of your name.” It is as though it said: “Make us rise, Lord, for works; help us by the strength of your arm to labor; and deliver us from the snares prepared against us.”

The mind’s intention ought to retain this petition during the office of Prime.

Here, however, at Terce, the verse says: “Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, my God and Savior.” It is as though it said: “You have helped us until the present time; help us also henceforth. We have not yet reached the goal toward which we are striving—that is, midday, at which you feed us and at which you recline, according to the Song of Songs. Do not abandon us on this journey, nor despise us, our saving God.”

Then “Kyrie eleison” and “Christe eleison” follow.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Prayer Celebrated by the Assembly of the Brothers through Several Daily and Nocturnal Courses

[Col. 1175A]

There is a priest on earth who must intercede daily for himself and for the people of God. And there is a priest in heaven who does not need to intercede, yet nevertheless wishes to do so and intercedes daily for us.

The priest who is on earth neither wishes nor is able to say that he is without sin, since John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

Nevertheless, although he is a sinner, his conscience ought not to reproach him, provided that he is a sinner only to the extent that he recognizes sin among the people on earth. That people is less burdened by sins in some cases and more heavily burdened in others.

For those who commit lesser sins [Col. 1175B] and for himself, the priest prays when he says “Kyrie eleison” and the Lord’s Prayer, in which no one can excuse himself unless he truthfully says: “And forgive us our debts.”

Then the priest continues with the pattern of prayer that Paul enumerates, saying: “Supplications, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings,” and the rest that follows.

Therefore Ambrose says in his exposition of the same epistle:

“Above all,” he says, “I beg you to know what is especially necessary for you to understand, so that you may properly know what it is fitting to do. He says: ‘Prayers, supplications, petitions.’”

And shortly afterward:

“Either we ask that good things be given to us by God—this he called prayers—or that we be released from evils—this he called supplications.”

And again, shortly afterward:

“Those things that oppose this are many and persistent. One is the devil’s deception, which in various ways seeks to turn us away from the good; another is the distress of sufferings, which seems to be present in us. Through these we are excluded from good things and are often confined, against our purpose, in things that are not suitable for us.

“But it is necessary that we, who endure a great struggle concerning this, have recourse to the Lord, who is powerful enough by his aid to quiet all those things that contribute to our distress.”

This he said about petitions.

And again, below:

“Thanksgiving is offered for things that have already been granted; and you are taught for whom these things ought to be done: ‘For all human beings.’ He commanded them to be concerned in common for all human beings.”

And again, below:

“Then he proceeds to those who seem to be highest among human beings: ‘For kings,’ he says, ‘and for all who are in positions of authority.’”

Our books, however, have supplications first and prayers afterward. Our prayer follows this order.

The first verse after the Lord’s Prayer is: “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you.” In this verse there is supplication, through which forgiveness from evils is requested.

When he says, “Heal my soul, because I have sinned against you,” he asks for the Lord’s medicine, so that he may be freed from sickness.

The second verse is: “Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation.” In this verse we ask for good things; this belongs to prayer.

The third is: “Turn, Lord—how long?—and be gracious toward your servants.” In this verse we ask that everything opposed to our good may be overcome through the Lord’s help. This belongs to petition.

Concerning this verse Augustine says in his exposition of the psalms:

“Turn, Lord—how long?—and be gracious toward your servants: it is the voice of those who endure many evil persecutions in this world, and who become known as shackled in heart through wisdom, yet who, even when compelled by evils, do not flee from the Lord to the good things of this age.”

The fourth should be, “Let them confess to you, O Lord,” which pertains to thanksgivings. Up to this point prayer has been offered, according to the Apostle, for all human beings. Then follows prayer “for kings and all who are in positions of authority, so that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all piety and chastity.” For there are within our Church [Col. 1176B] those who commit minor offenses; nevertheless, the preceding prayer is necessary for them. There are also those who commit greater offenses, for whom it is necessary to add the psalm, “Have mercy on me, O God,” which properly pertains to penitents. In another sense: the preceding prayer is for minor sins, while the psalm is for greater ones.

Finally, the priest rises in the place of that priest who is in heaven, who daily intercedes for us, and standing he says a prayer. This prayer follows at every season—that is, at Easter, Pentecost, on Sundays, and on feast days. To recall the resurrection of that priest whose place he occupies, he rises from his reclining position and, standing, says this prayer. Yet previously he prays lying down with the others, since he is a sinner and is prostrate with sinners; and because he occupies Christ’s place, he says [Col. 1176C] the special prayer while standing. This special prayer of priests, which in a certain way displays the freedom and glorification of the kingdom to come, and yet also shows that he will always be an intercessor there for us, is used throughout all the feast days mentioned.

The remainder of the prayer is omitted, since there is no sinner there, nor will there be. If someone wishes to say that this prayer takes the place of Christ’s intercession—he who daily intercedes for us with the Father—why does it say, “Through our Lord Jesus Christ”? Let him be told that Christ, who is naturally in the Father, and through whom humanity was assumed into God because of the one and same person of the Son of God, deigned to become for us the door through which we, our prayers, and all our good things pass to the Father. Therefore the priest rightly addresses his prayer to [Col. 1176D] God the Father “through our Lord Jesus Christ,” because through him he received the grace to discharge to his brothers and fellow disciples the ministry of Christ’s intercession in turn, and to recall and bring it back to memory.

The greeting precedes this prayer, and the blessing follows it, which in turn is followed by the thanksgiving. After his resurrection the Lord greeted the disciples; he greeted them again and blessed them on the Mount of Olives. They, giving thanks, worshiped in the place where his feet had stood.

That the same prayers should be celebrated in the evening hour as at none is written in the Council of Laodicea, chapter eighteen: the same office of prayers must always be performed at none and at evening. According to this [Col. 1177A] chapter, prayer should be celebrated in the same manner on feast days and on other days, both in the evening and at the ninth hour. As I think, we may similarly speak of the third and sixth hours.

After the evening and morning offices, which are performed for the dead, we customarily sing in its place the psalm, “Have mercy on me, O God,” and “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.” It is sixth in the order of the Psalms, yet it is entitled “for the octave.” This is because we, who are in the sixth age of the world, ought through this psalm to ask God on behalf of the seventh and eighth ages that we may escape the torments due to the wicked in those designated errors. Augustine says of it in the prologue to the same psalm:

“The eighth day of judgment will come. On it, assigning to each person what is due according to his merits, it will transfer the saints no longer to temporal works but to eternal life, while it will condemn the wicked [Col. 1177B] forever.”

Fearing this condemnation, the Church prays in this psalm, saying, “O Lord, rebuke me not in your anger.” Bede likewise says in his book *On Times*:

“This is the octave, for which the sixth psalm is entitled. I believe that, in the six ages of this world, supplication must be made for the seventh or eighth age of this world. In it the righteous will receive joys, but the reprobate punishments; therefore this psalm begins, continues, and ends in great dread: ‘O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury.’”

# CHAPTER V  
## On Sext

Of the three repetitions of sext, or none, I have supplied what I could in the course of prime and terce, concerning the readings and responsories. These present three repetitions [Col. 1177C] establish us in the service of the Lord, or fortify us against the enemy’s ambushes, through the seventh, eighth, and ninth hours—yet in such a way that at none itself the remaining three repetitions begin, carrying us through to the end of the day.

It remains to consider, from the condition of the time, the verse that is said at sext. The condition of the time is midday, when the sun is at the center of heaven and provides the earth with its fiercest heat. This same condition signifies the perfection of the minds of devout people, whose fervor is so joined to the invisible fire that it is nourished by its delight and illumined by the light of understanding.

At the same hour Peter went up into the upper room and desired to eat. At prime are the beginnings of the virtues, at terce their progress, and at midday [Col. 1177D] their perfection. Some verses of the course of sext announce this perfection. The first section says:

“My soul has failed for your salvation, and I have placed my hope exceedingly in your word.”

The second says:

“How I have loved your law, O Lord! It is my meditation all the day.”

The third says:

“My eyes have failed for your salvation and for the word of your righteousness.”

A verse displays the condition of such minds, saying:

“The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me there in a place of pasture.”

Where we say, “The Lord governs me,” the translation adopted by Saint Jerome from the Hebrew truth has, “The Lord feeds me.” Whoever is fed by the Lord through the coming of his Spirit is likewise governed by him—that is, the Spirit of God makes him delight in those ways that accord with reason and lead by the straight path to the strongly fortified city of Jerusalem. He lacks nothing, as the Apostle Paul says: “I can do all things in him who strengthens me”; “All things work together for him according to God.” He endures prosperity and adversity with equal composure; and therefore what follows is:

“In a place of pasture he has placed me,”

whether this means an abundance of intellectual things in the present, or in the future, everlasting joy and glory, where there will be the satisfaction of every joy without end.

# CHAPTER VI  
## On None

None contains the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth hours. The condition of the time when none is celebrated signifies that the fervor of study which the mind exercised in the height of the virtues has grown somewhat lukewarm because of the temptations that arise. [Col. 1178B] Hence Gregory says in his *Moralia on Job*:

“Vices, while they tempt us, humble the virtues progressing in + us.”

Just as the sun then descends from the center to the lower regions, so the mind, when it is tempted, descends from the height of intimate joy to consider its own nature and fragility, and sees how easily it may set.

Paul was being tempted when he said:

“Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh, an angel of Satan to buffet me.”

Our present teacher Paul shows here for what reason the elect person is tempted. In what follows he makes known the distress he suffered from the temptation, saying:

“For this reason I asked the Lord three times that it might depart from me.”

In my opinion, unless Satan’s thorn had caused him distress, he would not have prayed to God that it depart from him.

Some verses of the course of none sound the same prayer. The first section says:

“Tribulations and distress have found me; your commandments are my meditation.”

Augustine explains this in the same psalm:

“Let them rage, let them persecute, provided that the commandments of God are not abandoned, and that from those very commandments even those who rage may be loved.”

The second says:

“Many are those who persecute and trouble me, yet I have not turned aside from your testimonies.”

The third says:

“I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost; seek your servant, because I have not forgotten your commandments.”

A verse of the present course recalls the temptation signified by the sun’s decline:

“Cleanse me, O Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others.”

The aforementioned Augustine explains this in the eighteenth psalm:

“Take an evil thought from my heart; drive away from me the evil counselor. This is: ‘Cleanse me from my hidden faults, and spare your servant from those of others.’”

# CHAPTER VII  
## On the Evening Synaxis

We read in Ezra, as we have already mentioned, that the people of God confessed the Lord four times by day and four times by night. From the words of the lord Bede, in his exposition of the same Ezra, we learn that it is the opinion of the holy Church, in accordance with that custom, that it celebrates four offices by day and four by night.

For it is not without reason that we who serve God renew our vigils four times during the night, since those who served the world divided the night into four watches in their camps, lest the camps be broken into by enemies lying in ambush. We customarily call our four watches during the night evening, compline, nocturns, and matins.

From the etymology of the name “evening” we can learn that the evening office belongs to the night. Isidore says in his book *Etymologies*:

“The evening office is at the beginning of the night; it is named from the evening star, which rises as night begins.”

Augustine likewise says in the twenty-ninth psalm:

“In the evening weeping will remain.”

What does “in the evening weeping will remain” mean? Evening occurs when the sun sets. From this we may infer, when we observe feast days, that we ought to observe them from evening to evening, so that we must lawfully keep them from the setting of the sun until its next setting.

This condition of the night represents the weeping of those sinners for whom the true sun has set. They must mourn their five bodily senses, which are accustomed to obey in sinning, so that at matins—that is, when their sins have been escaped and the sun begins once more to rise for them, for whom it set in the evening—they may rejoice.

Hence the same author, in the psalm mentioned above:

“In the evening weeping will remain, and in the morning rejoicing,”

when the light that had set for sinners begins to rise for the faithful.

+ It also represents in another way the condition of those who are oppressed by some illness through which they approach death. For the more they fear dying and receiving the true sentence for their sins, the more they bring before the eyes of their death the carnal impulses generated through the five bodily senses, and mourn them.

Fear commonly takes possession of the minds of people when they approach death, as it is written of the Lord himself—although he did not fear because of infirmity, but in accordance with the economy of salvation—“he began to be sorrowful and distressed.” Nevertheless, there are many who rejoice at matins, when they will rise from the dead because of their fellowship in Christ’s Resurrection.

Having passed through these two interpretations, we must come to our daily practice. Our daily practice requires us to sing five psalms at the evening synaxis. For who does not know, although we pray to the Lord through four hours, how many obstacles and how many sorrows occupy the mind of the righteous during the day?

The eyes bring before it alluring forms, which enter the soul without the will of the righteous person and therefore distress it. In the same way, words of detraction or luxury enter through the ears and likewise bring trouble to the mind. The nostrils too are not strangers to this pestilential messenger. The mouth cannot excuse itself unless it sins. Everyone knows when words are criminal, when they are idle, and the other such things by which the mind is polluted through the mouth.

The hands and feet, without doubt, often touch what makes the soul worse through thought. But because by daily inclination we tend toward darkness through these five senses, it is necessary that at the beginning of night we ask God’s forgiveness for them.

These are the five senses that in the morning we commend to the Lord to be directed, saying:

“Direct, O Lord, our hearts, senses, and speech, and the works of our hands.”

Among “senses,” “speech,” and “works” the five bodily senses are included. The heart must be discussed separately when, if the Lord grants it, we come to the hymn of Mary.

Because of these five senses—for perhaps we were not worthy that they should be directed in all things according to the Lord’s pleasure—five psalms are sung so that we may be forgiven. We customarily sing these five psalms antiphonally.

As the three-part history relates in book 10, chapter 9, the use of antiphons in the churches first began to be practiced through Ignatius, bishop of Antioch. For it relates as follows:

“Yet it must be said from where the practice began, that antiphons should be sung in the Church. Ignatius, the third bishop of Antioch in Syria after the Apostle Peter, who also lived with the apostles themselves, saw a vision of angels, how through antiphons they sang hymns to the Holy Trinity. He is therefore believed to have handed on the form of the vision to the Church of Antioch, and from there it passed to all the churches.”

Antiphon means “reciprocal voice.” An antiphon is begun by one member of one choir, and [continues] in response to its accord [the printed wording is incomplete]. The psalm is sung by two choirs. For the antiphon itself—that is, the antiphon—joins the two choirs together.

As the soul is better than the body, so the song of the soul is better than that of the body. Therefore we must consider what the soul’s antiphon is. It seems to us that it is the virtue of love, which joins the works of two brothers together.

Are psalms referred to works? The antiphon refers to that love by which each person offers his work to his brother. For example: one reads and learns doctrine in school, while another sows in the field. At the time of the harvest, the teacher offers doctrine to the sower, and the sower bread to the teacher.

The antiphon alternates between two choirs, because charity cannot be less than something existing between two. The singers signify this reciprocal charity when they raise the antiphons alternately from each side.

These two choirs were represented by the wings of the living creatures extended toward one another, which Ezekiel saw as a figure of the coming of Christ and the New Testament. The joining of the two wings is the antiphon, which takes the place of charity.

Hence Gregory writes in his seventh homily on the same Ezekiel:

“For while he offers the word of preaching and drives away the darkness of ignorance from my heart by the light of truth, and while I, because perhaps he is oppressed by the powerful person of this world, offer him the comfort of my protection and rescue him from violent hands, we in turn extend our wings to one another, so that by affection and reciprocal assistance we may touch one another through the good that we have received.”

Therefore the first shepherd rightly admonishes us, saying:

“The end of all things will draw near. Therefore be prudent and watchful in prayers; above all, maintain continual mutual charity among yourselves, because charity covers a multitude of sins.”

After this follows the reading delivered by the shepherd. It is the reading that the shepherd ought diligently to administer to his household.

I once heard responsories sung in certain places after the evening reading; they are contained in some antiphonaries. But among others, and now in nearly all places, a verse follows the reading in conjunction with it. I often turn over in my mind whether a responsory ought to be sung after the evening reading: why should it not be sung in the same way after the morning reading?

As I considered this, it occurred to me that just as the hymn of Zechariah excludes the responsory after the morning reading, so the hymn of holy Mary excludes the responsory after the evening reading.

The verse would have to be discussed here, but since we begin these offices at Septuagesima, we cannot at this point say anything about the verse that we customarily say in the evening office before saying something about the Alleluia that is sung at Septuagesima.

On that same evening and during the following night, the Alleluia runs through all the offices of the cantor. We act in this way concerning the Alleluia when we store it away in its treasuries—that is, in the hearts of the elect and in the voices of the angels—just as a lover ordinarily acts toward a beloved who is about to undertake a long journey: he kisses his mouth, neck, eyes, forehead, and the rest.

Let this brief statement suffice concerning the Alleluia, which we repeat so often because we love it and because it is soon to be stored away.

We must speak of the verses used on the other Sundays at night and on the six days of the week. On Sunday nights we customarily say:

“Let my evening prayer ascend to you, O Lord, and let your mercy descend upon us.”

On the other nights we customarily say:

“Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.”

These verses have one purpose. The Sunday verse, by its words, shows that the evening prayer is being performed. Every verse ought to be such that it either recalls the condition of the office or the condition of the time, as do those sung concerning the Lord’s passion and resurrection.

The daily verse, however, in its latter words, although they are not sung, reveals the same thing by saying:

“The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.”

Because of these words the aforementioned verse, “Let my prayer be directed,” is begun, but I do not know why they are not sung. Perhaps it is because the singers dislike that they do not fit their melodies.

With this verse incense is offered, which the Lord commanded to be offered. It is written in the book of Exodus:

“You shall place the altar opposite the veil that hangs before the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat that covers the testimony, where I shall speak with you. Aaron shall burn fragrant incense upon it: in the morning, when he arranges the lamps, he shall burn it; and when he sets them in place in the evening, he shall burn the everlasting incense before the Lord,”

and so forth.

Let the high priest, who occupies Aaron’s place in the Church, attend to who ought to offer incense to the Lord upon the altar.

After this follows the hymn of holy Mary. Just as the five psalms lament that the five bodily senses have sinned, so the hymn of holy Mary chastises the thoughts that have lifted themselves up in empty boasting during the prosperity of the day, saying:

“He has scattered the proud in the mind of their heart; he has cast down the powerful from their throne.”

Up to this point, apart from the Sunday verse, we have described the condition of people who are struck by some negligence and therefore have cause to mourn. But now we must speak of those who triumph in the Lord and nevertheless offer him evening praise through the five psalms that we customarily sing on Sunday nights.

Just as Sunday night proved victorious through the Lord’s resurrection, so the psalms sung on it resound with the victory of the Lord’s elect and with his praise.

The first psalm, “Blessed be the Lord my God,” contains David’s victory over Goliath. The following psalms resound with the praise of God.

Of the second Augustine says in his exposition of the Psalms:

“I will exalt you, my God and king, and I will bless your name forever and ever. You see that the praise of God has begun; the praise itself is carried through to the end of the psalm.”

Of the third he says:

“Behold, the psalm sounds. Whose voice is it? If you wish, it is yours: the voice of one exhorting his soul to praise God and saying to himself, ‘Praise the Lord, my soul.’”

And of the fourth:

“It is said to us, ‘Praise the Lord.’ This is said to all nations, not only to us. And this voice, sounding in every place, is heard by the churches from the readers individually. Yet one voice of God above all does not cease, so that we may praise him. And as though we were asking why we ought to praise God, see what reason he gives: ‘Praise the Lord,’ he says, ‘because he is good.’”

The fifth psalm contains the praise of Jerusalem, which has been restored after its pilgrimage. Of it the same author says in the same work:

“What will you do, O Jerusalem? Labor and groaning pass away. What will you do? Will you plow? Will you sow? Will you plant anew? Will you sail? Will you conduct business? What will you do? Must you still be occupied in those works, even though they are good and come from mercy? Consider your number; consider your fellowship on every side. See whether anyone is hungry to whom you may offer bread; see whether anyone is thirsty to whom you may give a cup of cold water; see whether anyone among you is now a stranger whom you may receive in hospitality; see whether there is anyone sick whom you may visit; see whether anyone is quarrelling whom you may reconcile; see whether anyone is dying whom you may bury. What, then, will you do? Praise the Lord together, O Jerusalem.”

The lord Bede thus expounds the hymn of holy Mary in his homilies:

“Let us therefore turn over the words of the Gospel reading in frequent meditation and always retain in mind the examples of the blessed Mother of God, so that, found humble in God’s sight and submissive to our neighbors with the honor due to them, we may deserve to be exalted with her into everlasting joy. Let us carefully strive lest the favor of those who praise us improperly lift us up, when we see that she maintained an unshaken constancy of humility amid words of true praise.

“If an immoderate desire for temporal things delights us, let us remember that our Judge sends the rich away empty. If temporal affliction should trouble the mind, let us recall that he also exalts the humble. Let us never despair of obtaining forgiveness for our offenses, because his mercy extends from generation to generation for those who fear him.

“Let no one, amid the evils he has committed, be overtaken by the more serious guilt of impenitence, because God resists the proud. Separating them from the lot of the blessed, he scatters them through various places of punishment according to the variety of their sins.

“By the Lord’s generosity it comes about that, if we continually recall the deeds and words of blessed Mary, the practice of chastity and the works of virtue may continually persevere in us. For an excellent and most salutary custom has arisen in the holy Church: her hymn is sung daily by all with the psalmody of evening praise, so that through this the more frequent remembrance of the Lord’s incarnation may kindle the minds of the faithful toward devotion, and the examples of his mother, recalled again and again, may strengthen them in steadfast virtue.

“It has also pleased us that this should appropriately be done at evening, so that our mind, wearied during the day and stretched by various thoughts, may, as the time of rest approaches, gather itself together into unity of contemplation. Having been salutarily warned, it may then cleanse through the prayers and tears of the night whatever superfluous or harmful thing it has contracted through the wandering of the day.”

After this hymn, on Sunday nights, in some places the Kyrie eleison is said, as I heard at Rome, and afterward the collect; in some places only the collect follows.

Just as we omit kneeling in recalling our resurrection, so on those nights we omit the tearful prayers of the present life that we customarily utter while kneeling. As was demonstrated above from Augustine’s words, in that heavenly Jerusalem, where the resurrection is true, no prayer for miseries will be practiced in reality.

Therefore only the collect follows, which the priest customarily delivers while standing on Sunday nights, in remembrance of the future resurrection. Since we are in the present age, it is necessary for us to be fortified by the prayers of holy priests. And because in a certain way we recall the feast of the citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, we ought to celebrate it with greater joy and security than when we celebrate our pilgrimage.

Since at Septuagesima we began this institution [or precaution], we wish to append the words of Saint Augustine on Septuagesima, which he gives in his exposition of the psalm, “Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem”:

“After the seventy years, then, when Jeremiah prophesied that the city of Jerusalem would be restored, and when this came to pass so that an image of future things might be signified there, it was signified to us that after all this revolving of time, which turns according to the number seven, our future city will exist in eternity in a single day. For in that dwelling time does not revolve, because it does not slip away from its inhabitants.”

From the words of blessed Augustine we are taught that Septuagesima signifies the present time, which revolves according to the number seven, while the Easter days that follow Septuagesima signify the future homeland.

# CHAPTER VIII  
## On Compline

Compline is so called because in it the daily use of food or drink, which is necessarily taken for the support of the body, or ordinary conversation, is completed. Hence among monks there is also the practice, derived from the Rule of Saint Benedict, of fortifying the enclosure of the mouth through this office and making the monks abstain from common conversation until they return again to their tasks.

For this part of the night can rightly be called the “time of silence,” in which everything falls silent. Among those who divide the night into seven parts, the first part is called twilight, the second evening, and the third the time of silence, which we are now discussing. I think it can be called this because everything becomes silent during it.

In this office four psalms are recalled up to the verse. In the four psalms we commend the four elements of our body to the Lord. The verse makes this clear, saying:

“Keep me, O Lord, as the apple of your eye; protect me under the shadow of your wings.”

Everyone who has even a little understanding recognizes how many more dangers can assail a person externally while sleeping than while awake.

In a certain way this office is suited to the commendation by which a person commends himself to God when he passes from the world. Sleep is an image of death. For just as the mind of a dead person is separated from mortal things and the miseries of this world are consigned to oblivion, so in a certain way the spirit of one who sleeps is separated from its customary thoughts and from every temporal duty.

Augustine shows this in one verse of the first psalm, which is sung at compline:

“In peace, in the same place, I will sleep and rest.”

It is rightly hoped by such people that the mind will be wholly separated from mortal things and that the miseries of this world will be forgotten—something that is fittingly and prophetically signified by the terms “falling asleep” and “sleep.” There the highest peace can be interrupted by no disturbance. But this is not yet possessed in this life; it must be hoped for after this life.

The second psalm continues up to the verse in which Christ gave up his spirit on the cross. In it we desire to be conformed to his sleep—that is, so that the limbs may rest while the heart keeps watch.

The third psalm, “He who dwells in the shelter,” is full of words of prayer that implore the Lord’s protection. According to Roman usage, it is also sung on Good Friday after the reading in which, according to Hosea, our mortification is shown in imitation of Christ, together with the resurrection after two days.

Through this psalm the composer of the office admonishes us that in all dangers and tribulations, according to its words, our mind should be intent on beseeching God. And because our sleep bears some likeness to the sleep of those who, under the Lord’s protection, have passed from the present age, the same [Col. 1184D] psalm is sung at our compline.

The fourth psalm likewise recalls in some way the intention of those who are in tribulation and yet pass from tribulation into peace, saying:

“In the nights lift up your hands in the holy place.”

Hence Augustine says in his exposition of the same psalm:

“Night is a sorrowful thing; day is a joyful thing.”

And shortly afterward:

“Bless the Lord, then. When? In the nights. When did Job bless him, when the night was sorrowful? Everything he possessed was taken away; his children, whom he had preserved, were taken away. How sorrowful a night! But let us see whether he did not bless him in the nights: ‘The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has happened. Blessed be the name of the Lord.’”

The verse that follows, as we have stated, displays the entire work of the office—that is, the petition for the Lord’s protection amid the dangers of the night.

The peace desired by the soul of the one praying is shown by the hymn that follows, the hymn of holy Simeon: namely, that it may rest from every disturbance of this world. Simeon prayed for this when he desired to pass from this life to the other life and said:

“Now dismiss your servant, O Lord, according to your word, in peace.”

From this hymn we are clearly taught that in the present commendation we are conformed to those who have died in the Lord. Therefore after this commendation it is not appropriate to drink or eat, or to do anything of the sort that does not pertain to the rest of the limbs and to withdrawal into the body's state of repose.

And because thereafter there is no suitable conversation of people speaking with one another, nor discussion—which is necessary after the reading, when the eyelids are becoming heavy and the eyes draw sleep—reading ceases.

That time signifies what is written:

“They shall all be taught by God,”

and what the Apostle says:

“Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed.”

And because, according to the order of Ezra, a reading is necessary in this office, so that there may be reading four times during the night, devout men customarily read a lesson before the present office.

Just as Mary, who anointed the Lord with ointment, anticipated doing what was to be done at his tomb if his body were found, so a reading, through its instruction, anoints devout souls before the commendation of sleep.

# CHAPTER IX  
## On the Nocturnal Office

[Col. 1185C] In the nocturnal office we first say:

“O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.”

Then follows the Gloria.

When earlier we had gathered during the night, we commended ourselves to the Lord, closed our mouths, and afterward each of us in a certain way rested alone in his own tomb, standing in mind before the Lord alone, for whom words are not necessary because he knows all thoughts.

But now, because we have gathered again to confess the Lord, we ask him to open our lips by his direction and to cause our mouth to open for his praise.

Then follows the invitatory. In it the common assembly of the brothers calls together all who dwell everywhere, so that they may be roused and come to confess the Lord, as the second verse of the invitatory sounds:

“Let us anticipate his presence, you will say, in confession, and let us sing joyfully to him in psalms.”

Then follow twelve psalms, without an antiphon, with three glorifications of the Holy Trinity, arranged in three divisions of four psalms each.

Sunday night recalls the Lord’s resurrection to our memory. It is called Sunday because the Lord glorified it by his resurrection. For he did not rise from the dead alone, but all his elect also rose—whether those who existed from the beginning of the world before his incarnation, or those who will exist until the end of the world.

Therefore the Apostle Paul says:

“He was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Because in his resurrection he wished to signify the resurrection of all the elect, he therefore said, “by the resurrection of the dead.”

We recall the resurrection of all these on Sunday nights.

The condition of our Church is distinguished by three stages: under the natural law, under the Mosaic law, and under the law of evangelical grace. Although many saints existed under the natural law, the twelve patriarchs flourished above all, so much so that twelve tribes were later descended from them.

Just as in the New Testament the Christian people were propagated from the twelve apostles, so in the Old Testament the people specially belonging to God came from the twelve patriarchs.

These twelve psalms recall the first year of the visitation of the vineyard, in which the useless fig tree stood. So that we may not be useless, we recall the twelve psalms in imitation of the honorable conduct of the holy patriarchs.

We sing them divided according to the number four, because there are four virtues by which we believe the holy patriarchs worshiped the Holy Trinity: prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance. These virtues are not separated from one another. Wherever one of them is present, the other three must always be present.

Hence Augustine says in his letter to Jerome:

“Moreover, if prudence exists only when it is also brave, just, and temperate, then surely wherever it is present it has the others with it. Likewise, fortitude cannot be imprudent, intemperate, or unjust. Likewise, temperance must be prudent, brave, and just. Likewise, justice does not exist unless it is prudent, brave, and temperate, so that wherever one of them is truly present, the others are likewise present; but where the others are absent, that one is not true, even if in some way it may appear similar to them +.”

The following three psalms, with an antiphon, recall the second year, in which the Lord visited his vineyard through the law, while the useless fig tree still remained.

So that we may not be useless, we sing three psalms in order to share in the company of the three classes of elect who existed under the Mosaic law: namely, lawgivers, psalmists, and prophets.

This is the distinction between the twelve psalms sung without an antiphon and the three sung with an antiphon: it is the distinction between the twelve patriarchs, who were pilgrims and hoped for the inheritance that their descendants later possessed, and those same descendants who inherited the land promised to their fathers.

[Col. 1186D] The twelve patriarchs gloried in the promises, but their descendants gloried more in what they had received. The three final psalms, with the Alleluia, recall the third year in the New Testament, while the barren fig tree remains barren and the grace of the Gospel already shines forth. We praise the Lord in the primitive Church from the Jewish people; in the next age we praise him from the Gentiles; and likewise at the restoration of the Jewish people, so that our fig tree may bear fruit—that is, our people, whom by the examples of the holy Fathers we cultivate through words and conduct. The difference between those three psalms sung with antiphons and these three sung with the Alleluia is the difference between those who had a testament destined to be changed and those who have a testament that is not to be changed. Greater clarification is found in the New Testament than in the Old.

[Col. 1187A] We celebrate the resurrection of all these in our Sunday observance, and believe that we shall become participants in it. Gregory says in his homily that the three stages of the aforementioned periods are signified by the three years during which the Lord sought fruit from the fig tree and found none.

When we remember those who have departed from the world, we dig a trench around the fig tree, because we humble ourselves down to the dust of death; and we add manure when we recall our sins. Here it must be explained what difference there is between the arrangement of the present readings and that of those readings administered by the pastors to their own people. The readings sung by the pastors admonish the members of the household and those who are knowledgeable not to fail. [Col. 1187B] Just as wood is added to wood on the hearth so that the fire may not die out, so fiery words spoken by the pastors are added to the fiery understanding of the members of the household, so that they may not fail. The readings in the nocturnal office represent the readings that used to take place in the schools of the Fathers, where the unlearned were instructed and were permitted to ask about matters concerning which they were uncertain.

We have presented examples of these in the little book *On the Office of the Mass*, and here we offer one. It is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

> Now these were nobler than those in Thessalonica, for they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.

The very uncertainty that exists in the minds of hearers before they arrive at full understanding [Col. 1187C] is signified by the arrangement of the night. There is one variation concerning the verse: in this office it occurs in a different order from that in the other offices. In the other offices the verse follows the reading; in this one it precedes it. The purpose of the verse is to show the whole intention that the choir maintains in its office. Since the end contains the future outcome, whether evil or good, the verse is appropriately placed after the office has been completed and before the special prayer. In this office, however, because one sits for the reading after the psalms, the verse precedes the reading. No one doubts that sitting is some rest for the weary, and almost a foretaste of leisure. Therefore, because God does not despise the prayers of the afflicted, it was established that the prayer should immediately follow the bodily affliction, in the form of the verse.

The nine readings unite us with the life of the nine orders [Col. 1187D] of angels. The nine responsories unite us with the joys of those same nine orders of angels. And since we must pray before we reach their company, the verse of the choir’s common prayer is celebrated before the reading.

The first verse says, “I remembered your name in the night,” and so forth; the words themselves show why we have risen from our condition. The second verse says, “At midnight I arose.” This shows at what hour of the night one ought to rise. But because we are negligent about the time at which our fathers were accustomed to rise, we do not dare to lie; we change this verse and say another: “For you enlighten my lamp.” The third verse says, “Be exalted, O Lord.” This clearly recalls the New Testament [Col. 1188A], in which Christ exalted the humanity he had assumed to the heavens through his power.

Since we have said that one ought to rise at midnight in the nocturnal office, we must confirm our statement from the words of Saint Augustine and Jerome. David says in the psalm “Blessed are the undefiled” at what time he himself was accustomed to rise to give thanks to the Lord: “At midnight I arose.” And elsewhere: “I rose before dawn and cried out.” Augustine renders this: “I rose before the dead of night and cried out.” Many codices do not have “in the dead of night,” but “before dawn”; scarcely one has been found that doubles the preposition, namely, “before the dawn.”

“Before dawn,” therefore, here means the nocturnal time that is not yet mature—that is, not yet opportune—for doing anything while keeping vigil. In common speech it is also called an inconvenient hour. “The dead of night,” that is, midnight, is likewise the time when one ought to rest. It was undoubtedly so called because it is inconvenient for the activities of those who keep vigil. The ancients called what was opportune *tempestivum* and what was inconvenient *intempestivum*, deriving the words from *tempus*, “time,” not from that *tempestas* which in Latin usage now means a disturbance of the sky. Historians nevertheless readily use this word when they say “at that time,” meaning that what they wish to be understood is “at that time.”

Thus Jerome too writes in his book *The Life of Paula*:

> After the Alleluia had been sung, by which sign they were summoned to the assembly, no one was permitted to remain seated. The first to arrive, or one of the first, covered for the others, encouraging them to undertake the work by modesty and example, not by fear. In the morning, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, in the evening, and at midnight, they sang the psalter in order.

Likewise, in his letter to the virgin Demetrias:

> Now I shall speak only to the virgin—that is, considering only those things that are not outside you but within you. Besides the order of the psalms and prayer, which you must always perform at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, at evening, at midnight, and in the morning, determine how many hours you ought to devote to learning Holy Scripture and how much time to reading—not as a burden, but for the delight and instruction of the soul.
