When you have completed these periods, and the concern of your soul has frequently roused you to bend your knees, keep wool always in your hands: draw out the threads with your thumb from the warp, or let the spindles turn in their bowls to twist the weft; gather the spun threads into a ball or arrange them for weaving, and so forth.

[Col. 1188D] Again, in his letter to another woman concerning the education of her daughter:

> Let an elderly virgin of proven faith, morals, and chastity be placed over her; let her teach her and accustom her by example to rise at night for prayers and psalms, to sing hymns in the morning, and at the third, sixth, and ninth hours to stand in battle array like a warrior of Christ, and, having kindled her lamp, to offer the evening sacrifice. Let the day pass in this way; let the night find her laboring. Let prayer follow reading, and reading follow prayer.

These examples are sufficient for us to demonstrate at what hour one ought to rise in the nocturnal office. Here, too, let the three watches of the vigils come to an end—watches divided and observed in three-hour periods. At the fourth watch, when Lucifer has already risen, having shaken off the torpor of our weariness, let us soberly and vigorously await [Col. 1189A] the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who by his resurrection made us joyful and gave us the pattern of our own resurrection. The fathers longed for that resurrection, but it has been fulfilled in us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. We recall those ends in the morning office until the resurrection of our bodies.

## CHAPTER X. On the Morning Office

The morning office brings before our minds the period of the New Testament, that is, from the beginning of baptism to the full reward that God promised with an oath to Abraham and his descendants forever. For at that time, namely in the morning, the children of Israel were baptized in the Red Sea, as Exodus relates:

> It happened, he says, during the morning watch; and behold, the Lord, looking upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud, killed their army, overturned the wheels of their chariots, and so forth.

When these men were killed, the children of Israel were baptized. What the morning watch is, Bede shows in his treatise on Mark, where he discusses the fourth watch of the night:

> And around the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking upon the sea.

Military watches and guard-posts are divided into three-hour periods. When, therefore, he says that the Lord came to them during the fourth watch of the night, he shows that they had been in danger throughout the whole night and that help was provided for them at the end of the night. A little later he says:

> But when any righteous person has raised his mind toward the light of heavenly protection and the gifts of eternal recompense, he sees, as though Lucifer had suddenly risen amid the shadows of night [Col. 1189C], the one who announces the coming day. For Lucifer is said very often to illuminate three hours of the night, that is, the entire morning watch. And the Lord will be present, granting, once the dangers of temptation have been put to rest, the full confidence of freedom through his protection.

This period, that is, baptism, was prefigured in Noah’s ark, in which a few—that is, eight souls—were saved. The apostle Peter teaches that this preceded us as a type of our baptism, saying:

> In which a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water; and now baptism, in the likeness of this figure, saves us also, and so forth. +

Just as there were eight souls in the ark then, so we can find eight orders of the elect in the period of baptism. The first order is the primitive Church existing among the Jewish people; the second is that same primitive Church entering among the Gentiles; the third is the believing Gentiles; the fourth is the repentant Jewish people; the fifth consists of those who will exist in the time of Antichrist; the sixth, seventh, and eighth consist of those who will universally be gathered from Asia, Europe, and Africa, and who will enjoy a greater peace than the Church now enjoys.

Hence Gregory says:

> That net is then filled universally, when, at the end of the world, the totality of the human race is brought to completion.

The first psalm displays the primitive Church, which was reformed and built up by Christ’s preaching, with him already reigning, as he himself says: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” The first and second verses make this clear: “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty; the Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself.” The first shows Christ reigning; the second, the building up of his members, saying: “For he established the world, and it shall not be moved.”

What this psalm contains we learn from the words of Saint Augustine in his exposition of its title. He begins as follows:

> In the title we are, as it were, warned at the threshold what we should seek inside. It is therefore inscribed in this way: “A praise-song, by David, on the day before the Sabbath, when the earth was founded.”

And a little later:

> When all who believe throughout the whole earth are immovable in faith, the earth has been founded. Then the human being is made in the image of God; this is signified by that sixth day in Genesis. But how did God make him? How was the earth founded? Christ came to found the earth. For no one can lay another foundation than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus. +

Upon this foundation the apostolic Church was first founded. It came to the other nations, announcing to them Christ’s advent and commanding them to rejoice in him and serve him. Hence the same author, mentioned above, says in his exposition of Psalm 99:

> “Rejoice, then, to the Lord, all the earth.” Does the whole earth hear my voice now? And yet the whole earth has heard this voice: “The whole earth already rejoices to the Lord,” and what does not yet rejoice will rejoice. For the blessing, beginning from Jerusalem, extends through all nations, and so forth.

From these words we perceive our calling in the second psalm through the preaching of the apostles; and in the third we offer our goodwill to the apostles’ calling and say: “O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the light. My soul has thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh has thirsted for you.”

The title of the psalm shows that the present psalm is sung in the person of the Gentiles. The psalm itself has this title: “By David, when he was in the desert of Idumaea.” Augustine explains it in this way in his exposition of the same psalm:

> By the name Idumaea this present age is understood. For Idumaea was a certain nation of wandering people, where idols were worshiped.

Noah’s ark, which contained eight souls, had two chambers. Concerning this, the same author mentioned above writes in the fifteenth book of *The City of God*:

> It is certainly possible that someone may explain these matters more suitably for us, and another in another way, provided that everything said is referred to this city of God, of which we are speaking, journeying in this wicked age as in a flood; provided that the one who explains them does not wish to depart far from the intention of the one who wrote them.

For example, if someone were to understand what is written here—“you shall make it with lower chambers, two-chambered and three-chambered”—in a way different from what I said in that work, namely that the Church is gathered from all nations: that it is called “two-chambered” because of the two kinds of human beings, circumcision and uncircumcision, whom the Apostle also calls Jews and Greeks, and so forth.

Because it will happen before the persecution of Antichrist that the people from uncircumcision and circumcision will become one in faith, two psalms are contained in the third order under a single antiphon. [Col. 1191A] The things contained in the psalm “May God have mercy on us” designate both peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile peoples.

After these have been joined together, the tribulation of Antichrist will come. Nabuchodonosor preceded it as a figure, and he will cast the three sons of Noah, as it were three young men, into the furnace of tribulation. God not only delivered them from his wickedness because they were elect, but they will also bless the Lord in the likeness of the three young men. Therefore, whereas in the other psalms we are accustomed to say “Alleluia,” in this blessing we use Latin words, in order to commend the tribulation that the saints will suffer in the days of the aforementioned Antichrist—or that they now suffer from his members. It is not necessary there to sing “Glory to the Father and to the Son,” because in the blessing itself we commemorate the same Holy Trinity, saying: “Let us bless God the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit.”

We have said concerning “Glory to the Father” that the blessed Jerome wrote of its use to Pope Damasus. After this, according to Daniel, there will be a certain period of rest, for he says:

> Blessed is the one who waits and reaches the days of one thousand three hundred and thirty-five.

The blessed Jerome explains this as follows:

> Blessed, he says, is the one who, after Antichrist has been killed, waits beyond the one thousand two hundred and ninety days—that is, three and a half years—for forty-five days, during which the Lord and Savior will come in his majesty.

In that period of rest, the praise of God contained in three psalms will be celebrated: “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” “Sing to the Lord a new song,” and “Praise the Lord in his sanctuary,” by the whole human race [Col. 1191C] that escapes the tribulation. This human race was propagated from the three sons of Noah.

Hence Augustine writes in the aforementioned fifteenth book of *The City of God*:

> The ark was three-chambered because all nations were restored after the flood from the three sons of Noah.

Or it may be understood in another way, as the same Augustine writes in the forty-seventh question of his *Questions on the Gospels*. He says:

> I think that those three kinds that are taken up are also represented by the three names of holy men whom the prophet Ezekiel foretells as the only ones to be delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job. Noah seems to pertain to those through whom the Church is governed, just as the ark was guided through the waters by him, and the ark bore the figure of the Church. Daniel, because he chose a celibate life—that is, because he despised earthly marriage—in order, as the Apostle says, to live without anxiety, thinking about the things of God, signifies the class of those who are at leisure, yet exceedingly strong in temptations, so that they may be taken up. Job, because he had a wife, children, and abundant possessions of earthly things, belongs to the class to which the millstone has been assigned; nevertheless, they too must be exceedingly strong in temptations, as he was. Otherwise they cannot be taken up. Nor do I think that there are any other classes of human beings of which the Church consists than these three.

Because these are to share and possess together the one virtue, namely patience, three psalms are sung under a single antiphon or Alleluia, inviting us to their fellowship. Then follows the reading, which is recited in the choir as a fraternal admonition; it will always be pleasing so long as the Church dwells in the present age.

Afterward follows a verse suited to that time, for it says: “The Lord has reigned,” and so forth. Then what the Apostle says will take place: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father.” When he hands the kingdom over to God, he joins it to his own eternal kingdom—to himself, who is God.

The hymn of the prophet Zechariah recalls the reward promised to Abraham: that we should serve the Lord without fear, in holiness and righteousness, all our days. Such service is now found among the few who are already perfect; but then it will be celebrated by all the elect, because all will be perfect.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Nocturnal Office for Each Night

[Col. 1192B] The Sunday night recalls the citizens of Jerusalem from the beginning of the world to its end; the nights of the ordinary days recall the pilgrimage of mortals and their estrangement from their homeland while dwelling among enemies. And because there are twelve hours in the night, during which we need to be fortified by the Lord’s protection, we sing twelve psalms. Because this watchfulness is serious throughout the six ages of the world, we join the psalms with six antiphons. And because the six ages of the world are brought to completion in three periods—namely, the period of the natural law, of the written law, and of the law of grace—three readings are read and three responsories are sung.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Morning Office for Each Night

On Sunday nights, by means of five antiphons, we recall the condition of the Church from the beginning of its apostolic establishment to the perfection of the elect who will come at the end of the world. On ordinary nights, however, we recall the same condition in another way, through the changing of the psalms and canticles from Monday through Saturday.

The first psalm, “Have mercy on me, O God,” contains the conversion of penitents. The converted Jews, who are assigned to the primitive Church, frequently employed the power of this psalm when they repented at Peter’s preaching and were pierced in heart. Concerning them it is written in the Acts of the Apostles:

> When they heard these things, they were pierced in heart and said to Peter and the other apostles, “What shall we do, brothers?” But Peter said to them, “Repent,” he said, “and let each one of you be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.”

In a similar way, on the following nights the same psalm calls us who have been converted from a Gentile way of life to repentance. Enough has been said about the present psalm. Concerning the others—“O God, my God, to you I keep vigil from the light,” “May God have mercy on us,” “Praise the Lord from the heavens,” “Sing to the Lord,” and “Praise the Lord in his sanctuary”—we have already spoken. It remains to return to Monday and proceed through the changing of the psalms and canticles.

First, we must observe that just as the psalm and the canticle are assigned to one night in the office, so in their subject matter and meanings they are alike. The psalm “Give ear to my words” has this title: “For the one who receives the inheritance.” Augustine explains it as follows:

[Col. 1193A]

> The Church is therefore understood, for it has received the inheritance, eternal life through our Lord Jesus Christ, so that it may possess God himself. Clinging to him, it is blessed, in accordance with the saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance.”

The primitive Church received this inheritance, living in the present age together with the apostles. The canticle of the prophet Isaiah is sung in its person:

> I will confess to you, O Lord, because you were angry with me; your anger has turned away, and you have comforted me, and so forth.

This canticle recalls the time when the first standard of the holy Cross was raised. Hence earlier in the same prophet it is written:

> And he will raise a sign among the nations, and he will gather the scattered of Israel, and so forth.

Jerome explains this in the same work:

> “On that day”—that is, at that time, of which the preceding passage also spoke, when the root of Jesse rises as a sign for the peoples, or to rule the nations—“the Lord will again extend his hand,” so that, contrary to those Judaizers among us, Israel may not be saved only at the end of the world when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, but we should understand all these things as referring to the first coming.

And a little later:

> He will therefore raise the sign of the cross among all the nations, and he will first gather the people of Israel from the synagogues of the Jews, so that the apostles might fulfill the Savior’s command, when he said: “Go to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.”

In the continuation of the same book he shows what the canticle concerns, saying:

> You who had previously said in the wilderness, when you came up from the land of Egypt and the Red Sea was dried up, “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously magnified”: now, when the tongue of the Egyptian sea has been struck, its river dried up, cut through, and humbled, glorify the Lord and say: “I will confess to you, O Lord, because I deserved anger and fury. I have obtained your mercy. For you are my Savior”—that is, Jesus. I will no longer trust in idols, nor fear what ought not to be feared; you are my strength and my praise.

The difference between the psalm and the canticle is the difference between the works of the righteous person and thanksgiving: the psalm displays the works of the righteous person after conversion, as in the present psalm: “For to you I shall pray, O Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice. In the morning I shall stand before you and see,” and so forth; the canticle gives praise to God for the same work.

The verse after the reading on ordinary nights recalls the time when the reward will be repaid by the Lord to the righteous after the labor of the present age. The verse says: “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy,” and so forth. Augustine explains it in his exposition of the same psalm from which it is taken:

[Col. 1193D]

> Then, anticipating by hope those good things that are to come and counting them as though they had already happened, he says: “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy.” Thus, amid these nocturnal labors and pains, prophecy has been kindled for us like a lamp in a dark place, until the day dawns and Lucifer rises in our hearts. For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Then the righteous will be filled with that good which they now hunger and thirst for, while walking by faith and journeying away from the Lord. Hence it is also said: “You will fill me with joy at your countenance”; “in the morning they will stand and contemplate.”

And, as other interpreters have said: “We have been satisfied in the morning with your mercy.” Then they will be satisfied, just as he says elsewhere: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.” Hence it is said: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” And the Lord himself says: “I will show myself to him.” Until this happens, nothing good is sufficient for us, nor should it be sufficient, lest our desire remain on the way.

And a little later:

> We have been filled in the morning with your mercy, and we have exulted and rejoiced [been glad] in all our days. That day is a day without end; all those days are together. +

What follows on ordinary nights after the hymn of Zechariah, which introduces us after the resurrection of our bodies into eternal life, is indicated by the customary prayer: sinners hope through repentance for all those good things.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Tuesday

Tuesday recalls the time when the Church was persecuted by wicked emperors who tried to take away the apostles’ gain, so that they would not generate spiritual children. That period extended especially from Nero’s first persecution to the time of Diocletian and Maximian. The psalm shows which saints suffered at that time, saying: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation,” and so forth.

The verses that follow demonstrate no less the sadness that the holy Church had because it was openly permitted to generate Christ in the hearts of the elect. The holy Church escaped from this tribulation and sings the canticle that Hezekiah sang after he had been delivered from Sennacherib and after God had visited him with the scourge of illness, lest his heart be lifted up because of the victory granted to him. Hence he also says:

> The living, the living will confess to you, as I do today; the father will make your truth known to his children.

For he too wept because he grieved over the loss of his children.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Wednesday

Wednesday recalls the time when the holy Church was exalted above all its enemies. We can learn this from the title of the psalm sung on that day. Its title is:

> To the end: a psalm of David; a song of Jeremiah and Ezekiel from the people of the captivity, when they began to depart.

This psalm is sung in the person of those who look toward the return to Jerusalem and the liberty of God’s people. Just as the Jews were once freed from Babylonia and led to Jerusalem, so our Church was freed from the hand of the wicked emperors and granted liberty in the time of the emperor Constantine.

Therefore it exults in the canticle that Hannah, the mother of Samuel, sang after she had been delivered from the affliction caused by her rival Peninnah:

> My heart has exulted in the Lord, and my heart has been exalted in my God.

From that time, after the Roman state and power had been subjected to apostolic men and Christian emperors, the mouth of the Church was widened over its enemies, namely pagans and faithless Jews. This widening continues to the present day. May God grant that it continue for a long time and that what the Apostle says may be fulfilled:

> Until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, and so all Israel will be saved.

## CHAPTER XV. On Thursday

This stage receives the Jewish people and the Gentile people under one rod, that is, under one rule. Because the Jewish people are to be received in this stage, the psalm sung on Thursday is said to be from the prayer of Moses. Its title is:

> A prayer of Moses, the man of God.

The canticle follows:

> Let us sing to the Lord.

They sang this song long ago as a figure of the future victory that they will receive when what the Lord said in the Gospel is fulfilled:

> From now on you will not see me until you say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.”

## CHAPTER XVI. On Friday

Friday is celebrated in memory of the Passion of our Savior. The psalm sung on that day has this title:

> By David himself, when his son was persecuting him.

Augustine speaks of this title in the prologue to the same psalm:

> Let us therefore recognize how Christ was persecuted by his son. For he had sons concerning whom he said: “The sons of the bridegroom do not fast as long as the bridegroom is with them; but when the bridegroom has been taken away, then the sons of the bridegroom will fast.” Therefore the apostles are the sons of the bridegroom, and among them the persecutor Judas is the devil.

Thus Christ is about to proclaim his Passion in this psalm. The canticle likewise sounds forth his Passion, saying:

> He has horns in his hands; there his strength is hidden.

Jerome explains this as follows:

> The standards and trophies of the cross—and in those horns his strength is hidden. And a little later: On the cross, therefore, his strength was hidden for a short time, when he said to the Father, “My soul is sorrowful unto death,” and “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”; and on the cross, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.”

This is the fifth night after Monday. Just as on the fifth psalm on Sunday nights the contempt of Nabuchodonosor and the victory of the three young men are celebrated, among whom there was a fourth figure resembling the Son of Man, so now, in the fifth place, the contempt of the whole world and the victory of that supreme and only triumphant one are celebrated, whose appearance was once seen among the three young men. His Passion is rightly commemorated above all on Friday, because it was accomplished on that day.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Saturday
Sabbath recalls the memory of the elect among the Jews, who will be joined to the Church at the end of the world. The Sabbath which carnal Jews pretended, and still pretend, to observe, faithful Jews will keep in truth at the end. The psalm sung on it bears this title: “A psalm of a song for the Sabbath day.” From the psalm’s title, the psalm is appropriately assigned to the Sabbath [Col. 1196A]. How it corresponds to the Jewish people is demonstrated by a certain verse, which says: “Upon a ten-stringed psaltery, with song and harp.” Augustine explains this in the following way:

“You have now heard of the ten-stringed psaltery. The ten-stringed psaltery signifies the ten commandments of the Law. But one must sing upon it, not merely carry the psaltery; for the Jews also have the Law: they carry it, but do not sing. Who are those who sing? Those who practice it. Those who practice it with sadness do not yet sing. Who are those who sing? Those who do good with cheerfulness,” and so forth.

We believe that this will occur among the Jewish people when that people becomes one with the holy Church—what blessed Augustine now relates concerning the holy Church.

The song that follows, “Hear, O heavens,” shows how it suits the Sabbath and the Jewish people [Col. 1196B]. The lord Bede explains this in the second book of his treatise on Luke:

“They used to gather in the synagogues on the Sabbath, so that, in accordance with the Lord’s command, ‘Be still and know that I am God,’ they might withdraw from worldly business and sit with a quiet heart to meditate on the precepts of the Law. The indication that this observance is to be carried out daily has continued in the Church up to the present, because in certain places it has been customary to recite on the Sabbath the song of Deuteronomy, in which the condition of the entire ancient people is contained—namely, what they deserved from an offended God and what from a propitious one. Otherwise it would be out of order for the songs composed from the words of the prophets to be sung on the earlier days of the week, and Moses’ final song afterward.”

It is useful for the work of this composition if we consider, from the meanings and understanding of the psalms of the Lord’s night office at Matins [Col. 1196C], how the psalms and songs assigned to the six days of the week are linked together. The first psalm, “The Lord reigns,” demonstrates the Lord’s reign after his resurrection, concerning which he himself says: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.” Conversely, “Have mercy on me, O God” concerns the repentance of a dead man because of sin, but also of one reviving through the good fragrance that he received from the messengers of God’s words. For Christ came to die and rise from the dead on behalf of this man, as he himself makes clear in the Gospel, saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners,” and again: “For I have come to save what was lost.” To put it more plainly, he rose so that we might rise: his resurrection occurred through an immortal body [Col. 1196D], whereas ours occurs through repentance. Therefore, just as “The Lord reigns” is sung on Sundays and feast nights as the counterpart of his resurrection, so it is fitting that “Have mercy on me, O God” be sung on the following nights as the counterpart of our resurrection.

Because the aforementioned psalm, “The Lord reigns,” contains two things—the reign of Christ received through the triumph of the cross, and the establishment of the holy Church, which is not to be moved from its position—the psalm for Monday, and the song associated with it, that is, the psalm “The Lord reigns,” are attached because of the building of the Church.

The psalm “Give ear to my words” contains the voice of the Church, which at the beginning was joined to the apostles. Augustine says of it in the fifth psalm: “The voice of the Church is in this psalm, + called to the inheritance of the Lord: ‘Give ear to my words, O Lord.’” The one called upon invokes the Lord, so that, with his help, she may pass through the wickedness of this age and her song may reach him [Col. 1197A].

“Let me give thanks to you, O Lord,” as was demonstrated above, likewise represents the same Church.

The psalm “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth” contains the choir of preachers who, fearing none of the threats of rulers, roused the Church from Babylon to serve the Lord alone. What that same choir suffered from the citizens of the Babylonian city is clarified by the psalm “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.”

The song does not conceal the distress of King Hezekiah, who said: “I said, in the middle of my days I shall go to the gates of hell,” and the rest that follows. Hezekiah, the good and just king, is counted among the body of preachers [Col. 1197B]. The present song sufficiently indicates the distress of the present Church; concerning this distress the verse says: “I shall recall all my years in the bitterness of my soul.”

The psalm “O God, my God” contains the voice of the gentile people, which awakens from the sleep of the soul after the illumination brought by the preachers. What sleep it is from which it awakens when it says, “O God, my God, to you I keep watch at dawn,” is clarified by the aforementioned Augustine in his exposition of the same psalm:

“But we must take care lest our soul itself should sleep. The sleep of the soul is bad; the sleep of the body is good, for by it the body’s health is restored. The sleep of the soul is to forget its God. Whatever soul has forgotten its God is asleep.”

And below:

“O God, my God, to you I keep watch at dawn; my soul thirsted for you [Col. 1197C]. Behold that wilderness of Idumea: see how it thirsts here.”

And shortly afterward:

“When the soul thirsts, it thirsts for the fountain of wisdom.”

From that fountain of wisdom our souls will be filled, as another psalm says: “They shall be filled with the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your delights.” Wisdom, therefore, must be thirsted for; righteousness must be thirsted for.

The psalm for Wednesday sings of the same return—from forgetfulness of God to remembrance of him, as though from Babylon to Jerusalem. In that same psalm a thirst similar to that in the psalm “O God, my God” is mentioned. This psalm begins: “Water its furrows; multiply its offspring.” Hence the same author as above, in his exposition of the psalm “Praise is fitting for you, O God,” says:

“We see, they believe; and from those who believe, others believe; and from those, still others believe. It is not enough for one person merely to become faithful and win one person [Col. 1197D].”

The song “My heart exulted in the Lord” clearly shows that the holy Church is above Babylon.

The psalm “May God have mercy on us,” in which the Jewish people are gathered through the voices of the preachers saying, “Let the peoples give thanks to you, O God,” corresponds to the psalm for Thursday, “Lord, you have become our refuge,” which bears the title “A prayer of Moses, the man of God.” The song “Let us sing to the Lord” appropriately answers it.

The hymn of the three boys, “Bless the Lord,” brings the Lord’s Passion and his triumph back to our remembrance. Nebuchadnezzar signifies the devil; his ministers, who kindled the flame of the fire in the furnace, were the Jews crying, “Crucify, crucify!” The three boys were thrown into the furnace of fire [Col. 1198A], for it was destined that Christ should endure the fury of the Jews’ burning rage.

There were three boys who confessed the Lord with one voice. Three pure sacraments came forth from the man Christ in his Passion—spirit, water, and blood—which together reveal one Christ. The appearance of a fourth was in the furnace, “like the likeness of the Son of God.” For the body of Christ, assumed from the Virgin Mary, was hanging or being buried. The bodies of the boys were not corrupted in the furnace; it was destined that Christ’s body would not be corrupted by the decay of death. The three boys were delivered from the furnace; Christ was delivered from the lion’s mouth.

For this sacrament, as I believe, I heard “Bless the Lord” sung during the Easter vigil in the Church of Tours, after the readings. All who wish to live piously suffer persecution [Col. 1198B] and belong to the body of the three boys who were thrown into the furnace; Christ is the head of that body. Those who inflict persecutions belong to the body of the devil, of which Nebuchadnezzar was a member, as are all persecutors up to the greatest member, Antichrist.

And rightly, in the fifth order, the escape of the elect from their persecutors is recalled, because they can kill the body, which is governed by the five senses; but beyond that they have no power.

The psalm for Friday, as we have stated, and the song retain the Passion of Christ.

“Praise the Lord from the heavens,” “Sing to the Lord,” and “Praise the Lord in his holy places” show the activity of the holy Church after the persecution has been completed. This is contained in the verse: “It is good to give thanks to the Lord and to sing psalms to your name, O Most High” [Col. 1198C].

The song “Hear, O heavens, what I speak,” although it contains two things—namely, the Lord’s reward for good deeds and his recompense for offenses—is nevertheless directed, because of the Sabbath rest on which it is sung, toward those who enjoy good peace after persecution in our Church. Concerning them the verse says: “But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the cord of his inheritance.”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Sunday Nights at Matins from Septuagesima to Easter

On the Sunday nights from Septuagesima to the Lord’s Pasch, two psalms are changed at Matins: “Have mercy on me, O God” and “Give thanks to the Lord.” Through these two psalms those who are not yet perfect are instructed [Col. 1198D]—even in the degree to which human beings can be perfect here. Paul spoke of them: “Let all who are perfect think this way.” It is not appropriate for preceptors and teachers to remove from them either fear or hope.

The psalm “Have mercy on me, O God,” which echoes the voice of the repentant sinner, impresses upon us sinners the fear that we ought to have in our present pilgrimage concerning God’s vengeance. Let us mourn our sins in the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God.” After mourning, love will come—the love that through the Spirit, who consoles the hearts of mourners, casts out fear.

And therefore, because after anguish of heart and the condemnation of guilt love usually provides confidence to approach the Lord, let us ascend in the hope of the lot of the elect toward good works [Col. 1199A] by which God is praised, and let us say to one another: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good.”

These two steps are written about in Deuteronomy:

“You shall not take as a pledge the lower or the upper millstone, because he has placed his soul in your keeping.”

Saint Gregory explains this as follows:

“For sometimes we say ‘to take’ when we mean ‘to remove.’ Thus those birds eager to snatch are called hawks.”

And shortly afterward:

“The debtor’s pledge is the sinner’s confession. A pledge is taken from a debtor when the confession of sin is already held from the sinner. The upper and lower millstone are hope and fear.”

And again, a little later:

“In the confession of the sinner, hope and fear must therefore constantly be joined, because he hopes for mercy in vain if he does not also fear; and he fears justice [Col. 1199B] in vain if he does not also have confidence in mercy.”

And again:

“He removes the upper millstone if, when someone weeps over sin, he says: ‘You will not receive forgiveness for what you have done.’ He removes the lower if he flatters the sinner and says: ‘Do evil as much as you wish.’ For God is merciful and ready to forgive,” and so forth.

The psalm “The Lord reigns” instructs the perfect, such as the apostles were. “Have mercy on me, O God” instructs the fragile and weak, who ought to weep and mourn; this signifies the season of Septuagesima.

It seems appropriate to our smallness, because of the number seventy that encompasses our pilgrimage, that, together with the Alleluia and the elevation of the psalm “The Lord reigns,” “Glory to God in the highest” should be introduced into his treasures until the day of the Church’s exultation through the resurrection of our Head.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the Verses Used in Lent until the Passion of the Lord

[Col. 1199C]

It has often been said that the psalm “He who dwells in the help of the Most High” instructs those who, placed in the contest, set their hope in the Lord and implore all their help from him. For the holy Church is engaged in a greater contest during the days of Lent than at any other time. Therefore, during that season, she frequently uses this psalm in the verses, since it signifies the Lord’s protection and help.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Passion of the Lord

The days of the Lord’s Passion are counted as the two weeks before the Lord’s Pasch. It is not without reason [Col. 1199D] that his Passion is recalled during two weeks, since that same Passion is written and represented in the two periods of this world.

An example from the first period is Noah, who became drunk with wine, lay naked, was dishonored by one son, and honored by two. An example from the period already under the Law is this: “And your life shall hang before you; you shall fear night and day, and you shall not trust in your life.”

During those days, in the responsories alone, we lose for eleven days the glory of the holy Trinity, because one must come to the Passion of Christ through humility. The Passion and persecution, insofar as they are presently visible, concern the mass taken from Adam. The crowds who came to meet the Lord on Palm Sunday as he descended from the Mount of Olives signify this transformation into humility [Col. 1200A].

The hymn “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit” recalls the glory of the holy Trinity. Because the Son of God and the Son of Man are one person, and because he had come to suffer, the holy Church conforms herself to her Head and remains silent about his glorification until he is exalted [Col. 1200B] through the triumph of victory.

This prior humiliation, and the subsequent exaltation, are shown by one verse of Psalm 109, which says: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore he shall lift up his head.” The Lord drank from this torrent on the way, because in passing he tasted death; and therefore he lifted up his head, because what he had placed in the tomb by dying, he raised above the angels by rising.

Although it is properly fitting that, because of the humiliation of our Head, we should for the present omit the glorification of the holy Trinity—in which the Son of Man is honored because of the unity of the person of the Son of God—it can also be understood simply as reminding us that there was once a time when the hymn mentioned was not said in our Church.

Saint Jerome wrote about this same hymn to Pope Damasus. Similar is what Pope Innocent wrote: that Mass is not celebrated on Good Friday or on Holy Saturday. Nevertheless, a Mass is celebrated—the Mass celebrated by the apostles, namely, by the Lord’s Prayer alone.

If he wished to show by his words that the sacraments were entirely not celebrated, so that they should in no way be celebrated, no one among us observes this [Col. 1200C]. But so that the people, who needed to be refreshed on that day, might have the Lord’s Body as their foundation, and so that the Mass of the apostles might nevertheless be recalled to our memory, the same Mass is celebrated.

This need not be done on Holy Saturday, because everyone remains fasting until the night when the Mass of the Lord’s resurrection is celebrated.

From the day on which we omitted “Glory to the Father” there are two weeks—that is, fourteen days—until the Lord’s Pasch. The day of Pasch itself belongs to the third week, in which all the lost glorification is restored.

In the third period, that of the Law of grace, all the benefits awaited by our fathers are returned to the Church. They had been held in the enclosures of hell during the period of the natural law and during the period of the written Law.

Nor is it contrary to truth if the days of the Lord’s Passion, celebrated over two weeks, recall to our memory, as though through two periods, the grumbling of those who were winning the heavenly kingdom by their merits [Col. 1200D] and yet had been humbled in the enclosures of hell until the third week of the Law of grace.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday

The institutor of the office wished, as far as possible, to conform us by his instruction to the Passion of Christ, to the circumstances of the apostles, who were bound during the time of the Passion, and also to separate us from the behavior of the persecutors.

First, it must be said that all teaching by the pastor is silent in the Church on these days—that is, on the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, and Holy Saturday [Col. 1201A]. “O Lord, open my lips” is not said; no blessing is given to the readers; no instruction concerning the reading is supplied at Matins; and after the hymn of Zechariah the prayer is not directed in the customary manner by the pastor.

These things are not done because our pastor, Christ, has departed, and the rams of the flock, who had already been predestined to become pastors of the Church, have been scattered.

The lesser ministers perform their office in the figure of the disciples, who perhaps were less recognized as Christ’s disciples, and in the figure of the women who could be present at Christ’s humiliation.

Some singers are accustomed to omit the verse before “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel,” because no reading precedes it; they ought not to do this. They perform their own office, but the pastor’s office is kept silent.

They do not sing the Invitatory [Col. 1201B], to teach the avoidance of an evil gathering, such as occurred among the Jews concerning the killing of Christ. The nearer the Passion approaches, the more they humble themselves in their office.

Therefore, on these nights or days, they entirely omit “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.” Every salutation is absent during these three days or nights, to avoid the deadly salutation such as the devil Judas practiced.

Furthermore, the lofty signals made with bronze vessels are put aside, and the sound of wood, necessarily struck to summon the people to the Church, is everywhere more subdued than the sound of bronze [Col. 1201C].

A more humble practice of the Roman Church in ancient times may also be signified by this—especially when it was hiding in crypts because of persecutors. For younger Rome, which in ancient times was governed under one Lord together with ancient Rome, still retains the use of wood, not because of a shortage of bronze but because of its antiquity.

And because our Savior’s humiliation through burial is celebrated for three days, it is fitting that the humiliation of our office should follow for three days—namely, Thursday, Friday, and Saturday.

The nine psalms, nine readings, and nine responsories celebrated over three nights signify that the Lord, descending to the lower regions of the earth, snatched three classes of human beings from there and led them over into the fellowship of the nine orders of angels.

These three classes are distinguished in the Gospel by those who are in the field, those who are at the mill, and those who are in bed. And because these three classes are believed to have existed under the natural law, in the period of the written Law, or in the period of the prophets [Col. 1201D], they are rightly recalled over three nights. Because of the nine orders of angels, whose names we read through the number nine, their restoration to the fellowship of those same angels is celebrated.

Augustine explains these three classes of the elect in the forty-seventh section of his Book of Questions on the Gospels:

“Who are the two in one bed, the two women grinding together, and the two in the field, of all of whom one will be taken and one left? Three classes of human beings seem to be signified here.

“One is the class of those who choose leisure and repose, occupied neither with worldly business nor with ecclesiastical affairs; their repose is signified by the name ‘bed’ [Col. 1202A].

“Another is the class of those established among the peoples and governed by teachers, carrying on the affairs of this world. He signified them by the name of women, because, as he said, it is advantageous for them to be guided by the counsels of the knowledgeable; and he called them ‘grinding’ because of the circuit and rotation of temporal business. Yet he said that they were grinding together insofar as from those very possessions and affairs they provide resources for the uses of the Church.

“The third is the class of those who work in the ministry of the Church, as in God’s field, concerning which agriculture the Apostle speaks.”

Because we believe that these three classes existed in every period of time, and because, although they were elect, they descended to the enclosures of hell, while in these days the Lord descended to take them away from there and join them to the activity, knowledge, and joy of the angels, it is not without reason that the nocturnal offices are celebrated with nine psalms [Col. 1202B], which pertain to activity; nine readings, which pertain to knowledge of God’s works; and nine responsories, which pertain to the songs of the holy angels.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Extinguishing of the Lights

The extinguishing of the church’s light during these nights appears to us to be adapted to the Sun of righteousness himself, who was extinguished and buried for three days and three nights.

The Sun, who is Christ, illuminated his Church by day and by night, so that in the prosperity of day she might know how to exalt herself moderately, and in the adversity of night endure with equanimity.

The sun that illuminates the present world traverses its circuit by day and night in twenty-four hours [Col. 1202C]. Altogether, three days and nights contain seventy-two hours. For that many disciples Christ sent out, two by two, to preach before his face.

Accordingly, during each night of the aforementioned days, twenty-four lights are kindled. And because that sun signifies our Sun, which set on the evening of the Passion, by means of the light that we can kindle and extinguish we somehow represent the rising and setting of the true Sun, like the rising and setting of the physical sun.

Our Church is illuminated by twenty-four lights, and with each song in which we ought to rejoice, we descend into sadness, because our true Sun has set. Thus, as though with each hour, the sun’s decline increases until complete extinction.

This is done three times, because the Lord’s burial is recalled over three days. During the day this fire is renewed [Col. 1202D]. For it cannot otherwise be restored for the benefit of our Church unless it receives fuel from three sides.

Concerning this Gregory says in the *Moralia*:

“For corporeal fire, in order to be fire, needs corporeal fuel. When it must be preserved, it is undoubtedly nourished by heaped-up wood; nor can it remain unless kindled and replenished.”

+ It is rekindled because of our weakness, since without light we cannot perform our offices in the Church. Otherwise, it would be more fitting for it to remain extinguished after the first extinction until the glory of the resurrection and the renewal of the New Testament.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Three Psalms Sung in the Night Office during the Seven Baptismal Days

[Col. 1203A]

The three psalms sung on the Sunday night of the Lord’s resurrection demonstrate the works of three days that the Lord promised, according to Luke, to accomplish in the present age.

Luke says:

“On that very day some Pharisees came, saying to him: ‘Go away and depart from here, because Herod wants to kill you.’ And he said to them: ‘Go and tell that fox, “Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected.” Nevertheless, I must travel today and tomorrow and the following day, because it is not possible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.’”

He promised that he would perform these three works—casting out demons, completing healings, and being perfected on the third day [Col. 1203B]—and immediately afterward he speaks of his Passion, which was to take place in Jerusalem.

Concerning the casting out of demons he says, according to John: “Now is the judgment of this world.” Saint Augustine explains this in the forty-ninth sermon on the same Gospel of John:

“Setting aside that judgment at the end, when the living and the dead will finally be judged, the devil possessed the human race and held the guilty under the bond of sins. He ruled in the hearts of unbelievers; he deceived and dragged them captive into worship of the creature while abandoning the Creator. But through faith in Christ, established by his death and resurrection, and through his blood, poured out for the forgiveness of sins, thousands of believers are freed from the devil’s rule, joined to Christ’s body, and, under one Head [Col. 1203C], are enlivened as faithful members by his one Spirit. This he called judgment: this separation, this expulsion of the devil from those redeemed by him.”

The same Evangelist John speaks of this expulsion shortly afterward: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.”

This is the first day of which the Lord speaks according to Luke: “Behold, I cast out demons today.” The first antiphon shows this day; it says: “I am who I am, and my counsel is not with the ungodly.”

This is the judgment, that is, the separation of which John speaks, so that the faithful, with whom the Lord’s counsel is, may be separated from the ungodly.

The first psalm, “Blessed is the man,” shows the same thing. It first describes what blessedness must flee and what it must seek, and afterward likewise describes the expulsion of the ungodly, saying: “Not so the ungodly, not so, but like dust [Col. 1203D] which the wind drives from the face of the earth,” and the rest that follows.

The second antiphon shows what the Lord said he would complete on the following day, according to Luke—namely, healings. What these healings are, John explains immediately after saying, “Behold, the prince of this world will be cast out,” by adding: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things after me.”

Augustine explains this in the sermon mentioned above:

“He did not therefore refer this to a diversity of human beings, but to the integrity of creation—or certainly to every class of human beings, whether in all languages, in every age, or in every rank of good.”

And shortly afterward:

“That he might be their head, and they his members.”

The second antiphon speaks of this: “I asked my Father; he gave me the nations as an inheritance” [Col. 1204A]. Those whom he drew after him are the nations that the Father gave the Son as an inheritance.

The third antiphon touches upon the perfection that the Lord promised he would complete on the third day. The third day is when he leads those from whom he cast out the devil and whom he restored to health, through the joining of his body, into the fellowship of the holy angels.

The antiphon says: “I slept, and took my rest, and I rose again.” Christ rose, but not alone. Those who appeared to many in the holy city on the day of his resurrection bore witness to this through their resurrection.

The Head has risen; it is necessary that the members follow. Therefore Paul did not say: “Who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification by the resurrection of the dead Jesus Christ our Lord,” but said: “By the resurrection of the dead” [Col. 1204B].

The institutor of the office could not have shown the individual works of the three days more appropriately than through three psalms and three antiphons.

All these things were fulfilled in the Lord’s resurrection: the devil was cast out from the faithful; they were joined to the Head; the Head rose; and human nature, in his resurrection, was joined to the nature of the angels, although it was exalted far above all angels.

Angels can be everywhere through swift passage, both in heaven and on earth. That human nature, according to the arrangement made by the very same person, could, whenever he wished, be on earth and be raised into heaven through the triumph of immortality.

The nature of angels does not need food, drink, clothing, or any vehicle by which to travel; nor did that human nature need these things afterward [Col. 1204C]. Hence the Apostle said: “And even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, now we know him no longer in that way.”

Through these three days our catechumens are instructed as members of Christ: first, when the devil is cast out through exorcism and renunciation; then, when health is perfected in them through faith; finally, when they are justified through the laying on of the bishops’ hands.

Christ’s resurrection is our justification. We rise there with Christ where we are justified. Indeed, through these three days, as through three antiphons—the first separating us from the ungodly, the second joining us to Christ the Head, and the third making us rise through justification—we have entered the Church.

I speak from the person of the neophytes: the following baptismal days and nights [Col. 1204D] show how we ought to live in the Church itself according to Christ’s teaching.

The days signify Christ’s resurrection. Therefore, because Christ rose on one day, our offices run through those seven days as though it were still the Lord’s Day. In the Sacramentary we sing: “It is truly worthy and just, right and salutary, to proclaim you at all times, but especially and more gloriously on this day.” The singers sing daily: “This is the day which the Lord has made.”

We celebrate one and the same day through the baptismal sacraments over seven days, when the elect throughout the whole course of this life do not turn aside through works of darkness from their Head, who rose in such a way that he will never again die.

Just as the day recalls the Lord’s resurrection [Col. 1205A], so we recall his burial. If we have made seven days into one day because of the perpetual resurrection of good works, we ought to adapt the preceding nights as though to one day.

A three-day burial preceded the Lord’s resurrection, and a three-day burial precedes our justification. “For we were buried with him,” the Apostle says, “through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life.”

For one who dies and is buried can commit no sin. Night signifies a time of rest, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The night is coming, when no one can work.”

Although this is here said indiscriminately of good and evil works, we can nevertheless understand night as the time when a person rests from wicked works [Col. 1205B].

We recall this rest, in which we cease from evil and remain watchful in good, through the three psalms performed in the night office during the baptismal days.

When we are plunged three times into the water, we are buried with Christ in his three-day tomb. The person who sings three psalms at night is the one who keeps in mind that he has been buried with Christ and has therefore died to sin.

He has died to sin who does not commit sin. The person who sings during the day, “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it,” is the one who perseveres in innocence and good works.

And because we must earnestly meditate on these things and strive for them as long as we remain in the present age—that is, until the seventh day comes, on which the soul is separated from the body—let us sing during the day: “This is the day [Col. 1205C] which the Lord has made,” and let us celebrate the Lord’s burial at night.

And if many of us do not recall this mortification of the flesh, which is signified by the three psalms, and the justification signified by the office of one color, let us at least recall it in those who have recently been baptized.

Alternatively: those who are baptized with a simple heart receive the sevenfold Spirit, which the prophet Isaiah sings as resting uniquely upon our Lord Jesus Christ.

If it were not believed that those who are baptized could receive that same Spirit, the bishops who perform the laying on of hands would not implore that it be sent upon the neophytes.

To sing in harmony with that sevenfold Spirit, we celebrate our gatherings over seven days with greater religious devotion and care than usual. On each day [Col. 1205D] we strive to sing in harmony with one of the gifts.

We avoid laziness, lest we be rebuked according to the Lord’s word: “We have sung to you, and you have not danced.”

The Holy Spirit arrives as a new guest and exercises a song of indescribable joy—namely, of wisdom and understanding, counsel and fortitude, knowledge and piety, and fear of the Lord.

The host who receives him ought to dance to this song through faith, hope, and love.

Because of this reciprocity, on each day we sing something, whether in a responsory or in the Alleluia from the psalm “Give thanks to the Lord,” which recalls God’s goodness and mercy forever; and at night we sing three antiphons or Alleluias with three psalms.

Every Christian ought to honor the Holy Spirit through faith, hope, and love. Each gift of the Holy Spirit has these three sisters [Col. 1206A]; and all seven have these three sisters, as does each individual gift.

We can test this by an example from our own experience: if seven brothers had three sisters, those sisters would belong to all and to each individually.

To recall the one Spirit who works all these things, we observe one day in religious devotion over seven days. To recall his seven gifts, the days are multiplied by the number seven. And to recall our faith, hope, and love, which according to the Apostle must remain with us until the end of the world, who says, “But now faith, hope, and love remain,” we sing three psalms at night until the seventh day.

The baptismal sacraments extend to the completion of seven days because the newly baptized are enriched by the sevenfold Spirit [Col. 1206B]. Or else, because the totality of time, which revolves through the completion of seven days, is signified by seven days, during which every Christian must strive so that no one is alienated from faith, hope, and love, even if he cannot attain all the other good works.

Or else because every elect soul, departing from the body, immediately finds the Sabbath and has its work completed, since God completed his work on the seventh day.

Afterward, in the following period, the leaves of growing trees are multiplied and recalled, as it were, through the good conduct of various works expressed in many psalms.

We give thanks to God, who placed in the hearts of his servants the ordering of our offices in such a way that the people of God can almost be instructed from them as from a reading.

We have it written in the Roman Order [Col. 1206C] that “Kyrie eleison” or “Christe eleison” is not to be said at any office during the aforementioned days, but that without repetition we should sing: “This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.”

The priest customarily says only the Collect at the end of the office. If what we are doing were already present in reality, it would not be said, since the priest’s prayer exists in hope. It follows that what is held may be strengthened, and what is not yet held may be received.

Concerning this matter Augustine says in his treatise on Psalm 148:

“Our praise contains joy; our prayer, a groan. Something has been promised us that we do not yet possess; and because the one who promises is truthful, we rejoice in hope. Yet because we do not yet possess it, we groan in longing. It is good [Col. 1206D] to persevere in longing until what has been promised comes, the groaning passes away, and praise alone takes its place. Whatever prayer is offered by those who truly celebrate Easter—whether in the collect or in the chamber of the heart—is offered so that what has been promised, and is not yet possessed, may come in place of the longing that Saint Augustine mentions. The priest’s prayer is therefore celebrated.

“In what follows he likewise shows what joy holy Church recalls throughout all the days of Pentecost. ‘Because of these two periods,’ he says, ‘one which exists now in the tribulations and temptations of this life, and the other which will then exist in perpetual security and exultation, the celebration of two periods has also been instituted for us, before Easter and after Easter. That which is before Easter signifies the tribulation in which we now are; but what we now celebrate after Easter signifies the blessedness in which we shall afterward be. Therefore, in celebrating what is before Easter, we also enact it; but in celebrating what is after Easter, we signify what we do not yet possess. For that period we exercise ourselves in fasts and prayers; this period, with the fasts relaxed, we spend in praises.

“‘This is the Alleluia that we sing, which, as you know, is interpreted in Latin as “Praise the Lord.” Therefore that period is before the resurrection, while this period is after the Lord’s resurrection; and this period signifies the future life, which we do not yet possess, because what we signify after the Lord’s resurrection we shall possess after our resurrection. For both things have been prefigured and demonstrated for us in our Head. The Lord’s Passion shows us the life of present necessity, since we must labor and suffer tribulation and, finally, die. But the Lord’s resurrection and glorification show us the life that we shall receive when he comes to repay what is due to the worthy: evil to the evil and good to the good.

“‘For now all the wicked can sing Alleluia with us. But if they persevere in their wickedness, they will be able to say the song of our future life with their lips; yet they cannot obtain the life itself that will then exist in the reality now signified, because they were unwilling, before it came, to meditate upon and possess what was going to come. Now, therefore, brothers, we exhort you to praise the Lord; and this is what we all say when we say Alleluia: Praise God.’”

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### A Repetition Concerning the Greater Litany

[Col. 1207C]

When I wrote about the greater litany earlier, that is, in the first book of this work, I had not yet read that it had been instituted by Saint Gregory. I said that it had been instituted for two reasons: namely, because of the impending wars that could arise at that time, and for the preservation of the crops. But after I read Saint Gregory’s decree, I took care to insert it here in the same form in which it is read in the volume of his letters. After it, I likewise took care to append a certain letter to the emperor Phocas, in which it is shown that at that time the borders of the Romans were being ravaged by the Lombard people.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### The Statements That Follow from the Letters of Gregory

[Col. 1207D]

In the name of God our Savior Jesus Christ, in the sixth indiction, on the twenty-third day of the month of November, during the time of the lord and most blessed Pope Gregory, Phocas and Leontia Augusta were crowned in the seventh year, in the palace called Secundianas. The emperor Maurice was killed together with all his male sons, namely Theodosius, already crowned, Tiberius, Peter, Paul, and Justinian, and also Peter, the brother of the aforementioned Maurice Augustus, as well as certain nobles who adhered to him: namely, the patrician Constantine, the curator of the Placidias, and Gregory, the prince’s notary.

The image of the aforementioned Phocas and Leontia Augusta came to Rome on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, and an acclamation was made for them in the Lateran, in the Julian basilica, by all the clergy and senate: “Hear us, O Christ: life to Phocas Augustus and to Leontia Augusta.” Then the lord, most blessed and apostolic Pope Gregory, ordered that the image itself be placed in the oratory of Saint Caesarius within the palace.

It is fitting, dearest brothers, that we fear at least the scourges of God that we ought to have feared would come, now that they are present and have been experienced. May sorrow open for us the way of conversion, and may the punishment we are already suffering dissolve the hardness of our hearts. For, as was foretold with the prophet as witness, the sword has reached even to the soul. Behold, the whole people is struck by the sword of heavenly wrath, and individuals are suddenly destroyed by slaughter; sickness does not precede death, but, as you see, death outruns the delays of sickness. Each person who is struck is carried away before he can turn to the lamentation of repentance.

Consider, therefore, what sort of person arrives before the sight of the strict Judge when he has no time to mourn what he has done. For the inhabitants are not taken away piecemeal, but fall together: houses are left empty, parents look upon the funerals of their children, and their own heirs precede them to destruction. Therefore let each one of us flee to the lamentation of repentance while there is time to weep before the blow. Let us recall before the eyes of our mind whatever we have committed through error, and let us punish by weeping what we have wickedly done. Let us go before his face in confession, and, as the Prophet admonishes, let us lift our hearts together with our hands to God.

To lift the heart to God together with the hands means to raise the devotion of our prayer together with the merit of good action. He certainly gives confidence to our trembling—he gives it—who cries out through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live.” Let no one despair because of the enormity of his sins. For three days of repentance washed away the long-standing offenses of the Ninevites, and the converted thief purchased the rewards of life even at the very sentence of his death.

Let us therefore change our hearts and presume that we have already received what we ask. The Judge is bent more quickly toward prayer if the petitioner is corrected from his wickedness. Since the sword of so great a punishment is impending, let us persist in unremitting weeping. For the importunity that is usually displeasing to human beings pleases the judgment of truth. For the pious and merciful God wishes pardon to be demanded from him by prayers, since he does not wish to become angry to the extent that we deserve.

For this reason he says through the Psalmist: “Call upon me in the day of your tribulation, and I shall rescue you, and you shall glorify me.” He is therefore his own witness, since he desires to show mercy to those who call upon him, having himself instructed us to call upon him.

Therefore, dearest brothers, with contrite hearts and corrected actions, let us come tomorrow at first light to the sevenfold litany, according to the arrangement set out below, with devout and tearful minds. Let none of you go out into the fields for earthly work; let no one presume to conduct any business, so that, gathering at the church of the holy Mother of the Lord, we who have all sinned together may together bewail the evil things we do, in order that the strict Judge, when he sees us punishing our faults, may himself spare us from the sentence of the condemnation he has proposed.

It follows:

The litany of the clergy shall go out from the church of Saint John the Baptist.

The litany of the men, from the church of Saint Marcellus the martyr.

The litany of the monks, from the church of the martyrs John and Paul.

The litany of the handmaids of God, from the church of the blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian.

The litany of married women, from the church of the blessed Peter and the martyr Stephen.

The litany of widows, from the church of the blessed martyr Vitalis.

The litany of the poor and children, from the church of the blessed martyr Cecilia.

In the following letter it will be shown that the litany can undoubtedly be understood to have been instituted because of the urgency of wars. From the character of the time, we also infer that it was necessary for preserving the crops.

### Gregory to Phocas Augustus

[Col. 1209B]

It is pleasant to consider, with joy and great acts of thanksgiving, how many praises we owe to the almighty Lord, because, after the yoke of sorrow was removed, we have reached a time of freedom under the protection of your imperial benevolence. For the fact that Your Serenity did not find a deacon of the apostolic see remaining in the palace according to ancient custom was not due to my negligence but to the gravest necessity. While all the ministers of our church were shrinking from and avoiding those crushed and harsh times in fear, none of them could be charged with going to the royal city and remaining in the palace.

But after they learned that, by the grace of almighty God, your Clemency had reached the summit of imperial power, they too, prompted by joy, hastened to come to your feet, although previously they had been very much afraid to go there. Yet since some of them are so weakened by old age that they can scarcely endure the journey, while others are deeply occupied with ecclesiastical responsibilities, I judged the bearer of this letter suitable for attending upon your piety. He was the first of all the defenders, is well known to me through long familiarity, and has been approved in life, faith, and conduct. With the Lord as author, I therefore made him a deacon and hastened to send him, so that, when he finds a suitable opportunity, he may report to your Clemency everything that is happening in those regions.

I ask that Your Serenity deign to incline your pious ears to him, so that you may be able to show us mercy all the more quickly, the more truly you learn of our affliction through his report. For we cannot adequately express in any words of petition how, by daily swords and by how many incursions of the Lombards, we have now been oppressed for thirty-five years. But we trust in almighty God that he will complete for us the good things of his consolation that he has begun, and that he who has raised up pious rulers in the commonwealth will extinguish cruel tyrants.

Therefore may the Holy Trinity preserve your life for many years, so that we may enjoy longer the benefit of your benevolence, which we received only after delay.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### A Repetition Concerning the Alleluia Sung at Mass, the Garment of the Subdeacons, the Kyrie Eleison, and the Lord’s Prayer, from a Letter of Saint Gregory

When my smallness wrote about the office of the Mass, what follows was hidden from me in the same way as what I said earlier about the greater litany. I had not yet read what I afterward found in a letter of Saint Gregory: at what time the Alleluia was first sung at Mass in the Roman Church, and the other matters that will be made clear in the words of his letter to John of Syracuse. Once I found these things, I could not pass them over without introducing them here, although not in the appropriate place, since it was more suitable for them to be written in the office of the Mass than in the nocturnal office. The text of the letter follows.

### Gregory to John, Bishop of Syracuse

A certain man who came from Sicily told me that some of his friends—whether Greeks or Latins, I do not know—were murmuring, as though out of zeal for the holy Roman Church, about my arrangements, saying: “How does he govern the Church of Constantinople when in every respect he follows its customs?”

When I asked him, “Which of its customs do we follow?” the answer was: “Because you have arranged for the Alleluia to be said at Masses outside the season of Pentecost; because you have arranged for the subdeacons to proceed stripped of their garments; because you have arranged for the Kyrie eleison to be said; and because you have arranged for the Lord’s Prayer to be said immediately after the canon.”

I replied: “In none of these matters have we followed another Church. For the Alleluia to be said here is said to have been brought from the Church of Jerusalem through the tradition of blessed Jerome, in the time of Pope Damasus of blessed memory.”

And shortly afterward:

“I arranged for the subdeacons to proceed stripped of their garments because this was an ancient custom of the Church. But it pleased one of our pontiffs—I do not know which one—to order them to proceed clothed. For did your Churches receive their tradition from the Greeks? From where, then, do they have it today that subdeacons proceed in linen tunics, unless they received this from their mother, the Roman Church?

“As for the Kyrie eleison, we neither said nor say it as it is said by the Greeks. Among the Greeks everyone says it together; among us it is said by the clergy and answered by the people. The Christe eleison is likewise said the same number of times, although among the Greeks it is not said at all. At daily Masses we omit the other things that are usually said and say only Kyrie eleison and Christe eleison, so that we may remain somewhat longer in these words of supplication.

“We say the Lord’s Prayer immediately after the prayer because it was the custom of the apostles to consecrate the sacrificial offering with that prayer alone. It seemed very inappropriate to me to say over the offering the prayer composed by a scholar, and not to say over the body and blood of our Redeemer the tradition that our Redeemer himself composed. Among the Greeks, moreover, the Lord’s Prayer is said by the entire people, whereas among us it is said only by the priest.

“In what respect, then, have we followed the customs of the Greeks? We have either restored our ancient customs or established new and useful ones, and in these we are not shown to imitate others. A foolish person is one who thinks himself foremost because he refuses to learn the good things he sees in others.

“Therefore, when occasion arises for Your Charity to go to the city of Catania or to the Church of Syracuse, let Your Charity, through conversation, instruct those whom you believe or understand may have murmured about this matter, and, as though on another occasion, do not cease instructing them. For concerning the Church of Constantinople, who could doubt that it is subject to the apostolic see? Both the most pious lord emperor and our brother, the bishop of that same city, constantly profess this.

“Nevertheless, if either that Church or another has anything good, I am prepared to imitate it—and my inferiors, whom I prohibit from unlawful things—in what is good. For he is foolish who thinks himself foremost because he scorns to learn the good things he has seen.”

From this letter we learn that whatever good we can learn from other Churches, we should not despise. We also learn that at some time Mass was celebrated in the Roman Church without the Alleluia. Whether at that time the Tracts were sung on all Sundays, and after the Alleluia had been adopted were reserved only for the Sundays from Septuagesima onward, I do not know.

I know one thing: from the fact that the Alleluia became widespread, it is evident that in ancient times it was sung by Saint Augustine and in the Roman and Constantinopolitan Churches during the days of Pentecost, in order to recall the joy of the resurrection of the saints.

There remains something that presses upon my mind and calls for inquiry: just as the Alleluia is sung at Mass on Sundays and feast days, should it likewise be sung on ordinary days, or not? Perhaps we can be instructed by the present writing of Saint Gregory. Since Saint Gregory says, “At daily Masses we omit the other things that are usually said and say only Kyrie eleison and Christe eleison,” we can understand that the Alleluia was not sung by him on ordinary days in the office of the Mass.

## CHAPTER XXVII  
### On the Completion of the Days of Pentecost

When the Lord ascended into heaven, he commanded his disciples not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father, which they had heard from his mouth: “For John baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit, not many days from now”—that is, after ten days. They rightly await ten days, because it was to happen that, after ten days, they would receive more perfectly the mystery of the number ten, when the Holy Spirit came.

Thus Luke relates: “But remain seated here in the city until you are clothed with power from on high.” Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and, lifting up his hands, he blessed them. And it happened that, while he blessed them, he withdrew from them and was carried into heaven. And they worshiped him and returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually [Col. 1211D] in the temple, praising God and blessing the Lord.

To sit in the city means to think, with a silent and tranquil mind, upon the Lord’s promises and not to depart from the condition of perpetual peace; to strengthen the senses of the body so that death may not enter through them; and to consider that one must restore oneself wholly and intact to God. This means having within oneself the four elements intact, in the condition in which God provided them, being turned wholly toward the love of God with all one’s heart, soul, and mind, and knowing that the image of the Holy Trinity has been marked upon oneself.

If anyone desires to possess this denarius within himself, and recognizes that he possesses something less than it, he ought to worship the Lord and pray that he may grant it to him. And if he feels that, through charity—which casts out fear—he can obtain it, let him remain in the temple, praising and blessing God. This is to await for ten days the promise of the Father, to desire continually the wholeness of one’s creation, and to desire knowledge of one’s Creator.

The apostles received this denarius more fully and perfectly than they had possessed it before, on the day of Pentecost. Saint Augustine was admonished by the Holy Spirit with the same command before he departed from the body, when he requested that ten days be granted to him for meditating upon himself and his own affairs. It is written in his Life:

“For he had ordered that the very few psalms of David concerning repentance be written out. While lying in bed during the days of his illness, he kept looking at and reading these booklets, which had been placed opposite him against the wall, and he wept abundantly and continually. And, so that his concentration might not be disturbed by anyone, about ten days before he departed from the body he asked us who were present that no one should enter to see him except during those hours when the physicians entered to examine him or when food was brought to him.”

Thus far from the Life of Saint Augustine +.

Alternatively:

The same Saint Augustine writes in the seventeenth sermon on John:

“The great and universal fast is to abstain from iniquities and unlawful pleasures of the world. This is perfect fasting: that, renouncing impiety and worldly desires, we should live temperately and justly in this world.
