The Apostle adds what reward he assigns to this fast, and continues: ‘Awaiting that blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of the blessed God and our Savior Jesus Christ.’

“In this world, therefore, we celebrate something like a fortieth period of abstinence when we live well, when we abstain from iniquities and unlawful pleasures. But because this abstinence will not be without reward, we await that blessed hope and the revelation of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. When that hope has become reality, we shall receive the reward, the denarius.

“And shortly afterward:

“‘The denarius, therefore, which takes its name from the number ten, is given; and joined to the forty, it becomes fifty. Hence we celebrate the Forty before Easter with labor, but the Fifty after Easter with joy, as a reward already received. For to this labor of good work, which belongs to the number forty, is added the denarius of rest and blessedness, so that it becomes fifty. The Lord Jesus himself signified this much more clearly when, after his resurrection, he remained on earth with his disciples for forty days. On the fortieth day, when he had ascended into heaven, after ten days had been completed, he sent the reward of the Holy Spirit +.’”

For on the tenth day after the Lord’s Ascension, that is, during the vigils of Pentecost, holy Church celebrates baptism and conducts the litany before the solemn Masses. She prays either that she herself may deserve to enjoy the coming of the Holy Spirit, as the apostles enjoyed him when they were baptized by him at Pentecost, or that the neophytes may persevere in the unity of the Church.

Afterward the aforementioned Church sings “Glory to God in the highest,” following the example of the apostles, who, before receiving the Holy Spirit, were in the temple, continually praising God and blessing the Lord.

Although, after setting aside the Church’s office, I had not intended to say anything in these writings, yet because the subject of baptism arose during this festival, I wished to show my willingness to learn something about the things carried out around the baptisteries.

I now turn to the three psalms sung on the night of Pentecost. It seems to me that the difference between these three psalms, which are sung at Pentecost, and the three sung at the Lord’s Easter lies in the distinction between the baptism received by the apostles through water and the baptism received through the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost, concerning which the Lord said to them: “But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”

They had already been baptized with water; they had already received the Holy Spirit. Yet afterward they were told: “But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit.”

Concerning baptism with water, Augustine says in his letter to Seleucianus:

“Then, when he went out from Jerusalem with his disciples into Judea and remained there with them, he baptized—not by himself, but through his disciples. We understand that they had already been baptized, either with John’s baptism, as some think, or, what is more credible, with Christ’s baptism. For he would not have avoided the ministry of baptizing in order to have baptized servants through whom he might baptize others, since he did not avoid the ministry of that memorable humility when he washed their feet.”

That they received the Holy Spirit before the day of Pentecost, John makes clear when he says: “When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were closed.” And shortly afterward: “When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them,’” and the rest.

They had already received the Holy Spirit for the forgiveness of sins. But there still remained the gift that they had not yet received, though they were going to receive it on the day of Pentecost: namely, that they might confirm their preaching with signs of miracles, that they might not fear the rage of their persecutors, that they might not be ensnared by the bond of earthly desire, and that they might not be shaken by any error.

We believe that Peter had already been baptized when he denied the Lord at the voice of a servant girl. The same is true of Thomas, who doubted the Lord’s resurrection.

Just as two baptisms are then read of among the apostles—one through water and the other through the baptism of the Holy Spirit—so today there are two kinds of elect in our Church who have been baptized. One kind is in the active life; the other is in the contemplative life. These two kinds were signified by Martha and her sister Mary. The Lord assigned Mary the better part, but Martha was not reproved, because her part is good.

This distinction can be found in the antiphons that are sung at the Lord’s Easter and at Pentecost. At the Lord’s Easter the first antiphon says: “My counsel is not with the ungodly.” The first at Pentecost says: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent rushing wind.” A violent wind usually scatters the dust of the earth.

There is a great difference between the gift of God that separates the faithful from the ungodly and the gift that cleanses earthly thoughts from the breast. There the second antiphon says: “I asked my father.” Here it says: “Strengthen, O God, what you have worked in us, from your holy temple which is in Jerusalem. Alleluia, alleluia.”

In the same way, there is a difference between those who are appointed to the inheritance of the Lord because they are faithful, yet remain in the active life, and those who have rejected all earthly things and pray to God not to return to them, but to strengthen his gift in them, so that they may always sing Alleluia to God from the temple that is in Jerusalem.

There the third antiphon says: “I slept and took my rest, and I rose again.” Here the third says: “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth.” For Christ rose from death, and we too can rise daily from vices; and it can truly be said to us: “Do not grieve the Spirit of God.”

This antiphon, which says, “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created,” earnestly prays for the Spirit of God to come, so that the spirit of pride may rule neither in our thoughts nor in our words, but that the Spirit of God may lead both through his creation. As it is written in the Gospel: “When they seize you and lead you away, do not consider beforehand what or how you should speak; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you.”

It prays that the face of the earth may be renewed, so that the new person may confess that he has been justified not by himself but by the grace of God.

Just as at the Lord’s Easter the three psalms recall the works of Christ on the three days, so too they recall these same works at the coming of the Holy Spirit. To demonstrate that there is one work in the miraculous power of the whole Holy Trinity, one order of psalms is contained both in the Lord’s resurrection and in the coming of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1214C]

But Christ works less in some and more in others. For star differs from star in glory.

What we said at Easter concerning the following baptismal nights, we also say here: the three psalms recall the Lord’s three-day burial, especially in those who have recently been buried with the Lord. This is done for seven days because of the sacrament of the present life and because of the seventh day that the souls of the saints receive when stripped of their bodies, or because of the sevenfold Holy Spirit, who nourishes his own with different food on each day.

The three psalms can also recall the three virtues—faith, hope, and charity—without which no one can please God.

We also connect with this the banquet that each gift, like each brother, prepares for its fellow guests throughout the seven days, and the three virtues, like three sisters feasting together, from the first book of Saint Gregory’s Morals:

“For, to review briefly these very gifts of the sevenfold Spirit, one day belongs to wisdom, another to understanding, another to counsel, another to fortitude, another to knowledge, another to piety, and another to fear. For knowing is not the same as understanding, since many have knowledge of eternal things but are by no means able to understand them.

“Wisdom therefore prepares a banquet on its day, because it refreshes the mind with hope and certainty concerning eternal things. Understanding prepares a banquet on its day, because, by penetrating what has been heard, it enlightens the heart’s darkness while refreshing it. Counsel offers a banquet on its day, because, by preventing the soul from rushing headlong, it fills it with reason. Fortitude prepares a banquet on its day, because, by fearing no adversity, it sets foods of confidence before the trembling mind. Knowledge prepares a banquet on its day, because in the belly of the mind it overcomes the fast of ignorance. Piety offers a banquet on its day, because it fills the heart’s inward parts with works of mercy. Fear prepares a banquet on its day, because, while pressing upon the mind so that it does not become proud over present things, it strengthens it concerning future things with the food of hope.

“But in this banquet of the children, I see something that must be investigated: they feed one another. For each individual virtue is greatly weakened if one virtue does not support another. Wisdom is lesser if it lacks understanding; and understanding is very useless if it does not rest upon wisdom. For when it penetrates higher things without the weight of wisdom, its own lightness lifts it up only to make it fall more heavily.

“Counsel is worthless when it lacks the strength of fortitude, because what it discovers through deliberation, lacking the power to act, it does not bring to completion. Fortitude is also greatly undermined unless it is supported by counsel, because the more it sees that it can do, the more disastrously a virtue without the moderation of reason rushes headlong.

“There is no knowledge if it does not possess the usefulness of piety, because, while neglecting to carry out the good things it has learned, it binds itself more tightly for judgment. Piety too is very useless if it lacks the discernment of knowledge, because, when no knowledge illuminates it, it does not know how to show mercy.

“Fear itself, moreover, if it does not also possess these virtues, certainly rises to no work of good action. For, while it trembles at everything, it remains sluggish through its very strength and is deprived of every good.

“Since, therefore, virtue is refreshed by virtue through alternating service, it is rightly said that the children feast with one another. And when one supports another so that it may be lifted up, they prepare a banquet, as though a numerous offspring were to be fed on its appointed days.”

It follows:

“And they sent and called their three sisters, that they might eat and drink with them.”

When our virtues recognize hope, faith, and charity in everything they do, the working children, as three, call their sisters to the banquet, so that faith, hope, and charity may rejoice in the good work that each virtue administers. They receive strength as though from food, becoming more confident through good works; and when, after food, they desire to be infused with the dew of contemplation, they become, as it were, drunk from the cup.

It is not contrary to the truth if the three psalms are sung during the nights of the neophytes either because of the Lord’s burial, as we have mentioned, or because of faith, hope, and charity, which every Christian ought to possess from the very beginning of his understanding.

## CHAPTER XXVIII  
### On the Hour of the Baptistery on Saturday, or on the Vigil of Pentecost

It should be noted that holy Church now celebrates baptism at the hour of the day when the angel of the Lord came to Cornelius, announcing to him that his prayers and almsgiving had risen as a memorial before God, and telling him to send for Peter, who would baptize him. At that same hour the baptizer Peter came to Cornelius to baptize him.

For Peter questioned Cornelius, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “I ask, therefore, for what reason did you send for me?” And Cornelius said: “Four days ago, until this hour, I was praying at the ninth hour in my house,” and the rest.

Peter immediately instructed him in the creed of faith, as is contained in the aforementioned Acts, and at once the Holy Spirit fell upon all who heard the word. When this had happened, Peter replied: “Can anyone forbid water, so that these should not be baptized who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” And he ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ.

Therefore, at that time around the primitive Church, baptism was celebrated at the ninth hour, so that both that Church and its imitator, which exists today, might retain in mind that it ought to baptize in the death of Christ, who at the ninth hour gave up his spirit.

Our Church now maintains this custom on the vigil of Pentecost, prefigured by Cornelius, who, in order to deserve to receive baptism, was praying and fasting in his house at the ninth hour.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### On the Octave Days of Pentecost
Fifty days after the Lord’s Pascha—that is, the entire season of Pentecost—figure that joy which will exist in the life to come: either because the number forty, multiplied by its parts, makes fifty, or because forty contains the perfection of good works, and if ten, which represents the reward of works, is added to that number, it makes fifty; or whatever other explanation there may be, this is held without doubt: that the present fifty days signify the future rest, security, and joy. The seven days that follow recall the coming of the sevenfold Spirit, or our joy, in which we rejoice with the newly baptized, who are indeed being formed into the body of Christ.

We have written in our official books, “After the octave of Pentecost”; therefore we must discuss the same written notice. It is sufficiently clear that Pentecost expresses the number fifty. My simplicity does not know what “octaves” Pentecost may have, but since this festival—which, as we have said, recalls the coming of the Holy Spirit and received the name Pentecost from the reward of the newly baptized—the very octaves that can correspond to this mystery had retained the name borne by the first day of this festival.

How the octaves correspond to the coming of the Holy Spirit, or to the regeneration of the new person, we may gather some spark of light from the words of Saint Augustine in *The Sermon on the Mount*. After enumerating the sayings of the eight Beatitudes, he says, among other things:

> The eighth returns, as it were, to the beginning, because it shows and proves what has been completed and perfected.

And shortly afterward:

> There are therefore seven things that bring to perfection; for the eighth clarifies and demonstrates what is perfect, so that through these steps the others may be perfected, and the remaining ones may begin again, as it were, from the beginning.

It therefore seems to me that the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit, of which Isaiah speaks, also corresponds to these steps and sayings. And again:

> This eighth saying, which returns to the beginning and declares the perfected human being, perhaps signifies both circumcision on the eighth day in the Old Testament and the Lord’s resurrection after the Sabbath—which is certainly the eighth day and also the first—and the celebration of the octave festival days, which we celebrate in the regeneration of the new person.

Thus far Augustine.

The eighth day is also the first, according to the pattern of the eight Beatitudes. The first Beatitude says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” The eighth says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” These sayings pertain to the regenerated: those who are poor in this life for the sake of the kingdom of heaven must persevere to the end of life and receive the kingdom for which they labored here.

The baptism of the neophytes, although it takes place on Saturday, pertains to the baptism which the apostles received on the day of Pentecost. Its eighth day is the following Sunday, which we customarily call the octave of Pentecost. These are the festival days which blessed Augustine mentioned above as the octaves of the regenerated person.

The difference between our baptism and that of the apostles is that they were first baptized with water, then received the Holy Spirit once through Christ’s breathing while Christ was still on earth, and finally received him from heaven on the day of Pentecost. We, however, are baptized together in the presence of the bishop and receive the Holy Spirit through the bishop’s laying on of hands.

By imitating Christ’s death and resurrection, we ought to consider the completion of our baptism on Sunday, lest the members precede the head. And, following the practice of the primitive Church, we should consider the gift of the Holy Spirit on that same day at the third hour. Although, because of certain circumstances arising from the instability of the world, baptism or the laying on of hands is sometimes celebrated on different days or at different hours, nevertheless, because of the sacrament which it contains, it is assigned to those same days and hours.

For if the apostles received the Holy Spirit at the third hour because they were going to preach faith in the Holy Trinity, let us also turn this over in our minds: that at the same hour we received that same Spirit, in whom the Trinity is joined and who reveals that same Trinity.

Our baptism is in some way more closely related to the apostles’ baptism than to Christ’s baptism. Christ was not baptized in order to wash away his own sins, but for the sake of the pattern of his members, because there could be some in the future who would take pride in their innocence and think that baptism was not necessary for them. Therefore Christ’s baptism, although he was without sin, came first, so that no one deceived by foolish security might perish without baptism.

The Holy Spirit did not come upon Christ’s baptism in the form of a dove in order then to give him a gift which he did not possess; rather, he did so to show that he is present in our baptism and, through the simplicity of the dove, to demonstrate Christ’s simplicity and purity.

The apostles were baptized so that their sins might be wiped away in baptism, just as ours are; and therefore the Holy Spirit came to them through fire, because the rust of sin could cling to them through their weakness, and the power of the Holy Spirit wished to consume it forever.

For the power of fire consumes one material and restores and warms another: it consumes wood, but restores the substance of our body. So too the fire of the Holy Spirit consumes the rust of sins and warms our soul to the love of God and neighbor.

These two effects are the two denarii which the Lord gave to the innkeeper, according to the Evangelist Luke, on the following day—that is, on the second day—after he had bound up the wounds of the half-dead man, as though on the second day after baptism. There are rightly two, signifying the order of love, because one cannot love God who does not love one’s neighbor; nor does one rightly love one’s neighbor who does not love him for God’s sake.

Just as in baptism we are conformed to Christ’s death and burial, so in receiving the Holy Spirit we are conformed to the life-giving Spirit, who works in us the right order of love.

Because Christ’s death is remembered as having been completed at the ninth hour, those who are baptized into Christ’s death are baptized at the ninth hour. And because of the mystery of Christ’s burial, which is recalled on Saturday, Christ’s body is baptized on Saturday, so that after this burial it may rise on Sunday. For we ought to celebrate the beginning of the resurrection from Sunday.

Let that Sunday be the beginning of the new person who rose from the dead; and again, let it be his burial when the soul passes into rest without the body on Saturday, when the garments of the baptized are changed; and let the reception of their bodies be celebrated in the octave of Pentecost.

Or let the octave of Pentecost be celebrated for this reason: the work of the sevenfold Spirit is completed when it displays the perfected person, of whom the Apostle said: “If anyone does not stumble in speech, this is a perfect man.” Let the work of the sevenfold Spirit be celebrated for seven days, and on the eighth day its completion, manifestation, and glorification.

If this is so, the eighth day rightly recalls that same glorification in our offices; it returns to the beginning, as does the first day. Therefore, just as we celebrated the majesty of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, so we celebrate it in the octave of the same festival, so that, by recalling his gifts as often as possible, his love may deign to pour itself more abundantly into our hearts, until, according to the Gospel’s meaning, “the three measures of flour” are leavened into one, and everything that we think, understand, or live is referred to his love.

In commemoration of these three measures of flour, we sing three psalms at the night office on that same night, and we sing “Alleluia” until the end of the present Sunday. For this is how the festival is celebrated by the authority of divine law: from evening to evening, that is, from sunset to sunset.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Coming of the Lord

We wrote in the earlier books that preparation for the Lord’s coming begins in the fifth week and the fourth week before the Lord’s Nativity: in the fifth week because of the five ages of the world, in which there were elect people who believed, hoped for, and loved the Lord’s coming; in the fourth because of the four orders of books, namely, the Law, the Psalms, the Prophets, and the beginning of the Gospel.

Although Moses’ book recounts that elect men existed in the first, second, and third ages of the world, Moses wrote that whole book at the time assigned to the giving of the Law.

We also added that another interpretation could initiate the Lord’s coming in the fifth or fourth week, following the authorities of the Lectionary, Antiphonary, and Missal, whose author we believe to have been blessed Pope Gregory.

Both periods indicate to us a reasonable preparation: the five senses of the human being, which are present in our body, and the four elements of which our body consists. But now we add a third interpretation, which is no less appropriate to preparation for the Lord’s coming.

We say that there are two orders of righteous people in our Church who strive to prepare themselves to receive the coming Lord: one order strives in secular life, the other in spiritual life.

We can understand the order of secular people from what the reading says in the fifth week before the Lord’s Nativity:

> For this reason, the days are coming, says the Lord, when they will no longer say, “As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt,” but rather, “As the Lord lives, who brought out and led the offspring of the house of Israel from the land of the North.”

+ The Lord brought up the children of Israel from the land of the North when they returned from Babylonia to Judea. But the Lord more truly brings our good secular people to Judea—that is, to true confession—from the confusion of Babylonia, when he frees them from the power of the devil and from his body.

This happens through baptism, which faithful secular and spiritual people share. Those who suffer the harshness of the North in their minds are members of the devil. Just as the whole devil with his head in his body is worse than one of his members, so we have been freed from the devil’s power more fully than the children of Israel were from the kings of the Chaldeans.

The Gospel recalls these secular people in the reading that is read in the aforementioned fifth week. It recounts that the Lord fed five thousand men with five loaves. Bede explains this in his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke:

> There were about five thousand men, because there are five senses of the outward person. The five thousand men who followed the Lord signify those who, while still living in a secular condition, know how to use well the outward things they possess. They are rightly fed with five loaves, because such people still need to be instructed by the precepts of the Law.

+ The offices of the cantors and priests which are celebrated in the sacramentary, and which begin in the fourth week before the Nativity, raise spiritual people through the four Gospels toward a higher perfection. Hence the Epistle read on that same day says:

> Knowing that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep; for our salvation is now nearer than when we believed.

Of these spiritual people the aforementioned Bede says in the aforementioned book:

> For those who renounce the world completely are four thousand and are fed with seven loaves—that is, they are elevated by Gospel nourishment and instructed by spiritual grace. I think that the difference between them is mystically signified by the fact that five gilded columns were ordered to be made at the entrance of the tabernacle, but four before the sanctuary, that is, the Holy of Holies: beginners are chastened by the Law so that they may not sin, whereas the perfect are admonished through grace to live more devotedly for God.

Typically, through the song which is renewed in the fourth week before the Lord’s Nativity, we understand the joy of the minds of the perfect. If through the five weeks those people are signified who still lament recent sins through repentance, then through the four weeks we rightly understand those who advance with spiritual joy from virtue to virtue, in which the God of gods will be seen in Zion.

These two orders existed in the Old Testament, and they exist now. The renewal of the song signifies the joy of the elect, who rejoice greatly at the coming of their beloved Lord.

To them belongs the verse sung at evening:

> “Drop down, heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain the righteous one; let the earth be opened, and let it bring forth the Savior.”

They are the perfect heavens; they are the clouds. They announce subtle things, like dew, concerning the Lord’s Incarnation when they explain, “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” They rain down more substantial things when they narrate how Joseph betrothed Mary, how Christ was born in Bethlehem, how he was found in a manger, and other such matters.

The earth was opened: namely, the womb of the holy virgin Mary, without harm to her virginity; and it brought forth the shoot of the fragrance of the whole world, whose good odor spreads throughout the world.

Now many hearts of the faithful are warmed by the voice of preachers, and they bring forth true faith in Christ: joy, peace, patience, and the other shoots which the Holy Spirit makes fruitful.

Another verse at the morning office says:

> “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.”

This means: strive after good works and pious thoughts. The aforementioned verse recalls this ministry, which preachers ought to undertake during the days of the Lord’s coming.

Although good servants watch for the coming of their Lord with joy, they recall an even greater joy in his presence. For this reason we reserve certain elements of our office until the presence of the Lord’s Nativity, namely, “Glory to God in the highest” and the splendid vestment of the dalmatics—if indeed the practice is now as I have seen it performed in certain places.

The Apostle Paul indicates the preparation necessary for us in the aforementioned Epistle, which is read in the fourth week before the Lord’s Nativity:

> “The night has passed, but the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light. Let us walk honorably as in the day, not in revelry and drunkenness, not in sleeping chambers and indecencies, not in strife and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ.”

Just as a subject’s mind is moved more and more toward the care of receiving his superior through repeated and more frequent messages, so we are moved more and more toward concern for our preparation to receive the Lord through the renewal of the song.

Therefore, eight days before the Nativity of the Lord, nearly the entire text of the responsories and antiphons is renewed, so that through this we may be stirred more frequently to cleanse away all the refuse of shameful and earthly thoughts and prepare a worthy dwelling—adorned, that is, with pious thoughts—for the King of kings and Lord of lords.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the Nativity of the Lord

Although the Son of God was the only-begotten Son, he wished to join brothers to himself. He descended to the human race and assumed a human being in order to make brothers for himself, despising no one whom he recognized as obedient to the commands of his precepts, but receiving him in a brother’s place.

As has often been said, the time of the present age is divided into three periods: the period of the natural law, the period of the written Law, and the period of the New Testament.

Three outstanding men existed under the natural law: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Although many were like them, God himself very frequently recalls in Scripture that he is specially their God, saying: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”

To these three we assign three psalms of the first section of the nocturnal office, especially since these three are placed first in Christ’s genealogy. Through them we bring to remembrance all the elect fathers who lived under the natural law, and through Christ’s coming were joined to the choir of the holy angels, so that, just as the angels rejoice with the Holy Trinity, they too might rejoice with it.

The second section recalls those whom Christ made his brothers from the Mosaic Law, who were exercised by the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets. He likewise led them into the fellowship of the holy angels, so that they too might rejoice with the Holy Trinity.

He also adopted brothers for himself in the New Testament, through the primitive Church, through the obedience of the Gentiles, and through Jewish recognition.

Because his coming honored these people more than the earlier fathers, so that, if they are found worthy, when they depart from the world they are immediately transferred to heaven and joined to the fellowship of the holy angels—something the fathers had long awaited while murmuring within the chambers of hell—therefore “Alleluia” is celebrated in those antiphons which recall them, as in:

> “He called upon me, Alleluia,”

and again:

> “The Lord made it known, Alleluia.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Octaves at the Nativity of the Lord

The octaves are celebrated because the first days converge, just as one Sunday converges with another, and they are celebrated with the same rite. When subsequent good works return to the first, we in some manner celebrate octaves.

There was such great misery among human beings before Christ’s coming that no one attained the same innocence which the first human being possessed before he sinned. Circumcision, too, which is celebrated on the eighth day, was performed in remembrance of the first innocence—that is, so that the mind might be circumcised from every carnal thought—although it is itself also a figure of future people.

Through baptism Christ restored this same innocence to the human race; therefore on the eighth day, that is, on Sunday, the resurrection from baptism is recalled.

The difference between those who first imitate human innocence and those who existed in the Old Testament is this: although the latter were righteous, they were nevertheless held within the chambers of hell before Christ’s coming; the former enter the kingdoms of heaven.

And because our Redeemer wishes to lead us to a better condition than the one possessed by the first Adam, an eighth day is still awaited, which will come in the resurrection of bodies.

The first Adam was so innocent that he could sin if he wished. We receive innocence through baptism in such a way that we can sin and can will to sin; but after receiving our bodies, no one will be able, and no one will wish, to sin.

Therefore, since the octaves were instituted so that they might return to the first, we must consider what returns to the first day of the Nativity in the octaves of the Lord.

On the first day of the Nativity he came forth from the Virgin’s womb and was found in a manger wrapped in cloths. Did he come forth again from the Virgin’s womb on the eighth day and was he found in the manger, with the things read as having been spoken by the angels on the first day celebrated again? Nevertheless, we can find in what way the eighth day appropriately corresponds to the first.

We understand two purposes in Christ’s Nativity: first, that Christ came to human beings; second, that human beings came to Christ.

Augustine says concerning this in the first book of *On Christian Doctrine*:

> For one does not move toward him, who is present everywhere, by movements through places, but by good zeal and good conduct. We cannot do this unless Wisdom itself deigns to accommodate itself even to our great weakness, so that it might provide us with an example of living. It could not do so otherwise than in a human being, since we too are human beings. But because, when we come to Wisdom, we act wisely, while, when it comes to us, it is thought by proud people to have acted foolishly; and because, when we come to it, we grow strong, while, when it comes to us, it is considered weak: “the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings, and the weakness of God is stronger than human beings.” Since it is itself our homeland, it also made itself the way to the homeland for us. And although it is everywhere present to the sound and pure inner eye, it deigned to appear even to the bodily eyes of those whose eye was weak and unclean. Because the world could not know God through wisdom in the wisdom of God, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe. Therefore it is said to have come to us not by moving across distances of place, but by appearing to mortals in mortal flesh. It came there where it was, because it was in this world, and the world was made through it.

We celebrate Christ’s coming to human beings on the day of his Nativity; we celebrate human beings’ coming to Christ in his octaves.

This is easily recognized from the antiphons sung at the morning office. The first antiphon at the Nativity of the Lord, “The woman in childbirth has brought forth the king,” speaks specifically of the Lord’s Nativity. The first antiphon in the octave of the Lord says, “O wondrous exchange.” When it says “exchange,” it shows that one thing is given and another received. Christ gave his divinity and received our humanity. We celebrate what he gave in his Nativity, and what he received in the octave.

The members joined to the head rejoice together in the present festival. If anyone wishes to consider the following antiphons, he can recognize that the antiphons of the Lord’s Nativity specifically display his birth, while those of the Lord’s octave display the joining of his members.

In the antiphon “When you were born,” the Lord is called from the person of a human being; and at the end a human being speaks to God: “We praise you, our God.” The third, “The bush which Moses had seen,” speaks from the person of the members to the Mother of God: “Intercede for us.” The fourth again has at the end: “We praise you, our God.”

The fifth preserves the words of John the Baptist, by which he demonstrated the benefit given to us from Christ’s coming, saying:

> “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

The antiphon sung in the Gospel both displays the Lord’s presence among human beings and the assumption of the human being by him. For it says:

> “A wondrous mystery is declared: today the natures are renewed.”

How the natures are renewed Gregory Nazianzen explains in his book *On the Second Epiphanies*, saying:

> What is done concerning us, or for us? A new and unheard-of exchange of natures takes place, and God becomes human.

And shortly afterward:

> The Son of God began to be the son of a human being—not being changed from what he was, but assuming what he was not—so that the one who could not be contained might be contained, and through the intervening flesh, as though through a veil placed between, might speak with us. For it was not possible for this corruptible and fragile nature of ours to bear the unmingled nature of his divinity. Therefore things that are unmixed are mingled, and not only is God joined to our birth, or the heavenly mind to flesh, or the timeless one to time, but childbirth is joined to virginity, suffering is reconciled to the impassible, and the cup of death is offered to the immortal.

The antiphon continues:

> “What he was, he remained.”

That is, the Word, who wished to manifest himself to us through the material of flesh, remained what he had been: unchangeable light and eternal God, not changed into any creature.

It continues:

> “And what he was not, he assumed.”

These words display the assumption of the human being, since Christ deigned to assume a human being into one and the same person of God. Therefore the members of the head are rightly said to have passed into God.

Hence Augustine says in his twenty-sixth sermon on John:

> What, then, is it to believe in him? It is to love by believing, to cherish by believing, to go into him by believing, and to be incorporated into his members.

It continues:

> “Suffering neither mixture nor division.”

That is, he did not suffer the mixture which Sabellius asserts, making the Father and the Son one person; nor the division which Arius babbles.

Concerning the Lord’s circumcision, the labor of the holy interpreters makes me abundantly secure.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Theophany and the Ὑπαντή [Hypapante, the Presentation]

We omit one element in the Theophany from those which we celebrate at the Lord’s Nativity: namely, the invitatory.

It has often been said that the institutor of the office wished, as far as he could, to bring every action of that time back to our memory in the customary office, when the events we recall took place.

Therefore, because he wished to distinguish in this way our good invitation—by which the faithful are invited and encouraged to pray to God—from the invitation of Herod, who gathered the scribes and rulers of the Jews in order to learn where Christ would be born, intending to kill him, he omitted the invitatory of the present office.

The present nocturnal office strives to make known to us three notable events manifested through Christ’s coming: the coming of the Magi, Christ’s baptism, and the miracle performed by Christ from water.

The second and third are recalled briefly in the third nocturn and in the antiphon “Today the Church is joined to the heavenly Bridegroom.” But it sings openly and fully of the coming of the Magi in the two preceding nocturns.

This also seems especially appropriate to the order of the other offices. The office sung on the night of his Nativity, however, resounds with his infancy. The memory recalled through the offices of the cantors concerning the Lord’s octave and his circumcision sends forth sparks concerning his infancy, and similarly concerning what takes place in the Ὑπαντή.

It was therefore appropriate that the present office should touch especially on the events performed around his infancy.

Moreover, apostolic men were striving to transfer the general baptism from the present festival to the festivals of Pascha and Pentecost. Many therefore strove to frequent this festival because many believe that the Lord was baptized by John at this festival.

Hence it can appear that the present office speaks briefly of his baptism and fully of the coming of the Magi.

To make these matters clearer, I insert what Saint Leo the pope wrote concerning the aforementioned festivals, saying in the eighth chapter of the *Decretals*:

> The order of the events to be accomplished temporally through Jesus Christ our Lord took its beginning from the Incarnation of the Word. Thus there is one time when, with the angel announcing it, the blessed Virgin Mary believed that she would conceive through the Holy Spirit and conceived; another when, with her virgin integrity preserved, the child was born and was announced to the shepherds amid the rejoicing of the heavenly ministers; another when the infant was circumcised; another when the legal sacrifice was offered for him; another when the three Magi, stirred by the brilliance of the new star, arrived from the East in Bethlehem and worshiped the little child, venerating him through the mystical offering of gifts. Nor are the days the same on which he was taken away from the wicked Herod by a divinely ordered transfer to Egypt, or on which, after the persecutor’s death, he was called from Egypt to Galilee. Among these various acts of dispensation, bodily growth also proceeded. The Lord grew, as the Evangelist testifies, in the advances of age and grace.

The third nocturn of the present festival recalls three stages of believers: the Jewish people before the reception of the Gentiles; the Gentile people after the rejection of the Jewish people; and again the Jewish people at the end of the world.

In the first nocturn the understanding of the Magi is recalled: they understood that Christ was God. In the second nocturn the same understanding is recalled in which they perceived that Christ was king. In the third, the understanding is recalled in which they perceived that Christ had come in order to teach human beings that, through his baptism, it was necessary for them to be baptized, and through baptism to die to their father the devil, to his works, and to his pomps. In Christ’s baptism his death and burial are recalled.

We recall this third section through the Mass Introit chants from the octave of the Theophany until the Presentation of the Lord, unless the season of Septuagesima should anticipate us.

The first Introit after the octave of the Theophany, according to the order of our Antiphonary, is:

> “Upon a high throne I saw a man seated, whom a multitude of angels worship.”

This is the vision of the apostles and apostolic men: namely, that they should understand in their minds that the same Lord who was worshiped by the Magi as an infant, and whose presentation is awaited at this time until the fortieth day after his Nativity, governs the heavenly powers and is worshiped by them.

The second is:

> “Let the whole earth worship you, O God.”

This pertains to the multitude of believers: the one whom the three Magi first worshiped is afterward worshiped by all believers from Asia, Africa, and Europe.

Now, around the week in which the Presentation of the Lord is celebrated, this is sung:

> “Worship him, all his angels.”

Hence the Apostle says:

> “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth.”

Ambrose explains this in his Epistle to the Philippians:

> For this is granted to him: that all should worship him, and that all should confess Jesus Christ as God, made so in the glory of God the Father—that is, possessing such glory as it is right for one who claims God as his Father to possess, because of the union which he has with the Only-Begotten.

And shortly afterward:

> The invisible heavenly powers.

Peter also says concerning this same Son of God:

> “Having gone into heaven, angels, authorities, and powers having been subjected to him.”

Hence Bede says in his treatise on the same Epistle of Peter:

> No one doubts that the angels and all the powers and authorities of the heavenly Father were always subject to the Son of God, whom, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, they praise, fear, and worship as the one God without beginning. But blessed Peter rightly judged that it was necessary to remind us that the humanity he assumed was exalted through resurrection to such great glory that, by an incomparable height, it is placed above the power of every angelic dignity.

This Introit either contains the Ὑπαντή within itself or possesses the beginning of the same Ὑπαντή within its eight days, unless Septuagesima should come beforehand through the anticipation of Pascha.

The aforementioned Introits suggest the benefits Christ has bestowed on us to gladden our hearts. Therefore, with two of them, we sing the offertories “Rejoice.” We ought to rejoice because Christ’s benefits not only free us from the lower hell but also from the chambers of hell and lead us as far as the vision of eternal glory.

Hence the verse of the responsory sung in the week of the Ὑπαντή says:

> “For the Lord has built Zion, and he will be seen in his glory.”

Augustine says concerning this in his exposition of the Psalms:

> But when he comes to judge with his angels, when all nations will be gathered before him—

And shortly afterward:

> “The Lord has built Zion, and he will be seen in his glory”—he who was first seen there in his weakness.

From this verse we can conjecture that the institutor of the offices wished to indicate that the Lord’s presentation in the temple should stir us to present ourselves to him and to the Father.

The forty days during which the Lord’s presentation is awaited display the entire condition of the holy Church here in the present age, during which she must labor throughout the four parts of the world to fulfill the ten commandments of the Law—that is, to live justly and devoutly in this age while awaiting the blessed hope, when she will see the Lord in his glory and the choirs of angels worshiping God.

The same perseverance in good devotion is figured by the long tunic which Joseph wore as a prefiguration of Christ’s body and which we clerics wear, either in daily use or in the Church.

Through it we admonish the people of God to strive to cover themselves with good works until the end of the world. Hence Gregory says in the first book of the *Moralia*:

> For what is the long tunic but completed action? Just as a long tunic extending downward covers the body to the ankle, so a good action covers a person before the eyes of God until the end of life.

To carry lighted candles in one’s hands at the Ὑπαντή means that, at the presentation of oneself, each person brings his works with him, in which he may appear bright and shining in the assembly of the holy angels.

In their commemoration, the number nine is celebrated in the nocturnal office of the Ὑπαντή.

After the offices just mentioned, when Septuagesima arrives, we change the song of joy into one of tribulation, so that from it we may draw into our memory the disposition to which we ought to be bound according to our merits, and so that through the guidance of humility we may arrive at the Lord’s Passion.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Octaves of the Theophany

Christ was born temporally from the Virgin Mary, not for his own sake, as though he then began to exist when previously he did not exist. Before all times he was with the Father, through whom all these times were created. Rather, he was born so that a new light might appear to our minds, through which we might return to our Creator, since we were in darkness.

In the same way he was baptized, not because he needed baptism in order to wash away sins which he did not possess, but to give his Church a pattern of how she should seek to have her sins washed away. Hence he himself said in the Gospel:

> “For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.”

Christ died so that his body, which is the holy Church, might die to death. The human race had previously been dead to God because it obeyed death: we lived for death when we served it; we die to death when we renounce it.

To recall that Christ suffered for this reason—that we might die to sin—on the Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper our mortification is also recalled in certain offices, and the Lord’s Passion is read.

Hence it was said in the book already written concerning the fifth variation:

> If the days after Friday had followed in which it was necessary to grieve, perhaps we would have celebrated the octave of the Lord’s Passion—that is, through the celebration of the office we would have recalled that we ought earnestly to die to death.

A person dies to lust when he preserves chastity; he dies to envy when he possesses chastity; he dies to unbelief when his heart is cleansed by faith.

In the two readings read on the Friday of the Lord’s Passion, we observe two deaths celebrated on the same day. The reading from Exodus reveals Christ’s death; that from Hosea, the death of his members, concerning whom Paul says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires.” The Tract that follows the readings, “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High,” describes the whole protection by which the saints, placed in combat, are aided by the Lord. It is especially fitting to meditate on this psalm when someone approaches dangers and is surrounded by ambushes or afflictions, like a beast entangled in many snares, so that this may be heard from the Lord: “He will call upon me, and I will answer him; I am with him in tribulation.” For this reason it is now sung in the person of the members, because the Lord did not disdain to assume their feeling in himself. It is also sung on each night, because of nocturnal fears, or because sleep bears the likeness of death.

[Col. 1227C] In the Passion of our Savior, the wall of enmity was broken, and the two peoples were joined in one cornerstone; but this could not happen unless the Gentile people had first died to the death of vices. Since we have not proposed to investigate these matters here, but humbly beseech that they may have been implanted by that Spirit who breathes where he wills, we must now return to the subject at hand.

In the Theophany we celebrate how the Lord was sought by the Magi, found, and worshiped; how the guests rejoiced at the wedding; and how he was baptized. We can discern all these things from the antiphons sung at Matins. In its octave, the event for which Christ was baptized is celebrated—that is, our washing, through which our sins are cleansed. Such is the antiphon from the first day of the octave of the Theophany: “Renewing the old man, the Savior”; and from the second: “You who purify human defilements in spirit and fire.” A diligent investigator will be able to find the same meaning in what follows.

Since there are two commandments of love, namely of God and of one’s neighbor, just as by honoring the baptism of Christ, our God and Savior, we celebrated it at the Theophany, so let us also celebrate our baptism, already begun in our Head, in the octave of the Epiphany. That is, let us recall for what reason Christ was baptized: namely, because it was necessary that we should be baptized. And what benefit baptism brings, the antiphons show in the octave of the Theophany. Hence one of them says: “When the Lord had been baptized, the remission of our sins took place.”

The Meeting (Ὑπαντή) does not have an octave, because Christ was presented in the temple according to the Law. No teacher compels us on this account to present our infants in the temple on the fortieth day after their birth.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Birthdays of the Saints

What the birthdays of the saints are, we can learn from a single responsory sung on the feast of blessed Stephen. The responsory says: “Yesterday the Lord was born on earth, so that Stephen might be born in heaven.”

The birthdays of the saints reveal their births, by which they are born into fellowship with the nine orders of angels and into fellowship with the holy Fathers of the natural law, the written law, and the New Testament. Because of the glory of the New Testament, there are antiphons from the third period, “Alleluia,” such as these:

[Col. 1228B]

“The horns of the righteous will be exalted, Alleluia.”

“Light has risen for the righteous, Alleluia.”

“They kept his testimonies and his commandments, Alleluia.”

On the feasts that we commemorate, we commemorate by the number nine; standing, we pray while recalling the holy fellowship of the angels and holy Fathers who are already in everlasting joy.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Octaves of the Birthdays of the Saints

We customarily celebrate the octaves of certain saints’ birthdays—namely, those whose feast is held in greater renown among us—for example, the octaves of the apostles Peter and Paul and of the other saints, whose custom various Churches observe in celebrating octaves.

If we are unable to celebrate the birthdays of all the saints, how much less their octaves? We need not discuss which Churches honor one octave or another, but what the octaves themselves signify to us.

On the birthdays of the saints, we frequently celebrate those receptions in which the souls of the saints are received when they depart from the body. Augustine speaks of these receptions in his forty-sixth sermon on John:

“Just as, then, there are different custodians for those who are active in + offices, so there are different custodians of the dead and different merits of those who will rise. The poor man was received; the rich man was received—but the former in Abraham’s bosom, the latter where he thirsted and could not find even a drop of water. All souls, therefore”—I say this to instruct your charity—“when they have departed from the world, have their various receptions; the good have joy, and the wicked [Col. 1228D] torments. But when the resurrection has taken place, the joy of the good will be greater, and the torments of the wicked more severe, when they will be tormented together with the body.

“The holy patriarchs, prophets, apostles, martyrs, and good believers have been received in peace, yet all will still receive at the end what God promised. For the resurrection of the flesh, the destruction of death, and eternal life with the angels have also been promised: all of us together will receive these things. But the rest that is given immediately after death, if someone is worthy of it, each person receives when he dies. The patriarchs received it first—consider how long they have been at rest; the prophets afterward; the apostles more recently; the holy martyrs much more recently; and good believers every day. Some have been in this rest for a very long time, others not so long, others for fewer years, and others only recently. But when all awaken together from this sleep, they will receive what was promised +.”

On the birthdays of the saints, we rejoice together with the rest mentioned; on their octaves, however, with the resurrection of their bodies.

How worthy the eighth day is of honor, and what mystery it contains, the book of Leviticus shows. Hesychius the presbyter treats of this same Leviticus in his sixth book. Leviticus says:

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel: From the fifteenth day of this seventh month shall be the feast of Tabernacles for seven days to the Lord. The first day shall be called most solemn and most holy: you shall do no servile work on it, and for seven days you shall offer holocausts to the Lord; the eighth day also shall be most solemn [Col. 1229B] and most holy.”

Hence the aforementioned Hesychius says:

“He called the first of the seven days most solemn and most holy. For one who knows how to use present things as a tabernacle, the first day—that is, the beginning and origin—begins with the sanctification of rest. Therefore he very appropriately says: ‘You shall do no servile work,’ because those who regard the things that are in the world as a tabernacle and as transitory things serve no one in the world. He also commanded holocausts to be offered for seven days, showing that a perfect way of life ought to be followed throughout the whole period. When, therefore, we have passed through this present life, then we shall have the most solemn and most holy eighth day, namely, the age to come.”

And below:

“On the first day there is rest, and on the eighth day there is rest—not on the seventh, although he had proposed that the feast be celebrated with the number of seven days, but on the eighth. The first reason is that those who hold the Law according to the letter are not permitted to celebrate the feast. For the one who holds the Law according to the letter has been separated from the new people; it is the one who knows how to receive the Law according to the spirit and honor the eighth day, which, as we have said, signifies the resurrection of the dead.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Observance of Days throughout the Year

Where Saint Jerome explains the passage in Galatians, “You observe days and months and seasons and years. I fear that perhaps I have labored among you in vain,” he then adds the judgment of Christians against those who wish to object to us that we observe days and seasons—an objection for which novel Christians are rebuked by Paul.

Among other things, he says as follows:

“Let someone say: If it is not permitted to observe days, months, seasons, and years, then we too incur the same accusation when we observe the fourth day of the week, Parasceve, the Lord’s Day, the fast of Lent, the feast of Easter, the joy of Pentecost, and, according to the variety of regions, the various seasons established in honor of the martyrs.

“To this, the person who answers simply says: The days of Jewish observance are not the same as ours. For we do not celebrate the Passover of unleavened bread, but the Passover of the resurrection and the cross; nor do we count seven weeks toward Pentecost according to the custom of Israel, but we venerate the coming of the Holy Spirit. And so that the faith of the people gathered together might not grow weaker in Christ, certain days have therefore been appointed, so that we might all come together at the same time—not because that day on which we assemble is more solemn, but so that, on whatever day we ought to assemble, greater joy might arise from seeing one another.

“But the person who attempts to answer the opposing question more acutely affirms that all days are equal, and that Christ is not crucified only on Parasceve and raised only on the Lord’s Day, but that every day is holy because of the resurrection, and that he is always consumed in the flesh of the Lord. Fasts and assemblies on particular days, however, were instituted by prudent men for those who devote themselves more to the world than to God and cannot—or rather do not wish to—assemble in the church throughout the whole course of their lives and offer to God the sacrifice of their prayers before their human activities. For how many people are there who always practice even these few appointed times of prayer or fasting? Thus, although we are permitted either always to fast or always to pray, and, while rejoicing, continually to celebrate the Lord’s Day by receiving the Lord’s body, it is not likewise lawful for the Jews at every time to sacrifice the lamb, observe Pentecost, erect tabernacles, or fast every day.”

After the enumeration of the seasons that were observed at the time when blessed Jerome wrote these words, he gives the reason why Christians do not incur guilt by observing the seasons mentioned. The person who answers simply says that the days of Jewish observance are not the same as ours, together with the other words that follow.

And again below:

“But the person who attempts to answer the opposing question more acutely affirms that all days are equal, and that Christ is not crucified only on Parasceve and raised only on the Lord’s Day, but that every day is holy because of the resurrection, and that he is always consumed in the flesh of the Lord.”

The preceding defense, in which it is said that the days observed among us are not the same as those observed among the Jews, offers us some additional support. For this reason, during the time of the Lord’s Passion, we omit the customary greeting, because Judas falsely greeted the Lord; and we omit kneeling in prayer on Parasceve, which is done for the Jews, because they knelt while mocking Jesus; and we omit it in the prayer of the twelve readings, when the Passion of the three boys in the furnace is recalled, because, together with the faithless, they refused to worship the statue of Nebuchadnezzar with bended knee; and we omit the invitatory on the days of the Lord’s Passion, when they gathered for their wicked counsels concerning the Lord’s death.

Similarly, at the Theophany we omit the invitatory, when Herod gathered the Jewish sages with an evil purpose to inquire where Christ would be born.

We observe the fourth day of the week, Parasceve, the Lord’s Day, the fast of Lent, the feast of Easter, the joy of Pentecost, and, according to the variety of regions, the various seasons established in honor of the martyrs.

We observe the fourth day because, as Augustine says to Casulanus, on that day the Jews gathered and took counsel concerning the death of the Savior. We observe Parasceve because the same Savior suffered on it.

Since these days had anciently been observed according to the rite of the Roman Church, it became customary on those days to change the offices and celebrate Mass at the ninth hour, so that the people from outside might gather together when some new matter arose for which prayer was required, and for which the observance was being held.

Hence the aforementioned Jerome says above:

“Fasts and assemblies on particular days were instituted by prudent men for those who devote themselves more to the world than to God and cannot—or rather do not wish to—assemble in the church throughout the whole course of their lives and offer to God the sacrifice of their prayers before their human activities. For how many people are there who always practice even these few appointed times of prayer or fasting?” and so forth.

From the Roman Order we have the day of Saturday among the days observed, although Jerome did not count it [Col. 1231B] in the order of days of observance. For we know from many authors that Saturday, like the fourth day and Friday, was included among the days of fasting by the Romans. We also often find the office changed on it, as on the fourth and sixth days of the week; and especially on that day a blessing is given, because it is the day that the Lord blessed, and because it properly signifies the Holy Spirit, who is sevenfold.

Although the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, since God is spirit, and although the Father is holy and the Son is holy, the spirit of both is nevertheless called by the proper name “the Holy Spirit.”

Saturday was observed in different ways among the Easterners, among some Westerners, and also in the city of Rome. Saint Augustine treated this matter sufficiently in his letter to the presbyter Casulanus. I shall insert a few passages here:

“Concerning the difference,” he says to Casulanus, “from Urbicus: Let it not persuade you to praise the Christian city because it fasts on Saturday in such a way that you are compelled to condemn the Christian world because it eats.”

And again, from the reply of Saint Ambrose in the same letter, he says:

“When I am here, I do not fast on Saturday; when I am in Rome, I fast on Saturday. Whenever you come to a Church, observe its custom, if you do not wish either to suffer scandal or to cause it.”

It is written in the Life of blessed Ambrose that Ambrose himself fasted on the other days of the week, but ate on Saturday and Sunday.

Why he ate on Saturday or Sunday, the aforementioned Augustine shows in the aforementioned letter, writing about Saturday as follows:

“But on which days one ought not to fast, and on which one ought to fast, I do not find defined by a commandment of the Lord or of the apostles. And consequently I believe that—not for the sake of attaining the truth, which faith attains, or the righteousness in which the beauty of the king’s daughter is inward—but nevertheless for the sake of signifying eternal rest, where the true Sabbath is, relaxation is more fitting than restriction through fasting.”

And below:

“There are two things that cause us to hope for the blessedness of the righteous and the end of all misery: the death and the resurrection of the dead. In death there is rest, concerning which it is said through the prophet: ‘My people, enter your chambers; hide yourselves for a little while, until the Lord’s anger has passed.’ But in the resurrection there is perfect happiness in the whole human being, that is, in flesh [Col. 1232A] and spirit.

“From this it came about that, to signify both of these things, it was not thought appropriate to use the labor of fasting, but rather the joy of eating—except on the one paschal Saturday, on which, as we have said, the mourning of the disciples, because of the memory of what had happened, had to be signified by a longer fast.”

This understanding can be appropriately applied when we celebrate the feasts of the saints: at their earlier feasts we rejoice together with the souls of the saints, and at the octaves of those same saints, with the resurrection of their bodies.

For this reason all the Romans formerly used to fast on every Saturday, whereas Augustine has now said that one Saturday is to be observed. I speak of this in the past tense because I do not know how they conduct themselves now.

If any of the bishops wishes to imitate Ambrose, he will not in any respect be excluded from the fellowship of the saints. Let the people be instructed according to Saint Augustine, where he says in the aforementioned letter:

“Gladly obey your bishop in this matter; do not resist, and follow what he does without any scruple or dispute.”

+ So that every dispute may be absent from contentious people on account of these different fasts, provided that faith, hope, and charity are held in unity—things which all the teaching of the prophets and the knowledge of the Scriptures serve—Saint Augustine often repeats this verse in the aforementioned letter:

“The queen stood at your right hand, clothed in a golden garment, surrounded by variety.”

Among us also, in certain places, one day is observed—namely, Monday—which was not assigned for observance by the aforementioned authors, Saint Innocent, Saint Ambrose, Saint Augustine, or blessed Jerome. Our princes still sometimes commend it in fasting when a three-day fast, like that of the Ninevites, is proclaimed.

This, as I think, may derive its rule from Paul’s preaching, who said: “One person judges one day to be above another; another judges every day alike.”

Nevertheless, in explaining this, Ambrose says nothing about the other days; he introduces the fourth and sixth days of the week, in accordance with the custom maintained by the people known to him at that time.

Yet those fulfill what Paul says more truly who fast between the Lord’s Day and the third day of eating, on the intervening Monday; then again between the third day of the week and the fifth day of eating, they fast on Wednesday; and again between the fifth day of the week and the seventh day of eating, they fast on Friday. The Lord’s Day is prohibited for fasting in the book properly called the Canons.

Saint Augustine explains the reason for this prohibition in the aforementioned letter to Casulanus:

“To fast on the Lord’s Day,” he says, “is a great scandal, especially since the detestable heresy of the Manichaeans, which is very much and most clearly contrary to the Catholic faith and the divine Scriptures, has become known. They established this day for their hearers as though it were a lawful day for fasting, and consequently fasting on the Lord’s Day came to be regarded as something more horrifying.”

Saint Jerome places one Lent among the observances; we observe three Lents: before the Lord’s Easter, around the feast of Saint John, and before the Lord’s Nativity.

Let it be frequently practiced among us by devout minds. In Saint Jerome it is clear that the heretic Montanus established that observance of three Lents among his followers—that is, three Lents each year.

Among us too there is no doubt that we ought to prepare ourselves at the Lord’s coming through many pious works.

The birthdays of the saints are observed among us. Concerning these Augustine says in the aforementioned letter:

“On all the Lord’s Days, and throughout the fifty days after Easter, and on the solemn days of the martyrs in various places, and on every feast, people eat. We are accustomed, after the octave of the Lord’s Nativity, to celebrate the octaves of Saint Stephen, Saint John the Evangelist, and the Innocents, so that through the singing of those octaves we reach almost to the vigils of the Theophany.”

Concerning the fast that we undertake before the Lord’s Ascension, it is clear from which author it derives its beginning, and there is nothing to say about it, since the same blessed Augustine says:

“For in matters concerning which divine Scripture has established nothing certain, the custom of the people of God and the institutions of our ancestors are to be held as law.”

Nevertheless, we cannot say that nothing was written by the holy authorities concerning the joy of the days of Pentecost.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. When the Divine Mysteries Are Celebrated, with What Reverence and Fear One Should Stand in Church

Since we have briefly touched upon the birthdays of the saints, it is useful to append the words of Saint John Chrysostom, so that through them he may admonish me how I ought to restrain myself from superfluous words and laughter when I stand before the holy altar.

The same author says in his twelfth homily on the Epistle to the Hebrews:

“The priest of God stands, offering the prayer of all; but you laugh, fearing nothing? He, trembling, offers a prayer for you, but you despise it? Do you not heed the Scripture that says, ‘Woe to those who despise’? Do you not tremble? Do you not collect yourself?

“When you are about to enter a royal palace, you compose and adorn yourself in your clothing, your eyes, your gait, and everything else; but when you are about to enter here, where there truly is a royal palace, and one such as the heavenly palace is, do you laugh?

“I know indeed that you do not see; nevertheless hear this: the angels are present everywhere, and especially in the house of God they stand before the King, and all things are full of those bodiless powers.

“This speech is addressed also to women. In the presence of men they do not dare to do this so readily; and if they do, it is not always, but only at a time of relaxation. Here, however, you both veil yourself and cover your head.

“Tell me, woman: do you laugh while sitting in church? You entered to confess your sins, to fall prostrate before God, to ask and plead for your offenses, and you do this with laughter? How, then, will you be able to propitiate him?

“And what evil is laughter?” he says. “Laughter is not evil.”

“Is it therefore not evil?”

“It is evil—indeed, very evil—when it occurs at an unsuitable time, or rather, at an inopportune moment. Laughter has been given to us so that, when we have seen friends after a long time, we may do this; and when we see some offenders who are afraid, we may encourage them with laughter—not so that we may compel ourselves to laugh and always laugh. Laughter is present in our soul so that the soul may at times have relief, not so that it may be dissipated.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. Again on the Tonsure of Clerics

[Col. 1234A]

I remember saying earlier, with some doubt, whether the crown of our clerics first received its form from Saint Peter or from his successors, namely, the bishops of the city of Rome.

Later I found an authority on this matter in Beda, the servant of God, in his History of the English, chapter twenty-one, from a letter of Ceolfrid the abbot to Aytan, king of the Picts.

It is indeed permissible for us to profess that the difference in tonsure does not harm those whose faith in God is pure and whose charity toward their neighbor is sincere, especially since we never read that the Catholic Fathers had any controversy over the difference in tonsure, any more than they had a controversy over the difference concerning Easter or the faith.

Nevertheless, among all the tonsures that we have found either in the Church or throughout the human race, I would rightly declare that none should be followed and embraced more than the one worn on his head by him to whom the Lord said, when he confessed him: “You are Peter.”

And I believe that none should rightly be abominated and detested by all the faithful more than the one worn by him to whom the same Peter said, when he wished to purchase the grace of the Holy Spirit:

“May your money be with you in perdition, because you thought that the gift of God could be obtained with money. You have no share or lot in this word.”

Yet we are not tonsured into a crown for the reason that Peter was tonsured in this way, but because Peter was tonsured in this way in memory of the Lord’s Passion. Therefore we too, who desire to be saved through that same Passion, carry with him the sign of that Passion on the crown of our head, that is, on the highest part of our body.

For just as the whole Church, because it became the Church through the death of its Life-giver, customarily carries the sign of his holy cross on its forehead, so that it may frequently be defended from the assaults of evil spirits by the protection of this banner and may be taught by this repeated reminder that it too ought to crucify its flesh with its vices and desires, so it is also fitting that those who, whether by possessing the vow of a monk or the rank of cleric, must bind themselves for the Lord with the stricter reins of continence should also display on their heads the form of the crown that he himself wore in his Passion—a crown of thorns, which he bore in order to carry and remove from us the thorns and thistles of our sins.

Each person should display this form through his tonsure, so that even by the appearance of his forehead he may show that he is willing and ready to endure all mockery and reproach for him, and may signify that he always awaits the crown of eternal life which God promised to those who love him, and that, in order to receive it, he scorns both the adversities and the prosperities of the world.

The same Beda says of the tonsure in the Life of the Venerable and Most Holy Bishop Cuthbert:

“After, with the Lord’s help, he had received the yoke of Christ’s service and Peter’s form of tonsure in the shape of the crown of thorns encircling Christ’s head,” and so forth.

Let this suffice to demonstrate what the aforementioned servant of God, Beda, thought concerning the originator of our crown.

## CHAPTER XL. Again, on the Hour at Which Mass Should Be Celebrated by Those Who Are Free to Attend

[Col. 1235A]

We stated in the words of this work that the apostolic men prohibited the celebration of Mass before the third hour; nevertheless, I added what I had seen—namely, that Pope Leo recently celebrated Mass at dawn.

It was added in the Pontifical Deeds that Mass should be celebrated around the third hour for this reason: because at that same hour the Lord was crucified by the tongues of the Jews.

We add also, because of our established custom, that Mass may reasonably be celebrated at the sixth hour, since at the sixth hour of the day the Lord was crucified by the hands of his persecutors; likewise at the ninth hour, because then he gave up his spirit.

It is clear that Mass is celebrated [Col. 1235B] chiefly in remembrance of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ. That it is celebrated in his commemoration is manifest from the very words read in the canon:

“Whenever you do these things, you shall do them in remembrance of me.”

Hence we too are mindful, O Lord, we your servants and also your holy people, of the blessed Passion of Christ your Son, our Lord and God, as well as his resurrection from the dead and his glorious Ascension into heaven.

The things performed in the celebration of Mass after the canon has been begun recall the Lord’s Passion and resurrection and his Ascension into heaven. I have touched upon all these matters that occurred to me when I wrote about the office of the Mass.

Afterward I remembered that Saint Gregory had made known to us that Cassius, bishop of Narnia, came at the third hour to the solemn celebrations of Mass. I diligently sought to insert this here, to remind myself that, although I had seen the Apostolic Leo celebrate Mass at dawn, as well as other priests in the Roman Church, Saint Gregory had nevertheless not forgotten that Mass ought to be celebrated at the third hour.

This is especially so since the same pope reports in his homily delivered in the basilica of Saint Sebastian on the saint’s feast that Cassius the bishop had been commanded, through a certain priest, to persist in the work he was doing, with our Lord Jesus Christ saying:

“Do what you are doing; work at what you are working on. Let your hand not cease, let your foot not cease. On the birthday of the apostles you will come to me, and I will give you your reward.”

+ What that bishop was doing, the same Saint Gregory makes clear in the same homily: namely, that he celebrated Mass every day.

He also reveals below at what hour he went to Mass, saying:

“When he had heard these things, the bishop prostrated himself in prayer with great contrition of heart; and although he had come to offer the sacrifice at the third hour, because of the length of his extended prayer he prolonged it until the ninth hour.”

As I think, Saint Gregory wished the celebration of Mass to take place at the same hour that he knew to be acceptable to the Lord, through the exhortation made by him to that bishop, whom he said had come at the third hour to the solemn celebrations of Mass—while nevertheless preserving the established practice concerning the ninth hour on days of abstinence.

For if Mass is celebrated at other hours according to an established practice, there is some reason by which those hours may be defended. Such is the case at the Nativity of the Lord, when Mass is celebrated at night because of the birth of the Bread that is now eaten daily from the altar, or because of the concert of the angels, as we have already related.

On that same morning Mass is celebrated because of the rising of the new light, or because of the shepherds’ visit to the Lord’s manger, where they found food with which the souls of the saints are daily refreshed.

Similarly, we have offices established at the feasts of John the Evangelist and John the Baptist at the first light of day. Each of them offered to God within himself a kind of singular sacrifice from his mother’s womb—that is, from the moment he received the light of this world.
