John the Evangelist offered the sacrifice of virginity from the beginning of this light; John the Baptist offered the sacrifice of abstinence, for he drank neither wine nor strong drink and remained a Nazirite throughout his life.

On the holy night of the Lord’s Resurrection we celebrate Mass because of that same resurrection, which was completed on that night, and because of the visit of the holy women to the Lord’s tomb.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the Burial Rites of the Dead
Lord Bede openly explains in the funeral rites of Saint Cuthbert how a deceased priest ought to be clothed. For he writes as follows concerning his funeral rites:

[Col. 1236C]

“After, therefore, Cuthbert, the bishop of holy memory, had completed the communion, raised his eyes and hands to God, and commended his soul to him, he breathed forth his spirit and, sitting without a groan, died in the *Life of the Fathers*. Carried by sailors to our island, his whole body raised, his head wrapped in a napkin, the offering placed upon his holy breast, clothed in priestly vesture, prepared in his shoes to meet Christ, wrapped in a waxed shroud, and having a mind rejoicing with Christ.”

There can be no doubt that this was also the custom of the Roman Church in this matter, as it was among the English, especially since the Anglo-Saxons had received their first bishop Augustine from that Church, and at that time the Roman Church was especially renowned because of the authority of its most learned bishop Gregory. Later they received from the same Church the archbishop Theodore, highly skilled in both languages, Greek and Latin.

But I began to wonder what the lord Bede meant when he said, “prepared in his shoes to meet Christ”: whether he meant that Cuthbert would rise again in that same clothing, or in the good morals signified by clothing.

Meanwhile, I began to think about Christ: whether he was clothed in any garments after he rose from the dead; and, if he was, whether he ascended into heaven with those garments, or only with his natural body, which was spiritual. I began to consider whether he appeared clothed to those two men who saw him on the road, when they thought him to be a stranger; also to Mary Magdalene, when she believed him to be the gardener; likewise to the disciples, when he ate and drank with them; or whenever he appeared to them.

I also considered that the angels had appeared clothed. Thus it is written concerning them according to John: “She saw angels in white sitting.” And on the day of his assumption into heaven it is written: “Behold, two men stood beside them in white garments, and they said: ‘This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.’” Here I do not know whether he was clothed at that time or not. For we know that the angels said that he would come to judgment in the form in which he then ascended into heaven.

In the same way I thought that, when he was transfigured on the mountain, he did not lose his garments, but that they became white as snow.

After this it occurred to me that the first human beings, Adam and Eve, were naked before they sinned; and our Redeemer came to restore us to their condition, though to a far better one. After they sinned, God made tunics of skins for them.

Without prejudice to the faith, although I do not know whether human beings will come clothed in the manner in which Christ appeared after the resurrection and the angels were seen, or naked as the first human beings were, I nevertheless believe that no deformity will exist in spiritual bodies capable of offending or causing disgust to spiritual eyes.

Amid these uncertainties I thought of reading Augustine’s *City of God* and his letter to Paulinus concerning the care to be taken for the dead. I excerpted a few passages from it. From them it can nevertheless be understood that we ought to perform funeral rites for our dead more for our own salvation than for theirs; that, if funeral rites have not been performed, this causes no harm to those who have died in Christ; and that whoever performs funeral rites for them does so out of love for the one who promised that their bodies would rise again.

The same man says in the first book of *The City of God*, chapter twelve:

“Many Christian bodies, therefore, the earth did not cover; but no one separated any of them from heaven and earth, which is wholly filled by the presence of him who knows from where to raise up what he created. Indeed, it is said in the psalm: ‘They gave the dead bodies of your servants as food to the birds of heaven, the flesh of your saints to the beasts of the earth. They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.’ And shortly afterward: ‘Although these things appear harsh and dreadful in the sight of human beings, the death of his saints is precious in the sight of the Lord.’ Therefore all these things—the care of the corpse, the arrangement of burial, and the procession of the funeral rites—are more consolations for the living than aids for the dead.”

Again, in the same book, chapter thirteen:

“Nevertheless, the bodies of the dead are not for that reason to be despised and cast aside, especially the bodies of the just and faithful, which the Holy Spirit used as organs and vessels for every good work. For if a father’s clothing and ring, or anything of that kind, is dearer to descendants in proportion as their affection for their parents is greater, then certainly the bodies themselves ought not to be despised, since we carry them in a far more intimate and closely joined manner than any garments. For these bodies belong not to ornament or assistance applied from without, but to the very nature of the human being.

“Therefore the funerals of the just of old were cared for with dutiful devotion, funeral rites were celebrated, and burial was provided; and, while they were alive, they themselves entrusted to their sons the burial or even the transfer of their bodies. Tobias, too, is commended by the testimony of the angel for having pleased God by burying the dead.

“The Lord himself, destined to rise on the third day, praises and commends for proclamation the good deed of the devout woman who poured costly ointment over his limbs and did this for his burial. And those who received his body from the cross and carefully and honorably covered and buried it are commendably commemorated in the Gospel.

“Yet these authorities do not teach that any sensation exists in corpses; rather, they signify that the bodies of the dead also belong to the providence of God, to whom such offices of devotion are pleasing, on account of the faith by which the resurrection is affirmed. Here too one profitably learns how great the reward may be for alms that we provide to the living and conscious, if even what is done in the form of attentiveness and service to the lifeless limbs of human beings is not lost with God.”

From these words of Saint Augustine it is evident that we ought to celebrate funeral rites around the bodies of dead human beings because God wishes to raise them again.

The funeral rites of the dead are therefore manifest, and the human affection that ought to be shown in connection with the funeral rites of the dead has also been made manifest. Now we must speak of the evening, night, and morning offices.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the Offices for the Dead

We have it written in a certain Sacramentary that the offices for the dead are to be performed on the third, seventh, and thirtieth days. I do not understand this as though someone who wishes to perform the offices for the dead on the third day ought to pass the preceding two days without supplications; or that someone who does so on the seventh day should keep the office during the six preceding days; or that someone who does so on the thirtieth day should spend twenty-nine days in idleness. Rather, when it is said that the offices for the dead are celebrated on the third day, this may be understood in two ways: either that on the third day within the seven, and on the seventh within the thirty, the offices for the dead are celebrated more solemnly than on the other days; or that the third day completes that observance. We say the same concerning the seventh and thirtieth days.

For these three periods we shall set forth the authority of the Holy Scriptures. In the Book of Wisdom it is said concerning funeral rites:

“My son, pour out tears for the dead, and, as though he had suffered grievous things, begin to mourn; and, according to judgment, attend to his body, and do not neglect his burial. Because of the carrying-away, bear his mourning bitterly for one day, and console yourself because of the sadness; and make mourning according to his merit for one day, or two lest there be detraction.”

Here, first, he said that because of the carrying-away one should bear mourning for one day, and afterward, lest there be detraction, for one or two days; thus he introduces three days into mourning.

Through the third day of the commended deceased we may recall to mind the third day of the Lord’s resurrection, so that by this same number we may pray for our dead person, that he may deserve, through the remission of sins, to become a participant in Christ’s resurrection.

According to the Septuagint, the Ninevites fasted for three days so that, in Christ’s glorification through his resurrection from the dead, their sins might be blotted out. Hence Augustine says in his book *Questions on Genesis*:

“Nor should we believe that the Seventy Interpreters, whom the Church is accustomed to read, were in error when they did not say forty days, but three days, and that Nineveh would be overthrown.”

And shortly afterward:

“They placed three days, although they were not unaware that forty days were read in the Hebrew books, so that it might be understood that sins were dissolved and wiped away in the glorification of our Lord Jesus Christ. Of him it was said: ‘He was handed over because of our offenses, and he rose again for our justification.’ The glorification of the Lord is recognized both in the resurrection and in the ascension into heaven.”

The second celebration for the dead, on the seventh day, has authority in the passage recalled from Genesis:

“Joseph had chariots and horsemen in his company, and a very large crowd was formed. They came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is situated beyond the Jordan, and, celebrating funeral rites with great and vehement mourning, they completed seven days.”

Hence the aforementioned Augustine writes in the aforementioned book of *Questions*:

“And he mourned for his father seven days. I do not know whether mourning for nine days is found celebrated anywhere in Scripture for any of the saints; among the Latins this is called a *novendial* observance. Therefore it seems to me that those Christians who maintain this number in connection with their dead should be prohibited from doing so, since it belongs more to pagan custom.”

The seventh day, however, has authority in the Scriptures. Thus it is written elsewhere: “The mourning of the dead is for seven days, but the fool mourns all the days of his life.”

The number seven, on account of the mystery of the Sabbath, is especially a sign of rest. Therefore it is rightly offered to the dead as to those who are resting.

+ The third observance is performed on the thirtieth day. Aaron and Moses lead us to this authority. Concerning it, it was said in the writing about the Mass:

“For this reason we contend on behalf of our dead, so that they may be able to become participants in those whom Christ recalled from the prison of hell. In that commemoration we likewise celebrate offices for them, just as they are celebrated on those days when Christ descended into hell and on which he is believed to have died.”

For we cannot understand that all those who depart from the body immediately enter the kingdoms of heaven, or that others are received into other places of custody.

Thus we perform the offices for the dead in one manner. There are also places in which, generally for all the dead, prayer is offered at the evening and morning offices throughout the year, except at Pentecost and on feast days. There are others in which Mass is celebrated daily for the same persons. There are still others in which, at the beginning of the month, nine psalms, nine lessons, and an equal number of responsories are sung for them.

What this signifies Augustine shows in his book to Paulinus concerning the care to be taken for the dead:

“Supplications for the spirits of the dead are not to be omitted. They are to be made for all the deceased within the Christian community, even when their names are not spoken, whom the Church has received under a general commemoration, so that those who in this life lack parents, children, or any relatives or friends may be aided by one pious common mother. But if these supplications, which are made for the dead with right and devout faith and devotion, were lacking, I think that it would profit their spirits nothing if their lifeless bodies were placed in any holy places.”

## CHAPTER XLIII. Repetition Concerning the Three Baptismal Psalms

We said above that, through the nights, the three baptismal psalms recall to us the three works of Christ: the expulsion of demons, the effect of healings, and our resurrection, together with the Lord’s three-day burial. In another way, the offices of the baptismal days signify the Holy Spirit’s leading into the land of uprightness; and the three psalms of the nights signify faith, hope, and charity.

But now we add that in the works of darkness, or in the night, there are three original vices: the devil’s suggestion, the pleasure of the flesh, and the consent of the mind. Because of these three vices, in place of the three virtues—faith, hope, and charity—we sing three psalms, by which the aforementioned vices may be driven away from our catechumens.

How the office ought to be celebrated on the Lord’s Sunday night, which is the eighth day after the Lord’s Easter, is shown by the preceding words, in which the eight beatitudes, the work and perfection of the sevenfold Spirit, and the eight weekdays of the regenerated human being are recounted.

## CHAPTER XLIV. Repetition Concerning the Antiphon “The River’s Impetus,” Which Is Sung at the Theophany

[Col. 1240C]

People are accustomed to murmur concerning the psalm “Our God is our refuge,” asking why it is placed in the third division in an inverted order. Concerning this we speak as follows, following the order of the Gospel.

The Magi came to adore the Lord before he was baptized. Therefore the offices celebrated in the first division signify Christians and, in a certain manner, imitate the gifts and services of the Magi. The Magi offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh. For just as gold is the pre-eminent metal, so this gift is assigned to the pre-eminent office, namely, the royal one. Through this gift offered to Christ, royal power may be signified, coming to Christ with all its subjects. This is what the antiphons of the second division signify.

Frankincense, burned by fire, gives off a sweet fragrance and belongs to the ministry of priests. The frankincense then offered to Christ can signify the priests and religious ministers of the Church, who were to offer Christ the frankincense of prayers from the fire of their hearts.

Through myrrh the entire company of the elect may be signified. Myrrh is a burning spice. Whoever is prepared in mind to die with Christ for Christ’s name offers myrrh. In this company are gathered the people and populace who are marked out in the antiphons: “Offer to the Lord, sons of God”; “All the nations whom you have made”; and “Come, let us adore.”

The third division, moreover, celebrates Christ’s baptism; hence we sing in it the responsory “In the Form of a Dove” and “Today in the Jordan.”

[Col. 1241A]

The antiphon “The River’s Impetus” shows the hearts of the apostles filled with the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost. Afterward they preached baptism always and everywhere. The third division, through its psalms, contains the event that occurred at the time when the apostles preached baptism. The psalm “Our God is our refuge” corresponds to this event.

The antiphon shows how the Holy Spirit gladdened the apostles so that through baptism they might sanctify the Lord’s tabernacle. The other verses indicate that worldly people acted against this, as in these verses:

“Therefore we will not fear when the earth is shaken and the mountains are moved into the heart of the sea. Its waters roared and were troubled; the mountains were shaken by his strength.”

The psalm “Sing to the Lord” shows that all the gods of the nations are demons. Again, concerning the ferocity of pagan unbelievers and the joy of believers, it says:

“Let the sea and its fullness be stirred; the fields and all that is in them will rejoice,”

and so forth.

“The Lord has reigned; let the earth rejoice; let the many islands be glad”—these verses show the preaching of the apostles and likewise the overthrow of idols. Thus the verse says:

“His flashes have illumined the world; the earth saw and was shaken. The mountains melted like wax before the face of the Lord, before the face of the Lord, all the earth.”

And in what follows:

“Let all who worship carved images be confounded.”

## CHAPTER XLV. Repetition Concerning the Verse, and Concerning Pentecost and the Chalice

The verse has this distinctive feature: it arouses the hearts of those singing to seek the face of the Lord in prayer. For this reason it very often precedes the prayer.

The verse said in the nocturnal office, before the prayer that precedes the lesson, is intended to make the hearts of those present attentive to the lesson. It is known that sitting belongs more to security than standing. For security produces negligence among the lazy. Therefore the prayer precedes sitting, so that the Lord’s protection may rescue our hearts from every deceptive sense of security.

Before the hymns “Magnificat” and “Blessed Be the Lord God of Israel,” the verse precedes them because we ought to be as watchful and attentive to the words of those hymns as we are in prayer. In the other courses it precedes the final prayer.

Prayer and blessing are always at the end, before the brothers separate, each going to his own place. This practice follows the custom of the ancient Church. Thus it is read in the Acts of the Apostles concerning Paul, when he departed from Ephesus and told the Ephesians that they would no longer see his face:

“And when he had said these things, he knelt down with all of them and prayed.”

Likewise, when he departed from Tyre:

“They all accompanied us, with their wives and children, as far as outside the city; and, kneeling on the shore, we prayed. And when we had said farewell to one another, we went aboard the ship; but they returned to their own homes.”

The final prayer is therefore celebrated collectively at the very end, so that each person, returning to his own place fortified by such a shield—that is, common prayer—may be protected against every adversity.

Saint Ambrose called this prayer a *postulation*, or petition. Augustine likewise assigns the *postulation* to the prayer of the Mass, which the priest is accustomed to say after communion. This prayer is everywhere followed by blessing and thanksgiving. For this is what the words “Let us bless the Lord” and “Thanks be to God” signify. Both of these are to be referred to thanksgiving, with which Paul concludes the other prayers.

## CHAPTER XLVI. Repetition Concerning Pentecost

After the matters described above, I again found an authentic and clear passage of Ambrose concerning the fifty days after Easter. I preferred to introduce it here, although not in its proper place, rather than pass it over through negligence.

Ambrose says in his exposition on Luke:

“Our predecessors handed down to us that all fifty days of Pentecost are to be celebrated like Easter.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore throughout these fifty days the Church knows no fasting, just as on the Sunday on which the Lord rose; and all the days are like Sunday.”

## CHAPTER XLVII. Repetition Concerning Pentecost

Recently, as I think, it was shown to me by him who opens what no one closes what may reasonably be said concerning the Lord’s body placed on the altar and the chalice from his side, without prejudice to the teaching of those who wish otherwise and better to explain to me how and why the bread ought to be placed differently on the altar, and the chalice beside it.

The altar is the cross of Christ, from the place where it is written in the canon:

“Therefore, remembering…”

until the chalice is wrapped in the deacon’s cloth, in the manner of Joseph, who wrapped the Lord’s body in a shroud and napkin.

Concerning this altar Bede says in the second book of his exposition on the Apocalypse:

“Another edition has ‘upon the altar,’ because upon the altar of the cross he offered his golden censer, that is, his immaculate body, conceived by the Holy Spirit, to the Father for us.”

The bread spread upon the altar shows the Lord’s body extended upon the cross, which we eat. The wine and water in the chalice show the sacraments that flowed from the Lord’s side on the cross, namely blood and water, with which our Lord gives us drink.

Concerning this drink the aforementioned Ambrose says mystically in the aforementioned book:

“I also ask why we do not find that he was pierced before his death, but find that he was pierced after death, unless perhaps so that it might be shown that his blood was to be our drink and that we might understand the mystical order: not the sacraments of the altar before baptism, after baptism, but baptism first, and then the cup.”

And shortly afterward:

“For water and blood came forth: the one to cleanse, the other to redeem. Let us drink our price, so that by drinking we may be redeemed.”

[Col. 1243]

# THE BOOK OF SYMPHOSIUS AMALARIUS, PRIEST AND CHOREPISCOPUS OF METZ, ON THE ORDER OF THE ANTIPHONARY

## PROLOGUE

### On the Order of the Antiphonary

For a long time I was distressed because the Antiphonaries in our province disagreed with one another. The modern ones followed a different order from the old ones, and I did not know what ought to be retained. It pleased him who gives generously to all to free me from this uncertainty.

When I found an abundance of Antiphonaries in the monastery of Corbie—namely, three volumes of the nocturnal office and a fourth containing only the diurnal office—I attempted to spread my sails from the sea of curiosity toward the harbor of tranquility.

For when I was sent to Rome by the holy and most Christian emperor Louis to the holy and most reverend Pope Gregory concerning the volumes mentioned above, that same pope said to me:

“I do not have an Antiphonary that I can send to my son, the lord emperor, because Wala, when he served here on some embassy, took with him to Francia the copies that we had.”

I compared the volumes mentioned above with our Antiphonaries and found that they differed from ours not only in order, but also in wording and in the number of responsories and antiphons—many of which we do not sing.

For in many matters I found that our volumes had been arranged more reasonably than those. I wondered how it had happened that the mother and daughter differed so greatly from one another.

In one of the volumes of the aforementioned Antiphonaries I found that, among the material contained below, the work had been arranged in ancient times by Adrian the Apostolic.

[Col. 1243C]

I learned that our volumes were somewhat older than that volume of the city of Rome. Nevertheless, in some places I recognized that ours could be corrected by them, while in other places ours had been arranged more reasonably and appropriately, as I have said.

I therefore took a middle course between the two: I did not depart from our books where they were better arranged, and where they could be corrected by the volumes of the city, whether in order or in wording, I did not neglect the correction.

Where our modern singers had more reasonably arranged their offices according to authentic words—dividing the antiphons among the weekdays, as well as the responsories, and assigning to each vigil on the feasts of the saints its own antiphons—I first wrote the Roman order and then that of our singers.

Where I found such an order lacking, we added it from both sets of volumes, as the weekdays and weeks before the Nativity of the Lord and the Easter week will demonstrate.

Where the order of the responsories and antiphons in the volumes examined appeared to differ from the order of the books from which they had been taken, and from the agreement supported by reason, I did not hesitate to follow in our Antiphonary those things that seemed to correspond to the history and reason of this or that feast.

Where it seemed to me that something was written more suitably in the Roman Antiphonary than in ours, I wrote R. in the margin, on account of the city of Rome; where it was in ours, I wrote M., on account of the city of Metz; where my own judgment thought that something could be arranged more reasonably than in either of them, I wrote I. C., on account of indulgence and charity.

For this reason I ask singers not to despise our work before examining it according to the order of the books and the coherence of reason. If they find that it agrees less well with the order of the books or with reason in any respect, let them extend indulgence to my inexperience. Otherwise, let them not disdain to eat our vegetables, which a red earthenware dish sets before them.

[Col. 1244B]

In the verses which someone may find almost entirely changed, if he should deem the present volume worthy of frequent use, the priest of God Elisagarus [Helisachar] labored and toiled. He was exceptionally learned and most devoted to reading and divine worship, and was also first among the leading men of the palace of the most excellent Emperor Louis.

Not only he, but also all the learned men whom he was able to summon to himself, labored in the present undertaking.

Although the verses that had been most carefully altered were joined to their responsories, I did not hesitate, while passing through the earlier Antiphonaries, to insert into our Antiphonary whatever verses I found suitable, just as I found them inserted.

It must be noted that it is necessary for our Antiphonary to have verses different from the Roman one, because we sing our responsories in a different order from the Romans.

They begin the responsory from the beginning; when the verse has been completed, we shape the responsory with the completed verse around its sides, and thus make one body out of two bodies.

Therefore we must seek verses whose meaning agrees with the middle portions of the responsories, so that one sense may arise from the words of the responsory and the words of the verse.

The aforementioned and glorious priest Elisagarus took care of this. For that reason he strove to gather from different books verses suited to the responsories, which we and many others desire to use in the nocturnal office.

In all these matters I am supported by the assent of the supreme and most holy Apostolic Gregory, who answered the question of Saint Augustine by saying that, from wherever he wished to gather ecclesiastical offices, he could freely collect or insert them into the Roman order and assign them for the use of his people.

Thus it is written in the *History of the English*, book one, chapter five.

Augustine’s question:

“Since there is one faith, why are there different customs among the Churches? One custom of Masses is observed in the Roman Church, and another in Gaul.”

Pope Gregory replied:

“Your Fraternity knows the custom of the Roman Church in which you remember having been nourished. But it pleases me that, whether in the Roman Church, or in the Churches of Gaul, or in any Church, you have found something that may please almighty God more, you should carefully select it and pour it into the Church of the English, which is still new in the faith, as a special institution gathered from many Churches.

“For things are not to be loved on account of places, but places on account of good things. Therefore select from each Church whatever is devout, religious, and right; gather these things as into a bundle and establish them as a custom among the minds of the English.”

Thus far the blessed Gregory.

In many places I noted at the beginning the names of the responsories and antiphons according to the order of the Antiphonary of the City, and alongside them, in the second order, according to the order of our custom, so that the psalmist might have both before his eyes and sing whichever his judgment preferred.

It should be noted that the volume we call the Antiphonary has three names among the Romans. What we call the Gradual they call the Cantatory; among them it is still contained in one volume according to the ancient custom in certain Churches.

They divide the following part under two names. The part that contains the responsories is called the Responsorial, and the part that contains the antiphons is called the Antiphonary.

I followed our custom and placed responsories and antiphons together according to the order of the seasons in which our solemnities are celebrated.

### On the Matters About Which I Received Answers from the Masters of the Roman Church

[Col. 1245C]

I asked the archdeacon Theodore of the holy Roman Church, whom the Apostolic Lord had requested to instruct me according to my question concerning the order of the Roman office, how many verses the Roman Church sang in the responsory “Looking from Afar.” He replied: “Two.”

I asked why he had sung two, contrary to the usual custom, in that responsory. He replied: “Because of the honor of the great feast.”

Later I found not only three verses in this responsory, “Looking from Afar”—as it is contained in our Antiphonary—but also in many other responsories, either two or three written in the Roman Antiphonary.

It seemed to me that the following explanation could be given for so many verses. When it happens that one responsory is sung twice or three times in one week, or in several weeks, and two or three suitable verses are attached to it, one may be sung on one night, another on the next, and the third on the third.

I asked which order of responsories was celebrated on the Sunday night that we usually call the Octave of Easter. The answer was: “The ninth; on it we sing from the authority.”

I asked similarly about the office of Pentecost. The answer was: “We sing nine, as on the other Sundays during the nights.”

I asked the aforementioned archdeacon in what order they sang the responsories after the octave of Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord. The answer was:

“On the octave of Pentecost we begin to read the Book of Kings. In that same first week we sing responsories from the Psalms; in the following weeks until the month of August, from the history of the Kings.

“In the first week of August we read Solomon, and we sing responsories from the Psalms. In the following weeks until the month of September, from Solomon.

“In the first week of September we read Job and sing responsories from the Psalms; in the next two weeks, from Job; in the final week of that month, from Tobit.

“In the first two weeks of October, from Judith, Esther, and Ezra; in the final two weeks of that month, from Maccabees.

“In the first week of November we read from the Prophets and sing responsories from the Psalms. In all the remaining weeks until the Advent of the Lord, from the Prophets.”

I asked whether the Roman masters said anything during the interval between the nocturnal and morning offices. The answer was given to me:

“Nothing; but immediately after the nocturnal office they say, ‘O God, come to my assistance.’”

They do not sing the Lord’s Prayer after the nocturnal psalms, but say some chapter such as this:

“Through the intercession of the blessed prince of the apostles Peter, may the Lord save and protect us.”

They often conclude the nocturnal office with eight responsories and nine lessons.

I asked whether they sang “Te Deum laudamus” on Sunday nights. The answer was:

“Only on the birthdays of bishops do we sing ‘Te Deum laudamus.’”

Here we insert how we found it written concerning the authority of Adrian the Apostolic:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the Responsorial of the cycle of the year according to the seasons, of the thrice-blessed and Apostolic lord Adrian, pope, in the seventh indiction.”

Likewise at the end:

“This work the supreme pontiff, lord Adrian, renews for himself as a memorial throughout the ages.”

I marked with an obelus the “Alleluia” that follows the psalm “I will confess to you, Lord” at the Lord’s Easter evening office. I wrote it as I found it in the Roman order, although in our order it seems superfluous.

Previously I wrote in a little book called the *Official* about the season of Septuagesima, about the mystery of that number, and about the other offices celebrated in the Church throughout the year, whether nocturnal or diurnal.

Now, since I am about to speak, by God’s mercy, about the order of the Antiphonary, I wish to write something in summary, as a kind of handbook concerning the nocturnal offices alone and those commonly called the *Courses*.

When these matters have been recalled to memory, may the mind be renewed toward desire for the heavenly homeland; may it remember how it was recalled to that homeland, how it is recalled daily, and how, through each hour of the night and day, it can serve the Lord through these same courses and, on the last day, render its vows, because the five senses of its virginity have preserved their beauty and their attire for their bridegroom.

When my mind touches upon these affections, which I wish to note below for each course, I am moved by the sweetness of love for God, love of neighbor, and the eternal homeland, as well as by the presence of our Savior.

At the same time, it must be noted that my mind withdraws from human assistance and establishes itself in the help of the Lord; it is separated from earthly and perishable things and joined to heavenly and spiritual things.

## CHAPTER I. Here Begins the Annotation on the Nocturnal and Diurnal Offices Commonly Called the Courses
The restoration and renewal of the state of our innocence was given back to us in Christ’s resurrection. Therefore, since we are about to speak, as the Lord grants, about the nocturnal and diurnal offices, we must begin with the Lord’s night, which by his resurrection he preferred to all other nights. On the Lord’s night, appropriately, according to the custom of the Roman Church, rising from sleep, we first say, “[Lord, open my lips]” [Col. 1247B], and after this verse we glorify the holy Trinity, which is to be glorified for things past, present, and future.

Afterward the cantor’s trumpet gives the signal through the invitatory antiphon, so that Christians everywhere may be roused and hasten to the school of the teachers and shepherds of the Churches. Hence the lord Bede, in his treatise on Luke, says concerning a verse of the invitatory psalm:

“But when, singing with the Prophet, ‘Come, let us adore and fall down before the Lord; let us weep before the Lord who made us,’ I seek fellow-workers in this same task, I bring doves to the altar.”

After this antiphon twelve psalms are sung before the lessons and responsories. The number twelve contains within itself the totality of time and of things. In the twelve psalms, among ecclesiastical men [Col. 1247C], the memory of the holy Fathers who cultivated the Lord’s vineyard before the Law is instilled. Through this number those who come to the nocturnal office are instructed that, from the beginning of the world, the Lord had preachers in his Church who cultivated God’s people by their labors, so that through Christ’s resurrection they might seek a return to their own homeland.

The first psalm, “Blessed is the man,” in a certain manner sings of Abel, a just man whose blood was shed as a type of Christ’s blood. And the psalm, “[Lord my God, in you I have hoped],” speaks of Noah, his son, and their wives, who were saved through water. And “[Save me, Lord, for the holy man has failed]” speaks of Abraham, who alone resisted worshiping idols while the others fell into it.

Then follows the verse. [Col. 1247D] A verse is that song through which the mind’s attention is turned back toward another attention, as though it were a kind of official arrangement directing the mind’s journey by a sweet melody from one affection to another: for example, from psalmody to a lesson; from the solitude of all the Churches to one’s own conscience—a conversion learned in the responsories; and again from psalmody to the evangelical hymn, or to the Lord’s Prayer, whose customary prologue is “[Lord, have mercy, and Christ, have mercy],” or to the prayer ordinarily spoken by the priest alone.

This state of mind is demonstrated in many Churches through the position of the body. In many Churches, at the beginning of the singing called the verse, the choir turns toward the altar. After the verse, three lessons follow with [Col. 1248A] their responsories.

Our Church rightly passes from the worship of Abraham to the school of discipline. Abel and Enoch were holy and just men; but they were not called fathers of the nations, nor fathers of Christ, nor were they set forth as a sign of the faith of the Gentile people. Abraham is placed by the evangelist Matthew at the beginning of Christ’s genealogy. Abraham is called the father of many nations. Abraham received the sign of the faith that is in the foreskin.

Such a farmer’s teaching must be received and retained. For the state of time also admonishes us to celebrate lessons and responsories from Abraham. At the sixth hour of the day it is read in Matthew’s Gospel that Abraham entered upon his farming; but at midnight we are admonished to go forth before the Lord, following the example of the Psalmist, who says: “I came before you at dawn”—that is, [Col. 1248B] at midnight. At times our weakness is accustomed to postpone this until cockcrow.

It is fitting that the memory of those dead who died in Christ should be recalled during the night, since their passing and rest are compared with the night, as the Gospel says: “The night will come, when no one can work.”

Through the psalms the work of the preachers is shown; through the lessons, doctrine. In this order we follow the text of the evangelist Luke, who says: “I have composed the first account, O Theophilus, about all that Jesus began to do and teach.” The teaching of preachers seeks imitators. For this reason the cantor rises from his seat and raises his voice in the responsory, so that he may rouse the minds that have heard the teaching to good works. Devout minds rise through devotion to good [Col. 1248C] works in the responsory, so that they may answer the exhorter.

The order of the exhortatory office requires that something precede the exhortation which may focus the hearer’s attention and move him to follow, as is plainly shown when the usefulness of reading the divine Scriptures precedes the cantor’s exhortatory voice. And so that the exhorter’s mind may in no way be lifted up by arrogance because of the prompt response of his subjects, he is restrained by the verse, in which he alone must labor. When this has been done, he is reminded by his own labors and his own conscience that he must know himself to be measured before Christ’s tribunal, not by the opinion of the people and of his disciples.

[Col. 1248D] In ancient times the “Glory” was not sung after the verse; instead, the responsory was repeated. This order is consistent with reason: whoever began to become an exhorter for the sake of returning to the heavenly homeland should persevere in that work to the end. But the hymn was added by the modern Apostolics “[Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit]” after the verse, by which we are admonished always to praise the Creator for all his gifts and benefits.

The number of lessons and responsories celebrated on the Lord’s night clearly shows that the choir of holy preachers exhorts us, through Christ’s resurrection, toward that homeland and fellowship—namely, toward the heavenly Jerusalem and the nine orders of angels. These cannot be divided more properly or equitably than by the number three, through the intervals of the psalms of the three vigils, in which the three times named in the Gospel are recalled: [Col. 1249A] the first watch, the second watch, and the third watch.

In the first watch the future resurrection in Christ is recalled of those who cultivated the Lord’s vineyard before the Law; in the second, that of those who lived after the Law was given until Christ’s coming; in the third, that of Christ’s disciples. For Christ’s excellence is sung with “Alleluia” in the final three psalms.

The division of these psalms is as follows:

“Preserve me, Lord”: it recalls those of the Levitical order who rest in Christ.

“Hear, Lord, my justice”: the rest of judges.

“I will love you, Lord”: the palm of the kings of the Old Testament.

“The heavens declare”: the preachers of the New Testament.

“May the Lord hear you in the day of tribulation”: the triumph of the Christian martyrs.

“Lord, in your strength”: the enduring kingdom of spiritual [Col. 1249B] kings.

These persons are members of that head whose kingdom is recalled in the psalm, “The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty.”

The difference between the three Sunday nocturns and the three sung on the other nights when there is a feast of the saints is that the former recall the resurrection of bodies, while the latter recall the blessedness of holy souls, which they receive when they become citizens of the heavenly spirits and of the good.

## CHAPTER II. On the morning office during the Sunday nights

The morning office of the Sunday nights admonishes ecclesiastical men to consider how, first, after Christ’s resurrection, when [Col. 1249C] the darkness of errors and vices had been driven away, the primitive Church rose to the light of true faith, which is in the New Testament; how, at a later time, it would join to itself the Church from the Gentiles; and how thereafter the two Churches together would have to be tested by tribulations, found approved through patience, and through this testing reach heavenly blessedness.

The first verse of the first psalm of the morning office demonstrates that Christ reigned after his resurrection and clothed himself with beauty and strength. The second verse shows that the world was established—that is, that the apostles were strengthened by Christ’s resurrection and ascension into heaven, as well as by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit.

The second psalm shows their purpose: to join many to themselves from Judea, so that there might be one and the same faith among teachers and [Col. 1249D] subjects, one salvation, and one glorification.

The third psalm admonishes us to understand that, after the salvation of the Jews, the same salvation would reach the Gentiles. The psalm “[God, my God, to you I keep watch from the light]” is sung from the person of the Gentiles.

Meanwhile, after Judea has been rejected, it too will again be gathered through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, and one Church will be made from two peoples. Therefore the two present psalms—“[God, my God, to you I keep watch from the light]” and “[May God have mercy on us]”—are not divided, so that they may be a sign of that time when there will be no distinction between the faith of the Gentile and Jewish peoples.

The Church, united from two peoples, will prosper through patience, as Scripture says: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous men.” For tribulation produces patience.

[Col. 1250A] The three youths cast into the furnace, whose hymn is sung in the fifth order of psalms, remained patient in tribulation. They did not yield to the threats of King Nebuchadnezzar and his servants. By their steadfastness they prefigured the steadfastness of those saints who, in the time of Antichrist, will not yield to his snares and threats, but will persevere in the Catholic faith.

They will be patient in tribulation, will be found approved through patience, and through testing will be blessed in hope. Of them it is written: “Blessed are those who wait and reach the thousand three hundred and thirty-five days.” Hope, however, does not exist without faith and charity.

Therefore in our Church three psalms are sung together, filled with the praise [Col. 1250B] of God. These three psalms teach that the saints will live after Antichrist’s death in the steadfastness of faith, the blessedness of hope, the joy of love, and inseparable unity.

After these psalms a lesson is sung. For at that time spiritual food will not be lacking in the Church, food that will increase the joy once begun.

After this lesson the verse “[The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty]” is said. This verse teaches us that the elect will once again recount Christ’s triumph after Antichrist’s death—Christ who, during Antichrist’s time, was silent as though in hiding places.

Just as, after Christ’s disciples had grieved over his death, their minds were renewed in joy by his resurrection, so that they might meditate on the verse “The Lord has reigned,” so after Christians have grieved over Antichrist’s persecution, [Col. 1250C] their minds will be renewed in joy by his death, so that they may sing: “[The Lord has reigned; he has clothed himself with beauty].”

After this time the hymn “[Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people]” follows. Just as, when Zechariah sang this hymn, Christ’s first coming was near, so in the final time of which I spoke above, his second coming will be near. In it the saints will serve the Lord without fear, liberated from the hand of their enemies, in holiness and righteousness before him all their days; and the other good things attributed to God’s elect will also be fulfilled, things sung in the present hymn.

This continues through the verses which properly resound concerning John, namely, “And you, child, prophet,” and what follows.

## CHAPTER III. [Col. 1250D] On the nocturnal office of the ordinary nights

The number of psalms used in the nocturnal office on ordinary nights—twelve—urges the clergy to pray for their own sins and for those whose offerings sustain the Church.

It is written in John’s Gospel: “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

Through the twelve psalms a universal admonition is given to the clergy, that they intercede for the offenses of the peoples, which are committed in the night. Through the state of night the character of sins is understood, as Paul says in his Epistle to the Thessalonians:

“For you are all [Col. 1251A] sons of light and sons of day; you are not of night or of darkness. Therefore let us not sleep as the rest do, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night; and those who are drunk, are drunk at night. But since we belong to the day, let us be sober.”

We are debtors, because we live from the offerings of the faithful, to intercede both for their sins and for our own. Concerning this matter Saint Gregory writes in his homily:

“Let us consider what condemnation it is to receive here, without labor, the reward of labor. Behold, we live from the offering of the faithful; but do we labor for the souls of the faithful? We take for our support what the faithful offered for the redemption of their sins, yet we do not labor against those same sins, as we ought, either through the diligence of prayer or through [Col. 1251B] preaching.”

Brothers, in the nocturnal office let us sing as many psalms as there are hours in the equinoctial night, and from the condition of the time let us learn that we are debtors, obligated to intercede for the sins of those whose offerings sustain us.

From the six antiphons, which the choirs repeat in turn after each verse, we are admonished to direct our purpose toward the perfection of good works, since we are debtors to intercede for the sins of others. If we do this, the offering of the faithful received by us will not be dangerous or blameworthy, as the Gospel says: “The laborer is worthy of his food.”

Let us also remember the sentence of the apostle James: “Confess your sins to one another, pray for one another, that you may be saved; for the continual prayer of a righteous person has great power.”

We have inserted here [Col. 1251C] the character of those sins which are so easily forgiven, from the writings of our holy father Bede. In this judgment, however, there must be discernment, so that we confess our daily and light sins to one another among our equals and believe that these daily sins are remitted through prayer.

Saint Augustine likewise writes in the *Enchiridion*: “As for the daily, brief, and light sins without which this life is not lived, let the daily prayer of the faithful make satisfaction.”

## CHAPTER IV. [Col. 1251D] On the number of lessons and responsories of the nights mentioned above

It has often been repeated that responsories follow lessons because of ecclesiastical discipline, which does not wish to have hearers of the Law alone in its school, but doers also. Saint Gregory writes in his replies to Augustine:

“For even in spiritual matters, so that they may be arranged wisely and prudently, we can draw an example from bodily matters as well.”

From military watches we learn what we are to understand from the three lessons and responsories. Saint Ambrose says:

“Imitate the soldiers of this age, and consider yourself a soldier of Christ. The commanders established in their army that, while the soldiers slept, the camp should be guarded through three watches of the night. The fourth is at the time of morning, when we sing the morning office.”

During the three watches mentioned, guards are appointed who protect the bodies and equipment of the sleeping soldiers. In secular warfare [Col. 1252A] the soldiers sleep in turn and keep watch in turn. But in the warfare of Christians it is said in Mark’s Gospel: “What I say to you, I say to all: Watch.”

The three lessons and three responsories on ordinary nights signify to the holy people that the clergy of God’s Church are intent on this purpose: through the lesson—that is, through their teaching—and through the responsory—that is, through a great cry of the mind in preaching and exhorting—to urge God’s people to keep watch, lest the Lord of the house come suddenly, whether late, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning, and find him sleeping.

For if the lord of the house comes, according to Luke, in the second watch, or if he comes in the third watch, and the door is immediately opened to him when he knocks, those servants are blessed.

This is the intention of God’s clergy: if someone, overcome by deep [Col. 1252B] sleep, has been negligent in the first watch, let him await the Lord returning from the wedding feast with diligent care in the second watch. And if he has also been negligent in the second watch, let him at least be found awake in the third.

It must be noted that every faithful soul, on whatever day it is stripped of the body, receives the seventh day of the week, and the resurrection of the holy bodies awaits the eighth day. Thus whatever faithful soul awakens from the deep sleep of negligence through ecclesiastical care—whether in the first watch, the second, or the third—immediately reaches the morning time in the fourth watch.

As I understand it, the holy Roman Church specifically signifies this to us through its custom. Whenever it sees the office proceeding to maturity in whatever order or number of lessons, it abandons [Col. 1252C] the nocturnal office and begins the morning office, as I have heard. For it is dangerous to transgress the limits of the Fathers: that is, unless we rise either at dawn, according to the authority of the prophet David, or, according to the custom of our weakness, at cockcrow.

## CHAPTER V. On the morning office of the ordinary nights

Because man is a part of the world, he is called by the Greeks μικρόκοσμος (*mikrokosmos*), that is, “a smaller world.” Therefore the entire sequence of human birth is rightly compared with the stages of time.

Night is so called because it harms human sight or human affairs, or because thieves and robbers find in it an opportunity to harm others. The ignorance of the mind, which commonly arises from the darkness of sins, is compared with night.

Concerning this sin [Col. 1252D] Saint Augustine says in the *Enchiridion*:

“We sin for two reasons: either because we do not yet see what we ought to do, or because we do not do what we already see ought to be done. Of these two, the former is the evil of ignorance; the latter, of weakness.”

For those whose minds have been blinded by ignorance of sins, ecclesiastical men pray that they may recover their senses and recognize their sins. Through the merits of the saints intervening, Christ in his mercy is accustomed to visit such minds, in a certain manner, at the morning hour.

Morning is the withdrawal of darkness and the coming of dawn. At that time the sun approaches the upper regions in order to drive darkness from the surface of the earth. When the sun arrives, the gloom of ignorance is driven from the human mind, [Col. 1253A] as happened with Peter when he wept bitterly, and when God sent the prophet Nathan to David so that he might acknowledge his sin.

When dawn was already approaching, David said: “I have sinned against the Lord.” For such a state of converted minds, the holy Church sings at the morning hour the psalm “[Have mercy on me, God],” which David sang after he recognized his sin.

In this psalm the faith that purifies hearts indicates the remission of sins through the Creed, saying: “I believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, the communion of saints, the forgiveness of sins.”

Just as in the psalm “[The Lord has reigned],” which is sung in the free night, the condition [Col. 1253B] of those who persevere in the course begun after baptism is recalled, so in the psalm “[Have mercy on me, God],” which is sung in the servile nights, the condition of those who turn aside from their course after baptism is recalled—those who are afterward corrected and enlightened through the prayers of the faithful.

After the morning time comes dawn. Dawn is like the small light of day just beginning. Unless this period belongs to the night, there will not be the seven divisions of the night which the teachers enumerate: twilight, evening, the time of silence, deep night, cockcrow, morning, and dawn.

Of this same hour it is said in the Gospel: “On the first day of the week they come to the tomb very early.” The same hour is also called morning. John likewise writes concerning this hour: “Mary came in the morning, while it was still dark.” And Mark, as quoted above: “Whether late, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning.”

All the psalms placed in the second order on ordinary [Col. 1253C] nights echo something concerning morning.

The first says: “[For you I will pray, Lord; in the morning you will hear my voice; in the morning I will stand before you].”

The second: “[Send forth your light and your truth].”

The third: “[You will delight the goings forth of morning and evening].”

The fourth: “[In the morning may he pass away like grass; in the morning may he blossom].” And again: “[We have been filled in the morning].”

The fifth: “[Make me hear in the morning].”

The sixth: “[To proclaim your mercy in the morning].”

In this psalm hope is at work. In the first, evils are avoided; in the second, good things are desired through hope. Although the penitent possesses hope, nevertheless, from the night—that is, from sin—he has reason to grieve. Concerning this grief the Apostle says: “The grief that is according to God produces repentance leading to lasting salvation.” This grief is itself part of the night.

[Col. 1253D] In the third order two psalms are joined together. In these two the commandment of love, which is double, is celebrated.

In the first psalm the man instructed in the love of God says: “[God, my God, to you I keep watch from the light]”—that is, after the darkness has withdrawn, the dawn of faith and the daylight of restoration have shone upon me through good hope; I keep watch for you, and through the love by which I am carried away toward you, “My soul thirsts for you; how greatly my flesh also thirsts for you.”

In this psalm the love of God is recalled; in the second psalm, love of neighbor. These two commandments are not separated by any intervening element. Therefore no separation is found between these two psalms.

Divine Scripture says: “God chastises every son whom he receives.” This man, whose condition is now recalled, was [Col. 1254A] first tested and overcome. God now wishes him to be tested again and to conquer, and to possess the triumph of victory.

For the sake of teaching and admonition, the canticles follow—those which our fathers sang after they had been tested and God had granted them triumph.

The first canticle says: “[I confess to you, Lord, because you were angry with me].” You have heard the scourging; hear the triumph: “Your anger has turned away, and you have consoled me.” And again: “I will act confidently, and I will not fear.” And again: “Rejoice and praise, O dwelling-place of Zion.”

The second canticle was sung by Hezekiah after he recovered from illness.

The third was sung by Hannah after her rival had been humbled and Hannah herself exalted through the birth of her son.

The fourth was celebrated after the Egyptians who were pursuing God’s people had been overthrown.

The fifth was sung by the prophet Habakkuk. [Col. 1254B] Concerning him Jerome says:

“Meanwhile, according to the literal sense, the prophet complains against the Lord: why does Nebuchadnezzar lay waste the temple and Judah; why is Jerusalem, once the city of the Lord, destroyed; why does the people cry out and not receive an answer; why does the people, oppressed by the Chaldeans, cry aloud to the Lord and not receive salvation; why has the prophet himself, or the people, in whose person he now speaks, continued to live and been brought to this point, so that he sees the wickedness of the enemies and his own labor; why does injustice prevail against him?”

And he says this from the anguish of his mind, not knowing that gold is refined in fire and that the three youths came out of the furnace purer than they had entered.

And further:

“Our Lord, knowing the weight and measure of his mercy, sometimes does not hear [Col. 1254C] the one who cries out, in order to test him and provoke him more strongly to pray; and, as though refined by fire, he makes him more righteous and purer.”

The sixth was sung by Moses, who was troubled because of the Jews, who provoked his spirit. It concludes in this way:

“Praise the Lord, you nations, his people, for he will avenge the blood of his servants; he will repay vengeance upon their enemies, and he will show mercy to the land of his people.”

After these victory songs, the person of one exhorting to the praise of God is introduced, according to the voice of the Psalmist:

“In the Lord my soul shall be praised; let the meek hear and rejoice. Magnify the Lord with me, and let us exalt his name together.”

In this order he begins to exhort his companions and fellow citizens to praise the holy Trinity, which is distinct in three persons and joined in one and the same substance.

[Col. 1254D] Therefore the three psalms, full of divine praise, which are sung in place of this exhortation, are sung in our Church without any interruption.

After these psalms, which bring the Psalter to an end and show the human being perfectly restored, a lesson follows. For the perfect human being is especially pleased to teach and admonish the negligent, after the manner of David, who recalls the renewal of his mind in three verses:

“Create in me a clean heart, O God”;

“Do not cast me away from your presence”;

“Restore to me the joy of your salvation.”

Immediately he adds: “I will teach the unrighteous your ways, and the impious will be converted to you.”

After the lesson the verse follows. Our region has been accustomed throughout all ordinary nights to sing in this order, above [Possibly: always] [Col. 1255A] the verse “We have been filled in the morning with your mercy.”

In the Roman Antiphonary, however, I found several verses. Therefore it began to sing this verse at the morning office:

“Lord, I will meditate on you,” on Monday and Tuesday;

“We have been filled with your mercy,” on Wednesday and Thursday;

“Make me hear in the morning,” on Friday and Saturday.

All these verses pray for the good things of the Lord, which are necessary for retaining each person who has been converted in mind at the morning hour, whether for the present conversion or for the future morning expected in the resurrection.

After these steps we ascend to our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who visited and accomplished the redemption of his people.

An apostrophe is made from the man converted through repentance to the evangelical man who exhorted him to praise [Col. 1255B] the holy Trinity for the benefits granted to the convert. He says:

“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited human misery and accomplished its redemption, as he spoke through the mouth of the saints.”

Through their mouth he promised that on whatever day the impious person should be converted from his impiety, all his injustices would be consigned to oblivion. He also fulfilled the oath that he swore to Abraham our father: that he would give himself to us, that is, so that, liberated without fear from the hand of our enemies, we might serve the Lord in righteousness and holiness.

As though he were saying, the ecclesiastical man says: “This man who was weak has certainly been restored to health. All the parts of the night, by whose darkness he had been obscured, have been driven away. Let us give thanks to God, because from now on he will be able to serve the Lord and walk honorably, [Col. 1255C] as is fitting in the day.”

The gifts of God recalled in this hymn are received in part by the holy Church at the Lord’s first coming, but she will receive them more fully at his second coming.

## CHAPTER VI. On the courses of the day
Properly speaking, the common people call the whole day—the presence of the sun above the earth—“day.” [Col. 1255D] From this definition it may be understood that a day of twelve hours ought to begin at sunrise and end at sunset. Morning is a certain boundary between night and day. Dawn and the rising of the sun are called morning, as I stated earlier, in the Gospel: “While it was still dark.” And again it is said: “Very early on the first day of the week they came to the tomb, when the sun had already risen.” And again: “The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard,” having agreed with the laborers for a denarius for the day. From this “day” it is understood that, in its proper place, morning belongs to the day. It is written in another Gospel: “If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble.”

The assembly of the holy brothers, which gathers at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours, recalls in its office the condition of those who, after the washing of water—or after receiving health through repentance—run without turning back along the way of the Lord, that is, through his law, all the way to evening, meaning to the end of their life. Concerning this course Paul said in his final days: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith.”

[Col. 1256A] Indeed, the psalm *Blessed are the undefiled* is full of holy conduct, by which everyone ought to walk who strives to fulfill the law of the Lord. The psalm *Save me, O God, by your name*, which is placed before Psalm 118, is not placed there as though it were necessary only for that part of the day called the first hour, but for the whole period of the day.

Let the person who begins to walk in the law of the Lord know that on one side he has a lion and on the other a dragon: a lion in open persecutions, a dragon in ambushes. When the Ziphites lay in wait for David in order to seize him and hand him over to Saul, who wanted to kill him, he sang this psalm. And when we begin, at the first hour of the day, to avoid the persecutions and ambushes of the devil, let us sing this psalm [Col. 1256B] for the whole journey of the day: “Save me, O God, by your name, and deliver me by your strength.” Why? “For strangers have risen up against me,” and so forth.

For what do those walking along the road wish to pray, if not what the following verse shows, saying: “Turn back the evils upon my enemies, and in your truth destroy them”? In this psalm prayer has been offered for the protection of both sides of the road.

In the first part of the psalm *Blessed are the undefiled*, we enter upon the way of the Lord. What the purpose of walking is, we learn from the words of Saint Augustine. Among other things, in his exposition of this psalm he says:

> For surely the one who exhorts does this: he arouses the will of the person with whom he is dealing toward that for which the address of exhortation is employed. Why, then, are we addressed so that we may wish for what we cannot wish for, [Col. 1256C] unless it is because everyone indeed desires blessedness, but very many do not know by what way it is reached? Therefore this man teaches it when he says, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord.” As though he were saying: “I know what you want; you seek blessedness. If, then, you wish to be blessed, be undefiled.” Everyone wants the former, but few want the latter, without which one does not reach what everyone wants. But where will anyone be undefiled except in the way? And in what way except in the law of the Lord?

We have committed ourselves to the discourse of this law through the first part of Psalm 118 at the first hour of the day. Through the second part we anticipate the second part of the day. As in the first part, so in this one we make mention of the law of the Lord: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law.” And again: “Remove from me the way of iniquity, * [Col. 1256D] and in your law have mercy on me.”

The verse that follows, “Rise up, O Lord, help us,” just as the psalm *Save me, O God, by your name* does, belongs to the whole span of the day’s journey. This verse likewise belongs to the prayer that the Lord may be the helper and deliverer of his flock throughout the entire course of the journey, because of his mercy.

The third part of the aforementioned psalm is celebrated at the third hour of the day, and there too mention is made of the law of God, saying: “Set before me, O Lord, the way of your ordinances.” And again: “Give me understanding, and I shall search out your law,” and so forth.

The fourth part of the psalm is sung for the fourth hour of the day. There too mention is made of the law of the Lord: “My portion, O Lord, [Col. 1257A] I said, is to keep your law.”

The fifth part of the psalm is sung for the fifth hour of the day. There too mention is made of the law of the Lord: “Their heart is congealed like milk, but I have meditated on your law.” And again: “The law of your mouth is good for me.”

The reading that is read at each of the offices teaches this: whenever holy men have gathered, besides the good works that each of them diligently strives to perform, they should be refreshed freely by divine conversation.

In the sixth part of the psalm we enter upon the sixth hour of the day. There mention is made of the law of the Lord: “The wicked have told me tales, but not according to your law.” And again: “If your law had not been my meditation,” and so forth.

The seventh part of the psalm is sung for the seventh hour of the day. There mention is made of the law of the Lord: “How I have loved your law, O Lord; it is my meditation all day long.” [Col. 1257B]

The eighth part of the psalm is sung for the eighth hour of the day. There too mention is made of the law of the Lord: “I have hated the wicked, but I have loved your law.”

At the ninth hour of the day the ninth part of the psalm is sung. There we have the law of the Lord: “Your righteousness is righteousness forever, and your law is truth.”

The tenth part of the psalm is sung for the tenth part of the day. There mention is made of the law of the Lord: “See my humiliation and deliver me, for I have not forgotten your law.”

The eleventh part of the psalm is sung for the eleventh hour of the day. There too we have the law of the Lord: “I have hated and abhorred iniquity, but I have loved your law.” And again: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, O Lord.”

At the twelfth hour of the day the Lord gives his laborers the promised denarius.

I recently wrote in the *Official Book* about the evening hour [Col. 1257C], according to the etymology of its name: that, according to its etymology, the evening hour is after sunset and belongs to the night. If anyone celebrates the evening office at that hour from which it derives its etymology—that is, when the star called Vesper appears—the *Official Book* contains what I was able to understand about it. We, however, very often celebrate the evening office before sunset.

For that order to be celebrated in our Church which is described in the Book of Ezra—“Four times a day they confessed their sins to the Lord”—the evening office must be counted as part of the day. Lord Bede says, from the written account of this history, that the custom arose in our Church of having four readings recited to the brothers during the day. This is possible only if the evening reading [Col. 1257D] is counted as belonging to the day, together with the readings at the ninth, sixth, and third hours. At the first hour no reading is recited.

We begin the first office of the day at sunrise. We perform the evening synaxis around the twelfth hour, which is near the end of the day. The end of the day can signify the end of every human being, for “day” is used for the whole duration of a person’s life. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day; the hour is coming when no one can work.”

Saint Augustine says the following when he expounds the Gospel passage concerning the five wise virgins, whose devotion I wished to compare with that of those who sing the five psalms at evening:

> For when the Lord was secretly [Col. 1258A] questioned by the disciples about the consummation of the age, among the many things he said, he also said this: “Then the kingdom of heaven will be likened to ten virgins,” and so forth.

And below:

> It seems to me, therefore, that the five virgins signify continence divided according to the five senses from the allurements of the flesh. The soul’s appetite must be restrained—that is, from the pleasure of the eyes, the pleasure of the ears, the pleasure of smelling, of tasting, and of touching. But because this continence is practiced partly before God, so that he may be pleased by the interior joy of conscience, and partly before human beings, merely so that human glory may be gained, five are called wise and five foolish. Both groups are nevertheless virgins, because both possess continence, although they rejoice in opposite sources of stimulation.

Those who rejoice before God in glorying over their works [Col. 1258B] have walked during the day in his law; they are called wise virgins. These wise virgins will have lamps in their hands with oil when the bridegroom comes at the end of the world. The lamps signify good works, which each person carries with himself when he has performed them and has not sought a deceptive reward for them.

In the same way the psalms signify good works. In the place of the five virgins, during the final part of the day the choir sings five psalms, as though each person were carrying with him the good works he has performed through the five bodily senses. With these, as with lamps containing oil within them, they hasten to come out to meet the bridegroom.

For the one who strives to come out to meet the bridegroom arranges the steps of ascent in his heart. Therefore it is not without foresight that the fifteen psalms [Col. 1258C] of ascent are included in the evening office. And because these are insufficient for the number of seven days, others are added—those left over from the other offices.

After these psalms follows the mutual conversation of the saints through the reading, so that they may be reminded how to renew and compose the adornment of their souls, and prepare themselves as each person ought to be adorned when entering the presence of a king.

The verses that follow—that is, “Evening prayer” and “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight”—knock at the door of the chamber where the king sits. For in the Roman Antiphoner I found the verses “I will exalt you, my God and my king” and “Great is our Lord.” But the verses I have preferred clearly demonstrate, as far as possible, the whole devotion of the evening office.

After this, in the Gospel hymn [Col. 1258D] sung by Saint Mary, the choir of virgins recalls that it ought to strive to reach the place to which the Virgin of virgins went before it—that is, into the presence of the Savior.

After Saint Mary heard the archangel’s greeting and retained his words in her heart, she sang the present hymn, namely, *My soul magnifies the Lord*. For this reason she said of herself: “Because he has looked upon the lowliness of his handmaid; for behold, from now on all generations will call me blessed.”

Likewise, if the choir of virgins, after hearing the words of the Gospel saying, “Take care not to practice your righteousness before people, in order to be seen by them,” retains them in its heart, it will be called blessed by everyone.

The same matter is written in the Gospel of Luke:

> A certain woman from the crowd raised [Col. 1259A] her voice and said to him: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts that nursed you.” But Jesus said to her: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it.”

Saint Mary is called blessed because she heard the angel’s greeting; the choir of virgins is called blessed because it heard from the Lord the Gospel pronouncement written above and kept it.

Let the choir of virgins sing the hymn that the Virgin of virgins sang, and strive with every effort to enter the place to which Saint Mary arrived.

## CHAPTER VII. On Compline

After the seven offices have been recalled—of which the Prophet says, “Seven times a day I have given praise to you,” and elsewhere, “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise shall always [Col. 1259B] be in my mouth,” and another Scripture says, “The righteous man falls seven times a day and rises again”—there remains an eighth, which is called Compline.

In it lies the highest perfection of the other offices. For what the seven stages of the offices accomplish through progress, the eighth displays as perfect, that is, completed.

This office belongs to the night, but because of the effect indicated by its name, it is placed at the end of the other offices. In it eating, drinking, conversation, and every common activity are brought to an end; all the limbs are abandoned by human protection and entrusted to God alone, who neither sleeps nor slumbers.

Sleep is an image of death. Therefore, in this office we sing certain psalms that we customarily sing on the night of the Sabbath, when the Lord rested in the tomb, and which he himself sang on the cross, and which our Church sings in the office for the dead.

The psalm *When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me* is sung on the aforementioned Sabbath night. It is sung at Compline because of the prayer it contains: “In peace, in the same place, I shall sleep and rest.”

The psalm *In you, O Lord, I have hoped* was sung by Christ [Col. 1259C] on the cross and ends in this office at the place where he commended himself to the Father, saying: “Into your hands I commend my spirit.”

The psalm *He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High* is a shield against the devil’s ambushes. I cannot explain how many hidden dangers may assail those who are sleeping through the devil himself, through his members, and through the dangers of worms and wild beasts. Against these dangers the present psalm contains fitting words in its prayer: “His truth will surround you with a shield; [Col. 1259D] you will not fear the terror of the night.”

Indeed, we truthfully say to our Savior: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk; you will trample the lion and the dragon.”

I do not remember whether I wrote this in the *Official Book* or elsewhere. Concerning the meaning of the order of the chant, which the mercy of the Lord supplied to me—if it is true—at the time when I was praying for the office of Compline, I am therefore not reluctant to write it here, although it more properly belongs to the time when the tract *He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High* is sung.

The tract *He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High* admonishes us that whenever the devil wishes to persuade us to succumb to human tongues—to him through gluttony, empty glory, and greed—the words of this psalm should repeatedly [Col. 1260A] revolve in our hearts. In it is written: “You are my protector and my refuge, my God; I will hope in him, for he has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word.”

At the beginning of Lent the Gospel is read in which the Lord was tempted. Who conquered our temptation by his own temptation? He did so to remind us that, especially at that season, the devil sets himself upon tempting the servants of Christ. The tract, however, shows us what wall we ought to set against his temptation.

After forty days—that is, on Good Friday—the same tract is sung according to the ancient custom of the Roman Church. This preserves the order of times and events. For after the Lord had fasted for forty days, the devil began to tempt him, and sang to him verses from the [Col. 1260B] present tract. Defeated, he withdrew for a time, until he would return again—not now to tempt, but to persecute through his members, as he is read to have done in the Passion that follows the tract.

When we are persecuted by the devil’s members even unto martyrdom, we ought nevertheless to repeat the words of the tract, which say: “He has delivered me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word, from the arrow flying by day, from the activity that walks in darkness, from ruin and the demon of noonday.”

The fourth psalm is also sung at Compline because of the words it contains: “In the nights lift up your hands toward the holy place and bless the Lord.”
