There are four elements for which protection is requested. For this reason we sing four psalms, or because among the [Col. 1260C] ancients four watches were observed during the night.

Our petition in the present Compline is refined by the verse: “Guard me, O Lord, as the apple of the eye; protect me beneath the shadow of your wings.”

So that the wearied limbs may enjoy repose, Holy Church believes that it will receive this more abundantly if it commemorates the Gospel-man Simeon. Therefore it sings the hymn that Simeon sang after he saw and received Christ and prayed for everlasting peace.

In this office and at Prime there is no reading-conversation. Nevertheless, our Church has the custom that after the office of Prime the brothers gather together for a reading, and likewise before this office. Reading is a kind of refreshment of the mind.

At Prime the Lord’s flock is directed upon the way so that it may come to pasture. Let it work first, so that afterward it may be filled with refreshment at the third hour.

In this [Col. 1260D] office, however, everything is completed, as I said above. This begins with the first psalm, where it says: “In peace, in the same place, I shall sleep and rest,” and in the second: “Into your hands I commend my spirit.”

After this commendation there is no order for the customary conversation to follow; only a petition for protection is to be offered in prayer.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Office *Looking from Afar*

Because of the verse placed before the evening synaxis, “Drop down, you heavens, from above,” I likewise place before the singers’ offices concerning the Lord’s Advent the following verses, which run throughout the entire season of the Lord’s Advent in the nocturnal, morning, and evening offices.

[Col. 1261A] I have not proposed to speak about each individual responsory, but about the individual offices of the Sunday nights.

The first two responsories, namely, *Looking from afar* and *I was watching in a night vision*, establish at the beginning of the book the person of that Christ who is God and man and universal king. The holy Church now strives to proclaim his coming far and wide.

In the first responsory the cantor introduces the words or deeds of John the Forerunner. In the person of John one may say, “Looking from afar”—that is, from as far away as heaven is distant from earth. John himself says of himself: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth”; but of Christ: “He who comes from heaven is above all.”

What he saw while looking is added: “Behold, I see the power of God coming.”

Saint Gregory speaks of this same power in his homily, in the person of the Forerunner: [Col. 1261B]

> Considering both his humility and the power of his divinity, he says: “He who is of the earth speaks of the earth,” and so forth.

It follows: “And a cloud covering the whole earth.” That is: “I see the darkness of ignorance covering the earthly hearts of the Jews, who do not recognize the God who is present under the name of Christ.”

This responsory recalls the divine nature in Christ. John says: “Make straight the way of the Lord.” Saint Gregory explains this as follows:

> The way of the Lord is made straight to the heart when the word of truth is heard humbly.

Thus far Gregory. When the word of truth enters the heart, Christ enters the human mind; when that same word is heard humbly, the human heart goes out to meet Christ. This meaning is recalled in the responsory that says: “Go out to meet him.”

It follows: “And say, ‘Tell us whether you are the one [Col. 1261C] who is to reign over the people of Israel.’”

Clearly, the Forerunner sends his disciples to Christ so that they may say to him: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” Hence blessed Gregory says:

> Since you deigned to be born for human beings, indicate whether you will also deign to die for human beings.

It is not without reason that the question placed in the responsory is compared with John’s question. For the one who did not know whether Christ would deign to die for the people of Israel or descend alone into the chambers of the underworld could [have been ignorant] whether Christ wished to reign over the people of Israel himself or through others, as he did through many.

In the second responsory the human birth is revealed, when it says: “And behold, the Son of Man comes in the clouds of heaven.” From there it answers the preceding responsory, which asks whether Christ ought to reign [Col. 1261D] over the people of Israel.

This responsory says: “And kingship and honor were given to him,” not merely so that he might reign over the people of Israel, but so that the Jewish tribe, the people of Israel, and every language might serve him.

Once the sign has been placed in a prominent position—that is, once the king who is God and man has been revealed—let the following responsories proceed in order through the books and histories wherever we encounter this plainly.

Here it must be noted that the words concerning the Savior’s second coming and those concerning his first have been placed indiscriminately in the Antiphoner. For many things concerning the Lord’s first coming, and many concerning his second, have been prophesied among the things sung at the Lord’s Advent.

After the two responsories prescribed above follows: “I beseech you, Lord, send the one whom you are going to send,” from our collection. For this is the first [Col. 1262A] in the arrangement of the books.

After this follows: “Hear the word of the Lord.” Although it comes later in the sequence of responsories, *Behold, a virgin shall conceive*, it nevertheless has some appropriateness for being placed first. In it a response is made to Moses’ supplication, when he says: “I beseech you, Lord, send the one whom you are going to send,” through the words: “Hear the word of the Lord, nations.” And below: “Our Savior will come.”

It is also fitting that the responsories which foretell the conception of Saint Mary should be placed together. The responsory *Behold, a virgin shall conceive* plainly prophesies the appearance of Saint Mary; the following one, *The angel Gabriel was sent*, shows that the things prophesied are now present.

*Hail, full of grace* maintains the order of the sequence. The composed responsory *Receive the word, Virgin Mary*, harmonizing with those above, [Col. 1262B] was transferred from the Roman Antiphoner into ours.

The order requires that after the Gospel responsories there follow the apostolic one: *We await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ*.

Because of the order of the responsories already begun, the responsories for Terce, Sext, and None follow.

The same prologue that stands at the beginning of the third volume, which among the Romans is called the *Antiphoner*, is placed before the first antiphons—namely, “On that day the mountains shall drip sweetness,” and “Rejoice,” together with the others that follow in our Antiphoner.

The same order of antiphons runs in our Antiphoner as is contained in the Roman one, up to the antiphon *The angel of the Lord announced to Mary*. Then follows the order that we received from the Metz Antiphoner.

In this office I changed the antiphons [Col. 1262C] from the city of Metz’s Antiphoner into our Antiphoner. On Wednesday, in the aforementioned Antiphoner, we find the antiphon *One mightier than I is coming after me*, from the words of Saint John the Baptist. In the following week there is the antiphon *A voice crying out*, from the prophet Isaiah.

I reserved them for the time when the Gospel concerning John is read, from which the antiphons themselves were taken. From the prophet Isaiah I placed *A shoot shall come forth from the root of Jesse* on Wednesday of the first office. In particular, on Wednesday and Friday of Advent I placed antiphons from the prophets, because these days have existed from the beginning in the prophecy concerning Christ and the Church.

On Wednesday the sun and moon were placed in the sky; these belong to the prophecy concerning Christ and the Church. On Friday the human being who was the form of the future Adam [Col. 1262D] was created.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Responsory *Jerusalem, Your Salvation Will Come Quickly*

The earlier responsories were sung in the person of the households of God—that is, in the person of ecclesiastical men. Therefore some responsories, rejoicing in the benefit bestowed upon them, speak in the first person. Such is the first responsory: “Behold, I see the power of God coming”; and the second: “I was watching in a night vision, and behold, the Son of Man comes in the clouds of heaven”; and *We await the Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ*.

Moses himself speaks in his own person to the Lord, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, send the one whom you are going to send.”

But in the present week either the ecclesiastical [Col. 1263A] choir speaks, or some prophetic discourse acts as messenger to Jerusalem, which was once the metropolis and the city of the great King, and through Jerusalem to the leaders of the whole renowned congregation of God.

The absence of Christ cannot be remembered without sadness. The present responsories therefore speak as though consoling the people concerning the coming of their King and defender: “Jerusalem, your salvation will come quickly.”

This is spoken to the city of Jerusalem in the same manner: “Behold, the Lord will come, and all his saints with him.”

The fourth, *As a mother comforts her children*, comforts the citizens and neighbors of Jerusalem.

The fifth, *Jerusalem, you will plant a vineyard on your mountains*, from Jeremiah, comforts the captives who were in Babylon.

The sixth, *Virgin Israel*, again from Jeremiah, comforts [Col. 1263B] the ten tribes over which the house of Ephraim ruled. According to the order of Jeremiah’s prophecy, these two stand in the aforementioned sequence.

The responsory *The Lord will go forth from Samaria* makes mention of Bethlehem, from which the kings who ruled God’s people originated, namely David and Christ, the King of kings.

The responsory *Bethlehem, city of the Most High God* declares the dominion of the King of kings; therefore I placed it after the preceding one.

The responsory *Behold, the Lord our protector will come* contains the lineage of kings; therefore it follows the responsory concerning Bethlehem.

The antiphons proceed in order according to the Roman Antiphoner up to *Blessed are you among women*. Then follows the order of the Metz Antiphoner.

Wherever I could, I inserted antiphons that contain proclamation, explanation, and consolation [Col. 1263C] for Jerusalem—that is, for the primacy that desires the Lord’s coming.

## CHAPTER X. On the Responsories *Rejoice in the Lord Always* and *Behold, the Lord Will Appear*

In the Metz Antiphoner that I read, the responsory *Rejoice in the Lord* is not contained there; I transferred it from the Roman Antiphoner into ours.

Through the present responsories the messenger of God now speaks to the poor and to the people, who are easily oppressed by the powerful. Just as in the earlier responsories he consoled the dignity of power, so in these he consoles the subject people.

The responsory *Rejoice in the Lord* is full of words of consolation.

*Behold, the Lord will appear* fixes at the beginning the King of kings who is going to free the poor and afflicted [Col. 1263D] from the hand of secular power.

Both matters are demonstrated by the present responsories: the deliverer who is to come for the poor, and that he will come in the near future.

The second responsory strives to do this: *The time for him to come is near*. The third does so: *He who is to come*. The fourth also: *Egypt, do not weep*.

I transferred *A star will rise* from the other responsories into the fifth position, so that from it it might be clarified who the ruler is who was mentioned in the preceding responsory: “Before whose presence the abysses are moved.”

The following responsories are the same as those contained in the other Antiphoners. An exception is *Let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult*, which consoles the hearts of the poor above all.

The antiphons follow the order of the Roman Antiphoner [Col. 1264A] up to the antiphon *This is the testimony*. Then comes the order of the Metz Antiphoner. During this week I strove to insert antiphons from the Gospel proper, and from the prophets those that most greatly console the fainthearted.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Responsories *Blow the Trumpet in Zion*

In this week the Roman volumes contain mixed together responsories that we customarily sing on the Sunday having the first responsory *Blow the trumpet*, and those that we sing distinctly on the following nights during the week.

I passed over the confused order and tried to arrange the number of responsories, which is distinguished in our practice from Sunday night through each weekday, as follows.

The present responsories and those of the following week [Col. 1264B] strive to gather a multitude of people, so that they may be present and ready to receive the Lord of lords.

Therefore many contain *Behold*, which is an adverb of demonstration, as in the responsory *Blow the trumpet in Zion; behold, our God the Savior*; and in the responsory *Cry out with strength: behold, our God whom we awaited*; and in the responsory *Behold, the fullness of time will now come*.

The first responsory, *Blow the trumpet in Zion*, reminds the citizens that they should know of the king’s coming and announce it to their neighbors.

The second responsory, *Consider how great and glorious he is*, admonishes the citizens to consider that the one who enters to save the nations is greater than kings.

The third responsory, *The scepter will not be taken away from Judah*, teaches that the kings of the Jews would [Col. 1264C] fail in their own time.

The fourth, *Cry out with strength*, announces to the city of Jerusalem that the king awaited for a long time is at the doors.

The fifth admonishes the citizens to clothe themselves in worthy garments to receive so great a king—that is, to fast on the twenty-fourth day.

It should be noted that this responsory was sung in Gaul on the eighteenth day of the tenth month. In its place I found written in the Roman Antiphoner, “on the twenty-fourth day of the tenth month.” I also asked the apostolic Gregory about it. He replied: “We do not sing it on the eighteenth day of the tenth month, but on the twenty-fourth.”

The sixth responsory, *Behold, the fullness of time will now come*, shows the manner in which the greatest king enters.

I adapted the next three responsories to correspond with the Gospel that is read on the Sunday [Col. 1264D] proper to them.

The Gospel says in the person of John the Baptist: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way of the Lord,’” as the prophet Isaiah says.

The seventh responsory says: *Our King Christ will come, whom John preached as the Bridegroom who was to come.*

The Gospel says: “He who comes after me was made before me; I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.”

The eighth responsory says: *Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world; behold him of whom I said to you, ‘He who comes after me was made before me.’*

The ninth responsory says: *I must decrease, but he must increase. He who comes after me was made before me; I am not worthy to untie his sandal.*

The antiphons proceed in order according to the Roman [Col. 1265A] Antiphoner up to the antiphon *Behold, the Lord will appear*.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Antiphons of the Weekdays in the Week Immediately Before the Nativity of the Lord

For seven days the antiphons of Matins are renewed in all the Antiphoners before the Nativity of the Lord—that is, from the first antiphon, *Blow the trumpet in Zion*, on Sunday night, up to the first antiphon, *Judea and Jerusalem*, on Saturday night.

The sevenfold Spirit, whose work is the conception and birth of Saint Mary, is recalled to our memory through the number seven. Hence the prophet Isaiah is also read during this same week. He enumerates the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit on Friday, when the first human being [Col. 1265B] was created, whom the second human being now came to restore.

The repeated use of the number seven corresponds to our journey, by which we must go out to meet the infant Christ, so that through it we may learn that it is necessary for us to pray for the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit. Renewed and adorned by these gifts, we can worthily present ourselves to the mysteries of Christ’s birth.

For the same Holy Spirit overshadowed Saint Mary, so that she herself might receive and bear him—that is, Christ our Lord—and become his dwelling place.

As I said, I did not find the responsories divided by weekdays by the ancient Fathers; therefore I shall be silent about them.

I found *A little child will be born for us* among the responsories that begin with *Blow the trumpet in Zion* in the Roman [Col. 1265C] Antiphoner, and placed among the weekdays in the Metz Antiphoner, as I think, because it is written in the Antiphoner in the future tense: *A little child will be born for us*.

For we read the prophet Isaiah, from whom this responsory was taken, and it was found in both the Hebrew translation and the Septuagint that the statement there is in the past tense: *A child has been born for us*.

We followed the prophet and wrote it on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, when the words of the responsory are read in the nocturnal office and in the reading at Mass—especially since I had previously heard it sung at the Nativity of the Lord, though it was sung in the form in which it has been sung until now, *A little child will be born for us*. We have changed it according to the prophet Isaiah: *A child has been born for us*.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Antiphons That Begin with “O”

The antiphons sung during the present week with the hymn of holy Mary, all of which have an *O* at the beginning, show us a certain marvelous and inscrutable sign being celebrated in these days. Concerning this sign the prophet Isaiah says: “For this reason the Lord will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son.” Concerning that birth John the Baptist says: “Whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen.” *O* is an interjection of wonder. By means of this *O*, the cantor wished to indicate that the words that follow concern some marvelous vision, one more suited to the mind’s rumination than to a preacher’s narration.

[Col. 1266A] And since this wonder was produced through the conception and birth of holy Mary, the antiphons mentioned are more appropriate to the hymn of holy Mary than to that of Zechariah. And if anyone wishes to add an eighth antiphon on account of the perfection of the sum, he has an evident rationale, which Saint Augustine writes concerning the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, saying: “Blessed, therefore, are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” This eighth saying returns to the beginning and declares the perfected human being.

The first antiphon among the eight presently under discussion in the arrangement of the Antiphoner, entitled “[O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High],” is partly taken from the book of Jesus son of Sirach and partly from the book of Wisdom, commonly called Solomon’s. For that book marvelously praises wisdom.

[Col. 1266B] Thus it is written in the book of Jesus son of Sirach concerning the praise of wisdom: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature.” We must not think that the Lord possesses the members and bodily features of a human being in the way a human being does. Rather, because of the various works that he performs in individual human beings, human members are named in relation to him, since he does not cease each day to perform what he created all at once.

Hands are ascribed to him, as in the passage: “Your hands made me and fashioned me,” because he continually generates the Son from his own substance. A womb is ascribed to him, as in: “Before the morning star I begot you.” When he grants wisdom and upright speech for the manifestation of human beings, a mouth is ascribed to him, as here: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High.”

And again from Isaiah: “Then you will delight in the Lord,

[Col. 1266C] and I will raise you above the heights of the earth, and I will feed you with the inheritance of Jacob your father. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken.” Concerning the end of this chapter Saint Jerome wrote in the sixteenth book of his commentary on Isaiah, saying: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken,” so that just as in the hands we understand a work, in the feet a movement, in the womb generation, and in the ears and eyes hearing and sight, so in the mouth of God we understand speech. Otherwise, the simple and unchangeable nature of God is always and everywhere.

It follows: “[You reach mightily from end to end and dispose all things gently].” In the aforementioned book this is contained as follows: “Wisdom overcomes wickedness; therefore she reaches mightily from end to end and disposes all things gently. I loved her and sought her from my youth.”

According to what precedes in the present book,

[Col. 1266D] these words may be understood historically. For it is written: “He himself gave me true knowledge of the things that are, so that I might know the arrangement of the earth, the powers of the elements, the beginning and the consummation and the middle of times, and reflection upon all things, and the rest that follows.” And shortly afterward: “Whatever things are hidden and unforeseen I learned, for the artisan of all things taught me wisdom.” And below: “Wisdom is better than all things that are mutable.”

She reaches everywhere because of her purity. What reaches everywhere because of its purity reaches everywhere from the end of each work of which it is the craftsman to the end of another perfect work.

Concerning this wisdom Saint Augustine says in his work Against the Arians:

[Col. 1267A] “But where is the wisdom of God”—which is Christ, concerning whom it is written, “He reaches from end to [end] mightily and disposes all things gently”? Since, therefore, the Son is also everywhere, where was he to be sent? He reaches mightily from end to end because he is never resisted, nowhere resisted, and resisted by no one. He disposes all things gently—that is, without dispute, without shouting, without anguish, without weariness.

This will suffice for the present. For the rest, let us attempt to portray the cantor’s feeling concerning the birth of Christ.

O how marvelous you are among human beings, O Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High, even into human conversation! You reach mightily from end to end, because you are eternal, reign everywhere, and cannot be overcome. You came forth from the mouth of the Most High when you appeared visibly to human beings.

[Col. 1267B] Hence you yourself said: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world.” For the apostle Paul says of you: “For Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes.” You appeared in Christ; in him you brought the law to its end and fulfilled it—not only in him but also in all who believe in him.

You reach from the man Christ, who is the end of the law, to the end of those who believe in him, so mightily that the strong armed man finds no breach or opening through which he may enter the fold of his chosen flock.

What the prophet David foretold long ago has been fulfilled: “You, Lord, will preserve us and guard us from this generation forever; the wicked walk about.”

Again, O Wisdom, you reach mightily from end to end when, from Christ—who came at the end of the world and fulfilled the law—to the consummation of the age, you are

[Col. 1267C] with your disciples, so that all adversaries cannot resist or contradict the mouth and reason that you gave them. And in one and the same Spirit you gently dispose all the gifts of the Holy Spirit for them.

Since the present antiphons adorn with their sweetness the seven or eight days in which the sevenfold Spirit is commemorated—the Spirit who always dwelt in Christ as man from the moment he began to be man, and the Word became flesh in order to dwell among us—it is fitting that I demonstrate, insofar as I can, how consonant each of them is with the individual stages of the Holy Spirit.

Although a different order of the present antiphons is found written in the Roman Antiphoner and in the Metz Antiphoner, the first antiphon, “O Wisdom,” corresponds to the first stage, the spirit of wisdom. For it is one thing to have wisdom and another to understand.

[Col. 1267D] Many have a taste for eternal things, but are altogether unable to understand them. The wisdom that is in Christ powerfully refreshes the mind with certainty and hope concerning eternal things, and maturely orders all things. Supreme wisdom is in Christ; the wisdom found in other human beings is a spark of supreme wisdom.

The second antiphon presents Christ as a marvelous doorkeeper: what he closes, no one opens, and what he opens, no one closes. Thus it is written concerning him in the Apocalypse: “Thus says the holy and true one, who has the key of David: he opens and no one shuts; he shuts and no one opens.”

This is understood as follows: “Who has the key of David”—that is, royal power, either because he was born from David’s stock, or because [Col. 1268A] David’s prophecy was disclosed through Christ’s dispensation.

“He opens and no one shuts; he shuts and no one opens.” The secrets of divine law are opened to the faithful and closed to unbelievers by Christ’s power alone.

This antiphon is suited to the stage of the spirit of understanding. The spirit of understanding that is in Christ penetrates hidden things by the sharpness of its light and illuminates the darkness of the heart. For this is what the one who opens when he wishes accomplishes—what no one can close. Christ is the true light that enlightens every human being.

The third antiphon says: “O Emmanuel, our king and lawgiver.” What is more marvelous to say than that God should be with human beings, eat and drink with them, and answer their questions whenever they wish?

He himself is King David, not temporally but eternally. He is, in a certain sense, another Moses, who [Col. 1268B] gives us a law enduring through ages of ages. We who are from the nations awaited him; he will save us forever.

This antiphon corresponds to the third stage, the spirit of counsel. The spirit of counsel that is in Christ, by providing in advance, fortifies his members so that they do not fall headlong. This is the task of a king and lawgiver: to rule according to reason the people subject to him, to foresee what they ought to do and what they ought to avoid.

Christ is the Counselor, the Mighty God.

The fourth antiphon presents itself with marvelous praise and, in a certain sense, ineffably. It says that the root of Jesse stands as a sign for the peoples, that kings are silent in his presence, and that the nations will entreat him.

For thus it sings: “O Root of Jesse, who stand upon the cross, in whose hands are horns, and who are a sign for the peoples, when the sun was darkened, [Col. 1268C] the earthquake occurred, the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened.”

“Before whom kings will hold their mouths”—that is, the rulers of this age, who, with their rhetoric and dialectic, will be silent when the preaching of the holy cross and the holy Gospel arrives. Hence on this day the nations have been stirred up to preach the Crucified One.

This antiphon is suited to the fourth stage, the spirit of fortitude. The spirit of fortitude that is in Christ makes one unafraid of adversity and grants confidence to the trembling mind.

For from the root of Jesse arose King David, that is, the strong of hand. This king, strong of hand, stands as a sign for the peoples—namely, the Lord Jesus Christ crucified upon the cross—so that many may look toward him and wish to be protected under his strength.

Those who are kings in name only hold their mouths before him,

[Col. 1268D] because they can neither undertake nor dare to enter into conflict with his strength. Therefore many nations stream to him, entreating his protection.

The fifth antiphon marvels at the unheard-of one who rises—one who is not changed from day to day according to the alternation of the seasons, as things ordinarily are, but is eternal, whose sun illuminates not only the eyes of the body but also those of the mind. For righteousness belongs to the sight of the mind.

This antiphon corresponds to the fifth stage, the spirit of knowledge. The spirit of knowledge that is in Christ knows what to punish mercifully and what to forgive mercifully. Christ is the rising of knowledge rooted in charity. It is the work of righteousness alone to render knowing the eyes of the mind that contemplate.

The sixth antiphon recounts a marvelous event,

[Col. 1269A] namely, that the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire from the bush, while the bush was not consumed.

This antiphon corresponds to the sixth stage, the spirit of piety. The spirit of piety that is in Christ mercifully spares those who inflict evil upon him.

Moses was filled with that Spirit, concerning whom it is written that he was the meekest of all human beings. Yet no one is meeker than Christ. Christ, who lived among the Jewish people, shone in the flame of fire. He performed miracles, forgave sins to the humble, the quiet, and those who trembled at the word of the Lord. But the thorny thickets of the proud hearts of the Jews were not burned—those who plotted ambushes and persecutions against Christ. Nevertheless, Christ’s piety endured all these things, even to the point that he prayed on the cross for his persecutors.

[Col. 1269B] The seventh antiphon recalls the King of the nations and, in a marvelous way, places a stone at the head of the corner. We believe this stone to be living, and he wishes this to be his work, as the antiphon says: that he should make both into one—that is, join together two walls coming from different directions, from the Jewish people and from the Gentile people, and make one Church.

This antiphon corresponds to the seventh stage, the spirit of fear. The spirit of fear that is in Christ makes the nations fear, as it is written: “The nations will fear your name, Lord, and all the kings of the earth your glory.”

The eighth, “O Virgin of virgins,” intimates the Church’s wonder at the marvelous birth, saying: “Daughters of Jerusalem, why do you marvel at me? This mystery that you behold is divine.”

This antiphon shows that the man who assumed flesh from Mary is alone perfect among other human beings, because [Col. 1269C] in him alone dwells the sevenfold Spirit mentioned above.

Concerning this matter Saint Augustine writes in the first book of his work On the Sermon on the Mount. “There are therefore seven things that bring perfection, for the eighth clarifies and displays what is perfect.”

If anyone is pleased by the order of the present antiphons contained in the Roman Antiphoner, he will find it set out under the following heading in our Antiphoner.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the Office “Sanctify Yourselves”

The present office strives to indicate the appointed day of the Lord’s birth and the salvation that the birth itself brings with it, after the manner of Moses’ admonition. Moses commanded the people to sanctify themselves before the Lord descended upon the mountain.

Thus it is written [Col. 1269D] in Exodus, chapter nineteen:

“Go to the people,” the Lord said to Moses, “and sanctify them today and tomorrow. Let them wash their garments and be ready on the third day. For on the third day the Lord will descend before all the people upon Mount Sinai.”

And below:

“Moses came down from the mountain to the people and sanctified them. When they had washed their garments, he said to them: ‘Be ready on the third day; do not approach your wives.’”

Many in our Church follow this sanctification. But those who have been reborn spiritually ought to wash their garments spiritually—that is, cleanse away their committed sins through tears and compunction—so that they may meet the Lord’s descent without offense.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the Birth of the Lord

[Col. 1270A]

I found two nocturnal offices placed on one and the same night in the Roman Antiphoner. The first office, after the antiphon “[The Lord said to me],” had the antiphons “[Like a bridegroom]” and “[Grace has been poured forth].” The second had “[He placed his tabernacle in the sun]” and “[Lift up, eternal gates].”

Therefore I asked a certain cleric educated from infancy in the holy Roman Church why these two offices had been placed on one night: one proceeding through the antiphons “The Lord said to me,” “Like a bridegroom,” and “Grace has been poured forth”; and the other having as its first antiphon “The Lord said to me,” its second “[He placed it in the sun],” and its third “[Lift up, [Col. 1270B] eternal gates].”

He replied: “The office that has as its second antiphon ‘He placed it in the sun’ and as its third ‘Lift up’ is customarily sung by the Apostolicus at the vigils and in the church of Saint Mary at the Crèche without an invitatory.

“The other, which has as its second antiphon ‘Like a bridegroom,’ the clerics customarily sing in the church of Saint Peter, with the invitatory ‘Christ is born for us,’ at night, when the people customarily rise for the office.

“For this reason we placed first in our Antiphoner the antiphons that proceed through the second antiphon, ‘He placed his tabernacle in the sun,’ since that office is first celebrated by the Apostolicus at the vigils, and afterward the one whose second-place antiphon is ‘Like a bridegroom,’ in the church of Saint Peter at night.”

According to the order of the psalms and the beauty of the melody, the antiphons

[Col. 1270C] themselves suit the night of the Lord’s birth. We customarily sing them during the Lord’s octave, and the Apostolic man sings them at the first vigils in the church of Saint Mary Major.

The antiphon “[He placed his tabernacle in the sun]” is placed in the same psalm and at the same verse as the antiphon “[Like a bridegroom].” The antiphon “[Beautiful in form]” is placed at the same verse as “[Grace has been poured forth].” Their melodies are more beautiful than those that follow them. The same is true of the rest of the subsequent antiphons according to that order, in which the second is “He placed his tabernacle in the sun.”

The difference is that the antiphons of the third nocturn do not have *Alleluia* at the end or in the middle.

It should be noted that the three nocturns recall the three periods of the whole world: the period of the natural law, the period of the law given through Moses, and the period of grace.

The third nocturn,

[Col. 1270D] which recalls the grace of the New Testament, ought to have antiphons with *Alleluia* if they are sung at the time when the Lord’s resurrection is regularly celebrated by the faithful—that is, around the morning hour.

But the nocturns celebrated at the first vigils frequently end before midnight. In that part of the night the Lord’s resurrection is not celebrated except at Easter, on account of the mystery appropriate to it. Therefore the others are customarily without *Alleluia*, as those sung at the first vigils are in this place.

Nor do those sung at the morning office at the stated hour have *Alleluia*, as can be seen in our Antiphoner, which has the antiphons according to the Roman Antiphoner at the first vigils and at the morning office, except for one in the Gospel, “[It happened with the angel].”

[Col. 1271A] The aforementioned cleric of the holy Roman Church told me that at the Lord’s birth the antiphon “When the sun has risen” was sung by the holy Roman Church with the hymn of Zechariah. Yet I found it written in the Roman Antiphoner with the hymn of Zechariah on the night when the responsory “Sanctify yourselves today” is sung—a responsory that we customarily sing with the hymn of holy Mary on the preceding night of the Lord’s birth according to the flesh.

But the antiphons celebrated on that same night around the singing of the people and afterward have *Alleluia* in the third nocturn, as in “[He called upon me, Alleluia]” and “[Let the heavens rejoice and the earth exult before the face of the Lord, Alleluia, Alleluia. The Lord has made it known, Alleluia].” All the antiphons sung at the morning office also have

[Col. 1271B] *Alleluia*.

The responsories of that same night follow the custom practiced by household servants of kings and emperors when they come into the presence of the king: each offers the king whatever he is able to offer. They offer different gifts, but equally desire to reconcile themselves to the king’s favor and to please him.

So too the responsories offer to King Christ the thoughts of many minds, painted in varied colors and with manifold thanksgiving. They give thanks by praising holy Mary, because she brought forth in her lap the one whom the heavens cannot contain. They give thanks because the King of the heavens deigned to assume flesh from a virgin, in order to recall fallen humanity to heaven, at which the army of angels rejoices. They give thanks because through his birth the heavens—that is, the preachers—have become honey-sweet through the sweetness of spiritual understanding.

If I am not mistaken, anyone who seeks this feeling will find it expressed through many responsories concerning the present birth of the Lord.

The number of lessons and responsories, as well as of the antiphons of the nocturnal office, admonishes us to bless the Lord, praise him, and give thanks to him, because he wished his Word to become flesh in order to gather fallen humanity into the fellowship of the nine orders of angels.

I arranged the antiphons at the morning hour so that the first should show the birth of Christ from the virgin Mary—namely, “The woman who gave birth has brought forth a king”—and also the perpetual virginity of that same holy Mary. The following antiphons are taken from the Gospel, and likewise from the order of the saints’ festivals.

[Col. 1271D] It should also be noted here that just as through the number nine, which is celebrated at the Lord’s birth, we give thanks for God’s descent even to our humiliation, so through the same number we give thanks at the festivals of the saints, since they are worthy to ascend to the height of heaven, where the angels dwell.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the Evening Offices at the Lord’s Birth and at the Birthdays of the Saints

When I was young, I saw cantors celebrate the evening assembly preceding the day of a solemnity with more splendid singing and greater glory than the following evening of the feast day. Sometimes, indeed, [Col. 1272A] the songs of the saints’ festivals were celebrated on the preceding evening, and on the following evening those of ordinary weekdays.

Nevertheless, in the Antiphoners we had written for the day of the Lord’s birth and for the birthdays of the apostles Peter, Paul, and Andrew, there were antiphons suitable and appropriate to those days at the evening office following the day on which the Mass of their birthdays was celebrated. There we sang them, as we still do.

I, trained in the ancient custom, began to consider why the antiphons for the birthdays of the saints had not been established for the preceding evenings, during which, at the other festivals of the saints, I heard more glorious singing and saw a larger gathering of people and a more splendid office of lights than on the following evenings.

By God’s mercy I discovered that the celebration of evening solemnities was arranged more reasonably [Col. 1272B] by the ancient writers who composed the antiphons than by modern cantors.

Even now, when asked about the evening assembly, they commonly say that “Blessed be the Lord my God” belongs to Sunday. If they had wished to observe that the psalms of this evening had been placed at the end of the evening psalms, they would never say this. For the one who arranged the evening psalms undoubtedly began composing the order of the evening psalms from Sunday, and not from the end of the week.

Therefore “[The Lord said to my Lord]” belongs to Sunday; “[I loved him because the Lord will hear the voice of my prayer]” to Monday; “[I rejoiced at the things that were said to me]” to Tuesday;

[Col. 1272C] “[Unless the Lord builds the house]” and “[I will confess to you, Lord, with all my heart]” to Friday; “[Blessed be the Lord my God]” to Saturday.

Unless this order is maintained, it will not be true, according to the exposition of Lord Bede, that what is written in Ezra took place: “Four times a day they confessed to the Lord,” that is, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and in the evening.

Those who wish to celebrate antiphons from the Gospels read on the Sundays properly celebrate them in the morning office belonging to Sunday and at the evening office in which the psalm “[The Lord said to my Lord]” is sung.

If the antiphons are too numerous, they may indifferently be said on each of the weekdays for as long as the same Gospel is being read.

At festivals of the saints and other solemnities, if the evening offices are celebrated late, so that the sun has passed toward setting, the antiphons of the feast day may properly be said at the preceding evening office, because we have it written: “You shall celebrate your feasts from evening to evening,” that is, from sunset to sunset.

But if someone wishes to say that, although the sun has not yet passed toward setting, nevertheless, because we are performing the office in memory of this or that solemnity, that solemnity is already being celebrated in our minds, then we properly perform the office whose solemnity is being celebrated in our minds. We give thanks to God for the love of those minds, because charity, which believes all things, makes all things acceptable before God.

The composer of the Antiphoner, who placed the evening antiphon “[With you is dominion]” and the others [Col. 1273A] that follow it at the end of the day of the Lord’s birth, after the other offices had been celebrated, intended to indicate that this evening belonged more to the feast of the Lord’s birth than did the preceding evening before sunset.

Is this the rationale in the festivals of the apostles and the other saints: that the evening at the end of their birthday, after the other offices have been celebrated, belongs more to their natal day than does the preceding evening before sunset?

I have written about the twelve nights in the preface to the Lectionary, and I intend to write about them in the commentary on the daytime office.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning the Feast of Saint Stephen, the Protomartyr

I said above, with ancient custom supplying the rationale, that I had prescribed that the antiphons of [Col. 1273B] the third nocturn, which is sung around the fourth watch of the night, should have *Alleluia*, and likewise that the morning antiphons of the great festivals should have it. This is not found at the feast of Saint Stephen, Saint John, or the Innocents.

There are festivals whose offices are celebrated at night around the evening hour, which are commonly called proper offices; and in the later part of the night another office is sung, either for the proper weekday or for the common offices of the saints.

Thus, I think, the ancients acted concerning those festivals whose antiphons in the morning office do not have *Alleluia*.

The antiphons that we customarily sing in the nocturnal office at the festivals of the saints and that begin, “His delight was in the law of the Lord, day and night,” were, I think, selected by the *mordis* [read: *modernis*, “moderns”] from the multitude

[Col. 1273C] of antiphons that we have written in our Antiphoner from the Roman one. If anyone wishes to read them, he will find that they were not established from the beginning in the form in which they are sung among us.

I arranged the responsories as the rationale taught, according to the order of the history and events. Wherever I changed words from the Roman Antiphoner, I placed an *R* in the margin of the same page opposite them.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the Feast of Saint John

At the feast of Saint John I found six responsories, to which we prefix three—namely, [Col. 1273D] “The just man shall flourish like the lily,” “This is the man who performed great works before God,” and “This man accomplished everything that God commanded him”—so that we may make three nocturns.

In the last responsory, namely, “In the midst of the Church,” a triple *neuma* is sung contrary to the custom of the other responsories, and its verse and the *Gloria* are prolonged with a *neuma* beyond the usual practice.

This was not done by our predecessors without reason. Through it they wished to suggest some teaching to us, one that perhaps could exceed the minds of the cantors, some of whom are often changed from transitory things to eternal things and rejoice more in eternal than in transitory things.

The aforementioned *neuma* occurs among the other words around the word “understanding.” When the cantor comes to “understanding,” perform the *neuma*—that is, fix your step upon things that stand and remain.

What does this mean? It certainly wishes to teach you that, if you should ever arrive at understanding, in which divinity and eternity are perceived, you should, through the desire of your mind, pray for delays [Col. 1274A] there.

For if you have understood those things, you will delight in remaining there, in the things over which you will rejoice—that is, you will be glad without transitory words.

Understanding was within the inward parts of John, providing him with a kind of belch, when he said: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.”

The verse, “[The Lord sent his hand and touched my mouth],” speaks as though John were answering someone who questioned him.

“From where, John, did you receive this understanding, at which the cantors perform a *neuma*?”

He answers: “The Lord sent his hand and touched my mouth.”

“Why,” I ask, “do you perform a *neuma* in this verse, cantor?”

He replies: “Because this sending of the hand and touching of the mouth must be perceived through understanding.”

The singing of “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit” ought by that very power to praise the Holy Trinity by which God is in some way [Col. 1274B] perceived—that is, by understanding.

We must not force the Roman verses so that the meaning at the end of the verse agrees with the meaning at the side of the responsory. The holy Roman Church and our region do not sing the responsories and verses according to one order.

Among them, the principal cantor finishes the responsory in the first order. The assistant cantors respond in the same manner. Then the principal cantor sings the verse. When the verse is finished, the assistant cantors begin the responsory a second time from the beginning and carry it through to the end.

Then the principal cantor sings “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” When this is finished, the assistant cantors enter the responsory around the middle and carry it through to the end.

Finally, the principal cantor begins the responsory from the beginning and carries it to the end. When this is finished, the assistant cantors [Col. 1274C] repeat the responsory a third time from the beginning and carry it through to the end.

Therefore, because the assistant cantors sing the responsory three times, the *neuma* around the word “understanding” is threefold. It belongs to the assistant cantors to sing the *neuma* because of the strength of the joined voices.

From the beginning, responsories were sung three times by the cantors; the responsories concerning the Lord’s Passion show this order. For “Glory” was not sung with the responsories from the beginning.

We also have another verse written in our Antiphoner whose meaning agrees with the side of the responsory, so that if anyone should regard singing the *neuma* as superfluous, he may have a verse suitable for singing according to our custom.

The *neuma* may also be understood in another way as pertaining to the cantors around the word “understanding.”

[Col. 1274D] Most cantors strive to please through sound, and are thereby less imbued with intellectual matters. Their ignorance can be strained out by the *neuma* around the word “understanding.”

*Neuma* is Greek and is interpreted as “mute,” as the grammarian Comminianus says. For the *neuma* strikes foolish cantors on the forehead at the word “understanding,” when it shows them to delight only in sound concerning the understanding of the Scriptures.

Modern cantors also sing this *neuma* in the responsory “[He descended from the heavens],” and at the word “[the structure of the world].” At that word the *neuma* can appropriately fit.

By that *neuma* they indicate that the school of cantors finds great difficulty in explaining in words how the one who was born today from the virgin Mary fashioned and adorned the world, and how he himself is the light and beauty of the entire structure of the world.

The same meaning is found in the verse “[Like a bridegroom, the Lord came forth from his chamber].” It is impossible for the school of cantors to narrate the order of Christ’s procession from the Virgin’s womb, which is compared to a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the Lord’s Octave

We customarily sing only one nocturnal office at the Lord’s birth. Therefore, of the two that are celebrated by the Roman Church and are written in the Roman Antiphoner and in ours for the night of the Lord’s birth, we sing one during the Lord’s octave.

We wrote the morning antiphons for that same night as we found them in the Roman Antiphoner.

[Col. 1275A] What I heard

[Col. 1275B] What I heard from Roman clerics about the octaves of the Lord and of the saints, and what our region practices concerning them, I have partly written in the little book on the Office, and I am attempting partly to write in the little book on the Daytime Office.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the First Sunday after the Lord’s Birth

The antiphon “[The child Jesus]” is taken from the Gospel passage that contains the section after Simeon’s office. This was entirely completed before the arrival of the Magi. Therefore it should occupy a place on the Sunday before Epiphany, when the Gospel from which it was taken is read.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning Epiphany, That Is, Appearance or Manifestation
The antiphon, “[To Christ has dominion been given,]” I found [Col. 1275C] in the Roman Antiphoner among the antiphons for the Nativity of the Lord, and in the Metz Antiphoner among the antiphons for the Epiphany; for in its meaning it is appropriate to both feasts. I also found the antiphon “[Behold, he has come]” among those for the Nativity of the Lord, to which feast it is appropriate, as can be recognized from the Introit of that day itself. Therefore I assign it to the first evening synaxis, and “[To Christ dominion has been given]” to the evening of the day of the Epiphany itself.

Our region at the present service is accustomed to omit one element of the customary order, namely, the invitatory. The invitatory is the psalm “[Come, let us exult in the Lord].” By it the brothers are summoned together and taught what they ought to do after they have assembled. “Come,” it says, “let us exult in the Lord; let us jubilate to God our salvation. Let us come before [Col. 1275D] his face with confession, while the acceptable time remains.” Then it gives the reasons why we ought to come before his face with confession: “For God is a great Lord, and in his hand are all the ends of the earth, and he himself beholds the heights of the mountains.” Again the psalm teaches us what we should do: “Come,” it says, “let us adore and fall prostrate, and let us weep before the Lord, who made us.” And with powerful exhortation it presses us, saying: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts, as the children of Israel did, who saw the works of the Lord for forty years and, because of the hardness of their hearts, did not enter into the Lord’s rest.”

I heard this psalm celebrated at Constantinople, in the church of Hagia Sophia, at the beginning of Mass. [Col. 1276A] The present solemnity contains a twofold mention of the words used for adoring the Lord. One refers to the Magi, who truly sought the Lord in order to adore him and greet him with gifts; the other refers to Herod, who deceitfully said to the Magi: “Go and inquire diligently about the child; and when you have found him, report to me, so that I too may come and adore him.” The goodwill of the Magi, who were ordinary men, is to be imitated by us. The deceitfulness of Herod, who appeared to be a prince and king among the Jewish people, is to be avoided.

Because of this admonition and correction, it may reasonably be appropriate for the present service that the psalm “[Come, let us exult in the Lord]” be omitted from the first order of psalms and placed in the sixth order. The six antiphons in the two nocturns recall [Col. 1276B] the service of the Magi concerning Christ’s birth.

The three Magi who came to the Lord on this night were, through their mystical gifts, representatives of the Gentile people who dwell on the mainland and in the islands. Their three gifts prefigured Christ’s threefold character, namely, that of king, priest, and mortal man, as well as the three functions of Christ’s members, namely, wisdom, the power of prayer, and the mortification of the flesh. The gifts of the Magi carried the representation of these three functions.

From the gift of frankincense, the first antiphon says: “[Bring offerings to the Lord, sons of God,]” to the islands of the priests who inhabit the earth: “Bring offerings to the Lord, sons of God”—you can therefore be called sons of God because you are priests. What they ought to bring is understood: frankincense. It is as though it said: “[Col. 1276C] Bring the power of your prayer to Christ, since through him your prayers are directed to God the Father.” Frankincense is appropriate to the priesthood.

From the gift of gold, the second antiphon is addressed to the wise and understanding: “[Sing to our God, sing; sing to our king, sing wisely].” Through gold, wisdom is offered. For it is written: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise.” Gold is appropriate to God and to a king.

From the gift of myrrh, the third antiphon speaks of the whole mortal people who strive toward better things: “Let all the earth adore you and sing to you; let it sing a psalm to your name, O Lord.” The present antiphon is as though saying: “Let all the earth adore you and sing to you through the mortification of the flesh,” and let it say to you: “For your sake we are put to death all day long.” Myrrh is appropriate as an embalming spice for the bodies of the dead. [Col. 1276D]

This vigil speaks of the nations that dwell on the mainland; the second vigil speaks of those who dwell in the islands. Through the first antiphon it speaks of the wise: “[The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts].” Kings are called kings because they rule themselves and others; they are therefore called wise.

Through the second antiphon it speaks of the whole people: “[All the nations that you have made will come and adore before you, O Lord].”

Through the third antiphon the priests exhort one another and say: “[Come, let us adore him, for he is the Lord our God].”

The third vigil, however, speaks of Christ’s baptism. The third vigil usually brings the New Testament back to our memory. The New Testament, moreover, [Col. 1277A] was founded through baptism.

In the third vigil the mission of the Magi is completed. In the earlier vigils the words of the Magi are spoken concerning the future: “[Let all the earth adore you].” And again: “[The kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts].” But in this vigil, in which the New Testament is recalled, the whole earth sings to the Lord in the present through the repeated Alleluia, and says to its subjects: “[Adore the Lord].” And again, they say: “Let the many islands rejoice; adore the Lord.”

The psalm “[Our God is our refuge]” is placed in this vigil because it recalls the disturbance of the people who were troubled on account of the preaching of the New Testament and wished to resist the apostles’ preaching. Yet, by God’s providence, the force of the river, supplied through the apostles [Col. 1277B] by the ministry of the baptistery, overcame the agitation of earthly people and gladdened the city of God. For this city of God also consists of inhabitants of the mainland and the islands.

In the New Testament the Church says to those who have been baptized in Christ and dwell on the mainland, through the second psalm: “[Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth];” and through the antiphon: “[Adore the Lord in his holy court].” To those who dwell in the islands it says, through the third psalm: “[The Lord reigns; let the earth exult; let the many islands rejoice];” and through the antiphon: “[Adore the Lord, all his angels].”

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Responsories

In the order of the responsories we have written first [Col. 1277C] the responsory “[The day has been sanctified];” then “[Shine forth, Jerusalem];” for it is written according to the translation of the Seventy. In the Hebrew, however, it reads: “[Arise, shine, for your light has come].”

It is taken from the prophet Isaiah, and it recounts the illumination of the holy Church through Christ’s coming. If it is necessary to speak in the manner truly appropriate to the Magi, as Saint Ambrose says—for those who had seen Christ had understood Christ—we ought to understand that the Magi had been made into Jerusalem. For they would not have understood Christ unless they had been illuminated by him.

After this comes the third responsory from the same prophet, according to the order of the historical narrative: “[All will come from Sheba, bringing gold and frankincense].” In the Magi whom we believe to have been envoys of the whole world, we can understand all those who come from [Col. 1277D] Sheba. Through those who come from Sheba—that is, from captivity—to the Lord, we understand the multitude of the nations turning to the Lord.

Sheba, as Saint Jerome says in his commentary on the prophet Isaiah, book seventeen, is the entire province in which the regions of Midian and Ephah are located. Sheba is interpreted as “conversion” or “captivity.” And all those coming from captivity, bringing through their conversion the gold of faith and the frankincense of sacrifice, will not be content merely with their own salvation through these gifts; they will advance so that they may proclaim God’s salvation to others. Thus far Jerome.

After these two come the responsories from the Gospel, according to the order of the Gospel narrative, which recounts the order of the Magi’s arrival, [Col. 1278A] the offering of their gifts, and also declares that the stimulus for their journey was the appearance of a new star. After their departure from Herod, it also declares that the same star remained their guide as far as the house where Christ was.

After this narrative I placed in the third nocturn the responsories concerning Christ’s baptism, and finally those concerning the miracle of water changed into wine, according to the order of events.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Antiphons at Matins

It must first be noted that it is the intention of the singers on this night chiefly to celebrate what first took place in the present solemnity, namely, the arrival of the Magi. Therefore, in the present antiphons, I endeavored, in accordance with the sequence of the responsories, to arrange antiphons [Col. 1278B] concerning the arrival of the Magi. And where reason required that songs be sung concerning the other solemnities recalled on this night, I did not hesitate to write them.

The first antiphon, “[Begotten before Lucifer],” points to the present solemnity, namely, the Lord’s manifestation.

The second, “[Your light has come, Jerusalem],” shows through its prophecy what fruit the holy Church would receive from the Lord’s manifestation.

The third, from the same prophecy, “[Those who oppressed you will come to you],” recalls the gain of the holy Church.

The fourth, “[The seas and the rivers],” which is taken from the hymn of the three youths, resounds concerning the Lord’s baptism.

In fifth place is placed the antiphon “[The Magi saw the star],” which is the first item in the Gospel narrative concerning the arrival of the Magi. [Col. 1278C]

The antiphon “[Today, to the heavenly bridegroom]” recalls the three present solemnities. The following antiphons, as I have indicated, make known the arrival of the Magi and preserve the text of the Gospel from which they are taken.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the First Sunday after the Epiphany

I write two antiphons in this place, namely, “[Take the child and his mother],” and “[Return to the land of Judah].” They are taken from the Gospel “[When Herod had died],” which is read on this same Sunday. That Gospel contains Christ’s return from Egypt after the arrival of the Magi and before he was baptized.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Octave of the Theophany

[Col. 1278D] Just as the school of singers strives at the Epiphany to celebrate the arrival of the Magi, so it strives in the octave of the Epiphany to celebrate Christ’s baptism, as though he had been baptized on that very day. For this reason I did not hesitate to write an antiphon from the Gospel, as I first heard it sung: “[Today John rejoices].”

It should be noted that where the antiphons concerning the solemnity of the Magi come to an end, there I began to write antiphons that resound concerning Christ’s baptism and then extend toward the octave of the Epiphany. For there are more antiphons than it is necessary to celebrate in a single night of the octave. Nor have so many been written concerning the arrival of the Magi that, by singing them in order, we could reach the octave of the Epiphany.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the First Sunday after the Octave of the Epiphany

[Col. 1279A]

On the first Sunday after the octave of the Epiphany, the miracle that the Lord performed with water on the Epiphany itself is celebrated; therefore here we write antiphons from that same Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Responsories Taken from the Psalter

We ought not to be reluctant concerning the responsories from the Psalms, nor should the hearers find it tedious if I recite them in their order. It is evident that the chastisement of the body through fasting, the humbling of the mind, and the love of Christ exclude the devil from the enclosure of the holy Church.

The devil was excluded before the Lord’s birth by these obstacles; he is also excluded at the time of Christ’s birth [Col. 1279B] by Christ’s own presence. The devil is saddened because he has been excluded; the Church rejoices because Christ has entered the world. Thus the angel sang to the shepherds: “For behold, I bring you good news of great joy, because today a Savior has been born for you.”

The devil is saddened by the peace of the Church; the choir of angels sings in joy: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” All the saints admonish the Church to rejoice in the present festival, which they solemnly celebrate, just as the angel sang to the shepherds so that they might rejoice at seeing with bodily eyes the Savior who had been born.

One of them, namely Gregory of Nazianzus, explains the order of joy in his homily on the second Epiphany. “Let us rejoice,” he says, “in Christ’s baptism, and celebrate the feast, [Col. 1279C] not indulging the belly but exulting in spirit.”

Concerning this, a certain Greek teacher says in his second homily on the Book of Numbers:

“Paul says: ‘Let everything be done decently and in order.’ Paul, however, as a minister of the Gospel, wants the Christian to be orderly not only in his actions but also in his very appearance. And a little later:

“‘If any one of us is concerned with food and drink and directs all his care toward secular matters, but assigns one or two complete hours of the entire day to God and comes to church for prayer, or hears the word of God in passing, while devoting his principal care to worldly concerns and the belly, that person does not fulfill the command that a human being should proceed according to his proper order.’”

Thus far the Greek teacher.

By transgressing this present command, many, by devoting themselves to the service of the belly, fall into sin during the festive days of the Nativity and Epiphany of the Lord. The devil is always ready, so that when the shepherd has withdrawn for a little while, he may seize an unwary sheep.

For we believe that Christ is always present wherever two or three have been gathered in his name; so too in the Church during the festivals mentioned above, which rejoices in his coming. Therefore, because the joy of the festivals has been received chiefly in his name, with the angel himself singing before them, Christ is around his people and guards them.

When the festivals have been celebrated, the Church must take care of itself in another way, either because it is still on pilgrimage, or because during the festive days the spirit of joy, through human frailty [Col. 1280A] and the natural tendency of the body, has declined into concern for and preoccupation with the belly and its pleasures.

We must fight against this. Therefore the responsories from the Psalms follow; they contain abundant prayer and begin with the first psalm of penitents, namely: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.”

Again, the present period—from the festival of the Theophany until Septuagesima—recalls the devotion and ministry of preachers, from the Church’s first preachers to those of the final days of the New Testament. The letters of the supreme preacher, Paul, which are read at this same time, signify the same thing to us.

Prayer is appropriate to preachers, so that their preaching may have an open door. Concerning the order of the psalms for the common Sunday nights and weekdays, in both the daytime [Col. 1280B] and nighttime offices, I have written in the little book on the Office.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Office of Saint Marcellus

Concerning Saint Marcellus I found one responsory in the Roman Antiphoner, namely, “[This is truly the servant of God].” This responsory is often sung on the festivals of the other supreme pontiffs.

Where the Metz Antiphoner has “[And therefore, placed in the contest],” the Roman contains “[And therefore, placed in prayer].” While reading Saint Augustine’s sermon on Penance, I found the phrase “[saints placed in the contest].” Therefore I did not change what our Church long ago began to sing, namely: “[And therefore, placed in the contest, he became the confessor of the Lord Jesus Christ].”

For just as I found it written, so I write it here: “Both,” he says, [Col. 1280C] “are written most truly: ‘Whoever is born of God does not sin,’ and what we read in the same Epistle of John: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.’ The former is said of the first beginnings of the new person; the latter, of the remnants of the old. We do both in this life. Gradually the newness advances, and as the oldness gradually gives way, the new succeeds it. But while both are being enacted, we are in the contest.”

In the present responsory for the festival of Saint Marcellus, it is written: “[And therefore, placed in the stable].”

Why the responsory “[This is truly the servant of God]” should have this particular form on the festival of Saint Marcellus, I shall explain in the words of the Lord Bede, which he excerpted from the Life of Saint Marcellus in his Martyrology:

“On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of February is the birth-day [Col. 1280D] of Saint Marcellus, pope, who, by order of the emperor Maximinus [Maxentius], was first beaten with clubs and expelled from the presence of the one whom he was rebuking. Then, hearing that he was making into a church the house of Saint Lucina, which he himself had condemned to confiscation because she had given property from her possessions to Christians, and that he was celebrating Mass there, he ordered platforms to be constructed in that church, in the middle of the city, for the animals of the public stable. He assigned the same bishop to the stable for the service of the animals, under public guard.”

I have inserted many offices of saints from the Roman Antiphoner into our Antiphoner that the Metz Antiphoner does not have. I considered why I should omit them, since they are supported by the same authority as those which we find written in the Metz Antiphoner, namely, that of our holy mother, the Roman Church. [Col. 1281A]

We have also added a few items that are contained only in our region, such as the antiphons for Saint Medard and Saint Maurice. Both are designated by the signs prescribed in the prologue to the Antiphoner.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the ὑπαντή (Meeting)

Formerly, when the Metz Antiphoner was the only one known to me, I found in it antiphons over the nocturnal psalms for common virgins that did not seem to me appropriate to the festival of the Presentation of the Lord in the Temple. I began to seek antiphons from various places that would be suitable for the festival mentioned [Col. 1281B] above, and I began to sing them with my brothers in the choir.

Afterward I found proper antiphons in the Roman Antiphoner, and I placed both sets in our Antiphoner. If anyone possesses the Roman ones, let him sing them; if anyone does not possess them, let him see whether those I have written can be fitted into their proper places.

I wrote the responsories from the Roman Antiphoner and added “[This one who has arrived—no one knows his name].” I found the antiphons at Matins arranged in a different order in the Metz and Roman Antiphoners. That order itself is written in our Antiphoner. In the second order I wrote the same antiphons according to the order of the Gospel narrative.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Office of Septuagesima

[Col. 1281C] It must first be noted whose condition is celebrated from the Nativity of the Lord until Septuagesima, and from Septuagesima until the middle of Lent.

The generation of Christ and the generosity of the holy preachers are celebrated from the Nativity of Christ until Septuagesima. From Septuagesima onward, the generation of those who desire to emerge from captivity and from the distress of the present pilgrimage is celebrated, until the generation of Christ is born again around the paschal mysteries.

The generation of Christ and the generosity of his preachers have, for the most part, departed from the present age, so that they may reign with the angels before God. The time of such a departure is called night, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The night is coming, when no one can work.”

The present Church, [Col. 1281D] which is on this pilgrimage, recalls during the night of Septuagesima the glory celebrated among the citizens who have departed; during the day it recalls those who are held in captivity and sigh to return to freedom. Among those constrained by the sorrow of captivity, the brightness of the Alleluia is not celebrated; among those who have departed, the Alleluia is celebrated, because they do not cease from praising God.

In the Antiphoners the first responsory is: “Alleluia: while it is present, they imitate it.” As far as the name Alleluia is concerned, we cannot say, “While the present one is here, they imitate it.” Alleluia is neuter in gender. It is possible that Alleluia should be understood as referring to some thing, and that “while the present one is here, they imitate it” should be indicated. [Col. 1282A]

For the history from which the present responsory is taken teaches what the pronoun refers to. It is written there as follows:

“O how beautiful is the chaste generation with glory! For its memory is immortal, since it is known both to God and to human beings. When it is present, they imitate it; when it has withdrawn, they desire it; and, crowned forever, it triumphs.”

The order of the words is sound if the noun is placed first and the pronoun referring to it is supplied afterward. Therefore I placed this responsory in this order:

“Alleluia, a good name is better than great riches,”

so that a noun might precede that to which “they imitate it” could refer.

Concerning this good name, the lord Bede writes in his exposition of the Proverbs of Solomon:

“A good name, therefore, is the name of religion, which is rightly preferred to worldly riches. For even if someone were to gain the whole world, he would rightly despise it so greatly that his name might be written in heaven, and his memory fixed eternally among the angels and among holy people. This is the beautiful and chaste generation whose memory is fixed among the angels and among holy people.”

The responsory speaks of this generation: “While it is present, they imitate it.” Until the night of Septuagesima, it seemed to us that we had it present, because we frequently celebrated it with the Alleluia in many offices from the Nativity of the Lord until that time.

The first responsory, “[Alleluia, a good name],” is placed first as though it were a sign set upon a mountain, toward which travelers ought to direct their attention. The whole intention of the singers on this night is to magnify the name Alleluia. [Col. 1282C]

The second responsory begins: “While the present one is here, they imitate it.” This name Alleluia must be understood as referring to the thing itself, that is, to the words of the history saying:

“O how beautiful, glorious, and chaste is the spiritual generation! While it is present, they imitate it; and when it has withdrawn, they desire it.”

Who are these, if not the sons and daughters remaining in the present age?

The third responsory, in its Alleluia, recalls the praise of wisdom, as though it said:

“O praise of wisdom, you alone hold the chief place in the sight of the Lord. Through you all things were made.”

In that responsory the mother who has been left here in the world to complete the body of Christ speaks to the things themselves. It seems appropriate to me to turn toward our offspring, which is placed in distress, and to celebrate praise for it in Latin, [Col. 1282D] sympathizing with its tribulation:

“You, praise of wisdom, return to your treasures,”

that is, to the gathering of our offspring, with the Hebrew language, which triumphs before the Lord; for there the angels will bless you.

The fourth responsory is from the same body, as are several responsories.

The fifth responsory, “[Remain with us today],” is taken from the Book of Judges. It is written in the nineteenth chapter as follows:

“There was a certain Levite, dwelling at the side of Mount Ephraim, who took a wife from Bethlehem in Judah. She left him and returned to her father’s house in Bethlehem, and remained with him for four months. Her husband followed her.”

And below:

“On the fourth day, rising at night, there is no doubt that the woman’s husband wished to depart.” His father-in-law detained him.

And again below:

“His father-in-law spoke to him again: ‘Consider that the day is declining toward sunset and evening is approaching. Remain with me today also, and spend the day joyfully; tomorrow you shall depart to go to your home.’”

In its Alleluia this responsory contains the praise of charity. This son-in-law withdrew on the fifth day from the common joy that he had shared with his father-in-law. The responsory “[Remain with us today]” occupies the fifth region.

From this order, the remaining responsories repeatedly pray that the Alleluia may return again to the present Church when the bridegroom deigns to rise from the dead.

The sixth responsory is taken from Tobit. It is written as follows:

“But the angel said to him: ‘I will lead him back to you safe and sound, your son.’ [Col. 1283B] Tobias answered and said: ‘May you travel well, and may the Lord be on your journey, and may his angel accompany you.’”

And again:

“For I believe that the good angel of God accompanies him and orders well everything that happens around him, so that he may return to us with joy.”

This touches upon a consolation that we did not hear in the preceding responsories, namely: “that you may return to us again with joy.” It is as though it said:

“May the good angel of the Lord accompany your journeys with the glorious celebration of the Alleluia and order them well; and when the time of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ comes, and the beautiful, glorious, and chaste generation is born again through the baptismal mysteries, may he return to us with joy, and may the Alleluia be heard from our mouths throughout all the Churches.”

The seventh responsory, “[May your years be multiplied by the Lord],” [Col. 1283C] has almost the same meaning. It can appropriately be followed by the responsory “[I will declare your name to my brothers].” It is as though our mother, who commended the Alleluia among the heavenly citizens and again prays for its coming, were saying:

“When the Alleluia has returned to me, I will declare your name to my brothers.”

This is followed by the responsory “[It is good to confess].” In it what it means to declare and praise the name Alleluia is made clear.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Sexagesima

The present responsories are appropriate both to the present celebration, namely, Septuagesima, and to the condition of the seasons, namely, the beginning of the year. In them the misery of humanity is revealed: how it deserved captivity. The beginnings of creation are also sung.

Spring is the beginning of the year. During it responsories are sung that are taken from the Histories of the first holy fathers, through whom the holy religion was renewed in the earliest times after the condemnation of the first mass.

The responsories of Sexagesima remind us sufficiently of the happy creation of the first human being and of his extremely miserable transformation, namely, from light into darkness and from happiness into misery. This can be indicated by two responsories: “[While the Lord was walking in the paradise],” and “[By the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread].”

I arranged the responsories of this conclusion according to the sequence of the history from which they were taken.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the Antiphons at Matins on Sexagesima

[Col. 1284A]

The name Sexagesima descends obliquely from Septuagesima. Sexagesima is derived from the numbers six and ten. In the reckoning of numbers, there are ten between Septuagesima and Sexagesima. In the customary naming of our books, however, there are no more than seven days between Septuagesima and Sexagesima. This was not named so without providential purpose.

Whoever wishes to investigate the mystical meanings will find the number ten in the number seven, that is, the apprehension of the Ten Commandments in the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.
