Septuagesima is completed, as has often been said, on the Saturday called Closed Easter. Sexagesima falls on the Wednesday called Mid-Easter. For there are three complete days from Wednesday to Saturday. This gives us to understand that if someone seeks the remission of sins worthily and orderly at the beginning of his conversion, he will attain contemplation of the Holy Trinity.

Our fathers were in captivity for seventy years; toward the end of the reckoning of Septuagesima they deserved to be recalled from captivity. That captivity prefigured the captivity of the Christian people, which it suffers under the devil and his ministers. This is lamented in the psalm “[Have mercy on me, O God].”

The psalm “[Have mercy on me, O God]” is numbered fifty; that number begins with the number five. For our sin is gathered through the five senses.

The psalm “[Give thanks to the Lord]” is numbered one hundred seventeen. By this number the everlasting kingdom of God is signified. Whoever, in the psalm “[Have mercy on me, O God],” makes satisfaction by repenting and publicly confessing his sins in a foreign land deserves to be recalled and restored to the kingdom of Christ through the psalm “[Give thanks to the Lord].” [Col. 1284C]

The first antiphons from the psalm “[Have mercy on me, O God]” recall the penitent’s act of satisfaction. We sin for two reasons: either when we leave undone what we ought to do, or when we do what we ought not to do; against both of these we must fight. For the sin of transgression the first antiphon cries: “Have mercy on me, O God, and cleanse me from my transgression, for against you alone have I sinned.” Once the mind has received this spark of light through the gift of the Holy Spirit and perseveres in crying out the words of the antiphon, it has already begun to return from captivity.

After the present psalm, that is, “[Have mercy on me, O God],” follows the psalm “[Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good].” The beginning of this psalm, the one hundred seventeenth, and the conclusion of the fiftieth psalm correspond: both parts recall God’s benefits. The beginnings of the fiftieth psalm and the endings of the one hundred seventeenth psalm also answer one another. In the beginning of the fiftieth psalm there is confession of sins for the washing away of sins; at the end of the one hundred seventeenth there is joyful confession for benefits received and thanksgiving. So great is God’s mercy toward penitents that they are received from the degree of fear into the degree of piety, and from the degree of humility into the degree of exaltation. [Col. 1284D]

The first antiphons from the psalm “[Have mercy on me, O God]” recall the saying: “The righteous person is first the accuser of himself.” [Col. 1285A] The antiphons from the psalm “[Give thanks to the Lord]” follow the order of the Gospel, which says:

“When you are invited, go and recline in the last place, so that when the one who invited you comes, he may say to you, ‘Friend, move up higher’; then you will have glory before all those reclining with you.”

In accordance with this saying, the verses of the antiphons of the present psalm rise upward: those who are recalled to the Church through repentance ought to ascend by the steps of humility.

The antiphon “[I will confess to you]” pertains to joy, as Cassiodorus says in his commentary on the same psalm:

“We briefly declare that we should understand this most joyful confession as poured forth after the benefits have been received.”

But the remaining antiphons [Col. 1285B] of the following psalms proceed according to the order of the sequence of each individual psalm. When, by God’s mercy, we come to the places where the order has changed, we shall say there what the Lord grants.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On Quinquagesima

Quinquagesima, descending obliquely, stands at the third degree from Septuagesima. Abraham also existed in the third age of the world.

Quinquagesima takes its name from the number five. The number five is appropriate to the external human being, who is enlivened through the five senses, whether toward good or toward evil.

The fiftieth psalm has the voice of a penitent; the fiftieth year is placed in the jubilee. Quinquagesima receives its answer on the very day of the Lord’s resurrection. For from Quinquagesima there are fifty days until the Lord’s Easter. Whoever prays for sin during Quinquagesima obtains joy at the Lord’s Easter.

I found the responsories concerning Noah that have a place in this order joined in the Roman Antiphoners with the ancient responsories for Lent. I have nothing to say about this joining, especially since in this matter I follow the modern practice in our Church, who placed them before Abraham together with the responsories of Quinquagesima.

According to the sequence of the history, the order is that those concerning Noah be inserted between the responsories about Adam and Abraham. I shall provide an opportunity for understanding how the sacramental significance of the forty days and nights during which the heavens were opened corresponds to the present week, from the words of Saint Augustine as I found them in the volume of Eugippius, chapter sixty-one:

“It rained for forty days and forty nights, because all guilt of sins under the Ten Commandments of the Law is taken away throughout the whole world, which is contained in four parts. For ten multiplied by four makes forty. Whether, therefore, that guilt which pertains to the days and is contracted from the prosperity of worldly things, or that which pertains to the nights and is contracted from the adversity of worldly things, it is washed away through the sacrament of heavenly baptism.”

Those who are to be renewed through baptism ought to touch upon the patterns of the numbers forty and six. Through baptism the first human being, Adam, dispersed through the four parts of the world, is recalled to one body, the body of Christ. The body of Christ is read as having been constructed over forty-six years. Concerning this mystery, from Augustine’s words we have a written account in the little book on the Office, in the place where it speaks of Wednesday, which is called the beginning of the fast.

From the present Wednesday there are forty-six days until the public baptism. Although the order does not require that the responsory “[Forty days and nights]” be sung first on that same Wednesday, nevertheless, according to the order of the history, it is sung first on the Sunday night whose week contains the Wednesday that begins the fast.

According to the order of the history, and according to the sacramental meaning fashioned from the reckoning of the number forty, the responsories concerning Noah have an appropriate place at Quinquagesima, before Abraham. I arranged the responsories concerning Abraham as before, according to the order of the history, and finally [Col. 1286B] placed two from the Gospels that are read in the same week.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Antiphons at Matins on Quinquagesima

In this order the antiphon says: “According to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.” In it forgiveness is sought for what we have done against the law of the Lord.

On the preceding Sunday we pleaded for those things because we failed to do what we ought to have done; on this Sunday we plead for those things because we did what we ought not to have done.

After these two antiphons, thanksgiving is given in the antiphon from the second psalm, as though the mind believed that it had obtained what it had requested. Thus Cassiodorus says in the commentary mentioned above:

“You are my God, and I will confess to you; you are my God, and I will exalt you.”

In the first clause he says, “I will confess to you,” which pertains to thanksgiving; in the second, “I will exalt you,” because the Lord Christ, who returns good for evil, is exalted through the preaching of the blessed among all the nations.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Lent

The people of Metz customarily sing the invitatory in the middle of Lent: “Do not let it be in vain for you to rise early before daylight,” because the Lord has promised a crown to those who keep vigil. This antiphon contains an exhortation appropriate to the present season. Therefore it seemed fitting to me to place it at the beginning of the chapter on the Lenten season.

The responsories for Lent are the keys to the title concerning the conduct and condition of the whole of Lent. [Col. 1286D] For during these days we ought to correct our behavior, fast, weep, pray, be patient, keep watch, repent, and give alms more than at other times of the year. In this catalogue, human uncleanness is wiped away, and the human person is washed from every defilement.

It seemed to me that the responsories concerning fasting should be arranged as follows: first should stand, “Let us amend for the better what we have sinned through ignorance.” The order is this: if someone wishes to undertake the path of conversion, he should first put away his vices. What should be done afterward is shown by the second responsory, “In fasting and weeping.” What the devout mind obtains through this discipline is shown by the third responsory, “The season of fasting will open for us the gates of Paradise.”

For after the responsories [Col. 1287A] that preach fasting, another manner of cleansing follows—that is, through a penitent heart—and also a third, namely, through almsgiving. Therefore the responsories concerning fasting are placed first, because the Lenten season is especially consecrated to fasting.

I removed the responsory “Father, I have sinned against heaven” from this place and placed it in the week when the Gospel from which it was taken is read. According to our custom, I added after these responsories the responsories for Terce, Sext, and None, which I wrote in two orders.

Our region is accustomed to sing at Terce for two weeks, “Make me a participant, O God,” and the others that are inscribed in the Metz Antiphoner. The aforementioned responsory is mentioned in the Life of Saint Ambrose. He himself relates what meaning the aforesaid verse recalled to him [Col. 1287B] in his prayer: namely, that God should make him a participant, during the Lenten season, with all those who fear him, when the revelation concerning the holy martyrs Gervasius and Protasius was made to him.

Indeed, I found other, shorter responsories in the Roman Antiphoner. I wrote both orders in our Antiphoner, for at times we sing these and at times the others.

Lent is named from the number forty. This designation stands in fourth place after its source, namely Septuagesima, and reaches its perfection on the Lord’s Supper, when the brothers’ feet and the floors of the churches are washed. Truly, whoever has diligently submitted himself for forty days to the discipline set forth in the Lenten responsories will undoubtedly be found, on the Lord’s Supper, to have devoted himself to the worship of purity.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the antiphons at Matins during Lent

[Col. 1287C]

The first antiphon at Matins says: “Create in me a clean heart, O God; renew a right spirit within my inward parts.” For the present antiphons, like the other offices belonging to this day, instruct those who abstain concerning the kind of intention they ought to manifest before God during the time of their amendment.

The antiphon “Create in me a clean heart, O God” asks for right thinking in the person who abstains. For what is expressed by “Create in me a clean heart, O God” is repeated in “Renew a right spirit within my inward parts.” A right spirit belongs to a clean heart; “create” and “renew” ask for one and the same thing.

The antiphon “O Lord, save me; O Lord, grant prosperity” asks, through the interjection “O”—that is, through great desire—that the Lord save the person who abstains from sins, and that what seems harsh and storm-tossed during the days of abstinence, the Lord may make tranquil, bearable, and serene. In other words, may the Lord grant this prosperity to those who abstain, so that in the abstinence they have begun during this season they may persevere to the end.

The third antiphon, “Thus will I bless you in my life,” asks that, having been firmly established in the things I mentioned above, one should afterward devote himself to good works. For this is what it means to bless the Lord: to apply oneself vigilantly to good works. And thereafter, “I will lift up my hands,” in prayer in the form of a cross.

So that the wind of pride may not overthrow such a structure, the fourth antiphon asks for a spirit of humility and a contrite soul, and that, through these offerings and sacrifices, the Lord may receive the soldier.

The fifth antiphon, “Praise the Lord, heavens of heavens,” follows the order of the psalm. The sun and moon are excepted, since they are reserved for the story of Joseph.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the responsories sung concerning Isaac and Jacob

The responsories concerning Isaac and Jacob stand after Abraham, their father, according to the order of the story. I likewise arranged these according to the order of the story.

At the end of the present responsories stands the responsory “Father, I have sinned against heaven,” because of the Gospel read on the Saturday of the present week, from which it was taken. [Col. 1288B] This responsory appropriately stands after the responsories concerning Jacob, which recall an exile returned from exile: Jacob, of course, returned from exile to his homeland.

The compiler of the offices could have placed the designation “Thirtieth” in this order according to the quantity of the numbers. But because the designations Septuagesima, Sexagesima, and Quinquagesima are prefaces to Lent, and because this designation runs through the entire season of fasting until the Lord’s Pasch, the subsequent designations cease with that one—that is, with Lent.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the antiphons at Matins

The first antiphon says: “O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.” [Col. 1288C] In this week the consolation is recalled that the people of God heard through the mouths of the prophets Haggai and Zechariah after the tribulation they suffered under King Ahasuerus. The renewal of that people’s mind toward the joy of rebuilding the Temple is recalled through the present antiphons.

After the work had been interrupted and then begun again, the antiphon “O Lord, open my lips” is said. This custom is still observed in the Church. After a conversation has been interrupted, a conversation during the nighttime repeats the present verse again.

The antiphon follows: “The right hand of the Lord has shown strength.” The right hand of the Lord exercised this strength so that the Lord’s house might begin to be rebuilt, and the Lord became its helper.

The people, rescued from the furnace that Ahasuerus had prepared for them—namely, another Nebuchadnezzar—rightly sing to God the antiphon “Let us sing the hymn of the three young men.” Many adversaries wished to trouble the people of God so that they would not build the house of God; but because this had been established by the Lord, they could not destroy the work. This is recalled by the antiphon “He established them forever and for ages of ages.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the responsories concerning Joseph

Joseph’s brothers worshiped Joseph, because the time was coming when the Church would worship Christ. Therefore the invitatory antiphon “Let us worship God” should be placed before his responsories.

I arranged the responsories concerning Joseph according to the sequence of the story.

## CHAPTER XL. [Col. 1289A] On the antiphons at Matins

The first antiphon is “Deal kindly,” or, as some say, “Deal kindly.” This is not contained in the proper translation from which the Antiphoner was taken, but rather: “Deal kindly according to your good will, O Lord.”

In this week the completion of the walls of Jerusalem, which took place under Nehemiah, is recalled. Prayer for this completion anticipates it in the present antiphon, which says: “Deal kindly according to your good will, O Lord, so that the walls of Jerusalem may be built.”

The opposition of Nehemiah’s adversaries, who wished to disrupt that work, is explained in the Book of Ezra. But the Lord resisted them, while Nehemiah exhorted them: “Do not fear their presence; remember the great and terrible Lord.” [Col. 1289B] In place of this saying the antiphon is sung: “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear what man can do to me.”

On this night two antiphons are moved from their order. One is the antiphon which, according to the order of the verses, ought to stand after the antiphon “It is good to hope in the Lord,” as the beginning of the psalm. The other is “Sun and moon,” which, descending from the beginning of the psalm, ought to stand before the antiphon “He established them forever.” When the order is reversed, the former stands first and the latter afterward.

This consoles the brothers in the great tribulation they suffered from those rising up against them. They must remember God alone and not fear man. Therefore, according to the verse “In tribulation I called upon the Lord,” stands the antiphon of greatest consolation, “The Lord is my helper.” For hope is accustomed to smile upon the lukewarm.

Those who think they must defend themselves against an impending enemy need to say the antiphon “May God have mercy on us and bless us.” This is read in the lower portions of the aforementioned story: “When all our enemies heard it, all the nations around us were afraid and reflected among themselves.”

This sentence can appropriately be applied to the antiphon “The fire forgot the force of its power, so that your young men might be delivered unharmed.” The fury of the fire that was directed against Nehemiah and his young men among all the nations around Jerusalem was quieted when the wall of Jerusalem had been completed.

This antiphon, “The fire forgot the force of its power,” may also be understood specifically of Joseph’s inviolable chastity. When his mistress burned with desire for him, the force of the lustful fire was extinguished in Joseph, [Col. 1289D] so that the innocent young man remained unharmed.

The antiphons from the psalm “Praise the Lord from the heavens” began to proceed in order; but this order is changed at the verse “Praise him, sun and moon.” This was done because of the correspondence between the responsories concerning Joseph and this antiphon, which makes some mention of Joseph’s dream, in which he saw the sun and moon worshiping him—a prophecy concerning Christ.

Since this antiphon was held back from its order until this night for the reason stated, the order required that after the praise of the angels there should follow the praise of the heavens of heavens and of all the waters. According to the order, the antiphon “He established them” then follows, standing in an appropriate place according to the fittingness of its interpretation.

## CHAPTER XLI. On mid-Lent

[Col. 1290A]

The responsories concerning Moses proceed through the sequence of the story as far as the responsories concerning Joshua. Among the responsories concerning Joshua, I found one concerning the prophet Micah, namely, “My people, what have I done to you?” I identified it beforehand by its proper author, from whom it was taken.

It is appropriate to the present place because it portrays the preceding story.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the antiphons at Matins

The present antiphons are adapted to the times of Moses and Joshua, and also to the times of Nehemiah. On the night when these antiphons are sung, the responsories concerning Moses and Joshua are sung.

Moses taught the offering of sacrifice [Col. 1290B] to God. The first antiphon speaks of sacrifice: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness.”

The times of the ancient fathers are repeated in Nehemiah’s story. Among other things, the following is written there concerning the time of Joshua: “You gave them kingdoms and peoples, and you cast lots for them, so that they might possess the land of Zion,” and so forth. Where the lot intervenes, human counsel departs; where human counsel or refuge is absent, there is hope in the Lord alone. Concerning this the antiphon says: “It is good to hope in the Lord.”

And below: “The sons came and possessed the land, and you humbled the inhabitants of the land before them.” The meaning of the last psalm, “May God have mercy on us,” is close to this sentence. Hence the antiphon is: “May God, our God, bless us, and may he bless us.” For the sons possessed the land through blessing.

Then all the inhabitants of the land whom God humbled before the sons of Israel feared the Lord. And below, continuing the earlier passage: “In the time of their tribulation they cried out to you, and you heard them from heaven; and according to your many mercies you gave them saviors, who saved them from the hand of their enemies.” The words of this sentence harmonize with the words of the antiphon: “You are powerful, O Lord, to rescue us and to deliver us from the hand of death.”

In what follows in the aforementioned story comes a catalogue of the Jewish kings who sinned against the Lord. In response, the antiphon is sung in this order: “Kings of the earth and all peoples, praise God.”

The aforementioned antiphons fit the times of Nehemiah. Thus it is written in the lower portions of the story: “We will establish commandments over ourselves, to give a third of a shekel each year for the work of the house of our God, for the bread of the Presence, and for the continual sacrifice on Sabbaths, new moons, festivals, and holy days, and for sin offerings, to make atonement for Israel.” This sentence corresponds to the antiphon “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness.”

It continues: “The rest of the people cast lots, to take one part out of ten of those who would dwell in Jerusalem.” Those who read the history of Ezra know that these people, who now cast lots for those who would dwell in Jerusalem, and Nehemiah, placed their trust in heavenly hope alone, both on the way and in their homeland. Therefore, in their person, the antiphon is rightly sung: “It is good to hope in the Lord.”

And below it continues: “The people blessed all the men who had willingly offered themselves to dwell in Jerusalem.” For these words stands the antiphon “May God, our God, bless us.”

At the end of the book comes the following: “Of the sons of Joiada son of Eliashib, his son-in-law was Sanballat the Horonite, whom I drove away from me. Remember them, O my God, against those who defile the priesthood,” and so forth.

In his mind Nehemiah was singing the antiphon “You are powerful, O Lord; rescue us,” since he had driven away the son-in-law of the ruler. He did not fear death at the hands of man, because he was struggling against worldly powers so that the priesthood might not be defiled.

After this, the story follows with Nehemiah’s establishment of the entire order of God’s ministers. In place of this intention of Nehemiah, the antiphon may be sung: “Kings of the earth and all peoples, praise God, because his name alone has been exalted.” [Col. 1291B]

I shall repeat what I omitted above concerning the order of the antiphons that concern blessing. From the Sunday on which the mouth of the Church already refrains from the Alleluia—that is, from Sexagesima until the responsories concerning Joseph—there are three antiphons concerning the aforesaid blessing: “Blessed are you in the firmament of heaven”; “Sing a hymn, and exalt exceedingly”; and “Let us sing the hymn of the three young men.”

These three antiphons recall the three young men praising the Holy Trinity in the furnace.

The antiphon “In a spirit of humility,” which is sung during Lent, is a kind of preaching to the whole Church for the entire period of Lenten affliction.

The antiphon at Septuagesima, “Let the earth bless the Lord, and let all that springs up from it sing a hymn to him,” humbly joins human praise with the praise of the angels. Alleluia is the song of the angels in heaven. This is shown in the Apocalypse of the apostle John.

The blessing from which the antiphon “Let the earth bless the Lord” was taken is the praise of human beings placed in tribulation, signifying that the fellowship of the holy angels is with those who suffer for God.

With the three young men in the fiery furnace a figure like the Son of God was seen. For the sake of this significance, during Septuagesima the antiphon is mingled with the continual Alleluia: “Let the earth bless the Lord, and let all that springs up from it sing a hymn to him.”

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the Passion of the Lord

Concerning the number of nights belonging to the celebration of the Lord’s Passion, and concerning the omission of the Gloria, I have spoken in the previously mentioned official booklet.

During the two weeks before the Lord’s Pasch, wherever the compiler of the Antiphoner was able to gather sayings appropriate to the Lord’s Passion, he set them to a melody suitable for that season—that is, a mournful one—according to the number of necessary responsories and antiphons.

I moved the antiphons concerning Mary’s ointment from the first feria of the Metz Antiphoner to the seventh feria. For that anointing was celebrated on that day, namely, the day before Palm Sunday.

On Palm Sunday I found the antiphon “With angels and children in blessing,” and in some sources “The Lord, seeing”; for Lauds, “Let them be confounded.” It seemed to me that “Let them be confounded” suited the Chaldeans and Jews who kindled the fire of anger, [Col. 1292A] while “With angels and children” suited those who praise the Lord from the heavens.

On the Lord’s Supper I gathered the responsories in which the Lord foretold to his disciples his betrayal, what he did in prayer, and what Judas, by contrast, did in plotting and betraying him. Those that I found excerpted from the Gospel I placed according to the order of the Gospels; the others I tried to arrange according to the sequence of events.

On the night of Good Friday I moved from the Lord’s Supper a responsory concerning the prophet Isaiah, “Behold, we have seen him,” which properly belongs to the time of the Cross. It is followed by one concerning the prophet Jeremiah, “I have delivered my beloved soul into the hands of the wicked.” I placed these two from the prophets first.

Among the sequence of the following responsories is inscribed a responsory concerning the prophet Isaiah, “I stretched out my hands.” We did not sing this [Col. 1292B] on these nights, but on the feast of Saint Andrew. I therefore placed it in this order because it was found in the Roman Antiphoner.

The others were composed by the masters of the holy Roman Church. In them the remorse of his betrayal is repeatedly expressed, and the pain of his crucifixion goads the hearts of the faithful.

In the final two from the Gospel, the events that occurred at the end concerning his Passion are celebrated, up to the celebration of his burial on Good Friday.

On Holy Saturday his burial is recalled in some responsories, while in others there are the lamentation and weeping of those grieving over his unjust death.

## CHAPTER XLIV. On the extinguishing of lights around the Lord’s burial

The custom of our Church is maintained for three nights—that is, Thursday, which is called the Lord’s Supper; Friday, which is called Good Friday; and Saturday, which is called Holy Saturday—that the church lights be extinguished during the night.

Concerning the custom of our holy mother, the Roman Church, I questioned the archdeacon Theodore of that Church, namely, the Roman Church. He replied:

“I am accustomed to be with the Apostolic One at the Lateran when the office of the Lord’s Supper is celebrated. Nothing concerning the extinguishing of lights is observed there on that same night.

“On Friday no lamp or candle is kept lit in the church at Jerusalem for as long as the Apostolic Lord performs the solemn prayers there, or for as long as the Cross is being venerated. Nevertheless, on that day a new fire is kindled, from which fire is reserved until the nocturnal office.”

Both customs proceed along a reasonable path. Our custom, which extinguishes the candle and lamp lights for three nights, teaches us to turn from joy to sadness, from gladness to mourning. Everyone knows that the Church’s joy is signified by the light of candles and lamps. In the same way, singing belongs more to the delight and joy of minds than to grief and mourning.

For three nights the lights are extinguished, containing within themselves, together with their days, seventy-two hours. Through this present extinguishing, the extinguishing of the joy that is recalled as having taken place in the hearts of Christ’s disciples is signified for as long as Christ lay in the tomb.

Or it signifies that extinguishing of joy which took place in the hearts of the apostles [Col. 1293A] after the Lord’s betrayal until he entered to them through closed doors, showed them his hands and feet, and ate before them.

And appropriately the lights are extinguished at the place where the singing is renewed, so that it may be understood that at every moment of some unexpected joy there was always an obstacle of sadness. Concerning this matter and the number of candles, we have a written account in the official booklet.

Since on Friday, according to Roman custom, the new light is rekindled, this is its rationale: on that same day the sun was darkened from the sixth hour to the ninth hour. In imitation of that darkness, the customary lights in the church are extinguished and then renewed, because around the ninth hour the light of the sun returned to illuminate the world.

For three hours it did not give its light, preaching to the world that for three days and three nights its Creator and Maker would darken himself in the tomb. And because of the common necessity, it is rekindled on that same day in the holy Roman Church, so that food may be cooked from it and it may be reserved for the necessary use of the night.

On that same night, namely Sunday, which belongs to Christ’s resurrection, all the lights are renewed to signify the mystery. Because of the sacrament of the Lord’s burial and resurrection on Sunday night, the proper order is clear: when the office belonging to Christ’s resurrection is reached, a new and enduring fire should arise to illuminate the entire church.

This is what I mean when I say that fire should be reserved from Friday, so that the candle placed in the place of the pillar of fire may be lit for blessing—the candle that was illuminated at the beginning of the blessing. [Col. 1293C] When it has been blessed, the second candle should be lit from it.

The other lights should remain extinguished until the final litany, which belongs to the Mass office of the Lord’s resurrection. Then the lights of the church and of the newly baptized should be lit, so that it may be signified that, through Christ’s resurrection from the earth, the whole world is to be illuminated.

## CHAPTER XLV. On the resurrection of the Lord

Concerning the number of psalms during the Paschal nights, I have written what I could in the aforementioned booklet called the official.

In our Antiphoner is found the order of antiphons and responsories for the Paschal days that is found in the Roman Antiphoner. In that order I did not find the antiphons that we customarily sing at night on the Lord’s Resurrection over the nocturnal psalms: “I am who I am”; “I asked my Father”; and “I slept.”

I do not know from where the people of Metz collected them. I know one thing: their words harmonize with Christ’s resurrection.

The first antiphon, “I am who I am,” shows that the crucified Christ is God, and that God’s will is not with the impious who wished to extinguish Christ, but with those Jews who truly persevered in God’s law, as Peter and Paul did.

The antiphon “I asked my Father” teaches that the Gentile people were added to Christ’s flock through his Passion.

The third, “I slept,” shows Christ’s resurrection.

I found distinct responsories in the Metz Antiphoner for each feria through Thursday. It seemed reasonable to me that, since five ferias had assigned responsories, Friday and Saturday should not lack this particularity.

According to the order of the Gospel, I ought to have placed at the beginning the responsory “When the Sabbath had passed.” But because of the excellence of the melody and the manifest explanation of the Lord’s resurrection, I placed at the beginning, according to the practice of many Antiphoners, “The angel of the Lord descended from heaven.” It is followed by two according to the Gospel text: “When the Sabbath had passed,” and “The angel of the Lord spoke to the women.”

## CHAPTER XLVI. On Monday

Mary Magdalene declares the Lord’s resurrection. [Col. 1294B] “The Lord brought you in” is appropriate to the Jews. “From the mouth of the prudent” agrees with the preceding words, namely, with honey and the law of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Tuesday

“Jesus our Lord rising” resounds with the Lord’s resurrection. “With great power” celebrates the steadfastness of the first preachers. “If you have risen with Christ” draws ministers to the place where the victor of the contest is.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On Wednesday

On Wednesday there is still an address to the Jews, who are now invited to the kingdom of Christ. Christ is the lion [Col. 1294C] from the tribe of Judah and the root of David, who conquered and opened the gates of heaven to his own.

The responsory “Purge out the old leaven” contains these words: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed; therefore let us feast in the Lord.” Concerning this feast the offertory sung on that day says: “Man ate the bread of angels.”

The responsory “Christ, rising from the dead” manifests the completed victory of Christ and of the primitive Church.

## CHAPTER XLIX. On Thursday

“They have taken away my Lord” was taken from the Gospel read on Thursday.

In the responsory “Rejoice with me, all you who love the Lord,” Mary seeks the Lord around the tomb [Col. 1294D] and finds him. The Lord was buried in the tomb.

In the responsory “A people of possession,” mention is made on this feria of the people who were acquired from the uncircumcision by Christ’s blood.

## CHAPTER L. On Friday

The responsory “The good shepherd has risen” shows that the one who rose was he who, on the sixth day, laid down his life for his sheep.

On the sixth day the baptism of the Gentiles is recalled.

In the responsory “You are worthy, O Lord,” the chief preachers offer worthy praises to Christ. For he whose blood was poured out for our redemption is worthy to reveal the mysteries of Scripture that were foretold concerning that same redemption.

The responsory “It has been given to me” [Col. 1295A] was excerpted from the proper Gospel.

## CHAPTER LI. On Saturday

“The angel showed me a fountain of living water.”

It speaks as though those who have been baptized in Christ, who are newly born lambs, were speaking to the Church, and today return to the fountains in order to remove their white garments.

The responsory “All of you who have been baptized in Christ: you have put on Christ” is added to them.

## CHAPTER LII. On the glorious office performed around the evening stations during Paschal Week in the Roman Church

It is solemnly known that our mother, the Roman Church, sings three psalms before the hymn of the Gospel, and two afterward, at different altars in different places. Most often, however, this is done at the Cross and at the fonts, as we state from the writings that preserve the Roman order in various booklets.

It is likewise known that, at the end of the psalms, we customarily say a verse before the prayer that we ordinarily make by bending the knees or lowering the face toward the ground. Through the verse we are warned of some change and renewal of mind that includes the posture of prayer.

We have a written account of this same verse in the official booklet and in the prologue to this work. Here it is necessary to say about it those things by which it may be understood why the custom of the holy Roman Church omits the verse during the Paschal days and establishes another chant in its place.

The Paschal day, which is celebrated for seven days as though it were one day, proclaims to us through the order of its office that time of which Jesus Christ said in the Gospel of John: “Again I will see you, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you; and on that day you will ask me nothing.”

By praying, we ask for what we do not yet have. This will not be necessary when the hearts of the elect rejoice, and no one will take their joy from them, and it will not be necessary for them to ask for anything.

So that we may already rejoice in hope concerning what we await to receive in reality, the verses that customarily call our mind back to the introduction of some prayer are removed during the Paschal days. In their place, at certain daytime courses, the responsory “This is the day that the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” is sung.

[Col. 1295D]

The exultation and joy of which the present responsory speaks become clearer in our minds if they are pronounced among us in a clearer language, namely Hebrew. Therefore, at the station where the Apostolic One celebrates the evening office, Alleluia is sung with the full supplement and excellence of verses and sequences.

In the other daytime offices the responsory “This is the day” is sung in place of the verses.

At the evening office, after three psalms, one Alleluia is sung before the hymn of Saint Mary; after the fourth, one; after the fifth, one. These pertain to the Cross and to the fonts.

For in the Roman Order, on the very day of the Lord’s resurrection, the psalm “When Israel went out” is found repeated. This is done because of the many altars of that place where the station is held on that day.

On Wednesday, too, the responsory “This is the day that the Lord has made” is found clothed in chant after two Alleluias, to show that it had originally been established in place of the verses, but that by apostolic dignity Alleluia was substituted for them.

For the same reason it happened that many verses of Alleluia are sung in the Greek language in the aforementioned office.

On Friday the responsory “This is the day that the Lord has made” is inserted between two Alleluias, as I suppose, because of the places of the stations, which are first designated by lowly places and afterward by noble ones.

Concerning these places it is written in the Roman Order: “Until the eighth day of Easter, according to Roman custom, we celebrate the aforementioned course. At night we customarily sing the verses.”

We know that the two cycles of time—day and night—are distinguished by the Lord in the Gospel of John: “If anyone walks during the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world; but if anyone walks during the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

During the day—that is, in the better portion of this world—we presume to rejoice in hope of the future reality. During the night—that is, in the worse portion of this world—we fear, saying the verse: “Lest we stumble by presuming upon the hope that can be corrupted in us through our frailty, unless the Lord guards us.”

We sing the same psalms at each evening office because one and the same day is being celebrated. At the nocturnal office we recall those that we customarily celebrate on each Sunday night.

## CHAPTER LIII. [Col. 1296C] On the responsories entitled “concerning authority,” from the person of the believing Synagogue
The responsories entitled “On Authority” recall the entrance of the apostles into the Church, which was gathered from the Jews into the faith of the New Testament. They are therefore likewise entitled “On Authority,” because the apostles—whose character is sung in these responsories—became, in Christ’s place, the founders of the Jewish and Gentile Church.

The first responsory, “I bore fruit like a vine” (*Ego sicut vitis fructificavi*), gently gathers a portion of the Jewish people into the unity of the faith. For Wisdom speaks in this responsory—the Wisdom of whom the Lord says to the apostles: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom.” That Wisdom addresses the Jewish people gently and sweetly through the mouths of the apostles, saying: “[Come over to me, all you who desire me]” (*Transite ad me, omnes qui concupiscitis me*) [Col. 1296D]—that is, you who desire wisdom—“and be filled from my generations” (*et a generationibus meis adimplemini*), that is, from the mysteries which are revealed through us apostles at this time.

In many Antiphonaries this responsory is found in second place: “[You have become beautiful and gracious; your height is like an unfailing palm]” (*Speciosa facta es et suavis, altitudo tua similis palmae indeficienti*). We place it in third place because of the responsory’s correspondence, “[Good delight]” (*Delectatio bona*), with the first.

This second responsory, through praise of Wisdom, urges its hearers to approach the teachers of wisdom. Wisdom is good delight; in the works of her hands are many riches.

The third responsory, “[You have become beautiful]” (*Speciosa facta es*), can in a certain way harmonize with the fearful spirit [Col. 1297A] of the hearers, who do not trust that they can ascend to the height of the palm or be compared with its unfailing greenness. The height and beauty of the apostles’ wisdom are likened to the palm’s height and beauty. From their company there was once Peter, who said to the Lord: “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man.”

The fourth responsory comes to the aid of such a lament, saying: “Coming from Lebanon, how beautiful you have become, and the fragrance of your garments is above all spices” (*Veniens a Libano quam pulchra facta es, et odor vestimentorum tuorum super omnia aromata*). It is as though one were saying to an inexperienced hearer: “Do not be afraid. When you come from the Lebanon of baptism, you will be beautiful, and the fragrance of your garments will be above all the spices of the Old Testament.”

After these follows the fifth responsory from the Apocalypse: “[I heard a voice in heaven like the voice of a great thunderclap: Our God shall reign, and so forth]” (*Audivi vocem in coelo tanquam vocem tonitrui magni, Regnabit Deus noster, et caetera*). In this responsory [Col. 1297B] there is an address to the baptized, and the victory of Christ is recalled—he who said: “Take courage; I have conquered the world.”

The sixth follows: “[I heard the voice of many angels in heaven, saying: Fear the Lord and give him glory]” (*Audivi vocem in coelo angelorum multorum, dicentium: Timete Dominum, et date claritatem illi*). It is as though one were saying: “Fear him and give him glory whose victory resounded for you in the preceding responsory, because Christ himself, who rescued you from the kingdom of the devil and made you his kingdom, is the one who made heaven and earth, the sea, and the fountains of waters.”

In the first responsories, the joining of the hearers and their leaders into one faith is narrated. In the following responsories, the Church that has now been gathered is shown the mystery of the bridegroom and bride, from whom it itself was begotten. The bride herself is Jerusalem; therefore this bride is frequently recalled by the name Jerusalem, so that through this the singers’ minds may be turned in these responsories toward the primitive Church, which first began to grow in Jerusalem. [Col. 1297C]

The seventh responsory, “[One of the seven angels spoke to me]” (*Locutus est ad me unus ex septem angelis*), presents the person of some distinguished hearer saying to his fellow citizens: “One of the seven”—that is, one of the perfect preachers—“spoke to me: Come, I will show you the new bride, the wife of the Lamb.” This is plainly to say: “I will show you that mystery which exists in Christ and in the Church.”

The eighth responsory narrates what he saw when he looked: “[See Jerusalem descending from heaven, adorned with pure gold, and so forth]” (*Vide Hierusalem descendentem de coelo, ornatam auro mundo, et caetera*). I therefore saw Jerusalem descending from heaven because one of the angels said to me: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.” [Col. 1297D]

In the remaining responsories, the beauty of Jerusalem’s structure is narrated. All this must be understood mystically of spiritual buildings and the heavenly Jerusalem. In the ninth, its gate is described; in the tenth, its streets; in the eleventh, it is disclosed that Jerusalem itself is the great heavenly city, which nevertheless is still retained in this world as God’s tabernacle.

In the twelfth, it is made clear that the people of Israel who believe in God sing praises to God in that same city in which David once reigned and sang praises to God with his singers.

In the thirteenth, following the example of Moses, who through the words of the responsory “[Teach your children]” (*Docete filios vestros*) admonished the people before his death to keep the Lord’s law in memory, the Christian people descended from circumcision are admonished to teach their descendants to keep the Christian law in memory.

In accordance with the character of the offices that contain the person of the primitive Church, these responsories ought to be sung for three weeks.

## CHAPTER LIV. On the responsories of the psalms with Alleluia, in the person of the daughter

The present responsories, which are entitled “of the psalms,” endeavor to show the intention of those who once dwelt in Babylon—that is, in the confusion of this world—and who afterward desired to be recalled from there through the preaching, prayer, and teaching of those preachers who descended from Jerusalem [Col. 1298B] to visit them.

For this reason the first responsory is taken from the psalm: “[By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion]” (*Super flumina Babylonis, illic sedimus et flevimus dum recordaremur Sion*). The same responsory continues: “[If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand forget me]” (*Si oblitus fuero tui, Hierusalem, obliviscatur me dextera mea*). This responsory displays the fervent zeal of the Gentiles after their conversion, to such an extent that the speaker wishes evil upon himself if thereafter he should forget his mother Jerusalem.

The second responsory, “[With my whole heart I have sought you]” (*In toto corde meo exquisivi te*), could have been placed first according to the meaning of its words, since it explains the heart of a certain Gentile, such as Cornelius had. But, as I said above, to make the entire sequence of these responsories clear, the first responsory is taken from the aforementioned psalm, in which there is great lamentation because of the barriers [Col. 1298C] of Babylonian captivity.

In the third responsory, “[Lead me in the path of your commandments]” (*Deduc me in semita mandatorum tuorum*), the way out of Babylon and entry into Jerusalem is requested.

The one who was Babylon confesses his error in the fifth responsory: “[The waters saw you, O God; the waters saw you, and they were afraid]” (*Viderunt te aquae, Deus, viderunt te aquae, et timuerunt*). It is as though he were saying: “As long as I was rightly compared with a brute animal, I could not see you. Now that I and my people have been endowed with rational understanding, we see that you are God, and we are afraid.”

How this happened is clarified in what follows: “The clouds gave forth a voice.” This people first heard that voice at Ephrata, as the sixth responsory says, because Christ was born there: “She was found in the fields of the Gentiles.” Those who descended from Jerusalem worshiped God with the people who had been recalled from Babylon, in his Church. In that Church the feet of the Lord—that is, the evangelical visions—remain.

After the feet of the Lord had stood among the Gentile people, the inhabitants of the city of Babylon began to mock him and tried to tear him away from his station. In the seventh responsory they say to him: “[Sing us a hymn]” (*Hymnum cantate nobis*). The proud and arrogant Babylonian wants amusements and pleasures to be provided for him from God’s songs.

The answer to them should be: “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” I am surprised that “Alleluia” was added to the wicked mockery—“[Sing us a hymn, Alleluia]” (*Hymnum cantate nobis, Alleluia*). In its place I changed it to: “[Alleluia, Babylon said]” (*Alleluia, ait Babylon*).

The eighth responsory is sung in defense against these Babylonians: “[Judge my judgment]” (*Judica judicium meum*) [Col. 1299A]; and again the ninth: “[Deal with your servant]” (*Fac cum servo tuo*).

After this persecution comes the Lord’s deliverance. The tenth responsory speaks of this deliverance: “[Let those who have been redeemed by the Lord now speak]” (*Dicant nunc qui redempti sunt a Domino*).

The eleventh responsory reveals what they should say: “[It is good to give thanks to the Lord and sing psalms]” (*Bonum est confiteri Domino, et psallere*). Why? Because the Lord has delivered us from all our tribulations.

The twelfth responsory follows: “[O God, I will sing a new song to you]” (*Deus, canticum novum cantabo tibi*). Cassiodorus says of this in his exposition of the psalm “Blessed be the Lord my God”:

“He comes,” he says, “to the second order, in which, after deliverance from spiritual wickedness and savage peoples, the Prophet promises to give thanks to God through a new song.”

And further:

“It is rightly called new because, since he was not received by the Jews, to whom he had been promised as the one who would come, he passed over to the Gentiles.” [Col. 1299B]

It continues:

“On a ten-stringed psaltery I will sing to you.”

And further:

“The ten-stringed psaltery is the Decalogue, which was given to the tribes of the Hebrews. And to show that both Testaments have one author, he pledged that he would sing psalms to Christ the Lord in both.”

The present Church is not content that it alone should sing to God; through the thirteenth responsory it prefers to proclaim his name throughout the whole world: “[I will declare your name to my brothers]” (*Narrabo nomen tuum fratribus meis*).

The fourteenth responsory shows what he says to his brothers: “[Bless the Lord in the churches]” (*In ecclesiis benedicite Dominum*). In this responsory he separates the faithful from the assemblies of heretics and wicked people, and asks that God be praised in the churches, in which [Col. 1299C] there is one faith and the teaching of the apostles.

Again, the fifteenth responsory—“[Sing to God; sing a psalm to him]” (*Cantate Deo, psalmum dicite ei*)—urges the peoples, confidently relying with faithful minds upon what they have heard, to celebrate God’s praises with hymn-like rejoicing.

For this reason these responsories are taken from the psalter, which has ten strings. In these, love of God is signified by three, and love of neighbor by seven, so that through the responsories of the psalter the offspring may declare that it loves the bridegroom of its mother and its mother, and that it speaks and responds to the city of Jerusalem, which dwells in heaven.

The three daytime offices—namely, “[Sing to the Lord]” (*Cantate Domino*), “[A voice of gladness]” (*Vocem jucunditatis*), and “[Hear, O Lord, my voice]” (*Exaudi, Domine, vocem meam*)—recall the same periods that are commemorated through these responsories.

Therefore one does nothing wrong by singing these responsories for three weeks, that is, from the office “[Sing to the Lord]” (*Cantate Domino*) until Pentecost, with the feast of Christ’s Ascension duly preserved and celebrated.

Nor do I criticize the custom of our Church, which, out of love for Christ’s exaltation in heaven and desire for that kingdom to which he has already gone before us, sings the responsories of the Ascension for ten days.

The responsories of the psalms may end at whatever time the cantor reasonably judges. They may not properly begin before the Sunday on which the Introit “[Sing to the Lord a new song]” (*Cantate Domino canticum novum*) is sung.

## CHAPTER LV. On the feasts of the saints

[Col. 1300A]

I inserted the offices of the saints that are celebrated during the days of Pentecost into our Antiphonary, between the responsories “On Authority” and the responsories “of the Psalms,” about which I have now written. For some of those periods in which the feasts of the saints that I mentioned above are celebrated commonly occur before the responsories of the psalms are sung.

## CHAPTER LVI. On the vigils of the Ascension of the Lord

I arranged the responsories of the Ascension of the Lord according to this sequence, which, as it seems to me, follows the order of the events concerning that Ascension. At the beginning I placed those that contain a certain preliminary address of Christ to the disciples concerning his Ascension, arranged in the order written below.

The first is “[It is time for me to return to him who sent me]” (*Tempus est ut revertar ad eum qui me misit*); the second, “[Let not your heart be troubled]” (*Non turbetur cor vestrum*); the third, “[I will not leave you orphans]” (*Non relinquam vos orphanos*). Through these three the hearts of the disciples are consoled, so that they may not be troubled by his Ascension, since his return is undoubtedly promised again after ten days.

In the fourth responsory, “Exalt yourself, Lord, in your strength” (*Exaltare, Domine, in virtute tua*), the disciples address Christ in the manner of speech with which Mother Church spoke beforehand in the Song of Songs: “Flee, my beloved; be like a gazelle and a young stag upon the mountains of spices.” It is as though she were saying:

“Since, instructed by you, we believe that you came forth from the Father and [Col. 1300C] came into the world, where for our sake you suffered many scourges at the hands of the faithless—those who love the world—and were not honored in the world as was fitting; now, especially since we have heard from you that it is necessary for you to go and send us your Paraclete, while a hymn is owed to you in Zion, leave the world and go to the Father.

“You will be exalted in strength; your Paraclete will come and teach us about your glorification, which you have with your Father. Meanwhile we shall sing and chant Alleluia.”

After this concord between teacher and disciples, the Teacher commends the disciples to the Father in the fifth responsory: “Father,” he says, “when I was with them, I guarded those whom you gave me.”

In the four responsories that follow, the Ascension of the Lord into heaven itself is narrated. In the responsory “[After his passion]” (*Post passionem*) [Col. 1300D], the person of the singers speaks to the congregation, narrating to it the order of Christ’s ascension.

In the Roman Antiphonary I found the responsory “Men of Galilee” (*Viri Galilaei*), which we were not reluctant to record in our Antiphonary. If anyone wishes to sing it among the nocturnal responsories, it is available there.

At the very end is placed “[All the beauty of the Lord has been exalted above the stars]” (*Omnis pulchritudo Domini, exaltata est super sidera*). Christ’s body in reality has already been exalted above the stars; his members, that is, are there in hope, where the head is in reality. Therefore the responsory “[All the beauty of the Lord]” is not placed in the last position without reason: there the perfect and supreme reception of the Lord’s beauty above the stars is narrated.

The antiphons over the psalms at matins preserve the sequence of the history that is written in the Gospels and in the Acts of the Apostles.

## CHAPTER LVII. The nocturnal office for the feast of Pentecost

First, it should be noted that there are three antiphons—namely, “[Suddenly there came a sound from heaven]” (*Factus est repente de coelo sonus*), “[Confirm this, O God]” (*Confirma hoc Deus*), and “[Send forth your Spirit]” (*Emitte spiritum tuum*)—which our region sings but which the Romans do not sing. We copied them from the Metz Antiphonary into ours.

Concerning the order of this office—that is, the nocturnal office for the feast of Pentecost—and how it is celebrated among the Romans, I have written in the prologue to this little work. The Roman Church completes the entire number of psalms and responsories that we customarily sing on the other Sundays’ nights. Concerning the number that our region follows in certain places, we have written in the official booklet. [Col. 1301B]

Because of the baptismal mysteries, we complete the nocturnal offices with three psalms during the eight days at the end of Pentecost week. I have written there whatever I could, as I mentioned, in the official booklet. It remains only to write here the order of responsories preserved by our Antiphonary.

The first responsory, “[When the days of Pentecost were fulfilled]” (*Dum complerentur dies Pentecostes*), shows that the company of the disciples was together in a certain upper room and was awaiting Christ’s promise. It also shows figuratively how Christ’s promise would come, namely, in the likeness of the sound of a mighty wind.

The second, “[The Holy Spirit proceeding from the throne]” (*Spiritus sanctus procedens a throno*), explains what the sound of the mighty wind would serve: the Holy Spirit proceeding from the throne. This sound of the mighty wind awakens hearts so that they may attend to the work of the Holy Spirit, who invisibly entered the breasts of the apostles.

The third responsory, “[Suddenly there came from heaven the sound of a mighty wind arriving, where they were sitting, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit]” (*Factus est repente de coelo sonus advenientis spiritus vehementis, ubi erant sedentes, et repleti sunt omnes Spiritu sancto*), has this additional feature in its teaching, beyond the two preceding responsories: it demonstrates that the apostles were filled with the Holy Spirit.

The fourth, “[The Spirit of the Lord has filled the whole world, and that which contains all things has knowledge of speech]” (*Spiritus Domini replevit orbem terrarum, et hoc quod continet omnia, scientiam habet vocis*), has this additional feature beyond the others: it demonstrates that knowledge of the speech of various languages was given to the disciples through the coming of the Holy Spirit.

The fifth, “[Divided tongues appeared to the apostles like fire]” (*Apparuerunt apostolis dispartitae linguae tanquam ignis*), shows what we did not hear in the preceding responsories: namely, that fiery tongues sat upon the apostles.

The sixth responsory, “[They were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they began to speak as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance]” (*Repleti sunt omnes Spiritu sancto, et coeperunt loqui prout Spiritus sanctus dabat eloqui illis*), shows that a certain work had been completed. I call it a work that the Holy Spirit fashioned through his coming upon the apostles: namely, that they should become preachers of his activity. The present responsory shows this in its words, saying: “And they began to speak as the Holy Spirit gave them utterance.”

Up to this point the history of the present feast has been explained. The remaining responsories—that is, “[On the last day of the feast]” (*Ultimo festivitatis die*) and “[I no longer call you servants]” (*Jam non dico vos servos*)—are taken from the Lord’s sayings in other places. Nevertheless, in their text they contain certain words concerning the present feast, as “[On the last day of the feast]” includes, among other things: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom they were going to receive.” And “[I no longer call you servants: receive the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, within you]” (*Jam non dico vos servos, accipite Spiritum sanctum in vobis paracletum*).

For this reason these occupy the seventh and eighth places in our Antiphonary.

The responsory “[The Lord was teaching them discipline and wisdom]” (*Disciplinam et sapientiam docebat eos Dominus*) declares no small part of the work of the Holy Spirit. For it declares three great things: first, that the Lord taught them discipline and wisdom; second, that he strengthened the grace of his Spirit in them; third, that he filled their hearts with understanding.

Concerning discipline, Saint Augustine explains in the seventeenth sermon of his exposition of Psalm 18 as follows:

“He also added instruction; or, as more books have it, discipline. But the discipline that the Greeks call *paideia* [παιδεία] our Scriptures customarily place where instruction through hardships is to be understood, according to the saying: ‘For whom the Lord loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives.’ This is commonly called *disciplina* in ecclesiastical writings, translated from the Greek where *paideia* is read.

“For this word, placed in the Greek text, occurs in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the Latin interpreter says: ‘All discipline for the present seems not to be of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it will yield the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it.’

“Whoever, then, receives sweetness from God—that is, whoever is graciously inspired by him with delight in what is good—or, to explain this more plainly, whoever receives from God love of God and, for God’s sake, love of neighbor, must certainly pray earnestly that this gift may be increased in him so greatly that for its sake he not only despises other pleasures but also endures every kind of suffering.”

Thus far Augustine.

In the responsory, wisdom follows discipline. Wisdom is what makes one savor eternal things and labor and work earnestly for them. This order follows the custom of our school: first our students are trained through discipline, and afterward they become wise through wisdom.

Nor is this custom absent from the teaching of Christ, who said: “Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things and thus enter into his glory?” Saint Augustine said above that discipline concerns salutary scourges, which lead a person to receive God. Christ initiated us into these, as we heard above: “Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer these things?” [Col. 1302D]

By wisdom, however, we mean the disposition of those who savor eternal things. Those who savor eternal things strive, amid prosperity and adversity alike, to seize the path by which they may arrive at heavenly glory.

The responsory follows this same order: it says that the Lord first taught the disciples discipline and afterward nourished them through wisdom with hope of eternal things. The grace of healings and cures, and the working of miracles, which he had granted them before his passion, he strengthened in them through the coming of his Spirit and through the understanding that he first gave them when he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures. In this way he filled their hearts more perfectly.

Because this responsory in a certain way declares the supreme work of the Holy Spirit, let it also occupy the last place among the responsories of the present feast.

The antiphons over the matins follow the order of the history. The antiphon at the blessing, “[Fountains and everything that moves in the waters]” (*In benedictione fontes, et omnia quae moventur in aquis*), corresponds to the baptismal fonts.

Here it should be noted that we are accustomed, at the beginnings of feast days—for example, at the Lord’s Pasch, his Ascension, and the present feast—to sing Alleluia over the psalms at matins and on the other following nights, except at the blessing.

Why is this? It is because on the nights in which the event itself is celebrated, the singers strive to declare the history of the present feast; whereas on the other nights we recall our devotion, which we ought always and everywhere to maintain for God’s benefits, which we receive from his resurrection, his Ascension, and the coming of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 1303B]

Why, according to our custom, the antiphons are sung at the blessing is written in the Official Booklet: namely, because that hymn, “[Bless]” (*Benedicite*), recalls the time of the greatest tribulation that is to come. Since the Latin language is humbler than Hebrew and Greek, in that humbler language the time of the greatest humility and affliction is recalled through the antiphon in its own language: “[At the blessing]” (*In benedictione*).

## CHAPTER LVIII. On the responsories of the psalms

Concerning the responsories of the psalms, I wrote in the prologue to this work what then seemed worth writing to me. Therefore I am not reluctant to write some of it again [Col. 1303C], since I have come to the sequence of times in which we customarily sing them.

The churches of our region, following their customary and most usual practice, sing them from the octave of Epiphany until Sexagesima. It is, however, the custom of our humility among our people to sing them both there and here—that is, from the octave of Pentecost until the Kalends of July.

I heard them sung in this order when I seemed to be a boy, before Albinus, the most learned teacher of our entire region. Delighted and strengthened by his authority, after I had been given the freedom to sing what seemed appropriate to me, I began to sing them at the time written above, that is, from the octave of Pentecost until the Kalends of July.

After this, when I came to Rome in the year 831 from the Incarnation of the Lord, in the ninth indiction, under the rule of the lord and most pious emperor Louis [Col. 1303D], and during the apostolate of the most glorious apostolic lord Gregory, I asked learned men of our holy mother Church about the order of the responsories from the feast of Pentecost until Advent.

They answered me: “During the first week, before the responsories of Kings, we sing the responsories of the Psalms. Likewise before the responsories of Wisdom, likewise before the responsories of Job, and likewise before the responsories of the prophets.”

If I had heard this order from earlier times, I would not sing one order and write about another. For a rationale can be given for the order of the psalms before Septuagesima such as the following; and similarly for the responsories sung between the octave of Pentecost and Advent.

The days from the Nativity of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany recall the presence of the bridegroom with the bride. Likewise, the days from the Lord’s Resurrection until the octave of Pentecost. For concerning these days it seems to have been written: “Can the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them?”

But the days from the octave of Epiphany until Septuagesima, and from the feast of Pentecost until Advent, recall the days about which it is again written in the Gospel: “But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast.”

At Septuagesima another order of days is renewed, one that seems to bring greater affliction upon the Church. A person who is captive and exiled suffers greater affliction than one who, within his homeland, awaits the arrival of the bridegroom.

The period from the octave of Pentecost until Advent signifies that humiliation which holy Church customarily endures under its own dominion because of the absence of its bridegroom. In order that we may act wisely and deliberately during such a period, we frequently repeat the responsories of the psalms. Through them we are admonished to humble ourselves at that time under the hand of the mighty God, to fast, and to pray, so that we may be rescued from the dangers that threaten and preserved soberly until the Lord’s coming.

One must fast at that time, because the bridegroom has been taken away from us, as has the joy of his face. Fasting and prayer provide one remedy: they overcome the temptations of unclean spirits and human beings.

Through these two virtues the bridegroom shows us that a cure is provided against a certain illness, saying: “This kind cannot go out by anything except by fasting and prayer.”

During the days mentioned above, which recall the presence of the bridegroom with the bride, holy Church, following the custom of her ancestors, is more devoted to larger feasts than at other times. Therefore on those days the devil does not have as much opportunity as he desires to stain the souls of honorable people through Ceres and Liber.

When those days have ended, humanity, steeped in ancient custom and carnal pleasure, is drawn by its appetite toward the permitted feasts of the festival days. One must not obey it, because the bridegroom has been taken away; rather, one must be worn down and fast. For this to be done, prayer must also be added.

Is this not the reason that teaches us to sing the responsories of the psalms, which contain more prayers than the other books, during the times mentioned? And, so that we may be instructed further that they belong to a time of repentance, the first responsory is taken from the psalm that was first assigned among those called the penitential psalms.

## CHAPTER LIX. On the feast of Saint John the Baptist

The present feast has antiphons and responsories from the prophecy of Jeremiah and Isaiah, and from the Gospel. Jeremiah and John were both sanctified in their mothers’ wombs, and both became very powerful preachers against adversaries. Therefore the words spoken to Jeremiah are appropriately assigned to John the Baptist.

The antiphons taken at the present feast from Isaiah [Col. 1305A] the prophet properly belong to the person of Christ Jesus. But because John the Baptist deserved to become his precursor and to be sanctified from his mother’s womb, the antiphons also in a certain way suit him: “The Lord called me from the womb” (*Dominus ab utero vocavit me*); “He put my mouth in place, forming me from the womb” (*Posuit os meum, formansque me ex utero*); and “Kings will see, and princes will arise” (*Reges videbunt, et consurgent principes*).

I noted the responsories and the antiphons at matins according to the order of the Gospel, as I believe. But this too must be investigated: why do the antiphons of the feasts of the apostles in the third nocturn, and the antiphons at matins, have Alleluia at the end, whereas these do not?

We can observe two reasons here. The first is that the antiphons of the third nocturn and the antiphons at matins strike the mind of the hearer so that it may attend to the thought that the glory under the time of the grace of the New Testament is greater than it was under the time of the natural law and the law of the letter. For John’s birth occurred before the Lord’s Resurrection, whereas the apostles’ birth in heaven occurred after the glorification of the Church through the new gift of the Holy Spirit. Therefore these antiphons are not adorned with Alleluia, while those are.

The second reason is one that I discover from the Roman Antiphonary that has reached us. At the most distinguished feasts of the saints, it is the custom of our holy mother, the Roman Church, to conduct two offices during the night; these offices are entitled “Of the Vigils.”

The first, which is sung at the beginning of the night, is performed without Alleluia; the other, which begins around midnight and ends during the day, has Alleluia in the antiphons of the third nocturn and in the antiphons [Col. 1305C] at matins.

The first seems to recall the time when, around the apostolic choir, the legal custom was observed and Sabbaths were celebrated; the second recalls the time when those things had been entirely set aside and the Lord’s Resurrection began to be celebrated on Sundays, as we see today.

The offices of the primitive Church provided not only what was strictly necessary for the New Testament, but also what could assist the weakness of the inexperienced Church and resist Jewish falsehood in its introduction. Therefore the things now performed in our Church in commemoration of that time when the new was mixed with the old—which Paul in the Epistle to the Philippians counted as refuse—are not as distinguished as those that recall the time when only those things began to be observed that pertain to the New Testament.

Therefore the former are performed without Alleluia, while the latter, which pass onward to fellowship with the holy angels, have Alleluia in their antiphons placed near the end.

That this understanding was always held at the beginning among the perfect is shown by the words of the presbyter Bede in his exposition of Luke:

“The prudence of the righteous,” he says, “is not to presume upon righteousness from works of the law, but to seek salvation from faith, so that although they are placed under the law and fulfill the commands of the law, they nevertheless understand that they are to be saved by the grace of God through Christ.”

I have written about the order of the nocturnal and matutinal offices in the Official Booklet.

## CHAPTER LX. On the vigils of the apostles Peter and Paul

[Col. 1306A]

I have written in the Official Booklet whatever I could concerning the number of psalms, antiphons, and responsories. But because I have now written in our Antiphonary two vigils that are not contained in the Metz Antiphonary, and have changed the order of the responsories, a few things must be said here.

From the Roman Antiphonary I placed two vigils in our Antiphonary. The apostolic lord customarily conducts the first at the beginning of the night, without an invitatory, because at that hour the people are not invited to the vigils.

The people are invited to the vigils at that hour of the night of which the prophet David said: “I rose before dawn and cried out.” If anyone wishes to learn what hour that is, let him read Saint Augustine on Psalm 18; there he will find that “before dawn” is used for midnight. At that hour the clergy and people enter for the second vigil, and the invitatory is sung.

I wrote the responsories according to our custom, following the sequence of the events and the order of the history from which they were taken. In the antiphons I followed the order of the Roman Antiphonary, both in the vigils of Saint Peter and in the vigils of Saint Paul.

Why antiphons are sung over the evening psalms at the end of the feast day is written in the office for the Nativity of the Lord.

## CHAPTER LXI. On the vigil of Saint Lawrence

In the vigil of Saint Lawrence I found two nocturnal offices in the Roman Antiphonary. I inserted the same order [Col. 1306C] in our Antiphonary.

## CHAPTER LXII. On the vigil of Saint Mary on the day of her Assumption

Likewise, as above, I found two nocturnal offices in the Roman Antiphonary for the vigil of Saint Mary on her Assumption. Therefore we too placed double offices for the feast in our Antiphonary.

## CHAPTER LXIII. On the vigil of Saint Andrew

In the vigil of Saint Andrew I found, as above, double nocturnal offices, and I followed this in our Antiphonary. I wrote several proper responsories and antiphons of the saints from the Roman Antiphonary, which I did not find in the Metz Antiphonary.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On the common responsories of the saints

[Col. 1306D]

I entitled the common responsories of all the saints according to the Roman Antiphonary. After these I wrote separately concerning the apostles, the martyrs, and the confessors. Again, concerning the saint who was not called a bishop.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the offices for the dead

After the offices of the saints I inserted the office for the dead. For many pass from the present age and are immediately joined to the saints. For them the office is conducted according to the customary practice.

But the one who is least in that kingdom is greater than the saint who is in the present age.

## CHAPTER LXVI. On the anniversaries of bishops

[Col. 1307A]

A reason has been given why the office for the dead is added after the offices of the saints: namely, because the righteous who have died live freely without the danger of ambushes by the ancient enemy and hope for better things. Nevertheless, the office established for the dead is conducted for them, as was indicated above.

The righteous who are still living in the flesh, however piously they may live, can always be anxious and watchful lest, becoming sluggish through some deceit of the devil or through their own negligence, they be weakened in their right course.

## CHAPTER LXVII. On the office at the dedication of a church

After the office of the bishops there is inserted the office by which the places properly called churches are dedicated. Unless there has first been a bishop, the dedication of a church does not follow. The bishop completes the office by which the places of the church are dedicated.

For the bishop who blesses is greater than the house that is blessed.

Since I have mentioned the dedication of a church, it is appropriate for me to speak about the office sung at the dedication of the church of Saint Michael, which office stands in its proper place, namely, on the third day before the Kalends of October.

I confess that in the nocturnal office there I placed antiphons that are properly assigned to the dedication of churches in general; and I did not do this on my own. I heard Albinus, the most learned teacher of our region, whom I often mention, sing them at that feast.

Some responsories that were written for that feast in many Antiphonaries [Col. 1307C] and sung by many foolish singers, I heard him reject. I did not write them in our Antiphonary; instead, I appointed responsories from various offices in their place, although these do contain some mention of the ministries of the angels. I arranged them in the order that the rationale and history of the books indicate.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. On the antiphons that are taken from the daily Gospels
After the office by which a church is dedicated, I wrote antiphons from the Gospels, concerning which I asked the teachers of the Roman Church whether they sang them. They replied, “Not at all.” Nevertheless, our teachers say that they received them from them through the first teachers who taught the melody of Roman chant within the boundaries of the Franks. God knows whether these men are deceiving us, or whether those who boasted that they had received them from the teachers of the Roman Church had themselves been mistaken, or whether the Romans had lost them through carelessness and negligence, or whether they had never sung them. Nevertheless, we sing them because of their salutary words and because of the authority of our singers, who pride themselves on using the expertise of chant through practice.

## CHAPTER LXIX. On invitatory antiphons

After this I wrote the invitatory antiphons that proceed through the Sunday nights, and I wrote them in sequence according to the arrangement of the psalm, “[Come, let us rejoice in the Lord].” As for the ordinary weekday nights, I wrote them before Septuagesima.

## CHAPTER LXX. On the antiphons of the three young men

[Col. 1308A]

After the invitatory antiphons comes the order in which the antiphons of the three young men are to be written. I arranged them in no other way than according to the order of the other antiphons.
