Although all these things begin with the octave of Pentecost, as do also the responsories from the Psalms, Kings, Solomon, Job, and those that follow, I did not wish to intermingle with them the offices of the saints, so that the offices of the saints and the offices for ordinary days might readily be found in our Antiphoner. For the Romans also place the offices for ordinary days at the end of all their official books, except for the chapters concerning the Gospels.

Here it should be noted that, especially on the Sunday nights from the octave of Pentecost until the Advent of the Lord, the Romans sing antiphons from the histories of the books from which the responsories have been taken, or the Alleluia with the hymns of Zechariah and holy Mary. I placed these same antiphons at the head of the responsories. At that time I did not remember that the hour of the seventh day of the week, when the psalm “Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle” is sung at vespers, belongs more frequently to the preceding week than to the following one.

It is evident that, from Christ’s resurrection, the day and the night have their beginning. For the night of the following day cannot be said to have begun before the sun of the preceding day has been brought to its setting; and before that setting the evening assembly is very frequently celebrated, at which the psalm “Blessed be the Lord my God,” and the following psalms, are sung. [Col. 1308C] Therefore it is appropriate to write the antiphons belonging to the Sunday night for that night when the responsories from Kings are sung after the responsories. I say the same concerning the other responsories and antiphons. Therefore I ask that, if anyone should deign to copy our little works, he may deign to write these at the end of the responsories.

## CHAPTER LXXI. On the responsories entitled “of Kings”

As I said above, so I heard from the teachers of the Roman Church: namely, that in the first week, before the responsories of Kings, responsories from the Psalms should be sung, by which the beginning again of the season of fasting and prayer is signified. What harm is there to the order if it should happen that the responsories of Kings are sung for seven weeks, or six, or five, before the month of August, or if responsories from the Psalms and four from Kings are sung for two or three weeks, since at this time there must be instruction and teaching in humility and submission?

When this instruction has been completed, a suitable period of four weeks remains for recalling the examples of the holy Fathers—namely, Samuel, David, Elijah, and Elisha. All these persons, according to the sequence of the history, are found in the responsories and antiphons entitled “of Kings.” I have tried to arrange, according to the order of the history, the responsories and antiphons that we sing in our Antiphoner. We sing them especially at the time when it is fitting to go into battle. David was a warlike man.

## CHAPTER LXXII. On the responsories entitled “of Solomon,” or “of Wisdom”

[Col. 1309A]

I have endeavored to arrange the responsories of Solomon and of Wisdom, like those above, according to the order of the history. Here the sequence of the offices proceeds according to the canonical order. The time of Solomon is concluded in the books of Kings; responsories from Wisdom are joined to him because he was supremely wise. David was vigorous in military affairs, Solomon more vigorous than all others in wisdom; for a wise man is also called strong.

Hence the poet Horace says:

> Strong and wholly smooth and rounded in himself.

He who excels in wisdom is rightly called strong. Of this it is written: “Wisdom conquers wickedness.”

These two months are strongest in heat, as certain verses relate:

> In the solstice, burning Cancer bears July’s star;  
> The fervent Lion scorches the month of August with fire.

From the tradition of the holy Fathers we learn that it belongs properly to wisdom to provide fervor to those who carry it out. To give one example among many, Jerome says in his letter to Nepotian about the life of monks and clerics: “Moreover, the Shunammite woman is called *coccinea* in our language”—that is, scarlet—“to signify that she is hot with wisdom and fervent with divine reading.”

Therefore it seems fitting that in the hot month of August the responsories of Wisdom should be sung, so that through their singing we may be instructed that those who have received some spark of wisdom ought to pray for its increase from the highest and perfect Wisdom that dwells in heaven, in accordance with the words of the present responsories: “Send forth, O Lord, Wisdom from the seat of your greatness.” And again: “Give me, O Lord, Wisdom, the attendant upon your thrones.”

The heat of the month admonishes and instructs us, through the responsories, to thirst for the fervor and love of wisdom. In these two months the strength, beauty, and height of wisdom—as far as concerns the history of the Israelite people in the Old Testament—reach their conclusion. This is demonstrated more clearly from the histories of Ezra and the First Book of Maccabees, when I come to them in sequence.

## CHAPTER LXXIII. On the responsories of Job and Tobit

In the month of September, according to the teaching of the Roman Church, we sing responsories from the Psalms in the first week, those of Job in the second and third, and those of Tobit in the fourth, because of the necessary reminder of the affliction that we ought to recall during the days of our sojourn.

Job was chosen from among the Gentile people; Tobit deserved to be tested in captivity and was found approved. Both were scourged for the crown of patience, and both were found approved through patience. For this reason their memory is celebrated together in one month.

When the number of responsories is lacking—namely, the number nine—sufficient responsories from Job may be added to complete the number nine; in these pain and lamentation are contained. Neither of them had been exalted to the height of kingship. For this reason they do not possess separate months, but are concluded in one month, in which we recall the kingdom of the Assyrians.

As I learned from those who dwell in the eastern region, the month of September is particularly unhealthy. Therefore the responsories of Job and Tobit are sung in September, so that the sick may learn in that month, following the example of the blessed Fathers Job and Tobit, to endure God’s scourges patiently.

For Easterners report that, because of the abundance of new crops and the freshness of must, bodies that consume them are changed into sickness, as a certain versifier sings, with September filled by the abundance of must:

> Under your star, Virgin, September fattens Bacchus.

As far as concerns the history sifted out through the responsories of the present time, the kingdom of the Assyrians concludes in the responsories of Tobit. The responsories of Judith, Ezra, and Esther, up to the responsories of the Maccabees, belong to the period of the Persians and Medes.

## CHAPTER LXXIV. On the responsories of Judith, Ezra, and Esther

The books of Tobit, Judith, and Esther are not received into the canon among the Hebrews. Nevertheless, since we read them in the Church, we sing responsories from them.

Thus Eusebius writes in his *Chronicle* concerning Judith: “Cambyses, second king of the Persians, for eight years. They say that he is called by the Hebrews ‘the second Nebuchadnezzar,’ under whom the history of Judith was written.”

Concerning Esther he writes: “The seventh Artaxerxes, for forty years.” Some assert that what is written about Esther and Mordecai took place under this king, but I do not think so. Ezra would never have been silent about Esther, since he writes that at this time Ezra and Nehemiah returned from Babylon, followed by the events that are reported as having been accomplished by them.

Up to this point divine Scripture contains the sequence of the times. The aforementioned Eusebius records that what is written about Mordecai and Esther belongs to the time of Artaxerxes, who was the eleventh of the Persian kings, saying:

> The eleventh of the Persians was Artaxerxes, surnamed Mnemon, son of Darius and Parysatis, for forty years.

Under this king, it seems to me, the history contained in the Book of Esther was completed. For he is the one who is called Ahasuerus by the Hebrews and Artaxerxes by the Seventy interpreters.

Concerning this king, Saint Jerome writes in his exposition of Ezekiel as follows:

> Artaxerxes, surnamed Mnemon, son of Darius and Parysatis, reigned for forty years. He is called Ahasuerus by the Hebrews. Under him the history of Mordecai and Esther is related, when the entire Jewish people, delivered from the danger of death, recovered its former liberty.

From the second year of Darius to the end of Ahasuerus there are 155 years and four months; added to the preceding 234 years, these make 389 years and four months.

Therefore, according to the order of the history, after Judith a responsory of Ezra should be arranged, and after this the responsories of Esther. I have taken pains to arrange these and the preceding responsories, as usual, according to the sequence of the history. In these responsories the kingdom of the Persians and Medes reaches its conclusion. We sing these responsories—those of Judith, Ezra, and Esther—in the first part of the month of October.

## CHAPTER LXXV. On the responsories of the Maccabees

The history of the Maccabees records the times and kingdoms of the Greeks. I also took care, as far as I could, to arrange these responsories according to the order of the history.

I did not find the responsory “[I will break the bonds of my people]” in the Book of Maccabees. Therefore I placed it among the responsories in which it is necessary to cry out about any kind of tribulation.

The kingdom of the Medes preceded the kingdom of the Greeks. What I mentioned above as having failed in the office of the month of August—the strength and beauty of the people of Israel—will be shown here from the history of Ezra and from the Book of Maccabees.

It is written in the First Book of Ezra:

> Many also of the priests and Levites, and the leaders of the families and the elders who had seen the former temple before it was founded, wept with a loud voice when they saw this temple before their eyes. And many, shouting for joy, raised their voices; no one could distinguish the voice of the joyful shouting from the voice of the people’s weeping.

And again in the First Book of Maccabees:

> Woe is me! Why was I born to see the ruin of my people and the ruin of the holy city, and to sit there while it is given into the hands of enemies, and the sanctuary into the hands of foreigners? Its temple has become like a man without honor. Its vessels of glory have been carried away captive; its young men have been slaughtered in the streets, and its youths have fallen by the sword of enemies. What nation has not inherited its kingdom? All its adornment has been taken away.

The responsories of Judith, Ezra, and Esther, which belong to the times of the Persians and Medes, and the responsories of the Maccabees, which belong to the times of the Greeks, are concluded in one month because the kingdoms of the Medes and Greeks signified a lesser power than the kingdoms of the Assyrians and Romans. For how much lower and more insignificant were these two kingdoms—the Medes and Greeks—than the Assyrians and Romans!

Orosius makes this clear in the first book of his histories, saying:

> By an ineffable ordering, throughout the four quarters of the world four principal kingdoms were distinguished, rising in successive degrees: the Babylonian kingdom in the east, the Carthaginian in the south, the Macedonian in the north, and the Roman in the west. Between the first and the last—that is, between Babylonian and Roman—there came, as between an old father and a young son, the African and Macedonian kingdoms, brief and intermediate, admitted by the power of time, not by right of inheritance, as guardians and administrators.

I think it has been sufficiently shown from the history written above why the responsories of so many histories are concluded in one month.

## CHAPTER LXXVI. On the responsories of the prophets

In the month of November, according to the custom of the Roman Church, we sing responsories from the Psalms in the first week and from the prophets in the following three weeks.

The historical order should not be sought in the prophets. It is not the custom of the prophets to follow the order of histories, but rather the touch of the Holy Spirit, who breathes wherever he wills; and when you hear his voice, you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.

These responsories, in place of various messengers, are sent ahead by the Holy Spirit before the coming of Christ. In no books of the Old Testament is the admonition of the Holy Spirit to the people—that they should turn back to God—found so frequently as in the prophets. Therefore, since the salvation of the world is near—namely, in the month of December—it is necessary that the same admonition be celebrated frequently in November.

When the time called the Advent of the Lord arrives, the things that speak more clearly about Christ’s birth are read and sung. None of the prophets prophesies about Christ’s birth as clearly and openly as Isaiah. Therefore he is read during the Advent of the Lord. The responsories also follow this arrangement, resounding most explicitly about Christ’s birth.

All the prophets prophesied about Christ. Therefore in November their books are read, and responsories are taken from them. Jeremiah, who speaks at greatest length about the Lord’s Passion, is reserved until the time of the Passion. Nevertheless, one reading from him is read on the fifth Sunday before the Lord’s Nativity.

The month of November corresponds in a certain way to the kingdom of the Romans. The kingdom of the Assyrians was, though from afar, a certain foreshadowing of the kingdom of the Christian people. For the latter is eternal, whereas the former was temporal.

The prophets sowed during the times of the Assyrian, African, and Greek kingdoms what Christians gather in the time of the Roman Empire. Therefore it is right that we who are Christians, and who were so called from Christ in the time of that empire, should mention those holy men who sowed for our work the harvest that we gather and by which we are nourished.

This is fitting at no time more than in the month of November, which is joined and related to December, in which Christ was born. He brought the sowing of the prophets to maturity and gave us the power to gather it.

When the responsories of the preceding kingdoms have ended, the order requires that the responsories of the prophets follow—those who labored for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

To show more clearly what I wish to make known, let a portion of the history of the aforementioned presbyter Orosius concerning this matter be written:

> From the first year of the reign of Ninus until Babylon began to be restored by Semiramis, sixty-four years intervened. And from the first year of Proca, when he began to reign, until the founding of the city by Romulus, there were likewise sixty-four years. Thus, while Proca was reigning, the seed of future Rome was sown, although its shoot was not yet visible. In that same year of the reign of Proca, the kingdom of Babylon failed.

And below:

> Babylon was finally overthrown by King Cyrus at the time when Rome was first liberated from the domination of the Tarquinian kings. For by one and the same correspondence of times, the former fell and the latter rose. The former then first suffered the domination of foreigners; the latter then first spurned even the arrogance of its own people. The former, dying then, as it were, left an inheritance; the latter, coming to maturity, then recognized itself as heir. Then the East fell, and the empire of the West arose.

And again below:

> Babylon, 1,164 years after it had been founded by the Medes and their king Arbatus, was stripped by its prefect of its wealth and kingdom and deprived of its king. Yet it afterward remained unharmed for some time. Similarly, Rome, after the same number of years—that is, 1,164—was attacked by the Goths and their king Alaric, and, though its prefect was present, was stripped of its wealth; yet it still retains its kingdom and remains unharmed in its rule.

Although in the secret decrees the entire order of correspondence between the two cities was preserved, so that there the prefect Arbatus invaded its kingdom and here its prefect Attalus attempted to reign, nevertheless in this case alone the impious attempt was rightly rendered void by a Christian emperor.

Therefore I have thought that these matters ought especially to be recalled, so that, when so great a secret of the ineffable judgments of God has been partly revealed, those who foolishly murmur about Christian times may understand that one God arranged the times, both at the beginning of Babylon and at the end of the Roman Empire; that it is due to his clemency that we live, but that the misery of our life is due to our intemperance.

Behold: Babylon and Rome had similar origins, similar power, similar greatness, similar periods, similar blessings, and similar evils; yet they did not have a similar end or a similar downfall. Babylon lost its kingdom; Rome retains it. Babylon was deprived of its king by his death; Rome is secure with its emperor unharmed.

And why is this? Because there the shame of lust was punished in the king, whereas here the most continent justice of the Christian religion was preserved in the king. There, without reverence for religion, the license of fury fulfilled the greed of the will; here there were Christians who spared, Christians whom they spared, and Christians for whose memory and in whose memory mercy was shown.

The kingdom of the Christian people will endure without end. For this was the aim of the Roman kingdom: that the whole world should come together and unite, so that the census of the whole world might be recorded for one Augustus. By God’s authorship this has been accomplished for the Christian people. He is named throughout the whole world; he is truly and perpetually registered to the one Christ.

It will not prove empty what the prophet said:

> Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.

And in the Gospel of Mark:

> The Gospel must first be preached to all nations.

## CHAPTER LXXVII. On responsories collected from various offices

I found certain responsories scattered through various nocturnal offices that did not fit with the others. Among them are “[I will break the bonds of my people],” which I found among the responsories of the Maccabees, although it is not found in the history of the Maccabees; and “[My sins, like arrows, have been fastened in me],” which I found among those taken from the Psalms, although it itself was not taken from the Psalms.

The same reasoning applies to the other responsories that follow. Collected together and placed as one group, they have been set in our Antiphoner after the responsories of the prophets.

I also collected together certain antiphons that correspond to the season of confession. We customarily sing them on the nights when the prescribed fast is observed, and during the fasts of the four seasons of the year.

## CHAPTER LXXVIII. On antiphons transformed by conformity of sound into Alleluia

Some antiphons were collected after the responsories, and their melody was reduced to a single Alleluia joined to itself, so that on the Sunday nights only the Alleluia might be heard over the morning psalms, in remembrance of the joy of the future resurrection that remains on the eighth day.

The hymn of the three young men is excepted; concerning it we have written in the little official book.

## CHAPTER LXXIX. On the order for the burial of any Christian

I found in the Roman and Metz Antiphoners an order written concerning how it is appropriate to perform the office at the end of human life and concerning the burial of the dead. From both I collected what seemed correct to me and suitable to a reasonable course, and, having reduced these materials into a single body, I placed them under one text at the end of our Antiphoner.

## CHAPTER LXXX. On the responsories formerly sung before the hymn of holy Mary

[Col. 1314C]

In an ancient Roman Antiphoner I found responsories for vespers, which I had sometimes heard being sung and had sung myself. But since most of our region did not sing them, and I could find no reason for singing them before the hymn of holy Mary, when they were not sung before the hymn of Zechariah, I omitted them.

But now, because I have found them in the Roman Antiphoner, I append them here.

At the Advent of the Lord: responsory, “You will arise, Lord; you will have mercy on Zion, for it is the time to have mercy on her, for the time has come.”

At the Nativity of the Lord: responsory, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Alleluia.” Verse: “The Lord is God, and he has shone upon us.”

At the Epiphany: responsory, “The sanctified day has shone upon us, Alleluia, Alleluia.” Verse: “Come, nations, and adore the Lord, Alleluia, Alleluia.”

On Sunday nights: responsory, “How greatly your works are magnified, O Lord.” Verse: “You have made all things in wisdom; the earth is filled with your works, O God.”

And again, until vespers: responsory, “How greatly your works are magnified, O Lord.” Verse: “You have made all things in wisdom,” as above.

On weekdays: responsory, “Our help is in the name of the Lord.” Verse: “Who made heaven and earth,” for the two weeks before Lent.

During Lent: responsory, “Bring my soul out of prison, that I may confess your name, O Lord.” Verse: “My escape has perished, and there is no one who seeks my soul.”

In the following two weeks: responsory, “Be for us, O Lord, a tower of strength against the face of the enemy.”

In the final two weeks: responsory, “How long will my enemy be exalted over me? Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God.” Verse: “Those who trouble me will rejoice if I am shaken, but I have hoped in your mercy.”

During the Easter days: responsory, “Alleluia, Alleluia.” Verse: “Sing a new song to the Lord; let all the earth sing to the Lord.”

At the Ascension of the Lord: “Alleluia, Alleluia.” Verse: “God has ascended amid jubilation, and the Lord amid the sound of the trumpet.”

During the days of Pentecost: responsory, “Alleluia, Alleluia.” Verse: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak, Alleluia, Alleluia.”

On the feasts of the saints: responsories from the proper responsories that are sung at night.

[Col. 1315]

# THE EXCERPTS OF SYMPHOSIUS AMALARIUS, PRESBYTER OF METZ AND CHOREPISCOPUS, ON THE OFFICE OF THE MASS

(Baluz., *Capitularies*, from a manuscript of St. Gall in Switzerland.)

## HERE BEGIN THE EXCERPTS ON THE ROMAN ORDER AND ON THE FOUR PRAYERS OF THE BISHOPS OR OF THE PEOPLE AT MASS

[Col. 1315B]

We set out beforehand the chapters of the following little work, so that if someone, being ignorant of the lowliness of this work, should undertake it as though it were worthy, and afterward find it worthless, he may not, driven to repentance, say to himself or to those standing around him: “If I had known the rusticity of this work, I would never have devoted the labor of my eyes to it.” Let him now see at the beginning what follows through to the end. And if, for the sake of reading, he should fall into some nausea, let him not be ungrateful only toward the one who arranged it, but also toward himself, since, having recognized its lowliness, he nevertheless chose to examine it to the very end.

I. This must be made clear: the things we celebrate in the office of the Mass before the Gospel reading look toward the first coming of the Lord, up to the time when he was hastening toward Jerusalem to suffer.

II. The Introit, however, looks toward the company of the prophets. We rightly touch upon them here, since, as Augustine says, Moses was a minister of the Old Testament.

III. The *Kyrie eleison* looks toward those prophets who lived near the Lord’s coming; among them were Zechariah and his son John.

IV. The *Gloria in excelsis Deo* looks toward the company of angels who announced the joy of the Lord’s birth to the shepherds.

V. The first Collect looks toward what the Lord was doing around the age of twelve, when he went up to Jerusalem, sat in the Temple among the teachers, and listened to them and questioned them.

VI. The Epistle pertains to John’s preaching.

VII. The Responsory pertains to the goodwill of the apostles, when they were called by the Lord and followed him.

VIII. The Alleluia pertains to the joy of their minds, which they possessed because of his promises or because of the miracles that they saw being performed by him or through his name.

IX. The Gospel pertains to his preaching up to the time mentioned above.

[Col. 1316B]

X. From that point onward, what is done in the office of the Mass looks toward the period extending from the Sunday when the children went out to meet him up to his Ascension and Pentecost.

XI. The prayer that the priest says from the Secret through “Nobis quoque peccatoribus” signifies the prayer that Jesus practiced on the Mount of Olives.

XII. What is done afterward signifies the time when the Lord lay in the tomb.

XIII. When the bread is placed into the wine, it demonstrates the Lord’s soul returning to his body.

XIV. What is celebrated afterward signifies the greetings that Christ gave to his disciples.

XV. The breaking of the offerings signifies the breaking that the Lord performed for his two disciples at Emmaus.

## On the Roman order and on the station in the church

The men stand on the southern side and the women on the northern, so that it may be shown that, through the more perfect sex, the stronger saints are always placed in the greater temptations of the heat of this world, while through the weaker and more fragile sex the weaker are placed in a more suitable location.

This also pertains to what John saw in his Apocalypse: a mighty angel who placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth. For the stronger members are stationed in the greater dangers, and the others in those appropriate to them.

## On the entrance of the bishop

The bishop enters from the left and crosses to the right. We are all one body of Christ; therefore it is fitting that the bishop, entering the church, should imitate his head, Christ, entering the world.

Our Savior touched the left side because he assumed what is temporal; but he was tending toward the right and teaching the Church to do the same, since by the resurrection he raised the flesh that he had assumed to the right hand of God and caused his Church to sit with him in the heavenly places, as the apostle Paul says, because “he raised us together and made us sit together in the heavenly places.”

Hear what Solomon says about the right and the left:

> Length of days are in her right hand, and in her left are riches and glory.

If we desire to live for a long time, let us tend toward the right—that is, toward the life to come—and on the left we shall have riches and glory, that is, the sufficiency of the present life.

## On the deacons and the bishop’s other ministers

No more than seven deacons, an equal number of subdeacons, and an equal number of acolytes enter with him, carrying no more than three censers.

It is often written, and made clear in many places, that the universality of the Church is signified by the number seven, since, when its parts are multiplied, it makes twelve: three times four is twelve, and four times three is twelve. From the number twelve of the patriarchs and apostles the universal Church is propagated.

If you ask why there may not be six, four, or two in this order, I will answer that God delights in an odd number.

“Why,” you ask, “does God delight in an odd number?”

I say: because an odd number cannot be divided, and God does not wish division to be admitted into his Church. An even number can be divided, as six into three, four into two, and two into one. We do not accept one in the order mentioned above as an even number because God does not wish division and schism to be admitted into his Church.

Although the apostles had said nothing about seven deacons ordained by them, from that time the apostles, or the successors of the apostles, decreed throughout all the Churches that there should be seven deacons, who would be in a more elevated rank than the others and would stand closest to the altar, like the columns of the altar: seven on account of the seven perfect men, five on account of the five books of Moses, three on account of hope, faith, and charity, and one on account of the unity of the Church.

## On the carrying of candles

As many deacons as there are, so many candlesticks are carried, because joy of eternal life and perpetual light are promised to the whole Church that labors and imitates Christ.

This is clearly declared in John’s Apocalypse, when the Lord says to the negligent one:

> Repent and do the first works. But if not, I am coming to you, and I will move your candlestick from its place.

That is: if you do not repent, I will deprive you of the gift of the promised light.

## On the carrying of the censer

The censer is also carried, signifying the body of Christ, as it is written in the same Apocalypse:

> Another angel came and stood before the altar, holding a golden censer.

This has been explained in the following way: he appeared, that is, in the presence of the Church, himself made into a censer, from which God received the fragrance of sweetness and was reconciled to the world.

## On the bishop, now presented at the altar

The bishop, coming before the altar, first adores the holy things, and afterward gives the kiss of peace to the priests and deacons, because he imitates the one of whom the prophet wrote:

> His dominion will be multiplied, and there will be no end of his peace.

First the bishop adores the holy things because the mercy of the one from whom peace, concord, and the kingdom of Christ reign within us must first be bestowed.

He kisses two priests because he himself is the cornerstone who joined two walls into one, coming from opposite sides, and gave peace to those who were far away and to those who were near.

## On “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit”

After peace has been given, he attributes glory to the holy Trinity, as though saying: “We return glory to God the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, because he has deigned to show us in the last times the peace that he foretold through his holy prophets.”

When he says, “As it was,” the deacons proceed to the altar, then return again to the bishop and stand upright. This signifies that they—namely, the apostles—gave themselves over to death in order to be united to Christ’s body.

In this verse the variety of multiple times is demonstrated: “as it was in the beginning,” referring to the past; “and now,” to the present; “and always,” to the future and the eternal; and “world without end,” to the great duration of the ages.

Hence Origen:

> Whenever “ages of ages” are mentioned, perhaps, although the matter is unknown to us, some limit of a state is nevertheless indicated by the Lord, as though the first three expressions referred to time, and the latter ones to the ages of the faithful who pass away.

“Under the altar” is said by hyperbaton in the testimony concerning the name of Christ. I did not see them being killed beneath the altar, but I saw the souls of those who had been killed beneath the altar—that is, under the testimony of the name of Christ.

When the prophetic verse is said, the bishop goes to the altar and kisses it, because Christ came into the world through the mouths of the prophets and proceeded to the Passion.

## On the station of the deacons

The deacons first stand bowed before the altar with the bishop until “as it was,” because the choir of the holy martyrs remains in the valley of tears before the final tribulation.

Afterward, crowned through martyrdom, they stand upright, liberated and already secure from every persecution. God has wiped their eyes away from every tear, every pain, and every hunger; therefore they stand forever before the Lord.

## On the station of the bishop
The bishop, however, always remains inclined until the prophetic verse, because Christ did not anticipate the time at which he had been foretold through the mouths of the prophets. For at the time when the prophets foretold it, he came into the world for the Passion; and therefore, with the prophetic verse, he goes to the altar, because he imitates Christ, showing the people that everything the prophets foretold concerning Christ’s Passion was true and was accomplished in its proper time, as is clearly read in the prophecy of Daniel:

“Seventy weeks,” he says, “have been shortened concerning your people and your holy city, so that transgression may be brought to completion, sin may reach its end, iniquity may be blotted out, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, the vision and the prophet may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed” (Daniel IX).

And again below:

“He will confirm the covenant with many for one week, and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering will cease” (ibid.).

When he says, “everlasting righteousness may be brought in,” he speaks of Christ’s coming. When he says, “the Holy of Holies may be anointed,” he speaks of Christ’s baptism. When he says, “he will confirm the covenant with many for one week,” he speaks of John’s proclamation, Christ’s preaching, and the calling of the apostles. When he says, “in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering will cease,” he speaks of Christ’s Passion and resurrection.

When he says “seventy weeks,” these are 475 solar years. Seven years are assigned to one week. He calls them shortened because, out of 475, he makes 490. He removes the intercalary periods from the 475 solar years and sets apart those months and years that can be produced by the intercalations. Intercalations occur over 175 years; these must be divided by twelve, since there are twelve months in a year. Twelve times fourteen makes 168—that is, fourteen years—which you must add to the aforementioned 475 years, making 489. From the 175, seven months remain beyond the 168. Add these seven months to the 489 years, and the ninetieth year begins; in that year the Lord ascended the cross.

Therefore the prophet said, “He will confirm the covenant with many for one week,” because during it John preached, the apostles came together in faith, and in the middle of the week Christ Jesus was killed. The seven months added to the 489 years are referred to, in a syntactically uncertain sentence, as concerning him who submitted himself to the Father even unto death and addressed his mother concerning this expectation, saying:

“Woman, what is this to you and to me? My hour has not yet come” (John II).

The bishop, immediately after he has adored the holy things, proceeds to the right side of the altar and stands upright facing east; the deacons stand behind him, one after another, more on the right and fewer on the left. The bishop stands at the right side of the altar because Christ preached a kingdom in which everything is on the right and there is nothing left. He also stands upright because he came to rule his own with an iron rod—that is, with inflexible justice. He stands facing east because, as he himself indicates, he did not seek to do his own will but the will of him who sent him, as it is written: “Because he came down from heaven, not to do his own will” (John VI), and so forth. He never looks backward but always gazes upon the face of the Father. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I know where I came from and where I am going” (John VIII).

Thus Christ must preach both the heavenly kingdom and the subjugation of sins beneath his feet, look toward eternal things, and keep temporal things behind him. The deacons stand behind him because, as we have said, they can appropriately be compared with the choir of martyrs: they minister at the holy altar and bear the dalmatics that military usage once employed. These same deacons went before the altar because martyrs existed in the Old Testament; now they stand behind because, after the Lord’s birth, no one worthy of martyrdom is crowned any less gloriously.

Some of them stand on the right and some on the left because many who followed the contemplative life were crowned through martyrdom, while many from the active life proceed to the crown of martyrdom. An example containing both ways of life can be found in two men. Clement of Alexandria, writing about James the brother of John, relates a memorable story (Eusebius, book II, chapter 9, from Rufinus’s translation):

“And the man,” he says, “who had handed him over to the judge for martyrdom, moved by what had happened, himself also confessed that he was a Christian. Both were led together to punishment; and as they were being led along, the other asked James on the way to forgive him. After a brief deliberation, James said, ‘Peace be with you,’ and kissed him. Thus both were beheaded together.”

James led the contemplative life, because none of them claimed anything as his own. There is no doubt that his companion was leading the present life, although together with him he entered, marked out by martyrdom, into the glory of the heavenly kingdom. Those who lead the contemplative life flourish with a greater number of virtues than those who lead the active life, insofar as they can be compared with Martha and Mary: the one ministering in the active life, the other sitting in the contemplative life.

The candles are first lit by the acolytes outside the church and are carried into the church by the acolytes. At first the candles go ahead; after they have arrived at the altar, they are placed behind. Both arrangements signify that the teachers of the Church existed as illuminators before the Lord’s birth and afterward as well. Acolytes are called “kindlers of lights.” They are carried in the hands because those whom they fill with knowledge must never cease to raise them up by good examples.

The same candles are held in the hands of the acolytes until the *Kyrie eleison*; then they are placed on the pavement and stand with fixed position. So teachers ought not to leave the uneducated people from their hands before the people subject to them know how to say, “Lord, have mercy on me, a sinner.” To say this in deed is, as I have been taught by my teacher: “I recognize myself as wretched, and therefore I ought to implore the Lord’s mercy.”

Then they stand by themselves in the church and illuminate the church, since it is right that one who has already been taught by a teacher should, in the teacher’s place, teach the Church. These too, as we said, stand more numerous on the right and fewer on the left. We understand this to signify the same thing that we said above concerning the deacons.

After the first prayer, the candles are placed before the altar—not now on either side as before, but mixed together in order, each behind the next, to the last—because there are some who abandon everything and bind themselves to the contemplative life. Most lead the active life and care for earthly matters. Nevertheless, as far as they can, by giving alms and keeping vigils, they strive to hasten to the Church. Our Church holds both groups together in a mixed arrangement.

It may also be understood that the candles are placed in order before the altar so that the ministers may run freely to the ambo and minister around the altars. The Gospel, which is carried nearer to the bishop, shows that it is itself the way by which we go to the kingdom of God.

## The Bishop’s Sitting

That this signifies the repose of souls after the prayer, what is signified by the priests sitting with him, and what is signified by his facing the people, shows that he has been given authority to examine their deeds.

After the first prayer, which we call the *precation*, the bishop sits facing the people, and the priests sit with him. In that prayer itself we understand a good wish for the Church, as though he were saying to the people: “I have desired the good of the Church, and therefore I sit. If you wish to possess the repose of souls, seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and eternal necessities will be added to you; afterward you will find rest.”

To stand is to remain still engaged in the struggle and to pray. After victory, however, comes sitting and judging. The priests sit with him, since their ministry is to proclaim the same thing. Concerning them Paul says: “Let the presbyters be held worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in the word of God” (1 Timothy V).

After the first prayer he stands facing the people, to show himself to the people after he has manifested himself to the Lord and his deeds, prayed for himself and his own, prayed for good things for the people, and rendered praise to God: namely, to have the work of examining the deeds of his people, determining who among them is considered worthy and who unworthy.

## The Episcopal Seat

The higher place is assigned to bishops so that they may preside over and, as it were, guard the people. For what is called *episcopus* in Greek is interpreted in Latin as *superintentor*—an overseer—because he presides and watches over. Just as a higher place is made for a vine-dresser to guard the vineyard, so a higher place has been made for bishops.

And from this dangerous and lofty place a dangerous account must be rendered, unless we stand here with such a heart that, in humility, we are beneath your feet and pray for you.

## The Epistle

Christ was a minister, for he said: “I did not come to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matthew XX). John was a subordinate minister, who said: “This was he of whom I said, ‘He who is to come after me has been made before me.’” He did not ascend to the higher step, which the one who is going to read the Gospel usually ascends, in order to show that he was a subordinate minister, because John was not worthy to untie the strap of the sandals of the one whose words are read in it.

The cantor, however, may ascend without distinction. He ascends higher because Christ was set above John. He stands on the same level because John was regarded as his equal. He stands lower because he came to be baptized by John. The one who sings the responsory does not ascend higher than the one who reads the lesson; he stands in the same place. If he ascends higher, it is understood according to the modes described above.

It is called a responsory because, while one sings, the others respond. One—Christ—sang, that is, he called Peter and the other apostles. They responded because they imitated Christ. Therefore the responsory is appropriate to the calling of the apostles. He alone sings the verse because Christ, spending the night apart, prayed alone, as in the Gospel: “But he was spending the night in prayer” (Luke VI).

When the deacon ascends to read, he asks the bishop’s blessing and receives the Gospel from the altar. Two candlesticks and two censers, or one, go before him. What this signifies has already been stated. The deacon stands facing south, toward which men customarily gather. He first asks the bishop’s blessing. The bishop gives it to him: “May the Lord be in your heart and on your lips.”

The incense placed in the censer signifies the prayer of the saints. Hence the Prophet says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm CXL).

The deacon says, “The Lord be with you.” The people turn toward the east and pray to God that they may rightly understand what they are about to hear. Each person makes the sign of the holy cross on his forehead, so that through the sign of the holy cross they may be armored, and no fantasy of the devil’s deceit may find an entrance into their hearts and carry away the seed of the Gospel from their souls.

After this the staffs are put down from their hands. The Jews gave a reed to Jesus in his right hand, placed a crown of thorns on his head, greeted him, and, kneeling, worshiped him in mockery. We, however, fleeing their consent, should put down the staff that they raised in pride, and at that same hour should hold neither a crown nor any other covering upon our head.

If someone should suddenly enter the church at that hour, we do not greet him or kneel in prayer until the Gospel has been read.

Alternatively, we may understand the staff as human assistance. Hence Jeremiah also says: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man” (Jeremiah XVII), and so forth. Priests in the Church can be our staffs, since they ought to pray for us. We place that prayer in the place of the staff.

Sometimes we use that staff, and sometimes we do not. When we have Christ at hand, no staff is necessary. If, because of our sins, he has withdrawn, it is necessary to seek a staff—that is, the prayers of the saints.

Therefore, when the priest prays and performs the offices of other teachers, we hold staffs in our hands. When the words of Christ himself speak to us, we do not hold staffs in our hands. This shows that it is not difficult for Christ himself to teach his people. For where Christ speaks directly, we do not need Peter, Paul, or another teacher, because he himself is the one master who is in heaven.

## Why the Deacon in the Ambo Faces South

The deacon stands facing south when proclaiming the words of the Gospel because he speaks to those of whom Paul said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Corinthians VI). When the sun turns toward the south, it is usually hotter and higher. This signifies that the Church, fervent in spirit in the love of God, has been raised to the great summit of the virtues.

Concerning this region the Song of Songs says:

“Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday” (Song of Songs I).

In that same region the bride seeks him, recognizing that he lies at midday—that is, among those whose hearts burn with love of God and love of neighbor. These are the people of whom the Gospel speaks: those who, hearing the word in a good and excellent heart, retain it and bear fruit with patience.

Certainly, when we customarily sit for the lessons of teachers, the face of our teacher is more intent upon the one who can learn more perfectly than upon those who learn less perfectly—not because he wishes his teaching for them alone, but because he wants those who have a slower understanding to be taught again by the one who can more quickly discover the true meaning in the teacher’s instruction. We do not say this in such a way that those behind are excluded from the holy Gospel, but so that the less educated may be educated through teachers.

You who have climbed the lofty summit of ministry,

The higher the things you seek, the more moderate you must be.

As much as you bend toward the ground, so much do you become near to heaven.

For the mind that seeks lofty things will hold these lowly things,

And the inner step by which it wishes to descend rises.

The hostile serpent rejoices if you fall, O gracious one;

The angel of the High-throned One does not rejoice if you are [textually uncertain].

You command the lofty cups to ascend the threshold of Olympus.

## The Extinguishing of the Candles

After the Gospel has been read, the candles are extinguished. The candles signify the teachers of the Church. What does it mean that they are extinguished after the Gospel, except that none of the teachers can surpass the words of the holy Gospel? It is also plainly shown that, once the holy Gospel has been closed, the teaching of the teachers has been extinguished.

## The Creed in God

After Christ has spoken to his people (the Legend reads *locutus*), it is right that they should profess their belief more sweetly and attentively. Thus it is fitting that, after the Gospel, the people, having heard Christ’s words, should proclaim the intention of their faith with a splendid voice. The Christian religion is believed in the heart for righteousness, while confession with the mouth is made for salvation.

## The Presentation of the Corporal and the Chalice at the Altar

After the Gospel has been read, the subdeacon comes carrying on his left arm a chalice into which the people’s small vessels are to be received, and a corporal above the chalice. The deacon takes the corporal and places it on the altar, and likewise places the chalice there after receiving the small vessels.

The Lord Jesus himself is the subdeacon and the deacon. He is the subdeacon when he opened the book and read; he is the deacon when he said: “The Son of Man did not come to be ministered to, but to minister” (Matthew XX). He himself carries the chalice and the corporal.

Without anyone compelling him, he came to Jerusalem as the hour of his Passion approached, bearing the chalice on his left arm and the corporal above it, because what he suffered was temporal, not eternal. The corporal may not be made from any other cloth than linen. Linen, through many processes, reaches its whiteness. It signifies the very purpose of the Lord’s Passion. The chalice signifies that Passion in which he received our small vessels.

## Recapitulation Concerning the Lord’s Passion

The Lord’s Passion is narrated twice in this little book: once in the Gospel, and again in what still remains and is enacted at the altar. Why is this? Because Jesus was crucified twice: first by the tongues of the Jews, and afterward on the cross. Thus Mark says “the third hour”—that is, by the tongues of the Jews—whereas, as the other Evangelists relate, he was crucified by their hands at the sixth hour.

## The Offering

Christ the Lord is priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek. Melchizedek, king of Salem—that is, king of peace—offered bread and wine as a prefiguration of the true priest Christ, who offered to God the Father true bread, that is, his spotless body, and wine, that is, his blood. In his figure our Church today offers bread and wine in the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood.

Those who disdain to offer offerings disdain—although not with a living voice—to confess that they have been redeemed by Christ’s Passion and to commit that same Passion to memory, unless there happens to be some cause temporarily preventing them from doing so.

They offer with *fanones*, because we read that a cloth was used in the Lord’s Passion. *Fanones* are made from linen. Linen is used in many ways in Holy Scripture for the exercise of the Passion. Therefore they hold the offerings with clean *fanones*, to show that they have received the holy and catholic faith: to lay down their lives for their brothers, and not merely their souls, but pure souls, not polluted by any heresy but cleansed by charity.

Hence the Apostle says: “And if I deliver my body to be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians XIII).

Last of all, the priests and deacons offer, but only bread. The archdeacon alone customarily completes the offerings of those who came before, pouring water into the chalice and into the bishop’s small vessel. This shows that Christ’s body is one and that what he did, he did for all.

Thus in the Gospel, when Peter alone answered on behalf of all the disciples after the Lord asked them, “Who do you say that I am?” (Matthew XVI), he said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” What they all answered in their hearts, Peter alone expressed with a living voice.

The fact that the priests offer in the last place is not without a mystery. In his Apocalypse, John saw one like a son of man in the midst of seven candlesticks, and in him he saw the condition of the whole present Church, what it would be. After describing this, he says: “His feet were like brass, as in a burning furnace” (Revelation I).

By the fiery feet he means the Church of the last time, which will be tested and proved more emphatically through afflictions. The ministry of priests is to be strong in the Church, so that each may pray for himself and for the people. Because they are stronger in the Church, they offer last, signifying the Church, since in the last time there will be Antichrist, and the Church will suffer far more injuries than the present Church does.

If one wishes to hear why men offer before women, it is said to be because the primitive Church, under oppression when Christians were not yet fully established, suffered more injuries than the present Church now suffers. Women offer in the middle because, as is plainly evident, there is great silence in the Church. Thanks be to God, Christianity flourishes greatly in these times, especially because the ruling power is Christian.

The ministry of priests and deacons is to minister at the altar and around the altar. Therefore they alone approach the altar, since their ministry concerns the altar.

## How the Bishop’s Ministers—the Deacons and Subdeacons—Stand Around the Altar During the Hour of Mass

Concerning those who minister during the hour of Mass.—At the time when Mass is celebrated, the deacons stand behind the bishop, and the subdeacons before his face. It is known that Christ said to his disciples: “You will all suffer scandal because of me on this night” (Matthew XXVI). Just as Christ foretold, they fled from him that same night.

Accordingly, at this hour the secondary ministers of the altar withdraw from the bishop’s presence, signifying that the apostles were absent for a time, yet waiting behind, because after the Passion they followed him. What does it mean to stand behind? Without doubt, it means to follow the one who is ahead.

After the angelic hymn, the subdeacons stand inclined until it is said: “And to us sinners also.” Then they rise for the first time and stand in the place where they had stood before, because the disciples and the women followed the Lord to the place of crucifixion—not merely following, but also weeping.

Jesus turned and said: “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but over yourselves and over your children” (Luke XXIII). The women wept as though for a sinner, but the Lord himself showed that they ought not to weep over him, but over themselves, since they were sinners.

And what sort of ministry should the subdeacons be understood to have when they stand inclined, if they do not pray and weep for their own sins? Tropologically, the subdeacons are inclined because they have gone astray. They stand upright through confession, and again look upon the bishop’s face after he says: “And to us sinners also.”

How could the disciples and women close their eyes so as not to see hanging on the cross the Lord whom they loved so greatly? The subdeacons remain in that sight until the chalice is surrounded with the *fanon*. Then at last they withdraw, to prepare the chalices in which the Lord’s body is to be honorably preserved.

You will hear how long they stood beneath the cross. Luke says:

“This man approached Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus, and, having taken it down, wrapped it in a linen cloth. The women who had come with him from Galilee followed, saw the tomb, and how his body had been placed. Returning, they prepared spices and ointments; and on the Sabbath they kept silence” (Luke XXIII).

The women prepared spices and ointments with which the Lord’s body might be embalmed, so that it would not be reduced to dust. The subdeacons, after they see the chalice surrounded with linen, go and prepare clean chalices or linens in which they may receive the Lord’s body, so that it may not fall to the ground and turn to dust.

The women kept silence on the Sabbath. In the same way, the subdeacons wait until the Lord’s Prayer and what pertains to that prayer have been completed. The Sabbath is appropriately adapted to the Lord’s Prayer, in which there are seven petitions. For by the seventh day of the Sabbath the sevenfold Spirit is understood. Or this may be understood with reference to the Lord’s Prayer, which is adapted to the Sabbath. The silence of the Sabbath signifies the repose of the mind, which is given through the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. These gifts we ask for in the Lord’s Prayer.

Therefore the ministers of the Church rest at that hour. The deacons plainly remain inclined until the Lord’s Prayer is completed. The subdeacons rise when they hear, “And to us sinners also”; they signify those to whom Christ said: “But you, remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke XXIV), namely, the apostles.

Their continuing inclination signifies their perseverance in prayer, so that they might receive the Lord’s promise. He expressly commanded them to await in Jerusalem the promised Holy Spirit until Pentecost. They stand inclined until the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer are completed. Of them it is also read above that they ministered to him as far as the tomb, and afterward prepared the spices.

Those who bear their type withdraw from the altar to prepare the ministry when they hear: “For ever and ever. Amen.”

## Verse

Behold here the tomb of Christ which you see as the altar.

From here, seek with your mind the lofty heights above.

The linen cloths marvel together, as you pray, blazing,

In harmony with the Lord. Meditate on these things devoutly.

Disciples, lower your faces toward the ground;

The holy ranks of mothers show this to you.

Let us all stand humbly with the women

Continually before the gracious angelic faces.

## Why “Therefore, O Lord” Is Sung Secretly

It was the custom of our fathers that those who offered prayer should give praise to God. Therefore what we say in a loud voice before “Therefore, O Lord” belongs to the praise of our Creator, so that it may be plainly shown to everyone who can distinguish these things. In this part we are told to give thanks to God, and the angelic creation is declared to praise its Creator, each in its appropriate ministry.

Afterward comes “Therefore, O Lord,” namely, the priests’ special prayer. In it the priest prays specially for certain people, as he does for the Apostolicus, and afterward, when he says “of your servants and handmaids,” and immediately after he has poured out a prayer for his own people, he turns generally to pray for everyone, adding: “and of all who stand around,” and other things of the same kind.

Insofar as this prayer specifically concerns the priest, the priest alone enters into it and sings it secretly. He follows the command of his teacher, who says: “But when you pray, enter into your room” (Matthew VI), and so forth.

This custom remains in our Church to this day: if anyone offers a prayer, he offers it specially. He raises his voice enough to admonish himself concerning what he ought to ask in the secrecy of his heart. Nor is it without reason that this custom is maintained among Christians. Without doubt, it is because Christ prayed alone. Hence Matthew says: “And having dismissed the crowd, he went up the mountain alone to pray” (Matthew XIV).

## Concerning the Crosses in “Therefore, O Lord”

Six crosses are completed in this prayer, so that, just as the works of God are perfect, so the body of that same God and our Lord Jesus Christ may be understood as perfect. For the number six is perfect when its parts are combined.

This is signified by the fact that the final cross is made with the offering: he who came to suffer for the whole Church, whose body submitted to the Passion even to the touch of the cross.

### Alternatively

The five rows of crosses made before the sixth, when the chalice is touched with the offering, signify the five ages of the world before the Lord’s birth. The sixth signifies the time remaining from the Lord’s birth to the end of the world.

The chalice being touched once with the offering signifies that the Lord ascended the cross once, so that the torment occurring throughout the five ages of the world might come to an end. By the offering raised in the hand the prophets are signified: they raised the true bread, Christ, in their hands when they openly proclaimed his Incarnation. Hence Isaiah says: “Behold, a virgin will conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah VII).

When the deacon sees the cross being made and begun, he goes to raise the chalice and holds it raised together with the bishop until he says: “For ever and ever.” Then he places the chalice on the altar and wraps it in a cloth.

Joseph, having received the body of Jesus, wrapped it in a clean linen cloth and placed it in his own tomb. We therefore place this present deacon, because of his corresponding ministry, in the type of Joseph, or more generally in the type of those who receive the mysteries of Christ with a chaste heart.

The deacon who holds the chalice raised with the bishop places it on the altar because Joseph took the Lord’s body down from the cross and placed it in the tomb. As we said, the deacon wraps the chalice in a cloth because Joseph wrapped the body in a clean linen cloth.

On the altar itself—that is, in the tomb—the corporal lies. By it is understood the larger linen cloth with which the Lord’s entire body was covered in the tomb. By the cloth that covers part of the chalice, the *sudarium*, we understand the cloth that covered part of the Lord’s head and did not cover another part, as is the custom among the Jews; and it remains on the altar, that is, in the tomb.

This action continues until the three sections are completed: the prologue concerning the prayer that follows, “Our Father,” and “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord.” For the Lord rested in the tomb for three days.

Afterward, the Lord’s body having been mixed with wine, and peace having been announced, the Lord’s body is removed from the altar, because on the third day the soul that had descended to the underworld to free the righteous vivified the members of the body, returned to the body, and the Lord’s body was no longer found in the tomb.

Therefore, since the whole human being rose together, it is right that the Lord’s chalice be immediately removed from the altar together with the offering.

## The Names of the Four Prayers of the Bishops or the People at Mass

The first prayer is sometimes called a prayer and sometimes a collect. It is plainly called a prayer because good things are requested for the people. It is called a collect because the people begin to gather together as one.

May it please your fraternity, dearest brother, that I use the authority of Saint Augustine in this little work. He divides this office into four kinds: supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings, recalling them in this way.

Everything done in the office of the Mass before the offerings are placed on the altar is called a supplication. He distinguishes supplication from deprecation and imprecation in this way: supplication is when one wishes good things for the people; deprecation is when one prays that evil be avoided and that one cease from sins; imprecation is when one wishes evil—that is, curses.

The first prayer spoken by the bishop is called a supplication, namely, a good wish for the people. For we said that the Introit belonged to the office of the prophets, because through the mouths of the prophets Christ entered the world. He not only entered but also assumed flesh and became human, deriving his bodily origin from the holy patriarchs.

One of these patriarchs greatly desires and commends his coming to his people, saying: “The scepter will not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself will be the expectation of the nations” (Genesis XLIX). Again: “I will await your salvation, O Lord” (ibid.). Likewise: “I beseech you, Lord, send the one whom you are going to send” (Exodus IV).

The holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, desires this good when she answered the angel: “Let it be done to me; behold, the handmaid of the Lord, according to your word,” so that he might proceed from her virginal womb who would save his people from their sins (Luke I).

## The Secret Prayer

It is called the secret because the bishop offers a secret prayer over the offering, asking that God be willing to look upon the offering that has been set forth and assign it to the future consecration. It is known that the reason for making a secret prayer over the offering is so that Christ’s body may be made from it.

## The Breaking of the Offerings

The breaking of the offerings signifies the breaking that the Lord performed for the two at Emmaus. For this reason some bishops, when they communicate with one another, customarily make three portions from one offering, as a type of these three: Christ, Cleopas, and, as they say, Luke.

Just as there are many Churches throughout the whole world because of different places, yet there is one holy catholic Church because of one faith, so there are many offerings because of the vows of those who offer, yet there is one bread because of the unity of Christ’s body.

If you ask why the entire offering is not placed in the chalice, since it is established that the Lord’s whole body rose—part still to rise, part already living so as no longer to die, part mortal, and yet in heaven—the Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians III).

## Concerning the Peace Announced Before the Body and Blood of the Lord Are Mixed
The peace pronounced by the bishop or priest before the Lord’s body is placed into the blood may be understood in two ways. First, that peace may be understood as the peace given to the righteous at the same time when Christ’s soul descended into hell, rescued all the faithful from it, and God wiped away every tear from their eyes, so that they would no longer have [Col. 1329A] pain or mourning, but would live in God’s peace, by which the angels were reconciled with him, forever.

Or certainly, that peace may be understood as the peace given to Christ’s body when his soul returned to it: just as the soul was never troubled by its death, so the body should no longer be troubled by its transformation; rather, both should enjoy that peace, so that they may always rejoice in eternal immortality. It is not unreasonable if, through the touch by which the lips of the chalice are touched, we understand at the same time that passage of Scripture: “And he breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. II), so that the restoration of life may be read as belonging to the member to which life was first given.

Certainly, it also accords with reason that, since there are four senses in the head, the lips of the chalice are touched on four sides, either because Christ’s resurrection is hoped for from the four quarters of the world. [Col. 1329B] Hence it is written: “Come from the four winds, and breathe upon these slain, and let them live again” (Ezek. XXXVII).

Just as, after the children cried out, “Hosanna, blessed is he who comes,” certain Gentiles who did not yet belong to God sought through Philip, who was the mouth of the lamp, to see Jesus—by which it was signified that the Gentiles would become the Lord’s body through faith—so also, when this bread is first placed on the altar, it is understood that the Lord’s body will be made from it. Let us hear what the Lord answers concerning those Gentiles already mentioned: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone” (John XII). By this he plainly shows that unless he himself dies, the Gentile race will not become his body.

Likewise, pure bread could not previously become his body unless the priest’s sacrament of the Lord’s passion were recalled [Col. 1329C] and the sign of the cross were performed over it.

### Again, concerning the Secret

Christ sought solitude in prayer. How much more ought we not to seek it, since we are surrounded on every side by the tumult of vices and by worldly custom? It is useful that the priests’ entire special prayer be secret, so that we do not consider how our voice and the arrangement of our speech may please an earthly people, but only how the mind of the one praying may agree with God alone. From the point at which the bishop says the Secret up to the Agnus Dei, Augustine calls the whole section “prayers.”

### Concerning the Preface

[Col. 1329D]

The Preface is so called as if it were a prelude. For this prayer, which is called the Preface, is the prelude to the whole following prayer that is begun. “Te igitur” extends up to the Agnus Dei. This prayer follows the custom of the prayer of our fathers, who used to offer praises to the Lord in prayer.

Thus Daniel prayed: “O Lord our God, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a strong hand, and made for yourself a name, as it is this day” (Dan. IX). And shortly afterward: “Let your anger and your fury, I beseech you, be turned away from your city,” and so forth. First he praised the Lord because he had brought his people out of harsh servitude; afterward he pleaded concerning their present tribulation.

### Concerning the Blessing after Communion

[Col. 1330A]

Augustine calls this prayer after Communion a petition. It is called “after Communion” because it follows after the people have received Communion. It is called “over the people” because the people are then blessed, so that they may conform to our holy Gospel.

After prayer and Communion comes the blessing, because after Christ had prayed on the cross, eaten before his disciples, and given them the remaining portions, he raised his hands and blessed them (Luke XXIV). “And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he withdrew from them, and was carried up into heaven.” Our blessing is indeed a petition before the Lord, asking that he graciously bless us.

After giving the blessing, the bishop returns to his place. Then the deacon announces: “Go, the Mass is ended.” [Col. 1330B] He speaks to the people in the likeness of the angels who said to the apostles: “This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven” (Acts I), and so forth. What does “Go, the Mass is ended” mean, my brother, except: “Go in peace to your homes. A prayer has been dispatched for you to the Lord, and through the angels, who are called messengers, it has been brought into the presence of the divine majesty”?

The people answer: “Thanks be to God.” Augustine calls this response “thanksgiving.” The holy Church does this in the apostolic manner: the apostles, after worshiping Jesus, returned to Jerusalem with great joy (Luke XXIV). Hear how the apostles give thanks to God: “And they were continually in the temple, praising and blessing God, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.”

### How Certain Prayers and Crosses Are to Be Performed in the *Te igitur*

[Col. 1330C]

“Therefore, most merciful Father, through Jesus Christ your Son, our Lord, we humbly ask and entreat you to accept and bless these gifts.”

Here he makes the sign over the offering and the chalice three times—not under a single cross, but separately, making one cross for each:

“These + gifts, these + offerings, these + holy and unblemished sacrifices.”

“First, what we offer to you for your holy Catholic Church: may you graciously grant her peace, guard her, unite her, and govern her throughout the whole world, together with your servant, our pope, that man.”

“Remember, Lord, your male and female servants, that man and that woman”—here the names of the living are commemorated, if desired, but not on the Lord’s Day, except as on the other days—“and all those standing around, whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is recognized, [Col. 1330D] who offer you this sacrifice of praise for themselves and all their own, for the redemption of their souls, for the hope of their salvation and well-being, and who render their vows to you, the eternal, living, and true God.

“Joining in communion and venerating the memory, first, of the glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of your blessed apostles and martyrs: Peter, Paul, Andrew, James, John, Thomas, James, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon, and Thaddaeus; Linus, Cletus, Clement, Sixtus, Cornelius, Cyprian, Lawrence, Chrysogonus, John and Paul, Cosmas and Damian.

“If it is the feast of saints, let him say here: ‘And celebrating the day of the birth of that blessed man, or of those blessed men,’ and of all your saints, [Col. 1331A] whose merits and prayers grant that in all things we may be fortified by the help of your protection, through Christ our Lord.”

Here he bows toward the altar, saying:

“Therefore, Lord, we ask you graciously to accept this offering of our service, and also of your whole household; dispose our days in your peace, command that we be rescued from eternal damnation and numbered among the flock of your elect, through Christ our Lord.”

Here he raises himself upright and blesses only the offering:

“Which offering, O God, we ask you to make blessed +, approved +, ratified +, reasonable, and acceptable in every respect”—here he signs both, that is, the offering and the chalice—“so that it may become for us the body + and blood + of your beloved Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

“Who, on the day before he suffered, [Col. 1331B] took bread in his holy and venerable hands, and with his eyes raised toward heaven, to you, God his almighty Father, giving you thanks, blessed + it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take this, all of you, and eat from it. For this is my body.’

“In the same way, after supper had ended, taking also this excellent chalice into his holy and venerable hands, again giving you thanks, he blessed + it and gave it to his disciples, saying: ‘Take this, all of you, and drink from it. For this is the chalice of my blood, of the New and eternal Testament, the mystery of faith, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me.’

“Therefore, remembering, Lord, we, your servants, and also your holy people, the blessed passion of Christ your Son, our Lord and God, [Col. 1331C] as well as his resurrection from the dead and his glorious ascension into heaven, offer to your splendid majesty, from your gifts and what you have given us”—here he signs only the offering four times, and on the fifth occasion makes a single cross over the chalice—“a pure + victim, a holy + victim, an unblemished + victim, the holy + bread of eternal life, and the + chalice of everlasting salvation.

“Upon these gifts may you deign to look with a favorable and serene countenance and accept them, just as you deigned to accept the gifts of your righteous servant Abel, the sacrifice of our patriarch Abraham, and what your high priest Melchizedek offered to you: a holy sacrifice, an unblemished victim.”

Here he bows again beside the altar, saying:

“We humbly beseech you, almighty God.”

Here he prays privately whatever he wishes. Then he says:

[Col. 1331D]

“Command that these gifts be carried by the hands of your angel to your sublime altar, into the presence of your divine majesty.”

Here he rises, saying:

“So that all of us who, through participation in this altar, have received the most holy body and blood of your Son may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace, through Christ our Lord.”

Here two prayers are said: one over the diptychs [perhaps *diptycha*], the other after the reading of the names. This is done only on ordinary days or on *agendis* days:

“Remember also, Lord, those whose names have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace.”

And they are recited. Then, after they have been recited, he says:

“To them, Lord, and to all who rest in Christ, we beseech you to grant a place of refreshment, light, and peace, through Christ our Lord.” [Col. 1332A]

“To us also, your sinful servants, who hope in the abundance of your mercies, graciously grant some share and fellowship with your holy apostles and martyrs: with John, Stephen, Matthias, Barnabas, Ignatius, Alexander, Marcellinus, Peter, Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia, Anastasia, and with all your saints. Admit us into their company, we ask, not weighing our merits but generously granting pardon, through Christ our Lord.”

Here the archdeacon rises, comes forward, wraps the chalice in a small cloth, and raises it toward the lord pope.

“Through him, Lord, you always create all these good things.”

Here he signs both, that is, the offering and the chalice, three times, making one cross each time:

“You sanctify +, [Col. 1332B] give life to +, bless +, and grant them to us.”

Here the lord pope raises the two offerings as far as the rim of the chalice and touches it with the offerings, while the archdeacon holds it:

“Through him, and with him, and in him, to you, God the almighty Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, is all honor and glory.”

Then he says aloud:

“For ever and ever.”

They answer:

“Amen.”

Then he places the offerings back on the altar and says aloud:

“Let us pray.”

Then he says:

“Instructed by saving commands and formed by divine teaching, we dare to say:

“‘Our Father, who are in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come’”—up to “deliver us from evil.”

Then the lord pope, with no sound intervening, says this prayer:

“Deliver us, we beseech you, Lord, from all evils, past, present, and future; and through the intercession of the blessed and glorious ever-virgin Mary, Mother of God, and of your holy apostles Peter and Paul and Andrew, and of your holy first martyr Stephen, and of your blessed confessors Hilary, Martin, and Benedict”—here he names whichever and however many saints he wishes to commemorate—“together with all the saints, graciously grant peace in our days, so that, aided by the help of your mercy, we may always be free from sin and secure from every disturbance, through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son.”

Then he says:

“May the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ be always with you.”

They answer:

“And with your spirit.”

Then he gives the peace to the altar or to the paten. The people likewise give the peace to one another.

When the lord pope says, “May the peace of the Lord be always with you,” he does not place the holy portion into the chalice, as is customary among other priests when they break the bread and say the Agnus Dei. [Col. 1332D] After the fraction has been completed, the apostolic lord receives Communion: he bites off a portion for himself and places the remainder into the chalice, making the sign of the cross with it three times over the chalice without saying anything. Thus he partakes from the chalice, while the archdeacon holds it.

When the apostolic lord descends from the altar, the people begin to receive Communion. The Communion antiphon is sung. After Communion and the antiphon have been completed, the lord pope then rises, comes to the altar, and greets it in a loud voice, saying:

“The Lord be with you.”

They answer:

“And with your spirit.”

Then he gives the prayer:

“May what we have received with the mouth, Lord, be grasped by the mind, and may a temporal gift become for us an everlasting remedy, through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

[Col. 1333]

## Letters of Symphosius Amalarius
