(Apud Acherium, *Spicilegii*, volume III, p. 330, and from Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*.) (G)*

### First Letter: Amalarius to Jeremiah, Archbishop of Sens, Concerning the Name of Jesus

[Col. 1333A]

“To the most illustrious Father and keenest rhetorician, Jeremiah the prophet, Amalarius in our Jerusalem.”

They write the name of our Savior Jesus with an aspiration, though I do not know the reason for this. I know that it is not unknown to you—if the aspiration is placed after the I in the name *Iesus* for some reason—that you should explain this to your son, if you have the opportunity. I know that, if such a reason exists, it will be present in the storehouse of your mind and flow from there to me.

Before the lord Charles most recently went to Rome, I heard the priests of our Gaul pronounce the name “Gisus,” which agreed neither with the Hebrews nor with the Greeks. Since that time I have heard “Iesus,” which, in my opinion, agrees with [Col. 1333B] the Hebrews, whose leader Jesus prefigured our Jesus by his name, as Sedulius says:

> Even then the stars, having rendered service, saw Jesus who was to come, his name having been sent beforehand.

For the Greeks write that name with these letters: Ι.Ϲ.; and they read it as ΙΗϹΟΥϹ. Therefore it seems to me—unless you think otherwise—that it ought to be written with Ι, Η, and Ϲ, or Σ, as we read *Ihesus*. I ask you to instruct me with which letters I ought to write the aforementioned name.

### Second Letter: Jeremiah to Amalarius

The philosopher Porphyry writes the name *IESU* in his acrostics in Latin in this way: *IHESUS*. We know that he was highly skilled in both languages. He uses the Greek letter Η for the long [e], which the Greeks always pronounce in their own language as a long [i], while the Latins pronounce it as a long [e].

Imitating the Hebrews in another respect, we pronounce *Iesus* not with an aspiration, but by writing it with the Greek Η.

### Third Letter: Amalarius to Jonah, Bishop

“To a father deeply attached to his son: in your view, with which of the forms shown below is the name of Jesus more correctly written, ΙΗϹ or ΙΗΣ?”

But he replied, he says: “Just as Χ and Ρ, Greek letters, are joined to the appropriate Latin letters above to write the name of Christ, so Ι and Η, added to the appropriate Latin letter, write ΙΗΣ.”

### Fourth Letter: Amalarius to Rantgarius, Bishop

[Col. 1333D]

“Amalarius to Rantgarius, most reverend bishop of the city of Noyon.”

I remember being asked by your fatherhood how I understood what is written in the Lord’s institution: “This is the chalice of the blood of the New and eternal Testament, the mystery of faith.” Since I discovered that you wished to know how I understood it, I therefore briefly explain in writing what I think.

There was a chalice of the Old Testament, concerning which it is written in Exodus, chapter 98: “Moses therefore took half of the blood and put it into bowls; but the remaining part he poured upon the altar” (Exod. XXIV, 6). And shortly afterward: “This is,” he said, “the blood of the covenant which the Lord has made with you concerning all these words” (Luke XXII, 17).

The Lord completed this chalice at his supper, according to Luke, who says: “And taking the chalice, he gave thanks and said: Take this and divide it among yourselves. For I tell you that I will not drink of the fruit of the vine until the kingdom of God comes.” The chalice of the Old Testament overflowed with the blood of irrational animals. That blood was a figure of the true blood of Christ.

He himself inaugurated for us that chalice—that is, the chalice in which we drink Christ’s blood—at the supper just mentioned, after the earlier chalice had been completed, as Luke records in what follows: “Likewise also the chalice, after he had supped, saying: This is the chalice of the New Testament in my blood, which shall be poured out for you” (Luke XX).

“This chalice is a figure of my body, in which is the blood that will flow from my side to fulfill the old law. Once it has been poured out, the New Testament will henceforth exist, because a new and innocent blood—that is, the blood of a sinless man—will be poured out for the redemption of humanity, something that had not previously been done with the blood of any irrational animal.

“This blood is new, because it was poured out for our salvation. It is not the blood of an irrational animal but of a rational human being. Therefore it is called the blood of the New Testament, because once it was poured out, the old things passed away and new things came to be.

“It is called the blood of the eternal Testament because the New Testament will not be changed into another testament, as the Old was changed into the New.

“It is called the mystery of faith because, for the one who believes that he has been redeemed by that blood and becomes an imitator of Christ’s passion, it is effective for salvation and eternal life. Hence the Lord says: ‘Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves’ (John VI, 54). That is: unless you become participants in my passion and believe that I died for your salvation, you shall not have life in yourselves.

“*Mysterium* is Greek for ‘secret’ in Latin, because this faith is hidden in the hearts of the elect; therefore it is called the secret of faith.

“The mystery of faith is faith,” as Augustine says in Letter 23 to Bishop Boniface: “Therefore, just as in a certain sense the sacrament of Christ’s body is Christ’s body, and the sacrament of Christ’s blood is Christ’s blood, so the sacrament of faith is faith.” Likewise we may say: “This is the chalice of my blood, of the New and eternal Testament,” as if he were saying: “This is my blood, which is given for you, so that henceforth the New and eternal Testament may be received and maintained from me.”

It follows: “The mystery of faith.” You ought to believe this—that is, you ought to have this faith—so that through it you may receive the forgiveness of all your sins.

### Fifth Letter to Hetto, Monk

[Note: [Col. 1335D] “To Hetto.” Perhaps this is Hetto or Hectus, who was abbot of Echternach and afterward bishop of Trier.]

Your fraternity has graciously instructed me to name for you the author who distinguishes between *seraphin* when it is neuter and when it is masculine. I cannot immediately recall everything that you have read or that I have read concerning those ranks. Nevertheless, I shall now produce the author who distinguishes between *cherubin* in the neuter and masculine genders, as well as the author who says that *seraphim* with *m* is masculine and with *n* neuter.

I think that among the Greeks *cherubin* and *seraphin* end with the same final letters. Jerome says [Col. 1335B] in the third book of his commentary on Ezekiel:

> “Although many think that *cherubin* is said in the neuter gender and plural number, we ought to know that *cherub* in the singular is masculine, and that its plural, *cherubim*, is of the same gender—not because there is sex among God’s ministers, but because each is called by different genders according to the particular character of its language. Angels are called in the plural *Malachim*, and *cherubim* and *seraphim* are of the same gender and number.” [Col. 1335C]

Here Saint Jerome says that “we ought to know” this because he was speaking Latin to Latins. He himself was a Latin, and Paula and her daughter Eustochium were Latins. From this we can understand that we Latins ought to retain the names of those ministers in the masculine gender, in accordance with the Hebrew authority that Jerome interpreted.

And when he says, “not because there is sex among God’s ministers, but because each is called by different genders according to the particular character of its language,” we understand from this that the aforementioned ministers are of another gender in a foreign language.

Bede says in the first book *On the Tabernacle and Its Vessels*:

> “In the singular number it is called *cherub*, but in the plural *cherubin*, and it is a masculine noun. Yet Greek usage placed *cherubin* in the neuter gender, changing the letter *m* into *n*. But our translator, following the Hebrew language, placed it in the masculine gender.”

I shall show again where that same translator, Jerome, places *seraphin* in the neuter gender. In the book he wrote on the seraphim (chapter 6, near the beginning), he writes what is read in Isaiah, among other things:

> “None of the prophets except Isaiah saw seraphim standing around God, nor are the seraphim themselves read of elsewhere.”

Your Charity knows that when he said “standing,” he used the neuter gender for “those seraphim.” [Col. 1336A] We also have no small authority from the custom of the Church, which is accustomed [Col. 1336A] to say daily in the prayer offered over the table: “Blessed seraphim.”

[Note: [Col. 1336D] From this letter Amalarius is shown to have been a priest.]

### Sixth Letter to Guntradus

“Amalarius to Guntradus, beloved son in the discipline of Christ.”

My son, I remembered that your powerful intellect had asked why I did not guard myself more carefully, so that immediately after consuming the sacrifice I would not spit. You added that you had not seen the other priests do this—that is, spit immediately after eating the Eucharist.

When I heard this from you, I neither said much to you nor considered answering you on this subject; I regarded such a question as worthless. But now, while traveling, I have been troubled [Col. 1336B] by my affection for you, lest some false suspicion remain in your heart. You might think that I did this deliberately against our religion. Since I did not want you to remain in any error born of ignorance, especially because I sensed that you thought I was acting against the custom of religious priests, I preferred to shape my mind for you from the road rather than allow your ardent intellect to remain longer in a useless suspicion.

First attend, my son, to Paul’s statement: “The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one” (I Cor. II, 15). If what concerns the spirit remains in its proper order, the things done through the body are rightly judged, since the same Apostle says: “All things are clean to the clean” (Tit. I, 15). [Col. 1336C]

There are many who observe bodily cleanliness according to the custom of the Pharisees, yet from their minds proceed the unclean things that the Lord reckons in the Gospel, saying: “From the heart come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies. These are the things that defile a person” (Matt. XV, 20).

Spittle is not included among these, nor does it proceed from the evil thought that defiles a person. Spittle is natural to us; it proceeds from us without sin, and its expulsion benefits our health. Without insulting religious people, we do what Christ did for our salvation, as the Gospel teaches: “The Lord made clay from spittle and spread it on the eyes of the man born blind” (John IX, 6). And again, according to Mark: “He put his fingers into his ears, and, spitting, touched his tongue” (Mark VII, 32). [Col. 1336D]

The Lord’s body has been consecrated for the eternal salvation of human beings. The expulsion of spittle provides temporal health. We seek temporal health so that we may more readily attain eternal salvation. What serves eternal salvation is not contrary to the Lord’s institution.

Although the Apostle said, “When I am weak, then I am strong and powerful” (II Cor. XII, 10), he nevertheless cared for his health, as we know from the instruction he gave Timothy: “Drink no longer water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (I Tim. V, 29).

[Col. 1337A]

My son, in your reproach you showed that you disliked my spitting for no other reason than that you had seen the other priests refrain from spitting for a longer time after the sacrifice. Since you are still a very young boy, you have not seen many priests. Perhaps those whom you have most often seen are associated with hunters, who are accustomed to wash their hands of the fresh blood of their buffaloes and goats, as ordinary people also do when they approach the common table.

I do not say this because we ought not to venerate the Lord’s body above all foods, but because, if it has been venerated by the inner person, whatever is done naturally by the outer person is attributed to the Lord’s honor.

Although the keenest judgment of your childhood did not show me what displeased you, nevertheless, I think I see what displeases you: my spittle—that is, you think I am casting out the body I have received together with the spittle.

My son, your father’s mind does not think in this way. I beseech him who says through the Psalmist: “I will guard my strength toward you” (Ps. LVIII, 10).

If a phlegmatic person takes care of his health, he will more frequently attend to expelling phlegm. A phlegmatic person is not prohibited from advancement to the sacred orders. Paul did not fail to know that harmful and excessive humors would often have to leave a person; yet when he rejected a proud, angry, drunken, violent bishop who was greedy for shameful profit, he did not reject a phlegmatic one.

Perhaps you animal beings, puffed up with bodily cleanliness, can see harmful faults in your hidden imagination—faults that the Apostle Paul perhaps could not see in the Holy Spirit. God forbid, my son.

If I could refrain from spitting long enough to satisfy you, so that they would have nothing to criticize in me, I would willingly take care of this, as the Apostle commands: “Providing what is good not only before God but also before all people” (Rom. XII, 17).

But since this is difficult for me, I nevertheless trust in the Lord: if my mind is pure and humble in his sight, he will cause the body to enter my soul for its vivification, and what must leave for the body’s health he will cause to leave without loss to the soul.

If anyone does not believe that he can do this if he wishes, he does not believe that he is omnipotent. And whoever does not hope that he wishes this does not accept Paul’s statement: “Who desires all people to be saved” (I Tim. II, 4)—that is, those who are destined for salvation.

My son, remember what you used so often to say to me: “Unless the Lord guards the city, in vain does he watch who guards it” (Ps. CXXVI, 2). [Col. 1337D] If any scruple about the matter mentioned still clings to your mind, do not hide it from your father while he lives. Hold fast to what you hold; may the Lord multiply for you the understanding of these matters, beyond what you know how to ask.

Concerning the body of the Lord that we receive, I must say something, although the example does not correspond exactly to the present matter. [Col. 1338A]

The emperor Valentinian said to soldiers who wished to choose a colleague for him: “It was yours to make me emperor; it is mine to choose as colleague whom I wish.”

So, in truth, it is yours to wish for and ask the Lord for a pure heart; it is his to diffuse his body through our limbs and veins for our eternal salvation. For he himself said when he gave the bread to the apostles: “This is my body, which will be given for you” (Luke XXII, 19).

His body moves about on earth when and where he wished, and when and where he wishes. Even after his Ascension he did not disdain to show himself to the Apostle Paul in the temple at Jerusalem, which was on earth: “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Ps. XXIII). The whole earth, remaining in its created condition, blesses the Lord.

Only an evil will makes its vessel unclean for receiving the Lord. I say this so that, if something should leave my mouth from the Lord’s body without my knowledge or consent, you will not think me alien to the Christian religion, as though I held the body of my Lord in contempt, [Col. 1338B] or as though that body were directed to a place where he did not wish, or does not wish, to come.

Through this body our soul lives, as the same Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in yourselves” (John IV, 54). If that body itself is life for us, it is not taken away from it because of our separation, wherever what it possesses from itself may be; and from itself it grants that to us.

My son, tell your priests to beware lest a single word of what the Lord spoke in the Gospel depart from their hearts, since that word itself is life for us, just as consecrated bread is. The Lord says in the Gospel: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John VI, 64). [Col. 1338C]

I am commanded in the Law: “If anything remains of the lamb, I shall burn it with fire” (Exod. XXIX, 34). That lamb prefigured the flesh of Christ. The remains of the lamb that seemed destined to be burned with fire are the mysteries of the divinity, which cannot be grasped by us but must be received, at the Lord’s command, with the fire of charity in the heavenly offering.

I entrust everything to that fire—the fire of charity—so that by it my vices may be consumed and good affections may be received.

Thus, when the Lord’s body has been received with good intention, I should not debate whether it is invisibly taken up into heaven, or retained in our body until the day of burial, or exhaled into the air, or leaves the body with the blood, or is emitted through the pores, since the Lord says: “Everything that enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the sewer” (Matt. XV, 17).

[Col. 1338D]

This alone must be guarded against: that I do not receive it with the heart of Judas, that it not be held in contempt, and that it be most beneficially distinguished from ordinary foods.

Concerning the other matter for which you reproached your father, I do not now answer in every respect. Perhaps the Lord will grant that I may one day see you again in some way and speak with you about it face to face.

For the present I say: “Tell me, my son, why did you not sing to your father that Virgilian verse:

> ‘Cold [is it], O boys; flee from here, a snake lies hidden in the grass.’”

The canons prescribe (Apostolic Canon 9, according to the interpretation of Dionysius Exiguus; Council of Antioch I, canon 2) that all who enter a church should receive Communion. If they do not receive Communion, they must state the reason why they do not; if it is reasonable, they are to be excused, but otherwise they are to be excommunicated. [Col. 1339A]

I have discovered that you fixed the anchor of your mind in the open sea and not in the harbor; you fixed it in Gennadius, bishop of Marseille. I urge you instead to fix it in the safest harbor, Augustine, whose testimony is accepted throughout all the churches.

Gennadius urged you to receive Communion especially on Sundays. Perhaps it was not his custom to celebrate Mass every day. For if it had been, he would not have urged you to receive Communion especially only on Sundays.

It is the custom of certain Greek priests to prepare and sanctify themselves from Thursday onward for the celebration of Mass. It may happen that we commit a sin on Tuesday or Wednesday that is not washed away until after Sunday has ended. Therefore we do not rightly receive Communion on every Sunday. And it may happen that we please God on each day of a week in which it is lawful to taste and see how sweet the Lord is. [Col. 1339B]

One ought not to remain long absent from so beloved a guest, whom two of the disciples compelled to stay with them on the day of his resurrection at Emmaus.

Flee, my son, from the open sea to Augustine, the safe harbor. For he says to you in his letter to Januarius (Letter 118):

> “Perhaps someone among them settles the dispute more correctly who urges them to remain in the peace of Christ. Let each person do what he devoutly believes ought to be done according to his faith. Let neither of them shrink from the body and blood of the Lord; rather, let them strive together [Col. 1339C] to honor the most salutary sacrament. For Zacchaeus and the centurion did not quarrel with each other, nor did either place himself above the other: one of them joyfully received the Lord into his house, while the other said, ‘I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof’” (Luke XIX, 5; Matt. VIII, 8).

My son, if you know yourself to be a sinner, you ought not to drive the Lord away from you; rather, satisfy him through repentance and receive him in a contrite and humbled spirit. If you are righteous, receive him joyfully. If you are weak, ask him for health, and fall on your face before his feet, like one of the ten lepers, giving thanks, so that he may say to you: “Rise and go, for your faith has saved you” (Luke XVI, 19).

Do not postpone turning to him from day to day, because on whatever day you turn and groan, you will be saved. [Col. 1339D] According to Augustine, when you see that a devout affection is in you, receive the Lord’s body, so that it may grant you everlasting life. Do not postpone it until Sunday, because you do not know whether you will reach that day.

### Concerning the Observance of Lent

[Col. 1340A]

[Note: [Col. 1339D] Thus Amalar concludes Book III in the manuscript codex.]

The practice of many people must also be guarded against. For many who think they are fasting are accustomed, as soon as they hear the signal, to eat at the ninth hour; yet they must in no way be considered to have fasted if they have eaten before the evening office has been celebrated. For one must hasten to the Masses, and afterward, having heard the solemn rites of the Masses or the evening office, and having first distributed alms, one should go to food. If, however, someone is constrained by some necessity and is unable to come to Mass, he should reckon the evening hour, complete his prayer, and break his fast.

It must also be known that on each Sunday during Lent, apart from those who are excommunicated, the sacraments of the body and blood of Christ [Col. 1340B] are to be received by all the faithful; and on the Lord’s Supper, at the vigils of Easter, and on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, all the faithful must partake without exception. All the days of Easter week are likewise to be observed with equal devotion. The people must therefore be admonished not to approach the most holy sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood carelessly, nor to abstain from it excessively, but with all diligence and prudence to choose a time when they will abstain from marital intercourse, cleanse themselves from vices, adorn themselves with virtues, devote themselves to almsgiving and prayer, and thus approach so great a sacrament.

## LETTER VII. TO AN ANONYMOUS BISHOP

[Col. 1340C]

We believe that your faith is sufficient, since you seek in Christ Jesus that the narrow and arduous path of understanding appropriate to you in the Lord and to the priestly name may be opened. For you have been chosen by the Lord for this office on the basis of preceding merits and distinguished virtues, although in many people the grace of Christ is proved by those works, while, when the merit of conduct and life is absent, the gifts of God alone bear fruit. Nevertheless, since you are shown to be loved by the Lord above others, since you have fulfilled the works of the law, and since you dwell in grace and hasten toward the eminent love of the knowledge and understanding of God conversing with you, and since, with distinguished thoughts present, you wish to know what you have become, it will disclose to you the sacraments of the whole Church as it directs, preserving their order and place and teaching you what you ought to observe and how [Col. 1340D] you ought to observe it—provided that you do not call the zeal of this recent exhortation an injury, and are not ashamed to be for a little while the lesser, when you say that, having set yourself aside as lowly, you possess the privilege of dignity.
